The problem belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency bugs where external actions (liquidations) are not reflected in internal contract state, leading to incorrect assumptions in subsequent logic. To remediate, the contract should either update its stored debt and collateral amounts when a liquidation occurs, allow closePosition() to handle partial repayments based on the current outstanding debt, or explicitly prevent the function from being called after liquidation and provide a separate recovery path. In any case the fix must ensure that the contract’s view of the position stays consistent with the actual Compound balances, so that users can reliably close or unwind their positions without unexpected reverts.

title: `Position` contract allows to interact with positions that are liquidated
description: `Position` contract allows to interact with positions that are liquidated. Because of that user can loose funds.
poc:
When new position is created, the amount of tokens that were supplied as collateral [are saved](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/utilities/poolsUtility/Position.sol#L412) as well. Later, when the user wants to close position, they will [redeem that amount](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/utilities/poolsUtility/Position.sol#L220). If a user wants to add collateral to avoid liquidation or for any other reason, they can call `increaseMargin`, which will [increase their bath token amount](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/utilities/poolsUtility/Position.sol#L238) that is used as collateral for the position.

In this case, if `Position bathToken` collateral is liquidated, that means that their debt becomes 0 and if they call `closePosition`, then the call will revert, as it will need to [`redeem`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/main/contracts/utilities/poolsUtility/Position.sol#L220) `bathToken` amount that the `Position` contract doesn’t control anymore.

So in this case, if the user will call `increaseMargin`, just after it was liquidated, then the provided collateral will never be possible to withdraw, as `closePosition` will always revert.

Example:

1. User has open position for bathUSDC, with an amount of 1000 bathUSDC.

2. Their position is under liquidation so they want to `increaseMargin` with 100 USDC more.

3. Liquidation happens before `increaseMargin` was called, so the `Position` contract bathUSDC balance is now 0 and `increaseMargin` mints 100 bathUSDC more.

4. `increaseMargin` increased the position’s bath amount to 1100.

5. The user realized that they couldn’t save position and now want to get back collateral, they call `closePosition`.

6. `closePosition` reverts when redeeming as a `Position` contract that doesn’t have 1100 bathUSDC, only 100 USDC.

As a result, the user’s 100 USDC is locked and can be used only as collateral for borrowing.
bug_full: The Position contract manages leveraged positions that are represented by a bath token used as collateral. When a position becomes under‑collateralised the protocol liquidates it, which transfers the bath token balance out of the Position contract and sets the debt to zero. The contract, however, continues to store the original amount of bath tokens in its internal accounting and does not check the liquidation status before allowing further interactions. As a result a user can call increaseMargin after liquidation; the function mints additional bath tokens and updates the internal amount, but the contract no longer holds any of the original bath tokens because they were already removed during liquidation. When the user later calls closePosition, the function attempts to redeem the total recorded amount of bath tokens. Since the contract’s actual balance is insufficient, the redemption call reverts and the transaction fails. From the user’s perspective the sequence looks like: they add extra USDC as collateral, the transaction succeeds, but when they try to close the position they receive a revert error and their newly added USDC becomes locked inside the contract with no way to withdraw it. The impact is that funds are effectively frozen for any position that is liquidated while a margin‑increase transaction is pending or is executed afterwards, violating the expectation that added collateral can always be reclaimed. This issue occurs under the condition that liquidation happens between the user’s request to increase margin and the contract’s state update, creating a race condition between external liquidation and internal accounting. All users with open positions are affected, and the protocol’s trustworthiness is harmed because collateral that should be refundable becomes unusable. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena when the auditors examined the flow of liquidation, increaseMargin and closePosition and observed that the contract does not guard against interactions with already liquidated positions. The bug is subtle because the increaseMargin call succeeds, giving the impression that the operation was successful, while the failure only manifests later during closePosition, making it hard to notice without thorough testing. The root cause is the absence of a liquidation‑status check and the reliance on an internal counter that can become out of sync with the actual token balance. To remediate, the contract should forbid any margin‑increase or position‑closing actions once a position has been marked as liquidated, reset the internal collateral counter after liquidation, and verify that the contract holds enough bath tokens before attempting a redemption. This aligns the contract’s state with the protocol’s accounting rules and restores the guarantee that users can always retrieve their collateral when a position is not liquidated.

title: `Position._borrowLimit` doesn’t use exisiting collateral in case if user doesn’t have any `_bathToken`
description: `Position._borrowLimit` doesn’t use exisiting collateral in case if user doesn’t have any `_bathToken`.
bug_full: The Position._borrowLimit function is responsible for determining how many borrowing loops a user must perform and what percentage of the maximum allowed amount can be borrowed for a given leverage target. The routine first checks whether the caller already holds a balance of the specific bath token that is being used as collateral (the variable _minted). If that balance is non‑zero, the function calls _maxBorrow to retrieve the amount of collateral that can be leveraged and adds it to the loop calculation. However, when the user does not own any of the target bath token, the condition _minted != 0 evaluates to false and the code falls back to a simple calculation that only multiplies the desired asset amount by the collateral factor. This logic ignores any other bath tokens that the user may have supplied as collateral in previous positions. Consequently, the borrow limit is underestimated whenever a user mixes different bath tokens, because the existing collateral from other assets is never taken into account. The root cause is a narrow collateral check that relies solely on the balance of the current bath token instead of querying the Comptroller for overall account liquidity (getAccountLiquidity) or aggregating collateral across all supplied assets. An attacker or an unwary user can trigger the bug by first opening a position with one bath token (for example bathUSDC) and then attempting to open a second position with a different bath token (such as bathETH). The second position will calculate its borrowing capacity without considering the already deposited bathUSDC collateral, leading to a lower borrow limit than the protocol actually permits. From the user’s perspective this manifests as a situation where the UI reports that the borrow limit has been reached or that no borrowing power is available, even though the user has deposited collateral elsewhere; attempts to borrow the expected amount may return zero or a smaller amount, and the position may be forced into an unintended liquidation path. The issue is difficult to notice because the function behaves correctly when only a single bath token is used, and typical unit tests may not cover cross‑asset scenarios. The vulnerability belongs to the class of collateral accounting omissions, where cross‑asset collateral is not incorporated into risk calculations. To remediate the problem the borrow limit logic should query the Comptroller for the total liquidity of the account (using getAccountLiquidity) and, when the returned liquidity is non‑zero, incorporate the maximum borrowable amount from all existing collateral tokens, for example by calling _maxBorrow for each relevant bath token or by using the _liq value directly in the loop calculation. This ensures that the borrowing capacity reflects the full set of assets the user has supplied, aligning the protocol’s risk model with its intended business logic and preventing users from being incorrectly blocked from borrowing or from experiencing unexpected shortfalls.

title: Potential infinite loop in `_borrowLimit` function
description: The infinite loop vulnerability could cause the `openPosition` functionality to become unresponsive or fail, negatively affecting the performance and usability of the whole system.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded iterative calculation inside the internal view function that determines how many borrowing loops are required to reach a target leveraged amount. The function uses a while loop that continues as long as the accumulated asset amount is less than or equal to the desired amount, and each iteration reduces the amount that can be borrowed by multiplying the previous loop borrow amount with the collateral factor. When the collateral factor is below roughly sixty‑six percent and the requested leverage is high, the multiplication quickly drives the loop‑borrowed value toward zero. Because the loop condition only checks the total asset amount against the target and never enforces a minimum borrow amount or a maximum iteration count, the loop can continue indefinitely once the borrow amount becomes zero or a value that no longer increases the total enough to reach the target. This results in the openPosition workflow becoming unresponsive: a transaction that calls openPosition will consume gas until it runs out, the user sees no position created, balances appear unchanged, and the contract may lock funds until the transaction is reverted or the block gas limit is hit. The root cause is the lack of a termination guarantee for the while loop combined with a decreasing geometric series that can converge to a value smaller than one unit of the token’s smallest denomination. The issue manifests only under specific parameter combinations – typical collateral factors around 70 % work fine, but lower factors such as 50 % with high leverage cause the series to require hundreds of iterations, effectively an infinite loop. It was discovered during a security audit when the auditors added console logs and observed that the loop ran for an extremely large number of iterations, eventually exhausting gas. The bug is hard to notice because for most realistic market settings the loop terminates after a few iterations, giving a false sense of safety. From a security perspective the flaw belongs to the class of unbounded loop or arithmetic convergence bugs that can lead to denial‑of‑service conditions. The impact is primarily a denial of service for users attempting to open leveraged positions and potential loss of gas fees; it does not directly enable fund theft but can freeze user assets while the transaction is pending. The affected parties are any user of the protocol who tries to open a position with a low collateral factor or high leverage, as well as the protocol itself because the functionality becomes unusable. To remediate the issue the algorithm should be redesigned to avoid iterative borrowing altogether, for example by deriving a closed‑form expression for the borrowing limit, or by adding a hard cap on the number of loop iterations and a minimum acceptable loop‑borrowed value that forces the loop to exit safely. Additionally, input validation that rejects collateral factors below a safe threshold for the requested leverage can prevent the condition from arising. Implementing these mitigations restores predictable execution, prevents gas exhaustion, and aligns the contract’s behavior with the expected business logic that a user’s leveraged position should be created within a bounded number of steps.

title: Attack on rounding errors to get risk free profit
description: When users `buy()` from `RubiconMarket`, their `spend` is rounded down. Tokens with small decimals, such as WBTC and GUSD, are vulnerable to rounding error attack. Attackers can exploit it to get risk free profit.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price calculation performed by the market contract when a user calls the buy() function. The contract computes the amount of payment token (spend) as the product of the requested quantity and the offer's buy amount divided by the offer's pay amount, using plain integer division. Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, the result is always rounded down. This rounding down means the buyer pays slightly less than the exact proportional price for the tokens they receive. The issue becomes exploitable when the traded assets have a small number of decimal places, such as WBTC (8 decimals) or GUSD (2 decimals), and when the quantity chosen does not divide evenly by the price denominator. An attacker can repeatedly execute small‑size purchases that each incur a tiny rounding loss for the market but a tiny gain for the attacker. By aggregating many such trades, the attacker can extract a risk‑free profit that exceeds the gas costs of the operation. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are counter‑intuitive: the attacker’s USDC balance increases after buying WBTC, or the amount of USDC spent appears lower than expected, while other participants see their token reserves shrink without a corresponding loss of value. The root cause is the use of floor division instead of a ceiling or exact rounding method, violating the accounting assumption that the exchange rate is applied precisely. The bug was discovered during a formal audit of the RubiconMarket contract when the auditors inspected the buy() implementation and crafted test cases that demonstrated profit accumulation on low‑decimal tokens. Because each individual rounding error is very small, it can be easy to miss in casual testing or manual review, especially when the amounts involved appear negligible. The vulnerability affects any market pair where the price ratio and token decimals allow a non‑zero remainder in the division, effectively any token pair with low precision or large price disparity. The impact is a systematic loss of value from the market’s liquidity pool, undermining trust in the protocol and potentially draining funds from honest participants. To remediate the issue the spend calculation should be performed with rounding up, for example by adding the denominator minus one before division or by using a safe math library that provides ceiling division. This change ensures that the buyer always pays at least the exact proportional amount, preserving the intended economic invariants of the exchange.

title: Zero reward rate calculation impedes low-decimals token distributions
bug_full: The vulnerability is an integer‑division precision error in the reward‑rate calculation of the BathBuddy contract. The contract computes a linear reward distribution by dividing the total reward amount by the configured rewardsDuration. Because Solidity’s SafeMath division truncates any fractional part, when the reward amount is smaller than the duration (or when the token has a low number of decimals, such as an 8‑decimal WBTC token), the division yields a reward rate of zero. This occurs whenever reward.div(rewardsDuration) evaluates to zero, which forces the owner to either shorten the distribution period or increase the reward amount to obtain a non‑zero rate. The bug can be exploited by an attacker or a careless owner who sets a reward amount just below the duration, causing the contract to record a zero reward rate while still appearing to have an active distribution. As a result, users who expect to earn rewards see no increase in their token balances; the UI may show a pending reward but the actual balance remains unchanged after the distribution period elapses. The impact is that legitimate participants receive no rewards, effectively nullifying the incentive mechanism and potentially leading to loss of trust in the protocol. The issue manifests only under specific parameter combinations and is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error – the reward calculation silently returns zero. It was discovered during a security audit when a test case demonstrated that providing a reward amount slightly below the number of seconds in a year (approximately 31.5 million) resulted in a yearly reward of zero, whereas a slightly higher amount produced the expected reward. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic precision or rounding bugs that arise from integer division without scaling. To remediate, the reward‑rate formula should be performed with increased precision, for example by multiplying the reward amount by a large scaling factor (such as 10**8) before division, or by using a fixed‑point arithmetic library, ensuring that fractional rates are preserved and that a non‑zero reward is distributed even for low‑decimal tokens.

title: `RubiconMarket: buy
description:
In the `buy` function of the `RubiconMarket` contract, a fee is subtracted on taker trades. The default `feeBPS` is set to `1` which is equivalent to a fee of `0.01%` or `0.0001` in decimal form.

For tokens like gUSD with a low decimal precision of [2](https://etherscan.io/token/0x056fd409e1d7a124bd7017459dfea2f387b6d5cd), no fees will be taken on 3 figure trades since Solidity will round down the result to 0.
poc:
The taker fee is calculated in the `buy` function of the `RubiconMarket` contract on [L338](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/RubiconMarket.sol#L338) and also in the `calcAmountAfterFee` function on [L583](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/RubiconMarket.sol#L583).

The following reasoning also apply to the maker fee on [L346](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/RubiconMarket.sol#L346) and [L586](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-rubicon/blob/511636d889742296a54392875a35e4c0c4727bb7/contracts/RubiconMarket.sol#L586).

Let’s take, for example, a 500 gUSD trade. Mathematically the fee would be: `500 * 0.0001 = 0.05`.

In solidity, for a token with 2 decimal places, we would get: `amount * feeBPS / 100_000 = 50000 * 1 / 100_000 = 0` cause it rounds down to 0.

It would allow a user to not pay any taker and/or maker fee on 3 figure trades.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑rounding error that occurs when the RubiconMarket contract calculates taker or maker fees for tokens that have a very low decimal precision, such as gUSD which uses only two decimals. The contract stores the fee rate as basis points (feeBPS) with a default value of 1, representing a fee of 0.01 % (0.0001 in decimal). When a trade amount is expressed in the token's smallest unit and the fee is computed using integer division (amount * feeBPS / 100_000), the result is rounded down to the nearest integer. For a token with two decimals, a three‑figure trade like 500 gUSD is represented as 50000 units; the calculation 50000 * 1 / 100_000 yields 0, so the fee becomes zero. This happens because the fee amount is smaller than one token unit, and Solidity’s integer arithmetic discards any fractional remainder. An attacker can deliberately trade amounts that fall below the fee‑unit threshold, thereby avoiding any fee payment. The impact is that the protocol loses expected fee revenue and creates an unfair advantage for users who trade low‑decimal tokens in small volumes, potentially undermining the economic model of the market. The issue manifests only when the traded token has low decimal precision and the trade size is insufficient to generate at least one fee unit; high‑precision tokens (e.g., 18‑decimal ERC‑20s) are unaffected. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee calculation logic and noticed that the rounding behaviour was not considered for tokens with fewer than 18 decimals. The bug is subtle because fee collection works correctly for the majority of tokens, so the missing fee is not obvious unless a low‑decimal token is used. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful trade with no fee deducted, leading to confusion when the expected fee amount is not reflected in the transaction receipt or balance change. Users expect a small fee to be taken, but instead the fee field is zero, making it appear that the protocol is giving away free trades. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the computed fee is non‑zero (e.g., by adding a require statement after fee calculation) or reject tokens whose decimal precision is too low for the chosen fee basis points. Alternatively, the fee formula could be re‑engineered to use higher‑precision arithmetic or a different scaling factor so that a fee is always representable as at least one token unit. This class of bug falls under integer‑division rounding errors that lead to under‑charging or loss of revenue in financial smart contracts.

title: The curve of short leverage position is not smooth and may cause users to open positions that are different from expectations
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the calculation of short leveraged positions when the contract permits a 1x leverage value for short trades. In the current design the internal leverage check allows a short position with exactly one‑times leverage, but the borrowing routine interprets a 1x request as a request for the maximum amount of collateral that can be borrowed according to the collateralisation factor. Consequently, a user who supplies 1,000 USDC as collateral and selects a short leverage of 1.0x receives a borrowed amount equal to the full 70 % collateral factor (700 USDC worth of WBTC), which is then sold for 700 USDC, leaving a total position of 1,700 USDC. The same total position is obtained when the user selects a leverage of 1.7x, because the borrowing logic simply multiplies the excess leverage (leverage‑1) by the collateral amount, yielding the same 700 USDC borrow. Intermediate values such as 1.3x produce a smaller borrowed amount (300 USDC) and therefore a smaller final position (1,300 USDC). This creates a non‑monotonic, “unsmoothed” curve where the extreme low‑leverage (1.0x) and high‑leverage (1.7x) points produce identical exposure. The root cause is the combination of an overly permissive leverage validation for shorts and a borrowing formula that does not treat the 1x case as a no‑borrow scenario. An attacker does not need to exploit a traditional code‑execution flaw; the issue is purely economic. By selecting 1.0x, a user unintentionally opens a highly leveraged position, exposing them to liquidation risk and potential loss of funds while believing they are only marginally leveraged. The problem manifests whenever a short position is opened with a leverage value at or near the lower bound of the allowed range and the protocol uses a collateral factor below 100 %. Users see the leverage selector in the UI, expect a proportional increase in position size as leverage rises, but may observe that a 1.0x short yields the same balance as a 1.7x short, leading to confusion and possible financial harm. The issue was discovered during a systematic test suite that iterated over several leverage values and logged the borrowed amount; the test revealed identical borrowed amounts for 1.0x and 1.7x. Because the discrepancy is subtle and only appears in the numeric outcome of a trade, it can be easily missed by manual inspection or by users who do not compare multiple leverage settings. To remediate, the contract should either forbid 1x leverage for short positions, thereby ensuring that any allowed short leverage results in a strictly increasing borrowed amount, or the borrowing calculation should be adjusted so that a 1x request results in zero borrowing (i.e., the user only supplies collateral without taking a loan). Either approach restores the expected monotonic relationship between leverage and resulting position size and prevents users from unintentionally opening overly risky positions.

title: Both buyAllAmountWithLeverage and sellAllAmountWithLeverage always revert
description: Both `buyAllAmountWithLeverage` and `sellAllAmountWithLeverage` always revert. **So all users cannot open a leveraged position**.
bug_full: The contract provides two public functions, buyAllAmountWithLeverage and sellAllAmountWithLeverage, that are intended to let a user open a leveraged long or short position. Both functions start by checking whether the contract already holds any of the bath token that will be used as collateral. The check is performed by reading the ERC‑20 balance of the bath token for the Position contract (uint256 _minted = IERC20(_bathToken).balanceOf(address(this))). If the balance is non‑zero the code calls an internal helper _maxBorrow, which queries the Compound‑style comptroller for the contract’s liquidity (comptroller.getAccountLiquidity). The helper then requires that the reported liquidity (_liq) be greater than zero, otherwise it reverts with "_maxBorrow: LIQUIDITY == 0". Because a freshly deployed Position contract has never supplied collateral to the comptroller, its liquidity is always zero. An attacker can therefore send a single wei of the bath token to the newly created Position contract before a user invokes the leveraged function. The tiny transfer makes the balance check succeed, causing the contract to call _maxBorrow, which immediately hits the liquidity‑zero require and reverts the whole transaction. As a result every attempt to open a leveraged position fails, effectively a denial‑of‑service or griefing attack. From the user’s point of view the UI reports a transaction failure; the user expects to receive a new leveraged position but instead sees a reverted transaction and no change to their balances. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Position contract when the control flow around collateral detection was examined. It is subtle because the contract appears to have a valid collateral‑check path, yet the check relies on a mutable token balance that can be manipulated with an insignificant amount of tokens. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect collateral verification leading to forced revert” and violates the business assumption that a user can always open a leveraged position when they provide sufficient collateral. The recommended fix is to replace the token‑balance test with a direct query to the comptroller (comptroller.getAccountLiquidity) to determine whether collateral has already been supplied, thereby preventing an attacker from triggering the revert by sending a trivial token amount.

title: Incorrect fee handling in `Position.sol's` Market `Buy`/`Sell` functions
description: The incorrect fee handling in the `Position.sol` market buy and sell functions can lead to improper fee deductions and wrong trade execution.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect fee handling logic inside the internal marketBuy and marketSell functions of the Position contract. In the current implementation the contract calculates a fee based on the requested fill amount, subtracts that fee from the amount passed to the market, and then forwards the original full amount to the RubiconMarket buyAllAmount call. This results in the fee being applied twice: once manually in Position and again by the market’s own fee mechanism. On the sell side a similar mistake occurs: the function adds a fee to the minimum fill amount when querying the market for the required pay amount, then later recalculates a fee in asset terms and may transfer an extra amount from the user to cover the duplicated fee. The root cause is a misunderstanding of the v2 trade specification, which states that fees should not be accounted for inside Position but should be deducted from the input amount before the market call. Because the code still performs fee calculations, trades executed through Position._marketBuy or Position._marketSell for v2 markets will over‑charge users. An attacker or a careless user can exploit this by initiating trades that appear normal but result in a higher effective fee, causing the user to receive fewer tokens than expected or to lose additional assets when the contract pulls extra tokens to cover the duplicated fee. The impact is financial loss for traders, incorrect accounting for the protocol, and potential failure of trades when the contract’s balance is insufficient after the extra fee deduction. The issue manifests whenever a position is opened or closed via the rubiconSwap helper, i.e., any call that triggers _marketBuy or _marketSell. All participants who rely on the Position contract – end‑users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the contract’s accounting no longer matches the business logic that fees are taken only once. The problem was discovered during a formal audit and reproduced in the Position.t.sol test suite, where the fee calculations were observed despite the sponsor’s guidance that v2 trades should not include them. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert; it simply yields a slightly reduced output, making it easy to miss without detailed accounting checks. To remediate, the fee‑related code should be removed from both _marketBuy and _marketSell, allowing the RubiconMarket to handle fees exclusively, or the fee should be deducted from the user‑provided input amount before the market call in accordance with the v2 specification. This aligns the contract with the intended fee model, restores correct accounting, and prevents users from unintentionally paying double fees.

title: MKTU-3 | Pending Borrowing Fees Brick Withdrawals
description:
It is possible for user’s withdrawals to revert because the pending borrowing fees are attributed to
the user’s withdrawal but have not yet been added to the poolAmount.
In cases where there is a significant amount of unpaid borrowing fees this can become a non-trivial
issue for users attempting to withdraw.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/GMX-4/blob/033061d771f2b327c2fbd4ab59e960109ee85dc2/test/guardian/PoCs.ts#L520
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the accounting of borrowing fees in a leveraged trading pool. When a user opens a leveraged position, the protocol accrues borrowing fees over time. These fees are recorded as pending but are not immediately transferred into the pool’s total liquidity (poolAmount). The withdrawal routine, however, treats the pending fees as if they have already been deducted from the user’s withdrawable balance. Consequently, the contract attempts to send an amount that is larger than the actual pool balance because the pending fees have not been added to the pool yet. If the pending fee amount is sizable, the transfer fails and the transaction reverts, preventing the user from receiving any funds. This situation arises whenever a user with a large outstanding borrowing fee attempts to withdraw, or when many users collectively generate a high volume of unpaid fees that remain pending. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test reproducing the revert condition. It can be difficult to spot because the front‑end may display a correct balance for the user, giving the impression that a withdrawal will succeed, while the underlying contract state lacks sufficient liquidity to cover the fee‑adjusted amount. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style failure: users see their withdrawal requests fail, funds appear to be “stuck,” and confidence in the protocol’s accounting is eroded. The bug belongs to the class of fee‑settlement or accounting race conditions where pending liabilities are subtracted from user balances before the corresponding assets are made available. To remediate the problem, the protocol should either separate the claiming of borrowing fees from the withdrawal path, ensuring fees are settled into the pool before they are deducted, or modify the withdrawal logic to only apply pending fees after they have been transferred to the pool, thereby guaranteeing that the pool always holds enough liquidity to satisfy the adjusted withdrawal amount.

title: SWPU-1 | Max Price Used For Swap Pricing
description:
The getLatestPrice function is used to get prices for swaps, however, this will return the custom
price for the token if any is set. In the case of a MarketIncrease long order, the min and max price for
the customPrice are both the max of the primaryPrice. The inverse can be true using a
MarketDecrease short order.
This way users can get more favorable execution while swapping for the index token during a Market
order.
This invalidates the implemented protection where the inToken is supposedly valued at the minimum
price and the outToken is valued at the max price:
cache.amountOut = cache.amountIn * cache.tokenInPrice.min / cache.tokenOutPrice.max;
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the price‑retrieval routine used during token swaps. The contract calls a function that returns the latest price for a token, but if a custom price has been set, the function returns that value without distinguishing between the minimum and maximum bounds that are required for safe pricing. In a MarketIncrease long order the code assigns both the minimum and maximum price of the custom price to the maximum of the primary market price. The same inverted logic applies to a MarketDecrease short order. Because the swap calculation assumes the input token is valued at the minimum price and the output token at the maximum price, using the same maximum value for both sides lets a user obtain a more favorable exchange rate than intended. An attacker can trigger this condition by submitting a market order while a custom price is present, causing the contract to compute amountOut as amountIn multiplied by tokenInPrice.min (which is actually the maximum primary price) divided by tokenOutPrice.max (which may be the true minimum). The result is an inflated amountOut, effectively giving the attacker extra tokens or reducing the protocol’s received value. This flaw manifests only when a custom price is defined and the order type forces the min and max bounds to collapse to the same extreme value. It is difficult to notice because the price values themselves appear valid and the price‑check logic passes; the error lies in the misuse of the bounds rather than an outright invalid number. The impact is a breach of the accounting assumptions that the protocol relies on: funds can disappear from the pool, liquidity providers may suffer losses, and the overall token economics become inconsistent. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended protection logic (inToken valued at the minimum price, outToken at the maximum price) with the actual values supplied by getLatestPrice. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce that the input token price always uses the true minimum price, never the maximum primary price, and should reject or ignore custom prices that would cause the min and max bounds to be identical. In practice this means separating the handling of custom prices for the two bounds, adding explicit checks that tokenInPrice.min ≤ tokenInPrice.max, and ensuring that market order logic does not overwrite the minimum bound with a maximum value. By restoring the correct price range the swap calculation regains its intended safety guarantees and prevents users from receiving unexpectedly high payouts or the protocol from losing value.

title: SWOU-1 | LimitSwaps Unnecessarily Delayed
description:
The validateOracleBlockNumbers function for LimitSwaps does not allow oracle block numbers to
be equal to the orderUpdatedAtBlock. This is in contradiction to the oracle block validation for
increase and decrease orders.
Additionally, this unnecessarily requires that limit swaps be executed at a delayed block number,
when the current block number may provide a more favorable execution for the trader.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a boundary‑condition error in the oracle block validation logic for limit swap orders. The contract’s validateOracleBlockNumbers function requires the minimum oracle block number to be strictly greater than the block at which the order was last updated (orderUpdatedAtBlock). This differs from the validation used for increase and decrease orders, which allow equality. As a result, when the oracle reports a block number that is exactly equal to orderUpdatedAtBlock, the limit swap is considered invalid and must be postponed to a later block. Traders therefore experience an unnecessary delay; the current block may offer a more favorable price, but the order cannot be executed until a subsequent block, potentially causing missed profit or execution at a worse price. The issue occurs whenever a limit swap is created or updated and the oracle’s latest block coincides with the order’s update block. It affects any user who relies on timely limit‑swap execution, the protocol’s economic efficiency, and overall user confidence. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the validation logic across order types and identified the inconsistent inequality. Because the condition is subtle, it may not be obvious during normal testing unless the exact block equality case is exercised, making it hard to notice. The impact is economic rather than a direct loss of funds: users may see their expected trade not happen, balances remain unchanged, or they receive a worse execution price than anticipated. To remediate, the contract should relax the check to allow equality by using a greater‑than‑or‑equal comparison (minOracleBlockNumbers.areGreaterThanOrEqualTo(orderUpdatedAtBlock)). This aligns the limit‑swap validation with other order types and removes the unnecessary execution delay, restoring the intended business logic that a limit order can be filled as soon as the oracle price satisfies the trader’s conditions.

title: DOU-1 | Minimum Output Amount Griefing
description:
A malicious actor can observe a user’s triggerPrice for their stop-loss (among other order types)
approaching and shift price impact in the user’s market (or in the user’s virtual inventory) such that
their minimum output becomes invalidated and the order gets canceled.
In some cases this could cause significant grief to users who would have otherwise exited the
market. A malicious actor may stand to benefit from this by holding MarketTokens and grieving
traders within that market.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a minimum‑output‑amount griefing flaw that allows a malicious participant to invalidate a user’s stop‑loss (or similar) order by manipulating the price impact that the protocol uses to calculate the expected output. The root cause is the reliance on a static minimum‑output check that is evaluated at execution time against a price impact that can be altered by external trades. An attacker who can observe the user’s trigger price can deliberately trade against the market or adjust the user’s virtual inventory just before the order is executed, causing the actual amount that would be received to fall below the user‑specified minimum. When this condition is not met, the protocol cancels the order instead of completing the trade. From the user’s perspective the order appears to have been placed correctly, the trigger price is reached, but the transaction reverts with a cancellation and the user sees no change in their balance – the expected exit never happens, funds remain locked, and the user may be forced to stay in a losing position. This situation occurs whenever a stop‑loss with a minimum‑output constraint is used in a market where price impact can be influenced by other participants, especially when the attacker holds a significant amount of the market token and can profit from keeping traders in the market. The affected parties are any traders relying on stop‑loss or similar protective orders, as well as the protocol itself, which may suffer reputational damage and reduced confidence. The issue was discovered during a security audit by the Guardian team through logical analysis of the order‑execution flow; it is subtle because the UI typically only shows that the order was cancelled without explaining that the minimum‑output check failed, making it hard for users to diagnose. To mitigate the problem the protocol should clearly document this behavior, implement monitoring for abnormal price‑impact manipulations, and consider redesigning the minimum‑output logic – for example by using time‑weighted average prices, widening slippage tolerances, or adding anti‑manipulation safeguards that limit how much price impact can be altered immediately before execution. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “output‑validation griefing” where dynamic market conditions can be weaponized to cause legitimate orders to fail, violating the user’s expectation that a triggered stop‑loss will reliably liquidate the position.

title: KEY-1 | Wrong Key For Pool Adjustment
description:
The poolAmountAdjustmentKey function in Keys.sol uses the POOL_AMOUNT key instead of the
POOL_AMOUNT_ADJUSTMENT key.
There are luckily no catastrophic consequences as this is an int value and the poolAmountKey is a
uint, however, it poses a significant risk to any future changes and would cause confusion/potential
issues for those reading using the POOL_AMOUNT_ADJUSTMENT key.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mismatched storage key used in the pool amount adjustment routine of the contract. The function that should record a signed integer representing a pool adjustment mistakenly writes the value under the unsigned POOL_AMOUNT key instead of the intended POOL_AMOUNT_ADJUSTMENT key. This occurs because the constant name was copied incorrectly, causing the mapping that stores protocol state to receive the adjustment data in the wrong slot. As a result, any logic that later reads POOL_AMOUNT_ADJUSTMENT will retrieve a default value (typically zero) while the actual adjustment is hidden under POOL_AMOUNT, which is interpreted as an unsigned total pool amount. The root cause is a simple naming error that goes unnoticed due to the similarity of the two identifiers and because both keys exist in the same storage mapping. Exploitation is indirect: when the contract processes pool adjustments, the wrong key prevents the adjustment from being applied to the accounting calculations. Consequently, the protocol may report an unchanged pool size, leading to inaccurate user balances, incorrect fee distribution, or faulty liquidation triggers. The impact is primarily on accounting correctness; users may see their expected refunds or position sizes remain unchanged, or the protocol may allocate funds based on stale data. The bug manifests whenever the poolAmountAdjustmentKey function is invoked, which happens during any pool rebalancing or manual adjustment operation. All participants that rely on accurate pool accounting – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s risk engine – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the function implementation against the specification. It is hard to notice because the contract compiles and runs without reverting, and the incorrect key does not cause an immediate runtime error; the symptom is a subtle discrepancy in reported numbers. The recommended remediation is to replace the POOL_AMOUNT constant with POOL_AMOUNT_ADJUSTMENT in the adjustment function, ensuring that signed adjustment values are stored in the correct mapping entry. This aligns the implementation with the intended accounting model, restores the integrity of balance calculations, and prevents future confusion or bugs that could arise from the mismatched key. The problem belongs to the class of key‑misuse or storage‑slot errors, where a developer uses an incorrect identifier for a data structure, leading to logical inconsistencies and potential financial misreporting.

title: IPU-1 | Price Impact Double Counted
description:
When increasing a position, PositionUtils.validatePosition is called after incrementing the OI for the
position increase. However, the validation will re-compute the price impact amount based on this
updated OI.
The resulting cache.priceImpactUsd in isPositionLiquidatable would be inaccurate to the actual price
impact experienced. Therefore some positions may be errantly prevented from being opened with
this validation.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a price‑impact miscalculation that occurs when a trader tries to increase an existing position. The contract first updates the global open interest (OI) to reflect the additional size and then calls PositionUtils.validatePosition. The validation routine recomputes the price‑impact amount using the already‑updated OI, effectively counting the impact of the new order twice. Because the cached priceImpactUsd value used by the isPositionLiquidatable check is derived from this double‑counted figure, the protocol may incorrectly flag a position as liquidatable or reject a legitimate increase. The root cause is the ordering of operations: the OI delta is applied before the price‑impact validation, so the validation logic works on a state that already includes the delta instead of the previous state. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; the bug manifests automatically for any position increase that pushes the price‑impact calculation over the protocol’s threshold. The impact is that users see their transaction revert or be blocked even though the actual market impact is within allowed limits, leading to lost trading opportunities and potential frustration. The condition occurs only during position‑increase calls where the validation step follows the OI update; closing or opening a brand‑new position does not trigger the issue. All traders who rely on the protocol’s risk engine are affected, as are the protocol’s liquidity and reputation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noticed that the price‑impact cache did not match the expected value after an OI change. It is hard to notice because the price‑impact formula itself is correct; the discrepancy appears only in the validation path, which may only surface for larger order sizes. To fix the problem the validation should be performed against the pre‑update OI, or the price‑impact calculation should be adjusted to subtract the delta that has already been accounted for, ensuring that the cached priceImpactUsd reflects the true incremental impact. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of state‑ordering errors where a contract validates after mutating a critical variable, leading to double counting or stale‑state checks. From a user’s perspective the UI may show an error like “position cannot be opened – price impact too high” even though the displayed price impact on the front‑end is lower, creating a mismatch between expectation (the trade should succeed) and reality (the trade is rejected).

title: DPU-1 | Token Amount Added To USD Value
description:
The estimatedRemainingCollateralUsd is incremented by a token amount rather than a token amount
multiplied by a price:
estimatedRemainingCollateralUsd += params.order.initialCollateralDeltaAmount().toInt256();
As a result, the main effect is estimatedRemainingCollateralUsd is much smaller than it should be
and the position is more likely to get closed out in its entirety unexpectedly due to the
MIN_COLLATERAL_USD check.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting miscalculation in the collateral accounting logic of the GMX synthetics contract. Instead of converting the newly added collateral amount from token units to its USD equivalent, the code increments the variable estimatedRemainingCollateralUsd with the raw token amount returned by params.order.initialCollateralDeltaAmount(). This omission of the price multiplication causes the estimated USD collateral to be dramatically lower than the true value of the deposited tokens. The root cause is a unit‑conversion error: the contract treats a token quantity as if it were already expressed in USD, violating the fundamental assumption that collateral must be measured in a common monetary unit before any safety checks are applied. When the underestimated estimatedRemainingCollateralUsd is later compared against the protocol constant MIN_COLLATERAL_USD, the check can fail even though the user has supplied sufficient token collateral. As a result, the position may be flagged as under‑collateralised and the system may trigger a full liquidation, closing the trade unexpectedly and potentially wiping out the user’s funds. This condition occurs whenever a user adds collateral through an order that invokes the faulty increment, which includes most normal deposit actions. All participants who rely on the contract’s collateral accounting – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the bug can cause premature liquidations and loss of capital. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the auditor noticed that the addition operation used a token amount directly instead of applying the current price feed. The bug is subtle because the contract still records a positive collateral balance, so on‑chain explorers and UI dashboards may show a non‑zero token balance, masking the fact that the internal USD accounting is wrong. The failure mode can be described as a “unit conversion accounting bug” that leads to “funds disappear” symptoms: users expect their added collateral to protect their position, but the system treats it as insufficient and liquidates the position, resulting in a zero or dramatically reduced balance. To remediate the issue, the contract should first obtain the market price of the collateral token, multiply the token delta by this price to obtain a proper USD value, and then add that value to estimatedRemainingCollateralUsd. This change restores the invariant that the USD‑denominated collateral estimate accurately reflects the true economic value of the deposited tokens, preventing false triggers of the MIN_COLLATERAL_USD safety check and preserving the intended liquidation logic.

title: EDPU-1 | Users Are Negatively Affected By The Price Spread
description:
When the positiveImpactAmount is calculated during a deposit, the _params.priceImpactUsd is
divided by the tokenPrice.max to be converted into an outToken amount. However the token amount
is converted back to a USD amount when incrementing the mintAmount,
positiveImpactAmount.toUint256() * _params.tokenOutPrice.min.
This means that users are negatively impacted by the price spread because they receive less
positive impact than they otherwise would have.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mis‑calculation of the positive impact amount that is applied when a user makes a deposit. The contract first converts the USD price impact into an out‑token amount by dividing the reported price impact (priceImpactUsd) by the maximum token price (tokenPrice.max). This step is correct for obtaining the maximum possible token quantity. However, when the contract later adds this token quantity to the mint amount, it converts the token amount back to USD using the minimum token price (tokenOutPrice.min) instead of the maximum price. Because the minimum price is lower than the maximum price, the conversion yields a smaller USD value, effectively reducing the positive impact that the user receives. The root cause is the inconsistent use of max and min price parameters during the two conversion steps, which creates a hidden price spread penalty. An attacker does not need to perform any special action; the bug is triggered automatically whenever a deposit is processed, as the contract follows the flawed formula. The impact is that users receive fewer minted tokens or lower USD‑valued rewards than they expect, leading to a discrepancy between the UI‑displayed expected amount and the actual amount credited. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a lower balance after a deposit, or a missing refund/bonus that should have been credited. The issue was discovered by the Guardian audit of the GMX Synthetics contracts while reviewing the deposit logic. It can be hard to notice because the calculations appear mathematically sound and the UI may still show the original price impact, masking the loss caused by the spread. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where inconsistent conversion rates cause under‑allocation of funds. To fix the problem the contract should use the same price direction for both conversions – specifically, multiply the positiveImpactAmount by the maximum out‑token price (tokenOutPrice.max) when converting back to USD, ensuring users receive the full positive impact without being penalised by the spread.

title: GLOBAL-1 | Liquidations When Features Disabled
description:
It is possible for a state to arise where liquidations are enabled but other order types are disabled.
For example, increase orders can be disabled and a user is unable to add collateral to their position.
Fees will accumulate until a user’s position is liquidatable which leads to loss of funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical inconsistency in the liquidation module of the protocol that permits liquidations to be executed even when other order types required for margin maintenance, such as increase orders, are globally disabled. The root cause is that the contract maintains separate enable flags for liquidations and for order types that allow users to add collateral, and it does not enforce a dependency between them. As a result, a user who finds the increase‑order feature turned off cannot submit a transaction to increase the collateral of an existing position. Meanwhile, fees continue to accrue on the position, gradually eroding the margin ratio. When the accumulated fees push the position below the liquidation threshold, the protocol’s liquidation routine is still allowed to run and automatically closes the position, transferring the remaining collateral to liquidators. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are that they are unable to add more collateral through the UI, they see fees growing on their dashboard, and then, without any warning, their position disappears and they receive no refund. The impact is a loss of funds for the affected user and a breach of the protocol’s economic guarantees, because the system assumes users can always top up collateral to avoid liquidation. This condition occurs only when the global flag for liquidations is true while the flag for increase orders (or other margin‑adjusting order types) is false, a state that can arise after a governance change or a feature rollout that disables certain order types. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the interactions between feature toggles and safety checks. It can be hard to notice because liquidations themselves are expected behavior, and the inability to add collateral may be hidden behind a UI element that simply disables a button, making the failure mode appear as a normal liquidation. The appropriate remediation is to add a cross‑dependency check that prevents liquidations from being triggered when any order type required for margin maintenance is disabled, or to provide an emergency mechanism that allows users to add collateral even when normal order pathways are turned off. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “inconsistent state‑dependent safety checks” where access control or feature flags are not consistently applied across related protocol functions, leading to unintended loss of funds.

title: OCL-1 | Lack Of Sequencer Uptime Check
description:
Even with the heartbeat validation, it may be prudent to validate that the Sequencer is active to
prevent stale pricing.
This would avoid any scenarios where price movement triggers an update within the heartbeat
duration but the new price is not reported to the L2, allowing traders to take advantage of stale
pricing.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing verification that the off‑chain price sequencer is currently operational before the contract accepts a new price update. The contract relies only on a heartbeat timestamp to infer that a price feed is alive, but it does not check whether the sequencer that actually pushes price data to L2 is still up. If the sequencer crashes or becomes unreachable, the heartbeat may still be considered valid for the duration of its timeout window, allowing the contract to accept a price that has not been refreshed. An attacker or a trader can then submit a transaction that reads the stale price, execute trades, or open positions based on outdated market data, effectively exploiting the lag between the last genuine price and the time the contract records it. The impact is that users may receive trades at prices that no longer reflect the market, leading to unexpected losses, liquidations, or arbitrage opportunities for malicious actors. This condition occurs when the sequencer stops sending updates but the heartbeat timer has not yet expired, which can happen during network partitions, sequencer maintenance, or denial‑of‑service attacks on the sequencer node. All participants that rely on the contract for accurate pricing – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions of price is fresh are violated. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the keeper logic and noticed that the sequencer uptime flag was never consulted. It can be hard to notice because the contract still emits a valid heartbeat event, so external monitoring tools may report the system as healthy while the price feed is actually frozen. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit check that the sequencer is reported as active (for example by querying a status flag or requiring a recent sequencer‑specific update) before accepting any price change, and to document the keeper’s behavior when the sequencer is down so that operators can react appropriately. In generic terms this is a stale‑data or time‑of‑check‑time‑of‑use (TOCTOU) bug where the contract trusts a timing signal without confirming the underlying data source is alive, breaking the business rule that trades must be executed against up‑to‑date market prices.

title: CHAIN-1 | Hardcoded Chain ID
description:
In the Chain.sol file, uint256 constant public ARBITRUM_CHAIN_ID = 42161; is hardcoded.
From a comment in Oracle.sol, the codebase wishes to be impervious to a change in the chain ID:
// it might be possible for the block.chainid to change due to a fork or similar
However in the event that the Arbitrum chain ID changes, the currentBlockNumber and getBlockHash
functions will not return the appropriate Arbitrum values, potentially causing drastic effects on the
exchange.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a hard‑coded numeric identifier for the Arbitrum network (the constant value 42161) that is used by the contract to decide which block number and block hash to return. The root cause is that the developers encoded the expected chain identifier directly in the source code instead of reading the dynamic block.chainid value or exposing a configurable parameter. If the Arbitrum network ever changes its chain identifier – for example during a protocol upgrade, a hard fork, or a migration to a new L2 instance – the functions that rely on the constant will continue to return data that corresponds to the old identifier. As a result, calls to the currentBlockNumber or getBlockHash methods will produce stale or zero values, breaking the accounting assumptions of the exchange that depend on accurate block information. An attacker who can trigger a fork or who interacts with a deployment on a network that reuses the same contract bytecode but with a different chain ID could cause the exchange to settle trades using incorrect block data, leading to mis‑priced executions, missing refunds, or balances that appear unchanged. The impact is therefore a potential loss of funds for traders, liquidity providers, and any user relying on the exchange’s pricing logic. The issue manifests only when the underlying chain identifier diverges from the hard‑coded constant, a condition that is rare in normal operation and therefore easy to miss during testing because the contract behaves correctly on the current Arbitrum mainnet. The problem was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer read a comment indicating an intention to be resilient to chain‑id changes and noticed the contradictory hard‑coded value. Because the bug is environment‑dependent, it may not surface in unit tests or local simulations, making it subtle to detect. To remediate the issue, the constant should be replaced with a configurable variable that can be set at deployment or updated via governance, or the contract should simply read block.chainid at runtime. This change removes the reliance on a static identifier and aligns the contract’s logic with the actual network it is executing on, eliminating the risk of returning incorrect block numbers or hashes and preserving the integrity of the exchange’s financial calculations.

title: POSU-1 | Negative PnL Ignored In Sufficient Collateral Check
description:
The PnL of the remaining position is no longer accounted for during the
willPositionCollateralBeSufficient check.
In the case where the remaining position PnL is positive, this avoids errantly counting profit towards
the remaining position’s collateral.
However, in the case where the remaining position PnL is negative, this check fails to consider that
the remaining PnL could make the actual value backing the position significantly smaller than the
minCollateralUsdForLeverage.
It may be prudent to consider the PnL of the remaining position, only when it is in a loss. This way
the negative PnL, which would be subtracted from the collateral in the position, is taken into account.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the collateral verification logic that determines whether a position has enough margin to remain open after a partial closure. The function willPositionCollateralBeSufficient currently ignores the profit and loss (PnL) of the remaining portion of the position. When the remaining PnL is positive, the omission does not cause a problem because the profit would only increase the effective collateral. However, when the remaining PnL is negative, the check fails to subtract this loss from the collateral value, causing the protocol to treat an under‑collateralised position as sufficiently collateralised. This logical flaw can be triggered whenever a trader reduces the size of a losing position. An attacker could deliberately open a leveraged position, incur a loss, then partially close it to reduce the notional while keeping the negative PnL hidden from the collateral check. The contract would then allow the position to stay open despite the actual margin falling below the required minCollateralUsdForLeverage threshold. The impact includes the risk of unexpected liquidations, potential loss of user funds, and erosion of the protocol’s solvency guarantees. Users experience the symptom of a position that appears open and correctly sized in the UI, yet the system does not warn about insufficient margin; they may later see a liquidation or a missing refund. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who identified that the PnL term is omitted from the sufficient‑collateral condition. It is hard to notice because the check passes for positive PnL cases and the UI does not expose the underlying margin calculation. To remediate, the collateral verification should incorporate the remaining position’s PnL, but only when that PnL is negative, thereby ensuring that any loss is deducted from the effective collateral before comparing against the minimum required margin. This adjustment restores the intended accounting invariant that the total value backing a position must always cover the leverage requirement, preventing money from disappearing due to an unchecked loss.

title: GLOBAL-2 | Block Re-org Attack
description:
In the event of a block re-org a malicious trader may see that price has moved against them and
decide to get their order canceled rather than recorded.
Consider the following scenario:
Bob sees the keeper execute his MarketIncrease in block A
The block re-org occurs over a period of 1 minute
Bob sees the re-org is happening and sees that the execution of his order has since lost money
and gets his tx to cancel the order recorded in block B which will come before block A.
Bob can make his tx cancel his MarketIncrease by having it send the tokens necessary for the
MarketIncrease order elsewhere.
Bob’s order is canceled rather than executed since it did not net him any profit.
Notice that there are likely many ways to exploit the two-step execution process during a re-org.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a block re‑organization (re‑org) attack that targets the two‑step order execution flow used by the protocol. In the first step a keeper contract executes a MarketIncreaseorder and records the execution in a block (block A). In the second step the order can be cancelled or settled in a later transaction. Because the execution and cancellation are separate on‑chain actions, an attacker who monitors the mempool can exploit a temporary fork of the chain. When a re‑org occurs, the attacker observes that the price movement recorded in block A would cause the order to lose value. The attacker then submits a cancellation transaction that is included in a block (block B) that becomes part of the canonical chain before block A is finalized. By sending the tokens required for the MarketIncrease elsewhere, the attacker forces the protocol to treat the order as cancelled rather than executed, effectively nullifying the trader’s position and preventing any profit. This attack can be carried out within the time window of the re‑org, typically on the order of a minute, and requires the attacker to be able to front‑run the cancellation transaction so that it is mined earlier than the original execution. The impact is that honest traders may lose expected profits or see their orders disappear, leading to a mismatch between the UI (which may briefly show a successful execution) and the final state (where the order is cancelled and funds are not credited). The protocol’s accounting assumptions – that an executed order cannot be retroactively cancelled – are violated, breaking the integrity of the order book and potentially eroding user trust. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the protocol does not enforce finality checks or atomicity across the two steps. It is difficult to notice because the UI often shows the order as executed and then silently removes it after the re‑org, providing no explicit error message. To mitigate the risk, the protocol should either freeze all pending orders during a detected re‑org, enforce that execution and settlement occur within a single atomic transaction, or add a finality delay that only confirms orders after a sufficient number of confirmations. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “re‑org race conditions” where separate state‑changing operations can be reordered by the consensus layer, allowing an adversary to manipulate the order of state updates to their advantage.

title: GLOBAL-3 | Multiple Read-only Reenterancies
description:
There are several instances where a user may gain control over the order execution tx before the
dataStore has been properly updated.
Firstly, in the SwapOrderUtils.swap function, the SwapUtils.swap is executed before the swap order
is removed from the dataStore. Since the swap can have shouldUnwrapNativeToken == true the
order.receiver will get called upon receiving the output of the swap.
Since native token transfers forward 200,000 gas (from the test environment) the receiver will have
ample gas to potentially exploit any system building on top of GMX V2 and relying on the swap order
in the dataStore.
Similarly in the OrderUtils.cancelOrder function, the orderVault.transferOut is executed before the
order is removed from the dataStore.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a read‑only reentrancy bug that occurs in two order‑handling functions of the GMX V2 synthetic module. In the swap path, the contract calls the external SwapUtils.swap function before it removes the corresponding order from the persistent data store. When the swap is configured to unwrap the native token, the swap output is sent to order.receiver, which is an external address that can execute arbitrary code. Because the native token transfer forwards a large amount of gas (200,000 gas in the test environment), the receiver contract can re‑enter the GMX V2 system while the original order is still recorded in the data store. A similar pattern exists in the cancelOrder path where orderVault.transferOut is performed before the order entry is deleted. The root cause is the ordering of operations: an external call is made while the contract’s internal state still reflects the old order, allowing a malicious receiver to invoke functions that assume the order is still valid. An attacker can exploit this by deploying a contract as the order receiver, receiving the swap output or the transferred funds, and then calling back into the protocol to execute the same order again, to claim additional rewards, to manipulate position sizing, or to drain funds that should have been accounted as already processed. The impact is that funds may be transferred multiple times or orders may be processed out of the intended sequence, leading to potential loss of user assets and breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol. The issue manifests whenever a swap is executed with shouldUnwrapNativeToken set to true or when an order is cancelled and the vault transfer is performed before the order entry is cleared. Any user who places a swap or cancellation order that triggers these code paths is affected, as well as downstream contracts that rely on the correctness of the order store. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the ordering of state‑changing calls and identified that the contract performs read‑only external calls before updating its own storage. Because the external calls do not modify the contract’s own storage directly, the problem can be subtle and may not be caught by simple static analysis or by testing only successful paths. The recommended mitigation is to reorder the logic so that the order is removed from the data store (using OrderStoreUtils.remove) before any external call such as SwapUtils.swap or orderVault.transferOut is executed. This eliminates the stale state window and prevents a malicious receiver from re‑entering with an outdated view of the order. In generic terms the fix follows the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern: perform all internal state updates (effects) before interacting with external contracts (interactions).

title: It is possible to steal the unallocated part of every delegation period budget
description:
Attacker can monitor the standard proposals distribution and routinely steal each low activity period remainder by submitting a `transfer to self` proposal and voting a dust amount for it.

Since the criteria for the final slate update is that any increase in total funding votes casted is enough, the attacker’s costs are negligible, while the remainder funds during some periods can be substantial enough for the attacker to setup such a monitoring. I.e. as funds are constant share of the treasury, while activity can differ drastically, a situation when there are less viable proposals then funds can routinely happen over time.

The assumption of the current logic is that such unallocated funds will be returned to the treasury, but it will not be the case as the cost of stealing such funds is close to zero.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a budget‑leakage flaw that allows an attacker to capture the portion of a delegation period’s funding that is not allocated to any winning proposal. The root cause is that the slate‑validation logic only requires the sum of funding votes of a new slate to be greater than the current one and does not enforce any minimum voting power for individual proposals. Because of this, a proposer can submit a proposal that requests the remaining tokens and attach only a dust amount of governance votes. During periods of low voting activity the total votes cast for legitimate proposals may be far below the available budget, leaving a sizable remainder. An attacker monitors the end of each screening period, creates a “transfer‑to‑self” proposal, votes with the minimal dust, gets the proposal included in the top‑ten list, and then updates the top slate. The update succeeds because the new slate has a higher total funding‑vote sum, even though the attacker’s proposal contributes virtually no voting power. As a result the attacker can withdraw the unallocated funds for almost no cost. The impact is that treasury funds disappear from the protocol, reducing the amount available for genuine funding proposals and breaking the economic assumptions of the system. Users who expect their proposals to receive the full budget may see smaller payouts or missing refunds, and the overall health of the protocol’s funding mechanism is compromised. The issue manifests only when voting participation is low enough that the allocated votes do not consume the whole budget, which can happen repeatedly over time. It was discovered during a formal audit that examined the slate‑selection algorithm and noticed that proposals with zero or negligible funding votes are still considered valid as long as they are present in the top‑ten list. The flaw is subtle because the dust votes appear harmless and the contract does not explicitly reject proposals with insufficient voting power, making the problem easy to overlook in testing. To remediate the bug the protocol should introduce a minimum accepted vote power for any proposal that can be included in the final slate, reject proposals with zero or trivially small funding votes, and optionally enforce that the total allocated tokens must equal the available budget or that unallocated funds are automatically returned to the treasury. Implementing such checks restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents attackers from siphoning leftover funds.

title: Delegate rewards system is unfair to delegates with less tokens and reduces decentralization
description: Reduces decentralization significantly and discourages delegates with less token power to vote.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the delegate reward mechanism of the funding contract, which calculates rewards based on the square of each delegate’s voting power rather than a linear proportion. This mathematical choice creates a disproportionate allocation where delegates that hold a large amount of tokens receive a vastly higher share of the reward pool, while delegates with modest token balances receive only a negligible portion. The root cause is the use of a quadratic formula (reward ∝ votes²) for distributing rewards, which was likely intended for a different incentive model but was applied to delegate payouts without proper justification. An attacker or any large token holder can exploit this by simply voting with a high token balance, thereby receiving a reward that approaches the total pool, effectively “stealing” rewards from smaller participants. In the provided proof‑of‑concept, a delegate with 350 million tokens received roughly 98 % of the rewards, whereas a delegate with 50 million tokens received only about 2 %. The impact is a severe reduction in decentralization: smaller delegates are discouraged from participating because their expected returns are far below what a linear or square‑root (quadratic voting) distribution would provide. This condition manifests during the reward claim phase after a distribution period has ended, and it affects all participants who have delegated votes, including token holders, proposal creators, and the overall governance ecosystem. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a test compared the actual reward distribution against a linear baseline and highlighted the extreme skew. Because the contract functions correctly according to its code, the problem is subtle and may not be obvious from a superficial functional test; it requires analysis of the economic model and reward formulas. To remediate, the reward calculation should be replaced with a linear proportion (reward ∝ votes) or a quadratic‑voting style where rewards are proportional to the square root of votes, thereby aligning incentives with decentralization goals and ensuring that smaller delegates receive a fairer share of the pool. This class of bug falls under “economic incentive misalignment” or “reward distribution skew” and violates the expected business logic that rewards should reflect contribution proportionally rather than amplifying the power of large holders. From a user’s perspective, a small delegate may see their balance remain almost unchanged after claiming rewards, leading to confusion and disappointment when they expected a meaningful payout.

title: `_updateBucketExchangeRateAndCalculateRewards` reward calculation accuracy loss
description:
Divide first and then multiply, which has precision loss. The loss depends on the denominator, which is at most `denominator - 1`.  
Although `Maths.wdiv rounded` adopted in _updateBucketExchangeRateAndCalculateRewards, reduce the loss, but theoretically `interestFactor` loss is about `interestEarned_ / 2`.  
This means that the more interest are earned, the more users lose.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reward‑calculation rounding error that occurs in the function that updates a bucket’s exchange rate and then computes the reward for the caller. The contract first divides a value that represents the change in exchange rate by the amount of interest earned and only afterwards multiplies the result by the burn factor and a constant reward multiplier. Because Solidity uses integer arithmetic, dividing before multiplying truncates any fractional part, causing a loss of precision that can be as large as one unit less than the denominator. Although the code uses a helper that performs a rounded division (Maths.wdiv), the loss is still roughly half of the interest earned, meaning that the more interest a user generates, the larger the shortfall in the reward they receive.
