            ITalosOptimizer optimizer,
            BoostAggregator boostAggregator,
            address strategyManager,
            FlywheelCoreInstant flywheel,
            address owner
        ) public returns (TalosBaseStrategy) {
            return new TalosStrategyStaked( // @audit-issue Reorg Attack
                    pool,
                    optimizer,
                    boostAggregator,
                    strategyManager,
                    flywheel,
                    owner
                );
        }

[Link to Code](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/talos/TalosStrategyStaked.sol#L28)

Even more, the reorg can be a couple of minutes long. So, it is quite enough to create the `TalosStrategyStaked` and transfer funds to that address using the `deposit` method; especially when someone uses a script and not doing it by hand.

Optimistic rollups (Optimism/Arbitrum) are also suspect to reorgs. If someone finds a fraud, the blocks will be reverted, even though the user receives a confirmation.

The same issue can affect factory contracts in Ulysses omnichain contracts as well, with more severe consequences.

You can refer to this issue previously reported, [here](https://code4rena.com/reports/2023-04-frankencoin#m-14-re-org-attack-in-factory), to have a better understanding of it.
bug_full: The issue is a deterministic contract‑creation pattern that becomes unsafe when the underlying blockchain can experience short‑term reorganizations. A factory function uses the plain CREATE opcode (via the Solidity `new` keyword) to deploy a new strategy contract, and the resulting address is calculated only from the caller address and its nonce. On rollup chains such as Arbitrum, Optimism or Polygon, blocks can be reverted a few minutes after they are published if a fraud proof is submitted. When a deployment transaction is included in a block that later gets rolled back, the contract address disappears from the state. If a user or an automated script has already sent funds to that address in the same or a subsequent transaction, the funds are transferred to an address that no longer hosts the intended contract. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful confirmation and the deposited amount appears to be in the new strategy, but after the reorg the balance is zero, shares are missing, or the contract cannot be interacted with. The root cause is the reliance on a non‑finalized deployment address without any safeguard against chain reorganization. The vulnerability can be exploited by an attacker who either forces a fraud proof on an optimistic rollup or simply waits for a natural reorg, causing the deployment block to be invalidated after the user’s deposit. The impact ranges from temporary loss of visibility (funds appear to disappear) to permanent loss if the address is later taken over by another contract or becomes inaccessible, breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol (deposit should always be redeemable for shares). The problem is especially relevant for scripts that combine contract creation and fund transfer in a single transaction, because the deposit may be executed before the network reaches finality. It was discovered during a security audit that referenced earlier reports of re‑org attacks on factory contracts. The bug is hard to notice because the transaction receipt reports success and no explicit error is emitted; only after the chain finalizes does the contract vanish. The recommended mitigation is to use CREATE2 with a fixed salt so that the address can be pre‑computed and verified after finality, or to separate deployment from funding and only accept deposits after the block is finalized. Adding a finality check, using a trusted factory that records deployments, or employing a timelock before allowing deposits also reduces the attack surface. In short, the vulnerability belongs to the class of “re‑org‑sensitive deterministic deployment” bugs that violate the protocol’s expectation that a newly created contract will persist for the lifetime of the deposited funds.

title: Replenishing gas is missing in `_payFallbackGas` of `RootBridgeAgent`
description: The call `_payFallbackGas` is used to update the user deposit with the amount of gas needed to pay for the `fallback` function execution. However, it doesn’t replenish gas. In other words, it doesn’t deposit the `executionGasSpent` into `AnycallConfig` execution budget.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fallback handling of the RootBridgeAgent contract, specifically in the internal function that is supposed to reimburse gas after a cross‑chain fallback execution. When a fallback is triggered, the contract records the amount of gas that was spent and attempts to update the user’s deposit by subtracting the calculated cost (minExecCost) from the settlement record. However, the function never calls the AnycallConfig mechanism that would actually replenish the execution budget with the withdrawn gas. As a result, the contract’s internal gas pool is reduced without being refilled, leaving the bridge without enough gas to pay for subsequent fallback or cross‑chain calls. The root cause is a missing call to the gas‑replenishment routine (_replenishGas) after the contract withdraws gas from the port; the code only performs a subtraction on the settlement mapping and then returns. An attacker or a malicious user can deliberately invoke the anyFallback entry point with a payload that consumes a large amount of gas, causing the contract to deduct a substantial amount from the user’s deposit while never restoring the execution budget. Over time this can deplete the bridge’s gas reserve, leading to denial‑of‑service conditions where further cross‑chain settlements fail, or it can cause forced reverts when the remaining gas balance is insufficient for the next operation. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are subtle: a user may see their deposit reduced after a settlement, yet the expected refund or successful completion of the cross‑chain operation does not occur, and later attempts to bridge assets may simply return false or revert without a clear error message. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the Anycall gas management logic and noticed that the _payFallbackGas routine lacked any replenishment call. It is hard to notice because the function appears to correctly deduct gas, and the missing top‑up does not generate an explicit error; the failure only manifests later when the bridge runs out of gas. To remediate the problem the contract should, after withdrawing the required amount from the port, unwrap the token (if applicable) and invoke the _replenishGas function so that the execution budget in AnycallConfig is increased by the same amount that was deducted from the user’s settlement record. This ensures that the bridge’s gas accounting remains balanced and that future fallback executions have sufficient budget, preserving the intended business logic that gas spent on a fallback is reimbursed to the system rather than disappearing.

title: `migratePartnerVault`
description: In the `migratePartnerVault()` method, if `vaultId == 0` it means it’s an illegal address; but the Id of the vaults starts from 0, resulting in the first vault being mistaken as an illegal vault address.
bug_full: The contract contains a logical validation error in the migratePartnerVault function. The function is intended to replace the current partner vault with a new one, but it first checks whether the supplied vault address is recognised by calling factory.vaultIds(newVault) and rejecting the call if the returned identifier equals zero. The developers also use the identifier value zero as a sentinel that represents an illegal or uninitialised vault address. However, the factory that stores vault identifiers assigns identifiers starting at zero because the vault array is populated without a placeholder entry for address(0). Consequently, the very first vault that is added to the system receives the identifier 0, which is indistinguishable from the sentinel value used to flag an illegal vault. When an owner attempts to migrate to this first vault, the check incorrectly interprets the identifier as unrecognised and reverts with UnrecognizedVault, preventing the migration. This bug manifests whenever the first vault – the one with index zero – is the target of a migration, effectively locking the contract out of upgrading to that vault. From a user perspective the partner vault address remains unchanged, any expected balance transfers or claimOutstanding calls are never executed, and the UI may show that a migration request failed without a clear reason. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for the contract owner: they cannot move to the first vault, which may hold funds or be required for future upgrades, potentially leaving assets inaccessible or the protocol unable to evolve. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the migration logic with the factory’s addVault implementation and noticed the mismatch between the sentinel usage and the zero‑based indexing. The problem is subtle because zero is a common default value in Solidity and developers often rely on it as a “null” indicator, making the bug easy to overlook in code reviews. To remediate, the factory should reserve the zero index for a dummy entry (e.g., push address(0) into the vault array during construction) or the migration function should use a different sentinel such as checking for address(0) directly, or compare against a mapping that distinguishes between “not present” and a legitimate identifier (for example by using a separate boolean flag or by starting identifiers at 1). In essence, the contract must avoid conflating a valid identifier with a sentinel value, thereby restoring the ability to migrate to any legitimate vault, including the first one, and eliminating the denial‑of‑service risk.

title: `BranchBridgeAgent._normalizeDecimalsMultiple` will always revert because of the lack of allocating memory
description: `BranchBridgeAgent._normalizeDecimalsMultiple` will always revert because of the lack of allocating memory
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing memory allocation for the dynamic array that stores normalized deposit amounts inside the internal function that converts a list of token amounts to a common decimal representation. The function declares a return variable of type uint256[] memory named deposits but never creates a concrete array instance before writing to it. As a result, when the loop attempts to assign deposits[i] the EVM detects an invalid memory reference and the transaction reverts. This occurs every time the function is invoked, which typically happens as part of the bridge workflow that normalizes user deposits before they are forwarded to the destination chain. Because the revert happens before any state changes, the bridge call fails, leaving the user’s transaction unprocessed and the funds remain with the sender. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a submitted deposit that never appears on the destination chain, balances stay unchanged, or the transaction remains pending and eventually fails. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for the entire bridging protocol: no deposits can be processed, effectively freezing cross‑chain transfers and breaking the business logic that assumes successful accounting of normalized amounts. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the reviewers examined the implementation of the decimal‑normalisation helper and noticed that the return array was never instantiated. It can be hard to notice because the function is internal, has no external visibility, and the code looks syntactically correct; only at runtime does the missing allocation surface as a revert. The bug belongs to the class of uninitialized dynamic array errors, where a developer forgets to allocate memory for a return variable before populating it. To remediate, the function should allocate the deposits array with a length equal to the input deposits array (e.g., deposits = new uint256[](_deposits.length)) before entering the loop, ensuring that each element can be safely written. After the fix, the bridge can correctly compute normalized amounts, maintain accounting integrity, and allow users to see their expected balances after a successful deposit.

title: `vMaia` Lacks of override in `forfeitBoost`
description: Lack of override in `forfeitBoost`. When needed, `forfeit` will `underflow`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incomplete function override in the vMaia contract, which inherits from ERC4626PartnerManager. The contract deliberately disables the ability to claim a boost by providing an empty claimBoost implementation, but it fails to provide a matching empty forfeitBoost implementation. The base UtilityManager.forfeitBoost function subtracts the supplied amount from the caller’s userClaimedBoost mapping and then attempts to transfer the boost tokens. Because vMaia never records a claimed boost for a user, the userClaimedBoost entry is typically zero. When the parent contract invokes forfeitBoost – for example during a forced exit or a partner‑vault cleanup – the subtraction operation is performed on a zero balance, causing an arithmetic underflow. In Solidity versions that enforce checked arithmetic, this underflow triggers a revert, meaning the forfeit transaction fails and the user’s operation is blocked. The impact is that users of the vMaia contract may be unable to complete a forfeit, leading to funds that appear to be locked, denial‑of‑service for affected accounts, and a mismatch between expected and actual contract state. The issue manifests whenever the protocol logic calls forfeitBoost, which can happen during routine vault management or when a user attempts to withdraw after a boost has been applied. All participants that interact with the vMaia contract – including regular users, partner vault operators, and the protocol itself – are potentially affected because the contract’s accounting assumptions (that a boost can be safely forfeited) are violated. The problem was identified during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the inheritance hierarchy and noticing that claimBoost was overridden with an empty body while forfeitBoost was left untouched. Because the empty override is subtle, the bug can be missed during manual testing; the function appears to exist but does not contain the protective logic required for this specific implementation. To remediate the issue, the contract should explicitly override forfeitBoost with an empty implementation or with logic that safely handles the case where no boost has been claimed, thereby preventing the subtraction from a zero balance and eliminating the underflow risk. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of inheritance‑related override bugs where a derived contract unintentionally inherits unsafe behavior from a base contract, leading to arithmetic errors and unintended reverts.

title: `updatePeriod`
description: If there is a `weekly` that has not been taken, it may result in an insufficient minting of `HERMES`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the weekly emission routine of the HERMES token contract, specifically in the updatePeriod function that is responsible for minting new tokens each week. The function determines whether additional tokens need to be minted by comparing the contract's current token balance with a calculated required amount that includes the new weekly emission, growth, and the DAO share. The root cause is a logical accounting error: the balance check uses the contract's raw token balance, which may still contain the previous week’s allocation that has not yet been withdrawn by the flywheelGaugeRewards contract because its gaugeCycle can be longer than one week. Consequently, the required amount is underestimated, and the contract may skip minting when it actually needs to create more tokens. An attacker or any user can trigger updatePeriod after a new week has started but before the pending weekly allocation is taken, causing the contract to believe it has sufficient balance and therefore not mint the shortfall. When the gauge later attempts to claim the pending weekly reward, the contract lacks enough HERMES, leading to a shortfall in the distribution. From the user’s perspective this manifests as missing or zero weekly rewards despite the protocol advertising a regular emission; the UI may show that the weekly reward was scheduled but the wallet receives nothing. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s economic guarantees: token holders receive fewer tokens than promised, the DAO receives a reduced share, and overall accounting integrity is compromised. The issue occurs only when the gauge’s withdrawal interval exceeds the weekly period, making it a conditional bug that can be hard to notice because the balance‑check logic appears correct under normal timing. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit through logical analysis of the emission schedule. To remediate, the contract should adjust the required‑balance calculation to account for any pending weekly allocation that remains in the contract, for example by subtracting the outstanding weekly amount from the balance before comparison or by tracking pending rewards in a separate variable. This ensures that the minting logic always creates enough tokens to satisfy both the growth and DAO share obligations, restoring correct accounting and preventing reward shortfalls.

title: `_decrementWeightUntilFree` has a possible infinite loop
description: In the loop of the `_decrementWeightUntilFree()` method, the position of `i++` is wrong, which may lead to an infinite loop.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an infinite‑loop condition in the internal function that reduces a user’s weighted stake until a target free weight is reached. The loop iterates over a list of gauges using an index variable `i`. Because the increment statement `i++` is placed inside a conditional block that only executes when the user’s weight for the current gauge is non‑zero, the index is never advanced when `userGaugeWeight` equals zero. In that case the loop condition `i < size && (userFreeWeight + totalFreed) < weight` remains true, the same gauge is examined repeatedly and the function never exits. This logical error originates from an incorrect loop structure: the increment is not guaranteed on every iteration, violating the basic invariant that a for‑loop must progress. An attacker or any caller can trigger the condition simply by providing a user address that has at least one gauge with a zero weight, which is allowed by the protocol because there is no guard against `getUserGaugeWeight[user][gauge] == 0`. When the function is invoked, the contract’s execution will consume gas indefinitely until the block gas limit is reached, causing a denial‑of‑service for that transaction and potentially locking the caller’s funds if the call is part of a larger workflow. The impact is therefore a loss of availability for any operation that relies on `_decrementWeightUntilFree`, and could also prevent users from withdrawing or rebalancing their positions, leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds from the user’s perspective. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the control‑flow was examined and the misplaced increment identified. It can be hard to notice because typical usage patterns involve non‑zero gauge weights, so the loop appears to work correctly in most tests, while the edge case with zero weight silently creates a hang. The proper fix is to ensure the loop index is incremented on every iteration, for example by moving `i++` outside the `if (userGaugeWeight != 0)` block or by restructuring the loop to use a `while` with an explicit increment after the conditional logic. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect loop termination” or “missing iterator advancement” bugs that break expected termination guarantees and lead to denial‑of‑service conditions.

title: The user is enforced to overpay for the `fallback` gas when calling `retryDeposit`
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the gas‑reserve check applied to the retryDeposit function of the BranchBridgeAgent contract. The function is intended to allow a deposit owner to add additional ETH to an existing cross‑chain deposit and then trigger a fallback call if needed. A modifier called requiresFallbackGas is attached to both new‑deposit functions and retryDeposit. This modifier invokes an internal routine that simply verifies that the amount of ETH sent with the transaction (msg.value) is greater than a constant MIN_FALLBACK_RESERVE multiplied by the current gas price. The check works for a brand‑new deposit because the entire gas reserve must be supplied up‑front. However, when retryDeposit is used to top up a deposit that already holds some gas, the modifier does not take the previously deposited amount into account. Consequently, the caller must send an amount of ETH that is at least MIN_FALLBACK_RESERVE regardless of how much gas is already available in the deposit. In practice this forces the user to overpay for the fallback gas; the user expects to send only the shortfall (for example 0.05 ETH) but the transaction reverts unless they also include an additional 0.1 ETH to satisfy the generic check. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a transaction failure with a message about insufficient gas, and the only way to succeed is to increase the sent value, leading to an unexpected loss of funds. The impact is financial: deposit owners lose the extra ETH they had to provide, which reduces the efficiency of the bridge and may discourage participation. The issue manifests only when a deposit has already been created and the fallback has not yet been triggered, i.e., during a retry after a remote execution failure. It was discovered during a formal audit of the Anycall gas‑management logic, where the auditor noticed that the fallback‑gas verification does not differentiate between initial deposits and top‑ups. The bug is subtle because the modifier appears reasonable and the contract does not refund excess gas on failure, making the overpayment easy to overlook. Conceptually, the problem belongs to the class of “incorrect resource accounting” bugs where a safety check is applied without considering the current state, leading to unnecessary cost enforcement. The recommended remediation is to replace the generic modifier on retryDeposit with a state‑aware check that adds the existing deposited gas to the newly supplied msg.value before comparing against MIN_FALLBACK_RESERVE, or to remove the modifier entirely for the top‑up path. This change ensures that only the true shortfall must be supplied, aligning the contract’s behavior with user expectations and preserving the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Depositing gas through `depositGasAnycallConfig` should not withdraw the `nativeToken`
description: `DepositGasAnycallConfig` can deposit the gas fee externally, but it should not withdraw the `nativeToken`. This prevents gas from being deposited.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the gas‑deposit routine used by the RootBridgeAgent when interacting with the Anycall cross‑chain executor. The contract exposes a public payable function called depositGasAnycallConfig that is intended to allow an external caller to fund the bridge with native gas. Internally the function forwards the received ether to a helper _replenishGas, which first calls wrappedNativeToken.withdraw to unwrap an amount of wrapped native token and then forwards the same amount to the Anycall configuration contract via a deposit call. The root cause is that the logic assumes the gas to be deposited is always held as wrapped native token, even when the caller supplies raw ether directly. Consequently the withdraw step attempts to take the same amount from the contract’s wrapped token balance, which either fails because the balance is insufficient or unnecessarily reduces the contract’s native token holdings. When the withdraw succeeds, the native token that the caller sent is effectively burned, and the Anycall contract receives no net gas credit. This mismatch prevents the intended gas deposit, leading to a situation where a user who sends ETH to fund execution receives no usable gas credit; the UI may show a successful transaction but the bridge later cannot pay for cross‑chain calls, causing calls to revert with “InsufficientGasForFees” or similar errors. The impact is a loss of usable gas funds, potential execution failures, and a confusing user experience where funds appear to disappear after a deposit. The issue manifests whenever depositGasAnycallConfig is called with a non‑zero msg.value, i.e., any external gas funding attempt. It affects any participant trying to fund the bridge, including end‑users, relayers, and protocol operators who rely on the gas‑deposit mechanism. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the RootBridgeAgent’s gas management functions, where the auditor noticed that the withdraw call was unnecessary and contradictory to the purpose of the external deposit path. The problem is subtle because the withdraw and deposit calls use the same amount, making the net effect appear neutral in static analysis, yet at runtime the wrapped token balance is altered, breaking accounting assumptions. To remediate, the contract should either remove the wrappedNativeToken.withdraw call when handling external msg.value, or add proper deposit logic that directly credits the native token amount to the Anycall configuration without unwrapping. In conceptual terms, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect asset handling” or “mis‑matched token conversion” where a function both withdraws and deposits the same amount, resulting in a net loss of the underlying asset and violating the protocol’s accounting invariants.

title: When the `anyExecute` call is made to `RootBridgeAgent` with a `depositNonce` that has been recorded in `executionHistory`, `initialGas` and `userFeeInfo` will not be updated, which would affect the next caller of `retrySettlement`.
description: The wrong `userFeeInfo` will be used when `retrySettlement` is called directly.
bug_full: The contract contains a state‑management flaw in the bridge agent that can lead to incorrect gas accounting when a user invokes the retrySettlement function. The agent stores two mutable variables, initialGas and userFeeInfo, which are populated at the start of the anyExecute call and cleared at the end of that call after the execution fee has been paid. The logic in retrySettlement assumes that a zero value of initialGas means the function is being called directly by a user, while a non‑zero value indicates it is being invoked internally by anyExecute. This assumption breaks when anyExecute is called with a depositNonce that has already been recorded in executionHistory. In that situation anyExecute returns early before reaching the cleanup code that would reset initialGas and userFeeInfo. Consequently the stale values remain in storage. If a user then calls retrySettlement, the function sees initialGas != 0 and therefore uses the stale userFeeInfo that was set for the previous execution. This stale fee information can be lower than the required minimum fallback reserve, causing the call to revert with InsufficientGasForFees, or it can be higher, allowing the user to execute retrySettlement without sending any ether, effectively receiving a free transaction. The impact is that users may lose the ability to retry a settlement, experience unexpected reverts, or unintentionally obtain a fee‑free execution, breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees and potentially exposing the bridge to economic abuse. The bug is triggered only when the early‑return path of anyExecute is taken, which is easy to miss during testing because the normal execution flow correctly clears the variables. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between anyExecute, executionHistory, and retrySettlement. To remediate the problem the contract should either restrict retrySettlement so it can only be called by the authorized AgentExecutor, or explicitly delete or reset initialGas and userFeeInfo before any early return when the nonce has already been processed. Either approach ensures that stale fee data cannot be reused, restoring the intended invariant that retrySettlement either receives fresh user‑provided gas parameters or reverts safely.

title: In `ERC20Boost.sol`, a user can be `attached` to a gauge and have no boost balance.
description: When a user with a boosted gauge becomes deprecated, the user can transfer their boost tokens. When the same gauge is reintroduced to the active gauge list, the user will boost it again, even if their boost token balance is zero.
bug_full: The contract allows a user to attach boost tokens to a gauge, recording the highest per‑gauge boost as the user’s overall boost balance. The function that recomputes this balance, updateUserBoost, mistakenly iterates only over gauges that are currently active. When a gauge is moved to the deprecated list, the loop skips it, causing the user’s recorded boost to be recomputed as zero because no active gauge contributes a positive value. The protocol then treats the user’s entire token balance as free, allowing a transfer of tokens that are still logically attached to the now‑deprecated gauge. After the deprecated gauge is later re‑added to the active list, the user remains attached to that gauge even though their token balance is zero, so the system believes the gauge is still boosted while no tokens actually back it. This inconsistency can be exploited by a malicious user who deliberately deprecates a gauge, calls updateUserBoost to reset their boost to zero, transfers the tokens, and then triggers the gauge’s reinstatement, ending up with a gauge that appears to have a boost without any underlying tokens. The impact is a breach of the accounting guarantees of the protocol: funds that should be locked for boosting become transferable, leading to potential loss of boost value, inaccurate reward distribution, and erosion of trust in the gauge‑boost mechanism. The bug manifests only when a gauge transitions between active and deprecated states and the user invokes the boost‑update routine in that window. Any holder who has previously attached tokens to a gauge is affected, as the UI may still show the gauge as boosted while the user’s balance appears normal, making the problem hard to notice. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the logical flaw in the updateUserBoost implementation was identified. To remediate, the boost‑recalculation logic must consider every gauge a user has ever attached to, regardless of its current status, or the protocol must prevent boost balance reset when a gauge is deprecated. In short, the vulnerability is a state‑inconsistent boost accounting bug that lets users transfer tokens that are still logically allocated, violating the intended business rule that attached boost tokens are non‑transferable until they are truly free.

title: `BoostAggregator` owner can set fees to 100% and steal all of the user’s rewards
description: Users who use `BoostAggregator` will suffer a 100% loss of their rewards.
bug_full: The BoostAggregator contract contains a privileged economic parameter called protocolFee that determines what portion of a user’s accrued rewards is taken by the protocol. The contract exposes a function setProtocolFee(uint256 _protocolFee) that can be called only by the contract owner. The function checks only that the supplied fee does not exceed a constant DIVISIONER, which represents 100 % of the reward pool. Because the check allows the fee to be set exactly to DIVISIONER, the owner can raise the fee to the maximum value, effectively configuring the contract to keep the entire reward amount. When a user later calls the withdrawal or claim function, the contract calculates the user’s payout as reward × (DIVISIONER ‑ protocolFee)/DIVISIONER. With protocolFee equal to DIVISIONER, the numerator becomes zero and the user receives no tokens, while the full reward amount is transferred to the owner’s address. This behaviour can be triggered at any time after a user has deposited tokens, simply by the owner invoking setProtocolFee with the maximum value. All participants who rely on the public BoostAggregator instance are affected, because the contract is intended to be used by anyone without trusting the owner. From the user’s perspective the UI may still show the staked amount and indicate that rewards have been earned, but when the user attempts to claim the reward the transaction succeeds and the received amount is zero, creating the impression that the protocol “eats” the rewards. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditor noticed that the onlyOwner gate did not prevent a fee of 100 % and that the fee is applied globally to every user’s withdrawal. The vulnerability is subtle because the contract does not emit a warning or revert; it merely returns a zero payout, which can be mistaken for a normal “no reward” situation. The bug belongs to the class of owner‑controlled parameter manipulation where a privileged role can set an economic variable to an extreme value, breaking the intended accounting guarantees. To remediate the problem the contract should either remove the owner’s ability to change the fee after deposits, enforce a maximum fee well below 100 %, store the fee that was in effect at the time each user deposited and use that per‑user fee on withdrawal, or move fee governance to a decentralized mechanism with proper timelocks and caps. Implementing any of these fixes restores the invariant that users receive at least a portion of their earned rewards and prevents the owner from stealing the entire reward pool.

title: `vMaia` is ERC-4626 compliant, but the `maxWithdraw` & `maxRedeem` functions are not fully up to EIP-4626’s specification
bug_full: The vMaia vault claims ERC‑4626 compliance but its maxWithdraw and maxRedeem view functions do not respect the contract’s withdrawal‑pause logic. According to EIP‑4626, these functions must return zero whenever withdrawals or redemptions are globally disabled, for exampleduring a paused unstake period. In vMaia the functions simply return balanceOf[user] regardless of the current month or the 1st Tuesday window that governs when withdrawals are allowed. The root cause is that the pause condition, which is enforced in the internal beforeWithdraw hook, is never consulted by the read‑only maxWithdraw and maxRedeem methods. As a result, external callers – typically front‑ends or other contracts – receive a non‑zero “maximum withdrawable” amount even when the protocol has deliberately disabled withdrawals for the month. From a user’s perspective the UI will display a positive withdrawable balance, leading the user to expect a successful withdrawal, but any actual withdraw call will revert because beforeWithdraw will block the operation. This mismatch can cause confusion, failed transactions, loss of trust, and may be exploited by malicious contracts that rely on the view functions to calculate profit or to trigger other logic under the false assumption that funds are freely withdrawable. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by comparing the implementation against the EIP‑4626 specification. It is subtle because the view functions do not affect on‑chain state and therefore do not trigger a revert, making the problem invisible to simple transaction testing. The proper fix is to add a check of the global withdrawal window inside maxWithdraw and maxRedeem – returning balanceOf[user] only when the current timestamp falls within the allowed 1st Tuesday (UTC+0) of the month, and returning 0 otherwise – thereby aligning the contract with the specification and ensuring that users see accurate withdrawable amounts.

title: Protocol fees can become trapped indefinitely inside the Talos vault contracts
description:
Talos strategy contracts all inherit logic from `TalosBaseStrategy`, including the function `collectProtocolFees`. This function is used by the owner to receive fees earned by the contract.

Talos vault contracts should be expected to work properly for any token that has a sufficiently liquid Uniswap pool. However, certain ERC20 tokens [do not revert on failed transfers](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/2.x/api/token/erc20#SafeERC20), and instead return `false`. In `TalosBaseStrategy#collectProtocolFees`, tokens are transferred from the contract to the owner using `transfer`, and the return value is not checked. This means, that the transfer could fail silently; in which case `protocolFees0` and `protocolFees1` would be updated without the tokens leaving the contract. This function is inherited by any Talos vault contract.

This accounting discrepancy causes the tokens to be irretrievably trapped in the contract.
bug_full: Talos vault contracts inherit a function collectProtocolFees that allows the contract owner to withdraw accumulated protocol fees. The function transfers the fee tokens using the ERC20 transfer method but does not check the boolean return value. For ERC20 tokens that follow the OpenZeppelin standard of returning false on failure instead of reverting, a failed transfer is silently ignored. The accounting variables protocolFees0 and protocolFees1 are still decreased, so the contract records that the fees have been paid even though the tokens remain locked inside the vault. This mismatch creates a situation where protocol fees become permanently trapped, because there is no alternative mechanism to retrieve them and the owner cannot later claim the missing balance. The issue appears only when the vault holds a token whose transfer implementation does not revert on insufficient allowance, insufficient balance, or other transfer restrictions. It was discovered during a code audit that flagged the missing safeTransfer check. The bug is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the owner receives a successful receipt, while the on‑chain balance of the vault still contains the fee amount. From a user perspective the protocol appears to have paid out fees, but the expected token balance in the owner’s wallet does not increase, leading to missing refunds or zero payouts. This is an instance of an unchecked ERC20 transfer, a class of accounting‑logic bugs where state is updated before confirming external token movement. The proper fix is to use a safe transfer wrapper such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library, which reverts on a false return and therefore prevents the state from diverging from the actual token balances.

title: A lack of slippage protection can lead to a significant loss of user funds
description: Talos strategy contracts interact with Uniswap V3 in multiple areas of the code. However, none of these interactions contain any [slippage control](https://dacian.me/defi-slippage-attacks#heading-no-slippage-parameter). This means, the contract, and by extension, all users who hold shares, can lose a significant value due to liquid pools or MEV sandwich attacks every time any of the relevant functions are called.
poc:
In each of the below instances, a call to Uniswap V3 is made. Calls `amount0Min` and `amount1Min` are each set to `0`, which allows for a **100% slippage tolerance**. This means, that the action could lead to the caller losing up to 100% of their tokens due to slippage.

[`TalosBaseStrategy#deposit`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/talos/base/TalosBaseStrategy.sol#L201-L210):

```solidity
(liquidityDifference, amount0, amount1) = nonfungiblePositionManager.increaseLiquidity(
    INonfungiblePositionManager.IncreaseLiquidityParams({
        tokenId: _tokenId,
        amount0Desired: amount0Desired,
        amount1Desired: amount1Desired,
        amount0Min: 0, // @audit should be non-zero
        amount1Min: 0, // @audit should be non-zero
        deadline: block.timestamp
    })
);
```

[`PoolActions#rerange`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/talos/libraries/PoolActions.sol#L73-L87):

```solidity
(tokenId, liquidity, amount0, amount1) = nonfungiblePositionManager.mint(
    INonfungiblePositionManager.MintParams({
        token0: address(actionParams.token0),
        token1: address(actionParams.token1),
        fee: poolFee,
        tickLower: tickLower,
        tickUpper: tickUpper,
        amount0Desired: balance0,
        amount1Desired: balance1,
        amount0Min: 0, // @audit should be non-zero
        amount1Min: 0, // @audit should be non-zero
        recipient: address(this),
        deadline: block.timestamp
    })
);
```

[`TalosBaseStrategy#init`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/talos/base/TalosBaseStrategy.sol#L135-L149):

```solidity
(_tokenId, _liquidity, amount0, amount1) = _nonfungiblePositionManager.mint(
    INonfungiblePositionManager.MintParams({
        token0: address(_token0),
        token1: address(_token1),
        fee: poolFee,
        tickLower: tickLower,
        tickUpper: tickUpper,
        amount0Desired: amount0Desired,
        amount1Desired: amount1Desired,
        amount0Min: 0, // @audit should be non-zero
        amount1Min: 0, // @audit should be non-zero
        recipient: address(this),
        deadline: block.timestamp
    })
);
```

[`TalosBaseStrategy#_withdrawAll`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/talos/base/TalosBaseStrategy.sol#L353-L361):

```solidity
_nonfungiblePositionManager.decreaseLiquidity(
    INonfungiblePositionManager.DecreaseLiquidityParams({
        tokenId: _tokenId,
        liquidity: _liquidity,
        amount0Min: 0, // @audit should be non-zero
        amount1Min: 0, // @audit should be non-zero
        deadline: block.timestamp
    })
);
```
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing slippage protection in every interaction that the Talos strategy contracts have with Uniswap V3. In each call to the Uniswap non‑fungible position manager the parameters amount0Min and amount1Min are hard‑coded to zero, which effectively sets the slippage tolerance to 100 %. The root cause is that the contract does not expose any mechanism for the caller to specify a minimum acceptable amount of each token, and the audit team observed that the developers left the defaults at zero. An attacker can exploit this by performing a front‑running or sandwich attack: the attacker moves the pool price just before the strategy transaction is mined, causing the amount of token0 or token1 that the contract receives to be dramatically lower than the amount it expected to deposit, withdraw or rebalance. Because the contract accepts any amount, the transaction will still succeed, but the strategy may end up with far fewer assets than anticipated, potentially as low as zero. The impact is a loss of value for every user who holds shares in the strategy, as the share price will drop and users may receive little or nothing when they try to withdraw. The issue manifests whenever any of the vulnerable functions – deposit, rerange, init or withdrawAll – are executed, especially in volatile market conditions or when MEV bots are active. All token holders, the protocol’s liquidity pool and any downstream contracts that rely on the strategy’s balances are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit by Code4rena, which flagged the zero values as a missing slippage check. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it simply yields an unexpected token amount, so the UI may show a successful deposit while the user’s balance later appears reduced or the withdrawal returns almost nothing. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a missing slippage guard or unchecked price slippage in automated market maker interactions. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are a deposit that seems to succeed but results in fewer shares, a withdrawal that returns far less than expected, or a sudden disappearance of funds from the strategy. Users expect to receive at least the quoted amount of tokens, but the reality may be a near‑zero payout. To remediate the issue the contract should allow callers to provide non‑zero amount0Min and amount1Min values, or otherwise compute acceptable minimums based on a price oracle or a configurable slippage percentage, and enforce those limits before executing the Uniswap call.

title: The `RestakeToken` function is not permissionless
bug_full:
The vulnerability lies in the restakeToken function of the UniswapV3Staker contract, which is intended to be callable by anyone after an incentive period ends so that third‑party services can automatically re‑stake a user’s NFT and preserve reward accrual. The implementation passes a boolean flag named isNotRestake as true to the internal _unstakeToken routine, even when the external call is restakeToken. Inside _unstakeToken the access check is written as `if ((isNotRestake || block.timestamp < endTime) && owner != msg.sender) revert NotCalledByOwner();`. Because isNotRestake is always true for restakeToken, the condition collapses to `owner != msg.sender`, causing the transaction to revert whenever the caller is not the token’s owner, regardless of the block timestamp. This logical error effectively makes restakeToken non‑permissionless, contradicting the protocol’s design assumption.

The root cause is a mismatched flag semantics: the flag was meant to indicate whether the call is a genuine restake (allowing any caller after the incentive ends) but the code treats the flag as a “not‑restake” indicator. The flag is never set to false in the public restakeToken entry point, so the owner‑only restriction is always enforced.

An attacker or, more realistically, a legitimate third‑party automation service can exploit this by attempting to call restakeToken on behalf of another user and will be blocked by the revert. The exploit does not require malicious intent; any external actor trying to batch‑restake tokens will fail. The impact is that users cannot rely on automated re‑staking, leading to delayed re‑stake actions, loss of pending rewards, reduced issuance of bHermes utility tokens, and overall lower yield for liquidity providers. Third‑party aggregators that depend on permissionless restaking are also unable to provide cost‑effective batch operations, increasing gas costs for users.

The bug manifests only after the incentive’s end time has passed, when the protocol expects the restakeToken function to be open to anyone. It affects token owners who expect their positions to continue earning rewards without manual intervention, as well as any external service that attempts to act on their behalf. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a unit test demonstrated that a non‑owner (Charlie) could not restake Alice’s token, causing the transaction to revert with NotCalledByOwner(). The problem is subtle because the function name and documentation suggest open access, yet the boolean flag silently enforces owner‑only access.

To remediate the issue, the simplest fix is to pass false for the isNotRestake flag when calling _unstakeToken from restakeToken, thereby disabling the owner check for legitimate restake calls. A more robust solution is to rename the flag to isRestake and invert the logic, making the intent clearer and reducing the chance of future misuse. In either case, the access control condition should be rewritten to allow any caller after the incentive end time while still protecting owners from premature unstaking.

In summary, this is a classic case of improper access control caused by an incorrectly used boolean flag, resulting in a permissioned function that should be permissionless. The bug leads to missing rewards, lower protocol utility token distribution, and higher transaction costs, and can be fixed by correcting the flag usage or refactoring the access‑control logic.

title: Some functions in the Talos contracts do not allow user to supply `slippage` and `deadline`, which may cause swap revert
description:
In the following functions, except `TalosBaseStrategy.redeem()`, the minimum `slippage` is still hardcoded to `0`, not allowing the user to specify their own slippage parameters. This can expose users to sandwich attacks due to unlimited slippage.

Additionally, it also does not allow users to supply their own `deadline`, as the `deadline` parameter is simply passed in currently as `block.timestamp`, in which the transaction occurs. This effectively means, that the transaction has no deadline; which means that a swap transaction may be included anytime by validators and remain pending in `mempool`, potentially exposing users to sandwich attacks by attackers or MEV bots.

  * `TalosBaseStrategy.redeem()` [Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/talos/base/TalosBaseStrategy.sol#L269)
  * `TalosStrategyVanilla._compoundFees()` [Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/talos/TalosStrategyVanilla.sol#L148)
  * `TalosBaseStrategy.init()` [Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/talos/base/TalosBaseStrategy.sol#L147)
  * `TalosBaseStrategy.deposit()` [Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/talos/base/TalosBaseStrategy.sol#L208)
  * `TalosBaseStrategy._withdrawAll()` [Link](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/talos/base/TalosBaseStrategy.sol#L359)
poc:
Consider the following scenario:

  1. Alice wants to swap 30 BNB tokens for 1 BNB and later sell the 1 BNB for 300 DAI. They sign the transaction calling `TalosBaseStrategy.redeem()` with `inputAmount = 30 vBNB` and `amountOutmin = 0.99 BNB` (`$`1 slippage).
  2. The transaction is submitted to the `mempool`; however, Alice chose a transaction fee that is too low for validators to be interested in including their transaction in a block. The transaction stays pending in the `mempool` for extended periods, which could be hours, days, weeks, or even longer.
  3. When the average gas fee drops far enough for Alice’s transaction to become interesting again for miners to include it, their swap will be executed. In the meantime, the price of BNB could have drastically decreased. They will still at least get 0.99 BNB due to `amountOutmin`, but the DAI value of that output might be significantly lower. They have unknowingly performed a bad trade due to the pending transaction they forgot about.

An even worse way, is this issue can be maliciously exploited is through MEV:

  1. The swap transaction is still pending in the `mempool`. Average fees are still too high for validators to be interested in it. The price of BNB has gone up significantly since the transaction was signed, meaning Alice would receive a lot more ETH when the swap is executed. But that also means that their `minOutput` value is outdated and would allow for significant slippage.
  2. A MEV bot detects the pending transaction. Since the outdated `minOut` now allows for high slippage, the bot sandwiches Alice, resulting in significant profit for the bot and significant loss for Alice.

The above scenario could be made worse for other functions where slippage is not allowed to be user-specified. When combined with the lack of a deadline check, MEV bots can simply immediately sandwich users.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of hard‑coded swap parameters in several Talos contract functions, namely a fixed minimum slippage of zero and a deadline that is automatically set to the current block timestamp. Because the slippage value cannot be supplied by the caller, the contract effectively accepts any amount of price movement between the time the transaction is signed and the time it is executed. Likewise, using block.timestamp as the deadline means the transaction has no expiration; it can remain in the mempool indefinitely until a validator includes it. This combination creates a situation where a user‑initiated swap may be executed far after the intended price, exposing the user to unlimited slippage and allowing a front‑running or sandwich attacker to profit. The root cause is the omission of user‑controlled parameters and the absence of a deadline check in functions such as redeem, deposit, init, _withdrawAll and _compoundFees. An attacker can monitor pending transactions, wait for a favorable price shift, and then insert a higher‑priced trade before the victim’s transaction is mined, or simply let the victim’s transaction sit for a long period while market conditions deteriorate. The impact is that the user may receive far fewer assets than expected, effectively losing value even though the transaction succeeds; from the UI perspective the user sees a successful swap but the received amount is much lower or the expected profit disappears. This issue manifests when a user submits a transaction with a low gas price that causes it to linger in the mempool, or when the network experiences volatile price movements. All participants who interact with the affected functions—regular users, liquidity providers, and protocol integrators—are at risk. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined the contract’s parameter handling and noticed the hard‑coded values. It can be difficult to detect because the transaction does not revert; instead it silently yields an unfavorable rate, which may be attributed to market volatility rather than a contract flaw. The proper remediation is to expose slippage and deadline as configurable arguments, validate that the deadline has not passed, and enforce the user‑provided slippage tolerance before executing the swap, thereby aligning contract behavior with standard DeFi expectations and preventing unlimited price exposure.

title: Removing more gauge weight than it should be while transferring `ERC20Gauges` token
description: The `_decrementWeightUntilFree()` function is not well implemented. If there are deprecated gauges, it would remove more gauge weight than it should be while transferring `ERC20Gauges` token.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal function that decrements a user’s gauge weight when ERC20Gauges tokens are transferred. The routine iterates over all gauges attached to a user and stops when the sum of the user’s already free weight plus the weight freed in the current loop reaches the amount that should be transferred. However, the loop condition mistakenly adds the variable that tracks weight freed from each individual gauge (userFreed) to the user’s free weight, instead of using the aggregate weight that should be deducted from the total system weight (totalFreed). Because deprecated gauges are still iterated but their weight is not added to totalFreed, the condition can become true before the required amount of live gauge weight has been accounted for, causing the function to continue freeing weight from deprecated gauges as well. As a result, when a user attempts to transfer a specific amount of voting weight, the contract may remove far more weight than intended, zeroing out the user’s remaining gauge balances and reducing the global weight accounting incorrectly. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome – a partial transfer leaving some voting power intact – is violated; the user sees their balance drop to zero and their delegated votes disappear, even though they only transferred a fraction of their holdings. The bug is triggered only when a user holds weight in both live and deprecated gauges and initiates a transfer that requires freeing weight; the presence of deprecated gauges makes the loop condition inaccurate. It was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a targeted unit test demonstrated that after removing a deprecated gauge and transferring 100 weight, the contract erroneously freed the full 200 weight, wiping both gauges. The issue is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error; the state simply reflects a missing balance, which can be mistaken for normal zero‑balance behavior. To remediate, the loop condition must be rewritten to compare the required weight against the sum of userFreeWeight and totalFreed, ensuring that only live gauge weight contributes to the total weight reduction, and the function should stop once the exact amount to be transferred has been freed. This correction restores the intended accounting invariant that only the transferred amount of voting power is deducted, preserving user balances and protocol weight integrity.

title: Maia Governance token balance dilution in `vMaia` vault is breaking the conversion rate mechanism
description:
Once a user deposits `Maia` ERC-20 tokens into the `vMaia` ERC-4626 vault, they are eligible to claim 3 kinds of utility tokens: `bHermes Weight` and `Governance` and `Maia Governance` (`pbHermes`, partner governance). On each deposit, new Maia Governance tokens (`pbHermes`) are [minted to the vault in proportion to the deposited amount](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/maia/tokens/ERC4626PartnerManager.sol#L235-L246), but those tokens are [never burned on withdrawal](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/maia/tokens/ERC4626PartnerManager.sol#L248-L256). This naturally dilutes the vault’s `pbHermes` token balance during the course of users depositing & withdrawing `Maia` tokens. Furthermore, a malicious user can dramatically accelerate this dilution by repeatedly depositing & withdrawing within a single transaction.

_Note that the vault’s `bHermes Weight` and `Governance` token balances are not diluted during this process._

However, the [ERC4626PartnerManager.increaseConversionRate(...)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/maia/tokens/ERC4626PartnerManager.sol#L215-L229) method (which `ERC4626PartnerManager` is the base of the `vMaia` contract) relies on the vault’s `pbHermes` token balance and therefore, imposes a lower limit on an increased `pbHermes<>bHermes` conversion rate to avoid underflow, see [L226](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/maia/tokens/ERC4626PartnerManager.sol#L226): `min. rate = vault balance of pbHermes / Maia tokens in the vault`. Meanwhile, the upper limit for a new conversion rate is given by [L219](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/maia/tokens/ERC4626PartnerManager.sol#L219): `max. rate = vault balance of bHermes / Maia tokens in vault`.

As a consequence, the `vMaia` vault owner’s ability to increase the conversion rate is successively constrained by user deposits & withdrawals, up until the point where the dilution of `pbHermes` reaches the `vault balance of pbHermes > vault balance of bHermes`, which leads to complete DoS of the [ERC4626PartnerManager.increaseConversionRate(...)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/maia/tokens/ERC4626PartnerManager.sol#L215-L229) method.
bug_full: When a user deposits Maia ERC‑20 tokens into the vMaia ERC‑4626 vault, the contract mints a proportional amount of Maia Governance tokens (pbHermes) to the vault. These pbHermes tokens represent a partner‑governance share that can later be exchanged for bHermes weight tokens at a rate that the vault owner may increase using the increaseConversionRate function. The function calculates a minimum acceptable conversion rate as the vault’s current pbHermes balance divided by the total Maia tokens held, and a maximum rate based on the bHermes balance. Because the implementation never burns any pbHermes tokens when a user withdraws Maia, the total pbHermes supply in the vault only grows on deposits and never shrinks on withdrawals. Consequently, each deposit‑withdraw cycle dilutes the pbHermes balance relative to the bHermes balance. An attacker can amplify this effect by repeatedly depositing and withdrawing within a single transaction, rapidly inflating the pbHermes supply while the bHermes balance stays constant. When the diluted pbHermes balance becomes larger than the bHermes balance, the minimum conversion‑rate formula yields a value that exceeds the maximum allowed rate, causing increaseConversionRate to revert with an under‑backing error. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: the vault owner can no longer raise the conversion rate, breaking the intended economic model and preventing users from receiving the expected higher bHermes rewards. The issue is triggered only when the ratio of pbHermes to Maia tokens exceeds the ratio of bHermes to Maia tokens, which can be reached through normal user activity but is accelerated by a malicious actor. The vulnerability affects the vault owner, token holders, and any protocol component that relies on the conversion‑rate mechanism. It was discovered during a formal audit by observing the token‑balance dynamics in a test that repeatedly performed deposit‑withdraw cycles and then called increaseConversionRate, which consistently reverted once the dilution threshold was crossed. The bug is subtle because the vault’s token balances appear normal; only the internal accounting ratio is violated, making it easy to overlook in casual testing. The root cause is a missing burn of pbHermes on withdrawal, leading to an accounting mismatch that violates the assumption that pbHermes supply is always backed by bHermes. The recommended fix is to burn the appropriate amount of pbHermes when Maia is withdrawn, restoring the intended one‑to‑one backing relationship and preventing the dilution that leads to the conversion‑rate DoS. This class of bug can be described as a token‑dilution or under‑collateralisation vulnerability, where minted utility tokens are not correspondingly destroyed, breaking invariant checks that depend on token ratios.

title: Claiming outstanding utility tokens from `vMaia` vault DoS on `pbHermes<>bHermes` conversion rate > 1
description:
Once a user deposits `Maia` ERC-20 tokens into the `vMaia` ERC-4626 vault, they are eligible to claim 3 kinds of utility tokens: `bHermes Weight` and `Governance` and `Maia Governance` (`pbHermes`, partner governance), via the [ERC4626PartnerManager.claimOutstanding()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/maia/tokens/ERC4626PartnerManager.sol#L89-L97) method ( `ERC4626PartnerManager` is the base of the `vMaia` contract). The conversion rate between the utility tokens and [vMaia tokens minted on deposit](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/maia/tokens/ERC4626PartnerManager.sol#L235-L246) can be increased (and **only** increased) by the contract owner via the [ERC4626PartnerManager.increaseConversionRate(...)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/maia/tokens/ERC4626PartnerManager.sol#L215-L229) method.

However, the [checkWeight, checkGovernance & checkPartnerGovernance](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/maia/vMaia.sol#L66-L88) modifiers in the `vMaia` contract do not account for this conversion rate and therefore implicity only allow a conversion rate of 1.

As a consequence, as soon as the conversion rate is increased to > 1, a call to [ERC4626PartnerManager.claimOutstanding()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/maia/tokens/ERC4626PartnerManager.sol#L89-L97) will inevitably revert due to subsequent calls to the above modifiers. Since the conversion rate can [only be increased](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/maia/tokens/ERC4626PartnerManager.sol#L217) and the `vMaia` vault contract is not upgradeable, the `claimOutstanding()` method is subject to **permanent DoS**.

Of course, the user can still claim a reduced amount of utility tokens (according to a conversion rate of 1) via the [PartnerUtilityManager.claimMultipleAmounts(...)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/maia/PartnerUtilityManager.sol#L115-L124) method (`PartnerUtilityManager` is the base of the `ERC4626PartnerManager` contract), but this still implies a loss of assets for the user since not all utility tokens they are eligible for can be claimed. Furthermore, this workaround doesn’t help when the user is a contract which implemented a call to the `claimOutstanding()` method.
bug_full: An analysis of the vMaia vault reveals a denial-of-service condition affecting the ERC4626PartnerManager.claimOutstanding() function. When a depositor places Maia tokens into the vMaia ERC-4626 vault they become entitled to three utility tokens (bHermes weight, governance and partner governance). The amount of each token is calculated using a conversion rate that the contract owner can increase, but never decrease, via increaseConversionRate(). The vMaia contract overrides three internal modifiers – checkWeight, checkGovernance and checkPartnerGovernance – with implementations that only verify that the caller’s share balance is at least the raw amount requested plus any previously claimed amount. These overridden checks ignore the current conversion rate and therefore implicitly assume a rate of 1. As soon as the owner raises the conversion rate above 1, the internal accounting performed by claimOutstanding() produces a required amount that exceeds the caller’s raw share balance. The overridden modifiers then trigger an InsufficientShares revert, causing claimOutstanding() to fail. Because the conversion rate can only be increased and the vault contract is not upgradeable, the failure is permanent: users can no longer claim the full amount of utility tokens through the intended single-call interface. A fallback path exists via PartnerUtilityManager.claimMultipleAmounts(), which allows claiming only the portion of tokens that corresponds to a rate of 1, but this results in a loss of entitlement and does not help contracts that rely on claimOutstanding(). From a user perspective the symptom is that a transaction that previously returned three token balances now reverts, or the UI shows zero tokens received despite a positive deposit. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by reproducing the scenario in a Forge test that increased the conversion rate and observed the revert. The bug is subtle because the overridden modifiers appear to perform a standard insufficient shares check, yet they do not incorporate the dynamic conversion factor that other parts of the system use. The vulnerability belongs to the class of incorrect state validation after parameter change or rate-dependent accounting mismatch. The proper fix is to remove the three faulty modifiers from vMaia and rely on the correct implementations already present in ERC4626PartnerManager, which correctly factor in the conversion rate when validating claims.

title: Unstaking `vMAIA` tokens on the first Tuesday of the month can be offset
description:
According to [project documentation](https://v2-docs.maiadao.io/protocols/overview/tokenomics/vMaia) and [natspec](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/maia/vMaia.sol#L23-L24):

Users can stake their MAIA tokens at any time, but can only withdraw their staked tokens on the first Tuesday of each month.

NOTE: Withdraw is only allowed once per month, during the 1st Tuesday (UTC+0) of the month.

The implementation that keeps the above invariant true is dependent on at least one user attempting to unstake their `vMAIA` on the first chronological Tuesday of the month. But if nobody unstakes on the first Tuesday, then, on the second Tuesday of the month, the conditions are met and users can unstake them. Again, if no one unstakes on the second Tuesday, then the next Tuesday after that will be valid. So on and so forth.

Not respecting the declared withdraw/unstaking period and limitation is a severe protocol issue in itself. The case is also not that improbable to happen. If good enough incentives are present, there will be odd Tuesdays where nobody will unstake, thus creating this loophole.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a temporal‑window enforcement flaw in the vMAIA unstaking logic. The protocol promises that users may withdraw their staked MAIA tokens only on the first Tuesday of each month, and only once per month. However, the contract’s check for a valid withdrawal day relies on a condition that becomes true after any Tuesday once the first Tuesday of the month has been observed by at least one user. If no user initiates a withdrawal on the first Tuesday, the contract does not reset the condition, and the subsequent Tuesday satisfies the check, allowing withdrawals on the second, third, or any later Tuesday of the same month. This occurs because the implementation uses a generic "isTuesday" predicate together with a state flag that is only set when a withdrawal is attempted on the first Tuesday, rather than explicitly verifying that the current date is the first Tuesday of the month. An attacker can exploit this by staking tokens, ensuring that no other participant withdraws on the first Tuesday (for example by coordinating a delay or by simply waiting), and then withdrawing on a later Tuesday, thereby bypassing the intended restriction. The impact is that the tokenomics and incentive schedule of the protocol are broken: users can claim rewards or exit positions at times that were meant to be prohibited, potentially leading to an uneven distribution of rewards, altered supply dynamics, and loss of confidence in the protocol’s rules. The bug manifests only when the first Tuesday passes without any withdrawal; under normal conditions where at least one user withdraws on that day, the contract behaves as documented, making the issue easy to miss during testing. It was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors added a test that warped the blockchain timestamp to the first Tuesday, deliberately avoided a withdrawal, and then advanced to the next Tuesday, observing that the contract still permitted a withdrawal. The difficulty in noticing the problem stems from the fact that most test suites exercise the happy‑path scenario and do not simulate the edge case of a missed first‑Tuesday withdrawal. To remediate, the contract should replace the generic Tuesday check with a precise "isFirstTuesdayOfMonth" function that computes the first Tuesday of the month from the supplied timestamp and verifies that the current day falls within that 24‑hour window, independent of any prior withdrawals. This change enforces the intended temporal invariant directly in the code, eliminating reliance on external state and preventing the loophole that permits withdrawals on any later Tuesday.

title: Wrong consideration of `blockformation` period causes incorrect `votingPeriod` and `votingDelay` calculations
description:
In `GovernorBravoDelegateMaias.sol` contract, there are wrong calculations in [MIN_VOTING_PERIOD](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/governance/GovernorBravoDelegateMaia.sol#L18), [MAX_VOTING_PERIOD](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/governance/GovernorBravoDelegateMaia.sol#L21C29-L21C46), [MIN_VOTING_DELAY](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/governance/GovernorBravoDelegateMaia.sol#L24) and [MAX_VOTING_DELAY](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/governance/GovernorBravoDelegateMaia.sol#L27) because of the incorrect consideration of the `blockformation` period.

The contracts will be deployed on Ethereum mainnet Chain too. In an Ethereum mainnet chain, the blocks are made every 12 seconds but the `votingPeriod` and `votingDelay` variables have used 15 seconds while calculating their values.

For example:

`MIN_VOTING_PERIOD` is considered for 2 weeks:

       uint256 public constant MIN_VOTING_PERIOD = 80640; // About 2 weeks

2 weeks (in seconds) = 1,209,600  
Considered Ethereum `blockformation` time in seconds = 15

Therefore, `MAX_VOTING_PERIOD` = `1,209,600 / 15` = 80,640 (blocks).

This is how the calculations have arrived for other `votingPeriod` and `votingDelay` state variables. However, Ethereum `blockformation` happens every 12 seconds and it is confirmed in the below sources:  
[Reference-01](https://chainstack.com/protocols/ethereum/#Performance)  
[Reference-02](https://ycharts.com/indicators/ethereum_average_block_time)

The correct calculation should be with 12 seconds as `blockformation` period.

For example:  
2 weeks (in seconds) = 1,209,600  
Actual Ethereum `blockformation` time in seconds = 12

Therefore, `MAX_VOTING_PERIOD` = `1,209,600 / 12` = 100,800 (blocks).

Total number of block differences for a 2 week duration = `100,800 - 80,640 = 20,160 ~ 5.6` hours. This much time difference will affect the function validations, which will cause unexpected design failure.

[MIN_VOTING_PERIOD](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/governance/GovernorBravoDelegateMaia.sol#L18), [MAX_VOTING_PERIOD](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/governance/GovernorBravoDelegateMaia.sol#L21C29-L21C46), [MIN_VOTING_DELAY](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/governance/GovernorBravoDelegateMaia.sol#L24) and [MAX_VOTING_DELAY](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/governance/GovernorBravoDelegateMaia.sol#L27) are used in functions which are further explained as below:

    File: src/governance/GovernorBravoDelegateMaia.sol

    56    function initialize(
    57        address timelock_,
    58        address govToken_,
    59        uint256 votingPeriod_,
    60        uint256 votingDelay_,
    61        uint256 proposalThreshold_
    62    ) public virtual {
    63        require(address(timelock) == address(0), "GovernorBravo::initialize: can only initialize once");
    64        require(msg.sender == admin, "GovernorBravo::initialize: admin only");
    65        require(timelock_ != address(0), "GovernorBravo::initialize: invalid timelock address");
    66        require(govToken_ != address(0), "GovernorBravo::initialize: invalid govToken address");
    67        require(
    68            votingPeriod_ >= MIN_VOTING_PERIOD && votingPeriod_ <= MAX_VOTING_PERIOD,
    69            "GovernorBravo::initialize: invalid voting period"
    70        );
    71        require(
    72            votingDelay_ >= MIN_VOTING_DELAY && votingDelay_ <= MAX_VOTING_DELAY,
    73            "GovernorBravo::initialize: invalid voting delay"
    74        );

             // some code

At [L-68 and L-72](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/governance/GovernorBravoDelegateMaia.sol#L68-L72), these state variables are used to validate the conditions in the `initialize()` function, which can be called only once. These incorrect values make the conditions at L-68 and L-72 obsolete and the conditions will not work as expected by design.

Furthermore, the [MIN_VOTING_PERIOD](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/governance/GovernorBravoDelegateMaia.sol#L18), [MAX_VOTING_PERIOD](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/governance/GovernorBravoDelegateMaia.sol#L21C29-L21C46), [MIN_VOTING_DELAY](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/governance/GovernorBravoDelegateMaia.sol#L24) and [MAX_VOTING_DELAY](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/governance/GovernorBravoDelegateMaia.sol#L27) variables are used in the below setter functions, which for sure will not work as per the expected design:

    397  function _setVotingDelay(uint256 newVotingDelay) external {

    413  function _setVotingPeriod(uint256 newVotingPeriod) external {
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mis‑calculation of the governance timing parameters in the GovernorBravoDelegateMaia contract. The contract defines constant bounds for votingPeriod and votingDelay in terms of block numbers, assuming that each Ethereum block is produced every 15 seconds. In reality the Ethereum mainnet block time averages about 12 seconds. Because the constants are derived by dividing the intended time windows (for example two weeks = 1,209,600 seconds) by 15 instead of 12, the resulting block counts are about 20,160 blocks (roughly 5.6 hours) lower than they should be. This off‑by‑approximately‑5‑hour error propagates to the MIN_VOTING_PERIOD, MAX_VOTING_PERIOD, MIN_VOTING_DELAY and MAX_VOTING_DELAY constants. These constants are used in the initialize function to validate the supplied votingPeriod and votingDelay values and also in setter functions that allow the admin to change them later. As a result, legitimate parameter values that correspond to the intended two‑week voting period are rejected because they exceed the incorrectly low maximum, while values that pass the check correspond to a shorter real‑time voting window. An attacker could exploit this by submitting proposals with the minimum allowed period, which under the flawed calculation is shorter than the governance design expects, reducing the time community members have to review and vote on proposals. Conversely, the bug can prevent proper deployment of the governor if the correct parameters are supplied, causing the contract to revert during initialization and breaking the DAO’s governance setup. The impact is on the protocol’s governance integrity: proposals may be decided faster than intended, potentially allowing malicious or rushed changes, and the DAO’s token holders may lose the expected protection window. The issue affects any user or role that interacts with the governance contract, including proposers, voters, and the admin who sets timing parameters. It was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, where the auditors compared the hard‑coded block‑time assumption with publicly known Ethereum block times and identified the discrepancy. The bug is subtle because block time is an off‑chain environmental constant that is easy to overlook, and the contract does not expose the underlying assumption, making the error invisible in normal operation. To fix the issue, the constants should be recomputed using the correct 12‑second block interval, or the contract should store timing parameters in seconds and convert to blocks at runtime, ensuring that the validation logic matches the actual network conditions. This correction restores the intended two‑week voting period and appropriate voting delay, aligning the contract’s behavior with the DAO’s governance design and preventing timing‑related attacks.

title: If `HERMES` gauge rewards are not queued for distribution every week, they are slashed
description: In order to queue weekly `HERMES` rewards for distribution, `FlywheelGaugeRewards::queueRewardsForCycle` must be called during the next cycle (week).
