If a cycle has passed and no one calls `queueRewardsForCycle` to queue rewards, cycle gauge rewards are lost as the internal accounting does not take into consideration time passing, only the last processed cycle.
poc:
Rewards are calculated for the current cycle and last stored cycle only, with no intermediary accounting: 

Visual example:
    
     0 1 2 3 4 5 6  (epoch/cycle)
    +-+-+-+-+-+-+-+
    |Q|Q|Q| | |Q|Q|
    +-+-+-+-+-+-+-+

Up until epoch 2 `queueRewardsForCycle` (Q) was called, for cycle 3 and 4 nobody calls, on cycle 5 `queueRewardsForCycle` is called again, but cycle 3 and 4 rewards are not taken into consideration.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a time‑dependent accounting flaw in the reward distribution mechanism of the MaiaDAO ecosystem. Rewards for each gauge are supposed to be queued each cycle by calling the external function queueRewardsForCycle (via BaseV2Minter.updatePeriod). The contract’s internal state only records the last processed cycle and does not automatically account for cycles that have elapsed without a queue call. Consequently, if a weekly (or 12‑hour for UniswapV3 gauges) window passes without anyone invoking queueRewardsForCycle, the rewards that should have been distributed for those missed cycles are silently dropped from the accounting ledger. This happens because the reward calculation uses only the current cycle and the previously stored cycle, ignoring any intermediate periods, so the missed rewards are never added to any user’s balance. An attacker or simply an inactive participant could cause the loss by refraining from calling the function, and because the function has no access control and offers no direct incentive for callers, there is no guarantee that the call will happen on time. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that expected weekly rewards appear as zero, balances do not increase, and liquidity providers receive no compensation for the missed period, even though they supplied liquidity. The impact is a reduction of earned yield, potential loss of liquidity incentives, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s reward logic. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the auditors examined the FlywheelGaugeRewards contract and observed that the accounting logic does not handle skipped cycles, as demonstrated by a visual example where cycles 3 and 4 receive no queued rewards. The problem is hard to notice because there is no explicit error or revert; the contract simply records no reward, making the disappearance of funds appear as a normal “no reward” condition. To remediate, the protocol should introduce a mechanism that either automatically snapshots and accrues rewards for any missed cycles or provides a fallback that can be triggered by anyone (potentially with a small incentive) to process pending cycles. On‑chain automation tools such as Chainlink Automation could be employed to guarantee that queueRewardsForCycle is called within the required window, or the accounting model could be redesigned to compute rewards based on elapsed time rather than relying on a single periodic call. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “periodic update missing” or “deadline‑dependent reward slashing” vulnerabilities, where failure to perform a scheduled state transition results in loss of economic value.

title: Ulysses omnichain - User Funds can get locked permanently via making a callout without deposit
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Ulysses omnichain multicall router when a user invokes a no‑deposit multicall (funcId 0x02 or 0x03). In this flow the router calls the internal functions _approveAndCallOut or _approveMultipleAndCallOut and deliberately passes address(0) as the settlement initiator. Consequently the settlement record that is created in the root bridge stores its owner field as the zero address. The contract logic that governs settlement redemption and retry explicitly checks that the owner is not the zero address; if it is, both redeemSettlement and _retrySettlement revert or return false. When the cross‑chain callout to the destination branch fails – for example due to insufficient gas or a revert on the branch – the settlement remains in a Failed state but its owner is still zero. Because the owner cannot be identified, the user is unable to invoke a retry or a redeem operation, leaving the tokens that were transferred to the root bridge permanently locked. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears to have succeeded, their balance on the source chain drops to zero, yet no output tokens are received on the destination chain, creating a confusing “funds disappeared” symptom. The issue occurs only for the no‑deposit multicall endpoints; normal multicall calls that include a deposit correctly set the owner and are not affected. The root cause is a missing ownership assignment – a classic zero‑address ownership bug – which violates the protocol’s accounting invariant that global and local token supplies must remain 1:1. The invariant is broken because locked global tokens remain in the root bridge while no corresponding local tokens are minted for the user. The problem was uncovered during a manual audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test reproducing the failure: after forcing a fallback on a failed settlement, the redeem function reverted with SettlementRedeemUnavailable because the settlement owner was address(0). The bug is subtle because address(0) is a valid sentinel value in many contracts and the checks for settlement status do not surface the missing owner until a user attempts to recover funds. The recommended fix is to replace the hard‑coded address(0) with the actual recipient address (outputParams.recipient) when calling the approval and call‑out functions, thereby ensuring the settlement record contains a valid owner and can be retried or redeemed if the cross‑chain execution fails.

title: Ulysses omnichain - `addbridgeagentfactory` in `rootPort` is not functional
description:
The `addbridgeagentfactory` function is responsible for adding a new bridge agent factory to the `rootPort`.

However the current implementation is faulty. The faulty logic is in the following line:

```solidity
bridgeAgentFactories[bridgeAgentsLenght++] = _bridgeAgentFactory;
```

A couple of problems here: The function is attempting to access an index that does not yet exist in the `bridgeAgentFactories` array; this should return an out of bounds error. The function also does not update the `isBridgeAgentFactory` mapping; once a new bridge agent factory is added, a new Dict item with a key equal to the address of new bridge agent factory and value of true is added. This mapping is then used to enable toggling the factory, i.e. enabling or disabling it via the `toggleBridgeAgentFactory` function.

Impact: The code hints that this is a key governance action. It does not work at the moment; however, with regards to impact, at this moment it is unclear from the code what the overall impact would be to the functioning of the protocol. That is why it is rated as medium rather than high. Feedback from sponsors is welcome to determine severity.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance function that registers a new bridge‑agent factory in the root port contract. The implementation attempts to store the new factory address by writing to bridgeAgentFactories[bridgeAgentsLenght++] = _bridgeAgentFactory; however the array bridgeAgentFactories has not been pre‑allocated at that index, so the write accesses an element that does not exist. Solidity therefore throws an out‑of‑bounds exception and the transaction reverts. In addition, the function never sets the corresponding entry in the isBridgeAgentFactory mapping to true, which is the flag used by other contract logic (for example toggleBridgeAgentFactory) to recognise a valid factory. The root cause is a combination of incorrect array indexing (using post‑increment on a length variable instead of push) and an omitted state update. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; any privileged caller (the contract owner or DAO) who attempts to add a new factory will experience a revert, meaning the protocol cannot extend its set of bridge agents. The impact is that the governance mechanism for onboarding new cross‑chain agents is effectively broken, preventing future upgrades or additions and potentially freezing the ability to route assets through new chains. The failure manifests as a transaction that reverts with "index out of bounds" and from the user’s perspective the admin sees no new factory appear in the list, while the UI may still show the old factory count unchanged. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the test suite attempted to call addBridgeAgentFactory and observed the revert. Because the function is intended to be a simple administrative action, the bug can be easy to miss during manual review; the code compiles and the function is protected by onlyOwner, so reviewers may assume it works without exercising the array operation. The correct fix is to register the factory in the mapping (isBridgeAgentFactory[_bridgeAgentFactory] = true) and to append the address to the dynamic array using push, then increment the length counter if a separate counter is kept. This aligns the implementation with the pattern used in other ports and restores the intended governance flow. In generic terms the bug belongs to the class of “improper dynamic array handling and missing state registration”, which can lead to out‑of‑bounds errors and inconsistent internal bookkeeping, breaking business logic that relies on accurate factory enumeration.

title: `BribesFactory::createBribeFlywheel` can be completely blocked from creating any `Flywheel` by a malicious actor
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the BribesFactory contract creates a new bribe Flywheel. When createBribeFlywheel is called, it deploys a FlywheelCore instance with its flywheelRewards parameter set to the zero address. Immediately afterwards it calls FlywheelCore.setFlywheelRewards to replace the placeholder with a freshly deployed FlywheelBribeRewards contract. The setFlywheelRewards function reads the token balance of the current flywheelRewards address and, if the balance is greater than zero, attempts to transfer that amount to the new rewards contract. However, the function does not verify whether the current flywheelRewards address is the zero address. Because the Solmate ERC20 implementation used for reward tokens permits transfers to address(0), an attacker (or any user who unintentionally burns tokens) can send a tiny amount of the reward token to the zero address before any Flywheel is created. When the factory later tries to create a Flywheel, setFlywheelRewards will try to pull the token balance from address(0). The transfer from the zero address fails, causing the whole transaction to revert. As a result, the creation of any bribe Flywheel is blocked, effectively a denial‑of‑service on the reward‑distribution mechanism. This issue manifests only when the reward token allows transfers to the zero address and when a non‑zero balance exists at that address at the moment of Flywheel creation. It affects any protocol that relies on the BribesFactory to launch new bribe contracts, including third‑party projects that adopt MaiaDAO’s factory, because users may have already burned tokens, unintentionally preventing new bribes from being set up. The problem was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena through static analysis and a concrete proof‑of‑concept that transferred one wei of a mock ERC20 token to address(0) and observed the transaction revert with an arithmetic error. The bug is subtle because developers typically treat the zero address as a burn destination and do not expect it to hold a token balance, and the revert message does not directly point to the missing zero‑address check. To remediate, the setFlywheelRewards function should first check that the existing flywheelRewards address is not zero before attempting any token transfer, or the protocol should use an ERC20 implementation that disallows transfers to the zero address, such as OpenZeppelin’s ERC20, or add explicit validation in token contracts to reject transfers to address(0). This change prevents the accidental or malicious token balance at the zero address from causing a revert, restoring the ability to create new bribe Flywheels and preserving the intended reward flow.

title: A user can call `callOutSigned` without paying for gas by reentering `anyExecute` with Virtual Account
description: `Virtual account` can perform external calls during the root chain execution process. If it calls `callOut` at the Arbitrum Branch Bridge Agent, the call `anyExecute` in Root Bridge Agent will be reentered. The call `lock` will not work if a user initiates the process on another branch chain. Call `_payExecutionGas` will not charge gas for the reentrancy call. Meanwhile, the storage variables `initialGas` and `userFeeInfo` will be deleted. As a result, no gas will be charged for the original call.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy based gas‑payment bypass that occurs when a virtual account invokes the bridge function callOutSigned on an Arbitrum branch and, during the same transaction, re‑enters the Root Bridge Agent’s anyExecute function. In the normal flow anyExecute records the amount of gas deposited by the user in two storage slots (initialGas and userFeeInfo) and later calls an internal routine _payExecutionGas to charge the user for the gas actually consumed. Because the virtual account can trigger a second call to anyExecute before the original call reaches the payment step, the second (re‑entered) call executes _payExecutionGas, which immediately deletes the storage variables initialGas and userFeeInfo. When control returns to the original call, the payment logic sees initialGas equal to zero and userFeeInfo cleared, so the routine returns without charging any gas. The root cause is the reliance on mutable storage that is not protected against re‑entrancy; the contract assumes that the values stored before the execution phase will remain unchanged until the payment phase, which is false when a re‑entrant call can delete them. An attacker can exploit this by creating a virtual account that calls callOutSigned, causing the re‑entrancy, and thereby obtain free execution of arbitrary bridge logic. The impact is that the protocol loses the expected execution fees, potentially allowing an attacker to drain the fee pool or to execute expensive operations without paying, undermining the economic model of the bridge. The bug manifests only when the call originates from a virtual account and the call path includes a re‑entrant anyExecute; normal users who interact directly with the bridge do not see the issue. Affected parties include the bridge operator, any users whose fees are subsidised by the protocol, and the overall security of the cross‑chain messaging system. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of the _payExecutionGas function and noticed that it deletes the state before the payment calculation, which becomes problematic under re‑entrancy. It is hard to notice because the contract appears to charge fees correctly in single‑call scenarios, and the deletion of storage variables is a legitimate step in the normal flow, masking the re‑entrancy side effect. The recommended fix is to avoid persisting these values in contract storage across the execution phase; instead they should be copied into memory (local variables) at the start of anyExecute so that a re‑entrant call cannot overwrite or delete them. More generally, the contract should employ a re‑entrancy guard or redesign the payment logic to be atomic and independent of mutable storage, thereby preventing the gas‑payment bypass class of bug often referred to as “re‑entrancy with state‑clearing before fee settlement”. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a transaction that should have deducted a gas fee shows no fee deduction, or the bridge reports that the operation succeeded without any cost, contradicting the expectation that the user pays for execution.

title: Incorrect accounting logic for `fallback` gas will lead to insolvency
description: Incorrect accounting logic for `fallback` gas will lead to insolvency.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect accounting of gas reserves for fallback executions in a cross‑chain call system, which can cause the gas budget to become insolvent. The root cause is that the contract adds any excess execution gas to a fee accumulator (accumulatedFees) instead of reserving that amount for the subsequent fallback call on the opposite chain. When the root chain pays execution gas, the code computes the available gas as the deposited amount minus the amount already earmarked for bridging out, then replenishes the exact minimum execution cost and treats the remainder as fees. No gas is set aside for the fallback step. A symmetric mistake exists on the branch chain: after paying execution gas, the surplus is transferred to the recipient, and the fallback routine does not replenish gas or deduct the required fallback reserve from the stored gas pool. Consequently, when a fallback is later required, the contract checks the stored gas reserve, finds it insufficient, and either reverts or proceeds without enough gas, leading to a situation where the system cannot fund the fallback transaction. This can be exploited by triggering a call that consumes more than the expected execution gas, causing the excess to be absorbed into fees and depleting the pool that should have covered the fallback. The impact is that legitimate fallback calls fail, users may receive no refund or see their balances reduced to zero, and the protocol may become unable to complete cross‑chain operations, effectively locking funds. The condition occurs whenever the execution phase uses more gas than anticipated, leaving no reserved gas for the fallback phase on either the root or branch chain. All participants that rely on the fallback mechanism – callers, recipients, and the overall protocol – are affected because the accounting error breaks the fundamental assumption that gas can be safely transferred between phases. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by reviewing the gas accounting logic and noticing that the fallback reserve was never deducted from the deposited gas pool. It is subtle because normal executions that stay within expected gas limits appear to work, masking the problem until edge‑case gas consumption is triggered. To fix the bug, the contract should explicitly subtract the minimum fallback gas cost from the deposited gas amount (or from the remaining gas pool) and ensure that any excess execution gas is either returned to the caller or correctly accounted for without compromising the fallback reserve. In other words, the accounting should treat fallback gas as a reserved liability rather than as surplus fees, preserving solvency across both chains and preventing funds from disappearing or refunds from being missed.

title: `VirtualAccount` cannot directly send native tokens
description: Certain functions require native tokens to be sent. These functions will revert.
poc: According to the Sponsor, `VirtualAccounts` can “call any of the `dApps` present in the Root Chain (Arbitrum) e.g. Maia, Hermes, Ulysses AMM and Uniswap.” However, this is not the case, as `call()` is not `payable` and thus cannot send native tokens to other contracts. This is problematic because certain [functions](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/ulysses-omnichain/BaseBranchRouter.sol#L58-L62) require native token transfers and will fail.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a contract that acts as a virtual account for users and provides a generic call() method to interact with other dApps on the Arbitrum root chain. The call() function is not marked payable, which means it cannot forward any native token (ETH) that a caller might attach to the transaction. Many external contracts, such as Maia, Hermes, Ulysses AMM and Uniswap, expose functions that explicitly require a native token transfer as part of their execution. Because the virtual account’s call() cannot forward value, any attempt to invoke those functions from the virtual account results in a revert. The root cause is a missing payable modifier on the forwarding function combined with a looped call architecture that makes it unsafe to simply add payable to the existing method – the same msg.value could be unintentionally reused across multiple calls, leading to potential under‑ or over‑payment. An attacker or a regular user may assume that the virtual account can act as a fully‑featured proxy and therefore try to deposit funds or execute trades that need ETH; the transaction will fail silently at the contract level, leaving the user with a failed transaction and possibly a confusing UI where no error message is displayed. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style limitation: users cannot perform any operation that requires native token transfer through the virtual account, effectively blocking access to certain features of the integrated dApps and breaking the business logic that assumes the virtual account can act as a fully‑functional wallet. This condition occurs whenever a user calls a function that expects value to be sent, and it affects all participants who rely on the virtual account for cross‑contract interactions, including end‑users, liquidity providers, and protocol operators. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit by Code4rena, where test cases that attempted to invoke payable functions from the virtual account consistently reverted. The problem can be hard to notice because the call() interface looks generic and the lack of a payable modifier does not raise a compiler warning; only runtime testing reveals the failure. To remediate, the contract should introduce a dedicated forwarding function that is explicitly payable and forwards the exact amount of msg.value to each target, or redesign the loop to handle per‑call value safely, ensuring that native tokens can be transferred without reusing msg.value across multiple calls. This aligns the implementation with the expected accounting model where the virtual account can send and receive native tokens, restoring correct user experience and protocol functionality.

title: `unstakeAndWithdraw` inside `BoostAggregator` could lose `pendingRewards` in certain cases
description: When `BoostAggregator`’s `unstakeAndWithdraw` is triggered, it will try to unstake the uniswap NFT position token from the staker and get the pending rewards. If conditions are met, it will update the strategy and protocol rewards accounting, claim the rewards for strategy and finally, withdraw the NFT position tokens from the staker. However, if `pendingRewards` is lower than `DIVISIONER`, the accounting will not happen and can cause reward loss.
bug_full: The BoostAggregator contract contains a reward‑distribution flaw in its unstakeAndWithdraw function. When a user calls this function the contract first unstakes the Uniswap V3 NFT position, calculates the pending rewards as the difference between the current tokenIdRewards value and the stored tokenIdRewards snapshot, and then checks whether the pending amount is greater than a constant DIVISIONER before performing any accounting or claim. If the pending rewards are lower than DIVISIONER, the conditional block is skipped, meaning no protocol fee is taken and no claim is issued. The function then proceeds to withdraw the NFT token back to the user. Later, when the same NFT is deposited again through the onERC721Received callback, the contract overwrites tokenIdRewards with the current value from the Uniswap staker before staking the token. Because the earlier small pending rewards were never recorded or transferred, they become permanently inaccessible – the accounting entry is lost and the user’s balance does not reflect those rewards. The root cause is the use of a hard threshold (pendingRewards > DIVISIONER) combined with an unconditional reset of the rewards snapshot on re‑staking, which together truncate small reward amounts. An attacker or a careless user can trigger the unstake flow when the accrued reward is just below the threshold, causing the protocol to silently discard those rewards. The impact is a loss of legitimate reward tokens for the user and a reduction of protocol‑level fees, effectively making funds disappear from the expected accounting. This situation occurs only when the pending reward amount is small enough to fail the > DIVISIONER test and the NFT is subsequently restaked through BoostAggregator. Affected parties include any user who stakes NFTs via BoostAggregator and the protocol that relies on accurate reward accounting. The issue was discovered during a formal audit (Code4rena) by reviewing the reward‑claim logic and noticing that the snapshot update in onERC721Received overwrites unclaimed amounts. It can be hard to notice because the UI may simply show that the user received “0” rewards after unstaking, which matches the contract’s behaviour, and there is no explicit error or event indicating that a small amount was dropped. From the user’s perspective the expectation is that all accrued rewards are transferred on unstake, but in practice the balance may stay unchanged or show a zero payout, and later re‑staking the same position causes the missing rewards to vanish entirely. The bug belongs to the class of reward‑truncation or conditional accounting errors, where a threshold prevents proper handling of low‑value amounts. To remediate the issue the contract should either always claim the pending rewards regardless of size, or adjust the accounting so that the protocol fee is taken from the full amount and the remainder is transferred to the user. Removing the DIVISIONER check or moving the tokenIdRewards snapshot update to occur after the reward claim would prevent the loss of pending rewards and ensure that the accounting remains consistent with business logic that all earned rewards must be distributable.

title: `UlyssesToken.setWeights`
description:
The [ERC-4626](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4626) paradigm of deposit/mint and withdraw/redeem, where a **single** underlying asset amount can always be converted to a number of vault shares and vice-versa, breaks as soon as there are **multiple weighted** underlying assets involved.

While it’s easy to convert from shares to asset amounts using the weight factors, it’s hard to convert from asset amounts to shares, in case they are not exactly distributed according to the weight factors.

In the Ulysses protocol this was solved the following way:

  * On `UlyssesToken.deposit(...)` every asset amount is converted to shares and the **smallest** of them is the one received for the deposit, see [ERC4626MultiToken.convertToShares(…)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/erc-4626/ERC4626MultiToken.sol#L200-L207). As a consequence, excess assets provided on the deposit are lost for the user and cannot be redeemed with the received shares.
  * On `UlyssesToken.withdraw(...)` every asset amount is converted to shares and the **greatest** of them is the one required to withdraw the given asset amounts, see [ERC4626MultiToken.previewWithdraw(…)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/erc-4626/ERC4626MultiToken.sol#L250-L255). As a consequence, less assets than are entitled to, according to the share count, can be withdrawn from the vault incurring a loss for the user.

One might argue that this issue is of low severity, due to user error and the user being responsible to only use asset amounts in accordance with the vault’s asset weights. However, the asset weights are not fixed and can be changed at any time by the owner of the `UlyssesToken` contract via the [setWeights(…)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/ulysses-amm/UlyssesToken.sol#L88-L105) method. That is what makes this an actual issue.

Consider the scenario when a user is about to deposit/withdraw assets not knowing their respective weights have changed, or even worse the deposit/withdraw transaction is already in the `mempool`, but the call to `setWeights(...)` is executed before. Depending on the new asset weights, this will inevitably lead to a loss for the user.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the UlyssesToken vault implements the ERC‑4626 multi‑asset model with weighted underlying tokens. In a standard ERC‑4626 vault a single underlying amount can be deterministically converted to a share amount and back, but when several assets are weighted the conversion becomes ambiguous. The contract resolves this ambiguity by taking the smallest share amount when converting a deposit to shares and the largest share amount when converting a withdrawal request to shares. Consequently, any excess assets supplied during a deposit are silently discarded, and any shortfall during a withdrawal leaves the user with fewer assets than their share balance entitles them to. The root cause is the use of a naïve min/max selection instead of a proportional allocation that respects the weight vector. The problem is amplified because the owner can change the weight vector at any time via the setWeights function. If a user submits a deposit or withdraw transaction based on the old weights and the owner updates the weights before the transaction is mined, the contract will compute a different share amount, causing the user to receive fewer shares than expected on deposit or to retrieve fewer assets than expected on withdraw. From the user’s point of view the symptoms are missing tokens after a deposit – the user sees that the amount of shares received is lower than anticipated and that the surplus assets cannot be redeemed later – or a shortfall when trying to withdraw, where the received token amounts are smaller than the user’s balance would suggest. The impact is a loss of user funds that is not signaled by a revert; the contract simply accepts the assets and mints a reduced share count, making the bug hard to notice during normal operation. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which added a PoC test that demonstrated the loss when the weight vector is altered between transaction submission and execution. This class of bug can be described as a weighted multi‑token accounting error or conversion rounding/under‑allocation flaw that violates the fundamental accounting invariant of ERC‑4626 that one unit of underlying should map to a predictable amount of shares. To remediate the issue the deposit function should only transfer the exact token amounts required for the computed share count, mirroring the logic of the mint function, and the withdraw function should transfer the full set of assets the user is entitled to based on their share balance, mirroring the redeem function. Alternatively, the contract could enforce immutability of the weight vector for the duration of pending transactions or adopt a proportional share calculation that does not discard excess assets.

title: Removing a `UniswapV3Gauge` via `UniswapV3GaugeFactory` does not actually remove it from the `UniswapV3Staker`. The gauge still gains rewards and can be staked too
description:
Gauge factories have a [`BaseV2GaugeFactory::removeGauge`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/gauges/factories/BaseV2GaugeFactory.sol#L130-L137) that removes the indicated gauge and marks it as deprecated for the corresponding [`bHermesGauges` and `bHermesBoost`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/gauges/factories/BaseV2GaugeManager.sol#L100-L103) token contracts.

However, removing a `UniswapV3Gauge` with `UniswapV3GaugeFactory` does not actually remove it from the `UniswapV3Staker`. The gauge still remains and existing users that staked can still gain the exact same benefits from it.

What is worse, is that staking to the gauge can still happen. Any new users that stake cannot receive a share of the generated fees (plus boost), as it is impossible to vote for the deprecated gauge.
poc:
A step by step execution flow was shown above.

The lack of active gauge check can be observed in any of the staking flow functions:

  * [restakeToken](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/uni-v3-staker/UniswapV3Staker.sol#L340-L348)
  * [stakeToken](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/uni-v3-staker/UniswapV3Staker.sol#L465-L473)
  * [_stakeToken](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/uni-v3-staker/UniswapV3Staker.sol#L475-L519) (called by the above 2)

Also, there is no [`BaseV2GaugeFactory::afterCreateRemoved`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/gauges/factories/BaseV2GaugeFactory.sol#L125-L137) type of `callback` existing.

A theoretical POC would be as:

  * A `UniswapV3Gauge` is created via `UniswapV3GaugeFactory` (it is also automatically attached to the existing `UniswapV3Staker`).
  * Users vote for it via `bHermesGauges`.
  * A team decided to remove the existing `UniswapV3Gauge` for a newer version.
  * A team calls `BaseV2GaugeFactory::removeGauge` that does not remove the gauge from the `UniswapV3Staker`, while also deprecating it in `bHermesGauges`.
  * The now deprecated and faulty removed `UniswapV3Gauge` still receives fees from the `UniswapV3Staker`.
  * New users stake to the removed `UniswapV3Gauge`, but will not receive any bribe rewards; creating a situation where the first depositors gain the later ones.
bug_full: The issue is a gauge deprecation flaw in the UniswapV3 staking system. When a UniswapV3Gauge is removed through the UniswapV3GaugeFactory, the factory only marks the gauge as deprecated in the associated bHermesGauges and bHermesBoost contracts, but it does not update the UniswapV3Staker contract that actually distributes fees and boost rewards. As a result the gauge remains registered inside the staker, continues to accrue fees, and the public staking functions (stakeToken, restakeToken and the internal _stakeToken) do not check whether the gauge is active. Consequently an attacker or any user can still stake new liquidity positions into a gauge that the protocol intends to retire. Existing stakers keep receiving the full fee share and boost, while new stakers receive no bribe rewards because the gauge can no longer be voted for, creating a situation where early participants profit at the expense of later users. The impact is a mis‑allocation of rewards, loss of expected earnings for new participants, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that only active gauges generate incentives. The flaw manifests whenever BaseV2GaugeFactory::removeGauge is called for a UniswapV3Gauge; the staker’s internal mapping and bribe depot are never cleared and there is no after‑remove callback to deactivate the gauge. Users see the gauge still listed in the UI, are able to stake, but notice that their reward balance stays at zero or that they receive no fee share despite staking. The problem was uncovered during a security audit that examined the gauge removal flow and noticed the absence of an active‑gauge check in the staking functions. It is difficult to spot because the contract continues to emit events and transfer fees, giving the impression that the gauge is still functional, while the voting mechanism silently disables new reward distribution. To remediate the issue the protocol should implement a post‑removal hook (BaseV2GaugeFactory::afterCreateRemoved) that calls a function in UniswapV3Staker to clear the bribe depot for the removed gauge, add an explicit active‑gauge verification in the staking entry points, and adjust the boost calculation so that deprecated gauges no longer provide extra rewards. These changes would align the on‑chain state with the intended deprecation, prevent further staking into inactive gauges, and restore correct reward accounting.

title: `ERC4626PartnerManager.checkTransfer` does not check `amount` correctly, as it applies `bHermesRate` to `balanceOf[from]`, but not `amount`.
description: `ERC4626PartnerManager.checkTransfer` does not check `amount` correctly, as it applies `bHermesRate` to `balanceOf[from]`, but not `amount`.
poc:
`ERC4626PartnerManager.checkTransfer()` is a modifier that will be called to ensure that the `from` account has sufficient funding to cover `userClaimedWeight[from]`, `userClaimedBoost[from]`, `userClaimedGovernance[from]`, and `userClaimedPartnerGovernance[from]` before the transfer occurs:

However, `bHermesRate` is applied to `balanceOf[from]`, but not to `amount`. This is not right, since `amount` is not in the units of `userClaimedWeight[from]`, `userClaimedBoost[from]`, `userClaimedGovernance[from]`, and `userClaimedPartnerGovernance[from]`; but it’s in the units of shares of `ERC4626PartnerManager`.

The correct way to check, would be to ensure `balanceOf[from]-amount * bHermesRate` >= `userClaimedWeight[from]`, `userClaimedBoost[from]`, `userClaimedGovernance[from]`, and `userClaimedPartnerGovernance[from]`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ERC4626PartnerManager contract’s checkTransfer modifier, which is intended to guarantee that a sender has enough underlying assets to satisfy four separate claim balances (userClaimedWeight, userClaimedBoost, userClaimedGovernance, and userClaimedPartnerGovernance) before a token transfer is allowed. The logic mistakenly multiplies the sender’s total balance (balanceOf[from]) by the conversion factor bHermesRate, but it does not apply the same factor to the amount being transferred. Because the amount parameter is expressed in share units rather than the underlying asset units used by the claim balances, the check effectively compares an inflated underlying balance with the unchanged claim totals. This unit mismatch means that a user can transfer a larger number of shares than the protocol expects, while the contract still believes the underlying balance remains sufficient. An attacker can craft a transfer that reduces the true underlying balance below the claimed amounts, yet the check passes, allowing the user to withdraw or move assets that should be locked. The impact is a potential loss of collateral for the protocol: users may end up with more withdrawable shares than they are entitled to, leading to under‑collateralisation of the claim pools and possible depletion of funds that other participants rely on. The flaw manifests whenever the checkTransfer modifier is invoked – typically on any ERC4626PartnerManager transfer – and only when the transferred amount is non‑zero. All participants who hold claim balances are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken; the protocol itself may suffer a shortfall. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit through manual review of the modifier’s arithmetic, highlighting a logical error rather than a runtime exception. It can be hard to notice because the code appears to perform a straightforward subtraction and multiplication, and the missing conversion does not trigger a revert; the bug only surfaces under specific transfer sizes that expose the unit mismatch. To remediate, the modifier should convert the share amount to the underlying unit using bHermesRate before subtracting it from the sender’s balance, i.e., compute the effective underlying balance as balanceOf[from] – amount * bHermesRate and then compare this value against each claimed weight. This ensures that the transfer check respects the same unit system as the claim balances, restoring the intended accounting guarantees and preventing unauthorized fund extraction.

title: Branch Strategies lose yield due to wrong implementation of time limit in `BranchPort.sol`
description: Branch Strategies lose yield due to a wrong implementation of the time limit in `BranchPort.sol`. This results in missed yield for branch strategies, less capital utilization of the platform, and ultimately a loss of additional revenue for the protocol’s users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the time‑limit enforcement of a branch strategy contract. The contract is supposed to grant each strategy a fixed daily budget that resets every 24 hours. The current implementation updates the timestamp of the last management call on every invocation of the manage function, even when the call occurs before the 24‑hour window has elapsed. Because the reset of the remaining daily limit is tied to the difference between the current block timestamp and this stored timestamp, each early call pushes the reset point further into the future. As a result the daily budget may never be refreshed for an entire day, causing the strategy to miss out on the unused portion of its allocated budget. This bug belongs to the class of time‑window handling mistakes where a periodic quota is incorrectly refreshed. It can be exploited simply by calling manage at a sub‑optimal interval – for example calling it 36 hours after the first call instead of the required 24 hours – which causes the contract to treat the second call as the start of a new window and leaves the previous day's unused budget permanently unclaimed. The impact is a reduction in yield for the affected strategy, lower capital utilization on the platform and consequently less revenue for protocol users who expect the full daily budget to be available. The condition under which it occurs is any scenario where a strategy calls manage more than once within a 24‑hour period without exhausting its full daily limit. All participants that rely on the strategy’s performance – developers, investors and end‑users – are affected because the contract silently discards potential earnings. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the _checkTimeLimit function and noticed that the timestamp update was placed outside the conditional reset block. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an error; it simply yields lower returns, which can be mistaken for normal market variation. The correct fix is to move the assignment of the last‑managed timestamp inside the branch that resets the daily limit, or to separate the concepts of “last reset” and “last call” using an additional state variable, ensuring that the daily budget is refreshed only after a full 24‑hour interval regardless of intermediate calls. This restores the intended accounting logic where the daily limit is either fully replenished after each day or proportionally calculated based on elapsed time, preventing loss of yield and aligning contract behavior with user expectations of a daily budget that is always available.

title: DoS of `RootBridgeAgent` due to missing negation of return values for `UniswapV3Pool.swap`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way RootBridgeAgent processes the return values from UniswapV3Pool.swap. UniswapV3Pool.swap returns signed int256 amounts that are negative for exact‑input swaps. The official Uniswap documentation and reference implementation explicitly negate these values before converting them to an unsigned uint256. In RootBridgeAgent the internal functions _gasSwapIn and _gasSwapOut forward the raw int256 amounts directly to uint256 without applying the required negation. When the negative int256 is cast to uint256 the result becomes a very large positive number. This large number is then passed to SafeCastLib.toUint128 in anyExecute and _manageGasOut, where the conversion overflows and triggers a revert. Because the gas‑swap logic is used by virtually every external entry point – anyExecute, callOut, callOutAndBridge, callOutAndBridgeMultiple and others – the overflow aborts the whole call flow, preventing the bridge agent from completing its cross‑chain operations. The bug therefore manifests as a denial‑of‑service condition for the Ulysses Omnichain: users attempting to bridge gas or execute cross‑chain messages see their transactions fail, balances remain unchanged, and no gas is transferred. The issue occurs whenever an exact‑input swap is performed, which is the normal mode for the bridge’s gas‑swap routine, and it affects all participants that rely on the bridge – executors, users, and the protocol itself. The problem was discovered during a security audit when the auditors simulated a negative return value from a mock Uniswap pool and observed an overflow revert in CoreRootRouter.addBranchToBridgeAgent. The bug is subtle because the overflow happens deep inside a library cast, making the failure appear as a generic “overflow” error rather than a logical mistake in swap handling. The correct mitigation is to apply the same negation that Uniswap’s own router uses – i.e., return uint256(-(zeroForOne ? amount1 : amount0)) – before casting to uint256, ensuring that only positive amounts are passed to SafeCastLib. By fixing the sign handling the overflow disappears, the gas‑swap functions return realistic values, and the bridge regains its ability to move gas and process cross‑chain calls.

title: Governance relies on the current `totalSupply` of `bHermes` when calculating `proposalThresholdAmount` and `quorumVotesAmount`
description:
```solidity
As people mint `bHermes`, the `bHermesVotes`’ `totalSupply` grows; and `quorumVotesAmount` to execute the proposal also grows. But it shouldn’t, because new people can’t vote for it. This behavior adds inconsistency to the voting process, because it changes the threshold after creating the proposal.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the governance contract calculating the proposal threshold amount and the quorum votes amount by directly reading the current totalSupply of the bHermes governance token each time the values are needed. Because bHermes is an ERC4626DepositOnly token that mints additional governance tokens whenever a user calls deposit() or mint(), the totalSupply is a mutable value that can increase after a proposal has already been created. The contract does not snapshot the totalSupply at the moment of proposal creation; instead it calls govToken.totalSupply() inside getProposalThresholdAmount() and getQuorumVotesAmount(). Consequently, the required number of votes for a proposal to be accepted can change dynamically as new tokens are minted. This creates an inconsistency: new token holders are unable to vote on existing proposals, yet their minting activity raises the thresholds that existing voters must meet. An attacker or any participant who can trigger token minting after a proposal is submitted can inflate the totalSupply, thereby raising the proposalThreshold and quorumVotes values and potentially making it impossible for the proposal to reach the required voting power. Conversely, if the totalSupply were to decrease (which is not the case here), thresholds could drop unexpectedly. The impact is that proposals may never achieve quorum despite having sufficient voter support at the time of creation, leading to stalled governance decisions, loss of confidence, and possible centralization if only large token holders can afford to mint enough tokens to manipulate thresholds. The issue occurs whenever a proposal is open and any subsequent deposit or mint operation is performed on the bHermes token. All participants in the protocol—token holders, delegators, and the governance system itself—are affected because the voting logic no longer reflects the intended static voting power snapshot. The problem was discovered during a manual code audit that identified the use of govToken.totalSupply() in the threshold‑calculation functions and recognized that the totalSupply changes over time. The bug is subtle because the functions appear to return reasonable values and there is no explicit warning that the thresholds are mutable; only by tracing the token minting path does the inconsistency become apparent. To remediate the issue, the governance contract should capture the totalSupply at the moment a proposal is created and store it within the Proposal struct. Subsequent calls to getProposalThresholdAmount() and getQuorumVotesAmount() must then use this stored snapshot rather than the live totalSupply. This change ensures that the voting thresholds remain constant for the lifetime of each proposal, preserving the intended accounting assumptions and preventing manipulation of quorum requirements through token minting.

title: Inconsistencies in reading the encoded parameters received in the `_sParams` argument in `BranchBridgeAgent::clearTokens`
description:
```solidity
Token addresses could be computed wrong, which could lead to the tokens getting stuck in the root chain.
```
poc:
```solidity
The function [clearTokens()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/ulysses-omnichain/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L565-L634) is called from the [BranchBridgeAgentExecutor::executeWithSettlementMultiple() function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/ulysses-omnichain/BranchBridgeAgentExecutor.sol#L116-L157), which is used when the settlement flag is 2 “Multiple Settlements”.

As per the [documentation about the messaging layer written in the `IBranchBridgeAgent` contract](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/ulysses-omnichain/interfaces/IBranchBridgeAgent.sol#L112-L136), [when the flag is 2, the structure of the token info is as follows](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/ulysses-omnichain/interfaces/IBranchBridgeAgent.sol#L135):

 -         - ht = hToken
 -         - t = Token
 -         - A = Amount
 -         - D = Destination
 -         - b = bytes
 -         - n = number of assets
 -         ________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________________
 -        |            Flag               |           Deposit Info           |             Token Info             |   DATA   |  Gas Info   |
 -        |           1 byte              |            4-25 bytes            |        (105 or 128) * n bytes      |   ---	   |  16 bytes   |
 -        |                               |                                  |            hT - t - A - D          |          |             |
 -        |_______________________________|__________________________________|____________________________________|__________|_____________|

 -        | callOutMulti = 0x2            |  1b(n) + 20b(recipient) + 4b     |   	     32b + 32b + 32b + 32b      |   ---	   |     16b     |
```

3 of the 4 parameters encoded in `_sParams` ([hTokens](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/ulysses-omnichain/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L582-L593), [amounts](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/ulysses-omnichain/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L604-L612) and [deposits](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/ulysses-omnichain/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L613-L621)) read the whole 32 bytes and [tokens read only 20 bytes](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/main/src/ulysses-omnichain/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L594-L603).
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an inconsistent way of decoding the packed parameters that are passed to the clearTokens function of the BranchBridgeAgent contract. The messaging specification for a multiple‑settlement flag defines each field – including the token address, amount, and destination – as a full 32‑byte word. In the implementation, however, the hToken, amount and deposit values are extracted by reading the entire 32‑byte slot, while the token address is extracted by slicing only the lower 20 bytes of the slot. Because the code manually computes the start and end offsets for each entry, the mismatch between a 32‑byte read and a 20‑byte read shifts the subsequent offsets, causing the next token address to be read from the wrong position in the calldata. As a result, the address that the contract believes to be the token contract is often an unrelated value, which leads to calls being made against a non‑existent or wrong token contract. When the bridge later attempts to transfer or clear those tokens, the transfer either reverts or silently succeeds without moving any funds, effectively locking the tokens on the root chain. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a settlement the expected token balance is missing, the UI may show a zero balance or a failed refund, and the user receives nothing even though the transaction succeeded. The bug affects any participant that relies on the clearTokens routine – token holders, bridge operators, and the protocol itself – because it can cause permanent loss of assets. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the auditors compared the on‑chain encoding logic with the documented message format and noticed that the slice used for token addresses (`_sParams[...+12:...]`) only reads 20 bytes. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error; the incorrect address is simply used in a low‑level call, making the failure hard to detect without deep inspection of the calldata layout. The appropriate remediation is to standardize the decoding process: treat every parameter as a 32‑byte word, extract the full word, and then cast the lower 20 bytes to an address, or alternatively use Solidity’s abi.decode with a struct that matches the specification. This ensures that all offsets remain aligned and that token addresses are computed correctly, preventing assets from becoming irretrievable.

title: `UlyssesPool.sol` does not match `EIP4626` because of the preview functions
description:
```solidity
According to EIP4626, `previewDeposit()`, `previewRedeem()` and `previewMint()` must include a fee in the returned value:

1. `previewDeposit` “MUST be inclusive of deposit fees. Integrators should be aware of the existence of deposit fees.”
2. `previewRedeem` “MUST be inclusive of withdrawal fees. Integrators should be aware of the existence of withdrawal fees.”
3. `previewMint` “MUST be inclusive of deposit fees. Integrators should be aware of the existence of deposit fees.”
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract's previewDeposit, previewMint and previewRedeem functions do not account for the deposit or withdrawal fees that are applied in the actual deposit, mint and redeem flows. According to EIP‑4626, these preview functions must be inclusive of fees so that callers can correctly estimate how many shares they will receive or how many assets they need to provide. In UlyssesPool.sol the contract inherits a default implementation where each preview function simply returns the input value unchanged. However the concrete implementation of beforeDeposit, beforeMint and afterRedeem calls internal functions ulyssesAddLP and ulyssesRemoveLP that apply a fee before calculating the final share or asset amount. Because the preview functions bypass this fee logic, a user or integrator that queries previewDeposit(1000) will be told they will receive 1000 shares, while the actual deposit will deduct a fee and return fewer shares. The same mismatch occurs for previewMint and previewRedeem, causing users to underestimate the amount of assets required to redeem a given number of shares. This discrepancy can be exploited by malicious actors who rely on the preview values to craft transactions that appear to satisfy the required amounts, only to have the transaction revert or to receive less value than expected. The impact includes loss of user confidence, potential financial loss when users approve insufficient token amounts, and non‑compliance with the EIP‑4626 standard, which may break integrations with wallets, DeFi aggregators, or other protocols that assume fee‑inclusive previews. The issue manifests whenever the contract is used for deposit, mint or redeem operations while the preview functions are called to estimate outcomes; it does not depend on any particular external state. All users, front‑ends, and third‑party services that display preview values are affected because they present inaccurate information. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by comparing the contract's implementation against the EIP‑4626 specification and noticing that the preview functions were left untouched despite the presence of fee logic in the core functions. The bug is subtle because preview functions are read‑only and may not be exercised in typical unit tests, and the UI may simply show the raw input value, making the discrepancy easy to overlook. The correct remediation is to override previewDeposit, previewMint and previewRedeem in UlyssesPool.sol so that they invoke the same fee calculation used in beforeDeposit, beforeMint and afterRedeem, returning the fee‑adjusted share or asset amount. This brings the contract back into compliance with the EIP‑4626 standard and ensures that users see accurate estimates of the value they will receive or need to provide.

title: Deploy flow of `Talos` is broken
description:
```solidity
The `Talos` protocol can’t be deployed in a right way.
```
poc:
```solidity
`TalosBaseStrategy` needs `TalosManager` to be passed in the constructor:

    constructor(
        IUniswapV3Pool _pool,
        ITalosOptimizer _optimizer,
        INonfungiblePositionManager _nonfungiblePositionManager,
        address _strategyManager,
        address _owner
    ) ERC20("TALOS LP", "TLP", 18) {
        ...

        strategyManager = _strategyManager;
        
        ...
    }
```

But `TalosManager` needs `Strategy` to be passed into the constructor:
```solidity
   constructor(
        address _strategy,
        int24 _ticksFromLowerRebalance,
        int24 _ticksFromUpperRebalance,
        int24 _ticksFromLowerRerange,
        int24 _ticksFromUpperRerange
    ) {
        strategy = ITalosBaseStrategy(_strategy);
        
        ...
    }
```
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the deployment process of the Talos protocol, where the core contracts are arranged in a circular dependency that prevents a successful deployment. The TalosBaseStrategy contract expects an address of a TalosManager to be supplied in its constructor, storing this address as the strategy manager. Conversely, the TalosManager contract requires the address of a strategy contract to be passed to its own constructor, assigning it to an internal strategy reference. Because each contract’s constructor needs the other contract’s address, there is no way to instantiate either contract without already having the other deployed, creating a dead‑end initialization loop. This design flaw originates from the lack of a separate initialization or setter function that could break the circular reference after deployment. When a developer attempts to deploy the system, the transaction reverts or the deployment script fails, leaving the protocol unusable. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that the strategy or manager contract is missing, that balances remain zero, or that no interactions are possible because the core contracts never exist on chain. The impact is functional rather than financial: the protocol cannot be launched, users cannot deposit funds, and any planned token minting or liquidity provision never occurs. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors examined the constructor signatures and identified the mutual requirement. It can be hard to notice because the code compiles without errors and the circular dependency only manifests at deployment time, a stage that may be skipped in unit tests that mock addresses. To remediate the problem, the contracts should be refactored to remove the constructor‑based circular reference, for example by deploying one contract first, then calling a setter or an initialize function on the other contract to register the counterpart’s address, or by using a proxy pattern that allows post‑deployment wiring of the references. This class of bug is commonly known as a circular dependency or initialization order flaw, which violates the basic assumption that each component can be instantiated independently before being linked together, leading to a broken deployment flow and a non‑functional protocol.

title: Improper array initialization causes an index “out of bounds” error
description:
```solidity
In `createPools` of `UlyssesFactory.sol`, the return parameter `poolIds` is used to store new pool Ids after creation. However, it has not been initialized. This causes an index “out of bounds” error when `createPools` is called.
```
poc:
```solidity
Any test that calls `ulyssesFactory.createPools(...);` will cause an index out of bounds.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is an out‑of‑bounds write caused by an uninitialized dynamic array that is used to collect the identifiers of newly created pools. In the factory contract, the function that creates multiple pools declares a return variable (poolIds) of type uint256[] but never allocates storage for it before writing to its elements. Because Solidity initializes dynamic arrays with length zero, any attempt to assign a value at index 0 or higher triggers a runtime revert with an "index out of bounds" error. This happens whenever the createPools function is called with a non‑zero length, which is the normal case when a user wants to create one or more pools. The root cause is the missing allocation statement (e.g., poolIds = new uint256[](length)). An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; any caller can invoke the function and cause the transaction to revert, effectively denying service to legitimate users. From a user’s perspective the UI may report that pool creation failed, no new pool appears, and any funds sent with the transaction are returned because the transaction reverts, leading to confusion and loss of expected functionality. The protocol is affected because the factory cannot reliably deploy pools, breaking the business logic that assumes successful pool creation and proper accounting of pool identifiers. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit where test cases that called createPools repeatedly triggered the revert. It can be hard to notice because the compiler does not emit a warning for an uninitialized return array, and the error only appears at runtime when the function writes to the array. The bug belongs to the class of improper array initialization or missing memory allocation errors, which violate assumptions about array length and lead to out‑of‑bounds access. To remediate, the contract should allocate the array with the correct size before populating it, for example by inserting poolIds = new uint256[](length) at the start of the function, ensuring that each index is valid and the function can return the expected list of pool IDs without reverting.

title: NFT withdrawal grief
description: A lienee whose NFT is not currently on loan may be prevented from withdrawing it.
poc: A lienee who wishes to withdraw his NFT calls `withdrawNftWithInterest()` which tries to [`IERC721.safeTransferFrom()` the NFT](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-particle/blob/1caf678bc20c24c96fc8f6b0046383ff0e9d2a6f/contracts/protocol/ParticleExchange.sol#L183), which reverts if the NFT is not in the contract (being on loan). A griefer might therefore sandwich his call to `withdrawNftWithInterest()` with a `swapWithEth()` and a `repayWithNft()`. [`swapWithEth()` removes the NFT from the contract](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-particle/blob/1caf678bc20c24c96fc8f6b0046383ff0e9d2a6f/contracts/protocol/ParticleExchange.sol#L460), which causes the following `withdrawNftWithInterest()` to revert. For this, the griefer has to [pay `lien.credit + lien.price`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-particle/blob/1caf678bc20c24c96fc8f6b0046383ff0e9d2a6f/contracts/protocol/ParticleExchange.sol#L440). But this is [returned in full in `repayWithNft()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-particle/blob/1caf678bc20c24c96fc8f6b0046383ff0e9d2a6f/contracts/protocol/ParticleExchange.sol#L509-L512), [minus `payableInterest`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-particle/blob/1caf678bc20c24c96fc8f6b0046383ff0e9d2a6f/contracts/protocol/ParticleExchange.sol#L502) which is [nothing, since the loan time is zero](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-particle/blob/1caf678bc20c24c96fc8f6b0046383ff0e9d2a6f/contracts/libraries/math/MathUtils.sol#L24-L25).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that allows a malicious participant to block a legitimate NFT owner (the lienee) from withdrawing their token even when the token is not currently on loan. The contract’s withdrawNftWithInterest() function assumes the NFT is still held by the contract and directly calls IERC721.safeTransferFrom() to move the token to the caller. Because the function does not verify that the NFT remains in the contract at the moment of execution, an attacker can intervene by first calling swapWithEth(), which removes the NFT from the contract, and then immediately invoking withdrawNftWithInterest(). When the transfer is attempted, the safeTransferFrom call reverts because the NFT is no longer owned by the contract, causing the withdrawal to fail. The attacker then calls repayWithNft(), which returns the full amount they paid (lien.credit + lien.price) minus any payableInterest – which is zero when the loan duration is zero – effectively refunding the attacker’s expense. As a result, the legitimate owner sees no NFT returned, receives no error indicating a loan is active, and is left unable to retrieve their asset, creating a grief attack. This issue occurs only when the contract permits new loans to be taken on an NFT that the owner might want to withdraw later; there is no mechanism for the lienee to lock the NFT against new loans. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between swapWithEth(), withdrawNftWithInterest() and repayWithNft() and identified a sandwich‑style exploit. It can be hard to notice because the revert only happens under a specific ordering of calls and the attacker’s net cost is zero, so the contract appears to function correctly in normal use. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s business logic: users expect to be able to withdraw their NFT when it is not on loan, but the contract can silently prevent this, effectively making the NFT disappear from the user’s perspective. To remediate, the protocol should allow a lien to be marked as “non‑loanable” so that no new swapWithEth() calls can extract the NFT while a withdrawal is pending, and/or add an explicit ownership check right before the safeTransferFrom call and protect the function with a re‑entrancy guard. Conceptually, the fix restores the invariant that an NFT can only be transferred out if the contract still holds it, and gives the owner a way to opt‑out of future loans, thereby eliminating the grief vector.

title: `addCredit` DOS Attack
description: `addCredit` DOS Attack.
poc:
`addCredit()` can be called by anyone, and the `msg.value` is as small as `1 wei`.

Users can modify Lien at a small cost, causing the value stored in `liens[lienId]=keccak256(abi.encode(lien))` to change. By front-run, the normal user’s transaction `validateLien()` fails the check, thus preventing the user’s transaction from being executed.

The following methods will be exploited (most methods with `validateLien()` will be affected). For example:

  1. Front-run `auctionBuyNft()` is used to prevent others from bidding.
  2. Front-run `startLoanAuction()` to prevent the lender from starting the auction.
  3. Front-run `stopLoanAuction()` is used to stop Lender from closing the auction.   
etc.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by the addCredit function being callable by any address with no minimum ether requirement. Because addCredit updates the stored hash of a lien (liens[lienId] = keccak256(abi.encode(lien))) without restricting the caller, an attacker can send a transaction with as little as 1 wei, change the hash, and then front‑run a legitimate transaction that later calls validateLien. The validateLien check compares the current hash with the expected value, so the altered hash makes the check fail and the subsequent transaction reverts. This pattern can be repeated to block normal users from executing any function that relies on validateLien, such as auctionBuyNft, startLoanAuction, stopLoanAuction, and other loan‑related operations. From a user perspective the symptom is that a bid, auction start, or auction stop appears to fail with no obvious reason, often reverting with a generic error and leaving the user with no received NFT or loan progress. The impact is a loss of functionality rather than direct loss of funds, but it effectively freezes the protocol’s core workflows and can be used to harass participants or manipulate market outcomes. The condition occurs whenever an attacker can submit an addCredit transaction before a legitimate user’s transaction, which is feasible because the function lacks access control and accepts any msg.value, making it cheap to spam the network. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of lien validation and noticed that the hash‑based integrity check could be subverted by an uncontrolled state change. The problem is subtle because the addCredit function appears harmless and the small ether amount does not raise gas‑price alarms, so the denial of service can remain hidden until a user experiences unexpected reverts. To remediate the issue the addCredit function should be restricted to the borrower, a minimum msg.value should be enforced, and optionally a time‑based modification interval should be added to prevent rapid successive updates. These changes restore the integrity of the lien hash and ensure that only authorized parties can modify credit information, eliminating the front‑run vector that leads to denial of service.

title: New treasury rate should not affect existing loan
poc:
Consider the following scenario:

1. Alice and Bob have an active loan with an accumulated interest of 1 ETH and `_treasuryRate = 5%`.
2. The admin suddenly changes the `_treasuryRate` to `50%`. Now, if Alice claims the interest, she needs to pay 0.5 ETH to the treasury and keep 0.5 ETH.
3. Alice can either accept it and keep 0.5 ETH interest or front-run the admin transaction and claim before the `_treasuryRate` is updated.

The point is, Alice only agreed to pay a `5%` treasury rate at the beginning, so the new rate should not apply to her.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a mutable global treasury fee rate that is applied to the calculation of interest payouts for every loan, regardless of when the loan was originated. The contract stores the treasury rate in a single state variable that can be altered by the owner through the setTreasuryRate function. Because the rate is read at the moment a borrower claims accrued interest, any change performed while loans are still active retroactively modifies the fee that those loans must pay. This design flaw originates from the fact that the fee percentage is not captured at loan creation and is not stored per‑loan, allowing the owner to increase the rate after a loan has been issued. An attacker with owner privileges can raise the rate from a low value (for example 5 %) to a much higher value (such as 50 %) while borrowers still have outstanding interest. When a borrower later calls the claim function, the contract deducts the new, higher treasury share from the accrued interest, resulting in a dramatically reduced net payout. The borrower may either accept the reduced amount or attempt to front‑run the owner’s transaction and claim before the rate change is mined, but in either case the original agreement is violated. The impact is that borrowers receive less than expected, potentially losing a large portion of their earned interest, and the protocol’s economic guarantees are broken, eroding user trust. The issue manifests whenever the owner invokes setTreasuryRate while there exist active loans; it affects all participants with open positions, including lenders and borrowers who rely on the advertised fee schedule. The problem was identified during a Code4rena audit that examined the treasury fee logic and noticed that the rate variable is not immutable per loan. It can be difficult to detect in normal operation because the UI typically displays the current treasury rate, not the rate that applied when a loan was opened, and the fee is only deducted at claim time, making the discrepancy appear as a sudden, unexplained loss. The bug belongs to the class of “mutable global parameter affecting existing contracts” or “parameter drift” vulnerabilities, where a contract‑wide setting is changed after dependent state has been created. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a mismatch between the expected net interest (e.g., a 5 % fee) and the actual amount received (e.g., a 50 % fee), often observed as a sudden drop in the balance after claiming interest or even a zero payout when the fee exceeds the accrued amount. To remediate the issue the treasury rate should be recorded in each loan’s data structure at the moment the loan is created, making it immutable for the life of that loan, or a timelock should be introduced to prevent immediate changes, or the contract should prohibit rate changes while any loan is active. Storing the rate per loan preserves the originally agreed‑upon fee and aligns the implementation with the protocol’s economic model, eliminating the possibility of retroactive fee escalation.

title: Burning an NFT can be used to block voting
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way voting power snapshots are calculated in a governance contract that uses NFTs as voting tokens. When a member burns their NFT, the contract records the burn timestamp and prevents voting in the same block by checking if the last burn timestamp equals the current block timestamp. However, the snapshot used to determine a voter’s power for a proposal is taken from the previous block (values.proposedTime‑1). An attacker can therefore front‑run a legitimate call to the function that finalises a vote (accept) by first executing a burn transaction in the same block. The burn updates the timestamp, causing the subsequent accept call to hit the revert condition, even though the snapshot still reflects the voter’s pre‑burn power. Because the revert aborts the accept transaction, the proposal cannot be finalised, effectively denying service to the voting process for that block. The attack can be amplified by minting a dummy NFT with zero voting power and burning it immediately, which does not alter the total voting power but still triggers the timestamp check, allowing an adversary to block accept calls without sacrificing any voting weight. This issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when a test case reproduced the scenario by front‑running an accept transaction with a zero‑power NFT burn, causing the contract to revert with CannotRageQuitAndAcceptError. The problem is subtle because the revert only occurs when two specific actions happen in the same block, a condition that may not be obvious during normal operation, and the contract’s comments suggest the check is intended to prevent a different exploit, masking the denial‑of‑service side effect. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a transaction that unexpectedly reverts, leaving the proposal in a pending state and preventing the expected outcome of a successful vote. The impact is a potential stall of governance decisions, as any party member can block the acceptance of proposals for at least one block, and repeated use could undermine confidence in the protocol’s decision‑making process. The root cause is the combination of a block‑level timestamp check with a snapshot that does not account for burns occurring in the same block. To remediate the issue, the contract should either move the timestamp validation to the proposal‑creation step, redesign the snapshot mechanism to incorporate burns that happen in the same block, or otherwise ensure that a voter’s power cannot be used after a burn without causing a revert. Such changes would eliminate the ability to front‑run a burn to block voting while preserving the intended protection against vote manipulation.

title: Rage quit modifications should be limited to provide stronger guarantees to party members
description:
Party hosts can arbitrarily change the rage quit settings overriding any existing preset.

Rage quit is implemented in the `PartyGovernanceNFT` contract by using a timestamp. Leaving aside the cases of permanent settings (which, of course, cannot be changed) this implementation allows a more flexible feature than a simple enable/disable toggle. The timestamp represents the time until rage quit is allowed. If the timestamp is still in the future, then rage quit is enabled. If it is in the past, the feature is disabled.

This setting can be changed at will by party hosts. At any moment and without any restriction (other than the permanent enabled or disabled, which cannot be modified), the party host is allowed to change the value to **any arbitrary date**. This means that an already scheduled setting that would allow rage quit until a certain future date, can be simply overridden and changed by the party host.

A party member can feel secure knowing it has the option to rage quit until the defined timestamp in `rageQuitTimestamp`. However, any party host can arbitrarily reduce or completely disable the feature, ignoring any preset.

This is particularly concerning, as it defeats the purpose of having a programmable expiration date of the rage quit feature. The allowed modifications should ensure members are covered at least until the agreed timestamp (i.e. extend it or leave it as it is to disable rage quit the moment the timestamp expires), or provide better guarantees against arbitrary changes.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the ability of party hosts to arbitrarily modify the rage‑quit expiration timestamp in the PartyGovernanceNFT contract. The contract stores a single uint256 called rageQuitTimestamp that represents the moment until which a member may invoke the rage‑quit function; any timestamp in the future enables the feature, while a past timestamp disables it. Because the setter for this value is exposed to the host role without any additional constraints, a host can at any time replace the existing timestamp with an arbitrary date, including a date in the past or a date that shortens the remaining window. This design flaw originates from missing access‑control logic that would otherwise enforce monotonicity, delay, or limited reduction of the parameter. An attacker who controls a host account can therefore disable or truncate the rage‑quit period after members have relied on the originally advertised deadline, effectively stripping them of the right to exit the party. The impact is that members who expect to be able to quit before a known deadline may find the function reverting or doing nothing, leaving their tokens locked and potentially exposing them to unfavorable governance decisions or loss of value. The issue manifests whenever a host invokes the timestamp‑setting function before the previously announced deadline, except for the immutable permanent‑enabled or permanent‑disabled modes which are explicitly protected.
