The bug is subtle because price feeds continue to provide valid numbers, so the contract appears to function normally; only the underlying accounting diverges, making it hard to detect without comparing pre‑ and post‑event token balances. The recommended remediation is to document the expected behavior for each corporate action, extend the price‑feed interface to include a split‑ratio or conversion factor, and modify the token minting/burning logic to automatically adjust user balances or apply a scaling factor in valuation calculations whenever a split, reverse split, merger, or similar event is announced. By treating the situation as a corporate‑action accounting class of bug, the protocol can preserve the invariant that token holdings correctly reflect the holder’s entitlement after any market‑structure change.

title: DPCU-3 | Collateral Prioritized Over PnL
description: In the payForCost function, the collateral token is prioritized over the secondary token when making payments. As a result, a user’s collateral could be unexpectedly reduced when their is substantial PnL or price impact in the secondary token available to cover the cost. This can be especially unexpected for costs such as negative price impact which would commonly be thought of as affecting the execution price and being deducted from the PnL.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the payForCost routine where the contract’s accounting logic always selects the collateral token as the first source of funds when settling a cost, even if the user holds a sufficient amount of secondary‑token profit and loss (PnL) that could cover the expense. This ordering bias causes the user’s collateral balance to be reduced unexpectedly whenever a cost such as negative price impact is incurred while the secondary token has a sizable positive PnL. The root cause is a simplistic token‑selection algorithm that does not evaluate the availability of secondary‑token balances before drawing from collateral, thereby violating the intended accounting assumption that profit in the secondary token should be used to offset costs. An attacker or a regular user can trigger the issue by opening a position that generates PnL in the secondary token and then causing a cost event (for example, a trade that incurs negative price impact). When payForCost is called, the contract will debit the collateral token first, decreasing the user’s margin even though the secondary token could have paid the fee. The impact is a loss of collateral that may lead to reduced margin, unexpected liquidation risk, or simply a user‑visible discrepancy where the UI shows a healthy PnL but the collateral balance drops to zero or near zero. The bug manifests only during execution of payForCost and only when both a cost exists and the secondary token holds enough PnL to cover it; otherwise the normal flow applies. All participants who supply collateral – typically traders and liquidity providers – are affected because their funds can disappear without a clear on‑chain event indicating a fee deduction. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noticed that the cost‑payment logic prioritized collateral without any conditional check. It can be hard to spot because the UI usually displays PnL and collateral separately, and users naturally assume that a negative price impact will be deducted from the profit side rather than the margin side. To remediate, the contract should be refactored so that secondary‑token balances are evaluated and used before touching collateral, or the documentation must explicitly state that collateral will be prioritized. In generic terms, this is a resource‑allocation bug where the wrong asset class is chosen for fee settlement, leading to accounting inconsistencies and unexpected fund depletion. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a sudden reduction of the collateral balance after a trade that otherwise appears profitable, contradicting the expectation that “my profit should cover the cost”.

title: MKTU-3 | Shorts Arbitrarily Pay Stable Funding To Longs
description: In the event that OI is balanced for longs/shorts, shorts will arbitrarily pay longs because of the definition of result.longsPayShorts: result.longsPayShorts = cache.longOpenInterest > cache.shortOpenInterest. Normally, the fundingUsd would be 0 in this case as the resulting fundingFactorPerSecond is 0 when the OI is balanced. However when there is a stable funding factor configured the fundingFactorPerSecond will be nonzero when the OI is balanced. Therefore when there is a stable funding factor configured, shorts will arbitrarily pay longs the stable funding factor. This causes an incentive to stop shorting and join the long side to collect funding fees rather than pay them. Even though OI is already balanced, which undermines the point of funding fees.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic logic error in the funding calculation of a synthetic market where short positions are supposed to pay funding to long positions when open interest (OI) is imbalanced. The contract determines the direction of payment with the expression result.longsPayShorts = cache.longOpenInterest > cache.shortOpenInterest. When the long and short OI are exactly equal, the normal funding factor per second becomes zero, so no funding should be transferred. However, the protocol allows a stable funding factor to be configured, which forces fundingFactorPerSecond to remain non‑zero even when OI is balanced. Because the comparison uses a strict greater‑than operator, the condition evaluates to false for equal OI, but the subsequent update‑per‑size‑delta logic still applies the stable funding factor, causing shorts to arbitrarily pay longs. This creates an unintended incentive for traders to abandon short positions and switch to longs solely to collect the stable funding fee, undermining the purpose of funding fees which are meant to balance long and short exposure. The flaw can be exploited by any participant who can detect that the market has a configured stable funding factor and that long and short OI are equal; they can open or maintain a long position and receive funding from shorts without the market being imbalanced. The impact is economic: short traders lose funds they would not have paid under the intended model, liquidity on the short side may evaporate, and the market’s price‑discovery mechanism can be distorted. The condition occurs whenever the market is configured with a non‑zero stable funding factor and the OI snapshot shows equal long and short exposure, which may happen frequently in a balanced market. All users of the market – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the funding mechanism no longer enforces its designed risk‑sharing property. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the security researcher “Guardian”, who noticed that the funding calculation did not correctly handle the stable‑funding configuration in the balanced‑OI branch. It is subtle because the funding amount appears to be zero in many scenarios, and the code path looks correct at a glance; only when the stable factor is active does the hidden transfer become visible, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the update‑per‑size‑delta logic should be bypassed when a stable funding factor is present and the long and short OI are equal, or the comparison should be adjusted to treat equality as a no‑payment case, ensuring that fundingFactorPerSecond is forced to zero whenever OI is balanced regardless of the stable configuration. This restores the intended economic invariant that funding only flows when there is an imbalance between longs and shorts.

title: `ValidatorWithdrawalVault.distributeRewards` can be called to make operator slashable
description: An attacker can call `distributeRewards` right before `settleFunds` to make `operatorShare < penaltyAmount`. As a result, the validator will face loses.
poc:
`ValidatorWithdrawalVault.distributeRewards` can be called by anyone. It’s purpose is to distribute validators rewards among the stakers protocol and the operator. After the call, the balance of `ValidatorWithdrawalVault` becomes 0.

`ValidatorWithdrawalVault.settle` is called when a validator is withdrawn from beacon chain. In this case, the balance of the contract is used to [find operatorShare](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-stader/blob/main/contracts/ValidatorWithdrawalVault.sol#L62). If it’s less than the accrued penalty by the validator, then operator is slashed.

Because `distributeRewards` is permissionless, then next situation is possible:

  1. Operator decided to withdraw a validator. At the moment of that call, the balance of `ValidatorWithdrawalVault` is not 0 and `operatorShare` is 1 eth. Also the validator accrued 4.5 eth of penalty.
  2. A malicious user sees when 32 eth of a validator’s deposit is sent to the `ValidatorWithdrawalVault` and frontruns it with `distributeRewards` call. This makes balance to be 32 eth.
  3. `operatorShare` will be 4 eth this time (permissionless) and the penalty is 4.5, so the user is slashed.
  4. In this case, if a malicious user didn’t call `distributeRewards`, then the slash would not occur.

Also in same way, a permissioned operator can call `distributeRewards` to get their rewards when they are going to be slashed. As permissioned validators are not forced to have collateral to be slashed, they rescued their earnings; otherwise, they would have been sent to the `pool`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a public function that distributes validator rewards, which can be invoked by any address. Because the function has no access control, an attacker can call it immediately before the contract’s settlement routine that is executed when a validator is withdrawn from the beacon chain. The reward‑distribution call empties the contract’s balance and reduces the amount that will later be used to compute the operator’s share. During settlement the contract compares the operator’s share with the accrued penalty for the validator; if the share is lower than the penalty, the operator is slashed. By front‑running the withdrawal and draining the vault, a malicious user can force the operator’s share to fall below the penalty, causing an unexpected slash. This situation can also be abused by a dishonest operator who calls the reward‑distribution function just before settlement to harvest rewards and avoid being slashed. The issue occurs only when a validator withdrawal is pending, the vault holds the validator’s deposit and accrued rewards, and the distributeRewards function is callable by anyone. Affected parties include the operator, stakers who delegated to the validator, and the protocol itself because slashing reduces confidence in the economic model. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between distributeRewards and settle, noticing that the former resets the vault balance without any restriction. The bug is subtle because the function’s name suggests a harmless accounting operation, and there is no obvious indication that calling it can change the outcome of a later settlement. From a user’s perspective the operator expects to receive the correct reward and avoid a slash, but after the exploit the operator receives a slash and the protocol’s funds appear to disappear, violating the expected accounting guarantees. Conceptually the fix is to restrict the reward‑distribution function to a trusted role, or to redesign the settlement logic so that it uses a snapshot of the balance taken before any external calls, thereby preventing a malicious actor from altering the amount used for the slash calculation.

title: `ValidatorWithdrawalVault.settleFunds` doesn’t check amount that user has inside `NodeELRewardVault` to pay for penalty
description: `ValidatorWithdrawalVault.settleFunds` doesn’t check amount that user has inside `NodeELRewardVault` to pay for penalty. That value can increase operator’s earned amount, which can avoid slashing.
poc:
When a validator withdraws from beacon chain the `ValidatorWithdrawalVault.settleFunds` function is called. This function calculates amount that a validator [has earned](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-stader/blob/main/contracts/ValidatorWithdrawalVault.sol#L62) for attestations as a validator. So only the balance of this contract [is considered](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-stader/blob/main/contracts/ValidatorWithdrawalVault.sol#L99).

The function [fetches penalty amount](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-stader/blob/main/contracts/ValidatorWithdrawalVault.sol#L64). This penalty amount contains [of 3 points](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-stader/blob/main/contracts/Penalty.sol#L111): `_mevTheftPenalty`, `_missedAttestationPenalty` and `_missedAttestationPenalty`.

In this case, if the penalty amount is bigger than the validator’s earning on `ValidatorWithdrawalVault`, the [SD collateral is slashed](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-stader/blob/main/contracts/ValidatorWithdrawalVault.sol#L66-L69).

Now, we need to understand how validator receives funds in this system. All attestation payments come to `ValidatorWithdrawalVault`, while `mev`/`block` proposal funds are coming to `SocializingPool` or `NodeELRewardVault` (depends on user’s choice). So actually, `_missedAttestationPenalty` is responding to `ValidatorWithdrawalVault` earning, while `_mevTheftPenalty` is responding to `NodeELRewardVault` earnings.

That means, `NodeELRewardVault` balance should also be checked in order to find out how many earnings a validator has and they should be also counted when applying the penalty.

Simple example:

  1. A validator wants to exit.
  2. An operator earning is 0.1 eth inside `ValidatorWithdrawalVault`.
  3. The accrued penalty is 0.11, which means the user will be slashed.
  4. The operator also has `NodeELRewardVault` where their operator’s reward is 0.05 eth.
  5. As result, the user has enough balance to cover penalty, but they were still penalized.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the settlement routine that is executed when a validator withdraws its stake from the beacon chain. The function responsible for this, settleFunds, calculates the total penalty that must be deducted from the validator’s earnings and then checks whether the validator’s balance in the ValidatorWithdrawalVault is sufficient to cover that penalty. The logic, however, only looks at the balance held in the ValidatorWithdrawalVault and completely ignores any earnings that may be stored in the separate NodeELRewardVault, which holds rewards originating from MEV or block‑proposal activities. Because the penalty amount is composed of three components – the MEV theft penalty, the missed‑attestation penalty, and another missed‑attestation penalty – the MEV theft portion is directly tied to the operator’s rewards that reside in NodeELRewardVault. When the total penalty exceeds the amount present in the ValidatorWithdrawalVault but the combined balance of both vaults would actually be enough, the contract proceeds to slash the validator’s SD collateral as if the funds were insufficient. This mismatch between the accounting of distributed earnings and the penalty enforcement creates an unfair loss of funds for the validator. The issue manifests during the exit flow, specifically when settleFunds is called and the penalty calculation is performed. It affects any validator whose earnings are split across the two vaults, meaning both the validator (as a user) and the operator can experience unexpected slashing or loss of rewards. The problem was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, which examined the settlement logic and noticed that the NodeELRewardVault balance was never taken into account when verifying that the penalty could be covered. The bug is subtle because the protocol’s UI may display a total balance that appears sufficient, yet the internal check only validates a subset of that balance, leading to silent slashing without an obvious error message. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after initiating a validator exit, the expected refund is reduced or the collateral is unexpectedly taken, contradicting the expectation that the validator should receive the full amount of its accumulated earnings. This class of vulnerability can be described as an incomplete balance verification or accounting mismatch across multiple contract storage locations. To remediate the issue, the settlement logic should aggregate the validator’s total earnings from both the ValidatorWithdrawalVault and the NodeELRewardVault before applying the penalty, or the penalty calculation should be refactored to reference a unified accounting source that reflects all sources of reward. By ensuring that the full set of available funds is considered, the protocol can prevent unjustified slashing and preserve the intended economic guarantees.

title: No bidder has incentive to bid in the Auction except doing last-minute `MEV` due to fixed `endBlock`
description: No bidder has incentive to bid in the Auction except doing last-minute `MEV` due to fixed `endBlock`.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic‑incentive flaw in the auction mechanism where the contract sets a fixed block number as the auction end time (endBlock) and never adjusts it after a bid is placed. Because the deadline cannot be extended, rational participants recognize that bidding early provides no advantage; instead, they wait until the final block to submit their transaction. This creates a strong incentive for validators or MEV operators who can control transaction ordering in the last block to submit a bid that out‑competes all earlier offers. The root cause is the absence of an anti‑sniping or dynamic‑extension rule, which means the auction’s price‑discovery process is vulnerable to last‑minute manipulation. An attacker can exploit this by monitoring the auction, preparing a transaction with a slightly higher bid, and ensuring it is included in the last block using front‑running or priority‑gas‑auction techniques. When the attacker’s transaction is mined, the auction ends with a price that is often lower than what would have been achieved under a fair, competitive bidding process. The impact includes reduced revenue for the protocol, unfair treatment of honest bidders, and erosion of trust in the auction’s economic guarantees. The issue manifests whenever an auction is created with a static endBlock, as shown in the createLot function that assigns endBlock = block.number + duration and never updates it. All bidders, including regular users, may experience the symptom of seeing no early bids accepted and only a sudden surge of activity at the final block, leading to unexpectedly low final prices. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined the auction’s incentive structure and recognized the classic “last‑minute sniping” pattern common to fixed‑deadline auctions. Because the contract still functions technically—accepting bids and transferring tokens—the flaw can be subtle and may not raise immediate alarms until the economic consequences become apparent. To remediate, the auction should incorporate a dynamic end time that extends by a predefined interval (for example, one hour) each time a new highest bid is received, or employ other anti‑sniping mechanisms such as minimum bid increments, a grace period, or a commit‑reveal scheme. These changes restore the intended competitive environment, ensuring that bidders have a genuine incentive to participate throughout the auction rather than only at the last moment, and they align the contract’s behavior with the protocol’s economic design.

title: Chainlink’s `latestRoundData` may return a stale or incorrect result
description:
Chainlink’s `latestRoundData` is used here to retrieve price feed data; however, there is insufficient protection against price staleness.

Return arguments other than `int256 answer` are necessary to determine the validity of the returned price, as it is possible for an outdated price to be received. See [here](https://ethereum.stackexchange.com/questions/133242/how-future-resilient-is-a-chainlink-price-feed/133843#133843) for reasons why a price feed might stop updating.

The return value `updatedAt` contains the timestamp at which the received price was last updated, and can be used to ensure that the price is not outdated. See more information about `latestRoundID` in the [Chainlink docs](https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds/api-reference#latestrounddata). Inaccurate price data can lead to functions not working as expected and/or loss of funds.
bug_full: Chainlink’s latestRoundData function returns a tuple that includes the price (answer) and a timestamp (updatedAt). In the examined contract the price is used to calculate balances and supply, but the timestamp is ignored. Because there is no validation that the returned price is recent, the contract may accept a stale or otherwise incorrect price when the underlying Chainlink feed stops updating, is delayed, or is deliberately frozen. The root cause is the absence of a check that block.timestamp minus updatedAt is within an acceptable delay (MAX_DELAY). An attacker who can cause the feed to become outdated, for example by exploiting a network outage or by feeding a compromised aggregator, can make the contract read an old price. The contract will then perform accounting with that outdated value, leading to mis‑priced deposits, withdrawals or token minting. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal price, but the transaction may settle with a much higher or lower amount, resulting in unexpected loss of funds, zero refunds, or balances that appear to disappear. The issue manifests whenever the Chainlink feed does not update within the expected interval, which can happen intermittently and is difficult to detect because the contract does not emit any warning and the function call succeeds. The vulnerability was identified during a manual audit that compared the function signature with the Chainlink documentation and noticed that the updatedAt field was never used. Because the bug does not cause a revert by itself, it can remain hidden until a stale price leads to a financial discrepancy. The proper mitigation is to treat latestRoundData as a signed data structure and explicitly verify that the timestamp is recent, for example by requiring block.timestamp - updatedAt <= MAX_DELAY, and optionally checking that the roundId has increased and that the answer is non‑zero. This ensures that only fresh, trustworthy price data is used for critical accounting, preventing funds from being mis‑allocated.

title: DPCU-4 | Non-zero Effect On Pool Value
description: When the index token is the same as the PnL token, the positive price impact amount deducted from the position impact pool is maximized (round up division & divide by min price) meanwhile the deduction amount for the pool is minimized (round down division & divide by max price). Similarly, when the index token is the same as the collateral token, the negative price impact amount added to the position impact pool is minimized (multiplied by the min price and divided by the max price) while the pool amount delta is not. This creates a tendency for positive price impact to err on the side of increasing the pool value as stated in the comment on line 171. Because of the unequal effects on the impact pool amount and the pool amount there is an immediate non-zero impact on the pool value. This behavior opens up the possibility for market depositors to manipulate price impact and absorb the position impact pool value. Such a manipulation can be straightforward when the index token is the same as either the collateral token or PnL token.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic and pricing asymmetry that creates a non‑zero net change in the pool’s total value whenever the index token coincides with either the profit‑and‑loss (PnL) token or the collateral token. The contract calculates positive price impact by converting a USD amount to token units using a rounded‑up division and the minimum price, while the amount deducted from the position impact pool is computed with a rounded‑down division and the maximum price. Conversely, for negative price impact the conversion uses the minimum price multiplied by the USD amount and divided by the maximum price, but the pool delta is not adjusted symmetrically. Because the two conversions use different price references and opposite rounding directions, the amount added to the main pool does not exactly cancel the amount removed from the impact pool, resulting in a small but immediate increase (or decrease) of the pool’s recorded value. This imbalance can be exploited by market depositors who deliberately trade when the index token matches the collateral or PnL token, allowing them to manipulate the price‑impact calculation and siphon value from the position impact pool. The effect is subtle; the discrepancy stems from rounding bias and price selection rather than an outright arithmetic overflow, making it hard to notice during casual testing because the deviation may be only a few wei per transaction but can accumulate over many trades. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting assumptions—namely that price impact should be neutral overall—are violated, leading to inflated pool balances, unexpected loss of funds for other participants, and potential erosion of trust in the system. The issue was discovered during a formal audit that examined the impact‑pool accounting logic and identified the comment on line 171 describing the tendency for positive price impact to increase pool value. To remediate, the contract should use a single, consistent price reference (either the min or max price, but the same for both sides) when converting USD values to token amounts for both positive and negative price impact, and apply symmetric rounding (e.g., always round down or use exact integer arithmetic) so that the net effect on the pool value is zero. This change restores the intended accounting invariants and prevents manipulators from extracting value through the described price‑impact asymmetry.

title: `Vault.claimRewards` can break if Convex changes the operator
description: `Vault.claimRewards` assumes that CVX will always get minted to the Vault (if there is a CRV reward). If CVX does not get minted, the claim will fail, preventing payout of CRV and extra rewards. Looking at the Convex code there can be the case where the operator has changed, causing no mint to happen.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑claim function of the Vault contract, which assumes that the Convex CVX token contract will always mint the expected amount of CVX when a CRV reward is present. The CVX contract’s mint function checks that the caller is the current operator (the Booster contract) and, if the operator has changed – for example after a protocol shutdown or upgrade – it simply returns without minting any tokens and without reverting. Because the Vault does not verify that the mint actually succeeded, it proceeds with calculations that include a non‑existent CVX amount, then attempts to transfer CVX to the caller. When the mint silently fails, the CVX balance of the Vault does not increase, the subsequent transfer transfers zero tokens, and the AMPHClaimer receives an incorrect (zero) CVX value. As a result the user’s claim transaction appears to succeed but the user receives no CRV, no CVX and no AMPH rewards, effectively losing access to accumulated rewards. This condition occurs only when the Convex operator has been changed, which can happen during a shutdown scenario that Convex deliberately supports. All users who try to claim rewards while the operator mismatch exists are affected, although their deposited principal remains safe. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the call chain from Vault.claimRewards through BaseRewardPool to the CVX mint function and noticing the silent return path. The bug is hard to notice because the external call does not revert, so the transaction does not throw an error and the missing rewards are not obvious without checking token balances. Conceptually, the flaw is a reliance on an external side‑effect without validation – a classic missing‑return‑value check. To remediate, the Vault should record the CVX balance before invoking the mint, compare it after the call, and revert or handle the case where no CVX was minted, ensuring that reward distribution only proceeds when the expected tokens are actually available. This change restores the intended accounting logic that rewards must be fully minted before they are transferred, preventing the “funds disappear” symptom where users see a successful claim but receive zero tokens.

title: Reorg attack on user’s Vault deployment and deposit may lead to theft of funds
description:
`VaultDeployer` deploys instances of the `Vault` contract using `create`, where the address derivation depends on the sender’s address (= `VaultDeployer`) and its nonce.

Although the system is intended to be deployed on Ethereum, there still have been instances of chain reorgs in its PoS era : [ref](https://decrypt.co/101390/ethereum-beacon-chain-blockchain-reorg).

The frequency and depth of reorgs only increases in alternative L1s and L2s such as polygon and optimism, where reorgs have reached 100+ block depth : [ref](https://protos.com/polygon-hit-by-157-block-reorg-despite-hard-fork-to-reduce-reorgs/).
poc:
In a scenario in which a user’s `Vault` deplyoment and deposit is included fully within a reorg, an attacker is able to frontrun the user’s `Vault` deployment, effectively stealing the `Vault` instance at that particular address, include the user’s deployment (which will deploy a new `Vault` at a new, unrelated address) and his deposit to the **originally deployed`Vault`**, and finally backrun the user’s deposit by pulling funds from the `Vault`.

In order to pull off this attack successfully, the attacker needs to take care of some details:

  1. When frontrunning the `Vault` deployment, he must call `VaultDeployer.deployVault()` through a malicious contract under his control which implements the minimal interface to allow calls the `Vault` makes to the `VaultController` to not revert. Notice that this malicious `VaultController` could allow only deposits to go through in the `Vault`, but disallow withdrawals by returning `false` when `Vault` attempts to call `CONTROLLER.checkVault` within `Vault.withdrawERC20`.
  2. When frontrunning the `Vault` deployment, the attacker must set the `Vault`’s minter to the victim’s address, in order for the deposit to successfully go through within the `Vault`.

Once the victim’s deposit has been executed, the attacker can chose to pull the user’s funds from the compromised `Vault` by calling `Vault.controllerTransfer` through his malicious `VaultController`

Given the high impact of this finding but its low likelihood, I’m submitting this as a medium severity issue.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract that creates user vaults uses the CREATE opcode, which derives the new contract address from the deployer’s address and its current nonce. Because the address is therefore predictable and tied to the deployer’s transaction ordering, an attacker can manipulate the blockchain’s canonical history during a block reorganization to front‑run the deployment, obtain the same address, and later steal the funds that the user intended to deposit. The root cause is the combination of (i) deterministic address generation via CREATE, (ii) reliance on a single transaction being included in the canonical chain, and (iii) the possibility of deep chain reorgs on PoS Ethereum and especially on L1/L2 networks where reorgs of dozens or hundreds of blocks have been observed. An attacker who observes a pending user transaction that calls the vault deployer and then deposits into the freshly created vault can, before the reorg resolves, submit a competing transaction that also calls the deployer from a contract they control. By doing so they cause the same address to be created under their control, optionally setting the vault’s minter to the victim’s address so that the victim’s deposit succeeds. When the victim’s deposit transaction is later included in the canonical chain, the funds are transferred into the attacker‑controlled vault. The attacker’s malicious controller can then block withdrawals and invoke a privileged transfer function to move the deposited tokens out of the vault, effectively stealing them. From the user’s point of view the expected outcome – a newly created vault that holds their deposited tokens – is replaced by a vault that appears to accept the deposit but immediately empties, leaving the user with no balance and no receipt of funds. The impact is loss of user funds and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, because the protocol assumes that a vault deployed at a given address is owned by the user who initiated the deployment. The attack only succeeds when the deployment and deposit are both included in a block that later becomes orphaned during a reorg deep enough for the attacker’s competing block to become the canonical one. It is therefore more likely on networks with frequent or deep reorgs, such as Polygon or Optimism, but can also occur on Ethereum’s PoS chain under rare conditions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the deployment flow and considered the effect of chain reorganizations on deterministic address generation. It is subtle because the contract code itself does not contain an obvious flaw; the problem emerges only when the external environment (block finality) is taken into account, making it easy to overlook in standard unit tests. The recommended mitigation is to replace CREATE with CREATE2 and compute a unique salt from immutable parameters such as the vault identifier, the intended minter, and the caller’s address, thereby decoupling the vault address from transaction ordering and preventing an attacker from reproducing the same address in a competing block. In broader terms the bug belongs to the class of “deterministic address front‑run under reorg” vulnerabilities, where predictable contract addresses enable an adversary to hijack a newly created contract and siphon assets.

title: When Convex pool is shut down while collateral type is `CurveLPStakedOnConvex`, users unable to deposit that asset and protocol lose the ability to accept the asset as collateral further
description: When Convex pool of an asset that has `CurveLPStakedOnConvex` collateral type is shut down, users can no longer deposit that asset into vault since it would always revert on Convex booster `deposit` function, called during vault’s `depositERC20` process. With lack of method to update it, protocol would the ability to accept it as collateral even as plain LP without staking. Also users that use the asset as collateral may face risk of being liquidated. This is also applicable when Convex itself shutdown their booster contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs when a Convex pool that backs an asset registered in the vault with the collateral type CurveLPStakedOnConvex is shut down, either by the pool itself or by the Convex booster contract. The vault’s depositERC20 function always calls the Convex booster’s deposit method, assuming the pool is active. When the pool is closed, the booster call reverts, causing every subsequent deposit of that LP token to fail. Because the contract does not provide a mechanism to change the collateral type or pool identifier after a shutdown, the protocol loses the ability to accept the same token even as a plain, unstaked LP token. Existing vaults that already hold the token remain marked as “staked” via the isTokenStaked flag. During liquidation the vault checks this flag and attempts to withdraw from Convex; if the pool is shut down the withdrawal fails and the liquidation routine aborts, potentially leaving an under‑collateralised position un‑liquidated. The root cause is a hard‑coded dependency on an external Convex contract and a static collateral metadata configuration that is not updated when the external service becomes unavailable, combined with a stale staking state flag that is not cleared on full withdrawal. Exploitation does not require an attacker; the condition is triggered automatically when Convex shuts down a pool, which can happen as part of normal protocol upgrades or emergency actions. The impact is two‑fold: new users cannot deposit the asset, receiving a revert message such as “pool is closed”, and existing vaults may be unable to liquidate, risking loss of collateral value. From the user’s perspective the UI will show that a deposit transaction fails, that the expected balance does not increase, or that liquidation attempts produce no result despite an apparent deficit. The issue is difficult to notice because deposits work correctly until the external pool is disabled, and there is no on‑chain indicator that the collateral type should be treated as a simple token. The bug belongs to the class of external‑dependency shutdown handling errors and stale state flag inconsistencies, similar to “dependency lockout” or “incorrect accounting after external contract failure”. To remediate the problem the protocol should allow an admin to update the collateral metadata – switching the collateral type to Single and resetting the pool identifier to zero when a pool is shut down – and the vault’s withdraw function should clear the isTokenStaked flag when the entire balance is withdrawn, ensuring that liquidation logic reflects the true staking state. These changes restore the ability to accept the token as plain collateral and guarantee that liquidation can proceed correctly.

title: GSU-2 | getExecutionGas Needs to Account for Callback Gas
description: The GasUtils.getExecutionGas function sets aside a minHandleErrorGas amount to handle the subsequent error logic. However, this amount does not take into account the conﬁgured callback gas limit for an order in the event of a cancellation/freezing.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the gas‑budgeting logic of the execution engine, specifically the GasUtils.getExecutionGas routine. This function reserves a constant amount of gas, called minHandleErrorGas, to cover the error‑handling path that runs after an order is cancelled or frozen. The root cause is that the calculation of this reserve ignores the callback gas limit that is configured for each order. When an order is cancelled or frozen, the protocol invokes a user‑defined callback whose gas consumption may be larger than the fixed minHandleErrorGas value. Because the reserved gas is insufficient, the callback can run out of gas, causing the error‑handling code to abort prematurely. An attacker or a malicious user can trigger a cancellation or freezing of an order that has a high callback gas requirement, forcing the execution to hit the gas shortfall. The immediate impact is that the order’s cancellation does not complete correctly: funds that should be returned to the user remain locked, the order may stay in a frozen state, and the protocol’s accounting can become inconsistent. From the user’s perspective the UI may show the order as cancelled while the balance displayed for the user does not change, or the user may receive a zero refund despite expecting a full return of collateral. This condition occurs only during the post‑execution phase of an order when the configured callback gas limit exceeds the hard‑coded minHandleErrorGas reserve. It primarily affects traders who place orders with custom callbacks, as well as the protocol itself because stuck orders can reduce liquidity and erode trust. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who identified that the gas reservation logic did not incorporate the per‑order callback limit. The bug is subtle because normal test cases use low‑gas callbacks, so the shortage does not manifest, and the transaction simply reverts without a clear error message, making it hard to spot in routine testing. To remediate the problem the gas‑budgeting function should be modified to add the order’s configured callback gas limit to the minHandleErrorGas calculation, ensuring that enough gas is always available for both the callback and the subsequent error handling. In broader terms this is a classic insufficient‑gas accounting flaw, where the contract underestimates the gas needed for downstream logic, leading to failed callbacks and potential loss of funds.

title: GLOBAL-2 | Saved Callback Keeper Grieﬁng
description: Saved callback contracts will be executed on liquidation and ADL orders which are entirely funded by the keeper/protocol without any remuneration from the user. Additionally, the saved callback contract will be given the maximum callback gas limit upon liquidation or ADL. This way malicious traders may grief the keeper by creating numerous positions that become liquidatable simply to force the keeper to expend the maximum callback gas limit. Notice that a malicious trader may also be able to directly extract value from the keeper with gas tokens upon a liquidation or ADL callback since this execution gas is subsidized by the protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service and economic‑grief issue that arises from the way the protocol handles saved callback contracts during liquidation and automatic‑deleveraging (ADL) events. When a position is liquidated or an ADL order is executed, the protocol invokes a user‑provided callback contract and supplies it with the maximum allowed callback gas limit. Because the gas for this callback is paid entirely by the keeper or the protocol and not reimbursed by the user whose position is being liquidated, a malicious trader can open a large number of positions that are deliberately made liquidatable. Each of those positions triggers the saved callback, forcing the keeper to spend the full gas stipend on code that may be intentionally inefficient or even contain gas‑token tricks that refund part of the spent gas to the attacker. The root cause is the absence of any accounting or remuneration mechanism that ties the callback gas cost to the collateral of the liquidated position, combined with the protocol’s policy of granting the maximum gas limit regardless of the actual work performed. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly creating and then liquidating positions, or by submitting ADL orders that target vulnerable callbacks, thereby inflating the keeper’s gas bill without any compensation. The impact is that the keeper’s operational costs increase dramatically, potentially exhausting its gas budget, leading to missed liquidations, delayed ADL actions, and ultimately loss of funds for honest users because the protocol may be unable to maintain its risk‑management guarantees. The condition under which the bug manifests is any liquidation or ADL execution that references a saved callback contract; it affects the keeper service, the protocol’s treasury, and indirectly all users whose positions rely on timely liquidations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the callback handling logic and identified that the gas stipend is fixed and unpaid by the user. It can be hard to notice because the callback execution appears to succeed from the user’s perspective, while the hidden cost is borne by the keeper, and the protocol’s accounting does not surface the excessive gas consumption. To remediate, the protocol should either cap the gas supplied to callbacks based on the actual work needed, or charge the liquidated position’s remaining collateral for any gas beyond a reasonable threshold, effectively remunerating the keeper for excessive gas usage. This class of bug can be described as an unchecked external callback with unbounded gas subsidy, leading to grief attacks and economic drain on service providers. From a user’s point of view, the symptoms may include the keeper failing to process liquidations, delayed order execution, or the protocol reporting unusually high gas costs, while the trader who triggered the liquidation sees no penalty beyond the loss of their position. The expectation that the keeper’s gas is covered by the protocol is violated, resulting in a scenario where “funds disappear” from the keeper’s budget and the protocol’s safety mechanisms are weakened.

title: OCL-1 | Chainlink Feed Manipulation
description: In the event that a conﬁgured Chainlink price feed is outdated the order execution transaction will not occur due to a PriceFeedNotUpdated revert. A malicious trader may observe that the price feed is outdated and submit a market order that includes a token requiring that price feed. The trader’s order will not be executed as the price feed is outdated. The trader can then observe that the chainlink prices have been updated with a transmit transaction and choose to cancel their order if price has not moved favorably in the time that the price feed was outdated.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s reliance on a single Chainlink price feed that must be refreshed within a predefined interval for order execution to succeed. When the feed becomes stale, the contract deliberately reverts the transaction with a PriceFeedNotUpdated error, preventing the market order from being processed. This behaviour is intended as a safety check, but it creates an attack surface because a malicious trader can monitor the timestamp of the feed, detect that it is outdated, and deliberately submit a market order that is guaranteed to revert. After the feed is updated by a legitimate transmit transaction, the attacker can observe the new price and, if the price movement is unfavorable, cancel the pending order or submit a new order that takes advantage of the price change. The exploit therefore allows the attacker to waste the victim’s gas, create a denial‑of‑service condition for honest traders, and potentially front‑run the market by timing order cancellations around feed updates. The issue manifests only when the price feed fails to update within the expected window, which may occur due to network latency, oracle downtime, or intentional manipulation of the feed’s update schedule. All participants that rely on the affected market – including regular traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s accounting logic – are affected because their orders may appear to be submitted but never execute, leading to confusion, unexpected zero balances, or missing refunds. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the contract does not contain any fallback or graceful degradation path for stale feeds and that the revert message alone does not alert users to the underlying cause. Because a revert is an expected outcome in many smart contracts, the bug can be difficult to spot in production without explicit monitoring of feed freshness. To remediate the issue, the contract should incorporate explicit freshness checks before attempting execution, automatically freeze or cancel orders that cannot be fulfilled due to an outdated feed, emit clear events indicating the reason for cancellation, and optionally fallback to an alternative price source or a time‑buffered price to ensure continuity of service. By treating the stale‑feed condition as a first‑class error state rather than a simple revert, the protocol can preserve user expectations (order should execute or be cancelled) and prevent malicious actors from exploiting timing gaps in the oracle update cycle.

title: MKTU-4 | Unwieldy Claimable Collateral Controls
description: In the claimCollateral function the claimableFactor is the maximum of the claimableFactorForTime and claimableFactorForAccount. Therefore in the case where capped negative price impact is manipulated and claimable collateral ought to be used at the protocol's discretion to punish the manipulator, the controls will be insuﬃcient. Consider the following: A malicious trader manipulates reference prices to take advantage of negative PI capping. Many other traders are capped in the same timekey as this one malicious trader. The other traders ought to be able to claim their collateral at a later date, but the malicious trader should never have their claimableFactor updated. The current controls are not well suited for this scenario since every non-malicious trader would have to have a manual per-account claimableFactorForAccount conﬁgured. In the case where there are many innocent traders in this timekey this may be impractical, especially in times of market volatility. The controls should be ﬂipped such that the single malicious trader can be punished with a more constrictive claimableFactorForAccount.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the collateral‑claiming routine of the protocol, where the amount of collateral a user may withdraw is governed by a variable called claimableFactor. The contract computes this factor as the maximum of two sub‑factors: claimableFactorForTime, which reflects a global time‑based limit, and claimableFactorForAccount, which is intended to impose a stricter, per‑account restriction for malicious actors. Because the logic uses the mathematical maximum, the resulting claimableFactor is always the less restrictive of the two values. Consequently, when a trader manipulates reference prices to exploit the negative price‑impact (PI) capping mechanism, the protocol cannot apply a tighter per‑account cap; the global time‑based limit dominates and the malicious trader can still claim the full amount of collateral that should have been withheld. This design flaw emerges specifically in scenarios where many honest traders share the same timekey as the attacker and the protocol expects to punish only the attacker by lowering its claimableFactorForAccount. The per‑account factor would have to be configured individually for each honest user, which is impractical during volatile market conditions. From a user’s perspective, an attacker sees their balance increase unexpectedly after a price‑impact manipulation, while other participants may later discover that the protocol’s collateral pool is depleted, leading to missing or zero balances where funds were expected. The impact is a potential loss of protocol funds and a breach of the accounting assumptions that collateral should be locked when price manipulation is detected. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the claimCollateral function and noticed that the max operation contradicts the intended punitive behavior. It is subtle because the code appears to enforce a safety check, yet the choice of max silently disables the stricter per‑account rule. To remediate the problem, the contract should either replace the max with a minimum operation when the per‑account flag is enabled, or invert the logic so that claimableFactorForAccount acts as a tighter ceiling. Introducing an explicit boolean such as isClaimableFactorForAccountEnabled would allow the protocol to decide when the restrictive per‑account factor should override the global one, ensuring that malicious traders cannot bypass the intended collateral lock.

title: GLOBAL-3 | Unbounded Virtual Inventory Price Impact
description: There is no lower bound on how negative price impact can be during swaps or position orders due to the virtual inventory. In virtual inventories where there are many markets, it is possible to build up large imbalances over time as users may be incentivized with positive impact from their direct pool to make deposits or orders that ultimately increase the disparity in the virtual inventory. The resulting extreme disparity in the virtual inventory will lead to signiﬁcant negative impact without bound for unsuspecting users. The most likely outcome is that deposits and orders that would compute price impact from the virtual inventory will simply be cancelled due to their acceptable price or minimum amounts being unfulﬁllable.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded negative price impact that originates from the protocol’s virtual inventory mechanism. The virtual inventory is a bookkeeping construct used to smooth pricing across many synthetic markets, but the contract does not enforce any lower bound on how much negative impact the virtual inventory can contribute when calculating swap or position order prices. Over time, especially in environments with many markets, users are incentivised to place deposits or orders that generate positive impact on the direct pool while simultaneously pushing the virtual inventory further out of balance. Because the virtual inventory can accumulate arbitrarily large imbalances, the price‑impact formula may produce extremely negative adjustments. When a user submits a trade, the contract checks whether the resulting price satisfies the user‑specified acceptable price or minimum amount. If the virtual‑inventory‑derived impact is so large that the price falls below the user’s limit, the transaction is either cancelled or fails to meet the minimum amount condition. From the user’s perspective this appears as a swap that is rejected with a “price too low” error, a deposit that seems to be accepted and then disappears, or an order that executes at a dramatically worse rate than expected. The impact is that legitimate users may be unable to trade, may receive far worse execution prices, or may see their orders silently cancelled, eroding confidence in the protocol and potentially causing financial loss if a trade is forced through at an unfavorable price. The issue manifests whenever the virtual inventory has built up a significant imbalance, which can happen gradually as many participants interact with multiple markets without any safeguard on the magnitude of negative impact. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the price‑impact calculation lacks a ceiling for negative adjustments. It can be hard to notice because normal slippage checks already exist, so occasional rejections are expected; however, the underlying cause is a systemic accounting error that only becomes apparent after the virtual inventory drifts far from equilibrium. To remediate the problem the protocol should introduce a lower bound on the negative price impact that can be applied from the virtual inventory, or separate the virtual‑inventory impact factor and cap it independently from the direct pool impact. By limiting how much the virtual inventory can worsen a price, the contract will prevent unbounded negative adjustments, ensure that trades either execute within reasonable bounds or fail gracefully, and restore alignment with the intended economic model of the synthetic markets.

title: GSU-1 | Incorrect Decrease Gas Estimation
description: When estimating the gas needed for a decrease order in estimateExecuteDecreaseOrderGasLimit, 1 is added to gasPerSwap instead of adding 1 to the swap length to account for the extra swap due to decreasePositionSwapType.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the gas‑estimation routine used for decrease orders. When the contract builds the gas limit for a decrease order it calls estimateExecuteDecreaseOrderGasLimit and adds a constant of 1 to the variable gasPerSwap instead of adding the extra unit to the total number of swaps that will be performed. Decrease positions that require an additional swap because of the decreasePositionSwapType therefore have one swap less gas accounted for. The root cause is a misinterpretation of the extra swap as a per‑swap cost rather than an additional swap count. An attacker does not need to exploit the bug directly; any user who submits a decrease order will experience a transaction that may run out of gas and revert because the estimated gas limit is lower than the actual consumption. The impact is that the decrease operation fails, the user’s position remains unchanged, and the gas spent on the failed transaction is lost. This situation occurs only when a decrease order triggers the special swap type, i.e., when the protocol must execute an extra swap to unwind the position. Affected parties are end‑users who attempt to reduce or close positions and the protocol itself, which may appear unreliable or experience denial‑of‑service for decrease actions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the GMX Synthetics contract where the gas‑estimation logic was examined and the off‑by‑one was identified. Because gas estimation is an internal helper, the problem can be hard to notice until a transaction repeatedly fails with an out‑of‑gas error despite seemingly sufficient gas limits. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a decrease request submitted, but the transaction reverts and the user receives no refund or position change, often seeing a “out of gas” error and a loss of the gas fee. The bug belongs to the class of gas‑estimation errors where the formula does not correctly account for all execution steps, leading to under‑allocation of gas. To fix the issue the estimator should increase the swap length by one (or otherwise add the extra swap to the total gas calculation) instead of incrementing gasPerSwap, ensuring the gas limit covers the additional swap required by decreasePositionSwapType.

title: GLOBAL-1 | Positive Impact Misrepresented
description: During both increase and decrease orders, forPositiveImpact is determined based upon the priceImpactUsd being greater than 0, however this is based on the priceImpactUsd after it has been capped. In the event that the position impact pool is empty and the positive price impact value is capped to 0, the fees will be calculated with a forPositiveImpact of false, meanwhile the action does indeed balance the pool.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the fee‑calculation routine of a synthetic trading contract. The contract decides whether an order should be treated as a positive‑impact (rewarding the trader with configured fees) by checking if the variable priceImpactUsd is greater than zero. However this check is performed after priceImpactUsd has been limited by a cap that forces the value to zero when the position‑impact pool is empty. Consequently, when the pool is empty and a trader’s order would actually provide a positive impact to the pool, the capped priceImpactUsd becomes zero, the forPositiveImpact flag is set to false, and the fee logic treats the order as a negative impact. The fee calculation therefore applies the wrong fee formula, typically reducing or removing the reward that should have been granted. This mis‑representation occurs during both increase and decrease order paths and is triggered only when the impact pool has no remaining capacity. Users are affected because they may see their expected fee reward disappear or be charged an unexpected fee, leading to a discrepancy between the protocol’s accounting assumptions (that positive impact actions are rewarded) and the actual outcome (fees are deducted). The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended fee policy with the implementation logic and noticed that the flag was derived after the cap, contradicting the design specification. It is subtle because the priceImpactUsd value still appears non‑negative, so the flag logic looks correct at first glance, and the error only manifests when the pool is empty – a state that may not be exercised frequently in normal testing. To fix the problem, the contract should evaluate the forPositiveImpact condition before applying the cap to priceImpactUsd, ensuring that actions that truly balance or improve the pool are recognised and the correct fee schedule is applied. This change restores the intended economic incentive model and prevents users from receiving zero or reduced rewards when they should be credited.

title: If someone becomes a GSC member, they may become un-kickable forever
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way voting power is queried from voting vault contracts that are used to determine membership in the Arcade Governance Steering Committee (GSC). The BaseVotingVault contract implements a function called queryVotePower that, instead of merely reading a user’s historical voting balance, calls an internal findAndClear routine which both returns the most recent balance and deletes older entries that are older than a configurable staleBlockLag. This state‑mutating read is then used by two privileged functions in the GSC vault: proveMembership, which aggregates voting power from a list of vaults to admit a new member, and kick, which recomputes the aggregated voting power of an existing member and removes them if it falls below a threshold. Because findAndClear erases historical entries, an attacker can deliberately inflate the size of the voting‑power history by repeatedly delegating and redelegating tiny amounts of tokens over many blocks. Each delegation creates a new entry in the vault’s history. After the attacker has accumulated thousands of entries, they withdraw all tokens from the vault, causing their actual voting power to drop below the required threshold. When an honest participant later calls kick on the attacker, the kick function invokes queryVotePower on the attacker’s vault, which now attempts to clear thousands of historical entries in a single transaction. The gas required to iterate over and delete all those entries exceeds the block gas limit, causing the transaction to revert with an out‑of‑gas error. As a result, the attacker remains a GSC member even though they no longer hold any voting power, effectively becoming “unkickable”. The impact is severe: a permanently privileged member can repeatedly re‑enter the GSC, accumulate enough members to control a majority of the committee, and subsequently approve malicious proposals that can drain treasury funds or alter protocol parameters. The issue affects any user who can become a GSC member, the GSC governance process, and the overall security of the Arcade protocol. It was discovered during a formal security audit when the auditors observed that queryVotePower performed a state‑changing operation and that the kick function could be forced to run out of gas by inflating the vault’s history. The problem is subtle because the function name suggests a read‑only query, and the gas exhaustion only manifests after a large number of history entries have been created, which is not obvious during normal operation. The recommended mitigation is to replace the call to findAndClear with a pure read‑only find operation (as used in the queryVotePowerView function) so that membership checks and kick calculations never modify historical data. Alternatively, the contract could limit the number of stored history entries or provide a separate view‑only function for governance checks. In user‑facing terms, a member who should be removed sees the kick transaction fail with an out‑of‑gas error, while the attacker continues to appear as a valid GSC member and can still propose and vote on actions, even though they hold no underlying tokens. This breaks the expected invariant that only accounts with sufficient voting power can retain GSC privileges, leading to a denial‑of‑service and potential governance takeover.

title: `_syncVotingPower` can revert in underflow in `NFTBoostVault.sol` and `ARCDVestingVault.sol`
description: `_syncVotingPower` can revert in underflow in `NFTBoostVault.sol` and `ARCDVestingVault.sol`.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow that can occur in the internal function responsible for synchronising a delegatee's voting power when the voting power of a user is reduced. The function calculates the change in voting power as a signed integer, and when the change is negative it attempts to subtract the absolute value of the change from the delegatee's current voting power using the expression delegateeVotes - uint256(change * -1). Because there is no check that delegateeVotes is at least as large as the amount being subtracted, a situation where the reduction exceeds the delegatee's existing voting power triggers a uint256 underflow, causing the transaction to revert. This bug appears in two vault contracts that manage boosted voting power for NFTs and vesting grants. It manifests when an NFT with a high multiplier is withdrawn or when an admin revokes a grant, both of which can cause a large negative change. From a user's perspective the symptom is a transaction that fails with an "execution reverted" error at the moment they expect a withdrawal, a grant revocation, or a voting power update; the user sees no funds returned and the expected vote count does not change. The root cause is the unchecked subtraction of a potentially larger value than the current balance, a classic example of an integer underflow bug in smart contracts. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the voting‑power synchronisation logic and identified the unsafe cast from a signed to an unsigned integer without a safety guard. It can be hard to notice because the underflow only occurs in edge cases where the reduction is larger than the current delegated votes, which may not be exercised in normal test scenarios. Exploitation does not require sophisticated tooling; any user who holds a boosted NFT or a vesting grant can trigger the underflow by withdrawing the asset or by an admin revoking the grant, causing the transaction to revert and effectively denying service to the affected account. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: users cannot withdraw their NFTs or have their grants revoked, and the protocol's voting tally may become inconsistent because the update never happens. The bug violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that voting power can only be decreased down to zero, not below. A proper fix is to ensure that before performing the subtraction the contract verifies that delegateeVotes is greater than or equal to the absolute change, and if not, to set the new voting power to zero or use a saturating subtraction that prevents underflow. This change restores the intended business logic that voting power can be reduced but never become negative, eliminating the revert and allowing normal withdrawals and revocations.

title: Proposal vote power can be easily manipulated
description:
`ArcadeGSCCoreVoting` can be a target of vote manipulation. An attacker might be able to take a huge loan (even uncollateralized) for a single block before creating a proposal.

When voting, only this single block is checked when calculating the `votingPower`. This may lead to an attacker being able to execute arbitrary proposals with minimal risks involved.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the governance contract determines a voter’s power by querying a voting vault with the block number stored in the proposal’s created field, which is set to block.number - 1. This design only captures the token balance at a single block prior to proposal creation. An attacker can obtain a large amount of the governance token through a short‑term loan that is outstanding during that specific block, create a proposal, and then cast votes that are weighted by the inflated balance. Because the contract does not aggregate balances over time, the borrowed tokens are counted as legitimate voting power for the entire voting period, after which the loan can be repaid with little or no cost. The exploit can be carried out with a normal, even uncollateralized, loan that lasts only the one block needed for the snapshot, bypassing the intended flash‑loan mitigation. When the manipulated vote reaches the required quorum, the attacker can push any proposal through, including proposals that execute arbitrary code or change critical protocol parameters, potentially leading to loss of funds or unauthorized state changes. The issue appears only when a proposal is created and a vote is cast in the same block window; it affects all participants of the governance system because the integrity of the voting outcome is compromised. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined how voting power is calculated and noticed that the snapshot mechanism does not protect against single‑block balance changes. It is difficult to notice in normal testing because the contract behaves correctly for typical token holders and the single‑block snapshot seems reasonable at first glance. The vulnerability belongs to the class of governance vote‑power manipulation bugs caused by insufficiently robust voting‑power oracles that rely on a single‑block snapshot rather than a time‑weighted average. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a proposal being approved despite no visible large voter, or a proposal passing with an unexpectedly low number of votes, contradicting the expectation that only long‑term token holders influence decisions. The recommended mitigation is to replace the single‑block snapshot with a time‑weighted average (TWAP) or another multi‑block checkpointing scheme so that a temporary balance spike cannot dominate the voting power calculation.

title: User voting power is not synchronized after multiplier changes
description:
User voting power is not synchronized after multiplier changes.
If the manager decreases the multiplier for a token, users’ voting power will not be affected.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a governance system that grants voting power based on a token‑specific multiplier. When a manager modifies the multiplier for a given NFT, the contract stores the new multiplier but does not automatically adjust the voting power of users who have already registered the NFT as a boost. The root cause is that the function responsible for changing the multiplier only updates a mapping of token address and token id to a multiplier value and emits an event, while the users' boosted voting power is cached in a separate registration structure. The contract provides an auxiliary function that can recompute voting power for a list of addresses, but this function requires the caller to supply the exact user addresses and is limited to fifty addresses per call. Because the contract does not maintain a reverse index from token id to the set of users that rely on that token, the manager cannot reliably determine which users need to be refreshed, and users can simply avoid being included in the update call. Consequently, after a multiplier reduction, a user’s voting power remains at the higher, outdated value, giving them more influence than the protocol intends. This discrepancy is invisible to the user interface; the UI continues to display the same voting power, so the problem is hard to notice without explicit inspection of the multiplier change and a manual query of the cached voting power. The impact is that governance proposals may be decided with inflated votes, undermining fairness and potentially allowing a malicious actor to sway outcomes by deliberately lowering multipliers after votes have been cast. The issue manifests whenever a multiplier is changed after users have registered the corresponding NFT, which can happen at any time the manager exercises their privilege. All participants in the governance process—wardens, token holders, and the protocol itself—are affected because the integrity of the voting tally is compromised. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit that included unit tests reproducing the scenario where a user’s voting power remained unchanged after the manager called the multiplier‑setting function. The difficulty in spotting the bug stems from the fact that the contract’s design intentionally snapshots voting power at proposal creation, and the update mechanism is optional and not automatically triggered. To remediate the issue, the contract should maintain a mapping from each token id to the list of users that have delegated that token, and the setMultiplier function should iterate over that list (or emit an event that off‑chain services can use) to recompute and store the correct voting power for every affected user, or alternatively compute the boosted voting power lazily at query time so that it always reflects the current multiplier. This change would align the on‑chain accounting with the intended business logic that voting power must be proportional to the active multiplier, eliminating the possibility of stale, inflated votes.

title: Users who have claimed before the update on the merkle tree will have no shares of the rewards afterward
description: Users who have claimed before an update on the merkle tree in [ArcadeAirdrop](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-arcade/blob/main/contracts/token/ArcadeAirdrop.sol) are not going to be able to claim the extra rewards. The reward tokens will be left stuck in the contract, waiting for the manager to reclaim them.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect claim‑tracking mechanism in the ArcadeAirdrop contract that prevents users who have already claimed rewards from receiving any additional tokens when the merkle root is later updated. The root cause is a simple check that reverts if the caller’s address has a non‑zero entry in the claimed mapping (claimed[msg.sender] != 0). This logic assumes a static merkle tree and does not consider that the entitlement of a user may increase after a new merkle root is set. When the contract owner changes the merkle root to raise the reward amount, the contract still sees the early claimer as having already claimed and blocks any further withdrawal, causing the transaction to revert with AA_AlreadyClaimed. An attacker does not need to act; the bug is triggered automatically whenever the protocol updates the merkle tree after some users have claimed. The impact is that early claimers lose the extra portion of their rewards, while the additional tokens remain locked in the contract and can only be reclaimed by the manager, effectively “funds disappear” from the user’s perspective. This situation occurs only under the condition that a merkle root update happens after at least one user has claimed, and it affects all users who claimed before the update as well as the overall trustworthiness of the airdrop mechanism. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the claim implementation and identified the if‑statement that blocks further claims. It can be hard to notice because many airdrop contracts use a similar pattern for single‑use claims, and the audit may assume the merkle root is immutable. From the user’s point of view, the UI shows a transaction failure, no tokens are transferred, and the expected balance increase does not happen, contradicting the expectation that a larger reward amount should be claimable. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “incomplete state tracking for incremental entitlement” where the contract records only a boolean or total claimed amount without accounting for future entitlement changes. The proper fix is to store the amount already claimed per user and allow a new claim of the difference between the current entitlement (derived from the latest merkle root) and the previously claimed amount, similar to the approach used in the ReputationBadge contract where total grant and claimed amount are tracked separately. This change would enable users to claim additional rewards after a merkle root update and prevent tokens from becoming permanently stuck in the contract.

title: `ArcadeTreasury.sol` allowance may be overriden
description: Direct use of `IERC20(token).approve(spender, amount);` causes the same `spender` allowances to be overridden by each other.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an ERC20 allowance overwrite flaw that occurs because the contract calls IERC20(token).approve(spender, amount) each time an approval is needed. The approve function sets the spender's allowance to the exact amount supplied, replacing any previously granted allowance instead of adding to it. This design choice is the root cause: the internal _approve helper does not read the current allowance before calling approve, and the public gscApprove function also invokes approve with the raw amount. As a result, when multiple approval functions such as approveSmallSpend, approveMediumSpend or approveLargeSpend target the same spender, the last call silently overwrites the earlier allowance. An attacker who controls the GSC_CORE_VOTING_ROLE can exploit this by first granting a large allowance to a spender and then issuing a subsequent approval with a tiny amount (for example 1 wei), which reduces the spender's effective allowance to that tiny value. The impact is that legitimate spenders may find their allowance unexpectedly reduced, causing token transfers to fail with “transfer amount exceeds allowance” errors, or they may be unable to spend any funds at all. From the user’s perspective the UI may still show that an approval transaction succeeded, but the allowance displayed later is zero or far lower than expected, leading to confusion and potential denial‑of‑service for the protocol’s treasury operations. The condition under which this occurs is any sequence of approval calls that target the same spender without using an additive allowance pattern. The affected parties include the treasury contract, any external contracts or users that rely on the allowance to move tokens, and the protocol’s governance participants who expect consistent spending limits. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the reviewers noticed the direct use of approve and the lack of accumulation logic. It can be hard to notice because approve does not revert on overwrite and the contract emits no warning; the only symptom is a changed allowance value that may only be observed later when a transfer fails. The bug belongs to the class of ERC20 allowance overwrite or race‑condition vulnerabilities, where cumulative allowances are incorrectly handled. To remediate, the contract should read the existing allowance and approve the sum of the old allowance and the new amount, or use the ERC20 increaseAllowance function, thereby ensuring that each approval adds to the previous allowance instead of replacing it. This change restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents accidental or malicious reduction of spend limits.

title: `DAY_IN_BLOCKS` is incorrect
description:
The day in blocks is calculated with the block time as 13.3 seconds in CoreVoting.sol.: `uint256 public constant DAY_IN_BLOCKS = 6496;`, but since moving to proof of stake, block times are fixed to 12 seconds per block. [Reference](https://ethereum.org/en/developers/docs/consensus-mechanisms/pos/#:~:text=Whereas%20under%20proof%2Dof%2Dwork,block%20proposer%20in%20every%20slot).

This results in an incorrect calculation of the `lockDuration` and `extraVoteTime`, which is used in setting the total duration of a proposal should be active and also the max vote time.

The time difference can be calculated:

`3*24*60*60 / 13.3` = 19488.721804511 (`lockDuration` with 13.3 seconds).  
`3*24*60*60 / 12` = 21600 (`lockDuration` with 12 seconds).  
21600 - 19488.7 = 2111.3  
`2111.3*12 / (60*60)` = 7.03 (difference in hours for `lockDuration`).

`5*24*60*60 / 13.3` = 32481.203007519 (`extraVoteTime` with 13.3 seconds).  
`5*24*60*60 / 12` = 36000 (`extraVoteTime` with 12 seconds).  
36000 - 32481.2 = 3518.8  
`3518.8*12 / (60*60)` = 11.72 (difference in hours `extraVoteTime`).
