If the underlying protocol changes – for example a hard‑fork that reduces the block interval, a shift to a different consensus client, or any future upgrade that alters the average block production rate – the stored BLOCK_TIME will no longer reflect reality. Consequently the reserve calculations become inaccurate: the contract may report a higher or lower amount of assets than actually exist, leading to users receiving too little or too much when they withdraw, trade, or claim rewards. From a user’s perspective this can appear as a missing refund, a balance that suddenly drops to zero, or pricing that no longer matches market expectations. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the constructor contains a modifier that does not affect any state and that BLOCK_TIME is treated as a permanent constant despite being derived from a mutable network property. The issue is subtle because block times are relatively stable on mainnet, so the bug does not manifest immediately and may only become visible after a protocol change or over a long period of operation. The presence of an unused modifier also adds unnecessary complexity and may mislead developers into believing that additional security checks are performed during construction. To remediate the problem the contract should avoid hard‑coding a fixed block interval; instead it can query the timestamp of the latest block, use an oracle, or allow the BLOCK_TIME value to be updated by a governance mechanism at regular intervals. The ReentrancyGuard initialization can be performed without a custom modifier, simplifying the constructor. By making the time‑conversion logic dynamic, the accounting functions will continue to produce correct reserve values even if the network’s block production rate changes, preserving the integrity of user balances and protocol economics.

title: Identifying publications using its ID makes the protocol vulnerable to blockchain re-orgs
description:
In the protocol, publications are uniquely identified through the publisher’s profile ID and the publication’s ID. For example, when a user calls `act()`, the publication being acted on is determined by `publicationActedProfileId` and `publicationActedId`:
```solidity
Types.Publication storage _actedOnPublication = StorageLib.getPublication(
    publicationActionParams.publicationActedProfileId,
    publicationActionParams.publicationActedId
);
```

However, as publication IDs are not based on the publication’s data, this could cause users to act on the wrong publication in the event a blockchain re-org occurs.

For example:

  * Assume the following transactions occur in separate blocks:

    * Block 1: Alice calls `post()` to create a post; its publication ID is 20.
    * Block 2: Bob is interested in the post, he calls `act()` with `publicationActedId = 20` to act on the post.
    * Block 3: Alice calls `comment()` separately, which creates another publication; its publication ID is 21.
  * A blockchain re-org occurs; block 1 is dropped in place of block 3:

    * Alice’s comment now has the publication ID 20 instead of 21.
  * Bob’s call to `act()` in block 2 is applied on top of the re-orged blockchain:

    * This causes him to act on the comment instead of the post he intended to, as it now has the publication ID 20.

In this scenario, due to the blockchain re-org, Bob calls `act()` on a different publication than the one he wanted. This could have severe impacts depending on the action module being called; if the action module is used to collect and pay fees to the publisher and referrals (eg. [`MultirecipientFeeCollectModule.sol`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-lens/blob/main/contracts/modules/act/collect/MultirecipientFeeCollectModule.sol)), Bob could have lost funds.

Note that this also applies to [`comment()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-lens/blob/main/contracts/LensHub.sol#L247-L255), [`mirror`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-lens/blob/main/contracts/LensHub.sol#L270-L278) and [`quote()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-lens/blob/main/contracts/LensHub.sol#L293-L301), as they can be called with reference modules with sensitive logic as well.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the protocol’s reliance on a numeric publication identifier that is assigned solely based on the order of transactions for a given profile. Because the identifier is not derived from the publication’s immutable content, a blockchain re‑organization can change the mapping between an identifier and the underlying post, comment, mirror or quote. In a typical scenario Alice creates a post that receives identifier 20, Bob later calls act() with that identifier expecting to interact with the post, and Alice subsequently creates a comment that receives identifier 21. If a re‑org replaces the block containing Alice’s post with a later block that includes the comment, the comment is reassigned identifier 20 while the original post disappears from the canonical chain. When Bob’s act() transaction is finally executed on the reorganized chain, the identifier 20 now points to the comment, causing Bob to act on the wrong publication. This mismatch can trigger fee‑collection modules that assume the identifier uniquely identifies the intended creator, potentially diverting fees to an unintended recipient and resulting in a loss of funds for the user. The issue manifests only when a re‑org reorders or replaces publication‑creation transactions, which may happen in edge cases involving multiple authorized executors for a profile or transaction replacement. From a user’s perspective the UI will still display the same numeric identifier, but the content behind that identifier has changed, leading to symptoms such as “my collect fee went to the wrong creator” or “the action I performed affected a different post than I selected”. The problem is difficult to notice because the identifier appears stable and the protocol does not verify that the content associated with an identifier matches the caller’s expectation. The root cause is an identifier‑mismatch race condition caused by mutable identifiers that are not bound to immutable data. To remediate, the protocol should use a content‑derived reference, such as a keccak256 hash of the publication’s data, in addition to or instead of the sequential identifier when performing actions. This ensures that even if the numeric identifier is reassigned, the content hash will not match and the action can be rejected, preserving the intended accounting logic and preventing unintended fee transfers.

title: `tryMigrate`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the migration routine of the FollowNFT contract after the V2 upgrade. The function tryMigrate is intended to copy legacy follow information into the new storage layout, but it does not verify whether the caller’s profile is already recorded as a follower in the new mapping. Because the new mapping _followTokenIdByFollowerProfileId is initialised to zero for all pre‑upgrade followers, an attacker who was already following a profile before the upgrade can invoke the public follow() function before the migration transaction is executed. By front‑running the migration or by holding the profile NFT and the follow NFT in separate addresses, the attacker can cause follow() to succeed, creating a new follow token while the old token remains recorded in the legacy data structures. When tryMigrate is later called for the same profile, it writes a new entry into _followTokenIdByFollowerProfileId and increments the internal _followerCount without clearing the previous entry in _followDataByFollowTokenId. The result is a corrupted state where the same logical follower is counted twice, the follower count is inflated, and functions that rely on the internal mappings – such as isFollowing or removeFollower – behave inconsistently. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are confusing: the UI may show the correct follower count for a profile, yet the contract reports a higher count; a user who believes they have unfollowed may still be able to call unfollow a second time, or may see that isFollowing returns false while the contract still holds a stale follow token. The impact is primarily logical – the protocol’s accounting of followers becomes unreliable, which can affect reputation, reward distribution, or any feature that depends on accurate follower metrics. The issue appears only after the V2 upgrade and before a successful migration of each legacy follower, and it is exploitable by any holder of a pre‑upgrade follow token. It was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a Foundry test reproduced the double‑counting and demonstrated that the contract’s state can be corrupted. The bug is subtle because the follower count variable is incremented in an unchecked block, so the overflow is not obvious, and the duplicated mapping entries are not directly visible through standard getters. The proper fix is to add a guard in tryMigrate that checks whether the profile already has a non‑zero entry in _followTokenIdByFollowerProfileId (or that the target follow token’s originalFollowTimestamp is already set) and aborts the migration if the profile is already following. Additionally, the migration should clear any stale data associated with the old follow token to restore a consistent state. This change restores the invariant that a profile can follow a given profile at most once and that follower counts accurately reflect unique followers.

title: Users cannot unfollow if they do not own the FollowNFT of the `followTokenId` used for their profile
bug_full: The vulnerability is an authorization mismatch in the unfollow workflow of a social protocol that uses wrapped Follow NFTs. When a user initiates a follow, the contract allows the operation to succeed if the caller has been granted follow approval for a specific follow token identifier, even if the caller does not own the underlying Follow NFT. The follow logic checks a mapping that records which profile identifier is authorized to use a given follow token, and it accepts an external approval from the NFT owner. However, the subsequent unfollow function repeats a stricter ownership check: it requires the transaction executor to be the owner of the Follow NFT, or to have a direct approval or an operator approval for that NFT. Because the unfollow check does not consider the earlier follow‑approval mapping, a user who followed via an approved token but does not hold the NFT cannot satisfy the permission test. As a result, the unfollow call reverts with a DoesNotHavePermissions error. This can be exploited by an attacker who owns a Follow NFT and deliberately approves another address to follow a target profile. The victim can follow the target, see the follow reflected in the UI, but later attempts to unfollow will fail, leaving the follow relationship permanently active unless the NFT owner intervenes. The impact is that users lose control over their social connections, experience a mismatch between UI expectations (the unfollow button appears but the transaction fails) and on‑chain state, and may be forced to rely on a third party to remove the follow. The condition occurs whenever the follow was performed using an approved Follow NFT rather than direct ownership, which is a legitimate use case supported by the protocol’s follow‑approval mechanism. The affected parties are any profile owners who do not hold the Follow NFT for the token they used, as well as the broader protocol because the broken permission model undermines the intended autonomy of users. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the permission checks of the follow and unfollow functions and noticed the asymmetry between the two code paths. It can be hard to notice because the follow operation succeeds, giving the impression that the permission model is consistent, while the unfollow path silently diverges. The conceptual fix is to align the unfollow permission logic with the follow approval mapping, allowing a caller who was authorized to follow via an approved token to also be authorized to unfollow, or to add an explicit check that the caller matches the profile that initiated the follow. In other words, the contract should treat follow and unfollow symmetrically with respect to ownership and approvals, ensuring that a user who can follow a profile can also later remove that follow without needing the NFT owner’s intervention.

title: Users can unfollow through `FollowNFT` contract when LensHub is paused by governance
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an inconsistencybetween the LensHub contract and the per‑profile FollowNFT contracts regarding the protocol pause state. LensHub defines a global pause flag (ProtocolState.Paused) and protects its public unfollow function with a whenNotPaused modifier, meaning that when governance pauses the system users should be unable to call unfollow. However, each profile that has followers is represented by a separate FollowNFT contract that implements its own removeFollower and burn functions. These functions invoke the internal unfollow logic but do not check the LensHub pause flag before executing. As a result, when the LensHub contract is paused, a follower can still call FollowNFT.removeFollower or FollowNFT.burn (for example by wrapping the follow NFT and invoking the function) and successfully remove the follow relationship. The root cause is the missing pause guard in the FollowNFT contract, creating a cross‑contract state mismatch where the pause enforcement is not enforced uniformly. An attacker or any regular follower can exploit this by simply calling the NFT contract directly, bypassing the hub’s pause check. The impact is that governance loses the ability to freeze follow‑related state changes, allowing users to alter follow relationships during a pause, which may be used to manipulate on‑chain metrics, disrupt expected protocol behavior, or undermine confidence in the pause mechanism. The issue manifests only when the LensHub contract is in the Paused state; under normal operation both paths work as intended. Affected parties include profile owners who expect their follower list to be immutable during a pause, followers who may unintentionally change their follow status, and the protocol itself because the pause is intended to be a safety valve. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit when the test suite demonstrated that hub.unfollow reverted with a pause error while FollowNFT.removeFollower succeeded, confirming the inconsistency. The problem can be hard to notice because the pause modifier is present on the hub function, leading developers to assume that all follow‑related actions are automatically blocked when the protocol is paused. To remediate, the FollowNFT contract should incorporate the same whenNotPaused guard used by LensHub, either by adding a modifier that queries the hub’s state or by routing all unfollow actions through the hub so that the pause check is applied centrally. This aligns the contract’s behavior with the intended business logic that no follow‑related state changes should occur while the protocol is paused, restoring the integrity of the pause mechanism and preventing unexpected unfollow actions during emergency shutdowns.

title: Whitelisted profile creators could accidentally break migration for V1 profiles
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the migration process for legacy V1 profiles in the Lens protocol. During an upgrade, the batchMigrateProfiles() function recreates each V1 profile by minting a new handle NFT on the LensHandles contract and linking it to the profile. For handles that end with the ".lens" suffix, the function strips the suffix (except for the special LENS_PROTOCOL_PROFILE_ID) and then calls lensHandles.migrateHandle() to mint the handle. Whitelisted profile creators, however, are allowed to call LensHandles.mintHandle() and create any handle they choose. If a whitelisted creator mints a handle that matches the stripped version of a V1 profile before the migration runs, the subsequent call to migrateHandle() will attempt to mint an already‑existing token. Because ERC‑721 tokens cannot be minted twice, the call reverts with the error "ERC721: token already minted" and the batchMigrateProfiles() transaction aborts for that profile. The impact is that the affected V1 profile cannot be migrated to V2, leaving the profile owner unable to use the upgraded functionality; from the user’s perspective the migration appears to fail, the UI may show no change or an error, and the expected new handle NFT is never received. This issue only manifests when a whitelisted profile creator pre‑emptively mints a colliding handle, a scenario that is not obvious during normal operation and therefore can be hard to notice. It was discovered during a formal audit by reproducing the flow in a test contract that first creates a V1 profile, then mints the same handle via mintHandle(), and finally calls batchMigrateProfiles(), which reverts as expected. The root cause is the lack of a validation step that prevents mintHandle() from creating handles that already exist in the legacy namespace, combined with the migration logic that assumes those handles are unavailable. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a rule—either on‑chain or off‑chain—that disallows the creation of handles that correspond to any existing V1 profile, ensuring that the migration step can always mint the required handle without collision. This class of bug is a handle‑collision or namespace‑collision issue that breaks upgrade paths and violates the business assumption that each profile’s handle is unique and immutable across versions.

title: Inconsistent encoding of arrays in `MetaTxLib`
description:
According to the EIP-712 specification, arrays are encoded by concatenating its elements and passing the result to `keccak256`:

> The array values are encoded as the `keccak256` hash of the concatenated encodeData of their contents (i.e. the encoding of `SomeType[5]` is identical to that of a struct containing five members of type `SomeType`).

An example of a correct implementation can be seen in `validateUnfollowSignature()`, where the `idsOfProfilesToUnfollow` array is passed to `keccak256` after using `abi.encodePacked()`:
```solidity
keccak256(abi.encodePacked(idsOfProfilesToUnfollow)),
```
However, some other functions in `MetaTxLib` encode arrays differently, which differs from the EIP-712 specification.

Some functions do not encode the array at all, and pass the array to `abi.encode()` alongside other arguments in its struct. For example, in `validatePostSignature()`, the `postParams.actionModules` array is not encoded by itself:
```solidity
abi.encode(
    Typehash.POST,
    postParams.profileId,
    keccak256(bytes(postParams.contentURI)),
    postParams.actionModules,
    _hashActionModulesInitDatas(postParams.actionModulesInitDatas),
    postParams.referenceModule,
    keccak256(postParams.referenceModuleInitData),
    _getAndIncrementNonce(signature.signer),
    signature.deadline
)
```
Other instances of this include:

* `mirrorParams.referrerProfileIds` and `mirrorParams.referrerPubIds` in `validateMirrorSignature()`
* `publicationActionParams.referrerProfileIds` and `publicationActionParams.referrerPubIds` in `validateActSignature()`
* All functions that use `_abiEncode()`, namely `validateCommentSignature()` and `validateQuoteSignature()`

Secondly, the `validateChangeDelegatedExecutorsConfigSignature()` function encodes the `delegatedExecutors` and `approvals` arrays using `abi.encodePacked()`, but do not pass it to `keccak256`:
```solidity
abi.encode(
    Typehash.CHANGE_DELEGATED_EXECUTORS_CONFIG,
    delegatorProfileId,
    abi.encodePacked(delegatedExecutors),
    abi.encodePacked(approvals),
    configNumber,
    switchToGivenConfig,
    nonce,
    deadline
)
```
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an inconsistent handling of dynamic array arguments when constructing the EIP‑712 struct hash inside the MetaTxLib library. According to the EIP‑712 specification, any array field must be encoded by first concatenating the ABI‑encoded representation of each element, then hashing the concatenated data with keccak256, and finally inserting that hash into the overall struct encoding. In several functions – for example validatePostSignature, validateMirrorSignature, validateActSignature, validateCommentSignature, validateQuoteSignature and validateChangeDelegatedExecutorsConfigSignature – the code either passes the raw array directly to abi.encode, or uses abi.encodePacked without the required keccak256 step. This deviation means that the struct hash calculated by the contract does not match the hash that a signer would have produced when following the official EIP‑712 rules. The root cause is a misunderstanding of how arrays should be represented in the typed data hash, leading to a mismatch between the off‑chain signing process and the on‑chain verification logic. An attacker can exploit this mismatch by crafting a signature for one set of array contents while the contract interprets a different set, effectively allowing the attacker to replay a signature with altered array data or to have a signature accepted for actions the signer never intended. For instance, a malicious actor could submit a meta‑transaction that appears to authorize a specific list of action modules, but because the contract hashes the raw array, the verification succeeds even if the signed list is shorter or contains different module addresses, resulting in unauthorized module execution. The impact includes unauthorized state changes such as posting content with unintended modules, mirroring with forged referrer IDs, or changing delegated executor configurations without proper consent, which can undermine protocol integrity and potentially lead to loss of reputation or funds. The flaw manifests whenever a meta‑transaction that includes an array argument is signed and verified through the affected functions; any user, integrator, or dApp relying on these signatures is affected. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit by Code4rena, where the auditors compared the library’s encoding against the EIP‑712 reference implementation and noted the divergence. The problem is subtle because signatures may still be accepted for simple cases without arrays, and the UI typically does not expose the underlying hash computation, making the bug hard to detect through normal testing. To remediate, each function should first encode the array with abi.encodePacked, then hash the result with keccak256, and finally include that hash in the abi.encode call that builds the struct hash, thereby aligning the on‑chain verification with the EIP‑712 specification. This correction restores deterministic hashing, prevents signature replay or forgery with altered array data, and ensures that users receive the expected behavior – namely that a signed meta‑transaction is only accepted if the exact array contents match the signer’s intent.

title: EIP-712 typehash is incorrect for several functions in `MetaTxLib`
bug_full: The issue is a mismatch between the EIP‑712 typehash strings used in the MetaTxLib library and the actual parameters of the corresponding meta‑transaction functions in LensHub. Each function that accepts a signed payload – setProfileMetadataURIWithSig, postWithSig, commentWithSig, quoteWithSig and mirrorWithSig – defines a struct that is signed off‑chain according to the EIP‑712 standard. The contract then reconstructs the struct hash using a hard‑coded typehash constant and verifies the signature. In several cases the constant was built from an incorrect type definition: the name of a string field was written as "metadata" instead of "metadataURI", address and bytes array fields were labelled as "collectModule" and "collectModuleInitData" while the struct actually contains "actionModules" and "actionModulesInitDatas", and array fields in the MirrorParams struct were singularized in the typehash. Because the typehash encodes both the field names and their order, the hash computed inside the contract does not correspond to the hash that the signer produced. As a result, a legitimate signature will be rejected, causing the transaction to revert, and an attacker could potentially craft a signature that matches the wrong typehash and be accepted for unintended data. The vulnerability manifests whenever a user tries to execute a meta‑transaction that relies on a signed payload – the UI will show a transaction failure or “signature invalid” error, and the expected state change (profile metadata update, post creation, comment, quote or mirror) does not occur. The affected parties are any LensHub users who rely on signed meta‑transactions, as well as the protocol itself because the broken verification undermines the trust model of off‑chain signatures. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors compared the Solidity structs with the hard‑coded typehash strings and noticed the discrepancy. It can be hard to spot because the code compiles and the signatures appear syntactically correct; the error only surfaces at runtime when the hash mismatch causes verification to fail. The recommended remediation is to amend each typehash constant so that its field list, names and ordering exactly match the corresponding struct definition used by the function. Aligning the typehashes restores correct EIP‑712 hashing, ensures that only properly signed payloads are accepted, and prevents denial‑of‑service or potential signature‑spoofing attacks.

title: Token guardian protection doesn’t account for approved operators in `approve`
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the token‑guardian protection mechanism that is intended to block any transfer or approval of tokens owned by an address that has enabled the guardian. In the current implementation the `approve` function only checks whether the caller (`msg.sender`) has the guardian enabled and rejects the call if the caller is the token owner with guardian active. However, the ERC‑721 standard also permits an address that has been granted operator rights through `setApprovalForAll` to call `approve` on behalf of the token owner. Because the guard check does not verify the guardian status of the token’s actual owner, an approved operator can still set or change approvals for a token whose owner has the guardian enabled. The exploit proceeds by first having the owner grant operator rights to a third party, then the owner enables token guardian, and finally the operator (or any address that can disable its own guardian) calls `approve` for the owner’s token. The call succeeds, allowing the operator to designate a new approved address or clear an existing one, effectively bypassing the intended protection. This results in the owner losing the guarantee that their tokens cannot be approved for transfer, exposing the tokens to unauthorized transfers and potential theft. The issue manifests whenever a token‑guardian‑enabled address has previously set an operator via `setApprovalForAll`; it does not require any special permissions beyond the ability to call `approve` as an operator. Users, token owners, and any protocol relying on the guardian to secure assets are affected because the security assumption that guardian‑enabled accounts are immutable with respect to approvals is violated. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that included a Foundry test reproducing the scenario, and it can be subtle because the `approve` function still works for operators, making the guardian appear functional while it is not. The bug belongs to the class of “incomplete access‑control checks” where a protective condition is applied only to the caller and not to the resource owner, leading to a privilege‑escalation style bypass. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that after enabling token guardian, the approved address of their NFT can still be changed or cleared by an operator, contrary to the expectation that no approvals should be possible. To remediate the issue the `approve` logic should also verify that the token’s owner does not have token guardian enabled, for example by adding a check on `_hasTokenGuardianEnabled(_ownerOf(tokenId))` alongside the existing caller check. This change ensures that both direct owners and delegated operators are prevented from modifying approvals when the owner’s guardian is active, restoring the intended security guarantees.

title: Users can self-follow via `FollowNFT::tryMigrate`
description:
Users are not supposed to be able to self-follow on Lens v2, but they are able to bypass the restriction. This can also affect modules or newer functionalities that count on this behaviour.

Migration is an [Area of specific concern](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-lens#areas-of-specific-concern) for the devs, and this can easily be prevented with a simple check.

This can’t be undone without any upgrade.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a logic bypass that allows a Lens profile to follow itself after migrating a follow NFT from version 1 to version 2. In Lens v2 the normal follow function (FollowLib::follow) contains an explicit check that reverts when the follower profile identifier equals the followed profile identifier, preventing self‑follow. However, the migration pathway implemented in FollowNFT::tryMigrate does not repeat this validation, so when a user who already owns a V1 follow NFT that points to their own profile calls the migration function (typically via hub.batchMigrateFollows), the contract silently records the relationship as a valid follow on V2. The root cause is the missing comparison between the followerProfileId and the _followedProfileId inside the tryMigrate implementation. An attacker who controls a V1 follow NFT for their own profile can exploit this by invoking the migration, resulting in a self‑follow that bypasses the intended business rule. The impact is primarily logical: protocols, modules, or analytics that assume a profile can never follow itself may produce incorrect reputation scores, recommendation lists, or incentive calculations. From a user perspective the UI may unexpectedly display that the user is following themselves, contradicting the expectation that a profile cannot follow its own address. The issue manifests only when a self‑follow NFT exists on V1 and the owner initiates a migration to V2; it does not affect regular follow operations that already enforce the restriction. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, which added a test that migrates a known self‑follow NFT and then asserts that the contract reports the profile as following itself. Because the normal follow path already blocks self‑follow, developers may assume the invariant holds globally, making the bug easy to overlook. The vulnerability belongs to the class of missing validation or state‑transition inconsistencies, where a function that changes contract state fails to enforce the same invariants as other entry points. To remediate, the tryMigrate function should include a guard that checks if the follower profile identifier equals the target profile identifier and aborts the migration (for example, by returning 0 or reverting with a SelfFollow error). This simple addition restores the protocol’s guarantee that a profile cannot follow itself and prevents downstream modules from encountering unexpected self‑follow relationships.

title: Users can make any user follow them via `FollowNFT::tryMigrate`
description:
Follows in Lens v2 can be checked via `isFollowing()`, which returns the internal storage variable `_followTokenIdByFollowerProfileId[followerProfileId]` and can’t be manipulated by an unauthorized party via any of the follow/unfollow functions, as they have proper access control checks.

This is also prevented on token transfers in Lens v2. If user A wraps their follow token and transfer it to user B, it doesn’t mean that user B is following user A.

But using the `tryMigrate()` it is possible to “force” someone to follow another user without their consent.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the follow‑migration mechanism of Lens v2, where the public function tryMigrate can be invoked by any caller through the hub contract and is able to modify the internal mapping that records which profile follows which other profile. The root cause is that tryMigrate updates the _followDataByFollowTokenId structure without enforcing that the caller is the legitimate owner of the follow token or that the migration is authorised by the profile holder. Because the function only checks that the profile NFT and the follow NFT are held by the same address, an attacker can simply transfer a legacy (V1) follow NFT to a victim, satisfy the ownership check, and then trigger tryMigrate to associate the victim’s profile ID with the attacker’s followed profile ID. This results in a “fake” follow: the victim’s profile is recorded as following the attacker even though the victim never executed a follow transaction. The exploit can be carried out by anyone who can call the hub’s batchMigrateFollows or tryMigrate functions, making it trivial to force a follow relationship without consent. The impact is primarily social‑graph corruption – users see that they are following an account they never chose, which can be used for spam, reputation manipulation, or phishing. Although no funds are directly stolen, the protocol’s trust model is weakened because follow relationships are assumed to be user‑initiated. The issue manifests when a V1 follow token is transferred to a target address and the migration function is subsequently called; the isFollowing view returns true for the victim’s profile, creating a silent state change that is hard to detect because the UI only shows the follow status and does not reveal the underlying migration call. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a test case demonstrated that after transferring a follow NFT to a victim and invoking batchMigrateFollows, the victim’s profile automatically followed the attacker. The problem is difficult to notice because the follow status changes without any user‑visible transaction from the victim’s perspective, and the migration function returns 0 on failure without emitting an event, providing no audit trail. To remediate, the migration logic should be restricted to the actual token owners or to a whitelist of trusted accounts, optionally requiring an opt‑in flag from the profile owner. Additionally, the contract should emit a detailed event whenever a migration is rejected or succeeds, and it should verify that the follow token being migrated has not been transferred away from its original owner before updating the follow mapping. By tightening access control and improving observability, the protocol can prevent unauthorized follow assignments and preserve the integrity of the social graph.

title: Blocked follower can keep follow with `batchMigrateFollows`
bug_full: During the Lens V2 migration, the public function batchMigrateFollows allows anyone to migrate a set of V1 follows to V2. The internal tryMigrate function copies the follow relationship and burns the old Follow NFT, but it does not verify whether the follower profile has been blocked by the target profile. Consequently, if a profile has previously blocked a follower and the follower has not yet migrated, an attacker (or the blocked user themselves) can invoke batchMigrateFollows and cause the blocked follower to be recorded as following the target profile in V2. The contract emits a Followed event and updates the internal follower count, making the block ineffective. This breach occurs only when the follower owns both the Profile NFT and the original Follow NFT, because the migration logic requires the two tokens to be in the same account. The issue was discovered during a security audit by writing a test that first blocks a set of followers and then calls batchMigrateFollows, observing that the blocked accounts appear as followers after migration. The bug is hard to notice because the migration function is intended to be a harmless state transfer and the block check is performed elsewhere in the normal follow flow, not in the migration path. The impact is a violation of the platform’s access‑control guarantees: users who are explicitly blocked can still become followers, potentially leading to spam, unwanted notifications, and loss of trust in the protocol’s moderation mechanisms. The vulnerability belongs to the class of missing authorization checks during state migration. The proper fix is to add a verification step in FollowNFT.tryMigrate (or in the migration library) that queries the hub’s block list and aborts the migration when the follower is blocked, or to automatically unfollow blocked profiles during migration.

title: Borrowers can avoid liquidations, if ERC777 token is configured as an `emissionToken`
description:
If a borrower is `undercollateralized` then he can be liquidated by a liquidator by calling the `MErc20.liquidateBorrow` function. `liquidateBorrow` function calls the `MToken.liquidateBorrowFresh` in its execution process. Inside the `liquidateBorrowFresh` function the `MToken.repayBorrowFresh` is called which verifies whether repayment of borrowed amount is allowed by calling the `Comptroller.repayBorrowAllowed` function. The `repayBorrowAllowed` function updates the `borrower eligible rewards` by calling the `MultiRewardDistributor.updateMarketBorrowIndexAndDisburseBorrowerRewards`.

The `MultiRewardDistributor.updateMarketBorrowIndexAndDisburseBorrowerRewards` function calls the `disburseBorrowerRewardsInternal` to distribute the multi rewards to the `borrower`. The `disburseBorrowerRewardsInternal` calls the `sendReward` function if the `_sendTokens` flag is set to `true`.

`sendReward` function is called for each `emissionConfig.config.emissionToken` token of the `MarketEmissionConfig[]` array of the given `_mToken` market.

`sendReward` function transfers the rewards to the `borrower` using the `safeTransfer` function as shown below:
    
    token.safeTransfer(_user, _amount);

Problem here is that `emissionToken` can be `ERC777` token (which is backward compatible with ERC20) thus allowing a `malicious borrower` (the `recipient contract` of rewards in this case) to implement `tokensReceived` hook in its contract and revert the transaction inside the hook. This will revert the entire `liquidation` transaction. Hence the `undercollateralized borrower` can avoid the liquidation thus putting both depositors and protocol in danger.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a liquidation bypass that can be triggered when a market is configured to distribute rewards using an ERC777 token as the emission token. During a liquidation, the protocol calls the liquidateBorrow function, which eventually invokes a reward distribution routine that transfers the configured emission tokens to the borrower via a safeTransfer call. Because ERC777 tokens are backward compatible with ERC20, the safeTransfer call succeeds from the token contract’s perspective, but ERC777 also executes a tokensReceived hook on the recipient contract. A malicious borrower can deploy a contract that implements this hook and deliberately reverts inside it. When the hook reverts, the entire reward transfer reverts, causing the whole liquidation transaction to revert as well. Consequently, an under‑collateralized borrower can avoid having their collateral seized, leaving the protocol with potentially unrecoverable bad debt and exposing depositors to loss. The issue arises only when the emission token is an ERC777 token and the borrower’s address is a contract capable of rejecting the transfer via the hook. It was discovered during a formal audit of the Moonwell protocol where the reward distribution logic was examined and the interaction with ERC777 hooks was identified as a flaw. The problem is subtle because ERC777 tokens appear as standard ERC20 tokens, so developers may assume safeTransfer is sufficient to guarantee a successful transfer. The bug violates the accounting assumption that liquidation always succeeds in seizing collateral and repaying the debt, breaking the protocol’s risk model. To remediate, the protocol should restrict emission tokens to pure ERC20 tokens that lack transfer hooks, or redesign the liquidation flow to separate reward distribution from the core collateral seizure, ensuring that a failure in reward transfer does not revert the liquidation itself.

title: Missing check for the max/min price in the `chainlinkOracle.sol` contract
description:
The `chainlinkOracle.sol` contract specially the `getChainlinkPrice` function using the aggregator v2 and v3 to get/call the `latestRoundData`. the function should check for the min and max amount return to prevent some case happen, something like this:

<https://solodit.xyz/issues/missing-checks-for-chainlink-oracle-spearbit-connext-pdf>

<https://solodit.xyz/issues/m-16-chainlinkadapteroracle-will-return-the-wrong-price-for-asset-if-underlying-aggregator-hits-minanswer-sherlock-blueberry-blueberry-git>

If a case like LUNA happens then the oracle will return the minimum price and not the crashed price.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing sanity check on the price value returned by the Chainlink oracle in the getChainlinkPrice function. The function only verifies that the answer is greater than zero and that the timestamp is non‑zero, but it never compares the retrieved price against the minAnswer and maxAnswer limits that Chainlink aggregators expose as circuit‑breaker thresholds. These thresholds are designed to signal that a feed has frozen or that the price has moved beyond a reasonable range; when they are hit the aggregator will continue to return the last valid extreme value (the minimum or maximum answer). Because the contract does not enforce any bound, a stale or extreme price can be propagated to downstream logic that relies on the oracle for collateral valuation, liquidation triggers, or payout calculations. An attacker who can cause the underlying feed to hit its minAnswer or maxAnswer – for example by exploiting a market crash or by feeding manipulated data to the Chainlink node – can make the oracle return a price that is far lower or higher than the true market value. The protocol may then treat a healthy position as under‑collateralised, trigger unnecessary liquidations, or compute refunds that are zero or dramatically incorrect, leading to loss of user funds. This condition occurs whenever the Chainlink feed reaches its built‑in circuit‑breaker limits and the contract is called without additional checks. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit that referenced similar problems in other Chainlink adapter contracts. It is hard to notice because the function appears to return a valid, non‑zero price and the basic require statements pass, so developers may assume the price is trustworthy even when it is an extreme stale value. The proper mitigation is to retrieve the minAnswer and maxAnswer from the aggregator (or define protocol‑specific safe price windows) and add explicit require statements that the answer lies strictly between those bounds before converting it to 18‑decimal format. By enforcing these limits the contract prevents the propagation of frozen or out‑of‑range prices, preserving the accounting assumptions of the protocol and protecting users from unexpected zero balances, sudden liquidation, or missing refunds. This class of bug is generally known as a missing oracle sanity check or price sanity validation failure, which violates the business logic that prices must stay within reasonable, expected ranges.

title: `excuteProposal` can fail due to Wormhole guardian change
description:
Wormhole governance can change signing guardian sets. If this happens between a proposal is queued and a proposal is executed. The second verification in `_executeProposal` will fail as the guardian set has changed between queuing and executing.

This would cause a proposal to fail to execute after the `proposalDelay` has passed. Causing a lengthy re-sending of the message from `Timelock` on source chain, then `proposalDelay` again.
poc:
To execute a proposal on `TemporalGovernor` it first needs to be queued. When queued it is checked that the message is valid against the Wormhole bridge contract:

    File: Governance/TemporalGovernor.sol
    
    295:    function _queueProposal(bytes memory VAA) private {
    296:        /// Checks
    297:
    298:        // This call accepts single VAAs and headless VAAs
    299:        (
    300:            IWormhole.VM memory vm,
    301:            bool valid,
    302:            string memory reason
    303:        ) = wormholeBridge.parseAndVerifyVM(VAA);
    304:
    305:        // Ensure VAA parsing verification succeeded.
    306:        require(valid, reason);

After some more checks are done the message is [queued by its wormhole hash](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/main/src/core/Governance/TemporalGovernor.sol#L338-L339).

Then, after `proposalDelay`, anyone can call `executeProposal`.

Before the proposal is executed though, a second check against the Wormhole bridge contract is done:

    File: Governance/TemporalGovernor.sol
    
    344:    function _executeProposal(bytes memory VAA, bool overrideDelay) private {
    345:        // This call accepts single VAAs and headless VAAs
    346:        (
    347:            IWormhole.VM memory vm,
    348:            bool valid,
    349:            string memory reason
    350:        ) = wormholeBridge.parseAndVerifyVM(VAA);

The issue is that the second time the verification might fail.

During the wormhole contract check for validity there is a check that the correct guardian set has signed the message:

    79:        /// @dev Checks if VM guardian set index matches the current index (unless the current set is expired).
    80:        if(vm.guardianSetIndex != getCurrentGuardianSetIndex() && guardianSet.expirationTime < block.timestamp){
    81:            return (false, "guardian set has expired");
    82:        }

But(!), Wormhole governance can change the signers:

     76:    /**
     77:     * @dev Deploys a new `guardianSet` via Governance VAA/VM
     78:     */
     79:    function submitNewGuardianSet(bytes memory _vm) public {
                // ... parsing and verification
    
    104:        // Trigger a time-based expiry of current guardianSet
    105:        expireGuardianSet(getCurrentGuardianSetIndex());
    106:
    107:        // Add the new guardianSet to guardianSets
    108:        storeGuardianSet(upgrade.newGuardianSet, upgrade.newGuardianSetIndex);
    109:
    110:        // Makes the new guardianSet effective
    111:        updateGuardianSetIndex(upgrade.newGuardianSetIndex);
    112:    }

Were this to happen between `queueProposal` and `executeProposal` the proposal would fail to execute.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the TemporalGovernor contract validates a Wormhole VAA (Verified Action Approval) twice: once when a proposal is queued and again when the same proposal is executed after the configured proposalDelay. The first check stores only the hash of the VAA, not the full VAA or the guardian set that signed it. During execution the contract calls wormholeBridge.parseAndVerifyVM on the supplied VAA and compares the guardianSetIndex inside the VAA with the current guardian set index maintained by the Wormhole bridge. If the Wormhole governance has rotated to a new guardian set between the queue and the execute step, the guardianSetIndex in the stored VAA no longer matches the active set, causing the second verification to return false with the error "guardian set has expired". As a result the proposal reverts and never reaches the intended state change. This can happen naturally when the Wormhole network updates its guardian set, or it could be triggered deliberately by an attacker who times a guardian set change to coincide with a pending proposal. The impact is that any governance action that relies on the queued proposal – such as releasing funds from a timelock, updating protocol parameters, or executing upgrades – will fail to execute after the delay, forcing the proposer to resend the message, wait another delay period, and potentially lose the intended timing of the action. Users observing the UI will see that their proposal remains in a "queued" state even after the delay has elapsed, and transaction attempts to execute will revert with a generic verification failure, giving the impression that the proposal is stuck or that the system is broken. The issue was discovered during a code audit that examined the double verification logic and the guardian set handling in the Wormhole bridge contract. It is subtle because the verification code appears correct in isolation; the problem only manifests when an external governance event (guardian set rotation) occurs between the two calls, a scenario that is not obvious from a simple static analysis. The bug belongs to the class of time‑dependent external dependency mismatches, where a contract assumes that an off‑chain authority’s state remains static across a time window. To remediate, the contract should either store the complete VAA (or a hash that uniquely identifies the full VAA) at queue time and verify against that immutable data during execution, or limit the second verification to fast‑tracked proposals where the guardian set cannot change, or redesign the logic so that the guardian set index is captured and compared against the stored value rather than the current live set. By anchoring the verification to immutable data, the protocol can guarantee that a queued proposal remains executable regardless of subsequent Wormhole governance changes, restoring the expected behavior that a proposal queued today will either succeed after the delay or be explicitly cancelled, not silently fail.

title: Malicious `emissionToken` could poison rewards for a market
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the MultiRewardDistributor contract distributes accrued rewards across multiple emission configurations. For each market, the contract iterates over an array of MarketEmissionConfig structures and, for every configured reward token, calls an internal sendReward function that performs a SafeERC20.safeTransfer to the user. The SafeERC20 wrapper reverts the whole transaction if the token transfer fails. Consequently, if any emission token is malicious or implements a transfer function that deliberately reverts – for example by blacklisting the recipient or by being upgraded to a contract that always throws – the entire reward‑distribution call aborts. Because the loop does not catch individual transfer failures, the pending reward balances stored in the emissionConfig remain unchanged, effectively locking the rewards for that user forever. The issue can be triggered whenever a user has unclaimed rewards for a market that includes a poisoned emission token and the contract attempts to claim those rewards. Affected parties include borrowers and suppliers who rely on the reward mechanism, as well as the protocol itself, which loses the ability to distribute incentives and may see user confidence erode. The problem was uncovered during a formal audit by reproducing the scenario with a deliberately malicious token that reverts on every transfer; the test showed that the claimReward call reverted and no tokens were transferred. The bug is subtle because the token may appear legitimate – standard ERC20 interfaces pass static analysis – and only exhibits the failure at runtime, especially when the token implements blacklist logic (as seen in USDC or USDT). From a user’s perspective the symptom is a claim transaction that reverts with an error such as “No transfer for you”, leaving the user’s reward balance unchanged and appearing as if the protocol “refused to pay” or “eats the rewards”. This violates the core business logic that accrued rewards should be claimable and that the accounting of distributed tokens remains consistent. To remediate, the contract should either allow an admin to remove or disable a faulty emission configuration, or it should isolate each token transfer inside a try/catch block (or low‑level call with a gas stipend) so that a failure of one token does not revert the entire batch. Additionally, the protocol could validate emission tokens before acceptance, ensuring they do not contain blacklist or revert‑on‑transfer behavior, and provide a recovery path for users whose rewards were locked due to a previously added malicious token.

title: Only `guardian` can change `guardian`
description:
`guardian` is mentioned as an area of concern in the [docs](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell#overview):

> Specific areas of concern include:
> 
>   * TemporalGovernor which is the cross chain governance contract. Specific areas of concern include delays, **the pause guardian** , …
> 

`guardian` is a role that has the ability to pause and unpause `TemporalGovernor`. In code, it uses the `owner` from OpenZeppelin `Ownable` as `guardian`. The issue is that [`Ownable::transferOwnership`](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/access/Ownable.sol#L81-L86) is not overridden. Only `guardian` (`owner`) can transfer the role.

This can be a conflict of interest if there is a falling out between governance and the guardian. If the `guardian` doesn’t want to abstain, governance only option would be to call [`revokeGuardian`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/main/src/core/Governance/TemporalGovernor.sol#L205-L221) which sets `owner` to `address(0)`. This permanently removes the ability to pause the contract which can be undesirable.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the way the TemporalGovernor contract assigns the pause‑guardian role. The contract inherits OpenZeppelin Ownable and treats the contract owner as the guardian, but it does not override the standard Ownable.transferOwnership function. Consequently, only the current guardian (the owner) can call transferOwnership to change the guardian address. Governance, which is expected to be able to replace or update the guardian, is therefore unable to do so because any attempt to invoke transferOwnership from the governance contract reverts with the generic “Ownable: caller is not the owner” error. This design creates a conflict of interest: if the guardian decides to act maliciously— for example by pausing the TemporalGovernor and refusing to unpause— the governance process cannot replace the guardian to restore normal operation. The only recourse for governance is to call revokeGuardian, which sets the owner to address(0) and permanently disables the pause functionality, potentially leaving the protocol without an emergency stop mechanism. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit where a test case demonstrated that a proposal submitted by governance could not transfer the guardian role. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without warnings and the owner‑only restriction is a standard pattern; auditors may assume that governance has a back‑door to change privileged roles. Exploitation occurs when the guardian pauses the contract and then either refuses to unpause or blocks governance from updating the guardian, resulting in users seeing the contract stuck in a paused state, transactions reverting, and funds becoming inaccessible. The impact is a loss of the emergency‑pause safety valve, which violates the protocol’s security assumptions and can lead to funds being effectively frozen. The bug belongs to the class of role‑management access‑control flaws where a privileged role is not properly governed by the intended authority. To remediate, the contract should override transferOwnership so that either the governance contract or a multi‑signature mechanism can change the guardian, or introduce a dedicated function that restricts guardian updates to a defined set of actors while preserving the ability for governance to intervene when needed.

title: `TemporalGovernor` can be bricked by `guardian`
description:
When a `guardian` pauses `TemporalGovernor` they [lose the ability to pause again](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/main/src/core/Governance/TemporalGovernor.sol#L283). This can then be reinstated by governance using [`grantGuardiansPause`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/main/src/core/Governance/TemporalGovernor.sol#L188-L198).

However `grantGuardiansPause` can be called when the contract is still paused. This would break the assertions in [`permissionlessUnpause`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/main/src/core/Governance/TemporalGovernor.sol#L256) and [`togglePause`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/main/src/core/Governance/TemporalGovernor.sol#L289): `assert(!guardianPauseAllowed)`.

Also, `TemporalGovernor` [inherits from OpenZeppelin `Ownable`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/main/src/core/Governance/TemporalGovernor.sol#L27). There the `owner` has the ability to [`renounceOwnership`](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/access/Ownable.sol#L73-L75).

This could cause `TemporalGovernor` to end up in a bad state, since [`revokeGuardian`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-moonwell/blob/main/src/core/Governance/TemporalGovernor.sol#L205-L221) call that has special logic for revoking the guardian.

There is the ability to combine these two issues to brick the contract:

  1. `guardian` pauses the contract.
  2. governance sends an instruction for `grantGuardiansPause` which the `guardian` executes (while still paused). This step disables both `permissionlessUnpause` and `togglePause`. Though the contract is still rescuable through `revokeGuardian`.
  3. `guardian` calls `renounceOwnership` from `Ownable`. Which disables any possibility to execute commands on `TemporalGovernor`. Hence no more ability to call `revokeGuardian`.
bug_full: The TemporalGovernor contract contains a logical dead‑lock that can be triggered by a combination of actions from the designated guardian and the contract owner. The vulnerability arises because the function that re‑enables the guardian’s ability to pause (grantGuardiansPause) can be executed while the contract is already in a paused state. When this occurs the internal flag guardianPauseAllowed is set to true, which violates the assertions in both permissionlessUnpause and togglePause that require the flag to be false. Consequently those functions become permanently unusable. The problem is compounded by the fact that TemporalGovernor inherits OpenZeppelin Ownable, allowing the current owner – which may be the guardian – to renounce ownership. Once ownership is renounced the contract loses the privileged account that is able to call revokeGuardian, a special routine that could otherwise reset the guardian flag and restore pause control. The resulting state is a contract that remains paused, has guardianPauseAllowed set to true, and has no owner, meaning no party can invoke revokeGuardian, permissionlessUnpause, or togglePause. From a user’s perspective proposals cannot be executed, balances appear unchanged, and any expected refunds or state changes never occur. The issue was discovered during a security audit by analysing the pause‑related state transitions and noticing that the assertions were not protected against being triggered after a paused grantGuardiansPause call. It is difficult to spot because each function works correctly in isolation; only the specific sequence of pausing, granting pause rights while paused, and renouncing ownership leads to the dead‑lock. The impact is a medium‑severity risk where the protocol can be effectively bricked, locking funds and preventing governance actions. To remediate, the grantGuardiansPause function should be guarded with a whenNotPaused modifier (or equivalent check) to prevent it from being called while the contract is paused, and the ownership‑renounce and transfer functions should be overridden so that only governance can change the owner, preserving the ability to call revokeGuardian. Additionally, reconsidering the necessity of the assert(!guardianPauseAllowed) may simplify the logic and avoid unintended dead‑locks.

title: `fastTrackProposalExecution` doesn’t check `intendedRecipient`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fastTrackProposalExecution function of the TemporalGovernor contract. This function allows the contract owner (referred to as the guardian) to bypass the normal proposal‑queue flow and immediately execute a Verified Action Approval (VAA) by calling the internal _executeProposal routine with a flag that overrides timestamp checks. In the regular queueProposal path the contract validates that the VAA’s intendedRecipient field matches the address of the TemporalGovernor itself, preventing VAAs that are meant for other contracts from being processed. However, _executeProposal does not repeat this check, so when fastTrackProposalExecution is used the intendedRecipient verification is completely omitted. As a result, a guardian can submit a crafted VAA that claims to target any contract on the same chain, and the TemporalGovernor will blindly forward the payload to the specified address. This can be exploited by constructing a VAA that calls privileged functions on another contract – for example, changing the admin of a token, withdrawing funds, or altering trusted sender lists – and then invoking fastTrackProposalExecution while the governor is paused. The impact is that an attacker with guardian privileges (or a compromised guardian key) can execute arbitrary state‑changing actions that were never intended to be authorized by the TemporalGovernor, potentially leading to loss of funds, unauthorized admin changes, or disruption of protocol governance. The bug manifests only when the fast‑track path is used, which is typically reserved for emergency situations; under normal operation the intendedRecipient check protects the contract. Users may notice unexpected behavior such as their balances becoming zero, admin addresses changing without consent, or proposals that should have been rejected being applied instantly. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included unit tests reproducing the fast‑track execution with an incorrect intendedRecipient. It is hard to notice because the fast‑track function is rarely exercised, and developers may assume that the existing check in the queue flow is sufficient for all entry points. To remediate the problem the _executeProposal routine should enforce the same intendedRecipient == address(this) requirement as the queueProposal path, ensuring that any VAA processed – whether through the normal queue or the fast‑track shortcut – is explicitly addressed to the TemporalGovernor contract. This change restores the intended security boundary and prevents the contract from acting as a proxy for arbitrary cross‑chain messages.

title: `fastTrackProposalExecution` should only be callable when `TemporalGovernor` is paused
description:
The function `fastTrackProposalExecution` is supposed to be used by the `TemporalGovernor` owner during periods of emergency, when the contract is paused to fast track a certain proposal (queue and execute a proposal directly without delay or voting), with gaol of ensuring the protocol safety.

But the function `fastTrackProposalExecution` is missing the `whenPaused` modifier which means it can be called at any time to fast track any proposal and not just when the `TemporalGovernor` is paused.

I submit this issue as only Medium risk because only the `TemporalGovernor` owner can call the `fastTrackProposalExecution` function (and i suppose that the owner is trusted and will not execute malicious actions), but this issue still goes against the intent of the governance process in which the members of the DAO are supposed to propose, vote and execute the proposals in a permissionless and decentralized manner and where the owner should not be able to execute actions on the protocol without the agreement of the members (except for those emergency situation of course).
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing pause guard on a privileged function that is intended to be used only during emergency situations. The contract defines a function that allows the owner to fast‑track the execution ofa governance proposal, bypassing the normal voting delay. Because the function does not include the whenPaused modifier, the owner can invoke it at any moment, even when the TemporalGovernor is fully operational. This flaw originates from an oversight in the access‑control logic: the only restriction is the onlyOwner check, while the intended temporal restriction (only when the contract is paused) is absent. An attacker who gains control of the owner account, or a malicious owner, could call the function to execute arbitrary proposals without community approval, effectively overriding the DAO’s voting process. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s decentralised governance model; proposals may be executed without a vote, leading to unexpected state changes, loss of funds, or actions that contradict the community’s intent. The issue manifests whenever the owner calls the function while the contract is not paused, which is the default operating condition. All DAO participants, token holders, and any users relying on the governance timeline are affected because they may see proposals executed instantly, funds transferred without consent, or protocol parameters altered without a vote. The problem was discovered during a formal audit when reviewers compared the function’s comment – which explicitly states it should be used only when paused – with the actual code and noticed the missing whenPaused modifier. The bug is subtle because the function is already restricted to the owner, so a casual review might assume the owner will act responsibly; however, the lack of a pause check means the contract’s safety guarantees are not enforced programmatically. To remediate, the function should be protected by the whenPaused modifier (or an equivalent check) so that it can be called only during an emergency pause, restoring the intended governance flow where proposals are queued, voted on, and executed by the community. In broader terms, this is a governance‑process bypass bug where privileged actions are not constrained by the contract’s state, allowing unauthorized fast‑track execution of proposals and violating the accounting assumptions that proposals require a delay and community approval before affecting protocol state.

title: Proposals which intend to send native tokens to target addresses can’t be executed
description:
* In `TemporalGovernor` contract: any verified action approval (VAA)/proposal can be executed by anyone if it has been queued and passed the time delay.
  * But if the proposal is intended to send native tokens to the target address; it will revert since `TemporalGovernor` contract doesn’t have any balance, as there’s no `receive()` or payable functions to receive the funds that will be sent to the proposal’s target address.
  * So any proposal with a value (decoded from `vm.payload`) will not be executed since the  
`target.call{value:value}(data)` will revert.
bug_full: The TemporalGovernor contract allows any verified action approval (VAA) to be queued and later executed by calling target.call{value:value}(data). The vulnerability arises because the contract does not implement a receive() or any payable fallback function, meaning it cannot hold native ether. When a proposal includes a non‑zero value – for example, a governance action that should transfer 1 ether to a recipient – the execution step attempts to forward that value from the governor’s balance. Since the contract’s balance is always zero, the low‑level call reverts, causing the entire proposal to fail. This defect is a classic case of missing payable handling that leads to a value‑transfer failure. An attacker or any user can submit a proposal that includes a value field; the proposal will pass the queue and time‑delay checks, but execution will always revert, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service vector against any governance action that requires sending native tokens. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – receiving ether or seeing the treasury move funds – never happens; the UI may show the proposal as “executed” in the sense that the queue advanced, yet the recipient’s balance remains unchanged and the transaction reverts silently. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a test that queued a proposal with a 1 ether payload and observing that executeProposal reverted due to insufficient funds. Because the revert only occurs at execution time, the problem can be hard to notice during normal operation where most proposals do not involve value transfers. The impact is medium severity: it prevents legitimate treasury movements, may block essential protocol upgrades that rely on ether transfers, and can be abused to stall governance. The proper remediation is to add a receive() payable function (or a fallback payable) to allow the governor contract to accept ether, and optionally add a balance check before attempting a value‑transfer call to ensure the contract holds enough native tokens. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “missing payable fallback leading to value‑transfer revert” and violates the accounting assumption that the contract’s balance is sufficient to cover outgoing transfers, breaking the expected invariant that a queued proposal will execute exactly as specified.

title: Initial deploy won’t succeed because of too high `initialMintAmount` for USDC market
description: At the time of deploy, deployer initializes token markets with initial amount to prevent exploit. At least USDC and WETH markets will be initialized during deploy. But `initialMintAmount` is hardcoded to `1e18` which is of for WETH (1,876 USD), but unrealistic for USDC (1,000,000,000,000 USD). Therefore deploy will fail.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a hard‑coded constant named initialMintAmount that is set to 1 ether (1e18) and applied uniformly to every token market during contract deployment. This value is appropriate for tokens with 18 decimal places such as WETH, where 1e18 represents roughly 1,876 USD, but it is completely unsuitable for tokens with a different decimal precision, most notably USDC which uses 6 decimals. When the deployment script attempts to approve and mint the same 1e18 amount of USDC, the underlying token contract interprets the request as one trillion USDC (1,000,000,000,000 USDC), far exceeding any realistic balance or supply. Consequently the approve or mint call reverts, causing the whole deployment transaction to fail. The issue manifests only at deployment time, when the initializer loop iterates over each configured market and executes an approval followed by a mint of the constant amount. The affected parties are the deployer, the protocol team, and any future users because the protocol cannot be launched on mainnet or any environment where the token decimals differ from 18. The problem was discovered during a security audit that reviewed the deployment script and noticed the universal use of the constant without accounting for token‑specific decimal units. It can be hard to spot because the constant looks innocuous and the code path is executed only once, so routine unit tests on a local network with mock tokens that also have 18 decimals may pass unnoticed. The impact is a denial‑of‑service at the deployment stage: the contract never becomes live, funds cannot be allocated, and the protocol’s launch is blocked. From a user’s perspective the UI would never show the new market, and any expectation that the protocol is ready would be unmet, leading to confusion or perceived “missing” functionality. The bug belongs to the class of configuration‑driven arithmetic errors, specifically the misuse of a fixed token amount across assets with heterogeneous decimal precision. To remediate, the deployment configuration should allow an explicit initialMintAmount per token, derived from each token’s decimals, or the script should compute the correct amount dynamically. This change ensures that the approval and mint calls succeed for every market, allowing the protocol to be deployed safely.

title: Incorrect address is set as Wormhole Bridge, which breaks deploy
description: Wormhole Bridge will have incorrect address, which disables whole TemporalGovernance contract and therefore administration of Moonbeam. But during deployment markets are initialized with initial token amounts to prevent exploits, therefore TemporalGovernance must own this initial tokens. But because of incorrect bridge address TemporalGovernance can’t perform any action and these tokens are brick. Protocol needs redeployment and loses initial tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a misconfiguration of the Wormhole bridge address used by the TemporalGovernance contract on the Base network. The contract stores a constant WORMHOLE_CORE that should point to the Wormhole Token Bridge on the target chain. In the testnet deployment the address is set to 0xA31aa3FDb7aF7Db93d18DDA4e19F811342EDF780, which is the address of the bridge on Base testnet but has no contract code on Base mainnet. When the governor tries to execute a cross‑chain proposal it calls wormholeBridge.parseAndVerifyVM(...). Because the address contains no code, the external call reverts, causing the entire proposal execution to fail. TemporalGovernance is therefore unable to perform any of its privileged actions, including approving underlying tokens and minting the initial mTokens that are required to bootstrap the markets. The deployer supplies a certain amount of USDC, WETH and other assets to the governor so that the markets can be initialized with a non‑zero balance and avoid exploit windows. Since the governor cannot run its initialization logic, those tokens remain locked in the governor’s balance and are effectively lost. The protocol loses the ability to administer markets, and the whole deployment becomes unusable until the contract is redeployed with the correct bridge address. The issue was discovered during a code audit when the reviewers examined the configuration table for Wormhole chain IDs and noticed that the Base network entry used an address that does not contain a contract. The bug is subtle because the deployment transaction itself succeeds; the failure only appears later when a proposal is executed, which may be interpreted as a generic “proposal reverted” error rather than a configuration problem. The class of bug is an external‑contract address misconfiguration that leads to calls to a non‑existent contract, breaking cross‑chain functionality and causing permanent token lock‑up. From a user perspective, attempts to initialize a market result in no tokens being minted, balances stay at zero, and the UI may show that the proposal failed without any obvious reason. Users expect the governor to mint initial tokens and enable trading, but instead they see no change in their balances and the protocol appears dead. The recommended fix is to replace the WORMHOLE_CORE constant with the correct Wormhole core address for the target network (0xbebdb6C8ddC678FfA9f8748f85C815C556Dd8ac6 for Base Goerli) and to add proper validation that the address contains contract code before accepting it. Adding a fallback check or a deployment‑time assertion would prevent the same class of error in future deployments.

title: Incorrect chainId of Base in deploy script will force redeployment
description: Incorrect chainId of Base in deploy parameters results in incorrect deploy and subsequent redeployment.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect network identifier used in the deployment configuration for the Base blockchain. In the ChainIds contract the constant baseChainId is set to 84531, while the official Base mainnet chain id is 8453. The deployment routine reads block.chainid at runtime and uses it to look up a mapping chainIdToWormHoleId that provides the Wormhole identifier and selects configuration data such as trustedSenders and cToken settings. Because the stored constant does not match the actual chain id, the lookup either returns a default or an unrelated entry, causing the deployed Addresses contract to reference wrong dependency addresses. When the script is executed on Base, the contracts are either deployed with incorrect references or the deployment appears to succeed but the contracts behave incorrectly, which later forces a redeployment to correct the state. From a user perspective the contract may appear unresponsive, refunds may be missing, balances may stay at zero, or expected functionality simply does not work, violating the expectation that a deposit or transaction will be reflected on‑chain. The issue only manifests when deploying to the Base network; on other chains the constant may be correct or unused. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the declared constant with the official Base documentation, highlighting a mismatch that does not cause a compile‑time error and therefore can be hard to notice without functional testing. This class of bug is a configuration mismatch or incorrect network identifier that breaks address resolution logic. The recommended remediation is to update the baseChainId constant to the correct value 8453 and adjust any related Wormhole mapping entries so that the mapping chainIdToWormHoleId is populated with the proper key. After correcting the constant the deployment will resolve the correct addresses, avoid unnecessary redeployments, preserve protocol state and protect user funds.

title: It’s not possible to liquidate deprecated market
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an inability to liquidate positions that reside in a market that has been deprecated. In the original Compound design the Comptroller’s liquidateBorrowAllowed function consulted the borrowGuardianPaused flag – a flag that is set when a market is taken out of service – and allowed liquidation of such markets despite the fact that they no longer accept new borrows. In the Moonwell fork the code that performed this check was removed and the function now only validates that both the borrowed and collateral tokens are listed and that the borrower has a shortfall. Because a deprecated market is still listed but has its collateral factor set to zero, its borrowGuardianPaused flag true, and its reserve factor at the maximum, the short‑fall check never passes for a borrower who is under‑collateralised in that market. Consequently, a liquidator calling liquidateBorrow will receive an error (typically INSUFFICIENT_SHORTFALL) and the transaction reverts, meaning the risky position cannot be closed. The root cause is the missing conditional that treats a deprecated market as liquidatable regardless of shortfall. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker (or any borrower) can open a borrow in a market that later becomes deprecated, let the position become under‑collateralised, and rely on the fact that no one can liquidate it.
