An attacker can therefore call VaultFactory.deployVault, supply a legitimate‑looking Vault implementation, but point the Vault to malicious TwabController and PrizePool contracts that they control. Once deployed, the Vault appears authentic to users and front‑ends because the factory’s mapping marks the Vault address as genuine. Users interacting with the Vault – depositing tokens, checking balances, or expecting prize draws – are unknowingly using compromised components. The malicious TwabController can falsify historical balance snapshots, causing the protocol to calculate a user’s chance of winning incorrectly, while the malicious PrizePool can redirect prize tokens, award them to attacker‑controlled addresses, or simply withhold them. From the user’s perspective the symptoms may be subtle: a deposit may appear successful, balances may show the expected amount, but later the user receives no prize, the prize token balance becomes zero, or a withdrawal returns less than expected. The impact is a loss of deposited funds, theft of prize tokens, and erosion of trust in the fairness of the draw mechanism. This issue manifests whenever a front‑end or a user relies solely on the VaultFactory’s authenticity check and does not independently verify the provenance of the linked TwabController and PrizePool contracts. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the logical flow of the deployVault function and noticing that the auxiliary contracts are not gated by any factory verification. The problem is hard to notice because the UI typically displays only the Vault address as “verified”, and the malicious components can behave correctly during normal operations, only deviating when a prize is distributed. The appropriate remediation is to introduce dedicated factories for TwabController and PrizePool, record the addresses of contracts they deploy, and modify VaultFactory.deployVault to assert that the supplied _twabController and _prizePool were created by those factories. By enforcing immutable, factory‑verified dependencies, the protocol restores the intended security boundary and prevents attackers from injecting malicious business logic into otherwise authentic Vault contracts. This class of bug is an insecure composition pattern where dependent contracts are not validated, leading to trust‑boundary violations and potential fund loss.

title: The exchange rate change in the case of Lossy Strategy will cause the Vault to be under-collateralized for generic ERC4626 Yield Vaults
bug_full: The vulnerability is an exchange‑rate drift that occurs when a principal‑token (PT) Vault interacts with a generic ERC4626 yield vault that employs a lossy strategy. The PT Vault calculates the number of yield‑vault shares to burn during a withdrawal by calling a view function that converts the requested asset amount to shares using the current exchange rate. This conversion relies on the yield vault’s maxWithdraw view, which simply maps the static amount of assets held by the vault to the owner’s share balance. In a lossy strategy, the actual withdraw operation can incur a loss – for example because the underlying strategy charges a fee or suffers slippage – so the amount of assets that can be withdrawn is lower than the static value reported by maxWithdraw. Because the PT Vault determines the share amount before the loss is realized, it burns more shares than necessary to deliver the requested assets. The excess shares are effectively taken from later withdrawers, diluting their holdings and causing the PT Vault to become under‑collateralized. From a user’s perspective the expectation is that withdrawing a given number of assets will cost a proportional amount of PT shares, but the user may see a larger share deduction, a missing refund, or even a balance that drops unexpectedly to zero. The issue manifests only when the underlying strategy is lossy and the PT Vault does not re‑evaluate the exchange rate after the loss is applied. It affects all participants in the PT Vault, the protocol’s accounting guarantees, and any funds that rely on the vault’s share‑to‑asset conversion. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the withdrawal flow and noticing that the view‑based exchange rate does not reflect potential losses. It is hard to notice because the view function appears correct and no explicit error is emitted when the loss occurs; the discrepancy only shows up in the share accounting after the transaction. The bug belongs to the class of “exchange‑rate drift” or “share dilution due to lossy withdrawal” vulnerabilities, where a contract assumes a static price per share while the underlying asset value can decrease during the same operation. To remediate the issue the contract should guarantee that the price per share of the yield vault never decreases, or it should incorporate loss‑aware logic that adjusts the number of shares to burn after the actual withdraw amount is known, or restrict the PT Vault to only use strategies that are loss‑free for withdrawals.

title: Silent overflow could alter computation when calculating the `vaultPortion` in the `PrizePool` contract
description:
If an overflow happens, the computed value of the vault portion will be a totally different value than what should really be; which would end up causing the rewards to disperse and be lower for the draw that was used to compute the vault portion.

Note: Even though the bot reported issues about downcasting variables, it didn’t mention this specific unsafe casting; which if an overflow occurs, could cause a huge impact on the calculation of the vault portions.
poc:
When computing the `vaultPortion` to the PrizePool over a specific duration in draw, the values of the `vaultContributed` & `totalContributed` variables are computed on the DrawAccumulatorLib library, and they are computed and returned as `uint256` values.

The issue is, that in the `PrizePool::_getVaultPortion()` the `vaultContributed` & `totalContributed` variables are unsafely cast from uint256 to int256, which could lead to a silent overflow if any of the two original values don’t fit on an `int256`.

As a result of a silent overflow, the computed value of the vault portion will be a totally different value than what should really be; which would end up causing the rewards to disperse and be lower for the draw that was used to compute the vault portion.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unsafe down‑cast from uint256 to int256 in the PrizePool::_getVaultPortion function. The function receives vaultContributed and totalContributed values that are calculated as uint256 by DrawAccumulatorLib. When these values exceed the maximum positive value that fits in a signed 256‑bit integer (2^255‑1), the implicit conversion to int256 wraps around silently, producing a negative or drastically smaller number. Because the contract later uses the signed value in the formula that determines the vault portion of the rewards, the resulting vaultPortion is far from the intended proportion. An attacker or any participant who triggers a draw with sufficiently large contributions can cause the overflow, leading to a vault portion that is either zero or an unexpectedly low fraction. Consequently the pool distributes less reward to winners and the protocol’s vault receives an incorrect share, breaking the economic assumptions of the prize‑pool model. The bug manifests only when the accumulated contributions grow beyond the signed integer limit, which may happen after many draws or a single very large deposit. Users notice the problem as lower‑than‑expected prize amounts or missing vault fees; the UI may show normal draw results while the underlying accounting is off. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which identified the unsafe cast while reviewing the DrawAccumulatorLib integration. Because the overflow does not revert and produces a plausible numeric result, it can be difficult to detect without explicit checks or test cases that push the limits. The vulnerability belongs to the class of integer overflow caused by unsafe type conversion (down‑casting) from an unsigned to a signed integer. The proper mitigation is to replace the implicit cast with a safe conversion that verifies the value fits within int256, for example by using OpenZeppelin’s SafeCast library or by performing an explicit bounds check before the cast. Ensuring the vaultPortion calculation always uses values that cannot overflow restores the intended reward distribution and preserves the protocol’s financial guarantees.

title: Improper handling of cases when withdrawable assets = 0
description:
Improper handling of cases when withdrawable assets = 0.
The vault will not function correctly.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect handling of the situation where the amount of assets that can be withdrawn from the underlying yield vault is zero. The contract calculates an exchange rate by dividing the withdrawable assets by the total supply of shares. When the withdrawable amount is zero the code falls back to returning a constant representing a 1‑to‑1 ratio. As a result the vault is reported as collateralized even though it holds no liquid assets. This occurs because the conditional that checks both total supply and withdrawable assets only skips the division when the withdrawable amount is zero, but then returns the constant without considering the lack of assets. An attacker or any user can trigger this state by draining the yield vault so that its balance becomes zero; the vault will still report a healthy collateralization flag. Consequently, downstream logic that relies on the collateralized flag – such as withdrawal limits, fee calculations, or liquidation protection – will behave as if the vault is fully funded, allowing further deposits or preventing legitimate safeguards. Users may see their balances unchanged while the system believes they can withdraw, leading to a false sense of security and potential loss of funds if the protocol later attempts to honor withdrawals that cannot be satisfied. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors wrote unit tests that forced the withdrawable amount to zero and observed that the exchange rate returned the asset unit and the collateralized check returned true. The bug is subtle because the return value of the exchange rate function is a constant that matches the expected unit value in normal operation, making the failure mode blend with legitimate cases. The proper fix is to treat the zero‑withdrawable case as a non‑collateralized condition, either by removing the special‑case check or by explicitly returning a rate of zero and setting the collateralized flag to false. In generic terms the problem belongs to the class of “incorrect edge‑case handling for division by zero” or “misleading status flag when a resource amount is zero”.

title: Vault contribution calculations wrongly include the current round when claiming prizes
description: When claiming prizes, the higher the contribution percentage of the given vault, the higher the odds of a user contributing to that vault receiving a prize. Because the vault contributions are wrongly calculated, a vault gets credit for distributions that haven’t actually been made yet. A vault can swing the odds in its favour by contributing prize tokens to the prize pool in a recent round before claiming prizes (based on a normal value of alpha). This is particularly important when considering prize tiers that occur frequently (the highest tiers).
poc:
A draw is closed by the draw manager by calling `closeDraw`. During this process, new liquidity is distributed among the tiers to be available for prize claims:

```solidity
_nextDraw(_nextNumberOfTiers, uint96(_contributionsForDraw(lastClosedDrawId + 1)));
```

In the above line, the contributions are calculated based on `lastClosedDrawId + 1` because `lastClosedDrawId` has not yet been incremented. It is incremented at the end of the `_nextDraw` method.

A prize is claimed when a vault calls (via a claimer) `claimPrize`. In this process, the contribution percentage of the vault is calculated because it affects the winning region (i.e. odds) for a user:

```solidity
(SD59x18 _vaultPortion, SD59x18 _tierOdds, uint16 _drawDuration) = _computeVaultTierDetails(
      msg.sender,
      _tier,
      numberOfTiers,
      lastClosedDrawId
    );
```

As can be seen above, the vault portion is calculated based on `lastClosedDrawId`, which is the value which was incremented when closing the draw previously. This method makes the following underlying call:

```solidity
vaultPortion = _getVaultPortion(
      _vault,
      uint16(drawDuration > _lastClosedDrawId ? 0 : _lastClosedDrawId - drawDuration + 1),
      _lastClosedDrawId + 1,
      smoothing.intoSD59x18()
    );
```

This calculates the value dispersed between a start and end draw INCLUSIVE. Therefore, this is actually calculating the vault contributions based on the current in-progress round as well, which hasn’t yet been dispersed to the tiers. In fact, it also wrongly increments the start round ID.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the calculation of a vault’s contribution share that is used when a prize is claimed. The contract determines the portion of the prize pool that belongs to a vault by querying contributions over a range of draw IDs. Because the range is defined as inclusive of both the start and end IDs and the end ID is taken as lastClosedDrawId + 1, the calculation unintentionally includes the draw that is currently being processed but whose liquidity has not yet been distributed to the tiers. As a result the vault is credited with contributions that do not exist, inflating its contribution percentage and therefore its odds of winning a prize. An attacker can exploit this by depositing prize tokens into a vault immediately after a draw is closed and before calling claimPrize. The deposit is counted in the contribution share for the just‑closed draw, giving the vault a higher chance to win the next prize tier, especially for high‑frequency tiers. The impact is a distortion of the intended fair‑odds mechanism: users who rely on the advertised probability may receive fewer prizes, while the manipulating vault captures a disproportionate share of rewards. The bug manifests only when a vault calls claimPrize after a draw has been closed; the condition is that the contract’s internal lastClosedDrawId has already been incremented but the contribution query still uses lastClosedDrawId + 1. The affected parties are any participants who claim prizes through vaults, the protocol’s fairness guarantees, and ultimately the token holders whose rewards are mis‑allocated. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors compared the draw‑closing logic with the contribution‑query logic and noticed the mismatch in the draw ID boundaries. Because the calculation is performed inside a library call and the off‑by‑one error does not produce an obvious revert, it can remain hidden from casual testing and from users who only see the final prize outcome. The correct fix is to adjust the start and end draw IDs passed to _getVaultPortion so that the range excludes the in‑progress draw – i.e., use lastClosedDrawId as the end ID and subtract the draw duration without the extra +1 on the start ID. This aligns the contribution share with only the draws that have actually been settled, restoring the intended probability model. In generic terms the bug belongs to the class of incorrect accounting of time‑based contributions or off‑by‑one range error that leads to an over‑estimation of a participant’s stake and consequently to unfair reward distribution. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a vault that just added funds appears to have a higher chance of winning, while other users may see their expected prize amount reduced or receive no prize despite contributing a significant amount.

title: Loss of precision leads to under-collateralized
description: Since `_yieldVault` mostly calculates `shares` and uses `round down` when depositing, there is often a `1 wei` loss of precision, which can cause the `vault` to go into under-collateralized mode by mistake.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision‑loss rounding error that can push a yield‑backed vault into an under‑collateralized state. The contract calculates the current exchange rate by taking the maximum withdrawable assets reported by the underlying yield vault and then applying a round‑down conversion to shares. Most yield vaults round down when converting shares to assets, which means the value returned by maxWithdraw is often one wei smaller than the actual amount that was deposited. Because the exchange‑rate function uses this rounded‑down value directly, the computed rate can fall just below the expected asset‑per‑share unit. When the rate drops below that threshold the vault’s internal check marks the vault as not collateralized, preventing further deposits while still allowing withdrawals. This situation occurs most often on the first deposit after the vault has earned profit, especially when the vault is non‑exclusive and therefore subject to the rounding behavior of the underlying share accounting. The impact is that users attempting to deposit see their transaction revert or the UI indicate that the vault is “not collateralized”, even though only a single wei of accounting discrepancy exists. From the user’s perspective the balance appears unchanged, the expected deposit amount is not reflected, and the protocol may appear broken or unsafe. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test logged a one‑wei loss after a deposit and the collateralization flag switched to false. Because the discrepancy is only one wei, it is easy to miss in normal operation, yet the business logic treats any shortfall as a fatal under‑collateralization, violating the invariant that total assets should always cover total shares. The bug belongs to the class of rounding‑error or precision‑loss accounting bugs that break financial invariants. To remediate the problem the exchange‑rate calculation should be adjusted to compensate for the rounding loss, for example by adding one wei to the maxWithdraw value or by using a ceiling rounding mode when converting shares to assets, thereby ensuring the computed rate never falls below the required unit and the vault remains correctly collateralized.

title: Vault does not conform to ERC4626
description: Vault does not conform to ERC4626 which may break external integrations.
poc:
The ERC4626 specification states that `maxDeposit` MUST return the maximum amount of assets deposit would allow to be deposited for receiver and not cause a revert, which MUST NOT be higher than the actual maximum that would be accepted.

Similarly, `maxMint` MUST return the maximum amount of shares mint would allow to be deposited to receiver and not cause a revert, which MUST NOT be higher than the actual maximum that would be accepted.

The PoolTogether V5 Vault connects to an external ERC4626-compliant Vault (`_yieldVault`) and deposits incoming assets in it. This means, that `maxDeposit` and `maxMint` of the PoolTogether Vault must be constrained by the `maxDeposit` and `maxMint` of the external Vault.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a PoolTogether V5 Vault that implements the ERC4626 tokenized vault interface but provides non‑conforming implementations of the maxDeposit and maxMint view functions. According to the ERC4626 specification, maxDeposit(address) must return the exact maximum amount of assets that can be deposited for a given receiver without causing a revert, and this value must never exceed the true capacity of the underlying vault. Likewise, maxMint(address) must return the maximum number of shares that can be minted for a receiver under the same constraints. In the examined contract, both functions simply check an internal collateralisation flag and, when true, return type(uint96).max – a constant that represents the largest value that fits in a 96‑bit unsigned integer – regardless of the actual limits of the external yield vault that the PoolTogether Vault forwards deposits to. The root cause is that the implementation ignores the capacity reported by the connected ERC4626‑compliant yield vault (_yieldVault) and therefore over‑estimates the amount that can be safely deposited or minted. An external caller that queries maxDeposit or maxMint will be told that an arbitrarily large amount can be supplied, and may attempt to deposit that amount. When the underlying yield vault cannot accept the requested assets because its own maxDeposit or maxMint is lower, the transaction reverts. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a huge “maximum deposit” number, the user approves a large amount, but the transaction fails and no assets are transferred, leading to confusion and a perception that the protocol is broken. This bug can also break integrations that rely on the ERC4626 interface to compute safe deposit limits, potentially causing downstream contracts to lock funds or to abort operations. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by comparing the contract’s behaviour against the ERC4626 specification. It is hard to notice because the functions return a plausible large number and only manifest as a failure when a deposit is actually attempted. The vulnerability belongs to the class of ERC4626 compliance errors where maxDeposit/maxMint do not reflect the true capacity of the underlying asset manager. To remediate, the contract should query the external vault’s maxDeposit and maxMint for the given receiver, then return the lesser of that value and type(uint96).max, as shown in the recommended code changes. This ensures that the reported limits are accurate, prevents unexpected reverts, and restores compatibility with any ERC4626‑aware tooling or contracts.

title: `Claimer.claimPrizes` can be front-runned in order to make losses for the claim bot
description: `Claimer.claimPrizes` can be front-runned in order to make losses for the claim bot.
poc:
All prizes in the system should be claimed during the draw period. Anyone can call the `claimPrizes` function for any winner and prize. But the idea of protocol is to incentivize claim bots to do all claims instead of users. These should benefit from batching claims together in 1 call.

Also the `Claimer` contract is using `vrgda` which can increase/decrease fee for the claimer, depending of amount of already claimed prizes. That actually means, that in case not enough prizes are claimed in some point of time, then the fee will be increased to incentivize more bots.

So as bots will try to batch a lot of prize claims together, that means that they will spent a lot on gas. A malicious actor can see which prizes the bot is going to claim and front-run them with the last prize in the list. As a result, [claiming will fail](https://github.com/GenerationSoftware/pt-v5-prize-pool/blob/4bc8a12b857856828c018510b5500d722b79ca3a/src/PrizePool.sol#L434-L436) and the bot will face losses.

Another reason why a malicious actor can do that is to make `vrgda` to provide bigger fees. They can create a bot that will block claims of other bots with a big amount of claims in the batch, in order to wait and get better prices and claim those prize by themself and receive fees.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the batch claim function of the prize‑distribution contract, where a single transaction can claim multiple prizes for a winner. The function processes each prize sequentially and does not verify that a prize has already been claimed before attempting to transfer it. Because the contract uses a variable‑rate fee mechanism (VRGDA) that adjusts the fee based on the number of unclaimed prizes, the fee for the next claim can increase if earlier prizes remain unclaimed. An attacker who can observe a pending claim‑bot transaction can submit a competing transaction that claims the last prize in the bot’s batch just before the bot’s transaction is mined. When the bot’s transaction reaches the already‑claimed prize, the internal call fails, causing the whole batch to revert for that prize while the gas already spent on earlier successful claims is not reimbursed. From the bot’s perspective the transaction appears to have succeeded partially, but the expected fee payment is missing and the gas cost is higher than anticipated, effectively “money disappears” from the bot’s balance. This situation can also be abused to manipulate the VRGDA fee: by deliberately blocking a large batch of claims, an attacker can force the fee to rise, then submit their own claim when the fee is favorable, extracting a larger reward while other bots incur losses. The issue manifests only during the draw period when prizes are claimable and when bots attempt to batch many claims in a single transaction. It primarily affects automated claim bots that rely on the batching incentive, but it also harms the protocol’s economic model because fees may be distorted and users may experience delayed or failed prize distribution. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena through static analysis of the claimPrizes flow and the dynamic fee logic. It is subtle because the failure occurs after some successful claims, so the transaction does not outright revert, making the loss of fee revenue and extra gas consumption easy to overlook. To remediate the problem the contract should check whether a prize has already been claimed before attempting the transfer and, if so, return early from the batch loop while emitting an event that records the skipped prize. This prevents unnecessary fee calculations and avoids the revert that wastes gas. Additionally, redesigning the fee calculation to be independent of the remaining prize count or limiting batch sizes can reduce the incentive for front‑running attacks.

title: Curve Read-only Reentrancy can increase the price of some CurveStableCollateral
description:
If the curve pool of a CurveStableCollateral is a Plain Pool with a native gas token, just like eth/stETH pool: <https://etherscan.io/address/0xdc24316b9ae028f1497c275eb9192a3ea0f67022#code>  
The price can be manipulated by Curve Read-only Reentrancy.

A example is eth/stETH pool, in its `remove_liquidity` function:
bug_full: The vulnerability is a read‑only reentrancy issue that can be exploited in Curve pools that are implemented as Plain Pools containing a native gas token, such as the ETH/stETH pool. The problem originates from the fact that certain view‑only functions, for example the price calculation performed during a collateral valuation, invoke external calls that can be re‑entered. Because the external call is allowed to execute before the view function finishes, an attacker can trigger a re‑entrancy during the price query and manipulate the pool’s internal balances. By calling a function like remove_liquidity, which internally performs a static call to the pool’s pricing logic, the attacker can cause the price oracle to read a temporarily inflated price after the pool’s state has been altered in the attacker’s favor. This inflated price is then used by the protocol to assess the value of the CurveStableCollateral, allowing the attacker to borrow more assets or avoid liquidation. The impact is that the protocol may accept collateral that appears to be worth more than it truly is, leading to potential under‑collateralisation, loss of funds, or liquidation cascades when the price reverts to its correct level. The condition for exploitation is that the collateral contract relies on a Curve pool that permits read‑only re‑entrancy and that the attacker can invoke a function that triggers the vulnerable view call, typically during a liquidity removal or similar operation. All users who deposit the affected collateral, as well as the protocol that relies on its price feed, are affected because the price discrepancy can cause unexpected borrowing limits or sudden loss of collateral value. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the collateral contract and the Curve pool’s pricing functions. It is difficult to notice because the re‑entrancy occurs in a view context, which does not directly modify storage, and therefore standard re‑entrancy detection tools that focus on state‑changing calls may miss it. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the UI may display a higher collateral value or allow a larger loan amount than expected, and later the displayed balance may drop to zero or a much lower amount after the price correction, leading to confusion and potential liquidation. The bug belongs to the class of read‑only reentrancy or price‑oracle manipulation vulnerabilities, where an attacker leverages a re‑entrant call in a supposedly non‑mutating function to distort accounting. To remediate the issue the protocol should eliminate external calls from view functions used for price calculation, employ staticcall with re‑entrancy guards, or move the price logic to a trusted oracle that does not depend on mutable pool state. In conceptual terms the fix is to ensure that price queries are atomic and cannot be interfered with by any external contract during their execution, thereby preserving the integrity of the collateral valuation.

title: `CTokenV3Collateral._underlyingRefPerTok` should use the decimals from underlying Comet
description: `CTokenV3Collateral._underlyingRefPerTok` uses `erc20Decimals` which is the decimals of `CusdcV3Wrapper`. But it should use the decimals of the underlying Comet.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect decimal scaling when the contract calculates the amount of reference units that correspond to one unit of collateral token. The function responsible for this conversion calls a generic fixed‑point helper (shiftl_toFix) and supplies the number of decimals taken from the ERC‑20 wrapper (erc20Decimals). However, the exchange rate returned by the wrapper is expressed in terms of the underlying Comet token, whose decimal precision is defined by comet.decimals(). Because the wrapper’s decimals can differ from the underlying token’s decimals, the shift operation applies an erroneous factor, causing the computed _underlyingRefPerTok value to be either too large or too small. This mis‑scaling propagates to every place where the protocol evaluates the value of deposited collateral, the amount of underlying that can be redeemed, or the health factor used for liquidation. An attacker who can supply collateral or trigger a redemption can exploit the mismatch to receive more underlying assets than entitled, or to force a liquidation on honest users by making the protocol think their collateral is worth less than it actually is. The impact is a distortion of accounting that may lead to loss of funds, incorrect liquidation, or unfair reward distribution. The bug manifests whenever the contract reads the exchange rate from the wrapper – essentially any operation that relies on _underlyingRefPerTok – and it is especially problematic for tokens whose wrapper and underlying decimals differ (for example, a 6‑decimal wrapper for an 8‑decimal underlying). The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors compared the expected scaling against the implementation and noticed the mismatch. Because the numbers involved are large integers and the error is a constant shift, the problem does not produce obvious runtime errors and can remain hidden until a detailed review of the arithmetic is performed. To remediate the issue, the contract should replace the use of erc20Decimals with comet.decimals() when calling shiftl_toFix, ensuring that the reference‑per‑token conversion respects the true precision of the underlying asset. This change restores correct accounting, prevents users from seeing zero or unexpectedly low refunds, and aligns the protocol’s financial logic with its intended business rules.

title: `RTokenAsset` price estimation accounts for margin of error twice
description: `RTokenAsset` estimates the price by multiplying the BU (basket unit) price estimation by the estimation of baskets held (then dividing by total supply). The issue is that both BU and baskets held account for price margin of error, widening the range of the price more than necessary.
poc:
* Both `tryPrice()` and `lotPrice()` use this method of multiplying basket unit price by basket range then dividing by total supply
  * BU price accounts for oracle error
  * As for the basket range - whenever one of the collaterals is missing (i.e. less than baskets needed) it estimates the value of anything above the min baskets held, and when doing that it estimates for oracle error as well.

Consider the following scenario:

  * We have a basket composed of 1 ETH token and 1 USD token (cUSDCv2)
  * cUSDCv2 defaults and the backup token AAVE-USDC kicks in
  * Before trading rebalances things we have 0 AAVE-USDC
  * This means that we’d be estimating the low price of the ETH we’re accounting for margin of error at least twice:

    * Within the `basketRange()` we’re dividing the ETH’s `low` price by `buPriceHigh`
    * Then we multiply again by `buPriceLow`

(There’s also some duplication within the `basketRange()` but that function isn’t in scope, what is is scope is the additional margin of error when multiplying by `buPriceLow`).
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑conservative price estimation bug in the RTokenAsset contract. The contract computes a token price by multiplying a basket‑unit (BU) price estimate with an estimate of the number of baskets held, then dividing by total supply. Both the BU price estimate and the basket‑range estimate independently incorporate the oracle’s margin of error. When a collateral is missing and a backup token is used, the basketRange function applies the low oracle price (including its error margin) and then the overall price calculation multiplies this low price again by buPriceLow, which already contains the same error margin. As a result the margin of error is counted twice, widening the reported price range far beyond what the underlying assets justify. This can be exploited when a collateral shortfall occurs: an attacker or market condition that triggers the backup token path causes the protocol to report an artificially low price for the primary asset. Users redeeming or trading RTokens may therefore receive fewer underlying assets than expected, or the protocol may appear under‑collateralised and refuse withdrawals. The issue manifests only under conditions where at least one collateral is below its required amount and the backup asset is engaged, because only then does basketRange apply the low‑price estimate. Token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s risk model are affected because the accounting assumptions about asset value are broken. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the tryPrice and lotPrice functions and traced the double application of oracle error through basketRange. It is subtle because the contract still returns a price that looks plausible; the problem is the inflated uncertainty band, which may not be obvious from UI displays that only show a single price figure. The correct fix is to separate the error handling: compute either the BU price with its margin of error or the basket range with its margin, but not both. A dedicated price‑estimation function should apply the oracle error exactly once, ensuring that the final price reflects the true worst‑case value without double counting. This aligns the implementation with the intended accounting model where the protocol’s collateral value is bounded by a single, well‑defined error term, preventing users from receiving less value than the protocol’s guarantees and preserving the integrity of the financial logic.

title: Possible rounding during the reward calculation
description: Some rewards might be locked inside the contract due to the rounding loss.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding loss in the reward accounting logic of the staking wrapper. The contract tracks cumulativerewards per share using an integer multiplier (one) and updates it with the expression (delta * one) / totalSupply. Because Solidity performs integer division, any fractional part of the reward per share is truncated. When the function _claimAndSyncRewards is invoked frequently (on every deposit, transfer, or withdrawal), the truncated fractions accumulate and remain in the contract balance instead of being credited to users. This results in rewards that are effectively locked and never distributed, causing users to receive less than the expected amount – in extreme cases almost half of the entitled reward may be lost. The issue occurs whenever the reward token has fewer decimals than the underlying token or when the total supply is large relative to the reward amount, such that delta * one is not an exact multiple of totalSupply. The affected parties are token holders who rely on the contract to distribute staking rewards, as well as the protocol that promises a certain annual yield. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward synchronization routine and identified the division operation as a source of precision loss. The bug is subtle because the contract’s balance still grows, but the per‑share accounting does not reflect the missing fractions, making the discrepancy hard to notice without detailed accounting. To remediate, the contract should either use a higher precision multiplier, retain the remainder from the division and carry it forward to the next reward sync, or employ a fixed‑point arithmetic library that preserves fractional rewards. By ensuring that all reward fractions are eventually accounted for, the protocol can avoid locking funds and maintain the promised reward distribution.

title: `depositWithPermit` and `mintWithPermit` are allowed to be called by the permit creator only
description: Functions `depositWithPermit` and `mintWithPermit` are allowed to be called by the permit creator only. Not any other contracts will be able to execute these function on behalf of signer.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns two entry points, depositWithPermit and mintWithPermit, that are intended to let a token holder sign an ERC20 permit off‑chain and then let any other address submit that signature to the vault in order to approve and deposit tokens on the signer’s behalf. In the current implementation the contract forwards the permit call with msg.sender as the _owner argument. Because msg.sender is the address that is executing depositWithPermit, the contract only accepts permits that were signed by the same address that is calling the function. Consequently, a third‑party relayer, a contract, or any other caller cannot use a permit that was signed by a different user. The root cause is the misuse of msg.sender instead of the intended _receiver (or a separate owner parameter) when invoking the internal _permit helper. This mistake defeats the purpose of the permit mechanism, which is to separate signature creation from transaction execution. An attacker or honest user who expects to delegate a deposit can experience a failure: the permit verification will succeed only when the signer and the caller match, so a relayer’s transaction will be rejected, leaving the user with a signed message that cannot be used and potentially causing a denial‑of‑service situation. From the user’s point of view the UI may show a “deposit failed” or “approval failed” error even though a valid signature was provided, and the expected outcome – the vault balance increasing – does not happen. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended business logic (permit‑based delegation) with the actual code path and noticed that the owner argument was hard‑coded to msg.sender. The bug is subtle because the contract still compiles and the permit call itself succeeds; the problem only appears when the caller is not the signer, which may not be covered by simple unit tests. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect authorization parameter” or “owner‑parameter misuse” bugs, where a function forwards a privileged operation using the caller’s address instead of the designated beneficiary. To fix the issue the contract should replace msg.sender with the _receiver address (or an explicit owner parameter) when calling _permit, ensuring that the permit’s owner matches the address that signed the message and that any third party can safely submit the signed permit on behalf of the signer. This change restores the intended delegation flow, aligns the contract with ERC20Permit semantics, and prevents users from seeing silent failures or having to perform an extra on‑chain approval transaction.

title: Transfer of Vault tokens can cause accounting errors in other contracts
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Vault contract’s custom token transfer logic. Instead of using the standard ERC20::_transfer implementation, Vault::_transfer forwards the share movement to a TwabController contract. During this process the amount of shares to be moved, originally a uint256, is forcibly down‑cast to a uint96 before being passed to the controller. The TwabController, however, stores each account’s balance in a uint112 variable. When the share amount exceeds the maximum value that fits in a uint96 – for example when a user deposits the maximum uint96 value twice, resulting in a balance that is larger than uint96 can represent – the down‑cast silently wraps around, producing a much smaller number. The controller therefore records only the wrapped‑around amount as having been transferred, while the Vault contract still believes the full amount was moved. This mismatch creates an accounting error that can be exploited by an attacker who first deposits a large amount of shares, then initiates a transferFrom that triggers the underflow, and finally performs an additional transfer of the remaining balance. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the transfer succeeded and the balance decreased, yet the receiving contract or protocol records a lower amount than expected, effectively allowing the attacker to retain extra shares that were never accounted for. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees: token holders may see their balances incorrectly reduced, integrators that rely on the transferred amount may receive fewer shares than they should, and the overall token supply accounting can become inconsistent, potentially leading to fund loss or unfair advantage. The bug occurs only when share amounts cross the uint96 boundary, which is not obvious because the underlying storage type (uint112) can hold the larger value, masking the problem. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit through a Foundry test that deliberately minted the maximum uint112 amount, performed two maximum‑size deposits, and then observed that a subsequent transfer only moved a uint96‑sized chunk while the Vault still reported the full balance. The underflow is silent – no revert or error is emitted – making it hard to notice in normal operation. To remediate the issue the conversion should be performed with OpenZeppelin’s SafeCast library, which reverts on overflow, or the contract should avoid down‑casting altogether by aligning the storage type with the cast size or by using a larger integer type for the transfer function. In essence, the bug is a classic unsafe integer down‑cast leading to silent underflow and accounting inconsistency in token transfer logic.

title: Inconsistent behavior for canary claims in the `claimer`
description: Inconsistent behavior for canary claims in the `claimer`.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way the Claimer contract calculates the fee that must be paid for each prize claim. When a user invokes claimPrizes, the contract determines a per‑claim fee by calling _computeFeePerClaim with three arguments: the maximum fee for the tier, the number of claims being processed in the current transaction (claimCount), and the total number of claims that have already been recorded in the prize pool (prizePool.claimCount()). The contract, however, ignores the existence of so‑called canary claims – a special class of claims that are also tracked by the prize pool via prizePool.canaryClaimCount(). Because the canary count is omitted from the denominator of the fee calculation, the resulting feePerClaim is derived from an incomplete view of the pool’s claim state. Depending on the exact fee formula, this can cause the fee to be either higher or lower than intended. In practice, a user may see a normal prize amount but be charged an unexpected fee, or the protocol may collect less revenue than its accounting model predicts. The issue manifests whenever any canary claim has been recorded before or during a batch claim operation; the inconsistency appears only under that condition, making it easy to miss during routine testing because normal claims without canary activity behave correctly. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which compared the fee logic against the pool’s accounting assumptions and noticed the missing canary component. It is hard to notice from a UI perspective because the contract does not emit a separate event for the fee discrepancy; users simply observe that the net amount received after fees does not match the expected value based on the pool’s published fee schedule. The root cause is a logical oversight: the fee calculation treats canary claims as if they did not exist, violating the invariant that total claims (regular plus canary) should be used for fee distribution. To remediate the issue, the fee computation should be adjusted to include prizePool.canaryClaimCount() in the total claim count, effectively treating canary claims as regular claims for fee purposes. This aligns the fee logic with the protocol’s accounting model, restores predictable fee behavior, and prevents potential exploitation where an attacker could manipulate the fee by creating or timing canary claims to affect subsequent fee calculations.

title: Permanent funds lock in `StargateRewardableWrapper`
description: The staked funds might be locked because the deposit/withdraw/transfer logic reverts.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the StargateRewardableWrapper contract, which wraps a Stargate LP staking contract to provide reward‑bearing ERC20 tokens. Every token transfer, deposit or withdrawal triggers an internal call to _claimAssetRewards, which simply forwards a zero‑amount deposit to the external staking contract. The staking contract’s deposit function invokes updatePool, a routine that calculates pending rewards based on the global variable totalAllocPoint. If an administrator of the Stargate staking contract later sets the allocation points of the pool to zero – for example by calling set(0,0) – totalAllocPoint becomes zero. The next time updatePool runs, the expression stargatePerBlock * pool.allocPoint / totalAllocPoint triggers a division‑by‑zero and the transaction reverts. Because the wrapper does not contain any fallback or emergencyWithdraw logic, the revert propagates back to the wrapper’s deposit, withdraw and transfer functions, making them permanently unusable. From a user’s perspective a withdrawal attempt simply fails with a revert, the UI shows an error, and the user’s balance appears unchanged, leading to the impression that “my funds disappeared” or “I cannot get my money back”. The issue only manifests after the admin action; under normal conditions the wrapper works correctly, which makes the bug easy to miss during testing. The impact is that any user who has deposited through the wrapper becomes unable to retrieve their staked assets, effectively locking the funds indefinitely. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the wrapper and the staking contract and identified the division‑by‑zero path in updatePool. To remediate the issue the wrapper should detect the emergency condition and avoid calling the staking contract’s reward‑claiming path; _claimAssetRewards should simply return zero, and the wrapper should expose an emergencyWithdraw function that calls stakingContract.emergencyWithdraw to pull the underlying LP tokens back to users. This change restores the ability to recover funds even when the staking pool’s allocation points are zero, aligning the implementation with the expected business logic that users can always withdraw their deposited assets.

title: CurveStableMetapoolCollateral.tryPrice returns a huge but valid high price when the price oracle of pairedToken is timeout
description: The CurveStableMetapoolCollateral is intended for 2-fiattoken stable metapools. The metapoolToken coin0 is pairedToken and the coin1 is lpToken, e.g. 3CRV. And the `config.chainlinkFeed` should be set for paired token.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the CurveStableMetapoolCollateral contract derives a price range for a metapool token when it queries the price of the paired token from a Chainlink feed. The contract calls a helper function that returns a low and a high estimate based on the oracle price and a configured error margin. This call is wrapped in a try‑catch block with an empty catch clause, and the high estimate is pre‑initialised to the constant FIX_MAX, the maximum representable unsigned fixed‑point value. If the Chainlink feed does not respond within the configured timeout, the helper function reverts. Because the catch block is empty, the revert is silently ignored and the high estimate remains FIX_MAX while the low estimate stays at zero. The subsequent accounting routine multiplies the paired token balance by this inflated high price, and the Fixed‑point multiplication routine propagates FIX_MAX without overflow. Consequently the aggregate high asset‑under‑management (aumHigh) becomes FIX_MAX, and the final high price of the metapool token is computed as aumHigh divided by the total supply. For any supply greater than one token the division succeeds, yielding a gigantic but mathematically valid price that is far higher than the true market value. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately causing the oracle to time out— for example by disabling the feed or flooding it— and then invoking functions that rely on the inflated price, such as minting, redeeming, or refreshing collateral. The protocol will treat the over‑valued assets as worth far more than they actually are, allowing the attacker to extract excess funds or to cause other participants to receive far fewer assets than expected. From a user’s perspective the UI may display an unexpectedly large token price or a sudden loss of balance after a refresh, contradicting the expectation that the price reflects market reality. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the reviewer noticed the empty catch block and the propagation of FIX_MAX through the accounting logic. It is difficult to spot because the contract does not revert; instead it returns a seemingly valid price range, albeit one that is absurdly high, so normal error monitoring may miss it. The proper remediation is to avoid swallowing the error: the try‑catch should be removed or the catch should re‑throw, allowing the caller (for example the refresh function) to handle the failure. Alternatively, the contract could provide a safe fallback price or abort the price calculation when the oracle is unavailable, ensuring that the price range never collapses to the maximum representable value. This class of bug is a silent‑failure price oracle fallback error that leads to extreme price inflation and breaks the accounting invariants of the protocol.

title: The Asset.lotPrice doubles the oracle timeout in the worst case
bug_full: The vulnerability is a time‑based price decay mismatch in the Asset.lotPrice calculation. The contract stores the timestamp of the last successful price refresh in a variable called lastSave, but the refresh() function writes block.timestamp instead of the oracle feed’s updateTime. The lotPrice function later computes a delta as the difference between the current block.timestamp and lastSave and applies different branches depending on whether the delta is within the oracle timeout, beyond the oracle timeout but before the combined oracleTimeout+priceTimeout, or after the full timeout. Because lastSave is set to the block time at the moment the refresh succeeds, a scenario can arise where the oracle feed itself is already at the end of its timeout window when the refresh occurs. In that case the delta measured by lotPrice will be larger than the oracle timeout, causing the contract to treat the price as decaying, yet the decay start point is effectively shifted by an additional priceTimeout. Consequently the effective timeout for a stale price becomes roughly twice the intended oracle timeout in the worst case. This can be exploited by forcing the tryPrice() call to revert (for example by feeding a stale or missing price) so that the contract falls back to the historical price path. An attacker does not need to manipulate the contract directly; simply causing the oracle to be stale for a period that aligns with the refresh timing triggers the double‑timeout condition. The impact is that users querying the lot price may receive a zero or dramatically reduced price after the extended timeout, leading to failed trades, unexpected zero refunds, or assets being priced incorrectly. From the user’s perspective the UI may suddenly show a lot price of 0 or a price that drops far more than expected, contradicting the assumption that the price will remain valid for the configured oracle timeout. The bug affects any participant that relies on the lot price for buying, selling, or collateral valuation, effectively breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions about price freshness. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the interaction between refresh() and OracleLib’s timeout check was examined; the mismatch in timestamp sources was identified as a logical flaw that is easy to miss because it only manifests after a specific timing alignment and does not produce an immediate error. The bug is hard to notice because the price appears correct for the first timeout period and then silently decays, which can be mistaken for normal market movement. To remediate the problem the contract should either start the decay as soon as the delta exceeds the oracle timeout or, more robustly, store the oracle’s updateTime in lastSave instead of block.timestamp, thereby aligning the decay logic with the oracle’s own timing and preventing the effective timeout from being doubled.

title: User can’t redeem from RToken based on CurveStableRTokenMetapoolCollateral when any underlying collateral of paired RToken’s price oracle is offline
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an arithmetic overflow in the price‑validation routine of a Curve stable metapool collateral contract that supports RToken pairs. The contract obtains the low and high price bounds of the paired RToken by calling the RTokenAsset.price() oracle. When any underlying collateral of that paired RToken experiences a timeout or other failure, the oracle returns a legitimate but extreme price range: the low bound is a non‑zero value derived from the true price, while the high bound is set to the maximum representable fixed‑point value (FIX_MAX). The refresh logic of CurveStableRTokenMetapoolCollateral then attempts to compute a midpoint with the expression `uint192 mid = (low + high) / 2`. Because the addition of a normal low value and FIX_MAX exceeds the 192‑bit capacity, the operation overflows and triggers a revert. This overflow is not caught by any try/catch block, so the entire `refresh()` call reverts. Since the RToken’s `redeemTo` and `redeemCustom` functions invoke `assetRegistry.refresh()` at the start of the redemption flow, any user attempting to redeem their RToken while the paired token’s oracle is offline will experience an immediate transaction failure. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a failed redemption, no assets are transferred, and the balance appears unchanged, contrary to the expectation that the redemption would succeed and return the underlying stablecoins. The impact is that token holders are unable to withdraw their funds, the protocol may be marked IFFY, and liquidity can become effectively frozen. The issue was discovered during a security audit that linked this contract to a previously reported oracle‑timeout bug. It is difficult to notice because the overflow only manifests under the rare condition of an extreme high price, which does not occur during normal operation. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic overflows in fixed‑point calculations that are triggered by edge‑case oracle responses. A proper fix involves protecting the midpoint calculation from overflow, for example by using unchecked arithmetic with a safe division after a subtraction, or by overriding the `_anyDepeggedOutsidePool` check to compute the midpoint with a method that cannot overflow (such as using `Fix.plus` or splitting the addition). Additionally, the contract should gracefully handle the case where the high price equals FIX_MAX instead of asserting that the low price must be zero, thereby preventing a revert and allowing the protocol to mark the collateral as IFFY without blocking redemption entirely.

title: RTokenAsset price oracle can return a huge but valid high price when any underlying collateral’s price oracle timeout
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the RTokenAsset oracle aggregates prices of its underlying collateral assets. When the price oracle of any single collateral reverts – for example because of a timeout – the low‑price function returns (0, FIX_MAX), where FIX_MAX is the maximum representable fixed‑point value. The aggregation logic in BasketHandler treats the high component as a valid bound and multiplies it by the quantity of the affected collateral. Because Fixed.safeMul propagates FIX_MAX without overflow, the resulting basket high price becomes FIX_MAX while the low price is reduced proportionally to the share of the failing asset. The RTokenAsset then computes its own price as the average of the low and high values, and the internal check only requires low != 0 and high != FIX_MAX. Consequently, the high price that reaches the RToken level is a huge but still valid number, and the average price can be dramatically inflated. An attacker who can trigger a timeout in any underlying oracle can therefore cause the RToken price feed to report an artificially high value. This inflated price can be used to mint new RTokens at a cheap collateral cost or to redeem existing tokens for less than their true value, leading to under‑collateralisation of the protocol. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected token price spikes, redemption transactions that return far less than expected, or balances that appear to shrink without a clear on‑chain error. The issue occurs only when at least one collateral oracle reverts and the basket range top is lower than the total RToken supply, a condition that can happen after a haircut or when the system is already under‑collateralised. The bug is hard to notice because the high price passes the explicit sanity check (it is below FIX_MAX) and no transaction reverts, so the protocol continues operating with a wildly inaccurate price. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by analysing the price‑aggregation code paths and the handling of FIX_MAX values. To remediate the problem the protocol should enforce a stricter validation of the basket unit price – for example by requiring the low and high prices returned from BasketHandler to be non‑zero and strictly less than FIX_MAX – and propagate an error when any underlying asset reports an invalid price. Alternatively, the aggregation logic could reject or fallback when a collateral oracle times out, ensuring that the composite price never incorporates a FIX_MAX bound that can inflate the RToken price.

title: `Asset.lotPrice` only uses `oracleTimeout` to determine if the price is stale.
description: `OracleTimeout` is the number of seconds until an oracle value becomes invalid. It is set in the constructor of `Asset`. And `Asset.lotPrice` uses `OracleTimeout` to determine if the saved price is stale. However, `OracleTimeout` may not be the correct source to determine if the price is stale. `Asset.lotPrice` may return the incorrect price.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of using a single contract‑level variable called 'oracleTimeout' to decide whether the cached price stored by Asset.lotPrice is still fresh. The root cause is that the Asset contract assumes that all collateral implementations share the same timeout for their underlying price feeds, but many collaterals aggregate several feeds, each with its own timeout, or override the timeout via a different function. Because lotPrice only checks the elapsed time against 'oracleTimeout', it may treat a price as valid even when one of the constituent feeds has already expired. An attacker can trigger this situation by causing one of the feeds to stop updating while the other feed continues, causing the cached price to become stale for that feed. When lotPrice falls back to the savedLowPrice / savedHighPrice branch, it returns a price that no longer reflects the current market. This stale price can be used by the protocol to compute liquidation thresholds, collateral ratios, or loan repayments, leading to under‑collateralisation, unexpected liquidations, or users receiving zero or incorrect payouts. The bug manifests whenever the delta between the current block timestamp and the last saved price exceeds the timeout of any feed that is shorter than the generic 'oracleTimeout', but the contract still believes the price is fresh. All users who interact with assets that rely on Asset.lotPrice – borrowers, lenders, and liquidators – are potentially affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between Asset.lotPrice and various collateral implementations such as NonFiatCollateral and CurveStableCollateral, revealing that those collaterals use multiple feeds with distinct timeouts that are never consulted by lotPrice. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit any warning when a feed expires; the only visible symptom is that the returned price may be unexpectedly high or low, or that a liquidation may occur at a price that seems unrelated to market data. The appropriate fix is to abstract the timeout into a virtual function (e.g., actualOracleTimeout) that each collateral can override to return the correct composite timeout, or to redesign lotPrice to query each feed’s individual timeout before deciding whether to use the cached price. In generic terms, this is a stale‑oracle‑validation bug where the contract relies on an incorrect invariant about oracle freshness, violating the business logic that a price must be up‑to‑date before it is used for accounting.

title: StaticATokenLM transfer missing _updateRewards
description: Transfer missing `_updateRewards()`, resulting in the loss of `from`’s reward.
bug_full: The contract implements a reward‑distribution mechanism where a global accumulator (often called _accRewardsPerToken) must be refreshed each time a token holder's balance changes. Functions that change balances through minting or burning correctly invoke an internal routine that updates this accumulator before adjusting individual user snapshots, ensuring that pending rewards are recorded for the account that caused the change. However, the transfer and transferFrom pathways invoke a hook that only updates the per‑user snapshots after the balance move and completely omit the call that refreshes the global accumulator. As a result, when a holder sends tokens to another address, the contract records the new balances but calculates the pending rewards based on a stale accumulator value. The pending reward that should belong to the sender is therefore implicitly transferred to the recipient along with the token amount. From a user’s perspective the token balance appears correct, but the expected reward amount either drops to zero or is lower than anticipated, leading to the perception that “my rewards disappeared” after a transfer. This flaw can be exploited by an attacker who deliberately transfers tokens (or triggers many small transfers) to move the victim’s accrued rewards to an address they control, effectively stealing value that was supposed to be claimable by the original holder. The issue manifests every time a transfer or transferFrom is executed while the incentives controller is set, affecting any token holder who relies on the reward accrual logic. It was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the token transfer hook and noticing the missing update call. The bug is subtle because the token transfer succeeds and balances look normal; only the reward accounting is off, which may only be observed when a user attempts to claim or view their pending rewards. To remediate the problem the transfer hook should first invoke the global reward‑update routine before updating individual user snapshots, mirroring the logic used in mint and burn operations. This class of vulnerability belongs to reward‑accounting or state‑synchronisation bugs where a global accounting variable is not refreshed prior to a state transition, causing reward leakage and breaking the protocol’s economic guarantees.

title: `_claimRewardsOnBehalf
description: Incorrect determination of maximum rewards, which may lead to loss of user rewards.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect determination of the maximum reward amount that can be transferred when a user (or a third party) calls the internal function that claims rewards on behalf of an address. The contract keeps an accounting variable that accumulates each user’s unclaimed rewards through internal calculations, but the actual reward tokens are stored partly in an external Incentives Controller contract rather than in the main contract’s balance. When the claim function is invoked without the forceUpdate flag, it reads the contract’s token balance (REWARD_TOKEN.balanceOf(address(this))) and, if the calculated reward exceeds that balance, it silently reduces the reward to the available balance and then resets the user’s unclaimed reward counter to zero. Because the external controller still holds the missing tokens, the accounting entry for the user becomes larger than the real token holdings, and the excess amount is effectively lost. An attacker can trigger a claim on behalf of a victim while the contract’s balance is insufficient, causing the victim’s pending reward to be truncated and the internal record cleared, resulting in permanent loss of the victim’s accrued rewards. This issue manifests whenever the contract’s reward token balance is lower than the sum of all users’ unclaimed rewards and a claim is performed without forcing an update that would pull the missing tokens from the Incentives Controller. Affected parties include any token holder with pending rewards, the protocol’s economic model, and any downstream applications that rely on accurate reward accounting. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the reward accounting logic with the actual token flow and identified that the _updateRewards and _updateUser functions only compute values without transferring tokens, while the claim function assumes the contract’s balance reflects the total rewards. The bug is subtle because the balance‑capping check appears reasonable at first glance, yet the mismatch between internal accounting and external token storage can go unnoticed until a user experiences a shortfall in the claimed amount. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a certain amount of pending rewards, but after initiating a claim the received amount can be zero or lower than expected, violating the expectation that all displayed rewards will be transferred. The flaw belongs to the class of reward‑distribution accounting errors where external token sources are not synchronized with internal state, leading to truncation or loss of funds. To remediate the issue the contract should only apply the balance‑cap logic when forceUpdate is true, or it should first pull the missing rewards from the Incentives Controller into the contract before performing the cap, and finally it must adjust the unclaimed reward record to reflect any shortfall rather than clearing it entirely.

title: Lack of protection when caling `CusdcV3Wrapper._withdraw`
description:
When unwrapping the `wComet` to its rebasing `comet`, users with an equivalent amount of `wComet` invoking `CusdcV3Wrapper._withdraw` at around the same time could end up having different percentage gains because `comet` is not linearly rebasing.

Moreover, the rate-determining `getUpdatedSupplyIndicies()` is an internal view function inaccessible to the users unless they take the trouble creating a contract to inherit CusdcV3Wrapper.sol. So most users making partial withdrawals will have no clue whether or not this is the best time to unwrap. This is because the public view function [underlyingBalanceOf](https://github.com/reserve-protocol/protocol/blob/9ee60f142f9f5c1fe8bc50eef915cf33124a534f/contracts/plugins/assets/compoundv3/CusdcV3Wrapper.sol#L225-L231) is only directly informational when `amount` has been entered as `type(uint256).max`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the _withdraw function of the CusdcV3Wrapper contract, which converts a user’s wrapped token (wComet) back into the underlying rebasing token (comet) without any slippage or timing protection. Because comet’s supply index rebases in a non‑linear fashion, the amount of comet received for a given wComet balance depends on the current baseSupplyIndex, which changes with the protocol’s supply rate and elapsed time. The function first reads the user’s underlying balance via underlyingBalanceOf, which internally calls convertStaticToDynamic and getUpdatedSupplyIndicies. These view functions are internal and not directly exposed to regular users, so a user cannot determine whether the current index will give a favorable conversion rate. When multiple users withdraw around the same block, each may receive a different percentage of comet for the same amount of wComet, leading to unexpected gains or losses. The contract also performs a conservative rounding step that favours the wrapper, transferring (amount/10)*10 of the underlying token and then calculating the burn amount based on the change in the wrapper’s principal. This rounding, combined with the dynamic index, can cause the wrapper to retain a few wei more than the user expected, effectively reducing the user’s net return. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a lower than expected amount of comet after unwrapping, occasional zero‑value withdrawals when the calculated amount rounds down to zero, or a discrepancy between the displayed wComet balance and the actual comet received. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the withdrawal flow and noted that the only public view of the conversion rate (underlyingBalanceOf) is only accurate when the caller requests the maximum possible amount, leaving partial withdrawals without reliable information. The problem is hard to notice because the rounding differences are small (often a few wei) and the protocol’s rebasing mechanics are not obvious to end users. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “missing slippage protection and opaque price oracle” vulnerabilities, where a contract performs a value conversion based on an internal, time‑varying index without exposing the index to callers or allowing them to set acceptable bounds. The impact is financial: users may lose part of their expected return, and the protocol could be perceived as unfair or exploitable, especially if an attacker times withdrawals to benefit from favorable index movements. The vulnerability affects any holder of wComet who attempts a partial withdrawal, including regular users, integrators, and downstream contracts that rely on predictable conversion rates. A proper fix would introduce explicit slippage parameters to the _withdraw call (e.g., a minimum acceptable comet amount or a maximum acceptable wComet burn), expose the current conversion index through a public view function, and optionally enforce a more neutral rounding scheme. By allowing users to specify acceptable bounds, the contract would prevent unexpected loss due to index drift and make the withdrawal process transparent and auditable.

title: Lack of protection when withdrawing Static Atoken
description:
The Aave plugin is associated with [an ever-increasing exchange rate](https://github.com/reserve-protocol/protocol/blob/9ee60f142f9f5c1fe8bc50eef915cf33124a534f/contracts/plugins/assets/aave/StaticATokenLM.sol#L26). The earlier a user wraps the AToken, the more Static Atoken will be minted and understandably no slippage protection is needed.

However, since the rate is not linearly increasing, withdrawing the Static Atoken (following RToken redemption) at the wrong time could mean a difference in terms of the amount of AToken redeemed. The rate could be in a transient mode of non-increasing or barely increasing and then a significant surge. Users with an equivalent amount of Static AToken making such calls at around the same time could end up having different percentage gains.

Although the user could always deposit and wrap the AToken again, it’s not going to help if the wrapping were to encounter a sudden surge (bad timing again) thereby thwarting the intended purpose.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing slippage guard in the StaticATokenLM contract when a user withdraws a static aToken that represents a time‑varying exchange rate to the underlying aToken. The contract stores an ever‑increasing exchange rate, but the rate does not grow linearly; it can enter periods of stagnation or very slow growth before a sudden surge. The _withdraw function converts the amount of static tokens the caller wants to burn into a dynamic amount of underlying aTokens using the current rate, but it does not enforce any minimum‑out or maximum‑in constraint. Consequently, if a user initiates a withdrawal while the rate is temporarily flat, the calculation yields fewer aTokens than the user would expect based on earlier or later rates. Because the function accepts either a staticAmount or a dynamicAmount without a sanity check, two users withdrawing the same amount of static tokens at nearly the same block can receive different percentages of the underlying asset. The impact is that holders of StaticAToken may see their balances shrink unexpectedly, receive less than the advertised redemption value, or experience a lower percentage gain after an RToken redemption. This situation occurs whenever the exchange rate is in a transient non‑increasing phase and the caller does not specify a slippage tolerance. All users who wrap aTokens into StaticAToken, as well as the protocol that relies on predictable redemption values, are affected. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the rate() function and the arithmetic in _withdraw, noting that the contract never checks that the computed dynamic amount meets a user‑defined threshold. The bug is subtle because the rate is generally upward‑trending, so developers and users may assume that any withdrawal will be proportional to the amount of static tokens held, overlooking the brief periods when the rate plateaus. The class of bug is a missing slippage protection or unchecked exchange‑rate volatility, similar to price‑oracle‑dependent contracts that lack min‑out guarantees. From a user perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal but the displayed aToken balance is lower than expected, or the user may receive zero tokens when they anticipated a payout. To remediate, the contract should allow callers to specify a minimum acceptable amount of aTokens (or a maximum amount of static tokens to burn) and revert the transaction if the current rate would produce a result below that threshold, thereby providing deterministic protection against rate‑stagnation scenarios.

title: Potential Loss of Rewards During Token Transfers in StaticATokenLM.sol
description:
This issue could lead to a permanent loss of rewards for the transferer of the token. During the token transfer process, the `_beforeTokenTransfer` function updates rewards for both the sender and the receiver. However, due to the specific call order and the behavior of the `_updateUser` function and the `_getPendingRewards` function, some rewards may not be accurately accounted for.

The crux of the problem lies in the fact that the `_getPendingRewards` function, when called with the `fresh` parameter set to `false`, may not account for all the latest rewards from the `INCENTIVES_CONTROLLER`. As a result, the `_updateUserSnapshotRewardsPerToken` function, which relies on the output of the `_getPendingRewards` function, could end up missing out on some rewards. This could be detrimental to the token sender, especially the `Backing Manager` whenever `RToken` is redeemed. Apparently, most users having wrapped their `AToken`, would automatically use it to issue `RToken` as part of the basket range of backing collaterals and be minimally impacted. But it would have the Reserve Protocol collectively affected depending on the frequency and volume of RToken redemption and the time elapsed since `_updateRewards()` or `_collectAndUpdateRewards()` was last called. The same impact shall also apply when making token transfers to successful auction bidders.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward accounting logic of the StaticATokenLM contract during ERC20 token transfers. When a transfer is executed, the internal hook _beforeTokenTransfer calls _updateUser for both the sender and the receiver. Each _updateUser invocation queries pending rewards through _getPendingRewards with the third argument set to false. This flag disables the "fresh" branch that pulls the latest reward balance from the external INCENTIVES_CONTROLLER and updates the accumulated rewards per token (accRewardsPerToken). As a consequence, the snapshot of rewards per token stored for the user (_userSnapshotRewardsPerToken) is calculated on stale data, omitting any rewards that accrued since the last explicit call to _updateRewards or _collectAndUpdateRewards. The sender therefore records fewer unclaimed rewards than they are entitled to, while the receiver may inadvertently receive a higher snapshot, effectively transferring reward value without an explicit claim. The issue manifests only when the incentives controller is configured, the token has a non‑zero balance, and a transfer occurs without a preceding call to update the reward state. Users see no immediate error; balances appear correct, but later reward claims are lower than expected, leading to a silent loss of accrued incentives. The problem was identified during a manual audit that traced the call order inside _beforeTokenTransfer and noticed that the fresh flag was never set, causing the reward‑accrual branch to be skipped.
