3. User calls [callOut()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/BaseBranchRouter.sol#L83) to communicate through the branch BridgeAgent (that was deactivated):

```solidity
File: BaseBranchRouter.sol
83:     function callOut(bytes calldata _params, GasParams calldata _gParams) external payable override lock {
84:         IBridgeAgent(localBridgeAgentAddress).callOut{value: msg.value}(payable(msg.sender), _params, _gParams);
85:     }
```

4. Here is the execution path of the call from [callOut()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/BaseBranchRouter.sol#L83) function in [BaseBranchRouter](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/BaseBranchRouter.sol) contract:

1. Branch chain to EP: `callOut() => callOut (branch bridge agent - that was deactivated) => _performCall => send`
2. EP to Root chain: `receivePayload => lzReceive => lzReceiveNonBlocking => _execute => executeNoDeposit => execute (Router) => logic` continues based on custom Router’s implementation

There are few important points to note here:

1. Calls (No deposit calls) can occur through both [callOut()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L195) and [callOutSigned()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L262).
2. Adding the modifier [requiresBridgeAgent()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/BranchPort.sol#L547C1-L550C6) check is critical here, as communication between user’s custom Branch chain to Root chain routers is still active.
3. Incoming calls to [lzReceive()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L578) are not fine from user’s custom Root Router, since that still allows no deposit router-router communication through the deactivated branch bridge agent.
4. Incoming calls to [lzReceive()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L578) are fine from admin [CoreRootRouter](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/CoreRootRouter.sol#L186), since such calls will be made to manage bridgeAgents, factories, strategy tokens and port strategies in the BranchPort.
5. Outgoing calls from function [callOutSystem()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/f5ba4de628836b2a29f9b5fff59499690008c463/src/BranchBridgeAgent.sol#L180) are fine since the function is only used to respond back to the root chain when an incoming call from root to branch occurs to manage bridgeAgents, factories, strategy tokens and port strategies.
6. Preventing outgoing no deposit calls are important because user’s custom Root Router can communicate with other chains for various purposes such as bridging of tokens from Arbitrum (Root) to another branch chains like Avalanche, Fantom and many more. This is crucial since the call for bridging between Arbitrum and Avalanche originates from a branch bridge agent that is considered inactive.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing activity verification for branch bridge agents that have been disabled through the administrative removeBranchBridgeAgent function. When an admin toggles a bridge agent off, the BranchPort contract updates its internal isBridgeAgent mapping to false, signalling that the agent should no longer be used for cross‑chain communication. However, the BranchBridgeAgent functions callOut and callOutSigned, which are responsible for sending “no deposit” messages to the root chain, do not check the current activation status of the agent in the port. Likewise, the inbound handler for no‑deposit payloads (the branch side of lzReceiveNonBlocking) processes messages without confirming that the originating bridge agent is still recognised as active. As a result, a deactivated bridge agent can still be invoked by a user or a malicious contract to emit arbitrary no‑deposit calls that reach the root router. An attacker who knows the address of a disabled agent can call the public callOut function on the branch router, which forwards the request to the inactive agent, bypasses the missing require, and triggers cross‑chain execution on the root side. Because no funds are transferred, the exploit may not immediately show a loss of tokens, but it can cause unauthorized state changes, execute arbitrary logic in custom root routers, or manipulate protocol configuration, effectively breaking the trust model of the bridge. The issue appears only after the admin has deliberately disabled a bridge agent, and it is observable when users notice that calls they expect to be blocked are still being processed, or when unexpected actions occur on the root chain despite the agent being marked inactive. The problem was uncovered during a security audit that examined the lifecycle of bridge agents and identified that the deactivation path does not propagate to the callOut and inbound no‑deposit verification steps. The bug is subtle because the bridge continues to function for no‑deposit messages, which do not involve token transfers, making the abnormal behavior easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should enforce a check that the bridge agent is currently recognised as active in the BranchPort before any outbound no‑deposit call is performed and before processing inbound no‑deposit payloads. This can be achieved by adding a require statement that queries the port’s isBridgeAgent mapping, similar to the existing checks for deposit calls. Additionally, the root side should maintain a mirrored active flag or perform a cross‑chain verification to ensure consistency, thereby preventing deactivated agents from being used for any cross‑chain communication.

title: `BaseBranchRouter._transferAndApproveToken` may revert in some cases
description:
In [the bot-report.md for [M-04] Return values of `approve()` not checked](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/bot-report.md), it describes that “by not checking the return value, operations that should have marked as failed, may potentially go through without actually approving anything”, but the following contents of this submission is different.

If the token’s `approve` does not return a value, like [USDT](https://etherscan.io/token/0xdac17f958d2ee523a2206206994597c13d831ec7#code#L199), then `ERC20(_token).approve` will revert. Because ERC20 comes from solmate/tokens/ERC20.sol, its `approve` is defined as `function approve(address spender, uint256 amount) public virtual returns (bool)` where the return value is bool type with a size of 1 byte. The bytecode compiled by the solidity compiler from `ERC20(_token).approve` will check whether the return size is 1 byte. If not, revert will occur.

This will cause all functions calling `_transferAndApproveToken` to revert. This includes [callOutAndBridge](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/BaseBranchRouter.sol#L88) and [callOutAndBridgeMultiple](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/BaseBranchRouter.sol#L104).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service style bug that occurs when the contract calls the ERC20 approve function on a token that does not return the expected boolean value. The internal helper _transferAndApproveToken first transfers a deposit using safeTransferFrom and then calls ERC20(_token).approve(_localPortAddress, _deposit). The ERC20 implementation from solmate expects the call to return a 1‑byte boolean; the Solidity compiler inserts a check that the returned data length equals 1. Tokens such as USDT implement approve without a return value, so the low‑level call returns an empty byte array. The length check fails and the call reverts, causing the whole _transferAndApproveToken function – and any external function that invokes it, like callOutAndBridge and callOutAndBridgeMultiple – to revert. This means that a user attempting to bridge or deposit a non‑standard token experiences a transaction failure, sees no token transfer, and receives an error instead of the expected approval. The issue was discovered during a formal audit and reproduced with a Foundry test that called ERC20(USDT).approve, which reverted, while an interface call or a safeApprove wrapper succeeded. The bug is hard to notice because most ERC20 tokens follow the standard and return a boolean, so developers often omit explicit return‑value checks. The root cause is the assumption that all ERC20 tokens conform to the standard return signature, combined with the lack of a safe wrapper that tolerates missing returns. The impact is limited to denial of service for affected tokens; funds are not stolen because the transaction reverts, but users cannot complete the intended operation, leading to a poor user experience and potential loss of confidence. The fix is to replace the raw approve call with a safeApprove utility (for example, solady’s SafeTransferLib.safeApprove) that performs a low‑level call, accepts empty return data, and only reverts on a true failure. By using such a wrapper the contract no longer relies on the token returning a boolean, restoring compatibility with non‑standard tokens and preventing unexpected reverts.

title: If `RootBridgeAgent.lzReceiveNonBlocking` reverts internally, the native token sent by relayer to RootBridgeAgent is left in RootBridgeAgent
description: [v2 adapterParams](https://layerzero.gitbook.io/docs/evm-guides/advanced/relayer-adapter-parameters#airdrop) are used to send messages, which means that the relayer will send native token to RootBridgeAgent before [RootBridgeAgent.lzReceive](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/RootBridgeAgent.sol#L423) is called. However, if an exception occurs inside [lzReceiveNonBlocking](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/RootBridgeAgent.sol#L434-L439), `lzReceive` will [not revert (except for ARB branch)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/RootBridgeAgent.sol#L430). In this way, the native token sent to RootBridgeAgent will stay in RootBridgeAgent. Malicious users can steal these native tokens by sending some messages.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way RootBridgeAgent handles incoming cross‑chain messages that carry native token fees via LayerZero v2 adapter parameters (airdrop). When a relayer forwards a message, it first transfers the specified native token amount to the RootBridgeAgent contract and then invokes the lzReceive function. Inside lzReceive the contract forwards the call to lzReceiveNonBlocking using an excessivelySafeCall and records the boolean success flag. If lzReceiveNonBlocking encounters an internal error – for example because a downstream call to the bridge executor reverts – the success flag becomes false. The code deliberately checks the caller (msg.sender) and only reverts when the caller is the ARB branch; for all other branches the transaction continues without reverting. As a result the native token that the relayer sent remains locked in the RootBridgeAgent balance. Because the transaction does not revert, no error event is emitted and the leftover ether is not obvious to observers. A malicious actor can later craft a second message with the fallback flag enabled. When this message is processed, the fallback routine _performFallbackCall is executed and it forwards the entire contract balance (including the previously stranded native token) back to the caller via the LayerZero endpoint. Consequently the attacker can drain the ether that was meant to pay relayer fees. The issue occurs only when messages are sent with v2 adapter parameters, when lzReceiveNonBlocking fails without triggering the fallback path, and when a subsequent fallback‑enabled message is processed. It affects the bridge protocol, any user who pays relayer fees, and the overall economic model because fees disappear from the contract. The problem was discovered during a security audit by tracing the execution flow of lzReceive and reproducing the failure scenario. It is hard to notice because the failure is silent – the transaction succeeds, the contract balance grows, and no explicit revert or event signals the loss. To remediate, the lzReceive function should either revert on any internal failure regardless of the caller or explicitly return the native token to the original message sender when success is false. Additionally, the contract should avoid using address(this).balance as the call value without accounting for any remainder, and it should emit an event whenever native tokens are refunded or reclaimed, ensuring transparent accounting.

title: Depositors could lose all their deposited tokens
description: All user deposited assets, both, hTokens and underlyingTokens are at risk of getting stuck in a BranchPort if the address of the depositor gets blacklisted in one of all the deposited underlyingTokens.
bug_full: The issue is an atomic batch redemption flaw in the bridge contract that prevents a depositor from retrieving any of their deposited assets when the depositor address is blacklisted by at least one of the underlying ERC20 tokens. The contract’s redeemDeposit function is hard‑coded to send each token back to msg.sender, which must be the original depositor address, and it does not allow the caller to specify an alternative recipient. When a blacklisted token rejects the transfer to the original address, the transfer call reverts, causing the entire for‑loop that processes all tokens to revert. Because the redemption is performed atomically – all tokens are transferred in a single transaction – the failure of a single token aborts the whole operation, leaving every token (both the blacklisted one and the other non‑blacklisted tokens) locked inside the BranchPort contract. This situation can be reproduced by depositing multiple tokens, including a token that implements a blacklist, then blacklisting the depositor address before calling redeemDeposit. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit by constructing a test that blacklists the recipient and observing that the redemption transaction reverts and the balances of the depositor remain unchanged while the BranchPort retains the tokens. It is hard to notice because the contract appears to work correctly for normal users; only when a blacklist is triggered does the failure surface, and the error message is a generic revert from the token contract rather than an explicit indication that the bridge logic is at fault. The impact is that users whose address is blacklisted – either intentionally or due to a compliance rule – lose access to all of their deposited assets, effectively causing funds to disappear from their perspective. The affected parties are depositors, the bridge protocol, and any downstream applications that rely on the ability to retrieve assets. The root cause is the lack of flexibility in the redemption path and the assumption that all token transfers will succeed, which violates the accounting invariant that each deposited token can be returned independently. To remediate, the redemption function should be modified to accept a receiver address supplied by the caller and use that address for each token transfer, allowing users to direct funds to an unblocked address or to a contract that can handle the blacklist situation. This change restores the ability to recover assets even when some tokens reject transfers to the original depositor, preserving the bridge’s safety guarantees and preventing total loss of funds.

title: Message channels can be blocked resulting in DoS
description:
The communication channel between a branch chain and a destination chain can be blocked by exploiting the ability to specify arbitrary gas parameters for the destination chain function calls. As Ulysses implements a non-blocking pattern, forcing the destination chain calls to revert creates an undesirable “in blocking” state.

In addition, as the requisite functions to clear the blocked channel were not implemented, the channel will remain blocked until a successful manual call to the blocked endpoint’s `retryPayload` (with appropriate gas parameters).

As this vulnerability is created by the confluence of multiple underlying issues these have been split into three Root Causes for clarity:

  * Issue A: User can specify any gas params [against best-practice guidelines](https://layerzero.gitbook.io/docs/evm-guides/best-practice#gas-for-message-types).
  * Issue B: The protocol implements a non-blocking implementation pattern for `lzReceive` and doesn’t handle the “in-blocking scenario”.
  * Issue C: The protocol doesn’t implement the `ILayerZeroUserApplicationConfig` functions as recommended.

It should also be noted that this can be exploited to cause economic damage to the protocol. In it’s current state the [manual call](https://github.com/LayerZero-Labs/LayerZero/blob/48c21c3921931798184367fc02d3a8132b041942/contracts/Endpoint.sol#L127-L142) to `Endpoint::retryPayload()` is the only way to clear the channel. If the griefer were to initiate a high payload size call on a low-cost branch like Polygon zkEVM or Optimism, then the team will need to pay the gas fees to process the griefing payload at the higher gas cost on Arbitrum.

Due to the ability to consistently (and at a low cost) block communication between the root chain and branch chain (which can only be unblocked through a manual intervention) the issue has been evaluated to high.
bug_full: The issue is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises when a user can supply arbitrary gas parameters for a LayerZero cross‑chain call. Because the Ulysses protocol relies on a non‑blocking pattern, it assumes that the destination contract’s lzReceive function will always succeed. When a caller sets the gasLimit to an extremely low value, the remote lzReceive call runs out of gas and reverts. The LayerZero endpoint then stores the failed payload and marks the channel as "in‑message‑blocking". Subsequent messages to the same destination chain are automatically rejected with the error "LayerZero: in message blocking", effectively halting all cross‑chain communication for that pair of chains. The protocol does not implement the ILayerZeroApplicationConfig interface, so it lacks the forceResumeReceive function that would normally allow the contract to clear the blocked state. The only available remediation is a manual call to Endpoint.retryPayload, which must be performed by the protocol team and incurs the full gas cost on the destination chain. This creates a scenario where an attacker can repeatedly trigger the blockage with cheap payloads on low‑cost branch chains (e.g., Polygon zkEVM or Optimism) and force the team to pay high gas fees on the root chain (e.g., Arbitrum) to unblock the channel. From a user perspective the symptoms are silent: a transaction to add a token or bridge assets appears to succeed on the source chain, but the token never appears on the destination chain, balances remain zero, and further bridge attempts fail without obvious on‑chain errors. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit through a proof‑of‑concept test that deliberately set gasLimit to 1, causing an out‑of‑gas revert on the remote side and confirming the blocking behaviour. The problem is hard to notice because the source‑chain transaction does not revert, and the failure only manifests as a missing asset on the destination chain. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum gas limit based on a reliable gas estimate before forwarding the message, reject user‑provided gas values that are too low, inherit from the official NonblockingLzApp example to correctly handle failed deliveries, and implement the ILayerZeroApplicationConfig interface so that forceResumeReceive can be used to programmatically clear a blocked channel without manual intervention.

title: Incorrect flag results to `_hasFallbackToggled` always set to false on `createMultipleSettlement`.
description: Function `_hasFallbackToggled` would be set to false on `createMultipleSettlement` regardless of user intentions.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect handling of the fallback flag in the multi‑asset settlement function. The contract receives a boolean parameter that indicates whether the caller wants a fallback mechanism, but the code that builds the payload always writes the same byte value regardless of the boolean. Specifically, the expression `_hasFallbackToggled ? bytes1(0x02) & 0x0F : bytes1(0x02)` evaluates to `bytes1(0x02)` in both branches, and later the receiving chain checks `payload[0] == 0x82` to decide if a fallback is enabled. Because the payload never contains `0x82`, the fallback condition is never true. The root cause is a logical error: the ternary operator does not produce distinct values and the bitwise mask does not change the constant, while the verification logic expects a different flag value. An attacker or a user cannot trigger the fallback even when they explicitly request it, which means that if the remote execution fails the transaction will revert without the safety net, potentially leaving funds locked or causing unexpected failures in downstream integrations. The bug manifests whenever `createMultipleSettlement` (or its internal helper) is called, independent of the boolean supplied, so any user who relies on the fallback feature is affected. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing test payloads with a simple contract and observing that the comparison against `0x82` always returned false. The issue is subtle because the flag appears to be configurable in the interface, yet the on‑chain logic silently ignores the choice, making it easy to miss during manual review. To remediate, the payload encoding must be corrected so that the true branch emits the distinct fallback flag (for example `bytes1(0x82)`) and the false branch emits the normal flag (`bytes1(0x02)`), and the receiving contract’s flag check should be aligned with these values. This change restores the intended business logic that a user who opts‑in to a fallback receives protection against remote execution failures, preserving expected accounting and preventing silent loss of funds.

title: Incorrect source address decoding in RootBridgeAgent and BranchBridgeAgent’s `_requiresEndpoint` breaks LayerZero communication
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect decoding of the source address in the cross‑chain messaging logic of the RootBridgeAgent and BranchBridgeAgent contracts that rely on the LayerZero endpoint. When a bridge agent sends a message it builds the _destination parameter by concatenating the remote contract address followed by its own address. The receiving agent, however, extracts the sender address from the last 20 bytes of the _srcAddress field supplied to lzReceive, assuming that those bytes contain the remote contract address. In reality LayerZero (and its mock implementation) places the caller address in the first 20 bytes and the remote address in the second 20 bytes, so the receiver always reads its own address instead of the true remote sender. This mismatch triggers a LayerZeroUnauthorizedCaller revert, causing every cross‑chain call to fail. The bug occurs whenever the agents attempt to communicate across chains, i.e. any call that goes through the _requiresEndpoint modifier or the internal _requiresEndpoint function. It affects all users who try to bridge tokens, the protocol’s liquidity, and any role that depends on successful inter‑chain messaging because the bridge becomes inoperable and assets become permanently locked on the source chain. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors instantiated the contracts with the LayerZero endpoint mock and observed that the validation always reverted despite correct configuration. It is hard to notice because the transaction that initiates the bridge may appear to succeed on the source chain, but the destination chain silently reverts, leaving the user with no received tokens and no obvious error message in the UI. From a user’s point of view the symptom is that a bridge operation completes on the sending side but the expected token balance on the receiving side remains unchanged or becomes zero, and no refund is issued. The bug belongs to the class of address‑encoding or message‑format mismatches in cross‑chain protocols, where the sender and receiver disagree on the layout of the address payload. To fix the problem the contracts must decode the source address from the first 20 bytes of _srcAddress (or adjust the encoding to match the receiver’s expectation) and update the requiresEndpoint checks accordingly. Adding integration tests with the official LzEndpointMock that verify correct address extraction will prevent the regression.

title: `ArbitrumCoreBranchRouter.executeNoSettlement` can’t handle `0x07` function
description: `ArbitrumCoreBranchRouter.executeNoSettlement` can’t handle the `setCoreBranchRouter` function.
poc:
ArbitrumCoreBranchRouter extends CoreBranchRouter and overrides its `executeNoSettlement` function. `CoreBranchRouter.executeNoSettlement` [can handle the 0x07 function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/CoreBranchRouter.sol#L140-L146), but `ArbitrumCoreBranchRouter.executeNoSettlement` [can’t](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-maia/blob/main/src/ArbitrumCoreBranchRouter.sol#L168-L170).

I believe this is because previously `CoreBranchRouter.executeNoSettlement` also [didn’t handle 0x07 function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-05-maia/blob/54a45beb1428d85999da3f721f923cbf36ee3d35/src/ulysses-omnichain/CoreBranchRouter.sol#L278-L280) and when support for it was added, ArbitrumCoreBranchRouter was not updated with new function.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ArbitrumCoreBranchRouter contract, specifically in its overridden executeNoSettlement function. This function is responsible for dispatching internal calls based on the function selector that is passed in the calldata. The parent contract CoreBranchRouter includes explicit handling for the selector 0x07, which corresponds to the setCoreBranchRouter function that updates the address of the core branch router. When the CoreBranchRouter implementation was extended, the child contract ArbitrumCoreBranchRouter replaced executeNoSettlement but failed to copy the new case for selector 0x07. As a result, any transaction that tries to invoke setCoreBranchRouter through the Arbitrum router is not recognised; the call falls through the dispatch logic and is effectively ignored or may trigger a generic revert. This omission is a classic example of an incomplete override where a child contract does not stay in sync with newly added functionality in its parent. An attacker or a legitimate user can exploit the bug by sending a calldata payload with the 0x07 selector to the Arbitrum router. Because the router does not process the selector, the intended update of the core branch router address never occurs. The immediate impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: the protocol can no longer change its routing configuration, which may prevent cross‑chain messages from being forwarded correctly and could cause funds to become stuck or misrouted. From a user’s perspective the UI may report that the transaction succeeded, yet the router address remains unchanged, leading to confusing symptoms such as “my router update did nothing” or “messages are not being delivered”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the executeNoSettlement implementations of the parent and child contracts and noticed that the child version omitted the newly added case. It is hard to notice because the selector handling is internal, there are no public events emitted for the missing case, and typical unit tests may only cover the parent implementation. To remediate the problem the child contract should be updated to include support for the 0x07 selector, either by calling the parent’s implementation (using super.executeNoSettlement) or by replicating the same dispatch logic. This ensures that the setCoreBranchRouter function can be executed correctly on Arbitrum, restoring the ability to reconfigure routing and preventing the denial‑of‑service scenario.

title: Chain support cannot be removed or cleared in bridge contracts
poc:
1. Admin configs the destination address in SourceBridge by calling `setDestinationChainContractAddress("optimism", destinationAddress)`.
2. Admin decides to remove support for Optimism.
3. Admin calls `setDestinationChainContractAddress("optimism", address(0))`, but this will actually store the string for the zero address `0x0000....000`.
4. The check `bytes(destContract).length == 0` will fail and messages will still be routed.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an immutable chain‑support configuration in both the source and destination bridge contracts. The contracts store the address of the remote contract as a string in a mapping for the source bridge and store a keccak256 hash of the string for the destination bridge. The source bridge validates support by checking that the stored string has a non‑zero length, while the destination bridge validates support by checking that the stored hash is not equal to bytes32(0). Because any address, including the zero address, is converted to a non‑empty string and any hash of a non‑empty string can never be bytes32(0), there is no way to clear the entry or mark a chain as unsupported after it has been added. Consequently, an owner (or an attacker who gains owner privileges) can call setDestinationChainContractAddress with address(0) or addChainSupport with a dummy address, but the checks will still treat the chain as supported. When a user invokes burnAndCallAxelar, the bridge will burn tokens on the source chain, assume the destination contract exists, and attempt to forward the message. Since the stored destination address resolves to the zero address string, no contract on the destination chain can receive the call, and the minted side never occurs, resulting in permanent loss of the burned tokens. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined how configuration values are stored and validated. It is subtle because the length‑based check appears to guard against an empty entry, yet the string representation of address(0) is 42 characters long, so the check passes silently. The bug belongs to the class of “immutable configuration / inability to deregister” errors, where a system lacks a proper removal or disable function for critical mappings. Users experience the symptom of tokens disappearing after a bridge transaction, with no error message indicating a missing destination. The impact is loss of funds and the inability for the protocol to deprecate a compromised or obsolete chain, violating expected business logic that a bridge operator should be able to stop supporting a chain. The recommended remediation is to add explicit removal functions that delete the mapping entries (or reset them to a sentinel value) and to adjust the validation logic to treat an empty string or a zero hash as unsupported. A more robust design would store addresses as address types rather than strings, eliminating the need for length checks and allowing a clear address(0) sentinel to be recognized as “unsupported”.

title: All bridged funds will be lost for the users using the account abstraction wallet
description: Users with account abstraction wallets have a different address across different chains for same account, so if someone using an account abstraction wallet bridge the asset, assets will be minted to wrong address and lost permanently.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the bridge contract assuming that the caller address (msg.sender) is identical on every EVM‑compatible chain. When a user employs an account abstraction (AA) wallet, the contract address that represents the wallet is generated independently on each chain, so the same logical account has different on‑chain addresses. The source bridge builds a payload that encodes msg.sender as the recipient on the destination chain and then forwards this payload to the Axelar gateway. On the destination side the execute function decodes the payload and mints the bridged tokens to the address that was supplied – the source‑chain AA wallet address. Because that address does not exist or is not owned by the user on the target chain, the minted tokens are effectively locked forever, resulting in a permanent loss of funds. This issue is triggered whenever a user with an AA wallet initiates a bridge operation through the affected contract; the user expects the tokens to appear in their wallet on the destination chain, but the balance remains zero and no error is emitted, making the problem easy to miss. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the payload construction and the decode logic, revealing the implicit cross‑chain address equality assumption. It belongs to the class of cross‑chain address‑mismatch or “wrong recipient” bugs, where a contract blindly forwards a sender address without verifying that the address is valid on the target network. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful bridge transaction, the source balance would be burned, yet the destination wallet would show no incoming funds, contradicting the expectation of a received refund or minted tokens. The impact is the irreversible disappearance of assets for any AA‑wallet holder, potentially affecting millions of users and billions of dollars as indicated by the Safe wallet statistics. To remediate the issue the bridge should not rely on msg.sender as the destination address; instead it must let the caller explicitly provide a destination address that is verified to belong to the caller on the target chain, and it should warn AA‑wallet users that the automatic address mapping is unsafe. A deterministic deployment approach cannot guarantee identical addresses across chains because each chain’s state and opcode set differ, so the safe fix is to decouple address selection from the source‑chain address entirely.

title: Two different transactions can result in the same `txnHash` value, thus breaking the approval process of transaction minting
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the bridge contract generates a unique identifier for incoming cross‑chain transactions. The internal function that processes a payload computes a transaction hash (txnHash) by hashing only four fields: version, the source sender address, the amount and a nonce. Because the source chain identifier and the source contract address are omitted from the hash input, two distinct messages that happen to contain identical values for those four fields will produce the exact same txnHash. When this occurs, the mapping that stores the Transaction struct (txnHashToTransaction) and the mapping that records the approval threshold (txnToThresholdSet) are indexed by the colliding hash. The later message overwrites the earlier entry, effectively discarding the original approval data. This breaks the intended multi‑signature or multi‑approval process for minting tokens through the bridge. An attacker who controls a contract on a different source chain can deliberately craft a payload that matches the version, sender, amount and nonce of a legitimate transaction, causing a hash collision. The malicious payload will replace the stored threshold, allowing the attacker’s transaction to be minted without the required number of approvals, or it can prevent a legitimate transaction from ever reaching the required approvals, resulting in a denial‑of‑service condition. The impact is medium severity because it can lead to unauthorized token minting, loss of trust in the bridge, and potential financial loss for users who rely on the bridge’s guarantees. The issue manifests only when two separate source chains (or two different source contracts on the same chain) submit payloads with identical version, sender, amount and nonce values. All participants that depend on the bridge’s approval logic – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors noticed that the nonce check only prevents reuse of a nonce for the same source address, but does not prevent different source addresses from reusing the same nonce together with identical other fields. Because the collision is deterministic and does not raise an explicit error, it can be hard to notice in normal operation; the overwritten mapping entry silently replaces the previous one. The recommended remediation is to extend the payload that is hashed to include the source chain identifier and the source contract address, ensuring that each incoming transaction has a globally unique hash. Alternatively, the contract could use a composite key that incorporates these fields directly in the mapping, or store a separate identifier alongside the hash. By making the identifier truly unique, the approval process will no longer be vulnerable to collision, and the bridge will correctly enforce the required number of approvals before minting. From a user’s perspective the bug may appear as a mint transaction succeeding without any visible approvals, or as a legitimate mint request failing because the required approvals seem to have vanished, leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds. This class of bug falls under hash‑collision or identifier‑collision vulnerabilities, where insufficient entropy in a unique key allows distinct operations to be treated as the same, breaking business logic that assumes uniqueness.

title: Scores.sol: Incorrect computation of user’s score when alpha is 1
description:
The formula for a user’s score depends on the `xvs` staked and the `capital`. One core variable in the calculation of a user’s score is `alpha` which represents the weight for `xvs` and `capital`. It has been stated in the [documentation](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-09-venus/blob/main/contracts/Tokens/Prime/README.md#rewards) that `alpha` can range from 0 to 1 depending on what kind of incentive the protocol wants to drive (XVS Staking or supply/borrow). Please review **_Significance of α_** subsection.

When `alpha` is 1, `xvs` has all the weight when calculating a user’s score, and `capital` has no weight. If we see the Cobb-Douglas function, the value of `capital` doesn’t matter, it will always return 1 since `capital^0` is always 1. So, a user does not need to borrow or lend in a given market since `capital` does not have any weight in the score calculation.

The issue is an inconsistency in the implementation of the Cobb-Douglas function.

Developers have added an exception: `if (xvs == 0 || capital == 0) return 0;`  
Because of this the code will always return 0 if either the `xvs` or the `capital` is zero, but we know this should not be the case when the `alpha` value is 1.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an edge‑case error in the score‑calculation routine that implements a Cobb‑Douglas function for the Venus protocol. The function is supposed to combine a user’s XVS stake (xvs) and supplied/borrowed capital (capital) using a weight parameter alpha that ranges from 0 to 1. When alpha equals 1 the specification states that the capital term should have zero weight, meaning the score should be computed solely from the xvs amount (capital^0 evaluates to 1). The contract, however, contains a guard clause that returns 0 whenever xvs or capital is zero (if (xvs == 0 || capital == 0) return 0;). Because this clause does not take alpha into account, the routine incorrectly returns a score of zero whenever capital is zero even though the mathematical model predicts a non‑zero result (xvs^1 * 0^0 = xvs). The bug was discovered during a security audit when a test case set alpha to 1, supplied a non‑zero xvs balance and a zero capital value, and observed that calculateScore returned 0 instead of the expected xvs‑derived score. The issue is subtle because the early‑return appears reasonable for most alpha values and the zero‑capital case is rarely exercised in normal operation, making it easy to miss during manual testing. Exploitation occurs when the protocol or an attacker configures alpha to 1 (or close to 1) and a user’s capital is zero; the user’s on‑chain score and consequently their reward allocation become zero despite holding a substantial XVS stake. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a score of 0 or no reward distribution, contradicting the expectation that staking XVS alone should generate rewards. This breaks the accounting assumptions of the reward system, potentially leading to loss of incentives for legitimate participants and mis‑allocation of rewards. The affected parties are all users who rely on XVS‑only incentives, the protocol’s reward distribution logic, and any auditors or developers reviewing the contract. The recommended fix is to modify the guard clause so that it only returns 0 when either xvs or capital is zero *and* alpha is not equal to 1, or to enforce that alpha is strictly between 0 and 1 (exclusive) and handle the zero‑capital case explicitly. By correcting the conditional logic the function will respect the documented behavior of the Cobb‑Douglas formula and compute the correct score when capital has no weight.

title: DoS and gas griefing of calls to Prime.updateScores
description: `updateScores()` is meant to be called to update the scores of many users after reward alpha is changed or reward multipliers are changed. An attacker can cause calls to `Prime.updateScores()` to out-of-gas revert, delaying score updates. Rewards will be distributed incorrectly until scores are properly updated.
bug_full: The contract provides a function that iterates over a list of user addresses to refresh each participant’s score after a change in reward parameters. The loop is written with a manual index variable that is incremented only inside an unchecked block after the main logic. When the function encounters a user whose score has already been marked as updated for the current round, it executes a `continue` statement before reaching the unchecked increment. Because the increment is skipped, the index does not advance and the loop repeats the same iteration indefinitely until the transaction runs out of gas. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running a legitimate call with a separate call that updates a single already‑updated address, causing the subsequent call to hit the `continue` path for that address and never move past it. The result is an out‑of‑gas revert that prevents the rest of the users from being processed. This denial‑of‑service and gas‑griefing condition occurs only when the input array contains at least one address that is already up‑to‑date for the current scoring round. The affected parties are token holders who expect their scores to be refreshed and rewards to be distributed correctly, as well as any caller of the update function who may lose a large amount of gas. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the loop’s increment was placed after a `continue`, creating a scenario where the loop could stall. The bug is subtle because the code otherwise appears normal; the failure manifests as a generic out‑of‑gas error rather than an explicit revert, making it easy to overlook during testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of loop‑control errors that can cause infinite or unbounded iteration, leading to denial‑of‑service. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that after a change in the reward multiplier the pending rewards remain zero or unchanged, contrary to the expectation that they should increase. The protocol’s accounting assumption that scores are refreshed each round is violated, resulting in incorrect reward calculations. The proper fix is to ensure the loop index is always incremented regardless of whether a `continue` is taken, for example by moving the increment into the for‑header (`for (uint256 i = 0; i < users.length; ++i)`) or by placing the increment before the `continue` statement. This eliminates the possibility of the loop stalling and prevents the out‑of‑gas denial‑of‑service and gas‑griefing attack.

title: The `owner` is a single point of failure and a centralization risk
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a design flaw where the contract’s administrative functions are restricted to a single owner address, which in this deployment is a single externally owned account (EOA) or a single timelock contract. Because only one key or one contract can execute privileged actions such as initializing token lists, changing the primary token, or sweeping tokens, the system creates a single point of failure and a centralization risk. The root cause is the use of the onlyOwner modifier without any multi‑signature or role‑based fallback, meaning that control is not distributed among multiple parties. An attacker who compromises the owner’s private key, or who gains control over the timelock contract, can invoke any of the privileged functions and, for example, replace the token list, set a malicious token as the prime token, or transfer arbitrary amounts of ERC‑20 tokens to an address of their choice. This can result in loss of user funds, unauthorized token swaps, or a complete freeze of the liquidity provider because the owner could also disable further initialization. The exploit can be carried out at any time after deployment, as soon as the attacker obtains the owner credentials, and does not require any special conditions beyond key compromise. All users of the PrimeLiquidityProvider contract are affected because the contract holds pooled assets that are meant to be managed by a decentralized governance process; the centralization undermines the trust model and may cause users to receive zero refunds or see their balances disappear. The issue was identified during a manual audit that flagged the presence of onlyOwner functions without any additional governance safeguards. It can be hard to notice because the contract appears to be governed by a timelock, yet the timelock itself is a single address that can be controlled by a single entity, and the code does not enforce any multi‑party approval. The recommended remediation is to replace the single‑owner model with a multi‑signature wallet or a role‑based access control system where critical functions require approval from several independent parties, thereby removing the single point of failure and aligning the contract with decentralized governance expectations. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of centralization and ownership concentration vulnerabilities, where privileged operations are gated by a single authority, leading to potential fund theft, protocol manipulation, or service interruption if that authority is compromised or unavailable.

title: EXTH-1 | Lack of Contract Existence Check
description: The low-level call returns a success boolean of true if the target contract does not exist. As a result, the migration may not detect some failed external calls, leading to loss of funds for users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing contract‑existence verification before performing a low‑level call during the migration process. Because Solidity’s low‑level call returns a boolean that is true whenever the call does not revert, it also returns true when the target address contains no contract code. The root cause is that the migration contract assumes a true return value guarantees successful execution, but it does not check whether the callee actually exists. An attacker or a simple deployment mistake can cause the migration to invoke a non‑existent contract, for example when a token address is mistyped or the old contract has been self‑destructed. The call will succeed silently, the boolean will be true, and the migration logic will continue as if the external operation (such as a token transfer or state update) succeeded. Consequently, user funds may be sent to an address with no code and become unrecoverable, or the expected state change (e.g., balance update) will not happen. This situation occurs whenever the migration code uses low‑level .call or .call{value:…} without first confirming that address.code.length > 0. All users who rely on the migration to move their assets are affected, as are the protocol’s reputation and financial integrity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that flagged the absence of an existence check. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert, no error event is emitted, and the UI may simply show a successful migration while the balance on the destination contract remains unchanged. The proper fix is to add a contract‑existence guard – for example, require(address(target).code.length > 0) – before any low‑level call, or to replace low‑level calls with interface calls that automatically revert when the target contract does not exist. This change ensures that a missing contract is detected early, preventing silent loss of funds and preserving the expected accounting logic of the migration.

title: EXTH-2 | Lack Of safeTransfer For Arbitrary Token
description: In the makeExternalCalls function, the arbitrary refundToken is transferred using the transfer function, however safeTransfer should be used to avoid potential loss if the token chooses to return false rather than reverting upon failure.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of the standard ERC20 transfer function when the contract attempts to send an arbitrary refund token in the makeExternalCalls routine. Transfer simply forwards the call to the token contract and assumes success, but many ERC20 implementations deviate from the specification by returning a boolean value instead of reverting on failure. Because the code does not check the returned boolean, a token that returns false will cause the contract to believe the transfer succeeded while no tokens are actually moved. This can be exploited by an attacker who supplies a malicious or non‑standard token as the refundToken; the token’s transfer function can silently fail, allowing the contract to retain the funds that should have been refunded. The impact is that users requesting a refund may receive nothing, see their balances unchanged, or observe a successful transaction in the UI while the funds remain locked in the contract. The issue manifests only when the refundToken does not follow the expected revert‑on‑failure behavior, which is common for older or custom tokens. All participants who rely on the refund mechanism – typically end‑users and any downstream protocol that assumes refunds are honoured – are affected. The flaw was identified during a manual audit that highlighted the lack of a safety wrapper around external token transfers. Because the failure is silent, it can be difficult to notice without explicit return‑value checks or extensive testing with a variety of token contracts. The proper remediation is to replace direct calls to transfer with a safeTransfer pattern (for example, OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20.safeTransfer) that validates the boolean result and reverts on failure, thereby guaranteeing that either the tokens are transferred or the transaction aborts. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “unchecked external call” or “ERC20 transfer return‑value” bugs, where the contract assumes success without verification, breaking accounting assumptions and leading to potential loss of funds.

title: GLOBAL-2 | LayerZero Message Blocking
description:
LayerZero implements blocking functionality such that when a transaction on the destination chain fails, before any new transactions can be executed, the failed transaction has to be retried until success. A malicious user can submit a deposit or withdrawal they know will fail, and will prevent all other deposits and withdrawals from occurring, leading to loss of protocol functionality and loss of funds for those who already deposited. Some methods a malicious user can use to force such a scenario include but are not limited to:
1) Broker is allowed for Vault on srcChain but disallowed on the VaultManager on dstChain. The configuration of these two contracts aren’t atomic.
2) depositTo for an address that is blacklisted for the collateral token. When the blacklisted address triggers a withdraw action, the Vault withdrawal will revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from LayerZero's default blocking mode, which requires a failed cross‑chain transaction on the destination chain to be retried before any new messages are processed. When a malicious actor deliberately initiates a deposit or withdrawal that is guaranteed to revert on the destination chain, the LayerZero endpoint marks the message as failed and blocks the entire outbound queue. Because the protocol relies on the blocking behavior, no further deposit or withdrawal messages can be delivered until the failing message is successfully retried, which in practice may never happen if the underlying condition (such as a mismatched broker permission or a blacklisted address) remains unchanged. This design flaw allows an attacker to freeze the protocol’s core functionality: legitimate users attempting to deposit collateral or withdraw funds see their transactions remain pending, UI balances stay unchanged, and the system appears unresponsive. The impact is a loss of protocol availability and potential loss of funds that were already deposited but cannot be withdrawn because the retry mechanism is stuck. The issue occurs only when the contract configuration on the source and destination chains is not atomic – for example, the source vault permits a broker while the destination vault manager does not, or a withdrawal is triggered by an address that is blacklisted for the collateral token, causing an automatic revert. The affected parties include any user of the deposit or withdrawal functions, the protocol operators who cannot process new requests, and ultimately the ecosystem that depends on timely cross‑chain asset movement. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined the interaction between LayerZero's messaging layer and the protocol’s vault contracts, noting that the blocking semantics are rarely exercised in normal operation and therefore can be overlooked. The difficulty in spotting the bug arises because the system behaves correctly until a deliberately failing message is injected; there is no explicit error flag indicating that the message queue is halted, only the absence of progress. To remediate the issue, the protocol should adopt LayerZero's non‑blocking pattern, which decouples message failure from the processing of subsequent messages and stores failed messages in a retry queue that can be handled off‑chain or by an admin. Additionally, the contract should ensure that permission settings and blacklisting rules are synchronized across chains, or that any operation that could revert is guarded with pre‑checks before invoking the cross‑chain call. By moving to a non‑blocking architecture and tightening configuration consistency, the protocol can prevent a single malicious transaction from halting all cross‑chain activity and protect user funds from being unintentionally locked.

title: Insufficient validation of new Fertilizer IDs allow for a denial-of-service (DoS) attack on `SeasonFacet::gm` when above peg, once the last element in the FIFO is paid
poc:
[This coded PoC](https://gist.github.com/carlitox477/1b0dde178288982f4e25d40b9e43e626) can be run by:
1. Creating file `Beantalk/protocol/test/POCs/mint0Fertilizer.test.js`
2. Navigating to `Beantalk/protocol`
3. Running `yarn test --grep "DOS last fertilizer payment through minting 0 fertilizers"`
bug_full: The vulnerability is an insufficient validation of newly minted Fertilizer NFT identifiers that allows a self‑referential entry to be inserted into the FIFO queue used for tracking outstanding fertilizer bonds. The root cause lies in the push logic of the Fertilizer FIFO: when a Fertilizer with zero amount is minted twice, the condition that prevents duplicate identifiers checks only for a strictly greater balance (s.fertilizer[id] > amount) instead of a greater‑or‑equal check, so the second insertion is accepted even though the amount is zero. This creates a node whose next pointer references itself, meaning the pop routine can never advance past this element because getNext returns the same id and the activeFertilizer subtraction is zero. When the Bean price is above the peg, the Sun contract calls rewardToFertilizer, which iterates over the FIFO list using a while loop that expects each pop to eventually reach the end of the queue. Encountering the self‑referential node causes the loop to run indefinitely, blocking the execution of SeasonFacet::gm and effectively halting the season step. The impact is a denial‑of‑service: the protocol cannot progress to the next season, harvests stop, and users see transactions hanging or reverting, with no new rewards being distributed. The condition only manifests after the protocol has fully recapitalized the stolen liquidity and the Bean price remains above peg, because only then does rewardToFertilizer get invoked and the last element of the queue is processed. All participants—farmers, token holders, and the DAO—are affected because the core economic cycle is frozen. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test which minted two zero‑amount Fertilizers and observed the infinite loop. It is hard to notice because a zero‑amount Fertilizer appears harmless and the FIFO structure otherwise behaves correctly, so the self‑reference does not raise an obvious error flag. The bug violates the business logic that each Fertilizer entry must be payable and removable, breaking the accounting assumption that the total active fertilizer amount will eventually be reduced to zero. The recommended fix is to change the duplicate‑id guard to use a greater‑or‑equal comparison (>=) so that a zero‑amount insertion does not create a duplicate entry, thereby preventing the self‑referential node and restoring the ability of pop to terminate the loop. In broader terms, this is a classic queue‑corruption vulnerability where inadequate input validation permits the creation of a cyclic linked list, leading to infinite iteration and service denial.

title: GLPM-3 | Additional Ether Lost
description: If the provided msg.value is greater than the executionFee * migrationItems.length then the excess Ether is not refunded to the user and can be used by the user who calls the migrate function next.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑payment and missing‑refund bug in the migration function of the contract. When a caller invokes migrate and supplies a msg.value that exceeds the required execution fee multiplied by the number of migration items, the contract does not return the surplus Ether to the caller. The root cause is the absence of a validation check that enforces msg.value to equal executionFee * migrationItems.length and the lack of a refund mechanism for any excess amount. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately sending more Ether than required; the contract will retain the extra funds, which become available to the next address that calls migrate, effectively allowing the attacker to capture Ether that should have been refunded. The impact is a loss of user funds: a user who overpays sees a reduced balance after the transaction, and the subsequent caller can withdraw the unrefunded Ether, leading to unintended transfer of value. This condition occurs only when the supplied Ether is greater than the exact fee needed for the migration batch; normal calls with exact payment are unaffected. All participants who can call migrate – typically any external account – are potentially affected, especially those who unintentionally overpay. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee calculation logic and noticed the missing equality check and refund path. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and appears successful, while the excess Ether silently disappears from the sender’s balance, producing a subtle discrepancy that may only be observed when comparing expected versus actual post‑transaction balances. To remediate, the contract should enforce that msg.value matches the exact required fee and, if any surplus is detected, automatically refund the difference to the caller before proceeding with the migration logic. This aligns the implementation with standard accounting principles that require precise payment handling and prevents unintended fund loss, restoring trust that users receive exactly the amount they expect to pay and no more.

title: GLPM-4 | User Forced To Deposit Both Tokens
description: In RewardRouter.sol for GMX V1, function unstakeAndRedeemGlp() requires that _glpAmount > 0: require(_glpAmount > 0, "RewardRouter: invalid _glpAmount"); In the GlpMigrator contract, if a user wants to only redeem for a the long token in a market, and leaves the GlpRedemption short with migrationItem.short.glpAmount = 0, the migration will fail due to the above revert. This is unexpected behavior as it forces users to not only populate the migrationItem.short.token to match the market's short token, but also set a miniscule amount of glpAmount to redeem for the short token to avoid migration failure. The same behavior applies if a user wants to solely redeem for the short token in a market, and leave the long token untouched.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a strict input validation in the RewardRouter contract of GMX V1, where the function unstakeAndRedeemGlp() contains a require statement that enforces the supplied GLP amount to be greater than zero (require(_glpAmount > 0, "RewardRouter: invalid _glpAmount")). In the migration workflow implemented by the GlpMigrator contract, a user may wish to redeem only the long token or only the short token of a market. When the migration request sets the GLP amount for the opposite side to zero – for example, leaving migrationItem.short.glpAmount equal to 0 while redeeming the long token – the call to unstakeAndRedeemGlp() for the zero‑amount side triggers the require check and reverts the entire migration transaction. This behavior forces users to artificially populate a non‑zero GLP amount for a token they do not intend to receive, effectively compelling them to deposit both tokens even when only one is desired. The issue is discovered during a security audit that examined the migration logic and identified the mismatch between the contract’s expectations and the intended user flow. It is subtle because the revert message only mentions an invalid amount, offering no direct hint that a zero amount is disallowed for a token that the user deliberately omitted. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show the migration attempt as successful, but the transaction fails, leaving balances unchanged and providing no refund or token transfer – the user expects to receive the long token but receives nothing, or sees a “transaction reverted” error without a clear explanation. The impact is primarily a denial‑of‑service or usability problem: users cannot perform single‑sided redemptions without adding a minuscule, unnecessary amount, which may lead to confusion, extra gas costs, or accidental token transfers. The affected parties are any GMX V1 users performing token migrations, as well as the protocol’s migration tooling that relies on this function. The root cause is the hard‑coded requirement that GLP amounts be non‑zero, which does not align with the legitimate use case of zero‑amount redemptions. To remediate the issue, the migration logic should be adjusted to detect a zero GLP amount for either side and simply skip the corresponding unstakeAndRedeemGlp() call, allowing the migration to proceed with only the intended token. This change restores the expected business logic where users can redeem a single token without being forced to provide a dummy amount, eliminating the unexpected revert and aligning contract behavior with user expectations.

title: GLPM-5 | Reduced Burn Fee Can Be Larger Than Current
description: GMX is choosing to reduce the burn fee to further incentivize migration from GMX V1 to its latest GMX V2 system. However, there is no guarantee that the reducedMintBurnFeeBasisPoints is less than or equal to the current mintBurnFeeBasisPoints. The burn fee can be increased to be larger than its current value, causing users to redeem less tokens than expected.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑validation flaw in the migration logic of the GMX protocol. When the system attempts to lower the mint‑burn fee for users moving from GMX V1 to V2, it relies on a modifier called withReducedRedemptionFees that updates the fee based on a parameter named _reducedMintBurnFeeBasisPoints. The contract does not enforce that this new fee value must be less than or equal to the existing mintBurnFeeBasisPoints. As a result, a caller with permission to set the reduced fee can inadvertently or maliciously provide a value that is higher than the current fee. This mis‑configuration causes the burn fee applied during token redemption to increase instead of decrease, so users receive fewer tokens than they expect. The issue manifests when the migration function is executed and the fee‑update branch is taken; the condition that should compare the new fee to the old one is missing, allowing the fee to be set to any arbitrary basis‑point value. Users are affected because the UI may display a “reduced fee” message while the on‑chain calculation actually burns a larger portion of their tokens, leading to a discrepancy between displayed expectations and actual outcomes. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee‑adjustment logic and noticed the absence of a safety check. It can be hard to notice because the fee reduction is advertised, yet the contract does not validate the direction of change, and the resulting loss appears only after redemption, when users see a smaller token balance or receive zero tokens for a given amount. The impact is a financial loss for migrating users and a breach of trust in the protocol’s fee transparency. To remediate, the modifier should include a comparison such as bool shouldUpdateFees = _reducedMintBurnFeeBasisPoints < mintBurnFeeBasisPoints; and only apply the update when the new fee is strictly lower, thereby preserving the intended incentive structure and preventing accidental fee inflation.

title: GLPM-6 | Lists With Different Lengths
description: The externalCallTargets and externalCallDataList are used to call an external protocol with user-passed data. However, externalCallDataList may have a different length than externalCallTargets, potentially causing an out-of-bounds error or the incorrect data being used for a particular target. Similarly, refundTokens and refundReceivers may be different lengths, potentially causing an out-of-bounds error or funds being sent to an unintended receiver.
bug_full: The contract exposes a function that accepts two parallel arrays for making external calls – a list of target addresses (externalCallTargets) and a list of calldata blobs (externalCallDataList) – as well as two parallel arrays for handling refunds – a list of token contracts (refundTokens) and a list of receiver addresses (refundReceivers). The implementation iterates over each array assuming that the corresponding entries line up by index, but it does not verify that the lengths of the paired arrays are equal. As a result, if a caller provides mismatched lengths, the loop may read past the end of the shorter array, causing an out‑of‑bounds access that can revert the transaction, or it may pair a target with the wrong calldata or a token with the wrong receiver. This misalignment can lead to external protocol calls being executed with incorrect data, which may trigger unintended behavior in the called contract, and it can cause refunds to be sent to an unintended address or not sent at all. The vulnerability is rooted in the lack of input validation for parallel array lengths, a common class of bug where related data structures are not kept in sync. It is exploitable whenever a user can control the contents of these arrays – an attacker can deliberately craft mismatched inputs to cause a revert (denial‑of‑service) or to redirect funds to an address they control. The impact includes loss of user funds, failed migrations, and broken accounting assumptions because the protocol expects each token to be refunded to a specific receiver. The issue manifests under the condition that the migration function is called with arrays of differing sizes, which may happen unintentionally due to UI bugs or maliciously by an adversary. Users affected are token holders attempting to migrate, the protocol that relies on correct refunds, and any external contracts called with malformed data. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the absence of length checks for these arrays. It can be hard to notice because the contract may still execute when the shorter array is accessed only up to its length, silently pairing wrong elements without an immediate error, leading to subtle fund misdirection. To remediate, the contract should enforce that each pair of parallel arrays has identical length before entering the processing loops, for example by adding require statements that compare externalCallTargets.length with externalCallDataList.length and refundTokens.length with refundReceivers.length. This validation ensures that every target has a matching calldata entry and every token has a matching receiver, preserving the intended business logic and preventing out‑of‑bounds errors or incorrect fund transfers.

title: GLOBAL-3 | Centralization Risk
description: Throughout the smart contract system there is a lack of validation to prevent privileged addresses from taking malicious actions or even committing errors that have drastic consequences. Executing malicious withdrawals, settlements, ADLs, and liquidations. No validation that the liquidationFee = liquidatorFee + insuranceFee. No validation that the ratio of positionQtyTransfer to costPositionTransfer is accurate to the adlPrice provided. No validation that tokens being actively used as collateral cannot be removed from support, causing liquidations and insolvency. No validation that trade.notional = trade.tradeQty * trade.executedPrice in the executeProcessValidatedFutures function. No cap on configured values such as the maxWithdrawalFee and liquidationFeeMax. No cap on the liquidationFee as the liquidationFeeMax is unused at the contract level.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a systemic lack of input validation and safety checks that gives privileged addresses unchecked authority over critical financial operations. Because the contracts do not verify that fees, ratios, or collateral constraints are correct, a privileged actor can submit malformed parameters that bypass accounting rules. For example, the liquidation fee is not required to equal the sum of the liquidator fee and the insurance fee, the ratio between transferred position quantity and transferred cost is not checked against the advertised ADL price, and the trade notional is not enforced as the product of trade quantity and executed price. Additionally, there is no cap on configurable values such as maximum withdrawal fee or liquidation fee, and the maximum liquidation fee variable is never consulted, allowing arbitrarily large fees to be set. Tokens that are being used as collateral can be removed from the list of supported assets without any guard, which can trigger unexpected liquidations and potentially render the protocol insolvent. These omissions mean that a privileged address – typically the contract owner or an admin role – can execute malicious withdrawals, settlements, automatic debt liquidations (ADLs), and liquidations that do not respect the protocol’s economic assumptions. The impact is that users may see their balances reduced unexpectedly, receive zero or partial refunds, have positions liquidated despite sufficient collateral, or lose funds to inflated fees. The issue manifests whenever a privileged function is called, especially during withdrawal, liquidation, or trade settlement, and it affects every participant who relies on the protocol’s accounting integrity, including traders, lenders, and liquidity providers. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted missing require statements and unchecked arithmetic in the privileged pathways. Because the contract behaves as designed – it simply lacks the necessary checks – the problem can be subtle and may not produce obvious error messages; the UI may show successful transaction receipts while the underlying accounting is corrupted. To remediate, the protocol should introduce explicit validation of all fee relationships, enforce correct ratio calculations for position transfers, ensure that trade notional matches quantity times price, prevent removal of active collateral assets, and apply sensible caps to configurable fee parameters. These safeguards would transform the privileged functions from unrestricted power blocks into well‑constrained operations that preserve user funds and maintain the intended economic model.

title: MKTM-1 | Incorrect updatedAt Assigned
description: In the updateMarketUpload functions for both the perp prices and sumUnitaryFundings the lastMarkPriceUpdated and lastFundingUpdated are set to the block.timestamp. However, these attributes ought to be set to the perpPrice.timestamp and sumUnitaryFunding.timestamp as these are the timestamps from which the data was recorded. Using the block.timestamp for the lastFundingUpdated and lastMarkPriceUpdated values is not in line with the logic in the Ledger.executeProcessValidatedFutures function where the lastFundingUpdated is assigned to the trade.timestamp rather than the block.timestamp.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect timestamp assignment in the market upload functions that handle perpetual price updates and sum unitary funding updates. Instead of recording the timestamp that originates from the uploaded market data (perpPrice.timestamp or sumUnitaryFunding.timestamp), the contract stores the current block.timestamp in the state variables lastMarkPriceUpdated and lastFundingUpdated. This mismatch occurs because the Ledger.executeProcessValidatedFutures routine expects the lastFundingUpdated field to reflect the trade timestamp, not the block timestamp, and therefore the contract’s logic diverges from the intended accounting model. An attacker or even a benign user can exploit this by triggering market uploads at arbitrary times; the contract will believe the price or funding data is newer than it actually is, causing downstream calculations that rely on these timestamps—such as funding rate settlements, price oracle validation, and trade profit‑loss computation—to use stale or artificially shifted time references. The impact is that funding payments may be applied at incorrect intervals, leading to over‑ or under‑payment, and price updates may appear out of sync with the real market, potentially resulting in traders receiving unexpected funding amounts or seeing their positions settle with wrong rates. The condition under which the bug manifests is any execution of the updateMarketUpload functions for perpetual prices or sum unitary fundings; each call writes block.timestamp to the tracking fields. All participants who rely on accurate funding timestamps—traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the accounting assumptions of “funding is calculated from the exact moment the data was recorded” are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the contract’s timestamp handling does not follow the pattern used elsewhere in the Ledger module. Because timestamps are internal and not directly exposed in the UI, the problem can be hard to notice; users may only observe symptoms such as missing funding payments, unexpected zero balances after a trade, or price charts that seem to jump. The bug belongs to the class of state‑variable misassignment or timestamp mismatch errors, where a contract records an incorrect source of truth for time‑sensitive data. To remediate, the contract should assign the data’s own timestamp to the tracking variables (e.g., cfg.setLastFundingUpdated(data.timestamp) and cfg.setLastMarkPriceUpdated(data.timestamp)) so that the ledger’s execution logic aligns with the actual moment the market data was captured, restoring correct funding calculations and price update sequencing.

title: LGR-5 | Potential For Trapped Deposits
description: In the event that the accountDeposit function execution reverts, there is no recourse for the user to recover their deposit in the vault. The accountDeposit function may revert if the AccountDeposit data carries a brokerHash or tokenHash & srcChainId that does not agree with the configuration in the vaultManager contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a deposit‑trapping condition in the cross‑chain vault. When a user calls accountDeposit, the function validates that the supplied brokerHash, tokenHash and srcChainId match the configuration stored in the vaultManager contract. If any of these identifiers are inconsistent, the call reverts. Because the contract does not provide a fallback or withdrawal path for deposits that reverted, the ether or token that was transferred to the vault before the revert becomes permanently locked. The root cause is the lack of a recovery mechanism after a failed cross‑chain deposit and the reliance on a single external validation that can cause a revert. An attacker or a misconfigured client can trigger the revert by supplying incorrect identifiers, causing the transaction to fail while the user's funds remain in the vault with no way to be withdrawn. The impact is that users may lose access to their deposited assets; from the UI perspective the deposit appears to have been sent, but the balance shown by the vault remains unchanged or zero, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust. The condition occurs only when the deposit transaction reaches the point of validation and the data does not align with the vaultManager configuration; normal deposits with correct data succeed. All participants who rely on the vault for cross‑chain liquidity—individual users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because trapped funds reduce available liquidity and break accounting assumptions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the error‑handling paths of the accountDeposit function and noted the absence of any method to retrieve funds after a revert. Because the failure manifests as a silent loss of funds rather than an explicit error message, it can be hard to notice without tracing internal state changes. The bug belongs to the class of “funds‑locking due to unchecked revert” or “incomplete error recovery” vulnerabilities, where a contract accepts value before performing a check that may revert, but does not provide a compensating withdrawal function.
