To remediate, the contract should either perform the validation before accepting funds, or implement a user‑initiated claim/withdraw function that allows the depositor to retrieve assets when a deposit transaction fails, possibly with a retry or timeout mechanism. Adding proper event emission and UI feedback for failed deposits would also align user expectations (the user expects the deposit to be credited, but receives nothing) with actual contract behavior.

title: LGR-6 | Insurance Account May Become Insolvent
description: When liquidatable accounts cannot cover the liquidatorFee with their remaining margin, all positions in the account and the remaining margin balance are transferred to the insurance fund. In times of volatility, several accounts may become insolvent and all have their positions transferred to the insurance account. The insurance account may then find itself to be insolvent, in which case ADL will not be sufficient to remedy the situation. The insurance account is also intended to cover insolvent accounts where the settled PnL is more negative than the account margin. This behavior can also be a pathway for the insurance account to become insolvent, especially when combined with receiving positions from insolvent accounts.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the insurance account that is intended to act as a safety net for liquidated positions that cannot be fully covered by the remaining margin of a trader. When a trader’s account becomes liquidatable and the residual margin is insufficient to pay the liquidator fee, the protocol transfers all open positions together with the leftover margin into the insurance fund. In periods of high volatility, many accounts may simultaneously fail to meet the fee requirement, causing a cascade of position transfers into the insurance pool. Because the insurance pool is not equipped with an automatic replenishment mechanism and because the auto‑deleveraging (ADL) process may not be able to unwind the incoming positions quickly enough, the total value of assets held by the insurance account can fall below the liabilities it must cover. This creates a state of insolvency where the insurance fund cannot honor the promised payouts for users whose positions were supposed to be protected. The issue is rooted in the protocol’s accounting logic that assumes the insurance pool will always retain enough capital after absorbing failed accounts, an assumption that breaks down when multiple insolvent accounts are processed together. Exploitation does not require a direct attack; an adversary could deliberately trigger a large number of liquidations—by, for example, creating market pressure or submitting under‑collateralised orders—to force the insurance pool into a deficit. The impact is that users expecting a refund or compensation may receive nothing, balances displayed in the UI may appear as zero or missing, and the overall trust in the protocol can be eroded because the promised safety net fails. The condition manifests only under extreme market stress, making it difficult to observe during routine testing or normal operation. The flaw was identified during a security audit performed by the Guardian team, who noted that the logical flow of liquidation and fee handling does not include a contingency for the insurance fund’s capital depletion. Because the problem only appears when several accounts become insolvent at once, it can be missed by standard unit tests that cover single‑account scenarios. To remediate the issue, the protocol should introduce a capital‑buffer strategy for the insurance pool, such as automatic deposits when the fund’s balance approaches a predefined threshold, limits on the amount of positions that can be transferred in a single block, or enhancements to the ADL mechanism to ensure it can reliably unwind large position volumes. In essence, the design must be changed so that the insurance account is never relied upon to cover more loss than its available capital, thereby preserving the economic guarantees made to users.

title: GLOBAL-5 | Liquidations When Deposits Paused
description: When the Vault is paused, functions deposit and depositTo are prevented from being processed. As a result, the protocol can reach a state where liquidations can occur while deposits are paused, preventing users from keeping their positions solvent.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical inconsistency in the pause mechanism of the vault contract. When the vault is placed in a paused state, the deposit and depositTo functions are deliberately blocked to prevent new collateral from being added. However, the liquidation routine remains active, allowing the protocol to liquidate under‑collateralised positions even though users are unable to increase their collateral. This mismatch occurs because the pause flag is only checked in the deposit pathways and not in the liquidation entry point, creating a gap in state management. An attacker or any external actor does not need to exploit code execution; the exploit is triggered simply by invoking the pause function, after which any existing risky positions can be forced into liquidation without the user having a chance to remedy the shortfall. The impact is that users may lose a portion of their collateral or see their positions closed unexpectedly, leading to a reduction of funds that appear to “disappear” from their perspective. The condition arises whenever the protocol administrator pauses the vault – for example during an emergency or upgrade – while there are still open positions that are close to the liquidation threshold. All users with open leveraged positions are affected because they cannot add more margin, yet the system still enforces liquidation rules. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the pause semantics and noticed that the liquidation function did not reference the paused state. Because the behaviour only manifests under the specific circumstance of a paused vault with borderline positions, it can be easy to miss in routine testing where deposits and liquidations are exercised together. The bug belongs to the class of “inconsistent state handling” or “partial pause” vulnerabilities, where a global safety switch does not uniformly guard all critical operations. From a user’s point of view the UI may show a normal balance, but after the pause the position is liquidated and the displayed collateral drops to zero or a much lower amount, contradicting the expectation that pausing should protect the user from further loss. To remediate, the contract should either also block liquidation while the vault is paused, or at minimum emit clear documentation and warnings that liquidation can still occur, allowing users to withdraw or close positions before a pause is enacted. Conceptually the fix is to ensure that any operation that can change a user’s financial state respects the paused flag, thereby preserving the intended safety guarantees of the pause feature.

title: GLOBAL-6 | Lacking Storage Gaps
description: There are several Component abstract contracts that intend to be parents of upgradeable contracts, however they lack an appropriate _gap storage variable. For example, the LedgerComponent contract is an abstract contract that is meant to be inherited by upgradeable contracts, however there is a ledgerAddress storage variable defined in the LedgerComponent followed by no gap variable in the event that more variables would be added to the LedgerComponent contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing storage gap in abstract contracts that are intended to be used as base contracts for upgradeable implementations. Upgradeable contracts rely on a fixed storage layout that must remain compatible across contract versions. When a base contract does not reserve unused storage slots through a _gap variable, any future addition of state variables in that base contract or in contracts that inherit from it can shift the storage layout. This shift causes new variables to occupy storage slots that were previously used for existing data, leading to storage collisions. An attacker or a careless developer can exploit this by deploying an upgraded version that introduces new state variables without accounting for the missing gap, causing critical data such as addresses, balances, or configuration flags to be overwritten. The impact may include corrupted ledger addresses, incorrect balance values, failed refunds, or even loss of funds if the overwritten data controls token transfers. The issue manifests only when a contract is upgraded to a version that adds new storage variables to a base contract lacking a gap; in a static deployment the bug remains dormant. All users of the protocol, including token holders and integrators, are affected because the corrupted state can lead to unexpected UI behavior such as zero balances, missing payouts, or transactions reverting. The problem was discovered during a manual audit where the auditor inspected the inheritance hierarchy and noted the absence of a reserved storage array in the LedgerComponent abstract contract. Because the bug does not produce immediate runtime errors, it can be hard to notice until an upgrade is performed and the state appears inconsistent. The proper remediation is to add a storage gap, typically declared as uint256[50] private __gap;, in each abstract contract that may be extended in the future. This reserves a buffer of storage slots that can be used for new variables without altering the layout of existing slots, preserving upgrade safety and preventing accidental overwriting of critical data.

title: OPMAN-1 | Risk Of DoS
description: In the _futuresTradeUploadData function, a batch of trades are uploaded in a single transaction which allows a single malicious trade to DoS the entire batch if it reverts. For example, one trade in the batch could have an invalid symbolHash, which would cause the executeProcessValidatedFutures execution to revert. Similarly, in the _eventUploadData function, a batch of events are uploaded to be processed in a single tx which allows a single invalid event to DoS the entire batch.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) risk that arises when a batch of trades or events is uploaded to the contract using the _futuresTradeUploadData or _eventUploadData functions. The root cause is that the contract processes the entire batch in a single atomic transaction and does not perform per‑item validation or graceful error handling. Consequently, if any single entry in the batch is malformed—such as a trade containing an invalid symbolHash or an event that fails a required check—the internal call to executeProcessValidatedFutures reverts, causing the whole transaction to revert. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately inserting a malicious or invalid trade or event into an otherwise valid batch, causing the transaction to fail and preventing all other legitimate entries from being processed. The impact is a complete blockage of batch processing: users who submit batches see their transactions revert, receive no confirmation, and observe that expected trades or events are not recorded, effectively halting the protocol’s normal operation and potentially delaying market activity. This condition occurs whenever a batch upload is performed and at least one element does not satisfy the contract’s validation rules. The affected parties include protocol operators, traders, and any users relying on timely batch processing, as their funds remain unprocessed and the UI may display generic transaction failure messages without indicating the specific offending entry. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the batch handling logic and identified the lack of defensive checks. It can be hard to notice because the failure manifests as a generic revert of the whole transaction, making it difficult to pinpoint the single bad entry in large batches. To remediate, the contract should incorporate validation of each trade or event before execution, skip or isolate invalid items, or use try/catch patterns to ensure that a single malformed entry does not abort the entire batch. Implementing such defensive logic restores the expected behavior where valid trades are processed even if some entries are erroneous, aligning the implementation with the business assumption that a batch upload should not cause a total service outage due to one bad record.

title: ATPH-4 | DoS On Average Entry Price
description: When a position is updated after a trade, the average entry price is calculated using calAverageEntryPrice. However, if the openingCost and currentHolding are of the same sign, the calculation of position.averageEntryPrice = halfDown16_8(-openingCost, currentHolding).toUint128() will revert with a SafeCastOverflow. This is because halfDown16_8(-openingCost, currentHolding) will return a negative int which cannot be cast to a uint. This can occur if the currentHolding exceeds the openingCost for a short position, because halfDown16_8 will round the quotient to -1 on else { quotient -= 1; }; Note that if halfDown16_8 is modified to round up on a 0 quotient, the issue can still occur if currentHolding exceeds the openingCost for a long position, because halfDown16_8 will round the quotient to 1 and the currentHolding is also positive.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/OrderlyEVMContractsSuite/blob/4e216c2befe63c5379059f9359a7b3a0da008a71/test/GuardianPOC.t.sol#L397C5-L501C6
bug_full: The contract calculates a trader’s average entry price after each trade by calling a helper function that returns a signed integer and then casting the result to an unsigned 128‑bit value. When the signed result is negative, the SafeCast library throws an overflow exception, causing the whole transaction to revert. This situation arises when the sign of the opening cost and the sign of the current holding are the same and the absolute value of the holding exceeds the absolute value of the opening cost. In a short position, for example, a larger negative holding compared to a negative opening cost makes the helper function round the quotient down to –1; the subsequent cast to uint fails. The same pattern can appear for long positions if the rounding logic is altered to round up, producing a positive quotient of 1 while the holding is also positive. Because the revert happens inside the price‑averaging routine, any subsequent attempt to update the position – including closing, adding margin, or executing a new trade – will fail, effectively denying service to the affected account. From a user’s point of view the transaction simply “fails” or “reverts”, the UI may show an error, and the trader sees no change in balance or position despite submitting a valid order. The impact is that funds become locked in the position and the protocol’s accounting logic is broken for the affected market, especially those with low price assets where small trade sizes cause the opening cost to round to –1 or 1. The bug was uncovered during a systematic audit that exercised edge‑case trade sizes and examined the rounding behavior of the halfDown16_8 function. It is difficult to notice because the overflow only triggers under a narrow combination of sign and magnitude, which does not appear in typical larger‑trade scenarios. To remediate the issue the contract should either avoid casting a signed intermediate to an unsigned type, enforce a minimum trade size that prevents the rounding to –1/1, adjust the rounding algorithm to never produce a negative intermediate for short positions (or a positive one for long positions) when the signs match, or add explicit checks before the cast and handle the edge case gracefully. In short, the vulnerability belongs to the class of arithmetic‑overflow and unsafe‑type‑conversion bugs that can be exploited to cause a denial‑of‑service on position updates.

title: VAULT-1 | Allowed Token Contract Address Added
description: The documentation for setAllowedToken states that the function is supposed to “Add contract address for an allowed token given the tokenHash.” However, setAllowedToken only adds or removes the tokenHash from the allowedTokenSet. As a result, the address for the token is never added to the allowedToken mapping. Deposits and withdrawals will revert as the zero address does not have function safeTransferFrom, and continue to revert until changeTokenAddressAndAllow is called, which according to the documentation is an "unusual case on Mainnet".
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the documented behavior of the vault’s setAllowedToken function and its actual implementation. Documentation claims that calling setAllowedToken with a token hash will add the corresponding token contract address to an internal allowedToken mapping, thereby enabling deposits and withdrawals for that token. In practice, the function only updates a set that tracks allowed token hashes (allowedTokenSet) and never stores the token’s contract address in the allowedToken mapping. Consequently, the mapping entry remains the zero address. When a user later attempts to deposit or withdraw the token, the vault calls safeTransferFrom on the zero address, which lacks the required ERC‑1155/721 interface, causing the transaction to revert. This failure persists until an administrator manually invokes changeTokenAddressAndAllow, a procedure described as an “unusual case on Mainnet”. The bug affects any user or protocol component that relies on the vault to support a newly added token, leading to a situation where users see their deposit or withdrawal attempts fail silently, often receiving generic revert messages and no funds movement. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a “deposit failed” or “withdrawal reverted” error, while the expected outcome—successful token transfer—does not occur. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the function’s code against its specification and identified that the token address parameter was missing. It can be hard to notice because the function name and comments suggest correct behavior, and the zero address is not immediately obvious in transaction logs. The root cause is a logical omission: the contract never writes the token address to the allowedToken mapping. To remediate, setAllowedToken should be extended to accept a token address argument and assign it to allowedToken[_tokenHash] = _tokenAddress, ensuring that subsequent safeTransferFrom calls target a valid contract. This aligns the implementation with its intended specification and restores the ability for users to deposit and withdraw allowed tokens without requiring the exceptional changeTokenAddressAndAllow path.

title: ATPH-2 | Half Rounding Improperly Handles 0 Quotient
description: Orderly utilizes the halfUp and halfDown methods to round the quotient up or down on the magnitude of the fractional part. However, the edge case of a 0 quotient will cause the division to return a mathematically incorrect result. For example, consider the function call halfUp16_8(10, 11) int256 quotient = dividend / divisor = 10 / 11 = 0 int256 remainder = dividend % divisor = 10 % 11 = 10 if (10 * 2 >= 11) { if (quotient > 0) { quotient += 1; } else { quotient -= 1; <- quotient = 0 - 1 = -1 } } The returned quotient is -1 although 10 / 11 = 0.909 is not supposed to be a negative number and should round to 1.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/OrderlyEVMContractsSuite/blob/4e216c2befe63c5379059f9359a7b3a0da008a71/test/GuardianPOC.t.sol#L523
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect rounding implementation in the contract's half‑up/half‑down helper functions. These functions compute a quotient by integer division and then adjust it based on the remainder. When the dividend is smaller than the divisor, the integer division yields a quotient of 0. The adjustment logic checks whether twice the remainder is greater than or equal to the divisor and, if so, attempts to round up. The code mistakenly treats a zero quotient as a negative case and subtracts one, producing a quotient of –1. This violates the mathematical expectation that a positive fraction such as 10/11 should round to 1, not –1. The root cause is the conditional if (quotient > 0) { quotient += 1; } else { quotient -= 1; } which does not handle the zero‑quotient edge case correctly. An attacker can trigger the bug by calling any function that relies on these rounding helpers with inputs where the dividend is less than the divisor but the remainder is large enough to satisfy the rounding condition. The contract will then store or return a negative amount where a positive amount is expected, potentially causing accounting mismatches, failed withdrawals, or loss of funds if the negative value is later used in token transfers or fee calculations. The issue appears only when the division result is zero and the remainder is at least half of the divisor, a situation that can arise in normal market operations such as small order sizes or price updates. Users of the protocol—traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—may see balances become negative, refunds disappear, or transactions revert unexpectedly. The bug was discovered during a systematic audit that exercised the rounding functions with edge‑case inputs; it is easy to miss because the code path is rarely executed in typical test vectors and the negative result may be masked by later unsigned‑integer casts. To remediate, the rounding logic should increment the quotient whenever the rounding condition is met and the original quotient is non‑negative, i.e., replace the else branch with a no‑op or ensure quotient >= 0 before adding one. This aligns the implementation with the standard half‑up rounding rule and prevents the creation of spurious negative values, restoring correct accounting and protecting user funds.

title: ATPH-3 | Average Entry Can Be Rounded In User’s Favor
description: When rounding operations are performed, it is safer for the protocol to round against the users so that there is a smaller likelihood of needing to use the insurance fund or ADL. The average entry price is calculated using position.averageEntryPrice = halfDown16_8(-openingCost, currentHolding).toUint128() which rounds up if the fractional part is greater than half, and down otherwise. When a trader is long, it is possible for the entry price to round down which would provide the user a superior entry as they want to buy as low as possible. When a trader is short, it is possible for the entry price to round up which would provide the user a superior entry as they want to sell as high as possible.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol computes the average entry price for a newly opened position. The contract uses a function called halfDown16_8 that rounds the result of the division of the opening cost by the current holding: if the fractional part of the quotient is greater than one half, the value is rounded up, otherwise it is rounded down. Because the rounding direction is applied uniformly, it unintentionally benefits the trader depending on the trade side. For a long position the rounding down operation reduces the recorded entry price, meaning the trader appears to have bought at a lower price than the market, which improves the eventual profit. Conversely, for a short position the rounding up operation raises the recorded entry price, making it look as if the trader sold at a higher price, again improving profit. This bias can be exploited by repeatedly opening positions that trigger the favorable rounding, especially with small position sizes where the fractional component is more likely to cross the half‑threshold. The impact is economic: the protocol may collect less fees, may need to draw from its insurance fund or perform automatic deleveraging more often, and overall the accounting assumptions about fair entry pricing are violated. The issue occurs each time a position is opened and the average entry price is calculated, affecting any trader who opens a position in the direction that benefits from the rounding rule. It primarily affects traders (who receive a better entry price) and the protocol (which loses potential revenue). The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the price‑calculation logic and identified the direction‑dependent rounding as a source of bias. Because rounding is a subtle numerical operation, the problem can be hard to notice; the differences are often a few wei and may not be visible in normal UI displays, yet they accumulate over many trades. To remediate the issue the protocol should adjust the rounding strategy to always round against the user: for long positions round up, and for short positions round down, or adopt a neutral rounding method such as round‑toward‑zero. This change removes the systematic advantage and restores the intended economic balance of the system.

title: GLOBAL-4 | Vault Can Be Drained On Specific Chain
description: Because a withdrawal message can be sent to a Vault on any supported chain, a malicious user can deposit in a Vault on one chain and withdraw from a vault on another chain. This can be used to drain the Vault on a chain, forcing other users to withdraw their liquidity on other chains.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract's withdrawal routing does not enforce that the chain on which a user deposited matches the chain from which they withdraw. Because the withdrawal message can be addressed to any supported chain, a malicious actor can deposit assets into a Vault on Chain A, then craft a withdrawal request that targets the Vault on Chain B. The Vault on Chain B will release the assets even though no corresponding deposit exists on that chain, effectively creating unbacked liquidity. By repeating this across many users, the attacker can drain the entire balance of the Vault on the targeted chain, leaving honest users unable to retrieve their funds on that chain and forcing them to withdraw on other chains where the liquidity may be insufficient. The issue arises from missing validation of the origin chain identifier in the withdrawal logic, a design oversight in the cross‑chain messaging layer. It is exploitable whenever the system accepts a withdrawal request that includes a chain identifier supplied by the caller without checking that the caller’s deposit record exists on that chain. The impact is loss of funds for users of the drained chain, disruption of the protocol’s liquidity guarantees, and potential loss of confidence in the cross‑chain bridge. The condition occurs only on chains that share the same Vault contract code and accept external withdrawal messages; it does not affect chains where withdrawals are internally restricted. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit of the cross‑chain messaging flow, where the auditor noted that the withdrawal function did not compare the deposit chain with the withdrawal chain. The bug can be subtle because the contract appears to work correctly for honest users who withdraw on the same chain they deposited, and the cross‑chain nature hides the mismatch from simple unit tests. To remediate, the protocol should bind each deposit to a specific chain identifier and enforce that any subsequent withdrawal can only be executed on that same chain, or alternatively require a proof of deposit on the target chain before releasing funds. This class of bug is a cross‑chain accounting mismatch, similar to “unrestricted withdrawal destination” or “cross‑chain replay” vulnerabilities. From a user’s perspective, a legitimate user may see their balance on a particular chain become zero after an attacker drains the Vault, receiving no funds when attempting to withdraw, contrary to the expectation that their deposited assets are always available on the chain where they deposited.

title: LGR-3 | User Can Withdraw Entire Collateral When Open Position
description: Before creating a position, a user is required to deposit a balance sufficient for their position size. Upon the call to executeWithdrawAction, there is validation that the withdraw amount is not greater than the balance. However, there is no validation at the contract level in the executeWithdrawAction function that restricts a user from withdrawing their entire balance once they have an open position. If a user’s position is in loss, the user could simply withdraw their entire collateral and not risk losing any of their balance during settlement. This terribly disrupts the operations of the protocol as funds won’t be available to pay profitable traders.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/OrderlyEVMContractsSuite/blob/4e216c2befe63c5379059f9359a7b3a0da008a71/test/GuardianPOC.t.sol#L183
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked withdrawal of the entire collateral while a trader still holds an open position. The contract requires a user to deposit enough margin before opening a position, and the withdraw function only verifies that the requested amount does not exceed the recorded balance. However, it does not enforce any rule that the position must be closed or remain safely collateralised before the funds are released. Consequently, a trader whose position is underwater can call the withdraw routine and extract the full amount of collateral, leaving the position without any margin to cover potential losses. This can be exploited by first opening a leveraged position that moves against the trader, then immediately invoking the withdraw action; the contract will approve the request because the balance check passes, and no liquidation or margin‑call logic is triggered. The impact is that the protocol loses the funds needed to settle profitable counterparties, potentially causing unpaid profits, reduced liquidity, and even insolvency of the pool. The flaw manifests only when a user has an active position and attempts to withdraw; it does not appear during normal closed‑position flows, making it easy to overlook during casual testing. All participants who rely on the protocol’s guarantee that positions are fully collateralised are affected, including other traders and the protocol’s treasury. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that exercised withdrawal paths with open positions and observed that the contract allowed a full balance extraction. It is subtle because the basic balance‑comparison check looks correct, masking the missing business‑logic validation that ties withdrawals to position health. To remediate, the withdraw routine should incorporate a check that the remaining collateral after the withdrawal would keep the position above the liquidation threshold, possibly by requiring the caller to supply a price feed or by internally recomputing the position’s health before releasing funds. In generic terms, the bug is a missing collateral‑safety guard in a margin‑withdraw function, leading to a scenario where “funds disappear” from the protocol when a losing trader withdraws all their margin, violating the expected accounting invariant that open positions are always fully backed.

title: VAULTM-1 | Funds Will Be Locked On Hard Fork
description: In the VaultManager contract, token balances are stored in mappings such as tokenBalanceOnchain or tokenFrozenBalanceOnchain. These mappings take a token hash and a chainID and point to a token balance. If a chain were to experience a hard fork that chainID will change. This will result in the token balance being inaccessible as there will be a difference between what is being stored in state and the actual chainID of the chain.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the VaultManager contract records token holdings. Balances are stored in a double‑mapping that uses both a token identifier and the blockchain's chainID as keys. When a hard fork occurs the chainID of the network changes, but the contract continues to reference the old chainID in its storage. As a result the mapping entry that holds a user’s tokens no longer matches the current chainID, making the stored balance effectively invisible to the contract logic. Users attempting to withdraw or view their balance will see a zero or missing amount even though the funds are still locked in the contract’s state. This situation can arise any time a chain experiences a hard fork that alters its chainID, which is a rare but possible event for networks that support upgrades via fork. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the accounting model and noticed the reliance on a mutable external identifier. It is difficult to detect in normal testing because the chainID is constant on a stable network, so the bug only manifests under fork conditions that are not reproduced in typical test environments. The impact is that token holders lose access to their assets until the protocol implements a migration or the fork is reversed, effectively locking funds and breaking the economic guarantees of the system. To remediate the problem the contract should provide an owner‑only migration function that can re‑associate balances from the old chainID to the new one, or redesign the accounting to avoid using chainID as part of the storage key, for example by using a per‑chain registry or by abstracting the identifier behind a version‑agnostic layer. By doing so the protocol ensures that balances remain reachable after a fork and users receive the expected token amounts instead of an empty balance.

title: LGR-4 | Large Withdrawals Can Fail
description: In the executeWithdrawAction function, there is a check to ensure that the withdraw.fee is less than the maxWithdrawFee. However the maxWithdrawFee is a fixed value that will be used for all withdrawals. While the withdraw.fee will be a percentage based on the size of the individual withdraw. Because the two are inherently misaligned, there is a risk that large withdraws will fail as their withdraw.fee will be greater than the maxWithdrawFee. Users in this scenario will need to break up their withdrawals into multiple smaller withdrawals leading to operational inefficiency.
bug_full: During execution of the withdraw action, the contract compares the calculated fee for the requested amount with a constant maxWithdrawFee that is stored as a fixed absolute value. The fee itself is derived from a percentage of the withdrawal amount, so as the amount grows the fee grows proportionally. When the percentage‑based fee exceeds the constant cap, the require statement fails and the transaction reverts. This mismatch between a percentage‑based fee and an absolute maximum creates a situation where large, legitimate withdrawals are rejected while small withdrawals succeed. The condition is triggered only for amounts large enough that fee > maxWithdrawFee, which may not be covered by typical unit tests that use modest values. Users experience the failure as an unexpected “withdrawal failed” error, often seeing no funds transferred and sometimes being forced to split the intended amount into several smaller withdrawals to stay under the fee cap. The impact is operational inefficiency, increased gas costs, and potential loss of confidence because the protocol does not honour the expected ability to withdraw any amount up to the user's balance. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the fee validation logic and noticed the static nature of the cap. It can be hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly for normal‑sized withdrawals, and the failure only appears at scale. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect fee limit enforcement” or “misaligned fee validation” where business rules expressed as percentages are compared against fixed thresholds. To remediate, the max fee should be expressed as a percentage of the withdrawal amount (or the check should compare percentages rather than absolute values), ensuring that the fee never exceeds a configurable proportion of the withdrawn sum. This change restores the intended behavior that any withdrawal amount can be processed as long as the fee remains within the allowed percentage, eliminating the need for users to manually fragment their withdrawals.

title: SIG-1 | Signature Malleability
description: The verify function uses ecrecover without any validation that the s value is from one half of the valid s range, therefore it is possible for signatures to be maliciously replayed with a different s. At present, the OperatorManager is the only address that can perform this signature malleability, however, the opportunity should be removed.
bug_full: The vulnerability is signature malleability in the contract's signature verification routine. The verify function calls ecrecover directly and does not enforce that the s component of the ECDSA signature lies in the lower half of the curve order. Because the Ethereum specification allows two valid signatures that differ only by the s value (s and curveOrder‑s), an attacker who can supply a signature with the alternative s can produce a different, yet still valid, signature that recovers the same signer address. In the current implementation the only entity that can trigger this is the OperatorManager contract, which means the operator could replay a previously signed message with a modified s value and have the contract accept it as a fresh authorization. This can be exploited by constructing the complementary s value for any existing signed message and submitting it to functions that rely on the verify routine, effectively bypassing any nonce or replay protection that assumes a unique signature. The impact is that authorized actions such as order placement, fund transfer, or state changes could be executed multiple times or by an unauthorized party if the operator colludes, leading to potential loss of funds or incorrect protocol state. The issue appears whenever the contract validates signatures without the s‑range check, i.e., for every call to the verify function. Users of the protocol may notice that transactions they did not initiate are processed, or that funds are moved without a corresponding new signature from them. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the verification code against best‑practice libraries and identified the missing s‑value restriction. Because the contract still recovers the correct address, the problem is subtle and may not be evident from simple testing; only a careful review of the ECDSA specification reveals the malleability. The recommended remediation is to replace the raw ecrecover call with a vetted library such as OpenZeppelin’s ECDSA, which enforces the low‑s rule and also checks the v value, thereby eliminating the possibility of signature replay with an alternative s. In broader terms, this is a classic case of signature malleability where the cryptographic primitive is used without proper canonicalisation, breaking the assumption that each signed message has a unique representation. Fixing the issue restores the integrity of the authorization flow and prevents the operator or any attacker from forging a different signature that still passes verification.

title: `fetchPrice` can return different prices in the same transaction
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price‑feed contract’s state‑machine logic that decides which oracle value to return from the function fetchPrice. When the primary Chainlink oracle reports a price that deviates by more than fifty percent from the previous round and the secondary (fallback) oracle is not configured, the contract moves its internal status to bothOraclesUntrusted and returns the stored lastGoodPrice. Immediately afterwards, because the fallback address is still zero, the next execution of fetchPrice checks that Chainlink is no longer broken or frozen and, without re‑evaluating the large deviation, switches the status back to usingChainlinkFallbackUntrusted. As a result the second call in the same transaction (or the same block) returns the current Chainlink price, which can be dramatically higher than the lastGoodPrice returned earlier. The root cause is an incomplete guard: the code only verifies the deviation when setting bothOraclesUntrusted, but it does not prevent the status from being reverted to a state that trusts Chainlink again, nor does it require the presence of a fallback oracle before marking bothOraclesUntrusted. Consequently, an attacker can trigger a >50 % price swing, cause the first fetchPrice call to emit a stale, low price, and then invoke fetchPrice again to obtain the fresh, high price. By using the stale price to redeem collateral or open a loan and the fresh price to open a new position, the attacker can extract profit through arbitrage, effectively making funds disappear from the protocol’s accounting. The issue manifests only when three conditions hold simultaneously: (1) the fallback oracle address is zero, (2) the Chainlink price change exceeds the 50 % threshold between two consecutive rounds, and (3) the contract’s status transitions from usingChainlinkFallbackUntrusted to bothOraclesUntrusted and back within the same transaction. Users of the protocol – borrowers, lenders, and any external contracts that rely on fetchPrice – are affected because they may receive inconsistent price data, leading to unexpected liquidation, loss of collateral, or unintended profit for an attacker. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by reproducing the scenario with mock Chainlink feeds and observing that fetchPrice returned different values on successive calls in a single test. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the large price deviation is rare, and the contract appears to function correctly when a fallback oracle is present. The fix requires adding explicit checks that a fallback oracle exists before marking bothOraclesUntrusted, ensuring that the large‑deviation guard remains active after a status change, and preventing the contract from reverting to a trusting state without re‑validating the price similarity. In practice this means augmenting the _bothOraclesLiveAndUnbrokenAndSimilarPrice and _bothOraclesSimilarPrice helpers with fallback‑address checks, inserting an extra guard in the bothOraclesUntrusted branch to return lastGoodPrice when a deviation is still present, and generally tightening the state‑machine so that price‑consistency is enforced across successive fetchPrice calls.

title: Redemptions are inconsistent with other cdp’s operations
description:
Most actions that modify the (ICR) of a Collateralized Debt Position (CDP) must adhere to specific regulations to maintain the system’s stability. For instance, closing a CDP or decreasing its collateral is not permitted if it would trigger the system’s recovery mode, or if the system is already in that mode.

However, the rules for redemptions are less stringent. The only conditions are that both the system and the CDPs undergoing redemption must have an TCR and ICR above the MCR. So, it is possible to redeem a cdp that is actually helping the system to stay healthy.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistency in the redemption logic of a Collateralized Debt Position (CDP) system that allows a user to redeem collateral even when the redemption would push the Total Collateral Ratio (TCR) of the whole protocol below the Minimum Collateral Ratio (MCR) and consequently trigger Recovery Mode (RM). The root cause is that the contract only checks that the system TCR and the individual CDP's Individual Collateral Ratio (ICR) are above MCR before allowing a redemption, while other CDP operations such as closing a position or decreasing collateral also enforce a rule that the action must not cause the system to enter RM. Because this additional safeguard is missing for redemptions, an attacker can deliberately select a CDP that is currently helping the system stay healthy, redeem a large amount of eBTC, and cause the overall collateralization to drop below the safety threshold. The exploit works by calling the redemption function with a quantity large enough to reduce the total collateral pool; the contract does not reject the transaction, the CDP is removed from the sorted list, and the system’s TCR is recomputed below MCR, automatically switching the protocol into Recovery Mode. The impact is that the protocol becomes under‑collateralized, future operations such as opening new CDPs or borrowing may be blocked, and users may see the UI display a recovery‑mode warning, loss of ability to redeem further, or unexpected zero balances for their positions. This condition occurs only when the system is close to the MCR and a redemption is performed that would cross the threshold; it is most relevant for CDPs that hold a significant share of the collateral and for scenarios where bad‑debt redistribution is large. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a proof‑of‑concept test demonstrated that after a price drop the TCR remained above MCR, but a subsequent redemption caused the TCR to fall below MCR and the system entered RM. The bug is hard to notice because the redemption fee and economic deterrents mask the logical flaw, and the protocol’s normal operation does not surface the inconsistency unless a large redemption is attempted. To fix the problem, the redemption pathway should be extended with the same pre‑condition checks used for other CDP modifications: it must reject any redemption that would cause the system TCR to dip below MCR, and it should only allow redemptions during Recovery Mode if they help the system exit that state. This aligns the redemption logic with the protocol’s accounting assumptions that no single operation may jeopardize overall collateral health, thereby preventing funds from disappearing or the system from unintentionally entering recovery mode.

title: Attacker can utilize function `CdpManager.redeemCollateral`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the CdpManager.redeemCollateral function, which is responsible for converting a user’s debt into EBTC and returning the corresponding amount of stETH collateral. The function processes CDPs in ascending order of their nominal collateralization ratio (NICR), starting with the smallest CDP that meets the minimum collateralization requirement (MCR). For each iteration, the internal routine _redeemCollateralFromCdp either fully repays a CDP, setting its debt and collateral to zero, or partially repays it, leaving a residual debt and collateral. The implementation attempts to save gas by deferring the removal of fully repaid CDPs from the SortedCdps list until after the redemption loop, using a batchRemove call. However, when a CDP is only partially repaid, the code immediately reinserts that CDP into the sorted list with its new NICR value. Because the fully repaid CDPs have not yet been removed, the partially repaid CDP can be placed in an incorrect position relative to the still‑present fully repaid entries. This temporary violation of the sorted order invariant means that the list no longer reflects a true ascending NICR sequence. An attacker can exploit this by supplying crafted upper and lower hint parameters to the redeemCollateral call, forcing the partially repaid CDP to be inserted at a deliberately wrong spot while the batch removal of fully repaid CDPs is pending. The resulting misordering can cause subsequent redemption operations to select CDPs out of the intended priority, potentially leading to users receiving no collateral, receiving less than expected, or having their CDPs incorrectly flagged for redemption despite maintaining a healthy collateralization ratio. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show a successful redemption transaction but the user receives zero stETH, or the CDP appears out of order in the list, contradicting the expectation that redemption always returns the appropriate amount of collateral. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors observed that the SortedCdps list was not updated consistently within the loop, and a proof‑of‑concept demonstrated the ordering break. The issue is subtle because the invariant is only violated for a short window, and normal operation restores the correct order after the next redemption, making it easy to miss in routine testing. Conceptually, the fix is to postpone the reinsertion of the partially repaid CDP until after the batch removal of fully repaid CDPs has completed, ensuring that the sorted list remains consistent throughout the operation. This class of bug falls under “inconsistent state updates in ordered data structures” and violates core accounting assumptions that the protocol relies on to guarantee fair and predictable redemption ordering.

title: The way fees are accounted can break the sorted list order
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way eBTC accounts for protocol fees when using the corrected‑stake mechanism borrowed from Liquity. Initially the total stake of all CDPs equals the total collateral because no fees have been taken. When the value of the underlying stETH rises, the protocol extracts a portion of the increase as a fee. This fee is deducted directly from the total collateral pool while the total stake value remains unchanged, because the corrected‑stake formula uses a snapshot of total collateral that is not updated after the fee deduction. Consequently, the stake assigned to a newly opened CDP is calculated as (collateral * totalStakesSnapshot) / totalCollateralSnapshot. Since totalCollateralSnapshot has been reduced by the fee but totalStakesSnapshot has not, the resulting stake for the new CDP is artificially higher than the stakes of older CDPs. The higher stake translates into a lower Nominal Individual Collateral Ratio (NICR) for the new CDP, causing its NICR to fall below that of older positions. The sorted list that orders CDPs by descending NICR therefore loses its monotonic property: older CDPs can appear after newer ones, breaking the unique insertion point invariant. This order break can be triggered whenever a positive rebase generates fees, which is a normal condition for the protocol, and it becomes visible after several fee events or after opening many CDPs in quick succession. The affected parties are all borrowers and liquidators that rely on the sorted list for correct redemption order; they may experience unexpected redemption sequencing, higher fees than anticipated, or even denial‑of‑service if the list becomes sufficiently disordered. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are subtle: a newly opened CDP may show a collateral ratio that is lower than older CDPs, the UI may display out‑of‑order rankings, and redemption transactions may fail or return less collateral than expected. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditor wrote a test that opened a hundred CDPs, applied a large stETH price increase to generate fees, and then observed that the NICR ordering assertion failed. The bug is hard to notice because the list appears correctly sorted until the fee‑taking event occurs, and the discrepancy only manifests in the relative ordering of NICR values, which is not directly visible in most front‑ends. The root cause is an accounting inconsistency: the fee deduction changes the denominator of the stake calculation without a corresponding update to the numerator, violating the invariant that stake is proportional to collateral. This class of bug can be described as a “sorted‑list order violation caused by inconsistent state updates in fee accounting”. To remediate the problem the protocol must redesign the fee and debt redistribution logic so that totalStake and totalCollateral remain proportionally aligned after fee collection. Possible approaches include updating the totalStake snapshot when fees are taken, using a pure proportional distribution that does not rely on corrected stake, or redesigning the data structure to tolerate temporary order violations. In any case, the fix must ensure that the ordering invariant of the CDP list is preserved, preventing unfair fee distribution, unexpected collateral ratio drops, and potential DOS scenarios.

title: When calling LeverageMacroBase.doOperation to open a CDP, the POST CALL CHECK may use the wrong cdpId
description:
After [LeverageMacroBase.doOperation](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-badger/blob/main/packages/contracts/contracts/LeverageMacroBase.sol#L118-L124) is used to open a new CDP, there will be a [POST CALL CHECK](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-badger/blob/main/packages/contracts/contracts/LeverageMacroBase.sol#L169-L183), which is used to check the new CDP. However, the current implementation incorrectly assumes that [the index of the new CDP is the last one](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-badger/blob/main/packages/contracts/contracts/LeverageMacroBase.sol#L173). In this case, there may be two impacts:

  1. The check that should be passed cannot be passed, causing tx revert and waste of gas.
  2. The check that should not have been passed was passed, which may result in funds losses from `this` contract or caller.
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs in the LeverageMacroBase contract when the function doOperation is used to open a new collateralized debt position (CDP) and a post‑call check of type openCdp is requested. The code records the number of CDPs owned by the contract before the new CDP is created (initialCdpIndex = sortedCdps.cdpCountOf(address(this))) and later assumes that the newly created CDP will be stored at the last index of the owner’s list. It then retrieves the CDP identifier with sortedCdps.cdpOfOwnerByIndex(address(this), initialCdpIndex). This assumption is incorrect because the SortedCdps data structure stores CDPs in descending order of their nominal collateral ratio (NICR). If the newly created CDP has a lower NICR than an existing CDP, it will be inserted earlier in the list, meaning its index is not the last one. Consequently the post‑call check reads the wrong CDP – either the previous CDP or an unrelated one. The impact is two‑fold: (1) the check may fail even though the newly created CDP satisfies the expected parameters, causing the transaction to revert and waste gas; (2) the check may succeed with mismatched data, allowing the contract or the caller to believe that the CDP has the expected debt, collateral or status, which can lead to unintended fund transfers or loss of assets from the contract. The bug manifests only when the contract already owns at least one CDP and a second (or later) CDP is opened whose NICR is not the highest, which is why it is not observed for the first CDP and can be hard to notice during normal testing. The affected parties are the protocol that relies on LeverageMacroBase for flash‑loan‑backed leverage operations, any user or contract that invokes doOperation with an openCdp post‑check, and the funds locked in the CDP manager. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors traced the index calculation and identified the mismatch between the recorded count and the actual position of the new CDP in the sorted list. This class of bug is an off‑by‑one or index‑misalignment error caused by an incorrect assumption about the ordering of a linked list data structure. From a user perspective the symptoms are unexpected transaction reverts when opening a second CDP, or successful transactions that later show incorrect debt or collateral values, potentially resulting in missing funds or failed repayments. The correct mitigation is to capture the CDP identifier returned by borrowerOperations.openCdp and store it in a dedicated storage slot, then use that exact identifier in the post‑call check instead of recomputing an index. After the check the slot should be cleared. Alternatively, the contract could compute the proper index using the CDP manager’s nextCdpNonce or a similar deterministic method that respects the sorted order. This eliminates the reliance on the “last index” assumption and restores the integrity of the post‑call validation.

title: Batched liquidations doesn’t distribute bad debt on next batches in the list
bug_full: The vulnerability is a batch‑liquidation accounting flaw in the LiquidationLibrary of the Badger protocol. When the CDPManager calls batchLiquidateCdps in normal mode, the function iterates over each CDP, calculates a synchronized collateral‑to‑debt ratio (ICR) that includes any pending debt redistribution, and then performs the liquidation. If a CDP in the batch generates bad debt, the library records that debt in a global redistribution index but does not update the index before processing the next CDP in the same batch. Consequently the next CDP is evaluated with a stale debt value, causing the liquidation to treat the position as if less debt existed. The liquidator and the CDP owner therefore receive a larger share of collateral than they should, while the missing portion of bad debt is never redistributed to the remaining stakers. This error only manifests when multiple CDPs are liquidated in a single transaction and at least one of them creates bad debt; it does not appear in single‑CDP liquidations or in recovery mode where a different path is taken. The impact is that protocol accounting becomes inconsistent: users may see unexpectedly high collateral returns, the protocol’s total bad debt is understated, and honest stakers are forced to absorb the undistributed debt later. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation flow, where the auditor noticed that the redistribution accumulator (_debtIndex) is only updated after the whole batch, not after each individual liquidation, leading to a 3 % loss of bad‑debt redistribution per batch. Because the contract still reports a successful liquidation and the discrepancy is only visible in aggregate accounting, the bug can be hard to detect in normal testing. The correct mitigation is to apply the pending bad‑debt redistribution to the global index after each liquidation inside the batch, or to recalculate the synchronized ICR for every CDP using the updated index before proceeding to the next iteration. In other words, the redistribution step must be performed incrementally rather than once at the end of the batch, ensuring that every CDP sees the current debt state and that no portion of bad debt is omitted from the redistribution pool.

title: A safe that has been created using version `1.40=<` will not be compatible with Brahma
poc:
Consider the following:

  * Alice has a safe setup.
  * Alice wants to integrate their safe into the Brahma ecosystem.
  * Alice calls `WalletRegistry.registerWallet` and this call succeeds.
  * Alice decides they want to implement the guard contract provided by the Brahma ecosystem, `SafeModeratorOverridable.sol`
  * Alice calls `GnosisSafe.setGuard(address(SafeModeratorOverridable))`.
  * This will fail because of this new require statement in Safe contracts `v1.4.0=<`:

```solidity
    function setGuard(address guard) external authorized {
            if (guard != address(0)) {
                require(Guard(guard).supportsInterface(type(Guard).interfaceId), "GS300");
            }
```
Because the `SafeModeratorOverridable.sol` does not support the `EIP-165` interface:
```solidity
    source: contracts/src/core/SafeModeratorOverridable.sol

    contract SafeModeratorOverridable is AddressProviderService, IGuard {
```
This means that every Safe created with version 1.4.0 or up, can not implement the guard contract, which is a fundamental part of the way the `ConsoleAccounts` function.
bug_full: An incompatibility arises when a Gnosis Safe that was deployed with contract version 1.4.0 or newer is later registered in the Brahma ecosystem. The GuardManager module introduced in version 1.4.0 adds a runtime check that any guard contract passed to setGuard must implement the ERC‑165 interface and return true for the Guard interface identifier. The Brahma‑provided guard implementation SafeModeratorOverridable implements IGuard but does not inherit ERC165 nor expose supportsInterface, so the require statement reverts with error code GS300. As a result, after a successful call to WalletRegistry.registerWallet, the owner of the safe cannot attach the required guard, and the safe does not become a functional consoleAccount. From the user’s perspective the registration UI reports success, but subsequent attempts to enable the guard produce a transaction failure and the account loses the expected moderation capabilities, effectively disabling a security layer. The issue is triggered only for safes whose bytecode includes the new ERC‑165 guard check, i.e., version 1.4.0 and above, and only when the guard contract does not conform to ERC‑165. It affects any user or protocol that relies on Brahma’s consoleAccount model, potentially leading to denial‑of‑service or loss of policy enforcement, although funds remain in the safe. The problem was uncovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the integration flow between Brahma and external safes. The bug is subtle because the registration step succeeds and the incompatibility surfaces later, making it easy to miss during functional testing. To remediate the situation the guard contract should be upgraded to implement ERC‑165 and correctly report support for the Guard interface, or the Brahma integration should be adjusted to accept non‑ERC‑165 guards, or the safe version used by Brahma should be downgraded to a pre‑1.4.0 release that does not enforce the interface check. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of interface‑compatibility mismatches where a contract assumes a certain standard (ERC‑165) that downstream contracts do not satisfy, leading to runtime reverts and broken business logic.

title: `SubAccount` operator can steal funds via the gas refund mechanism
description:
The `SubAccount` operator can steal funds from the SubAccount Gnosis Safe via the Gnosis Safe gas refund mechanism, since the trusted validator signatures do not include the following parameters that are included in the `Safe.sol` `execTransaction` function:

  * `uint256 safeTxGas`
  * `uint256 baseGas`
  * `uint256 gasPrice`
  * `address gasToken`
  * `address payable refundReceiver`

This allows the operator to call `execTransaction` with these parameters set to send all the Ether or a chosen ERC-20 token held in the SubAccount Gnosis Safe to the operator’s address.
poc:
One of the operators, who is an owner on the SubAccount Gnosis Safe, calls `execTransaction` on the Gnosis Safe with valid `to`, `value`, `data`, `operation`, and `signatures` parameters which is allowed by the current policy configured on the SubAccount, and therefore the trusted validator will also sign.

However, the operator will also populate `execTransaction` function parameters related to gas refunds (`safeTxGas, baseGas, gasPrice, gasToken` and `refundReceiver`), to values that transfer to themselves Ether or ERC-20 tokens held in the SubAccount Gnosis Safe.

The transaction is executed, and in the `handlePayment` [function call](https://github.com/safe-global/safe-contracts/blob/main/contracts/Safe.sol#L229) within the Gnosis Safe execution, the Ether or ERC-20 tokens will be transferred to the address the operator specified in the `refundReceiver` parameter.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked gas‑refund path in the SubAccount wrapper around a Gnosis Safe. The policy validator that authorises transactions only signs the core parameters (to, value, data, operation, signatures) and deliberately omits the five gas‑related fields that the Safe’s execTransaction function expects: safeTxGas, baseGas, gasPrice, gasToken and refundReceiver. Because these fields are not part of the signed payload, an operator who is also an owner of the SubAccount can supply arbitrary values when calling execTransaction. By setting refundReceiver to their own address and configuring safeTxGas, baseGas, gasPrice and gasToken so that the Safe’s internal handlePayment routine treats the call as a gas‑refund payment, the operator can cause the Safe to transfer all Ether or any ERC‑20 token balance to the attacker’s address. The exploit works whenever the policy permits the operator to invoke execTransaction with a valid signature, which is the normal case for SubAccount owners. From a user’s perspective the safe appears to have executed a legitimate transaction, but after execution the balance may be reduced to zero or the expected refund is missing, leading to the perception that my funds disappeared or the refund never arrived. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the PolicyValidator contract, where the absence of the gas‑refund parameters in the signed data was identified as a logical gap. It is difficult to notice because the Safe’s refund mechanism is rarely exercised in typical usage, and the transaction still passes all signature checks, giving a false sense of security. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external payment parameters or gas‑refund manipulation vulnerabilities, where a contract’s accounting assumptions are broken by allowing unverified fields to dictate fund movement. To remediate, the validator must include safeTxGas, baseGas, gasPrice, gasToken and refundReceiver in the data that is covered by the trusted validator’s signature, ensuring that any attempt to alter the refund destination or amount would invalidate the signature. Properly constraining these parameters restores the intended invariant that only the explicitly approved recipient can receive funds, preventing operators from siphoning assets via the refund path.

title: Protocol is not `EIP712` compliant: incorrect typehash for `Validation` and `Transaction` structures
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of incorrect EIP‑712 type‑hash constants for the data structures that are used when signing messages in the protocol. EIP‑712 requires that the hash of a struct’s type definition (the type‑hash) be calculated from the exact fields and order of the current struct. In this contract the constants TRANSACTION_PARAMS_TYPEHASH and VALIDATION_PARAMS_TYPEHASH were generated from two obsolete structs – ExecutionParams and ValidationParams – that were removed during a refactor, while the code now uses the newer Transaction and Validation structs. Because the type‑hashes no longer match the actual structs, any signature that is verified against these constants is checked against the wrong schema. This mismatch can be exploited by an attacker who creates a signature that is valid for the old schema but not for the intended Transaction or Validation data, potentially causing the contract to accept malformed or replayed messages, or to reject legitimate ones. The impact is that users may experience transaction failures, refunds that never arrive, or funds becoming locked because the contract believes a signature is invalid when it is actually correct for the current struct, breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol. The issue manifests whenever a signed transaction or validation is processed – essentially every call that relies on EIP‑712 verification – and therefore affects all participants, including safe owners, executors, and any third‑party services that rely on the contract’s correctness. The flaw was discovered during a security audit when the auditors compared the stored type‑hash constants with the expected keccak256 strings derived from the current struct definitions and found a mismatch. It is easy to miss because the constants are opaque 32‑byte values and the tests only asserted equality with the old strings, providing no coverage of the actual encoding logic. To remediate, the type‑hash constants must be recomputed from the up‑to‑date Transaction and Validation structs, the contract code updated to use the new constants, and comprehensive tests added to ensure the hashes always reflect the current struct definitions. This brings the contract back into compliance with EIP‑712 and restores the integrity of signature verification, preventing accidental fund loss or denial of service caused by mismatched signatures.

title: Module transactions will always fail because incompatible with Safe 1.5.0
description:
GnosisSafe has concept of module. Trusted modules of GnosisSafe contract can execute arbitrary transactions without signatures once enabled. That’s the main purpose of protocol: to allow the execution of some defined action (like swap on DEX) without signatures via registering such an action in Policy commitment. Then, execute this action via Executor or Main Account without need of delegatee’s signatures, and also allow one to register SubAccounts and manage them via Main Account.

Therefore, ExecutorPlugin and Main Account are enabled as modules. The main problem is that all transactions executed via module will fail, meaning SubAccount is just another GnosisSafe without additional utility. When assessing the severity, I took into consideration protocol specific: protocol is about adding new functionality.

Users also have access to SafeSub-accounts that reduce their risk from the protocol by isolating their interactions.

But core functionality of protocol regarding ExecutorPlugin and SubAccounts doesn’t work. Due to this reasoning I submit it as High, despite there is no financial loss.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the Gnosis Safe module execution flow and the Guard contract interface used by the Brahma protocol. Gnosis Safe allows trusted modules to submit transactions without user signatures by calling execTransactionFromModule. This function first invokes Guard.checkModuleTransaction and expects the call to return a bytes32 guardHash, which is later passed to Guard.checkAfterExecution. In the Brahma deployment the Guard contracts (SafeModerator or SafeModeratorOverridable) implement an older version of IGuard that declares checkModuleTransaction without a return value. When execTransactionFromModule calls the newer interface, the Solidity ABI decoder attempts to read a bytes32 from the call’s return data, but the called function emits no data. This mismatch triggers a decoding error and causes the whole execTransactionFromModule call to revert. Consequently, any transaction submitted through a registered module – including the ExecutorPlugin and SubAccount modules that are essential for the protocol’s “execute without signatures” feature – will always fail. From a user perspective, attempts to trigger a swap, withdraw funds, or any other module‑driven action result in no on‑chain activity; the UI may show a pending transaction that never confirms, or the user may see a failure message such as “execution from module failed”. The protocol’s promise of isolated SubAccounts that reduce risk is therefore broken, as those SubAccounts cannot perform any operation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the auditors inspected the Guard interface and observed that the implementation did not match the expected signature, then reproduced the failure with a minimal Remix test that demonstrated a revert on decoding an absent return value. The bug is subtle because the contract compiles without errors – the interface mismatch is only revealed at runtime – and because the failure occurs inside a low‑level call that is not directly visible in higher‑level transaction logs. The class of bug is an ABI incompatibility or interface mismatch leading to a forced revert, a common pattern when a contract expects a return value that the callee does not provide. To remediate, the Guard contracts must be updated to implement the current IGuard interface, adding a bytes32 return value to checkModuleTransaction (typically a hash of the transaction parameters) and ensuring that checkAfterExecution receives a matching guardHash. Once the interface aligns, module‑initiated transactions will execute as intended, restoring the protocol’s core functionality and allowing users to rely on SubAccounts for risk‑isolated interactions.

title: The Liquidity mining callpath sidecar owner can pull native tokens from the `Dex`
description: The owner of the liquidity mining sidecar can pull the native coins that are stored in the `CrocSwapDex` to reward the users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked payable function in the liquidity‑mining sidecar contract that allows the contract owner (or any caller, because the governance check is commented out) to declare a reward schedule without actually providing the native tokens required for that schedule. The root cause is the absence of a validation that the amount of ether sent with the call (msg.value) matches the total reward amount calculated from the weeklyReward parameter and the number of weeks covered. Because the function setConcRewards (and the analogous setAmbRewards) is marked payable but does not contain a require statement that enforces msg.value to equal the expected reward total, the caller can specify any reward amount while sending zero or insufficient ether. When the protocol later distributes rewards, it pulls the native coins from the balance of the CrocSwapDex contract, which holds the pool’s native token reserves. Consequently, the sidecar can drain those reserves, effectively allowing the owner to “pull” native tokens from the Dex and either keep them or distribute less than promised. This manifests to users as missing or zero refunds: a user expects a weekly reward but receives nothing, or sees their balance unexpectedly reduced after a distribution event. The issue occurs whenever setConcRewards or setAmbRewards is invoked without the proper ether attached, which is possible because the access control check is disabled and the payable modifier does not enforce any value transfer. The problem was discovered during a security audit when reviewers noticed the payable functions lacked any msg.value verification and the governance restriction was commented out, indicating a logical oversight rather than a coding mistake. The flaw can be hard to spot because the functions appear to accept payments, leading developers to assume callers will send the correct amount, and the reward distribution logic may work correctly until the Dex balance is exhausted, at which point the failure becomes apparent. To remediate, the contract should enforce that msg.value equals the total reward amount calculated from the weeklyReward and the number of weeks, and it should reinstate proper access control so that only authorized governance can set reward parameters. This aligns the contract with standard safe‑payment patterns and prevents unauthorized extraction of native tokens, preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the liquidity‑mining program.

title: If `dt` is not updated accurately, `timeWeightedWeeklyPositionInRangeConcLiquidity_` might be updated incorrectly
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the time‑weighted liquidity accrual routine of a concentrated liquidity pool. The routine iterates over weekly intervals, using a variable named dt to advance the loop’s time cursor. When a tick’s exit timestamp falls after the next weekly boundary (tickTracking.exitTimestamp > nextWeek), the code enters an else branch that sets tickActiveEnd to nextWeek but fails to recompute dt. Consequently dt retains its initial value, which is either nextWeek‑time or block.timestamp‑time, both of which are larger than the actual elapsed interval (tickActiveEnd‑tickActiveStart). Because dt is too large, the while loop advances the time cursor by a bigger step than it should, resulting in fewer iterations than required. Each skipped iteration omits the addition of (tickActiveEnd‑tickActiveStart) * liquidity to the timeWeightedWeeklyPositionInRangeConcLiquidity_ mapping. This mapping feeds the reward calculation in claimConcentratedRewards, so an under‑recorded time‑weighted liquidity leads to an under‑payment of rewards. Users therefore receive less reward than they earned, sometimes seeing a zero or unexpectedly low amount when they expect a full payout. The bug manifests only when a tick exits after the next week boundary, a relatively rare edge case that can be missed during normal testing because the loop still executes and rewards are merely reduced, not eliminated. It was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditor noted the missing dt update in the else block. The issue belongs to the class of “incorrect iterator update” or “time delta miscalculation” bugs that break accounting assumptions about continuous accrual. Fixing the problem requires assigning dt = tickActiveEnd - tickActiveStart (or equivalently dt = tickActiveEnd - time) inside the else branch so that the loop’s time cursor matches the actual end of the active period, ensuring all weeks are accounted for and rewards are calculated correctly. Updating dt also guarantees that tickTrackingIndexAccruedUpTo_ is set correctly, preserving the integrity of the tick‑tracking state.

title: Rewards cannot be transferred when calling protocol command
bug_full: The vulnerability is a payable‑modifier mismatch in the protocol command flow used to configure liquidity‑mining rewards. The public entry point CrocSwapDex::protocolCmd is declared payable and forwards the call, together with any attached ether, to a proxy contract via delegatecall. The proxy then invokes LiquidityMiningPath::protocolCmd, which decodes the command and calls setConcRewards or setAmbRewards. Because LiquidityMiningPath::protocolCmd is not marked payable, the EVM reverts any transaction that includes a non‑zero msg.value, causing the reward‑setup command to fail. The root cause is that the developer assumed the payable attribute of the outer function would automatically apply to the delegated implementation, but payable is not inherited across delegatecall boundaries. An attacker or even a legitimate protocol authority can trigger the failure simply by sending ether with the command, which results in a revert and prevents the rewards from being funded. The impact is that liquidity providers expecting weekly rewards may see no reward allocation, the UI may display “reward setup failed” or simply show zero balances, and the protocol’s incentive mechanism is effectively broken until the bug is fixed. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to setConcRewards or setAmbRewards through the protocol command interface that includes a positive callvalue. The affected parties are the protocol administrators who manage reward distribution and the users who rely on those rewards. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the command pattern and noticed the missing payable keyword in the delegated contract. It can be hard to notice because delegatecall forwards msg.value transparently, and the function signatures appear identical, leading developers to assume the inner function can accept ether. The bug belongs to the class of payable‑mismatch or value‑forwarding errors in delegatecall architectures, where a non‑payable implementation rejects ether sent by a payable caller. To remediate, the LiquidityMiningPath::protocolCmd function should be marked payable, or the command flow should be redesigned to ensure no ether is sent when the inner function is non‑payable. Once corrected, reward‑setup transactions will succeed, funds will be transferred as intended, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about reward distribution will be restored.

title: Accrued liquidity can be lost and never be recovered for a given tick period.
