description: Accrued liquidity can be lost and never be recovered for a given tick period due to not incrementing `tickTrackingIndex`, which sets the tick end timestamp to `nextweek` and will start accruing liquidity for next tick period.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the time‑weighted liquidity accrual logic of the LiquidityMining contract. When a liquidity provider exits a concentrated position at exactly the timestamp that marks the end of the current weekly tick (the variable nextWeek), the contract evaluates the condition `if (tickTracking.exitTimestamp < nextWeek)`. Because the comparison is strict, the branch that should increment the internal tickTrackingIndex and calculate the elapsed time (dt) is not taken; instead the else branch runs, setting tickActiveEnd to nextWeek and moving to the next tick period without updating the index. As a result the accrued liquidity for that tick is never recorded in `tickTrackingIndexAccruedUpTo_`, effectively causing the provider’s earned rewards to disappear. This bug occurs only when the exit timestamp equals the boundary of the next tick, a situation that can be triggered deliberately by timing an exit to the exact week‑end or happen unintentionally if the user’s transaction lands on that precise second. The affected parties are liquidity providers who rely on the contract to credit their time‑weighted rewards, as well as the protocol itself because the accounting invariants are broken and total rewards may be under‑distributed. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the `accrueConcentratedPositionTimeWeightedLiquidity` function and noticing that the tick index is never incremented for the boundary case. It is hard to notice because the loss is silent – no revert or error is emitted, only the expected reward amount is missing, which may appear as a normal zero‑reward situation. The bug violates the business logic that each tick’s liquidity must be fully accounted before the contract advances to the next period, breaking the assumption that accrued liquidity is always captured. The recommended fix is to change the comparison to `<=` so that the index is incremented when the exit timestamp is exactly equal to nextWeek, ensuring the correct dt calculation and proper crediting of accrued liquidity. Conceptually, the fix restores proper tick progression and guarantees that no liquidity is lost due to boundary timing, aligning the contract’s accounting with its intended reward model.

title: Positions that are not eligible for rewards will affect the reward income of eligible positions
description: When calculating reward distribution, the contract uses the current position’s liquidity time weight divided by the total liquidity time weight of the pool, instead of the total liquidity time weight of the pool that meets the reward conditions. This means that if there is a large amount of liquidity in the pool that is not eligible for rewards, the total weekly reward distribution will be much less than the `rewardPerWeek`, which should not be expected.
bug_full: The contract distributes weekly rewards based on each position’s liquidity‑time weight divided by the pool’s total liquidity‑time weight. The calculation mistakenly includes the weight of every position in the pool, even those that do not satisfy the reward eligibility criteria (for example, positions that lack a required lock period or do not meet a token‑type condition). Because the denominator contains ineligible liquidity, the share allocated to eligible positions is diluted. An attacker or any participant can add a large amount of liquidity that is deliberately made ineligible for rewards, which inflates the total weight and reduces the proportion of rewards that eligible positions receive. In practice this means that a user who expects to receive the full `rewardPerWeek` amount may see only a fraction of it – in the reported test the reward was reduced to roughly one‑quarter of the intended amount. The issue manifests whenever the pool contains a mix of eligible and ineligible positions, which is a common scenario for concentrated‑type reward programs that impose conditional restrictions. Users with legitimate positions experience lower payouts, potentially receiving nothing if the ineligible weight overwhelms the pool. The protocol’s economic model is broken because the reward accounting no longer matches the advertised distribution schedule, leading to loss of trust and possible token value erosion. The problem was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a test where an extra position that does not meet the reward conditions was added, and the observed reward transfer to the contract was far below the expected weekly amount. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error; it simply distributes a smaller amount, which can be mistaken for normal variance. The correct fix is to adjust the reward‑distribution formula so that the total weight used in the denominator only aggregates the liquidity‑time weight of positions that satisfy the reward conditions, thereby ensuring that only eligible liquidity competes for the reward pool. This change restores the intended accounting semantics and prevents reward dilution caused by unrelated liquidity.

title: Some tokens enable the direct draining of all approved `ERC20Votes` tokens
description:
There’s an appropriately invalidated finding found by the bots during the bot race about the [unsafe use of `transferFrom` on non-standard ERC20 tokens](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-ens/blob/main/bot-report.md#d24-unsafe-use-of-erc20-transfertransferfrom). The finding is mostly invalid because, here, we’re using `ERC20Votes` tokens, not `ERC20` ones; hence the mentioned tokens like USDT aren’t good arguments.

I would like to argue, however, that the recommendation that would’ve been true here would be to wrap the `transferFrom` calls in a `require` statement, as the `transferFrom` functions used in `ERC20Votes` are still from the inherited `ERC20` interface and therefore could be returning a boolean (`transferFrom(address from, address to, uint256 amount) returns bool`, see [OpenZeppelin’s implementation](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/4.x/api/token/erc20#ERC20-transferFrom-address-address-uint256-)), instead of reverting, depending on the existence of such an `ERC20Votes` token. The assumption of an `ERC20Votes` token returning `true` or `false` instead of reverting will be used in this argumentation and be considered a possibility; especially since the list of potential `ERC20Votes token`s used by this contract isn’t specified (`ENSToken` isn’t enforced). Also, see [these posts](https://discord.com/channels/810916927919620096/1159158237325697166/1160653235703521451) from the Discord channel:

Question by J4X — Hey @nickjohnson, are we correct to assume that this will only be deployed on ethereum?

Answer by nickjohnson — By us, yes, but consider the goal of the audit to be against any wrapped erc20votes token, not just `$`ens.

**About this finding:**

This finding is the second one in a series of 2 findings using a similar set of arguments, but the first is used here as a chain:

1. Some tokens break accounting by enabling the free minting of `ERC20MultiDelegate` tokens.
2. Some tokens enable the direct draining of all approved `ERC20Votes` tokens.

Some parts are similar between the two findings, but because they each deserved their own analysis and “should fix” - argumentation, they are submitted as separate findings.

Draining all `ERC20Votes` tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the ERC20MultiDelegate contract interacts with an external ERC20Votes token through the standard transferFrom function. The contract assumes that transferFrom will either succeed and return true or revert on failure, but it does not explicitly check the boolean return value. If an ERC20Votes implementation deviates from the typical OpenZeppelin behaviour and returns false instead of reverting when a transfer cannot be performed, the ERC20MultiDelegate logic proceeds as if the transfer succeeded. This silent failure enables an attacker who has been granted an unlimited allowance on the ERC20Votes token to call delegateMulti with arbitrary source and target identifiers and mint any amount of ERC20MultiDelegate tokens for themselves without actually moving the underlying votes tokens. Once the attacker holds these freshly minted delegate tokens, they can invoke delegateMulti again, this time using the newly created balances as sources to pull the approved ERC20Votes tokens from the proxy contracts that back each delegate ID. The result is a complete draining of all ERC20Votes tokens that were approved for the ERC20MultiDelegate contract, effectively moving the funds from the proxy contracts to the attacker’s address. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that their vote‑token balance suddenly drops to zero while the attacker’s balance increases, and the accounting of the multi‑delegate token appears inconsistent because the delegate balances no longer correspond to any underlying votes tokens. The issue occurs only when the external token’s transferFrom returns false on failure, when the attacker has an allowance set, and when the contract does not enforce a require on the return value. It affects any holder of the ERC20Votes token who approves the ERC20MultiDelegate contract, as well as the protocol that relies on correct accounting of delegated voting power. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit when a mock ERC20Votes token was crafted to return false on failed transfers, demonstrating that the contract’s logic does not guard against this edge case. The problem is hard to notice because most ERC20 implementations revert on failure, so developers rarely add explicit checks for the boolean return. To remediate the issue the contract should either wrap every transferFrom call in a require that checks the returned boolean, or replace the call with a safeTransferFrom pattern that reverts on failure, thereby ensuring that any unsuccessful token movement aborts the delegate operation and prevents unauthorized minting and draining of funds. In essence, the bug is a classic unchecked return‑value vulnerability in token transfer logic that leads to accounting breakage and potential fund loss.

title: `FULL_RESTRICTED` Stakers can bypass restriction through approvals
bug_full: The vulnerability is an access‑control bypass in the StakedUSDe contract that allows a fully restricted (blacklisted) staker to withdraw or redeem their USDe tokens despite the protocol’s intention to lock those funds. The contract inherits from OpenZeppelin ERC4626, which defines a redeem function that lets an approved address act on behalf of the token owner. In the overridden _withdraw internal function the code only checks whether the caller or the receiver has the FULL_RESTRICTED_STAKER_ROLE, but it never checks the actual token owner (the _owner parameter). Consequently, a blacklisted user can call approve on a third‑party address, and that address can invoke redeem with the blacklisted user as the owner. The _beforeTokenTransfer hook also blocks direct transfers from restricted addresses unless the destination is the zero address (burn), but it does not affect the redeem path, so the restriction is effectively bypassed. This flaw can be exploited by any blacklisted staker who first approves another address and then lets that address call redeem, resulting in the full amount of locked USDe being transferred to the approved address. The impact is that the compliance mechanism intended to freeze assets is ineffective; restricted users can still extract their funds, violating legal and business rules and potentially exposing the protocol to regulatory risk. The issue occurs whenever a fully restricted address has granted an allowance to another address and the protocol relies on the _withdraw check to enforce the lock. Affected parties include the blacklisted stakers, the protocol operators who expect the blacklist to enforce asset freezes, and any third parties that might be tricked into receiving withdrawn funds. The bug was discovered during a security audit through a Foundry test that demonstrated the full blacklist withdrawal scenario. It is hard to notice because the contract correctly blocks direct transfers and direct withdraw calls, giving a false sense of security, while the indirect redeem path remains unchecked. To fix the issue, the _withdraw function must also verify that the token owner does not hold the FULL_RESTRICTED_STAKER_ROLE, and the contract should ensure that any ERC4626 operation that moves assets on behalf of an owner respects the restriction, effectively extending the access control check to the owner parameter as well. This class of bug is an access‑control bypass caused by incomplete validation of privileged roles during delegated operations, leading to unexpected fund movement where users expect their balance to remain locked.

title: Soft Restricted Staker Role can withdraw stUSDe for USDe
description:
A requirement is stated that a user with the `SOFT_RESTRICTED_STAKER_ROLE` is not allowed to withdraw `USDe` for `stUSDe`.

The code does not satisfy that condition, when a holder has the `SOFT_RESTRICTED_STAKER_ROLE`, they can exchange their `stUSDe` for `USDe` using `StakedUSDeV2`.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns an access‑control flaw in the StakedUSDe contract where the soft‑restricted staker role is intended to be prohibited from withdrawing USDe in exchange for stUSDe, but the implementation does not enforce this restriction. The contract checks only the FULL_RESTRICTED_STAKER_ROLE for both the caller and the receiver before reverting the operation, leaving out any verification of the SOFT_RESTRICTED_STAKER_ROLE. As a result, a user who has been granted the soft‑restricted role – typically through a blacklist manager – can still call the redeem or withdraw functions, which internally invoke the same _withdraw logic, and receive their original USDe plus any accrued rewards. This behavior contradicts the documented policy that soft‑restricted accounts may deposit but may not withdraw, creating a mismatch between expectations and reality. The issue is triggered after a user is blacklisted with the soft‑restricted role and then attempts to redeem or withdraw; the contract’s condition evaluates to false and the operation proceeds, allowing the user to extract funds that the protocol intended to lock. The impact is that the protocol’s risk‑mitigation controls are bypassed, potentially enabling malicious or sanctioned accounts to move assets, undermining compliance and exposing the system to financial loss or reputational damage. The flaw was discovered during a Code4rena audit by writing tests that first assign the soft‑restricted role to an account and then invoke redeem and withdraw, observing that the calls succeed and the balances are transferred as expected. The problem is subtle because the role name suggests a restriction, the documentation explicitly states withdrawal is disallowed, and the code only checks a different role, making the bug easy to overlook without targeted testing. To remediate, the access‑control check should be extended to include hasRole(SOFT_RESTRICTED_STAKER_ROLE, caller) (or receiver) in the same conditional that reverts with OperationNotAllowed, thereby aligning the contract’s behaviour with its specification and preventing soft‑restricted accounts from exchanging stUSDe for USDe. This class of bug falls under improper access control where a privilege check is incomplete, leading to unintended privilege escalation and violation of business logic that assumes locked funds cannot be withdrawn by certain roles.

title: users still forced to follow previously set cooldownDuration even when cooldown is off
description:
The `StakedUSDeV2` contract can enforces coolDown periods for users before they are able to unstake/ take out their funds from the silo contract if coolDown is on. Based on the presence of the modifiers `ensureCooldownOff` and `ensureCooldownOn`, it is known that the coolDown state of the `StakedUSDeV2` contract can be toggled on or off. In a scenario where coolDown is on (always turned on by default) and Alice and Bob deposits, two days after Alice wants to withdraw/redeem. Alice is forced to wait for 90 days before completing withdrawal/getting her tokens from the silo contract because Alice must call coolDownAsset()/coolDownShares() fcns respectively. Bob decides to wait an extra day.

On the third day, Bob decides to withdraw/redeem. Contract admin also toggles the coolDown off (sets cooldownDuration to 0), meaning there is no longer a coolDown period and all withdrawals should be sent to the users immediately. Bob now calls the redeem()/withdraw() fcn to withdraw instantly to his address instead of the silo address since there is no coolDown.

Alice sees Bob has gotten her tokens but Alice cant use the redeem()/withdraw() because her `StakedUSDeV2` were already burned and her underlying assets were sent to the silo contract for storage. Alice cannot successfully call `unstake()` because her `userCooldown.cooldownEnd` value set to ~ 90 days. Now Alice has to unfairly wait out the 90 days even though coolDowns have been turned off and everyone else has unrestricted access to their assets. Alice only crime is trying to withdraw earlier than Bob. This is a loss to Alice as Alice has no StakedUSDE or the underlying asset for the no longer necessary 90 days as if the assset is volatile, it may lose some fiat value during the unfair and no longer necessary wait period.

If cooldown is turned off, it should affect all contract processes and as such, withdrawals should become immediate to users. Tokens previously stored in the USDeSilo contract should become accessible to users when the cooldown state is off. Previous withdrawal requests that had a cooldown should no longer be restricted by a coolDown period since coolDown now off and the coolDownDuration of the contract is now 0.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑inconsistency bug in the StakedUSDeV2 vault that forces users who started a withdrawal while the cooldown mechanism was active to remain locked out even after the contract administrator disables the cooldown by setting cooldownDuration to zero. The root cause is that the unstake() function only checks whether the current block timestamp is greater than the user‑specific cooldownEnd value that was recorded when the user called cooldownAssets() or cooldownShares(). It does not consider the global cooldownDuration flag, nor does the admin function that disables the cooldown clear or override existing cooldownEnd timestamps. Consequently, when the admin toggles the cooldown off, any pending cooldown entries remain unchanged and the require block in unstake() still reverts because block.timestamp is still earlier than the stored cooldownEnd, effectively locking the user’s underlying assets in the silo contract for the originally scheduled 90‑day period. An attacker (or any user) can exploit this by waiting for the admin to turn the cooldown off after they have already initiated a cooldown, then attempting to withdraw immediately; the contract will reject the request, forcing the user to wait the full original period while other users can withdraw instantly. The impact is that affected users lose timely access to their funds, potentially suffering market‑price loss or liquidity issues, and the protocol’s promised “instant withdrawal when cooldown is off” guarantee is broken. This condition occurs only after the cooldown has been turned on by default, a user has initiated a cooldown withdrawal, and later the admin disables the cooldown. All users with pending cooldowns are affected, while users who have not started a cooldown are not. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the ensureCooldownOff modifier on withdraw/redeem functions with the logic inside unstake() and noticed that the latter does not respect the global cooldown flag. It can be hard to notice because the contract’s public interface suggests that disabling the cooldown makes withdrawals immediate, yet the internal state for existing cooldowns is never updated. The proper fix is to modify unstake() (or the admin toggle) so that when cooldownDuration is zero, pending cooldown entries are either cleared or the timestamp check is bypassed, allowing immediate withdrawal from the silo and aligning the contract’s behavior with ERC‑4626 expectations and the protocol’s stated policy.

title: Malicious users can front-run to cause a denial of service
description: Malicious users can transfer `USDe` token to `StakedUSDe` protocol directly lead to a denial of service (DoS) for StakedUSDe due to the limit shares check.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic denial‑of‑service that arises when a malicious actor can transfer USDe tokens directly into the StakedUSDe contract without invoking the deposit function. The contract calculates the number of shares to mint using a formula that divides the amount of assets by the total assets held by the contract (totalAssets) plus a constant, and then checks that the resulting share amount is at least a minimum threshold (MIN_SHARES = 1 ether). Because totalAssets is derived from the token balance of the contract, a direct transfer increases the denominator while the totalSupply of shares remains unchanged. This dilution makes the share conversion factor arbitrarily small. When the attacker sends a small amount, for example 1 ether, the next legitimate user attempting to deposit any reasonable amount receives fewer than the required minimum shares, causing the deposit call to revert with a MinSharesViolation error. The impact is that legitimate users are unable to stake USDe, their transactions fail, and the protocol becomes effectively unusable, constituting a denial of service. The condition occurs whenever the contract permits arbitrary ERC20 transfers into its balance and enforces a non‑zero minimum share requirement. All users who try to deposit after the malicious transfer are affected, while existing share holders retain their balances but cannot receive new shares. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a test that performed a direct token transfer followed by a normal deposit, which consistently reverted. The problem is subtle because the token transfer itself does not revert and the share calculation appears correct under normal operation; only the interaction between external balance changes and the minimum‑share guard reveals the flaw. From a user perspective the symptom is a transaction that reverts with an obscure “MinSharesViolation” error, leaving the user with no new shares and an unchanged token balance, contrary to the expectation that a deposit of thousands of ether would succeed. This bug belongs to the class of share‑dilution or accounting‑invariant violations that enable front‑run denial‑of‑service attacks. To remediate the issue the contract should either enforce a minimum deposit amount that cannot be bypassed by external transfers, prevent direct token transfers into the contract, or redesign the share calculation to rely on an internal accounting variable rather than the raw token balance, thereby eliminating the possibility of share dilution and ensuring that the minimum‑share check does not unintentionally block legitimate deposits.

title: `MinterContract::payArtist` can result in double the intended payout
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the royalty payout function of the MinterContract, where the validation of the split percentages does not correspond to the actual calculation of artist royalties. An admin can set the primary split between artist and team to any values that sum to 100 percent, and the contract stores the artist address percentages that were previously proposed and accepted. When payArtist is called, the function only checks that the stored artist percentage plus the two team percentages supplied in the call equal 100. If the admin later changes the primary split so that the artist percentage becomes zero while the team percentage becomes 100, the check still passes because 0 + teamperc1 + teamperc2 = 100. However, the payout calculation still uses the stale artist address percentages, which still sum to the original artist allocation (for example 100 percent). As a result the contract sends the full royalty amount to the artist based on the old allocation and also sends the full amount to the team based on the new allocation, effectively paying out up to double the intended amount. This can be exploited by any party with admin rights: they first set an artist‑only split, have the artist addresses accepted, then switch the split to team‑only and invoke payArtist. The contract will transfer the full royalty pool to both parties, draining the contract balance. The issue occurs whenever the primary split is altered after artist address percentages have been accepted but before a payout is executed. It affects the protocol’s financial integrity, the admin role, the artist and team beneficiaries, and ultimately any users relying on correct royalty accounting. The bug was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, which reproduced the double payout with a Foundry test. It is hard to notice because each individual transfer appears correct – the artist receives the expected amount and the team receives the expected amount – while the total exceeds the contract’s available balance, leading to an unnoticed loss of funds. The flaw belongs to the class of accounting or logic errors where validation and state used for computation diverge. To remediate, the contract should verify that the sum of the stored artist address percentages matches the current artist allocation before performing any payout, or it should recompute artist royalties based on the current split, and optionally reset or re‑validate artist address percentages whenever the primary split changes.

title: The `RandomizerVRF` and `RandomizerRNG` do not produce hash value.
poc:
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/8b518196629faa37eae39736837b24926fd3c07c/smart-contracts/RandomizerVRF.sol#L66>
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/8b518196629faa37eae39736837b24926fd3c07c/smart-contracts/RandomizerRNG.sol#L49>
bug_full: During the fulfillment of a randomness request, the RandomizerVRF and RandomizerRNG contracts assign a tokenHash by casting the abi‑encoded random words and token identifier directly to bytes32. This cast truncates the encoded data to the first 32 bytes, effectively storing only the first element of the random array and ignoring the tokenId contribution. Consequently the tokenHash is not a cryptographic hash but merely the raw random number (or its truncated representation). The specification and documentation require tokenHash to be a keccak256 hash of the random data, ensuring a uniform 256‑bit distribution and uniqueness across tokens. Because the implementation skips the hash step, tokenHash values can collide, the entropy range may be smaller than the full uint256 space, and subtle biases such as monobit bias are not mitigated. The bug manifests when the oracle returns a random word and the contract calls setTokenHash; any user who mints an NFT expects a unique, unpredictable hash identifier, but may observe duplicate hashes or hashes that appear to be the raw random number. The issue was discovered during a code audit that compared the contract against the documented behavior. It can be hard to notice because the stored value still looks random and the contract functions correctly from a purely functional standpoint, masking the violation of the invariant that tokenHash must be a hash. The impact is primarily on protocol correctness: downstream logic that relies on hash uniqueness for provenance, rarity calculations, or anti‑collusion measures may be weakened, and the reduced entropy could be exploited to predict token identifiers. The affected parties include token owners, the protocol that issues NFTs, and any integrators that assume a proper hash. The recommended remediation is to replace the bytes32 cast with a keccak256 hash of the concatenated random words and tokenId, thereby restoring the intended distribution, eliminating collisions, and complying with the specification.

title: Vulnerability in `burnToMint` function allows double use of NFT
description: The current implementation of the `burnToMint` function in the `NextGenCore.sol` smart contract permits a contract holder to both burn and sell the same NFT, effectively exploiting it to mint a new NFT. This leads to potential fraudulent activities when trading the NFT.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical ordering flaw in the burn‑to‑mint workflow of the NextGenCore contract. The function that is supposed to destroy an existing NFT and then issue a new one performs the minting step before the burn. Because the internal _mintProcessing routine calls _safeMint, which can invoke external code on the recipient contract, an attacker can execute arbitrary logic between the mint and the burn. By deploying a malicious contract that receives the newly minted token, the attacker can transfer or sell the original token before it is actually burned. In practice the attacker lists the NFT for sale, receives a purchase offer, then calls burnToMint. The contract mints a replacement token to the attacker’s contract, and during the _safeMint callback the attacker moves the original token to the buyer or another address, effectively allowing the same NFT to be used twice – once as a sold asset and once as a burned token that is replaced by a new one. This results in the buyer receiving nothing while the attacker keeps the proceeds from the sale and also obtains the newly minted NFT, causing a loss of funds and a breach of trust in the marketplace. The issue manifests whenever burnToMint is invoked with a recipient that is a contract capable of executing code on receipt, and when the collection is configured to allow burn‑to‑mint operations. It affects token owners, buyers, and the overall protocol because accounting assumptions about one‑to‑one correspondence between burned and minted tokens are violated. The flaw was discovered during a Code4rena audit through manual code review and a crafted test that demonstrated the re‑entrancy‑like behavior. It is subtle because the mint and burn occur in the same transaction, making the state appear consistent at the end of execution, and the external call is hidden inside the safe‑mint routine. The proper fix is to apply the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern: perform the burn before any external call, update the collection supply counters, and only then mint the new token, or alternatively guard the function with a non‑reentrant modifier and avoid calling _safeMint on contracts that could manipulate the token before it is destroyed. This ensures that the original NFT cannot be transferred or sold after the burn request, preserving the intended one‑to‑one token lifecycle.

title: On a Linear or Exponential Descending Sale Model, a user that mints on the last `block.timestamp` mints at an unexpected price.
description: A user can mint a token at an incorrect price and lose funds if they mint on the last authorized `block.timestamp` during a Linear or Exponential Descending Sale Model.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the time‑based pricing logic of a descending sale model. The contract determines the mint price by checking whether the current block.timestamp lies between the allowlist start time and the public end time using strict greater‑than (>) and less‑than (<) comparisons. Because the final timestamp (publicEndTime) is excluded, the getPrice() function falls back to the fixed‑price branch and returns the initial collectionMintCost instead of the expected collectionEndMintCost. This logic error occurs both in the price‑calculation routine and in the mint() function, which also uses an inclusive lower bound but an exclusive upper bound for the public sale window. When a user’s transaction is mined exactly at the publicEndTime, the contract treats the sale as finished and applies the original high price. The user therefore pays more than the advertised final price, losing funds or receiving a price that does not match the sale’s advertised schedule. The impact is financial loss for any participant who mints at the exact last second of the sale, erosion of trust in the pricing mechanism, and potential reputational damage for the protocol. The condition is rare because it only triggers at a single block timestamp, making it easy to overlook during testing; the bug may only appear in production when a miner includes a transaction with a timestamp equal to publicEndTime. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the conditional boundaries of the descending sale logic. It belongs to the broader class of boundary‑condition bugs where exclusive comparisons cause incorrect branch selection. From a user’s perspective the UI may display the advertised lower price for the final period, but the transaction receipt shows a higher amount deducted, leading to confusion such as “I expected a cheap mint but I was charged the full price”. To remediate, the contract should replace the > and < operators with >= and <= in the relevant else/if branches so that the final timestamp is included in the descending price calculation, ensuring the price returned at publicEndTime matches the collectionEndMintCost. This change aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that the price linearly or exponentially descends to the final price at the end of the sale period.

title: Auction payout goes to `AuctionDemo` contract owner, not the token owner
description:
At the end of an auction in `AuctionDemo`, the highest bidder claims the token, which transfers the token from the token owner to the auction winner. In the same transaction, the token owner should receive the auction payout.

However, the function `AuctionDemo::claimAuction()` sends the payout to the `AuctionDemo` contract owner.

This behavior deviates from the listed [invariant](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/tree/main?tab=readme-ov-file#main-invariants):

The highest bidder will receive the token after an auction finishes, the owner of the token will receive the funds and all other participants will get refunded.

1. Auction is started, Alice deployed the `AuctionDemo` contract and Cecilia approved the `AuctionDemo` contract to transfer her tokens to the winning bidder.
2. Auction is completed. The highest bid was Bob.
3. Bob claims his winnings. The token is transferred from Cecilia to Bob. The bid from Bob is sent to Alice and Cecilia gets nothing.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a payout misdirection in the auction contract. When the highest bidder calls the claim function, the contract correctly transfers the NFT from the original token holder to the winner, but the ether that represents the winning bid is sent to the owner of the AuctionDemo contract instead of the actual token owner. The root cause is a logical error: the claimAuction implementation uses the contract’s Ownable.owner() (or a variable that references the contract owner) as the recipient of the proceeds, confusing it with the token’s owner address. An attacker does not need to do anything special; any participant can trigger the bug simply by calling claimAuction after the auction ends. The impact is that the legitimate token owner loses the auction revenue, receiving zero ether, while the contract owner unexpectedly gains the funds. This occurs whenever the token being auctioned is owned by an address different from the contract owner, which is the typical case in a marketplace where creators list their own NFTs. The affected parties are the token owners, bidders who expect the seller to be paid, and the overall protocol reputation because the business rule that “the token owner receives the funds” is violated. The issue was discovered during a functional test that verified ether balances after a claim; the test showed that the contract owner’s balance increased while the token owner’s balance remained unchanged. The bug can be hard to notice because the NFT transfer succeeds and the UI may only display the token changing hands, hiding the missing payout. To fix the problem, the contract should retrieve the current owner of the token (for example by calling IERC721.ownerOf(tokenId)) and direct the payable call to that address, ensuring that the auction proceeds are sent to the rightful seller. This correction restores the intended accounting invariant that the seller receives the bid amount and all other participants are refunded appropriately, preventing funds from disappearing or being sent to an unintended party.

title: Artist signatures can be forged to impersonate the artist behind a collection
description:
Artist signatures can be forged, making it possible to sign any message, while “proving” that it was signed by any address.

This can be done to impersonate any address from any artist, breaking a core protocol functionality, and losing users’ trust. The signature can’t be deleted by anyone, nor the artist address, once the collection is signed.

This also breaks one of the [main invariants of the protocol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/tree/main#main-invariants):

Properties that should NEVER be broken under any circumstance:

  * Only artists can sign their collections.

Evaluated as Medium since it breaks a core contract functionality, and a main invariant, regardless of trusted roles. As any collection admin can impersonate any legit address, which should be consider a way to “escalate their authority beyond their role” [as mentioned on the Access Control and Permissions Attack Ideas](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/tree/main#attack-ideas-where-to-look-for-bugs).
poc:
`setCollectionData()` allows to set the artist address when the current `collectionTotalSupply == 0`:

  * [NextGenCore.sol#L149](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/main/smart-contracts/NextGenCore.sol#L149)
  * [NextGenCore.sol#L150](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/main/smart-contracts/NextGenCore.sol#L150)

The problem is that it doesn’t check that the param `collectionTotalSupply` passed is != 0. Meaning that the function can be executed multiple times to change the artist address, as long as the total supply is zero:

  * [NextGenCore.sol#L148](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/main/smart-contracts/NextGenCore.sol#L148)
  * [NextGenCore.sol#L153](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/main/smart-contracts/NextGenCore.sol#L153)

So, it can be called first to set a fake artist address to call `artistSignature()` to sign the collection:

  * [NextGenCore.sol#L257](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/main/smart-contracts/NextGenCore.sol#L257)

And then call `setCollectionData()` again to set the legit artist address.

Once the signature is set, it can’t be changed, nor the artist address, as it will always fall under the `else` clause:

  * [NextGenCore.sol#L162](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/main/smart-contracts/NextGenCore.sol#L162)
  * [NextGenCore.sol#L258](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/main/smart-contracts/NextGenCore.sol#L258)

The following coded POC shows how it can be done.
bug_full: An artist signature forgery vulnerability exists in the collection management contract. The contract allows a collection administrator to call setCollectionData with a total supply of zero. Because the function does not enforce that collectionTotalSupply be greater than zero, the administrator can change the stored artist address while the collection is still unfinalized. An attacker can first set a malicious address as the artist, invoke artistSignature to record a signature that is stored as coming from the malicious address, and then call setCollectionData again with a non‑zero total supply and the legitimate artist address. The signature entry is immutable after it is written, so the on‑chain record shows that the legitimate artist signed the collection even though the signature was produced by the attacker. This breaks the protocol invariant that only the true artist can sign a collection, enables impersonation of any artist, and undermines user trust because collectors see a signed collection that was never authorized by the real creator. The flaw is triggered whenever a collection is created with a totalSupply of zero and the administrator has permission to modify the artist field; it does not require any privileged role beyond the collection admin. Because the signature is stored on‑chain without an explicit link to the address that produced it, the forgery is difficult to detect by casual inspection – the signature appears to be valid and the artist address matches the expected value after the second call. The impact includes potential loss of reputation for artists, confusion for buyers who may purchase under false pretenses, and the inability to retroactively correct the forged signature. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the input validation of setCollectionData. To remediate, the contract should enforce that collectionTotalSupply be non‑zero before allowing any change to the artist address, or lock the artist field after the first assignment, and ensure that artistSignature can only be called when the stored artist address matches the caller’s address. In general, this class of bug is an improper state transition that permits privileged data (artist identity) to be altered after a dependent immutable action (signature) has been performed.

title: Auction winner can prevent payments via `safeTransferFrom` callback
description:
An auction winner can decide to conditionally revert the `claimAuction()` execution.

This leads to the following impacts:

  * Other bidders can’t get their funds back
  * The protocol doesn’t receive the funds from the winning bid

This can lead to permanent loss of funds if the adversary decides to. As a drawback, they can’t get the NFT.

But nevertheless, they can use their control over the function to ask for a ransom, as the sum of other bids, plus the protocol earnings can be higher than the maximum bid itself and the damaged public image of the protocol for losing users funds.

It also breaks one of the [main invariants of the protocol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen#main-invariants):

Properties that should NEVER be broken under any circumstance:

  * The highest bidder will receive the token after an auction finishes, **the owner of the token will receive the funds** and **all other participants will get refunded**.

Evaluated as Medium, as despite of the possibility of permanent assets lost, and breaking a main invariant, the adversary will have to take a loss as well; or persuade the participants via a ransom.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises when the auction contract settles an auction by first calling IERC721.safeTransferFrom to move the token to the winning bidder and only afterwards attempts to forward the winning bid amount to the seller and to refund the other participants. Because safeTransferFrom invokes the onERC721Received callback on the recipient contract, a malicious winner that is itself a contract can deliberately revert inside that callback. The revert propagates to the entire claimAuction transaction, causing the NFT transfer, the payment to the protocol owner, and all refunds to be rolled back. This happens only after the auction has been declared finished and the winner calls claimAuction, so the protocol assumes the transfer will succeed. The affected parties are the seller (who never receives the proceeds), the other bidders (who never get their deposits back), and the protocol itself (which loses the ability to collect its fees and to release the token). The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the claimAuction implementation, where the auditor noticed that the safeTransferFrom call is not protected against a reverting receiver. It is easy to miss because safeTransferFrom is a standard ERC‑721 function and developers often trust that the receiver will not revert, overlooking the fact that any contract can implement ERC721Receiver and abort the call. The impact is that funds can become permanently locked and the token remains unclaimed, breaking the protocol’s invariant that the highest bidder receives the token, the seller receives the funds, and all other participants are refunded. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a failed claim transaction, the winner would not receive the NFT, bidders would see no refund, and the seller would see no payment, contrary to the expectation that claiming the auction always succeeds. The bug belongs to the class of callback‑revert or external‑call‑ordering vulnerabilities, where a contract performs a state‑changing external call before completing its own internal accounting. To remediate the issue the NFT transfer should be isolated from the payment logic, for example by moving the token transfer to a separate function that can be called after the funds have been safely distributed, or by using a pull‑payment pattern for refunds and seller proceeds, and by handling possible reverts from safeTransferFrom with try/catch or by using a non‑reverting transfer method.

title: If an airdrop happens before a mint the price could skyrocket
description: As explained by the [docs](https://seize-io.gitbook.io/nextgen/nextgen-smart-contracts/features#minting-process), several steps can occur during the minting process. However, an airdrop before `salesOption` 3 can lead to price inflation.
poc:
Under `salesOption` 3, [getPrice](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/main/smart-contracts/MinterContract.sol#L536) returns:
    
```solidity
return collectionPhases[_collectionId].collectionMintCost
    + ((collectionPhases[_collectionId].collectionMintCost / collectionPhases[_collectionId].rate) * gencore.viewCirSupply(_collectionId));
```

This is the increased rate based on the NFTs **already in circulation**. If an airdrop occurs before a mint with `salesOption` 3, the price will be much higher than intended.

Example:

Steps | Option | NFTs | Price | Rate  
---|---|---|---|---  
1 OG users | Airdropped | 20 NFTs | free | -  
2 Whitelisted | Sales 3 | 10 NFTs | 1 ETH | 10 (0.1 ETH increase)  
3 Public | Sales 1 | 70 NFTs | 2 ETH | -  
  
With the current three steps, after the airdrop, `salesOption` 3 should start at 1 ETH and gradually increase to 2 ETH. Afterward, it should mint at a constant rate of 2 ETH.

However, when sales option 3 starts, [getPrice](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/main/smart-contracts/MinterContract.sol#L536) will return 3 ETH instead of 1 ETH. This will cause the initial users to pay an inflated price, which was not intended by the owner and can harm their reputation. It’s also unfair to the users, as these so-called special (whitelisted) users will pay increased prices.

_Note: see [original submission](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen-findings/issues/381) for math breakdown provided._

Gist [here](https://gist.github.com/0x3b33/558b919a57101e7a0942e557a464078a). 

Add to remappings - `contracts/=smart-contracts/` and run it with `forge test --match-test test_airdrop --lib-paths ../smart-contracts`.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the mint price calculation in the MinterContract uses the total number of NFTs reported by gencore.viewCirSupply as the basis for a linear price increase when salesOption 3 is active. Because the function does not differentiate between NFTs that were minted through the public sale and those that were distributed via an airdrop, an airdrop that occurs before the first sale under salesOption 3 artificially inflates the circulating supply. The price formula adds collectionMintCost plus (collectionMintCost / rate) multiplied by the circulating supply, so each airdropped token adds an extra (collectionMintCost / rate) to the price of every subsequent mint. An attacker or even an honest contract owner who triggers an airdrop before the sale can cause the first whitelisted users to see a price that is significantly higher than the intended starting price (for example 3 ETH instead of 1 ETH). The impact is economic: users pay more than advertised, the protocol appears to overcharge, and the reputation of the project may suffer. The condition occurs whenever salesOption 3 is selected and an airdrop is executed before any minting under that option. The affected parties are the whitelisted or early buyers who expect a low, predictable price, as well as the protocol owners who intend a fair pricing curve. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the minting flow and the price‑calculation code, noticing that the circulating‑supply variable can be increased by external airdrop calls. It is hard to notice because the price function itself does not emit warnings and the airdrop is a legitimate operation, so the inflated price looks like a normal progression of the pricing curve. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑dependent pricing logic” or “economic manipulation via mutable supply counters”. To fix the problem, the contract should keep a separate counter for airdropped tokens and subtract that amount from the value returned by viewCirSupply when computing the price, or otherwise base the price on the number of tokens minted through the sale rather than total supply. This ensures that airdropped NFTs do not affect the price curve, preserving the intended economics and preventing users from receiving a higher price than expected.

title: `getPrice` `salesOption` 2 can round down to the lower barrier, skipping the last time period
description: [getPrice](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/main/smart-contracts/MinterContract.sol#L530) in `salesOption` 2 can round down to the lower barrier, effectively skipping the last time period. In simpler terms, if the price is scheduled to decrease over 4 hours, it will decrease for 2.999… hours and then jump to the price at the end of the 4th hour.
poc:
[getPrice](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/main/smart-contracts/MinterContract.sol#L530) uses [this else-if calculation](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/main/smart-contracts/MinterContract.sol#L553) to determine whether it should return the price as an equation or just the final price.
    
```solidity
if (((collectionMintCost - collectionEndMintCost) / rate) > tDiff) {
    price = collectionPhases[_collectionId].collectionMintCost - (tDiff * collectionPhases[_collectionId].rate);
} else {
    price = collectionPhases[_collectionId].collectionEndMintCost;
}
```

The `if` statement’s method of division by `rate` is incorrect, as it results in rounding down and incorrect price movements. This can cause the price to jump over the last time period, effectively decreasing faster than intended.

Example:

Values |   
---|---  
`collectionMintCost` | 0.49 ETH  
`collectionEndMintCost` | 0.1 ETH  
`rate` | 0.1 ETH (per hour)  
`timePeriod` | 1 hour - 3600 sec  
  
Hour 0 to 1 - 0.49 ETH.  
Hour 1 to 2 - 0.39 ETH - as it crosses the 1st hour, the price becomes 0.39 ETH.  
Hour 2 to 3 - 0.29 ETH - same here.  
It should go from 3 to 4 to 0.19 ETH, but that step is missed, and it goes directly to 0.1 ETH - the final price.  
Hour 3 to 4 - 0.10 ETH - the final price.

Gist [here](https://gist.github.com/0x3b33/ab8a384f9979c4a9b7c4777be00a78de).

Add `contracts/=smart-contracts/` to mappings and run it with `forge test --match-test test_changeProof --lib-paths ../smart-contracts -vv`.

Logs:
    
    [PASS] test_changeProof() (gas: 745699)
    Logs:
      4900000000000000000
      3900000000000000000
      2900000000000000000
      1000000000000000000
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one rounding error in the price‑calculation routine used for salesOption 2. The function determines whether the current time difference (tDiff) falls within the linear decay period by comparing the integer division of (collectionMintCost‑collectionEndMintCost) by the rate against tDiff. Because Solidity integer division always rounds down, the expression ((collectionMintCost‑collectionEndMintCost) / rate) yields a value that is one unit smaller when the exact number of elapsed periods matches the intended final step. The conditional uses a strict greater‑than comparison, so when tDiff equals the exact number of periods the condition evaluates to false and the code jumps to the else branch, returning the final collectionEndMintCost prematurely. As a result, the price schedule skips the last intermediate price point and jumps directly to the final price, for example moving from 0.29 ETH to 0.10 ETH instead of the expected 0.19 ETH at the fourth hour. This can be exploited by a buyer who initiates a purchase exactly at the boundary of the last period and pays less than the contract’s intended price, leading to revenue loss for the seller and an imbalance in the economic model of the protocol. The issue manifests only when the elapsed time aligns with the exact number of decay intervals; in other cases the price appears to follow the schedule, making the bug hard to notice without precise testing. Users observing the UI may see the price drop to the final amount earlier than advertised, causing confusion such as “I expected to pay 0.19 ETH but the contract charged 0.10 ETH”. The bug was discovered during a formal audit and reproduced with a Forge test that logged the price values at each hour. Fixing the problem requires adjusting the conditional to include equality (changing > to >=) or redesigning the arithmetic to avoid integer‑division rounding, for example by multiplying before dividing or using a ceiling function. Conceptually, the fix ensures the linear decay schedule is evaluated correctly for the final interval, preserving the intended price progression and preventing premature price jumps.

title: Bidder Funds Can Become Unrecoverable Due to 1 second Overlap in `participateToAuction`
description: Bidder funds may become irretrievable if the `participateToAuction()` function is executed after `claimAuction()` during a 1-second overlap.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race condition that can leave a bidder’s ether permanently locked in the auction contract. The contract allows a participant to place a new bid with participateToAuction as long as the current block timestamp is less than or equal to the auction end time, while the winner can call claimAuction as soon as the timestamp is greater than or equal to the same end time. Because the two functions use opposite inequality operators, there exists a one‑second overlap after the auction officially ends during which both functions are callable. When the winner invokes claimAuction first, the contract marks the auction as claimed, transfers the token to the highest bidder and refunds every recorded bidder by iterating over the stored bids. If a later bidder manages to call participateToAuction within the overlap, their bid is recorded after the claim loop has already executed. The claimAuction logic does not include a subsequent refund step for bids added after it runs, and the contract’s cancelBid and cancelAllBids functions are disabled after the auction ends. Consequently, the newly submitted funds become trapped in the contract with no withdrawal path. This situation can be triggered by an attacker who quickly submits a bid immediately after the winner’s claim, or unintentionally by a legitimate user who is unaware of the narrow timing window. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after submitting a bid they receive no confirmation, their wallet balance drops, and later they see no refund or token transfer – effectively “my funds disappeared”. The impact is loss of ether for any bidder caught in the overlap and erosion of trust in the auction protocol. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the temporal checks and state transitions of the auction lifecycle. It is difficult to notice because the window is extremely short and typical test suites do not simulate concurrent calls at the exact block boundary. The proper mitigation is to enforce a strict “less than” condition for participateToAuction, or to set a separate flag that disables new bids once claimAuction has been executed, and to implement a pull‑payment or withdrawal pattern that allows any bid submitted after a claim to be reclaimed safely. In short, the bug belongs to the class of time‑based race conditions that break accounting assumptions and cause funds to become unrecoverable.

title: Unchecked return value of low-level `call()/delegatecall()`
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract uses low‑level call or delegatecall to transfer ether but never checks the boolean success value returned by the call. The Solidity language returns false when the external call runs out of gas, reverts, or the recipient’s fallback reverts, yet the code proceeds as if the transfer succeeded. This pattern appears in multiple functions that pay the auction owner, refund bidders, distribute royalties, and withdraw contract balance. Because the return value is ignored, a failed transfer does not revert the transaction; the contract continues execution, potentially leaving funds locked in the contract or causing the intended recipient to receive no ether. An attacker or a malicious recipient can cause the call to fail deliberately by using a fallback function that reverts or consumes all gas, thereby preventing the payment while the contract state is already updated to reflect that the payment was made. The impact is that users may see their refunds or royalty payments disappear, balances shown in the UI remain unchanged, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions that payments are always successful are violated. The issue manifests whenever the contract attempts to send ether via call without checking success, which occurs during auction settlement, royalty distribution, and admin withdrawals. It affects all participants: bidders expecting refunds, artists expecting royalties, the contract owner expecting withdrawals, and any user relying on the financial flows. The problem was discovered during a static analysis audit that flagged the unchecked call pattern. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; only the missing ether can be observed after the fact. The proper fix is to verify the boolean result of each call and revert on failure, or to use a safer transfer pattern such as OpenZeppelin’s Address.sendValue, which includes a require on success. Treating the unchecked call as a class of unchecked low‑level call bug helps prevent money from silently disappearing or refunds failing.

title: User funds sent in excess are not refunded
bug_full: The contract contains three payable functions that accept Ether to mint or burn tokens. Each function checks that the amount of Ether sent (msg.value) is at least the price required for the operation, but it does not enforce an exact match nor does it return any surplus Ether when the caller sends more than the minimum. The root cause is a missing refund mechanism after the price check; the code simply records the full msg.value in an internal accounting variable (collectionTotalAmount) and proceeds with the mint or burn logic. An attacker or an honest user can exploit this by deliberately over‑paying, for example by using a wallet that adds extra gas‑related padding or by mis‑calculating the price off‑chain. Because the contract never sends the excess back, the extra funds become permanently locked in the contract balance. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, but the user’s wallet shows a higher-than‑expected deduction and no corresponding token benefit for the extra amount, leading to a symptom such as “my balance decreased more than the price of the mint” or “I received no refund for the extra ETH”. The impact is financial loss for any user who over‑pays, and it also skews the protocol’s accounting, inflating the recorded collection totals without a corresponding increase in minted assets. The issue manifests whenever msg.value exceeds the exact price calculation, which can happen due to UI rounding errors, manual entry mistakes, or malicious over‑payment. It affects all participants who interact with the minting or burning functions, including end‑users and the protocol’s revenue model. The vulnerability was identified by an automated static analysis tool that flagged the absence of a refund path after a payable check. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; the contract simply retains the extra Ether silently. To remediate, the functions should either require msg.value to equal the exact price (using a strict equality check) or, after performing the core logic, calculate any surplus and transfer it back to the sender using a safe call or transfer pattern, ensuring that the internal accounting only reflects the net amount actually paid for the service. This aligns the contract’s behavior with typical payment‑for‑service expectations and prevents unintended fund lock‑up.

title: `ODSafeManager#allowSAFE`
description:
“According to the GEB framework, the proxy contracts (`ODProxy`) are designed to interact with the Safe Manager (`ODSafeManager`) through the Proxy Action contract (`BasicActions`). The pivotal function, `allowSAFE()`, is responsible for granting an address the capability to manage the Safe. Unfortunately, the `BasicActions` contract lacks the implementation of the `allowSAFE()` function. Consequently, the proxy contract is unable to execute `allowSAFE()`, leading to the inaccessibility of several critical functions for authorized users.

The functionality of essential operations such as `modifySAFECollateralization()`, `transferCollateral()`, `transferInternalCoins()`, `quitSystem()`, `enterSystem()`, `moveSAFE()`, `removeSAFE()`, and `protectSAFE()` is currently halted due to the inability to allow users to manage the Safe.

In addition to the absent `allowSAFE()` implementation, the following functions are also not yet implemented in the `BasicActions` contract and these functions are not directly executable by proxy contract: `allowHandler()`, `modifySAFECollateralization()`, `transferCollateral()`, `transferInternalCoins()`, `quitSystem()`, `enterSystem()`, `moveSAFE()`, `removeSAFE()`, and `protectSAFE()`.”
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incomplete implementation of the proxy‑action layer that connects an ODProxy contract to the ODSafeManager contract. In the GEB architecture the BasicActions contract is expected to expose a set of helper functions – most notably allowSAFE() – that forward calls to ODSafeManager so that a proxy can grant an address permission to manage a SAFE. Because BasicActions does not contain an implementation of allowSAFE() (and also omits other functions such as allowHandler, modifySAFECollateralization, transferCollateral, transferInternalCoins, quitSystem, enterSystem, moveSAFE, removeSAFE and protectSAFE), any attempt by a proxy to execute these actions results in a revert. The root cause is therefore a missing function definition in the delegate‑call contract, which breaks the expected delegation flow: the proxy calls ODProxy.execute, which forwards the payload to BasicActions, but BasicActions cannot forward the call to ODSafeManager because the selector is not recognised. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload – the mere use of the standard UI or script that tries to call allowSAFE through the proxy will fail, producing a SafeNotAllowed revert. The impact is a functional denial‑of‑service for legitimate users: they cannot grant permission to a SAFE, and consequently cannot invoke critical operations such as modifying collateralisation, transferring collateral or internal coins, moving or removing a SAFE, or protecting a SAFE. From the user’s point of view the interface may show a “Allow” button, but the transaction reverts and the user sees no change in ownership or balances; funds remain locked in the SAFE and the user receives no confirmation that the permission was granted. This condition occurs whenever a user interacts with the protocol through an ODProxy that relies on the current BasicActions implementation. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by executing unit tests that attempted to call allowSAFE via the proxy and observed the expected revert. The bug is subtle because the contract compiles without errors and the missing functions are not referenced directly in the proxy code, making it easy to overlook during code review. The proper remediation is to add concrete implementations of allowSAFE and the other missing actions in BasicActions, or to deploy a new BasicActions contract that includes these selectors and point the proxy to it. Once the functions exist, the proxy can successfully delegate the call to ODSafeManager, restoring the ability for users to manage their SAFEs and re‑enabling the full suite of protocol operations.

title: Old permissions in handlerCan mapping are still attached to the safeHandler of a transferred safe
description: A safe is associated with a unique safeHandler. This safeHandler can give permissions to addresses through the [allowHandler()](https://github.com/open-dollar/od-contracts/blob/f4f0246bb26277249c1d5afe6201d4d9096e52e6/src/contracts/proxies/ODSafeManager.sol#L112) function which stores these approvals/disapprovals in the [handlerCan](https://github.com/open-dollar/od-contracts/blob/f4f0246bb26277249c1d5afe6201d4d9096e52e6/src/contracts/proxies/ODSafeManager.sol#L41) mapping. Now let’s say there is a safeHandler which has permissioned some addresses in the handlerCan mapping. When this safe is transferred to a new owner, the previous permissions that were added to the safeHandler are still attached to it without the new owner realizing it.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a stale‑authorization bug in the ODSafeManager contract. Each safe is linked to a unique safeHandler, and the contract stores per‑handler permissions in a mapping called handlerCan. When the owner of a safe calls allowHandler, the handlerCan entry for that safeHandler is set to allow certain caller addresses. The contract’s transferSAFEOwnership function updates the safe’s owner but does not clear or re‑key the handlerCan entries, so the permissions that were granted by the previous owner remain attached to the same safeHandler after the safe is transferred. As a result, the former owner can still invoke functions that check handlerAllowed for the transferred safe, effectively bypassing the new owner’s intended access control. This can be exploited by the previous owner to perform actions such as calling quitSystem with the new owner’s safe handler, moving debt or funds to the new owner without consent, or otherwise manipulating the safe’s state. The impact is that the new owner may lose control over their safe, see unexpected transactions, or suffer loss of assets, while the protocol’s accounting assumptions about exclusive ownership are violated. The bug manifests whenever a safe is transferred via safeTransferFrom, which triggers the after‑token‑transfer hook that calls transferSAFEOwnership; the hook does not reset handlerCan. Any user who receives a safe under the assumption that no handlers are authorized will be surprised when previously authorized addresses can still act, leading to symptoms such as unauthorized withdrawals, unexpected state changes, or missing balances. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the warden demonstrated that permissions persisted after transfer. It is hard to notice because the mapping is public and the contract does not emit an event indicating a permission reset, so the new owner receives no warning. The proper fix is to make handlerCan a three‑dimensional mapping that also keys on the safe owner, or to explicitly clear or reinitialize the handlerCan entries for the safeHandler during transfer, mirroring the behavior already implemented for the safeCan mapping. By ensuring that permissions are tied to the current owner, the contract will enforce the intended access control and prevent the previous owner from retaining privileged rights after a transfer.

title: Updating `SafeManager` address in the `Vault721` will disable NFV minting
description:
* `Vault721` contract is the ERC721 “Non-fungible Vault” (NFV) that manages all SAFEs ownership, transfers, and approvals via the ERC721 standard, the minter of the NFV is the `ODSafeManager` contract.
  * `ODSafeManager` contract acts as interface to the SAFEEngine to facilitate the management of SAFEs; such as opening safes,modifying SAFE collateral, moving SAFE collateral, etc.
  * When a user opens a SAFE via `ODSafeManager.openSAFE` function; a NFV will be minted to the user where it will have the same id as the SAFE id so that the ids of any of them can be used interchangeably in the system, and the `_safeId` is the state variable that tracks the number of the opened safes/and minted NFV by the `ODSafeManager` contract.
  * The initial value of the `_safeId` is zero; and it will be incremented with each opened SAFE.
  * But a problem will be caused if the governance change the `ODSafeManager` address via `Vault721.setSafeManager`; as this will result in adding a new deployed safe manager where it will have the `_safeId` set to zero, which will result in breaking the synchronization between the `_safeId` and the last minted NFV id (breaking an invariant).
  * But how could this be a problem? Well, this will result in **disabling SAFE opening and NFV minting:**

    1. The old safe manager contract has a `_safeId` of 1000, and this matches the id of the last minted NFV, so the next NFV id supposed to be 1001, and that should match the value of `_safeId`.
    2. The governance decided to change the safe manager address (with a new deployed one) with extra/updated features; so the `_safeId` of the new `ODSafeManager` will be zero.
    3. Now a user tries to open a SAFE; so the `_safeId` will be incremeted by 1 (and will equal one) and when the `Vault721.mint` is called to mint a NFV; the function will revert as it’s requested to mint a NFV with id=`_safeId`=1, and this NFV has been already deployed by the old safe manager contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑synchronisation error that occurs when the address of the contract responsible for creating SAFEs (the ODSafeManager) is changed through the Vault721.setSafeManager function. Vault721 is an ERC‑721 contract that mints a non‑fungible vault (NFV) token for every SAFE opened, using the internal counter _safeId from the ODSafeManager as the token identifier. The original ODSafeManager starts its _safeId at zero and increments it each time a SAFE is opened, so the value of _safeId always matches the id of the most recently minted NFV. When governance upgrades to a new ODSafeManager instance, the new contract also starts its _safeId at zero because its storage is fresh. This breaks the invariant that the SAFE id and the NFV token id are identical. As a result, when a user later calls ODSafeManager.openSAFE, the new manager increments its _safeId to one and asks Vault721 to mint a token with id 1, which already exists from the previous manager. The mint call reverts, preventing the creation of a new SAFE and the associated NFT. The impact is that users cannot open new SAFEs, their expected NFT never arrives, and the protocol loses the ability to add new positions, potentially locking funds that depend on new SAFEs. The bug is discovered during an audit that examined the setSafeManager function and noticed that the new manager does not inherit the previous _safeId state. It is hard to notice because changing an address looks harmless and the failure only appears after an upgrade when the counter diverges. The issue belongs to the class of upgrade‑induced state‑migration bugs where invariant assumptions across contracts are violated. To remediate, the new ODSafeManager should be initialised with a _safeId that reflects the total number of already minted NFVs (for example, highest token id + 1) or a dedicated migration function should copy the relevant counters from the old manager. Alternatively, Vault721 could expose the current minted count and the manager could read it on deployment, ensuring the counters stay in sync and future SAFE openings succeed.

title: Mismatch between the SAFE generated debt and the amount of the system tokens minted for the user
description:
When the user generates a debt against his collateral (when he locks a collateral first) in `BasicActions.generateDebt`:
* First the user requests a debt of a value `_deltaWad`.
* Then this requested value is modified by the `_getGeneratedDeltaDebt` function: where the requested debt by the user is updated by comparing the coin balance of the SAFE (which is minted when the user generates a debt) with the requested debt; if the requested debt exceeds the coin balance of the SAFE; the requested debt value is modified by calculating the needed `deltaDebt` that would be enough to exit wad amount of COIN tokens with the current coins balance of the SAFE.
* Then a debt is going to be generated for the SAFE with this modified debt value (by updating the SAFE’s collateralization by the `SAFEEngine`):
```solidity
_modifySAFECollateralization(
    _manager,
    _safeId,
    0,
    _getGeneratedDeltaDebt(_safeEngine, _safeInfo.collateralType, _safeInfo.safeHandler, _deltaWad)
);
```
* Then the user (EOA) will be minted system tokens of a value equals to the original value requested by him not the updated value generated by the `_getGeneratedDeltaDebt` function, and this is done via `_exitSystemCoins` function which will in turn call the `__coinJoin.exit` function:
```solidity
_exitSystemCoins(_coinJoin, _deltaWad * RAY);
```
So as can be seen; the values doesn’t match; as the modified `_deltaDebt` that is used to update the `safe.generatedDebt` (via `BasicActions._modifySAFECollateralization` function) might be of a value lesser/larger (depending on the rate and coins balance of the safe) than the actual minted tokens; so when the user wants to repay the SAFE debt his minted tokens might not be enough to do so.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mismatch between the amount of debt recorded for a SAFE and the amount of system tokens that are minted and transferred to the user when the user calls generateDebt. The root cause is that the internal helper _getGeneratedDeltaDebt adjusts the requested debt based on the SAFE’s existing COIN balance and the accumulated rate, and the adjusted value is passed to SAFEEngine to update the SAFE’s generatedDebt. However the original request value (_deltaWad) is later used unchanged in the call that exits COIN tokens to the user. Because the adjusted debt can be smaller or larger than the original request, the protocol ends up either minting more tokens than the debt that was recorded or minting fewer tokens than required to cover the recorded debt. This inconsistency can be triggered whenever a user generates debt while the SAFE already holds some COIN balance, which is a normal situation after partial repayments or previous exits. The affected parties are any user who creates or modifies a SAFE through BasicActions.generateDebt and the protocol itself, because the accounting invariant between generatedDebt and minted tokens is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the data flow through _generateDebt and identified that the two calls use different values. It is hard to notice because both external calls succeed and no revert is emitted; the mismatch only becomes visible later when the user attempts to repay the debt or when the protocol checks the total outstanding debt, leading to unexpected insufficient balance errors or leftover debt that cannot be cleared. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the requested amount of tokens was received, but later the repayment transaction fails or the SAFE remains under‑collateralized, effectively causing funds to disappear or become unrecoverable. The bug belongs to the class of invariant‑violation or arithmetic‑inconsistency bugs where state updates are not performed atomically with the corresponding token transfer. The correct fix is to compute the adjusted delta once, store it in a local variable, and use that same value both for the SAFEEngine debt update and for the token exit, ensuring that the amount of minted COIN exactly matches the recorded generatedDebt. Aligning these two operations restores the accounting guarantees of the protocol and prevents users from being unable to repay or from extracting excess tokens.

title: Decimal Limitation in CamelotRelayer and UniV3Relayer Contract Deployment
description: The current design of the CamelotRelayer and UniV3Relayer contracts limits its compatibility to only those `_quoteTokens` that have a decimal count of 18 or fewer. If an attempt is made to deploy the contract with a token having more than 18 decimals as the `_quoteToken`, the contract deployment will fail due to an underflow issue during the multiplier calculation. This poses no financial risk but restricts the contract’s adaptability in the wider DeFi ecosystem, preventing its use with tokens that have more than 18 decimals.
poc:
The restriction emerges from the constructor, where the `multiplier` is deduced as `18 - IERC20Metadata(_quoteToken).decimals()`.
```solidity
multiplier = 18 - IERC20Metadata(_quoteToken).decimals();
```
For tokens like [`YAMv2`, which possess 24 decimals](https://etherscan.io/token/0xaba8cac6866b83ae4eec97dd07ed254282f6ad8a), the computation would attempt `18 - 24`, which results in an underflow, making the contract deployment unsuccessful.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a decimal‑precision limitation in the constructor of CamelotRelayer and UniV3Relayer. The contracts compute a variable called multiplier as 18 minus the number of decimals reported by the quote token. Because multiplier is declared as an unsigned integer, the subtraction underflows when the token reports more than 18 decimals, causing the constructor to revert and the contract deployment to fail. This occurs only at deployment time, before any user funds are locked, so there is no direct financial loss, but it prevents the protocol from being instantiated with tokens such as YAMv2 that use 24 decimals. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the auditors attempted to deploy the contracts with a high‑decimal token and observed an unexpected revert. The bug is subtle because the source code compiles without warnings and the arithmetic looks innocuous; the underflow only manifests for a specific class of tokens, making it easy to miss in manual testing. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a transaction to create a new relayer simply fails, leaving no contract address and no visible error message in the UI, which may be interpreted as a “missing contract” or “deployment bug”.
