When other liquidators (even this liquidator belongs to protocol) writes to repay and erase the rest 200 USD bad debt, he cannot because [removeCollateralTo validates share > 0, if share is 0, revert](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-initcapital/blob/a53e401529451b208095b3af11862984d0b32177/contracts/core/PosManager.sol#L235).
    
```solidity
    _require(_shares > 0, Errors.ZERO_VALUE);
```

If the underlying collateral is WLP, the second liquidation aims to write off bad debt does not work as well because if all WLP is transferred out, calling [_harvest and unwrap again is likely to revert](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-initcapital/blob/a53e401529451b208095b3af11862984d0b32177/contracts/core/PosManager.sol#L265).
    
```solidity
    _harvest(_posId, _wLp, _tokenId);
    IBaseWrapLp(_wLp).unwrap(_tokenId, _amt, _receiver);
```

The bad debt permanently inflates the totalAssets() in lending pool and inflates the total debt to not let other users borrow from protocol because of the borrow cap checks.

Also, the lender suffers the loss because if the bad debt is not repaid, the lender that deposit cash into the lending pool is lost.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the liquidation logic of a lending pool that allows a liquidator to seize a borrower’s collateral – either pool shares or wrapped liquidity provider tokens (WLP) – and use the seized value to repay the borrower’s outstanding debt. The code deliberately takes the minimum of the available collateral and the amount needed to cover the bad debt, then requires that at least one share remains after the transfer (the check _require(_shares > 0, Errors.ZERO_VALUE)). When the market price of the collateral falls such that the total value of the borrower’s shares is lower than the debt, a liquidator can only partially cover the debt before the collateral is fully exhausted. After the collateral is completely seized, any remaining unpaid portion of the debt is marked as bad debt, but the protocol lacks any mechanism to write off or otherwise handle this residual amount. Subsequent attempts to clear the debt fail because the share‑validation check rejects a zero‑share operation, and the WLP unwrapping path also reverts when there is no token left to unwrap. As a result, the bad debt stays permanently recorded, inflating the pool’s totalAssets() and total debt metrics, preventing other users from borrowing due to borrow‑cap constraints, and causing lenders who supplied assets to suffer unrecoverable losses. The issue is observable from a user’s perspective as a position that appears to have been fully liquidated yet still shows an outstanding debt balance, borrow limits that are unexpectedly hit, and a lending pool that reports higher total assets than the actual cash on hand. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the auditors noticed that after a full‑collateral liquidation the contract reverted on further debt‑clearing calls. It is difficult to notice because the initial liquidation transaction succeeds and no explicit error is emitted; the problem only surfaces when a second liquidation or a debt‑write‑off is attempted. To remediate the issue, the protocol should introduce a pathway to handle residual bad debt, such as a donation function that allows external parties to supply assets to offset the loss, or an explicit loss‑socialisation mechanism that can clear the bad debt even when no collateral remains. Additionally, the share‑validation logic should be relaxed to permit zero‑share operations when the intent is to erase bad debt, and the WLP unwrapping routine should gracefully handle empty balances. Implementing these changes would restore accounting consistency, prevent artificial inflation of pool metrics, and protect lenders from silent capital erosion.

title: API3 oracle timestamp can be set to future timestamp and block API3 Oracle usage to make code revert in underflow
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price‑reading function of the Api3OracleReader contract, which assumes that the timestamp returned by the API3 data feed is always less than or equal to the current block timestamp. The function retrieves a price and a timestamp from the oracle and then checks that the data is not stale by evaluating block.timestamp - timestamp <= maxStaleTime. If the oracle relayer supplies a timestamp that is slightly in the future – which is allowed by the API3 server as long as it is less than one hour ahead of the current block time – the subtraction underflows because Solidity performs unchecked arithmetic on unsigned integers. The underflow produces a very large number, causing the stale‑time check to fail and the transaction to revert with the MAX_STALETIME_EXCEEDED error. This revert blocks any further calls to the price function, effectively halting price retrieval for all tokens that rely on this reader. From a user perspective the UI may show a price of zero, missing balances, or failed swaps because the contract cannot obtain a valid price. The impact is not a direct loss of funds, but a denial‑of‑service condition that can freeze protocol operations that depend on up‑to‑date oracle data. The issue occurs whenever the relayer updates the data feed with a future timestamp within the one‑hour window permitted by the onlyValidTimestamp modifier, and the contract’s maxStaleTime parameter is set to a value that would normally allow the data. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the logical assumptions of the timestamp comparison. The bug is subtle because the future timestamp is a legitimate state for the oracle and the underflow only manifests when the contract performs the subtraction, which may not be obvious during normal testing. To remediate, the contract should first verify that the oracle timestamp is not in the future before performing the stale‑time subtraction, or use a safe subtraction that treats future timestamps as fresh data, thereby preventing the underflow and ensuring that price reads succeed even when the oracle reports a slightly ahead timestamp.

title: Admin configuration isAllowedForCollateral
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol determines the amount of cash that a lending pool holds when calculating collateral credit. After a user deposits assets and receives pool shares, the contract allows a caller to add collateral through a function that checks the admin‑controlled configuration flag isAllowedForCollateral. This check correctly prevents a disallowed token, such as a highly volatile token A, from being used directly as collateral. However, the cash amount of the pool is later derived from the raw ERC‑20 balance of the pool contract via the syncCash function, which can be invoked indirectly through a flash‑loan style call. An attacker who can mint an unlimited amount of token A can simply transfer a large quantity of the token to the pool, trigger a flash callback, and then cause syncCash to update the internal cash variable to the inflated token balance. Because the collateral valuation formula converts pool shares to token value using the cash amount (total assets = cash + debt), inflating cash artificially raises the perceived value of existing shares without changing the share count. Consequently, the attacker’s collateral credit is dramatically increased, allowing them to borrow the entire pool balance and generate massive bad debt. This exploit works even though the admin has explicitly disabled token A as collateral, because the restriction only applies to the explicit collateralize function and does not protect the indirect cash accounting path. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the admin configuration and the flash‑loan mechanism. It can be hard to notice because the admin flag appears to enforce the intended policy, yet the protocol’s accounting model trusts external token balances, creating a hidden attack surface. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that the protocol suddenly allows borrowing amounts far beyond the visible collateral, leading to situations where funds disappear from the pool, borrowers can withdraw all assets, and lenders suffer unexpected losses. The bug belongs to the class of “collateral valuation manipulation” or “cash accounting bypass” vulnerabilities, where external token transfers can corrupt internal accounting. To remediate the problem the protocol should maintain an internal ledger for cash that is only updated through controlled deposit functions, and it should prevent the syncCash routine from being called from a flash‑loan context or any untrusted external call. By decoupling cash accounting from raw token balances and restricting the flash‑loan pathway, the protocol can enforce the admin’s collateral policy and protect against inflation attacks.

title: collectLiquidity
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the liquidity collection function of a position manager contract that only permits the caller (msg.sender) to receive the withdrawn tokens. The function accepts a single token identifier and internally forwards the collected amounts to the transaction origin without allowing the caller to specify an alternative recipient address. This design flaw becomes critical when the caller is listed on a token‑specific blacklist, for example the USDC blacklist. Because the contract cannot direct the withdrawn USDC to a non‑blacklisted address, the transfer of that token fails, and the subsequent attempt to collect the paired asset (such as WETH) is also aborted, leaving part of the liquidity permanently locked in the contract. The root cause is the absence of a recipient parameter, which forces the contract to use msg.sender as the sole destination, violating the expectation that a user can retrieve both assets of a liquidity position regardless of external token restrictions. An attacker or a malicious user could exploit this by deliberately placing a legitimate LP on a blacklist, causing the LP’s withdrawal transaction to revert or to return zero for the blacklisted token while still receiving the other token, effectively stealing the ability to recover the full position. The impact is a partial loss of funds: the user sees a successful transaction but receives less than expected, often observing a zero balance for one of the assets, while the other asset is transferred correctly. This situation occurs during the post‑decreaseLiquidity step when the user calls collectLiquidity, and only under the condition that the caller’s address is prohibited from receiving one of the tokens involved. All liquidity providers who might be blacklisted are affected, as are protocols that rely on this contract for safe fund extraction. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementation with reference contracts such as UniswapV3Pool.collect, which expose a recipient argument to avoid this problem. The bug is subtle because the function signature appears normal and the failure manifests only when a blacklist is triggered, making it easy to miss during standard testing. The recommended remediation is to extend the function signature to include an address recipient parameter and forward the collected amounts to that address, mirroring the behavior of established reference implementations. This change restores the ability to route tokens around blacklist restrictions, aligns with expected business logic that a user should receive the full amount of both assets, and prevents accidental locking of funds.

title: reclaimLiquidity
bug_full: The contract allows a liquidity provider (LP) to signal that its supplied liquidity should be reclaimed by calling a function that records a renewalCutoffTime. The intended flow is that after this timestamp the LP can withdraw the funds because any existing loan should either be voluntarily closed by the borrower or become eligible for forced liquidation once the loan term expires. However, the openPosition function does not check the renewalCutoffTime or the remaining loan term before allowing a new loan to be created. As a result, a borrower can close an existing position shortly before the loan term ends, immediately open a new position, and thereby reset the loan start time. Because liquidatePosition only permits forced closure after block.timestamp exceeds lien.startTime + LOAN_TERM, the borrower can perpetually avoid liquidation by repeatedly closing and reopening. This timing loophole lets the borrower occupy the LP’s liquidity indefinitely, effectively locking the funds and preventing the LP from retrieving them even after reclaimLiquidity has been called. From the LP’s point of view the UI may still show the liquidity as “locked” or “in use” despite having initiated a reclaim, leading to confusion and potential financial loss. The impact is medium severity: the LP’s capital is tied up for an unbounded period, reducing liquidity availability and possibly harming the protocol’s economic model. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between reclaimLiquidity, liquidatePosition, and openPosition and noticed that the renewalCutoffTime is never consulted when opening a new loan. The bug is subtle because the contract’s functions appear to work correctly in isolation; only the combination of timing checks across multiple calls reveals the flaw. To remediate the problem the openPosition function should enforce a restriction that prevents new loans from being created if the current time is earlier than renewalCutoffTime plus the original loan term (plus a small safety buffer). Alternatively, a flag could be introduced to permanently disable new loans after a reclaim request. Both approaches close the timing gap and ensure that once an LP signals reclamation, the borrowed liquidity cannot be extended indefinitely, restoring the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: malicious borrowers can follow reclaimLiquidity
bug_full: The vulnerability is a boundary‑condition error in the renewal‑time check that governs when a borrower may add premium to an outstanding loan. The contract stores a timestamp called lien.startTime that marks when the loan was created, and a separate value called renewalCutoffTime that is set to the block timestamp when a liquidity provider (LP) calls reclaimLiquidity. The addPremium function is supposed to be blocked once the renewalCutoffTime is greater than the loan’s start time, preventing the borrower from extending the loan after the LP has indicated an intention to retrieve its liquidity. However, the code uses a strict greater‑than comparison (renewalCutoffTime > lien.startTime). If the borrower manages to execute addPremium in the same block where the LP sets renewalCutoffTime, the two timestamps become equal. Because the check does not reject the equality case, the borrower can successfully call addPremium, resetting lien.startTime to the current block timestamp. The subsequent liquidatePosition function contains a condition that requires lien.startTime < renewalCutoffTime in order to allow liquidation. With the timestamps equal, this condition fails and the function reverts with Errors.LiquidationNotMet, meaning the LP’s attempt to close the position and retrieve its liquidity is blocked. The exploit is carried out by monitoring the mempool, front‑running the LP’s reclaimLiquidity transaction, and submitting addPremium(0) in the same block. From the user’s perspective the LP sees a transaction revert, their balance remains unchanged, and the expected liquidity never returns, creating the impression that funds have disappeared or that the protocol is unresponsive. The affected parties are the liquidity providers who cannot reclaim their capital, the borrowers who can keep an unhealthy position indefinitely, and the protocol’s overall capital efficiency. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the subtle equality case was overlooked because the comparison appeared logically correct at first glance. It is hard to notice because the condition only fails in the narrow scenario where the timestamps match, which is rare without an active attacker. The bug belongs to the class of off‑by‑one or boundary‑condition errors in access‑control logic. The recommended fix is to change the comparison to a greater‑or‑equal check (renewalCutoffTime >= lien.startTime), ensuring that when the timestamps are equal the addPremium call is also rejected. This limits the borrower to at most one premium addition after a reclaim and prevents indefinite postponement of liquidation, restoring the expected behavior that LPs can retrieve their liquidity once they signal reclamation.

title: Zero amount token transfers may cause a denial of service during liquidations
description: Some ERC20 implementations revert on zero value transfers. Since liquidation rewards are based on a fraction of the available position’s premiums, this may cause an accidental denial of service that prevents the successful execution of liquidations.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises when a liquidation routine attempts to transfer a reward amount that is exactly zero. Some ERC20 token contracts are written to revert any transfer call with a value of zero, even though the ERC20 specification does not require this behaviour. In the affected protocol the liquidation reward is calculated as a fraction of the premiums earned on the liquidated position; when the fraction evaluates to zero the contract still invokes the token's transfer function with a zero amount. Because the token reverts, the entire liquidation transaction fails, leaving the under‑collateralised position un‑liquidated. This can be exploited by an attacker who either selects a token that is known to revert on zero transfers or manipulates the premium calculation so that the reward becomes zero, thereby blocking the liquidation of any position that uses that token. The impact is that users cannot rely on the protocol to automatically resolve risky positions, which may lead to prolonged exposure of collateral, potential insolvency of the pool, and loss of confidence. The condition occurs whenever a liquidation is triggered for a position that involves a token with the zero‑transfer revert behaviour and the computed reward is zero. All users who open positions with arbitrary ERC20 tokens, as well as liquidators and the protocol itself, are affected because the system does not enforce an allow‑list of safe tokens. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the reviewers noticed that the reward calculation could produce a zero value and that the subsequent safeTransfer call did not guard against it. It is easy to miss because zero‑value transfers are often assumed to be no‑ops and many popular tokens silently accept them; only a subset of non‑standard tokens will revert, making the failure appear sporadic. To remediate, the contract should check that any amount passed to a token transfer is greater than zero before invoking the external call, or use a wrapper that safely ignores zero amounts. Adding an explicit >0 guard not only prevents the revert but also saves a small amount of gas. More robustly, the protocol could maintain an allow‑list of ERC20 tokens that are known to support zero‑value transfers, or redesign the reward logic to guarantee a minimum non‑zero reward. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a liquidation transaction that reverts with no reward paid, leaving the UI to show that the position remains open and that the expected liquidation reward is zero, contrary to the expectation that the protocol will automatically liquidate risky positions and compensate the liquidator.

title: Dangerous use of deadline parameter
description: The protocol is using `block.timestamp` as the deadline argument while interacting with the Uniswap NFT Position Manager, which completely defeats the purpose of using a deadline.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of using the current block timestamp as the deadline argument when calling the Uniswap NonfungiblePositionManager from the ParticlePositionManager contract. The deadline field in Uniswap functions is intended to give callers a safety window: a transaction that is mined after the supplied deadline is rejected, protecting users from stale or front‑run executions. By hard‑coding deadline = block.timestamp, the contract effectively disables this protection because the check deadline >= block.timestamp always succeeds in the same block. The root cause is a design mistake where the developer assumed that passing the current timestamp would enforce a time limit, but it merely mirrors the present block time and provides no future buffer. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a higher‑gas transaction that changes the pool state (e.g., price manipulation or liquidity removal) just before the victim’s transaction is mined, knowing that the victim’s transaction will not be rejected for being outdated. Consequently, the user may lose expected liquidity, receive worse slippage, or see their position altered without the intended deadline safeguard. This issue manifests every time ParticlePositionManager.mint, increaseLiquidity, or decreaseLiquidity forwards a deadline to Uniswap without allowing the caller to specify a future timestamp. All users who rely on the contract to manage their Uniswap V3 NFT positions are affected, as the protocol’s accounting assumptions about time‑bounded execution are violated. The problem was identified during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the function signatures and noticing that block.timestamp was directly passed as the deadline parameter. It can be hard to notice because the deadline parameter exists, giving a false sense of security, and the UI may display a deadline value that appears correct while it actually offers no protection. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit deadline parameter to each liquidity‑management function, validate that it is greater than the current block timestamp by a reasonable margin, and forward this user‑controlled value to the underlying Uniswap calls. This restores the intended safety window and aligns the contract’s behavior with the expected business logic of protecting users from stale or front‑run transactions.

title: Increase liquidity in close position may not cover original borrowed liquidity
description: When a position is closed, there is no check to ensure that the effective added liquidity covers the original borrowed liquidity from the LP.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the closing flow of a leveraged liquidity position in a decentralized finance protocol. When a user or contract initiates a close operation, the system adds liquidity back to the pool on behalf of the borrower but does not verify that the amount of liquidity actually returned (cache.liquidityAdded) is at least equal to the amount originally borrowed (lien.liquidity). The root cause is the absence of a safety check after the call to the Uniswap‑style increaseLiquidity function, combined with reliance on a complex on‑chain price calculation that can suffer from rounding or precision errors. Because the protocol trusts the calculated value without a post‑condition, an attacker could manipulate the pool price—potentially via a flash loan or a large trade—so that the mathematical formula under‑estimates the required repayment. In such a scenario the effective liquidity added may fall short of the borrowed amount, leaving the protocol under‑collateralized. From a user perspective the position appears to be closed successfully, yet the expected refund or returned liquidity is missing or reduced to zero, causing confusion and potential loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the missing require statement and considered the edge case where Uniswap’s deterministic math could be off by a small margin, which could be amplified by market manipulation. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error when the shortfall occurs; the transaction simply completes, making the loss invisible in normal logs. To remediate, the closing routine should enforce a post‑condition such as require(cache.liquidityAdded >= lien.liquidity) or include a small tolerance buffer to account for rounding, thereby guaranteeing that the borrowed liquidity is fully covered before the position is considered closed. This class of flaw belongs to the broader category of insufficient repayment checks in lending or leveraged liquidity contracts, where accounting assumptions about asset returns are not enforced, leading to potential fund disappearance and breach of protocol financial guarantees.

title: Add premium doesn't collect fees
description: Fees are applied to premiums when a new position is opened, but the same mechanism is not enforced when margin is added to an existing position.
poc:
A user can skip paying part of the fees by bundling two operations in a single transaction:

  1. A call to `openPosition()` with the minimal required amount of `marginFrom` so that `amountReceived + amountToBorrowed + marginTo >= collateralTo`.
  2. A call to `addPremium()` to provide the required premiums to cover for eventual fees.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a fee‑collection bypass that occurs when a trader adds premium to an already opened position. The contract applies a fee schedule only during the initial openPosition call, where the required margin and borrowed amount are used to compute fees. The addPremium function, however, does not repeat this calculation and therefore does not deduct any fees from the premium that is supplied later. The root cause is that the fee‑accrual logic is hard‑coded in the opening routine and omitted from the premium‑addition routine, leaving a gap in the accounting path. An attacker can exploit this by first opening a position with the minimal margin that satisfies the collateral requirement, then immediately calling addPremium in the same transaction (or later) to supply the remaining premium without paying the expected fees. Because the fee is not taken, the protocol receives less revenue than it should, giving the attacker an economic advantage and potentially harming liquidity providers who rely on fee accruals. The issue manifests whenever a user calls addPremium after opening a position, especially when the two calls are bundled together, which makes the missing fee invisible to the UI – the trader sees the expected premium amount transferred but receives no fee deduction, and the protocol’s accounting shows a shortfall. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared fee handling across entry points and noticed that the premium‑addition path lacked any fee logic. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to only move funds and does not emit any fee‑related events, so developers may assume fees are handled elsewhere. To remediate, the same fee schedule used in openPosition should be applied inside addPremium: determine the correct token based on the zeroForOne flag, multiply the premium amount by the FEE_FACTOR, and accrue the resulting fee to the appropriate liquidity position, ensuring that every premium transfer is subject to the same accounting rules. This aligns the contract with the intended business logic that all margin‑related operations incur fees, preserving protocol revenue and preventing traders from bypassing fee obligations.

title: Modifying the loan term setting can default existing loans
description: Protocol admins can modify the loan term settings. This action can inadvertently default existing loans created under different terms.
poc:
Let’s say the current configured loan term in ParticlePositionManager is 2 weeks.

  1. A user creates a new position, expecting it to last at least 2 weeks.
  2. The owner of the LP calls `reclaimLiquidity()` to stop it from being renewed.
  3. The protocol changes the loan term setting to 1 week.
  4. The user is liquidated after 1 week.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the protocol stores the loan term as a single global parameter that can be changed by admins, and the liquidation logic reads this global value when determining whether a loan has expired. Because the original loan term that was in effect when a position was opened is not recorded in the loan’s data structure, a later change to the global loan term can cause an existing loan to be considered overdue earlier than the borrower expected. This happens because the contract compares the loan’s start time plus the current LOAN_TERM against block.timestamp, rather than using the term that was valid at the time of loan creation. An attacker (or any admin) can exploit this by updating the loan term to a shorter duration after a loan has been opened, then triggering liquidation after the new, shorter period has elapsed. The impact is that borrowers may see their positions liquidated prematurely, resulting in loss of collateral or unexpected debt repayment, while lenders may receive liquidation proceeds earlier than intended. The condition occurs whenever the governance or admin modifies the LOAN_TERM variable, which is intended to be a rare operation but can be executed at any time. All participants who have active loans – borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions about loan duration are violated. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the liquidation condition and noticed that the loan term is not persisted per loan. It can be hard to notice because the contract’s UI may still display the original term, and the change only manifests when a loan is liquidated, making the discrepancy subtle. The proper fix is to store the loan term value in each loan’s data structure (e.g., lien.loanTerm) at creation time and use that stored value when calculating the loan’s expiry, ensuring that the original agreement is honored regardless of later configuration changes. This change aligns the bug with the class of “configuration‑driven state inconsistency” or “global parameter mutation affecting per‑instance logic”. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a borrower who expects a two‑week loan may be liquidated after one week, seeing their collateral seized and receiving no refund. The expectation of a stable loan duration is broken, leading to funds disappearing unexpectedly. The vulnerability does not rely on a direct code exploit but on governance‑level parameter changes, making it a business‑logic flaw rather than a classic code injection.

title: Liquidation condition should not factor the liquidation reward into the premiums
description: The premiums used to determine the liquidation condition have the liquidation reward already discounted, potentially causing a lien to be considered underwater while technically it is not.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting order flaw in the liquidation logic of the protocol. The contract determines whether a position is eligible for liquidation by comparing the premium amounts that are available to the amounts owed to the liquidity providers. However, before this health check is performed the code already subtracts the liquidation reward from the premium balances. Because the reward has been deducted early, the remaining premium may appear insufficient to cover the owed amounts, causing the condition to evaluate as true even when the full premium would have been enough. This mis‑ordering can cause a lien that is actually solvent to be flagged as underwater, allowing a liquidator to trigger liquidation prematurely. The root cause is the placement of the reward calculation and subtraction before the liquidation condition check, combined with the fact that the liquidation reward factor is mutable by an admin, which can be altered to increase the reward and further tighten the condition. An attacker acting as a liquidator can monitor positions that are still healthy, invoke the liquidation function, receive the reward, and leave the liquidity provider with a shortfall because the protocol pays out less than the amount owed after the premature reward deduction. The impact is that liquidity providers may receive less than their entitled fees, borrowers may see their positions liquidated despite being adequately collateralised, and overall trust in the protocol’s accounting is eroded. The issue manifests whenever the liquidation check runs – typically at the moment a position reaches the time‑based or premium‑based threshold – and is especially pronounced after an admin changes the LIQUIDATION_REWARD_FACTOR. Users experience symptoms such as a liquidation button becoming active while their dashboard still shows a healthy balance, or receiving a smaller payout after liquidation than expected. The bug belongs to the class of business‑logic errors where health‑check calculations are performed on already‑adjusted state, leading to incorrect risk assessment. It was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors traced the flow of premium values and noticed that the reward subtraction occurred before the condition evaluation, a subtle mistake that does not raise immediate compile‑time warnings. Detecting the problem in production can be difficult because the contract’s external view may still report sufficient premiums, and only the internal ordering reveals the shortfall. The proper fix is to perform the liquidation condition check using the full, unadjusted premium amounts, and only after confirming that liquidation is justified should the contract deduct the liquidation reward and distribute it to the liquidator. Additionally, the protocol should protect the reward factor from arbitrary changes or enforce caps that preserve the health invariant. By correcting the order of operations and securing the reward parameter, the protocol will ensure that only truly underwater positions can be liquidated and that liquidity providers receive the full amount they are owed.

title: Impossible to open a position with a large `marginTo`
description:
`marginTo/From` is a way to both cover your position and increase your premium when opening a position. There is however a unintended limit on how much `marginTo` you can provide when opening a position.

When doing the swap to increase leverage, the `amountToMinimum` (minimum received amount) is calculated:

[`ParticlePositionManager::openPosition`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-particle/blob/main/contracts/protocol/ParticlePositionManager.sol#L212):
```solidity
collateralTo - cache.amountToBorrowed - params.marginTo, // amount needed to meet requirement
```
As you see here, a `marginTo > collateralTo - cache.amountToBorrowed` will underflow this calculation. Thus there is no way to provide a bigger margin than this.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract computes the minimum amount that must be received from the swap when a user opens a new position. The calculation subtracts the user‑provided margin for the "to" side (marginTo) from the difference between the total collateral that will be supplied (collateralTo) and the amount that is already borrowed (cache.amountToBorrowed). The expression collateralTo - cache.amountToBorrowed - marginTo is performed using unchecked arithmetic. If marginTo is larger than collateralTo - cache.amountToBorrowed, the subtraction underflows, causing an arithmetic error that reverts the transaction. As a result, a trader who tries to open a position with a large marginTo – for example to increase the premium or to provide extra safety – cannot do so; the call to openPosition fails and the user receives no position, no token transfers, and no refund. This situation can be reproduced by supplying a marginTo that is just one unit higher than the allowed maximum, which triggers a stdError.arithmeticError revert. The issue is difficult to spot because the underflow only occurs for a narrow range of inputs and the revert message does not clearly indicate that the problem is caused by an oversized margin, making it appear as a generic arithmetic failure. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic or input‑validation errors where user‑controlled parameters are directly used in subtraction without proper bounds checking. From a business‑logic perspective the contract incorrectly treats marginTo as part of the expected swap output, violating the assumption that the premium should be accounted for separately from the swap amount. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style limitation: legitimate users cannot open positions with the desired margin, potentially reducing protocol utility and allowing an attacker to block certain trades by forcing the contract into a state where any attempt to use a large margin reverts. The fix is to stop counting marginTo toward the expected swap output, for example by clamping the subtraction to zero when marginTo exceeds the available collateral, or by moving marginTo out of the amountToMinimum calculation entirely and validating it against protocol limits before performing the subtraction. Implementing safe‑math checks or explicit require statements that enforce marginTo ≤ collateralTo - cache.amountToBorrowed will prevent the underflow and restore the intended functionality of opening positions with arbitrary, but safe, margin values.

title: openPosition
description:
In `openPosition()`, it allows `token0PremiumPortion` and `token1PremiumPortion` to be 0 at the same time.

In this case, if `tokenId` enters `out_of_price`, for example, `UpperOutOfRange`, anyone might be able to input:
    
```solidity
    marginFrom = 0
    marginTo = 0
    amountSwap = 0
    zeroForOne = false
    liquidity > 0
```

Note: `amountFromBorrowed + marginFrom == 0`, so `fees == 0`

To open a new Position, borrow Liquidity, but without paying any fees. It’s basically a no-cost loan.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the openPosition function of the particle position manager contract. The function permits both token0PremiumPortion and token1PremiumPortion to be set to zero simultaneously. When a token identifier (tokenId) falls into an out‑of‑price category such as UpperOutOfRange, the fee calculation relies on the premium portions; if both are zero the computed fees become zero. An attacker can therefore call openPosition with marginFrom = 0, marginTo = 0, amountSwap = 0, zeroForOne = false and a positive liquidity amount while also passing tokenFromPremiumPortionMin = 0 and tokenToPremiumPortionMin = 0. Because amountFromBorrowed + marginFrom equals zero, the contract records no fees and grants the requested liquidity as a no‑cost loan. This flaw occurs only when the price range check classifies the token as out of range, and it is triggered by the absence of a validation rule that enforces a minimum premium portion. Users experience a situation where they receive borrowed liquidity but see no fee or premium values in the position data, contradicting the expectation that opening a leveraged position incurs a fee. The protocol’s economic model is violated because fee revenue is lost and an attacker could repeatedly open fee‑less positions, potentially eroding the incentive structure and draining available liquidity. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a test case that opened a position under the described parameters and observed zero token0Premium and token1Premium values while liquidity was transferred. The bug is subtle because zero premium values are not explicitly prohibited by the contract and the frontend only enforces a minimum of 1‑2 %, making the problem easy to miss in casual testing. The recommended remediation is to add a requirement that token0PremiumPortion and token1PremiumPortion each meet a defined minimum threshold (for example, a constant MIN_FROM_PREMIUM_PORTION and MIN_TO_PREMIUM_PORTION) before allowing the position to be opened, thereby guaranteeing that a non‑zero fee is always collected.

title: Position can be opened even when the particle position manger does not hold the Uniswap V3 Position NFT
bug_full: The vulnerability is an authorization flaw in the Particle Position Manager that allows a user who has merely approved the manager as an operator for their Uniswap V3 position NFT to have that position opened, decreased or leveraged by a third party without the NFT actually being transferred into the manager contract. The root cause is that the contract’s modifier only checks that the caller is approved or the owner of the token (using the standard isAuthorizedForToken check) and does not verify that the manager contract itself holds the NFT at the time the liquidity‑changing functions are called. Because approval is a normal step in many workflows, an attacker can exploit the situation by approving the manager (or by the user approving it unintentionally) and then calling the openPosition or decreaseLiquidity functions on behalf of the original NFT owner. The attacker can reduce the original liquidity, open a leveraged position for the duration of the loan term, and maintain a sufficient premium to avoid liquidation. This results in the original owner being unable to reclaim their liquidity through the expected reclaimLiquidity call, effectively losing control over part of their funds while the borrower profits from the leveraged trade. The issue manifests whenever a user grants operator approval to the Particle Position Manager but does not transfer the NFT into the manager; under those conditions any address that can invoke the manager’s functions can manipulate the position. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of approval versus ownership checks and identified that the contract never asserts that the manager is the current holder of the NFT before performing external calls to the Uniswap V3 pool. It can be hard to notice because approval is a legitimate action and developers may assume that approval implies consent to borrow, overlooking the fact that ownership transfer is required for actual control of the position. From a user’s perspective the symptoms include seeing their LP token balance shrink, receiving no tokens when attempting to reclaim liquidity, or observing that their position has been leveraged without any explicit transaction from them. The business logic that the NFT holder must be the party providing liquidity is violated, breaking accounting assumptions that each LP token corresponds to a specific amount of underlying assets. To remediate the issue the contract should include an explicit check that the Particle Position Manager is the current owner of the NFT before allowing any increase, decrease, or leverage operation, and should only permit these actions after the NFT has been transferred into the manager. This ensures that approval alone is insufficient to manipulate the position and restores the intended security model where only the actual holder of the NFT can affect its liquidity.

title: Malicious lender can manipulate the fee to force borrower pay high premium
description:
When user creates a position, the fee is snapshot is queried from uniswap v3 position manager when [preparing leverage](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-particle/blob/a3af40839b24aa13f5764d4f84933dbfa8bc8134/contracts/libraries/Base.sol#L132)
    
```solidity
    function prepareLeverage(
        uint256 tokenId,
        uint128 liquidity,
        bool zeroForOne
    )
        internal
        view
        returns (
            address tokenFrom,
            address tokenTo,
            uint256 feeGrowthInside0LastX128,
            uint256 feeGrowthInside1LastX128,
            uint256 collateralFrom,
            uint256 collateralTo
        )
    {
        int24 tickLower;
        int24 tickUpper;
        (
            ,
            ,
            tokenFrom,
            tokenTo,
            ,
            tickLower,
            tickUpper,
            ,
            feeGrowthInside0LastX128,
            feeGrowthInside1LastX128,
            ,
    
        ) = UNI_POSITION_MANAGER.positions(tokenId);
```

and stored in the lien struct
    
```solidity
// prepare data for swap
(
	cache.tokenFrom,
	cache.tokenTo,
	cache.feeGrowthInside0LastX128,
	cache.feeGrowthInside1LastX128,
	cache.collateralFrom,
	collateralTo
) = Base.prepareLeverage(params.tokenId, params.liquidity, params.zeroForOne);
```

then [stored in the liens struct](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-particle/blob/a3af40839b24aa13f5764d4f84933dbfa8bc8134/contracts/protocol/ParticlePositionManager.sol#L247)
    
```solidity
// create a new lien
liens[keccak256(abi.encodePacked(msg.sender, lienId = _nextRecordId++))] = Lien.Info({
	tokenId: uint40(params.tokenId), // @audit
	liquidity: params.liquidity,
	token0PremiumPortion: cache.token0PremiumPortion,
	token1PremiumPortion: cache.token1PremiumPortion,
	startTime: uint32(block.timestamp),
	feeGrowthInside0LastX128: cache.feeGrowthInside0LastX128,
	feeGrowthInside1LastX128: cache.feeGrowthInside1LastX128,
	zeroForOne: params.zeroForOne
});
```

then when the position is closed, the [premium interested paid depends on the spot value of the fee](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-particle/blob/a3af40839b24aa13f5764d4f84933dbfa8bc8134/contracts/protocol/ParticlePositionManager.sol#L442)
    
```solidity
// obtain the position's latest FeeGrowthInside after increaseLiquidity
(, , , , , , , , cache.feeGrowthInside0LastX128, cache.feeGrowthInside1LastX128, , ) = Base
	.UNI_POSITION_MANAGER
	.positions(lien.tokenId);

// calculate the amounts owed since last fee collection during the borrowing period
(cache.token0Owed, cache.token1Owed) = Base.getOwedFee(
	cache.feeGrowthInside0LastX128,
	cache.feeGrowthInside1LastX128,
	lien.feeGrowthInside0LastX128,
	lien.feeGrowthInside1LastX128,
	lien.liquidity
);
```

If the fee increased during the position opening time, the premium is used to cover the fee to make sure there are incentive for lenders to deposit V3 NFT as lender.

As the comments point out:

// calculate the the amounts owed to LP up to the premium in the lien  
// must ensure enough amount is left to pay for interest first, then send gains and fund left to borrower

However, because the fee amount is queried from position manager in spot value, malicious lender increase the liquidity to that ticker range and then can swap back and forth between ticker range to inflate the fee amount to force borrower pay high fee / high premium, while the lender has to pay the gas cost + uniswap trading fee.

But if the lender [adds more liquidity](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-particle/blob/a3af40839b24aa13f5764d4f84933dbfa8bc8134/contracts/protocol/ParticlePositionManager.sol#L118) to nft’s ticker range, he can collect the majority of the liqudity fee + collect high premium from borrower (or forcefully liquidated user to take premium).
bug_full: When a borrower creates a leveraged position the contract queries the current fee growth values from the Uniswap V3 position manager and stores them in the lien record. These snapshot values are later used, at the moment the position is closed, to calculate the premium that the borrower must pay to the lender. The logic assumes that the fee growth observed at opening reflects the natural market fee accumulation over the borrowing period. However, because the contract reads the fee growth as a spot value without any caps or averaging, a malicious lender can artificially inflate the fee growth inside the same tick range. By adding a large amount of liquidity to the NFT’s tick range and performing rapid swaps within that range, the lender drives up the feeGrowthInside values before the borrower closes the position. When the contract later computes the owed premium, it uses the inflated fee snapshot, causing the borrower to pay a much higher premium than would be justified by normal market activity. From the borrower’s perspective the UI may show that the expected refund or remaining collateral is lower than anticipated, or that a surprisingly large fee is deducted at close, even though price movements appear modest. The impact is an economic loss for the borrower while the lender extracts additional premium, potentially without any real risk other than gas and swap fees. The vulnerability manifests whenever the fee snapshot is taken at position opening and later used directly for premium calculation, i.e., for any position that relies on the stored feeGrowthInside values. It affects all users who borrow against a Uniswap V3 NFT and any lender who can control liquidity in the same tick range. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of fee data between the Uniswap position manager and the protocol’s lien struct. It is hard to notice because fee growth is expected to change over time and the contract does not perform sanity checks on the magnitude of the change, making the manipulation blend with normal fee accrual. To remediate the problem the protocol should stop using the raw spot fee value for premium calculation; instead it could cap the premium, use a time‑weighted average fee, or otherwise limit how much fee growth can affect the borrower’s payment. This class of bug is an economic manipulation or fee‑inflation vulnerability, where a privileged participant can influence a metric that determines another participant’s cost, breaking the intended accounting assumptions of the system.

title: Excess tokens that are not accounted in the token premium portion stuck in the `ParticlePositionManager`
description: Excess tokens from margins provided by traders when opening position could become stuck inside the `ParticlePositionManager` due to precision loss when calculating the token premium portion.
bug_full: The issue is a rounding and precision loss bug that occurs when the contract computes the token premium portion for a new position. The premium is calculated by multiplying the net margin by a fixed scaling constant called BASIS_POINT (currently set to 1,000,000) and then dividing by the collateral amount. The result is cast to a 24‑bit unsigned integer before being stored in the lien structure. Because the scaling factor is relatively small compared to the typical 18‑decimal token precision, the division discards fractional bits. When the premium amount is small relative to the collateral, the truncation can leave a few wei or micro‑units of the token unaccounted for. These leftover units are not included in the lien’s accounting and therefore remain locked inside the ParticlePositionManager contract after the position is liquidated, liquidity is reclaimed, and the treasury is withdrawn. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a test that opened a position, added premium, liquidated the position, reclaimed liquidity and finally inspected the token balances of the manager. The test showed that after the full lifecycle a small amount of USDC (about 1,123 units) and a larger amount of WETH (about 5.16e11 wei) stayed in the manager contract. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after closing a position the expected refund is slightly lower than anticipated, sometimes appearing as a zero return for very small amounts, and the protocol’s internal balance shows an unexplained dust of tokens. The vulnerability belongs to the class of fixed‑point arithmetic rounding errors that generate “dust” that cannot be reclaimed by normal flows. Although each individual occurrence is tiny, the dust can accumulate over many transactions and effectively reduce the total assets under management, harming liquidity providers and the protocol’s economic model. The bug manifests whenever a token with high decimal precision is used and the premium calculation involves the low‑resolution BASIS_POINT scaling combined with a uint24 storage type. It is hard to notice because the amounts are small and may be dismissed as normal rounding variance. The recommended mitigation is to increase the scaling factor (for example using a larger BASIS_POINT value) or store the premium portion with a wider integer type to preserve more fractional precision. Additionally, providing an explicit “sweep dust” function would allow the protocol owner to recover any residual tokens that become trapped. Implementing these changes would align the accounting with the business logic that all premium tokens should be either allocated to the lien or returned to the user, eliminating the hidden loss of funds.

title: AddLiquidity and decreaseLiquidity missing slippage protection
description:
When user mint NFT add liquidity, user can specify two parameter, params.amount0Min and params.amount1Min
    
```solidity
    // mint the position
    (tokenId, liquidity, amount0Minted, amount1Minted) = Base.UNI_POSITION_MANAGER.mint(
        INonfungiblePositionManager.MintParams({
            token0: params.token0,
            token1: params.token1,
            fee: params.fee,
            tickLower: params.tickLower,
            tickUpper: params.tickUpper,
            amount0Desired: params.amount0ToMint,
            amount1Desired: params.amount1ToMint,
            amount0Min: params.amount0Min,
            amount1Min: params.amount1Min,
            recipient: address(this),
            deadline: block.timestamp
        })
    );
```

If the minted amount is too small, transaction revert [in this check](https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-periphery/blob/697c2474757ea89fec12a4e6db16a574fe259610/contracts/base/LiquidityManagement.sol#L88) in Uniswap position manager when adding liquidity.
    
```solidity
(amount0, amount1) = pool.mint(
	params.recipient,
	params.tickLower,
	params.tickUpper,
	liquidity,
	abi.encode(MintCallbackData({poolKey: poolKey, payer: msg.sender}))
);

require(amount0 >= params.amount0Min && amount1 >= params.amount1Min, 'Price slippage check');
```

However, when adding liquidity, the parameter [amount0Min and amount1Min is set to 0](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-particle/blob/a3af40839b24aa13f5764d4f84933dbfa8bc8134/contracts/libraries/LiquidityPosition.sol#L195).
    
```solidity
// increase liquidity via position manager
(liquidity, amount0Added, amount1Added) = Base.UNI_POSITION_MANAGER.increaseLiquidity(
	INonfungiblePositionManager.IncreaseLiquidityParams({
		tokenId: tokenId,
		amount0Desired: amount0,
		amount1Desired: amount1,
		amount0Min: 0,
		amount1Min: 0,
		deadline: block.timestamp
	})
);
```

As Uniswap V3 docs highlight:

<https://docs.uniswap.org/contracts/v3/guides/providing-liquidity/mint-a-position#calling-mint>

> We set amount0Min and amount1Min to zero for the example - but this would be a vulnerability in production. A function calling mint with no slippage protection would be vulnerable to a frontrunning attack designed to execute the mint call at an inaccurate price.

If the user transaction suffers from frontrunning, a much less amount of token can be minted.

Same issue happens when user decrease liquidity:
    
```solidity
    function decreaseLiquidity(uint256 tokenId, uint128 liquidity) internal returns (uint256 amount0, uint256 amount1) {
        (amount0, amount1) = Base.UNI_POSITION_MANAGER.decreaseLiquidity(
            INonfungiblePositionManager.DecreaseLiquidityParams({
                tokenId: tokenId,
                liquidity: liquidity,
                amount0Min: 0,
                amount1Min: 0,
                deadline: block.timestamp
            })
        );
    }
```

The amount0 and amount1Min are set to 0.

When MEV bot frontruns the decrease liquidity, much less amount0 and amount1 are released.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing slippage protection when a contract adds or removes liquidity from a Uniswap V3 pool through the non‑fungible position manager. In the minting flow the caller can supply amount0Min and amount1Min, which are intended to guarantee that at least a certain amount of each token is received despite price movement. However, the contract hard‑codes these parameters to zero both when increasing liquidity and when decreasing liquidity. Because the check in the Uniswap position manager only verifies that the actual amounts are greater than or equal to the supplied minima, a zero value disables the price‑slippage guard entirely. An attacker, typically an MEV bot, can front‑run the transaction after the user’s transaction is submitted but before it is mined, causing the pool price to shift. The pool will then mint or release a smaller amount of token0 and token1 than the user expected, yet the transaction will not revert because the minimum checks are satisfied (zero ≥ zero). From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the liquidity addition succeeded, but the received token balances are noticeably lower, sometimes appearing as if the funds “disappeared” or the refund is missing. The impact is a loss of value for the liquidity provider; the protocol’s accounting assumptions that the supplied amounts match the user’s intent are violated, potentially eroding trust in the platform. The issue occurs whenever the contract’s addLiquidity or decreaseLiquidity functions are invoked with hard‑coded zero minima, which is the case in the audited code base. It was discovered during a security audit that referenced Uniswap documentation warning that using zero slippage parameters is unsafe in production. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not fail, so developers may not notice the reduced token amounts without explicit balance checks. The proper remediation is to expose amount0Min and amount1Min as user‑controlled parameters or to compute safe minimums based on the expected price range, thereby re‑enabling the slippage check before calling the position manager. This aligns the implementation with the intended security model of Uniswap V3 and prevents front‑running attacks that would otherwise cause unexpected token loss.

title: `CultureIndex.sol#dropTopVotedPiece
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the dropTopVotedPiece function of the CultureIndex contract, which is responsible for taking the currently highest‑voted art piece from a max‑heap and auctioning it off. The function first retrieves the top‑voted piece, then checks whether the accumulated vote weight for that piece meets a quorum that is calculated as a percentage of the total voting token supply at the moment the piece was created. Because the quorum value is derived from the dynamic totalSupply of the ERC20 voting token, an attacker can inflate the token supply by purchasing additional voting tokens through the ERC20TokenEmitter contract. After inflating the supply, the attacker creates a bogus art piece; the inflated supply also inflates the piece’s quorum requirement. The attacker then casts enough votes to make the bogus piece the highest‑voted entry in the max‑heap, but deliberately keeps the vote count below the newly‑inflated quorum threshold. When the AuctionHouse calls dropTopVotedPiece, the require statement fails because totalVoteWeights[pieceId] is lower than piece.quorumVotes, causing the transaction to revert. Since the max‑heap still reports the same bogus piece as the top entry, no other piece can ever become the top‑voted candidate, effectively locking the drop mechanism. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate art pieces that have reached their own quorum can never be dropped, users see the UI stuck on the same top‑voted piece, auctions do not start, and participants are forced either to vote for the bogus piece to push it over its quorum, to create new pieces and restart voting, or to wait indefinitely. The issue affects all participants of the protocol – artists, voters, the AuctionHouse, and any downstream contracts that rely on timely drops – and can lead to lost revenue, increased gas costs, and a degraded user experience. The problem was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which included a reproducible proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrates the top‑voted piece remaining undroppable. The bug is subtle because the contract correctly enforces the quorum check for the piece it is trying to drop, yet it does not account for the possibility that the top‑voted piece itself may never satisfy its quorum, a scenario that is not obvious from normal operation. The vulnerability belongs to the class of ranking‑based denial‑of‑service bugs where ordering logic (max‑heap) is decoupled from eligibility criteria (quorum), allowing a malicious or accidental configuration to block progress. To remediate, the protocol should either (1) redesign the quorum calculation to be independent of the mutable total token supply, (2) modify the drop logic to iterate over the heap until a piece that satisfies its quorum is found, (3) introduce an admin or DAO‑controlled escape‑hatch that can forcibly drop or remove a stuck piece, or (4) enforce that a piece cannot become the top‑voted entry unless it already meets its quorum, thereby preventing a quorum‑locked state.

title: The quorumVotes can be bypassed
description:
This vulnerability allows for the minting and auctioning of an art piece that has not met the required quorum. It enables malicious voters to influence outcomes with fewer votes than what is stipulated by the protocol. This undermines a key invariant of the protocol:

An art piece that has not met quorum cannot be dropped.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the calculation and storage of the quorum threshold for an art piece within a governance‑driven protocol. When a new piece is created, the contract records the total voting power (totalVotesSupply) by reading the current total supply of two voting tokens and then stores a derived quorumVotes value as a fixed fraction of that supply. Because the protocol uses a block‑based clock for vote checkpoints, the total token supply can increase later in the same block after the piece creation transaction has been executed. The stored quorumVotes therefore reflects an outdated, underestimated voting power, sometimes even zero, while the real voting power at the end of the block is higher. An attacker who can back‑run the createPiece transaction can purchase additional governance tokens in the same block, causing the contract to believe the piece meets the quorum when it actually does not. This allows the attacker to invoke the dropTopVotedPiece function and mint or auction the art piece without satisfying the intended quorum invariant. The impact is that pieces can be dropped, minted, or auctioned without genuine community approval, breaking a core business rule that only pieces with sufficient votes may be removed, potentially leading to misallocation of funds, loss of trust, and economic damage to token holders. The issue manifests when the creationBlock and the stored quorumVotes are used for later checks instead of recomputing the quorum from the token supply at the end of that block. It affects any user who expects their vote to count toward quorum, the protocol’s governance process, and any party relying on the integrity of the drop mechanism. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit where the auditors observed that the contract stored the quorum value at creation time and demonstrated the exploit with a test that back‑runs a token purchase in the same block, showing the quorum value being recorded as zero. The problem is subtle because the stored values appear consistent at the moment of creation and no error is thrown, making it easy to miss during casual testing. The recommended remediation is to stop persisting quorumVotes at creation and instead compute it on demand using the token’s getPastTotalSupply function for the piece’s creationBlock, ensuring the quorum reflects the true voting power at the block’s end and preventing supply manipulation within the same block from affecting the quorum calculation.

title: Since buyToken function has no slippage checking, users can get less tokens than expected when they buy tokens directly
description: Users can buy NontransferableERC20Token by calling `buyToken` function directly. At that time, the expected amount of tokens they will receive is determined based on current supply and their paying ether amount. But, due to some transactions (such as settleAuction or another user’s buyToken) which is running in front of caller’s transaction, they can get less token than they expected.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing slippage protection in the buyToken function of a token emission contract that uses a variable rate gradual Dutch auction (VRGDA) pricing model. The contract calculates the amount of tokens a user should receive based on the current supply and the ether sent, but it does not verify that the amount does not fall below a user‑specified minimum before the transaction is finalized. Because the VRGDA price rises when the token supply gets ahead of the schedule, any transaction that is mined before the user’s purchase – for example a front‑running buyToken call from another user or a settleAuction call that internally invokes buyToken – can increase the price and therefore reduce the number of tokens the original caller receives. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a larger purchase transaction that is placed in the same block ahead of the victim’s transaction, causing the price to jump and the victim’s expected token amount to shrink. The impact is that users see a lower token balance than anticipated; they may send a fixed amount of ether expecting, say, 4.87 tokens but receive only about 4.43 tokens, effectively losing part of their purchase value. This situation occurs only when a user calls buyToken directly and there is no slippage check; it does not affect calls made through settleAuction, which intentionally bypasses the check. All participants who rely on the contract to deliver a predictable token amount – individual buyers, the protocol’s economic model, and any downstream applications – are affected. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors wrote a test that simulated a front‑run scenario and observed the token amount decreasing without any error. It is hard to notice because the price increase is an intended behavior of the VRGDA algorithm, so a reduced token amount may be mistaken for normal market dynamics rather than a contract flaw. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running or slippage‑related vulnerabilities where the contract fails to enforce a minimum output amount. To remediate, the contract should accept a slippage tolerance parameter from the caller and revert the transaction if the actual token amount falls below the expected amount, while preserving the intended behavior for internal calls such as settleAuction. Adding this check would align the contract with standard best practices for token sales and protect users from unexpected loss of tokens.

title: ERC20TokenEmitter will not work after a certain period of time
description: The `timeSinceStart` in the `vrgdac.xToY` function will revert over a certain value, resulting in the `ERC20TokenEmitter#buyToken` function always revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a time‑dependent arithmetic failure in the VRGDAC pricing module used by the ERC20TokenEmitter contract. The module calculates the amount of tokens that can be bought by converting a desired token amount (Y) to a required payment (X) using a function that takes the elapsed time since the sale started (timeSinceStart) as an input. The implementation relies on fixed‑point (wad) arithmetic and assumes that timeSinceStart stays within a range where the intermediate values remain non‑zero. When the sale is far behind its target schedule, the elapsed time can grow large (for example more than three hundred and sixty‑five days). At that point the calculation of the exponential term or a division by a value that has been reduced to zero triggers a revert with the error 'UNDEFINED'. Because the ERC20TokenEmitter#buyToken function calls vrgdac.xToY with block.timestamp‑startTime as timeSinceStart, any call after the threshold causes the whole transaction to revert, preventing token purchases. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a failed transaction or a button that does nothing, and the user receives no tokens even though they expected to acquire them. The impact is that the token sale becomes effectively frozen for all participants, halting revenue for the DAO and preventing new holders from joining. The issue appears only after a prolonged period of low sales activity, which makes it easy to miss during short‑term testing. It was discovered during a formal audit when the tester reproduced the failure by initializing the VRGDAC with realistic parameters and setting timeSinceStart to 400 days, causing the yToX call to return 'UNDEFINED'. The root cause is precision loss and division‑by‑zero in the fixed‑point math of the VRGDAC pricing formula. To remediate the problem the pricing function should be rewritten to clamp or cap timeSinceStart, use safe fixed‑point operations that avoid zero denominators, or redesign the VRGDAC algorithm so that it never reaches a state where a parameter becomes zero regardless of how far behind schedule the sale is. Applying such a fix restores the ability for users to buy tokens at any point in time and aligns the contract behaviour with the expected business logic that token purchases should always succeed while the sale is active.

title: positionMapping for last element in heap is not updated when extracting max element
description:
During the extraction of the max element through the function [extractMax()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-revolutionprotocol/blob/d42cc62b873a1b2b44f57310f9d4bbfdd875e8d6/packages/revolution/src/MaxHeap.sol#L156), the `positionMapping` for the last element in the heap tree is not updated when the last element is equal to its parent.

These are the following impacts:

1. MaxHeap does not function as intended and breaks its expected functionality due to element being incorrectly indexed in the heap.
2. When a new element is inserted to that index, the incorrectly indexed element accesses the new element’s itemId during value updates
3. Downward heapifying will work incorrectly leading to the parent having a value smaller than its child. Thus, further breaking not only the maxHeap tree but also the binary tree spec.
4. Error in this heapifying will lead to the incorrectly indexed element being extracted.

**Note: Point 3 in the impacts above breaks an invariant of the MaxHeap tree mentioned in the README.**
    
The MaxHeap should always maintain the property of being a binary tree in which the value in each internal node is greater than or equal to the values in the children of that node.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect update of the internal position mapping when the maximum element is removed from a binary max‑heap implementation. The contract stores each item’s identifier in a heap array and keeps a separate positionMapping that records the current index of each identifier. During extractMax the last leaf element is moved to the root and the heap size is decremented, but if the moved element has the same priority value as its parent, the code never updates positionMapping for that element. As a result the mapping continues to point to the old leaf index while the element now resides at the root. This mismatch causes subsequent operations – insert, updateValue and any downward heapify – to read or write using a stale index. When a new element is inserted, the stale entry may be overwritten, leading to two different identifiers sharing the same recorded position. Updating a value then uses the wrong index, causing upward or downward heapify to operate on unrelated nodes, which can violate the max‑heap invariant (a parent value smaller than a child). The impact is that the contract may return a non‑maximum element from extractMax, expose incorrect rankings, and potentially allow an attacker to manipulate ordering or extract lower‑valued items. The bug manifests only when the last element’s priority equals its parent’s priority, a condition that is easy to miss because the heap appears to contain the correct values in the array and valueMapping, while the hidden positionMapping is wrong. It was discovered during a manual audit that traced the state of the heap after extraction and observed that positionMapping still referenced the old leaf index. The issue is hard to notice because the visible heap array and value mapping remain consistent, and the failure only appears in later operations that rely on the position mapping. From a user perspective, a call to extractMax may return an unexpected lower‑value item, and a subsequent insert may appear to overwrite an existing entry, leading to missing or duplicated identifiers. The bug belongs to the class of data‑structure indexing errors where auxiliary bookkeeping structures are not kept in sync with the primary structure. The correct fix is to ensure that after moving the last leaf to the root, the positionMapping for the moved element is always updated to the new root index, and to handle the special case where the leaf value equals its parent’s value. Updating the mapping restores the invariant that each identifier’s recorded position matches its actual location in the heap, thereby preserving the max‑heap property and preventing incorrect ordering or extraction.

title: MaxHeap.sol: Already extracted tokenId may be extracted again
description: `MaxHeap.sol#extractMax` function only decreases the `size` variable without initializing the `heap` state variable. On the other hand, `MaxHeap.sol#maxHeapify` function involves the `heap` variable for the out-of-bound index which will contain dirty non-zero value. As a result, uncleared dirty value of `heap` state variable will be used in the process and already extracted tokenId will be extracted again.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a max‑heap implementation used to store token identifiers. The extractMax function removes the element at the root, decrements the size counter and moves the last element to the root, but it never clears the storage slot that previously held the last element (heap[size] after the decrement). Because the slot is left with its old non‑zero value, subsequent calls to maxHeapify may read this stale entry when calculating the right child index (right = 2*pos+2). If right equals the former size, the algorithm accesses an out‑of‑bound index that still contains the previously extracted tokenId. This dirty value is then compared against legitimate entries, causing the heap to consider the already‑extracted tokenId as the maximum again. The root cause is the missing initialization of the vacated heap slot, combined with a maxHeapify routine that does not guard against reading beyond the current size. An attacker or a malicious admin can trigger the bug by extracting all items, inserting new items with lower values, and then updating a value so that maxHeapify is invoked. The heap will incorrectly return the old tokenId, effectively allowing the same token identifier to be extracted twice. From a user’s perspective the protocol promises a fresh tokenId on each extraction, but the UI may show a duplicate NFT or a balance that appears unchanged, violating the expectation that each token is unique. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees: duplicate token issuance can lead to double‑spending, incorrect reward distribution, or loss of trust in the system’s fairness. The issue appears only under specific conditions – when the heap becomes empty, new items are added with lower priority, and a value update forces a heapify that reads the stale slot – making it easy to miss in casual testing. It was discovered during a formal audit by writing a test that extracts all items, reinserts smaller‑value items, updates a value, and observes that the previously extracted tokenId reappears. The bug is subtle because the heap still functions correctly for many sequences, and the out‑of‑bound read does not cause a revert, only a logical error. The proper fix is to clear the vacated slot after decrementing size (e.g., set heap[size] = 0) and/or adjust the maxHeapify bounds check to ensure it never reads indices equal to or greater than the current size. This prevents stale data from influencing the ordering logic and restores the guarantee that each extraction yields a previously unseen tokenId.

title: Anyone can pause AuctionHouse in `_createAuction`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the auction creation flow of the AuctionHouse contract. When the public function settleCurrentAndCreateNewAuction is called, it internally invokes a private routine that attempts to mint a new NFT for the upcoming auction. The minting operation is wrapped in a try/catch block; if the mint call throws, the catch clause executes a pause on the AuctionHouse contract. Although the code checks that the remaining gas is at least a hard‑coded threshold before attempting the mint, an attacker can deliberately inflate the gas consumption of the mint function by supplying an art piece with a large metadata payload or by specifying many creators. Each additional creator triggers a storage write inside a loop, and copying large metadata also consumes significant gas. By constructing an art piece with a modest number of creators (for example ten) the attacker can exceed the 750 000‑gas threshold, causing the mint call to run out of gas. The out‑of‑gas exception is caught by the generic catch clause, which then calls the internal _pause function, effectively freezing the entire auction system. This pause can be triggered by any user who can call settleCurrentAndCreateNewAuction, not only privileged roles. The impact is that the contract stops creating new auctions, bids cannot be placed, and any funds locked in ongoing auctions become inaccessible until the contract is manually unpaused by an authorized account. From a user’s perspective the UI will show that after an auction ends no new auction appears, the contract appears “paused”, and balances that should have been updated remain unchanged. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the gas‑griefing surface of the mint routine and verified that the gas‑left check does not guarantee safety against deliberately expensive mint operations. The bug is subtle because the pause is a legitimate response to a caught error, making it easy to overlook that an attacker can force that error path. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of unchecked external call failures leading to unintended state changes, specifically a denial‑of‑service via out‑of‑gas manipulation. The recommended mitigation is to narrow the catch clause to only handle explicit error strings, thereby allowing out‑of‑gas exceptions to propagate and not trigger a pause, or to redesign the minting logic to have deterministic gas usage or to move the pause out of the catch block entirely.

title: `ERC20TokenEmitter::buyToken` function mints more tokens to users than it should do
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ERC20TokenEmitter.buyToken function where the amount of governance tokens to mint for the buyer and for the creator are calculated independently using getTokenQuoteForEther. Each call to getTokenQuoteForEther reads the current emittedTokenWad, which reflects the token supply before either portion is minted.
