Because the two calculations are performed sequentially but the state variable emittedTokenWad is only updated after both results are obtained, the second call uses the same supply value as the first call. This breaks the VRGDA (variable rate gradual Dutch auction) pricing model that expects a single token quote based on the total ETH being spent. As a result, the sum of the tokens minted for buyer and creator exceeds the amount that would be minted if the total ETH payment were quoted once, effectively inflating the token supply and allowing users to obtain more tokens per ETH than intended. The bug can be triggered whenever buyToken is executed with a non‑zero creatorRateBps and entropyRateBps, i.e., any purchase that splits the payment between the treasury and the creator. An attacker can repeatedly purchase tokens, causing the protocol to mint extra tokens and dilute existing holders, while the treasury receives the correct ETH amount, leading to a mismatch between the economic model and the actual token distribution. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test comparing getTokenQuoteForEther(100 ETH)+getTokenQuoteForEther(500 ETH) against getTokenQuoteForEther(600 ETH) showed the former to be larger, confirming over‑minting. The problem is subtle because the contract still transfers the expected ETH amounts and the token balances increase, so a casual inspection may not reveal the pricing deviation. To remediate, the function should first compute the total ETH that will be used to purchase governance tokens, call getTokenQuoteForEther once to obtain a single token amount, and then allocate that amount proportionally between buyer and creator, or alternatively update emittedTokenWad after the creator’s portion is minted before calculating the buyer’s portion. This restores the VRGDA invariant and prevents unintended token inflation. Users may notice that they receive more tokens than the price curve suggests, or that the total supply grows faster than the schedule, indicating a breach of the intended accounting logic.

title: Since art pieces’ size is not limited, attacker may block AuctionHouse from creating and settling auctions
description: **Note:** _there is another bug (calling`verbs.getArtPieceById` in a loop in `_settleAuction`), but this issue focuses on a different attack vector for creating DoS attack, so in this submission, I assume that the bug is fixed (that is, `verbs.getArtPieceById` is not called in a loop, but cached before it)._
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the fact that the contract does not enforce any size limits on the string fields stored in the ArtPieceMetadata structure. Because the metadata strings can be arbitrarily long, an attacker can submit an art piece whose description or other text fields contain a payload of several megabytes. When such a piece is used to create an auction, the contract writes the huge string into storage during the _createAuction call and later reads it again during _settleAuction. Writing a large amount of data triggers the expensive sreset opcode (approximately 2 900 gas per zero‑byte) instead of the cheaper sset, causing the gas consumption of both the creation and settlement functions to approach or exceed the block gas limit (around 30 million gas for creation and 22 million gas for settlement in the reported PoC). As a result, the transaction either runs out of gas or becomes prohibitively expensive, effectively preventing the protocol from creating new auctions or settling existing ones. This denial‑of‑service condition can be triggered without any additional exploits; the attacker simply needs to be able to call the function that registers a new art piece. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that a transaction to create an auction reverts with an out‑of‑gas error, or that after an auction has ended the settlement transaction never succeeds, leaving the auction in a perpetual pending state and locking the bidders’ funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the tester measured gas usage while supplying a very long string of null bytes and observed that the gas cost grew linearly with the payload size. The problem is subtle because the contract’s logic appears correct and the metadata is not used for any on‑chain computation, so developers may not anticipate that storage size alone can break the system. The appropriate mitigation is to treat the metadata as untrusted user input and enforce a maximum byte length for each field, or to store only a hash or IPFS CID on‑chain and keep the full description off‑chain. By limiting the length of the metadata, the gas cost of creating and settling auctions remains bounded, preserving the protocol’s ability to process auctions and protecting users’ funds.

title: Once EntropyRateBps is set too high, can lead to denial-of-service
description: Once entropy is set too high, the remaining ETH used to invoke `buyToken` is very small, which can lead to the protocol permanently being stuck.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when the protocol’s entropyRateBps parameter is configured to a value that is too high. The contract splits the ETH collected in an auction between creators and a token purchase step. A high entropyRateBps causes the calculation of paymentAmount for each creator to consume almost all of the creatorsShare, leaving a very small remainder (creatorsShare‑ethPaidToCreators). When this remainder falls below the protocol‑defined minPurchaseAmount, the subsequent call to the ERC20TokenEmitter’s buyToken function reverts with INVALID_ETH_AMOUNT, preventing the token minting and the start of the next auction round. This situation can be triggered by the contract owner or any privileged account that is allowed to set entropyRateBps (and creatorRateBps) within the setter’s nominal bounds, so the misconfiguration is not prevented by existing checks. The impact is that the protocol becomes permanently stuck: no new auctions can be created, bidders cannot acquire tokens, and the ETH already transferred to creators is effectively locked in the contract, violating the business expectation that each auction round will conclude with token distribution and fresh bidding. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case set entropyRateBps to 9999 and reservePrice to 0.005 ether, causing the settlement transaction to revert. It is hard to notice because the setter functions accept the high value without error, and the failure only manifests after the settlement step, not during bidding, making the symptom appear as an unexpected revert rather than a configuration problem. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the amount remaining for token purchase (creatorsShare‑ethPaidToCreators) is greater than minPurchaseAmount before invoking buyToken, or impose a tighter relationship between entropyRateBps, creatorRateBps, and the reserve price so that the remainder can never drop below the minimum purchase threshold. This fixes the logical flaw by ensuring the accounting assumptions of the protocol remain valid and prevents the protocol from entering a deadlocked state where funds disappear from the user’s perspective and no tokens are minted.

title: It may be possible to DoS AuctionHouse by specifying malicious creators
description: **Note:** *there is another bug in `AuctionHouse::_settleAuction` that causes DoS (querying `verbs.getArtPieceById` too many times), but this submission describes another issue and from now on, **I assume that`verbs.getArtPieceById` is not called in loop in `_settleAuction`***.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition that can be triggered during the settlement phase of an auction when the contract iterates over a list of creators and attempts to transfer ETH or ERC20 tokens to each of them. The root cause is that the settlement logic in AuctionHouse::_settleAuction does not impose any limit on the number of creator entries and performs a direct value transfer to every creator address without protecting against malicious fallback functions. An attacker can create an auction that lists a large number of creator contracts whose receive() function contains an infinite loop or otherwise consumes all available gas. When settleCurrentAndCreateNewAuction is called after the auction ends, the contract executes a loop that calls each creator’s receive() to distribute rewards. The malicious contracts cause the transfer to stall, consuming an excessive amount of gas (the proof‑of‑concept shows a difference of roughly 20.5 million gas when 100 malicious creators are used versus a single honest creator). Because the gas required exceeds the block gas limit or the transaction runs out of gas, the settlement transaction reverts, leaving the auction in an unsettled state. From a user’s perspective the auction never finalises, bidders cannot claim their winnings, and expected reward payments appear to disappear or remain unclaimed. The issue affects any participant that relies on the auction to close, including bidders, creators, and the protocol itself, which may lose revenue and reputation. The problem was discovered during a formal audit when the researchers crafted a test contract with an infinite‑loop receive() and measured the gas consumption during settlement. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because typical auctions involve only a few honest creators whose fallback functions execute quickly, masking the underlying scalability flaw. To remediate the issue the protocol should either cap the number of creators that can be specified for an auction or, preferably, change the reward distribution model from a push‑based approach to a pull‑based one, such as providing a separate claimRewards function that each creator can call independently. This eliminates the need for the settlement routine to iterate over potentially untrusted contracts and prevents a single malicious creator from halting the entire auction process.

title: `encodedData` argument of `hashStruct` is not calculated perfectly for EIP712 singed messages in `CultureIndex.sol`
description: Encoding of `encodedData` is not done correctly for the verification of EIP712 signed messages.
poc: All of the link mentioned above. Also Read [this](https://ethereum.stackexchange.com/questions/125105/signing-an-array-whit-eth-signtypeddata-v) Ethereum exchange conversation.
bug_full: The contract implements an off‑chain vote that is signed using EIP‑712 typed data. The verification routine builds a struct hash by calling abi.encode with the raw pieceIds array, the voter address, a nonce and a deadline, and then hashes the result with keccak256. According to the EIP‑712 specification, dynamic arrays must be represented by the keccak256 hash of their tightly packed encoding, not by the raw array itself. Because the code feeds the un‑hashed array directly into the struct hash, the resulting digest does not faithfully bind the exact list of piece identifiers to the signature. This mismatch creates a logical vulnerability: a signature that appears valid for one set of pieceIds can be accepted for a different set, or an attacker can craft a signature that passes verification while the on‑chain vote records a different array. The bug is triggered whenever a voter calls the internal _verifyVoteSignature function with a non‑empty pieceIds array, which is the normal path for every vote. Users experience the problem as unexpected signature rejections or, conversely, as votes being counted for items they never selected, effectively breaking the trust model of the governance process. The issue was discovered during a formal audit (Code4rena) where the auditor noted that the struct hash should use keccak256(abi.encodePacked(pieceIds)) instead of the raw array. It is subtle because the ecrecover call succeeds and no explicit error is thrown; the contract simply records an incorrect vote, making the defect hard to spot through ordinary testing. The appropriate remediation is to hash the pieceIds array before inserting it into the typed‑data struct, ensuring that the EIP‑712 digest uniquely represents the exact data the signer intended. This change restores the cryptographic binding between the signed message and the vote payload, preventing forgery, replay, or accidental mis‑recording of votes and aligning the implementation with the EIP‑712 standard.

title: All Rage Trade functions allow sending tokens
description:
All three approved functions on Rage Trade (depositTokens(), withdrawTokens() and redeemTokens()) allow for a receiver argument to be included, which sends the resulting tokens to that address. The corresponding Controller assumes that all tokens are withdrawn to the Sentiment account that called the function.  
The three functions that can be called on Rage Trade have the following signatures:  
• depositToken(address token, address receiver, uint256 amount)  
• redeemToken(address token, address receiver, uint256 amount)  
• withdrawToken(address token, address receiver, uint256 amount)  
Each of these functions contains a receiver argument, which can be passed any address that will receive the outputted tokens.  
The DNGMXVaultController incorrectly assumes in all cases that the outputted tokens will be received by the Sentiment account in question, regardless of what is entered as a receiver.  
Accounting on user accounts can be thrown off (intentionally or unintentionally), resulting in mismatches between their assets array and hasAsset mapping and the reality of their account.  
This specific Impact was judged as Medium for multiple issues in the previous contest:
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in three public functions of the Rage Trade contract – depositToken(address token, address receiver, uint256 amount), redeemToken(address token, address receiver, uint256 amount) and withdrawToken(address token, address receiver, uint256 amount). Each function allows the caller to specify an arbitrary receiver address that will receive the tokens resulting from the operation. The DNGMXVaultController, which maintains an internal accounting of each Sentiment account’s assets, incorrectly assumes that the tokens will always be transferred back to the Sentiment account that invoked the function (msg.sender). Consequently, the controller updates the assets array and the hasAsset mapping based on the caller’s address, regardless of the actual receiver supplied in the transaction. This mismatch can be triggered whenever a user (or an attacker) passes a receiver that differs from msg.sender, either intentionally or by mistake. When the mismatch occurs, the on‑chain accounting state no longer reflects the real token holdings: the assets list may still contain the token, the hasAsset flag may stay true, but the tokens are actually sitting in a different address. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that a deposit appears to succeed while the expected balance does not increase, a withdrawal or redemption shows a zero or reduced balance, or the UI displays assets that are no longer owned. The impact is a medium‑severity accounting inconsistency that can be abused to hide token movements, create false asset reports, or potentially divert funds to an address controlled by an attacker. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Sentiment January Update where the auditor noticed that the controller’s logic never validates the receiver argument against msg.sender. The bug is subtle because the functions themselves correctly transfer tokens; the failure lies in the separate accounting module that does not cross‑check the destination address, making the problem easy to overlook during functional testing. To remediate, the controller (or any decoding logic that interprets calls to Rage Trade) must verify that the receiver argument equals msg.sender before accepting the operation, and reject or flag any deviation. In practice this means adding an explicit check on the decoded data and, if the receiver differs, either reject the call or adjust the accounting to reflect the true recipient. By aligning the accounting with the actual token flow, the protocol restores consistency between reported assets and real holdings, preventing misleading balances and protecting users from inadvertent loss or malicious redirection of tokens.

title: Using one controller for two addresses could
description:
The DNGMXVaultController is intended to be used as a controller for two separate contracts when interacting with Rage Trade. While individual contracts check for signature collisions, there is no protection in this Controller. If the contracts end up with functions with colliding signatures, this may enable users to call illegal functions and get around the protocol safeguards.
While most of Sentiment's Controllers correspond to one contract, the DNGMXVaultController is one controller that will support two separate contracts: DepositPeriphery and WithdrawPeriphery.
While signature collisions are unlikely, they do happen. For this reason, the Solidity compiler stops code from compiling in the case of a collision. This ensures that there will not be issues in any EVM bytecode. Because Sentiment controllers approve function calls based on signatures, they can be sure that, for any given contract, they will only be approving the function they are intending.
However, once multiple contracts are managed by one controller, there are no compiler checks across these contracts for colliding signatures. The result is that there is the potential for a function signature on one contract that is approved, due to a matching signature on the other contract.
There is the potential for users to get access to non-permitted functions if there is a signature collision.
This is a security risk in this specific case, but is also a more global suggestion for Sentiment. While two contracts on one Controller one time is unlikely to cause a problem, the practice of loading multiple contracts onto on Controller should be avoided, as the risks will increase as this is performed.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a single controller contract that is responsible for routing calls to two distinct periphery contracts – a DepositPeriphery and a WithdrawPeriphery – when interacting with the Rage Trade protocol. The controller authorises function calls solely by matching the 4‑byte function selector (the method signature hash) without taking the target contract address into account. Solidity only enforces selector uniqueness within a single contract, so when two separate contracts are managed by the same controller there is no compile‑time guarantee that their selectors are distinct. Consequently, if the DepositPeriphery and the WithdrawPeriphery each implement a function whose selector collides, the controller will mistakenly approve the call for the wrong contract. An attacker who discovers such a collision can craft a transaction that appears to invoke an allowed function on one contract but is actually executed on the other, potentially bypassing the protocol’s safeguards. This could allow a user to invoke privileged or state‑changing functions that were never intended to be reachable through the controller, such as withdrawing funds, altering accounting variables, or disabling security checks. The issue manifests only when both contracts contain at least one overlapping selector, which may happen after a contract upgrade, the addition of new features, or simply by coincidence because selector collisions, while rare, are possible. All participants that interact with the vault – depositors, withdrawers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the controller’s mis‑routing can lead to unexpected loss of assets, zero balances, or failed refunds that appear to the user as “my funds disappeared” or “the withdrawal returned nothing”. The problem was uncovered during a manual security audit that examined the controller’s design and recognised that the lack of per‑contract selector validation creates an authorization bypass. It is difficult to detect in routine testing because the function selectors are opaque bytes and typical unit tests focus on functional correctness within each contract, not on cross‑contract selector overlap. The recommended remediation is to split the DNGMXVaultController into two independent controller contracts, each dedicated to a single periphery contract, or to implement a strict mapping that ties each allowed selector to a specific contract address. This eliminates the possibility of accidental selector collisions and restores the intended one‑controller‑per‑contract security model, ensuring that users receive the expected behavior – deposits go to the deposit contract and withdrawals go to the withdrawal contract – without the risk of unauthorized function execution.

title: (previously M-06)
description:
For an empty phase, both the endingRoundId and startingRoundId will be 0.
And the roundCount should be 0 instead of 1.
https://github.com/equilibria-xyz/perennial-mono/blob/e801b6eecae6ca609597710d2980bd26184a2ef8/packages/perennial-oracle/contracts/types/ChainlinkRegistry.sol#L77-L82
When empty phases are involved, the result of getRoundCount() will be incorrect, and therefore OracleVersion will also be incorrect.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the ChainlinkRegistry contract calculates the number of rounds in a phase. When a phase contains no price data – an empty phase – both the startingRoundId and endingRoundId are stored as zero. The existing logic, however, assumes that a non‑zero endingRoundId always indicates a populated phase and increments the roundCount by one regardless of the actual data. Consequently, for an empty phase the roundCount is reported as 1 instead of the correct value 0. This off‑by‑one error propagates to the getRoundCount() function, which then returns an incorrect count and causes the derived OracleVersion to be wrong. The impact is that any downstream contract or protocol component that relies on the OracleVersion for price validation, slashing, or settlement may treat stale or non‑existent data as current, potentially leading to incorrect pricing, failed settlements, or unintended economic outcomes. The bug manifests only when a phase transitions without any round submissions, a situation that can occur during network upgrades, data feed pauses, or when the oracle source temporarily stops providing updates. It was discovered during a manual audit of the Perennial oracle integration, where the auditor noticed that the roundCount did not match the expected state for phases with no data. The issue is subtle because the roundCount field still holds a plausible positive integer, making the discrepancy easy to overlook without explicit checks for empty phases. To remediate the problem the contract should include a special case: if endingRoundId equals zero, the phase must be treated as empty and the roundCount set to zero, and getRoundCount() should return this corrected value. This adjustment restores the integrity of the OracleVersion calculation and aligns the contract’s accounting with the intended business logic that an empty phase contributes no rounds to the oracle history.

title: (previously M-02 in fix review)
description: https://github.com/equilibria-xyz/perennial-mono/blob/e801b6eecae6ca609597710d2980bd26184a2ef8/packages/perennial-oracle/contracts/types/ChainlinkAggregator.sol#L50-L76
bug_full: The contract contains a conditional branch that treats a price‑feed phase as empty when the stored startingRoundId equals zero. In the current implementation the constructor or initialization logic guarantees that startingRoundId is always set to a non‑zero value, so the condition can never be true. The root cause is an assumption in the code that a zero startingRoundId is a possible state, even though the surrounding logic enforces a non‑zero invariant. If, contrary to the design, startingRoundId were ever zero, the contract would consider the phase empty, potentially returning a default price of zero or triggering a revert when callers request the latest round data. This could cause downstream protocols that rely on the oracle to receive an unexpected zero price, fail their own calculations, or halt execution, leading to user‑visible symptoms such as missing price updates, failed transactions, or funds being locked because a trade cannot be priced. The vulnerability manifests only under the unreachable condition where startingRoundId is zero, which does not occur in the deployed code, making it hard to observe in testing. It was discovered during a systematic audit that flagged the empty‑phase check as a potential logical error. Because the branch is never exercised, the issue may be overlooked unless the code is closely examined for invariant violations. The recommended remediation is to remove the unreachable check or replace it with an explicit assert that startingRoundId is never zero, thereby eliminating dead code and clarifying the contract’s assumptions. Conceptually, this is a defensive‑programming flaw where an impossible state is handled as if it were valid, which can lead to incorrect accounting or denial‑of‑service if the invariant were ever broken.

title: Poor validation or prices reported by Chain-
description:
The GMXAdapter contract integrates with Chainlink feeds, however prices reported by Chainlink feeds are not thoroughly validated. This exposes the protocol to the negative impact of extreme market events, possible malicious activity of Chainlink data feeders or its contracts, potential delays, and outages.
The _getChainlinkPrice function of GMXAdapter reads a price from a Chainlink feed and ignores the updatedAt value returned by latestRoundData (GMXAdapter.sol#L192):
```solidity
(, int answer, , , ) = assetPriceFeed.latestRoundData();
if (answer <= 0) {
    revert InvalidAnswer(address(this), answer);
}
```
Besides the answer, latestRoundData also returns updatedAt, the timestamp of when the round was updated. Chainlink Price Feeds do not provide streaming data. Rather, the aggregator updates its latestAnswer when the value deviates beyond a specified threshold or when the heartbeat idle time has passed. Due to outages or malicious activity of Chainlink data feeders, prices may be delayed or even become stale.
latestRoundData also returns roundID and answeredInRound values, which can be used to check for price reporting round completeness. However, the values are ignored and not validated, which exposes the protocol to any Chainlink issues with completing price reporting rounds.
Also, the answer is not checked against reasonable price limits: while there's a check for a zero or negative price, an invalid price may still be above zero.
By not checking the updatedAt value, GMXAdapter becomes exposed to outages in Chainlink or malicious activity of its data feeders, which may lead to incorrect pricing during liquidations or any other activity that uses the PriceType.REFERENCE price type.
In case a Chainlink price feed has failed to finalize a round, GMXAdapter won't detect a stale or an invalid price, which will affect all operations that use the reference price type.
In case a price that's outside of the reasonable limits of an asset is reported (due to an outage in Chainlink or malicious activity), GMXAdapter will fail to detect such price. As a result, any operation that uses the reference price type will be impaired.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation of Chainlink price feed metadata in the GMXAdapter contract. The contract calls latestRoundData and only checks that the returned answer is greater than zero, ignoring the updatedAt timestamp, roundID and answeredInRound fields, and not enforcing that the price lies within reasonable min/max bounds. Because Chainlink aggregators only update when the price moves beyond a threshold or after a heartbeat, a stale or deliberately manipulated price can remain unchanged for an extended period. If the feed experiences an outage, a delay, or a malicious data feeder submits a fabricated answer, the GMXAdapter will still accept the stale or out‑of‑range price and use it as the reference price for liquidations, margin checks, and any other operation that relies on accurate market data. This can cause liquidations to be triggered at incorrect values, users to receive wrong settlement amounts, or the protocol to open positions based on a price that no longer reflects the market, potentially leading to loss of funds or unfair advantage for an attacker. The issue manifests whenever a price round has not been finalized, when updatedAt is older than the expected heartbeat, or when the price exceeds the asset’s logical bounds but remains positive. It affects all participants that interact with the protocol through the GMXAdapter, including traders, liquidators, and any contract that reads the reference price. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the adapter’s price‑retrieval logic and noted the absence of checks that are recommended by Chainlink’s own feed monitoring guidelines. The bug is subtle because the returned price may appear numerically valid, making it difficult to detect without explicit timestamp or round completeness verification. To remediate, the adapter should verify that updatedAt is recent relative to the feed’s heartbeat, ensure answeredInRound is at least equal to roundID, and compare the answer against the feed’s configured minAnswer and maxAnswer limits, rejecting any price that fails these checks before it is used in protocol calculations.

title: GMX Reward Router's claimForAccount() can
description:
When claimFees() is called, the Controller automatically adds WETH to the user's account. However, in the case where no fees have accrued yet, there will not be WETH withdrawn. In this case, the user will have WETH added as an asset in their account, while they won't actually have any WETH holdings.
When a user calls the GMX Reward Router's claimFees() function, the RewardRouterController confirms the validity of this call in the canCallClaimFees() function:
```solidity
function canCallClaimFees()
    internal
    view
    returns (bool, address[] memory, address[] memory)
{
    return (true, WETH, new address[](0));
}
```
This function assumes that any user calling claimFees() will always receive WETH. However, this is only the case if their stake has been accruing.
Imagine the following two actions are taken in the same block:
• Deposit assets into GMX staking
• Call claimFees()
The result will be that claimFees() returns no WETH, but WETH is added to the account's asset list.
The same is true if a user performs the following three actions:
• Call claimFees()
• Withdraw all ETH from the WETH contract
• Call claimFees() again
A user can force their account into a state where it has WETH on the asset list, but doesn't actually hold any WETH.
This specific Impact was judged as Medium for multiple issues in the previous contest:
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the GMX Reward Router's claimFees workflow, where the RewardRouterController unconditionally reports that a call to claimFees will deliver WETH regardless of whether any fees have actually accrued. The controller's canCallClaimFees function always returns a tuple containing the WETH address, signalling that the caller should receive WETH. When a user invokes claimFees in a situation where no fees are due—such as immediately after depositing assets in the same block, or after withdrawing all WETH from the WETH contract and then calling claimFees again—the function returns zero WETH. Nevertheless, the AccountManager logic later adds the token to the account's asset list based solely on the controller's token list, without checking the account's actual token balance. As a result, the user's account records WETH as an owned asset while the on‑chain balance of WETH for that account remains zero. This discrepancy is exploitable: an attacker can deliberately trigger a claimFees call under fee‑less conditions to pollute the asset list with a zero‑balance token, potentially confusing UI displays, breaking accounting assumptions, and causing downstream contracts that rely on accurate asset enumeration to behave incorrectly. The impact is classified as medium because the immediate loss of funds does not occur, but the inaccurate accounting can lead to mis‑reporting, faulty risk calculations, or future integration bugs as the protocol expands. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the Reward Router and AccountManager interaction, where the auditor observed that the asset‑list update routine did not verify token balances before insertion. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the transaction succeeds, and the only symptom is the presence of a token with a zero balance, which may be overlooked in routine testing. The proper fix is to modify the _updateTokensIn function (and its invocation order) so that a token is added to an account's asset list only if the account's balance for that token is greater than zero. This change eliminates the creation of “fake” assets and restores consistency between the on‑chain token balances and the accounting metadata, thereby preserving the integrity of risk assessments and UI representations.

title: No check if Arbitrum L2 sequencer is down in
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing verification of the Arbitrum L2 sequencer status when the GLPOracle contract reads a Chainlink price feed. The oracle function getEthPrice only checks that the reported timestamp is not older than one day and that the price value is positive, but it does not query the Chainlink sequencer status feed that indicates whether the L2 sequencer is currently operational. On Arbitrum, when the sequencer is down the data feed may continue to return a price that appears fresh because the timestamp is still recent, yet the price can be stale or even deliberately manipulated by an attacker controlling the off‑chain data source. Because the contract assumes the price is reliable, a malicious actor can exploit the sequencer downtime to submit a price that is higher than the true market value, allowing borrowers to obtain larger loans than they should be able to collateralise, or submit a lower price to prevent liquidations of under‑collateralised positions. The impact is therefore a distortion of the protocol’s accounting logic: users may receive more funds than intended, or avoid liquidation when they should be liquidated, breaking the economic guarantees of the lending system. The condition occurs whenever the Arbitrum sequencer experiences an outage and the contract does not perform the required sequencer‑up check. It affects any participant that relies on the GLPOracle for price information, including lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the implementation against Chainlink’s recommended pattern for L2 feeds. It is subtle because the existing stale‑price check passes – the timestamp is still within the allowed window – so developers may not notice that the price is effectively unreliable. To remediate, the contract should incorporate the Chainlink sequencer status feed and revert when the sequencer is reported as down, following the example code in the Chainlink documentation. This change restores the assumption that price data is fresh and trustworthy, re‑aligning the protocol’s accounting with its intended risk model and preventing attackers from exploiting sequencer outages to manipulate loan terms or liquidation outcomes.

title: PreviewRedeem may under-price the value of
description:
previewRedeem will return an incorrect result based on address(0)
If you get the partnership the fee changes, the address could change the value
This may enable: Unfairer (bps wise), liquidations when they shouldn't happen, also will enable marginally higher profit for liquidators as they may be able to benefit from the reduction of the fee
A user may get liquidated earlier, and the accounting would be incorrect
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the previewRedeem view function, which calculates the amount a user would receive when redeeming their position. The function mistakenly bases part of its fee calculation on the zero address (address(0)) instead of using the actual account or partnership address that determines the applicable fee. When a partnership’s fee changes, the zero‑address placeholder causes the preview to return a value that is lower than the true redemption amount. This under‑pricing can lead to several adverse outcomes: users may appear to be under‑collateralised and be liquidated earlier than warranted, liquidators can obtain a marginally higher profit because the fee reduction inflates the perceived liquidation incentive, and the protocol’s internal accounting becomes inconsistent with the real economic state. The issue manifests only when previewRedeem is called for a partnership whose fee has been altered, and the contract relies on address(0) as a fallback for fee lookup. Because previewRedeem is a read‑only function, the discrepancy is not immediately visible on‑chain and may only be observed through mismatched UI displays or unexpected liquidation events. The flaw was identified during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noted that the logic does not correctly reference the caller’s account to determine the fee tier. Detecting the problem can be difficult because the function does not modify state and the incorrect values may be subtle, especially when the fee change is small. To remediate the issue, the fee lookup should be performed using the actual partnership or user account context rather than a hard‑coded zero address, ensuring that the preview calculation reflects the true fee schedule and preserves the protocol’s accounting invariants. This class of bug falls under incorrect fee‑parameter handling and price‑preview miscalculation, which can cause funds to disappear from a user’s perspective, refunds to be lower than expected, and overall trust in the protocol’s liquidation logic to be eroded.

title: Risk with Liquidation
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the liquidation function transfers the vault token (pvGLP) to the liquidator using transferFrom, but the subsequent redemption of that token is gated by an approval check that only allows whitelisted addresses, active partners, or direct EOAs (msg.sender == tx.origin). Because liquidators are typically contracts that are not whitelisted and not marked as active partners, the redemption call reverts with UNAUTHORIZED, leaving the liquidator unable to convert the received pvGLP into underlying assets. This situation can occur during periods of high volatility when a vault becomes under‑collateralized and the protocol relies on third‑party liquidators to restore solvency. The impact is that liquidations may be delayed or fail, causing the vault to remain unsafe, potentially leading to loss of funds for depositors or the protocol. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the liquidation flow, where the author noticed that the internal _isEligibleSender check restricts redemption to a narrow set of callers. The problem is subtle because the liquidation transaction itself succeeds, giving the impression that the operation completed, while the follow‑up redemption silently fails, which may not be obvious from logs. To remediate, the redemption logic should either accept the liquidator as an authorized caller, use a pull‑based redemption that does not require the liquidator’s approval, or redesign the flow so that the protocol itself, rather than the liquidator, performs the final asset transfer. This class of bug falls under “authorization bypass in post‑liquidation redemption” or “restricted redemption after token sweep”. From a user perspective, a liquidator sees the vault token arrive in its balance but cannot claim the underlying assets, resulting in a zero payout despite a successful liquidation event. Depositors may notice that their vault remains under‑collateralized after a liquidation attempt, contrary to the expectation that the protocol automatically resolves the shortfall.

title: Tokens not owned by an account can be added
description:
In the controllers RewardRouterController, RewardRouterV2Controller and DNGMXVaultController the function canCall can return in tokenIn a token address that has actually not been received by the account. If the account did not have the token before, then the token is added to the asset list of the account even if the account does not hold the token at all.
• in RewardRouterController: in canCallCompound(), WETH is added to tokensIn but no tokens are sent to the account as a result of the call to the Reward Router's function compound()
• in RewardRouterV2Controller: in canCallRedeem() the token redeemed is added to tokensIn, but the router's function unstakeAndRedeemGlp() allows to send the tokens to a 3rd party receiver instead of the caller. In such a case, no tokens are sent to the account.
• in DNGMXVaultController: in canWithdraw() the token redeemed is added to tokensIn, but the DN GMX vault's functions redeemToken() and withdrawToken() allow to send the tokens to a 3rd party receiver instead of the caller. In such a case, no tokens are sent to the account.
There can be tokens in the list of assets of an account that the account doesn't own.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an asset‑list inflation bug that allows a user’s account to be recorded as holding a token that was never transferred to that account. The root cause lies in the controller contracts RewardRouterController, RewardRouterV2Controller and DNGMXVaultController, where the helper function canCall builds a list called tokensIn based on the assumption that the underlying router or vault call will always credit the caller with the token being processed. In reality the router’s compound function, the GLP unstakeAndRedeem function and the vault’s redeemToken/withdrawToken functions each accept an optional third‑party receiver address. When a caller invokes these functions through the controller, the token can be sent to an arbitrary address instead of the caller, yet canCall still adds the token’s address to the caller’s asset list. This mismatch can be triggered whenever a user executes a compound, redeem or withdraw operation that forwards the token to another address, for example when using a proxy contract, a relayer, or a malicious receiver. An attacker could deliberately specify a third‑party receiver to cause the caller’s asset list to contain a token with a zero balance. From a user’s perspective the UI may display that the account holds a certain token, while the actual balance shown on‑chain is zero, leading to confusion such as “my token appears in my portfolio but I cannot see any amount”. The impact is primarily an accounting inconsistency: downstream logic that relies on the asset list to decide eligibility, fee calculation or reward distribution may behave incorrectly, potentially allowing actions that should be blocked or causing mis‑reporting of portfolio values. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the controller logic, where the auditor noticed that canCall unconditionally pushes token addresses into tokensIn without verifying the post‑call balance. The bug is subtle because the token transfer itself succeeds, but the destination is not the caller, so standard balance checks elsewhere do not flag the problem. To remediate, the controller should either (1) require that the router/vault functions always credit the caller, removing the optional receiver parameter, (2) perform an explicit balance check after the external call and only add the token to tokensIn if the caller’s balance increased, or (3) redesign canCall to return only tokens that are guaranteed to be owned by the caller, eliminating the assumption that every invoked operation results in token receipt.

title: BalancedVault may unable to rebalance when makerLimit was decreased
description:
In _adjustPosition(), it is expected that makerLimit will always be greater than currentMaker. That should be the case in normal circumstances. However, the makerLimit can be changed by the productOwner at anytime. When the makerLimit is changed to a lower value, _adjustPosition will revert at L298 due to underflow.
https://github.com/equilibria-xyz/perennial-mono/blob/3d2c5f16fb4f65f25ecf1f2cb2a5f89448415beb/packages/perennial-vaults/contracts/BalancedVault.sol#L291-L299
The makerLimit can be changed by the productOwner at anytime:
https://github.com/equilibria-xyz/perennial-mono/blob/3d2c5f16fb4f65f25ecf1f2cb2a5f89448415beb/packages/perennial/contracts/product/UParamProvider.sol#L236-L23
bug_full: The BalancedVault contract contains a rebalancing routine called _adjustPosition that assumes the configurable parameter makerLimit will always be greater than the current amount of maker tokens (currentMaker). This assumption holds only while the makerLimit remains unchanged. However, the productOwner role is allowed to modify makerLimit at any time, including lowering it below the currentMaker value. When makerLimit is decreased, the arithmetic that calculates the new maker allocation underflows, causing the function to revert at line 298. The revert stops the rebalancing process, meaning the vault cannot adjust its exposure to the maker side. From a user perspective, deposits may appear to be accepted but later transactions fail, withdrawals may be blocked, and the vault may report a stale or zero balance for the maker side. The impact is that the vault can become stuck, preventing users from moving funds, and potentially leading to loss of confidence or capital being effectively frozen until the limit is raised again or the contract is upgraded. The issue manifests only when the productOwner reduces makerLimit while there is a non‑zero currentMaker position, a scenario that can occur during normal governance actions or malicious manipulation of the limit. It was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s state‑transition logic, where the auditor noted the unchecked reliance on makerLimit > currentMaker and verified that a lower limit triggers an underflow revert. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit a specific error message for the underflow, and the failure only appears during a rebalancing call, which may be infrequent, making it hard to notice in routine testing. Conceptually, the fix is to add explicit validation that makerLimit is not set below currentMaker, or to guard the arithmetic with safe‑math checks that handle the case where makerLimit < currentMaker, for example by capping the maker allocation to the new limit or by postponing rebalancing until the limit is increased. This class of vulnerability falls under improper handling of mutable configuration parameters that break invariant assumptions, leading to arithmetic underflow and denial‑of‑service conditions in financial smart contracts.

title: BalancedVault sophisticated active users may deposit or withdraw at the last minute before the new oracle version to escape loss or snatch profits
description:
The PNL of a position is settled every time a new price is posted.
The BalancedVault is designed to be split 50/50 between long and short, but the actual effective position sizes can be different. Therefore, every new price comes with a profit or loss.
When there is a significant amount of profit added to the holdings by the update, a sophisticated user can monitor the price update very closely, maybe even frontrun the price update transaction and deposit to the BalancedVault, and exit right after the update.
By doing so, the user would be able to take a portion of the profit.
Vice versa, if there is an upcoming price movement that causes a loss to the BalancedVault, the user would be able to escape the loss.
The root cause for this issue is that the strategy is asynchronous, but the vault is synchronous.
The pending PNL of the asynchronous strategy is predictable, which creates an opportunity for active users to use this knowledge against inactive users.
We are not including the Vault in this release as it needs a rewrite mainly due to issue M2.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a timing‑based profit‑extraction flaw in the BalancedVault contract. The vault settles the profit‑and‑loss (PNL) of its underlying asynchronous strategy every time a new price is posted by the oracle, but the settlement logic is executed synchronously within the vault’s deposit/withdraw functions. Because the pending PNL of the asynchronous strategy can be predicted from the upcoming price update, a sophisticated actor can monitor the pending oracle transaction, front‑run it, and manipulate their position around the exact moment the vault records the new PNL. In practice the attacker watches for a large positive price movement, deposits funds into the vault just before the price update transaction is mined, and then withdraws immediately after the update, thereby capturing a slice of the newly recorded profit that rightfully belongs to all vault participants. Conversely, when a price movement is expected to generate a loss, the attacker can withdraw before the update, escaping the loss while the remaining participants absorb it. This attack is possible whenever a significant price change is about to be posted, i.e., during the narrow window between the oracle’s price calculation and the vault’s synchronous PNL settlement. The affected parties are any users of the BalancedVault, especially passive investors who cannot react as quickly as the attacker; they may see their expected returns reduced or their balances unexpectedly lower. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the asynchronous nature of the strategy with the vault’s synchronous accounting and identified the predictable pending PNL as an exploitable surface. The flaw is hard to notice because the vault’s accounting appears correct after each update, and the profit taken by the attacker is indistinguishable from normal earnings; only a detailed timing analysis reveals the discrepancy. Conceptually, this is a front‑running race condition where deposit/withdraw actions can be timed around oracle updates to steal profit or avoid loss, violating the intended 50/50 long‑short risk sharing and the accounting assumptions that all participants share gains and losses proportionally. To remediate the issue the vault should be redesigned so that PNL settlement is decoupled from immediate user actions, for example by introducing a commit‑reveal scheme, a delay or lock‑up period for new deposits, or by making the strategy’s PNL calculation atomic with the vault’s state update, thereby preventing users from exploiting predictable pending PNL. In user‑facing terms, a user may notice that after depositing just before a price change they receive an unexpectedly high return, while other users see their balances shrink or their expected refunds disappear, indicating that the vault’s profit distribution logic can be gamed through precise timing.

title: (previously M-05)
description:
When there are multiple new phases at L63, they will all start with round.roundId.
As a result, sync() -> getRoundCount() will revert, as the startingRoundId of the last phase for the next phase can be larger than its latestRoundId.
https://github.com/equilibria-xyz/perennial-mono/blob/e801b6eecae6ca609597710d2980bd26184a2ef8/packages/perennial-oracle/contracts/ChainlinkFeedOracle.sol#L58-L76
https://github.com/equilibria-xyz/perennial-mono/blob/e801b6eecae6ca609597710d2980bd26184a2ef8/packages/perennial-oracle/contracts/types/ChainlinkAggregator.sol#L59-L76
poc:
Given:
Last phase: 3
Last phase startingRoundId: (uint256(3) << 64) + 1
Last phase latestRoundId: (uint256(3) << 64) + 3
Last phase startingVersion: 10
Current phase: 5
Current aggregator roundId: 1
Current proxy roundId: (uint256(5) << 64) + 1
L63, the first iterate:
The second iterate, L65 startingRoundId: (uint256(5) << 64) + 1;
ChainlinkAggregator.sol#L74, latestRoundId: (uint256(4) << 64) + 1;
ChainlinkAggregator.sol#L75, latestRoundId - startingRoundId will revert.
bug_full: The contract implements a Chainlink‑based price oracle that aggregates data from a Chainlink aggregator. Each time the underlying Chainlink aggregator moves to a new phase, the oracle stores a startingRoundId that encodes the phase number in the high 64 bits of the round identifier. The sync() function walks through the stored phases and calls getRoundCount() to determine how many rounds are available in the current phase. The calculation inside getRoundCount() subtracts the stored startingRoundId from the latestRoundId reported by the aggregator. When more than one new phase appears between two consecutive sync() calls, the stored startingRoundId for the newest phase is set to the roundId of that phase (for example (phaseId<<64)+1), while the latestRoundId reported by the aggregator still belongs to the previous phase (for example (previousPhaseId<<64)+N). Because the startingRoundId of the new phase is numerically larger than the latestRoundId of the previous phase, the subtraction underflows and the function reverts. This means that sync() cannot progress across multiple phase jumps, causing the oracle to stop updating its price feed. From a user perspective the protocol that relies on this oracle will see stale or missing price data, transactions that depend on fresh prices may fail, and funds that would be liquidated or settled based on the price may become stuck. The bug is triggered only when the Chainlink aggregator advances through two or more phases before the oracle’s sync() routine is invoked – a situation that is rare but possible during rapid network upgrades or when the off‑chain updater is delayed. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a proof‑of‑concept that constructs a scenario with a last phase (id 3) and a current phase (id 5) where the calculated round count overflows and the transaction reverts. The problem is subtle because normal operation with a single phase transition works correctly, so the failure does not appear in routine tests. To remediate the vulnerability the contract should validate the relationship between startingRoundId and latestRoundId for each phase, reject attempts to sync more than one phase at a time, or redesign the round‑count logic to correctly handle phase boundaries, for example by passing an explicit list of startingRoundIds and ensuring that latestRoundId is never smaller than its corresponding startingRoundId. By enforcing these checks the oracle will continue to update across phase changes without reverting, preserving the integrity of price data for all downstream users.

is lost because there is no such method in GMXFuturesPoolHedger to locked
ERC20 token.
The trader fee discount that is airdropped to the GMXFuturesPoolHedger contract
is lost because there is no such method in GMXFuturesPoolHedger to locked
ERC20 token.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing claim mechanism for referral rebates that GMX distributes to the GMXFuturesPoolHedger contract. When the contract creates an increase‑position request it passes a hard‑coded referral code (bytes32("LYRA")), which according to GMX’s referral program triggers a discount for the trader and a rebate that is paid to the referrer in ERC20 tokens (e.g., GMX, esGMX, or native ETH/AVAX). The GMX protocol therefore sends the rebate to the address of the GMXFuturesPoolHedger contract. However, the contract does not implement any function that allows an admin or any authorized party to withdraw or lock those ERC20 tokens. As a result, the rebate tokens become permanently stuck in the contract balance. The issue arises whenever a position is opened with the referral code, i.e., under normal operation of the protocol, and it affects the protocol’s revenue model because the expected referral fees never reach the treasury or the intended beneficiaries. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a discount was applied to the trade but the corresponding rebate balance remains zero, contradicting the expectation that a portion of the fees should be credited back. The problem was discovered during a manual audit review of the contract’s source code, where the absence of any claim or withdraw function was noted. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the tokens simply sit idle, and standard testing may not check the contract’s token balance after a rebate is sent. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “unclaimed token lock” or “missing withdrawal” vulnerabilities, where a contract receives external assets but lacks a safe path to transfer them out. To remediate, the contract should be extended with an admin‑only claim function that can transfer any ERC20 token held by the contract to a designated address, thereby allowing the protocol to retrieve the airdropped GMX trading fee refunds and any other stuck referral tokens. This change restores the intended economic flow, aligns the on‑chain accounting with the business logic of the referral program, and prevents future loss of rebate funds.

title: GMXFuturesPoolHedger uses payable.transfer
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the use of payable(msg.sender).transfer to return excess Ether to the caller in the GMXFuturesPoolHedger contract. Transfer forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas to the recipient, which is sufficient for a simple externally owned account but insufficient for most smart contract receivers that may need more gas to execute fallback or receive functions. When the caller is a contract, the transfer call can run out of gas and revert, causing the entire transaction to fail. As a result, the contract’s balance remains locked because the fallback logic that should return the funds never completes. This issue occurs whenever the contract attempts to send the entire remaining balance back to msg.sender after a hedge operation or after posting a collateral order, as shown in the two code snippets. The root cause is the reliance on Solidity’s transfer primitive, which imposes a hard‑coded gas limit and does not handle errors gracefully. An attacker or any user interacting through a contract can trigger the failure simply by being a contract address, leading to a situation where users expect a refund or excess collateral to be returned but receive nothing, and the UI may display a zero balance while the funds are still held by the pool. The impact is that funds become effectively unattainable for those contract users, breaking the accounting assumptions of the futures pool and potentially undermining trust in the protocol. The issue was identified during a manual audit that highlighted the unsafe pattern of using transfer for arbitrary recipients. It can be hard to notice because the failure manifests only when the recipient is a contract, which may not be exercised in basic testing with EOAs. The recommended remediation is to replace transfer with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas and checks the returned success flag, or to use OpenZeppelin’s Address.sendValue utility, which safely forwards Ether and reverts on failure. By adopting this pattern, the contract ensures that refunds are reliably delivered regardless of the recipient’s type, preserving the intended financial flows and preventing locked funds.

title: longScaleFactor for an expired board can be
bug_full: The vulnerability is a timing manipulation of the liquidity pool’s net asset value (NAV) that allows a board beneficiary to artificially inflate the longScaleFactor used for option settlements. The root cause lies in the way the contract updates the protectedQuote when processing queued deposits. When processDepositQueue() is called, the totalQueuedDeposits are reduced by the processed amount, but the protectedQuote is recomputed as (NAV + processedDeposits) multiplied by (DecimalMath.UNIT - lpParams.adjustmentNetScalingFactor). Because the adjustment factor is less than one, the protectedQuote is decreased by only a fraction of the processed deposit, while the NAV is increased by the full deposit amount. This creates a net increase in NAV that is not reflected in the protectedQuote, causing the subsequent calculation of liquidity.longScaleFactor to be higher than it should be. An attacker who can call the public functions processDepositQueue() and settleExpiredBoard() in the same transaction can front‑run a large initiateDeposit() call, process the deposit queue to boost NAV, and then settle the expired board while the inflated longScaleFactor is still in effect. The inflated factor is stored in scaledLongsForBoard and later multiplied with each long position’s amount during settlement, giving the attacker’s board a larger payout. Other boards that settle later, especially around withdrawal events where the protectedQuote reduction is smaller, receive a lower longScaleFactor and therefore a reduced payout. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that a beneficiary sees an unexpectedly high payout, while other participants see smaller or even zero payouts for otherwise identical positions. The impact is a zero‑sum redistribution of funds: the attacker’s board gains at the expense of other board settlements, effectively stealing value from them. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between deposit queue processing and board settlement logic. It is hard to notice because the NAV change is internal to the contract and the longScaleFactor is only observed later during settlement, making the manipulation subtle and not directly flagged by simple balance checks. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑inconsistent accounting” or “timing‑dependent scaling factor manipulation”. To remediate, the protocol should restrict processDepositQueue() and its counterpart processWithdrawalQueue() to a trusted keeper or a time‑locked mechanism, enforce a minimum interval (e.g., 24 hours) between queue processing and board settlement, and ensure that the protectedQuote adjustment mirrors the full impact of processed deposits and withdrawals so that NAV remains consistent for scaling calculations.

title: GMXFuturePoolHedger does not implement
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing payable receive fallback in the GMXFuturePoolHedger contract, which prevents the contract from accepting the execution fee that the GMX PositionRouter refunds when an increase‑or‑decrease‑position request is cancelled. The root cause is that the PositionRouter’s cancelIncreasePosition and cancelDecreasePosition functions call an internal helper that withdraws WETH to ETH and then uses the low‑level .send operation to transfer the execution fee to the address supplied by the caller – in this case the hedger contract. Because the hedger contract does not implement a receive() or payable fallback function, the .send call fails silently, returning false, and the contract simply discards the refunded fee. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; it is triggered automatically whenever a pending order is cancelled, for example when the keeper cannot meet the slippage constraints. The impact is that the execution fee, which is meant to be reimbursed to the hedger, is permanently lost, leading to a shortfall in the contract’s accounting and potentially reducing the funds available for future hedging operations. This shortfall may manifest to users as missing refunds, unchanged balances after a cancellation, or unexpected depletion of the contract’s ETH holdings. The issue occurs only under the condition that a pending increase or decrease request exists and the cancelPendingOrder function is called after the minimum cancellation delay has passed. The affected parties are the GMXFuturePoolHedger contract itself, its owners, and any protocol participants who rely on the hedger to manage positions and receive fee refunds. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s interface with the GMX documentation and observed that the refund path did not include a payable fallback, while the PositionRouter explicitly sends ETH. The bug is hard to notice because the .send operation does not revert on failure and the contract does not emit an event indicating the loss, so the transaction appears successful even though the fee is not received. To remediate the issue, the hedger contract should implement a receive() external payable {} (or a payable fallback) so that it can accept ETH transfers, and optionally check the return value of the .send call or use a safer transfer method. This change restores the intended refund flow, aligns the contract’s behavior with the GMX specification, and prevents silent loss of execution fees, thereby preserving the financial integrity of the hedging pool.

title: No check for active Arbitrum and optimistic
description:
The protocol wants to deploy Arbitrum and optimism
Chainlink recommends that all Optimistic L2 oracles consult the Sequencer Uptime
Feed to ensure that the sequencer is live before trusting the data returned by
If the Arbitrum Sequencer goes down, oracle data will not be kept up to date, and
thus could become stale. However, users are able to continue to interact with the
protocol directly through the L1 optimistic rollup contract. You can review Chainlink
docs on L2 Sequencer Uptime Feeds for more details on this.
As a result, users may be able to use the protocol while oracle feeds are stale. Then
outdated price can be used to settle trade.
If the Arbitrum or optimism sequencer goes down, the protocol will allow users to
continue to operate at the previous (stale) rates.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract does not verify that the Arbitrum or Optimism sequencer is active before using price data from the Chainlink L2 Sequencer Uptime Feed. The root cause is the absence of a check on the sequencer's uptime status; the contract reads the latestRoundData but never validates the answer or the timestamp. As a result, if the sequencer goes down, the feed stops updating and the contract continues to use the last reported price, which may be stale. An attacker or any user can then execute trades or settlements with outdated prices, causing trades to settle at rates that no longer reflect the market. This can lead to users receiving less value than expected, balances being reduced unexpectedly, or funds being transferred at a disadvantageous rate. The condition occurs whenever the L2 sequencer experiences downtime longer than the grace period defined by the protocol; the contract does not block operations during that window. The affected parties include any user interacting with the protocol on the affected L2, as well as the protocol itself because its accounting assumptions are violated. The issue was identified during a security audit that reviewed the integration with Chainlink L2 feeds and noted the missing sequencer availability guard. It is easy to miss because the contract functions normally when the sequencer is up, and the stale price may not be obvious until a significant market move occurs. The bug belongs to the class of oracle availability checks missing, where external data sources are trusted without confirming their freshness. From a user perspective the UI may show a normal price feed, but after a sequencer outage the trade execution may result in a zero or unexpectedly low refund, or a balance that appears to have vanished. The recommended fix is to add a helper that reads the sequencer's latestRoundData, checks that the answer indicates the sequencer is live and that the data timestamp is within an acceptable grace period, and revert the transaction with a specific error when the sequencer is unavailable. Implementing this check restores the protocol’s guarantee that only up‑to‑date price information is used for settlements.

title: canHedge() does not check short exposure nor
bug_full: The function canHedge() in the GMXFuturesPoolHedger contract is intended to act as a gatekeeper that decides whether the LiquidityPool may issue new options based on the available hedging capacity in the GMX Vault. The implementation checks the remaining base‑asset liquidity and compares it with the absolute difference between the expected hedge and the current hedge (absHedgeDiff). However, the logic only validates the long‑side depth and completely omits any verification of the short‑side depth. Moreover, the amount of options that are about to be sold (the amountOptions parameter) is never taken into account when calculating the required market depth. As a result, when the pool attempts to increase a short exposure – for example when expectedHedge is negative and deltaIncreasing is true – the function may still return true because the missing short‑side check does not detect that the vault lacks sufficient quote‑asset liquidity. This flaw allows the LiquidityPool to issue options under extreme market conditions where the underlying vault cannot provide the necessary hedge. An attacker or even a regular user can trigger the vulnerability simply by invoking the standard option‑issuance flow; the contract will believe hedging is possible and will mint the option, but later the pool will be unable to offset the position, leading to under‑collateralisation. The practical impact includes potential loss of user funds, missing refunds, or options that cannot be exercised, effectively causing balances to disappear or become zero after settlement. The issue manifests whenever the market depth buffer condition is evaluated only for the long side while the short side is stressed, especially when deltaIncreasing indicates a trade that expands a negative delta. All participants that rely on the pool – option buyers, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions that each issued option is backed by sufficient hedge are violated. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noted that the canHedge() routine does not reference the amountOptions argument and lacks a symmetric check for the short side. Because the function returns a simple boolean without any UI warning, the bug can be hard to notice; users see no error message and assume the pool is safely hedged. To remediate, the contract should perform an additional market‑depth verification for the short side by fetching the remaining quote‑asset amount from the GMX Vault, incorporate the pending option amount into the absHedgeDiff calculation, and ensure that both long and short exposures respect the configured marketDepthBuffer. This change restores the intended invariant that option issuance only proceeds when the vault can fully hedge the net delta, preventing the loss of funds and preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: Swap fees are not applied to collateralDelta
description:
Missing inclusion of swap fees can lead to inaccuracies in hedging when adjusting
long positions on GMX.
_collectSwapFees() is used to calculate the swap fee and deduct it from the token
output amount in the GMX Vault contract on line 545. GMXFuturesPoolHedger does
not include the swap fee when it calculates the collateralDelta for long positions
in _decreasePosition() and _increasePosition().
GMXFuturesPoolHedger does not accurately adjust the hedge position.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an accounting omission where the swap fee charged by the GMX vault is not taken into account when the GMXFuturesPoolHedger computes the collateralDelta for long positions. The contract calls _collectSwapFees to determine the fee and deduct it from the token output amount, but the hedger’s _increasePosition and _decreasePosition functions calculate the collateralDelta without subtracting this fee. As a result the hedge position is adjusted with a slightly higher collateral amount than it should be. This mis‑calculation occurs every time the hedger creates or reduces a long position through the PositionRouter, i.e. during normal rebalancing of the pool. The root cause is a missing reference to the fee value in the collateralDelta formula, a logical flaw discovered during a manual audit of the code base. Because swap fees are typically a small percentage, the error does not produce an obvious overflow or revert, making it hard to notice in routine testing; the balances appear correct on a per‑transaction basis but drift over time, leading to cumulative over‑collateralisation or under‑collateralisation. From a user perspective the symptoms may include unexpected slippage, lower net returns, or positions being liquidated earlier than expected, as the protocol believes more collateral is available than actually is after fees. The impact is medium severity: inaccurate hedging can erode pool profitability, expose liquidity providers to loss, and undermine confidence in the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue violates the business logic that the net amount received by the vault after fees must equal the amount used as collateral for the hedge. To remediate, the swap fee should be subtracted from the collateralDelta before invoking createIncreasePosition or createDecreasePosition on the PositionRouter, ensuring that the fee is reflected in the net collateral transferred. This aligns the hedger’s accounting with the vault’s fee model and restores correct hedge sizing.

title: GMXFuturesPoolHedger's getHedgingLiquidity()
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that reports hedging liquidity for the futures pool. It calculates pending delta liquidity based on a theoretical model that assumes the current hedge position is already at the target leverage and that market prices are static. The root cause is that the calculation does not incorporate the mark‑to‑market value of the existing hedge, ignoring any unrealized profit or loss and any drift in leverage that occurs as the market moves. Consequently, the pendingDeltaLiquidity value can be significantly higher or lower than the actual amount of free quote assets that are truly available for new hedges. When the protocol uses this inflated figure to decide whether a new option position can be opened, it may allow positions that cannot be subsequently hedged because the real free liquidity is insufficient. An attacker or a regular user can exploit this by opening large positions during periods of substantial unrealized P&L on the hedge; the contract will report enough liquidity, the trade will be accepted, and later the hedge will fail, leaving the pool exposed to delta‑originated losses. The impact can be severe: the pool may become under‑collateralised, users may receive no payout, balances can appear to disappear, and in extreme cases the protocol could become insolvent. The condition occurs whenever the hedging position accrues unrealised gains or losses, when leverage parameters change, or when market prices shift between the time the theoretical liquidity is computed and the time it is used. All participants that rely on the pool – liquidity providers, option traders, and end‑users – are affected because the protocol’s risk‑control mechanisms are bypassed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of liquidity calculations and identified a mismatch between the theoretical values and the actual NAV after accounting for unrealised P&L. It is hard to notice because the UI shows a non‑zero pendingDeltaLiquidity and the contract emits no error, giving the impression that sufficient funds are available, while internally the freeLiquidity metric is already exhausted. To remediate, the contract should compute hedging liquidity using mark‑to‑market values of the current hedge, i.e., include the realised and unrealised P&L and any leverage drift, so that pendingDeltaLiquidity accurately reflects the true amount of quote assets that can be allocated to new hedges. This adjustment restores the intended risk‑management guarantees and prevents positions from being opened that the pool cannot safely hedge.

title: New SHORT_CALL_QUOTE positions hedging
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect interpretation of the delta direction when opening SHORT_CALL_QUOTE positions in the futures pool hedger. The pool’s canHedge function receives a boolean flag called deltaIncreasing that indicates whether the trade will increase the pool’s net delta. For a short call sold against quote collateral the pool delta actually increases, because the pool acquires a call option with positive delta regardless of the collateral type. However, the openPosition flow passes false for this flag when calling sendShortPremium, treating the operation as if it were decreasing delta. The canHedge logic contains a shortcut that returns true when !deltaIncreasing && expectedHedge >= 0, which is satisfied for SHORT_CALL_QUOTE trades even though the expected hedge is positive and the pool delta is growing. As a result the hedging capacity check that would normally compare the required hedge against the pool’s available base asset liquidity is bypassed. Consequently a user can open a SHORT_CALL_QUOTE position of any size, even when the pool does not have enough base asset to hedge the added delta. The protocol may therefore become partially unhedged, effectively selling naked call options. This exposure can generate rapid, delta‑driven losses across the entire protocol because the hedge cannot be performed later. The flaw manifests every time a user calls openPosition for a SHORT_CALL_QUOTE option, which internally invokes _routeLPFundsOnOpen, sendShortPremium and _checkCanHedge with the wrong deltaIncreasing value. All participants that rely on the pool’s hedging guarantees – liquidity providers, option holders and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the hedging logic, where the relationship between option type, collateral type and delta direction was examined and found to be inverted. It is subtle because the transaction succeeds without a revert, making the problem invisible to users until the pool’s balance shows unexpected losses or the hedge buffer is exhausted. The bug belongs to the class of risk‑management logic errors where a sign or flag is mis‑applied, leading to an incorrect eligibility check for hedging. From a user perspective the symptoms are that a short call quote trade appears to execute normally, but later the pool may report missing funds, zero hedge capacity, or unexpected loss of collateral, contradicting the expectation that the protocol will always be able to hedge sold options. The proper fix is to pass true for deltaIncreasing when the option being sold is a call, regardless of whether the collateral is quote or base, or to redesign the canHedge function to compute the delta impact from the option type instead of relying on an external flag, thereby ensuring that the hedge capacity check is always performed for SHORT_CALL_QUOTE positions.

title: [WP-M1] getRewards() can be triggered by
description: ConvexRewardPool#getReward(address) can be called by any address besides the owner themself. The reward tokens will only be added to the assets list when getReward() is called.
