To remediate the issue, the protocol should stop enforcing the MAX_RESOURCE_LIMIT constraint at the L1 entry point and instead enforce ordering and gas limits within the L2 sequencer, or redesign the metering so that buying the maximum gas incurs a cost that is significantly higher than a typical user’s deposit. This would restore the intended censorship‑resistance property and prevent cheap front‑running attacks that cause bridge deposits to revert.

title: contract with only IOptimismMintableERC20 in-
description:
If a custom contract implements only the IOptimismMintableERC20, but no the ILegacyMintableERC20, the contract is not compatible with the StandardBridge, as the bridge uses the l1Token function from the legacy interface implementation of OptimismMintableERC20 using the interface IOptimismMintableERC20.

Also, the StandardBridge, which uses the OptimismMintableERC20 has _isOptimismMintableERC20 function, which checks whether the given token address is implementing OptimismMintableERC20. The function will be true if either of token implements only one of the interfaces, it will return true.

However, if the given token passes the _isOptimismMintableERC20, the legacy function l1Token will be called on the token. If the token does not implement the legacy interface, the call will fail.

Therefore, the token which only implements IOptimismMintableERC20, but not the ILegacyMintableERC20, is not compatible with StandardBridge.

Any custom contract without l1Token function will not be compatible with StandardBridge
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the token interface that a custom ERC20 contract implements and the expectations of Optimism's StandardBridge. A token that implements only the IOptimismMintableERC20 interface does not provide the legacy l1Token function defined in ILegacyMintableERC20. The bridge contains a helper called _isOptimismMintableERC20 that returns true if the token implements either of the two interfaces, not necessarily both. When the helper returns true for a token that implements only the new interface, the bridge proceeds to call the legacy l1Token function on the token. Because the function is absent, the external call reverts, causing the bridging transaction to fail. This incompatibility can be exploited unintentionally: an attacker could deploy a token that pretends to be Optimism‑mintable but lacks the legacy function, causing any user attempting to deposit or withdraw through the StandardBridge to experience a revert and potentially see their balance unchanged while believing the operation succeeded. The impact is that users cannot move the affected token across L1 and L2, leading to a perception that funds have disappeared or that refunds are missing. The issue occurs whenever a token contract is registered with the bridge and only the new interface is present; it does not depend on specific input values, but on the presence or absence of the legacy function. Developers of custom tokens, users of those tokens, and the bridge operator are all affected because the bridge will reject the token at runtime despite passing the initial interface check. The problem was discovered during a logical audit of the bridge’s token validation code, where the auditor noted that the interface detection logic does not enforce the presence of both required functions. The bug is subtle because the contract compiles without errors and the interface check returns true, so the failure only appears at execution time, making it hard to notice without targeted testing. To remediate the issue, the bridge’s _isOptimismMintableERC20 function should be tightened to require that a token implements both IOptimismMintableERC20 and ILegacyMintableERC20, or the bridge should conditionally call l1Token only after confirming the legacy interface is present. Alternatively, token developers can add a minimal ILegacyMintableERC20 implementation that returns the correct L1 token address, ensuring compatibility with the StandardBridge.

title: Can get around hats per level constraints us-
description:
Each hat has the ability to mint 2^16 = 65,536 direct children. The id of the next child to be minted is saved in _hats[_admin].lastHatId and is incremented with each new child created. Once it hits 65,536, no more children can be created, as // use the overflow check to constrain to correct number of hats per level. However, this check can be bypassed by using phantom levels. The basic idea is that there is nothing stopping an admin from creating a new hat and setting the admin to a non-existent path, using intermediate hatIds of 0 to accomplish this.
Here's an example to make it more concrete:
• I am a topHat with domain 0x00000001
• I have created all 65,536 possible children (0x1.0001 to 0x1.ffff)
• But nothing is stopping me from setting 0x1.0000.0001 as the admin and continuing to create hats
• This hatId cannot possible exist (because no hatId immediately following a 0000 can actually be minted)
• Therefore, it is functionally the same as having 0x1 as the only admin
• This user can then continue to create children from 0x1.0000.0001.0001 to 0x1.0000.0001.ffff
• This can be repeated at each level, creating the ability to have unlimited direct children
The constraints around the number of direct descendants that an individual hat can have can be easily violated.
A simple change to the targetThreshold fails to propagate through to the safe's threshold, which causes all transactions to revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the hierarchical hat system where each hat is allowed to mint at most 2^16 (65,536) direct child hats. The contract stores the identifier of the next child to be minted in a mapping called _hats[_admin].lastHatId and increments this counter on each creation. When the counter reaches the maximum, an overflow check is intended to stop further minting at that level. However, the check only validates the counter for the immediate admin and does not verify that every element of the admin path actually corresponds to an existing hat. Because there is no requirement that each intermediate hat in the path have a positive maxSupply (i.e., be a real hat), an admin can create a new hat and deliberately set its admin to a non‑existent path that contains zero‑filled segments (for example, 0x1.0000.0001). This “phantom hat” does not exist in the hierarchy, but the contract treats the supplied admin address as valid and permits minting children under it. By repeating this trick at each level, the attacker can bypass the 65,536 direct‑children limit indefinitely, effectively creating an unlimited number of hats. The exploit proceeds as follows: (1) the attacker, who holds top‑level admin rights, mints all 65,536 children of a legitimate top hat; (2) the attacker creates a new hat and sets its admin to a fabricated identifier that includes a zero segment, which the contract does not reject; (3) the contract accepts the new admin and allows the attacker to mint another full set of 65,536 children under this phantom hat; (4) steps 2‑3 are repeated recursively, yielding an unbounded supply of hats. This breaks the core business assumption that each hat can only have a bounded number of direct descendants, leading to potential governance dilution, spam attacks, excessive gas consumption, and denial‑of‑service conditions for any component that relies on the hierarchical limit. The flaw manifests whenever an authorized admin can specify an arbitrary admin path during hat creation, which is typical in the contract’s design. All participants that depend on the hat hierarchy – including regular users, governance mechanisms, and downstream contracts – are affected because the system’s accounting and weight calculations become unreliable. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the admin‑validation logic and noticed the absence of a check for the existence of each hat in the path. It is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an obvious error; instead it silently permits creation of hats with identifiers that never existed, making the problem hard to detect from the UI or simple transaction logs. The recommended remediation is to augment the isAdminOfHat() function (or equivalent) with a verification that every hat along the supplied admin path has a positive maxSupply, ensuring that only real hats can be used as administrators. Additionally, the logic that reconciles the safe’s threshold should be corrected so that any change to the targetThreshold is properly propagated, preventing unintended reverts. By enforcing these checks, the protocol regains its intended bounded‑children property and restores confidence in its governance model.

title: If signer gate is deployed to safe with more
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic error in the HatsSignerGate deployment routine that assumes a Gnosis Safe can have at most five existing modules. When the gate is attached to a safe that already contains more than five modules, the constructor queries the safe with getModulesPaginated(...,5) and records the length of the returned array as the number of existing modules. Because the pagination limit truncates the list, the recorded count is lower than the actual number of modules. The gate then stores enabledModuleCount = recordedCount + 1 and later, during each transaction, it recomputes a hash of the first enabledModuleCount modules and compares it with a hash that includes enabledModuleCount+1 modules. The extra module that was omitted earlier causes the two hashes to differ, triggering a revert with SignersCannotChangeModules. As a result, every transaction submitted through the safe reverts, effectively freezing the safe and preventing signers from moving funds. The issue manifests only when the safe already has more than five modules at the moment the gate is attached; a fresh safe or one with five or fewer modules works as intended. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the HatsSignerGate contract, where the auditor noticed the hard‑coded pagination limit and the mismatch in module counting logic. It is hard to notice because the deployment does not emit a warning and the contract documentation only contains a comment advising against attaching the gate to a safe with more than five modules, without enforcing it programmatically. The vulnerability belongs to the class of pagination‑related state‑mismatch bugs that lead to denial‑of‑service conditions. From a user perspective, the UI will show transactions failing with a generic revert, balances remaining unchanged, and no obvious indication that the problem is a module‑count overflow. The expected behavior is that a transaction executes and updates the safe’s state; the actual behavior is an immediate revert, leaving funds locked. The proper mitigation is to add an explicit check during deployment that queries the safe for more than five modules and reverts if the count exceeds the safe limit, thereby preventing the gate from being attached to an incompatible safe. This enforcement eliminates the mismatch and restores normal operation.

title: attacker can perform malicious transactions
bug_full: The vulnerability is a flawed reentrancy guard in the safe's execTransaction flow. The contract maintains a counter _guardEntries that is incremented in checkTransaction and decremented in checkAfterExecution. The intention is that the counter should be non‑zero during execution, preventing a second call from bypassing the guard. However, the logic increments the counter before the external call and decrements it after, and the decrement is performed unconditionally. An attacker can craft a sequence of nested transactions that cause the counter to be incremented twice but decremented only once, leaving the guard at a non‑zero value while the internal guard address has been overwritten to zero. By first submitting a transaction (Tx1) that sets the guard address to zero and then, within the same execution, calling execTransaction on a second transaction (Tx2) that restores the guard, the attacker can execute Tx2 while the guard check believes the contract is still protected. Because the guard value is temporarily zero, the safe permits the second transaction to run without the intended protection, allowing the attacker to modify the threshold, move funds, or perform other malicious actions. The issue occurs only when a re‑entrant call is made during execTransaction; normal single‑step executions appear safe. Users may notice that a transaction that should have been rejected proceeds, or that funds are transferred without proper signature verification. The bug belongs to the class of reentrancy guard mis‑implementation where the entry/exit counters are not symmetrically updated under nested calls. It was discovered during a manual audit of the guard module by checking the arithmetic of _guardEntries and testing re‑entrancy scenarios. The problem is subtle because the counter does not underflow, so the guard does not trigger an error, making the flaw easy to miss in basic testing. The recommended fix is to invert the counter updates: decrement the guard in checkTransaction and increment it in checkAfterExecution, or otherwise ensure that the guard state cannot be altered to zero during a nested call. This change guarantees that any re‑entrant execTransaction will always see a non‑zero guard and will be blocked, preserving the intended security guarantees.

title: Owners can be swapped even though they
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the HatsSignerGateBase contract where the post‑execution verification routine (checkAfterExecution) does not validate that the set of safe owners remains unchanged after a multisig transaction. Because the contract only checks that certain module variables have not been altered, a group of colluding signers can exploit the missing owners check by invoking a delegatecall to a malicious contract that performs a swapOwner operation. The swapOwner function is normally guarded by a loop that only permits replacement of an owner whose signer hat is no longer active; however, by executing the swap through a delegatecall after the main transaction has completed, the guard is bypassed. This allows the attackers to replace legitimate owners with cooperating signers while the original signers still retain their hats, effectively hijacking the ownership set without triggering any revert or explicit error. The impact is that the multisig security model is broken: unauthorized parties can gain control over the safe, approve further transactions, and potentially drain funds or alter protocol parameters. The issue manifests only after a transaction has been executed, so users observing the UI may see the list of owners change unexpectedly, or notice that proposals are approved by signers who should not have authority. The affected parties include any protocol or DAO that relies on HatsSignerGateBase for owner management, as well as the funds protected by the safe. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the contract’s state‑validation logic and identified the absence of an owners comparison step. It is difficult to notice because the contract does not emit an event or revert when owners are swapped, and the existing checks give a false sense of safety. To remediate, the contract should perform a pre‑flight snapshot of the owners array and compare it to the post‑flight state, rejecting any transaction that alters the owner set, analogous to the existing module‑state checks. This class of bug can be described as an insufficient post‑execution state validation or ownership‑swap bypass, where business logic assumes immutability of critical governance participants but fails to enforce it programmatically. Users may experience symptoms such as “my DAO’s owner list changed without my action” or “proposals are being approved by unknown signers”, indicating that the underlying accounting of signer rights has been violated.

title: middle level admins can steal child trees be-
description:
In normal scenario middle level admins can't relink a child tree to another tree and when code link a tree it checks that the old and new admin is in the same tree(have same tippy hat). But middle level admins can bypass this buy using unlink logic.
A middle level admin can perform this actions: (x -> y) means x is admin of y (y linked to x)
1. Suppose we have this tree: Root0 (admin0) -> H1 (Admin1) -> H2 (Admin2) -> Root3 (Admin3) -> H4 (Admin4). (H1, H2, H4 are hats and Root0 is tophat and Root3 is "root tree")
2. Now Admin2 wants to remove (Root3 -> H4) tree from higher level admins(Admin1) access.
3. Admin2 would create new TopHat Root1 and link it to H2. (H2 -> Root1).
4. Now Admin2 would change the link of Root3 from H2 to Root1 by calling relinkTopHatWithinTree(Root3, Root1). Because Admin2 is admins of the H2 and both Root3 and Root1 is linked to the H2 so this action would be possible.
The tree would become: (Root0 -> H1 -> H2 -> Root1 -> Root3 -> H4)
5. Now Admin2 would call unlinkTopHatFromTree(Root3) and unlink Root1 from Root0 tree. Because Admin2 created Root1 he would become admin of the Root1 and would be only one that have admin access to Root3. (Root1 -> Root3 -> H4)
Simple unlinking can't always make middle level admin to be new admin so middle level admin should perform one relink and then unlink.
Middle level admin can steal the child trees and become the solo admin of them.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass in the hierarchical admin system that manages "hats" (sub‑trees) within a protocol. The contract enforces that a relink operation may only connect two trees when the old and new administrators belong to the same parent tree, and that an unlink operation may be called by any admin of the target tree. Because the checks do not verify that the caller is the top‑level (tippy‑hat) administrator, a middle‑level admin can combine a relink followed by an unlink to detach a child subtree and become its sole administrator. The root cause is insufficient access‑control validation in the functions relinkTopHatWithinTree and unlinkTopHatFromTree: they only confirm tree membership, not the caller’s hierarchical position. An attacker (a middle‑level admin) can first create a new top‑hat node, relink the target child tree to this new node (which is allowed because both trees share the attacker’s current admin), and then unlink the child tree from the original hierarchy. After these steps the attacker is the only admin of the stolen subtree, effectively stealing control of any permissions, assets, or governance rights that reside under that subtree. This can be exploited whenever a middle‑level admin has the ability to invoke both relink and unlink functions, which is typical in normal operation of the protocol. The impact is that the original higher‑level admins lose exclusive control over the affected child trees, potentially leading to unauthorized asset transfers, permission changes, or governance actions. Users of the protocol may notice that previously managed hats disappear from their admin view, that they can no longer perform actions on certain sub‑trees, or that balances and permissions under those hats behave unexpectedly (e.g., “my admin panel shows no access to a subtree I used to control”). The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logical flow of tree manipulation functions. It is hard to notice because each individual function appears to enforce a same‑tree rule, giving a false sense of safety; only the combination of two calls creates the bypass. To remediate, the contract should enforce that only the top‑level (tippy‑hat) admin can perform unlink operations, and that relink operations may only move a subtree upward toward the top‑level admin, not laterally to a sub‑level tree owned by the caller. In other words, the access control must be tightened to require the caller to be the highest authority in both the source and destination trees, preventing middle‑level admins from hijacking child trees.

title: Unbound recursive function call can use un-
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded recursive traversal of a hierarchical hat structure that can cause unlimited gas consumption and eventual out‑of‑gas reverts. The contracts maintain a tree of hats where each hat may be linked to a parent hat in another tree. Functions that need to resolve administrative rights, image URIs, top‑level domains or circular‑link checks walk up this tree by calling themselves recursively or looping without any hard limit on the depth of the hierarchy. Because the recursion depth is directly proportional to the number of linked hats, an attacker or even a legitimate administrator can create a very deep chain – for example linking two trees each containing a thousand hats – which pushes the total depth to two thousand levels. When a user invokes a view or state‑changing function that relies on this traversal, the EVM must execute a number of calls proportional to the depth. If the depth exceeds the gas that can be supplied in a single transaction, the call runs out of gas and reverts, leaving the contract in a broken state for the affected hats. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are a transaction that simply fails with an out‑of‑gas error, a UI that shows no image for a hat, or even a balance that appears unchanged or zero after an operation that should have transferred funds. The impact is that any action that depends on the recursive lookup – such as checking whether an address is an admin of a hat, fetching metadata, or validating that no circular links exist – becomes impossible, effectively freezing functionality for those hats and potentially preventing legitimate fund movements. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the recursive logic and identified the lack of a depth guard. It is hard to notice because the functions work correctly for shallow trees and only fail when the hierarchy grows unusually large, a condition that may not be exercised in typical test scenarios. The flaw violates the core business assumption that hat look‑ups are inexpensive and that the hierarchy will remain shallow. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce a maximum allowed depth for any hat tree, maintain the current depth as state, and reject actions that would cause the depth to exceed this threshold. Additionally, the recursive algorithm could be replaced with an iterative approach that includes explicit gas‑budget checks, or the logic could be refactored to limit the number of external calls per transaction, thereby preventing unbounded gas consumption and ensuring that hat‑related operations remain usable regardless of tree size.

title: Usage of HSG for existing safe can brick safe
description:
The HatsSignerGateFactory allows for deployment of HSG / MHSG for existing safes. I believe the intention is to let the user call enableModule() and setGuard() on the safe after deployment with the HSG / MHSG address.
This can result in unmatching values of maxSigners in the HSG and number of valid signers of the safe. That will prevent further interaction with the safe rendering it unusable.
If a safe has 10 owners with valid hats, and a HSG / MHSG is deployed with a value of maxSigners < 10 and this HSG / MHSG is wired to the safe, the checks for validSignerCount <= maxSigners will revert in the HSG.
These checks are present in reconcileSignerCount and claimSigner. However reconcileSignerCount is a core function that is called by checkTransaction(), the pre-flight check on the safe transaction.
The safe will not be able to execute any transaction until the number of valid signers is lowered (some hat wearers give up their hats / some hats turns invalid ...)
bug_full: The issue originates from the HatsSignerGate (HSG) or its multi‑signer variant (MHSG) being deployable for an already existing Gnosis Safe without verifying that the module’s configured maximum number of signers (maxSigners) matches the current number of valid owners on the safe. The HSG contract enforces a rule that the count of valid signers must never exceed maxSigners; this rule is checked in functions such as reconcileSignerCount and claimSigner, which are invoked during the safe’s pre‑flight transaction validation (checkTransaction). When a safe that already has, for example, ten owners with valid hats is wired to an HSG instance whose maxSigners parameter is set to a lower value (e.g., eight), every subsequent transaction triggers the validation logic, the condition validSignerCount <= maxSigners fails, and the transaction reverts. Because the safe’s core transaction path always calls these checks, the safe becomes effectively unusable – no further transaction can be executed until the number of valid signers is reduced, which typically requires owners to lose their hats or otherwise become invalid, an event that may never occur. From a user’s perspective the safe appears to be “bricked”: the UI shows the safe as active, but any attempt to send funds, execute a module function, or even view a transaction status results in a silent failure or a revert error, leaving the balance locked and owners unable to perform expected actions such as withdrawals or upgrades. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit of the Hats protocol where the interaction between the factory‑deployed HSG and existing safes was examined. It is subtle because the deployment of the module itself succeeds and the mismatch only manifests later during transaction execution, making it easy to overlook during testing. The bug belongs to the class of configuration‑driven access‑control mismatches where a module’s internal limits are not reconciled with the host contract’s state, violating the accounting assumption that the safe’s signer set will always be within the module’s allowed range. To remediate, the contract should either allow the safe owner to adjust the maxSigners value after deployment or, preferably, include a safety check in the factory or enableModule flow that validates the module’s maxSigners against the current valid signer count before the module is attached. This ensures that the safe cannot be rendered inoperable by an improperly configured HSG instance.

title: The Hats contract needs to override the ERC1155.balan
bug_full: The Hats contract inherits the ERC1155 standard but only overrides the single‑token balance query (balanceOf) to enforce business rules: when a hat is inactive or a wearer is not eligible the function deliberately returns zero. The batch version of the query (balanceOfBatch) is left untouched and therefore reads the raw internal mapping _balanceOf directly, bypassing the eligibility checks. As a result, callers can obtain a non‑zero balance for a hat that the contract’s own logic treats as unavailable. This inconsistency can be exploited by an attacker who queries balanceOfBatch for his address and a hat ID that is inactive or for which he is ineligible; the function will return the stored token amount even though the single‑token view reports zero. Other contracts or off‑chain services that rely on balanceOfBatch for accounting, access control, or reward distribution may incorrectly assume the user holds a valid hat and grant privileges, transfer rights, or distribute funds. The impact is a violation of the protocol’s accounting assumptions, potential unauthorized actions, and user confusion because the UI (which typically uses balanceOf) shows no ownership while a batch query reveals a positive balance. The bug manifests only when the hat state is inactive or the wearer fails the eligibility test, and only for callers that use the batch interface; normal single‑token queries behave as intended. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the overridden functions against the ERC1155 base implementation. The issue is subtle because balanceOfBatch is rarely called directly and its implementation appears correct at a glance, making the discrepancy easy to miss. To remediate, the contract should override balanceOfBatch and apply the same _isActive and _isEligible checks for each (owner, id) pair, returning zero whenever the hat is inactive or the wearer is not eligible. This class of bug—partial overriding of inherited state‑exposing functions—creates inconsistent visibility of token balances and breaks the intended business logic of conditional ownership.

title: [Medium][Outdated State] _removeSigner in-
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the multi‑signer removal routine of the HatsSignerGate contract. The function that deletes a signer (_removeSigner) decides whether to decrement the stored signerCount based on a comparison between the number of currently valid signers (validSignerCount) and the previously recorded signerCount (currentSignerCount). The original logic uses an equality check (validSignerCount == currentSignerCount) to decide that the count should stay unchanged, otherwise it subtracts one. This approach fails when a signer that was previously inactive becomes active before another signer is removed. In that situation validSignerCount increases while currentSignerCount remains unchanged, causing the equality test to be false and the function to incorrectly reduce the signerCount by one. As a result the contract’s internal threshold – the number of signatures required to approve actions – is set to a lower value than the actual number of active signers. An attacker who can trigger the state transition (e.g., by re‑activating a dormant signer and then invoking removeSigner for a different signer) can cause the contract to accept fewer signatures than intended, potentially allowing unauthorized transactions or governance actions. The bug manifests only after a specific sequence of state changes, making it easy to miss during casual testing because the signer list appears correct at a glance. It was discovered during a formal audit of the Hats Protocol by the auditor Sherlock, who noted that the condition does not account for an increase in validSignerCount. From a user’s perspective the UI may still display three active owners, but the contract will only require two signatures, leading to unexpected approvals and possible loss of control over funds. The issue belongs to the class of accounting or state‑synchronisation bugs where on‑chain bookkeeping diverges from the logical model. The recommended fix is to replace the equality check with a greater‑than‑or‑equal comparison (validSignerCount >= currentSignerCount) or to recompute the signerCount directly from the current set of active signers, ensuring that the threshold always reflects the true number of valid signers.

title: If a hat is owned by address(0), phony signatures can be accepted
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the multisig contract validates signers through a hat‑ownership check. The contract recovers the signer address from each ECDSA signature using ecrecover and then calls isValidSigner, which ultimately checks whether the recovered address owns a specific hat by calling the Hats contract’s balanceOf function. Because ecrecover returns address(0) when presented with a malformed signature (for example a v value other than 27 or 28), the recovered address can be zero. The Hats contract’s balanceOf implementation does not guard against address(0); it simply reads the stored balance and, if the hat is marked active and the wearer is eligible, returns a positive balance. Consequently, if a hat is ever transferred to address(0) – whether intentionally for supply adjustments, accidentally during a burn, or through a mis‑mint – the balance lookup will report that address(0) “wears” the hat. The isValidSigner check therefore treats address(0) as a valid signer, allowing any attacker to craft a phony signature that resolves to address(0) and have it accepted as a legitimate approval. This breaks the intended majority‑of‑signers rule, enabling transactions to be executed with fewer than the required number of distinct owners. In a 2‑of‑3 configuration, a single malicious party could approve arbitrary transfers, effectively stealing funds. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the signature‑validation flow and noticed the well‑known ecrecover edge case combined with the lack of an address(0) guard in the hat‑ownership logic. It is subtle because a hat owned by address(0) is an unusual state that most developers do not anticipate, and the contract does not emit any warning or revert when such a balance is queried. From a user’s perspective, a transaction that should be rejected due to insufficient signatures is instead processed, leading to unexpected fund movement or loss. The bug belongs to the class of “invalid signer acceptance due to zero‑address ownership” and is related to improper input validation and off‑by‑one errors in owner‑management loops. To remediate, the countValidSignatures routine should explicitly reject a recovered signer of address(0), the Hats.balanceOf function should revert when the queried wearer is address(0) (mirroring OpenZeppelin’s ERC721 guard), and any loops that iterate over owner arrays should use the correct upper bound (i.e., iterate to ownerCount, not ownerCount‑1) to ensure all owners are examined. These changes restore the integrity of the multisig’s signature counting and prevent phantom signers from being accepted.

title: targetThreshold can be set below minThreshold
bug_full: The vulnerability arises because the contract permits the target threshold parameter to be set to a value lower than the already‑configured minimum threshold. When the minimum threshold is set, the code checks that it does not exceed the current target threshold, enforcing the invariant minThreshold <= targetThreshold. However, the complementary check is missing when the target threshold is later updated: the setter only verifies that the new target does not exceed the maximum number of signers, but it does not ensure that it remains at least as high as the existing minimum threshold. Consequently, an authorized caller can unintentionally or maliciously lower the target threshold below the minimum. When the contract later calls reconcileSignerCount() to synchronize the safe’s required number of signers, it writes this lower target value into the safe’s threshold. Because the safe now requires fewer signatures than the protocol’s defined minimum, any transaction that validates the minimum requirement will reject, causing all operations that depend on the safe to fail. From a user’s perspective this appears as transactions that never execute, error messages about insufficient signers, or a complete freeze of the protocol’s functionality, often with balances appearing unchanged while the system is effectively locked. The issue manifests only after the target threshold is changed after the minimum threshold has been set, and only if the caller does not perform an additional validation. Affected parties include protocol operators, signers, and end‑users who rely on the safe to move funds; funds may become inaccessible because no valid transaction can satisfy the mismatched thresholds. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the validation logic of the two setter functions and identified the asymmetric checks. It can be hard to notice in routine testing because the setter accepts the new value without reverting, and the failure only becomes visible later when a transaction is attempted and the safe rejects it. The root cause is an inconsistency in parameter validation: the contract enforces minThreshold <= targetThreshold when setting the minimum, but omits the reverse check when setting the target. The recommended remediation is to add a guard in the target‑threshold setter that ensures the new value is not less than the current minThreshold, keeping both checks symmetric. This class of bug belongs to parameter‑validation inconsistencies that break business‑logic invariants, leading to a state where accounting assumptions (minimum required signers) are violated and the protocol’s operation is effectively halted.

title: Changing hat toggle address can lead to unintended toggle
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the mechanism that controls whether a hat (a permission token) is active or inactive through a toggle address. A hat stores its current on/off status in local storage, while the toggle address – which can be either an externally owned account (EOA) or a contract – is responsible for updating that status. When the toggle address is a contract, it can change the status by returning a false value from its getHatStatus() function. However, the contract that manages hats does not automatically synchronize the local storage with the contract’s returned value. Consequently, if an admin changes the toggle address from a contract to an EOA without first invoking a function that forces a status check (such as checkHatToggle()), the local storage still reflects the previous true state. The admin may believe the hat is turned off because the contract toggle reported false, but after the address change the hat reverts to the stale true value, effectively turning the hat back on. This discrepancy can be exploited: a malicious actor can observe the admin’s transaction that changes the toggle address, then front‑run a transaction that relies on the hat being off, thereby using a hat that should be disabled. The impact is severe for any system that relies on hats for critical access control, such as multisignature wallets or governance modules, because an unintentionally re‑enabled hat can grant unauthorized signing rights or execution privileges. The issue manifests only when the toggle address is a contract that has changed its status without the admin explicitly syncing the state, and then the address is switched to an EOA. It is difficult to notice because the user interface may still display the hat as disabled, while the on‑chain state has silently flipped back to enabled after the address change. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the changeHatToggle() function and identified the missing synchronization step. To remediate, the changeHatToggle() implementation should invoke a status‑synchronization routine (e.g., checkHatToggle()) before overwriting the toggle address, ensuring that the latest status is recorded in local storage. More generally, the bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency vulnerabilities where external state changes are not reflected in internal storage before a critical configuration change, violating the expected accounting invariant that a permission’s status remains unchanged unless explicitly altered by the owner.

title: Owners of linked tophats cannot have eligibility changed
description:
Tophats that are linked to new admins are supposed to behave like normal hats, rather than tophats, but their eligibility variable will be permanently set to address(0). This turns off the badStanding functionality, which allows all owners of the hat to be immune to punishments from their admins.
When a Tophat is linked to a new admin, the assumption is that it will behave like any other immutable hat. From the docs:
a tophat that has been linked (aka grafted) onto another hat tree is no longer considered a tophat
However, while most hats are not able to have their toggle or eligibility set to the zero address (which is carefully checked against in createHat()), tophats will always have them set to the zero address.
Since these hats are immutable, even when they are linked, there is no way to change the values of these two variables. They are permanently set to address(0).
This is especially problematic for eligibility, as even the local value of badStandings that can be used if the event that there is no external contract is set in _processHatWearerStatus(), which can only be called if eligibility is either an EOA that calls setHatWearerStatus() or a contract that implements the IHatsEligibility interface.
This causes major problems for admins of linked tophats, as while they are expected to behave like other immutable hats, instead will not give the admin the privileges they need.
Admins controlling linked tophats cannot turn off the eligibility of wearers who misbehave, giving tophat owners extra power and breaking the principle that linked tophats are no longer considered tophats.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns hats that are designated as tophats and later linked (or grafted) onto a different hat tree. In the Hats protocol a tophat is created with its eligibility and toggle addresses permanently set to address(0) because tophats are immutable by design and the createHat function explicitly forbids non‑zero values for these fields. Documentation states that once a tophat is linked it should behave like any other immutable hat, losing its special tophat status. However, the implementation does not update the stored eligibility or toggle addresses after the link operation. As a result the eligibility variable remains address(0) forever, which disables the badStanding functionality that relies on a valid eligibility contract or an EOA to call setHatWearerStatus. Consequently, admins of a linked tophat cannot turn off the eligibility of wearers who misbehave, nor can they toggle the hat’s active state. From a user perspective an admin may invoke the expected admin functions, but the contract silently ignores the request, leaving misbehaving wearers still authorized and giving the tophat owners unintended extra power. The issue manifests whenever a tophat is grafted onto another hat tree; any subsequent attempt to modify eligibility or toggle will have no effect because the stored address is permanently zero. The affected parties are the admins of linked tophats, the hat wearers who should be punishable, and any protocol that relies on the badStanding mechanism for security or governance. The flaw was discovered during a security audit when the auditor compared the documented behaviour of linked tophats with the actual contract code and observed that the eligibility field never changes after linking. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the operation simply does nothing, leading developers to assume the function works as described. The root cause is an immutable configuration bug: the protocol treats the tophat’s eligibility and toggle as immutable even after the hat’s type changes, violating the intended privilege model. To remediate, the contract should allow a one‑time update of the eligibility and toggle addresses at the moment a tophat is linked, for example by introducing a configuration flag that permits these fields to be set once and cleared when the hat is unlinked. This change would restore the admin’s ability to enforce badStanding rules, align the implementation with the documented behaviour, and prevent privilege escalation where admins lose control over wearer eligibility.

title: Hats can be overwritten
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the hat creation routine that does not verify whether the supplied admin identifier already corresponds to an existing hat. When a child hat is instantiated with an admin that has not been created yet, the internal mapping stores the child entry under the future admin’s identifier. Later, when the missing admin is finally created, the same storage slot is reused and the child’s record is overwritten with the new admin data. Because the contract assumes that a hat, once created with immutable flags, cannot be altered, this overwrite allows an attacker who controls the admin hierarchy to modify properties of a supposedly immutable child hat – for example, increasing its maxSupply from 10 to 20. The exploit proceeds in four steps: (1) a child hat is created under a non‑existent admin with immutable settings; (2) the missing admin hat is created afterwards; (3) the same child identifier is created again, this time with different parameters; (4) the contract’s view function shows that the child hat ID is unchanged but its stored attributes (such as maxSupply) have been replaced. From a user’s perspective the expected behavior – a hat that cannot be changed after deployment – is violated; users may see the supply of a hat they thought immutable suddenly increase, leading to unexpected token minting or loss of scarcity, which can be leveraged to rug participants. The issue affects any wearer who can create hats in their subtree, the protocol’s accounting guarantees, and any downstream applications that rely on hat immutability. It was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a test that creates a child hat, then creates its admin, and finally re‑creates the child, confirming that the stored maxSupply changes. The bug is subtle because the mapping key collision is hidden by the hierarchical naming scheme, and developers may assume that the admin existence check is implicit. To remediate, the contract should enforce that an admin hat exists before it can be referenced as a parent, for example by requiring that the admin’s maxSupply (or another non‑zero field) is set, thereby preventing the creation of child hats under undefined admins and preserving the intended immutability guarantees.

title: Hats.uri function can be DOSed by providing large strings
description:
The Hats.uri function returns a JSON representation of a hat's properties.
The issue is that the length of the details and imageURI string can be so big that the function consumes more than the maximum amount of gas. This would cause the transaction to revert.
Also a malicious user can just make the length so big that the transaction becomes very expensive. This would cause unnecessary expenses to anyone calling the function which is basically a loss of funds.
The attack is only feasible on a low cost chain (so not on the ETH mainnet) because the attacker needs to set the large string which costs a lot of gas.
So let us consider Polygon which has a block gas limit of 30 million gas.
Furthermore I used this site to calculate the gas costs for the Polygon Network: https://www.cryptoneur.xyz/gas-fees-calculator
So in order to DOS the Hats.uri function we must make it consume >30m Gas.
It is not possible to set the details field to such a large string directly in one transaction because it would cost >30m Gas.
So we need to slowly increase the length of the details field using the Hats.changeHatDetails function.
Increasing the length by so much that the Hats.uri function consumes an extra 1m Gas costs at most 15m Gas (I tested this but obviously I cannot paste the code here because it would be ridiculously big).
At most we would have to spend 30 * 15m = 450m Gas to execute the attack.
Using the calculator I linked, this costs ~92 USD at the time of writing this.
This is within reach of an attacker. Also we must consider that gas prices may drop in the future.
So the attacker can DOS the Hats.uri function or cause anyone calling it to spend up to 30m Gas which is ~6 USD on Polygon.
Also the attacker can make the hat immutable after performing the attack such that the string cannot be changed anymore.
bug_full: The Hats contract exposes a public uri() function that builds a JSON string containing the hat's details and imageURI fields. Because the implementation does not enforce any upper bound on the length of these two strings, the amount of gas required to concatenate and return the JSON grows linearly with the total character count. On chains with relatively high block gas limits, such as Polygon (≈30 million gas per block), an attacker can repeatedly call the changeHatDetails() method to append small chunks to the details field, eventually inflating the stored string to a size that makes a single call to uri() exceed the block gas limit. When the oversized uri() is invoked, the transaction runs out of gas and reverts, effectively denying service to any user or off‑chain service that relies on the metadata endpoint. Even if the call does not revert, the gas cost can rise to several million units, translating to several dollars of expense for callers. The problem is rooted in the lack of input validation for unbounded string storage, a common class of denial‑of‑service vulnerability caused by unchecked data size in view‑type functions that nevertheless consume gas when executed on‑chain. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that measured gas consumption for increasingly large strings and identified the point where the gas usage surpasses the network’s block limit. It can be hard to notice because developers often assume that view functions are cheap and ignore the fact that they still consume gas when called from another contract or via a transaction. The impact is that legitimate users may see transactions fail with “out of gas”, may be charged unexpectedly high fees when fetching metadata, and the protocol may become unusable if the hat is later made immutable, locking in the oversized data. To remediate, the contract should enforce a reasonable maximum length for the details and imageURI fields at the point of modification, rejecting inputs that would cause excessive gas consumption, or alternatively store large assets off‑chain and reference them via a fixed‑size hash. This prevents the metadata function from being abused to drain gas or block access to hat information, preserving both economic efficiency and availability of the service.

title: Depositing GNS might revert before reaching
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical accounting error in the deposit routine of a GNS‑based vault contract. The function validates that the projected total amount of GNS after a new deposit does not exceed a hard‑coded ceiling (maxGNSDeposited) by checking totalAssets() + assets against the limit before any protocol fees are deducted. Because the fee subtraction (sendDepositFees) occurs only after the check, the contract may reject a deposit that would actually keep the net balance under the maximum once fees are accounted for. This mismatch can cause the transaction to revert with the message "GNS deposits more than max" even though the user’s effective deposit (assets minus fees) would be permissible. The bug manifests when the vault’s current assets are close to the threshold and any non‑zero fee is applied, a situation that is easy to miss during normal testing because most deposits succeed far from the limit. An attacker could deliberately push totalAssets() near the ceiling, then trigger a small deposit that, after fees, would be acceptable, but the premature check would cause the transaction to revert, effectively denying service to legitimate users and freezing new liquidity inflows. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on deposits, potential loss of expected staking rewards, and user confusion as the UI reports a generic max‑deposit error while no funds are transferred. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who noted that the mint function performs the same threshold validation only after all amounts—including fees and rewards—are accounted for, indicating the deposit logic is inconsistent. The problem is hard to notice because the revert only occurs under edge‑case balances and the error message does not reveal that fees are the cause. To remediate, the contract should compute the net deposit amount (assets minus fees) before comparing against maxGNSDeposited, or move the threshold check to after the fee deduction, mirroring the safe pattern used in the mint function. This aligns the contract’s accounting with its business rule that the total stored GNS must never exceed the configured maximum, preventing false reverts and preserving expected deposit functionality.

title: gDAIPriceSource and VoltGNSPriceSource will
description:
gDAIPriceSource and VoltGNSPriceSource#getPrice returns the share value in terms of DAI. If DAI were to depeg then the vault would continue to give out loans under the assumption that DAI is still worth $1.
/gDAIPriceSource.sol#L17-L19
Here we see that the price source simply returns the current share price in terms of DAI. This works fine if DAI remains pegged to $1. In the event that DAI depegs then the valuation of the gDAI collateral will be completely wrong and will result in the protocol taking on a lot of bad debt.
This issue also affects VoltGNSPriceSource because GNS will be greatly overvalued
Protocol will take on a large amount of bad debt if DAI depegs
bug_full: An issue exists in the price‑oracle contracts used by the vault, namely gDAIPriceSource and VoltGNSPriceSource. Both contracts expose a getPrice function that returns the current share price expressed directly in DAI units and implicitly treats one DAI as equal to one US dollar. This design works while DAI remains tightly pegged, but it lacks any reference to an external DAI/USD feed. Consequently, if DAI deviates from its $1 peg, the valuation of gDAI collateral (and of GNS collateral through VoltGNSPriceSource) becomes inaccurate. An attacker or market event that causes DAI to depeg can therefore allow a borrower to obtain a loan based on an inflated collateral value. The protocol records the loan as fully collateralised in DAI terms, but when the DAI price falls the underlying collateral is worth less than the outstanding debt, creating bad debt for the vault. The problem manifests whenever the DAI/USD price moves away from 1, especially during rapid depegs, and it affects all participants that rely on the vault’s accounting – borrowers who think they are over‑collateralised, lenders who expect their loans to be backed, and token holders who trust the protocol’s solvency. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the price source code, where the getPrice implementation simply returned the share price without any sanity check or oracle reference. Because DAI has historically been stable, the bug can be easy to overlook and may only surface under stress conditions. To remediate, the contracts should incorporate a reliable DAI/USD price feed such as the Chainlink oracle, adjust the share price calculation to reflect the true USD value of DAI, and add safeguards that reject loan issuance when the external price deviates beyond an acceptable tolerance. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that collateral value in USD always exceeds the borrowed amount, preventing the vault from silently accruing bad debt.

title: VoltGNSPriceSource does not consider with-
description:
VoltGNS can have a withdraw fee that is taken when it is withdrawn. If this is the case then the value of VoltGNS should take this withdraw fee into consideration to properly value the collateral.
/VoltGNSPriceSource.sol#L23-L25
Here the exchange ratio of the vault and GNS price are used directly without considering the withdraw fee to remove the GNS from the vault.
Collateral will be valued incorrectly when there is a fee, leading to potentially bad loans
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price‑calculation component that determines the value of VoltGNS collateral for vault loans. The contract reads the exchange ratio between the vault’s native token and GNS and applies it directly to compute the collateral price, but it ignores any withdraw fee that the vault may charge when GNS is taken out. The root cause is a missing step in the accounting logic: the fee amount is never deducted from the effective amount of GNS that can be realized, so the reported collateral value is higher than the true realizable value. An attacker can exploit this by opening a loan when the vault’s withdraw fee is non‑zero, receiving a collateral valuation that assumes the full GNS amount is available. The borrower then withdraws the GNS, pays the fee, and the protocol still believes the loan is over‑collateralised. If the market price of GNS falls or the fee is large, the loan becomes under‑collateralised, potentially leading to a loss for the protocol when the position is liquidated. The impact is that the protocol may issue loans that are not fully backed, resulting in bad debt, reduced liquidity, and possible erosion of user confidence. The condition for the bug to manifest is any configuration where the vault defines a withdraw fee greater than zero; if the fee is zero the calculation happens to be correct. All participants who rely on the vault – borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting mismatch can cause unexpected liquidations or missing funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the price source contract, where the auditor noticed that the fee‑related state variable was never read in the valuation function. It can be hard to notice because the price feed appears to return a sensible market price and the fee may be a small percentage, so the over‑valuation may not be obvious in routine tests. To remediate, the price source should query the vault for the current withdraw fee, compute the net amount of GNS that can actually be extracted, and use that net amount in the collateral valuation formula. This adjustment aligns the reported collateral value with the real amount that can be realised after fees, restoring correct accounting and preventing loans from being under‑collateralised. The bug belongs to the class of collateral‑mispricing or accounting‑omission vulnerabilities, where a fee or cost is omitted from the valuation of assets, breaking the protocol’s financial invariants and leading to potential fund loss.

title: swapToGNS doesn't add any slippage protec-
description:
The uniswapV3Swap call doesn't implement any kind of slippage protection allowing it to be sandwich attacked.
#L195-L196
We can see here that it calls the swap with not slippage protection at all. This allows the caller to sandwich attack the trade and steal all the DAI being swapped.
DAI being swapped can be stolen via sandwich attack
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that forwards a token swap to the Uniswap V3 router. The call supplies the amount of DAI to be exchanged for GNS but does not include any constraint on the acceptable execution price. Because the Uniswap V3 swap interface allows the caller to specify a price limit (or amountOutMinimum) and the implementation omits this parameter, the transaction is executed at whatever price the pool offers at the moment of execution. An attacker can therefore place a higher‑priced trade immediately before the victim’s transaction (front‑run) and a lower‑priced trade immediately after (back‑run), creating a classic sandwich attack. The victim’s swap proceeds at a severely unfavorable rate, causing the output GNS to be transferred to the attacker or the DAI to be drained from the contract. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the swap transaction succeeded, but the expected GNS balance is zero or far lower than anticipated, and the DAI that was supposed to be exchanged appears to have vanished. The issue is discovered during a manual audit where the call site was inspected and the missing slippage parameter was noted. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the Uniswap router does not emit an explicit error when price deviates; only the economic outcome is abnormal. The root cause is the absence of a price‑limit check, which violates the business assumption that a swap should not execute at a price worse than a user‑defined tolerance. To remediate, the contract should calculate an acceptable minimum amount of GNS (or a maximum price for DAI) based on a configurable slippage percentage and pass this value to the Uniswap V3 swap call, ensuring that the transaction reverts if the market moves beyond the allowed range. This class of bug is commonly referred to as missing slippage protection and can lead to fund loss through sandwich attacks.

title: Protocol fees will make some liquidations un-
description:
When calculating liquidator discount it always uses _minimumCollateralPercentage instead of the the actual collateralization of the debt. If the debt goes too far underwater then the protocol fees will be higher than the actual discount making it unprofitable to liquidate.
ol#L389-L393
When calculating liquidator discount it always uses _minimumCollateralPercentage.
This means that the liquidatorDiscount will be incorrect if the actual ratio is lower than the minimum ratio. Since it takes fees based on liquidatorDiscount it could cost the liquidator more in VOLT than they would receive in collateral.
Example: Assume _minimumCollateralPercentage = 150%. This gives a liquidator discount of 33%. Now imagine that a position being liquidated only has a collateralization of 110%. This gives a liquidator discount of 9%. Since the protocol takes half, it will take 16.33% of the collateral which will make the liquidation unprofitable.
It might seem impossible for the percentage to get low enough to make this an issue but in the event the sequencer goes down liquidations would be delayed.
Liquidations are unprofitable if debt is too far underwater
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the liquidator discount in the liquidation routine of the protocol. Instead of using the actual collateralisation ratio of a debt position, the code always references a static _minimumCollateralPercentage constant (for example 150%). This static value determines the discount that the liquidator receives and the portion of the collateral that the protocol takes as fees. When a position’s real collateral ratio falls below the minimum – for instance a ratio of 110% when the minimum is 150% – the computed discount is far smaller than it should be (9% instead of the expected 33%). Because the protocol still extracts fees based on the discount, it can end up taking a larger share of the collateral (16.33% in the example) than the liquidator’s net gain, making the liquidation unprofitable. The issue manifests most clearly when a debt becomes deeply underwater, which can happen if the sequencer experiences downtime and liquidations are delayed, allowing the collateral ratio to deteriorate further. Under these conditions a liquidator who expects to receive a profitable amount of collateral after paying protocol fees may instead receive less than the cost of the liquidation, resulting in a net loss. Users affected include liquidators who attempt to execute the liquidation and borrowers whose positions may remain unliquidated despite being undercollateralised, potentially leading to larger defaults. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation logic, where the auditor noted that the discount calculation never referenced the dynamic collateral ratio. The bug is subtle because for typical, well‑collateralised positions the static minimum yields a correct discount, so the problem only appears in extreme underwater scenarios that are not frequently exercised in tests. To remediate, the discount should be derived from the actual collateral percentage of the position at the time of liquidation, and fee extraction should be bounded to ensure that the liquidator’s net reward remains non‑negative. This change aligns the accounting with the business rule that liquidators must be incentivised to act and prevents the protocol from unintentionally taking more value than it should, thereby restoring correct economic incentives and preventing loss of funds during liquidation.

title: Adversary can DOS vault repayments by mak-
description:
payBackToken will revert if the repayment amount is greater than the amount of debt owed by the vault. Adversary can DOS repayments by making a dust payment and causing a revert.
ol#L261-L273
VoltaVault#payBackToken requires that the repayment amount is less than or equal to the amount of debt owed by the vault. This can be frontrun with dust repayment to cause repayment to revert.
Adversary can prevent repayment
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the vault’s repayment routine where the function that accepts token repayments enforces a strict check that the repayment amount must be less than or equal to the current debt of the vault. This check is performed without accounting for the possibility that a preceding tiny (dust) repayment can reduce the recorded debt just enough to make a subsequent legitimate repayment amount exceed the new debt balance. An adversary can exploit this by front‑running a legitimate repayment transaction with a minimal dust payment that lowers the vault’s debt by a small amount. When the original repayment transaction is later executed, the amount it tries to repay – originally equal to the full debt – now exceeds the updated debt, causing the contract to revert. The revert prevents the repayment from being processed, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition for any user attempting to clear their debt. This issue manifests whenever a repayment transaction is pending and an attacker can insert a dust repayment before it, which is feasible in public mempools where transaction ordering can be manipulated. The affected parties include any borrower or user of the vault who wishes to repay their debt, as well as the protocol itself because blocked repayments can lead to stale debt, inaccurate accounting, and potential loss of confidence. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the repayment logic and identified that the strict inequality check could be triggered by a front‑run dust payment. The problem is subtle because the contract behaves correctly for normal repayments; only under the specific timing of a preceding tiny repayment does the revert occur, making it easy to miss in standard testing. To remediate the issue, the repayment logic should be adjusted to handle over‑payment gracefully – for example by capping the repayment amount to the outstanding debt or by allowing the function to accept amounts greater than the debt and automatically reducing the excess to zero – thereby preventing a revert and ensuring that legitimate repayments cannot be blocked by an adversarial dust transaction. This class of bug falls under improper input validation and denial‑of‑service through transaction ordering, where business logic assumes a static debt amount during the execution of a repayment, violating the accounting invariant that repayments must always be accepted up to the owed amount.

title: Initial user of voltGNS vault can abuse round-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a share‑to‑asset ratio manipulation in an ERC4626‑style vault that allows the first participant to distort the price of vault shares by making a large off‑chain token donation after the initial share minting. The root cause lies in the way the vault calculates shares: when totalSupply is zero the contract uses an initial conversion that treats assets and shares as 1:1, but after the first tiny deposit the totalSupply becomes non‑zero while the totalAssets value can still be increased by a direct token transfer that bypasses the deposit logic. Because the deposit function does not enforce a minimum deposit amount or burn any of the initially minted shares, an attacker can deposit a single wei of the underlying token, receive one wei of vault shares, and then send a massive amount of tokens directly to the vault. This inflates totalAssets without increasing totalSupply, so the share price collapses. When a regular user later deposits a normal amount, the contract’s _convertToShares routine computes shares as assets × totalSupply / totalAssets (with rounding), resulting in the user receiving only a fraction of the expected shares. In the concrete scenario the attacker’s donation of 1e18 wei causes a subsequent 2e18 wei deposit to be converted into just one wei of shares, meaning the user’s claim covers only half of the vault’s holdings and they lose roughly 0.5e18 tokens. The impact is a direct loss of funds for any depositor after the attack, an unfair profit for the attacker, and a breach of the accounting guarantees that vault shares represent a proportional claim on assets. The issue manifests only on a freshly deployed vault where totalSupply is initially zero and where the contract permits arbitrary token transfers into its balance; it does not appear when the vault already has a healthy share supply. All participants who trust the vault’s share‑based accounting – including end‑users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that recognized the pattern as a known ERC4626 “share‑skew” problem, which can be subtle because the UI may still display a successful deposit while the user actually receives an almost negligible amount of shares, leading to unexpected zero balances or dramatically reduced withdrawals later. The bug is hard to notice because the contract does not emit warnings about abnormal share‑to‑asset ratios and the rounding error is hidden in the arithmetic. To remediate the issue, the contract should either burn a small amount of shares when totalSupply is zero (for example, sending 10 000 wei of the freshly minted shares to the zero address), enforce a minimum deposit size, prevent direct token transfers that bypass the deposit function, or adjust the initial conversion logic to account for future donations so that the share price cannot be artificially depressed. Conceptually, the fix restores the invariant that each share always represents a consistent proportion of the vault’s underlying assets, thereby eliminating the opportunity for an attacker to profit from a “donation‑induced” share price manipulation.

title: voltGNS.mint doesn't allow to mint for first
bug_full: The contract’s mint function contains a guard clause that requires the total amount of assets held by the contract to be greater than zero before any new shares can be minted. This condition is evaluated at the very start of the function, causing the transaction to revert whenever the contract’s balance is still empty. The root cause is a logical error: the contract treats a zero‑balance state as invalid for minting, even though the first depositor is supposed to create the initial liquidity pool. An attacker or even a benign user who is the first to interact with the contract will be unable to call mint because the require(totalAssets() > 0) statement fails, resulting in a revert and no shares being issued. From a user’s perspective the UI may display an unexpected error or simply show that the transaction failed, leaving the user with no minted tokens and possibly a loss of gas. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for onboarding the first participant, which can stall the protocol’s launch or require a manual pre‑funding step (for example sending a single wei of the underlying token) to bypass the check. This issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s public interface, where the auditor noted that the mint logic could never succeed on an empty contract. It can be hard to notice because many test environments start with a pre‑seeded balance, masking the problem until deployment on a fresh network. The bug belongs to the class of “initialization guard” or “zero‑balance restriction” vulnerabilities, where business logic incorrectly assumes a non‑zero state before the first operation. To fix the issue the require statement should be removed or altered to allow minting when totalAssets() equals zero, possibly by handling the first deposit as a special case that initializes the pool without violating any accounting invariants. By allowing the first mint, the protocol’s intended flow—deposit, mint shares, and stake—behaves as expected, and users receive the shares they anticipate rather than seeing a silent failure.

title: voltGNS.compound is not called for
description:
compound is not called for voltGNS.withdraw and redeem. User lose funds because of that.
voltGNS.compound is harvesting rewards from gnsVault, then swap them into GNS and then stake them back to the vault. Because of this totalAssets is increasing and stakers earn more GNS. This function is called at the top of deposit and mint function, but it's not called inside withdraw and redeem. Because of that, users that are going to withdraw from voltGNS are losing some funds.
Lose of funds for withdrawers.
bug_full: The vulnerability in the VoltGNS contract stems from the fact that the internal function responsible for harvesting and restaking reward tokens – referred to as compound – is invoked at the beginning of deposit and mint operations but is omitted from the withdraw and redeem paths. The contract is designed so that compound first claims accrued GNS rewards from the external gnsVault, swaps the rewards into GNS, and then stakes the newly obtained GNS back into the vault. This process increases the reported totalAssets value, which represents the amount of GNS that all stakers are entitled to claim. When a user initiates a withdrawal or a redemption, the expected accounting flow assumes that totalAssets already reflects the most recent reward harvest. Because compound is not called, the totalAssets figure remains stale and does not include the latest rewards. Consequently, the amount of GNS calculated for the withdrawing user is based on an outdated lower balance, causing the user to receive fewer tokens than they are mathematically entitled to. The impact is a loss of accrued rewards for any participant who withdraws or redeems before a deposit or mint triggers a compound call. This condition occurs every time withdraw or redeem is executed, affecting all users of the protocol who rely on accurate reward distribution. The issue was identified during a manual audit that compared the code paths of deposit, mint, withdraw and redeem and noticed the missing compound invocation. It can be difficult to detect in normal operation because the contract’s external view of totalAssets still grows over time, and the discrepancy only becomes visible when a user’s withdrawal amount is lower than expected, often appearing as “missing funds” or “rewards not received”. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where state‑updating functions are not called in all relevant execution paths, breaking the invariant that totalAssets must always reflect the current reward balance before any user‑facing transfer. To remediate the problem, the withdraw and redeem functions should be amended to invoke the compound routine before calculating the user’s share, thereby ensuring that the reward balance is up‑to‑date and that users receive the full amount of GNS they have earned.

title: PerpDepository has no way to withdraw prof-
description:
PerpDepository has no way to calculate or withdraw any profits made by the vault.
By design stakes are entitled to a portion of the profits generated by the delta-neutral strategy. The issue is that the vault never implements a way to withdraw profits to stakers, resulting in loss of revenue for them.
See summary.
Profits owed stakers will be trapped in the contract and they will lose that portion of their revenue
bug_full: The vulnerability in the PerpDepository contract is a missing profit settlement mechanism. Stakers are entitled by design to a share of the profits generated by the delta‑neutral strategy, but the contract does not implement any function to calculate those profits nor a way to transfer them to the stakers. The root cause is an omission in the contract’s accounting logic: after the strategy produces a positive delta, the resulting revenue is recorded in the vault’s balance but never exposed through a withdrawal interface. An attacker does not need to actively exploit code execution; the flaw is passive – any profit that accrues becomes permanently trapped, preventing users from receiving the expected revenue. The impact is that stakers see no increase in their claimable balance even after a profitable period; from a user perspective the UI may show the same staked amount, no reward, or a zero‑return message, contradicting the expectation of earning a share of the strategy’s gains. This condition occurs whenever the vault records profit, which is any time the underlying delta‑neutral position yields a positive outcome. All participants who have deposited stakes are affected because their entitled portion of the profit is effectively lost. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the auditor noted the absence of any public or internal function that computes or distributes profit to stakeholders. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract may still accept deposits and allow withdrawals of the principal, giving the impression that it works correctly, while the silent loss of accrued profit remains hidden. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “missing settlement or withdrawal logic” and violates the fundamental accounting assumption that earned revenue must be claimable by its owners. To remediate the issue, the contract should be extended with a correctly scoped function that (i) determines each staker’s proportional share of the accumulated profit, (ii) updates internal accounting to reflect the distribution, and (iii) transfers the calculated amount to the staker, ensuring that the profit is no longer trapped in the contract.

title: PerpDepository.netAssetDeposits variable
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the PerpDepository contract tracks the amount of base assets that have been deposited by users. A single state variable, netAssetDeposits, is increased when a user deposits assets and decreased when a user withdraws assets. The contract assumes that the amount a user can withdraw will never exceed the value stored in netAssetDeposits, effectively treating the variable as a perfect accounting ledger that matches the value of minted UXD tokens one‑to‑one with the underlying asset. However, the value of the underlying asset (for example WETH) can change between the time of deposit and the time of redemption. When the price drops, a user who redeems the same amount of UXD tokens receives more base asset than was originally recorded in netAssetDeposits. The withdrawal function checks if the requested amount is greater than netAssetDeposits and reverts with an underflow error if it is. Consequently, the transaction fails, the user receives no assets, and the UXD tokens remain unredeemed. From the user’s perspective the expectation is that redeeming 1200 UXD will return the equivalent value in WETH, but instead the transaction reverts and the user sees no change in balance, creating the impression that funds have disappeared or are locked. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s accounting logic, where the auditor noticed that netAssetDeposits is never adjusted for price fluctuations and is not used elsewhere in the protocol. The bug is subtle because the variable name suggests it represents the net amount of assets held, yet it does not reflect the actual vault balance after price movements, making the underflow condition easy to miss in normal operation. The impact is medium: users who attempt to withdraw after a price change may be unable to redeem their UXD tokens, effectively locking their funds and undermining confidence in the protocol’s accounting integrity. The affected parties are all UXD token holders and the protocol itself, as the accounting inconsistency can lead to a loss of usability and potential loss of funds if no recovery mechanism exists.
