The bug manifests only when an order is delayed and the underlying token’s price‑feed deviates from its historical value, a situation that is difficult to detect because the on‑chain price appears correct at the moment of execution, masking the fact that the order’s intended price snapshot was ignored. From a user’s perspective the UI may show an order that was filled, but the resulting balance may be lower than expected, refunds may be zero, or liquidation may occur unexpectedly. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the oracle integration logic. To remediate the problem, the contract should either lock the price at order submission using the archive oracle or replace all live price‑feed references with the archive oracle for price determination, ensuring that delayed orders are always evaluated against the price that existed when they were created. This change restores the integrity of the pricing model and aligns execution outcomes with user expectations and protocol economics.

title: EmptyFeedPrice will cause orders to be can-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic error in the order handling routine of the GMX exchange contract where a specific oracle error, EmptyFeedPrice, is not recognised as an empty‑price condition. The contract’s _handleOrderError function only treats errors that satisfy OracleUtils.isEmptyPriceError or match the InvalidKeeperForFrozenOrder selector as reasons to revert the transaction; all other errors trigger a cancellation of the pending order. Because EmptyFeedPrice is omitted from the empty‑price check, when an oracle feed returns a zero price the error is not classified as an empty‑price error. Consequently the contract proceeds to cancel the order instead of reverting it. This behaviour occurs whenever the price feed becomes empty or reports zero, which can happen during oracle downtime, network congestion, or feed manipulation. Users who have submitted market orders, especially close‑position orders, may see those orders silently cancelled, leaving positions open and exposing them to adverse price movements or liquidation. From the user’s perspective the UI may show the order status changing to “canceled” or the order disappearing from the order book, and the expected refund or position closure never occurs, effectively causing funds to disappear or be lost. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noted that other oracle errors correctly trigger a revert while EmptyFeedPrice does not. The bug is subtle because a zero price is an edge case and the cancellation path does not emit a distinct error, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate the problem the EmptyFeedPrice selector should be added to the list of errors recognised by OracleUtils.isEmptyPriceError, ensuring that the contract reverts on this condition just like other empty‑price errors, thereby preserving the intended order lifecycle and protecting user funds. The flaw belongs to the class of improper error handling or missing error classification bugs, where an exceptional condition is not mapped to the correct control‑flow branch, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a zero price must abort the operation rather than silently cancel it.

title: Insufficient oracle validation
bug_full: An insufficient oracle validation vulnerability exists in the price‑feed module of the protocol. The contract retrieves price data from a Chainlink oracle using the latestRoundData() call, but it completely ignores the timestamp fields returned by the oracle. Because there is no freshness or staleness check, a price that is minutes or hours old can be accepted as current. This situation arises when the off‑chain OCR (Off‑Chain Reporting) node fails to push a new update in time, leaving the last signed price unchanged. An attacker or simply a network outage can therefore cause the contract to continue using an outdated price. When a trader opens or closes a position, the protocol calculates profit and loss based on the stale price, which may be significantly different from the real market price. As a result the trader may be liquidated prematurely, receive a smaller profit, or even incur a loss that should not have occurred, while other participants in the liquidity pool bear the unintended cost. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a liquidation or a zero‑balance event even though the market appears stable, or a refund that is lower than expected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the oracle integration code and noticed that the timestamp variable is never used. The bug is hard to notice because the price value itself is signed and appears authentic; only the missing time validation creates the risk, which does not surface in normal functional tests that use fresh mock data. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “stale data acceptance” or “missing freshness validation” bugs, where external data is trusted without verifying its recency. To exploit the flaw, an adversary can block or delay the OCR feed, wait for the contract to cache the last price, and then trigger trades that profit from the discrepancy between the stale price and the actual market. The impact is financial loss for traders and erosion of confidence in the protocol’s accounting logic. The recommended mitigation is to introduce a configurable staleness threshold (for example, a maximum number of seconds) and reject any price whose timestamp is older than the current block time minus that threshold. Adding this check restores the intended business rule that only recent, signed prices may be used for PnL calculations, preventing unintended liquidations and protecting user funds.

title: Malicious order keepers can trigger the cancellation of any order by providing oracle prices from blocks unrelated to the order
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic flaw in the order execution path of the protocol where a keeper that supplies oracle price data from blocks that are outside the order's allowed block range can cause the order to be cancelled instead of retried. Each order records the minimum and maximum block numbers that its oracle data must fall within. When a keeper provides a price array together with block numbers that are larger than the expected block, smaller than required, or simply not within the recorded range, the contract calls internal revert functions such as OracleBlockNumbersAreLargerThanExpected, OracleBlockNumbersAreSmallerThanRequired, or OracleBlockNumberNotWithinRange. The surrounding error‑handling logic only treats empty or malformed price arrays as retryable conditions; it does not catch these specific block‑number reverts. As a result the execution flow interprets the revert as a fatal failure and marks the order as cancelled. A malicious or careless keeper can therefore repeatedly submit out‑of‑range oracle data, forcing the protocol to cancel legitimate orders. This denial‑of‑service style attack prevents the order from being executed at the intended price, which may leave a user’s position unprotected and lead to an unexpected liquidation. The impact is that users see their orders change to a cancelled state, lose the expected protection or profit, and may suffer loss of funds when a position is liquidated because the protective order never executed. The issue manifests whenever the keeper network includes an actor that can manipulate the block numbers attached to the oracle payload, which is plausible in a decentralized keeper system. It was discovered during a security audit when the auditor noticed that the three revert functions for block‑number validation were not covered by any try‑catch or fallback handling. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit a distinct error to the user; the order simply disappears from the pending list, making it hard to trace back to a block‑number mismatch. The bug belongs to the class of improper error handling that turns a recoverable validation failure into an irreversible cancellation, effectively a denial‑of‑service vector against order execution. To remediate, the contract should either catch these specific revert reasons and treat them as retryable errors, or perform explicit block‑number checks before invoking the oracle logic and revert the transaction with a clear message instead of cancelling the order. By ensuring that out‑of‑range oracle data does not automatically trigger cancellation, the protocol can preserve order integrity and protect user positions.

title: Missing checks for whether a position is still an ADL candidate or not
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing per‑position eligibility checks in the auto‑deleveraging (ADL) execution path. The ADL handler currently validates only exchange‑wide profit‑and‑loss (PnL) thresholds before attempting to reduce a trader’s position, but it does not verify that the specific position is still a valid ADL candidate at the moment of execution. This gap arises because the keeper first builds a list of candidate positions based on a snapshot of market data, then later submits a transaction that calls AdlHandler.executeAdl(). If the keeper experiences a delay – for example due to a CPU spike, network latency, or sequencer retries – the trader may have already partially closed or reduced the position. Because the contract lacks a fresh check, the ADL logic proceeds to reduce the position again, potentially over‑reducing it or forcing a size that would become negative. The code only aborts when the reduction would make the size negative, but it does not prevent an unnecessary reduction that harms the user. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker controlling the ADL keeper (or any entity that can trigger the ADL transaction) can wait for a window after the candidate list is generated, then let a user shrink their position, and finally submit the ADL transaction, causing the contract to apply the global PnL rule to a position that is no longer eligible. The impact is loss of user capital, unexpected position size changes, and possible liquidation of a position that the user believed was safe. This occurs under conditions where there is a time gap between candidate selection and transaction confirmation, typically in high‑load environments or when the keeper’s execution is delayed. All users with open leveraged positions are affected, as the protocol’s risk‑management guarantees are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended ADL flow with the actual implementation and noticed the absence of a per‑position eligibility view. It can be hard to notice because the contract still reverts on obvious errors (negative size) and the global PnL checks succeed, so the transaction appears legitimate while silently harming the user’s balance. The recommended fix is to introduce a view function that determines whether a given position is still eligible for ADL at execution time and to revert the transaction if the position no longer meets the criteria. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “missing state validation” or “stale data usage” where a contract relies on outdated off‑chain information to make on‑chain decisions, violating accounting assumptions that a position’s risk profile remains unchanged between selection and enforcement. From the user’s perspective, the UI may show a normal trade execution, but after the ADL transaction the displayed position size may drop to zero or a lower value than expected, and the user receives no refund or compensation for the unintended reduction. The expectation that a closed or reduced position will remain untouched is broken, leading to funds disappearing or being incorrectly seized by the ADL mechanism.

title: Oracles are vulnerable to cross-chain replay attacks
bug_full: The vulnerability is a cross‑chain replay weakness in the oracle signature scheme. The contract computes a constant SALT at deployment by hashing the chain identifier (block.chainid) together with a static string. This SALT is then used as the only domain separator for all price signatures, without appending the current chain identifier to each signed message. Because the SALT is immutable, a signature created on the original chain remains valid on any forked chain that reuses the same contract address, even though the fork may have a different chain identifier. When a hard fork occurs – for example a transition from proof‑of‑work to proof‑of‑stake – the forked chain presents a new chainid but the oracle contract still verifies signatures against the old SALT. Consequently, keepers on the forked chain can replay oracle prices that were signed on the original chain. These replayed prices may be completely inaccurate for the forked environment (e.g., a token that is not yet supported on the fork may be priced at zero), leading to erroneous execution prices and potentially wrongful liquidations of user positions. The impact is that users may see their collateral liquidated or their balances reduced despite no real market movement, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions and exposing funds to loss. The issue manifests only after a chain split where the same contract code and address exist on both chains, and it is difficult to notice because signature verification appears to succeed and no explicit chain‑specific check is performed. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the oracle’s construction and signature verification logic. To remediate, the protocol should incorporate the current block.chainid into each signed payload, either by recomputing the SALT per message or by appending the chain identifier as a separate field in the signature, ensuring that a signature is bound to the specific chain on which it is used. This change prevents replay of stale oracle data across forks and restores the integrity of price feeds for all participants.

title: Missing checks for whether Arbitrum Sequencer is active
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing health check for the Arbitrum Sequencer when the protocol reads price data from Chainlink price feeds. The contract assumes that the price returned by the feed is always up‑to‑date, but on Arbitrum the Sequencer is responsible for ordering and finalising L2 transactions, including the updates that Chainlink nodes push to the feed. If the Sequencer goes offline, submitted transactions are not processed and the price feed can become stale. Because the contract does not verify the Sequencer status before using the price, an attacker or a malicious keeper can submit orders while the Sequencer is down, receive a price that reflects an earlier market state, and have those orders executed at a price that no longer matches reality. This situation can be especially damaging if a stablecoin such as USDC de‑pegs during the outage; the stale price would allow users to trade at a price that no longer exists, potentially draining funds or creating arbitrage opportunities. The impact is that users may see a normal price on the UI, place a trade expecting the quoted price, but receive an execution price that is far off, leading to unexpected loss of assets, incorrect accounting, and erosion of trust in the protocol. The condition under which the bug manifests is any period when the Arbitrum Sequencer is inactive or experiencing a failure, which can be intermittent and may not raise obvious on‑chain errors because the price feed call still returns a value. All participants who rely on accurate pricing – traders, keepers, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the contract’s oracle integration against Chainlink’s recommended best practices, which explicitly advise checking the Sequencer status on L2 networks. The bug is subtle because the contract’s code path appears normal; there is no revert or error, only a silent use of outdated data, making it hard to detect without monitoring Sequencer health. To remediate, the contract should query a dedicated Chainlink Sequencer status feed (or an equivalent on‑chain indicator) before accepting or executing any order, and reject or pause order processing while the Sequencer is reported as offline. This aligns the implementation with the intended security model of preventing stale price usage and preserves the economic guarantees of the platform.

title: Fee receiver does not get paid when collateral is liquidated
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑distribution logic error that occurs during the liquidation of a position. When a position is liquidated and the collateral left after covering the outstanding funding fee is sufficient, the contract’s liquidation routine calculates the amount that should be sent to the pool but fails to allocate the portion of the position fees that belongs to the designated fee receiver. The root cause is that the function getLiquidationValues builds a PositionFees struct named _fees but never populates its fields in the branch where the remaining collateral amount is zero. Consequently the function returns an empty fee structure and the subsequent code that would transfer the fee receiver’s share is skipped. An attacker or any user who can trigger a liquidation can therefore cause the fee receiver to receive zero fees while the entire remaining collateral, including the fee amount, is transferred to the pool. The impact is a loss of revenue for the fee receiver, which may be a treasury, a third‑party service, or a token holder that relies on those fees. From a user’s point of view the liquidation appears to succeed – the position is closed and the pool balance grows – but the expected fee payout never arrives, leading to accounting mismatches such as “my fee balance stayed at 0” or “the pool received more than it should”. This condition only manifests when the liquidation path takes the else‑branch that sets remainingCollateralAmount to zero and does not explicitly set the fee fields. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the DecreasePositionCollateralUtils contract, where the reviewer noticed that the _fees variable was declared but never assigned before being returned. Because the contract does not emit an error or revert, the bug can be subtle and may go unnoticed unless fee balances are reconciled. To remediate the problem the fee calculation should be performed before the early return, the _fees struct must be populated with the correct fee receiver amount, and the liquidation flow should ensure that the fee transfer step is always executed regardless of the collateral amount. In other words, the fee‑splitting logic must be split correctly and the function must not exit prematurely, guaranteeing that the fee receiver’s share is paid as intended.

title: Virtual impacts can be trivially bypassed via multiple small orders
bug_full: The vulnerability is a virtual‑price‑impact bypass that allows an attacker to avoid the intended deterrent against oracle price manipulation by fragmenting a large order into many smaller orders that each fall below the virtual‑impact threshold. The root cause lies in the pricing logic which only applies the virtual inventory impact when the calculated virtual price impact for a single order exceeds a threshold derived from that order’s USD delta. Because the check is performed per‑order and does not aggregate the size of multiple orders from the same user or across different accounts, a series of sub‑orders can each satisfy the condition "priceImpactUsdForVirtualInventory <= thresholdPriceImpactUsd" and therefore receive the lower of the virtual or real impact. An attacker can therefore submit a batch of small trades within the same block, manipulate the oracle price in between or before the batch, and have each trade execute with minimal impact, effectively bypassing the protection that was meant to keep the overall position price‑impact high. The impact is that the attacker can move the market price in their favour, extract value from other participants, or cause the protocol’s accounting to diverge from expected economic guarantees. This scenario occurs whenever virtual inventory is enabled, the virtual impact for a single order is below the threshold, and the contract processes multiple orders in the same block – a situation common in high‑frequency or batch trading environments. All users of the market, as well as the protocol’s liquidity providers, are affected because the price they see may be artificially favorable for the attacker while later trades suffer unexpected slippage or loss. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the getPriceImpactUsd function and identified that the conditional return path ignores cumulative impact. It is hard to notice because each individual transaction appears to have a normal, low price impact, and the aggregate effect only becomes visible after many trades have been executed. To remediate, the virtual price impact calculation should be applied unconditionally or the threshold logic should consider the total position size across all orders from a single account or across the block, ensuring that splitting an order does not reduce the overall impact. In user‑facing terms, a trader may observe that a large intended purchase executes with almost zero slippage, then see the market price shift dramatically after a flurry of small trades, leading to unexpected losses or perceived “free” trades. This class of bug is a threshold‑bypass or cumulative‑impact evasion flaw that violates the protocol’s economic assumptions about price impact and oracle safety.

title: Collateral tokens that cannot be automatically swapped to the PnL token bypass slippage checks
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a slippage‑checking flaw that appears when a position is closed using the flag that requests an automatic swap of the collateral token into the profit‑and‑loss (PnL) token. The contract stores a single slippage parameter, minOutputAmount, expressed in units of the PnL token. When the swap succeeds the contract adds the secondary output amount to the primary output amount and the slippage check is applied to the total PnL token amount. However, if the swap fails – for example because the collateral token is paused or the external swap handler reverts – the code catches the error, emits a SwapReverted event and returns the original collateral token unchanged. Because the slippage limit is defined only for the PnL token, the returned collateral token is never compared against the user‑specified minOutputAmount. Consequently the user can be forced to accept any amount of collateral token that the market offers at the moment of failure, incurring the full price‑impact slippage even though they had set a protective minimum. This situation can be triggered deliberately by an attacker who makes the swap revert, or unintentionally by a token pause, and it only occurs for orders that have the SwapCollateralTokenToPnlToken flag enabled. Affected parties are the end‑users who placed the resting order, the protocol that records the position, and any liquidity providers whose balances may be altered unexpectedly. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the DecreasePositionCollateralUtils contract, where the control flow for a failed swap was examined and the absence of a slippage guard was noted. It is subtle because the contract still emits a SwapReverted event, giving the impression that the operation was handled safely, while the economic consequence – a potentially large loss of value – is hidden from the user interface. From the user’s point of view the expectation is that the order will either execute with at least the specified minOutputAmount of PnL token or revert entirely; instead the user may receive the original collateral token at a worse rate, seeing a zero or reduced profit where a profit was expected, effectively making funds disappear. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect slippage enforcement on fallback paths” or “missing validation on alternative execution branches”. To remediate the problem the contract should convert the USD value of the secondary output amount into the primary output amount and apply the slippage check against the combined total, or redesign the slippage mechanism to accept a minimum amount expressed in the token that will actually be transferred in every possible execution path.

title: Limit orders are unnecessarily delayed by a block due to oracle block number restrictions
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one block delay in the execution of limit and stop‑loss decrease orders caused by overly strict oracle block number validation. When a user creates a limit or stop‑loss order, the contract records the block number at which the order was placed. To guarantee that the price data used for triggering the order is fresh, the validation logic requires that both the primary price (the earlier price in the price range) and the secondary price (the later price) reported by the oracle have block numbers strictly greater than the order’s block. In practice this means that the price range covering the block in which the order was submitted cannot be used; the order must wait for the next price range, effectively skipping one oracle update. The root cause is the use of a single "latestUpdatedAtBlock" threshold for both price points instead of allowing the primary price to be equal to the order block while only the secondary price must be newer. An attacker does not need to act; the bug is triggered automatically when a user’s order relies on the immediate next oracle update. The exploitation scenario is straightforward: a user submits a stop‑loss at price 100, expecting the order to be filled as soon as the oracle reports a price crossing that threshold in the next block range. Because the contract rejects the price range that includes the order’s block, the order is forced to wait for the following range, where market conditions may have moved unfavorably. This can lead to a larger price impact penalty, higher slippage, or even execution at a price far from the user’s intended trigger, resulting in financial loss or dissatisfaction. The issue manifests only when the oracle provides price updates in discrete block‑aligned ranges and the order type is LimitIncrease, LimitDecrease, or StopLossDecrease. Users placing such orders experience a delay that appears as a pending order despite the market already meeting the trigger condition; the UI may show the order as still open while the expected execution never occurs at the optimal price. The bug was discovered during a systematic audit of the GMX synthetic contracts, where the validation function DecreaseOrderUtils.validateOracleBlockNumbers and IncreaseOrderUtils.validateOracleBlockNumbers were examined and the unnecessary strictness was identified. It is subtle because the contract does not revert; it simply postpones execution, making the problem easy to miss without careful analysis of block‑level price data. To remediate, the validation should be relaxed so that the primary price may have a block number equal to the order’s block, and only the secondary price needs to be strictly greater. This change aligns the oracle data requirements with the intended business logic that the order should be triggerable as soon as the price crosses the threshold, eliminating the artificial one‑block delay and restoring expected user experience while preserving safety against stale price data.

title: Slippage is not respected if PnL swap associated with position decrease fails
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the logic that handles the conversion of profit‑and‑loss (PnL) tokens after a position is decreased. When a user requests to swap the PnL token for another asset, the contract invokes an external swap routine that checks slippage limits. If the swap succeeds, the output amount is compared against the minimum amount specified by the order. However, if the swap reverts – for example because the market is temporarily disabled, the price impact exceeds the allowed slippage, or an intermediate token is paused – the contract falls back to a helper function that directly transfers the raw output token to the user without performing any slippage verification. This omission means the user may receive fewer tokens than the minimum they expected, potentially even zero tokens, while the transaction is still considered successful from the protocol’s perspective. The flaw is a missing validation step in the error‑handling path, effectively bypassing the accounting guarantees that the protocol relies on to protect users’ funds. Exploitation requires an attacker (or a market condition) to force the swap to fail, which can be achieved by manipulating market liquidity, pausing a token, or submitting a transaction with extreme price impact. Under those conditions the contract will still send the (possibly reduced) output amount, violating the user’s expectation that the protocol enforces the slippage bound. Affected parties include any user who decreases a position and opts for a PnL token conversion, as well as the protocol itself because the accounting invariant that the USD value of the output token must meet the order’s minimum is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the DecreaseOrderUtils._handleSwapError function and noticed that the transferOut call does not reference the order’s minOutputAmount. It can be hard to notice because the fallback path is only exercised when external swaps fail, a scenario that may not be covered by typical unit tests. To remediate, the contract should recompute the USD value of the output token after a swap failure and compare it against the order’s minimum acceptable amount, reverting the transaction if the value is insufficient. In broader terms, this is a classic case of missing validation in an error‑handling branch, leading to a “slippage bypass” or “unchecked fallback transfer” bug that can cause users to receive less than expected, effectively making funds disappear from the user’s perspective.

title: Global position-fee-related state not updated until after liquidation checks are done
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical ordering flaw in the liquidation workflow of the GMX synthetic position contract. When a trader submits a liquidation order, the contract first checks whether the position is liquidatable by calling a function that evaluates the current funding and borrowing multipliers. However, the global state that stores these fee‑related multipliers is only refreshed after the liquidation check, via a call to PositionUtils.updateFundingAndBorrowingState. Because the check runs on stale data, a position that meets the liquidation criteria in the current block is mistakenly considered safe and the liquidation is aborted. The contract then proceeds to update the global state, but the missed liquidation is only re‑evaluated in the next block, at which point the correct multipliers are applied and the position may finally be liquidated. This delay means that a position that should have been closed immediately can remain open for an extra block, exposing the trader and the protocol to a larger loss than the intended liquidation penalty. The impact is that users see their margin erode more than expected, balances can drop to zero or become negative, and the protocol’s risk parameters are effectively weakened for the duration of the delay. The issue manifests only when a liquidation order is processed in the same block where funding or borrowing rates change, which is a common scenario in volatile markets. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the sequence of state updates and liquidation checks. The bug is subtle because the contract eventually updates the fee state, so on‑chain explorers show the correct values after the transaction, making the premature check hard to spot without tracing execution order. To remediate, the contract should update the funding and borrowing state before performing any liquidation eligibility checks, ensuring that the decision is based on the most recent fee multipliers. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of state‑dependency ordering errors, where a contract’s logic relies on stale global variables, leading to incorrect business‑logic outcomes such as delayed liquidations, unexpected fund loss, and broken accounting assumptions.

title: Position fees are still assessed even if the ability to decrease positions is disabled
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of continuous assessment of position fees – both borrowing and funding – even after the protocol’s feature flags have disabled the ability to create or execute orders that would normally allow a trader to reduce or close a position. The root cause is that fee accrual is calculated solely based on elapsed time using timestamps retrieved from the data store, without checking whether the order‑creation or order‑execution features are paused. Consequently, when a keeper disables these features, traders are still considered to hold open positions and the contract keeps adding borrowing and funding charges each second. An attacker (or a malicious keeper) can trigger the pause, leaving existing positions open while fees keep growing, eventually draining the trader’s margin and causing liquidation without any fault on the trader’s side. From the user’s perspective the UI will refuse to place a closing order – often showing a message that order placement is disabled – yet the account balance continues to shrink and may reach zero, leading to unexpected liquidation. The impact is loss of funds for any user with an open position at the time of the pause, erosion of trust in the protocol’s safety guarantees, and potential regulatory concerns because the system violates the expectation that closing a position stops further fee accrual. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the feature‑flag checks in order‑creation and order‑execution functions with the fee‑calculation utilities, revealing that the latter ignore the pause state. It is hard to notice because fee accrual is a background process; users may not see the incremental fee increase until the balance is significantly reduced or liquidation occurs. To remediate, the fee‑tracking logic should incorporate the same feature‑flag checks used for order handling, pausing the update of cumulative borrowing and funding factors when order creation or execution is disabled, or alternatively allowing a forced closure path that settles fees up to the pause moment. This aligns the accounting model with the protocol’s business logic that fees are only owed while a position is actively tradable, preventing money from disappearing silently and preserving the intended economic guarantees of the platform.

title: Positions cannot be liquidated once the oracle price drops to zero
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a liquidation dead‑lock that occurs when an asset’s oracle price becomes zero. The contract treats a zero price as an invalid value and explicitly reverts in both the on‑chain Chainlink price feed handling and the off‑chain secondary price lookup. Because the liquidation routine reads the current price from these oracle helpers, any attempt to liquidate a position when the price is zero triggers a revert, preventing the liquidation transaction from completing. This situation can be triggered if the underlying market crashes to zero, if a malicious actor manipulates the price feed to return zero, or if a bug in the price feed pushes a zero value through. When liquidation is blocked, the position remains open while the protocol continues to accrue losses and fees, which can eventually render the exchange insolvent. Users who hold leveraged positions expect that a falling price will trigger liquidation and protect their collateral; instead they see no action, their collateral may be drained over time, and they receive no liquidation event or payout. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the oracle integration code, where the explicit `revert EmptyFeedPrice` and `revert OracleUtils.EmptyLatestPrice` checks were observed. Because a zero price is an extreme edge case, it is rarely exercised in testing, making the bug easy to overlook. To remediate, the protocol should introduce a fallback liquidation path that does not rely on a non‑zero price, such as using the last known non‑zero price, a default minimal price, or a separate liquidation oracle that can handle zero values. This change would ensure that positions remain liquidatable under all price conditions, preserving the accounting invariants and protecting user funds.

title: Trades in blocks where the bid or ask drops to zero use outdated prices
bug_full: The vulnerability is an oracle price selection flaw that treats a price value of zero as a sentinel indicating that no price has been set. In the contract, the getLatestPrice function first checks a secondary price and, if it is not empty, returns it; otherwise it falls back to a primary (older) price. The emptiness check is implemented by treating a price of zero as empty. When a market event causes the secondary price to legitimately become zero – for example when the bid or ask drops to zero in a given block – the function incorrectly discards this valid zero price and returns the stale primary price instead. This means that any position closed in the first block where the price touches zero is settled using the outdated non‑zero price, giving the exiting trader a more favorable execution at the expense of the liquidity pool and the counter‑party. The issue occurs only when the secondary price is zero while the primary price is still non‑zero, which is a rare but possible scenario in volatile markets. It affects all participants who rely on the oracle for pricing, including liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself, because the accounting assumptions that the price reflects the current market are violated. The bug was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor noticed that the sentinel logic conflated a legitimate zero price with an empty price, leading to incorrect trade settlement. It is hard to notice because zero prices are uncommon and the contract does not emit an explicit error; the UI may display a zero price, yet the trade proceeds as if the price were still the previous value, creating a silent financial discrepancy. The correct mitigation is to replace the overloaded zero sentinel with an explicit flag or a distinct sentinel value that unambiguously indicates the absence of a price, ensuring that a zero price is treated as a valid market value. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “sentinel misuse” or “invalid sentinel handling” bugs, where a legitimate data value is overloaded as a special marker, leading to logic that misinterprets valid inputs and produces accounting errors such as funds disappearing from the pool or trades being settled at an unintended price.

title: PnL is incorrectly counted as collateral when reducing a position
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way GMX calculates the remaining collateral of a position when the position is partially reduced. The contract adds the full unrealized profit‑and‑loss (PnL) amount to the collateral balance before comparing it against the protocol‑defined minimum collateral threshold (MIN_COLLATERAL_USD). Because profit is counted as part of the collateral, a trader who holds a large positive PnL can invoke a partial‑close operation and withdraw almost all of the actual collateral, leaving only a single wei of the collateral token in the position while the profit is still counted as collateral. The check therefore reports that the position still satisfies the minimum collateral requirement even though the real, risk‑covering collateral is essentially zero. If the market price then experiences a sudden downward gap – a common occurrence in crypto markets – the position incurs a loss that exceeds the tiny amount of real collateral, causing the liquidity pool to absorb the shortfall. The protocol has no mechanism for a keeper to automatically lower the leverage of such an under‑collateralised position; the only remediation is a liquidation that may happen much later, by which time the pool may have already suffered a loss. This flaw was discovered during a formal audit of the PositionUtils.willPositionCollateralBeSufficient function, where the code adds values.positionPnlUsd to the remainingCollateralUsd before applying the minimum‑collateral test. The issue is subtle because the UI and on‑chain queries continue to display a healthy collateral ratio as long as the position remains profitable, making the problem hard to notice until a price shock occurs. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated – collateral is supposed to be an independent safety buffer, not a function of unrealised gains – leading to potential fund loss for the pool and other traders. To remediate, the profit component should be excluded from the collateral‑sufficiency check; the protocol may still perform a separate health check that includes PnL, but the minimum‑collateral enforcement must rely solely on the actual collateral deposited. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a position appears to have sufficient collateral while the displayed collateral amount is effectively zero, and after a price drop the position may be liquidated with an unexpectedly large loss, contradicting the expectation that “my profit protects my collateral”.

title: Users that have to claim collateral more than once for a given time slot may get the wrong total amount
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting error that occurs when a user attempts to claim collateral more than once for the same time slot while the claimable factor changes between claims. The contract calculates an adjusted claimable amount by applying a factor to the raw claimable amount, transfers the appropriate portion to the user, and then records the amount that has been claimed. However, instead of persisting the original claimable amount, the code mistakenly stores the factor‑adjusted total as the claimed amount. As a result, the remaining claimable balance is computed as adjustedClaimableAmount minus the previously recorded claimedAmount, which can become zero even though the user is still entitled to additional collateral. This flaw is triggered when a keeper modifies the claimableFactor after an initial claim and the user initiates a second claim for the same slot. In the example, a user first claims 1 ETH with a factor of 1.0, which is recorded correctly. Later the factor is reduced to 0.5 and the user’s claimable amount increases to 2 ETH, but the contract stores the adjusted amount (1 ETH) as the claimed total, causing the remaining claimable amount to be calculated as zero. Consequently the user receives no additional funds despite being owed 0.5 ETH, leading to a shortfall in the user’s balance and a mismatch in the protocol’s collateral accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noted that the state update uses the wrong variable. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the transfer succeeds; the user only observes that the expected extra collateral never arrives, which may be attributed to normal market behavior. The bug belongs to the class of state‑update or accounting bugs where an incorrect variable is persisted, causing under‑payment. To remediate, the contract should store the original claimableAmount (the amount before factor adjustment) as the claimed collateral amount, and then compute the remaining claimable balance using the correct values. This ensures that subsequent claims correctly reflect the total entitlement, preserving user funds and maintaining accurate protocol accounting.

title: boundedSub() might fail to return the result due to incorrect underflow check
description:
The goal of boundedSub() is to bound the result regardless what the inputs are to prevent overflows/underflows. However, the goal is not achieved for some cases.
As a result, boundedSub() still might underflow and still might revert. The goal of the function is not achieved.
As a result, the protocol might not be fault-tolerant as it is supposed to be - when boundedSub() is designed to not revert in any case, it still might revert. For example, function MarketUtils.getNextFundingAmountPerSize() will be affected.
boundedSub() is designed to always bound its result between type(int256).min and type(int256).max so that it will never overflow/underflow:
cts/utils/Calc.sol#L116-L135
It achieves its goal in three cases:
1) Case 1: if either a or b is zero or the signs are the same there should not be any overflow.
2) Case 2: a > 0, and b < 0, and a-b > type(int256).max, then we need to return type(int256).max.
3) Case 3: a < 0, and b > 0, and a - b < type(int256).min, then we need to return type(int256).min which essentially is checking a < 0 && b + a <= type(int256).min, a wrong condition to check. Because of using this wrong condition, underflow cases will not be detected and the function will revert instead of returning type(int256).min in this case.
To verify, suppose a = type(int256).min and b = 1, a-b needs to be bounded to prevent underflow and the function should have returned type(int256).min.
However, the function will fail the condition, as a result, it will not execute the if return a - b;
As a result, instead of returning the minimum, the function will revert in the last line due to underflow. This violates the property of the function: it should have returned the bounded result type(int256).min and should not have reverted in any case.
The following POC in Remix can show that the following function will revert:
```solidity
function testBoundedSub() public pure returns (int256){
return boundedSub(type(int256).min+3, 4);
}
```
boundedSub() does not guarantee underflow/overflow free as it is designed to be.
As a result, the protocol might break at points when it is not supposed to break. For example, function MarketUtils.getNextFundingAmountPerSize() will be affected.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a utility function that performs a bounded subtraction on signed 256‑bit integers. The function is intended to guarantee that the result never exceeds the limits of int256, returning int256.max or int256.min when an overflow or underflow would occur, and therefore never revert. The implementation checks three cases: identical signs or zero, positive a with negative b exceeding the maximum, and negative a with positive b exceeding the minimum. The third check uses the condition `a < 0 && b + a <= type(int256).min`, which is logically incorrect. When a equals int256.min and b is a small positive number, the true underflow condition is `a <= type(int256).min + b`, but the implemented condition fails, allowing the subtraction `a - b` to be executed and causing the EVM to revert due to an arithmetic underflow. This flaw means that boundedSub can still revert, breaking the assumption that it is fault‑tolerant. The bug propagates to higher‑level logic such as MarketUtils.getNextFundingAmountPerSize, which relies on boundedSub to compute funding amounts per position size. Consequently, legitimate calls to funding calculations may unexpectedly revert, leading to user‑facing symptoms like missing funding values, zero balances shown in the UI, or transactions that fail without a clear error message. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the GMX codebase, where the auditor observed that a test case `boundedSub(type(int256).min+3, 4)` caused a revert. The problem is subtle because the function appears to handle most overflow/underflow scenarios, and only a specific edge case triggers the failure, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the underflow check must be corrected to `if (a < 0 && a <= type(int256).min + b) return type(int256).min;` so that the function returns the minimum value instead of reverting. This change restores the intended guarantee that boundedSub always returns a bounded result, preserving protocol stability and preventing unexpected reverts that could halt market operations or degrade user experience.

title: Deposits/Withdrawals/Orders will be canceled when execution fails during disabled state
description:
The protocol has the ability to enable/disable operations such as deposits, withdrawals and orders. If the above operations are disabled:
1. Users will not be able to create/cancel the operations
2. Keepers will not be able to execute the operations
However - on execution failure, cancellation will succeed even if the feature is disabled. Therefore - keepers executing operations that are disabled will cancel them and make the user pay execution fees. (loss of funds)
Let us use deposits as an example. Other operations behave in a similar way.
Consider the following scenario:
1. Bob creates a deposit using createDeposit
2. GMX disabled deposits because of maintenance.
3. Keeper executed Bobs deposit
4. Bobs deposit is cancelled and the execution fee is paid to the keeper from Bobs pocket.
5. GMX finished maintenance and enables again the deposits
Execution will fail in the following check:
cts/exchange/DepositHandler.sol#L144-L150
The revert will be caught in the catch statement and _handleDepositError will be
/contracts/exchange/DepositHandler.sol#L102-L113
_handleDepositError will call DepositUtils.cancelDeposit which does not have
-synthetics/contracts/exchange/DepositHandler.sol#L181-L203
Users lose execution fee funds and have to deposit again.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑validation flaw that allows a user’s operation to be cancelled and the execution fee to be taken even when the protocol has deliberately disabled that operation. The contract maintains a global flag that can disable deposits, withdrawals or order execution for maintenance. Normal logic prevents users from creating or cancelling these actions and prevents keepers from executing them while the flag is off. However, when a keeper attempts to execute a disabled operation and the call reverts, the catch block invokes an internal error‑handling routine that calls a generic cancel function. This cancel function does not re‑check the disabled flag, so it proceeds to cancel the operation and transfers the keeper’s execution fee from the user’s balance. An attacker (or any keeper) can therefore trigger a disabled operation, cause it to fail, and still collect the user’s fee without the user receiving the intended service. The impact is a loss of execution fees for users and the need to repeat the operation after maintenance ends. The issue manifests only when an operation is disabled, a keeper forces execution, and the execution reverts; under normal successful execution the disabled check works correctly. Users experience a cancelled deposit (or withdrawal/order) with no funds deposited and a deduction of gas or execution fees, contrary to the expectation that a disabled state should block any fee‑incurring activity. The bug is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert outright – it succeeds in cancelling the operation, so the UI may simply show “deposit cancelled” without highlighting that a fee was taken. The root cause is missing access‑control or state validation in the error‑handling path, a classic example of an unchecked state transition in a fallback routine. To remediate, the contract should propagate the disabled‑state error through the catch block and add explicit disabled‑state checks inside the internal cancel functions, ensuring that cancellation cannot occur while the feature is turned off. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that no fees are charged when operations are deliberately paused.

title: Keeper can make deposits/orders/withdrawals fail by providing limited gas
bug_full: The vulnerability is a gas‑griefing flaw that allows a privileged keeper to deliberately cause the execution of deposits, orders or withdrawals to run out of gas, forcing the internal try block to revert while still leaving enough gas for the catch block to run. The contract records the amount of gas available at the start of the function, then calls an internal _execute* method inside a try/catch. Because the code does not enforce a minimum gas reserve for the try statement, a malicious keeper can supply just enough gas that 63/64 of the supplied amount is consumed by the called function, triggering an out‑of‑gas exception, while the remaining 1/64 is sufficient to execute the catch clause. The catch clause treats the failure as a normal cancellation, pays the keeper the execution fee and any incentive rewards, and marks the deposit/order/withdrawal as cancelled. This behaviour can be repeated for every pending operation, effectively allowing the keeper to cancel all user‑initiated actions and collect all associated fees. The impact is that users see their deposits or orders disappear, balances may become zero, expected refunds or order completions never occur, and the protocol loses revenue that was intended to fund its operations. The issue manifests whenever a keeper is authorized to call the execute functions and the system imposes a maximum callback gas limit (for example 2,000,000 gas) that is large enough for the catch path but insufficient for the full execution path. Because the failure is handled gracefully by the contract, the problem is hard to notice from the UI – users simply observe cancellations or missing funds without an explicit error. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by analysing the gas accounting logic and creating a proof‑of‑concept that deliberately under‑funds the call. It belongs to the class of out‑of‑gas manipulation or gas‑griefing bugs in contracts that rely on try/catch without proper gas safety checks. To remediate, the contract should enforce a gas buffer that guarantees the try block cannot run out of gas, for example by requiring that gasleft() exceeds a predefined threshold before invoking the internal function, or by restructuring the logic so that fees are only paid after successful execution. Additionally, the protocol could avoid rewarding keepers on failed executions or move fee payment out of the catch path, thereby eliminating the economic incentive for the attack.

title: Multiplication after Division error leading to precision loss
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision loss bug that originates from performing integer division before multiplication in fixed‑point arithmetic. In the market utility code the funding amount is calculated as (sizeOfLargerSide / Precision.FLOAT_PRECISION) * durationInSeconds * fundingFactorPerSecond. Because Solidity uses integer division, the division by the 10**30 constant truncates any fractional part, discarding valuable precision. The truncated intermediate value is then multiplied by other factors, and the same imprecise result is reused to compute fundingUsdForLongCollateral and fundingUsdForShortCollateral. A similar pattern appears in the position utility where sizeDeltaInTokens is derived from a division that loses fractions before being used to calculate positionPnlUsd. The root cause is the order of operations: dividing first reduces the magnitude of the numerator, causing the remainder to be lost permanently, and subsequent multiplications cannot recover the lost bits. An attacker or a user with a large position can amplify the rounding error, leading to systematic under‑payment or over‑payment of funding, incorrect collateral allocation, and inaccurate profit‑and‑loss reporting. The impact is primarily on traders and liquidity providers who rely on precise accounting; they may see their expected funding amount reduced, their collateral balance appear lower than anticipated, or their PnL displayed incorrectly, potentially triggering unexpected liquidations. The bug manifests whenever the contract computes fundingUsd, fundingUsdForLongCollateral, fundingUsdForShortCollateral, or positionPnlUsd using the described arithmetic pattern, which is a common scenario in the protocol’s accounting flow. It was discovered during a manual audit that inspected arithmetic expressions and identified the division‑first pattern as a source of rounding error. The issue is subtle because each individual rounding loss is small and may not be visible in isolated tests, but the errors accumulate over many transactions, creating a drift that is hard to notice from the user interface. To remediate the problem the arithmetic should be reordered so that all numerators are multiplied together before a single division by the product of denominators, preserving full precision. Using a dedicated fixed‑point library or increasing the intermediate precision can also mitigate the loss. Conceptually the fix restores the invariant that funding and PnL calculations are mathematically exact within the chosen precision, aligning the implementation with the protocol’s business logic that assumes accurate accounting of user balances.

title: when execute deposit fails, cancel deposit and keeper loses execution fee
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of execution fees when a deposit operation fails during the executeDeposit function of a keeper‑driven protocol. The contract deducts a portion of the execution fee at the beginning of executeDeposit, assuming that the remaining gas will be sufficient to cover the subsequent cancellation step if an error occurs. When an internal call throws later in the execution flow, the internal helper _handleDepositError is invoked, which in turn calls DepositUtils.cancelDeposit to reimburse the keeper for the execution fee. Because the failure may happen after most of the gas has been consumed, the amount of gas (and therefore the fee) left for the cancellation call is very small. As a result, the keeper receives little or no compensation for the work performed, effectively losing the execution fee that was initially taken. This situation can be exploited by an attacker who deliberately triggers a revert in the later stages of executeDeposit, causing keepers to repeatedly execute failing deposits and incur fee losses, thereby draining keeper incentives and potentially discouraging participation. The impact is primarily economic: keepers receive insufficient remuneration, which may reduce the reliability of the keeper network and indirectly affect users whose deposits are cancelled without proper fee handling. The issue manifests only when a deposit fails after a substantial amount of gas has been spent, and it is observable from the user’s perspective as a cancelled deposit with no fee refund, contrary to the expectation that the keeper should be fully compensated. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined the error‑handling path of executeDeposit and noticed that the cancellation routine does not reserve enough gas for fee payment. It is subtle because the contract does appear to pay a fee, but the amount is insufficient, making the loss easy to overlook in normal operation. To remediate the issue, the protocol should increase the minimum execution fee required for a deposit to ensure that enough gas remains for a successful cancellation, and any excess fee should be refunded to the user when the deposit succeeds. Conceptually, the fix involves reserving a safety margin of gas for error paths and separating keeper compensation from user‑paid fees, thereby preventing fee erosion on failed deposits.

title: The oracle price could be tampered due to missing duplicate price index check
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation for duplicate price indexes in the oracle’s price‑setting routine. When the contract receives a batch of compacted price values it trusts the accompanying index array to identify each price entry, but it does not verify that the indexes are unique. As a result, a malicious actor – for example a compromised order keeper – can craft a transaction that supplies the same index for two different price entries, modify the second entry after the signatures are generated, and still have the contract accept the tampered data because the signature verification only checks the signed values, not the uniqueness of the indexes. This flaw allows the attacker to alter the effective primary price that the protocol uses for vault valuations, liquidation triggers and market pricing. The impact is that the protocol may compute a price that is higher or lower than the genuine market price, leading to incorrect collateral valuations, unintended liquidations, and ultimately the theft of funds from vaults or markets. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to the oracle’s setPrices (or the internal _setPrices) function when multiple price entries are supplied; if the caller provides a compacted price index array containing duplicates, the contract will silently accept it. Users, token holders, and the protocol itself are affected because the price feed no longer reflects the true market state, breaking the accounting assumptions that each token price is uniquely identified. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test script demonstrated that after signing a set of prices, an attacker could change the second price while re‑using the same index, and the contract would still report a blended price that differed from the signed values. The bug is hard to notice because the resulting price may still lie within an expected range, so no obvious error is emitted and the UI may simply show a slightly off price. To remediate, the contract should enforce that each price index appears only once in the submitted batch, rejecting any transaction that contains duplicate indexes, or redesign the data structure to map prices directly to unique identifiers, thereby restoring the integrity of the oracle’s price calculation and preventing price tampering.

title: getAdjustedLongAndShortTokenAmounts()Incorrect calculation in adjustment logic
description:
The function getAdjustedLongAndShortTokenAmounts() attempts to balance the long and short pool amounts for a market which has the same long and short token. However, the calculations are incorrect and may result in an unbalanced pool or a reverted transaction.
There are two equivalent bugs which occur depending on which pool is larger (long vs short). The bug occurs due to incorrect values being used in the if-statements.
The first issue is occurs on line 395 where the diff is compared to poolLongTokenAmount. This is the incorrect value, instead longTokenAmount should be used.
For the case where diff < poolLongTokenAmount
• if longTokenAmount < diff it will overflow on line 396
• if longTokenAmount >= diff this case behaves correctly For the case where diff >= poolLongTokenAmount
• if longTokenAmount >= diff the result is an unbalanced pool since we are attributing too many tokens to the long amount.
• if longTokenAmount < diff this case behaves correctly
The same issue occurs on line 404 for the case when there is a deficit in short tokens.
There are two different negative impacts stated in the above depending on the conditions. The first is an overflow that will cause the transaction to revert.
The second impact is more severe as it will cause an unbalanced pool to be created. The impact is the deposit will have a significant price impact. The most noticable case is the initial deposit. The first deposit will will have diff = 0 and poolShortTokenAMount = poolLongTokenAmount = 0. The impact is line 408-409 is executed which attributes all funds to the short pool and none to the long pool.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that attempts to equalise the amounts of a long and a short token pool when both tokens are identical. The logic uses an incorrect variable when comparing the difference between the pools, specifically it compares the difference to the total amount of tokens already in the long pool (poolLongTokenAmount) instead of the amount contributed by the user (longTokenAmount). This mistake causes two distinct failure modes. In the first mode, when the user‑provided amount is smaller than the calculated difference, the subtraction operation underflows, triggering a revert and causing the transaction to fail even though the user supplied sufficient funds. In the second mode, when the user‑provided amount is larger than the difference, the function attributes an excessive number of tokens to the long side, resulting in an unbalanced pool where the short side receives too few tokens. The most visible manifestation occurs on the initial deposit: because both pool balances start at zero, the branch that should split the deposit equally instead assigns the entire amount to the short pool, leaving the long balance at zero. From a user perspective this appears as a missing or zero long token balance after a successful deposit, or as an unexpected transaction revert. The impact includes distorted pricing because the pool’s accounting no longer reflects the true supply of each side, leading to a significant price impact for subsequent trades and potentially harming liquidity providers. The bug is triggered whenever a market uses the same token for both long and short positions and the pools have differing sizes, conditions that are common in synthetic or leveraged products. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the adjustment routine and identified the mismatched variable usage. The issue can be hard to notice because the surrounding code appears logically sound and the overflow only occurs for specific value ranges, while the imbalance may initially seem like a normal market fluctuation. The proper fix is to replace the erroneous comparisons with the user‑provided amount (longTokenAmount) and to recompute the adjusted amounts based on that value, ensuring that the difference is reduced symmetrically and that no underflow or over‑allocation can occur. In broader terms, this is a classic example of an arithmetic mis‑use bug in pool rebalancing logic that violates the fundamental accounting invariant that the total deposited amount must be split proportionally between the long and short sides.

title: _validateRange in Config does not check the input value against boundaries
description:
_validateRange in Config does not check the input value as described value is within the allowed range. However in the function itself the value is only used in sending revert message, but not used in any check against a pre-set boundary.
function does not verify the input value is within an expected range
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Config contract where the internal helper function _validateRange is intended to enforce that a supplied configuration value lies within a predefined minimum and maximum bound. In practice the function only incorporates the supplied value into a revert message string and never performs an actual comparison against the stored limits. Consequently any caller can provide an arbitrary uint256 value and the contract will accept it as valid. This missing validation stems from a developer oversight: the logical check that should compare the input to the allowed range was omitted, leaving only the error‑reporting code. Exploitation is straightforward – any external transaction that triggers a configuration update calling _validateRange can supply out‑of‑bounds values, such as extreme leverage limits, fee percentages, or timing parameters. Because the protocol relies on these parameters to maintain economic safety and correct accounting, setting them to unreasonable values can break liquidation logic, cause fee calculations to overflow or underflow, or otherwise distort the expected behavior of the system. Users may observe symptoms like unexpectedly high fees, zero refunds, or balances that appear to disappear after a configuration change. The bug manifests whenever a public or privileged function forwards a value to _validateRange; there is no conditional guard that prevents values outside the intended interval. All participants of the protocol – administrators, traders, and liquidity providers – are potentially affected because the misconfiguration can jeopardize the integrity of the entire platform. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer examined the source code and noted that the function name and revert message suggested validation, yet no actual range check existed. The problem is subtle because the presence of a revert message gives the impression that validation occurs, and typical unit tests may not cover extreme boundary cases, allowing the flaw to remain hidden. To remediate, the contract should retrieve the appropriate minimum and maximum limits for the specific configuration key and explicitly compare the input value against these bounds, reverting with a clear error if the value falls outside the allowed interval. This correction restores the intended safety guarantees and aligns the implementation with the documented business logic that configuration parameters must stay within defined ranges.

title: There is no market enabled validation in Swap and CreateAdl
description:
There is no market enabled validation in Swap and CreateAdl activities.
Controller may execute activities for disabled market in Swaphandler and CreateAdlHandler
Activities can still be performed on an disabled market
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing validation that a market is enabled before executing swap or create ADL (auto‑deleveraging) operations. The contract’s controller functions forward requests to the SwapHandler and CreateAdlHandler without checking the market’s enabled flag. As a result, an attacker or any user can invoke these functions for a market that the protocol has deliberately disabled, for example during maintenance, after a security incident, or when the market is paused due to insufficient liquidity. Because the handlers do not re‑verify the market status, the transaction proceeds as if the market were active, allowing token swaps or ADL positions to be created on a market that should be inert. This breaks the business assumption that disabled markets cannot be interacted with, potentially leading to unexpected price exposure, loss of funds, or execution of trades at stale or manipulated rates. The impact is that users may see their swaps succeed on a market that is supposed to be offline, causing confusion (e.g., user expects the market to be disabled but the trade goes through) and exposing the protocol to economic risk. The issue is discovered during a manual audit of the controller logic, where the absence of a call to MarketUtils.getEnabledMarket was noted. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it simply behaves correctly from a technical standpoint while violating the intended state‑machine rules. The proper fix is to introduce an explicit enabled‑market check in both the swap and create‑ADL pathways, typically by retrieving the market properties through a utility that reverts when the market is disabled, and aborting the operation if the check fails. This aligns the implementation with the intended access‑control model and prevents execution on markets that are not meant to be active.

title: Denial-of-Service in the liquidation flow re-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that appears in the liquidation workflow of a lending protocol when an offer is created with an excessively high loan‑to‑value (LTV) parameter. The root cause is that the contract does not validate the magnitude of the LTV value, which can cause the internal share calculation to become zero or produce a value that overflows the arithmetic used in the price() function. When the share is zero, the price() routine attempts a division or modulo by zero; when the share is non‑zero but the LTV is astronomically large, the estimated value computation overflows. Both situations trigger a revert during the liquidation step, preventing the contract from completing the liquidation and leaving the collateral NFT locked inside the protocol forever. An attacker can exploit this by submitting an offer with a deliberately inflated LTV, allowing a borrower to obtain a loan that later cannot be liquidated, effectively freezing the collateral. The impact is that the borrower’s NFT never returns, the loan remains in an unresolved state, and the protocol loses the ability to enforce its risk model, which may erode user trust and lead to financial loss if the frozen asset cannot be recovered. The condition occurs only when the liquidation function calls price() on a loan whose parameters were derived from an offer with an out‑of‑range LTV; it is not triggered during normal borrowing or repayment paths. The affected parties include borrowers who expect their collateral to be returned after liquidation, lenders who rely on the protocol to recover assets, and the overall protocol which assumes that liquidation will always succeed. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Sherlock, who wrote a test case that supplied a borrow amount of 1e40 together with an LTV of 1e61, causing the share to be zero and the price() call to revert. The bug is subtle because the LTV field is user‑controlled and the overflow only manifests under extreme values that are not exercised in typical usage, making it easy to overlook without targeted testing. To remediate the problem, the borrowing logic should enforce a reasonable upper bound on LTV and ensure that the lender’s share is strictly greater than zero before proceeding. Additionally, the price() function should include explicit checks for division by zero and use safe arithmetic that caps values to prevent overflow. By treating this as a class of arithmetic‑overflow denial‑of‑service vulnerability, developers can apply generic safeguards such as input validation, safe‑math libraries, and invariant checks to avoid similar failures in other financial calculations.

title: Refunding logic with multiple deposits is first
description:
There is no accounting to keep track of which deposits are being used to pay bounties. This means that after all deposits have expired, the first user to refund their deposit will get more funds.
nager/Implementations/DepositManagerV1.sol#L171-L179
Available funds are simply calculated by taking the current balance of the bounty contract and subtracting the locked balance. This works well for single deposits but doesn't when there are multiple deposits from multiple funders. When this occurs it will cause a first mover take all situation.
Example: User A and User B both makes 10,000 USDC deposits to an Ongoing bounty, bringing the total funds of the bounty to 20,000 USDC. After some time the bounty is closed. By the time it's closed, it has paid out 10,000 USDC in awards leaving it with 10,000 USDC. User A and B both wait until their deposits are expired.
Now User A requests a refund from his deposit. This refunds all 10,000 USDC to User A leaving none for User B. As a result, User A has effectively forced User B to pay all the awards.
Reward logic is first mover take all
bug_full: Refund logic in the bounty contract does not keep per‑depositor accounting, so when several users have deposited funds and the bounty is later closed, the contract calculates the refundable amount as the contract balance minus the locked balance. This calculation works for a single deposit but becomes incorrect when multiple deposits exist. After the bounty pays out part of the rewards, the remaining balance is shared among the depositors. Because the contract does not record how much each depositor contributed, the first depositor who invokes the refund function receives the entire remaining balance, leaving the other depositors with zero refund. The vulnerability appears when at least two deposits are present, the bounty has been closed, some rewards have been paid, and the deposit lock period has expired. Users expect to receive back only their own contribution, but instead one user can take all leftover funds, effectively forcing the other contributors to bear the cost of the awards. This is an accounting or financial‑logic error that manifests as a first‑mover‑take‑all race condition. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the refund implementation and noticed that the available funds are derived from a global balance rather than per‑depositor records. The issue can be hard to notice because the refund function behaves correctly for a single depositor and the test suite may not include scenarios with multiple funders. The impact includes loss of funds for honest depositors, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential legal or reputational consequences. The proper fix is to maintain explicit accounting of total funded amount versus total paid amount and to track each depositor’s share, so that a refund distributes the remaining balance proportionally or equally among all eligible depositors rather than giving it all to the first caller.

title: Resizing the payout schedule with less items
bug_full: The contract allows an administrator to replace the payout schedule by providing a new array of payout amounts and a token address. In addition to the numeric schedule, three parallel metadata arrays – tierWinners, invoiceComplete and supportingDocumentsComplete – store per‑item information. The implementation creates new temporary arrays sized to the length of the new payout schedule and then copies the existing values from the old metadata arrays into the new ones using three separate for‑loops. The loops, however, iterate over the length of the original arrays (tierWinners.length, invoiceComplete.length, supportingDocumentsComplete.length) instead of the length of the newly allocated arrays. When the new schedule contains fewer items than the previous schedule, the old arrays are longer than the new ones. The loops therefore attempt to write beyond the bounds of the newly created arrays, causing a runtime exception and reverting the entire transaction. This bug manifests only when the schedule is resized to a smaller size; expanding the schedule works because the new arrays are at least as large as the old ones. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer attempted to shrink the schedule and observed an unexpected revert without an explicit error message. It can be hard to notice because the function otherwise appears to succeed for normal updates, and the revert does not expose which loop caused the failure. The impact is that the contract cannot be re‑configured to a reduced payout schedule, potentially locking the protocol in an undesired state and preventing future payouts that rely on a smaller schedule. Administrators, bounty participants and any downstream contracts that depend on the schedule may be affected because the contract cannot reflect the intended payment plan. The vulnerability belongs to the class of array‑index‑out‑of‑bounds or improper‑length handling bugs, where code assumes two arrays have identical lengths without verifying the relationship after a resize operation.
