From a user perspective the UI may show a successful schedule edit request but the transaction fails silently, leaving the schedule unchanged and possibly causing confusion such as “my schedule update did not go through” or “the system says my payout plan was saved but I still see the old amounts”. To fix the issue the copy loops must iterate only up to the minimum of the old and new array lengths, or they should copy from the old array into the new one using the new array’s length as the bound. This ensures that when the schedule is reduced, only the overlapping entries are transferred and no out‑of‑bounds write occurs, allowing the contract to accept smaller payout schedules safely.

title: useLoan doesn't allow liqudator to specifiy
description:
useLoan doesn't allow the liquidator to specify a max price they are will to pay for the collateral they are liquidating. On the surface this doesn't seem like an issue because the price is always decreasing due to the dutch auction. However this can be problematic if the chain the contracts are deployed suffers a reorg attack. This can place the transaction earlier than anticipated and therefore charge the user more than they meant to pay. On Ethereum this is unlikely but this is meant to be deployed on any compatible EVM chain many of which are frequently reorganized.
See summary.
Liquidator can be charged more than intended
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the loan liquidation routine where the function that executes a liquidation (useLoan) does not expose a parameter that lets the liquidator set a maximum acceptable price for the collateral being purchased. The root cause is that the contract assumes the Dutch‑auction price will only move downward, and therefore omits any slippage or price‑cap check. An attacker who can cause a blockchain reorganization can cause the liquidation transaction to be mined in an earlier block than originally intended. Because the auction price is higher in earlier blocks, the liquidator ends up paying more than the price they expected, effectively over‑paying for the collateral. This can be exploited by submitting a liquidation transaction with a gas price that makes it likely to be included in a block that is later re‑ordered, or by a malicious miner who deliberately reorders blocks. The impact is a financial loss for the liquidator, reduced profitability of the liquidation process, and potentially a distortion of the protocol’s incentive model. The condition occurs on any EVM‑compatible chain where block reorgs are common; on Ethereum the risk is low but on chains with frequent reorganizations the risk is material. The affected parties are liquidators, borrowers (who may see their collateral sold at an inflated price), and the protocol itself because the economic assumptions of the auction are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the loan contract where the liquidation flow was examined and the missing price‑cap parameter was noted. It is subtle because the price curve is monotonic decreasing, so developers may assume no protection is needed; the only visible symptom is that a liquidator receives a receipt showing a higher payment than anticipated, or that the profit margin is unexpectedly negative. The bug belongs to the class of “missing slippage protection” or “price‑cap omission” in auction‑based liquidation mechanisms. To remediate, the contract should be modified to accept a maximum price (or slippage tolerance) from the liquidator and revert the transaction if the current auction price exceeds that limit. This restores the expected economic behavior and prevents over‑payment caused by chain reorgs.

title: Adversary can utilize a large number of their
bug_full: The vulnerability is an interest‑distribution flaw in the loan contract’s sendInterests routine. The function calculates the amount to send to each provision by adding the provision’s principal to either a minimal‑interest share (interests / loan.nbOfPositions) when the loan is repaid early, or a proportional share (interests * provision.amount / loan.lent) otherwise. Because the minimal‑interest case divides the total minimal interest equally among all positions, an attacker can inflate the number of provisions by creating many of their own small provisions. By doing so, the denominator loan.nbOfPositions becomes large, causing each legitimate lender to receive only a tiny fraction of the minimal interest that was promised by the loan terms. The attack works only when the loan is repaid before the accrued interest exceeds the minimal‑interest threshold, i.e., when interests == loan.payment.minInterestsToRepay. In that scenario the contract treats the repayment as a “spam‑offer” anti‑DoS measure and distributes the minimal interest uniformly, regardless of the relative size of each provision. As a result, a lender who expects a 10 % APR on a 1000 USDC loan may receive as little as 1 % APR because the attacker has split the loan into ten provisions of 20 USDC each, each entitled to only 10 USDC of minimal interest, while the attacker’s own provisions capture the remaining 90 USDC. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a small interest payment (e.g., “interest received: 10 USDC”) instead of the expected larger amount, leading to confusion and perceived loss of yield. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the ClaimFacet.sol source by the auditor Sherlock, who noted that the division by loan.nbOfPositions is not bounded and that no check exists on the relative size of provisions. The flaw is subtle because the code appears to protect against spam offers, and the abnormal interest distribution only becomes visible when an attacker deliberately creates many provisions, a situation that may not occur in normal operation. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce that no single provision is disproportionately larger than others, or replace the equal‑share minimal‑interest formula with a proportional calculation based on each provision’s amount, and optionally cap the total number of provisions. Such changes would align the interest distribution with the economic expectations of lenders and prevent the dilution of legitimate interest payments.

title: minOfferCost can be bypassed in certain sce-
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the minimum‑interest guarantee that is intended to protect lenders from spam loan requests that would otherwise generate interest payouts smaller than the cost of claiming them. The contract stores a global value called minInterestsToRepay and checks it only when the total accrued interest exactly equals this threshold. If the accrued interest is greater than the threshold, the function sendInterests distributes the payout proportionally to each provision using the formula provision.amount + (interests * provision.amount) / loan.lent. Because the proportional formula is based on the absolute size of each provision rather than on the per‑position minimum, a provision that represents a very small fraction of the total loan can receive an amount that is below the guaranteed minimum. This situation arises when the loan has multiple provisions and at least one provision’s share is smaller than 1 / n, where n is the number of provisions. For example, with a minimum interest of 1e18 and two provisions of 25 % and 75 % of the loan, the total minimum interest is 2e18. If the accrued interest reaches 2.001e18, the proportional calculation gives 0.5e18 to the first provision and 1.5e18 to the second, violating the per‑position minimum of 1e18 for the first provision. An attacker can trigger this condition by creating many small provisions or by waiting until the interest just exceeds the minimum, causing some lenders to receive less interest than expected. The impact is that lenders may receive payouts that are lower than advertised, potentially making the loan unprofitable and opening the protocol to denial‑of‑service attacks where spam loans generate insufficient compensation. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the sendInterests function, where the conditional branch for interests == minInterestsToRepay was noted and the subsequent proportional calculation was examined. The issue is subtle because the contract appears to honor the minimum when the interest equals the threshold, but the guarantee disappears once the interest exceeds it, making the problem easy to miss in testing. To remediate the issue, the protocol should enforce a per‑provision minimum that is derived from the smallest allowed provision size, or restrict provision amounts so that no provision can be smaller than 1 / (2n) of the total loan. Alternatively, the payout formula could be adjusted to guarantee that each provision receives at least the minimum interest regardless of the overall interest level. This class of bug falls under incorrect financial guarantee enforcement and rounding errors in interest distribution, where the business logic that each lender must receive a minimum return is violated, leading to user‑facing symptoms such as “my interest payout is lower than expected” or “my balance shows zero when I should have received a refund.”

title: If auction price goes to 0, NFT might become
description:
There are certain ERC20 tokens which revert on zero value transfers (e.g. LEND). If an NFT's price drops down to 0, nobody will be able to claim it as the transaction will always revert.
The time of loan.auction.duration passes. The NFT's price is 0. Alice tries to purchase/ claim it, however the ERC20 token on which the auctions is going reverts on 0 value transfers. The NFT becomes stuck forever and no one can take the rights of it.
Consider the following scenarios: 1.
The ERC20 used in the auction is pausable. Throughout the auction, the token gets paused. Now, the auction is still going, the price is dropping and no one is able to claim it. The ERC20 doesn't get unpaused up until the auction ends. Since no one was able to purchase the NFT during the auction, its price now is 0. Since the token reverts on zero value transfers, the NFT is stuck forever.
2.
Alice is looking at NFT auction which is coming near its end. Alice is looking to purchase the NFT for as little as possible and starts monitoring the mempool, so in case someone tries to buy it, she can front-run the transaction and get the NFT herself. At this point Alice getting the NFT should be guaranteed. However, there aren't many other active users/ they aren't paying attention to said NFT. Little time goes by, auction ends and price is set to 0. Alice is happy she can claim the NFT for free. However, the token reverts on 0 value transfers and now no one can claim it and the NFT is lost forever.
NFT might be lost forever
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the auction mechanism that permits the winning price of an NFT to fall to zero while the contract still expects to transfer the payment token to the seller. Certain ERC20 tokens, such as LEND, are implemented to revert any transfer call with a value of zero. When the auction duration expires and the price calculation reaches zero, the claim function attempts to execute a token transfer of amount zero. Because the token’s transfer method explicitly rejects zero‑value transfers, the transaction reverts, preventing the transfer from completing. As a result the NFT remains locked inside the auction contract and cannot be claimed by any participant, effectively rendering the asset inaccessible. This situation can arise under normal price‑decay logic, when the token is paused during the auction, or when no bidder is willing to pay a positive amount and the price algorithm continues to decrease. The affected parties include bidders who expect to acquire the NFT for free, the original seller who cannot receive payment, and the protocol that loses the ability to enforce ownership transfer, potentially harming user trust and causing loss of value. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined token compatibility and edge‑case price handling. It is subtle because zero‑value transfers are often assumed to be no‑ops and therefore not explicitly guarded against, making the failure mode easy to overlook in testing. To remediate, the auction should enforce a minimum payable amount greater than zero (for example, one wei) or include a special case that bypasses the token transfer when the price is zero, or restrict the use of tokens that revert on zero transfers. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “zero‑value transfer reversion” errors that break business logic when a financial operation is expected to succeed with a zero amount, violating the accounting assumption that a zero price means a free claim rather than a transaction failure.

title: when issuer set new winner by calling set-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑reset omission in a tiered bounty contract that allows a new tier winner to inherit previously set verification flags and therefore bypass required invoice or supporting‑document checks. The contract stores boolean flags invoiceComplete[tier] and supportingDocumentsComplete[tier] that are set to true by an off‑chain oracle once the designated winner submits the required paperwork. When the bounty issuer calls setTierWinner to replace the winner of a given tier, the function only overwrites the tierWinners mapping and does not reset either of the verification flags. As a result, if the previous winner had already satisfied the invoice requirement, the flag remains true after the winner is changed, and the new winner can claim the prize without providing the invoice or supporting documents that the bounty rules demand. This flaw originates from the missing reset logic in setTierWinner and the reliance on external off‑chain state updates without a corresponding on‑chain invalidation step. An attacker who can act as the issuer, or who can convince the issuer to change the winner after the flags are set, can exploit the bug by selecting themselves (or another colluding address) as the new winner and immediately calling the claim function, receiving the payout while the contract believes the invoice requirement is already satisfied. The impact is that funds may be released without the intended compliance checks, breaking the accounting assumptions of the bounty program, potentially causing financial loss for the issuer and eroding trust in the protocol. The issue manifests only when the issuer changes a tier winner after the invoiceComplete or supportingDocumentsComplete flag for that tier has been marked true; it does not affect the initial winner selection flow. All parties that rely on the bounty’s verification process – the issuer, legitimate participants, and any downstream users of the protocol – are affected because the contract’s business logic no longer enforces the required documentation. The problem was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that setTierWinner updates only the winner mapping and does not touch the verification flags, a subtle state‑management bug that may be missed by functional tests that never change winners after verification. The bug is hard to notice because the UI typically shows only the current winner and the claim button, while the internal flags are hidden, so a user may see a prize being paid out without any request for an invoice, leading to confusion. To remediate, the setTierWinner function should explicitly reset invoiceComplete[tier] and supportingDocumentsComplete[tier] to false (or require a fresh verification step) whenever the winner is changed, ensuring that the new winner must satisfy all required conditions before receiving funds. This aligns the contract’s behavior with the intended business rule that each winner must independently provide the required documentation.

title: Adversary can block NFT distribution on tiered
description:
Bounties limit the number of NFT deposits to five. An adversary can block adding NFTs by assigning NFTs to tiers that don't exist.
nager/Implementations/DepositManagerV1.sol#L113-L131
DepositMangerV1#fundBountyNFT passes the user supplied _data to TieredBountyCore#receiveNft
plementations/TieredBountyCore.sol#L41-L42
_data is decoded and stored in _tier allowing the user to specify any tier they wish.
An adversary can abuse this fill all eligible nft deposit slots with nfts that can't be claimed by any tier. This allows them to effectively disable nft prizes for any tiered bounty. Using a large enough tier will make it impossible to ever claim the nfts because it would cost too much gas to set a large enough payout schedule
Adversary can effectively disable nft prizes for any tiered bounty
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked tier identifier in the NFT deposit flow of a tiered bounty contract. When a user calls the deposit function, the contract forwards a user‑supplied data blob to the core contract, which decodes the blob and stores the value as the target tier for the NFT. Because the core contract does not verify that the supplied tier index corresponds to an existing tier (i.e., it does not compare the index against the length of the tierWinners array), an attacker can deliberately specify a tier number that is outside the valid range. By repeatedly depositing NFTs with such out‑of‑range tier identifiers, the attacker can fill all five allowed NFT slots with tokens that are associated with a non‑existent tier. Once the slots are occupied, legitimate participants are unable to add NFTs that belong to real tiers, and the bounty’s NFT reward distribution becomes effectively blocked. From a user’s perspective the expected reward never appears; the UI may show that the bounty has reached its NFT limit while no claimable NFTs exist, leading to confusion and a perception that “funds disappear” or “rewards are missing”. The issue occurs whenever the deposit function is invoked with arbitrary data and the contract’s tier validation is omitted, which is the case in the current implementation. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the data handling path from DepositManagerV1#fundBountyNFT to TieredBountyCore#receiveNft. The problem is subtle because the tier field is not directly visible in the UI and the contract does not emit an explicit error when an invalid tier is used; instead the NFTs are silently stored in an unreachable bucket. The bug belongs to the class of “unchecked input leading to out‑of‑bounds state” and violates the business logic that each tier must have a bounded set of winners and associated rewards. To remediate, the core contract should enforce that the supplied tier index is less than the length of the tierWinners array (or otherwise within the defined tier range) before accepting the NFT, thereby preventing the creation of unreachable reward slots and preserving the intended distribution mechanism.

title: Adversary can break NFT distribution by de-
description:
Bounties limit the number of NFT deposits to five. An adversary can block adding NFTs by repeatedly depositing and withdrawing an NFT.
plementations/BountyCore.sol#L64-L93
All bounties use BountyCore#refundDeposit to process refunds to user. This simply transfers the NFT back to the funder but leaves the nftDeposit. This uses up the deposit limit which is current set to 5. Since the deposit cap is used up by deposits that have been refunded the slots can't be used to distribute legitimate NFTs to the bounty claimant.
Adversary can block legitimate NFT distribution
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical state‑management flaw in the bounty contract that limits each bounty to a maximum of five NFT deposits. When a user requests a refund, the contract’s refundDeposit function transfers the NFT back to the caller but fails to remove the corresponding entry from the internal nftDeposits storage. Because the deposit slot remains marked as occupied, the contract believes the deposit limit has been reached even though the NFT has left the contract. An adversary can exploit this by repeatedly depositing an NFT and immediately invoking the refund function, thereby consuming a slot each time. After five such cycles the deposit cap is exhausted, preventing any further legitimate NFT deposits and consequently blocking the distribution of reward NFTs to bounty claimants. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for the NFT reward mechanism: users who expect to receive a reward find that no slots are available, the UI may show “no NFTs left” or a claim transaction reverts, and the protocol’s promised functionality is broken. The issue occurs only when refunds are processed; it does not affect other asset transfers. It affects all participants of the bounty system – funders, claimants, and the protocol itself – because the core business logic assumes that a refunded NFT frees up a slot. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of BountyCore.sol where the refund logic was examined and the mismatch between token transfer and internal accounting was observed. The bug can be hard to notice because the outward‑facing behavior (the NFT is returned) appears correct, while the hidden accounting state silently fills up. To remediate, the refund function should delete the deposit identifier from nftDeposits and adjust any counters so that the slot becomes reusable, restoring the intended invariant that the number of active deposits never exceeds the configured limit.

title: Carousel.mintRollovers potentially mints 0 shares
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs in the rollover minting routine of a carousel‑style vault where a user‑submitted deposit is processed together with a relayer fee. When the amount of assets supplied for a queued rollover item is exactly equal to the relayer fee, the calculation that determines how many vault shares to mint results in zero shares because the net assets to mint are computed as deposited assets minus the relayer fee. This edge case causes the vault’s total value locked (TVL) for the affected epoch to remain zero. The contract later calls a previewWithdraw function that derives the entitled share amount by dividing the user’s assets by the epoch’s final TVL. With a final TVL of zero, the division triggers a revert due to a division‑by‑zero error. As a consequence the rollover queue cannot progress; the stuck item can only be removed manually by the queue owner, otherwise the queue remains frozen for the remainder of the epoch. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the mintRollovers loop and identified that the condition checking for sufficient assets only guards against assets being lower than the relayer fee, but does not prevent the case where assets equal the fee, leading to a zero‑share mint. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error when zero shares are minted; instead the failure manifests later as a revert in a seemingly unrelated previewWithdraw call, making it hard to trace back to the original minting step. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a transaction that appears to succeed, followed by a later withdrawal attempt that reverts with a division‑by‑zero error, and an apparent loss of balance where the user’s vault share balance remains zero despite having deposited assets. The root cause is an arithmetic edge case in the share‑minting formula combined with insufficient validation of the epoch’s TVL before invoking previewWithdraw. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce that the net assets to mint are strictly greater than zero, for example by checking that deposited assets exceed the relayer fee before proceeding, or by verifying that the epoch’s final TVL is non‑zero prior to calling previewWithdraw. Adding an explicit guard against zero‑share minting and handling the zero‑TVL scenario gracefully would prevent the queue from becoming permanently stuck and preserve the expected accounting guarantees of the vault.

title: Arbitrum sequencer downtime lasting before and beyond epoch expiry prevents triggering depeg
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the inability to trigger a depeg event when the Arbitrum sequencer experiences downtime that starts before an insurance epoch ends and continues past the epoch expiry. The contract’s triggerDepeg function obtains the current price of the pegged asset through getLatestPrice, which first checks the sequencer status via a Chainlink uptime feed. If the sequencer is reported as down, or if the grace period after it comes back up has not elapsed, getLatestPrice reverts with SequencerDown or GracePeriodNotOver. Because triggerDepeg relies on this price, any attempt to call it while the sequencer is down fails, preventing the depeg from being recorded. The protocol also provides a triggerEndEpoch function that can be called after the epoch expires. This function does not verify whether a depeg could have been triggered during the expiry window; it simply ends the epoch if the vault addresses are set. Consequently, a malicious participant controlling the collateral vault can wait until the sequencer is down, let the epoch expire, and then call triggerEndEpoch to close the epoch without a depeg. The contract then distributes the premium payments to the collateral vault, even though the insurance condition (price falling below the strike) could not be proven because the price oracle was unavailable. From the user’s perspective, premium‑vault participants see no insurance payout – their balance remains unchanged or becomes zero – while collateral‑vault participants unexpectedly receive the premium, creating a mismatch between expected and actual outcomes. The issue is a business‑logic flaw that assumes the price oracle will always be available at epoch boundaries, ignoring the edge case where the sequencer is down. It was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that getLatestPrice reverts on sequencer downtime and that triggerEndEpoch lacks any guard against this situation. The bug is hard to spot because it only manifests during a rare combination of sequencer outage and epoch expiry; under normal conditions the contracts behave correctly and no explicit error is shown to users. To remediate the problem, the protocol should introduce a post‑expiry challenge period during which anyone can submit evidence (e.g., Chainlink round IDs) that the sequencer was down and that the price crossed the strike, allowing a depeg claim before the epoch can be closed without a depeg. Additional checks in triggerEndEpoch to ensure that a depeg was either triggered or provably impossible would also close the loophole, restoring the intended accounting guarantees and preventing unfair premium extraction.

title: VaultFactoryV2#changeTreasury misconfigures the vault because the setTreasury subcall uses the wrong variable
bug_full: The vulnerability is a misconfiguration bug in the VaultFactoryV2.changeTreasury function where the contract updates the treasury address of a pair of vault contracts using the internal state variable treasury instead of the function argument _treasury. The root cause is a simple variable naming mistake: the sub‑calls IVaultV2(vaults[0]).setTreasury(treasury) and IVaultV2(vaults[1]).setTreasury(treasury) reference the factory’s stored treasury address rather than the new address supplied by the caller. Because the function is protected by a timelock, the incorrect treasury address can remain in place for at least three days before it can be corrected, and the bug is not obvious from the emitted AddressWhitelisted event or the whitelist calls that succeed. An attacker does not need to exploit the bug directly; the issue manifests when the controller contract later attempts to distribute premium and collateral fees via premiumVault.sendTokens and collateralVault.sendTokens, which rely on the vaults’ treasury address to receive funds. Since the vaults were configured with the wrong treasury, the token transfer sub‑calls can fail, causing the triggerDepeg routine to abort. This failure prevents time‑sensitive depeg payouts from being executed, meaning users who are entitled to a refund or premium may receive nothing, see their balances unchanged, or experience a zero‑payout UI message. The impact is that valid depegs are missed, funds become effectively locked, and the protocol’s financial guarantees are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Sherlock team, and it can be hard to notice because the function appears to perform the expected whitelist and emits an event, while the incorrect variable usage does not trigger a revert. To remediate, the setTreasury calls should be changed to pass the _treasury argument, ensuring the vaults are configured with the intended treasury address. Conceptually, the fix restores correct parameter propagation and eliminates the logic error that caused the accounting mismatch between expected and actual treasury destinations.

title: Null epochs will freeze rollovers
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the rollover mechanism of a vault that allows users to carry forward a position from one epoch to the next. The contract checks whether a user has received a payout in the previous epoch before minting new shares for the rollover. The check is implemented as `if (entitledShares > queue[index].assets)`, which only permits minting when the calculated entitled shares are strictly greater than the assets that were originally locked. In normal epochs a payout reduces the user’s assets, so entitledShares exceeds the original amount and the condition passes. However, when a null epoch occurs – an epoch in which no payout is generated because there were no qualifying participants or the vault deliberately skips a payout – the entitledShares value equals the original assets. Because the condition requires a strict greater‑than relationship, the check fails, preventing the minting of rollover shares. As a result, the rollover process halts after the null epoch, effectively freezing the user’s position and preventing any further rollovers. The impact is that users who expected their position to continue automatically find their funds locked in the vault with no way to advance to the next epoch, leading to a loss of expected earnings and potential liquidity issues. The bug is triggered only when a null epoch is produced, which may be rare and therefore easy to miss during testing; the logic appears correct for typical epochs, so the failure mode is subtle. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the `Carousel.sol` contract, where the auditor noticed that the condition does not account for the case where entitledShares equals assets. The problem belongs to the class of off‑by‑one or boundary‑condition errors in financial state transitions, where a comparison operator does not correctly handle equality cases. From a user’s perspective the UI would show that the rollover button is disabled or that the transaction reverts, while the user expects the position to roll over automatically and may see their balance remain unchanged across epochs. To fix the issue the comparison should be relaxed to allow equality, i.e., `if (entitledShares >= queue[index].assets)`, ensuring that rollovers continue even when no payout occurs in the previous epoch. This change aligns the contract logic with the intended business rule that a null epoch should not interrupt the continuity of a position.

title: Inconsistent use of epochBegin could lock user funds
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race‑condition caused by inconsistent handling of the epoch start timestamp (epochBegin) in two separate parts of the contract. One function, triggerNullEpoch, checks that the current block timestamp is strictly less than epochStart and reverts if the epoch has already begun, while a modifier used by the deposit function checks that the timestamp is strictly greater than epochBegin and reverts if the epoch has already started. Because the two checks treat the equality case differently, both functions can be executed in the same block when block.timestamp equals epochBegin. In that scenario an attacker (or any user) can call triggerNullEpoch first, which records a final total value locked (finalTVL) for the epoch, and then call deposit in the same block. The deposit succeeds and increases the pool’s TVL, but finalTVL remains unchanged because it was already set by triggerNullEpoch. When emissions are later calculated, the contract divides the allocated emissions by finalTVL. If finalTVL is zero or does not reflect the newly deposited assets, the division either yields an incorrect (often zero) emission amount or triggers a division‑by‑zero revert. The withdraw function then attempts to transfer both the user’s shares and the calculated emissions; if the emission calculation reverts, the whole withdraw call fails, effectively locking the user’s deposited assets in the contract. This bug manifests only when the epoch begins exactly at the block timestamp and the two calls happen in the same block, making it hard to notice during normal testing because each function works correctly in isolation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the logical conditions of the epoch checks and identified the mismatch. It belongs to the class of temporal logic bugs where boundary conditions are handled inconsistently, leading to state‑inconsistent updates and arithmetic errors. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a deposit that appears successful, followed by a withdrawal that either returns zero emissions or reverts with an error, leaving the user’s balance unchanged or appearing as “funds disappear”. The business logic that assumes emissions are proportionally distributed based on the final TVL is violated, breaking accounting guarantees. The recommended remediation is to make the epochHasNotStarted modifier use a greater‑than‑or‑equal comparison (>=) so that the equality case is handled consistently, or to restructure the epoch lifecycle to ensure finalTVL is updated after any deposits that occur at the epoch start. This change prevents the race condition, ensures correct emission calculations, and eliminates the possibility of funds becoming permanently unwithdrawable.

title: Non-whitelisted tokens cannot be added if the token limit is reached
description:
Non-whitelisted tokens cannot be deposited to a bounty contract if too many whitelisted contracts were deposited.
The DepositManagerV1.fundBountyToken function allows depositing both whitelisted and non-whitelisted tokens by implementing the following check:
1. if a token is whitelisted, it can be deposited without restrictions;
2. if a token is not whitelisted, it cannot be deposited if openQTokenWhitelist.TOKEN_ADDRESS_LIMIT tokens have already been deposited.
However, while the token addresses limit requirement is only applied to non-whitelisted tokens, whitelisted tokens also increase the counter of token addresses: both non-whitelisted and whitelisted token addresses are added to the tokenAddresses set.
Bounty minters may not be able to deposit non-whitelisted tokens after they have deposited multiple whitelisted ones.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mis‑implemented token address limit in the bounty contract’s DepositManagerV1.fundBountyToken function. The contract is designed to allow unlimited deposits of whitelisted tokens while restricting the number of distinct non‑whitelisted token addresses that can be deposited, using a constant TOKEN_ADDRESS_LIMIT. However, the implementation adds every token address—whether whitelisted or not—to a single tokenAddresses set and then applies the limit check only to non‑whitelisted tokens. As a result, each whitelisted token also increments the global counter, and once the combined count reaches the configured limit, any subsequent attempt to deposit a non‑whitelisted token is rejected. This logic flaw can be exploited by an attacker who first deposits enough whitelisted tokens to fill the limit, thereby preventing legitimate users from adding their own custom or non‑whitelisted tokens to a bounty. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the token‑deposit functionality: users expecting to fund a bounty with a specific token receive a transaction that reverts or is silently ignored, leaving their balances unchanged and causing the bounty to remain unfunded with the desired asset. The condition occurs whenever the total number of distinct token addresses stored in the contract reaches TOKEN_ADDRESS_LIMIT, regardless of their whitelist status. Affected parties include bounty minters, token issuers, and any participants relying on the ability to deposit arbitrary assets into the bounty system. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended business rule (limit applies only to non‑whitelisted tokens) with the actual state‑tracking logic. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit a distinct error for whitelisted versus non‑whitelisted rejections, and the limit appears to work correctly for whitelisted tokens, masking the hidden restriction on other tokens. To remediate, the contract should maintain separate accounting for whitelisted token addresses or exclude them from the tokenAddresses set used in the limit comparison, ensuring that only non‑whitelisted token counts contribute to the enforcement of TOKEN_ADDRESS_LIMIT. This adjustment restores the intended behavior where whitelisted tokens are unrestricted and non‑whitelisted tokens are limited only by the explicit cap, eliminating the unintended denial‑of‑service scenario.

title: Malicious user can make rolloverQueue never be processed
description:
rolloverQueue is shared by all epochs. For each round of epoch, mintRollovers will process rolloverQueue from the beginning. A normal user calls enlistInRollover to enter the rolloverQueue, and in the next round of epoch, he will call delistInRollover to exit the rolloverQueue. In this case, rolloverQueue.length is acceptable. However, malicious user can make the rolloverQueue.length huge, causing the relayer to consume a huge amount of gas for every round of epoch.
Carousel will send relayerFee to relayer in order to encourage external relayer to call mintRollovers. Malicious user can make external relayer unwilling to call mintRollovers. Ultimately, rolloverQueue will never be processed.
Let's assume the following scenario:
relayerFee is 1e18. The current epochId is E1, and the next epochId is E2. At present, rolloverQueue has 10 normal user QueueItem. Bob has deposited 1000e18 assets before the start of E1, so balanceOf(bob, E1) = 1000e18.
1. Bob creates 1000 addresses, each address has setApprovalForAll bob. He calls two functions for each address:
Carousel.safeTransferFrom(bob, eachAddress, E1, 1e18)
Carousel.enlistInRollover(E1, 1e18, eachAddress), 1e18 equal to minRequiredDeposit.
2. rolloverQueue.length equals to 1010(1000+10).
These 1000 addresses will never call delistInRollover to exit the rolloverQueue, so no matter whether these addresses win or lose, their QueueItem will always be in the rolloverQueue. In each round of epoch, the relayer has to process at least 1000 QueueItems, and these QueueItems are useless. Malicious users only need to do it once to cause permanent affects.
When a normal user loses in a certain round of epoch, he may not call delistInRollover to exit the rolloverQueue. For example, he left the platform and stopped playing. In this case, rolloverQueue.length will become larger and larger as time goes by.
Carousel contract will not send any relayerFee to the relayer, because these useless QueueItem will not increase the value rthquake/src/v2/Carousel/Carousel.sol#L447). Obviously, calling mintRollovers has no benefit for the relayer. Therefore, no relayer is willing to do this.
The relayer consumes a huge amount of gas for calling mintRollovers for each round of epoch. In other words, as long as the rolloverQueue is unacceptably long, it is a permanent DOS.
bug_full: Thevulnerability stems from the contract using a single, global rolloverQueue array that stores all pending rollover requests across every epoch. When a round of an epoch finishes, the mintRollovers function iterates from the beginning of this array to process each QueueItem. A normal user enlists in the queue, then later delists to remove their entry, keeping the queue length manageable. However, a malicious actor can flood the queue with a large number of dummy entries by creating many addresses, approving the main account, transferring the minimum required deposit to each address and calling enlistInRollover for each one. Because these dummy entries never call delistInRollover, they remain in the queue indefinitely. The relayer that is incentivised to call mintRollovers receives a fixed relayerFee that is calculated based on the number of useful QueueItems processed. When the queue is filled with thousands of useless items, the gas required to iterate over the entire array grows dramatically while the fee does not increase, making the call unprofitable for any external relayer. Consequently, relayers stop invoking mintRollovers, the rolloverQueue is never processed, and the protocol enters a permanent denial‑of‑service state where rollover operations cannot be completed. This affects all participants: normal users cannot have their assets rolled over to the next epoch, relayers lose expected revenue, and the overall protocol may halt, breaking business logic that assumes rollovers are always executed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the queue handling logic and fee model. It is subtle because the queue length appears normal under regular usage, and the gas cost is only revealed when the queue is artificially inflated, making the problem easy to overlook in routine testing. The root cause is the lack of per‑epoch segregation and cleanup of the rollover data structure, combined with a fee mechanism that does not account for processing overhead. To remediate, the queue should be restructured into a mapping from epoch identifiers to separate arrays (or other bounded data structures), allowing the mintRollovers function to process only the relevant epoch’s items and preventing a single epoch from being poisoned by unrelated entries. Additional safeguards such as queue length caps, pruning of stale entries, or dynamic fee adjustments could further mitigate the risk.

title: User deposit may never be entertained from deposit queue
bug_full: The contract maintains a depositQueue that is processed by a relayer using a loop that iterates from the end of the array towards the beginning, effectively implementing a FILO (first‑in‑last‑out) stack. When the queue length grows beyond a small threshold (the code limits processing to the last ten entries), the loop stops after handling the most recent deposits and never reaches the earliest entries. As a result, a deposit that was the first element in the queue can remain forever at the front of the list if new deposits keep arriving faster than the relayer can process the whole queue. The root cause is the combination of the while condition "(length - _operations) <= i" and the decrementing index, which together prevent the loop from traversing the full array when the queue is large. An attacker does not need to act actively; the issue is triggered simply by a high volume of deposits that outpace the relayer’s processing cadence. The impact is that the affected user never receives the minted shares that should correspond to their deposit, their balance in the contract stays unchanged, and the funds stay locked in the depositQueue indefinitely. From the user’s point of view the UI shows a successful deposit transaction but later shows no increase in share balance or any receipt of tokens, creating the impression that the funds have vanished. The problem occurs whenever the deposit queue length exceeds the number of entries the relayer processes in one call and additional deposits are added before the relayer can finish a full sweep. All depositors are potentially affected, especially those who deposit early during periods of high traffic, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about every deposit being eventually minted are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the queue‑processing function, where the auditor noticed that the loop logic favoured recent entries and that early entries could be skipped. It is hard to notice in normal testing because small queues behave correctly and the bug only manifests under load. To remediate the issue the contract should either switch to a FIFO (first‑in‑first‑out) processing model, increase the number of entries processed per call, or expose a user‑controlled dequeue function that allows a depositor to remove or trigger processing of their own entry regardless of its position in the queue. Implementing any of these fixes would ensure that every deposit is eventually processed and that users receive the shares they expect.

title: changeTreasury() Lack of check and remove old
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the changeTreasury function that is intended to replace the treasury address for a given market. The implementation fails to verify that the new treasury address differs from the current one and mistakenly calls setTreasury with a contract‑level variable instead of the supplied _treasury argument. Moreover, the function does not remove the previous treasury from the vault whitelist before adding the new address. As a result, if the caller supplies the same address as the current treasury, the whitelist call may unintentionally revoke the whitelist status of that address, leaving the market without a valid treasury. When a different address is supplied, the old treasury remains whitelisted, meaning it retains permission to interact with the vaults and potentially withdraw or manage funds that should now be controlled by the new treasury. This flaw can be exploited by an attacker who either re‑uses the existing treasury address to cause the whitelist to be cleared, or by a malicious former treasury holder who continues to have whitelist privileges after a legitimate change, allowing unauthorized fund movements. The impact includes loss of control over market funds, unexpected zero balances for users, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that only the designated treasury may receive fees or perform privileged actions. The issue manifests whenever changeTreasury is called, which is gated only by the onlyTimeLocker modifier; no additional checks prevent misuse. All participants that rely on the treasury – protocol operators, market creators, and end‑users – are affected because the treasury’s authority is either unintentionally removed or improperly retained. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the control flow of treasury updates and identified missing validation and cleanup steps. It can be hard to notice because the function emits a successful event even when the whitelist state is incorrect, and the contract does not revert on the duplicate‑address case, leading to silent misconfiguration. The proper remediation is to add a check that the new treasury differs from the current one, explicitly revoke the old treasury’s whitelist status on both vaults, and invoke setTreasury with the supplied _treasury parameter. This ensures that only the intended address holds whitelist privileges and that the treasury role is correctly transferred without leaving residual permissions.

title: mintRollovers should require entitledShares
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the mintRollovers function where the contract decides whether to perform a rollover based on a fee‑coverage check. The code currently compares the queued asset amount (queue[index].assets) with the relayer fee and, if the queued amount is insufficient, it skips the rollover for that user. However, the actual amount that the user is entitled to receive – entitledShares – can be larger than the queued amount while still being sufficient to cover the relayer fee. Because the function uses the wrong variable for the fee check, it may incorrectly skip a rollover even when the user has enough shares to pay the fee. The same mistake propagates to the calculation of assetsToMint, where the contract subtracts the relayer fee from queue[index].assets instead of from entitledShares. As a result, a user who is already profitable may see the expected minting operation omitted, receiving no new tokens or refunds despite meeting the fee requirement. This discrepancy appears to the user as a missing payout or a zero balance after a rollover, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that entitledShares represent the user’s claim. The issue occurs only in scenarios where entitledShares exceeds the queued asset amount but is still greater than or equal to the relayer fee, a condition that may not be exercised in typical test suites, making the bug hard to notice. It was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who observed that the fee‑coverage logic did not align with the definition of entitledShares. The bug does not enable direct theft of funds, but it leads to incorrect business logic where users lose expected earnings. To remediate, the fee check and the assetsToMint computation should be rewritten to use entitledShares instead of queue[index].assets, ensuring that the rollover proceeds whenever the user’s actual entitled amount can cover the relayer fee.

title: Vault Factory ownership can be changed instantly
bug_full: The vulnerability is an ownership‑change bypass that defeats the intended timelock protection in the VaultFactoryV2 contract. The contract inherits OpenZeppelin Ownable, which exposes a public transferOwnership function guarded only by the onlyOwner modifier. Although the contract defines a changeOwner function that is restricted to a timelock contract via onlyTimeLocker, it never overrides or disables the inherited transferOwnership function. As a result, the current owner (or any address that gains control of the owner key) can call transferOwnership directly and replace the owner address in a single transaction, without waiting for the configured delay period. This happens because the access control for ownership change is split between two functions with different modifiers, creating a conflict where the more permissive path remains reachable. An attacker who compromises the owner key can instantly seize control, reconfigure markets, change oracles, whitelist malicious controllers, or otherwise manipulate critical protocol parameters. Users of the protocol expect that any critical change will be delayed, giving them time to react, but the bypass makes the delay ineffective, leading to a situation where funds may be redirected or protocol rules altered before users can intervene. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the declared security model (timelock‑only changes) with the actual Solidity inheritance hierarchy and modifier usage. It can be hard to notice because the changeOwner function appears to enforce the correct policy, while the inherited transferOwnership function is hidden behind the OpenZeppelin library and may not be examined closely. To remediate, the contract should override transferOwnership and restrict it to the timelock contract (e.g., by adding onlyTimeLocker), or remove the public onlyOwner version entirely, ensuring that ownership can only be transferred through the delayed mechanism. This class of bug is an access‑control misconfiguration that allows privilege escalation and violates the business assumption that critical governance actions are subject to a time‑based safety window. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show a pending ownership change that should take hours or days, yet the owner switches instantly, causing unexpected loss of control and potentially leading to missing refunds, zeroed balances, or other abnormal behavior.

title: function lockCapital() doesn't filter the expired
description: when a lending loan defaults, then function lockCapital() get called in the ProtectionPool to lock required funds for the protections bought for that lending pool, but code doesn't filter the expired protections first and they may be expired protection in the active protection array that are not excluded and this would cause code to lock more fund and pay fund for expired defaulted protections and protection sellers would lose more funds. This lockCapital() code: ```solidity function lockCapital(address _lendingPoolAddress) external payable override onlyDefaultStateManager whenNotPaused returns (uint256 _lockedAmount, uint256 _snapshotId) { /// step 1: Capture protection pool's current investors by creating a snapshot of the token balance by using ERC20Snapshot in SToken _snapshotId = _snapshot(); /// step 2: calculate total capital to be locked LendingPoolDetail storage lendingPoolDetail = lendingPoolDetails[ _lendingPoolAddress ]; /// Get indexes of active protection for a lending pool from the storage EnumerableSetUpgradeable.UintSet storage activeProtectionIndexes = lendingPoolDetail .activeProtectionIndexes; /// Iterate all active protections and calculate total locked amount for this lending pool /// 1. calculate remaining principal amount for each loan protection in the lending pool. /// 2. for each loan protection, lockedAmt = min(protectionAmt, remainingPrincipal) /// 3. total locked amount = sum of lockedAmt for all loan protections uint256 _length = activeProtectionIndexes.length(); for (uint256 i; i < _length; ) { /// Get protection info from the storage uint256 _protectionIndex = activeProtectionIndexes.at(i); ProtectionInfo storage protectionInfo = protectionInfos[_protectionIndex]; /// Calculate remaining principal amount for a loan protection in the lending pool uint256 _remainingPrincipal = poolInfo .referenceLendingPools .calculateRemainingPrincipal( _lendingPoolAddress, protectionInfo.buyer, protectionInfo.purchaseParams.nftLpTokenId ); /// Locked amount is minimum of protection amount and remaining principal uint256 _protectionAmount = protectionInfo .purchaseParams .protectionAmount; uint256 _lockedAmountPerProtection = _protectionAmount < _remainingPrincipal ? _protectionAmount : _remainingPrincipal; _lockedAmount += _lockedAmountPerProtection; unchecked { ++i; } } unchecked { /// step 3: Update total locked & available capital in storage if (totalSTokenUnderlying < _lockedAmount) { /// If totalSTokenUnderlying < _lockedAmount, then lock all available capital _lockedAmount = totalSTokenUnderlying; totalSTokenUnderlying = 0; } else { /// Reduce the total sToken underlying amount by the locked amount totalSTokenUnderlying -= _lockedAmount; } } } ``` As you can see code loops through active protection array for that lending pool and calculates required locked amount but it doesn't call _accruePremiumAndExpireProtections() to make sure active protections doesn't include any expired protections. if function _accruePremiumAndExpireProtections() doesn't get called for a while, then there would be possible that some of the protections are expired and they are still in the active protection array. This would cause code to calculated more locked amount and also pay fund for those expired defaulted protections too from protection sellers. (also when calculating the required token payment for the protection code doesn't check the expiration too in the other functions that are get called by the lockCapital(), the expire check doesn't exists in inner function too) see summery.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the lockCapital function of the ProtectionPool contract, which is responsible for locking the required amount of capital when a lending loan defaults. The function iterates over the activeProtectionIndexes set to calculate the total amount that must be locked, but it fails to remove or ignore protections that have already expired. The root cause is the omission of a call to the internal routine _accruePremiumAndExpireProtections, which updates the active set by expiring outdated protections. Because expired entries remain in the active list, the calculation includes their protectionAmount even though they are no longer valid. An attacker or any party that triggers a default after the expiration period can cause lockCapital to lock more funds than necessary, effectively draining capital from the pool and forcing protection sellers to pay for protections that should have expired. This over‑locking can lead to a situation where the total underlying sToken balance is reduced to zero, leaving legitimate protection buyers without the expected coverage and causing the pool to lose liquidity. The issue manifests when a loan defaults while the expiration routine has not been executed for a while, and the contract is in an unpaused state with the onlyDefaultStateManager modifier allowing the call. Users experience symptoms such as their protection token balance decreasing unexpectedly, refunds or payouts being zero despite having paid premiums, or the pool’s available capital disappearing. The bug is a business‑logic flaw that stems from stale state data: the contract relies on an outdated active protection array without filtering out expired entries, violating accounting assumptions that only active protections should contribute to locked capital. It was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noted that the function does not invoke the expiration logic before performing the aggregation. The problem can be hard to notice because the function appears to perform its intended calculations and does not revert; the incorrect over‑locking only becomes visible under specific default scenarios. To remediate, the contract should invoke _accruePremiumAndExpireProtections (or an equivalent expiration check) before iterating over active protections, or explicitly skip entries whose expiration timestamp has passed, ensuring that only valid, unexpired protections are considered when locking capital.

title: ControllerPeggedAssetV2: outdated price may
description: prices may be used. The following checks are performed for the chainlink price feed: trollers/ControllerPeggedAssetV2.sol#L299-L315 As you can see the updatedAt timestamp is not checked. So the price may be outdated. The price that is used by the Controller can be outdated. This means that a depeg event may be caused due to an outdated price which is incorrect. Only current prices must be used to check for a depeg event.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an outdated price feed usage in the ControllerPeggedAssetV2 contract. The contract reads a Chainlink price feed but never validates the updatedAt timestamp, meaning the price returned may be arbitrarily old. The root cause is the absence of a freshness check; the code extracts the price, startedAt and answeredInRound values but ignores the updatedAt field, so a stale price can be accepted as current. An attacker or any external condition that causes the Chainlink oracle to stop updating (for example a network outage or a deliberate feed pause) can leave the stored price unchanged for an extended period. When the controller later evaluates a de‑peg condition, it will compare the stale price against the target peg. Because the price is not recent, the comparison can incorrectly signal a de‑peg event even though the market price is still stable. This false de‑peg can trigger protocol‑wide actions such as liquidation, collateral seizure, or emergency shutdown, effectively freezing user funds or causing unnecessary loss. The issue manifests whenever the price feed becomes stale and the controller’s de‑peg check runs, which may be sporadic and hard to reproduce. All participants who rely on the controller – token holders, lenders, borrowers, and any downstream contracts – are affected because they may see their balances reduced, withdrawals blocked, or collateral liquidated without a genuine market event. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who inspected the price‑retrieval function and noticed that the updatedAt value was never compared to block.timestamp. Because the contract does not emit any warning about stale data, the bug can remain hidden until a de‑peg is incorrectly triggered, making it difficult to diagnose from the UI where users simply observe a sudden loss of funds or a “de‑peg” flag. The correct mitigation is to treat this as a price‑staleness check: define a reasonable time window (for example a few minutes) and revert the transaction if updatedAt is older than block.timestamp minus that limit. By enforcing a freshness constraint, the controller will only act on recent, trustworthy prices, preserving the intended business logic that de‑peg events reflect real market movements rather than outdated oracle data.

title: ControllerPeggedAssetV2: triggerEndEpochfunc-
description: tion can be called even if epoch is null epoch leading to loss of funds An epoch can be resolved in three ways which correspond to the three functions available in the Controller: triggerDepeg, triggerEndEpoch, triggerNullEpoch. The issue is that triggerEndEpoch can be called even though triggerNullEpoch should be called. "Null epoch" means that any of the two vaults does not have funds deposited. In this case the epoch should be resolved with triggerNullEpoch such that funds are not transferred from the premium vault to the collateral vault. So in triggerEndEpoch is should be checked whether the conditions for a null epoch apply. If that's the case, the triggerEndEpoch function should revert. The assumption the code makes is that if the null epoch applies, triggerNullEpoch will be called before the end timestamp of the epoch which is when triggerEndEpoch can be called. This is not necessarily true. triggerNullEpoch might not be called in time (e.g. because the epoch duration is very short or simply nobody calls it) and then the triggerEndEpoch function can be called which sends the funds from the premium vault into the collateral vault: trollers/ControllerPeggedAssetV2.sol#L172-L192 If the premium vault is the vault which has funds and the collateral vault does not, then the funds sent to the collateral vault are lost. Loss of funds for users that have deposited into the premium vault.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the epoch‑resolution logic of the ControllerPeggedAssetV2 contract. The contract defines three functions that can close an epoch: triggerDepeg, triggerEndEpoch and triggerNullEpoch. A "null epoch" occurs when one of the two vaults – the premium vault or the collateral vault – holds no assets for the given epoch. In that situation the protocol is supposed to call triggerNullEpoch, which simply marks the epoch as resolved without moving any funds. However, the implementation of triggerEndEpoch does not verify whether a null epoch condition is present. It assumes that triggerNullEpoch will always be invoked before the epoch’s end timestamp, an assumption that is not guaranteed. Consequently, if the null‑epoch condition is true and nobody calls triggerNullEpoch in time (for example because the epoch duration is very short or because no participant triggers the call), an attacker or any external caller can invoke triggerEndEpoch after the epoch end. The function will then transfer the total assets from the premium vault into the collateral vault even though the collateral vault has a zero balance. Because the collateral vault is expected to hold collateral, the transferred funds become unrecoverable, effectively disappearing from the protocol. Users who deposited into the premium vault therefore see their balances reduced to zero or receive no payout, contrary to the expectation that their funds are either returned or used as collateral. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who noted that the missing guard allows the function to be called in an invalid state. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the bug only manifests when a vault’s TVL is zero, a condition that may not occur frequently and does not produce an explicit error. The proper fix is to add a guard at the start of triggerEndEpoch that checks both vaults for non‑zero total assets for the epoch and reverts with a clear error (for example VaultZeroTVL) when a null epoch is detected, thereby forcing callers to use triggerNullEpoch for those cases. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of state‑validation errors where a function proceeds without confirming that pre‑conditions hold, leading to unintended fund movement and loss of accounting integrity.

title: Controller doesn't send treasury funds to the
description: The Controller contract sends treasury funds to its own immutable treasury address instead of sending the funds to the one stored in the respective vault contract. Each vault has a treasury address that is assigned on deployment which can also be updated through the factory contract: But, the Controller, responsible for sending the fees to the treasury, uses the immutable treasury address that it was initialized with: It's not possible to have different treasury addresses for different vaults. It's also not possible to update the treasury address of a vault although it has a function to do that. Funds will always be sent to the address the Controller was initialized with.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a misrouting of treasury fees caused by the Controller contract using a fixed, immutable treasury address that was set at the time the Controller was deployed. The root cause is that the Controller does not query the associated Vault contract for the current treasury address, even though each Vault stores its own treasury address that can be changed through the factory. Because the Controller always references its own hard‑coded address, any attempt to update a Vault’s treasury address – or to deploy multiple Vaults with distinct treasury destinations – has no effect on where the fees are sent. An attacker or a protocol maintainer could change a Vault’s treasury address expecting the fees to be redirected, but the Controller will continue to forward the funds to the original address, effectively leaving the intended treasury empty. This can be exploited by deploying a Vault with a legitimate treasury, then later updating the Vault’s treasury to a malicious address; the Controller will still send the fees to the original address, causing the malicious address to never receive the expected revenue, while the original address continues to collect fees. The impact is that protocol revenue may be locked in an unintended account, vault owners may see their treasury balances remain zero despite fee accrual, and users may notice that expected refunds or payouts never arrive. The condition under which this occurs is any situation where the Vault’s treasury address differs from the Controller’s immutable address – either because multiple Vaults are used or because the Vault’s treasury has been updated after deployment. All parties that rely on correct fee distribution – the protocol, vault operators, and end‑users – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the Controller’s fee‑sending logic with the Vault’s treasury management functions and noticed the hard‑coded reference. It is subtle because the transaction succeeds; there is no revert or error, only a silent misdirection of funds, making it easy to overlook in testing. To remediate, the Controller should retrieve the treasury address from the Vault at the moment of fee transfer, or maintain a mapping of Vault‑to‑treasury addresses that can be updated in sync with the Vault’s own setter function. This change ensures that fees are always sent to the currently configured treasury, preserving the intended accounting and preventing funds from disappearing into an unexpected address.

title: Stuck emissions for nullified epochs
description: If either the premium and / or collateral vault has 0 TVL for an epoch with emissions, those emissions will not be withdrawable by anyone. The finalTVL set for a vault with 0 TVL (epoch will be nullified) will be 0. As a result, emissions that were allocated to that vault are not withdrawable by anyone. It's admittedly unlikely to happen since the emissionsToken is expected to be Y2K which has value and is tradeable. Emissions cannot be recovered.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of reward emissions for epochs in which a vault’s total value locked (TVL) is zero. When an epoch is created with a non‑zero emissions allocation but the associated premium or collateral vault reports a TVL of zero, the protocol marks the epoch as nullified and records a finalTVL of zero for that vault. Because the accounting logic ties withdrawable emissions to the finalTVL, a zero finalTVL causes the allocated emissions to become permanently inaccessible – no participant can claim them and the tokens remain locked in the contract. This situation can arise when the emissions token, although expected to have market value (e.g., Y2K), is paired with a vault that has no underlying assets at the epoch boundary. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the epoch finalisation and reward distribution code, where the auditor noticed that the withdrawal path checks only for a positive finalTVL before allowing a claim. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error or revert; instead, it silently records a nullified epoch, leading users to believe that rewards will be claimable later. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that after an epoch ends, the expected reward balance remains unchanged or appears as zero, even though the protocol’s dashboard shows that emissions were allocated for that period. The impact is a loss of potentially valuable tokens for any user who relied on the emissions, effectively “funds disappear” for that epoch. The problem affects any participant who interacts with a vault that can reach a zero TVL state, including liquidity providers and protocol treasury managers. Additionally, an edge case exists where both premium and collateral vaults are empty; the current logic only marks the collateral vault as nullified, leaving the premium vault in an inconsistent state. To remediate, the contract should include a recovery mechanism that detects nullified epochs and redirects the unclaimed emissions back to a treasury or a designated safety pool, and it should ensure that both vaults are correctly marked when they are simultaneously empty. This aligns the accounting model with the business expectation that allocated emissions are either claimable or safely reclaimed, preserving the integrity of the reward distribution system.

title: Protection can be bought in late pools, allow multiple times
description:
A buyer can buy a protection for a pool that's already late on a payment. The buyer can pay the minimal premium and get a higher chance of getting a compensation. Protection sellers may bear higher losses due to reduced premium amounts and the increased chance of protection payments.
The protocol allows lenders on Goldfinch to get an insurance on the funds they lent. The insurance is paid after a repayment was late. The protocol doesn’t allow protection buyers to buy protections for pools that’s already late to disallow buyers abusing the protections payment mechanism. To do this, the _verifyLendingPoolIsActive function checks the current status of a pool and reverts if it’s late.
However, poolStatus is cached and can be outdated when the function is called, since it's not updated in the call. Pool statuses are updated in assessStates and assessStateBatch, which are triggered on schedule separately. This allows buyers to buy protections in pools that's already late in Goldfinch but still active in Carapace.
Consider this scenario:
1. A pool is in the active state after assessStates is run.
2. Before the next assessStates call, the pool gets into the late state, due to a missed repayment. However, in the protocol, the pool is still in the active state since assessStates hasn't been called.
3. The malicious buyer front runs the next assessStates call and submits their transactions that buys a protection with the minimal duration for the pool. The _verifyLendingPoolIsActive function passes because the pool's state hasn't been updated in the contracts yet.
4. The assessStates call changes the status of the pool to LateWithinGracePeriod, which disallows buying protections for the pool.
5. If the pool eventually gets into the default state (chances of that is higher since there's already a late payment), the malicious buyer will be eligible for a compensation.
Protection buyers can increase their chances of getting a compensation, while buying protections with the minimal duration and paying the minimal premium. Protection sellers will bear increased losses due to reduced premium amounts and the increased chance of a compensation.
1. _verifyLendingPoolIsActive checks the current status of a pool and reverts if it's not active: ProtectionPoolHelper.sol#L412-L415
2. Pool statuses are cached and are stored in DefaultStateManager: DefaultStateManager.sol#L278-L280
3. Pool statuses are updated in DefaultStateManager.assessStates: DefaultStateManager.sol#L119
4. DefaultStateManager.assessStates is not called by ProtectionPool.buyProtection: ProtectionPool.sol#L162
bug_full: The vulnerability allows a protection buyer to purchase insurance for a lending pool that has already become late, by exploiting a stale pool‑status cache. The contract stores the current state of each pool in a cached variable inside the DefaultStateManager. This cached value is only refreshed when the assessStates (or assessStateBatch) function is executed, which occurs on a scheduled basis and is not invoked automatically by the protection‑purchase flow. The helper function _verifyLendingPoolIsActive checks the cached status and reverts if the pool is not marked as active. Because the cache may be outdated, an attacker can front‑run the next assessStates call, submit a buyProtection transaction while the cache still reports the pool as active, and pay only the minimal premium for a short‑duration protection. After the assessStates call runs, the pool status is updated to LateWithinGracePeriod, which normally blocks new protections, but the buyer’s protection remains valid. If the pool later defaults, the buyer receives a compensation payout that was obtained with an artificially low premium, while the protection seller suffers a higher loss than intended. This flaw occurs only when a repayment is missed between two assessStates executions and an adversary can time their transaction before the state refresh. It affects any lender or protocol participant relying on the insurance mechanism, as well as the protocol’s economic model that assumes premiums reflect risk. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the logical flow of state updates with the actual contract code. It is subtle because the UI and on‑chain view may still show the pool as active, leading developers to believe the safety check is sufficient. To remediate, the verification routine should trigger an immediate state assessment (for example by calling DefaultStateManager._assessState) or otherwise ensure the pool’s status is up‑to‑date before allowing a protection purchase, thereby preventing the purchase of insurance for already‑late pools. In essence, the bug is a classic stale‑state or cache‑invalidation problem that breaks the intended business rule that protections can only be bought for pools that are currently active, leading to unfair compensation and potential financial loss for sellers.

title: If unlocked capital in pool falls below minRequiredCapital
bug_full: The vulnerability is a pricing logic error in the protection‑purchase flow of a capital pool. The contract calculates a risk factor based on total unlocked capital, leverage ratio and a minimum required capital threshold. When the risk factor cannot be computed, the PremiumCalculator falls back to a fixed minimum premium. The canCalculateRiskFactor function returns false not only when the leverage ratio is out of the allowed window, but also when the total unlocked capital is lower than the configured minRequiredCapital. This latter condition should make protection expensive or unavailable because the pool is under‑collateralised, yet the fallback treats it the same as an out‑of‑range leverage case and offers the cheapest possible premium. An attacker can trigger this situation by withdrawing most of the sellers’ funds or by locking a large portion of capital, causing the unlocked capital to drop below the threshold while the leverage ratio remains within bounds. Under those circumstances a buyer can purchase protection at a price that does not reflect the heightened risk, effectively receiving cheap insurance when the pool is almost empty. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a very low premium and the user expects to obtain protection at a normal cost, but the contract silently sells it for the minimum amount, violating the business rule that low capital should increase risk and price. The impact is that the protocol may issue under‑priced protection, leading to a situation where claim payouts exceed the available capital, potentially draining the pool and harming all participants. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the premium‑calculation branch and identified that the same fallback flag is used for three distinct failure modes, including insufficient capital. It is hard to notice because the fallback to a minimum premium is a legitimate response for leverage‑ratio violations, so the additional condition appears innocuous. The correct mitigation is to prevent protection purchases when unlocked capital is below the minimum required amount, or to compute a premium that reflects the higher risk instead of using the minimum premium placeholder. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that protection pricing scales with pool solvency and ensures that users cannot obtain cheap protection when the pool lacks sufficient backing.

title: Protection too expensive when some capital is locked
description:
The leverage ratio is computed as a ratio of unlocked capital to total protections. This means that each protection position which has locked capital is effectively counted twice: once to lock up capital, and once again to decrease the leverage ratio. This can lead to situations where a pool is very well capitalized to sell more protection, but cannot do so.
Consider: Pool has $1.1 million in deposits, and $1 million in protection positions. All pools have late payments, and so $1 million is locked. Pool now has $100k in unallocated deposits, but its leverage ratio is 100k / 1.1M ~ 0.09. Depending on the leverage floor, protection will either be really expensive or cannot be bought at all, even though the pool is well-capitalized.
Compare: If all pools defaulted and the $1M was lost, then the pool would have $100k in deposits and $0 in protection positions, and protection would be very cheap. The situation with locked capital should be treated similarly.
Protection is very expensive or impossible in some situations where it should be cheap.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting mis‑calculation in the way the protocol derives its leverage ratio for protection sales.
