The ratio is defined as unlocked capital divided by total protection exposure, but the implementation counts protection positions that have already locked capital twice: once as a reduction of available capital (because the capital is locked) and again as part of the denominator that lowers the ratio. As a result, when a pool contains a large amount of locked protection, the computed leverage ratio can drop to a very low value even though the pool’s total deposits are high. This condition occurs whenever there are late‑payment or settlement events that cause protection positions to lock capital, and the protocol enforces a leverage floor that determines the minimum acceptable ratio for offering new protection. An attacker or even a regular user who opens a protection position that locks a substantial amount of capital can therefore push the ratio below the floor, making new protection either prohibitively expensive or completely unavailable. From a user’s point of view the UI may display abundant pool balance, but attempts to purchase protection either fail with a “leverage too low” error or return an unexpectedly high premium, contradicting the expectation that a well‑capitalized pool should provide cheap protection. The impact is primarily economic: legitimate protection buyers are unable to obtain coverage at reasonable cost, which can erode confidence in the protocol, reduce market liquidity, and potentially cause loss of revenue for the pool operators. The bug was discovered during a systematic audit of the Carapace protocol, where the auditor observed that the leverage calculation did not differentiate between locked and free capital. The issue is subtle because the total deposit figure looks healthy, so a superficial check of pool balances does not reveal the problem. The correct fix is to adjust the leverage‑ratio formula so that only unlocked (free) capital is used in the numerator and locked protection exposure is excluded from the denominator, or otherwise ensure that locked capital is not counted twice. In generic terms this is a double‑counting accounting error that violates the business logic that protection pricing should be proportional to truly available capital.

title: If a lendingPool is added to the network while already late
description:
If a lending pool is added to a protection pool, the defaultStateManager sets the currentState to late without setting the late timestamp. This can enable anyone in the network to be able to call the _assessState once more and mark the pool as default.
defaultStateManager uses _assessState function to transfer between states.
However, in case an underlying pool is called by _assessState for the first time when it is added to the protocol. The _assessState function sets the currentState to late without updating the lateTimestamp which will remain zero. The attacker can exploit this to move the pool to the default state where it locks the lending pool and renders it unusable.
While it is checked that when pools are added to the ReferenceLendingPool inside _addReferenceLendingPool that the pools should be in Active state, if in the time between the addition of a pool and the first time call of _assessState the pool goes from Active to Late, this attack can be performed by the attacker.
DefaultStateManager.sol#L370-L375
An attacker can render an underlying lending pool unusable.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑transition flaw in the DefaultStateManager used by the lending protocol. When a new lending pool is added to a protection pool while the pool is already in a Late condition, the manager’s _assessState routine sets the pool’s currentState to Late but fails to record the associated lateTimestamp, leaving that timestamp at zero. Because the timestamp is never initialized, the contract believes the pool has been Late for an indefinite period. An attacker can then invoke _assessState a second time; the logic interprets the missing timestamp as a cue to progress the pool from Late to Default, which permanently locks the underlying lending pool and prevents any further deposits, withdrawals or repayments. The bug occurs only in the narrow window between the addition of a pool to the ReferenceLendingPool (where the code checks that the pool is Active) and the first execution of _assessState after the addition, if the pool’s state changes to Late during that interval. All participants that rely on the pool – borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the pool becomes unusable and any funds locked inside may become inaccessible. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noted that the lateTimestamp field was never updated on the initial Late transition, a detail that is easy to miss because the contract still reports a Late state and no explicit error is thrown. The problem is hard to notice because the state variable appears correct while the timestamp, an internal accounting field, silently stays at its default value, allowing the default transition to be triggered later without obvious warning signs. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of improper initialization or missing guard conditions in state‑machine implementations, where a transition does not fully initialise all required metadata, leading to an unintended escalation path. From a user perspective the symptoms are a sudden inability to interact with the pool – attempts to deposit or withdraw revert, the UI shows the pool as locked or defaulted, and balances appear unchanged despite expected activity. To remediate the issue the _assessState function should treat the first transition to Late as a special case, explicitly setting the lateTimestamp and preventing a second immediate transition to Default. Additional safeguards such as checking that a Late timestamp is non‑zero before allowing a move to Default, or restricting who can call _assessState after pool addition, would close the attack surface.

title: secondary markets are problematic with how locking works
description:
Seeing that a pool is about to lock, an attacker can use a flash loan from a secondary market like Uniswap to claim the share of a potential unlock of capital later.
The timestamp a pool switches to Late can be predicted and an attacker can use this to call assessState which is callable by anyone. This will trigger the pool to move from Active/LateWithinGracePeriod to Late calling lockCapital on the ProtectionPool:
ProtectionPool.sol#L365-L366
File: ProtectionPool.sol
365:
/// step 1: Capture protection pool's current investors by creating a snapshot of the token balance by using ERC20Snapshot in SToken
366:
_snapshotId = _snapshot();
This records who is holding sTokens at this point in time. If the borrower makes a payment and the pool turns back to Active, later the locked funds will be available to claim for the sToken holders at that snapshot:
DefaultStateManager.sol#L500-L505
File: DefaultStateManager.sol
500:
/// The claimable amount for the given seller is proportional to the seller's share of the total supply at the snapshot
501:
/// claimable amount = (seller's snapshot balance / total supply at snapshot) * locked capital amount
502:
_claimableUnlockedCapital =
503:
(_poolSToken.balanceOfAt(_seller, _snapshotId) *
504:
lockedCapital.amount) /
505:
_poolSToken.totalSupplyAt(_snapshotId);
From docs:
If sellers wish to redeem their capital and interest before the lockup period, they might be able to find a buyer of their sToken in a secondary market like Uniswap. Traders in the exchanges can long/short sTokens based on their opinion about the risk exposure associated with sTokens.
Since an sToken is a fungible ERC20 token, it is fairly easy to bootstrap the secondary markets for protection sellers.
If there is a Uniswap (or similar) pool for this sToken, an attacker could potentially, using a flash loan, trigger the switch to Late and since they will be the ones holding the sTokens at the point of locking they will be the ones that can claim the funds at a potential unlock.
An attacker can, using a flash loan from a secondary market like Uniswap, steal a LPs possible share of unlocked tokens. Only paying the risk of the flash loan fee.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a permission flaw in the state‑assessment routine of the protection pool. The contract exposes a function (assessState) that any address can invoke, and this function can trigger the pool to transition from an Active or LateWithinGracePeriod state to a Late state. When the transition occurs, the pool calls lockCapital, which creates an ERC20Snapshot of the sToken balances (the protection token representing sellers' stakes). The snapshot records the exact token holdings at the moment of locking and later uses those balances to calculate each seller’s claimable share of any unlocked capital. Because assessState is publicly callable, an attacker can predict the exact block timestamp when the pool will switch to Late, obtain a large amount of sTokens instantly via a flash loan from a secondary market such as Uniswap, and call assessState within the same transaction. The flash‑loaned sTokens become the holder of the snapshot balance, so the attacker is recorded as owning a proportional share of the total supply at that snapshot. When the pool later unlocks capital, the claimable amount is computed solely from the snapshot data, allowing the attacker to claim the portion of unlocked funds that would normally belong to legitimate sellers. The impact is that an attacker can siphon a significant share, potentially the entire unlocked capital, from honest participants. This occurs only when the pool is about to enter the Late state, a condition that can be forecasted from on‑chain timestamps. The affected parties are the sellers who expect to redeem their capital and interest, as well as the protocol that relies on correct accounting of claimable amounts. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the accessibility of assessState and the interaction with the snapshot mechanism. It is difficult to notice because the snapshot and lock happen atomically within a single transaction, leaving no obvious on‑chain flag that the balance was artificially inflated by a flash loan. From a user’s perspective, a legitimate seller may see their sToken balance drop after a transaction and later find that the claimable amount returned by the contract is zero, while an attacker receives an unexpected payout. The bug belongs to the class of “flash‑loan‑induced snapshot manipulation” or “unauthorized state transition” vulnerabilities, where public functions allow an attacker to temporarily acquire assets, trigger a state change, and exploit accounting that assumes static token holdings. To remediate, the assessState function should be restricted to a trusted role or made internal, preventing arbitrary callers from initiating the lock. Alternatively, the protocol could require that snapshot balances be taken only from holders that have maintained their position for a minimum period, or decouple the claim calculation from a single‑transaction snapshot. In any case, the fix must ensure that the snapshot cannot be manipulated by transient flash‑loaned tokens, thereby preserving the intended proportional distribution of unlocked capital.

title: Growing of totalSupply after successive locking cycles
description:
In a protection pool, after enough cycles of locking capital/depositing, totalSupply can grow to overflow uint256.
ProtectionPool.sol#L589-L606
_getExchangeRate() can become arbitrarily small after a funds locking, since locked funds are subtracted from totalSTokenUnderlying; This means that new depositors can get a lot more shares than depositors from before funds locking.
This behavior is correct, because otherwise previous depositors would have an oversized share of the new capital. However this has the negative effect of growing totalSupply exponentially, eventually reaching type(uint256).max and overflowing (reverting every new deposit).
Protocol can come to a halt if totalSupply reaches type(uint256).max.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked exponential growth of the token totalSupply in the protection pool contract. The contract calculates an exchange rate by dividing the underlying amount of staked tokens (totalSTokenUnderlying) by the current totalSupply. When a locking cycle occurs, the locked funds are subtracted from totalSTokenUnderlying while totalSupply remains unchanged, causing the exchange rate to become arbitrarily small. As a result, each subsequent deposit mints a disproportionately large number of shares because the tiny exchange rate translates a modest deposit amount into a huge share amount. Over many successive locking cycles this minting process inflates totalSupply exponentially until it reaches the maximum value of a uint256, at which point any further minting operation overflows and reverts. The overflow halts the protocol because new deposits cannot be processed, effectively freezing the system for all users. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the protection pool’s accounting logic, where the auditor observed that the exchange rate could shrink without bound after repeated locks. It is difficult to notice in normal testing because the overflow only manifests after a large number of cycles, far beyond typical usage patterns. From a user’s perspective, deposits that previously succeeded start failing with a revert, and earlier depositors may see their share balances unexpectedly balloon while later users receive zero shares because the transaction reverts. The bug violates the fundamental accounting assumption that the totalSupply should represent a bounded share of the underlying assets. To remediate, the token design should incorporate a regular rebasing mechanism or enforce a lower bound on the exchange rate, thereby preventing the exchange rate from collapsing and ensuring totalSupply cannot grow unchecked. Alternative mitigations include capping the amount of shares minted per deposit, using safe‑math checks for overflow, or redesigning the accounting model so that locked funds do not reduce the denominator of the exchange rate calculation.

title: Freezing of the protocol when totalSTokenUnderlying becomes zero
description:
In some cases the protocol can contain zero funds while having a non-zero totalSupply of STokens. In that case the protocol will not be able to accept any new deposits and any new protection buys, thus coming to a halt, unless all STokens are burned by their respective holders.
In the case lockCapital has to lock all available capital:
ProtectionPool.sol#L415-L419
totalSTokenUnderlying becomes zero, but totalSupply is still non-zero since no SToken have been burned. Which means that new deposits will revert because blob/main/contracts/core/pool/ProtectionPool.sol#L602-L605
And convertToSToken tries to divide by _getExchangeRate();
ProtectionPool.sol#L602-L605
Also all new protection buying attempts will revert because _leverageRatio is zero, and thus under leverageRatioFloor.
The protocol comes to a halt, unless every SToken holder burn their shares by calling withdraw after enough cycles have passed, returning to the case totalSupply == 0.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a protocol‑wide freeze that occurs when the contract’s accounting variable that tracks the total underlying assets backing the synthetic token (totalSTokenUnderlying) drops to zero while the total supply of the synthetic token (SToken) remains non‑zero. The root cause is the lack of a safeguard that prevents the underlying balance from being fully drained without simultaneously burning all outstanding STokens. When totalSTokenUnderlying becomes zero, the function that converts deposited assets into STokens attempts to compute an exchange rate by dividing by this zero value, which triggers a division‑by‑zero revert. In parallel, the leverage ratio derived from the same underlying amount becomes zero, falling below the protocol’s minimum leverageRatioFloor and causing protection‑buying functions to revert as well. An attacker or any user who can withdraw enough capital can therefore trigger this state by emptying the pool and leaving holders with unburned STokens. Once the state is reached, any subsequent deposit or protection purchase reverts, effectively halting the protocol until every SToken holder manually burns their tokens by calling withdraw after the required cycle delay. The impact is a complete loss of usability: users cannot add new funds, cannot purchase protection, and existing liquidity becomes locked, undermining confidence in the platform. The condition only manifests after a series of withdrawals that exhaust the underlying balance, a scenario that may be rare and therefore hard to notice during normal operation. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the conversion logic and identified that the contract does not enforce a minimum underlying reserve. From a user’s perspective the UI will show a normal deposit screen, but the transaction will revert with an obscure error, leading the user to see “deposit failed” or “protection buy failed” without an obvious reason, contrary to the expectation that deposits should always succeed when funds are available. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑state‑inconsistency errors where invariant relationships between token supply and backing assets are broken. To remediate, the contract should enforce a non‑zero minimum reserve (for example, a small constant such as 1e6 wei) or require that totalSTokenUnderlying can only reach zero when totalSupply is also zero, and the exchange‑rate calculation should gracefully handle a zero‑underlying case rather than dividing by it. This ensures that the protocol remains operational and that users’ expectations of being able to deposit or buy protection are met.

title: Some protection buyers might not be able to renew their protection
description:
Some protection buyers will never be able to renew their protection due to delayed expiration processing.
We show below how some buyers will not be able to renew their protection due to delayed expiration process caused by the wrong implementation of verifyAndAccruePremium(). Due to the bug, they might miss the deadline and grace period for renewal.
1) First the verifyBuyerCanRenewProtection() function checks whether it is too late to renew the protection (before the grace period expires). In addition, verifyBuyerCanRenewProtection() also checks whether there exists an expired protection with the same lending pool and position token ID at protectionBuyerAccounts[msg.sender].expiredProtectionIndexByLendingPool[_protectionPurchaseParams.lendingPoolAddress][_protectionPurchaseParams.nftLpTokenId] in L371. If such an existing expired protection is not there, renewal will be rejected.
ProtectionPoolHelper.sol#L360-L399
2) In order for the expired protection to be stored in protectionBuyerAccounts[msg.sender].expiredProtectionIndexByLendingPool[_protectionPurchaseParams.lendingPoolAddress][_protectionPurchaseParams.nftLpTokenId], the expireProtection() must be called at L1004 of function _accruePremiumAndExpireProtections().
ProtectionPool.sol#L963-L1021
3) the expireProtection() function stores such expired protection at L311-315:
ProtectionPoolHelper.sol#L293-L321
4) However, before expireProtection() can be called, function verifyAndAccruePremium() needs to be called first to decide whether a protection has expired or not (L990).
ProtectionPool.sol#L963-L1021
5) However, when there is no payment for a while, for example, when the last payment is made before a protection P starts (_latestPaymentTimestamp < _startTimestamp), P will not be considered as expired see L215-220 of verifyAndAccruePremium() below:
ProtectionPoolHelper.sol#L201-L284
6) Therefore, if there is no payment for a long time, then verifyAndAccruePremium() will always consider a protection P has not expired. expireProtection() will never process it. So the actually expired protection will not be stored in protectionBuyerAccounts[msg.sender].expiredProtectionIndexByLendingPool[_protectionPurchaseParams.lendingPoolAddress][_protectionPurchaseParams.nftLpTokenId]. The buyer for P will not be able to renew P because verifyBuyerCanRenewProtection() will fail to find an existing expired protection P. If there is no payment for a long time, then the buyer for P might miss the deadline and grace period and will never be able to renew P anymore.
Some protection buyers might never be able to renew their protections due to delayed expiration processing as a result of a bug of verifyAndAccruePremium(). getActiveProtections() might return some protections that are supposed to have expired, but not processed due to the above bug.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a delayed expiration processing bug that can prevent protection buyers from renewing their coverage. The root cause lies in the verifyAndAccruePremium function, which incorrectly assumes that a protection has not expired when no premium payments have been made for an extended period. Specifically, when the latest payment timestamp is earlier than the protection start timestamp, the function returns early without marking the protection as expired, even if the current block timestamp is past the scheduled expiration. Because expireProtection is never invoked, the expired protection is not recorded in the buyer's expiredProtectionIndex mapping. The renewal logic in verifyBuyerCanRenewProtection checks this mapping to confirm that an expired protection exists before allowing a renewal. When the expired entry is missing, the renewal call is rejected, causing the buyer to miss the renewal deadline and the subsequent grace period. This situation can occur for any buyer whose protection experiences a long gap without premium payments, such as when the last payment is made before the protection start date or when payments stop entirely. Affected parties include individual users purchasing protection, the protocol that relies on timely renewals for risk management, and any downstream contracts that assume expired protections are correctly cleared. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the protection pool contracts, where the auditor observed that getActiveProtections could return protections that should have been expired but were still listed as active. The bug is subtle because the contract appears to function normally when payments are regular; only after a prolonged inactivity does the logic diverge, making it hard to notice without targeted testing of edge‑case payment timelines. The impact is that users may be unable to extend or replace their protection, potentially leaving them exposed to uncovered risk and causing loss of expected coverage. To fix the problem, verifyAndAccruePremium should be revised to correctly detect and flag expirations even when no payments have been made after the start timestamp, ensuring that expireProtection is called and the expired protection is stored, thereby allowing the renewal pathway to operate as intended. This class of bug falls under improper state transition handling and stale‑state checks, where a contract fails to update its internal accounting when a condition (expiration) is met but a related trigger (payment) is absent.

title: Account that is affiliated with a plugin can some-
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the staking module’s reliance on external plugins to signal stake changes during a slash operation. The module iterates over all registered plugins, calling IPlugin(plugin).requiresNotification() to decide whether to invoke notifyStakeChange. This call is performed without a try‑catch guard, assuming it never reverts. A malicious or colluding plugin can deliberately revert the requiresNotification() call when it observes that a particular account’s stake is about to be reduced. By front‑running the slasher’s slash() transaction, the plugin flips its internal flag so that requiresNotification() reverts, causing the entire slash() call – which internally invokes _notifyStakeChangeAllPlugins – to revert as well. After the slash transaction fails, the plugin restores its normal state, allowing the slashing attempt to be sandwiched between two plugin state changes. Because the protocol also permits accounts to periodically renew withdrawal requests when a withdrawalDelay is configured, the colluding account can keep a withdrawal window open. If the withdrawal window expires before the protocol’s PLUGIN_EDITOR removes the offending plugin, the account can execute exit() while the plugin is in its normal state, withdrawing the full stake without ever being slashed. This creates a scenario where a staker can evade penalties, effectively stealing the protocol’s security guarantees. The issue is subtle because the plugin behaves correctly most of the time; only under the specific timing of a slash does it misbehave, making detection difficult. The impact includes loss of slashing enforcement, potential fund loss for the protocol, and erosion of trust in the staking mechanism. The root cause is the unchecked external call to requiresNotification and the protocol’s design that allows a plugin to influence the outcome of a critical security operation. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the missing try‑catch around requiresNotification and the possibility of state manipulation by a plugin. To remediate, the staking module should protect the requiresNotification call with a try‑catch block, treat a failure as a non‑notification (or abort the slash safely), or redesign the slashing flow to be independent of plugin state, ensuring that a plugin cannot cause the slash to revert and that withdrawal windows cannot be abused to bypass penalties.

title: slash calls can be blocked, allowing malicious
description:
A malicious user can block slashing by frontrunning slash with a call to stake(1) at the same block, allowing him to keep blocking calls to slash while waiting for his withdraw delay, effectively bypassing the slashing mechanism. StakingModule's checkpointProtection modifier reverts certain actions, like claims, if the accounts' stake was previously modified in the same block. A malicious user can exploit this to intentionally block calls to slash. Consider the following scenario, where Alice has SLASHER_ROLE and Bob is the malicious user.
1. Alice calls slash on Bob's account.
2. Bob sees the transaction on the mempool and tries to frontrun it by staking 1 TEL. (See Proof of Concept section below for a simplified example of this scenario)
If Bob stake call is processed first (he can pay more gas to increase his odds of being placed before than Alice), his new stake is pushed to _stakes[address(Bob)], and his latest checkpoint (_stakes[address(Bob)]._checkpoints[numCheckpoints - 1]) blockNumber field is updated to the block.number. So when slash is being processed in the same block and calls internally _claimAndExit it will revert due to the checkpointProtection modifier check (See code snippet below).
```solidity
modifier checkpointProtection(address account) {
    uint256 numCheckpoints = _stakes[account]._checkpoints.length;
    require(numCheckpoints == 0 || _stakes[account]._checkpoints[numCheckpoints - 1]._blockNumber != block.number, "StakingModule: Cannot exit in the same block as another stake or exit");
    _;
}
```
Bob can do this indefinitely, eventually becoming a gas war between Alice and Bob or until Alice tries to use Flashbots Protect or similar services to avoid the public mempool. More importantly, this can be leveraged to block all slash attempts while waiting the time required to withdraw, so the malicious user could call requestWithdrawal(), then keep blocking all future slash calls while waiting for his withdrawalDelay, then proceed to withdraws stake when block.timestamp > withdrawalRequestTimestamps[msg.sender] + withdrawalDelay. Therefore bypassing the slashing mechanism. In this modified scenario:
1. Alice calls slash on Bob's account.
2. Bob sees the transaction on the mempool and tries to frontrun it by staking 1 TEL.
3. Bob requests his withdraw (requestWithdrawal())
4. Bob keeps monitoring the mempool for future calls to slash against his account, trying to frontrun each one of them.
5. When enough time has passed so that his withdraw is available, Bob calls exit or fullClaimAndExit
Slashing calls can be blocked by malicious user, allowing him to request his withdraw, wait until withdraw delay has passed (while blocking further calls to slash) and then withdraw his funds. Classify this one as medium severity, because even though there are ways to avoid being frontrun, like paying much more gas or using services like Flashbots Protect, none is certain to work because the malicious user can use the same methods to their advantage. And if the malicious user is successful, this would result in loss of funds to the protocol (i.e funds that should have been slashed, but user managed to withdraw them).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running blockage of the slashing mechanism in the StakingModule contract. The contract uses a checkpointProtection modifier that reverts any claim or exit that occurs in the same block in which the account’s stake was modified. Because the modifier checks the most recent checkpoint block number against block.number, an attacker who observes a pending slash transaction can submit a stake(1) call in the same block, causing the checkpoint to be updated to the current block. When the slash function later invokes the internal _claimAndExit routine, the modifier detects that the account was modified in the same block and reverts with the message StakingModule: Cannot exit in the same block as another stake or exit. By repeatedly front‑running every slash attempt, the attacker can keep the slash function failing, then request a withdrawal, wait for the withdrawalDelay, and finally exit the stake, effectively withdrawing funds that should have been slashed. The attack works only when the attacker can get his transaction mined before the slash transaction in the same block, which can be achieved by paying higher gas fees or using private‑mempool services. The impact is that the protocol loses the amount that would have been confiscated by slashing, undermining the economic security model. The issue is discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a PoC that disables automining to force both transactions into the same block. It is hard to notice because the revert message appears as a normal protection check and does not directly indicate a malicious front‑run, and the behavior only manifests under specific timing conditions. The affected parties are the protocol itself, any slasher role holder who expects to penalize misbehaving accounts, and honest stakers whose security relies on slashing. The recommended mitigation is to provide a version of the claim‑and‑exit logic that bypasses the checkpointProtection check when called from the slash function, or to redesign the protection so that it does not interfere with legitimate slashing calls. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of transaction‑ordering attacks that exploit intra‑block state checks, leading to denial of service on critical protocol functions and loss of expected penalties.

title: Front Run of addBlackList() function
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of two related weaknesses in a staking‑based vault contract. First, the contract allows a user to be blacklisted through a privileged function, after which a separate function removes any funds that belong to the blacklisted address. The contract only protects the removal (exit) operation with a checkpoint guard that prevents multiple exits in the same block, but it does not protect the staking operation. Because the staking function can be called repeatedly within a single block, the historical balance query that reads the amount staked at a given block returns the value from the first checkpoint of that block. When an attacker sees a pending blacklist transaction in the mempool, they can front‑run it by submitting a higher‑gas transaction that stakes (or simply withdraws) their tokens before the blacklist takes effect. The stale checkpoint reading makes the contract believe the user’s stake is lower than it actually is, allowing the attacker to withdraw more than the protocol expects to be locked. This front‑run can also be performed by bribing the block producer with extra ETH to the coinbase address. The second weakness is the inaccurate historical balance function: because multiple stake calls in the same block are not prevented, the function that reports the amount staked at a specific block returns only the first checkpoint, under‑reporting the true stake. Downstream components such as a vault that rely on these historical readings for accounting, fee calculation, or risk management will receive incorrect data, potentially causing the vault to make unsafe decisions, misallocate rewards, or expose user funds to loss. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a blacklist transaction is observed, the user may still be able to withdraw their tokens, or the vault may display a lower balance than actually deposited, leading to confusion and possible loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the blacklist, exit protection, and the checkpoint‑based staking module. It is subtle because the contract appears to enforce a single‑exit‑per‑block rule, yet it unintentionally permits multiple stakes, which only manifests when multiple stake calls occur in the same block – a scenario that is not obvious during normal testing. The recommended mitigation is to apply the same checkpoint‑protection modifier to the staking function, ensuring that both staking and exiting are limited to one operation per block, and to document this limitation clearly. By synchronising the protection, the stale‑checkpoint problem is eliminated, historical balance queries become reliable, and front‑running of blacklist actions is no longer feasible.

title: Withdraw delay can be bypassed
description:
```solidity
StakingModule has core feature around staking, claim and withdraw. All these
features has core and essential mechanism which is delayed withdrawal. In ideal
scenario, user will stake X amount of token and will call requestWithdrawal when
user want to withdraw his/her stake. requestWithdrawal will record user's request
to withdraw and allow this user to withdraw only after withdrawalDelay is passed
and during withdrawalWindow only. User can call requestWithdrawal in well advance
before staking and this will allow user to bypass withdrawalDelay.
Withdraw locking/delaying is core feature of this contract and it can be exploited
very easily.
User can call requestWithdrawal before staking tokens and this will set user's
withdrawalRequestTimestamps. Once withdrawalDelay is passed user can easily
stake and unstake without locking time.
One would suggest that easy fix is to check staked > 0 during call to
requestWithdrawal and that should solve this issue. No, it will not. Assume staked>0
check is added in requestWithdrawal then user will stake 1 wei and call
requestWithdrawal and this will result in almost same scenario.
Why would this happen? Because there is no relationship between stake and
withdrawalRequestTimestamps.
withdrawalDelay can be bypassed
```
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the delayed‑withdrawal mechanism of a staking module. In the intended design a user who has staked tokens must first call requestWithdrawal, which records a timestamp and then forces the user to wait a configured withdrawalDelay before being able to pull the funds during a limited withdrawalWindow. The flaw arises because the contract stores the withdrawal request timestamp independently of the amount that is actually staked, and it never clears or updates this timestamp when the user later stakes tokens. Consequently an attacker can call requestWithdrawal before any tokens are deposited, simply wait for the delay period, then stake a minimal amount (even 1 wei) and immediately invoke the withdrawal functions without ever observing the intended lock‑up period. The exploit proceeds as follows: (1) call requestWithdrawal with zero balance, (2) advance blockchain time until the withdrawalDelay has elapsed, (3) stake a tiny amount of the token, (4) call the claim or exit function and retrieve the stake instantly. From the user’s perspective the UI may indicate that a withdrawal request is pending and that a waiting period is required, yet the user can receive the full amount right away, violating the expectation of a delayed exit. This bypass undermines the economic security model of the protocol, allowing participants to avoid the intended cooling‑off period that may be required for slashing, reward distribution, or other protocol invariants. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the tester crafted a proof‑of‑concept that called requestWithdrawal before staking and observed that the subsequent fullClaimAndExit succeeded without any additional waiting. The problem is subtle because the requestWithdrawal function appears harmless—it merely records a timestamp—and there is no explicit check that the caller actually holds a positive stake at the time of the request. To remediate the bug the contract should tie the withdrawal request to the current staked balance, for example by rejecting requestWithdrawal when the caller’s stake is zero, and more importantly by resetting or clearing withdrawalRequestTimestamps whenever the user’s stake amount changes (e.g., on any successful stake or unstake). This ensures that a fresh request must be made after a genuine staking action, restoring the intended delay enforcement and preserving the protocol’s security guarantees.

title: Lender can take borrower's collateral before
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the loan lifecycle that allows a lender to withdraw the borrower’s collateral before the borrower has missed the first scheduled payment. The contract determines whether a loan is in default by calling TellerV2.isLoanDefaulted, but this check ignores the grace period that should apply until the first payment due date. When the market parameters are configured so that the payment default duration is shorter than the payment cycle – for example a payment cycle of 3600 seconds and a default window of only 1 second – the default condition becomes true immediately after the bid is accepted. Because the default check does not consider that the first payment is not yet due, the lender can invoke CollateralManager.withdraw and seize the collateral almost instantly, even though the borrower has not had any opportunity to make a repayment. This situation can be triggered by any market operator who can set the payment cycle and default values, and the operator may also be the lender, creating a potential abuse vector. From the borrower’s perspective the UI will show that the collateral balance has vanished, the expected repayment window is still in the future, and attempts to withdraw or view the collateral result in an error such as “No collateral balance for asset”. The impact is that the borrower loses the pledged assets without having defaulted, breaking the economic assumptions of the protocol, eroding trust, and effectively causing funds to disappear. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that added a test case reproducing the scenario: after configuring a tiny default duration, the test accepted a bid and then, after skipping only the default seconds, called withdraw and verified that the collateral was taken. The bug is subtle because the default logic works correctly for later payments, so developers may not notice that the first payment deadline is excluded from the calculation. To remediate, the default‑checking routine must be updated to incorporate the timestamp of the first payment due date, similar to the logic in TellerV2.calculateNextDueDate, ensuring that a lender can only liquidate after the borrower has missed the first payment by the configured default period. Additionally, the contract should enforce sensible minimum values for the payment default duration to prevent configurations that make immediate liquidation possible or that disable liquidation entirely.

```solidity
LenderCommitmentForwarder#updateCommitment overwrites ALL of the

2) User A's commitment is close to expiry so they call to update their
```

bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the LenderCommitmentForwarder.updateCommitment function, which replaces the entire commitment record with a new struct supplied by the caller. While the function enforces that the principal token address and market identifier remain unchanged, it does not protect the other fields, notably the maxPrincipal (the amount of capital the lender is willing to expose). Because the implementation overwrites the whole struct, a lender who intends only to modify a non‑financial attribute such as the expiration timestamp can unintentionally reset the maxPrincipal to its original value. This design flaw creates a race condition: if a lender submits an update transaction to extend the expiry of a commitment, a malicious borrower can observe the pending transaction, front‑run it with a loan that consumes the full committed amount, and then, after the update is mined, the commitment’s maxPrincipal is restored to the original value. The borrower can repeat the process, effectively borrowing twice the amount the lender intended to expose. The impact is that the lender becomes over‑committed, potentially losing funds if the collateral value drops or if the protocol cannot cover the excess loan. The issue manifests whenever a commitment is updated and the transaction ordering allows an adversary to interleave a loan request between the update and its final state. It affects any user who relies on the commitment’s amount field to reflect their true exposure, as well as the overall protocol’s accounting and risk models. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the function’s intent (updating a single field) with its actual behavior (overwriting all fields). It can be hard to notice because the function appears to perform a benign update and the overwritten amount may match the previous value, masking the over‑commitment until the second loan is executed. To remediate, the contract should separate mutable and immutable fields: provide a dedicated method for extending expiry that leaves the amount untouched, and introduce an increaseAmount (or increaseApproval‑style) function that only raises the maxPrincipal without resetting it. Additionally, the updateCommitment function should validate that the amount field is either unchanged or explicitly increased, rejecting any transaction that would reduce or reset it unintentionally. This approach restores the intended business logic that a lender’s commitment amount cannot be altered without their explicit consent, preserving accounting integrity and preventing front‑run over‑commitment attacks.

bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the FeeBuyback contract's submit() function, which repeatedly calls SafeERC20.safeApprove to grant the referral contract an allowance equal to the contract's Telcoin balance. SafeERC20 enforces a rule that an ERC20 token's allowance can only be set from zero to a non‑zero value, or from a non‑zero value back to zero, to prevent the well‑known race condition of changing allowances. The submit() implementation assumes that the referral contract will consume the entire allowance in a single call to increaseClaimableBy(). If the referral contract uses only part of the allowance, a non‑zero allowance remains. On the next invocation of submit(), the contract attempts to approve the same non‑zero allowance again without first resetting it to zero. SafeERC20 then reverts with the message "SafeERC20: approve from non-zero to non-zero allowance". This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: after a partial consumption of the allowance, any further calls to submit() fail, preventing the fee‑buyback mechanism from executing. The impact is that the protocol cannot distribute or buy back fees, user‑facing interfaces may show transactions that revert or appear to do nothing, and expected refunds or token swaps never occur. The issue manifests only when the referral contract does not fully use the granted allowance, which may be rare in normal operation and therefore easy to miss during testing. It was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the approval pattern and cross‑checked it against the SafeERC20 library requirements. The bug is hard to notice because the first call succeeds and the contract appears functional until a partial allowance scenario arises. To remediate, the contract should reset the allowance to zero before granting a new non‑zero amount, or use increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance patterns, or transfer tokens directly without relying on an external contract to consume the full allowance. This change aligns the contract with the standard ERC20 approval safety model and restores reliable operation of the fee‑buyback process.

title: The createMarket transaction lack of expira-
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the market‑creation function of the Bond Protocol, which calculates the market duration (length) and the maximum payout based on the current block timestamp at the moment the transaction is executed. Because the function does not enforce any expiration or deadline check, a transaction that is submitted by a user can remain pending in the mempool for an arbitrarily long period before being mined. When the transaction finally executes, block.timestamp may be far later than the time the creator intended, causing the computed length to become much shorter than expected. The contract then derives the maximum payout as capacity × depositInterval ÷ length. A dramatically reduced length inflates the maxPayout value, often by orders of magnitude, while the capacity and deposit interval remain unchanged. Consequently, an attacker can call the purchase function immediately after the market is created and receive a payout that is far larger than the economic model anticipates. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that a purchase yields an unexpectedly huge amount of payout tokens, sometimes draining the market’s reserve and leaving other participants with no tokens to claim. The impact is a loss of funds for the market owner and any subsequent participants, as the protocol’s accounting assumptions about bounded payouts are violated. The issue occurs whenever the createMarket transaction is delayed beyond the intended start time and the attacker can act before the market owner manually closes the market. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the createMarket logic with Uniswap’s addLiquidity function, noting the absence of the “ensure(deadline)” modifier that protects against stale transactions. The bug is subtle because the transaction passes all other validation checks; only the passage of time changes the internal arithmetic, making it hard to detect without explicit deadline enforcement. To remediate, the contract should require a deadline parameter and enforce that block.timestamp is not greater than this deadline at the point of market creation, or alternatively compute market length from an explicit start timestamp supplied by the creator and validate that the resulting length falls within acceptable bounds before calculating maxPayout. This prevents the length from collapsing to a tiny value and stops the inflation of the payout ceiling.

bug_full: The vulnerability is a financial‑logic error in the market creation routine of the bond protocol where the equilibrium price – the oracle price after applying the configured base discount – is not used when calculating the market capacity for quote‑denominated markets. The contract computes capacity by multiplying the quoted capacity by a scale factor and dividing by the raw oracle price, while the discounted price (the equilibrium price) is only applied later when the price is stored for other purposes. Because the discount is omitted in the capacity formula, the effective price used is higher than intended, which reduces the computed capacity and consequently the maximum payout that can be allocated to a single user. This mis‑calculation occurs during the internal _createMarket function in both OFDA and OSDA implementations whenever the market is created with capacityInQuote set to true. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the BondBaseOFDA.sol and BondBaseOSDA.sol contracts, where the auditor observed that the discount logic appears in the price‑decimals calculation but not in the capacity computation. The bug is subtle because the contract still compiles and functions, but the resulting maxPayout value is smaller than the economic design expects, leading to user‑visible symptoms such as “my purchase limit is lower than advertised”, “I have to split my bond purchase into multiple transactions”, and “extra gas fees due to additional calls”. Affected parties include any user attempting to acquire a large amount of bond tokens, the protocol’s liquidity efficiency, and potentially the protocol’s reputation for accurate pricing. The impact is primarily economic: users receive fewer payout tokens per transaction, may incur higher transaction costs, and the market may experience reduced trading efficiency. The flaw belongs to the class of mis‑applied discount or price‑adjustment bugs where a financial factor is omitted from a critical formula, violating the assumption that the equilibrium price reflects the true cost basis. To remediate, the discounted price should be calculated first (price.mulDivUp(ONE_HUNDRED_PERCENT‑baseDiscount, ONE_HUNDRED_PERCENT)) and then used as the divisor in the capacity computation, ensuring that capacity and maxPayout reflect the intended equilibrium price. This correction restores the expected maximum payout, aligns the contract’s accounting with its business logic, and eliminates the need for users to fragment trades.

description:

```solidity
an unfair advantage.
```

bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a price‑validation routine that retrieves a Chainlink data feed on an L2 network such as Arbitrum but fails to verify whether the L2 sequencer is currently operational. Because the function does not call the sequencer‑up flag or any equivalent health check, it treats the returned price as fresh even when the underlying sequencer is down and the feed may be stale or deliberately frozen. The root cause is the omission of a required safety guard that Chainlink recommends for L2 deployments: checking the sequencer status before accepting a price. An attacker who can induce a sequencer outage—or who can manipulate the feed during a downtime window—can cause the contract to accept an outdated price as if it were current. By submitting transactions that rely on this stale price, the attacker may obtain an unfair advantage, for example by borrowing against an inflated collateral value or liquidating positions at a manipulated rate. The impact is a potential loss of funds for honest users, distortion of the protocol’s accounting, and erosion of trust in the price oracle integration. The flaw manifests whenever the contract calls the price‑validation function while the Arbitrum sequencer is offline; it does not depend on any particular user action, only on the network condition. All participants that rely on the price—depositors, borrowers, liquidators—are affected because the protocol may make decisions based on incorrect market data. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementation against Chainlink’s L2 sequencer‑feed guidelines. It is subtle because the price value itself appears syntactically correct and no revert occurs, so developers may assume the feed is reliable. To remediate, the contract should incorporate the standard sequencer‑up check (e.g., calling the `isSequencerUp` function or inspecting the `roundId` flag) and reject or pause price updates when the sequencer is reported down. This aligns the code with the generic class of bugs where external state is assumed valid without verification, leading to stale‑data acceptance and financial mis‑calculation. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that transactions that depend on price data may succeed but produce unexpected outcomes such as receiving a lower refund, an unexpected liquidation, or a sudden change in collateral valuation, contrary to the expectation that the price feed is always up‑to‑date.

title: Minting doesn't control for resulting zero shares
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the mint functions of the nwToken adapter for both Ether and ERC20 underlying assets. When a user calls mint with a positive amount of underlying, the contract converts that amount to nwToken shares using _convertToAsset, which performs integer division and rounds down. If the supplied amount is smaller than the current exchange rate denominator, the conversion yields zero shares. The code does not verify that the resulting share amount is greater than zero before calling the internal _mint routine. Consequently the transaction completes, the user's underlying tokens are transferred to the contract, but no nwTokens are minted, leaving the user with a net loss of the deposited assets. This can happen whenever the exchange rate is such that the smallest deposit that can be expressed in whole shares exceeds the amount sent, for example with very low deposits or after the exchange rate has increased. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the mint logic and noticed the absence of a post‑conversion positivity check. It is subtle because the transaction does not revert and emits the usual Mint event with a zero amount, which may be overlooked by UI layers; users may see that their balance of nwTokens did not increase and may assume the operation failed without realizing their funds are now held by the contract. The impact includes direct loss of user funds, potential downstream failures in systems that assume a positive share balance, and reputational damage to the protocol. The bug belongs to the class of “round‑down to zero” arithmetic errors and unchecked post‑condition failures in token minting. To remediate, the contract should enforce a non‑zero share result, for example by adding require(assetTokenAmount != 0, "Zero shares") after conversion, or by defining a minimum mint amount that guarantees at least one share. This ensures that any transaction that would otherwise produce zero shares reverts, protecting users from inadvertent asset loss.

title: token() function should return the address of
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the token() view function of the migrated wrapper contract (nwToken). After the migration from a Compound cToken to a new wrapper token, the function still returns the constant COMPOUND_TOKEN, which is the address of the original cToken, instead of returning the address of the wrapper itself (address(this)). This mismatch causes the governance routine that enables a cash group to reject the supplied asset rate oracle. Specifically, the internal _updateAssetRate routine reads the token address from the rate adapter via AssetRateAdapter(rateOracle).token() and asserts that it matches the asset token recorded in the TokenHandler. Because token() yields the old cToken address while the asset token entry now points to the nwToken address, the require check fails and the transaction reverts. The bug therefore prevents the protocol from successfully enabling cash groups for the migrated currencies, blocking the creation of nToken proxies, halting fCash trading, and potentially leaving user deposits unable to be minted or withdrawn. The issue is discovered during an audit of the Notional migration code, where tests showed that all four migrated tokens were instantiated with the old cToken address passed as COMPOUND_TOKEN. From a user’s perspective the UI would appear to accept a new token but subsequent actions would silently fail, often presenting generic “invalid rate oracle” errors or simply no response, leading users to see missing balances or an inability to trade. The problem is subtle because the token() function is expected to return an address, and returning a different but still valid address does not raise compile‑time warnings; only runtime validation catches the inconsistency. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect reference after upgrade” or “stale address reference” vulnerabilities, where a contract continues to expose a legacy identifier after its logical role has changed. To remediate, the token() implementation should be changed to return the contract’s own address (address(this)) so that the rate oracle correctly reflects the new wrapper token, aligning the on‑chain registry with the actual asset and allowing cash groups to be enabled without error.

```solidity
150000000 wei.
Bob can obtain all excess funds from the contract this way as long as
_checkSupplyInvariant() allows.
Since that's excess funds only, setting the severity to be medium.
redeemUnderlying() calls _convertToAsset() to get nwToken amount from the
underlying amount requested:
te/contracts/external/adapters/nwToken.sol#L116-L127
function redeemUnderlying(uint redeemAmount) external nonReentrant override
returns (uint) {
if (redeemAmount == 0) return NO_ERROR;
require(finalExchangeRate != 0);

_transferUnderlyingToSender(redeemAmount);

_convertToAsset() always rounds down:

I.e. the shares required for the given amount of underlying are rounded down and
so some amount of underlying within the same shared count can be obtained for

```
bug_full: redeemUnderlying suffers from a rounding‑down error when converting an underlying amount to the corresponding token shares. The private function that performs the conversion multiplies the requested underlying by a fixed‑point precision constant and then divides by the current exchange rate using integer division. Because Solidity discards the remainder, the result is always rounded down. Consequently the contract calculates fewer token shares than are actually required to cover the requested underlying amount. When a user mints tokens by supplying underlying and later calls redeemUnderlying for an amount that is just slightly larger than the exact value represented by those shares, the contract burns the rounded‑down share count and transfers the full requested underlying. The difference, often a few wei, is transferred to the caller for free. This behavior can be repeated as long as the internal supply invariant check does not reject the state, allowing an attacker to accumulate small but unbounded excess withdrawals. The bug manifests in any nwToken where the underlying asset has more decimal places than the wrapped token (for example ETH with 18 dp and cETH with 8 dp) and where the exchange rate precision requires a high‑precision divisor. Users experience the symptom of receiving slightly more underlying than they expected, e.g., a redeem of 1 ETH may return 1 ETH + 150 wei. The protocol’s accounting assumptions that each share represents a fixed proportion of the underlying are violated, breaking the invariant that total underlying equals total shares times the exchange rate. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the conversion routine and noticed the lack of a rounding‑up adjustment. It is hard to notice because the discrepancy is tiny per transaction and may be masked by normal rounding behavior in other parts of the code. The recommended mitigation is to change the conversion to round up (for example by adding the denominator‑1 before division) or to enforce an exact share calculation, and to tighten the supply‑invariant check to reject states where the contract holds less underlying than the outstanding shares imply. This class of vulnerability is commonly referred to as a rounding‑error or integer‑division truncation bug that leads to under‑collateralization and unintended fund leakage.

title: Bid submission vulnerable to market parameters
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race‑condition/parameter‑manipulation issue in the bid submission flow of the lending marketplace. When a borrower sends a transaction that calls the internal _submitBid function, the contract fetches several loan terms—payment cycle, APR, default duration, expiration time, payment type and the calculated payment‑cycle amount—from the MarketRegistry at the moment the transaction is executed. Because these values are read from a mutable registry rather than being locked in the transaction, a market owner who can modify the registry while the bid transaction is still pending in the mempool can change any of those parameters before the transaction is mined. As a result the borrower may be bound to a loan that differs from the terms they expected when they signed the transaction. An attacker can set the default duration or payment cycle to zero, causing the loan to be considered in default immediately after acceptance, which enables the market owner to liquidate the collateral and effectively steal it. The impact is that borrowers can lose their collateral without having had a chance to repay, and the loan’s accounting (payment schedule, interest calculation) no longer matches the user’s expectations. The issue manifests only when the market owner changes registry values between transaction submission and execution, a situation that is common in environments with high mempool activity or where the owner has incentive to front‑run. It is difficult to notice because the transaction itself does not revert and the on‑chain state appears consistent; the discrepancy is only visible after the loan is created, when the borrower sees an unexpected payment schedule or an immediate default. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running or sandwich‑style attacks that exploit mutable external configuration during a pending transaction. To mitigate the problem the contract should capture the relevant market parameters as inputs to _submitBid (or as part of the signed payload) and compare them against the current registry values, reverting the transaction if any mismatch is detected. This ensures that the borrower explicitly consents to the exact terms that will be applied, preventing silent changes that could lead to loss of funds.

title: EMI last payment not handled perfectly could
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect handling of the final equal‑monthly‑installment (EMI) payment in a loan contract. The contract calculates the amount due for a repayment cycle by first determining a maximum cycle owed value (maxCycleOwed). For the last payment cycle it sets maxCycleOwed to the sum of the remaining principal and accrued interest, then scales this amount by the proportion of time elapsed (owedTime) over the full payment cycle length. When a borrower makes the last payment early – for example a few minutes before the scheduled due date – owedTime is smaller than the full cycle, causing the computed owedAmount to be lower than the true total of principal plus interest. The code then assigns duePrincipal_ as the minimum of (owedAmount minus interest) and the remaining principal. Because owedAmount is understated, duePrincipal_ becomes smaller than the full principal, and the subsequent check paymentAmount >= _owedAmount fails. Consequently the loan state is not updated to PAID, the borrower’s collateral remains locked, and the lender can later trigger a default and withdraw the collateral. The impact is that a borrower who appears to have repaid the loan loses the collateral for a negligible unpaid amount, while the lender receives the principal, interest, and the seized collateral. This edge‑case occurs only when the final EMI is submitted before the end of its payment window; normal on‑time or late payments do not expose the flaw. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the repayment logic and identified the ternary expression and min‑function combination as a source of mis‑calculation. It is hard to notice because the discrepancy is small and only manifests under the specific timing of an early final payment, which many users may not test. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect settlement calculation for terminal payment periods” and violates the fundamental accounting assumption that the last payment must settle the entire outstanding balance regardless of elapsed time. To remediate, the contract should treat the last payment cycle as a full settlement, either by bypassing the time‑proportional scaling for the final cycle or by directly using the sum of remaining principal and interest as the amount due, ensuring the paymentAmount >= _owedAmount condition can be satisfied and the loan state transitions to PAID, thereby returning the collateral to the borrower.

title: defaulting doesn't change the state of the loan
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑inconsistency bug in the loan lifecycle where a defaulted loan is not marked as closed in the core loan contract (TellerV2) when the collateral is seized through the CollateralManager. The root cause is that the CollateralManager’s default‑handling branch only transfers the collateral to the lender and emits an event, but it never updates the loan status stored in TellerV2, which remains in the ACCEPTED state. Because the loan state is unchanged, the protocol still permits the lender to call the payment function and the borrower to continue sending repayments even though the loan has technically defaulted and the collateral is no longer available. An attacker (or a malicious lender) can exploit this by waiting for a loan to default, invoking the collateral claim, and then front‑running a pending repayment transaction to collect the payment while also keeping the seized collateral. The impact is that funds may be double‑spent: the lender receives both the late payment and the collateral, and the borrower may continue paying for a loan that is already considered defaulted, leading to wasted gas and potential loss of trust. This condition occurs whenever a loan becomes overdue and the CollateralManager’s default branch is executed; it does not depend on any special flags beyond the default check. All participants in the loan – the borrower, the lender, and any third‑party observers – are affected because the loan’s public status does not reflect its true condition, breaking accounting assumptions that a defaulted loan is closed and its collateral is either held or transferred. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Teller protocol where the flow of state updates across contracts was examined; it is subtle because the collateral transfer succeeds and the event is emitted, giving the appearance that the default handling completed, while the underlying loan record remains unchanged. Detecting the bug requires tracing cross‑contract state changes rather than looking at a single function. The recommended remediation is to move the default‑handling logic into TellerV2 so that the loan status is explicitly set to a CLOSED or DEFAULTED enum before the collateral is transferred, or to add a call from CollateralManager that updates the loan state in TellerV2. This class of bug is generally known as a state‑synchronisation or accounting inconsistency, where business logic (default → close loan) is not enforced at the data‑layer level. From a user’s perspective the UI may still show the loan as active, the borrower may see that payments are accepted but receive no acknowledgment that the loan is already defaulted, and the lender may notice that the collateral claim succeeded while the loan still appears payable, leading to confusion and potential financial loss.

title: bids can be created against markets that doesn't
bug_full: The contract allows a lender to submit a bid that references a market identifier without first checking whether that market has been created in the MarketRegistry. As a result a bid can be recorded against a non‑existent market. When the market is later created the bid can be accepted by the lender, but the stored loan parameters contain a paymentCycle of zero (because the PaymentType defaults to EMI which is represented by the value 0) and a default duration of zero. The loan logic later uses these fields in division operations when calculating the amount owed and when checking whether a loan is defaultable or liquidatable. Because the divisor is zero the calculations revert, causing the functions isLoanDefaulted, isLoanLiquidateable and repayLoanFull to either return false or throw a division‑by‑zero error. Consequently the loan can never be closed, the borrower’s collateral remains locked forever and the lender cannot recover the principal. The issue only manifests after a market is created and the bid is accepted, making it easy to miss during a superficial review that only looks at bid creation. It was discovered during a systematic audit that exercised the bid lifecycle with a market that did not exist at the time of bid submission. The bug belongs to the class of “missing existence checks leading to invalid state transitions” and violates the fundamental accounting assumption that every loan must have a well‑defined repayment schedule and default parameters. From a user’s perspective the borrower sees that the loan cannot be repaid and the collateral never returns, while the lender sees that the loan cannot be liquidated or reclaimed. The protocol’s financial safety guarantees are broken because funds become permanently inaccessible. The recommended remediation is to enforce a market‑existence validation when a bid is submitted and to ensure that paymentCycle and defaultDuration are non‑zero before a loan is instantiated, rejecting bids with zero APY or providing sensible defaults that prevent division‑by‑zero errors.

title: last repayments are calculated incorrectly
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the final repayment amount for loans whose total duration is not an exact multiple of the configured payment‑cycle length. The contract determines that the current cycle is the last one by checking whether the remaining loan time (durationLeftOnLoan) is less than a full payment‑cycle or whether the sum of principal and accrued interest is less than or equal to the per‑cycle payment amount. This logic assumes that the loan will always end exactly at a cycle boundary. When a loan spans a fractional number of cycles – for example a loan of 1,000 units with a duration of 2.5 cycles – the condition becomes true one cycle too early. As a result, the borrower is required to pay the entire remaining principal plus interest in the second cycle instead of the expected smaller installment (e.g., 600 instead of 400). The bug was discovered during an audit test that created such an “irregular” loan, advanced the blockchain time to the end of the first cycle, performed a repayment, and then observed that the second repayment demanded the full remaining balance. The issue is hard to notice because most loans in practice are configured with durations that are multiples of the payment‑cycle, so the erroneous branch is rarely exercised in normal testing. It violates the business logic that each installment should be bounded by the agreed payment‑cycle amount and that the final installment should only cover the leftover amount, not the whole loan. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a schedule like 400 + 400 + 200, yet the contract forces a payment of 600 on the second cycle, leading to unexpected loss of funds, possible liquidation of the borrower’s collateral, and a mismatch between displayed and actual balances. The affected parties include borrowers who may be forced to over‑pay or be liquidated, lenders who could see irregular cash‑flows, and the protocol itself which may lose credibility. The root cause is the misuse of a time‑based comparison to identify the last payment cycle and the reliance on a ceiling division in the EMI calculation that always rounds up the number of cycles, ignoring partial periods. A proper fix involves either rejecting loan requests whose duration is not an exact multiple of the payment‑cycle, or revising the EMI and last‑cycle logic to correctly handle partial cycles – for example by computing the exact remaining time and adjusting the maximum payable amount for the final period. Removing the flawed last‑payment‑cycle flag or replacing it with a calculation based on the actual remaining principal and interest would align the contract’s behavior with borrower expectations and restore the intended accounting guarantees.

title: setLenderManager may cause some Lenders
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract records the lender for each loan after an NFT is claimed. When a lender claims a loan NFT, the code sets the bid.lender field to the address of the current lender manager contract. Later, when a borrower repays the loan, the getLoanLender function checks whether the stored lender address equals the address of the current lender manager; if it does, the function returns the owner of the NFT from the manager, otherwise it returns the stored address directly. This design works only as long as the lender manager address never changes. If the contract owner calls setLenderManager to point to a new manager, the stored bid.lender still contains the old manager address. Consequently, the equality test fails, getLoanLender returns the stale old manager address, and the repayment is transferred to that outdated contract. Because the old manager is no longer the active component that tracks NFT ownership, the funds become inaccessible or can be captured by whoever controls the old contract, leading to a loss of lender assets. The issue is a classic stale reference or upgrade‑ability logic bug: a mutable contract address is used as an identifier for a dynamic role, and the code does not update existing loan records when the identifier changes. Exploitation is straightforward – any party with permission to call setLenderManager (typically the contract owner) can switch the manager after loans have been issued, causing subsequent repayments to be misrouted. From a user perspective, a lender who expects to receive a repayment may see the transaction succeed on‑chain but the funds never appear in their wallet, or the protocol may show a zero balance for that lender. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of repayment logic and identified the mismatch between stored lender addresses and the current manager reference. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit an error; the transfer simply goes to an address that no longer participates in the protocol, making the symptom appear as a silent loss of funds. The recommended mitigation is to stop using the mutable manager address as a sentinel value. Instead, a constant placeholder (referred to as MAGIC_NUMBER) should be stored in bid.lender to indicate that the true lender is the NFT owner managed by the lender manager. The getLoanLender function would then compare against this constant rather than the current manager address, ensuring that the ownership lookup remains correct even after the manager contract is upgraded. This approach eliminates the stale reference and restores correct routing of repayments, aligning the contract’s accounting with its business logic that lenders should receive their due payments regardless of manager upgrades.

title: A borrower/lender or liquidator will fail to withdraw collateral due to gas limit
bug_full: The vulnerability is a gas‑exhaustion denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when a borrower submits a bid with an unbounded number of collateral items. In the TellerV2 contract the submitBid function accepts an array called _collateralInfo, but it does not enforce any limit on the length of this array. Each element of the array is stored in a mapping that tracks collateral addresses and then later, when a borrower, lender, or liquidator attempts to withdraw the collateral, the CollateralManager iterates over the entire set of stored collateral addresses in a for‑loop inside the internal _withdraw function. Because the loop runs once for every collateral entry, a malicious or careless borrower can supply enough ERC20, ERC721 or ERC1155 assets to make the total gas consumption of the withdrawal transaction exceed the block gas limit. When the gas limit is hit, the transaction reverts and the collateral remains locked in the escrow. The impact is that legitimate participants – the borrower, the lender, or a liquidator – may be unable to retrieve or claim their assets even though the loan is repaid or liquidated, effectively freezing funds. The issue manifests only when the number of collateral entries is large enough to push the gas usage of the withdrawal or liquidation call beyond the available gas; normal‑size bids with a few collateral items work as expected. The affected parties are any user of the protocol who relies on the ability to reclaim collateral, including borrowers, lenders and third‑party liquidators. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the loops in CollateralManager and noticed the absence of any size check on the _collateralInfo parameter. It can be hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly for typical usage and only fails under extreme, but possible, input sizes, which may not be covered by standard tests. The root cause is the combination of an unrestricted input array and an unbounded iteration over that array during a state‑changing external call. To remediate the issue the protocol should enforce a reasonable maximum number of collateral items per bid, or redesign the withdrawal logic to process collateral in batches or via a pull‑based pattern that does not require iterating over an arbitrarily large collection in a single transaction. By limiting the array length or using pagination, the gas consumption of the withdrawal path becomes predictable and the risk of funds being permanently locked is eliminated.

title: updateCommitmentBorrowers does not delete
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of the Solidity delete operator on a mapping that stores an EnumerableSet data structure. EnumerableSet is a complex type that internally contains a dynamic array and a mapping used to track element existence. When the contract LenderCommitmentForwarder calls updateCommitmentBorrowers, it executes delete commitmentBorrowersList[_commitmentId]; expecting to remove all previously authorized borrower addresses for a given commitment. However, delete only resets the top‑level struct fields and does not clear the inner mapping that records which addresses are members of the set. Consequently, the stale addresses remain recorded as members of the set even though the external view of the set appears empty. An attacker or any previously authorized borrower can still invoke LenderCommitmentForwarder.acceptCommitment and receive a loan because the contract’s internal check uses the still‑populated EnumerableSet. This flaw was discovered during a manual audit when a test function demonstrated that after deleting a set, previously added addresses were still reported as present by the contains method.
