To remediate, the contract should explicitly reject assets with LTV = 0 from being treated as collateral, add a sanity check that the net borrow limit is greater than or equal to the existing borrow before performing subtraction, and enforce a hard cap on the borrow amount derived from protocol parameters. In broader terms, this is a classic case of unchecked arithmetic combined with missing validation of input parameters, leading to an underflow and a breach of the protocol’s financial safety model.

title: Loss of user funds - unchecked Return of ERC20
description:
Silently failing transfers can result in a partial or total loss of the users investment.
Some ERC20 Tokens do not revert on failure of the transfer function, but return a bool value instead. Some do not return any value. Therefore it is required to check if a value was returned, and if true, which value it is. This is not done on some places in these contracts.
The DebtIssuanceModulev2, which is required to issue or redeem tokens whenever there is a LeverageModule involved uses the invokeTransfer function of the Invoke library to transfer ERC20 Tokens from the SetToken to the user.
invokeTransfer is encoding the Calldata for the regular transfer function of ERC20 tokens and passes it together with the target (ERC20 token address) the SetTokens generic invoke function, which in turn uses functionCallWithValue from the Openzeppelin Address Library. This method is bubbling up a possible revert of the call and returning the raw data.
The generic invoke is returning this raw data, however in invokeTransfer the return value of invoke is ignored and not used. As some ERC20 Tokens do not revert on a failed transfer, but instead return a false bool value, the stated behaviour can lead to silently failing transfers.
This is inside the DebtIssuanceModulev2 used to:
1. Transfer The "debt" (borrowed) Tokens to the user at Issuance
2. Transfer back the main component Tokens (e.g. aTokens) to the user at Redemption
If such a Transfer silently fails, the funds will remain inside the setToken contract and the user has no chance to recover them.
In the issuance event the user receives the SetTokens but not the borrowed Tokens, which he has to repay when he wants to redeem the tokens. (Results in Loss of the "Debt")
In the redemption event the user repays his debt & burns his Set Tokens, but never receives his original Tokens back. (Total Loss of investment)
Possible Loss of all/part of the Investment for the User
Usage of invokeTransfer inDebtIssuanceModulev2:
cts/protocol/modules/v1/DebtIssuanceModuleV2.sol#L283
cts/protocol/modules/v1/DebtIssuanceModuleV2.sol#L315
invokeTransfer function ignores return value of invoke:
cts/protocol/lib/Invoke.sol#L66-L78
invoke uses functionCallwithValue and returns the raw return Data (which is ignored in this case):
cts/protocol/SetToken.sol#L197-L212
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked return value of ERC20 token transfers performed by the DebtIssuanceModuleV2. The module uses a generic invoke function that forwards the calldata for the standard ERC20 transfer and receives the raw return data from OpenZeppelin's functionCallWithValue, but the invokeTransfer wrapper discards this data. Many ERC20 implementations do not revert on a failed transfer; instead they return a boolean false or no value at all. Because the contract does not verify that a returned boolean exists and is true, a transfer can silently fail while the external call itself reports success. This situation can occur during both issuance, where borrowed tokens are supposed to be sent to the user, and redemption, where the user should receive back the underlying assets after repaying debt. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful transaction, the SetToken is minted or burned as expected, but the user receives no borrowed tokens on issuance or receives zero of the original tokens on redemption. The accounting logic of the protocol assumes that the token balances have moved; when the transfer silently fails the funds remain locked inside the SetToken contract, leading to partial or total loss of the user’s investment and an unrecoverable debt position. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the invokeTransfer implementation and noted that the returned data from the low‑level call was never examined. It is hard to notice because no revert is emitted, no event signals the failure, and the contract’s external behavior (transaction success) masks the internal loss. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external call return‑value errors, specifically the failure to validate ERC20 transfer success. To remediate, the contract should validate the presence and truthiness of the returned data, for example by using OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library and its safeTransfer function, which automatically reverts on false returns or missing data. This ensures that any transfer failure propagates as a transaction revert, preserving the expected business logic that users receive their tokens or that the protocol aborts the operation.

title: no validation to ensure the arbitrum sequencer
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation step that fails to verify whether the Chainlink sequencer on an Arbitrum layer‑2 network is operational before the contract reads price data. The root cause is that the contract directly calls latestAnswer on the collateral and borrow price oracles and scales the returned values without checking the sequencer status flag provided by Chainlink. When the sequencer is down, the oracle continues to return the last stored answer, which appears fresh to the contract even though it is stale. An attacker who can detect a sequencer outage can trigger a rebalance transaction while the price feed is frozen; the protocol will then compute collateral and borrow values based on outdated prices. Because the stale price may be significantly different from the current market price, the rebalance can be forced into a loss‑making position, causing users to lose collateral or be liquidated unfairly. This condition occurs only during periods when the Arbitrum sequencer is offline, a situation that is not obvious from the UI because the price values still display numbers and no error is emitted. All participants who rely on the protocol’s pricing – borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself – are affected, as the accounting assumptions that collateral value equals the market value are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the absence of a sequencerUp check in the price‑retrieval logic. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit warnings; the stale price is indistinguishable from a legitimate update without external monitoring. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit sequencer status verification (for example, using Chainlink’s sequencerUp() function or checking the answer’s timestamp) before using the oracle values, and to fallback or pause operations if the sequencer is reported down. By ensuring that only fresh, verified price data is used, the protocol can maintain correct accounting and prevent forced loss‑making rebalances.

title: Relying solely on oracle base slippage param-
description:
AaveLeverageStrategyExtension relies solely on oracle price data when determining the slippage parameter during a rebalance. This is problematic as chainlink oracles, especially mainnet, have upwards of 2% threshold before triggering a price update. If swapping between volatile assets, the errors will compound causing even bigger variation. These variations can be exploited via sandwich attacks.
AaveLeverageStrategyExtension.sol#L1147-L1152
```solidity
function _calculateMinRepayUnits(uint256 _collateralRebalanceUnits, uint256 _slippageTolerance, ActionInfo memory _actionInfo) internal pure returns (uint256) {

    return _collateralRebalanceUnits
        .preciseMul(_actionInfo.collateralPrice)
        .preciseDiv(_actionInfo.borrowPrice)
        .preciseMul(PreciseUnitMath.preciseUnit().sub(_slippageTolerance));
}
```
When determining the minimum return from the swap, _calculateMinRepayUnits the true value and the oracle value can be systematically exploited via sandwich attacks. Given the leverage nature of the module, these losses can cause significant loss to the pool.
Purely oracle derived slippage parameters will lead to significant and unnecessary losses
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the AaveLeverageStrategyExtension contract relying exclusively on the price reported by a Chainlink oracle to compute the slippage tolerance used in the _calculateMinRepayUnits function during a rebalance. Because Chainlink price feeds on mainnet only update when the price moves beyond a roughly 2 % threshold, the oracle price can be stale when the strategy swaps between volatile assets. The stale price is multiplied by the user‑provided slippage tolerance, producing a minimum expected return that is higher than what the market will actually deliver. An attacker can observe the pending rebalance transaction, execute a front‑running trade that moves the market price, and then execute a back‑running trade (a sandwich attack) that forces the swap to execute at a worse rate. The contract will still consider the trade acceptable because the oracle price has not yet reflected the price movement, causing the pool to receive fewer collateral units than expected. This loss is amplified by the leveraged nature of the strategy, potentially draining a significant portion of the pool’s assets. The issue manifests when the rebalance is triggered while the oracle price is outdated, which is common during periods of high volatility or when the price feed’s update threshold is large. Users of the protocol experience unexpected reductions in their deposited collateral, lower returns, or even zero refunds after a rebalance, contrary to the expectation that the slippage parameter protects them. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined the slippage calculation logic and recognized that no external price verification or dynamic slippage adjustment was performed. It is difficult to notice because the contract code appears to use a standard oracle‑based price and a configurable slippage tolerance, giving the impression of safety, while the underlying price staleness is invisible to on‑chain observers. The vulnerability belongs to the class of oracle‑dependent slippage mis‑estimation bugs that enable sandwich attacks. To remediate, the contract should allow a trusted keeper to supply a custom slippage value and enforce that this custom value does not deviate from the oracle price by more than a small, predefined threshold, thereby providing tighter, more reactive control while still limiting the risk of malicious keeper behavior.

title: Chainlink price feed is deprecated, not suffi-
bug_full: The contract calculates collateral and borrow valuations by calling the Chainlink price feeds through the deprecated latestAnswer function inside the internal _createActionInfo routine. Because latestAnswer returns only the raw price without any timestamp or round identifier, the implementation does not verify whether the returned value reflects the most recent round or whether the data is stale. As a result, if the price feed has not been updated for a period of time, the contract will continue to use an outdated price when computing the collateralPrice and borrowPrice fields. This stale or potentially invalid price propagates through the rest of the protocol, causing mis‑valuation of user positions. An attacker or a benign market condition can therefore trigger scenarios where a borrower appears over‑collateralised when in fact the true market price is lower, or vice‑versa, leading to unexpected liquidations, denial of withdrawals, or the ability to borrow more assets than should be allowed. The issue manifests whenever _createActionInfo is invoked – typically during rebalance, borrow, repay or liquidation checks – and the underlying Chainlink feed has not produced a fresh round. All participants who rely on accurate pricing, including lenders, borrowers and the protocol itself, are affected because the accounting assumptions that collateral value equals price × amount are violated. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that flagged the use of the deprecated latestAnswer call and the absence of any freshness checks. It can be hard to notice because the price value may still look plausible; without a timestamp the contract has no way to detect that the data is old, so the bug does not raise explicit errors but silently skews calculations. The recommended remediation is to replace latestAnswer with the newer latestRoundData interface, capture the roundId, answeredInRound and updatedAt fields, and enforce that answeredInRound is at least the current roundId and that updatedAt is non‑zero (and optionally within an acceptable time window). This ensures that only fresh, verified price data is used for valuation, restoring the integrity of the protocol’s accounting logic and preventing funds from disappearing or being liquidated incorrectly.

title: The protocol does not compatible with token
description:
The protocol does not compatible with token such as USDT because of the Approval Race Protection
the protocol is intended to interact with any ERC20 token and USDT is a common one
Q: Which ERC20 tokens do you expect will interact with the smart contracts? The protocol expects to interact with any ERC20.
Individual SetToken's should only interact with ERC20 chosen by the SetToken manager.
when doing the deleverage
https://github.com/IndexCoop/index-protocol/blob/86be7ee76d9a7e4f7e93acfc533216ebef791c89/contracts/protocol/modules/v1/AaveV3LeverageModule.sol#L31
first, we construct the deleverInfo
```solidity
ActionInfo memory deleverInfo = _createAndValidateActionInfo(
    _setToken,
    _collateralAsset,
    _repayAsset,
    _redeemQuantityUnits,
    _minRepayQuantityUnits,
    _tradeAdapterName,
    false
);
```
then we withdraw from the lending pool, execute trade and repay the borrow token
```solidity
_withdraw(deleverInfo.setToken, deleverInfo.lendingPool, _collateralAsset, deleverInfo.notionalSendQuantity);

uint256 postTradeReceiveQuantity = _executeTrade(deleverInfo, _collateralAsset, _repayAsset, _tradeData);

uint256 protocolFee = _accrueProtocolFee(_setToken, _repayAsset, postTradeReceiveQuantity);

uint256 repayQuantity = postTradeReceiveQuantity.sub(protocolFee);
_repayBorrow(deleverInfo.setToken, deleverInfo.lendingPool, _repayAsset, repayQuantity);
```
this is calling _repayBorrow
```solidity
/**
 * @dev Invoke repay from SetToken using AaveV2 library. Burns DebtTokens for SetToken.
 */
function _repayBorrow(ISetToken _setToken, ILendingPool _lendingPool, IERC20 _asset, uint256 _notionalQuantity) internal {
    _setToken.invokeApprove(address(_asset), address(_lendingPool), _notionalQuantity);

    _setToken.invokeRepay(_lendingPool, address(_asset), _notionalQuantity, BORROW_RATE_MODE);
}
```
the trade received (quantity - the protocol fee) is used to repay the debt
but the required debt to be repaid is the (borrowed amount + the interest rate)
suppose the only debt that needs to be repaid is 1000 USDT
trade received (quantity - the protocol fee) is 20000 USDT
only 1000 USDT is used to repay the debt
because when repaying, the paybackAmount is only the debt amount
https://github.com/aave/aave-v3-core/blob/29ff9b9f89af7cd8255231bc5faf26c3ce0fb7ce/contracts/protocol/libraries/logic/BorrowLogic.sol#L204
```solidity
uint256 paybackAmount = params.interestRateMode == DataTypes.InterestRateMode.STABLE
    ? stableDebt
    : variableDebt;
```
then when burning the variable debt token
https://github.com/aave/aave-v3-core/blob/29ff9b9f89af7cd8255231bc5faf26c3ce0fb7ce/contracts/protocol/libraries/logic/BorrowLogic.sol#L224
```solidity
reserveCache.nextScaledVariableDebt = IVariableDebtToken(
    reserveCache.variableDebtTokenAddress
).burn(params.onBehalfOf, paybackAmount, reserveCache.nextVariableBorrowIndex);
```
only the "payback amount", which is 1000 USDT is transferred to pay the debt, the excessive leftover amount is (20000 USDT - 1000 USDT) = 19000 USDT
but if we look back into the repayBorrow function
```solidity
/**
 * @dev Invoke repay from SetToken using AaveV2 library. Burns DebtTokens for SetToken.
 */
function _repayBorrow(ISetToken _setToken, ILendingPool _lendingPool, IERC20 _asset, uint256 _notionalQuantity) internal {
    _setToken.invokeApprove(address(_asset), address(_lendingPool), _notionalQuantity);

    _setToken.invokeRepay(_lendingPool, address(_asset), _notionalQuantity, BORROW_RATE_MODE);
}
```
the approved amount is 20000 USDT, but only 1000 USDT approval limit is used, we have 19000 USDT approval limit left
according to
https://github.com/d-xo/weird-erc20#approval-race-protections
Some tokens (e.g. OpenZeppelin) will revert if trying to approve the zero address to spend tokens (i.e. a call to approve(address(0), amt)).
Integrators may need to add special cases to this logic if working with such a token.
USDT is such token that subject to approval race condition, without approving 0 first, the second approve after first repay will revert
second and following repay borrow will revert if the ERC20 token is subject to approval race condition
bug_full: The vulnerability is a compatibility problem between the Index protocol’s deleverage module and ERC‑20 tokens that implement an approval‑race‑protection mechanism, such as USDT. The root cause lies in the way the module handles token allowances when repaying a borrow on Aave. After a trade, the contract approves the full amount of tokens received (for example 20,000 USDT) to the Aave lending pool, then calls the Aave repay function. Aave only consumes the exact debt amount (for example 1,000 USDT) and ignores the surplus, leaving a large unused allowance (19,000 USDT) on the token contract. Tokens with approval‑race‑protection require that any change to a non‑zero allowance first be reset to zero; otherwise a subsequent approve call will revert. Because the protocol does not reset the allowance to zero before issuing a new approve for the next repayment, the second and later calls to _repayBorrow revert when the token is USDT or any token with the same protection. An attacker does not need to be involved – the bug manifests automatically during normal operation. The impact is that a user who initiates a deleverage expecting to receive the excess funds will see the transaction fail, leaving their SetToken in a partially deleveraged state and potentially locking funds in the protocol. The issue occurs only when the repay token is subject to approval‑race‑protection and when multiple repay cycles are required, which is common for leveraged strategies that repeatedly rebalance. It was discovered during a manual audit of the AaveV3LeverageModule when tracing the flow of allowances and comparing the approved amount with the amount actually consumed by Aave’s BorrowLogic. The problem is subtle because the first repayment succeeds, giving the impression that the logic is correct, while the hidden leftover allowance only triggers a failure on subsequent calls. To remediate, the protocol should follow the safe‑approve pattern: before setting a new allowance, first call approve(token, spender, 0) to clear the previous allowance, then call approve with the desired amount, or use OpenZeppelin’s safeIncreaseAllowance / safeDecreaseAllowance utilities. This change ensures compatibility with all ERC‑20 tokens, restores the expected behaviour where users receive the correct post‑trade funds, and prevents unexpected reverts that could freeze assets.

title: User would liquidate his account to sidestep
description:
A single user could open a massive maker position, using the maximum leverage possible (and possibly reach the maker limit), and when a lot of takers open take positions, maker would liquidate his position, effectively bypassing the taker invariant and losing nothing apart from position fees. This would cause takers to be charged extremely high funding fees (at the maxRate), and takers that are not actively monitoring their positions will be greatly affected.

In the closeMakeFor function, there is a modifier called takerInvariant.
```solidity
function closeMakeFor(
    address account
)
    public
    nonReentrant
    notPaused
    onlyAccountOrMultiInvoker(account)
    settleForAccount(account)
    takerInvariant
    closeInvariant(account)
    liquidationInvariant(account)
{
    _closeMake(account, amount);
}
```
This modifier prevents makers from closing their positions if it would make the global maker open positions to fall below the global taker open positions. A malicious maker can easily sidestep this by liquidating his own account. Liquidating an account pays the liquidator a fee from the account's collateral, and then forcefully closes all open maker and taker positions for that account.
```solidity
function closeAll(address account) external onlyCollateral notClosed settleForAccount(account) {
    AccountPosition storage accountPosition = _positions[account];
    Position memory p = accountPosition.position.next(_positions[account].pre);
    // Close all positions
    _closeMake(account, p.maker);
    _closeTake(account, p.taker);
    // Mark liquidation to lock position
    accountPosition.liquidation = true;
}
```
This would make the open maker positions drop significantly below the open taker position, and greatly increase the funding fee and utilization ratio.

ATTACK SCENARIO
• A new Product (ETH-Long) is launched on arbitrum with the following configurations:
– 20x max leverage (5% maintenance)
– makerFee = 0
– takerFee = 0.015
– liquidationFee = 20%
– minRate = 4%
– maxRate = 120%
– targetRate = 12%
– targetUtilization = 80%
– makerLimit = 4000 Eth
– ETH price = 1750 USD
– Coll Token = USDC
– max liquidity (USD) = 4000*1750 = $7,000,000
• Whale initially supplies 350k USDC of collateral (~200ETH), and opens a maker position of 3000ETH ($5.25mn), at 15x leverage.
• After 2 weeks of activity, global open maker position goes up to 3429ETH (~6mn); and because fundingFee is low, people are incentivized to open taker positions, so global at 80% utilization. Now, rate of fundingFee is 12%
• Now, Whale should only be able to close up to 686ETH ($1.2mn) of his maker position using the closeMakeFor function because of the takerInvariant modifier.
• Whale decides to withdraw 87.5k USDC (~50ETH), bringing his total collateral to 262.5k USDC, and his leverage to 20x (which is the max leverage)
• If price of ETH temporarily goes up to 1755 USD, totalMaintenance = 3000 * 1755 * 5% = $263250. Because his totalCollateral is 262500 USDC (which is less than totalMaintenance), his account becomes liquidatable.
• Whale liquidates his account, he receives liquidationFee * totalMaintenance = 20% * 263250 = 52650 USDC, and his maker position of 3000ETH gets closed. Now, he can withdraw his remaining collateral (262500 - 52650 = 209850) USDC because he has no open positions.
• Global taker position is now 2743ETH (~4.8mn); and global maker position is 429ETH (~750k)
• Whale has succeeded in bypassing the takerInvaraiant modifier, which was to prevent him from closing his maker position if it would make global maker position less than global taker position.

Consequently,
• Funding fees would now be very high (120%), so the currently open taker positions will be greatly penalized, and takers who are not actively monitoring their position could lose a lot.
• Whale would want to gain from the high funding fees, so he would open a maker position that would still keep the global maker position less than the global taker position (e.g. collateral of 232750 USDC at 15x leverage, open position = ~2000ETH ($3.5mn)) so that taker positions will keep getting charged at the funding fee maxRate.

User will close his maker position when he shouldn't be allowed to, and it would cause open taker positions to be greatly impacted. And those who are not actively monitoring their open taker positions will suffer loss due to high funding fees.
bug_full: A vulnerability exists in the funding‑fee enforcement logic of the perpetual product where a maker can bypass the takerInvariant check by liquidating his own account. The takerInvariant modifier is intended to prevent a maker from closing a position that would cause the total open maker volume to fall below the total open taker volume, thereby protecting takers from excessive funding fees. The root cause is that the liquidation pathway (closeAll) closes both maker and taker positions for the account and marks the account as liquidated without invoking the takerInvariant modifier. Consequently, a malicious maker who holds a very large maker position can deliberately become under‑collateralised, trigger self‑liquidation, receive the liquidation fee, and force the global maker volume to drop dramatically while the global taker volume remains high. This state drives the funding fee calculation to its maximum rate (maxRate), causing all remaining taker positions to be charged extremely high funding fees, often up to 120 % per period. The exploit can be carried out when the maker has opened a position close to the maximum allowed leverage, has enough collateral to become liquidatable, and can invoke the liquidation function. The affected parties include takers who see their funding fees spike unexpectedly, users who may lose value in their positions, and the protocol itself which suffers from unfair fee distribution and potential loss of trust. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s closeMakeFor and liquidation functions, where the interaction between the takerInvariant modifier and the liquidation flow was identified as a logical gap. The problem is subtle because liquidation is a legitimate operation that rewards the liquidator, so the bypass does not raise an immediate error and may be overlooked during testing. From a user perspective, a taker may notice that the funding fee displayed in the UI jumps from a normal rate (e.g., 12 %) to the maximum rate (120 %) without any market event, and may see their position value erode rapidly despite no price movement. The maker, on the other hand, can close a large position that the protocol should have prevented, receive a liquidation fee, and withdraw the remaining collateral, effectively profiting from the fee spike. This class of bug can be described as an invariant‑bypass through an alternative state‑changing function, a common pattern where access‑control or safety checks are applied only to a subset of entry points. To remediate the issue, the protocol should enforce the takerInvariant (or an equivalent maker‑to‑taker balance check) on all paths that can reduce maker exposure, including liquidation, or redesign the fee model so that self‑liquidation does not create a disproportionate advantage. Additional mitigations include introducing a per‑account maker limit to prevent any single user from controlling a large share of the maker side, and allocating a portion of the liquidation fee to the protocol treasury to remove the incentive for self‑liquidation. Implementing these changes would restore the intended funding‑fee equilibrium and protect takers from unexpected fee spikes.

title: Market Allows Zero Amount Positions Which
description:
When adjusting positions, it correctly calculates the amount and respects limits, but it runs into a problem when dealing with a zero amount in the openMake and closeMake functions. This problem occurs when the Vault doesn't wish to change any position but still communicates a "0" amount to the product, resulting in revert and halting the rebalancing process.

When decreasing a position, the Market Vault calculates the available room and permits only the closing of positions up to the point where the maker equals the taker. If the market's taker is greater than the maker, the amount is deemed as zero.
Conversely, when increasing a position, the Vault checks if the product's maker limit is exceeded. If it is, the Vault assigns the amount as zero. Following this, the Vault executes the closeMake and openMake functions using the calculated amount.

However, an issue arises with the Vault's openMake and closeMake functions operating with a zero amount. Even though the Vault might not want to open or close any position, it still calls the product with a "0" amount. This leads to the modifiers throwing an error, and the rebalancing process gets stuck.

In such cases where maker limit is exceeded in product or takers > makers vaults rebalancing will be stuck. Therefore, I'll call it as high
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the market vault invoking product functions with a zero‑amount parameter during rebalancing operations. When the vault calculates the amount to open or close a position, it may determine that the amount is zero because either the maker limit of the product is exceeded or the market taker balance exceeds the maker balance. Instead of skipping the call, the vault proceeds to execute the openMake or closeMake functions with this zero amount. The product contracts contain modifiers that reject calls with a zero amount, causing the transaction to revert. This revert halts the rebalancing loop, leaving the vault unable to adjust positions further. The issue manifests when the rebalancing logic expects a non‑zero amount to be processed, but the business rules legitimately result in zero, such as when no position change is required or limits are hit. From a user perspective, a rebalance transaction appears to be submitted but then fails with a revert, the UI shows no change in balances, and the protocol may appear frozen or unresponsive. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for the market: liquidity providers cannot have their positions rebalanced, potentially leading to stale pricing, reduced capital efficiency, and loss of confidence. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of amount calculations and the interaction with product modifiers. It is subtle because a zero amount seems harmless, yet the product’s internal checks treat it as an invalid operation, making the failure easy to miss without thorough testing. The root cause is a lack of input validation in the vault: it does not guard against zero‑amount calls before invoking external functions. To remediate, the vault should detect a zero amount and simply return from the openMake or closeMake routine without making the external call, effectively treating the situation as a no‑op. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that a zero amount means no position change, preventing the revert and restoring normal rebalancing behavior. The vulnerability belongs to the class of zero‑value call validation errors, where improper handling of edge‑case inputs leads to contract reverts and service interruption.

title: Payoff definitions that can cross zero price
description:
The price that is returned by an Oracle can be transformed by a "Payoff Provider" to transform the Oracle price and implement different payoff functions (e.g. 3x Leveraged ETH, ETH*ETH).
According to the documentation, any payoff function is supported:
https://docs.perennial.finance/mechanism/payoff

The problem is that this is not true.
Payoff functions that transform the Oracle price such that the transformed price can cross from negative to positive or from positive to negative are not supported.
This is because there is a location in the code, where there is division by currentPrice:
perennial-vaults/contracts/balanced/BalancedVault.sol#L487
Thus there is a risk of division-by-zero if the price was allowed to cross the 0 value.

In contrast to what is specified in the Docs, not all payoff functions are supported which can lead to a situation where it causes division-by-zero and thereby DOS.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the payoff transformation logic of the Perennial BalancedVault. A Payoff Provider takes the price returned by an external Oracle and applies a user‑defined payoff function (for example 3× leveraged ETH or ETH × ETH) before the price is used in the vault’s accounting. The contract assumes that the transformed price is always non‑zero, as documented, and later divides by the variable `currentPrice`. If the payoff function is capable of producing a value that can become zero or change sign—i.e., cross from positive to negative or vice‑versa—the division operation may encounter a zero divisor. When `currentPrice` equals zero the transaction reverts, causing a denial‑of‑service condition that prevents further deposits, withdrawals, or fee calculations. This situation can arise whenever the underlying oracle price moves such that the payoff formula evaluates to zero, which is possible for leveraged or quadratic payoffs when the underlying asset price approaches the breakeven point of the formula. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the vault contract, where the line performing `amount / currentPrice` was identified as unsafe for payoff functions that are not strictly positive. The bug is subtle because the documentation explicitly states that "any payoff function is supported," leading developers to assume safety, while the actual code does not enforce a non‑zero invariant. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a transaction that suddenly fails with a division‑by‑zero revert, balances that appear unchanged after an operation, or a vault that becomes unresponsive, contrary to the expectation that a deposit or withdrawal will succeed and the user will receive the correct amount. The impact is limited to vaults employing such risky payoff definitions, but it can affect any participant who interacts with those vaults, potentially locking funds until the contract is upgraded. To remediate the issue the protocol should either restrict the set of allowed payoff functions to those that guarantee a strictly positive transformed price, or introduce an explicit guard that detects a zero `currentPrice` and substitutes a safe fallback value (for example setting it to 1) or reverts with a clear error message. Updating the documentation to reflect the supported payoff classes and adding runtime checks will prevent the division‑by‑zero scenario and restore reliable operation of the vault.

title: Leveraged trader with small collateral can
description:
A highly leveraged trader (around max leverage) with small collateral can autoliquidate position to create a riskless position.

As we can see in closeTake function:
perennial-mono/packages/perennial/contracts/product/Product.sol#L246-L256
• maintenanceInvariant is not enforced, meaning that extraction of takerFee can make the position go unhealthy
perennial-mono/packages/perennial/contracts/collateral/Collateral.sol#L128-L129
• minimum liquidation incentive equals liquidationFee * minCollateral. Which is constant and equal to 0.5 DSU on arbitrum products such as: https://arbiscan.io/address/0x5E660B7B8357059241EAEc143e1e68A5A108D035

We can deduce that a highly leveraged trader, with very small collateral (0.5 DSU) can create a riskless position lasting until next settlement by auto liquidating.

Example: Maintenance factor is 2% Liquidation fee is 5% Taker fee is 0.1% Funding fee is 0%
Alice has a 50x leverage taker position opened as authorized per maintenance invariant:
Alice collateral: 0.5 DSU Alice taker position: notional of 25 DSU
To create the riskless position Alice does in the same tx:
• closes the taker position (and by paying the takerFee makes her position instantly liquidatable)
• liquidates her position withdrawing the whole 0.5 DSU collateral

For the rest of the oracle version Alice has a 25 DSU position with 0 collateral. Which means that in the end of the period:
• if positive Pnl: Alice gets it added to her collateral, and can withdraw some gains
• if negative Pnl: It gets induced upon the protocol as shortfall: https://github.com/perennial/contracts/collateral/types/OptimisticLedger.sol#L62-L73

If Alice has multiple such positions on multiple accounts, considerable amounts can be stolen this way from the protocol.
Alice obtains a riskless position, inducing potential shortfall on the protocol
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw that allows a highly leveraged trader with a very small amount of collateral to create a risk‑free position by self‑liquidating within a single transaction. The root cause lies in the contract’s failure to enforce the maintenance invariant after fee extraction: the taker fee taken during a close operation can reduce the effective collateral below the required threshold, yet the contract does not prevent the position from remaining open. Additionally, the liquidation incentive is a constant value (liquidationFee multiplied by a minimum collateral amount) that does not scale with the size of the position, enabling a trader to withdraw the entire tiny collateral while leaving the notional exposure untouched. Because the protocol adds positive PnL to an account’s collateral even when that account has zero collateral, the invariant that a position must always retain some risk is violated. An attacker can exploit this by opening a max‑leverage position with the minimum allowed collateral (for example 0.5 DSU on Arbitrum), then in the same transaction closes the position, pays the small taker fee which instantly makes the position liquidatable, and immediately triggers liquidation to pull out the full collateral. After liquidation the account holds a notional exposure of 25 DSU with zero collateral, which appears to the user as a “riskless” position. At the end of the settlement period, if the market moves against the trader, the negative PnL is recorded as a shortfall on the protocol’s optimistic ledger, effectively stealing funds from the system. This issue manifests when a trader uses maximum leverage, the contract does not check the maintenance invariant after fee deduction, and the liquidation incentive remains a fixed 0.5 DSU. It affects leveraged traders, the protocol’s liquidity pool, and any users relying on the protocol’s accounting integrity. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the closeTake function and the collateral handling logic, where the missing invariant check and the constant liquidation incentive were identified. The problem is subtle because the UI may show that the collateral has been withdrawn and the position appears closed, yet the underlying notional exposure persists, leading to unexpected zero‑balance accounts that can still generate profit or loss. From a user perspective the symptoms include seeing the collateral disappear while the position remains open, receiving no refund when expecting one, or observing the protocol’s total collateral shrink without a clear transaction. To remediate, the contract should enforce that a position cannot become collateral‑free at any point, disallow adding positive PnL to an account with zero collateral, and make the liquidation incentive proportional to the actual risk rather than a fixed constant, thereby preserving the invariant that every open position retains some minimum collateral.

title: Accounts will not be liquidated when they
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the liquidation routine that can prevent an under‑collateralised account from being liquidated. The contract reads the total collateral amount before calling product.closeAll, which deducts a close‑position fee from the account’s balance. The fee that is later transferred to the liquidator is calculated as the minimum of the pre‑close total collateral and the product of collateralForFee and the liquidation fee. Because the pre‑close total collateral is higher than the actual balance after the fee deduction, the calculated fee may exceed the remaining collateral. When the contract then attempts to debit the account with this oversized fee, an underflow occurs and the transaction reverts, leaving the account un‑liquidated. This situation arises when totalMaintenance multiplied by the liquidation fee is greater than the account’s total collateral, i.e., when the account should be liquidated according to the protocol’s risk parameters. The bug primarily affects users who hold highly leveraged positions, liquidators who try to execute a liquidation, and the protocol itself because positions that should be closed remain open, exposing the system to potentially massive losses. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation logic, where the auditor noticed that the collateral value used for fee calculation was fetched before the closeAll call and therefore did not reflect the post‑fee balance. The problem is subtle because normal liquidations succeed; only when the fee deduction pushes the balance below the calculated fee does the underflow trigger, making it easy to miss in routine testing. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a position that has fallen far below the maintenance margin does not trigger a liquidation event; the UI may show the account as still active while the underlying collateral is insufficient, leading to a false sense of security. The bug belongs to the class of “stale state usage in financial accounting” or “incorrect collateral accounting during liquidation”. To remediate the issue the contract should recompute the current collateral after product.closeAll, or otherwise cap the fee to the actual remaining balance before attempting the debit, ensuring that the liquidation can proceed without causing an underflow. This correction restores the intended business logic that accounts with insufficient collateral are forcibly closed and that liquidators receive the correct compensation.

title: Unintended Vault Operation Due to Product
description:
Vault operation can behave unexpectedly when products settle and skip versions in their oracles. This problem arises when the vault assumes a non-existent version of a product, leading to miscalculations in the _assetsAtEpoch() function. This inaccuracy can affect the distribution of shares among depositors, redeemers, and claimers, disrupting the balance of the market.

When a product progresses to a new version of its oracle, it first settles at the current version plus one, then jumps to the latest version. For instance, if a product's latest version is 20 and the current version is 23, the product will first settle at version 21 and then jump from 21 to 23, bypassing version 22. This process can lead to unintended behavior in the vault, particularly if the vault's deposited epoch points to the bypassed version, which can result in a potential underflow and subsequent rounding to zero.

Consider this scenario: A vault is operating with two markets, each having two products. Let's assume the vault has equal positions and collateral in both markets, with all assets priced at $1 for simplicity. Also, assume that Market0 contains product A and product B, while Market1 contains product C and product D.
The latest version of product A is 20, while the vault's latest epoch is 2, which corresponds to version 20 for product A. Similarly, the latest version of product C is 10, with the vault's latest epoch at 2, corresponding to version 10 for product A.
Assume there are no positions created in product C, D, and also no deposits made to the vault, meaning the vault has not opened any positions on these products either. The oracle version for product C, D gets updated twice consecutively. Since there are no open positions in product C, D, their products will progress to version 12 directly, bypassing version 11.

This circumstance renders the epoch stale, which will lead to miscalculations in deposits, claims, and redemptions. During the _assetsAtEpoch() function, the vault incorrectly assumes that there is a version 11 of product C, D. However, these products have skipped version 11 and advanced to 12. Since the latest version of product C, D is greater than the version the vault holds, the vault presumes that version 11 exists. However, as version 11 doesn't exist, the _accumulatedAtEpoch will be the negative of whatever was deposited. This leads the vault to incorrectly assume a large loss in that market. Consequently, depositors can gain more shares, while redeemers and claimers may receive fewer shares.

If the above scenario happens, vault users can incur extreme losses on claim and redeem operations and depositors can earn uneven shares.
perennial-mono/packages/perennial/contracts/product/Product.sol#L84-L130 settle
perennial-mono/packages/perennial/contracts/interfaces/types/PrePosition.sol#L133-L136 if no open positions in preposition settle version is current version
perennial-vaults/contracts/balanced/BalancedVault.sol#L376
perennial-vaults/contracts/balanced/BalancedVault.sol#L823-L843 checks for +1 version, if latestVersion > currentVersion, it assumes vault lost all the funds in that market.
perennial-vaults/contracts/balanced/BalancedVault.sol#L797-L805
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the vault’s accounting routine that assumes a product version always increments by exactly one. When a product’s oracle advances by more than one version, the vault continues to reference the intermediate version that never existed. This mismatch occurs in the _assetsAtEpoch() function, where the vault reads the accumulated value for a version that was skipped. Because the contract treats the missing version as if it were present, it calculates a negative accumulated amount, which is then rounded to zero. The resulting zero balance is interpreted as a total loss for that market, causing the share‑allocation algorithm to inflate the number of shares granted to new depositors while reducing the amount returned to claimers and redeemers. The bug is triggered only when a product settles at the current version plus one and then jumps directly to a later version, a situation that can happen when there are no open positions for that product and the oracle updates twice in quick succession. Users experience symptoms such as receiving far fewer tokens than expected on claim or redemption, or unexpectedly high share counts on deposit. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the BalancedVault contract, where the version‑checking logic was found to rely on a +1 comparison instead of verifying the actual stored version for the epoch. Because the erroneous calculation may produce a zero balance that looks legitimate, the problem can remain hidden until a version skip occurs. The vulnerability belongs to the class of version‑skipping or underflow/rounding bugs in financial accounting logic. To remediate, the vault should compare the epoch’s recorded product version with the product’s latest version and handle any gaps explicitly, rather than assuming loss when the latest version exceeds the current version by one. This change eliminates the false assumption of a non‑existent version and restores correct share distribution across all vault participants.

title: Users can be forced to claim assets at bad
description:
In balanced vault contract, anyone can call claim assets for other accounts; malicious users could abuse this function to force other users to receive less assets than they expect.

When claiming asset, pro rate, in which users will receive less assets than expect, will be applied when total collateral is less than total unclaimed amount. So after redeeming shares and converting it to assets, users might not want to claim assets right away in this scenario, for they will receive less token amount. However, other users can force them to claim via claim() function because there is no restrict on this function to claim for other accounts.

Users will be forced to receive less assets in some scenarios.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a balanced vault contract where the claim() function does not enforce any access control, allowing any address to invoke it for an arbitrary account. The contract determines the amount of assets to return to a user by applying a pro‑rate formula that reduces the payout when the vault's total collateral is lower than the sum of all unclaimed amounts. Users who have redeemed shares and converted them to assets may intentionally postpone calling claim() to avoid receiving a reduced amount, expecting to claim the full entitlement later. Because the function can be called by anyone, a malicious actor can force the victim's account to be claimed immediately, triggering the pro‑rate reduction and causing the victim to receive fewer tokens than expected. This situation occurs whenever the vault becomes under‑collateralized, for example after large withdrawals or adverse market movements. The affected parties are token holders of the vault, whose balances may be decreased without consent, and the protocol's accounting guarantees are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the claim() entry point and noted the missing require(msg.sender == account) check. The bug is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it simply transfers a smaller amount, which can be mistaken for normal fee or market variation. The flaw belongs to the class of missing‑authorization or forced‑execution bugs, where an external actor can trigger a state‑changing operation on behalf of another user. Exploitation steps are: (1) attacker observes that total collateral is less than total unclaimed amount; (2) attacker calls claim(victimAddress) on the vault; (3) the vault applies the pro‑rate reduction and transfers the reduced asset amount to the victim; (4) the victim's expected balance is lower than anticipated, potentially leading to loss of value or inability to meet downstream obligations. From the user's perspective the UI may show that a withdrawal was processed but the received token amount is unexpectedly small or zero, contrary to the amount displayed before the claim. The business logic that assumes users can claim their full entitlement is violated, breaking the accounting assumptions of the vault. The recommended remediation is to enforce that only the owner of the account can invoke claim(), for example by adding require(msg.sender == account) or by using a standard ownership pattern, thereby preventing third parties from forcing a claim on behalf of another user.

title: Liquidators can prevent users from making
description:
The Perennial protocol has a paused state in which all operations are paused. The protocol can be unpaused by privileged accounts. But when this unpause happens the liquidators can frontrun and liquidate user positions before those users get a chance to make their positions healthy.

perennial-mono/packages/perennial/contracts/collateral/Collateral.sol#L108-L135
The pauser address can pause the perennial protocol using the Controller.updatePaused function. Once the protocol is paused all these operations cannot be done by users:
• Open/close/modify current make or take positions on a product.
• Deposit or withdraw collateral.
• Liquidate under-collateralized positions.

Though, real prices from oracles will surely move up or down during this paused period. If the oracle prices go down, the users won't be allowed to add more collateral to their positions or close their positions. Hence their positions will get under-collateralized (based upon real prices).

Once the protocol is unpaused the liquidators can front-run most users and liquidate their positions. Most users will not get a chance to make their position healthy.

This results in loss of funds for the users.

Perennial also has the concept of settlement delay. Any position opened/closed at oracle version n is settled at oracle version n + 1. This also alleviates the frontrunning liquidation issue. While validating an account's health before liquidation, the protocol only considers the current maintenance requirement for the account (not the next). This makes users more prone to getting front-runned and liquidated.

By front-running any collateral deposit or position closure of a legitimate user which became under-collateralized during the paused state, the liquidator can unfairly liquidate user positions and collect liquidation profit as soon as the protocol is unpaused. This causes loss of funds to the user.

```solidity
Collateral
external
nonReentrant
notPaused
notZeroAddress(account)
isProduct(product)
collateralInvariant(account, product)
{
    _products[product].creditAccount(account, amount);
    token.pull(msg.sender, amount);
    emit Deposit(account, product, amount);
}
```

```solidity
Product
public
nonReentrant
notPaused
onlyAccountOrMultiInvoker(account)
settleForAccount(account)
closeInvariant(account)
liquidationInvariant(account)
{
    _closeTake(account, amount);
}
```

```solidity
public
nonReentrant
notPaused
onlyAccountOrMultiInvoker(account)
settleForAccount(account)
takerInvariant
closeInvariant(account)
liquidationInvariant(account)
{
    _closeMake(account, amount);
}
```
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the Perennial protocol handles its paused state and the subsequent unpause transition. When the protocol is paused, all user‑initiated actions such as opening, modifying, or closing positions, depositing or withdrawing collateral, and even liquidations are blocked. However, the price feeds from the oracles continue to update during this period. If the oracle price moves against a user’s position, the position can become under‑collateralized while the user is still unable to add collateral or close the position because the contract is paused. When the privileged account later calls the unpause function, the protocol immediately re‑enables all operations, including liquidations, but does not provide any protection against a liquidator submitting a liquidation transaction before the affected user can react. Because the liquidation check only uses the current maintenance requirement and does not consider the next oracle version (the settlement delay), a liquidator can front‑run a legitimate user’s pending deposit or close transaction and force a liquidation as soon as the contract is unpaused. This race condition allows the liquidator to capture the liquidation profit while the user loses the collateral that would otherwise have been saved by a timely deposit or closure. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after the protocol resumes, their position is suddenly liquidated, their balance may drop to zero, and they receive no refund or warning despite having attempted to act. The impact is a loss of funds for users and an unfair advantage for liquidators. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the pause logic and liquidation invariants, noting that the pause mechanism does not extend to the liquidation path after unpause and that the health check does not account for the upcoming oracle version. The bug is hard to notice because the pause feature is generally assumed to protect users from any adverse actions, yet the contract’s state transition inadvertently opens a narrow window for exploitation. Conceptually, the fix is to introduce a grace period after unpausing during which liquidations remain disabled, allowing users to restore the health of their positions, and to adjust the health‑check logic to consider the next oracle version’s maintenance requirement, thereby eliminating the front‑running liquidation opportunity.

title: BalancedVault doesn't consider potential break
description:
In case of critical failure of any of the underlying markets, making it permanently impossible to close position and withdraw collateral all funds deposited to balanced Vault will be lost, including funds deposited to other markets.

As Markets and Vaults on Perennial are intended to be created in a permissionless manner and integrate with external price feeds, it cannot be ruled out that any Market will enter a state of catastrophic failure at a point in the future (i.e. oracle used stops functioning and Market admin keys are compromised, so it cannot be changed), resulting in permanent inability to process closing positions and withdrawing collateral.

BalancedVault does not consider this case, exposing all funds deposited to a multi-market Vault to an increased risk, as it is not implementing a possibility for users to withdraw deposited funds through a partial emergency withdrawal from other markets, even at a price of losing the claim to locked funds in case it becomes available in the future. This risk is not mentioned in the documentation.

Users funds are exposed to increased risk compared to depositing to each market individually and in case of failure of any of the markets all funds are lost. User has no possibility to consciously cut losses and withdraw funds from Markets other than the failed one.
poc:
Consider a Vault with 2 markets: ETH/USD and ARB/USD.
1. Alice deposits to Vault, her funds are split between 2 markets
2. ARB/USD market undergoes a fatal failure resulting in maxAmount returned from _maxRedeemAtEpoch to be 0
3. Alice cannot start withdrawal process as this line in redeem reverts:
```solidity
if (shares.gt(_maxRedeemAtEpoch(context, accountContext, account))) revert BalancedVaultRedemptionLimitExceeded();
```
bug_full: The vulnerability in BalancedVault is an emergency‑withdrawal omission that allows a single catastrophic failure of any underlying market to lock all user funds deposited in a multi‑market vault. The root cause is that the vault assumes every integrated market remains operable and does not provide a fallback path when a market becomes permanently unable to close positions or return collateral. When a market’s internal logic reports a maximum redeemable amount of zero, the redemption function checks this value and reverts with a BalancedVaultRedemptionLimitExceeded error, preventing any withdrawal attempt regardless of how many healthy markets remain in the vault. An attacker or a natural failure – for example, an oracle outage, compromised admin keys, or a bug that makes a market’s closing function unusable – can trigger this state, causing the vault’s redemption limit to be zero. Exploitation consists of forcing or waiting for one market to enter this dead state, after which every user who has deposited assets across the vault is unable to start the withdrawal process; any transaction to redeem shares will revert, leaving the user’s balance unchanged on‑chain while the UI may still display the deposited amount. The impact is a total loss of access to funds: users cannot consciously cut losses, cannot withdraw from the unaffected markets, and the protocol offers no mechanism to recover the locked assets. This condition occurs only when at least one market reaches a permanent failure mode, a scenario that is plausible in permissionless environments where external price feeds and market contracts can be compromised. All depositors in the vault, as well as the broader protocol, are affected because the vault aggregates assets and treats them as a single pool. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the redemption flow and identified that the contract does not handle the edge case where _maxRedeemAtEpoch returns zero. The problem is hard to notice because normal operation never triggers the revert, and the documentation does not warn users about the systemic risk. To remediate, the vault should implement a partial or emergency withdrawal mechanism that allows users to extract funds from markets that remain functional, even if it means accepting a loss on the locked portion, or at a minimum clearly disclose the risk of total loss in the user documentation. Conceptually, this bug belongs to the class of “cascading lock‑up due to dependent component failure” and violates the accounting assumption that each market’s collateral can be independently reclaimed, breaking the expectation that users can always withdraw their deposited assets.

title: ChainlinkAggregator: binary search for roun-
description:
When a phase switchover occurs, it can be necessary that phases need to be searched for a roundId with a timestamp as close as possible but bigger than targetTimestamp.
Finding the roundId with the closest possible timestamp is necessary according to the sponsor to minimize the delay of position changes:
The binary search algorithm is not able to find this best roundId which thereby causes unintended position changes.
Also it can occur that the ChainlinkAggregator library is unable to find a valid roundId at all (as opposed to only not finding the "best").
This would cause the Oracle to be temporarily DOSed until there are more valid rounds.

Let's look at the binary search algorithm:
perennial-oracle/contracts/types/ChainlinkAggregator.sol#L123-L156
The part that we are particularly interested in is:
perennial-oracle/contracts/types/ChainlinkAggregator.sol#L139-L149

Let's say in a phase there's only one valid round (roundId=1) and the timestamp for this round is greater than targetTimestamp.
We would expect the roundId that the binary search finds to be roundId=1.
The binary search loop is executed with minRoundId=1 and maxRoundId=1001.
All the above conditions can easily occur in reality, they represent the basic scenario under which this algorithm executes.

minRoundId and maxRoundId change like this in the iterations of the loop:
minRoundId=1
maxRoundId=1001
->
minRoundId=1
maxRoundId=501
->
minRoundId=1
maxRoundId=251
->
minRoundId=1
maxRoundId=126
->
minRoundId=1
maxRoundId=63
->
minRoundId=1
maxRoundId=32
->
minRoundId=1
maxRoundId=16
->
minRoundId=1
maxRoundId=8
->
minRoundId=1
maxRoundId=4
->
minRoundId=1
maxRoundId=2

Now the loop terminates because minRoundId + 1 !< maxRoundId.
Since we assumed that roundId=2 is invalid, the function returns 0 (maxTimestamp=type(uint256).max):
perennial-oracle/contracts/types/ChainlinkAggregator.sol#L153-L155

In the case that latestRound.roundId is equal to the roundId=1 (i.e. same phase and same round id which could not be found) there would be no other valid rounds that the ChainlinkAggregator can find which causes a temporary DOS.
As explained above this would result in sub-optimal and unintended position changes in the best case. In the worst-case the Oracle can be temporarily DOSed, unable to find a valid roundId.

This means that users cannot interact with the perennial protocol because the Oracle cannot be synced. So they cannot close losing trades which is a loss of funds.
The DOS can occur since the while loop searching the phases does not terminate:
perennial-oracle/contracts/types/ChainlinkAggregator.sol#L88-L91
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the binary‑search routine used by the ChainlinkAggregator library to locate a round identifier (roundId) whose timestamp is the smallest value that is still greater than a supplied targetTimestamp during a phase switchover. The algorithm assumes that a valid round exists both below and above the search interval and therefore discards the lower bound (minRoundId) once the loop condition minRoundId + 1 < maxRoundId fails. In edge cases where a phase contains only a single valid round and the initial maxRoundId is set to a large, invalid value, the loop narrows the interval until maxRoundId becomes an invalid round while minRoundId still points to the only valid round. Because the implementation never checks whether minRoundId itself satisfies the timestamp condition, it returns a sentinel value (0 with maxTimestamp set to type(uint256).max) instead of the correct roundId. This mis‑behaviour can be triggered when the targetTimestamp is earlier than the timestamp of the sole valid round, a situation that commonly occurs during phase transitions. As a result, the Oracle is unable to fetch a price feed, causing the Perennial protocol to be temporarily unable to synchronize the price oracle. Users experience symptoms such as an inability to close losing trades, UI components showing no price data or a zero price, and positions remaining open despite expectations that they should be settled. The impact ranges from sub‑optimal position changes to a full denial‑of‑service where funds cannot be withdrawn until a new valid round appears. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who identified that the binary‑search loop does not terminate correctly for the single‑round scenario and that the returned sentinel value is indistinguishable from a legitimate “no data” condition, making the bug hard to notice in normal operation. The root cause is an off‑by‑one / boundary‑condition error in the search algorithm. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit check after the loop to verify whether minRoundId yields a timestamp greater than the target; if it does, the function should return the proxy roundId derived from minRoundId instead of falling back to maxRoundId. Only when both bounds are invalid should the function return 0. This change ensures that the algorithm correctly handles the edge case, prevents the temporary DOS, and restores the expected accounting behavior of the Oracle.

title: Missing Sequencer Uptime Feed check can
description:
When the Arbitrum sequencer is down and then comes back up, all Chainlink price updates will become available on Arbitrum within a very short time.
This leaves users no time to react to the price changes which can lead to unfair liquidations.

Chainlink explains their Sequencer Uptime Feeds here.
Quoting from the documentation:
To help your applications identify when the sequencer is unavailable, you can use a data feed that tracks the last known status of the sequencer at a given point in time. This helps you prevent mass liquidations by providing a grace period to allow customers to react to such an event.

Users are still able in principle to avoid liquidations by interacting with the Arbitrum delayed inbox via L1, but this is out of reach for most users.
Users can get unfairly liquidated because they cannot react to price movements when the sequencer is down and when the sequencer comes back up, all price updates will immediately become available.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the absence of a check on the Arbitrum sequencer uptime status before the protocol consumes Chainlink price updates. The contract assumes that price data is always reliable and does not verify whether the L2 sequencer was recently offline. When the sequencer experiences a downtime and later resumes, Chainlink publishes a batch of previously withheld price updates almost instantly. Because the protocol does not enforce a grace period or a confirmation that the sequencer has been stable for a certain interval, the liquidation engine processes these sudden price spikes as if they occurred in real time. An attacker or a natural sequencer outage can therefore trigger a cascade of liquidations: users who were unable to add collateral while the sequencer was down receive liquidation notices the moment the sequencer comes back up, even though the market price had not moved during the outage. From the user’s point of view the UI shows a liquidation event with no preceding price movement, the expected ability to top‑up collateral is missing, and the balance of the position drops to zero. The impact is unfair loss of collateral for leveraged traders and a potential erosion of trust in the protocol’s risk management. The issue appears only during the specific window when the sequencer transitions from offline to online, making it easy to miss in routine testing because price feeds appear correct after the transition. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented Chainlink Sequencer Uptime Feed with the contract’s actual logic and found no reference to it. The root cause is a missing external health‑check integration, which is a class of bug where a system relies on a data source without validating its availability status, leading to a time‑of‑check‑time‑of‑use (TOCTOU) style race condition. To remediate, the protocol should query the Chainlink Sequencer Uptime Feed, require that the sequencer has been continuously up for a configurable grace period before accepting new price updates for liquidation calculations, and optionally pause liquidation during the transition window. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that users should have a reasonable window to react to price changes after a sequencer outage, preserving the accounting assumptions of gradual price movement and collateral safety.

title: If long and short products has different maker
description:
In a market scenario where long and short products carry different position fees, continuous rebalancing could potentially deplete the vault's funds. This situation arises when closing positions incurs a maker fee, which gradually eats away at the collateral balance. The rebalancing cycle continues until the fee becomes insignificant or the collateral balance is exhausted.
If a market's long and short products have different position fees, continuous rebalancing could be an issue. A significant position fee difference might deplete all funds after repeated rebalancing.
Consider a scenario with one market, where the long product has a 0% maker fee (position fee), and the short product a 10% maker fee. A vault holding 100 positions divided across these markets, with 50 short and 50 long positions, and collateral balances of 50-50 each, is presented.
Now, suppose the vault and the product are entirely in sync (meaning they're of the same version). If someone deposits 100 assets into the vault, it would distribute that deposit, adding 50 to both product's collateral balances, bringing them to 100 each. The vault then increases its position to 100 to maintain the 1x leverage. The long market would match this since it has no maker fee, but the short market would lose 5 from its collateral due to the fee charged by the openMake operation. As a result, the market now has 95 in the short market and 100 in the long market collateral. This imbalance triggers a rebalancing operation via sync().
After the second call to sync(), the collateral balances would be 97.5 in both markets, and the markets would reduce their positions to maintain the 1x leverage. The long market would reduce its position to 97.5, but when the short market does the same, the closeMake operation's fee charge reduces the short market collateral market. This imbalance again allows a call to settle...
As seen if the difference between the products are high the rebalance will start eating the vaults collateral balance by paying redundant maker fees.
The above scenario assumes only one market with two products. If there are two markets, the situation could be more troublesome due to the additional fee charges and potentially higher losses.
Since the vaults funds can be drained significantly if certain cases are met (high makerFee set by market owner and big collateral balance differences between markets or directional exposure on vault causing the collateral balance differences higher than usual so more funds to rebalance hence more fee to pay). I'll label it as high.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a vault that maintains a 1x leveraged exposure across a market’s long and short products while assuming that the maker (position) fee applied to opening and closing positions is identical for both sides. In reality, a market may configure different maker fees for the long and short products – for example, a 0% fee on the long side and a 10% fee on the short side. When the vault receives a deposit, it allocates collateral equally to both products and then increases its total position to match the deposited amount. The long side can increase its position without fee loss, but the short side incurs a maker fee during the openMake operation, reducing its collateral. The vault’s sync() routine detects the resulting imbalance and attempts to rebalance by adjusting positions on both sides. Each rebalance triggers another openMake or closeMake call, and because the short side still pays a fee while the long side does not, the collateral on the short side is further reduced. This cycle repeats: after each sync the vault’s collateral on both sides converges to a lower value, but the fee on the short side continues to be deducted, gradually draining the vault’s total funds. The issue manifests when the fee differential is significant, the vault holds a large collateral imbalance, or the vault’s directional exposure amplifies the amount that must be rebalanced. Users who deposit assets expect their balance to remain stable or grow proportionally with market performance, yet they observe their collateral slowly decreasing, sometimes to zero, without any explicit loss event. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined the rebalancing logic and noticed that the positionFee parameter was not incorporated into the sync calculations. Because the fee loss per iteration can be small, the drain may appear negligible at first and only become evident after many cycles, making it hard to detect in short‑term testing. To remediate the flaw, the vault should either enforce that both products use the same maker fee or modify the rebalancing algorithm to explicitly account for each product’s positionFee when calculating the required collateral adjustments, thereby preventing unnecessary fee payments and protecting the vault’s capital.

title: BalancedVault.sol: Early depositor can ma-
bug_full: The vulnerability is an exchange‑rate manipulation and rounding‑down bug in the BalancedVault implementation. An attacker can make an initial deposit that is so small that it mints only a single share (or a few shares). Because the vault calculates share amounts using the formula shares = amount * totalSupply / totalAssets with integer division, the share price is directly tied to the ratio of totalAssets to totalSupply. After minting the minimal share balance, the attacker transfers a large amount of the underlying asset directly to the vault contract, bypassing the deposit function. This external transfer increases totalAssets while totalSupply remains almost unchanged, causing the exchange rate to drop dramatically. When a later user deposits a normal amount, the vault computes the number of shares to mint using the same floor division. Due to the skewed ratio, the computed share amount is rounded down to zero, so the user’s transaction succeeds in sending assets to the vault but the user receives no shares. From the user’s perspective the balance of shares stays at zero even though the vault now holds a large amount of assets, effectively stealing the deposited funds. The impact is loss of funds for any depositor that follows the attacker, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential financial damage as the vault’s accounting assumptions are broken. The condition for exploitation requires that the attacker can (1) make a tiny initial deposit that mints the smallest possible share amount, and (2) transfer additional assets directly to the vault before other users deposit. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case was added that performed exactly this sequence and observed that the victim’s share balance was zero while the vault held more than two ether of assets. The bug is hard to notice because normal deposit paths work correctly and external token transfers are not usually considered in the share‑minting logic; the rounding error only becomes visible when the asset‑to‑share ratio is extreme. To remediate, the vault should prevent arbitrary external asset transfers from affecting totalAssets, enforce that share calculations use rounding up or a minimum share amount, or add a safeguard that the exchange rate cannot be manipulated below a safe threshold. In essence, the contract must treat the exchange rate as a protected invariant and ensure that share minting cannot be reduced to zero by external asset injections, thereby preserving the intended accounting relationship between assets and shares.

title: BalancedVault.sol: claim can be impossible
description:
When a user redeems his shares, he then needs to call the claim function to actually claim his assets.
This will downstream call the _rebalancePosition function with the claimAmount as an argument.
Under some circumstances the _rebalancePosition function can revert due to unsigned integer underflow, making it impossible to claim assets.
This condition is not permanent but can only be solved by sending additional assets to the Vault causing a loss of funds.
Assume the following situation:
_assets() = 5e18
_totalUnclaimed = 10e18
unclaimed of user1 = 5e18
When user1 calls claim, pro-rata claiming applies and the actual claimAmount is equal to 5e18*10e18/10e18=5e18.
Now let's look at the vulnerable line:
packages/perennial-vaults/contracts/balanced/BalancedVault.sol#L474
_totalAssetsAtEpoch would be equal to 0:
packages/perennial-vaults/contracts/balanced/BalancedVault.sol#L684-L690
Thereby the line in _rebalancePosition reverts due to unsigned integer underflow (0 - claimAmount),
You can add the following test to BalancedVaultMulti.test.ts which is a modified version of the existing gracefully unwinds upon insolvency test:
```
it('reverts upon pro rata claim', async () => {
    // 1. Deposit initial amount into the vault
    await vault.connect(user).deposit(utils.parseEther('50000'), user.address)
    await vault.connect(user2).deposit(utils.parseEther('50000'), user2.address)
    await updateOracle()
    await vault.sync()
    // 2. Redeem most of the amount, but leave it unclaimed
    await vault.connect(user).redeem(utils.parseEther('40000'), user.address)
    await vault.connect(user2).redeem(utils.parseEther('20000'), user2.address)
    await updateOracle()
    await vault.sync()
    // 3. An oracle update makes the long position liquidatable, initiate take close
    await updateOracle(utils.parseEther('20000'))
    await long.connect(user).settleAccount(vault.address)
    await short.connect(user).settleAccount(vault.address)
    await long.connect(perennialUser).closeTake(utils.parseEther('700'))
    await collateral.connect(liquidator).liquidate(vault.address, long.address)
    // // 4. Settle the vault to recover and rebalance
    await updateOracle() // let take settle at high price
    await updateOracle(utils.parseEther('1500')) // return to normal price to let vault rebalance
    await vault.sync()
    await updateOracle()
    await vault.sync()
    // 6. Claim should be pro-rated
    await vault.claim(user2.address)
})
```
The user is at least temporarily unable to claim his assets and the situation needs to be solved by sending additional assets to the Vault (of which the user most likely does not get the majority back with the claim) -> loss of funds
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the claim workflow of a balanced vault contract. When a user redeems their share tokens they must subsequently call the claim function to receive the underlying assets. The claim implementation forwards the requested claimAmount to an internal routine called _rebalancePosition. This routine calculates the amount of assets available for the current epoch using a variable that represents the total assets at the epoch (_totalAssetsAtEpoch). Under normal operation this value is positive, but after a liquidation event the vault can end up with _totalAssetsAtEpoch equal to zero while there are still unclaimed shares recorded in the system.
