The code then attempts to subtract the claimAmount from zero (0 - claimAmount) using an unsigned integer, which triggers an under‑flow revert. Because the revert occurs inside the internal rebalance call, the external claim transaction fails and the user is unable to retrieve any of their assets. The condition is not permanent; it can be cleared only by sending additional assets into the vault so that _totalAssetsAtEpoch becomes larger than the pending claimAmount. This extra injection dilutes the value of the original claim and may cause the user to receive less than expected, effectively resulting in a loss of funds. The bug appears only after a specific sequence: deposits by multiple users, partial redemption leaving a large unclaimed balance, an oracle price shift that makes the long position liquidatable, execution of liquidation and settlement steps, and finally a rebalance attempt while the epoch‑level asset counter is still zero. The affected parties are any vault participants who have unclaimed balances after a liquidation, as well as the protocol itself because the locked funds reduce overall liquidity and can erode trust. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors added a test reproducing the described sequence and observed that the claim transaction reverted with an unsigned integer underflow. It is hard to notice in ordinary usage because the revert only manifests under the precise combination of liquidation and pending unclaimed shares, which may not be exercised in routine operations. Conceptually the bug belongs to the class of accounting‑state mismatches where a contract assumes a non‑zero balance before performing a subtraction, leading to arithmetic underflow. The user‑facing symptom is that the UI shows a claimable amount but the transaction fails, leaving the user’s balance unchanged or showing zero assets received. The expected behavior – a user redeems shares and receives the proportional amount of underlying tokens – is violated; instead the claim is impossible until external assets are injected, breaking the business logic that guarantees proportional redemption. The proper fix is to guard the subtraction by ensuring that claimAmount never exceeds the epoch‑level total assets, for example by adding a require check or by adjusting the accounting so that _totalAssetsAtEpoch is updated before the subtraction, thereby preventing the underflow and allowing claims to succeed under all conditions.

title: Malicious trader can bypass utilization buffer
description:
A malicious trader can bypass the Utilisation buffer, and push utilisation to 1 on any product.
Perenial products use a utilization buffer to prevent taker side to DOS maker by taking up all the liquidity:
packages/perennial/contracts/product/Product.sol#L547-L556
Makers would not be able to withdraw if utilization would reach 100% because of takerInvariant which is enforced during closeMake:
packages/perennial/contracts/product/Product.sol#L535-L544
A malicious trader can bypass the utilisation buffer by first opening a maker position, open taker position and close previous maker position. The only constraint is that she has to use different accounts to open the maker positions and the taker positions, since perennial doesn't allow to have maker and taker positions on a product simultaneously.
So here's a concrete example:
Let's say the state of product is 900 USD on the maker side, 800 USD on the taker side, which respects the 10% utilization buffer.
Example
Using account 1, Alice opens up a maker position for 100 USD, bringing maker total to 1000 USD.
Using account 2, Alice can open a taker position for 100 USD, bringing taker to 900 USD, which respects the 10% utilization buffer still.
Now using account 1 again, Alice can close her 100 USD maker position and withdraw collateral, clearing account 1 on perennial completely.
This brings the utilization to 100%, since taker = maker = 900 USD.
This is allowed, since only takerInvariant is checked when closing a maker position, which enforces that utilization ratio is lower than or equal to 100%.
Any trader can bring the utilization up to 100%, and use that to DoS withdrawals from Products and Balanced vaults for an indefinite amount of time. This is especially critical for vaults, since when any product related to any market is fully utilized, all redeems from the balanced vault are blocked.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition that allows a malicious trader to push the utilization ratio of a Perennial product to 100 % and consequently block withdrawals and vault redemptions. The product enforces a utilization buffer (for example a 10 % safety margin) only when a taker position is opened; the check is performed by the takerInvariant modifier, which ensures that the ratio of taker to maker collateral stays below the buffer limit. However, when a maker position is closed, the contract only verifies that the utilization does not exceed 100 % – it does not re‑apply the buffer constraint. Because the buffer is not enforced on maker‑close operations, an attacker can exploit the sequence: (1) open a maker position with one account, (2) open a taker position with a second account while staying inside the buffer, (3) close the original maker position using the first account. After step 3 the taker and maker totals become equal, driving the utilization to exactly 100 %. At this point the takerInvariant condition is still satisfied (it allows ≤ 100 %), so the transaction succeeds, but the product’s liquidity is fully consumed. Any subsequent attempt to withdraw maker collateral or to redeem from a balanced vault fails because the protocol treats a fully utilized product as out of liquidity, effectively DoS‑ing the withdrawal path. The impact is that users cannot retrieve their deposited funds, vault participants see their redemption requests revert, and the protocol’s economic guarantees are broken because the accounting assumption that a safety buffer protects against total exhaustion is violated. The issue manifests only when the attacker can maintain separate maker and taker accounts – a restriction enforced by the contract – and when the product’s buffer logic is limited to taker‑side actions. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the invariant checks and noticed the asymmetry between opening and closing flows. The bug is subtle because the contract appears to enforce a utilization limit, yet the limit is applied inconsistently, making the failure mode easy to miss in testing. To remediate, the same buffer check that limits taker openings must also be applied when a maker position is closed, ensuring that utilization never exceeds the configured safety margin regardless of the operation type. This change restores the intended protection against liquidity exhaustion and prevents the DoS scenario where funds appear to disappear or become unrecoverable due to a full utilization state.

title: LenderActions's moveQuoteToken can create
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the moveQuoteToken function of the lending pool contract. The function allows acaller to shift quote‑token liquidity from one price bucket to another, optionally crossing the Lowest Utilized Price (LUP) threshold. During this operation the contract applies an unutilized deposit fee when the movement goes from a bucket priced at or above LUP to a bucket priced below LUP. The fee is deducted from the moved amount, which reduces the total amount of deposits recorded in the pool. However, the function does not verify that after the fee deduction the pool’s total debt remains lower than the total deposits, a condition that is required for the LUP calculation to be mathematically sound. The Deposits.getLup routine assumes debt ≤ total deposits; if debt exceeds deposits, the LUP value becomes inconsistent with the underlying accounting tree. Moreover, moveQuoteToken only checks that the High Threshold Price (HTP) does not exceed the new LUP when moving to a higher‑indexed bucket, but it omits the additional safeguard present in the removeQuoteToken path that also aborts when debt > total deposits. Consequently, a rare corner case can arise where an unutilized deposit fee shrinks the deposit sum enough that poolState.debt > Deposits.treeSum(deposits), while the LUP may be forced below the HTP due to the bounded LUP calculation. This breaks the core pricing logic of the pool: loan‑book limits become mis‑aligned, interest calculations may use an incorrect price floor, and users may see their expected refunds or available liquidity disappear or be reduced to zero. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that after moving assets the pool balance is lower than before, or that no liquidity is available for borrowing even though no withdrawals were performed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the LenderActions contract, where the auditor noticed that the safety check present in removeQuoteToken was not replicated in moveQuoteToken and that the fee‑adjusted deposit amount could violate the debt‑vs‑deposit invariant. Because the condition depends on a specific combination of bucket prices and fee rates, it is unlikely to be triggered in normal operation, which is why the severity was assessed as medium. Nevertheless, the bug is hard to notice because the pool continues to operate and only the internal accounting becomes inconsistent, leading to subtle mispricing rather than an outright revert. The proper remediation is to add the same invariant check used in removeQuoteToken – ensuring that when debt is non‑zero it never exceeds the total deposits – and to retain the existing HTP‑vs‑LUP validation for all move directions. By enforcing both conditions, the contract guarantees that LUP remains a valid price floor and that the pool’s accounting stays coherent, preventing the described loss of funds or unexpected zero‑balance symptoms.

title: Wrong Inflator used in calculating HTP to de-
description:
When accruing Interest, the interest is added according to the deposits in all buckets upto the lower of LUP and HTP prices' buckets. But HTP is wrongly calculated in the accrueInterest function.
All major functions in Pool.sol use _accrueInterest which makes a call to PoolCommons.accrueInterest to accrue the interest for all deposits above the minimum of LUP and HTP prices, which means upto the lower of the LupIndex and HTPIndex because indexes move in the opposite direction of prices. Here in accrueInterest function, the accrualIndex is calculated as the higher of LUPIndex and HTPIndex to make sure interest is calculated for all deserving deposits above min(HTP price, LUP price) ie. max(LUP index, HTP index).
using the newInflator which incorporates the newly accrued interest into the HTP calculation, whereas the LUP is calculated with old values. The accrualIndex is set to max(LUP index, HTP index). then.
Assume that the LUP price > HTP price. So, LUP index < HTP index. Hence, for the interestEarningDeposit all the deposits above the HTP index will be considered.
But the value of HTP index is wrong now because it is calculated using new Inflator which means that the new Interest has been added in calculation of HTP already and thus the derived HTP index will be lower in value (which means upper in the bucket system). Assume that still after this LUP index < HTP index
Now since the old LUP index and new HTP index is used in the max(LUP index, HTP index) function, and LUP index is still < HTP index (ie. LUP price > HTP price) thus the deposits that were between the old HTP index and the new HTP index have been left out of the interestEarningDeposit calculation.
I talked to the developers about this discrepancy between new HTP and old LUP being used, and they said "I can see the argument in favor of using the prior inflator here to be totally precise."
Also, one of them said, "It should be computed using the debt prior to the interest accrual itself, as it's determining the the minimum amount of deposit onto which that interest would be applied"
This means that the htp index has been underestimated because it has been made lower (ie. upper in the bucket system) and thus the deposits that lie between the old HTP index and new HTP index have not been considered for calculating interestEarningDeposit when they should have been considered because before the interest accrual itself, those deposits were under the deserving max(LUP index, HTP index) bracket.
This means interestEarningDeposit has been underestimated and later calculations at PoolCommons.sol#L253 for lender Factor have become wrong.
This is a logic mistake and leads to wrong values for the lenderFactor.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical miscalculation in the interest‑accrual routine of the pool contract. When the system accrues interest it determines a range of deposit buckets that should receive the newly earned amount by taking the lower of the two price thresholds, the LUP (lowest usable price) and the HTP (highest threshold price). The implementation computes an accrual index as the maximum of the LUP index and the HTP index, because indexes move opposite to prices. The bug arises because the HTP index is derived using the new inflator, which already incorporates the interest that is being accrued in the current call, while the LUP index is still based on the old inflator. When the market condition is such that the LUP price is higher than the HTP price (i.e., LUP index < HTP index), the new inflator makes the HTP index artificially lower in the bucket ordering. Consequently, deposits that lie between the old HTP index and the newly calculated HTP index are omitted from the interestEarningDeposit calculation. This omission leads to an under‑estimation of the total interest that should be credited to lenders, which then propagates to an incorrect lenderFactor value used elsewhere in the protocol. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a lender’s balance grows slower than expected, sometimes appearing to receive no interest for a period, and the reported lender factor is lower than the advertised rate. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who traced the discrepancy through the accrueInterest function in Pool.sol and the subsequent calculations in PoolCommons.sol. The bug is subtle because it does not cause a transaction to revert or produce an obvious error; it only affects accounting in specific price configurations, making it easy to miss in routine testing. The correct mitigation is to compute the HTP index with the prior (old) inflator, i.e., before the new interest is applied, ensuring that the max(LUP index, HTP index) correctly captures all deposits that are eligible for the current interest period. By using the old inflator for HTP, the protocol will include the previously omitted deposits, resulting in accurate interest accrual and a proper lenderFactor calculation.

title: KickerActions uses wrong check to prevent
description:
The kickWithDeposit function in KickerActions has a check to prevent users having deposits below the LUP to use those deposits for kicking loans, but this check is flawed.
The mentioned check evaluates if the bucketPrice used by the kicker is below the LUP. But the problem here is that the LUP used in this check is the new LUP that is calculated after incorporating the removal of the deposit itself and the debt changes. Thus, this check can be easily bypassed because the new LUP is bound to move lower and thus may cross past the bucketPrice used.
Consider a situation :
1. The kicker has deposits in a bucketPrice below LUP
2. Now he calls kickWithDeposit using this deposit
3. The new LUP is calculated after removing this deposit and adding the debt changes for kickPenalty etc.
4. This will make the LUP decrease and thus now LUP < bucketPrice that the user input
This way this check can be bypassed. According to the developers, the check was in place to prevent kickers from using deposits below the LUP to kick loans but this is not fulfilled.
This breaks protocol functionality because now anyone can deposit below LUP and use that to kick valid user loans. The kickWithDeposit function was only made to help depositors get their deposits back if some loans are blocking the withdrawl due to the LUP movement. But the current implementation allows anyone to kick those loans that were originally not eligible for liquidation.
This is a high severity issue because it griefs users off their funds by liquidating them, even when they were not eligible for liquidation.
bug_full: An improper validation in the kickWithDeposit function allows a user who holds a deposit in a bucket whose price is below the current lowest usable price (LUP) to bypass the intended protection and trigger a kick on loans that are not eligible for liquidation. The function first removes the caller’s deposit and applies the kick penalty, then recomputes the LUP based on the new state. The check that is supposed to reject kicks when bucketPrice < LUP mistakenly compares bucketPrice against this newly computed LUP instead of the pre‑kick LUP. Because the removal of the deposit and the added debt typically push the LUP downward, the condition can become false after the state change, letting the transaction continue. An attacker can therefore call kickWithDeposit with a deposit that is originally below LUP, cause the LUP to drop, and successfully liquidate a loan that should have remained safe. This results in unauthorized liquidation, causing borrowers to lose collateral or incur unexpected debt, and effectively griefs users by stealing value from loans that were not meant to be liquidated. The issue appears only when the kicker’s deposit resides in a bucket below the current LUP and the function’s logic updates the LUP before performing the eligibility check. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the economic invariants of the protocol. The bug is subtle because the code contains a check that looks correct at a glance, but the ordering of state updates makes the check ineffective, and typical unit tests that do not simulate the exact sequence may miss it. To remediate, the validation should be moved to the beginning of the function or rewritten to compare bucketPrice with the LUP calculated before any state modifications, ensuring that deposits below the LUP cannot be used to kick protected loans. This class of vulnerability is an improper state‑dependent validation, where the order of operations breaks a business rule and allows economic manipulation. From a user’s perspective, a borrower may see their loan liquidated with no warning, receiving a zero or reduced balance, while the kicker receives the liquidation reward. The protocol’s accounting assumptions that only loans above LUP are liquidatable are violated, leading to loss of funds and reduced trust in the system.

title: Lenders lose interests and pay deposit fees
bug_full: The vulnerability is a slippage‑related deposit‑fee bug in the pool's addQuoteToken function. The contract calculates the Lowest Utilization Price (LUP) at the moment the transaction is executed and compares it with the bucket index supplied by the lender. If the supplied index is higher than the LUP index, the code treats the deposit as being below the minimum price and applies a deposit fee while also preventing the deposited amount from earning interest. Because the LUP is derived from the pool's current debt, any other deposit that changes the debt between the time the user signs the transaction and the time it is mined can move the LUP upward. The function does not provide any slippage protection or a way for the caller to specify a maximum acceptable LUP, and the expiry parameter only guards against stale transactions, not against price movement. Consequently, a lender can unintentionally deposit below LUP, lose the expected interest, and be charged a fee without any explicit warning. This situation is especially likely when many lenders act in the same block or when a large (whale) deposit or a malicious front‑runner raises the LUP just before the victim's transaction is included. From the user's perspective the UI may show that the deposit was accepted, but the balance after the transaction is lower than expected, interest accrues at zero, or a portion of the amount disappears as a fee, leading to confusion and the impression that funds have vanished. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the pool contract logic, where the relationship between the LUP calculation and the deposit fee condition was examined and found to lack any safeguard against price slippage. The bug is hard to notice because the contract does not emit a distinct event for the fee, and the fee is deducted silently as part of the internal accounting, so standard transaction receipts do not highlight the loss. To remediate the problem the protocol should introduce slippage protection: the caller should be able to specify a maximum acceptable LUP (or a minimum acceptable index) and the transaction should revert if the on‑chain LUP at execution exceeds that bound. Alternatively, the fee logic could be moved to a separate step that requires explicit user consent. Implementing such a check would align the contract's behavior with the economic expectation that a lender only pays fees when they knowingly accept the price, thereby preventing accidental loss of interest and unexpected fee charges.

title: Due to excessive HTP check moveQuoteTo- multiple times
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical ordering flaw in the moveQuoteToken function of the lending pool contract. The function is intended to let a depositor shift quote‑token deposits from one price bucket to another, a capability that is essential for risk management and yield optimisation. The code performs a safety check that the protocol’s high‑price threshold (HTP) must not exceed the low‑price threshold (LUP) after a move. However, this check is executed after the source bucket’s deposit has been removed but before the destination bucket’s deposit is added back. At that intermediate point the LUP can temporarily drop below the HTP, causing the condition vars.htp > lup_ to be true and the transaction to revert with LUPBelowHTP. The intended invariant – that HTP be less than or equal to LUP in the final state – is therefore enforced on a transient state, making the check excessively strict. The bug manifests when a user attempts to move a sizable amount from a lower‑index bucket to a higher‑index bucket (i.e., to a higher price bucket). The removal of a large deposit can lower the LUP enough that the temporary inequality triggers, even though the final state after the addition would satisfy the invariant. As a result, legitimate deposit‑management operations become unavailable, especially for large deposits, preventing users from repositioning funds to mitigate risk. From the user’s perspective the UI reports a failure (often with the error LUPBelowHTP or InsufficientLP) and the expected outcome – the deposit appearing in the target bucket – does not occur; the funds remain locked in the original bucket, leading to missed opportunities to avoid liquidation or capture yield. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who noted that the check’s placement contradicts the protocol’s design described in the Ajna white‑paper. It is hard to notice because the failure only occurs under specific conditions (large moves to higher price buckets) and may appear as an occasional “random” revert. The impact is medium: it does not expose funds to theft, but it can cause financial loss for depositors who cannot react quickly to market changes. The proper fix is to move the HTP‑vs‑LUP validation to after the destination bucket’s deposit has been added, or to relax the condition to compare HTP with the LUP that would result after the full move, possibly by using the initial LUP for fee calculations. This adjustment ensures the invariant is checked on the final state, restoring the intended functionality of dynamic deposit management without compromising protocol safety.

title: D3VaultFunding.userWithdraw() does not have minTokenAmount
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the D3VaultFunding contract’s userWithdraw function, which allows a caller to request a token withdrawal without providing any slippage protection such as a minTokenAmount parameter. The function calculates the amount to be transferred by calling an internal _getExchangeRate routine that derives the exchange rate from mutable on‑chain variables: the current cash balance, total borrows, total reserves and withdrawn reserves. Because these variables can be altered by any transaction that executes before the withdrawal completes, an attacker can perform a sandwich attack – inserting a malicious transaction that inflates or deflates the cash or reserve values immediately before the victim’s withdraw call is processed. The exchange rate then becomes unfavorable, causing the amount computed by userWithdraw to be lower than the user expects. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal but the received token amount is unexpectedly small or even zero, leading to a discrepancy between the expected and actual balances. This issue affects any user who calls userWithdraw directly, as well as the protocol’s overall liquidity and accounting integrity, since the protocol assumes that the exchange rate reflects a fair market value at the moment of withdrawal. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who noted the absence of a minimum‑amount check and the direct use of a mutable exchange rate, a pattern commonly associated with price‑manipulation or sandwich attacks. The problem can be hard to notice because the function appears to transfer the correct amount based on an internal calculation, yet the calculation itself can be manipulated without any explicit error. To remediate, the contract should introduce a minTokenAmount argument (or an equivalent slippage limit) and verify that the computed amount meets this threshold before proceeding with the transfer. Additionally, the exchange rate should be derived from a more stable source or locked in before any state‑changing operations to prevent front‑running manipulation. This class of bug is generally categorized as missing slippage protection or price‑oracle manipulation, leading to potential fund loss, incorrect accounting, and user dissatisfaction.

title: Possible loss of Funds
description:
Transfers at Liquidation may silently fail, causing collateral be paid out withoud debt being paid, or liquidator not getting collateral.
in D3VaultLiquidation.sol:liquidate the caller pays the outstanding debt, and received the collateral tokens with a discount in exchange. However, the transfer of the tokens to pay the debt, as well as the transfer of the collateral Tokens are using the transferFrom function of the ERC20 interface instead of safeTransferFrom (which is used in other functions). Moreover, the return value of this function is not checked. As not all ERC20 tokens revert on a failed transfer, this could lead to a silent failure of a transfer. As the function will go on in this case this could lead to the liquidation to finish with either:
• The debt not being paid, but the collateral still paid to the caller --> Loss of protocol funds!
• The debt being repaid by the caller, but the collateral is not transferred --> Loss of user funds!
Possible loss of user or protocol funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation routine of the D3VaultLiquidation contract where token transfers are performed with the ERC20 transferFrom function instead of the safer safeTransferFrom variant and the return value of transferFrom is not inspected. Because many ERC20 implementations do not automatically revert on a failed transfer but simply return false, the contract can continue execution even when the debt‑payment transfer or the collateral‑transfer fails. This silent failure can manifest in two harmful ways: the caller may repay the outstanding debt while the collateral never reaches them, resulting in a loss of user funds; or the collateral may be transferred to the caller while the debt repayment never occurs, causing a drain of protocol reserves. The issue appears only during liquidation calls, when the contract attempts to move arbitrary ERC20 tokens that may have non‑standard behavior. It was uncovered during a manual audit that compared the safeTransferFrom usage in other functions with the unchecked transferFrom in liquidate. The problem is difficult to detect because no exception is thrown and no explicit error is logged, so the transaction appears successful from the caller’s perspective even though the accounting state is inconsistent. Users may notice that after a liquidation they receive no tokens despite paying debt, or that the protocol’s debt ledger shows a reduction while the collateral balance remains unchanged. The root cause is the lack of proper error handling for token transfers, violating the assumption that a successful call guarantees token movement. To remediate, the contract should replace transferFrom with safeTransferFrom (or otherwise verify the boolean return) for both the debt‑payment and collateral‑payment steps, ensuring that any failure reverts the whole liquidation and preserves the intended accounting invariants.

title: Limit index isn't checked in repayDebt, so user
description:
repayDebt() resulting LUP _revertIfPriceDroppedBelowLimit() check is not
performed in the case of pure debt repayment without collateral pulling.
LUP will move (up or no change) as a result of debt repayment and repayDebt()
have limitIndex_ argument. As a part of multi-position strategy a user might not be
satisfied with repay results if LUP has increased not substantially enough.
I.e. there is a user control argument, it is detrimental from UX perspective to
request, but not use it, as for any reason a borrower might want to control for that
sake of other loans of that borrower.
Unfavorable repayDebt() operations will be executed and the borrowers, whose
strategies were dependent on the realized LUP move, can suffer a loss.
Probability of execution is high (no prerequisites, current ordinary behavior), while
the probability of the following loss is medium, so placing the severity to be
medium.
There is a limitIndex_ parameter in repayDebt():
ool.sol#L208-L232
```solidity
function repayDebt(
    address borrowerAddress_,
    uint256 maxQuoteTokenAmountToRepay_,
    uint256 collateralAmountToPull_,
    address collateralReceiver_,
    uint256 limitIndex_
) external nonReentrant {
    ...
    RepayDebtResult memory result = BorrowerActions.repayDebt(
        auctions,
        buckets,
        deposits,
        loans,
        poolState,
        borrowerAddress_,
        maxQuoteTokenAmountToRepay_,
        collateralAmountToPull_,
        limitIndex_
    );
```
Currently _revertIfPriceDroppedBelowLimit() is done on collateral pulling only:
external/BorrowerActions.sol#L365-L375
```solidity
if (vars.pull) {
    // only intended recipient can pull collateral
    if (borrowerAddress_ != msg.sender) revert BorrowerNotSender();
    // an auctioned borrower in not allowed to pull collateral (even if
    collateralized at the new LUP) if auction is not settled
    if (result_.inAuction) revert AuctionActive();
    // calculate LUP only if it wasn't calculated in repay action
    if (!vars.repay) result_.newLup = Deposits.getLup(deposits_, result_.poolDebt);
    _revertIfPriceDroppedBelowLimit(result_.newLup, limitIndex_);
}
```
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the repayDebt function of a lending protocol that accepts a limitIndex_ argument intended to protect borrowers from unfavorable changes in the Lowest Utilized Price (LUP) during a repayment operation. The root cause is that the internal check _revertIfPriceDroppedBelowLimit() is only executed when collateral is pulled, and is omitted when the function is used solely for debt repayment without collateral extraction. Consequently, when a borrower calls repayDebt with collateralAmountToPull_ set to zero, the contract still computes a new LUP based on the reduced pool debt, but it never validates that this new LUP respects the caller‑provided limitIndex_. An attacker or a careless borrower can therefore trigger a repayment that moves the LUP in a direction that is insufficient for their broader multi‑position strategy, leading to unexpected losses or missed profit opportunities. The exploit scenario is straightforward: a borrower supplies a limitIndex_ expecting the transaction to revert if the LUP after repayment is lower than the limit, but because the check is missing, the transaction succeeds regardless of the LUP movement. From the user’s perspective the symptoms may include a repayment that appears to have succeeded while the expected price improvement does not occur, resulting in a stagnant or even deteriorated position, zero collateral being returned when it was anticipated, or a strategy that relied on the LUP shift failing silently. The issue manifests whenever repayDebt is invoked without pulling collateral, which is a common case because the function does not require any prerequisite beyond the repayment amount. Borrowers who depend on the LUP change for other loans or for rebalancing are affected, as the protocol’s accounting assumptions about price protection are violated. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the code paths for repayment with and without collateral pulling and noticed the missing call to the price‑limit guard. It can be hard to notice because the function signature includes the limitIndex_ parameter, giving the impression that the limit is always enforced, and the missing check does not produce an obvious on‑chain error. The recommended remediation is to compute the new LUP after the repayment and invoke _revertIfPriceDroppedBelowLimit() with the supplied limitIndex_ in the same way it is done for the collateral‑pull branch, thereby restoring the intended safety check while allowing the check to be omitted only when both repayment and pull are disabled to save gas.

title: Then getAmountsForDelta function at Underlying.sol does not match UniswapV3
description:
The function getAmountsForDelta() at the Underlying.sol contract is used to
compute the quantity of token0 and token1 to add to the position given a delta of
liquidity. These quantities depend on the delta of liquidity, the current tick and the
ticks of the range boundaries. Actually, getAmountsForDelta() uses the sqrt prices
instead of the ticks, but they are equivalent since each tick represents a sqrt price.
There exists 3 cases:
• The current tick is outside the range from the left, this means only token0
should be added.
• The current tick is within the range, this means both token0 and token1 should
be added.
• The current tick is outside the range from the right, this means only token1
should be added.
The issue on the implementation is on the first case, which is coded as follows:
```solidity
if (sqrtRatioX96 <= sqrtRatioAX96) {
    amount0 = SafeCast.toUint256(
        SqrtPriceMath.getAmount0Delta(
            sqrtRatioAX96,
            sqrtRatioBX96,
            liquidity
        )
    );
}
```
The implementation says that if the current price is equal to the price of the lower
tick, it means that it is outside of the range and hence only token0 should be added
to the position.
But for the UniswapV3 implementation, the current price must be lower in order to
consider it outside:
```solidity
if (_slot0.tick < params.tickLower) {
    // current tick is below the passed range; liquidity can only become in range
    // by crossing from left to right, when we'll need _more_ token0 (it's becoming more valuable) so user
    // must provide it
    amount0 = SqrtPriceMath.getAmount0Delta(
        TickMath.getSqrtRatioAtTick(params.tickLower),
        TickMath.getSqrtRatioAtTick(params.tickUpper),
        params.liquidityDelta
    );
}
```
Reference
When the current price is equal to the left boundary of the range, the uniswap pool
will request both token0 and token1, but arrakis will only request from the user
token0 so the pool will lose some token1 if it has enough to cover it.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that calculates the token amounts required to add liquidity when a specific liquidity delta is requested. The implementation decides which token(s) to request based on a comparison between the current square‑root price and the square‑root price of the lower tick of the range. It uses a "less‑than‑or‑equal" (<=) check, treating the situation where the current price is exactly equal to the lower bound as being outside the range and therefore only requesting token0. In the reference Uniswap V3 implementation the condition is a strict "less‑than" (<) comparison, meaning that when the price equals the lower bound the pool is considered inside the range and both token0 and token1 must be supplied. Because of this off‑by‑one boundary error, when the price is precisely at the lower tick the Arrakis contract asks the user for token0 only, while the Uniswap pool expects both tokens. The pool consequently receives insufficient token1, leading to a shortfall of token1 in the pool’s accounting. From a user perspective the symptom is that a liquidity‑adding transaction may complete with only token0 transferred, the expected token1 never arrives, and the pool’s balance appears reduced or the transaction may later revert due to the missing token. The impact is a potential loss of token1 value for the protocol and for liquidity providers, as the pool becomes under‑collateralised for that asset. This edge case occurs only when the current price exactly matches the lower boundary of the liquidity range, a condition that is rarely exercised in typical testing and therefore easy to miss. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by comparing the contract’s logic with the official Uniswap V3 reference code. The bug belongs to the class of boundary‑condition or off‑by‑one errors in financial calculations that break accounting assumptions. The recommended remediation is to replace the <= comparison with a strict < comparison, aligning the contract’s behaviour with Uniswap V3 and ensuring that both token0 and token1 are requested when the price sits on the lower bound.

title: Lack of rebalance rate limiting allow operator to drain vault
description:
Operators of Arrakis vaults are constrained by the checks defined in
SimpleManager.sol, these checks prevent them from causing too much of a fund
loss on a single rebalance call (check univ3 pool price deviation, enforce minimum
swap slippage parameters).
However since there is no rate limiting for an operator to call rebalance on
SimpleManager, an operator can simply drain the vault by applying the accepted
slippage a hundred times in one transaction.
There are mostly two safety measures for preventing an operator to extract vault
funds when calling rebalance:
• Check pool price deviation for mints: By checking that a pool price is close to
a price given by a chainlink feed, operator is prevented from adding liquidity to
a pool at a really unfavorable price, and backrun later to extract vault funds
• Check slippage parameters for swap (_checkMinReturn): By checking that a
minimum amount of tokens is returned to the vault after the swap, it is
preventing the operator to swap tokens at a too unfavorable price. Min
amount out enforced in ArrakisV2:
rrakisV2.sol#L341-L363
As stated by the sponsor, in a public trustless setup, these slippage parameters
should be restricted to ~1%.
However since an operator is not rate limited for the number of calls she can do on
SimpleManager.rebalance, she can simply call it multiple times in a very short
timespan, extract an arbitrarily large share of vault funds.
Vault funds can be drained by a malicious operator.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an absence of any rate‑limiting mechanism on the rebalance function of the Arrakis vault manager contract. The manager enforces two safety checks – a pool price deviation check against a Chainlink feed and a minimum‑return slippage check – which are intended to prevent an operator from executing a single rebalance that would cause an excessive loss of funds. However, because the contract does not restrict how many times an operator can invoke rebalance within a single transaction or over a short time window, an attacker can call the function repeatedly, each call satisfying the individual slippage constraints (typically around one percent). By chaining a large number of such calls, the cumulative effect can drain an arbitrarily large portion of the vault’s underlying assets. The exploit works by having a malicious operator submit a transaction that contains many sequential rebalance calls; each call swaps tokens at the maximum allowed slippage, moves assets out of the pool, and returns just enough tokens to pass the minimum‑return check. From the user’s perspective the vault balance may suddenly drop to zero, withdrawals may fail, and the UI may show missing or empty balances despite the contract reporting successful rebalances. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that noted the lack of any counter‑measure on the frequency of rebalance calls. It is hard to notice because each individual rebalance appears legitimate and passes all existing checks, masking the cumulative loss. The impact is a potential loss of all deposited funds for every participant in the vault, undermining trust in the protocol and exposing users to financial harm. The affected parties include vault depositors, the protocol’s governance, and any downstream contracts that rely on the vault’s assets. To remediate, the contract should enforce a rate‑limit on the number of rebalance invocations per block or per time interval, or better, enforce a cumulative loss limit by comparing the total underlying value before and after a rebalance batch and rejecting the transaction if the loss exceeds a predefined threshold. This change would align the implementation with the intended business logic that rebalance operations should only cause minimal, bounded slippage and should not be exploitable for large‑scale fund extraction.

title: Min deposit protection during rebalancing can be bypassed in multi-tier
description:
Arrakis vault implements a slippage protection during rebalancing, but it does not
protect when multiple feeTiers are used.
akis/blob/main/v2-core/contracts/ArrakisV2.sol#L408-L409
can be used to check that liquidity is added around a given price (acts like a
slippage protection), when used on one pool.
However when aggregated on multiple pools as it is done here (over same tokens
but multiple fee tiers), it does not protect the user, as pools can be imbalanced in
different directions, and funds can be provided in the same proportion but provide
liquidity at a worse price,
Example:
Arrakis vault handles the price range 1200-2000 on WETH-USDC in fee tiers [0.3%,
0.5%], price of WETH sits at 1600.
Alice sees that Bob the operator tries to rebalance the pool and thus provides
liquidity on both ranges
Alice front runs Bob transaction, driving the price of WETH-USDC on fee tier 0.3%
to 1200, and on fee tier 0.5% to 2000.
Bob executes his operation, and provides bigger amounts of WETH and USDC to
provide same liquidity (worse prices), and so the slippage checks out.
Alice back runs the operation and makes a nice profit.
v2-manager-templates/contracts/SimpleManager.sol#L189-L194
So the sandwiching is limited by the deviation parameter (1%). This issue still holds,
since maybe Bob wanted to enforce a stricter deviation for his rebalance (0.5%)
using this check, and fails to do so.
Bob makes an unfortunate rebalance to the profit of a sandwich.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the minimum‑deposit slippage protection that Arrakis V2 vaults apply when rebalancing liquidity across Uniswap V3 pools. The contract checks that the amount of liquidity added to a single pool stays within a predefined price deviation, which works as a safeguard against large price moves for that pool. However, when the vault aggregates several pools that share the same token pair but have different fee tiers, the protection is performed independently for each tier and does not consider the combined effect of the deposits. Because each tier can be moved in opposite directions, an attacker can manipulate the price on each pool separately, supply liquidity at a worse overall price, and still satisfy the per‑tier slippage check. In practice, an operator (Bob) initiates a rebalance that adds liquidity to both a 0.3 % and a 0.5 % fee tier within a price range of 1200‑2000 for WETH‑USDC while the market price sits at 1600. An adversary (Alice) front‑runs the transaction, driving the price on the low‑fee tier down to 1200 and on the high‑fee tier up to 2000. Bob’s rebalance then adds larger amounts of WETH and USDC to meet the same target liquidity, but because the price checks are performed per tier, the operation appears to respect the 1 % deviation limit and therefore passes. Alice subsequently back‑runs the transaction, captures the price discrepancy, and extracts profit. The impact is that liquidity providers may receive a worse execution price than expected, effectively losing value, while the protocol’s rebalancing logic can be gamed for profit. The issue manifests only when a vault uses multiple fee tiers for the same token pair and relies on the existing per‑tier deviation check; it does not appear in single‑tier deployments, making it easy to overlook. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended aggregate price protection with the actual implementation. It is hard to notice because each individual check looks correct and the contract emits no explicit warning when the aggregate price deviates. To remediate, the vault should compute the effective price impact across all fee tiers and enforce a combined slippage constraint, or alternatively enforce stricter per‑tier deviation limits that account for cross‑tier imbalances. In other words, the minimum‑deposit protection must be applied to the total deposited amounts grouped by fee tier, ensuring that the overall price does not move beyond the operator’s intended tolerance. This class of bug falls under “inconsistent multi‑pool slippage validation” where per‑component checks do not guarantee system‑wide safety, leading to potential fund loss and unfair trade execution.

title: outdated variable is not effective to check multiple chainlink feeds
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the ChainLinkOraclePivot contract validates the freshness of two distinct Chainlink pricefeeds. The contract stores a single timeout value, called outdated, and applies the same check to both feeds when retrieving their latest round data. In practice the two feeds have very different update frequencies: the MATIC/ETH feed on Polygon updates roughly once every 24 hours (heartbeat 86400 seconds) while the ETH/USD feed updates every few seconds (heartbeat 27 seconds). Because the contract uses one generic threshold, setting outdated to the short interval causes the long‑interval feed to be considered stale far too often, leading to frequent reverts with the message “ChainLinkOracle: priceFeedA outdated.” Conversely, setting outdated to the long interval permits the short‑interval feed to be accepted even when its data is several minutes old, allowing stale prices to be used in the pivot calculation. An attacker can exploit this mismatch by triggering a transaction after the long‑interval feed has not been refreshed within the short timeout, causing the contract to revert and potentially denying service, or by using the high timeout to feed a deliberately outdated short‑interval price that skews the derived price used for swaps, minting, or redemption. The impact is that the protocol may compute an incorrect price, leading to users receiving less value than expected, arbitrage opportunities for malicious actors, or loss of funds for liquidity providers. The issue manifests whenever the _getLatestRoundData function is called, which is the normal path for price queries, and it affects any user or contract that relies on the oracle’s output – essentially the entire protocol’s economic logic. The problem was discovered during a manual audit when the tester observed that the same outdated variable was applied to feeds with disparate heartbeats, and that the test suite showed frequent reverts for the MATIC/ETH feed. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit a distinct event for stale data; the only symptom is an occasional revert or, more subtly, a price that is silently stale, which may only be observed as an unexpected token price or a missing refund. The bug belongs to the class of “stale‑data validation errors” where heterogeneous external data sources are guarded by a single timeout, violating the assumption that all sources update at the same rate. To remediate, the contract should maintain separate freshness thresholds for each feed, ideally derived from each feed’s advertised heartbeat, or rely on Chainlink’s built‑in stale‑answer protection. This ensures that each price is validated against an appropriate timeout, preventing both unnecessary reverts and acceptance of outdated prices, thereby preserving correct accounting and user expectations.

title: Update to managerFeeBPS applied to pending fees
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way manager fees are calculated in the ArrakisV2 contract. The contract stores a single managerFeeBPS variable that represents the percentage of collected UniV3 fees that are owed to the manager. When fees are harvested – either through the burn() function or during a rebalance – the internal _applyFees routine multiplies the pending fee amounts by the current managerFeeBPS and credits the result to the manager’s balance. Because the fee calculation reads the managerFeeBPS value at the moment of execution, any change to this variable retroactively influences all pending fees that have not yet been claimed. The manager (or any address that can call setManagerFeeBPS) can therefore call setManagerFeeBPS to increase the fee rate up to the contract‑wide maximum of 10,000 basis points (100 %) immediately before a fee collection event. This manipulation causes the pending fees that were expected to be split between stakers and the manager to be diverted entirely to the manager’s balance. The root cause is the absence of a snapshot or checkpoint of the fee rate at the time the fees become pending; the contract relies on a mutable global variable instead of a per‑epoch or per‑collection immutable value. Exploitation is straightforward: the manager monitors the contract for accumulated fees, then invokes setManagerFeeBPS with a high value, and finally triggers a rebalance or burn that invokes _applyFees, causing the inflated fee rate to be applied to the pending amounts. The impact is that stakers receive less or no share of the fees they are entitled to, effectively losing revenue that should have been distributed to them. This can happen at any time when there are unclaimed fees and the manager has permission to adjust the fee rate, which is allowed by design as long as the new rate does not exceed the hard‑coded 10,000 bps limit. The affected parties are the liquidity providers (stakers) who expect a proportional share of the protocol fees, as well as the overall protocol economics because the fee distribution model is broken. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the fee‑distribution logic and noticed that the managerFeeBPS variable is read directly during fee application without any historical locking. It can be hard to notice because the fee‑change function appears benign, respects the maximum bound, and the contract does not emit any warning that pending fees will be re‑evaluated under the new rate. From a user’s perspective, a staker may see their expected fee reward drop to zero after a rebalance, or notice that the manager’s balance suddenly jumps while their own pending balance remains unchanged. The bug belongs to the class of “retroactive state‑dependent fee manipulation” or “mutable parameter applied to pending accruals”. To remediate, the contract should capture the current managerFeeBPS value at the moment fees become pending (e.g., when they are first recorded) and use that immutable snapshot for subsequent distribution, or it should enforce that the fee rate can only be changed after all pending fees have been settled, effectively checkpointing fees before any update to the fee parameter. This ensures that fee calculations remain consistent with the expectations of stakers and prevents a manager from arbitrarily seizing pending fees.

title: D3Oracle will return the wrong price if the
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the D3Oracle contract consumes price data from a Chainlink price feed. Chainlink price feeds enforce a hard minimum and maximum answer: when the true market price falls below the configured minimum, the feed returns the minimum value instead of the actual price, and similarly returns the maximum value when the market price exceeds the upper bound. The D3Oracle implementation retrieves the latest round data and only validates that the reported price is greater than zero, that the data is recent, and that the round identifier is not stale. It never checks whether the price lies within the expected minimum‑and‑maximum range defined by the feed. Consequently, during extreme market conditions such as a rapid crash or a price spike, the oracle may supply the capped minimum or maximum price, and the contract will accept it as a legitimate market price. This incorrect price propagates through the getPrice() and getOriginalPrice() functions, which are used by D3VaultFunding, D3VaultLiquidation and D3UserQuota modules. As a result, calculations that depend on the price – for example collateral valuation, liquidation thresholds, funding limits and user quota enforcement – are performed with a distorted value. From a user’s perspective the protocol may appear to accept a deposit or loan at a normal rate, but later the system may liquidate the position at an unfavorable price, or allocate an incorrect quota, leading to unexpected loss of funds or denial of service. The impact is medium severity because the bug does not allow arbitrary fund theft on its own, but it can cause systematic under‑collateralisation and premature liquidations, especially during volatile market events, thereby eroding user confidence and potentially draining protocol reserves. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the auditor noticed that the price validation logic only checks for a positive price and does not enforce the feed’s documented bounds. The problem is subtle because the price value is still non‑zero and the timestamp check passes, so the contract behaves as if the data were correct, making the bug hard to detect through simple testing. To remediate the issue the contract should compare the retrieved price against the known minimum and maximum answers of the Chainlink feed (or a reasonable sanity range) and revert if the price falls outside this interval. Adding such bounds validation restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents the protocol from acting on artificially capped prices.

title: When swapping 18-decimal token to 8-decimal
description:
Here is the poc:
```solidity
uint256 payFromToken = d3Proxy.buyTokens(
    address(d3MM),
    user1,
    address(token1),
    address(token2),
    0,
    abi.encode(swapData),
    block.timestamp + 1000
);
assertEq(payFromToken, 0);
```
It may cause unexpected loss
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a decimal‑precision mismatch when a user swaps a token that uses 18 decimal places for a token that uses only 8 decimal places through the D3Trading contract. The buyTokens function calculates the amount of the source token that must be transferred (payFromAmount) based on the quoted price and the target amount. Because the target token has fewer decimals, the intermediate calculation can produce a value that is smaller than one unit of the 18‑decimal token. Solidity integer division truncates any fractional part, so the resulting payFromAmount becomes zero. The contract then proceeds with the swap assuming a non‑zero payment, but the recorded payment amount is zero. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed – the contract may emit events and update balances – yet the user receives no tokens or, in some implementations, the contract may still debit the user’s balance, effectively causing a loss of funds. The issue is triggered only when the swap size is sufficiently small that the required 18‑decimal token amount falls below the smallest representable unit after conversion to the 8‑decimal token. It is therefore a conditional bug that manifests under low‑value swaps or when the price feed is unfavorable. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the D3Trading.sol source code, where the auditor noticed that the function does not guard against a zero payFromAmount after the conversion step. The bug can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it simply records a zero payment, which may look legitimate in logs, and the loss only becomes apparent when users observe missing balances or receive no output tokens. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of rounding or precision errors in financial smart contracts, where mismatched token decimals lead to under‑flow or truncation. The impact is a potential loss of user funds and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, as the contract’s internal accounting assumes that a positive amount of the source token is always transferred. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a minimum non‑zero payment amount – for example, by checking if payFromAmount equals zero after the calculation and, if so, setting it to the smallest possible unit (1) or rejecting the transaction with a clear error. This ensures that either a minimal amount is transferred or the swap is aborted, preserving the integrity of the protocol’s financial logic and preventing silent loss of funds.

title: liquidationTarget is not set when removing
description: It may not remove pool successfully.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a missing state update during the liquidity removal process of a decentralized exchange pool. Specifically, when a user invokes the function that removes liquidity, the internal variable that records the address or identifier of the liquidation target is never assigned. This omission means the contract lacks the necessary reference to direct the withdrawn assets to the correct recipient or to trigger the appropriate accounting steps. As a result, the removal transaction may complete without reverting, but the expected transfer of tokens does not occur, leaving the user’s balance unchanged and the pool in an inconsistent state. The root cause is a logical oversight in the removal routine where the liquidationTarget field is not set before the final settlement logic executes. Exploitation is straightforward: any participant attempting to withdraw liquidity will experience a failed or silent removal, effectively locking their funds in the pool. In a worst‑case scenario, an attacker could repeatedly trigger removal attempts to keep the pool in a broken state, preventing other liquidity providers from exiting and potentially causing a loss of confidence in the protocol. The issue manifests only when the removal path is taken; normal trading operations remain unaffected. It primarily affects liquidity providers who expect to receive their proportional share of assets after calling the removal function, as well as the protocol itself, which relies on accurate accounting for solvency and fee distribution. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined state transitions and noticed that the liquidationTarget variable remained unset after a removal call. Because the contract does not emit a specific error or event for this condition, the bug can be hard to detect through standard testing or transaction monitoring. To remediate the issue, the removal logic should be amended to explicitly assign the correct liquidation target before any asset transfers or accounting updates are performed, and additional checks or events should be added to verify that the target is set, ensuring that withdrawals either succeed fully or revert with a clear error message. This class of bug falls under improper state initialization and can lead to funds disappearing from the user’s perspective, refunds not being issued, and overall accounting breakdown within the pool.

title: borrow amount recorded in AssetInfo and
description: The last pool's repay() / finishLiquidation() will be blocked, since the record.amount will be larger than the info.borrowAmount, which will cause a underflow in info.totalBorrows = info.totalBorrows - realDebt;
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch that occurs when the amount recorded for a borrowed asset in the pool’s internal AssetInfo structure exceeds the borrowAmount stored in the corresponding info record. This discrepancy originates from an incorrect update of the borrow tracking fields during borrowing, interest accrual, or reserve adjustments, causing the recorded amount to be larger than the official borrow amount. When a borrower later calls repay() or when the protocol attempts to finish a liquidation, the contract tries to reduce the totalBorrows field by the real debt amount. Because totalBorrows is smaller than the real debt due to the earlier over‑recording, the subtraction underflows. In Solidity 0.8 this underflow triggers an automatic revert, blocking the repayment or the final step of liquidation. The bug manifests only after a specific sequence: a borrower takes a loan, the price of the collateral asset changes dramatically, interest is accrued, part of the borrowed token is burned or otherwise removed, and then a liquidation is initiated. Under these conditions the internal accounting becomes inconsistent, leading to a revert. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are that a repayment transaction fails with an underflow error, the liquidation process never completes, and funds appear to be stuck in the pool despite the UI showing a zero or reduced balance. Both borrowers and liquidators are affected because they cannot close positions or recover collateral, and the protocol’s overall health is jeopardized as outstanding loans cannot be settled. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a proof‑of‑concept test that deliberately drives the price oracle, accrues interest, burns tokens and triggers liquidation. It is hard to notice because the mismatch only surfaces after a long series of state changes and does not appear in simple unit tests. The proper fix is to ensure that the recorded borrow amount never exceeds the stored borrowAmount, by correcting the logic that updates AssetInfo during borrowing, interest accrual, and reserve updates, and by adding sanity checks before performing subtraction on totalBorrows. In broader terms the bug belongs to the class of arithmetic underflow caused by inconsistent state updates in loan accounting, which violates the fundamental invariant that totalBorrows must always be greater than or equal to the real debt of a position.

title: parseAllPrice not support the tokens whose
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the price‑parsing routine that normalises token amounts to a fixed 18‑decimal representation. The code assumes that every ERC‑20 token has a decimal count less than or equal to 18 and computes a correction factor as 18 minus the token’s declared decimals. When a token such as NEAR, which uses 24 decimals, is supplied, the subtraction 18 - tokenDecimal underflows because tokenDecimal is larger than 18. In unsigned arithmetic this produces a very large positive integer, causing the subsequent division or multiplication to overflow or revert. As a result, the parseAllPrice function cannot handle tokens whose decimal precision exceeds 18, and any operation that depends on this function – including buying, selling, or providing liquidity – will fail with a revert. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for users attempting to trade high‑precision tokens: trades are rejected, balances remain unchanged, and liquidity cannot be added for those assets. This behaviour contradicts DODO v3’s advertised compatibility with all standard ERC‑20 tokens, misleading users into believing that any token can be traded. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined edge‑case token configurations. It may be difficult to notice in routine testing because the majority of deployed tokens use the common 18‑decimal standard, so the failure only surfaces with the relatively rare high‑decimal tokens. To remediate the problem, the contract should avoid the fixed‑18 assumption and instead compute a scaling factor based on the absolute difference between the token’s decimals and a chosen base (for example 36) or use safe arithmetic that handles both positive and negative differences without underflow. By correcting the decimal normalisation logic, the protocol will regain its intended ability to price and trade any ERC‑20 token regardless of its decimal precision, restoring expected user experience where a trade either succeeds or fails for reasons unrelated to decimal handling.

title: Wrong assignment ofcumulativeBid for Range-
description:
Wrong assignment of cumulativeBid for RangeOrder state. In D3Trading, the getRangeOrderState function is returning RangeOrder (get swap status for internal swap) which is assinging wrong toTokenMMInfo.cumulativeBid which suppose to be cumulativeBid not cumulativeAsk. The error lies in the assignment of roState.toTokenMMInfo.cumulativeBid. Instead of assigning tokenCumMap[toToken].cumulativeAsk, it should be assigning tokenCumMap[toToken].cumulativeBid.
File: D3Trading.sol
```solidity
roState.toTokenMMInfo.cumulativeBid =
    allFlag >> (toTokenIndex) & 1 == 0 ? 0 : tokenCumMap[toToken].cumulativeAsk;
```
This wrong assignment value definitely will mess up accounting balance, resulting unknown state will occure, which is not expected by the protocol. For one case, this getRangeOrderState is being used in querySellTokens & queryBuyTokens which may later called from sellToken and buyToken. The issue is when calling _contructTokenState which can be reverted from PMMRangeOrder when buy or sell token.
File: PMMRangeOrder.sol
```solidity
// B
tokenState.B = askOrNot ? tokenState.B0 - tokenMMInfo.cumulativeAsk : tokenState.B0 - tokenMMInfo.cumulativeBid;
```
When the tokenMMInfo.cumulativeBid (which was wrongly assign from cumulativeAsk) is bigger than tokenState.B0, this will revert. This wrong assignment value definitely will mess up accounting balance, resulting unknown state will occure, which is not expected by the protocol. For example reverting state showing a case above.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic error in the accounting path of the D3Trading contract where the cumulative bid amount for a range order is incorrectly populated with the cumulative ask value. The function getRangeOrderState builds a RangeOrder structure that includes a field toTokenMMInfo.cumulativeBid. Instead of reading tokenCumMap[toToken].cumulativeBid, the code reads tokenCumMap[toToken].cumulativeAsk when the flag for the destination token is set. This mis‑assignment propagates to the PMMRangeOrder contract, where the cumulativeBid field is used to compute the remaining token balance (B0 - cumulativeBid). If the mistakenly assigned cumulativeAsk is larger than the stored base balance B0, the subtraction yields a negative value and the contract reverts with an out‑of‑bounds error. The bug therefore breaks the fundamental accounting invariant that cumulativeBid must never exceed the available token balance. It is triggered whenever a user invokes sellToken or buyToken on a pair that has an active range order and the destination‑token flag is active, causing getRangeOrderState to return the malformed RangeOrder. From a user perspective the symptom is a transaction that unexpectedly reverts, often with a generic “insufficient balance” or “revert” message, and the UI may show that the intended trade did not occur while the user’s balance appears unchanged or, in some edge cases, temporarily reduced to zero. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the D3Trading contract where the auditor examined the data flow from getRangeOrderState to the token‑state construction in PMMRangeOrder and identified the mismatched variable name. Because the erroneous value is only used in a subtraction that may succeed for many typical orders, the bug can remain hidden until a specific order with a large cumulativeAsk is processed, making it difficult to notice in routine testing. The appropriate remediation is to replace the assignment with the correct cumulativeBid source, i.e., set roState.toTokenMMInfo.cumulativeBid to tokenCumMap[toToken].cumulativeBid when the flag is set. This restores the correct accounting relationship, prevents unexpected reverts, and aligns the contract with its intended business logic that bids and asks are tracked separately. The flaw belongs to the class of bugs known as incorrect state assignment or accounting mismatch, where a variable representing one financial dimension is mistakenly populated with another, violating protocol invariants and leading to transaction failures and potential loss of user confidence.

title: D3VaultFunding#checkBadDebtAfterAccrue
description:
D3VaultFunding#checkBadDebtAfterAccrue makes the incorrect assumption that a collateral ratio of less than 1e18 means that the pool has bad debt. Due to how collateral and debt weight affect the collateral ratio calculation a pool can have a collateral ratio less than 1e18 will still maintaining debt that is profitable to liquidate. The result of this is that the after this threshold has been passed, a pool can no longer be liquidate by anyone which can lead to continued losses that harm both the LPs and the MM being liquidated.
D3VaultFunding.sol#L382-L386
```solidity
if (balance >= borrows) {
    collateral += min(balance - borrows, info.maxCollateralAmount).mul(info.collateralWeight).mul(price);
} else {
    debt += (borrows - balance).mul(info.debtWeight).mul(price);
}
```
When calculating the collateral and debt values, the value of the collateral is adjusted by the collateralWeight and debtWeight respectively. This can lead to a position in which the collateral ratio is less than 1e18, which incorrectly signals the pool has bad debt via the checkBadDebtAfterAccrue check.
Example:
Assume a pool has the following balances and debts:
Token A - 100 borrows 125 balance
Token B - 100 borrows 80 balance
Price A = 1
collateralWeightA = 0.8
Price B = 1
debtWeightB = 1.2
collateral = 25 * 1 * 0.8 = 20
debt = 20 * 1 * 1.2 = 24
collateralRatio = 20/24 = 0.83
The problem here is that there is no bad debt at all and it is still profitable to liquidate this pool, even with a discount:
ExcessCollateral = 125 - 100 = 25
25 * 1 * 0.95 [DISCOUNT] = 23.75
ExcessDebt = 100 - 80 = 20
20 * 1 = 20
The issue with this is that once this check has been triggered, no other market participants besides DODO can liquidate this position. This creates a significant inefficiency in the market that can easily to real bad debt being created for the pool. This bad debt is harmful to both the pool MM, who could have been liquidated with remaining collateral, and also the vault LPs who directly pay for the bad debt. Unnecessary loss of funds to LPs and MMs
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect bad‑debt detection mechanism in the D3VaultFunding contract. The function checkBadDebtAfterAccrue assumes that a collateral‑to‑debt ratio (CR) lower than 1e18 automatically means the pool has entered bad‑debt territory and should be blocked from further liquidation. This assumption is wrong because the contract applies collateralWeight and debtWeight when computing the weighted collateral and weighted debt that feed the CR. The weighting can push the CR below the 1e18 threshold even when the underlying raw collateral exceeds the raw debt, meaning the position is still economically liquidatable with a profit after discount. When the weighted CR falls below the threshold, the check flags the pool as having bad debt and disables external liquidators; only the DODO protocol itself is allowed to perform liquidation. As a result, external participants cannot liquidate the pool, the pool remains stuck, and the remaining collateral cannot be recovered. Over time this can turn a merely weighted‑ratio mismatch into real bad debt, causing losses that are ultimately borne by liquidity providers and market makers. The issue manifests after an accrual step where the weighted CR drops below 1e18, which can happen even though the raw balances show excess collateral (for example, a pool with 125 balance vs 100 borrow on token A and 80 balance vs 100 borrow on token B, with weights 0.8 and 1.2, yields a weighted CR of 0.83 but still has 23.75 units of excess collateral after discount). Users observing the pool will see that liquidation attempts from external accounts fail, their LP shares may lose value, and no refunds are issued despite apparent surplus collateral. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who traced the logic of the weighted CR calculation and identified the mismatch between the economic reality and the contract’s binary bad‑debt flag. The problem is subtle because the CR value itself looks low, which normally signals risk, yet the underlying accounting still permits profitable liquidation; this discrepancy can be missed if only the weighted CR is inspected. The correct mitigation is to base the bad‑debt check on the raw, un‑weighted collateral and debt values, or to remove the weight factors from the CR comparison so that the contract only flags true bad‑debt situations where raw collateral is insufficient to cover raw debt. By aligning the check with the actual economic state, external liquidators can continue to operate, preventing unnecessary loss of funds and preserving the integrity of the vault’s accounting.

title: D3UserQuote#getUserQuote queries incor-
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the quota calculation performed by the D3UserQuote#getUserQuote function. Inside a valuation loop the code iterates over a list of tokens and, for each token, retrieves the associated asset address, the user's balance of that asset, and the market price from an oracle. The intention is to convert the token balance to a common value using the exchange rate returned by d3Vault.getExchangeRate for the current token, and then aggregate the result into a usedQuota variable. However, a typographical error causes the function to call d3Vault.getExchangeRate with the identifier token instead of the loop variable _token. Because token refers to a different scope (often the last token processed or an uninitialized value), the exchange rate applied does not correspond to the asset being evaluated. This mismatch leads to an incorrect conversion of the token balance, typically under‑estimating the usedQuota. Since the protocol uses usedQuota to enforce a risk‑mitigating quota, an underestimated usedQuota makes the system believe the user has consumed less risk than they actually have, allowing the user to open positions that are larger than intended. The impact is that positions can become oversized and over‑risk, potentially causing liquidation losses that affect the user, the protocol’s capital pool, and any lenders relying on the quota enforcement. The bug manifests whenever getUserQuote is called, i.e., during any operation that queries a user’s quota, and it affects all users whose balances are evaluated in the loop. It was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noticed the variable name mismatch while reviewing the valuation logic. The error is subtle because the surrounding arithmetic appears correct and the code compiles without warnings; only a careful inspection of variable scopes reveals the problem. Detecting the issue at runtime is difficult because the returned quota may still be a plausible number, especially if token and _token happen to have similar exchange rates for certain assets. To remediate the issue, the call to d3Vault.getExchangeRate must be changed to use the loop variable _token, ensuring that each token’s specific exchange rate is applied. Additional safeguards such as unit tests that compare expected quota values across multiple tokens and static analysis rules that flag mismatched identifiers can help prevent similar bugs. In user‑facing terms, a user may see a quota that is far lower than expected, leading to confusion when the UI reports that they can open larger positions than the protocol’s risk model intends, or conversely, they may observe that their positions are being liquidated unexpectedly because the system mis‑calculated their risk exposure.

title: Protocol is completely incompatible with USDT
description:
USDT will revert if the current allowance is greater than 0 and an non-zero approval is made. There are multiple instances throughout the contracts where this causes issues. In some places this can create scenarios where it becomes impossible to liquidate and/or borrow it.
See summary.
USDT may become impossible to liquidate or borrow
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the fact that the USDT token does not follow the standard ERC20 approve semantics. USDT’s implementation reverts any call to approve when the current allowance for a spender is greater than zero and the caller attempts to set a new non‑zero allowance in a single transaction. Throughout the protocol, several functions that interact with USDT – such as liquidation, borrowing and any internal token transfer that requires setting an allowance – invoke approve with a non‑zero value without first resetting the existing allowance to zero. Because the approve call reverts, the whole transaction fails, leaving the user’s balance unchanged and preventing the intended operation. This situation can arise whenever a user or the protocol tries to approve USDT for a contract that already has a non‑zero allowance, which is a common pattern in many DeFi contracts that assume standard ERC20 behaviour. The impact is that positions containing USDT may become impossible to liquidate, borrowers may be unable to open or repay loans, and overall protocol risk management can be compromised. Users experience symptoms such as “liquidation failed”, “borrow transaction reverted”, or “no funds were transferred despite a successful UI request”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the auditor observed repeated approve calls to USDT and noted the revert condition. It is hard to notice because most ERC20 tokens allow direct non‑zero allowance updates, so developers often omit the zero‑reset step.
