The vulnerability belongs to the class of state‑validation bugs where critical protocol state (liquidation status) is not checked before allowing fund movements, breaking business logic that assumes funds cannot be withdrawn while a position is being liquidated. From a user perspective the symptoms are missing or zero balances after a withdrawal attempt, protocol balance dropping unexpectedly, and error messages such as “ERC20: transfer amount exceeds balance”. The recommended fix is to add explicit require statements (or modifiers) that ensure neither partyA nor partyB is marked as liquidated before permitting deallocation, transfer allocation, or close‑position operations, and to ensure that any balance‑changing operation updates the relevant nonce so that stale signatures become invalid.

title: partyB can leverage emergency mode for quick profit
description:
A partyB can exploit the system by requesting the activation of emergency mode when they have an open position that partyA is reluctant to close. In the interim, partyB can take advantage of any open quotes with an expected open price below the current market rate. Once partyB is granted emergency status, they can immediately close these trades for a quick profit.
Suppose Alice, acting as partyB, has an ongoing position with a counterparty, partyA, who has refrained from closing the position. Sensing the need for an intervention, Alice appeals to the protocol for the activation of emergency mode.
However, just before the transaction granting emergency status is processed, Alice conducts a quick sweep for any open quotes where the proposed open price is less than the current market rate. Alice stumbles upon a quote where partyA offers a LONG position on 100 units of ETH at an expected open price of $2000 each. Given that the prevailing market price for ETH stands at $2010, Alice promptly takes advantage of the opportunity by opening that quote. As soon as Alice is granted emergency status, she can close the trade and immediately pocket a neat profit of $1000 [(2010-2000) x 100] within quick operations.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an emergency‑mode mechanism that, when activated by a participant (partyB), grants that participant the ability to close any open positions in the system without restriction. Because the contract does not tie the emergency status to a specific counter‑party, partyB can request emergency mode while a counter‑party (partyA) still holds an open position that the counter‑party is unwilling to close. During the short window between the request and the transaction that actually sets the emergency flag, partyB can front‑run the system and open new quotes that are priced favorably relative to the current market price. In the described scenario, partyB discovers a quote offering a long position at an expected open price lower than the market price, opens the quote, and once emergency status is granted, immediately closes the trade, pocketing the price difference as profit. The root cause is the overly broad permission granted by emergency mode and the lack of atomicity between the request and the enforcement of the mode. Exploitation requires only that an open quote with a price advantage exists and that the attacker can submit a transaction before the emergency flag is set. The impact is a direct financial loss for the counter‑party whose position is closed at an unfavorable price, erosion of trust in the protocol’s fairness, and potential systemic abuse if many participants repeat the pattern. The condition under which it occurs is when a party with an open position is reluctant to close, an emergency mode can be requested, and the contract permits opening new quotes while the request is pending. The affected parties are any users who rely on the emergency mechanism for safety, especially those holding positions opposite the requester, as well as the protocol itself, which may suffer reputational damage. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of the emergency‑mode function and identified that the status is granted globally rather than per‑counter‑party. It can be difficult to notice because the emergency mode is intended as a protective feature, and the profit‑making step happens in a very short time window that may not be covered by typical test cases. To remediate, the emergency status should be scoped to the specific counter‑party whose position is being protected, or the contract should prevent opening new quotes after an emergency request, enforce atomic state changes, or require explicit consent from the opposite party before allowing closure of positions under emergency mode. In user‑facing terms, a trader may see their open quote filled at a price they did not expect, or notice that their counterpart suddenly closes a position and walks away with a profit, while the trader’s balance is reduced accordingly.

title: Quotes that have already been liquidated can be liquidated again in some cases
description:
LiquidationFacetImpl.liquidatePartyB is used to liquidate PartyB, which directly adds partyBAllocatedBalances[partyB][partyA] to allocatedBalances[partyA] (core/contracts/facets/liquidation/LiquidationFacetImpl.sol#L294-L296). In this way, the liquidation against PartyB has been completed. The main purpose of LiquidationFacetImpl.liquidatePositionsPartyB is to remove the OpenPosition of both parties (symmio-core/contracts/facets/liquidation/LiquidationFacetImpl.sol#L369). If this function is not called, the OpenPosition of both parties will always exist. The reasons for not calling it maybe:
- symmetrical/blob/main/symmio-core/contracts/facets/liquidation/LiquidationFacetImpl.sol#L373) is 0, there is no incentive for liquidator.
2. Liquidator (bot) is not working due to downtime/network issues.
3. Intentionally not called.
4. tx is deferred processing (pending in mempool), resulting in [here](https://githcts/facets/liquidation/LiquidationFacetImpl.sol#L318-L322) revert.
Afterwards, if PartyA is liquidated due to quote with other PartyB, LiquidationFacetImpl.liquidatePositionsPartyA will process the quotes with the original PartyB. These quotes should have been removed.
For simplicity, the numbers mentioned below will not be exact values, it is just to describe the issue. Suppose the following scenario:
There are 3 users: PartyA(A1), PartyB(B1), PartyB(B2). The symbol is ETH/USDT.
allocatedBalances[A1]=1000
partyBAllocatedBalances[B1][A1]=1000
partyBAllocatedBalances[B2][A1]=1000
1. A1 created a short quote1 via PartyAFacet.sendQuote. pendingLockedBalances[A1]=500. The current symbol price is 100.
2. B1 opens quote1 via PartyBFacet.lockAndOpenQuote. lockedBalances[A1]=500, partyBLockedBalances[B1][A1]=500. [LibQuote.addToOpenPositions](https://ntracts/facets/PartyB/PartyBFacetImpl.sol#L253) will add quote1 to the OpenPositions array of both parties. The status of quote1 is QuoteStatus.OPENED.
3. As time goes by, the price dumps to 50. B1 can be liquidated.
4. The liquidator initiates liquidation against B1 via LiquidationFacet.liquidatePartyB. allocatedBalances[A1]=1000+partyBAllocatedBalances[B1][A1]=2000, partyBAllocatedBalances[B1][A1]=0.
5. liquidatePositionsPartyB is not called, so the OpenPositions array of both parties still contains quote1, and its status is still QuoteStatus.OPENED.
6. A1 thinks that the price will continue to dump, and creates a short quote2. pendingLockedBalances[A1]=500. The current price is 50. Because allocatedBalances[A1]=2000 at this time, when the price pump to 200, A1 will be liquidated.
7. B2 opens quote2. lockedBalances[A1]=500, partyBLockedBalances[B2][A1]=500. The OpenPositions array of A1 contains quote1 and quote2. The OpenPositions array of B2 only has quote2.
8. As time goes by, the price pumps to 200. A1 can be liquidated.
9. The liquidator initiates liquidation of A1. This process requires 3 calls: Liquida-tionFacet.liquidatePartyA/setSymbolsPrice/liquidatePositionsPartyA. The /symmio-core/contracts/facets/liquidation/LiquidationFacet.sol#L28) of setSymbolsPrice is calculated off-chain. From the flow of the ain/symmio-core/muon/crypto_v3.js#L238-L267) function in crypto_v3.js, all quotes in the OpenPositions array of A1 will be calculated into upnl. Because quote1 was opened when the price was 100, and the current price is 200, so B1 is profitable. This means that B1 that has been liquidated can also be allocated part of allocatedBalances[A1]. This is obviously unreasonable. This is a loss of part of the funds for B2.
Quotes that have already been liquidated can be liquidated again in some cases.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a double‑liquidation logic error that allows a quote which has already been settled for one counter‑party to be processed again when the opposite side of the position is later liquidated. The root cause is the separation of two functions in the liquidation facet: liquidatePartyB, which transfers the counter‑party’s allocated balance to the liquidator, and liquidatePositionsPartyB, which is responsible for removing the quote from the OpenPositions arrays of both parties. When liquidatePositionsPartyB is omitted – for example because the incentive for the liquidator is zero, the liquidator bot is offline, the call is intentionally skipped, or the transaction reverts while pending – the quote remains marked as QuoteStatus.OPENED in the OpenPositions list. Later, when PartyA is liquidated, the liquidation routine iterates over all quotes recorded in PartyA’s OpenPositions array, including the stale quote that should have been cleared. The calculation of unrealised P&L (upnl) therefore includes a quote that has already been settled, causing the protocol to allocate part of PartyA’s balance to the already‑liquidated PartyB. This results in an unreasonable redistribution of funds: the newly opened counter‑party (e.g., B2) may lose part of its expected allocation, and the overall accounting of the protocol becomes inconsistent. From a user’s perspective the UI may still display the quote as open after the first liquidation, leading the user to believe the position is still active, while in reality the funds have already been transferred. When the second liquidation occurs the user sees an unexpected reduction in balance or a missing refund, contradicting the expectation that only the current open quotes affect the outcome. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation facet, where the auditor observed that the OpenPositions array was not cleared after a successful liquidation and that subsequent liquidation calculations incorrectly included those stale entries. The bug is subtle because the allocatedBalances appear correct after the first liquidation, masking the lingering stale quote; only a deeper inspection of the position‑tracking data structures reveals the inconsistency. To remediate the problem the contract should ensure that the removal of open positions is performed atomically with the balance transfer, either by merging liquidatePartyB and liquidatePositionsPartyB into a single transaction or by adding a guard that prevents already‑settled quotes from being considered in later liquidation calculations. Additional safeguards such as explicit state flags for settled quotes or checks that an OpenPosition entry has not been previously liquidated before inclusion in upnl computation would also mitigate the risk. The fix must be designed to handle large OpenPositions arrays without causing out‑of‑gas errors, possibly by processing the array in chunks or by using more gas‑efficient data structures.

title: Malicious PartyB can block unfavorable close
description:
Malicious PartyB can block close position requests that are unfavorable toward them by intentionally choose not to fulfill the close request and continuously prolonging the force close position cooldown period, causing a loss of profits for PartyA.
If PartyA invokes the requestToClosePosition function for an open quote, the quote's status will transition from QuoteStatus.OPEN to QuoteStatus.CLOSE_PENDING. In case PartyB fails to fulfill the close request (fillCloseRequest) during the cooldown period (maLayout.forceCloseCooldown), PartyA has the option to forcibly close the quote by utilizing the forceClosePosition function.

Malicious PartyB could abuse this by blocking PartyA from closing their positions against them when the price is unfavorable toward them. For instance, when PartyA is winning the game and decided to close some of its positions, PartyB could block the close position request to deny PartyA of their profits and prevent themselves from losing the game.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic flaw that allows a malicious counter‑party (PartyB) to indefinitely block a user’s (PartyA) request to close an open position. The contract marks a quote as CLOSE_PENDING when PartyA calls requestToClosePosition and then expects PartyA to be able to invoke forceClosePosition after a fixed cooldown period. The cooldown check is implemented by comparing the current block timestamp with quote.modifyTimestamp plus a configured delay. However, quote.modifyTimestamp is updated not only when the close request is created but also by many other functions, including LibQuote.closeQuote, which is called whenever PartyB partially fulfills a close request. By calling fillCloseRequest with the smallest possible filledAmount, PartyB can trigger closeQuote, which resets quote.modifyTimestamp to the current block time. This action effectively restarts the cooldown timer, preventing the condition block.timestamp > quote.modifyTimestamp + cooldown from ever becoming true. Consequently, PartyA’s forceClosePosition call reverts with “Cooldown not reached”, and the position remains open despite PartyA’s intention to close it. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a pending close request, the expected profit does not appear, and the account balance stays unchanged, leading to confusion and potential loss of earnings. The issue occurs whenever PartyB can invoke fillCloseRequest after a close request has been made, which is possible for any quote that permits partial fills. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of timestamps across contract functions and identified that modifyTimestamp is used for multiple unrelated purposes. Because modifyTimestamp is a legitimate field updated throughout the contract’s lifecycle, the problem is subtle and may not be obvious from surface‑level testing. The proper mitigation is to decouple the timestamp used for the force‑close cooldown from the general modifyTimestamp. Introducing a dedicated variable such as requestClosePositionTimestamp that is set only when PartyA initiates a close request and is never altered by other functions eliminates the ability for PartyB to reset the cooldown. The forceClosePosition function should then compare the current block timestamp against this new variable plus the configured delay. This change isolates the cooldown logic, restores the intended guarantee that PartyA can eventually force close a position, and prevents malicious parties from indefinitely blocking closures.

description:
The insolvency check (isSolventAfterOpenPosition) within the openPosition function does not consider the locked balance adjustment, causing the user account to become insolvent immediately after the position is opened. As a result, the affected users will lose their CVA and liquidation fee locked in their accounts.

leverage = price × quantity / lockedValues.total()
When opening a position, there is a possibility that the leverage might change different market price compared to the one at the moment the user requested. Thus, the purpose of Line 163 above is to adjust the locked values to maintain a
The issue is that the insolvency check at Line 150 is performed before the adjustment is made.
Assume that the adjustment in Line 163 cause the locked values to increase. The insolvency check (isSolventAfterOpenPosition) at Line 150 will be performed with old or unadjusted locked values that are smaller than expected. Since smaller locked values mean that there will be more available balance, this might cause the system to miscalculate that an account is not liquidatable, but in fact, it is actually liquidatable once the adjusted increased locked value is taken into consideration.
In this case, once the position is opened, the user account is immediately underwater and can be liquidated.
The issue will occur in the "complete fill" path and "partial fill" path since both paths adjusts the locked values at Line 185
Users might become liquidatable immediately after opening a position due to an incorrect insolvency check within the openPosition, which erroneously reports that the account will still be healthy after opening the position, while in reality, it is not. As a result, the affected users will lose their CVA and liquidation fee locked in their accounts.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect solvency validation that occurs inside the function responsible for opening a new trading position. The contract calls an insolvency check (isSolventAfterOpenPosition) before it updates the locked balance that represents the collateral required for the newly opened position. Because the check uses the old, unadjusted locked values, it may incorrectly report that the account remains solvent. After the function later adjusts the locked values – often increasing them due to price changes or leverage calculations – the account’s actual collateral becomes insufficient and the account is instantly underwater. This mismatch allows the protocol’s liquidation mechanism to trigger immediately after the position is opened, causing the user to lose the CVA and the liquidation fee that were previously locked in the account. The issue manifests when the locked‑value adjustment at line 163 (or the analogous adjustment in the partial‑fill path) increases the required collateral. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a successful position opening followed by an unexpected liquidation event; the user may see their balance drop to zero or notice that the expected refund or collateral is missing. The bug belongs to the class of post‑state‑change solvency validation errors, where the order of operations leads to a false‑negative insolvency result. It was discovered during a manual audit of the openPosition logic, where the auditor observed that the insolvency check was performed before the balance update, a subtle mistake that can be overlooked because the check itself passes. The problem is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error at the time of the check, and the subsequent liquidation appears as a normal protocol action. To remediate the issue the solvency check should be performed after the locked balances have been adjusted, or the check should be recomputed with the updated collateral values, ensuring that the account’s health is evaluated against the true post‑open state. This change restores the intended business logic that a user’s position should only be liquidated if the account is genuinely under‑collateralized after all state changes have been applied.

title: Suspended PartyBs can bypass the withdrawal restriction
description:
Suspended PartyBs can bypass the withdrawal restriction by exploiting fillCloseRequest function. Thus, an attacker can transfer the ill-gotten gains out of the protocol, leading to a loss of assets for the protocol and its users.
ontracts/facets/Account/AccountFacet.sol#L26
File: AccountFacet.sol

```solidity
28:

29:
}
30:
31:

32:
address user,
33:
uint256 amount
34:

35:
AccountFacetImpl.withdraw(user, amount);
36:
emit Withdraw(msg.sender, user, amount);
37:

```
When a user is suspended, they are not allowed to call any of the withdraw functions (withdraw and withdrawTo) to withdraw funds from their account. These withdrawal functions are guarded by the notSuspended modifier that will revert if the user's address is suspended.
ontracts/utils/Accessibility.sol#L73
File: Accessibility.sol

```solidity
75:

"Accessibility: Sender is Suspended"
```

However, suspected PartyBs can bypass this restriction by exploiting the fillCloseRequest function to transfer the assets out of the protocol. Following describe the proof-of-concept:
1) Anyone can be a PartyA within the protocol. Suspended PartyBs use one of their wallet addresses to operate as a PartyA.
2) Use the PartyA to create a new position with an unfavorable price that will immediately result in a significant loss for any PartyB who takes on the position. The partyBsWhiteList of the new position is set PartyB address only to prevent some other PartyB from taking on this position.
3) Once PartyB takes on the position, PartyB will immediately incur a significant loss, while PartyA will enjoy a significant gain due to the zero-sum nature of this game.
4) PartyA requested to close its position to lock the profits and PartyB will fill the close request.
5) PartyA calls the deallocate and withdraw functions to move the assets/gains out of the protocol.
In the event of an attack, the protocol will suspend the malicious account and prevent it from transferring ill-gotten gains out of the protocol. However, since this restriction can be bypassed, the attacker can transfer the ill-gotten gains out of the protocol, leading to a loss of assets for the protocol and its users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a permission bypass that allows an address that has been marked as suspended to move assets out of the protocol despite the presence of a withdrawal restriction. The protocol enforces a notSuspended modifier on the public withdraw and withdrawTo functions, which checks a storage flag and reverts if the caller is suspended. However, the functions that create and close trading positions – openPosition and fillCloseRequest – do not include this modifier. A malicious PartyB can first have its address suspended, then act as a PartyA to open a position that forces a counterpart PartyB to take a loss. When the counterpart fills the close request, the protocol credits the suspended PartyB with the profit through fillCloseRequest, and because the function lacks the notSuspended guard the protocol later allows the suspended address to call withdraw or withdrawTo and transfer the ill‑gotten gains out of the system. The exploit works whenever a suspended address is able to be the counter‑party in a position and later invoke fillCloseRequest, which can be triggered by any PartyB that accepts the position. The impact is a loss of assets for the protocol and its users, as the protocol’s intended safeguard – preventing suspended accounts from extracting funds – is effectively circumvented. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the suspension logic and the position‑closing workflow; the auditor noted that the suspension check was missing on functions that can credit balances. The bug is subtle because the withdrawal functions themselves behave correctly, so a simple test of calling withdraw from a suspended address would appear to work, masking the deeper flow that can still move funds. Conceptually, this is a classic case of incomplete access control where a security‑critical state (suspended) is not propagated to all entry points that can affect balances. From a user’s perspective, a user who has been suspended expects that no further transfers can be made, yet after a position is closed the user sees a successful withdrawal and the protocol’s total balance shrinks unexpectedly. The business logic that “suspended accounts cannot extract value” is violated, breaking accounting assumptions of zero‑sum settlement. The recommended fix is to add the notSuspended modifier to both openPosition and fillCloseRequest (and any other functions that can credit a user’s balance) so that a suspended address cannot participate in profit‑generating actions, thereby restoring the intended security invariant.

title: Imbalanced approach of distributing the liquidation fee within setSymbolsPrice function could be exploited
description:
The imbalance approach of distributing the liquidation fee within setSymbolsPrice function could be exploited by malicious liquidators to obtain the liquidation fee without completing their tasks and maximizing their gains. While doing so, it causes harm or losses to other parties within the protocols.
A PartyA can own a large number of different symbols in its portfolio. To avoid out-of-gas (OOG) errors from occurring during liquidation, the setSymbolsPrice function allows the liquidators to inject the price of the symbols in multiple transactions instead of all in one go.
Assume that the injection of the price symbols requires 5 transactions/rounds to complete and populate the price of all the symbols in a PartyA's portfolio. Based on the current implementation, only the first liquidator that calls the setSymbolsPrice will receive the liquidation fee. Liquidators that call the setSymbolsPrice function subsequently will not be added to the AccountStorage.layout().liquidators[partyA] listing as Line 88 will only be executed once when the liquidationType is still not initialized yet.

..SNIP..

priceSig.upnl &&

A malicious liquidator could take advantage of this by only setting the symbol prices for the first round for each liquidation happening in the protocol. To maximize their profits, the malicious liquidator would call the setSymbolsPrice with none or only one (1) symbol price to save on the gas cost. The malicious liquidator would then leave it to the others to complete the rest of the liquidation process, and they will receive half of the liquidation fee at the end of the liquidation process.
Someone would eventually need to step in to complete the liquidation process. Even if none of the liquidators is incentivized to complete the process of setting the symbol prices since they will not receive any liquidation fee, the counterparty would eventually have no choice but to step in to perform the liquidation themselves. Otherwise, the profits of the counterparty cannot be realized. At the end of the day, the liquidation will be completed, and the malicious liquidator will still receive the liquidation fee.
Malicious liquidators could exploit the liquidation process to obtain the liquidation fee without completing their tasks and maximizing their gains. While doing so, many liquidations would be stuck halfway since it is likely that no other liquidators will step in to complete the setting of the symbol prices because they will not receive any liquidation fee for doing so (not incentivized).
This could potentially lead to the loss of assets for various parties:
• The counterparty would eventually have no choice but to step in to perform the liquidation themselves. The counterparty has to pay for its own liquidation, even though it has already paid half the liquidation fee to the liquidator.
• Many liquidations would be stuck halfway, and liquidation might be delayed, which exposes users to greater market risks, including the risk of incurring larger losses or having to exit at an unfavorable price.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incentive‑distribution flaw in the liquidation workflow, specifically in the setSymbolsPrice function that is used to inject price data for a liquidated party’s portfolio. The root cause is that the contract records the first caller of setSymbolsPrice as a liquidator and assigns the entire liquidation fee to that address, while subsequent callers are not added to the liquidators list because the liquidationType flag is already set and the push operation on line 88 is executed only once. When a liquidation requires several transactions to provide prices for many symbols, a malicious actor can call setSymbolsPrice with only one or a few symbols, receive the full fee, and then abandon the remaining price submissions. Other liquidators who later complete the price injection receive no fee, which removes their economic incentive to finish the process. As a result, liquidations can become stuck halfway, forcing the counter‑party or the protocol itself to complete the liquidation without any reward, leading to higher gas costs, delayed exits, and potential loss of assets for users. The issue manifests when liquidationType is initially NONE and the price‑setting phase spans multiple blocks or transactions. It affects any participant that relies on timely liquidation – liquidators expecting fair compensation, counterparties whose positions are being closed, and end‑users whose collateral may be at risk. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state‑transition logic of the liquidation facet. It is subtle because the first call appears to work correctly and no revert is thrown for later calls, making the missing fee distribution easy to overlook. The bug belongs to the class of incentive‑misalignment or reward‑splitting vulnerabilities, where the contract’s accounting assumptions about proportional contribution are violated. From a user perspective the symptoms are delayed liquidation, unexpected zero reward for participants who performed work, and the need for the affected party to pay the full liquidation fee themselves, contrary to the expectation that fees are shared among contributors. A proper fix is to redesign the fee allocation so that each liquidator receives a share proportional to the number of symbol prices they supplied, for example by tracking contributions and applying a proportional multiplier such as the existing partyBPositionLiquidatorsShare variable, thereby restoring balanced incentives and preventing liquidations from stalling.

title: Liquidators will not be incentivized to liquidate
description:
Liquidating certain accounts does not provide a liquidation fee to the liquidators. Liquidators will not be incentivized to liquidate such accounts, which may lead to liquidation being delayed or not performed, exposing Party B to unnecessary risks and potentially resulting in greater asset losses than anticipated.

The liquidatorShare and partyBPositionLiquidatorsShare variables will both be zero, which means the liquidators will get nothing in return for liquidating PartyBs. As a result, there will not be any incentive for the liquidators to liquidate such positions.
Liquidators will not be incentivized to liquidate those accounts that do not provide them with a liquidation fee. As a result, the liquidation of those accounts might be delayed or not performed at all. When liquidation is not performed in a timely manner, PartyB ended up taking on additional unnecessary risks that could be avoided in the first place if a different liquidation incentive mechanism is adopted, potentially leading to PartyB losing more assets than expected.
Although PartyBs are incentivized to perform liquidation themselves since it is the PartyBs that take on the most risks from the late liquidation, the roles of PartyB and liquidator are clearly segregated in the protocol design. Only addresses granted the role of liquidators can perform liquidation as the liquidation functions are guarded by onlyRole(LibAccessibility.LIQUIDATOR_ROLE). Unless the contracts are PartyB upon registration OR liquidation functions are made permissionless, PartyBs are likely not able to perform the liquidation themselves when the need arises.
Moreover, the PartyBs are not expected to be both a hedger and liquidator simultaneously as they might not have the skillset or resources to maintain an infrastructure for monitoring their accounts/positions for potential late liquidation.
bug_full: The contract implements a liquidation routine that is supposed to reward addresses holding the LIQUIDATOR_ROLE with a liquidation fee when they liquidate an insolvent Party B position. The code calculates a variable called liquidatorShare only when a specific condition is true: the absolute value of the available balance (interpreted as a uint256) must be smaller than the locked loss factor of the Party B account. If this condition fails, the execution follows an else branch that explicitly sets both liquidatorShare and the per‑position liquidator share to zero. Consequently, when the loss incurred by Party B exceeds the predefined liquidation fee threshold, the liquidator receives no compensation for performing the liquidation. This logical branch was discovered during a manual audit of LiquidationFacetImpl.sol, where the else clause at line 269 was identified as assigning zero values. The root cause is an incentive‑calculation design that only awards a fee under a narrow scenario, ignoring cases where the loss is larger than the fee, thereby violating the business assumption that liquidators are always compensated for their work. Exploitation does not require an attacker; the protocol itself will invoke the liquidation function under the described conditions, resulting in a liquidator‑free liquidation. The impact is that liquidators, who are the only actors authorized to call the liquidation function, have no economic reason to act, leading to delayed or omitted liquidations. Delayed liquidations increase the exposure of Party B to further market moves, potentially causing greater asset loss than originally anticipated. The issue manifests when the deficit in the Party B account is large enough that the condition `uint256(-availableBalance) < lockedBalance.lf` evaluates to false. From a user perspective, a liquidation transaction may appear successful, yet the liquidator’s balance remains unchanged and no fee is transferred, contradicting the expectation that a liquidation yields a reward. Because the protocol separates the roles of Party B and liquidator, Party B cannot perform the liquidation themselves, and the lack of incentive is not immediately obvious from the UI. The bug belongs to the class of “incentive‑misalignment” or “reward omission” vulnerabilities, where business logic that should guarantee compensation fails under certain state conditions. To remediate, the incentive mechanism should be redesigned to guarantee a non‑zero fee for any liquidation, for example by always allocating a fixed percentage of the account’s credit‑value‑adjusted (CVA) loss to the liquidator, or by introducing a fallback fee when the primary calculation yields zero. This change would restore the economic motivation for liquidators, ensure timely liquidations, and align the protocol’s risk‑management assumptions with its actual behavior.

title: emergencyClosePosition can be blocked
description:
The emergencyClosePosition function can be blocked as PartyA can change the position's status, which causes the transaction to revert when executed.
Activating the emergency mode can be done either for a specific PartyB or for the entire system. Once activated, PartyB gains the ability to swiftly close positions without requiring users' requests. This functionality is specifically designed to cater to urgent situations where PartyBs must promptly close their positions.
Based on the PartyBFacetImpl.emergencyClosePosition function, a position can only be "emergency" close if its status is QuoteStatus.OPENED.
contracts/facets/PartyB/PartyBFacetImpl.sol#L312
File: PartyBFacetImpl.sol
309:
function emergencyClosePosition(uint256 quoteId, PairUpnlAndPriceSig memory upnlSig) internal {
310:
AccountStorage.Layout storage accountLayout = AccountStorage.layout();
311:
Quote storage quote = QuoteStorage.layout().quotes[quoteId];
312:
require(quote.quoteStatus == QuoteStatus.OPENED, "PartyBFacet: Invalid state");
..SNIP..
As a result, if PartyA knows that emergency mode has been activated, PartyA could pre-emptively call the PartyAFacetImpl.requestToClosePosition with minimum possible quantityToClose (e.g. 1 wei) against their positions to change the state to QuoteStatus.CLOSE_PENDING so that the PartyBFacetImpl.emergencyClosePosition function will always revert when triggered by PartyB. This effectively blocks PartyB from "emergency" close the positions in urgent situations.
PartyA could also block PartyB "emergency" close on-demand by front-running PartyB's PartyBFacetImpl.emergencyClosePosition transaction with the PartyAFacetImpl.requestToClosePosition with minimum possible quantityToClose (e.g. 1 wei) when detected.
PartyB could accept the close position request of 1 wei to revert the quote's status back to QuoteStatus.OPENED and try to perform an "emergency" close again. However, a sophisticated malicious user could front-run PartyA to revert the quote's status back to QuoteStatus.CLOSE_PENDING again to block the "emergency" close for a second time.
During urgent situations where emergency mode is activated, the positions need to be promptly closed to avoid negative events that could potentially lead to serious loss of funds (e.g. the protocol is compromised, and the attacker is planning to or has started draining funds from the protocols). However, if the emergency closure of positions is blocked or delayed, it might lead to unrecoverable losses.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the emergencyClosePosition function in the PartyB facet, which is intended to allow a privileged PartyB to close an opened position instantly when the protocol enters emergency mode. The function checks that the quote's status is exactly QuoteStatus.OPENED before proceeding. Because the check does not accept the alternative status QuoteStatus.CLOSE_PENDING, a malicious PartyA can manipulate the quote status to CLOSE_PENDING by calling requestToClosePosition with the smallest possible quantity (for example 1 wei) either before the emergency mode is activated or by front‑running the PartyB transaction. When the status becomes CLOSE_PENDING, the require statement in emergencyClosePosition fails and the transaction reverts, effectively blocking the emergency close operation. This is a classic state‑dependent race condition where the legitimate state transition performed by PartyA interferes with the emergency path of PartyB. The impact is that positions that should be liquidated to protect funds remain open, leaving the protocol exposed to further loss during a crisis such as an ongoing attack or market crash. The issue manifests only when emergency mode is active and when an adversarial PartyA can submit a transaction that changes the quote status before PartyB’s emergency transaction is mined. Users experience the symptom of a “failed emergency close” – they expect their position to be closed and their balance to be updated, but the transaction reverts and the on‑chain balance stays unchanged, giving the impression that funds have disappeared or are locked. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the contract logic, where the auditor noticed that the status check was overly restrictive and could be manipulated through a front‑running transaction. It is hard to notice because the requestToClosePosition function is a normal part of the protocol and the status transition to CLOSE_PENDING is a legitimate state in regular operation; only the combination with emergency mode creates the problem. The vulnerability belongs to the class of front‑running and state‑dependency bugs that break business‑logic assumptions about invariant states during privileged operations. To remediate the issue, the emergencyClosePosition function should be relaxed to accept both OPENED and CLOSE_PENDING statuses, or the protocol should enforce an atomic state change that cannot be overridden by a competing transaction, thereby ensuring that emergency closures can always be executed when needed.

title: Hedgers are not incentivized to respond to
description:
Hedgers could intentionally force the users to close the positions themselves via the forceClosePosition and charge a spread to earn more, which results in the users closing at a worse price, leading to a loss of profit for them.
How fillCloseRequest function works?
For a Long position, when PartyB (Hedger) calls the fillCloseRequest function to fill a close position under normal circumstances, the hedger cannot charge a spread because the hedger has to close at the user's requested close price (quote.requestedClosePrice).
If the hedger decides to close at a higher price, it is permissible by the function, but the hedger will lose more, and the users will gain more because the users' profit is computed based on long profit = closing price - opening price.
Under normal circumstances, most users will set the requested close price (quote.requestedClosePrice) close to the market price most of the time.
In short, the fillCloseRequest function requires the hedger to match or exceed the user's requested price. The hedger cannot close at a price below the user's requested price in order to charge a spread.
contracts/facets/PartyB/PartyBFacetImpl.sol#L256
function fillCloseRequest(
..SNIP..
if (quote.positionType == PositionType.LONG) {
require(
closedPrice >= quote.requestedClosePrice,
"PartyBFacet: Closed price isn't valid"
)
How forceClosePosition function works?
For a Long position, the forceCloseGapRatio will allow the hedger to charge a spread from the user's requested price (quote.requestedClosePrice) when the user (PartyA) attempts to force close the position.
The upnlSig.price is the market price and quote.requestedClosePrice is the price users ask to close at. By having the forceCloseGapRatio, assuming that forceCloseGapRatio is 5%, this will create a spread between the two prices (upnlSig.price and quote.requestedClosePrice) that represent a cost that the users (PartyA) need to "pay" in order to force close a position.
contracts/facets/PartyA/PartyAFacetImpl.sol#L253
function forceClosePosition(uint256 quoteId, PairUpnlAndPriceSig memory upnlSig) internal {
..SNIP..
if (quote.positionType == PositionType.LONG) {
require(
upnlSig.price >=
quote.requestedClosePrice +
(quote.requestedClosePrice * maLayout.forceCloseGapRatio) /
1e18,
"PartyAFacet: Requested close price not reached"
);
..SNIP..
LibQuote.closeQuote(quote, filledAmount, quote.requestedClosePrice);
Issue with current design
Assume a hedger ignores the user's close request. In this case, the users (PartyA) have to call the forceClosePosition function by themselves to close the position and pay a spread.
The hedgers can abuse this mechanic to their benefit. Assuming the users (PartyA) ask to close a LONG position at a fair value, and the hedgers respond by calling the fillCloseRequest to close it. In this case, the hedgers won't be able to charge a spread because the hedgers are forced to close at a price equal to or higher than the user's asking closing price (quote.requestedClosePrice).
However, if the hedger chooses to ignore the user's close request, this will force the user to call the forceClosePosition, and the user will have to pay a spread to the hedgers due to the gap ratio. In this case, the hedgers will benefit more due to the spread.
In the long run, the hedgers will be incentivized to ignore users' close requests.
The hedgers will be incentivized to ignore users' close requests, resulting in the users having to wait for the cooldown before being able to force close a position themselves. The time spent waiting could potentially lead to a loss of opportunity cost for the users.
In addition, hedgers could intentionally force the users to close the positions themselves via the forceClosePosition and charge a spread to earn more, which results in the users closing at a worse price, leading to a loss of profit for them.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mis‑aligned incentive in the position‑closing workflow. The contract offers two paths for closing a long position: fillCloseRequest, which can only be executed by the hedger and requires the closing price to be at least the user‑requested price, and forceClosePosition, which can be invoked by the user after a cooldown and permits the closing price to be higher than the requested price by a configurable forceCloseGapRatio. Because the forceClosePath adds a spread that is paid to the hedger, a hedger can simply ignore the user’s original close request, wait for the cooldown, and force the user to close through forceClosePosition. The user then receives a closing price that is artificially inflated by the gap ratio, reducing the calculated profit (closing price minus opening price) and effectively transferring value to the hedger. This behavior occurs whenever a user submits a close request with a price close to market and the hedger chooses not to fill it. The affected parties are the users who expect to close at the quoted price and the protocol that assumes fair price execution. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the price checks in fillCloseRequest and forceClosePosition and identified that the latter permits a hidden spread only in the force‑close path, making it easy to miss in casual testing. The impact is that users may see their expected profit disappear, receive a lower net payout, or experience opportunity‑cost loss while the hedger gains extra margin. To remediate, the gap ratio should be removed so that forceClosePosition closes at the actual market price, or the protocol should penalize hedgers for not responding to close requests, or only allow a spread when the hedger actively fulfills the request. Aligning incentives eliminates the ability for a hedger to force a user to pay an extra spread and restores the intended accounting logic where profit equals closing price minus opening price.

title: Position value can fall below the minimum acceptable quote value
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the quote‑closing logic of the exchange contract. The protocol defines a minimum acceptable quote value (for example 5 USD) that must be preserved for any open position. This invariant is normally enforced by a require statement that checks the total locked value of the quote before allowing further operations. However, when a user submits a close request and then cancels it, the contract changes the quote status to CANCEL_CLOSE_PENDING and enters a branch that resets the quote to an OPENED state without re‑evaluating the minimum‑value condition. If the counter‑party (Party B) proceeds to fill the close request partially, the same branch is executed and the validation is skipped, allowing the remaining position value to fall below the configured threshold. As a result, the position can end up with a value that is too small for the liquidation engine to operate profitably; liquidators may refuse to act because the fee would be negligible, leaving the position exposed to market volatility and potentially causing users to lose more than expected. From the user’s perspective the position may appear to have a very low or zero balance, liquidation attempts fail, and refunds are missing, contradicting the expectation that a cancelled close request prevents further fills. The issue manifests only when a close request is cancelled and the opposite party still chooses to fill it partially; normal order execution paths still enforce the minimum‑value check, making the bug easy to miss during casual testing. The problem was discovered during a systematic audit of the quote‑management library, where the conditional flow was examined and the missing require statement was identified. Fixing the bug requires adding the minimum‑value validation to the CANCEL_CLOSE_PENDING branch, ensuring that after any partial fill the remaining locked value is still above the protocol‑defined minimum. This restores the accounting invariant, prevents positions from slipping into an uneconomical state, and preserves the intended liquidation guarantees.

In Lines 157, 159, and 161 above, a malicious user could make the numerator smaller than the denominator (LibQuote.quoteOpenAmount(quote)), and the result will be zero due to a rounding error in Solidity.
In this case, the quote.lockedValues will not decrease and will remain the same. As a result, the locked balance of the account will remain the same even though a certain amount of the position has been closed. This could cause the account's locked balance to be higher than expected, and the errors will accumulate if it happens many times.
When an account's locked balances are higher than expected, their available balance will be lower than expected. The available balance affects the amount that users can withdraw from their accounts. The "silent" increase in their locked values means that the amount that users can withdraw becomes lesser over time, and these amounts are lost due to the errors.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error in the closeQuote function of the LibQuote library. When a quote is partially closed the contract calculates the reduction of each locked component (cva, mm, lf) by multiplying the component by the filledAmount and dividing by the total open amount of the quote. Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, if the filledAmount is sufficiently small the product becomes smaller than the denominator and the division yields zero. As a result the computed lockedValues remain unchanged even though the position is considered closed. A malicious or careless user can submit a close request with a tiny filledAmount, causing the subtraction term to be zero and leaving the account’s locked balances unchanged. The locked balance therefore stays higher than the actual exposure, which reduces the account’s available balance and limits the amount that can be withdrawn. Over repeated executions the discrepancy accumulates, effectively making funds silently disappear from the user’s perspective. The issue occurs only when the filledAmount is small relative to the quote’s open amount and the locked components are also small enough that the multiplication does not overflow the denominator. All participants in a quote – both parties and any third‑party liquidity providers – are affected because the accounting invariant that locked collateral matches the open position size is broken. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of LibQuote.sol where the division expressions were examined and it was observed that they could round down to zero. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an error; the balances simply do not change, so the loss is silent and only becomes apparent after many close operations. The flaw belongs to the class of integer‑division rounding errors that cause accounting inconsistencies. From a user’s point of view the expected behavior is that a portion of the locked collateral is released after closing a trade, but in practice the locked amount remains unchanged, the withdrawable balance is lower than expected, and the UI may show ‘no refund’ or ‘available balance decreased’. To remediate the issue the contract should validate that the filledAmount is large enough to produce a non‑zero reduction, or use a rounding‑up calculation, or restructure the accounting so that the reduction is computed with full precision before division. Ensuring that the reduction cannot be zero unless the position is fully closed restores the invariant that locked values accurately reflect the remaining open amount.

title: Liquidating a turned solvent Party A does not credit profits
bug_full: During the multi‑step liquidation process a logical flaw allows a party that has become solvent again (referred to as Party A) to lose any realized profit earned during that liquidation. The liquidation routine first checks the available balance of Party A and, if it is non‑negative, marks the liquidation as a normal type and records a liquidation fee. When the contract iterates over Party A's open positions, losses are correctly deducted from the counter‑party (Party B) and the profit amount is calculated, but the code only adds that profit to Party B’s allocated balance. After all positions are closed the contract unconditionally resets Party A’s allocated balance to zero without first crediting the realized profit. As a result the protocol retains the profit that should belong to Party A, effectively making the funds disappear from the user’s perspective. This bug is triggered when a liquidation is started while Party A is still solvent, i.e., after setSymbolsPrice has been called and the liquidation type is set to NORMAL, and then liquidatePositionsPartyA processes the positions. The affected party is the solvent trader (Party A) who expects to receive the profit from the closed positions; instead the UI shows a zero or unchanged balance, contradicting the expectation of a positive payout. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation facet where the flow of balance updates was examined. It can be hard to notice because a zero balance after liquidation may be considered normal, masking the fact that a profit was never credited. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting or settlement bugs where profit/loss accounting is incomplete, leading to loss of funds. To remediate, the implementation should add the realized profit to Party A’s allocated balance before resetting the balance, and the accounting logic should ensure that total unrealized profit and loss are reconciled with allocated balances for both parties.

title: Consecutive symbol price updates can be multiple times
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the liquidation workflow that permits a liquidator to update the market prices of the symbols underlying a distressed Party A’s positions multiple times during a single liquidation process. The contract function that records symbol prices, setSymbolsPrice, only checks that the unrealized profit‑and‑loss (upnl) and totalUnrealizedLoss values supplied by the liquidator match the values stored in the liquidation details. Because these two numeric fields remain unchanged after a partial liquidation, the contract does not prevent the liquidator from calling setSymbolsPrice again with a new price snapshot. An attacker can therefore liquidate one of Party A’s open positions, then submit a fresh price signature reflecting the current market for the remaining symbols, and finally liquidate the next position. Each time the price is refreshed, Party B – the counter‑party to Party A – receives the full loss amount plus any credit‑value adjustment (CVA), effectively receiving more funds than the total collateral originally locked by Party A. In the demonstrated scenario, Party B receives 130 USDT while Party A only locked 100 USDT, creating a 30 USDT shortfall that is recorded as bad debt in the protocol. The issue occurs only when Party A is insolvent, the liquidation is performed in multiple calls, and the market is volatile enough that symbol prices change between calls. It affects all participants: Party A loses the remainder of its collateral, Party B receives excess profit, and the protocol’s treasury suffers an unrecoverable loss. The flaw was uncovered during a security audit by constructing a test that performed two consecutive liquidations with an intervening price update. Because the upnl and loss fields stay constant, the price change appears legitimate and therefore the bug can be subtle and easy to miss in routine testing. From a user perspective the symptoms are unexpected extra payouts to the counter‑party and a sudden drop in the protocol’s balance, i.e., “my protocol lost funds after liquidation” or “the counter‑party got more than it should”. The root cause is the lack of a state guard that ties the price snapshot to the entire liquidation lifecycle; the contract does not record how many positions remain or lock the price data after the first liquidation step. To remediate, the protocol should either forbid any further calls to setSymbolsPrice once a liquidation has begun, or it should store the count of open positions at the start of liquidation and only allow price updates while that count is unchanged. In practice this means adding a check that either (a) the liquidation status is marked as “finalised” before permitting price changes, or (b) the price update function validates that no positions have been settled since the last snapshot. By enforcing a single immutable price view for the whole liquidation, the protocol prevents the profit‑inflation attack and restores correct accounting of collateral and fees.

title: Party B liquidation can expire, causing the
description:
The liquidation of Party B can get stuck if the liquidation timeout is reached and the positions are not liquidated within the timeout period.
The insolvent Party B's positions are liquidated by the liquidator via the liquidatePositionsPartyB function in the LiquidationFacetImpl library. This function requires supplying the QuotePriceSig memory priceSig parameter, which includes a timestamp and a signature from the Muon app. The signature is verified to ensure the priceSig values were actually fetched the trusted Muon app.
The signature is expected to be created within the liquidation timeout period. This is verified through the validation of the priceSig.timestamp, as seen in lines 318-322. Failure to do so, i.e., providing a signature that's created after the liquidation timeout, results in the signature being treated as expired, thereby causing the function to revert and rendering the liquidation of Party B stuck.
Party A's locked balance is not decremented by the liquidatable position. Party B's liquidations status is stuck and remains set to true, resulting in the notLiquidated and notLiquidatedPartyB modifiers to revert.
```solidity
308: function liquidatePositionsPartyB(
309:     address partyB,
310:     address partyA,
311:     QuotePriceSig memory priceSig
312: ) internal {
313:     AccountStorage.Layout storage accountLayout = AccountStorage.layout();
314:     MAStorage.Layout storage maLayout = MAStorage.layout();
315:     QuoteStorage.Layout storage quoteLayout = QuoteStorage.layout();
316:
317:     LibMuon.verifyQuotePrices(priceSig);
318:     require(
319:         priceSig.timestamp <=
320:         maLayout.partyBLiquidationTimestamp[partyB][partyA] + maLayout.liquidationTimeout,
321:         "LiquidationFacet: Expired signature"
322:     );
323:     require(
324:         maLayout.partyBLiquidationStatus[partyB][partyA],
325:         "LiquidationFacet: PartyB is solvent"
326:     );
327:     require(
328:         block.timestamp <= priceSig.timestamp + maLayout.liquidationTimeout,
329:         "LiquidationFacet: Expired price sig"
330:     );
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a time‑bound liquidation dead‑lock in the Party B liquidation flow. When an insolvent Party B is supposed to be liquidated, the liquidator must call liquidatePositionsPartyB with a price signature (QuotePriceSig) that contains a timestamp signed by the trusted Muon app. The contract checks that the signature timestamp is not later than the stored liquidation deadline (maLayout.partyBLiquidationTimestamp + liquidationTimeout) and also that the current block time is within liquidationTimeout of the signature. If the liquidation process is not completed before the timeout expires, any later signature will fail the timestamp check, causing the function to revert with “Expired signature”. Because the contract never clears maLayout.partyBLiquidationStatus[partyB][partyA] (which stays true) or resets the stored liquidation timestamp, subsequent attempts to liquidate are blocked by the notLiquidatedPartyB modifier. Consequently Party A’s locked balance is never decremented and Party B’s positions remain marked as liquidated but are in fact not processed. This dead‑lock can be triggered simply by waiting out the timeout or by an attacker deliberately delaying the price feed, resulting in funds that should be released staying locked, users seeing transactions revert, and the protocol being unable to recover the insolvent position. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the timestamp validation logic and noticed the absence of any status‑reset mechanism after the timeout. It is hard to notice because the revert message appears legitimate (“Expired signature”) and the liquidation status flag remains true, so later calls fail silently without obvious state changes. The bug belongs to the class of “time‑dependent state‑locking” or “expiration‑based dead‑lock” vulnerabilities, where a timeout condition prevents a required state transition and the contract does not provide a recovery path. To remediate, the contract should clear the liquidation status and timestamp when the timeout is reached, allow a new liquidation attempt, or redesign the validation to accept older signatures or to automatically cancel the liquidation request after the timeout, thereby preventing the lock‑up of funds and restoring expected behavior where a user expects a liquidation to succeed or to receive a refund of the locked balance.

title: Fee collector can grief the protocol by with-
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting underflow that occurs when the fee collector withdraws all accumulated trading fees from a shared balance mapping that is also used to store refundable fees for Party A. The protocol records trading fees collected during quote creation in the same balances structure that holds Party A and Party B balances. When a quote is cancelled or expires, the contract attempts to return the previously collected trading fee to Party A by adding the fee to Party A’s allocated balance and subtracting the same amount from the fee collector’s balance. If the fee collector has previously withdrawn those fees, the fee collector’s balance becomes insufficient and the subtraction triggers an unsigned‑integer underflow, causing the transaction to revert. An attacker who controls the fee collector role can deliberately withdraw the full fee pool, then trigger a quote cancellation or expiration (or wait for a natural expiration) to cause the underflow and effectively deny service to the protocol. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on any function that needs to return trading fees – including quote cancellation requests, forced cancellations, position openings, and quote expiration – leaving users unable to close or modify positions and potentially locking funds. The condition arises only when the fee collector’s balance is lower than the fee that must be returned, which may not be obvious during normal operation because fees are usually present. The affected parties are the protocol itself, all participants who rely on quote lifecycle operations (Party A, Party B, and any downstream users), and any funds that become inaccessible while the protocol is stuck. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the SYMM contract suite when the auditor noticed that the same storage slot was used for both fee collection and fee refunds without any safeguard. It is hard to notice because the underflow only manifests when the fee collector’s balance is drained, a scenario that may not be exercised in standard tests. To remediate, the protocol should separate the accounting of fees that are permanently earned by the fee collector from fees that may need to be returned, track the refundable portion explicitly, and enforce that withdrawals can only remove fees that are no longer refundable. Additionally, a balance‑sufficiency check or safe‑math subtraction should be added before attempting to return fees. From a user’s perspective, a transaction that should refund a trading fee instead fails with a revert, leaving the user with no refund and possibly an error message such as “transaction reverted”. The expectation that a cancelled quote returns the fee is violated, resulting in a situation where “funds disappear” or “refund is missing”, which is a classic symptom of an accounting underflow bug.

title: Liquidators can prevent users from making
description:
The Symmetrical protocol has various paused states in which different operations are paused. The protocol operations can be unpaused by privileged accounts. But when this unpause happens the liquidators can frontrun and liquidate user positions before those users get a chance to make their positions healthy.
ontracts/facets/control/ControlFacet.sol#L242-L295
The privileged addresses can pause the symmetrical protocol fully/partially using the pausability functions in ControlFacet. Once the protocol is paused all these operations cannot be done by users:
• deposit
• withdraw
• allocate
• deallocate
• sendQuote
• lockQuote
• openPositions
• liquidations
• etc
Though, real prices from oracles will surely move up or down during this paused period. If the oracle prices go down, users won't be allowed to allocate more collateral or close their positions. Hence their positions will get under-collateralized (based upon real prices).
Once the protocol is unpaused the liquidators can front-run most users and liquidate their positions. Most users will not get a chance to make their position healthy.
This results in loss of funds for the users.
By front-running any collateral allocation or position closure of a legitimate user which became under-collateralized the paused state, the liquidator can unfairly liquidate user positions and collect liquidation profit as soon as the protocol is unpaused. This causes loss of funds to the user.
Also, on unpause, it is unlikely that any human users will be able to secure their positions or MEV/liquidation bots capture the available profit. Hence the loss is certain.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a timing‑based liquidation flaw that appears when the Symmetrical protocol is placed in a paused state and later unpaused. The root cause is that the pause mechanism disables all user‑initiated actions such as depositing collateral, withdrawing, allocating or deallocating positions, and even sending or locking quotes, while still allowing external price feeds to update oracle values. Because the protocol’s collateralisation checks are based on the latest oracle prices, a price movement during the pause can render a user’s position under‑collateralised even though the user is unable to add more collateral or close the position. When the privileged account calls the unpause function, the protocol immediately re‑enables the liquidation function. Liquidators, who monitor the unpause transaction, can submit a liquidation transaction in the same block and therefore front‑run legitimate users who have not yet had a chance to react. This results in the user’s position being liquidated and the liquidator collecting the profit, while the user loses the expected collateral or profit. From the user’s point of view the symptom is a sudden loss of funds or a zeroed balance after the protocol resumes, often without any warning that a liquidation occurred. The impact is a loss of funds for any user whose position became under‑collateralised during the pause, a breach of the protocol’s economic fairness guarantees, and a potential erosion of trust in the system. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the pause‑unpause flow and identified that liquidation is not gated by any grace period after unpause. It can be hard to notice because pausing is generally perceived as a protective measure, and developers may assume that no adverse events can happen while the system is paused. However, the continuous oracle updates invalidate that assumption. To remediate the problem, the protocol should introduce a configurable grace period after unpause during which liquidation calls are rejected, giving users a window to add collateral or close positions before liquidators can act. This change aligns the contract’s behaviour with the intended safety guarantees of the pause feature and prevents unfair, front‑run liquidations that cause fund loss.

title: Liquidating pending quotes doesn't return trad-
description:
When a user is liquidated, the trading fees of the pending quotes aren't returned.
When a pending/locked quote is canceled, the trading fee is sent back to party A, e.g.
ore/contracts/facets/PartyA/PartyAFacetImpl.sol#L136
ore/contracts/facets/PartyA/PartyAFacetImpl.sol#L227
But, when a pending quote is liquidated, the trading fee is not used for the liquidation. Instead, the fee collector keeps the funds:
These funds should be used to cover the liquidation. Since no trade has been executed, the fee collector shouldn't earn anything.
Liquidation doesn't use paid trading fees to cover outstanding balances. Instead, the funds are kept by the fee collector.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the liquidation path of a decentralized trading protocol. When a user has a pending or locked quote, the protocol normally refunds the trading fee to the quote creator when the quote is cancelled. However, if the user is liquidated while a quote remains pending, the fee that was previously paid is not returned or applied to the liquidation; instead it is retained by the fee collector. The root cause is a missing transfer of the pending‑quote fee in the liquidation routine, which assumes that no fee needs to be handled because no trade was executed. An attacker or any party that can trigger liquidation of a user with pending quotes can therefore cause the fee collector to keep those funds, effectively stealing the fee amount. The impact is that the liquidated user loses the fee that should have been either refunded or used to offset the debt, leading to a higher net loss and a situation where the protocol’s accounting no longer balances. This condition occurs only when liquidation is performed while there are outstanding pending quotes; normal cancellation of quotes works correctly. The affected parties are users who place quotes and later become liquidated, as well as the protocol itself because the fee collector receives funds it should not earn, breaking trust in the fee model. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the fee handling logic of quote cancellation and liquidation and noticed the discrepancy. Because the fee is transferred to a contract address rather than the user, the loss may not be immediately visible in the UI, making it hard to notice without inspecting internal balances. To fix the problem, the liquidation code should be amended to either (i) return the pending‑quote fee to the quote creator when the user is not the one being liquidated, or (ii) apply the fee toward the liquidator’s debt when the liquidated party is the fee payer. This aligns the behavior with the intended accounting model where fees are either refunded or used to cover outstanding obligations, preventing unintended fund loss and preserving protocol honesty.

title: _account_for_withdraw_liquidity rounding in
description:
Vault implementers should be aware of the need for specific, opposing rounding directions across the different mutable and view methods, as it is considered most secure to favor the Vault itself during calculations over its users. If (1) it’s calculating how many shares to issue to a user for a certain amount of the underlying tokens they provide or (2) it’s determining the amount of the underlying tokens to transfer to them for returning a certain amount of shares, it should round down. If (1) it’s calculating the amount of shares a user has to supply to receive a given amount of the underlying tokens or (2) it’s calculating the amount of underlying tokens a user has to provide to receive a certain amount of shares, it should round up.
When the user extracts liquidity, due to the existence of share, the calculation has precision errors, should pay special attention to the rounding direction. Users withdraw a specific amount of liquidity, user shares should be rounded up, subtract 1 more shares, to avoid spending more than they earn, resulting in the eventual run out of the vault.
_amount_to_lp_shares calculates the amount of share to be subtracted, which should round up, otherwise the user account share will be 1 more than it actually is, and the difference will gradually become larger as users interact with vault over time, eventually run out of the vault.
Rounding in the wrong direction, when users withdraw liquidity, the shares are greater than actual value, and gradually accumulate as interactions, eventually causing the vault to be run out of and unable to repay all the liquidity.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect rounding direction applied in the vault’s share‑to‑liquidity conversion logic. The vault is supposed to favour its own accounting by rounding down when it calculates how many shares to issue for a deposit and rounding up when it determines how many shares must be burned to return a specific amount of underlying tokens on withdrawal. In the implementation the function that computes the number of shares to subtract during a withdrawal (_amount_to_lp_shares) rounds down instead of up. As a result the user’s share balance is recorded as slightly higher than the actual value of the underlying assets they are withdrawing. Each withdrawal therefore consumes fewer underlying tokens than the recorded shares imply. The discrepancy is tiny per transaction but accumulates over many interactions, eventually causing the vault’s total token balance to be insufficient to honour all outstanding shares. This can be exploited by repeatedly withdrawing small amounts, allowing an attacker to gradually drain the vault because the contract believes it still holds enough assets to cover the inflated share balances. The impact is that funds may disappear from the vault, legitimate users may receive less than expected or experience failed withdrawals, and the protocol can become insolvent. The condition under which the bug manifests is any user‑initiated liquidity extraction where the contract uses the faulty rounding logic to compute the share reduction. All participants who hold shares in the vault are affected, including depositors, withdrawers, and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended rounding policy with the actual implementation and identified the mismatch. It is hard to notice because each individual rounding error is small and does not raise an exception; only after many withdrawals does the cumulative error become apparent. The proper fix is to change the rounding direction in the share‑subtraction calculation to round up, and to audit all related conversion functions to ensure a consistent policy: round down when issuing shares for deposits and round up when burning shares for withdrawals. By aligning the implementation with the intended accounting model, the vault will maintain correct invariant relationships between total underlying tokens and total shares, preventing the gradual loss of liquidity and preserving user expectations that the amount withdrawn matches the share value.

title: Vault._amount_per_base_lp_share should also
description: Unstoppable's vault consists of two types of pools. The safety module pool is designed to bear the first loss risk. So the bad debt is first covered by the safety. Liquidity Providers have the choice to provide liquidity in the "Base LP" pool or the "Safety Module" pool. The Safety Module pool takes a first loss risk protecting the Base LP in exchange for a higher share of the trading and accruing interest. However, if the safety module liquidity is insufficient, the base liquidity is also used to cover the bad debt. But Vault._amount_per_base_lp_share never take bad debt into consideration, leading to loss of funds. When calling Vault.withdraw_liquidity, it uses Vault._account_for_withdraw_liquidity to calculate the withdraw share. If the base pool is chosen, it calls self._amount_per_base_lp_share. And it directly uses self.base_lp_total_amount to calculate the shares without considering the. Suppose that base_lp_total_amount is 100 and safety_module_lp_total_amount is 100. The bad_debt is now 150 and total_debt_amount is 0. The available liquidity is. Consider the following situations. • The total share of base liquidity is 100 shares, with Alice and Bob each having 50 shares. • Alice calls withdraw_liquidity to withdraw 50 tokens from the base pool. • Bob also wants to withdraw the liquidity but he fails since the available. If the amount of bad debt is more than safe module liquidity, the withdrawal of base liquidity becomes unfair. Early liquidity providers have the advantage of being able to withdraw the full amount, while other liquidity providers are unable to withdraw any liquidity, resulting in a loss of funds for them.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the vault contract that manages two liquidity pools – a Base LP pool and a Safety Module pool. The Safety Module is intended to absorb the first loss, protecting the Base LP providers. When the safety module does not have enough liquidity to cover the bad debt, the protocol is designed to draw the remaining loss from the Base LP pool. However, the internal function that calculates how much each Base LP share is worth, _amount_per_base_lp_share, ignores the outstanding bad debt entirely. It simply divides the total amount of base liquidity by the total number of base shares, assuming that the full base amount is still available. Consequently, when bad debt exceeds the safety module’s balance, the calculation reports a higher per‑share value than the actual recoverable amount. An attacker or any user does not need to perform a special action – the flaw manifests automatically when the vault’s bad debt grows beyond the safety buffer and a later liquidity provider attempts to withdraw. The first providers who withdraw before the shortfall are able to claim the full nominal amount, while subsequent providers receive far less or nothing at all, even though they hold the same number of shares. From a user’s perspective the UI will show a normal share balance, but the withdrawal transaction returns zero tokens or a dramatically reduced amount, violating the expectation that “my share should be worth the same amount as everyone else’s”. This leads to an unfair distribution of funds, a loss of capital for later providers, and breaks the accounting assumption that each share represents an equal claim on the pool’s assets. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who noted that the function never references the bad_debt variable. It is difficult to spot because the function’s name and simple arithmetic appear correct in isolation, and the problem only surfaces under the specific condition of excessive bad debt, which may not be exercised in routine tests. The proper remediation is to adjust the per‑share calculation to subtract the portion of bad debt that cannot be covered by the safety module, as illustrated in the recommended code snippet. By accounting for the net available base amount, the vault will correctly reflect the reduced value of each share and prevent the loss of funds for later liquidity providers.

title: The Vault._update_debt() function should be
description: The Vault._update_debt() should be executed before the interests rate are modified by the Vault.set_variable_interest_parameters() function. The Vault._update_debt() function helps to accrue interest since the last update. The execution path: 1. It calls the function Vault._debt_interest_since_last_update(_debt_token) in order to calculate the token debt interest. 2. The Vault._debt_interest_since_last_update() function uses the Vault._current_interest_per_second() function in order to get the interest per second. 3. The Vault._current_interest_per_second() calls Vault._interest_rate_by_utilization() in order to get the interest rate. 4.
