The Vault._interest_rate_by_utilization() function calls the Vault._dynamic_interest_rate_low_utilization() or Vault._dynamic_interest_rate_high_utilization depending on the switch utilization. 5. The Vault._dynamic_interest_rate_low_utilization() is executed and it calls the Vault._min_interest_rate(). 6. Then, the Vault._min_interest_rate() function gets the value from the [self.interest_configuration_address][0]. So in the step 6, it gets the interest from the interest_configuration, then the interests are used in order to calculate the token debt. The Vault._update_debt() accrue interest since the last update, the function should be executed before the admin change the interest configuration via Vault.set_variable_interest_parameters() function. The reason is that the time that has already passed must be taken with the previous interest before the admin changes to the new interests rate. The protocol should accrue interest since the last update before change the interest rate configuration. If the admin change the interest rate, the new interest rate should be applied to the future time not to the time that has already passed. The time that has already passed should use the previous interest. It is unfair for the users because users expects interests changes to be applied after they were changed not to the past time the _update_debt has not been executed. • The Vault._update_debt() function. • The Vault._debt_interest_since_last_update function. • The Vault._current_interest_per_second() function. • The Vault._interest_rate_by_utilization() function. • The Vault._dynamic_interest_rate_low_utilization() function. • The Vault._dynamic_interest_rate_high_utilization() function. • The Vault._interest_configuration() function. • The Vault.set_variable_interest_parameters() function.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ordering of state updates inside the Vault contract when the administrator modifies the variable interest parameters for a given debt token. The contract provides a function, Vault._update_debt(address), that accrues interest on outstanding debt based on the interest rate that was in effect since the last update. The interest rate itself is read from a configuration stored in the contract and is accessed through a chain of internal calls: _debt_interest_since_last_update → _current_interest_per_second → _interest_rate_by_utilization → either _dynamic_interest_rate_low_utilization or _dynamic_interest_rate_high_utilization, which finally reads the rate from the interest configuration. The administrative function set_variable_interest_parameters updates this configuration, but the current implementation does not invoke _update_debt before the configuration change. Consequently, when the admin changes the rates, the subsequent call to _interest_rate_by_utilization immediately returns the new rate, and any interest that should have been accrued for the elapsed time up to the moment of the change is calculated with the new rate instead of the old one. This ordering flaw means that past time is charged at a future interest rate, violating the expectation that interest changes apply only to future periods. Users therefore may see their debt increase unexpectedly, receive lower refunds, or observe balances that do not match the interest they anticipated. The issue is particularly harmful because it can be triggered by any admin action, and the contract does not emit a warning or revert; the mis‑calculation is silent, making it hard to detect from the UI where only the final balance is shown. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑dependent calculation ordering” or “interest rate update ordering” vulnerabilities, where a state‑changing operation is performed before dependent state is reconciled. It was discovered during a manual audit that traced the call graph of the interest accrual logic and identified the missing _update_debt call. To remediate, the set_variable_interest_parameters function should first call _update_debt for the affected token address, thereby locking in the correct interest for the elapsed period, and only then overwrite the interest configuration. This ensures that the protocol accrues interest using the previous rate for past time and applies the new rate solely to future intervals, preserving fairness and aligning with user expectations of how interest changes work.

title: Vault multihop swaps for any token pair will
description: The Unstoppable SwapRouter’s add_path() function stores the same swap path for swapping from "token1" to "token2" and from "token2" to "token1". If the swap path starts with the token1 address, swaps from token2 to token1 will fail, and vice versa. The administrator must call SwapRouter add_path() to add support for swaps that use multiple Uniswap pools (multihop swaps). The path provided is a sequence of token addresses and pool fee amounts. The path is stored in the self.paths hashmap using the provided token1 and token2 addresses as the keys. The path is stored twice, once for each ordering of those keys such that the stored path can be accessed easily without sorting the keys. When a path stored in the Unstoppable Vault is used for a swap, it is obtained by indexing the hashmap first with the address of the input token for the swap: path: Bytes[66] = self.paths[_token_in][_token_out]. But, because of the logic in add_path() described above, the first address in the obtained path could be either _token_in or _token_out. In the case that it is _token_out, the swap will fail as described below. The stored path is passed along for use by the Uniswap V3 SwapRouter which assumes that the first 2 addresses in the path define the first pool to use. The SwapRouter uses Path.decodeFirstPool() to extract the first address, and it is the first return value thus interpreted as tokenIn for the swap: (address tokenIn, address tokenOut, uint24 fee) = data.path.decodeFirstPool(); In the case that the first token address in the path is actually the intended output token for this swap, the Uniswap V3 SwapRouter will attempt to transfer the input amount of the output token and fail because it does not have any allowance to access the Unstoppable SwapRouter contract's balance of the output token. The planned margin trading functionality will not work as intended when multihop swaps are required between the margin/debt token and the position token. Since such swaps will work in one direction but fail in the other, traders would either be unable to obtain the desired position or, in the worst case, be unable to exit the also be unable to force exit of over-leveraged positions.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the Unstoppable SwapRouter stores and retrieves multihop swap paths for a pair of tokens. When an administrator calls add_path() the function receives a byte‑encoded path that lists token addresses and pool fees, and it stores this exact byte sequence in a two‑dimensional hashmap using the two token addresses as keys. To make look‑ups convenient the implementation writes the same path twice, once under the key order (token1, token2) and once under (token2, token1). The critical mistake is that the stored byte sequence is not reordered to match the direction of the lookup. Consequently, when a swap is requested in the opposite direction of the originally added path, the router fetches a path whose first address is the intended output token rather than the input token. The Uniswap V3 SwapRouter interprets the first two addresses of the path as the first pool’s tokenIn and tokenOut, so it attempts to pull the output token from the contract’s balance. Because the contract holds no allowance for that token, the transfer fails and the whole swap reverts. This problem only appears for multihop swaps (paths longer than a single pool) because single‑hop swaps happen to work regardless of the ordering. The impact is that users trying to trade in one direction can open a position, but the reverse trade – which is required for closing or liquidating a leveraged position – will fail, potentially locking funds and preventing forced exits of over‑leveraged positions. The issue is triggered whenever a multihop path is added via add_path() and later used for the reverse token pair, i.e., when the first address in the stored path does not equal the token supplied as _token_in. Affected parties include any trader using the margin‑trading feature, the vault that holds users’ collateral, and ultimately the protocol’s liquidity and reputation. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the SwapRouter’s add_path logic, where the auditor noticed that the same raw path was stored for both key orders without adjusting its orientation. It can be hard to notice because successful one‑way swaps give the impression that the router works correctly, and the failure manifests only as a generic revert with an allowance error, offering little insight into the underlying cause. To remediate, the add_path function should derive the token pair directly from the supplied path, store a correctly ordered version for the forward direction, and additionally store a reversed copy for the opposite direction, ensuring that the first address always matches the input token of the lookup. Comprehensive tests for both directions of multihop swaps should be added to prevent regression. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a transaction that reverts with a message such as “transfer amount exceeds allowance” while the expected token balance remains unchanged, leading to confusion because the user expected a successful swap or a refund of their position but receives nothing.

title: MarginDex::execute_limit_orderwill always re-
description: All calls to the MarginDex's execute_limit_order will always revert due the limit order being cleared in storage ahead of a call to remove_limit_order. The execute_limit_order function includes the following logic... The limit order is being set to empty(LimitOrder) in storage. Then a call to self._remove_limit_order is called for the same _uid. remove_limit_order has the following logic... The newly-empty order is read from storage, and it's associated account is used fetch the limit_order_uids. The issue is that this account is the zero address, which is the default value after the order was cleared in the preceding function. This will cause the uids array to be empty, and the loop will revert when i == len(uids) - 1. This means that all calls to execute_limit_order will revert, and no limit orders can be executed, which is a major piece of functionality for the protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the limit‑order execution path of the MarginDex contract. When a user invokes execute_limit_order, the function first overwrites the stored LimitOrder struct with an empty value. Immediately afterwards it calls an internal helper _remove_limit_order passing the same order identifier. The removal routine reads the now‑cleared order from storage to obtain the associated account address, which is then used to look up the list of order identifiers (limit_order_uids) belonging to that account. Because the order was cleared, the account field contains the default zero address. Consequently the lookup returns an empty uid array and the subsequent loop attempts to access an element at index i == len(uids)‑1, triggering a revert. This sequence means that every call to execute_limit_order reverts, effectively preventing any limit order from being executed. The root cause is the premature clearing of the order before the removal logic can retrieve the correct account information, a classic case of improper state mutation order leading to a denial‑of‑service condition. The impact is that users with pending limit orders see their orders remain in a pending state indefinitely, funds may be locked, and the protocol loses a core trading capability. The issue manifests whenever a limit order exists and execute_limit_order is called, regardless of the caller’s role. It affects all participants who rely on limit‑order execution, including traders and liquidity providers. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit of the contract’s order‑management functions, where the revert pattern was observed but the underlying storage mutation order was not immediately obvious. The problem can be hard to notice because the revert does not expose a clear error message; it simply aborts the transaction, making it appear as a generic failure. To remediate, the contract should avoid clearing the order before invoking the removal routine; instead it should first retrieve the necessary account information, perform the uid list cleanup, and only then delete or zero‑out the order entry. This adjustment restores the correct logical flow, ensures that the account address is valid when accessed, and prevents the unintended revert, thereby re‑enabling limit‑order execution and preserving protocol functionality.

title: Users trying to reduce their positions with
description: Reducing the users' positions with market orders will always revert due to a wrong value assigned to the min_amount_out variable when swapping part of the funds out. In the Vault contract, there is the reduce_position function, which is called by the users to reduce their positions. When the function is called, the min_amount_out variable used by UniswapV3 as a slippage protection is calculated with the following code: When the function receives a min_amount_out equal to 0, it means the user wants to reduce the position with a market order (for example, to reduce it right now). But in that case, some slippage is calculated to bring some protection to the swap. That protection is calculated with the function _market_order_min_amount_out which basically does the following: The important part (for us) in that code is the call to _quote_token_to_token, which basically queries the price relation of both tokens and multiply it by the _amount_in var. But... if we check the original function (the one I wrote at the beginning of this section), the value passed as _amount_in to _market_order_min_amount_out is the position_amount value instead of the amount of the position to be reduced (contained in the var _reduce_by_amount). And since in the _swap function we are swapping only the _reduce_by_amount amount and position_amount is always greater than _reduce_by_amount, the _min_amount_out value that we send in the _swap function will be always greater than the greatest amount out we could receive, making the _swap function to always revert thus making the reduce_position to revert also. Users won't be able to reduce their positions using market orders, potentially making them to lose funds due to not being able to reduce their positions in the right moment (since they should use non-market orders, which may not be right thing for their situation).
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Vault contract’s reduce_position function, which allows a user to shrink an existing leveraged position. When a caller supplies a min_amount_out of zero, the function interprets this as a request for a market order – i.e., the user wants the contract to swap the specified portion of the position immediately without specifying a price limit. To protect the user from excessive slippage, the contract calls an internal helper _market_order_min_amount_out that computes a minimum acceptable output amount based on the amount of input tokens that will be swapped. However, the implementation mistakenly passes the total position size (position_amount) to this helper instead of the actual amount that the user intends to reduce (_reduce_by_amount). Because the swap routine later only exchanges the smaller _reduce_by_amount, the calculated min_amount_out is artificially inflated – it is larger than any realistic amount that could be received from the trade. When the swap is executed, the UniswapV3 router checks that the actual output meets or exceeds the supplied min_amount_out; the condition fails and the router reverts the transaction. Consequently, the outer reduce_position call also reverts, preventing the user from executing a market‑order reduction at all. This bug manifests whenever a user attempts a market‑order reduction (min_amount_out == 0) and the reduction amount is less than the total position, which is the normal case. Affected parties include any holder of a position in the Vault, the protocol that relies on timely position adjustments, and ultimately the funds that may become locked because users cannot exit or downsize their exposure when market conditions demand it. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher identified as Sherlock, who traced the flow of variables and observed that the swap always reverted under the described conditions. The problem is subtle because the function signature and external behavior appear correct – the contract accepts a market order flag – yet the internal slippage calculation uses the wrong variable, leading to a silent failure that only surfaces as a transaction revert. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a “reduce position” action that instantly fails, with no tokens transferred and possibly an error message like “transaction reverted”. Users expect their position to shrink and their collateral to be returned, but instead they receive nothing and may be forced to place a limit order, which could be unsuitable in volatile markets. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect parameter usage in slippage protection calculations”, a common source of unintended reverts in DeFi swap integrations. To remediate, the contract should compute the minimum output amount based on the exact amount being swapped (_reduce_by_amount) or adjust the slippage logic to reference the correct variable. In conceptual terms, the fix is to align the slippage protection input with the actual trade size, ensuring that the min_amount_out never exceeds the maximum possible output, thereby allowing market‑order reductions to succeed without violating the router’s safety checks.

title: Blocklisted address can be used to lock the
description: Blocklisted address can be used to lock the option token minter's fund. When deploy a token via the teller contract, the contract validate that receiver address is not address(0). However, a malicious option token creator can set a seemingly favorable strike price and pick a blocklisted address and set the blocklisted address as receiver. https://github.com/d-xo/weird-erc20#tokens-with-blocklists. Some tokens (e.g. USDC, USDT) have a contract level admin controlled address blocklist. If an address is blocked, then transfers to and from that address are forbidden. Malicious or compromised token owners can trap funds in a contract by adding the contract address to the blocklist. This could potentially be the result of regulatory action against the contract itself, against a single user of the contract (e.g. a Uniswap LP), or could also be a part of an extortion attempt against users of the blocked contract. Then user would see the favorable strike price and mint the option token using payout token for call option or use quote token for put option. However, they can never exercise their option because the transaction would revert when transferring asset to the receiver for call option and transferring asset to the receiver for put option when exercising the option. The user's fund that used to mint the option are locked. Blocklisted receiver address can be used to lock the option token minter's fund.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a blocklist‑related logic flaw that allows a malicious option token creator to lock the funds of users who mint option tokens. When the teller contract deploys a new option token it only verifies that the receiver address is not the zero address, but it does not check whether the receiver is on a contract‑level blocklist that some stablecoins and other tokens maintain. An attacker can therefore choose a strike price that looks attractive and set the receiver to an address that is already blocklisted (or later add the newly created option contract address to the blocklist). When a user later tries to exercise the option, the underlying token transfer to the receiver is rejected because the token contract enforces a blocklist rule that forbids any transfer to or from a blocked address. The transaction reverts, the option cannot be exercised, and the assets that were supplied as collateral during minting remain permanently locked in the option contract. This situation can arise under several conditions: the token used for payout or quote is a blocklist‑enabled token (e.g., USDC, USDT), the blocklist is managed by an admin who can add arbitrary addresses, or a regulator or extortionist forces the addition of the option contract to the blocklist. The affected parties are the option token minters, any users of the protocol who rely on exercising their options, and the protocol itself because locked funds reduce liquidity and trust. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the teller’s receiver validation logic with the known blocklist behavior of certain ERC‑20 tokens. It is difficult to notice because the contract appears to accept any non‑zero address, and the blocklist enforcement happens inside the external token contract, not in the teller code, so a superficial test may not reveal the transfer failure until an exercise attempt is made. The impact is a loss of user funds, potential regulatory freeze, and a vector for extortion, as users see a favorable strike price, mint the option, and later find that their balance becomes zero when trying to exercise. To remediate, the deployment flow should include a check that the receiver address is not present on the token’s blocklist, and the protocol should consider adding an expiry mechanism that allows the minter to burn the option token and reclaim the collateral if the receiver never becomes reachable. Conceptually, the fix is to enforce business‑logic constraints that the receiver must be a valid, non‑blocked address and to provide a fallback recovery path for locked collateral, thereby eliminating the blocklist‑induced lockup scenario.

title: Loss of option token from Teller and reward
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a loss of both the option token held in the Teller contract and the associated reward token from the OTLM contract when the option reaches its expiry while the underlying layer‑2 (L2) sequencer is unavailable. The contract enforces expiry by comparing the current block timestamp with the stored expiry value and, if the timestamp is greater or equal, it reverts any attempt to exercise the option. Likewise, the reward‑claiming function checks the same condition and returns zero when the option has expired. Because L2 networks such as Arbitrum and Optimism rely on a sequencer to produce new blocks, a sequencer outage halts block production and therefore prevents users from submitting a transaction before the on‑chain expiry moment. When the sequencer is down at the exact time the option would otherwise be exercised, the user cannot send the exercise transaction, the contract treats the option as expired, and the reward function yields zero. From the user’s perspective the option token becomes worthless and the expected reward balance remains unchanged or is reported as zero, contrary to the expectation that the token can be exercised and the reward claimed. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the expiry checks and cross‑referenced known sequencer downtimes on Optimism Bedrock and Arbitrum, highlighting that the protocol’s business logic assumes continuous L2 availability. The problem is subtle because the contract code itself is correct; the failure mode emerges only from external infrastructure downtime, making it easy to overlook during testing. The impact is a loss of funds for option holders and liquidity providers, undermining the incentive model of the OTLM reward system. The affected parties include any user who holds an option token on the Teller contract, the protocol that issues rewards, and ultimately the overall trust in the system. To mitigate the issue, the protocol should incorporate an external sequencer‑up‑time feed, such as Chainlink’s L2 sequencer data, and introduce a grace period that extends the exercise window or allows reward claims when the sequencer is reported as down. This change would decouple the expiry logic from the immediate availability of block production and preserve user funds during temporary L2 outages.

title: Use A's staked token balance can be used to
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting mix‑up that occurs when the token used for staking (the stake token) is the same ERC‑20 token that is later used as the payout token for option‑token rewards. Because the contract does not keep separate balances for staked tokens and for payout tokens, the reward‑minting routine draws directly from the pool that also holds users’ staked deposits. In practice, a user who has staked, for example, 100 USDC can later see part of that 100 USDC deducted when another user’s reward is minted, because the contract treats the whole USDC balance as available for both purposes. The root cause is a missing check that the stake token and the payout token are distinct, combined with a single accounting variable (totalBalance) that aggregates both kinds of funds. An attacker does not need to perform any special call; simply claiming a legitimate reward when the pool contains insufficient free USDC will cause the contract to consume a portion of another user’s stake to satisfy the minting operation. After the pool is depleted in this way, any subsequent call to the emergencyUnstakeAll function reverts due to an insufficient token balance, preventing the affected user from withdrawing their original stake. From the user’s point of view the expected behavior – “I stake 100 USDC and later I can withdraw the same 100 USDC (plus any earned rewards)” – is violated; instead the UI may show a successful reward claim but later the withdrawal transaction fails, leaving the user’s balance unchanged or showing a zero‑return. The impact is that funds can become permanently locked for users who stake a token that also serves as the payout token, effectively causing a loss of the staked capital. This issue was discovered during a manual audit of the OTLM contract logic, where the auditor observed that the same token address could be supplied for both roles and that the contract never distinguishes the two balances. The bug is subtle because the token contract reports a single total balance, making it easy to assume that the pool always has enough liquidity for both staking and rewards. To remediate, the protocol should either enforce that the stake token and the payout token are different assets, or introduce separate accounting structures that track staked balances and reward‑payout balances independently, ensuring that reward minting never draws from users’ locked stakes. Conceptually, this is a classic “double‑spending of accounting pool” or “shared‑resource accounting” flaw, where a single pool is used for two mutually exclusive purposes without proper isolation, leading to unintended depletion of user funds.

title: IERC20(token).approve revert if the underly-
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s use of the standard IERC20 approve function to set an allowance for a payout token. The code assumes that every ERC20 token complies with the original specification by returning a boolean value from approve. However, several widely‑deployed tokens, most notably USDT, deviate from the spec and do not return any value. The protocol’s ERC20 wrapper (solmate) checks the return data and expects a boolean; when the token omits the return, the wrapper interprets the missing data as a failure and triggers a revert. This mismatch causes any transaction that attempts to call approve on a non‑standard token to fail, while other token operations such as safeTransfer and safeTransferFrom continue to work because they use safe wrappers that do not rely on a return value. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors attempted to approve USDT as a payout token and observed an unexpected revert. It is difficult to notice in normal testing because most test suites use well‑behaved tokens that return a boolean, masking the problem until a non‑standard token is introduced. When the revert occurs, the contract cannot set the allowance needed for subsequent transfers, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition: users expect to receive a payout but the transaction reverts and no funds are moved, effectively making the payout token unsupported. The impact is limited to the inability to use certain ERC20 tokens as payout assets, which can break business logic that assumes any ERC20 token can be approved. The affected parties include protocol operators who may list unsupported tokens, users awaiting payouts, and any downstream contracts that rely on the allowance being set. To remediate the issue, the contract should replace direct calls to approve with a safeApprove pattern that does not require a boolean return, or otherwise handle tokens that do not follow the original ERC20 specification. By using a safe wrapper, the contract can gracefully handle both standard and non‑standard tokens, ensuring that allowance setting succeeds or fails in a controlled manner without reverting the entire transaction.

title: Division before multiplication result in loss of
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic precision loss caused by performing a division before a multiplication when calculating per‑token rewards. In the reward‑per‑token function the contract first computes rewardsToApply as ((block.timestamp‑lastRewardUpdate)*rewardRate)/REWARD_PERIOD, which uses integer division. When the elapsed time since the last update is small – for example a few seconds – and the reward period is fixed to one day, the product of elapsed time and rewardRate is often smaller than REWARD_PERIOD, so the division truncates to zero. The subsequent multiplication by the token’s decimal scaling factor cannot recover the lost value, and the final addition to rewardsPerTokenStored adds zero. This problem is amplified for tokens with low decimal precision (e.g., USDC with 6 decimals or Gemini USD with 2 decimals) because the scaling factor (10**stakedTokenDecimals) is small, making the overall reward amount even smaller. As a result, users who expect to earn a proportional reward may receive no additional tokens; their balance appears unchanged after an update, effectively causing “funds disappear” from the user’s perspective. The issue occurs whenever the reward update function is called frequently with short time intervals, which can happen naturally in a high‑frequency staking environment or be induced by an attacker who repeatedly triggers the update to keep the calculated reward at zero. The affected parties are stakers, the protocol’s reward distribution logic, and any downstream applications that rely on accurate accounting of earned rewards. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward calculation formula and identified the order of operations as a source of truncation error. It can be hard to notice because the loss may be small for a single update and only becomes evident over many updates or when using low‑decimal tokens, where the expected reward is already modest. Conceptually, the fix is to avoid division before multiplication: compute the product of rewardsToApply and the decimal scaling factor first, then perform a single division by totalBalance, or use a fixed‑point arithmetic library that preserves precision throughout the calculation. By reordering the arithmetic or increasing the intermediate precision, the contract will correctly accrue rewards even for short elapsed intervals and low‑decimal tokens, aligning the actual behavior with the intended business logic of proportional reward distribution.

title: Debt is not updated when removing margin
description: Debt is not updated when removing margin from a position. Traders are allowed to remove margin/collateral from their positions: vy#L528-L546. As you can see, the position can only have collateral removed if it is not liquidable: vy#L487. The problem is that the total_debt_shares[_debt_token] is not updated when checking whether the position is liquidable nor when calling remove_margin. You can see on the following links the progression of the function calls to calculate whether a position is liquidable or not: vy#L444 vy#L1142 vy#L1099 vy#L1111 vy#L1117C16-L1117C16. As seen, total_debt_shares[_debt_token] is not updated to the current total_debt_shares[_debt_token] by calling _update_debt and therefore a stale total_debt_shares[_debt_token] is used to calculate whether a position is liquidable. Allowing positions that are in fact liquidable remove margin because the debt is not updated. Not updating the debt before removing collateral (margin) from your position does allow a trader to remove collateral from a liquidable position.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a stale‑debt calculation that occurs when a trader removes margin (collateral) from an existing position. The contract checks whether a position is liquidable before allowing margin removal, but it bases this check on the global variable total_debt_shares for the debt token. Because the function removeMargin does not invoke the internal routine _update_debt, the value of total_debt_shares may be outdated – it does not reflect debt that has accrued in other positions since the last update. Consequently, the liquidation test uses a stale, lower debt figure, incorrectly concluding that the position is safe. An attacker can therefore call removeMargin on a position that is actually under‑collateralised, withdraw collateral that should remain locked, and leave the protocol with insufficient backing for the outstanding debt. The impact is a potential loss of funds for lenders and a breach of the protocol’s accounting invariants: the total collateral no longer covers the total debt, breaking the core guarantee of solvency. This condition appears only when debt shares have changed elsewhere (for example, after other users borrow or repay) and the victim’s position has not been refreshed. The affected parties include any trader who holds a position, the protocol’s liquidity pool, and downstream users who rely on the protocol’s safety. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the margin‑removal workflow, where the auditor traced the call chain from the liquidability check through the debt‑share calculations and noticed that _update_debt was never called. The bug is subtle because the function does perform a liquidability check, giving the impression that the safety guard is active, yet the underlying data is stale, making the check unreliable. To remediate, the contract should refresh the debt accounting at the start of the removeMargin function – typically by invoking _update_debt – or otherwise ensure that total_debt_shares reflects the current state before any liquidation or margin‑removal logic is executed. This aligns the implementation with the intended accounting model, preventing users from withdrawing collateral from positions that are truly liquidable and preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: FixedStrikeOptionTeller: create can be invoked
description:
block.timestamp == expiry but these option tokens cannot be exercised even in the same transaction. The create function has this statement:
```solidity
if (uint256(expiry) < block.timestamp) revert Teller_OptionExpired(expiry);
```
The exercise function has this statement:
```solidity
if (uint48(block.timestamp) >= expiry) revert Teller_OptionExpired(expiry);
```
Notice the >= operator which means when block.timestamp == expiry the exercise function reverts. So if a user claims his rewards using OTLM.claimRewards or OTLM.claimNextEpochRewards when block.timestamp == expiry, he receives the freshly minted option tokens but he cannot exercise these option tokens even in the same transaction (or same block). Moreover, since the receiver does not possess these freshly minted option tokens, he cannot reclaim them either (assuming reclaim function contains the currently missing optionToken.burn statement). Option token will be minted to user but he cannot exercise them. Receiver cannot reclaim them as he doesn't hold that token amount. This leads to loss of funds as the minted option tokens become useless. Also the scenario of users claiming at expiry is not rare.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a timestamp boundary inconsistency between the token creation (mint) path and the token exercise (redeem) path in the FixedStrikeOptionTeller contract. When a user calls the claim function at the exact moment when block.timestamp equals the option expiry, the create logic checks that expiry is not in the past using a strict less‑than comparison (if expiry < block.timestamp revert). Because the equality case passes, the contract mints fresh option tokens to the caller. However, the exercise function validates the same expiry with a greater‑than‑or‑equal comparison (if block.timestamp >= expiry revert). Consequently, when block.timestamp is exactly equal to expiry, any attempt to exercise the newly minted tokens in the same transaction or block reverts. The user ends up holding option tokens that cannot be exercised, and because the reclaim function (which would normally burn the tokens) does not include a burn step for this edge case, the tokens cannot be reclaimed either. This results in a loss of value: the user receives tokens but cannot realize the underlying payoff, effectively making the minted tokens useless. The issue manifests whenever a user claims rewards at the expiry timestamp, a situation that is not rare in practice because users often trigger claims at the end of an epoch. It was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s reward‑claiming and exercise flows, where the auditor noticed the mismatched comparison operators. The bug is subtle because both checks appear correct in isolation; only when the two functions are exercised together at the boundary does the problem surface, making it easy to miss in standard testing that does not target the exact expiry moment. The vulnerability belongs to the class of off‑by‑one or boundary‑condition errors that violate the business logic assumption that minted options are immediately exercisable. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that the claim succeeded and the option balance increased, yet any subsequent attempt to exercise those options returns a transaction revert, leaving the balance unchanged and the expected payout missing. To remediate, the contract should enforce a consistent timestamp rule: either forbid minting at expiry (use <= in the create check) or allow exercising at expiry (use > in the exercise check). Adding a burn step in the reclaim path for tokens minted at expiry would also prevent them from becoming permanently locked.

title: stake() missing set lastEpochClaimed when
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the staking function does not initialise the per‑user lastEpochClaimed variable when a user stakes for the first time (i.e., when their previous stake balance is zero). Because lastEpochClaimed remains at its default value (zero), the internal _claimRewards routine treats the user as having unclaimed rewards for every epoch from 0 up to the current epoch. When the user later calls stake again or tries to claim rewards, the contract iterates over a potentially very large range of epochs, consuming a linear amount of gas. As the protocol progresses and the epoch counter grows, the loop can exceed the block gas limit, causing the transaction to revert with an out‑of‑gas error. This prevents new stakers from successfully staking or claiming rewards, effectively locking their funds and breaking the expected accounting that rewards are claimed only for epochs that have not yet been settled. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the staking contract where the code path for a zero‑balance user was examined and the missing assignment to lastEpochClaimed was identified. The bug is subtle because the stake function appears to update rewardsPerTokenClaimed correctly, so the omission does not raise a compiler warning and only manifests after many epochs have elapsed. From a user’s point of view the UI may show a normal staking transaction but the transaction fails with a high gas consumption or an out‑of‑gas error, and the user may see that no rewards are received even though they have been staking for a long time. The problem belongs to the class of “state‑initialisation” or “missing bookkeeping” bugs that break accounting invariants. The recommended fix is to set lastEpochClaimed[msg.sender] to the current epoch when a user with zero balance stakes for the first time, thereby aligning the stored epoch marker with the rewards per token snapshot and preventing the unnecessary loop. After the fix, new stakers will start with lastEpochClaimed equal to the current epoch, so future reward claims will only iterate over epochs that actually have unclaimed rewards, keeping gas usage bounded and preserving protocol safety.

title: claimRewards() If a rewards is too small, it
bug_full: The contract calculates a user’s epoch reward by multiplying the difference between the cumulative rewards per token at the end of the epoch and the amount already claimed, then multiplying by the user’s stake balance and finally dividing by 10 raised to the number of decimals of the staked token. Because Solidity uses integer division, when the numerator is smaller than the denominator the result is rounded down to zero. Some ERC20‑like payout tokens reject a transfer of exactly zero tokens and revert the transaction. Consequently, when the computed reward for a particular epoch is zero, the call to payoutToken.approve followed by optionTeller.create triggers a revert, preventing the claimRewards() function from completing. The revert not only blocks the current claim but also stops any later epoch claims because the contract’s state remains unchanged and the option teller never receives the expected reward amount. Users therefore see no tokens credited for the epoch, may receive an error message, and are unable to claim future rewards, effectively freezing their accrued earnings. The issue appears only when the reward amount is very small – for example, when rewardsPerTokenEnd is only marginally higher than userRewardsClaimed – a situation that can arise in later epochs as the reward pool diminishes or when a user’s stake is tiny relative to the token’s decimal precision. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined the reward‑distribution logic and noticed the assumption that a zero‑value transfer would be a no‑op. It is subtle because a zero reward seems harmless, yet the token’s strict transfer implementation causes a hard failure that can be missed in basic testing. To remediate, the contract should detect a zero reward before attempting any token interaction and simply return without performing an approve or create call, or it should adjust the reward formula to avoid rounding to zero, or ensure that the payout token used supports zero‑value transfers. This change restores the ability of users to claim subsequent epochs and prevents the protocol from becoming stuck due to a single negligible reward calculation.

title: Funds can be stolen from the FixedStrikeOptionTeller
bug_full: The vulnerability is an integer‑division rounding error in the collateral calculation for put options. When the contract computes the required quote‑token collateral as (amount * strikePrice) / 10**payoutTokenDecimals, the product amount * strikePrice can be smaller than the denominator if the payout token has many decimals or the amount is low. Because Solidity uses integer division, the result is truncated toward zero, yielding a requiredCollateral value of zero. The contract then attempts to transfer zero quote tokens from the caller, succeeds silently, and mints the requested amount of option tokens. An attacker can repeatedly call the create function with such parameters, minting an arbitrary number of put‑option tokens without providing any collateral. After the options expire, the attacker can call reclaim and receive the quote‑token collateral that was originally supplied by honest users who created options with proper collateral. This leads to under‑collateralized options, loss of user funds, and potential draining of the protocol’s quote‑token reserves. The issue occurs whenever amount * strikePrice < 10**payoutTokenDecimals, which is common for tokens with high decimal precision (e.g., 18‑decimal payout tokens) combined with modest strike prices. Any address can act as the malicious receiver, so all participants in the option market are at risk. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, where the logical flow of the create function was examined and the edge case of integer division was identified. It is hard to notice because the code path appears to enforce a transfer of the exact collateral amount, yet the zero‑value transfer passes the balance‑difference check without raising an error. To remediate, the contract should enforce a non‑zero collateral requirement, use ceiling division or a safe‑math library that rounds up, and add explicit validation that requiredCollateral > 0 before proceeding. Additionally, the calculation could be performed with higher precision or by checking that amount * strikePrice does not overflow the denominator, thereby preventing free minting of options and preserving the economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: optionTokens can be expired even though the
description: epoch is not over. When deploying an optionToken the parameter expiry is rounded down to the “nearest day at 0000 UTC” but since the end of an epoch is calculated by the epochDuration and the exact time the epoch has started and the optionToken was created, this can lead to an epoch still being active but the corresponding optionToken to be already expired. When starting a new epoch, the variable epochStart is set to the current time (block.timestamp) and the end of the epoch is calculated by adding the epochDuration to the epochStart variable. The optionToken of the new epoch is deployed with the parameter expire calculated based on the current time stamp, the timeUntilEligible and the eligibleDuration. (uint48(block.timestamp) + timeUntilEligible + eligibleDuration). However, the actual expiry is set to the “nearest day at 0000 UTC” before the token is deployed. Since the epochDuration can be as close as 1 second to the sum of timeUntilEligible + eligibleDuration, this can lead to an epoch still being active but its optionToken to be already expired. Example: epochDuration = 7 days, timeUntilEligible = 0, eligibleDuration = 7 days + 12 hours. New epoch is launched on the 01.01.2024 at 11:45 am. => epochStart = block.timestamp = 01.01.2024 at 11:45 am, epochEnd = epochStart + epochDuration = 08.01.2024 at 11:45 am. Initial expire = block.timestamp + timeUntilEligible + eligibleDuration = 08.01.2024 at 11:45 pm, but expiry is rounded down to 08.01.2024 at 00:00 am, so option has already expired. Users that wait until the epoch has ended to claim their rewards expecting the options to be exercisable for 12 hours after the epoch end cannot claim their options since they are expired already and lose out on all the value the options would have had, which can be significant depending on the current price of the payoutToken.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a time‑rounding error that can cause an option token to be considered expired before the associated epoch has finished. When a new epoch is started the contract records the current block.timestamp as epochStart and computes epochEnd by adding the configured epochDuration. At the same time the option token for that epoch is deployed with an intended expiry equal to block.timestamp plus timeUntilEligible plus eligibleDuration. Before the token is created the contract rounds this expiry down to the nearest midnight UTC (00:00) of the same day. If the sum of timeUntilEligible and eligibleDuration is close to the epochDuration, the rounding down can move the expiry timestamp earlier than epochEnd. Consequently the option token is marked expired while the epoch is still active. Users who wait until the epoch ends – expecting the option to be exercisable for the additional eligible period – find that the contract rejects their claim because the token is already expired. From the user’s perspective the UI shows the option as available, they attempt to claim after the epoch, but receive no payout and their balance remains unchanged, contrary to the expectation that a reward should be received. The impact is a loss of potential value for token holders; the options become unusable and the associated payout value is forfeited. The bug occurs only under specific timing conditions, namely when epochDuration is less than or equal to the sum of timeUntilEligible and eligibleDuration and the rounding operation truncates the expiry to the start of the day. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between epoch timing logic and expiry calculation. The issue is subtle because rounding timestamps to a day boundary is a common practice and may appear harmless, yet it creates an off‑by‑one‑day (or hour) discrepancy that violates the protocol’s business rule that options remain exercisable for the full eligibleDuration after the epoch. The class of bug is a date‑truncation or rounding‑down error in time‑sensitive smart contracts. To remediate the problem the expiry calculation should be rounded up to the next midnight UTC, or the contract should avoid rounding altogether and enforce that the expiry is always later than epochEnd, thereby preserving the intended exercisable window and preventing users from losing their rewards.

title: Owners will incur loss and bad debt if the
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic incentive flaw in the limit‑order fulfillment flow. The contract allows the order owner to pay the gas required to execute a swap and then expects each user to reimburse the owner by sending a fee when they later call claimOrder to retrieve the swapped tokens. Because the fee is collected only at claim time, the owner bears the upfront gas cost. If the market price of the swapped token collapses, the token value becomes lower than the fee that the user would have to pay, so rational users simply abandon the order and never call claimOrder. The code in claimOrder correctly handles refunds of excess ETH or wrapped native tokens, but it does not enforce any pre‑payment or collateral, so the owner cannot recover the gas already spent. This situation can be exploited by anyone holding an order: after the price crash they can do nothing, and the owner’s gas expense remains unreimbursed, creating bad debt. The impact is financial loss for the order owner, potentially eroding trust in the protocol if many orders remain unclaimed. The condition occurs when token prices drop sharply after the order is filled, making the fee per user higher than the token’s residual value. The affected parties are the order owners who fund the execution and any protocol participants relying on the fee model for sustainability. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the economic model rather than a code‑level flaw; it is subtle because the function appears to handle fee transfers correctly, masking the underlying incentive misalignment. Detecting the problem requires looking at the flow of funds over time, not just at individual transactions, which is why it may be missed in standard testing. The recommended mitigation is to collect the fee in advance—either by requiring users to deposit an estimated gas fee before the order is fulfilled or by using a collateral mechanism—so that the owner is guaranteed reimbursement, and any excess can be refunded after the claim. In broader terms, this is a class of ‘fee‑prepayment’ or ‘economic‑incentive’ vulnerability where the party that bears execution cost does not have a reliable mechanism to recover it, leading to loss of funds when participants can opt out after execution.

title: Owner unable to collect fulfillment fee from
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic rounding error that can cause the claimOrder function to attempt to transfer a zero amount of the output token. The function calculates each user’s share of the total output using integer division: owed = (totalTokenOut * depositAmount) / totalTokenDeposited. Because Solidity discards any fractional part, a user who contributes a very small amount relative to the batch total may receive an owed value of zero, especially when the two tokens have different decimal precisions (for example, SHIB with 18 decimals and USDC with 6 decimals). When the calculated owed amount is zero, the subsequent call to tokenOut.safeTransfer(user, owed) tries to transfer 0 tokens. Some ERC‑20 implementations reject zero‑value transfers and revert the transaction. The revert prevents the user from successfully calling claimOrder, which in turn blocks the contract owner from collecting the fulfillment fee that is normally taken from the user’s claim. This situation occurs under conditions where the batch contains a large total deposit, the user’s deposit is tiny, and the output token has lower precision, causing the division to truncate to zero. The affected parties are small traders who receive no payout, the protocol owner who loses the expected fee, and potentially the overall protocol if many such reverts cause a denial‑of‑service condition. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic of the fee distribution logic. It can be hard to notice because the formula appears mathematically correct, yet the integer division semantics are subtle and the zero‑transfer edge case is not always tested. The bug belongs to the class of “rounding‑to‑zero” or “integer‑division truncation” errors that violate accounting assumptions that each participant receives a non‑zero share proportional to their contribution. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful claim request but then either display an error message or simply not credit any tokens, contradicting the expectation that a claim always yields a positive amount. To remediate, the contract should guard against zero transfers by checking that owed > 0 before invoking safeTransfer, or by using a rounding‑up strategy or a minimum‑payout threshold that ensures a non‑zero amount is transferred when possible.

title: getGasPrice() doesn't check Arbitrum l2
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a gas‑price oracle function that reads a Chainlink fast gas price feed on an Arbitrum L2 network but fails to verify the status of the L2 sequencer before using the value. The root cause is the omission of a check against the dedicated sequencer‑uptime feed that Chainlink provides for L2 environments. Because the function only validates that the timestamp of the price data is recent, it can still accept a price that is technically fresh yet originates from a feed that is considered unreliable when the sequencer is down. An attacker who can cause the Arbitrum sequencer to stop or who can manipulate the feed during a sequencer outage can therefore supply a falsified gas price. By calling getGasPrice, the contract may return this manipulated price instead of the safe owner‑defined fallback, allowing the attacker to under‑pay for gas‑related operations or to cause other contracts that rely on the price to behave incorrectly. The impact includes potential economic advantage for the attacker, incorrect accounting of gas costs, and possible loss of funds for users who trust the returned price. The condition under which the bug manifests is any period when the Arbitrum sequencer is offline or its status feed reports a failure; during such periods the fastGasFeed may still return a value that passes the stale‑timestamp check, leading the function to use it. All participants that depend on the gas price – including end‑users, contract owners, and the broader protocol – are affected because they receive a price that does not reflect the true network state. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s oracle integration, where the auditor noted the absence of a sequencer‑status verification step that is recommended by Chainlink documentation for L2 feeds. The bug can be subtle because the timestamp check alone gives the impression that the data is fresh, masking the fact that the underlying L2 environment is not processing transactions. To remediate, the contract should query the sequencer‑uptime feed and reject or fallback to the owner‑set price whenever the sequencer is reported as down, following the example code provided by Chainlink for L2 sequencer feeds. This class of bug falls under missing reliability checks for off‑chain data sources in L2 contexts, where a feed’s freshness does not guarantee its validity when the underlying sequencer is unavailable. From a user perspective, the contract may return a gas price that is unexpectedly low or zero, leading to failed transactions or unexpected costs, contrary to the expectation that the price reflects the current network conditions.

title: User can sandwich pool writeOff and profit
description:
A user can scan the mempool for pool writeoffs and profit by front-running and back-running it.
iFIL's value is based on the ratio of iFIL minted and InfinityPool#totalAssets.
Upon a user write-off, totalBorrowed is decreased, decreasing the pool's totalAssets (and therefore decreasing iFIL's price). A user can be monitoring the mempool and profit off of user write-offs.
Attack scenario
Let's consider there are only 2 equal stakers in InfinityPool. Both of them have 500 iFIL and totalAssets == 2000 (basically iFIL/wFIL ratio is 1:2) A borrower, whose principal was 200 wFIL, has been liquidated and will now be written off. (For simplicity of the example, let's consider no funds were recovered) 1 of the stakers can do the following to make a profit:
1. Scan the mempool for the write-off transaction.
2. When they see the transaction pending, they front-run it, selling all of their stake (leaving only 500 iFIL in circulation and 1000 wFIL in the pool)
3. The write-off transaction executes and it now lowers totalBorrowed by the borrower's principal. This also lowers the pool's totalAssets, making them 1000 - 200 = 800
4. The user can now deposit their 1000 wFIL back and they will be minted ((1000 / 800) * 500) = 625 iFIL
In the end, although the 2 users had equal stakes, the one who didn't take any action is left with 500 iFIL (equal to 800 wFIL) The user who did sandwich the transaction is left with 625 wFIL (equal to 1000 wFIL) The user who performed the sandwich attack not only didn't lose any money (unlike the other user), but will also now earn a bigger % of the fees from InfinityPool, although the initial investment of the 2 users was the same.
A user may profit off from innocent users by performing sandwich attacks.
bug_full: The vulnerabilityis a front‑running / back‑running sandwich attack on the InfinityPool write‑off mechanism. When a borrower is liquidated, the pool executes a write‑off that reduces totalBorrowed and consequently lowers totalAssets, which in turn reduces the iFIL price (iFIL = totalSupply * totalAssets ratio). Because the price is derived from the pool’s totalAssets at the moment of minting, an attacker who monitors the mempool can detect the pending write‑off transaction, front‑run it by selling all of their iFIL stake before the write‑off is processed, and then back‑run by depositing the received wFIL after the write‑off has lowered totalAssets. The attacker’s deposit is minted at a higher iFIL‑per‑wFIL ratio, giving them more iFIL than they would have received without the sandwich. The other honest stakers receive the same amount of iFIL as before, but the value of their iFIL is now a smaller share of the pool’s assets, effectively diluting their position and reducing their future fee earnings. The attack can be carried out whenever a write‑off transaction is pending and the pool does not enforce any ordering protection or deposit lock‑up. It affects any user who holds iFIL in the pool, as well as the protocol’s economic fairness because it allows profit extraction from innocent participants. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the pool’s accounting logic, where the relationship between totalBorrowed, totalAssets, and the iFIL minting formula was examined and found to be manipulable by transaction ordering. The problem is subtle because the price impact is not emitted as an explicit error; the pool’s state appears consistent, yet the relative value of each holder’s iFIL changes silently. To mitigate the issue, the protocol should prevent the attacker from changing its position between the write‑off and the subsequent deposit, for example by locking deposits for a period, applying a fee on deposits or withdrawals that offsets the arbitrage gain, or by redesigning the write‑off accounting to use a time‑weighted average price or a commit‑reveal scheme that removes the ability to front‑run. In short, the bug is a classic sandwich/price‑manipulation vulnerability arising from a mutable price oracle based on instantaneous pool balances.

title: DOS all signatures and verification from agent-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition affecting the credential verification flow of agents in the GLIF system. Agents must present a signed credential that is validated by the modifier _validateAndBurnCred, which calls agentPolice.isValidCredential and then agentPolice.registerCredentialUseBlock. The registerCredentialUseBlock function records the signature as used by storing the hash of the (v,r,s) tuple together with the current block number. The only access control performed is a check that the caller’s agent id matches the credential’s subject field: if (IAgent(msg.sender).id() != sc.vc.subject) revert Unauthorized(). Because there is no verification that msg.sender is an authorized agent address registered in the system, an attacker can deploy a contract that implements the IAgent interface and returns any chosen id. By front‑running a legitimate agent’s transaction, the attacker can call registerCredentialUseBlock with the same v,r,s values extracted from the pending transaction but with the subject set to the attacker‑controlled id. The check passes, the signature is marked as used, and the original agent later finds its credential rejected as already spent. This prevents the agent from executing actions that require a fresh credential, such as repaying debt or borrowing WFIL, effectively putting the agent into a default state. The issue occurs whenever an agent submits a transaction that includes a signed credential and the transaction is observable in the mempool; the attacker must be able to submit a transaction in the same block before the legitimate one. All agents are potentially affected because the flaw is systemic, and the impact is a loss of functionality rather than direct loss of funds, though prolonged denial can lead to financial penalties. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the credential handling logic, where the lack of proper access control on registerCredentialUseBlock was identified as a logical oversight. The bug is hard to notice because the signature validation itself succeeds and the only failure appears later as an “Unauthorized” revert, which may be misinterpreted as a user error. The recommended fix is to enforce that msg.sender is a registered agent, for example by checking the router’s agent registry or by restricting the function to calls originating from the agent contract itself, thereby preventing phantom agents from abusing the credential‑use tracking. In generic terms, this is a privilege‑escalation and replay‑prevention bypass that enables a denial‑of‑service attack on credential‑based operations.

title: SimpleRamp will not burn any excess iFIL it
bug_full: The SimpleRamp contract is designed to eliminate any surplus iFIL tokens that may reside in the contract after a user‑initiated transfer, thereby keeping the internal accounting of iFIL balances consistent. The intended behaviour, as described in the comment, is to burn the total amount of iFIL held by the contract after the transfer, which would include both the newly transferred tokens and any tokens that were already present (the "excess"). However, the implementation calculates the amount to burn as the difference between the contract's current iFIL balance and the balance recorded before the transfer (balanceOfBefore). Because the transfer adds exactly the amount that was just transferred, this difference equals the transferred amount only, leaving any pre‑existing excess untouched. The root cause is an incorrect accounting formula that assumes the contract never held iFIL before the operation, ignoring the possibility of leftover tokens. An attacker or a careless user could deliberately or inadvertently send extra iFIL to the contract; the contract will then burn only the expected amount and retain the surplus. This retained surplus skews the contract’s accounting, potentially allowing the protocol to believe it has burned more iFIL than it actually has, which can lead to mismatched accounting, incorrect fee calculations, or even unauthorized withdrawals if the protocol relies on the burned amount to release funds. The issue manifests whenever the contract holds any iFIL prior to the burn step, such as after a previous operation that left residual tokens, or when a user sends more than the expected amount. It affects all participants that interact with SimpleRamp, including end‑users expecting their excess iFIL to be destroyed, the protocol that depends on accurate accounting for security and economic guarantees, and auditors who rely on the contract’s comments for correctness. The problem was discovered during a manual audit where the comment and the actual code were compared, revealing a mismatch between the intended burn logic and the implemented calculation. Because the contract still performs a burn, there is no immediate revert or error, making the bug subtle and easy to overlook until accounting discrepancies surface in later audits or financial reports. To resolve the issue, the burn call should be changed to destroy the entire iFIL balance held by the contract after the transfer, for example by invoking iFIL.burn(address(this), iFIL.balanceOf(address(this))). This ensures that any excess tokens are removed, restoring the intended invariant that the contract never retains iFIL after processing a request, and thereby preserving correct accounting and protocol safety.

title: when rate will be changed for Pool then users
description: will pay for all previous epochs accrding to new rate When rate will be changed for Pool then users will pay for all previous epochs accrding to new rate When agent borrows funds from pool, then is should pay interests according to the rate. Currently this rate is minimum(gcred 100), but it can be changed and then gcred of account will be changed and rate will be changed. Once it will be done, that means that user should pay for the previous epochs using this new rate. This is incorrect. Another point, which should be considered is that when agent is liquidated, then penalty rate is used. And again user pays with this penalty rate for all previous epochs, where he was not malicious. This is also incorrect. User pays more fees.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting error that causes borrowers and liquidated users to be charged interest or penalty fees for past epochs using a rate that was changed after those epochs occurred. The contract stores a single global rate for the pool and a single penalty rate for liquidations, and it applies these values whenever it calculates accrued fees. When an administrator or governance action updates the pool rate or the liquidation penalty, the contract does not preserve the historical rate that was in effect during earlier epochs. Consequently, the interest calculation for all previous periods is recomputed with the new, higher rate, and the liquidation penalty is retroactively applied to the entire borrowing history instead of only to the epoch in which the liquidation event happened. An attacker who can influence the rate parameters can therefore cause borrowers to over‑pay, extracting additional value from honest users. The impact is that users see higher total interest than expected, balances are reduced more than anticipated, and liquidation penalties appear inflated even when the user behaved correctly. This situation occurs whenever the pool rate or penalty rate is modified after a borrowing position has been opened or after a liquidation has taken place. All participants who have active loans or have been liquidated are affected, including lenders who rely on correct fee accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee‑calculation logic and noticed that the contract references the current rate rather than a snapshot of the rate at the time each epoch was recorded. The bug is subtle because the contract still reports correct fees for the current epoch, so the discrepancy only becomes visible when aggregating totals over multiple epochs, making it easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate the problem, the protocol should store the rate value that was active for each epoch (or each loan) and use that stored snapshot when computing accrued interest. Likewise, the liquidation penalty should be applied only to the epoch in which the liquidation occurs, with the penalty rate captured at that moment. By decoupling historical fee calculations from mutable global parameters, the contract will honor the original economic assumptions and prevent users from being over‑charged.

title: PoolRegistry#upgradePoolshould call SimpleRamp#refres
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the upgrade process of a liquidity pool that is paired with a ramp contract responsible for converting iFIL shares into wFIL and for recovering stray FIL. When the pool is upgraded, the registry transfers all liquid assets to the new pool instance but does not automatically invoke the ramp’s external function refreshExtern, which is required to re‑bind the ramp to the freshly created pool. Because refreshExtern is left to be called manually by any external actor, there is a window of time after the upgrade during which the ramp still references the old pool’s state. The ramp calculates redemption amounts using the old pool’s totalAssets function, which adds the pool’s current asset balance, totalBorrowed and other accounting fields. After an upgrade the old pool’s totalBorrowed is typically low or zero, while the new pool holds the bulk of the assets. Consequently, when a user calls redeem on the ramp during this window, the conversion formula uses an outdated, low totalBorrowed value and returns far fewer wFIL than the user’s iFIL share entitlement. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, but the received wFIL amount may be near zero, violating the expectation that redeeming iFIL yields a proportional amount of wFIL. A second, related issue appears when a user invokes recoverFIL while the ramp is still linked to the old pool. The recoverFIL logic sends any FIL held by the ramp back to the pool address stored in the ramp, which at this moment points to the deprecated pool contract. The sent FIL becomes locked in the old pool, which no longer receives deposits or withdrawals, making the funds effectively unrecoverable. Both problems arise only after a pool upgrade and before refreshExtern is executed, creating a race‑condition‑like state where the ramp operates on stale references. The bug is subtle because the UI typically shows correct share balances and does not indicate that the underlying pool address has changed; users only notice the discrepancy when the redemption yields an unexpectedly low amount or when recovered FIL disappears. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the upgrade flow, where the auditor noted that the registry’s upgradePool function does not include a call to ramp.refreshExtern. The class of bug can be described as a state‑desynchronisation after contract upgrade, leading to incorrect accounting and permanent fund loss. To remediate, the upgradePool implementation should be amended to invoke oldPool.ramp.refreshExtern() immediately after the asset transfer, or the ramp should enforce a guard that blocks any redeem or recoverFIL calls until it has been refreshed, thereby ensuring that all calculations reference the current pool state and that funds are not sent to an obsolete contract.

title: Only newAgent can call Agent.migrateMiner, but
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the upgrade workflow of the Agent contract used by the GLIF pool system. When an agent owner invokes AgentFactory.upgradeAgent, the factory deploys a new Agent instance, records the new address in the old agent’s storage (oldAgent.newAgent) and transfers all liquid assets to the new contract via decommissionAgent. After this step the protocol expects the new Agent to call Agent.migrateMiner for each miner that was registered to the original agent, thereby transferring miner ownership to the upgraded contract. However, the migrateMiner function contains a strict access‑control check that only permits the address stored in newAgent to be the caller (if (newAgent != msg.sender) revert Unauthorized()). In practice the newly deployed Agent contract does not implement a public migrateMiner entry point, so it cannot invoke the function on the old contract. Consequently the call always reverts, leaving miners permanently registered to the decommissioned agent. The root cause is a mismatch between the intended caller (the owner of the new agent) and the enforced caller (the new agent contract itself), combined with the absence of a corresponding method in the new contract. This logical flaw can be exploited by an attacker who controls the upgrade process to block miner migration, effectively freezing the ability of miners to change ownership and potentially causing reward loss or fund immobility. The impact is that users who expect their miners to be migrated after an upgrade see no change – the UI may show a “Migrate” button that returns no error but the miner remains bound to the old agent, leading to confusion and possible financial loss. The issue manifests only after a successful upgrade where decommissionAgent has set newAgent and transferred assets; before the upgrade the function works as intended. All agents, their owners, and any miners registered to them are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumes that miners can be migrated seamlessly during upgrades. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit (Sherlock) that examined the upgrade path and noticed that the access check does not align with the actual caller capabilities. It is hard to notice because the revert message is generic (“Unauthorized”) and the UI does not surface the failure, making the bug appear as a silent “nothing happened” symptom. To remediate, the access control should be relaxed to allow the owner of the new agent (or an authorized admin) to invoke migrateMiner, for example by comparing msg.sender to IAuth(newAgent).owner() instead of the newAgent address, or by providing a proxy function in the new contract that forwards the call. This adjustment restores the intended upgrade flow, ensures miners can be migrated, and prevents funds or rewards from becoming inaccessible.

title: Bypassing the isOpen modifier in the pools
description: Bypassing the isOpen modifier in the pools Currently, GLIF has a modifier isOpen that "pauses" the interaction with several functions from the pool, some of them are: borrow , pay , deposit and mint . This modifier can be set to false for several reasons, upgrading and agent, or simply because there is a security issue and you need to pause the system. This modifier can be actually bypassed by triggering either receive or fallback in the pool contract, because they call the internal function to deposit instead of the external one that has the modifier. System can still be interacted with when it must be paused. This could cause issues when the contract is paused.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an access‑control bypass that allows interactions with a pool contract even when the contract’s pause flag (the isOpen modifier) is set to false. The pool is designed to block external functions such as borrow, pay, deposit and mint when the system is paused, typically during upgrades, emergency response or security incidents. However, the contract also implements a receive and a fallback function that forward incoming ether to an internal deposit routine. This internal routine does not carry the isOpen modifier, so an attacker can send ether directly to the contract address or trigger the fallback by calling a non‑existent function, causing the internal deposit logic to execute while the external entry points remain blocked. The root cause is the separation of the external, guarded functions from the internal logic that is unintentionally exposed through the generic ether‑receiving entry points. Exploitation consists of sending a transaction that hits the receive or fallback entry, which then calls the internal deposit code and updates user balances, borrows, or other state changes despite the pause. The impact is that funds can be moved, new positions opened, or existing loans repaid while the protocol is supposed to be frozen, breaking the expectation that no state changes occur during a pause. This can lead to financial loss, inconsistent accounting, and erosion of trust because users may believe the system is halted while it continues to process value. The condition occurs whenever the isOpen flag is false and the contract still accepts ether; any user or malicious actor can trigger the bypass without needing special privileges. The affected parties include regular users who rely on the pause mechanism, the protocol operators who assume the pause provides safety, and any downstream contracts that interact with the pool. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor observed that the receive/fallback functions called the same internal deposit routine used by the public deposit function, but without the pause guard. Because the bypass uses standard ether transfer mechanisms, it may be difficult to notice in normal operation; the contract appears paused in the UI, yet transactions succeed silently. The bug belongs to the class of “modifier bypass” or “access control circumvention via internal function exposure”. To remediate, the pause guard should be applied to the internal deposit routine as well, or the receive/fallback functions should be disabled or redirected to a guarded entry point, ensuring that no state‑changing logic can be reached when isOpen is false.

title: Agents might not be able to prevent being liq-
