description: Agents might not be able to prevent being liquidated (defaulted) GLIF uses a modifier isOpen to upgrade the pools and to prevent from interacting with specific functions like borrow , pay , or deposit . be in the pay function. That is basically the function were you repay your principal/borrowed amount + interest. In the case the the contracts are paused, agents will fail to pay back their borrowed amount falling in default states. Agents will fall to repay debt and they will be entering default/administration if any pool is paused and it is not being upgraded
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of a generic pause modifier (isOpen) on the function that processes loan repayments (pay). The contract is designed to pause a pool during upgrades by setting isOpen to false, which blocks any function that carries the modifier. Because the repayment function is also protected by this modifier, borrowers are unable to submit a repayment transaction when the pool is paused. This creates a situation where a borrower who has an outstanding principal plus accrued interest cannot clear the debt, even though the protocol intends to allow repayment at any time. If the pool remains paused for a sufficient period, the borrower’s debt stays outstanding, triggering the protocol’s default or liquidation logic. The impact is that agents (borrowers) may be forced into default or administration without having the opportunity to settle their obligations, potentially leading to loss of collateral, reduced confidence in the protocol, and financial loss for both borrowers and lenders. The condition under which the bug manifests is any time the pool is paused – either by an admin or automatically during an upgrade – and a borrower attempts to call the pay function. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the pause mechanism and core business functions. It can be hard to notice because pausing is generally assumed to be a safety measure that temporarily halts all activity, and developers may overlook that repayment is a critical path that must remain available. From a user’s perspective, the UI would show a transaction failure or a generic “function not allowed” error when trying to repay, leaving the displayed debt unchanged and possibly showing a warning of impending liquidation. The expectation that a borrower can always repay to avoid liquidation is violated, resulting in money disappearing from the borrower’s balance and the protocol’s accounting becoming inconsistent. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of improper access‑control or business‑logic flaws where a global pause flag blocks essential state‑changing operations. The recommended remediation is to remove the isOpen modifier from the repayment function or to implement a separate exemption that allows pay to be called even when the pool is paused, ensuring that borrowers can always settle their debt regardless of upgrade status.

title: Back-run new deployments / front-runrefreshRoutes
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race condition between contract upgrades and the refreshRoutes function that updates internal references to the latest deployed contracts. GLIF's architecture stores addresses of core components (poolRegistry, agentPolice, agentFactory, wFIL) in each contract that calls refreshRoutes. When an upgrade is performed, the new implementation is deployed and registered, but the calling contract must invoke refreshRoutes in the same transaction to replace the stale addresses with the new ones. If the refreshRoutes call is omitted or executed in a separate transaction, an attacker can observe the pending upgrade, front‑run a transaction that relies on the old addresses, or back‑run after the upgrade to interact with the previous version before the references are updated. This allows the attacker to exploit any residual state or known vulnerabilities in the old contract, or to profit from state that existed before the upgrade (e.g., withdrawing funds, calling privileged functions). The impact is that users may lose funds, receive unexpected zero refunds, or experience incorrect routing of calls, because the system continues to point to an outdated contract that may be compromised. The condition occurs whenever a contract in the GLIF registry is upgraded without an atomic refreshRoutes call; it is especially dangerous when the upgraded contract fixes a security issue, because the old version may still be reachable for a short window. The affected parties include any user interacting with the upgraded contracts, the protocol itself (its accounting and routing logic), and any role that relies on the registry addresses (agents, miners, etc.). The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the codebase, where the auditor noted that refreshRoutes is a separate external function and not enforced to be called together with upgrades. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract continues to compile and function, and the stale address is only visible through internal storage; normal UI interactions may appear normal until an attacker exploits the window. The bug belongs to the class of “upgrade‑time race condition” or “stale pointer” vulnerabilities, where a contract holds a cached address that is not synchronously updated with the source of truth. To remediate, the upgrade process should be designed to update the stored addresses atomically, for example by integrating the refresh logic into the upgrade transaction, using a constructor or initializer that fetches the latest registry values, or by restricting external calls to refreshRoutes and ensuring they are executed immediately after deployment. By guaranteeing that the system never operates with outdated component addresses, the protocol can prevent front‑running or back‑running attacks that would otherwise allow an attacker to manipulate funds or bypass security patches.

title: Agent owners can lose funds if agent is up-
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a permanent fund lockup that can occur when an agent contract is upgraded while a deposit or payment transaction is being performed. The root cause is the checkVersion modifier that compares the version stored in the agent with the version reported by the central AgentDeployer contract. When the deployer is upgraded to a new version, the modifier reverts any call that requires the agent to be on the current version, effectively freezing almost all state‑changing functions on the old agent, including any function that could move or withdraw the contract’s ether balance. An attacker does not need to act maliciously; a legitimate upgrade triggered automatically by the protocol or by an administrator can happen in the same block as a user’s transfer. In the described scenario, Alice, who owns an agent, sends ether to the agent and intends to call the pay function to settle a debt. If the upgradeAgent call occurs before the pay call is executed, the checkVersion guard blocks the pay function and any other migration routine, leaving the ether trapped in the old agent instance. Because the old agent can no longer interact with the new version and there is no built‑in migration path, the funds become unrecoverable; the UI would show that the deposit succeeded but later the balance appears stuck or zero when trying to withdraw, violating the user’s expectation that the money can be used or refunded. This issue affects any agent owner, users relying on the agent for payments, and the overall protocol liquidity, as locked funds reduce available capital. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the version‑checking logic and identified that the upgrade path does not include a balance migration mechanism. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert; it simply succeeds in sending ether, yet the subsequent state‑changing calls are blocked, making the loss apparent only later when withdrawal attempts fail. To remediate the issue, the contract should provide a safe migration function that allows the owner (or an authorized entity) to transfer the ether balance from the old agent to the newly upgraded agent, or the version check should be relaxed for deposit and migration operations, ensuring that funds are never stranded after an upgrade.

title: Agent version update resets agent state
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑reset bug that occurs when an Agent contract is upgraded to a newer version through the AgentFactory. During the upgrade process the factory deploys a fresh Agent instance, copies the identifier, owner, operator and request key, transfers the Ether balance and marks the old contract as decommissioning. However, three critical storage variables – faultySectorStartEpoch, administration and defaulted – are never copied to the new instance. Because these variables remain at their default zero or false values in the freshly deployed contract, the upgraded Agent appears to be in a clean, good‑standing state even if it previously recorded a defaulted loan, an ongoing administration period, or a faulty sector start epoch. The root cause is the upgrade logic’s omission of explicit migration for these fields; the Solidity compiler does not automatically copy storage from one contract to another, and the upgrade function only migrates a subset of the state. An attacker who controls the Agent owner (or an authorized administrator) can trigger an upgrade and thereby erase evidence of defaults or administrative penalties, effectively resetting the accounting view of the Agent. The impact is that the protocol’s risk model can be subverted: defaulted positions may be hidden, penalties may disappear, and downstream contracts that rely on the defaulted flag for liquidation or reward distribution will behave as if the Agent is healthy. This condition manifests only when the version number of the AgentDeployer is higher than the current Agent version and the caller passes the ownership or administration checks. Users of the protocol see a discrepancy between the expected state (e.g., a defaulted flag should remain true, a repayment schedule should still be overdue) and the UI, which now shows the Agent as active and in good standing, often with no visible penalties or missing refunds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the upgrade function against the Agent’s storage layout and identified the missing assignments. It can be hard to notice because the balance transfer succeeds and the contract continues to operate, so no immediate error is thrown; only a careful inspection of the state after upgrade reveals the reset. To remediate, the upgrade routine must explicitly read the values of faultySectorStartEpoch, administration and defaulted from the old Agent and write them into the newly deployed contract before completing the migration, ensuring that the logical accounting state is preserved across versions.

title: Just-in-Time depositor can take interests with-
description:
The SPs pay the protocol interests via the pay function. The depositor can monitor mempool for pay call transactions and steal the interests with sandwich attack. The attacker monitors the mempool for pay transactions and can launch the following sandwich attack.
1. Frontrun with a transaction that deposits a large amount of assets to InfinityPool. This will mints the attacker a large amount of iFIL shares.
2. The pay transaction gets executed and the interests are distributed to depositors. The attack will get a large portion of the interests because he holds a large amount of the iFIL shares.
3. Backrun with a withdraw transaction to exit and profit. The attacker can steal a large portion of the protocol income. The severity is set to high because this is an ongoing impact and will render the protocol useless for depositors.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a sandwich‑style front‑running attack on the protocol’s interest‑distribution mechanism. When the protocol calls its pay function, it distributes accrued interest to all current iFIL share holders proportionally to their share balance. Because the contract does not enforce any lock‑up period or snapshot of balances before the distribution, an attacker can monitor the mempool for the pending pay transaction, then front‑run it with a large deposit that mints a massive amount of iFIL shares. At the moment the pay transaction executes, the attacker’s inflated share balance entitles them to a disproportionately large slice of the interest pool. Immediately after the distribution, the attacker back‑runs a withdraw transaction to redeem the newly minted shares and capture the stolen interest. This sequence can be performed within a single block, allowing the attacker to siphon a significant portion of the protocol’s income without altering the contract code. The root cause is the lack of a temporal restriction or balance snapshot that separates interest accrual from recent deposits, making the share‑based accounting vulnerable to manipulation of transaction ordering. The impact is that legitimate depositors receive less interest than expected, potentially seeing their balances grow slower or not at all, while the attacker profits at the protocol’s expense. Over time, repeated exploitation can erode the protocol’s revenue stream and render the service unattractive for users. The issue manifests whenever the pay function is called and there is no enforced delay between deposit and withdrawal; it is especially exploitable in environments with high transaction‑ordering freedom, such as public mempools. It was identified during a manual audit of the interest‑distribution logic, where the auditor noted that the contract does not prevent a depositor from immediately withdrawing after a pay call. The problem can be subtle because the attacker’s profit appears as a normal interest payout, making it hard to distinguish from legitimate earnings. To remediate, the protocol should introduce a lock‑up period that prevents newly deposited shares from being withdrawn until after at least one interest distribution cycle, or alternatively compute interest based on a snapshot of balances taken before the pay transaction executes. This change would break the attack vector by ensuring that an attacker cannot temporarily inflate their share balance to capture the current interest pool, thereby preserving the intended accounting guarantees and protecting depositor funds.

title: Faulty interest calculations force agents to
bug_full: The vulnerability is an interest‑accrual miscalculation that allows an agent to overpay interest when they increase their borrowed principal before any interest has been settled. The contract tracks the last block for which interest was paid in a field called epochsPaid. When a borrow() call is executed the principal is increased, but epochsPaid is never updated, so the subsequent interest formula continues to use the old block number as the start of the accrual period. As a result the interest is computed on the new, larger principal for the entire elapsed time since the previous payment, effectively charging interest on the additional amount for a period it was not actually borrowed. An attacker can exploit this by borrowing an initial amount, waiting for the intended interest period, then borrowing again immediately before calling pay(). The contract will then calculate interest on the summed principal over the full period, leading to a fee roughly twice the expected amount. The impact is that users (agents) are forced to transfer more FIL tokens to the treasury than the protocol specification dictates, causing unexpected loss of funds and eroding trust in the lending pool. The condition occurs whenever a borrower calls borrow() multiple times without an intervening pay() that would reset epochsPaid. It affects any participant who tries to increase their loan size before settling interest, and consequently the protocol’s accounting and fee collection mechanisms. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the borrow() implementation and noticed that epochsPaid was never written after a borrow, a fact confirmed by a proof‑of‑concept test that compared interest collected in two scenarios with identical block intervals but different borrow patterns. The bug is subtle because the contract still records the correct principal and the interest calculation itself is mathematically sound; the error lies in stale state, which may not be obvious from external transaction receipts. To remediate, the contract should record the accrued interest up to the current block and then update epochsPaid to the current block number whenever borrow() changes the principal, ensuring that subsequent interest calculations start from the most recent accrual point. This class of bug belongs to state‑inconsistency or accounting‑logic errors where a temporal accounting variable is not refreshed after a state‑changing operation, leading to over‑charging or fund loss. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a second borrow the expected refund or repayment amount is lower than anticipated, often appearing as “my balance became zero” or “I paid double the interest”. The protocol’s promise of interest being charged only for the time each amount is outstanding is violated, breaking the economic model of the lending pool.

title: Agent can prevent liquidation/administration/default
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded iteration over an agent’s list of registered pools that can be exploited to prevent the platform from liquidating, administrating, or defaulting an agent. The contract allows any agent to add an arbitrary number of pool identifiers to its internal array via a function that simply pushes the pool ID without any limit. When the system needs to check whether an agent is behind its repayment schedule, a modifier calls an internal view function that retrieves the full list of pool IDs for the agent and iterates over each entry to compare the epochs paid with the current block number minus a target window. Because the array can grow without bound, the gas required for the loop grows linearly with the number of pools. If an attacker registers the agent with a very large number of pools – even borrowing a negligible amount from each – the iteration can exceed the block gas limit on the Filecoin network, causing an out‑of‑gas revert. The revert aborts the onlyWhenBehindTargetEpoch check, meaning the platform never detects that the agent is overdue, and consequently never triggers liquidation, administration, or default logic. From a user’s perspective the pools that funded the agent see no liquidation event, their balances remain unchanged, and the expected recovery of funds never occurs, effectively leaving funds locked or lost. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the reviewer noticed that the addPoolToList function does not enforce any cap and that the liquidation path iterates over the entire pool list. It is hard to notice in normal testing because the code works correctly with a modest number of pools; the gas exhaustion only appears when the list becomes very large, a condition that may not be exercised in typical unit tests. This class of bug belongs to unbounded‑iteration denial‑of‑service vulnerabilities that break business‑logic enforcement. To remediate the problem the protocol should impose a reasonable maximum on the number of pools an agent can be associated with, or redesign the accounting checks to avoid iterating over a potentially huge array (for example by using pagination, off‑chain aggregation, or a mapping with per‑pool counters). Limiting the size of the list or changing the algorithm ensures that liquidation and default mechanisms remain executable within the available gas, preserving the safety of pool funds.

title: Shutting down a pool will prevent exits
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that blocks all user exits from the InfinityPool when the contract’s shutdown flag is activated. The pool exposes a public boolean isShuttingDown that is set to true to halt new deposits and borrow operations, and the flag is designed to be irreversible. The root cause is that the same flag is also used inside the liquidity query function getLiquidAssets, which returns zero whenever isShuttingDown is true. The withdraw flow of the SimpleRamp first converts the requested asset amount to shares and then calls an internal _processExit routine. _processExit checks that the amount of assets the user wants to receive does not exceed the pool’s liquid assets by calling pool.getLiquidAssets(). Because getLiquidAssets returns 0 during shutdown, any non‑zero withdrawal request triggers the InsufficientLiquidity revert, causing the transaction to fail. An attacker who controls the shutdown mechanism (typically the protocol owner or governance) can therefore freeze all user funds simply by toggling the shutdown flag, even if the pool still holds the underlying assets. The impact is that users attempting to redeem their positions see their transactions revert, receive no funds, and observe unchanged balances in the UI – effectively “funds disappear” from the user’s perspective. This condition occurs whenever isShuttingDown is true, regardless of the actual amount of assets held by the pool, and it affects every staker, borrower, and any external integrator that relies on the exit path. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the pool’s state‑transition logic, where the interaction between the shutdown flag and the liquidity calculation was examined. It can be hard to notice because the shutdown flag is intended to protect the protocol from further deposits, so developers may assume that existing liquidity remains withdrawable; the early return of zero is subtle and only manifests when a withdrawal is attempted. The bug belongs to the class of improper state gating or logic coupling, where a single flag incorrectly governs multiple independent functionalities, leading to a denial‑of‑service of withdrawals. To remediate, the shutdown flag should be decoupled from the liquidity query: either remove the conditional return of zero, introduce a separate flag that only pauses deposits/borrows, or explicitly allow exits while the pool is shutting down. The fix must ensure that getLiquidAssets reflects the true on‑chain balance even when deposits are disabled, thereby restoring the ability for users to withdraw their funds safely.

title: Operator can backrun owner to avoid chang-
bug_full: The vulnerability is an access‑control race condition that allows the current operator of a contract to block the owner from changing the operator role. The contract defines a transferOperator function that is protected by a modifier permitting both the owner and the operator to call it. The intended workflow is a two‑step process: the owner calls transferOperator to set a pendingOperator address, and the pending operator must later accept the role. Because the operator is also authorized to invoke transferOperator, the operator can observe the owner’s transaction that sets pendingOperator and immediately submit a competing transaction that overwrites pendingOperator with the zero address or with its own address. By doing so the operator prevents the pending operator from ever being accepted, effectively locking the owner out of the operator‑change mechanism. This can be exploited whenever the owner attempts to replace an operator; the malicious operator simply back‑runs or front‑runs the owner’s call and resets the pendingOperator value. The impact is that the owner loses the ability to rotate or remove a potentially compromised operator, leaving the contract under the control of a single party. Users of the protocol may be exposed to misbehaviour, fund‑locking, or other malicious actions because the operator role often has privileged permissions such as fund withdrawal or contract upgrades. The condition occurs only during the operator‑change procedure and only when the operator is monitoring the blockchain for the owner’s transaction. The affected parties are the contract owner, the operator, and indirectly all users who rely on the protocol’s security guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the access modifiers and the state‑transition logic of the operator management functions. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to be owner‑only at a glance, and typical unit tests may not simulate the race condition where two parties call the same function in quick succession. The proper fix is to restrict transferOperator so that only the contract owner can call it, removing the operator from the onlyOwnerOperator modifier, or to split the function into separate owner‑only and operator‑only calls that cannot interfere with each other. Conceptually, this is a privilege‑escalation and role‑management flaw where a privileged party can override another privileged party’s intended state change, violating the business logic that the owner should be able to reassign the operator at any time.

title: AgentPolice._writeOffPools doesn't consider
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation routine of the AgentPolice contract, specifically the internal function that writes off pool balances when an agent is liquidated. The routine calculates each pool's share of the recovered funds by summing only the principal amounts owed by the agent to each pool and then distributing the total recovered amount proportionally to those principals. It completely ignores any accrued interest that the pools are entitled to receive. Because the function does not account for interest, the amount sent to each pool can be lower than the total debt (principal plus interest) that the pool expects. In a scenario where two pools have equal principal but different interest repayment status, the proportional share based on principal alone may allocate insufficient funds to the pool that still owes interest, while the excess is sent to the agent’s owner. This misallocation occurs whenever an agent is liquidated and the _writeOffPools function is invoked, which is the normal path for handling defaulted agents. The affected parties are the liquidity pools that lose expected interest revenue, the lenders who rely on that interest, and the protocol’s accounting integrity, as balances no longer reflect the true obligations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the liquidation logic and noticed that the interest component was never incorporated into the write‑off calculation. It is subtle because the code appears to correctly proportionally allocate funds based on principal, a common pattern, making the omission of interest easy to overlook. The impact is a systematic under‑payment of interest to pools, resulting in lost earnings for pool participants and an unintended surplus that is transferred to the agent’s owner, which can erode trust in the protocol’s fairness. To remediate the problem, the write‑off routine should be modified to compute each pool’s total outstanding debt as principal plus accrued interest, either by querying an oracle or by extending the accounting data, and then distribute the recovered amount proportionally to that total debt. This ensures that pools receive the full amount they are owed, preserving correct financial accounting and preventing excess funds from being misdirected.

title: Due to excessive HTP check moveQuoteTo- multiple times
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the moveQuoteToken function of the Ajna pool contract. The function is intended to let a depositor relocate a portion of their quote‑token deposit from one price bucket (fromIndex) to another (toIndex) in order to manage risk and capture yield. Before the function completes, it removes the specified amount from the source bucket, computes the new Lowest Utilised Price (LUP) based on the reduced deposit, and then checks whether the Highest Threshold Price (HTP) – derived from the loan book – exceeds this intermediate LUP. If HTP is greater, the transaction reverts with LUPBelowHTP. The root cause is that the HTP‑vs‑LUP validation is performed after the removal but before the addition of the same amount to the destination bucket. Logically the protocol only needs to ensure that HTP ≤ LUP both before the move starts and after the move finishes; checking the condition in the middle creates an artificial barrier. Consequently, when a depositor attempts to move a large amount upward (from a lower‑price bucket to a higher‑price bucket), the temporary state often violates HTP ≤ LUP, causing the call to revert even though the final state would be valid. This makes moveQuoteToken unavailable for a substantial share of active debt‑management operations, especially for big deposits. From the user’s perspective the transaction fails with a LUPBelowHTP error, no LP tokens are minted in the target bucket, and the funds remain locked in the original bucket, giving the impression that the protocol is refusing to move their money. The impact is that depositors cannot reposition their quote‑token holdings in response to market shifts, which can lead to missed yield opportunities or exposure to liquidation risk; in extreme cases the inability to move funds quickly may result in actual financial loss. The issue manifests only under specific conditions: a move from a lower index to a higher index, a deposit size large enough that its removal pushes the interim LUP below the current HTP, and the presence of a non‑zero deposit fee that may further reduce the moved amount. It was discovered during a manual audit of the LenderActions contract, where the auditor observed that the revert condition was placed between the removal and addition steps. The bug is subtle because the contract does eventually satisfy the HTP ≤ LUP condition after the full move, so a superficial test that only checks final state would not catch it. To remediate, the HTP check should be moved to after the destination bucket has been credited, or the condition should be relaxed to compare HTP against the LUP that would result after the complete transfer. Alternatively, the fee calculation could be based on the initial LUP, avoiding a change in LUP that triggers the revert. In any case, the fix must ensure that the moveQuoteToken operation is allowed whenever the protocol’s invariant HTP ≤ LUP holds both before and after the transfer, rather than during the intermediate step.

title: Limit index isn't checked in repayDebt, so user
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the repayDebt function of the lending protocol where a user‑provided limitIndex parameter is intended to bound the acceptable change of the Lowest Usable Price (LUP) after a repayment. The contract currently invokes the internal _revertIfPriceDroppedBelowLimit check only when collateral is being pulled, but skips this verification when the transaction consists solely of debt repayment. As a result, a borrower can submit a repayment request with a specific limitIndex expecting the transaction to revert if the new LUP exceeds that limit, yet the call proceeds unchecked. The root cause is the conditional placement of the price‑limit validation inside a branch that is executed only for collateral pulls (vars.pull) and omitted from the pure repayment branch (vars.repay). An attacker or a careless borrower can therefore trigger a repayment that moves the LUP upward or leaves it unchanged, contrary to the borrower’s expectations. This can be exploited by invoking repayDebt with a non‑zero limitIndex while setting collateralAmountToPull to zero, causing the function to skip the price‑limit check. The protocol will accept the repayment, update the pool debt, recalculate the LUP, and allow the new LUP to be higher than the borrower’s specified bound. Borrowers who rely on a predictable LUP movement for multi‑position strategies may find that subsequent loans become under‑collateralized or that liquidation thresholds are crossed, leading to a loss of funds or failed arbitrage opportunities. The issue manifests whenever a user performs a pure debt repayment without pulling collateral, which is a common operation with no additional prerequisites, making the execution probability high. All borrowers who use the limitIndex argument, especially those with complex strategies spanning several loans, are affected because the protocol silently violates the accounting assumption that the limitIndex protects against unfavorable price shifts. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the BorrowerActions contract where the code path for repayment was examined and the missing call to _revertIfPriceDroppedBelowLimit was noted. It can be difficult to notice in testing because the transaction succeeds and the UI typically reports a successful repayment, while the subtle LUP drift only becomes apparent later when other positions suffer. To remediate the issue, the same LUP validation logic used for collateral pulls should be executed after the repayment calculation, i.e., compute the new Lup from the updated pool debt and invoke _revertIfPriceDroppedBelowLimit with the supplied limitIndex before finalizing the repayment. Skipping the check only when both repayment and pull are absent is acceptable for gas optimisation, but any path that changes the pool debt must enforce the limit. In summary, the bug is a missing price‑limit guard in a repayment‑only flow, leading to unexpected LUP changes, potential loss of borrower funds, and a breach of the protocol’s financial safety guarantees.

title: LenderActions's moveQuoteToken can create
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that moves quote tokens between price buckets in the lending pool. The routine applies an unutilized deposit fee when a token is moved from a bucket priced at or above the Lowest Utilised Price (LUP) to a bucket priced below LUP. This fee reduction can shrink the total amount of deposits recorded for the pool. The core accounting model of the pool assumes that the total debt is always lower than the total deposits, an invariant that is enforced in other functions such as removeQuoteToken by checking that poolState.debt does not exceed the sum of deposits stored in the deposits tree. In moveQuoteToken this invariant is not re‑checked after the fee adjustment; the code only verifies that the High Threshold Price (HTP) does not exceed the new LUP. Consequently, when the fee reduces deposits enough to make poolState.debt greater than the deposits tree sum, the pool enters an inconsistent state where LUP is calculated based on a debt amount that is larger than the available deposits. This breaks the fundamental pricing logic, allowing the pool to report more liquidity than actually exists and potentially permitting loans to be issued with insufficient collateral. The bug can be triggered only when the token move crosses the LUP boundary and a non‑zero deposit fee is applied, making the scenario rare but still exploitable. An attacker could craft a moveQuoteToken call that satisfies these conditions, causing the invariant violation and then proceeding to borrow against an overstated liquidity pool, leading to under‑collateralised positions and possible loss of funds for lenders. From a user perspective the symptoms may appear as an unexpected reduction in deposited balance, loans being approved despite insufficient collateral, or withdrawals failing because the pool believes it has less capital than it really does. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that moveQuoteToken lacked the debt‑greater‑than‑deposits check present in removeQuoteToken. Because the condition is uncommon, the inconsistency does not immediately surface, making it hard to detect through routine testing. The recommended remediation is to add the same invariant check used in removeQuoteToken – reverting the transaction if poolState.debt is non‑zero and exceeds Deposits.treeSum(deposits_) after the fee adjustment – and to combine this with the existing HTP versus LUP validation. Restoring this check re‑establishes the accounting guarantees and prevents the pool from entering the erroneous state.

title: Wrong Inflator used in calculating HTP to de-
description:
When accruing Interest, the interest is added according to the deposits in all buckets upto the lower of LUP and HTP prices' buckets. But HTP is wrongly calculated in the accrueInterest function.
All major functions in Pool.sol use _accrueInterest which makes a call to PoolCommons.accrueInterest to accrue the interest for all deposits above the lower of LUP and HTP prices, which means upto the lower of the LupIndex and HTPIndex because indexes move in the opposite direction of prices. Here in accrueInterest function, the accrualIndex is calculated as the higher of LUPIndex and HTPIndex to make sure interest is calculated for all deserving deposits above min(HTP price, LUP price) ie. max(LUP index, HTP index).
using the newInflator which incorporates the newly accrued interest into the HTP calculation, whereas the LUP is calculated with old values. The accrualIndex is set to max(LUP index, HTP index). then.
Assume that the LUP price > HTP price. So, LUP index < HTP index. Hence, for the interestEarningDeposit all the deposits above the HTP index will be considered.
But the value of HTP index is wrong now because it is calculated using new Inflator which means that the new Interest has been added in calculation of HTP already and thus the derived HTP index will be lower in value (which means upper in the bucket system). Assume that still after this LUP index < HTP index
Now since the old LUP index and new HTP index is used in the max(LUP index, HTP index) function, and LUP index is still < HTP index (ie. LUP price > HTP price) thus the deposits that were between the old HTP index and the new HTP index have been left out of the interestEarningDeposit calculation.
I talked to the developers about this discrepancy between new HTP and old LUP being used, and they said "I can see the argument in favor of using the prior inflator here to be totally precise."
Also, one of them said, "It should be computed using the debt prior to the interest accrual itself, as it's determining the the minimum amount of deposit onto which that interest would be applied"
This means that the htp index has been underestimated because it has been made lower (ie. upper in the bucket system) and thus the deposits that lie between the old HTP index and new HTP index have not been considered for calculating interestEarningDeposit when they should have been considered because before the interest accrual itself, those deposits were under the deserving max(LUP index, HTP index) bracket.
This means interestEarningDeposit has been underestimated and later calculations at PoolCommons.sol#L253 for lender Factor have become wrong.
This is a logic mistake and leads to wrong values for the lenderFactor.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the interest‑accrual routine of the pool contract. When the pool accrues interest it must consider all deposits that lie above the lower of the LUP (lowest usable price) and HTP (highest target price) buckets. The implementation determines the accrual index as the maximum of the LUP index and the HTP index. However the HTP index is calculated with the new inflator, which already incorporates the interest that is being accrued in the same transaction, while the LUP index is calculated with the old inflator. In scenarios where the LUP price is higher than the HTP price (so the LUP index is lower than the HTP index) the new inflator makes the HTP index artificially lower (i.e., moves it upward in the bucket ordering). As a result the max(LUP index, HTP index) uses a stale LUP index together with an underestimated HTP index, causing the range of deposits between the old HTP index and the new HTP index to be omitted from the interestEarningDeposit calculation. Those omitted deposits receive no interest for that period, which leads to an under‑estimation of the total interest earned and consequently an incorrect lenderFactor value used later in the protocol. The bug is discovered during a manual audit of the Pool.sol and PoolCommons.sol code, where the auditor observed that the HTP calculation used the newly updated inflator instead of the prior value. The issue is subtle because the majority of deposits are still correctly accounted for; only deposits that fall in the narrow bucket range affected by the index shift are impacted, making the discrepancy hard to notice in normal testing. From a user perspective the symptom is that a lender’s balance may not increase as expected after an interest period, or the reported APY appears lower than advertised, effectively causing funds to disappear for the affected deposits. The root cause is the misuse of the inflator state when computing the HTP index, violating the accounting assumption that interest should be applied only after the correct bucket range has been identified. The recommended fix is to compute the HTP index using the old inflator (the value before the current interest accrual) so that the max(LUP index, HTP index) reflects the true set of deposits that are eligible for interest. By aligning both indexes to the same pre‑interest state, the interestEarningDeposit calculation will include all deserving deposits and the lenderFactor will be accurate.

title: PositionManager & PermitERC721 do not comply with EIP-4494
description:
The Scope QA explicitly stated an expectation for the contract/code under inspection to comply with EIP-4494. However, the PermitERC721 and PositionManager contracts do not satisfy the requirements of the EIP-4494 standard. Specifically, they lack the implementation of the IERC165 interface and do not indicate support for the 0x5604e225 interface. These discrepancies mark the contracts as non-compliant with the EIP-4494 standard, which could lead to potential interoperability issues.
According to the specifications of the EIP-4494 standard, they lack the crucial implementation of the IERC165 interface and do not support the 0x5604e225 interface, both of which are mandatory according to the EIP-4494 standard.
Quoting the EIP: This EIP requires EIP-165. EIP165 is already required in ERC-721, but is further necessary here in order to register interface of this EIP. This enables them to interact accordingly. The interface of this EIP (as defined in EIP-165) is 0x5604e225. Contracts implementing this EIP MUST have the supportsInterface function return true when called with 0x5604e225.
The absence of the IERC165 implementation and lack of support for the 0x5604e225 interface in accordance with the EIP-4494 standard have several potential implications:
1. The PositionManager & PermitERC721 contracts do not comply with the EIP-4494 standard.
2. This discrepancy could hamper the contracts' interoperability with other systems and smart contracts, as third-party contracts would be unable to identify their adherence to the EIP-4494 standard.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a failure to comply with the EIP‑4494 standard for ERC‑721 tokens that support gas‑less approvals via a signed permit. The root cause is that both the PermitERC721 and PositionManager contracts omit the implementation of the ERC‑165 introspection interface (IERC165) and consequently do not report support for the interface identifier 0x5604e225, which EIP‑4494 mandates. Because the contracts lack a supportsInterface function that returns true for this identifier, external callers, libraries, or other smart contracts cannot reliably detect that the token implements the permit functionality. An attacker or a benign integrator attempting to use the permit flow will invoke the permit function or query supportsInterface; the call will either revert or return false, causing the off‑chain signature to be ignored. The practical impact is that users expecting a gas‑less approval experience receive no approval, their allowance remains zero, and UI elements such as “Approve with signature” appear to do nothing. This breaks interoperability with marketplaces, aggregators, or wallet SDKs that rely on EIP‑4494 to perform permit‑based approvals, potentially forcing users to fall back to on‑chain approve transactions that are more expensive and slower. The issue manifests whenever a contract or dApp checks for EIP‑4494 compliance via ERC‑165 or attempts to call the permit method; under those conditions the contract behaves as if the feature is absent. The affected parties include token holders, developers integrating the token into other protocols, and any third‑party service that assumes standard compliance. The problem was discovered during a scoped quality‑assurance audit that explicitly required EIP‑4494 compliance; the auditor inspected the bytecode and source for the presence of IERC165 and the required interface ID and found them missing. Because the bug does not cause immediate loss of funds, it can be subtle: the contract appears functional, yet certain advanced workflows silently fail, making it hard to notice without targeted testing. To remediate the issue, the contracts should inherit from IERC165, implement the supportsInterface function, and ensure that calling supportsInterface with 0x5604e225 returns true. Additionally, the contracts must expose the permit function according to the EIP‑4494 specification so that off‑chain signatures are correctly processed. By aligning with the standard, the token regains compatibility with the broader ecosystem and restores the expected user experience of gas‑less approvals.

title: Lenders lose interests and pay deposit fees due to LUP/HTP slippage
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the deposit function of a lending pool where a lender supplies quote tokens through the addQuoteToken() entry point. The contract determines the current Lowest Utilization Price (LUP) and Highest Threshold Price (HTP) at the moment the transaction is executed and compares the supplied bucket index with the calculated LUP index to decide whether a deposit fee should be applied. Because the function does not offer any slippage protection, a lender cannot specify a maximum acceptable LUP or HTP value. Consequently, if the pool state changes between the time the transaction is signed and the time it is mined – for example due to other lenders depositing large amounts or a malicious actor front‑running the transaction – the spot LUP may increase. When the transaction finally settles, the supplied index can be interpreted as being below the new LUP, triggering an automatic fee deduction and preventing the deposited amount from earning interest. From the user’s perspective the deposit appears to succeed, but the resulting LP balance is lower than expected, interest accrues at a reduced rate, or the user receives a fee charge that was not disclosed. The issue is a classic price‑slippage or race‑condition bug where the contract relies on a mutable on‑chain price without allowing the caller to bound the acceptable change. It was discovered during a manual audit of the pool’s source code, where the auditor noticed that the expiry parameter only guards against stale transactions and does not protect against LUP/HTP movement. The problem can be hard to notice because the fee is applied silently inside the addQuoteToken logic, and the UI may simply show a smaller token balance without explaining the cause. To remediate, the contract should introduce slippage protection – for example by letting the caller provide a maximum acceptable LUP index or by reverting the transaction if the current LUP exceeds the user‑specified threshold. This change would align the implementation with the business rule that deposits below the minimum LUP/HTP should be rejected rather than silently penalised, restoring user confidence and preventing unintended loss of funds.

title: SetToken can't be unlocked early.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract’s early‑unlock logic depends on a variable raiseTargetPercentage being exactly zero. The function setRaiseTargetPercentage enforces a requirement that the new value be greater than zero, so the variable can never be set back to zero after it has been assigned a non‑zero value. Moreover, the unlock function does not clear raiseTargetPercentage, leaving the non‑zero value persisted across subsequent rebalances. Consequently, the internal predicate _canUnlockEarly, which checks that all targets are met and raiseTargetPercentage == 0, will never evaluate to true after the first positive assignment. This prevents a manager from ending a locked rebalance early, effectively keeping the SetToken locked for the full rebalance duration or indefinitely if the manager repeatedly initiates rebalances with a non‑zero raiseTargetPercentage. From a user’s perspective the token appears to remain locked, withdrawals return no tokens, and expected refunds are missing, violating the expectation that an early unlock should be possible when targets are satisfied. The issue occurs whenever a manager calls setRaiseTargetPercentage with a positive value—a normal operation—and later attempts to unlock early. It was discovered during a manual audit of the AuctionModule’s rebalance flow, where the relationship between raiseTargetPercentage and the early‑unlock guard was examined. The bug is subtle because the contract only reverts with a generic error message, making it hard to notice until a manager experiences unexpected lock‑up. The recommended remediation is to reset raiseTargetPercentage to zero inside the unlock function (or modify the setter to allow zero) so that the early‑unlock condition can be satisfied after each rebalance, aligning the implementation with the intended business rule that managers may keep the raise target at zero to permit early exit or raise it temporarily and then clear it.

title: Because of rounding issues, users may not be
bug_full: The contract implements a voting power system that converts a user's token claim into voting tokens using the formula (tokenAmount * voteFactor) / fractionDenominator. Because Solidity performs integer division, any fractional part is discarded. When a claim is granted in a single step that is an exact multiple of fractionDenominator, the conversion yields the expected number of voting tokens. However, when the same total claim is split across multiple adjustments – for example, an initial airdrop of 1000 tokens followed by an owner‑initiated adjust() that raises the claim to the same 1000 tokens – each individual conversion may round down to zero voting tokens. The user therefore accumulates fewer voting tokens than required for the later withdrawal step, which burns voting tokens equal to tokensToVotes(totalClaimed). In the example, the user needs to burn 1 voting token (2000*5/10000) but has received 0 voting tokens from both the initial grant and the adjustment, so the withdrawal reverts. The bug manifests whenever the voteFactor is not an exact multiple of fractionDenominator and claims are issued or increased in separate stages. It affects any participant who relies on the voting token balance to satisfy the burn condition, effectively locking their claim and preventing fund withdrawal. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the token‑to‑vote conversion logic; it is subtle because the rounding loss is invisible in the UI – the user sees a correct token balance but the voting token balance remains zero, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual ability to withdraw. The problem belongs to the class of integer‑division rounding bugs in financial calculations, where loss of precision breaks accounting invariants. To remediate, the protocol should avoid a separate voting‑token accounting layer and instead compute voting power directly from the unclaimed token amount, or use a higher‑precision representation (e.g., fixed‑point arithmetic) or a rounding‑up strategy that guarantees the required voting tokens are always minted. By aligning the voting power calculation with the actual token balance, the contract will preserve the invariant that a user can always burn the exact amount of voting tokens needed to withdraw their claim.

title: In PriceTierVesting there is no check if the Se-
description: Price from oracle on L2s can be invalid/stale if the sequencer is down. This could lead to users being able to claim tokens that they should not be able to claim. If the sequencer of the L2s were to go offline the Chainlink oracle may return an invalid/stale price. This could lead to users being able to claim tokens that they should not be able to claim. tier price, this would have unlocked all tokens to be claimable. If the sequencer the oracle would still return the high price even though the price is lower now and not all tokens should be claimable. It should always be checked if the sequencer is up before consuming any data from Chainlink. For more details on L2 Sequencer Uptime Feeds check the Chainlink docs(https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds/l2-sequencer-feeds) specify more details. Receivers can claim tokens they should not be able to claim
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the PriceTierVesting contract where the calculation of the vested token fraction relies on a Chainlink price feed without first confirming that the L2 sequencer feeding that data is operational. When the sequencer goes offline, the Chainlink oracle continues to return the last recorded price, which may be significantly higher than the current market price. Because the contract does not verify sequencer uptime, it consumes this stale price as if it were fresh, causing the getVestedFraction function to compute an inflated vesting ratio. As a result, a user who calls the claim function during a sequencer outage can receive the full token allocation instead of the proportion dictated by the vesting schedule. This flaw can be exploited by any participant who monitors the sequencer status and triggers a claim while the feed is stale, effectively allowing unauthorized token claims and diluting the token supply. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions: tokens that should remain locked become claimable, leading to potential loss of value for other token holders and undermining confidence in the distribution mechanism. The issue manifests only under the condition that the L2 sequencer is down; under normal operation the price feed returns correct data and the contract behaves as intended. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the vesting logic and external price feeds, noting the absence of a sequencer‑up check that Chainlink explicitly recommends for L2 feeds. The bug is subtle because the price value itself appears valid, and there is no on‑chain indication that the data is stale, making it easy to miss during routine testing. To remediate, the contract should query the Chainlink Sequencer Uptime Feed before using any price data and revert the transaction if the sequencer is reported as down, thereby ensuring that vesting calculations only use fresh, reliable price information. This class of issue falls under the broader category of oracle‑stale‑data vulnerabilities, where contracts trust external data without validating its freshness, leading to incorrect business‑logic outcomes such as users receiving more tokens than they are entitled to, balances unexpectedly jumping to full amounts, and the overall token economics being compromised.

title: SafeERC20.safeApprovereverts for changing ex-
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the misuse of OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20.safeApprove function inside the CrosschainDistributor contract. SafeERC20.safeApprove is designed to be called only when setting an initial allowance from zero to a non‑zero value or when resetting an existing allowance back to zero; any attempt to change a non‑zero allowance directly to another non‑zero amount triggers a revert. In the contract, the internal function _allowConnext calls token.safeApprove(address(connext), amount) each time the total amount of tokens to be distributed is updated via the _setTotal function. Because the allowance to the Connext contract is already non‑zero after the first distribution, subsequent calls to _setTotal try to overwrite that allowance with a new non‑zero value, causing SafeERC20.safeApprove to revert. This logical error means that any attempt by an airdrop owner to adjust the total token amount after the initial setting will fail, effectively locking the ability to modify the airdrop parameters. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: external protocols that rely on the ability to change the total airdrop amount cannot do so, and users may see the expected total not updating, receive zero tokens despite a positive balance, or experience transaction failures without an obvious reason. The bug is discovered during a security audit (Sherlock) by reviewing the allowance handling code and noting the explicit warning comment in SafeERC20.safeApprove. It can be hard to notice because the call to safeApprove looks syntactically correct and the revert only occurs when the allowance is already non‑zero, a condition that may not be exercised in simple unit tests. To remediate, the contract should replace safeApprove with safeIncreaseAllowance or safeDecreaseAllowance when adjusting the allowance, or explicitly reset the allowance to zero before calling safeApprove with the new amount. This aligns the implementation with the ERC20 allowance best practices and restores the intended functionality of updating the total airdrop amount without causing transaction reverts.

title: CrosschainDistributor: Not paying relayer fee
description:
CrosschainDistributor is not paying relayer fee when calling xcall to claim tokens to other domains. The transaction will not be relayed on target chain to finnalize the claim. User will not receive the claimed tokens unless they bump the transaction fee themself. In _settleClaim, the CrosschainDistributor is using xcall to claim tokens to another domain. But relayer fee is not payed.
```solidity
id = connext.xcall(
    // <------ relayer fee should be payed here
    _recipientDomain, // destination domain
    _recipient, // to
    address(token), // asset
    _recipient, // delegate, only required for self-execution + slippage
    _amount, // amount
    0, // slippage -- assumes no pools on connext
    bytes('')
);
```
Without the relayer fee, the transaction will not be relayed. The user will need to bump the relayer fee to finnally settle the claim by following the instructions here in the connext doc. User will not receive their claimed tokens on target chain.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing relayer fee when the CrosschainDistributor contract invokes Connext's xcall function to transfer claimed tokens to another domain. The contract assumes that the xcall call will automatically cover the relayer fee, but the fee argument is omitted, so the cross‑chain message is under‑funded. As a result the Connext relayer does not forward the message to the destination chain, and the claim never finalises. From the user's perspective the UI reports that the claim transaction was submitted successfully on the source chain, but the expected token balance on the target chain remains unchanged or zero, leading to confusion and the impression that the tokens disappeared. The issue occurs whenever the internal _settleClaim function is executed, i.e., for any user‑initiated claim. It affects all users of the protocol who rely on cross‑chain token distribution, and it undermines the protocol’s promised functionality. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of funds and noticed that the xcall call did not include any fee parameter. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no error is emitted; the only symptom is the lack of token receipt on the destination chain. The root cause is a business‑logic error: the contract does not calculate or forward the required relayer fee, violating Connext’s accounting assumptions that each cross‑chain message must be paid for. To remediate, the contract should query the appropriate relayer fee from Connext (or a fee oracle) and include that amount in the xcall call, or allow the user to supply the fee, ensuring that the message is fully funded and the claim can be relayed and settled.

title: price is calculated wrongly in BoundedStep-
poc: • A manager wants to switch stablecoins. He wants to buy DAI and Sell USDT at a price of minimum and initial price of 1 and increasing to 1.05. • Technically, the price is not 1, but rather 1e-12 because of decimals 1e6/1e18 (1e6 in WAD) With the right formula • If he uses the scalingFactor of 2, the priceChange at t0 would be 0 • Therefore bidder would have to pay 1e18 DAI for 1e6USDT. With the wrong formula • If he uses the scalingFactor of 2, the priceChange at t0 would 1 (1e18 in WAD) instead of 0 • Therefore the price would increase by a magnitude 1e12. • Therefore, bidder would pay approximately 1e18 DAI for 1e6 * 1e12 USDT. • Attacker could take 1e12 (1 trillion USDT) with one DAI in a flash. • Or if there's not enough liquidity e.g if there's only 1m USDT, then he'll pay 1e-12 DAI. That's less than a penny. bizzyvinci My bad, I agree with Med cause the catastrophe is bounded by min and max value. pblivin0x My bad, I agree with Med cause the catastrophe is bounded by min and max value. I think we all agree this should be de-escalated to a Medium hrishibhat Result: Medium Has duplicates Considering this a valid medium based on the Escalations have been resolved successfully! Escalation status: • IAm0x52: accepted pblivin0x The remediation for this issue is open for review here https://github.com/IndexCoop/index-protocol/pull/25 The fix to the formula is here: https://github.com/IndexCoop/index-protocol/blob/839a6c699cc9217c8ee9f3b67418c64e80f0e10d/contracts/protocol/integration/auction-price/BoundedStepwiseExponentialPriceAdapter.sol#L73 IAm0x52 Fix looks good. scalingFactor is now applied via wadMul which fixes this order of operation issue.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic‑order‑of‑operations mistake in the price calculation routine of the BoundedStepwiseExponentialPriceAdapter contract. The intended formula for the price change is scalingFactor multiplied by (e^x − 1), where e^x is expressed as a fixed‑point WAD value and the subtraction of one (WAD) normalises the exponential term. Because the implementation omitted parentheses, the code evaluates scalingFactor * e^x − WAD, which first multiplies the exponential expression by the scaling factor and only then subtracts the constant one. This subtle precedence error means that when the time bucket is zero – the moment when e^0 = 1 and the price should equal the initial price – the computed price change is not zero but scalingFactor − 1. Consequently the returned price is offset by exactly scalingFactor − 1 WAD units. The bug manifests whenever the price adapter is used to derive auction or rebalance prices, especially at the start of a price window or when the elapsed time is a multiple of the bucket size. Users experience symptoms such as an initial price that is higher or lower than expected, receiving or paying an amount that does not match the quoted rate, or seeing balances disappear after a trade because the protocol charges a dramatically inflated price. For example, with an initial price of 100 and a scaling factor of 11, the correct price starts at 100, but the buggy calculation starts at 110, a ten‑unit error that compounds as the exponential grows. In extreme cases the error can cause a trader to pay a trillion times more than intended or, conversely, to acquire a huge amount of assets for a negligible payment, effectively draining or inflating protocol funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor examined the getPrice logic and noticed that the subtraction of WAD was placed outside the multiplication, a mistake that is easy to miss because the code compiles and the error only appears for the edge case of a zero time bucket. Detecting the problem requires careful reasoning about fixed‑point arithmetic and testing of boundary conditions, which are often omitted in standard test suites. The appropriate remediation is to enforce the correct order of operations, either by adding explicit parentheses around (expExpression − WAD) before multiplying by scalingFactor, or by using a dedicated wad multiplication helper that performs the subtraction first. This change restores the intended price dynamics, ensures that the initial price matches the configured value, and prevents the protocol from exposing users to unintended financial loss or gain.

title: No check for sequencer uptime can lead to
description: When purchasing from dutch auctions on L2s there is no considering of sequencer uptime. When the sequencer is down, all transactions must originate from the L1. The issue with this is that these transactions use an aliased address. Since the set token contracts don't implement any way for these aliased addressed to interact with the protocol, no transactions can be processed during this time even with force L1 inclusion. If the sequencer goes offline during the the auction period then the auction will continue to decrease in price while the sequencer is offline. Once the sequencer comes back online, users will be able to buy tokens from these auctions at prices much lower than market price. See summary. Auction will sell/buy assets at prices much lower/higher than market price leading to large losses for the set token
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns Dutch auction contracts deployed on layer‑2 networks that rely on the L2 sequencer being continuously operational. The contract does not verify that the sequencer is up during the auction window. When the sequencer goes offline, all user‑initiated transactions must be routed through the L1 bridge, which uses an address aliasing mechanism. The set‑token contracts that receive auction bids are not programmed to recognise or accept calls originating from these aliased addresses, so any bid submitted while the sequencer is down is rejected or silently ignored. Because the auction price‑decrement logic runs on‑chain regardless of transaction availability, the price continues to fall while no participant can place a valid order. When the sequencer is restored, the auction can be completed at a price that is far below the current market value, allowing a buyer to acquire assets at a deep discount, or conversely allowing a seller to receive an inflated price if the auction is a sell‑side. From a user perspective the UI may show a normal‑looking auction, but attempts to submit a bid return no confirmation, or the transaction appears to be stuck, and later the user sees that the final price was unexpectedly low or high. The impact is a potential loss of value for the set‑token holders, as the protocol may sell assets for far less than market price or buy them for far more, eroding the net asset value of the fund. The condition occurs only when the L2 sequencer experiences downtime during the auction period; the bug is not triggered on a healthy sequencer. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the auction flow, where the auditor noticed that the contract never checks the sequencer status and that the L1‑to‑L2 message handling does not accommodate the address alias used by the bridge. The problem can be hard to notice because the price curve appears normal and the auction may complete successfully after the sequencer recovers, masking the fact that the price was manipulated while the system was unavailable. The vulnerability belongs to the class of availability‑dependent logic errors or sequencer‑downtime exploitation where on‑chain state changes continue while off‑chain or cross‑layer transaction paths are blocked. To remediate, the contract should query the sequencer’s uptime (or a reliable L2 availability oracle) at each price‑update step and abort or invalidate the auction if any downtime is detected, or alternatively whitelist the aliased address so that L1‑originated bids are accepted. In short, the bug violates the business assumption that every price tick can be acted upon by a participant; when that assumption is broken, the auction can settle at a price that does not reflect market reality, leading to unexpected loss of funds.

title: Full inventory asset purchases can be DOS'd
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial-of-service condition in the auction-style component purchase function. The contract requires that the quantity requested in a bid does not exceed the current auctionQuantity, enforced by a require statement. When a legitimate user submits a bid that exactly matches the total remaining balance of the component (i.e., they intend to buy the whole inventory), the transaction passes the check only if the auctionQuantity has not been altered. Because the check is performed at execution time, a malicious actor can submit a preceding transaction that purchases a tiny fraction of the component. This front‑run reduces auctionQuantity just enough that the later “buy‑all” bid now exceeds the available quantity, causing the require to fail and the transaction to revert. The attacker does not need to own a large amount of the component; a minimal bid is sufficient to block the larger purchase. The impact is that legitimate buyers are unable to acquire the component they intended to purchase; their transaction reverts, they lose the gas spent, and the auction may be stalled, allowing the attacker to wait for a more favorable price in a Dutch‑auction setting. The condition occurs only when a user attempts to purchase the entire remaining balance; normal partial purchases are unaffected. The affected parties are any users trying to buy the full inventory, the protocol that relies on timely sales, and potentially downstream contracts that expect the component to be transferred. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the bid‑validation logic, where the strict “_componentQuantity <= auctionQuantity” check was observed to lack a safe “buy‑all” sentinel. It can be hard to notice because the require statement appears correct for typical bids, and the edge case of a full‑balance purchase is rarely exercised in testing. To remediate, the contract should allow a special value (e.g., type(uint256).max) to represent “all remaining” or should compute the effective quantity as the minimum of the requested amount and the current auctionQuantity, thereby eliminating the race condition. This change removes the ability for a front‑runner to force a revert by shrinking the available quantity by a negligible amount.

title: Exponential and logarithmic price adapters
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the exponential and logarithmic price adapters used by the auction contract. These adapters rely on the expWad and lnWad functions, which are implemented assuming 18 decimal fixed‑point precision. When the component token and the quote token have different decimal places, for example 18‑dp WETH sold against 6‑dp USDT, the adapter scales the price with a simple scalingFactor that matches the quote token decimals. Because expWad and lnWad are executed on values that are far smaller than 1e18, the assembly implementation collapses to a linear relationship instead of the intended exponential curve. As a result the calculated price is off by a factor proportional to the decimal mismatch. The contract then calls _calculateQuoteAssetQuantity, which multiplies the component amount by the incorrect price using preciseMul or preciseMulCeil. From a user’s perspective the sell order appears to succeed, but the amount of quote tokens received is significantly lower than expected, sometimes even zero. This breaks the economic assumptions of the auction, allowing a seller to receive an unfair price or an attacker to manipulate the curve to obtain a better rate. The issue manifests only when the token pair has mismatched decimals and the price change magnitude is small enough for the linear regime of expWad/lnWad. It was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who observed in Remix that expWad(1e6)‑WAD equals 1e6, expWad(5e6)‑WAD equals 5e6, etc., indicating a perfect linear scaling. The difficulty in spotting the bug stems from the fact that the core mathematical functions are written in low‑level assembly, hiding the precision loss from typical static analysis tools. To remediate the problem the scalingFactor should be normalised to 18‑dp precision before being applied, and the price calculation should use preciseMul after the exponentiation, ensuring that expWad and lnWad operate on full‑precision values and only the final result is scaled down to the quote token decimals. This change restores the intended exponential pricing behaviour and prevents users from receiving incorrect or missing funds.

title: Target raises can be highly damaging for dutch
description: Multi-component dutch auctions are fundamentally incompatible with target raises and will lead to inefficient pricing causing loss to set token. The AuctionRebalanceModuleV1 allows targets to be increased when all component targets have been met and there is still excess quote token. When combined with multiple components, it his highly likely that these target raises will lead to inefficient pricing which will cause loss to the set token. Consider the following a set token has the following composition that has target raises enabled: 40% USDC 30% WBTC 30% WETH The manager wishes to rebalance the set to the following using USDC as the quote token: 20% USDC 40% WBTC 40% WETH Assume the WETH portion of the execute within the first hour of the auction. The WBTC on the other hand doesn't execute until 12 hours in. Assume there is excess quote so the target is increased. The issue is that now because of the change in time, the WETH auction is now well above the market price. This buys the WETH for a large loss compared to the market price of WETH. Pricing after target raises will likely be heavily skewed from market prices for some components lead to set token losses
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way multi‑component Dutch auctions handle target raises within the AuctionRebalanceModuleV1. When a set token is configured with target raises, the module permits the target amount of the quote token to be increased after all component targets have been satisfied while there is still excess quote token remaining. In a multi‑component auction the different assets settle at different times; for example the WETH portion may be executed early in the auction while the WBTC portion may only settle many hours later. Because the contract does not reset the rebalanceStartTime when the target is raised, the later‑executing components continue to use the original auction start time and therefore trade at a price that is no longer aligned with the current market. This creates a situation where the price for the later component becomes heavily skewed, often far above the market price, causing the protocol to purchase the asset at an inflated cost. The impact is a loss of value for the set token: holders see the token NAV drop, the protocol may acquire assets at a discount to the set token’s own valuation, and the overall token price can appear to fall unexpectedly. The issue manifests only when target raises are enabled, the auction contains multiple components, and there is excess quote token that triggers a target increase. It is difficult to notice because the price deviation can be mistaken for normal market volatility and no explicit error is emitted. The bug was discovered during a formal audit of the rebalancing logic, where the auditor observed that the start time was never refreshed after a target raise, leading to stale pricing. To remediate the problem the contract should reset rebalanceStartTime whenever a target raise occurs, effectively restarting the Dutch auction for the remaining components so that each trade is priced against the current market. Alternatively, disabling target raises for multi‑component auctions would also prevent the mispricing scenario.

title: Malicious users can exploit the auction and
description: The SetToken can be minted and redeemed by anyone when it is not locked during rebalancing. This can allow malicious users to front-run and back-run the bidders and manipulate the auction outcome. When rebalancing, the token manager can configure if the SetToken is locked or not. If the SetToken is not locked, anyone can mint and redeem the SetToken using BasicIssuanceModule. The token manager can also configure the pricing mechanism via the priceAdapter. There are some mechanisms: • BoundedStepWise adapters: like Dutch Auction which the price can increase/decrease over time. Let's see an example: The current price of WETH is 1940 USDC. Total supply of the SetToken is 10. A Set Token with component WETH and current unit(1 WETH) wants to achieve target unit (0.5 WETH - 975 USDC). • Current unit: 1 WETH => Current notional: 10 WETH • Target unint: 0.5 WETH - 975 USDC => Target notional: (5 WETH - 9750 USDC) To achieve this, it needs to sell WETH to buy USDC. The manager starts rebalancing using linear price curve: start at $2000, lower to minimum $1900, take steps of $0.1 every minute. It also chooses USDC as the quote token. Assuming when the price of WETH reaches 1950 USDC, a bidder bids for all of the available WETH for the rebalance process, which is 0.5 WETH per Set Token or 5 WETH in total for 9750 USDC (5*1950). The expected result should be that the SetToken will meet the target and the rebalancing process will finish. The end position will be: • Expected position: 0.5 WETH - 975 USDC => Expected notional (5 WETH - 9750 USDC) However, the module is deployed on mainnet and polygon, a malicious user can front-run the bidder and mint the SetToken to make profit and disrupt the auction. The malicious user mints 10 SetToken using 10 WETH. It increases the total supply of the SetToken to 20. • After the malicious user front-run the bidder: – Current unit: 1 WETH => Current notional: 20 WETH. – Target unit: 0.5 WETH - 975 USDC => Target notional: (10 WETH - 19500 USDC) • After bidder bids 5 WETH for 9750 USDC: – Current: 0.75 WETH - 487.5 USDC => Current notional: (15 WETH - 9750 USDC) After that, the malicious user can back-run the bidding transaction and redeem his 10 SetToken for 7.5 ETH and 4875 USDC. Malicious user balance: • Before: 10 WETH = 19400 USDC • After: 7.5 WETH + 4875 USDC = 7.5 * 1940 + 4875 = 19425 USDC. The malicious user can make a profit of 25 USDC and disrupt the auction because the auction cannot finish as it should be. He cannot make a profit directly by bidding because the bidder may need to be whitelisted by the manager. In conclusion, if the price of auction is above the market price and a bid is placed, a malicious user can front-run and back-run the bidder and make a profit and disrupt the auction in the unlocked rebalancing process. The malicious user can make a profit and prevent the auction from meeting the target and finishing.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the ability to mint and redeem the SetToken while a rebalancing auction is in progress, provided the token manager has not locked the SetToken.
