The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditor observed that the _processPositionGlobal function modifies pending positions without applying the usual limit checks, and that the invariant only guards against underflow. Because the overflow only occurs under the rare combination of an invalid oracle version and a maker value near its limit, it can remain hidden until the market suddenly stops processing updates, making it hard to detect in normal operation. To remediate the flaw, the contract should introduce an “openable” value analogous to the existing “closable” safeguard, calculate the maximum allowable increase for a position, and enforce that the sum of settled position and openable amount never exceeds the global maker limit or utilization constraints. This ensures that both decreases and increases respect the market’s accounting invariants, preventing overflow and the resulting market lock‑up.

title: KeeperOracle.request adds only the first pair
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the KeeperOracle.request function, which is responsible for registering market and account pairs that need to be called back when a specific oracle version settles. The function checks whether the current oracle version (identified by a timestamp) has already been recorded and, if so, returns immediately before adding the new market and account to the internal callback sets. Because the early‑return statement is placed before the calls that push the market address into the global callback set and the account address into the local callback set, only the first request made for a given version is stored. Subsequent requests that occur in the same oracle version are silently ignored, meaning those markets and accounts never receive the settlement callback. This logical ordering error occurs whenever two or more requests are issued within the same timestamp – a situation that is highly probable in a multi‑market environment where the same KeeperOracle instance is shared. The impact is that affected markets do not execute their update logic and accounts do not receive the expected settlement, leading to missing or delayed state changes, potential fund lock‑up, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a request was submitted but the balance remains unchanged, or a market appears to have not been settled despite the oracle version having settled. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the request implementation, where the early‑return logic was identified as preventing the registration of additional callbacks. It is difficult to notice because the function still emits events and updates the version mapping, giving the impression that the request succeeded, while the crucial registration step is omitted. The bug belongs to the class of state‑update ordering errors or premature‑exit bugs, where a condition causes the function to exit before essential side‑effects are performed. To remediate the problem the addition of the market and account to the callback lists must be performed before the early‑return check, or the logic should be restructured so that the version check does not bypass the registration step. By ensuring that every request, regardless of whether the version has already been recorded, adds its pair to the callback sets, the protocol will correctly invoke settlement callbacks for all markets and accounts as intended, preserving the expected business logic and preventing funds from disappearing or settlements from being missed.

title: KeeperOracle.commit will revert and won't work
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the KeeperOracle contract that aggregates price‑feed requests from multiple Market contracts. When an oracle version is ready, KeeperOracle.commit iterates over every market that called request for that version and invokes each market’s update function via an internal _settle call. The update function is protected by a whenNotPaused modifier, so if any market in the callback list is paused, its update call reverts. Because commit does not isolate individual failures, the revert propagates and causes the entire commit transaction to fail. As a result, the oracle becomes temporarily bricked: no market can receive a price update, trading on all markets that share the same KeeperOracle stops, and the protocol cannot progress to the next oracle version. This also blocks the intended upgrade path for the oracle provider, which requires the latest version of the previous provider to be committed before a switch can be finalized. An additional, related issue is that the callback loop has no cap on the number of markets that can be queued for a given version. If many markets are authorized, the gas required to iterate through the list may exceed the block gas limit, causing commit to run out of gas and revert even when no market is paused. The root cause is the lack of error handling around the market.update call and the absence of a limit on callback queue size. Exploitation is straightforward: an admin or an attacker who can pause a single market can freeze all other markets that rely on the same KeeperOracle, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition. Users experience symptoms such as trades failing to settle, positions remaining open despite expected closure, balances appearing unchanged, and refunds not being issued because the price feed never updates. The impact is a loss of functionality across the protocol, potential locking of user funds, and an inability to upgrade or replace the oracle provider, which undermines the protocol’s reliability and trust. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer examined the commit logic and noticed that a revert in any market’s update would abort the whole process. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the revert only occurs when a market is paused—a state that may be rare or only temporary—so the problem can remain latent until an admin action triggers it. To remediate, the commit routine should catch and ignore individual market reverts, for example by wrapping the update call in a try/catch block, or by filtering out paused markets before invoking update. Additionally, the contract should enforce a reasonable limit on the number of markets that can be added to the callback queue per oracle version, or restrict the total number of authorized markets, to prevent gas‑limit exhaustion. These changes would isolate failures, preserve the ability of unaffected markets to continue trading, and maintain the upgrade path for the oracle provider.

title: No check for active L2 Sequencer
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the absence of a check for the active L2 sequencer when retrieving price data from Chainlink on roll‑up networks such as Arbitrum. In the TradingModule contract the function that returns a price pair calls the Chainlink oracles and validates only that the reported timestamps are within a configured freshness window and that the numeric values are positive. On L2, however, when the sequencer is down the whole chain is effectively paused; block timestamps stop advancing while the last oracle round remains unchanged. Because the contract does not query the SequencerUptimeFeed or any equivalent status indicator, the freshness check still passes and the stale price is treated as current. An attacker can therefore trigger a situation where the sequencer is halted, wait for the price feed to become outdated, and then execute trades or vault operations that rely on the outdated rate. Users interacting with the SingleSidedLPVaultBase or CrossCurrencyVault contracts will see their expected refunds or profit calculations deviate dramatically – for example a user may expect a positive return but receives zero or even a loss because the protocol is using a price that no longer reflects the market. The impact is a loss of funds for honest participants and an unfair advantage for a malicious actor who can manipulate the timing of trades around sequencer downtime. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s oracle handling logic against Chainlink’s recommended pattern, which explicitly includes a sequencer‑status guard. The bug is subtle because the on‑chain price freshness assertions still succeed, so no revert or obvious error is emitted, making it hard to notice from routine testing. To remediate, the contract should incorporate the standard Chainlink sequencer‑uptime check (for example by calling the SequencerUptimeFeed and reverting when the sequencer is reported down) before using any price data. This ensures that stale rates are never accepted, preserving the accounting assumptions of the vaults and protecting user balances from disappearing due to outdated oracle information.

title: reinvestReward() generates dust totalPool-
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the vault accounting logic treats rewards that are reinvested without minting new vault shares. In the vault, a depositor receives a number of shares that represent a proportional claim on the total pool of assets. The share amount is calculated as lpTokens multiplied by the current totalVaultSharesGlobal divided by totalPoolClaim, or, for the very first deposit, by a fixed internal precision constant. Because the calculation uses integer division, a deposit that is smaller than the internal token precision can be rounded down to zero shares. When totalVaultSharesGlobal is zero, any subsequent deposit will also result in zero shares, regardless of the amount deposited, because the denominator (totalPoolClaim) is non‑zero while the numerator (totalVaultSharesGlobal) remains zero. The reinvestReward() function exacerbates this problem: it adds the reward amount to totalPoolClaim but deliberately does not increase totalVaultSharesGlobal. If reinvestReward() is called before any user has deposited (or after all users have withdrawn, leaving totalVaultSharesGlobal at zero), the contract state ends up with a positive totalPoolClaim and a zero totalVaultSharesGlobal – a “dust” condition. From that point on, any new deposit will be evaluated against a zero‑share pool, causing the share calculation to round down to zero. Users therefore see their deposited tokens converted into no vault shares, meaning they receive no ownership stake, cannot withdraw rewards, and may even fail collateral checks that rely on vault shares as collateral. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the vault’s reward‑reinvestment flow, where the auditor noticed that the function updates only one side of the accounting equation. It is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error; the symptom is simply that deposits appear to succeed but the user’s balance of vault shares remains zero, which can be missed unless the share balance is explicitly inspected after a deposit. The root cause is a combination of integer‑division rounding (dust) and missing invariant enforcement in reinvestReward(): the function should never allow totalPoolClaim to increase while totalVaultSharesGlobal stays at zero. The recommended fix is to add a guard that requires totalVaultSharesGlobal to be greater than zero before allowing reward reinvestment, or to mint a proportional amount of vault shares alongside the increase of totalPoolClaim, thereby preserving the invariant that totalPoolClaim and totalVaultSharesGlobal grow together. This ensures that every token deposited translates into a non‑zero share amount and that the vault’s accounting remains consistent, preventing users from losing their stake or the protocol from entering an abnormal state.

title: BalancerWeightedAuraVault.sol wrongly assumes
description:
BalancerWeightedAuraVault.sol which is used specifically for weighted balancer pools wrongly uses totalSupply all the time to get the total supply of the pool, but this would not be true for newer weighted pools.

Balancer pools have different methods to get their total supply of minted LP tokens, which is also specified in the docs here https://docs.balancer.fi/concepts/advanced/valuing-bpt/valuing-bpt.html#getting-bpt-supply. The docs specifies the fact that totalSupply is only used for older stable and weighted pools, and should not be used without checking it first, since the newer pools have pre-minted BPT and getActualSupply should be used in that case. Most of the time, the assumption would be that only the new composable stable pools use the getActualSupply, but that is not the case, since even the newer weighted pools have and use the getActualSupply. To give you few examples of newer weighted pools that use getActualSupply https://etherscan.io/address/0x9f9d900462492d4c21e9523ca95a7cd86142f298 https://etherscan.io/address/0x3ff3a210e57cfe679d9ad1e9ba6453a716c56a2e https://etherscan.io/address/0xcf7b51ce5755513d4be016b0e28d6edeffa1d52a the last one also being on Aura finance. Because of that, the interaction with newer weighted pools and also the future weighted pools would not be accurate since the wrong total supply is used and calculations like _mintVaultShares and _calculateLPTokenValue would both be inaccurate, which would hurt the protocol and the users.

Impact is a high one since the calculation of shares and the value of the LP tokens is very important for the protocol, and any miscalculations could hurt the protocol and the users a lot.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect assumption in BalancerWeightedAuraVault.sol that the totalSupply function of a Balancer weighted pool always returns the current amount of minted BPT (Balancer Pool Tokens). In reality, Balancer introduced newer weighted pools that pre‑mint BPT and expose the actual circulating supply through a separate getActualSupply function. The contract unconditionally calls totalSupply to obtain the pool’s token supply, which is only valid for legacy stable and weighted pools. When the vault interacts with a newer weighted pool, the totalSupply value may be stale or represent a different accounting figure, causing the internal calculations that determine how many vault shares to mint (_mintVaultShares) and how to value LP tokens (_calculateLPTokenValue) to be inaccurate. An attacker or any user does not need to perform a complex exploit; the bug is triggered automatically whenever a deposit or withdrawal is processed against a newer weighted pool. The impact is that users may receive fewer vault shares than they are entitled to on deposit, or the protocol may credit excessive shares, leading to a mismatch between the recorded vault balance and the actual underlying assets. This mismatch can manifest to the user as a missing or reduced balance after a transaction, a withdrawal that returns less than expected, or, in extreme cases, a withdrawal that appears to succeed while the protocol’s accounting shows a deficit. The issue occurs only when the vault is connected to a newer weighted pool – for example, pools deployed at addresses 0x9f9d900462492d4c21e9523ca95a7cd86142f298, 0x3ff3a210e57cfe679d9ad1e9ba6453a716c56a2e, or 0xcf7b51ce5755513d4be016b0e28d6edeffa1d52a – all of which use getActualSupply. It affects the protocol’s accounting logic, liquidity providers who deposit through the vault, and any downstream users relying on correct share valuation. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that cross‑referenced the Balancer documentation on BPT valuation and observed that the contract never checks which supply method to use. Because totalSupply still returns a numeric value, the bug does not cause immediate reverts or obvious errors, making it hard to notice without detailed analysis of pool versions. To remediate, the contract should first detect whether the target pool implements getActualSupply (e.g., via ERC165 or interface detection) and use that method for newer pools, falling back to totalSupply only for legacy pools. This pattern of relying on an outdated external contract interface is a generic class of bug where assumptions about third‑party contracts become invalid after upgrades, leading to incorrect financial calculations and potential loss of funds.

title: Some curve pools can not be used as a single
description:
For single sided curve strategy contest docs says that any curve pool should be ok to be used. However, some pools are not adaptable to the Curve2TokenPoolMixin abstract contract.

The contract assumes the existence of three types of pool scenarios. In one scenario, the pool address itself serves as the LP token. In another scenario, the LP token is obtained by querying the lp_token() or token() function. However, in some cases where potential integration with Notional is possible, certain pools lack a direct method to retrieve the underlying LP token. For instance, the sETH-ETH pool, which presents a promising option for a single-sided strategy in ETH vaults, does not offer public variables to access the underlying LP token. Although the pool contract contains the token variable that returns the LP token of the pool, this variable is not publicly accessible. Consequently, in such cases, querying the LP token directly from the pool is not feasible, and it becomes necessary to provide the LP token address as input.

Here the example contracts where neither of the options are available: sETH-ETH: https://etherscan.io/address/0xc5424b857f758e906013f3555dad202e4bdb4567 hBTC-WBTC: https://etherscan.io/address/0x4ca9b3063ec5866a4b82e437059d2c43d1be596f All curve pools that can be used as a single sided strategy for notional leveraged vaults considered to be used but some pools are not adaptable thus I will label this as medium.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incompatibility between the Curve2TokenPoolMixin abstract contract used by the Notional single‑sided strategy and certain Curve pool implementations. The abstract contract expects to be able to obtain the LP token address in one of three ways: (i) the pool contract itself is also the LP token, (ii) the pool exposes an lp_token() or token() view function, or (iii) the pool provides a public variable named token that returns the LP token. Some Curve pools, such as the sETH‑ETH pool (0xc5424b857f758e906013f3555dad202e4bdb4567) and the hBTC‑WBTC pool (0x4ca9b3063ec5866a4b82e437059d2c43d1be596f), do not expose any of these interfaces; the token variable exists only internally and is not marked public. As a result, when the strategy contract is instantiated with such a pool, it cannot automatically discover the LP token address. The constructor therefore leaves the LP token address unset (zero) or requires the caller to supply it manually. If the address is left unset, subsequent calls that mint, transfer, or withdraw LP tokens will interact with the zero address, causing transactions to revert or, in some edge cases, silently succeed with no effect. Users who deposit assets into the vault expecting a single‑sided exposure to the pool will see their balances remain unchanged, receive no LP tokens, or be unable to claim withdrawals, effectively locking their funds. The issue manifests only when a vault is configured to use a Curve pool that does not conform to the assumed interface, i.e., when the pool lacks a public method to retrieve its LP token. It was discovered during a manual audit of the Notional Update 4 codebase, where the documentation claimed “any Curve pool should be ok,” but testing against the mentioned pools revealed the missing interface. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles and passes basic unit tests; the failure appears only at runtime when the pool address is supplied, making it easy to overlook. To remediate, the strategy should treat the LP token address as an explicit constructor argument supplied by the trusted vault owner, and the internal logic that attempts to auto‑detect the token should be removed. This change eliminates the reliance on a specific pool ABI and ensures that the contract can correctly interact with any Curve pool, preserving expected accounting behavior and preventing user funds from becoming inaccessible.

title: depositFromNotional function is payable, which
description:
The function depositFromNotional used in BaseStrategyVault.sol is payable, which means that it should accept Ether, but in reality it will revert every time when msg.value is > than 0 in any of existing strategy.

depositFromNotional is a function used in BaseStrategyVault.sol for every strategy, to deposit from notional to a specific strategy. As you can see this line/blob/main/leveraged-vaults/contracts/vaults/common/BaseStrategyVault.sol#L166-L173 which means that it is expected to be used along with msg.value being > than 0. This function would call _depositFromNotional which is different on any strategy used, but let's take the most simple case, since all of them will be the same in the end, the case of CrossCurrencyVault.sol. In CrossCurrencyVault.sol, _depositFromNotional would later call _executeTrade ontracts/vaults/CrossCurrencyVault.sol#L184 which would use the TradeHandler b/main/leveraged-vaults/contracts/vaults/common/BaseStrategyVault.sol#L124 If we look into the TradeHandler library, _executeTrade would delegatecall into the implementation of TradingModule.sol to executeTrade function, as can be seen here ontracts/trading/TradeHandler.sol#L41-L42 If we look into the executeTrade function in TradingModule.sol we can see that this function does not have the payable keyword, which mean that it will not accept msg.value > than 0 https://githding/TradingModule.sol#L169-L193 The big and important thing to know about delegate call is that, msg.sender and msg.value will always be kept when you delegate call, so the problem that arise here is the fact that the calls made to depositFromNotional with msg.value > 0, would always revert when it gets to this delegatecall, in every strategy, since the function that it delegates to, doesn't have the payable keyword, and since msg.value is always kept through the delegate calls, the call would just revert. This would be the case for all the strategies since they all uses _executeTrade or _executeTradeWithDynamicSlippage in a way or another, so every payable function that would use any of these 2 functions from the TradeHandler.sol library would revert all the time, if msg.value is > 0.

Impact is a high one, since strategy using pools that need to interact with Ether would be useless and the whole functionality would be broken.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a payable‑function mismatch that occurs in the depositFromNotional workflow of the BaseStrategyVault contract. depositFromNotional is declared payable and therefore accepts Ether, but it forwards the call to a strategy‑specific _depositFromNotional implementation which eventually invokes TradeHandler._executeTrade (or _executeTradeWithDynamicSlippage). These helper functions use delegatecall to execute the executeTrade function defined in TradingModule.sol. Because delegatecall preserves msg.sender and msg.value, the Ether sent to depositFromNotional is still attached when the delegatecall reaches executeTrade. However executeTrade is not marked payable, so the EVM rejects any call that carries a non‑zero msg.value and reverts the transaction. The root cause is the inconsistent payable modifier across the call chain: an outer function is payable while the ultimate implementation that receives the call is not. An attacker or any user who tries to deposit Ether through depositFromNotional will see the transaction revert, receiving an “execution reverted” error and no change to their balance. This behaviour breaks the intended business logic that certain strategies need Ether to interact with external pools, effectively rendering those strategies unusable. The issue manifests whenever depositFromNotional is invoked with msg.value > 0 on any strategy that relies on TradeHandler’s delegatecall path, which includes all current strategies in the codebase. Users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself are affected because deposits cannot be processed, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition for Ether‑based strategies. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that traced the call flow from BaseStrategyVault.sol through TradeHandler and TradingModule.sol and noticed the missing payable keyword on executeTrade. It can be hard to notice because the outer function’s payable attribute gives the impression that the whole call chain can handle Ether, while the revert only occurs deep inside a delegatecall, which may be overlooked in testing. The bug belongs to the class of “payable delegatecall mismatch” or “inconsistent payable modifiers” that violate accounting assumptions that a deposit of Ether should increase the contract’s balance. To remediate, the executeTrade function should be marked payable, or alternatively the payable keyword should be removed from depositFromNotional if the protocol does not intend to accept Ether through that path. Ensuring that every function in the delegatecall chain shares a consistent payable status will prevent the revert and restore the expected behavior where a user’s Ether deposit is correctly recorded and used by the strategy.

title: Emergency withdraw might not be enough if
description:
that it can be called when a balancer pool enables "enableRecoveryMode" and maybe it can be called when the pool has an exploit and it needs to be unwinded immediately. However, if the actual pool is a nested pool that has an another pool lp as its underlying and that pool has the exploit or "enableRecoveryMode" toggle on then the emergency withdraw will not be able to exit the position properly since the actual pool that has the emergency issue is the nested pool.

Assume that there is a CPS-wstETH-rETH, WETH weighted pool where as this weighted pool has only 2 tokens which is the weth token and the cps-wsteth-reth bpt token. If the emergency withdraw is called the vault will receive those two tokens. However, if the actual problem (maybe exploit or recovery mode toggle on) happens in the underlying pool then the emergency withdraw will not be able to cover the emergency situation.

It is likely to have these type of pools and it might make sense to deposit them. However, the emergency withdraw should be properly seated for these type pools. Pool that has a notional finance assets is listed is eligible for single sided strategy, and in such pools the emergency withdraw can be broken I will label this as medium.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the emergency‑withdraw mechanism of a Balancer‑style vault that supports nested pools. The function is designed to let an authorized emergency role pull out all assets from a pool when a critical condition such as enableRecoveryMode or an on‑chain exploit is detected. The flaw arises because the implementation only extracts the top‑level pool’s tokens – in the example a weighted pool that holds WETH and a BPT token representing an underlying CPS‑wstETH‑rETH pool – and does not recursively unwind any underlying pool that may itself be in recovery mode or compromised. Consequently, if the underlying pool is the one experiencing the emergency, the vault receives the outer tokens but the assets locked inside the inner pool remain inaccessible. This situation can occur whenever a pool is composed of another pool’s LP token, a pattern that is common for composable finance products. Users who have deposited into such nested structures, as well as the protocol’s liquidity providers and governance, are affected because their funds may appear to be withdrawn while in reality a portion of the capital stays trapped, leading to a loss of available liquidity and potential financial loss. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the emergency‑withdraw function and Balancer’s enableRecoveryMode flag, noting that the code does not check or propagate the emergency call to nested pools. The bug is subtle: the transaction does not revert and the vault’s balance shows the expected top‑level tokens, so developers and auditors may assume the emergency exit succeeded, while the hidden inner assets are silently frozen. To remediate, the emergency exit logic should be extended to detect nested pool relationships and either recursively call the underlying pool’s emergency withdraw or provide a mechanism for the emergency role to unwind the entire composition in a single operation. This change restores the intended safety guarantee that an emergency withdraw fully recovers all user funds, regardless of pool nesting, and aligns the contract’s behavior with the business rule that users must be able to retrieve their assets when a pool is flagged for recovery or compromised.

title: ETH can be sold during reinvestment
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic flaw in the token validation routine that is meant to stop a vault from selling its native ETH during the reinvestment process. The contract implements an internal function that returns true for tokens that are considered invalid reward assets, and the reinvestment code checks this function before allowing a trade. In the Curve implementation the function lists Deployments.ALT_ETH_ADDRESS – a sentinel value (0xEeeeeEeeeEeEeeEeEeEeeEEEeeeeEeeeeeeeEEeE) that is not the actual address used for ETH in trades. The trading utility, however, represents ETH with either Deployments.WETH (the wrapped token) or Deployments.ETH_ADDRESS (address(0)). Because the validation list does not contain these real ETH identifiers, a call to the reinvestment function can still pass an ETH trade, meaning the bot can sell the vault’s ETH balance. The Balancer implementation suffers a similar problem: it only blocks Deployments.WETH but omits Deployments.ETH_ADDRESS, so a direct ETH trade also bypasses the guard. The flaw is discovered during a manual audit that compared the token constants used in the guard with those used by the trading helper. It is subtle because the guard appears to reference an ETH constant, giving a false sense of protection, and the code paths that actually perform the trade are hidden in a utility library. When the guard is bypassed, the vault may unintentionally or maliciously sell its non‑reward ETH assets during reinvestment, reducing the vault’s ETH holdings. From a user’s perspective the deposited ETH may disappear or the balance shown after a reinvestment may be lower than expected, leading to confusion such as “my vault balance is zero after a trade” or “I expected a refund but got nothing”. The impact is a loss of user funds and a breach of the accounting assumptions that the vault never trades its base ETH during reinvestment. The issue occurs whenever the reinvestment function is invoked with a trade that involves ETH, which is common in automated strategies that harvest rewards and then reinvest. To remediate, the guard should explicitly list both Deployments.WETH and Deployments.ETH_ADDRESS (or the canonical ETH constant used by the trading library) as invalid reward tokens, ensuring that any attempt to trade ETH during reinvestment is rejected. This change restores the intended invariant that the vault’s ETH cannot be sold during the reinvestment step, aligning the contract’s behavior with its business logic and protecting user assets.

title: BPT LP Token could be sold off during re-investment
description:
BPT LP Token could be sold off during the re-investment process. BPT LP Tokens must not be sold to external DEXs under any circumstance because:
• They are used to redeem the underlying assets from the pool when someone exits the vault
• The BPTs represent the total value of the vault

Within the ConvexStakingMixin._isInvalidRewardToken function, the implementation ensures that the LP Token (CURVE_POOL_TOKEN) is not intentionally or accidentally sold during the reinvestment process.
ontracts/vaults/curve/ConvexStakingMixin.sol#L64
File: ConvexStakingMixin.sol
```solidity
function _isInvalidRewardToken(address token) internal override view returns (bool) {
    return (
        token == TOKEN_1 ||
        token == TOKEN_2 ||
        token == address(CURVE_POOL_TOKEN) ||
        token == address(CONVEX_REWARD_POOL) ||
        token == address(CONVEX_BOOSTER) ||
        token == Deployments.ALT_ETH_ADDRESS
    );
}
```
For non-composable Balancer pools, the pool tokens do not consist of the BPT token. Thus, it needs to be explicitly defined within the _isInvalidRewardToken function.
ontracts/vaults/balancer/mixins/AuraStakingMixin.sol#L38
File: AuraStakingMixin.sol
```solidity
function _isInvalidRewardToken(address token) internal override view returns (bool) {
    return (
        token == TOKEN_1 ||
        token == TOKEN_2 ||
        token == TOKEN_3 ||
        token == TOKEN_4 ||
        token == TOKEN_5 ||
        token == address(AURA_BOOSTER) ||
        token == address(AURA_REWARD_POOL) ||
        token == address(Deployments.WETH)
    );
}
```
Per the sponsor's clarification below, the contracts should protect against the bot doing unintended things (including acting maliciously) due to coding errors, which is one of the main reasons for having the _isInvalidRewardToken function. Thus, https://discord.com/channels/812037309376495636/1175450365395751023/1175781082336067655
LP tokens (BPT) might be accidentally or maliciously sold off by the bots during the re-investment process. BPT LP Tokens must not be sold to external DEXs under any circumstance because:
• They are used to redeem the underlying assets from the pool when someone exits the vault
• The BPTs represent the total value of the vault
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unintended ability for the vault’s reinvestment routine to sell the Balancer Pool Token (BPT) that represents the total value of the vault. The root cause is an omission in the _isInvalidRewardToken function, which is supposed to enumerate all token addresses that must never be transferred to external decentralized exchanges during reward‑swapping. For certain non‑composable Balancer pools the BPT address is not included in this whitelist, so the contract treats the LP token like any other reward token and permits a swap. An attacker or a buggy automation bot can therefore invoke the reinvestment path, trigger a swap that sends the BPT to a DEX, and receive another asset in return. Because BPT tokens are required to redeem the underlying assets when a user exits the vault, selling them removes the redemption right and effectively destroys the vault’s claim on its underlying liquidity. From the user’s perspective the vault balance appears to shrink or become zero after a reinvestment, and a withdrawal request may return no assets or only a fraction of the expected amount. The impact is a loss of funds for all vault participants, a breach of the accounting invariant that the vault’s token supply equals the value of the pooled assets, and a potential loss of confidence in the protocol. The issue manifests only during the reinvestment step when reward tokens are processed; if the BPT token is not explicitly blocked, the swap proceeds silently, making the bug hard to notice because no explicit error is thrown and the token transfer may be recorded as a normal trade. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the ConvexStakingMixin and AuraStakingMixin contracts, where the reviewer observed that the BPT address was missing from the invalid‑token list. To remediate, the contract should be updated so that the BPT token address is added to the _isInvalidRewardToken return condition, thereby preventing any swap or transfer of the LP token during reinvestment. Additional safeguards such as explicit checks before token transfers and restricting the swap function to known reward tokens can further harden the system against accidental or malicious token sales.

title: Leverage Vault on sidechains that support Curve
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the Leverage Vault contracts deployed on Arbitrum and Optimism incorrectly identify the version of the Curve pool they interact with. The constructor sets IS_CURVE_V2 only when the chain ID equals the Ethereum mainnet constant; on side‑chains the flag remains false even when the pool implements the Curve V2 interface. Because the flag is false, the internal _joinPoolAndStake function always calls the Curve V1 add_liquidity signature, which does not accept the use_eth boolean. Curve V2 pools expect the caller to indicate whether native ETH is being supplied; when the flag is missing the call defaults to use_eth = false, causing the pool to try to pull WETH from the vault and then unwrap it. The vault, however, only holds native ETH and never provides WETH, so the pool’s internal transfer logic reverts. As a result, any deposit transaction to the vault on those side‑chains fails, users see their transaction revert and receive no LP tokens, and the vault’s core deposit functionality is effectively broken. This condition occurs only on deployments where the contract is not on Ethereum mainnet, i.e., on Arbitrum and Optimism, and only for pools that are of the Curve V2 type. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the constructor logic and the pool‑joining code, where the conditional check against a hard‑coded mainnet chain ID was noted. Because the failure manifests as a revert during a deposit, it may be missed if testing is performed only on mainnet or if only Curve V1 pools are used. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect chain‑specific feature flag” or “version‑detection mismatch” that leads to calling an incompatible external contract interface. The impact is a loss of revenue for the protocol since users cannot deposit, and the vault cannot generate fees. To remediate, the contract should correctly detect the pool version on each supported chain, for example by probing for a V2‑only function such as gamma() or by using a registry that works on side‑chains, and set IS_CURVE_V2 accordingly before invoking add_liquidity. This ensures the correct function signature with the use_eth flag is used, allowing native ETH deposits to succeed.

title: Division by Zero in CvgRewards::_distributeCvgRewards
bug_full: The vulnerability is a division‑by‑zero error that occurs in the reward distribution routine of the CVG staking system. When the internal function that aggregates the total weight of all gauges (_setTotalWeight) computes a sum of zero – which can happen if no gauge receives any vote – the variable totalWeightLocked is set to zero. Later, the function _distributeCvgRewards reads this value into a local variable _totalWeight and uses it as the divisor in the expression (stakingInflation * gaugeWeight) / _totalWeight for each gauge. Because Solidity does not allow division by zero, the transaction reverts, aborting the entire distribution loop. The revert prevents the protocol’s state machine from advancing to the next cycle state (State.CONTROL_TOWER_SYNC). As a result, the cycle never reaches the unlock phase, and any CVG tokens that users have locked in NFT positions remain permanently non‑withdrawable. The impact is a denial‑of‑service that effectively freezes user funds and stops reward accrual, violating the protocol’s accounting assumption that total weight is always positive for proportional reward calculation. The bug manifests only when the total weight is exactly zero, a condition that may be rare in normal operation and therefore easy to miss during testing; the failure appears as a generic transaction revert or a “LOCKED” error when calling burnPosition, without an obvious indication of a division‑by‑zero. It was discovered during a manual audit of the reward logic, where the auditor noticed that the code does not guard against a zero divisor. The issue belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic errors that lead to runtime exceptions and can be exploited by an attacker who deliberately ensures that no gauge receives votes, thereby forcing totalWeightLocked to zero and freezing all locked CVG. To remediate, the contract should detect a zero total weight before performing the division and treat the reward for that cycle as zero, or skip the distribution loop entirely, allowing the cycle to progress and users to eventually unlock their tokens. This simple guard restores the intended business logic that rewards are proportional to gauge weight while preserving the ability to withdraw locked assets.

title: LockPositionService::increaseLockTime Inaccurate
description:
LockPositionService::increaseLockTime uses block.timestamp for locking tokens, resulting in potential over-extension of the lock period. Specifically, if a user locks tokens near the end of a cycle, the lock duration might extend an additional week more than intended. For instance, locking for one cycle at the end of cycle N could result in an unlock time at the end of cycle N+2, instead of at the start of cycle N+2. This means that all the while specifying that their $CVG should be locked for the next cycle, the $CVG stays locked for two cycles.
The function increaseLockTime inaccurately calculates the lock duration by using block.timestamp, thus not aligned to the starts of cycles. This discrepancy leads to a longer-than-expected lock period, especially when a lock is initiated near the end of a cycle. This misalignment means that users are unintentionally extending their lock period and affecting their asset management strategies.
Scenario:
• Alice decides to lock her tokens for one cycle near the end of cycle N.
• The lock duration calculation extends the lock to the end of cycle N+2, rather than starting the unlock process at the start of cycle N+2.
• Alice's tokens are locked for an additional week beyond her expectation.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inaccurate calculation of the lock expiration time in the LockPositionService increaseLockTime function. The contract determines the unlock timestamp by adding a user‑specified lock duration to the current block.timestamp, which is a raw Unix time value that does not necessarily align with the protocol’s weekly cycle boundaries. Because the calculation does not round the start time to the beginning of the next week, a lock that is created shortly before the end of a cycle can be extended by almost an entire additional week. In practice this means that a user who intends to lock tokens for one cycle may find their assets remaining locked until the end of the following cycle, effectively extending the lock by one extra week. The bug occurs whenever the lock is initiated in the tail end of a cycle, i.e., when block.timestamp is close to the cycle’s cutoff. It affects any holder of the CVG token who uses the increaseLockTime function, because their expected unlock date is longer than advertised, leading to unexpected immobilisation of funds, missed withdrawal windows, and potential loss of yield or liquidity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the time‑based logic of the service and identified that the lock duration calculation does not incorporate a modulo operation to align with the weekly period. The problem is subtle because the transaction succeeds and the contract records a valid future timestamp, so there is no explicit error; however, the UI may display the intended unlock cycle while the on‑chain state reflects a later timestamp, making the discrepancy hard to notice without inspecting the raw unlock time. This class of bug belongs to time‑alignment or rounding errors in smart contracts that rely on periodic intervals. To remediate the issue the lock time should be normalized to the start of the next week, for example by computing (block.timestamp % WEEK) + lockDuration and then adding the remainder needed to reach the next multiple of WEEK, ensuring that the lock always expires at the beginning of the intended cycle. Conceptually the fix forces the lock period to be a whole number of weeks, matching user expectations and the protocol’s accounting rules, and prevents tokens from disappearing from the user’s control for an unintended extra week.

title: Delegation Limitation in Voting Power Management
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a voting‑power delegation mechanism that enforces two immutable caps: a maximum number of token IDs that may be delegated to a single address (maxTokenIdsDelegated) and a maximum number of delegatees that a single token may assign (maxMgDelegatees). The function delegateMgCvg is intended to both create a new delegation and to modify or delete an existing one, but it first checks the two caps before any state change. When either cap is already reached, the require statements reject the call with the errors TOO_MUCH_DELEGATEES or TOO_MUCH_MG_TOKEN_ID_DELEGATED, even if the caller only wants to adjust the percentage of an existing delegation or to remove a single delegatee. Consequently, token owners cannot increase, decrease, or delete a specific delegation once the limits are hit, forcing them to either leave the delegation unchanged or to remove all of their delegations at once. This inflexibility can arise after the DAO changes the caps downward, after many users have already delegated to the same address, or simply when the hard limits are reached during normal operation. From a user’s perspective the UI will still display the existing delegation, but any transaction that attempts to change the percentage or to revoke a single delegatee will revert, leading to the expectation “my vote should be updated” being violated by a silent failure. The impact is that voting power becomes effectively locked, governance participation may be reduced, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about dynamic delegation are broken. The issue was discovered during a security audit and reproduced with unit tests that deliberately hit the caps and then attempted updates, which consistently reverted. It is hard to notice because the function signature suggests full CRUD capability, yet the cap checks silently block updates without a clear UI warning. The bug belongs to the class of “hard‑cap delegation lock” or “immutable limit update blockage” where business‑logic constraints prevent legitimate state transitions. To remediate, the contract should separate the creation of new delegations from the modification of existing ones, allowing updates to an existing delegatee even when the overall delegatee count is at its maximum, or provide a dedicated function that bypasses the cap checks for updates and removals while preserving the overall limit on distinct delegatees.

title: cvgControlTower and veCVG lock timing
description:
When creating a locked CVG position, there are two more or less independent locks that are created. The first is in lockingPositionService and the other is in veCVG. LockingPositionService operates on cycles (which are not finite length) while veCVG always rounds down to the absolute nearest week. The disparity between these two accounting mechanism leads to conflicting scenario that the lock on LockingPositionService can be expired while the lock on veCVG isn't (and vice versa). Additionally tokens with expired locks on LockingPositionService cannot be extended. The result is that the token is expired but can't be withdrawn. The result of this is that the expired token must wait to be unstaked and then restaked, cause loss of user yield and voting power while the token is DOS'd.
Cycles operate using block.timestamp when setting lastUpdateTime on the new cycle in L345. It also requires that at least 7 days has passed since this update to roll the cycle forward in L205. The result is that the cycle can never be exactly 7 days long and the start/end of the cycle will constantly fluctuate.
Meanwhile when veCVG is calculating the unlock time it uses the week rounded down as shown in L328.
We can demonstrate with an example:
Assume the first CVG cycle is started at block.timestamp == 1,000,000. This means our first cycle ends at 1,604,800. A user deposits for a single cycle at 1,400,000. A lock is created for cycle 2 which will unlock at 2,209,600.
The lock on veCVG does not match this though. Instead its calculation will yield:
(1,400,000 + 2 * 604,800) / 604,800 = 4
4 * 604,800 = 2,419,200
As seen these are mismatched and the token won't be withdrawable until much after it should be due to the check in veCVG L404.
This DOS will prevent the expired lock from being unstaked and restaked which causes loss of yield.
The opposite issue can also occur. For each cycle that is slightly longer than expected the veCVG lock will become further and further behind the cycle lock on lockingPositionService. This can also cause a dos and yield loss because it could prevent user from extending valid locks due to the checks in L367 of veCVG.
An example of this:
Assume a user locks for 96 weeks (58,060,800). Over the course of that year, it takes an average of 2 hours between the end of each cycle and when the cycle is rolled over. This effectively extends our cycle time from 604,800 to 612,000 (+7200). Now after 95 cycles, the user attempts to increase their lock duration. veCVG and lockingPositionService will now be completely out of sync:
After 95 cycles the current time would be:
612,000 * 95 = 58,140,000
Whereas veCVG lock ended:
612,000 * 96 = 58,060,800
According to veCVG the position was unlocked at 58,060,800 and therefore increasing the lock time will revert due to L367
The result is another DOS that will cause the user loss of yield. During this time the user would also be excluded from taking place in any votes since their veCVG lock is expired.
Unlock DOS that cause loss of yield to the user
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between two independent lock accounting mechanisms used by the protocol. When a user creates a locked CVG position, LockingPositionService records the lock in terms of cycles that are advanced based on block.timestamp, while the veCVG contract determines the unlock time by rounding down to the nearest whole week. Because the cycle length in LockingPositionService is not a fixed 7‑day interval – it requires only that at least seven days have passed before a new cycle can be started – the actual cycle duration drifts over time. Meanwhile veCVG always snaps the unlock timestamp to an exact multiple of a week. This drift creates scenarios where the LockingPositionService lock is considered expired while the veCVG lock is still active, or the opposite. When the LockingPositionService lock is expired but the veCVG lock is still active, the protocol blocks the user from withdrawing the tokens because the veCVG contract rejects the operation, and the tokens cannot be extended either. Conversely, when veCVG reports an earlier unlock than LockingPositionService, attempts to extend the lock are reverted by veCVG checks. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are a token that cannot be withdrawn or restaked, a balance that appears unchanged, zero yield accrual, and loss of voting power despite the expectation that the lock has expired. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition that forces the user to wait for an unstake‑and‑restake cycle, resulting in lost yield and reduced governance influence. The issue occurs under normal operation whenever cycles are not exactly seven days, which is effectively always due to the reliance on block.timestamp and the asynchronous roll‑over logic. All CVG token holders who rely on locking for yield or voting are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the lock‑expiration logic in both contracts and identified the divergent time calculations. It is hard to notice because each contract functions correctly in isolation and the inconsistency only manifests after multiple cycles, making it appear as a rare edge case. The recommended remediation is to align the two mechanisms by using a single, deterministic time base – for example, adopting the week‑rounded approach used by veCVG for both contracts or replacing block.timestamp‑based cycles with an absolute measurement that guarantees exact seven‑day periods. By synchronising the lock accounting, the protocol can prevent the lock‑expiration mismatch, eliminate the denial‑of‑service scenario, and restore expected yield and voting behavior.

title: SdtRewardReceiver#_withdrawRewards has
bug_full: The vulnerability is a slippage‑check bypass that occurs in the reward‑withdrawal function when the contract swaps SDT for cvgSDT. The code obtains the minimum acceptable output (_min_dy) by calling the pool’s get_dy view function and passes that value directly to the exchange call. Because get_dy computes the exact amount that would be received given the pool’s current balances, it reflects the state at the moment of execution, not the state at the time the user’s transaction was created. An attacker who can front‑run or sandwich the withdrawal can modify the pool’s reserves just before the exchange call, causing the price to shift dramatically. When get_dy is invoked after the attacker’s manipulation it returns a much lower output amount, which the contract then uses as the minimum acceptable amount. Consequently the exchange call never reverts and the user’s swap executes at the manipulated price, often delivering far fewer cvgSDT tokens than expected or even zero. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful reward withdrawal but the token balance either remains unchanged or drops far below the anticipated amount, violating the expectation that a minimum‑output check protects against adverse price movement. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that get_dy is a relative output calculated at runtime and therefore cannot serve as a reliable slippage guard. The bug is hard to spot because the code appears to enforce a safety check, yet the check is effectively a no‑op under adversarial conditions. The impact is that SDT rewards can be sandwiched and the entire reward balance may be lost, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions that rewards are exchanged at a fair rate. The affected parties are any user withdrawing rewards, the protocol’s reward distribution logic, and token holders who rely on accurate accounting. To remediate the problem the contract should allow the caller to specify a concrete _min_dy value or use an external price oracle or time‑weighted average price that is not manipulable within the same transaction, thereby restoring a genuine slippage protection mechanism.

title: Division difference can result in a revert
description:
Different ordering of calculations are used to compute ysTotal in different situations. This causes the totalShares tracked to be less than the claimable amount of shares
ysTotal is calculated differently when adding to totalSuppliesTracking and when computing balanceOfYsCvgAt. When adding to totalSuppliesTracking, the calculation of ysTotal is as follows:
```solidity
uint256 cvgLockAmount = (amount * ysPercentage) / MAX_PERCENTAGE;
uint256 ysTotal = (lockDuration * cvgLockAmount) / MAX_LOCK;
```
In balanceOfYsCvgAt, ysTotal is calculated as follows
```solidity
uint256 ysTotal = (((endCycle - startCycle) * amount * ysPercentage) / MAX_PERCENTAGE) / MAX_LOCK;
```
This difference allows the balanceOfYsCvgAt to be greater than what is added to totalSuppliesTracking
This breaks the shares accounting of the treasury rewards. Some user's will get more than the actual intended rewards while the last withdrawals will result in a revert
totalSuppliesTracking calculation
cts/Locking/LockingPositionService.sol#L339-L345
In increaseLockTimeAndAmount
cvg/contracts/Locking/LockingPositionService.sol#L465-L470
_ysCvgCheckpoint
cvg/contracts/Locking/LockingPositionService.sol#L577-L584
balanceOfYsCvgAt calculation
cvg/contracts/Locking/LockingPositionService.sol#L673-L675
poc:
startCycle 357
endCycle 420
lockDuration 63
amount 2
ysPercentage 80
Calculation in totalSuppliesTracking gives:
```solidity
uint256 cvgLockAmount = (2 * 80) / 100; == 1
uint256 ysTotal = (63 * 1) / 96; == 0
```
Calculation in balanceOfYsCvgAt gives:
```solidity
uint256 ysTotal = ((63 * 2 * 80) / 100) / 96; == 10080 / 100 / 96 == 1
```
Example Scenario
Alice, Bob and Jake locks cvg for 1 TDE and obtains rounded up balanceOfYsCvgAt. A user who is aware of this issue can exploit this issue further by using increaseLockAmount with small amount values by which the total difference difference b/w the user's calculated balanceOfYsCvgAt and the accounted amount in totalSuppliesTracking can be increased. Bob and Jake claims the reward at the end of reward cycle. When Alice attempts to claim rewards, it reverts since there is not enough reward to be sent.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an inconsistency in the way the contract computes the total amount of coverage shares (ysTotal) in two separate code paths. In the function that updates the global tracking of total supplies, the calculation multiplies the locked amount by the percentage, divides by the maximum percentage, and then multiplies the lock duration before dividing by the maximum lock period. In the view function that reports a user’s balance at a given cycle, the same variables are multiplied together first and then divided twice, effectively changing the order of integer division. Because Solidity performs integer division with truncation, the two formulas can produce different results when the intermediate product is not an exact multiple of the divisor. The result is that the balance reported by balanceOfYsCvgAt can be larger than the amount that was actually added to totalSuppliesTracking. This accounting mismatch allows a malicious user to lock a very small amount, obtain a rounded‑up balance from the view function, and later claim more rewards than the treasury has recorded. When the contract finally tries to distribute the rewards, the recorded total is insufficient and the transaction reverts, leaving the last claimant unable to withdraw. The issue manifests only when the arithmetic yields a fractional component – for example, with a lock duration of 63 cycles, an amount of 2 tokens and an 80 % percentage, the tracking calculation yields zero while the balance function yields one. Users see a normal reward balance in the UI, but the claim either succeeds with an unexpectedly high payout or fails with a revert, creating confusion and potential loss of funds. The bug was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who exercised the functions with edge‑case values and observed the divergence. It is hard to notice because the discrepancy is hidden behind integer rounding and only appears with small amounts; the UI does not expose the internal totalSuppliesTracking value. The flaw belongs to the class of arithmetic precision or rounding bugs that break accounting invariants. To remediate the issue, the contract should use a single, canonical formula for ysTotal in all places, ensuring that multiplication and division are performed in the same order and that any rounding is applied consistently. Optionally, the code could employ a higher‑precision intermediate type or explicit rounding logic to guarantee that the reported balance never exceeds the tracked total, thereby preserving the integrity of the reward distribution mechanism.

title: Adjusting "I" will create a sandwich opportunity
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an on‑chain parameter named "I" (the internal price coefficient) that is modified by a privileged function called adjustPrice. Because the function updates the coefficient instantly, the price used for subsequent swaps changes in a single block. An attacker, typically an MEV bot, can observe the pending adjustPrice transaction, execute a trade just before the price update (selling the base token at the old, higher price), allow the price to be adjusted, and then immediately execute a reverse trade (buying the base token at the new, lower price). This sandwich pattern extracts the price differential as profit, which is effectively a loss for the liquidity providers whose deposits are re‑priced by the adjustment. The exploit works whenever the admin or maintainer calls adjustPrice with a new I value, and it does not require any special permissions beyond being able to submit a transaction in the same block. The affected parties include liquidity providers who see their token reserves shrink, regular users who may receive worse swap rates, and the protocol itself which suffers from unfair capital extraction. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the tester simulated a front‑run scenario: the test transferred base tokens, performed a sell, called adjustPrice, and then performed a buy, observing that the bot’s final base token balance exceeded its initial balance while the pool reserves decreased. The problem is subtle because the price change appears legitimate and the admin role is trusted, so developers may not anticipate that an immediate parameter shift can be arbitraged. Moreover, the profit is hidden in the swap outputs rather than explicit token transfers, making it harder to spot without detailed accounting. To remediate, the contract should either restrict adjustPrice to a timelocked or slowly ramping mechanism (e.g., updating I over several seconds or blocks) or move the function behind a private RPC that limits public mempool visibility, thereby reducing the window for front‑running. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “instant parameter change leading to sandwichable price updates”, where a privileged state change creates a temporary arbitrage window that can be exploited by MEV bots, resulting in unexpected profit for the attacker and loss of value for honest participants.

title: First depositor can lock the quote target value
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the initialization of a dual‑token liquidity pool that allows the first liquidity provider to set the internal quote‑target variable to zero. When the pool is empty (totalSupply == 0) the contract computes the number of shares for the depositor and then derives the quote target by multiplying those shares with a scaling factor (1e18) using a floor‑division routine. Because the multiplication is performed as target * d / (10**18), a very small initial deposit can produce a shares value that, after scaling, rounds down to zero. The quote target is stored as a uint112, so a zero value is accepted. Subsequent deposits update the quote target by adding DecimalMath.mulFloor(_QUOTE_TARGET_, mintRatio) to the existing target; since the existing target is zero, the multiplication also yields zero and the target never increases, regardless of how much additional quote liquidity is supplied. This condition persists for the lifetime of the pool because the update formula always multiplies the current target, which remains zero. The impact is that the pool’s swap logic, which relies on a non‑zero quote target to calculate pricing and slippage, becomes effectively disabled for the quote side. Users attempting to trade quote tokens receive no price impact, swaps may revert or return zero output, and liquidity providers cannot earn fees because the pool cannot process quote‑side trades. The issue affects all participants of the pool – the initial depositor, later liquidity providers, and any trader interacting with the pool – and can be exploited by an attacker who makes a minimal initial deposit to lock the quote side of the market. The flaw was discovered during an audit by testing the contract with tiny deposit amounts; the zero quote target was not obvious from the UI because the pool appears to have reserves, but the internal target variable is silently zero, making the problem hard to notice without inspecting the on‑chain state. To remediate, the contract should use a calculation that preserves precision for small deposits, such as applying a ceiling division, enforcing a minimum non‑zero quote target, or scaling the quote balance with the correct decimal factor before the floor operation. In essence, the bug is a rounding‑to‑zero error in the initialization of a financial invariant, leading to a locked or unusable quote side of the pool.

title: Share Price Inflation by First LP-er, Enabling
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inflation of the LP share price that occurs during the very first deposit of a DODO GasSavingPool. When the pool is empty the contract calculates the initial number of shares by taking the minimum of the base‑token value and the quote‑token value supplied by the depositor. Because this calculation does not enforce a minimum total supply, an attacker can create a situation where the totalSupply of LP tokens is only one wei. After the attacker has minted a modest amount of shares (for example 1001 shares) they immediately sell almost all of them, keeping only a single wei of LP token. The attacker then donates a very large amount of base and quote tokens and calls the sync routine, which inflates the reserves while the totalSupply remains at the tiny one‑wei level. Subsequent calls to buyShares compute a mintRatio based on the ratio of the new input amounts to the inflated reserves. The contract multiplies this mintRatio by the totalSupply to determine how many new shares to mint. Because totalSupply is only one wei, the mintRatio would need to be greater than 1000 wad to satisfy the internal require that the minted amount be larger than 1000. Normal users provide input amounts that are far smaller than this threshold, so the _mint function reverts with the error “MINT_AMOUNT_NOT_ENOUGH”. From a user’s perspective a transaction that should give them new LP tokens simply fails, no shares are received and the balance remains unchanged, which is contrary to the expectation that buying shares always succeeds. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the core liquidity‑adding function: after the attacker’s manipulation, any attempt to buy shares with a reasonable amount of capital is rejected, effectively freezing the pool and preventing further liquidity provision, swaps, or flash‑loan operations. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case (test_mint1weiShares_DOSx1000DonationVolume) reproduced the exact sequence of actions and observed the revert. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the contract behaves correctly when the pool is already initialized; the bug only manifests under the specific edge case of the first deposit combined with a malicious follow‑up donation. The root cause is the reliance on a minimum‑value formula for initial share minting and the lack of a safeguard against an extremely low totalSupply, which together allow the share price to be inflated arbitrarily. To remediate the problem the initialization logic should be changed so that the first 1001 LP tokens are minted to the zero address, as done in Uniswap V2, making it prohibitively expensive to manipulate the share price. Alternatively, the contract could enforce a minimum totalSupply or use a more robust pricing formula that does not depend on a mutable totalSupply during the first deposit. Implementing such a fix restores the expected invariant that buying shares always yields a positive amount of LP tokens and prevents the denial‑of‑service scenario.

title: Balancer LP valuation methodologies use the
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the way the Olympus RBS 2.0 contract values Balancer liquidity‑provider (LP) tokens. The code calls the Balancer pool’s totalSupply() function to obtain the total amount of LP tokens and then divides the pool’s asset valuation by this number to derive a per‑token price. In many Balancer pool implementations totalSupply() does not return the true circulating supply; it reports a theoretical maximum supply that can be orders of magnitude larger than the actual amount of LP tokens held by users. The correct metric is getActualSupply(), which reflects the real number of tokens that exist after fees, rebasing or other internal accounting adjustments. Because the contract relies on the wrong function, the derived LP price can be dramatically under‑ or over‑valued. When the RBS system uses this distorted price to calculate the backing per OHM, it may decide to buy or sell assets at prices that are far from market reality, leading to large financial losses for the protocol and its participants. The issue appears only when a pool’s totalSupply diverges from its actual supply – a condition that is not obvious from the contract’s external behavior. Users may notice that RBS transactions execute at unexpected rates, that LP token balances seem normal while the protocol’s accounting shows a sudden loss, or that the protocol appears to “sell at a loss” without any obvious error. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the RBS valuation logic, where the auditor compared on‑chain data from several Balancer pools and observed a mismatch between the reported max supply and the real supply. The bug is hard to spot because the contract does not revert or emit an error; it simply uses a number that looks plausible but is mathematically incorrect for valuation. To remediate the issue, the contract should query getActualSupply() for each Balancer pool, using a try‑catch block to handle pools that do not implement the function, and fall back to a safe default only when the actual supply cannot be obtained. This change ensures that the LP valuation reflects the true amount of tokens in circulation, preserving the integrity of the RBS pricing model and preventing inadvertent loss of funds.

title: Possible incorrect price for tokens in Balancer
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the price calculation for tokens that are part of Balancer StablePools when the pool’s amplification factor (amp) is being updated. The price oracle function getTokenPriceFromStablePool obtains the amplification factor by calling getLastInvariant, which returns the amp value that was used for the most recent invariant calculation. During an admin‑initiated amplification parameter update, the current amp can diverge from the last recorded amp because the pool gradually transitions to a new amp value over a defined time window. As a result, the oracle continues to use a stale amp value while the pool’s internal swap logic already uses the evolving current amp. This mismatch leads to an incorrect computation of the invariant and consequently an inaccurate token price. An attacker or any user querying the price feed while the amp update is in progress can receive a price that is either too high or too low. If the price is used for critical operations such as collateral valuation, liquidation thresholds, or trade execution, the mispricing can cause users to receive fewer tokens than expected, trigger premature liquidations, or enable arbitrage that drains funds from the protocol. The issue manifests only during the amplification update window, which may last several hours, making it easy to miss in routine testing because the price feed behaves correctly before and after the window. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the Balancer price feed contract, where the code path for fetching the amp factor was compared against the pool’s swap implementation. The problem is subtle because the price feed still returns a deterministic value; however, the underlying assumption that the amp factor is static is violated. To remediate, the oracle should retrieve the current amplification parameter directly via the pool’s getAmplificationParameter (or an equivalent view) and recompute the invariant with that up‑to‑date amp value, mirroring the logic used in the pool’s swap functions. This change ensures that price calculations remain consistent throughout any amp transition, preserving accounting integrity and preventing users from seeing unexpected zero balances or receiving an incorrect refund amount.

title: Incorrect deviation calculation in isDeviating-
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a deviation‑checking routine that is intended to ensure that a live price (for example a spot price from Uniswap V3) does not stray too far from a reference time‑weighted average price (TWAP). The implementation mistakenly measures the deviation by comparing the larger of the two values to the smaller one, using the larger value as the denominator. In mathematical terms it evaluates ((max‑min) * maxDeviation) / max > allowedBps, which corresponds to |max‑min|/max rather than the correct |max‑min|/reference (the TWAP). This root‑cause is a logical error in the _isDeviating helper, which is invoked by isDeviatingWithBpsCheck. Because the denominator is the larger value, the allowed price band becomes asymmetric: the upper bound can be higher than the intended limit while the lower bound remains correct. An attacker can therefore push the spot price above the permitted deviation without triggering the revert, effectively bypassing the price‑integrity guard. The impact is that price‑oracles may report manipulated values, downstream contracts that rely on the oracle (such as lending, liquidation, or swap logic) may execute with distorted prices, and users may receive less favorable trade outcomes or suffer loss of collateral. The bug manifests whenever the contract calls isDeviatingWithBpsCheck to compare a current value against a TWAP, which is a common pattern in oracle validation code. All participants that trust the protocol’s price feed – traders, liquidity providers, and token holders – are potentially affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Deviation.sol library, where the auditor noticed that the calculation did not match the documented intention of measuring deviation from the mean. The problem is subtle because the function still returns a boolean based on a percentage, so a superficial test may appear to pass, hiding the asymmetric allowance. To remediate, the deviation logic should be rewritten to compute the absolute difference between the two values, divide by the reference (the TWAP), and compare the result against the maximum basis‑points threshold. This aligns the check with the intended business rule that the price may deviate by at most X bps from the TWAP, restoring symmetric bounds and preventing price manipulation.

title: BunniPrice.getBunniTokenPrice doesn't include
description:
BunniPrice.getBunniTokenPrice doesn't include fees into calculation, which means that price will be smaller. BunniPrice.getBunniTokenPrice function should return usd cost of bunniToken_. After initial checks this function actually do 2 things:
• validate deviation
• calculates total cost of token
Let's check how it's done to calculate total cost of token. It's done using _getTotalValue function. So we get token reserves using _getBunniReserves function and the convert them to usd value and return the sum. _getBunniReserves in it's turn just fetches amount of token0 and token1 that can be received in case if you swap all bunni token liquidity right now in the pool. The problem is that this function doesn't include fees that are earned by the position. As result total cost of bunni token is smaller than in reality. The difference depends on the amount of fees there were earned and not returned back. Also when you do burn in the uniswap v3, then amount of token0/token1 is not send back to the caller, but they are added to the position and can be collected later. So in case if BunniPrice.getBunniTokenPrice will be called for the token, where some liquidity is burnt but not collected, then difference in real token price can be huge. Price for the bunni token can be calculated in wrong way.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price‑oracle function that is supposed to return the USD value of a Bunni token. The function calculates the token price by fetching the current reserves of the underlying Uniswap V3 position and converting those amounts to USD, but it fails to add any fees that have been earned by the position and not yet collected. This omission is the root cause: the helper routine that obtains the reserves only reports the amounts that would be received if the entire liquidity were swapped instantly, ignoring both accrued protocol fees and the fees that remain pending after a burn operation. Because of this, the computed price is systematically lower than the true economic value of the token. An attacker or a careless user can exploit the discrepancy by relying on the understated price when performing trades, redemptions, or any logic that depends on the oracle, potentially causing the protocol to issue or accept tokens at a value that is below market reality. The impact manifests as users receiving less USD value than expected when they redeem or sell Bunni tokens, protocol accounting becoming inaccurate, and the possibility of financial loss for liquidity providers. The bug appears whenever the Uniswap V3 position has accumulated fees – a condition that becomes more likely over time and especially after liquidity is burned without immediately collecting the pending fees. All token holders, liquidity providers, and any component that trusts the BunniPrice.getBunniTokenPrice output are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the price‑calculation logic was examined and the missing fee inclusion was identified as a logical flaw. It can be hard to notice because the price still looks plausible and the deviation grows gradually as fees accumulate, making the error subtle until large fee balances are present. To remediate the problem, the price‑oracle should be modified to incorporate both the fees that have already been collected and the fees that are currently owed to the position before converting the reserves to USD, ensuring that the returned price reflects the full economic value of the token. This class of bug is a fee‑omission error in an on‑chain price oracle, leading to under‑pricing, broken accounting assumptions, and potential loss of funds for users who rely on the reported price.

title: Inconsistency in BunniToken Price Calculation
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistency between the price deviation check and the actual LP token price calculation in the Bunni protocol. The internal _validateReserves function compares a reserves‑to‑TWAP ratio that includes both on‑chain token reserves and any uncollected protocol fees, while the functions that compute the LP token value (such as _getTotalValue and getProtocolOwnedLiquidityReserves) deliberately ignore those uncollected fees and rely only on the raw reserves. Because the deviation check therefore uses a higher, fee‑inflated ratio, it can deem the pool state as acceptable even when the true reserve balance deviates significantly from the historical TWAP. An attacker can exploit this mismatch by allowing fees to accumulate (or by artificially creating fee‑like balances) so that the deviation check passes, while the price calculation under‑estimates the amount of value actually held in the pool. When the protocol later uses the underestimated reserve values to price LP tokens, it may over‑price the tokens, allowing the attacker to mint or redeem LP tokens at a favorable rate, effectively extracting value from the pool. The impact is a potential loss of funds for users who rely on the displayed LP token price, as the protocol may pay out more than the underlying assets justify, leading to a drain of protocol‑owned liquidity. The issue manifests when the pool has non‑zero uncollected fees and the TWAP observation window is such that the fee‑adjusted ratio stays within the allowed deviation threshold.
