All participants who hold or trade Bunni LP tokens are affected, especially those interacting with protocol‑owned liquidity pools. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the logic of the deviation validator with the price aggregation functions and noticed that the former adds fee amounts while the latter does not. It is subtle because the deviation check still succeeds, giving a false sense of safety, and the price computation uses a straightforward spot‑reserve formula that appears correct at first glance. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where inconsistent state views lead to price manipulation opportunities. From a user perspective the UI may show a higher LP token value, users may receive less underlying assets when withdrawing, or the protocol may appear to have excess liquidity that later disappears. The root cause is the mismatched inclusion of uncollected fees in the validation step versus their exclusion in the valuation step. To remediate, the protocol should align the two calculations: either include uncollected fees in both the deviation check and the price computation, or exclude them from both, ensuring that the ratio used for validation matches the ratio used for pricing. Additionally, relying solely on spot reserves for LP pricing is risky; incorporating a more robust oracle or a fee‑adjusted TWAP would further mitigate manipulation risk.

title: Price can be miscalculated.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price‑feed strategy contract where the functions that are supposed to return a median price incorrectly handle the case of exactly two non‑zero oracle values. The code checks the length of the filtered price array and, if it is less than three, assumes that a median cannot be calculated and returns the first non‑zero price. This assumption is wrong because a median can be derived from two values – either by averaging the two middle entries or by applying the existing median routine, which already supports an even‑length array. Consequently, when two non‑zero prices are present and they differ enough to be considered deviated, the contract returns the first price instead of the true median. The root cause is a logical misconfiguration in the length check and an early return that bypasses the proper median calculation. An attacker or any user does not need to perform any special actions; the bug is triggered automatically whenever the price feed supplies exactly two valid prices, which can happen during sparse oracle updates or when some sources return zero. The impact is that downstream contracts that rely on the median price – such as trading, liquidation, or collateral valuation modules – will receive a price that is either too high or too low. From a user perspective this may appear as a trade being executed at an unexpected rate, a refund amount being zero, or a balance suddenly dropping to zero because the protocol used a wrong price for accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the SimplePriceFeedStrategy contract, where the auditor noticed the length‑check logic and verified that the median routine can handle two elements. The bug can be hard to notice because the contract still reverts for arrays smaller than three, giving the impression that the check is intentional, and the deviation logic masks the problem when more than two prices are present. To remediate the issue the length condition should be relaxed to allow two non‑zero prices and the function should fall back to the median calculation rather than returning the first element. Updating both getMedianPriceIfDeviation and getMedianPrice to use a "< 2" check and then compute the median restores correct price feed behavior and aligns with the intended business logic of providing a fair market price.

title: Price calculation can be manipulated by intentionally reverting price feeds
description:
Price calculation module iterates through available price feeds for the requested asset, gather prices of non-revert price feeds and then apply strategy on available prices. This allows attackers to let some price feeds revert to get advantage from any manipulated price feed. Here we have some methods that attackers can abuse to intentionally revert price feeds.

1. UniswapV3 price feed UniswapV3Price.sol#L210-214
```solidity
// Get the current price of the lookup token in terms of the quote token
(, int24 currentTick, , , , , bool unlocked) = params.pool.slot0();
// Check for re-entrancy
if (unlocked == false) revert UniswapV3_PoolReentrancy(address(params.pool));
```

In UniswapV3 price feed, it reverts if current state is re-entered. An attacker can intentionally revert this price feed by calling it from UniswapV3's callback methods.

2. Balancer price feed BalancerPoolTokenPrice.sol#L388 BalancerPoolTokenPrice.sol#487 BalancerPoolTokenPrice.sol#599 BalancerPoolTokenPrice.sol#748
```solidity
// Prevent re-entrancy attacks
VaultReentrancyLib.ensureNotInVaultContext(balVault);
```

In BalancerPool price feed, it reverts if current state is re-entered. An attacker can intentionally revert this price feed by calling it in the middle of Balancer action.

3. BunniToken price feed BunniPrice.sol#L155-160
```solidity
_validateReserves(
    _getBunniKey(token),
    lens,
    params.twapMaxDeviationsBps,
    params.twapObservationWindow
);
```

In BunniToken price feed, it validates reserves and reverts if it doesn't satisfy deviation. Since BunniToken uses UniswapV3, this can be intentionally reverted by calling it from UniswapV3's mint callback.

Usually for ERC20 token prices, above 3 price feeds are commonly used combined with Chainlink price feed, and optionally with averageMovingPrice. There are another two points to consider here:

1. When average moving price is used, it is appended at the end of the price array. OlympusPrice.v2.sol#L160
```solidity
if (asset.useMovingAverage) prices[numFeeds] = asset.cumulativeObs / asset.numObservations;
```

2. In price calculation strategy, first non-zero price is used when there are 2 valid prices: getMedianPriceIfDeviation - SimplePriceFeedStrategy.sol#L246 getMedianPrice - SimplePriceFeedStrategy.sol#L313 For getAveragePrice and getAveragePriceIfDeviation, it uses average price if it deviates.

Based on the information above, here are potential attack vectors that attackers would try:

1. When Chainlink price feed is manipulated, an attacker can disable all three above price feeds intentionally to get advantage of the price manipulation.

2. When Chainlink price feed is not used for an asset, an attacker can manipulate one of above 3 spot price feeds and disable other ones.

When averageMovingPrice is used and average price strategy is applied, the manipulation effect becomes half:
(P+ΔX)+(P) / 2 = P + ΔX/2 ; P = MarketPrice; ΔX = ManipulatedAmount
Attackers can disable some of price feeds as they want with ease, they can get advantage of one manipulated price feed.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way the protocol aggregates multiple on‑chain price feeds to compute an asset price. The aggregation module iterates over a list of feeds, collects the values from any feed that does not revert, and then applies a strategy that may select the first non‑zero price, the median, or an average depending on configuration. Because the logic silently discards feeds that revert instead of aborting the whole calculation, an attacker who can cause a chosen feed to revert can control which subset of feeds is actually used. The root cause is the combination of two design choices: (1) price‑feed contracts such as the UniswapV3, Balancer, and Bunni feeds contain explicit re‑entrancy checks that revert when their internal state is re‑entered, and (2) the aggregation routine treats a revert as a non‑fatal event and simply skips the offending feed. An attacker can trigger the re‑entrancy checks by invoking the vulnerable feed from a callback (for example, the UniswapV3 pool’s callback or a Balancer vault action) and deliberately cause the feed to revert. Once the feed reverts, the aggregator ignores it and proceeds with the remaining feeds, which may include a manipulated spot feed or a Chainlink feed that the attacker has already compromised. The price that is finally returned can therefore be skewed, often by a factor proportional to the difference between the manipulated feed and the true market price. When an average‑moving‑price feed is also used, the manipulation effect is reduced but still present because the average is computed over the remaining valid prices. This flaw manifests whenever the protocol relies on the aggregated price for critical operations such as liquidations, collateral valuations, swaps, or fee calculations. From a user’s perspective the symptoms can include unexpected liquidation at a price far from the market, swaps that return far less than expected, or refunds that appear to be zero. Users expect the protocol to use a reliable, consensus price, but instead they receive a price that has been artificially altered because some feeds were forced to revert. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer observed that the price‑feed contracts contain re‑entrancy guards that can be triggered externally and that the aggregation code does not propagate those errors. The bug is hard to notice because occasional feed failures are normal in decentralized environments, and the silent omission of a feed does not raise an explicit alarm, making the price deviation appear as a normal market fluctuation. Conceptually, the problem belongs to the class of oracle aggregation vulnerabilities where the failure handling logic allows an attacker to bias the result by removing trustworthy inputs. The recommended mitigation is to change the aggregation routine so that any revert from a feed causes the whole price calculation to revert, or to enforce a quorum of feeds that must succeed before a price is accepted, and to redesign the individual feeds to avoid re‑entrancy checks that can be externally triggered. By ensuring that a missing or reverted feed is treated as a fatal error, the protocol can prevent an attacker from selectively discarding honest feeds and thereby preserve the integrity of its pricing logic.

title: getReservesByCategory() when useSubmodules
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the view function getReservesByCategory which aggregates reserve information for a given category. When a category is configured to use submodules (useSubmodules == true) the implementation unconditionally performs a staticcall to the address of each installed submodule using the selector stored in data.submoduleReservesSelector. The code does not verify that this selector is non‑zero. For categories such as protocol‑owned‑treasury the selector is intentionally set to bytes4(0) because the treasury does not expose a reserves function. Because the check is missing, the staticcall is executed with a zero selector, causing the call to revert. The revert propagates out of getReservesByCategory, so any external caller that queries the affected category receives an exception instead of a list of reserves. This behaviour can be triggered simply by calling getReservesByCategory(toCategory('protocol-owned-treasury')). The root cause is an unchecked assumption that every submodule that is enabled also provides a valid selector, which is not true for categories that deliberately omit the selector. Exploitation consists of invoking the view function with a category that has useSubmodules true but an empty selector, resulting in a denial‑of‑service for that query path. The impact is that users, front‑ends, and other contracts cannot retrieve treasury balances, leading to missing or zero values in UI dashboards and potentially breaking downstream accounting logic that expects reserve data. The bug affects any caller of getReservesByCategory, including regular users, protocol integrators, and auditors who rely on accurate reserve reporting. It was discovered during a systematic audit when a test case that added a treasury submodule caused the function to revert, emitting a SPPLY_SubmoduleFailed error. The issue is subtle because the function is marked view and does not modify state, so developers may not anticipate a revert, and the empty selector value looks innocuous. The correct mitigation is to add a guard that only performs the submodule staticcall when data.submoduleReservesSelector is not equal to bytes4(0), as shown in the recommended code change. By skipping the call for empty selectors the function will return the expected reserve list (which may be empty) instead of reverting, restoring correct accounting behaviour and preventing denial‑of‑service attacks.

title: Inability to Re-add oldToken After Execution of setNewTokenAndReplace
description:
The D3MakerFreeSlot contract's setNewTokenAndReplace() function, when executed, permanently removes the oldToken information without clearing its index from state.priceListInfo.tokenIndexMap. This oversight prevents the re-addition of the oldToken using either setNewTokenAndReplace() or setNewToken() methods.

The setNewTokenAndReplace() function is designed to replace an existing token with a new token in a slot, thereby saving gas. However, this function only removes the oldToken's information from state.tokenMMInfoMap and does not clear its index from state.priceListInfo.tokenIndexMap. Consequently, the system behaves as if the oldToken is still present, preventing its re-addition.

Once an oldToken is replaced, it cannot be re-introduced into the system using standard methods, potentially leading to operational inefficiencies or the need for workaround solutions.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incomplete cleanup bug in the D3MakerFreeSlot contract that prevents a previously used token from being re‑added after the setNewTokenAndReplace() function has been called. The function is intended to replace an existing token with a new one while saving gas, but it only deletes the old token’s data from the tokenMMInfoMap structure. It fails to clear the old token’s entry in the priceListInfo.tokenIndexMap, which still records the old token’s index as a non‑zero value. Because the contract treats any non‑zero index as an indication that the token is already present, subsequent calls to setNewTokenAndReplace() or setNewToken() that try to re‑introduce the old token are rejected with the HAVE_SET_TOKEN_INFO error. This occurs every time the replacement function is executed, meaning the old token becomes permanently locked out of the pool. The impact is that the protocol can no longer list or trade the original token, leading to operational inefficiencies, potential loss of liquidity, and the need for work‑arounds such as redeploying the contract. The issue is discovered during a security audit by Sherlock, who added a test that shows the old token’s index remains set after replacement and that attempts to add it again revert. The bug is subtle because the visible token data appears removed, yet an internal mapping still holds a stale reference, making it easy to miss during casual inspection. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the token as missing, but any attempt to add it back results in an error or no change, violating the expectation that a token can be swapped out and later restored. The class of bug is a state‑inconsistency or stale reference error, where a contract does not fully clean up all related storage entries. The correct remediation is to modify setNewTokenAndReplace() so that it also sets priceListInfo.tokenIndexMap[oldToken] to zero, thereby fully clearing the old token’s presence and allowing it to be added again in the future.

title: swap() will be reverted if path has more tokens
description:
swap() will be reverted if path has more tokens, the keepers will not be able to
successfully call swapForTau().
In test/SwapAdapters/00_UniswapSwapAdapter.ts:
```solidity
// Get generic swap parameters
const basicSwapParams = buildUniswapSwapAdapterData(
["0xyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy",
"0xzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzz"],
[3000],
testDepositAmount,
expectedReturnAmount,
0,
).swapData;
```
We will get:
0000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000024f49cbca
0000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000056bc75e2d63100000
0000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000055de6a779bbac0000
yyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy000bb8zzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzz
Then the swapOutputToken is _swapData[length - 41:length - 21].
But if we have more tokens in path:
```solidity
const basicSwapParams = buildUniswapSwapAdapterData(
["0xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx",
"0xyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy",
"0xzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzz"],
[3000, 3000],
testDepositAmount,
expectedReturnAmount,
0,
).swapData;
```
000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000024f49cbca
0000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000056bc75e2d63100000
0000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000055de6a779bbac0000
xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx000bb8yyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy
yyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyyy000bb8zzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzzz
swapOutputToken is _swapData[length - 50:length - 30], the swap() function will
be reverted.
The keepers will not be able to successfully call SwapHandler.swapForTau().
Someone will get a reverted transaction if they misuse UniswapSwapAdapter.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a deterministic revert in the swap() function of the UniswapSwapAdapter when the token swap path contains more than two tokens. The root cause is the use of hard‑coded byte offsets to extract the output token from the encoded swap data, assuming a fixed path length of two hops. When a multi‑hop path is supplied, the calculated slice (length‑41:length‑21) no longer points to the correct token identifier; instead the code reads an incorrect segment (length‑50:length‑30) and the subsequent logic fails, causing the transaction to revert. An attacker or a careless user can trigger this condition simply by providing a longer path, which results in a denial‑of‑service for the keepers that invoke SwapHandler.swapForTau(). The impact is that legitimate swap attempts are aborted, users see no received tokens, balances remain unchanged, and the protocol cannot fulfill its intended exchange operation. This occurs only when the adapter is called with a path array longer than two elements, a scenario that is uncommon in typical two‑token swaps but possible in complex routing strategies. The affected parties include protocol keepers, end‑users who rely on automated swaps, and any component that expects a successful token exchange. The issue was discovered during an audit test that constructed swap parameters with three tokens and observed a revert. It can be hard to notice because most test cases use two‑token paths, so the bug remains hidden until a multi‑hop swap is attempted. To remediate, the contract should either enforce a maximum of two pools, dynamically compute the offset based on the actual path length, or decode the calldata using proper ABI utilities and verify that the output token balance meets the amountOutMinimum requirement before proceeding. This change eliminates the fixed‑offset assumption and restores correct behavior for any valid path length, preventing unexpected reverts and ensuring that users receive the expected token amounts.

title: Mint limit is not reduced when the Vault is burning
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the function that decreases the amount of tokens a vault is allowed to mint after it burns TAU on behalf of a user. The contract keeps a mapping called currentMinted that records how many tokens each address has minted against its mint limit. When a vault burns tokens, the function _decreaseCurrentMinted is supposed to subtract the burned amount from the vault’s own entry in currentMinted so that the vault regains the freed mint capacity. Instead, the code reads the minted amount from currentMinted[account] (where account is the user whose tokens are being burned) but then writes the subtraction result to currentMinted[msg.sender] (the vault). Because the vault is the caller, msg.sender does not equal account, and currentMinted[account] is typically zero for the user. Consequently the vault’s currentMinted entry is reduced by zero, leaving the vault’s mint limit unchanged. This mistake also allows a user to transfer TAU to another address before burning, causing the condition accountMinted >= amount to be false and bypassing any reduction logic entirely. The bug can be exploited to permanently lock a vault’s mint capacity: after a series of burns the vault never regains the space to mint new tokens, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service on token issuance. Users may notice that after burning, the vault cannot mint additional tokens even though the protocol’s accounting assumes the mint limit should have increased; expected behavior (“burn frees up mint quota”) is not observed, leading to missing or delayed token allocations. The issue appears only when the vault acts as a burner on behalf of a user or when tokens are transferred between accounts before burning, making it easy to miss during casual testing because no transaction reverts and no explicit error is emitted. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the mint‑limit accounting logic. Fixing the problem requires correcting the key used when reading and writing the currentMinted mapping – for example, using currentMinted[msg.sender] for both read and write – or redesigning the function to explicitly handle vault‑user relationships and edge cases. In broader terms, this is a state‑inconsistency bug where accounting variables are updated with the wrong address, violating the protocol’s invariant that burned tokens should free up mint capacity.

title: Account can not be liquidated when price fall by 99%
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow that occurs during the liquidation process when the price of the underlying asset drops by ninety‑nine percent or more. The liquidation routine first computes a theoretical amount of collateral to seize without any discount (collateralToLiquidateWithoutDiscount) by dividing the debt to liquidate by the crashed price. Because the price is extremely low, this intermediate value becomes very large. The contract then applies a liquidation discount to obtain the actual collateral to liquidate, but it still calculates the liquidation surcharge using the original large value instead of the discounted amount. When the surcharge exceeds the discounted collateral, the subsequent subtraction (collateralToLiquidate minus liquidationSurcharge) underflows, causing the transaction to revert with a panic code. This edge case is not triggered in normal market conditions, so it can be missed by routine testing. An attacker who can force a severe price drop, for example by manipulating the oracle, can cause liquidation attempts to fail, leaving under‑collateralised accounts un‑liquidated and potentially exposing the protocol to bad debt. From a user perspective the liquidator sees the transaction revert and receives no reward, while the borrower’s unhealthy position remains unchanged, contradicting the expectation that liquidation always succeeds. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case simulated a ninety‑nine percent price crash and observed a revert. It is hard to notice because the arithmetic works correctly for typical price movements and only fails in extreme scenarios. The bug belongs to the class of financial‑formula underflow errors where derived values are not bounded before being used in subsequent calculations. The recommended fix is to compute the surcharge on the actual amount that will be taken, for example by using the minimum of the discounted collateral and the undiscounted estimate, ensuring the surcharge can never be larger than the collateral to be transferred. This change restores the invariant that collateralToLiquidate minus surcharge is non‑negative, allowing liquidation to succeed under any price condition.

title: A malicious admin can steal all users collat- eral
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked administrative ability to replace the price‑oracle wrapperthat the protocol relies on for valuing user collateral during liquidation. The contract that manages price feeds allows the owner (a multisig admin) to call an updateWrapper function and set any address as the new oracle wrapper for a given underlying asset, without any timelock, governance vote, or additional validation. Because the liquidation routine fetches the external price from this wrapper to compute how much collateral can be seized, a malicious wrapper can return a manipulated price that makes the protocol believe a user’s collateral is worth far less than it actually is. The attacker‑controlled wrapper is programmed to detect the attacker’s address (via tx.origin) and, when invoked, to report a price that triggers the liquidation logic to treat the user’s entire debt as liquidatable, thereby allowing the attacker to call liquidate on any account and transfer the full amount of collateral to themselves while paying only a negligible amount of the protocol’s native token for the fee. This breach violates the core accounting assumption that price data is trustworthy and immutable during a liquidation window. The exploit can be carried out at any time the admin chooses to replace the wrapper, and it affects every user who has deposited collateral, as well as the protocol’s fee‑splitting mechanisms and any third‑party liquidators that rely on correct pricing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the PriceOracleManager and BaseVault contracts, where the lack of a delay or access restriction on the wrapper update stood out as a logical flaw. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the price feed appears to function correctly for honest users, and the liquidation checks only validate that the collateral received meets a minimum exchange‑rate threshold, not that the price source is authentic. To remediate the problem, the protocol should enforce a timelocked governance process for any price‑oracle update, separate the admin role from price‑feed management, and add sanity checks that the new wrapper contract conforms to expected interfaces and cannot be arbitrarily controlled by a single address. Implementing these controls restores the integrity of the price feed, prevents an admin from silently swapping in a malicious oracle, and protects user collateral from being drained through manipulated liquidation calculations.

title: SwapHandler.sol: Check that collateral token cannot be swapped
description:
The SwapHandler.swapForTau function checks that the collateralToken cannot be
sent to the SwapAdapter for trading:
```solidity
ntracts/Vault/SwapHandler.sol#L54-L56
```
There exist however ERC20 tokens that have more than one address. In case of
such a token, the above check is not sufficient. The token could be swapped
anyway by using a different address.
The check that collateral cannot be swapped can be bypassed for tokens with
multiple addresses.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the swapForTau function of the SwapHandler contract, which is intended to prevent the protocol's collateral token from being sent to an external SwapAdapter for trading. The function performs a simple equality check against the stored collateral token address and rejects swaps that use that exact address. However, certain ERC20 tokens can be represented by more than one contract address – for example, proxy contracts, wrapped versions, or token clones that share the same underlying asset. Because the check only compares the literal address, an attacker can supply an alternative address that points to the same token, bypassing the restriction. When the function receives this alternate address, it treats the token as non‑collateral, forwards it to the SwapAdapter, and the adapter swaps the tokens for TAU or another asset. This effectively removes the collateral from the vault without the protocol’s accounting noticing the loss. The impact is a reduction or complete disappearance of user‑locked collateral, leading to under‑collateralisation of positions, potential liquidation of loans, and loss of funds for all users of the vault. The issue manifests whenever swapForTau is called with a token address that is not the exact stored address but represents the same underlying token; it can be triggered by any actor who can invoke the function, including malicious users. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the SwapHandler source code, where the reviewer noted that the protection relied solely on address equality and did not consider token identity. The bug is hard to notice because typical unit tests use the canonical token address, and the contract appears to block the collateral token at first glance. To remediate, the contract should verify that the collateral balance does not change as a result of the swap – for example by recording the balance before the call and asserting it is unchanged afterwards – or enforce a whitelist of tokens that are allowed to be swapped, thereby preventing any token that could represent the collateral from being sent to the adapter. This class of bug falls under the broader category of insufficient asset identity validation, where a contract assumes a single address uniquely identifies a token, leading to logical errors in accounting and security checks. From a user perspective, the symptom is that after attempting a swap, the displayed collateral balance may drop to zero or an expected refund may be missing, contrary to the expectation that the collateral remains locked. The protocol’s business logic that collateral must stay untouched is violated, breaking the accounting guarantees that underpin the system’s safety.

title: stETH/ETH chainlink oracle has too long of a heartbeat
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s reliance on a Chainlink stETH/ETH price feed that updates only once every 24 hours and tolerates a 2 % deviation before triggering an update. The function that calculates the OHM token price calls this feed to derive the amount of stETH that should be returned to a user after an arbitrage operation. Because the feed can remain stale for up to a full day, the on‑chain price used for settlement may diverge from the actual market price by as much as two percent. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the contract uses the outdated price to compute the expected wstETH amount, then transfers the calculated amount to the user while sending any excess to the treasury. If the real market price has moved unfavourably relative to the stale feed, the user receives less stETH than they are entitled to, effectively losing a portion of their funds. This situation can be exploited by an attacker who monitors market movements, waits for a significant price shift, and then triggers a withdrawal while the oracle is still reporting the old price, thereby capturing the difference. The impact is a systematic under‑payment to users, potentially amounting to a loss of up to two percent per transaction, and it affects any participant who deposits or withdraws stETH through the vault, as well as the protocol’s overall trustworthiness. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer examined the getTknOhmPrice function and noted the long heartbeat and high deviation threshold of the stETH/ETH feed. The problem is subtle because the discrepancy is small and does not generate explicit errors; users simply see a smaller balance returned than expected, which may appear as a normal rounding loss. To remediate the flaw, the contract should replace the stETH/ETH feed with a feed that has a shorter heartbeat and tighter deviation limits, such as the stETH/USD feed, or implement additional sanity checks that compare multiple oracle sources before finalising the payout. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of oracle‑staleness or price‑feed‑deviation vulnerabilities, where outdated pricing data leads to incorrect financial calculations and unintended fund loss. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a withdrawal that returns less stETH than anticipated, contradicting the expectation that the contract will honour the current market value of their assets.

title: Normal users could be inadvertently grieved
description:
The contract check on the withdrawn ratios of OHM and wstETH against the
current oracle price could run into grieving naive users by taking any wstETH
shifted imbalance as a fee to the treasury even though these users have not gamed
the system.
Here is a typical scenario, assuming the pool has been initiated with total LP equal
pricing match up with manager.getOhmTknPrice() or manager.getTknOhmPrice(),
i.e. 100 OHM to 1 wstETH or 0.01 wstETH to 1 OHM. The pool token balances in
each step below may be calculated via the Constant Product Simulation after each
swap and stake.)
OHM token balance: 100_000
wstETH token balance: 1_000
Total LP: 10_000
1. A series of swap activities results in the pool shifted more of the LP into
wstETH.
OHM token balance: 90_909.1 wstETH token balance: 1_100 Total LP: 10_000
2. Bob calls deposit() by providing 11 wstETH where 1100 OHM is minted with
stakes with 909.09 OHM and 11 wstETH and proportionately receives 100 LP.)
OHM token balance: 91_818.19 wstETH token balance: 1_111 Total LP: 10_100
User's LP: 100
3. Bob changes his mind instantly and proceeds to call withdraw() to remove all
of his LP. He receives the originally staked 909.09 OHM and 11 wstETH. All
OHM is burned but he is only entitled to receive 909.09 / 100 = 9.09 wstETH
since the system takes any arbs relative to the oracle price for the Treasury
and returns the rest to the owner.
OHM token balance: 90_909.1 wstETH token balance: 1_100 Total LP: 10_000
User's LP: 0
Bob suffers a loss of 11 - 9.09 = 1.91 wstETH (~ 17.36% loss), and the system is
ready to trap the next user given the currently imbalanced pool still shifted more of
the LP into wstETH.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s withdrawal routine that validates the proportion of OHM and wstETH returned to a liquidity provider against the current oracle price. When the pool’s token ratio has drifted from the oracle reference – for example after a series of swaps that increase the wstETH share – the contract treats the entire deviation as a fee payable to the treasury. This logic does not distinguish between price changes caused by external arbitrage and the user’s own recent deposit. Consequently, a user who deposits a balanced amount of OHM and wstETH and then withdraws immediately after the pool has become imbalanced will receive less of the token they originally supplied. In the illustrated scenario, Bob deposits 11 wstETH together with the corresponding amount of OHM, receives 100 LP tokens, and then withdraws his LP. Because the pool now holds a higher proportion of wstETH than the oracle price predicts, the contract calculates that Bob is entitled to only 9.09 wstETH and transfers the remaining 1.91 wstETH to the treasury as a fee. From the user’s perspective the expectation – “I should get back the 11 wstETH I just supplied” – is violated; the user sees a shortfall in the received balance without any explicit error, which may be mistaken for normal slippage. The impact is a direct loss of funds for ordinary liquidity providers and a potential erosion of trust in the protocol, while the treasury unintentionally accrues assets from users who have not performed any arbitrage. The issue manifests whenever the pool’s internal token reserves diverge from the oracle‑derived price, i.e., after any swap activity that shifts the constant‑product curve. It was discovered during a manual audit that simulated pool states revealed a systematic over‑charging of users based on the current oracle price rather than on the user’s entry snapshot. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit a warning or revert; the loss appears as a silent fee, making it hard to detect without detailed accounting. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of “oracle‑price‑based fee miscalculation” bugs where fee logic is tied to a global price reference instead of the individual user’s entry conditions. A proper fix would involve recording the exact amounts of OHM and wstETH contributed at deposit time, taking a snapshot of the pool’s state, and computing any treasury fee only on the differential that exceeds the user’s expected share, thereby preventing the treasury from seizing assets that belong to honest users.

title: SetLimit does not take into account burned tokens
description:
The function setLimit() may not be able to sufficiently restrict mint ability of
manager.
The setLimit() function reverts when newLimit_ < deployedOhm, mintOhmToVault
will revert if deployedOhm + amount_ > ohmLimit + circulatingOhmBurned. If the
value of circulatingOhmBurned is high, and the admin can only set the limit above
deployedOhm, they could end up in a state where they cannot limit the amount the
vault is allowed to burn sufficiently. I.e. the vault is always able to mint at least
circulatingOhmBurned new tokens.
so this value could grow arbitrarily high.
Lack of control of admin on mint ability of manager.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical accounting flaw in the contract that governs the OHM token minting limits. The setLimit() function is intended to let the admin restrict how many new tokens the manager can mint, but it only checks that the new limit is greater than or equal to the amount of tokens already deployed (deployedOhm). The minting function, mintOhmToVault(), however, allows minting as long as deployedOhm plus the requested amount does not exceed the sum of the configured limit (ohmLimit) and the amount of tokens that have been burned and are tracked in circulatingOhmBurned. Because circulatingOhmBurned is added to the limit check, a large burned‑token balance effectively raises the ceiling for minting. When the admin tries to lower the limit after a substantial number of tokens have been burned, the contract still permits the vault to mint at least the burned amount, and the burned amount can grow without bound. This means the admin cannot reliably cap the total supply, leading to uncontrolled inflation. The issue manifests whenever the admin calls setLimit() with a value lower than the current deployed supply while circulatingOhmBurned is non‑zero. Users may notice that the token supply keeps increasing despite the protocol’s stated cap, or that refunds or balances appear larger than expected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the logic of setLimit() with mintOhmToVault() and identified the missing accounting for burned tokens. It is hard to notice because the mint function does not revert and appears to respect the limit, while the extra term silently expands the allowed supply. To remediate, the limit enforcement should be aligned with the minting check: either incorporate circulatingOhmBurned into the setLimit() calculation, enforce a hard cap on total minted tokens regardless of burned amount, or reduce circulatingOhmBurned when new tokens are minted, ensuring that the admin’s limit truly bounds the overall supply.

title: Multiple functions aren't payable so quotes may fail
description:
There are multiple functions that use quotes but that aren't payable. This breaks
their compatibility with some quotes. As the 0x docs state: Certain quotes require
a protocol fee, in ETH, to be attached to the swap call.
The following flows use a quote but the external/public starting function isn't
payable:
RollerPeriphery
1) redeem
Periphery
1) removeLiquidity
2) combine
3) swapPT
4) swapYT
5) issue
See summary.
Functions won't be compatible with certain quotes causing wasted gas fees or bad
rates for users
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a set of external or public functions that are not marked payable even though they accept a quote object which, for certain quote providers, requires an ETH protocol fee to be attached to the call. The root cause is the omission of the payable modifier on functions such as redeem, removeLiquidity, combine, swapPT, swapYT and issue, which are part of the RollerPeriphery contract. When a user supplies a quote that mandates a fee, the contract attempts to forward the quote without the necessary ETH value, causing the low‑level call to revert. This can be exploited by an attacker who supplies a quote that includes a fee expectation, causing the transaction to fail and the user to lose the gas spent on the call, or by front‑running the transaction to force a worse swap rate because the fee cannot be paid and the quote fallback may select a sub‑optimal path. The impact is that users may see their swap or liquidity operation revert with no token movement, experience unexpectedly high gas costs, or receive a worse execution price because the intended quote could not be used. The issue manifests only when a quote type that requires a protocol fee is used; standard quotes that do not need ETH pass without problem, making the bug easy to miss during normal testing. Affected parties include any user interacting with the affected functions, the protocol’s liquidity providers who may lose fee revenue, and the overall trustworthiness of the platform. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s public interface with the 0x documentation on quote requirements. Because the functions appear syntactically correct and the fee requirement is hidden inside the quote data, developers may not notice the missing payable attribute until a failing transaction occurs in production. To remediate the issue, each external function that forwards a quote should be declared payable and should forward the attached ETH value to the quote execution call, or the contract should be refactored to separate fee handling from the core logic, ensuring that any required protocol fee is explicitly collected and passed along. This class of bug falls under the broader category of improper handling of external payable calls, where a contract’s interface does not match the payment expectations of the called service, leading to transaction reverts, wasted gas, and potential financial loss for users.

title: Multiple functions may leave excess funds in contract
description:
Periphery#combine may leave excess underlying in the contract due to _fromTarget
unwrapping to underlying and the quote may not swap them all.
When using arbitrary tokens to swap to underlying the contract always moves in
the full amount specified. There is no guarantee that the quote will consume all
tokens. As a result the contract may leave excess sell tokens in the contract but it
should return then to the receiver.
These functions include:
RollerPeriphery
1) deposit
Periphery
1) swapForPTs
2) addLiquidity
3) issue
RollerPeriphery#RollermintFromUnderlying uses adapter.scale and previewMint to
determine the amount of underlying to transfer. The roller code will mean that
previewMint will always perfectly reflect the exact exchange rate into the roller.
However adapter.scale varies by adapter and isn't guaranteed to be exact. The
result is that _transferFrom may take too much underlying. Since this underlying is
wrapped to target the contract should return all excess target to receiver.
See summary.
Token may be left in the contract and lost
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a systematic failure to return excess tokens that remain in the contract after a swap or mint operation. The root cause is the reliance on external quote calculations and adapter scaling factors that are not guaranteed to consume the full amount of input tokens. Functions such as Periphery#combine, deposit, swapForPTs, addLiquidity, issue and RollerPeriphery#RollermintFromUnderlying transfer the full amount specified by the caller, then invoke a quote or previewMint that may return a smaller amount because of rounding, slippage or imprecise scaling. Because the code does not check the residual balance after the quote, any leftover sell tokens or wrapped target tokens stay locked in the contract instead of being sent back to the user. An attacker or a regular user can trigger this condition simply by providing a token amount that the quote cannot fully swap, for example when using arbitrary tokens with volatile rates or adapters with non‑exact scale values. The impact is that users may see their expected refund or minted amount reduced, while the missing portion silently disappears from their wallet and is retained by the contract. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction but the balance after the operation is unchanged or lower than expected, leading to confusion such as “my deposit returned nothing” or “my liquidity addition left my tokens stuck”. The issue occurs whenever the contract performs a full‑amount transfer followed by a quote that does not guarantee full consumption, which includes the listed functions that handle deposits, swaps, liquidity addition and token minting. It was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who noted that the logic assumes the quote will always match the transferred amount and therefore omitted any cleanup step. The bug is hard to notice because the leftover amount can be small, no events are emitted for the retained tokens, and the contract’s accounting appears correct from a high‑level perspective. To remediate, each function should calculate the actual amount received from the quote or previewMint and explicitly transfer any surplus tokens back to the caller before exiting, or enforce exact‑swap constraints and proper slippage checks. Conceptually this belongs to the class of “excess fund retention” or “unreturned token” bugs, where a contract fails to honor the principle that all user‑supplied assets must either be used as intended or returned, violating basic accounting assumptions of the protocol.

title: Periphery#_swapPTsForTarget won't work correctly
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal function _swapPTsForTarget of the Periphery contract. The function is intended to convert principal tokens (PTs) into the protocol's target token by first redeeming mature PTs and, if redemption is not possible, performing a Balancer swap. The implementation checks only whether the maturity scale (mscale) is greater than zero and then proceeds to call the divider.redeem path. However, it does not verify whether the adapter has its redeemRestricted flag set for the given maturity. When an adapter marks redemption as restricted, the redeem call reverts or fails, but the function does not fall back to the Balancer swap branch. As a result, the swap operation returns zero target tokens while the PT balance may be lost or remain locked in the contract. This situation occurs only for PTs that are mature and belong to an adapter that has redemption restricted, which is a valid state for some adapters. Users attempting to swap under these conditions experience a failed transaction or receive no target tokens, contrary to the expectation that the swap will always deliver the target amount. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who noted that the code path for mature PTs lacks the redeemRestricted guard present in the analogous _removeLiquidity function. The bug is subtle because typical test scenarios use adapters without redemption restrictions, so the failure does not appear in standard unit tests. The vulnerability belongs to the class of logical/accounting errors where a required state check is omitted, leading to an invalid operation and potential fund loss. To remediate, the function should incorporate a check similar to _removeLiquidity: if the adapter’s level indicates redeemRestricted, the contract should skip the redeem call and either retain the PT balance or execute an alternative swap path, ensuring that the user either receives the expected target tokens or retains control over their PTs.

title: fillQuote uses transfer instead of call which may break
description:
Transfer will always send ETH with a 2300 gas. This can be problematic for
interacting smart contracts if gas cost change because their interaction may
abruptly break.
See summary.
Changing gas costs may break integrations in the future
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the use of Solidity's transfer function to send ETH within the fillQuote routine. Transfer forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas to the recipient, which historically was sufficient for simple wallet contracts but is no longer guaranteed after gas cost changes introduced by protocol upgrades such as EIP‑1884. Because the amount of gas required to execute a fallback or receive function can increase, the fixed stipend may become insufficient, causing the ETH transfer to revert. This failure can happen whenever fillQuote attempts to forward funds to an external contract that needs more than 2300 gas, for example a token wrapper, a decentralized exchange router, or a user‑controlled contract with complex logic. When the transfer reverts, the whole fillQuote transaction aborts, leaving the caller without the expected refund or execution result. From a user perspective the symptom is that a trade or operation appears to succeed but the user receives no funds, sees a zero balance, or encounters a transaction that suddenly fails without a clear error message. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the ETH‑sending path and recognized that relying on transfer is brittle under evolving gas economics. It is difficult to notice because the contract works correctly on current networks, and the failure only manifests after a gas‑cost change or when interacting with a contract that deliberately consumes more gas. The bug belongs to the class of “fixed‑gas‑stipend transfer failures” and violates the business assumption that funds can always be forwarded safely to any participant. The recommended remediation is to replace transfer with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas (or a calibrated amount) and checks the returned success flag, while ensuring that re‑entrancy is not introduced because the contract only holds the caller’s funds. By using call, the contract becomes resilient to future gas cost adjustments and to recipients that require more execution gas, preventing silent fund loss and denial‑of‑service scenarios.

title: sponsorSeries() method fails when user want to swap
description:
sponsorSeries() fails when user want to use swapQuote to swap for stake token to
sponsor a series.
stake is token that user need to deposit (technically is pulled) to be able to sponsor
a series for a given target. User has option to send SwapQuote calldata quote and
swap any ERC20 token for stake token. Below is the code that doing transferFrom()
of stakeToken not sellToken()
```solidity
if (address(quote.sellToken) != ETH) _transferFrom(permit, stake, stakeSize);
if (address(quote.sellToken) != stake) _fillQuote(quote);
```
Expected behaviour of this function is to pull sellToken from msg.sender when
address(quote.sellToken) != stake. For example- stake token is WETH. User want
to swap DAI for WETH in sponsorSeries(). In this case, user would be sending
SwapQuote.sellToken = DAI and swapQuote.buyToke = WETH and expect that
fillQuote() would swap it for WETH. This method will fail because sellToken not
transferred from msg.sender.
sponsorSeries() fails when address(quote.sellToken) != stake
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the sponsorSeries() function that allows a user to provide a SwapQuote in order to exchange an arbitrary ERC20 token (sellToken) for the required stake token before sponsoring a series. The implementation mistakenly calls _transferFrom on the stake token address instead of on the sellToken when the sellToken is not ETH. Specifically, the code executes if (address(quote.sellToken) != ETH) _transferFrom(permit, stake, stakeSize); followed by if (address(quote.sellToken) != stake) _fillQuote(quote);. As a result, when a user supplies a sellToken that differs from the stake token (for example DAI as sellToken and WETH as stake token), the contract attempts to pull WETH from the caller’s wallet even though the caller only holds DAI and has not approved WETH. The transferFrom therefore fails, causing the entire sponsorSeries() call to revert. The root cause is a logical error in token selection: the function uses the stake token variable for the allowance transfer instead of the sellToken variable, and it does not calculate or transfer the exact amount of sellToken required to obtain the needed stakeSize. Exploitation is straightforward: any user trying to sponsor a series using a swapQuote with a non‑stake sellToken will experience a failed transaction, receiving no refund or sponsorship, and seeing UI symptoms such as “transaction failed”, “insufficient allowance”, or “no tokens received”. The impact is that legitimate users cannot use alternative tokens to fund sponsorships, potentially reducing protocol adoption and causing frustration. The condition occurs only when quote.sellToken is neither ETH nor the stake token, making the bug invisible in cases where the sellToken equals the stake token. All users who attempt this flow are affected, while the protocol’s accounting assumptions—namely that the sellToken will be transferred and swapped to produce the required stake amount—are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the token transfer logic and identified the mismatched variable usage. It may be hard to notice because the function succeeds for the common case (sellToken equals stake token or ETH) and provides no explicit error message for the failure path. The recommended remediation is to replace the current transferFrom call with one that pulls the sellToken from msg.sender for an amount sufficient to achieve at least stakeSize of the stake token, and to ensure proper allowance checks and accurate amount calculations before invoking the swap. In broader terms, this is a token‑selection logic bug that leads to failed swaps and broken sponsorship flows.

title: User can prevent liquidations by frontrunning
description:
User can prevent liquidations by frontrunning the tx and decreasing their debt so that the liquidation transaction reverts.
In the liquidation transaction, the caller has to specify the amount of debt they want to liquidate, _debtAmount. The maximum value for that parameter is the total amount of debt the user holds:
In _calcLiquidation(), the contract determines how much collateral to liquidate when _debtAmount is paid by the caller. In that function, there's a check that reverts if the caller tries to liquidate more than they are allowed to depending on the position's health.
The goal is to get that if-clause to evaluate to true so that the transaction reverts.
To modify your position's health you have two possibilities: either you increase your collateral or decrease your debt. So instead of preventing the liquidation by pushing your position to a healthy state, you only modify it slightly so that the caller's liquidation transaction reverts.
Given that Alice has:
• 100 TAU debt
• 100 Collateral (price = $1 so that collateralization rate is 1) Her position can be liquidated. The max value is:
(1.3e18 * 100e18 - (100e18 * 1e18 * 1e18)/1e18)/1.3e18 = 23.07e18 (leave out liquidation discount for easier math)
The liquidator will probably use the maximum amount they can liquidate and call liquidate() with 23.07e18. Alice frontruns the liquidator's transaction and increases the collateral by 1. That will change the max liquidation amount to:
(1.3e18 * 100e18 - 101e18 * 1e18)/1.3e18 = 22.3e18.
That will cause _calcLiquidation() to revert because 23.07e18 > 22.3e18.
The actual amount of collateral to add or debt to decrease depends on the liquidation transaction. But, generally, you would expect the liquidator to liquidate as much as possible. Thus, you only have to slightly move the position to cause their transaction to revert.
User can prevent liquidations by slightly modifying their position without putting it at a healthy state.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running manipulation that allows a borrower to prevent a pending liquidation by making a tiny adjustment to their position after the liquidation transaction has been submitted but before it is executed. The liquidation function requires the caller to specify the amount of debt to liquidate (_debtAmount) and internally computes the maximum debt that can be liquidated based on the current health of the position. If the supplied amount exceeds this maximum, the contract currently reverts the whole transaction. Because the maximum is calculated from the on‑chain collateral and debt values at the moment of execution, a malicious borrower can submit a separate transaction that either adds a small amount of collateral or repays a small portion of debt, thereby lowering the computed maximum just enough that the originally requested _debtAmount becomes larger than the new limit. When the liquidation transaction is finally mined, the check fails and the transaction reverts, leaving the borrower’s position unchanged and the liquidator without any reward. This flaw occurs whenever a liquidation is attempted on an under‑collateralized account and the borrower can front‑run the liquidation with a higher‑gas transaction that slightly improves the health factor without reaching a fully healthy state. The affected parties are the borrowers, who can avoid liquidation, and the liquidators, who lose expected profit and may be forced to retry at higher cost. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation logic, where the auditor noticed that the contract uses a strict revert instead of capping the liquidation amount. It can be hard to notice because the borrower’s balance appears to improve only marginally, yet the liquidation fails silently, giving the impression that the protocol is protecting users rather than exposing a logical error. The bug belongs to the class of transaction‑ordering or front‑running vulnerabilities combined with improper input validation, specifically a denial‑of‑service style liquidation denial. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a “liquidation failed” message or simply no change in collateral, while the user expected the position to be partially closed and the debt reduced. The business logic that assumes a liquidation will always succeed when the health factor is below the threshold is violated, breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol. The recommended fix is to change the liquidation routine so that if the requested debt exceeds the maximum, the contract does not revert but instead proceeds with the maximum allowable amount, or otherwise caps the value before performing the transfer. This eliminates the incentive for a borrower to manipulate the transaction ordering and restores the intended liquidation behavior.

title: QVBaseStrategy::reviewRecipients() doesn't
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the multi‑manager review mechanism of the QVBaseStrategy contract. The function reviewRecipients allows pool managers to submit a status (Accepted or Rejected) for a pending recipient and increments a counter for that specific status. When the counter for a given status reaches the configured reviewThreshold, the contract immediately overwrites the recipient’s stored status with the new value, without checking the recipient’s current status or the total distribution of reviews across all possible statuses. Consequently, if different managers submit conflicting reviews, the last status that reaches the threshold will replace any previous status, even if the overall majority of managers have voted the opposite way. For example, with five managers and a threshold of two, three rejections followed by two acceptances will result in the recipient being marked Accepted, because the Accept status reaches the threshold after the Rejected status has already been set. This logic flaw allows a coalition of a minority of managers to flip a recipient’s status after a majority has already decided, breaking the intended consensus rule. The impact is that recipients may be incorrectly marked as eligible to receive funds, leading to misallocation of pool assets, potential loss of trust, and violation of the protocol’s business rules that assume a majority decision. The issue manifests only when multiple managers review the same recipient with different outcomes and the threshold is low enough for both statuses to be reached independently. It is difficult to notice because each status update emits a legitimate event and passes the threshold check, so the contract appears to behave correctly on a per‑call basis while the overall decision logic is corrupted. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reviewRecipients implementation and constructed a test case where the status was overwritten after the threshold was met for a second time. To remediate, the contract should track the total number of reviews per status and only update the stored recipientStatus when a status not only reaches the threshold but also represents the prevailing outcome, or it should prevent further overwrites once a status has been set unless an explicit reset is performed. In essence, the bug is a consensus‑override logic error that allows status flipping and should be fixed by adding proper majority checks or immutable status once finalized.

title: QVBaseStrategy contract : recipient reviewStatus
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the recipient registration and review workflow of the QVBaseStrategy contract. When a new recipient registers, their status moves from None to Pending and the pool manager can later change the status to Accepted by calling reviewRecipients, provided the number of reviews for that specific status reaches a predefined reviewThreshold. The contract stores the number of reviews for each recipient and status in a mapping called reviewsByStatus. The flaw appears when an already‑accepted recipient updates their application. The _registerRecipient function changes the status from Accepted back to Pending, but it does not reset the counter reviewsByStatus[recipientId][Status.Accepted]. Consequently, the next time the pool manager reviews the same recipient and votes for the Accepted status, the stored counter may already be equal to or above the threshold, causing the contract to immediately set the status to Accepted again without requiring the full amount of new votes. This logic error allows a recipient to bypass the intended review threshold, effectively “re‑accepting” with fewer or even zero additional votes. From a user perspective the symptom is that a recipient appears to be approved instantly after re‑registration, even though the pool manager has not performed a full review; funds may be allocated to that recipient under the false assumption that a proper quorum was reached. The issue is triggered only when an accepted recipient re‑registers with new terms; it does not affect first‑time registrations or rejected applicants. It primarily affects the protocol’s governance model, the pool manager’s ability to enforce review policies, and any users or investors relying on the correctness of recipient selection. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s state‑transition logic, where the reviewer noticed that the reviewsByStatus mapping was never cleared on status change. Because the contract emits the same events as in the normal flow, the problem can be subtle and may not be evident from logs alone, making it hard to detect in production. To remediate the issue, the _registerRecipient function should reset the review counter for the previous status (e.g., set reviewsByStatus[recipientId][Status.Accepted] to zero) whenever a recipient’s status is changed from Accepted back to Pending, ensuring that a fresh quorum is required for any subsequent acceptance. This correction restores the intended invariant that a recipient must accumulate a full set of reviews for each new acceptance round, preserving the protocol’s security and economic guarantees.

title: [M-01] Allocation can start before registra-
description:
The way that timestamps are set or specifically, validated right now allows Allocation to start before Registration ends. I havent git a clear answer from the this can potentially break some stuff in QVBaseStrategy and DonationVotingMerkleDistributionBaseStrategy.
If _registerRecipient is called while Allocation is active on both QVBaseStrategy and DonationVotingMerkleDistributionBaseStrategy This can completely modify the effects of reviewRecipients and rewrite the status of already 'reviewed' recipients. This can cause rewards being falsely distributed or even stuck as well.
Of course there is a check to see if the caller is a member of the pool. Since the members are 'trusted' then the likelihood is low, thus the impact will be medium, if those roles are not to be trusted, then impact can potentially be high.
Recipient statuses can be modified and altered causing funds to sent falsely or get stuck.
This is the check to validate timestamps in both strategies. As we can see, it allows allocationStartTime to be less than registrationEndTime.
```solidity
if (
    block.timestamp > _registrationStartTime || _registrationStartTime > _registrationEndTime
    || _registrationStartTime > _allocationStartTime || _allocationStartTime > _allocationEndTime
    || _registrationEndTime > _allocationEndTime
) revert INVALID();
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a timestamp validation flaw that permits the allocation phase of a quadratic voting or donation‑merkle distribution pool to begin before the registration phase has officially ended. The contract’s current checks only ensure that the registration start time is before the registration end time and that the allocation start time is before the allocation end time, but they omit a rule that the registration end must not be later than the allocation start. Because of this missing condition, an attacker who is a trusted pool member can invoke the _registerRecipient function while the allocation window is already active. Doing so rewrites the status of recipients that have already been reviewed, allowing the attacker to alter their eligibility, trigger rewards to be sent to unintended addresses, or cause rewards to become permanently stuck. The impact is medium when only trusted members can call the function, but it could become high if the role is compromised or mis‑assigned. The issue manifests when the deployment parameters are set such that _registrationEndTime > _allocationStartTime, a situation that may not be obvious during normal testing because most deployments use non‑overlapping windows. From a user’s perspective, a recipient may see a reward that never arrives or see funds disappear from the pool without explanation. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the timestamp checks in QVBaseStrategy and DonationVotingMerkleDistributionBaseStrategy. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the windows overlap, and the logic that processes rewards assumes the registration phase is already closed before allocation begins. The proper fix is to add an explicit validation that the registration end time must be less than or equal to the allocation start time, causing the transaction to revert if the windows overlap. This change restores the intended lifecycle ordering, prevents status tampering during allocation, and ensures that rewards are distributed only to recipients that were properly reviewed during the registration period.

title: The RFPSimpleStrategy._registerRecipient()does
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the RFPSimpleStrategy contract where the internal function responsible for registering a recipient, _registerRecipient, does not correctly handle the input data when the pool is created with the useRegistryAnchor flag set to true. The contract expects the calldata to contain a recipient address, a proposal bid amount and optional metadata, but the implementation only decodes a subset of those fields, leaving the recipient address undefined. As a result the function reverts with the custom error RECIPIENT_ERROR whenever a user attempts to register, effectively blocking any registration. This occurs because the conditional branch that should decode the full tuple (address recipientId, address recipientAddress, uint256 proposalBid, Metadata) is either missing or incorrectly written, so the required recipientAddress is never extracted. An attacker or a careless pool creator can trigger the issue simply by deploying a pool with useRegistryAnchor=true; no special privileges are needed. Once the pool is live, any attempt by a profile member to register as a recipient fails, causing the pool to have zero registered recipients. Consequently, any funds deposited into the pool remain unallocated and become effectively trapped, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that every funded pool will have at least one recipient to receive allocations. The problem was discovered during a targeted audit test that created a pool with the flag enabled and observed that registerRecipient consistently reverted with RECIPIENT_ERROR. The bug is subtle because the same function works correctly when the flag is false, so the failure only appears under a specific configuration, making it easy to overlook during casual testing. To remediate the issue, the strategy must be updated to decode the full data structure when useRegistryAnchor is true, extract the recipient address, and perform the necessary authorization checks before proceeding. In conceptual terms the fix is to ensure that the registration logic correctly parses all expected parameters regardless of the flag, thereby restoring the ability for users to register and for funds to be distributed as intended. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after depositing funds they see no recipients appear, their balance remains unchanged, and attempts to join the pool are met with an error stating that the recipient is invalid, which contradicts the expectation that they should be able to register and receive allocations.

title: QV strategy cannot receive native token
description:
See summary
Cannot use QV strategy with native token.
https://github.com/allo-protocol/allo-v2/blob/main/allo-v2/contracts/strategies/qv-base/QVBaseStrategy.sol#L574
Notice the lack of a receive() method, which is also lacking in QVSimpleStrategy. In https://github.com/allo-protocol/allo-v2/blob/main/allo-v2/contracts/strategies/rfp-simple/RFPSimpleStrategy.sol#L500 . https://github.com/allo-protocol/allo-v2/blob/main/allo-v2/contracts/core/Allo.sol#L516 . Tracing the definitions, it invokes the strategy with call(gas(), to, amount, gas(), 0x00, gas(), 0x00) (in SafeTransferLib). I.e.: it invokes it with empty calldata, and will therefore try to call receive() and revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing payable entry point in the quadratic voting (QV) strategy contracts, which prevents the contracts from accepting native blockchain tokens (e.g., ETH). The root cause is that the QVBaseStrategy, QVSimpleStrategy, and related strategy implementations do not define a receive() function or a payable fallback, while the core Allo contract transfers native tokens using a low‑level call with empty calldata. Because the call supplies no data, the EVM looks for a receive() function to handle the incoming value; when none is present, the call reverts. An attacker or any user who attempts to fund a QV strategy with native tokens triggers this revert, causing the transaction to fail and the funds to remain with the sender. The impact is that legitimate users cannot deposit native tokens into the QV strategy, breaking expected functionality such as reward distribution or stake deposits that rely on native token transfers. This condition occurs whenever the Allo core contract invokes SafeTransferLib to move native tokens to a strategy that lacks a payable entry point, typically during deposit or reward payout phases. The affected parties include protocol participants who intend to use native tokens with QV strategies, the protocol itself because the business logic assumes the strategy can receive funds, and developers who may mistakenly believe the strategy is compatible with native assets. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that traced the token transfer path and noticed the absence of a receive() implementation in the strategy contracts. It can be hard to notice because the contracts compile and work correctly with ERC20 tokens, and the failure only manifests when native tokens are used, which may not be exercised in standard test suites. To remediate, the strategy contracts should be updated to include a payable receive() function (or a payable fallback) that simply accepts the incoming value, allowing the low‑level call to succeed. This change restores the intended behavior where users can send native tokens to the strategy and receive the expected accounting outcomes, such as successful deposits, correct reward calculations, and proper balance updates, aligning the implementation with the protocol’s financial assumptions.

title: The 1-second overlap between the during-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a timing overlap that occurs when the contract checks for an active allocation period and the condition that the allocation has ended using the same block.timestamp value. Because the EVM provides timestamps in seconds, while the protocol logic appears to have been written assuming millisecond precision, there exists a one‑second window where both the _checkOnlyActiveAllocation and _checkOnlyAfterAllocation modifiers evaluate to true in the same block. In practice this means a distribute() call can be executed at the exact moment the allocation period is considered finished, and a vote submitted in the same block after the distribution can still modify the final vote tally. The attack scenario is straightforward: a pool manager schedules a distribution based on the current vote distribution, then an attacker (or a colluding miner) submits a last‑minute vote that shifts the percentage of votes in favor of one recipient. The distribution already sent funds according to the old percentages, leaving a residual amount that no longer matches any recipient’s share. Because the contract does not provide a mechanism to withdraw this leftover amount, the funds become permanently locked in the pool. The impact is a partial loss of the pooled capital, affecting all participants who contributed funds and expected their share to be fully claimable. The bug manifests only when the block timestamp exactly equals the allocation end time, a condition that is rare on chains with long block times but becomes certain on roll‑ups or when miners deliberately order transactions to create the overlap. It was discovered during a manual audit of the QVSimpleStrategy contract, where the auditor noticed that the timestamp checks used inclusive comparisons and that the documentation implied millisecond precision. The issue is hard to notice because it requires a precise alignment of block timing and transaction ordering, which does not happen in typical usage. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce a strict separation between the allocation phase and the distribution phase, for example by using a > comparison for the after‑allocation check or by introducing a dedicated withdrawal function that allows any leftover balance to be reclaimed. This eliminates the one‑second overlap and ensures that no funds can become permanently inaccessible due to timing edge cases.

title: Problems with tokens that transfer less than
description:
Several things that can go wrong with this:
1. An attacker can put dust of this token in a wallet, and then call allo.fundPool() with type(uint256).max of this token. If the pool has not already been funded, then poolAmount will not be at type(uint256).max despite nothing being in the pool. It is now not possible to fund the pool.
2. Someone can do this in the DonationVotingMerkleDistributionVaultStrategy to set someones claim of this token to type(uint256).max . It is now impossible for anyone else to donate this token to them.
Pools cannot work with such tokens
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of ERC‑20 tokens whose transfer function does not move the exact amount requested, such as fee‑on‑transfer or dust‑limited tokens. The contract assumes that calling fundPool with the sentinel value type(uint256).max will either fully fund the pool or be rejected if the pool is already funded. Because the token may deduct a fee or round down the transferred amount, the actual balance that reaches the pool is lower than the requested max value. An attacker can exploit this by first sending a negligible amount of the problematic token (dust) to the pool contract and then invoking allo.fundPool() with type(uint256).max. The pool’s internal accounting records a poolAmount that is not equal to type(uint256).max, even though the pool appears unfunded, and the contract subsequently refuses any further funding attempts because it believes the pool is already at its maximum capacity. A similar issue appears in the DonationVotingMerkleDistributionVaultStrategy, where an attacker can set a beneficiary’s claim amount to type(uint256).max by exploiting the same token transfer discrepancy, effectively preventing any other donor from contributing that token to the same claim. The impact is that pools become permanently unfundable, donations cannot be made, and users may see their expected refunds or claim balances remain zero despite having contributed, leading to loss of confidence and potential financial loss. This condition occurs only with tokens that do not conform to the strict ERC‑20 transfer semantics expected by the protocol; it is triggered when the contract does not verify the actual amount transferred after each call. The affected parties include token donors, claimants, and any protocol component that relies on the pool’s funding logic. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fundPool logic and identified that the code does not check the return value of the token transfer, allowing the discrepancy to go unnoticed. Because the contract does not emit an explicit error when the transferred amount is lower, the problem can be subtle and may only surface after a pool becomes stuck. To remediate, the protocol should either reject tokens that implement transfer fees or otherwise modify the logic to explicitly verify that the amount received matches the amount requested, avoid using type(uint256).max as a sentinel for unlimited funding, and add defensive checks that revert when the transferred amount is insufficient. In short, the bug is a classic “incorrect handling of non‑standard ERC‑20 tokens” that leads to dead‑locked funding flows and broken claim calculations.

title: QVSimpleStrategy: If someone fund a pool when
description:
Allo::fundPool can be called by anyone at anytime, and it will increase the BaseStrategy.poolAmount via BaseStrategy::increasePoolAmount().
https://github.com/allo-protocol/allo-v2/blob/main/allo-v2/contracts/core/Allo.sol#L339-L345
