The BaseStrategy.poolAmount storage variable is used to determine the payout of each recipient by QVBaseStrategy::_getPayout:
https://github.com/allo-protocol/allo-v2/blob/main/allo-v2/contracts/strategies/qv-base/QVBaseStrategy.sol#L559-L574
When the fund is distributed by the pool manager via QVBaseStrategy::_distribute, the paidOut flag for the recipientId whose share was distributed will be set to be true.
https://github.com/allo-protocol/allo-v2/blob/main/allo-v2/contracts/strategies/qv-base/QVBaseStrategy.sol#L458
The problem occurs when some funds are added when some funds are distributed.
In the case, the funds will be partially or fully locked.
If some funds are added after the distribution is started, the added funds may be locked.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the quadratic voting (QV) pool strategy where the public function fundPool can be invoked at any moment, even after the distribution phase has begun. The contract stores the total amount of tokens available for a voting round in a variable called poolAmount, and the payout for each recipient is calculated from this value when the internal function _getPayout is executed. During distribution, each recipient that receives their share is marked with a paidOut flag, preventing further payouts for that identifier. Because the poolAmount variable remains mutable, an attacker or any user can add additional funds after the first payout has been processed. The distribution logic does not re‑evaluate the newly added balance nor does it clear the paidOut flags, so the extra tokens become effectively locked in the contract – they stay in the poolAmount storage but are never allocated to any recipient. This situation can occur whenever fundPool is called while _distribute is in progress or after it has already completed for some recipients. The impact is that legitimate participants receive less than the expected reward, and the protocol may lose funds that become unrecoverable unless a special recovery function is added. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a healthy pool balance, yet the expected refund or reward is zero or lower than anticipated, leading to confusion and loss of trust. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the Allo V2 contracts, where the interaction between fundPool and the payout calculation was examined and the mismatch was identified. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the funds simply remain idle, making the bug appear as a silent accounting error rather than an outright failure. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “post‑distribution mutable state” or “locked‑funds” vulnerabilities, where state that should be immutable after a settlement phase is still writable, breaking the accounting invariants of the system. The recommended remediation is to either restrict fundPool so it can only be called before the distribution starts, or to implement a recoverFund mechanism similar to other strategies that allows the contract owner or pool manager to withdraw any funds that become locked after distribution, thereby restoring the intended economic flow.

title: _distribute() function in RFPSimpleStrategy
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal _distribute function of the RFPSimpleStrategy contract. The function is responsible for paying a selected recipient for a milestone. It first retrieves the pool balance (poolAmount) and the recipient's proposalBid, then checks if recipient.proposalBid > poolAmount and reverts with NOT_ENOUGH_FUNDS if true. The check is intended to ensure that the pool has enough tokens to cover the payment. However, the actual amount to be transferred is calculated as (recipient.proposalBid * milestone.amountPercentage) / 1e18, i.e., a fraction of the proposalBid defined by the milestone percentage. Because the check uses the full proposalBid instead of the fractional amount, after the first milestone the poolAmount is reduced while the proposalBid remains unchanged. When the second milestone is processed, the condition recipient.proposalBid > poolAmount becomes true even though the required payment for that milestone is smaller than the remaining pool balance. The function then reverts, causing a denial-of-service: subsequent milestones cannot be paid, funds stay locked in the contract, and the pool manager is unable to fulfill the funding schedule. The issue appears only when the total proposalBid equals the initial pool amount and the milestones are split into multiple percentages; it is not obvious because the revert message suggests a generic not enough funds error, while the pool actually holds sufficient tokens for the remaining milestones. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of the funds-availability check. It is hard to notice because the check looks syntactically correct and the contract does not expose the intermediate calculation, so developers may assume the guard is sufficient. To remediate, the guard should compare the exact amount to be transferred (recipient.proposalBid * milestone.amountPercentage / 1e18) against poolAmount, or alternatively track the remaining bid amount per recipient. This class of bug falls under incorrect fund-availability validation or mis-calculated payment guard, which can lead to denial-of-service and locked funds. From a user perspective, after the first milestone the recipient receives the expected payment, but on the second milestone the transaction reverts and the UI may show an error like insufficient funds even though the pool still holds tokens, leaving the recipient with no further payouts and the pool manager unable to complete the project.

title: Recipient cannot always claim expected do-
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the DonationVotingMerkleDistributionVaultStrategy contract where the _afterAllocate function records the amount a donor intends to allocate as the claimable balance for a recipient without verifying the actual amount received by the vault. This faulty assumption works for standard ERC20 tokens but fails for tokens that implement a transfer fee (fee‑on‑transfer or tax tokens). When such a token is donated, the Permit2.permitTransferFrom call transfers the requested amount, but the token contract deducts a fee, so the vault’s balance increases by less than the requested amount. The contract then adds the full requested amount to the claims mapping, inflating the claimable balance. Recipients attempting to claim their funds receive less than expected, sometimes nothing, because the vault does not hold enough tokens to satisfy the recorded claim. The issue occurs whenever a non‑standard token with a non‑zero transfer fee is used, affecting donors, recipients, and the overall protocol’s accounting integrity. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of _afterAllocate and identified the unchecked assumption about transfer amounts. The bug is hard to notice because the transfer call succeeds and does not revert, giving the impression that the operation was successful, while the shortfall remains hidden in the contract’s accounting. To remediate, the contract should measure the vault’s token balance before and after the transfer, compute the actual amount received, and update the claim with that real amount, or alternatively reject tokens that charge a transfer fee. This correction aligns the recorded claim with the true token balance, preventing recipients from receiving fewer tokens than they are promised and preserving the protocol’s financial correctness.

title: Allo#_fundPool
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑rounding underflow caused by integer division in the _fundPool function. The contract calculates feeAmount = (_amount * percentFee) / getFeeDenominator(), where getFeeDenominator returns 1e18 and percentFee is expressed with 18‑decimal precision (e.g., 1e15 for 0.1 %). Because Solidity uses integer arithmetic, any _amount that is smaller than getFeeDenominator/percentFee will produce a feeAmount of zero after division. For example, depositing 9 GeminiUSD (9e2 units) with a 0.1 % fee yields (9e2 * 1e15) / 1e18 = 0, so no fee is transferred to the treasury. The contract does not enforce a minimum funding amount, allowing an attacker to repeatedly call fundPool with small amounts, each time avoiding the fee, and eventually accumulate an arbitrary total pool balance without ever paying the protocol fee. This can be exploited on low‑cost L2 networks where many tiny transactions are cheap. The impact is loss of revenue for the protocol and a distortion of the intended economic model; users may see their pool funded but the protocol’s fee accounting shows zero fees collected, breaking the assumption that every deposit contributes a proportional fee. The issue appears only when the deposited amount is below the fee‑threshold; larger deposits incur the correct fee. It affects any pool that uses a token with standard 18‑decimal precision and any user who can split a larger deposit into many sub‑deposits. The bug was discovered during manual code review of the fee calculation logic. It is subtle because the code looks correct at a glance and the zero‑fee result is not an explicit error; the contract simply records a fee of zero, which may go unnoticed in normal operation. The proper fix is to enforce a minimum deposit amount or to round the fee calculation up (e.g., using a ceiling division) or to require that feeAmount be at least one token unit when percentFee > 0. This class of bug is a rounding/precision underflow that occurs when fee calculations are performed with integer division without safeguards for small values.

title: CREATE3 is not available in the zkSync Era.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of the CREATE3 library on the zkSync Era network, where the underlying address calculation for CREATE2 differs from Ethereum. CREATE3 assumes that the address returned by its getDeployed function matches the address that will be produced by a subsequent CREATE3.deploy call, following the standard Ethereum CREATE2 formula. On zkSync Era, however, the CREATE2 derivation incorporates an additional keccak256("zksyncCreate2") prefix and a different ordering of the sender, salt, bytecode hash and constructor input hash. Because the library does not account for these differences, the pre‑calculated address (preCalculatedAddress) is incorrect, while the actual deployed contract resides at a different location. The registry then records the wrong address as the anchor, causing the anchor registration logic to point to an address that contains no code. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the anchor address as registered, but any interaction with that address fails silently, balances appear unchanged, and refunds or other expected actions do not occur. The impact is that users cannot perform anchor‑related operations, potentially leading to locked funds or failed transactions. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors compared the zkSync Era documentation with the behavior of the CREATE3 library and reproduced the mismatch on the testnet. It is hard to notice because the contract compiles and the deployment transaction succeeds, yet the address stored in the registry does not correspond to the deployed bytecode, a subtle runtime inconsistency. The bug belongs to the class of address‑derivation mismatches caused by platform‑specific CREATE2 semantics. To remediate the problem the contract should replace CREATE3 with a direct CREATE2 implementation that follows zkSync Era’s address formula, use type(Anchor).creationCode for the bytecode, and adjust the address‑computation routine accordingly. This ensures that the pre‑calculated address matches the actual deployed address, restoring correct anchor registration and preventing user‑visible failures such as missing balances or failed refunds.

title: Anchor contract is unable to receive NFTs of
bug_full: The Anchor contract is designed to act as a wallet attached to a user profile, allowing the profile owner to execute arbitrary calls and to receive native ether through its receive() fallback. However, the contract does not implement the ERC721Receiver or ERC1155Receiver interfaces, specifically the onERC721Received and onERC1155Received functions required by the ERC721 and ERC1155 safe transfer mechanisms. When an external account or a protocol attempts to transfer an NFT to the Anchor using safeTransferFrom or when a token is minted directly to the contract with a safeMint function, the ERC721/ERC1155 token contract invokes the receiver hook on the destination. Because the Anchor contract lacks these hooks, the call reverts, causing the transfer to fail. This root cause is a missing implementation of the standard receiver callbacks, not a compilation error, so the contract appears syntactically correct but fails at runtime. An attacker does not need to exploit a vulnerability; the issue is that any legitimate attempt to deposit an NFT will be rejected, effectively preventing the Anchor from holding the intended assets. The impact is that profile owners expecting to store high‑value NFTs in their Anchor will see their transactions revert, leading to a loss of functionality and potential financial loss if the protocol assumes the Anchor can custody NFTs. The problem manifests whenever safeTransferFrom, safeMint, or any ERC1155 safeTransfer is used, and it affects all users, the protocol that relies on the Anchor for NFT‑based features, and any third‑party strategy that tries to send NFTs to the contract. The issue was discovered during a manual audit review of the contract’s source code, where the absence of the required receiver functions was noted. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors and includes a receive() function for ether, which may give a false impression that all token types are supported. To remediate, the contract should inherit from IERC721Receiver and IERC1155Receiver (or the OpenZeppelin equivalents) and implement onERC721Received and onERC1155Received to return the correct selector values, thereby satisfying the ERC721 and ERC1155 safe transfer specifications. Once these callbacks are added, the Anchor will be able to accept NFTs as intended, aligning the contract’s behavior with user expectations that a wallet can hold both ether and tokenized assets.

title: fundPool does not work with fee-on-transfer
description:
In _fundPool, the parameter for increasePoolAmount is directly the amount used in the transferFrom call.
re/Allo.sol#L516-L517
```solidity
_transferAmountFrom(_token, TransferData({from: msg.sender, to: address(_strategy), amount: amountAfterFee}));
_strategy.increasePoolAmount(amountAfterFee);
```

When _token is a fee-on-transfer token, the actual amount transferred to _strategy will be less than amountAfterFee. Therefore, the current approach could lead to a recorded balance that is greater than the actual balance. fundPool does not work with fee-on-transfer token
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fundPool routine that records the amount of tokens added to a strategy pool. The function takes a parameter called amountAfterFee and passes it directly to a low‑level transferFrom call, then immediately forwards the same value to the strategy’s increasePoolAmount method. This logic assumes that the token transfer will deliver exactly amountAfterFee to the strategy contract. However, for fee‑on‑transfer (also known as tax or deflationary) tokens, the token contract deducts a portion of the transferred amount as a fee, so the actual number of tokens arriving at the strategy is lower than amountAfterFee. Because the contract records the higher, expected amount without verifying the real balance change, the recorded pool balance can become larger than the true token balance held by the strategy. The mismatch can be triggered whenever a user calls fundPool with a token that implements a transfer fee, which includes many popular DeFi tokens. Users who deposit such tokens see their pool share increase according to the advertised amount, but the underlying token balance is smaller. Later, when withdrawals or profit calculations rely on the recorded pool amount, the protocol may allow users to claim more tokens than are actually available, leading to a shortfall of funds, incorrect accounting, and potential loss of assets for other participants. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Allo V2 codebase when the auditor noticed that the amount passed to increasePoolAmount was taken directly from the input rather than from the observed token balance change. The bug can be subtle because the transferFrom call does not revert; it simply transfers a reduced amount, so the contract’s state appears consistent at the time of deposit. Only when the discrepancy surfaces during later accounting or withdrawal operations does the problem become evident. To remediate the flaw, the contract should measure the actual token balance received by the strategy – for example by recording the token balance before the transfer, performing the transfer, then measuring the balance after and using the difference as the argument to increasePoolAmount. This ensures that the recorded pool amount always matches the real token holdings, preserving the protocol’s accounting invariants and preventing users from receiving more tokens than were deposited.

title: Exponential Inflation of Voice Credits in Quadratic
description:
In the given code snippet, we observe a potential issue in the way voice credits are being accumulated for each recipient. The specific lines of code in question are:
```solidity
function _qv_allocate(
    ...
) internal onlyActiveAllocation {
    ...
    uint256 creditsCastToRecipient = _allocator.voiceCreditsCastToRecipient[_recipientId];
    ...
    // get the total credits and calculate the vote result
    uint256 totalCredits = _voiceCreditsToAllocate + creditsCastToRecipient;
    ...
    //E update allocator mapping voice for this recipient
    _allocator.voiceCreditsCastToRecipient[_recipientId] += totalCredits;
    //E @question should be only _voiceCreditsToAllocate
    ...
}
```

We can see that at the end :
```solidity
_allocator.voiceCreditsCastToRecipient[_recipientId] = _allocator.voiceCreditsCastToRecipient[_recipientId] + _voiceCreditsToAllocate + _allocator.voiceCreditsCastToRecipient[_recipientId];
```

Here, totalCredits accumulates both the newly allocated voice credits (_voiceCreditsToAllocate) and the credits previously cast to this recipient (creditsCastToRecipient). Later on, this totalCredits is added again to voiceCreditsCastToRecipient[_recipientId], thereby including the previously cast credits once more

Proof of Concept (POC):
Let's consider a scenario where a user allocates credits in three separate transactions:
1. Transaction 1: Allocates 5 credits
• creditsCastToRecipient initially is 0
• totalCredits = 5 (5 + 0)
• New voiceCreditsCastToRecipient[_recipientId] = 5
2. Transaction 2: Allocates another 5 credits
• creditsCastToRecipient now is 5 (from previous transaction)
• totalCredits = 10 (5 + 5)
• New voiceCreditsCastToRecipient[_recipientId] = 15 (10 + 5)
3. Transaction 3: Allocates another 5 credits
• creditsCastToRecipient now is 15
• totalCredits = 20 (5 + 15)
• New voiceCreditsCastToRecipient[_recipientId] = 35 (20 + 15)

From the above, we can see that the voice credits cast to the recipient are exponentially growing with each transaction instead of linearly increasing by 5 each time. Exponential increase in the voice credits attributed to a recipient, significantly skewing the results of the voting strategy( if one recipient receive 15 votes in one vote and another one receive 5 votes 3 times, the second one will have 20 votes and the first one 15) Over time, this could allow for manipulation and loss of trust in the voting mechanism and the percentage of amount received by recipients as long as allocations are used to calculate the match amount they will receive from the pool amount.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a double‑counting logic error in the allocation routine that updates a recipient's voice‑credit balance. When the function processes a new allocation it first reads the existing credits for the recipient, adds the newly allocated amount to obtain a variable called totalCredits, and then adds totalCredits to the stored balance. Because totalCredits already contains the previous balance, the stored balance is increased by the sum of the new credits and the old credits, effectively adding the old credits a second time. This causes the voice‑credit tally to grow exponentially rather than linearly with each allocation. The bug can be triggered whenever the internal allocation function is called, which means any participant who repeatedly allocates credits to a recipient can inflate that recipient's voting power far beyond the intended amount. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a recipient receiving far more votes than they actually allocated – for example, three allocations of five credits each result in a reported balance of thirty‑five credits instead of fifteen. The inflated voting power skews the outcome of the quadratic voting mechanism and distorts the calculation of match amounts that are derived from the vote totals, potentially leading to unfair distribution of pooled funds and loss of trust in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the allocation logic, where the auditor noticed that the mapping update line added both the new allocation and the existing balance. It is subtle because the numbers increase in a plausible way, making it easy to overlook the exponential growth without detailed testing. The proper fix is to update the recipient’s balance by adding only the newly allocated voice credits, i.e., increment the stored value by the allocation amount alone, eliminating the double addition of the previous balance. This correction restores linear growth of voice credits, preserves the intended voting economics, and prevents manipulation of the matching pool.

title: RFPSimpleStrategy milestones can be set mul-
description:
The setMilestones function in RFPSimpleStrategy contract checks if MILESTONES_ALREADY_SET or not by upcomingMilestone index. if (upcomingMilestone != 0) revert MILESTONES_ALREADY_SET(); But upcomingMilestone increases only after distribution, and until this time will always be equal to 0. It can accidentally break the pool state or be used with malicious intentions.
1. Two managers accidentally set the same milestones. Milestones are duplicated and can't be reset, the pool needs to be recreated.
2. The manager, in cahoots with the recipient, sets milestones one by one, thereby bypassing totalAmountPercentage check and increasing the payout amount.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the milestone configuration function of the RFPSimpleStrategy contract. The function is intended to be callable only once to establish a fixed schedule of payouts, but it guards this restriction by checking the upcomingMilestone index. Because upcomingMilestone is initialized to zero and is only incremented after the first distribution, the condition `if (upcomingMilestone != 0) revert MILESTONES_ALREADY_SET()` never triggers during the initial configuration phase. As a result, multiple managers—or a single manager acting repeatedly—can invoke setMilestones repeatedly before any distribution occurs. This permits the creation of duplicate milestone entries and, more critically, allows a manager colluding with a recipient to add milestones one by one, thereby bypassing the totalAmountPercentage validation that ensures the sum of all payouts does not exceed the allocated pool. The impact includes over‑payment of funds, corruption of the pool’s internal state, and the inability to reset or correct the milestone list without recreating the entire pool. The issue manifests when a pool is freshly deployed and funded but before the first payout; any attempt to set milestones at that stage will succeed regardless of prior calls. Users of the protocol—such as token holders, project owners, and recipients—may observe unexpected behavior: the pool may appear to have been funded correctly, yet payouts exceed the intended amount, or the pool may become unusable and require redeployment. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state‑guard logic of the setMilestones function and identified that the guard relied on a variable that does not change until after distribution, making the check ineffective. Because the contract does not emit explicit warnings or revert on duplicate milestone creation, the problem can be subtle and may only be noticed after funds have been misallocated. To remediate, the contract should verify that the milestones array is empty before allowing a new configuration, for example by checking `if (milestones.length > 0) revert MILESTONES_ALREADY_SET()`. Alternatively, the contract could permit resetting milestones only when they are not actively in use, by ensuring the first milestone’s status is None before deleting the existing list. This class of bug is a state‑initialization guard failure, where an improper condition allows re‑initialisation of critical protocol parameters, leading to accounting violations and potential financial loss.

title: minOfferCost can be bypassed in certain sce-
description: minOfferCost is designed to prevent spam loan requests that can cause the lender to have positions that cost more gas to claim than interest. Due to how interest is calculated right after this minimum is passed it is still possible for the lender to receive less than the minimum. ClaimFacet.sol#L94-L106 ```solidity function sendInterests(Loan storage loan, Provision storage provision) internal returns (uint256 sent) { uint256 interests = loan.payment.paid - loan.lent; if (interests == loan.payment.minInterestsToRepay) { // this is the case if the loan is repaid shortly after issuance // each lender gets its minimal interest, as an anti ddos measure to spam offer sent = provision.amount + (interests / loan.nbOfPositions); } else { /* provision.amount / lent = share of the interests belonging to the lender. The parenthesis make the calculus in the order that maximizes precison */ sent = provision.amount + (interests * (provision.amount)) / loan.lent; } loan.assetLent.checkedTransfer(msg.sender, sent); } ``` When a loan has generated more than the minimum interest amount the method for calculating the interest paid is different and depending on the size of the provisions it may lead to provisions that are under the guaranteed minimum. Example: Assume the minimum interest is 1e18. A loan is filled with 2 provisions. The first provision is 25% and the second is 75%. Since there are two loans the total minimum interest for the loan is 2e18. After some time the paid interest reaches 2.001e18 and the loan is paid back. Since it is above the minimum interest rate, it is paid out proportionally. This gives 0.5e18 to the first provision and 1.5e18 to the second provision. This violates the minimum guaranteed interest amount. Minimum interest guarantee can be violated
bug_full: The contract implements a minimum interest guarantee (minOfferCost) that is intended to protect lenders from spam loan requests that would otherwise generate interest payouts smaller than the cost of claiming them. The guarantee is enforced by checking whether the total accrued interest equals the configured minimum (minInterestsToRepay). If the loan is repaid shortly after issuance, a fixed minimal amount is distributed to each lender; otherwise the contract distributes interest proportionally based on each provision's share of the total lent amount. The vulnerability arises because the proportional formula does not enforce the per‑provision minimum when the loan contains multiple provisions and the total interest is only slightly above the global minimum. When the number of provisions n is greater than one, a provision that represents less than 1/n of the total loan can receive an amount that falls below the guaranteed minimum, even though the overall interest exceeds the threshold. An attacker can create many small provisions or manipulate the timing of repayment so that the total interest is just above the minimum, causing each individual lender to be paid less than expected. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a lower‑than‑advertised payout: a lender who expects to receive at least the minimum interest sees a reduced amount, sometimes even zero, despite the loan being fully repaid. This breaks the economic assumptions of the protocol, reduces incentives for lenders, and may open the system to spam attacks because the anti‑DDoS safeguard no longer holds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the sendInterests function, where the conditional branch for the “interest equals minInterestsToRepay” case was examined and the subsequent proportional calculation was found to ignore the per‑provision floor. The bug is subtle because the total interest appears to satisfy the minimum, so a superficial check of the contract’s state would not reveal the under‑payment of individual provisions. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce a per‑provision minimum that is derived from the smallest allowed provision percentage, or restrict provision sizes so that no single provision can be smaller than 1/(2n) of the total loan. Alternatively, the distribution logic could be rewritten to guarantee that each provision receives at least minInterestsToRepay/n, regardless of the proportional share, thereby preserving the intended anti‑spam guarantee.

title: If auction price goes to 0, NFT might become
description: There are certain ERC20 tokens which revert on zero value transfers (e.g. LEND). If an NFT's price drops down to 0, nobody will be able to claim it as the transaction will always revert. The time of loan.auction.duration passes. The NFT's price is 0. Alice tries to purchase/ claim it, however the ERC20 token on which the auctions is going reverts on 0 value transfers. The NFT becomes stuck forever and no one can take the rights of it. Consider the following scenarios: 1. The ERC20 used in the auction is pausable Throughout the auction, the token gets paused. Now, the auction is still going, the price is dropping and no one is able to claim it. The ERC20 doesn't get unpaused up until the auction ends. Since no one was able to purchase the NFT during the auction, its price now is 0. Since the token reverts on zero value transfers, the NFT is stuck forever. 2. Alice is looking at NFT auction which is coming near its end. Alice is looking to purchase the NFT for as little as possible and starts monitoring the mempool, so in case someone tries to buy it, she can front-run the transaction and get the NFT herself. At this point Alice getting the NFT should be guaranteed However, there aren't many other active users/ they aren't paying attention to said NFT. Little time goes by, auction ends and price is set to 0. Alice is happy she can claim the NFT for free. However, the token reverts on 0 value transfers and now no one can claim it and the NFT is lost forever. NFT might be lost forever
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an auction contract that accepts payment in an ERC20 token whose transfer function deliberately reverts when the transferred amount is zero. The auction logic permits the price of the listed NFT to decay to zero as the auction timer expires. When the price reaches zero, a buyer – often a user trying to claim the NFT for free – initiates a purchase transaction that attempts to transfer 0 tokens to the seller. Because the underlying token rejects zero‑value transfers, the transaction reverts, the transfer never occurs, and the auction contract does not record a new owner. Consequently the NFT becomes permanently locked in the contract with no way to transfer ownership, effectively disappearing from the protocol’s usable assets. The root cause is a mismatch between the token’s transfer semantics and the auction’s price‑floor logic: the contract does not enforce a minimum non‑zero price nor does it handle the special case where the token rejects a zero‑amount transfer. Exploitation is straightforward – an attacker or even a passive participant can simply wait until the auction timer runs out and the price naturally falls to zero, then attempt to claim the NFT; the claim will always revert, leaving the token‑locked NFT stuck forever. The impact is that the NFT is lost to the protocol, users cannot retrieve or sell the asset, and the overall trust in the auction mechanism is eroded. This condition occurs only when the auction is denominated in a token that has a hard‑coded revert on zero transfers (for example LEND) and when the auction’s price‑decay algorithm allows the price to reach zero, possibly compounded by a paused token that cannot be unpaused before the auction ends. All parties that might interact with the auction – bidders, the original NFT owner, and the protocol itself – are affected because the asset becomes unrecoverable. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined token compatibility and identified that the contract did not guard against zero‑value transfers. It is easy to miss because zero‑value transfers are rarely exercised in normal operation and the UI may display a “Buy for 0” button that appears legitimate, while the underlying transaction fails silently. To remediate, the auction should enforce a minimal price greater than zero (for example one wei) or include explicit handling for zero‑price cases, and it should reject tokens that revert on zero transfers or wrap the transfer call with a conditional that bypasses the revert. In broader terms, this is a business‑logic deadlock caused by an incompatibility between token transfer semantics and auction price decay, leading to a situation where funds or assets disappear from the user’s perspective despite the contract appearing to function correctly.

title: fee calculations
description: in/concentrator/contracts/Multipool.sol#L722-L746, these LOCs don't allow underflow/overflow, but refering to https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core/issues/573 which allows underflow/overflow. This will lead to some transactions will revert. • some user transactions will revert. ```solidity if (liquidity > 0) { ( uint256 feeGrowthInside0X128Pending, uint256 feeGrowthInside1X128Pending ) = _getFeeGrowthInside( IUniswapV3Pool(position.poolAddress), slots[i].tick, position.lowerTick, position.upperTick ); pendingFee0 += uint128( FullMath.mulDiv( feeGrowthInside0X128Pending - feeGrowthInside0LastX128, liquidity, ) ); pendingFee1 += uint128( FullMath.mulDiv( feeGrowthInside1X128Pending - feeGrowthInside1LastX128, liquidity, ) ); } ```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee‑accumulation logic of the Multipool contract where pending fees are calculated using a subtraction of two 128‑bit fee‑growth values followed by a FullMath.mulDiv operation. The code assumes that the current feeGrowthInside value is always greater than or equal to the previously stored feeGrowthInsideLast value, an invariant that holds for the original Uniswap V3 implementation. However, a known issue in the Uniswap V3 core (issue 573) permits the fee‑growth counters to underflow or overflow due to wrap‑around arithmetic. Because Solidity 0.8+ enforces checked arithmetic by default, the subtraction feeGrowthInsideX128Pending - feeGrowthInsideX128LastX128 will revert when an underflow occurs. Consequently, any user transaction that triggers the pending‑fee calculation while the counters have wrapped will revert, preventing the user from claiming accrued fees. From the user’s perspective the transaction fails with no obvious error, the UI may show that the pending fee balance remains zero or that a withdrawal attempt simply reverts, leading to confusion and the impression that funds are missing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that cross‑referenced the contract’s source with the Uniswap core bug report. It is subtle because the code itself contains no explicit overflow checks and the underflow condition is rare, only appearing after a specific sequence of pool interactions that cause the fee‑growth counters to wrap. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic underflow/overflow vulnerabilities where implicit assumptions about monotonic counters are violated. To remediate, the fee‑growth subtraction should be performed inside an unchecked block, allowing the wrap‑around behavior to match the Uniswap core’s design and preventing the transaction from reverting. This change restores the intended accounting semantics, ensuring that users can successfully claim their pending fees even when the underlying counters have wrapped.

title: emergency_shutdownrole is not enough for emer-
poc: To get a coded PoC, make the following modifications to the test case: lob/main/Cooler/src/test/Clearinghouse.t.sol#L125 //rolesAdmin.grantRole("cooler_overseer", overseer); rolesAdmin.grantRole("emergency_shutdown", overseer); • Run the following test command (to just run a single test test_emergencyShutdown()): forge test --match-test test_emergencyShutdown The test will fail with the ROLES_RequireRole() error.
bug_full: The contract implements an emergencyShutdown function that is intended to deactivate the protocol and optionally return any held stablecoins (sDAI and DAI) to a treasury. The function is protected by the onlyRole("emergency_shutdown") modifier, so an account with that role is expected to be able to call it. Inside the function the code reads the balances of sDAI and DAI and, if they are non‑zero, calls defund(token, amount) to transfer the assets out. However, the defund function itself is guarded by onlyRole("cooler_overseer"). Because the emergencyShutdown function does not have the cooler_overseer role, the internal call to defund reverts with a ROLES_RequireRole error unless the caller also holds the overseer role. As a result, an account that only has the emergency_shutdown role cannot successfully execute the shutdown; the transaction fails before the active flag is set to false and before the Deactivated event is emitted. This mismatch between the external role check and the internal role requirement creates a logical flaw that effectively disables the emergency shutdown mechanism. The impact is that during a crisis the protocol may remain active, funds could stay locked in the contract, and users may be unable to retrieve their assets because the expected shutdown path is blocked. The bug manifests whenever an emergency_shutdown role holder attempts to invoke emergencyShutdown without also being a cooler_overseer, which is a realistic scenario because the two roles are defined for distinct responsibilities. The issue was discovered during an audit when a test case granted only the emergency_shutdown role to an overseer address and observed a revert with the ROLES_RequireRole error. It can be hard to notice because the function signature and external modifier appear correct, and the failure occurs only after the internal defund call, which may be overlooked during a quick code review. To remediate the problem the logic should be decoupled: either remove the defund calls from emergencyShutdown and perform defunding in a separate transaction, or move the defunding code to an internal helper that does not carry a role restriction, allowing the shutdown function to complete its primary purpose without requiring the overseer role. In either case the contract must ensure that the emergency_shutdown role alone is sufficient to deactivate the protocol as intended, preserving the intended safety guarantees and preventing a denial‑of‑service style failure where the protocol cannot be halted.

title: Lender is able to steal borrowers collateral by
description: Say a user has 100 collateral tokens valued at $1,500 and they wish to borrow 1,000 debt tokens valued at $1,000 they would would call: (values have simplified for ease of math) requestLoan("1,000 debt tokens", "5% interest", "10 loan tokens for each collateral", "1 year") ,! If a lender then clears the request the borrower would expect to have 1 year to payback 1,050 debt tokens to be able to receive their collateral back. However a lender is able to call provideNewTermsForRoll with whatever terms they wish: i.e. provideNewTermsForRoll("loanID", "10000000% interest", "1000 loan tokens for each collateral" , "1 year") ,! They can then follow this up with a call to rollLoan(loanID): During the rollLoan function the interest is recalculated using: ```solidity function interestFor(uint256 amount_, uint256 rate_, uint256 duration_) public pure returns (uint256) { uint256 interest = (rate_ * duration_) / 365 days; return (amount_ * interest) / DECIMALS_INTEREST; } ``` As rate_ & duration_ are controllable by the borrower when they call provideNewTermsForRoll they can input a large number that the amount returned is much larger then the value of the collateral. i.e. input a rate_ of amount * 3 and duration of 365 days so that the interestFor returns 3,000. This amount gets added to the existing loan.amount and would make it too costly to ever repay as the borrower would have to spend more then the value of the collateral is worth to get it back. i.e. borrower now would now need to send 4,050 debt tokens to receive their $1,500 worth of collateral back instead of the expected 1050. The extra amount should result in more collateral needing to be sent however it is calculated using loan.request.loanToCollateral which is also controlled by the lender when they call provideNewTermsForRoll, allowing them to input a value that will result in newCollateralFor returning 0 and no new collateral needing to be sent. ```solidity function newCollateralFor(uint256 loanID_) public view returns (uint256) { Loan memory loan = loans[loanID_]; // Accounts for all outstanding debt (borrowed amount + interest). uint256 neededCollateral = collateralFor(loan.amount, loan.request.loanToCollateral); // Lender can force neededCollateral to always be less than loan.collateral return neededCollateral > loan.collateral ? neededCollateral - loan.collateral : 0; } ``` As a result a borrower who was expecting to have repay 1050 tokens to get back their collateral may now need to spend many multiples more of that and will just be forced to just forfeit their collateral to the lender. Borrower will be forced to payback the loan at unfavourable terms or forfeit their collateral.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic manipulation bug that allows a lender to arbitrarily increase the debt and alter the collateral‑to‑debt ratio of an existing loan, effectively forcing the borrower to forfeit their collateral. The root cause is the absence of any access control or validation on the functions that let a lender propose new loan terms (provideNewTermsForRoll) and subsequently execute a roll (rollLoan). Because the interest rate, loan duration and the loan‑to‑collateral factor are supplied by the caller and are later used directly in the interestFor and newCollateralFor calculations, a malicious lender can supply extreme values – for example a 10 000 000 % interest rate and a loan‑to‑collateral multiplier that makes the required additional collateral evaluate to zero. When rollLoan is invoked, the contract recomputes the total amount owed by multiplying the original principal by the inflated interest, producing a debt that far exceeds the value of the pledged collateral. At the same time, newCollateralFor returns zero additional collateral because the lender‑controlled loanToCollateral parameter forces the needed collateral calculation to be less than the already posted collateral. From the borrower’s point of view the UI will still show that the loan is active, but the repayment amount displayed suddenly jumps from the expected 1 050 debt tokens to several thousand, while the system indicates that no extra collateral is required. The borrower therefore faces a choice: either attempt to repay an amount that is economically impossible or surrender the collateral for nothing. This scenario can occur whenever a loan is in a state that permits rolling and the lender is able to call the term‑changing functions, which is typical in many lending protocols that allow renegotiation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noticed that the functions lack any restriction on who may call them and that the arithmetic uses unbounded user‑controlled parameters. The bug is subtle because the calculations themselves are mathematically correct; the problem only manifests when the inputs are maliciously extreme, making it easy to overlook during normal testing. To remediate the issue the contract should restrict rollLoan (and the term‑setting function) to an authorized entity such as the contract owner or a governance module, and it should enforce sensible bounds on interest rates, durations and loan‑to‑collateral ratios. Additionally, the protocol should require explicit borrower consent before any term change takes effect, and it should validate that the new required collateral is never less than the amount already posted. By applying these controls the protocol can prevent lenders from unilaterally imposing unaffordable repayment terms and protect borrowers from losing their collateral unexpectedly.

title: gOhm stuck forever if call claimDefaulted on
description: 1. Bob calls Clearinghouse.lendToCooler to make a loan collateralized by 1000 gOhm. 2. Bob defaults on the loan 3. Immediately after default, Eve calls Cooler.claimDefaulted on Bob's loan. 4. The gOhm is transferred to the Clearinghouse 5. There is no way to burn or transfer it. (In fact, defund() can be used to transfer literally any token except gOhm back to the treasury.) However, the gOhm can now be stolen using the exploit in #1, potentially in the same transaction as when Eve called Cooler.claimDefaulted(). Anyone can very easily make all defaulted gOhm get stuck forever. Cooler.claimDefaulted sends the collateral to the lender, calls onDefault #L325 Clearinghouse.onDefault does nothing ouse.sol#L265 Although Clearinghouse.defund() can be used to send any other token back to the treasury, it cannot do so for gOhm ouse.sol#L340
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of gOhm tokens used as collateral in the Clearinghouse loan system. When a borrower defaults and an external actor calls Cooler.claimDefaulted, the contract moves the gOhm collateral to the Clearinghouse contract. However, the Clearinghouse’s onDefault function is empty and the defund routine, which is intended to return any token to the treasury, explicitly excludes gOhm. As a result the gOhm becomes permanently locked inside the Clearinghouse with no mechanism to transfer, burn, or otherwise recover it. This logical flaw arises because the code assumes all ERC‑20 tokens can be handled by defund, but a hard‑coded exception for gOhm prevents that. An attacker can trigger claimDefaulted on any defaulted loan, even without being the lender, causing the collateral to be trapped. The impact is that lenders expecting to receive their collateral after a default receive nothing, effectively losing the value of the gOhm and breaking the protocol’s accounting invariant that collateral can be reclaimed. The issue manifests only after a default event for loans that used gOhm as collateral and when claimDefaulted is invoked, which any address can do. Users see their balances drop to zero and receive no refund, a symptom that can be mistaken for a scam. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the default handling logic and noticed that defund does not support gOhm. Because the failure is silent—no revert or error is emitted—the bug can be hard to notice unless the specific token is tested. To remediate, the contract should either restrict claimDefaulted to be callable only by the original lender, or extend the onDefault/defund logic to include a safe transfer or burn path for gOhm, ensuring that collateral can always be reclaimed or properly accounted for.

title: Lender can front-run rollLoan and call
description: After a loan is created, the lender can provide new loan terms via provideNewTermsForRoll. If they are reasonable, the user can then accept them. However this opens up a risky scenario: 1. User A borrows from lender B 2. Lender B proposes new suitable terms 3. User A sees them and calls rollLoan to accept them 4. Lender B is waiting for this and sees the pending transaction in the mempool 5. Lender B front-runs user A's transaction and makes a new call to provideNewTermsForRoll will an extremely high interest rate 6. User A's transaction now executes and they've accepted unfavorable terms with extremely high interest rate User may get mislead in to accepting unfavorable terms and overpaying interest
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running race condition that occurs when a borrower accepts new loan terms offered by a lender. After a loan is created, the lender can call provideNewTermsForRoll to propose updated terms, such as a different interest rate. The borrower then calls rollLoan to accept those terms. Because the contract does not record a bound on the interest rate at the moment the borrower signs the transaction, a malicious lender (or any actor with the ability to submit a transaction) can observe the pending rollLoan transaction in the mempool, submit another provideNewTermsForRoll call with an extremely high interest rate, and have that transaction mined before the borrower’s rollLoan. When the borrower’s transaction finally executes, the contract sees the latest terms – the inflated interest rate – and the borrower unintentionally accepts them. This leads to the borrower overpaying interest, potentially paying far more than expected, and seeing their effective loan cost increase dramatically. The issue is triggered only when the borrower relies on off‑chain information about the proposed terms and the contract does not enforce that the terms have not changed between proposal and acceptance. It primarily affects borrowers who use the rollLoan feature, but any lender can exploit the same mechanism to extract higher fees from users. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of provideNewTermsForRoll and rollLoan and noticed the absence of a maximum‑interest check. It can be hard to notice because the user interface typically shows the proposed terms at the time of viewing, and the borrower may not realize that the terms can be altered in the short window before the transaction is mined. To remediate the issue, the rollLoan function should require the borrower to specify the maximum interest rate they are willing to accept, and the contract must enforce that the current terms do not exceed this limit before applying them. Additional mitigations could include a commit‑reveal scheme or a time‑locked acceptance period to prevent immediate overwriting of terms. By bounding the acceptable interest rate, the protocol ensures that borrowers receive the terms they saw and prevents malicious front‑running that would otherwise cause unexpected high interest charges and financial loss.

title: Denial-of-Service in the liquidation flow re-
description: If the loanTovalue value of the offer is extremely high, the liquidation flow will be reverted, causing the collateral NTF to persist in the contract forever. The platform allows users to sign offers and provide funds to those who need to borrow assets. In the first scenario, the lender provided an offer that the loanTovalue as high as the result of the shareMatched is 0. For example, if the borrowed amount was 1e40 and the offer had a loanToValue equal to 1e68, the share would be 0. BorrowLogic/BorrowHandlers.sol#L47 As a result, an arithmetic error (Division or modulo by 0) will occur in the price() function at line 50 during the liquidation process. AuctionFacet.sol#L34-L55 In the second scenario, if the lender's share exceeds 0, but the offer's loanToValue is extremely high, the price() function at line 54 may encounter an arithmetic error(Arithmetic over/underflow) during the estimatedValue calculation. AuctionFacet.sol#L54 Poof of Concept kairos-contracts/test/BorrowBorrow.t.sol ```solidity function testBorrowOverflow() public { uint256 borrowAmount = 1e40; BorrowArg[] memory borrowArgs = new BorrowArg[](1); (, ,uint256 loanId , ) = kairos.getParameters(); loanId += 1; Offer memory offer = Offer({ assetToLend: money, loanToValue: 1e61, duration: 1, expirationDate: block.timestamp + 2 hours, tranche: 0, collateral: getNft() }); uint256 currentTokenId; getFlooz(signer, money, getOfferArg(offer).amount); { OfferArg[] memory offerArgs = new OfferArg[](1); currentTokenId = getJpeg(BORROWER, nft); offer.collateral.id = currentTokenId; offerArgs[0] = OfferArg({ signature: getSignature(offer), amount: borrowAmount, offer: offer }); borrowArgs[0] = BorrowArg({nft: NFToken({id: currentTokenId, implem: nft}), args: offerArgs}); } vm.prank(BORROWER); kairos.borrow(borrowArgs); assertEq(nft.balanceOf(BORROWER), 0); assertEq(money.balanceOf(BORROWER), borrowAmount); assertEq(nft.balanceOf(address(kairos)), 1); vm.warp(block.timestamp + 1); Loan memory loan = kairos.getLoan(loanId); console.log("price of loanId", kairos.price(loanId)); } ``` The loan position will not be liquidated, which will result in the collateral NTF being permanently frozen in the contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that appears during the liquidation phase of a loan when the loan‑to‑value (LTV) parameter of an offer is set to an extremely high value. The root cause is the lack of validation on the LTV field, which allows a lender to create an offer where the calculated share of the lender becomes zero or where arithmetic operations in the price() function overflow. When the borrower accepts such an offer, the loan is recorded normally, but later, when the protocol attempts to liquidate the position, the price() routine performs a division by the lender share (which is zero) or multiplies values that exceed the uint256 range, causing a division‑by‑zero exception or an arithmetic overflow. The transaction reverts, so the liquidation does not complete and the collateral NFT remains locked inside the contract forever. This impact is felt by the borrower, who loses access to the collateral, by the lender, who cannot recover the loaned assets, and by the protocol, whose liquidation mechanism is effectively broken for the affected loan. The condition occurs only when an offer’s LTV is set to a value such that shareMatched evaluates to zero or when the LTV is so large that the estimatedValue calculation overflows; it is triggered during the price() call that is part of the liquidation flow. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case deliberately used a borrow amount of 1e40 together with an LTV of 1e61, causing the price() function to revert with a division‑by‑zero error. Because the error only manifests with extreme, seemingly unrealistic parameters, it can be easy to miss in normal functional testing, and the revert provides no explicit indication that the collateral is permanently frozen. From a user’s perspective the UI would show the loan as still active, the borrower would see no liquidation event, and the NFT balance of the contract would increase while the borrower’s balance stays at zero, contradicting the expectation that the collateral would be sold or returned. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic errors that lead to denial‑of‑service, specifically division‑by‑zero and overflow in financial calculations. To remediate the issue the protocol should enforce a sensible upper bound on the LTV value during offer creation and ensure that the lender’s share is always greater than zero before any price calculation is performed. Adding explicit safe‑math checks and reverting with a clear error message when the parameters are out of range will prevent the liquidation flow from being aborted and keep collateral assets accessible.

title: useLoan doesn't allow liqudator to specifiy
description: useLoan doesn't allow the liquidator to specify a max price they are will to pay for the collateral they are liquidating. On the surface this doesn't seem like an issue because the price is always decreasing due to the dutch auction. However this can be problematic if the chain the contracts are deployed suffers a reorg attack. This can place the transaction earlier than anticipated and therefore charge the user more than they meant to pay. On Ethereum this is unlikely but this is meant to be deployed on any compatible EVM chain many of which are frequently reorganized. See summary. Liquidator can be charged more than intended
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation routine of the loan contract, where the function that executes a liquidation (useLoan) does not give the liquidator any control over the maximum price they are willing to pay for the seized collateral. In a typical Dutch‑auction style liquidation the price of the collateral is programmed to fall over time, so a liquidator normally expects to pay less if the transaction is mined later. However, on blockchains that experience frequent chain reorganisations, a transaction that is submitted with the expectation of being mined after the price has dropped can be pulled into an earlier block when the chain is re‑orged. Because the contract does not enforce a ceiling on the price, the liquidator may end up paying a higher price than intended, effectively over‑paying for the collateral. This can happen when the underlying chain has low finality or is subject to malicious re‑org attacks that reorder pending transactions. The affected parties are the liquidators themselves, who lose value, and indirectly the protocol users who rely on predictable liquidation economics. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the economic assumptions of the liquidation flow and noticed the missing price‑cap parameter. It is subtle because the price is designed to only decrease, so developers may assume that over‑payment cannot occur, making the bug easy to overlook in testing. The impact is a financial loss for the liquidator, potentially eroding confidence in the protocol’s fairness and opening a vector for attackers to manipulate liquidation outcomes by inducing re‑orgs. To remediate, the contract should be modified to accept a maximum acceptable price from the liquidator and enforce that the actual price used in the liquidation does not exceed this bound, reverting the transaction otherwise. This change restores the economic guarantee that a liquidator will never pay more than the price they have explicitly approved, aligning the implementation with the intended auction model and protecting users from unexpected price spikes caused by chain‑level reordering.

title: Adversary can utilize a large number of their
description: The minimal interest paid by a loan is scaled by the number of provisions that make up the loan. By inflating the number of provisions with their own provisions then can cause legitimate lenders to receive a much lower interest rate than intended. ClaimFacet.sol#L94-L106 ```solidity function sendInterests(Loan storage loan, Provision storage provision) internal returns (uint256 sent) { uint256 interests = loan.payment.paid - loan.lent; if (interests == loan.payment.minInterestsToRepay) { // this is the case if the loan is repaid shortly after issuance // each lender gets its minimal interest, as an anti ddos measure to spam offer sent = provision.amount + (interests / loan.nbOfPositions); } else { /* provision.amount / lent = share of the interests belonging to the lender. The parenthesis make the calculus in the order that maximizes precison */ sent = provision.amount + (interests * (provision.amount)) / loan.lent; } loan.assetLent.checkedTransfer(msg.sender, sent); } ``` If a loan is paid back before the minimal interest rate has been reached then each provision will receive the unweighted minimal interest amount. This can be abused to take loans that pay legitimate lenders a lower APR than expected, cheating them of their yield. Example: A user wishes to borrow 1000 USDC at 10% APR. Assume the minimal interest per provision is 10 USDC and minimum borrow amount is 20 USDC. After 1 year the user would owe 100 USDC in interest. A user can abuse the minimum to pay legitimate lenders much lower than 10% APR. The attacker will find a legitimate offer to claim 820 USDC. This will create an offer for themselves and borrow 20 USDC from it 9 times. This creates a total of 10 provisions each owed a minimum of 10 USDC or 100 USDC total. Now after 1 year they owe 100 USDC on their loan and the repay the loan. Since 100 USDC is the minimum, each of the 10 provisions will get their minimal interest. 90 USDC will go to their provisions and 10 will go to the legitimate user who loaned them a majority of the USDC. Their APR is ~1.2% which is ~1/9th of what they specified. Legitimate users can be cheated out of interest owed
bug_full: The vulnerability is an interest‑distribution flaw in the loan contract that allows an attacker to dilute the interest paid to legitimate lenders by inflating the number of loan provisions (positions). The contract calculates a minimal interest amount that is paid to each provision when the loan is repaid before the accrued interest reaches the configured minimum (interest == loan.payment.minInterestsToRepay). In this branch the code adds a fixed minimal interest share that is divided by loan.nbOfPositions, the total number of provisions, regardless of each provision’s size. An adversary can create many small self‑provision entries, each holding a tiny amount of the loan, thereby increasing nbOfPositions dramatically. When the loan is repaid early, the minimal‑interest path is triggered and each provision receives only the tiny per‑position share, so the attacker’s self‑provisions collectively capture almost all of the minimal interest while the genuine lender receives a fraction far below the advertised APR. This can be exploited by repeatedly borrowing the minimum amount, creating a chain of self‑provisions, and then repaying the loan after the minimal‑interest threshold is met. The impact is a severe reduction of the effective annual percentage rate for honest lenders, potentially dropping from the promised 10 % to around 1 % or less, effectively stealing yield. The condition for exploitation is that the loan is repaid before the accrued interest exceeds the minimal‑interest threshold and that the attacker can add a large number of provisions to the same loan. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the loan repayment logic, where the division by loan.nbOfPositions in the minimal‑interest branch was identified as a source of disproportionate interest allocation. The flaw is subtle because the minimal‑interest path is intended as an anti‑ddos safeguard and is rarely exercised, so developers may assume it cannot be abused. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the size of each provision is comparable, limit the number of provisions per loan, or, more robustly, calculate the minimal‑interest share proportionally to each provision’s amount rather than equally dividing by the count. This ensures that even when the minimal‑interest branch is taken, each lender receives interest commensurate with their contribution, preserving the intended APR and preventing yield dilution.

title: The fees are incorrectly updated in the_deposit
description:
In _deposit and _withdraw function of Multipool contract, fee0 and fee1 are calculated from the accrued fee amounts to update feeGrowth of contract and send the protocol fee to the owner. However, these calculations are incorrect and do not align with the collected fees from the positions. It allows attacker break the protocol fees.
In function withdraw, all accrued fees from Uniswap V3 pool will be collected (tokensOwed0After and tokensOwed1After). However, fee0 and fee1 are updated by tokensOwed0After - tokensOwed0Before and tokensOwed1After - tokensOwed1Before.
It is incorrect because in cases where tokensOwed0Before > 0 or tokensOwed1Before > 0, fee0 and fee1 end up being smaller than the collected fees. Consequently, when _upFeesGrowth is executed, it will send smaller protocol fees than expected.
Therefore, an attacker can exploit this vulnerability and undermine the protocol fees by minting minuscule amounts to all positions within the Multipool contract.
This is possible since anyone can mint for any positions in UniSwapV3 pools (the owner of position is recipient). This causes the fees of each position to be accrued beforehand, resulting in tokensOwed0Before and tokensOwed1Before becoming close to tokensOwed0After and tokensOwed1After. Then the majority of protocol fees will be lost (solvent in the reserve).
Scenario:
1. Attacker mints minuscule amounts to all positions within the Multipool contract to accrue fees for these positions.
2. The attacker then calls the earn() function to collect and update fees. In this scenario, tokensOwed0Before and tokensOwed1Before become equal to tokensOwed0After and tokensOwed1After (withdrawing 0 liquidity). As a result, fee0 and fee1 become 0, leading to the loss of these protocol fees.
Similar to _deposit function.
Protocol will lose its fees.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the Multipool contract updates its protocol fee accounting during deposit and withdrawal operations. Instead of recording the total fees that have been collected from the Uniswap V3 pool, the contract computes the fee increments (fee0 and fee1) as the difference between the post‑operation owed token amounts (tokensOwed0After, tokensOwed1After) and the pre‑operation owed amounts (tokensOwed0Before, tokensOwed1Before). When a position already has a non‑zero owed balance, this subtraction yields a value that is smaller than the actual fees accrued, and in the extreme case where the owed balances are unchanged the computed fee increment becomes zero. The root cause is an incorrect accounting formula that assumes no prior fee balance, ignoring the fact that Uniswap V3 positions can accumulate fees before the Multipool contract interacts with them. An attacker can exploit this by minting a very small amount of liquidity to every position that the Multipool contract tracks, thereby forcing each position to accrue a tiny fee balance before any deposit or withdrawal occurs. Because the attacker can then call the contract’s earn() function (or trigger a withdrawal with zero liquidity), the tokensOwed values before and after the operation become almost identical, causing fee0 and fee1 to be calculated as zero. Consequently, the internal _upFeesGrowth routine distributes no protocol fees to the owner, and the fees that should have been transferred remain trapped in the pool’s reserves. This results in a loss of revenue for the protocol and reduces the expected compensation for the contract owner. The issue manifests only when there are pre‑existing fee balances on positions, a condition that is not obvious from the UI; users may see that fees have been accrued but the protocol’s fee balance does not increase, leading to confusion. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑handling logic, where the auditor noticed that the fee growth calculation did not match the total collected fees. It is hard to notice because the contract still updates its feeGrowth variable, but the amount added is silently smaller than it should be, and no explicit error is thrown. To remediate the problem, the fee calculation should be changed so that fee0 and fee1 are set directly to the total collected amounts (tokensOwed0After and tokensOwed1After) or, alternatively, the prior owed balances should be added back to the growth calculation, ensuring that the protocol receives the full amount of fees that were actually earned. This aligns the accounting with the business logic that the protocol must capture a fixed percentage of all fees generated by the underlying Uniswap V3 pool.

title: Checking `bool` return of ERC20 `approve` and `transfer` breaks protocol for mainnet USDT and similar tokens which don't return true
description:
Checking `bool` return of ERC20 `approve` and `transfer` breaks protocol for mainnet USDT and similar tokens which [don't return true](https://etherscan.io/token/0xdac17f958d2ee523a2206206994597c13d831ec7#code) even though the calls were successful.

Protocol won't work with mainnet USDT and similar tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract assuming that the ERC20 functions approve and transfer always return a boolean value indicating success and explicitly checking that return with a require statement. In reality, several widely‑deployed tokens on Ethereum mainnet, most notably USDT, implement the ERC20 interface without returning any value; they simply revert on failure and otherwise return nothing. Because the contract treats the absent return data as false, the require condition fails even though the token operation succeeded. This mismatch is triggered whenever the contract invokes approve or transfer on a token that does not conform to the optional boolean‑return ERC20 standard. Exploitation does not require a crafted payload; merely using a non‑standard token such as USDT is enough to cause the call to revert and break the protocol’s workflow. The impact is that legitimate users cannot deposit, withdraw, or otherwise move USDT through the protocol, leading to failed transactions, missing balances, and potentially funds being locked if the revert occurs after partial state updates. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Portico contract where the auditor observed require(token.transfer(...)) patterns and verified the token’s source code, noting the lack of a return statement. Because the failure manifests as a generic transaction revert without a clear error message, developers and users may see only “operation failed” in the UI, making the root cause hard to diagnose. The appropriate mitigation is to stop relying on the boolean return and instead use a wrapper that correctly handles both standard and non‑standard ERC20 tokens, such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library or Solmate’s SafeTransferLib, which perform low‑level calls and verify success based on the call’s success flag and return‑data length. By abstracting the transfer logic, the protocol can safely interact with any ERC20 token, preserving the expected business logic that a successful transfer updates the user’s balance as intended.

title: Possible precision loss in_checkpositionsRange
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision loss in the private function that validates a position range. The function receives a signed 24‑bit integer representing the total range and another signed 24‑bit integer representing the tick spacing. It checks three conditions, one of which is (( _range / 2 ) % _tickSpacing != 0) or a non‑zero offset. Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, when the range is an odd number the expression _range / 2 drops the fractional part. For example, with a range of 9 and a tick spacing of 3, the division yields 4 instead of the mathematically correct 4.5, and the subsequent modulo operation evaluates to 1. This incorrect remainder causes the overall validation to succeed or fail in ways that were not intended. The root cause is the use of integer division before the modulo operation, which loses precision and leads to a wrong comparison. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a range that is not a multiple of the tick spacing but that passes the flawed check because the truncated half‑range produces a non‑zero remainder. As a result, positions that should be rejected as invalid are accepted, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions about position granularity. The impact includes potential misallocation of liquidity, incorrect fee calculations, and the possibility of funds being locked or lost if downstream logic assumes a correctly aligned range. The bug manifests only when the range is odd or when the half‑range is not an exact multiple of the tick spacing, so it may remain hidden under typical test cases that use even ranges. Users of the contract, including traders opening positions and the protocol’s risk engine, are affected because the contract may record positions that do not respect the defined tick grid. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the security researcher, who noticed that the expression could truncate fractional values and produce unexpected modulo results. It is hard to notice because the code compiles without warnings and the condition appears syntactically correct; only careful reasoning about integer arithmetic reveals the flaw. To fix the problem the validation should avoid dividing before applying the modulo, for example by checking that the full range is a multiple of the tick spacing and that the range divided by two is also a multiple, using a multiplication‑based check or by casting to a larger integer type before division. In conceptual terms the bug belongs to the class of integer‑division‑precision‑loss errors that break range‑validation logic, leading to situations where a user expects a refund or a correct position but receives nothing or sees an unexpected zero balance because the contract accepted an invalid configuration.

title: The deposit - withdraw - trade transaction
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing expiration‑timestamp (deadline) validation in the core deposit‑withdraw‑trade flow of the protocol. The contract functions that handle user deposits, withdrawals and trade executions do not enforce a deadline parameter, unlike the reference implementation in Uniswap V2 where a modifier ensure(deadline) checks that deadline >= block.timestamp and reverts with an EXPIRED error if the transaction is stale. The root cause is the omission of this time‑bound check in the internal logic, allowing a transaction that was signed by a user to remain pending in the mempool indefinitely. An attacker or even a benign network delay can cause the transaction to be mined long after the user submitted it, at which point market prices may have moved dramatically. Because the trade is time‑sensitive, executing it after a significant price shift results in the user receiving a far worse execution price, potentially turning a profitable trade into a loss, or causing the user’s deposited liquidity to be allocated at an unfavorable rate. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction but the resulting balance is lower than expected, or the trade appears to have been executed at a price far from the quoted rate, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. The issue affects any participant who relies on the contract’s deposit, withdraw or trade functions – typically traders, liquidity providers and end‑users of the protocol. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s flow against known patterns such as Uniswap’s router, where the deadline check is explicitly present. The bug can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it simply executes with stale data, making the problem appear as normal slippage or market movement rather than a contract flaw. To remediate, the contract should introduce a deadline argument to the relevant external functions and apply a modifier similar to ensure(uint deadline) that requires deadline >= block.timestamp, reverting with an appropriate error if the transaction is expired. This restores the intended time‑bound guarantee, prevents execution of outdated trades, and aligns the protocol with established best practices for time‑sensitive DeFi operations.

title: Wrong auctionPrice used in calculating BPF to
description:
1. bucketTake() function in TakerActions.sol calls the _takeBucket()._prepareTake() to calculate the BPF.
8cbd972a66b3b50e3/ajna-core/src/libraries/external/TakerActions.sol#L416
8cbd972a66b3b50e3/ajna-core/src/libraries/external/TakerActions.sol#L688
2. In _prepareTake() function, the BPF is calculated using vars.auctionPrice which is calculated by _auctionPrice() function.
```solidity
function _prepareTake(
    Liquidation memory liquidation_,
    uint256 t0Debt_,
    uint256 collateral_,
    uint256 inflator_
) internal view returns (TakeLocalVars memory vars) {
    vars.auctionPrice = _auctionPrice(liquidation_.referencePrice, kickTime);
    vars.bondFactor = liquidation_.bondFactor;
    vars.bpf = _bpf(
        vars.borrowerDebt,
        collateral_,
        neutralPrice,
        liquidation_.bondFactor,
        vars.auctionPrice
    );
```
3. The _takeBucket() function made a judgment after _prepareTake()
```solidity
// cannot arb with a price lower than the auction price
if (vars_.auctionPrice > vars_.bucketPrice) revert AuctionPriceGtBucketPrice();
// if deposit take then price to use when calculating take is bucket price
if (params_.depositTake) vars_.auctionPrice = vars_.bucketPrice;
```
so the root cause of this issue is that in a scenario where a user calls Deposit Take(params_.depositTake ==true) ,BPF will calculated base on vars_.auctionPrice instead of bucketPrice.
And then, BPF is used to calculate takePenaltyFactor, borrowerPrice, netRewardedPrice and bondChange in the _calculateTakeFlowsAndBondChange() function and direct impact on the _rewardBucketTake() function.
8cbd972a66b3b50e3/ajna-core/src/libraries/external/TakerActions.sol#L724
8cbd972a66b3b50e3/ajna-core/src/libraries/external/TakerActions.sol#L640
```solidity
vars_ = _calculateTakeFlowsAndBondChange(
    borrower_.collateral,
    params_.inflator,
    params_.collateralScale,
    vars_
);
_rewardBucketTake(
    auctions_,
    deposits_,
    buckets_,
    liquidation,
    params_.index,
    params_.depositTake,
    vars_
);
```
Wrong auctionPrice used in calculating BFP which subsequently influences the _calculateTakeFlowsAndBondChange() and _rewardBucketTake() function will result in bias.
Following the example of the Whitepaper(section 7.4.2 Deposit Take) BPF = 0.011644 * (1222.6515-1100 / 1222.6515-1050) = 0.008271889129 The collateral purchased is min{20, 20000/(1-0.00827) * 1100, 21000/(1-0.01248702772 )* 1100)} which is 18.3334 unit of ETH. Therefore, 18.3334 ETH are moved from the loan into the claimable collateral of bucket 1100, and the deposit is reduced to 0. Dave is awarded LPB in that bucket worth 18. 3334 · 1100 · 0. 008271889129 = 166. 8170374. The debt repaid is 19914.99407 DAI
Based on the current implementations: BPF = 0.011644 * (1222.6515-1071.77 / 1222.6515-1050) = 0.010175. TPF = 5/4*0.011644 - 1/4 *0.010175 = 0.01201125.
The collateral purchased is 18.368 unit of ETH. The debt repaid is 20000 * (1-0.01201125) / (1-0.010175) = 19962.8974DAI Dave is awarded LPB in that bucket worth 18. 368 · 1100 · 0. 010175 = 205.58.
So, Dave earn more rewards38.703 DAI than he should have.
As the Whitepaper says: " the caller would typically have other motivations. She might have called it because she is Carol, who wanted to buy the ETH but not add additional DAI to the contract. She might be Bob, who is looking to get his debt repaid at the best price. She might be Alice, who is looking to avoid bad debt being pushed into the contract.
