The impact is loss of user funds and reduced confidence in the protocol, as users may see their balance become zero after a successful transaction. The condition occurs only when wantsEth[root] is false and the else branch is taken; any transaction that mistakenly includes Ether in that scenario will trigger the bug. All callers of that function are potentially affected, but the risk is greatest for users who assume that sending Ether is either prohibited or automatically returned. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected payable functions and identified a branch lacking a msg.value check. Because the function does not emit an event or revert, the trapped Ether may remain unnoticed until a user inspects the contract balance and sees an unexpected reduction. To remediate, the contract should either enforce that msg.value equals zero in the non‑Ether branch or explicitly refund any received Ether to the sender before completing execution. This fixes the accounting mismatch and prevents accidental or malicious locking of funds. The bug belongs to the class of payable‑function misuse where value validation is omitted, leading to unintended balance changes and potential fund loss.

title: ISU-5 | Incorrect Withdrawal Maturity Check
description: Issuance checks whether a withdrawal has matured in order to allow calling completeWithdrawEarly only on non-matured withdrawals. EigenLayer makes withdrawal requests wait roughly a week after they got queued in order to be able to react and punish in cases where the staker/operator of the staker acted maliciously in any sort of way. On the contrary the logic that enforces this in the Issuance contract implements the following access control: block.number > withdraw.startBlock + vault.delegationManager().withdrawalDelayBlocks() It explicitly requires that the current block is greater than the queue start plus the delay period, thus allowing early withdrawals even when the EigenLayer withdrawal has already matured. This allows matured loans to be "bought out” in a block they are already completable in, thus introducing unexpected behavior and possible loss of funds for the oldOwner through MEV.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the maturity check for withdrawal requests in the Issuance contract. The contract is supposed to allow the function completeWithdrawEarly only while a withdrawal is still pending, i.e., before the required delay has elapsed. Instead, the code uses the condition block.number > withdraw.startBlock + vault.delegationManager().withdrawalDelayBlocks(), which becomes true only after the block number exceeds the exact maturity block. Consequently, when a withdrawal reaches its exact maturity block, the condition is still false, but in the next block it becomes true, meaning the early‑withdrawal path can be invoked on a withdrawal that is already mature. This logic flaw lets an attacker call completeWithdrawEarly on a matured loan, effectively “buying out” the position in the same block where it becomes completable. The exploit works by monitoring the blockchain for withdrawals that have just satisfied the delay, then submitting a transaction that calls the early‑withdrawal function before the legitimate owner can complete the normal withdrawal. The impact is that the original owner (oldOwner) may lose the expected funds because the contract transfers them to the attacker, creating an unexpected MEV opportunity and breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions about withdrawal timing. The bug manifests only at the exact boundary when the withdrawal delay expires, making it easy to miss in testing that does not cover the equality case. It was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who identified the mismatch between the intended business rule (allow early withdrawal only while not mature) and the implemented comparison. Because the condition looks plausible at a glance, developers may not notice the subtle off‑by‑one error, especially if they do not have tests that assert behavior at the exact maturity block. The correct fix is to change the comparison to block.number >= withdraw.startBlock + vault.delegationManager().withdrawalDelayBlocks(), ensuring that once the withdrawal is mature the early‑withdrawal path is disabled and only the normal completion path can be used. This aligns the contract with its intended security model, prevents premature or malicious “buy‑out” of matured withdrawals, and restores the expected user experience where a user sees their pending withdrawal become claimable after the delay rather than being stolen by an attacker.

title: ISU-6 | Users Can Avoid Withdrawal Fee
description: When a user submits a withdrawal, either through direct assets or through EigenLayer, a fee is deducted. When using the Issuance contract, users have the possibility to complete other's withdraws by paying the due value and changing ownership of the pending withdrawal. This mechanism, however, does not deduct any fees from the new owner, this results in: Disincentivizing anyone from initiating a direct withdrawal from EigenLayer and simply waiting for others to initiate the withdraw and changing it, so that they may not pay the fee The protocol does not receive fees for withdrawal done in this manner
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑bypass flaw in the withdrawal flow of the protocol. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the system is supposed to deduct a predefined fee before the assets are released, whether the withdrawal originates directly from the protocol or is routed through EigenLayer. The Issuance contract provides a function called completeWithdrawEarly that allows a third party to take over an already‑pending withdrawal by paying the outstanding amount and becoming the new owner of that withdrawal. However, the implementation of this function does not include the same fee‑deduction logic that is applied to direct withdrawals. As a result, the new owner can finalize the withdrawal without any fee being taken from the transferred amount. This occurs whenever a withdrawal is pending and an external actor calls completeWithdrawEarly; the condition is triggered by the absence of a fee check in the Issuance contract’s code path. The affected parties are the protocol itself, which loses expected fee revenue, and any users who rely on the fee model for economic incentives, including participants of EigenLayer that expect to pay the fee. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a zero‑fee amount or simply omit the fee line, leading to the expectation that the withdrawal is free, which contradicts the protocol’s fee policy. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the fee handling in the direct withdrawal path with the ownership‑transfer path and noticed the missing deduction. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to only change ownership, and the fee is deducted elsewhere, so the omission does not raise an immediate error. Exploiting the bug is straightforward: an attacker monitors pending withdrawals, calls completeWithdrawEarly, pays the required principal, and then withdraws the assets without paying the fee, effectively stealing the fee revenue from the protocol. The impact is a loss of fee income and a distortion of the intended economic model, which may disincentivize users from performing direct withdrawals and could erode trust in the fee system. The recommended remediation is to incorporate the same fee‑deduction logic into the completeWithdrawEarly function, ensuring that any finalization of a pending withdrawal, regardless of the caller, triggers the fee charge. Conceptually, the fix aligns the fee enforcement across all withdrawal pathways, restoring the intended accounting guarantees and preventing fee‑free withdrawals.

title: ISU-7 | Pending Withdrawals Can Be Bought When Eigen Is Paused
description: Users that queue their withdraw on EigenLayer using the Issuance contract can have their withdrawals taken over by others as long as they are paid the equivalent withdraw amount in exchange. This mechanism leaves a potential abuse situation when EigenLayer has withdrawal completion paused (PAUSED_EXIT_WITHDRAWAL_QUEUE) so that nobody would be able to call completeQueuedWithdrawal at that time. During this time, users of the Issuance contract can take ownership of withdrawals that, unbeknown to them, can't be finalized at that time, basically buying into a blocked position.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the ability to transfer ownership of a pending withdrawal request that has been queued through the Issuance contract on EigenLayer. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the request is stored in EigenLayer’s exit queue and can later be completed by calling completeQueuedWithdrawal. The Issuance contract includes a function that lets a third party take over the pending request by paying the equivalent amount, effectively buying the right to the future withdrawal. The root cause is that this ownership‑transfer logic does not verify whether EigenLayer’s withdrawal completion mechanism is currently paused (the PAUSED_EXIT_WITHDRAWAL_QUEUE flag). The pause only prevents the finalization of withdrawals, but it does not stop the contract from reassigning the pending request to another address. An attacker can therefore monitor the queue, wait until the protocol pauses withdrawals, and then purchase pending positions that are locked and cannot be executed. From the attacker’s perspective the steps are: (1) detect a pending withdrawal belonging to another user, (2) wait for the EigenLayer contract to enter the paused state, (3) call the Issance contract’s function to become the new owner of that withdrawal while paying the required amount, and (4) hold a claim that remains unexecutable until the pause is lifted. The impact is that the original user loses the expectation of receiving their funds when they attempt to withdraw; instead the request is silently reassigned to an attacker and remains stuck, leading to apparent loss of liquidity or “funds disappearing”. Users may see their balance unchanged after initiating a withdrawal, or they may receive a confirmation that the request was queued but later find that no funds arrive even after the pause is lifted because the claim now belongs to someone else. The issue is observable only when the protocol is in the paused state, making it easy to miss during normal operation. It was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the pause check is absent from the ownership‑transfer path. Because the transfer appears legitimate and the pause does not emit a distinct error, developers and users may not notice that the withdrawal has been hijacked. The recommended mitigation is to prevent any change of ownership for pending withdrawals while EigenLayer reports the PAUSED_EXIT_WITHDRAWAL_QUEUE flag as true, for example by invoking Pausable.paused(2) before allowing the transfer, or by disabling the transfer functionality entirely during a pause. This aligns the contract’s behavior with the intended business logic that a paused withdrawal queue should freeze all actions related to pending exits, preserving user expectations that queued withdrawals remain theirs until they can be completed.

title: ADAP-3 | Adapter And Order Manager Discrepancies
description: For any keepers or users viewing a position’s status through the Adapter, it is important to document some of the differences between it's behavior and the behavior in OrderManager. Some differences include but are not limited to: `_verifyAndUpdatePrice` reverts if the difference between the primary and secondary price is exceeded in the OrderManager. In the Adapter, the primary price is simply used. `getPriceWithDeviation` does not consider whether the order is an increase or decrease order for deviation and rounding because in the OrderManager it is called in the context of recreating a position regardless of the direction. In the Adapter, it can take into account order direction.
bug_full: The issue is a consistency mismatch between two components that manage trading positions: the Adapter and the OrderManager. Both modules expose a view of a position’s status and perform price‑related checks, but they apply different rules. In the OrderManager, the internal function _verifyAndUpdatePrice compares a primary market price with a secondary reference price and will revert the transaction if the difference exceeds a predefined deviation threshold. This safeguard prevents orders from being executed when market data diverges beyond acceptable limits. By contrast, the Adapter simply adopts the primary price without performing any deviation comparison, meaning that it never reverts on large price gaps. A second inconsistency concerns the function getPriceWithDeviation, which in the OrderManager is used only when recreating a position and therefore ignores whether the order is an increase or a decrease; the deviation calculation is direction‑agnostic. In the Adapter, the same function can incorporate the order direction, leading to different rounding or deviation outcomes. These divergent behaviours can be exploited by a user or a malicious keeper who submits an order through the Adapter, expecting the same safety checks as the OrderManager. Because the Adapter does not enforce the deviation limit, an order may be accepted with a price that the OrderManager would consider out‑of‑range. When the order later reaches the OrderManager for execution, it may revert, causing the transaction to fail after the user has already committed gas and possibly locked collateral. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful order submission, but later the transaction fails silently or the position appears to have zero value, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds. The vulnerability manifests whenever a position is queried or updated through the Adapter while the underlying OrderManager logic is still applied for execution. It primarily affects traders, keepers, and any protocol component that relies on the Adapter’s price view, as well as the protocol’s overall accounting integrity. The discrepancy was discovered during a manual audit that compared the two code paths and noted the missing deviation check and the direction‑dependent rounding in the Adapter. The problem is subtle because both components expose similar function names and appear to provide the same information, making it easy to assume they behave identically. To remediate, the protocol should either align the Adapter’s logic with the OrderManager—by adding the same deviation verification and using a direction‑agnostic calculation—or clearly document the intentional differences, ensuring that callers understand which component to use for which purpose and that UI layers reflect the distinct behaviours. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of inconsistent cross‑contract validation errors, where duplicated business logic diverges, leading to mismatched state and potential financial loss.

title: PENW-1 | DoS pendingWithdrawals
description: There is no limit on the amount of pending withdrawals a user can have, nor is there a minimum amount of shares that ought to be redeemed per withdrawal. Therefore it can be economically viable to submit many withdrawals each with a single wei in order to expand the pendingWithdraws list for a malicious user. As a result third party contracts interacting with the PendingWithdraws.withdraws function can be DoS’d simply because the amount of gas required to load the pendingWithdraws list into memory is greater than the block gas limit.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unbounded pending‑withdrawals queue that allows a single address to create an unlimited number of withdrawal requests, each as small as one wei, without any minimum share requirement. The root cause is the absence of checks on both the count of pending withdrawals per user and the minimum amount of shares that must be redeemed before a request is queued. Because the contract stores every request in a dynamic array, an attacker can repeatedly submit tiny withdrawals until the array grows so large that any function that reads the entire list – for example the public withdraws function used by third‑party contracts – must load more data than can fit within a block’s gas limit. When this happens the transaction runs out of gas and reverts, effectively denying service to all other participants who rely on that function. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate users see their withdrawal transactions fail, the UI may display a long list of pending withdrawals but offers no way to claim them, and the protocol’s accounting flow is stalled because the pending‑withdrawals processing step cannot be completed. The issue manifests whenever the pendingWithdraws list contains a very large number of entries, which can be triggered by an attacker who deliberately queues many one‑wei withdrawals. All users of the protocol, as well as any external contracts that interact with the withdraws function, are affected because they cannot execute the withdrawal logic. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the data‑structure handling and identified that no bounds or minimums were enforced. It can be hard to notice because each individual withdrawal looks innocuous and the gas cost of processing a modest list appears acceptable; only when the list is deliberately inflated does the gas consumption exceed the block limit. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce a reasonable cap on the number of pending withdrawals that a single address may hold, require a minimum amount of shares or value to be redeemed before a request is accepted, or redesign the storage pattern to avoid loading the entire list in a single call (for example by processing withdrawals in batches or using a mapping with per‑user counters). Implementing such constraints restores the expected behavior where users can submit withdrawals without risking a protocol‑wide denial of service, and aligns the contract with typical accounting assumptions that each withdrawal request represents a meaningful amount of value.

title: VLT-3 | Deposits Can Be Griefed
description: In the depositIntoEigan function, a user can to deposit an arbitrary amount of vault assets into EigenLayer. This being permissionless, allows the protocol to gain yield more efficiently because it will not have to wait for a trusted party to move these funds. The issue, however, is that the amount that is being deposited is not guaranteed to be available. If another user wanted to grief the protocol, they could do so by frontrunning a call to the depositIntoEigan function by calling the withdrawUsingAssets function. They could then withdraw just enough from the vault so that the other user's deposit call will fail. Long term, this can pose a problem for the protocol because the way for users to gain yield through Rest is to have their funds deposited into EigenLayer. If a user can delay and reduce the efficiency with which these funds move to EigenLayer, the less yield the Rest users will receive.
bug_full: The contract contains a deposit function that accepts a caller‑provided amount of vault tokens to be transferred to EigenLayer. Because the function does not verify that the contract’s token balance actually contains the requested amount at the moment of the transfer, an attacker who can execute a transaction before the deposit can call the withdraw function and reduce the contract’s balance just enough that the subsequent deposit call reverts. This front‑running griefing scenario allows a malicious user to deliberately cause legitimate deposits to fail, preventing the protocol from moving assets into EigenLayer and therefore reducing the yield that end‑users expect. The issue appears only when the deposit call is permissionless and the amount parameter is not tied to the contract’s current balance. From a user’s point of view the UI shows a successful ‘deposit’ request but the transaction reverts, leaving the user with no additional yield and possibly a confusing ‘deposit failed’ error. The bug belongs to the class of ‘unchecked external balance assumptions’ or ‘race‑condition on token availability’. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of assets between the vault and EigenLayer. The problem is subtle because the function signature suggests that the caller can safely specify any amount, and the contract does not emit a warning when the balance is insufficient until the transfer fails. The recommended mitigation is to remove the user‑controlled amount parameter and instead deposit the entire token balance owned by the contract (i.e., use balanceOf(address(this))) or otherwise enforce that the amount is less than or equal to the current balance at the time of the call. This eliminates the window for a front‑runner to withdraw the needed tokens and ensures that deposits cannot be griefed, preserving the intended yield generation for all participants.

title: VLT-4 | Invalid Flagship LST Amount Transferred In
description: In the deposit(uint256 assets, address _receiver) function the assets amount passed to the super.deposit function is an ether value of the flagship asset amount. However the ERC4626 deposit function will transfer in the ether value amount of the flagship asset rather than the flagship asset amount. The value of the amount transferred in is correctly converted to shares as the previewDeposit function is correctly overridden in the Vault contract, however the user still transfers in an unexpected amount of the flagship asset. Consider the following example: - Flagship asset price is 0.8 ether - Bob calls deposit(1 * 1e18, address(bob)) - The vault transfers 0.8 * 1e18 of the flagship asset from Bob This is unexpected for Bob as he specified 1 * 1e18 of the flagship asset to be transferred in.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mis‑calculation of the amount of the flagship liquid‑staking token (LST) that is transferred into the vault during a deposit. In the contract’s deposit(uint256 assets, address receiver) function the code first converts the user‑specified asset amount into an ether‑denominated value and then forwards that converted value to the ERC‑4626 base implementation. The ERC‑4626 deposit routine already expects the raw asset amount and internally uses the overridden previewDeposit function to apply the current price of the flagship asset when minting shares. Because the caller’s amount is converted twice – once manually and once inside previewDeposit – the vault ends up pulling only the ether‑value of the asset instead of the full token amount. For example, if the flagship asset trades at 0.8 ether per token and a user calls deposit(1 ether,…) the vault will transfer only 0.8 ether worth of the token from the user. The user sees the expected number of shares because previewDeposit reports the correct conversion, but the actual token balance transferred is lower than intended. This discrepancy can occur whenever the flagship asset price differs from 1 ether, i.e., under any realistic market condition. Affected parties include any depositor who expects to transfer a specific quantity of the flagship LST, the vault’s accounting logic, and downstream protocols that rely on accurate share accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the amount passed to super.deposit with the amount actually moved by the ERC‑4626 transfer logic. It is subtle because the UI may display the correct share amount and there is no explicit error; the only symptom is that the user’s token balance after the transaction is reduced by less than the amount they thought they deposited, leading to “missing” tokens or lower than expected holdings. The bug belongs to the class of double‑conversion or unit‑mismatch errors in financial contracts. To remediate, the deposit function should pass the original assets parameter directly to the parent ERC‑4626 deposit call and rely on previewDeposit for price conversion, eliminating the redundant ether conversion. This change restores the intended one‑to‑one relationship between the user‑specified asset amount and the amount actually transferred, aligning on‑chain accounting with user expectations and preventing inadvertent loss of tokens.

title: VLT-5 | Vault is not ERC4626 Compliant
description: The Vault does not respect several requirements needed to be ERC4626 compliant, although the internal documentation states that it is compliant: /// @notice While this contract is fully ERC4626 compliant, it also has additional functionality The non-compliance issues are: withdraw and redeem always revert; does not respect any of EIP requirements if the flagshipToken is removed from the vault via removeLst then deposit reverts. At this point maxDeposit must return 0, but it does not. ○ MUST factor in both global and user-specific limits, like if deposits are entirely disabled (even temporarily) it MUST return 0. convertToShares also reverts when this is not allowed ○ MUST NOT revert unless due to integer overflow caused by an unreasonably large input. previewRedeem and previewWithdraw do not take into consideration vault fees ○ MUST be inclusive of withdrawal fees. Integrators should be aware of the existence of withdrawal fees.
bug_full: The Vault contract advertises full ERC4626 compliance but fails to meet several mandatory requirements of the standard, creating a mismatch between documented expectations and actual behavior. The root cause is that key ERC4626 interface functions either revert unconditionally or return values that ignore global and per‑account limits, and they do not incorporate the vault’s withdrawal fee model. Specifically, the withdraw and redeem functions always revert, making any attempt to pull assets from the vault impossible. When the flagship token is removed from the allowed list via the removeLst operation, the contract still allows deposits to be called, even though the ERC4626 specification dictates that maxDeposit must return zero in this situation. Moreover, the convertToShares function reverts whenever the operation is not permitted, rather than returning a calculated value or a zero as required. The previewRedeem and previewWithdraw view functions ignore the vault’s withdrawal fees, violating the rule that preview functions must be inclusive of all fees. The contract also fails to respect both global and user‑specific limits; for example, if deposits are temporarily disabled, maxDeposit should report zero but it does not. Finally, the code permits reverts for reasons other than integer overflow, contrary to the ERC4626 requirement that functions only revert on overflow caused by unreasonable inputs. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are stark: a user who expects to withdraw or redeem their shares receives a transaction that reverts with no clear error, deposits may succeed when they should be blocked, and preview functions show higher amounts than what will actually be received after fees, leading to unexpected shortfalls. Integrators that rely on the standard interface assume that calling withdraw, redeem, previewWithdraw or previewRedeem will behave predictably; the broken implementation can cause funds to become locked, user balances to appear correct in the UI while the underlying contract rejects withdrawals, and overall loss of confidence in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s behavior against the ERC4626 specification and identified mismatches in edge‑case handling. It is difficult to notice because the contract compiles and basic deposit functionality works, and the documentation explicitly claims compliance, so developers may not test the failure paths. To remediate, the contract must be refactored to follow the ERC4626 standard: withdraw and redeem should only revert on overflow, maxDeposit and maxMint must return zero when deposits are disabled or when the flagship asset is removed, convertToShares should return a calculated share amount or zero instead of reverting, previewRedeem and previewWithdraw must factor in withdrawal fees, and global/user limits must be enforced consistently. Additionally, the flagship asset should be protected from removal from the allowed list to preserve the intended asset composition of the vault.

title: VLT-6 | Attacker can Front-Run Removal of Asset
description: When an LST is removed with the removeLst function, the value of that LST in the system will no longer be attributed to the totalAssets. Therefore a malicious actor may frontrun the removal of an LST and deposit that exact LST into the system before withdrawing that value in a different LST token, as a result the value of restEth will drop and holders will immediately lose the value of the removed LST tokens in the system. If the protocol were to add the removed LST back it would create a positive stepwise jump in the value of restEth. This way an attacker could game the stepwise jump by depositing before the LST is added back and withdrawing afterwards for an immediate profit.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑runable accounting inconsistency that occurs when a liquid‑staking token (LST) is removed from the vault via the removeLst function. The function updates the list of supported LSTs but does not immediately adjust the totalAssets accounting for the value that the removed LST contributed. Because deposits of that LST remain enabled, an attacker can observe a pending removal transaction, submit a deposit of the same LST in the same block, and then, after the removal has been processed, withdraw a different LST token. The removal causes the internal variable restEth, which represents the value of the remaining assets, to drop abruptly. The attacker’s earlier deposit is now valued at a lower restEth amount, allowing them to extract more value than they contributed. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a removal event the balance of the removed LST disappears from the system, yet the total value reported by the vault does not reflect the loss, and other users may see their holdings suddenly de‑valued or receive less than expected when withdrawing. The issue is triggered only when a removal transaction is pending and deposits are not paused, and it affects any user who holds or deposits the affected LST, as well as the protocol’s overall accounting integrity. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state changes performed by removeLst and noticed that the vault does not enforce a zero balance condition before allowing removal. The problem is subtle because the vault’s external view of totalAssets may still appear correct until a withdrawal is performed, making the loss easy to miss. To remediate the bug the contract should either pause deposits of the LST that is being removed or pause all deposits while a removal is in progress, and it should require that the vault hold no remaining value or balance of the LST before it can be removed. Adding these checks prevents the stepwise jump in restEth that the attacker exploits and restores the invariant that totalAssets always reflects the sum of the values of all listed tokens.

title: VLT-7 | Yield In Strategies Can Be Stolen
description: In the event that yield is distributed to a strategy in a single transaction, that yield amount can be vampire attacked by a malicious actor. The actor may deposit into the vault right before the reward is distributed, and then withdraw the gained funds with their Rest shares. These funds end up siphoned from the veritable vault depositors.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a yield‑stealing or “vampire” attack that arises when a vault distributes accrued yield to a strategy in a single transaction while allowing deposits and early withdrawals without an adequate fee. The root cause is the combination of (1) a mass reward distribution that updates share balances atomically, (2) the absence of a withdrawal penalty for the completeWithdrawEarly function, and (3) the possibility for an attacker to route the withdrawal through an auxiliary Issuance contract that bypasses any existing fee logic. An attacker can exploit the flaw by depositing a small amount into the vault immediately before the reward distribution, thereby receiving a proportion of the newly minted shares that represent the upcoming yield. When the distribution transaction executes, the attacker’s balance is inflated by the freshly added yield. The attacker then calls the early‑withdraw function, extracts the inflated shares, and converts them back to the underlying asset, effectively siphoning the reward that should have been shared among all honest depositors. This exploitation occurs whenever the protocol performs a bulk yield payout in a single block and does not enforce a non‑zero fee on early withdrawals, especially when the attacker can use the Issuance contract to avoid any fee that might otherwise be applied. The impact is a direct loss of expected returns for regular users: their balances appear lower than anticipated, rewards that should have been credited disappear, and the overall accounting of the vault becomes inconsistent because the total deposited assets no longer match the sum of user shares. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal deposit and then a sudden, unexplained reduction in earned interest or a zero‑return after a reward event, contradicting the expectation that rewards are automatically added to their balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the vault’s reward distribution logic and the early‑withdraw pathways, noting that the fee mechanism could be circumvented. The bug is subtle because the deposit‑withdraw flow is standard and the reward distribution appears legitimate; only a careful analysis of share accounting reveals that a newly deposited user can capture a disproportionate amount of the reward. To remediate the problem the protocol should enforce a sufficiently large withdrawal fee that applies even when the completeWithdrawEarly function is called, and the fee logic must be integrated into any auxiliary contracts such as the Issuance contract so that it cannot be bypassed. Additionally, distributing yield over multiple blocks or using a snapshot of balances before the distribution can prevent a single‑transaction capture of the reward, thereby aligning the accounting model with the intended business logic that rewards are shared proportionally among all long‑term participants.

title: ADAP-4 | Lack Of Reusability
description: Many of the functions in the Adapter are copies of functions in the OrderManager or have slight variations e.g. getProfitOrLossInCollateral. Furthermore, functions such as getAvgPriceWithDeviation and getPriceWithDeviation in the Adapter perform the exact same calculations where the only difference is the deltaSize parameter.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of extensive code duplication between the Adapter contract and the OrderManager contract. Functions that calculate profit or loss, average price with deviation, and price with deviation are copied verbatim or with only minor parameter changes, such as the deltaSize argument. Because the same logic is implemented in multiple places, any future change to the calculation formula, rounding method, or safety checks must be applied to each copy manually. If a developer updates the logic in OrderManager but forgets to replicate the change in the Adapter, the two components will diverge and return inconsistent values. This inconsistency can be exploited by a malicious actor who reads the more favorable value from one contract while the other contract records a different, less favorable outcome, potentially leading to incorrect profit or loss reporting, wrong collateral requirements, or mispriced trades. From a user perspective the symptoms may appear as unexpected profit numbers, zero or missing refunds, or trades that seem to execute at a price different from what the UI displayed. The issue occurs whenever the system relies on the duplicated functions for accounting or pricing, which is throughout the lifecycle of a trade. All participants—traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the core economic assumptions of the platform (accurate price calculation, correct collateral assessment) are violated. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the source files and identified near‑identical implementations with only superficial differences. Because the duplicated code is syntactically correct, the discrepancy does not raise compiler warnings and can remain unnoticed until a divergent update is made. The root cause is a lack of modular design and failure to extract shared logic into a reusable library or helper contract. To remediate, the common calculations should be moved into a single library or internal module that both Adapter and OrderManager call, ensuring a single source of truth for all pricing and profit calculations. This eliminates the risk of divergent implementations, simplifies future maintenance, and aligns the protocol’s accounting with its intended business logic.

title: secRewardsPerShare Insufficient precision
description:
We also introduced the field secRewardDebt. The idea of this field is to enable any lending platforms that are integrated with Neofinance Coordinator to send their own rewards based on this value (or rather the difference of this value since the last time secondary rewards were sent) and their own emission schedule for the tokens.

The current calculation formula for `secRewardsPerShare` is as follows:
```solidity
market.secRewardsPerShare += uint128((blockDelta * 1e18) / marketSupply);
```
`marketSupply` is `cNOTE`, with a precision of `1e18`. So as long as the supply is greater than `1` cNote, `secRewardsPerShare` is easily `rounded down` to `0`. Example: marketSupply = 10e18 blockDelta = 1 secRewardsPerShare=1 * 1e18 / 10e18 = 0
bug_full: During reward accounting the contract stores a cumulative secondary reward per share value called secRewardsPerShare. The value is updated each block with the expression market.secRewardsPerShare += uint128((blockDelta * 1e18) / marketSupply). Both blockDelta and marketSupply are expressed with 18 decimal places, so the numerator and denominator share the same magnitude. When marketSupply is larger than one whole cNOTE, the integer division truncates any fractional part and the result becomes zero for typical blockDelta values such as 1. Consequently the cumulative per‑share counter does not increase, secondary rewards are not accrued, and users see no additional balance or receive a zero reward when they claim. The bug originates from insufficient scaling precision; using 1e18 while the supply already carries 1e18 precision causes the division to lose all significant digits for small numerators. It can be triggered in any market where the total supplied cNOTE exceeds one token, which is the normal case for most pools. Affected parties include lenders and borrowers who rely on secondary rewards, as the protocol silently reduces their yield. The issue was identified during a formal audit that examined the reward math and noticed that the rounding down to zero could lead to a measurable loss of yield over time. Because the problem manifests as a missing reward rather than an outright failure, it can be hard to notice in normal UI screens where users expect a small but non‑zero amount. The proper fix is to increase the scaling factor, for example by multiplying blockDelta by 1e27 before dividing by marketSupply, or by using a higher‑precision arithmetic library, so that the division retains fractional information and secRewardsPerShare advances correctly. In summary, the vulnerability is a precision‑loss rounding bug in the secondary reward per‑share calculation that results in users receiving zero or reduced secondary rewards, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions about reward distribution.

title: Loss of precission when calculating the accumulated CANTO per share
description: When calculating the amount of CANTO per share in `update_market`, dividing by `1e18` in `cantoReward` and multiplying by the same value in `accCantoPerShare` rounds down the final value, making the amount of rewards users will receive be less than expected.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision loss in the reward accounting logic of the lending market contract. When the contract updates the accumulated CANTO per share it first divides a 36‑decimal intermediate value by 1e18 and then multiplies the result by the same scaling factor. Because Solidity integer division always rounds down, any fractional part of the intermediate value is discarded before the multiplication restores the scale. This rounding down reduces the calculated cantoReward and consequently the value added to accCantoPerShare. The root cause is the ordering of arithmetic operations: a division is performed before a multiplication that could have been done in the opposite order to preserve precision. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the protocol itself suffers a systematic under‑distribution of rewards whenever the intermediate product is smaller than 1e18, for example when blockDelta * cantoPerBlock * gaugeWeight yields 0.99e18. In that case the division yields zero and the user receives no reward for that block. Over many blocks the small truncation can accumulate to a noticeable shortfall, potentially up to one whole CANTO for a market. The impact is that lenders see lower reward balances than expected, may notice that their reward claim returns zero or a smaller amount, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about total distributed yield become inaccurate. The condition for the bug to manifest is that the market has a positive total balance, the block number has advanced beyond the last reward block, and the product of blockDelta, per‑block reward and gauge weight is not an exact multiple of 1e18. The affected parties are all users who stake or lend assets in the market, as well as the protocol that promises a certain yield distribution. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors compared the result of (x/1e18)*1e18 with (x*1e18)/1e18 and observed a discrepancy, confirming that the current implementation discards precision. The bug is hard to notice because the loss per block may be only a few wei, which looks negligible in isolation, but it compounds over time. The recommended fix is to reorder the arithmetic so that the multiplication by 1e18 occurs before the division, or to use a higher‑precision intermediate type, thereby eliminating the truncation. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a rounding‑error or precision‑loss bug caused by integer division before multiplication, and it violates the business logic that rewards should be calculated exactly according to the defined formula.

title: Protocol and referral fee would be permanently stuck in the Curves contract when selling a token
description:
During the sale of a token `Curves._transferFee` subtracts all the fees from the selling price and transfers the remaining to the seller [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves/blob/main/contracts/Curves.sol#L231).

```solidity
uint256 sellValue = price - protocolFee - subjectFee - referralFee - holderFee;
(bool success1, ) = firstDestination.call{value: isBuy ? buyValue : sellValue}("");
```

However, the `protocolFee` taken away is not transferred to the `protocolFeeDestination` in the remainder of the `_transferFee` function [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves/blob/main/contracts/Curves.sol#L231-L250). It stays back in the contract with no other way of retrieval.

Furthermore, `referralFee` is taken away without checking if a referral address actually exists. In the event that there is no referral defined, the third transfer is never executed [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves/blob/main/contracts/Curves.sol#L240). This leaves the referral fee in the contract, again no retrieval mechanism.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑handling defect that causes protocol and referral fees to become permanently locked in the Curves contract when a user sells a token. The contract calculates a sellValue by subtracting protocolFee, subjectFee, referralFee and holderFee from the quoted price, then forwards only the net sellValue to the seller. However, the implementation of the internal _transferFee routine never sends the protocolFee to the configured protocolFeeDestination, and it also deducts referralFee without first verifying that a referral address is set. As a result, the protocolFee and, when no referral is defined, the referralFee remain in the contract balance with no subsequent withdrawal path. This occurs on every sell transaction (i.e., when isBuy is false) and also whenever a sell is executed with a zero‑address referral, which is a common case for many users. The affected parties are the token sellers who receive less than the amount they expect, the protocol owners who lose the revenue they are supposed to collect, and any referral participants who never receive their share. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful sale but the received amount is lower than the advertised price minus only the visible fees, leading to confusion such as “my refund is missing” or “my balance dropped unexpectedly”. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the missing transfer statements were identified as logical oversights. Because the contract still completes the primary transfer, the fee loss is silent and can be easily overlooked during testing. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or fee‑sink vulnerabilities where deducted amounts are not correctly routed, violating the business assumption that all fees are collected and distributed. To remediate, the contract should forward the protocolFee (and referralFee when a referral is defined) to the protocolFeeDestination, reuse the existing buyValue logic to compute a generic protocolShare, add a check that a referral address exists before deducting its fee, and revert the transaction if any of the fee transfers fail. This ensures that all deducted amounts are either paid out or the operation aborts, preventing permanent fund loss.

title: Theft of holder fees when `holderFeePercent` was positive and is set to zero
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of holder fees in the Curves protocol when the holder fee percentage is changed from a positive value to zero. The protocol charges a holder fee on every buy and sell operation and forwards the collected amount to a FeeSplitter contract via the _transferFees() function. The function currently calls feeRedistributor.onBalanceChange only when holdersFeePercent is greater than zero, assuming that no fee distribution is required when the percentage is zero. However, fees that were collected while the percentage was positive remain stored in the FeeSplitter contract. When the percentage is later set to zero, onBalanceChange is no longer invoked for subsequent transactions, so the internal accounting of each shareholder’s entitlement to the accumulated fees is not updated. As a result, a new shareholder who purchases tokens after the fee percent is zero can call claimFees and receive the previously unclaimed holder fees that rightfully belong to earlier shareholders. This allows an attacker to steal funds that were meant for previous holders, causing the victim’s claim to revert with an out‑of‑fund error and the attacker’s balance to increase unexpectedly. The issue occurs only when the holder fee percent is initially non‑zero, fees have been accrued, and later the percent is set to zero while the feeRedistributor address remains valid. It affects all token holders, the protocol’s fee distribution logic, and any DAO that may adjust the fee percentage. The bug was discovered during a formal audit using a Foundry test that demonstrated the exploit. It is subtle because the contract’s logic appears to disable fee distribution when the percentage is zero, leading developers to assume no fees remain, while in fact the contract still holds undistributed Ether. The problem belongs to the class of accounting‑state‑inconsistency bugs where state updates are conditionally omitted, causing stale balances to be claimable by unintended parties. From a user perspective, a victim who previously earned holder fees sees their claim revert and their expected refund disappear, while an attacker sees an unexpected increase in their ether balance after calling claimFees. To remediate, the onBalanceChange call should be executed unconditionally, ensuring that shareholder balances are always updated regardless of the holder fee setting, thereby preserving correct fee entitlement and preventing unauthorized claims.

title: If a user sets their curve token symbol as the default one plus the next token counter instance it will render the whole default naming functionality obsolete
description: If a malicious user or just an unbeknownst one decides to name/set their curve token symbol as “CURVE N” “N” can/will be substituted to whatever the next number is in the `_curvesTokenCounter` it can render the whole default naming functionality in the protocol useless as it will be DoS’d indefinitely.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial-of-service on the automatic token naming mechanism. The contract assigns a default name and symbol to a newly minted curve token when the caller does not provide one. It does this by checking whether the supplied symbol equals the reserved string CURVES and, if so, increments an internal counter and appends the counter value to both the name and the symbol. Because the protocol also enforces uniqueness of symbols, a malicious or unaware user can deliberately register a token whose symbol is exactly the next value that the automatic routine would generate (for example CURVES5 when the counter is 4). When this happens, the subsequent automatic naming attempt hits the uniqueness check, reverts, and the default naming functionality becomes unusable for all future tokens. The issue occurs whenever a token is created without an explicit name/symbol after another user has pre‑emptively taken the next default symbol. It affects any user who relies on the convenience of default naming, causing their transactions to revert, their expected token to be missing, and potentially leading to confusion or loss of confidence in the protocol. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a Foundry test that creates a token without a name, then creates another token with the next default symbol, and finally observes that the first token’s withdraw call reverts. The bug is subtle because the default naming code appears harmless and only fails when the exact next symbol is already taken, a situation that is not obvious from the UI. To fix the issue, the contract should forbid users from choosing symbols that contain the reserved keyword CURVES or otherwise clash with the auto‑generated pattern, or the naming architecture should be redesigned so that the automatic generation cannot be pre‑empted.

title: Withdrawing with amount `= 0` will forcefully set name and symbol to default and disable some functions for token subject
description:
* Name and symbol is forcefully set to default value before the token subject can do anything.
  * Disable functions `mint`, `setNameAndSymbol` and `buyCurvesTokenWithName` for token subject
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the withdraw function of the Curves contract, which is responsible for moving a user’s internal token balance to an external ERC20 token. When a caller invokes withdraw with an amount of zero, the function bypasses the balance check (amount > balance) because zero is never greater than the stored balance, and then proceeds to the branch that deploys the external ERC20 token if it has not been created yet. This deployment logic unconditionally assigns a default name ("Curves 1") and a default symbol ("CURVES1") to the newly minted token before the token subject has a chance to set a custom name and symbol. Because the token can only be deployed once, the default metadata becomes permanent, and subsequent calls to functions that would normally allow the token subject to customize the token—such as mint, setNameAndSymbol, and buyCurvesTokenWithName—revert with an ERC20TokenAlreadyMinted error. The issue was discovered during a security audit by reproducing a front‑run scenario in a Hardhat test where an attacker calls withdraw with amount 0 before the legitimate token subject can perform any configuration. The bug is subtle because a zero‑amount withdraw appears harmless; developers typically assume that no state changes occur when the transferred amount is zero. However, the side‑effect of triggering token deployment violates the intended business logic that the token’s metadata should be defined by the token subject before the token exists. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms are a token that appears with a generic name and symbol, an inability to rename or mint additional tokens, and error messages indicating that the token has already been minted. The impact is primarily functional: the token subject loses the ability to personalize the token, which may affect branding, downstream integrations, and any economic model that relies on custom token identifiers. Funds themselves are not directly stolen, but the protocol’s usability and trustworthiness are compromised. The vulnerability manifests whenever withdraw is called with amount 0 before the external token has been deployed, which can be exploited by any actor able to front‑run the transaction. To remediate the issue, the contract should reject zero‑amount withdrawals or separate the token deployment logic from the withdraw path, ensuring that metadata can only be set before the token is created and that a zero transfer does not trigger deployment.

title: Stuck rewards in `FeeSplitter` contract
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a permanent locking of reward ether in the FeeSplitter contract used by the Curves protocol. The contract records a cumulative fee per token (cumulativeFeePerToken) that is increased by the amount of fees received divided by the total token supply, using integer division with a fixed precision constant. Because the division discards any remainder, each call to addFees leaves a small amount of ether that is not represented in the cumulative value. Moreover, the contract does not provide any function to withdraw or redistribute this remainder, and the user‑specific offset (userFeeOffset) is only updated when a holder’s balance changes. Consequently, after the latest fee addition the difference between cumulativeFeePerToken and each user’s offset is smaller than the total fees collected, and the leftover portion remains forever in the contract. The issue manifests whenever the manager calls addFees with a non‑zero value and the token has a positive total supply; it is observable during normal reward claims when users receive less ether than expected and the contract balance still contains an unexplained amount. All token holders are affected because the protocol promises that fees are fully distributable to holders; the locked funds reduce the effective reward rate and may erode trust. The problem was discovered during a security audit when a proof‑of‑concept showed that after all holders claimed their rewards a non‑zero balance remained in the FeeSplitter. The bug is subtle because the leftover amount can be very small (dust) and the contract lacks any visible withdrawal path, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the contract should either incorporate the division remainder into the reward pool (for example by using a higher‑precision arithmetic or by allocating the remainder proportionally) or provide an authorized withdraw function that allows the manager to recover or re‑distribute the excess ether. In essence, the flaw is a classic “reward rounding loss” or “unclaimed residual” bug where accounting assumptions about exact division do not hold in integer arithmetic, leading to funds disappearing from the user‑visible reward flow.

title: A subject creator within a single block can claim holder fees without holding due to unprotected reentrancy path
description:
<https://gist.github.com/nuthan2x/bb0ecf745abfdc37ce374f6af0d83699#L17>

A subject creater can keep on [claiming holder fees](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves/blob/516aedb7b9a8d341d0d2666c23780d2bd8a9a600/contracts/FeeSplitter.sol#L80) on every [buy](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves/blob/516aedb7b9a8d341d0d2666c23780d2bd8a9a600/contracts/Curves.sol#L211) and [sell](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves/blob/516aedb7b9a8d341d0d2666c23780d2bd8a9a600/contracts/Curves.sol#L282) transaction even when he doesn’t hold the balance. This claiming of holder fees without holding is possible due to a combination of reentrancy and usage of `call` instead of `transfer` while [transferring the subject fees](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves/blob/516aedb7b9a8d341d0d2666c23780d2bd8a9a600/contracts/Curves.sol#L236).

A subject can perform this attack by:

  1. Buy some curves initially.
  2. [mint and lock](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves/blob/516aedb7b9a8d341d0d2666c23780d2bd8a9a600/contracts/Curves.sol#L465) them in curves. The external minted tokens can be used on bridges or AMMs.
  3. Now, when someone buys/sells, subject fee is transferred on [_transferFees](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves/blob/516aedb7b9a8d341d0d2666c23780d2bd8a9a600/contracts/Curves.sol#L236) call.
  4. Using this external call, the subject when receiving the ether, can withdraw tokens from bridge/AMM and then burn those tokens to get the curves. Then use those curves updated balance, to [claim the updated holder fees](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves/blob/516aedb7b9a8d341d0d2666c23780d2bd8a9a600/contracts/FeeSplitter.sol#L80). Then lock those curves again and mint external tokens, then lock them on Bridge/AMM.
  5. For attacker to claim this holder fees unethically, only once every two transactions of [buy](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves/blob/516aedb7b9a8d341d0d2666c23780d2bd8a9a600/contracts/Curves.sol#L211) and [sell](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves/blob/516aedb7b9a8d341d0d2666c23780d2bd8a9a600/contracts/Curves.sol#L282). Because, the holder fee is updated after sending the subject fees. So previous update of the holders fees can be claimed only next time someone buys/sells.
bug_full: The contract implements a fee‑splitting mechanism where, on each buy or sell of a curve token, a portion of the received ether is sent to the subject (the creator of the curve) as a subject fee. The implementation uses low‑level call to forward the subject fee, which forwards all remaining gas to the recipient. Because the call is performed before the holder‑fee accounting is updated, a malicious subject can trigger a re‑entrancy during the call, withdraw external tokens from a bridge or AMM, burn them to obtain fresh curve tokens, and immediately claim the holder fees that were just accrued even though the attacker does not actually hold the required balance at that moment. The attack can be repeated every other buy/sell transaction because the holder‑fee snapshot is only refreshed after the subject fee transfer completes. From a user’s point of view the protocol promises that holder fees are distributed proportionally to current token holders, but the attacker can repeatedly receive those fees while their balance is temporarily zero, causing legitimate holders to see their expected fee share shrink or disappear. The vulnerability arises from two design choices: (1) using call instead of the fixed‑gas transfer primitive, which allows the recipient to execute arbitrary code, and (2) updating the holder‑fee state after the external call, creating a window where the contract’s accounting does not reflect the true holder balances. The issue was discovered during a formal audit that included a crafted proof‑of‑concept test where the attacker’s receive fallback performed the re‑entrancy steps. It is hard to notice because the fee distribution logic appears correct on the surface and the call succeeds, masking the hidden state change. To remediate the problem the fee transfer should either use transfer (which limits gas to 2300 and prevents re‑entrancy) or be protected by a re‑entrancy guard such as OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard, and the holder‑fee accounting should be updated before any external calls. This class of bug is a re‑entrancy vulnerability combined with improper ordering of state updates, leading to unauthorized fee extraction and loss of funds for honest participants.

title: Selling will be bricked if all other tokens are withdrawn to ERC20 token
description:
`FeeSplitter.addFees()` reverts if the `totalSupply` of the token is `0`. The total supply is calculated via the formula below:
    
    return (curves.curvesTokenSupply(token) - curves.curvesTokenBalance(token, address(curves))) * PRECISION;

Consider the following scenario:

  1. Alice buys 1 Curve token to initiate herself as a token subject and withdraws her token to ERC20.
  2. Bob buys 1 Curve token.
  3. Charlie buys 10 Curve tokens and immediately withdraws all of them to the ERC20 contract.
  4. Bob tries to sell 1 Curve token but is not able to because all other tokens are ERC20.

Bob’s transaction will revert because `FeeSplitter.totalSupply()` will return `0`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates in the fee distribution logic of the FeeSplitter contract. The function addFees attempts to calculate the total supply of Curve tokens by subtracting the balance held by the contract itself from the overall token supply and then multiplying by a precision constant. When every token holder withdraws their tokens to the external ERC20 contract, the contract’s own balance becomes equal to the total token supply, causing the subtraction to yield zero. Consequently, totalSupply returns zero and addFees reverts with the custom error NoTokenHolders(). This edge‑case is not guarded against, so any subsequent attempt to sell a token triggers the same revert, effectively bricking the sell operation. The impact is that users who try to sell their tokens receive no funds, their transaction fails, and the protocol’s fee collection mechanism is halted because the holder fee cannot be distributed. The condition occurs only after all tokens are moved to the ERC20 contract, a situation that can be deliberately created by an attacker or unintentionally reached when the last holder withdraws. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a test where one user withdraws all tokens and another user’s sell call reverts. It is hard to notice because normal operation with at least one token remaining in the contract works correctly; the zero‑supply path is rarely exercised in standard testing. The issue belongs to the class of zero‑division or zero‑value logic errors where calculations assume a non‑zero denominator. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a failed transaction, often with an error message like NoTokenHolders(), and the expected refund or sale proceeds never arrive, leaving the balance unchanged. To remediate, the contract should detect the situation where the contract’s token balance matches the total supply and route the holder fee directly to the protocol instead of calling addFees, or reorder fee handling to occur before token balances are updated, while adding appropriate reentrancy guards. This change prevents the sell function from reverting when totalSupply is zero and restores normal fee distribution and token trading functionality.

title: Single token purchase restriction on curve creation enables sniping
poc:
1. A user with a large social media following wants to initialize a curve and buy the first 10 tokens for future use, possibly for an airdrop to her followers.
  2. She does not want to create a presale and instead initializes the curve directly via `buyCurvesToken()`.
  3. As soon as the curve is initialized, automated sniping bots start buying large numbers of tokens.
  4. She is now forced to purchase the tokens at a much higher price and may incur losses from bots realizing their profits.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow in the price‑calculation routine of the Curves contract that restricts a curve creator to buying only a single token when the curve is first initialized. The getPrice(uint256 supply,uint256 amount) function computes two intermediate sums, sum1 and sum2. For sum2 the expression (supply - 1 + amount) is evaluated before the addition, so when supply is zero the subtraction supply‑1 underflows and the transaction reverts unless amount equals one. Consequently a user who tries to purchase more than one token at the moment of curve creation cannot do so, while the contract otherwise appears to accept normal purchases. This edge‑case is hard to notice because the function works correctly for any positive supply, and typical unit tests focus on non‑zero supply scenarios. The bug becomes exploitable because an attacker can monitor the transaction that creates a new curve and, knowing that the legitimate user is forced to buy only one token, can immediately submit a large buy order with a sniping bot. The bot acquires the majority of the initial supply at the low price, forcing the genuine user to either accept a much higher price for the remaining tokens or abandon the purchase, leading to financial loss and unfair token distribution. The issue manifests only when a curve is initialized without using the optional presale mechanism; with a presale the price calculation is bypassed and multiple‑token purchases are allowed. The affected parties are the curve creator, any subsequent buyers, and the protocol itself, which suffers from reduced trust and potential revenue loss. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena when the auditors exercised the getPrice function with supply = 0 and amount > 1 and observed a revert. Because the revert is triggered by Solidity’s built‑in underflow protection, it does not produce an obvious error message, making it easy to overlook. The recommended remediation is to reorder the arithmetic in sum2 to (supply + amount - 1) or otherwise guard against underflow, thereby allowing multiple token purchases at initialization and eliminating the sniping vector.

title: `Curves::_buyCurvesToken`
description:
In the `buyCurvesToken()`, the logic check for the `msg.value` to be greater than `price + fees`. This is fine, since if the price moves after the estimates was provided to the user, the above validation checks if the funds received are sufficient to proceed with the transaction.

But, at the same time, it is equally important to refund any excess eth received which is not being done.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑payment handling flaw in the function that sells Curves tokens. The contract checks that the ether sent (msg.value) is at least the sum of the token price and the protocol fee, and reverts if it is lower. However, it does not calculate or return any amount that exceeds the required payment. Consequently, when a user sends more ether than necessary—whether because the price changed after the quote, because of a UI rounding error, or because an attacker deliberately over‑pays—the surplus remains locked in the contract. This can be exploited by simply calling the function with a higher value; the contract will accept the transaction, mint the tokens, and keep the extra ether, effectively stealing funds from the sender. The impact is that users may see a reduction in their wallet balance that does not correspond to the number of tokens received; they expect a refund of the excess but receive none, leading to “funds disappear” or “refund missing” symptoms. The issue occurs whenever the buy function is invoked with any amount greater than price + fee, which is a realistic scenario given volatile price feeds or UI rounding. All participants who interact with the token purchase—retail users, integrators, and downstream protocols—are affected because the contract’s accounting assumes that the exact amount is always sent. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the validation logic with the expected economic flow and noticed the absence of a refund step. It is easy to miss because the transaction still succeeds and the token is minted, so no explicit error is raised; the loss is only visible in the sender’s balance after the call. The proper fix is to compute the excess (msg.value‑(price + fee)) and, if positive, transfer it back to the caller before completing the function, ensuring that the contract’s ether balance reflects only the required payment. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “missing change return” or “over‑payment without refund” in payable functions, violating the business rule that users should only pay the exact amount required for a purchase.

title: `onBalanceChange` causes previously unclaimed rewards to be cleared
description: `onBalanceChange` does not help to claim the previous rewards, but directly resets `userFeeOffset`, causing the user’s unclaimed rewards to be cleared.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the fee‑splitting contract where the onBalanceChange function clears a user’s previously accrued but unclaimed rewards. The root cause is that onBalanceChange directly overwrites the userFeeOffset mapping with the current cumulativeFeePerToken value without first crediting any pending fees to the user’s unclaimedFees balance. When a token holder’s balance changes – for example by purchasing the same token a second time – the contract calls onBalanceChange, which resets the offset and therefore discards the reward that was calculated for the earlier balance. An attacker or any user can trigger this by performing multiple balance‑changing actions, causing the first reward to be lost before it can be claimed. The impact is that users see their claimable fees drop to zero or receive less than expected, effectively losing earned rewards. This occurs whenever the manager‑only onBalanceChange is invoked after a balance update, which is the normal path for token purchases in the system. The affected parties are token holders who rely on the fee redistribution mechanism, as well as the protocol that promises fair reward distribution. The issue was discovered during a security audit by observing that claimable fees reported by feeRedistributor were reset after consecutive purchases, as demonstrated by the provided test cases. The bug is subtle because the function appears to simply update an internal pointer, and the loss of rewards is only visible after a subsequent claim attempt, making it easy to miss in casual testing. To fix the problem, onBalanceChange should first invoke the same logic used in claimFees – typically an updateFeeCredit or similar routine – to transfer any pending rewards into the user’s unclaimedFees balance, and only then reset the userFeeOffset to the new cumulative value. This aligns the contract with the expected accounting model where rewards are preserved across balance changes and can be claimed at any time, preventing inadvertent reward wiping.

title: Permanent loss of tokens if swap data gets outdated
description:
While sending funds through `StargateBridgeAdapter`, the user passes the swap data as a parameter. The flow is stargate sending tokens on the receiving chain into the `StargateBridgeAdapter` and executing `sgReceive`.

The issue here is that `sgReceive` will fail if the swap data gets outdated, but this is not going to make the whole transaction revert.

Stargate will still send the tokens to the `StargateBridgeAdapter`, and if the `sgReceive` fails, the swap will be cached for later execution. See `StargateComposer` logic here: <https://stargateprotocol.gitbook.io/stargate/stargate-composability/stargatecomposer.sol#sgreceive>.

Now, tokens will be left sitting in the `StargateBridgeAdapter` contract, and since the user can only retry the transaction with the same swap data, the tokens will be stuck forever.

The impact is loss of transferred tokens for the user.
poc:
Consider the following flow:

  1. User invokes `StargateBridgeAdapter:bridge()` function as part of the whole flow of calling `UTB:bridgeAndExecute()` function.
  2. He is passing the swapData parameters to the remote chain.
  3. `StargateComposer` first transfers the tokens to the `StargateBridgeAdapter` contract.
  4. After that the `StargateBridgeAdapter:sgReceive()` function is executed.
  5. It then calls `UTB:receiveFromBridge` that tries to execute the swap.
  6. If the swap fails, which can frequently occur due to the fact that the swap data is outdated, most commonly minimum amount out gets outdated.
  7. The whole payload gets stored inside the `StargateComposer` contract, and the tokens are left in the `StargateBridgeAdapter` contract.
  8. As the user can only retry the transaction with the same payload, the tokens will be stuck forever.
  9. An example of StargateComposer contract can be seen on: <https://stargateprotocol.gitbook.io/stargate/developers/contract-addresses/mainnet#ethereum>

Note: The application needs to use the `StargateComposer` contract as opposed to StargateRouter because it is transferring funds with payload, i.e. it executes `sgReceive` on the receiving chain. You can only use `StargateRouter` directly if you’re sending funds empty payload. More on it: <https://stargateprotocol.gitbook.io/stargate/stargate-composability>
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a permanent token lock that can occur when a cross‑chain swap is performed through the StargateBridgeAdapter contract. When a user initiates a bridge transaction, the source chain sends the tokens together with a payload that contains swapData to the destination chain. On the destination chain the StargateComposer forwards the tokens to the StargateBridgeAdapter and invokes its sgReceive function, which in turn calls the user‑defined receiveFromBridge routine to execute a token swap. The root cause is that the swap logic relies on parameters such as a minimum amount‑out that are calculated off‑chain at the time the transaction is signed. If market conditions change between the signing moment and the execution moment – for example a sharp price movement or a sudden slippage increase – the provided swapData becomes outdated and the swap reverts. Because sgReceive is called inside a cross‑chain message handler, the revert does not unwind the whole Stargate message; instead the message payload is cached inside the StargateComposer contract for later retry. The tokens that were transferred to the BridgeAdapter remain there, and the cached payload can only be retried with the same stale swapData. Consequently the swap will fail again and the tokens stay locked indefinitely, effectively disappearing from the user’s balance. From the user’s perspective the bridge transaction appears to have succeeded on the source chain, but on the destination chain the expected output (for example a received token amount or a successful swap) never arrives and the balance shown by the UI remains unchanged or shows zero for the transferred asset. The impact is a loss of the user’s own funds; no other parties are directly harmed, but the protocol’s reputation suffers because cross‑chain operations are expected to be atomic. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, with a proof‑of‑concept provided by the researcher known as the Warden, who demonstrated that a market shock can trigger the failure path. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert on the source chain and there is no explicit error emitted to the user, making it hard to notice without deep inspection of the cached payload. To remediate the problem the receiveFromBridge call should be wrapped in a try/catch block; if the swap reverts, the contract must transfer the received tokens back to the original sender or allow the payload to be cleared with updated swap parameters. This change restores the expected atomicity of the bridge‑swap flow and prevents permanent token loss. The vulnerability belongs to the class of cross‑chain composability bugs where downstream execution failures are not propagated back to the originating transaction, leading to asset lock‑up.

title: Users can use the protocol freely without paying any fees by calling the `DecentEthRouter::bridgeWithPayload
description: Users can use the protocol without paying any fees.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unauthorized fee bypass in the DecentEthRouter contract. The function bridgeWithPayload, which is supposed to be invoked only by the DecentBridgeAdapter, lacks any access control checks. Because the contract does not verify the caller, any external account can call bridgeWithPayload directly. The function performs the bridging operation and normally charges a protocol fee, but when called by an arbitrary user the fee calculation or transfer is skipped, allowing the user to move assets across the bridge without paying the required fee. This can be exploited by constructing a transaction that calls bridgeWithPayload with the desired payload; the transaction will succeed, the assets will be transferred, and no fee will be deducted from the sender or collected by the protocol. The impact is economic: the protocol loses expected fee revenue, creates an unfair advantage for attackers, and may undermine the incentive model that funds security and maintenance. The issue occurs whenever the bridgeWithPayload function is invoked by an address other than the authorized DecentBridgeAdapter, which is not prevented by any modifier or require statement. All users of the protocol, as well as the protocol owners, are affected because the fee revenue stream is compromised. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that reviewed the router’s permission model and noticed the absence of a caller restriction. It can be hard to notice because the function still performs its primary bridging logic correctly, and the missing fee may not be obvious unless fee accounting is explicitly checked. The recommended remediation is to add proper access control, such as restricting the function to calls from the DecentBridgeAdapter contract, or using an onlyAdapter modifier, thereby ensuring that fee collection logic is always executed. In generic terms, this is a classic missing‑access‑control vulnerability that enables fee‑free operation, violating the business rule that every bridge transaction must pay a fee. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a transaction that should have reduced the user’s balance by the fee instead leaves the balance unchanged, leading to a situation where “the user expects a fee to be taken but receives zero”. The bug breaks the accounting assumptions of the protocol and can be classified as an economic bypass rather than a direct asset theft.

title: Missing access control on UTB:receiveFromBridge allows UTB swaps to be executed without spending bridge fees while bypassing fee/swap instruction signature verification
description:
