Users can abuse the public [`UTB:receiveFromBridge`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-decent/blob/011f62059f3a0b1f3577c8ccd1140f0cf3e7bb29/src/UTB.sol#L311) function’s lack of access control to directly call the internal [`UTB:_swapAndExecute`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-decent/blob/011f62059f3a0b1f3577c8ccd1140f0cf3e7bb29/src/UTB.sol#L134) function.

This bypasses the [`UTB:retrieveAndCollectFees`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-decent/blob/011f62059f3a0b1f3577c8ccd1140f0cf3e7bb29/src/UTB.sol#L228) modifier, which is used to collect fees from UTB users and validate fee and swap instructions via [`UTBFeeCollector:collectFees`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-decent/blob/011f62059f3a0b1f3577c8ccd1140f0cf3e7bb29/src/UTBFeeCollector.sol#L44) in all other public swap/bridge functions (namely [`UTB:swapAndExecute`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-decent/blob/011f62059f3a0b1f3577c8ccd1140f0cf3e7bb29/src/UTB.sol#L115) and [`UTB:bridgeAndExecute`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-decent/blob/011f62059f3a0b1f3577c8ccd1140f0cf3e7bb29/src/UTB.sol#L266)).

This allows users to execute inter-chain swaps without spending bridge fees, using instructions that have not been signed by a validator key. Unsigned additional payloads can also be included in the swap instruction’s `payload` element, which would then be executed by the [`UTBExecutor:execute`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-decent/blob/011f62059f3a0b1f3577c8ccd1140f0cf3e7bb29/src/UTBExecutor.sol#L19) function.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a public function named receiveFromBridge in the UTB contract that forwards its arguments directly to an internal routine called _swapAndExecute. This routine is normally protected by the retrieveAndCollectFees modifier, which enforces payment of bridge fees and validates that the swap and execution instructions are signed by a trusted validator. Because receiveFromBridge lacks any access control or modifier, any external account can invoke it and cause _swapAndExecute to run without the fee collection step and without signature verification. The root cause is the omission of an authorization check that assumes only the bridge infrastructure will call receiveFromBridge, while the code does not enforce that assumption. An attacker can therefore craft a SwapAndExecuteInstructions structure containing arbitrary swap parameters and a payload, call receiveFromBridge, and have the contract execute the payload and perform the swap while paying zero fees and using unsigned instructions. This enables several attack scenarios: (1) fee bypass, where the protocol’s fee collector never receives the expected ether or token amount, resulting in revenue loss; (2) unauthorized execution of arbitrary calldata, allowing the attacker to trigger any function on a target contract, such as minting NFTs or transferring tokens without permission; (3) breaking of accounting invariants because the protocol assumes that every cross‑chain swap is accompanied by a validated fee payment. From a user’s perspective the swap appears to succeed – the expected token balances change and the target action (for example an NFT mint) occurs – but the fee‑collector balance remains unchanged, which is contrary to the protocol’s documented behavior. The issue is observable only when the receiveFromBridge function is called directly, a path that is not exercised by normal UI flows, making it easy to overlook during testing. It was discovered by the Code4rena audit team through manual review of public entry points and confirmed with a Forge proof‑of‑concept that demonstrated fee‑free swaps and execution of arbitrary payloads. The bug belongs to the class of missing authorization / access‑control vulnerabilities that also lead to signature verification bypasses. To remediate the problem the contract should restrict receiveFromBridge to calls from the trusted bridge contract (e.g., using onlyBridge modifier or making the function internal), re‑apply the retrieveAndCollectFees modifier, and enforce that swap instructions are signed before execution. By restoring proper access control and validation, the protocol will once again guarantee that fees are collected and that only authorized swap instructions are processed, preserving both economic security and functional correctness.

title: Potential loss of capital due to fixed fee calculations
description:
The `StargateBridgeAdapter` relies on a fixed fee calculation (0.06% of the current Stargate fee), but as explained in the Stargate documentation, fees can be automatically adjusted to meet demand. ([here](https://stargateprotocol.gitbook.io/stargate/v/user-docs/tokenomics/protocol-fees))

This reward can be adjusted ([StargateFeeLibraryV02.sol#L68](https://github.com/stargate-protocol/stargate/blob/c647a3a647fc693c38b16ef023c54e518b46e206/contracts/libraries/StargateFeeLibraryV02.sol#L68)) to “To incentivize users to conduct swaps that ‘refill’ native asset balances”. A problem arises because the `StargateBridgeAdapter` doesn’t account for this variable fee.

Then the callback function (triggered on the target chain) will receive a token amount greater than `amountIn`. [StargateBridgeAdapter.sol#L207](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-decent/blob/011f62059f3a0b1f3577c8ccd1140f0cf3e7bb29/src/bridge_adapters/StargateBridgeAdapter.sol#L207)
    
    IERC20(swapParams.tokenIn).approve(utb, swapParams.amountIn);

As you can see, here the difference between the received amount [StargateBridgeAdapter.sol#L188](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-decent/blob/011f62059f3a0b1f3577c8ccd1140f0cf3e7bb29/src/bridge_adapters/StargateBridgeAdapter.sol#L188) and `swapParams.amountIn` gets lost in the adapter.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the bridge adapter assuming a static fee model when interacting with the Stargate protocol. Stargate’s fee mechanism is designed to be dynamic: the protocol can automatically increase the fee percentage to incentivize users to perform swaps that replenish native asset balances. The adapter, however, calculates the expected fee as a fixed 0.06 % of the current fee and uses the original input amount (swapParams.amountIn) when approving tokens for the downstream contract. When the Stargate fee is adjusted upward, the callback on the destination chain receives a token amount (amountLD) that is greater than the originally supplied amountIn. Because the adapter only approves swapParams.amountIn, the surplus tokens that arrived in the callback are never transferred to the intended recipient contract. From the user’s perspective this manifests as a missing or reduced balance after a bridge swap – the UI may show that the transaction succeeded, yet the expected refund or received amount is lower than anticipated, sometimes appearing as a zero payout. The issue is a logical accounting error: the contract’s accounting assumes a constant fee and therefore does not account for the variable fee component, leading to a discrepancy between the amount sent and the amount forwarded. This discrepancy can cause permanent loss of capital for any user who initiates a swap while the fee is higher than the static assumption, as the excess tokens remain locked in the adapter contract with no mechanism to retrieve them. The bug was discovered during a security audit (Code4rena) by reviewing the fee handling logic and noticing that the adapter does not use the actual amount received (amountLD) when approving the token transfer. The problem is subtle because fee adjustments happen automatically on-chain and are not visible to end‑users, making the loss easy to overlook unless the balance after the swap is carefully inspected. To remediate the issue, the adapter should approve the full amount that arrives in the callback (amountLD) rather than the originally requested amountIn, ensuring that all tokens received from Stargate are correctly forwarded to the downstream contract. This change aligns the contract’s accounting with the dynamic fee model and prevents inadvertent capital loss caused by the mismatch between expected and actual token amounts.

title: DecentEthRouter.sol#_bridgeWithPayload
poc:
Example:

1. Alice wants to swap and bridge some tokens from Ethereum to Arbitrum.
2. For simplicity we’ll assume that LZ will need 0.1 ETH in order to pay for gas fees.
3. Alice sends 0.5 ETH instead.
4. The flow of functions is executed and the extra 0.4 ETH is refunded from LZ to `refundAddress`, which is set to `msg.sender`, which is `DecentBridgeAdapter`.
5. Alice loses here 0.4 ETH forever, as there is no way to withdraw and send the ETH from the `DecentBridgeAdapter` to Alice.
bug_full: The issue is an incorrect refund address configuration in the cross‑chain bridging flow of DecentEthRouter. When a user calls bridgeAndExecute, the contract ultimately invokes LayerZero (LZ) through the internal function _bridgeWithPayload. LZ requires a LzCallParams struct that contains a refundAddress used to return any excess native token that was supplied for gas. The code sets this refundAddress to msg.sender, which in this execution context is the DecentBridgeAdapter contract. Because DecentBridgeAdapter does not implement any mechanism to withdraw or forward received ETH, any surplus gas payment is permanently locked in that contract. The root cause is the misuse of msg.sender instead of the user‑specified refund address that is passed through the bridgeAndExecute call. An attacker or any user can trigger the bug simply by over‑paying the gas amount when bridging tokens; the extra ETH is sent to LZ, LZ refunds the surplus to the adapter, and the funds become unrecoverable. This leads to a situation where a user expects a refund of unused gas but receives nothing, seeing their balance reduced by the over‑paid amount while the UI shows a successful bridge. The problem occurs only when the bridging path uses DecentEthRouter with DecentBridgeAdapter and when the supplied msg.value exceeds the actual gas needed on the destination chain. All users who bridge assets through this path are affected because the protocol’s design states that no native value should remain in the contracts after execution. The bug was discovered during a manual audit by analyzing the flow of refundAddress and noticing that the adapter lacks any withdrawal function, making the trapped funds invisible in normal operation. It is hard to notice because the refund happens on the source chain after the cross‑chain call completes, and there is no event or balance change visible to the user apart from the missing ETH. Conceptually, the fix is to replace the msg.sender reference with the refund address supplied by the caller (the user) when initiating the bridge, or to add a safe withdrawal mechanism that forwards any refunded ETH back to the original sender. This class of bug falls under improper handling of refund destinations in cross‑chain messaging, which can lead to fund lock or loss despite correct bridging logic.

title: MarginTradingHook users could potentially be DOSed
poc:
Consider the next scenario:

1. Alice creates a contract that she would use as the caller of `MarginTradingHook`. Since Alice planning to work only with ERC20 tokens, she doesn’t implement the `receive` or payable `fallback` function on her contract.
2. Alice using a contract in combination with `MarginTradingHook` for her trading activity for some time.
3. Bob sends to `MarginTradingHook` 1 wei of wrapped native token.
4. Now each call from Alice’s contract to `MarginTradingHook` functions that include the `refundNative` modifier would revert since `MarginTradingHook` unwraps 1 wei of `WNATIVE` and tries to send it to the Alice contract. Since the last one can’t accept native transfers - calls revert.

Bob could effectively continue DOS even if native funds were withdrawn by other users, by spamming dust amount txs each block, at the same time Alice could lose funds on her active positions due to changing market conditions.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a modifier that automatically attempts to unwrap any wrapped native token balance held by the contract and then forwards the resulting native currency to the caller of the function. Because the modifier does not check whether the caller is capable of receiving native transfers, it will try to send native ether even when the caller is a contract without a payable fallback or receive function. When a malicious actor deposits a tiny amount of wrapped native token (for example, 1 wei) into the contract’s balance, every subsequent call that uses the modifier will trigger the unwrap and native transfer, causing the call to revert due to the recipient’s inability to accept ether. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate users who interact with the contract through their own contracts that are not payable will see their transactions fail, receive a generic “call failed” error, and be unable to execute further trading actions. The impact is that users may lose the ability to manage open positions, potentially suffering losses from market movements, while the attacker can repeatedly spam dust amounts of wrapped native tokens to keep the contract in a reverted state. The issue occurs only when the contract holds a non‑zero wrapped native balance and the caller lacks a payable fallback, conditions that are not obvious during normal operation and therefore easy to overlook. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the refund logic of the hook contract. The problem is subtle because the modifier appears to provide a helpful refund mechanism, yet the requirement that the transfer succeed is enforced with a hard revert, making even the smallest amount of wrapped native token a vector for attack. To remediate, the contract should make the native refund optional—e.g., by adding an explicit flag that callers can enable when they expect a native transfer—or remove the mandatory success check, or otherwise ensure that only callers capable of receiving native ether are targeted. In essence, the bug is a classic unchecked external call combined with an implicit assumption about the caller’s ability to receive ether, leading to a denial‑of‑service through dust‑level token injection.

title: `fillOrder` not properly cancel order when collateral of position is empty
description: When `fillOrder` is triggered, and the order’s collateral size inside the position manager is empty, it should change the order status to canceled. However, due to mistakenly updating memory data instead of the storage `__orders` data, it will not be canceled properly.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑inconsistency bug in the order‑cancellation logic of the fillOrder function. When the function is called and the collateral amount of the associated position is zero, the intended behaviour is to mark the order as cancelled, emit a CancelOrder event and stop further processing. However, the implementation copies the order struct from storage into a memory variable, updates the status field on that memory copy, and then returns. Because only the memory copy is modified, the persistent storage entry in the __orders mapping remains unchanged, leaving the order status as Active. This occurs because the developer mistakenly wrote to a temporary memory object instead of the storage slot that holds the order data. An attacker or any caller can exploit the bug by invoking fillOrder on an order whose collateral is empty; the contract will emit a cancellation event, leading the user to believe the order is no longer executable, while the order actually stays active in storage. Consequently, a later call to fillOrder (or any function that processes active orders) can fill the order, causing unexpected token transfers, potential loss of funds, or execution of trades that the user thought were cancelled. The impact is that users see a CancelOrder event and expect their order to be dead, but the protocol still treats it as live, breaking accounting assumptions and violating the business rule that an empty‑collateral position should automatically cancel pending orders. The bug manifests only when the collateral size is zero at the moment fillOrder is executed; under normal collateral conditions the function proceeds correctly. All participants who can call fillOrder – typically the order executor or any external caller – are affected because the storage state does not reflect the emitted event. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the flow of order status updates and noticed that the status assignment was performed on a memory variable rather than the storage mapping. It can be hard to notice because the contract does emit the correct event, giving the impression that the state change succeeded, and the function returns early, so no further logic runs to reveal the inconsistency. The proper fix is to write the new status directly to the storage entry, e.g., __orders[_orderId].status = OrderStatus.Cancelled, and to avoid using a memory copy for state mutations. This aligns the on‑chain state with the emitted events and restores the intended invariant that orders with zero collateral are automatically cancelled.

title: SwapType.CloseExactOut balance check too strict can be DOSed
description: SwapType.CloseExactOut balance check too strict can be DOSed.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises in the contract’s callback that finalises a swap when the swap type is CloseExactOut. The code checks that the contract’s balance of the output token after the swap is exactly equal to the amount that was requested (swapInfo.amtOut) using a strict equality comparison. This equality test is the root cause: it assumes that the token balance will match the requested amount precisely, ignoring the fact that other transactions, rounding errors, fee deductions or front‑running swaps can change the balance by a tiny amount. An attacker can exploit the condition by submitting a small, preceding swap that slightly alters the pool’s token ratio, causing the contract’s balance to be marginally higher or lower than the expected value (for example 1000.1 USDC instead of 1000 USDC). When the victim’s CloseExactOut transaction executes, the equality check fails, the require statement reverts with a slippage‑control error, and the whole operation is aborted. The impact is that legitimate users who are trying to close a position receive no funds, see a transaction revert, and the protocol becomes unable to process further CloseExactOut swaps, effectively a denial‑of‑service on that functionality. The condition occurs only when the swap type is CloseExactOut and the contract attempts to verify the exact output amount; any deviation, however small, triggers the revert. The affected parties are users who rely on closing positions, the protocol’s liquidity pools that may become stuck, and any downstream contracts that expect the swap to succeed. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the CoreCallback logic and identified that the equality comparison is overly strict for a slippage check. It can be hard to notice because developers often use equality checks for exact amounts, assuming the token transfer will be deterministic, yet in a live DeFi environment token balances are subject to minor variations. To remediate, the equality check should be relaxed to a greater‑than‑or‑equal comparison (or a tolerance‑based check) so that receiving slightly more than the requested amount does not cause a revert, and the slippage logic should be rewritten to use a configurable tolerance rather than an exact match. This class of bug—strict equality slippage validation—breaks the expected business logic that a user’s position can be closed as long as the protocol receives at least the requested amount, leading to unexpected zeros, missing refunds, and a broken accounting flow.

title: LP unwrap / wrap is fully broken if master chef contract has insufficient reward token and block decollateralize wlp and wlp liquidation
description: LP unwrap / wrap is fully broken if master chef contract has insufficient reward token.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when the LP wrapper contract attempts to unwrap or wrap liquidity provider (LP) tokens and the external MasterChef contract (or its extra rewarder) does not hold enough reward tokens to satisfy the transfer that is hard‑coded in the wrapper’s logic. The root cause is an unchecked assumption that the MasterChef contract will always have a sufficient balance of the primary reward token (MOE) and any extra reward token (e.g., USDC) before calling safeTransfer. When the wrapper calls the internal _modify function of MasterChef during deposit, withdraw, harvest or claim, the code unconditionally executes a safeTransfer of the calculated reward amount to the wrapper contract. If the reward accounting indicates that the wrapper is entitled to, for example, 10 000 MOE but the MasterChef contract only holds 9 000 MOE, the safeTransfer reverts, causing the entire transaction to revert. Because the wrapper does not catch this failure, the subsequent steps that would normally release the underlying LP tokens are never reached. Consequently, any user‑initiated LP unwrap, decollateralization of wrapped LP (wLP), or liquidation that relies on the wrapper’s withdraw function will fail with a revert, leaving the user’s LP tokens locked in the wrapper contract and the protocol’s liquidation mechanism stalled. The impact is that users see their withdrawal transaction fail, their UI shows no change in balance, and the protocol cannot process liquidations, potentially leading to capital being stuck and market participants losing confidence. This condition manifests only when the external reward contracts are under‑funded, a state that may be hard to detect during normal operation because the reward balances are managed off‑chain or by a separate team, and the wrapper contract does not expose the reward balance before attempting the transfer. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which traced the call flow from the wrapper to MasterChef’s _modify function and identified the unconditional transfer as a single point of failure. The bug belongs to the class of external‑dependency transfer reverts, where a contract’s business logic depends on another contract’s token balance without proper checks, leading to a DoS. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is a transaction that appears to succeed in the UI but then reverts with an error, resulting in “no funds received” or “withdrawal failed” messages, even though the user expected to receive their LP tokens back. To remediate, the wrapper should use the emergencyWithdraw path when a regular withdraw fails, or it should first verify that the MasterChef and extra rewarder contracts have sufficient token balances, or gracefully handle the transfer failure by skipping reward distribution while still releasing the underlying LP. This change removes the hard dependency on external reward balances and restores the ability for users to retrieve their assets even when reward contracts are under‑funded.

title: DOS possible while stopping a rental with erc777 tokens
description: If an order involves erc777 token for a pay order then in the `tokensReceived` callback the renter can create DOS situation resulting in the lender’s assets being stuck in the rental safe.
poc:
[ERC777 token standard](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-777) which is backward compatible with `erc20` implies that on the transfer of the tokens the recipient can implement a `tokensReceived` hook to notify of any increment of the balance.

Now suppose a pay order is created with an erc777 consideration asset as there is no restriction on that and also the eip specifies that

The difference for new contracts implementing ERC-20 is that tokensToSend and tokensReceived hooks take precedence over ERC-20. Even with an ERC-20 transfer and transferFrom call, the token contract MUST check via ERC-1820 if the from and the to address implement tokensToSend and tokensReceived hook respectively. If any hook is implemented, it MUST be called. Note that when calling ERC-20 transfer on a contract, if the contract does not implement tokensReceived, the transfer call SHOULD still be accepted even if this means the tokens will probably be locked.

So the `tokensReceived` hook is optional for a `transfer/transferFrom` call. Hence sending the assets from the lender’s wallet to the escrow contract shouldn’t be an issue.

Now when the rental period is over or in/between, the `stopRent` method in stop policy is called, which calls `settlePayment` in escrow module. Now on the token transfer

```solidity
(bool success, bytes memory data) = token.call(
    abi.encodeWithSelector(IERC20.transfer.selector, to, value)
);
```

The `tokensReceived` hook if implemented by the renter, would be called and they could just revert the tx inside the `tokensReceived` hook which would mean that the assets lent by the lender are locked forever.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that can occur when a rental agreement uses an ERC777 token as the payment asset. ERC777 tokens extend the ERC20 interface with a tokensReceived hook that is executed on the recipient side of a transfer. In the RE‑NFT protocol the stopRent function ultimately calls escrow.settlePayment, which performs a low‑level call to token.transfer to move the lender's assets out of the escrow contract. If the token being transferred implements the ERC777 tokensReceived hook, the hook is invoked on the renter’s contract because the renter is the recipient of the transfer. A malicious renter can code the hook to revert the transaction, causing the low‑level call to return false and the whole stopRent execution to fail. As a result the lender’s funds remain locked in the escrow contract indefinitely. The root cause is that the protocol accepts any ERC20‑compatible token without checking whether the token also follows ERC777, and it relies on the ERC20 transfer semantics while using a low‑level call that does not guard against callback reverts. The issue can be exploited simply by creating a rental order with an ERC777 token and then, when the rental period ends, invoking stopRent; the renter’s tokensReceived implementation will revert and prevent the settlement. The impact is that the lender cannot retrieve the lent assets, the protocol cannot finalize the rental, and users may see balances that never change even though the rental has ended. The condition occurs only when the consideration token is an ERC777 token that implements a malicious tokensReceived hook and when stopRent is executed. The affected parties are the lenders who provide assets, the renters who can trigger the revert, and the overall protocol which loses the ability to enforce its accounting rules. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the interaction between ERC777 callbacks and the escrow’s low‑level token transfer. It is hard to notice because ERC777 is backward compatible with ERC20 and many developers assume that a standard transfer will never invoke external code. The recommended mitigation is to forbid ERC777 tokens as consideration, for example by maintaining a whitelist of allowed assets, or by using a safe transfer pattern that either rejects tokens with callbacks or implements its own tokensReceived handler to ensure the transfer cannot be reverted. In user terms the symptom is that after ending a rental the UI still shows the lender’s balance locked in the escrow and no refund is received, contrary to the expectation that the funds would be returned immediately.

title: Risk of DoS when stoping large rental orders due to block gas limit
description:
When an order is created on Opensea the `Create::validateOrder()` policy method is used to ensure the order is configured correctly. Currently there is no maximum limit to the number of `offers` in the input `ZoneParameters`, which allows orders to contain an arbitrary amount of ERC-721 and ERC-1155 items to a rental order.

If a large enough rental order is successfully created, there is a risk that it won’t be able to be stopped by calling the `Stop::stopRent()` due to the amount of gas required exceeding the block gas limit. This would prevent the escrow from settling the order and leave the order permanently in a rental state. This also means any ERC-721 and ERC-1155 tokens in the order would not be able to be reclaimed.

This situation arises under the following conditions:

* The call to stop a rental order uses more gas than the call to create a rental order
* The call to create the rental order is successful
* The call to stop a rental order uses more gas than the block gas limit
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that can occur when an order created on the marketplace contains an unbounded number of offered ERC‑721 or ERC‑1155 items. The contract’s Stop::stopRent() function iterates over the full list of offers to return the assets to the escrow and to settle the rental. Because the order validation logic does not enforce a maximum length for the offers array, an attacker (or a careless user) can create a rental order with thousands of items. When the rental period expires and the owner calls stopRent, the gas required to process all those items can exceed the block gas limit. The transaction then runs out of gas and reverts, leaving the escrow in a perpetual rental state. From the user’s perspective the rental appears to remain active, no refund is received, and the NFTs remain locked in the contract, which may look like the protocol is refusing to return the assets. The issue is discovered during a security audit that fuzz‑tested the order creation and stop functions, showing that the gas consumption of stopRent can be higher than that of order creation and can surpass the typical Ethereum block gas limit (≈30 million). The problem is hard to notice because normal orders contain only a few items and therefore the gas usage stays well below the limit; only unusually large orders trigger the failure. The root cause is the lack of a constraint on the size of the SpentItem[] offer array, which makes the gas cost of stopping a rental order unbounded. The impact is that funds or NFTs may become permanently unrecoverable, breaking the business logic that rentals must be terminable and that assets can be reclaimed after the rental period. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “unbounded input leading to gas exhaustion” or “DoS via block gas limit”. The recommended mitigation is to enforce a reasonable maximum number of offers (for example 500‑1000) in the order validation step, rejecting orders that exceed this threshold, thereby guaranteeing that stopRent will always fit within the block gas limit.

title: DoS of Rental stopping mechanism
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial-of-service condition in the rental lifecycle of the protocol. The contract allows administrators to toggle the activation flag of hook functions that are called at the start (onStart) and at the end (onStop) of a rental. When a rental is created the lender and the renter supply a hook address; the protocol stores this address and later calls the onStart hook during creation and the onStop hook when the renter wants to stop the rental. The code checks the global hook status before invoking onStop and reverts with Shared_DisabledHook if the flag for that hook is false. Because the flag can be changed by an admin at any time, an administrator can disable the onStop hook after a rental has already begun. When the renter later calls stopRent, the contract sees the flag as disabled, triggers the revert, and the transaction fails. As a result the rental cannot be closed, the lender’s NFT remains locked in the renter’s safe and any ERC20 payment that was escrowed stays in the escrow contract. The impact is that funds are effectively frozen until the admin re-enables the hook or a contract upgrade is performed, which constitutes a denial-of-service for both lenders and renters. The condition occurs only when an admin disables the onStop hook while a rental that uses that hook is active; it does not affect rentals that never used a hook or where the onStop hook was never enabled. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the hook-status bitmap logic and verified that the onStart and onStop hooks are not independent. The bug is subtle because the revert happens only after a legitimate stopRent call, so users see a generic “hook disabled” error rather than an obvious loss of funds, making it easy to overlook during functional testing. The proper fix is to decouple the activation status of onStart and onStop, or to make the onStop hook immutable for the lifetime of a rental, ensuring that a rental created with an active onStart hook can always be stopped regardless of later admin actions. In generic terms the flaw belongs to the class of “state-dependent external callback disabling” or “admin-controlled callback denial-of-service” bugs, where business logic assumes that a callback will always be available but the protocol permits it to be turned off, breaking accounting assumptions that a rental must be able to terminate and release assets.

title: Incorrect ordering for deletion allows to flash steal rented NFT’s
description: User’s can flash steal NFT’s circumventing any restrictions imposed on the NFT
bug_full: The vulnerability is an ordering flaw in the stopRent function of a rental marketplace that handles ERC721 and ERC1155 assets. When a renter attempts to stop a rental, the contract first transfers the rented NFT back to the caller before it verifies that a corresponding rental order actually exists in storage. Because the existence check is performed only after the external token transfer, a malicious contract can exploit the onReceived callback that is triggered by the NFT transfer to create a valid rental order during the same transaction. By calling stopRent with a deliberately non‑existent order identifier, the attacker receives the NFT immediately, can invoke any function on it, and thereby bypasses the lender‑defined hook contracts that are supposed to restrict how the NFT may be used. After performing the unauthorized actions, the attacker creates the missing order (for example by replaying a previously signed Seaport order) so that the final existence check succeeds and the stopRent execution continues without reverting. The impact is that the attacker gains temporary, unrestricted control over the rented NFT within a single transaction, allowing actions such as interacting with on‑chain games, calling arbitrary selectors, or otherwise violating the business logic that assumes the NFT remains locked or subject to specific hooks. The asset must be returned by the end of the transaction, so there is no permanent loss of funds, but the protocol’s security guarantees around rental restrictions are broken. This flaw occurs whenever stopRent is invoked with an order that does not yet exist and the contract follows the current sequence of transfer‑then‑check. It affects lenders who rely on the protocol to enforce usage restrictions, renters who expect their assets to be protected, and any downstream contracts that assume the NFT cannot be manipulated during a stop operation. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors observed that the external call to _reclaimRentedItems occurs before STORE.removeRentals, and they demonstrated a proof‑of‑concept where a flash‑steal of a restricted NFT is possible. The bug is subtle because the transfer appears to succeed and the order is later added, making the exploit invisible without tracing the callback flow. Conceptually, this is an instance of improper ordering of external calls and state updates, a variant of reentrancy where the contract’s internal invariants are violated before they are checked. To remediate, the contract should verify the existence of the rental order at the very start of stopRent, move the NFT transfer after the verification, or employ a reentrancy guard that prevents state changes from being influenced by callbacks. By ensuring that no external call occurs before the contract’s internal consistency checks, the flash‑steal vector is eliminated and the intended restriction logic is restored.

title: Upgrading modules via `executeAction`
description: All assets from rentals pre-upgrade will be locked. Users can’t recover them as old rentals can’t be stopped.
bug_full: The issue is an upgrade‑lockout bug that occurs when the protocol upgrades a storage module through Kernel.executeAction while there are still active rental agreements. The upgrade routine reconfigures policies and initializes the new module but does not migrate any on‑chain state or provide a mechanism to stop or withdraw assets that are held by the old module. As a result, assets that were escrowed for rentals created before the upgrade remain locked in the previous contract instance, and the rental cannot be terminated because the stopRent function is no longer reachable. Users therefore experience a situation where they expect to receive their escrowed funds after a rental expires, but the balance shown by the UI stays unchanged or appears as zero for the new module, while the old contract still holds the tokens. The vulnerability was discovered during an audit by writing a proof‑of‑concept test that upgrades the PaymentEscrow module, fast‑forwards time past the rental expiration, and then attempts to stop the rental, which reverts, confirming that the funds are inaccessible. The root cause is the lack of a migration path or a pre‑upgrade safety check that ensures all rentals are either stopped or have a bounded maximum duration before the upgrade is allowed. This condition can be hard to notice because the upgrade transaction itself succeeds without error, giving the impression that the system is functional, while the hidden state in the old contract is silently unreachable. The impact is that renters and lenders who had active rentals at the time of the upgrade lose access to their escrowed tokens, effectively a denial‑of‑service and potential loss of funds. The bug belongs to the class of upgrade‑related state incompatibility bugs, where a proxy or modular contract is replaced without reconciling existing data. To remediate, the protocol should either enforce that no rentals are active before allowing an upgrade (for example by introducing a maximum rental duration and pausing new rentals), or implement a migration interface such as a migrate() function that lets users transfer their rental state and escrowed assets to the new module, or provide an emergency withdrawal path in the old module so that locked funds can be reclaimed.

title: Assets in a Safe can be lost
description:
The `Guard.sol` contract is enabled on Safe’s and uses the [`_checkTransaction`](https://github.com/re-nft/smart-contracts/blob/3ddd32455a849c3c6dc3c3aad7a33a6c9b44c291/src/policies/Guard.sol#L195-L293) function to ensure that transactions that the Safe executes do not transfer the asset out of the Safe.

The `checkTransaction` function achieves this by isolating the function selector and checking that it is not a disallowed function selector. For instance: `safeTransferFrom`, `transferFrom`, `approve`, `enableModule`, etc.

The list does not, however, check for calls to `burn` the token, neither does it check if it is a `permit`. The sponsor has noted the following:

The [Guard](https://github.com/re-nft/smart-contracts/blob/3ddd32455a849c3c6dc3c3aad7a33a6c9b44c291/src/policies/Guard.sol) contract can only protect against the transfer of tokens that faithfully implement the ERC721/ERC1155 spec.

But this does not acknowledge the fact that an ERC721/ERC1155 implementation can still be an honest implementation and have extra functionality. In particular, the `burn` function is a common addition to many ERC721 contracts, usually granted through inheriting `ERC721Burnable`.

For example, the following projects all have a `burn` function, and Safe’s protected by `Guard.sol` that hold these NFTs will be vulnerable to loss of assets via a malicious renter:

* [Pudgy Penguins](https://etherscan.io/address/0xbd3531da5cf5857e7cfaa92426877b022e612cf8#writeContract)
* [Lil Pudgies](https://etherscan.io/address/0x524cab2ec69124574082676e6f654a18df49a048#writeContract)
* [Oh Ottie](https://etherscan.io/address/0x7ff5601b0a434b52345c57a01a28d63f3e892ac0#code#F3#L45)

These are three that are in the top 10 projects on Opensea at the time of writing.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Guard contract that is attached to a Gnosis Safe used by the rental protocol. The Guard’s _checkTransaction routine validates each transaction by extracting the function selector and rejecting a hard‑coded list of selectors that correspond to token transfer operations such as safeTransferFrom, transferFrom, approve, enableModule and similar. The root cause is that the whitelist of disallowed selectors does not include functions that destroy tokens, namely burn and burnFrom, nor does it consider the permit function that can grant approvals via signatures. Because the Guard only blocks outward transfers, a malicious renter who has temporary control of the Safe can invoke the burn function on an ERC721 or ERC1155 token that implements ERC721Burnable or a custom burn method. The call passes the selector check, is executed, and the token is permanently destroyed. The impact is the loss of the underlying asset: the owner’s balance shows zero, the UI no longer displays the NFT, and the protocol cannot recover the burned token. This occurs whenever a Safe protected by the current Guard holds a token contract that exposes a burn or burnFrom entry point and a renter is able to submit a transaction calling that selector. The affected parties are the token owners, renters, and the overall protocol that assumes assets remain recoverable while rented. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case attempted to execute a burn selector and observed that the Guard did not revert the transaction as expected. The problem is subtle because burning does not involve a transfer event; it simply removes the token from existence, making it easy to miss in logs or UI monitoring. To remediate, the Guard should be extended to include explicit checks for burn, burnFrom and, where appropriate, permit selectors, rejecting any transaction that attempts to invoke these functions while a rental is active. Adding these selectors to the disallowed list restores the intended protection that assets cannot leave or be destroyed while under rental, aligning the contract’s behavior with the business logic that assets must remain intact for the duration of the rental agreement.

title: `Guard::checkTransaction` restricts native ETH transfer from user’s safes
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Guard::checkTransaction function of the ReNFT safe implementation. The guard enforces a rule that transaction calldata must be at least four bytes long in order to guarantee the presence of a function selector. This rule is appropriate for contract calls that invoke a specific function, but it unintentionally blocks native ETH transfers because such transfers are encoded with an empty data field (zero‑byte calldata). When a safe owner attempts to move ETH out of a safe using a simple value‑only call, the guard evaluates the data length, finds it less than four, and reverts with the error GuardPolicy_FunctionSelectorRequired. The root cause is an overly strict input validation that assumes every transaction carries a selector, ignoring the legitimate case of a value‑only transfer. Exploitation is straightforward: any attempt to execute a native ETH transfer from a ReNFT safe is automatically rejected, causing the transaction to fail and the ETH to remain locked inside the safe. The impact is that users cannot withdraw or forward ETH from their safes, leading to stuck funds, broken user expectations (users expect to send ETH and receive a successful transaction, but instead see a revert and unchanged balances), and reduced confidence in the protocol’s reliability. This condition occurs whenever the Guard::checkTransaction function processes a transaction with data.length == 0, which is the normal encoding for native ETH transfers. The affected parties are the owners of ReNFT safes, any protocol component that relies on the guard for transaction validation, and ultimately the end‑users who expect to move ETH. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case demonstrated that a standard Gnosis safe could send ETH while a ReNFT safe could not, and the revert error pointed to the guard’s selector check. The bug is subtle because the safe’s receive() function correctly accepts inbound ETH, so the problem only appears on outbound transfers, making it easy to miss in casual testing. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of input‑validation bugs where legitimate edge‑case inputs are rejected due to an assumption about data format. To remediate, the guard should be modified to allow data.length == 0 for value‑only transfers, either by skipping the selector requirement when the calldata is empty or by explicitly handling native ETH transfers as a special case. This change restores the expected behavior that a safe can both receive and send ETH, aligning the contract with standard accounting assumptions and preventing funds from becoming inaccessible.

title: The owners of a rental safe can continue to use the old guard policy contract for as long as they want, regardless of a new guard policy upgrade
description:
Policy contracts such as Guard.sol can be upgraded when needed. However, there is a vulnerability in existing implementation of Guard policy, that allows a rental safe contract to use the outdated Guard.sol for an unlimited amount of time.

This compromises the security of the rental wallet because unsafe transactions that are checked and reverted in the new guard policy contract can be directly bypassed and permitted in rental safe contract using an old guard policy.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an upgrade‑ability oversight in the rental‑safe guard policy system. When the protocol upgrades the Guard.sol contract, the safe continues to reference the previous Guard address because the Guard implementation never verifies that it is still listed as an active policy in the Kernel contract. The root cause is the absence of an active‑policy check in the Guard.checkTransaction function and in the internal helper functions that rely only on view calls to storage without any access control. As a result, a rental safe that has not executed the migration delegate call can keep using the old Guard logic indefinitely. An attacker (or any user) can exploit this by deploying a new Guard with stricter rules – for example blocking delegate calls, disallowing certain function selectors or extensions – while safes still bound to the old Guard will bypass those new restrictions. From the user’s perspective a transaction that should be reverted (e.g., a delegate call to an unapproved contract) is accepted and executed, leading to the expectation that the safe is protected but in reality the protection is missing. The impact is a weakened security model for the rental wallet: unsafe transactions may be processed, funds could be moved in ways the protocol intended to forbid, and the fairness of the rental marketplace is compromised because some safes operate under old, more permissive rules while others are forced to comply with the new policy. The condition occurs whenever the protocol executor upgrades the Guard via Kernel.activatePolicy / Kernel.deactivatePolicy and the safe owner does not invoke the whitelisted migration contract to update the stored guard address. The issue was discovered during an audit that examined the upgrade flow and observed that Guard.checkTransaction does not query Kernel for its active status, allowing the old guard to remain functional even after deactivation. The problem is subtle because the contract still compiles and transactions succeed, giving no obvious error signal; only a careful review of the policy‑activation logic reveals the gap. The recommended remediation is to add an isActive verification in Guard.checkTransaction (for example by calling Kernel.getPolicyIndex and confirming the address appears in Kernel.activePolicies) and to enforce migration of safes to the new guard, ensuring that deactivated policies cannot be used to validate transactions.

title: Protocol does not implement EIP712 correctly on multiple occasions
description: Being not EIP712 compliant can lead to issues with integrators and possibly DOS.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect implementation of the EIP‑712 typed data hashing scheme in several contract functions. Instead of concatenating the type description strings with abi.encodePacked, the code uses abi.encode, which adds length prefixes and padding, producing a type hash that differs from the canonical EIP‑712 hash. Because the contract verifies signatures against this malformed hash, any order or message signed off‑chain with the correct EIP‑712 encoding will be rejected by the on‑chain verifier. This mismatch can cause integrators to experience failed transactions, denial‑of‑service conditions, and potentially locked funds when a rental order cannot be processed. The issue appears when a user creates a rental order, signs the order off‑chain, and submits it to the protocol; the contract computes a wrong type hash, the signature verification fails, and the transaction reverts, leaving the user with no confirmation and possibly with assets still escrowed. The bug was discovered during a formal audit when a test compared the contract‑generated hash with a hash generated using the correct encodePacked method and observed a mismatch. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles and runs normally; the failure only surfaces during signature verification, which may not be exercised in routine unit tests, making it hard to notice. To remediate, the contract must replace every abi.encode call used for constructing EIP‑712 type hashes with abi.encodePacked, ensuring that the concatenated type strings match the EIP‑712 specification. This change restores proper signature validation, allowing orders to be accepted, funds to flow as intended, and integrators to rely on standard EIP‑712 tooling.

title: paused ERC721/ERC1155 could cause stopRent to revert, potentially causing issues for the lender.
description: Many ERC721/ERC1155 tokens, including well-known games such as Axie Infinity, have a pause functionality inside the contract. This pause functionality will cause the `stopRent` call to always revert and could cause issues, especially for the `PAY` order type.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the interaction between the protocol’s stopRent function and external ERC721 or ERC1155 tokens that implement a pause mechanism. When a lender invokes stopRent (or stopRentBatch) the protocol attempts to reclaim the rented NFTs by delegating a call to the safe, which in turn calls reclaimRentalOrder to transfer each token back to the lender. If the underlying NFT contract is paused, the ERC721/1155 transfer functions revert, causing the delegated call to fail and the entire stopRent transaction to revert. This situation occurs only when the rented asset’s contract is in a paused state, which can happen for legitimate reasons (e.g., a game pausing trading) or could be triggered by an attacker who gains control over the token’s pause flag. From the user’s perspective the lender sees a transaction revert and the renter’s reward calculation continues to accrue, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual earnings; the UI may indicate that the rental was stopped while the NFT balance remains unchanged or appears to be zero. The impact is a temporary denial‑of‑service for the lender who cannot retrieve their asset, and a potential over‑payment to the renter because the protocol continues to calculate rewards as if the rental were still active. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised stopRent with known paused tokens such as AxieInfinity’s contract. It is hard to notice because the pause logic resides in an external contract and the protocol’s own code does not check for transfer success beyond the revert, so the failure is only observable when a pause is active. The bug belongs to the class of external call failures caused by state‑dependent token contracts, specifically a “paused token transfer revert” that breaks downstream accounting. To remediate, the protocol should decouple the NFT reclamation from the stopRent call, for example by recording a timestamp when stopRent is requested and performing the actual token transfer later (pull‑based) after the token is unpaused, or by using a whitelist of tokens that are known not to pause. This redesign prevents the immediate revert, ensures that lenders can eventually recover their assets, and keeps reward calculations aligned with the actual rental period.

title: `RentPayload`’s signature can be replayed
description: A malicious user could potentially fulfill all `PAY` orders that own the same value of `zonehash`.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a replayability flaw in the rental protocol where the signature attached to a RentPayload can be reused to satisfy multiple PAY orders that share the same zonehash. The root cause is that the RentPayload structure does not contain any field that uniquely identifies a single order, such as a nonce or the order hash, and the contract’s validation logic only checks that the signature is authentic and not expired. Because there is no replay protection, an attacker who obtains a valid, unexpired payload and its signature can submit the same payload to any number of PAY orders that have identical metadata, causing the contract to accept each submission as a distinct fulfillment. Exploitation proceeds by first creating or observing a PAY order with a given metadata set, then extracting the payload and signature from the order’s extraData. The attacker then calls the fulfillment function repeatedly, passing the same payload and signature for each target order. Since the signature verification succeeds each time and the expiration check still passes, the contract records each fulfillment and transfers the rental earnings to the attacker. The impact is that lenders lose the expected rental payments, the escrow balance is drained, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken – funds that should be allocated to distinct lenders are instead captured by a single malicious renter. This condition occurs whenever multiple PAY orders are created with identical OrderMetadata, which is likely because the metadata fields (order type, duration, hooks, extra data) are simple and often repeated. All participants – lenders, renters, and the protocol itself – are affected because the financial outcome is altered without any visible error; from a user’s point of view the UI may show rentals being fulfilled as normal, but the expected balances for lenders remain unchanged or become zero, and the attacker sees unexpected earnings. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case demonstrated that extraData fields were identical across orders from different lenders and that stopping the rentals removed the orders from storage while still allowing the same payload to be reused. The flaw is hard to notice because the signature verification passes and there is no explicit replay check, so normal transaction logs do not reveal abnormal behavior. To remediate, the RentPayload should include a unique identifier such as the orderHash (or a nonce) and the contract must verify that each payload has not been used before processing a fulfillment. This change ensures that each rental order can only be satisfied once, restoring the intended one‑to‑one relationship between a payload signature and a specific rental agreement and preventing unauthorized multiple earnings.

title: Lender of a PAY order lending can grief renter of the payment
description:
In a PAY order lending, the renter is payed by the lender to rent the NFT. When the rent is stopped, [`Stop.stopRent()`](https://github.com/re-nft/smart-contracts/blob/3ddd32455a849c3c6dc3c3aad7a33a6c9b44c291/src/policies/Stop.sol#L265), transfers the NFT from the renter’s Safe back to the lender and transfers the payment to the renter.

To transfer the NFT from the Safe, [`_reclaimRentedItems()`](https://github.com/re-nft/smart-contracts/blob/3ddd32455a849c3c6dc3c3aad7a33a6c9b44c291/src/policies/Stop.sol#L166) is used, which makes the Safe contract execute a delegatecall to `Stop.reclaimRentalOrder()`, which is inherited from [`Reclaimer.sol`](https://github.com/re-nft/smart-contracts/blob/3ddd32455a849c3c6dc3c3aad7a33a6c9b44c291/src/packages/Reclaimer.sol#L71). This function uses [`ERC721.safeTransferFrom()`](https://github.com/re-nft/smart-contracts/blob/3ddd32455a849c3c6dc3c3aad7a33a6c9b44c291/src/packages/Reclaimer.sol#L33) or [`ERC1155.safeTransferFrom()`](https://github.com/re-nft/smart-contracts/blob/3ddd32455a849c3c6dc3c3aad7a33a6c9b44c291/src/packages/Reclaimer.sol#L43) to transfer the the NFT.

If the recipient of the NFT (the lender’s wallet) is a smart contract, the `safeTransferFrom()` functions will call the `onERC721Received()` or `onERC1155BatchReceived()` callback on the lender’s wallet. If those functions don’t return the corresponding magic bytes4 value or revert, the transfer will revert. In this case stopping the rental will fail, the NFT will still be in the renter’s wallet and the payment will stay in the payment escrow contract.
bug_full: In this contract a PAY‑order rental allows a lender to transfer an NFT to a renter and to receive a payment when the rental is stopped. The stop operation is implemented in Stop.stopRent() which calls an internal function _reclaimRentedItems(). That function makes the renter’s Safe contract execute a delegatecall to Stop.reclaimRentalOrder(), which in turn invokes ERC721.safeTransferFrom() (or ERC1155.safeTransferFrom()) to move the rented NFT back to the lender’s address. The safeTransferFrom() variant performs a callback on the recipient – onERC721Received() for ERC721 or onERC1155BatchReceived() for ERC1155 – and expects the contract to return a specific magic bytes4 value. If the lender’s address is a smart contract that either does not implement the required callback, returns an incorrect value, or deliberately reverts, the safeTransferFrom() call reverts. Because the revert is not caught, the whole stopRent() transaction fails. As a result the rental order remains stored, the NFT stays inside the renter’s Safe, and the payment that should have been released from the escrow contract stays locked. From the user’s perspective the renter sees that the expected payment never arrives (their ERC20 balance is unchanged) while the NFT is still in their wallet, which contradicts the expectation that stopping the rental returns the asset and releases the funds. The vulnerability is rooted in an unsafe external call during asset reclamation: the protocol assumes the recipient of the NFT will always accept the safe transfer, but it does not verify or handle failures. It can be exploited by a malicious lender who deploys a contract with a faulty onERC721Received() that reverts, thereby causing a denial‑of‑service on the stopRent() function and griefing the renter by withholding the payment. The impact is a temporary loss of the rental payment and a potential freeze of the NFT in the renter’s safe; the renter can continue to use the NFT but cannot claim the agreed compensation. The issue manifests only when the lender is a contract with a non‑compliant ERC721 receiver, and it is triggered when the rental period ends or when either party calls stopRent(). It was discovered during a formal audit by constructing a BadWallet contract that disables the onERC721Received() callback, causing the stopRent() call to revert. The problem is subtle because safeTransferFrom() is normally considered safe and developers may assume the lender will be an EOA or a well‑behaved contract, so the failure path is rarely exercised. Mitigation strategies include separating the asset reclamation from the stop operation so that each party can claim their assets independently, modifying _reclaimRentedItems() to ignore transfer failures and allow the rental to be marked stopped, or replacing ERC721.safeTransferFrom() with ERC721.transferFrom() when the recipient is known to be able to hold the token without the receiver check. For ERC1155 the safeTransferFrom() cannot be avoided, so additional checks or a different reclamation flow are required. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “unsafe external callback during token transfer” and violates the business logic that stopping a rental must always return the NFT and release the payment, breaking accounting assumptions of the protocol.

title: Blocklisting in payment ERC20 can cause rented NFT to be stuck in Safe
description:
When a rental is stopped, [`Stop.stopRent()`](https://github.com/re-nft/smart-contracts/blob/3ddd32455a849c3c6dc3c3aad7a33a6c9b44c291/src/policies/Stop.sol#L265) transfers the rented NFT back from the renter’s Safe to the lender’s wallet and transfers the ERC20 payments from the payment escrow contract to the respective recipients (depending on the type of rental, those can be the renter, the lender, or both).

To transfer the ERC20 payments, [`PaymentEscrow.settlePayment()`](https://github.com/re-nft/smart-contracts/blob/3ddd32455a849c3c6dc3c3aad7a33a6c9b44c291/src/modules/PaymentEscrow.sol#L320) is called.

`PaymentEscrow.settlePayment()` will use [`_safeTransfer()`](https://github.com/re-nft/smart-contracts/blob/3ddd32455a849c3c6dc3c3aad7a33a6c9b44c291/src/modules/PaymentEscrow.sol#L100) (via `_settlePayment()` and `_settlePaymentProRata()` or `_settlePaymentInFull()`) to transfer the ERC20 payments to the recipients:

  * If the rental was a BASE order, the payment is sent to the lender.
  * If the rental was a PAY order and the rental period is over, the payment is sent to the renter.
  * If the rental was a PAY order and the rental period is not over, the payment is split between the lender and the renter.

If either the payment recipient or the payment escrow contract are blocklisted in the payment ERC20, the transfer will fail and `_safeTransfer()` will revert. In this case the rental is not stopped, the rented NFT will still be in the renter’s Safe, and the payment will still be in the payment escrow contract.

Blocklisting is implemented by several stablecoins issued by centralized entities (e.g. USDC and USDT) to be able to comply with regulatory requirements (freeze funds that are connected to illegal activities).

There are multiple scenarios that can have impact here:

A. The renter of a PAY order rental is blocklisted: Even if the renter is already blocklisted before making the rental, the rental can still start, but ending the rental will not be possible, so the lender loses the rented NFT (it will be stuck in the Safe) and at least temporarily loses access to the payment (it will be stuck in the payment escrow, but a protocol admin could recover it).

B. The lender of a BASE order rental is blocklisted: Ending the rental will not be possible, so the lender loses the rented NFT and the payment. However, it is unlikely that the lender has been blocklisted arbitrarily during the rental or wasn’t aware of the blocklisting before the rental, so this scenario seems unlikely.

C. The payment escrow contract becomes blocklisted during the rental (if it were blocklisted before the rental, the rental couldn’t start): In this case the lender loses the rented NFT and the payment is lost. However, it seems unlikely that the payment escrow contract becomes blocklisted.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a payment‑transfer blocklist issue that can cause a rented NFT to become permanently locked in the renter's Safe when the rental is stopped. The Stop.stopRent function calls PaymentEscrow.settlePayment which uses an internal _safeTransfer helper to move ERC20 tokens from the escrow to the designated recipient. If the ERC20 token implements a blocklist and either the recipient address or the escrow contract itself is on that list, the _safeTransfer call reverts. Because the payment transfer is part of the same atomic transaction that also returns the NFT, the revert aborts the entire stopRent execution, leaving the NFT in the renter's Safe and the payment still held in the escrow. This occurs when a rental is being terminated – either after the rental period for a PAY order or when a lender manually stops a BASE order – and any involved party becomes blocklisted during or before the stop. The affected parties are the lender, who loses access to the NFT and the expected payment, and the renter, who may not receive a refund; the protocol’s accounting assumptions that assets are always returned on stop are violated. The issue was discovered during a security audit that added a mock blocklist to a test ERC20 and observed that stopRent reverted, leaving the rental state unchanged. It is hard to notice because the UI may still show the rental as active and balances appear unchanged, giving the impression that nothing went wrong, while the underlying transaction has failed. The bug belongs to the class of atomic‑transfer failures caused by token‑level restrictions that break business‑logic invariants. To remediate, the contract should separate the NFT return from the payment transfer, using a non‑reverting transfer helper that records a failed payment for later claim, or require the lender and renter to claim their assets in separate functions, ensuring that a blocklisted payment does not prevent the NFT from being returned.

title: Blacklisted extensions can’t be disabled for rental safes
description: Safe owners can enable modules on their safes only if those modules are whitelisted, this check is also done on disabling modules, which poses a problem. This guarding logic is handled in `_checkTransaction` in `Guard.sol`. If a module is whitelisted and a safe owner enables it on his safe, later protocol admins find out that the module has a serious bug and should be blacklisted so no more rental safes are affected, at this point the safe owner has no way of disabling that module as it is blacklisted, and his safe will be vulnerable to exploitation forever, putting all the safe’s possessions at risk.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the guard logic that validates both enabling and disabling of modules (extensions) against a single whitelist stored in the contract. When a safe owner enables a module, the contract checks that the module address is present in the whitelist, which is the intended behaviour. However, the same whitelist check is also applied when a user attempts to disable a module. If the protocol administrators later remove the module from the whitelist because a critical bug is discovered, the module becomes blacklisted but remains enabled on any safe that previously added it. Because the disable function still requires the module to be whitelisted, any subsequent attempt by the safe owner to remove the module reverts, leaving the malicious or buggy module permanently active. This situation can be exploited by an attacker who knows the module’s vulnerability: the attacker can interact with the still‑enabled module to drain assets, modify state, or otherwise compromise the safe’s holdings. The impact is that the safe’s possessions are exposed to theft or unauthorized actions for as long as the module stays enabled, and the safe owner has no on‑chain mechanism to remediate the situation. The condition occurs only after an admin toggles the whitelist flag to false for a module that has already been enabled; before that point, disabling works as expected. Safe owners, renters, and any user of the protocol who relies on the safety of their assets are affected, while the protocol itself suffers reputational damage and potential loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a test that enables two whitelisted extensions, blacklists them, and then verifies that a disable call reverts. It is hard to notice because the UI typically shows a generic transaction failure without indicating that the failure is due to a blacklist check, and the problem only manifests after an administrative blacklist action, which may be infrequent. The bug belongs to the class of improper access‑control or whitelist misuse where enable and disable permissions are conflated, resulting in a permanent lock‑in of a module. From the user’s perspective the safe appears to refuse to remove the extension, the transaction reverts, and the safe continues to show the module as enabled, contradicting the expectation that a user can always disable a module they added. To fix the issue the contract should separate the checks for enabling and disabling: disabling should be allowed regardless of whitelist status, or a dedicated list of non‑disableable modules (such as a stop‑policy list) should be consulted instead of the generic whitelist. This change restores the ability of safe owners to remove any previously added module and prevents permanent exposure to vulnerable extensions.

title: Impossible to change managed wallets with `proposeWallets` after first rejection
poc:
The scenario for this issue to occurs is straightforward :

  * `mainWallet` make a request to `proposeWallets` to change the main and confirmation wallets which sets `proposedMainWallet != address(0)`.
  * `confirmationWallet` doesn’t like the change so he calls `receive` function with insufficient amount of ETH to refuse the change. After `receive` call, `activeTimelock` is set to `uint256.max` but `proposedMainWallet` is still different from `address(0)`.
  * `mainWallet` tries to call `proposeWallets` again by it will always revert because `proposedMainWallet != address(0)`.
  * Both main and confirmation wallets can never be changed again.
bug_full: The contract implements a two‑step wallet change process where the main wallet proposes new main and confirmation addresses and the confirmation wallet must either accept by sending at least 0.05 ether or reject by sending less. The receive function that handles the confirmation correctly updates the timelock but fails to clear the proposal state when the confirmation wallet rejects. As a result the variable that stores the proposed main wallet remains set to a non‑zero address. The subsequent proposeWallets function contains a guard that requires the proposedMainWallet to be address(0) before a new proposal can be recorded, causing every later call to revert with the message "Cannot overwrite non-zero proposed mainWallet." This bug occurs only after the first rejection, i.e., when the confirmation wallet sends insufficient ether, and it permanently blocks any further wallet updates. Both the main wallet and the confirmation wallet are affected because they can no longer change the governance addresses, which may prevent migration, recovery, or emergency actions and can effectively freeze the protocol’s administrative controls. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state transitions of the wallet‑change workflow and noticed that the reject path does not reset the proposal variables. It is easy to miss because the receive function appears to handle the rejection case by setting the timelock to the maximum value, giving the impression that the proposal has been cleared, while the hidden state remains. The vulnerability belongs to the class of state‑stuck bugs where a failed operation leaves mutable storage in an inconsistent state. From a user perspective the UI may show a successful proposal submission, then a rejection, but any subsequent attempt to propose a new wallet results in an unexpected revert, violating the expectation that a rejected proposal can be resubmitted. The recommended fix is to reset both proposedMainWallet and proposedConfirmationWallet to address(0) in the reject branch of the receive function, mirroring the reset performed in the successful changeWallets path, thereby ensuring that the contract returns to a clean state and future proposals are accepted.

title: The user who withdraws liquidity from a particular pool is able to claim more rewards than they should by carefully selecting a `decreaseShareAmount` value such that the `virtualRewardsToRemove` is rounded down to zero
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic rounding error in the reward accounting logic of the staking contract. When a user calls the internal function that decreases their share, the contract computes the amount of virtual rewards that should be removed using integer division: virtualRewardsToRemove = (user.virtualRewards * decreaseShareAmount) / user.userShare. Because Solidity truncates the result toward zero, a sufficiently small decreaseShareAmount can make this expression evaluate to zero even though the user actually has a positive virtual reward balance. The subsequent calculation of claimableRewards subtracts virtualRewardsToRemove from rewardsForAmount, and if virtualRewardsToRemove is zero the full rewardsForAmount is considered claimable. As a result the user can withdraw liquidity in many tiny steps, each time forcing the virtual‑reward subtraction to round down to zero and thereby claiming rewards that are supposed to remain unclaimed. This over‑claims virtual rewards, leading to a loss of protocol funds. The condition occurs whenever decreaseShareAmount is non‑zero but small enough that the product of virtualRewards and decreaseShareAmount is less than user.userShare, which is common for large share values. All liquidity providers who can invoke the decrease function are affected, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about “some rewards are virtual and cannot be claimed” are violated. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the arithmetic in _decreaseUserShare and noticing that the only validation on decreaseShareAmount is a non‑zero check. The bug is subtle because rounding down is a normal consequence of integer division and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when virtualRewardsToRemove becomes zero, making it easy to miss in testing. The proper mitigation is to change the calculation to round up the virtualRewardsToRemove value (for example by using a ceiling division or adding a check for a non‑zero remainder) or to enforce a minimum decreaseShareAmount that guarantees a non‑zero subtraction. By ensuring that virtual rewards are always deducted, the contract will honor the business rule that virtual rewards are not claimable, restoring correct reward distribution and preventing users from receiving more tokens than they are entitled to.

title: Persistent Contract Call revert prevents finalizing a ballot
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unhandled revert in the DAO governance contract when finalizing a ballot of type CALL_CONTRACT. The function _executeApproval invokes an external contract via ICalledContract(ballot.address1).callFromDAO(ballot.number1) without wrapping the call in a try/catch block. After the external call, the internal function _finalizeApprovalBallot attempts to mark the ballot as finalized by calling proposals.markBallotAsFinalized(ballotID). Because Solidity reverts the whole transaction when an external call fails, the markBallotAsFinalized line is never reached if the external contract reverts. This creates a state inconsistency where an approved ballot remains unfinalized, effectively locking the governance flow. The root cause is missing error handling for external calls and placing the finalization step after a potentially failing operation. An attacker can exploit this by proposing a CALL_CONTRACT ballot that points to a contract deliberately designed to revert in its callFromDAO function. Once the ballot receives enough YES votes, the DAO will attempt the external call, encounter a revert, and abort the transaction, leaving the ballot in an approved but not finalized state. The impact includes a denial‑of‑service condition for the DAO: further proposals may be blocked, expected actions such as token transfers or state changes never occur, and users see the ballot still listed as active despite voting having concluded. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the proposal still open, no tokens are moved, and the expected ContractCalled event is missing, leading to confusion and the impression that the system is broken. The issue occurs only during the finalization step of an approved CALL_CONTRACT ballot and only when the external contract call fails; normal successful calls do not trigger the bug, making it easy to miss in standard testing. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit when reviewers noticed an “unhandled revert” comment and verified that the finalization flag was not set after a failing call. The bug belongs to the class of unhandled external call failures that cause partial state updates and governance deadlocks. To remediate, the external call should be wrapped in a try/catch construct so that a revert does not abort the surrounding transaction, and proposals.markBallotAsFinalized should be executed regardless of the call outcome. Emitting the ContractCalled event can be placed outside the try block or emitted conditionally. This ensures that approved ballots are always marked finalized, preserving the DAO’s ability to continue operating even when a called contract misbehaves.

title: Creation of token whitelisting proposals can be DOS’d
description: The creation of token whitelisting proposals isn limited to 5 proposals; after which it is DOS’d until proposals are voted on and finalized.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial-of-service condition in the DAO’s token-whitelisting proposal mechanism. The contract enforces a hard cap of five pending token-whitelisting proposals. Because proposals remain pending until they are voted on and finalized, an attacker who can submit five proposals can fill the queue with spam or malicious entries. Once the limit is reached, any further call to create a new token-whitelisting proposal reverts with the message \"The maximum number of token whitelisting proposals are already pending\". This behaviour occurs regardless of whether the existing proposals have any votes, and there is no privileged function to cancel or prune pending proposals. Consequently, legitimate users who wish to add new tokens are blocked, the protocol’s ability to expand its token list is halted, and the governance process is effectively frozen until the existing proposals are resolved. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a test that creates six proposals; the sixth proposal fails as expected, demonstrating the DOS vector. The problem is subtle because a limit of five proposals may appear reasonable, yet the lack of a cleanup or removal path makes the condition exploitable in practice.
