If a holder calls distribute just before the owner changes the token list, the distribute loop will iterate over the old length of distributableERC20s while the entitlement array still reflects the previous size. When the owner’s transaction executes, the length of distributableERC20s is increased or decreased, causing the loop to read an index that no longer exists in erc20EntitlementPerUnit. This triggers an “index out of bounds” revert, effectively bricking further distributions for all holders until the owner re‑adds the missing token or fixes the array mismatch. In a second scenario, a malicious holder can front‑run the owner’s setDistributableERC20s call, invoke distribute with a subset of the holder list (e.g., 90 % of the holders) and claim the rewards for the existing tokens. After the owner’s transaction adds a new token, the attacker back‑runs a distribute call that includes the remaining holder, allowing the same holder to claim the newly added token’s rewards while also retaining the previously claimed rewards. This results in a double‑claim situation where one participant receives more than its fair share, reducing the amount available to the other participants. If the owner removes a token from the list, any balance of that token held by the contract becomes inaccessible until the token is re‑added, leading to potential loss of rewards. The vulnerability was discovered during a formal audit when a proof‑of‑concept test reproduced the out‑of‑bounds revert and demonstrated the double‑claim flow. The issue is subtle because the revert only occurs under a specific sequence of owner and holder transactions, making it easy to miss during routine testing. The impact includes possible loss of rewards for honest holders, unfair enrichment of a malicious holder, and a denial‑of‑service condition that halts reward distribution. The affected parties are all token holders, the protocol’s reward logic, and any users relying on the fairness of the distribution mechanism. To remediate, the contract should restrict setDistributableERC20s to be callable only after a distribution period has fully elapsed, enforce that the length of distributableERC20s and erc20EntitlementPerUnit remain synchronized, and optionally pause distribution while the token list is being updated. This ensures that reward calculations remain consistent, prevents out‑of‑bounds errors, and eliminates the opportunity for double claims or bricking the distribution process.

title: Withdrawal from NFTs can be temporarily blocked
bug_full: The contract implements a batch withdrawal routine that iterates over a dynamic array of managed NFT contracts (ManagedNFTs) starting from a stored cursor called nextWithdrawal. The routine calculates a limit as the smaller of the requested number of withdrawals plus the current cursor and the current length of the ManagedNFTs array, then loops from nextWithdrawal up to that limit, calling each NFT’s withdrawBalancesTo function. After the loop the cursor is set to the last index processed and, if the cursor equals the array length, it is reset to zero and a WithdrawalFinished event is emitted. The vulnerability arises because the reset logic only triggers when nextWithdrawal is exactly equal to ManagedNFTs.length. If, for any reason, nextWithdrawal becomes larger than the array length – for example when a subset of NFTs has already been withdrawn and then some NFTs are released from the array, or when a malicious actor front‑runs a release transaction and forces a re‑entrancy call to withdrawFromManagedNFTs from within an ERC721 callback – the cursor will never satisfy the equality check. Consequently the loop condition (i < limit) will evaluate to false for all subsequent calls, the function will exit without processing any NFTs, and the cursor will remain stuck at a value that exceeds the array bounds. This state effectively blocks further revenue withdrawals from all managed NFTs, creating a denial‑of‑service condition for the protocol’s revenue pool. From a user perspective the contract’s balance appears unchanged after a withdrawal attempt, refunds that should be sent to the protocol’s treasury remain missing, and the UI may show “no funds withdrawn” or a zero‑change message despite the presence of underlying token balances. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit when the researchers constructed a proof‑of‑concept that leveraged the onERC721Received callback to invoke withdrawFromManagedNFTs while the ManagedNFTs array was being modified, demonstrating that the cursor can be driven past the array length. The bug is subtle because the out‑of‑range cursor only manifests after a specific sequence of partial withdrawals followed by NFT releases, a scenario that may not be exercised in normal operation and therefore can be missed by simple unit tests. The root cause is an off‑by‑one reset condition that assumes the cursor will never exceed the array length, ignoring that the array can shrink independently of the cursor. To remediate the issue the reset logic should be changed to reset the cursor whenever it is greater than or equal to the current array length (i.e., if nextWithdrawal >= ManagedNFTs.length) before emitting the WithdrawalFinished event. This ensures that any out‑of‑range cursor is safely wrapped to zero, restoring the ability to process future withdrawals and preventing the revenue lock‑up. The vulnerability belongs to the class of state‑inconsistent indexing bugs where mutable collection size and iteration pointers become desynchronized, leading to functional dead‑locks and potential loss of funds.

title: PrincipalToken is not ERC-5095 compliant
description: Protocols that try to integrate with Spectra, expecting `PrincipalToken` to be ERC-5095 compliant, will face an array of issues that may damage Spectra’s brand and limit Spectra’s growth in the market.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a deviation from the ERC‑5095 token standard in the PrincipalToken contract, which leads to non‑compliant behaviour for several core functions. Specifically, the redeem and withdraw functions do not honour the ERC‑20 allowance flow required by the standard: a spender that has been granted allowance over a holder’s principal tokens cannot successfully call redeem or withdraw on behalf of the holder, causing the call to revert even though the allowance exists. In addition, the maxWithdraw function violates the specification by reverting when the contract is paused, whereas ERC‑5095 mandates that it must never revert and should instead return zero when withdrawals are disabled. Likewise, maxRedeem fails to return zero when the contract is paused, returning a non‑zero value that suggests redemption is possible when it is actually blocked. The root cause is an incomplete implementation of the ERC‑5095 interface: the contract lacks the necessary checks for allowance‑based redemption/withdrawal and does not handle the paused state according to the standard’s requirements. An attacker or any third‑party contract that relies on the allowance mechanism can be blocked from redeeming or withdrawing tokens, resulting in a denial‑of‑service condition for delegated users. Integrators that assume ERC‑5095 compliance may call maxWithdraw or maxRedeem expecting a safe zero value during a pause, but instead encounter a revert, causing transactions to fail and potentially leaving funds inaccessible until the pause is lifted. This issue manifests whenever the token is paused or when a spender with a valid allowance attempts to act on behalf of a token holder. Users, protocol developers, and any downstream applications that depend on correct ERC‑5095 semantics are affected because they may experience failed withdrawals, unexpected reverts, or an inability to redeem tokens through approved contracts, undermining trust in the protocol and harming its reputation. The problem was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which wrote targeted test cases that demonstrated the missing allowance support and improper pause handling. The bug can be subtle because direct calls by the token owner succeed, masking the failure path for delegated calls, and because developers may not anticipate that a paused state should return zero rather than revert. To remediate the issue, the redeem and withdraw functions must be updated to check for ERC‑20 allowances and allow burning of tokens by an approved spender, and the maxWithdraw and maxRedeem functions must be modified to never revert and to return zero whenever withdrawals or redemptions are globally disabled, such as when the contract is paused. In broader terms, this is a classic case of non‑compliant token standard implementation, where missing allowance handling and incorrect pause semantics break expected accounting logic, leading to user‑visible symptoms like transaction failures, zero balances remaining unchanged, and an inability to retrieve funds through delegated contracts.

title: All yield generated in the IBT vault can be drained by performing a vault deflation attack using the flash loan functionality of the Principal Token contract
bug_full: The vulnerability is a flash‑loan‑driven vault deflation attack that allows an adversary to drain all yield that has accumulated in the interest‑bearing token (IBT) vault. The root cause lies in two interacting design choices: the PrincipalToken contract exposes a flashLoan function whose maxFlashLoan implementation returns the entire IBT balance of the contract, and the ERC4626‑style vault calculates its share price as totalAssets divided by totalShares, falling back to a default price of one when both totals are zero. When the PrincipalToken holds the full supply of IBT shares, an attacker can borrow the whole balance via a flash loan, redeem every share in the vault for the underlying assets, and then mint back the same amount of shares plus the flash‑loan fee at the default price of one. Because the vault’s share price has been reset to the default value, the attacker receives the underlying assets at a price lower than the original share price, effectively extracting the difference – the accrued yield – while repaying only the flash‑loan fee. This sequence leaves ordinary users with a dramatically reduced share value and a loss of all previously earned interest, and in extreme cases may also erode part of the principal. The attack can be carried out entirely on‑chain in a single transaction, making it difficult to detect from external monitoring; the share price appears normal until the moment it is reset, and the flash‑loan repayment masks the malicious activity. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a Foundry proof‑of‑concept test reproducing the exploit. It is hard to notice because the vault’s fallback pricing logic is not obvious and the flash‑loan interface does not restrict the amount that can be borrowed. To mitigate the problem, the flashLoan function should record the IBT rate before the loan and verify that the rate has not decreased after repayment, or otherwise enforce a limit on the flash‑loanable amount or protect the vault against price resets. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of flash‑loan‑enabled price‑manipulation vulnerabilities that arise from unchecked borrowing limits combined with vault pricing mechanisms that default to a constant when emptied, leading to loss of user funds and broken accounting assumptions.

title: Missing unwrap configuration when withdrawing cross-chain in the `depositYBLendSGLLockXchainTOLP`
description:
The `depositYBLendSGLLockXchainTOLP()` function attempts to lend into Singularity, then withdraws the Singularity tokens cross-chain to lock and participate on the destination chain. The Singularity tokens are wrapped as TOFT tokens to facilitate cross-chain transfer.

```solidity
uint256 fraction =
    _depositYBLendSGL(data.depositData, data.singularity, IYieldBox(yieldBox), data.user, data.lendAmount);

// wrap SGL receipt into tReceipt
// ! User should approve `address(this)` for `IERC20(data.singularity)` !
uint256 toftAmount = _wrapSglReceipt(IYieldBox(yieldBox), data.singularity, data.user, fraction, data.assetId);
```

This function calls `_withdrawToChain()` with the `unwrap` parameter set to false, indicating that TOFT-wrapped Singularity tokens will not be unwrapped upon receipt on the destination chain.

```solidity
_withdrawToChain(
    MagnetarWithdrawData({
        yieldBox: yieldBox,
        assetId: data.assetId,
        unwrap: false,
        lzSendParams: data.lockAndParticipateSendParams.lzParams,
        sendGas: data.lockAndParticipateSendParams.lzSendGas,
        composeGas: data.lockAndParticipateSendParams.lzComposeGas,
        sendVal: data.lockAndParticipateSendParams.lzSendVal,
        composeVal: data.lockAndParticipateSendParams.lzComposeVal,
        composeMsg: data.lockAndParticipateSendParams.lzParams.sendParam.composeMsg,
        composeMsgType: data.lockAndParticipateSendParams.lzComposeMsgType,
        withdraw: true
    })
);
```

However, the [`TapiocaOptionLiquidityProvision.lock()`](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tap-token/blob/20a83b1d2d5577653610a6c3879dff9df4968345/contracts/options/TapiocaOptionLiquidityProvision.sol#L187) function attempts to acquire YieldBox’s shares of the original Singularity tokens. Therefore, upon receiving wrapped Singularity tokens on the destination chain, it should unwrap these tokens to facilitate the execution of subsequent actions.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect configuration of the unwrap flag during a cross‑chain withdrawal performed by the depositYBLendSGLLockXchainTOLP function. The function first lends assets into the Singularity protocol, wraps the resulting Singularity receipt tokens into TOFT (a cross‑chain wrapper), and then calls the internal _withdrawToChain routine to move the wrapped tokens to a destination chain where they are intended to be locked by the TapiocaOptionLiquidityProvision.lock method. However, the call to _withdrawToChain explicitly sets the unwrap parameter to false, meaning the TOFT‑wrapped Singularity tokens arrive on the destination chain still wrapped. The lock() implementation subsequently attempts to acquire YieldBox shares of the original (unwrapped) Singularity tokens, and therefore fails because it receives the wrapped version instead. This mismatch between the expected token type and the actual token delivered constitutes a logical flaw in the cross‑chain workflow. An affected user initiates a deposit expecting their funds to be lent, transferred, and locked on the target chain; instead, the transfer completes but the lock step cannot locate the required unwrapped tokens, resulting in either a revert or a silent no‑op. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful on the source chain, yet the expected lock does not occur, balances may appear unchanged, and no participation in the destination protocol is recorded. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by tracing the data flow from the deposit function through the wrapper and withdrawal calls and noticing that the unwrap flag was hard‑coded to false while the downstream lock logic requires unwrapped assets. Because the failure happens after the cross‑chain message is sent, it can be difficult to detect through simple UI checks; the UI may only show that the transaction was mined without indicating that the lock failed. The impact is medium severity: users may lose the ability to lock their assets, effectively rendering their deposited funds unusable or stuck, and the protocol’s promised cross‑chain liquidity provision is broken. The bug belongs to the class of configuration‑mismatch or token‑wrapping errors where wrapped assets are not correctly unwrapped before being used in downstream logic, violating accounting assumptions that the same token type is available after transfer. The correct remediation is to set the unwrap flag to true when calling _withdrawToChain, ensuring that the TOFT tokens are automatically converted back to the original Singularity tokens on the destination chain, or alternatively to modify the lock() function to accept wrapped tokens. Either approach restores the intended flow: lend → wrap → cross‑chain transfer → unwrap → lock, aligning the actual token state with the protocol’s expectations and preventing users from seeing “nothing happened” after a deposit.

title: `tOLP` positions created through `MagnetarAction.Permit` can be stolen
description:
This issue is a combination of three other issues:

* `MagnetarAction.TapToken` integration will leave tokens stuck in `Magnetar` contract.
* A lot of calls in `MagnetarAction.Permit` enables anyone to steal whitelisted tokens held by `Magnetar`.
* Anyone can take any whitelisted tokens approved to `Magnetar`.

In short, the first issue describes that, due to how `MagnetarAction.TapToken` is setup, it will leave the `tOLP` position a user creates through [`TapiocaOptionBroker::participate`](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tap-token/blob/20a83b1d2d5577653610a6c3879dff9df4968345/contracts/options/TapiocaOptionBroker.sol#L301) stuck in the `Magnetar` contract. As it mints the position to `msg.sender` which will be the `Magnetar` contract:

```solidity
File: tap-token/contracts/options/TapiocaOptionBroker.sol

301:    oTAPTokenID = oTAP.mint(msg.sender, lockExpiry, uint128(target), _tOLPTokenID);
```

The two following ones:

Firstly, describes how anyone can take any tokens that are in the `Magnetar` contract by granting themselves permissions to transfer any whitelisted tokens in using `MagnetarAction.Permit`. Because of how [`MagnetarStorage::_checkSender`](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/Magnetar/MagnetarStorage.sol#L93-L97) validates that the first argument in the calldata to `MagnetarAction.Permit` is the same as `msg.sender`. This together with that a lot of the calls allowed through `MagnetarAction.Permit` (`IYieldBox::setApprovalForAll`, `IYieldBox::setApprovalForAsset`, `IERC20::approve`, and `IERC721::approve`) have `address to`; i.e. the operator/approvee as the first argument. Hence, any user can approve themselves to transfer tokens out of the contract.

Secondly, by using `MagnetarAction.OFT`; which allows anyone to transfer tokens out of `Magnetar` (and steal any approved tokens to `Magnetar`) since there is an unvalidated call done to any whitelisted contract in [`MagnetarAction.OFT`](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/Magnetar/Magnetar.sol#L325-L333).

The contract is not in itself supposed to hold any tokens; in itself these issues are not that severe by themselves. However, these issues combined allows an attacker to steal the position completely. Since the first one makes the position be stuck in `Magnetar` and the two last ones makes it not actually stuck, but retrievable by anyone.

If a user uses `MagnetarAction.TapToken` to create their position they can have their position and/or rewards stolen.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a combination of three related flaws in the Magnetar module of the Tapioca option system. First, when a user creates a tOLP position through the participate function, the contract mints the newly created token to msg.sender, which in this context is the Magnetar contract itself, causing the position to be held inside Magnetar instead of the user’s wallet. Second, the MagnetarAction.Permit function validates that the first argument of the calldata matches msg.sender, but many of the permitted calls (such as setApprovalForAll, setApprovalForAsset, ERC20 approve and ERC721 approve) treat that first argument as the address to be approved. Because the check only compares the caller address, any external actor can craft a Permit call that grants themselves approval over any whitelisted token stored in Magnetar. Third, the MagnetarAction.OFT function allows an unrestricted call to any whitelisted contract without additional validation, enabling an attacker to invoke the previously approved transfer functions and move the tokens out of Magnetar. When these three issues are combined, an attacker can first cause a user’s tOLP position to become stuck in Magnetar, then use Permit to approve themselves as the operator for that token, and finally use OFT to transfer the token to their own address, effectively stealing the position and any associated rewards. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome – receiving a tOLP token and being able to claim rewards – is replaced by a missing token, a zero balance, and an inability to withdraw, which may appear as a silent loss because the contract is not supposed to hold tokens and the discrepancy is not obvious. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by constructing a test that creates a position, invokes Permit to set self‑approval, and then extracts the token via OFT, demonstrating that the token can be transferred out by any address. The issue is hard to notice because the token being held in Magnetar does not raise an alarm and the approval logic appears to be correctly scoped at first glance. To remediate the problem the contract should allow the caller to specify a receiver for minted positions, tighten the Permit function to restrict which calls can be authorized and ensure the approved address is validated against the intended target, and remove or heavily guard the generic OFT call so that arbitrary transfers cannot be performed without explicit permission. In essence, the bug is an authorization bypass and improper ownership assignment that violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions, leading to potential loss of user funds.

title: Spearbit finding “It is possible to exercise TAP option an extra time compared to lock duration” not fixed
description:
The finding itself is a follow up on the C4 finding [#189](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-07-tapioca-findings/issues/189). The description of the issue can be found in the Spearbit report.

The mitigation introduced in the [PR](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tap-token/pull/155) seems lost in the code base at audit here.

Quoting the impact from the Spearbit report:

Lenders with active oTAP positions will receive oTAP shares from the DSO program every week that their position remains locked, proportional to their positions share of the total supplied locked liquidity in the respective market
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw that allows a participant to exercise a TAP option more than once for a single lock period, effectively claiming an extra distribution of oTAP shares. The contract is supposed to grant one weekly reward to each lender whose liquidity is locked for the defined duration, but the state that records whether the option has already been exercised is either missing or was unintentionally removed during a previous code change. Because the contract does not enforce a single‑exercise rule, an attacker can call the exerciseOption function at the end of the first eligible epoch, receive the entitled oTAP shares, and then, after the epoch advances, call the same function again on the same locked position and receive a second batch of shares. This can be performed by following the steps demonstrated in the test: lock liquidity for a period slightly longer than a week, participate in the option program, wait until the first epoch ends and exercise the option, advance to the next epoch, and invoke exerciseOption a second time before exiting the position. The impact is that the attacker receives more oTAP tokens than the protocol’s accounting assumes, inflating their reward and potentially draining the DSO reward pool, which harms other lenders and undermines the economic model of the protocol. The issue manifests only when a position spans at least one full epoch and the caller interacts with the contract across epoch boundaries; it does not affect positions that are never exercised or that are withdrawn before an epoch ends. Lenders, protocol operators, and any user relying on the promised weekly reward distribution are affected because the over‑issuance distorts the expected share of rewards. The bug was originally identified by a Spearbit audit, a mitigation was merged in a pull request, but the fix was later lost from the code base, allowing the condition to reappear. It is hard to notice because the contract still permits a successful exercise call and does not revert; the extra reward may only be observed by comparing expected versus actual oTAP balances after multiple epochs. To remediate, the contract should re‑introduce a reliable tracking mechanism (e.g., a mapping of lock IDs to a boolean flag) that marks an option as exercised and prevents any subsequent calls for the same lock period, or otherwise enforce that exerciseOption can be called at most once per lock duration. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that each locked liquidity share yields exactly one weekly reward, preserving accounting integrity and preventing unauthorized extra token minting.

title: anyone with a `Pearlmit` approval to transfer `TapToken` can have their funds stolen
bug_full: An authorization bypass occurs in the transferFrom function of the TapToken contract. The function first checks the standard ERC20 allowance between the token holder (from) and the caller (spender). If the allowance is insufficient, the code falls back to calling Pearlmit.transferFromERC20, passing the token holder, the recipient, the TapToken contract address, and the transfer amount. Pearlmit validates the allowance against msg.sender, which in this context is the TapToken contract itself. Consequently, any user who has previously granted an allowance to the TapToken contract in Pearlmit unintentionally authorizes the contract to move their tokens on its own behalf. An attacker can invoke transferFrom on TapToken with the victim as the source address; the fallback path sees the TapToken contract as an approved spender and transfers the victim’s tokens to the attacker. The victim’s balance drops to zero while the attacker’s balance increases by the same amount, producing the symptom of 'my TAP balance disappeared' or 'I received no tokens after a transfer'. This exploit is triggered only when a holder has a non‑zero Pearlmit allowance for the TapToken contract and another party calls transferFrom on TapToken for that holder. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the conditional logic and confirming the behavior with a test that approved the TapToken contract in Pearlmit and then performed a transferFrom from a third address, resulting in token theft. The bug is hard to notice because the fallback path is rarely exercised, the revert condition checks a different error flag, and the UI shows a successful transfer without indicating that the source address was not the caller. The vulnerability belongs to the class of incorrect authorization checks or privilege escalation across contracts, where an external contract’s allowance logic is applied to the wrong actor. To remediate, the fallback to Pearlmit should be removed or the allowance verification should be performed against the original spender (the address that initiated transferFrom) rather than the TapToken contract, ensuring that only explicitly approved spenders can move tokens. Properly restricting the fallback or adding explicit checks would prevent unauthorized token movement and restore confidence that balances cannot be stolen through indirect allowance approvals.

title: `depositRepayAndRemoveCollateralFromMarket` function of MagnetarAssetModule can’t be used on behalf of user
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the depositRepayAndRemoveCollateralFromMarket function of the MagnetarAssetModule contract. The function is intended to allow an authorized caller to act on behalf of a user specified in the data.user field, after passing a sender check that permits either the user themselves or a whitelisted address. However, when the function proceeds to pull the underlying ERC‑20 tokens, it calls the internal _extractTokens helper with msg.sender as the source address instead of data.user. This mismatch means that the contract attempts to transfer tokens from the caller’s wallet rather than from the intended user’s wallet. The root cause is an authorization logic error: the check correctly validates that the caller is allowed to act for the user, but the subsequent token extraction does not respect that validation and mistakenly uses the global transaction sender. An attacker or any whitelisted third party can invoke the function with a victim’s address in data.user, expecting the victim’s tokens to be used, but the contract will instead try to debit the attacker’s balance. If the attacker does not hold enough of the asset or has not granted sufficient allowance, the transaction will revert, causing a denial‑of‑service for the legitimate user. Conversely, if the attacker does have a balance, the tokens will be taken from the wrong address, leading to unexpected loss of funds for the caller. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful call while the user’s balance remains unchanged, or the transaction may fail with an “insufficient balance” error even though the user has enough tokens. The issue violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that tokens supplied in a deposit originate from the declared user, breaking the expected flow of collateral management and repayment. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the sender check and token extraction logic. It can be hard to notice because the function name and the presence of a data.user parameter suggest correct behavior, and typical unit tests may only cover the case where msg.sender equals data.user. The proper fix is to replace the msg.sender argument in the call to _extractTokens with data.user, ensuring that tokens are drawn from the authorized user’s balance and that allowance checks are performed against the correct address. This correction aligns the token source with the authorization logic and restores the intended business rule that only the designated user’s assets are used in the deposit‑repay‑remove‑collateral workflow.

title: Options can be exercised preemptively due to timing delays
poc:
The attack is carried out in the following steps. Lets assume the current epoch has JUST started, and is epoch 1. Let’s assume the netAmount for this epoch is 100.

1. Alice calls `participate`. The `netAmount[2]` (next epoch) is increased by her deposit amount of 100.
2. Alice waits 1 week.
3. Alice then calls `exerciseOption`. Lets assume `newEpoch()` hasn’t been called yet.
4. Alice passes the `OneEpochCooldown` check. Alice gets assigned rewards. Alice’s rewards are = `100 * gaugeTotalForEpoch / netAmount[1], which is = 100 * total / 100 = total`.
5. The other depositors who hadn’t collected their rewards yet cannot collect them anymore. This is because there are not enough tokens for the rewards anymore. This is because the contract used `netAmount[1]` as the denominator while there are more than `netAmount[1]` shareholders collecting rewards.

Since this allows users to collect rewards in the same epoch and break the accounting, and can be timed very effectively, this is a high severity issue.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the time‑based cooldown that protects option exercise and the epoch‑based accounting that determines reward eligibility in the TapiocaOptionBroker system. When a participant mints an otap position, the contract records the block.timestamp of creation and enforces a OneEpochCooldown by checking that the current timestamp is at least one full epoch (seven days) after the entry time. Separately, the contract tracks the amount of liquidity expected for each epoch in a mapping called netDepositedForEpoch, and rewards are calculated using the net amount of the epoch that is currently active. Because the cooldown uses block.timestamp while the accounting uses the epoch index, a narrow timing window appears at the moment an epoch finishes but before the internal epoch counter is incremented by the newEpoch function. An attacker can participate at the very beginning of an epoch, wait exactly one epoch duration, and then call exerciseOption before the epoch number is updated. The timestamp check passes, but the contract still believes it is in the previous epoch for accounting purposes, so the attacker’s reward calculation uses the net deposit of the epoch they just entered instead of the next epoch. This allows the attacker to claim rewards that belong to the same epoch they just funded, effectively double‑dipping. The impact is that the claimed rewards drain the pool, leaving honest participants with reduced or zero payouts, and the contract may run out of reward tokens altogether. The bug manifests only when the epoch transition is delayed, which can be hard to notice because the timestamp guard appears correct and the epoch increment is an internal state change that many tests do not hit at the exact boundary. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the logical relationship between the cooldown and the epoch accounting. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a participant can exercise an option after a week and receive the full gauge reward, while other users later see their balances unchanged or even reduced to zero, contrary to the expectation that rewards are distributed only after the epoch ends. The issue belongs to the class of time‑epoch synchronization bugs, a form of race condition where two state variables that should evolve together diverge, leading to incorrect accounting. The recommended remediation is to align the cooldown check with the epoch index rather than raw timestamps, for example by rejecting exercise calls when the current epoch number has not yet advanced beyond the participant’s entry epoch, or by updating the netDepositedForEpoch mapping before reward calculation. This ensures that rewards are only claimable after the accounting epoch has officially progressed, restoring the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: `depositYBLendSGLLockXchainTOLP` function of the MagnetarAssetXChainModule will not work because it transfers Singularity tokens to the user before `_withdrawToChain`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the depositYBLendSGLLockXchainTOLP function of the MagnetarAssetXChainModule. The function is designed to lend Singularity tokens, wrap the received tokens into a TOFT receipt, and then send the wrapped tokens across chains using the internal _withdrawToChain routine. The root cause is a logical ordering error: after wrapping, the contract immediately transfers the newly minted TOFT tokens to the caller (the user) before invoking _withdrawToChain, which expects the contract itself to hold the TOFT tokens (or YieldBox shares) in order to withdraw them to the destination chain. Because the tokens have already been sent to the user, the contract’s balance of TOFT and the corresponding YieldBox shares is zero at the moment _withdrawToChain attempts to pull them, causing the withdrawal call to revert. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; any user calling depositYBLendSGLLockXchainTOLP will trigger the revert, making the function unusable. The impact is that legitimate users cannot complete the intended cross‑chain lock‑and‑participate flow: the transaction fails, no tokens are locked on the target chain, and the user receives no receipt of a successful deposit. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a “deposit” button, the transaction appears to be submitted, but after mining the user sees either a reverted transaction or a missing balance change, contrary to the expectation that their funds are now participating on another chain. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the control‑flow was examined and it was observed that the contract transfers assets before the cross‑chain withdrawal step. The bug is subtle because the token transfer itself succeeds, and only later does the contract attempt an operation that fails due to an empty balance, which may be mistaken for a network or gas issue. The class of bug is a “premature asset transfer” or “incorrect asset custody ordering” that violates the accounting assumption that the contract must retain custody of assets until they are dispatched to another chain. To remediate, the wrapped TOFT tokens should be deposited back into the YieldBox under the contract’s own address after wrapping, ensuring that _withdrawToChain can successfully pull the required shares. This change restores the intended flow: the contract keeps custody, withdraws to the destination chain, and only then releases or locks the assets as designed.

title: `_lockOnTOB` function of MagnetarMintCommonModule will not work due to the missing approved asset for YieldBox before depositing
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a token‑locking routine that attempts to move singularity tokens from a user into a YieldBox vault without first granting the vault permission to transfer those tokens. The function extracts the tokens from the user, then calls YieldBox.depositAsset, specifying the contract itself as the source address. YieldBox expects an allowance for the singularity token from the contract, but because the contract never calls safeApprove (or any approve) on the token, the allowance remains zero. When YieldBox tries to pull the tokens, the ERC‑20 transfer fails and the deposit reverts, causing the entire lock operation to abort. This flaw occurs whenever the lock flag is true and a non‑zero fraction of tokens is intended to be locked, which is the normal path for users who want to participate in the option broker. The impact is that legitimate users see their transaction revert, receive no confirmation that their tokens are locked, and may be confused by a missing balance change or an unexpected error message. From the user’s perspective the UI may indicate that the lock request was submitted, but the on‑chain state shows no token movement and the contract does not hold any shares, effectively breaking the business logic that assumes tokens are deposited and locked. The issue was discovered during a code audit that examined the flow of token handling and identified that the approval step was omitted before the external call to YieldBox. Because the failure happens inside a low‑level external contract call, the revert may appear as a generic “transfer failed” error, making it hard to pinpoint without tracing the allowance state. The bug belongs to the class of missing‑allowance or approval‑order errors, where a contract attempts to transfer ERC‑20 tokens it does not have permission to move. To remediate, the contract should explicitly approve the YieldBox contract for the exact amount of singularity tokens before invoking depositAsset, ensuring the vault can pull the tokens successfully. After adding the approval, the lock function will behave as intended, allowing users to lock their tokens and receive the corresponding YieldBox shares, restoring the expected accounting and protocol guarantees.

title: Incorrect return value of function `BaseTapiocaOmnichainEngine._payNative`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the overridden internal function that is supposed to collect the native token fee required for sending LayerZero messages. The contract BaseTapiocaOmnichainEngine inherits the OAppSender logic where the function _payNative(uint256 _nativeFee) is expected to return the exact amount of native tokens that were supplied by the caller, because the caller may need to pay more than the single _nativeFee value when several messages are bundled in one transaction. In the current implementation the function simply checks that msg.value is at least _nativeFee and then returns the input parameter _nativeFee instead of the full amount of native tokens actually sent (msg.value). This mismatch means that when the caller provides enough native tokens to cover the aggregate fee for multiple messages, the contract’s accounting records only the smaller _nativeFee value. Downstream logic that relies on the returned fee may therefore believe that insufficient fee was paid, causing the transaction to revert with NotEnoughNative or to silently skip the cross‑chain calls. From a user’s perspective the transaction may appear to succeed, but the expected cross‑chain operation does not happen, or the user may see an unexpected revert even though they sent enough native tokens. The issue is triggered only when more than one LayerZero message is dispatched in a single transaction, a scenario that is common in the Magnetar and Tap token contracts that batch calls through BaseTapiocaOmnichainEngine. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the fee‑handling logic. It is hard to notice because the function signature matches the parent contract and a single‑message test passes; the problem only surfaces under multi‑message conditions. Conceptually the bug belongs to the class of incorrect return‑value or accounting errors where a function reports a lower amount than actually transferred, breaking the contract’s financial invariants. To fix the issue the function should return msg.value (the total native tokens supplied) after confirming that it meets or exceeds the required fee, thereby aligning the reported fee with the real amount paid and restoring correct accounting for multi‑message batches.

title: Magnetar’s `mintBBLendSGLLockTOLP` reverts when `lock` is set to false
poc:
During the `lock` function call, we see that the Magnetar contract tries to credit itself the NFT tokens.
```solidity
tOLPTokenId = ITapiocaOptionLiquidityProvision(lockData.target).lock(
    participate ? address(this) : user, singularityAddress, lockData.lockDuration, lockData.amount
);
```
However, if the lock functionality is skipped, then the Magnetar contract will not own the tokens since this step will not be run. Users will be forced to raw send the NFT position to the magnetar contract which is unsafe since the Magnetar contract is not designed to hold tokens.
bug_full: The Magnetar contract provides a modular workflow through the mintBBLendSGLLockTOLP function, allowing a caller to optionally lock a newly minted USDO position in a TOLP (liquidity provision) contract and then optionally participate in a TOB (option broker) contract. The vulnerability arises when the caller disables the lock step (lockData.lock = false) but still enables the participation step (participateData.participate = true). In that scenario the function still attempts to approve and call the participate routine on the TOLP NFT that it expects to own, because the internal _lockOnTOB routine only transfers the NFT to the Magnetar contract when the lock flag is true. When the lock is skipped, the NFT remains in the caller’s wallet, so the subsequent approve/participate call fails with a revert because the contract does not hold the required token ID. The root cause is a missing conditional branch that reconciles ownership of the TOLP NFT when the lock step is omitted; the code assumes a lock always precedes participation. An attacker (or any user) can trigger the bug by calling mintBBLendSGLLockTOLP with lock=false and participate=true, causing the transaction to revert after the minting and before any funds are transferred. The impact is that legitimate users cannot complete the intended workflow, they lose the gas spent on the failed transaction, and the protocol’s user experience is broken. In the worst case a user might be forced to manually transfer the NFT to the Magnetar contract, a step that the contract is not designed to accept and could lead to assets being locked or lost. The issue manifests only when the combination of flags results in a participation request without a preceding lock, making it easy to miss during testing because each step works correctly in isolation. The bug belongs to the class of workflow‑state inconsistencies where conditional logic does not correctly enforce prerequisite state, leading to ownership mismatches. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a transaction that “failed” or “reverted” with no NFT received, even though the user expected a successful participation and possibly a reward token. To remediate, the contract should either enforce that lockData.lock must be true whenever participateData.participate is true, or modify the _participateOnTOLP routine to pull the NFT from the caller when the lock step was skipped, thereby ensuring the contract holds the token before calling the option broker. This correction restores the logical consistency of the modular workflow and prevents unexpected reverts.

title: Magnetar unwrap operations broken due to bad ownership and checks
poc: The fact that Magnetar isn’t designed to hold tokens is evident from the fact that any user can just call the unwrap function from magnetar and burn up any tokens it is currently holding. So the absence of the transferring of the token to the Magnetar contract itself causes an issue.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the unwrap workflow of the Magnetar contract, where the function that is supposed to return a user’s underlying assets is unable to do so because the contract never takes custody of the tokens it attempts to burn. In the TOFT implementation the internal _unwrap routine first calls _burn(msg.sender, amount) and then withdraws the same amount to a destination address. However, Magnetar’s _processWrapOperation invokes the unwrap selector without first transferring the caller’s tokens into the Magnetar contract, so the contract is not the owner of the tokens it tries to burn. As a result the burn succeeds (or can be forced) while the corresponding assets are never withdrawn, effectively destroying the user’s balance. A second flaw is the use of _checkSender, which validates that the first argument of the unwrap call – the destination address – matches msg.sender. Because the destination is not the token owner, this check does not enforce any real ownership constraint and can even prevent legitimate use cases where the user wants to receive the assets at a different address. An attacker, including a MEV bot, can front‑run a legitimate unwrap request, call the unwrap function themselves, and cause the tokens to be burned while the contract never holds them, leading to loss of funds. The issue manifests whenever a user calls the Magnetar contract’s wrap/unwrap interface expecting their tokens to be returned; instead the user sees their balance reduced to zero and receives no refund. The bug was discovered during a formal audit that examined the call flow and ownership checks. It is hard to notice because the function signatures appear correct and the contract does not store user tokens, so the missing transfer step is not obvious from a superficial review. The problem belongs to the class of token custody and authorization bugs where ownership is assumed without proper transfer and where sender validation is applied to the wrong parameter. To remediate, the contract should first transfer the caller’s tokens into its own balance before invoking the internal _unwrap routine, thereby ensuring it actually owns the tokens it burns, and the _checkSender verification for unwrap should be removed or rewritten to validate the true token owner rather than the destination address. This would align the contract’s behavior with user expectations that an unwrap operation returns the underlying assets and would prevent accidental or malicious token destruction.

title: `twAML` weights can be griefed by burning tokens
poc: Users can directly burn tokens due to `OTAP`’s open burn function as evident from the linked code. This prevents `exitPosition` being called in the `TOB` contract and thus, never resets the `twAML` values.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an open token burn function that allows any holder of OTAP tokens to destroy their token after they have participated in the voting and weighting mechanism. The TOB contract relies on the existence of the token to later call exitPosition which resets the twAML weight entries. Because the burn function is unrestricted, a malicious user can burn their token before the lock expires, causing the exitPosition call to revert and leaving the twAML entry permanently altered. The twAML values are used to compute average magnitude, divergence and ultimately the discount that participants receive when exercising options. As a result, the weight contributed by the burned user remains in the pool indefinitely, skewing the calculation for all other participants. This can be triggered at any time after a user has locked liquidity, and the effect persists for the lifetime of the pool because there is no mechanism to clean up stale entries. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the TOB and TOLP contracts when the interaction between the burn function and the exitPosition logic was examined. It is subtle because the burn operation itself succeeds and appears legitimate, while the downstream failure only occurs later when the system attempts to reference the burned token. The impact is that an attacker can grief other users by permanently biasing the weighting algorithm, potentially reducing their rewards or increasing the cost of exercising options. The bug belongs to the class of incomplete state cleanup after external token destruction or unrestricted token burn leading to stale accounting entries. To remediate, the burn function should be restricted so that only the TOB contract or other authorized contracts can invoke it, or the exitPosition logic should be hardened to handle missing tokens gracefully, for example by checking token existence before attempting to burn or by resetting the twAML entry independently of the token. From a user perspective the UI may still show voting power after a token is burned or the expected discount may be zero, which contradicts the expectation that burning a token ends participation and resets weights. The failure mode is effectively a permanent distortion of accounting that causes rewards to disappear or discounts to be miscalculated.

title: A single second in an epoch makes an user eligible for the entire epoch’s rewards
poc:
The situation can be created in the following manner:

1. Say the current timestamp is 100. Say the epoch is scheduled to end at 200. Alice creates a lock with the lock duration of 101 seconds.
2. The expiry epoch is calculated as 2, since epoch 1 ends at 200 but the position expires at 201.
3. Thus, Alice is eligible to collect rewards for epoch 2 even though she only spends 1 second in that epoch locked.
4. Alice can then take out her TOLP token the moment timestamp passes 201. However since the current epoch (2) is `<=` the expiry epoch (2), she can claim rewards later as well.
5. Alice waits until the next epoch start at 300 and claims her option rewards.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a temporal inconsistency between two contracts that manage locked liquidity provider tokens and option rewards. One contract records the lock duration in seconds, while the other interprets the same lock period in epoch units (weeks). When a user creates a lock that expires a few seconds after an epoch boundary, the lock expiry timestamp is converted to an epoch number that belongs to the new epoch. The exitPosition function checks the raw timestamp and therefore allows the user to withdraw the locked token as soon as the lock expires, even if only a single second of the new epoch has passed. At the same time, the exerciseOption function checks the position’s liveness by comparing the current epoch with the epoch‑derived expiry week, and it still considers the position active for the entire new epoch. Consequently, the user can withdraw the token while still being eligible to claim the full epoch’s option rewards. This mismatch lets a participant earn rewards without having any tokens locked for the majority of the epoch, effectively draining the reward pool and giving an unfair advantage. The issue occurs only when the lock expiry falls inside an epoch rather than exactly at its end, and it is triggered by the differing time‑base checks in the two contracts. All participants in the protocol, the reward distribution mechanism, and token holders are affected because the reward accounting is violated. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the lock‑expiration logic of the two contracts and identified the contradictory conditions. It is subtle because each function individually appears to enforce the correct expiration rule, making the inconsistency easy to overlook. To remediate the problem, the contracts should adopt a single, consistent time representation for lock periods—either both should use epoch units or both should use seconds—and the active‑position check should be aligned with the withdrawal check so that a position cannot be both expired and reward‑eligible at the same time. This would restore the intended business logic that rewards are only distributed to users who keep their tokens locked for the full duration of an epoch.

title: Rescue request timestamp not reset in `TapiocaOptionLiquidityProvision.sol` contract
description:
In order to put an asset in rescue mode, the admin first needs to call `requestSglPoolRescue`. This will start a cooldown period and the rescue can only be triggered after the cooldown period has passed. This is evident from the code in the `activateSglPoolRescue` function.
```solidity
if (block.timestamp < sglRescueRequest[sgl.sglAssetID] + rescueCooldown) revert RescueCooldownNotReached();
```
The issue is that once the rescue has been carried out, the value in `sglRescueRequest[sgl.sglAssetID]` is not reset. This means if the same asset is added back in, it will now not have any cooldown anymore. The contract will treat the asset as if the rescue request is still ongoing.

The `requestSglPoolRescue` cannot be called to reset the cooldown, since the value stored is non `0`. Since this bypasses a protection mechanism put in place by the devs, this is a medium severity issue.
poc: The problem arises when an asset is rescued, and then added back in. `sglRescueRequest[sgl.sglAssetID]` is left untouched, and so after being added back in it can be immediately rescued without any cooldown time.
bug_full: An admin‑controlled rescue mechanism is intended to protect a single‑asset liquidity pool by requiring a cooldown period after a rescue request is submitted. The contract stores the block timestamp of the request in a mapping keyed by the asset identifier. When the admin later calls the activation function, the code checks that the current block.timestamp is greater than the stored timestamp plus a fixed cooldown; if not, the call reverts. The vulnerability arises because, after a successful rescue, the stored timestamp is never cleared or reset. Consequently, if the same asset is later re‑added to the pool, the mapping still contains the old timestamp, which is already older than the current time, so the cooldown check passes immediately. This allows the admin to bypass the intended waiting period and perform another rescue without delay. The root cause is a missing state‑cleanup step in the rescue activation function, leaving stale data that defeats the protection logic. An attacker with admin privileges can exploit this by rescuing an asset, re‑depositing it, and then invoking the rescue again instantly, effectively removing assets from the pool repeatedly. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees: assets can be withdrawn without respecting the designed safety window, potentially leading to unexpected loss of liquidity or manipulation of pool balances. The issue manifests only when an asset that has been rescued is later re‑introduced; otherwise the cooldown works as expected. Users of the protocol may notice that after a rescue, the asset can be rescued again immediately, contrary to the documented waiting period, resulting in 'funds disappear' or 'rescue works instantly' symptoms. The flaw was identified during a manual audit that examined the rescue workflow and observed that the mapping entry was never cleared. Because the contract does not emit an event or otherwise signal the reset, the problem can be subtle and may go unnoticed in normal operation. The recommended remediation is to delete or zero‑out the mapping entry for the rescued asset within the activate rescue function, ensuring that any subsequent addition of the asset starts a fresh cooldown cycle. This aligns the implementation with the intended security model and prevents the cooldown bypass.

title: `_internalRemoteTransferSendPacket
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical ordering error in the internal remote transfer routine that handles refunds when the amount requested on the source chain exceeds the amount actually debited. The function first overwrites the requested amount with the debited amount and only afterwards attempts to transfer the difference back to the caller. Because the subtraction uses the already‑overwritten value, the computed difference is always zero, so the contract never sends the excess funds back. This occurs only when _lzSendParam.sendParam.amountLD is greater than amountDebitedLD_, a condition that should trigger a partial refund. The bug is caused by mutating the send parameters before calculating the refund, a classic case of state‑update‑order misuse. An attacker (or any user) can exploit the flaw by initiating a cross‑chain transfer with a deliberately larger amount than the contract will actually lock, expecting the contract to return the surplus. Instead, the contract retains the surplus, effectively stealing the extra tokens from the user. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transfer but the wallet balance does not increase by the expected refund amount, or the user receives zero tokens when a partial refund was promised. The impact is a loss of funds for any participant who relies on the refund logic, undermining trust in the protocol’s accounting and potentially violating business rules that require accurate settlement of cross‑chain transfers. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the refund path and noticed that the transfer call used a zero amount. It can be hard to notice because the surrounding code appears to handle the edge case correctly, and the zero‑amount transfer does not revert, so no explicit error is emitted. The proper fix is to perform the transfer of the difference before mutating the send parameters, ensuring the correct amount is calculated and sent back to the caller. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect state mutation order leading to zero‑value refunds” and should be addressed by reordering operations or by using a temporary variable to hold the original requested amount for the refund calculation.

title: Unordered Nonces open up to further MEV risks
description:
While a great effort was made to mitigate out of order nonce execution, the reality is that since `PermitC` allows unordered nonces, then nonces could be executed out of order. This opens up more problems than the original Permit Exploit. The original Permit exploit allowed to effectively always make multi-operations revert. This new scenario instead allows to use the order of nonces that will cause the most damage.

The most basic example would be using the reverse order to keep allowances to be non-zero. This may open up to more exploits, an example being claiming `TAP`, `twTAP` or rewards to router addresses by keeping the allowance as non-zero. Additionally, any time more than one Permit is issued, a race condition is available. This race condition would allow an exploiter to consume the nonces out of order, and then causes the transaction to revert. This, in contrast to the previous iteration, allows all possible sequences of combinations of allowances to determine the final result, while the original permit operation would allow only the proper sequence to be executed (with pauses between each step).

This additional risk can create scenarios in which outstanding allowance is left, which could incorrectly signal the willingness to claim tokens or the willingness to allow a target to bridge funds at a different time than intended. It’s worth reiterating how `Signatures` can be executed as soon as made available on any mempool, whether a L2 or LayerZeros system.
poc:
* Victim signs Permit A, B and C.
  * Notice how any of the permutations of `[A, B, C]` could be used out of order.
  * Front-runner will execute those signatures at whichever order is best for them to leak the most value.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s PermitC function allowing permits to be submitted with non‑sequential (unordered) nonces. Because the contract does not enforce that a higher nonce must be processed after a lower one, an attacker who observes a set of signed permits (for example Permit A, B and C) can reorder their execution in the mempool. This reordering creates a race condition where the attacker front‑runs the original user and consumes the permits in an order that maximises profit. By executing the permits in reverse order, the attacker can keep token allowances non‑zero after each step, which may enable unauthorized claims of TAP, twTAP or other reward tokens, or allow a malicious router address to bridge funds that the user never intended to approve. The core reason is that the contract’s accounting assumes permits will be processed in the order they were signed, but the nonce check only verifies uniqueness, not monotonicity. Consequently, the contract may revert a transaction after some permits have already altered state, leaving dangling allowances that appear to signal permission to spend when none was intended. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after signing several permits they may see their allowance unexpectedly remain positive, or they may notice that claimed rewards disappear or that a transaction they signed reverts while their balances are unchanged. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the auditors examined the PermitC implementation and identified that the nonce ordering check was insufficient. It is difficult to notice because permits are signed off‑chain and the ordering problem only manifests when multiple permits are submitted in the same block, a scenario that is not obvious during normal testing. The impact is medium‑severity: it can lead to loss of token value, unauthorized reward claims, and potential bridging of funds to attacker‑controlled contracts, affecting any user who signs more than one permit and the protocol’s overall security guarantees. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce that each macro (approval operation) can only approve a given spender once, and any revocation should be performed without requiring a signed permit – either by consuming the allowance via a transferFrom call or by providing an operator‑only function that resets the allowance to zero. This eliminates the ability to reorder permits to keep allowances alive and removes the race condition that enables the MEV exploit.

title: Same contract multi permits fundamentally cannot be solved via the chosen standards
description:
The finding is a direct follow up to: `All cross-chain USDO and TOFT flows using approvals may be susceptible to permit-based DoS griefing` from the Spearbit report.

Since permits are signatures, they will be available to anyone monitoring the chain. They will be usable by anyone, since the goal of permit is allowing some other `msg.sender` to broadcast the signature and have it work.
poc:
Due to this, the current architecture is still subject to front-run exploits via the following:

* Monitor the mempool for any sequence of permit signatures.
* Execute all of the signatures before the transaction.

Any time, more than one permit is signed to the same token, for example, to Add Exact Allowance and Revoke it, front-running the calls will burn the approvals and reset the allowance down to `0`.

The transaction, which may have worked had only one of the signatures been front-run, is unable to function as the last signature for revoking will be broadcasted right after the first one. This effectively means that the only architecture that could be used for Tapioca is single signature, with no revokes, which doesn’t seem to be the case at this time.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a permit‑based denial‑of‑service that arises when a contract accepts multiple permit signatures for the same token, typically one to grant an exact allowance and another to revoke it. Because a permit is simply a signed message that can be submitted by any address, the signature is publicly visible in the mempool and can be replayed by an attacker. An adversary can monitor the mempool, detect a pending permit that will increase an allowance, and immediately broadcast a revocation permit that resets the allowance to zero before the original transaction is mined. This front‑run sequence causes the allowance to be cleared, so the subsequent cross‑chain operation that depends on the increased allowance reverts. The impact is that legitimate users and operators experience failed transactions, funds remain locked in the contract, and the protocol’s cross‑chain flows become unreliable. The issue occurs whenever the design relies on permits for both granting and revoking approvals, especially in exact‑allowance patterns where rounding errors may also be present. All participants who depend on permit‑based approvals – end‑users, trusted operators, and the protocol itself – are affected because the contract’s accounting assumptions (that an allowance can be safely increased and then decreased) are violated. The problem was discovered during a security audit that traced the logical flow of permit usage and identified that the revocation step can be front‑run, a scenario that is difficult to notice because the permit signatures themselves are valid and the contract does not differentiate between a legitimate sender and an attacker. To remediate, the contract should avoid using permits for revocation, employ try‑catch around permit calls, enforce a strict 0→X→0 allowance lifecycle via a dedicated renounceAllowance function, and consider granting higher allowances while handling rounding errors in share‑to‑amount conversions. By ensuring that only grant permits are used and that revocations are performed by the contract itself rather than by external signatures, the front‑run attack surface is eliminated and the protocol’s accounting integrity is restored.

title: Incorrect decoding in `decodeLockTwpTapDstMsg`
description:
The decoding applied in `decodeLockTwpTapDstMsg` is incorrect as there are more than one combination of bytes that would result in the same result.

This is due to: `uint96 duration = BytesLib.toUint96(BytesLib.slice(_msg, userOffset_, durationOffset_), 0);` , which uses length `== durationOffset_` which is 32 instead of 12.

`uint256 amount = BytesLib.toUint256(BytesLib.slice(_msg, durationOffset_, _msg.length - durationOffset_), 0);` uses the length of the message, instead of 32 which would be the maximum size of a u256.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the message‑decoding routine used by the TapTokenCodec contract, specifically the function decodeLockTwpTapDstMsg. The routine extracts a 96‑bit lock duration and a 256‑bit token amount from a byte array, but it uses incorrect slice lengths when calling the BytesLib helper. The first slice uses the offset value (durationOffset_) as the length, which is 32 bytes, instead of the required 12 bytes for a uint96 field. The second slice uses the remaining length of the message (_msg.length‑durationOffset_) as the length for the amount, rather than the fixed 32‑byte size of a uint256. Because of these mismatched lengths, multiple distinct byte patterns can be interpreted as the same decoded values, creating an ambiguous mapping between the encoded payload and the decoded struct. An attacker can craft a malformed encoded message that passes the decoder without reverting yet yields a duration or amount different from what the sender intended. This can cause the protocol to lock tokens for a shorter or longer period than expected, or to credit/debit an incorrect token amount, potentially leading to funds being locked indefinitely, released prematurely, or transferred to the wrong party. The issue manifests whenever an external party supplies an encoded lock‑tap message to the contract – for example, when users interact with a token‑locking feature or when other contracts forward such messages. All participants that rely on the correctness of the decoded duration and amount – including token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s accounting logic – are affected. The flaw was discovered during automated fuzzing with Medusa and Recon, which generated a test case that decoded a message, re‑encoded it, and observed that the two byte arrays differed despite the decoder reporting success. The problem is subtle because the decoder does not throw an error; it simply reads the wrong region of memory, making the bug hard to spot through manual code review or simple unit tests. To remediate the issue, the slice calls must be changed to use the exact field sizes: the duration slice should be limited to 12 bytes and the amount slice should be limited to 32 bytes. This ensures that each field is read from the intended portion of the payload, eliminating the ambiguous decoding and restoring the contract’s intended accounting guarantees. From a user’s perspective, the bug may appear as a situation where a lock transaction that should hold tokens for, say, 30 days instead releases them after a few hours, or where the amount shown in the UI does not match the amount actually locked, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust in the protocol.

title: `burst
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal function that forwards a call with an optional ether value. When the caller supplies a positive _actionValue and sets _allowFailure to true, the contract executes the external call but deliberately suppresses any revert handling. The code only extracts the revert message when the call fails and _allowFailure is false; when _allowFailure is true the failure is ignored and the function simply returns. Because the ether that was attached to the call is transferred before the success check, a failed call leaves the transferred ether locked inside the contract. The contract does not automatically refund this ether to the original sender. Instead, the only way to retrieve the stuck ether is through an owner‑only rescueEth() function, which may be executed at a later time. Until the owner rescues the balance, any address that can invoke other contract functions can draw on the retained ether to perform further actions, effectively allowing a malicious actor to siphon the funds. This issue occurs whenever a user invokes the burst entry point (or any wrapper that uses _executeCall) with a payable action that is permitted to fail. The affected parties are the users who expect their ether to be returned on a failed action, as well as the protocol that relies on correct accounting of deposited funds. The problem was identified during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the control flow of the call‑forwarding routine. It is subtle because the contract does retain a positive balance after a failed allowed call, which may appear normal, and the presence of a rescue function can give a false sense of safety. However, the retained ether can be repurposed by an attacker to execute arbitrary calls, leading to loss of user funds and a breach of the protocol’s financial guarantees. The bug belongs to the class of “improper value handling on external call failure” or “stuck ether due to missing refund logic”. To remediate, the contract should track the total ether supplied for the batch of actions, verify that the contract’s balance after execution matches the expected leftover, and explicitly return any remaining ether to msg.sender before exiting. This can be achieved by accumulating the expected value, checking for mismatches, and performing a final call that forwards the entire contract balance back to the caller, ensuring that no ether remains unintentionally locked in the contract.

title: After `unregisterSingularity
bug_full: The contract allows the contract owner to call unregisterSingularity, which removes the mapping entry for a given singularity and deletes the associated asset identifier without first verifying whether any user positions are still locked in that pool. The function only checks that the singularity is registered and that it is in rescue mode, then proceeds to delete activeSingularities[singularity] and sglAssetIDToAddress[sglAssetID] and to pop the identifier from the singularities array. Because the totalDeposited field of the pool is not examined, a pool that still holds user‑locked shares can be unregistered. When a user later calls unlock, the function reads activeSingularities[_singularity] which now contains default zero values after the deletion. Consequently the unlock logic cannot locate the original lock position, the transfer call is never executed, and the user’s shares remain permanently locked in the contract. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful UnregisterSingularity event, but attempts to withdraw result in no token movement, balances appearing unchanged, or a silent failure. The impact is that funds become inaccessible, violating the protocol’s accounting guarantees that deposited assets can always be withdrawn. The issue occurs whenever the owner unregisters a singularity while any deposits exist, which can happen in normal rescue scenarios or through malicious misuse of the owner privilege. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the state‑cleanup logic and noticed the absence of a guard on totalDeposited. The bug is subtle because the function emits an event that suggests successful cleanup, and the contract does not revert or throw an error, making the loss of withdrawability easy to overlook. The vulnerability belongs to the class of improper state cleanup or invariant violation bugs, where a contract removes critical bookkeeping data without ensuring that dependent operations remain valid. To remediate, the unregister function should enforce that activeSingularities[singularity].totalDeposited is zero (or otherwise ensure that no locked positions exist) before deleting the pool data, thereby preserving the ability for users to unlock and retrieve their tokens and maintaining the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: `TapiocaOptionBroker.participate
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the participate function of the option broker contract where the wrapper used to transfer an ERC721 token, pearlmit.transferFromERC721, is called with msg.sender as the owner argument. The ERC721 transfer routine internally checks that the supplied owner address matches the actual owner of the token (via ERC721.ownerOf). Because msg.sender may be an approved operator rather than the true owner, the ownership check fails and the transfer reverts, causing the whole participate call to abort. This bug belongs to the class of incorrect parameter usage leading to an authorization denial‑of‑service condition. It can be exploited simply by any user who has been granted approval to manage a token but is not the token’s recorded owner; such a user attempts to call participate, the contract attempts the transfer with the wrong owner, the require statement in the ERC721 implementation fails, and the transaction reverts with a TransferFailed error. The impact is that legitimate participants are unable to lock their NFT positions, resulting in a user‑facing symptom where the transaction reverts, no new option tokens are minted, and balances appear unchanged – users expect their participation to succeed but receive nothing. The condition occurs whenever the participate function reaches the transfer step, regardless of the contract’s paused state, and affects any role that relies on approved operators, namely regular users and potentially the protocol’s front‑end that assumes successful participation. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the token transfer logic and noticing the mismatch between the approved operator and the required owner parameter. It may be hard to notice because the revert message is generic (TransferFailed) and the approval check earlier in the function passes, giving the impression that the call should succeed. The correct fix is to supply the actual token owner to the wrapper, for example by calling tOLP.ownerOf(_tOLPTokenID) as the first argument, or by using the standard ERC721.transferFrom method which internally handles approved operators. By aligning the owner argument with the token’s true owner, the transfer succeeds, the participation proceeds, and the protocol’s business logic – locking a position and issuing option tokens – is restored, preserving the expected accounting invariants and preventing funds from being unintentionally locked or lost.

title: Adding reward tokens to `twTap` could cause pending cross-chain claim rewards msg to be stuck
description:
```solidity
if (
    (claimedAmount_.length - 1) // Remove 1 because the first index doesn't count.
        != claimTwTapRewardsMsg_.sendParam.length
) {
    revert
```
The process of cross-chain claim is as follows: The B chain is the main chain, which the `twTap` is deployed. And the user is on the chain A.

1. The user calls `TapOFT.sendPacket` with `MSG_CLAIM_REWARDS` message on the chain A.
2. The LZ replays the message on the chain B, which will call the `TapTokenReceiver._claimTwpTapRewardsReceiver` function.
3. `TapTokenReceiver._claimTwpTapRewardsReceiver` function will send every reward token to the chain A by LZ `TapTokenSender(rewardToken_).sendPacket`.
poc: The issue is that, if after step 1 the LZ message sent, a new reward token is added to the `twTAP` on the chain B, then step 2 will be revert in the `TapTokenReceiver._claimTwpTapRewardsReceiver` function. So this message will be stuck in the LZ indefinitely.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a cross‑chain reward‑claiming logic error that can cause a pending LayerZero (LZ) message to revert and become permanently stuck. The contract on the destination chain (chain B) checks that the length of the claimed amount array, minus one for a placeholder index, exactly matches the length of the send‑parameter array contained in the incoming claim message. This strict equality assumption is based on the set of reward tokens being static. If a new reward token is added to the twTap contract on chain B after the user has already submitted a claim request from chain A, the stored token list grows. When the LZ relayer delivers the message and the receiver function _claimTwpTapRewardsReceiver executes, the length check fails because claimTwTapRewardsMsg_.sendParam now has a different size than claimedAmount_.length‑1. The function reverts, causing the LZ packet to be rejected and left in the outbound queue indefinitely.
