bug_full: The vulnerability is an incompatibility between the PendlePowerManager contract and the latest PendleRouterV3 implementation. The manager contract was written against an older version of the Pendle router where the functions addLiquiditySingleSy and removeLiquiditySingleSy accepted five parameters and did not require a limit argument. In PendleRouterV3 the function signatures were changed to include an additional LimitOrderData parameter, which changes the function selector. Because the manager continues to call the old selector, the router cannot find a matching function and reverts with the error RouterInvalidAction. This mismatch is the root cause: a breaking change in the external contract interface that was not reflected in the dependent contract. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; any user attempting to open a farm position (which triggers addLiquiditySingleSy) or close a position (which triggers removeLiquiditySingleSy) will cause the transaction to revert. The impact is that legitimate users are unable to deposit or withdraw liquidity through the power farm, leading to a denial‑of‑service situation where funds appear to be locked because the transaction fails before any state change. From the user’s perspective the UI will show a failed transaction, often with a generic revert message, and the expected balance update (e.g., receipt of LP tokens or refund of underlying assets) never occurs. The issue manifests whenever the contract interacts with the router on any supported chain, i.e., under normal operation of the lending protocol. It affects all participants of the protocol who rely on the power farm feature, including borrowers, lenders, and the protocol’s revenue model. The problem was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors executed unit tests against both the old router address and the V3 router address; the test against V3 consistently reverted, revealing the selector mismatch. The bug can be hard to notice because the Solidity compiler does not flag mismatched external calls, and the revert only occurs at runtime when the router is called, which may be mistaken for a generic business‑logic error. The vulnerability belongs to the class of interface‑incompatibility or breaking‑change bugs caused by external contract upgrades without corresponding updates in dependent contracts. To remediate, the manager should be updated to use the new function signatures, supplying a valid LimitOrderData struct (or a zero‑filled placeholder if limits are not needed), and optionally include a version check to select the appropriate selector for older routers. Alternatively, the protocol could restrict itself to a single router version and deprecate support for the older interface, ensuring that all calls match the router’s ABI. This fix restores correct liquidity addition and removal, allowing users to open and close positions without unexpected reverts, and aligns the contract with the current Pendle router specification.

title: `PendlePowerFarmToken:: totalLpAssetsToDistribute` may lead to temporary DOS due to price growth check being skipped during deposit
description: Random actors, malicious or not, can DOS the Pendle `PowerFarm` vault by sending rewards to it through `PendlePowerFarmToken::addCompoundRewards()` or `PendlePowerFarmController::exchangeRewardsForCompoundingWithIncentive()`. This results in all users being unable to access their positions or open new ones for a set amount of time imposed by `PendlePowerFarmToken::_validateSharePriceGrowth()`.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a temporary denial‑of‑service condition in the Pendle PowerFarm vault that arises from a mismatch between reward addition and share‑price validation. The vault tracks user positions with a share price that is allowed to grow only at a rate proportional to elapsed time, enforced by a private function that reverts when the current share price exceeds a calculated maximum. When an actor calls the function that adds compound rewards, the contract increases the total assets to be distributed but does not immediately mint corresponding shares or update the share price before the validation step that runs after the function body. As a result the newly added rewards are invisible to the share‑price calculation, causing the share price to appear to have jumped beyond the permitted growth limit. Subsequent calls that rely on the same validation modifier – including deposits, withdrawals and manual sync – all revert with an InvalidSharePriceGrowth error until enough time passes for the maximum allowed price to catch up. This means users see their transactions fail, balances remain unchanged, and they cannot open new positions or withdraw existing ones, effectively locking funds in the vault for weeks. The issue can be triggered by any address that can call the reward‑addition function, even without malicious intent, because the function does not restrict the amount of rewards that can be added. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit where a test case demonstrated that after a large reward deposit, deposits and withdrawals reverted for up to eight weeks. The problem is subtle because the reward‑addition function appears benign and the share‑price check is hidden inside a modifier that executes after the function body, making it easy to overlook that the pending rewards are not accounted for in the price calculation. The vulnerability belongs to the class of share‑price growth validation bypasses that lead to temporary DOS in tokenized vaults that separate asset accounting from share accounting. To remediate, the contract should convert incoming rewards into shares at the moment they are added, or move the share‑price validation to occur after the share price has been updated, ensuring that the growth check reflects the true state of the vault and preventing the revert condition from being triggered unintentionally.

title: Incorrect calculation of lending shares in `_withdrawOrAllocateSharesLiquidation` can lead to revert and failure to liquidate
description:
When liquidating a user, `_withdrawOrAllocateSharesLiquidation()` can be called which checks if a pool is large enough to pay out the liquidator, and if not, then the liquidator is allocated shares that can be used to withdraw at a later time when the pool is large enough. There are two scenarios in which the pool will not be large enough to pay out the liquidator:

1. The obvious scenario where the pool simply doesn’t contain enough tokens to cover the withdraw amount.
2. So many tokens are borrowed out of the pool that there isn’t enough available to pay out the liquidator.

Note: If there are some tokens available but not enough to cover the entire withdraw amount, then those tokens are transferred, dropping the total pool to `0`, and the rest are allocated as shares.

However, if these scenarios were ever to arise, the `_withdrawOrAllocateSharesLiquidation()` function would not work as expected. This is due to how it calculates the lending shares (`totalPoolInShares`) of the total pool:
When liquidating, it will calculate the `totalPoolInShares` like this (with amount being the total pool):
```solidity
lendingShares = (totalDepositShares * amount) / pseudoTotalPool - 1;
```
However, calculating the lending shares this way will cause the `_compareSharePrices()` to revert on the `syncPool` modifier. Specifically the check on
```solidity
_validateParameter(
    _lendSharePriceBefore,
    lendSharePriceAfter
);
```
This is because `_maxSharePrice` is passed in as false to `calculateLendingShares()`, which subtracts one.
```solidity
uint256 totalPoolInShares = calculateLendingShares(
            {
                _poolToken: _poolToken,
                _amount: totalPoolToken,
                _maxSharePrice: false
            }
        );
```
However, because we are withdrawing, it should be set to true so that it adds one. In all other areas where `calculateLendingShares()` is being used, the functions that focus on withdrawing have `_maxSharePrice: true` and the depositing functions have `_maxSharePrice: false`:
[`withdrawOnBehalfExactAmount` on `WiseLending.sol`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-wise-lending/blob/79186b243d8553e66358c05497e5ccfd9488b5e2/contracts/WiseLending.sol#L874).
[`_preparationsWithdraw` on `MainHelper.sol`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-wise-lending/blob/79186b243d8553e66358c05497e5ccfd9488b5e2/contracts/MainHelper.sol#L154).
[`_handleDeposit` on `WiseCore.sol`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-wise-lending/blob/79186b243d8553e66358c05497e5ccfd9488b5e2/contracts/WiseCore.sol#L119).
When `_maxSharePrice` is set to true, the `_validateParameter()` check will pass.

Even if the `_validateParameter()` check did not exist, if `_maxSharePrice` is left as-is (set to false), any subsequent liquidations through `_withdrawOrAllocateSharesLiquidation()` would revert with panic due to an underflow. This is because (as stated above), liquidating when the pool is not large enough to pay out the liquidator will drop the total pool to `0` and issue the remainder as shares. Therefore, any subsequent calls to liquidate when the total pool is `0` will underflow:
```solidity
//amount is totalPoolToken which in this scenario = 0;
shares = amount * totalDepositShares / pseudoTotalPool - 1
```
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect calculation of lending shares during the liquidation path of the WiseLending protocol. When a liquidator attempts to withdraw or allocate shares because the pool does not contain enough tokens to cover the full repayment, the internal function `_withdrawOrAllocateSharesLiquidation` calls `calculateLendingShares` with the flag `_maxSharePrice` set to false. This flag causes the formula `lendingShares = (totalDepositShares * amount) / pseudoTotalPool - 1` to subtract one from the computed share amount. In normal withdrawal code the flag is set to true, which adds one and ensures the share‑price validation in `_compareSharePrices` passes. With the flag false, the validation `_validateParameter(_lendSharePriceBefore, lendSharePriceAfter)` fails, causing the transaction to revert. Even if the validation were removed, the subtraction can produce an under‑flow when the pool balance has been reduced to zero after a partial payout, because the calculation then attempts to subtract one from a zero value. The bug is triggered only in edge cases where the pool is exhausted or heavily borrowed, making it easy to miss during routine testing. From a user perspective the liquidator expects to receive compensation in the form of shares, but the call reverts and no shares are issued, effectively leaving the liquidator with no reward and potentially locking funds in the protocol. Borrowers and the overall protocol are also affected because failed liquidations prevent the system from recovering bad debt, undermining the accounting guarantees of the lending pool. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a Foundry test that simulates a mock pool liquidation failed. The root cause is the misuse of the `_maxSharePrice` flag in the share‑price calculation, a classic example of an off‑by‑one error in financial accounting logic. The recommended fix is to change the flag to true for the liquidation withdrawal path, aligning the calculation with other withdrawal functions and preventing the under‑flow and validation revert. This correction restores the intended behavior where the liquidator receives newly minted shares when the pool cannot pay out immediately, preserving the protocol’s economic model and preventing unexpected transaction failures.

title: Current heartbeat implementation may lead to a prolonged DoS for Chainlink Oracles
description: Currently, if there are 50 fast updates followed by no updates, a Chainlink Oracle will be considered dead, even though it’s normal behavior. Chainlink Oracles update either after some time has passed or upon a price change.
bug_full: An availability check in the OracleHelper contract treats a Chainlink price feed as dead when the internal counter records fifty consecutive fast updates followed by a period with no updates. Chainlink feeds are designed to emit updates only when the price changes or after a configurable time interval; therefore a normal situation where the price remains stable for many hours can trigger the dead‑oracle flag. The root cause is a heartbeat implementation that relies on the number of recent updates rather than on the native Chainlink heartbeat or timestamp, and the recalibrate function can be invoked by any address, allowing an attacker to repeatedly force the dead‑oracle state. An attacker can call recalibrate after a sequence of legitimate updates, causing the contract to mark the feed as dead and subsequently reject price queries. When the feed is considered dead, the lending protocol stops accepting collateral valuations, leading to loan creation failures, liquidation delays, or complete denial of service for users trying to interact with the protocol. This condition occurs after a sequence of fast price changes (up to fifty) followed by a period of price stability, which is a common market scenario. All participants that rely on the oracle – borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself – are affected because price information becomes unavailable. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena using a forked mainnet test that simulated a block range with no updates, revealing that the dead‑oracle detection returned true even though the feed was operational. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit errors; instead it silently reports the oracle as dead, making it hard to notice until price‑dependent functions stop working. The proper fix is to replace the custom heartbeat logic with Chainlink’s native heartbeat mechanism, and to restrict access to the recalibrate function so that only authorized entities can trigger it, preventing accidental or malicious DoS. In generic terms, this is a false‑positive availability detection flaw in an oracle integration, where an incorrect liveness check leads to a denial‑of‑service condition.

title: Precision loss in the calculation of the fee amounts and fee shares inside the `_preparePool` function of the `MainHelper` contract
description: Low fee amounts and fee shares are calculated in the preparation part due to the precision loss.
poc:
Solidity rounds down the result of an integer division, and because of that, it is always recommended to multiply before dividing to avoid that precision loss. In the case of a prior division over multiplication, the final result may face serious precision loss as the first answer would face truncated precision and then multiplied to another integer.

The problem arises in the pool’s preparation part before applying the LASA algorithm. After cleaning up the pool, the next step is to update the pseudo amounts and adding the corresponding fee shares of that pool.

If we look deeply at the function `_updatePseudoTotalAmounts()` we can see the fee shares calculation procedure is presented as:
```solidity
uint256 amountInterest = bareIncrease
    / PRECISION_FACTOR_YEAR;

uint256 feeAmount = amountInterest
    * globalPoolData[_poolToken].poolFee
    / PRECISION_FACTOR_E18;
```
We can see there is a hidden division before a multiplication that makes round down the whole expression. This is bad as the precision loss can be significant, which leads to the pool printing less `feeAmount` than actual.

Also, it is better to mention that some protocols implement this method to have an integer part of the division (usually in time-related situations). But we can clearly see that this pattern is used in the calculation of `feeAmount` at which the precision matters. Furthermore, the mentioned error will escalate, especially when the `bareIncrease` is bigger but close to the `PRECISION_FACTOR_YEAR` amount. The precision loss becomes more serious at lower discrepancies (such as `1.2 ~ 2` magnitudes of `PRECISION_FACTOR_YEAR`).

As for the Proof of Concept part, we can check this behavior precisely. You can run this code to see the difference between the results:
```solidity
function test_precissionLoss() public {

    uint x = (PRECISION_FACTOR_YEAR * 3)/ 2; // This number represents the `bareIncrease`
    uint256 poolFee = 789600000000000000000000; // This number represents the `poolFee`

    uint256 amountInterest = x
        / PRECISION_FACTOR_YEAR;

    uint256 feeAmount1 = amountInterest
        * poolFee
        / PRECISION_FACTOR_E18;

    uint256 feeAmount2 = (x * poolFee) / (PRECISION_FACTOR_YEAR * PRECISION_FACTOR_E18);
    
    console.log("Current Implementation ", feeAmount1);
    console.log("Actual Implementation ", feeAmount2);
}
```
The result would be: (for 1.5 of `PRECISION_FACTOR_YEAR`):
```
Current Implementation  789600
Actual Implementation  1184400
```
Thus, we can see that the actual implementation produces less fee amount than the precise method. This test shows a big difference between the two calculated fee amounts in the LASA algorithm.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision‑loss arithmetic bug that occurs in the pool preparation logic of the MainHelper contract, specifically inside the _preparePool routine when the function _updatePseudoTotalAmounts calculates fee amounts. The code first divides the raw increase (bareIncrease) by a yearly precision constant, producing amountInterest, and then multiplies amountInterest by the pool fee before dividing by a second precision constant. Because Solidity uses integer arithmetic, the initial division truncates any fractional part, and the subsequent multiplication cannot recover the lost precision. This ordering of division before multiplication therefore yields a feeAmount that is systematically lower than the mathematically correct value. The bug can be exploited by submitting transactions where bareIncrease is close to the precision factor, causing the intermediate division to round down to zero or a very small integer, which in turn reduces the recorded feeAmount. As a result, the protocol under‑pays fees, leading to revenue loss for fee recipients and inaccurate accounting for liquidity providers. The issue manifests when the pool is being prepared before the LASA algorithm runs, and it affects any user or contract that relies on the fee calculation for rewards, refunds, or profit sharing. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by manually reviewing the arithmetic expressions and confirming the effect with a proof‑of‑concept test that compared the current implementation with a corrected version that multiplies before dividing. The bug is hard to notice because the numbers appear plausible and the discrepancy only becomes evident with specific input ranges where the division truncates a non‑zero remainder; typical UI displays simply show a smaller fee balance without indicating the underlying rounding error. The class of bug is a rounding/precision loss error caused by improper ordering of integer division and multiplication. To fix the issue, the calculation should be reordered so that the multiplication with the pool fee is performed before any division, for example feeAmount = bareIncrease * poolFee / (PRECISION_FACTOR_E18 * PRECISION_FACTOR_YEAR), or by using a higher‑precision arithmetic library. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that expected fee rewards or refunds are lower than anticipated, sometimes appearing as zero when the user expects a positive amount, violating the business logic that fees are proportional to the increase in pool value.

title: A user can lose more value than he specifies in the spread when he enters a `PowerFarm`
poc:
1. A user enters the market with `$1000` of WBTC and specifies a spread of 105%.
2. At the end of the transaction the comparison is done against `$950`. So the actual value he gets can be between `~$904.76` and `$950` and the transaction would pass.
3. The user may lose between `$0` and `$45.24` (`950 - 904.76`).
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect handling of the user‑specified spread in the PowerFarm leverage logic, which can cause a user to receive less value than the minimum guaranteed by the spread. The root cause is that the contract applies the allowed spread to the deposit amount during the UniswapV3 swap on Arbitrum and then later compares the post‑transaction ETH value against a baseline that has already been reduced by the same spread. Consequently, the comparison in the exit routine uses ethValueBefore that reflects the minimum allowed value rather than the actual initial deposit, while ethValueAfter is scaled by the spread a second time. An attacker (or any user) can exploit this by simply entering a position with a spread such as 105% and a $1000 deposit; the contract will accept a final value as low as roughly $904.76, allowing the user to lose up to $45.24 even though the spread was intended to protect against losses below $950. The impact is a reduction of user funds beyond the promised protection, effectively breaking the accounting assumption that the spread limits loss on both entry and exit. The bug manifests when a user enters or exits a PowerFarm on Arbitrum, because the code path that performs the token‑to‑ETH conversion applies the reverseAllowedSpread and then re‑applies the allowed spread during the final value check. Users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself are affected because the financial guarantees of the farm are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the mismatch between the intended spread logic and the actual implementation, and it is subtle because the transaction still succeeds and the loss appears as a normal market variation rather than an explicit error. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit a warning when the final value is lower than the true expected minimum, and the revert only triggers when the post‑transaction value falls below the already‑reduced baseline. The proper fix is to store the original deposit amount before any spread adjustment and use that unmodified value to compute ethValueBefore, while applying the spread only to the final comparison, thereby ensuring that the minimum protected value is correctly enforced. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of incorrect financial constraint enforcement, where protective parameters are applied inconsistently, leading to unintended fund loss.

title: User’s attempt to deposit & withdraw reverts due to the calculation style inside `_calculateShares
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one rounding error inside the internal function that converts a value into share units (_calculateShares). The function deliberately subtracts one unit when rounding down in favour of the protocol. When the pool’s pseudo total amount and the total deposit shares become small – typically when they fall below one ether – the subtraction causes the computed lend share price to be marginally higher than the protocol‑defined maximum (1e18 wei). The share‑price validation routine (_compareSharePrices) checks that the new lend share price does not exceed the current maximum and that the borrow share price does not decrease. Because the rounded‑down calculation produces a lend share price of 1e18 + 1, the validation fails and the transaction reverts. This manifests during normal user actions such as depositing additional collateral after an initial deposit or withdrawing an amount that would leave the pool balance just under the threshold. Users experience a revert with no obvious error message, see their transaction fail, and may be unable to add collateral to avoid liquidation or withdraw their full balance, leading to potential loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit where a series of deposit and withdraw tests with varying ether amounts consistently triggered reverts for specific value combinations. It is hard to notice because it only appears for certain edge‑case amounts and the share‑price discrepancy is a single wei, which is not visible in typical UI displays. The bug belongs to the class of rounding‑induced arithmetic errors that break invariant checks in financial smart contracts. To fix the problem the rounding adjustment should be removed or the pseudo total pool variable should be kept in sync with total deposit shares, ensuring that the computed share price never exceeds the allowed maximum. In conceptual terms the solution is to eliminate the off‑by‑one bias or adjust the validation thresholds so that the invariant holds for all possible pool states.

title: M-05 | Borrowers Exposed To Gas Grieﬁng
description: In the initializeNewLoan function a promissoryNote is minted to the lender using the INFTYERC721V1.mint function, which relies on safeMint. As a result if the lender address is home to a contract, the onERC721Received function will be invoked at that address. The contract at the lender address may have malicious logic implemented for the onERC721Received function to waste the borrower’s gas, causing a loss of native tokens for the user.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates in the loan initialization routine where a promissory note NFT is minted to the lender using the ERC721 safeMint function. SafeMint follows the ERC721 standard by invoking the onERC721Received callback on the recipient address if the recipient is a contract. When the lender address is a contract, the callback is executed in the context of the borrower’s transaction. A malicious lender contract can implement onERC721Received with logic that deliberately consumes excessive gas or reverts, causing the borrower’s transaction to either fail or incur a much higher gas cost than expected. This situation is known as gas griefing: the borrower loses native tokens (gas) without receiving any benefit, and the loan creation may not complete. The issue occurs only when the lender is a contract, not when it is an externally owned account, and it is triggered during the initializeNewLoan function. The affected parties are borrowers who initiate loans and the protocol that relies on successful loan creation. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined the minting flow and recognized the external call introduced by safeMint as a potential attack surface. Because safeMint is a common pattern, developers may overlook the fact that the callback can be controlled by an adversary, making the bug subtle and hard to detect through simple testing. To remediate, the contract should replace safeMint with the internal _mint function, which does not perform an external call, or otherwise restrict lenders to EOAs or enforce a gas stipend on the callback. Conceptually, the fix removes the untrusted external invocation that enables the borrower to be forced to pay arbitrary gas, thereby aligning the implementation with the intended business logic that minting a promissory note should not expose the borrower to additional costs. From a user perspective, a borrower may see a transaction that appears to create a loan but either reverts with an out‑of‑gas error or succeeds with an unexpectedly high gas fee, leading to the perception that “my funds disappeared” or “the loan creation cost way too much”. The expectation that minting an NFT is a cheap, internal operation is violated, resulting in a denial‑of‑service‑like effect on the loan workflow.

title: M-06 | Block Stuﬃng Risk
description: If the block.timestamp is a few seconds before the beginning of a new hour and User A sends a tx to pay back their full loan amount, the lender may stuff blocks on the network until the next hour begins. As a result, the borrowers debt to be repaid will increase and the borrowers tx will no longer close the loan. Immediately the borrower will have to pay an additional period of interest. More insidiously, the borrower may not realize that the loan remains open and as a result may be unexpectedly liquidated.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a time‑dependency flaw in the loan repayment logic that allows a lender or a miner to increase the borrower’s outstanding debt by manipulating the block.timestamp around an hourly boundary. The contract calculates the amount of interest owed based on the current hour and expects the borrower to send a transaction that exactly matches the debt at that moment. When a borrower submits a repayment transaction a few seconds before the start of a new hour, an attacker can “stuff” the chain with a rapid succession of blocks whose timestamps advance into the next hour, which is permitted within the protocol’s timestamp tolerance. Because the contract re‑evaluates the debt after the block containing the repayment is mined, the interest for the new hour is added, making the previously sufficient repayment amount insufficient. Consequently the loan remains open, the borrower is charged an additional period of interest, and the protocol may automatically liquidate the position because the required collateral no longer covers the increased debt. This situation is hard to notice because the borrower sees a successful transaction that appears to have repaid the full amount, yet later observes unexpected interest accrual or a liquidation event. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between block.timestamp and repayment amount calculations. It belongs to the class of “block‑timestamp manipulation” or “time‑window” bugs, where business logic assumes a monotonic, predictable time source that can be subtly shifted by miners. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful repayment, but the balance later drops to zero or a liquidation warning appears, violating the expectation that paying the full amount closes the loan. To remediate the problem the contract should decouple repayment amount from the exact timestamp by allowing callers to indicate a desire to repay the full outstanding debt, letting the contract compute the required amount internally, or by using a more robust time measurement such as block numbers or cumulative interest that cannot be altered by a single block’s timestamp. This change ensures that the repayment transaction will close the loan regardless of when the block is mined, eliminating the block‑stuffing attack surface.

title: M-01 | Risk Of Function Selector And Storage Collision
description: The BlastOnboarding contract is itself a proxy, however it has several declared storage variables and functions. As a result the contract is prone to storage and function selector collision.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a storage and function selector collision in the BlastOnboarding contract, which acts as a proxy but also declares its own state variables and functions. Because a proxy is expected to forward calls to an implementation contract and keep only a minimal set of storage slots, any additional variables in the proxy occupy slots that the implementation also expects to use. Likewise, if the proxy defines functions whose 4‑byte selectors match those of functions in the implementation, the proxy will intercept calls that were meant for the implementation. An attacker can exploit this by invoking a function that appears to belong to the logic contract; the proxy’s own version will be executed, potentially reading or writing to a storage slot that controls critical parameters such as admin address or fund balances. This can lead to unauthorized upgrades, loss of control over the contract, or misdirection of funds. The issue manifests when a bootstrapper (logic) contract is deployed behind the BlastOnboarding proxy and its selector set overlaps with the proxy’s functions, or when the implementation expects storage slots that the proxy has already occupied. All participants that rely on the onboarding process – the protocol, its users, and any funds held during the onboarding phase – are at risk. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the proxy’s storage layout and function signatures with those of typical implementation contracts and noticed the mismatch. Because the proxy still appears functional and the collisions do not raise compile‑time errors, the bug can remain hidden until a specific function call triggers the wrong code path. The recommended remediation is to redesign the proxy so that it contains only the essential storage (e.g., implementation address) using reserved or unstructured slots, and to ensure that no function in the proxy shares a selector with any function in the implementation. A systematic verification of selector uniqueness and storage slot allocation should be performed before any future bootstrapper is linked to the proxy.

title: M-02 | Predictable MagicLP Salt
description: The salt used to deploy the new MagicLP contract in the factory is based upon replicable values that any malicious user may pass in. This way a malicious actor may observe two transactions in the mempool and intentionally get their transaction ordered between them. Transaction 1: Create pool at address A Transaction 2: Send additional funds to pool at address A The attacker may create the exact same pool at address A and end up with the funds in their pool. Currently there is no high impact risk as the owner of the clone does not have any special privileges, but this may be unexpected for the user creating the pool.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a predictable address generation flaw in the MagicLP factory contract. The factory creates new pool contracts using the CREATE2 opcode with a salt that is derived solely from values supplied by the caller, such as the token pair or other deterministic parameters. Because the salt does not incorporate any unpredictable element like the caller’s address, an attacker can calculate in advance the exact address at which a legitimate pool will be deployed. When a user submits a transaction to create a pool, the attacker can monitor the mempool, see the pending creation request, and submit a competing transaction that uses the same salt before the legitimate one is mined. By doing so, the attacker’s transaction creates a clone at the same deterministic address, effectively “stealing” the address that the user expects. After the attacker’s pool exists at that address, the second transaction – which the user intended to fund their own pool – sends ether or tokens to the address that now belongs to the attacker’s contract. From the user’s perspective the address shown in the UI matches the expected pool address, but the funds are received by an attacker‑controlled contract, leading to missing balances, zero refunds, or funds that appear to disappear. The issue occurs whenever the factory relies on a fully predictable salt and the attacker can front‑run the creation transaction, which is feasible in public mempools where transaction ordering can be influenced. The affected parties are any user who creates a new MagicLP pool and any protocol that relies on the integrity of pool ownership, because the unexpected redirection of funds can erode trust. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the factory’s address‑derivation logic and identified that the salt does not include msg.sender, making it trivially reproducible. The problem is subtle because the deployed address looks correct and the contract does not expose privileged functions, so the misdirection of funds may not be immediately obvious. To remediate the issue, the factory should incorporate an unpredictable component into the CREATE2 salt, such as the caller’s address, a per‑user nonce, or a hash of the transaction hash, ensuring that only the intended creator can pre‑compute the pool address. This change prevents an attacker from being able to pre‑emptively deploy a contract at the same address and protects users from losing funds due to address hijacking.

title: M-03 | previewAddLiquidity Disagrees With _adjustLiquidity
description: In the _adjustAddLiquidity function the baseAdjustedInAmount and quoteAdjustedInAmount are adjusted without considering tokens that may be sitting in the MagicLP contract and unaccounted for in the reserves. Therefore the result from _adjustAddLiquidity contradicts the result retrieved from previewAddLiquidity when there are excess tokens sitting in the MagicLP contract as the previewAddLiquidity function accounts for the current token balance of the lp contract. As a result in some cases the resulting baseAdjustedInAmount and quoteAdjustedInAmount users would expect to pay using the previewAddLiquidity function will not line up with the baseAdjustedInAmount and quoteAdjustedInAmount that are paid in actuality.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mismatch between the previewAddLiquidity helper and the internal _adjustAddLiquidity routine used when a user adds liquidity to the MagicLP pool. The previewAddLiquidity function reads the current token balances of the pool contract and includes any tokens that are sitting in the contract but are not reflected in the recorded reserves. In contrast, _adjustAddLiquidity computes the baseAdjustedInAmount and quoteAdjustedInAmount based solely on the stored reserve values, ignoring any excess tokens that may have been transferred to the pool outside of the normal add‑liquidity flow. Because of this discrepancy, the amounts shown to the user during the preview step – the amounts the user expects to provide – can differ from the amounts that the contract actually requires and deducts when the transaction is executed. The issue manifests when stray tokens accumulate in the pool contract, for example due to direct transfers, failed withdrawals, or previous bugs that left residual balances. Under those conditions a user may see a preview indicating that a certain amount of base and quote tokens will be needed, but the transaction will either pull a larger amount, reject the transaction, or leave the user with an unexpected residual balance. The impact is that users can lose funds, experience unexpected slippage, or be unable to add liquidity as intended, breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the preview calculation with the actual execution path and noticed inconsistent results when the pool held extra tokens. It can be hard to notice because the UI typically shows only the preview values and the contract does not emit explicit warnings about hidden balances; the discrepancy only appears in edge cases where the pool’s token balance diverges from its recorded reserves. To remediate, the _adjustAddLiquidity logic should be updated to incorporate the actual token balances of the pool, or the preview function should be aligned to use the same reserve‑only view, ensuring both paths calculate adjusted amounts from the same source of truth. This class of bug falls under accounting mismatches and state‑inconsistency errors, where on‑chain accounting diverges from off‑chain or helper‑function expectations, leading to incorrect fund handling and broken business logic.

title: M-04 | Blast Point Remunerations May Be Gamed
description: In the BlastOnboarding contract users may deposit their token balances and will be remunerated with the points they would have otherwise received if they didn't deposit into the contract. These point remunerations will occur off-chain at undisclosed times. However if a user is able to predict, recognize a pattern, or guess within a reasonable range when the distributions will occur they could deposit before the distribution and withdraw after the distribution to receive more Blast Points than they otherwise would have by simply depositing into the BlastOnboarding contract for the entire period or simply holding the native yield tokens for the entire period. The same may occur with a malicious Liquidity Provider for the MagicLP contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the BlastOnboarding contract’s off‑chain Blast Point remuneration mechanism. Users can deposit their token balances into the contract and are promised points that they would have earned had they not deposited. The contract does not enforce any lock‑up period or on‑chain verification of the holding duration, and the point distributions are performed off‑chain at times that are not disclosed on the blockchain. Because the distribution schedule can be observed, inferred from past patterns, or guessed within a reasonable window, an attacker can time a deposit to occur shortly before a distribution and then withdraw immediately after the distribution is executed. By doing so the attacker receives the points that would have been awarded for the short deposit period in addition to the points they would have earned by simply holding the tokens for the whole period, effectively double‑counting the reward. This timing manipulation can be repeated for each distribution cycle, inflating the attacker’s Blast Point balance far beyond the intended amount. The impact is a distortion of the reward economics: the attacker gains an unfair advantage, the total supply of Blast Points may be inflated, and other honest participants receive a smaller share of the reward pool. The issue manifests when the off‑chain remuneration occurs and the attacker can predict or approximate its timing; it affects any user of the BlastOnboarding contract as well as malicious liquidity providers interacting with the MagicLP contract, because the same reward logic applies. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the reward calculation relies on an off‑chain event without any on‑chain constraints, making it a classic timing or front‑running attack on off‑chain reward distribution. The problem is subtle because the point allocation is not recorded on‑chain, so normal blockchain analytics do not reveal the manipulation, and the contract’s public interface does not indicate any lock‑up requirement. To remediate, the contract should require that deposited amounts be locked for a minimum period before they become eligible for point remuneration, or the point distribution should be performed on‑chain with a deterministic, verifiable schedule that cannot be guessed. Alternatively, the off‑chain process could be made unpredictable (e.g., using a secure randomness source) and the contract should enforce that only users who have continuously held tokens for the full reward interval receive points. In user‑facing terms, an affected user would see an unexpectedly high Blast Point balance after a short deposit, or notice that other participants’ points appear lower than expected, indicating that the reward system has been gamed. This class of bug is generally referred to as a timing attack on off‑chain reward distribution or a deposit/withdraw manipulation that violates the intended accounting assumptions of the protocol.

title: M-05 | Disabled Native Yield Tokens Cause Loss Of Funds
description: If the owner does not want to enable native yield for a token with function setTokenEnabled, that token will have the default mode which is AUTOMATIC for WETH and USDB. When a token is in AUTOMATIC mode, the balance of the token in the contract increases as yield is gained. However, the DegenBox contract is unable to support rebasing tokens: /// @notice The BentoBox is a vault for tokens. The stored tokens can be ﬂash loaned and used in strategies. /// Yield from this will go to the token depositors. /// Rebasing tokens ARE NOT supported and WILL cause loss of funds. /// Any funds transfered directly onto the BentoBox will be lost, use the deposit function instead. As per the comment above, rebasing tokens are not compatible with the DegenBox and will cause loss of funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the DegenBox (also known as BentoBox) vault handles token yield modes. When the contract owner disables native yield for a token using the setTokenEnabled function, the token falls back to the default AUTOMATIC mode for certain assets such as WETH and USDB. AUTOMATIC mode assumes that the token balance inside the vault will increase automatically as the token generates yield. However, DegenBox is not designed to work with rebasing tokens – tokens whose total supply changes on‑chain and therefore alter the apparent balance without an explicit transfer. Because the vault’s internal accounting treats balances as static, a rebasing token that is placed in AUTOMATIC mode causes the recorded balance to diverge from the actual token supply. If a user or a contract sends such a token directly to the DegenBox address instead of using the official deposit function, the vault silently accepts the transfer but cannot correctly track the rebasing adjustments. As a result, the deposited funds become unrecoverable: users see a zero or incorrect balance in the UI, withdrawals fail, and the token amount appears to disappear from the system. This situation can be triggered whenever the owner disables native yield for a token that is not compatible with rebasing, or when any participant mistakenly transfers tokens directly to the vault. The issue is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error; the loss manifests only when a user attempts to interact with the affected balance later, making it hard to detect during normal operation. The root cause is the lack of a safe “VOID” mode that would prevent the vault from accepting rebasing tokens when yield is disabled, combined with the assumption that AUTOMATIC mode is safe for all tokens. To remediate the problem, the protocol should introduce a VOID yield mode that can be set by the owner for tokens that should not accrue automatic yield, enforce that all token transfers go through the deposit function, and add explicit checks that reject rebasing tokens or tokens in AUTOMATIC mode when native yield is disabled. This would align the vault’s accounting model with the token’s behavior and prevent accidental loss of user funds.

title: M-01 | Overlap Between Payment And Default Periods
description: Since the hoursElapsed is rounded down in the getLoanAmountDue function and the loan.duration check uses strictly greater than, loan payments are only disabled an entire hour after the end date of a loan. Therefore during this time a borrower may still pay back their loans and may frontrun the liquidation tx to do so.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one time‑boundary error in the loan repayment logic. The contract calculates the elapsed time in whole hours by rounding down the actual elapsed seconds, and then checks whether the loan has passed its duration with a strict greater‑than comparison (hoursElapsed > loan.duration). Because the rounded value equals the loan duration exactly at the moment the loan reaches its scheduled end, the condition evaluates to false and the contract still permits a repayment. This creates a one‑hour window after the official due date during which a borrower can still submit a payment that would normally be rejected. An attacker can exploit this window by front‑running the liquidation transaction: the borrower observes a pending liquidation, quickly repays the loan within the overlap period, and thereby prevents the liquidation from succeeding. The impact is that lenders may lose the ability to liquidate defaulted positions, potentially leaving the protocol with uncollected debt and undermining the expected penalty mechanisms. The issue manifests only after the loan’s end timestamp, before the next whole‑hour tick, and affects any role that relies on the default detection – primarily borrowers (who can avoid liquidation) and lenders (who may not receive the expected recovery). The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the time‑rounding logic with the default condition and identified the mismatch. It is subtle because the contract uses hour‑level granularity, so tests that only check a few seconds after expiry may not reveal the problem, and the UI may still display the loan as active, giving a false sense of security. To fix the issue, the default check should be changed to a greater‑than‑or‑equal comparison (hoursElapsed >= loan.duration) or the elapsed time calculation should be performed with exact timestamps, eliminating the rounding gap. This class of bug belongs to time‑boundary or off‑by‑one errors that cause payment windows to overlap with default periods, violating the business rule that a loan becomes non‑payable exactly when it is overdue.

title: M-02 | Errant Origination Fee Validation
description: In the setLoanOriginationFee function the _loanOriginationFee basis points value is intended to be capped at a maximum of 10%, however the validation asserts that the _loanOriginationFee is less than 10_000, which represents 100% in basis points.
bug_full: The contract contains a logic error in the function that sets the loan origination fee. The business rule requires the fee to be capped at ten percent of the loan amount, which corresponds to a maximum of 1,000 basis points. However, the implementation validates the supplied fee by asserting that it is less than 10,000 basis points, a limit that actually represents one hundred percent. Because the comparison uses the wrong constant, any fee value up to 9,999 basis points (approximately 99.99%) passes the check. This mistake originates from an off‑by‑order‑of‑magnitude validation, where the intended upper bound was mistakenly multiplied by ten. An attacker who can invoke the fee‑setting function—typically an admin or a compromised privileged account—can therefore set an exorbitant origination fee. When a borrower requests a loan, the contract deducts the configured fee from the disbursed amount; with a fee near 100 % the borrower receives only a tiny fraction of the expected funds, effectively losing the majority of the loan value. From the user’s perspective the UI may display a reasonable percentage (e.g., “10 %”) or simply show the fee amount, but the underlying contract permits a far higher fee, leading to unexpected zero or near‑zero balances after borrowing. The impact is financial loss for borrowers, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential reputational damage. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that compared the documented fee cap with the actual Solidity require statement and identified the mismatched constant. Because the bug resides in a single comparison, it may not be obvious during normal operation unless a fee is deliberately set to an extreme value, making it easy to overlook in testing. The proper remediation is to adjust the validation to enforce that the fee is strictly less than 1,000 basis points (or equal to 1,000 if the policy allows exactly ten percent) and to ensure that any future changes to fee limits are reflected consistently across documentation, UI, and contract checks. Adding comprehensive unit tests that verify the fee cannot exceed ten percent and reviewing access control for the fee‑setting function further mitigates the risk.

title: M-03 | Paused State Leads To Forced Defaults
description: When the owner pauses the NFTYFinanceV1 contract, borrowers cannot repay their loans and therefore may be forced to default and lose their NFT collateral.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a pause‑related access control flaw in the NFTYFinanceV1 contract that prevents borrowers from executing the loan repayment function when the contract owner activates the paused state. The root cause is that the makeLoanPayment function is guarded by the same pause modifier that is intended to halt only non‑essential operations, so when the contract is paused the repayment path is unintentionally blocked. An attacker or even a well‑meaning owner can trigger the pause, after which any borrower with an outstanding loan is unable to submit a payment transaction; the transaction reverts and the loan remains outstanding. Because the protocol’s accounting assumes that borrowers can always repay before the loan term expires, the inability to pay forces the loan into default according to the contract’s logic, which then automatically seizes the NFT collateral that backs the loan. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome – a successful repayment and retention of the NFT – is replaced by a situation where the UI shows the loan balance unchanged, the repayment button is disabled, and eventually the collateral disappears from the user’s wallet. This issue is discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the pause mechanism and core financial functions. It can be hard to notice because pausing is generally regarded as a safety feature, and the contract’s documentation may not highlight that repayment is also paused, leading developers and auditors to assume that only administrative functions are affected. The impact is financial loss for borrowers, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential liability for the protocol operators, as users may be forced to lose valuable NFTs without any chance to settle their debt. The bug belongs to the class of “paused‑state forced default” or “emergency‑stop misuse” vulnerabilities, where an emergency control unintentionally disables critical user‑initiated actions, breaking business logic that relies on continuous availability of payment pathways. To remediate the issue the contract should decouple the pause protection from the repayment function, either by exempting makeLoanPayment from the pause modifier or by introducing a separate pause flag that only affects non‑critical operations, ensuring that borrowers retain the ability to settle their loans even when the protocol is in an emergency state.

title: M-04 | Zero Platform Fee Can DoS New Loans
description: In the setLoanOriginationFee function there is not validation that the _loanOriginationFee is not 0, therefore the platformFee that is taken from new loans can be 0 when the loanOriginationFee is set to 0. Some ERC20 tokens choose to revert upon transferring a 0 amount, however there is no check that the platformFee is nonzero before attempting to transfer this amount to the platformWallet.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation for the platform fee amount in the loan creation flow. When the loanOriginationFee parameter is set to zero, the calculated platformFee for a new loan also becomes zero. The contract then attempts to transfer this zero‑value fee to the platformWallet without checking that the amount is non‑zero. Certain ERC20 token implementations deliberately revert when a transfer of 0 tokens is requested. Because the transfer is executed unconditionally, a zero‑fee loan triggers a revert in the token contract, causing the entire initializeNewLoan transaction to fail. This failure prevents the loan from being recorded, effectively a denial‑of‑service (DoS) against new loan issuance. The issue occurs whenever the platform fee can be configured to zero, either by an administrator or through a governance action, and when the underlying token follows the “revert on zero transfer” rule. Users attempting to borrow see their transaction revert, receive no loan, and may be confused why the operation fails despite providing sufficient collateral. The protocol’s accounting assumptions that a fee will always be collected are violated, breaking the expected flow where the platform receives a non‑zero compensation for each loan. The bug belongs to the class of input‑validation and zero‑value transfer errors, where unchecked parameters lead to unexpected reverts in external token contracts. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the setLoanOriginationFee function and noted the absence of a non‑zero check before the fee transfer. The problem can be subtle because a zero fee may be a legitimate configuration in some business models, and developers might assume that transferring zero tokens is a no‑op. To remediate, the loan initialization code should conditionally execute the fee transfer only when the computed platformFee is greater than zero, or the token interface should be wrapped with a safe‑transfer helper that skips zero‑value calls. This change restores the ability to create loans with a zero fee without causing a revert, eliminating the DoS vector while preserving intended fee logic.

title: M-06 | Lacking LP Validations Allows For Malicious Intent
description: Anyone can create a pool with the same base/quote tokens as well as the same params (i, k) as an 'oﬃcial' MIMSwap pool. An attacker could create such pools to steal liquidity away, or even worse implement such pools with rug pull functions. Since the Router does not validate the lp address, router functions can be used to interact with these malicious LPs. Attackers may interact with router functions intentionally to populate etherscan with transactions to their malicious pool. Users who see this may check the pool and see that the base/quote token and other params are correct, and end up interacting with that LP instead of the oﬃcial one. In fact, there may not even be an oﬃcial lp yet, i.e. attackers frontrun the creation of the LP once they know the address of the base/quote tokens. This often happens when a memecoin is launched with no frontend or oﬃcial site stating the correct lp address.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing validation step in the router contract that allows any address to be used as a liquidity‑pool (LP) target without confirming that the address corresponds to the official pool registered in the factory. Because the router does not check the pools mapping in the factory, an attacker can deploy a malicious LP that uses the same base and quote token pair and identical parameters (i and k) as a legitimate MIMSwap pool. Once the fake pool exists, the attacker can call router functions such as addLiquidity, removeLiquidity, or swap with the malicious LP address. From a user’s perspective the pool appears correct – the token symbols, pair, and parameters match the expected values – so a user may interact with it believing it is the official pool. When the user deposits funds or performs a swap, the malicious contract can execute a rug‑pull or otherwise divert the assets, resulting in the user receiving no tokens, seeing their balance drop to zero, or observing a missing refund. The issue is most likely to be exploited when a new memecoin is launched without an official frontend that publishes the correct LP address, or when an attacker front‑runs the creation of the official pool and registers a fake pool first. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the router’s interaction with LP addresses and noted the absence of any verification against the factory’s registry. The flaw can be hard to notice because the on‑chain data (token addresses, parameters) looks identical to the legitimate pool, and there is no explicit warning in the UI. To remediate, the router should retrieve the expected LP address from the factory’s pools mapping for the given token pair and compare it with the supplied address, rejecting the call if they differ. This validation enforces that only the officially registered pool can be used, preventing malicious pools from being leveraged to steal liquidity or execute rug pulls, and restores confidence that the protocol’s accounting assumptions – that each token pair maps to a single, trusted pool – are upheld.

title: M-07 | Governor Contract Does Not Conﬁgure Blast Points
description: The blast governor contract does not conﬁgure blast points, this will cause the contract to miss out on points that can later be used to receive an airdrop of tokens from blast. “Blast Points are distributed automatically every block to EOAs and smart contracts based on their balance of ETH, WETH, and USDB. Speciﬁcally, EOAs and smart contracts earn Points at a rate of 0.06504987 Points/Block/ETH (around 0.03252493376 Points/second/ETH).” Since the contract is meant to hold eth as it collects yields from other contracts, it will not be able to accrue points based on its eth balance.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a configuration omission in the governor contract that prevents it from registering with the Blast Points system. Blast Points are an on‑chain incentive mechanism that automatically distributes points to externally owned accounts (EOAs) and contracts based on the amount of ETH, WETH, or USDB they hold, at a rate of roughly 0.065 points per block per ETH. The governor contract is designed to hold ETH collected as yield from other contracts, so it should be eligible to earn points that can later be redeemed for an airdropped token allocation. However, because the contract never calls the BlastPoints.configure() function—typically invoked in the constructor—it never registers its balance with the Blast Points protocol. As a result, the contract’s ETH balance is invisible to the points calculation engine, and the contract misses out on accruing any points. This omission is a classic business‑logic or incentive‑misconfiguration bug rather than a direct code‑execution flaw. Exploitation does not involve an attacker manipulating the contract; the impact arises automatically as the protocol operates, leading to a loss of future token rewards that were expected by the protocol’s governance and its participants. The issue manifests whenever the governor contract holds a non‑zero ETH balance, which is the normal operating condition after yield collection. All users, token holders, and the protocol itself are affected because the anticipated airdrop could have been used to fund further development or to reward participants. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s intended functionality with the Blast Points integration documentation. It can be hard to notice because the points are not stored on the contract itself; they are tracked off‑chain by the Blast system, so the contract’s state appears normal while silently missing out on rewards. The proper remediation is to add a call to BlastPoints.configure()—for example, in the constructor—so that the governor contract registers its address and begins earning points in line with its ETH holdings. This aligns the contract with the intended incentive model and restores the expected reward flow, ensuring that the protocol can claim its rightful share of the airdropped tokens.

title: Pool Creation Failure Due to WETH Transfer Compatibility Issue on Some Chains
bug_full: The vulnerability originates in the router contract that creates a liquidity pool for native tokens by wrapping the received ether into a wrapped token (WETH) and then moving that wrapped token to the newly deployed pool. The router calls the ERC20 safeTransferFrom function with the router contract itself as the source address (address(this)) and the pool clone as the destination. On most networks the standard WETH9 implementation contains a special case that skips allowance checks when the source address equals the caller, allowing the transfer to succeed without an explicit approval. However, on several chains such as Blast, Wrapped Arbitrum and Wrapped Fantom the WETH contract does not include this shortcut and follows the generic ERC20 logic, which requires a non‑zero allowance for any transferFrom call. Because the router never sets an allowance for itself, the call reverts with an insufficient‑allowance error. This mismatch causes the createPoolETH function to fail, preventing the pool from being created and causing the transaction to revert. From a user perspective the UI reports a failed pool creation, no pool address is returned, and the ether that was sent is refunded by the revert, leading to confusion and a perception that funds have disappeared. The issue is discovered during a security audit when the team executed a forked test on the Blast network and observed the transferFrom revert. It is hard to notice because the same code works on Ethereum, Optimism, Polygon and BSC where the standard WETH9 contract is deployed, so the problem only appears on less common chains with non‑standard wrapped token contracts. The bug belongs to the class of incompatibility with non‑standard ERC20 implementations, specifically the misuse of transferFrom for a self‑transfer without prior allowance. The correct mitigation is to replace the safeTransferFrom call with a direct safeTransfer (or an equivalent withdraw‑and‑transfer pattern) so that the router does not rely on an allowance bypass that may not exist. By doing so the router can move the wrapped ether to the pool on any chain regardless of the WETH implementation, restoring the intended business logic that a user who supplies native ether receives a newly created pool and corresponding liquidity shares.

title: Tokens yeild can not be set to claimable.
description: The enabling of yeild on rebasing tokens can be permanently DOS-ed.
poc:
Abracadabra uses this signature for the configure function for the rebasing function of WETH and USDB
    
    function configure(YieldMode) external returns (YieldMode);

But the actual signature for this is:
    
    function configure(YieldMode yieldMode) external returns (uint256)

And it returns the balance of caller

So if the balance of contract is above 2, this function becomes unusable and can’t configure the yeild to be claimable.

The following function always fails:

This can be exploited by attacker by donating a very little amount of eth to the magicLP, blastOnBoarding and now the blastOnBoarding can’t make yeild claimable when the following function is invoked.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that prevents a rebasing token from being switched into the claimable yield mode. The root cause is a mismatch between the expected Solidity function signature used by the onboarding contract and the actual signature implemented in the Blast token registry. The onboarding code calls IERC20Rebasing.configure(YieldMode) assuming the function returns a YieldMode enum, but the real implementation returns a uint256 representing the caller’s balance. When the contract’s balance exceeds a small threshold (greater than two wei), the call to configure no longer matches the expected return type and the transaction reverts, leaving the token permanently in a non‑claimable state. An attacker can exploit this by sending a tiny amount of ether to the magicLP or BlastOnboarding contract, raising its balance just enough to trigger the failure. Once the configure call fails, the internal function enableTokenClaimable never succeeds, so the onboarding contract cannot mark the token as supported for claimable yields. From a user’s perspective the UI will show that deposits are disabled, expected refunds or yield claims return zero, and balances appear frozen even though no funds are lost. The issue occurs during deployment or any later attempt to enable claimable mode, and it affects any user trying to deposit or claim yields on the affected token, as well as the protocol’s accounting logic that assumes yields can always be made claimable. The bug was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors compared the function signatures in the Blast codebase with those used in the onboarding contract and observed that a small ETH donation caused the configure call to fail. The problem is subtle because the function compiles and appears to work for zero‑balance contracts, making it easy to miss in basic testing. To remediate, the contract must be updated to use the correct configure signature from the Blast codebase, ensuring the return type matches the implementation, or the logic should be rewritten to avoid relying on the faulty call. After fixing the signature, the token can be set to YieldMode.CLAIMABLE and normal deposit and claim flows resume, restoring the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Miscalculation in addLiquidity of Router results in unauthorized spending of tokens
poc:
1. MagicLP has (500 USDC, 500 DAI) reserves and balances, 100 shares
2. Victim calls addLiquidity for (1000 USDC, 1000 DAI) , min 200 shares
3. Attacker frontrans and donates (1000 USDC, 500 DAI) to the LP
4. addLiquidity() executes:
5. baseInAmount = 1500 + 1000 - 500 = 2000 USDC
6. quoteInAmount = 1000 + 1000 - 500 = 1500 DAI
7. baseIncreaseRatio = 2000 / 500 = 4
8. quoteIncreaseRatio = 1500 / 500 = 3
9. quoteAdjustedInAmount = 1500 DAI
10. baseAdjustedInAmount = 500 * 3 = 1500 USDC

Therefore LP::buyShares() is called with (1500, 1500) for 200 shares instead of (1000, 1000)

User has now put an extra ($500,$500) of unauthorized funds in the contract. They may or may not be aware of it when the TX is executed. Note that funds put in the LP are obviously in risk of impermanent loss alongside any other economic, systemic and security-related risks. This is a simple example to prove the point but could be tweaked for different tokens (more or less volatile), amounts and ratios.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a miscalculation in the router’s addLiquidity function that causes the contract to request more base and quote tokens from the caller than the amounts originally supplied. The root cause is a reversed use of the pool’s token balances and reserves: the code adds the caller‑provided amount to the current token balance and then subtracts the reserve, instead of adding the reserve to the caller amount and subtracting the balance. This inverted formula makes the required input amount increase as the pool’s existing balance grows. An attacker can exploit this by first donating tokens directly to the liquidity pool, inflating the pool’s balance. When a victim subsequently calls addLiquidity, the router computes an inflated baseAdjustedInAmount and quoteAdjustedInAmount, transfers the extra tokens from the victim, and mints the requested shares. The impact is unauthorized spending of the victim’s tokens – the user ends up sending more assets than they intended, even though they receive the expected number of shares, which may appear larger due to the attacker’s donation. The issue occurs only when the pool has a higher balance than its recorded reserve at the moment addLiquidity is executed, a condition that can be created by a malicious donor. It affects any user of the router who adds liquidity after such a donation, and it also appears in the previewAddLiquidity view function, though with lower immediate financial impact. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the adjustment logic and identified the swapped variables. It is hard to notice because the UI typically shows the share amount received, which may even be higher, masking the extra token loss; there is no explicit warning that more tokens were taken. To fix the problem, the formula should be corrected to compute the required amount as reserves plus the caller amount minus the current balance, and an invariant check should be added to ensure the adjusted amounts never exceed the original inputs. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of arithmetic mis‑use and incorrect accounting of token reserves, leading to violations of the core invariant that a contract must not spend user funds without explicit consent. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a transaction that appears to succeed, the share balance increases, but the token balance of the user drops by more than the amount they approved, effectively causing funds to disappear or be taken without clear justification.

title: Loss of assumed functionality of the Onboarding contract in a highly-sensitive area
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the onboarding contract that bootstraps funds for a reward staking pool. After deployment the contract creates a LockingMultiRewards instance, grants it an allowance to transfer the entire pool of LP shares and then transfers ownership to the protocol owner. A function called setStaking allows the owner to replace the staking contract before the onboarding process is marked as ready. The function simply overwrites the internal staking address and emits an event, but it does not reset the ERC20 allowance that was previously granted to the old staking contract, nor does it grant the same allowance to the newly assigned contract. Because the staking contracts rely on this allowance to pull tokens when users claim rewards, the omission means that after the owner swaps the staking address the new contract has no permission to move the bootstrap pool shares. Consequently any claim transaction directed at the new pool reverts due to an insufficient allowance error. Users experience a situation where they attempt to claim rewards and receive nothing, or the transaction fails with a revert, even though the protocol UI indicates that rewards are available. The issue is triggered only when the owner invokes setStaking before the ready flag is set; after ready the function is blocked, but the damage is already done if a migration was attempted. The affected parties include token holders who cannot retrieve their earned rewards, the protocol that loses functional correctness, and the owner who may be unable to complete a legitimate migration. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the contract’s state‑transition logic and noticed that allowance management was not tied to the staking address change. It is subtle because the function appears to perform a harmless address update, and the missing allowance calls are not obvious without tracing token transfer paths. The problem belongs to the class of allowance‑management or token‑approval bugs, where a contract fails to keep token permissions in sync with mutable contract references. To remediate, the setStaking function should first revoke the previous allowance by calling safeApprove with a zero amount on the old staking contract, then grant the full pool share allowance to the new staking contract, or alternatively the ability to change the staking contract should be removed entirely to avoid inconsistent state. Properly updating the allowance restores the expected behavior where users can claim rewards from the newly assigned staking pool without encountering reverts, aligning the contract’s business logic with its accounting assumptions.

title: A user’s tokens could be locked for an extended duration beyond their intention and without their control
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the locking function determines the unlock timestamp by adding a fixed lockDuration to the next epoch timestamp, which is always the start of the following reward period. Because the contract does not allow the caller to specify a deadline or to lock until a chosen future time, a transaction that is submitted close to the end of the current epoch can be mined in the next epoch, causing nextEpoch to advance by an additional week (or the length of rewardsDuration). As a result the calculated unlock time is shifted by an additional week, potentially preventing users from accessing their LP tokens when needed. The issue arises from the absence of a deadline parameter and from the reliance on nextEpoch() rather than the current epoch when computing the lock expiry. Exploitation does not require malicious intent; it occurs naturally when network conditions such as high gas prices, validator latency, or temporary censorship delay the inclusion of the lock transaction. When the transaction finally executes in a later block, the contract records a lock that expires at nextEpoch + lockDuration, which may be one or more epochs later than the user expected. The impact is a temporary freeze of funds: the user sees their staked balance disappear from the unlocked pool, receives no rewards until the extended lock ends, and may be unable to withdraw for an extra week, which can cause missed loan repayments or other time‑sensitive operations. The bug affects any participant who stakes and locks tokens, especially those who act near epoch boundaries, and it was discovered during a manual audit that examined the lock‑creation logic and compared it with typical deadline patterns used in swap functions. The problem is subtle because the contract still enforces a lock and the extra delay is only visible after the transaction is mined, making it easy to attribute to normal network latency. The appropriate remediation is to allow the caller to provide a latestUnlockTime or deadline argument, or to compute the unlock timestamp based on the current epoch rather than the next one, thereby preventing unintended extensions of the lock period. This class of issue belongs to the broader category of \"missing deadline / time‑bound parameter\" bugs that can lead to unintended state changes and temporary loss of asset availability.

title: MagicLpAggregator always returns lower than correct answer, leading to arbitrage loss
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the MagicLpAggregator contract derives the price of a liquidity‑provider (LP) token for a pair of closely‑tied assets. The contract fetches the latest price from two separate oracles, normalises them to a common decimal base and then selects the smaller of the two values (the “minAnswer”). It subsequently assumes that the combined reserve of both tokens is worth this single minimum price and returns minAnswer * (baseReserve + quoteReserve) / totalSupply as the LP token price. The root cause is the logical mistake of treating two assets with potentially different market values as if they shared a single price, effectively undervaluing the pool whenever the two underlying prices diverge, even by a few basis points. An attacker can exploit this by purchasing LP tokens at the artificially low price, redeeming the underlying assets from the pool, and selling them on the open market at their true market values. In the example where token A trades at $0.99 and token B at $1.00, the aggregator reports an LP price of $1.98 instead of the correct $1.99, allowing a trader to buy $198 000 worth of LP tokens, withdraw the assets and sell them for $199 000, pocketing a $1 000 profit. The impact is a systematic loss for honest LP holders whose positions are de‑valued, and for any protocol that relies on the aggregator’s output as collateral valuation – it may lend more than the real worth of the LP tokens, exposing the system to liquidation or insolvency. The flaw manifests whenever the two underlying assets are not perfectly price‑aligned, which is common even for supposedly pegged tokens that experience minor fluctuations. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that examined the pricing logic and identified the misuse of the minimum oracle value. It can be hard to notice because the code appears conservative (using the lower price) and the deviation is often small, so UI displays may only show a slight discrepancy that users might attribute to rounding. To remediate, the contract should compute the LP token value as a weighted sum of each reserve multiplied by its own oracle price, i.e., (basePrice * baseReserve + quotePrice * quoteReserve) / totalSupply, or provide separate lower‑bound and upper‑bound oracle feeds for collateral purposes. This corrects the accounting assumption that the pool’s total value equals the sum of reserves priced at a single uniform rate, eliminating the arbitrage window and aligning the on‑chain price with the true market valuation. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the displayed LP token price is marginally lower than expected, leading to fewer tokens received on purchase or a lower redemption amount, contrary to the expectation that the LP token reflects the exact combined value of its underlying assets.

title: Permanent loss of yield for stakers in reward pools due to precision loss.
