poc:
* Reward pool offers WBTC rewards
* Epoch has just started,
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision loss that occurs when the contract computes the per‑second reward rate by dividing the total reward amount by the remaining epoch time using Solidity integer division. Because Solidity discards any fractional remainder, the calculated rewardRate is rounded down, and the truncated fraction is never recovered. Later the contract multiplies this rounded rate by the elapsed time to determine the amount of rewards to distribute, which means the lost fraction is permanently removed from the pool. The root cause is the lack of a scaling factor (such as 1e18) or any rounding‑up mechanism before the division, so the arithmetic operates on whole numbers only. This can be exploited indirectly: every time a new reward amount is notified, the contract silently discards up to (_remainingRewardTime‑1) units of the token, which translates into a material loss of value for stakers. For a one‑week epoch the worst‑case loss is 604,799 token base units; with USDC this is roughly $0.6, while with WBTC it can exceed $400 per epoch. The loss is shared proportionally among all participants, so each staker receives less than the advertised yield. The condition under which it occurs is any reward notification where the remaining time is non‑zero, which is essentially every epoch. All users who stake in the reward pool, as well as the protocol that promises those rewards, are affected because the promised returns are not delivered. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the reward calculation logic and noticing that the amount is divided before being multiplied, leading to a remainder that is never accounted for. It is hard to notice because the missing amount often appears as dust – a small fraction of a token – and the UI typically shows only the final reward balance, not the intermediate arithmetic. The proper fix is to store the rewardRate in a higher‑precision format, for example by scaling the amount by 1e18 before division, or by using a rounding‑up division, so that the fractional component is preserved and the total distributed reward matches the intended amount. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of fixed‑point arithmetic errors where integer division causes permanent loss of value, resulting in users receiving fewer rewards than expected, a discrepancy that violates the protocol’s economic guarantees and can erode trust in the system.

title: Factory::create
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the factory contract's create function, which builds a new MagicLP clone using LibClone.cloneDeterministic with a salt derived from tx.origin and the pool parameters. Because tx.origin reflects the original external account that started the transaction, it can be identical for different calls that are queued on an optimistic roll‑up such as Blast. An attacker who can observe the pending transaction queue and later cause a chain re‑organization can submit a transaction that uses the same tx.origin and identical arguments, causing the deterministic address calculation to produce the same clone address as the legitimate deployment. As a result the attacker can pre‑emptively deploy a contract at that address or overwrite the expected instance, gaining control over the LP contract that was intended for the original user. This breaks the assumption that each pool address is unique to its creator and that only the creator can initialize it. The impact is that the malicious party may seize ownership, redirect fees, or lock user funds, leading to loss of assets or incorrect accounting where users see a pool that returns zero or does not accept deposits. The issue manifests only on chains with probabilistic finality where pending transactions can be reordered, such as optimistic roll‑ups, and when the factory relies on tx.origin instead of msg.sender or an explicit creator field in the salt. It was discovered during a manual audit of the Abracadabra Money periphery contracts by reviewing the create function and noting the use of tx.origin. The problem is subtle because tx.origin is often assumed to be unique per user, and deterministic deployment patterns are commonly trusted, so the bug may not be evident until a re‑org scenario is simulated. The proper mitigation is to construct the deterministic salt using the actual caller (msg.sender) or an explicit creator address that cannot be spoofed by a re‑ordered transaction, ensuring that each deployment address is bound to the transaction that performed it. This class of bug falls under insecure deterministic contract deployment and misuse of tx.origin for authentication, which can lead to address collision attacks and unauthorized control of deployed contracts.

title: Adjusting ” _I_ ” will create a sandwich opportunity because of price changes
description:
Because `MagicLP` is forked from DODO, we will check DODO documentation to understand this contract. From [DODO documentation](https://docs.dodoex.io/en/developer/contracts/dodo-v1-v2/dodo-v1-v2-integration-guide), the ” _I_ ” is the “i” value in here and it is directly related with the output amount a trader will receive when selling a quote/base token:

![img](https://i.imgur.com/UpeLbGg.png)

Adjusting the value of ” _I_ ” directly by calling `setParameters()` function will influence the price. This can be exploited by a MEV bot, simply by trading just before the `setParameters()` function and exiting right after the price change. The profit gained from this operation essentially represents potential losses for the liquidity providers who supplied liquidity to the pool.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the MagicLP contract, which inherits the pricing logic from the DODO protocol. The contract exposes a public setParameters() function that allows the pool owner to modify the internal variable referred to as “I”. This variable is directly used in the formula that determines the amount of output tokens a trader receives when swapping either the quote or base token. Because the price calculation depends on I, any change to I instantly alters the effective exchange rate offered by the pool. The root cause is that the contract does not protect the I update from being observed and front‑run, nor does it enforce a gradual ramp‑up or a trading pause while the parameter is being changed. An attacker, typically a MEV bot, can monitor the mempool for a pending setParameters transaction, execute a trade just before the parameter change at the pre‑change price, and then execute a second trade immediately after the change at the new, more favorable price. This sandwich pattern extracts the price differential as profit, which is effectively a loss for the liquidity providers whose capital underpins the pool. The impact is that LPs see their share value decrease, users may receive a worse price than expected, and the protocol’s economic guarantees are weakened. The issue manifests whenever the owner calls setParameters without additional safeguards; it can happen at any time the pool parameters are adjusted. All participants who rely on the pool’s price – especially liquidity providers and traders – are affected. The problem was identified during a security audit by tracing the DODO documentation, recognizing that the I variable is tied to the output amount, and noting that the contract permits unrestricted updates. The bug is subtle because the price shift appears as a normal market movement and does not raise an explicit error, making it easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate, the protocol should restrict I updates to a trusted context, employ private RPC endpoints to hide the transaction from public mempools, introduce a timelock or multi‑step ramp‑up that gradually changes I, and temporarily disable trading while parameters are being modified. These measures remove the immediate arbitrage window and protect liquidity providers from sandwich exploitation, aligning the contract’s behavior with the intended accounting assumptions of stable pricing and fair market access.

title: Missing Return Statement in `_getReserves` Function in `MagicLpAggregator` Contract
description: The `MagicLpAggregator` contract contains a flaw within the `_getReserves` function where it fails to return the reserve values fetched from the `pair` contract. This oversight results in the `latestAnswer` function always returning zero, which can have severe implications for any systems that depend on this contract for accurate liquidity pool pricing data.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing return statement in an internal helper function that is supposed to fetch the two reserve balances from a liquidity‑pair contract. Because the function does not return the values it reads, the caller receives the default uninitialized values, which are zero. The root cause is a simple coding oversight: the developer assigned the reserves to local variables but never emitted them as the function’s output. When the public `latestAnswer` view reads these reserves, it multiplies the zero values by scaling factors and then uses them to compute a price or other oracle metric. Consequently the oracle always reports a zero answer. This can be exploited by any downstream contract or off‑chain system that trusts the aggregator for accurate pool pricing. By feeding a perpetual zero price, an attacker could trigger unwanted behavior such as unnecessary liquidations, failed trades, or mis‑allocation of funds in protocols that rely on the price feed. The impact is that users see a price of zero, trades may revert or be priced incorrectly, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about non‑zero liquidity are violated. The bug manifests every time `latestAnswer` is called after deployment, regardless of the actual state of the underlying pair. It affects all participants that read the aggregator – token holders, traders, and any smart contracts that use the price as an input. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit where the code was examined for logical correctness. It is hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors, the function executes silently, and the zero result may be interpreted as a legitimate value in a test environment. The class of bug is a missing return / default‑value misuse, where uninitialized variables propagate as zero. From a user’s perspective the UI would display a price of 0 or a missing quote, leading to confusion when a trade shows no value or a dashboard shows an empty field. The expectation is that the oracle returns the current reserves and a derived price, but the reality is that it always returns zero. To fix the issue the `_getReserves` function must explicitly return the two reserve variables after reading them from the pair contract, ensuring that the caller receives the actual on‑chain balances. This change restores correct price calculation and aligns the contract’s behavior with its intended accounting logic.

title: `MagicLpAggregator` can be incompatible with potential integrators due to incorrect `latestRoundData` function
bug_full: The MagicLpAggregator contract implements the Chainlink AggregatorV3Interface function latestRoundData but returns hard‑coded zero values for roundId, startedAt, updatedAt and answeredInRound while only forwarding the price answer. This deviation from the standard interface means that any downstream contract that follows the common pattern of reading the price and then checking the updatedAt timestamp for freshness will see an updatedAt of 0. Because 0 is always less than the current block timestamp minus the allowed staleness window (for example one hour), the freshness check fails and the downstream contract reverts with a “stale price feed” error. The root cause is the omission of proper propagation of the timing metadata from the underlying Chainlink feed; the aggregator simply discards those fields instead of copying them. An attacker does not need to perform any special action – the vulnerability is triggered automatically whenever an integrator calls latestRoundData and applies a staleness guard, which is a best‑practice pattern used by many protocols. The impact is that protocols that rely on MagicLpAggregator for price information cannot obtain a valid price feed, causing transactions that depend on the price (such as swaps, collateral valuations, or liquidation checks) to fail. From a user’s perspective the transaction reverts with a “stale price feed” message, the UI may show no price or an error, and expected actions like a trade or loan approval are blocked. The issue occurs under the condition that the integrator performs the typical updatedAt < block.timestamp - 1 hour check, which is true for virtually all production deployments that enforce freshness. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit when a test case called latestRoundData, extracted the returned timestamps, applied the standard freshness logic and observed an immediate revert. Because the function signature matches the expected interface, the problem can be subtle and may not be caught by simple compilation or interface checks; only runtime inspection of the returned values reveals the inconsistency. To remediate the issue the aggregator should retrieve the full round data from the underlying base or quote oracle and return the exact roundId, startedAt, updatedAt and answeredInRound values, thereby conforming to the Chainlink specification and allowing integrators’ freshness checks to succeed. In broader terms this is a metadata propagation bug in an oracle wrapper, where missing or incorrect timestamp fields break downstream accounting assumptions about data freshness, leading to integration failures and potential loss of service for users.

title: MagicLpAggregator doesn’t consider the decimal of MagicLP
description:
We can know that the `MagicLpAggregator` can serve as the `price source` for `MagicLP shares` when the prices of `base` and `quote` tokens are similar.
    
MagicLpAggregator would be used to price MagicLP collateral for Cauldrons. 
Something to note is that the MagicLP Oracle is only meant for closed-together price pool. 
It's just that the oracle is not meant to be used for any kind of MagicLP, just for closely priced tokens like MIM/USDB.

There’s no assurance that we can use `MagicLpAggregator` for `base` and `quote` tokens with only `18 decimals`. The `MagicLP` token has the same `decimal` as the `base` token. However, the `MagicLpAggregator` does not account for this `decimal`, resulting in incorrect `prices` when the `decimal` of the `base` token is not `18`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the MagicLpAggregator contract that is used as a price source for MagicLP share tokens. The aggregator normalises the answers from the base and quote price oracles and the reserves of the underlying pool to 18 decimal places, but it deliberately skips the decimal adjustment for the MagicLP token itself. Because the MagicLP token inherits the decimal count of the base token, any pool whose base token does not use 18 decimals will cause the final price calculation to be scaled incorrectly. The root cause is the omission of a scaling factor that should convert the LP token total supply (and implicitly its share value) to the same 18‑decimal basis as the other inputs. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a MagicLP whose base token has fewer (or more) than 18 decimals, causing the aggregator to report a price that is orders of magnitude larger or smaller than the true value. When the reported price is used by Cauldrons or other lending contracts to value collateral, the protocol may accept insufficient collateral, allow over‑borrowing, or trigger wrongful liquidations, leading to loss of user funds. The issue manifests whenever MagicLpAggregator is employed for a MagicLP whose underlying base token deviates from the 18‑decimal standard; it does not affect pools where both tokens are 18‑decimal. Users depositing MagicLP as collateral will see their share price appear dramatically inflated (e.g., 8 000 000 USD instead of 8 USD) and may receive unexpected liquidation or borrowing limits. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing mock contracts with mismatched decimals and observing the price output. It is hard to notice because the contract returns a numeric value that looks syntactically correct and the mismatch only becomes apparent when comparing against expected economic values. The correct fix is to treat the MagicLP token as another decimal‑sensitive asset: multiply the LP total supply (or equivalently the reserves) by 10 ** (18 - lpDecimals) before using it in the price formula, ensuring all components share the same 18‑decimal basis. This brings the reported price back in line with the true economic value and restores reliable collateral valuation.

title: Less base tokens are transferred when selling quote tokens due to the precision loss that occurred in `_GeneralIntegrate
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision‑loss arithmetic bug in the pricing routine that calculates how many base tokens are returned when a user sells quote tokens. The core of the problem lies in the internal function that performs a curve integral, where a division is executed before a multiplication. Because Solidity integer division always rounds down, the intermediate result loses fractional units before it is multiplied by the fee factor, causing the final amount of base tokens to be systematically lower than the mathematically correct value. This issue appears whenever the curve parameter R differs from 1, which triggers the branch that calls the integration helper, and when the fee coefficient k is non‑zero. An attacker or a regular trader can invoke the sellQuoteToken path and receive fewer base tokens than the market price dictates. From the user’s perspective the UI will show a smaller credit than expected – for example a trader may expect to receive 21,888 base tokens but only receives 17,164, a discrepancy of roughly 27.5 %. The shortfall translates into missing refunds, reduced balances, or unexpected zero‑output in extreme cases, breaking the accounting assumptions of the liquidity pool. The bug was uncovered during a formal audit when the auditors compared the contract’s output with a mathematically precise reference implementation and observed a large deviation. The error is hard to spot because the rounding occurs inside a helper that uses DecimalMath utilities, and the loss is only evident with certain parameter ranges; normal test values may not expose the under‑payment. To remediate the issue the calculation should be reordered so that multiplication precedes division, using a high‑precision scaling factor (e.g., 1e18) and avoiding floor division on intermediate results. By computing the penalty term as (k * V0²) / (V1 * V2) and applying the scaling only at the final step, the contract can preserve the intended precision and ensure that users receive the correct amount of base tokens, restoring the integrity of the pricing logic and the protocol’s financial accounting.

title: Staking contract is not able to support native USDB/WETH
description: Loss of yield if USDB/WETH is used as reward token.
poc:
From what I understood from the protocol team, they want to support any ERC20 tokens that are considered safe/well known. I believe USDB/WETH falls into this category.

Both USDB and WETH yield mode are AUTOMATIC by default. `LockingMultiRewards.sol` uses internal accounting to track all rewards that are accrued for users. For instance, when users stake `amount`, `stakingTokenBalance` will increase by `amount` and user’s balance will increase by `amount` accordingly. Rewards that are distributed to users are based on these internal accounting values.

The issue here is that,

1. If USDB/WETH tokens are used as reward tokens, the accrued yield due to automatic rebasing are lost as they cannot be claimed.
2. If protocol team has not used such tokens as reward tokens yet and becomes aware of this, then it means that they will not be able to use these tokens as reward tokens.
bug_full: The issue is that the staking contract is unable to correctly handle native rebasing ERC20 tokens such as USDB or WETH when they are used as reward tokens. The contract records user stakes and reward entitlements using internal accounting variables that are updated only when explicit transfer or mint operations occur. Rebalancing tokens that operate in AUTOMATIC mode increase the holder's balance through a protocol‑level rebase, but the contract does not contain a mechanism to claim or pull the newly created tokens into its reward pool. As a result, any yield generated by the automatic rebasing of USDB or WETH never reaches the contract and is effectively lost. This problem manifests whenever a protocol operator configures a rebasing token as a reward token, because the contract assumes that reward balances can be tracked solely by the static amount recorded at deposit time. Users who stake expecting to receive the additional rebasing yield will see their reward calculations remain flat, leading to a discrepancy between the expected increase in token holdings and the actual amount received. The impact is twofold: stakers receive less than the advertised reward, and the protocol loses the ability to advertise these popular rebasing assets as viable incentives. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the reward accounting logic and identified that the contract never invokes the token’s claim function or any pull‑mechanism for rebasing yields. The flaw is subtle because the contract accepts any ERC20 token without immediate errors, and the missing yield only becomes apparent when the token’s balance grows autonomously, a behavior that is not visible in the contract’s internal state. To remediate the issue, the contract should be extended to allow the reward token to be set to a CLAIMABLE mode and implement a routine that periodically or on‑demand claims the rebasing surplus and adds it to the internal reward pool, ensuring that the automatic yield is captured and distributed to stakers as intended.

title: `LockingMultiRewards` contract on Blast does not configure gas yield nor token yield mode.
description: The Abracadabra team configures gas yield for all contracts in the Blast L2 except for the `LockingMultiRewards` contract. Therefore, gas yields accrued on the `LockingMultiRewards` staking contract since deployment will be lost as it was never configured using `BlastYields.configureDefaultClaimables`. If the contract holds native yield reward tokens in ERC20 such as WETHRebasing or USDB then these rewards will also be lost.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing configuration of the Blast yield system for the LockingMultiRewards staking contract deployed on the Blast L2 network. The contract’s constructor never calls BlastYields.configureDefaultClaimables, which is required to enable the contract to claim the gas fees that are automatically accrued to it by the Blast protocol, nor does it set up any token‑yield claimables such as WETHRebasing or USDB that might be distributed as native rewards. The root cause is a simple omission in the initialization code: while every other contract in the Abracadabra suite explicitly enables the gas‑yield mode, this contract’s constructor only validates input parameters and sets internal variables, leaving the yield mode disabled. Because the contract can still be used for staking, users will spend gas to deposit, lock, and claim rewards, but the protocol will never be able to retrieve the gas‑fee rebate that Blast would otherwise allocate to the contract. Consequently, the accrued gas fees are permanently locked in the protocol’s internal accounting and cannot be claimed by the contract owner or redistributed to stakers. If the contract also holds native reward tokens, those tokens will remain unclaimed for the same reason, effectively leaking value from the protocol. The issue manifests whenever the contract is deployed on Blast and any user interacts with its staking functions; the contract operates normally from a functional standpoint, so the problem is not obvious from the UI. Users may notice that, despite staking, they receive no extra “gas rebate” or token reward that other contracts provide, leading to a discrepancy between expected and actual returns. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the initialization patterns of all Abracadabra contracts and identified the absence of the Blast yield configuration call. It can be hard to detect because the contract does not revert or emit errors; the missing yields are simply never credited, which may be interpreted as a normal lack of additional rewards. To remediate, the constructor (or an admin‑only initialization function) should invoke BlastYields.configureDefaultClaimables with the appropriate parameters to enable gas‑yield mode, and a separate admin function should be added to allow the protocol to claim accumulated gas and token yields. Optionally, the contract should also be examined for the need to configure Blast points if the protocol intends to distribute them. By properly configuring the yield system, the protocol will recover the gas rebates and any native token rewards, aligning the contract’s behavior with the intended economic model and preventing inadvertent value loss.

title: User can grief bootstrap process by sending the cap amount of unlocked tokens to it.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic error in the token cap enforcement of the onboarding contract. The contract maintains separate counters for locked and unlocked token amounts and a global cap per token. When a user deposits tokens, the code checks whether the total amount of that token stored in the contract exceeds the cap, but it compares the cap against the sum of locked and unlocked tokens (totals[token].total) instead of the amount that is actually locked (totals[token].locked). Because of this, an attacker can fill the cap by depositing the maximum allowed amount with the lock flag set to false. Those tokens are recorded as unlocked, leaving the locked counters at zero. The bootstrap function later reads only the locked balances to provide initial liquidity to a new pool. If the locked counters are zero, the bootstrap creates a pool with zero base and quote amounts, causing the pool creation to either revert due to insufficient output or emit a liquidity event with zero shares. As a result, legitimate users cannot contribute locked tokens, the onboarding process stalls, and the protocol cannot launch the intended liquidity pool. The issue manifests when the contract is in the Opened state and a user deposits tokens without locking them up, reaching the cap. It affects any participant who expects the bootstrap to succeed, as they will see no liquidity, possible transaction reverts, and a missing pool. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined the relationship between caps and locked balances. It is hard to notice because the deposit function succeeds and the cap check does not raise an error, giving the impression that the contract is operating normally, while the hidden invariant that bootstrap relies on is silently broken. The fix is to enforce the cap against the locked total instead of the overall total, ensuring that only tokens that will be used for bootstrapping count toward the cap. This change restores the intended accounting invariant and prevents a denial‑of‑service where an attacker can grief the bootstrap process by exhausting the cap with unlocked tokens.

title: `asdRouter.sol` is at risk of DOS due to vulnerable implementation of `NOTE` address
description: `asdRouter.sol` is at risk of DOS due to vulnerable implementation of `NOTE` address.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the router contract stores the NOTE token address in an immutable state variable that is set only once in the constructor. In the Canto ecosystem the underlying NOTE token can be upgraded by deploying a new NOTE contract and updating the cNOTE contract’s underlying() view. Because the router never queries cNOTE.underlying() and continues to use the original noteAddress, any function that relies on this variable – such as swaps between asdUSDC and NOTE or cross‑chain compose – will reference a contract that no longer implements the expected interface after the upgrade. Calls to the stale address revert or silently fail, preventing users from completing swaps. From a user’s perspective a transaction that should deliver NOTE either reverts with an error or completes without delivering any tokens, appearing as if the funds vanished or the swap returned zero. This is a classic hard‑coded address or immutable configuration bug, a form of denial‑of‑service that only manifests after a governance‑driven change of the NOTE token address. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the router implementation with the recommended pattern of using cNoteToken.underlying(). The problem is subtle because the address change is expected to be rare, so normal testing does not trigger the failure, making it easy to overlook. The impact is medium: users cannot swap to or from NOTE until the router is redeployed with the correct address, which can be done by the protocol team. The proper fix is to replace the immutable noteAddress variable with a call to the cNOTE contract’s underlying() view each time the address is needed, or to store a mutable reference that can be updated by an authorized admin. This aligns the router with the ecosystem’s design that NOTE may be redeployed, eliminating the denial‑of‑service condition.

title: `ASDRouter` didn’t call `ASDUSDC.approve`
description: The function ‘ASDRouter#lzCompose()’ never succeeds. The receiver can only receive `ASDUSDC` token when the call of ‘ASDRouter#lzCompose()’ is done.
bug_full: The vulnerability in the ASDRouter contract is an allowance omission that prevents the router from swapping deposited ASDUSDC for NOTE. When a user calls lzCompose, the router first deposits wrapped USDC into the ASDUSDC token and then attempts to swap the resulting ASDUSDC for NOTE by calling the external crocSwapAddress contract. However, the router never calls ASDUSDC.approve for the crocSwapAddress, leaving the allowance at zero. Because the DEX contract requires a non‑zero allowance to execute transferFrom, the swap call reverts internally and the router catches the failure, refunds the ASDUSDC to the caller, and does not mint or transfer any NOTE. The root cause is the missing approve call in the router’s constructor and in the internal _swapOFTForNote function. The bug can be triggered every time lzCompose is executed, because the allowance condition is always false unless the contract is manually approved. Users are affected because they expect to receive NOTE or ASD tokens after depositing USDC, but instead their balance remains unchanged or they receive a refund, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual outcomes. The issue was discovered during a security audit and reproduced with unit tests that logged a zero allowance while the router held a positive ASDUSDC balance. It is hard to notice because the outer transaction does not revert; only internal logs show the failure, and from a UI perspective the operation appears successful while delivering no value. The impact is medium severity: funds are not stolen, but the protocol’s core deposit‑and‑swap flow is broken, preventing users from acquiring the intended token and potentially reducing confidence in the platform. The appropriate fix is to grant the DEX contract a sufficient allowance, typically by calling ASDUSDC.approve(crocSwapAddress, type(uint).max) in the router’s constructor or immediately before the swap, ensuring that the external contract can transfer the required amount of ASDUSDC.

title: Removing token from the whitelist may cause DoS due to limited USDC amount
description: Users won’t be able to withdraw `USDC` tokens from `asdUSDC`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a whitelist‑based restriction in the withdraw function of the asdUSDC contract. The function first checks that the USDC version supplied by the caller is present in the whitelistedUSDCVersions mapping before allowing a token burn and a transfer of the underlying USDC. Because the contract counts all deposited USDC balances – regardless of their whitelist status – toward the total supply of asdUSDC, removing a USDC version from the whitelist does not automatically clear its stored balance. When the contract owner later removes a previously whitelisted USDC version that still holds a non‑zero balance, users who hold asdUSDC that were originally backed by that version can no longer specify it in the withdraw call. Consequently, they are forced to withdraw using only the remaining whitelisted versions. If other users exhaust the available USDC of the remaining version, the remaining asdUSDC holders find the contract unable to satisfy their withdrawal request, triggering a revert with either “ASDUSDC: USDC version not whitelisted” or “ASDUSDC: Not enough USDC balance”. From a user’s perspective the expectation that a token can be redeemed for its underlying asset is violated; the UI may show a successful burn but the actual USDC transfer fails, leaving the user with a zero balance or an unchanged asdUSDC balance and no refund. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition where funds become effectively locked and the protocol’s accounting assumptions – that each asdUSDC token is fully backed by withdrawable USDC – are broken. This issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logical flow of the withdraw routine and identified that the whitelist check does not consider the residual balance of a removed version. The problem is subtle because whitelist removal is a normal administrative action and the contract does not emit a warning when a version with a remaining balance is disabled, making the under‑collateralisation easy to overlook. The bug belongs to the class of whitelist‑driven asset‑lock vulnerabilities, where access control on withdrawal paths creates a mismatch between recorded total supply and actually withdrawable assets. To remediate, the contract should either eliminate the whitelist requirement for withdrawals, enforce that a version can only be removed after its balance is zero, or provide a migration path that allows holders to claim their share from the removed version through an alternative mechanism, thereby preserving the invariant that every asdUSDC token remains fully redeemable.

title: Balance check during `MagicSpend` validation cannot ensure that `MagicSpend` has enough balance to cover the requested fund
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the MagicSpend contract where the validation step checks the contract's external balance (address(this).balance) against the requested withdrawal amount, but does not keep a record of funds that have already been earmarked for other pending withdrawals. The root cause is that the contract relies on the current on‑chain balance instead of an internal state variable that reflects the net available balance after accounting for all validated UserOperations in the same batch. When the EntryPoint batches several UserOperations that use the same MagicSpend paymaster, each operation passes validation because the contract balance appears sufficient for the individual request. However, during the execution loop the contract attempts to transfer the summed withdrawals, and if the total exceeds the actual balance, the second (or later) withdrawal fails in postOp, causing a revert and leaving the user with no funds. This can be exploited by an attacker or a careless bundler who includes multiple operations that together drain more than the contract holds, effectively causing a “funds disappear” scenario where users see a successful transaction in the UI but receive zero payout. The impact includes failed withdrawals, loss of expected refunds, potential reputation damage for the paymaster, and possible locking of funds if the contract does not handle the revert gracefully. The condition for the bug to manifest is when the EntryPoint processes a batch of UserOperations against a MagicSpend contract whose balance is lower than the sum of the requested withdraw amounts. All users of the paymaster, the contract owner, and any protocol relying on the paymaster are affected because they may not receive the promised funds. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a proof‑of‑concept demonstrated two operations withdrawing 100 and 150 wei from a contract with only 200 wei, causing the second operation to revert. The problem is subtle because each validation passes, so developers may not notice the inconsistency until execution fails, and typical UI feedback may only show a generic transaction failure without indicating an accounting error. To remediate, the contract should maintain an internal accounting variable that tracks the remaining balance after each validated withdrawal, decrementing it during validation and using it for subsequent checks. Alternatively, a limit such as maxWithdrawDenominator can be enforced to cap each withdrawal to a fraction of the current balance, reducing the chance of over‑withdrawal. In general, the fix requires moving from a pure balance check to a stateful balance accounting pattern that prevents race conditions and ensures that the contract can always satisfy the total amount of pending withdrawals.

title: Users can front run the signature of the paymaster operation leading to some problems
bug_full: The vulnerability is a signature‑replay race condition in the MagicSpend paymaster contract that implements the EIP‑4337 paymaster interface. The contract reuses the same cryptographic signature that authorises a user’s withdraw request as the signature that is consumed by the validatePaymasterUserOp function when a transaction is sponsored by the paymaster. Because the signature (and the associated nonce) can be presented only once, a malicious user can submit a normal withdraw call directly to the contract before the bundler includes the paymaster‑sponsored user operation. By front‑running the withdraw transaction, the attacker consumes the nonce, causing the subsequent call to validatePaymasterUserOp to revert due to an already‑used signature. This results in the paymaster refusing to sponsor the user’s transaction, effectively a denial‑of‑service attack on the paymaster’s reputation. The issue occurs only when the attacker can control transaction ordering, for example by sending a higher‑gas‑price transaction that gets mined first. It affects any user who relies on the paymaster to cover gas costs, as their operation will fail unexpectedly and they will see no gas being paid, even though the withdraw succeeded. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the withdraw function and the paymaster validation logic, and it is subtle because the two functions appear unrelated and the reuse of the signature is not obvious without tracing the nonce handling across both entry points. The bug is hard to notice in standard unit tests because it requires a specific ordering of external transactions, a scenario that typical testing frameworks do not simulate. Conceptually, the fix is to separate the authorisation domains: use a distinct signer or a different nonce space for withdraw operations and for paymaster validation, ensuring that a signature cannot be replayed across the two functions. By enforcing unique signatures for each operation, the race condition is eliminated and the paymaster can reliably sponsor transactions without being vulnerable to front‑run attacks that would otherwise cause unexpected reverts and damage to protocol trust.

title: The `shortOrder` verification bug on the `RedemptionFacet::proposeRedemption`
description:
The `BidOrdersFacet::bidMatchAlgo()` allows a `shortOrder` to be partially matched and leave its `ercAmount * price < minAskEth` due to the [`DUST_FACTOR` constant](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-dittoeth/blob/91faf46078bb6fe8ce9f55bcb717e5d2d302d22e/contracts/facets/BidOrdersFacet.sol#L190) (as long as its corresponding `shortRecord` is maintaining enough `ercDebt + shortOrder`’s `ercAmount` to keep the position `>=` the `minShortErc` threshold).

The redemption process enables redeemers to redeem their `ercEscrowed` for `ethCollateral` on target `shortRecords`. If a `shortRecord` was partially filled, the `RedemptionFacet::proposeRedemption()` must guarantee that the corresponding `shortOrder` maintains the `ercAmount` `>=` `minShortErc`. In other words, if the `shortOrder`’s [`ercAmount` is less than the `minShortErc` threshold](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-dittoeth/blob/91faf46078bb6fe8ce9f55bcb717e5d2d302d22e/contracts/facets/RedemptionFacet.sol#L111), the [`shortOrder` must be canceled](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-dittoeth/blob/91faf46078bb6fe8ce9f55bcb717e5d2d302d22e/contracts/facets/RedemptionFacet.sol#L113) from the order book. Otherwise, the `shortRecord` position will be less than the `minShortErc` threshold when the order is matched again.

Subsequently, the small `shortRecord` (`short` position) will not incentivize liquidators to liquidate it even if it is liquidable, leaving bad debt to the protocol.

I discovered that the `proposeRedemption()` improperly verifies the proposer (redeemer)‘s inputted [`shortOrderId` param](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-dittoeth/blob/91faf46078bb6fe8ce9f55bcb717e5d2d302d22e/contracts/facets/RedemptionFacet.sol#L81), allowing an attacker to specify the `shortOrderId` param to another `shortOrder`’s id that does not correspond to the target redeeming `shortRecord`.

The vulnerability can bypass the `minShortErc` threshold verification process on the `shortOrder` corresponding to the processing `shortRecord`, eventually allowing an attacker to leave a small `shortRecord` position that disincentivizes liquidators from liquidating the position. Furthermore, the small `shortRecord` also disables the redemption mechanism from redeeming it for `ethCollateral`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the RedemptionFacet.proposeRedemption function where the shortOrderId supplied by the caller is used to load an order from storage before the function verifies that the order actually belongs to the shortRecord being redeemed. Because the contract first checks whether the loaded shortOrder.ercAmount is below the protocol‑defined minShortErc threshold and only then validates the association (shortRecordId and shorter address), an attacker can supply the identifier of a different shortOrder that satisfies the amount check. The malicious caller therefore bypasses the cancellation logic that would normally remove a shortOrder whose ercAmount is too small. As a result a partially‑filled shortRecord can be redeemed while its corresponding shortOrder remains on the order book with ercAmount < minShortErc. This leaves the shortRecord position below the minimum size required for liquidators to be incentivised, causing the protocol to accumulate bad debt and preventing the redemption mechanism from returning ethCollateral to the user. The bug manifests when a shortRecord is in a PartialFill state, its shortOrder amount is below minShortErc, and the caller can control the shortOrderId argument. Users experience transactions that appear successful but receive no ETH, or see their short positions remain unliquidated despite being under‑collateralised. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the redemption flow, where the order‑book integrity check was found to be performed after the amount comparison, making the mismatch hard to notice because the function still reverts only on a later check. The class of bug is an order‑book reference integrity flaw that allows parameter tampering to bypass business‑logic thresholds. The proper fix is to move the validation of shortOrder.shortRecordId and shortOrder.addr immediately after loading the order, before any comparison with minShortErc, and to cancel the order if its amount is below the threshold. This restores the invariant that every shortRecord on the book satisfies the minimum size requirement and that liquidation incentives remain intact.

title: Can manipulate the `C.SHORT_STARTING_ID` `ShortRecord` of the `TAPP`
description: Attackers can make it so that risky debts are not liquidated, and unliquidated risky debts can accumulate over the long term.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an ID‑reuse and state‑corruption bug in the handling of ShortRecord NFTs that represent short positions for the TAPP (Treasury‑Aggregating‑Protocol‑Pool) contract. When a ShortRecord is fully liquidated the library function LibShortRecord.deleteShortRecord moves the constant identifier C.SHORT_STARTING_ID into a reusable‑ID list, but the complementary function LibShortRecord.fillShortRecord never restores that identifier to the active list. Consequently, if an attacker mints a ShortRecord NFT and transfers it to the TAPP contract, the internal createShortRecord call reuses the same C.SHORT_STARTING_ID and overwrites the original ShortRecord stored for the TAPP. This overwriting changes the collateral amount, the ERC‑debt balance and the debt‑rate of the TAPP’s short position without any visible on‑chain event that indicates a problem. The root cause is the missing state transition for the identifier after a partial liquidation path where the TAPP absorbs leftover short debt; the contract assumes the ID is unavailable, but it remains in the reusable pool. An attacker can exploit the bug by: (1) creating a ShortRecord NFT, (2) transferring the NFT to the TAPP address, (3) causing the contract to allocate the same C.SHORT_STARTING_ID for the new record, and (4) thereby overwriting the TAPP’s existing short record. The impact is that risky debts that should be liquidated remain unliquidated, allowing them to accumulate over time. From a user perspective the symptoms are unexpected changes to a short position: the displayed collateral may drop to zero or differ from the expected amount, the debt balance may be altered, and liquidation attempts may appear to succeed while the protocol’s accounting shows no reduction in risk. This situation can lead to funds being effectively locked or lost, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about collateralisation ratios are violated. The bug manifests only when a ShortRecord NFT is transferred to the TAPP contract while the C.SHORT_STARTING_ID is present in the reusable list, a condition that arises after certain partial liquidation flows. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a series of partial and full liquidation scenarios and observing that the TAPP short record could be manipulated after an NFT transfer. The issue is subtle because the contract’s external behaviour (liquidation calls) still returns success, and the internal identifier reuse is not exposed in events, making it hard to notice without deep state inspection. The recommended remediation is to prevent ShortRecord NFTs from being transferred to the TAPP contract, or to ensure that any identifier removed from active use is properly cleared from the reusable pool before it can be reassigned. In broader terms this is a classic example of improper management of freed identifiers leading to state injection, similar to use‑after‑free bugs in traditional software, and it breaks the invariant that each short position is uniquely associated with a stable identifier.

title: The `colRedeemed` variable is wrongly retrieved in `LibBytes::readProposalData` function
bug_full: The vulnerability is a bit‑masking error in the low‑level data‑extraction routine used by the protocol. In the LibBytes.readProposalData function the 11‑byte field that stores the amount of collateral already redeemed (colRedeemed) is extracted from a 32‑byte word with inline assembly. The code shifts the word right by 80 bits to align the desired bytes and then attempts to mask the lower 11 bytes, but it mistakenly uses the add operation with a constant mask instead of the logical and operation. As a result the constant mask is added to the shifted value, producing a number that is larger than the true 11‑byte value. This incorrect colRedeemed value is later fed into the RedemptionFacet.claimRedemption logic, which relies on the field to calculate how much collateral a user can claim. Because the protocol believes a larger amount of collateral has already been redeemed, it may under‑pay the user, reject a legitimate claim, or, depending on the surrounding accounting checks, allow a user to claim more than they are entitled to. The bug manifests only when the proposal data is read – typically during a redemption transaction – and is invisible to callers because the assembly code compiles without warnings and the surrounding Solidity code treats the returned value as a normal uint88. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, which added a small test contract that compared the faulty assembly expression with the correct one and observed a discrepancy. The problem is hard to notice because the misuse of add versus and looks syntactically correct and the resulting number may still be within plausible ranges, especially when the high‑order bits of the shifted word are zero. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees: users may receive an incorrect redemption amount, potentially leading to loss of funds or unintended profit. The vulnerability belongs to the class of bit‑masking or data‑extraction bugs where an arithmetic operator is used instead of a bitwise operator, causing wrong values to be read from packed byte structures. To remediate the issue the assembly line should be changed to use and with the same mask (colRedeemed := and(0xffffffffffffffffffffff, shr(80, fullWord))) so that only the intended 11 bytes are kept. This correction restores the integrity of the colRedeemed field, ensuring that redemption calculations reflect the true state of collateral and that users receive the amount they expect.

title: `transferShortRecord`: Can transfer a newly created `ShortRecord` using a previously minted NFT
description: Can move the newly created `ShortRecord` using the NFT that was minted in the past.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the transferShortRecord routine that moves a ShortRecord together with its associated NFT. The function retrieves the NFT entry from storage and then looks up the ShortRecord using the NFT's shortRecordId, but it never verifies that the NFT's tokenId still matches the ShortRecord's tokenId. When a ShortRecord is closed, the NFT is not burned and the mapping fields (owner, shortRecordId) are left unchanged. If the protocol later re‑creates a new ShortRecord using the same shortRecordId and mints a fresh NFT with the same tokenId, the stale NFT entry still points to the old shortRecordId. Because the transfer function does not check the tokenId, any address that previously obtained approval for the old NFT can call transferFrom and cause the newly created ShortRecord to be transferred along with the bridge credit collateral. An attacker therefore exploits the bug by first obtaining approval for an NFT, waiting for the original short to be closed, triggering the creation of a new short with the same identifier, and finally invoking the transfer, which moves the collateral to the attacker’s address. The impact is unauthorized movement of funds that belong to the original short creator, breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol and potentially leading to loss of user collateral. The issue manifests only when a shortRecordId is reused after closure and the NFT remains in the mapping; it is hard to notice because the UI still shows the same NFT owned by the same address and the shortRecordId appears unchanged, giving a false impression that nothing has changed. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a test that re‑uses the shortRecordId and verifies that an approved third party can still transfer the new short. To remediate, the contract should either burn the NFT or clear its mapping fields when a ShortRecord is closed, and it must enforce a check that the NFT's tokenId equals the ShortRecord's tokenId before allowing any transfer. Additionally, reusing shortRecordIds while an NFT still exists should be prohibited, or the NFT should be required to be re‑minted with a fresh identifier, thereby preventing stale approvals from being leveraged to move new collateral.

title: `oracleCircuitBreaker`: Not checking if price information of asset is stale
description: `oracleCircuitBreaker`: Not checking if price information of asset is stale.
bug_full: An oracle circuit breaker is intended to reject invalid Chainlink data before it is used in price calculations. In the examined contract the function that retrieves an asset price checks that the round identifier is non‑zero, that the reported price is positive and that the timestamp is not in the future, but it never verifies that the timestamp is recent with respect to a configured stale‑limit. The helper oracleCircuitBreaker performs the same incomplete validation and omits the stale‑limit check as well. As a result, if a Chainlink feed for a given asset stops updating, the contract will continue to accept the last reported price indefinitely. Traders who rely on the on‑chain price will then execute swaps, liquidations or collateral checks against a stale value, which can cause them to receive far less assets than expected, trigger unnecessary liquidations, or allow an attacker to front‑run a transaction with a deliberately outdated price. The bug manifests whenever the block timestamp exceeds the stored timestamp plus the asset‑specific chainlinkStaleLimit, a condition that is not currently detected. All users that interact with price‑dependent functions, as well as the protocol’s overall accounting, are affected because the economic assumptions of “price reflects current market” are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the validation logic against the intended design of a circuit breaker. It is subtle because the existing checks appear to protect against obvious errors (zero price, future timestamp) and therefore the stale‑price scenario can go unnoticed until a price feed actually stalls. The proper fix is to store a maximum age for each asset (chainlinkStaleLimit) and to add a condition that rejects the price when block.timestamp is greater than timeStamp plus that limit, both in getOraclePrice and in oracleCircuitBreaker. This ensures that only fresh oracle data is used and restores the intended safety guarantees of the price feed.

title: `ShortOrders` can be created with `ercAmount == minAskEth/2`, increasing the gas costs for matching large orders and disincentivizing liquidators from liquidating them
description: A user can create a `ShortOrder` with `ercAmount == minAskEth/2` by matching the `ShortOrder` with a bid that fills it up to `minAskEth/2` and exiting the `ShortRecord` leaving only `minAskEth/2` in the `ShortOrder` with an empty `ShortRecord`.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the creation of a ShortOrder whose ERC20 amount (ercAmount) is only half of the protocol‑defined minimum ask amount (minAskEth). The contract’s validation routine checkShortMinErc() verifies that an order meets the minimum size but fails to ensure that the order being examined is not already marked as Cancelled. Because cancelled orders are still stored in the order book, an attacker can first create a short order, cancel it, and then reuse its identifier to submit a new bid that partially fills the order only up to minAskEth/2. After the partial fill, the associated ShortRecord is exited, leaving an empty ShortRecord while the ShortOrder remains with ercAmount equal to minAskEth/2. From a user’s perspective the order appears in the market but carries a dust‑sized amount that cannot be efficiently matched; liquidators attempting to close large positions encounter unexpectedly high gas consumption and may be discouraged from performing liquidations. The impact is an increase in gas costs for matching large orders, a potential denial‑of‑service vector that hampers the protocol’s liquidation mechanism, and a deviation from the intended accounting guarantees that each short must meet the minimum ask threshold. The issue manifests whenever the dust factor is set to 0.5 (or any value that permits a half‑size order) and when the contract reuses order identifiers without checking the Cancelled flag. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a test that creates a tiny short order, cancels it, and then exits the short record while the tiny order persists. The bug is hard to notice because the order still satisfies the basic non‑zero amount check and passes the minAsk validation due to the halved value, making it look like a legitimate order. The recommended remediation is to extend the validation logic to reject orders whose type is Cancelled before applying the minimum‑size check, ensuring that cancelled orders cannot be reused to create undersized positions. Conceptually, this is a state‑inconsistency bug where stale order metadata is reused, violating the protocol’s invariant that every active short must respect the minimum ask amount, leading to accounting anomalies and increased operational costs.

title: Using cached price to create a proposal reduce the efficacity of redemptions for asset peg
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the redemption workflow using a cached oracle price instead of a fresh market price when evaluating short positions. In Ditto, oracle prices are refreshed only when an action related to shorts, such as a liquidation, is executed. The liquidation facet explicitly calls the oracle update before processing the short, but the redemption facet does not trigger an update and instead reads the price via LibOracle.getPrice, which returns the last cached value. This design creates a time‑of‑check‑to‑time‑of‑use (TOCTOU) mismatch: the collateral ratio of a short is calculated with a stale price that may no longer reflect the current market during periods of high volatility. An attacker can submit a redemption proposal after a rapid price movement, while the cached price still shows a higher collateral value. The contract then believes the short is sufficiently collateralised, allowing the attacker to redeem the short at a 1:1 exchange rate based on the outdated price. The protocol consequently hands out assets that are under‑collateralised, eroding the peg of the stable asset and potentially generating bad debt. The impact is that the protocol’s treasury can lose value, users may receive less value than expected, and the overall peg stability is compromised. The issue manifests when the market price changes quickly between the last oracle update (triggered by a liquidation) and a subsequent redemption transaction. All participants who rely on the redemption mechanism – short holders, liquidity providers, and end‑users – are affected because the protocol may dispense assets that are not fully backed. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the conditions for oracle updates and noticed that redemption does not satisfy the update clause. It is subtle because the UI shows a successful redemption and the price feed appears correct elsewhere, making the loss of peg appear unrelated to the transaction. The bug belongs to the class of stale‑oracle‑data or price‑caching vulnerabilities, where a contract uses outdated external data for critical financial calculations. From a user perspective, a redemption may complete normally, but later the stablecoin price deviates, balances may appear unchanged or lower than expected, and the protocol may show missing collateral. To remediate, the redemption logic should obtain a fresh price by calling a function that forces a spot oracle read, such as LibOracle.getSavedOrSpotOraclePrice, or otherwise ensure that the price is updated before the collateral ratio is computed. This eliminates the reliance on stale data and restores correct accounting for redemption operations.

title: If a redemption has `N` disputable shorts, it is possible to dispute `N-1` times the redemption to maximize the penalty
description:
Ditto is a decentralized CDP protocol allowing users to get stablecoins (called dUSD here) against LST (Liquid Staking Tokens like stETH or rETH) collateral. Depositing LST grant dETH, a shares representing the value deposited in ETH. Users can then open different kind of positions: bids, asks or shorts, each one having its own orderbook.

Ditto implemented a mechanism called Redemption, idea borrowed from [Liquity](https://docs.liquity.org/faq/lusd-redemptions). Redemption allows anyone to redeem dUSD for a value of exactly 1 USD by calling out shorts with very bad CR (collateral ratio) and closing them. This helps the protocol to keep a healthy global market CR, shorters to not be liquidated, and dUSD holders to redeem dUSD with no loss in case of dUSD trading below 1 USD.

Users can propose multiple shorts to be redeemed at once if they meet certain conditions ([see Constraints in doc](https://dittoeth.com/technical/redemptions#proposing-a-redemption)). The shorts must be sorted from lowest CR to highest CR, and all CRs must be below a CR of 2. If a proposal do not properly follow these rules, anyone can dispute the proposal by showing a proof-short: all proposal shorts with a CR higher than the proof become invalid.

For each invalid short, a penalty is applied to the redeemer (and awarded to the disputer). The penalty calculation is based on the CR difference between the `disputeCR` (proof) and the `currentProposal.CR` (lowest invalid CR):

_Note: please see scenario in warden’s[original submission](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-dittoeth-findings/issues/110)._

The issue is located in this part of the mechanism and is pretty easy to understand. Let’s imagine 4 shorts in a list of shorts: … `< CR1 < CR2 < CR3 < CR4 <` … `CR1 = 1.1, CR2 = 1.2, CR3 = 1.3, CR4 = 1.4`, and all have an `ercDebt` of 1 ETH.

Redeemer propose `[CR2, CR3, CR4]` to redeem.

Disputer sees that there is in fact CR1 that is lower than all the proposed shorts.

Disputer could dispute the proposal by giving CR1 as a proof, and CR2 as the invalid CR, which would also invalid all higher CRs in the proposal. This would give (let’s take `callerFeePct` value from tests, 0.005 or 0.5%):

  1. `penaltyPct =` `min( max(0.005, (1.2 - 1.1)/1.2 ), 0.33) = min( max(0.005, 0.091), 0.33) = 0.091`.
  2. `penaltyAmt =` `(1 + 1 + 1)ETH * 0.091 = 3 * 0.091 = 0.273 ETH`.

The vulnerability lies in the fact that the disputer can dispute this proposal 3 times:

  * 1st: dispute CR4 with CR1.
  * 2nd: dispute CR3 with CR1.
  * 3rd: dispute CR2 with CR1.

By doing this, the disputer will get penalty applied 3 times, and in some case, the total penalty using this trick will be higher than the penalty when disputing the whole proposal at once, as shown in the coded proof of concept.

For CR1:

  1. `penaltyPct =` `min( max(0.005, (1.4 - 1.1)/1.4 ), 0.33) = 0.214`.
  2. `penaltyAmt =` `1 ETH * 0.214 = 0.214 ETH`.

For CR2:

  1. `penaltyPct =` `min( max(0.005, (1.3 - 1.1)/1.3 ), 0.33) = 0.142`.
  2. `penaltyAmt =` `1 ETH * 0.142 = 0.142 ETH`.

For CR3:

  1. `penaltyPct =` `min( max(0.005, (1.2 - 1.1)/1.2 ), 0.33) = 0.091`.
  2. `penaltyAmt =` `1 ETH * 0.091 =` `0.091 ETH`.

`sum of penaltyAmt = 0.447 ETH`.

We can see here how more beneficial it to adopt the second strategy.
poc:
Copy [this gist](https://gist.github.com/InfectedIsm/036947553bdfc984a19b929eea4aade5) to `test/Redemption.t.sol` and run the tests by executing `forge test -vvv --mt AuditDisputeRedemption`.

You’ll get that output, showing that disputing redemptions one by one give a higher penalty:

Running 2 tests for test/Redemption.t.sol:RedemptionTest
[PASS] test_AuditDisputeRedemptionAllAtOnce() (gas: 2213036)
Logs:
  redeemer reward: 7.69230769230769231e21

[PASS] test_AuditDisputeRedemptionOneByOne() (gas: 2250699)
Logs:
  redeemer reward: 3.846153846153846155e21
  redeemer reward: 4.166666666666666665e21
bug_full: The issue is a logical flaw in the redemption dispute mechanism of a decentralized CDP protocol that allows a disputer to claim the penalty reward multiple times from a single redemption proposal. The protocol requires redemption proposals to list short positions sorted by increasing collateral ratio (CR) and to include only shorts whose CR is below a global threshold. When a proposal omits a short with a lower CR than any of the listed shorts, an attacker can submit a dispute using that omitted short as the proof‑short. The contract then marks every short in the proposal with a CR higher than the proof as invalid and awards a penalty based on the difference between the proof CR and the lowest invalid CR. Because the contract does not enforce that the dispute targets the highest invalid index, the attacker can repeat the dispute three times, each time using the same proof‑short but a different invalid short, thereby receiving three separate penalty payouts. The cumulative penalty obtained by splitting the dispute can exceed the penalty that would be awarded if the whole proposal were disputed at once, effectively allowing the attacker to “double‑dip” on the same set of shorts. This flaw occurs whenever a redemption proposal contains more than one short and there exists a lower‑CR short that is not part of the proposal, which is a common situation given the sorting requirement. The affected parties are the redeemer, who receives a lower reward than expected, and the protocol, which loses additional funds to the disputer. The vulnerability was uncovered during an audit by constructing a proof‑of‑concept test that compared the reward when disputing all shorts at once versus disputing them one by one, revealing a higher total penalty in the latter case. The problem is subtle because each individual dispute appears to calculate a correct penalty, and the contract does not track whether a short has already been used as a proof, making the cumulative over‑payment easy to miss in a superficial review. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of incentive‑gaming or “partial claim” exploits where a protocol’s accounting assumes a single, atomic claim but permits repeated partial claims. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a redemption transaction yields a smaller dUSD reward or even zero, while the disputer’s address shows an unexpectedly large increase in ETH balance. The business logic that redemption should preserve the protocol’s overall collateral ratio and fairly compensate participants is violated because the same collateral is effectively penalised multiple times. The recommended mitigation is to enforce that the index of the last invalid short in the proposal must not exceed the proof‑short’s CR; specifically, the contract should revert if proposal[N‑1].CR is less than or equal to disputeCR, preventing the attacker from selecting a lower‑CR proof for a subset of the proposal and thereby eliminating the ability to split the penalty across multiple disputes.

title: Valid redemption proposals can be disputed when bad debt occurs by applying it to a SR outside of the proposal
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the accounting of bad debt and the protocol’s state‑tracking timestamp. When the system incurs bad debt, the debt is spread across all short positions by raising a global debt rate (ercDebtRate). The internal routine that applies a portion of this debt to an individual short record (updateErcDebt) correctly increases the short’s recorded debt and updates its collateral‑to‑debt ratio (CR), but it fails to refresh the short’s last‑updated timestamp (updatedAt). Because the timestamp is unchanged, external logic that relies on the freshness of a short’s state – such as the disputeRedemption check that compares CRs at the moment a redemption proposal is challenged – can be tricked into using stale CR data. An attacker can therefore create a legitimate redemption proposal, wait for bad debt to be socialized, and then invoke a function (proposeRedemption) that internally calls updateErcDebt on a short that is not part of the proposal. This action pushes the short’s CR below the required threshold without moving the updatedAt marker. When the attacker later disputes the redemption, the protocol believes the short in the proposal is under‑collateralized and awards the attacker the penalty fee, effectively stealing funds that should have been returned to the original redeemer. The issue manifests only when bad debt occurs and when a redemption proposal is later disputed; it does not appear during normal redemption execution because the timestamp remains unchanged. Users experience the symptom of a redemption that should succeed but instead results in an unexpected penalty, or they see their balance reduced without a clear reason. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑stale‑timestamp” or “inconsistent accounting” vulnerabilities, where a financial invariant is violated because a bookkeeping field is not updated alongside a value change. It is hard to notice because the debt update is internal and the timestamp field is not directly displayed in most UI components, so the discrepancy does not raise an immediate alarm. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which added a test that showed the updatedAt field remained identical before and after a proposal that triggered a debt update. To remediate, the protocol should either update the updatedAt field every time updateErcDebt modifies a short, or ensure that disputeRedemption re‑evaluates the short’s debt and CR by calling updateErcDebt on the relevant record before performing the collateral check. Either approach restores the invariant that any change to a short’s financial state is reflected in its freshness metadata, preventing the attacker from exploiting stale CR values to claim penalties.

title: In case a gauge weight reduction is performed via `GaugeController::change_gauge_weight`, it is possible that all functions will stop functioning permanently for that gauge
description: If the weight of a given gauge has been manually changed using the `GaugeController::change_gauge_weight` function, all functions related to that gauge might become permanently DoSed.
poc: This issue has been reported in [this](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-verwa-findings/issues/206) and [this](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-verwa-findings/issues/386) report from the previous Code4rena audit of the codebase. However, by the looks of it, no fix has been applied in order to mitigate it, so it is still present.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a permanent denial‑of‑service condition that can be triggered when the weight of a gauge is reduced using the GaugeController.change_gauge_weight function. The root cause lies in the accounting logic that updates the bias and slope of a point (pt) representing the gauge’s voting power. When the new weight causes the change in slope (d_slope) to be larger than the current pt.slope, the contract attempts to subtract a larger value from a smaller one, which results in an underflow or a negative slope that is not properly clamped. Because the contract does not guard against this situation, subsequent calls that rely on a valid pt.slope – such as deposit, withdraw, or reward distribution – revert or behave incorrectly, effectively rendering the gauge inoperable. An attacker or any user with permission to call change_gauge_weight can deliberately lower the gauge weight, causing the slope underflow and freezing all gauge‑related functions. The impact is that users can no longer interact with the affected gauge: deposits return no tokens, withdrawals fail, and rewards are never distributed, leading to locked or disappearing funds from the perspective of the end‑user. This condition occurs only after a weight reduction event; normal operation with unchanged or increased weight does not exhibit the problem, which makes it hard to notice during routine testing. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit and reported in two public issue trackers, but no remediation has been applied. From a user’s point of view the UI may show a zero balance, missing rewards, or transactions that simply do nothing, contradicting the expectation that a gauge should continue to accept deposits and issue rewards. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic underflow/overflow errors in state‑update logic, specifically when a subtraction is performed without checking that the minuend is larger than the subtrahend. To fix the problem the contract should enforce a lower bound of zero on pt.slope (and similarly on pt.bias) before performing the subtraction, for example by checking if pt.slope >= d_slope and otherwise setting pt.slope to zero. This ensures that the gauge’s accounting variables never become negative, preserving the ability of all gauge functions to operate after a weight change.

title: `GaugeController::remove_gauge` will always revert whenever the gauge it’s being called or has any weight attached to it
description: `GaugeController::remove_gauge` will always revert when it is called for gauges with weight that is `!= 0`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance function that removes a gauge from the system. When the function is invoked for a gauge that currently holds a non‑zero weight, the transaction always reverts. The root cause is the order in which state variables are mutated: the implementation first clears the gauge type mapping for the target gauge and only afterwards calls the internal routine that subtracts the gauge’s weight from the global accounting structures. Because the gauge type has already been set to zero, the internal routine reads an invalid type index (effectively -1) and performs arithmetic on mappings that no longer correspond to a real gauge type. This leads to an under‑flow or arithmetic panic (code 0x11) and forces the whole call to revert. An attacker or honest governor cannot successfully remove an active gauge; the contract will reject the operation and the gauge remains registered with its weight still accounted for. From a user’s perspective the transaction fails with a generic panic error, the UI may still display the gauge as present, and the expectation that the gauge will be deleted is not met. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on governance actions: any urgent need to retire a gauge requires an additional proposal to work around the bug, delaying protocol upgrades or fund reallocation. The issue is discovered during a formal audit and reproduced with a test that expects a panic when remove_gauge is called after voting for weight. It is hard to notice because the function works correctly for gauges with zero weight, so the failure only appears under specific state conditions. The bug belongs to the class of state‑mutation‑order errors that cause arithmetic under‑flow or invalid indexing, similar to “remove‑before‑cleanup” patterns. To fix the problem the contract should invoke the weight‑removal routine before clearing the gauge type, or otherwise preserve the original gauge type while performing the subtraction, ensuring that the accounting updates reference a valid type. This change restores the intended behavior where a gauge can be removed regardless of its current weight, eliminating the revert and allowing governance to manage gauges safely.

title: Issue from previous audit still present: Gauge can have bigger weight than was intended by protocol
description:
[M-01 from previous audit is still present](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-verwa-findings/issues/294). In this issue, the sponsor said [they fixed it](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-verwa-findings/issues/294#issuecomment-1698755740). I tried to check how it was fixed, but the link doesn’t work for me.

But `change_gauge_weight` function [still exists](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-neobase/blob/main/src/GaugeController.sol#L346-L348) which makes it possible to reproduce this. Also `remove_gauge_weight` function is present, that allows [to completely remove gauge](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-neobase/blob/main/src/GaugeController.sol#L378-L380) and i think that fix was to remove `change_gauge_weight` function.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unrestricted gauge weight modification mechanism that allows a gauge to acquire a weight larger than the protocol intends. The root cause is the presence of a public function that can change a gauge's weight without adequate access control or validation of the new weight against protocol limits. Because the function remains in the contract, an attacker or any privileged caller can invoke it to inflate the weight of a chosen gauge, and a separate function can even remove the gauge entirely. This can be exploited by calling the weight‑change function with an arbitrarily high value, causing the reward distribution algorithm to allocate a disproportionate share of rewards to the manipulated gauge. The impact is a distortion of the accounting model: users who expect a fair share of rewards may receive less, while the manipulated gauge may drain the reward pool, effectively causing funds to disappear from the perspective of honest participants. The issue manifests whenever the weight‑change function is executed, which can happen at any time because there is no guard preventing excessive values. All participants in the protocol, including token holders, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts that rely on correct gauge weighting, are affected. The problem was originally identified in a prior audit (referred to as M‑01) and was claimed to be fixed, but the function still exists in the current codebase, indicating that the fix was not applied. Because the weight values are stored on‑chain and the UI may simply display the current weight, the over‑allocation can be subtle and may only become apparent when the reward pool is unexpectedly depleted or when users notice that their expected rewards are lower than anticipated. To remediate the issue, the change_gauge_weight function should be removed entirely or, if retained, must be protected by strict access controls and enforce that any new weight respects the protocol’s maximum allowed weight, ensuring that the accounting invariants remain intact. This class of bug falls under improper access control and unchecked arithmetic in governance‑related state updates, leading to reward misallocation and potential loss of funds.

title: Improper adjustment of Lending Ledger configuration
description:
The `LendingLedger` utilizes an approximation system (to evaluate the time that has elapsed between two block numbers) which contains adjustable values. Additionally, it permits the governance to adjust the `cantoPerBlock` value of multiple epochs at any time.

The way these values are adjusted is insecure and thus can cause them to retroactively apply to markets that have not yet been updated.

In the case of the `LendingLedger::setBlockTimeParameters`, a notice exists within the `LendingLedger::update_market` function that warns that:
