This logic error occurs whenever a withdraw or repay is executed before a deposit or borrow in the same day, or when the day boundary is crossed and the reset runs after the increase. The root cause is the incorrect ordering of the reset and increment operations, which prevents the intended replenishment of the daily caps. An attacker could exploit this by repeatedly triggering withdrawals or repayments to cause the reset to overwrite the counters, thereby keeping the daily limits artificially low and preventing legitimate users from depositing or borrowing, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition. Users may observe that after a successful withdrawal they are immediately blocked by a DailyLendIncreaseLimit error, or that repayments do not restore borrowing capacity, even though the contract’s UI suggests they should. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena through manual code review and logical analysis of the daily‑limit handling. It is subtle because the increment statements appear correct in isolation, but the subsequent reset masks their effect, making the bug easy to miss in testing. The proper fix is to adjust the order of operations: either move the reset call before the increment, or ensure the increment is applied after the reset so that the daily counters reflect the net change correctly. In conceptual terms, the bug belongs to the class of state‑invariant violations where a mutable accounting variable is unintentionally overwritten, breaking the protocol’s business logic that assumes daily limits are replenished after withdrawals or repayments.

title: Liquidation reward sent to msg.sender instead of recipient
description:
```solidity
When performing liquidation the liquidator will fill the `LiquidateParams` containing the liquidation details. The issue here is that instead of sending the liquidation rewards to the `LiquidateParams.recipient`, the rewards will be sent to `msg.sender`.

The liquidation rewards will be sent to `msg.sender` instead of the recipient, any external logic that relies on the fact that the liquidation rewards will be sent to recipient won’t hold; this will influence the protocol’s composability.
```
poc:
```solidity
In order to keep the system safe the liquidator can and is incentivised to liquidate unhealthy positions. To do so the `liquidate()` function will be fired with the appropriate parameters. One of those parameters is the `address recipient;`; the name is quite intuitive for this one, this is where the liquidation rewards are expected to sent.

But if we follow the `liquidation()` function logic, the rewards will not be sent to recipient address. This [piece of code](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/435b054f9ad2404173f36f0f74a5096c894b12b7/src/V3Vault.sol#L741-L742) handles the reward distribution.
    
    (amount0, amount1) =
        _sendPositionValue(params.tokenId, state.liquidationValue, 
        state.fullValue, state.feeValue, msg.sender); 

We can see that `msg.sender` is being used instead of `params.recipient`.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reward misdirection flaw that occurs during the liquidation process of a lending vault. When a liquidator invokes the liquidation routine, the contract receives a structure containing a recipient address that is intended to receive the liquidation rewards. However, the implementation mistakenly forwards those rewards to the caller of the function (msg.sender) instead of the designated recipient. The root cause is the use of the global caller variable rather than the explicit recipient field when invoking the internal value‑transfer helper. An attacker can exploit this by simply calling the liquidation function themselves, thereby receiving the full reward that should have been sent to another party, such as a third‑party contract or a user‑specified address. The impact is that any external logic that assumes rewards will be delivered to the recipient – for example composable strategies that rely on forwarding rewards to a treasury or a staking contract – will fail, leading to unexpected loss of funds for the intended beneficiary. This condition manifests whenever the liquidation function is executed, regardless of the health of the position, as long as the caller supplies a recipient address. The affected parties include liquidators, users who delegate liquidation rewards to a separate address, and any downstream protocol components that depend on correct reward routing. The issue was discovered during a manual code review where the auditor compared the parameter usage against the expected business logic and identified the mismatch. It can be hard to notice because the transaction still succeeds and the caller receives a reward, which may appear correct on the surface; only the mismatch between the intended recipient and the actual receiver reveals the flaw. To remediate, the contract should replace the use of msg.sender with the explicit recipient field when calling the internal reward distribution function, ensuring that the reward is sent to the address supplied in the liquidation parameters. This aligns the implementation with the intended accounting model where rewards are allocated to a designated party rather than the transaction originator, preserving composability and correct fund flow.

title: Users’s tokens stuck in `AutoCompound` after Vault is deactivated
description:
```solidity
Users’s tokens stuck in `AutoCompound` after Vault is deactivated.
```
bug_full: The AutoCompound contract allows the contract owner to enable or disable a vault through the setVault function. When a vault is active, a user can deposit a Uniswap V3 position token (NFT) into the vault and later withdraw any leftover token balances using withdrawLeftoverBalances. The function first determines the current owner of the NFT by calling nonfungiblePositionManager.ownerOf. If the stored vault flag for that owner is true, the code replaces the owner variable with the vault’s internal ownerOf result, otherwise it expects the caller to be the NFT owner. The vulnerability arises because the contract does not prevent the owner from deactivating a vault while there are still non‑zero balances recorded in the positionBalances mapping. When the vault is deactivated, vaults[owner] becomes false, the function falls back to the check owner == msg.sender, but the owner variable still points to the vault address (the address that originally held the NFT). Consequently the condition fails and the function reverts with Unauthorized, leaving the user’s token balances permanently locked inside the contract. This bug can be exploited simply by an attacker who is the contract owner: after users have deposited positions, the owner can call setVault with _active = false, causing any subsequent withdrawal attempts to revert and the funds to become inaccessible. The impact is that users lose access to their leftover token0 or token1 amounts, effectively “funds disappear” from their perspective; the UI would show a successful deposit but later attempts to claim refunds return zero or throw an error. The issue manifests only after a vault transition from active to inactive, which is why it may be missed during normal testing that only covers the active path. It affects all participants who rely on AutoCompound’s withdrawal mechanism, breaking the business logic that leftover balances should always be withdrawable. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by reproducing the scenario with a mocked call that forces the ownerOf query to return a non‑vault address after deactivation, causing the revert. The problem is hard to notice because the revert message is generic and the function otherwise works correctly when the vault remains active. To remediate, the contract should either forbid deactivating a vault while any positionBalances entry is non‑zero, or modify withdrawLeftoverBalances to correctly resolve the true token holder after deactivation (for example by checking the original depositor or by allowing the vault to forward withdrawals). In conceptual terms, this is a state‑transition access‑control bug where deactivating a component invalidates a later permission check, leading to locked assets.

title: Lack of safety buffer in `_checkLoanIsHealthy` could subject users who take out the max loan into a forced liquidation
description:
```solidity
The `_checkLoanIsHealthy` function is used in the `V3Vault` to assess a user’s given position and determine the health factor of the loan. As there is no safety buffer when checking the health factor of a given position, users could be subject to a negative health factor if there are minor movements in the market which could result in liquidation or in the worst case scenario, an attacker could force a liquidation on a user and profit by sinking their position in the Uniswap pool.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the absence of a safety margin when the V3Vault contract evaluates a borrower’s health factor in the internal `_checkLoanIsHealthy` routine. The function compares the current collateral‑to‑debt ratio directly against the liquidation threshold without any buffer, allowing a user who borrows up to the maximum permitted amount to hover extremely close to the liquidation point. Because the health check does not require a cushion, even a minor adverse price movement—such as a small shift in the underlying Uniswap pool price caused by a flash‑loan swap—can push the health factor just below the threshold, triggering an immediate liquidation. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately creating a tiny market impact, for example by borrowing a large amount of WETH, swapping it for USDC to depress the WETH/USDC price, and then calling the vault’s `liquidate` function while the borrower’s position is still technically over‑collateralised according to the UI. The attacker profits by seizing the collateral that would otherwise have remained safe. The impact is that legitimate borrowers lose part or all of their deposited collateral despite seeing a “healthy” loan in the front‑end, and the protocol suffers reputational damage because users experience forced liquidations that appear unjustified. The issue occurs whenever a borrower takes the maximum loan allowed by the contract’s collateral factor and the market experiences any small price deviation; it is especially relevant for assets with low volatility buffers or when large flash‑loan attacks are possible. The affected parties include borrowers, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself, as the loss of user funds can reduce overall trust. The flaw was discovered during a Code4rena audit, where a proof‑of‑concept test demonstrated that a malicious actor could flash‑loan WETH, manipulate the pool price, and liquidate a victim’s position that had borrowed the full collateral value. The problem is subtle because the health factor may still read as above the threshold before the price shift, making it hard to notice without detailed simulation. The bug belongs to the class of “missing safety buffer” or “liquidation threshold mis‑check” vulnerabilities, where accounting assumptions about collateral adequacy are violated. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a healthy loan, the user expects the collateral to remain safe, but after a tiny market move the protocol liquidates the position, the user receives no funds back, and the collateral disappears. To remediate, the contract should introduce a configurable safety buffer (for example, allowing borrowing only up to 75 % of the 80 % liquidation threshold) and enforce this buffer both at loan issuance and during liquidation checks, ensuring that even small market fluctuations cannot immediately trigger liquidation.

title: Wrong global lending limit check in `_deposit` function
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect accounting check in the internal _deposit function of a lending protocol. The function verifies that the total amount of assets lent does not exceed a global lending limit, but it mistakenly compares the raw totalSupply value, which represents lender share tokens, directly against the globalLendLimit that is expressed in asset units. Because share tokens and assets are not equivalent, the contract must first convert totalSupply to an asset amount using the protocol's conversion routine (e.g., _convertToAssets) before performing the limit comparison. The root cause is a missing unit conversion step, leading to a mismatch between the metric being checked (shares) and the metric that defines the limit (assets). When the lending exchange rate is greater than one – a normal condition after interest accrues – the converted asset value is larger than the share count, meaning totalSupply will appear smaller than the global limit even though the actual assets lent have already surpassed it. Consequently, the contract allows deposits that push the total assets beyond the intended ceiling. This can be exploited by an attacker who deposits a large amount, causing the share count to increase modestly while the underlying asset exposure grows disproportionately, thereby bypassing the global limit. The protocol may then lend more assets than it is designed to support, increasing the risk of insolvency, unexpected liquidation, or inability to honor withdrawals. The issue manifests when users attempt to deposit after the protocol has technically reached its global lending capacity; the UI may still indicate that deposits are allowed, leading to user confusion as their balances appear normal but later withdrawals fail or the protocol’s health deteriorates. The bug was discovered during a formal audit (Code4rena) by comparing the logic in _deposit with the correct implementation in the maxDeposit view function, which performs the necessary conversion. It is subtle because the share count alone does not raise an alarm, and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the asset limit is exceeded. To remediate, the contract should compute the current asset exposure by converting totalSupply with the latest lend exchange rate and then compare that asset value against globalLendLimit, mirroring the logic used in maxDeposit. This ensures that the protocol enforces its intended risk parameters and prevents over‑lending.

title: User might execute `PositionToken` of token set by previous token owner
description:
The `AutoRange.configToken()` function updates the state variable `positionConfigs` for a `tokenId` and callable by the owner of the `tokenId`. However, in the call to `AutoRange.execute()`, the state variable `positionConfigs` for the `tokenId` is used in setting the local variable `PositionConfig memory config` without any further check to ensure the config has been set by the current owner of the `tokenId`.

This in some way could affect the swapcall on the token position such that the protocol does not receive any incentive.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a missing ownership check on the position configuration used by the AutoRange contract. When a token holder calls configToken, the contract stores a PositionConfig struct in the mapping positionConfigs keyed by the tokenId. This mapping is never cleared or re‑validated when the token is transferred to a new owner. Consequently, the execute function later reads positionConfigs[params.tokenId] without confirming that the configuration was set by the current token owner. An attacker who previously owned the token can therefore set a malicious or outdated configuration, transfer the token, and let the new owner trigger execute with the stale config. The stale config may point to an attacker‑controlled vault, use incorrect tick ranges, or disable the incentive mechanism, causing the protocol to miss expected fees or to execute swaps with the wrong parameters. From a user’s perspective the transaction may complete but yield no reward, or the UI may show a normal swap while the underlying accounting shows zero incentive, leading to confusion and potential loss of value. The issue manifests after a token transfer and before the new owner re‑configures the position, and it affects any operator or vault that is authorized to call execute. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the flow between configToken and execute and noticing that the config is not tied to the current owner. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an event when the config becomes stale, and front‑end checks can be bypassed, making it hard for users to notice that the stored configuration no longer belongs to them. The proper mitigation is to either clear the positionConfigs entry on token transfer, store the owner address inside the PositionConfig and verify it inside execute, or require the new owner to explicitly set a fresh configuration before any automated execution. By enforcing that the configuration originates from the current token holder, the protocol can guarantee that incentive calculations and swap parameters remain consistent with the owner’s expectations, preventing unintended fund routing or incentive loss.

title: `V3Vault` is not ERC-4626 compliant
description: Protocols that try to integrate with Revert Lend, expecting `V3Vault` to be ERC-4626 compliant, will multiple issues that may damage Revert Lend’s brand and limit Revert Lend’s growth in the market.
bug_full: The V3Vault contract is intended to implement the ERC‑4626 tokenized vault standard, but several of its view functions do not conform to the specification, creating a compliance bug that can surface as unexpected transaction failures for users and for any protocol that integrates assuming standard behavior. The root cause lies in the way the contract calculates the maximum amounts that can be deposited, minted, withdrawn, or redeemed. Specifically, the maxDeposit and maxMint functions only consider the global lend limit and ignore the daily lend increase limit, returning a non‑zero value even when the daily limit has been reached. Likewise, maxWithdraw and maxRedeem compute their results based solely on the caller’s share balance without properly capping the amount at the vault’s currently available liquidity, which can cause the functions to report a higher limit than what can actually be withdrawn. When a user attempts to deposit more than the daily limit, the contract reverts with a DailyLendIncreaseLimit error because the maxDeposit value is misleading; similarly, a redemption or withdrawal may revert with an InsufficientLiquidity error when the caller’s balance exceeds the liquid assets in the vault. From the user’s perspective this appears as a situation where “my deposit fails even though I have approved enough tokens” or “my redeem call returns less than my share balance or reverts unexpectedly”, violating the expectation that the max* view functions accurately reflect the actionable limits. The issue is discovered during a formal audit where test cases were written to compare the contract’s return values against the ERC‑4626 reference implementation, revealing mismatches that would be hard to notice in production because the functions are read‑only and do not emit events, so developers may assume they are correct without testing edge cases. The impact is medium severity: it does not directly steal funds, but it can block legitimate user actions, cause integration failures for other protocols, and damage the reputation of Revert Lend by breaking the advertised standard compliance. The bug belongs to the class of “standard compliance violations” where a contract’s public interface does not honor the invariants defined by a widely adopted tokenized‑vault interface, leading to accounting inconsistencies and user‑experience problems. To remediate, the maxDeposit and maxMint functions should be updated to return the lesser of the global lend limit remaining and the daily lend increase limit, while maxWithdraw and maxRedeem must compare the caller’s balance with the vault’s available liquidity and return the smaller of the two, thereby aligning the contract with the ERC‑4626 specification and preventing unexpected reverts.

title: Users’ newly created positions can be prematurely closed and removed from the vault directly after they are created
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic flaw that allows a newly created loan position to be closed and removed from the vault immediately after creation by calling the repay function with a zero amount. When a user creates a position, the contract stores a Loan struct with debtShares set to 0 and registers the NFT in the vault’s ownedTokens mapping. The repay implementation does not require the repayment amount to be greater than zero and treats the case where the current debt shares equal the repaid shares as a full repayment. Because both values are zero for a fresh position, the condition currentShares == shares evaluates to true, triggering the internal _cleanupLoan routine. This routine removes the NFT from the vault’s storage, deletes the loan record and transfers the NFT back to the user, effectively erasing the position. An attacker can exploit this by calling repay(TEST_NFT,0,false) on any freshly minted position, causing the vault to believe the loan is fully repaid even though no debt existed. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style griefing: the original user’s NFT is returned, the position disappears, and any subsequent attempt to borrow against that NFT reverts with an unauthorized error because the contract no longer recognises the position. The issue occurs only for positions that have zero debt, i.e., immediately after creation and before any borrow operation. All users who create a position are potentially affected, and any external actor can trigger the exploit without needing special permissions. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit and confirmed with a Forge test that reproduces the griefing scenario. It is hard to notice because a zero‑value repay call appears innocuous and the contract does not emit any warning; the state transition silently deletes the loan. The bug belongs to the class of insufficient input validation leading to incorrect state transitions, specifically treating a zero‑value operation as a successful full repayment. From a user’s perspective the NFT that was expected to stay locked in the vault is suddenly back in their wallet, yet attempts to borrow fail, violating the expectation that a newly created position can be used to obtain credit. The correct mitigation is to add explicit validation in the repay function that rejects calls with amount == 0 or that target loans with zero debtShares, and to revert with a clear error before any state changes are performed. This prevents the premature cleanup and preserves the intended lifecycle of loan positions.

title: Repayments and liquidations can be forced to revert by an attacker that repays minuscule amount of shares
description:
At the moment, both `repay` and `liquidate` calls will fail if the amount of shares that the transaction attempts to repay exceeds the outstanding debt shares of the position, with `RepayExceedsDebt` and `DebtChanged` errors respectively.

This enables an attacker to keep repaying very small amounts, such as 1 share, of the debt, causing user/liquidator transactions to fail.

The attack exposes risks for users who are close to the liquidation theshold from increasing their position’s health, and also from self-liquidating their positions once they’re already below the threshold.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service logic error in the repayment and liquidation pathways of the lending vault. The contract enforces a strict check that the number of shares supplied to a repay or liquidate call must not exceed the current outstanding debt shares of the position. When an attacker deliberately repays an extremely small amount of debt – for example one share – the remaining debt shares become slightly lower than the amount a legitimate borrower or liquidator later tries to repay (often the full debt amount). Because the contract does not allow an over‑payment and does not return any excess tokens, the subsequent call hits the RepayExceedsDebt or DebtChanged revert conditions and fails. This can be exploited by front‑running a borrower’s transaction: the attacker first makes a tiny repayment, then the borrower’s attempt to repay the full balance or to self‑liquidate reverts, leaving the position unable to improve its health factor or to be liquidated safely. The impact is that users close to the liquidation threshold may be forced into an involuntary liquidation by the attacker, or may be unable to rescue their position, potentially resulting in loss of collateral. The issue manifests after interest accrues and the debt is non‑zero, whenever an attacker can obtain a minimal amount of the repayment token and execute a repay of one share before the victim’s transaction is mined. It affects any borrower, liquidator, or protocol participant who relies on the ability to repay or liquidate a position. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit through crafted test cases that simulated front‑running scenarios. It is hard to notice because a repayment of a single share appears harmless and the contract’s error messages (RepayExceedsDebt, DebtChanged) do not clearly indicate a denial‑of‑service condition. The flaw belongs to the class of over‑payment handling or input‑validation bugs where the contract does not tolerate excess repayment amounts. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a transaction revert with an unexpected error, the expected health‑factor improvement never occurs, and the collateral may be seized unexpectedly. To remediate, the repayment function should accept any amount, cap the effective repayment at the outstanding debt shares, and return any surplus tokens to the caller. Likewise, liquidation should be allowed with an amount up to the current debt shares without requiring an exact match, preventing the attacker from forcing a revert by shrinking the debt by a tiny amount.

title: `AutoExit` could receive a reward calculated from the entire position’s fund even if `onlyFee` is true in `AutoExit.execute`
description: The owner of the NFT could end up paying more rewards to `AutoExit` than anticipated when `onlyFee` is set to true.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the AutoExit contract where the reward that is deducted from a liquidity provider’s position is calculated from a variable named feeAmount0/feeAmount1. In the normal flow these variables are intended to represent only the fees accrued by the Uniswap V3 position. However, the internal function _decreaseFullLiquidityAndCollect first calls decreaseLiquidity, which withdraws a portion of the underlying liquidity, and then calls collect, which returns the total amount of tokens that includes both the accrued fees and the assets that were just withdrawn by the decreaseLiquidity call. The contract then recomputes feeAmount0 and feeAmount1 by subtracting the amount returned from decreaseLiquidity, assuming the remainder corresponds solely to fees. When the onlyFee flag is set to true, AutoExit.execute subtracts a reward proportional to feeAmount0 and feeAmount1 from the user’s remaining balances. Because feeAmount incorrectly contains the withdrawn liquidity as well as the fees, the reward calculation mistakenly uses the entire position’s value instead of just the fee portion. An attacker controlling the operator role can trigger execute after a user has already called decreaseLiquidity, causing the operator to receive a larger reward than expected. From the user’s perspective the UI shows that the NFT position has been reduced more than anticipated, or that a refund is missing, even though the user only authorized fee collection. The impact is a loss of up to roughly two percent of the position value for the affected liquidity provider, while other participants remain unaffected. The issue appears only when onlyFee is true and the owner has previously decreased liquidity before the AutoExit execution. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the relationship between the feeAmount variables and the reward logic, noting that the naming of the variables masked the inclusion of withdrawn assets. The bug is hard to notice because the code comments refer to feeAmount as “fees only” and the collect call aggregates both fees and liquidity withdrawals, which is not obvious without deep inspection of Uniswap V3’s accounting model. To remediate, the contract should compute the fee amounts exclusively from the feeGrowthInside metric of the position, or otherwise separate the fee accounting from the liquidity withdrawal accounting, ensuring that the onlyFee path never incorporates assets that originated from a liquidity decrease. This aligns the reward calculation with the intended business logic that rewards should be based solely on accrued fees, preserving user expectations that setting onlyFee true limits deductions to fee earnings only.

title: Users cannot stop loss in AutoRange and AutoExit
description:
Users cannot stop loss in AutoRange and AutoExit, resulting in huge loss.
  * Users cannot withdraw their tokens and cut loss even when they choose no swap option.
bug_full: The issue is a loss‑prevention failure in the AutoRange and AutoExit automators. The contracts are designed to let a user withdraw their liquidity without performing a token swap by setting amountIn to zero. However, the internal function _validateSwap is invoked unconditionally, even when no swap is requested. _validateSwap checks that the current Uniswap V3 tick does not deviate from the time‑weighted‑average‑price (TWAP) tick by more than a configurable maxTickDifference. If the price move exceeds this threshold – which is limited to 200 ticks (approximately a 1 % change when the default is 100) – the function reverts with TWAPCheckFailed. Because the revert occurs after the liquidity has already been decreased and the tokens are ready to be returned, the whole transaction rolls back and the user’s withdrawal never happens. From the user’s perspective the transaction simply fails, the UI shows a generic error, and the expected balance does not change; the user cannot cut the loss and the funds remain locked, potentially incurring further loss as the market continues to move. The bug is rooted in the contract’s logic that treats the TWAP check as mandatory for every execution path, rather than only for actual swaps. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a test that mocks a 1 % price drop and observes that a no‑swap withdrawal reverts. The problem is subtle because the function name _validateSwap suggests it only applies to swaps, and the amountIn parameter being zero is not used to bypass the check. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “unconditional validation leading to denial‑of‑service” bugs, where a safety check intended for one operation blocks another legitimate operation. To remediate, the contract should skip the TWAP validation when amountIn is zero (i.e., when no swap is intended) or handle a false return from _hasMaxTWAPTickDifference without reverting, allowing the withdrawal to complete. Adjusting the maxTickDifference limit or making it optional per execution could also mitigate the risk, but the core fix is to decouple the loss‑cutting path from the swap‑only validation logic.

title: Missing L2 sequencer checks for Chainlink oracle
description:
Note: This finding was reported via the winning [Automated Findings report](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/main/bot-report.md). It was declared out of scope for the audit, but is being included here for completeness.

[337](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/ac520c5fedf4e1654c597a46efaf5a7c27295de1/src/V3Oracle.sol#L337)
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an absent access‑control check on the function that records price data from a Layer‑2 (L2) sequencer into a Chainlink oracle contract. The oracle contract, identified in V3Oracle.sol, is designed to accept price updates only from a trusted L2 sequencer that aggregates off‑chain data and signs the result. Because the contract does not verify that the caller is the authorized sequencer, any external address can invoke the update routine and supply arbitrary price values. This flaw originates from a missing sequencer‑identity validation step, which is a classic case of unchecked external input in a price‑feed contract. An attacker who can submit a transaction to the oracle can therefore inject a manipulated price, causing downstream protocols that rely on the oracle—such as lending, borrowing, or liquidation mechanisms—to compute incorrect collateral ratios, trigger unwarranted liquidations, or allow the attacker to withdraw more assets than entitled. The exploit is straightforward: the attacker calls the price‑update function with a crafted value, the contract records it without restriction, and the altered price propagates to all dependent contracts. The impact is financial loss for users, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential systemic risk if the oracle feeds multiple markets. The condition for the bug to manifest is any invocation of the price‑update entry point; there is no role‑based gating, so the attack can be performed by any account that can pay gas on the L2 network. The affected parties include protocol users (borrowers, lenders), the protocol’s treasury, and any third‑party contracts that reference the oracle. The issue was discovered by an automated static‑analysis tool that flagged the missing sequencer check, a finding that was reported in an automated findings report and marked out of scope for the broader audit. The problem can be subtle because normal operation with the legitimate sequencer appears functional, and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when an unauthorized update occurs, making the bug easy to overlook during manual testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce a strict access control mechanism—such as an onlySequencer modifier or a require statement that compares msg.sender against a stored, immutable sequencer address—ensuring that only the designated sequencer can submit price data. This change restores the intended trust model, prevents arbitrary price manipulation, and aligns the contract’s behavior with the business logic that assumes a single source of truth for market prices.

title: `V3Oracle` susceptible to price manipulation
description:
`V3Oracle::getValue()` is used to calculate the value of a position. The value is the product of the `oracle price * the amounts held in the position`. Price manipulation is prevented by checking for differences between Chainlink oracle and Uniswap TWAP.

However, the amounts (`amount0` and `amount1`) of the tokens in the position are calculated based on the current pool price (`pool.spot0()`), which means they can be manipulated. Since the value of the total position is calculated from `amount0` and `amount1` it can be manipulated as well.
poc:
Invoking `V3Oracle::getValue()` first calls the `getPositionBreakdown()` to calculate the `amount0` and `amount1` of the tokens in the position based on spot price:

```solidity
     (address token0, address token1, uint24 fee,, uint256 amount0, uint256 amount1, uint256 fees0, uint256 fees1) =
                getPositionBreakdown(tokenId);
```

Under the hood this calls `_initializeState()` which gets the current price in the pool: 

```solidity
    (state.sqrtPriceX96, state.tick,,,,,) = state.pool.slot0();
```

Based on this value the `amount0` and `amount1` (returned from `getPositionBreakdown()` are deduced:

```solidity
    function _getAmounts(PositionState memory state)
            internal
            view
            returns (uint256 amount0, uint256 amount1, uint128 fees0, uint128 fees1)
        {
            if (state.liquidity > 0) {
           ....
                (amount0, amount1) = LiquidityAmounts.getAmountsForLiquidity(
                    state.sqrtPriceX96, state.sqrtPriceX96Lower, state.sqrtPriceX96Upper, state.liquidity
                );
            }
           ....
        }
```

After that, the prices are fetched from Uniswap & Chainlink and compared.
    
```solidity
     (price0X96, cachedChainlinkReferencePriceX96) =
                _getReferenceTokenPriceX96(token0, cachedChainlinkReferencePriceX96);
     (price1X96, cachedChainlinkReferencePriceX96) =
                _getReferenceTokenPriceX96(token1, cachedChainlinkReferencePriceX96);
```

Finally, the value of the positions tokens and fees are calculated in the following formula:
    
```solidity
    value = (price0X96 * (amount0 + fees0) / Q96 + price1X96 * (amount1 + fees1) / Q96) * Q96 / priceTokenX96;
    feeValue = (price0X96 * fees0 / Q96 + price1X96 * fees1 / Q96) * Q96 / priceTokenX96;
    price0X96 = price0X96 * Q96 / priceTokenX96;
    price1X96 = price1X96 * Q96 / priceTokenX96;
```

Basically the position value is a product of 2 parameters `price0X96/price1X96` and `amount0/amount1`:

  * `price0X96/price1X96` - are the prices derived from the oracles. They are validated and cannot be manipulated.
  * `amount0/amount1` - are calculated based on the spot price and can be manipulated.

Since `amount0` and `amount1` can be increased/decreased if a malicious user decides to distort the pool price in the current block (through a flash loan for example), this will directly impact the calculated value, even though the price itself cannot be manipulated since it is protected against manipulation.

The check in the end `_checkPoolPrice()` only verifies that the price from the oracles is in the the acceptable ranges. However, this does not safeguard the value calculation, which as explained above also includes the `amounts` parameters.

It should be noted that `_checkPoolPrice` uses the uniswap TWAP price for comparison, which is the price over an extended period of time making it very hard to manipulate in a single block. And exactly this property of the TWAP price can allow an attacker to manipulate the spot price significantly, without affecting the TWAP much; which means the price difference won’t change much and `_checkPoolPrice` will pass.

A short example:

  * The `V3Oracle` has been configured to use a TWAP duration of 1 hour.
  * The TWAP price reported for the last hour is 4000 USDC for 1 WETH.
  * Bob takes a flash loan to distort the spot price heavily and call in the same transaction `borrow` | `repay` on a V3Vault (which call `V3Oracle.getValue()`).
  * Because of the price manipulation `amount1` and `amount0` are heavily inflated/deflated.
  * However this changes the TWAP value only a little (if at all), so the price validation passes.
  * The position value is calculated by multiplying the stable oracle price by the heavily manipulated amounts.
  * User repay/borrows at favorable conditions.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the V3Oracle.getValue() routine that derives the token amounts of a liquidity position from the pool’s current spot price (the value returned by slot0) and then multiplies those amounts by oracle‑derived prices to obtain the total position value. Because the spot price is taken directly from the pool state, an attacker who can temporarily distort the pool price – for example by using a flash loan to perform a large swap in the same block – can inflate or deflate amount0 and amount1. The contract later validates the oracle price against a Uniswap TWAP, but the TWAP aggregates price over a long interval and therefore does not reflect the instantaneous spot manipulation. Consequently the price check passes while the manipulated amounts cause the computed value to be far higher or lower than the true market value. This allows a malicious user to borrow more assets, repay less, or otherwise extract excess value from the protocol. The issue appears only when getValue() is called after a spot‑price distortion within the same transaction and when the TWAP window is longer than a single block, which is the typical configuration. All participants that rely on the oracle‑reported position value – lenders, borrowers, and any external contracts that read the value – are affected because the accounting logic can be tricked into believing a position is worth more than it actually is. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit by tracing the flow of getValue() and noticing that amount0/amount1 are calculated from the mutable spot price rather than the protected oracle price. The bug is subtle because the contract visibly checks the oracle price, giving the impression that price manipulation is impossible, while the hidden dependence on spot‑derived amounts is easy to overlook. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may include an unexpected jump or drop in the displayed position value, balances that appear to disappear or inflate, and fees that are calculated incorrectly. This class of bug can be described as a “spot‑price‑derived amount manipulation” where the accounting formula mixes a trusted price feed with an untrusted, manipulable quantity. The recommended mitigation is to compute amount0 and amount1 from the same oracle price used for valuation, or otherwise decouple the amount calculation from the instantaneous spot price, ensuring that both price and quantity components are sourced from tamper‑resistant data.

title: Tokens can’t be removed as a collateral without breaking liquidations and other core functions
description:
The core mechanism that Revert utilizes to prevent arbitrary tokens to be utilized as collateral is by the default setting of the `collateralFactor`. Since the `collateralFactor` for all tokens (besides the ones approved for usage in the system, and set by admins) is `0`, that means that no one can borrow against a collateral which hasn’t been approved.

The problem arises when admins would want a collateral removed from the system. There would be multiple reasons as to why this might be the case:

  * The underlying collateral has become too volatile.
  * The DAO in charge of Revert protocol decides to remove it as a collateral.
  * There has been some kind of a change in the mechanics of how that token operates and Revert wants it removed (e.g. upgradeable tokens, most-popular examples include USDC/USDT).

The only way in which this could be performed is to set the `collateralFactor` back to `0`, but this would break core mechanics such as liquidations.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the protocol’s reliance on a single numeric parameter, the collateralFactor, to both indicate whether a token is accepted as collateral and to scale the value of that collateral during liquidation. When a token is approved, its collateralFactor is set to a positive fixed‑point value; when the token is removed, the factor is reset to zero. The liquidation routine later computes the collateral value by multiplying the token’s market value by this factor and then divides the debt by the resulting collateral value to determine the liquidation amount. If the factor has been set to zero, the computed collateral value becomes zero, causing a division‑by‑zero operation that triggers a panic revert. Consequently, any loan that uses the delisted token as collateral can no longer be liquidated, and attempts to query loan health or perform liquidation will consistently revert. From a user’s perspective, borrowers see transactions fail with a generic “panic” error, their UI may report that the loan is unhealthy or that the collateral balance is zero, and lenders cannot recover their exposure because the protocol cannot enforce repayment through liquidation. The issue manifests only after an admin deliberately sets the collateralFactor of an already‑used token to zero, a scenario that can arise when the DAO decides to delist a volatile or upgraded token. It was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors exercised the setTokenConfig function to zero out a token’s factor and observed the resulting revert in the liquidation path. The bug is subtle because a zero factor intuitively appears to disable borrowing for that token, yet the same zero propagates into arithmetic that assumes a non‑zero divisor, making the failure hard to spot without testing edge cases. The root cause is the conflation of a whitelist flag with a scaling factor; the fix is to separate token eligibility from the numeric factor, for example by maintaining an explicit whitelist mapping and ensuring that liquidation calculations never divide by a value that can be zero, either by guarding against zero or by using a distinct “enabled” flag for collateral eligibility. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of arithmetic errors caused by improper handling of sentinel values in financial smart contracts, leading to broken accounting logic and potential loss of funds or frozen positions.

title: Dangerous use of deadline parameter
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of passing the current block timestamp (block.timestamp) as the deadline argument when calling the Uniswap V3 NonfungiblePositionManager contract. The deadline field in Uniswap’s position manager functions is intended to act as a time‑bound safeguard: the contract checks that the supplied deadline is greater than the current block timestamp and rejects the call if the deadline has already passed. By supplying block.timestamp, the check compares the same value against itself, which always succeeds and therefore provides no protection. This pattern appears in the AutoCompound::execute and V3Vault::_sendPositionValue functions, where the deadline parameter is hard‑coded to block.timestamp instead of being supplied by the caller or set to a future timestamp. The root cause is a misunderstanding of the deadline semantics, treating it as a placeholder rather than a security bound. An attacker, such as an MEV bot, can observe a pending transaction that includes an insufficient gas limit or is delayed for any reason, then later include the same transaction in a block after the original sender’s deadline would have expired – because the deadline check never expires, the transaction can be executed at the attacker’s discretion. This enables front‑running, sandwich attacks, or forced execution of stale liquidity operations, potentially resulting in users receiving less favorable swap rates, loss of accrued fees, or even complete loss of deposited liquidity if the attacker manipulates the execution order. The issue manifests when a user initiates a liquidity addition or removal and expects the deadline to protect against delayed execution; from the UI perspective the user may see their transaction succeed but later notice that the expected fees were not received or that the position was altered unexpectedly. The bug is subtle because the code appears to set a deadline, yet the value chosen nullifies the intended safety check, making it easy to overlook during code review. The proper remediation is to expose a deadline parameter on the affected functions and forward a future timestamp (e.g., block.timestamp + maxDelay) to the Uniswap calls, mirroring the pattern used in other parts of the codebase such as LeverageTransformer::leverageUp and V3Utils::_swapAndIncrease. By doing so, the contract regains the intended time‑bound protection, preventing malicious re‑execution of pending transactions and preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees around liquidity timing and fee distribution.

title: `dailyDebtIncreaseLimitLeft` is not updated in `liquidate`
poc: `dailyDebtIncreaseLimitLeft` was not incremented in `liquidate()`, see [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/435b054f9ad2404173f36f0f74a5096c894b12b7/src/V3Vault.sol#L685-L757).
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a missing state update in the vault’s liquidation routine. The contract tracks a daily limit called dailyDebtIncreaseLimitLeft, which represents the amount of assets that can be borrowed again on the same day. In the repay() function the limit is increased by the amount that has just been repaid, reflecting the business rule that repaid assets become available for new loans. However, the liquidate() function, which also returns assets to the vault as a form of repayment, does not adjust dailyDebtIncreaseLimitLeft. As a result, when a large number of positions are liquidated – especially with high asset values – the vault receives a surplus of assets that are not counted toward the daily borrowing allowance. This surplus causes the utilization rate to drop sharply because the protocol believes there is less borrowable capital than actually exists. The issue can be exploited by triggering many liquidations in a short period, effectively exhausting the daily debt‑increase budget and preventing legitimate borrowers from obtaining credit, which may lead to a denial‑of‑service condition and reduced earnings for lenders. The problem is subtle because the liquidation path appears to behave like a normal repayment, yet the accounting for the daily limit is omitted, making the discrepancy hard to detect without inspecting the internal state updates. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑state‑inconsistency errors where a financial invariant is not maintained across all code paths. From a user’s perspective, borrowers may see that their loan requests are rejected despite the vault holding ample collateral, and lenders may notice an unexpected drop in utilization metrics or see that their deposited assets are not being re‑lent. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the logic of repay() and liquidate() and noticing the missing increment. To remediate the problem, the liquidate() function should include the same increment of dailyDebtIncreaseLimitLeft that repay() performs – for example, adding dailyDebtIncreaseLimitLeft += state.liquidatorCost (or the amount of assets returned) after a successful liquidation – thereby restoring the intended accounting invariant and preventing the utilization rate from collapsing.

title: `AutoRange` execution can be front-ran to avoid protocol fee, causing loss for protocol
description:
When users configure their NFT within the `AutoRange` contract, they have 2 options for fee-handling:

  1. Protocol takes 0.15% of the entire position size.
  2. Protocol takes a higher fee of 2%, but only from the position’s collected fees.

The user sets `PositionConfig.onlyFees=false` for the first option, and `onlyFees=true` for the second option. When an operator calls the `AutoRange.execute()` function, they set the reward parameter `rewardX64` based on the user’s `PositionConfig`.

However, the execution can be front-ran by the user. They can change the `onlyFees` boolean, which changes the fee handling logic, while the `rewardX64` parameter set by the operator is unchanged.

The user can exploit this to their advantage by initially setting `onlyFees` to false, so that the operator will call the function with only 0.15% reward percentage. But when the operator sends their transaction, the user front-runs it by changing `onlyFees` to true. Now, the protocol only gets 0.15% of the fees collected when they initially intended to collect 0.15% of the entire position.
poc: See [the rewardX64 parameter](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/457230945a49878eefdc1001796b10638c1e7584/src/transformers/AutoRange.sol#L62) and [docs regarding fee source](https://docs.revert.finance/revert/auto-range#selecting-a-fee-source).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running race condition in the AutoRange contract that allows a user to manipulate the fee source after an operator has already calculated the reward parameter. The contract stores a boolean flag that determines whether the protocol fee is taken from the entire position size (0.15 %) or only from the fees collected by the position (2 %). When an operator calls AutoRange.execute they read the current flag, compute a rewardX64 value that matches the chosen fee source, and pass that value to the execution function. Because the flag is stored in mutable contract state, the user can submit a transaction that flips the flag after the operator’s transaction has been broadcast but before it is mined. The execution then proceeds with the original rewardX64 that was calculated for the first fee source, while the fee‑calculation logic now uses the second fee source. As a result the protocol receives only the small 0.15 % fee on the collected fees instead of the intended 0.15 % on the whole position, effectively reducing the protocol’s revenue. The issue occurs whenever there is a time gap between the operator’s transaction submission and its inclusion in a block, and any participant who can front‑run the transaction can exploit it. The affected parties are the protocol, which loses expected fee income, and potentially other users who rely on correct fee accounting. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena when the auditors examined the interaction between the onlyFees flag and the rewardX64 parameter and noticed that the flag could be changed without updating the reward calculation. The problem is subtle because the reward value appears correct at the time of submission, and typical unit tests do not simulate transaction ordering attacks, making the discrepancy easy to miss. To remediate the issue the contract should either lock the fee source for the duration of the execution, require the operator to provide separate reward values for each possible flag state, or recompute the reward inside the execute function based on the current flag, thereby eliminating the inconsistency between the stored flag and the pre‑computed reward. This class of bug falls under mutable‑state front‑running or transaction‑ordering dependency, where a user can alter a contract variable after an incentive parameter has been fixed, leading to unintended economic outcomes such as funds disappearing from the protocol’s fee pool or refunds being calculated with the wrong formula.

title: Incorrect liquidation fee calculation during underwater liquidation, disincentivizing liquidators to participate
poc: [Code snippet from `V3Vault._calculateLiquidation`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/435b054f9ad2404173f36f0f74a5096c894b12b7/src/V3Vault.sol#L1112-L1119).
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the liquidation fee for underwater positions in the V3Vault contract. According to the protocol specification, the fee that liquidators must pay to the reserve should be exactly ten percent of the outstanding debt, but the implementation mistakenly derives the fee from ten percent of the total position value (fullValue) instead. This mis‑calculation originates from using the expression fullValue * (Q32 - MAX_LIQUIDATION_PENALTY_X32) / Q32, which effectively applies a 90 % factor to the full position value, rather than applying the 10 % penalty to the debt amount. When a borrower’s collateral falls below the required threshold, the contract enters the liquidation branch that assumes the position is fully underwater. The code then sets liquidationValue to the full position value and computes liquidatorCost based on the erroneous penaltyValue. As a result, the liquidator receives a smaller reward than intended, sometimes even less than the cost of covering the debt, which disincentivizes participation in the liquidation process. In practice a liquidator may observe that the expected profit from a liquidation is missing or dramatically reduced, and the protocol may end up with positions that remain under‑collateralised because no one is willing to liquidate them. This can lead to systemic risk where the reserve cannot be replenished and borrowers retain debt that should have been cleared. The issue is discovered during a formal audit of the contract’s liquidation logic, where the auditor compared the white‑paper specification with the on‑chain code and identified the mismatch. It is subtle because the fee is still a percentage of a value, so the numbers appear plausible at a glance, and the contract does not emit a distinct event indicating the fee source. The proper fix is to compute the penalty as ten percent of the debt (debt * MAX_LIQUIDATION_PENALTY_X32 / Q32) and adjust liquidatorCost, liquidationValue and reserveCost accordingly, ensuring that the liquidator receives the correct incentive and the reserve receives the intended fee. This class of bug falls under “incorrect financial parameter calculation” and violates the accounting assumption that fees are proportional to debt, not to collateral value, breaking the expected economic model of the protocol.

title: Asymmetric calculation of price difference
description:
Price difference is calculated in 2 ways depending on whether `price > verified price` or not.

If `price > verified price`, this is the equation:
    
    (price - verified price) / price

Otherwise price is calculated with this equation:
    
    (verified price - price) / verified price

When the 2 equations above are graphed with `price = horizontal axis`, we get 2 different curves, see [here](https://www.desmos.com/calculator/nixha3ojz6).

The first equation produces a asymptotic curve (shown in red). The second equation produces a linear curve (shown in green). Therefore, the rate at which the price difference changes is different depending on whether `price > verified price` or not.
poc: Price difference of `+1` or `-1` from `verified price` are not symmetric:
bug_full: The vulnerability is an asymmetric calculation of the price difference used to decide whether a reported price is within an acceptable deviation from a verified oracle price. The contract applies two different formulas depending on the sign of the deviation: when the reported price is higher than the verified price it computes (price‑verifiedPrice)/price, while when the reported price is lower it computes (verifiedPrice‑price)/verifiedPrice. Because the denominator changes with the direction of the deviation, the resulting percentage difference is not symmetric – a deviation of +1 unit yields a smaller percentage than a deviation of –1 unit of the same magnitude. This asymmetry creates a non‑linear curve for upward deviations and a linear curve for downward deviations, as demonstrated by graphing the two equations. The root cause is a logical error in normalising the price delta: the contract should use a single, consistent denominator (typically the verified price) and take the absolute value of the delta. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a price that is slightly above the verified price, staying under the maximum allowed difference, while the same magnitude below the verified price would exceed the threshold and be rejected. Consequently the protocol may accept price updates that are farther from the true market price than intended, leading to mis‑pricing of collateral, incorrect liquidation triggers, and potential loss of funds for lenders or borrowers. The issue manifests during the price verification step whenever the contract compares the on‑chain price to the oracle price, affecting any user who relies on accurate price checks – for example borrowers, lenders, and anyone interacting with the lending market. It was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors plotted the two formulas and observed the mismatch. The bug is subtle because both formulas appear mathematically plausible and may pass simple unit tests that only check one side of the inequality, making it hard to notice without thorough analysis of both directions. To remediate, the contract should compute the absolute difference between price and verified price, divide by the verified price (or another constant denominator), and compare the result against the maximum allowed deviation, as shown in the recommended code snippet. This change restores symmetry, ensures that a deviation of +1 and –1 are treated identically, and aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that price deviations must be bounded uniformly regardless of direction.

title: Some ERC20 can revert on a zero value transfer
description:
Note: This finding was reported via the winning [Automated Findings report](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/main/bot-report.md). It was declared out of scope for the audit, but is being included here for completeness.

[728](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/ac520c5fedf4e1654c597a46efaf5a7c27295de1/src/V3Vault.sol#L728), [946](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/ac520c5fedf4e1654c597a46efaf5a7c27295de1/src/V3Vault.sol#L946), [226](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/ac520c5fedf4e1654c597a46efaf5a7c27295de1/src/automators/Automator.sol#L226), [272](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/ac520c5fedf4e1654c597a46efaf5a7c27295de1/src/transformers/AutoCompound.sol#L272), [88](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/ac520c5fedf4e1654c597a46efaf5a7c27295de1/src/transformers/LeverageTransformer.sol#L88), [91](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/ac520c5fedf4e1654c597a46efaf5a7c27295de1/src/transformers/LeverageTransformer.sol#L91), [872](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/ac520c5fedf4e1654c597a46efaf5a7c27295de1/src/transformers/V3Utils.sol#L872), [85](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/ac520c5fedf4e1654c597a46efaf5a7c27295de1/src/utils/FlashloanLiquidator.sol#L85), [98](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/ac520c5fedf4e1654c597a46efaf5a7c27295de1/src/utils/Swapper.sol#L98), [167](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-revert-lend/blob/ac520c5fedf4e1654c597a46efaf5a7c27295de1/src/utils/Swapper.sol#L167)
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the fact that some ERC20 token contracts revert when a transfer of zero tokens is attempted. The ERC20 specification does not mandate that a zero‑value transfer must succeed, yet many higher‑level contracts assume it behaves as a no‑op. In the examined code base, numerous functions—including vault deposits, automated compounding, leverage adjustments, flash‑loan liquidation and token swapping—invoke token transfer operations without first confirming that the amount to be moved is greater than zero. When the underlying token implements a strict check and reverts on a zero amount, the entire transaction that called the transfer also reverts. This can be exploited by an attacker who supplies or selects a token that follows this stricter behaviour, causing any protocol operation that may result in a zero‑value transfer to fail. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: users attempting to deposit, withdraw, rebalance or claim rewards may see their transactions revert, leading to missing balances, failed UI actions, or funds appearing to be locked. The issue manifests whenever a calculation yields zero—such as after rounding, when a user’s position is fully repaid, or when a liquidation yields no profit. All participants who interact with the protocol—token holders, borrowers, lenders, and automated bots—are affected because the contract does not gracefully handle the edge case. The problem was discovered by an automated findings tool that scanned the repository for transfer calls that could receive a zero amount, flagging them as potential revert sources. It is easy to miss because developers typically test only positive transfer amounts and assume zero transfers are harmless, so the failure does not surface in standard unit tests. To remediate, the contract should guard each token transfer with a condition that skips the call when the amount is zero, or employ a wrapper that catches and ignores zero‑value reverts, or rely on a token implementation that explicitly permits zero transfers. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “unchecked external call with unsafe input” where an external contract’s unexpected revert breaks internal logic, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a zero transfer does not alter balances.

title: The top tier prover can not re-prove
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the logic that allows a top‑tier prover to re‑prove a new block transition in the LibProving.proveBlock function. The contract is supposed to let a top‑tier prover submit a different transition after the previous one, provided that the new transition differs and several assert conditions are satisfied. The code contains an assert that checks ts.contestBond == 0, but the default value for ts.contestBond is set to 1 for gas‑saving reasons. Because the assert expects zero while the actual stored value is one, any attempt by a top‑tier prover to re‑prove a different transition triggers the assert and causes the transaction to revert. The root cause is a mismatch between the assumed initial state of the contestBond field and its real initialization. An attacker or honest participant can exploit this by simply invoking the re‑prove path; the transaction will fail even though the business logic permits the operation. The impact is that the top‑tier prover, often a guardian or privileged entity, cannot overwrite an existing proof with a new one, potentially stalling block finalisation or forcing reliance on lower‑tier provers. This occurs whenever the top‑tier prover calls proveBlock with a different transition while the stored tier state still has contestBond equal to its default of one. Users of the protocol, including block proposers and validators, are affected because their expected workflow—submitting a new proof and seeing the block progress—does not happen; from a UI perspective they may see a transaction revert, no change in balances, and no new block being verified. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a test case demonstrated that changing the assert to check for contestBond == 1 allowed the transaction to succeed. The bug can be hard to notice because the assert only fires in the specific re‑prove scenario, which may not be exercised in standard test suites, and the default value of one is not obvious without inspecting the tier initialization code. The correct fix is to align the assert with the actual default by checking ts.contestBond == 1, thereby allowing the top‑tier prover to re‑prove as intended and restoring the protocol’s expected block‑finalisation flow.

title: retryMessage unable to handle edge cases.
description:
The function `retryMessage()` is unable to handle some edge scenarios listed below.

1. Reverting or refunding a sender when the receiver is banned after the transaction is placed in a `RETRIABLE` state.
2. Message that is suspended after the transaction is placed in a `RETRIABLE` state.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the retryMessage function of the bridge contract, which is responsible for re‑executing cross‑chain messages that previously failed and were marked with the RETRIABLE status. The function only verifies that the message is still in the RETRIABLE state before attempting a second call, but it neglects two critical checks that can change after the message entered that state: whether the destination address has been placed on a ban list (addressBanned) and whether the message has been suspended via the proofReceipt mechanism. Because these conditions are not re‑evaluated, an attacker can manipulate the system by first causing a message to fail (for example, by providing insufficient gas), allowing it to become RETRIABLE, and then banning the target address or suspending the message before invoking retryMessage. When retryMessage is called, the contract will still try to invoke the call, potentially processing a message that should be blocked or ignoring a suspension that was intended to prevent execution. This can lead to several undesirable outcomes: a user may see a message that should have been refunded or rejected being processed, resulting in funds being transferred to a banned contract; a legitimate user may experience a permanent lock of their funds because the message remains in RETRIABLE without a proper refund path; or a malicious actor could replay a fake message on the destination chain, undermining the bridge’s trust model. The issue is subtle because the normal execution path (message succeeds or fails once) works as expected, and the missing checks only become relevant after the state transition to RETRIABLE, a scenario that many test suites overlook. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the reviewers examined the control flow of retryMessage and identified that proofReceipt[msgHash].receivedAt and addressBanned[_addr] are never consulted. To remediate the flaw, the retryMessage logic should be extended to re‑validate the ban list and suspension status before attempting the second call, and optionally the ban list feature could be removed or clarified to avoid confusion. By ensuring that a retriable message cannot be processed if its destination is banned or if the message has been suspended, the bridge will preserve its intended accounting guarantees and prevent unexpected fund movements or security breaches.

title: A recalled ERC20 bridge transfer can lock tokens in the bridge
description:
A recalling ERC20 bridge transfer can lock funds in the bridge if the call to mint tokens fail on the source chain. Depending on the Native token logic this could either be a permanent lock or a lock of an unknown period of time.

Example of how this can happen with the provided USDCAdapter:

USDC limits the amount of USDC that can be minted on each chain by giving each minter a minting allowance. If the minting allowance is reach minting will revert. If this happens in a recalled message the tokens together with the ETH value is locked.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that a recalled ERC20 bridge transfer can become permanently stuck when the minting step on the destination chain fails. The bridge contract attempts to mint the bridged token by calling a token adapter (USDCAdapter) that enforces a per‑minter minting allowance. When the allowance is exhausted, the adapter’s mint function reverts with \"mint amount exceeds minterAllowance\". If this revert occurs while processing a recalled message – a message that is being sent back to the source chain after a failure – the bridge’s internal logic does not provide an alternative path, so the transferred amount of USDC together with any attached native ETH remains locked inside the bridge contract. The root cause is the combination of a hard‑coded allowance check in the native token contract and the bridge’s assumption that minting will always succeed during a recall. Exploitation does not require an attacker; any user who initiates a bridge transfer that later needs to be recalled while the allowance is already maxed out will experience the lock. The impact is loss of access to the bridged tokens and the accompanying ETH, which may be permanent if the allowance is never freed, effectively a denial‑of‑service for those funds. The condition occurs only when (1) a user initiates a cross‑chain transfer of a token that has a capped minting supply, (2) the destination chain’s minting allowance for the bridge’s minter is already reached, and (3) the bridge attempts to recall the message, causing the mint call to revert. Users are affected because they expect the recalled transfer to credit their account, but instead see no balance change and their ETH remains unwithdrawable, violating the protocol’s accounting guarantees that every bridged amount is either minted or returned. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, and it is subtle because the minting failure only appears in the rarely exercised recall path, making it easy to miss in normal testing. To remediate, the bridge should include a fallback mechanism such as allowing the user to resend the message with new data, redeeming for the canonical token on the source chain, or providing a UI warning about the supply cap. In general, the class of bug is a “mint‑revert on recall” leading to token lock, a form of accounting inconsistency where the bridge’s state diverges from expected token balances.

title: There is no slippage check for the eth deposits processing in the `LibDepositing.processDeposits`
description:
The `LibDepositing.depositEtherToL2` function is called by the TaikoL1.depositEtherToL2 to deposit ether to the `L2 chain`. The maximum number of `unprocessed eth deposits` are capped at `_config.ethDepositRingBufferSize - 1` as shown here:
    
```solidity
        unchecked {
            return _amount >= _config.ethDepositMinAmount && _amount <= _config.ethDepositMaxAmount
                && _state.slotA.numEthDeposits - _state.slotA.nextEthDepositToProcess
                    < _config.ethDepositRingBufferSize - 1;
        }
```

The Taiko configuration states that `ethDepositRingBufferSize == 1024`. Hence the maximum unprocessed eth deposits allowed by the taiko L1 contract is `capped at 1023`.

When the L2 block is proposed by calling the `LibProposing.proposeBlock` function by the TaikoL1 contract, it processes the unprocessed `eth deposits` by calling the `LibDepositing.processDeposits`. But it is allowed to process `at most 32 eth deposits per block` as per the following conditional check in the `processDeposits` function.
    
```solidity
    deposits_ = new TaikoData.EthDeposit[(numPending.min(_config.ethDepositMaxCountPerBlock))];
```

Here the `ethDepositMaxCountPerBlock == 32` as configured in the `TaikoL1.getConfig` function.

And the `fee amount` for each of the `eth deposits` are calculated as follows:
    
```solidity
    uint96 fee = uint96(_config.ethDepositMaxFee.min(block.basefee * _config.ethDepositGas));
    
    uint96 _fee = deposits_[i].amount > fee ? fee : deposits_[i].amount;
    
    deposits_[i].amount -= _fee; 
```

Hence the `deposited eth amount` is deducted by the calculated `_fee amount` for the `eth deposit transaction`. If the basefee of the `L1 block` increases significantly then the maximum fee of `ethDepositMaxFee: 1 ether / 10` will be applied. Thus deducting that amount from the `transferred eth deposit to the recipient in L2`.

Now let’s consider the following scenario:

1. `nextEthDepositToProcess` is currently `100`.
2. `numEthDeposits` is `1060` currently.
3. The number of proposed L2 blocks required to process 1060th eth deposit is = 1060 - 100 / 32 = 30 L2 blocks.
4. As a result all the `above 30 L2 blocks` will not be proposed in a single L1 block and will require multiple L1 blocks for it.
5. If there is `huge congestion` in the mainnet during this time the `block.basefee` of the subsequent `L1 blocks` would increase. And this could prompt the maximum fee of `_config.ethDepositMaxFee` to be charged on the deposited amount (in the `LibDepositing.processDeposits` function, since subsequent L1 block would have a higher `block.basefee`) thus prompting loss of funds on the recipient.
6. For example let’s assume the depositor deposit `1.1 ether` and current gas fee is `0.01 ether`. Hence the recipient expects to receive approximately `1.09 ether` at the time of the deposit on L1. But when the deposit is processed in a subsequent L1 block, if the fee amount increases to the maximum amount of `0.1 ether` then the recipient will only get approximately `1 ether` only. This will cost the recipient a `loss of 0.9 ether`. If there was a slippage check a depositor can set for his eth deposits then he can prevent excessive gas costs during processing.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way TaikoL1 handles Ether deposits to the L2 chain. A user initiates a deposit by calling depositEtherToL2, which only records the amount on L1 and returns a transaction receipt. The actual transfer of the recorded amount to the L2 recipient is performed later by LibDepositing.processDeposits, which is triggered when a block is proposed. During processing the contract computes a fee as the minimum of a configured maximum fee and the product of the current block.basefee and a gas constant. Because the fee calculation uses the block.basefee at the moment of processing, any increase in the L1 basefee between the time the user signs the deposit transaction and the time the deposit is finally processed will raise the fee. The contract does not perform a slippage or fee‑tolerance check, so the deducted fee can grow up to the configured maximum of 0.1 ether per deposit. When the ring buffer for pending deposits reaches its limit (1024 entries) and only 32 deposits are processed per block, a backlog can form during periods of high network congestion. In such a scenario dozens of L1 blocks may pass before a particular deposit is processed, giving the basefee ample opportunity to spike. The practical impact is that the recipient receives less Ether than the sender expected; for example a user who deposits 1.1 ether while the basefee is low may anticipate receiving roughly 1.09 ether after a small fee, but if the basefee rises the contract may deduct the full 0.1 ether, leaving the recipient with only 1 ether. From the user’s point of view the UI will show a successful deposit transaction, but the balance on L2 will be lower than expected, sometimes appearing as a missing or zero amount. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the deposit logic and noticing the lack of a slippage guard. It is difficult to notice because the fee deduction is internal to the contract and does not emit a distinct event; the only symptom is an unexpected reduction in the received amount. The root cause is the separation of the deposit and processing steps combined with a fee calculation that depends on a mutable blockchain parameter without any user‑controlled bound. The recommended mitigation is to introduce a slippage check that compares the fee at processing time with the fee estimated at deposit time, reject the deposit if the fee exceeds a user‑specified tolerance, or move the fee calculation to the deposit transaction so that the amount transferred is deterministic. This would align the contract’s behavior with the user’s expectation that the amount they deposit is the amount the recipient receives, minus a predictable fee.

title: Bridge watcher can forge arbitrary message and drain bridge
description: The `bridge_watchdog` role can forge arbitrary messages and drain the bridge of all ETH and tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the bridge_watchdog role’s ability to call the suspendMessages function and manipulate the timestamp stored in the proofReceipt mapping. The contract treats any message whose receivedAt timestamp is non‑zero as proven, without verifying that the message has actually been validated by the off‑chain signal service. By first suspending a message (setting the timestamp to the maximum uint64 value) and then immediately unsuspending it (setting the timestamp to a non‑zero value such as the current block timestamp), a malicious bridge_watchdog can create a fabricated proof for an arbitrary message hash that has never been submitted or verified. Because the contract’s processMessage routine only checks the receivedAt field to decide whether a message is proven, the forged message is accepted as valid and the bridge releases the associated ETH or token assets to the destination address. This privilege escalation allows an attacker who controls the bridge_watchdog role to drain the bridge of all funds, effectively stealing user balances.
