The issue is triggered whenever the bridge_watchdog role is compromised or deliberately malicious; it does not require any other pre‑condition. Users are affected because they expect that only messages with genuine proofs can be processed, yet they may see their funds transferred to an attacker or notice that a message is marked DONE without having provided any proof. The bug was discovered during a security audit when the researchers wrote a proof‑of‑concept test that suspended and unsuspended a message, then called processMessage and observed that the bridge released funds despite the lack of a valid proof. The problem is subtle because the suspendMessages function appears to be a harmless administrative tool for pausing messages, and the timestamp field is reused as a proof flag, making the unintended side‑effect easy to overlook. To remediate the issue, the contract should ensure that unsuspending a message does not set a non‑zero timestamp unless the message has already been proven, or it should restrict the bridge_watchdog role to only modify a separate suspension flag without touching the proof receipt. Additionally, the logic that determines whether a message is proven should be decoupled from the suspension mechanism and should require an explicit proof from the signal service. By enforcing these checks, the bridge can prevent forged messages and protect user assets from being drained.

title: First block proposer check in the `LibProposing._isProposerPermitted` function is errorneous
bug_full:
The vulnerability is a logical error in the permission‑checking routine that decides whether a transaction may propose the first block after the genesis block. The private function _isProposerPermitted is intended to allow only a special address called proposer_one to submit the first block. The code first checks if the current block number equals one and, if so, verifies that msg.sender matches the resolved proposer_one address. However, after this check the function continues to evaluate a second condition that compares msg.sender against a generic proposer address resolved from the contract. If the generic proposer is set to a non‑zero address that differs from proposer_one, the final return statement evaluates to false, causing the function to reject the transaction even though the caller is the authorized proposer_one. The root cause is the missing early return or explicit true when msg.sender equals proposer_one, allowing the later generic check to override the intended permission.

An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the flaw itself prevents the legitimate proposer_one from successfully proposing the first block. When the generic proposer address is configured (which is common in production deployments), any attempt by proposer_one to submit the first block triggers a revert via L1_UNAUTHORIZED. This denial‑of‑service effect halts the block‑proposing pipeline, meaning the blockchain cannot progress beyond the genesis block. Subsequent blocks remain unproposed, effectively freezing the protocol and locking any funds that depend on block finalisation.

The condition occurs only for the very first block after genesis (slotB.numBlocks == 1) and only when the generic proposer address is non‑zero and does not match proposer_one. All other blocks are unaffected because the function falls back to the generic proposer check, which works as intended.

The affected parties are the protocol itself, its validators, and any users who expect the chain to start processing transactions. From a user‑interface perspective the symptom is that the UI shows no new block being produced, balances remain unchanged, and attempts to submit the first block result in a transaction that reverts with an “unauthorized” error. Users may see their funds appear to be stuck because the chain never advances.

The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the logical flow of the permission function was examined and the contradictory checks were identified. It can be hard to notice because the function superficially appears to enforce the correct rule for proposer_one, and the bug only manifests under a specific configuration that may not be exercised in basic unit tests.

To remediate the problem the function should return true immediately when msg.sender equals the resolved proposer_one address, or restructure the logic so that the generic proposer check is bypassed for the first block. In conceptual terms, the permission routine must give priority to the special first‑block proposer and not allow a later generic check to invalidate that permission.

This class of bug falls under improper access‑control logic, where multiple overlapping permission checks interfere with each other, leading to an unintended denial of service. It violates the protocol’s accounting assumption that the first block will always be producible by the designated proposer, breaking the expected flow of block finalisation and fund availability.

title: Incorrect __Essential_ init
description:
The EssentialContract.sol contract is inherited by the TaikoToken contract. This essential contract contains two __Essential_ init() functions, one with an owner parameter only (see [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-taiko/blob/f58384f44dbf4c6535264a472322322705133b11/packages/protocol/contracts/common/EssentialContract.sol#L109)) and the other with owner and address manager parameters (see [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-taiko/blob/f58384f44dbf4c6535264a472322322705133b11/packages/protocol/contracts/common/EssentialContract.sol#L95)).

The issue with the current code is that it uses the [__Essential_ init()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-taiko/blob/f58384f44dbf4c6535264a472322322705133b11/packages/protocol/contracts/common/EssentialContract.sol#L109) function with the owner parameter only. This would cause the [onlyFromOwnerOrNamed(“snapshooter”)](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-taiko/blob/f58384f44dbf4c6535264a472322322705133b11/packages/protocol/contracts/L1/TaikoToken.sol#L52) modifier on the [snapshot](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-taiko/blob/f58384f44dbf4c6535264a472322322705133b11/packages/protocol/contracts/L1/TaikoToken.sol#L52) function to not be able to resolve the snapshooter role since the address manager contract was never set during initialization, thus causing a revert.

Due to this:

1. Snapshooter role is denied from taking snapshots.
2. Timely snapshots for certain periods could have failed by the snapshooter since they would have required the owner to jump in by the time the issue was realized.
3. Correct/Intended functionality of the protocol is affected i.e. the snapshooter role assigned to an address cannot ever perform its tasks validly.
bug_full: During deployment the TaikoToken contract inherits EssentialContract which provides two overloads of __Essential_init. The implementation in TaikoToken calls the overload that accepts only an owner address, leaving the internal addressManager variable unset. The onlyFromOwnerOrNamed('snapshooter') modifier used on the snapshot() function first checks whether msg.sender is the contract owner or the address resolved for the role named 'snapshooter' via the AddressResolver. Because addressManager is still zero, the resolver's internal _resolve function reverts with RESOLVER_INVALID_MANAGER, causing the snapshot call to fail. As a result, any account granted the snapshooter role cannot execute snapshots; the transaction reverts and no state change occurs. This breaks the intended accounting flow where periodic snapshots record token balances, potentially preventing later reward calculations or governance decisions that rely on those snapshots. The bug manifests only when the snapshooter role is exercised, making it easy to miss during normal testing that focuses on owner functions. It was discovered during a security audit that inspected the initialization sequence and the modifier logic. The issue belongs to the class of initialization‑order or missing‑dependency bugs, where a contract is left in an incomplete state and later calls that depend on that state revert. From a user perspective, a snapshooter attempting to call snapshot sees a transaction revert with an error, receives no snapshot event, and may observe that expected balance snapshots are missing. The protocol’s reliability is reduced because the owner must manually intervene to perform snapshots, defeating the purpose of the dedicated snapshooter role. The recommended fix is to invoke the __Essential_init overload that accepts both the owner and the address manager address during TaikoToken initialization, ensuring the resolver can locate the snapshooter address and allowing snapshot() to succeed.

title: Bridged tokens would be lost if sender and receiver are contracts that don’t implement fallback/receive
description:
When a bridged token is received on the dest chain, `ERC20Vault.onMessageInvocation()` is being called. `onMessageInvocation()` always calls `to.sendEther(msg.value)` even when the `msg.value` is zero. `sendEther()` would attempt to call the contract with the value supplied and empty data. If the `to` address is a contract that doesn’t implement neither the fallback function nor receive then the entire transaction would revert.

The same issue occurs during recalling the message, if the sender is also a contract that doesn’t implement neither a fallback nor receive then the recalling would fail as well.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unconditional Ether transfer performed by the bridge's ERC20Vault when processing a cross‑chain token message. The function onMessageInvocation always invokes sendEther(msg.value) regardless of whether msg.value is zero. In Ethereum, even a call with value zero triggers the fallback/receive mechanism of the target address; if the target is a contract that does not implement either a fallback() external payable or receive() external payable function, the call reverts. Consequently, when the bridge attempts to deliver tokens to such a contract, the whole transaction reverts and the ERC20 tokens remain locked in the vault. The same logic is used when a message is recalled; if the original sender contract lacks a payable fallback, the recall also reverts, preventing the sender from retrieving the tokens. The issue is triggered whenever a bridged transfer is directed to a contract without a payable fallback, which can happen with zero‑value transfers (the common case for token‑only bridges) or with non‑zero ETH attached. Users experience the symptom that their token balance does not increase after a bridge operation, or that a recall operation fails and the tokens stay stuck. The protocol assumes that the bridge can always forward ETH, even when the amount is zero, which violates the accounting assumption that a zero‑value transfer is a no‑op. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a test contract that deliberately omits fallback/receive and observing that the bridge call reverts with ETH_TRANSFER_FAILED. The bug is subtle because a zero‑value call appears harmless and developers may overlook the requirement for a payable fallback. To remediate, the bridge should skip the sendEther call when the amount is zero, or modify sendEther to return early in that case, and provide a safe path for non‑zero transfers such as allowing the sender to forfeit the ETH or using a pull‑payment pattern. Properly handling the absence of a fallback prevents token loss and ensures that bridge operations succeed even when the destination contract does not accept ETH.

title: LibProposing:proposeBlock allows blocks with a zero parentMetaHash to be proposed after the genesis block and avoid parent block verification
poc: The test suite contains the TaikoL1TestBase:proposeBlock that creates new block proposals with a zero parentMetaHash. This is called multiple times at tests like test_L1_verifying_multiple_blocks_once and test_L1_multiple_blocks_in_one_L1_block at the TaikoL1.t.sol test file, demonstrating the lack of reversion if the parentMetaHash is not zero outside of the genesis block.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the block‑proposing routine of the LibProposing library, where the function that creates a new block checks that the supplied parentMetaHash matches the stored parentMetaHash only when the supplied value is non‑zero. Because there is no explicit validation that the supplied parentMetaHash itself is non‑zero after the genesis block, a proposer can submit a block whose parentMetaHash field is zero. This bypasses the intended parent‑block verification step, allowing the block to be accepted without a proper link to the previous block. The root cause is the missing sanity check on the params.parentMetaHash argument outside of the genesis context. An attacker can exploit this by crafting a proposal transaction that sets parentMetaHash to zero, causing the contract to skip the parent‑hash consistency test and accept the block. The impact is that the blockchain’s continuity can be broken: subsequent blocks may reference an invalid predecessor, leading to contestations, potential loss of funds locked in the disputed block, and a breakdown of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue manifests only after the genesis block, when normal blocks are expected to carry a non‑zero parentMetaHash; it does not appear during the initial block creation, making it easy to miss in casual testing. It was discovered by the Code4rena audit team through inspection of the test suite, which contains a test that repeatedly proposes blocks with a zero parentMetaHash without triggering a revert, demonstrating the flaw. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms may include seeing a newly proposed block appear in the UI with an empty or zero parent hash, unexpected contestation events, or funds that were expected to be released remaining locked. The bug belongs to the class of missing input validation or improper state transition checks, specifically a parent‑hash validation omission. To remediate, the contract should enforce that params.parentMetaHash is non‑zero for any block proposal that is not the genesis block, reverting with an appropriate error if the condition is violated, thereby restoring the guarantee that each block is cryptographically linked to its predecessor and preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: The decision to return the liveness bond depends solely on the last guardian
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the GuardianProver multisignature contract that is used to contest block proofs. When a guardian calls the approve function, the contract builds a hash that is signed by the required number of guardians. The hash is calculated only over the block metadata (_meta) and the transition data (_tran) and deliberately omits the proof object (_proof). After the required approvals are collected, the contract checks a condition based on the content of _proof.data to decide whether the liveness bond that was locked for the assigned prover should be returned. Because the proof data is not part of the signed hash, the last guardian that provides the final approval can arbitrarily choose any value for _proof, including a specially crafted 32‑byte payload that matches the constant RETURN_LIVENESS_BOND. Consequently the contract may transfer the liveness bond to the assigned prover (or withhold it) solely based on the last guardian’s choice, without consensus from the other guardians. This flaw occurs whenever a top‑tier proof is contested, the isTopTier flag is true, and the approval process reaches its final step. The affected parties are the guardians, the assigned prover who expects to receive the bond, and any users relying on the protocol’s economic guarantees. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the logical flow of the approve function and noticing that the proof data is never bound to the approval hash. It is hard to notice because the approval event looks normal and the proof is only examined later, so a malicious guardian can inject the desired payload after the approvals are recorded. The impact is that funds locked as a liveness bond can disappear or be returned incorrectly, breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol and potentially allowing a rogue guardian to steal or withhold the bond. From a user’s perspective the assigned prover may receive a bond they did not earn, or may see the bond remain locked even though the proof was approved, leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds. The bug belongs to the class of insufficient message binding or signature replay vulnerabilities, where critical data is omitted from the signed message, enabling unauthorized state changes. To remediate, the contract should include the proof (or at least the proof data) in the hash that guardians sign, for example by computing keccak256(abi.encode(_meta, _tran, _proof.data)). This ensures that all guardians collectively agree on the proof content and on whether the liveness bond should be returned, restoring the intended multisig consensus and preventing a single guardian from unilaterally deciding the bond outcome.

title: Proposers would choose to avoid higher tier by exploiting non-randomness of parameter used in getMinTier
description:
The issue exists for both `MainnetTierProvider.sol` and `TestnetTierProvider.sol`. For this report, we shall concentrate only on describing it via `MainnetTierProvider.sol`.

The proving tier is chosen by the [getMinTier()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-taiko/blob/main/packages/protocol/contracts/L1/tiers/MainnetTierProvider.sol#L66-L70) function which accepts a `_rand` param.
    
File: contracts/L1/tiers/MainnetTierProvider.sol

```solidity
66:    function getMinTier(uint256 _rand) public pure override returns (uint16) {
67:        // 0.1% require SGX + ZKVM; all others require SGX
68:        if (_rand % 1000 == 0) return LibTiers.TIER_SGX_ZKVM;
69:        else return LibTiers.TIER_SGX;
70:    }
```

If `_rand % 1000 == 0`, a costlier tier `TIER_SGX_ZKVM` is used instead of the cheaper `TIER_SGX`. The `_rand` param is passed in the form of `meta_.difficulty` [which is calculated inside](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-taiko/blob/main/packages/protocol/contracts/L1/libs/LibProposing.sol#L199-L209) `proposeBlock()`:
    
File: contracts/L1/libs/LibProposing.sol

```solidity
199:    // Following the Merge, the L1 mixHash incorporates the
200:    // prevrandao value from the beacon chain. Given the possibility
201:    // of multiple Taiko blocks being proposed within a single
202:    // Ethereum block, we choose to introduce a salt to this random
203:    // number as the L2 mixHash.
204:    meta_.difficulty = keccak256(abi.encodePacked(block.prevrandao, b.numBlocks, block.number));
205:    
206:    // Use the difficulty as a random number
207:    meta_.minTier = ITierProvider(_resolver.resolve("tier_provider", false)).getMinTier(
208:        uint256(meta_.difficulty)
209:    );
```

As can be seen, all the parameters used in L204 to calculate `meta_.difficulty` can be known in advance and hence a proposer can choose not to propose when `meta_.difficulty` modulus 1000 equals zero, because in such cases it will cost him more to afford the proof (sgx + zk proof in this case).
bug_full: The contract determines the minimum proof tier for a block by calling getMinTier with a pseudo‑random value derived from meta_.difficulty. The difficulty is calculated as keccak256 of block.prevrandao, the number of blocks being proposed in the same L1 block, and the current block number. All of these inputs are known to a proposer before they decide to submit a proposal, which means the resulting difficulty can be predicted in advance. The getMinTier function returns a cheaper tier unless the predicted difficulty modulo 1000 equals zero, in which case it forces the more expensive SGX+ZKVM tier. Because the condition is deterministic, a proposer can simply refrain from proposing when the modulo condition would trigger the higher tier, thereby avoiding the extra cost. This behaviour does not break the cryptographic security of the rollup, but it creates a subtle liveness problem: blocks that would have required the expensive tier may go unproposed, leading to longer intervals between finalized blocks and potentially higher fees for the few proposers who do submit. Users may notice that block finality is slower than expected or that their transactions remain pending for an unusually long time. The issue was discovered during a code audit that examined the tier selection logic and recognized that the randomness source is fully controllable by the proposer. It is hard to spot because the code appears to use a random value, yet the randomness is only pseudo‑random and derived from publicly known data. The proper mitigation is to replace the deterministic difficulty‑based selection with a source of true randomness, such as a verifiable random function (VRF), or to redesign the tier selection so that it cannot be influenced by proposers. In abstract terms, this is a predictability‑based economic manipulation vulnerability where a deterministic pseudo‑random parameter is used to decide a cost‑related tier, allowing actors to game the system by selectively opting out of costly outcomes.

title: Invocation delays are not honoured when protocol unpauses
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of invocation delays in a bridge contract when the protocol is paused and later unpaused. The contract defines pause() and unpause() functions that are tracked by whenPaused and whenNotPaused modifiers, but the processMessage() routine calculates the required waiting period using the block timestamp and a static invocationDelay value without accounting for any time the contract spent in a paused state. When a message is proven, the timestamp of receipt (receivedAt) is stored and the code later checks that block.timestamp is greater than or equal to receivedAt plus invocationDelay (plus an extra delay for non‑preferred executors). Because the pause does not adjust receivedAt or the remaining delay, the elapsed time while the contract is paused is counted as if the delay window continued to run. Consequently, after an unpause the required delay may have already been satisfied, allowing any caller – including a non‑preferred executor – to invoke processMessage immediately. This breaks the intended ordering where a preferred executor has exclusive access to the execution window, enabling front‑running attacks that can steal execution rewards or disrupt the expected economic incentives. The issue manifests only when the contract is paused during the waiting period, which can be rare and therefore easy to miss during testing. From a user’s perspective the UI may indicate that a message is ready for execution, yet the transaction either succeeds instantly after unpause or fails to respect the expected delay, leading to unexpected reward distribution or missing refunds. The root cause is the lack of a mechanism to track how much of the delay window has already elapsed before the pause and to resume the countdown after unpause. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between pause logic and time‑based checks in processMessage, noticing that the whenNotPaused modifier is not applied and that the timestamp comparison does not subtract paused time. To remediate, the contract should store the amount of time already spent in the valid wait window before a pause, record the timestamp of the last unpause, and adjust the delay calculation accordingly, similar to the approach used in pauseProving() and unpausing logic elsewhere in the protocol. This adjustment restores the intended delay semantics, prevents unauthorized front‑running, and aligns the contract’s behavior with its business logic around executor priority and reward distribution.

title: Taiko SGX Attestation - Improper validation in certchain decoding
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the SGX attestationmodule used by the Taiko network to verify remote SGX provers. During the certificate chain decoding step the contract extracts the notBefore and notAfter fields from each X.509 certificate and checks that the DER tag indicating the time format is either UTC time (0x17) or GeneralizedTime (0x18). The implemented condition for the notBefore tag is written as (notBeforeTag != 0x17 && notBeforeTag == 0x18), which can never be true because a value cannot be both different from 0x17 and equal to 0x18 at the same time. As a result the check always passes, allowing any arbitrary byte value to be used as the notBefore tag. The notAfter tag is correctly validated, but because the notBefore validation is effectively disabled, a malicious prover can craft a certificate with an invalid time encoding or with a deliberately chosen tag that bypasses the intended format check. This flaw is discovered during a manual audit of the AutomataDcapV3Attestation library, where the logical expression was identified as contradictory. The issue is subtle because the surrounding code appears to perform a standard certificate validity check, and the failure does not raise an explicit error; the function simply proceeds to the next verification steps, making the problem easy to overlook during testing. Exploitation follows a straightforward flow: an attacker with SGX hardware registers its instance via the registerInstance function, supplies a certificate chain where the first certificate contains a malformed notBefore tag, the faulty validation accepts the certificate, and the attestation process continues as if the certificate were well‑formed. Because the attestation is the foundation for trusting the prover’s zero‑knowledge proof generation, the network may accept proofs generated by a compromised or tampered SGX enclave. The practical impact includes loss of trust in the proof system, potential acceptance of invalid proofs, and indirect financial risk if downstream contracts rely on those proofs for fund transfers. The bug manifests when any prover submits a certificate chain; honest users see no immediate UI error, but later may observe that proofs appear to verify while the underlying hardware is not trustworthy, or that refunds or payouts based on those proofs are missing or incorrect. The affected parties are the protocol itself, any contracts that depend on the attestation, and ultimately end‑users whose assets are secured by the ZK proofs. The vulnerability belongs to the class of improper input validation or logical condition errors in cryptographic certificate handling. To remediate, the condition must be corrected to explicitly reject any tag that is not 0x17 nor 0x18 for both notBefore and notAfter fields, ensuring that only properly encoded time values are accepted. After fixing, the attestation will reject malformed certificates, restoring the intended security guarantees of the SGX prover registration process.

title: Malicious caller of `processMessage
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Bridge contract's processMessage function. After attempting to invoke the cross‑chain message, the code updates the message status to DONE on success or to RETRIABLE on failure. Regardless of the outcome, the function then pays a reward equal to the message fee to the caller if the caller is not the designated refund address. Because the reward payment is performed unconditionally, a malicious actor can deliberately cause the invoke call to revert by supplying just enough gas (using the 63/64 rule from EIP‑150) so that the external call fails and the message is marked RETRIABLE. The attacker, who is not the refundTo address, still receives the fee, effectively extracting funds without delivering the intended message. This can be repeated by repeatedly calling processMessage with manipulated gas limits, draining the bridge's fee pool. The issue appears only when the caller is a non‑refund address, the message execution fails, and the contract follows the reward branch. Users of the bridge, relayers, and the protocol's economic model are affected because fees that should compensate successful execution are paid out even on failure, breaking the accounting assumption that fees are earned only for successful processing. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit where a test contract deliberately consumed gas to trigger the failure path and observed that the attacker still received the fee. It is subtle because the reward logic is placed after the status update and does not check the return value of the invoke call, making it easy to overlook during code review. The proper mitigation is to condition the fee transfer on a successful invokeMessageCall result, or to defer any reward until after a successful retryMessage call, ensuring that fees are only paid when the message has been processed correctly. In practice the bug manifests as users seeing unexpected ether credited to their address after a failed cross‑chain call, while the intended recipient receives no value and the bridge's fee balance shrinks unexpectedly.

title: Freezed Chain will never be unfreeze since `StateTransitionManager::unfreezeChain` is calling `freezeDiamond` instead of `unfreezeDiamond`
description:
`StateTransitionManager::unfreezeChain` function is meant for unfreeze the freezed chain of passed `_chainId` param. While `freezeChain` function is meant for freeze the chain according to passed _chainId. But `freezeChain` and `unfreezeChain` both functions are calling same function `freezeDiamond` by same line `IZkSyncStateTransition(stateTransition[_chainId]).freezeDiamond()` by mistake. So both these function will only freeze the chain.

Also there is no other function inside `StateTransitionManager.sol` contract which is calling `unfreezeDiamond`. `unfreezeDiamond` is function defined in `Admin.sol` where the call is going since `IZkSyncStateTransition` also inherits IAdmin which have freezeDiamond and unfreezeDiamond both functions. But `unfreezeDiamond` is not called from `unfreezeChain` function. So freezed chain will never be unfreeze.

`unfreezeChain` also have wrong comment instead of writing unfreezes it writes freezes. It seems like dev just copy pasted without doing required changes.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic‑dispatch error in the StateTransitionManager contract where the function intended to unfreeze a previously frozen chain, unfreezeChain, mistakenly invokes the freezeDiamond routine instead of the correct unfreezeDiamond routine. This copy‑paste mistake causes both freezeChain and unfreezeChain to execute the same freeze operation, leaving any chain that has been frozen permanently frozen from the perspective of the manager contract. The root cause is an incorrect external call to IZkSyncStateTransition(stateTransition[_chainId]).freezeDiamond() and a mismatched comment that still describes the action as an unfreeze. Because the manager never calls unfreezeDiamond, the only way to reverse a freeze is through an alternative admin path that may be restricted or removed in future upgrades. An attacker or a benign user cannot exploit the bug directly, but the protocol suffers a denial‑of‑service condition: once a chain is frozen, the manager contract cannot unfreeze it, preventing further state transitions, transaction processing, or withdrawals on that chain. Users observing the UI will see the chain status remain “frozen” and may experience missing refunds, zero balances, or inability to interact with the network, contrary to the expectation that an admin can restore normal operation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended semantics of the two functions with their actual implementation and noticed that both functions called the same freeze routine and that the comment for unfreezeChain was inaccurate. The bug is subtle because the function signatures are identical and the erroneous call does not raise a compilation error, making it easy to overlook during code review. To remediate, the unfreezeChain function should be updated to call IZkSyncStateTransition(stateTransition[_chainId]).unfreezeDiamond() and its documentation should be corrected to reflect the unfreeze action. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “incorrect function dispatch” or “logic inversion” bugs where a function performs the opposite of its declared purpose, breaking business logic that assumes a frozen chain can be restored.

title: L2SharedBridge l1LegacyBridge is not set
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing initialization of the legacy bridge address in the L2SharedBridge contract. During the migration from L1ERC20Bridge to L1SharedBridge, the L2 side must be able to accept deposits that originated from the old L1ERC20Bridge. The initialize function receives a parameter _l1LegacyBridge and checks that it is not the zero address, but it never stores the value in the state variable l1LegacyBridge. As a result l1LegacyBridge remains address(0). When a user sends a deposit before the L1 contract is upgraded, the L2 contract calls finalizeDeposit which validates that the caller is the stored legacy bridge; because the stored address is zero, the validation fails and the deposit is rejected. This situation occurs only on the ERA chain where the else branch is executed, and only during the initialization phase after the contract is upgraded. Users experience a silent failure: they submit a deposit, receive no confirmation, and the funds appear to disappear or become locked. The protocol loses the ability to process legacy deposits, breaking the accounting assumption that every deposited token will eventually be claimable on L2. The issue was discovered during a code audit that compared the migration specification with the actual implementation and noticed that the assignment statement was missing. It is hard to notice because the contract compiles and the initialize function does not revert; the problem only manifests when a legacy deposit is attempted. The correct fix is to assign the provided legacy bridge address to the state variable inside the else block, ensuring that finalizeDeposit can correctly recognise messages from the old L1 bridge. In conceptual terms the bug is an uninitialized state variable leading to a validation bypass, a class of errors often referred to as missing assignment or zero‑address default bugs.

title: State transition manager is unable to force upgrade a deployed ST, which invalidates the designed safeguard for ‘urgent high risk situation’
description:
State transition manager (STM) will be unable to force upgrade a deployed ST against intended design for ‘urgent high risk situation’.

This invalidates the designed safeguard mechanism of an STM force upgrade and ST.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the StateTransitionManager (STM) contract’s inability to perform a forced upgrade of a deployed State Transition (ST) chain when an urgent high‑risk situation arises, contrary to the protocol’s documented safeguard. The root cause is a mismatch between the intended design and the actual implementation: STM never invokes the Admin facet’s upgradeChainFromVersion function, which is the only entry point that allows an ST to be upgraded by the manager, because no method in StateTransitionManager calls it. Additionally, the executeUpgrade function, which is restricted to the STM, is only reachable inside the internal _setChainIdUpgrade routine that runs during the initial createNewChain call; after the chain’s genesis this path is no longer available. Consequently, when a critical bug or security incident is discovered after deployment, the STM cannot trigger the upgrade that the documentation promises, leaving the vulnerable contract unchanged. This limitation can be exploited by an attacker who discovers a flaw in the ST contract and knows that the protocol cannot patch it, effectively keeping the system exposed to the original vulnerability. The impact is that the protocol loses its emergency response mechanism, potentially endangering user funds, breaking trust, and violating the business logic that assumes a privileged upgrade path for high‑risk scenarios. The condition occurs any time an upgrade is required after the chain’s initial deployment, i.e., whenever a high‑risk issue is identified post‑genesis. All participants who rely on the protocol’s security guarantees—protocol operators, auditors, and end‑users—are affected because the safeguard that should protect them is non‑functional. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditor demonstrated that the forced‑upgrade flow cannot be executed despite being described in the project documentation. The problem is subtle because the upgrade functions exist and are correctly access‑controlled, but the STM lacks any code path to reach them after deployment, making the missing capability easy to overlook. To remediate, the STM should be extended with a public or privileged method that can invoke either executeUpgrade or upgradeChainFromVersion on the target chain’s Admin facet, thereby restoring the ability to force an upgrade at any time. This class of bug falls under upgradeability flow omissions and privileged‑function accessibility mismatches, where the intended emergency upgrade mechanism is not wired into the contract’s logic, leading to a situation where “funds disappear” or “vulnerable code remains active” despite expectations of a rapid fix.

title: User might be able to double withdraw during migration
description: A user might be able to double withdraw during migration in some edge conditions: (1) if their withdrawal tx is included in a batch number the same or after `eraFirstPostUpgradeBatch`; (2) And if the user `finalizeWithdrawal` on the old L1ERC20Bridge.sol before L1ERC20Bridge.sol is upgraded.
bug_full: During the migration of the zkSync L1 bridge, the contract that finalizes ERC20 withdrawals checks whether the withdrawal originated from the legacy bridge only when the batch number of the L2 transaction is lower than a constant called eraFirstPostUpgradeBatch. If a user submits a withdrawal whose L2 batch number is equal to or greater than this constant, the _isEraLegacyWithdrawal function returns false and the legacy‑bridge status check is skipped. An attacker can exploit this by first calling finalizeWithdrawal on the old L1ERC20Bridge.sol before the bridge contract is upgraded, receiving the tokens, and then, after the upgrade and the migration of funds to the new L1SharedBridge.sol, calling finalizeWithdrawal again with the same withdrawal parameters. Because the legacy‑bridge status is no longer consulted, the second call succeeds and the same ERC20 amount is transferred a second time. The vulnerability is a double‑withdrawal or double‑spend condition that arises from an incomplete state transition during an upgrade, effectively a race condition between the legacy and new bridge contracts. It manifests only when the withdrawal transaction is included in a batch whose number is the same as or later than eraFirstPostUpgradeBatch and when the user finalizes on the old bridge before the upgrade completes. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the user’s wallet balance increases twice for a single withdrawal, while the protocol’s escrow balance is reduced by the same amount twice, leading to missing funds. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the migration steps and the logic that determines whether a withdrawal is considered legacy. Because the condition depends on a precise batch number and on the timing of contract upgrades, it can be easy to miss in standard testing and may only appear in edge‑case scenarios. The proper mitigation is to ensure that the legacy‑withdrawal status is always verified during and after the upgrade, for example by introducing a grace period during which any withdrawal is checked against the old bridge, or by preventing finalization on the old bridge once the upgrade batch is reached. This eliminates the possibility of bypassing the legacy check and prevents the double‑withdrawal attack.

title: `block.timestamp` used as swap deadline offers no protection
description:
`UniV3Utils::swap` performs a [swap](https://github.com/beefyfinance/experiments/blob/14a313b76888581b05d42b6f7b6097c79f3e65c6/contracts/interfaces/exchanges/UniV3Utils.sol#L20) with `deadline: block.timestamp`. This function is called by `StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap::_chargeFees` [L375](https://github.com/beefyfinance/experiments/blob/14a313b76888581b05d42b6f7b6097c79f3e65c6/contracts/protocol/concliq/uniswap/StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap.sol#L375), [L389](https://github.com/beefyfinance/experiments/blob/14a313b76888581b05d42b6f7b6097c79f3e65c6/contracts/protocol/concliq/uniswap/StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap.sol#L389) and `BeefyQIVault::_swapRewardsToNative` [L223](https://github.com/beefyfinance/experiments/blob/14a313b76888581b05d42b6f7b6097c79f3e65c6/contracts/protocol/qidao/BeefyQIVault.sol#L223).

The block the transaction is eventually put into will be `block.timestamp` so this [offers no protection](https://dacian.me/defi-slippage-attacks#heading-no-expiration-deadline).
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of using the current block timestamp (block.timestamp) as the deadline parameter for a token swap operation. Because the transaction that calls the swap will be mined in the same block whose timestamp is used, the deadline is effectively equal to the moment the transaction is executed, providing no time‑based protection. The root cause is a misuse of a time‑based guard: the contract assumes that setting deadline to block.timestamp will prevent execution after a certain time, but in practice the deadline is already satisfied when the transaction is included, so the check never filters out malicious ordering. An attacker who can submit a transaction in the same block can front‑run or reorder the swap, manipulate the price on the underlying pool, and cause the swap to execute at a significantly worse rate. This can lead to users receiving far fewer tokens than expected, fees being taken at an unfavorable price, or overall loss of value for the protocol’s vaults. The issue manifests whenever the swap utility is invoked, which includes fee charging in StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap and reward conversion in BeefyQIVault. Affected parties are the end‑users who deposit into the vault, the protocol that manages those funds, and any role that relies on accurate fee collection. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the swap logic and noted that the deadline parameter did not provide any real expiration window. It can be hard to notice because the code appears to set a deadline, satisfying the superficial expectation that a time limit exists, yet the deadline is effectively a no‑op. To remediate, the contract should accept a deadline supplied by the caller that is set to a future timestamp (e.g., block.timestamp + some buffer) and enforce that the swap only proceeds if the current block timestamp is less than this future deadline. This aligns the implementation with the intended protection against price manipulation and restores the intended business logic that swaps must complete within a reasonable time window.

title: Native tokens permanently stuck in `StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap` contract due to rounding in `_chargeFees`
description:
** `StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap::_chargeFees` converts LP fees into the native token then distributes the native tokens split between:
* the caller as a reward for initiating the harvest
* beefy protocol
* the strategist registered with the strategy

However due to [rounding during division](https://github.com/beefyfinance/experiments/blob/14a313b76888581b05d42b6f7b6097c79f3e65c6/contracts/protocol/concliq/uniswap/StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap.sol#L397-L404) some tokens are not distributed but instead accumulate inside the `StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap` contract where they are permanently stuck.

** Fees will accumulate inside the `StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap` contract where they are permanently stuck. Although the amount each time is small the effect is cumulative, especially given that this protocol is intended to be deployed on the many blockchains where Beefy currently operates.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error in the fee‑distribution routine of a passive Uniswap strategy. When the strategy harvests LP fees it converts the earned fees into the native token and then splits the resulting amount among three recipients: the caller who triggered the harvest, the Beefy protocol treasury, and the strategy’s strategist. The split is performed by multiplying the total native amount by each fee share and dividing by a fixed divisor. Because Solidity integer division truncates any fractional remainder, a small amount of native tokens can remain undistributed after the three transfers. This remainder is not sent to any recipient and instead stays in the strategy contract. Over a single harvest the leftover amount is tiny, but because the strategy is expected to run on many chains and harvest frequently, the leftovers accumulate over time, permanently locking native tokens inside the contract. The issue manifests when a harvest is executed; the caller receives the expected reward, the protocol and strategist receive their portions, but the strategy’s balance of the native token is non‑zero. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a harvest succeeded and that they earned rewards, yet the underlying contract holds a small amount of native token that never reaches any wallet, effectively causing funds to disappear from the protocol’s accounting. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by Cyfrin, which added a targeted test that deposited large amounts, generated LP fees, performed a harvest, and then asserted that the strategy’s native balance should be zero. The test failed, exposing the rounding remainder. The problem is subtle because the leftover amount is usually negligible per harvest and does not cause an immediate failure, making it easy to overlook in normal operation. It violates the business logic that all harvested fees must be fully accounted for and distributed, breaking the accounting invariants of the protocol. The recommended fix is to change the fee‑distribution logic so that the final recipient (the Beefy treasury) receives the total native amount minus the amounts already sent to the caller and strategist, thereby ensuring that any rounding remainder is transferred rather than left in the contract. This approach eliminates the permanent lock‑up of native tokens without altering the intended fee percentages. The vulnerability belongs to the class of integer‑division rounding bugs that cause residual balances to be stranded in smart contracts.

title: `StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap` gives ERC20 token allowances to `unirouter` but doesn't remove allowances when `unirouter` is updated
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a strategy contract that automatically grants unlimited ERC20 token allowances to a router address stored in a parent fee‑manager contract. When the contract is initialized, it calls a private function that executes forceApprove on both underlying tokens, setting the allowance for the current router to the maximum uint256 value. The router address is stored in a variable that can be changed at any time by the contract owner through an external setUnirouter function inherited from the fee‑manager. However, the contract never revokes the previously granted allowances when the router address is updated. The only mechanism to clear allowances is a panic function that must be called explicitly, and there is no automatic cleanup in setUnirouter. Consequently, after the owner changes the router, the old router contract retains the ability to transfer the strategy’s tokens without any further permission checks. An attacker who controls or compromises the old router can therefore invoke transferFrom on the token contracts and drain the protocol’s balances. From a user’s perspective this manifests as deposited funds suddenly disappearing, balances showing zero, or withdrawals failing without an obvious on‑chain error. The issue occurs whenever the owner updates the router address without also invoking the panic routine, which is a plausible operational scenario during upgrades or governance actions. All token holders who have deposited into the strategy are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumes that only the current router can move funds; the lingering allowance breaks this invariant and violates the expected accounting model. The flaw was identified during a manual security audit that examined the allowance management logic and noticed that setUnirouter does not include any allowance reset. It can be hard to detect in production because token allowances are not displayed in typical UI dashboards and the token balances may remain unchanged until the malicious router actively spends them. To remediate the issue the contract should either make setUnirouter virtual and override it in the strategy to revoke all token allowances before assigning a new router, or explicitly reset the allowances to zero within the same function. Using a safeApprove pattern that first sets allowance to zero before granting a new one would also prevent stale approvals from persisting. By ensuring that no stale approvals remain after a router change, the protocol restores its intended security guarantees and prevents unintended token transfers.

title: Update to `StratFeeManagerInitializable::beefyFeeConfig` retrospectively applies new fees to pending LP rewards yet to be claimed
description:
** The fee configuration `StratFeeManagerInitializable::beefyFeeConfig` can be updated via `StratFeeManagerInitializable::setBeefyFeeConfig` [L164-167](https://github.com/beefyfinance/experiments/blob/14a313b76888581b05d42b6f7b6097c79f3e65c6/contracts/protocol/beefy/StratFeeManagerInitializable.sol#L164-L167) while LP rewards are collected and fees charged via `StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap::_harvest` [L306-311](https://github.com/beefyfinance/experiments/blob/14a313b76888581b05d42b6f7b6097c79f3e65c6/contracts/protocol/concliq/uniswap/StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap.sol#L306-L311).

This allows the protocol to enter a state where the fee configuration is updated to for example increase Beefy's protocol fees, then the next time `harvest` is called the higher fees are retrospectively applied to the LP rewards that were pending under the previously lower fee regime.

** The protocol owner can retrospectively alter the fee structure to steal pending LP rewards instead of distributing them to protocol users; the retrospective application of fees is unfair on protocol users because those users deposited their liquidity into the protocol and generated LP rewards at the previous fee levels.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the fee configuration of the strategy manager can be changed while there are unclaimed LP rewards, and the harvest function calculates fees after the configuration change, causing the new higher fee to be applied retroactively to rewards that were earned under the previous lower fee rate. This happens because the setBeefyFeeConfig function is callable at any time and the harvest routine first reads the current fee configuration before claiming and charging fees, without first settling pending rewards. An attacker who controls the protocol owner role can increase the Beefy fee, then trigger or wait for a harvest, causing the higher fee to be deducted from the pending rewards before they are distributed to liquidity providers. The impact is that users receive less reward than expected, effectively losing part of their earned LP tokens or native tokens; the protocol can appear to charge higher fees but the loss is hidden because the reward amount is lower. The condition required is the presence of pending rewards and the ability of the owner to call setBeefyFeeConfig before harvest. The affected parties are LP providers who deposited liquidity and expect their rewards to be calculated with the fee rate that was in effect when the rewards accrued. The issue was identified during a security audit by Cyfrin, and it may be hard to notice because the fee change is a legitimate governance action and the harvest transaction still succeeds, only the fee amount is different. The bug belongs to the class of mutable‑parameter‑and‑order‑of‑operations vulnerabilities, where a state variable that influences accounting is changed after the accounting period but before settlement. From a user perspective the UI may show a normal harvest transaction but the received reward amount is unexpectedly low or zero, contradicting the expectation that my reward should be X. To fix the problem the fee‑setting function should be made virtual and overridden in the strategy so that before the fee configuration is updated the contract first claims any pending earnings and charges fees based on the old configuration; alternatively the contract could lock fee changes during harvest or enforce that fee updates only affect future rewards. This ensures that pending rewards are settled under the fee regime that was in effect when they were earned, preserving fairness and preventing retroactive fee theft.

title: Redemptions are blocked when L2 sequencers are down
poc:
**
1. Protocol X attempts to transfer 10,000 USDC from CCTP Domain A to CCTP Domain B.
2. CCTP Domain B is an L2 rollup that batches transactions for publishing onto the L1 chain via a centralized sequencer.
3. The L2 sequencer goes down; however, transactions can still be executed via forced inclusion on the L1 chain.
4. Protocol X implements the relevant functionality and attempts to redeem 10,000 USDC via forced inclusion.
5. The Wormhole CCTP integration does not consider the contract's aliased address when validating the `mintRecipient`, so the redemption fails.
6. Cross-chain transfer of this liquidity will remain blocked so long as the sequencer is down.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the redemption logic of the Wormhole‑CCTP integration on L2 rollups. The function that redeems tokens checks that the caller address exactly matches the stored mintRecipient using a direct equality comparison. On rollups such as Optimism and Arbitrum, transactions that are forced onto L1 are executed with an aliased version of the original L2 address – the L2 sequencer replaces the sender address with a deterministic alias. Because the contract does not consider this aliased address when performing the equality check, a legitimate redemption request that is forced through L1 during a sequencer outage fails the require statement and reverts with “caller must be mintRecipient”. The root cause is an incomplete sender validation that ignores the address‑aliasing mechanism required for maximum uptime. An attacker or a legitimate user can exploit the condition by triggering a forced inclusion while the L2 sequencer is down; the transaction will be accepted by the L1 bridge but the redemption will be blocked, leaving the cross‑chain payload – often a time‑sensitive liquidity infusion – unable to be executed. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on cross‑chain transfers: users see no funds arriving, the UI may display a redemption failure or a zero balance, and the protocol’s liquidity pipeline is stalled until the sequencer resumes. This occurs only when the L2 sequencer is unavailable and the contract relies on forced inclusion to bypass the sequencer, a scenario that is not covered by typical unit tests. The affected parties include any user or protocol that depends on the Wormhole‑CCTP bridge on L2 domains, as well as the protocol operators who expect continuous availability of cross‑chain liquidity. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, which identified that the address aliasing check was missing. It can be hard to notice because normal operation on a healthy sequencer passes the check, and the failure only manifests under outage conditions that are rarely simulated. To remediate, the validation should be expanded to accept either the original mintRecipient address or its aliased counterpart, ensuring that forced‑inclusion transactions are recognized as authorized. This class of bug falls under improper handling of address aliasing and insufficient sender authentication, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition that violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a valid VAA can always be redeemed.

title: Loss of funds due to malicious forcing of `mintRecipient` onto Circle blacklist when CCTP message is in-flight
poc:
**
1. Alice burns 10,000 USDC on CCTP Domain A to be transferred to her EOA on CCTP Domain B.
2. While this CCTP message is in-flight, an attacker withdraws a non-trivial amount of USDC, that was previously obtained from a recent exploit, from protocol X to Alice's EOA on CCTP domain B.
3. Law enforcement notifies Circle to blacklist Alice's EOA, which now holds stolen funds.
4. Alice attempts to redeem 10,000 USDC on CCTP Domain B, but minting fails because her EOA is now blacklisted on the USDC contract.
5. The 10,000 USDC remains burnt and cannot be minted on the target domain since the VAA containing the attested CCTP message can never be executed without the USDC mint reverting.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises when the address designated to receive minted tokens – the mintRecipient – becomes blacklisted by Circle while a cross‑chain transfer message (VAA) is still in‑flight. The contract logic requires the caller of redeemTokensWithPayload to match the stored mintRecipient, and it does not provide any mechanism to change that address after the VAA is emitted. Because Circle’s blacklist prevents the USDC contract from minting to a blacklisted address, the mint operation reverts and the VAA can never be executed. An attacker can exploit this by sending illicit or sanctioned funds to the intended recipient address, prompting Circle to place the address on its blacklist before the redemption transaction is submitted. The source chain burns the USDC, the VAA is delivered to the destination chain, but the destination mint fails, leaving the burned tokens unrecoverable. This scenario can occur whenever a malicious actor can force a legitimate recipient address onto the blacklist during the narrow window while the VAA is pending. The affected parties are the original sender of the cross‑chain transfer and the intended recipient, both of whom lose access to the transferred funds. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the Wormhole CCTP integration and Circle’s blacklisting policy, noting that the integration does not expose MessageTransmitter.replaceMessage and therefore cannot replace a VAA with a new mintRecipient. The problem is subtle because the failure manifests only as a silent revert of the mint step; users see no funds arrive and may not realize the underlying regulatory block. To remediate, the protocol should allow replacement of a VAA with a new mintRecipient before the VAA is consumed, or implement a governance‑controlled recovery path that can re‑mint the burned tokens when the original recipient is permanently blocked. This class of bug falls under immutable address enforcement combined with external compliance restrictions, leading to permanent loss of funds when the compliance rule changes after a message is in‑flight.

title: Silent overflow in `TrimmedAmount::shift` could result in rate limiter being bypassed
bug_full: The vulnerability is a silent overflow in the amount‑trimming library used by the NTT manager. The library provides a function that scales a token amount from one decimal precision to another and then casts the result to a 64‑bit unsigned integer because the target chain (Solana) only accepts uint64 token amounts. In the trimming function a check is performed to ensure the scaled value fits into uint64, but the shift function, which also performs scaling and casting, lacks this check. When the input amount is large enough that the scaled value exceeds 2^64‑1, the cast truncates the high bits without reverting, producing a much smaller amount. This truncated amount is then fed to the rate‑limiting logic, allowing an attacker to present an apparently small amount while actually moving a much larger value, effectively bypassing the rate limiter. The bug can be triggered whenever the shift function is called with a destination decimal precision that is lower than the source precision and the original amount is close to the uint64 ceiling. It affects any user or contract that relies on the rate limiter to enforce transfer caps, potentially allowing unchecked large transfers and loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual code review that compared the safety checks of related functions and noticed the missing overflow guard in shift. Because the overflow does not generate an error, it can be hard to notice; the contract continues to operate and the UI may show normal transaction success while the internal accounting is wrong, leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds. To remediate, the shift function should include an explicit verification that the scaled amount does not exceed the maximum uint64 value and revert with a clear error if it does, mirroring the check present in the trim function. This change restores the intended invariant that all token amounts fit within the target chain’s numeric limits and re‑enables the rate limiter to function correctly.

title: Disabled Transceivers cannot be re-enabled by calling `TransceiverRegistry::_setTransceiver` after 64 have been registered
bug_full: The issue is a logical ordering flaw in the registry function that manages transceiver contracts. The function first checks whether the total number of registered transceivers has reached the hard‑coded maximum of sixty‑four and reverts with a TooManyTransceivers error if the limit is hit. Only after this check does the code attempt to re‑enable a previously disabled transceiver by setting its enabled flag to true. When the registry is already full, the early revert prevents execution from reaching the enable branch, making it impossible to turn a disabled transceiver back on. This bug occurs only in the edge case where the maximum number of transceivers has been registered and at least one of them has been disabled, a situation that is unlikely under normal operation but can arise during upgrades or mis‑configuration. The affected parties are protocol administrators and any users relying on the transceiver for cross‑chain token transfers, because a disabled transceiver that cannot be re‑enabled may halt the flow of funds through that path. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit that examined the registration logic and noticed that the maximum‑capacity guard was placed before the enable‑logic block. It is hard to notice because the function appears to work correctly when adding new transceivers, and the enable path is only exercised in a rare scenario. From a user perspective, an admin attempting to enable a transceiver sees a transaction revert with TooManyTransceivers, while the UI may still display the transceiver as disabled, leading to confusion and the expectation that the enable action should succeed. The impact is that the protocol loses the ability to reactivate a transceiver without redeploying the contract, potentially freezing certain cross‑chain routes and violating the business assumption that disabled components can be safely re‑enabled. The bug belongs to the class of state‑gate ordering errors where a capacity check blocks legitimate state transitions. The recommended fix is to move the maximum‑transceiver validation inside the branch that handles new registrations, allowing the enable‑logic to execute even when the registry is full. Conceptually, the fix separates the concerns of adding a new transceiver from toggling the enabled flag of an existing one, ensuring that the latter remains reachable regardless of the registry size.

title: NTT Manager cannot be unpaused once paused
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an irreversible pause mechanism in the NTT Manager contract. The contract exposes a pause() function that can be called by the owner or a designated pauser, which correctly triggers the internal _pause() modifier and sets the contract’s paused flag. However, the source code does not provide a complementary unpause() function that would call _unpause() and clear the paused flag. Because the pause state can be entered but never left, any authorized actor who accidentally or maliciously invokes pause will render the manager permanently inactive until the contract is upgraded or redeployed. This creates a denial-of-service condition for the cross-chain token bridge: users attempting to send or receive tokens will see transactions revert with a “paused” error, UI components will display a paused status, and expected token transfers will not occur, giving the impression that funds have disappeared or are stuck. The issue arises from an incomplete implementation of the OpenZeppelin Pausable pattern, where the developer added the pause entry point but omitted the exit point. It is easy to miss during testing because the pause function works as intended and the contract passes basic functionality checks; the missing unpause only becomes apparent when the contract is actually paused. The problem was identified during a security audit that reviewed the manager’s state-control functions. To remediate, the contract should implement an unpause() external function protected by the same onlyOwnerOrPauser modifier, which calls the internal _unpause() routine, thereby restoring normal operation. Adding this function restores the expected lifecycle of the contract, prevents permanent denial of service, and aligns the implementation with standard pausable contracts.

title: Immutable gas limit within `WormholeTransceiver` can lead to execution failures on the target chain
description:
The Wormhole-specific Transceiver implementation uses an immutable [`gasLimit`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/Transceiver/WormholeTransceiver/WormholeTransceiverState.sol#L27) variable to calculate the Relayer delivery price. The underlying assumption here is that the gas consumed for transfers will always be static; however, this is not always the case, especially for L2 rollups such as Arbitrum, where gas is calculated as a function of the actual gas consumed on L2 and the L1 calldata cost that is effectively an L2 view of the L1 gas price. Please refer to the [Arbitrum docs](https://docs.arbitrum.io/inside-arbitrum-nitro#gas-and-fees) for more information on how gas is estimated.

In cases where L2 gas depends on the L1 gas price, extreme scenarios can occur where the delivery cost computed by the static gas limit is insufficient to execute a transfer on L2.

An immutable gas limit can give an extremely stale view of the L2 gas needed to execute a transfer. In extreme scenarios, such stale gas estimates can be insufficient to execute messages on a target chain. If such a scenario occurs, all pending messages with a stale gas estimate will risk being stuck on the target chain. While the gas limit can be changed via an upgrade, there are two issues with this approach:
1. Synchronizing a mass update across a large number of `NttManager` contracts might be difficult to execute.
2. Changing the gas limit has no impact on pending transfers that are already ready for execution on the target chain.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the WormholeTransceiver component that uses a hard‑coded gasLimit value to calculate the relayer delivery price for cross‑chain token transfers. The code assumes that the amount of gas required to execute a transfer on the destination chain is constant, but on Layer‑2 rollups such as Arbitrum the actual gas consumption is a function of the current L1 gas price and the amount of calldata that must be posted to L1. Because the gasLimit is immutable, the contract can retain a stale estimate that is too low when L1 gas prices rise or when the L2 execution model changes. When the static gas limit is insufficient, the relayer cannot provide enough gas to complete the message on the target chain, causing the message to remain pending indefinitely. From a user perspective the transfer appears to be submitted successfully, the UI shows a pending status, but the recipient never receives the funds and the sender’s balance remains unchanged, violating the expectation that a cross‑chain transfer will complete within a reasonable time. The impact is a loss of liveness for the NTT protocol: funds become effectively locked until an operator upgrades the contract and manually adjusts the gas limit, which does not retroactively rescue already‑stuck messages. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the gas estimation logic and compared it with the documented Arbitrum gas model. It is difficult to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit failure event; the only symptom is a growing backlog of pending messages. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of static configuration errors where a parameter that should reflect a dynamic network condition is hard‑coded. The proper mitigation is to make the gas limit mutable, allowing NTT managers or an automated oracle to update the value in response to changes in L1 gas price, or to compute the required gas per‑message at execution time. This change restores the accounting assumption that the relayer will always supply sufficient gas for successful delivery, preventing funds from disappearing into an unexecuted state.

title: Transceiver invariants and ownership synchronicity can be broken by unsafe Transceiver upgrades
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the upgrade mechanism of Transceiver contracts that are used by NTT Managers for cross‑chain message handling. A Transceiver is expected to keep two immutable references – the address of the NTT Manager and the address of the underlying NTT token – unchanged across upgrades. This guarantee is enforced by the internal virtual function _checkImmutables, which asserts that the manager and token addresses remain identical. However, the design allows a malicious or careless upgrade to bypass these checks in two ways: by overriding _checkImmutables in a custom implementation without calling the original validation, or by invoking Implementation._setMigratesImmutables(true), which disables the immutables verification for the subsequent upgrade. Because the Transceiver ownership model is synchronized with the NTT Manager owner – the manager’s transferOwnership function iterates over all registered transceivers and calls each transceiver’s transferTransceiverOwnership – any transceiver that changes its owner independently (through the public OwnableUpgradeable.transferOwnership function that is not overridden) can later be upgraded without the immutables check. When such a transceiver is upgraded to a version that points to a different NTT Manager or token, the invariant that all transceivers share the same manager address is broken. As a result, a later call to NttManagerState.transferOwnership reverts, because the manager detects that at least one registered transceiver is out of sync. Since transceivers cannot be deregistered, the manager becomes effectively frozen: the intended owner cannot change, cross‑chain transfers that rely on the manager may stop working, and token holders may see their balances remain unchanged while the protocol appears to be operational. The impact is a loss of control over the manager contract, potential locking of funds, and a breach of the business logic that assumes a single authoritative manager across all endpoints. The issue manifests only when a transceiver owner performs an upgrade that disables the immutables check, which can be subtle because the upgrade transaction itself looks legitimate and the invariant checks are hidden behind internal functions. It was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, which demonstrated a proof‑of‑concept where calling _setMigratesImmutables(true) allowed an upgrade that caused NttManagerState.transferOwnership to revert. The bug is hard to notice in normal testing because the manager’s ownership transfer appears to work until a mismatched transceiver is present. To remediate, the immutables verification functions should be made private (or otherwise non‑overridable) so that they cannot be bypassed, and the ability to disable the check via _setMigratesImmutables should be removed or restricted. Additionally, the public transferOwnership function of the transceiver should be overridden to enforce that only the NTT Manager can change transceiver ownership, preserving the intended synchronization of owners across the system.

title: Setting a peer `NttManager` contract for the same chain can cause loss of user funds
description:
** The current implementation of `NttManager::setPeer` allows the owner to set the NTT Manager as a peer for the same chain ID as the current chain. If the NTT Manager owner accidentally (or otherwise) sets an arbitrary address as a peer `NttManager` address for the same chain, this configuration would allow a user to initiate a transfer with the same target chain as the source chain, but such transfers will not get executed on the target chain (which is same as source chain).
** There is a potential loss of funds for the users. Even if the peer is subsequently removed, messages already sent from the source chain can never be executed. Any funds attached to those messages will be stuck in the `NttManager` contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the NttManager contract’s setPeer function, which permits the contract owner to register a peer NttManager address for any chain identifier, including the identifier of the chain on which the contract itself is deployed. Because the implementation does not enforce a check that the peer chain ID differs from the local chain ID, an owner (or an attacker who gains owner privileges) can configure the contract so that the peer for the current chain points to an arbitrary address, even the zero address. When a user later initiates a cross‑chain transfer and specifies the local chain as the destination, the NttManager treats the request as a normal cross‑chain operation: it locks the user’s tokens, emits a Wormhole message and updates the outbound rate‑limit accounting. However, because the registered peer address belongs to the same chain, the corresponding inbound processing on the destination chain never occurs – the inbound rate‑limit for that chain remains at zero and the message is effectively dropped. From the user’s perspective the transfer appears to succeed; the sender’s balance is reduced, but the intended recipient receives no tokens and the total supply of the token does not change. The funds become permanently locked in the NttManager contract unless the owner manually removes the mis‑configured peer and provides a separate recovery mechanism, which is not part of the current logic. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised the setPeer function with the local chain ID and observed that outbound limits were decremented while inbound limits stayed unchanged, confirming that messages were never processed. The bug is subtle because the contract’s UI and events suggest a successful transfer, and same‑chain cross‑chain transfers are uncommon, so developers may not anticipate this edge case. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of “incorrect cross‑chain routing validation” bugs, where a contract fails to validate that a peer belongs to a distinct network before accepting it as a routing target. To remediate, the setPeer function should reject any attempt to register a peer whose chain identifier matches the contract’s own chain ID, and the transfer function should include a guard that prevents sending to the same chain when the peer configuration is invalid. This validation restores the invariant that every emitted cross‑chain message must have a corresponding inbound handler on a different chain, thereby preventing user funds from disappearing into an unexecuted message queue.

title: Lack of a gas refund in the current design can lead to the overcharging of users and misaligned relayer incentives that can choke message execution
description:
** To understand gas handling, it is important to highlight a few key aspects of the current design:
1. On the target chain, Transceivers can either attest to a message or attest and execute a message. Transceivers up to the threshold attest to a message, while the Transceiver who will cause the threshold to be reached attests and executes a message.
2. Each transceiver quotes a gas estimate on the source chain. When quoting a price, no Transceiver knows if its peer on the target chain will simply attest to a message or both attest and execute a message. This means that every Transceiver quotes a gas estimate that assumes its peer will be executing a message.
Based on the two above facts, the following can be deduced:
1. If the threshold has not yet been reached, a sender is paying a delivery fee for every Transceiver, even ones that are attesting a message after it was already executed.
2. The sender is paying for a scenario where every Transceiver is responsible for executing a message on the target chain. In reality, only one transceiver will execute, and all others will attest.
3. If a relayer consistently calls a Transceiver before the threshold is reached, a relayer will earn more than is spent in terms of gas.
4. The above point incentivizes relayers to always be the ones to attest and not to execute. A clever relayer can simply query `messageAttestations` off-chain and skip a delivery if `messageAttestations == threshold - 1`, since a relayer spends less gas than what they charged on the source chain if they deliver before OR after a threshold is met.
**
1. Users are overcharged on the source chain without recourse due to the lack of a refund mechanism.
2. Relayers can choke message execution by skipping execution of the message that meets the attestation threshold. Current economic incentives benefit relayers if they skip this specific message.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic‑logic flaw in the Wormhole cross‑chain message delivery design where the system does not refund unused gas to the sender after a message has been attested by enough transceivers. The root cause is that each transceiver on the source chain quotes a gas estimate assuming its peer on the target chain will both attest to and execute the message, even though only the transceiver that reaches the attestation threshold actually performs the execution. Consequently, the sender is charged a delivery fee that covers the full gas estimate for every transceiver, including those that only attest and never execute. Because the protocol does not provide a mechanism to return the surplus gas, users are overcharged with no recourse.
