This mis‑alignment creates a perverse incentive for relayers: a relayer can monitor the number of attestations off‑chain and, when the count is one short of the threshold, deliberately skip the execution step, collect the quoted fee, and keep the difference between the quoted gas cost and the actual gas spent. By consistently acting before the threshold is reached, a relayer can earn more than it spends, and by skipping the execution of the message that would meet the threshold, it can effectively choke the message, leaving it unexecuted on the target chain. The impact is two‑fold: users see higher than expected fees and may never receive the intended cross‑chain transfer, while the protocol’s reliability is weakened because a malicious or profit‑seeking relayer can stall critical messages. The issue manifests whenever multiple transceivers are involved in attestation and the threshold has not yet been met, which is the normal operating condition for most messages. Both end‑users who pay the delivery fee and the protocol itself are affected because the economic model no longer guarantees that fees correspond to actual work performed. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, which highlighted the discrepancy between quoted gas and actual execution cost and noted that the existing `targetChainRefundPerUnitGasUnused` field returned by `DeliveryProvider::quoteEvmDeliveryPrice` is never used. The problem is subtle because the overcharging appears as a normal delivery fee and there is no explicit error or revert; only a careful analysis of the fee calculation reveals the excess. To remediate, the protocol should calculate the unused gas based on the `targetChainRefundPerUnitGasUnused` parameter and automatically refund the surplus to the sender’s address on the target chain, thereby aligning fees with real gas consumption and removing the incentive for relayers to skip execution. In broader terms, this is a class of bug where missing refund logic leads to overcharging and incentive distortion, breaking the expected accounting guarantees of a cross‑chain messaging system.

title: Access-controlled functions cannot be called when L2 sequencers are down
description:
** Given that rollups such as [Optimism](https://docs.optimism.io/chain/differences#address-aliasing) and [Arbitrum](https://docs.arbitrum.io/arbos/l1-to-l2-messaging#address-aliasing) offer methods for forced transaction inclusion, it is important that the aliased sender address is also [checked](https://solodit.xyz/issues/m-8-operator-is-blocked-when-sequencer-is-down-on-arbitrum-sherlock-none-index-git) within access control modifiers when verifying the sender holds a permissioned role to allow the functions to which they are applied to be called even in the event of sequencer downtime. The most pertinent examples include:
* [`PausableOwnable::_checkOwnerOrPauser`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/libraries/PausableOwnable.sol#L17-L24), which is called in the [`onlyOwnerOrPauser`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/libraries/PausableOwnable.sol#L9-L15) modifier, which itself is applied to [`PausableOwnable::transferPauserCapability`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/libraries/PausableOwnable.sol#L31-L39) and, more importantly, [`NttManagerState::pause`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/NttManager/NttManagerState.sol#L188-L191).
* [`OwnableUpgradeable::_checkOwner`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/libraries/external/OwnableUpgradeable.sol#L83-L90) which is called in the [`onlyOwner`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/libraries/external/OwnableUpgradeable.sol#L67-L73) modifier, which itself is applied to [`OwnableUpgradeable::transferOwnership`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/libraries/external/OwnableUpgradeable.sol#L92-L101), [`NttManagerState::upgrade`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/NttManager/NttManagerState.sol#L183-L186), [`NttManagerState::transferOwnership`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/NttManager/NttManagerState.sol#L193-L203), [`NttManagerState::setTransceiver`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/NttManager/NttManagerState.sol#L205-L228), [`NttManagerState::removeTransceiver`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/NttManager/NttManagerState.sol#L230-L242), [`NttManagerState::setThreshold`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/NttManager/NttManagerState.sol#L244-L257), [`NttManagerState::setPeer`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/NttManager/NttManagerState.sol#L259-L281), [`NttManagerState::setOutboundLimit`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/NttManager/NttManagerState.sol#L283-L286), [`NttManagerState::setInboundLimit`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/NttManager/NttManagerState.sol#L288-L291), and [`Transceiver::upgrade`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/Transceiver/Transceiver.sol#L66-L68).
* The [`onlyRelayer`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/Transceiver/WormholeTransceiver/WormholeTransceiverState.sol#L274-L279) modifier which is applied to [`WormholeTransceiver::receiveWormholeMessages`](https://github.com/wormhole-foundation/example-native-token-transfers/blob/f4e2277b358349dbfb8a654d19a925628d48a8af/evm/src/Transceiver/WormholeTransceiver/WormholeTransceiver.sol#L64-L105).
** Failure to consider the aliased sender address prevents the execution of admin or otherwise permissioned functionality on a chain where transactions are batched by a centralized L2 sequencer. Since this functionality could be time-sensitive, such as the urgent pausing of the protocol or the relaying of NTT messages, this issue has the potential to have a high impact with reasonable likelihood.
poc:
** While potentially unlikely, a possible scenario could include:
1. An attacker identifies an exploit in the NTT Manager’s protocol on the source chain and plans to bridge stolen funds to the Ethereum mainnet. Assume the source chain is an L2 rollup that batches transactions for publishing onto the L1 chain via a centralized sequencer.
2. The L2 sequencer goes down; however, transactions can still be executed via forced inclusion on the L1 chain. The Attacker could either have forced or waited for this to happen.
3. The Attacker exploits the protocol and initiates a native token transfer, kicking off the 24-hour rate limit duration. Assume the outbound rate limit is hit on the L2, but the inbound limit is not exceeded on the Ethereum mainnet.
4. Access-controlled functions are not callable since they do not check the aliased sender address, so admin transactions cannot be force-included from L1, e.g. pause the protocol.
5. The rate limit duration passes, and the sequencer is still down – the attacker completes the outbound transfer (assuming attestations are made) and relays the message on the Ethereum mainnet.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an access‑control bypass that appears only when a Layer‑2 rollup such as Optimism or Arbitrum experiences sequencer downtime. The contract’s permissioned modifiers (for example onlyOwner, onlyOwnerOrPauser, onlyRelayer) verify the caller by checking msg.sender against stored role addresses, but they do not account for the address‑aliasing mechanism that L2‑to‑L1 forced inclusion uses. When the sequencer is offline, a transaction can still be forced onto L1 with the sender address automatically transformed (aliased) to a different value. Because the modifiers ignore this aliased form, calls that should be allowed for owners, pausers or relayers are rejected, preventing any admin or privileged function from being executed during the outage. This happens because the root cause is a missing check for the aliased sender address in the access‑control logic. An attacker can exploit the situation by waiting for or inducing sequencer downtime, then using forced inclusion to submit a malicious transaction while the protocol’s admin functions remain inaccessible. The attacker may trigger a rate‑limit breach on the L2 side, initiate a token transfer, and rely on the fact that the protocol cannot be paused or upgraded until the sequencer returns, thereby extending the window for fund exfiltration or other harmful actions. The impact is that the protocol loses its ability to react to emergencies – users may see the system continue operating when it should be paused, upgrades cannot be applied, and relayer functions may fail, potentially leading to loss of funds or degraded security guarantees. The condition under which this occurs is specific: the L2 chain must support forced inclusion and employ address aliasing, and the sequencer must be down or otherwise unable to process normal batches. All privileged roles – owners, pausers, relayers – are affected because their functions become effectively locked. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the access‑control modifiers and compared them against the rollup’s forced‑inclusion documentation. It is hard to notice because normal operation on a healthy sequencer shows no problem; only under the rare sequencer‑down scenario does the bug surface, making it easy to miss in standard testing. To remediate, the contract should extend each access‑control check to also accept the aliased version of the caller address, for example by normalising the sender through the rollup’s aliasing utility before role verification, or by explicitly granting the aliased address the same role. As an additional mitigation, reducing the inbound rate limit on the affected chain to zero can prevent the attacker from completing a transfer while the sequencer remains down, limiting the window of exposure. In summary, the bug is a missing alias‑aware permission check that blocks critical admin actions during L2 sequencer outages, violating the protocol’s expectation that privileged functions remain callable at all times.

title: `Goldigovernor._getProposalState()` shouldn't use `totalSupply`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance contract’s internal function that determines a proposal’s final state. The function compares the number of votes in favor against a quorum calculated as one‑twentieth of the token’s totalSupply obtained from the liquidity pool contract at the moment the check is performed. Because totalSupply is a mutable value that can increase after the voting period has closed, the quorum threshold can rise unexpectedly. If additional tokens are minted or otherwise added to the pool after voting ends, a proposal that previously satisfied the quorum may suddenly fall below the new threshold. The logic then classifies the proposal as Defeated instead of Queued, causing the proposal to be blocked from execution. This flaw occurs during the state transition phase after the voting window, when the contract evaluates whether the proposal has met the quorum requirement. All participants who submitted votes, as well as the protocol that relies on timely execution of approved proposals, are affected because a legitimate governance decision can be silently invalidated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that identified the use of a live totalSupply call as a quorum source, a pattern that can lead to time‑dependent inconsistencies. It is hard to notice because the UI may initially display the proposal as Queued and later change to Defeated without any user‑initiated action, giving the impression of a random state flip. The impact includes potential governance paralysis, delayed or aborted upgrades, and loss of confidence among token holders. To remediate, the contract should capture a snapshot of totalSupply at the proposal’s start (or at the end of the voting period) and use that immutable value for the quorum check, or replace the dynamic totalSupply reference with a fixed quorum parameter stored per proposal. This change ensures that the quorum requirement remains constant throughout the proposal lifecycle, preserving the intended business logic that a proposal meeting the required vote count remains executable.

title: In `Goldivault.redeemYield()`, users can redeem more yield tokens using reentrancy
bug_full: The Goldivault contract allows a user to call redeemYield to burn a portion of their yield token (YT) and receive a proportional amount of underlying yield assets. The function first calculates a share based on the amount of YT to burn, then immediately calls the YT contract to burn the tokens, which updates the YT totalSupply but does not change the vault's balance of the underlying assets. After the burn, the contract iterates over each configured yield token and transfers a claimable amount calculated from the current vault balance multiplied by the share. If the YT contract implements a beforeTokenTransfer hook – for example an ERC777 style hook that is invoked during the burn – a malicious token can execute arbitrary code before the burn completes. By re‑entering redeemYield from within that hook, the attacker can call the function a second time while the vault’s underlying balance has not yet been reduced, but the YT totalSupply has already been lowered from the first call. This mismatch causes the second call to compute a larger claimable amount, allowing the attacker to receive more yield tokens than their proportional share. The vulnerability is a classic reentrancy bug triggered by an external callback, often referred to as a token‑hook reentrancy or callback reentrancy. It can be exploited whenever a yield token supports hooks and the Goldivault function does not protect against re‑entrancy, i.e., it lacks a nonReentrant modifier or does not follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern. The impact is that a malicious user can drain the vault’s yield assets, effectively stealing funds that belong to honest participants. The issue manifests under the condition that the contract is concluded, the delay period has passed, and the caller supplies a non‑zero amount. Users may notice that their redemption yields unexpectedly high amounts, while later the vault balance appears depleted or other users receive less than expected. The problem was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, who identified the logical flaw in the ordering of state changes and external calls. Because most ERC20 tokens do not have hooks, the reentrancy path is not obvious and may be missed during testing. To remediate, the contract should either add a nonReentrant guard to redeemYield, move all external token transfers after all internal state updates, or redesign the accounting to avoid relying on mutable external balances during the call. Implementing a reentrancy lock or adhering strictly to the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern will prevent the malicious hook from re‑entering the function and ensure that the amount of yield tokens claimed always matches the user’s true share, preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees.

title: Wrong validation in `Goldigovernor.cancel()`
bug_full: The Goldigovernor contract contains a flawed validation in its cancel() function that governs who may cancel a pending proposal and under what voting conditions. The function is intended to allow a proposal to be cancelled either by its original proposer or by any actor if the proposer’s voting power has fallen below the protocol’s proposalThreshold. Instead, the implementation first checks that the caller is the proposer and then reverts when the proposer’s prior votes are greater than the threshold. This logic mistakenly ties the ability to cancel exclusively to the proposer and also requires the proposer to have fewer votes than the threshold, which is the opposite of the intended rule. As a result, a proposer who loses voting power cannot cancel his own proposal, and third‑party users are never given the opportunity to cancel a proposal on behalf of the protocol. The bug is discovered during a manual audit of the governance contract where the conditional statement was flagged as “incorrect”. It may be hard to notice because the function still compiles and the revert message appears only when a proposer’s vote count exceeds the threshold, a situation that may not be exercised in typical test scenarios. When a proposal cannot be cancelled, the associated Timelock transactions remain queued indefinitely, preventing the protocol from withdrawing or modifying assets tied to those actions. This can lead to a dead‑lock where funds are effectively frozen, or worse, allow a malicious proposal to be executed because the community cannot intervene to stop it. Users observing the UI would see that a proposal stays in a “Pending” state even after the proposer’s voting power drops, and attempts to cancel return no feedback or an unexpected revert. The vulnerability belongs to the class of access‑control and business‑logic validation errors where the condition for a privileged operation is inverted or overly restrictive. To remediate, the cancel() function should be rewritten so that the proposer can always cancel their own proposal, while any other caller may cancel only if the proposer’s prior votes are below the proposalThreshold. This typically involves changing the require/revert logic to a combined check that permits cancellation when (msg.sender == proposal.proposer) || (GovLocks(govlocks).getPriorVotes(proposal.proposer, block.number‑1) < proposalThreshold).

title: Users wouldn't cancel their proposals due to the increased `proposalThreshold`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the cancel() function that validates a caller’s voting power against the current global proposalThreshold value. Because proposalThreshold is mutable through the setProposalThreshold() admin call, its value can be altered after a proposal has been created. When a proposer submits a proposal, the system records only the proposal data but does not snapshot the threshold that was in effect at that moment. If the multisig or any authorized entity later raises proposalThreshold above the proposer’s voting power, the subsequent call to cancel() will fail the threshold check and revert, even though the proposer originally met the requirement. This creates a scenario where a user who expects to be able to withdraw or cancel their own proposal finds the transaction rejected, the proposal remains active, and any associated funds or state remain locked. The impact is a breach of the governance business logic: proposals that should be cancellable become irrevocable, potentially leading to dead‑locked governance decisions, loss of confidence, and financial risk if proposals involve token transfers or escrowed assets. The condition occurs only when the threshold is increased after proposal creation and the proposer’s voting power lies between the old and new thresholds. It primarily affects proposers and any participants relying on the ability to cancel proposals, as well as the protocol’s overall integrity. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the interaction between setProposalThreshold() and cancel(). It can be hard to notice because the cancel function works correctly under normal circumstances; the failure only appears after an administrative change, which may not be exercised frequently in testing. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “state‑dependent access control” or “dynamic parameter misuse” where a permission check references a mutable global variable instead of a snapshot tied to the specific object. To remediate, the contract should cache the proposalThreshold value at the time the proposal is created and use that cached value for subsequent cancel eligibility checks, or redesign the cancel logic to rely on a separate, immutable criterion such as the proposer’s own voting power at proposal time. This ensures that the ability to cancel remains consistent with the expectations set at proposal submission and prevents the protocol from unintentionally locking proposals through administrative threshold adjustments.

title: `Goldilend.liquidate()` might revert due to underflow
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an inaccurate interest calculation performed in the repay function, where a rounding discrepancy causes the computed interest to be one unit lower than the contractual amount. When a borrower repays the full principal, the contract subtracts the repayment amount minus the rounded‑down interest from the global outstandingDebt variable. Because the interest is understated, the subtraction removes more debt than intended, leaving outstandingDebt smaller than it should be. Later, when another borrower’s position is liquidated, the liquidate function attempts to reduce outstandingDebt by the exact difference between the borrowed amount and the stored interest (the correct value). If outstandingDebt has already been reduced too far, this subtraction underflows, triggering a revert and preventing the liquidation. The issue manifests only when a repayment triggers the rounding error and a subsequent liquidation occurs before the debt accounting is corrected. Affected parties include borrowers who expect their loans to be liquidated when overdue, lenders relying on accurate debt accounting, and the protocol itself, which may become unable to clear bad debt, potentially locking funds. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the arithmetic of the FixedPointMathLib functions and identified that the rounding behaviour in mulWadUp could produce a lower interest value. The problem is subtle because the rounding error is small and only surfaces in aggregate accounting, making it easy to miss during normal testing. It violates the core business logic that total outstanding debt must always be at least the sum of each loan’s principal minus interest, breaking the accounting invariant and causing user‑facing symptoms such as liquidation transactions reverting with an underflow error and balances appearing inconsistent. The recommended remediation is to compute the exact debt to be repaid as borrowedAmount minus interest and to cap the subtraction against the current outstandingDebt, mirroring the safe pattern used in the repay function, thereby preserving the accounting invariant and preventing underflow reverts.

title: In `Goldigovernor`, wrong assumption of block time
description:
** In `Goldigovernor.sol`, voting period/delay limits are set with 15s block time.

```solidity
/// @notice Minimum voting period
uint32 public constant MIN_VOTING_PERIOD = 5760; // About 24 hours

/// @notice Maximum voting period
uint32 public constant MAX_VOTING_PERIOD = 80640; // About 2 weeks

/// @notice Minimum voting delay
uint32 public constant MIN_VOTING_DELAY = 1;

/// @notice Maximum voting delay
uint32 public constant MAX_VOTING_DELAY = 40320; // About 1 week
```

But Berachain has 5s block time according to [its documentation](https://docs.berachain.com/faq/#how-well-does-berachain-perform).

```
Berachain has the following properties:

- Block time: 5s
```

So these limits will be set shorter than expected.

** Voting period/delay limits will be set shorter than expected.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the assumed block production interval and the actual block time of the target blockchain. In the governance contract, the minimum and maximum voting periods as well as the voting delay are expressed as fixed numbers of blocks (5760, 80640, 1, and 40320 respectively) with the implicit assumption that each block takes roughly fifteen seconds. On Berachain, however, blocks are produced every five seconds. Consequently, the same block counts correspond to only one third of the intended real‑world duration. This mis‑calculation means that a voting period advertised as "about 24 hours" actually lasts only eight minutes, and a maximum period advertised as "about two weeks" lasts only about two days. The same compression applies to the voting delay, which may be far shorter than expected. An attacker or any participant can exploit this by submitting proposals under the belief that they have ample time to discuss and vote, only to find that the voting window closes much earlier. This can lead to rushed decisions, insufficient scrutiny, or the ability to front‑run proposals before other voters can react. The impact is a weakened governance process: token holders may miss the chance to cast votes, proposals may be executed without proper community oversight, and the protocol’s security assumptions based on a longer deliberation period are violated. The issue manifests whenever the contract is deployed on a chain whose block time differs from the fifteen‑second baseline, affecting all users who rely on the governance UI to show expected time frames. It was discovered during a static audit that compared the documented block time of Berachain with the hard‑coded constants. Because the constants are expressed in block numbers rather than timestamps, the problem can be subtle and may not be obvious from a superficial code review or UI testing that only shows block counts. To remediate, the contract should derive time‑based limits from the actual block interval, either by storing a configurable block‑time constant, using timestamps for period calculations, or by adjusting the constants to reflect the target chain’s five‑second block cadence. This aligns the on‑chain voting windows with the real‑world expectations expressed in the protocol documentation and prevents the governance process from being unintentionally accelerated.

title: M-01 | Fill Price Causes Funding And Utilization Discrepancy
description:
In the Position.validateTrade function the params.fillPrice is used to compute the marginValues,
which include the funding and utilization fees based upon that price. However the funding and
utilization fees should not be based upon the fillPrice, as this price includes a premium/discount
according to how the trade affects the market skew.
This will lead to shorts paying less fees when they push the skew increasingly short, or longs paying
more fees when they push the skew increasingly long.
Additionally, when the currentFundingAccruedComputed and currentUtilizationAccruedComputed is
accounted for the market with the recomputeUtilization and recomputeFunding functions these
values are based upon the pythPrice. As a result traders will experience a discrepancy in the amount
of funding and utilization fees paid to the market’s recorded funding and utilization accrued values.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the Position.validateTrade function calculates funding and utilization fees. Instead of using the oracle‑derived market price (oraclePrice/pythPrice), the function mistakenly relies on the trade fillPrice, which already incorporates a premium or discount that reflects how the trade shifts the market skew. Because fillPrice is skew‑adjusted, a trader who pushes the market deeper into a short or long bias receives a fee calculation that is artificially low or high respectively. Consequently, short positions that increase short skew pay less funding and utilization fees than they should, while long positions that increase long skew are over‑charged. The discrepancy becomes visible when the market’s recomputeUtilization and recomputeFunding functions later reconcile the accrued funding and utilization values using the unbiased oracle price; the on‑chain recorded accrued values no longer match the fees actually paid by traders. This mismatch can be exploited by deliberately trading in a direction that moves the skew, thereby reducing the fee burden and gaining an unintended profit margin. The impact is a distortion of fee revenue for the protocol, unfair cost distribution among participants, and potential erosion of trust in the market’s accounting logic. The issue manifests whenever a trade is executed that changes the market skew and the contract uses fillPrice for fee computation, which is typical for most trades. All market participants—traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the fee accounting is inaccurate. The flaw was uncovered during a manual audit that compared the fee calculation paths and identified the inconsistent price source. It is subtle because the fee formulas appear mathematically correct; the error lies in the choice of input price, making it easy to miss without a deep trace of the data flow. To remediate, the fee calculation should be refactored to use the oraclePrice (the unbiased market price) rather than the fillPrice when determining funding and utilization fees, ensuring that fees are based on a price that does not embed the trader‑induced skew. This aligns the fees with the protocol’s intended economic model and restores consistency between paid fees and recorded accrued values.

title: M-02 | Full Utilization DoS
description:
When computing the current utilization in the PerpMarket.getUtilization function if the backing
liquidity is over-utilized, e.g. delegatedCollateralValueUsd < 0, then a utilization of 100% is returned.
However when the backing liquidity is exactly 100% utilized, e.g. delegatedCollateralValueUsd == 0
then the function will attempt to divide the lockedCollateralUsd by the delegatedCollateralValueUsd,
resulting in a divide by 0 panic revert.
However, the risk of DoS is unlikely as the utilization is unlikely to be able to get to exactly 100%.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the market contract’s utilization calculation routine. The function that reports current utilization divides the amount of locked collateral by the amount of delegated collateral that backs the market. When the market is over‑utilized, the backing collateral value becomes negative and the function correctly caps the reported utilization at 100 %. However, when the market reaches exactly full utilization, the backing collateral value is zero. In this edge case the division operation attempts to divide by zero, which triggers a Solidity panic and reverts the transaction. The root cause is an insufficient guard condition that only checks for a negative backing value but does not handle the zero case. An attacker who can manipulate deposits, withdrawals, or price feeds to bring the delegated collateral value precisely to zero can cause any call that queries utilization – including trades, liquidations, or administrative actions – to revert, effectively denying service to all users of the perpetual market. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to reject transactions with no obvious reason, showing error messages such as “panic: division by zero” or simply failing without a clear explanation, leading to confusion and potentially halted trading activity. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition that does not directly steal funds but can freeze market operations, affect liquidity providers, traders, and the overall protocol reputation. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the market’s accounting logic, where the auditor noted that the conditional branch handling over‑utilization did not cover the exact‑zero scenario. Because reaching exactly 100 % utilization is unlikely in normal operation, the bug can be easy to overlook, especially if test cases only cover positive or negative collateral values. To remediate, the function should return a safe utilization value (e.g., 100 %) whenever the delegated collateral value is less than or equal to zero, thereby avoiding the division altogether. This change aligns the implementation with the intended business rule that utilization cannot exceed full capacity and restores reliable operation of the market contract.

title: M-03 | Wrong Feature Flag Used For Account Split
description:
In the splitAccount function the feature flag validation is performed with the
Flags.MERGE_ACCOUNT feature, meanwhile the Flags.SPLIT_ACCOUNT feature ought to be used.
This can allow an account which does not have permission to split their account to do so anyway.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect permission check in the contract function that separates a user’s holdings into two distinct accounts. Instead of verifying that the caller has the SPLIT_ACCOUNT feature flag, the code mistakenly checks for the MERGE_ACCOUNT flag. This mismatch means that any account that is authorized to merge accounts – a permission that is often granted for unrelated operations – will also be able to invoke the split operation, even if the protocol’s business rules forbid it. The root cause is a simple copy‑and‑paste or naming error in the feature‑flag validation logic, which bypasses the intended access control. An attacker can exploit this by calling the splitAccount function on an account that lacks explicit split permission but has the merge flag enabled. Because the contract believes the required flag is present, it proceeds with the split, reallocating assets between the newly created sub‑accounts. The impact is that funds can be moved or duplicated without proper authorization, breaking accounting invariants, potentially leading to loss of value for other users, and undermining trust in the protocol’s permission model. This condition occurs whenever the feature‑flag system is active and the MERGE_ACCOUNT flag is set for an address, which is common in many deployment configurations. Users who are not supposed to split their accounts may see unexpected new accounts appear, balances may shift unexpectedly, or refunds may be calculated incorrectly because the protocol assumes splits only happen under controlled circumstances. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the reviewer compared the flag used in the splitAccount function against the documented permission model and noticed the mismatch. It can be hard to notice because the code still performs a flag check, so superficial testing that only verifies a true flag passes will not reveal the problem; only a deeper review of the flag semantics exposes the flaw. To remediate, the contract should replace the MERGE_ACCOUNT flag check with the correct SPLIT_ACCOUNT flag, add explicit unit tests that assert only accounts with SPLIT_ACCOUNT can invoke the split, and consider centralising flag validation to avoid similar mistakes in the future. Conceptually, this is a mis‑configured access‑control bug where an incorrect capability identifier is used, allowing unauthorized execution of a privileged operation.

title: M-04 | flagReward Incorrectly Based On marginUsd
description:
In the validateNextPositionEnoughMargin function the Maintenance Margin is calculated through the
getLiquidationMarginUsd function. However the invocation wrongly passes in the nextMarginUsd to
compute the flagReward when it should be passing in collateralUsd.
The flagPosition function computes the flagReward based upon the collateralUsd of the position,
therefore using nextMarginUsd to compute the flagReward inaccurately accounts for the amount in
the liquidation check.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the flagReward used in the liquidation safety check of a synthetic market contract. The root cause is a mismatched argument passed to the getLiquidationMarginUsd helper: the validateNextPositionEnoughMargin function supplies the nextMarginUsd value where the collateralUsd of the position should be provided. Because the flagPosition routine derives the flagReward from the collateralUsd, using nextMarginUsd leads to a reward that does not reflect the true amount of collateral backing the position. An attacker or a regular user can trigger the faulty path when the protocol validates whether a proposed position change has sufficient margin. The contract will compute a maintenance margin that is either too low or too high, causing the flagReward to be mis‑estimated. Consequently, under‑collateralised positions may escape detection and avoid liquidation, or well‑collateralised positions may be flagged and liquidated prematurely. From the user’s perspective this manifests as unexpected liquidation events, missing refunds, or balances that appear to disappear after a trade. The issue is discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the variable used for the flagReward does not match the intended accounting model. It is subtle because the function names suggest a generic margin check, and the wrong variable still yields plausible numbers in simple scenarios, making the bug easy to overlook. The proper fix is to pass the collateralUsd amount as the second‑to‑last parameter to getLiquidationMarginUsd inside validateNextPositionEnoughMargin, ensuring the flagReward is derived from the correct collateral figure and that liquidation logic respects the intended financial guarantees.

title: M-05 | entryPrice Used To Validate Initial Margin
description: In the validateNextPositionIm function the getLiquidationMarginUsd function is used to compute the initial margin value that the position must uphold. However the initial margin value is computed based upon the newPosition.entryPrice rather than the oraclePrice. This is in direct contradiction to the price used to calculate and validate the maintenance margin for the position in the validateNextPositionEnoughMargin function, which uses the oraclePrice. This leads to a discrepancy in the validation performed on a position when validating a trade. The initial margin is validated based upon the entryPrice while the maintenance margin is validated based upon the oraclePrice.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mismatch in how the contract validates margin requirements for a new position. When a trade is being evaluated, the function that checks the initial margin (validateNextPositionIm) calculates the required liquidation margin by calling getLiquidationMarginUsd with the position's entryPrice – the price at which the position was originally opened. At the same time, the function that checks the maintenance margin (validateNextPositionEnoughMargin) uses the current oraclePrice to compute the required maintenance margin. Because the two checks rely on different price sources, the contract can deem a position sufficiently collateralised for the initial margin while the maintenance margin, based on the live oracle price, may actually be insufficient. This inconsistency arises from a logical error: the code re‑uses entryPrice where the up‑to‑date oracle price should be used. An attacker can exploit this by opening a position when the entryPrice is favourable but the oracle price is already moving against the position. The initial margin check will pass, allowing the trade to be accepted with less collateral than truly required. Later, as the oracle price diverges, the maintenance margin check will fail, causing the position to become under‑collateralised and subject to liquidation. From a user’s perspective the UI may display that the margin is adequate, yet the position can be liquidated unexpectedly, leading to a sudden loss of funds or a balance that drops to zero. The issue is discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noticed that the two validation functions use different price references. It can be hard to notice because each individual check appears correct in isolation; only when a price shift occurs does the inconsistency surface, making it easy to miss during routine testing. The bug belongs to the class of margin‑validation inconsistencies and oracle‑price misuse, where accounting assumptions about required collateral are violated. To remediate, the contract should compute the liquidation margin using the same oraclePrice that is used for the maintenance margin, ensuring both checks are based on a single, current market price. This alignment restores the intended safety guarantees and prevents positions from being accepted with insufficient collateral, thereby protecting users and the protocol from unexpected liquidations and fund loss.

title: M-14 | Endorsed Keeper May Receive Excessive Fees
description: In validateLiquidation, liqKeeperFee is calculated based on liqSize which is expected not to exceed maxLiquidatableCapacity. Therefore, getLiquidationKeeperFee is expected to calculate iterations = 1 and return liquidationFeeInUsd * 1. However, when an endorsed keeper performs a liquidation, liqSize may exceed maxLiquidatableCapacity. In this case, iterations could exceed 1, and the keeper will receive multiples of the keeperFee despite only performing one liquidation. For example, if liqSize = 10 but maxLiquidatableCapacity = 2, then the keeper will receive five times the keeperFee.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑payment of liquidation keeper fees that occurs when an endorsed keeper initiates a liquidation with a size larger than the protocol‑defined maxLiquidatableCapacity. The fee calculation routine assumes that a liquidation may need to be split into several iterations when the requested liquidation size exceeds the capacity, and it multiplies the base keeper fee by the number of iterations (typically computed as ceil(liqSize / maxLiquidatableCapacity)). For regular keepers this behaviour matches the number of actual liquidation steps, but the endorsed keeper contract is designed to perform a single liquidation regardless of size. Because the validation logic does not restrict liqSize for the endorsed keeper, the fee function still returns a fee multiplied by the iteration count, effectively rewarding the keeper multiple times for a single action. An attacker or any endorsed keeper can exploit this by submitting a liquidation request with an artificially large liqSize, causing the contract to calculate several iterations and pay out several times the intended keeperFee. The impact is a direct loss of protocol funds: the keeper receives excessive compensation while the liquidated user sees a higher-than‑expected fee deducted from their collateral, and the overall fee pool may be drained faster than intended. The condition is triggered only when the caller is the endorsed keeper address and the liquidation size exceeds the maxLiquidatableCapacity; normal keepers are not affected because they either split the liquidation or are limited by other checks. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the fee‑calculation function does not special‑case the endorsed keeper and that the iteration variable can grow beyond one. It is subtle because the fee amount appears correct for typical sizes and the over‑payment only becomes visible with unusually large liquidation requests, which may not be exercised in routine testing. To remediate, the fee routine should enforce a single iteration for the endorsed keeper (for example by forcing iterations=1 when msg.sender equals the endorsed keeper address) or the validation step should cap liqSize to the maxLiquidatableCapacity for that caller. This class of bug falls under reward‑multiplier or fee‑scaling errors where a reward is incorrectly proportional to an input that should be bounded, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each liquidation incurs exactly one keeper fee. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a liquidation transaction may deduct a much larger fee than expected, or the keeper’s balance may increase by an unexpectedly high amount, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust in the system.

title: M-15 | Utilization Rate Not Bounded Below 1
description: The documentation for the getUtilization function states that the collateralUtilization is between zero and one, however this is not true as the lockedCollateralUsd / delegatedCollateralValueUsd ratio is not guaranteed to be below one. While delegated collateral is locked when it’s value drops below the minimumCredit (e.g. lockedCollateralUsd), this does not guarantee that the delegatedCollateralValueUsd will always be greater than the minimumCredit. The delegatedCollateralValueUsd may fall below the minimumCredit based on price action as well as increases in the minimumCredit by the introduction of new positions. As a result the utilization can be above 1e18, which can lead to unexpected utilization fees as well as a DoS when computing the utilization rate with the getCurrentUtilizationRate function. If the utilization rate is allowed to hit > 3e18 then the highUtilizationRateInterest calculation is at risk of overflowing the uint128 and halting all order execution and liquidations in the BFP market.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the getUtilization function, which calculates the collateral utilization as the ratio of lockedCollateralUsd to delegatedCollateralValueUsd. The documentation claims this ratio is always between zero and one, but the implementation does not enforce an upper bound. When the market experiences adverse price movements or when new positions increase the minimumCredit requirement, delegatedCollateralValueUsd can fall below the amount of locked collateral. In such cases the utilization value can exceed 1e18 (i.e., 100%). This unbounded result propagates to the getCurrentUtilizationRate function and, more critically, to the highUtilizationRateInterest calculation that assumes the utilization stays below a safe threshold. If the utilization climbs above roughly 3e18, the multiplication performed in the interest formula overflows the uint128 type, causing the calculation to revert. The overflow halts order execution and liquidations across the BFP market, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition. Users observe that their trades or liquidation attempts fail silently, fees appear unusually high or zero, and balances remain unchanged despite attempted actions. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by the Guardian team, who noted the discrepancy between the documented bounds and the actual runtime behavior. It is difficult to detect in routine testing because the overflow only manifests under extreme market conditions that are rarely reproduced in a test environment. To remediate, the contract should explicitly cap the utilization result at 1e18 before it is used in downstream calculations, or employ safe‑math checks that detect and handle values exceeding the expected range. By enforcing this bound, the highUtilizationRateInterest computation remains within the uint128 limits, preserving normal order processing and liquidation functionality and aligning the implementation with the documented business logic that utilization must not exceed 100%.

title: M-16 | Lacking Execution Incentive During Periods Of High Gas Fees
description: In the test environment the maxKeeperFeeUsd is between $50 and $100, however this amount will be insufficient to incentivize the execution of orders and flagging of liquidatable positions during periods of high network usage and gas fees. The maxKeeperFeeUsd ought to be raised to sufficiently incentivize timely order execution and liquidation. Subsequently, some users may be unwilling to pay for extremely high execution costs during these times of high network usage. For these users it may be useful to have an order specific maximum keeper fee to limit the potential cost to their account’s margin.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an insufficient maximum keeper fee (maxKeeperFeeUsd) that is intended to compensate external keepers for executing orders and flagging liquidatable positions. The root cause is that the fee ceiling is set between $50 and $100, a value that is adequate only when gas prices are low. During periods of high network usage, gas costs for the keeperSettlementGasUnits (approximately 1.2 million gas) can exceed the capped reward, especially when the base fee rises to 40 gwei and ETH trades around $3,500. Because the reward no longer covers the execution cost, keepers have little economic incentive to submit the transaction, so orders remain unfilled and liquidations are not flagged. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the code; the failure emerges naturally when the market experiences congestion. The impact is that users may see their pending orders sit idle, their positions stay open despite being under‑collateralised, and eventual liquidations may occur at a worse price or not at all, effectively causing loss of funds or market instability. The condition occurs only when gas fees spike; under normal conditions the system appears to work, making the problem hard to notice in routine testing. All participants who rely on timely order execution – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the economic model assumes keepers will be paid enough to act. The issue was identified during a security audit that simulated high‑fee scenarios and observed that the keeper incentive ceiling was too low. From a user’s perspective the UI may show an order as “submitted” but no execution occurs, balances remain unchanged, and expected liquidation warnings never appear, leading to confusion and potential loss. The bug belongs to the class of incentive‑misalignment or fee‑cap bugs where a hard‑coded reward limit does not adapt to dynamic gas costs, breaking the accounting assumption that execution costs are always covered. To remediate, the protocol should raise the global maxKeeperFeeUsd to a level that comfortably exceeds the worst‑case gas cost (for example $200+ under the assumed conditions) and optionally expose a per‑order configurable fee ceiling so users can cap their exposure while still providing sufficient incentive for keepers.

title: M-17 | Gas Griefing With Settlement Hooks
description: Users can opt to use settle order hooks, called at the end of the settleOrder function. These hooks will be mainly used for splitting and merging accounts when settling orders. These hooks require explicit permissions from the account holders: _PERPS_MODIFY_COLLATERAL_PERMISSION. If a user commits an order with one of this hooks, they can front run the keeper order and remove the account permissions, reverting the transaction.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a gas‑griefing scenario that arises when a user includes a settlement hook in an order and the hook requires the _PERPS_MODIFY_COLLATERAL_PERMISSION. The settleOrder function calls the hook after the main settlement logic. Because the permission is checked only at hook execution, a malicious actor can submit a separate transaction that revokes the permission from the affected account after the order has been committed but before the keeper’s settleOrder transaction runs. By front‑running the keeper, the attacker ensures that when the hook is invoked it fails the permission check, causing the entire settleOrder transaction to revert. This revert wastes the gas paid by the keeper and prevents the order from being settled, effectively a denial‑of‑service attack on the keeper infrastructure. The issue occurs only when settlement hooks are used and the required permission can be altered by any party with authority over the account. Users of the protocol are not directly losing funds, but keepers experience unexpected gas loss and delayed order execution, which can affect overall protocol reliability. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between settlement hooks and permission management, noting that the permission state is not locked for the duration of settlement. The bug is subtle because the revert happens in a later transaction, not at order creation, and the failure appears as a generic transaction revert without a clear indication of the underlying permission change. To remediate, the contract should lock or snapshot the required permission when the order is created, move the permission verification to the beginning of settleOrder, or prevent external revocation of the permission until after the hook has completed. This would eliminate the ability for an attacker to cause a front‑run permission removal and stop the gas‑griefing attack.

title: M-18 | Order Cancellation Overcompensates Keepers
description: Upon cancelling an order, the keeper is compensated with the same fee they would receive for executing the order. However the gas cost necessary to execute an order is far more than the gas cost to cancel an order. Additionally, keepers will receive the keeperFeeBufferUsd as profit when cancelling an order, when this amount is meant instead to incentivize the execution of an order. As a result keepers receive far more profit for cancelling orders rather than executing them. Therefore, keepers will not only be overcompensated for cancellation, but highly incentivized to front-run users who are cancelling their own orders to cancel them on the user’s behalf and collect a fee from the user’s margin.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic incentive flaw in the order‑cancellation path of the BFP market contract. When a user submits a cancellation, the contract awards the keeper that processes the cancellation the same keeperFeeBufferUsd amount that is intended as a profit incentive for executing an order. Because the gas required to execute an order is substantially higher than the gas needed to cancel it, the fixed buffer represents a net profit for the keeper rather than a reimbursement of gas. Consequently the keeper receives a profit on cancellation that is larger than the profit they would earn from execution. This mis‑aligned fee calculation allows a malicious keeper to monitor pending cancellation requests, front‑run the user’s transaction and submit a cancellation on the user’s behalf, collecting the keeperFeeBufferUsd from the user’s margin. The user sees their order disappear and their margin reduced, while the keeper gains an unexpected reward. The issue manifests whenever the cancelOrder function is called and the contract’s fee logic does not differentiate between execution and cancellation. It affects any user who attempts to cancel an order, the keepers who can exploit the over‑payment, and the protocol which may lose economic efficiency and user trust. The flaw was identified during a manual audit that compared the gas cost assumptions of the execution path with the static fee applied to cancellations; the problem is subtle because the fee appears as a normal compensation and does not raise an explicit error, making it easy to overlook in functional testing. To remediate the issue the fee calculation should be split: a lower, gas‑reimbursement‑only fee for cancellations and a separate profit buffer reserved for execution, ensuring that keepers are not financially motivated to cancel orders instead of executing them.

title: M-19 | Sudden Block Fee Increases May Cause Insolvent Liquidations
description: New positions are validated when the order is settled by checking if the margin minus the fees will satisfy the initial and maintenance margin checks. This fees include order, keeper, flag and liquidation fees. The issue is that the calculations of these fees rely heavily on the block.basefee and eth price, the only parameters that the protocol can't control. This base fee can range from 10-15 Gwei in a normal market scenario, up to >600 Gwei when volatility is high. Therefore, users can open LONG positions when the block base fee is low, and get liquidated a few blocks later if the base fee increases, even if the market price moves in their favor. Potentially, this can cause an insolvent liquidation for small accounts since the base fee jump might be an unpredictable stepwise change.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the market contract validates new positions during order settlement. The contract computes the required initial and maintenance margins by subtracting a set of fees – order, keeper, flag and liquidation fees – from the user’s supplied margin. These fee amounts are calculated using the current block.basefee and the on‑chain ETH price, both of which are external variables that the protocol cannot control. Because block.basefee can jump from a typical 10‑15 gwei to several hundred gwei during periods of high volatility, the fee estimate may be dramatically lower at the moment a user opens a LONG position than it is a few blocks later. When the base fee spikes, the fee component of the margin calculation increases, causing the effective margin (margin minus fees) to fall below the maintenance threshold even though the market price may have moved in the trader’s favour. The contract then triggers a liquidation. For small accounts the sudden fee increase can consume more collateral than is available, resulting in an insolvent liquidation where the protocol cannot fully cover the loss. From the user’s perspective the experience is that a position that appeared safe and profitable is suddenly closed, the user receives no payout, and the account balance may drop to zero or a much lower value than expected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the margin‑checking logic, where the reliance on block.basefee was noted as an uncontrolled external factor. It is difficult to notice because the fee formulas themselves are mathematically correct; the problem only manifests when the underlying base fee changes abruptly, a condition that is not obvious from static analysis. To remediate the issue the protocol should decouple fee calculations from volatile on‑chain parameters, for example by increasing the minimum margin requirement (minMarginUsd) to a level that can absorb realistic base‑fee spikes, or by using a smoothed or capped fee model that does not react directly to each block’s base fee. By ensuring that the margin buffer accounts for possible fee volatility, the contract can avoid triggering unintended liquidations and protect users’ funds from disappearing unexpectedly.

title: M-20 | Risk Free Trade With Account Permissions
description: PoC Similarly to M-09, it is possible to make a short term risk free trade by preventing keepers from executing an account’s order by including a splitAccount callback where no keeper is granted the necessary _PERPS_MODIFY_COLLATERAL_PERMISSION for the fromId account. As a result, a malicious user may prevent an order from being executable in the block where the valid price data is accurate and only allow the order to go through once a significant period of time has passed and the user observes that the true current price of the index asset has moved in their favor. The order will only be executable with the outdated price, and therefore the user will realize a risk-free profit based upon how much price has diverged in the user’s favor since then.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a permission‑based execution flaw that enables a user to create a short‑term, risk‑free profit scenario by blocking the normal keeper from executing an order in the block where the price feed is accurate. The contract allows a user‑controlled splitAccount callback to be invoked before the keeper’s permission to modify collateral (_PERPS_MODIFY_COLLATERAL_PERMISSION) is verified. If the callback does not grant the required permission, the keeper is unable to finalize the order during that block, leaving the order pending with the price that was recorded at order creation. Because the price oracle updates only once per block, the pending order can later be executed with the stale price after the market has moved in the attacker’s favor. The attacker then triggers execution (or a different keeper with the proper permission does so) and the order settles at the outdated price, yielding a profit that does not expose the attacker to market risk. This situation occurs whenever an order includes a callback that can manipulate the permission check, typically in the same transaction that creates the order. The affected parties are the protocol’s economic model, honest traders, and any keeper that expects to execute orders promptly. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between callbacks and permission enforcement, noting that the failure path is silent and does not raise an explicit error, making it easy to overlook. The bug belongs to the class of “callback‑controlled permission bypass” or “execution gating via user‑controlled hooks”, which violates the assumption that orders are always executable with up‑to‑date price data. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that an order that should have been filled immediately remains pending, and later appears to fill at a price that no longer reflects the market, effectively giving the creator a free profit. To remediate the problem the contract should either increase the order fee to offset any potential arbitrage gain or, more robustly, remove the ability for users to influence order executability through callbacks, for example by wrapping callbacks in a try/catch block and ensuring that the required permission is granted before the order execution step is attempted.

title: M-21 | Lacking Incentive To Repay Debt
description: In the BFP market users can leave accounts with realized debtUsd and enough collateral to support that debtUsd without ever repaying the debt. The debt inside these accounts will be reported in reportedDebt as profits for the LPs, however the sUSD will never be returned and never increase the creditCapacity for the market since the debt is not repaid. Over time with many positions holding unpaid debt there is an increased risk of reducing the getWithdrawableMarketUsd to a point where traders are unable to withdraw their sUSD collateral or claim their sUSD profits.
bug_full: The BFP market contains a logical flaw that allows a trader to leave an account with a realized debt amount denominated in USD while still maintaining enough collateral to cover that debt, yet there is no mechanism that forces the trader to actually repay the debt. The system records the outstanding debt in the reportedDebt variable and treats it as profit for liquidity providers, but the corresponding sUSD is never returned to the market’s credit pool, so the market’s creditCapacity does not increase. Because the debt remains unpaid, the aggregate withdrawable market USD (getWithdrawableMarketUsd) can gradually shrink as more positions accumulate unpaid debt. This creates a situation where other participants may find that their sUSD collateral or expected profit cannot be withdrawn, effectively locking funds and reducing market liquidity. The root cause is the absence of any interest rate, penalty, or incentive tied to unpaid debt, which means the protocol does not enforce repayment or adjust accounting metrics to reflect the missing sUSD. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately opening a position, realizing a debt, and then simply abandoning repayment; the protocol will still count the debt as profit for LPs while the actual sUSD remains unavailable. Over time, as many accounts behave this way, the market may reach a state where getWithdrawableMarketUsd approaches zero, preventing honest traders from extracting their collateral or claiming earned sUSD. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the BFP market code, where the auditors observed that debt reporting and credit capacity updates were decoupled. The problem is subtle because the on‑chain numbers still show profit and sufficient collateral, so the liquidity shortfall is not immediately obvious to users or external observers. To remediate the flaw, the protocol should introduce a configurable interest rate or other economic penalty on any debt that remains unpaid beyond a reasonable period, thereby creating a financial incentive for traders to settle their obligations and ensuring that reportedDebt accurately reflects the amount of sUSD that can be reclaimed by the market. This change would align the accounting of profits with the actual availability of funds and protect the market from liquidity erosion.

title: M-06 | Merging Accounts May Fail For Multicollateral Positions
description: When merging accounts, the function executes getMatchingMarketCollateral which returns the matching margin collateral equal to market. This function will return a matching synthMarketId and fromAccountCollateral. If the fromId account has multiple collaterals, the getMatchingMarketCollateral function will only return the last collateral that matched. This means that the merge will transfer one collateral to the toId account, and leave the other 2 in the fromId account. The issue is that the merge will then transfer a portion of the collateral but the whole position size. If the last collateral that matched is the smallest one in terms of USD, then the toPosition might invalidate the Initial Margin check and revert.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/synthetix-pocs/blob/main/markets/bfp-market/test/integration/modules/team2PoCs.test.ts#L108
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs during the account‑merge operation of a multi‑collateral trading platform. When a user merges a source account (fromId) into a destination account (toId), the merge routine calls a helper that searches for collateral matching the market of the position. This helper returns a single collateral entry – specifically the last one that satisfies the market filter – together with its amount. If the source account holds several different collateral types, only the last matching collateral is selected, while the other collateral balances remain in the source account. The merge logic then transfers the selected collateral amount to the destination account but moves the entire position size, assuming that the transferred collateral fully backs the position. Consequently, the destination account may end up with a position that is under‑collateralised because the total USD value of the transferred collateral is smaller than required. The platform’s initial‑margin check, which validates that the collateral value covers the position risk, can therefore fail and cause the transaction to revert. This situation can be observed by users as a failed merge where the position appears to have moved but the expected collateral balance is missing or only partially present, leading to unexpected “insufficient margin” errors or a complete inability to trade after the merge. The issue is triggered only when the source account contains more than one collateral type and the last matching collateral is not the one with the highest USD value. It was discovered during a targeted audit that exercised the merge function with multi‑collateral accounts and observed that the collateral accounting did not reflect the full set of assets. The bug is subtle because the merge transaction does not emit an explicit warning about missing collateral; the revert occurs later during the margin check, making it hard to trace back to the merge logic. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of “partial asset transfer” or “incomplete collateral aggregation” bugs, where a function assumes a single asset representation while the underlying state may contain multiple assets. To remediate the issue, the merge routine should aggregate the balances of all collaterals belonging to the source account and transfer the total available amount to the destination account, or alternatively enforce that a merge is only allowed when a single collateral type is present. This ensures that the destination position is always fully backed and that the initial‑margin verification succeeds, preserving the expected accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: M-07 | Small Positions Accrue Bad Debt In The System
description: Users can set their own keeperFeeBufferUsd and limitPrice, potentially forcing bad debt into the system. This is because IM and MM have minimum values as follows: IM = 2% * position.size + fixed = 2% * p.size + 50 MM = 1% * position.size + fixed + liqFlagReward + keeper reward = 1% * p.size + 50 + liqFlagReward + keeper reward While the maximum value for keeperFeeBufferUsd is 100 USD. Currently, it's possible to place an order with keeperFeeBufferUsd > collateral > IM && MM, choosing the maximum keeperFeeBufferUsd and an unrealistic limitPrice, using it to cancel your order later and accrue bad debt of keeperFeeBufferUsd - collateral. Similarly users can submit orders that would decrease their position size by a trivial amount and avoid the liquidatable checks upon settlement, allowing the keeper fee to place their position in a liquidatable or even insolvent state.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a margin‑validation flaw that allows a trader to create a small position while declaring a keeper fee buffer that exceeds the actual collateral and the minimum initial and maintenance margin requirements. The protocol calculates the initial margin (IM) as 2 % of the position size plus a fixed 50 USD and the maintenance margin (MM) as 1 % of the position size plus the same fixed amount together with liquidation‑flag and keeper rewards. Because the keeperFeeBufferUsd parameter can be set by the user up to a hard‑coded maximum of 100 USD, a user can submit an order where keeperFeeBufferUsd is larger than the posted collateral while the collateral still satisfies the low IM and MM thresholds for a tiny position. By also providing an unrealistic limitPrice the order never fills; when the order is later cancelled the protocol attempts to charge the keeper fee from the account. Since the account’s collateral is insufficient, the system records a shortfall equal to keeperFeeBufferUsd minus the actual collateral, i.e., bad debt. A similar attack vector exists when a user submits an order that reduces the position size by a negligible amount, thereby bypassing the liquidation checks that run on settlement. The keeper fee is then applied to the already‑thin margin, pushing the account into a liquidatable or even insolvent state. The impact is that the protocol accrues unrecoverable debt, eroding the overall solvency of the market and potentially affecting all participants who rely on the pooled margin. The issue manifests whenever a trader can set a high keeper fee buffer and an extreme limit price, or when they can shrink a position just enough to avoid the liquidation guard while still being charged the keeper fee. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the relationship between user‑controlled fee buffers and the margin formulas, and it is subtle because the order appears normal on‑chain and the bad debt only becomes visible after cancellation or settlement, making it easy to miss in routine monitoring. To remediate the problem the protocol should raise the minimum margin requirement (minMarginUsd) so that the keeper fee can never exceed the protected margin, enforce that keeperFeeBufferUsd cannot be larger than the excess collateral after accounting for IM and MM, and reject orders whose limitPrice would make the order unfillable or whose fee would render the account liquidatable. In essence the fix is to tighten validation of fee buffers against actual collateral and to ensure that any fee charged is always covered by the account’s margin, thereby preventing the creation of bad debt and preserving the accounting invariants of the system.

title: M-08 | getFillPrice And validateLiquidation Revert Due To Division By 0
description: If skewScale is set to 0, arithmetic operations which divide by skewScale will revert. This occurs in the Order.getFillPrice and Position.validateLiquidation functions. While it is unlikely that skewScale will ever be set to 0, this is a possibility and is specifically handled in many areas of the codebase.
bug_full: An arithmetic vulnerability exists in the market contract where the variable skewScale is used as a divisor in the getFillPrice and validateLiquidation functions. If the contract owner or an upgrade sets skewScale to zero, any call that triggers these calculations will attempt to divide by zero, causing the EVM to revert the transaction. The root cause is the lack of a guard clause checking for a zero denominator before performing the division. An attacker could deliberately set skewScale to zero (if they have permission) or exploit a misconfiguration to cause legitimate users' orders or liquidation checks to fail. When the division occurs, the transaction reverts with a generic error, so users see no fill price, their order appears stuck, or liquidation attempts are rejected, leading to loss of expected execution and potential capital being locked. The issue manifests only when skewScale equals zero, a state that is unlikely in normal operation but is not prevented by the contract logic. All participants who interact with order filling or liquidation – traders, liquidators, and the protocol itself – are affected because their calls may revert unexpectedly. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined arithmetic expressions and identified the missing zero‑check. Because the revert message is generic, the bug can be hard to notice; developers may attribute the failure to other reasons such as insufficient liquidity. The proper fix is to add explicit validation that skewScale is non‑zero before performing division, or to replace the division with a safe math routine that returns a default value or reverts with a clear error when the denominator is zero. This class of bug falls under unchecked division or denominator validation errors, which violate the contract’s accounting assumptions that price calculations always produce a finite number. From a user perspective, the UI may show “transaction failed” or “order not filled” without a clear reason, while the user expects the order to be executed and the liquidation to succeed. The mismatch between expectation (order fills, liquidation proceeds) and reality (revert, no funds moved) constitutes a functional and financial failure.

title: M-09 | Risk Free Trade With Merge Callbacks
description: PoC Order execution with the settleOrder function requires that the priceUpdateData provided to parse the pythPrice is for the price update that satisfies the minimum and maximum times (commitmentTime + 12 seconds, commitmentTime + 60 seconds) as well as that the publish time of the price update that is sequentially previous to the provided price data took place before the minimum commitmentTime. Therefore only prices that satisfy these constraints may be used to execute an order while it is ready and not stale. A malicious user may prevent an order from being executable in the block where the valid price data is accurate and only allow the order to go through once a significant period of time has passed and the user observes that the true current price of the index asset has moved in their favor. The order will only be executable with the outdated price, and therefore the user will realize a risk-free profit based upon how much price has diverged in the user’s favor since then. The malicious user may prevent their order from being executable by registering a mergeAccounts hook as a callback where the user’s position as the fromAccount has sUSD collateral in addition to the market’s index as collateral and therefore reverts. When the malicious user wishes their order to be executable, e.g. they have determined that price has moved in a direction that is favorable to them, they may remove the sUSD collateral with the payDebt function, assuming they have a pre-existing position with debt, and execute their order with the outdated price.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a timing‑and‑callback manipulation that lets a malicious participant block the execution of a market order until the on‑chain price feed has moved in their favour, then force the order to settle with a stale price that still satisfies the contract's commitment‑time window. The root cause is that the settleOrder function only checks that the supplied price update falls within a fixed interval relative to a commitment timestamp, and it allows a user‑controlled mergeAccounts hook to run during execution. Because the hook can deliberately revert the transaction when the caller still holds a specific collateral configuration (sUSD together with the index asset), the order remains unexecutable even though a fresh, valid price update is available. When the attacker decides the market price has diverged enough, they remove the sUSD collateral using the payDebt function, causing the hook to stop reverting and allowing the order to settle with the previously‑valid but now outdated price. This results in a risk‑free profit equal to the price movement since the original commitment time, effectively letting the attacker capture value without bearing market risk. The impact is that the attacker can earn arbitrage‑like gains at the expense of other traders, undermining fairness and potentially draining liquidity from the market. The issue manifests when an order is ready for execution, the price feed provides a price within the allowed 12‑to‑60‑second window, but the attacker’s callback prevents settlement; later, after the price moves, the order finally executes with the old price, producing an unexpected profit for the attacker while other users see their orders delayed or filled at unfavorable rates. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between price‑timing checks and external callbacks, noting that the contract does not guard against user‑controlled reverts influencing order executability. It can be hard to notice because the contract’s own logic appears to enforce freshness of price data, and the revert originates from a legitimate hook that developers might expect to succeed. To remediate, the protocol should either remove the ability for users to influence order execution through callbacks, enforce that order settlement cannot be blocked by external code, or introduce economic disincentives such as higher order fees to make short‑term manipulation unprofitable. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “callback‑induced execution control” or “price‑staleness exploitation” where external hooks are used to manipulate the timing of state‑changing functions, violating the assumption that price data freshness alone guarantees fair settlement.

title: M-10 | Keeper Gas Fee Is Fixed While Execution Gas Is Not
description: Every keeper operation is rewarded with a specific keeper fee, where the gas units are fixed and the fee is calculated on the spot with: gas * gasPrice + keeperProfit. However, some operations can use much more gas than others.
