The L1 bridge contract calls a function that reads the current ezETH‑to‑ETH price and broadcasts it to the L2 side via a cross‑chain message. On L2 the price is stored in a variable that is later read by minting or deposit functions. Because the price is propagated only after the L1 transaction is mined, there is a time lag during which the price that will be applied on L2 is already known to observers but has not yet been written to the L2 contract. An attacker can monitor the L1 mempool, detect the pending price‑update transaction, extract the new price, and then submit a transaction on L2 that mints xezETH (or performs a deposit) using the stale price before the L2 contract processes the update. When the price update finally executes, the attacker can immediately sell the freshly minted xezETH on a market that reads the updated price, capturing the difference between the price at mint time and the price after the update. This front‑running or sandwich style exploit is possible whenever the price changes noticeably and the bridge does not enforce any protection against stale price usage. The impact is that an attacker can earn arbitrage profit at the expense of regular users, who may see lower returns, unexpected slippage, or even a reduction in the value of their deposited assets because the protocol’s accounting assumes the price is up‑to‑date. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of price information from L1 to L2 and identified that the update mechanism is not atomic and lacks validation of timeliness. The problem can be hard to notice because the price broadcast appears legitimate and the contract does not emit explicit warnings about stale data; only a careful analysis of the cross‑chain timing reveals the exploitable gap. To mitigate the issue the protocol should make the price update resistant to front‑running, for example by introducing a commit‑reveal scheme, adding a minimum delay between price publication and its use, requiring signatures with timestamps, or incorporating a price oracle that validates freshness on L2. Additional fees on L2 deposits can also reduce the incentive for exploitation, but a systematic design change that eliminates the reliance on a single pending transaction for price synchronization is the recommended fix.

title: Fetched price from the oracle is not stored in `xRenzoDeposit`
description: Failure to store the fetched price from the oracle in the storage variables of the `xRenzoDeposit` contract can result in several important issues.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a stale‑price bug in the xRenzoDeposit contract where the price fetched from the external oracle is not written back to the contract's persistent storage variables (lastPrice and lastPriceTimestamp). The root cause is that the getMintRate function only returns the fresh oracle price when the oracle address is non‑zero, but it never updates the storage slot with that price. Consequently, when the oracle address is later set to zero, the contract falls back to the previously stored price, which may be hours or days old. An attacker or even a regular user can exploit this by depositing after the oracle has been disabled; the contract will use the outdated price to calculate the amount of ezETH minted, leading to an inaccurate conversion rate. The impact includes users receiving fewer tokens than expected, apparent loss of value, and potential financial loss for depositors. The bug manifests whenever the oracle is defined, a price is fetched, and then the oracle address is cleared before the next deposit, or when the price‑update logic compares a new price against an old stored price, causing the divergence check to reject legitimate updates. All participants who interact with the deposit function—regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the accounting assumptions of a one‑to‑one price relationship are broken. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the getMintRate and updatePrice logic and noticing that the fetched oracle price is never persisted. It is hard to notice because the view function appears to return the correct, up‑to‑date price, masking the fact that subsequent state‑changing calls will rely on stale data once the oracle is disabled. The bug belongs to the class of stale‑data or cache‑inconsistency vulnerabilities, where on‑chain state is not synchronized with off‑chain inputs. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are deposits that yield unexpectedly low token amounts, balances that seem to disappear, or refunds that are zero despite a non‑zero input. The contract violates its business logic by assuming the stored price always reflects the latest market rate, which is no longer true. The recommended fix is to modify getMintRate (or a related internal function) so that when the oracle returns a newer price and timestamp, the contract updates lastPrice and lastPriceTimestamp accordingly before returning the values. This ensures that any subsequent calls, even after the oracle is removed, use the most recent price and that the divergence check compares against the true latest price, eliminating the stale‑price condition.

title: Incorrect exchange rate provided to Balancer pools
description:
The [`xRenzoDeposit`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol) contract, apart from being the entry point for deposits on L2s, also acts as a rate provider for Balancer pools on L2s, allowing them to determine the exchange rate between `xezWETH` and `WETH` tokens. Rate providers are crucial for Balancer pools to calculate token prices and determine yield protocol fees during joins and exits, as explained in the [Balancer documentation](https://docs.balancer.fi/reference/contracts/rate-providers.html).

However, the [`getRate()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L456) function in `xRenzoDeposit` does not provide the correct exchange rate. It simply returns the `lastPrice` state variable, which:

  * May be stale if `updatePrice()` or `updatePriceByOwner()` have not been called recently.
  * May be older than the rate provided by `oracle.getMintRate()`.
  * Can be different from the rate at which xezETH are minted in [`_deposit()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Bridge/L2/xRenzoDeposit.sol#L227), which uses the newest of the oracle and internal `lastPrice` values, opening up arbitrage opportunities.
poc:
1. `xRenzoDeposit` is set as the rate provider between `xezWETH` and `WETH` for a Balancer pool.
2. The price of `ezETH` relative to `ETH` changes on L1, but the receiver fails and `updatePrice()` is not called on `xRenzoDeposit`.
3. However, the oracle feed still provides accurate data.
4. A user executes an operation on a WETH/xezETH Balancer pool, which calls `getRate()` on `xRenzoDeposit` to fetch the price.
5. `getRate()` returns the stale price from the internal `lastPrice` variable.
6. The Balancer pool uses this incorrect rate for its calculations, leading to mispricing of `xezWETH` and potential manipulation.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the rate‑provider contract that supplies the price for the xezWETH/WETH Balancer pool on Layer‑2. The contract’s getRate() function simply returns a stored variable called lastPrice. This variable is only refreshed when the internal updatePrice() or updatePriceByOwner() functions are called, and it does not automatically reflect the most recent minting rate obtained from the external oracle. Consequently, if the price of ezETH on Layer‑1 changes and the update functions are not invoked, getRate() will return a stale value that may be older than the oracle’s current mint rate. The pool then uses this outdated rate to calculate token values during joins and exits, which violates the accounting assumptions that Balancer pools rely on for correct pricing and fee calculation. From a user’s perspective, a trader expects to receive a fair amount of xezWETH when swapping WETH, but because the pool is operating with an incorrect exchange rate, the output can be lower than expected, effectively causing funds to disappear or be undervalued. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the auditors observed that the rate provider did not align with the minting logic and could be stale. The bug is subtle because the contract still returns a numeric rate, so the pool appears functional, yet the hidden discrepancy can be exploited by an attacker who monitors oracle updates and submits trades when the internal lastPrice lags, capturing arbitrage profits. The impact is medium: mispricing can lead to financial loss for users and potential manipulation of the pool’s yield calculations, but it does not directly enable arbitrary code execution. The flaw occurs whenever the price on L1 changes without a corresponding call to updatePrice() on the L2 contract, a condition that can happen naturally in production. The affected parties include any user interacting with the Balancer pool, the protocol that relies on accurate pricing for fee distribution, and the overall ecosystem that expects correct token valuations. To remediate the issue, the getRate() function should be aligned with the minting logic by calling the oracle’s getMintRate() method, applying a staleness check (e.g., ensuring the timestamp is within an acceptable window), and returning that fresh rate instead of the potentially outdated lastPrice. This change ensures that the rate provider supplies a consistent and up‑to‑date price, restoring the integrity of the pool’s accounting and preventing arbitrage opportunities.

title: Pending withdrawals prevent safe removal of collateral assets
description:
The [`RestakeManager`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol) contract allows the admin to add and remove collateral tokens that are accepted for deposits into the protocol via the [`addCollateralToken()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L220) and [`removeCollateralToken()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L244) functions.

From the protocol team:

(In order to) remove a collateral token we can withdraw full and increase the withdraw buffer to let users withdraw it.

However, since users cannot be forced to claim their withdrawals, it is always possible that a significant amount of the collateral token remains in the `WithdrawQueue` indefinitely in outstanding withdrawals.

In that case, calling `removeCollateralToken()` for that token would break accounting in the protocol. The `ezETH` total supply would still reflect the amounts that were burned to initiate those withdrawals, but the token balance in the `WithdrawQueue` would no longer be counted towards the TVL.

The `RestakeManager` admin is unable to safely remove a collateral token. Removing the token anyway would inflate the `ezETH` mint and redeem rate compared to the actual backing collateral value.
poc:
Assume `token1` has a balance of `Y` in the `WithdrawQueue` from pending user withdrawals. If `removeCollateralToken(token1)` is called:

1. `token1` is removed from the `collateralTokens` array.
2. `token1` balance of `Y` is still in `WithdrawQueue` but no longer counted in `totalTVL`.
3. Mint rate for `ezETH` increases since `totalTVL` is lower but `ezETH` total supply is unchanged.
4. Redeem rate for `ezETH` also increases since `ezETH` is now redeemable for a larger share of the remaining collateral.

The mint and redeem rates for `ezETH` are now inflated compared to the true value of the collateral backing it, since `Y` worth of `token1` is not accounted for in `totalTVL` but is still effectively backing the `ezETH` that was burned to withdraw it.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the RestakeManager contract handles the removal of collateral tokens while there are still pending user withdrawals queued in the WithdrawQueue. When an admin calls removeCollateralToken for a token that has outstanding withdrawals, the contract deletes the token from the list of accepted collateral but does not clear or account for the amount that remains locked in the WithdrawQueue. This creates a mismatch between the protocol’s reported total value locked (TVL) and the actual collateral backing the ezETH token. Because the TVL calculation no longer includes the pending balance, the mint and redeem rates for ezETH are artificially inflated: the same amount of ezETH supply is now backed by a lower reported TVL, so new ezETH can be minted at a cheaper rate and existing ezETH can be redeemed for a larger share of the remaining collateral. The issue can be triggered whenever users have initiated withdrawals that they have not yet claimed and the admin decides to remove the associated collateral token, which is allowed by the current implementation. From a user’s perspective, the protocol appears to work normally – users can still claim their withdrawals later – but the pricing displayed in the UI shows higher mint/redeem rates, and users may receive more ezETH than the actual collateral would justify. This discrepancy violates the fundamental accounting assumption that every minted ezETH is fully backed by the sum of all collateral, including any amounts pending withdrawal. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the token removal logic and identified that the contract does not enforce a zero‑balance condition on the WithdrawQueue before allowing removal. The problem is subtle because the token removal function is rarely used, and the TVL drop may not be immediately obvious in dashboards, making the over‑issuance of ezETH easy to overlook. To remediate the issue, the protocol should either prevent removal of a collateral token while any pending withdrawals exist (for example by requiring claimReserve[token] to be zero) or modify the TVL calculation to continue counting the WithdrawQueue balance for tokens that have been removed until all withdrawals are settled. Either approach restores the invariant that the total supply of ezETH is always backed by the reported collateral, eliminating the risk of inflated mint/redeem rates and potential under‑collateralization.

title: stETH/ETH feed being used opens up to 2 way `deposit<->withdrawal` arbitrage
description:
The stETH/ETH oracle is not a exchange rate feed, it’s a Market Rate Feed, while other feeds are exchange rate feeds.

This opens up ezETH to be vulnerable to:

  * Market Rate Manipulations.
  * Sentiment based Price Action.
  * Duration based discounts.
poc:
This opens up to arbitrage anytime stETH trades at a discount (see Liquidations on the 13th of April).

Had withdrawals been open, the following could have been possible:

  * Deposit stETH before the Depeg (front-run oracle update).
  * Get ezETH.
  * Withdraw stETH after the depeg (1% a day, around 365% APR).

As well as:

  * stETH market depegs.
  * Deposit ETH for ezETH.
  * Withdraw stETH at premium (about 1% arbitrage, around 365% APR).
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of using a market‑rate oracle for the stETH/ETH pair as if it were a stable exchange‑rate feed in the ezETH contract. Because the contract prices deposits and withdrawals based on this market feed, the protocol assumes that one unit of stETH is always worth a fixed amount of ETH. In reality the feed reflects the current market price, which can deviate due to de‑pegs, sentiment‑driven swings or temporary discounts. When the market price diverges, a user can deposit stETH (or ETH) at the quoted rate, receive ezETH, and later withdraw the opposite asset at a more favorable rate, effectively extracting value from the price gap. The attack can be performed by front‑running the oracle update, depositing before a de‑peg and withdrawing after, or by depositing ETH when stETH trades at a premium and withdrawing stETH at a discount. The impact is that the protocol may lose large amounts of value, creating an apparent APR of several hundred percent for the attacker while honest users see their balances reduced or receive less value than expected. The condition for exploitation is any period where the stETH/ETH market price differs from the assumed exchange rate, which occurs frequently during market stress, liquidation events, or when the oracle is updated with delayed data. All participants—liquidity providers, token holders, and the protocol itself—are affected because the accounting assumptions are broken and the token’s peg is undermined. The issue was identified during a Code4rena audit that compared the oracle type with the contract’s pricing logic; the mismatch is subtle because the feed name suggests a price feed, yet its semantics are that of a market rate, making the bug easy to overlook. The vulnerability belongs to the class of oracle‑type mismatches that enable two‑way arbitrage between deposit and withdrawal functions. From a user’s perspective the contract advertises that depositing ETH or stETH yields ezETH at a fair rate, but after a price swing the user may withdraw and receive either zero or a far lower amount of the underlying asset, contrary to the expectation of a 1:1 value transfer. To remediate, the withdrawal path should be expressed in ETH, deposits should be priced using a pessimistic exchange rate, and the contract should incorporate slashing, discount and operational cost adjustments rather than relying on the raw market feed.

title: Incorrect handling of decimals in `LibLockedUnderlying::getPercentLockedUnderlying` results in an incorrect value being returned, affecting the temperature and Bean to maxLP gaugePoint per BDV ratio updates in each subsequent call to `SeasonFacet::gm` when `unripe asset supply < 10M`
description:
Due to the Barn Raise and the associated Beans underlying Unripe assets, the number of tradable Beans does not equal the total Bean supply. Within the calculation of L2SR, the term "locked liquidity" refers to the portion of liquidity in the BEAN:ETH WELL that cannot be retrieved through chopping until the corresponding Fertilizer is paid.

The exchange ratio for the corresponding underlying asset can be summarized in the following formula:

$$\frac{Paid Fertilizer}{Minted Fertilizer} \times \frac{totalUnderlying(urAsset)}{supply(urAsset)}$$

The second factor indicates the amount of the underlying asset backing each unripe asset, while the first indicates the distribution of the underlying asset based on the ratio of Fertilizer that is already paid.

When a user chops an unripe asset, it is burned in exchange for a penalized amount of the underlying asset. The remaining underlying asset is now shared among the remaining unripe asset holders, meaning that if another user tries to chop the same amount of unripe asset at a given recapitalization rate, they will receive a greater amount of underlying asset.

For instance, assume that:
* 50% of the minted Fertilizer is paid
* A current supply of 70M
* An underlying amount of 22M

If Alice chops 1M unripe tokens:
$$1,000,000 \times 0.50 \times \frac{22,000,000}{70,000,000} =$$
$$1,000,000 \times 0.50 \times 0.31428 =$$
$$1,000,000 \times 0.50 \times 0.31428 =$$
$$1,000,000 \times 0.15714285 = $$
$$157,142.85$$

If Bob then chops the same amount of tokens:
$$1,000,000 \times 0.50 \times \frac{22,000,000-157,142.85}{70,000,000 - 1,000,000} =$$
$$1,000,000 \times 0.50 \times \frac{21,842,857.15}{69,000,000} =$$
$$1,000,000 \times 0.50 \times \frac{21,842,857.15}{69,000,000} =$$
$$1,000,000 \times 0.50 \times 0.3165 =$$
$$158,281.57$$

Given that the assumption of chopping the total unripe asset supply in one step is highly unlikely, the Beanstalk Farms team decided to perform an off-chain regression based on the average unripe asset per unripe asset holder. This yields an approximation for the percentage locked underlying token per asset based on the current unripe asset supply. An on-chain look-up table is used to retrieve the values of this regression; however, the issue with its implementation lies in its failure to account for unripe token decimals when compared with the inline conditional supply constants [`1_000_000`](https://github.com/BeanstalkFarms/Beanstalk/blob/dfb418d185cd93eef08168ccaffe9de86bc1f062/protocol/contracts/libraries/LibLockedUnderlying.sol#L61), [`5_000_000`](https://github.com/BeanstalkFarms/Beanstalk/blob/dfb418d185cd93eef08168ccaffe9de86bc1f062/protocol/contracts/libraries/LibLockedUnderlying.sol#L62), and [`10_000_000`](https://github.com/BeanstalkFarms/Beanstalk/blob/dfb418d185cd93eef08168ccaffe9de86bc1f062/protocol/contracts/libraries/LibLockedUnderlying.sol#L63) as the intervals on which the iterative simulation was performed. Given these constants are not a fixed-point representation of the numbers they are intended to represent, [comparison](https://github.com/BeanstalkFarms/Beanstalk/blob/dfb418d185cd93eef08168ccaffe9de86bc1f062/protocol/contracts/libraries/LibLockedUnderlying.sol#L286) with the [6-decimal supply](https://github.com/BeanstalkFarms/Beanstalk/blob/dfb418d185cd93eef08168ccaffe9de86bc1f062/protocol/contracts/libraries/LibLockedUnderlying.sol#L60) will be incorrect.

Given that unripe assets have 6 decimals, `LibLockedUnderlying::getPercentLockedUnderlying` will tend to execute [this conditional branch](https://github.com/BeanstalkFarms/Beanstalk/blob/dfb418d185cd93eef08168ccaffe9de86bc1f062/protocol/contracts/libraries/LibLockedUnderlying.sol#L63-L173), producing an incorrect calculation of locked underlying whenever the supply of the unripe asset is below 10M.

In the given scenario, this error would cascade into an incorrect calculation of L2SR, affecting how the temperature and Bean to maxLP gaugePoint per BDV ratio should be updated in the call to [`Weather::calcCaseIdandUpdate`](https://github.com/BeanstalkFarms/Beanstalk/blob/dfb418d185cd93eef08168ccaffe9de86bc1f062/protocol/contracts/beanstalk/sun/SeasonFacet/Weather.sol#L68) within [`SeasonFacet::gm`](https://github.com/BeanstalkFarms/Beanstalk/blob/dfb418d185cd93eef08168ccaffe9de86bc1f062/protocol/contracts/beanstalk/sun/SeasonFacet/SeasonFacet.sol#L51).
poc:
A differential test (see Appendix A) was written to demonstrate this issue based on CSV provided by the Beanstalk Farms team. Modifications to the CSV include:
* Adding headers: recapPercentage, urSupply, lockedPercentage
* Generate a CSV without whitespaces
* Round the first column to 3 decimals
* For the third column, delete `e18` and round values to 18 decimals
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic/decimal handling error in the library function that calculates the percentage of locked underlying assets for unripe tokens. The function compares the current unripe token supply, which has six decimal places, against hard‑coded integer thresholds (1_000_000, 5_000_000, 10_000_000) that are not scaled to the same fixed‑point representation. Because the constants are interpreted as whole numbers while the supply is expressed with 6‑decimal precision, the conditional branch that should be taken for supplies below ten million tokens is selected incorrectly. As a result the function returns a percentage that is too high or too low, which propagates to the L2SR (locked‑to‑supply ratio) calculation used in the seasonal gauge update. The downstream effect is that the temperature metric and the Bean‑to‑maxLP gauge point per BDV ratio are updated with wrong values whenever the unripe asset supply is under ten million. From a user’s perspective the protocol may credit or debit an incorrect amount of beans when chopping unripe assets, leading to situations where a user expects a refund or reward but receives a smaller amount, or conversely where the protocol distributes more beans than intended. The bug appears only when the supply is small, making it easy to miss in normal operation where supplies are larger. It was discovered during a differential test that compared on‑chain outputs with an off‑chain regression table supplied by the team. The issue is hard to notice because the function is called indirectly through the seasonal update and the incorrect percentages are subtle numerical deviations rather than outright failures. The proper fix is to scale the inline supply thresholds by the token’s decimal factor (multiply by 10⁶) or to perform the comparison using values that share the same fixed‑point format. This aligns the conditional logic with the actual token precision and prevents the cascade of mis‑calculations. The vulnerability belongs to the class of fixed‑point arithmetic bugs where mismatched scaling leads to incorrect branching and downstream accounting errors.

title: Gauge point updates should be made considering the time-weighted average deposited LP BDV rather than instantaneous at the time of Sunrise
description:
Prior to the introduction of the Seed Gauge System, the Grown Stalk per BDV for whitelisted assets was static and could only be changed via governance. The Seed Gauge System now allows Beanstalk to target an amount of Grown Stalk per BDV that should be issued per Season, with Gauge Points being introduced to determine how the Grown Stalk issued that Season should be distributed between whitelisted LP tokens.

Gauge Points are updated every Season, when `LibGauge::stepGauge` is called within `SeasonFacet::gm`. This Gauge Point update is currently performed by [considering the instantaneous total deposited LP BDV](https://github.com/BeanstalkFarms/Beanstalk/blob/dfb418d185cd93eef08168ccaffe9de86bc1f062/protocol/contracts/libraries/LibGauge.sol#L115-L122) at the time of the `gm` call. However, this value can be subject to manipulation so the Seed Gauge System should instead use a time-weighted average deposited LP BDV over the previous Season duration.

Given the Gauge Points for a given whitelisted LP can only increase/decrease by one point per Season, and the Bean to max LP GP per BDV ratio is capped at 100%, the incentive to perform this attack is relatively low. However, a large deposit immediately before the Sunrise call, and withdrawal immediately after, could nonetheless result in manipulation meaning the Seed Gauge system does not work as intended.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the Seed Gauge System updates Gauge Points at each Season sunrise. Instead of basing the calculation on a time‑weighted average of the total deposited LP BDV over the previous Season, the contract takes a single instantaneous snapshot of the total deposited BDV at the exact block when the `gm` function (which calls `LibGauge::stepGauge`) is executed. Because this snapshot can be altered in the same block, an attacker can deposit a large amount of whitelisted LP tokens immediately before the sunrise call, inflate the instantaneous BDV, and then withdraw the tokens right after the update. The inflated BDV causes the Gauge Points to be calculated as if a higher amount of LP were continuously present, resulting in an oversized allocation of Grown Stalk for that Season. The impact is a mis‑distribution of rewards: honest participants receive less Grown Stalk than the protocol’s economics predict, while the attacker gains an unfair share of the reward pool. This manipulation can happen every time the Season advances, i.e., whenever `stepGauge` is invoked, and it only requires the ability to call deposit and withdraw functions around the sunrise transaction. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Cyfrin, where the logical dependence on an instantaneous value was flagged as a potential economic attack vector. The problem is subtle because the snapshot appears correct at the moment of execution and no explicit error is emitted, making it hard to detect from ordinary transaction logs. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a large, short‑lived deposit, the expected Grown Stalk per BDV is lower than anticipated, or the protocol seems to “lose” rewards for regular users. This class of bug falls under flash‑loan‑style economic manipulation where reward calculations rely on a single point‑in‑time state instead of a robust time‑averaged metric. The recommended mitigation is to replace the instantaneous BDV with a time‑weighted average computed over the entire previous Season, storing the BDV at the end of each block and updating the average whenever any function changes the total deposited BDV. By using a moving average, a single block’s deposit cannot disproportionately affect the Gauge Point calculation, restoring the intended fairness of the Seed Gauge System.

title: Gauge point constants in `InitBipSeedGauge` should be scaled by the ratio of deposited BDV
description:
The [current initial Gauge Point (GP) distribution](https://github.com/BeanstalkFarms/Beanstalk/blob/dfb418d185cd93eef08168ccaffe9de86bc1f062/protocol/contracts/beanstalk/init/InitBipSeedGauge.sol#L68-L69) is based solely on the grown stalk per season per BDV for each LP, whereas it should be determined by considering the deposited BDV per LP.

Considering the following math which underlies the behavior of the gauge system:
$$depositedBDVRatio(LP) = \frac{silo.totalDepositedBDV(LP)}{\sum_{wlpt}^{wlpt \in Whitelisted \ LP \ Tokens} silo.totalDepositedBDV} $$
$GP_{s}(LP) =$
1. $depositedBDVRatio(LP) > LP.optimalDepositedBDVRatio \land GP_{s-1}(LP) \leq 1gp \Rightarrow GP_{s}(LP) = 0$
2. $depositedBDVRatio(LP) > LP.optimalDepositedBDVRatio \land GP_{s-1}(LP) > 1gp \Rightarrow GP_{s}(LP) = GP_{s-1}(LP)- 1gp$
3. $depositedBDVRatio(LP) \leq LP.optimalDepositedBDVRatio \Rightarrow GP_{s}(LP) = GP_{s-1}(LP) + 1gp$

It can be seen that the formula relies on the previous $GP_{s-1}(LP)$, where $s$ indicates the current season number and deposited BDV ratio. Moreover, it is evident that the intention of this mechanism is to incentivize the Beanstalk protocol to have a pre-defined optimal deposited BDV ratio for each LP. Consequently, the initial assignment of GP should consider this intention.

An incorrect initial GP distribution can result in unintended initial behavior, which can take a significant amount of time to rectify given that gauge points can only increase/decrease by one point per season as defined in [`GaugePointFacet::defaultGaugePointFunction`](https://github.com/BeanstalkFarms/Beanstalk/blob/dfb418d185cd93eef08168ccaffe9de86bc1f062/protocol/contracts/beanstalk/sun/GaugePointFacet.sol#L26-L38).
poc:
```solidity
// InitBipSeedGauge.sol
uint128 beanEthGp = uint128(s.ss[C.BEAN_ETH_WELL].stalkEarnedPerSeason) * 500 * 1e12;
uint128 bean3crvGp = uint128(s.ss[C.CURVE_BEAN_METAPOOL].stalkEarnedPerSeason) * 500 * 1e12
```

As observed, the initial GP assignment is determined by the stalk earned per season before BIP-39, with the following values:
* BEAN:3CRV Curve LP: `3.25e6`
* BEAN:ETH Well LP: `4.5e6`

These values are not correlated with the total BDV deposited per LP. Consequently, the initial assignment of GP is made with incorrect values.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the Beanstalk protocol assigns initial gauge points (GP) to liquidity‑provider (LP) tokens during the InitBipSeedGauge initialization. Instead of basing the initial GP on the proportion of total deposited BDV that each LP contributes, the code mistakenly uses the amount of stalk earned per season (a value that existed before BIP‑39) multiplied by a constant factor. Because gauge points are intended to reflect the deposited BDV ratio – the fraction of the protocol’s total BDV that a particular LP holds – the current implementation creates a mismatch between the expected incentive structure and the actual allocation. The root cause is a missing scaling step: the GP calculation does not incorporate the depositedBDVRatio(LP) = silo.totalDepositedBDV(LP) / Σ totalDepositedBDV of all whitelisted LPs. As a result, an LP that has a small BDV share may receive a disproportionately high GP, while a large‑BDV LP may be under‑rewarded. Exploitation is not an active attack but a systemic misallocation that manifests immediately after contract deployment. Since the GaugePointFacet only permits GP to change by one point per season, correcting the imbalance can take many seasons, during which users experience rewards that diverge from the protocol’s economic model. From a user’s perspective, a depositor expects their gauge points – and thus future reward shares – to be proportional to the amount of BDV they supplied; instead they may see an unexpectedly low or high GP balance, leading to “reward amount is wrong” or “my points are zero” symptoms. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Cyfrin, who noted that the initial GP values (e.g., 3.25e6 for BEAN:3CRV and 4.5e6 for BEAN:ETH) have no correlation with the actual BDV totals. The bug is subtle because the numbers appear reasonable and the contract compiles without error, making it easy to overlook the missing proportionality check. To remediate, the initialization should first compute the total BDV across all whitelisted LPs, then assign each LP a GP equal to its BDV share multiplied by the standard GP unit (1e18), effectively scaling the GP by the depositedBDVRatio. This change restores the intended incentive alignment and prevents prolonged reward distortion.

title: Incorrect calculation of unmigrated BDVs for use in `InitBipSeedGauge::init`
description:
The current values for the [constants](https://github.com/BeanstalkFarms/Beanstalk/blob/dfb418d185cd93eef08168ccaffe9de86bc1f062/protocol/contracts/beanstalk/init/InitBipSeedGauge.sol#L35-L39) in `InitBipSeedGauge::init` are an estimation and not finalized. To correctly calculate the BDV, the Beanstalk Farms team simulates migrating all the remaining unmigrated deposits at the block in which BIP-38 was executed such that the change of BDV corresponding to the underlying asset in `BDVFacet::unripeLPToBDV` is considered and subject to the slippage incurred at the time of liquidity migration. The `deposits.json` file contains a list of outstanding deposits at the Silo V3 deployment block `17671557`, so the script considers all `removeDeposit` events after this point as deposits to be removed from the unmigrated BDV. By filtering from the Enroot fix deployment block `17251905`, if an account has removed its deposit after the Enroot fix but before Silo V3 was deployed, this would improperly assume the deposits have been migrated when they haven't. Additionally, given the script is forking mainnet at the BIP-38 execution block `18392690`, it is not correct to use `18480579` as the end block for event filtering.

The case has also been considered that, given the state changes will already have been applied, and assuming the migration transaction isn't top/bottom of block, it might be desirable to fork/filter up to the block before BIP-38 execution and check whether any migrations occurred before/after the migration transaction that need to be considered manually. After further inspection of the block in which the BIP-38 upgrade took place, it appears this is not necessary as no events were emitted.

An additional discrepancy in the unmigrated Bean BDV value was identified by the Beanstalk Farms team. After Silo V3, the implementation of `Sun::rewardToSilo` [increments the BDV](https://github.com/BeanstalkFarms/Beanstalk/blob/dfb418d185cd93eef08168ccaffe9de86bc1f062/protocol/contracts/beanstalk/sun/SeasonFacet/Sun.sol#L201-L204) by the amount of Bean issued to the Silo, but all previously earned Beans are not considered. Therefore, the value returned by `SiloExit::totalEarnedBeans` at the time of Silo V3 deployment should be added to the total.

The calculated unmigrated BDVs are incorrect, as shown below. The current implementation returns values that are smaller than they should be, meaning the total deposited BDV will fail to consider some deposits and be lower than intended.

Output of the current implementation:
```
unmigrated:  {
  '0x1BEA0050E63e05FBb5D8BA2f10cf5800B6224449': BigNumber { value: "3209210313166" },
  '0x1BEA3CcD22F4EBd3d37d731BA2D8893dB9d1Efab': BigNumber { value: "6680992571569" },
  '0xBEA0000029AD1c77D3d5D23Ba2D8893dB9d1Efab': BigNumber { value: "304630107407" },
  '0xc9C32cd16Bf7eFB85Ff14e0c8603cc90F6F2eE49': BigNumber { value: "26212521946" }
}
```

Corrected output:
```
unmigrated:  {
  '0x1BEA0050E63e05FBb5D8BA2f10cf5800B6224449': BigNumber { value: "3736196158417" },
  '0x1BEA3CcD22F4EBd3d37d731BA2D8893dB9d1Efab': BigNumber { value: "7119564766493" },
  '0xBEA0000029AD1c77D3d5D23Ba2D8893dB9d1Efab': BigNumber { value: "689428296238" },
  '0xc9C32cd16Bf7eFB85Ff14e0c8603cc90F6F2eE49': BigNumber { value: "26512602424" }
}
```
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an inaccurate calculation of the unmigrated Bean Deposit Value (BDV) that is used during the InitBipSeedGauge::init routine after the BIP‑38 upgrade. The root cause is two‑fold: first, the off‑chain script that simulates the migration of all remaining deposits uses hard‑coded block numbers that do not correspond to the actual Silo V3 deployment block (17671557) and the block at which the migration transaction is executed. By starting the event filter at the earlier Enroot fix block (17251905) and ending at a fixed block (18480579) the script mistakenly assumes some deposits have already been migrated when they have not, and it also fails to include any events that occur after the migration block. Second, the script ignores the additional Bean reward that the Sun::rewardToSilo function adds to the Silo’s BDV after Silo V3, because it only reads the current BDV without adding the totalEarnedBeans value that should be credited. As a result, the computed unmigrated BDV values are systematically lower than the true amounts, as demonstrated by the comparison between the current and corrected outputs. This mis‑calculation can be exploited indirectly: any downstream logic that relies on the unmigrated BDV – such as reward distribution, withdrawal calculations, or gauge weight assignments – will operate on an understated figure, causing users to receive fewer rewards or see reduced balances than they are entitled to. The impact is therefore a financial discrepancy that affects all depositors whose positions were not migrated at the time of the upgrade, as well as the protocol’s accounting integrity. The issue manifests only during the initialization phase of the gauge contract, after BIP‑38 execution, and only when the off‑chain migration script is run with the incorrect constants. It was discovered by the Cyfrin audit team while reviewing the InitBipSeedGauge source and the accompanying migration script, noticing that the script’s block range and reward handling did not match the on‑chain state. Because the problem lives in an off‑chain calculation, it does not produce obvious on‑chain errors and can remain hidden unless the resulting BDV totals are manually compared against expected values. To remediate the issue, the script should be updated to use the exact Silo V3 deployment block as the start of the RemoveDeposit event filter, replace the hard‑coded end block with the current block number at execution time, and augment the unmigrated BDV with the totalEarnedBeans value obtained from the Sun contract. This correction ensures that the unmigrated BDV reflects the true economic state, preserving accurate reward accounting and preventing users from receiving less than they should.

title: Locks can be created with expiry in the past
description:
Due to a silent overflow in [`SolidityV2ERC42069::lockToken`](https://github.com/SolidlyLabs/v2-core/blob/757b18ad05780d2af22018b0c2c9d59422dc59d3/contracts/SolidlyV2-memecore.sol#L387), a sufficiently large duration will cause the unlock date to be in the past. This could allow the caller to create a fraudulent lock, advertising that they have locked for the maximum duration but which can actually be withdrawn immediately. However, the impact is somewhat limited as this will be visible to anyone who calls [`SolidityV2ERC42069::getLock(s)`](https://github.com/SolidlyLabs/v2-core/blob/757b18ad05780d2af22018b0c2c9d59422dc59d3/contracts/SolidlyV2-memecore.sol#L459-L471) with the owner's address (perhaps in a UI). From the attacker's perspective, the extension functionality could ideally be used to wrap around at will, hiding this malicious intent; however, this is not possible due to the checked math revert when incrementing the date.

This bug has a high likelihood of being abused with a more limited impact; therefore, it is categorized as a medium-severity finding.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an integer overflow in the lock creation routine of the SolidityV2ERC42069 contract. When a caller supplies a very large lock duration, the contract adds the duration to the current block timestamp in 256‑bit arithmetic, then down‑casts the result to a 128‑bit unsigned integer that stores the unlock date. Because the cast occurs after the addition, the sum can exceed the maximum value representable in 128 bits (2^128‑1). The excess bits are silently discarded, causing the stored unlock date to wrap around to a value that is earlier than the current block timestamp, often zero. This means a lock that is advertised as having the maximum possible duration can actually be withdrawn immediately. The root cause is the unsafe down‑casting of a potentially overflowing sum, rather than performing the addition in the 128‑bit domain or checking for overflow before the cast. The bug can be triggered whenever the supplied duration is larger than (2^128‑1 – block.timestamp). An attacker can create a fraudulent lock, see the lock appear in the UI with an expiry of 0 or a past date, and then withdraw the locked tokens right away, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that locked tokens are unavailable until the recorded unlock time. The impact is limited because any observer can call getLock with the owner’s address and see that the lock’s expiry is in the past, making the deception visible. Nevertheless, the ability to create a lock that is effectively non‑existent undermines trust in the locking mechanism and could be abused in phishing or scam scenarios where users are led to believe their assets are secured for a long period. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, which added a test that locks tokens with a duration close to the maximum uint128 value and verifies that the stored date becomes zero. The overflow is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error; the lock simply appears to have an expiry of 0, which may be interpreted as “no lock” or “already expired” without further investigation. To remediate the problem, the contract should perform the addition in the 128‑bit space (e.g., cast block.timestamp to uint128 before adding the duration) or use safe arithmetic that checks for overflow before down‑casting. This ensures that the stored unlock date always reflects a future point in time and that the lock semantics cannot be bypassed.

title: Linea can permanently lock user ETH on L2 by censoring user transactions through the centralized sequencer
description: Linea can permanently lock user ETH on L2 by censoring user transactions through the centralized sequencer; as the Linea team control the sequencer they can choose (or be forced by a government entity) to censor any users by not including their L2 transactions when building L2 blocks. Additionally, there is no way for users to withdraw their L2 assets by [initiating an L1 transaction which would avoid the L2 censorship](https://solodit.xyz/issues/m-09-lack-of-access-to-eth-on-l2-through-l1-l2-transactions-code4rena-zksync-zksync-git). The combination of these factors means that users bridging assets over to Linea are completely at the mercy of the Linea team for their continued freedom to transact. This represents a significant downgrade from Ethereum's censorship resistance where even the OFAC censorship regime only had [38% enforcement](https://www.mevwatch.info) over the last 30 days. It should be noted however that this is a common defect [[1](https://youtu.be/Y4n38NPQhrY?si=88NeDOAsyA_kgVpo&t=167), [2](https://youtu.be/e8pwv9DIojI?si=Ru4oTdy0VM7S7Hmj&t=183)] with first-generation zkEVMs and de-centralized zk L2 sequencers are an active area of research [[1](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nF4jTEcQbkA), [2](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DP84VWng2i8)], so Linea is not an exceptional case in this regard.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the Linea zkEVM L2 relies on a single, centrally operated sequencer that decides which transactions are included in each L2 block. Because the sequencer is controlled by the Linea team, it can arbitrarily omit or censor any user‑submitted transaction. When a transaction that would move or withdraw ETH from the L2 is not included, the user has no alternative path to retrieve the funds because the contract does not expose a mechanism to initiate a withdrawal from L1 that bypasses the sequencer. Consequently, assets that have been bridged to Linea can become permanently inaccessible as long as the sequencer continues to refuse inclusion, effectively locking the ETH on L2. This situation occurs whenever the sequencer is instructed—either voluntarily by the operator or under external pressure such as a legal order—to block a specific address or transaction type. The affected parties are any user who has deposited ETH or other bridged tokens onto Linea, as well as the broader protocol that promises censorship‑resistant transaction finality. The issue was identified during a systematic security audit that examined the withdrawal flow and the governance model of the sequencer, noting the absence of a fallback L1‑only exit. The problem is subtle because the UI may simply show that a transaction is “pending” or “not confirmed” without indicating that the sequencer is deliberately ignoring it, making it hard for users to distinguish normal network congestion from intentional censorship. From a user perspective the symptom is that after attempting to withdraw, the balance shown on the L2 remains unchanged, or the user receives no funds despite a successful bridge transaction. This class of bug falls under “centralized sequencer censorship” and “withdrawal availability” defects, where the protocol’s design violates the expected accounting invariant that deposited funds must remain retrievable by the owner. An attacker—or a coercive authority—could exploit the sequencer by refusing to include the user’s withdrawal request, thereby freezing the assets indefinitely. To remediate, the protocol should either decentralize the sequencing process so that no single entity can unilaterally censor transactions, or implement a provably safe exit mechanism that allows users to trigger a withdrawal directly on L1, for example through a fraud‑proof or challenge‑based bridge that does not depend on L2 block production.

title: Users can't cancel or refund their source chain transaction if the destination chain transaction continually fails, causing loss of bridged funds
description:
Linea's messaging service allows users to bridge ETH between Ethereum L1 mainnet and Linea L2. The bridging process operates in 2 distinct transactions where the first can succeed and the second can fail completely independently of each other. In the first step of the bridging process on the source chain the user supplies their ETH to the messaging service contract on that chain together with some parameters. In the last step of the bridging process on the destination chain a delivery service ("postman") or the user themselves calls `claimMessage` or `claimMessageWithProof` to complete the bridging process. The last step of claiming the message is an arbitrary [call](https://github.com/Consensys/zkevm-monorepo/blob/364b64d2a2704567adac00e3fa428a1901717666/contracts/contracts/messageService/l1/L1MessageService.sol#L144-L154) with arbitrary calldata made to an address of the user's choosing. If this call fails for any reason the user may re-try claiming the message an infinite number of times. However if this call continues to revert (or if the `claim` transaction continually reverts for any other reason), the user:
* will never receive their bridged ETH on the destination chain
* has no way of initiating a cancel or refund transaction on the source chain
This scenario will result in a loss of bridged funds to the user.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a permanent fund lock that occurs when a user bridges ETH from Ethereum L1 to Linea L2 using the messaging service and the second transaction that finalises the bridge on the destination chain repeatedly fails. The root cause is the separation of the deposit step on the source chain from the claim step on the destination chain without any escrow, timeout or rollback mechanism. Because the contract only records the deposit and then relies on an arbitrary external call made by the claim transaction, there is no way for the user to cancel the operation or retrieve the deposited ETH if the call reverts each time. An attacker or a mis‑behaving destination contract can deliberately cause the claim to revert by providing malicious calldata or by making the target contract revert, which forces the claim transaction to fail indefinitely. The exploit consists of the user (or an attacker) initiating the bridge, then ensuring that every subsequent claimMessage or claimMessageWithProof transaction on the destination chain reverts; the protocol permits the user to retry infinitely but provides no alternative path to unwind the deposit. As a result the user never receives the bridged ETH on Linea, the UI may show a pending or “bridge completed” status while the balance on the destination chain remains zero, and the user has no method to initiate a cancel or refund on the source chain. This situation leads to a loss of funds for the user and undermines trust in the bridge, as the protocol’s accounting assumes that every successful deposit will eventually be matched by a successful claim. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of messages between the two chains and identified the missing cancellation logic. It can be hard to notice because the first transaction succeeds and emits events that suggest the bridge is working, while the failure only appears later when the user checks their destination balance. To remediate the problem the contract should implement a cancel or refund mechanism on the source chain that can be triggered after a configurable timeout or after a certain number of failed claim attempts, allowing the original depositor to retrieve their ETH. This change restores the expected invariant that deposited funds are either delivered to the recipient or can be reclaimed by the sender, eliminating the dead‑lock condition and aligning the bridge’s behaviour with standard accounting guarantees.

title: M-01 | NFT Marketplace Bidding Bait-And-Switch
description: Whenever a mirror ERC721 token is transferred, minted, or burned through ERC20 transfers, the order in which the mirror tokens are taken from the holder is LIFO (last in first out). This behavior can be abused in certain circumstance by a malicious actor to steal user funds when interacting with NFT marketplaces. The exact situation happens when a user that has a bid on a mirror NFT also sells a unit or more of base tokens from the same wallet. In that case, a malicious holder of the mirror NFT can make a profit and leave the user without the rare NFT. Attack scenario using the live [Asterix](https://opensea.io/collection/asterixlabs) collection as an example: Bob has one of the rarest NFTs, [1960](https://opensea.io/assets/ethereum/0x0000000000c26fabfe894d13233d5ec73f61cc72/1960) and waits for people to bid on it. At this point, Alice bids on it for 1.2938 WETH. The floor for the collection is 0.674 ETH and buying an NFT by buying the base tokens from the [liquidity pool](https://www.dextools.io/app/en/ether/pair-explorer/0x68e4af213c49f320175116bff189c9ca452ce29c?t=1714341972227) is 0.5671 ETH. Alice has another NFT, lowest rarity, and sells by selling a unit of base tokens. Since the collection is on Ethereum, the base swap transaction can be seen in the mempool. Bob sees the base unit sell and front-runs it with accepting Alice’s bid. Alice gets the rare 1960 ID and pays 1.2938 WETH, but immediately loses it as it was the last in and the base unit sell burns it, marking her a loss of 1.2938 - 0.5671 ETH. Bob quickly initiates several cycled mints/burns to reclaim the rare NFT. Even if Bob fails to reclaim it, Alice still suffered a loss of the rare NFT. The above case can also happen unintentionally, when a user bid is accepted exactly in the same block as him selling base tokens equivalent to a NFT, having the same financial loss.
poc: https://github.com/DanielGelfand/DN404-Team1/pull/2/files
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the DN404 contract synchronises mirror ERC721 tokens with ERC20 transfers. When a mirror token is transferred, minted, or burned as a result of an ERC20 operation, the contract selects the token to move using a last‑in‑first‑out (LIFO) rule: the most recently minted token is the first one removed from the holder’s balance. This ordering is contrary to the expected first‑in‑first‑out (FIFO) behaviour that most users assume for NFTs. The root cause is the internal stack‑like bookkeeping of mirror tokens, which does not preserve the chronological mint order. Because of this, an attacker can manipulate the timing of a bid acceptance and a base‑token sale to steal a rare NFT. The exploit works as follows: a user places a bid on a rare mirror NFT while simultaneously holding base tokens that can be swapped for ETH. When the user later sells a unit of those base tokens in the same transaction block or when the sell transaction is visible in the mempool, the contract’s LIFO logic treats the rare NFT as the last minted token and therefore burns it during the base‑token sale. A malicious participant monitoring the mempool can front‑run the bid acceptance, cause the sale to execute first, and end up with the rare NFT while the original bidder pays the full bid amount but receives nothing. The impact is a direct financial loss: the bidder’s WETH is transferred to the seller, but the rare NFT disappears from the bidder’s wallet, effectively turning a successful purchase into a loss of both the token and the paid funds. The condition required for the attack is the coexistence of an active bid on a mirror NFT and a base‑token sell operation originating from the same wallet within the same block or mempool window. All participants who rely on the marketplace – bidders, sellers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the trust model of “pay and receive the NFT” is broken. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the DN404 implementation, where the auditors observed that the internal token queue behaved like a stack rather than a queue, and that this behaviour could be triggered by normal marketplace interactions. The bug is subtle because the ordering is not exposed in the UI; users see a normal bid acceptance and a normal token swap, yet the rare NFT silently vanishes, making the problem hard to detect without deep inspection of the contract’s state changes. To remediate the issue, the synchronization logic should be changed to a FIFO scheme so that the earliest minted NFT is the first to leave the holder’s balance, or the risk should be clearly documented for integrators so that they can design around it. In abstract terms, this is a token‑selection ordering flaw that enables a bait‑and‑switch attack, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that assets are transferred in the order they were acquired, and leading to scenarios where “funds disappear” or “the expected NFT is missing” after a successful bid.

title: M-02 | Double NFT Minting Via AfterNFTTransfer Hook
description: Contracts that extend DN404 can implement the _afterNFTTransfer hook to be executed after any NFT token transfers, including minting and burning. An attacker can abuse any implementations that pass access to holders from within these hooks as there are situations when the _afterNFTTransfer function is called before the internal storage is committed, breaking CEI. Consider the following attack scenario in a system implementing the _afterNFTTransfe hook: An approver initiates a transfer to a user where direct transfers will be made. In the _afterNFTTransfer function the malicious attacker has an existing helper contract that directly transfers several ERC721 tokens to himself. Since this was done before the balanceOf equivalent was updated, after the initial execution is finalized, the malicious strategy will have a smaller ERC721 balance then the number of ERC721 it owns. As the attacker has less NFTs then they should by the ownedLength variable and because this ownedLength is used in determining how many NFT a user will have for their base token amount, the attacker can transfer any amount, even 0, to himself and the contract will mint him extra ERC721 tokens, the exact number that was sent by the helper contract. At this point, an attacker owns double the ERC721 tokens that he received, for half the amount of ERC20 base required to own that many.
poc: https://github.com/DanielGelfand/DN404-Team1/pull/1
bug_full: The vulnerability is a double‑minting flaw that arises from the way the DN404 contract executes its _afterNFTTransfer hook. The hook is intended to run after any NFT transfer, including minting and burning, but the implementation calls the hook before the contract updates the internal accounting that tracks how many NFTs a holder owns (the ownedLength variable). Because the state change that records the new balance is performed after the external call, an attacker can trigger a re‑entrancy‑like situation: when a legitimate transfer is initiated, the _afterNFTTransfer hook executes and the attacker’s malicious helper contract can transfer additional ERC‑721 tokens to the attacker’s address. At that moment the ownedLength value still reflects the pre‑transfer balance, so the contract later calculates the number of NFTs to mint based on a lower balance than the attacker actually holds. The contract therefore mints extra NFTs equal to the amount transferred by the helper, resulting in the attacker possessing twice the number of NFTs for roughly half the required ERC‑20 base token cost. This bug occurs whenever a direct NFT transfer (including minting) invokes the hook, because the hook is called before the ownedLength variable is updated. The affected parties are token holders and the protocol itself, as the inflated NFT supply undermines the economic model and can lead to loss of value for honest participants. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the ordering of state updates and external calls in the DN404 implementation; it is subtle because the hook appears to run “after” a transfer, yet the internal bookkeeping has not yet been committed, making the problem easy to overlook. The attack is hard to notice from the UI because the user may simply see that they received the expected NFTs, while the contract’s internal accounting is inconsistent, and the extra tokens are minted silently. To remediate the flaw, the _afterNFTTransfer logic should be moved to a separate loop that executes only after the ownedLength (and any other balance‑related state) has been fully updated, and no external calls should be made before the contract’s internal state reflects the transfer. This eliminates the re‑entrancy window and restores the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, preventing double minting and preserving the intended token economics.

title: M-03 | Address Initialization Allows Pools To Accumulate NFTs
description: Upon the first interaction with an address the address data flags are initialized, checking to see if the address holds any bytecode. If the account does not hold any bytecode at the time of account initialization then it receives only the _ADDRESS_DATA_INITIALIZED_FLAG flag. However if the address is later deployed to (e.g. a new pool is created at this address), the contract will not be excluded from ERC721 minting, as it will not automatically receive the _ADDRESS_DATA_SKIP_NFT_FLAG flag. As a result malicious actors may transfer tokens to an address where a pool for the token is about to be deployed to in order to avoid getting the address marked with the _ADDRESS_DATA_SKIP_NFT_FLAG. NFTs will then errantly be minted to and burned from the pool address upon liquidity modification and swaps. This creates a pool of NFTs which are not owned by end users, but instead locked up in a swap pool where a significant amount of them may not be able to move due to locked liquidity. In the case of a swap pool it would be possible for a flashloan to rescue potentially rare ERC721 tokens, however in the case of a locking contract or some other arbitrary integration these ERC721 tokens could be unintentionally locked for a significant amount of time.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way DN404 initializes address metadata the first time an address is touched. During this initialisation the contract checks whether the address contains bytecode; if it does not, the address receives only the _ADDRESS_DATA_INITIALIZED_FLAG flag. The design assumes that contracts deployed later will automatically acquire the _ADDRESS_DATA_SKIP_NFT_FLAG flag, which tells the system to ignore the address when minting ERC721 tokens. Because the flag is not added retroactively, a contract that is created after the first interaction – for example a new liquidity pool – remains without the skip‑NFT marker. An attacker can exploit this by sending ERC721 tokens to the future pool address before the pool contract is deployed. When the pool is later created, the address is still considered eligible for NFT minting, so any subsequent liquidity‑add or swap operation will unintentionally mint new NFTs to the pool address and later burn them during swaps. The result is a collection of NFTs that are owned by the pool contract rather than by end users. From a user perspective the symptoms are missing or zero balances in their wallet, unexpected reduction of NFT holdings after a swap, or the appearance of “ghost” NFTs that cannot be transferred out of the pool. The impact ranges from loss of rare NFTs to the inability to retrieve them because the pool’s liquidity may be locked for an extended period, making the tokens effectively inaccessible. The issue is triggered only when an address is first touched while empty of bytecode and later receives a contract deployment; it does not affect addresses that already had bytecode at initialisation. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the address‑initialisation logic, where the auditor noticed that the skip‑NFT flag is only set on first‑touch for contracts that already exist. It is subtle because the flag logic is hidden behind a low‑level data structure and the problem only manifests after a specific sequence of actions, making it easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate, the getSkipNFT function should explicitly check for the presence of bytecode on every call, regardless of whether the address has been initialised, or the protocol should provide a mechanism for trusted contracts to set the skip‑NFT flag after deployment. Documenting the risk and encouraging integrators to implement their own skip‑NFT checks can also mitigate accidental token locking.

title: M-04 | Missing tokenId Existence Check
description: When a tokenURI function is called in the fallback of the DN404 contract, it is never checked whether the given tokenId exists. According to the recommendation in EIP712, the tokenURI function should throw an error if the tokenId is not a valid NFT. This recommendation is followed in the OpenZeppelin ERC721 implementation contract as well as the ERC721A implementation.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked token identifier in the tokenURI function that is invoked from the fallback of the DN404 contract. When a caller supplies a tokenId that does not correspond to a minted NFT, the function proceeds without verifying the existence of that token and returns whatever data the fallback provides. The root cause is the absence of a guard clause that would normally call _exists(tokenId) or a similar check before constructing the URI, a pattern mandated by EIP‑721 and replicated in OpenZeppelin’s ERC721 and ERC721A implementations. An attacker can exploit this by querying tokenURI with arbitrary, non‑existent tokenIds. Because the contract does not revert, it may return a default or empty string, causing off‑chain services, marketplaces, or user interfaces to display missing or incorrect metadata. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a blank image, missing description, or a URI that points to an unexpected location, leading the user to believe the token is invalid or that the platform is broken. The impact is primarily informational: users lose confidence, third‑party services may misinterpret the token as valid, and automated scripts that rely on a successful revert to filter invalid IDs may behave incorrectly. The issue manifests whenever tokenURI is called with an identifier that has never been minted, which can happen during normal browsing of token collections, during batch queries, or when malicious actors deliberately probe the contract. All participants that rely on accurate NFT metadata – token owners, marketplace operators, and protocol integrators – are affected because the contract violates the ERC‑721 invariant that tokenURI must revert for unknown tokenIds. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s behavior against the ERC‑721 specification and noted the missing existence check. It is subtle because the function still returns a value, so no obvious error is thrown, making it easy to overlook during testing unless explicit negative‑case tests are written. The proper remediation is to insert a validation step that confirms the tokenId exists (for example, using _exists(tokenId)) and to revert with a custom error if the check fails. This aligns the contract with the standard tokenURI contract pattern and prevents the accidental exposure of empty or misleading metadata, preserving the integrity of the token’s accounting and user experience.

title: Inconsistent sequencer unexpected delay in DelayBuffer may harm users calling `forceInclusion`
description: Buffer unexpected delay due to sequencer outage is inconsistent.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the delay‑buffer logic that underpins the forceInclusion mechanism of Arbitrum’s SequencerInbox contract. The buffer is intended to record the amountof time a delayed message has been waiting because the sequencer is unavailable, and it is used to guarantee that a user can force‑include a message after a bounded number of blocks. The implementation calculates the unexpected delay by subtracting the last sequenced block number from the current block number, but it fails to also consider the oldest delayed message that has not yet been included. As a result, when messages are forced‑included out of order – for example when a later message is included before an earlier one – the buffer is not reduced correctly and may retain a value that is far larger than the true waiting time. This inconsistency can be triggered during a sequencer outage when several delayed messages accumulate and a user (or an attacker) chooses a non‑sequential inclusion order. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a transaction that should be force‑included after a few hundred blocks instead requires thousands of blocks, effectively locking the funds associated with the message for an unexpectedly long period. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style restriction on withdrawals or state updates, which harms end‑users, L3 game participants and any party relying on timely inclusion. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which provided a proof‑of‑concept test showing that the buffer value remains at the maximum (e.g., 7320 blocks) instead of decreasing to the expected threshold (e.g., 600 blocks) when inclusion order is altered. Because the buffer is an internal accounting variable, the problem can be subtle and may only be noticed when users experience unusually long waiting times or when the contract reverts with the ForceIncludeBlockTooSoon error. The root cause is an incomplete accounting of unexpected delay that leads to double‑counting or omission of delay periods. To remediate, the contract should track the total unexpected delay separately and compute it as the current block number minus the greater of the previously sequenced block number and the oldest undelivered delayed message. This ensures that each block of real sequencer downtime is counted exactly once and that the buffer is depleted consistently regardless of inclusion order. Applying the same correction that exists in the delayProofImpl function to the forceInclusion path eliminates the nondeterministic behavior and restores the intended guarantee that users can force‑include messages within a predictable timeframe.

title: `BOLDUpgradeAction.sol` will fail to upgrade contracts due to error in the `perform` function
description: An error in the `BOLDUpgradeAction.sol` contract prevents it from upgrading and deploying new BOLD contracts.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the upgrade helper contract that is responsible for cleaning up an old rollup before deploying a new BOLD contract. The cleanup routine iterates over the list of stakers, pauses the old rollup, and attempts to refund eligible stakers. The core flaw is the manipulation of the loop bound inside the for‑loop: when a staker qualifies for a refund the code decrements the local variable that stores the total number of stakers (stakerCount) while the loop index continues to increase. Because the loop condition is evaluated against the mutated stakerCount, the iterator can eventually exceed the actual number of staker entries that remain accessible through the rollup’s getter functions. This leads to an out‑of‑bounds array access when calling getStakerAddress(i), causing the transaction to revert with a panic error. The bug is triggered only when at least one staker meets the refund criteria and the contract attempts to modify the stakerCount during iteration, which is a realistic scenario for any rollup that has active participants. As a result, the upgrade action aborts, preventing the deployment of the new BOLD contracts and leaving the protocol in a frozen state. Users and protocol operators are affected because the expected upgrade does not happen, funds that should be refunded remain locked, and the system may appear unresponsive. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the test harness reproduced the panic by iterating over the real rollup contract on a forked mainnet. The problem is subtle because the loop logic appears correct at a glance; the decrement of stakerCount is intended to reduce the iteration range after a successful refund, but it unintentionally corrupts the loop invariant. The appropriate mitigation is to avoid mutating the loop bound while iterating. A safe fix is to iterate over a snapshot of the staker list, use a separate counter for processed refunds, or collect eligible staker addresses in a temporary array before performing refunds, ensuring that the original stakerCount remains unchanged during the loop. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “incorrect loop control” or “mutable iteration bound” bugs that can cause index out‑of‑range errors and abort critical state‑transition functions. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that an upgrade was submitted but never completes, balances stay unchanged, and no refund is received even though the protocol indicates that a refund should have been processed. The discrepancy between the expected successful upgrade and the actual failure is a direct consequence of the faulty loop logic.

title: All supplied WETH to Aave as a deposit by a Strategy will be irrecoverable
description: WETH supplied to Aave will be lost.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a logic flaw in the strategy that manages Aave V3 positions. After the strategy swaps collateral for WETH in order to repay a debt, it calculates whether any WETH remains unused (the "leftover" amount). If a leftover exists, the code calls an internal _supply function to deposit that WETH back into the Aave pool. The root cause is that the strategy’s withdrawal routine is limited to pulling only the collateral asset from Aave; it has no mechanism to retrieve a deposited WETH token. Consequently, any WETH that is mistakenly supplied becomes permanently locked in the Aave pool because the contract cannot issue a withdrawal request for that asset. An attacker does not need to perform any special action – the bug is triggered automatically whenever the swap output exceeds the required debt plus fee, which is a normal situation when market prices move favorably. The impact is that users who interact with the strategy expect any excess WETH to be returned to their wallet, but instead the funds disappear from the user’s perspective; the UI may show that the transaction succeeded while the user’s WETH balance is unchanged or reduced. This loss affects all participants of the protocol who rely on the strategy to manage their leveraged positions, breaking the accounting assumption that every token received by the contract can be reclaimed. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors traced the flow of the leftover WETH and noticed that the only withdrawal path targets collateral assets, not WETH. The problem is subtle because the deposit operation does not revert and there is no explicit error message, making the loss appear as a silent disappearance of funds. To remediate the flaw, the contract should stop depositing leftover WETH into Aave and instead use that amount to repay additional debt, or implement a proper withdrawal path for WETH. In either case the fix restores the intended business logic that excess WETH is either used to improve the loan‑to‑value ratio or returned to the user, preventing irreversible loss of assets.

title: Vault can be DoS
description: When `totalSupply = 0`, the attacker donates 1wei token, causing the number of shares to remain 0 at deposit time.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the vault’s share‑minting logic caused by an incorrect zero‑check in the internal conversion routine that translates deposited assets into vault shares. The function responsible for this conversion, often called toBase, only verifies whether the elastic component of the vault’s accounting structure (the total amount of underlying assets) is zero. It does not also verify that the base component, which represents the total supply of vault shares, is non‑zero. When the vault is freshly deployed its totalSupply (base) is zero. If an attacker makes a tiny deposit – for example 1 wei of the underlying token – the conversion routine sees a non‑zero elastic value, takes the else branch, and computes the number of shares as (elastic * total.base) / total.elastic. Because total.base is zero, the result is always zero, regardless of the deposited amount. Consequently the contract mints zero shares to the depositor, emits a Deposit event that appears normal, but the user receives no ownership tokens and the vault’s totalSupply remains zero. From that point onward any subsequent deposit will also be converted to zero shares, effectively locking the vault and preventing legitimate users from depositing or withdrawing assets. The attack does not directly steal funds; the assets remain in the vault, but the protocol becomes unusable, violating the business assumption that every deposit yields a positive share balance. This issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors examined the toBase implementation and noticed the missing check for total.base. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the event logs look successful, so users may think their deposit succeeded while their balance stays at zero. The fix is to extend the zero‑condition to include both components of the accounting pair – i.e., treat the situation as a zero‑state when either total.elastic or total.base is zero – ensuring that a deposit in a zero‑supply vault yields a one‑to‑one share allocation instead of zero. This change restores the invariant that a non‑zero deposit always results in a non‑zero share amount, preventing the denial‑of‑service scenario.

title: `StrategyLeverage.harvest` doesn’t account flashloan fee
description:
`StrategyLeverage.harvest` function checks position state. In case if position LTV is bigger than max LTV, then [extra debt is repaid](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-bakerfi/blob/main/contracts/core/strategies/StrategyLeverage.sol#L395) to decrease LTV back to normal.

In order to repay part of debt, flashloan is taken and contract [should pay fee for it](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-bakerfi/blob/main/contracts/core/strategies/StrategyLeverage.sol#L342).

So overall after adjusting our debt is decreased with `deltaDebt` but our collateral is decreased with `deltaDebt + fee`.

The problem is that this is not reflected in the [`newDeployedAmount` calculation](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-bakerfi/blob/main/contracts/core/strategies/StrategyLeverage.sol#L397-L399) as it thinks that both collateral and debt were decreased by `deltaDebt`.

As result of this, `newDeployedAmount` is bigger than it is in reality (in reality it is `newDeployedAmount - fee`), which means that later when some profit accrued, protocol [may not receive it](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-05-bakerfi/blob/main/contracts/core/strategies/StrategyLeverage.sol#L408-L416). For example if `profit is < fee`, then protocol won’t receive it and if `profit is > fee`, then protocol will receive management fee based on `profit - fee` amount.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the harvest routine of a leveraged strategy contract. When the position’s loan‑to‑value (LTV) exceeds the configured maximum, the function initiates a flash‑loan to repay part of the outstanding debt and bring the LTV back within limits. The flash‑loan incurs a fee that must be deducted from the strategy’s collateral. However, the implementation only subtracts the principal amount (deltaDebt) from both the debt and the collateral when computing the new deployed amount, completely ignoring the flash‑loan fee. As a result, the contract records a higher deployed amount than actually exists – the real deployed amount is lower by exactly the fee amount. This mis‑accounting becomes visible only when the strategy later realizes a profit that is comparable to or smaller than the flash‑loan fee. In such cases the protocol’s accounting logic believes more collateral is available than there truly is, causing the protocol to either miss the entire profit (if profit < fee) or to calculate management fees on a reduced profit (profit ‑ fee) instead of the full amount. The flaw is triggered only under the specific condition that a harvest call is made while the LTV is above the threshold, causing a flash‑loan‑based debt adjustment.
