An attacker or any user who triggers the first mint can therefore cause the contract to emit the entire supply instantly, or, depending on the exact arithmetic, the first mint may fail entirely, preventing any future minting. The impact is severe: the token’s economic model collapses, holders may receive an unexpected flood of tokens, market price can be destabilized, and the protocol loses control over inflation. The issue manifests only on the first minting call, making it easy to miss in routine testing that focuses on repeated mint cycles. It was discovered during a formal audit by Cyfrin, who noted that the timestamp variable was never set. The bug is hard to notice because the contract appears to work after the first mint, and the abnormal supply growth may only be observed after a short period of time. To remediate, the contract should set _lastMintTimestamp to the current block timestamp during deployment or the first invocation of setVestingFactor, ensuring that the time‑based mint calculation starts from a valid reference point. This change restores the intended gradual release of tokens and prevents the accidental minting of the full supply in a single day.

title: When recoverToken in DaiGoldAction contract is called, it does not update the status
description:
recoverToken function moves specific amount of TGLD from the auction contract to another and delete last epoch so that it can be reset and restart. The tokens get moved but the status nextAuctionGoldAmount is not subtracted, and this gives incorrect amount of TLGD tokens to the next epoch, and as a result, the bidders won't be able to claim their TGLD.

The next auction has incorrect number as auction amount which results in users not being able to claim tokens after the auction ends.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the recoverToken function of the DaiGoldAction contract. This function is intended to move a specified amount of TGLD tokens from the auction contract to a destination address and then delete the last epoch so that the auction can be reset and restarted. While the token transfer itself succeeds, the function fails to update the internal accounting variable that tracks the amount of gold allocated for the next auction, known as nextAuctionGoldAmount. Because this state variable is not decremented by the amount of tokens that were moved, the contract records an inflated gold amount for the subsequent auction epoch. When the next auction ends, the claim logic checks the recorded auction amount against the actual token balance, and the mismatch prevents bidders from successfully claiming their TGLD tokens. From a user’s perspective, after an auction finishes they may see a claim transaction revert or return zero, and their wallet balance remains unchanged even though they expect to receive tokens proportional to their bids. The issue occurs whenever recoverToken is invoked after an auction has concluded but before the next epoch begins, which is typically an administrative action. All participants who placed bids in the affected auction are impacted because they cannot retrieve their entitled tokens, effectively locking their funds. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by Cyfrin, where the logical flow of state updates was examined and the missing subtraction was identified. The problem is subtle because the token transfer itself does not emit an error, and the UI may show that tokens were moved, masking the underlying accounting inconsistency. This class of bug can be described as a state‑inconsistency or accounting error where external actions modify balances without synchronizing internal bookkeeping variables. To remediate the issue, the recoverToken implementation should explicitly subtract the transferred amount from nextAuctionGoldAmount (or otherwise reconcile the internal gold counter) before deleting the epoch, ensuring that the recorded auction amount matches the actual token supply for the next round. By aligning the on‑chain accounting with the token movements, the protocol restores the ability for bidders to claim their TGLD and preserves the integrity of the auction’s financial logic.

title: In staking contract, rewards distribution can be delayed by front-running distributeGold function
description:
In `TempleGoldStaking` contract, the reward distributer calls `distributeRewards` to by minting available TLGD from the token contract and updates reward rate based on the minted amount. However, the distribution works only after the distribution cooldown period is passed:
```solidity
if (lastRewardNotificationTimestamp + rewardDistributionCoolDown > block.timestamp) { revert CannotDistribute(); }
```

It uses `lastRewardNotificationTimestamp` as latest updated timestamp, which can be also updated by anyone who calls a public function `distributeGold`. By front-running this function, it prevents the distributor from updating reward rate.

More seriously, if `distributeGold` is called regularly before the distribution cooldown, rewards distribution can be prevented forever.

Reward distribution can be delayed.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running denial‑of‑service on the reward distribution mechanism of the staking contract. The contract uses a single timestamp variable, lastRewardNotificationTimestamp, to enforce a cooldown before new rewards can be minted and distributed. This timestamp is updated not only by the privileged distributeRewards function, which mints new tokens and recalculates the reward rate, but also by a public function called distributeGold. Because any address can call distributeGold, an attacker can submit a transaction that updates lastRewardNotificationTimestamp just before the cooldown expires. The distributeRewards function then checks if lastRewardNotificationTimestamp + rewardDistributionCoolDown > block.timestamp and reverts with CannotDistribute when the condition is true. By front‑running the legitimate distribution transaction with a call to distributeGold, the attacker forces the check to fail, causing the distribution to revert. If the attacker (or any user) repeatedly calls distributeGold before the cooldown period ends, the timestamp is continuously refreshed and the condition never becomes false, effectively preventing reward distribution forever. From a user’s perspective, stakers see their pending rewards remain at zero even though time has passed, and the UI shows no increase in balances or earned rewards. The impact is that the economic incentive model of the protocol is broken: funds may be minted but never reach stakers, leading to loss of trust and potential loss of value for participants. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, where the logical coupling of a public state‑changing function with a cooldown guard was identified as a flaw. It can be hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly when no adversarial transaction is present; the problem only surfaces under targeted front‑running or regular misuse of distributeGold. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running and timestamp manipulation vulnerabilities that result in a denial‑of‑service of critical protocol logic. To remediate, the contract should either restrict access to distributeGold (e.g., make it permissioned) or introduce a separate state variable that records the last reward distribution timestamp and is updated exclusively by distributeRewards. This separation ensures that only authorized reward updates affect the cooldown logic, preventing external actors from resetting the timer and blocking reward distribution.

title: Configuring compose option will prevent users from receiving TGLD on the destination chain
description:
Users are able to send their TGLD by calling `send` function of TempleGold contract. Since `SendParam` struct is passed from users, they can add any field including compose data into the message. However on the destination chain, in `_lzReceive` function, it blocks messages with compose options in it:
```solidity
if (_message.isComposed()) { revert CannotCompose(); }
```

This means that users who call `send` with compose option, they will not receive TGLD tokens on the destination chain.

Token transfer does not work based on the parameter and causes loss of funds for users.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the cross‑chain transfer of the TGLD token through the TempleGold contract. The contract exposes a public send function that accepts a user‑provided SendParam struct. Because the struct is supplied directly by the caller, a user can include any field, including the optional compose data that is intended for advanced messaging. On the destination chain, the internal _lzReceive function checks the incoming message and explicitly rejects any message that carries compose options by executing if (_message.isComposed()) { revert CannotCompose(); }. Consequently, when a user includes a compose option in the SendParam, the message is accepted on the source chain but is reverted on the destination chain, preventing the token transfer from completing. The root cause is the lack of validation of the compose flag in the send function, allowing malformed or unsupported messages to be forwarded to the remote endpoint. An attacker or an unwitting user can exploit this by simply adding a compose field to the parameters; the contract will forward the request, the remote side will revert, and the user’s TGLD will be deducted from the source balance while never arriving on the destination chain. The impact is a loss of funds for the sender, as the tokens appear to be sent but the recipient receives nothing, leading to a zero balance on the destination side and a reduced balance on the source side. This condition occurs whenever the send function is called with a SendParam that contains any compose data, which is not currently prohibited by the contract. All users of the bridge, as well as the protocol that relies on reliable cross‑chain accounting, are affected because the accounting assumptions of “sent equals received” are broken. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the handling of user‑controlled structs and the message validation logic on the remote chain. It can be hard to notice because the compose option is optional and may not be used in typical transfers, so the failure only appears for edge‑case inputs that include it. To remediate, the send function should either reject any SendParam that contains compose data by reverting early, or, preferably, the contract should construct the SendParam internally from a minimal set of user‑provided fields such as the amount, thereby eliminating the possibility of injecting unsupported options. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that a user’s funds are either transferred successfully or the transaction fails atomically, preserving user balances and protocol integrity.

title: In staking contract, resetting self delegation will reset vote weight to zero
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the staking contract’s handling of self‑delegation resets. When a delegate calls the function that clears their own delegation, the contract invokes an internal routine to update the delegate’s vote weight. This routine receives a new balance value of zero, which triggers a conditional block that resets the internal timestamp (stakingTime) and the last recorded share amount to zero. As a result, the delegate’s accumulated voting power, which should be based on the amount of tokens they still hold, is incorrectly cleared. The root cause is the misuse of a generic balance‑update path for a special case where the delegate’s own stake is not meant to change, causing the accounting logic to treat the delegate as if they have no stake. An attacker or any user can exploit this by resetting their self‑delegation immediately before a governance epoch ends, causing the delegate’s vote weight to start from zero for that epoch. This leads to a loss of voting influence, potentially altering the outcome of proposals or allowing a malicious actor to diminish a competitor’s voting power. The issue manifests only when the self‑delegation reset function is called while the delegate still holds a non‑zero balance; otherwise normal delegation changes behave correctly. Affected parties include any token holder who delegates to themselves, the governance process of the protocol, and any participants relying on vote weight for decision making. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by Cyfrin, where the logical flow of the update routine was examined and the unintended reset of stakingTime was identified. It can be hard to notice because the user interface still shows the correct token balance, yet the voting power displayed in governance dashboards drops to zero, creating a discrepancy that may be attributed to a UI glitch rather than a contract flaw. To remediate, the contract should separate the logic for self‑delegation resets from generic balance updates, preserving the existing stakingTime and share values when the delegate’s own balance remains unchanged, or pass the current balance instead of zero to the weight‑updating function. This ensures that vote weight continues to reflect the delegate’s actual stake, aligning with the protocol’s accounting assumptions that voting power is proportional to token holdings over time.

title: Incorrect end time setting for spice auction
description:
In `startAuction` function of `SpiceAuction` contract, the end time is set wrong.
```solidity
uint128 startTime = info.startTime = uint128(block.timestamp) + config.startCooldown;
uint128 endTime = info.endTime = uint128(block.timestamp) + config.duration;
```
Currently, `endTime` is set using `block.timestamp`, not `startTime` calculated above.

The auction end time becomes shorter than expected.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the auction end time in the SpiceAuction contract. When startAuction is called, the contract records a startTime as the current block timestamp plus a configured startCooldown, but it then sets endTime using the raw block.timestamp plus the auction duration. Because the startCooldown is ignored in the endTime computation, the resulting endTime can be earlier than the intended startTime, or at best shorter than the advertised auction length. This timing mismatch occurs whenever the startCooldown value is non‑zero or when the configured duration does not account for the cooldown period. As a result, an auction may close immediately after being created, preventing any bids from being placed. Users experience symptoms such as seeing the auction listed as finished right after initiation, receiving no opportunity to submit a bid, or observing that their expected participation window disappears. The root cause is a logical error: the contract uses block.timestamp for both start and end calculations instead of deriving endTime from the already computed startTime. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, which highlighted that the bug is subtle because the timestamps are close in value and may not be caught by simple unit tests that assume zero cooldown. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker can start an auction and rely on the premature end to deny competitors the chance to bid, effectively sabotaging the market mechanism. The impact is a loss of auction fairness, potential revenue loss for the protocol, and a degraded user experience, though funds are not directly stolen. The bug belongs to the class of timing or deadline miscalculations that break business logic assumptions about auction duration. To remediate, the endTime should be calculated as startTime plus the configured duration, ensuring the auction runs for the full intended period regardless of any start cooldown. This conceptual fix restores the correct accounting of time and aligns the contract behavior with user expectations that an auction lasts for the advertised duration.

title: No token recover mechanism when the auction ends without any bid
description:
In `SpiceAuction` contract, when an auction ends with no bids, the auction tokens are locked into the contract and can't be recovered. `recoverToken` function doesn't help recover the auction token because it limits recoverable amount to `balance - totalAllocation`.

The auction tokens can be stuck in the contract and can't be recovered, although this would be rare case.
bug_full: The contract implements an auction where a token is deposited as the auctioned asset. When the auction finishes, participants can claim allocations and the contract provides a recoverToken function intended to allow the owner to withdraw any surplus tokens. However, the recoverToken logic restricts the withdrawable amount to the contract's token balance minus the total amount that has been allocated to bidders. In the edge case where the auction ends without any bids, the total allocation is zero, but the internal accounting still treats the deposited auction token as part of the allocated pool, causing the computed withdrawable amount to be zero. As a result, the auction token remains permanently locked in the contract with no way for the seller or any privileged role to retrieve it. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the mere occurrence of an auction that receives no bids triggers the condition. The impact is that the seller loses access to the token they intended to sell, effectively causing the funds to disappear from their perspective. This situation can arise whenever market conditions lead to zero participation, which may be rare but is possible. The affected parties are the token owner who created the auction and any downstream protocol that expects the auctioned asset to be recoverable after a failed sale. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the token recovery path and identified that the balance‑minus‑allocation check does not account for the case of zero bids. Because the contract does not emit any event or revert, the token lock is silent, making it hard to notice until the owner attempts to recover the token and finds the balance unchanged. The bug belongs to the class of “locked‑asset” or “unrecoverable token” vulnerabilities, where accounting logic prevents withdrawal of assets that are no longer needed. To fix the problem, the recovery function should be adjusted to allow withdrawal of the entire auctioned token amount when total allocation is zero, or a separate fallback mechanism should be added that explicitly transfers the auction token back to the seller after an empty auction. This change restores the expected business logic that an unsold item can be reclaimed, aligning the contract’s behavior with user expectations that they can retrieve their token if no one bids.

title: M-07 | setFundingRate Unexpectedly Changes Funding
description: The setFundingRate function allows a permissioned address to update the maxFundingRate, which potentially caps the existing funding rate for pending funding fees. This action would affect funding fees that have accumulated in the past causing unexpected funding changes for users, which could ultimately lead to accounts being subject to unexpected liquidation as a result of receiving less funding fees than expected.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a function that lets a privileged address modify the protocol’s maximum funding rate without first reconciling the funding state that has already been accumulated for open positions. Because the function only updates a cap variable, the change is applied retroactively to funding fees that were calculated in previous intervals but have not yet been settled. As a result, users who expected a certain amount of funding payout – either a positive funding credit or a negative funding charge – may receive a different amount after the cap is altered. If the new cap reduces the funding credit, a trader’s effective margin can shrink, potentially pushing the position into liquidation even though the market price has not moved. Conversely, raising the cap could increase funding charges unexpectedly. The issue manifests whenever the permissioned address invokes the rate‑setting function after funding has accrued but before the protocol distributes or settles those fees. All traders with open positions are affected because the accounting assumption that funding fees are immutable after calculation is violated. The problem was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the behaviour of this function with a similar one that correctly distributes an impact pool before changing a related parameter. The bug is subtle because the function call appears harmless – it only changes a configuration value – and the UI typically shows the current funding rate, not the historical amounts that will be altered. To remediate, the contract should first settle or update the pending funding state for all positions before applying the new maximum funding rate, mirroring the pattern used in the impact‑distribution function. This ensures that previously accrued funding fees remain accurate and users receive the amounts they are entitled to, preserving the integrity of margin calculations and liquidation thresholds.

title: M-08 | MEV Bribes Allow Grieﬁng Of Keepers
description: On Avalanche C-Chain a user can use providers such as flashbots or snowsight to set the gas price to the lowest acceptable gas price and still have their transaction executed via a bribe. Inside of validateExecutionFee(), the validation for the execution fee checks if execution fee is less than gasLimit * tx.gasprice. Setting a lower tx.gasprice will allow a user to pay less than the expected amount for an execution fee and force the keeper to draw on treasury reserves to subsidize the transaction. It may be possible for a malicious actor to submit many orders this way in order to grief the keepers. Or users may use this to pay less execution fees on the exchange consistently.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑validation flaw that allows an attacker to submit a transaction with an artificially low gas price while still having the transaction executed through an external bribe mechanism such as Flashbots or Snowsight. The contract’s validateExecutionFee() routine only checks that the supplied execution fee is greater than or equal to gasLimit multiplied by tx.gasprice. Because there is no lower bound on tx.gasprice, a user can set the gas price to the minimum acceptable value, pay a fee that is smaller than what the keeper expects, and rely on a bribe to get the transaction mined. The keeper then has to draw the shortfall from the protocol’s treasury reserves in order to cover the actual gas cost. This situation can be reproduced repeatedly, allowing a malicious actor to submit many orders that underpay the execution fee, effectively griefing the keepers and draining treasury funds over time. The issue occurs on Avalanche C‑Chain where the transaction‑ordering service permits custom gas prices and where the exchange contracts rely on the simple gas‑price‑based fee check. Anyone who interacts with the exchange – keepers, treasury managers, and users – can be affected: keepers receive less compensation than expected, the treasury balance may shrink without obvious cause, and the overall economic model of the protocol can be compromised. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the fee‑validation logic and noticed the absence of a minimum‑gas‑price constraint. It can be hard to notice because the transaction still succeeds, the fee appears to satisfy the contract’s condition, and the underpayment is masked by the external bribe, making the loss invisible in normal transaction logs. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a minimum acceptable gas price and verify that tx.gasprice exceeds this threshold before accepting the execution fee, ensuring that the fee always covers the real gas cost and preventing keepers from being subsidised by the treasury. This class of bug is a missing‑parameter validation or under‑payment check that breaks the accounting assumptions of the protocol, leading to situations where users receive a transaction execution for far less than expected, keepers are under‑compensated, and funds appear to disappear from the treasury.

title: M-09 | Refund gas limit is not accounted for
description:
The payExecutionFee function refunds the leftover gas to the user **before** executing the external callback to refundExecutionFee. This gas refund doesn't take into account the fact that refundExecutionFee can use up to 500k gas. This will enable users to grief keepers, making their TX unproﬁtable. For Example:
1. User makes an order with 3m gas as execution fee.
2. Keeper executes that order with 3m gas (equal execution fee).
3. We reach payExecutionFee, where up to now 2m gas is used.
4. Keeper is payed 2m and the user is refunded 1m.
5. The refundExecutionFee triggers wasting 500k gas. In the current scenario the user only paid 2m gas for his order, but costed the keeper 2.5m gas.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/gmx-v2-1-team-2-pocs/tree/POC_UNRECORDED_GAS
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect gas accounting flaw in the payExecutionFee routine of the contract. The function refunds any unused execution gas to the user before it invokes the external callback refundExecutionFee, but it does not reserve gas for the callback itself. Because refundExecutionFee can consume up to roughly five hundred thousand gas, the refund calculation assumes that the remaining gas will be free, which is false. An attacker can exploit this by submitting an order with a modest execution fee, allowing the keeper to spend the full amount of gas while the contract only refunds a smaller portion to the keeper. In practice the keeper receives a payment that covers the gas used up to the refund point, but then the subsequent callback burns additional gas that is not compensated, causing the keeper to lose up to half a million gas per transaction. From the user’s perspective the order appears to have been executed successfully and the user receives a refund of the leftover gas, yet the keeper’s transaction becomes unprofitable and may be abandoned. The impact is a financial loss for keepers, reduced incentive for network participants to execute orders, and potential degradation of the protocol’s reliability. The issue manifests whenever payExecutionFee is called with a non‑zero leftover gas amount and the contract subsequently calls refundExecutionFee, which is the normal flow for every order execution. Both regular users and keepers are affected: users see a normal refund, while keepers incur unexpected gas costs. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the gas accounting logic and identified that the gas used by refundExecutionFee was not included in the keeper’s compensation calculation. Because the discrepancy is hidden inside internal accounting and does not produce an obvious on‑chain error, it can be difficult to notice without detailed gas‑usage tracing. The proper remediation is to adjust the gas‑usage model so that the base execution gas amount (EXECUTION_GAS_FEE_BASE_AMOUNT) accounts for the maximum gas that refundExecutionFee may consume, or to restructure the code so that the refund to the user occurs after the callback, ensuring that the keeper is always reimbursed for the full gas spent. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of gas‑refund miscalculations, where the contract’s accounting assumptions about remaining gas do not match the actual execution cost, leading to unintended loss of funds.

title: M-01 | No way for user to add cancellation receiver
description: When an order gets cancelled there is a check to see if the order has a cancellationReceiver. If it does the funds will be sent there, if not then the account will get the funds. This works well, however there is no way for a user to add a cancellationReceiver when creating an order. Preventing the use of this feature.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing capability in the order‑cancellation logic of the contract. When an order is cancelled the contract checks whether the order struct contains a non‑zero cancellationReceiver address; if it is set, the refunded funds are transferred to that address, otherwise the funds are sent back to the order creator’s address. The root cause is that the contract’s order‑creation function does not expose any parameter or setter that allows the user to specify a cancellationReceiver at the time the order is created. Consequently, every order is created with a default (zero) cancellationReceiver, which forces the fallback path to always credit the original order owner. An attacker does not need to exploit code execution; the issue can be triggered simply by creating an order and later cancelling it, expecting the refund to be routed to a different address. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that a user who intended the refund to be sent to a designated wallet (for example a cold‑storage address or a third‑party escrow) receives the funds in their own account or, if the contract logic later rejects the transfer, may see no refund at all. The impact is primarily a breach of user expectations and a loss of flexibility: users cannot implement custom refund flows, which may be required for compliance, multi‑sig wallets, or custodial services. The problem manifests whenever an order is created and later cancelled, under any network condition, because the missing field is immutable at creation time. It affects all participants who rely on the cancellationReceiver feature – typically traders, custodians, or protocol integrators that need to direct cancelled funds elsewhere. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the order lifecycle functions, where the auditor noted that the cancellationReceiver field is never populated. Because the contract still refunds funds correctly to the order owner, the omission can be subtle and may go unnoticed until a user explicitly tries to set a different receiver and observes that the contract ignores the request. To remediate, the order‑creation interface should be extended with an optional address argument for cancellationReceiver, and the contract should validate that the supplied address is non‑zero and not a contract that could reject funds. Adding this setter restores the intended business logic that cancelled funds can be routed to an arbitrary, user‑specified address, aligning the implementation with the protocol’s accounting assumptions and user expectations.

title: `TempleGoldStaking.getVoteWeight()` calculates vote weight of an account incorrectly
poc:
Let's suppose `halfTime` is 7 days.
- Alice stakes `100 ether` on May 3.
- Alice stakes `400 ether` again on May 17.
- She calls the `getVoteWeight()` function on May 18.
  The function returns `500 * 13 / (13 + 7)` instead of `100 * 13 / (13 + 7)`, which is 5 times greater than real vote power.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the vote‑weight calculation of the staking contract. The public function getVoteWeight reads the current token balance of an account and forwards it to an internal routine that determines voting power based on a time‑weighted formula. Inside the private routine, when the stored week number for the account is newer than the week that the contract considers as the last completed week, the code swaps the current weight parameters with a snapshot taken in the previous week. However, the routine continues to multiply the snapshot’s stake time by the *current* token balance instead of the balance that existed at the time of the snapshot. This mismatch creates a stale‑state‑mixing bug: the time component reflects an older, smaller stake while the amount component reflects a newer, larger stake. The bug can be exploited by a user who increases their token balance after a week boundary but before the contract updates the stored weight for the new week. By calling getVoteWeight during that interval, the user receives a vote weight that is artificially inflated because the calculation uses the larger, recent balance together with the older, more favorable stake‑time factor. In the provided example, a holder who originally staked 100 ether and later added 400 ether receives a vote weight computed as if the full 500 ether had been staked for the earlier 13‑day period, resulting in a five‑fold overestimation. The impact is that governance decisions can be swayed by participants who appear to have far more voting power than they legitimately earned, potentially compromising protocol security and fairness. The condition occurs whenever the contract’s internal week counter advances (block.timestamp / WEEK_LENGTH – 1) while the account’s stored weekNumber is still set to the newer week, causing the fallback to the previous weight snapshot. All token holders and the governance mechanism are affected because the inflated weights are visible in UI components that display voting power, leading users to see unexpectedly high numbers. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Cyfrin, which identified the logical inconsistency between the snapshot selection and the balance used. It is difficult to notice because the function returns a plausible‑looking number and basic unit tests may not cover the cross‑week transition scenario. The proper remediation is to ensure that when a previous weight snapshot is used, the corresponding previous balance snapshot is also applied, or to recompute the weight entirely from the stored snapshot data without mixing current balances. This class of bug belongs to time‑weighted accounting errors where stale state is combined with fresh state, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that vote weight should be derived from a consistent snapshot of both balance and staking duration.

title: Rewards are calculated as distributed even if there are no stakers, locking the rewards forever
poc:
Here's an example scenario:
Alice is `distributionStarter` and Bob is a person who wants to stake `Temple`.
- Alice calls the `distributeRewards()` function to mint TGLD for this contract.
  Let's suppose the minted TGLD is `7*86400 ether` to calculate simply. Then `rewardRate` becomes `1 ether`.
- After 24 hours, Bob stakes `10000` TGLD into the contract.
- After 6 days, Bob withdraw all staked TGLD and claim rewards. Then he gets `6*86400 ether`.

As a result, `86400 ether` is locked in the contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reward‑distribution accounting flaw that allows tokens to become permanently locked when the contract mints or distributes rewards before any user has staked. The root cause is that the internal function that computes the cumulative reward per token updates the last‑update timestamp unconditionally, while it only skips the reward‑per‑token calculation when the total supply of staked tokens is zero. Because the timestamp is still advanced, the contract’s accounting assumes that rewards have been earned over the elapsed period even though there were no participants to receive them. An attacker or any caller can exploit this by invoking the distributeRewards() function (or any function that triggers the reward update) while totalSupply is zero. The function mints a reward amount, sets a rewardRate, and records a new lastUpdateTime. Since no stakers exist, the rewardPerTokenStored value remains unchanged, but the elapsed time is recorded, causing the subsequent reward calculation to treat the minted amount as already distributed. When a legitimate staker later joins, the contract will calculate rewards based only on the period after the first stake, effectively discarding the earlier minted rewards. The impact is that a portion of the reward tokens becomes irretrievable; users who stake later receive less reward than the protocol intended, and the contract balance shows a permanent shortfall. This occurs whenever distributeRewards is called before any stake and later stakes are made, affecting all future stakers, the protocol’s incentive model, and any token holders expecting their rewards. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the reward‑distribution logic, where the auditor noticed that the timestamp update was not guarded by a totalSupply check. The bug is subtle because the rewardPerTokenStored value appears correct, masking the fact that the accounting window has moved forward, making the loss of tokens easy to overlook. To fix the problem, the contract should either prevent reward distribution when totalSupply is zero (by reverting the call) or modify the accounting so that the timestamp is not advanced unless there is at least one staker. This ensures that rewards are only accrued when there are participants to receive them, preserving the intended economic guarantees and preventing permanent loss of minted tokens.

title: M-01 | Launch Allows For Anchor Larger Than Target Width
description: In the launch function the anchor position can be more than 10 tick spacings wide as the setTicks call for the anchor position assigns the lower tick as the floor tick + one tick spacing, and the upper tick as the even tick spacing ahead of the active tick.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing boundary validation in the launch routine that permits the anchor range to exceed the protocol‑defined maximum width. In the current implementation the function that sets the lower and upper ticks derives the lower tick as the floor tick plus one tick spacing and the upper tick as an even multiple of the tick spacing ahead of the active tick, but it never checks that the distance between these two ticks respects the configured ANCHOR_WIDTH (for example ten tick spacings). Because of this omission an attacker or a careless user can invoke launch with parameters that cause the anchor to span a much larger price interval than intended. The oversized anchor dilutes the concentration of liquidity, creates a price band that may not intersect the market price, and can lead to extreme slippage or trades that return almost nothing. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal pool creation, yet after a trade the user may notice that the received amount is far lower than expected or that their balance appears unchanged because the pool’s price range is effectively out of sync with the market. The issue manifests whenever launch is called with a custom anchor and the contract does not enforce the width limit, affecting any participant who provides liquidity through that entry point as well as the overall capital efficiency of the protocol. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the tick‑calculation logic and identified that the lower‑tick and upper‑tick assignments lack a constraint on their separation. It can be hard to notice because the contract still compiles and the pool can be created; the problem only becomes visible when trading activity reveals abnormal price behaviour. The bug belongs to the class of range‑validation errors where boundary checks are omitted, leading to an “anchor width overflow”. To remediate the issue the launch function should explicitly verify that the lower tick is not lower than activeTick minus ANCHOR_WIDTH and that the upper tick does not exceed activeTick plus ANCHOR_WIDTH, or it should clamp the calculated anchor to the maximum allowed width before invoking setTicks. Enforcing these checks restores the intended business logic that liquidity must be concentrated within a predefined price band, preventing unexpected loss of funds, inefficient capital use, and user‑facing symptoms such as refunds of zero or negligible amounts.

title: M-02 | Floor Reserves Decrease After Sweep
description:
In the sweep function the liquidity for the anchor position is maintained, however the anchor position moves higher. Therefore more reserves will be required to maintain the same liquidity for the anchor position.
Therefore if there is not enough profit from the discovery position to overshadow this discrepancy, reserves will be taken from the floor to sustain the anchor liquidity while moving the anchor up.
This may be unexpected as it can unnecessarily reduce capacity by moving reserves up from the floor position to the anchor.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the sweep routine of a liquidity pool that manages an anchor position and a floor position. The routine is designed to keep the anchor position’s liquidity constant while moving the anchor price upward. Because the anchor’s price increases, the amount of reserves required to sustain the same liquidity grows. The implementation mistakenly bases the sweep on preserving liquidity rather than preserving the reserve balance of the anchor. When the profit generated by the discovery position is insufficient to cover the extra reserves needed for the higher anchor price, the contract automatically pulls reserves from the floor position to keep the anchor liquid. This results in a silent reduction of the floor’s reserve balance, decreasing the overall capacity of the pool without any explicit warning. From a user’s perspective the pool may still appear to have the same total liquidity, but the floor can no longer support the same volume of trades, leading to unexpected failures such as missing refunds, zero‑balance errors, or inability to execute large orders. The issue manifests whenever the sweep function is invoked while the anchor moves higher and the discovery position does not generate enough excess profit. It primarily affects liquidity providers and users who rely on the floor’s capacity, as well as the protocol’s economic guarantees. The problem was identified during a manual audit by the Guardian team, and it can be difficult to notice because the UI typically shows only the anchor’s liquidity metric, not the underlying reserve distribution. The root cause is a logical flaw in the sweep algorithm that ties reserve adjustments to liquidity targets instead of reserve targets. To remediate, the sweep should be rewritten to preserve the anchor’s reserve amount rather than its liquidity, accepting a minor reduction in anchor liquidity as a trade‑off, or alternatively to add explicit checks that prevent floor reserve depletion. This change restores the intended accounting invariants and prevents the floor from unintentionally losing capacity.

title: M-03 | Swap Fees Included In Circulating Supply
description:
The protocol deploys liquidity to Uniswap and earns fees in both reserve token and bAsset. The protocol owned bAssets and earned bAsset fees are not intended to be part of the circulating supply.
However, swap fees in bAsset are calculated as a part of the circulating supply during bump, sweep and slide. The reason of this is circulating assets is calculated with bAssetsCirculating = BPOOL.totalSupply() - BPOOL.balanceOf(address(BPOOL));.
Previously, bAsset fees were in the BPOOL and they were excluded while subtracting the balance of BPOOL. But after remediations, those fees are in the MarketMaking contract and not excluded.
The newly issued tokens during bump is calculated based on the bAssetsCirculating, and more tokens will be issued due to this.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an inaccurate accounting of the protocol’s circulating bAsset supply, which leads to the unintended minting of additional tokens during supply‑adjustment operations such as bump, sweep and slide. The protocol calculates the circulating amount of bAssets with the expression bAssetsCirculating = BPOOL.totalSupply() - BPOOL.balanceOf(address(BPOOL)). This formula was originally correct because any bAsset fees collected from swaps were held inside the BPOOL contract itself and therefore automatically excluded by the subtraction of the pool’s own balance. After a remediation step, however, the swap fees are transferred to a separate MarketMaking contract. Because the circulating‑supply calculation still only subtracts the BPOOL balance, the fees residing in MarketMaking are mistakenly counted as part of the circulating supply. Consequently, when the protocol determines how many new tokens to issue during a bump (or similar) event, it uses an inflated bAssetsCirculating value and mints more tokens than the economic model intends. The impact is a dilution of existing token holders, a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions, and potential loss of trust as the token supply can grow without a corresponding increase in underlying assets. The issue manifests whenever the bump, sweep or slide functions are executed after fees have been moved to the MarketMaking contract, i.e., under normal operating conditions after the fee‑remediation. It affects all participants who rely on the token’s supply integrity – token holders, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts that assume a correct supply figure. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the supply‑adjustment logic, where the auditor noticed that the fee‑holding contract was no longer accounted for in the circulating‑supply formula. The problem is subtle because the extra tokens are minted in small increments that may blend with normal supply growth, making the discrepancy hard to spot without a detailed supply audit. To remediate, the circulating‑supply calculation should be updated to also subtract the balance of bAssets held by the MarketMaking contract (or any other contract that can own protocol‑issued bAssets) before determining the amount to mint. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect circulating‑supply accounting” or “fee‑inclusion inflation” vulnerabilities, where protocol‑owned assets that are not meant to be counted as circulating are inadvertently included, leading to over‑issuance and economic distortion. From a user’s perspective, the symptom may appear as an unexpected increase in total token supply, a perceived loss of value per token, or a situation where a user expects a certain amount of newly minted tokens based on fee accrual but receives a larger, unexplained amount, effectively diluting their holdings.

title: M-04 | Interest Free Credits Intra-Day
description:
The getTimeslot function returns the unix timestamp at the end of the day as today, and this is used while calculating daily interests during credit borrowing.
For example, when the current time is 14:05:00, today is considered as 23:59:59. Because of today is considered as the end of the day, the time between 23:59:59 and the exact borrow time are interest free.
If a user gets a credit on June 1st at 00:00:01 for only 1 day:
- Today is June 1st 23:59:59
- Credit end time is June 2nd 23:59:59
User will basically get 2 days credit by paying only 1 day interest.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract's getTimeslot function, which returns the Unix timestamp representing the end of the current calendar day (23:59:59) and uses this value as the reference point for daily interest calculations on borrowed credits. Because the function treats the entire remaining portion of the current day as a full day of credit, any loan taken after midnight but before the end of the day accrues interest for only one full day while actually being usable for almost two days. For example, a borrower who obtains a one‑day credit at 00:00:01 on June 1st sees the contract record "today" as June 1st 23:59:59 and sets the credit expiry to June 2nd 23:59:59. The borrower therefore enjoys roughly 48 hours of credit while paying interest for only a single day. This discrepancy occurs whenever the loan duration is expressed in whole days and the contract does not adjust the expiry to account for the partial day that has already elapsed. The affected parties are borrowers, who receive more credit than they pay for, and the protocol, which loses expected interest revenue. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the interest‑calculation logic, where the off‑by‑one‑day behavior was identified as a subtle accounting error that does not raise immediate runtime exceptions, making it easy to overlook. From a user perspective the symptom is that the UI shows a one‑day loan term, yet the borrower can use the loan for nearly two days without additional charges, violating the expectation that interest is charged for the exact period of usage. The bug belongs to the class of time‑boundary miscalculations, specifically an incorrect handling of day‑level timestamps that leads to interest‑free periods. To remediate, the contract should either add an extra day to the expiry timestamp when initializing a loan to cover the remainder of the current day, or redesign getTimeslot to return the start of the next day so that interest is calculated on the actual elapsed time. Clear documentation of this behavior can also mitigate user confusion, but a code‑level fix is recommended to preserve the protocol's revenue model.

title: M-05 | Extra Interest Charged When Extending Credit
description:
The remediation of M-H-03 is performed via adding current day to remaining days when a user extends their credit. However, the parent finding was only causing problem when a new credit is issued with 0 added days in the last day.
Current remediation charges additional one day credit when users extend their credit regardless of when the extension is performed.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unintended extra interest charge that occurs whenever a borrower extends an existing credit line. The root cause is a remediation step that adds the current calendar day to the remaining credit duration each time an extension is performed, regardless of when the extension is requested. This logic was introduced to fix a separate issue (M-H-03) that only manifested when a new credit was issued with zero added days on the final day of the term. However, the added day is now applied indiscriminately, so even extensions made well before the term expires receive an additional day of credit. Because interest is calculated on a per‑day basis, the extra day translates directly into higher accrued interest. An attacker does not need to exploit a code flaw; the contract’s own arithmetic produces the over‑charge. The impact is that borrowers see a higher interest amount than expected, their effective loan cost increases, and the protocol may appear to charge hidden fees. This situation occurs whenever a user calls the credit‑extension function, especially on the last day of the loan when the original remediation intended to add zero days. All users of the credit facility are affected, and the discrepancy may be visible in the UI as a lower net amount received after extension or an unexpected increase in the interest field. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the intended business logic (interest should only reflect the actual extended period) with the implemented calculation. It can be hard to notice because the extra day adds only a small amount of interest, which may be masked by rounding or by users not closely tracking daily interest accruals. To remediate, the contract should either prohibit extensions that would result in zero added days on the final day, or modify the extension logic to add only the actual number of days requested rather than automatically appending the current day. Clear documentation of this behavior to borrowers would also mitigate confusion. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where a formula incorrectly adds time units, leading to over‑charging and a breach of the expected financial contract semantics.

title: M-06 | Decrease Position Prevented
description:
The anchor and floor positions can be disjoint, and price may be between the two positions. When a user attempts to decreasePosition, the floor reserves will be removed before the swap.
If price is between the two positions, Uniswap will revert during the swap since there is no liquidity below the anchor as the floor was removed temporarily. Consequently, the user will be unable to decreasePosition and unwind their leverage.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inability for a leveraged trader to successfully call the decreasePosition function when the market price sits between two internally defined price levels called the anchor and the floor. The contract removes the floor reserves before executing the token swap that is required to unwind the position. If the price is between the anchor and the floor, there is no liquidity available below the anchor after the floor reserves have been taken out, so the external Uniswap swap reverts due to insufficient liquidity. This temporary liquidity gap is caused by the design choice that the floor and anchor positions can be disjoint and that the floor is removed prior to the swap. An attacker does not need to do anything special; any user who tries to decrease a leveraged position under these price conditions will experience a transaction revert and will be unable to close or reduce the position. The impact is that the user’s leveraged position remains open, potentially exposing them to further price movement and liquidation risk, while the protocol may end up with stuck positions and locked funds. The issue occurs only when the price drifts into the interval between the anchor and floor, a scenario that may not be exercised in normal testing, making it hard to notice. It was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team when reviewing the position‑management logic. From a user’s perspective the transaction simply fails with a generic swap‑failure error, the UI may show “transaction reverted” or “insufficient liquidity”, and the expected refund or reduced balance never arrives. This class of bug falls under liquidity‑management or state‑transition errors where the order of operations creates a temporary liquidity vacuum. To remediate the problem the contract should adjust (slide) the floor position before removing its reserves, or otherwise ensure that liquidity remains available for the swap. Monitoring the price relationship between anchor and floor and performing a slide when they become disjoint will prevent the revert and allow users to safely unwind their leverage.

title: While changing vote delegator from himself to another user, `_delegateBalances` should not be decreased
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the vote delegation logic of the staking contract. When a token holder delegates voting power to themselves, the contract records the holder’s own balance as part of their delegate balance. Later, if the same holder changes the delegate to a different address, the function that updates delegate balances subtracts the holder’s balance from the previous delegate’s total, even though the previous delegate was the holder themselves. This subtraction is performed unconditionally whenever the removed flag is true and the holder’s balance is greater than zero. The root cause is the absence of a check that excludes the self‑delegation case; the code assumes that any previous delegate should lose the user’s balance, but self‑delegation does not actually contribute to another party’s voting weight. An attacker or any user who follows the normal workflow can trigger the bug simply by first delegating to themselves and then switching to another delegate. The exploit results in the new delegate receiving less voting power than they should, while the former (self) delegate’s recorded balance is incorrectly reduced, leading to an overall mismatch in the protocol’s accounting of vote weight. The impact is a distortion of governance calculations: proposals may be decided with fewer votes than intended, and users may see their expected voting power disappear or be lower than anticipated. This condition occurs only when the user’s token balance is positive, they have previously set themselves as delegate, and they subsequently change the delegate to a different address. All token holders who use self‑delegation are affected, as are the governance mechanisms that rely on accurate delegate balances. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Cyfrin, who noted that the subtraction step does not consider the special case of self‑delegation. It can be hard to notice because the total token supply remains unchanged and the holder’s personal balance is still displayed correctly; only the derived voting power shown in governance UI may appear reduced, which may be attributed to other factors. To remediate the problem, the contract should add a condition that skips the subtraction when the previous delegate equals the caller (i.e., when the user was delegating to themselves). Conceptually, the fix ensures that self‑delegation does not affect any external delegate’s balance, preserving the intended accounting invariants and preventing vote weight loss. This class of bug falls under improper handling of edge cases in delegation logic, specifically failing to exclude self‑references when updating aggregate balances, leading to accounting inconsistencies and potential governance manipulation.

title: M-01 | Lacking Initial Tick Validation May Brick The Protocol
description: The BPOOL module is initialized with the starting values for activeTick and floorTick. The current validation only checks that activeTick > floorTick. At this moment, checkpointTick is also initialized with the same value as activeTick. The issue rises when initial activeTick value is not greater than floorTick + TS, as the active tick will be at the FLOOR range, ANCHOR range won't exist, and DISCOVERY range will be initialized with 0 liquidity. Additionally, if this initial setup is created, then no marketMaking operations can be executed, even if the price start trading upwards: • bump - checkpoint is at the FLOOR • sweep - Panic reverts when calculating liquidityPremium as liquidityA is 0 • slide - activeTick is above checkpoint
bug_full: The vulnerability is an initialization‑time logic error in the pool contract that fails to enforce a minimum distance between the floor tick and the active tick. During pool creation the contract only checks that activeTick is greater than floorTick, but it does not verify that activeTick is at least one tick‑spacing (TS) above floorTick. As a result, when the initial activeTick is set to a value that is not greater than floorTick+TS, the checkpointTick is copied from activeTick and ends up positioned in the FLOOR range. Because the ANCHOR range never materialises and the DISCOVERY range is created with zero liquidity, the pool starts in a state where no market‑making functions (bump, sweep, slide) can succeed. Any attempt to add liquidity or execute a trade triggers a panic: the sweep operation reverts while calculating liquidityPremium because liquidityA is zero, and the slide operation finds the active tick above the checkpoint, causing further failures. From a user’s perspective the pool appears to exist but every interaction returns an error or simply does nothing, leading to symptoms such as “adding liquidity fails with a revert”, “trades revert with panic”, or “the pool shows zero liquidity even though it should have initial funds”. The impact is that the protocol becomes effectively bricked – no trades can be executed, liquidity providers cannot deposit, and funds may become locked in a non‑functional pool. This condition occurs only when the pool is instantiated with malformed tick parameters; it is not detected by the existing checks and therefore can remain unnoticed until a user attempts the first operation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the lack of a floorTick+TS validation allowed the pool to start in an invalid state. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect initialization constraints” that violate accounting assumptions about price ranges and liquidity distribution. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce that the initial active tick is strictly greater than floorTick plus one tick‑spacing, for example by adding require(_initialFloorTick + TS < _initialActiveTick, "Invalid tick values"). This ensures that the checkpoint, anchor, and discovery ranges are correctly populated and that market‑making functions can operate as intended.

title: M-03 | Anchor Liquidity Heavily Reduced
description: The slide operation scales down the ANCHOR liquidity using the inverseLiquidityPremium as follows: liquidityA = uint128(uint256(liquidityA).divWad((inverseLiquidityPremium))); The issue arises when all (or most) of the circulating supply is collateralized, and the leverage factor is a very large number. This means the liquidityA can drop to unexpected low values, creating high slippage to the users currently trading. If slide is triggered when the price is at the ANCHOR range (normal scenario), the operation will effectively remove most of the liquidity from the active trading range, moving the active reserves to the FLOOR range. Although he capacity of the system is still increasing, any subsequent sales will move the active tick into the FLOOR, something the protocol wants to avoid. In order to restore the correct liquidity of the ANCHOR, price will need to trade up into DISCOVERY and receive surplus reserves. Although this might temporarily restore the liquidity, the slide operation will keep scaling down the ANCHOR every time its triggered, as long as liquidityA > liquidityThreshold.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a liquidity scaling defect in the slide operation that reduces the amount of liquidity allocated to the ANCHOR price range. The contract computes the new anchor liquidity by dividing the current liquidity by an inverseLiquidityPremium value, which becomes extremely large when the protocol’s leverage factor grows due to a high proportion of the circulating supply being used as collateral. Because the division can shrink the anchor liquidity to very low numbers, the active reserves are effectively moved out of the intended ANCHOR range and into the FLOOR range. This situation arises when the slide function is triggered while the market price is still inside the normal ANCHOR band, a scenario that occurs frequently in regular operation. As a result, traders experience unexpectedly high slippage, receive far less output than expected, or see their swaps appear to execute with no change in balance. The protocol’s design assumes that the ANCHOR range always holds sufficient liquidity to absorb trades; the bug violates this accounting invariant by allowing the anchor liquidity to collapse. The issue was discovered during a security audit by the Guardian team, who observed that under extreme collateralisation the leverage factor can become arbitrarily large and cause the liquidity scaling formula to produce near‑zero values. The problem is hard to notice because the overall system capacity may still be increasing, masking the fact that the active trading band has been emptied; users only see the symptom of excessive price impact or missing refunds. To remediate the defect, the protocol should bound the leverage factor, for example by adding a maximum value or by redesigning the getLeverageFactor calculation to include a configurable leverageRange that limits how much the ANCHOR liquidity can be reduced. This ensures that liquidityA never falls below a safe threshold and that the ANCHOR range continues to provide the expected depth for trades, preserving the economic guarantees of the system.

title: M-04 | Liquidity Premium Rounds Down To 0
description: The liquidity premium is used to calculate the liquidity of the DISCOVERY range, based on the ANCHOR range liquidity, during rebalances. The main goal is to scale DISCOVERY range liquidity based on the ratio depending on the tick distance of the active tick to the floor tick, and the TICK_PREMIUM_FACTOR. The issue involves the initialized value of TICK_PREMIUM_FACTOR. There is a discrepancy between the tests and the deploy script, as the tests use 4800 but the deploy script uses 4800e18. In case the 4800e18 value is used, it will cause the getLiquidityPremium calculation round to 0, whenever the tick difference is less than 4800. During a sweep and slide this issue will make DISCOVERY liquidity equal to the ANCHOR liquidity.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error in the calculation of the liquidity premium that scales the DISCOVERY range liquidity during a rebalance. The contract stores a constant called TICK_PREMIUM_FACTOR, which should be a plain integer value of 4800. However, the deployment script initializes this constant with 4800e18, i.e., 4800 multiplied by 10^18, while the unit tests use the correct 4800. Because the premium calculation divides the tick distance by TICK_PREMIUM_FACTOR using integer arithmetic, the inflated factor makes the divisor enormously large. When the active‑tick distance to the floor tick is smaller than 4800, the division result becomes zero, so the function getLiquidityPremium returns zero. Consequently, the DISCOVERY range receives no premium adjustment and its liquidity is set equal to the ANCHOR range liquidity during a sweep‑and‑slide operation. This deviation from the intended scaling logic can cause the protocol to expose more capital than designed, undermining risk controls and potentially leading to over‑allocation of funds to the DISCOVERY range. The issue manifests only when the tick difference is below the 4800 threshold, which is a common scenario during normal market movements, making it easy to miss because the contract does not revert or emit an error; it simply returns a zero premium silently. Users observing the UI may notice that the DISCOVERY liquidity appears identical to the ANCHOR liquidity, contrary to the expectation that it should be lower due to the premium factor. The problem was discovered during a security audit that compared the test configuration with the live deployment script and identified the mismatched constant initialization. To remediate, the TICK_PREMIUM_FACTOR should be set to the intended plain integer 4800, or the premium calculation should be adjusted to correctly handle the scaling factor and avoid integer‑division truncation. This class of bug falls under arithmetic precision and scaling errors, where an incorrectly sized constant leads to unintended zero‑rounding in financial formulas, breaking accounting assumptions about proportional liquidity distribution.

title: M-05 | Discovery Liquidity Increased Above MAX_DISCOVERY_RATIO
description: The ratio between the DISCOVERY and ANCHOR liquidity during a sweep operation should be capped by the MAX_DISCOVERY_RATIO (5x), following this logic: liquidityPremium = (liquidityPremium / liquidityA) > MAX_DISCOVERY_RATIO ? liquidityA * MAX_DISCOVERY_RATIO : liquidityPremium; The issue relies on the ratio liquidityPremium / liquidityA, as this division rounds down in Solidity. Therefore, every time this division rounds down to the value of MAX_DISCOVERY_RATIO (5), then liquidityPremium value is not updated, due to the > comparison. Because liquidityPremium on its own is larger than liquidityA * MAX_DISCOVERY_RATIO, this rounding issue allows the DISCOVERY liquidity to increase up to almost 7x the ANCHOR liquidity during sweep rebalancing.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the rebalancing logic that caps the ratio between discovery liquidity and anchor liquidity during a sweep operation. The protocol is supposed to enforce a maximum discovery‑to‑anchor ratio (MAX_DISCOVERY_RATIO) of five times by checking whether the computed ratio liquidityPremium / liquidityA is greater than the constant. In Solidity, the division of two unsigned integers truncates toward zero, so the result is rounded down. When the true mathematical ratio is slightly above five, the integer division yields exactly five. Because the code uses a strict greater‑than comparison, the condition fails and the cap is not applied. Consequently the discovery liquidity can grow to almost seven times the anchor liquidity, violating the intended accounting invariant. This can be triggered whenever the sweep function is called with liquidity values that cause the truncated division to equal the constant, which is a realistic scenario in normal operation. The impact is that the protocol may allocate an excessive amount of discovery liquidity, distorting fee distribution, exposing liquidity providers to higher risk, and potentially allowing an attacker to manipulate the pool’s balance or drain funds by repeatedly forcing oversized discovery allocations. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic of the rebalancing routine; it is subtle because the rounding behaviour is hidden behind a simple comparison and may not be caught by typical unit tests that use values where the division does not truncate. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the pool appears to have an unexpectedly large discovery side, leading to lower than expected returns or missing balances when they expect the discovery side to be limited to five times the anchor side. The bug belongs to the class of integer‑division rounding errors combined with off‑by‑one comparison mistakes, which break business‑logic constraints on financial ratios. The recommended remediation is to change the comparison to a greater‑than‑or‑equal check or to employ fixed‑point arithmetic that preserves the exact ratio before applying the cap, thereby ensuring the discovery liquidity never exceeds the defined maximum ratio.

title: M-06 | Bump Reverts Due To Lack Of Reserves
description: An edge case appears when the price is at DISCOVERY range, and all reserves from FLOOR and ANCHOR are borrowed. This could happen when there is heavy buying, and all bAssets are collateralized. If we try to trigger a bump operation, this will revert at this function: BPOOL.manageLiquidityFor(Range.DISCOVERY, Action.ADD, liquidityD); The issue is that when we try to mint liquidity in the Uniswap Pool, the calculation for the token amounts owed to the pool are rounded up: getAmount1Delta(sqrtRatioAX96, sqrtRatioBX96, uint128(liquidity), true). Due to the rounding up, more reserves are requested to be transferred in the uniswapV3MintCallback than available, preventing the bump operation from occurring.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when the protocol attempts to perform a bump operation while the price is inside the DISCOVERY range and the reserves allocated to the FLOOR and ANCHOR ranges have been completely borrowed. The bump logic calls BPOOL.manageLiquidityFor with an ADD action, which internally mints liquidity in a Uniswap V3 pool. The amount of token1 that must be supplied to the pool is calculated by getAmount1Delta with the round‑up flag set to true. Because the function rounds the required amount upward, it can request slightly more token1 than is actually available in the pool’s reserve balance. When all reserves are already borrowed, the contract does not have enough token1 to satisfy the rounded‑up request, causing the UniswapV3MintCallback to revert and the entire bump transaction to fail. This edge case is triggered only under heavy buying pressure that pushes the price into the DISCOVERY range and exhausts the collateralised bAssets, a situation that is rare in normal operation but can be induced deliberately. The impact is that any attempt to add liquidity through the bump mechanism will revert, effectively freezing the protocol’s ability to rebalance liquidity and potentially leaving users without the expected liquidity adjustments; from a user perspective the UI may show a failed bump transaction, no new liquidity appearing, or balances remaining unchanged despite a successful request. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noticed that the rounding behavior of the Uniswap library could exceed the actual reserve balance when reserves are fully depleted. The problem is subtle because the rounding only adds a minimal amount, which is invisible when reserves are plentiful, making it easy to miss in standard testing. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic‑rounding errors that lead to overallocation of assets and can be exploited to cause a DoS by exhausting reserves and then invoking the bump function. To remediate, the contract should compute the exact amount of token1 needed without rounding up, or cap the amount requested to the current reserve balance before calling manageLiquidityFor, as illustrated in the recommended code snippet. By ensuring that the requested reserves never exceed what is available, the bump operation can succeed even when the DISCOVERY range is fully utilized, restoring normal liquidity management and preventing the denial‑of‑service condition.

title: M-07 | Rebalance Threshold May Prevent Sliding Operation
description: The REBALANCE_THRESHOLD is a param set in the constructor of MarketMaking policy. This means that this param can be configured by the protocol. Although the current deployment script sets the initial value to 1, any value above this will cause unexpected behavior of the slide operation. This is due to the fact that if checkpoint and active ticks are less than 2 TS away from the floor tick, slide can't be triggered if the price trades into the FLOOR range (canSlide tick will be located below the floor tick). Therefore, the protocol won't be able to correctly rebalance the liquidity when there is heavy selling of bAssets.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a configurable rebalance threshold in the market‑making policy that can disable the slide operation used to shift liquidity when the price moves into the floor range. The threshold is stored in a constructor argument called REBALANCE_THRESHOLD and can be set to any positive integer by the protocol. The slide logic assumes the threshold equals 1, which guarantees that the canSlide tick is always at or above the floor tick when the active or checkpoint tick is within two tick‑spacing units of the floor. If the threshold is set to a value greater than 1, the calculation places the canSlide tick below the floor tick, causing the slide() function to return false even though the price has entered the floor range. As a result the market‑making contract cannot rebalance liquidity during periods of heavy selling of the base asset. Users observing the UI may see that their expected rebalancing or price‑adjustment actions never happen, balances appear unchanged, or the market seems stuck at a low price. The impact is that the protocol may lose the ability to provide liquidity, leading to higher slippage, potential loss of fees, and in extreme cases the floor price may be reached without corrective liquidity, exposing the pool to depletion. The condition occurs only when the REBALANCE_THRESHOLD parameter is configured above its intended value and the price moves close enough to the floor tick that the distance between checkpoint/active ticks and the floor tick is less than two tick‑spacing units. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the market‑making contract where the relationship between the threshold and the slide eligibility check was examined. It is subtle because the default deployment uses the correct value of 1, so normal testing does not reveal the failure, and the bug manifests only under specific market stress scenarios. The recommended fix is to remove REBALANCE_THRESHOLD from the constructor, hard‑code it as a constant equal to 1 inside the policy, and adjust any dependent calculations accordingly. This eliminates the configuration risk and ensures the slide operation can always be triggered when needed, preserving the intended liquidity‑rebalancing behavior.

title: M-08 | Incorrect Circulating Supply Calculation
description: The getCirculatingSupply function removes the current liquidity in bAssets from the total token supply. The goal is to determine how many bAssets can be sold into the pool. There are cases when this function returns an outdated value, due to the fact bAsset fees are not accounted for in the calculation. Consequently, the value returned might be slightly above the real value. During heavy selling of bAssets into the pool, the difference can increase as there will be more pending fees to claim. This can impact the off-chain systems for managing the operations, as the function will not return the correct state. Even if the system appears solvent using this getter function, a market making operation may revert as the real circulating supply is recalculated during the execution.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the getCirculatingSupply view function of the BaselineV2 contract. The function is intended to report the amount of bAssets that are freely tradable by subtracting the current liquidity held in the pool from the total token supply. However, the implementation ignores any pending protocol fees that have accrued on the bAsset side of the pool but have not yet been claimed. Because those fees are still part of the pool’s balance, they should be excluded from the circulating amount, but the function treats the entire pool balance as if it were already available for sale, leading to an over‑estimation of the true circulating supply. When the pool accumulates unclaimed fees – a situation that becomes common during periods of heavy selling – the returned circulating supply can be slightly higher than the real amount that can be sold without violating the pool’s invariant. The error is subtle because the over‑estimation may be only a few tokens in normal conditions, making it hard to notice on‑chain, and the function is read‑only, so no transaction reverts directly because of it. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the getter’s output with the actual pool state after fee‑generating trades. Exploitation follows a simple flow: an attacker (or any participant) triggers a large volume of bAsset sales, causing the pool to accrue significant pending fees; the getCirculatingSupply function then reports a value that includes those fees, leading off‑chain systems that rely on this number – such as market‑making bots or risk dashboards – to believe more assets are available for trade. When the bot attempts to execute a trade based on the inflated figure, the contract’s internal accounting recalculates the real circulating supply during execution, detects the shortfall, and reverts the transaction. From the user’s perspective this appears as a sudden “trade failed” or “market maker reverted” message, while the UI may still display a healthy supply figure, creating confusion and potential loss of trading opportunities. The affected parties include liquidity providers, market‑making bots, and any off‑chain monitoring service that uses the getter to assess solvency. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑state inconsistencies where derived metrics omit pending state changes, similar to rounding or fee‑omission errors. To remediate, the getter should be modified to add the amount of pending bAsset fees to the liquidity subtraction, ensuring that only truly free tokens are counted as circulating. This change restores alignment between the reported metric and the contract’s internal accounting, preventing false‑positive solvency reports and avoiding unnecessary transaction reverts.

title: M-09 | Initial Deployed Liquidity Missing Crucial Validations
description: For the V2 migration, the InitializeProtocol policy will be used. This will initialize the pool, mint the initial spot supply, setup credits and deploy the pool liquidity.
