The issue relies on the deployLiquidity function, as it only verifies the new deployed capacity is above the initial circulating supply. The missing validations are: • Verify the new liquidityD is not above MAX_DISCOVERY_RATIO, as the tick premium and leverage can be high. • Validate the spot supply is already minted, as the system might be insolvent and distributeSpot does not check this. • Validate credit is already setup, similar to spot, circulating supply will be minted and can make the system insolvent. Although there is some documentation about the steps for the V2 migration, the code does not enforce these steps, so there could be arbitrage attacks that can be triggered if the liquidity is not setup correctly.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the liquidity deployment step of the V2 migration process, specifically in the deployLiquidity function that is invoked by the InitializeProtocol policy. The function only checks that the newly deployed liquidity capacity exceeds the initial circulating spot supply, but it omits several critical safety checks. First, it does not verify that the new liquidity D value stays below the protocol‑defined MAX_DISCOVERY_RATIO, which is intended to bound tick premium and leverage. Second, it fails to confirm that the spot token supply has already been minted before liquidity is added, allowing the system to become insolvent because distributeSpot does not enforce this precondition. Third, it does not ensure that credit allocations are set up prior to liquidity deployment, meaning circulating supply could be minted without the corresponding credit backing, again risking insolvency. Because these validations are missing, an attacker can manipulate the initial liquidity parameters to create arbitrage opportunities or force the pool into a state where the accounting invariants are broken. For example, by deploying liquidity with an excessively high D value, the attacker can profit from price discrepancies caused by unchecked tick premiums. Similarly, if spot supply or credit is not minted, the pool may appear to have sufficient assets while actually lacking the necessary backing, leading to user balances that become zero or missing refunds when withdrawals are attempted. The issue manifests during the migration phase when the protocol transitions from V1 to V2, and only under conditions where the deployLiquidity call is executed without the missing pre‑checks. All participants that rely on the pool – liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself – are potentially affected because the core accounting assumptions are violated. The flaw was identified during a manual security audit that compared the documented migration steps with the actual code implementation and noticed the absence of enforcement for the documented safeguards. It can be hard to notice because the contract may still appear to function normally for small values, and the missing checks only cause observable problems when extreme or malicious parameters are supplied. To remediate, the deployLiquidity routine should be hardened by adding explicit assertions that (i) the proposed liquidity D does not exceed MAX_DISCOVERY_RATIO, (ii) the spot token supply has already been minted, and (iii) credit allocations are established before any liquidity is added. Additionally, the protocol should prevent any further minting of circulating supply after liquidity deployment to preserve accounting integrity. This class of bug falls under insufficient input validation and improper initialization sequencing, which can lead to financial loss, arbitrage exploitation, and broken business logic where users expect their funds to be available but receive zero or missing refunds.

title: M-10 | Virtual Liquidity Lower Than Expected
description: When the slide operation is triggered, the virtualLiquidityF is calculated based on the total collateral and the reserves removed from the FLOOR, using the lower and upper sqrtPrice of the entire range. In case the slide is executed when the active tick is in the FLOOR range, virtualLiquidityF will still use the upper sqrtPrice of the range, instead of the current price. This issue will cause the virtualLiquidityF to appear smaller than expected.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the calculation of the virtual liquidity metric (virtualLiquidityF) that is used during a slide operation in a concentrated liquidity pool. The contract computes virtualLiquidityF by taking the total collateral and the reserves removed from the FLOOR range and feeding them into a liquidity‑for‑amount‑1 formula that expects a lower and an upper sqrtPrice bound for the whole range. The root cause is that, when the slide is executed while the active tick lies inside the FLOOR range, the implementation mistakenly continues to use the upper sqrtPrice of the range as the price limit, instead of the current market sqrtPrice (or the minimum of the current price and the upper bound). This mis‑selection of the price bound leads to a lower virtualLiquidityF than the true amount of liquidity that should be represented. The bug can be exploited indirectly: because the virtualLiquidityF appears smaller, subsequent trades that rely on this metric may be rejected, experience higher slippage, or receive less favorable execution amounts. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that a trade may revert or return a smaller amount than expected, even though the on‑chain balances of the user have not changed, creating the impression that “funds disappear” or that the pool is “out of liquidity”. The condition under which the issue manifests is precisely when the slide operation is triggered while the active tick is within the FLOOR interval; outside of that scenario the calculation uses the correct price bound. The affected parties include any trader interacting with the pool, liquidity providers whose credit calculations depend on virtualLiquidityF, and the protocol itself because the accounting of available liquidity becomes inaccurate. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who observed that the virtualLiquidityF value was consistently lower than expected in the described scenario. The bug is subtle because the virtualLiquidityF value is an internal metric not directly displayed in the UI, so the discrepancy can go unnoticed until a trade fails or exhibits unexpected price impact. Conceptually, the issue belongs to the class of pricing‑formula bugs where an incorrect price bound is applied in a liquidity calculation, violating the assumption that the virtual liquidity should reflect the current market price. To remediate the issue the slide logic should be updated to use the actual current sqrtPrice (or the lower of the current price and the upper bound) when calling LiquidityAmounts.getLiquidityForAmount1, as illustrated in the recommended code snippet. This change restores the correct virtualLiquidityF value, aligns trade execution with user expectations, and prevents the unintended reduction of apparent liquidity.

title: M-11 | Operations Using Outdated Circulating Supply
description: When a credit is defaulted, its collateral is sent directly to the BPOOL contract through the _burnDefaultedCollateral function. This creates a temporary condition where the circulating supply is higher than expected, if the market making operations are executed before defaulting the expired loans. In the bump operation, an increased circulating supply will effectively mint more tokens than expected for the inflation basis.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inflation bug caused by the contract using an outdated view of the circulating token supply during market‑making operations. When a credit defaults, the _burnDefaultedCollateral function transfers the collateral directly to the BPOOL contract. This transfer temporarily inflates the recorded circulating supply because the defaulted amount has not yet been subtracted from the supply counter. If the bump (market‑making) operation is executed before the defaultOutstanding routine that reconciles the supply, the bump calculation reads the inflated supply and mints additional tokens based on that higher number. The extra tokens are created for the inflation basis, leading to unintended dilution of existing holders, inaccurate accounting, and potential loss of value for the protocol. The issue occurs only when the ordering of calls is such that the default handling is delayed relative to the bump, which can happen in normal operation if market‑making is triggered automatically after a loan expires. It primarily affects token holders, market makers, and any party relying on the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between default processing and supply‑adjusting functions. It is hard to notice because the supply discrepancy exists only for a short window and does not generate explicit error messages; the protocol appears to function normally while silently minting extra tokens. To remediate the issue, the contract should ensure that defaultOutstanding (or an equivalent supply‑reconciliation step) is executed at the beginning of any market‑making cycle, guaranteeing that the circulating supply used in the bump calculation reflects the true post‑default state. Conceptually, the fix enforces a correct ordering of state‑updates so that supply‑dependent calculations never operate on stale data, eliminating the unintended token creation and preserving the intended economic model.

title: M-12 | Arbitrage Attack After Slide Operation
description: The market making slide operation rebalances the liquidity structure when active tick goes below a certain threshold. In case the heavy selling pushes the price to the FLOOR, the slide operation will be the only range with reserves. When liquidity is added to the FLOOR, bAssets will be minted in this range. This scenario allows arbitrager to buy tokens at discount, trigger sweep/bump operations, and profit from it.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a price‑manipulation and arbitrage flaw that appears after the market‑making slide operation rebalances the pool when the active tick falls below a predefined threshold. When a large amount of selling pressure pushes the price down to the lowest allowed tick, called the FLOOR, the slide logic makes the FLOOR the only range that still holds reserves. Adding liquidity to this FLOOR range causes the protocol to mint bAssets exclusively in that range, creating a situation where the market price is artificially low while the pool still contains value. An attacker can detect this condition, purchase the under‑priced tokens from the FLOOR range, and then trigger the sweep or bump mechanisms that move the price back up, effectively extracting profit from the price discrepancy. The root cause is the slide operation’s failure to maintain a diversified liquidity distribution and its permissive minting of bAssets at the extreme price boundary, which violates the assumption that liquidity is spread across multiple price ranges. Exploitation requires a specific market state: heavy selling that drives the price to the FLOOR, activation of the slide rebalancing, and the presence of newly added liquidity in the FLOOR range. Under these conditions, the arbitrageur can buy tokens at a discount, cause the pool to sweep the cheap assets into higher price ranges, and realize a net gain at the expense of other participants. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may include seeing tokens purchased at a price far below market, unexpected jumps in the pool’s price after a trade, or a sudden loss of value for liquidity providers who expected their assets to be fairly priced. The issue is difficult to notice because it only manifests during extreme price movements and appears as a normal rebalancing event. It was discovered during a systematic audit of the slide operation logic, where the auditor identified that the floor‑only liquidity scenario enables a profitable arbitrage loop. To remediate the problem the protocol should enforce an initial liquidity layout that prevents the FLOOR from becoming the sole active range, add safeguards that block bAsset minting when the pool is at its price floor, and ensure that the slide operation maintains minimum liquidity across multiple ticks. In essence, the fix requires redesigning the slide rebalancing to preserve a spread of reserves and to reject liquidity additions that would concentrate all value at the price floor, thereby eliminating the discount arbitrage opportunity.

title: M-13 | Attackers Can Borrow With Zero Interest
description: Users can borrow reserve tokens by adding bAssets as collateral to the system and interests for these credits are paid upfront based on a daily rate and the baseline value. Credits are created based on the baseline value of the bAssets, and interests are also paid based on the baseline value when the credit is created. However, this baseline value only increases in time, which means that more reserves can be borrowed with the same collateral when the baseline value increases. And lastly, the protocol [has a check](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/baseline-team-2-pocs/blob/7aa793fec8884f284f09c2995b8da3bbe97a9a0a/src/policies/CreditFacility.sol#L125C1-L126C76) to ensure the borrow is legitimate (either extension of existing borrow or new borrow). But, this check is incorrect and a user can still borrow without extending and without increasing the collateral. Attackers can combine all of these to borrow zero interest credits: 1. Attacker buys bAssets or already holds. 2. Creates a very long term credit when the blv is as low as possible. The interest is paid at this step. 3. Waits for blv to increase. 4. Borrows again without increasing the collateral and without extending expiry. 5. This second borrow will transfer more reserves due to increased blv, but the interest will be 0. 6. Attacker can do it repetitively every time the blv increases. The attacker basically setup his future credits, and paid the interest for them at a very low price, making them effectively free.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic flaw that allows a borrower to obtain reserve tokens without paying any interest by exploiting the way the protocol calculates interest and validates borrow requests. Interest for a credit is charged only once at the moment the credit is created, using the baseline value (blv) of the collateral at that time. Because the protocol’s design lets the baseline value increase monotonically, the amount of reserves that can be drawn against the same collateral grows as the blv rises, while the previously paid interest remains fixed. In addition, the policy that checks whether a borrow operation is legitimate contains an incorrect condition: it permits a new borrow even when the caller does not extend an existing credit and does not add extra collateral. An attacker can therefore follow a multi‑step attack: first, acquire or already hold the required bAssets and open a very long‑term credit when the blv is at its lowest, paying the minimal interest required at that moment. Next, the attacker waits until the blv has increased. When the increase occurs, the attacker invokes the borrow function again without providing additional collateral or extending the credit’s expiry. The protocol’s accounting sees a higher baseline value and therefore releases more reserve tokens, but the interest calculation still references the original low‑interest credit, resulting in zero additional interest being charged. This process can be repeated each time the blv rises, allowing the attacker to continuously extract reserves at no cost. The impact is a loss of expected interest revenue for the protocol, a gradual draining of its reserve pool, and a breach of the economic assumptions that borrowers will always pay interest proportional to the amount borrowed. The issue manifests only after the baseline value has risen relative to the initial credit creation, so it may go unnoticed during normal operation because the upfront interest payment appears correct and the legitimacy check seems to enforce proper borrowing. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the credit facility’s policy logic and interest model. It is difficult to spot because the protocol’s design intentionally allows the baseline value to grow, and the interest‑free outcome is a side‑effect rather than an explicit error. To remediate, the protocol should reject borrow calls that are not extensions of an existing credit or that do not increase collateral, and it should compute interest based on the total outstanding credit or on the current baseline value rather than only on the baseline at credit creation. This would close the loophole that lets borrowers obtain free credit and restore the intended economic guarantees of the system.

title: M-14 | liquidityPremium Can Be A Discount
description: The liquidity premium calculated in function getLiquidityPremium() is calculated as follows: liquidityPremium_ = uint256(uint24(activeTick - BPOOL.floorTick())).divWad(TICK_PREMIUM_FACTOR). If the activeTick is less than TICK_PREMIUM_FACTOR away from the floor tick, then the function returns a proportion less than 100%. Consequently, when the returned proportion is multiplied by the target anchor liquidity in functions sweep() and slide(), the liquidity amount is decreased rather than increased. This results in unexpected liquidity structures when the active tick is less than 4800 ticks from the floor tick. For example, the anchor range liquidity is treated as the "top of book" liquidity, and is targeted to have a basis of 1/1000th of the floor liquidity. However consider a liquidity structure where multiple slides have taken place, and the active tick is 2400 ticks above the floor tick. Now the liquidityPremium is 2400 / 4800 = 0.5, resulting in a targeted anchor liquidity of 1/2000th. The targeted anchor liquidity in this case is less than the configured 1/1000th base ratio, and as the active tick moves closer to the floor tick the targeted anchor liquidity becomes even smaller, which ultimately creates much less price stability when the anchor range is below 4600 ticks in width. Additionally, liquidity is increasingly allocated away from where trading action will accumulate fees when the anchor is collapsing below a width of 4600 ticks.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol computes a liquidity premium in the getLiquidityPremium() routine. The function derives a proportion by dividing the distance between the current active tick and the floor tick by a constant factor (TICK_PREMIUM_FACTOR). When the active tick lies less than TICK_PREMIUM_FACTOR ticks above the floor tick, the resulting proportion is below 100 %. The code that later multiplies this proportion by the target anchor liquidity therefore applies a discount instead of a premium, shrinking the amount of liquidity that should be allocated to the anchor range. In practice this means that for active ticks within roughly 4 800 ticks of the floor tick the anchor position receives less than the configured minimum of one‑thousandth of the floor position liquidity. As the active tick moves closer to the floor, the targeted anchor liquidity can become arbitrarily small, causing the anchor range to provide far less depth than intended. The immediate impact is a degradation of price stability: the reduced anchor liquidity fails to absorb trading pressure, slippage rises and fee earnings for liquidity providers drop. Moreover, because the protocol continues to allocate liquidity away from the price region where fees are generated, the overall fee capture of the pool diminishes. The issue manifests only when the active tick is relatively close to the floor tick, a condition that can arise naturally as market price moves or can be forced by an attacker who manipulates the tick index. All participants who rely on the anchor’s stability – liquidity providers, traders and the protocol’s fee model – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the mathematical assumptions behind the premium calculation; it is subtle because the function name and the division operation suggest a “premium” but the sign of the result is not validated, so the bug can remain hidden while the UI still reports normal liquidity numbers. Detecting the problem requires inspecting the actual liquidity thresholds used in sweep() and slide() and comparing them against the documented 1/1 000th floor‑liquidity rule. To remediate the issue the premium calculation must be treated as a true premium: the resulting factor should never reduce the anchor liquidity below the configured minimum. A typical fix caps the premium at 1 × 10⁶ (i.e., 100 %) or adds a floor to the computed proportion, and then uses the corrected premium when determining the liquidityThreshold, as illustrated in the recommended code snippet. By enforcing this lower bound the protocol restores the intended price‑stability guarantees and prevents the anchor from collapsing into an ineffective, fee‑draining position.

title: M-15 | getLeverageFactor DoS
description: In the getLeverageFactor function the resulting leverageFactor is computed by dividing the totalCollateral by the _bAssetsCirculating - totalCollateral. However it is possible for the totalCollateral to be the entirety of the circulating supply in the event that every holder borrows against their bAssets. In this scenario the getLeverageFactor will revert with a divide by 0 panic. This results in a DoS for any call to the sweep or slide functions.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a division‑by‑zero error in the function that calculates the leverage factor. The contract computes leverageFactor as totalCollateral divided by (_bAssetsCirculating - totalCollateral). When every holder borrows against their bAssets, totalCollateral can become equal to the total circulating supply, making the denominator zero. The Solidity runtime then triggers a panic and reverts the transaction. This calculation is invoked by the sweep and slide functions, so any call to those functions after the denominator reaches zero will also revert, effectively denying service to all users. The issue appears only in the edge case where the protocol is fully collateralised, which may not be covered by typical tests, making it hard to notice. From a user perspective the UI shows a generic execution reverted or division by zero error and the expected actions such as sweeping accrued fees or sliding a position fail, leaving balances unchanged and funds seemingly locked. The bug does not directly steal assets, but it prevents legitimate operations, impacting borrowers, lenders and any participant that relies on the affected functions. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic of the leverage calculation. The root cause is the lack of a guard for a zero denominator. The recommended mitigation is to add an explicit check for the case where (_bAssetsCirculating - totalCollateral) equals zero and return the maximum allowed leverage factor or otherwise handle the situation without performing the division.

title: Staking ETH incorrectly assumes revert bubbling
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the EbtcLeverageZapRouter and its base contract interact with Lido's stETH contract when staking ETH. Both openCdpWithEth and adjustCdpWithEth invoke a low‑level call (address(stEth).call{value:_initialETH}("")) to deposit the supplied ETH into Lido. Low‑level calls return a boolean indicating success, but the router code ignores this return value and proceeds as if the deposit always succeeded. Lido can deliberately revert the deposit in two documented situations: when the protocol is paused (pauseStaking) or when a per‑block staking limit is exceeded. Because the router does not check the call result, a revert from Lido is silently swallowed, leaving the router’s balance unchanged while the surrounding CDP workflow – permits, flash‑loan handling, account synchronization, CDP initialization and eBTC minting – continues. Subsequent logic expects a positive stETH balance; when the balance is zero, internal checks such as _requireAtLeastMinNetStEthBalance or _requireZeroOrMinAdjustment fail, ultimately causing a later ERC20 transfer revert (e.g., "ERC20: transfer amount exceeds balance"). From the user’s perspective, they send ETH expecting it to be converted into stETH collateral for a new or adjusted CDP, but the transaction either reverts at a later stage or completes with the CDP in an inconsistent state and the user’s ETH effectively lost or locked in the router contract. The impact is a direct loss of the native ETH supplied for staking and a potential degradation of the CDP’s collateralisation, which can render the position under‑collateralised or unusable. The issue manifests only when Lido’s deposit function reverts – a condition that is rare but possible when the protocol is paused or the staking limit is hit. It affects any user interacting with the leverage zap router, the protocol’s accounting logic, and any downstream contracts that rely on correct collateral accounting. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit when a test case deliberately paused deposits in a mock Lido contract, revealing that the router did not propagate the revert and that funds were effectively lost. The problem is subtle because the transaction may still emit events and appear successful until a later require triggers a revert, making it easy to misattribute the failure to other components. The correct mitigation is to capture the boolean result of the low‑level call and require it to be true, or to replace the call with a direct interface call to Lido’s submit function that automatically bubbles up reverts. Additionally, after the call the contract should verify that the expected stETH balance increase is non‑zero before proceeding with the rest of the CDP workflow, ensuring that any deposit failure aborts the entire operation and refunds the user’s ETH.

title: M-16 | Risk Free Arbitrage Attack
description:
The main market making operations allow the protocol to rebalance the liquidity and bump the floor price, as long as solvency is maintained. Due to the fact that these operations can be executed in the same transaction, there is an arbitrage attack opportunity that will drain most of the initial reserves from the protocol, without any risk. Consider the following attack flow:
1. buy bAssets, pushing the price deep into DISCOVERY
2. trigger a sweep to distribute the surplus reserves into the ANCHOR and FLOOR ranges, and update checkpoint tick
3. call bump multiple times to catch up with the active tick.
4. sell all bAssets at a profit, removing a huge chunk of reserves liquidity.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a risk‑free arbitrage vector that stems from the protocol’s market‑making functions being callable repeatedly within a single transaction or block. The core logic of the protocol allows an operator to buy bAssets, which pushes the internal price deep into the DISCOVERY range, then immediately trigger a sweep that redistributes surplus reserves into the ANCHOR and FLOOR ranges and updates the checkpoint tick. Because there is no restriction on how many times the bump (price‑catch‑up) operation can be invoked, the attacker can call it multiple times in the same block, effectively moving the floor price upward without waiting for external market activity. After the price has been artificially inflated, the attacker sells the previously purchased bAssets at the new higher price, extracting a large amount of liquidity while the protocol’s reserves have been drained. This sequence can be executed atomically, so the protocol appears to have performed legitimate rebalancing steps, making the exploit hard to detect during normal operation. The impact is a rapid loss of the protocol’s initial reserves, breaking the solvency invariant that the market‑making module is supposed to maintain, and leaving liquidity providers and users with missing balances or zero‑value tokens. The condition required for the attack is the ability to invoke the liquidity‑rebalance and bump functions an unrestricted number of times within a single block; no rate‑limiting or per‑block call counter is present. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the market‑making flow and the checkpoint update logic. Because the operations are designed to be composable and are executed in the same transaction, the abnormal price movement does not generate external alerts, which is why the bug may remain unnoticed until a malicious actor exploits it. To remediate the problem, the protocol should enforce a limit on how many times the rebalancing or bump functions can be called per block, or introduce a mandatory time delay between successive calls, thereby preventing an attacker from performing the price‑manipulation loop in a single transaction. In generic terms, the bug belongs to the class of ‘unrestricted repeated state‑changing calls’ that enable risk‑free arbitrage and violate the accounting assumptions that reserve balances must remain sufficient after each market‑making step. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are sudden disappearance of liquidity, a floor price that spikes and then collapses, and balances that become zero or far lower than expected after a seemingly normal trade.

title: M-01 | claimed Value Not Assigned
description: In the claim function the claimed boolean is not assigned to true, therefore the system never indicates that the claim can occur. As a result arbitrary users can trigger multiple transfers to the winner and emit the Claim event several times.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing state update in the claim routine of the contract. The function is supposed to mark a reward as claimed by setting a boolean flag, but the code never assigns the flag to true. Because the flag remains false, the contract’s internal logic that should prevent further claims never triggers. Consequently any address can invoke the claim function repeatedly, causing the contract to execute the transfer logic multiple times and emit the Claim event each time. This allows an attacker or any user to drain the allocated payout by repeatedly receiving the same amount, effectively making funds disappear from the contract’s balance. The issue manifests whenever a user calls the claim function after the winning condition has been satisfied; there is no guard that checks whether the reward has already been claimed. The problem was identified during a manual audit that inspected the state transitions of the claim flow. It can be hard to notice because the function may appear to succeed – the transfer is performed and the event is emitted – yet the missing assignment is not obvious without tracing the state variable. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑variable not updated” or “missing flag” errors, which break accounting assumptions that each reward can be claimed only once. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that the winner has been paid, but the balance of the contract drops unexpectedly after each claim, and the same winner may receive the payout multiple times. To remediate, the contract should set the claimed flag to true immediately after a successful transfer (or use a modifier that checks and updates the flag atomically) so that subsequent calls are rejected.

title: M-02 | Reheat Sniping
description: The reheat function will buy YES and loop it when the random roll hits. However the random value is based upon the block.timestamp and block.prevrandao which are both deterministically available at the block in which the reheat transaction is recorded. In environments where front-running is possible, a malicious actor may create a contract which buys YES and reverts if the block.timestamp and block.prevrandao would not fulfill the random requirements. This way the attacker can detect owner transactions to reheat and frontrun them in the same block to buy YES right before the price increases as a result of the reheat. The attacker can then back run the reheat and sell their YES tokens if a reheat looping was performed for a risk free immediate profit.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the contract’s reheat function, which determines whether to purchase additional YES tokens and repeat the operation based on a pseudo‑random value derived from block.timestamp and block.prevrandao. Because both of these blockchain variables are known to miners, validators, or any actor observing the pending block, the randomness is effectively predictable. An attacker can therefore construct a contract that first simulates the random roll; if the simulated outcome would cause the reheat to loop (and thus raise the YES price), the attacker’s contract proceeds, otherwise it reverts. By monitoring the mempool for a legitimate user’s reheat transaction, the attacker can front‑run in the same block, buying YES tokens just before the price increase triggered by the reheat loop. After the reheat executes and the price has risen, the attacker back‑runs, selling the previously bought YES tokens at the higher price, capturing a risk‑free profit. This attack vector is a classic example of predictable‑randomness exploitation leading to front‑running or MEV extraction. It occurs only in environments where transaction ordering can be influenced, such as networks with active miners or bots that can submit multiple transactions in a single block. The affected parties include regular users who invoke the reheat function expecting a fair random outcome, as well as the protocol itself, which may suffer from distorted price dynamics and reduced trust. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the source of entropy used in the reheat logic and identified that the randomness source is fully deterministic at block inclusion time. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly from a functional standpoint; the reheat either loops or not as coded, but the economic side‑effect—price manipulation via front‑running—is subtle and only observable through abnormal profit patterns or unexpected price spikes. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms may appear as a sudden increase in the cost to acquire YES after a reheat, or a feeling that their transaction was “out‑priced” by an unknown party, even though the UI shows no explicit error. The vulnerability belongs to the broader class of predictable‑randomness and front‑running bugs, where reliance on on‑chain data for entropy enables malicious actors to pre‑emptively position themselves for profit. To remediate, the contract should replace block.timestamp and block.prevrandao with a source of randomness that cannot be known before transaction execution, such as a commit‑reveal scheme, a verifiable random function (VRF) from a trusted oracle, or introduce mechanisms that delay price impact until after a commitment period, thereby removing the deterministic advantage for front‑runners.

title: M-03 | Blast Yields Are Not Conﬁgured For YesArena
description: In the YesArena contract there is no configuration for gas yields, however the YesArena contract is likely to accrue a nontrivial gas expenditure during the game.
bug_full: The YesArena smart contract lacks any configuration or mechanism to handle gas yields that may be generated during gameplay. This omission originates from the contract not integrating the Blast gas‑rebate system, which is designed to accumulate and later allow the contract to claim refunds for gas spent on certain operations. Because the contract does not track or expose functions for claiming these yields, any gas rebates that would otherwise be credited remain unclaimed and effectively locked inside the contract. An attacker or even a regular user cannot exploit this directly to steal funds, but the economic impact is that the protocol and its participants incur higher net gas costs than necessary, reducing overall efficiency and potentially eroding user trust. The issue manifests whenever the YesArena game executes transactions that trigger gas‑yield generation – for example, during match creation, move submissions, or settlement – and the contract does not provide a way to retrieve the accrued rebate. Users may notice that their transaction receipts show higher gas consumption without the expected reduction in cost, or that the contract’s balance does not reflect any reclaimed gas. The vulnerability was identified during a systematic audit of the contract’s financial flows, where the absence of Blast‑related configuration stood out as a logical gap. It can be difficult to spot because the contract still functions correctly from a functional standpoint; the missing yields are a silent loss that does not cause outright failures. To remediate, the contract should be extended with appropriate state variables and public functions that record gas‑yield accruals and enable the owner or designated role to claim the accumulated gas refunds, aligning the implementation with the intended Blast yield model and restoring the expected economic behavior of the protocol.

title: M-04 | Lacking _buy Slippage Protection
description: In the _buy function there is no slippage protection configured in the swap call. This allows malicious actors to sandwich the reheat transaction’s swap and extract value from the system.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing slippage protection in the contract's internal _buy function that performs a token swap. Because the swap call does not specify a maximum acceptable price impact, an attacker can place a transaction immediately before (front‑run) and after (back‑run) the victim's purchase, forming a sandwich. The attacker manipulates the market price between the two swaps, causing the victim's swap to execute at an unfavorable rate. This can result in the user receiving far fewer tokens than expected, or in extreme cases the swap returning zero output, effectively making the user's funds disappear. The issue arises whenever the _buy function is invoked on a chain where transactions are visible in a public mempool, allowing the attacker to observe and reorder transactions. It affects any participant who calls the buy interface, including regular users and integrators, because the contract assumes the swap will execute at the quoted price. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the contract code, where the absence of a slippage parameter or deadline check was noted. The problem is subtle because the transaction may still succeed and emit no error, making the loss appear as a normal outcome rather than a contract failure. The bug belongs to the class of price‑manipulation vulnerabilities caused by unchecked swap parameters. To remediate, the contract should enforce a maximum slippage limit or use a deadline, and optionally query the expected output before executing the swap, reverting if the actual amount deviates beyond an acceptable threshold. Implementing these checks restores the intended accounting guarantees that a user’s purchase yields the expected amount of tokens and prevents the protocol from leaking value through sandwich attacks.

title: Incorrect comparison logic in post-operation checks
description:
The `_doCheckValueType` function, which is crucial for post-operation validation, contains reversed comparison logic for the `gte` (greater than or equal to) and `lte` (less than or equal to) operators. This reversal causes the function to perform the opposite checks than intended, potentially allowing operations to pass validation when they should fail, or fail when they should pass.

This issue could lead to:

  1. Incorrect validation of CDP (Collateralized Debt Position) states after operations.
  2. Potential manipulation of the system by exploiting these misaligned checks.
bug_full: An incorrect comparison logic bug exists in the post‑operation validation routine of the LeverageMacroBase contract. The internal function that checks a numeric condition against a stored threshold mistakenly uses the opposite relational operator for the greater‑than‑or‑equal (gte) and less‑than‑or‑equal (lte) cases. Specifically, when the operator is gte the code checks storedValue >= actualValue instead of actualValue >= storedValue, and when the operator is lte it checks storedValue <= actualValue instead of actualValue <= storedValue. This reversal means that the function can approve a transaction that should be rejected, or reject a transaction that should be allowed. The routine is invoked after every state‑changing operation on a collateralized debt position (CDP), such as adding collateral, borrowing, repaying, or withdrawing. Because the validation is inverted, a user may be able to push a CDP into an under‑collateralized state without triggering the safety check, potentially allowing liquidation or loss of funds, or conversely may see a legitimate operation fail with an unexpected revert. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the logic appeared syntactically correct and therefore escaped casual review; the error is subtle because the comparison symbols are visually similar and the surrounding code does not highlight the direction. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a transaction succeeding when the protocol’s risk parameters indicate it should have been blocked, or it may display an error message saying post check failed even though the operation meets the expected limits. This violates the core accounting assumption that post‑operation checks enforce the defined collateral ratios and debt limits. The issue belongs to the class of validation logic inversion bugs, where the intended relational condition is implemented backwards. The recommended remediation is to swap the operands in the gte and lte branches so that the actual value is compared to the stored threshold in the correct direction, and to add unit tests that cover boundary conditions for both operators. After correction the contract will correctly enforce CDP health, preventing unintended fund loss or protocol manipulation.

title: Delegations cannot be removed in some cases due to vulnerable `revokeDelegate()` implementation
description: An old borrower can use an old delegation to claim on behalf of a new borrower.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the inability to correctly revoke an NFT delegation when the original delegation was created with custom rights. In the loan contract, a borrower can call delegate() and forward a bytes32 _rights value to the external DelegateRegistry, which stores the delegation under a hash that incorporates those rights. When the loan ends and the collateral NFT is transferred to a new borrower, the protocol offers a revokeDelegate() function that is supposed to clear any existing delegation. However, revokeDelegate() always calls DelegateRegistry.delegateERC721 with an empty rights string, which generates a different storage key than the one used for the original delegation. Because the registry looks up delegations by the combined (delegate, collection, tokenId, rights) hash, the empty‑rights call does not match the previously stored entry and therefore leaves the original delegation untouched. As a result, the old borrower’s delegation remains active even after the NFT has changed ownership. An attacker who controls the original delegation can then invoke any functionality that relies on the delegation – for example claiming airdrops, event tickets, or other token‑based benefits – as if they were the new owner. From a user’s perspective the new borrower expects the delegation to be cleared, but the UI may still show that the NFT is delegated to the old address, or the user may notice that a ticket or reward is claimed by an unknown party. The impact is unauthorized claim of assets, loss of benefits, and potential reputational damage to the protocol because the accounting assumptions that a borrower’s delegation can be safely revoked are broken. The issue manifests only when custom rights are supplied during delegation; if the default empty rights are used, revokeDelegate works as intended. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the parameters passed to delegate() and revokeDelegate() and identified the mismatch in rights handling. The bug is subtle because the revoke function does not revert or emit an error – it simply performs a no‑op, making it easy to miss in testing. To remediate, revokeDelegate should accept the same rights parameter that was used during delegation (or retrieve it from storage) and pass that exact value to DelegateRegistry.delegateERC721, ensuring the correct delegation entry is removed. Alternatively, the contract could provide a dedicated revocation method in the registry that clears all rights for a given delegate, collection, and tokenId. This change restores the intended invariant that a borrower can always clean up previous delegations before transferring ownership, preserving the protocol’s security and accounting guarantees.

title: Wrong logic in `AUTO_COMPOUND` doesn’t allow for swap to token1
description: Protocol functionality broken
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the AUTO_COMPOUND action of the protocol’s liquidity‑management contract. The function is supposed to allow a user to compound earned rewards and optionally swap the compounded amount into a chosen target token before adding liquidity. The implementation contains a conditional branch that checks whether the target token is token0, which works correctly, but the alternative branch mistakenly tests if state.token0 == state.token1. Because a Uniswap‑style pool can never have the same address for token0 and token1, this condition is never satisfied for any real pool. Consequently, when a caller specifies token1 as the target token, the code falls through to the generic “compound without swap” path and never executes the intended swap. The root cause is a logic error: the developer compared two immutable pool token addresses instead of comparing the caller‑provided target token against state.token1. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; any user who tries to auto‑compound into token1 will experience the bug simply by invoking the function with params.targetToken set to token1. The impact is that the user’s expectation – receiving a swap into token1 as part of the auto‑compound – is not met; the funds remain in token0 or are added to the pool without conversion. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful auto‑compound transaction, but the balance of token1 does not increase, leading to perceived “missing funds” or “refund not received”. This flaw affects all participants who rely on the AUTO_COMPOUND feature, reduces the protocol’s utility, and can cause economic loss if users assume the swap occurred. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the conditional logic was examined and found to be unreachable. It is subtle because the code compiles and the branch appears syntactically correct, yet the condition can never be true, making it easy to overlook in testing. The recommended remediation is to replace the faulty comparison with params.targetToken == state.token1, thereby restoring the intended swap‑to‑token1 behavior. In broader terms, this is a classic example of an unreachable code path caused by an incorrect equality check, leading to a functional deviation from the protocol’s business logic and accounting assumptions about token conversion during auto‑compounding.

title: The signatures are replayable
description: User signed orders can be replayed
bug_full: The contract allows a user to sign an order that is later executed by an operator, but the signed order does not contain a nonce or any unique identifier and the execution function does not verify that the on‑chain parameters match the data the user signed. The validation routine only recovers the signer address from the signature and checks that the order has not been explicitly cancelled. Because the order hash is static, the same signature can be submitted repeatedly and the operator can arbitrarily change fields such as deadline, liquidity amount, target token, or swap data without breaking the signature check. An attacker who controls the OPERATOR_ROLE – either through key compromise, a breached backend API, or a software bug that re‑uses stored orders – can replay a previously signed order or craft a new execution that uses the old signature while supplying malicious parameters. This can lead to unexpected position adjustments, removal of liquidity, creation of extra NFTs, or loss of funds from the user’s wallet. From the user’s perspective the symptoms may be a sudden drop of token balances to zero, receipt of an extra NFT that holds no value, or a failed swap where the expected output is missing. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case signed an empty order struct and the contract executed it successfully, proving that the signed data is never compared to the execution payload. The bug is hard to notice because the signature verification passes, giving the impression that the transaction is authorized, while the underlying business logic – that the user’s intent is respected – is violated. The vulnerability belongs to the class of replayable signature or missing‑nonce bugs combined with insufficient parameter binding. To remediate, the order struct should include a nonce (or a unique order identifier) that is stored and marked as used after execution, and the execute function must compare every relevant field of the signed order with the parameters supplied by the operator, rejecting any mismatch. This ensures that each signed order can be used only once and that the operator cannot alter the user‑intended transaction details.

title: `_deductFees`
description: All main functionality risks reverting with tokens that revert on zero value transfers, via a transfer in `Common._deductFees()`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee‑deduction routine that is shared by the V3Automation and V3Utils modules. The function calculates a fee for each token amount by multiplying the amount by a fixed‑point fee rate (feeX64) and then dividing by the Q64 scaling constant. Because the calculation uses integer division, any situation where 0 < feeX64 * amount < Q64 yields a feeAmount of zero after rounding down. The implementation, however, unconditionally invokes SafeERC20.safeTransfer to send the calculated fee to the fee taker, even when feeAmount is zero. Certain ERC20 tokens, such as those that explicitly revert on zero‑value transfers, cause the safeTransfer call to revert the entire transaction. Consequently, any operation that relies on _deductFees – including swaps, deposits, withdrawals, or automated actions – may fail unexpectedly when the fee rounds to zero for a supported token. From the user’s perspective the transaction simply reverts, often with an error like “transfer amount must be greater than zero”, leaving the user with no token movement and a perception that the protocol is broken or that their funds are stuck. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors observed that the fee calculation could produce zero and that the subsequent transfer was not guarded by a >0 check. It is subtle because the fee being zero is a mathematically valid outcome, yet the contract assumes a transfer will always succeed. The impact is medium: it does not lead to loss of funds, but it prevents legitimate interactions with the protocol for affected tokens, effectively denying service. The bug belongs to the class of “unchecked zero‑value external calls” or “zero‑transfer reverts”. To remediate, the contract should conditionally execute the fee transfer only when feeAmount > 0, as illustrated in the recommended code snippet, thereby aligning the business logic (charging a fee only when it is non‑zero) with the token’s transfer semantics and restoring expected behavior.

title: The Protocol breaks the Allowance Mechanism of the NFTs
description: The user loses their approved entities
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol moves a position NFT between the token owner and the protocol contract. Each action that the platform performs calls ERC721.transferFrom (or safeTransferFrom) to temporarily take custody of the NFT and later return it to the original owner. According to the ERC721 specification, any transfer clears the per‑token approval stored in the _tokenApprovals mapping, effectively revoking all previously granted operator rights for that token. Consequently, an address that was previously approved by the owner – for example a delegate, a bot, or a third‑party service – loses its permission as soon as the protocol executes a transfer, even though the owner never revoked the approval themselves. This breaks the allowance mechanism that ERC721 users rely on for delegated management. The exploit scenario is straightforward: a user (Alice) approves another address (Bob) to manage her position NFT. Bob later interacts with the protocol to collect fees. When the protocol transfers Alice’s NFT to itself and back, the ERC721 transfer logic deletes the stored approval, so Bob’s allowance becomes zero. From Bob’s perspective the contract now rejects his calls with “Not approved”, and Alice is left without a delegated manager. The impact is that delegated fee collection, liquidity withdrawal, or any other automated action that depends on the prior approval can no longer be performed, potentially causing missed fee accruals or forced liquidation if market conditions move against the position. The issue manifests every time the protocol’s functions V3Utils.execute, V3Automation, or any other routine that invokes transferFrom on the NonfungiblePositionManager are called, because each transfer triggers the internal _transfer routine that deletes the token approval. The affected parties are the NFT owners, their approved operators, and the protocol itself, which unintentionally invalidates user‑granted permissions. The problem was discovered during a security audit that traced the flow of NFT transfers and observed that the allowance mapping was cleared after each protocol‑mediated move, contradicting the expectation that approvals persist across internal transfers. The bug is subtle because the transfer appears successful and the ERC721 Transfer event is emitted, while the loss of approval is silent and only surfaces when the previously approved address attempts to act. To remediate the issue, the protocol should avoid transferring ownership of the NFT altogether and instead rely on the isAuthorizedForToken modifier that checks _isApprovedOrOwner, or use the onERC721Received hook to retain the original approval state. Alternatively, the contract could request a blanket approval via setApprovalForAll, but that introduces broader risk. The core fix is to preserve the existing approval mapping when the protocol temporarily holds the NFT, ensuring that delegated operators retain their rights after the protocol’s operation completes.

title: Swapping logic would be broken for some supported tokens
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal swap routine that interacts with an external router to exchange one ERC‑20 token for another. After performing the swap, the function attempts to reset the token allowance by calling an internal safe‑approve helper with a zero amount. This pattern works for most ERC‑20 implementations, but some tokens – notably BNB and other “weird” ERC‑20 contracts – deliberately revert when the approve function is called with a value of zero. Because the swap code unconditionally executes the zero‑allowance reset, a transaction that involves such a token will hit a revert at the reset step, causing the entire swap to fail. The root cause is the assumption that every token complies with the ERC‑20 specification that permits approve(0) without error, combined with the fact that a dedicated helper (_safeResetAndApprove) that could work around the issue is never invoked in the swap path. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; simply initiating a swap with a token that rejects zero‑value approvals triggers the failure. The impact is that users attempting to trade the affected token receive no output – the UI may show a pending transaction that eventually reverts, leaving the user’s funds unchanged but the transaction costs are lost. In a broader sense, the protocol’s swapping feature becomes unusable for any supported token that enforces a non‑zero‑only approval policy, effectively breaking a core business function and opening a denial‑of‑service vector. The condition occurs whenever the amountIn is non‑zero, swapData is provided, and the token being swapped out does not allow approve(0). The issue was discovered during a code audit that compared the protocol’s allowance‑reset logic with the documented behaviour of tokens that revert on zero approvals. It is subtle because the failure happens after the external call to the router, making it appear as a generic swap failure rather than an allowance‑related bug. To remediate, the swap routine should either catch the revert from the zero‑allowance call and fall back to the safeResetAndApprove helper, or the protocol should explicitly reject tokens that do not support approve(0). Conceptually, the fix is to avoid assuming universal ERC‑20 compliance for allowance resets and to handle tokens with non‑standard approval semantics in a safe manner.

title: Multicall does not work as intended
bug_full: The Size protocol provides a multicall entry point that is meant to let a user combine several actions – for example a deposit of underlying borrow tokens followed by a repayment – in a single transaction. The intended behaviour is to bypass the normal borrowAToken cap check during the deposit, but to enforce an invariant after the batch finishes: the increase in the total supply of borrowAToken must never exceed the decrease in the total supply of the corresponding debt token. The implementation of this invariant is flawed because the multicall routine records the borrowAToken supply before and after the batch using the contract’s own balance (borrowAToken.balanceOf(address(this))) instead of the global totalSupply() value. When a user deposits via multicall, the contract’s own balance remains zero, so the recorded “supply before” and “supply after” both appear to be zero. Consequently the invariant check sees no increase and never enters the branch that would compare the increase to the debt reduction, even though the real total supply of borrowAToken has grown beyond the configured cap. This allows a malicious or careless user to deposit an amount that pushes the global borrowAToken supply over its cap, or to combine a large deposit with a repayment that mints extra borrowAToken without triggering a revert. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful deposit or repayment even though the protocol’s accounting rules should have blocked the operation; the user may see their borrow token balance increase unexpectedly or may be able to repay a loan that would otherwise be rejected due to the cap. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees: the borrowAToken cap, which is meant to limit exposure, can be bypassed, leading to token inflation, potential loss of value for other token holders, and a weakening of the protocol’s risk controls. The bug manifests only when the multicall path is used, particularly for deposit‑and‑repay pairs or for deposits alone, and only when the borrowAToken supply is close to the cap. It was discovered during a formal audit by analysing the state variables used in the invariant validation. The issue is hard to notice because the contract’s own token balance is naturally zero, making the faulty check appear correct at a glance. The proper fix is to measure the borrowAToken supply with totalSupply() both before and after the multicall, ensuring the invariant sees the true increase and reverts when the cap would be exceeded. Conceptually, this is an invariant‑violation bug caused by using an incorrect state snapshot in a batch operation, allowing a cap‑bypass and unintended token minting.

title: Users can not to buy/sell minimum credit allowed due to exactAmountIn condition
bug_full: The contract enforces a minimum credit amount of 5e6 units that can be borrowed or sold, but the validation logic in both the buy and sell market functions checks the raw cash amount supplied by the user (params.amount) against this credit minimum without taking into account the exactAmountIn flag and the conversion rate between cash and credit. When a user sets exactAmountIn to true for a buy operation, params.amount represents the cash they are willing to spend; the amount of cash required to obtain the minimum credit can be lower than the credit minimum after applying the rate per tenor, yet the code unconditionally reverts if params.amount is less than 5e6. The same mistake occurs for sell operations when exactAmountIn is false, causing the transaction to revert even though the cash amount would correspond to the minimum credit after conversion. This mismatch between the unit of measurement used in the check and the unit expected by the user prevents legitimate trades that meet the business rule of minimum credit, leading to a user‑facing symptom where the transaction fails with the error CREDIT_LOWER_THAN_MINIMUM_CREDIT, the user receives no credit or cash, and balances remain unchanged. The root cause is an improper input validation that ignores the conversion formula and the exactAmountIn flag, a classic example of a business‑logic validation bug where the wrong domain variable is compared. The issue manifests whenever a user attempts to buy or sell the smallest allowed credit using the exact amount mode, affecting any participant in the market – borrowers, lenders, or liquidity providers – and can reduce protocol usability and liquidity. It was discovered during a security audit when test cases attempted to execute a trade with the minimum credit amount and observed an unexpected revert. The bug can be hard to notice because the check appears reasonable at first glance, but it violates the accounting assumption that cash and credit are interchangeable after applying the rate. The recommended fix is to adjust the validation to compare the cash amount against the minimum credit only after applying the appropriate conversion when exactAmountIn is true, and to keep the original check for the opposite mode, thereby aligning the validation with the intended business rule and restoring the ability to trade the minimum credit amount.

title: Size uses wrong source to query available liquidity on Aave, resulting in borrow and lend operations being bricked upon mainnet deployment
bug_full: Size's credit market contracts contain a liquidity validation routine that reads the balance of the variablePool contract to decide whether enough assets are available for borrowing or lending. In Aave, however, the actual liquidity is stored in the aToken contracts, while the pool contract itself holds no underlying tokens. Because the code queries address(state.data.variablePool) instead of the aToken address, the reported liquidity is always zero on a live Aave deployment. Consequently, the require‑like check in validateVariablePoolHasEnoughLiquidity reverts whenever a user attempts to supply, borrow or withdraw, effectively bricking the core functionality of the protocol. The bug was uncovered during a security audit that compared the production Aave contracts with the PoolMock used in the test suite; the mock transfers assets to the pool contract, masking the problem in unit tests. The issue is hard to notice because the contract compiles and passes all local tests, and the revert message only mentions insufficient aToken liquidity, which may be interpreted as a transient condition. From a user’s point of view, a transaction that should result in a successful loan or deposit instead fails with a revert, leaving the user with no received funds and an unchanged balance, contrary to the expectation that the operation would succeed. The impact is a denial‑of‑service: users cannot interact with the credit market, and any integration that relies on these functions will appear broken, though no funds are directly stolen. The vulnerability belongs to the class of external‑protocol state mis‑reference bugs, where a contract queries the wrong contract for a critical invariant. The correct fix is to obtain the aToken address from the pool’s reserve data and query the underlying token balance of that aToken, thereby aligning the check with Aave’s actual accounting model. After the fix, the liquidity check reflects the true available amount, allowing borrow and lend operations to proceed as intended.

title: Inadequate checks to confirm the correct status of the sequence/`sequencerUptimeFeed` in `PriceFeed.getPrice`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price‑feed contract that relies on a Chainlink L2 sequencer uptime feed to decide whether the underlying sequencer is operational before returning a price. The contract reads two values from the feed: an answer flag where 0 means the sequencer is up and 1 means it is down, and a timestamp called startedAt that marks the moment the sequencer changed status. According to Chainlink documentation, when the feed is in an “invalid round” – for example because the sequencer status could not be updated due to network or oracle issues – the startedAt field is returned as 0 and the answer field is also 0. The contract implements two checks: it reverts if answer equals 1, and it reverts if the time elapsed since startedAt is less than a hard‑coded grace period of one hour. The logic assumes startedAt is always a non‑zero timestamp. In an invalid round, startedAt is 0, so the expression block.timestamp‑startedAt evaluates to the current block timestamp, which is always far larger than the grace period. Consequently the second check never triggers, and the function proceeds to return a price even though the sequencer status has not been confirmed. This flaw allows callers to obtain price data during periods when the sequencer may be down or the feed data is unreliable. Users of the contract – traders, liquidators, or any protocol component that depends on accurate pricing – may receive stale or incorrect prices, potentially leading to mis‑priced trades, unintended liquidations, or loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors noted that the grace‑period logic is ineffective when startedAt is zero. The bug is subtle because the code appears to enforce a safety window, yet the edge case of an invalid round silently bypasses it, making it easy to miss in casual testing. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit validation that reverts when startedAt equals 0, or to treat a zero timestamp as an invalid round and reject price queries until a valid round is observed. By ensuring that both the answer flag and the startedAt timestamp are validated, the contract will correctly block price retrieval while the sequencer status is uncertain, restoring the intended security guarantees of the price feed.

title: Users may incur an unexpected fragmentation fee in the `compensate`
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the compensate() function that lacks a user‑controlled minimum amount parameter. When a borrower calls compensate, the contract computes the amount to compensate as the smaller of the requested amount and the credit available in the debt‑related credit position. If the market state changes between the selection of the credit positions and the execution of compensate – for example, a preceding buyCreditMarket or sellCreditMarket transaction reduces the credit in the debt‑related position – the computed amountToCompensate becomes smaller than the total credit held in the compensating position. The remaining credit triggers the fragmentation fee logic, which charges the borrower a fee in collateral tokens. From the user’s perspective the balance of their collateral token drops unexpectedly, often showing a small but unexplained deduction after a compensate transaction that previously incurred no fee. This can happen in normal user flows whenever market activity modifies credit amounts, and it can be deliberately induced by a malicious actor who front‑runs the compensate call, executes a market trade that reduces the target credit, and forces the borrower to pay the unforeseen fee. The impact is a loss of funds that the user did not anticipate, breaking the expectation that compensate either fully settles the credit or costs nothing. The issue was discovered during a security audit through a proof‑of‑concept test that compared two scenarios: one where compensate was called directly after setting up matching credit positions (no fee) and another where an intervening market trade altered the credit amount (fee charged). The bug is subtle because the fee is conditional and often zero, making it easy to miss during casual testing. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of “partial execution with unexpected post‑condition fees” or “slippage‑induced fee exposure”. To remediate, the protocol should allow callers to specify a minimum acceptable compensation amount or a slippage protection flag that causes the transaction to revert if any fragmentation fee would be applied, thereby aligning the contract’s behavior with user expectations and preventing fee exploitation.

title: Neither `sellCreditMarket` nor `compensate` validates whether a credit position is for sale
description: A credit buyer could be forced to buy a `not for sale` credit position with no way to sell it passively, potentially suffering a loss due to missing an arbitrage opportunity.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation in the functions that handle secondary market operations for credit positions. Specifically, the sellCreditMarket and compensate functions do not verify that a credit position is actually marked as for sale or that the lender has not globally disabled sales of their positions. The root cause is that the code only checks the forSale flag when the caller is the current lender, but it fails to enforce the same check when the caller attempts to sell a credit position that has been explicitly marked as not for sale or when the lender has set the allCreditPositionsForSaleDisabled flag. As a result, an attacker who controls a credit position can invoke sellCreditMarket to transfer ownership of a credit that the original owner intended to keep unsold. The attacker can also use compensate to apply a non‑sale credit position to settle a debt, bypassing the intended restriction. Exploitation proceeds by first marking a credit position as not for sale (or disabling all sales for the lender) and then calling sellCreditMarket with that creditPositionId. Because the function does not reject the operation, the protocol transfers the credit to the buyer, who may be unaware that the position cannot be resold. The buyer then holds a credit that cannot be sold again, preventing them from exiting the position or participating in arbitrage, which can lead to a financial loss. This issue manifests whenever a credit position’s forSale flag is false or the lender’s global sale‑disable flag is true, and a party invokes the secondary market functions. It affects any user of the Size protocol who relies on the ability to control the tradability of their credit positions, including lenders, borrowers, and speculators. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that exercised the sellCreditMarket path with a credit marked not for sale and observed that the transaction succeeded despite the flag being false. The bug is subtle because the function does perform other checks (such as ownership and amount) and therefore appears to behave correctly at first glance; the missing sale‑status validation is easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should enforce that a credit position is transferable only if the lender’s allCreditPositionsForSaleDisabled flag is false and the specific credit’s forSale flag is true, and the same checks should be applied in the compensate function before allowing a credit to be used for debt repayment. This aligns the implementation with the business rule that a lender must be able to decide whether their credit can be sold or used for compensation, preventing unintended forced sales and protecting users from unexpected loss of liquidity or arbitrage opportunities.

title: Credit can be sold forcibly as `forSale` setting can be ignored via Compensate
description: Any credit position can be forcibly sold with the help of its borrower. This will be executed only when have expected profit; for example, when lender’s curve is not null and is above the market it is profitable to buy credit from them (lend to them at above market rates), but they might block it with the lack of free collateral and the `forSale = false` flag, which can be overridden by the corresponding borrower of this credit position. The impact of this forced sale is proportional to interest rate volatility and can be substantial. There are no additional prerequisites for the setup.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of the forSale flag on credit positions within the Size protocol. When a credit position is created through the createDebtAndCreditPositions routine, the implementation unconditionally sets the forSale attribute to true. Later, the Compensate action can be invoked with a special RESERVED_ID parameter. In this path the contract creates a fresh credit position by calling createDebtAndCreditPositions again, again with forSale set to true, and then substitutes the existing lender’s credit position with the newly created one. Because the new position is always marked as forSale, the original lender’s intention to keep the credit non‑transferable (by setting forSale to false or by disabling all credit positions for sale) is ignored. An attacker who is the borrower of the associated debt can therefore trigger a forced sale: after the Compensate call the credit can be purchased on the market through the BuyCreditMarket function, even though the lender had explicitly disabled the sale. The root cause is the failure to propagate the original forSale flag and the lack of a check that prevents a borrower from overriding a lender’s sale restriction. Exploitation requires only that the borrower can call Compensate with the reserved identifier and that the lender’s credit curve is above the current market rate, making the forced purchase profitable. When these conditions are met, the borrower can force the lender’s credit to be sold at a price that may be unfavorable to the lender, leading to a loss of expected interest income or even a reduction of the lender’s balance. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that a credit that was marked as not for sale disappears from the lender’s portfolio, the reported balance may drop to zero or a lower amount, and the lender receives no notification that a sale was forced. The issue is a class of authorization‑bypass or flag‑override bug where mutable state is unintentionally overwritten, breaking the business logic that a lender should control whether their credit can be transferred. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of credit creation and compensation and noticed that the forSale flag was hard‑coded to true in the compensation path. The problem can be subtle because the normal creation path also uses forSale true, so the overridden behavior blends with expected operations and may not raise an immediate alarm. The recommended remediation is to pass the original forSale value into createDebtAndCreditPositions when it is called from Compensate, or to add an explicit check that prevents the borrower from creating a credit position with forSale true when the target position was marked as not for sale. By preserving the lender’s flag, the protocol restores the intended invariant that only parties authorized to sell a credit can do so, eliminating the forced‑sale scenario.

title: Sandwich attack on loan fulfillment will temporarily prevent users from accessing their borrowed funds
description:
The protocol does not remove borrowed token liquidity from the aave pool once a loan is initiated. It only checks if there is enough available liquidity via the `validateVariablePoolHasEnoughLiquidity()` function. A user is expected to withdraw their funds after the loan is created. This means that a malicious user can sandwich loans that exceed the available liquidity in aave by depositing liquidity in a frontrun transaction and removing it in a backrun transaction. This way a user that takes out a loan will not be able to remove their funds until there is enough available liquidity in the pool.

Also note that liquidity may become unavailable via other factors, like external users removing liquidity from aave.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a liquidity‑validation flaw in the loan fulfillment flow where the protocol only checks that the Aave variable pool reports sufficient underlying token balance before completing a loan, but it never actually reserves or removes that liquidity from the pool. Because the contract transfers a borrow‑AToken representation to the borrower and relies on a subsequent pull‑based withdrawal, an attacker can front‑run a legitimate loan request by depositing a large amount of liquidity, causing the validation to succeed, and then back‑run by withdrawing the same liquidity before the borrower’s pull transaction executes. This sandwich pattern temporarily reduces the pool’s available liquidity below the amount owed to the borrower, so when the borrower attempts to withdraw their borrowed funds they receive nothing or a reduced amount, effectively locking the funds until enough liquidity returns. The issue occurs whenever a loan is created without an immediate debit of the underlying assets, and it can be triggered by any external actor who can manipulate the pool’s balance within the same block, including normal users withdrawing liquidity or other MEV actors. The affected parties are borrowers who expect to receive their loaned tokens immediately after the loan transaction, as well as the protocol which may appear to have insufficient liquidity, potentially harming its reputation and financial stability. The flaw was discovered during a code audit that examined the sellCreditMarket function and noticed that validateVariablePoolHasEnoughLiquidity only performs a view check without state mutation, and that executeSellCreditMarket transfers borrowAToken rather than the underlying token. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert and the loan appears successful, making the missing funds observable only later when the user attempts to pull the assets. Conceptually, this is an accounting‑consistency bug where the protocol’s internal accounting assumes liquidity has been reserved without actually doing so, violating the invariant that borrowed amounts must be backed by real pool assets.
