To remediate, the contract should debit the pool’s underlying token balance at loan creation (or use a pull‑over‑push pattern that atomically reserves liquidity) and optionally expose a multicall interface to combine loan creation and withdrawal in a single atomic step, thereby preventing the window where an attacker can manipulate the pool’s balance between the two operations.

title: Borrower is not able to compensate his lenders if he is underwater
description: A borrower of a loan could have other credit positions with borrowers that have healthy CRs which he could use to compensate his lenders to avoid liquidations and improve his CR. However, he is not able to do this via [`compensate()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-size/blob/8850e25fb088898e9cf86f9be1c401ad155bea86/src/Size.sol#L247) and he is forced to sell his credit positions via [`sellCreditMarket()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-size/blob/8850e25fb088898e9cf86f9be1c401ad155bea86/src/Size.sol#L188) or [`sellCreditLimit()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-06-size/blob/8850e25fb088898e9cf86f9be1c401ad155bea86/src/Size.sol#L172). The complications of this are described in the example below.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the compensate() function performs a post‑operation collateral‑ratio (CR) validation that reverts the transaction if the borrower’s CR is still below the liquidation threshold after the compensation. Because the check is performed after each individual compensate call, a borrower who needs to compensate more than one debt position in order to bring the overall CR back into the healthy range cannot do so. The borrower is forced to split the intended multi‑position compensation into separate transactions, each of which fails the underwater check, causing a revert. As a result the borrower cannot use his healthy credit positions to offset the unhealthy debt positions and must instead sell those credit positions on the market, potentially at a severe discount or when no buyers exist, increasing the risk of liquidation. The issue occurs when a borrower is underwater (CR < liquidation threshold) but holds one or more credit positions with healthy CR that could be used to improve the overall ratio. The root cause is the placement of the underwater validation after the compensation logic without considering that the CR may only become healthy after multiple compensations. The exploit is straightforward: an attacker (or any borrower) can trigger a revert by attempting to compensate a subset of debt positions while still underwater, preventing the intended risk mitigation. The impact is financial loss for borrowers, reduced protocol safety, and possible forced liquidation. It was discovered during a manual audit of the Size protocol where the state.validateUserIsNotUnderwater call was examined. The bug is subtle because the compensate function appears to succeed for a single position, leading developers to assume it works for multiple positions as well. The fix is to measure the CR before and after the compensation logic and only revert if the CR becomes worse, or to allow the transaction to succeed as long as the final CR after all intended compensations is healthy, possibly by moving the underwater check outside the loop or by aggregating compensations. This class of bug is an improper post‑condition check that prevents multi‑step state updates from reaching a safe state. From a user perspective the UI would show a transaction failure with a revert message, the borrower would see that his credit positions cannot be used to rescue the loan, and the balance of his credit tokens would remain unchanged while his loan remains underwater, leading to panic and potential liquidation.

title: `withdraw` should allow taking out borrowed assets regardless of collateral ratio
bug_full: The vulnerability is a business‑logic flaw in the withdraw() entry point of the Size protocol. After a user calls withdraw(), the contract unconditionally executes state.validateUserIsNotBelowOpeningLimitBorrowCR(msg.sender), which checks that the caller’s collateral ratio remains above the opening‑limit borrow collateral ratio (openingLimitBorrowCR). This check is appropriate when a user withdraws collateral because removing collateral reduces the collateral ratio, but it is incorrectly applied when the user withdraws the underlyingBorrowToken – the token that the user has already borrowed. Withdrawing a borrowed token does not change the collateral ratio, yet the contract still enforces the opening‑limit check. Consequently, if a borrower’s collateral ratio has fallen below the opening limit (for example due to market price movements or accrued interest), any attempt to withdraw the borrowed asset will revert, even though the asset is the borrower’s own debt token. The root cause is the unconditional invocation of the collateral‑ratio validation after every withdrawal, without distinguishing the token type being withdrawn. An attacker could manipulate asset prices or deliberately reduce a user’s collateral ratio to trigger this check and effectively lock the borrower’s loan tokens, creating a denial‑of‑service condition. From a user’s perspective the UI may report a successful transaction but the balance of the borrowed token remains unchanged, or the transaction may simply revert with an obscure error, leading to confusion such as “my funds disappeared” or “I cannot get my loan back”. The impact is medium severity because it prevents legitimate borrowers from retrieving their own borrowed assets, potentially causing loss of access to funds and undermining trust in the protocol’s accounting assumptions. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit through logical analysis of the withdraw flow. It is hard to notice because the same function works correctly for collateral withdrawals, so the failure only appears under specific collateral‑ratio conditions. The proper fix is to conditionally skip the opening‑limit collateral‑ratio validation when the token being withdrawn is the underlyingBorrowToken, allowing borrowers to withdraw their debt tokens regardless of the current collateral ratio while still protecting collateral withdrawals with the appropriate safety check.

title: Incorrect call argument in `THORChain_Router::_transferOutAndCallV5`, leading to grief/steal of `THORChain_Aggregator`’s funds or DoS
description: When transferring a token, which is of type fee-on-transfer, in `THORChain_Router::_transferOutAndCallV5`, the token is first deposited to the `THORChain_Aggregator` and then `THORChain_Aggregator::swapOutV5` is called with the same amount. The call will always revert if the `THORChain_Aggregator` does not have tokens or grief/steal (depending on the token) of `THORChain_Aggregator`’s tokens. An example of a fee-on-transfer token that is in the whitelist is `PAXG` ([see here](https://gitlab.com/thorchain/thornode/-/blob/develop/common/tokenlist/ethtokens/eth_mainnet_latest.json?ref_type=heads#L1870)) to view the loss of funds that are locked and waiting to be rescued in the `THORChain_Aggregator`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way THORChain_Router::_transferOutAndCallV5 handles tokens that charge a fee on each transfer (fee‑on‑transfer tokens). When the router moves a token from a user to the THORChain_Aggregator, it first deposits the requested amount and then immediately invokes THORChain_Aggregator.swapOutV5 with the same amount that was specified for the deposit. Because fee‑on‑transfer tokens deduct a portion of the transferred value, the aggregator actually receives less tokens than the amount passed to swapOutV5. The contract assumes that the full amount is available, so the subsequent call either reverts due to insufficient balance or, if the aggregator holds other tokens, the fee is unintentionally taken from those funds. This mismatch can cause user‑deposited assets to become permanently locked, enable an attacker to drain the aggregator’s balance, or render the swap function unusable, effectively a denial‑of‑service condition. The issue manifests only when a fee‑on‑transfer token is present in the router’s whitelist (for example PAXG) and a user initiates a transfer‑out operation. It affects any participant who deposits such tokens, the aggregator contract that holds the funds, and the overall protocol because the accounting assumptions about token balances are violated. The problem was uncovered during a Code4rena audit through a reproducible test that introduced a custom fee‑on‑transfer ERC20 token and observed that the router’s call to swapOutV5 always reverted or caused a loss of tokens. The bug is subtle because the initial transfer appears successful – the token contract emits a Transfer event and the router’s balance updates – yet the hidden fee is not reflected in the amount used for the subsequent call, making the discrepancy easy to miss in normal operation. To remediate the flaw, the router should employ a safe transfer routine that records the recipient’s pre‑transfer balance, performs the token transfer, then computes the actual amount received and uses that exact value when invoking swapOutV5. This approach guarantees that the protocol never assumes more tokens than were actually transferred, preventing both accidental fund loss and intentional griefing attacks. The class of bug can be described as an “incorrect handling of fee‑on‑transfer tokens leading to balance mismatch and unsafe external calls”, a common pitfall in DeFi contracts that interact with tokens that modify the transferred amount.

title: Due to the use of `msg.value` in for loop, anyone can drain all the funds from the `THORChain_Router` contract
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the router contract reusing the global msg.value amount inside a for‑loop that processes an array of transfer payloads. When a caller invokes batchTransferOutAndCallV5 with more than one TransferOutAndCallData element and the fromAsset field is set to address(0) (indicating an ether transfer), the internal _transferOutAndCallV5 function forwards the entire msg.value to the target address on each iteration. The function first attempts to call swapOutV5 on the supplied target; if that call returns false, a fallback path executes a low‑level send of msg.value to the same target. Because msg.value is not reduced after the first iteration, the contract ends up sending the full ether amount repeatedly, ultimately emptying its balance and transferring all funds to the attacker‑controlled address. The issue occurs only when the payload array length exceeds one and the attacker can set an arbitrary target address because the struct is not validated. From a user perspective the router appears to accept a payment but after the transaction the contract balance becomes zero and the user receives no funds, contradicting the expectation that the router will forward exactly the supplied amount. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the handling of aggregationPayloads and noticed that msg.value is used without accounting for per‑iteration consumption, leading to an unchecked value reuse pattern. The bug is subtle because the fallback logic includes a refund to msg.sender, yet in the batch scenario the first successful send already consumes the ether, so the refund path is never reached. This class of issue belongs to improper handling of external call results combined with reuse of a global value inside a loop, effectively creating a drain vector similar to a re‑entrancy exploit but without actual re‑entrancy. The impact is a complete loss of ether held by the THORChain_Router, affecting any user or protocol that relies on the contract for cross‑chain swaps. To mitigate the problem the contract should stop using msg.value inside the loop, introduce an explicit etherAmount field for each payload, and enforce that the sum of those amounts equals msg.value before processing. Additionally, the target address should be validated or a safe transfer pattern should be employed that limits the amount sent per iteration, ensuring that the router cannot be drained by a malicious batch call.

title: Vultisig should be burnable
description: The Vultisig token, as described in its documentation, is expected to include a burnable feature. However, the current implementation of the Vultisig token contract lacks the necessary functions to support token burning. This report identifies the impact of this missing functionality and provides a recommended solution to implement the burn feature. The vultisig stated that they forgot to add this functionality.
bug_full: The Vultisig token contract is advertised as having a burnable feature, meaning token holders should be able to destroy a portion of their balance to reduce total supply. However, the deployed contract does not contain any public burn or burnFrom functions, nor does it inherit from OpenZeppelin's ERC20Burnable. The root cause is a simple omission in the source code: the developer forgot to add the required functions after the contract was written. Because the contract compiles and passes basic ERC20 tests, the missing capability is not obvious during normal operation and may only be discovered by comparing the on‑chain behavior with the documentation or by an audit that checks for compliance with the stated tokenomics. As a result, users who expect to be able to burn tokens find that the UI shows a “burn” button that either does nothing or is absent, and any attempt to reduce supply fails silently. This violates the business logic that the token supply should be deflationary or adjustable, potentially leading to inflated circulating supply, misaligned incentives, and loss of trust in the protocol. The issue affects all token holders, the protocol’s economic model, and any downstream contracts that rely on a decreasing supply. Exploitation is not a classic attack but a functional failure: an attacker could claim that the token is deflationary while the supply cannot be reduced, misleading investors. The problem was identified during a Code4rena audit when the auditors compared the contract’s public interface with the documentation and noted the absence of burn functions. The bug is hard to notice because there are no runtime errors, and the contract otherwise behaves like a standard ERC20. The recommended remediation is to add standard burn(uint256) and burnFrom(address,uint256) functions that call the internal _burn routine and update allowances accordingly, or to inherit from OpenZeppelin’s ERC20Burnable module. Once added, token holders will be able to destroy tokens, the total supply will correctly reflect burned amounts, and the contract will align with its advertised specifications.

title: `claim` function lacks slippage controls for `amount0` and `amount1` returned by `pool.burn` function call
description: Because the `claim` function does not have slippage controls for `amount0` and `amount1` returned by the `pool.burn` function call, the `claim` function call can suffer from price manipulation on the associated Uniswap v3 pool. If a price manipulation frontruns the `claim` transaction, the claimed token amounts can be much less than what they should be.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a claim function that withdraws liquidity from a Uniswap V3 pool but does not enforce any slippage limits on the token amounts returned by the pool.burn call. Because the function simply accepts whatever amount0 and amount1 the pool reports, an attacker who can manipulate the pool price immediately before the claim transaction is mined can cause the pool to return far fewer tokens than the user’s logical entitlement. The root cause is the absence of a check similar to the one used in Uniswap’s decreaseLiquidity function, which validates that the returned amounts meet a minimum threshold supplied by the caller. An exploit proceeds by front‑running the claim transaction with a price‑impact trade that shifts the pool’s price curve, then allowing the claim to execute while the pool’s internal accounting still reflects the manipulated price. The claim function will then collect the reduced amounts, deduct fees, and transfer them to the user, who sees a successful transaction but receives a much smaller token balance – sometimes even zero – while the protocol still records the liquidity as removed. This situation can occur whenever the launch has succeeded, the user calls claim, and the pool’s price is susceptible to rapid changes, such as low‑liquidity environments. The affected parties are token holders who expect to receive their full share of liquidity and accrued fees, as well as the protocol that relies on accurate accounting of withdrawn assets. The issue was identified during a formal audit by Code4rena, and it can be difficult to notice because the transaction does not revert and the UI may simply display a “claim successful” message, hiding the fact that the amounts transferred are unexpectedly low. To remediate, the claim function should incorporate slippage controls – for example, requiring amount0 >= amount0Min and amount1 >= amount1Min – or otherwise validate the returned amounts against expected values before proceeding with fee deductions and transfers. This aligns the function with the standard Uniswap decreaseLiquidity pattern and restores confidence that users receive the correct token amounts, preventing money from disappearing due to price manipulation.

title: Transfer of `ILOPool` NFT token to different account allows for users to bypass the pool’s `maxCapPerUser` invariant
bug_full: The vulnerability is an invariant‑bypass caused by the way the ILOPool contract determines whether an investor already owns a position. The contract uses the ERC721 balance of the caller (balanceOf(recipient) == 0) to decide if a new NFT should be minted. Because an NFT can be transferred to another address, an investor can move their existing token to a second account, making the original address appear to have no NFTs. When the investor calls buy() from the original address again, the contract treats the caller as a new participant, mints a second NFT and creates a new position. The per‑user contribution limit (maxCapPerUser) is only checked against the raise amount stored in the newly created position, not against the total amount contributed by the same logical user across all of their positions. Consequently, the user can purchase raise tokens in excess of the intended per‑user cap by repeatedly transferring the NFT and opening fresh positions. This bypass allows a single participant to monopolize the pool’s hardCap, preventing other investors from buying in. The issue is discovered during a formal audit when a test demonstrated that after transferring the NFT, the balance of the original address becomes zero, yet the contract still permits another buy that exceeds the maxCapPerUser, and subsequent attempts by other users revert with a hard‑cap error. The bug is subtle because the contract’s logic appears to enforce the cap on a per‑position basis, which is a common pattern for NFT‑backed positions, and the transfer of ownership is a normal ERC721 operation that developers may not associate with contribution limits. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a sudden drop of their NFT balance to zero after a transfer, followed by the ability to buy more tokens than the protocol advertises as the maximum per user, and finally other users seeing their transactions fail with a hard‑cap error. The vulnerability belongs to the class of invariant‑bypass or accounting‑state‑splitting bugs where per‑entity limits are enforced on a mutable identifier rather than on an immutable user identity. To remediate, the contract should track contributions by a stable identifier (e.g., the original investor address) independent of NFT ownership, aggregate raise amounts across all positions owned by that identifier, and avoid using balanceOf as the sole condition for minting a new NFT. Implementing an internal mapping that records whether an address has ever purchased and summing raiseAmount across all its positions would restore the intended maxCapPerUser invariant and prevent the pool from being monopolized.

title: An attacker can flood the protocol with false offers to cause DoS
bug_full: The vulnerability is a resource‑exhaustion denial‑of‑service condition that arises from the protocol’s unbounded enumeration of offers during Chainlink automation upkeep. The contract stores every created offer in a global set and the checkUpkeep function iterates over the entire collection to build a batch of offers that need verification, payout or expiration. Because the contract allows any address to create an offer with only a flat fee and imposes no minimum on the maximum payment amount, an attacker can submit a large number of zero‑value offers that remain in the Pending state. These false offers consume the iteration budget and quickly fill the batch size limit, causing legitimate offers to be ignored by the automation agents. The impact is that users who expect their offers to be verified, to receive payouts, or to be expired on schedule see their offers stuck indefinitely, balances appear unchanged, and refunds never arrive. The issue is observed when the number of pending offers grows large enough that the for‑loop in checkUpkeep cannot reach the real offers before hitting the configured batch size. It affects all participants of the protocol – advertisers, responders and any party relying on timely verification or payout – because the protocol’s core business logic assumes that only economically meaningful offers will be present. The problem was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test creating hundreds of zero‑value offers with a single flat‑fee allowance. The bug is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error; it simply processes offers slower, which may be mistaken for normal latency. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of unchecked input validation leading to enumeration‑based DoS. The correct mitigation is to enforce limits on the number of active offers per address, require a minimum payment amount, or collect the flat fee at creation time and refund it only on cancellation or expiration, thereby preventing an attacker from flooding the system with cheap, useless offers.

title: Malicious creators can force advertisers to pay the flat fee by cancelling accepted offers
description:
The protocol charges a `flatFee` for all offers when they are accepted. Once accepted, the `flatFee` is sent to the protocol owner’s address and is NOT refunded under any circumstances, including cancellation or expiration.

While this could be intentional, there is another issue related to malicious creators. After acceptance, if the content creator does nothing, the offer expires after `Offer.payoutDate` and the funds are refunded to the advertiser except for the flat fee. Or the content creator can call `cancelOffer()` to cancel the offer.

Although it is understood that there exists an off-chain backend mechanism to manage creators, it is desirable to have an on-chain escrow feature for the creators as well. This would require creators to put up some collateral when they accept an offer, which would reimburse the advertiser for their loss if the creator breaks the deal.

The current implementation can lead to situations where advertisers incur losses due to the non-refundable flat fee and potential malicious behavior by content creators. This could result in a lack of trust and reduced participation in the protocol.

We evaluate the overall impact to be Medium because the accepting offer is handled by admin.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a non‑refundable flat fee that is transferred to the protocol owner at the moment an offer is accepted, combined with the absence of any on‑chain escrow or penalty mechanism for the content creator. The root cause is the contract’s business logic: once an offer is accepted the flat fee is deducted permanently, and the contract allows the creator to either cancel the offer via cancelOffer() or simply let the offer expire after the payoutDate without delivering the promised content. Because the contract does not require the creator to post collateral, there is no economic incentive for the creator to honour the deal, and the protocol does not reimburse the advertiser for the flat fee when the creator aborts. An attacker controlling a malicious creator can therefore accept an offer, then immediately call cancelOffer() or remain idle until expiration, causing the advertiser’s transaction to lose the flat fee while the remaining funds are returned. From the advertiser’s point of view the expected behaviour is that a cancelled or expired offer would refund the full amount, but in practice the flat fee is permanently lost, leading to a situation where the user sees a deduction from their balance and receives no compensation for the cancelled service. This issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the offer lifecycle and fee handling. It can be hard to notice because the non‑refundable fee may be documented as intentional, masking the economic impact of the creator’s ability to cancel without penalty. The impact is a medium‑severity loss of advertiser funds, erosion of trust in the platform, and reduced participation, especially since the acceptance flow is controlled by an admin. To remediate, the protocol should introduce an on‑chain escrow that requires creators to lock collateral when they accept an offer; this collateral would be released to the advertiser if the creator fails to fulfil the agreement, and the flat fee policy should be revisited to allow refunds in cases of cancellation or expiration, thereby aligning incentives and protecting advertisers from malicious creator behaviour.

title: Using a wrong fee percentage [Self-Reported]
description:
In the middle of the audit, the Tunnl team spotted a bug in the function `sendFunctionsRequest()`.
While the function calculates the `maxCreatorPayment`, it was using the `s_config.creatorFeePercentageBP` instead of `s_offers[offerId].creatorFeePercentageBP`.
This could potentially affect the payment amount to the content creators when there is a change in the configuration.

We evaluate the impact to be Medium because of the low likelihood.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a miscalculation of the creator fee when the contract processes a payment request in the function sendFunctionsRequest. Instead of using the fee percentage that is stored per‑offer (s_offers[offerId].creatorFeePercentageBP), the code reads the global configuration fee (s_config.creatorFeePercentageBP). This root cause stems from an incorrect reference to a state variable, causing the contract to apply a generic fee to every payment regardless of the specific agreement attached to each offer. An attacker or even a legitimate admin who changes the global fee after offers have been created can trigger the bug: subsequent calls to sendFunctionsRequest will compute maxCreatorPayment with the new global fee, resulting in creators receiving either less or more than the amount stipulated in their original offer. From a user perspective, a creator may notice that the expected payout (for example a 5 % share) is reduced to a lower percentage, or in extreme cases the payout may become zero if the global fee is set very high. The impact is economic – creators lose revenue and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about fixed per‑offer fees are violated, potentially leading to disputes and loss of trust. The condition for exploitation is the existence of a mutable global fee configuration and offers that rely on a different fee percentage; the bug manifests only after the global fee is altered post‑offer creation. The issue was discovered during an internal audit when the Tunnl team reviewed the payment logic and noticed the mismatched variable usage. It can be hard to notice because payments still succeed; the discrepancy appears only as a subtle deviation from expected amounts, which may be overlooked without explicit checks or tests. The proper fix is to replace the reference to the global fee with the per‑offer fee when calculating maxCreatorPayment, and to add unit tests that verify the fee used matches the offer’s stored percentage. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect parameter reference” or “configuration‑driven arithmetic error” that leads to wrong financial calculations.

title: Incomplete implementation of state transition from Pending to Expired
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incomplete implementation of a state transition in the offer lifecycle where a Pending offer is never moved to the Expired state. The contract’s performUpkeep function contains logic that assumes a Pending->Expired transition, revoking the advertiser’s allowance when the offer expires before acceptance. However, the outer loop processes only offers that have been added to the s_offersToUpkeep set, and the checkUpkeep routine populates this set exclusively with accepted offers. Because Pending offers are never inserted into the upkeep list, the conditional branch that would set the status to Expired is never reached for those offers. As a result, offers that remain pending past their acceptanceExpirationDate stay in the Pending state indefinitely, preventing the automatic revocation of escrowed funds and leaving the advertiser’s allowance locked. From a user perspective the symptom is an offer that appears to have passed its expiration date but never emits an Expired event, the advertised funds remain unavailable, and the UI may show the offer as still active or pending. The root cause is a mismatch between the state machine’s expected transitions and the data structure that drives upkeep processing, a classic example of a missing state‑transition trigger in a smart‑contract lifecycle. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that extracted all possible state transitions and compared them against the actual code paths, revealing that the Pending->Expired edge was never exercised. It can be hard to notice because the code for the transition exists and compiles correctly; only the runtime condition that would invoke it is never satisfied due to the incomplete upkeep set population. The impact is classified as medium: no immediate loss of funds occurs, but the business logic is broken, advertisers cannot reclaim locked allowances automatically, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about offer expiration are violated. The recommended remediation is to modify checkUpkeep (or the data‑structure management) so that Pending offers are also added to s_offersToUpkeep, ensuring that performUpkeep will evaluate and execute the Pending->Expired transition as intended, and to review other state transitions for similar omissions.

title: M-01 | No Storage Gaps In Upgradable Contracts
description:
The system uses upgradable contracts. The following parent contracts don’t use storage gaps, which will result in a corrupted storage if a variable is added/removed: Omnichain:
- [VaultOCCManager](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/omnichain-ledger-1/blob/d68be172d909441ee31674a6b3cd26b143adc8bd/contracts/lib/OCCManager.sol#L25-L118)
- [LedgerAccessControl](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/omnichain-ledger-1/blob/master/contracts/lib/LedgerAccessControl.sol)
- [OCCAdapterDataLayout and LzTestData](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/omnichain-ledger-1/blob/master/contracts/lib/OCCAdapterDatalayout.sol)
- [ChainedEventIdCounter](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/omnichain-ledger-1/blob/master/contracts/lib/ChainedEventIdCounter.sol)
- [MerkleDistributor](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/omnichain-ledger-1/blob/master/contracts/lib/MerkleDistributor.sol)
- [Valor](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/omnichain-ledger-1/blob/master/contracts/lib/Valor.sol)
- [Staking](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/omnichain-ledger-1/blob/master/contracts/lib/Staking.sol)
- [Revenue](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/omnichain-ledger-1/blob/master/contracts/lib/Revenue.sol)
- [Vesting](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/omnichain-ledger-1/blob/master/contracts/lib/Vesting.sol)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a storage layout incompatibility in contracts that use the proxy‑upgrade pattern. The parent contracts in the Omnichain system do not reserve unused storage slots (commonly called a storage gap). Because the upgradeable pattern relies on a fixed ordering of state variables, adding, removing or re‑ordering variables in a contract that lacks a reserved gap shifts the positions of existing variables in storage. When a new implementation is deployed, the shifted layout causes previously stored values – such as balances, access‑control flags, or configuration parameters – to be written to the wrong slots. As a result the protocol may read zero balances, lose permission settings, or execute with corrupted accounting data. The issue manifests only after an upgrade that modifies the storage layout; during normal operation the contract behaves correctly, making the problem hard to notice in testing. All participants that rely on the contract – users, token holders, stakers, and the protocol’s governance mechanisms – can be affected because corrupted state can lead to loss of funds, denial of service, or unintended behavior. The flaw was identified during a manual audit that inspected the inheritance hierarchy and observed the absence of the standard uint256[50] private __gap; pattern recommended for upgradeable contracts. Fixing the issue requires adding a reserved storage gap to each contract in the inheritance chain and ensuring that any future upgrades only append new variables after the gap, preserving the original layout. This class of bug is known as a storage‑layout incompatibility in upgradable proxy contracts and is mitigated by reserving storage slots and following strict versioning guidelines.

title: M-02 | Missing Validations For Grants
description:
grant only validates if the array params match in length, but there are some crucial validations that should be enforced to correctly grant tokens to a holder:
- Validate that the start and cliff times are in the future.
- Ensure that the cliff time is not before the start time.
- Ensure that the amounts being granted are greater than zero.
- duration > 0
- cliffTime < startTime + duration
Additionally, when the owner creates a regrant, it will add the new amount to the exiting grant, but it will overwrite the timestamps and durations. Setting a shorter duration can allow the user to claim all tokens immediately.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of insufficient validation when creating or updating token grants in a vesting contract. The contract only checks that the input arrays have matching lengths, but it does not enforce critical business rules such as requiring the start and cliff timestamps to be in the future, ensuring the cliff occurs after the start, guaranteeing that each granted amount is greater than zero, enforcing a positive vesting duration, and confirming that the cliff time is earlier than the sum of start time and duration. Because these checks are missing, an owner can create a grant with a start time that has already passed, a cliff that precedes the start, a zero or negative amount, or a duration of zero, all of which break the intended vesting schedule. Moreover, when the owner performs a regrant, the implementation adds the new amount to the existing grant but overwrites the original timestamps and duration fields. By supplying a shorter duration in the regrant, the owner can effectively accelerate the vesting schedule, allowing the beneficiary to claim the entire token balance immediately. This flaw can be exploited by an attacker who controls the grant creation or regrant functions: they can set malicious parameters that bypass the vesting logic, causing tokens to become instantly claimable or rendering a grant ineffective. The impact includes loss of the intended vesting protection, potential premature token release, and confusion for token holders who expect a delayed release but receive tokens instantly or see zero vesting periods. The issue manifests whenever a grant or regrant transaction is executed without the missing checks, which can happen in normal operation because the contract does not reject such inputs. All token holders who rely on the vesting mechanism are affected, as are the protocol’s reputation and any downstream contracts that assume proper vesting behavior. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s intended business logic against its actual parameter validation, revealing a mismatch. Because the contract still compiles and functions, the bug may be hard to notice unless the vesting schedule is examined closely or unexpected token releases are observed. The recommended remediation is to add explicit validation clauses that enforce future start and cliff times, a cliff that is not earlier than the start, positive non‑zero grant amounts, a duration greater than zero, and a cliff that occurs before the end of the vesting period. Additionally, the regrant logic should preserve the original timestamps and duration or require explicit approval before overwriting them, preventing accidental or malicious acceleration of vesting. By aligning the implementation with the intended vesting model, the contract will prevent premature token claims and maintain the expected accounting guarantees.

title: M-03 | Signatures in Valor can be reused
description: The TREASURE_UPDATER_ROLE can call Valor.dailyUsdcNetFeeRevenue to report for USDC revenue by using a signed message. However, there are no checks if the signature has already been used which allows for one signature to be reused unlimited times.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a replay‑type flaw in the Valor contract where the function that records daily USDC net fee revenue accepts a signed message from an address that holds the TREASURE_UPDATER_ROLE, but the contract does not keep any record of whether that signature has already been processed. Because there is no nonce, timestamp check, or replay‑prevention mechanism, the same cryptographic signature can be submitted an unlimited number of times. An attacker who possesses a valid signed payload – for example a report that claims a certain amount of USDC revenue – can call the function repeatedly, causing the contract to treat each submission as a fresh revenue event. This leads to the protocol’s accounting logic counting the same revenue multiple times, which may result in excess USDC being transferred to the treasury or to an attacker‑controlled address, depending on how the revenue distribution is implemented. The issue manifests whenever the TREASURE_UPDATER_ROLE or any address that can present a valid signature invokes the dailyUsdcNetFeeRevenue function; there is no condition that blocks subsequent calls with the same signature. Users of the protocol see inflated revenue figures, unexpected USDC balances, or refunds that do not match the actual activity. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the signature verification flow and noticed the absence of any replay protection. It can be hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly on the first submission, and the repeated calls may be spaced out or hidden among legitimate updates, making the over‑counting appear as normal revenue growth. Conceptually, the fix is to treat the signed message as a one‑time authorisation by adding a unique nonce (or a sequential identifier) to the signed data, storing a hash of used nonces, and rejecting any signature that references a nonce already marked as spent. This aligns the implementation with the standard replay‑attack mitigation pattern used for off‑chain signed authorisations and restores the integrity of the protocol’s accounting and fee distribution logic.

title: Attackers can prevent users creating an offer by frontrunning
description:
The protocol allows anyone to create offers with an offer ID provided by the user. While this design gives users the flexibility to choose their offer ID, it also introduces a problem.

The `createOffer` function checks if an offer with the provided ID already exists and reverts if it does.
```solidity
TunnlTwitterOffers.sol
function createOffer(bytes32 offerId, uint256 maxPaymentUsdc, uint32 acceptanceDurationSeconds, uint32 _offerDurationSeconds) external {
    require(offerId != bytes32(0), "Invalid offerId");
    require(s_offers[offerId].creationDate == 0, "Offer already exists"); //@audit Can be abused to prevent offer creation
    require(acceptanceDurationSeconds >= s_config.minAcceptanceDurationSeconds, "AcceptanceDuration is too short");
    require(_offerDurationSeconds >= s_config.minOfferDurationSeconds, "OfferDuration is too short");
```

Malicious actors can abuse this and prevent normal users from creating offers.

Example:
- Alice, an attacker, decides to harm the protocol's reputation.
- Alice allows the `flatFee` amount of USDC to the protocol and monitors the mempool.
- A legitimate user, Bob, tries to create an offer with ID="BOB".
- Alice sends a front-running transaction to create a fake offer with the same ID.
- Alice's fake offer is created, and Bob's transaction reverts because an offer with the same ID already exists.

The impact is amplified for the following reasons:
- The protocol does not require actual funding but only an allowance for the creation of offers. Anyone can create any number of offers with a single allowance of the `flatFee` amount of USDC.
- Alice can choose to disrupt only "big" offers from reputable advertisers.

While the attack is not economically beneficial for the attacker, it is quite feasible for a possible competitor to run this kind of malicious activity. Additionally, the protocol will be deployed on Base(L2), where gas costs will be minor.

We evaluate the impact to be Medium because the attack does not directly affect users' funds and is not economically beneficial for the attacker.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running denial‑of‑service caused by allowing callers to supply an arbitrary offer identifier (offerId) when creating an offer. The createOffer function only checks whether an entry with the supplied identifier already exists and reverts with "Offer already exists" if it does, but it does not bind the identifier to the transaction sender. Because the identifier is chosen off‑chain by the user, a malicious actor who monitors the mempool can submit a transaction that creates a fake offer with the same identifier before the legitimate user’s transaction is mined. When the victim’s transaction is later processed, the existence check fails and the call reverts, preventing the offer from being created. This issue occurs whenever an attacker can see a pending offer creation request, has enough allowance to pay the flat‑fee required for offer creation, and can submit a competing transaction with a higher gas price. The affected parties are advertisers and any users who rely on being able to create offers; from the user’s perspective the UI shows a transaction failure or a revert message, contradicting the expectation that the offer will be recorded. No funds are stolen, but the protocol’s reputation and the ability of large advertisers to launch campaigns are harmed because their offers cannot be created. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the offer creation logic, where the lack of a sender‑to‑identifier relationship was identified as a potential abuse vector. The issue can be difficult to notice because the function behaves correctly for unique identifiers; the failure only appears when an identifier collision is deliberately induced. To remediate, the contract should enforce that an offer identifier is either derived from the creator’s address or that the creator’s address is stored and subsequent creations with the same identifier are rejected unless they originate from the same sender. This binds the identifier to a specific user and eliminates the ability for an external party to pre‑emptively reserve identifiers, thereby closing the front‑running denial‑of‑service vector.

title: M-04 | Vesting Claims DoS’ed With OFT Token Update
description:
orderTokenOft is set in the OmnichainLedgerV1 initialize function, but admin can use setOrderTokenOft to update this token address at a later stage. There are a couple of issue that arise when performing this update:
- LedgerOCCManager does not contain an admin function to update the orderTokenOft address. If address is updated on OmnichainLedgerV1 and not in LedgerOCCManager, users will still be able to stake with the old token address.
- LedgerOCCManager will hold orderTokenOft tokens sent from vault chains. If the token address is updated, any withdraw or claim will fail as the contract does not have balance of the new token.
- When users request vesting claims, the unclaimedOrderAmount will be sent to the orderCollector. In case admin updates the orderTokenOft, user claims will be DoS'ed as the contract may not have sufficient amount of the new token to transfer the collector.
bug_full: A denial‑of‑service vulnerability exists in the vesting claim flow of the OmnichainLedger system because the address of the order token (orderTokenOft) can be changed in the OmnichainLedgerV1 contract while the LedgerOCCManager contract continues to reference the original address. The root cause is the lack of an administrative function in LedgerOCCManager to update the stored token address and the assumption that the token balance held by LedgerOCCManager will always correspond to the address returned by OmnichainLedgerV1. When an admin calls setOrderTokenOft on OmnichainLedgerV1, the new token address is recorded, but LedgerOCCManager still holds the old token balance and still accepts stakes using the old address. Consequently, any subsequent withdraw or vesting claim attempts are routed to the new token address, for which LedgerOCCManager holds no balance. The unclaimed order amount is sent to the orderCollector, but because the contract does not own the new token, the transfer fails and the claim transaction reverts or results in a zero transfer. From a user’s perspective, a claim transaction appears to succeed on‑chain but the user receives no tokens, their displayed balance remains unchanged, and the UI may show a generic failure message. Users expect to receive their vested OFT tokens after a claim, but instead they receive nothing, effectively locking their vested assets. The issue is discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the two contracts and identified the inconsistent token address handling. It can be hard to notice because the token address change is a rare administrative action and the failure manifests only after a claim, not during staking, making the symptom appear as a generic claim failure rather than a systemic bug. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “state‑inconsistent address update” bugs where mutable configuration is not propagated to all dependent components, breaking accounting assumptions. To remediate, the protocol should avoid changing the orderTokenOft address after deployment, or if a change is required, the LedgerOCCManager contract must be equipped with a synchronized setOrderTokenOft function that updates its internal reference and ensures that the new token balance is minted or transferred to match the previous token holdings, thereby preserving the integrity of staking and vesting operations.

title: M-05 | Staking esOrder Without Balance
description: ProxyLedger allows users to stake ORDER or esORDER. When the isEsOrder flag is set to true, users will effectively stake esORDER on the OmnichainLedgerV1 contract, but will also be charged ORDER tokens, due to the fact that vaultSendToLedger will deduct the staked amount from the user balance. Therefore, user will end up with an esORDER stake, and ORDER tokens will be sent to the LedgerOCCManager contract. Although user will be able to unstake, vest and re-claim the ORDER tokens, this is an unexpected behavior as esORDER staking should not be triggered directly. Additionally, if future upgrades give more reward weight to esORDER staking, users will be able to game the system by creating an esORDER stake with ORDER tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the staking entry point of the ProxyLedger contract, which permits a caller to indicate that the stake should be made with the synthetic token esORDER by setting the isEsOrder flag to true. When this flag is true the contract forwards the request to the OmnichainLedgerV1 contract, correctly crediting the caller with an esORDER position. However, the internal routine vaultSendToLedger that records the stake always deducts the amount from the caller's balance of the base token ORDER, regardless of the flag value. Consequently the user ends up holding an esORDER stake while the ORDER tokens that were supposed to be staked are instead transferred to the LedgerOCCManager contract. This behavior contradicts the intended business logic that esORDER staking should be a separate, optional pathway that does not consume ORDER tokens. The flaw originates from a missing conditional check that distinguishes between ORDER and esORDER when debiting the user’s balance, i.e., the contract treats both token types identically in the debit step. An attacker can exploit the bug by deliberately invoking stake(true) with any amount of ORDER, thereby converting ORDER into an esORDER position without actually providing esORDER tokens. The immediate impact is a loss of ORDER tokens from the user’s wallet, which appear as a zero or reduced ORDER balance in the UI while the esORDER balance rises unexpectedly. Users may notice that after staking they receive no ORDER tokens back, see their ORDER balance drop to zero, and yet a new esORDER stake is recorded. The issue manifests whenever a user attempts to stake using the esORDER flag, which can be done by any address interacting with the contract. It primarily affects token holders who wish to stake, the protocol’s accounting layer, and any downstream reward distribution that assumes correct token classification. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the staking flow, where the auditor observed that the debit operation did not respect the isEsOrder flag. The bug is subtle because the contract still records a successful stake and the UI may display the new esORDER balance, masking the hidden loss of ORDER tokens. To remediate, the staking function should explicitly use the ORDER token reference when the intention is to stake ORDER, and the isEsOrder parameter should be removed or its handling revised so that vaultSendToLedger only deducts the appropriate token type. In conceptual terms, the fix requires separating the accounting paths for the two token classes and ensuring that a synthetic token stake does not trigger a debit of the base token. This class of bug can be described as an incorrect token‑type handling or cross‑token debit error, leading to unintended token conversion and potential reward manipulation.

title: M-06 | Users May Receive Rewards For Only 1 Batch
description:
The intended batch flow is as follows:
1. Users redeem valor in batch A.
2. Batch A finishes.
3. A trusted role marks the batch as claimable.
Whenever a user redeems their valor or claim USDC, _collectUserRevenueForClaimableBatch is called to increase their withdrawable amount by adding the withdrawable amounts of the first claimable batch. If there are users that redeem their valor in between steps 2 and 3 from above (so batch A is finished and batch B is active) when they claim USDC when batch B becomes claimable they will be given the reward from only the first claimable batch even though they are entitled to rewards from two batches.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reward‑allocation logic error that causes a user to receive USDC rewards from only the first claimable batch, even when the user is entitled to rewards from multiple batches. The root cause is that the internal function that aggregates a user’s withdrawable revenue (_collectUserRevenueForClaimableBatch) adds the withdrawable amount of the first batch marked claimable and then stops, instead of iterating over all batches that have become claimable. This flaw appears when a user redeems valor after a batch has finished but before the next batch is marked claimable. The user then waits until the subsequent batch becomes claimable and calls the claim function; the contract only credits the reward from the earlier batch and ignores the reward earned in the later batch. As a result, the user’s balance is lower than expected, effectively causing part of the earned reward to disappear. The issue is triggered only under the specific timing condition where a user’s redemption occurs between the finish of one batch and the claimable marking of the next batch, and it is exposed when the user later claims after the second batch becomes claimable. All users who interact across batch boundaries are affected, leading to loss of earned rewards and potential erosion of trust in the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the batch‑claim flow and identified that the reward‑collection loop does not handle multiple claimable batches. Because the normal single‑batch path works correctly, the bug can be subtle and may only be noticed when users report that their reward amount is unexpectedly low or when they see a zero balance after claiming across batches. To remediate, the contract should be modified so that the reward‑collection routine aggregates the withdrawable amounts of every batch that is currently claimable for the user, ensuring that all earned rewards are credited before the transfer is executed. This change restores the intended accounting behavior where each user receives the full sum of rewards earned across all claimable batches.

title: M-01 | No Storage Gaps In Upgradable Contracts
description:
The system uses upgradable contracts. The following parent contracts don’t use storage gaps, which will result in a corrupted storage if a variable is added/removed: OFT:
- [OFTAdapterUpgradable](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/oft-team-1-pocs/blob/audit/contracts/layerzerolabs/lz-evm-oapp-v2/contracts/oft/OFTAdapterUpgradeable.sol)
- [OFTCoreUpgradable](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/oft-team-1-pocs/blob/audit/contracts/layerzerolabs/lz-evm-oapp-v2/contracts/oft/OFTCoreUpgradeable.sol)
- [OFTUpgradable](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/oft-team-1-pocs/blob/audit/contracts/layerzerolabs/lz-evm-oapp-v2/contracts/oft/OFTUpgradeable.sol)
- [OAppCoreUpgradable](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/oft-team-1-pocs/blob/audit/contracts/layerzerolabs/lz-evm-oapp-v2/contracts/oapp/OAppCoreUpgradeable.sol)
- [OAppReceiverUpgradable](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/oft-team-1-pocs/blob/audit/contracts/layerzerolabs/lz-evm-oapp-v2/contracts/oapp/OAppReceiverUpgradeable.sol)
- [OAppSenderUpgradable](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/oft-team-1-pocs/blob/audit/contracts/layerzerolabs/lz-evm-oapp-v2/contracts/oapp/OAppSenderUpgradeable.sol)
- [OAppUpgradable](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/oft-team-1-pocs/blob/audit/contracts/layerzerolabs/lz-evm-oapp-v2/contracts/oapp/OAppUpgradeable.sol)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing storage gap in a set of upgradable contracts that implement the OFT protocol. Upgradable contracts that use a proxy delegatecall pattern must preserve the exact order and size of state variables across upgrades. When a contract does not reserve unused storage slots (commonly called a storage gap), adding, removing, or reordering a variable in a future implementation shifts the storage layout. As a result, values that were stored in earlier slots are written to the wrong slot after an upgrade, corrupting the contract's state. This can cause token balances, configuration parameters, or access control flags to be overwritten with incorrect data. An attacker who can trigger an upgrade – either by possessing the upgrade role or by exploiting a governance flaw – can introduce a new variable that deliberately collides with an existing slot, causing the contract to lose or misreport balances, block withdrawals, or even allow unauthorized transfers. The impact is that users may see their balances become zero, refunds may not be sent, or the protocol may halt because accounting assumptions are broken. The issue manifests only when a new implementation is deployed; during normal operation the contract appears functional, making the bug hard to notice in testing. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the source code, where the auditor observed that none of the listed parent contracts contain the typical uint256[50] private __gap storage gap that is recommended for future‑proofing. Because the corruption occurs only after an upgrade, developers may not see any symptom until a later version is released, at which point funds can be irretrievably lost. The proper mitigation is to add a reserved storage gap in each upgradable contract, preserving a number of empty slots that can be used for future state variables without altering the layout of existing slots. This aligns the contracts with the standard upgradeable‑contract pattern and prevents storage‑collision attacks.

title: M-02 | Ordered Nonce Flag Should Only Be Set Once
description: The OrderOFT and OrderAdapter contracts are initialized with orderedNonce flag enabled, although owner can turn this flag on and off as pleased using setOrderedNonce. When orderedNonce is set to false, messages can be executed in any order, increasing the maxReceivedNonce. If the orderedNonce is turned on back again, there will be issues with messages that were not executed with lower nonces, as the only acceptable nonce will be maxReceivedNonce + 1.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns a mutable orderedNonce flag in the OrderOFT and OrderAdapter contracts. Theflag is intended to enforce that cross‑chain messages are processed strictly in increasing nonce order, but the contracts expose an owner‑only function setOrderedNonce that can toggle the flag on and off at any time. When the flag is set to false, the contracts relax the ordering requirement, allowing messages with any nonce to be executed. Each successful execution updates an internal maxReceivedNonce value to the highest nonce seen. If the owner later re‑enables orderedNonce, the contract resumes enforcing that only the next nonce (maxReceivedNonce + 1) may be accepted. Any previously unprocessed messages that have a lower nonce than maxReceivedNonce are then permanently rejected because the contract no longer permits gaps in the sequence. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: users who submitted messages while the flag was off may see their transactions never being executed, their funds remaining locked in the contract, and no error indicating why the message was dropped. The issue arises because the ordering logic assumes the flag’s state is immutable after deployment; toggling it breaks the invariant that all lower nonces must have been processed before a higher one. It is hard to notice because the flag change is an owner action that does not emit a warning about pending nonces, and the contract does not perform a sanity check when the flag is re‑enabled. The impact is limited to the protocol’s message‑passing layer but can affect any user relying on ordered delivery, leading to missing refunds, stalled cross‑chain transfers, or inconsistent accounting. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the lifecycle of the orderedNonce flag and its interaction with maxReceivedNonce. To remediate, the contract should either remove the ability for the owner to change the flag after deployment or restrict the function to only disable orderedNonce permanently, ensuring that once the strict ordering requirement is relaxed it cannot be reinstated and thereby preserving the nonce monotonicity invariant. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of mutable state‑control vulnerabilities where a security‑critical flag can be flipped, invalidating previously established protocol guarantees.

title: M-07 | Incorrect Calculation Of USDC Required Per Batch
description:
The Revenue contract tracks the amount of USDC tokens required per batch id, for users to redeem.
It uses the fixedValorToUsdcRateScaled to calculate the USDC amount based on the batch valor amount.
This USDC amount calculation is missing the VALOR_TO_USDC_RATE_PRECISION correction, so the value returned is greater than expect, thus invalid. Additionally, if the batch id is not claimable yet, the fixedValorToUsdcRateScaled value is not set (value 0), so all amounts will be 0 due to the multiplication.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the USDC amount required for a batch redemption in the Revenue contract. The contract stores a fixed conversion rate called fixedValorToUsdcRateScaled and multiplies it by the batch valor amount to derive the USDC requirement. However, the implementation omits a division by the constant VALOR_TO_USDC_RATE_PRECISION, which is necessary to adjust the units of the scaled rate. As a result, the computed USDC amount is larger than the mathematically correct value, causing users to be asked for more USDC than needed. In addition, when a batch has not yet become claimable, the fixedValorToUsdcRateScaled variable is left at its default value of zero. The multiplication with a zero rate yields a required USDC amount of zero, which prevents legitimate redemption because the contract treats the zero as an invalid or non‑claimable amount. The bug can be exploited by a malicious actor who submits a redemption request with an inflated USDC amount, causing honest users to either over‑pay or be blocked from claiming, effectively locking funds in the contract. The impact includes failed redemption attempts, potential loss of user funds due to over‑payment, and disruption of the protocol’s revenue accounting because the internal accounting assumes the wrong USDC requirement. The condition occurs whenever the contract calculates the required USDC for any batch, especially during the early phase before the rate is set or for any batch after the rate is set but the precision correction is missing. All users who interact with the redemption function are affected, but the most visible effect is on users trying to claim their rewards. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the on‑chain calculation with the expected mathematical formula and noticed a mismatch in units. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings and the UI may simply display a higher required amount without indicating the underlying scaling error. The proper fix is to incorporate a division by VALOR_TO_USDC_RATE_PRECISION after the multiplication, thereby normalising the units of the scaled rate, and to ensure that the rate is correctly initialised before any batch becomes claimable. Conceptually, this is a unit‑conversion or scaling‑factor omission bug, a common class of arithmetic errors where a multiplier is applied without the corresponding divisor, leading to inflated or zero results that break business logic such as refund calculations and accounting invariants. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a required USDC amount that is unexpectedly large or zero, the transaction may revert with an “insufficient amount” error, and the expected refund or redemption never arrives, violating the expectation that the contract will return the correct amount of USDC for a given batch.

title: M-08 | Incorrect Access Control For setTotalUsdcInTreasure
description: setTotalUsdcInTreasure was meant to be called by the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE and not the TREASURE_UPDATER_ROLE, as the latter will use dailyUsdcNetFeeRevenue which validates signatures and checks timestamps.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect access‑control configuration on the function that updates the recorded amount of USDC held in the protocol treasury. The function setTotalUsdcInTreasure was intended to be callable only by accounts that possess the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, which represents the highest level of governance authority. However, the contract mistakenly grants the TREASURE_UPDATER_ROLE permission to invoke this function. The root cause is a mismatched onlyRole modifier that does not enforce the intended admin‑only restriction. Because the TREASURE_UPDATER_ROLE is also used by the dailyUsdcNetFeeRevenue routine, which includes signature verification and timestamp checks, allowing this role to call setTotalUsdcInTreasure bypasses those protective checks. An attacker who can acquire the TREASURE_UPDATER_ROLE—through a compromised key, delegated permission, or any other means—can call setTotalUsdcInTreasure and arbitrarily set the total USDC balance reported by the contract. This manipulation can corrupt accounting, inflate or deflate the treasury balance, and consequently affect downstream fee calculations, reward distributions, and any logic that relies on the correct treasury total. Users may notice symptoms such as unexpected zero balances, missing fee rewards, or rewards that appear larger than expected, because the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated. The issue manifests whenever setTotalUsdcInTreasure is invoked, which under normal operation should be restricted to the admin role but is currently exposed to a lower‑privileged role. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit when the auditor observed that the access‑control modifier did not match the documented design. It can be hard to notice because the function itself may appear to work correctly and the role mismatch does not produce an immediate runtime error; the impact only becomes visible through incorrect accounting outcomes. To remediate the issue, the access‑control modifier on setTotalUsdcInTreasure should be changed to require onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE), ensuring that only the designated admin can modify the treasury total, and any additional validation logic from dailyUsdcNetFeeRevenue should be retained for functions that require it. This correction restores the intended governance hierarchy and prevents unauthorized manipulation of treasury accounting.

title: M-09 | Valor May Be Redeemed At An Undesirable Rate
description:
A user may observe that redeeming valor in batch A is quite profitable so they initiate a redeemValor request. However, due to their transaction taking quite a long time to be executed and delivered to the Orderly Network, their redeem request may now end up in batch B. In batch B the redeeming terms may not be as good as the user desired.
For example, a lot of valor accumulated without much profit or the admin called Valor.setTotalUsdcInTreasure to decrease the usdc. The user will not be able to stop the transaction and in result, they will redeem at undesirable rate.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the redeemValor function, which allows a user to exchange Valor tokens for USDC based on the exchange rate defined for the current batch. The contract does not bind a redemption request to the batch that was active at the moment the transaction was submitted. Consequently, if the transaction experiences a delay—such as network congestion, long execution time, or ordering latency—it may be mined and processed in a subsequent batch. Because the protocol permits the admin to modify the total USDC available in the treasure (for example via Valor.setTotalUsdcInTreasure) between batches, the exchange rate can change from the user’s expectation. An attacker or any user can therefore submit a redeem request while a profitable batch (batch A) is visible, but the transaction may be executed in batch B where the rate is less favorable, resulting in a lower amount of USDC received. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful redemption, yet the received amount is far below the anticipated value, appearing as if funds disappeared or the refund calculation is wrong. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the flow of batch‑dependent state and noticed the absence of a batch identifier in the redeem call. It is difficult to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit warning about batch changes, and the transaction receipt only indicates success, not the rate applied. The impact is financial loss for users who rely on the displayed rate, erosion of trust in the protocol’s accounting guarantees, and potential exploitation by users who deliberately time transactions to land in a more advantageous batch. The flaw belongs to the class of “state‑dependent race conditions” where mutable protocol parameters can be altered between request submission and execution. To remediate, the function should accept an explicit batchId argument and verify that the current batch matches this identifier, reverting the transaction if a mismatch is detected. This change forces the redemption to occur only under the exact batch conditions observed by the user, eliminating the possibility of an undesirable rate caused by batch migration.

title: M-10 | Claiming Rewards Possible When Distributor Paused
description:
According to the comments in MerkleDistributor:
Contract is pausable by owner. It allows to pause claiming rewards.
However, claimRewards doesn't have the whenNotPaused modifier. This is most likely because claimRewards calls function updateRoot which implements it. However, the call to updateRoot is conditional - it happens only if there is an upgrade possible. Otherwise, claiming is still possible - even in paused state.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a pause bypass in the MerkleDistributor contract. The contract is designed to be pausable by the owner, with the intention that when the pause flag is set, users should not be able to claim their Merkle‑based rewards. The claimRewards function, however, does not carry the whenNotPaused modifier. Instead it relies on an internal call to updateRoot, which does have the whenNotPaused guard, but that call is executed only when a root upgrade is possible. When the contract is paused and no upgrade is required, the conditional branch skips updateRoot, leaving claimRewards executable. This logical omission allows anyone to invoke claimRewards and receive rewards even though the contract is in a paused state. The root cause is the missing access‑control check on the external entry point and the conditional gating of the pause enforcement. An attacker can simply call claimRewards while the contract is paused, and the function will process the Merkle proof, transfer the allocated tokens, and update the user’s claimed bitmap. The impact is that the pause mechanism, which is expected to freeze reward distribution, is ineffective; funds that should be locked remain claimable, potentially leading to unexpected depletion of the reward pool. This occurs whenever the owner has called pause and the Merkle root does not need updating. Users, protocol operators, and token holders are affected because they rely on the pause to protect against further claims during emergencies or upgrades. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by reviewing contract comments and noticing the mismatch between the documented pause behavior and the actual code path. It can be hard to notice because the pause flag appears to work for other functions, and the claimRewards function still succeeds silently, giving the impression that the contract is functional while actually violating its security guarantees. To remediate, the claimRewards function should be protected directly with the whenNotPaused modifier, or the internal logic should be refactored so that pause enforcement is unconditional for any claim path. This aligns the implementation with the intended business rule that no rewards may be claimed while the distributor is paused, restoring trust in the protocol’s accounting and emergency controls.

title: M-11 | USDC Claims Will Fail When Using OFT Wrappers
description:
In order to make a batch claimable, admins need to update the totalUsdcInTreasure using dailyUsdcNetFeeRevenue. If the USDC amount added has 6 decimal precision (as most USDC tokens), then the user will receive a 6 decimal amount when the ClaimUsdcRevenueBackward payload is executed.
bool success = IERC20(usdcAddr).transfer(message.receiver, message.tokenAmount);
The protocol plans to allow claims in multiple chains, using both native USDC or OFT wrappers. The issue is that OFT tokens have 18 decimals by default. Therefore, users will receive less tokens than expected when using OFT wrappers (If the protocol launches on BSC, the pegged USDC token has 18 decimals).
Additionally, as the ProxyLedger will transfer native USDC tokens, it should use safeTransfer instead.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a decimal‑precision mismatch that occurs when users claim USDC revenue on chains where the protocol uses an Omnichain Fungible Token (OFT) wrapper instead of the native 6‑decimal USDC contract. Admins update the total USDC amount using a value expressed with six decimals, but the claim payload forwards that same raw amount to an OFT token that by default has 18 decimals. Because the contract does not rescale the amount, the transfer call sends a value that is interpreted as 18‑decimal units, effectively reducing the user’s payout by a factor of 10^12. The result is that a user who expects to receive, for example, 100.000000 USDC will actually receive 0.000000100000 USDC, appearing as a missing or dramatically reduced balance. This underpayment happens whenever the ClaimUsdcRevenueBackward function is executed on a chain that employs the OFT wrapper (such as BSC where the pegged USDC token is an OFT with 18 decimals). The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the claim logic and noticed that the transfer uses IERC20.transfer without safeTransfer and that the decimal handling was not adjusted for the wrapper token. The bug is subtle because the transaction succeeds, the UI may show a successful claim, and the user only notices that the received amount is far lower than expected, making it easy to miss without detailed balance checks. The impact is financial loss for any user claiming revenue, a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, and potential loss of trust in the multi‑chain revenue distribution mechanism. The root cause is the assumption that all USDC‑like tokens share the same 6‑decimal precision, which is invalid for OFT wrappers that default to 18 decimals, combined with the lack of safeTransfer which could hide failed transfers. To remediate, the protocol should deploy an OFT wrapper that overrides the decimals function to return 6, or explicitly convert the amount to the wrapper’s decimal space before calling transfer. Additionally, the contract should replace IERC20.transfer with a safeTransfer pattern that checks the return value and reverts on failure, ensuring that under‑payment or failed transfers are not silently ignored.

title: M-12 | getRemainingBalance Should Round Up
description:
Vestings are linearly unlocked after a cliff period during the release duration. Claimable balance of a vesting is calculated by subtracting the remaining balance from the total balance.
However, remaining balance of a vesting is calculated using the mulDiv formula from Math Library and this formula rounds down by default. Rounding down the remaining balance means rounding up the claimable balance.
Total claimable amounts will not be affected from this but intermediary claims will give users slightly more tokens than it should.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error in the vesting contract that determines how many tokens a user can claim at any point after the cliff period. The contract calculates the remaining balance of a vesting schedule using the mulDiv function from a standard Math library. By default mulDiv rounds the result down, which means the remaining balance is slightly smaller than the mathematically exact value. Because the claimable amount is derived by subtracting the remaining balance from the total allocated balance, a smaller remaining balance produces a claimable amount that is rounded up. Consequently, when a user makes an intermediate claim, the contract may credit the user with a few extra tokens compared to the intended linear release schedule. The issue is discovered during a formal audit that inspected the arithmetic of the vesting logic and noticed that the rounding direction favoured the claimant rather than the protocol. It is hard to notice because the total amount that can ever be claimed over the full vesting period remains unchanged; only the distribution of tokens across individual claim events is affected, so a casual test that only checks the final balance may miss the problem. The impact is that users can receive slightly more tokens earlier than expected, which can be abused to front‑run claims, distort the token supply curve, and undermine the economic assumptions of the protocol that rely on a smooth linear release. The bug manifests when the vesting schedule is queried for the claimable amount or when a claim transaction is executed after the cliff but before the end of the release duration. Any participant who interacts with the vesting contract – typically token holders with vested allocations – is affected because they may see a higher claimable balance in the UI and receive more tokens than the schedule intends. From a user‑facing perspective the symptoms are a claim transaction that returns a few extra tokens, a displayed claimable amount that is marginally higher than the linear formula would predict, and a remaining balance that appears lower than expected after the claim. The root cause is the use of a rounding‑down division in a formula that should round in favour of the protocol. To fix the issue the contract should invoke the mulDiv function with an explicit rounding‑up option, or otherwise adjust the arithmetic so that the remaining balance is rounded up (or the claimable amount is rounded down), ensuring that intermediate claims never exceed the schedule’s intended amount. This class of bug belongs to arithmetic precision or rounding‑direction errors, which are common in financial smart contracts where exact token accounting is required.

title: M-13 | Recall Can Be Frontrunned
description:
Owner has a right to recall a grant and this function returns unclaimed tokens to the owner from the holder. Returning unclaimed tokens:
1. Creates unfair situations between holders. Let’s assume there are two different holders with exact same cliff and release duration parameters but one of them claimed unlocked part of his vesting and the other didn’t claim anything yet. Recalling from both of these holders results in different user balances.
2. Creates a surface for frontrunning attacks. Users can frontrun the recall and claim their vestings’ claimable portion just before the recall.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a contract function that allows the contract owner to recall a grant by transferring any unclaimed tokens from a holder back to the owner. The function does not differentiate between tokens that are still locked and tokens that have already vested and are claimable by the holder.
