As a result, when the owner initiates a recall, a holder who has already claimed the vested portion retains those tokens, while a holder who has not yet claimed loses the entire unclaimed balance, even though part of that balance was already vested. This creates an unfair situation because two users with identical cliff and release parameters can end up with different post‑recall balances solely based on whether they exercised their claim earlier. Moreover, the recall can be front‑run: a malicious actor or even an honest holder can observe the pending recall transaction, submit a claim for the vested portion in the same block, and have that claim mined before the recall. The front‑runner therefore extracts the claimable tokens, leaving the owner to retrieve only the remaining locked tokens, effectively stealing the vested amount. The impact is a loss of expected funds for users who rely on the contract’s vesting logic, a breach of the accounting assumptions that vested tokens are protected until the owner explicitly revokes the grant, and a potential erosion of trust in the protocol. The issue manifests whenever the owner calls the recall function while there are pending claimable tokens for any holder, and it is exploitable by anyone able to monitor the mempool and submit a higher‑gas transaction. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the recall logic and identified that the function returns the full unclaimed balance without checking the already‑vested portion. It can be difficult to notice because the recall appears to be a standard administrative action and the loss of tokens may be attributed to normal vesting behavior rather than a malicious front‑run. To remediate, the contract should be changed so that recall only retrieves the portion of the grant that remains locked (i.e., tokens that are not yet vested) or introduce a separate function that explicitly excludes already‑vested tokens from being recalled. This adjustment restores the intended accounting guarantees, prevents unfair balance discrepancies, and eliminates the front‑running attack surface.

title: M-14 | Lack Of Withdraw Functions
description:
LedgerOCCManager, OCCManager (and potentially OmnichainLedgerV1) are expected to hold ORDER / USDC tokens which are burned or transferred when users claim.
The issue lies with the lack of a withdraw function for Owner to recover these tokens from the contract. Owner may wish to do this during a migration to a new contract.
Without a withdraw function, these tokens may become permanently stuck in the contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the absence of any mechanism that allows the contract owner to retrieve ERC‑20 tokens that remain locked in the contract after normal user operations such as claiming or burning. The contracts in question are designed to hold ORDER and USDC tokens temporarily; when a user claims, the tokens are supposed to be either burned or transferred out. However, because no withdraw function is implemented, any tokens that for any reason stay in the contract’s balance become inaccessible to the owner. This situation can arise during routine migrations to a newer contract version, when the owner may need to move residual token balances to the new deployment. The root cause is a missing public or only‑owner function that would invoke the ERC‑20 transfer method to send the remaining balance to a designated address. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker does not need to interact with the contract; the risk is that the legitimate owner is unable to recover the tokens, effectively causing permanent loss of funds. The impact is that users may see their expected refunds or token balances disappear from the user interface, while the contract still holds the assets, leading to a mismatch between on‑chain accounting and the protocol’s business logic. The condition occurs whenever tokens are left in the contract after a claim, a failed transfer, or during a migration event. All parties that rely on the contract’s ability to manage token flows—users, the protocol’s treasury, and the contract owner—are affected. The issue was identified during a manual audit that compared the contract’s intended token lifecycle with the actual exposed functions and noted the lack of any withdrawal entry point. Because the contract does not emit explicit errors or revert when tokens are stuck, the problem can be subtle and may only be discovered when balances are audited or when a migration is attempted. To remediate, the contract should be extended with a withdraw function restricted to the owner (or a governance role) that safely calls the ERC‑20 transfer method for each supported token, includes proper checks for successful transfer, and emits an event documenting the withdrawal. This aligns the implementation with the expected accounting model, prevents permanent token lock‑up, and restores confidence that the protocol can manage residual balances correctly.

title: Infinite loop in the `exitValidators()` prevents users from calling `requestUnstake()`
bug_full: When a user calls the requestUnstake() function to withdraw their staked ETH, the CasimirManager contract first checks whether the current expected withdrawable balance can satisfy all pending unstake requests. If the balance is insufficient, the contract invokes a private helper called exitValidators() with a count of validators that need to be exited. The exitValidators() implementation iterates over the stakedValidatorIds array using a while loop that decrements the count and increments an index only when the examined validator has status ACTIVE. The root cause of the vulnerability is that the loop does not advance the index when a validator’s status is not ACTIVE. Consequently, if the first validator in the list (or any validator examined while count is still positive) is not ACTIVE, the condition inside the if‑statement is never satisfied, the index remains unchanged, count never decreases, and the while loop runs forever. In practice the transaction consumes the caller’s entire gas limit and then reverts, leaving the user with no change to their balance. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a failed transaction, often reported as an out‑of‑gas error, and the expected ETH refund never arrives. This denial‑of‑service effect can be weaponised: a malicious actor with a small stake can front‑run a large staker’s requestUnstake, ensure that the first validator in the list is in a non‑ACTIVE state, and cause the whale’s unstake transaction to run out of gas, effectively delaying or blocking the withdrawal of a substantial amount of ETH. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Cyfrin, where the static analysis highlighted that the loop variables count and index are not updated in all execution paths. The bug is subtle because the loop appears correct when all validators are ACTIVE; only the edge case of a non‑ACTIVE validator triggers the infinite iteration, which may not be exercised by typical unit tests. The vulnerability belongs to the class of infinite‑loop denial‑of‑service bugs caused by missing loop‑control updates. To remediate, the code should guarantee progress on each iteration—by incrementing the index regardless of validator status, adding a break condition when no further ACTIVE validators exist, or refactoring the loop into a bounded for‑loop that safely exits. Proper handling ensures that requestUnstake either successfully exits enough validators or fails gracefully without exhausting gas, restoring the expected behavior where users can retrieve their funds after an unstake request.

title: Multiple unstake requests can cause denial of service because withdrawn balance is not adjusted after every unstake request is fulfilled
bug_full: The contract contains a denial‑of‑service style accounting bug in the function that processes pending unstake requests. The function iterates over a configurable number of requests with a while loop, and for each request it calls a helper that checks whether the request can be fulfilled based on the variable withdrawnEffectiveBalance. This variable represents the amount of ETH that the manager contract believes it can safely return to users. However, withdrawnEffectiveBalance is only adjusted after the loop finishes, not after each individual transfer. As a result, the loop may treat the balance as unchanged even though ETH has already been sent out in previous iterations. When multiple unstake requests are processed in a single call, the contract can therefore honour more requests than the actual withdrawable balance permits. The final accounting step attempts to subtract the total amount that was sent (unstakedAmount) from withdrawnEffectiveBalance and, if necessary, from an auxiliary unassignedBalance. If the summed amount exceeds the stale balance, the subtraction underflows or triggers a revert, leaving the transaction incomplete. From a user’s point of view the symptom is that a staker who initiates an unstake may see the transaction revert or may receive no ETH even though the request was accepted, effectively causing funds to disappear or become locked. The issue occurs only when the fulfillUnstakes function is called with a count that allows more than one request to be processed and when the pool’s effective withdrawable balance is smaller than the aggregate of those requests. It affects any participant who relies on timely refunds, the overall protocol’s ability to finalize a reporting period, and any downstream contracts that assume the manager’s balance accounting is sound. The bug was discovered during a manual audit by Cyfrin, which noted that the getNextUnstake helper uses a stale balance variable and that the loop does not update the balance after each transfer. The problem is subtle because each individual request appears valid when checked, masking the cumulative over‑draw. To remediate the issue the contract should either update withdrawnEffectiveBalance (and possibly unassignedBalance) after each successful transfer, or compute the remaining withdrawable amount before entering the loop and stop processing once that limit is reached. In either case the accounting must reflect the real ETH balance after every iteration, preventing the function from fulfilling more unstake requests than the contract can actually pay and eliminating the potential for a revert that blocks further operations.

title: Spamming `requestUnstake()` to cause a denial of service in the unstake queue
description:
**
- The function `requestUnstake()` allows users to request any amount, even `amount = 0`.
- The contract processes all unstake requests in a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue, handling earlier requests before later ones.
- The `remove()` function has a time complexity of O(n), which consumes gas.

This means an attacker could repeatedly call `requestUnstake()` to enlarge the unstake queue, causing the gas consumption of `fulfillUnstake()` to exceed the block gas limit.

** Excessive gas usage when calling `fulfillUnstake()` could exceed the block gas limit, causing a DOS.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by an unbounded unstake request queue. The contract’s requestUnstake function accepts any amount, including zero, and each call appends a new entry to a FIFO queue that is later processed by fulfillUnstake. The queue removal routine uses a linear‑time (O(n)) algorithm, so the gas required to iterate and delete entries grows proportionally with the number of pending requests. An attacker can repeatedly invoke requestUnstake with a zero amount, inflating the queue without any economic cost per call. As the queue becomes large, the gas needed for a single fulfillUnstake call can exceed the block gas limit, preventing the function from completing and effectively locking all legitimate unstake operations. This situation manifests to users as pending unstake requests that never resolve, UI elements that show a request but no balance change, and transactions that either revert or remain pending indefinitely. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the contract’s queue management logic and noticed the lack of a minimum unstake amount combined with an inefficient removal implementation. It is difficult to spot because each individual request consumes little gas and appears harmless, yet the cumulative effect can cripple the system. The bug belongs to the class of resource‑exhaustion or gas‑limit denial‑of‑service vulnerabilities, where unchecked data structures enable an attacker to consume all available gas. To remediate, the contract should enforce a non‑zero minimum unstake amount that makes spamming economically impractical, consider imposing a cap on the number of pending requests, and replace the O(n) removal with a constant‑time data structure or batch processing approach. These changes restore the expected behavior where users can request and receive refunds reliably, aligning the contract’s accounting with its business logic and preventing funds from becoming inaccessible due to a clogged queue.

title: Users could avoid loss by frontrunning to request unstake
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running exploitation path that allows a participant to avoid a loss that is automatically applied to all stakers when a validator is slashed. When a slash occurs the contract’s finalizeReport() function detects a negative change value, computes a loss amount and reduces the global rewardStakeRatioSum and the latestActiveBalanceAfterFee, effectively decreasing every user’s stake proportionally. The root cause is that the unstake mechanism permits a new unstake request to be created and fulfilled within the same reporting period, because the getNextUnstake() view function treats any request whose period field is less than or equal to the current reportPeriod as immediately fulfillable. Since unstake requests are processed in a FIFO queue, a malicious actor can observe a pending slash in the mempool, submit an unstake request, and have it satisfied before the loss accounting is applied, thereby withdrawing their stake at the pre‑slash value while the loss is still deducted from the remaining pool. This can be exploited by monitoring the mempool for slash reports, submitting an unstake transaction with a higher gas price, and ensuring the request is placed at the front of the queue or that the queue is empty, so the contract’s getNextUnstake() returns a fulfillable request in the same period. The impact is unfair loss distribution: honest stakers see their balances reduced, while the front‑runner retains the full amount and any accrued rewards, effectively stealing value from the protocol and other participants. The condition under which this occurs is any slashing event that triggers a negative change during a report period combined with the ability to create and satisfy an unstake request before the accounting update is finalized. All stakers, especially those who do not monitor the mempool, are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions—that losses are shared proportionally among all participants—are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Cyfrin, where the logic of the unstake queue and the period check was examined and identified as allowing immediate fulfillment. The bug is subtle because the loss is reflected only in a reduction of a global ratio variable, not in an explicit transfer, making it easy to miss in casual testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce a delay or waiting period for unstake requests so that they cannot be fulfilled in the same report period they are created, and optionally impose a small fee on unstake operations to discourage rapid front‑running. This change restores the intended accounting model where slashing losses are distributed fairly among all active stakers.

title: Centralization risks with a lot of power vested in the `Reporter` role
description:
** In the current design, the `Reporter`, a protocol-controlled address, is responsible for executing a number of mission-critical operations. Only `Reporter` operations include starting & finalizing a report, selecting & replacing operators, syncing/activating/withdrawing and depositing validators, verifying & claiming rewards from EigenLayer, etc. Also noteworthy is the fact that the timing and sequence of these operations are crucial for the proper functioning of the Casimir protocol.

** With so many operations controlled by a single address, a significant part of which are initiated off-chain, the protocol is exposed to all the risks associated with centralization. Some of the known risks include:

- Compromised/lost private keys that control the `Reporter` address
- Rogue admin
- Network downtime
- Human/Automation errors associated with the execution of multiple operations
bug_full: The vulnerability is a centralization risk caused by the design of the Casimir protocol where a single protocol‑controlled address, called the Reporter, is granted authority to perform a wide range of mission‑critical actions such as starting and finalizing reports, selecting and replacing operators, syncing, activating, withdrawing and depositing validators, and verifying and claiming rewards from EigenLayer. This concentration of power creates a single point of failure because the Reporter’s operations are largely initiated off‑chain and depend on the availability and correctness of the private key and the admin that controls it. If the private key is compromised, lost, or the controlling admin acts maliciously, an attacker can manipulate report lifecycles, replace honest operators with malicious ones, block validator deposits or withdrawals, and claim rewards that should belong to the protocol, effectively draining funds or freezing the system. The impact is that users may see their expected rewards disappear, their validator balances become zero, or withdrawals fail, leading to a loss of confidence and potential financial loss. The issue manifests whenever the off‑chain process that drives the Reporter fails, such as during network downtime, human error, or automation bugs, because no alternative mechanism exists to execute the required functions. The vulnerability was identified during a security audit that examined the contract’s access control model and noted the disproportionate authority assigned to a single address. It can be hard to notice in normal operation because the protocol behaves correctly as long as the Reporter functions as intended, masking the underlying trust assumption. To remediate, the protocol should reduce reliance on a single address by introducing multi‑signature control, continuous monitoring of off‑chain processes, and a clear migration path toward decentralized governance, thereby distributing authority and mitigating the risk of key compromise, rogue admin actions, or operational outages.

title: `ChainlinkUtil::getPrice` doesn't check for stale price
description:
** [`ChainlinkUtil::getPrice`](https://github.com/zaros-labs/zaros-core-audit/blob/de09d030c780942b70f1bebcb2d245214144acd2/src/external/chainlink/ChainlinkUtil.sol#L32-L33) doesn't [check for stale prices](https://medium.com/zaros-labs/chainlink-oracle-defi-attacks-93b6cb6541bf#99af).

** Code will execute with prices that don’t reflect the current pricing resulting in a potential loss of funds for users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing freshness validation in the function that retrieves a price from a Chainlink oracle. The contract calls the oracle’s latestRoundData but never checks the returned timestamp (updatedAt) against the feed’s expected heartbeat interval. Because the contract assumes the price is current, it may accept a value that has not been refreshed for a period longer than the oracle’s heartbeat. An attacker who can cause the feed to become stale, for example by delaying updates or by exploiting a temporary outage, can make the contract use an outdated price. When the stale price is used in calculations such as collateral valuation, liquidation thresholds, or margin requirements, the protocol may compute incorrect amounts, leading to unexpected liquidations, loss of user funds, or incorrect accounting balances. This issue manifests when a price feed has not been updated within its heartbeat window; the contract proceeds without reverting, so users see symptoms like their position being liquidated despite no market movement, balances dropping to zero, or refunds being calculated incorrectly. The bug was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, and it is subtle because the price value itself appears plausible and no explicit error is thrown. The root cause is the absence of a timestamp check, which violates the business logic that assumes oracle data reflects the current market. To remediate, the contract should compare the updatedAt timestamp to the feed’s heartbeat (or a configurable freshness threshold) and revert if the data is stale, thereby restoring the intended accounting guarantees and preventing funds from disappearing due to outdated price information.

title: Protocol operator can disable settlement for market with open positions, making it impossible for traders to close their open positions but still subjecting them to potential liquidation
description:
** `GlobalConfiguration::updateSettlementConfiguration` allows the protocol operator to disable settlement for markets without checking if those markets have open positions; this allows the operator to disable settlement for a market with open positions.

** The protocol can enter a state where traders who previously opened leveraged positions in a market are subsequently unable to close those positions. However these positions are still subject to liquidation since the liquidation code continues to function even when settlement is disabled.

Hence the protocol can enter a state where traders are unfairly severely disadvantaged; unable to close their open leveraged positions but still subject to liquidation if the market moves against them.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a configuration function that lets the protocol operator turn off settlement for any market without first verifying whether traders still hold open leveraged positions in that market. Because the check is missing, the operator can disable settlement after users have entered positions. When settlement is disabled, the contract that processes market orders rejects any attempt to close a position, reverting with a SettlementDisabled error. However, the liquidation routine does not consult the settlement flag and continues to evaluate and liquidate positions that remain open. Consequently, a trader who wishes to exit a losing position finds the close function unavailable, while the same position can still be forcibly liquidated by the protocol, potentially wiping out the trader’s collateral. This situation can arise whenever the operator disables settlement for a market that already has active positions, for example during maintenance or a governance action. The affected parties are the traders holding open positions, who expect to be able to close or unwind their exposure, and the protocol itself, which may be perceived as unfair or unsafe. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that included a concrete proof‑of‑concept test: after opening a BTC position, the test disabled settlement for the BTC market, attempted to close the position (which reverted), then forced a price move that made the position liquidatable and successfully liquidated it. From a user’s perspective the UI would show the market as closed or disabled, yet the trader’s balance would not change when trying to close, and later the trader could see a sudden loss of collateral due to liquidation. The bug belongs to the class of “inconsistent state transition” or “partial disablement” bugs where one contract pathway (closing) respects a disabled flag while another pathway (liquidation) ignores it, breaking the accounting invariants of the system. To remediate the problem the protocol should either forbid disabling settlement while any open positions exist, or modify the close‑position logic to remain functional even when settlement is disabled, ensuring that all state‑changing actions respect the same enable/disable flag and that traders can always unwind their positions safely.

title: Update to funding rate parameters retrospectively impacts accrued funding rates
description:
** On centralized perpetuals protocols funding rates are typically settled every 8 hours however on Zaros they "accrue" and are settled when the trader interacts with their position. The protocol owner also has the power to alter funding rate parameters which when altered apply retrospectively.

** Traders who are not frequently modifying their positions can be either positively or negatively retrospectively impacted by changes to the funding rate parameters. The retrospective application is unfair to traders because traders are under the impression that they are accruing funding rates at the current configuration parameters.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a retroactive funding‑rate calculation flaw in a perpetual futures protocol where funding accrues continuously but is only settled when a trader interacts with their position. Because the contract reads the current global funding parameters at the moment of settlement, any change to those parameters by the protocol owner is applied to the entire accrued amount, even for periods that occurred before the change. This design allows the owner to increase (or decrease) the funding velocity or other rate‑defining variables while positions remain open, causing the accrued funding to be recomputed with the new, higher (or lower) rates. Traders who keep their positions open for long periods without frequent interactions are especially vulnerable: when they finally close or withdraw, the settlement logic retroactively applies the updated parameters, resulting in a larger funding charge than the trader expected based on the parameters that were in effect when the position was opened. The impact is a loss of funds that appears as an unexpected reduction in the user’s balance after closing a position, often manifested as “my balance dropped more than the fees I paid” or “the funding fee suddenly jumped at settlement”. The issue occurs only when (1) funding is accrued but not settled on a regular schedule, (2) the protocol owner modifies funding‑rate‑related configuration while positions are open, and (3) the trader does not interact with the position during the interval. It primarily affects users who are inactive or who rely on the assumption that funding rates are calculated using the parameters that were active at the time of accrual. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that added a test case: the test opened a position, waited a week, changed the max funding velocity ten‑fold, and then closed the position, observing a noticeably lower final balance compared to the baseline where no parameter change occurred. The problem is subtle because the UI typically shows no funding charge until settlement, so users may not notice the discrepancy until after they have closed the position, making it hard to attribute the loss to a parameter change. To remediate, the protocol should either settle funding on a fixed interval (e.g., every eight hours) or freeze the funding parameters for each open position at the time of its last settlement, ensuring that subsequent configuration changes only affect new accrual periods. In decentralized environments where on‑chain governance may limit immediate parameter freezes, a hybrid approach of periodic settlement combined with a snapshot of parameters per position can mitigate retroactive re‑calculation and restore fairness to traders.

title: `SettlementBranch::_fillOrder` doesn't pay order and settlement fees if PNL is positive
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the SettlementBranch::_fillOrder function where the handling of order and settlement fees diverges depending on the sign of the calculated profit‑and‑loss (PNL). During PNL calculation the contract adds the order fee and settlement fee to the PNL value (line 161), effectively treating those amounts as a deduction from the trader's profit. However, when the resulting PNL is positive the execution follows the branch starting at line 204, which simply converts the positive PNL into a UD60x18 amount and deposits it into the trader's account without ever transferring the previously accounted fees to their designated recipients. The root cause is a missing fee‑payment step in the positive‑PNL path; the code only pays fees in the negative‑PNL branch where a loss is covered, leaving the positive‑PNL branch incomplete. An attacker or any user who can generate a profitable trade can trigger this branch, causing the protocol to retain the fee amounts that should have been sent to the order‑fee and settlement‑fee beneficiaries. The impact is that fee recipients receive less than they are entitled to, which can erode the economic incentives of the protocol, reduce funding for settlement operations, and potentially allow malicious actors to siphon fees over time. This condition occurs whenever the filled order results in a PNL greater than zero after the fee deduction step. Affected parties include the fee recipients (often the protocol treasury or third‑party partners), the protocol’s accounting layer, and indirectly any users relying on correct fee distribution for trust. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Cyfrin, where the logical flow of fee handling was examined and the asymmetry between the two branches was identified. It can be hard to notice because the contract still deposits the correct profit amount to the trader, so the transaction appears successful, and the missing fee transfers do not cause a revert or obvious error. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the expected profit, but the fee pool remains unchanged, leading to a discrepancy between expected and actual fee balances. Conceptually, this bug belongs to the class of “conditional fee omission” or “incorrect accounting of fees based on sign of profit”. To remediate, the contract should ensure that order and settlement fees are transferred to their recipients regardless of whether the PNL is positive or negative, typically by deducting the fee amounts from the net profit before depositing to the trader or by explicitly invoking the fee‑payment logic in both branches. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that fees are always owed, preserving accounting integrity and protocol security.

title: `ChainlinkUtil::getPrice` doesn't check if L2 Sequencer is down
description:
** When using Chainlink with L2 chains like Arbitrum, smart contracts must [check whether the L2 Sequencer is down](https://medium.com/zaros-labs/chainlink-oracle-defi-attacks-93b6cb6541bf#0faf) to avoid stale pricing data that appears fresh.

** Code will execute with prices that don’t reflect the current pricing resulting in a potential loss of funds for users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract's price retrieval function does not verify the operational status of the L2 sequencer before using the value returned by the Chainlink data feed. On L2 networks such as Arbitrum, the Chainlink price feed continues to return the last known price even when the underlying sequencer is offline. Because the contract assumes the returned price is fresh, it may execute trades, liquidations, or other financial logic with a stale price that appears recent. This situation arises whenever the sequencer experiences downtime, which can be caused by network congestion, maintenance, or an attacker deliberately disrupting the sequencer. An attacker does not need to manipulate the price feed directly; they only need to wait for or induce sequencer downtime, after which the contract will accept the unchanged price as current. Users interacting with the contract will see a normal price display in the UI, but the actual market price may have moved significantly, leading to unexpected losses, failed liquidations, or incorrect accounting. The issue was identified during a security audit by Cyfrin, which referenced known best‑practice guidance that L2 contracts must check the sequencer status. The bug is subtle because the price feed still returns a timestamp that looks recent, so developers and users may not notice that the data is stale. To remediate, the contract should query the dedicated Chainlink sequencer status feed and revert or pause operations when the sequencer is reported as down, or fallback to an alternative source. This class of bug falls under “stale oracle data due to missing health‑check” and violates the assumption that oracle data always reflects the current market state.

title: `ChainlinkUtil::getPrice` will use incorrect price when underlying aggregator reaches `minAnswer`
description:
** Chainlink price feeds have in-built minimum & maximum prices they will return; if due to an unexpected event an asset’s value falls below the price feed’s minimum price, [the oracle price feed will continue to report the (now incorrect) minimum price](https://medium.com/zaros-labs/chainlink-oracle-defi-attacks-93b6cb6541bf#00ac).

[`ChainlinkUtil::getPrice`](https://github.com/zaros-labs/zaros-core-audit/blob/de09d030c780942b70f1bebcb2d245214144acd2/src/external/chainlink/ChainlinkUtil.sol#L32-L33) doesn't handle this case.

** Code will execute with prices that don’t reflect the current pricing resulting in a potential loss of funds for users.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a price‑retrieval helper that reads a value from a Chainlink aggregator without verifying that the returned answer respects the feed’s built‑in bounds. Chainlink price feeds define a minimum (minAnswer) and maximum (maxAnswer) price; when an asset’s market price falls below the minimum, the oracle continues to emit the static minAnswer instead of the actual market price. Because the helper function does not check whether the fetched answer lies between minAnswer and maxAnswer, it may accept this stale minimum value as if it were current. An attacker who can trigger a sharp price drop—through market manipulation, a flash‑loan‑driven attack, or by exploiting a temporary oracle outage—can force the feed into its minimum‑price state. The contract then uses the incorrect price for downstream calculations such as swaps, collateral valuations, or liquidation triggers. From a user’s perspective the protocol appears to operate normally, but the user may receive far fewer tokens than expected, see a sudden loss of collateral, or be liquidated at an unfair price. The impact is a potential loss of funds for any participant that relies on the price, and it can also undermine the overall economic safety of the protocol. The issue occurs only when the underlying aggregator’s answer is outside the allowed range, a condition that is not obvious because the feed still returns a numeric value. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the price‑fetching logic and compared it against Chainlink’s documented behaviour. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit any warning or revert; the incorrect price silently propagates through the system. To remediate, the price‑retrieval function should explicitly compare the answer with the feed’s minAnswer and maxAnswer and revert if the answer is out of bounds, thereby preventing the use of a stale or capped price. This class of bug is a range‑validation omission in oracle integration, leading to accounting mismatches where the protocol’s accounting assumptions (that the oracle always reflects the true market price) are violated.

title: Users can easily bypass collateral `depositCap` limit using multiple deposits under the limit
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the enforcement of a collateral deposit cap that is intended to limit the total amount of a specific margin collateral that can be locked in the protocol. The contract implements a private check called _requireEnoughDepositCap which only compares the amount being deposited in a single transaction against the configured depositCap. Because the function does not consider the cumulative amount already deposited for that collateral type, an attacker can repeatedly call the deposit routine with amounts that are each individually below the cap. By chaining many such deposits, the attacker can push the total collateral balance far beyond the intended limit. This flaw originates from a logical error in the validation routine: it uses a simple greater‑than comparison on the incoming amount instead of verifying that the sum of the existing balance and the new amount stays within the cap. Exploitation is straightforward – a malicious user submits a series of small deposits, each passing the per‑transaction check, until the aggregate exceeds the cap. The impact is that the protocol’s risk controls are bypassed; the system may believe that sufficient collateral is present while in reality the cap has been violated, potentially leading to under‑collateralized positions, unexpected liquidations, or loss of funds for other participants. The condition occurs every time a deposit is made, regardless of who initiates it, and affects any user who interacts with the margin collateral module, as well as the protocol itself because its accounting assumptions are broken. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit by Cyfrin, where the auditors noted that the validation logic does not aggregate deposits. It can be hard to notice because each individual transaction succeeds and no error is emitted, so the breach of the cap is only visible when the total balance is inspected after many deposits. From a user’s perspective the symptom may be that they are able to deposit more than expected, or later the system may reject withdrawals or trigger liquidation despite apparent excess collateral, creating confusion when balances do not match the documented limits. The bug belongs to a class of cumulative limit enforcement errors where per‑action checks are insufficient to enforce a global constraint. To remediate the issue the _requireEnoughDepositCap function should be rewritten to retrieve the current total deposited amount for the given collateral type, add the new deposit amount, and revert if that sum exceeds the configured depositCap, thereby ensuring the cap is respected across all transactions.

title: Anyone can cancel traders' market orders due to missing access control in `OrderBranch::cancelMarketOrder`
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unauthorized state‑change caused by a missing access‑control check in the function that cancels market orders. The contract exposes an external function cancelMarketOrder that accepts a tradingAccountId, loads the associated market order and calls marketOrder.clear() before emitting a LogCancelMarketOrder event. Because the function does not verify that msg.sender is the owner of the supplied trading account, any address can invoke it with any valid tradingAccountId. An attacker can therefore call cancelMarketOrder, causing the target trader's pending market order to be cleared from the order book without the trader’s consent. This results in the order disappearing, the trader receiving no execution, and potentially missing a profitable trade or incurring additional gas costs to recreate the order. The issue occurs whenever the function is called, as there is no conditional check restricting the caller. It affects all users who hold trading accounts on the protocol, undermining the integrity of the order matching system and exposing traders to loss of expected outcomes. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by Cyfrin, where the logical flow of the function was examined and the absence of an ownership verification step was noted. Because the function appears to be a normal administrative operation and does not revert on unauthorized calls, the problem can be subtle and may only be noticed when orders vanish unexpectedly. The bug belongs to the class of missing authorization vulnerabilities, where privileged state‑changing functions are callable by anyone. To remediate, the function should load the trading account and verify that the caller matches the account owner before proceeding, for example by invoking a helper that checks sender against the stored owner address. This restores proper access control, prevents unauthorized cancellations, and aligns the contract with expected security and business‑logic assumptions that only the account holder can cancel their own orders.

title: Protocol operator can disable market with open positions, making it impossible for traders to close their open positions but still subjecting them to potential liquidation
description:
** `GlobalConfigurationBranch::updatePerpMarketStatus` allows the protocol operator to disable markets without checking if those markets have open positions; this allows the operator to disable a market with open positions.

** The protocol can enter a state where traders who previously opened leveraged positions in a market are subsequently unable to close those positions. However these positions are still subject to liquidation since the liquidation code continues to function even when markets are disabled.

Hence the protocol can enter a state where traders are unfairly severely disadvantaged; unable to close their open leveraged positions but still subject to liquidation if the market moves against them.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a market‑status validation flaw that allows the protocol operator to disable a perpetual market even when traders have open leveraged positions. The root cause is that the function responsible for changing a market's enabled flag does not verify whether any accounts hold non‑zero positions in that market, and the order‑execution path checks the market status and reverts with a PerpMarketDisabled error, while the liquidation routine ignores the disabled flag and continues to evaluate and liquidate positions. An attacker with operator privileges can therefore mark a market as disabled after users have opened positions; those users will find that attempts to close or reduce their positions are rejected, yet the same positions remain subject to the normal liquidation logic. When the market price moves against the trader, the protocol can liquidate the position, seizing the trader’s collateral, even though the trader was unable to voluntarily close the position. From the user’s point of view the UI shows a transaction failure when trying to close the trade, often with a message like “PerpMarketDisabled”, and the expected refund or profit does not arrive; later the user may see their balance reduced or their collateral taken without having been able to act. This situation violates the fundamental accounting assumption that a trader can always exit a position before liquidation, leading to unfair loss of funds and eroding trust in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a security audit through a targeted integration test that opened a position, disabled the market, attempted a close (which reverted), then forced a price move that made the position liquidatable and confirmed that liquidation succeeded. The bug can be hard to notice because disabling a market is a rare administrative action and the liquidation path still works, so the loss may only be observed after an adverse price movement. To remediate, the contract should either prevent disabling a market while any open positions exist, or it should allow users to close or reduce positions even when the market is marked disabled, while still permitting liquidation to protect the system’s solvency.

title: Liquidation leaves traders with unhealthier and riskier collateral basket, making them more likely to be liquidated in future trades
description:
** The protocol's proposed collateral priority queue with associated Loan-To-Value (LTV) is:
```
1 - USDz   - 1e18 LTV
2 - USDC   - 1e18 LTV
3 - WETH   - 0.8e18 LTV
4 - WBTC   - 0.8e18 LTV
5 - wstETH - 0.7e18 LTV
6 - weETH  - 0.7e18 LTV
```

This means that the protocol will:
* first liquidate the more stable collateral with higher LTV
* only after these have been exhausted will it liquidate the less stable, riskier collaterals with lower LTV

** When a trader is liquidated, their resulting collateral basket will contain less stable, more riskier collateral. This makes it more likely they will be liquidated in future trades.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a business‑logic flaw in the liquidation routine of the protocol where the algorithm prioritises the liquidation of the most stable collateral assets that have the highest loan‑to‑value (LTV) ratios before touching the less stable, lower‑LTV assets. Because the priority queue is ordered to exhaust high‑LTV, stable tokens such as USDz and USDC first, a trader who is liquidated ends up retaining a basket composed mainly of volatile assets like WETH, WBTC, wstETH and weETH. This happens because the liquidation function iterates through the priority list and only after the high‑LTV positions are fully seized does it start to liquidate the lower‑LTV positions. An attacker or any market participant can trigger a liquidation on a vulnerable trader, causing the protocol to strip away the safer collateral and leave only the riskier tokens. The impact is that the trader’s remaining collateral becomes more exposed to price swings, increasing the probability of a subsequent liquidation even if the original position was only marginally under‑collateralised. The condition occurs whenever a trader’s health factor falls below the liquidation threshold and the protocol’s liquidation queue is invoked. All users who provide collateral to the system are affected because the design flaw can repeatedly erode their safety buffer, potentially leading to a cascade of liquidations and loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the liquidation logic, where the auditor observed that the priority ordering contradicted typical risk‑mitigation practices. It may be hard to notice because the protocol still performs a liquidation and the user does receive some collateral back, but the returned assets are of a different risk profile, which is not immediately obvious from the UI. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that after a liquidation the displayed collateral balance is lower and consists of volatile tokens, and the user may see unexpected zero or near‑zero returns when trying to withdraw or trade the remaining assets. This violates the business assumption that liquidation should preserve the safest possible collateral mix to protect users from further loss. The conceptual fix is to invert the priority queue so that the protocol first liquidates the most volatile, low‑LTV assets, thereby preserving the higher‑LTV stable assets for the trader and reducing the chance of repeat liquidations.

title: Keeper fills market order using incorrect old `marketId` but newly updated position size when trader updates open order immediately before keeper processes original order
description:
** Consider the following scenario:
1) A trader creates an order for the BTC market with position size POS_SIZE_A
2) Some time passes and the order is not filled by the keeper
3) At the same time:
3a) The keeper attempts to fill the trader's current open BTC order
3b) The trader creates a transaction to update their order to a different market with position size POS_SIZE_B

If 3b) is executed before 3a) then when 3a) is executed the keeper will fill the order:
* for the incorrect old BTC market
* but with the newly updated position size POS_SIZE_B!

** The keeper will fill the order for an incorrect market with an incorrect position size.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race condition that allows a keeper to fill a market order using a market identifier that belongs to an earlier version of the order while applying the position size from a later version of the order. The contract stores the order parameters in a mutable structure and the fillMarketOrder function receives the marketId as an argument but does not verify that the stored order still has the same marketId at the moment of execution. When a trader submits an order for market A and, before the keeper processes it, submits a second transaction that overwrites the same order slot with a new market B and a different size, the keeper may later call fillMarketOrder with the original marketId (A). Because the contract reads the size from the current order storage, which now contains the size for market B, the fill is performed on market A with the size intended for market B. This mismatch can be exploited by a trader who deliberately updates the order to a different market and size, causing the keeper to open a position on an unintended market with an unexpected exposure. The impact is that the user ends up holding a position on a market they never intended, often with a size that does not match their expectation, which can lead to unwanted risk, potential liquidation, or loss of funds. The condition required for the bug to manifest is a specific ordering of transactions: the order‑update transaction must be mined before the keeper’s fill transaction, and the fill function must not re‑read or validate the marketId against the stored order. All traders who rely on the ability to modify open orders, as well as keepers and the protocol’s risk engine, are affected because the accounting assumptions that a filled order corresponds to the market and size originally requested are violated. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin through an integration test that simulated the exact transaction ordering. It is hard to notice because the fill transaction succeeds without reverting, and the UI may simply display a new position on the wrong market, making the problem appear as a normal trade rather than an error. The bug belongs to the class of time‑of‑check‑to‑time‑of‑use (TOCTOU) or stale‑state vulnerabilities where mutable order data is used after it has been changed. The recommended remediation is to add a check in SettlementBranch::fillMarketOrder that re‑validates the marketId against the stored order and reverts if they differ, or to make the order data immutable for the duration of the fill operation. By ensuring that the market identifier used for the fill matches the identifier stored at the moment the order was created, the protocol can prevent unintended cross‑market fills and preserve the integrity of user positions.

title: `TradingAccount::getAccountMarginRequirementUsdAndUnrealizedPnlUsd` uses incorrect price during order settlement
description:
** During order settlement `SettlementBranch::_fillOrder` uses an off-chain price provided by the keeper:

```solidity
File: SettlementBranch.sol
120:         ctx.fillPrice = perpMarket.getMarkPrice(
121:             ctx.sizeDelta, settlementConfiguration.verifyOffchainPrice(priceData, ctx.sizeDelta.gt(SD_ZERO))
122:         );
123:
124:         ctx.fundingRate = perpMarket.getCurrentFundingRate();
125:         ctx.fundingFeePerUnit = perpMarket.getNextFundingFeePerUnit(ctx.fundingRate, ctx.fillPrice);
```

All variables including `ctx.fillPrice` and `ctx.fundingFeePerUnit` are calculated based on this price.

But during the margin requirement validation in `TradingAccount::getAccountMarginRequirementUsdAndUnrealizedPnlUsd` the price input provided by the keeper is not used, instead this uses an index price:

```solidity
File: TradingAccount.sol
207:             UD60x18 markPrice = perpMarket.getMarkPrice(sizeDeltaX18, perpMarket.getIndexPrice());
208:             SD59x18 fundingFeePerUnit =
209:                 perpMarket.getNextFundingFeePerUnit(perpMarket.getCurrentFundingRate(), markPrice);
```

** All calculations in `TradingAccount::getAccountMarginRequirementUsdAndUnrealizedPnlUsd` may be incorrect as the price provided by the keeper may differ from the current index price. Hence during an order settlement `TradingAccount::getAccountMarginRequirementUsdAndUnrealizedPnlUsd` may return incorrect outputs.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a price‑source inconsistency that occurs during order settlement. When a keeper supplies an off‑chain price to SettlementBranch::_fillOrder, the fill price and funding fee per unit are computed with that price. Immediately afterwards TradingAccount::getAccountMarginRequirementUsdAndUnrealizedPnlUsd is called to validate the account’s margin requirement and to compute unrealized PnL. Instead of re‑using the keeper‑provided price, the function fetches the market’s index price via perpMarket.getIndexPrice and uses it to calculate a mark price. Because the off‑chain price can differ from the index price, the margin requirement and unrealized PnL may be calculated on a different price basis than the fill price that actually affected the position. This mismatch can cause the contract to report a lower margin requirement than is truly needed, allowing a trader to open or maintain a position with insufficient collateral, or to display an unrealized PnL that does not match the UI’s expectation. The bug manifests only during the settlement flow, i.e., when an order is filled and the margin check is performed; it does not affect other read‑only queries. All participants who rely on accurate margin checks – traders, liquidators, and the protocol itself – are potentially affected because the accounting assumptions that margin must cover the worst‑case price movement are violated. The issue was identified by the Cyfrin audit team through code review of the settlement and margin‑validation logic. It is subtle because both price sources are legitimate values, so the discrepancy does not raise an obvious error flag, and the resulting margin numbers may appear plausible while actually being incorrect. The proper fix is to pass the keeper‑provided off‑chain price into TradingAccount::getAccountMarginRequirementUsdAndUnrealizedPnlUsd (or to compute the mark price in the same way as SettlementBranch) so that the same price is used consistently for fill price, funding fee, margin requirement and unrealized PnL calculations. This aligns the accounting model with the business rule that margin must be evaluated on the price that actually settled the trade, preventing under‑collateralisation and ensuring that users see the expected PnL and margin numbers.

title: For extreme ratios, `getRatiosFromPriceSwap` will return data for which is impossible to converge into a reserve
description:
The Basin team has implemented look up table to fetch pre-calculated values, which are close to the `targetPrice` to decrease the complexity of `calcReserveAtRatioSwap` and `calcReserveAtRatioLiquidity` functions.

[Stable2LUT1](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-basin/blob/7d5aacbb144d0ba0bc358dfde6e0cc913d25310e/src/functions/StableLUT/Stable2LUT1.sol#L740) has a function `getRatiosFromPriceSwap`, which returns `PriceData` struct based on provided `price`.

We can see that in case of super extreme price, the function will revert with `LUT: Invalid price`, but there is also support for extreme prices, which we assume should work correctly, when such situation occurs.

We will investigate an edge case, which is present when we enter `if (price < 0.213318e6)` and price is above `0.001083e6`. In such situations, the function will return the following struct:

```solidity
PriceData(
    0.213318e6, // highPrice
    0.188693329162796575e18,
    2.410556040105746423e18,
    0.001083e6, // lowPrice                       
    0.005263157894736842e18,                      
    10.522774272309483479e18,
    1e18
);
```

If you notice, we have a large gap between `highPrice` and `lowPrice` and more precisely. The following results in large jump in reserves calculation when `updateReserve` which leads to skipping the target price sequentially, which moves away `pd.currentPrice` until we exit the `for` loop, which returns 0.

Here is an estimation of the impact based on the PoC which is below:

**For a ratio `~ 1:4.6` of the price of the tokens:**

  * We have a `targetPrice` of 212104 (0.21).
  * We end up with reserves for a price `44957 (0.04)`, which is `~ X5` less than the requested amount.
  * As result we receive `3623929482258792273`, instead of `2421185918213441156`, which is a big difference.
  * Note that we don’t return the compromised data, but this is the calculated value on the last iteration.
poc:
Place the following test inside `/test/beanstalk/BeanstalkStable2.calcReserveAtRatioLiquidity.t.sol` and run it with `forge test --mt "test_calcReserveAtRatioSwapSkipTarget" -vv`:

```solidity
function test_calcReserveAtRatioSwapSkipTarget() public view {
    uint256[] memory reserves = new uint256[](2);
    reserves[0] = 1e18;
    reserves[1] = 1e18;
    uint256[] memory ratios = new uint256[](2);
    ratios[0] = 4202;
    ratios[1] = 19811;

    // 4202 * 1e6 / 19811  = 212104 = 0.212 / 1  = 1 : 4.6
    //                                0.04  / 1  = 1 : 25    

    uint256 reserve1 = _f.calcReserveAtRatioSwap(reserves, 1, ratios, data);
    //console.log("Reserves 1 :", reserve1);
}
```

You can further add `console.log` inside the for loop of `calcReserveAtRatioSwap` and log `pd.currentPrice` on each update. Notice that each time, the current price is further away from the target. Here are logs:

```
Logs:
  We want  212104
  Lud Data High:  213318
  Lud Data Low:  1083
  Max step size:  1858346112180059079
  Scaled reserves when closest J:  2421185918213441156
  Scaled reserves when closest I:  188693329162796575
  Rate at iteration  0  is  209986
  Rate at iteration  1  is  215834
  Rate at iteration  2  is  205646
  Rate at iteration  3  is  223618
  Rate at iteration  4  is  192647
  Rate at iteration  5  is  247954
  Rate at iteration  6  is  156345
  Rate at iteration  7  is  320536
  Rate at iteration  8  is  83844
  Rate at iteration  9  is  409344
  Rate at iteration  10  is  42030
  Rate at iteration  11  is  291810
  Rate at iteration  12  is  106911
  Rate at iteration  13  is  401234
  Rate at iteration  14  is  44576
  Rate at iteration  15  is  306730
  Rate at iteration  16  is  94144
  Rate at iteration  17  is  409601
  Rate at iteration  18  is  41952
  Rate at iteration  19  is  291337
  Rate at iteration  20  is  107346
  Rate at iteration  21  is  400812
...
```
bug_full: The vulnerability originates in the lookup‑table based function that translates a requested price into a pre‑computed PriceData structure. When a caller supplies a price that lies in an extreme but not ultra‑extreme range (for example a price of roughly 0.212 × 10⁶, corresponding to a token ratio of about 1 : 4.6), the function selects a PriceData entry whose highPrice and lowPrice values are far apart – 0.213318 × 10⁶ versus 0.001083 × 10⁶. This large gap causes the subsequent reserve‑calculation routine (calcReserveAtRatioSwap or calcReserveAtRatioLiquidity) to iterate over a price‑adjustment loop that never converges to the target price. Each iteration moves the current price farther away from the desired value, eventually exiting the loop with a reserve estimate that is dramatically lower than expected – in the PoC the computed reserve is about five times smaller than the correct amount, and the function may even return zero. The root cause is the insufficient granularity of the lookup table for extreme price ratios, which provides data that does not guarantee a monotonic approach to the target price. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker can craft a swap request with a price in the problematic interval, causing the protocol to allocate far fewer tokens than the user should receive. From the user’s perspective the UI will show a successful swap, but the received token balance will be unexpectedly low or zero, violating the expectation that the swap amount matches the quoted price. The impact affects any participant performing swaps or providing liquidity on the Basin stable‑swap pool, leading to loss of value and broken accounting assumptions that reserves should reflect the quoted price. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit when a test case exercised the extreme‑ratio path and observed the divergent loop behaviour; it is subtle because the function does not revert and the lookup table appears to return a valid struct, making the failure easy to miss in casual testing. To remediate the problem the lookup table should be regenerated with finer granularity for extreme ratios, or the algorithm should include a safety check that aborts when the price gap exceeds a safe threshold, ensuring that the reserve‑calculation loop can always converge to the target price. In essence, the bug is a classic case of an out‑of‑range lookup leading to non‑convergent iterative computation, breaking the protocol’s financial guarantees.

title: In `Stable2LUT1::getRatiosFromPriceLiquidity`, in extreme cases, `updateReserve` will start breaking
poc:
Test case for underflow: paste the following inside `BeanstalkStable2LiquidityTest` and run `forge test --match-contract BeanstalkStable2LiquidityTest --mt test_calcReserveAtRatioLiquiditExtreme -vvvv`:

```solidity
function test_calcReserveAtRatioLiquiditExtreme() public view {
        uint256[] memory reserves = new uint256[](2);
        reserves[0] = 1e18;
        reserves[1] = 1e18;
        uint256[] memory ratios = new uint256[](2);
        ratios[0] = 8;
        ratios[1] = 1;

        uint256 reserve0 = _f.calcReserveAtRatioLiquidity(reserves, 0, ratios, data);
    }
```

Logs:

```
  Target Price:  125000
  Original Current Price:  1083
  --------------------------------
  Reserve before step:  2000000000000000000000
  --------------------------------
  Reserve:                2000000000000000000000
  Amount to decrease by:  893822359084720968727
  Current Price at iteration  0 1993
  Reserve:                1106177640915279031273
  Amount to decrease by:  887258462712414537152
  Current Price at iteration  1 10817
  Reserve:                218919178202864494121
  Amount to decrease by:  823610307119851952292
```

As you can see, the code attempts massive corrections to the reserve in order to achieve convergence, but the amount to decrease the reserve is too large and the function underflows.

Test case when lowering `lowPriceJ`: run the same test as before, but change `lowPriceJ` to `10e18`, for example purposes:

```solidity
if (price < 0.001083e6) {
                                    revert("LUT: Invalid price");
                                } else {
                                    return
                                        PriceData(
                                            0.27702e6, 
                                            0, 
                                            9.646293093274934449e18, 
                                            0.001083e6, 
                                            0, 
                                      ->    10e18, 
                                            1e18);
                                }
```

Logs:

```
Target Price:  125000
  Original Current Price:  1083
  --------------------------------
  Reserve before step:  10000000000000000000
  --------------------------------
  Reserve:                10000000000000000000
  Amount to decrease by:  158841687633952488
  Current Price at iteration  0 272070
  ...
  Reserve:                20736004517896372313
  Amount to increase by:  8588323693661738
  Current Price at iteration  254 131644
  END OF NEWTON's METHOD
```

The logs are compacted as they are very large, but the idea is this:

  1. Target price is again much larger than current price.
  2. During the first correction, the price moves by a very large amount, making it much larger than target price.
  3. Now `updateReserves` has to do corrections in the other direction (increase the reserve), so that the prices can converge on the target price, but this never happens, as Newton’s method ends after 255 iterations and leaves the loop.
  4. `calcReserveAtRatioLiquidity` will return 0, as `reserve` is never initialized anywhere, effectively making the function useless.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Stable2LUT1 contract, specifically in the getRatiosFromPriceLiquidity routine that calculates reserve adjustments using a Newton‑style iteration. When the market price is very close to the configured lowPrice (approximately 0.001083e6) while the target price is near the highPrice (around 0.27702e6), the algorithm sets pd.currentPrice to the lowPrice and scales the reserve with the factor lowPriceJ/precision. Because lowPriceJ is extremely large (e.g., 2000e18), the first correction step attempts to move the reserve by an amount that far exceeds the actual reserve balance. This oversized decrement drives the reserve value to zero and then attempts a further subtraction, triggering an arithmetic underflow panic and causing the function to revert. Even if lowPriceJ is reduced, the huge gap between lowPrice and highPrice makes the convergence loop diverge: the price overshoots the target, the algorithm flips direction, and after many iterations it aborts without ever reaching the desired price, ultimately returning a reserve of zero. The root cause is the combination of an unbounded price range and an excessively large scaling constant, which together produce correction steps that are mathematically unsound for extreme inputs. An attacker can deliberately invoke the function with a price just above the lowPrice threshold, causing the contract to revert and effectively deny service to any caller that relies on this liquidity calculation. The impact is that liquidity provisioning or rebalancing operations may fail, users see no change in their balances, and the protocol may be unable to compute correct reserves, potentially freezing funds or producing misleading zero‑reserve results. The issue manifests only under edge‑case price conditions, making it easy to miss during normal testing because typical price values stay well within the safe range. It was discovered by the Code4rena audit team through targeted unit tests that exercised extreme price values and observed the underflow panic. Fixing the problem requires both lowering lowPriceJ to a reasonable magnitude and narrowing the allowed price interval so that highPrice and lowPrice are much closer, thereby limiting the size of each correction step. A more robust solution would also involve adding explicit bounds on the reserve adjustment magnitude or redesigning the convergence algorithm to avoid large jumps altogether. From a user perspective the contract either reverts with a generic panic or silently returns a zero reserve, leading to symptoms such as "my transaction failed", "no liquidity was added", or "my balance stayed at zero despite a deposit". This class of bug is a numeric overflow/underflow caused by unbounded iterative correction in financial calculations, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that reserves must remain positive and converge to the target price.

title: `YieldEthStakingLido` lacks a limit on the max stake amount, which may result in the unstake exceeding `MAX_STETH_WITHDRAWAL_AMOUNT`, resulting in the token not being retrieved
bug_full: The vulnerability in the YieldEthStakingLido contract stems from the absence of any validation on the amount that can be staked, which later becomes the amount requested for withdrawal. Lido’s withdrawal queue imposes a hard per‑request ceiling called MAX_STETH_WITHDRAWAL_AMOUNT (currently 1,000 stETH). When a user stakes an amount that exceeds this ceiling – for example a leveraged position that translates to more than roughly $500,000 worth of stETH – the subsequent call to unstake triggers the unstETH.requestWithdrawals function with the full withdraw amount. Because the amount is larger than the allowed maximum, Lido’s requestWithdrawals reverts, the contract does not receive a valid withdrawal request identifier, and the user’s stETH remains locked inside the YieldEthStakingLido contract. From a user’s perspective the unstake transaction fails silently, the UI may show a successful transaction hash but the token balance does not change, leading to confusion and the expectation that a refund should be received while in reality nothing is returned. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s withdrawal logic with Lido’s documented limits; it is subtle because the staking path works correctly and only the withdrawal path fails, making the bug easy to miss unless the edge case of large stakes is exercised. The root cause is a missing check that the requested withdrawal amount respects Lido’s per‑request limit, effectively assuming that any amount can be withdrawn in a single call. This violates the business logic that each withdrawal request must be bounded, breaking accounting assumptions and potentially causing permanent loss of funds for users who have staked above the limit. The recommended mitigation is to introduce a checkStakeAmount routine in the base staking contract and enforce a safe maximum (for example half of MAX_STETH_WITHDRAWAL_AMOUNT) or to split large withdrawals into multiple requests, thereby ensuring that every unstake call complies with Lido’s withdrawal constraints.

title: `executeYieldBorrowERC20` calculates totalSupply using the wrong index
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that processes ERC20 yield‑borrow requests. Instead of using the asset’s supply index to determine the total amount of tokens that are available for borrowing, the code mistakenly multiplies the scaled cross‑supply by the group’s borrow index. This mis‑calculation produces an incorrect totalSupply value that is typically higher than the real supply. Because the subsequent checks that enforce asset‑level and staker‑level yield caps compare the requested amount against this inflated totalSupply, a borrower can pass the require statements even when the true caps have been exceeded. The root cause is a logical mix‑up of two similarly typed index variables – supplyIndex and borrowIndex – which are both stored in the contract’s data structures. The bug is triggered whenever executeYieldBorrowERC20 is called for an ERC20 asset, i.e., during any yield‑borrow operation. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to allow a borrow that should be rejected; the user may receive a larger loan than expected, or the protocol may later find that its accounting is out of balance, potentially leading to insufficient collateral, unexpected liquidations, or loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, and it can be hard to notice because the arithmetic expression looks syntactically correct and both indices are of the same numeric type, so a quick visual inspection may not reveal the semantic error. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect financial index usage” bugs, where a contract applies the wrong scaling factor to a monetary amount, breaking accounting assumptions and allowing caps or limits to be bypassed. To remediate the problem the totalSupply should be fetched with the asset’s supplyIndex rather than the group’s borrowIndex, ensuring that the cap checks reflect the true amount of tokens that can be borrowed. Conceptually, the fix restores the proper relationship between supply and borrow calculations, re‑establishing the intended safety checks and preventing borrowers from obtaining more tokens than the protocol’s yield‑cap policy permits.

title: PriceOracle has invalid checks on price staleness
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price oracle function that queries a Chainlink feed for an asset price. The contract attempts to guard against stale data by checking that the timestamp field updatedAt is not zero and that the answeredInRound value is greater than or equal to the roundId returned by the feed. Both of these checks are conceptually incorrect: a non‑zero updatedAt only proves that the feed has ever been updated, not that the answer is recent, and the answeredInRound field has been deprecated and no longer provides a reliable freshness guarantee. Because the contract does not compare the current block timestamp with the feed’s timestamp, it may accept a price that has not been refreshed for an extended period, such as beyond the heartbeat defined by the data provider. This flaw originates from a misunderstanding of the Chainlink aggregator API and from reusing legacy fields that no longer reflect the intended semantics. An attacker can exploit the issue by waiting until the feed becomes stale – for example, after a market move that the oracle has not yet reported – and then triggering a transaction that relies on the oracle’s price. The contract will accept the outdated price as valid, leading to calculations that are based on obsolete market data. Consequently, users may receive incorrect amounts, experience unexpected liquidations, or see their collateral valuation drop dramatically, effectively causing funds to disappear or be transferred under unfavorable terms. The problem manifests whenever the getAssetPriceFromChainlink function is called after the initial price has been set, because the two require statements will always succeed regardless of how old the price is. All participants that depend on the oracle – borrowers, lenders, traders, and any external contracts that read the price – are affected. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors compared the implementation against the official Chainlink documentation and identified the mismatch. The bug can be hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit warnings; the price appears to be a normal non‑zero value, yet it may be arbitrarily outdated, leading to subtle accounting errors that only surface under adverse market conditions. To remediate the problem, the contract should replace the current checks with a proper freshness validation, such as verifying that block.timestamp minus updatedAt is less than the asset‑specific heartbeat (for example, one hour for ETH/USD), and should drop the deprecated answeredInRound comparison entirely. By aligning the validation logic with the intended use of the Chainlink API, the oracle will reject stale answers, preserving the integrity of price‑dependent operations and preventing the loss of funds caused by outdated pricing data.

title: Risk of mass liquidation after pool/asset pause and unpause, due to borrow interest compounding implementation
bug_full: The vulnerability is a time‑dependent accounting error that allows borrow interest to continue compounding while a pool or a specific asset is paused, and then applies the accumulated interest in a single step when the contract is unpaused. The root cause lies in the interest‑updating routine, which calculates the new borrow index based on the last update timestamp stored in the asset data. When a pause is triggered, the validation functions correctly reject borrow, repay and liquidation calls, but they do not modify the timestamp used by the interest logic. Consequently, the function that updates the borrow index assumes that the full elapsed time between the last update and the moment of unpause has passed, even though borrowers were unable to make repayments during that interval. An attacker or any privileged actor who can pause the pool or an asset can therefore create a situation where, after an arbitrarily long pause, the debt of every variable‑rate borrower is inflated by the compounded interest that accrued while the contract was inert. When the pause is lifted, the inflated debt may immediately exceed the collateral value, triggering automatic liquidations that the borrowers cannot prevent because they were not allowed to repay while the contract was paused. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a sudden jump in the amount required to repay, an unexpected liquidation notice, or a rapid loss of collateral that appears to happen “out of nowhere” after the UI shows the pool as active again. The issue is hard to notice because the interest accrual is an internal accounting operation; the UI typically displays the same borrow balance before the pause, and only after unpause does the required repayment amount change dramatically, without an explicit error message. This bug belongs to the class of “interest accrual during disabled state” or “paused‑state compounding errors”, where time‑based financial calculations are performed even though the contract’s external actions are deliberately frozen. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the pause validation logic and the interest‑index update routine, noticing that the pause checks do not affect the timestamp used for interest calculation. To remediate the issue, the contract should record the moment a pause starts and either skip interest accrual for the paused interval or reset the last update timestamp when the pause ends, ensuring that borrowers are not charged interest they could not repay. By preventing interest from compounding while the contract is paused, the protocol eliminates the risk of mass, uncontrolled liquidations and aligns the accounting model with the intended business logic that pausing is an emergency measure, not a period for hidden fee accumulation.

title: If an isolated borrower/bidder is blacklisted by the debt token, risk of DOS liquidation/auction of the corresponding loan
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the interaction between an ERC20 token that implements a blocklist (for example USDC) and BendDAO's isolated liquidation and auction mechanisms. When a debt asset is blacklisted, the token contract rejects any transfer to or from the blocked address. The protocol’s IsolateLogic library assumes that transferring the previous bidder’s deposit back to them, or sending any surplus funds to the borrower after liquidation, will always succeed. In practice, if a bidder is added to the token’s blocklist after submitting a bid, the subsequent call to VaultLogic.erc20TransferOutBidAmount that attempts to return the old bid amount will revert because the token refuses to move funds to the blacklisted address. This revert aborts the entire auction transaction, preventing any further bids from being placed and effectively freezing the auction. A similar situation occurs when the borrower themselves is blacklisted: during the liquidation step, any excess bid amount that should be returned to the borrower triggers the same blocked‑transfer revert, causing the liquidation call to fail and leaving the loan in an unresolved state. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition that can lock collateral, stop the auction process, and prevent the protocol from recovering debt, thereby harming lenders, borrowers, and the overall health of the system. The issue manifests only when the debt token supports blocklisting and a participant in the auction or liquidation flow becomes blacklisted, a scenario that is rare but possible through governance actions or compliance enforcement. From a user perspective the symptoms are transaction reverts with messages indicating a blocked address, an auction that appears stuck with no new bids accepted, and liquidation attempts that never complete, leaving balances unchanged or appearing as zero despite expectations of a refund.
