The bug belongs to the class of token‑level access‑control failures that propagate into higher‑level protocol logic, creating a DoS vector. It is difficult to detect during normal testing because the blocklist is typically inactive, and the failure only surfaces when a blacklisted address is involved. The recommended mitigation is to guard the external token transfer with a try‑catch construct, or to redesign the flow so that transfers to potentially blocked addresses are optional, skipped, or routed through an intermediate contract that is not subject to the token’s blocklist. This change ensures that a failed transfer does not revert the whole auction or liquidation transaction, preserving protocol liveness even when participants are blacklisted.

title: Unhandled request invalidation by the owner of Etherfi will lead to stuck debt
description: The `owner` of Etherfi has the ability to invalidate withdrawal requests, which will DoS `YieldEthStakingEtherfi::protocolClaimWithdraw()` without ever repaying the debt. Additionally, Etherfi has a mechanism to manually claim the invalidated withdrawal, which will leave the withdraw request in a DoSed state in `YieldEthStakingEtherfi`.
poc:
`WithdrawRequestNFT::claimWithdraw()` from Etherfi [checks](https://github.com/etherfi-protocol/smart-contracts/blob/master/src/WithdrawRequestNFT.sol#L94) that the request is valid. The owner of `WithdrawRequestNFT` may [invalidate](https://github.com/etherfi-protocol/smart-contracts/blob/master/src/WithdrawRequestNFT.sol#L174) the request at any time and claim it for [itself](https://github.com/etherfi-protocol/smart-contracts/blob/master/src/WithdrawRequestNFT.sol#L135).

Thus, as withdrawals in `YieldEthStakingEtherfi` can not be canceled and there is no way to handle invalidated withdrawals, the debt from the nft will never be repaid if the owner claims the nft for itself. If the owner validates the request later, there will still be a period of unknown duration during which it’s not possible to repay the debt.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a privileged function that allows the contract owner of the Etherfi withdrawal request NFT to invalidate any pending withdrawal request and subsequently claim the NFT for themselves. Because the YieldEthStakingEtherfi contract assumes that a withdrawal request, once created, remains valid until it is processed, it does not contain any logic to handle the case where the request is marked as invalid. When the owner calls the invalidate function, the request’s status changes to an invalid state, but the protocol’s protocolClaimWithdraw() routine still attempts to settle the request based on the original assumptions. As a result, the call to protocolClaimWithdraw() reverts or becomes a no‑op, leaving the associated debt from the NFT unrepaid. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition where the debt remains outstanding indefinitely and users who submitted the withdrawal never receive their funds. The issue can be triggered at any time after a user creates a withdrawal request, simply by the owner exercising the invalidate‑and‑claim path. It affects all users of the Etherfi staking protocol who rely on the withdrawal mechanism, as well as the protocol’s accounting layer that expects the debt to be cleared once a withdrawal is processed. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the WithdrawRequestNFT contract, where the auditor observed that the owner has unrestricted power to invalidate requests and that YieldEthStakingEtherfi does not include any fallback or recovery logic for such a scenario. Because the invalidation is an owner‑only action, it may not be exercised in normal operation, making the bug easy to overlook until an intentional or accidental call occurs. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a withdrawal that appears to be pending forever, with no change to the user’s balance and no refund received, effectively causing “funds disappear” from the user’s point of view. The bug belongs to the class of authorization‑based request invalidation leading to a denial‑of‑service of debt repayment, violating the protocol’s business logic that every withdrawal request must eventually be settled and the corresponding debt cleared. To remediate the issue the protocol should introduce explicit handling for invalidated requests, such as allowing the protocol to cancel the request, repay the debt, or prevent the owner from invalidating requests after they have been created. Alternatively, the protocol could add a recovery path that detects an invalidated request and safely resolves the outstanding debt, ensuring that user withdrawals either complete or are refunded according to the intended accounting rules.

title: `wrapNativeTokenInWallet` is not compatible with Arbitrum's WETH implementation
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incompatibility between the generic wrapper routine used by the protocol and the specific implementation of the wrapped native token (WETH) on Arbitrum. The routine, called wrapNativeTokenInWallet, is intended to receive a native ether amount, call the WETH contract’s deposit function to mint an equivalent amount of wrapped token, and then move that token from the protocol’s vault to the user by invoking the ERC20 transferFrom method. On most chains the standard WETH9 contract includes a special case that skips the allowance check when the source address equals the caller (src == msg.sender). Because the vault contract itself is the caller, the allowance requirement is bypassed and the transfer succeeds. Arbitrum, however, deploys a custom WETH contract that does not contain this shortcut; its transferFrom implementation always checks the allowance mapping regardless of the caller. Since the vault never sets an allowance for itself, the call to transferFrom reverts with a token‑transfer‑failed error. Consequently, a user who sends native ether expecting to receive the wrapped version experiences a transaction that either fails outright or completes without delivering any WETH, leaving the user’s balance unchanged while the protocol appears to have accepted the deposit. The issue was discovered during a cross‑chain audit that compared the behavior of the wrapper function on multiple L2 networks. It is subtle because the same code works on Ethereum, Optimism, Polygon and BSC, leading auditors to assume correctness without testing the Arbitrum variant. The impact is medium: users on Arbitrum cannot successfully wrap native ether using this function, which breaks the intended deposit‑and‑receive flow and may cause confusion, loss of gas fees, and a perception that funds have disappeared. The bug violates the business logic that a deposit of native ether should result in an equivalent amount of wrapped token being credited to the sender. The root cause is the reliance on transferFrom’s src‑equals‑msg.sender shortcut, which is not part of the ERC20 standard and therefore not guaranteed across implementations. To remediate, the wrapper should use the standard transfer method after depositing, which does not require any allowance and works uniformly across all WETH contracts. This change eliminates the dependency on non‑standard behavior and restores the expected user experience where the deposited ether is instantly wrapped and transferred back to the user’s address.

title: Fixed title
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a strict equality check that assumes the contract will receive exactly the amount of ERC20 tokens that were requested to be transferred. In the function that processes incoming bids, the contract records its token balance before the transfer, executes a safeTransferFrom call, then records the balance after the transfer and requires that the post‑transfer balance equals the pre‑transfer balance plus the requested amount. This logic works for standard ERC20 tokens whose transfer function delivers the full amount, but it fails for fee‑on‑transfer tokens that deduct a portion of the transferred value as a fee. When such a token is used, the contract’s balance increases by less than the requested amount, causing the require statement to revert the whole transaction. The root cause is the assumption that the token transfer is fee‑free and that the balance delta will match the input amount, which is not true for tokens that implement a transfer fee. An attacker or any user can exploit this by attempting to deposit a fee‑on‑transfer token; the transaction will revert, preventing the deposit and effectively denying service to anyone trying to use that token with the protocol. The impact is that users see their transaction fail with an “invalid transfer amount” error, their token balance remains unchanged, and they lose the gas spent on the failed transaction. The protocol also cannot accept fee‑on‑transfer tokens unless the logic is adjusted, limiting the range of assets that can be used and potentially reducing liquidity. This issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the contract’s compatibility with fee‑on‑transfer tokens. It can be hard to notice because the balance‑difference pattern works for the majority of tokens, and the fee is only apparent when a token with a transfer tax is used. To remediate, the contract should either measure the actual amount received and adjust accounting accordingly, or explicitly reject fee‑on‑transfer tokens and document this limitation. In either case the strict equality check must be replaced with logic that does not assume a fee‑free transfer, thereby aligning the implementation with the business rule that the protocol must either support such tokens or clearly communicate that they are unsupported. From a user’s perspective, the expectation is that depositing 1,000 tokens results in a 1,000‑token increase in the contract’s balance; instead the contract receives only 950 tokens, the transaction reverts, and the user sees no change in their balance, leading to confusion and a perception that “funds disappear” even though the tokens were never actually transferred.

title: User are forced to borrow again in order to unlock their NFTs from `IsolateLending.sol`
description:
Isolated Margin Lending the BendDAO protocol will calculate the health factor based on a single collateral (one NFT), the liquidation of collateral will be achieved by selling the NFT through an auction mechanism.

However, the borrower who gets liquidated (his NFT is in the auction state) still able to repay his loan and close the auction, by triggering `IsolateLiquidation.sol#isolateRedeem()`. Each asset has a redemption threshold `redeemThreshold` to define the minimum debt repayment amount by the borrower.

File: IsolateLogic.sol#executeIsolateRedeem()

```solidity
vars.redeemAmounts[nidx] = vars.borrowAmount.percentMul(nftAssetData.redeemThreshold);
```

The `redeemThreshold` is updateable from `Configurator.sol#setAssetAuctionParams()` with a max value of `10_000`. In case the user calls `IsolateLiquidation.sol#isolateRedeem()` and `nftAssetData.redeemThreshold` is `10_000` (`MAX_REDEEM_THRESHOLD`). This will be set `scaledAmount` to zero.

File: IsolateLogic.sol#executeIsolateRedeem()

```solidity
loanData.scaledAmount -= vars.amountScaled;
```

This means the debt is fully paid; however,

1. The `loanData.loanStatus` will still be in active state `Constants.LOAN_STATUS_ACTIVE`.
2. The `erc721TokenData.LockerAddr` is not updated to `address(0)`.

So, the user is not able to withdraw his NFT from `BVault.sol` or even update the loan state and `LockerAddr` values through `IsolateLending.sol#isolateRepay()` due to [this check](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-benddao/blob/main/src/libraries/logic/ValidateLogic.sol#L498-L500)

Note: The only way the user can unlock his NFT is by borrowing again. This will increase `loanData.scaledAmount` again to greater than zero, and then he needs to repay that loan `IsolateLending.sol#isolateRepay()` to update the `erc721TokenData.LockerAddr` to `address(0)`. This will expose the user to the unnecessary risk of being liquidated again.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the isolated‑margin lending flow of the BendDAO protocol where a borrower can fully repay the debt of a loan that is backed by a single NFT, yet the protocol does not clear the internal loan state that ties the NFT to the loan. The root cause is the redeemThreshold parameter, which can be set to its maximum value (10_000). When the borrower calls the isolateRedeem function with this maximum threshold, the calculation of the required repayment amount yields zero, so the scaledAmount field of the loan is reduced to zero and the debt is considered paid. However, the loanStatus field remains in the active state and the erc721TokenData.LockerAddr still points to the vault contract. A later validation step in ValidateLogic checks that the loan is still active and that the locker address is non‑zero before allowing a withdrawal, causing the withdrawERC721 call to revert with an "asset already locked in use" error. From the user’s point of view the expectation is that after repaying the loan the NFT becomes freely withdrawable, but instead the user sees no change in the UI, the loan still appears active and the NFT cannot be transferred, effectively locking the asset. The issue only manifests when the redeemThreshold is set to its maximum, which can be done by the protocol owner through Configurator.setAssetAuctionParams or potentially by a malicious actor who can influence that parameter. Because the loan’s scaledAmount is zero, the protocol reports the debt as cleared, making the problem subtle and easy to miss during routine testing; the UI may show a zero balance while the backend still blocks withdrawals. The impact is that borrowers are forced to open a new loan on the same NFT to reset the locker address, exposing them to additional interest, fees, and the risk of being liquidated again. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena using a Foundry proof‑of‑concept that demonstrated the inability to withdraw after a full redeem. The recommended remediation is to add a state‑cleanup step that, when scaledAmount reaches zero, explicitly resets the locker address to address(0) and updates the loan status to a closed state, ensuring that the NFT can be withdrawn without requiring a new borrowing operation. This class of bug can be described as an incomplete state transition after debt settlement, where financial accounting is correct but asset‑ownership metadata remains stale, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a zero debt implies no collateral lock.

title: isolateRedeem
description:
One of the features of this protocol is that the borrower can redeem his loan (under the **Isolate Lending**) after his loan goes into auction state (before the end of the auction) by simply invoking `IsolateLiquidation.sol#isolateRedeem()`. However, in order to keep the liquidators incentivized to launch the auction for any bad debt, the borrower could get forced to pay them some fee (called `bidFine`).

The `bidFine` is defined by two factors `bidFineFactor` and `minBidFineFactor`, both of them are updatable from `Configurator.sol#setAssetAuctionParams()`,

In case admin set them to zero, when the borrower tries to redeem his loan this logic from `IsolateLogic.sol#executeIsolateRedeem()`:

File: IsolateLogic.sol#executeIsolateRedeem()

```solidity
(, vars.bidFines[vars.nidx]) = GenericLogic.calculateNftLoanBidFine(
  debtAssetData,
  debtGroupData,
  nftAssetData,
  loanData,
  vars.priceOracle
);
```

will set the value of `vars.bidFines[vars.nidx]` to zero. After that, the flow will enter this `IF` block to transfer the `bidFine` to the liquidator who launched the auction.

File: IsolateLogic.sol#executeIsolateRedeem()

```solidity
if (loanData.firstBidder != address(0)) {
  // transfer bid fine from borrower to the first bidder
  VaultLogic.erc20TransferBetweenWallets(
    params.asset,
    params.msgSender,
    loanData.firstBidder,
    vars.bidFines[vars.nidx]
  );
}
```

In case `params.asset` is one of Revert-on-Zero-Value-Transfers tokens (in scope), the transaction will revert because it is trying to transfer zero value `vars.bidFines[vars.nidx] == 0`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the loan redemption flow of the Isolate Lending feature. When a borrower attempts to redeem a loan that is already in auction state, the contract calculates a fee called bidFine that is meant to compensate the liquidator who started the auction. The fee amount is derived from two configurable parameters, bidFineFactor and minBidFineFactor, which can be set to zero by an administrator. If both factors are zero, the calculation returns a bidFine of zero. The redemption logic then unconditionally calls an ERC20 transfer function to move the bidFine from the borrower to the liquidator. Certain ERC20 tokens are implemented to revert any transfer with a value of zero. Because the code does not check whether the fee amount is greater than zero before invoking the transfer, the transaction reverts on those tokens. This makes the redemption transaction fail, preventing the borrower from exiting the auction and effectively locking the loan. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the isolateRedeem function and its interaction with configurable auction parameters. It can be hard to notice because many ERC20 implementations accept zero‑value transfers without error, so the bug only manifests with tokens that explicitly reject zero transfers. The impact is that borrowers may be unable to redeem their positions, leading to unexpected loss of access to their collateral and potential financial loss, while the protocol’s business logic – rewarding liquidators only when a fee is actually owed – is broken. The affected parties include borrowers, the protocol’s liquidity pool, and any liquidators relying on the fee mechanism. The root cause is a missing guard condition around the fee transfer. The recommended fix is to add a check that the calculated bidFine is greater than zero before attempting the ERC20 transfer, ensuring that zero‑value transfers are never executed and the redemption can proceed when no fee is due.

title: Updating asset collateral params can lead to liquidate borrowers arbitrarily
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the protocol’s ability for a privileged PoolAdmin to modify the collateral configuration of any asset at any moment through the Configurator.setAssetCollateralParams function. The health‑factor calculation in GenericLogic.calculateUserAccountData treats an asset as collateral only when its liquidationThreshold is non‑zero; the same threshold value is also used to add the asset’s value to the total collateral amount. Consequently, if the admin sets both collateralFactor and liquidationThreshold of a supplied asset to zero, the protocol instantly treats that asset as having no collateral value. The borrower’s health‑factor therefore drops to zero or below, regardless of market price movements, and the account becomes eligible for liquidation. A liquidator – often an MEV bot monitoring the blockchain – can then call crossLiquidateERC20, repay the borrower’s debt and seize the now‑unprotected collateral at the protocol‑defined discount. From the user’s perspective the supplied token balance appears unchanged in the UI, but shortly after the admin’s parameter change the borrower receives a transaction that transfers their collateral to an unknown address, effectively losing the funds. The impact is a sudden loss of collateral for any borrower who relied on that asset, erosion of trust in the protocol’s stability, and potential financial loss for users who cannot react in time. The issue occurs whenever the admin updates collateral parameters without any delay or safeguard, and it affects all borrowers with open positions that use the altered asset as collateral, as well as the broader ecosystem that expects collateral to remain stable during the life of a loan. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the health‑factor logic and identified that the same liquidationThreshold variable is used both for eligibility and for collateral valuation, allowing a zero‑value update to bypass any market‑based safety checks. The problem is subtle because changing a configuration parameter is a normal governance operation and does not immediately raise alarms; the health‑factor drop can be mistaken for a price shock, making the exploit hard to detect without tracing the parameter change. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a timelocked or buffered period before collateral parameters can be altered, prevent setting the liquidationThreshold to zero while loans are active, cache the parameters per loan at the time of borrowing, or require a multi‑step governance process that gives borrowers time to adjust their positions. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “configurable collateral parameter abuse” where on‑chain governance actions can be weaponised to force arbitrary liquidations, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that collateral value only changes due to market price fluctuations.

title: No check if Arbitrum/Optimism L2 sequencer is down in Chainlink feeds `PriceOracle.sol`
description:
Chainlink recommends that all Optimistic L2 oracles consult the Sequencer Uptime Feed to ensure that the sequencer is live before trusting the data returned by the oracle.

If the Arbitrum Sequencer goes down, oracle data will not be kept up to date, and thus could become stale. However, users are able to continue to interact with the protocol directly through the L1 optimistic rollup contract. You can review Chainlink docs on [L2 Sequencer Uptime Feeds](https://docs.chain.link/docs/data-feeds/l2-sequencer-feeds/) for more details on this.

This protocol uses `getPriceOracle()` everywhere and it sub call to [`PriceOracle.sol#latestRoundData()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-benddao/blob/main/src/PriceOracle.sol#L122). As a result, users may be able to use the protocol while Oracle feeds are stale. This could cause many problems, for example:

* A user has a loan with 100 tokens, valued at 1 ETH each, and no borrows.
* The Arbitrum sequencer goes down temporarily.
* While it’s down, the price of the token falls to 0.5 ETH each.
* The current value of the user’s loan is 50 ETH, so the liquidators should be able to liquidate this position because it is unhealthy.
* However, due to the stale price, the protocol lets the user keep borrowing.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing verification of the L2 sequencer uptime feed before the protocol consumes price data from a Chainlink oracle. Chainlink advises that contracts on Optimistic roll‑ups such as Arbitrum or Optimism must first confirm that the sequencer is active, because a down sequencer stops the publishing of fresh price updates and leaves the feed stale. In the examined contract the function that retrieves the latest price calls the Chainlink Aggregator’s latestRoundData() directly without checking the Sequencer Uptime Feed. Consequently, when the Arbitrum sequencer experiences a temporary outage, the price returned by the oracle remains at the last value before the outage. This stale price can be exploited by a borrower: if the market price of a collateral token drops while the sequencer is down, the protocol still sees the old higher price, believes the loan is healthy and permits further borrowing or prevents liquidation. From the user’s point of view the protocol appears to allow borrowing even though the collateral value has fallen, or a liquidation that should have occurred is silently ignored, leading to a mismatch between expected risk controls and actual behavior. The issue is discovered during a security audit (Code4rena) by reviewing the oracle integration pattern and noting the absence of the recommended sequencer check. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the price simply looks plausible, masking the fact that it is outdated. The impact is a medium‑severity economic risk: the protocol may lose funds if borrowers exploit stale prices to avoid liquidation or over‑borrow, affecting lenders, borrowers, and the overall health of the system. The proper mitigation is to follow Chainlink’s example code and add a sequencer‑active guard, for example by calling the Sequencer Uptime Feed’s latestRoundData() and reverting when the answer indicates downtime or when the data is within a grace period. This ensures that price reads are only accepted when the L2 sequencer is confirmed to be live, restoring the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: Major insolvency risk in `LiquidationLogic::executeCrossLiquidateERC721`
description: Whenever the price of a nft suffers a significant drop or the debt asset increases in price, there is a threshold after which liquidations are not profitable at all for the liquidator. Moreover, it does not offer the possibility of partial liquidation to at least partially mitigate this issue.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic design flaw in the cross‑liquidation routine for ERC‑721 collateral. The contract determines the amount of debt to be repaid by dividing the total outstanding debt by the number of NFTs held by the borrower, and then uses this per‑NFT price to calculate how much of the debt the liquidator must pay to acquire each token. Because there is no upper bound on the derived price, a situation where the market price of the NFT drops sharply or the price of the borrowed asset rises can cause the computed per‑NFT price to exceed the actual market value of the NFT. When a liquidator calls executeCrossLiquidateERC721 under those conditions, they are forced to pay an inflated amount for the NFT, resulting in a loss where the debt repaid is greater than the collateral value received. The contract also does not allow partial liquidation at a discounted price; even if the caller specifies only a subset of the borrower’s NFTs, each is still priced using the same unbounded formula, preventing the liquidator from limiting exposure. The impact is that liquidators may incur systematic losses, and if the protocol cannot recover the shortfall, the DAO treasury must cover the bad debt, eroding protocol funds. The issue manifests only when the health factor falls below one and the price oracle reports a significant depreciation of the NFT or an appreciation of the debt asset, conditions that can be reproduced in testing by artificially lowering the NFT price. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a test case demonstrated that after a 40 % price drop the calculated debt to liquidate was 112 % of the collateral value, making the trade unprofitable. The problem is hard to notice because under normal market conditions the division yields a reasonable price, and the code does not contain explicit sanity checks or caps. To remediate, the protocol should introduce a maximum per‑NFT price, similar to the discount‑capped repayment logic used for ERC‑20 collateral, or allow the liquidator to specify a maximum acceptable price and support partial liquidation at a discounted rate. By capping the price, the liquidator can at least recover part of the debt and the protocol can avoid generating bad debt that must be absorbed by the treasury. This class of bug belongs to the category of “unbounded price calculation in collateral liquidation” and violates the fundamental accounting assumption that the value of collateral sold must be at least equal to the debt repaid. From a user’s perspective, a borrower may see their NFT transferred away while the liquidator receives far less value than paid, and the protocol may need to allocate treasury funds to cover the shortfall, contrary to expectations that liquidations are always neutral or profitable for the liquidator.

title: Incorrect accounting of utilization, supply/borrow rates due to vulnerable implementation in `IsolateLogic::executeIsolateLiquidate`
bug_full: An incorrect accounting bug occurs in the isolated loan liquidation flow when the contract updates interest rates. During execution of IsolateLogic.executeIsolateLiquidate, the function calculates an extra amount that the liquidator must pay if the winning bid does not fully cover the outstanding debt. The implementation then calls InterestLogic.updateInterestRates with the sum of the total borrowed amount and the extra amount as the liquidityAdded parameter. Because the extra amount is already part of the repayment that will be transferred back to the pool, adding it again inflates the reported liquidityAdded value. The inflated liquidityAdded increases the variable availableLiquidityPlusDebt, which in turn reduces the computed assetUtilizationRate. A lower utilization rate makes the interest rate model return a higher borrow rate and supply rate than should apply to the actual pool state. The bug is triggered only when an isolated NFT loan is liquidated with an insufficient bid, i.e., when vars.totalExtraAmount is non‑zero. Users who provide the extra repayment see their loan cleared, but the protocol records a utilization that is artificially low, causing borrowers to be charged an unexpectedly low or high rate depending on the model, and lenders to receive a supply rate that does not reflect the true pool usage. From a user perspective the symptoms are a mismatch between the expected interest accrual and the observed APR, or a pool dashboard that shows utilization far below the actual borrowed amount. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the interest‑rate update logic and noticing that the extra repayment amount was double‑counted. It is hard to notice because the rates are calculated off‑chain and the discrepancy only appears after a liquidation event, which may be infrequent. The proper fix is to pass only the actual borrowed amount (vars.totalBorrowAmount) to updateInterestRates, thereby avoiding the double counting of the extra repayment. Conceptually the bug belongs to the class of accounting mis‑calculations where a repayment is added to both the liquidity increase and the debt reduction, leading to an inaccurate utilization metric and consequently incorrect interest rates.

title: It’s impossible to retrieve collected fines from the yield staking contract
description: No means to retrieve collected fines from the staking contract.
bug_full: The contract implements a yield‑staking system where a staker can be forced to unstake by a privileged botAdmin. When this forced exit occurs the protocol adds an "unstakeFine" to the amount the staker must repay. The repayment routine calculates the total debt as the sum of the original NFT debt and the fine (nftDebtWithFine). If the staker’s claimed yield covers the total, the excess is returned; otherwise the staker must transfer the shortfall. After the repayment the function sends only the original nftDebt back to the lending pool and updates internal accounting, while the fine amount remains in the contract’s balance. No subsequent function exists that allows the admin or any other role to transfer those accumulated fine funds out of the contract. Consequently, every time a forced unstake is performed, the fine is permanently locked inside the contract. This situation is discovered during a manual audit that traced the repayment flow and observed that the fine is never accounted for in any withdrawal path. The bug is subtle because the contract’s external balance simply grows; there is no event announcing the fine collection and the normal repay logic appears to succeed, so the trapped funds can be mistaken for normal contract reserves. The impact is that the protocol cannot realize the revenue it expects from fines, breaking the economic model and potentially discouraging the use of forced‑unstake mechanisms. Users experience a mismatch between the amount they are charged (the fine) and any visible benefit, as the fine disappears from their wallet but never reappears elsewhere. The issue manifests whenever botAdmin invokes the forced‑unstake path, i.e., under any condition that triggers an unstakeFine. A proper fix is to introduce a privileged function (e.g., collectFines or withdrawFine) that transfers the accumulated fine balance to a treasury or admin address, and to update the accounting so that the fine is explicitly recorded as protocol revenue. This change restores the intended flow of funds and prevents permanent loss of assets within the contract.

title: Borrower can prevent yield position repayment and closure by the bot
description: User may revoke the underlying asset approval from the yield contract and prevent the `botAdmin` from repaying and closing his position. As a result, the debt will not be repaid, leaving the protocol at a loss.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a repayment flow that can be blocked by the position owner, allowing the borrower to keep a debt outstanding and prevent the automated bot from closing the yield position. The contract’s internal _repay function first withdraws the accrued yield, compares it with the total debt plus any unstake fine, and if the yield is insufficient it calculates an extraAmount that must be transferred from the NFT owner to cover the shortfall. This transfer relies on the owner having granted an ERC20 allowance to the contract and is performed with a safeTransferFrom call. Because the repayment logic is tightly coupled with the NFT unlocking step, the bot assumes the transfer will succeed; however, a borrower can revoke the allowance immediately before the bot executes, causing the safeTransferFrom to revert or fail. When the transfer fails, the function does not reach the repayment and token‑unlocking steps, leaving the debt unpaid and the NFT locked. The issue manifests only when the collected yield is lower than the debt‑plus‑fine amount, a condition that can occur for under‑collateralised positions or during market downturns. The affected parties are the protocol itself and its lenders, as the unpaid debt continues to accrue interest, resulting in a loss of expected revenue. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the repayment logic and noticing the reliance on external token approvals without a fallback. It is subtle because the normal path (yield covering the debt) works correctly, so the failure only appears in edge cases where the borrower deliberately revokes approval. To remediate, the repayment and NFT unlocking logic should be decoupled: the contract should only unlock the NFT when no extraAmount is required, and when extraAmount is needed the token must remain locked until the owner explicitly repays the remaining balance, eliminating the need for a forced transfer from the owner during the bot’s execution. This design removes the dependency on mutable allowances and ensures that debt repayment cannot be blocked by the borrower, preserving protocol accounting integrity.

title: Changing auction duration will have effect on ongoing auctions
description: Auctions created before the auction duration was changed will have their duration shortened/extended, which may catch their participants off guard.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a time‑parameter mutation flaw in the auction module of the protocol. When a liquidation auction is created the contract stores only the start timestamp and later determines whether the auction has ended by adding the global variable auctionDuration to that start time each time a check is performed. Because auctionDuration can be changed by the PoolAdmin through setAssetAuctionParams, any change to this variable is immediately reflected in the calculation of the end timestamp for all auctions that are already in progress. Consequently, shortening the duration causes an ongoing auction to be considered finished earlier than participants expect, preventing borrowers from redeeming their debt and allowing the last bidder to claim the collateral prematurely. Extending the duration has the opposite effect, keeping funds locked longer than advertised. The root cause is the failure to store a fixed auctionEndTimestamp at the moment the auction is launched, violating the business assumption that the auction length is immutable once started. The issue can be exploited simply by the admin calling setAssetAuctionParams while an auction is active; no special permissions beyond the existing admin role are required. The impact is financial loss or unexpected behavior for borrowers and bidders, who may see the UI indicate that the auction is still open while the contract rejects their actions, or vice‑versa. The problem occurs only when the protocol allows the duration parameter to be modified after an auction has begun, and it affects any user who participates in that auction. It was discovered during a code audit that highlighted the dynamic recomputation of the end time. Because the contract does not emit a specific event about the change affecting ongoing auctions, the bug can be hard to notice until a participant experiences a premature failure. The correct mitigation is to calculate the absolute end timestamp once at auction creation and store it in immutable state, for example by assigning auctionEndTimestamp = block.timestamp + auctionDuration and using that stored value for all subsequent checks. This change aligns the implementation with the intended accounting model where each auction has a fixed deadline, eliminating the possibility for the admin to retroactively alter the timing of an active auction.

title: Updating fee factor may create issues for the protocol
description:
When the protocol fee is modified in the `Configurator` module:

  * The new fee percentage will be applied to the interest collected before the fee change.
  * The protocol will use the supply rate that was calculated using the old fee factor.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol fee (feeFactor) is updated in the Configurator module. When an administrator changes the feeFactor, the contract immediately applies the new percentage to the interest that has already been accrued, but it does not recompute the asset supply rate using the updated feeFactor. Consequently, the supply rate that determines future interest earnings for lenders continues to be calculated with the old feeFactor, while the treasury fee is taken with the new one. This mismatch creates an accounting inconsistency: the amount of interest credited to lenders is based on a stale rate, and the amount minted to the treasury may be higher or lower than intended. The issue can be exploited by an attacker who triggers a feeFactor change and then performs borrow or repay actions before the supply rate is refreshed, causing the protocol to either under‑collect fees (reducing treasury revenue) or over‑charge borrowers (inflating lender returns) depending on the direction of the change. The impact is subtle but significant: lenders may see their expected returns deviate from the protocol’s advertised rates, the treasury may be under‑funded, and overall incentive alignment can be broken. The bug manifests only when the feeFactor is modified; normal borrowing, repaying, or interest accrual operations do not expose it. It affects all participants that interact with the affected asset – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol’s treasury – because the accounting error propagates through every subsequent interest calculation. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the Configurator’s fee update flow, where the order of calls to updateInterestIndexs and updateInterestRates was examined and found to be inconsistent with the intended accounting model. The discrepancy is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error; the symptom is a silent drift in fee distribution that can only be observed by comparing expected versus actual treasury balances or supply rates. The correct mitigation is to ensure that after a feeFactor change the supply rate is recomputed using the new feeFactor before any further interest accrual, or to update the interest indexes first and then apply the new feeFactor, as demonstrated in the provided patch. In conceptual terms, the fix restores the invariant that fee calculation and supply‑rate calculation are always performed with the same feeFactor, eliminating the temporary inconsistency and preserving accurate accounting across the protocol.

title: Protocol should update interest rate after changing rate model in the configurator module
description: After updating the interest model, the protocol does not update the interest rate, resulting in interest being calculated at the old model rates for some time.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a stale‑interest‑rate condition that appears after the pool administrator updates the lending rate model through the Configurator module. The configurator writes the new rateModel address into the group data storage and emits an event, but it does not invoke the InterestLogic.updateInterestRates function that recomputes the interest index based on the new model. As a result, the protocol continues to calculate accrued interest using the previously cached model until another transaction that implicitly triggers an interest‑rate update (such as a borrow, repay or any action that calls updateInterestRates) occurs. The root cause is a missing state‑synchronisation step: the configuration change is not coupled with the necessary economic state refresh. An attacker or a careless admin can exploit this timing gap by switching to a more favorable rate model and then performing operations before the stale index is refreshed, causing borrowers to be charged less or lenders to receive less than expected. The impact is a mismatch between the rate displayed to users and the rate actually applied to their balances, leading to unexpected zero or reduced interest accrual, balances that appear lower than they should, and potential accounting inconsistencies across the protocol. The issue manifests only after a rate‑model change and persists until a subsequent interest‑rate‑updating transaction is executed, which may be minutes or hours later depending on activity. All participants that rely on accurate interest calculations – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol’s treasury – are affected because the financial accounting assumptions (that the stored rate model always reflects the applied formula) are violated. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the team observed that the Configurator’s executeSetAssetLendingRate function does not call the interest‑rate update routine, a pattern also present in Aave V2 and V3. The bug can be hard to notice because normal user interfaces show the newly set rate, yet the backend still uses the old formula, and the discrepancy only becomes visible after a period of inactivity or when users compare expected versus actual accrued interest. The recommended remediation is to invoke InterestLogic.updateInterestRates immediately after updating the rateModel, ensuring that the interest index is refreshed and that subsequent calculations use the new model. Conceptually, this is a configuration‑change‑without‑state‑synchronisation defect, a class of bugs where a parameter update is not propagated to dependent state, leading to stale data and incorrect financial outcomes.

title: Incorrect `unwrapNativeTokenInWallet` receiver address
description: If the user specifies native tokens as output assets, the protocol will mistakenly try to unwrap wrapped tokens from the `msg.sender` instead of the `receiver` address that was specified in the function call.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect handling of the receiver address when unwrapping wrapped native tokens back to the native token form. When a user requests a withdrawal or borrow of a native token and supplies a custom receiver address, the protocol first sends the wrapped version of the native token to that receiver via an ERC20 transfer. Afterwards it calls the internal function unwrapNativeTokenInWallet, which is supposed to pull the wrapped tokens from the address that actually holds them and then withdraw them to the same address. However, the function is invoked with msg.sender – the caller of the outer withdraw or borrow function – instead of the receiver that was specified in the parameters. As a result, the contract attempts to execute a transferFrom on the wrapped token contract using msg.sender as the source, even though the tokens reside in the receiver’s wallet. If msg.sender and receiver differ, the transferFrom fails, the subsequent withdraw call reverts with a generic token‑transfer‑failed error, and the user receives no native token. This bug manifests in the BVault, CrossLending and IsolateLending modules wherever native‑token output is supported, such as withdrawERC20, crossBorrowERC20 and isolateBorrow. The root cause is a misuse of msg.sender for asset ownership checks, a classic “receiver address confusion” where the contract assumes the caller also owns the assets being unwrapped. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker can trigger a withdrawal with a receiver address that is not the caller, causing the transaction to revert and effectively denying service to legitimate users who wish to receive funds at a different address. The impact is that users expecting their native token to be deposited into their chosen wallet see the transaction fail, their UI shows no balance change, and the protocol may appear unreliable. The issue is hard to notice because the code works correctly when the receiver equals msg.sender, which is a common test scenario; only when alternative receivers are used does the failure surface. The bug was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena when reviewing the flow of unwrapNativeTokenInWallet and noticing the mismatch between the address that receives the wrapped token and the address from which the contract tries to pull it. To remediate, the call to unwrapNativeTokenInWallet should pass the receiver address instead of msg.sender, ensuring the contract pulls the wrapped tokens from the correct holder before unwrapping. This aligns the asset flow with the intended business logic that a user who specifies a destination address should receive the native token there, preserving accounting integrity and preventing denial‑of‑service scenarios.

title: Users can evade the `yDUSD` vault’s withdrawal timelock mechanism
bug_full: The yDUSD vault implements an ERC4626 style withdrawal timelock that is intended to force a seven‑day waiting period after a user calls proposeWithdraw before the user can call withdraw. The contract stores each pending withdrawal in a mapping keyed by the caller address (msg.sender) and then, in the withdraw function, reads the pending amount and timestamp from withdrawals[msg.sender. However, the function also accepts an explicit owner parameter that determines whose shares are burned and whose underlying DUSD assets are transferred. Because the code never checks that the caller (msg.sender) matches the owner argument, an attacker can create a second address, call proposeWithdraw on that address to generate a valid withdrawal request, and then invoke withdraw with the attacker’s own address as the owner while still using the second address as msg.sender. The timelock check uses the timestamp stored under the second address, which satisfies the seven‑day condition, allowing the attacker to bypass the waiting period entirely. The attacker must also approve the second address to spend the attacker’s yDUSD shares, after which the internal _withdraw routine burns the attacker’s shares and transfers the attacker’s DUSD assets to the chosen receiver. This flaw breaks the core invariant that only the account that created the withdrawal request may withdraw after the timelock, effectively rendering the timelock meaningless. In practice a user expects to wait seven days before receiving funds, but an attacker can receive the assets instantly, leading to unexpected zero balances for the victim and potential loss of funds from the vault. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a test that creates two accounts, proposes a withdrawal with one, and then withdraws from the other without waiting. The bug is subtle because the withdraw function appears to enforce the timelock, yet the key used for the pending request is unrelated to the owner whose assets are moved. The vulnerability belongs to the class of authorization‑mix‑up bugs where access control checks are performed on the wrong variable. The recommended mitigation is to enforce that msg.sender equals the owner argument, or to store pending withdrawals keyed by the actual owner, and to revert if the two differ. This restores the intended security property that only the proposer can withdraw after the prescribed delay.

title: Changing the `slashingHandler` for `NativeVaults` will DoS slashing
description: Relevant code: [NativeVault::slashAssets](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-karak/blob/f5e52fdcb4c20c4318d532a9f08f7876e9afb321/src/NativeVault.sol#L308)
poc:
Let’s suppose the following scenario:

  1. SlashHandler `A` is set for key `Constants.DEAD_BEEF` in `assetSlashingHandlers`.
  2. 5 `NativeVaults` get deployed with this slash handler.
  3. SlashHandler `B` is set for `Constants.DEAD_BEEF`.
  4. These 5 `NativeVaults` would not be slashable until some measures are taken - either `A` restored or the vault’s implementations are updated.

Both approaches to fix this issue once it has occurred have their drawbacks:

  * If after **step 3**, more `NativeVaults` are created updating the allowlist will always cause some group of native vaults to be **unslashable**.
  * Changing the `NativeVault` implementations can only be done only 1 by 1, since the default vault implementation is for normal `Vault`.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition affecting the slashing mechanism of NativeVault contracts. The contract maintains a global allowlist mapping called assetSlashingHandlers that links an asset identifier (for example the constant DEAD_BEEF) to a slashing handler contract. When a vault is deployed it relies on the current entry in this mapping to perform slashAssets calls. Because the mapping entry can be changed by governance after vault deployment, the previously deployed vaults continue to reference the mutable global entry rather than an immutable handler address stored in the vault itself. If the entry is replaced with a different handler, the original vaults attempt to invoke a handler that no longer implements the expected interface or is no longer authorized, causing the slashAssets function to revert or silently fail. Consequently the vaults become unslashable – penalties that should be applied to misbehaving participants never occur and the assets remain locked in the vault. This situation can be triggered simply by executing a transaction that updates the slashing handler for a given asset after one or more NativeVaults have already been created. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the reviewers examined the slashAssets implementation and noticed that the handler address is mutable and not tied to each vault instance. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit a specific warning when slashing fails; from a user’s perspective the UI may show that a slash event was recorded but the vault balance does not change, leading to confusion. The impact is that the protocol’s risk‑mitigation guarantees are broken – funds that should be confiscated remain untouched, potentially allowing malicious actors to retain collateral and undermining trust in the system. The affected parties include any user who deposits assets into a NativeVault that was created before the handler change, as well as the protocol itself which relies on slashing to enforce correct behavior. To remediate the issue the slashing handler should be made immutable per vault, for example by storing the handler address in the vault at construction time, or by restricting changes to the global allowlist to periods when no vaults exist for the affected asset. Alternatively a migration function could be provided that updates all existing vaults to the new handler in a single atomic operation, ensuring that no vault becomes unslashable after a handler change.

title: A snapshot may face a permanent DoS if both a slashing event occurs in the `NativeVault` and the staker’s validator is penalized
description: The staker can still receive rewards even if their validators are empty.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the snapshot finalisation logic of the NativeVault contract that can permanently deny progress of a validator’s snapshot when a combined slashing event reduces the validator’s effective balance below the amount of shares the contract attempts to burn. The root cause lies in the internal _decreaseBalance() function, which calculates the number of shares to burn by converting the requested asset reduction to shares (using previewWithdraw) but does not verify that the resulting share amount does not exceed the holder’s current share balance. When a validator is first slashed by the NativeVault (for example 2 ETH) and then suffers a beacon‑chain slashing that removes the remaining effective balance (for example the full 32 ETH) within the seven‑day snapshot window, the snapshot processing code attempts to decrease the user’s balance by the full 32 ETH. Because the user’s share balance only represents the remaining 30 ETH after the first slashing, the burn operation tries to destroy more shares than exist, causing the transaction to revert. The revert aborts the _updateSnapshot() call, leaving the snapshot data structure in an unfinished state. From the user’s perspective the UI will show a snapshot that never completes, the validator appears to have zero balance yet the user continues to receive staking rewards, and further calls to validateSnapshotProofs() or validateExpiredSnapshot() are permanently blocked. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for the affected account: the user cannot finalise the snapshot, cannot withdraw or restake, and the protocol’s availability for that participant is impaired, although the total assets remain safe. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow from slashing events through snapshot validation to the share‑burning routine and identified the missing balance check. It is hard to notice because the failure only occurs under the rare combination of two slashing events whose total exceeds the user’s restaked balance within the snapshot period, a scenario that does not arise in normal operation. The bug belongs to the class of share‑accounting or arithmetic under‑burn errors where a conversion from assets to shares is performed without a safeguard against insufficient share balance. To remediate, the _decreaseBalance() implementation should cap the number of shares to be burned to the holder’s actual share balance (for example using Math.min(convertToShares(assets), balanceOf(nodeOwner))) before invoking the burn, thereby ensuring that the contract never attempts to destroy more shares than exist and allowing snapshots to complete correctly.

title: When malicious behavior occurs and DSS requests slashing against vault during 2 day period after `SLASHING_WINDOW` of 7 days is passed after staker initiates a withdrawal, token amount to be slashed is calculated to be higher than what it should be
poc:
The following steps can occur for the first described scenario where the DSS unfairly slashes more underlying token amount from the vault than it should be allowed.

  1. The vault holds `100` underlying tokens and has only one staker who owns `100` shares.
  2. On Day 0, the staker initiates his withdrawal for redeeming `50` shares.
  3. During the `SLASHING_WINDOW` of 7 days between Day 0 and Day 7, no malicious behavior occurs, and the DSS does not request any slashing against the vault.

     * Therefore, the staker’s withdrawal is safe and should not be slashable, and the staker should receive `50 * 100 / 100 = 50` underlying tokens for his withdrawal.
  4. On Day 8, a malicious behavior occurs, and the DSS with a 50% allowed slashing percentage requests to slash the vault.

     * The token amount to be slashed by the DSS is calculated to be `50% * 100 = 50` underlying tokens.
     * However, because the staker’s withdrawal initiated on Day 0 should not be subject to such slashing, the token amount to be slashed by the DSS should equal `50% * (100 - 50) = 25` underlying tokens.
  5. On Day 9, the `MIN_WITHDRAW_DELAY` of 9 days is passed after the initiation of the staker’s withdrawal so the staker finishes his withdrawal and does receive `50 * 100 / 100 = 50` underlying tokens from the vault.
  6. On Day 10, the DSS finalizes the slashing and slashes `50` underlying tokens calculated on Day 8, which is more than `25` underlying tokens that it should slash, from the vault. Therefore, the DSS unfairly slashes more underlying tokens from the vault than it should be allowed.

The following steps can occur for the second described scenario where the staker’s withdrawal can be unfairly slashed by the DSS even though it should not be slashed.

  1. The vault holds `150` underlying tokens and has two stakers in which Staker A owns `100` shares and Staker B owns `50` shares.
  2. On Day 0, Staker A initiates his withdrawal for redeeming `100` shares.
  3. During the `SLASHING_WINDOW` of 7 days between Day 0 and Day 7, no malicious behavior occurs, and the DSS does not request any slashing against the vault.

     * Therefore, Staker A’s withdrawal is safe and should not be slashable, and Staker A should receive `100 * 150 / (100 + 50) = 100` underlying tokens for his withdrawal.
  4. A malicious behavior occurs when 3 minutes are passed after Day 7 starts, and the DSS with a 50% allowed slashing percentage requests to slash the vault when 5 minutes are passed after Day 7 starts.

     * The token amount to be slashed by the DSS is calculated to be `50% * 150 = 75` underlying tokens.
     * However, because Staker A’s withdrawal initiated on Day 0 should not be subject to such slashing, the token amount to be slashed by the DSS should equal `50% * (150 - 100) = 25` underlying tokens.
  5. On Day 9, the `MIN_WITHDRAW_DELAY` of 9 days is passed after the initiation of Staker A’s withdrawal so the staker calls the `Vault.finishRedeem` function for finishing his withdrawal.
  6. When 5 minutes are passed after Day 9 starts, the DSS calls the `Core.finalizeSlashing` function for finalizing the slashing.
  7. Both Staker A’s `Vault.finishRedeem` transaction and the DSS’s `Core.finalizeSlashing` transaction are sent at the similar time, a malicious miner places and executes the DSS’s `Core.finalizeSlashing` transaction before Staker A’s `Vault.finishRedeem` transaction.
  8. When the DSS’s `Core.finalizeSlashing` transaction is executed, the DSS slashes `75` underlying tokens calculated in Step 4, which is more than `25` underlying tokens that it should slash, from the vault.
  9. When Staker A’s `Vault.finishRedeem` transaction is executed, Staker A receives `100 * (150 - 75) / (100 + 50) = 50` underlying tokens, which is less than `100` underlying tokens that it should receive for his withdrawal, from the vault. Therefore, Staker A’s withdrawal is unfairly slashed by the DSS even though it should not be slashed.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol calculates the amount of assets that can be slashed when a Decentralized Security Service (DSS) submits a slashing request against a vault. The slashing library fetches the vault's totalAssets value and multiplies it by the allowed slashing percentage, but totalAssets includes tokens that are already earmarked for a pending withdrawal. Because the withdrawal delay (MIN_WITHDRAW_DELAY) is defined as the sum of the slashing window (7 days) and a veto window (2 days), a staker who initiates a withdrawal after the 7‑day slashing window should be protected from any slashing that occurs later. However, during the 2‑day period after the slashing window expires, the DSS can still request a slashing, and the calculation mistakenly treats the pending withdrawal amount as part of the slashable pool. Consequently, the DSS may slash a larger portion of the vault's assets than the protocol intends, effectively stealing tokens that belong to the withdrawing staker. The problem is amplified by a race condition: when the MIN_WITHDRAW_DELAY finally passes, the staker calls Vault.finishRedeem to complete the withdrawal while the DSS calls Core.finalizeSlashing to finalize the slash. A malicious miner can order the finalizeSlashing transaction before the finishRedeem transaction, causing the vault to lose the over‑calculated slashed amount before the staker receives his funds. This results in the staker receiving fewer tokens than expected, the vault balance decreasing more than allowed, and the overall accounting assumptions of the protocol being violated. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the slashing logic and the timing relationships between the slashing window, veto window, and withdrawal delay. It is difficult to notice because the totalAssets function appears correct on its own and the timing edge case is subtle, only manifesting when a slashing request is made just after the slashing window and a miner front‑runs the finalization. To remediate, the protocol should exclude assets that are pending withdrawal from the slashable amount, either by adjusting the earmarked stakes calculation to use the vault balance after pending withdrawals are deducted or by deferring the calculation until finalizeSlashing after confirming that no protected withdrawals are in progress. Additionally, the finishRedeem function could be allowed to complete once the slashing window has passed without a pending slashing request, and the minimum withdrawal delay should only be enforced when a slashing request exists. These changes would align the slashing mechanism with the intended business logic that withdrawals initiated after the slashing window are not subject to penalties, restoring correct accounting and protecting user funds.

title: Delayed slashing window and lack of transparency for pending slashes could lead to loss of funds
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race‑condition and accounting inconsistency that arises from the two‑day veto window used for slashing vaults. When a slashing request is created, the protocol records the amount that should be removed from the vault based on the assets and share distribution at that moment. However, the actual transfer of the slashed assets is delayed by a configurable veto period, during which new deposits are still permitted. Because the slashing logic reduces the total assets of the vault without excluding deposits that occur after the request, any user who adds liquidity during the pending window is unintentionally subjected to the same proportional loss as the original shareholders. In the extreme case where a vault is fully slashed and its asset balance becomes zero while the share supply remains non‑zero, any subsequent deposit instantly loses all value, effectively allocating the new funds to previous shareholders at a zero‑price share. The root cause is the separation of the decision to slash from its execution combined with the absence of any on‑chain visibility of pending slashes. This lack of transparency means users cannot query whether a vault is currently queued for a slash, so they may unknowingly deposit into a vault that will lose value shortly after. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the slashing handler and observed that the handleSlashing function transfers assets from the vault after the delay, while the deposit function remains unrestricted. The problem is hard to notice because the UI does not display pending slashes and the share price only appears to drop after the slash finalizes, giving the impression of a normal market movement. The impact includes direct loss of funds for new depositors, misallocation of assets to earlier shareholders, broken accounting assumptions that total assets and total shares stay in sync, and erosion of trust in the protocol. The vulnerability affects all stakers who interact with vaults, the vault operators who manage deposits, and the overall protocol security posture. To remediate, the protocol should expose a getter that indicates whether a vault has a queued slash, pause or disable deposits while a slash is pending, and optionally prevent deposits when the vault’s asset balance is zero but shares still exist. Conceptually, the fix removes the time‑window race by synchronizing the state transition of slashing with deposit eligibility and by providing transparent observability of pending punitive actions.

title: Slashings will always fail in some cases
bug_full: The vulnerability originates in the vault’s slashAssets routine, which calculates the amount to be transferred to a slashing handler as the minimum of the vault’s current total assets and the amount requested by the core contract. After the two‑day veto window expires, the core contract calls slashAssets for each vault listed in a pending slash request. If, during the waiting period, the vault’s balance drops to zero – for example because another DSS has already slashed the vault or because pending withdrawals were completed – the Math.min operation returns zero. The function then proceeds to approve and invoke the external handleSlashing function with a zero amount. The slashing handler contains an explicit check that reverts when the amount is zero, causing the entire transaction that batches multiple vault slashes to fail. As a result, all other vaults in the same request remain unslashed, delaying or preventing the enforcement of penalties. This issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between requestSlashing, finalizeSlashing, and the vault’s slashAssets implementation. It is subtle because a zero transfer amount appears harmless, yet the downstream contract treats it as an error and reverts, breaking the atomicity of the batch operation. The impact is that operators may be unable to enforce slashing on misbehaving participants, users may see slashing transactions stuck or reverted, and the protocol’s economic security model is weakened because penalties can be delayed or missed. The problem occurs only when a vault’s balance becomes zero after a slash request has been queued but before it is finalized, which can happen in multi‑DSS environments or when withdrawals are processed during the veto period. The affected parties include the protocol’s governance committee, vault operators, and any users whose assets are subject to slashing. To remediate the issue, the slashAssets function should check that the computed transferAmount is greater than zero before approving the handler and invoking handleSlashing; if the amount is zero, the function should simply emit the Slashed event with a zero value and skip the external call, allowing the rest of the batch to continue unhindered. This change prevents the zero‑amount revert and restores the intended behavior of partial slashing without blocking other vaults.

title: Bringing a position from unsafe to safe by liquidation partially`
description: The CDPVault’s liquidation mechanism allows partial liquidations to temporarily bring unsafe positions back to a safe state. This can delay necessary liquidations if collateral prices continue to fall, potentially leading to increased risk and larger losses for the protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a liquidation‑logic flaw that allows a position that has become under‑collateralized to be made temporarily appear safe after a partial liquidation, thereby preventing further liquidations even if the market price continues to fall. The root cause is that the contract’s safety check (_isCollateralized) is performed after the debt has been reduced by the partial repayment, without accounting for the fact that the collateral value may still be insufficient under the original price trajectory. An attacker (or a borrower acting strategically) can trigger a partial liquidation that reduces the debt just enough to satisfy the liquidation‑ratio check, causing the contract to flag the position as safe. Because the position is now marked safe, any subsequent liquidation attempts – even with a lower repay amount – are rejected until the price drops far enough to satisfy the new, higher safety threshold. This can be exploited by deliberately performing a small partial liquidation to “reset” the safety flag, then allowing the collateral price to decline further, which delays the necessary full liquidation and may leave the protocol exposed to larger losses or insolvency. The impact is that lenders’ collateral may be insufficiently seized, leading to potential loss of funds, and the protocol’s risk parameters become ineffective. The issue manifests only when the system permits partial liquidations and the collateral price is volatile; it does not appear when positions are fully liquidated in one step. All participants who rely on the vault’s safety indicator – borrowers, lenders, and protocol governance – are affected because the UI and on‑chain checks will incorrectly report a safe state. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by reproducing a scenario where a position became unsafe, a partial liquidation was executed, and a subsequent liquidation attempt was rejected despite further price decline. It is hard to notice because the contract’s state variables correctly reflect the reduced debt, and the safety flag is updated according to the new debt, giving the impression that the position is healthy. The bug belongs to the class of “unsafe‑to‑safe state transition” or “partial liquidation safety check bypass” vulnerabilities, where business logic assumes that any liquidation that makes a position safe is sufficient, ignoring future price movements. From a user’s perspective, a borrower may see their position marked as safe after a partial liquidation and assume no further risk, while a lender may notice that their collateral value drops but no liquidation occurs, leading to unexpected zero recovery. To remediate, the liquidation function should either forbid partial liquidations that leave the position still under‑collateralized, keep the unsafe flag until the price recovers, or enforce a re‑evaluation of safety based on the pre‑partial state, ensuring that positions cannot be artificially marked safe without fully restoring the required collateralization ratio.

title: Wrong repayment amount used in `PositionAction::_repay`, forcing users to unexpectedly lose funds
description:
```solidity
PositionAction allows users to interact with their position in the CDP Vault through a proxy, on top of that it allows users to do certain actions before interacting with the position. An example of this is the `PositionAction::deposit`, which allows users to:

  1. Deposit collateral tokens directly into the position.
  2. Swap arbitrary tokens for collateral and the deposit into the position.

This is handled in `PositionAction::_deposit`, where if swap params exist, swap takes place and the returned amount is used when depositing into the position; else the user’s specified amount is used.

However, in `PositionAction::_repay`, this is not the case, where even if a swap took place, the amount sent to the vault/position is still the one specified by the user; which is wrong and inconsistent with the other functions’ API. This can cause unexpected behaviors and reverts when users try to interact with `PositionAction::repay`.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the PositionAction contract’s internal repayment routine. When a user calls the repay function with an auxiliary swap (for example, swapping USDC for the underlying collateral token), the contract performs the swap correctly but then continues to use the amount field supplied by the caller – often zero – instead of the actual amount of underlying token received from the swap. This mismatch means the contract approves and forwards an incorrect repayment amount to the vault, leaving the borrower’s debt unchanged while the swapped tokens are permanently transferred out of the user’s wallet. The root cause is a logical error: the function does not update the local amount variable after the swap, unlike the deposit path which correctly substitutes the swapped amount. Exploitation is straightforward: a user (or an attacker acting on behalf of a user) can invoke repay with a non‑zero auxSwap and set the amount parameter to zero; the swap will consume the user’s USDC, the contract will approve zero repayment, and the vault will record no reduction in debt. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are a drained USDC balance, unchanged collateral, and an unchanged debt figure – the user expects the debt to be reduced but receives nothing. This situation occurs only when the repay call includes a swap and the amount argument does not reflect the swap output. All borrowers using PositionAction through a proxy are affected because the bug is embedded in the shared library. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit that added integration tests with a Balancer pool to simulate realistic swaps. It is hard to notice because the function signature suggests the amount argument controls the repayment, and the swap itself succeeds, giving the impression that the operation completed correctly. The bug violates the core accounting invariant that the amount of underlying token sent to the vault must equal the debt reduction. The recommended fix is to capture the actual amount returned by the swap (or transferred directly) and use that value when approving and calling modifyCollateralAndDebt, mirroring the logic used in the deposit function. By doing so the repayment amount aligns with the tokens actually supplied, restoring the intended financial behavior and preventing silent loss of user funds.

title: `SwapAction::getSwapToken` will return wrong swap token for balancer `EXACT_OUT` swaps
description:
```solidity
As known, when doing a Balancer `EXACT_OUT` batch swap, assets should be passed in reverse order, this is thoroughly documented [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/main/src/proxy/SwapAction.sol#L176-L209).

Swapping in USDC for an exact amount out of BAL
    
    swapType = `EXACT_OUT` and `assets` = [BAL, WETH, DAI, USDC]:

However, in `SwapAction::getSwapToken`, for Balancer swaps it always returns the last asset in the assets array, which is correct for `EXACT_IN` but wrong for `EXACT_OUT`, where it should be the first asset in the assets array.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the helper routine that determines which token is considered the output of a Balancer batch swap. For Balancer swaps the contract always selects the last element of the assets array as the out‑token, which is correct for swaps of type EXACT_IN where the assets are ordered from input to output. However, for swaps of type EXACT_OUT the Balancer specification requires the assets to be supplied in reverse order, meaning the first element of the array represents the token that will be received. Because the routine does not account for this reversal, it returns the wrong token – the input token instead of the expected output token – whenever an EXACT_OUT swap is performed. The root cause is a misunderstanding of Balancer’s asset ordering rules and a hard‑coded assumption that the out‑token is always the last entry. An attacker or a careless user can exploit this by constructing an EXACT_OUT swap request; the contract will believe it has delivered the desired token while in reality it either retains the original token or sends the wrong asset. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that a swap transaction succeeded, but the balance of the expected token does not increase and the balance of the token that should have been spent may remain unchanged, leading to a situation where “funds disappear” or a “refund is missing”. The issue manifests only for Balancer swaps using the EXACT_OUT mode and when the contract later relies on the returned token identifier for bookkeeping, fee calculation, or further transfers. All participants who perform such swaps – end‑users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions are violated and the protocol may record incorrect asset flows. The bug was discovered during a manual audit when a test case demonstrated that getSwapToken returned the input token address for an EXACT_OUT swap, contradicting the documented asset ordering. It is subtle because the swap itself does not revert; the transaction appears successful, making the error easy to overlook without explicit checks. The proper remediation is to adjust the token‑selection logic so that when the swap type is EXACT_OUT the routine returns the first element of the assets array, and otherwise returns the last element, thereby aligning the implementation with Balancer’s specification and restoring correct accounting of received assets.

title: `INFLATION_PROTECTION_TIME` can not be up to a year as intended because it is hardcoded to `1749120350`
description:
```solidity
AURA rewards will be distributed at a lesser time than a year. In fact, if the `AuraVault.sol` contract is deployed 295 days after the completion of this audit, No aura rewards will be distributed. This is because the `INFLATION_PROTECTION_TIME` is hardcoded to `1749120350`.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a hard‑coded timestamp constant named INFLATION_PROTECTION_TIME that is set to the literal value 1749120350 inside the AuraVault contract. This constant is intended to represent a one‑year window after contract deployment during which AURA token rewards may be distributed to users who call the claim function. Because the value is fixed at compile time, the effective reward window is anchored to an absolute Unix time rather than being calculated relative to the block timestamp at deployment. As a result, if the contract is deployed after the hard‑coded moment – which, at the time of the audit, is less than 295 days away – the condition block.timestamp <= INFLATION_PROTECTION_TIME will immediately evaluate to false. Consequently, the branch that transfers the user‑specified AURA amount is never executed and the contract instead transfers the entire remaining AURA balance to the locker address. From a user’s perspective the expected AURA reward is missing; the UI may show a successful claim event but the user receives zero AURA tokens, while other rewards such as BAL may still be delivered. The impact is that participants who rely on the promised AURA incentives receive nothing, effectively breaking the protocol’s inflation‑protection incentive model and potentially discouraging future participation. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the constant definition and the subsequent timestamp comparison. It can be hard to notice because the numeric constant looks like any other configuration value and does not immediately reveal that it is already in the past.
