The proper mitigation is to replace the constant with an immutable variable that is initialized in the constructor as block.timestamp + 365 days, or otherwise make the protection period configurable at deployment time, ensuring the reward window always starts from the moment the contract becomes live. This change restores the intended business logic that users receive AURA rewards for up to one year after deployment, aligning the contract’s accounting assumptions with the protocol’s incentive design.

title: `PositionAction4626::increaseLever` will always revert
description:
```solidity
Users can use `PositionAction::increaseLever` to increase their positions’ leverage, i.e., increasing both the collateral and debt, by taking a flash loan and doing some swaps. At the end of the process, after swapping “borrow” tokens to underlying tokens they should be returned to the vault under the position’s “name”.

For ERC20 collateral positions, this is happening in `PositionAction20::_onIncreaseLever` (that gets called in `PositionAction::onFlashLoan`) which approves the vault to spend some amount and then returns the amount to be later sent using the following in `PositionAction::onFlashLoan`:
    
    // add collateral and debt
    ICDPVault(leverParams.vault).modifyCollateralAndDebt(
        leverParams.position,
        address(this),
        address(this),
        toInt256(collateral),
        toInt256(addDebt)
    );

However, for ERC4626 collateral positions, `PositionAction4626::_onIncreaseLever` is both approving the amount and depositing it into the vault under `address(this)` which IS NOT the position’s proxy but `PositionAction4626` contract as it is the flash loan callback function and isn’t delegated like `increaseLever`. When `_onIncreaseLever` finishes, it’ll try to deposit the collateral AGAIN in the vault using [this](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/main/src/proxy/PositionAction.sol#L416-L422); which will for sure revert, as the approval was spent and no funds are left to make the deposit.

This will cause `PositionAction4626::increaseLever` to always revert and never work, blocking users from leveraging their positions.
```
bug_full: PositionAction4626::increaseLever is intended to let a user raise the leverage of a vault position that uses an ERC4626 token as collateral. The function works by taking a flash loan, swapping the borrowed assets, approving the vault to pull the newly acquired collateral and finally depositing that collateral back into the vault under the position’s proxy address. In the ERC20‑based implementation the approval is granted to the vault and the subsequent deposit succeeds because the vault pulls the tokens from the proxy contract. In the ERC4626 implementation the internal helper _onIncreaseLever mistakenly approves the vault and immediately calls deposit on the vault using address(this) as the depositor. Because address(this) is the PositionAction4626 contract – the flash‑loan callback – the vault transfers the approved tokens to itself, consuming the allowance. After the helper returns, the outer logic attempts a second deposit of the same amount, assuming the allowance is still available. The allowance has already been spent, so the ERC20 transfer reverts with ERC20: insufficient allowance. The revert occurs every time increaseLever is called, effectively making the function unusable. The bug is a classic case of incorrect handling of token approvals and depositor identity, where the contract assumes that an approval granted to itself can be reused after it has already been consumed. It is discovered during a functional audit that exercised the increaseLever path for ERC4626 collateral and observed a deterministic revert. The issue is subtle because the same code path works for ERC20 collateral, so reviewers may overlook the difference in depositor semantics. The impact is that users cannot increase leverage on positions that use ERC4626 tokens, leading to a denial‑of‑service for those positions and potentially locking funds that users intended to leverage. The condition occurs whenever a user calls increaseLever on a position whose collateral token implements ERC4626, i.e., when the flash‑loan callback executes _onIncreaseLever. Affected parties include the position owners, the protocol’s liquidity providers and any downstream contracts that rely on leveraged positions. The fix is to stop the internal function from performing the deposit on behalf of the PositionAction4626 contract and instead return the raw collateral amount to the outer logic, which will then perform a single deposit under the correct proxy address. In other words, the contract should not consume the approval twice nor use the wrong depositor address. Correcting the flow restores the intended accounting where the vault receives the exact amount of newly minted collateral and the leverage increase succeeds.

title: `PoolAction::updateLeverJoin` wrongly updates `assetsIn` array, leading to `PositionAction4626::_onIncreaseLever` to always revert
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect handling of the token amount array that is passed to Balancer when a user tries to increase the leverage of a position whose collateral is an ERC4626 token. In the function that prepares the join parameters, a loop iterates over the list of pool assets and attempts to skip the Balancer pool token (BPT) while writing the upfront and flash‑loan amounts into the assetsIn array. The code uses a boolean flag (skipIndex) that is set only when the current asset equals the pool token, but the flag is applied to the index calculation before the check, causing the assetsIn array to be shifted incorrectly when the pool token is not present in the assets list. As a result, the loop overwrites the wrong entry in assetsIn, often duplicating the flash‑loan amount into a second position. When the updated parameters are later used by PositionAction4626::_onIncreaseLever, the mismatched amounts cause the Balancer vault to reject the join operation and the contract reverts with a BAL#506 error. This bug manifests whenever a user calls increaseLever with a Balancer pool that does not contain the BPT token at the expected index, which is common for ERC4626‑based collateral. The impact is that legitimate users cannot increase leverage on their positions, effectively locking their collateral and preventing further borrowing; from a UI perspective the transaction simply fails and the user sees no change in their balance or collateral, often interpreting it as a mysterious “funds disappear” or “refund missing” situation. The issue was discovered during a security audit by examining the logic of PoolAction::updateLeverJoin and reproducing the failure in an integration test that showed assetsIn being set to [49 ether, 49 ether] instead of the expected [49 ether, 0]. The bug is subtle because the loop appears to handle the BPT skip correctly, but the condition order and the use of the skip flag cause an off‑by‑one error only when the pool token is absent, making it easy to miss in casual testing. The proper fix is to determine the correct pool token address from the Balancer vault and pool ID, and to adjust the loop so that the skip logic is applied after confirming the asset is not the pool token, ensuring that assetsIn is indexed only for real tokens and that the BPT entry is never written to. Conceptually, the fix involves correctly aligning the assets array with the amounts array and avoiding overwriting entries, thereby restoring the intended accounting of token amounts and allowing increaseLever to succeed without unintended reverts.

title: `PositionAction4626::_onDecreaseLever` wrongly updates `tokenOut` forcing user’s funds to be stuck in the position action contract
description:
```solidity
Users can use `PositionAction::decreaseLever` to decrease the leverage of their positions when the collateral is an ERC4626, that position action interacts with `PositionAction4626::_onDecreaseLever`. With that, the protocol gives the ability to join/exit Balancer pools, leveraging down an ERC4626 position is handled in `PositionAction4626::_onDecreaseLever`.

This first step is that `tokenOut` is set to the redeemed 4626 amount; however, when `auxAction` exists, (i.e. the user wants to exit a Balancer pool), the `tokenOut` is updated to return the amount of the exit position, this poses multiple issues:

  1. If the token out from Balancer is not the same as 4626’s underlying this will wrongly update to another token’s amount.
  2. If the recipient is not in the position action contract, the tokens would be sent to another address, while it assumes that it received them.
  3. If the `token = 4626`’s underlying, the recipient is the user, and the amount of from Balancer is less than the redeemed `tokenOut`, the contract would set the `tokenOut` as the Balancer return amount, which is less than the original `tokenOut`. This will return the wrong `tokenOut` in `PositionAction::onCreditFlashLoan`, sending the user a residual amount less than the real amount (the POC below is for this scenario).

The user’s “extra” collateral amount will end up stuck in the position action contract forever.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the PositionAction4626::_onDecreaseLever routine that is invoked when a user decreases the leverage of a position whose collateral is an ERC4626 token and also supplies an auxiliary Balancer pool exit action (auxAction). The function initially records tokenOut as the amount of the underlying token redeemed from the ERC4626 vault. When an auxAction is present, the code overwrites tokenOut with the amount returned by the Balancer pool exit. This overwrite assumes that the Balancer exit token is identical to the ERC4626 underlying token and that the recipient of the exit tokens is the PositionAction contract itself. In reality the Balancer pool may return a different token, or the exit may be sent directly to the user. If the returned token differs, tokenOut is set to an incorrect amount; if the recipient is not the contract, the contract later assumes it received tokens that never arrived; and if the returned amount is smaller than the original redemption, tokenOut is reduced, causing the contract to believe it has transferred the full amount while a residual balance of the underlying token remains locked inside the PositionAction contract. The bug is triggered only when a decreaseLever call includes an auxAction that exits a Balancer pool, which is a common pattern for users who want to unwind leveraged positions. The impact is that a portion of the user’s collateral becomes permanently inaccessible – in the proof‑of‑concept the user loses roughly 20 ether worth of collateral that stays forever in the PositionAction contract. From the user’s perspective the UI may show the expected reduction in debt and collateral, but the final balance of the underlying token is lower than anticipated, leading to “funds disappear” symptoms. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a test that performed a decreaseLever with a Balancer exit and observing the residual token balance. It is hard to notice because the contract’s primary token balances appear zero, while the hidden residual is held in the underlying token’s balance, which is not displayed in typical dashboards. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or token‑out mismanagement vulnerabilities, where a contract incorrectly tracks the amount of tokens it should have transferred. The proper fix is to compute tokenOut after the auxiliary action by reading the contract’s actual balance of the underlying token (or by ensuring the recipient is the contract) and to handle cases where the Balancer exit token differs from the ERC4626 underlying token, thereby preventing any leftover collateral from being trapped.

title: `PoolAction::_balancerExit` returns wrong token out amount
description:
Users use `PoolAction::exit` to exit a Balancer pool position, it calls `_balancerExit` to do the job. It is expected to exit the pool and return the amount out of the token; however, it returns the whole recipient’s balance, without considering the case where the recipient is holding an amount of the same token from different sources. It’ll return an exaggerated amount rather than the amount out.

This will cause `PositionAction4626::_onDecreaseLever` to revert sometimes. In this case, the user is leveraging down, exiting a Balancer pool, and holds some `tokenOut` amount. In `PositionAction::onCreditFlashLoan`, `withdrawnCollateral` would be an unreal exaggerated amount, and the contract will try to send back `residualAmount` which will be greater than its balance.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the routine that processes a Balancer pool exit. When a user calls the generic exit function, the internal helper _balancerExit is supposed to calculate how many units of the requested token are transferred out of the pool and return that amount to the caller. Instead of measuring the net increase of the recipient’s token balance, the implementation simply reads the recipient’s entire token balance after the exit and returns that value. Consequently, if the recipient already owned some of the same token from previous operations, the returned figure includes both the pre‑existing balance and the newly received amount. This mis‑calculation inflates the reported out amount, sometimes by a factor of two or more. The bug was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a test that pre‑funded the user with the target token, performed a pool join, transferred the LP tokens to the contract, and then called exit; the test observed that the function reported 19 WSTETH when only 9 WSTETH were actually withdrawn. The root cause is an accounting error: the code does not capture the balance before the exit and therefore cannot compute the delta. An attacker or an unwary developer can exploit this by supplying a recipient address that already holds the token, causing downstream logic that relies on the returned amount – such as PositionAction4626::_onDecreaseLever – to receive an exaggerated value. The downstream contract then attempts to transfer a residual amount that exceeds its actual token holdings, triggering a revert and potentially leaving the user’s transaction incomplete. The impact is that leveraged positions may fail to close, funds may become temporarily locked, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken because the contract believes it has transferred more collateral than it actually did. The issue manifests only when the exit recipient has a non‑zero balance of the token being withdrawn; in pure fresh‑exit scenarios the bug is invisible, making it hard to notice in normal operation. From a user’s perspective the UI may show an unexpectedly large token balance after exiting, yet the transaction reverts or the protocol reports an error, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. The flaw belongs to the class of “incorrect token out amount calculation” or “balance‑delta mis‑reporting” bugs, which violate the invariant that the amount returned by a withdrawal function must equal the net token increase of the caller. The proper fix is to record the recipient’s token balance before invoking the Balancer vault, perform the exit, then compute and return the difference between the post‑exit and pre‑exit balances, ensuring that only the newly received tokens are reported.

title: `PendleLPOracle::_fetchAndValidate` uses Chainlink’s deprecated `answeredInRound`
description:
`PendleLPOracle` uses Chainlink to get the price of Pendle’s underlying asset in ETH; this is done using `_fetchAndValidate`. That function uses `answeredInRound`, which is deprecated according to [Chainlink docs](https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds/api-reference#latestrounddata).

Previously used when answers could take multiple rounds to be computed.

This results in invalid/wrong prices from Chainlink.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of using Chainlink's deprecated answeredInRound field in the function that fetches and validates price data for the Pendle LP oracle. The field was originally intended for cases where an answer could span multiple rounds, but Chainlink has removed support and now recommends using latestRoundData. Because answeredInRound may return stale or zero round identifiers, the oracle can accept outdated or malformed price data. An attacker who can influence the underlying Chainlink feed, or who can wait for a round where answeredInRound is not updated, can cause the oracle to return a price that is significantly higher or lower than the true market price. When the oracle supplies this incorrect price to the Pendle protocol, LP token valuations, collateral calculations, and trade settlements are performed with the wrong number, leading to users receiving too few tokens, excessive slippage, or even loss of funds. The issue manifests whenever the oracle calls _fetchAndValidate, which is executed on every price query, and it occurs under normal network conditions because the deprecated field still returns a value that passes the contract's checks. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit that compared the contract's implementation against the current Chainlink documentation. It is subtle because the returned price still looks like a plausible ETH value, so users and developers may not notice the discrepancy until a trade fails or a loss is observed. The proper fix is to stop using answeredInRound and instead rely on the latestRoundData call, checking that the round is fresh, the answer is non‑zero, and the timestamp is recent. This aligns the oracle with the recommended Chainlink interface and prevents the acceptance of stale or incorrect price data. In summary, the contract suffers from a deprecated‑API usage class of bug that leads to inaccurate price feeds, breaking the accounting assumptions of the Pendle protocol and potentially allowing financial loss.

title: Malicious actor can abuse the minimum shares check in `StakingLPEth` and cause DoS or locked funds for the last user that withdraws
description: The last user that tries to cooldown/withdraw his share will not be able to withdraw the full deposited amount.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a hard‑coded minimum‑shares guard that is enforced on every deposit and withdrawal in the StakingLPEth vault. The contract stores the total number of issued shares (totalSupply) and aborts any operation that would leave totalSupply greater than zero but smaller than a constant MIN_SHARES. Because the guard is applied after the underlying ERC4626 logic updates balances, a malicious actor can manipulate the share accounting so that the final user’s withdrawal would reduce totalSupply below the threshold, causing the _checkMinShares function to revert. In practice this means that the last participant who attempts to cooldown or withdraw their position may only receive (balance‑MIN_SHARES) and the remaining MIN_SHARES become permanently locked unless another user later deposits enough shares to raise totalSupply above the limit. The same check also interferes with the share‑conversion formula used during minting: when totalSupply is zero and a small amount of LP‑ETH is already present, the calculated share amount can fall below MIN_SHARES, causing the deposit to revert and effectively denying any new minting. An attacker can exploit this by back‑running a legitimate deposit with a tiny share mint, or by seeding the contract with a negligible amount of LP‑ETH before any user deposits, thereby forcing the share calculation to produce an insufficient amount. The impact is twofold: (1) a denial‑of‑service condition where legitimate users cannot withdraw their full funds, leading to locked capital and user frustration; (2) a denial‑of‑service on the deposit path, preventing new users from entering the vault unless they provide an astronomically large amount of assets. The issue manifests only when the totalSupply is close to the MIN_SHARES boundary, which is typically after the first few deposits or when the contract is freshly deployed. All participants—depositors, withdrawers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the economic guarantees of the vault are broken and the accounting assumptions that each share corresponds to a proportional claim on assets no longer hold. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit that examined the invariant checks around share accounting. It is subtle because the guard appears to protect against inflation attacks, yet it introduces a griefing vector that is not obvious from a superficial review of the code. The recommended remediation is to eliminate the minimum‑shares check or to pre‑fund the contract at deployment so that totalSupply never falls below the threshold, thereby removing the condition that can be triggered by an attacker. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “invariant‑violation checks that can be abused to create a state where legitimate operations revert”, a pattern that can cause funds to disappear from the user’s perspective or refunds to be partially missing.

title: `CDPVault.liquidatePosition`
bug_full: The contract contains a scaling mismatch that leads to an over‑payment of collateral during liquidation. Each position stores collateral in an internal representation that is multiplied by a factor called tokenScale, which reflects the token's decimal precision. Deposit, withdraw and collateral‑modification functions correctly convert between the external token amount and the internal amount by applying tokenScale, for example using wmul(abs(deltaCollateral), tokenScale) before transferring tokens. However, the liquidatePosition function skips this conversion and transfers the raw internal amount directly to the liquidator with token.safeTransfer(msg.sender, takeCollateral). When the collateral token has fewer than 18 decimals, tokenScale is less than 1e18, so the internal amount is larger than the true token amount. As a result, a liquidator can receive many times more tokens than the protocol intends to give, effectively draining collateral from the vault. The exploit works by creating a position with a low‑decimal token, forcing a price drop that makes the position under‑collateralised, and then calling liquidatePosition with a modest amount of debt. Because the transfer is unscaled, the liquidator receives an inflated amount of collateral (e.g., 1052 units instead of the expected 10.52 units). This loss is borne by other depositors, who may later be unable to withdraw their own collateral, as demonstrated when a user’s withdrawal reverts due to insufficient remaining balance. The issue appears only in the liquidation path, making it easy to miss during casual testing, and it violates the accounting assumption that the total collateral in the vault is conserved across operations. The bug was discovered through a targeted audit test that exercised liquidation with a token of 16 decimals. To remediate, the contract should apply the same tokenScale conversion when sending collateral to the liquidator, for example by transferring wmul(takeCollateral, tokenScale) instead of the raw amount, thereby restoring consistent unit handling across all entry points.

title: Unclaimed rewards handling issue in `AuraVault` contract functions
poc:
1. **User deposits assets:**

     * User calls `deposit(1000, receiver)`.
     * `totalAssets()` returns 10,000 (current balance in reward pool).
     * `previewDeposit(1000)` calculates shares based on 10,000 total assets.
     * Unclaimed rewards of 500 are not included, leading to an incorrect share calculation.
  2. **User mints shares:**

     * User calls `mint(100, receiver)`.
     * `totalAssets()` returns 10,000 (current balance in reward pool).
     * `previewMint(100)` calculates assets based on 10,000 total assets.
     * Unclaimed rewards of 500 are not included, leading to an incorrect asset calculation.
  3. **User withdraws assets:**

     * User calls `withdraw(1000, receiver, owner)`.
     * `totalAssets()` returns 10,000 (current balance in reward pool).
     * `previewWithdraw(1000)` calculates shares based on 10,000 total assets.
     * Unclaimed rewards of 500 are not included, leading to an incorrect share calculation.
  4. **User redeems shares:**

     * User calls `redeem(100, receiver, owner)`.
     * `totalAssets()` returns 10,000 (current balance in reward pool).
     * `previewRedeem(100)` calculates assets based on 10,000 total assets.
     * Unclaimed rewards of 500 are not included, leading to an incorrect asset calculation.
bug_full: The AuraVault contract implements the ERC4626 tokenized vault interface and relies on the totalAssets() view to report the amount of underlying assets that back each share. In the current implementation totalAssets() simply returns the balance of the underlying token held in the external RewardsPool, ignoring any rewards that the vault has earned but not yet claimed. Because the earned rewards are not added to the reported total, the preview functions used by deposit, mint, withdraw and redeem calculate share‑to‑asset ratios based on an incomplete asset pool. When unclaimed rewards exist, a depositor receives more shares than the actual value of the deposited assets, while a withdrawer may receive fewer assets for the same number of shares. This discrepancy can cause users to see unexpected share balances, receive zero or reduced refunds, or observe their vault balance appear correct while the accounting behind the scenes is off. The bug manifests whenever the vault has pending rewards – a condition that can arise at any time as the RewardsPool distributes incentives. All participants of the vault, including regular users and the protocol that depends on accurate accounting, are affected because the fundamental invariant that each share represents a proportional claim on the total assets is broken. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit by Code4rena, where the auditors compared the on‑chain balance with the expected reward accrual and noticed mismatched share calculations. It is subtle because the vault’s token balance looks normal and the missing rewards are not visible in the contract’s storage, making the error easy to overlook during casual testing. The proper remediation is to modify totalAssets() so that it adds the amount returned by the earned() call of the RewardsPool to the current balance, thereby ensuring that both claimed and unclaimed rewards are accounted for in every share‑related computation. This change restores the correct accounting relationship, prevents users from receiving an incorrect number of shares or assets, and aligns the vault’s behavior with the intended ERC4626 semantics.

title: Lack of Slippage Control in `AuraVault::deposit` and `AuraVault::mint` Functions Can Lead to Unexpected Financial Losses for Users
description: The `AuraVault` contract implements ERC-4626 vault functionality, allowing users to deposit assets and mint shares. However, the `deposit` and `mint` functions lack slippage controls, which can result in users receiving fewer shares or sending more assets than expected. This issue is similar to a previously reported bug in the `bHermes` contract, where the absence of slippage controls in the `ERC4626DepositOnly.deposit` and `ERC4626DepositOnly.mint` functions led to unexpected outcomes for users.
poc:
1. Alice wants to deposit 1000 units of an asset into the `AuraVault` contract and expects to receive at least 100 shares.
  2. Alice calls the `deposit` function with 1000 units of the asset.
  3. Due to slippage, Alice receives only 90 shares instead of the expected 100 shares.
  4. Alice loses value because she received fewer shares than expected.

Similarly, for the `mint` function:

  1. Bob wants to mint 100 shares and expects to send no more than 1000 units of the asset.
  2. Bob calls the `mint` function with 100 shares as the input.
  3. Due to slippage, Bob ends up sending 1200 units of the asset instead of the expected 1000 units.
  4. Bob loses value because he sent more assets than expected.
bug_full: An ERC‑4626 vault implementation called AuraVault allows users to deposit assets and mint shares, but the deposit and mint functions do not enforce any slippage limits. The functions calculate the number of shares (or required assets) using a preview call and then immediately perform the transfer without checking that the actual output meets a user‑defined bound. Because the price of the underlying asset can change between the preview and the execution, or because rounding errors can occur, a caller may receive fewer shares than expected when depositing, or may have to provide more assets than anticipated when minting. An attacker or a volatile market can exploit this by front‑running the transaction or by simply waiting for a price shift, causing the vault to mint shares at a less favorable rate. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, but the UI shows a lower share balance or a higher token balance deduction than was anticipated – for example, a user expects to receive 100 shares for 1 000 tokens but ends up with only 90 shares, or expects to spend at most 1 000 tokens for 100 shares but is charged 1 200 tokens. The impact is a direct financial loss for the depositor and a breach of the accounting guarantees that ERC‑4626 promises, potentially eroding trust in the protocol. The issue was identified during a security audit that compared the code to a known bug in the bHermes contract where the same lack of slippage protection caused similar outcomes. The problem is subtle because the functions follow the ERC‑4626 interface and do not revert on unfavorable conversion rates, making it easy to miss during functional testing. The recommended mitigation is to add explicit slippage parameters – a minimum number of shares for deposits and a maximum amount of assets for mints – and to require that the previewed amount satisfies these bounds before proceeding. This aligns the vault with best‑practice patterns for ERC‑4626 and prevents users from unintentionally losing value due to market movement or rounding.

title: DOS attack to `SwapAction.transferAndSwap`
description:
```solidity
SwapAction.transferAndSwap() will perform a _transferFrom to transfer the input tokens to the user proxy and then perform a swap via a router. When it uses an ERC20 permit transferFrom, an attacker can extract the v, r, s from the safePermit() call and frontruns it with a direct safePermit() with the same arguments. As a result, SwapAction.transferAndSwap() will fail due to the advancing of nonce. Effectively, this is a DOS attack.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the SwapAction.transferAndSwap workflow that relies on an ERC20 permit (EIP‑2612) to set an allowance before calling safeTransferFrom. The contract calls token.safePermit with the signature parameters supplied by the user and then immediately performs a safeTransferFrom. Because the permit mechanism uses a nonce that is incremented on each successful execution, an attacker who observes the pending transaction can front‑run it by submitting an identical safePermit call with the same v, r, s values. This front‑run consumes the nonce, so when the original transaction reaches the contract the safePermit call fails with an “invalid signature” error. The contract does not catch this failure and proceeds under the assumption that the allowance is in place, causing the whole transferAndSwap call to revert. The root cause is the lack of proper handling for permit failures and the reliance on a mutable nonce that can be exhausted by a malicious actor. Exploitation requires only the ability to monitor the mempool and submit a transaction with the same permit data before the victim’s transaction is mined. When the attack succeeds, the user’s swap does not execute; the transaction reverts, the user sees no token transfer or swap result, and may be left with an unchanged balance while the allowance may have been altered. This affects any user of the protocol who attempts to swap tokens via SwapAction.transferAndSwap, as well as the protocol itself because legitimate swaps can be blocked, harming liquidity and user trust. The issue was discovered during a security audit by reproducing a front‑running scenario in a Forge test that called safePermit directly before the proxy execution, confirming that the nonce increment caused the subsequent permit verification to fail. The problem is subtle because the allowance appears to be correctly set after the attacker’s transaction, yet the contract’s internal logic still aborts, making it easy to miss in casual testing. To remediate, the contract should treat the permit call as optional: either verify that the permit succeeded using a try‑catch block and fall back to checking the existing allowance, or require the caller to provide sufficient allowance beforehand. Using Permit2’s atomic permit‑and‑transfer function or adding explicit nonce checks can also prevent the race condition. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of signature‑replay or nonce‑race denial‑of‑service vulnerabilities where an attacker can invalidate a user‑supplied permit by consuming its nonce before the contract processes it, breaking the expected flow of token transfer and swap execution.

title: WhenNotPaused modifier in the CDPVault can be bypassed by users
description: Users can still execute deposit and withdraw functions when the CDPVault.sol is paused as against the design expectation by just calling the modifyCollateralAndDebt(...) function with the necessary parameters.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a pause bypass in the CDPVault contract. The contract is designed to stop all deposits and withdrawals when the DAO activates the pause flag, and this restriction is enforced by the whenNotPaused modifier on the public deposit and withdraw functions. However, both of these functions delegate the core state change to a separate function called modifyCollateralAndDebt, which is declared as public and does not carry the whenNotPaused guard. Because the helper function is publicly accessible, any user can invoke it directly with arbitrary parameters that mimic a deposit or a withdrawal even while the contract is paused. An attacker can therefore submit a transaction that calls modifyCollateralAndDebt with a positive deltaCollateral to add collateral or with a negative deltaCollateral to remove collateral, effectively bypassing the emergency stop. This can be done at any time after the pause is engaged, meaning the pause mechanism does not provide the intended safety window. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken: users expect that no collateral movements are possible during a pause, yet funds can still be moved, potentially leading to unexpected balance changes, loss of trust, or even draining of assets if combined with other bugs. The issue affects all participants of the protocol because any address can call the public function, and it is especially dangerous for the DAO that relies on the pause as a risk‑mitigation tool. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the pause modifier was only applied to the wrapper functions and not to the underlying state‑changing routine. The problem is subtle because the public helper function is not exposed through the user interface, so developers and users may assume that pausing is sufficient. The correct remediation is to either restrict modifyCollateralAndDebt to internal visibility so it cannot be called from outside the contract, or to add the whenNotPaused modifier to the function itself, ensuring that the pause flag is respected for every state‑changing entry point.

title: Incorrect calculation of `newCumulativeIndex` in function `calcDecrease`
description:
In the contract CDPVault.sol, the function calcDecrease calculates newCumulativeIndex in line 703 when amountToRepay < interestAccrued with profit which is:

```solidity
newCumulativeIndex =
(INDEX_PRECISION * cumulativeIndexNow * cumulativeIndexLastUpdate) /
(INDEX_PRECISION *
    cumulativeIndexNow -
    (INDEX_PRECISION * profit * cumulativeIndexLastUpdate) /
    debt); // U:[CL-3]
```

However, the profit contains the cumulativeQuotaInterest, so it can not be used to calculate newCumulativeIndex.

```solidity
if (amountToRepay >= cumulativeQuotaInterest) {
    amountToRepay -= cumulativeQuotaInterest; // U:[CL-3]
    profit += cumulativeQuotaInterest; // U:[CL-3]

    newCumulativeQuotaInterest = 0; // U:[CL-3]
}
```

For example, when the left amountToRepay can cover the interestAccrued, the newCumulativeIndex should be cumulativeIndexNow as in line 692, because: interestAccrued == (debt * cumulativeIndexNow) / cumulativeIndexLastUpdate - debt.

```solidity
if (amountToRepay >= interestAccrued) {
    amountToRepay -= interestAccrued;

    profit += interestAccrued;

    newCumulativeIndex = cumulativeIndexNow;
}
```

However, when the left amountToRepay = interestAccrued - 1, and profit will be cumulativeQuotaInterest+interestAccrued - 1. The calculation of newCumulativeIndex will be larger than cumulativeIndexNow because the cumulativeQuotaInterest+interestAccrued - 1 will be larger than interestAccrued which is totally wrong, since it exceeds the limit cumulativeIndexNow.

```solidity
newCumulativeIndex =
(INDEX_PRECISION * cumulativeIndexNow * cumulativeIndexLastUpdate) /
(INDEX_PRECISION *
    cumulativeIndexNow -
    (INDEX_PRECISION * profit * cumulativeIndexLastUpdate) /
    debt); // U:[CL-3]
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the CDPVault contract’s calcDecrease routine, where the new cumulative interest index (newCumulativeIndex) is derived from a formula that mistakenly incorporates the variable profit when the repayment amount is smaller than the accrued interest. Profit is a sum of the regular interest accrued and the cumulative quota interest, but the quota portion should not be used to adjust the index because it represents a separate reward stream. When a borrower attempts to repay an amount that is just one unit short of the total interest owed (amountToRepay = interestAccrued‑1), the contract adds this shortfall to profit, producing a profit value larger than the actual interest. The subsequent division computes a newCumulativeIndex that exceeds the current cumulativeIndexNow, violating the invariant that the index can never grow beyond the latest pool index. This mis‑calculation can be triggered whenever the repayment amount is insufficient to cover the full interest, a condition that occurs naturally as users make partial repayments over time. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the protocol reports an index that is higher than the pool’s base interest index, which may lead to inflated reward calculations for stakers or incorrect debt accounting for borrowers. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a test that forces the edge case where amountToRepay is one wei less than the accrued interest, revealing that cumulativeIndexLastUpdate becomes greater than cumulativeIndexNow – an impossible state under correct accounting. The bug is subtle because the numbers involved are large fixed‑point integers, so the overflow does not cause an immediate revert and may only be observable through detailed logs or mismatched balances. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of “incorrect state update due to misuse of intermediate accounting variables” and breaks the business rule that the cumulative interest index must be monotonic and bounded by the pool’s current index. The recommended fix replaces the profit term with the actual amountToRepay in the denominator of the index formula, ensuring that the index is updated only by the portion of repayment that truly reduces interest, and resets the remaining repayment amount to zero. This correction restores the invariant, prevents the index from exceeding its legitimate maximum, and aligns the contract’s accounting with the intended financial model.

title: `PositionAction.decreaseLever`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the leverage‑adjustment functions of the PositionAction contract, specifically the decreaseLever (and similarly increaseLever) routine that orchestrates a flash‑loan, debt reduction, collateral withdrawal and token swap. The core issue is an accounting error: the code calculates the flash‑loan amount (loanAmount) and the debt reduction amount (subDebt) directly from leverParams.primarySwap.amount, which already includes the protocol fee charged by the flash‑lender. Because the protocol fee is not subtracted, the contract attempts to borrow more underlying tokens than are actually available after fee deduction. Consequently, when the flash‑loan is repaid, the contract tries to return an amount that exceeds the borrowed principal plus fee, leading to insufficient allowance or balance checks and causing the transaction to revert. This flaw manifests only when the flash‑lender’s protocolFee is non‑zero; with a zero‑fee configuration the functions appear to work, making the bug easy to miss in tests that omit fee settings. An attacker does not gain direct access to funds, but a legitimate user attempting to decrease leverage will experience failed transactions, unexpected reverts, and may see collateral appear to be withdrawn but then not returned, effectively resulting in a “funds disappear” symptom from the user’s perspective. The impact is medium severity because it disrupts normal protocol operations and can cause loss of usability, though no ether is stolen. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the auditors introduced a 1 % protocol fee and observed that decreaseLever reverted due to insufficient allowance. The difficulty in spotting the issue stems from the subtlety of fee inclusion in the swap amount and the fact that the contract’s error messages reference allowance rather than the underlying miscalculation. To remediate, the contract must compute loanAmount as leverParams.primarySwap.amount minus the protocol fee (or equivalently scale down by the fee factor) and use the same corrected value for subDebt and for the amount to be repaid to the flash‑lender. This adjustment restores the accounting balance, ensures the flash‑loan is correctly sized, and prevents unexpected reverts when users adjust leverage.

title: In `CDPVault::liquidatePositionBadDebt`
description: The incorrect calculation affects the protocol’s profit assessment, resulting in potential losses for users, particularly in the interest portion.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation routine that handles bad‑debt positions. The function calculates the loss by taking the total debt, which is defined as principal plus accrued interest, and subtracting the amount that the liquidator repays. Because accrued interest is intended to be treated as profit for the protocol, including it in the loss computation reverses the accounting logic: when the repayment amount exceeds the principal, the contract records a loss instead of a profit. This mis‑calculation can be triggered whenever an unsafe position is liquidated through the `liquidatePositionBadDebt` entry point and the caller supplies a `repayAmount` larger than the outstanding principal debt. An attacker can deliberately choose such a repayment amount to cause the protocol’s profit accounting to show a deficit, effectively eroding the interest revenue that should belong to lenders or token holders. From a user perspective the symptoms are that after a liquidation the expected interest earnings disappear, the protocol may display a negative profit figure, or the liquidator receives less collateral than anticipated. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the loss computation logic and comparing it with the profit calculation used in the regular `liquidatePosition` function. The bug is subtle because the same `calcTotalDebt` helper is used throughout the contract, making the sign error easy to overlook, and the loss variable is only used for internal accounting, not directly exposed to external callers. To remediate the problem the loss should be calculated using only the principal component, i.e., `debtData.debt - repayAmount`, while the accrued interest should be recorded as profit. Adjusting the formula restores the intended accounting invariant that interest accrues as revenue and only the principal can be lost during a bad‑debt liquidation.

title: Because of the asset: `Share 1:1 Conversion`, if vault incurs a loss, the last user to withdraw will take the entire loss
description: Because of the 1:1 conversion rate in `PoolV3`, if the pool incurs a loss due to liquidation from borrowed asset through `CDPVault`, last user to withdraw will take the full loss.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the PoolV3 contract converts between shares and underlying assets when the total number of issued shares exceeds the actual asset balance. The contract uses a 1:1 conversion rate in the _convertToAssets function whenever totalSupply() is greater than or equal to totalAssets(). In a normal state this appears harmless, but if the vault suffers a loss – for example through a bad‑debt liquidation triggered by a CDPVault borrowing operation – the pool’s asset balance can drop below the number of outstanding shares. Because the conversion function then returns assets equal to shares without accounting for the shortfall, the first withdrawers can still redeem their full share value while the remaining share holders are forced to withdraw a smaller amount of assets than their share count would suggest. The last user to call withdraw therefore absorbs the entire loss, receiving fewer assets than expected or even triggering a revert due to a SafeCast overflow. This situation can be reproduced by depositing equal amounts from two users, inducing a liquidation that creates a 10 % asset deficit, and then withdrawing sequentially; the first user receives the full amount, while the second can only pull a reduced amount and the transaction fails. The impact is that honest participants lose part of their deposited capital, breaking the economic assumption that each share represents an equal claim on the pool’s assets. Users experience a mismatch between the share balance shown in the UI and the actual withdrawable amount, often seeing “balance becomes zero” or “withdraw returns less than expected”. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by adding a targeted unit test that simulates a bad‑debt liquidation and observes the asymmetric withdrawal results. It is subtle because the conversion logic looks correct under normal conditions and passes basic sanity checks; the problem only surfaces when the pool is under‑collateralised, a state that may not be exercised in routine testing. To remediate the flaw, the conversion routine must always compute assets proportionally to the current asset‑to‑share ratio, using rounding that favours the pool (e.g., rounding down) or by making withdrawals lossy so that any deficit is shared across all remaining share holders. In essence, the contract should treat the share‑to‑asset conversion as a variable exchange rate rather than a fixed 1:1 mapping whenever the pool’s asset balance is insufficient, thereby preserving fairness and preventing a single participant from bearing the entire loss.

title: Honest users could be permanently DOS’d from withdrawing their vested tokens/rewards
description: Potential permanent DOS to honest users [(or force the users to incur losses since some tech savvy users can notice this griefing attempt, but to stop this they’d have to withdraw early which forces them to incur losses](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/reward/MultiFeeDistribution.sol#L505-L525), since even if the vesting duration reduces there is no other method for the user to withdraw their tokens and it’s stuck in the protocol. Alternatively, if the user leaves the claiming of their tokens even after the vesting period and does not immediately withdraw; the chances of this happening heavily increases since with each day an entry to the `_userEarnings` array can be made.
poc:
[`ChefIncentivesController#Claim()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/reward/ChefIncentivesController.sol#L518) is a public function and callable by anyone. When claiming, there is a need to [vest the tokens](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/reward/ChefIncentivesController.sol#L546), now this vesting [directly vests to the `multifeedistributor`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/reward/ChefIncentivesController.sol#L560).

In [`MultiFeeDistribution#vestTokens()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/reward/MultiFeeDistribution.sol#L496-L529), there is a [logic](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/reward/MultiFeeDistribution.sol#L505-L525) to only allow _pushing_ a new entry for a user to his `_userEarnings` array once in a day. These rewards are then kept, and then after the vesting period a user can claim their rewards, where the `_userEarnings` array would be looped through.

Now from the links to the necessary functions attached, we can see that there is no minimum claimants to be made, asides the check that `RDNT` must be `>` `0`, however as little as `1` is allowed.

For active users that could earn even if little rewards per day, this then allows a malicious user to cause a permanent DOS to claiming their vested tokens, since all the attacker has to do, is once a day **for as long as the vesting duration query,_which could in valid scenarios be quite lengthy_** query [`ChefIncentivesController#Claim()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi/blob/57871f64bdea450c1f04c9a53dc1a78223719164/src/reward/ChefIncentivesController.sol#L518) while passing the user’s address. Then, when the user comes to withdraw their vested tokens, the loop OOG’s and then reverts due to the amount of entries in the `_userEarnings` array.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that can permanently prevent honest users from withdrawing tokens that have vested in the reward distribution contract. The root cause is that the claim function in the incentives controller is public and accepts an arbitrary beneficiary address, while the vesting routine in the fee distribution contract only permits a single entry to be pushed into a per‑user earnings array each day. Because there is no access control limiting the caller to the beneficiary, a malicious actor can invoke the claim function on behalf of a victim once per day for the entire length of the vesting period. Each call creates a new entry in the victim’s earnings array, even if the claimed amount is minimal. Over time the array grows to contain many daily entries, and when the legitimate user finally attempts to claim their vested tokens, the contract loops over the entire array. The loop becomes so large that it exceeds the block gas limit, causing an out‑of‑gas revert and effectively locking the user’s funds. From the user’s perspective the withdrawal transaction simply fails or runs out of gas, and the UI may show that the balance remains unchanged or that the reward amount is zero despite having earned tokens. The issue is hard to notice because the claim function appears to work correctly for small amounts and only fails later when the array size becomes excessive. The attack scenario requires the attacker to repeatedly call the public claim function with the victim’s address each day; no special privileges are needed. The impact is that users may be forced to withdraw early, incurring a loss, or may be unable to retrieve their tokens at all, undermining trust in the protocol. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined function visibility and the per‑day entry restriction. To remediate, the claim function should be restricted so that only the token holder can invoke it, for example by checking that msg.sender matches the beneficiary address or by adding an explicit access‑control modifier. Additionally, the contract could enforce a hard limit on the total number of earnings entries per user or provide a mechanism to prune stale entries, thereby preventing unbounded array growth and the associated gas exhaustion.

title: In `PositionActionPendle::_onDecreaseLever`, `tokenOut` is implemented incorrectly
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the internal function that handles a decrease‑lever operation for the Pendle position action. The function is supposed to return the amount of token that is sent back to the caller (tokenOut) after the collateral withdrawal. It correctly calls the withdraw routine, but it only assigns tokenOut when an auxiliary pool action is present (leverParams.auxAction.args.length != 0). When the auxiliary action array is empty, the function reaches the end without setting tokenOut, leaving the return variable at its default value of zero. As a result the contract reports that no tokens were returned even though collateral was withdrawn from the vault. This mismatch can be triggered whenever a user decreases leverage without specifying any extra pool exit action. From the user’s point of view the transaction appears successful, but the expected refund or token balance does not increase; the UI may show a successful decrease‑lever operation while the user’s wallet balance remains unchanged, effectively making the funds disappear from the user’s perspective. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by comparing the implementation with the analogous PositionAction4626 contract, which correctly returns the withdrawn amount regardless of the auxiliary action. The bug is subtle because the function does not revert or emit an error; it simply returns zero, which can be overlooked in testing if the auxiliary path is always exercised. The impact is medium: users may lose access to the withdrawn collateral, and the protocol’s accounting may become inconsistent, potentially affecting downstream calculations such as health factor or liquidation triggers. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect return value handling” or “missing fallback assignment” bugs, where a code path fails to initialise an output variable. To remediate, the function should always compute and assign tokenOut – for example by capturing the amount withdrawn from the vault and returning it even when leverParams.auxAction.args.length is zero, mirroring the logic used in PositionAction4626._onDecreaseLever. Adding an explicit else branch or moving the tokenOut assignment before the conditional resolves the accounting error and restores correct user balances.

title: Users of a vault can steal other user’s rewards when one vault’s `lastRewardTime` differs from another vault’s `lastRewardTime`
bug_full: The contract implements a multi‑vault reward distribution where each vault (pool) tracks its own lastRewardTime and accountedRewards. The bug arises because the reward calculation function uses the vault‑specific lastRewardTime to determine the elapsed duration, but it does not adjust the available reward pool to reflect that other vaults may have a more stale lastRewardTime. When a user modifies their position in one vault, that vault’s lastRewardTime is advanced while the other vaults keep their older timestamps. Later, when a user from the updated vault claims rewards, the calculation treats the entire global reward balance (depositedRewards minus the accountedRewards of the claiming vault only) as available, ignoring the fact that part of those rewards belong to the still‑stale vaults. Consequently the claiming vault can draw a fraction of rewards that should have been allocated to other vaults, effectively stealing them. This situation occurs whenever vaults are updated at different times – for example, when a debt change triggers handleActionAfter for a single vault – and a subsequent claim is made after the global reward period has progressed beyond the earliest lastRewardTime. Users of the affected vault see their expected rewards reduced or disappear, while the exploiting vault receives more than its proportional share, violating the accounting assumption that rewards are distributed proportionally to each vault’s allocation points. The issue was discovered during a code audit that examined the interaction between _updatePool and _newRewards and identified that the global availableRewards value was not reduced by the accountedRewards of other vaults. It is subtle because the contract still updates accountedRewards correctly for the calling vault, so the discrepancy only becomes visible when multiple vaults are active and claims are made at different times. The proper fix is to compute the per‑vault available reward as the vault’s share of depositedRewards minus its own accountedRewards, or to synchronize reward accounting across all vaults before any claim, ensuring that the global reward balance is correctly partitioned. This eliminates the ability for one vault to claim rewards that belong to another and restores the intended proportional distribution.

title: The debt in `EligibilityDataProvider::requiredUsdValue`
description: It does not align with the documentation and the eligibility criteria for rewards are lower than what is specified by the protocol.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mis‑calculation in the eligibility logic that determines whether a user qualifies for LOOP token emissions. The contract is supposed to require that a user lock LP tokens whose USD value is at least 5 % of the user’s total debt, as described in the protocol documentation. However, the implementation first multiplies the raw debt amount by the required deposit ratio, then converts the result to a USD value using the LP price, and finally applies a price‑tolerance ratio. Because the requiredDepositRatio (5 %) and the priceToleranceRatio (90 %) are applied after the conversion, the effective threshold becomes 5 % × 90 % ≈ 4.5 % of the total debt, not the documented 5 %. In other words, the contract checks that the locked LP amount is greater than roughly 4.5 % of the debt, which is lower than intended. The root cause is an ordering error in the financial formula: the deposit ratio is applied to the debt before the conversion to USD, and the tolerance ratio is applied on top of that, shrinking the required collateral. An attacker can exploit this by providing slightly less LP than required, still passing the eligibility test, and then claim LOOP emissions that were meant only for properly collateralised users. The impact is that the protocol may distribute rewards to under‑collateralised positions, eroding the economic model and potentially draining reward funds. This condition occurs whenever the `isEligibleForRewards` function is called, because it relies on the faulty `requiredUsdValue` calculation. The affected parties include the protocol itself, token holders who fund the emissions, and honest users who expect the rules to be enforced. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by comparing the on‑chain logic with the published documentation and with a reference implementation from Radiant Capital. It is hard to notice because the numbers involved are small percentages and the nested arithmetic hides the discrepancy; the contract still returns a non‑zero required value, so a superficial test may appear to work. To fix the problem, the required USD value should be computed by first converting the user’s total debt to USD, then applying the required deposit ratio, and finally comparing the result directly with the locked USD value, ensuring the threshold matches the documented 5 % of the total position. This aligns the code with the intended business rule and prevents reward leakage. The bug belongs to the class of financial‑formula errors where scaling factors are applied in the wrong order, leading to an eligibility check that is too permissive, causing users to receive rewards despite not meeting the advertised collateral requirement, which violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions and expected user experience where a user expects to need a 5 % lock but receives rewards with less.

title: `lastRPS` could be set to `0` accidentally
description: New reward distribution can not start automatically when `lastRPS` is set to `0` accidentally.
bug_full: The contract contains a logic flaw in the way it caches the previous reward rate. When a reward distribution finishes, the internal function _updateEmissions stores the current rewardsPerSecond value into the variable lastRPS and then sets rewardsPerSecond to zero. The subsequent function registerRewardDeposit is designed to restart a new distribution by copying lastRPS back into rewardsPerSecond, but it only does so if rewardsPerSecond is zero and lastRPS is greater than zero. If the claim function is called a second time after the distribution has already ended, _updateEmissions runs again and overwrites lastRPS with the now‑zero rewardsPerSecond, effectively erasing the cached rate. As a result, when new rewards are deposited, the condition lastRPS > 0 fails and rewardsPerSecond remains zero, so the reward stream never restarts. This can be triggered by any user who can invoke claim after the period has expired, causing future rewards to disappear even though tokens have been deposited. From a user’s perspective the UI will show that a deposit was made but subsequent claim attempts return zero tokens, balances stay unchanged and the expected reward accrual never occurs. The issue was uncovered during a security audit by reproducing the scenario in a unit test that called claim twice after the end time. It is subtle because lastRPS appears to be an internal cache and a zero value is not obviously erroneous, making the bug easy to miss in casual testing. The proper fix is to protect the update of lastRPS so it only occurs when rewardsPerSecond is non‑zero, or to ensure that registerRewardDeposit can recover the previous rate even if lastRPS has been cleared, thereby preserving the ability to restart reward distribution.

title: Incorrect address is used as `spender` for ERC20 permit signature verification
description: The failure of permit signature verification might revert the whole function. `PositionAction#increaseLever()` might revert if ERC20 permit signature is used as `permitParams`.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect address being supplied as the spender when verifying an ERC20 permit signature in the PositionAction contract. The contract’s increaseLever function calls safePermit on an ERC20 token, intending to grant the contract itself permission to transfer the user’s tokens. However, the implementation passes the destination address (the "to" parameter) as the spender argument instead of the contract’s own address (address(this)). Because the EIP‑2612 permit signature is bound to a specific spender, the signature generated for the user proxy does not match the spender used in the verification step, causing the permit verification to fail and the safePermit call to revert with “EIP2612: invalid signature”. This failure propagates up, causing the entire increaseLever transaction to revert. From a user’s perspective the operation that should increase leverage simply does not happen; the UI may show a generic error or no change in position size, leading the user to believe that their funds are stuck or that the protocol is malfunctioning. The issue is a classic case of a permit‑parameter mismatch, a subclass of authorization bugs where the signed allowance is checked against the wrong spender address. It is difficult to notice because the revert message is generic and developers may assume the permit logic is correct, especially when the same code path works for direct transfers that do not involve permits. The bug affects any user attempting to increase leverage via a permit‑based approval, as well as the protocol’s overall reliability, potentially enabling a denial‑of‑service attack where an attacker can force repeated reverts by supplying malformed permits. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit when the test suite exercised increaseLever with a valid permit signed for the user proxy; the transaction reverted, prompting investigation that revealed the spender mismatch. To remediate the issue, the contract should pass its own address (address(this)) as the spender argument to safePermit, ensuring that the permit signature aligns with the entity that will actually spend the tokens. This change restores correct permit verification, allowing the increaseLever function to succeed when provided with a valid signature and eliminating the unintended revert path.

title: `PoolV3#repayCreditAccount
description: Either the profit or the loss is calculated incorrectly, resulting in the treasury owns incorrect profit balance.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the profit and loss accounting performed by the PoolV3 contract when a credit manager calls repayCreditAccount. The function is supposed to mint lpETH shares to the treasury when a repayment yields profit, or burn shares from the treasury when a loss occurs. However, the implementation mistakenly uses the public convertToShares() helper, which calculates shares based on the ERC4626 exchange rate derived from total assets and total supply, instead of the internal _convertToShares() helper that enforces the pool’s 1:1 WETH‑to‑lpETH rate. Because the pool is designed to treat WETH and lpETH as having a one‑to‑one relationship, using convertToShares() can return a smaller number of shares than the actual amount of profit or loss. Consequently, when profit > 0 the treasury receives fewer lpETH shares than it should, and when loss > 0 the treasury may burn fewer shares than required, leaving an excess balance. This mis‑calculation can be triggered by any credit manager during a normal repayment flow, making it exploitable without special permissions. An attacker can repeatedly generate profit‑bearing repayments, causing the treasury to be under‑minted each time and effectively siphoning value to the attacker’s account. The impact is an incorrect treasury profit balance, which translates to missing or reduced profit distribution for users and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue manifests only during the repayCreditAccount call when profit or loss is non‑zero, and it affects the treasury, lenders, and any participants relying on accurate profit accounting. It was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the auditor noticed that the conversion used in deposit (which is 1:1) differed from the conversion used in repayment. The bug is subtle because both functions return a uint256 and appear interchangeable, so tests that only check for successful execution may not reveal the discrepancy. To remediate, the contract should replace every call to convertToShares() inside repayCreditAccount with the internal _convertToShares() function, thereby aligning the share calculation with the pool’s defined exchange rate and restoring correct profit and loss accounting. This class of bug is an accounting mismatch caused by inconsistent conversion logic, similar to rounding or unit‑conversion errors that break financial invariants. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that after a profitable repayment the treasury’s lpETH balance grows less than expected, profit payouts appear lower, or after a loss the treasury retains extra lpETH, leading to confusing UI numbers such as “profit received: 0” or “treasury balance unchanged despite loss”.

title: `PositionAction4626.sol#_onWithdraw` should withdraw from `position` CDPVault position instead of `address
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal withdrawal hook of the PositionAction4626 contract. The function _onWithdraw is intended to pull collateral from a specific CDPVault position supplied by the caller, as documented in the abstract PositionAction contract and as implemented by PositionAction20. Instead, the implementation calls ICDPVault(vault).withdraw(address(this), amount), which forces the vault to withdraw from the proxy contract itself (address(this)) rather than from the position address passed as a parameter. This mismatch between the documented contract interface and the actual code is the root cause of the bug. When a user or another contract invokes the withdraw operation on a position that is not owned by the proxy – for example, when a proxy is used to manage an external address’s CDP – the call appears to succeed but the collateral remains locked in the intended position because the vault never touched it. From the user’s perspective the UI may report a successful withdrawal and the transaction may emit no error, yet the expected token balance does not change, leading to confusion, apparent loss of funds, or an inability to retrieve collateral. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated: the system assumes that a successful withdraw reduces the collateral of the target position, but the bug leaves that position untouched while potentially draining the proxy’s own balance. This issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by comparing the behavior of PositionAction4626 with the reference implementations PositionAction20 and PositionAction, and by observing that unit tests covering withdrawals from unrelated positions failed. The problem is subtle because the withdraw call does not revert and returns a value, so standard testing that only checks for transaction success may miss the logical error. To remediate the issue the withdraw call must be changed to use the position argument (ICDPVault(vault).withdraw(position, amount)) so that the vault correctly debits the intended CDP. Aligning the implementation with the abstract contract’s specification restores the expected business logic, ensures that collateral accounting remains consistent, and allows proxies to manage arbitrary positions safely.

title: Rewards may be spread out among the wrong time period due to the way the protocol calculates it
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect reward‑distribution calculation that occurs when a second incentive is added while a previous incentive’s rewardsDuration has not yet finished. The contract’s internal function that notifies a new reward computes a leftover amount based on the remaining time of the current period and the current rewardPerSecond, then adds this leftover to the new reward amount and recomputes rewardPerSecond for the whole combined period. Because the leftover is blended into the new period, the original reward that should have been paid out during its own timeframe is delayed and partially re‑allocated to the later period. As a result, users who staked during the first incentive receive a smaller claimable amount than expected, and in some edge cases the rounding performed during the leftover calculation can cause a permanent shortfall of tokens. The bug is triggered whenever the _notifyReward function is called with block.timestamp less than the stored periodFinish, i.e., when a new incentive is introduced before the previous one expires. All participants who earned rewards in the earlier window are affected, because their balances may appear normal in the UI but the actual claimable amount is reduced, sometimes to zero, leading to a mismatch between expected and received rewards. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the reward queue logic and noticing that the contract mixes reward periods instead of keeping them isolated. It is hard to notice because the contract still reports a reward rate and does not emit an explicit error; users only see the symptom of missing or reduced tokens after claiming. The flaw violates the fundamental accounting assumption that each incentive’s rewardPerSecond should be distributed only within its own period. A proper fix is to store each incentive as a separate entry in a queue‑like structure, keep its periodFinish and rewardPerSecond independent, and advance a counter only after a period has fully elapsed, thereby preventing leftover amounts from being merged into a new period. This design ensures that rewards are allocated exactly according to the intended time windows and that early stakers receive the full amount they earned.

title: `BalancerOracle::update
description: Whenever `block.timestamp - lastUpdate > updateWaitWindow` and needs to update the price, it will return a stale price because it will fetch the price from the `lastUpdate` not the `currentUpdate`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price‑oracle update routine of a Balancer‑based contract. When the elapsed time since the last price refresh exceeds the configured updateWaitWindow, the update() function is invoked. Inside this function the code first checks that the waiting period has passed, then immediately copies the variable currentPrice into safePrice and records the current block timestamp as lastUpdate. Only after these assignments does the routine recompute currentPrice by aggregating token prices and pool invariants. Because safePrice is set before the fresh price calculation, it retains the price that was valid at the previous update – a stale value that may be minutes or hours old depending on how long the update was delayed. Consequently, any downstream logic that relies on safePrice (for example slippage checks, collateral valuation, or user‑visible price feeds) will operate on outdated data. This can cause users to receive incorrect quotes, experience unexpected losses, or see their balances appear unchanged while the market moves. The issue manifests whenever an update is triggered after the waiting window, especially if the call is delayed beyond a single window, leading to a price that is effectively two windows old. All participants that depend on the oracle – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the ordering of state updates and noted that the safePrice assignment uses the pre‑computed currentPrice rather than the newly calculated one. The problem is subtle because the contract does emit a new currentPrice, so a superficial check may suggest the oracle is up‑to‑date, while the value actually used for safety checks remains stale. To remediate, the logic should first compute the fresh currentPrice, then assign safePrice = currentPrice and finally update lastUpdate, ensuring that the safe price always reflects the most recent market data. This class of bug is a stale‑data or time‑of‑check‑time‑of‑use (TOCTOU) ordering error in oracle update mechanisms, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that price feeds are current at the moment they are recorded and used.

title: Bug in `claim` allows users who are disqualified to claim their previously earned emissions
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑claiming routine of the incentives controller. The function that users call to collect their earned emissions first checks whether the caller is still eligible for rewards by invoking the external eligibility provider. However, this check is performed before the contract refreshes the user’s eligibility status. The refresh logic, which recomputes eligibility based on the current price of the locked token and the required collateralisation ratio, is only executed later in the call chain by the helper function that updates the user’s eligibility data. Because the stale eligibility result is used to decide whether to revert, a user whose total value locked has fallen below the 5 % threshold after a price movement can still pass the initial check and continue through the claim flow. The contract therefore allows a disqualified participant to receive emissions that should have been blocked, effectively letting “malicious lockers” claim rewards that are no longer justified. This flaw manifests whenever the protocol’s eligibility mode is active (i.e., not disabled), the contract is not paused, and a price change or other state transition renders a previously eligible user ineligible before they submit a claim. From the user’s perspective the UI will show a successful claim and the wallet will receive tokens, even though the protocol’s accounting assumes the user should have been denied. The impact is a loss of funds from the reward pool, distortion of the incentive distribution, and a breach of the protocol’s economic guarantees. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the ordering of the two calls was examined and identified as inconsistent with the intended business logic. It can be difficult to spot because the transaction does not revert and the emitted events appear normal, so the bug does not raise an obvious error flag. The proper remediation is to ensure that the eligibility refresh occurs before any eligibility check, for example by swapping the order of the two calls or by integrating the refresh directly into the eligibility query. By doing so the contract will correctly revert when a user is no longer qualified, preserving the integrity of the reward accounting and preventing unauthorized emission claims.

title: Usage of `lastEligibleStatus` can cause user to miss out on rewards on `manualStopEmissionsFor` invocation
description: Invoking `manualStopEmissionsFor` can cause the user to miss out on rewards from vaults even after the user becomes eligible.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a logical assumption in the reward‑distribution routine that ties the user’s eligibility status to a cached flag called lastEligibleStatus. When the contract operates in FULL eligibility mode, the handleActionAfter function checks whether the user was previously eligible (lastEligibleStatus) and whether they are currently eligible (refresh). If both flags are true, the implementation assumes that all vault balances for that user have already been updated to reflect the latest state, and therefore it only updates the balance of the vault that triggered the call. This assumption breaks when the manualStopEmissionsFor function is invoked. manualStopEmissionsFor is a whitelisted operation that iterates over a list of vault tokens and forcibly sets each vault’s user balance and reward debt to zero, emitting a BalanceUpdated event for each token. Because the function directly manipulates the stored balances without updating the eligibility cache, a user can become eligible for rewards after their balances have been zeroed, but the cached lastEligibleStatus still reflects the pre‑stop state. Consequently, when handleActionAfter runs, it sees that the user is currently eligible and that they were previously eligible, and therefore it only refreshes the vault that caused the eligibility transition, leaving the other vault balances at zero. The practical effect is that the user’s rewards are accrued only for the single vault that was updated, while all other vaults silently stop earning rewards.
