From the user’s perspective the UI may show that they are eligible and that one vault is earning, but the total reward amount is lower than expected, or balances appear unchanged despite eligibility. The issue impacts any participant who holds positions in multiple vaults and relies on the protocol’s reward accounting, leading to under‑payment of earned rewards. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by tracing the interaction between manualStopEmissionsFor and the eligibility checks and noticing that the reward‑update logic does not re‑query all vault balances after a manual stop. The bug is hard to notice because the contract still emits events and the single updated vault behaves correctly, masking the silent loss in the other vaults. The flaw belongs to the class of reward‑accounting logic errors where stale eligibility state leads to inconsistent balance updates. To remediate the problem the lastEligibleStatus check should be removed or the manualStopEmissionsFor routine should trigger a full refresh of all registered balances for the affected user, ensuring that every vault’s reward debt is recomputed when eligibility changes.

title: Discrepancy between the `lastRewadTime` and the `lastAllPoolUpdate` can allow for incorrect reward distribution to pools if `registerRewardDeposit` deposits less assets
description: Incorrect reward distribution causing some pools to gain more while others to gain less.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an inconsistency between the global timestamp that records the last time any pool was updated (lastAllPoolUpdate) and the individual timestamp stored for each pool (lastRewardTime). The contract’s mass‑update routine always writes lastAllPoolUpdate = block.timestamp, regardless of whether the overall reward period has already expired. In contrast, the per‑pool update function caps the timestamp used for reward calculation at the current endRewardTime, which is the moment when the total unclaimed rewards are expected to be exhausted. When block.timestamp exceeds endRewardTime, the per‑pool timestamp is set to endRewardTime, which can be lower than the newly written lastAllPoolUpdate. This creates a state where a pool’s lastRewardTime is behind the global lastAllPoolUpdate. Subsequent calls that recompute endRewardTime use lastAllPoolUpdate as a base, effectively extending the reward window for pools whose lastRewardTime is still lower. If a small reward deposit is made after the original endRewardTime has passed, the contract may accept the deposit, recalculate a new endRewardTime based on the higher lastAllPoolUpdate, and allow the lagging pool to claim rewards for the interval between its old lastRewardTime and the new endRewardTime. As a result, some pools receive more tokens than were actually deposited while other pools receive less, breaking the intended 1:1 reward ratio. From a user perspective the symptoms are unexpected reward amounts: a user may see a higher than anticipated balance in one pool, while another user with an identical allocation sees a lower or zero pending reward. The issue is hard to notice because timestamps are normally assumed to be monotonic and synchronized across the contract; the discrepancy only appears in the edge case where a low‑amount deposit is made after the reward period has already elapsed. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the reward‑distribution logic and identified that the mass‑update routine does not respect the endRewardTime constraint. To remediate the problem the contract should either clamp lastAllPoolUpdate to endRewardTime when the latter is already reached, ensure that registerRewardDeposit cannot be called with an amount that would keep the new endRewardTime below the current block.timestamp, or redesign the reward‑time calculation so that global and per‑pool timestamps remain consistent, thereby preventing any pool from claiming rewards beyond the actual deposited amount.

title: Emission schedule is not followed and can cause unexpected allocation of rewards
bug_full: The contract implements a time‑based emission schedule that changes the rewards per second at predefined timestamps (startOffset). When the blockchain time passes a startOffset, the internal function setScheduledRewardsPerSecond advances the schedule index and calls _massUpdatePools to bring every pool up to date. The vulnerability lies in the accounting performed inside _massUpdatePools (and the helper _newRewards). The code calculates the newly accrued reward as duration * rewardsPerSecond, where duration is block.timestamp minus the pool’s lastRewardTime and rewardsPerSecond is the value that was in effect before the schedule change. Because the calculation does not split the time interval at the exact moment the new schedule becomes active, the old rewardsPerSecond is applied for the whole period up to the current block, ignoring the higher or lower rate that should have applied after the schedule transition. The root cause is an incorrect formula: instead of using oldRewardsPerSecond for the interval (lastUpdateStamp, newScheduleStartTimestamp) and newRewardsPerSecond for (newScheduleStartTimestamp, block.timestamp), the implementation uses a single term that assumes a constant rate. This can be exploited indirectly by any user who stakes tokens across a schedule boundary; the protocol will either over‑pay or under‑pay rewards depending on whether the new rate is higher or lower than the previous one. The impact is a deviation from the intended token distribution: users may receive fewer rewards than advertised, or the protocol may unintentionally mint extra tokens, draining its treasury over time. The bug manifests only when a schedule change occurs while pools have pending rewards – i.e., when block.timestamp exceeds startOffset and setScheduledRewardsPerSecond triggers a mass update. Stakeholders affected include token holders who expect a certain reward amount, the protocol’s economic model, and any downstream contracts that rely on accurate reward accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended emission formula with the actual implementation and noticed the missing split at the schedule boundary. It is subtle because the reward accrual still appears to work; the discrepancy may be small per block and only becomes noticeable after many blocks or when large reward rate changes occur, making it easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate, the reward calculation should be rewritten to explicitly account for the two intervals: oldRewardsPerSecond multiplied by (newScheduleStartTimestamp‑lastRewardTime) plus newRewardsPerSecond multiplied by (block.timestamp‑newScheduleStartTimestamp). This aligns the on‑chain accounting with the documented emission schedule and restores correct token economics. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect handling of time‑dependent rate changes” or “reward schedule transition miscalculation”, where a contract fails to adjust its accounting when a parameter that varies over time is updated.

title: `PositionAction.sol#onCreditFlashLoan` may have leftover tokens after conducting `leverParams.auxSwap`
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs in the PositionAction contract when a user executes a decreaseLever operation with the auxiliary swap (auxSwap) option enabled. The function onCreditFlashLoan first borrows a flash loan, repays CDPVault debt, withdraws collateral, and then performs a primary swap that is configured as an EXACT_OUT swap to obtain the exact amount of debt tokens needed to settle the flash loan. Because the primary swap may leave a small amount of collateral – the residualAmount – the contract attempts to handle this remainder. If auxSwap is enabled, the code performs an auxiliary swap that is configured as an EXACT_IN swap with a hard‑coded input amount. The exact amount of collateral remaining after the primary swap is not known in advance, so the auxSwap often consumes less than the available residual collateral. The leftover tokens are neither transferred to the residualRecipient nor sent elsewhere; they remain trapped in the PositionAction contract. This bug is a classic case of token leakage caused by mismatched swap semantics (EXACT_OUT followed by EXACT_IN) and an assumption that the residual amount can be predicted. It can be exploited unintentionally by users who expect to receive any leftover collateral after a lever reduction; instead, part of their assets become permanently inaccessible, effectively disappearing from their balance. The issue manifests only when auxSwap is enabled and the residualAmount is greater than zero, which depends on market conditions and the exact output of the primary swap. Affected parties include any user of the protocol who performs a decreaseLever with auxSwap, as well as the protocol itself because locked tokens reduce overall liquidity and may undermine trust. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the flow of token transfers and noticing that the contract does not account for the actual token balance after the auxSwap. It is subtle because the leftover amount can be small and the contract does not emit events or expose the trapped balance, making it easy to overlook during testing. The recommended remediation is to calculate the actual token balance of the primary swap asset held by the contract after the auxSwap and explicitly transfer the entire remaining balance to the residualRecipient, ensuring no tokens remain locked. This aligns the implementation with the intended accounting logic that any collateral not needed for debt repayment should be returned to the user, preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: `PositionAction.sol#_deposit` incorrectly checks `auxSwap.assetIn` should be equal to `collateralParams.targetToken`
description: `PositionAction.sol#_deposit` incorrectly checks `auxSwap.assetIn` should be equal to `collateralParams.targetToken`. This is incorrect, because `auxSwap.assetIn` should be the token used to swap for `collateralParams.targetToken`.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the deposit routine of the PositionAction contract where the function validates the auxiliary swap input token by asserting that auxSwap.assetIn must be exactly equal to the collateral configuration's target token. This check is conceptually wrong because auxSwap.assetIn represents the token that the user supplies to be swapped into the target token, not the target token itself. The root cause is a misunderstanding of the swap parameter semantics, leading to a logic error that rejects legitimate deposit attempts that involve swapping a different source token for the required collateral. An attacker or any user attempting to deposit using a supported source token will see the transaction revert, resulting in a denial‑of‑service condition where deposits cannot be processed. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a failed transaction, a missing or zero balance after the attempt, or an unexpected “no funds received” message even though the user sent tokens. The protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated because the contract expects to receive collateral after a successful swap, but the erroneous check prevents the swap from occurring, potentially leaving the protocol under‑collateralized if the issue is not addressed. The bug was discovered during a formal audit where the code comment describing the intended behavior conflicted with the actual equality check. It can be hard to notice because the check appears reasonable at a glance and the surrounding logic is complex, masking the semantic mismatch. The recommended remediation is to remove the equality assertion or replace it with a validation that ensures auxSwap.assetIn is a supported source token rather than forcing it to match the target token, thereby restoring the intended swap‑and‑deposit flow.

title: ChefIncentivesController caches `endRewardTime`, which is not required, and may cause issues during reward update
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a caching mechanism used to store the calculated end of the reward distribution period (endRewardTime) in the ChefIncentivesController contract. Instead of recomputing the end time on every pool update, the contract keeps a cached value for a duration defined by endingTime.updateCadence, which is set to two days. This design assumes that the parameters influencing the reward schedule – such as rewards per second or the set of registered reward tokens – remain unchanged during the cache window. In practice, these parameters can be altered by governance actions or by adding new reward tokens, causing the cached endRewardTime to diverge from the true value. When rewardsPerSecond is increased, the real end time becomes earlier than the cached value, but the contract continues to believe rewards are still available, leading to a situation where the internal logic caps the effective timestamp at the cached endRewardTime. Consequently, the pool’s _updatePool function may stop distributing rewards prematurely, leaving users with missing or reduced accruals. Conversely, if new reward tokens are added or the reward balance grows, the true end time shifts later, but the stale cache makes the contract think rewards are still being earned beyond the intended horizon. This can cause some pools to continue receiving rewards after they should have stopped, effectively stealing allocation from other pools and breaking the intended proportional distribution. The bug manifests only when a pool’s state is updated, which occurs on user‑initiated actions such as deposits, withdrawals, or harvest calls. Because updates are not performed on a regular schedule, the discrepancy can persist unnoticed for up to the cache interval, making the problem hard to detect during routine testing. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a sudden drop to zero rewards despite having staked for a period, or an unexpected surplus of tokens in a pool that should have stopped earning. The issue was identified during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors observed that the endRewardTime function returns a cached estimate that is not refreshed when key variables change. The root cause is the unnecessary caching of a value that depends on mutable state, violating the accounting assumption that reward distribution periods are deterministic given the current parameters. The recommended remediation is to eliminate the cache and recompute endRewardTime on each call, which is acceptable because the update function is only invoked on user interactions, so the gas savings from caching are negligible. By always using the fresh calculation, the contract will correctly stop reward accrual when the schedule ends and will prevent any pool from receiving rewards beyond its allocated share, restoring fairness and preserving protocol integrity.

title: `SwapAction.sol#balancerSwap` does not support native ETH as input token
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that performs a Balancer swap inside the SwapAction contract. Although the public swap entry point is marked payable and the contract correctly forwards msg.value when joining a Pendle pool, the internal balancerSwap routine calls balancerVault.batchSwap without attaching the received ether. As a result, when a user supplies native ETH as the input token for a Balancer swap, the contract does not pass that ETH to the Balancer Vault. The root cause is a missing value field in the external call, a classic “value‑not‑forwarded” bug. An attacker or honest user can trigger the issue simply by invoking swap with swapProtocol set to BALANCER and assetIn equal to the zero address (native ETH). The call will succeed at the contract level, but the Balancer Vault will receive zero ether, causing the swap to either revert due to insufficient input funds or to complete without actually exchanging any value. From the user’s perspective the transaction may appear to succeed, yet the expected output token is not received and the sent ETH either remains locked in the SwapAction contract or is returned to the sender, depending on the fallback logic. This breaks the business assumption that a payable swap will always transfer the supplied ETH to the underlying protocol, leading to a mismatch between user expectations (receiving swapped tokens) and reality (receiving nothing). The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor noted the comment “BUG. Does not pass msg.value.” It can be hard to notice because the function signature is payable and other pathways (e.g., Pendle joins) correctly forward value, giving a false sense of correctness. The proper fix is to include the value field in the batchSwap call, i.e., balancerVault.batchSwap{value: msg.value}(...), ensuring that any native ETH supplied by the caller is forwarded to Balancer. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of improper value forwarding bugs that violate accounting assumptions and can cause funds to disappear or swaps to fail silently.

title: `PositionAction20._onWithdraw` and `PositionPendle20._onWithdraw` also returns token amount in wrong scale
description: Withdraw operations will invariably revert due to insufficient funds if the collateral’s decimal deviates from 18.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the withdraw callback functions of two contracts, PositionAction20 and PositionPendle20, which are invoked when a user attempts to pull collateral from a vault. These callbacks return the amount of tokens that were withdrawn, but they assume that the token uses the standard 18‑decimal representation (wad) regardless of the actual decimal precision of the underlying collateral. When the collateral token has a decimal count different from 18, the returned value is scaled incorrectly: the contract reports a larger amount than it actually transferred. The vault then checks that it still holds enough balance to satisfy the reported amount, detects a shortfall, and reverts the transaction with an “insufficient funds” error. Consequently, any user trying to withdraw a token whose decimals deviate from 18 will experience a failed withdrawal, seeing either a transaction revert or a UI that shows no funds returned. This issue was uncovered during a manual audit that compared the implementation against known patterns (such as WP‑M2) and noticed that the tokenScale conversion step was missing. The bug is subtle because most test suites use 18‑decimal tokens, so the error does not surface under typical unit tests. It violates the fundamental accounting assumption that the amount reported by a contract matches the actual token balance change, breaking the protocol’s guarantee that users can retrieve their deposited assets. The proper fix is to convert the raw wad amount returned by the vault into the token’s native scale before returning it, typically by multiplying the wad amount by the tokenScale factor provided by the vault. This ensures that the reported amount reflects the true token quantity, preventing the insufficient‑funds revert and restoring correct withdrawal behavior.

title: Lack of slippage check while interacting with ERC4626 Vault in `PositionAction4626` could lead to users’ fund loss
description: Users’ funds loss from ERC4626 exchange rate change or manipulated.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the PositionAction4626 module that mediates deposits and withdrawals between a CDP vault and an ERC4626 vault. When a user supplies the underlying token of an ERC4626 vault as the target token, the contract automatically calls IERC4626.deposit to convert the underlying into vault shares, and later calls IERC4626.redeem to convert shares back into the underlying. Both calls are performed without any verification of the exchange rate or a minimum amount that the user expects to receive. The root cause is the absence of a slippage check – the code simply accepts the amount of shares returned by deposit and the amount of underlying returned by redeem, regardless of how the vault’s price per share may have moved between transaction submission and execution. Because ERC4626 vaults can change their share price due to other deposits, withdrawals, or even malicious manipulation of the vault’s accounting, an attacker can front‑run a pending transaction, alter the exchange rate, and cause the user to receive fewer shares on deposit or less underlying on withdraw. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are a missing or reduced balance after a seemingly successful operation: a deposit may appear to succeed while the user’s token balance stays unchanged or is lower than expected, and a withdrawal may return zero or a dramatically smaller amount of the destination token. The impact is a direct loss of funds for any user who interacts with PositionAction4626 using an ERC4626 underlying token, effectively breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol that the deposited amount equals the received collateral. The issue manifests whenever the contract path PositionAction._deposit → PositionAction4626._onDeposit or PositionAction._withdraw → PositionAction4626._onWithdraw is taken and the source or destination token differs from the vault’s collateral token. It was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the auditors noted that the deposit and redeem calls lack any comparison against a user‑provided slippage tolerance or a previewed amount. The problem is subtle because the ERC4626 interface does not revert on unfavorable rates; it simply returns the computed amount, and the surrounding contract does not perform any sanity check, making the loss easy to miss in normal testing. To remediate, the contract should allow callers to specify a maximum acceptable slippage and should use the previewDeposit and previewRedeem functions (or equivalent calculations) to compute the expected amount before executing the actual deposit or redeem. The transaction should then revert if the actual amount falls below the user‑defined threshold, thereby protecting users from exchange‑rate manipulation and ensuring that the protocol’s accounting remains sound.

title: Users can farm on zero-tax land if the landlord locked tokens before the LandManager deployment
bug_full: The vulnerability is an uninitialized plot metadata condition that allows a renter to stake a munchable on a landlord’s land with a tax rate of zero, effectively bypassing the protocol’s tax mechanism. The root cause is that LandManager::stakeMunchable does not verify that plotMetadata[landlord] has been set before recording the latestTaxRate in the toilerState structure. When a landlord has locked tokens in the LockManager before the LandManager contract is deployed and has not called triggerPlotMetadata or any function that updates the plot metadata, the currentTaxRate field remains at its default value of zero. A renter who stakes a token on such a plot captures this zero tax rate in the toilerState at the moment of staking. During subsequent farming, the calculation of schnibblesLandlord multiplies the total schnibbles earned by the stored latestTaxRate, which is still zero, so the landlord receives no tax while the renter receives the full amount. This situation occurs only until the renter farms again, at which point the contract updates the latestTaxRate from the now‑initialized plotMetadata, but the tax loss for the earlier period is permanent. The impact is that landlords lose expected revenue, the economic assumptions of the protocol are violated, and users can artificially inflate their schnibbles balance by farming on zero‑tax land. The bug is triggered when the landlord’s plot metadata has never been initialized after LandManager deployment and the AccountManager.forceHarvest function does not interact with LandManager to enforce metadata initialization. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the staking flow and noticed the missing check for plotMetadata existence. The issue can be hard to notice because the tax rate appears correct after the first harvest; only the initial period yields zero tax, which may not be obvious from normal operation. The appropriate fix is to add a validation that plotMetadata[landlord] is initialized (for example, checking that plotMetadata[landlord].lastUpdated is non‑zero or that currentTaxRate is non‑zero) before allowing a stake, and to ensure that the latestTaxRate in toilerState is always refreshed from the current plot metadata. This class of bug falls under uninitialized state leading to incorrect financial calculations, similar to zero‑value defaults causing revenue leakage. From a user’s perspective, a landlord may see “no tax collected” or “my balance did not increase” while a renter sees “my schnibbles balance is higher than expected” after farming on a plot that should have charged tax.

title: Multiplication overflow leading to memory corruption and incorrect register write-back
description: The unchecked multiplication of int32 values (rs and rt) and type conversion within the execute function in MIPS contract can result in an overflow, leading to the assignment of an incorrect value to the val variable in the step(…) function. This incorrect value is subsequently written to memory and the destination register in the step function. This can cause data corruption in contract and break of Proper MIPS contract functionality and storage
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked multiplication of two signed 32‑bit operands inside the MIPS execute function. Because the operation is performed inside an unchecked block and the result is directly cast to a 32‑bit unsigned value, an overflow is not detected. When the opcode 0x1C with function code 0x2 (MUL) is executed, the product of rs and rt can exceed the int32 range; the overflow wraps around and produces an incorrect 32‑bit pattern. This incorrect pattern is stored in the local variable val, which is later written to contract memory and back‑propagated to the destination register by the step function. As a result the contract’s simulated register file and memory become corrupted, breaking the expected MIPS semantics. The bug manifests only when the specific multiplication instruction is used with operand values that cause overflow, for example rs = 0x7fffffff and rt = 2. Any user or protocol component that invokes step with such an instruction will see unexpected register values, missing or wrong data in memory, and downstream logic that relies on those values may behave incorrectly or halt. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the execute implementation and noticed the unchecked int32 multiplication followed by a cast to uint32. Because the overflow does not trigger a revert, the symptom is subtle: the transaction succeeds, but the internal state is silently altered, making it hard to detect without explicit state checks or fuzzing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of arithmetic overflow leading to state corruption, a common pattern when safe‑math checks are omitted. To remediate, the multiplication should be performed in a wider signed type (e.g., int64), the result validated against the int32 bounds, and only then safely down‑cast, or a library such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeMath for signed integers should be used. Adding the overflow check restores the contract’s guarantee that register and memory values always reflect the mathematically correct result, preserving the protocol’s correctness and preventing silent data loss.

title: Missing address check for instructions LH and LHU
description:
Instruction processing cannot detect problems in time.

According to [this](https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/academic/class/15740-f97/public/doc/mips-isa.pdf), page 99, Section Restrictions, the address must be naturally aligned. If the least-significant bit of the address is non-zero, an Address Error exception occurs. However, in the contract, the address is not checked.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the MIPS virtual machine implementation used by the Optimism rollup, where the load‑halfword (LH) and load‑halfword‑unsigned (LHU) instructions do not enforce the two‑byte alignment requirement defined by the MIPS ISA. According to the official specification, any attempt to read a half‑word from an address whose least‑significant bit is set must raise an Address Error exception; the VM instead masks the address to a 4‑byte boundary before the memory read, effectively ignoring the alignment rule. This omission creates a situation where a contract can request a 16‑bit value from an odd memory location and receive data that is shifted, truncated, or silently zeroed, because the underlying hardware would normally reject the operation. An attacker who can influence the address used in a LH/LHU operation—typically by supplying crafted calldata or by manipulating internal offsets—can cause the VM to read from a misaligned address, leading to incorrect values being fed into the contract’s business logic. The impact ranges from subtle accounting errors, such as balances being calculated incorrectly or refunds being computed as zero, to more severe state corruption that could allow funds to be unintentionally locked or drained if the contract relies on precise half‑word values for permission checks or token accounting. The bug manifests only when the program accesses half‑word memory at an address with a non‑zero LSB; normal 4‑byte aligned accesses behave as expected, which makes the issue hard to notice during routine testing. Users may observe symptoms like a UI showing a zero balance after a deposit, a refund amount that is always zero, or unexpected reverts when a function that reads a uint16 is called. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit when reviewers compared the VM’s behavior against the MIPS ISA documentation and noted the missing alignment verification. Because the VM silently accepts the out‑of‑spec access instead of raising an exception, the bug can remain hidden until a specific misaligned address is exercised. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit check for the least‑significant bit of the target address in the LH and LHU implementations and to revert the transaction when the address is not two‑byte aligned, thereby restoring compliance with the MIPS specification and preventing malformed reads from corrupting contract state.

title: Addresses can be pre-populated with bad data
description: Inside `PreimageOracle.sol`, anyone can call the `loadPrecompilePreimagePart()` to load data into the contract. The problem is that anyone is able to specify the `address _precompile` parameter. This opens up the door for malicious users to pre-populate data and use it to validate wrong data.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the PreimageOracle contract, which stores fragments of pre‑image data that later contracts read to verify cryptographic proofs. The function loadPrecompilePreimagePart is deliberately public so that the op‑program can supply data for newly added precompiles without upgrading the oracle. However, the function accepts an arbitrary address parameter _precompile and does not verify that the address corresponds to a legitimate precompile that already exists on the chain. Because the storage key for a pre‑image is derived from the supplied address, a malicious actor can call loadPrecompilePreimagePart with a future precompile address, supply any byte sequence, and cause the internal flag preimagePartOk[key][offset] to be set to true. When a later contract invokes readPreimage with the same key, the require check that the pre‑image exists passes, and the contract returns the attacker‑controlled data. This enables the attacker to fabricate pre‑image data that will be accepted as valid during proof verification, effectively allowing invalid proofs to be marked as correct. The impact is that any protocol component that relies on the oracle for correct pre‑image data – for example the MIPS virtual machine implementation used by the rollup – may execute state transitions based on falsified inputs, leading to incorrect state updates, potential loss of funds, or violation of the protocol’s security guarantees. The issue manifests whenever a new precompile is planned but not yet deployed, or when a contract reads a pre‑image for an address that an attacker has pre‑populated. All users, validators, and sponsors that trust the oracle’s output are affected because they may observe transactions that appear successful while the underlying proof is bogus, resulting in unexpected balance changes or state mutations that contradict the expected business logic. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit when a test case demonstrated that loading data for a non‑existent precompile address succeeded and that readPreimage subsequently returned the injected data without error. The problem is subtle because the contract’s public interface appears legitimate and the flag check seems to guarantee existence, yet the existence condition can be satisfied by any address, making the bug easy to overlook in code review. To remediate, the oracle should restrict loadPrecompilePreimagePart to known, authorized precompile addresses, enforce that only a privileged entity (such as the op‑program or a designated sponsor) can set the flag, or require an explicit confirmation step before marking a pre‑image as valid. In essence, the bug is a classic case of unchecked input leading to unauthorized state injection, breaking the assumption that pre‑image data is immutable and trustworthy, and causing the system to accept fabricated proofs that should have been rejected.

title: Unvalidated memory access in `readMem` and `writeMem` functions
description:
The [`readMem()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-optimism/blob/main/packages/contracts-bedrock/src/cannon/MIPS.sol#L538C4-L584C6) and [`writeMem()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-optimism/blob/main/packages/contracts-bedrock/src/cannon/MIPS.sol#L592C3-L632C6) functions do not properly validate the memory address being accessed. This could lead to unauthorized access to memory outside the intended ranges, which could then allow a black hat to read or modify sensitive data, in creative ways. As the contract is using a `32-bit` address space `uint32` for `addresses` without implementing proper bounds checking, possibly then allowing access to the entire 4GB address space.

Specific attack vectors:

  * Overwriting the `preimageKey` and/or `preimageOffset` to gain unauthorized access to preimage data.
  * Manipulating the `pc` or `nextPC` values to alter program flows, even possible paths to bypass security checks.
  * Adjusting with intent the heap value to cause memory allocation issues.
  * Altering the `exitCode` or `exited` flags to prematurely terminate or continue execution inappropriately.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds memory access in the MIPS emulator used by the Optimism Bedrock contracts. The functions that read and write memory accept a 32-bit address but only verify that the address is 4-byte aligned; they never check that the address lies inside the memory region that the emulator reserves. Because the address space is 4 GB, an attacker can supply a value such as 0xFFFFFFFC and the assembly block will read or write the corresponding word from calldata without reverting. This allows the caller to overwrite critical fields stored in the emulator state – for example preimageKey, preimageOffset, the program counter (pc and nextPC), the heap pointer, or the exitCode and exited flag. By manipulating these values the attacker can cause the emulator to expose pre‑image data, change execution flow, allocate memory incorrectly, or terminate the program at an arbitrary point, effectively breaking the protocol’s accounting and potentially leading to loss of funds or unauthorized state transitions. The bug manifests whenever the step function is invoked with a crafted proof and state that includes a malicious address; the contract does not perform any additional validation beyond alignment, so the out-of-bounds access passes silently. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case deliberately attempted to read and write to a very high address and the contract did not revert, confirming the missing bounds check. Because the code only checks alignment, the problem can be subtle and may not be caught by standard unit tests that use only in-range addresses, making it hard to notice in normal operation. The proper mitigation is to introduce explicit upper-bound checks on the address argument in both readMem and writeMem, using a constant that reflects the actual size of the emulator’s memory layout, and to ensure that any future changes to the memory model also update this limit. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an unchecked memory index or out-of-bounds memory access, which violates the assumption that the emulator’s memory is a closed, well-defined array and breaks the integrity of the protocol’s state.

title: Panic in MIPS VM could lead to unchallengeable L2 output root claim
description:
Suppose we have a situation where the MIPS geth goes wrong and always panics. The vmStatus can only be either `UNFINISHED` or `PANIC`.

In the current execution bisection game system, the `UNFINISHED` state can not be used as the root claim; the `PANIC` state can always be attacked. So we can counter every bisection game at `SPLIT_DEPTH + 1`; none of the claims at `SPLIT_DEPTH` are challenged. Inductively, claims agreeing with `SPLIT_DEPTH` are not challengable.

In the current configuration, `SPLIT_DEPTH` is set to 30, so we can deny any dispute against the root claim at depth 0. If that were to happen, the state of the L2 output root could be hijacked and unrecoverable.

It’s unclear if there are easy methods to trigger panic in the MIPS VM.

One possible way is to leverage the privilege, as the batcher is currently controlled by a centralized trusted entity. Ordinary users cannot construct the batches and channels for the rollup, but the batcher can freely set the payload blob to L1.

A malicious batcher could compress a huge amount of zero blobs, upload them to L1, and force the MIPS VM to decompress them. Considering the limited memory resources of the MIPS VM and the absence of garbage collection in the MIPS go-ethereum, the VM could be very easily corrupted.
bug_full:
The vulnerability originates from the way the MIPS virtual machine (VM) used by the Optimism rollup reports its execution status. The VM can only return two states: UNFINISHED or PANIC. In the current bisection‑game dispute resolution, a claim that ends in the UNFINISHED state is not allowed to be used as the root claim, while a claim that ends in PANIC can always be attacked by the challenger. Because of this asymmetry, an attacker who can force the VM into a PANIC state can repeatedly counter every bisection step at a depth of SPLIT_DEPTH+1, preventing any challenge to the claim at SPLIT_DEPTH. The protocol sets SPLIT_DEPTH to 30, which means that once a PANIC is induced, the root claim at depth 0 becomes effectively unchallengeable. If a malicious actor succeeds in causing a PANIC, they can hijack the L2 output root, making the state of the rollup unrecoverable and potentially causing loss of funds for all users of the chain.

The root cause is twofold: first, the VM lacks a graceful handling of out‑of‑memory or other fatal errors and simply panics; second, the dispute‑resolution logic treats the PANIC state as always attackable, which unintentionally gives the attacker a deterministic way to block challenges. The attack vector relies on the batcher role, which is currently a centralized trusted entity that can construct arbitrary batch payloads. By compressing a massive number of zero‑filled blobs and submitting them to L1, the batcher can exhaust the limited memory of the MIPS VM, which has no garbage collection in the Go‑Ethereum implementation. The resulting memory exhaustion triggers a panic, and the subsequent bisection game can be forced to stop at the split depth, leaving the root claim untouched.

From a user’s perspective the symptoms are subtle: disputes may appear to be resolved instantly without any challenge, the rollup may stop producing new L2 state updates, and balances that depend on the disputed output may appear frozen or disappear. Users expect that a dispute can be challenged and resolved, but instead the protocol silently accepts a faulty root claim. The issue is hard to notice because a panic does not necessarily emit a clear error on‑chain; it merely changes the internal status flag, and the bisection logic proceeds as if the challenge succeeded.

The vulnerability was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the dispute‑resolution contracts and the interaction with the MIPS VM. The auditors noted that the split depth is an even number, which combined with the PANIC handling creates a deterministic loophole. To remediate the problem, the recommendation is to set the split_depth to an odd number, which breaks the deterministic counter‑strategy and restores the ability to challenge a PANIC claim. More robust fixes would include adding proper error handling in the MIPS VM, limiting batch payload sizes, and ensuring that the UNFINISHED state can be used as a fallback root claim when a panic occurs.

title: In some cases, proper `CLOCK_EXTENTSION` time cannot be ensured to generate the initial instruction trace
description: In some cases, a team will not be granted enough `CLOCK_EXTENSION` time to generate the initial instruction trace and perform a counter claim.
bug_full: The fault dispute game contract contains a boundary‑condition error in the clock‑extension logic that can leave a defending team with less than the required time to generate an execution‑trace bisection root claim and to submit a counter‑claim. The contract is supposed to grant an extra CLOCK_EXTENSION period to any team that needs to create a grand‑child claim at the split depth (SPLIT_DEPTH+1). When the remaining duration (nextDuration) is exactly equal to MAX_CLOCK_DURATION minus a single CLOCK_EXTENSION, the condition `if (nextDuration.raw() > MAX_CLOCK_DURATION.raw() - CLOCK_EXTENSION.raw())` evaluates to false, so the extension block is skipped. Because the code only applies the double extension when the condition is true, the defending team receives no additional time (or only a single extension) even though the protocol expects a double extension at that depth. This off‑by‑one style bug can be triggered deliberately by an opponent who times their move so that the clock reaches the exact threshold, or it can occur unintentionally in normal operation when the clock happens to be at that boundary. When the defending team runs out of time, the dispute is automatically resolved in favor of the attacking team, causing the defender’s claim to be rejected and any associated funds to be slashed or withheld. From a user perspective the symptom is that a claim that should be refundable or contestable is instead marked as lost, balances appear unchanged, and no refund is received despite the expectation that the protocol would allow a counter‑claim. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by examining the move() function and testing edge cases where the remaining clock time equals the extension threshold. It is hard to notice because the majority of test scenarios use values that are strictly greater than the threshold, so the bug only manifests at the precise boundary. The conceptual fix is to change the comparison to `>=` (or to compute the required extension period before the subtraction) and to ensure that the double CLOCK_EXTENSION is always applied when the next position depth equals SPLIT_DEPTH‑1, regardless of the exact remaining duration. This correction restores the intended safety margin, guarantees that both the execution‑trace root claim and the subsequent counter‑claim have sufficient time, and aligns the contract’s behavior with its business logic that assumes a minimum extension period for split‑depth disputes.

title: `MIPS` \- Incorrect implementation of SRAV instruction
description: Incorrect dispute game resolution - it will make `True` root claim to be `False`.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect implementation of the SRAV (shift right arithmetic variable) instruction in the MIPS‑based dispute‑game engine. The SRAV operation is defined to shift the value in register rt right by a count taken from the low‑order five bits of register rs; the count must be masked with 0x1F so that only values 0‑31 are used. The code implements the instruction as `rt >> rs` without applying the mask, and then sign‑extends the result. Because the Solidity shift operator follows the EVM rule that a shift amount greater than or equal to the word size yields zero, any rs value that has a bit set above the fifth position causes the shift count to be 32 or larger, producing a zero result regardless of the original rt value. This deviation from the MIPS specification means that when the dispute‑game logic uses SRAV to compute the expected root claim, a malicious or malformed rs can force the computed claim to be zero, turning a true root claim into false. The bug can be exploited by submitting a dispute where the shift amount is crafted with high bits set, causing the engine to resolve the game incorrectly and potentially allowing an invalid state transition. The impact is that the protocol may accept fraudulent outcomes, leading to loss of funds or security guarantees for users who rely on the dispute resolution. The condition occurs whenever the SRAV opcode (function code 0x07) is executed; it is triggered only if the shift amount register contains a value larger than 31, which can happen because the implementation does not enforce the 5‑bit mask. All participants in the dispute game—proposers, challengers, and any downstream contracts that depend on the game’s result—are affected because the final decision may be based on a wrong arithmetic result. The issue was discovered during a static analysis audit of the Optimism dispute‑game contract, where the auditor compared the implementation against the MIPS ISA reference and noticed the missing `& 0x1F` mask. The bug is subtle because the shift operation still compiles and runs without reverting, and the zero result may appear plausible in some edge cases, making it hard to detect through normal testing. The correct fix is to apply the five‑bit mask to the shift amount before performing the shift, i.e., compute `rt >> (rs & 0x1F)` and then sign‑extend the result, matching the MIPS definition. This change restores the intended arithmetic behavior, prevents the zero‑shift exploit, and ensures that dispute‑game outcomes reflect the true logical state of the system.

title: The LPP proposer may not be reimbursed their gas costs by the bonds at `MAX_GAME_DEPTH` because `step
poc:
1. Alice (honest proposer) and Bob (attacker) are engaged in a fault dispute game at `MAX_GAME_DEPTH`. Alice needs to counter Bob’s false claim.
2. Alice initializes and submits an LPP on the `PreimageOracle`, incurring significant gas costs in the process.
3. As soon as the challenge period ends, Bob calls `squeezeLPP()` to finalize the LPP.
4. Immediately after, Bob calls `step()` on the FaultDisputeGame contract, providing the necessary proof that uses Alice’s LPP data.
5. The `step()` function succeeds, countering the false claim. However, it assigns the large bond to Bob (`msg.sender`) instead of Alice.
6. Bob receives their bond back, griefing Alice of the reimbursement for her significant gas expenditure.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the FaultDisputeGame contract where the step() function awards the FDG bond to the caller without verifying that the caller is the entity that supplied the preimage data for a Large Preimage Proposal (LPP). Bonds in the Optimism fault‑proof system are deliberately sized at MAX_GAME_DEPTH to reimburse the proposer for the very high gas cost of submitting a max‑size LPP (approximately 150 million gas). The step() implementation sets parent.counteredBy = msg.sender, meaning any address can invoke step after the LPP data has been loaded into the preimage oracle and receive the reimbursement that was intended for the honest proposer. An attacker can therefore wait until the challenge period ends, call squeezeLPP() to finalize the LPP, and immediately call step() with the required proof, stealing the bond. From the user’s perspective the proposer sees that after spending a large amount of gas on the LPP they receive no refund; their balance remains unchanged while another participant gains the expected reward. This flaw was uncovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the alignment between the economic incentives described in the Optimism specifications and the actual contract logic. The issue is subtle because the step() function appears to work correctly and the bond transfer to msg.sender is the default expected behavior, making the misallocation easy to overlook. The root cause is a missing link between the preimage oracle’s data provider and the bond payout logic, resulting in an incentive‑misalignment and a front‑running style reward hijacking. The bug primarily manifests at MAX_GAME_DEPTH where the bond size is large enough to make the loss significant, but any step that reads from the oracle is vulnerable. To remediate, the contract should record the address that loaded the preimage (for example via a currentPreimageProposer variable) and use that address when assigning the bond, or restrict step() to be callable only by the original proposer, clearing the proposer record after use. This correction restores the intended guarantee that the party incurring the gas cost is reimbursed, preserving the economic security model of the protocol.

title: Honest party’s move could become invalid when re-org takes place
description: When block re-org takes place, honest party’s move could become invalid. A similar issue has been [raised](https://github.com/sherlock-audit/2024-02-optimism-2024-judging/issues/201) earlier, and this report shows two new scenarios, which the [fix](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/pull/10520/files#diff-d25b365609feaebe61ed8cf3547bd8f7fbe26aa6a5a30aab21788e9fad7a7c6a) fails to address.
poc:
A new parameter `_claim` has been added to ensure the target is the expected one, but this is still not enough.
    
    function move(Claim _disputed, uint256 _challengeIndex, Claim _claim, bool _isAttack) public payable virtual {

The factory uses create instead of create2 to deploy the proxy, consider the following scenario:

1. Evil Alice creates a invalid root claim A and game P.
2. Seemingly honest Bob attacks A with claim B in game P.
3. Seemingly honest Bob creates a valid root claim C and game Q.
4. Evil Alice attacks C with claim B(valid, same hash as step 2) in game Q.
5. Honest Coco defends B with claim D in game Q.

Alice and Bob are friends actually and they use another smart contract to interact with the factory and game. At the end of step 1 and 3, A,P and C,Q are stored in the contract, and in step 2 and 4, the contract executes `P.move(A,...)`and `Q.move(C,...)`. Coco simply uses an eoa at step 5.

Then reorg happens, transaction order becomes 34125. The address of game P and Q are swapped (since the deployed address is derived from sender and nonce). Now it will look like:

1. Seemingly honest Bob creates a valid root claim C and game Q.
2. Evil Alice attacks C with claim B(valid, same hash with step 4) in game Q.
3. Evil Alice creates a invalid root claim A and game P.
4. Seemingly honest Bob attacks A with claim B in game P.
5. Honest Coco defends B with claim D in game P.

Alice and Bob are still in their desired game but Coco will be in a wrong game. As a result, her bond will be lost.
    
    proxy_ = IDisputeGame(address(impl).clone(abi.encodePacked(msg.sender, _rootClaim, parentHash, _extraData)));
    ......
    instance := create(value, add(m, add(0x0b, lt(n, 0xffd3))), add(n, 0x37))

Suppose create2 is used to address the previous scenario, but within the same game, reorg could still impact the honest party. Consider the following scenario:

1. Evil Alice creates an invalid root claim A.
2. Honest Coco attacks A with claim B.
3. Evil Alice attacks A with an invalid claim X.
4. Evil Alice attacks B with the valid claim C.
5. Honest Coco defends C(the claim created in step 4) with claim D.
6. Evil Alice attacks A with an invalid claim E.
7. Evil Alice attacks E with the valid claim C (same hash as step 4).

Now reorg happens again, new transaction order is 1267534. Alice uses the previously mentioned contract call trick(store claim and index this time) so that her txs do not revert. Then at step 5, Coco’s tx will succeed since disputed hash is the same. But her defend will now imply C and E are both valid, so she’ll lose her bond again.

Chain reorgs are very prevalent in Ethereum mainnet, we can check [this](https://etherscan.io/blocks_forked) index of reorged blocks on etherscan.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way dispute‑game contracts are instantiated and how moves are linked to a specific game instance. The factory currently uses the CREATE opcode to deploy a proxy for each game, which means the address of the proxy depends on the sender address and the transaction nonce. When a chain re‑organisation reshuffles the order of transactions, the non‑deterministic address calculation can cause two games that were created in a particular sequence to swap their addresses. An honest participant who later calls the move function with a claim that is tied to a specific game may unintentionally interact with the wrong game because the contract resolves the address based on the now‑different nonce ordering. Consequently, the participant’s bond is forfeited even though the move would have been valid in the originally intended game. The same problem can also appear when CREATE2 is used: although the address becomes deterministic, the protocol still derives a claim hash only from the claim data and its position, without incorporating the parent claim hash. An attacker can submit identical claim hashes in multiple disputes and, by orchestrating a re‑org, cause the honest defender’s transaction to be evaluated against a different dispute where the same hash is considered valid for a different lineage. The exploit requires the attacker to control the ordering of transactions (for example by using a helper contract that stores claims and re‑submits them) and to reuse claim hashes across games. When the re‑org occurs, the honest party’s defend transaction succeeds against a disputed hash that now represents two conflicting claims, leading the protocol to treat the defender as having acted incorrectly and to slash the bonded amount. The impact is a loss of funds for honest users, erosion of trust in the dispute‑resolution mechanism, and potential economic incentives for malicious actors to trigger or profit from re‑orgs. The issue manifests only under re‑organisation conditions, which are common on Ethereum, and is difficult to detect because the contract logic behaves correctly when transactions are processed in the originally intended order; the mismatch appears only after the chain history is rewritten. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑binding” or “address‑binding” vulnerabilities where contract state is implicitly tied to transaction ordering or non‑deterministic deployment addresses. To remediate the problem, the factory should deploy proxies with CREATE2 (using cloneDeterministic) so that the address is fixed regardless of transaction ordering, and the claim hash calculation must be extended to include the parent claim hash (e.g., claimHash(child)=keccak256(claim,position,claimHash(parent)). The contract must then verify that the stored claimHash matches the expected value before allowing any move, ensuring that a claim cannot be replayed across different disputes. This change eliminates the reliance on transaction order and prevents an attacker from redirecting honest moves to an unintended game, thereby protecting bonded funds and preserving the integrity of the dispute resolution process.

title: The `MIPS` doesn’t implement `ADD`, `ADDI`, and `SUB` instructions correctly
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the arithmetic instruction emulation of a Solidity contract that mimics a 32‑bit big‑endian MIPS processor. According to the official MIPS ISA, the ADD, ADDI and SUB instructions must trigger an integer‑overflow exception when the signed result cannot be represented in 32 bits. The contract’s execute function performs these operations inside an unchecked block and simply returns the wrapped 32‑bit result, never reverting or emitting an error. The root cause is the use of unchecked arithmetic for these opcodes, which discards the overflow detection logic required by the specification. An attacker can craft a transaction that supplies operand values causing a signed overflow; the contract will silently wrap the result and continue execution as if the operation succeeded. Because the surrounding claim‑validation logic relies on the arithmetic result to decide whether a claim is valid, the wrapped result can make an otherwise invalid claim appear legitimate, or cause a legitimate claim to be rejected. This can be exploited during the challenge phase of the protocol: a malicious participant submits a claim with overflow‑prone values, the contract computes a wrapped sum or difference, and the protocol’s verifier accepts the forged claim, allowing the attacker to claim rewards or to block honest participants. The impact is the potential loss of funds, incorrect accounting of claims, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s correctness. The bug manifests whenever the contract executes ADD, ADDI or SUB with operands that would overflow a signed 32‑bit integer, which can happen in normal usage if large values are supplied or if an attacker deliberately chooses overflow‑inducing inputs. All users who rely on the claim system—depositors, challengers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the arithmetic guarantees they expect are violated. The issue was discovered during a formal audit that compared the contract’s behavior against the MIPS ISA specification and identified the missing overflow checks. Because the contract does not revert on overflow, the symptom is subtle: users see claims being accepted or rejected inconsistently, and balances may change without an obvious error message, making the problem hard to notice without deep inspection of the arithmetic implementation. The proper fix is to replace the unchecked addition and subtraction with safe arithmetic that checks for signed overflow and reverts with a defined exception, or to use Solidity’s built‑in checked arithmetic (by removing the unchecked block) and explicitly enforce the ISA’s overflow semantics. In broader terms, this is a classic integer‑overflow handling bug in an instruction‑set emulator, where the lack of proper overflow detection breaks the intended security guarantees of the surrounding protocol.

title: Attacker can continuously create games for not yet safe l2 blocks to prevent the update of anchor state
description: When creating a dispute game, the output root should be one of the safe l2 block’s. However, attacker can continuously create games for not yet safe l2 blocks. Honest party can no longer propose the root after it becomes safe, since UUID must be unique. As a result, no root can be successfully defended, the anchor state can no longer be updated and the fund on L2 will be frozen.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises from the way a dispute game identifier (UUID) is calculated when a claim is submitted for an L2 block. The contract generates the UUID from the game type, the claimed output root and optional extra data, but it deliberately omits any reference to the block’s parent hash or other block‑specific information. Because of this omission, an attacker can create a dispute game for a block that has not yet reached the safety threshold – a so‑called unsafe block – and obtain a UUID that will later be identical to the UUID that an honest participant would need to use when the same output root is claimed for the block after it becomes safe. The protocol enforces uniqueness of the UUID, reverting any attempt to create a second game with the same identifier. Consequently, once the attacker has occupied the identifier, the honest party is unable to propose the correct root after the block is finalized, the anchor state cannot be updated, and any funds that depend on that state become frozen. The attack can be carried out continuously: the attacker repeatedly creates games for each newly‑produced unsafe block, effectively locking the protocol’s state transition mechanism. This issue is discovered during a security audit that examined the logical flow of dispute creation and noticed that the UUID does not incorporate a block‑specific field. It is hard to notice because the contract appears to enforce a unique identifier correctly; the problem only manifests when the same root is reused for a later safe block, a scenario that is not obvious from the code alone. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a transaction to submit a claim for a safe block reverts with a “GameAlreadyExists” error, withdrawals fail, and balances that should become available remain at zero. The bug belongs to the class of identifier‑collision or insufficient‑entropy vulnerabilities that enable a denial‑of‑service by preventing legitimate state updates. To remediate the issue the UUID calculation should be extended to include the parent hash (or another unique block identifier), ensuring that each block’s claim yields a distinct UUID even when the output root is identical, thereby restoring the ability of honest participants to create dispute games and update the anchor state.

title: RToken can manipulate distribution to avoid paying DAO fees
description:
Revenue produced by RTokens is sold for both RSR and RTokens according to a distribution defined in the [`Distributor`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-reserve/blob/3f133997e186465f4904553b0f8e86ecb7bbacbf/contracts/p1/Distributor.sol). The `BackingManager` [splits](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-reserve/blob/3f133997e186465f4904553b0f8e86ecb7bbacbf/contracts/p1/BackingManager.sol#L247-L261) the collateral tokens to be sold proportionately to the RSR/RToken distribution ratio and sends them to the `rsrTrader` and `rTokenTrader`. When trades settle, the obtained RSR or RTokens are sent to the `Distributor`, which distributes them no longer according to the RSR/RToken ratio but to the different destinations for the specific token. The sum of all destinations for each token is used to derive the ratio.

The DAO fee is added to the RSR share of the initial split and paid when RSR is distributed.

However, the current implementation allows governance to manipulate the distribution settings without much effort in a way that can significantly reduce the amount of DAO fees paid.

This can be achieved through a combination of two different root causes:

  * an RSR destination can be added that prevents rewards from being immediately distributed
  * the RSR/RToken ratio is calculated twice: once in the `BackingManager`, and once in the `Distributor`, and it is can be modified between the two

Essentially, the distribution can be set in a way that temporarily accumulates RSR revenue in the `rsrTrader` according to one RSR/RToken ratio, and then later redistributed with a different ratio.
poc:
Assuming a 10% DAO fee, governance can execute the following steps to pay only about 1% in fees:

  1. Set the distribution such that `rsrTotal == 0` before DAO fees are added.
  2. Add the RSR token itself as a distribution target. Like stRSR, [RSR](https://etherscan.io/token/0x320623b8e4ff03373931769a31fc52a4e78b5d70#code) does not allow transferring to itself, so the distribution will always fail.
  3. 10% of revenue will accumulate as RSR in the `rsrTrader`.
  4. After some time, change the distribution such that `rTokenTotal == 0` and add another destination with non-zero `rsrDist` (e.g., `stRSR`).
  5. Remove RSR as a distribution target and call `rsrTrader.distributeTokenToBuy()`.
  6. Only 10% of the accumulated RSR will go to the DAO, which is effectively 1% of the total revenue.
  7. Repeat this process as needed.
bug_full: The vulnerability allows a malicious governance actor to manipulate the revenue distribution mechanism of the protocol in order to drastically reduce the amount of DAO fees that are actually paid out. The root cause is two‑fold: first, the Distributor contract permits an RSR destination to be added that cannot receive tokens immediately, causing the RSR revenue to be held temporarily in the rsrTrader contract; second, the RSR/RToken split ratio is calculated separately in the BackingManager and again in the Distributor, and the ratio can be altered between these two calculations. An attacker can therefore set the distribution so that the initial split sends a large portion of revenue to rsrTrader based on one ratio, then later change the distribution table and the ratio before the rsrTrader distributes its holdings, causing only a small fraction of the expected DAO fee to be transferred. This exploit can be carried out whenever governance has permission to modify the Distributor’s destination table and to invoke rsrTrader.distributeTokenToBuy. The impact is that the DAO receives far less fee revenue than the protocol’s economic model assumes, veRSR holders see reduced rewards, and overall accounting invariants are broken, effectively constituting a privilege‑escalation style attack that diverts protocol funds. From a user’s perspective the DAO fee payout appears unusually low or even zero despite normal revenue generation, leading to confusion and loss of trust. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between BackingManager’s split logic and the Distributor’s dynamic destination configuration. It is hard to notice because the fee calculation still occurs, but the amount transferred is silently reduced by the altered ratio, and the failing RSR destination does not raise an explicit error. To remediate the problem the protocol should forbid RSR (or any token that can be added as a self‑referential destination) from being used as a distribution token, lock the RSR/RToken ratio between the split and final distribution phases, and enforce that distribution destinations cannot be configured to reject incoming transfers, thereby preserving the intended fee‑on‑revenue model.

title: Broken assumptions can lead to the inability to seize RSR
description: The `seizeRSR` [function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-reserve/blob/main/contracts/p1/StRSR.sol#L424) takes RSR from the staking contract when `BackingManager` wants to sell RSR, but it does not have enough. In this case, the stakers can lose a portion of their stake in order to keep the system healthy. However, an issue arises from broken assumptions about `stakeRSR` and `totalStakes`, which will make the contract unable to seize due to revert.
poc:
Let’s assume the system becomes unhealthy, and the stakers will start unstaking their tokens in fear of an upcoming reset/seize. Then, the expected event comes, and the `BackingManager` tries to seize RSR from the staking contract.

This action is frontran however, with the last staker who:

  1. unstakes everything
  2. stakes one token
  3. stakes one token again

Let’s examine how does this break `seizeRSR`.

  1. During the `unstake` [call](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-reserve/blob/main/contracts/p1/StRSR.sol#L259):

     * `_payoutRewards` is called. Since `totalStakes` is still above `1e18`, `stakeRSR` can be increased and become greater than `totalStakes`. Let’s assume that `totalStakes` would be `1000e18` and `stakeRSR` would end at `1001e18` after this step.
     * Now, the `stakeRate` would be updated. Since `stakeRSR` is not zero yet, and so is not `totalStakes`, it would be set to

           uint192((totalStakes * FIX_ONE_256 + (stakeRSR - 1)) / stakeRSR)

which translates to

           uint192((1000e18 * 1e18 + (1001e18 - 1)) / 1001e18)

resulting in `999000999000999001`

     * `totalStakes` would be decreased in `_burn` by `1000e18` to zero, which would result in `stakeRSR` being set to zero
  2. During the `stake` [call](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-reserve/blob/main/contracts/p1/StRSR.sol#L227):

     * `payoutRewards` is skipped because it was already called in this block
     * `newTotalStakes` in `mintStakes` is calculated as `(stakeRate * newStakeRSR) / FIX_ONE`, which translates to `(stakeRate * (stakeRSR + rsrAmount)) / FIX_ONE` which translates to `(999000999000999001 * (0 + 1)) / 1e18` resulting in 0, meaning 0 tokens are minted and `totalStakes` remains 0
     * `stakeRSR` is increased by 1
  3. The second `stake` call will have the same effects

     * after this call, the `stakeRate` is `999000999000999001`, `totalStakes` is 0, and `stakeRSR` is 2 (note that this breaks [this assumption](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-reserve/blob/main/contracts/p1/StRSR.sol#L619-L620))
  4. Now we examine the important parts of the `seizeRSR` call

     * `stakeRSRToTake` is set to `(2 * rsrAmount + (rsrBalance - 1)) / rsrBalance`, which will result in 1 every time the we are not seizing more than half of the total balance of the contract
     * `stakeRSR` is therefore set to 1, and since it is non-zero, `stakeRate` is updated to `uint192((FIX_ONE_256 * totalStakes + (stakeRSR - 1)) / stakeRSR)`, which translates to `uint192((1e18 * 0 + (1 - 1)) / 1)` which comes to 0
     * the rest of the call is not important until it comes to

           emit ExchangeRateSet(initRate, exchangeRate());

     * Here, we can see that the call returns

           return (FIX_SCALE_SQ + (stakeRate / 2)) / stakeRate;

     * since `stakeRate` was updated to 0 before, the call will revert
bug_full: An inability to seize RSR occurs because the staking contract breaks the invariant that totalStakes and stakeRSR must be simultaneously zero. The contract calculates a stakeRate from totalStakes and stakeRSR and later uses this rate in seizeRSR to compute the amount of RSR to take. When totalStakes becomes zero while stakeRSR remains positive, the stakeRate is set to zero. The subsequent division by stakeRate in the exchangeRate calculation triggers a division‑by‑zero panic, causing seizeRSR to revert. The root cause is a rounding error in mintStakes: if the stakeRate is slightly below the threshold 5e17 and a very small amount (e.g., 2 wei) is staked after an almost complete unstake, the formula (stakeRate * newStakeRSR) / FIX_ONE evaluates to zero, leaving totalStakes at zero but increasing stakeRSR. An attacker who is the last staker can front‑run the BackingManager’s seizeRSR call, first unstaking almost all tokens and then staking the tiny amount in the same block. This sequence forces totalStakes to zero, makes stakeRSR non‑zero, and forces stakeRate to zero, so the seizeRSR call reverts with a panic code. From a user perspective the transaction simply fails with a “division or modulo division by zero” error, and the protocol is unable to recover RSR during an unhealthy state, potentially freezing funds and preventing the system from rebalancing. The issue only appears under very specific numeric conditions: stakeRate just below 5e17, the caller being the last staker, and the ability to front‑run the seize call. It was discovered during a formal audit when a PoC test reproduced the revert. The bug is hard to notice because normal staking and unstaking operations work correctly and the failure only manifests with extreme edge‑case values and transaction ordering. To remediate, the contract should enforce the invariant that if totalStakes is zero then stakeRSR must also be zero, for example by rejecting zero‑amount mints or by adding a check in _mint, and by updating seizeRSR to handle the zero‑stakeRate case safely (e.g., defaulting the rate to FIX_ONE). Alternatively, the stakeRate update logic could be guarded so that it is only performed when both totalStakes and stakeRSR are non‑zero. Ensuring these checks restores the protocol’s ability to seize RSR and prevents a denial‑of‑service condition.

title: The default Governor Anastasius is unable to call `resetStakes`
description:
The `StRSR` contract contains a function [`resetStakes`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-reserve/blob/main/contracts/p1/StRSR.sol#L490), which is used to reset the staking of a specific RToken system, when the stake rate becomes unsafe. When this happens, the `era` of the staking contract is incremented, which practically resets the `StRSR` token. Since this is a sensitive action, only governance can call this function.

The Reserve team provides a default and recommended `Governance` contract with `TimelockController`, which handles the proposal creation and execution. The contract also ensures that proposals created in a past era can not be queued or executed in the current era since the voting conditions can differ between eras. However due to this check, it is impossible for the `Governance` contract to call `resetStakes`, since the function would increment the era, and the following check whether the proposal was proposed in the same era would not hold and revert the transaction.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the interaction between the StRSR staking contract and the default Governor contract (named Anastasius) that is backed by a TimelockController. StRSR provides a resetStakes function that is intended to be called by governance when the staking exchange rate becomes unsafe; calling this function increments the internal era counter, effectively resetting the token state. The Governor implementation overrides the internal _execute method and performs a check called startedInSameEra that requires the proposal to have been created in the same era in which it is executed. In the current code the check is performed after the super._execute call, meaning the era is already incremented by resetStakes before the check runs. As a result the requirement fails and the transaction reverts, making it impossible for the Governor to successfully execute resetStakes. The root cause is therefore the ordering of the era‑validation logic relative to the state‑changing call, which violates the assumption that a proposal’s era does not change during execution. An attacker could exploit this by forcing the staking rate into an unsafe region (for example by flooding the contract with a large amount of RSR) and then relying on the fact that the governance process cannot reset the stakes, leaving the protocol in a prolonged unsafe state. The impact is that token holders may see the exchange rate drift far from its intended range, potentially devaluing their stakes or breaking accounting invariants, while the protocol loses the ability to recover from the unsafe condition. The issue manifests only when resetStakes is invoked through the Governor; direct calls by the contract owner would succeed, which makes the bug subtle and easy to miss during casual testing. It was discovered during a formal audit when a test case attempted to propose, queue and execute a resetStakes call and observed a revert with the message "TimelockController: underlying transaction reverted". The bug is hard to notice because the resetStakes function itself works correctly in isolation, and the era check is hidden inside the governance wrapper. The recommended remediation is to move the startedInSameEra requirement before the super._execute call, or otherwise adjust the validation so that proposals that intentionally change the era are allowed to proceed. Conceptually, the fix restores the invariant that a proposal may be executed if it was created in the same era, even when the execution itself updates the era, thereby re‑enabling the critical resetStakes operation and preserving the protocol’s safety guarantees.

title: Dutch auctions can fail to settle if any other collateral in the basket behaves unexpectedly
description:
When a Dutch auction that originated from the backing manager receives a bid, it [calls](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-reserve/blob/3f133997e186465f4904553b0f8e86ecb7bbacbf/contracts/plugins/trading/DutchTrade.sol#L222) `BackingManager.settleTrade()` to settle the auction immediately, which [attempts to chain](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-reserve/blob/3f133997e186465f4904553b0f8e86ecb7bbacbf/contracts/p1/BackingManager.sol#L92) into another `rebalance()` call. This chaining is implemented using a try-catch block that attempts to catch out-of-gas errors.

However, this pattern is not safe because empty error data does not always indicate an out-of-gas error. Other types of errors also return no data, such as calls to empty addresses casted as contracts and revert / require statements with no error message.

The `rebalance()` function interacts with multiple external assets and performs several operations that can throw empty errors:

  1. In `basketsHeldBy()`, which calls `_quantity()`, which in turn calls `coll.refPerTok()` (this function should in theory [never revert](https://github.com/3docSec/2024-07-reserve/blob/main/docs/collateral.md#refpertok-reftok), but in case it interacts with the underlying ERC20, its implementation may have been upgraded to one that does).
  2. In `prepareRecollateralizationTrade()`, which calls `basketRange()`, which also calls `_quantity()`.
  3. In `tryTrade()` if a new rebalancing trade is indeed chained, which calls `approve()` on the token via `AllowanceLib.safeApproveFallbackToMax()`. This is a direct interaction with the token and hence cannot be trusted, especially if the possibility of [upgradeability](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-reserve/tree/3f133997e186465f4904553b0f8e86ecb7bbacbf?tab=readme-ov-file#erc20-token-behaviors-in-scope) is considered.

If any of these operations result in an empty error, the auction settlement will fail. This can lead to the Dutch auction being unable to settle at a fair price.

Note: we have found [this](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-06-reserve-findings/issues/8) finding pointing out the very same issue in a previous audit, but this report highlights a different root cause in where the error originates.
poc:
1. A Dutch auction is initiated for rebalancing collateral.
2. After some time, a bidder attempts to submit a bid at fair market value.
3. `BackingManager.settleTrade()` is called by the trade contract.
4. The `rebalance()` function is called within the try-catch block.
5. The underlying ERC-20 of one of the collateral assets in the basket has an empty revert clause that currently throws when one of its functions is called.
6. The catch block receives an empty error and reverts the transaction.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a settlement failure in Dutch auctions that are triggered by the BackingManager when a bid is received. The contract attempts to settle the trade and immediately calls a rebalance function inside a try‑catch block that is designed to catch out‑of‑gas (OOG) errors. The root cause is the assumption that an empty revert data payload always indicates an OOG condition.
