In reality, many external calls – such as reading a collateral reference per token, calculating basket ranges, or approving ERC‑20 tokens – can revert without returning an error string, for example when a token contract is upgraded to throw on approve or when a collateral plugin deliberately reverts with a plain require. When any of these calls returns an empty error, the catch block mistakenly treats it as an OOG error and propagates a revert, causing the entire settlement transaction to fail. This can happen whenever a collateral asset in the basket exhibits an empty‑error revert during the rebalance chain, which is possible for any ERC‑20 that may be upgraded or for collateral plugins that are not guaranteed to be non‑reverting. The affected parties are bidders who expect their bid to be processed, the protocol that relies on timely auction settlement to rebalance collateral, and ultimately token holders whose collateral may remain locked or be priced incorrectly. The impact is that the Dutch auction may never settle at a fair price, leaving user balances unchanged, bids unfilled, and the protocol’s accounting out of sync. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the settlement flow and identified that the empty‑error catch logic does not reliably differentiate OOG from other revert reasons, a problem previously noted in earlier audits but with a different origin. The bug is hard to notice because an empty revert looks like a generic failure and does not provide a clear diagnostic message, making debugging obscure. To remediate, the pattern of catching empty errors for OOG should be removed; instead the contract should use a reserved‑gas approach or explicit error handling that does not rely on error data length, and external calls should be wrapped with safe‑approve utilities that handle arbitrary revert behaviours. By redesigning the settlement flow to avoid chaining rebalance inside the try‑catch or by ensuring all collateral contracts provide meaningful revert messages, the auction can reliably settle and the protocol’s accounting integrity is preserved.

title: Users can dodge losses due to StRSR era changes with instant operations
poc:
Alice is an StRSR token holder:

  * she notices that a transaction will soon cause RSR to be seized and the `stakeRate` will wrap to 1.0
  * she immediately initiates an `unstake`, so her funds are moved to the drafts bucket
  * immediately after the transaction that wraps the `stakeRate`, she calls `cancelUnstake`
  * Alice lost only the pro-rata RSR that was seized (which may be minimal) while others lost everything

A similar sequence can be performed to avoid losses on funds that are being unstaked by instead calling `cancelUnstake` first and `unstake` later.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the StRSR contract handles the two exchange rates – stakeRate and draftRate – that are bounded by a maximum value (MAX_STAKE_RATE and MAX_DRAFT_RATE, both equal to 1e27). When a seizeRSR call pushes either rate above its cap, the contract automatically starts a new era and resets the offending rate to its base value. This reset effectively wipes out the proportional share of the token holders that were holding the affected bucket, because the internal accounting assumes the previous rate is no longer valid. The root cause is that the two rates are wrapped independently and the contract does not enforce a simultaneous reset when only one of them exceeds its safe threshold. Consequently, an attacker who holds StRSR can observe an upcoming seizeRSR transaction that will trigger a rate wrap, and can front‑run or react in the same block by sandwiching the wrap with unstake and cancelUnstake calls. By moving their balance to the draft bucket before the wrap and then cancelling the unstake after the wrap, the attacker avoids the pro‑rata loss that is applied to all other holders. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that some participants see their StRSR balance drop to zero or receive a much smaller refund, while the attacker’s balance appears unchanged or only reduced by the minimal seized amount. The impact is an unfair redistribution of funds: honest stakers lose a portion of their value, whereas the attacker preserves almost all of theirs. This situation can only occur when the stakeRate or draftRate is close to the maximum bound, a seizeRSR transaction is about to be executed, and the attacker can issue the unstake/cancelUnstake sequence within the same block – conditions that are rare but not impossible, especially for large stakeholders with the ability to monitor pending transactions. The issue was discovered during a formal audit (Code4rena) by analysing the seizeRSR logic and noticing that the rate reset logic is not atomic across both rates. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the rate reset is an internal accounting change that does not emit a distinct event indicating a loss for individual users; the only observable effect is the sudden disappearance of balances for some accounts. The recommended mitigation is to treat the two rates as a single logical entity: either wrap both rates together when either exceeds its safe limit, or extend the resetStakes governance function so it can be called when draftRate is out of bounds as well. Making the reset atomic or adding explicit checks that prevent a user from performing unstake/cancelUnstake around a pending wrap would close the attack surface and restore the intended collective accounting model.

title: The time available for a canceled withdrawal should not impact future unstaking processes
description:
When `stakers` want to `unstake` their `StRSR`, they cannot `withdraw` `RSR` immediately.  
Instead, each `withdrawal` enters a `queue` and will become available after the `unstaking delay` period.  
This `queue` operates on a `FIFO` basis, meaning earlier `withdrawals` are processed before later ones.  
`Stakers` can also cancel their `withdrawals`, and the `RSR` will be `restaked` immediately.  
However, even canceled `withdrawals` can still impact future `withdrawal` requests.
bug_full: The contract implements a FIFO withdrawal queue for users who unstake their StRSR tokens. When a user initiates an unstake, a draft entry is pushed onto the queue with an "availableAt" timestamp that equals the current block time plus the global unstakingDelay. Users may later cancel a pending withdrawal; the cancellation logic simply advances a pointer (firstRemainingDraft) so that the cancelled entry is ignored for payout, but the entry itself remains in the array. The pushDraft routine, however, always reads the "availableAt" value from the last element of the array regardless of whether that element is still considered active. Consequently, if a cancelled draft still holds an old availableAt timestamp (for example from a previous 1‑day delay), any new draft pushed after a change in the global unstakingDelay will inherit the larger timestamp. This means that even after the admin reduces the delay and the user cancels earlier withdrawals, the contract continues to enforce the original, longer lock‑up period for subsequent withdrawals. The bug manifests when the unstakingDelay is lowered after a user has a pending (or cancelled) draft: the user expects the new, shorter delay but the contract still reports a later withdrawal time, effectively locking funds for longer than advertised. From a user’s perspective the UI will show a withdrawal that should be claimable after one hour, yet the transaction reverts or the claim button remains disabled, leading to confusion, panic, or accusations of a scam. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the withdrawal path and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that the delay applied to a draft reflects the current global setting. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case demonstrated that a cancelled draft from a previous delay continued to affect a new draft after the delay was changed. It is hard to notice because the cancellation appears to clear the queue, but the stale timestamp is hidden in the underlying storage and only surfaces when the next draft is created. The proper fix is to adjust the pushDraft logic so that it only considers the "availableAt" of the last draft that is still pending (i.e., when firstRemainingDraft is less than the current index). By resetting lastAvailableAt to zero for cancelled tails, new drafts will be scheduled using the current unstakingDelay, restoring the intended behaviour and preventing funds from being locked unexpectedly.

title: The `tradeEnd` in `BackingManager` isn’t updating correctly
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of the tradeEnd timestamp in the BackingManager contract. The contract stores a tradeEnd value for each trade kind and uses it in the rebalance function to prevent a new auction from being launched in the same block as the previous one. This logic works for batch auctions, where the auction always runs until its declared end time, but it is incorrect for Dutch auctions, which can finish earlier than the maximum auction length. Because the tradeEnd variable is set to the original endTime of the Dutch auction and never cleared or updated after the auction actually ends, the require check "tradeEnd[kind] < block.timestamp" continues to fail until the full maximum duration (up to one week) has elapsed. When the basket status temporarily becomes IFFY, the rebalance function cannot start a new auction even after the asset status recovers, because the stale tradeEnd value still blocks the call. An attacker could deliberately trigger an IFFY status or wait for a long‑running Dutch auction to finish early, causing the protocol to be unable to launch new Dutch auctions for days, which reduces efficiency and may affect availability if the fallback GnosisTrade mechanism is also paused. Users experience the symptom of no new Dutch auction appearing in the UI, even though the protocol is otherwise functional; they may see a prolonged period with no rebalancing activity and wonder why their expected price‑optimised trades are not occurring. The issue was discovered during a security audit by examining the rebalance guard clause and reproducing a scenario where an asset’s status flips to IFFY and back while a Dutch auction with a long duration is in progress. It is hard to notice because the require statement appears reasonable and only manifests under specific timing conditions that are not exercised in normal operation. The bug belongs to the class of state‑stale‑timestamp errors, where a contract retains outdated timing information that incorrectly restricts future actions. To fix the problem, the contract should reset or update tradeEnd after a Dutch auction settles, for example by assigning tradeEnd[kind] = block.timestamp or by clearing the entry when the auction ends, and the guard condition should be adjusted to consider the actual end of the auction rather than the maximum allowed duration. This change restores the ability to start new Dutch auctions promptly once the basket is ready, aligning the implementation with the intended business logic of continuous rebalancing without unnecessary downtime.

title: Potential uninitialized `entropySlots` reading in `getNextEntropy`, causing 0 entropy mint
description: The `getNextEntropy` function can be called at any time without waiting for the write entropy batches process to finish. This could lead to the function returning an uninitialized entropy value of `000000`, resulting in users losing funds to mint useless tokens and not being eligible for future airdrops as they get 0 shares. This vulnerability can severely impact the users’ trust and the protocol’s functionality.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the entropy generation contract allowing the public function that returns the next entropy value to be invoked before the internal batch‑writing process has populated the storage array that holds entropy slots. The contract tracks a current slot index and a last initialized index, but the getter does not verify that the current slot has been written. Consequently, when the function is called while currentSlotIndex is greater than or equal to lastInitializedIndex, the low‑level read returns the default value of zero (0x000000) instead of reverting. From a user’s perspective this manifests as a mint transaction that appears to succeed, emits an EntropyRetrieved event with a zero value, and results in a newly minted token that carries no share or value. The user therefore loses the ether or other assets spent on the mint, receives a token that is effectively worthless, and may become ineligible for future airdrops that depend on a non‑zero entropy share. The impact is economic loss for the individual user and erosion of trust in the protocol because the accounting assumptions – that each minted token corresponds to a positive entropy share – are violated. The issue can be reproduced by calling the getter immediately after deployment or during the window before the writeEntropyBatch routine finishes, as demonstrated by a test that expects the EntropyRetrieved event with a zero argument. The problem is subtle because the contract does not throw an error; it simply returns a default value that passes basic validation, making the failure easy to miss during casual testing. The appropriate mitigation is to enforce a guard that ensures the current slot index is strictly less than the last initialized index before reading the entropy, or to guarantee that the first batch is written in the constructor so that no uninitialized slot can ever be accessed. This class of bug falls under uninitialized storage access or unchecked state transition, where a function reads from a data structure before it is guaranteed to contain valid data, leading to logical errors and financial loss.

title: Funds can be locked indefinitely in NukeFund.sol
description:
* Permanent loss of funds.
* Dependency on user action.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a permanent fund lock condition caused by the contract’s exclusive withdrawal mechanism being tied to the nuke() function, which can only be executed by an NFT holder and burns the NFT as part of the claim. Because there is no alternative path for the contract owner or any other party to retrieve the remaining ether, the funds become irretrievable when either all NFTs have been burned or the remaining NFT owners never invoke nuke(). The root cause is a design decision that couples fund distribution to a state‑changing token burn without providing a fallback or emergency withdrawal. An attacker or even a benign user can trigger the lock by simply burning NFTs through the separate burn() function or by abandoning their NFTs, leaving the contract with a positive ether balance but no callable entry point to move it. The impact is a permanent loss of ether for the protocol and its participants; users expecting a refund or claim will see no transfer, their UI will show unchanged balances, and the protocol’s advertised fund distribution model fails. The condition occurs after the contract is deployed, once the NFT supply is reduced to zero or when the contract is paused, because nuke() is guarded by whenNotPaused. All NFT holders, the protocol team, and any investors are affected because the locked ether cannot be used for further operations or redistributed. The issue was discovered during a formal audit where the logic of fund extraction was examined and the lack of an alternative withdrawal path was identified as a critical edge case. It is hard to notice because normal operation (successful nuke calls) works as intended, masking the dead‑end scenario that only appears when the trigger token set is exhausted. The recommended remediation is to introduce an emergency withdrawal function for the contract owner or a timed fallback that allows the remaining ether to be reclaimed or redistributed when no eligible NFTs exist, thereby breaking the dependency on a user‑initiated burn. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a “withdrawal deadlock” or “funds lock due to missing exit path”, and it violates the basic accounting assumption that every deposited ether must have a reachable exit route.

title: A dev will lose rewards if after claiming his rewards he mints an NFT
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑update‑after‑external‑call bug in the DevFund contract that can cause a developer to receive fewer rewards than entitled when the developer’s contract executes a payable receive() function during the same transaction as a claim. The claim function calculates the pending amount, transfers the Ether to the caller, and only afterwards sets the caller’s rewardDebt to the current totalRewardDebt. If the caller’s receive() function immediately spends the received Ether to mint an NFT, the minting operation sends a fee back to DevFund, triggering its receive() logic. That logic increases totalRewardDebt before the caller’s rewardDebt is updated, so the caller’s stored rewardDebt becomes larger than it should be. As a result the next time rewards are calculated the pending amount is reduced, effectively stealing a portion of the originally claimed rewards. The issue occurs only when the airdrop has not started (the receive() path that updates totalRewardDebt is active) and when the developer’s contract performs a re‑entering call that sends Ether back to DevFund in the same transaction. Developers who intend to support the protocol by immediately using claimed funds to mint NFTs are affected; they may see their reward balance lower than expected or receive zero additional rewards after a claim. The bug was discovered during a manual audit by examining the order of operations in claim() and noticing that the external call precedes the state update, creating a re‑entrancy‑like race condition. It can be hard to notice because the contract works correctly when the developer does not perform a callback, and the loss only manifests under a specific sequence of actions. The proper mitigation is to follow the 'Checks‑Effects‑Interactions' pattern: update all internal accounting variables, including rewardDebt, before transferring Ether to the caller, or to use a pull‑payment model. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of improper state handling after external calls, which can lead to accounting inconsistencies and unintended loss of funds.

title: Lack of slippage protection in dynamic pricing mint function
description:
The `mintWithBudget` function uses a dynamic pricing mechanism without implementing slippage protection. Given the specific pricing parameters, this can lead to users paying more than anticipated for their NFTs, especially for larger mints or mints occurring later in a generation. Specific impacts include:

  * Unexpected cost increases for users, particularly for multi-NFT mints.
  * Potential for users to receive fewer NFTs than expected if prices rise during minting.
  * Possible transaction failures if the price increases beyond the user’s budget, wasting gas.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a lack of slippage protection in a mint function that uses a dynamic pricing formula. The contract calculates the price of each NFT inside a loop based on the current generation mint count, and it re‑evaluates that price for every iteration without fixing a maximum acceptable price or total cost before the transaction starts. Because the price can increase between the moment a user estimates the cost off‑chain and the moment the transaction is mined, the user may end up receiving fewer NFTs than expected or paying a higher average price per NFT. The root cause is the combination of a per‑mint price recomputation and the absence of any constraint on how much the price may change during execution. An attacker, or simply another participant, can mint a number of NFTs just before the victim’s transaction is included, causing the price to rise. When the victim’s transaction finally executes, the loop sees the higher price, consumes the supplied budget more quickly, and stops minting early. The impact is that users see a shortfall in the number of tokens they receive, a higher effective price per token, and in some cases a transaction failure if the budget is exhausted before the desired amount is minted, resulting in wasted gas. This situation occurs whenever the mint function is called with a budget that assumes a static price, especially for large batch mints or during periods of high demand when many participants are minting concurrently. The affected parties are the end‑users who expect a certain quantity of NFTs for a given amount of ETH, as well as the protocol’s reputation because users may perceive the contract as unfair or deceptive. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the minting loop and simulated a scenario where another user mints before the victim, revealing that the contract does not enforce any slippage limit. The problem can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it simply delivers fewer tokens than the user anticipated, which may only be observed after the UI displays the final token count. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are a mismatch between the expected and actual number of NFTs, a small leftover ETH balance, and an average price per NFT that is higher than the quoted price. This bug belongs to the class of dynamic‑pricing without slippage guard vulnerabilities, a form of front‑running or price‑manipulation risk. The recommended remediation is to add slippage protection: compute the total cost for the desired quantity before entering the loop, enforce a maximum acceptable price per token, or lock the price for the entire transaction, thereby preventing price drift during execution.

title: Incorrect check against golden entropy value in the first two batches
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect validation of a special "golden entropy" value during the generation of the first two batches of entropy slots. In the contract each uint256 storage slot holds thirteen concatenated entropy values, and the protocol specification states that the golden entropy value 999999 must never appear in the first two passes; it is only allowed to be inserted deliberately in the final pass. The implementation of writeEntropyBatch1 (and the analogous writeEntropyBatch2) attempts to enforce this rule with a require statement that checks the entire slot value against 999999. Because the slot contains thirteen separate entropies, the check only rejects a slot when the whole 256‑bit number equals 999999, which never happens. Consequently a slot that contains the forbidden value in any of its thirteen sub‑fields – for example a slot whose decimal representation ends with ...999999123345 – passes the require and is written to storage. This mismatch between the specification and the code allows the golden entropy to be recorded early, violating the intended rarity guarantees. An attacker can trigger the batch‑write functions repeatedly; when a pseudo‑random slot happens to embed the golden value, the contract does not revert, so the golden entity becomes available in the first two passes. The impact is that users may receive the overpowered "Golden God" entity far earlier than expected, breaking game balance, giving unfair advantage, and potentially distorting token‑economics that rely on the rarity of that entity. The condition occurs whenever the batch initialization functions are called, which is part of normal game setup, and therefore affects any player, the protocol’s economic model, and developers who assume the documented rarity. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the reviewer compared the documented rule with the source code and noticed that the validation was performed on the aggregate slot rather than on each individual entropy. The bug is subtle because the slot is a large number and the forbidden pattern can be hidden among other digits, making it difficult to detect through simple testing or log inspection. The recommended remediation is to decompose the slot into its thirteen constituent entropy values and assert that none of them equals 999999 before storing the slot, or to generate and validate each entropy separately and then pack them. This type of flaw belongs to the class of improper validation of composite data structures, often described as a partial‑value check or aggregate‑value validation error. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a player expects the rare golden entity to appear only at the final stage, but instead sees it immediately after starting the game, leading to confusion such as "I got the top‑tier character right away, is this a bug?" The discrepancy between expected rarity and actual occurrence highlights the underlying validation mistake.

title: TraitForgeNft: Generations without a golden god are possible
description: The golden god is the special entropy of 999,999. This entropy is set at `slotIndexSelectionPoint` and `numberIndexSelectionPoint` [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/EntropyGenerator/EntropyGenerator.sol#L19-L20). These are in the third part of the entropy list. When forging two NFTs it increases the current generations [`generationMintCounts`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/TraitForgeNft/TraitForgeNft.sol#L45). This means that less NFTs of that generation can be minted, as there are only 10,000 NFTs per generation. Therefore, the golden god might not be reached and no golden god for that generation exists.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the guarantee that each generation of TraitForgeNft NFTs will contain a unique "golden god" token, defined by a special entropy value of 999,999 that is stored at fixed positions called slotIndexSelectionPoint and numberIndexSelectionPoint in the entropy list. The contract tracks how many NFTs have been minted for a given generation through the generationMintCounts mapping, which is capped at 10,000 tokens per generation. Because the golden god’s entropy appears at a predetermined index that can be far behind the start of the list, the contract does not enforce that the golden god must be minted before the generation limit is reached. When users mint or, more importantly, forge NFTs, the generation count is increased without checking whether the golden god has already been created. Consequently, if enough NFTs are minted or forged before the entropy list reaches the golden god slot, the generation can become fully minted (10,000 tokens) while the golden god never materialises. This situation can be reproduced by first minting all tokens of generation one, forging them, then minting a small number of generation two tokens and forging the remaining generation‑one tokens, after which the second generation reaches its cap without ever encountering the golden god entropy. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a generation finishes with the expected number of NFTs but the promised rare "golden god" never appears; users who expected to receive or trade a golden god receive nothing, and the perceived rarity of the collection is broken. The impact is primarily economic and reputational: collectors may feel misled, secondary‑market values can drop, and the protocol’s marketing claim of a guaranteed special token per generation is violated. The flaw is subtle because the contract does not emit any warning or revert when the last token of a generation is minted, making the absence of the golden god only visible after the generation is exhausted. The issue was discovered during a formal audit that exercised extreme mint‑and‑forge sequences to exhaust the entropy list. To remediate, the minting and forging logic should include a guard that checks whether the golden god has been minted before allowing the final token of a generation to be created; if it has not, the transaction should revert or the contract should reserve the last slot for the golden god, ensuring that the special token is always minted within the generation’s supply limit. This change would transform the bug from a silent rarity violation into a deterministic guarantee aligned with the protocol’s stated business logic.

title: Discrepancy between nfts minted, price of nft when a generation changes & position of `_incrementGeneration`
description:
The report covers two bugs:

  * User pays the maximum price of the last generation when minting the 1st nft of the next generation.
  * Wrong positioning of `_incrementGeneration()` will lead to the user paying the starting price of 1st nft of `generation 1` even when the nft being minted is the 1st nft of a `different generation`.
bug_full: The contract implements a generational pricing scheme where each generation of NFTs has a fixed start price that increases by a per‑generation increment and, within a generation, each additional token raises the price by a per‑token increment. The vulnerability consists of two intertwined logical errors. First, the price‑calculation function uses the current generation’s mint count to compute the price even when the mint operation is about to cross the boundary to the next generation. Because the generation counter is incremented only after the price is read, the first token of a new generation is priced with the maximum price of the previous generation instead of the intended lower start price plus the per‑generation increment. Second, the internal mint routine increments the generation counter after updating the token identifier and mint count, but the check that triggers the increment is placed before the token‑id increment in one path and after in another, causing the mint count for the new generation to be incorrectly set to one while the price calculation still references the old generation’s count. The root cause is a misplaced call to the generation‑increment function and a price‑oracle that does not account for the generation transition. An attacker (or any user) can exploit this by simply minting the first NFT of a new generation, paying a price that is up to the maximum of the previous generation – a loss of several hundredths of ether per token. The impact is monetary over‑charging of users and a deviation from the economic model described in the whitepaper, potentially eroding trust and reducing revenue for the protocol. The bug manifests only when a generation reaches its maximum token supply and a new generation is about to start; it does not affect earlier mints within a generation. All participants who interact with the mint function – end‑users, the protocol’s revenue model, and any downstream contracts that rely on the pricing logic – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the on‑chain price calculation against the documented pricing schedule and observed a discrepancy at the generation boundary. It is subtle because the contract’s state updates appear correct at a glance, and the price function is read‑only, so the over‑charge is not obvious without tracing the exact order of state changes. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting or pricing logic errors caused by incorrect state transition ordering. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a normal mint button, but the amount of ether required suddenly spikes, leading to a situation where the user expects to pay a small price for the first token of a new generation but is charged a much larger amount, sometimes resulting in a failed transaction or an unexpected loss of funds. The correct fix is to reorder the generation increment so that it occurs before the price is calculated for the next mint, and to adjust the price‑calculation function to reference the upcoming generation’s start price when the mint count for the current generation is zero. This aligns the on‑chain price with the intended economic model and prevents users from being over‑charged at generation boundaries.

title: Lack of ability to make an some external function calls makes the DAO stage unreachable
description:
Switching to DAO phase in `NukeFund` is not possible. This vulnerability is on the boundary of scope because it makes it impossible to use the out-of-scope contract but the problem is in the contact inside the scope that is the owner of this external contract.

The `TraitForgeNft` contract is written in such a way that it can add and remove users from the airdrop. For this the NFT contract must have ownership over the airdrop contract.

Because of this, an additional function is created in `TraitForgeNft` to start the airdrop while other functions that can only be called by the owner (`setTraitToken`, `allowDaoFund`) are absent in `TraitForgeNft` contract. Which makes these functions impossible to call.

The first function may not be necessary (deployer can call it at deploy), but the second function must have its own handle in the `TraitForgeNft` contract since this function is used by `NukeFund` and can only be called after the start of the airdrop; that is, after the transfer of ownership to the `TraitForgeNft` contract.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing delegation path that prevents the DAO funding stage of the NukeFund workflow from ever being reached. In the system, the Airdrop contract is transferred to the ownership of the TraitForgeNft contract, and only the owner of Airdrop is allowed to invoke the external function allowDaoFund(). This function is required by NukeFund to signal that the DAO may receive its share of the developer funds after the airdrop has started. However, TraitForgeNft does not expose any public or external method that forwards a call to Airdrop.allowDaoFund(). As a result, when NukeFund executes its third‑stage distribution logic, the condition airdropContract.daoFundAllowed() is never true, causing the branch that would send the developer share to the DAO address to be skipped. Instead, the contract either sends the funds to the contract owner or leaves them unallocated, depending on the earlier branch. The root cause is a design oversight: the owner contract (TraitForgeNft) was written to manage airdrop start and user lists but omitted the delegate handle for the DAO‑funding function, even though the function is essential for the downstream NukeFund contract. The issue can be exploited indirectly: any participant expecting the DAO to receive its allocated ETH will see the allocation missing, and the DAO will never receive its share, breaking the intended economic model. The impact is a misallocation of developer revenue, potential loss of trust in the protocol, and funds that appear to “disappear” from the DAO’s perspective. The problem manifests after the airdrop has been started and ownership of the Airdrop contract has been transferred to TraitForgeNft, i.e., during the NukeFund’s dev‑share distribution phase. All parties that rely on the DAO receiving funds—protocol developers, DAO participants, and token holders—are affected. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit when the test suite attempted to call Airdrop.allowDaoFund() through the expected delegation path and found no callable function, confirming that the DAO stage is unreachable. Because the contract does not revert or emit an error, the missing call can be subtle and may only be noticed when the DAO balance remains zero despite successful airdrop execution. To remediate, the TraitForgeNft contract should implement a thin wrapper function, e.g., allowDaoFund(), that is restricted to the owner and forwards the call to the Airdrop contract. This restores the intended control flow, allowing NukeFund to detect that the DAO fund is allowed and to transfer the appropriate share. Conceptually, the fix re‑establishes the missing delegation link between the owner contract and the external DAO‑funding function, aligning the contract’s behavior with its business logic and accounting assumptions.

title: `Golden God` tokens can be minted twice per generation
description: The current implementation of the EntropyGenerator contract allows for the possibility of having two “Golden God” tokens (tokens with an entropy value of 999999) per generation. This duplicity undermines the intended uniqueness and rarity of the Golden God token, potentially disrupting the game’s economy and fairness. The predictability of one Golden God token, combined with the chance of a second one, could lead to exploitation and loss of player trust.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the possibility that two distinct “Golden God” tokens – defined by an entropy value of 999999 – can be minted within the same generation of the EntropyGenerator contract. The root cause is that the contract contains two independent pathways that can produce the exact same entropy value. The first pathway is a hard‑coded check in the private getEntropy function that returns 999999 when the slotIndex and numberIndex match a predefined selection point. The second pathway is the regular entropy calculation performed during a writeEntropyBatch3 call, where the slot value is divided and modulo‑ed to obtain a six‑digit number; if the underlying slot value happens to be chosen such that the resulting six‑digit number equals 999999, the same “Golden God” token is emitted again. Because the contract does not keep any state indicating that a Golden God token has already been issued for the current generation, the second pathway can succeed even after the predetermined token has been minted. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately crafting a batch write that inserts a slot value yielding 999999 after the initial token has been created, thereby forcing the contract to mint a second token of identical rarity. The impact is a breach of the intended uniqueness and scarcity of the Golden God token, which undermines the game’s economic model, allows a malicious actor to obtain an extra high‑value NFT, and can erode player trust in the fairness of the system. The condition occurs whenever a generation includes the predefined selection point and a subsequent writeEntropyBatch3 operation writes a slot that evaluates to the same six‑digit maximum. All participants who rely on the rarity guarantee – players, token holders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the token’s rarity is a core part of its value proposition. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the logic of getEntropy and the batch write function were examined side‑by‑side and the lack of a guard flag was noted. The bug can be hard to notice in normal operation because the duplicate token may appear only rarely, and the two code paths look unrelated; without explicit checks, the system silently violates its own accounting rules. To remediate, the contract should maintain a per‑generation boolean flag (or similar state) that records whether a Golden God token has already been minted and reject any further attempts to produce the 999999 entropy value. Alternatively, the entropy calculation could be adjusted to exclude the maximum value after the predetermined token is issued. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a player who expects only one “Golden God” NFT per generation may see two such NFTs appear in their wallet, leading to confusion and the perception that the game is unfair or possibly manipulated. This class of bug falls under duplicate‑unique‑token or double‑mint vulnerabilities, where insufficient uniqueness enforcement allows the same scarce asset to be created more than once, breaking business logic that assumes a single instance per epoch.

title: Imprecise token age calculation results in an incorrect nuke factor, causing users to claim the wrong amount
bug_full: The vulnerability is an imprecise token age calculation in the NukeFund contract. The function calculateAge determines the age of a token by first converting the time difference between the current block timestamp and the token creation timestamp into whole days using integer division (seconds / 60 / 60 / 24). Because Solidity performs integer division, any time difference smaller than one full day is truncated to zero, causing the variable daysOld to be zero. The subsequent formula multiplies daysOld by a performance factor, a denominator and an age multiplier, and then divides by 365. When daysOld is zero, the entire age value becomes zero, which is then used as the nuke factor for the claim calculation. As a result, the claim amount that a token holder can withdraw is dramatically lower than the amount dictated by the intended economic model; in extreme cases the claim may be zero. The bug manifests whenever a token is claimed within less than a full day after its creation, or whenever the time delta is small enough that the integer division rounds down to zero. Users experience the symptom of receiving less funds than expected, sometimes seeing a claim amount that is zero despite having a valid token. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a test comparing the current implementation with a precision‑preserving version showed an 11 % discrepancy in the computed age, leading to a proportionally larger nuke factor. The problem is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings about zero age, and the loss appears as a gradual under‑payment rather than an outright failure. The root cause is the order of operations: dividing before multiplying loses precision. The correct approach is to perform the multiplication first and only divide by the full denominator (seconds per year) after the product, preserving fractional days. Fixing the calculation restores the intended proportional claim amount and prevents users from losing funds due to rounding errors. This class of bug is a typical precision loss caused by premature integer division in financial formulas, often referred to as a rounding or truncation error.

title: Duplicate NFT generation via repeated forging with the same parent
description:
It is possible to get the same NFT (same generation, same entropy) when the forging is done with the same `parentId` multiple times. Although the number of times this action will be feasible is limited with the forging potential of the token it can still occur at least once.

Scenario:

  1. User A lists his/her NFT for forging.
  2. User B forges his/her NFT with the NFT from User A.
  3. The new NFT is created with the combined properties of the NFT1 and NFT2.
  4. User A lists his/her NFT for forging again.
  5. User B forges his/her NFT with the NFT from User A again.
  6. The NFT will be of the same generation and will have the same entropy as the one forged before.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a duplicate‑NFT generation flaw that occurs when the forging function of the TraitForge protocol is invoked multiple times with the same pair of parent tokens. The contract combines the entropy values of two NFTs by averaging them and assigns the result to a newly minted token of the next generation. Because the contract does not keep any record of which parent pairs have already been used, a user can list the same parent token for forging again and combine it with the same partner token, producing a new token that has exactly the same generation number and the same entropy value as the previously forged token. This happens whenever a parent token is relisted after a successful forge and the same partner token is supplied; the only limiting factor is the remaining forging potential of the tokens, but at least one duplicate can be created. The root cause is the absence of a uniqueness check for forged token pairs, meaning the protocol assumes that each forge operation is inherently unique, which is not enforced by the code. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly forging the same pair, thereby inflating the supply of NFTs that are supposed to be unique, breaking the scarcity model, and potentially manipulating market prices or reward calculations that depend on token rarity. From a user’s perspective the symptom is the appearance of two distinct token IDs that exhibit identical visual traits, entropy, and generation, contrary to the expectation that each forged NFT should be unique. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit when a test case demonstrated that the contract emitted the expected events for a second forge using the same parent, confirming that the duplicate was minted without any error. The bug is subtle because the contract’s normal event flow does not flag the duplication, and the UI may simply display another token entry, making it easy to overlook. To remediate the problem, the contract should maintain a mapping of already‑forged unordered token pairs (for example using keccak256 of the sorted IDs) and add a require statement that rejects any forge attempt involving a pair that has been used before. After a successful forge, the pair should be recorded in the mapping to prevent future duplicates. This change restores the intended uniqueness guarantee, aligns the protocol’s accounting with its business logic, and protects users from receiving duplicate NFTs that could devalue their collections.

title: NFTs mature too slowly under default settings.
description:
The Nuke Fund accumulates ETH from new mints and economic activity. After a 3-day maturity period, anyone can nuke their entity to claim a share of the ETH in the Fund. Every entity has a parameter, called `initialNukeFactor`, set on mint which represents how much of the Fund can be claimed on nuke. The maximum total `nukeFactor` is 50%, expressed as `50_000`.

The calculations of `finalNukeFactor` consist of `adjustedAge`, `defaultNukeFactorIncrease` and `initialNukeFactor`.

[NukeFund.sol#L145-L148](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L145-L148)
    
    uint256 initialNukeFactor = entropy / 40; // calculate initalNukeFactor based on entropy, 5 digits
    uint256 finalNukeFactor = ((adjustedAge * defaultNukeFactorIncrease) /
      MAX_DENOMINATOR) + initialNukeFactor;

The age is calculated via `calculateAge()` function.

[NukeFund.sol#L121-L131](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-traitforge/blob/279b2887e3d38bc219a05d332cbcb0655b2dc644/contracts/NukeFund/NukeFund.sol#L121-L131)
    
    uint256 daysOld = (block.timestamp -
      nftContract.getTokenCreationTimestamp(tokenId)) /
      60 /
      60 /
      24;
    uint256 perfomanceFactor = nftContract.getTokenEntropy(tokenId) % 10;
    uint256 age = (daysOld *
      perfomanceFactor *
      MAX_DENOMINATOR *
      ageMultiplier) / 365; // add 5 digits for decimals

The idea behind age calculations is quite simple: we calculate how many days have passed since token creation and convert that into years.

However, the default value of the `nukeFactorIncrease` set to 250 is extremely low. While [whitepaper](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1pihtkKyyxobFWdaNU4YfAy56Q7WIMbFJjSHUAfRm6BA) mentions that the fastest maturing NFT should mature (reach `nukeFactor` of `50_000`) in around 30 days and the slowest in 600 days, in reality it would take 4050 days for the best possible NFT to fully mature.

To showcase this let’s do some math:

To mature NFT must reach `finalNukeFactor` of `50_000`, the best possible NFT would have 25000 `initialNukeFactor` and `performanceFactor` of 9. 

  * `defaultNukeFactor` is set to 250
  * `finalNukeFactor = adjustedAge * defaultNukeFactorIncrease + initialNukeFactor`
  * `50000 = x * 250 + 25000`
  * `25000 = 250x`
  * `x = 100`
  * `adjustedAge = daysOld * performanceFactor / 365`
  * `100 = x * 9 / 365`
  * `9x = 100 * 365`
  * `x = 365000 / 9 = 4055`

For the best NFT to mature fully in 30 days, the `defaultNukeFactor` would need to be 135 times bigger, more precisely `33750`.

NFTs mature extremely slowly with default settings, to the point where `performanceFactor` of an NFT does not play any role and `finalNukeFactor` is determined solely by the `initialNukeFactor`.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mis‑parameterisation of the NFT maturity algorithm in the NukeFund contract. The contract calculates a final nuke factor that determines how much of the accumulated ETH a token holder can claim after a maturity period. The formula combines an adjusted age component with a default nuke‑factor increase and an initial nuke factor set at mint time. Because the defaultNukeFactorIncrease variable is hard‑coded to the very low value 250, the adjusted age contribution grows far slower than intended. Even the best possible NFT – one with the maximum initialNukeFactor (≈25 000) and the highest performanceFactor (9) – would need roughly 4 050 days to reach the maximum allowed nukeFactor of 50 000, whereas the protocol’s whitepaper states that full maturity should be achievable in about 30 days for the fastest NFTs and up to 600 days for the slowest. The root cause is therefore an incorrect constant that throttles the rate at which the adjusted age term adds to the final nuke factor, effectively rendering the performanceFactor irrelevant and making maturity depend almost entirely on the initialNukeFactor. An attacker does not need to exploit a code flaw; they simply wait, but users experience a severe mismatch between expected and actual returns. From a user’s perspective, after the advertised 30‑day period the UI still shows a near‑zero increase in claimable share, leading to confusion, disappointment, and the perception that funds have disappeared. The impact is that token holders receive far less ETH than promised, undermining the economic incentives of the protocol and potentially eroding trust. The issue manifests whenever the contract is deployed with the default settings and the ageMultiplier remains at its default of 1, affecting all NFT owners, the protocol’s revenue distribution, and any parties relying on the fund’s payout schedule. It was discovered during a formal audit and reproduced with a Foundry test that measured the nuke factor after 30 days and after 4 000 days, confirming the extreme slowdown. The bug is hard to notice because the arithmetic itself is correct; only the magnitude of the constant is wrong, which only becomes apparent over long time horizons. To remediate, the defaultNukeFactorIncrease should be increased to a value that aligns with the whitepaper’s maturity targets – at least 33 750 – or the formula should be redesigned to correctly scale the adjusted age contribution. Adjusting this parameter restores the intended business logic that NFTs mature within the promised 30‑600‑day window, ensuring that users receive the expected share of the fund and that the protocol’s accounting assumptions hold true.

title: Pause and unpause functions are inaccessible
description:
All in-scope contracts of TraitForge inherit from the [Pausable contract of OpenZeppelin](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/utils/Pausable.sol), a feature designed to allow the pausing and unpausing of contract functionalities in emergency situations or for maintenance. However, (parent) contracts do not expose the `_pause()` and `_unpause()` functions and the Pausable contract contains only internal pausing/unpausing functions.

As a result, despite inheriting the pausability feature, administrators are unable to utilize these critical controls to pause or resume the contract’s operations when needed, potentially leading to issues during periods requiring immediate intervention.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a missing external control for the pause mechanism in contracts that inherit OpenZeppelin's Pausable module. Although the contracts correctly inherit the internal _pause() and _unpause() functions and use the whenNotPaused modifier on critical functions, they never expose any public or external function that calls these internal methods. As a result, the designated administrator (typically the contract owner or an authorized role) cannot trigger a pause or resume operation, even in emergencies such as a discovered exploit or required maintenance. The root cause is a design oversight: the parent contracts expose only the internal hooks and omit a wrapper like pause() or unpause() guarded by an onlyOwner modifier. Exploitation is not a direct attack but rather a denial of defensive capability; an attacker who discovers a vulnerability can continue to interact with the contract because the legitimate operators are unable to halt activity. This leads to potential financial loss, continued state changes, and erosion of user trust, especially when users expect that the protocol can be paused to protect their assets. The issue manifests whenever the contract’s functions are guarded by whenNotPaused and the operators attempt to call a pause function that does not exist, resulting in no state change and no emitted Paused event. All users, token holders, and the protocol itself are affected because the safety valve is effectively disabled. The problem was identified during a manual audit that inspected inheritance hierarchies and noted the absence of public pause/unpause wrappers despite the presence of the Pausable base. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors and the Pausable logic appears to be present, giving a false sense of security. To remediate, the contracts should implement public pause() and unpause() functions that invoke the internal _pause() and _unpause() methods and restrict access to the contract owner or a designated role, thereby restoring the intended emergency stop capability and aligning the implementation with the business logic that assumes the ability to halt operations when needed.

title: Forger Entities can forge more times than intended
description:
As per [the docs](https://github.com/TraitForge/GitBook/blob/main/TraitForger%20Entity/Forge%20Potential%20.md):

> Entities’ Forge Potential is determined by the [5] digit in entropy. Each entity may have the ability to forge 0-9 times depending on its Forge Potential.

This means an entity with `forgePotential of 0` is infertile, an entity with `forgePotential = 1` can forge 1 time a year, an entity with `forgePotential = 2` can forge 2 times a year and so on.

The number of times an entity forges is tracked in the `forgingCounts` mapping. This mapping is incremented for both the `forgerTokenId` and `mergerTokenId` every time a successful forging happens thru `forgeWithListed`.

The `forgingCounts[]` of `mergerTokenIds` is handled correctly. The increment of `forgingCounts[]` precedes the condition check:
    
        forgingCounts[mergerTokenId]++;
            require(mergerForgePotential > 0 &&
        		        forgingCounts[mergerTokenId] <= mergerForgePotential,
        			      'forgePotential insufficient'
        );

However, Forger Entities `forgerTokenId` are able to exceed the forging limit due to increment of `forgingCounts[]` happening after the condition check. The check is made during the `listForForging` call, but the `forgingCounts[]` mapping is only incremented during `forgeWithListed` call. This allows the ‘Forger Entities’ to list one more time than intended.

This results in each Forger entity with non-zero `forgingPotential` having the ability to forge 2-10 times, instead of 1-9 times intended by the protocol.

As long as Forger Entities have a non-zero `forgingPotential`, the Entity is able to exceed the limit intended by `forgingPotential`.
poc:
Assume a Forger Entity of:
    
           _tokenIds = 123 
           forgingPotential = 1 (extracted from the 5th digit of entropy).
           Initial forgingCounts for tokenId 1 is 0.

**First Listing:**

  * During listing: `forgingCounts[123] = 0`
  * Check: `forgingCounts[123] <= forgePotential (0 <= 1)` => Pass
  * During forging: `forgingCounts[123]++` => 1 (during forging)

**Second Listing:**

  * During listing: `forgingCounts[123] = 1`
  * Check: `forgingCounts[123] <= forgePotential (1 <= 1)` => Pass
  * During forging: `forgingCounts[123]++` => 2

**Third Listing: (Reverts only at the third attempt)**

  * During listing: `forgingCounts[123] = 2` (during listing)
  * Check: `forgingCounts[123] < forgePotential (2 <= 1)` => Fail
  * During forging: forging does not proceed.

This shows a Forger Entity with a `forgingPotential` of 1 can forge 2 times. Similarly, a forger entity with `forgingPotential` of 9 can forge 10 times.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one logic error in the forging workflow of TraitForge entities. Each forger entity has a "forgePotential" value derived from entropy that is supposed to limit the number of times the entity can be used to forge per year – for example a potential of 1 should allow exactly one successful forge, a potential of 2 should allow two, and so on up to nine. The contract tracks how many times an entity has been used in a mapping called forgingCounts. For merger entities the count is incremented before the limit check, so the require statement correctly prevents exceeding the allowed number. For forger entities, however, the count is only incremented after the limit check, which is performed during the listForForging call. Because the check uses a "<=" comparison, the contract permits one additional listing before the count is finally incremented during forgeWithListed. Consequently a forger with a non‑zero forgePotential can be listed and forged one more time than the protocol specification permits. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the ordering of state updates and the condition logic. It is subtle because the increment occurs in a different function, making the off‑by‑one condition easy to overlook during casual testing. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that the entity has not yet reached its limit, and the user expects the forge operation to fail after the advertised number of uses, but instead the transaction succeeds an extra time, resulting in unexpected additional tokens or assets being minted. This violates the economic assumptions of the protocol, potentially inflating supply and giving unfair advantage to entities that can exceed their limit. The issue affects all forger entities with a forgePotential greater than zero, and therefore impacts any participant relying on the intended scarcity model. The recommended fix is to change the condition to a strict "<" comparison (forgingCounts[tokenId] < forgePotential) or to move the increment before the check so that the count accurately reflects the number of already‑performed forges. Implementing the fix restores the intended one‑to‑one relationship between forgePotential and actual forge operations, preventing unintended extra minting and preserving protocol integrity.

title: Users’ ability to nuke will be DoSed for three days after putting NFTs up for sale and canceling the sale
description: Users will not be able to nuke their NFTs for three days after canceling sale of their NFTs.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the reward‑claiming (nuke) mechanism of an NFT marketplace that requires a token holder to have possessed the token for at least three days before invoking the nuke function. The contract implements a hook called _beforeTokenTransfer that records the block timestamp of the last transfer in a mapping called lastTokenTransferredTimestamp. When a user lists an NFT for sale, the token is transferred to an internal EntityTrading contract; if the user later cancels the sale, the token is transferred back to the original owner. Because the hook unconditionally updates the timestamp whenever the from and to addresses differ, the transfer back from EntityTrading to the owner overwrites the previous timestamp even though ownership never truly changed from the user’s perspective. The nuke function later checks this timestamp to enforce the three‑day holding period, so the reset forces the user to wait another three days before they can claim the reward. This bug is triggered only when a token is listed for sale and the listing is cancelled, i.e., when the token moves through the EntityTrading contract. It affects any NFT holder who relies on the nuke reward, causing them to lose expected earnings or be forced to wait longer than the protocol’s advertised rules. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the transfer hook and its interaction with the sale‑cancellation flow. It is subtle because the transfer appears legitimate and the timestamp update is a common pattern, making the unintended side‑effect easy to overlook. Conceptually, the problem belongs to the class of state‑reset bugs caused by overly broad token‑transfer hooks that do not distinguish between user‑initiated transfers and internal bookkeeping moves. From a user’s point of view the UI may show that the NFT is eligible for nuke after three days, but after cancelling a sale the nuke button remains disabled and the transaction reverts, contradicting the expectation that the reward should be claimable. The business logic that “ownership for three days yields a reward” is violated because the contract mistakenly treats the internal transfer as a loss of continuous ownership. The recommended mitigation is to add explicit checks in _beforeTokenTransfer so that timestamps are not refreshed when the transfer involves the EntityTrading contract or when the transfer is part of a listing cancellation, thereby preserving the original holding period. Implementing these checks restores the intended accounting invariant and ensures that users receive rewards according to the protocol’s published rules.

title: There is no slippage check in the `nuke
description: NFT owners may receive significantly less nuke funds than they expected.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing slippage or minimum‑claim check in the contract function that distributes ETH to NFT owners when they invoke the nuke() operation. The function computes the amount a caller can receive by multiplying the current fund balance by a per‑token nuke factor and then subtracts that amount from the shared pool. Because the calculation uses the live fund value without enforcing a lower bound, a later transaction can consume a large portion of the pool before an earlier‑submitted transaction is executed, causing the earlier caller to receive only a fraction of the amount they expected. This situation arises from the root cause that the contract does not lock the fund amount at the moment a claim is initiated and does not verify that the resulting claim meets a minimum threshold. An attacker, or simply the natural nondeterministic ordering of transactions in the sequencer, can submit a competing nuke() call that is processed first; the first call drains a substantial part of the pool, and the second call, which may have been submitted earlier, ends up receiving a reduced payout (for example, a user expecting 5 ETH receives only 2.5 ETH). The impact is a financial loss for the affected NFT holder, who sees a smaller balance transferred to their address, potentially losing up to 50 % of the anticipated reward. The issue manifests whenever multiple NFT owners try to claim from the same fund in a short time window, especially when the fund size is limited and the nuke factor is high. It affects all participants who hold claim‑eligible NFTs, undermines the protocol’s fairness guarantees, and can erode user trust because the UI will show a successful claim transaction but the received amount will be far lower than the displayed estimate. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that simulated two competing claims and observed the discrepancy in the received ETH. It can be hard to notice because the contract emits a successful claim event and the transaction does not revert; only a careful comparison of expected versus actual payouts reveals the shortfall. To remediate, the contract should introduce a minimum‑claim amount validation (a slippage guard) that reverts the transaction if the computed claim falls below a reasonable threshold, or alternatively snapshot the fund balance at the start of the claim and allocate a fixed share per token, thereby preventing later transactions from reducing earlier expectations. This class of bug is commonly known as a slippage or front‑running‑prone payout calculation flaw, where the lack of a guard allows ordering attacks to diminish user rewards.

title: Incorrect `isApprovedForAll` check in the `NukeFund.nuke
description: Approved users can’t nuke the owner’s NFT.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the access‑control check of the NukeFund.nuke function. The function is intended to allow a caller who is either the token owner or an operator approved for all to trigger a burn of the specified ERC‑721 token. To enforce this, the code first calls nftContract.isApprovedOrOwner(msg.sender, tokenId), which correctly verifies that the caller is the owner or an approved operator. The second require statement is supposed to ensure that the NukeFund contract itself is authorized to transfer the token, either because it is the explicit approved address for the token or because the token owner has granted it an operator‑for‑all approval. However, the implementation mistakenly checks nftContract.isApprovedForAll(msg.sender, address(this)) – it asks whether the caller (msg.sender) has set an approval‑for‑all for the NukeFund contract. In the typical use case, the caller is an operator, not the token owner, so this condition is false even when the token owner has correctly approved the NukeFund contract. As a result, the transaction reverts with the message "Contract must be approved to transfer the NFT" despite the caller being legitimately authorized. The bug belongs to the class of incorrect authorization checks, where the wrong principal is queried for a permission, leading to a denial‑of‑service for approved users. Exploitation consists of an approved operator attempting to nuke a token and being blocked, which prevents the intended burning of the NFT and can leave the token permanently locked in the contract, effectively freezing any associated value or refund mechanism. The issue manifests whenever a user who is not the token owner but has been granted operator rights calls the nuke function; it does not depend on token state beyond standard ERC‑721 ownership. The affected parties are token owners, approved operators, and any protocol component that relies on the ability to destroy NFTs for fund reclamation or state cleanup. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the control flow of the nuke function and comparing it with the ERC‑721 internal approval logic. It can be hard to notice because the first require passes, giving the impression that the caller is correctly authorized, and the error only surfaces at the second check, which may be overlooked during manual testing. The correct fix is to replace the faulty isApprovedForAll call with nftContract.isApprovedForAll(nftContract.ownerOf(tokenId), address(this)), thereby checking that the token owner, not the caller, has granted the contract operator rights. This aligns the check with the ERC‑721 specification and restores the intended functionality, allowing approved operators to successfully trigger a burn and preventing unintended token lockup.

title: Excess ETH from `forgingFee` can get stuck in `EntityForging` under certain situations
description: ETH being permanently locked in the contract under certain situations.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the EntityForging contract accepts a forging fee that can be higher than the required amount and does not return the surplus, causing the extra ETH to become permanently locked in the contract. This occurs because the function that processes the forging payment only checks that the sent value is at least the required fee, but it does not enforce equality nor includes logic to refund any excess. An attacker or any user can exploit the bug by deliberately sending more ether than the fee, for example by calling forgeWithListed with a value of 1.1 ETH when the fee is 1 ETH. The contract records the payment, completes the forging operation, and retains the 0.1 ETH in its balance because there is no subsequent transfer back to msg.sender. The impact is a value leak: the protocol loses the overpaid ether permanently, reducing available funds and potentially affecting the economic incentives of the system. The condition under which this happens is when the caller overpays the forging fee, which may occur unintentionally due to UI rounding errors or intentionally as an attack. Users are affected because they expect to pay exactly the listed fee and to receive any change, but instead see their wallet balance reduced by the excess amount with no refund; from a UI perspective the transaction appears successful and the forged entity is created, yet the user’s ether disappears. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case deliberately sent an overpayment and observed that the EntityForging contract balance increased by the surplus amount. The bug is subtle because the contract still performs its primary function correctly, so the extra ether can be overlooked unless balances are audited. The vulnerability belongs to the class of incorrect payment handling or unrefunded overpayment bugs, where a contract fails to enforce exact payment or to return change. To remediate, the contract should either require the caller to send exactly the fee amount or, if overpayment is allowed, calculate the surplus and transfer it back to the sender immediately after the forging operation. Implementing such a check restores the intended accounting invariants and prevents ether from becoming permanently locked.

title: Each generation should have 1 “Golden God” NFT, but there could be 0
poc:
1. 10,000 NFTs get minted in a generation, so it’s time to increment to the next generation.
2. `TraitForgeNft` contract increments generation and calls the `initializeAlphaIndices` to set the location of the “Golden God”.
3. “Golden God” entropy is set in the last slot (770th), in the last 10 entropy slots.
4. The “Golden God” NFT is not mintable, as there needs to be more than 10,000 mints in the generation, which is not possible.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract selects the location of the special “Golden God” NFT for each generation. A pseudo‑random hash is used to compute a slot index as (hash % 258) + 512, which yields values from 512 up to 769, and a number index as hash % 13, which yields values from 0 to 12. The protocol stores entropies in a fixed‑size array of 770 slots, each holding 13 entropies, but only the first 10,000 entropies (the first 770 slots with the first four entries of the last slot) are actually mintable before the generation is incremented. Because the selection logic does not verify that the chosen entropy falls within the mintable range, a combination where the slot index equals 769 (the final slot) and the number index is greater than 3 points to one of the last ten entropies that are never minted. When the generation reaches its maximum mint count of 10,000, the contract automatically increments to the next generation and calls the initialization function, locking in the out‑of‑range selection. As a result, the “Golden God” NFT for that generation becomes permanently unmintable, violating the documented guarantee that each generation must contain exactly one such NFT. The bug is essentially an off‑by‑one or boundary‑condition error in the random index calculation. It can be triggered naturally by the modulo operation; no attacker needs to manipulate the hash. When it occurs, users see the generation end without receiving the expected rare token, leading to confusion or disappointment. The impact is limited to the loss of a unique, high‑value NFT; the total supply of 10,000 tokens per generation remains unchanged, but the rarity distribution is altered, potentially affecting the perceived fairness and economic value of the collection. The issue manifests only when the generation is full and the random selection lands on the disallowed region, making it rare and easy to miss during testing. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by comparing the implementation against the protocol’s documentation and noticing that the slot calculation could exceed the usable range. The bug is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an error and the UI simply proceeds to the next generation, giving the impression that everything worked as intended. The recommended mitigation is to add a boundary check that rejects or re‑rolls selections that would place the “Golden God” in the last slot beyond the first four positions, or to adjust the slot calculation to exclude the final slot entirely. In generic terms, this is a boundary‑condition error that leads to an unmintable special asset, often described as an “out‑of‑range entropy placement” or “lost guaranteed token due to slot overflow”. From a user’s perspective, after minting the last NFT of a generation they expect to see a Golden God appear in their wallet, but instead they receive nothing, causing a mismatch between expectation and reality.

title: `DropBox::tokenURI` returns data for non-existent `tokenId` violating `EIP721`
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ERC‑721 token contract’s tokenURI function, which is overridden to concatenate a base URI with the numeric token identifier and a .json suffix without first verifying that the supplied tokenId actually corresponds to a minted NFT. According to the ERC‑721 specification, tokenURI must revert when the queried token does not exist, because the URI is defined only for valid assets. The root cause is the omission of an existence check (such as _exists(tokenId) or _requireOwned(tokenId)) before constructing the metadata URL. As a result, any caller can request tokenURI for an arbitrary number, and the contract will return a syntactically valid string that points to a JSON file that may never be created or associated with a real token. An attacker or a careless front‑end can therefore retrieve metadata for non‑existent tokens, leading to integration problems: NFT marketplaces, wallets, or explorers that rely on tokenURI to display images and attributes may show broken links, empty images, or incorrect information, confusing users who expect a valid NFT. The issue manifests whenever tokenURI is called with a tokenId that has not been minted, which can happen during normal browsing, marketplace indexing, or when a malicious actor deliberately probes the contract with high tokenIds. The affected parties include token holders, potential buyers, marketplace operators, and any user interface that displays NFT metadata. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by Cyfrin, which compared the implementation against OpenZeppelin’s reference and the ERC‑721 standard and noted the missing validation. Because the function returns a string rather than reverting, the bug can be subtle: callers may assume the token exists simply because a URI is returned, and the contract does not emit an error that would flag the issue. To remediate, the tokenURI function should include a check that the tokenId is owned or exists before building the URI, for example by invoking _requireOwned(tokenId) or require(_exists(tokenId)). This brings the contract back into compliance with the ERC‑721 specification and prevents marketplaces from receiving misleading metadata, thereby preserving the expected user experience of seeing correct images and attributes for genuine NFTs.

title: Use upgradeable or replaceable `VRFHandler` contracts when interacting with Chainlink VRF
description:
** Cyfrin has been made aware by our private audit clients that Chainlink intends on bricking VRF 2.0 at the end of November 2024 such that "VRF 2.0 will stop working" even for existing subscriptions.

** All immutable contracts dependent on VRF 2.0 will be bricked when Chainlink bricks VRF 2.0. The same will apply in the future to immutable contracts depending on VRF 2.5 when/if Chainlink does the same to it.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an immutable smart contract that directly calls Chainlink VRF version 2.0 to obtain verifiable randomness. Because the contract is immutable, its address of the VRF coordinator and subscription parameters are hard‑coded at deployment and cannot be altered later. Chainlink has announced that VRF 2.0 will be decommissioned at the end of November 2024, meaning the VRF coordinator will stop responding to any request made through the old interface. When the deprecation occurs, any request sent from the immutable contract will either revert or return no random value, causing the contract’s randomness‑dependent logic to fail. This failure can manifest as a lottery never drawing a winner, a game not progressing, an NFT minting process that stalls, or any feature that expects a random number to be supplied. Users experience symptoms such as transactions that appear to succeed but never produce the expected outcome, balances that remain unchanged, or UI elements that stay empty because the backend never receives randomness. The impact is that the protocol’s core functionality is effectively bricked, potentially leading to loss of user trust, halted revenue streams, and in extreme cases, funds that are locked because the contract cannot progress to a state where they would be released. The issue is discovered through audit communication with the client, who was informed by Chainlink’s roadmap that VRF 2.0 will be retired, and the auditor recognized that immutable contracts cannot be patched to point to a newer VRF version. The problem is subtle because the contract may continue to work correctly until the deprecation date, giving a false sense of security, and the failure only becomes apparent when randomness requests silently stop returning data. Conceptually, this is a class of external‑dependency‑version‑lock bugs where a contract is permanently bound to a specific version of an off‑chain service that may be discontinued. The recommended mitigation is to introduce an intermediate VRFHandler contract that abstracts the VRF interaction. The handler can be either a replaceable immutable contract using VRFConsumerBaseV2Plus or an upgradeable contract using VRFConsumerBaseV2Upgradeable, allowing the owner to redeploy or upgrade the handler when a new VRF version is released. The immutable business logic contract would then call the handler’s stable API, and the handler would manage all VRF calls and callbacks, forwarding the random result back. This design insulates the core contract from future VRF upgrades, preserving functionality and preventing the bricking scenario.

title: Incorrect state update in `RiskOracle::_processUpdate`
description:
** Within the `RiskParameterUpdate` struct, there is a field [`bytes previousValue`](https://github.com/ChaosLabsInc/risk-oracle/blob/9449219174e3ee7da9a13a5db7fb566836fb4986/src/RiskOracle.sol#L15) that is intended to store the previous value of a parameter.
