The impact includes denial‑of‑service of withdrawals, potential abuse of short‑term credentials, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s access‑control model. The affected parties are lenders attempting to withdraw, the market contracts that rely on the hook, and any users whose funds may be temporarily locked. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit check that msg.sender is a registered hooked market before proceeding with credential validation, mirroring the pattern used in FixedTermLoanHooks. This change restores the intended access control, prevents arbitrary calldata from reaching external providers, and mitigates the front‑running and DoS vectors associated with the bug.

title: M-08 | GLV Read-only Reentrancy Risk
description: In the executeGlvWithdrawal function the withdrawal is performed with _processMarketWithdrawal before burning the glvWithdrawal.glvTokenAmount() from the glvVault. As a result any withdrawals which use shouldUnwrapNative token as true and receive weth will have the opportunity to exploit any systems which attempt to read the value of a GLV. This is because during this transfer of native tokens to the receiver address the GLV supply has not yet been reduced, but the amount of GM tokens in GLV has been reduced. The receiver then gains control over the transaction execution if it is a contract with a receive function. For example, any protocols attempting to use GLV as collateral can errantly count this collateral as being insufficient and allow incorrect liquidations since the GLV price is incorrectly reduced during this external transfer of native tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a read‑only reentrancy flaw that occurs in the executeGlvWithdrawal function when a withdrawal is performed with the shouldUnwrapNative flag set to true, causing the contract to transfer native tokens (WETH) to the receiver before the GLV token balance is burned. The root cause is the ordering of operations: the external call that sends WETH is executed while the internal accounting still reflects the original GLV supply, even though the amount of GM tokens backing the GLV has already been reduced. Because the transfer invokes the receiver's fallback or receive function, a malicious contract can re‑enter the execution flow and read the GLV state at a moment when the price calculation is inconsistent. An attacker can therefore observe a temporarily inflated GLV supply, compute a lower price for the GLV collateral, and cause downstream protocols that rely on that price (for example, liquidation engines) to mistakenly deem the collateral insufficient and trigger liquidations or other adverse actions. The impact includes incorrect liquidations, potential loss of user funds, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s accounting logic. The issue manifests only when withdrawals request native token unwrapping; contracts that do not implement a receive function are not affected, but any contract that can execute code on receipt of WETH can exploit the timing window. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the sequence of state updates and external calls. It is hard to notice because the external call appears benign – it merely transfers funds – and the reentrancy does not modify state directly, yet the inconsistent view of the GLV price can be leveraged by downstream logic. To remediate, the GLV token burn must be performed before any external transfer, i.e., update the internal GLV supply immediately after calculating the market token amount and before invoking ExecuteWithdrawalUtils.executeWithdrawal. This ensures that any subsequent external call observes a consistent and correct GLV balance, eliminating the read‑only reentrancy window and preserving the integrity of collateral valuation.

title: M-09 | User GLV Deposits Errantly Maximized
description: In the _getMintAmount function the poolValue used to compute the value of the depositor’s GM tokens is maximized to avoid applying a double spread from the GLV value computation. However the computation of the GLV value is not guaranteed to have a maximizing effect in excess of the maximizing effect experienced by the depositor. For example: • GLV is supports Markets A, B, and C • GLV totalSupply is 100 • GLV holds 10 GM A, 10 GM B, and 0 GM C • The minimum price of GM A is $1 and the maximum is $1.01 • The minimum price of GM B is $1 and the maximum is $1.01 • The minimum price of GM C is $1 and the maximum is $1.05 due to indexToken spread, trader pnl, impact pool amount, etc… • User A deposits 10 GM C tokens • The GLV value if minimized is $20, User A’s deposits is $10 if minimized, User A would receive 50 GLV tokens if both were minimized • The GLV value since it is maximized is $20.20, User A’s deposit is valued at $10.50 since it is maximized • As a result the maximization of both of these values positively affects User A such that they now receive $10.50/$20.20 * 100 ~= 51.98 GLV Due to the maximization of both values in this example, User A receives roughly 2 more GLV tokens than if the values were to not be maximized. Additionally, the same effect would apply if a user is simply depositing more $ value than the GLV currently holds, since the maximization would have a greater absolute value impact on the numerator than the denominator due to being applied for a larger size.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the deposit‑minting routine of the GLV pool, specifically the internal _getMintAmount function that determines how many GLV tokens a user receives for a given deposit. The routine calculates a poolValue using the maximum possible price for each underlying GM token in order to avoid a double spread when the GLV value itself is computed. However, the same maximized price is also applied to the user’s deposited value, which should be evaluated at the minimum price to prevent the user from benefiting from the spread. Because both the numerator (user deposit value) and the denominator (total pool value) are inflated by the same optimistic price, the resulting ratio is biased in the depositor’s favor. In practice, a user who deposits a token whose maximum price is significantly higher than its minimum – for example GM C with a $1.05 max versus $1 min – will receive more GLV tokens than a fair, market‑aligned calculation would grant. The audit discovered that when a user deposits an asset with a larger spread, the maximization of both values adds a larger absolute amount to the numerator than to the denominator, leading to an over‑issuance of roughly two extra GLV tokens in the illustrated scenario. This effect is subtle because the overall pool value also rises, so the ratio change is modest and can be missed by cursory checks or UI displays that simply show the minted amount without revealing the underlying price assumptions. The impact is economic: the protocol dilutes existing GLV holders, creates a profitable arbitrage window for depositors, and undermines the intended accounting invariants that the pool’s total supply should represent the true value of its underlying assets. The bug manifests whenever a deposit is processed, especially for assets with asymmetric price bounds, and it affects any user who interacts with the deposit function as well as downstream participants who hold GLV tokens. To remediate, the pool valuation should continue to use the maximum price to protect the protocol, but the user’s deposit valuation must be performed at the minimum price, ensuring that the rounding never favours the depositor. The same spread logic should be mirrored on withdrawals to avoid a reverse bias. By separating the price extremes for pool and user calculations, the protocol restores a neutral or protective bias and eliminates the over‑minting risk.

title: M-10 | Virtual Inventory Ignored On Withdrawal
description: When withdrawing from a GM market in GMX V2, no price impact is applied since the withdrawn tokens are taken at the ratio of pool balances of the backing liquidity for the market. However if the market is within a virtual inventory, this ratio which was withdrawn directly from the market may have a negative impact on the virtual inventory (VI), but is ignored since no price impact is applied on withdrawal. Consider the following scenario: • Markets A, B, and C are all backed by WETH/USDC and make up a VI • Market A holds $100 of WETH and $200 of USDC • Market B holds $200 of WETH and $100 of USDC • Market C holds $100 of WETH and $100 of USDC • The total VI balances are $400 WETH & $400 USDC, the VI is balanced • User A withdraws 50% of the GM supply from Market A • Market A now holds $50 of WETH and $100 of USDC, ignoring fees • The total VI balances are $350 WETH and $300 USDC, the VI is now unbalanced Since there is no way to be positively impacted for balancing the virtual inventory, no value can be directly extracted this way. Though this leads to cases where the virtual inventory is negatively imbalanced, affecting other users who experience subsequent negative impact within the same virtual inventory on swaps and deposits, but while failing to negatively impact the user who created the imbalance. Additionally, as the virtual inventory was implemented to disincentivize profitable manipulations in price impact across similar markets, ignoring the VI on withdrawals may allow a case where this is not sufficiently protected against, though none have been identified at this time.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of withdrawals from markets that participate in a shared virtual inventory (VI) in the GMX V2 protocol. When a user withdraws tokens from a market, the contract calculates the amount based solely on the actual pool balances of the backing liquidity, deliberately omitting any price‑impact adjustment. This logic is correct for isolated markets, but it fails when the market is part of a VI that aggregates the balances of several markets to provide a collective pricing surface. The root cause is that the withdrawal routine does not consult the virtual inventory state, so it ignores the effect that removing liquidity from one market has on the overall VI balance. Consequently, a user can withdraw a portion of the market’s supply, reducing the market’s on‑chain token holdings while leaving the VI’s aggregate balances out of sync. In the example, three markets A, B and C share a VI backed by equal amounts of WETH and USDC. After a user withdraws 50 % of the supply from Market A, the VI’s total becomes 350 WETH and 300 USDC, creating a negative imbalance. Because the protocol does not apply a negative price‑impact penalty on withdrawals, the withdrawing user experiences no loss – they receive the expected amount – while the imbalance silently degrades the pricing for subsequent swaps and deposits performed by other participants in the same VI. The impact is therefore indirect: other users face worse slippage, higher fees, or reduced returns, and the protocol’s economic model that relied on the VI to deter profitable price‑impact manipulation is weakened. This condition manifests whenever a market belonging to a VI allows withdrawals and the contract’s withdrawal path does not incorporate the VI’s aggregate state. It is difficult to notice because the transaction appears normal from the user’s perspective; the balance of the withdrawn market simply decreases, and there is no immediate error or loss visible to the withdrawing party. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit of the GMX V2 codebase, where the auditor observed that the virtual inventory was consulted for swaps and deposits but omitted for withdrawals. To remediate the problem, the withdrawal logic should be extended to reference the virtual inventory, compute the resulting imbalance, and apply an appropriate negative price‑impact or rebalance fee that reflects the cost imposed on the shared inventory. By doing so, the protocol would restore the intended economic protection, ensuring that any action that harms the VI also incurs a proportional cost to the actor, preserving fairness for all participants.

title: M-11 | GLV Oracle Count Wrong For Homogenous Markets
description: The estimateGlvDepositOraclePriceCount and estimateGlvWithdrawalOraclePriceCount functions add 2 constant oracle prices for every GLV. Additionally, the estimateGlvShiftOraclePriceCount is a static 4 oracle price feeds. However in the future it is planned that homogenous market GLV's may be supported. Therefore the oracle price count is consistently over-estimated for GLV's with homogenous markets. As a result users and shifts will unintentionally have to pay a higher margin to the keepers on every interaction with a homogenous market GLV.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect accounting of oracle price feeds used when estimating the margin that must be posted for interactions with Global Liquidity Vault (GLV) contracts that support homogeneous markets. The contract functions that calculate the required oracle price count add two fixed oracle price entries for every GLV and a static four oracle price entries for each shift operation. This hard‑coded approach was designed for the current market configuration, but the protocol roadmap includes support for homogeneous market GLVs where the actual number of distinct oracle feeds is lower. Because the code does not adjust the constant count, the estimated oracle price count is systematically higher than the true number of feeds. As a result, the margin that users must provide – and the fee that keepers receive – is inflated. Users therefore pay a larger execution fee or margin than the protocol’s economic model expects. The issue manifests only when a GLV with a homogeneous market is used, which may be a future or optional configuration, making it easy to overlook during normal testing. From a user’s perspective the transaction may appear to succeed but the deducted amount is larger than anticipated, or the transaction may revert because the supplied margin is insufficient for the over‑estimated requirement. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the fee‑calculation logic and identified the static addition of oracle price counts as a mismatch with the intended accounting rules. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit warnings about the over‑charge; the only symptom is an unexpected increase in the margin or fee. To remediate the issue the oracle price counting logic should be made dynamic or at least conditioned on the market type, ensuring that the number of oracle feeds added matches the actual feeds required for homogeneous markets. This adjustment will align the required margin with the protocol’s design, prevent users from paying excessive fees, and preserve the intended economic incentives for keepers.

title: M-12 | Insufficient Gas Forwarded For Refund
description: In the refundExecutionFee function the REFUND_EXECUTION_FEE_GAS_LIMIT is forwarded to the callbackContract when calling the refundExecutionFee value. However the transaction execution is not validated to have the necessary REFUND_EXECUTION_FEE_GAS_LIMIT with the gas left for the transaction. As the REFUND_EXECUTION_FEE_GAS_LIMIT is currently configured to 200,000 gas units and the refundExecutionFee call takes place at the end of action executions it is possible that keepers would not have provided enough gas to forward the entire limit. Instead 63/64 of the remaining gas left will be forwarded to the refundExecutionFee function call in these cases. This may cause unexpected reverts for integrating systems and result in mis-accounted funds. However this instance of not validating the gas left with the validateGasLeftForCallback is not as severe as the lack of this validation for the GLV callbacks, as the refund fee is configured with a lower gas limit and handles less funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an insufficient‑gas issue in the refundExecutionFee callback. The contract forwards a fixed gas limit of 200,000 units to the external callback contract, but it does not first verify that the transaction still has at least that amount of gas remaining. Because Solidity automatically caps the gas forwarded to a call at 63/64 of the gas left, if the refundExecutionFee call is executed after a series of actions that consume most of the supplied gas, the callback receives less than the required 200,000 gas. When the callback needs more gas than it receives, it reverts, causing the refund to fail. This failure can happen only in edge cases where the keeper or caller supplies just enough gas for the main actions but not enough for the final refund, making the problem hard to notice during normal testing. From a user’s perspective the expected refund never arrives, balances appear unchanged or zero, and the UI may show a successful transaction while the funds remain locked. The impact is mis‑accounted funds and a broken refund flow, which can undermine trust in the protocol even though the amount of funds at risk is limited by the lower refund gas limit. The issue was discovered during a security audit that highlighted the missing validateGasLeftForCallback check. Because the contract does not enforce a minimum gas threshold before invoking the refund, the bug can be reproduced by deliberately limiting the gas supplied to the transaction. The proper mitigation is to call validateGasLeftForCallback (or an equivalent check) before the refundExecutionFee call, ensuring that the remaining gas meets or exceeds the configured refund gas limit, thereby guaranteeing that the callback has sufficient execution resources and preventing unexpected reverts.

title: M-01 | MarketMaking Ignores Loops Capacity
description: Additional debt can now serve as capacity for the Baseline system in the Loops vault. This is accounted for in the CreditFacility but not in the MarketMaking contract. As a result the capacity checks between the CreditFacility and MarketMaking policies will not agree.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a capacity‑mismatch bug in the MarketMaking contract of the Baseline protocol. The contract is responsible for checking whether there is enough credit capacity before allowing new market‑making positions. The protocol’s CreditFacility correctly adds the total debt of the Loops vault (LOOPS.totalDebt()) to its accounting, treating that debt as part of the overall capacity pool. However, the MarketMaking contract omits this value when it computes its own capacity limits. As a result, the two components perform inconsistent checks: the CreditFacility believes there is less free capacity than actually exists, while MarketMaking believes there is more. This discrepancy can be exploited by an attacker who opens large positions through the MarketMaking interface, causing the system to allocate credit beyond the true safe limit because the MarketMaking contract does not account for the debt already present in the Loops vault. When the hidden debt later materialises, the protocol may become under‑collateralised, leading to potential liquidation of positions, loss of user funds, or denial of service for legitimate users who are incorrectly rejected by the CreditFacility’s stricter checks. The issue appears only when the Loops vault accumulates debt and a market‑making transaction triggers a capacity verification, which may be rare and therefore easy to miss during routine testing. It was discovered during a formal audit by the security team Guardian, who noticed that the capacity calculation in MarketMaking did not reference the Loops total debt variable. The bug is subtle because both contracts appear to enforce capacity limits, but the mismatch is not visible in UI or logs until an extreme edge case occurs, making it hard for operators to notice until a failure happens. To remediate the problem, the MarketMaking contract should be updated to include LOOPS.totalDebt() in its capacity computation, ensuring that both components share a consistent view of available credit. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that total allocated credit plus existing Loops debt never exceeds the protocol’s overall capacity, preventing over‑allocation and preserving the financial safety guarantees of the system.

title: M-02 | Vault Position Not Sum Of User Positions
description: Function getFundingSince is not perfectly precise, such that the decay of two time deltas X and Y is not the same as the funding decay of one time delta X + Y. This is important since chargeFunding only updates the last update timestamp for the vault position, not user positions. Consider this scenario where there is only one open position: 1) 10 seconds pass. 2) Vault is charged funding for 10 second decay. 3) 200 more seconds pass. 4) Vault is charged funding for 200 second decay; User is charged funding for 210 second delay. 5) User sends request to close their position. Ultimately, the latest position of the vault is not aligned with the latest position of the user due to the imprecision of getFundingSince. The position the user can reduce is greater than the latest vault position, causing an underflow when performing vault.position -= _positionToReduce. This can be harmful in the case there are multiple open positions, and a single depositor is left hanging and unable to close their position. Note that this issue is also applicable to the vault.debt -= debtToReduce_; calculation as the debt is also updated when funding is charged.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an imprecise implementation of the funding decay function used to update the vault’s accounting state. The function that calculates the elapsed funding since the last update does not preserve linearity: the decay computed for two separate time intervals X and Y does not equal the decay computed for the combined interval X+Y. Because the contract only updates the timestamp for the vault position when funding is charged, individual user positions retain an older timestamp. When a user’s position is later reduced, the contract applies a funding decay that assumes the longer combined interval, while the vault itself has only accounted for the shorter, separate intervals. This mismatch can cause the user’s calculated reducible position to be larger than the vault’s recorded position. When the contract attempts to subtract the user‑requested reduction from the vault’s position, an arithmetic underflow occurs because the vault’s position variable is smaller than the amount being subtracted. The same problem applies to the vault’s debt accounting, which is also updated only during funding charges. The bug manifests under specific timing conditions: a single open position, a pause long enough for the vault to be charged funding for a short interval, followed by a longer interval before the user attempts to close the position. In practice, the user may see their balance disappear, receive no funds when closing, or observe that the contract reports a negative or zero vault position while the user’s position appears still open. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the funding decay logic and the vault’s state‑update mechanisms. It is difficult to notice because the underflow only appears when the timing of funding charges and user actions align in a particular way, and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the subtraction wraps around. This class of bug falls under arithmetic underflow caused by inconsistent state updates and precision loss in time‑based calculations. To remediate, the contract should ensure that reductions never exceed the current vault position or debt, for example by capping the amount to reduce to the vault’s available balance, and by synchronizing the funding decay calculation for both vault and user positions or by updating user timestamps alongside the vault. In broader terms, the fix requires making the accounting logic deterministic and preventing any subtraction that could cause the stored totals to become negative, thereby preserving the protocol’s accounting invariants and preventing users from being unable to close positions or from experiencing unexpected loss of funds.

title: M-03 | Slide Causes Anchor To Disappear
description: In the slide function the reserves of the anchor position are added back to the anchor after potentially extending the Anchor further downwards with a call to _updateTicks. This can result in the Anchor position having little liquidity or disappearing entirely after the slide operation. This is because the price may have been set less than or equal to the lower end of the Anchor position, in which case there would be no reserves in the liquidity position. In this case the Anchor position would not be built up again until a sweep occurs, and in the meantime there can be erratic price fluctuations between the floor and discovery which may be far apart.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the slide routine that adjusts the Anchor liquidity position. When the function attempts to extend the Anchor downwards it first calls an internal tick‑update routine and then adds the reserves of the previous Anchor back to the new position. If the market price after the tick update is at or below the lower bound of the newly created Anchor, the liquidity bucket that should receive the reserves contains no tokens, effectively leaving the Anchor with little or no liquidity. Because the Anchor is the reference point for price discovery, its disappearance causes the protocol to fall back to the floor price and creates large, erratic price gaps between the floor and the discovery level. From a user perspective this manifests as sudden price jumps, missing liquidity on the UI, trades that execute at unexpected rates or even fail, and a perception that the market “disappears” for a short period. The issue occurs only when the slide operation pushes the Anchor below the current price and the price is already at the lower edge of the Anchor’s tick range. Liquidity providers, traders and any integrators that rely on continuous price discovery are affected because their positions may be exposed to volatile price swings and reduced depth. The problem was uncovered during a systematic audit of the slide logic, where the interaction between _updateTicks and the reserve‑re‑addition step was examined. It is subtle because the Anchor can re‑appear after a later sweep operation, so the disappearance may be transient and not immediately obvious in logs or simple tests. The root cause is an incorrect assumption that the Anchor will always retain some reserve after a downward slide; the code does not guard against the case where the price sits at the lower tick, resulting in a zero‑reserve bucket. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of liquidity‑position underflow or anchor‑disappearance bugs caused by improper handling of reserve allocation after tick adjustments. To remediate the issue the protocol should ensure that the Anchor is never placed below the active price, for example by keeping the Anchor at least one tick‑spacing above the current price, or by enforcing a minimum reserve amount when rebuilding the Anchor. This prevents the Anchor from vanishing and maintains a stable price discovery range, preserving expected market behavior and protecting users from unexpected price gaps.

title: M-04 | Incorrect Virtual Reserves Accounting
description: In the launch function the pessimisticCapacity includes the floor reserves when stretching the virtual reserves over the entire floor position to compute its worst case capacity. This incorrectly accounts for stretching out the floor reserves which would actually increase if the price were to rise to the upper floor tick. This was the original reason why the virtual reserves had to be stretched because they would not receive corresponding reserves in as price rose to the upper tick of the floor. This accounting is attempted to be fixed by leaving the bAssets of the floor position in the circulating supply, as if they had been swapped out of the floor as price rose. However this again does not account for the reserves of the floor increasing due to swap input amounts.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect accounting of virtual reserves during the launch routine of the protocol. When the contract stretches virtual reserves across the entire floor position to calculate a pessimistic capacity, it mistakenly treats the floor reserves as if they remain constant, even though those reserves would actually increase if the market price moves toward the upper floor tick. The original design stretched virtual reserves because they would not automatically receive additional real reserves as price rose, but the implemented fix tried to compensate by keeping the floor position's bAssets in the circulating supply, pretending they had been swapped out. This workaround still fails to account for the extra reserves that accrue from swap inputs when the price climbs, leading to an over‑optimistic estimate of how much capacity the pool has. As a result, the protocol may believe it is solvent while in reality it is under‑collateralised. An attacker or any user could trigger a price increase toward the upper floor tick and then execute large swaps or mint operations that exceed the true reserve backing, causing the pool to run out of assets and leaving users with missing balances or zero refunds. The issue manifests only during the launch phase and when the price moves into the upper floor range, making it easy to miss in normal operation because balances appear correct until the specific condition is met. It was discovered through a manual audit that examined the solvency check logic and identified that the floor‑position accounting does not reflect the dynamic growth of reserves. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect accounting of virtual reserves” or “capacity over‑estimation” bugs, which violate the fundamental accounting invariant that total assets must always cover total liabilities. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a price rise and a subsequent large trade, the expected refund or redemption amount is unexpectedly low or even zero, contrary to the expectation that the pool should honor the full amount. To remediate the problem the special floor‑position accounting should be removed and the original solvency check restored, with the only addition being the inclusion of the total debt value in the pessimistic capacity calculation, thereby ensuring that the capacity estimate correctly reflects all real reserves and outstanding obligations.

title: M-01 | Excess execution fee will be required
description: To deposit GM, the long token address must be 0. if (params.initialLongToken != address(0)) However, when estimating execution fees, the only way to not pay for a deposit is to have the long address equal to the market address. if (glvDeposit.market() == glvDeposit.initialLongToken()) Due to these conflicting statements, users depositing GM tokens will be required to pay an execution fee as if they were depositing the underlying asset.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns an inconsistency between the deposit validation logic and the execution‑fee estimation logic in a market‑deposit contract. When a user wants to deposit the synthetic GM token, the contract requires the initial long‑token address to be the zero address (address(0)). This check is implemented as `if (params.initialLongToken != address(0))` which rejects any non‑zero long token for a GM deposit. However, the fee‑estimation routine determines whether a fee should be waived by comparing the market address with the initial long‑token address: `if (glvDeposit.market() == glvDeposit.initialLongToken())`. Because the GM deposit forces the long‑token address to be zero, the condition never holds, and the contract treats the operation as a regular underlying‑asset deposit, charging the full execution fee. As a result, users depositing GM tokens are required to pay an excess fee that they do not expect. The issue manifests during the fee‑estimation step that runs before the transaction is sent, so the user sees a normal fee estimate in the UI but the transaction reverts or succeeds with a higher cost, effectively making funds disappear from the user’s perspective. The affected parties are any wallet or protocol participant attempting to deposit GM tokens; they lose additional ETH or gas that was not accounted for in the UI. The problem was discovered during a manual audit where the reviewer compared the deposit‑parameter checks with the fee‑calculation code and noticed the contradictory requirements. It is hard to notice because the fee‑estimation path is separate from the validation path, and the UI typically does not expose the internal condition that ties the market address to the long‑token address. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “fee‑miscalculation due to mismatched business rules” or “incorrect conditional logic leading to over‑charging”. To remediate, the contract should only apply the execution fee when an actual underlying long or short token is being deposited, i.e., when the initialLongToken (or initialShortToken) is non‑zero, and the fee‑waiver condition should be aligned with the validation rule that permits a zero address for synthetic token deposits. This change ensures that the fee estimation reflects the true cost of the operation and prevents users from unexpectedly paying extra fees.

title: M-02 | GLV Withdrawal Callback Gas Cost Ignored
description: For the GLV Withdrawal flow, the callback call is made at the end of GlvWithdrawalUtils::executeGlvWithdrawal(). Since the callback is made after payExecutionFee() is called, the gas used in the callback will not come out of the user’s execution fee and will instead be charged to GMX. The max callback gas limit is set to 3,000,000 for Arbitrum and 2,000,000 for Avalanche, which over time will cause GMX incur substantial losses.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper gas accounting flaw in the GLV withdrawal flow of the GMX protocol. After a user initiates a withdrawal, the contract executes GlvWithdrawalUtils::executeGlvWithdrawal which first calls payExecutionFee to deduct the user‑provided execution fee, and only then invokes a callback function. Because the callback is executed after the fee has already been paid, the gas consumed by the callback is not charged to the user’s execution fee but is instead billed to the GMX contract itself. The protocol sets a very high maximum gas limit for this callback – three million gas on Arbitrum and two million on Avalanche – so each withdrawal can cause a substantial amount of gas to be spent from GMX’s balance. Over many withdrawals, especially if an attacker repeatedly triggers withdrawals with heavy callback logic, the accumulated gas cost can become a significant loss for the protocol. The issue occurs whenever a GLV withdrawal is processed; it does not depend on any special input values other than the normal execution of the withdrawal path. Users are affected indirectly: they see their withdrawal complete as expected, but the protocol’s treasury loses ether or native token to cover the unexpected gas, which may eventually affect liquidity or fee distribution. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the ordering of internal calls and noticed that the callback was placed after the fee deduction, violating the intended accounting model where all gas costs should be covered by the user‑provided fee. The problem is hard to notice because the withdrawal appears successful from the user’s perspective – the UI shows a completed transaction and the user receives the expected assets – while the hidden gas expense is absorbed by the contract, making the loss invisible in normal transaction logs. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “gas mis‑allocation” or “callback after fee payment” vulnerabilities, where the contract’s internal accounting does not correctly attribute gas consumption. To remediate, the callback should be moved before payExecutionFee so that any gas used by the callback is deducted from the user’s execution fee, ensuring that the protocol does not unintentionally subsidize the callback execution. This change restores the intended economic model, prevents systematic erosion of the protocol’s funds, and aligns the contract’s behavior with user expectations that they pay for the full cost of their transaction.

title: M-03 | executionFee Should Be Updated
description: The createGlvWithdrawal function does not update the params.executionFee after recording the transferred wntAmount with recordTransferIn. As a consequence, users may not receive a full refund when the transferred wnt amount exceeds the provided input value. Furthermore, the validateExecutionFee function utilizes the provided params.executionFee instead of the actual transferred wnt amount, potentially causing the function to inaccurately revert even when the transferred amount is enough to cover execution costs.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the withdrawal routine of a GLV contract where the execution fee variable is not refreshed after the contract records the incoming WNT transfer. The createGlvWithdrawal function calls recordTransferIn to note the amount of WNT that has been moved into the contract, but it leaves params.executionFee unchanged. Consequently the later validateExecutionFee check compares the user‑supplied executionFee value with the required fee instead of the actual amount that was transferred. If the transferred amount is larger than the supplied fee, the contract may either under‑refund the user or revert the transaction even though enough WNT is available to cover execution costs. This bug manifests when a caller provides a lower executionFee than the amount that ends up being transferred, for example due to rounding, gas price fluctuations, or manual mis‑calculation. The affected parties are any user invoking the withdrawal function and the protocol itself because the mis‑accounted fee can lead to lost refunds or unnecessary transaction failures, breaking the expectation that a withdrawal returns the full remaining balance after fees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the flow of fee handling and noticed that the fee parameter was never updated after the transfer recording step. It can be hard to notice because the contract still accepts the transfer and only fails later in the validation step, producing a revert that appears unrelated to the fee logic. The impact is medium severity: users may receive less than the expected refund or see their withdrawal revert despite having supplied sufficient funds, leading to a loss of confidence and potential financial loss. The bug belongs to the class of fee‑miscalculation or accounting‑state‑inconsistency vulnerabilities, where a stored variable no longer reflects the true on‑chain state. From a user perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal request but then display a zero or reduced balance, or the transaction may simply revert with an obscure error, contradicting the expectation that the contract will return the full amount after deducting the execution fee. The correct remediation is to update params.executionFee (or recompute the fee) after recordTransferIn so that validateExecutionFee validates against the actual transferred amount, ensuring the refund calculation matches the real balance and preventing spurious reverts.

title: M-04 | GLV Used To Exit Illiquid Markets
description: GLV allows users to essentially swap between GM markets with no fees by triggering a GLV deposit of GM market A and triggering a GLV withdrawal of GM market B. An actor holding GM market A can observe that GM market A is locked due to pnlToPoolRatio validations or reserves validations and use GLV to exit their GM A tokens into GM B tokens. This will come at the expense of all other GLV holders, who are now left with the illiquid GM A tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the fee‑less cross‑market swap mechanism provided by the GLV contract, which lets a user deposit a token from one GM market (market A) and withdraw an equivalent amount of a token from another GM market (market B). The core problem is that GLV does not verify the liquidity or lock status of the underlying market from which the deposit originates before allowing a withdrawal from a different market. When market A becomes illiquid or is locked by internal checks such as pnlToPoolRatio or reserve validations, an attacker who still holds GM‑A tokens can still deposit those tokens into GLV and immediately withdraw GM‑B tokens, effectively escaping the locked market. This action leaves the remaining GLV participants with GM‑A tokens that can no longer be redeemed because the underlying market is frozen, so their balances appear unchanged while the value of those tokens is effectively trapped. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a user who tries to swap or withdraw GM‑A through GLV receives nothing or sees their balance stay the same, contrary to the expectation that the swap should always succeed without fees. The impact is a redistribution of value: the attacker gains liquid GM‑B tokens while other users are left holding illiquid GM‑A tokens, potentially resulting in loss of funds, reduced confidence in the protocol, and a breach of the accounting assumption that all GLV‑issued tokens remain equally redeemable. The issue manifests only when the underlying GM market is in a locked state, which may not be obvious from the GLV UI because the contract does not surface the lock condition. It was identified during a manual security audit (by Guardian) that examined the interaction between GLV and the GM market contracts. The flaw is subtle because the GLV contract’s external interface appears to work correctly, and the fee‑less nature masks the fact that a hidden liquidity check is missing. To remediate the problem, the protocol should either impose a withdrawal fee that makes the exploit uneconomical, or, more directly, prevent GLV deposits when the source GM market is flagged as illiquid or locked, ensuring that all swaps respect the underlying market’s state and that no participant can abandon a locked market at the expense of others.

title: M-05 | GLV Actions Cannot Be Simulated
description: The simulateExecuteGlvDeposit and simulateExecuteGlvWithdrawal functions have the onlyController modifier, however they are not exposed through the GlvRouter and therefore cannot be called.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns two internal simulation functions – simulateExecuteGlvDeposit and simulateExecuteGlvWithdrawal – that are intended to provide a read‑only preview of a GLV (Generalized Liquidity Vault) deposit or withdrawal. Both functions are protected by the onlyController modifier, which restricts calls to the contract’s controller address, but they are not linked to the public GlvRouter contract that external callers use to interact with the GLV system. Because the router does not expose any external entry point for these simulation methods, they cannot be invoked from off‑chain tools, front‑end interfaces, or other contracts. The root cause is a mismatch between the access control design (onlyController) and the contract architecture (router as the sole public gateway). An attacker does not need to exploit a classic code execution flaw; instead, the issue can be abused by any user or integrator who expects to call the simulation functions to estimate outcomes before committing real funds. When a user attempts to simulate a deposit or withdrawal through the usual UI or SDK, the call silently fails or returns no data, leading the user to believe the operation will succeed with certain parameters while in reality the system cannot provide the preview. This can cause users to submit transactions with incorrect assumptions, potentially resulting in unexpected slippage, insufficient gas, or even failed transactions that waste fees. The problem manifests whenever a caller tries to invoke the simulation functions directly or indirectly via the router – which, by design, does not forward those calls. The affected parties include end‑users, front‑end developers, and any protocol component that relies on accurate pre‑execution estimates for risk management or UI display. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the GLV contract suite, where the auditor noted the presence of the simulate functions but could not locate any public accessor. The bug is subtle because the functions compile without errors and appear in the source, yet they are effectively dead code from the perspective of external callers, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the simulateExecuteGlvDeposit and simulateExecuteGlvWithdrawal functions should be added to the GlvRouter’s public interface, either by exposing them directly or by providing a proxy that forwards calls while preserving the onlyController restriction. This change restores the intended simulation capability, aligns the access control model with the contract architecture, and prevents users from encountering silent failures when trying to preview GLV actions.

title: M-06 | GLV Used For Atomic Withdrawals
description: In the _processMarketWithdrawal function the collected glv amount is converted into a market token amount and withdrawn from the GLV address. However because the marketTokenAmount is determined during the time of execution, a user may abuse the GLV withdrawal to perform an atomic withdrawal while avoiding the atomic withdrawal fee. Consider the following scenario: - address(1) holds 1 GLV - User A holds 1000 GLV - The totalSupply of GLV is 1001 - User A creates a withdrawal for their 1000 GLV - User A watches for the keeper’s execution transaction and frontruns it to donate 50,000 GM tokens to the GLV in the same block - The keeper’s execution transaction now credits User A with 1000/1001 * 50,000 of these GM tokens for their GLV withdrawal - User A is able to withdraw their GM tokens in a single block while only paying the TwoStep swapPricing fee and 10 basis points for their loss to the initial deposit address
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the market withdrawal routine where theamount of market tokens to be returned to a GLV holder is calculated on‑chain using the current balance of the market token held by the GLV contract at the moment the keeper executes the withdrawal. Because the conversion uses a live balance rather than a snapshot or an internally recorded entitlement, an attacker can manipulate the balance in the same block as the withdrawal request. The attack works as follows: the attacker, who already owns a large portion of the GLV supply, creates a withdrawal request for their GLV tokens. Before the keeper’s transaction that processes the request is mined, the attacker front‑runs the transaction and transfers a large amount of the market token (for example GM) into the GLV contract. When the keeper finally executes the withdrawal, the contract computes the market token amount as the attacker’s GLV share of the total GLV supply multiplied by the newly inflated market token balance. Consequently the attacker receives a disproportionate share of the donated market tokens while only paying the standard two‑step swap pricing fee and a small basis‑point loss, effectively bypassing the intended atomic withdrawal fee. This manipulation is possible whenever the protocol relies on the external token balance for accounting and does not enforce a lock‑up or snapshot between request and execution. The impact is a loss of market token value from the protocol, unfair enrichment of the attacker, and reduced funds available to other GLV holders. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the reliance on balanceOf for entitlement calculation. It can be hard to notice because the balance change occurs in a single block and the fee calculation appears correct, masking the underlying over‑allocation. To remediate, the contract should record each holder’s market token entitlement at the time the withdrawal request is made, or use a snapshot of the market token balance before processing, or prevent external deposits to the GLV address between request and execution, thereby eliminating the ability to manipulate the conversion rate.

title: M-07 | GLV Trapped Funds Upon Disabled
description: In the createGlvWithdrawal function the validateGlvMarket validation uses true as the shouldBeEnabled configuration. Therefore users may not withdraw from the portion of a Glv that is a disabled Glv market. As a result when a market becomes disabled via the isGlvMarketDisabledKey key, users are not able to fully withdraw their deposited value from the Glv unless the keeper explicitly shifts all funds out of the disabled Glv market.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑dependent access control flaw in the GLV (global liquidity vault) withdrawal logic. The createGlvWithdrawal function calls a validator that checks the market’s enabled flag with a hard‑coded expectation that the market must be enabled (shouldBeEnabled = true). When a market is later marked as disabled via the isGlvMarketDisabledKey, the same validator still blocks any withdrawal request, even though users have previously deposited funds while the market was active. As a result, deposited assets become effectively trapped: a user who tries to withdraw after the market is disabled receives a reverted transaction or a zero amount, while the UI may still display a withdraw button, leading to confusion. The issue occurs only after the market transitions to the disabled state and only for withdrawal paths; deposits remain possible until the market is explicitly disabled. The root cause is the misuse of a generic “must be enabled” check for both deposit and withdrawal operations, without distinguishing that withdrawals should be permitted even when the market is disabled. This logical oversight was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s state‑machine handling. It is hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly while the market is active, and the failure manifests only after a state change that many users may not anticipate. The impact is that users lose access to their funds until a privileged keeper manually shifts the assets out of the disabled market, which may not happen promptly, effectively freezing user balances. To remediate, the validator should be adjusted to allow withdrawals regardless of the market’s enabled flag, while still preventing new deposits into a disabled market. Conceptually, this is a “withdrawal‑blocked‑when‑disabled” bug, a subclass of improper state validation that violates the expected accounting invariant that users can always retrieve assets they have contributed, even if the market is no longer active.

title: Yield deposits are susceptible to losses of up to 10\%
bug_full: The vulnerability is an excessive slippage exposure in the yield‑deposit and withdrawal workflow of the Smart Vault. When a user calls the depositYield or withdrawYield functions, the contract performs a series of intermediate decentralized‑exchange swaps and interactions with Gamma Vaults. After these operations the contract checks that the total collateral value has not fallen below ninety percent of the pre‑operation value using the condition postCollateralValue < 9 * preCollateralValue / 10. This check only guarantees that the collateral does not disappear completely; it still permits a loss of up to ten percent per operation. The root cause is that the slippage protection is coarse‑grained and tied to a fixed 10 % threshold, while the actual price impact of the swaps can be arbitrarily close to that limit. Because the system runs on Arbitrum with a centralized sequencer, traditional MEV does not exist, but latency‑driven bots can still front‑run predictable events such as liquidations and deliberately cause the swaps to execute at the worst‑case price, pushing the collateral drop to the allowed maximum. An attacker can therefore submit a transaction that forces the DEX swap to execute at a price that yields exactly a ten‑percent loss, or slightly less, causing the user’s deposited amount to be reduced by that amount. The impact is that users see less collateral returned than expected, balances appear lower, and the vault may be brought dangerously close to liquidation, jeopardising the safety of all participants. This condition occurs each time a deposit or withdrawal is performed, especially when market conditions are volatile or when a bot can manipulate the timing of the swaps. The affected parties are any depositor or withdrawer of the Smart Vault, as well as the protocol that relies on the vault’s collateralisation. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the slippage handling logic and identified that the 10 % guard is insufficient to protect against realistic price impact and MEV‑style manipulation. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert on any loss; it merely enforces a threshold, so the transaction succeeds and the user receives a reduced amount without an explicit error, making the loss easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should allow callers to specify a tighter maximum collateral drop (for example 1 % or 0.5 %) and expose configurable slippage limits for each intermediate swap, thereby preventing bots from exploiting the fixed 10 % ceiling. In broader terms, this is a classic case of inadequate slippage protection and insufficient validation of external price‑impact operations, leading to unintended fund loss and potential liquidation risk.

title: Hardcoded pool fees can result in increased slippage and failed swaps
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of hard‑coded pool fee values in the SmartVaultV4.swap function and in the internal USD‑deposit and withdrawal helpers of SmartVaultYieldManager. Instead of determining the appropriate Uniswap or Ramses pool fee dynamically, the code fixes the fee to 3000 for generic token swaps and to 500 for USDC/USDs swaps. This assumption is unsafe because the pool that carries the specified fee is not guaranteed to be the most liquid pool at any given time. When market conditions shift and a pool with the hard‑coded fee has low liquidity, the router will execute the trade against a thin order book, causing excessive price impact. The slippage can exceed the 10 % threshold that SmartVaultV4.significantCollateralDrop checks, which then reverts the transaction and prevents the vault from completing a yield deposit or withdrawal. For direct calls to SmartVaultV4.swap there is no explicit validation, so the vault can be pushed arbitrarily close to liquidation: the only safeguard is that the minimum amount out is set just enough to keep the collateralisation margin within 1 % of liquidation. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are confusing – a deposit transaction may revert with a generic “significant collateral drop” error, a withdrawal may return zero USDC, or a swap may appear to succeed but deliver far less output than expected, effectively making funds disappear. The issue was discovered during the CodeHawks contest audit (report M‑03) where the hard‑coded fee was flagged as a logical flaw. It is difficult to notice because the fee value itself looks innocuous and the router does not emit a warning when the selected pool is ill‑liquid; only the downstream validation or a failed transaction reveals the problem. Conceptually, this is a class of bug where static configuration (hard‑coded fees) leads to economic misbehaviour such as increased slippage, failed swaps, denial‑of‑service of deposits/withdrawals, and potential under‑collateralisation of the vault. The recommended remediation is to make the pool fee a parameter supplied by the caller or to query the router for the optimal fee, thereby aligning the swap with the most liquid pool and restoring the intended safety margins.

title: Insufficient validation of Chainlink data feeds
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of insufficient validation of Chainlink price feed data inside the PriceCalculator contract, which is responsible for converting token amounts to USD and vice‑versa. The contract calls AggregatorV3Interface.latestRoundData but does not verify any of the returned fields – round identifier, price value, timestamp or freshness. Because the contract trusts whatever data the feed returns, a stale or zero price can be accepted and used in the arithmetic that determines collateralisation and liquidation thresholds. An attacker or a simple feed outage can cause the feed to return an old round, a zero price, or a timestamp that is far in the past; the contract will still compute a conversion based on that stale value. Consequently, users may see their positions incorrectly marked as under‑collateralised, leading to unnecessary liquidations, loss of collateral, or creation of positions that are not sufficiently backed by assets. This situation occurs whenever the Chainlink feed is delayed, the L2 sequencer is down, or the feed contract returns malformed data – all conditions that are realistic on Arbitrum where sequencer uptime can affect feed reliability. All participants who rely on the price – borrowers, lenders, and token holders – are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions (that price data is fresh and non‑zero) are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted the lack of checks on the feed response. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit any warning or revert; the price simply appears plausible, yet it may be outdated, and the resulting liquidation or collateral shortfall manifests only as unexpected loss of funds. The proper mitigation is to add explicit validation of the round ID, ensure the price is non‑zero, verify that the update timestamp is present and not in the future, and enforce a maximum age (timeout) for the price data. Additionally, on L2 networks the contract should check the sequencer uptime feed to avoid using prices while the sequencer is offline. By performing these checks, the contract will reject stale or incorrect data, preserving the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: Potential stale data in `FundFlowController::performUpkeep` can lead to incorrect state updates
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classic time‑of‑check‑to‑time‑of‑use (TOCTOU) race condition in the FundFlowController contract. The checkUpkeep view function computes the amounts of tokens that are ready to be unbonded (nextGroupOpVaultsTotalUnbonded and nextGroupComVaultsTotalUnbonded) by iterating over vaults and inspecting the unbondingActive flag, which depends on the current block timestamp and each vault’s claim‑period end time. These computed values are then encoded and handed over to performUpkeep, which trusts the data and updates the protocol state accordingly. Because checkUpkeep and performUpkeep are executed in separate transactions, any delay between the two – for example due to network congestion, gas price spikes, or a maliciously delayed keeper – can cause the unbondingActive status of some vaults to change after the view calculation but before the state‑changing call. When performUpkeep finally runs, it may apply stale totals that no longer reflect the real on‑chain situation. As a result the contract can record too many or too few unbonded tokens. In practice this means that funds that should have become withdrawable after the claim period may remain locked, or conversely funds that should still be locked may be released prematurely. Users therefore experience a mismatch between expected balances and actual balances: a user who expects a refund after the vesting period may see a zero payout, or may see an unexpected increase in withdrawable balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Cyfrin, which noted that the contract relies on data produced by a view function rather than recomputing it at execution time. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert; the state simply diverges from reality, making it hard to detect without explicit accounting checks. The recommended mitigation is to recalculate the totalUnbonded values inside performUpkeep, or to add on‑chain validation that the passed values still match the current vault status before applying them. This eliminates the reliance on potentially stale data and restores the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: `WithdrawalPool::withdrawalBatches` array is only every increasing in size potentially leading to Denial Of Service
description:
** Every time withdrawals are finalized, a new batchId gets appended to `withdrawalBatches` array. Over time, this array is ever increasing and can lead to extremely large size. It is important to note that users can trigger a queuing of withdrawal by themselves.

** Potential denial of service of `getBatchIds` and `getFinalizedWithdrawalIdsByOwner`
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unbounded growth of the withdrawalBatches array in the WithdrawalPool contract. Every time a withdrawal is finalized the contract appends a new batch identifier to this array, but it never removes entries that have already been processed. Because users can trigger the queuing of withdrawals themselves, a malicious or even benign user can cause the array to become extremely large over time. Functions such as getBatchIds and getFinalizedWithdrawalIdsByOwner iterate over the entire withdrawalBatches array to assemble results. When the array size grows beyond a certain point, the gas required for these loops exceeds the block gas limit, causing the calls to revert or run out of gas. From a user perspective this manifests as a UI that fails to display any withdrawal history, shows empty results, or simply hangs when trying to view pending or finalized withdrawals, leading users to think their funds are missing or that the contract is broken. The root cause is a design flaw: the contract lacks any mechanism to prune or archive batches that have been fully processed, relying only on ever‑increasing storage. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of storage patterns and function complexity. It can be hard to notice because the array grows gradually; only after many withdrawals does the gas consumption become problematic, at which point the problem appears as an unexpected denial of service rather than a clear coding error. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition that prevents users from querying their withdrawal status and may effectively lock the withdrawal functionality, undermining the availability of the protocol. The affected parties include all users of the protocol, front‑end applications that rely on these view functions, and the protocol operators who cannot service requests. To remediate the issue the contract should implement a cut‑off calculation based on the indexOfLastWithdrawal and the first queued withdrawal, then delete or archive all batches up to that cut‑off on a regular basis, or replace the growing array with a circular buffer or other bounded data structure. This pruning restores the ability of view functions to execute within gas limits and prevents the denial‑of‑service scenario.

title: Attacker can deny users from depositing into priority pool by front-running call to StakingPool::depositLiquidity()
description:
** The `VaultControllerStrategy` contract is susceptible to a front-running attack that can prevent priority pool from depositing user funds into specific vaults of a strategy. The vulnerability lies in the `deposit` function, which uses a `globalState.groupDepositIndex` to track the current deposit state. An attacker can exploit this by front-running legitimate deposits by calling `depositLiquidity` that deposits unused deposits into a strategy.

The griefing attack works as follows:
1. Priority pool prepares a transaction to deposit funds, specifying a list of vault IDs.
2. An attacker observes this pending transaction in the mempool.
3. The attacker quickly submits their own transaction that uses unused staking pool deposits, using the same vault IDs but with a higher gas price.
4. The attacker's transaction is processed first, updating the `globalState.groupDepositIndex`
5. When the priority pool transaction is processed, it fails due to an `InvalidVaultIds` error, as the `globalState.groupDepositIndex` no longer matches the expected value.

** In certain scenarios, priority pool can be prevented from depositing user funds, effectively creating a denial of service condition for the deposit functionality. It is noteworthy that an attacker need not use his own funds to execute the attack but use the unused staking pool deposits (when available) to grief other depositors.
poc:
**
```typescript
it('front-running deposit to change deposit index', async () => {
    const {
      token,
      accounts,
      signers,
      adrs,
      strategy,
      priorityPool,
      stakingPool,
      stakingController,
      rewardsController,
      vaults,
    } = await loadFixture(deployFixture)

    await token.transfer(await stakingPool.getAddress(), toEther(100)) //depositing to represent unused liquidity in staking pool
    //@audit front-run priority pool deposit
    await stakingPool.connect(signers[2]).depositLiquidity([encodeVaults([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])]) // anyone can deposit this

    //@audit actual deposit is DOSed as the group deposit index has changed
    await expect(
      priorityPool.connect(signers[2]).deposit(toEther(100), false, [encodeVaults([0, 1, 3, 4])])
    ).to.be.revertedWithCustomError(strategy, 'InvalidVaultIds()')
})
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running race condition that allows an attacker to deny legitimate users from depositing liquidity into a priority pool. The deposit logic in the VaultControllerStrategy contract relies on a mutable global variable, globalState.groupDepositIndex, to represent the current batch of vault IDs that a deposit should target. When a user submits a transaction to the priority pool, the contract expects the global index to match the value calculated at the time of transaction creation. Because the index is updated by any call to StakingPool.depositLiquidity, an attacker who monitors the mempool can submit their own depositLiquidity transaction with a higher gas price, causing it to be mined first. This front‑run increments the global deposit index before the user’s transaction is processed, so the subsequent priority pool deposit fails with an InvalidVaultIds error. The attack does not require the attacker to provide their own funds; they can use unused staking pool deposits that are already present in the contract. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a reverted deposit transaction, often showing a custom error message and resulting in no funds being transferred to the intended vaults, contrary to the expectation that the deposit would succeed. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for the priority pool’s deposit functionality, potentially preventing users from allocating their liquidity and undermining confidence in the protocol’s reliability. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included transaction‑ordering tests and manual inspection of the deposit flow. It can be hard to notice because the failure only occurs under specific ordering of transactions and the error message does not directly indicate a front‑running problem. Conceptually, the fix is to eliminate reliance on a single mutable global index for coordinating deposits, for example by gating the depositLiquidity function to authorized callers or by redesigning the deposit mechanism to use per‑deposit identifiers or atomic checks that are resistant to order manipulation. This class of bug falls under front‑running and state‑injection vulnerabilities where shared mutable state can be altered between transaction submission and execution, breaking business logic that assumes a stable ordering of operations.

title: No way to recover principal if an operator is removed by Chainlink
description:
** Chainlink can remove operators from the [OperatorStakingPool](https://etherscan.io/address/0xa1d76a7ca72128541e9fcacafbda3a92ef94fdc5#code). This will stop the Operator from accruing any more rewards by removing their principal. Their principal is not lost however, it is still available though by calling `OperatorStakingPool::unstakeRemovedPrincipal`.

In the `OperatorVault` there is no call like this. If an OperatorVault got removed as operator in the chainlink staking pool the pool principal would be locked.

** The funds could eventually be recovered by an upgrade to the vault but that is a long process and until then, the vault behavior would be imperfect as the removed principal is included in the vault principal:
```solidity
function getPrincipalDeposits() public view override returns (uint256) {
    return
        super.getPrincipalDeposits() +
        IOperatorStaking(address(stakeController)).getRemovedPrincipal(address(this));
}
```
Thus the vault would appear as it had the principal but it wouldn't be withdrawable.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the OperatorVault contract that is used together with Chainlink's OperatorStakingPool. When Chainlink decides to remove an operator from the staking pool, the operator’s principal is no longer eligible for new rewards and must be reclaimed by calling the function unstakeRemovedPrincipal on the staking pool. The staking pool implements this recovery path, but the OperatorVault does not expose any mechanism to invoke it. Consequently, the principal that belongs to a removed operator becomes locked inside the staking pool. The vault’s view function getPrincipalDeposits adds the amount returned by getRemovedPrincipal to the normal principal balance, so from a user’s perspective the vault appears to hold the full amount of deposited capital. In reality that portion cannot be withdrawn because the vault lacks a call to unstakeRemovedPrincipal, leading to a mismatch between displayed balance and withdrawable funds. The issue manifests only after Chainlink removes the operator, which can happen as a result of protocol‑level governance, misbehaviour, or external triggers. Affected parties include any operator or token holder that relies on the OperatorVault to manage their staking capital, as their funds may become inaccessible while still being reported as available. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the integration between the vault and the Chainlink staking pool and noticed the missing recovery call. It is subtle because the UI or on‑chain queries will still show the expected principal amount, masking the fact that withdrawals will fail or return zero for the removed portion. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where a contract’s state representation diverges from the actual transferable assets. To remediate the issue, the vault should implement a function that allows the operator or the contract owner to invoke unstakeRemovedPrincipal on the staking pool, and the accounting logic should be adjusted to exclude removed principal from the reported deposit balance until it is successfully reclaimed. This change restores the ability to recover the locked capital and aligns the displayed balance with the true withdrawable amount.

title: `Vault::unbondingActive` can be out of sync with Chainlink and `FundFlowController` bonding
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one logic error in the function that reports whether a vault is still in its unbonding (claim) period. The contract exposes Vault::unbondingActive which returns true while the current block timestamp is strictly less than the claim period end returned by the stake controller. Other components – the Chainlink vault implementation and the FundFlowController – treat the claim period as inclusive, using a <= comparison. Consequently, at the exact moment when block.timestamp equals the claimPeriodEndsAt, Vault::unbondingActive incorrectly reports that the unbonding period has already finished. This mismatch is used in several critical paths: FundFlowController relies on unbondingActive to calculate total unbonded balances and to decide which withdrawal orders to process; VaultControllerStrategy::withdraw checks unbondingActive before calling vault.withdraw; and VaultControllerStrategy::_depositToVaults uses the flag to update totalRebonded. When the timestamp hits the claim period end, the withdraw routine believes the vault is no longer in an active claim period and therefore skips the withdrawal logic, resulting in a user‑initiated withdraw call that returns zero tokens even though the user’s balance is sufficient and the claim period is technically still open. The accounting variables totalUnbonded and totalRebonded become stale because deposits that should be counted as rebonded are ignored at the boundary moment. The issue manifests only at the precise block where the claim period ends, making it hard to notice in routine testing that does not target the boundary condition. It was discovered during a formal audit by comparing the semantics of the three related functions and confirming the discrepancy with a targeted test that sets the block timestamp to the claim period end and observes that no tokens are transferred. The bug violates the business logic that users should be able to withdraw any amount up to their deposited balance during the entire claim period, including the final second. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a normal balance, the withdraw button is enabled, but the transaction completes with no token transfer, leading to confusion and potential loss of confidence. The class of bug is an inclusive‑exclusive boundary mismatch, a common off‑by‑one error in time‑based state checks. The recommended fix is to align the comparison in Vault::unbondingActive with the other components by changing the strict less‑than operator to a less‑than‑or‑equal operator, thereby ensuring that the claim period is treated as inclusive across the whole system and that withdrawals at the exact end of the period succeed as intended.

title: Staking rewards susceptible to reward multiplier manipulation
description:
For staking in the Chainlink Operator and Community staking pools a staker is rewarded through the Chainlink [RewardVault](https://etherscan.io/address/0x996913c8c08472f584ab8834e925b06D0eb1D813). Here rewards are accrued per time staked.

There is however a twist to how the rewards work compared to the standard rewards design. To promote staying in your position for an extended period of time, Chainlink uses a `multiplier`. This goes from 0 to 1 over a period of 90 days (at time of writing). Just as you start staking you have a multiplier of 0, then it linearly increases to 1 over 90 days.

Were you to unstake during this period, the multiplier is reset and the forfeited rewards you should have earned are distributed to the other stakers.

This can be used to grief LinkPool stakers to reduce their rewards received rewarding stakers outside of LinkPool.

A user could iterate depositing a full vault (+ 1 LINK) and withdrawing a full vault to iterate through the whole current vault group. Thus resetting all the multipliers for the vaults.

A quick overview of the impact using current numbers from the community pool:

Current emission rate for community stakers is `~0.05 LINK/s`. The community vault is currently full with a total of `40875000 LINK` staked. This gives a gain per token per second of `0.05 / 40875000 =~ 1.2e-09`

LinkPool has a total stake `1324452 LINK`, ~3% of the pool.

As mentioned above, the multiplier period is `90 days` and the unbonding period is `4 weeks` which is the fastest you can reset the multiplier.

This gives a reward calculation:
```
perTokenPerS*(staked*0.2)*4 weeks =~ 783 LINK
```
To get the total forfeited you'll need to multiply with `1-(staked time/multiplier period)`:
```
perTokenPerS*(staked*0.2)*4 weeks*(1 - (4 weeks/90 days)) =~ 540 LINK
```
Hence in this case a total of 540 LINK would be lost. Note that this only applies to when the vaults start from 0 multiplier. If a vault was previously at `>90 days` there wouldn't be any forfeit hence the gain is only gotten the second time you do this for a vault group. As it is only then the multiplier is completely reset.

To see the profitability of this, the gained `540 LINK` is split into the pool:
```
540/40875000 = 1.3e-5 per held link
```
If a user has 100 vaults (with maximum deposit 15000 LINK each), this would gain them a total of 19 LINK which is in the ballpark of what the gas would probably cost of this.

Hence the attack vector is pretty small. However there is still a possibility for griefing or un-intended loss of rewards due to vaults having their multiplier unnecessarily reset.

Note, that this is taken with the current community staking pool distribution. The attack grows more profitable the larger the LinkPool stake is.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a reward‑multiplier manipulation in the Chainlink staking system. Stakers earn rewards from a vault that applies a linear multiplier that grows from 0 to 1 over a 90‑day period. When a vault is withdrawn before the multiplier reaches 1, the multiplier is reset to 0 and the unearned portion of the reward is redistributed to the remaining vaults. The contract does not restrict who can trigger a withdrawal for any vault, nor does it enforce any ordering on the withdrawal index. An attacker can therefore deposit the maximum amount into a vault, immediately withdraw it, and repeat the process for every vault in the pool. Each withdrawal forces the multiplier of that vault back to 0, causing the rewards that would have accrued during the elapsed staking time to be forfeited and shared with the other participants. From the point of view of a legitimate staker, the expected increase in reward over time is reduced; the user may see a lower reward balance or even a missing reward that was expected after a month of staking. The impact is a reduction of up to several hundred LINK for the targeted pool, which, when spread across many vaults, can amount to a noticeable loss for honest participants. The issue appears only when a vault is withdrawn before the 90‑day multiplier matures, which is the case during the four‑week unbonding period that the protocol allows. The flaw was discovered during a security audit performed by Cyfrin, who noted that the reward‑distribution logic does not verify that a withdrawal is the result of the vault owner’s intent and that the multiplier reset can be triggered repeatedly without cost. Because the reward reduction is a gradual accounting discrepancy, it may be difficult for users to notice; the UI simply shows a lower accrued reward amount, which can be mistaken for normal variance. The vulnerability belongs to the class of reward manipulation or economic griefing bugs, where business‑logic assumptions about monotonic reward growth are violated. To mitigate the issue, a withdrawal timelock could be introduced to prevent rapid deposit‑withdraw cycles, and the withdrawal index could be forced to rotate forward so that the same vault cannot be repeatedly targeted within a short window. These changes would preserve the intended incentive that rewards increase with staking duration and stop external actors from artificially resetting multipliers.

title: M-04 | Chainlink Price Lacks Price/Sequencer Validation
