An attacker could trigger a repayment, observe the unchanged high rate, and then open new positions that are priced incorrectly, effectively extracting excess value or causing LPs to receive less interest than they are entitled to. The impact includes inaccurate accounting, potential loss of interest revenue for liquidity providers, and distorted borrowing costs that may undermine the economic assumptions of the protocol. The issue manifests whenever payDebt is called, which occurs during normal debt settlement, and it affects all participants that depend on the interestRate: borrowers, LPs, and the protocol itself. It was discovered during a manual audit review of state‑update logic, where the auditor noticed that the interestRate variable is never assigned after the repayment step. The bug is subtle because the UI may continue to display the same rate, and the contract’s public view functions still return the stored value, making the inconsistency hard to spot without tracing internal state changes. To remediate, the contract should recalculate the utilizationRate after payDebt, derive the correct interestRate from it, and update the stored variable before the function exits, optionally emitting an event to signal the change. This aligns the on‑chain accounting with the intended business logic that interest rates must reflect the current market utilization, ensuring that rewards and borrowing costs are computed correctly.

title: M-11 | Interest Rates Not Accurate To Liquidity Updates
description:
The utilization fees in the Perps-V3 market are dependent on the amount of credit capacity
delegated to the market by the V3 core system, however the utilization rate does not update when
the amount of backing liquidity changes.
For instance, a delegator can undelegate from a vault which provides credit capacity to the Perps-V3
market and increase the utilization ratio. However this utilization update is not reflected in the
utilization rate until a updateInterestRate is triggered on the Perps-V3 side.
Therefore the interest rate that is charged can be misrepresentative of the actual amount of liquidity
utilized during these periods before an interest rate update is triggered.
A malicious LP could abuse this by minting sUSD directly before a interest rate update in the
Perps-V3 market, this way increasing the utilization ratio and forcing the the interest rate for all
traders to be higher over the next period.
The LP may then backrun the interest rate update and burn their sUSD that was minted.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑inconsistency bug in the Perps‑V3 market where the utilization‑based interest rate does not automatically reflect changes in the backing liquidity supplied by the V3 core system. The market calculates fees using a utilization ratio that depends on the amount of credit capacity delegated to it, but this ratio is only refreshed when the function updateInterestRate is explicitly called. Consequently, when a delegator removes (undelegates) liquidity, the actual utilization of the market increases, yet the stored utilization rate remains stale until the next manual update. This mismatch allows the reported interest rate to be lower or higher than the true economic condition, misleading traders about the cost of holding positions. A malicious liquidity provider can exploit the window between a liquidity change and the subsequent interest‑rate update by minting sUSD (the market’s synthetic asset) to artificially inflate the utilization ratio, thereby forcing a higher interest rate for all traders. After the higher rate is in effect, the attacker can back‑run the updateInterestRate call, burn the minted sUSD, and capture the excess funding fees earned during the inflated period. The impact is that traders may pay unexpectedly high funding costs, eroding their profits or causing losses, while the protocol’s accounting assumptions about fair interest rates are violated. The issue occurs whenever backing liquidity is altered—either added or removed—without an immediate call to updateInterestRate, which is the default behavior of the current implementation. All market participants, including traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself, are affected because the economic incentives are distorted. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit of the Perps‑V3 contracts, where the auditor noted that the utilization variable is only updated in a single external function rather than being tied to liquidity‑change events. The bug can be hard to notice because the interest rate appears to change only at discrete intervals, and the discrepancy may be small for short periods, making it blend with normal market volatility. To remediate, the protocol should ensure that any change to the delegated credit capacity triggers an immediate recalculation of the utilization ratio and updates the interest rate, effectively turning the utilization metric into a real‑time oracle. This aligns the reported rates with the actual liquidity state, restores correct accounting, and prevents manipulation through timing attacks. The class of bug is a delayed state update or stale oracle problem, where on‑chain economic parameters are not kept in sync with underlying resource changes, leading to inaccurate pricing and potential financial loss for users.

title: M-12 | Stepwise Jump After Update
description:
A trader's pending funding and interest are calculated based on an accrued value which is updated
each time positions are updated based on the current rate and elapsed time.
The issue lies when admin updates funding or interest rate parameters without first realizing the
accumulated funding/interest with the old parameters.
Any rate increase/decrease would directly affect the funding/interest that a user would have to pay
(positively or negatively).
For example:
T0: User opens position, market caches interestRate = 2%
T5: Admin adjusts interest rate gradient, market interest rate should increase to 3% but
InterestRate.update not performed so new rate is not stored.
T10: User closes position
Interest owed calculated using 2% rate -- (calculateNextInterest uses the last cached rate)
Instead user should have been charged 2% from T0-T5, and 3% from T5-T10.
bug_full: An on‑chain perpetual market calculates each trader’s pending funding and interest by multiplying an accrued factor with the current interest rate. The contract stores the last used rate in a cache and updates the accrued factor only when a specific internal function is called. The vulnerability occurs when an administrator changes the global funding or interest‑rate parameters without first invoking the function that recomputes the accrued funding using the old rate. Because the cached rate is not refreshed, the next funding or interest calculation continues to use the stale rate for the entire remaining lifetime of the position. Consequently, a trader who opened a position before the rate change is charged (or credited) with the old rate for the whole period, instead of the correct piece‑wise rate that should apply before and after the update. For example, a position opened at 2 % interest that should have been charged 2 % for the first five minutes and 3 % for the next five minutes is instead settled using 2 % for the full ten minutes. This mis‑calculation can be exploited by an admin who deliberately raises or lowers the rate shortly before a large position is closed, causing the protocol to collect less funding than intended or to over‑charge traders. The impact is financial: traders receive an unexpected refund or pay an unexpected fee, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about revenue per time interval are broken. The bug manifests only when a rate change occurs while positions are open and the recompute function is omitted; it is easy to miss because the UI shows the new rate, yet the on‑chain settlement uses the old cached value, leading to subtle discrepancies that appear only in settlement traces. The issue was identified during a systematic audit of the funding‑interest update flow. To remediate, the contract must call the internal recomputeFunding routine before any funding‑rate parameter is altered and must call updateInterestRate before any interest‑rate parameter is changed, ensuring that accrued values are materialised with the previous rate before the cache is overwritten.

title: M-13 | Partial Liquidators Not Fairly Rewarded
description:
Keepers that perform partial liquidations on flagged accounts may be responsible for liquidating
multiple open positions.
However, they only receive a static liquidateKeeperCost, as opposed to flagKeeperCost (received by
keeper that flags the account) which increases based on the number of open positions.
If the gas cost of liquidating multiple positions is greater than the reward, these partial liquidation
keepers may not be incentivized to perform the liquidations at all which is detrimental to the system.
On the other hand, the keeper that flags the account for liquidation receives flagKeeperCost
regardless of number of positions that were actually liquidated.
If the liquidation window happened to be small and only one out of many positions were liquidated,
the keeper still receives the cost of liquidating all open positions.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incentive mis‑alignment in the liquidation workflow of the Perps V3 protocol. When an account with multiple open positions is flagged for liquidation, a keeper that performs the flagging receives a reward (flagKeeperCost) that scales with the number of positions reported. In contrast, a keeper that actually executes the liquidation receives a fixed reward (liquidateKeeperCost) regardless of how many positions it has to close. Because the gas required to close several positions can exceed the static reward, partial‑liquidation keepers may find the operation unprofitable and may choose not to act. This creates a situation where under‑collateralized positions remain open, increasing the risk of systemic loss. The problem manifests whenever an account holds more than one position and the liquidation window is short, so that only a subset of positions can be liquidated before the deadline. The affected parties are the keepers, who receive unfair compensation, and the protocol users whose positions may stay liquidatable longer than expected, potentially leading to unexpected losses. The issue was identified during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noticed that the reward formula does not account for the actual work performed. It can be hard to spot because the static reward values appear reasonable in isolation, and the discrepancy only emerges under multi‑position liquidation scenarios. To remediate, the liquidateKeeperCost should be made dynamic, increasing proportionally to the number of positions actually liquidated, and the flagKeeperCost should be capped or otherwise limited so that flaggers are not over‑rewarded when few positions are actually liquidated. Aligning the reward structure restores the economic incentive for keepers to perform partial liquidations and preserves the protocol’s safety guarantees.

title: M-14 | validDistributorExists Not Checked
description:
The modifyCollateral function calls validDistributorExists which returns a boolean that indicates if a
distributor of the given collateral is set or not.
The modifyCollateral does not check if the returned boolean is true or false. Therefore if no
distributor is set, the flow will continue.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a collateral‑modification routine that invokes a helper function returning a boolean flag indicating whether a distributor contract has been registered for the supplied collateral type. The routine neglects to verify the returned flag before proceeding, so when the flag is false – meaning no distributor is configured – the execution continues as if a valid distributor were present. This missing pre‑condition check is the root cause: the contract does not enforce the invariant that a distributor must exist before collateral can be altered. An attacker or any user can trigger the modifyCollateral entry point with a collateral asset that lacks an associated distributor. Because the code assumes the distributor exists, subsequent logic may reference an uninitialized address, skip essential accounting steps, or emit events that do not reflect the true state. The practical impact is that the protocol’s accounting can become inconsistent, potentially allowing funds to be locked, withdrawn incorrectly, or left in an undefined state. Users may observe that after attempting to modify collateral they receive no confirmation, their balance appears unchanged, or later withdrawals fail because the internal bookkeeping no longer matches the on‑chain state. The issue manifests whenever modifyCollateral is called with a collateral token for which the system administrator has not set up a distributor, a situation that can arise during contract upgrades, misconfiguration, or malicious contract deployment. All participants who rely on correct collateral handling – lenders, traders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the invariant breach can compromise the safety of the entire margin system. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit that inspected the control flow of modifyCollateral and noticed that the boolean result of validDistributorExists was never used. It is easy to miss because the function call does not revert or emit an error, so the transaction appears successful even though the internal state may be corrupted. To remediate, the contract should explicitly check the boolean and revert with a clear error message when no distributor is set, for example by adding a require statement that validates the existence of the distributor before any state changes are performed. This restores the intended invariant and prevents the protocol from entering an inconsistent accounting state.

title: M-15 | Fill Price Funding And Interest Discrepancy
description:
In _settleOrder and updatePositionData, oldPosition's PnL is called with fillPrice, which computes
funding and interest based on fillPrice.
This is problematic for two reasons:
a) it causes a discrepancy with recomputeFunding which uses oraclePrice (see AsyncOrder.sol:
289).
b) Funding and interest should not be based upon fillPrice, as this price includes a
premium/discount according to how the trade affects the market skew.
As a result, shorts pay more fees when they balance the market and less when they imbalance the
market. Consider this scenario:
• order price = 1000
• short trade (positive price impact), fill price = 1010 => more fees are paid
• short trade (negative price impact), fill price = 990 => less fees are paid
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an accounting mismatch in the perpetual futures contract where the funding and interest components of a position’s profit‑and‑loss (PnL) are calculated using the trade’s fill price instead of the oracle price that represents the unbiased market value. In the _settleOrder function and in updatePositionData the code calls oldPosition.getPnl(fillPrice) which internally derives funding and interest from that price. Because the fill price incorporates a premium or discount that reflects the immediate impact of the trade on market skew, the resulting funding charge is not neutral: a short position that moves the market toward balance receives a higher fill price (e.g., 1010 when the order price is 1000) and therefore pays more funding, while a short that pushes the market further out of balance receives a lower fill price (e.g., 990) and pays less. The protocol’s recomputeFunding routine, used elsewhere, correctly bases its calculation on the oracle price, creating a discrepancy between the two paths. An attacker can exploit this by submitting trades that deliberately generate favorable price impact, thereby reducing the funding fees owed or inflating fees paid by counterparties, which distorts the intended incentive structure and can erode protocol revenue. The issue manifests whenever a position is settled or its data refreshed, i.e., during order execution and position updates, and it affects any trader who opens or closes a position, especially short positions that are sensitive to price impact. Because the fee calculation appears to succeed and the contract does not emit an explicit warning, the problem can be hard to notice; only a careful comparison of funding amounts against oracle‑based expectations reveals the inconsistency. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect reference price for financial calculations” or “price‑impact‑biased funding computation”. From a user perspective the symptom is that a trader may receive a higher‑than‑expected funding charge or a lower refund after closing a position, contradicting the expectation that funding should be independent of the immediate trade impact. The root cause is the misuse of fillPrice as the reference for funding and interest. The recommended remediation is to replace the fillPrice argument with the oracle price (or the runtime.currentPrice that mirrors the oracle) in both _settleOrder and updatePositionData, ensuring that funding and interest are derived from a market‑neutral price source. This aligns the accounting with the protocol’s design, restores fair fee distribution, and eliminates the incentive for price‑impact manipulation.

title: M-16 | Missing Access Control In payDebt
description:
Except for the payDebt function, all other external, state-modifying functions in the Perps-V3 system
have the access control: FeatureFlag.ensureAccessToFeature(Flags.PERPS_SYSTEM).
This could lead to unexpected behavior in the event that the system is paused through the removal
of access to flag feature.
Also, the payDebt function also does not check that the msg.sender is indeed the account owner,
allowing anyone to reduce debt and increase collateral for another account. It is unclear if this is
intended behavior.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the payDebt function of the Perps‑V3 contract suite. Unlike every other external state‑modifying entry point, payDebt does not enforce the global feature flag check FeatureFlag.ensureAccessToFeature(Flags.PERPS_SYSTEM). Consequently the function remains callable even when the Perps system is deliberately paused by revoking the flag. In addition, the function lacks any verification that the caller (msg.sender) is the owner of the account whose debt is being repaid, nor does it require a specific permission such as AccountRBAC._PERPS_MODIFY_COLLATERAL_PERMISSION. The root cause is therefore a missing access‑control guard that should both respect the system‑wide pause mechanism and validate the caller’s authority over the target account. An attacker can exploit this by invoking payDebt with arbitrary account identifiers. By supplying a positive payment amount, the attacker reduces the recorded debt of the victim account while simultaneously increasing its collateral balance, because the function credits collateral proportionally to the payment. This manipulation can be performed for any account, including those of honest users, without any on‑chain indication that the call originated from an unauthorized party. The impact is a breach of accounting integrity: debt figures become artificially low, collateral figures become artificially high, and the protocol’s risk parameters are distorted. Users may notice that their account shows a higher collateral amount or a lower debt after a transaction they never initiated, leading to confusion or potential loss of value if the protocol later liquidates the artificially inflated position. The issue manifests whenever the payDebt function is called, especially during periods when the Perps system is paused, because the missing feature‑flag guard bypasses the intended shutdown. It affects all account holders, liquidators, and the overall protocol security model, as the ability to modify another user’s financial state without permission undermines trust. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit that compared access‑control patterns across the contract’s external functions and flagged the inconsistency. Because the function performs legitimate‑looking arithmetic and emits no unusual events, the problem can be hard to spot in routine testing or by casual observers. To remediate, the function should be updated to include FeatureFlag.ensureAccessToFeature(Flags.PERPS_SYSTEM) to respect the pause state, and it should call Account.loadAccountAndValidatePermission with the appropriate permission constant to ensure that only the account owner or an authorized role can modify debt and collateral. This aligns the function with the contract’s overall security model and prevents unauthorized debt reduction and collateral inflation.

title: M-17 | Max Collateral Can Be Exceeded Through payDebt
description:
In the modifyCollateral function, the added collateral amount is validated through
globalPerpsMarket.validateCollateralAmount to ensure that the maximum collateral limit is not
exceeded.
However, in the payDebt function, this check is not performed, even though the function can increase
an account's sUSD collateral (as any excess over the amount used to pay debt is added to the
collateral).
Additionally, sUSD collateral may exceed the maximum amount through the realization of profits.
Moreover, the payDebt function lacks the validation to ensure that the maximum number of collateral
types per account is not exceeded, which is done through PerpsAccount.validateMaxCollaterals.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the perps market contract where the function that settles debt payments (payDebt) can unintentionally increase an account's sUSD collateral without enforcing the protocol‑defined limits on total collateral amount and on the number of distinct collateral types. In the normal collateral‑adjustment path (modifyCollateral) the contract calls globalPerpsMarket.validateCollateralAmount and PerpsAccount.validateMaxCollaterals to ensure that an account never holds more than the maximum allowed sUSD collateral and never exceeds the permitted variety of collateral assets. PayDebt, however, skips these checks. When a user supplies more sUSD than is required to clear the outstanding debt, the surplus is automatically credited to the account as additional collateral. Likewise, realized profits are added to the sUSD collateral balance. Because the validation steps are omitted, an attacker can repeatedly overpay debt or trigger profit realizations to push the sUSD collateral beyond the configured ceiling or to add extra collateral types, thereby breaching the risk parameters that the protocol relies on for liquidation and margin calculations. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated: positions may become under‑collateralised from the system’s perspective while appearing healthy to users, leading to potential liquidation failures, inaccurate risk metrics, and ultimately loss of funds for honest participants. This condition can occur any time a user calls payDebt with an amount larger than the debt owed, or when profit distribution logic adds sUSD to the account, and it affects any account holder as well as the overall market’s safety guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the validation logic across related functions and noticed the missing calls in payDebt. It is subtle because the UI typically shows the user’s balance increasing as expected after an over‑payment, giving no immediate indication that a protocol limit has been breached. To remediate, the payDebt implementation should invoke the same validation routines used by modifyCollateral—globalPerpsMarket.validateCollateralAmount to enforce the maximum collateral amount and PerpsAccount.validateMaxCollaterals to enforce the maximum number of collateral types—before crediting any excess sUSD as collateral. This ensures that all pathways that can increase collateral are subject to the same safety checks, preserving the intended accounting invariants and protecting users from unexpected collateral limit violations.

title: M-18 | Account Can Be Made Liquidateable By Cancelling
description:
Cancellation charges account with keeper fee. Which this can put the account into a liquidatable
state. This will result in immediate loss for user who could have withdrawn their funds otherwise.
Order’s cancel-ability can be controlled by manipulating the skew. In addition to the fee for
cancellation, the liquidation fees provide an added incentive to cancel the order which could even
cover the costs of the skew manipulation.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the cancellation flow of perpetual futures positions in the protocol. When a user cancels an open order, the system charges a keeper fee that is deducted from the account's collateral. The contract does not verify that the remaining collateral after this deduction stays above the liquidation threshold. Consequently, if the account was already close to the required margin, the additional fee can push the collateral ratio below the required level, causing the account to become liquidatable immediately after the cancellation. The root cause is an insufficient post‑cancellation collateral check combined with the ability to influence the market skew, which determines the size of the keeper fee and the liquidation incentive. An attacker can manipulate the skew to increase the fee or to make the order appear cancel‑able, then either force the user to cancel or wait for the user to cancel voluntarily. Once the fee is applied, the account’s health factor drops, and a keeper can liquidate the position, seizing the remaining collateral. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a normal cancellation action, but shortly afterwards the account is flagged as liquidatable and the user may see their balance reduced to zero or a failed withdrawal attempt, contrary to the expectation that cancelling simply removes the order without affecting funds. The impact is a direct loss of the user’s remaining margin, which could have been withdrawn safely if the cancellation had not triggered liquidation. This issue was discovered during a manual audit of the perps V3 contract where the cancellation logic was examined and the missing collateral validation was identified. It is hard to notice because the fee is a legitimate protocol charge and the liquidation occurs only under tight margin conditions, making it appear as a normal market event rather than a bug. To remediate, the contract should enforce a validation step after applying the keeper fee to ensure the account’s collateral ratio remains above the liquidation threshold, reject cancellations that would cause under‑collateralisation, and consider limiting the fee or protecting against skew manipulation that can artificially inflate the fee or liquidation incentive.

title: M-01 | MintUSD() Does Not Verify Market Capacities
description:
The mintUsd() function decreases the creditCapacity of the markets connected to the pool.
However, it does not verify if there is enough creditCapacity available to support the markets. As a
result, by using mintUsd, LPs can potentially push the markets below their minimumCredit.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the mintUsd function of the pool contract, which reduces the creditCapacity of each market linked to the pool when new USD is minted. The function lacks a verification step to ensure that the remaining creditCapacity after the reduction is still above the market's minimumCredit threshold. Because of this missing check, a liquidity provider (LP) can repeatedly call mintUsd and drive the creditCapacity of a market below its required minimum, effectively under‑collateralising the market. The root cause is an absent capacity‑validation guard, similar to the one used in delegateCollateral, that should prevent state transitions leading to a locked or insolvent market. An attacker can exploit the flaw by minting large amounts of USD in a single transaction or across multiple transactions, watching the creditCapacity drop until it breaches the minimumCredit limit. When this condition occurs, the market may become unable to honour withdrawals, positions may be forcibly liquidated, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions break, potentially resulting in loss of funds for users who rely on the market’s stability. The issue manifests only when the market’s creditCapacity is already close to its minimum and an LP initiates minting; under normal operating conditions with ample capacity the bug may remain unnoticed. It was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the behaviour of mintUsd with other functions that correctly enforce capacity constraints. The problem is subtle because the function does not revert or emit an obvious error; instead the state silently moves into an invalid region, making it hard to detect without explicit checks. To remediate, the contract should incorporate a verification step—such as calling a _verifyNotCapacityLocked routine—before decreasing creditCapacity, ensuring that the post‑mint capacity remains above the minimumCredit bound. This class of bug falls under missing invariant checks or capacity‑underflow errors, where business logic that guarantees sufficient collateral is not enforced, leading to unexpected zero balances, missing refunds, or funds disappearing from the market.

title: M-19 | Usage Of DEFAULT Price Tolerance
description:
getCurrentPrice from PerpsPrice.sol has a different staleness tolerances for different cases. In the
current cannon deployment, node's DEFAULT tolerance is settled as 1 hour.
Using a 1 hour price tolerance might lead to some attack vectors because user can maliciously
choose best price for their purpose from the last one hour to use.
Followings are some functions that uses DEFAULT tolerance and possible attack vectors that can be
used with them:
1. minimumCredit : This can be used to bypass checks (withdrawing collateral from market as an LP
when the minimumCredit is in the border)
2. isEligibleForLiquidation : Accounts that are liquidatable can settle order via bypassing this check.
3. reportedDebt : Can return not accurate values
4. View functions: Might be problematic for integrators.
The reason for decreased severity is because it requires no recent update in Pyth price within the
time period and because in order to create a large enough impact it requires good amount of price
change within one hour window.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the PerpsPrice contract determines price freshness. The function getCurrentPrice applies a default staleness tolerance of one hour, meaning that any price reported within the last sixty minutes is considered valid regardless of whether a newer price update has arrived. This default tolerance is used by several critical protocol functions – minimumCredit, isEligibleForLiquidation, reportedDebt and various view helpers – without additional verification. Because the tolerance is relatively long, an attacker can monitor the external price feed (for example Pyth) and wait until a price that is advantageous for a specific operation appears within the one‑hour window. When such a price is observed, the attacker can trigger a transaction that relies on the stale price, for instance withdrawing collateral as a liquidity provider when the minimumCredit check is borderline, or forcing a liquidation to succeed by bypassing the isEligibleForLiquidation guard. The reportedDebt view may also return a value that does not reflect the most recent market movement, leading integrators to make decisions based on inaccurate data. From a user perspective the symptoms can be confusing: a trader may see a liquidation succeed even though the account appears healthy, a liquidity provider may be able to pull out collateral that should be locked, or a dashboard may display a debt figure that is lower than the true obligation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the tolerance settings against the expected risk model of the protocol. It is subtle because the price data still looks recent – it is only older than the most recent feed update, which is not obvious without inspecting the tolerance constant. The impact is limited to scenarios where the price moves significantly within an hour; however, in volatile markets a large enough swing can cause material loss of funds or incorrect accounting. The recommended mitigation is to replace the generic DEFAULT tolerance with a stricter bound for functions that enforce security checks, and to introduce a dedicated STRICT tolerance for view functions that external integrators rely on. Protocol documentation should also warn integrators that view results may be stale if a strict tolerance is not enforced. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of price‑staleness or oracle‑tolerance weaknesses, where overly permissive time windows allow malicious actors to exploit outdated price information to bypass economic safeguards, resulting in unexpected fund movements and inaccurate protocol state.

title: M-20 | Unsafe Collateral Amount Because Of Fees
description:
When an order is settled, the account the order is committed for is charged orderFees. There are
validations in [AsyncOrder.validateRequest](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/perps-v3-1/blob/fd4c562868761bdcafb1a3dc080c3465e4e4de76/markets/perps-market/contracts/storage/AsyncOrder.sol#L333-L347) that the collateral value will not drop below the needed
margin after paying the fees.
The following must be true: currentAvailableMargin = [getRequiredMarginWithNewPosition](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/perps-v3-1/blob/fd4c562868761bdcafb1a3dc080c3465e4e4de76/markets/perps-market/contracts/storage/AsyncOrder.sol#L529-L583)() +
orderFees.
However, getRequiredMarginWithNewPosition returns 0 when a position is being reduced.
This makes the above expression equivalent to:
currentAvailableMargin = orderFees
This check is not sufficient. In the following scenario:
• required margin = $500
• currentAvailableMargin = $550
• orderFees = 100
The currentAvailableMargin = orderFees will pass, but after the account is charged the fees, its
margin will fall below the required margin and their positions will instantly become liquidatable.
bug_full: An unsafe collateral validation occurs during order settlement when the contract charges order fees. The system is supposed to ensure that after fees are deducted the account’s available margin remains above the required margin for the new position. The validation logic adds the order fees to the required margin returned by getRequiredMarginWithNewPosition and compares this sum to the current available margin. However, getRequiredMarginWithNewPosition returns zero whenever a position is being reduced, because a reduced position is assumed to need no additional margin. Consequently the check simplifies to verifying that the current available margin is at least equal to the order fees. In a scenario where the required margin is $500, the account has $550 available, and the order fees are $100, the check passes because $550 ≥ $100. After the fees are deducted, the account is left with $450, which is below the $500 required margin, making the position instantly liquidatable. The vulnerability therefore allows a trader to unintentionally fall below the margin requirement after a reduction trade, leading to unexpected liquidation and potential loss of collateral. The issue is triggered only when a position is reduced and fees are non‑zero, and it affects any user who relies on the margin check to avoid liquidation. It was discovered during a manual audit of the AsyncOrder contract where the margin validation code was examined. The problem is subtle because the function returning zero for reduced positions appears correct in isolation, and the additional fee deduction is not obvious in the validation expression. To remediate, the contract should perform a post‑fee margin check or adjust the required‑margin calculation to include fees, ensuring that the account cannot become liquidatable as a direct result of fee payment. This class of bug is an accounting‑logic error where the protocol’s safety check does not account for all state changes, breaking the business rule that a trader’s collateral must always cover the required margin after any operation.

title: M-21 | Vaults With Zero Delegation Prevent Liquidations
description:
The LiquidationAssetmanager contract contains an array of addresses known as
poolDelegatedCollateralTypes.
When an account undergoes liquidation, the distribution of its collateral takes place within the
distributeCollateral function of this contract.
This particular function iterates over all pool collateral types, or vaults, and executes
distributeRewards for each of them in proportion to the amount held by the vault.
By tracing the sequence of calls, we eventually arrive at the distribute function within
RewardDistributon.sol. In this function, an attempt to distribute a reward to 0 vault delegators will
result in an error and cause a revert.
bug_full: During the liquidation process the LiquidationAssetmanager contract iterates over every collateral type listed in the poolDelegatedCollateralTypes array and calls distributeRewards for each vault. The reward distribution is performed by the distribute function in RewardDistribution.sol, which assumes that the vault holds a positive amount of delegated collateral and that the reward amount is non-zero. When a vault has zero delegated collateral, the call to distribute attempts to allocate a reward to a set of zero delegators, causing an internal require or division by zero to fail and the whole transaction to revert. As a result the liquidation of the target account is aborted, leaving the user’s position un-liquidated even though it is under-collateralised. This behaviour can be triggered whenever any vault in the pool has a collateral balance of zero, which may happen if a delegator withdraws all collateral or if a newly created vault has not yet received any delegation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by tracing the call chain from LiquidationAssetmanager through distributeCollateral to RewardDistribution and observing the revert on zero-balance vaults. Because the revert occurs only in the edge case of zero collateral, it may not be obvious during normal testing and the error message does not indicate the underlying logic problem, making it hard to spot. The impact is that liquidations can be blocked, preventing the protocol from recovering under-collateralised positions, potentially locking funds and exposing the system to solvency risk. Users expect that a liquidation will either succeed or fail with a clear reason, but instead they see a generic transaction failure and their collateral remains unchanged. The vulnerability belongs to the class of unchecked external calls with zero-value assumptions or division-by-zero/revert on empty set bugs. To remediate the problem the contract should include an explicit check before invoking distributeRewards: if the vault's collateral amount is zero or the calculated reward amount is zero, the function should skip the distribution for that vault and continue with the next one. This guard restores the intended liquidation flow and ensures that the protocol's accounting assumptions are not violated.

title: M-02 | Price Impact Sandwich Attack
description:
Users who balance the skew can be sandwiched by an attacker who front runs and back runs the
call:
• The skew is at 1000
• The user tries to balance the skew by shorting -1000
• Attacker front runs the call and shorts -1000 (receives a positive price impact)
• User call goes through and the user imbalances the skew by -1000 (receives a negative price
impact)
• Attacker back runs the call and longs 1000 (receives a positive price impact)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a price‑impact sandwich attack that can be performed against users who attempt to rebalance a market skew in a perpetuals contract. The protocol maintains a net position (skew) that is expected to be close to zero; users can submit a transaction that shorts or longs an amount equal to the current skew in order to bring the market back to equilibrium. Because the contract calculates price impact based on the net change of the transaction, an attacker can front‑run the user’s balancing transaction, submit a trade of the same size in the opposite direction, and capture a positive price impact before the user’s trade is executed. When the user’s trade finally executes, the market is now imbalanced in the opposite direction, causing the user to receive a negative price impact and to move the skew further away from zero. The attacker then back‑runs with a trade that restores the original skew, again receiving a positive price impact. The net effect is that the attacker profits from the price impact while the user’s intended rebalancing fails, potentially leaving the user with a worse execution price, higher slippage, or even a loss of value. This scenario occurs whenever a user submits a transaction that directly manipulates the market skew without additional protection such as time‑weighted average price checks or strict slippage limits. It primarily affects traders who rely on the contract’s automatic skew‑balancing feature, and it can be exploited by any participant who can observe pending transactions in the mempool and submit their own trades with higher gas price. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the perps V3 contract where the price‑impact formula was examined and the ordering of state updates allowed the attacker to capture the impact before the user’s trade. The problem is subtle because the contract’s logic correctly updates the skew and price impact for each individual trade; the vulnerability only appears when multiple trades are sequenced in a single block, making it easy to miss in unit tests that consider isolated calls. To mitigate the risk, the protocol should inform users about the possibility of sandwich attacks and encourage them to set appropriate slippage tolerances, or alternatively redesign the price‑impact calculation to be based on a time‑weighted average or to lock the skew state for the duration of a user‑initiated rebalancing transaction. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of front‑running or sandwich attacks that exploit deterministic price‑impact formulas in DeFi markets, breaking the expectation that a balancing trade will improve the user’s position and instead causing the user to receive a worse price or lose value.

title: M-03 | newRequiredMargin Uses fillPrice
description:
In getRequiredMarginWithNewPosition, newRequiredMargin is calculated with fillPrice. This is
inaccurate as fillPrice includes a premium/discount, and therefore should only be used for PnL
calculations.
Otherwise, a new position might be within the required margin (based on fillPrice) but immediately
after settling it could be eligible for liquidation (which calculates margin based on oracle price).
This is also inconsistent with how oldRequiredMargin is calculated in the next step, which uses
currentPrice.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inaccurate margin calculation in the function that determines the required collateral for a new position. Instead of using the current oracle price, the code uses the fill price, which already incorporates a premium or discount applied at trade execution. Because the fill price deviates from the true market price, the required margin is underestimated. When the position is later settled, the protocol re‑evaluates margin using the oracle price; the previously sufficient collateral may now be insufficient, causing the position to become eligible for liquidation even though the trader was told the margin requirement was met at entry. This mismatch occurs whenever a non‑zero premium or discount exists, typically in volatile or low‑liquidity markets. Traders opening positions are directly affected because they may see a healthy margin on the UI, only to have their position liquidated shortly after, resulting in unexpected loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the margin logic for new positions with the logic used for liquidation and noticed the inconsistent price source. It is hard to notice because the initial margin check passes, so no error is raised at the time of opening, and the UI shows the expected collateral amount; the problem only surfaces later during settlement, making the failure appear as a sudden liquidation rather than a calculation error. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of accounting or price‑oracle mismatches where a contract uses two different price references for related financial checks, violating the assumption that margin requirements are based on the same market price used for liquidation. The correct fix is to replace the fill price with the current oracle price when computing the new required margin, ensuring that both entry and liquidation use a consistent price reference and that the protocol’s safety guarantees hold.

title: M-04 | Margin Liquidations Should Remove Pending Order
description:
During liquidateMarginOnly, the liquidated account may have a pending order which is not removed.
The order cannot be settled and if market price were to go outside of the priceLimit range, the order
can now be cancelled.
However, as the account has been liquidated, the cancel order settlement reward is charged as debt
to the account but may never be repaid. This debt will exist in the system as permanent bad debt.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑cleanup flaw that occurs during the margin‑only liquidation process of a perpetual futures contract. When the liquidateMarginOnly function is invoked on an account that still holds a pending order, the routine does not delete or settle that order. Consequently the order remains in the system even though the account’s collateral has been seized. Because the order is still considered active, it can later be cancelled by anyone. The cancellation logic charges a settlement reward to the account that originated the order; however, since the account has already been liquidated, the reward is recorded as a debt that the account can never repay. This creates a permanent bad‑debt entry in the protocol’s accounting ledger. The impact is that the protocol’s total liabilities become larger than its assets, effectively “money disappears” from the system and the affected user ends up with a negative balance that never resolves. The issue manifests only when a liquidation is performed on an account with an outstanding order, a situation that is not uncommon in highly leveraged trading environments. It affects any trader whose position is liquidated while they have open orders, as well as the overall health of the protocol because the unrecoverable debt reduces the net collateralization ratio. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the Synthetix Perps V3 codebase, where the auditor traced the liquidation flow and noticed that pending orders were never cleared. The problem is subtle because the UI typically shows that the account has been liquidated and may not display the lingering order, making the debt entry appear out of nowhere. From a security perspective the bug belongs to the class of order‑lifecycle management errors where state is left orphaned after a critical transition. To remediate the issue the liquidation routine should explicitly remove or settle any pending orders belonging to the liquidated account before finalizing the debt calculation, ensuring that no settlement reward is charged to an already‑closed position. This change restores accounting consistency and prevents the creation of permanent bad debt.

title: M-05 | Order Fee Calculation Uses The Wrong Price
description:
• The fillPrice is used in the calculateOrderFee function to calculate the notional.
• As the orderFee is a percentage taken from the notional a higher fillPrice will lead to a higher
orderFee and a lower fillPrice will lead to a lower orderFee.
This impacts long trades correctly, but short trades wrong:
• Long Trade:
• With a positive price impact the fillPrice decreases
• With a negative price impact the fillPrice increases
• Short Trade:
• With a positive price impact the fillPrice increases
• With a negative price impact the fillPrice decreases
Therefore a positive price impact on a short (trader balances the OI) increases the fillPrice and
therefore also the orderFee of the trader and vice versa.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect fee calculation in the perpetual trading contract where the notional amount for the order fee is derived from the fillPrice instead of the intended orderPrice. The fillPrice reflects the execution price after applying price impact, while the orderPrice represents the price before impact. Because the order fee is a fixed percentage of the notional, using the fillPrice causes the fee to vary with price impact. For long positions this behaviour unintentionally aligns with expectations: a positive price impact lowers the fillPrice and therefore reduces the fee, while a negative impact raises the fee. However, for short positions the relationship is inverted: a positive price impact (which occurs when a trader reduces open interest) raises the fillPrice, leading to a higher fee, and a negative impact lowers the fee. This mismatch means that short traders are charged more when the market moves in their favour, violating the intended accounting logic that fees should be based on the original order price. The issue can be exploited by deliberately creating or amplifying positive price impact on short trades, for example through coordinated trading or by submitting large orders that shift the fillPrice upward, thereby inflating the fee taken from the trader. The impact is financial loss for short traders, potential erosion of trust in the protocol’s fee model, and distortion of market incentives. The bug manifests whenever a short trade is executed with any non‑zero price impact, which is a common scenario in leveraged perpetual markets. Users experience the problem as unexpectedly high fees; a trader may see a fee that is larger than anticipated, reducing net proceeds or even turning a profitable trade into a loss. The discrepancy is subtle because the fee is expressed as a percentage of notional, so the calculation appears mathematically correct, and the problem only appears when comparing long and short fee behaviour. The flaw was identified during a systematic audit of the fee logic, where the auditor noticed that the fee formula referenced the fillPrice variable. To remediate the issue, the contract should compute the notional using the orderPrice – the price before impact – ensuring that fees are independent of the direction‑specific price impact and consistent across long and short positions. This correction restores the intended fee model, aligns with business logic that fees are a fixed proportion of the intended trade size, and prevents inadvertent over‑charging of short traders.

title: M-06 | Allow Liquidations While Market Is Disabled
description:
All state-modifying functions validate that the feature flag PERPS_SYSTEM is enabled before
allowing transactions to proceed. This includes liquidations, which implies that if the feature flag is
disabled, liquidations cannot be processed.
This is undesirable because open positions that become liquidatable while the feature flag is
disabled can lead to significant bad debt in the system.
Additionally, traders should be allowed to close their open positions even while the market is
disabled to avoid liquidations.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of a single feature flag, PERPS_SYSTEM, to gate every state‑modifying function in the perpetual contracts module, including both trading actions and liquidation logic. When the flag is turned off to disable a market, the contract also blocks the liquidation function and the user‑initiated position‑close function. Consequently, if a trader’s position becomes under‑collateralised while the market is disabled, the protocol is unable to trigger a liquidation or allow the trader to voluntarily close the position. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition that can lead to accumulated bad debt because the system’s accounting assumes that liquidations will always be possible for unsafe positions. The issue is discovered during a security audit that examined the gating logic of the PERPS_SYSTEM flag and noticed that no finer‑grained controls exist. It may be hard to notice because disabling a market is generally expected to pause new trades, not to prevent existing positions from being resolved, and typical test suites may not simulate the scenario where a market is disabled while positions are still open. The impact affects any user with an open position at the time of the disable, the protocol’s collateral pool, and ultimately the overall solvency of the system, as bad debt can erode the pool’s value. From a user’s perspective, attempts to close a position or to trigger a liquidation will revert with an error indicating that the PERPS_SYSTEM feature is disabled, leaving the user’s balance locked and potentially resulting in a loss of funds if the position continues to accrue losses. The bug belongs to the class of improper feature‑flag granularity and denial‑of‑service logic errors that break essential economic invariants. To remediate the issue, the contract should introduce separate flags or conditional checks that allow liquidation and position‑closing operations to remain active even when the market is paused, mirroring the approach used in other markets such as the BFP market, thereby preserving the protocol’s ability to enforce collateral requirements and protect user funds.

title: M-07 | Liquidation Rewards Should Not Use Fill Price
description:
getRequiredMarginWithNewPosition calculates the required margin for a new position by adding
possible liquidation rewards to the required margin for the position.
The issue lies with how the liquidation rewards are calculated using fillPrice instead of an oracle
price:
runtime.accumulatedLiquidationRewards = marketConfig.calculateFlagReward(
MathUtil.abs(newPositionSize).mulDecimal(fillPrice));
1. This in contradiction with how isEligibleForLiquidation is calculated which uses an oracle price.
2. fillPrice includes a premium/discount according to how the trade affects the market skew. This
would unfairly make shorts require a higher margin when they balance the market and less when
they imbalance the market.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol computes the liquidation reward that is added to the required margin when a trader opens a new position. The function that determines the required margin calls getRequiredMarginWithNewPosition, which adds a term called accumulatedLiquidationRewards. This term is calculated by multiplying the absolute size of the new position by the fill price of the trade and then passing the product to marketConfig.calculateFlagReward. The fill price reflects the execution price of the trade, which includes any premium or discount that results from the current market skew. In contrast, the eligibility check for liquidation (isEligibleForLiquidation) uses an external oracle price that represents the true market value without the skew‑induced adjustment. Because the liquidation reward is derived from the skew‑adjusted fill price, the required margin can be artificially inflated for short positions that help rebalance the market and artificially deflated for positions that increase imbalance. An attacker who can influence the market skew—by submitting large offsetting trades or by exploiting price impact—can therefore manipulate the fill price to lower the margin requirement for a risky position, making it easier to open under‑collateralised positions that can later be liquidated. When the manipulated position is later evaluated against the oracle‑based liquidation check, the protocol may deem it eligible for liquidation even though the trader appeared to have sufficient margin at entry. This mismatch can lead to unexpected liquidations, loss of user funds, and erosion of confidence in the protocol’s accounting logic. The issue appears only when a new position is opened and the required margin is recomputed; it does not affect existing positions that were opened before the bug was introduced. All market participants—traders, liquidators, and the protocol itself—are potentially affected because the margin calculation no longer reflects the true risk. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit of the margin‑calculation code, where the auditor noticed that the reward calculation referenced fillPrice while the liquidation eligibility logic referenced the oracle price, a discrepancy that is easy to overlook because both values are used elsewhere in the contract. The problem is subtle because the fill price is a legitimate source of price information for many calculations, so the inconsistency does not raise an immediate red flag. To remediate the issue, the liquidation reward should be computed using the same oracle price that the liquidation eligibility check uses, thereby aligning the margin requirement with the true market value and eliminating the incentive for price‑impact manipulation. In practical terms, users may notice that the margin they are asked to provide is higher or lower than expected, that positions are liquidated despite appearing well‑collateralised, or that their account balance drops unexpectedly after opening a trade. The bug belongs to the class of accounting mismatches where different parts of a protocol use inconsistent price sources, leading to incorrect risk assessments and potential fund loss.

title: M-08 | Liquidations May Liquidate LPs
description:
• When a trader is liquidated all of the trader's collateral is distributed to the LPs by reallocating it to
the distributor where the funds do not contribute to the LP's health.
• After that the positions of the trader (with negative PnL) are closed.
The totalDebt is calculated with the following formula and can be negative if the LPs currently make
a profit through trader losses: totalDebt = reportedDebt - marketDepositedCollateral
Here is an example of how a liquidation could influence this calculation:
• A trader owns $1000 collateral and has a position with a $700 loss
• Before the liquidation totalDebt = 300 - 1000 = -700 (LPs make profit)
• After the liquidation totalDebt = 0 - 0 = 0 (position is neutral)
As pools delegate to multiple markets it could be that other markets have a positive totalDebt and
this negative totalDebt is needed to balance the LP's health.
Therefore this reallocation of debt to the distributor may cause some LP positions to become
immediately unhealthy as they no longer are credited with the negative debt of the position (that was
liquidated now).
Their debt and collateral would then be socialized amongst the other LP positions, however these
positions would not receive the collateral rewards that would have gone to the liquidated account
through the distributor this way.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the liquidation routine of the perpetual market where, upon a trader’s liquidation, the entire collateral of the trader is transferred to a distributor contract instead of being accounted for in the liquidity providers' (LPs) health metrics. The protocol computes a pool‑level debt metric called totalDebt as reportedDebt minus marketDepositedCollateral. Because marketDepositedCollateral can be larger than reportedDebt, totalDebt may become negative, which effectively records a profit for LPs that offsets other positive debt positions across markets. When a liquidation occurs, the marketDepositedCollateral for the liquidated trader is reset to zero, which eliminates the negative component of totalDebt. Consequently, LPs that were relying on that negative debt to keep their health score above the required threshold suddenly see their health drop, their collateral balance shrink, and the expected reward distribution disappear. This situation can happen whenever a trader with a sizable loss is liquidated, especially in pools that delegate to multiple markets where some markets have positive totalDebt that depend on the negative totalDebt from the liquidated position for overall balance. The impact is that LPs may experience unexpected loss of collateral, health degradation, and potentially forced liquidation of their own positions, undermining confidence in the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who traced the liquidation flow and observed that the reallocation of debt to the distributor does not update the LP health state, making the problem subtle and easy to miss because the UI typically only shows the successful transfer of the trader’s collateral without highlighting the hidden health shift. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where state changes in one component are not reflected in dependent risk metrics, violating the business assumption that LPs retain their proportional share of collateral and risk exposure after a trader liquidation. From a user perspective, an LP may notice that after a liquidation event their health score drops, their balance appears lower than expected, and the reward payout that should have been received from the liquidated trader’s collateral is missing. To remediate the issue, the liquidation logic should be restructured so that marketDepositedCollateral is either distributed to LPs in a way that preserves their health calculations or the totalDebt formula is adjusted to prevent negative values from being unintentionally removed, ensuring that LPs’ risk and reward accounting remain consistent after any liquidation.

title: DAO name can be stolen by front-running calls to `MembershipFactory::createNewDAOMembership`
description:
When `MembershipFactory::createNewDAOMembership` is called, the newly created `MembershipERC1155` instance it is [associated](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/MembershipFactory.sol#L61) with a name, `ensname`:

```solidity
require(getENSAddress[daoConfig.ensname] == address(0), "DAO already exist.");
```

However, this call can be front-run by a malicious user who sees that another creator is setting up a One World Project membership token and "steals" their name by registering the same name before them.

Anyone can front-run the creation of a DAO membership. This could be used for creating honey pots or just to grief the DAO creator.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running name‑theft issue in the DAO membership creation flow. When a user calls the factory function to create a new DAO membership, the contract records the desired ENS name in a mapping and checks that the name is not already associated with an address by using a require statement. Because the check only verifies that the name is currently unused, a malicious actor who observes the pending transaction can submit their own transaction with the same ENS name before the original creator’s transaction is mined. The attacker’s transaction succeeds, registers the name, and the subsequent legitimate transaction fails the require check, causing it to revert. This results in the original creator being unable to register the intended DAO name, effectively “stealing” the name. The impact is that an attacker can hijack the branding of a DAO, create a honey‑pot contract under the expected name, or simply grief the intended creator by preventing the DAO from being launched under the chosen identifier. The issue manifests whenever the factory’s createNewDAOMembership function is called without additional verification that the caller is the rightful owner of the ENS name. It affects DAO creators, their future members, and the overall protocol reputation because users may be misled into interacting with a malicious contract that bears the expected name. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the name‑registration logic and identified that the uniqueness check does not bind the name to the caller’s address. The problem can be hard to notice because the transaction simply reverts with a generic “DAO already exist.” error, which may be interpreted as a transient naming conflict rather than an attack. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the ENS name is linked to the creator’s address, for example by storing a composite key of (creator, name) or by verifying that the caller is the owner of the ENS name before allowing registration. Alternatively, the system could allow any string as a name but internally use a unique identifier that incorporates the creator’s address, preventing another party from pre‑emptively claiming the same visible name. This class of bug falls under front‑running and name‑squatting vulnerabilities, where insufficient binding of identifiers to owners enables malicious actors to hijack resources that are expected to be exclusive.

title: DAO membership fees cannot be retrieved by the creator
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the DAO membership contract does not provide a mechanism for the DAO creator to withdraw the portion of the membership fee that is transferred to the DAO's MembershipERC1155 address. When a user calls joinDAO, the contract splits the tier price into a platform fee sent to the One World Project wallet and the remainder sent to the DAO's token contract. Because the token contract lacks any function that allows the creator (or any privileged role other than the generic EXTERNAL_CALLER) to move those funds, the tokens become permanently locked unless an external caller role manually invokes a generic callExternalContract function. This situation creates a funds‑lock bug: the creator expects to receive the membership revenue but sees no increase in their balance, while the token contract holds the ERC20 tokens. The issue arises from missing withdrawal logic and an incomplete access‑control design; the contract only defines a role for arbitrary external calls, but does not expose a dedicated rescue or withdraw function for the creator. An attacker who controls the EXTERNAL_CALLER role could potentially drain the locked funds, but even without malicious intent the creator is unable to retrieve the fees, breaking the economic model of the DAO. The problem manifests whenever a user joins the DAO and the tier price is transferred; the locked balance persists until the creator manually triggers an external call through the factory, which is not part of the intended workflow. Users see their payment succeed, but the DAO creator receives no funds, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual revenue. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the joinDAO flow and noted the absence of any getter or withdraw function for the DAO side of the split. Because the tokens sit in a contract that does not expose its balance, the issue can be easy to miss in manual testing unless the balance of the token contract is inspected. The recommended fix is to add a dedicated method, restricted to the DAO creator or an authorized role, that transfers the accumulated membership fees from the MembershipERC1155 contract to the creator’s address, or to integrate the fee handling directly into the joinDAO logic. This would align the contract’s behavior with the business expectation that the DAO creator receives the membership revenue and would eliminate the hidden escrow that currently locks funds.

title: Meta transactions do not work with most of the calls in `MembershipFactory`
description:
`MembershipFactory` uses a custom meta transactions implementation by inheriting `NativeMetaTransaction` which allow a relayer to pay the transaction fees on behalf of a user. This is achieved by following the same standard as ERC2771, where the user signs a transaction that is forwarded by a relayer and executed with the signing user's address appended to the `msg.data`.

Therefore, `msg.sender` cannot be used to retrieve the actual sender of a transaction as this will be the relayer in the case of [`NativeMetaTransaction::executeMetaTransaction`](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/meta-transaction/NativeMetaTransaction.sol#L33) being called. As already implemented [here](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/MembershipFactory.sol#L165-L185), the solution is to utilize a `_msgSender()` function that retrieves the signing user from the last 20 bytes of the `msg.data` in these cases.

For this reason, the following functions in `MembershipFactory` are problematic:
* `MembershipFactory::createNewDAOMembership` [[1](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/MembershipFactory.sol#L69), [2](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/MembershipFactory.sol#L84)].
* `MembershipFactory::joinDAO` [[1](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/MembershipFactory.sol#L129), [2](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/daomembershipFactory.sol#L130), [3](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/MembershipFactory.sol#L131), [4](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/MembershipFactory.sol#L132)].
* `MembershipFactory::upgradeTier` [[1](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/MembershipFactory.sol#L141), [2](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/MembershipFactory.sol#L142), [3](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/MembershipFactory.sol#L143)].

None of the above calls will work properly in combination when originated via `NativeMetaTransaction::executeMetaTransaction`, with `MembershipFactory::createNewDAOMembership` being the most problematic as it will create the DAO membership token with the `MembershipFactory` contract address as the `creator`. `MembershipFactory::joinDAO` and `MembershipFactory::upgradeTier` will most likely just revert as they require the `msg.sender` (`MembershipFactory`) to hold either `MembershipERC1155` tokens or payment `ERC20` tokens, which it shouldn't.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way MembershipFactory handles meta‑transactions. The contract inherits a custom NativeMetaTransaction implementation that follows the ERC2771 pattern: a relayer forwards a signed payload and the original signer’s address is appended to msg.data. Because of this forwarding, the Solidity global variable msg.sender reflects the relayer (or the factory contract itself when executeMetaTransaction is used) instead of the actual user who signed the request. The factory’s functions createNewDAOMembership, joinDAO and upgradeTier were written assuming msg.sender is the caller’s address and therefore use msg.sender to check ownership, token balances and payment allowances. When these functions are invoked through executeMetaTransaction, the checks read the factory’s address, causing the DAO membership token to be minted with the factory as the recorded creator, and causing joinDAO and upgradeTier to revert because the factory does not hold the required ERC1155 membership tokens or ERC20 payment tokens. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that a meta‑transaction to create a membership results in a token whose owner is the factory contract, that attempts to join a DAO return an error or revert, and that upgrades fail silently, leading to a perception that funds are lost or that the operation did nothing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended business logic (the user should be the creator and holder of the membership token) with the actual on‑chain behavior when meta‑transactions are used. It is hard to notice because the contract compiles and works correctly for direct calls; only when meta‑transactions are employed does the mismatch appear, and the failure manifests as a revert rather than an obvious mis‑assignment. This class of bug is a meta‑transaction sender‑context error, where code relies on msg.sender instead of a context‑aware helper such as _msgSender() that extracts the original signer from the calldata. The impact is medium severity: users cannot correctly create or join DAOs via relayers, which breaks the intended onboarding flow and may cause loss of user confidence or funds if payments are sent before the revert. The proper fix is to replace every usage of msg.sender in the affected functions with the provided _msgSender() helper, ensuring that ownership checks, token balance queries and payment transfers reference the true user address even when the call is relayed through executeMetaTransaction.

title: Tier restrictions for `SPONSORED` DAOs can be bypassed by calling `MembershipFactory::upgradeTier`
description:
If the DAO specified by the `daoMembershipAddress` parameter in a call to `MembershipFactory::upgradeTier` is registered as [`SPONSORED`](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/MembershipFactory.sol#L139), members can upgrade their tier by burning two lower tier tokens for one higher tier token. However, the [`tiers.minted`](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/libraries/MembershipDAOStructs.sol#L35) member of [`MembershipDAOStructs::DAOConfig`](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/libraries/MembershipDAOStructs.sol#L16) is not updated or validated against the configured [`tiers.amount`](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/libraries/MembershipDAOStructs.sol#L32), meaning that a DAO member can mint more higher tier tokens than intended by minting lower tier tokens and upgrading them.

The maximum number of memberships for a given tier can be circumvented by upgrading lower tier. Additionally, since `tiers.minted` is not decremented/incremented for the original and upgraded tiers respectively, no new tokens will be able to be minted for the lower tier.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting bypass in the membership tier management of SPONSORED DAOs. The contract tracks how many tokens have been minted for each tier through a `tiers.minted` counter that is supposed to be compared against a hard‑coded `tiers.amount` limit. When a member calls `MembershipFactory.upgradeTier`, the implementation burns two lower‑tier tokens and mints one higher‑tier token, but it never updates the `tiers.minted` values for either the source tier or the destination tier, nor does it validate that the destination tier’s `tiers.amount` limit is respected. As a result, an attacker can first fill a high tier up to its declared maximum, then acquire a few low‑tier tokens and upgrade them, causing the high tier’s effective supply to exceed the configured cap while the low tier’s minted counter remains unchanged. This can be exploited by any member of a SPONSORED DAO who can acquire the required lower‑tier tokens, typically by joining the DAO with a small amount of stake. The impact is that the protocol’s tier‑based access control and scarcity model are broken: users may receive more high‑tier memberships than intended, leading to over‑allocation of privileged rights, dilution of benefits, and potential loss of trust in the DAO’s governance rules. The condition occurs only for DAOs marked as SPONSORED, where the upgrade path is enabled, and only when the attacker has enough lower‑tier tokens to perform the upgrade. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that included a test case exercising the upgrade flow after the high tier reached its maximum; the test revealed that the `Tier full.` revert was bypassed and the balance of the high tier increased beyond the limit while the internal `minted` counters stayed unchanged. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an event or revert when the limit is exceeded during an upgrade, making the over‑minting invisible to external observers who rely on the `minted` state to enforce caps. To fix the problem, the upgrade logic must decrement the `minted` count of the source tier, increment the `minted` count of the target tier, and enforce that the target tier’s `minted` value never exceeds its `amount` limit before performing the mint. In user‑facing terms, a member expects that once a tier reports “Tier full” they cannot obtain additional tokens of that tier, yet they can still receive extra high‑tier tokens after an upgrade, effectively seeing their balance jump from the maximum to a higher number, while the UI still shows the tier as full. This constitutes a classic over‑minting or supply‑cap bypass bug that violates the intended accounting invariants of the membership system.

title: No membership restrictions placed on `PRIVATE` DAOs allows anyone to join
description:
[`MembershipDAOStructs::DAOType`](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/libraries/MembershipDAOStructs.sol#L6-L10) exposes the different types a DAO can have, namely `PRIVATE`, `SPONSORED`, and the default `PUBLIC` which has no restrictions. DAOs of type `SPONSORED` are open but require the use of all tiers, and while `PRIVATE` may be expected to impose further limitations on membership, this case is not handled and so it is possible for anyone to join these DAOs.

Even if a DAO creator specifies `DAOType.PRIVATE`, there is no possibility to place restrictions on which accounts are allowed to join.
bug_full: During the audit it was observed that the contract defines three DAO types – PUBLIC, SPONSORED and PRIVATE – but the joinDAO function does not contain any logic that restricts membership when the DAO type is set to PRIVATE. As a result, the only condition checked before allowing a new member is that the caller has approved the required token amount; there is no verification of an allow‑list, role, or any other identifier that would limit who can call joinDAO. Consequently, any address can call joinDAO on a DAO that the creator intended to be private. An attacker can simply approve the required token amount and invoke joinDAO, gaining membership rights that were supposed to be exclusive. This may allow the attacker to participate in governance proposals, access privileged functions, or claim benefits reserved for private members, thereby violating the business assumption that private DAOs are invitation‑only. The issue manifests whenever a DAO is created with DAOType.PRIVATE; no additional configuration is required to trigger the flaw.
