Users of the protocol, DAO creators, and members are affected because the privacy guarantee is broken and the protocol’s reputation may suffer. The problem was discovered through a targeted test that attempted to join a PRIVATE DAO with an arbitrary address and observed that the transaction does not revert. The bug is subtle because the UI and the DAO configuration display the private flag, giving the impression that membership is restricted, while the underlying contract logic does not enforce it. To remediate, the contract should introduce an explicit allow‑list or role‑based check that is evaluated in joinDAO for PRIVATE DAOs, ensuring that only approved accounts can become members. This change restores the intended access control and aligns the on‑chain behavior with the off‑chain expectations of privacy.

title: DAO membership can exceed `MembershipDAOStructs::DAOConfig.maxMembers`
description:
The [`MembershipDAOStructs::DAOConfig.maxMembers`](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/libraries/MembershipDAOStructs.sol#L18) field is intended as a cap to DAO membership, beyond which should not be exceeded; however, this is currently unused and there is no limit on how many members can join a DAO besides the limit for each respective tier.
Any number of members can join a DAO, limited only by the maximum amount for each tier.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked membership limit in a DAO contract. A configuration field called maxMembers is meant to cap the total number of participants that can join a DAO, but the contract never validates this value when new members are added. The root cause is that the joinDAO function does not read or compare the current member count against the maxMembers parameter, leaving the limit effectively unused. An attacker can exploit this by creating many wallet addresses and calling joinDAO repeatedly, thereby exceeding the intended cap. This can be done immediately after DAO creation, as the only restriction that remains is the per‑tier maximum, which may be much higher than the overall cap. The impact is that the DAO’s governance model is weakened: voting power becomes diluted, economic assumptions about member‑based fees or rewards are broken, and the protocol may allocate resources to more participants than it was designed for. Users who expect a limited community may see an unexpectedly large roster of members, and the protocol’s business logic that relies on a bounded member set no longer holds. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test was added that deliberately set maxMembers to one and then allowed two distinct accounts to join without any revert. Because the contract does not emit explicit warnings or UI messages about the cap, the problem can be hard to notice unless the member count is manually inspected. The recommended remediation is to enforce the maxMembers constraint by checking the current number of members before allowing a new join and reverting the transaction if the limit would be exceeded. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that the DAO cannot have more participants than the configured maximum, thereby preserving the integrity of voting weight and any fee‑distribution logic that depends on a fixed member pool.

title: Lowest tier (highest index) membership cannot be upgraded
description:
For `SPONSORED` DAOs, members are permitted to upgrade from a lower tier membership to a higher tier by burning two tokens within a call to [`MembershipFactory::upgradeTier`](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/smart-contracts-blockchain-1wp/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/MembershipFactory.sol#L135-L144). This logic attempts to [validate](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/MembershipFactory.sol#L140) that the current tier can be upgraded:
```solidity
require(daos[daoMembershipAddress].noOfTiers > fromTierIndex + 1, "No higher tier available.");
```
However, one important detail here to note is that the highest tier membership has the lowest tier index when [referenced](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/MembershipFactory.sol#L140-L142) within `MembershipFactory::upgradeTier`. Hence, the highest tier is denoted by `0` and the lowest tier with the highest index, `6`, meaning that the above validation is off-by-one. `7 > 6 + 1` is `false` and it is not possible to upgrade from the lowest tier (highest index) membership. Also note that attempted upgrades from the highest tier (lowest index) fail only due to a [revert on underflow](https://github.com/OneWpOrg/audit-2024-10-oneworld/blob/416630e46ea6f0e9bd9bdd0aea6a48119d0b515a/contracts/dao/MembershipFactory.sol#L142) when attempting to mint.
DAO members cannot upgrade the lowest tier memberships to higher tiers.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one logic error in the membership tier upgrade function of a DAO contract. The contract stores membership tiers in descending order, where the highest tier has index 0 and the lowest tier has the highest index (for example 6). When a member calls the upgrade function, the code checks whether a higher tier exists with the condition `require(daos[daoMembershipAddress].noOfTiers > fromTierIndex + 1, "No higher tier available.");`. Because the highest index already represents the lowest tier, adding 1 to the current index makes the comparison false for the lowest tier (e.g., 7 > 6+1 evaluates to false). Consequently, members holding the lowest tier cannot upgrade to any higher tier; the transaction reverts with the message “No higher tier available.” The same off‑by‑one mistake also causes an underflow when attempting to upgrade from the highest tier, leading to a revert during minting. The root cause is a misunderstanding of the tier indexing direction and an incorrect boundary check. Exploitation is straightforward: any user attempting to upgrade from the lowest tier will be blocked, effectively denying them access to higher‑privilege features that require a higher tier. The impact is functional rather than financial: users may burn tokens expecting an upgrade, receive no new tier, and see their transaction fail, which can be confusing and may lead to loss of confidence in the protocol. The bug manifests only when the `upgradeTier` call is made with the highest index; normal tier upgrades from intermediate tiers succeed, making the issue easy to miss during casual testing. It was discovered during a formal audit by Cyfrin, which added a targeted test case that reproduced the revert. The problem is hard to notice because the require statement appears to enforce a “higher tier exists” rule, yet the sign of the inequality is wrong for the chosen indexing scheme. The appropriate fix is to remove the unnecessary `+ 1` from the comparison, or otherwise adjust the logic to correctly reflect the tier ordering, ensuring that the condition simply checks that the total number of tiers is greater than the current index. This change restores the ability for members in the lowest tier to upgrade, aligning the contract behavior with the intended business logic that higher tiers grant additional rights and that members can progress by burning tokens.

title: DAO members have no option to leave
description:
`MembershipFactory` exposes methods to join a DAO and upgrade tiers within a `SPONSORED` type DAO; however, there is no logic directly exposed to DAO members to burn their membership token(s) if they decide to leave the DAO. The only role with permissions to execute this is `EXTERNAL_CALLER` who can do so on behalf of the user, presumably at their request.
DAO members cannot leave without the cooperation of `EXTERNAL_CALLER`.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that DAO members have no direct mechanism to burn their membership token and therefore cannot voluntarily leave a SPONSORED type DAO. The MembershipFactory contract provides functions for joining and tier upgrades, but the only entity authorised to call the internal burn routine is the EXTERNAL_CALLER role. Because the burn function is not exposed to token holders, a member must rely on an external actor to execute the burn on their behalf. This design flaw originates from missing access control that would allow the token owner to invoke the burn directly. An attacker or a negligent external caller could simply refuse to perform the burn, effectively trapping the member’s token and any associated rights or withdrawable assets. Exploitation consists of a member attempting to exit, submitting a request, and receiving no response because the privileged caller does not act, leading to a situation where the user sees no change in balance, cannot redeem their stake, and may perceive that their funds have disappeared. The issue manifests whenever a user who holds a membership token wishes to leave the DAO, regardless of the contract’s other functionality. It affects all token holders, the DAO’s governance model, and any downstream protocols that assume members can freely opt‑out. The problem was identified during a manual audit of the MembershipFactory’s public interface, where the absence of a member‑accessible burn function was noted as inconsistent with typical token economics. The bug is subtle because the UI may present a “join” button but no “leave” option, and the contract does not emit an explicit error, making it easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should expose a burn or withdraw function that is callable by the token owner (or by any address holding the token) and enforce proper checks to ensure only legitimate holders can destroy their membership. This aligns the implementation with the expected business logic that members can freely exit, preventing fund lock‑up and preserving trust in the protocol.

title: Gas griefing/attack via creating the proposals
description:
The timelock acts in a way that once the proposals are submitted, they need to be cancelled or executed. This behaviour opens up a griefing attack vector towards the owners of the vault in case at least `threshold` amount of owners’ private keys are exposed.
When the keys are exposed, the attackers can send as many transactions as they need to the network from the safe with different salts. Even if one of the transactions go through, funds can be stolen. The protocol defence mechanisms in these situations is (1) Pause guardian can cancel all the proposals (2) Cold signers can cancel proposals.
Both these defence mechanisms require gas usage from the victim’s accounts, and it is important to note that they can not use the funds inside the Kleidi wallet. This can lead to a gas war between attackers and the victims and can cause them to at least cause a griefing attack.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a gas‑griefing or denial‑of‑service weakness in the timelock component that manages proposals for a multi‑owner vault. The timelock stores scheduled operations until they are either executed or cancelled, but it does not provide a cheap mechanism to invalidate a large batch of pending proposals. When an attacker obtains the private keys of at least the threshold number of owners, they can submit an arbitrary number of proposals from the compromised safe, each with a distinct salt value. Because each proposal is recorded as a separate operation, the attacker can flood the timelock with thousands or even hundreds of thousands of entries. The root cause is the lack of an epoch or versioning scheme that would automatically render old proposals obsolete when the contract is paused or when a new governance period begins. Consequently, the only way for honest participants – the pause guardian or the cold‑signer owners – to remove the malicious proposals is to call the cancel function for each entry, which consumes gas from the victims’ external accounts. The victims cannot use the funds locked in the Kleidi wallet to pay for this gas, so they must spend their own ether to clear the queue. This creates a “gas war” where the attacker can out‑spend the defenders, effectively preventing the vault from being able to cancel or execute legitimate operations. If the attacker’s malicious proposal is eventually executed, it may transfer assets out of the vault, leading to direct financial loss. The attack scenario unfolds as follows: (1) attacker compromises enough owner keys, (2) attacker schedules a massive number of proposals with unique salts, (3) honest owners attempt to pause the contract or cancel the proposals, (4) each cancellation transaction requires gas, (5) the attacker can continue to schedule new proposals faster than the defenders can afford to cancel, (6) the vault becomes clogged, and (7) any successful execution of a malicious proposal results in stolen funds. The impact is two‑fold: a denial‑of‑service condition that blocks legitimate governance actions and a potential theft of assets if a malicious operation is executed. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a long list of pending proposals, an inability to clear them without paying high gas fees, and the possibility of seeing funds disappear after an unexpected execution. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors measured gas consumption for scheduling and cancelling large numbers of proposals and observed that cancelling each entry could cost several hundred million gas units. The problem is hard to notice because the timelock’s basic functionality works correctly; the flaw lies in the economic design rather than a code error. The recommended mitigation is to introduce epoch counters that advance whenever the contract is paused or a new governance period starts, and to incorporate the epoch into the operation hash. By doing so, all proposals from previous epochs become automatically invalid, eliminating the need for the defender to cancel each proposal individually and removing the gas‑griefing vector.

title: Wrong handling of call data check indices, forcing it sometimes to revert
description:
Cold signers can add call data checks as whitelisted checks that hot signers could execute without timelocks, the call data checks depend on the indices of the encoded call. However, the protocol invalidly handles these indices in 2 separate places:

  1. <https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/main/src/Timelock.sol#L1136>
  2. <https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-kleidi/blob/main/src/BytesHelper.sol#L50>

Where length is computed as `end index—start index`, which is usually wrong as index subtraction needs `+1` to be translated to a length. For most of the scenario, this is okay; however, if a parameter that is being checked filled all of its bytes then this would be an issue (PoC is an example). For example, a uint256 filling all of its 32 bytes. **NB:** This is not caught in the unit tests because there isn’t any test that checks this edge case, where a parameter that fills all its bytes is being checked.

This forces the whitelisted call to revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the handling of calldata slice indices used to whitelist calls that cold signers add for hot signers. The protocol computes the length of a slice as endIndex‑startIndex, but the correct length of a byte range is endIndex‑startIndex+1. This mistake appears in two places: the generic byte‑slicing helper and the timelock function that validates the length of each whitelisted calldata fragment. For most parameters the error is invisible because the checked data does not occupy the full byte width, however when a parameter exactly fills its allocated bytes – for example a uint256 with the maximum value that occupies all 32 bytes – the computed length is one byte short. As a result the contract rejects the calldata check with errors such as "CalldataList: Data length mismatch" or "End index is greater than the length of the byte string" and the subsequent whitelisted transaction reverts. The issue occurs when a cold signer registers a check that includes a full‑width value, and a hot signer later tries to execute the whitelisted call. Users experience a failed transaction, no token allowance is set, and the UI may show that the expected approval did not happen. The bug was discovered during a security audit because the existing unit tests did not cover the edge case where a parameter fills all its bytes. It is hard to notice in normal operation because most calls use smaller values and therefore pass the length check. The impact is primarily a denial‑of‑service for legitimate whitelisted actions; funds are not stolen but the protocol’s functionality is blocked. The fix consists of correcting the length calculation by adding one to the difference between end and start indices in both the slice helper and the timelock validation, and updating the require statements accordingly. This adjustment restores the intended accounting logic, ensuring that the byte range matches the actual data size and that whitelisted calls execute as expected.

title: `UpdateExpirattionPeriod`
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the timelock contract that prevents a scheduled operation from being executed after the expiration period has been reduced. When a proposal is created, the contract records a timestamp and expects the operation to be executable while the current block timestamp is between the recorded timestamp and the timestamp plus the expirationPeriod that was in effect at scheduling time. The contract includes a private function _afterCall that is invoked after an operation is executed. This function redundantly calls isOperationReady(id) to verify that the operation is still ready before marking the proposal as completed. However, isOperationReady uses the global expirationPeriod variable, which may have been changed by a prior call to updateExpirationPeriod. If the expirationPeriod is lowered after the proposal was scheduled but before execution, the second readiness check can fail because the new, shorter period makes the condition timestamp + expirationPeriod > block.timestamp false, even though the operation was originally ready. As a result, the execution reverts with "Timelock: operation is not ready" and the proposal remains in the live set, effectively becoming dead‑locked. The impact is that any scheduled upgrade, fund transfer, or governance action can become permanently unexecutable, locking assets or preventing protocol changes. This issue affects the protocol owner, any user relying on the timelock for delayed execution, and ultimately the security of the system because critical operations may be stalled. The bug was discovered during a security audit by reviewing the _afterCall implementation and noticing that the readiness check is performed after the expiration period may have been altered. It is hard to notice because the check appears harmless and only triggers under the specific edge case of reducing the delay, which is not a common operation in typical usage. The proper fix is to remove the redundant isOperationReady check from _afterCall or to store the original expiration period per proposal and use that for the final validation, ensuring that the completion marker is set without re‑evaluating the mutable global delay. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistent validation errors where a contract re‑validates a condition using a variable that may have changed after the original state was recorded, leading to unintended reverts and dead‑locked state.

title: Invalid handling of flash loan fees in `PositionAction::onCreditFlashLoan`, forcing it to always revert
description:
When users take a flash loan, an amount is sent to the receiver, and then some action takes place, after that action that sent amount is expected to be paid and some fee. Users can also call `PositionAction::decreaseLever` through a proxy, to “Decrease the leverage of a position by taking out a credit flash loan to withdraw and sell collateral”, after it is called, the flash loan lender sends the credit and calls `onCreditFlashLoan`, which handles all that logic.

This was reported in [Issue 524](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-07-loopfi-findings/issues/524), and a fix has been implemented. However, the fix is incomplete, and the `onCreditFlashLoan` will always revert when the fees are `>0`.

The fix added includes adding fees to the approval amounts:
    
    underlyingToken.forceApprove(address(leverParams.vault), subDebt + fee);
    underlyingToken.forceApprove(address(flashlender), subDebt + fee);

That fix still misses a point; the amount coming from the flash lender is constant, and that amount will be used to repay a position’s debt. The issue here is that all the amount is being used to repay without accounting for the extra fees that the flash lender will be requesting.

This causes `PositionAction::onCreditFlashLoan` to always revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way a flash‑loan based leverage‑decrease operation handles the lender’s fee. When a user invokes the decrease‑leverage function, the protocol obtains a credit flash loan from an external lender. The lender transfers a fixed principal amount to the contract and expects the same principal plus a non‑zero fee to be returned in the same transaction. The contract approves the lender to pull an amount equal to the principal plus the fee, but the internal logic that repays the position’s debt mistakenly uses the entire principal amount to settle the debt, completely ignoring the separate fee amount. Because the fee is not deducted from the repayment calculation, the contract ends the callback with insufficient token balance to cover the fee transfer. The ERC‑20 transfer that attempts to move the fee therefore fails, causing the onCreditFlashLoan callback to revert. This revert aborts the whole decrease‑leverage transaction, preventing the user from reducing their leverage and leaving the position unchanged. The issue manifests only when the flash‑loan fee is greater than zero, which is the normal case for any real lender, and it is triggered during the onCreditFlashLoan callback after the credit flash loan is issued. Users, the protocol’s credit manager, and the flash‑loan provider are all affected because legitimate leverage‑decrease attempts fail, potentially leading to a denial‑of‑service scenario where positions cannot be unwound. The flaw was discovered during a security audit when a test case that forced a non‑zero fee caused the transaction to revert with the message “ERC20: transfer amount exceeds balance”. The problem is subtle because the approval of the fee appears correct on the surface, yet the repayment arithmetic does not reserve any tokens for the fee, making the bug easy to miss in code review. To remediate the issue, the contract must adjust the amount of debt it repays by subtracting the fee, ensuring that after the principal is used to reduce the position’s debt, a separate transfer of the exact fee amount is performed to the lender. In conceptual terms, the fix requires proper accounting of flash‑loan fees in the repayment logic, guaranteeing that the contract retains enough balance to satisfy both principal and fee obligations before completing the callback. This class of bug falls under improper financial accounting in flash‑loan callbacks, where fee handling is omitted or mis‑calculated, leading to unexpected reverts and potential loss of functionality.

title: Invalid handling of risdual amount in `PositionAction::onCreditFlashLoan`, forcing it to revert
description:
Users can call `PositionAction::decreaseLever` through a proxy, to “Decrease the leverage of a position by taking out a credit flash loan to withdraw and sell collateral”. After it is called, the flash loan lender sends the credit and calls `onCreditFlashLoan`, which handles all that logic. When doing so, users are supposed to swap their collateral withdrawn into debt tokens so that the flash loan can be repaid.

The protocol tries to handle the residual amount from the swap (`swapped - paid debt`), by trying to repay extra debt for the designated position, using:
    
```solidity
if (residualAmount > 0) {
    underlyingToken.forceApprove(address(leverParams.vault), residualAmount);
    ICDPVault(leverParams.vault).modifyCollateralAndDebt(
        leverParams.position,
        address(this),
        address(this),
        0,
        -toInt256(residualAmount)
    );
}
```

However, this is invalid for 2 main reasons:

  1. This is trying to repay extra debt than what the user is trying to, which is passed in the `primarySwap.amount`.
  2. If the user tries to repay his whole debt using `decreaseLever` the TX will revert, as it’ll try to repay some nonexistent debt.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates in the flash‑loan callback that is executed when a user invokes the decreaseLever operation to lower the leverage of a position. After the flash loan supplies the required credit, the contract swaps the withdrawn collateral for debt tokens and calculates a residual amount as the difference between the amount obtained from the swap and the debt that must be repaid. The implementation then attempts to use this residual amount to repay additional debt by calling a vault function with a negative debt delta. This logic is flawed for two reasons. First, the residual amount may be larger than the actual outstanding debt of the position, so the contract tries to repay debt that does not exist. Second, when a user attempts to repay the entire debt in a single decreaseLever call, the residual amount becomes positive while the outstanding debt is already zero, causing the vault’s modifyCollateralAndDebt call to revert with a CallerNotCreditManagerException. The bug manifests whenever the swap yields any excess tokens – a common situation when market prices move or when the swap is executed with a generous limit. It affects any user who tries to reduce leverage, especially those who aim to fully close their debt, and it can also be triggered by an attacker who deliberately crafts a swap that leaves a residual amount, causing the transaction to revert and effectively denying service to legitimate users. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by executing a targeted integration test that performed a full‑debt repayment and observed the revert. It is hard to notice because the residual handling code is executed only after a successful flash‑loan and swap, and the revert surface‑level error does not clearly indicate that the problem lies in an over‑repayment calculation. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the leverage‑reduction request was submitted but then the transaction fails, leaving the user with no change in collateral or debt and only losing gas fees. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for leverage‑down operations and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that residual tokens can always be safely applied to debt repayment. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where post‑operation residual balances are incorrectly applied to state updates without proper validation. The correct mitigation is to stop using the residual amount to repay debt unconditionally. Instead, the contract should first check whether the position still carries outstanding debt; if it does, the residual may be applied to reduce that debt, otherwise the residual should be transferred to a designated recipient or returned to the caller. This change restores the intended invariant that debt repayments never exceed the actual debt and prevents unexpected reverts during leverage reduction.

title: `PositionAction4626.sol#_onWithdraw` should withdraw from position CDPVault position instead of `address
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal withdrawal routine of the PositionAction4626 contract. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the function _onWithdraw calls the CDPVault.withdraw method with address(this) as the recipient instead of the intended position address that actually owns the collateral. This mismatch causes the vault to transfer the withdrawn collateral back to the PositionAction4626 contract rather than to the user’s position, breaking the accounting invariant that a position’s balance should decrease by the withdrawn amount. The root cause is a simple parameter error: the code comments show a placeholder for the position argument, but the implementation mistakenly hard‑codes the contract’s own address. An attacker or any caller can trigger the faulty path, causing the protocol to move funds to an address that is not under the user’s control. The immediate impact is that the user receives no tokens despite a successful transaction, the UI may display a completed withdrawal while the user’s balance remains unchanged, and the withdrawn assets become locked inside the PositionAction4626 contract. This situation can also break downstream logic that expects the withdrawn amount to be available for further conversion if the destination token differs from the collateral, because the subsequent ERC4626 redemption step operates on a zero or incorrect amount. The bug manifests whenever a withdrawal is performed, especially when the destination token is not the native collateral token, as the contract attempts to redeem from the ERC4626 vault after the initial misdirected withdraw. The issue was discovered during a formal audit where the deposit path had already been corrected, but the withdraw path remained unchanged. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and emits no explicit error; only the missing token transfer and unchanged balances reveal the problem. To remediate, the withdraw call must be changed to pass the correct position address, i.e., ICDPVault(vault).withdraw(position, amount), ensuring that the collateral is sent to the rightful owner. Additionally, any logic that follows should reference the actual recipient rather than the contract itself, restoring the intended flow of funds and preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees.

title: `PositionActionPendle.sol#_onWithdraw` does not have slippage parameter `minOut` set
description: When performing withdraws on `PositionActionPendle` and exiting Pendle pools, users may lose funds due to not setting slippage.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the withdraw logic of the PositionActionPendle contract, specifically the internal function _onWithdraw that is used when a user exits a Pendle pool or an ERC4626‑compatible position. The function does not accept or enforce a slippage protection parameter such as minOut, which is a common safeguard that requires the amount returned by the pool to be at least a user‑specified minimum. Because the contract simply forwards the call to the underlying pool and accepts whatever amount the pool returns, a malicious actor or an adverse market movement can cause the pool to deliver fewer tokens than the user expects. An attacker who can front‑run the transaction or manipulate the price feed can cause the withdrawal to execute with a large price impact, resulting in the user receiving a reduced amount, sometimes even zero, while the transaction still reports success. The impact is that users lose part or all of the funds they intended to withdraw; from the UI perspective the balance shown after withdrawal is lower than expected, or the user receives no tokens despite a successful transaction. The issue appears only when the withdraw path goes through PositionActionPendle._onWithdraw, i.e., when withdrawing Pendle positions or ERC4626 positions, and it does not affect other contract functions. The problem was identified during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the withdraw implementation and noticing the absence of any minOut check. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; the only symptom is a smaller received amount, which may be attributed to normal market variation. To remediate, the contract should be modified to accept a minOut argument from the caller and to compare the actual amount received from the pool against this threshold, reverting the transaction if the amount is below the user‑specified minimum. This adds a standard slippage guard and aligns the contract with typical DeFi withdrawal patterns, preventing unexpected fund loss.

title: `PositionAction.sol#onCreditFlashLoan` may end up with stuck funds for `EXACT_IN` primary swaps
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the onCreditFlashLoan function of the PositionAction contract when it processes a decreaseLever action with a primary swap of type EXACT_IN. In this scenario the contract withdraws collateral, possibly from an ERC4626 vault or a pool, and swaps the entire withdrawn amount for the debt token. The swap output is then divided: part is used to repay the flash‑loan plus fee, and the remainder is sent to the CDPVault to reduce the outstanding debt. The CDPVault implementation caps any repayment to the current debt balance; if the amount being sent exceeds the debt, the excess tokens are not accepted and the internal modifyCollateralAndDebt call truncates the repayment. Because the PositionAction contract does not forward the surplus tokens to the user or emit an event, the excess debt tokens remain locked inside the PositionAction address where the user has no authority to retrieve them. This condition can occur whenever the amount of collateral withdrawn for the swap is larger than the user’s debt, which is feasible when the collateral is sourced from liquidity pools that may return more tokens than the debt amount. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears successful but the expected residual balance is missing; the user receives no refund and the contract balance shows an unexpected token holding that is inaccessible. The issue was identified during a code review of a recent diff that introduced the exact‑in handling path. It is hard to notice because the contract does not expose the leftover balance and the failure does not revert, so normal testing may not surface the loss of funds. The impact is that users can lose a portion of their collateral permanently, leading to medium‑severity financial loss and erosion of trust in the protocol. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect handling of over‑payment in debt repayment” or “residual token lock due to repayment caps”. The proper fix is to detect any surplus after the debt repayment calculation and transfer those tokens to the residualRecipient address instead of attempting to repay the CDPVault, or to redesign the repayment logic to return excess to the caller. Ensuring that the contract never holds unclaimed debt tokens and that events are emitted for residual transfers will prevent the funds from becoming stuck.

title: Inflated `GaugeV3` rewards when period is skipped
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an inflation of gauge rewards when a weekly accounting period is skipped. The gauge distributes rewards proportionally to the amount of liquidity that each position held inside a tick range during each 1‑week period. The calculation relies on the function periodCumulativesInside, which obtains the cumulative seconds‑per‑liquidity value for the period from the field endSecondsPerLiquidityPeriodX128 stored in the PeriodInfo struct. However, endSecondsPerLiquidityPeriodX128 is written by _advancePeriod and newPeriod to represent the cumulative value at the start of the next period, not the true end of the current period. When a period experiences no activity – no swaps, no liquidity additions or removals – the contract does not advance the period until a later call to _advancePeriod (for example via notifyRewardAmount). At that moment the stored endSecondsPerLiquidityPeriodX128 for the skipped period is set to a timestamp that is one week later than it should be, effectively adding an extra week of seconds‑per‑liquidity to the calculation. As a result, the formula that multiplies seconds‑per‑liquidity by the position’s liquidity over‑counts the time the position was in range, causing the rewards for that period to be roughly doubled. An attacker can exploit this by (1) creating a pool with minimal liquidity, (2) calling notifyRewardAmount right before the period boundary to lock in a reward amount, (3) allowing the next period to remain completely idle, and (4) later invoking _advancePeriod to record the inflated cumulative value and claim the overstated reward. The attacker receives the extra tokens while other LPs who had previously earned a legitimate share see their claim reduced or become unable to claim because the gauge balance has been drained. The bug manifests only when a period is skipped, which is a rare but possible scenario, especially for newly deployed or low‑activity pools. From a user perspective the symptom is that a participant’s expected reward is missing or reduced, while another address can withdraw roughly twice the amount that was originally deposited as gauge rewards. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by reproducing the scenario in a test suite that advanced time across multiple weeks without any pool interaction. It is hard to notice because the reward numbers still appear plausible and the condition of a completely idle week does not raise an obvious alarm. The proper fix is to distinguish between the cumulative value at the start and at the end of each period – for example by adding separate startSecondsPerLiquidityPeriodX128 and endSecondsPerLiquidityPeriodX128 fields – and to compute the end value using the exact period boundary rather than the next period’s start. This ensures that periodCumulativesInside always uses the correct time window, eliminating the extra week of seconds‑per‑liquidity and preventing reward inflation.

title: The fee for the protocol in the function `RamsesV3Pool::flash`
poc:
When calling the function [flash](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-10-ramses-exchange/blob/236e9e9e0cf452828ab82620b6c36c1e6c7bb441/contracts/CL/core/RamsesV3Pool.sol#L684-L725) on a RamsesV3Vault the caller initiates a flash loan. For the amount he flashes he needs to pay a fee. This fee is then divided between the protocol and the liquidity provider of the protocol. The issue arises from the fact how the share of the fees the protocol should get is calculated:
```solidity
uint256 pFees0 = feeProtocol == 0 ? 0 : paid0 / feeProtocol;
```
The feeProtocol is a number between 0 and 100 representing the % of fees the protocol should get, which is initially set to 80 meaning 80% of the fees should go to the protocol. With the current calculation and the initial value of 80, the protocol would only get 1/80 of the fees instead of 80% of the fees, contradicting the intended fee distribution and resulting in way less fees for the protocol than intended.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑split miscalculation in the flash‑loan function of the RamsesV3Pool contract. The protocol is supposed to receive a configurable percentage of the flash‑loan fee, expressed by the variable feeProtocol which ranges from 0 to 100 and represents the percent of the fee that belongs to the protocol (for example 80 means 80 % of the fee). The implementation, however, treats feeProtocol as a divisor and computes the protocol share as paid0 / feeProtocol (and similarly for token1). With the default value of 80 this yields only 1/80 of the fee instead of the intended 80 % of the fee. The root cause is an incorrect arithmetic formula that was carried over from an earlier version of UniswapV3 where feeProtocol was encoded using bit‑shifts; the conversion to a plain percentage was not updated. An attacker can exploit the bug by initiating a flash loan and paying a dramatically lower protocol fee, effectively reducing the cost of borrowing. The impact is that the protocol collects far less revenue than expected, which can erode its economic model and reduce incentives for liquidity providers, while users may see higher apparent returns because the fee that should go to the protocol is instead retained by the pool. The condition occurs whenever a flash loan is executed and feeProtocol is non‑zero; the error is deterministic for any fee amount. All participants in the protocol – the governing DAO, liquidity providers, and users – are affected because the fee distribution does not match the documented policy. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena when the auditors read the flash function and noticed the division instead of multiplication. It is subtle because the function still passes the official UniswapV3Pool specification tests, and the feeProtocol variable is otherwise used correctly in other parts of the code, making the bug easy to overlook. To remediate, the calculation should be changed to multiply the paid fee by feeProtocol and then divide by the appropriate denominator (e.g., 100 for a percent basis), ensuring that the protocol receives the intended percentage of the fee. This correction restores the intended economic split and aligns the contract behaviour with its documentation and business logic, preventing under‑collection of protocol fees.

title: M-01 | Insufficient Token Amounts Lead To Swap Error
description: When compounding rewards in _pairedLpTokenToPodLp, pairedLpTokens are swapped to pTKN via Uniswap's swapV2Single. However, if too little tokens are provided it may revert in Uniswap V2 with 'INSUFFICIENT_INPUT_AMOUNT' or INSUFFICIENT_OUTPUT_AMOUNT . This could be caused by a balance of 1 wei of pairedLpTokens. which after halving becomes 0 pTKNs. This small balance could be easily donated by an attacker looking to DOS the contract, or simply caused by leftover tokens from a previous transaction. As processing of rewards is called by every major flow, reverting could have serious implications such as preventing users from removing leverage and result in liquidations.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an insufficient‑input condition that triggers a swap failure in the contract function that converts paired LP tokens into pTKN tokens via Uniswap V2. The function first halves the amount of paired LP tokens before calling Uniswap's swapV2Single. When the original balance is extremely small – for example a single wei – the halving operation yields zero pTKN tokens. Uniswap V2 validates that the input amount and the expected output amount are non‑zero; if either check fails it reverts with the generic messages INSUFFICIENT_INPUT_AMOUNT or INSUFFICIENT_OUTPUT_AMOUNT. This situation can arise unintentionally from leftover dust after a previous transaction, or it can be deliberately induced by an attacker who donates a tiny amount of paired LP tokens to the contract with the aim of causing a denial‑of‑service. Because the reward‑compounding routine that performs this swap is invoked by every major user flow – including leverage removal and reward withdrawal – a single revert can block the entire operation, preventing users from exiting leveraged positions and potentially leading to forced liquidations. The issue affects any participant who relies on the contract to process rewards or unwind positions; from the user’s perspective the transaction simply fails, the UI reports an error, no tokens are received and the balance appears unchanged, contrary to the expectation that a withdrawal or leverage removal would succeed. The problem was identified during a manual audit by the Guardian team, and it is subtle because the revert messages are generic and the offending token amount is so small that it may be overlooked during testing. The bug belongs to the class of input‑validation and arithmetic‑underflow errors that produce a zero‑output swap. To remediate, the contract should verify that the token balance after any internal scaling is above a safe minimum before invoking the external swap, or it should adjust the scaling logic to avoid producing a zero output. Implementing an explicit minimum‑amount check or using a safe‑math library to guard against under‑flow would prevent the revert and eliminate the denial‑of‑service vector.

title: M-02 | Underflow In _updateAssetMetadataFromVault
description: Whenever _updateAssetMetadataFromVault is called, a vault's Collateral Backed Ratio (CBR) is updated and compared against its previous value. If the CBR decreased from the previous update, then the vault's utilization is also decreased based on _vaultAssetRatioChange. The issue occurs when _vaultAssetRatioChange is greater than 100%. This leads to an underflow when updating vaultUtilization[_vault]. Consider this example: • Vault's CBR decreased from 100e27 to 49e27 • _vaultAssetRatioChange: (100e27 * 1e27 / 49e27 ) - 1e27 = 1.04e27 • vaultUtilization[_vault]: 100 - (100 * 1.04e27 / 1e27) = underflow Such a drastic drop in CBR is unlikely but possible in vaults with obscure tokens (as Peapods is designed to be used permissionlessly). A revert in the update for one vault will cause DOS in all whitelisted vaults, and prevent liquidations in FraxlendPair vaults.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/peapods-1/pull/10/commits/336bec48aeb9065f048b9b98631cf8f585d25a3e
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unsigned integer underflow that occurs when the function that updates a vault's Collateral Backed Ratio (CBR) also tries to adjust the vault's utilization based on the change in asset ratio. The root cause is that the contract computes a variable called _vaultAssetRatioChange as a percentage of the previous CBR and then subtracts a proportional amount from vaultUtilization[_vault] without verifying that the subtraction will not exceed the current utilization value. When the CBR drops sharply, the calculated _vaultAssetRatioChange can become greater than 100 %, meaning the contract attempts to subtract more than the full utilization amount. Because Solidity’s default arithmetic on unsigned integers wraps on underflow, the subtraction wraps around to a very large number, causing the transaction to revert. An attacker can trigger this condition by forcing a large decrease in the CBR of a vault – for example, by manipulating the price of an obscure token used as collateral so that the CBR falls from 100e27 to 49e27. The contract then computes _vaultAssetRatioChange ≈1.04e27 (104 %), and the subsequent line vaultUtilization[_vault] = vaultUtilization[_vault] - (vaultUtilization[_vault] * _vaultAssetRatioChange / 1e27) attempts to subtract more than the existing 100 % utilization, leading to an underflow and a revert. The immediate impact is a denial‑of‑service: the revert stops the update for the affected vault and, because the update is performed in a loop over all whitelisted vaults, the failure blocks updates for every vault in the system. This also prevents liquidations from being executed on FraxlendPair vaults, potentially leaving unsafe positions unaddressed and exposing users’ funds to further risk. The condition only manifests when the CBR decrease is large enough to push the ratio change above 100 %, a scenario that is unlikely under normal market conditions but becomes feasible with low‑liquidity or volatile tokens that the protocol allows permissionlessly. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that exercised edge‑case values for CBR and observed a revert caused by an arithmetic underflow. It is hard to notice in routine testing because typical price movements do not produce a ratio change exceeding 100 %, and the revert appears as a generic transaction failure rather than a clear arithmetic bug. To remediate the problem the contract should guard against ratio changes above 100 % – for instance by capping _vaultAssetRatioChange at 1e27, using a signed integer for the delta, or adding an explicit underflow check before performing the subtraction. Conceptually the fix is to ensure that any adjustment to utilization never subtracts more than the current utilization, preserving the invariant that utilization remains within the 0‑100 % range. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that actions that trigger a vault update (such as deposits, withdrawals, or price feeds) suddenly fail with a transaction revert, the UI may show no change in utilization or display an error, and users may notice that liquidations are no longer being processed, leading to confusion and potential loss of confidence in the protocol.

title: M-03 | Precision Loss Leads To Reverts In TokenRewards
description: When a user receives shares from TokenRewards for the first time, _cumulativeRewards is called to update the user's rewards mapping with an excluded amount. This amount will be used to calculated the user's share of future rewards. The issue occurs in _cumulativeRewards: (_share * _rewardsPerShare[_token]) / PRECISION By rounding down the calculation, it is essentially excludes the user from 1 wei less of rewards, implying the user earned 1 wei more rewards. This will overtime lead to insufficient balance of rewards to transfer out, and DOS all functionality of the contract when that happens.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision loss caused by integer division rounding down when the contract updates a user’s cumulative rewardrecord. When a user receives shares for the first time, the internal function that records the excluded amount computes (_share * _rewardsPerShare[_token]) / PRECISION. Because Solidity performs integer division, any fractional part is discarded, effectively giving the user an extra 1 wei of reward that is never backed by the contract’s reward pool. Over many reward cycles this tiny over‑allocation accumulates, eventually exhausting the pool of rewards that the contract can transfer. When the contract later attempts to transfer the promised reward amount, the balance is insufficient and the transfer call reverts, causing all subsequent reward‑related functions to fail. This denial‑of‑service condition appears only after a user has been allocated shares and after enough reward periods have passed for the rounding error to become material. The affected parties are token holders who expect to claim rewards, as well as the protocol that relies on accurate accounting of reward balances. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward accounting logic and identified the use of a down‑rounding division without safeguards. It can be hard to notice because the discrepancy is only 1 wei per allocation, which is negligible in a single transaction and does not surface until the cumulative error grows large enough to deplete the reward reserve. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal reward balance, but when the user attempts to claim the reward the transaction reverts and no tokens are transferred, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. The bug belongs to the class of rounding or precision‑loss errors in financial smart contracts, where integer division without rounding‑up or proper scaling breaks accounting invariants. To fix the issue the calculation of the excluded amount should be performed with a rounding‑up strategy, for example by adding PRECISION‑1 before division or by using a library that guarantees ceiling division, ensuring that the contract never records more reward than it can actually pay out.

title: M-04 | Positions Are Lost When lendingPair Is Changed
description: When a new position is [initialized](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/peapods-2/blob/cebeb47138e5f029cefd698328dfbd33e90fbbea/contracts/lvf/LeverageManager.sol#L271), its lendingPair is set to the lending pair for the pod configured by the owner of the contract. However, adding and removing leverage always use the most recent lendingPair for the pod of the position instead of the pair at the time of it creation. This results in positions being lost when the owner changes the pair by calling [setLendingPair](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/peapods-2/blob/cebeb47138e5f029cefd698328dfbd33e90fbbea/contracts/lvf/LeverageManagerAccessControl.sol#L14-L19) because _removeLeverage will make the custodian remove collateral from the new pair where it doesn't have any.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the management of leveraged positions in a lending protocol where each position is expected to retain a reference to the specific lending pair that was active at the time the position was created. When a new position is initialized, the contract records the current lending pair for the pod and stores it in the position’s properties. However, the functions that add or remove leverage do not use this stored reference; instead they always query the most recent lending pair configured for the pod. If the contract owner later changes the pod’s lending pair via the setLendingPair function, subsequent calls to remove leverage will attempt to withdraw collateral from the newly set pair, which does not hold any of the position’s collateral. As a result, the custodial logic cannot locate the funds, and the position effectively becomes lost – the user’s collateral is stuck and the position may disappear from the UI. This flaw arises from a mismatch between per‑position state (the original lending pair) and global state (the latest lending pair) and is a classic case of stale‑reference or state‑inconsistency bug. Exploitation does not require malicious user interaction; it can be triggered simply by the contract owner updating the lending pair after positions have been opened and then users attempting to adjust leverage or withdraw. The impact is that users may see their position listed but receive no funds when they try to remove leverage, leading to apparent loss of assets and broken accounting assumptions that each position’s collateral is always reachable. The issue manifests only after the owner changes the lending pair and a user subsequently performs a leverage‑adjusting operation. It affects all users with active positions, the protocol’s custodial accounting, and any downstream services that rely on accurate position balances. The problem was identified during a manual audit that compared the initialization logic with the leverage‑adjustment logic and noticed the divergent source of the lending pair identifier. Because the contract does not emit a clear error when the withdrawal fails, the symptom may be subtle – the UI may still show the position, but the withdrawal transaction succeeds with no funds transferred, making the bug hard to detect without deep inspection of state variables. The correct mitigation is to store the lending pair identifier within each position’s immutable properties and reference that stored value whenever leverage is added or removed, ensuring that operations always target the pair that actually holds the collateral. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that a position’s collateral remains bound to the lending pair that was active at creation, preserving accounting integrity and preventing silent loss of funds.

title: M-05 | Flash Loan Repayments Fail During addLeverage
description: When adding leverage, the user provides pod tokens, and the corresponding pairedLpTokens are flash loaned. At the end of the transaction, this flash loan is repaid by borrowing pairedLpTokens from Fraxlend. However, the flash loan fee is not accounted for when borrowing from Fraxlend. The borrow amount from Fraxlend equals the flash loan amount unless users provide a greater overrideBorrowAmt. The Natspec comments regarding this variable is: "Override amount to borrow from the lending pair, only matters if max LTV is >50% on the lending pair". Since providing overrideBorrowAmt is not mandatory and there are no restrictions, the borrow amount from Fraxlend will usually be equal to _props.pairedLpDesired in most cases. However, this amount is equal to _d.amount, which is smaller than _flashPaybackAmt, causing the transaction to revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs in the addLeverage function that uses a flash loan to obtain paired liquidity provider tokens (pairedLpTokens). After the flash loan is taken, the contract attempts to repay it by borrowing the same amount of pairedLpTokens from the Fraxlend lending pool. The repayment logic mistakenly assumes that borrowing the principal amount is sufficient, ignoring the flash‑loan fee that must also be returned. Because the optional overrideBorrowAmt parameter is not required and is rarely set, the borrowed amount defaults to the exact flash‑loan principal (_props.pairedLpDesired). This amount matches the flash‑loan principal (_d.amount) but is smaller than the total amount that must be repaid (_flashPaybackAmt), which includes the fee. When the contract tries to settle the flash loan with an insufficient amount, the transaction reverts. The bug is a classic under‑payment or fee‑omission error in flash‑loan repayment logic, violating the accounting invariant that total borrowed funds plus fees must be returned. It manifests only when a user initiates an addLeverage operation that relies on flash loans, causing the transaction to fail and the user to lose only gas costs. Users see a failed transaction, no change in their leveraged position, and may be confused why their request to add leverage does not succeed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the repayment flow and noted that the fee component was never added to the borrow request. It can be hard to notice because the fee is typically a small percentage of the loan, so most test runs that use small amounts may not trigger a revert. The proper fix is to ensure that the minimum borrow amount from Fraxlend includes both the principal and the flash‑loan fee (i.e., _props.pairedLpDesired plus _d.fee) or to enforce that an appropriate overrideBorrowAmt is supplied whenever the fee would cause an under‑payment. By correcting the repayment calculation, the protocol restores its financial guarantees and users can successfully add leverage without unexpected reverts.

title: M-06 | Borrowers Pay For Paused Interest
description: FraxlendPair has a function pause which pauses all actions in the pair and a function pauseInterest which pauses interest accrual. When interest is paused, new interest will not be accumulated and that's expected. However, once unpaused, the current borrowers will have to pay interest for the duration from the moment the protocol was paused until the current block. Since the protocol may function normally and have just its interest paused, that means new lenders and borrowers may come and go. This will cause a huge interest misaccounting. For example, interest is paused on Monday. Some borrowers leave the pair. and new ones enter it right before it's unpaused the next Monday. Since the lastUpdated timestamp will be the first monday, the new borrowers will immediately owe interest for that one week they were not even part of the pair.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an interest‑pause accounting flaw in the FraxlendPair contract. The contract provides a pauseInterest flag that stops the accrual of interest while leaving the pair otherwise operational. When interest is paused the contract keeps the lastUpdated timestamp unchanged. When the flag is cleared, the contract calculates accrued interest from the old timestamp for every active borrower. Because the timestamp is not refreshed, borrowers that joined after the pause are charged interest for the whole pause period even though they were not present. This mis‑accounting can be triggered whenever the protocol owner pauses interest but continues to allow deposits, withdrawals or new loans. An attacker can open a loan immediately after the pause and, when interest is resumed, will be billed for the full paused interval, effectively paying interest for time they never used. The impact is that borrowers may see their debt increase unexpectedly, potentially paying a large amount of interest that was never earned by the protocol, which can erode trust and cause financial loss. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the pause logic. It is subtle because the UI shows normal balances and the pause flag appears to work, so the over‑charging is not obvious without inspecting the timestamp handling. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect state reset after feature toggle” or “time‑based accounting error”. The correct fix is to update the internal last‑interest‑accrual timestamp (currentRateInfo.lastTimestamp) to the current block timestamp when pauseInterest is set to false, or to prevent new positions while interest is paused. By resetting the timestamp, interest is only accrued from the moment the pause ends, aligning the accounting with the actual participation of each borrower.

title: M-15 | Feeds With > 18 Decimals Are Problematic
description: The price returned by the oracle is adjusted to 18 decimals with the following computation: _price18 = uint256(_price) * (10 ** 18 / 10 ** _decimals); Notice that the division here happens before the multiplication. This means that if the decimals of the feed are more than 18, the price will be rounded to 0 causing big problems for the assets pricing.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic precision error in the oracle price conversion routine. The contract receives a price value together with the number of decimals reported by the feed. To normalise the price to 18 decimals it computes _price18 = uint256(_price) * (10 ** 18 / 10 ** _decimals). Because the division 10 ** 18 / 10 ** _decimals is performed before the multiplication, the expression is evaluated using integer division. When the feed reports more than 18 decimals, the divisor 10 ** _decimals is larger than 10 ** 18, so the division yields zero. Multiplying the original price by zero results in a normalised price of zero. This zero price is then used throughout the protocol for valuation, collateral checks and trade execution. An attacker can trigger the condition by supplying a feed with a decimal count greater than 18, or by targeting an existing feed that already uses a high precision. With a zero price, the protocol may accept collateral that is effectively worthless, allow purchases at no cost, or calculate refunds as zero, causing users to lose funds or receive nothing. The issue appears only when the feed’s decimal field exceeds 18, which is uncommon for many mainstream price feeds, making the bug easy to overlook during testing. It was discovered during a manual audit of the oracle integration code, where the order of operations was examined. The problem is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error; the price simply becomes zero, leading to silent mispricing. The correct approach is to perform the multiplication first (price * 10 ** 18) and then divide by 10 ** _decimals, or to use a safe fixed‑point library that preserves precision. This change ensures that feeds with any number of decimals are correctly scaled to 18‑decimal representation, preventing the price from collapsing to zero and preserving the intended accounting logic of the protocol.

title: M-16 | addLiquidity Fails For Fee-On-Transfer Tokens
description: When addLiquidityV2 is called, an amount of _pairedLPToken is transferred into the contract, and the same amount is used to add liquidity in the DEX_HANDLER. However, if the pairedLPToken is a Fee-on-Transfer token, then the amount received would be less than expected due to a fee. Therefore, the DEX_HANDLER.addLiquidity call could fail due to insufficient tokens.
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs in the addLiquidityV2 function of the contract when it attempts to add liquidity for a token pair that includes a fee‑on‑transfer (FoT) token as the paired LP token. The function first transfers an amount of the paired LP token, denoted as _pairedLPToken, into the contract and then passes the same amount to the DEX_HANDLER.addLiquidity call, assuming that the contract now holds exactly that amount. Fee‑on‑transfer tokens deduct a small percentage on each transfer, so the actual balance that arrives in the contract is lower than the amount specified. Because the code does not verify the post‑transfer balance, it forwards the original, higher amount to the DEX handler. The DEX handler therefore receives fewer tokens than it expects, causing the addLiquidity call to revert due to insufficient token supply. This can be exploited by supplying any FoT token as the paired LP token; the transaction will fail, preventing users from successfully adding liquidity. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for liquidity provision: users attempting to deposit may see the transaction revert or, in some implementations, may lose the transferred tokens without receiving liquidity shares, effectively making funds disappear from the user’s perspective. The issue manifests only when the paired token implements a transfer fee, a condition that is not obvious from the contract’s interface and therefore easy to overlook during testing. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the expected token amount with the actual balance after transfer and noted the mismatch. It is hard to notice because most token pairs do not have transfer fees, and the contract does not emit explicit warnings about the shortfall. To remediate, the contract should query its actual token balance after the transfer (or use a safeTransfer pattern that returns the received amount) and pass that real balance to the DEX handler, or otherwise adjust the logic to accommodate fee‑on‑transfer behavior. In broader terms, this is a classic example of an accounting mismatch caused by assuming a token’s transfer is fee‑free, leading to incorrect liquidity calculations and potential loss of user funds.

title: M-17 | Single Token Pod Assumption
description: When getting price from the oracle, if the base token is a pod, _getBaseTokenInClPool is called. There it gets all assets from the pod and assumes the first token in the array is the base token. However, pods were designed to be multi-asset and able to be created permissionlessly. Therefore, if the first asset is not the intended base token, then serious integration issues would occur. Furthermore in the function _debondFromSelfLendingPod, an assumption is made that the selfLendingPod has only one token. If ever this assumption is broken, there would be integration errors with FraxlendPair and a possibility of stuck tokens in LeverageManager after debonding.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an implicit single‑token assumption made by the LeverageManager when it interacts with a SelfLendingPod. When the oracle is asked for the price of a base token that is itself a pod, the internal helper _getBaseTokenInClPool retrieves the full list of assets stored in the pod and blindly treats the first element of that array as the base token. Pods, however, are deliberately designed to be multi‑asset containers and can be created without permission, meaning the first asset may be any token that the creator chooses. A similar assumption appears in _debondFromSelfLendingPod, where the code proceeds as if the pod holds exactly one token. If a pod contains more than one token, the price returned by the oracle can be calculated from the wrong underlying asset, causing FraxlendPair to use an incorrect price in its accounting. When the debonding step runs, the contract may attempt to move tokens that are not present in the expected position, leaving assets stranded inside LeverageManager. The impact is that users may see unexpected zero balances, receive incorrect amounts on withdrawals or repayments, and the protocol may suffer from stuck funds that cannot be reclaimed automatically. This condition occurs only when a pod is used as the base token and the pod’s asset array does not match the single‑token expectation, which can happen at any time because pods are permissionlessly creatable. The affected parties include any user who opens leveraged positions through the protocol, the FraxlendPair contract that relies on correct pricing, and the LeverageManager that may end up holding orphaned tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the logical flaw of assuming the first asset is the base token without verification. It is hard to notice because the code does not emit explicit warnings and the bug only manifests with specially crafted multi‑asset pods, which are not part of the typical test suite. To remediate, the constructor should store the intended underlying token explicitly, similar to the existing UNDERLYING_TKN variable, and all functions that retrieve a base token from a pod must validate that the pod contains exactly the expected token or handle multiple tokens gracefully. In broader terms, this is a classic validation‑missing bug where an assumption about data structure size leads to incorrect business logic, breaking accounting invariants and potentially causing funds to disappear from the user’s perspective.

title: M-18 | Wrong Price Calculations If T0 Is baseToken
description: When the base token is one of the two tokens in the UNDERLYING_TKN_CL_POOL, it has to be token1. That's because _pricePTKNPerBase18 is calculated based on whether or not the base token is part of that pool by checking if it's token1. This means for pools where the base token is token0 the price will be wrongly flipped.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect price calculation that occurs when the designated base token of a liquidity pool is placed as token0 instead of token1 in the underlying token‑pair contract. The contract’s pricing routine assumes that the base token is always token1 and determines the price of the protocol token per base token (pricePTKNPerBase18) by checking the position of the base token. When the base token is actually token0, the routine mistakenly treats token0 as token1, causing the computed price to be inverted. This logical error originates from a hard‑coded assumption about token ordering rather than a dynamic check of the pool composition. An attacker or any user can exploit the flaw simply by interacting with a pool where the base token is token0; the contract will return a price that is the reciprocal of the correct value. Consequently, swaps, deposits, or withdrawals that rely on this price will yield dramatically incorrect amounts – users may receive far fewer tokens than expected, overpay with the base token, or see their balances reduced to near zero. The impact is financial loss for any participant who trades in affected pools, and it undermines the protocol’s accounting guarantees because the invariant that the protocol token is correctly valued against the base token no longer holds. The bug manifests only under the condition that the base token is included in the pool pair but occupies the token0 slot; pools where the base token is token1 behave correctly. It was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the price‑derivation logic and noticed the hard‑coded token1 check without a fallback for token0. The issue can be hard to notice because the contract may still execute without reverting, and the price discrepancy may only become apparent after a user observes an unexpected output amount or a sudden balance change. To remediate, the pricing function should be rewritten to determine the base token’s position dynamically, or enforce at pool creation time that the base token is always token1, thereby eliminating the assumption that leads to the flipped price. In broader terms, this is a class of “incorrect token ordering” bugs that cause arithmetic inversions in price calculations, breaking business logic that expects a stable exchange rate between the protocol token and its base asset. From a user’s perspective, the UI may display a price that is orders of magnitude off, a swap may return zero or negligible tokens, and the expected refund or received amount does not match the amount sent, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds.

title: M-19 | Improper Deadline For Fraxlend Swaps
description: Similarly to M-01, FraxlendPairCore::repayAssetWithCollateral() & FraxlendPairCore::leveragedPosition() does not allow a user to set the block.timestamp for their swap. This exposes users to MEV sandwich attacks, and can cause them to lose out on funds that would have been used to repay their debt.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper deadline handling in the FraxlendPairCore contract functions that perform swaps, specifically repayAssetWithCollateral and leveragedPosition. These functions internally use the current block.timestamp as the deadline for the Uniswap‑style swap, without exposing a parameter that allows the caller to set a custom deadline. The root cause is the omission of a user‑controlled deadline argument, which forces the swap to rely on the block timestamp at execution time. Because the deadline cannot be set by the user, a malicious actor (or any MEV bot) can observe a pending transaction, insert a higher‑priced transaction before it (the front‑run) and then insert a second transaction after it (the back‑run), creating a sandwich attack. In this scenario the attacker can manipulate the price of the asset being swapped, causing the user’s swap to execute at an unfavorable rate. As a result the user may receive less of the output token than expected, or the swap may fail to provide enough value to fully repay the outstanding debt. The impact is that the borrower can lose part of the collateral that was intended to cover the debt, potentially leaving the loan under‑collateralised and causing a loss of funds for the user. The condition occurs whenever a user initiates a repayment‑with‑collateral or a leveraged position that requires an internal swap, and the transaction is pending in the mempool long enough for an attacker to front‑run it. All participants who rely on these functions – borrowers, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the economic assumptions of the loan repayment logic are broken. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit that examined the swap pathways and noticed that the deadline parameter was hard‑coded to block.timestamp, a pattern known to be vulnerable to MEV. The bug can be hard to notice because the transaction may still succeed and the user only sees a smaller repayment amount or a slightly higher debt, which can be attributed to market volatility rather than a contract flaw. Conceptually, the fix is to expose a deadline argument that the caller can set, allowing the user to specify a reasonable time window for the swap and thereby preventing an attacker from arbitrarily extending the deadline to execute a sandwich. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of deadline‑or‑timestamp misuse leading to front‑running vulnerabilities, where missing user‑controlled timing controls break the intended accounting guarantees of a DeFi protocol. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as a missing or reduced refund, a repayment that does not clear the debt, or an unexpected reduction in the token balance after the transaction, contrary to the expectation that the swap will fully cover the loan. The failure mode is essentially a loss of funds due to an exploitable price manipulation path rather than a direct code error, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that the swap will execute at a fair market price within a bounded time window.

title: M-20 | FraxVault Incompatible With Non-Standard Tokens
description: The FraxlendPair contracts do not support non-standard tokens such as rebasing or fee-on-transfer tokens, whose balance changes during transfers or over time. If the Peapods team expects to support these tokens, then there will be accounting issues when interacting with FraxlendPair contracts.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the FraxlendPair contracts assuming that every ERC‑20 token behaves according to the standard specification, meaning that a transfer of X tokens always results in the sender’s balance decreasing by X and the receiver’s balance increasing by exactly X. This assumption is violated by non‑standard tokens such as rebasing tokens, which automatically adjust holder balances over time, and fee‑on‑transfer (or tax) tokens, which deduct a portion of the amount during each transfer. When a user deposits a token of this type into a FraxlendPair, the contract records the amount it believes was transferred based on the transfer call return value, but the actual token balance that the contract receives may be lower because of the hidden fee or a rebasing event. Consequently, the internal accounting of the vault becomes inconsistent with the real token holdings. An attacker or an unwary user can exploit this mismatch by depositing a fee‑on‑transfer token, receiving a smaller amount of credit than expected, and later attempting to withdraw or borrow against an inflated internal balance, leading to either loss of funds for the user or a shortfall in the vault’s reserves. The impact includes incorrect interest calculations, potential under‑collateralisation of loans, and the risk that users receive less than they deposited or that the protocol cannot honour withdrawals, effectively causing funds to disappear from the user’s perspective. This condition occurs whenever the FraxlendPair interacts with any token whose balance changes during a transfer or over time, and it affects all participants who deposit such tokens, including lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the expected token flow against the actual balance changes and noted that the contracts do not perform any post‑transfer balance verification. The problem is subtle because the transfer transaction itself does not revert and the token contract does not emit an explicit warning; the discrepancy only becomes visible when the vault’s accounting is later reconciled. To remediate the issue, the contract should verify the token balance of the vault before and after each transfer, adjust the recorded amount to reflect any fees or rebasing effects, or explicitly reject tokens that do not conform to the ERC‑20 standard. In broader terms, this is a classic case of assuming token invariance where none exists, leading to accounting bugs that break the fundamental guarantee that deposited assets are fully accounted for.

title: M-21 | removeLeverage Could Fail For Self-Lending Pairs
description: This bug was reported in a previous audit but does not seem to be fixed (see [https://hackmd.io/@tapir/SyxqzohUA#M-6-Removing-leverage-will-likely-fail-if-the-pod-token-needs-to-be-sold-for-the-borrowed-token-in-a-self-lending-scenario](https://hackmd.io/@tapir/SyxqzohUA#M-6-Removing-leverage-will-likely-fail-if-the-pod-token-needs-to-be-sold-for-the-borrowed-token-in-a-self-lending-scenario)) The issue remains that there is no natural Uniswap V2 market that exists to swap pod tokens for borrowed assets (from FraxlendPair), when the pair is self-lending. Furthermore, during _swapPodForBorrowToken in the removeLeverage flow, the entire amount of pod tokens received is passed as amountInMax for the swap --resulting in zero slippage protection. This could allow an attacker to deploy a pool to take advantage of this scenario and steal all pod tokens from a user.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the removeLeverage workflow of the Peapods contract, specifically in the internal function that swaps pod tokens for the borrowed asset when a leveraged position is being unwound.
