In self‑lending configurations the pod token and the borrowed token are effectively the same asset, meaning there is no external Uniswap V2 pair that can provide liquidity for the required conversion. The code nevertheless attempts to perform a swap by passing the entire amount of pod tokens received as amountInMax to the Uniswap router, which removes any slippage protection. Because the router is called with an unrestricted amountInMax, an attacker can create a malicious liquidity pool with a very unfavorable price, trigger the removeLeverage call for a victim, and cause the router to accept the swap at the manipulated rate. The result is that the victim’s pod tokens are transferred to the attacker’s pool, leaving the user with a zero or dramatically reduced pod‑token balance while still expecting a refund of their leveraged position. This flaw manifests only when the pod token must be sold for the borrowed token in a self‑lending scenario, i.e., during the _swapPodForBorrowToken step of removeLeverage. Users who have opened leveraged positions are directly affected, as their funds disappear without an explicit error. The issue was originally flagged in a prior audit but remains unfixed, making it hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it simply completes with an unexpected loss of assets, which may be interpreted as a normal outcome by a casual observer. To remediate, the contract should enforce a reasonable slippage limit on the swap, verify that a healthy Uniswap V2 market exists for the token pair before attempting the conversion, and add a fallback path or guard clause that prevents the swap when the market is missing or when the pair is self‑lending. By doing so the protocol restores the expected accounting invariant that a user’s pod‑token balance after removeLeverage matches the amount they are entitled to receive, eliminating the possibility of silent fund theft.

title: M-22 | USDC Blacklist Prevents Transfers
description: When the staking pool token is transferred it will call _setShares(), which will lead to _distributeReward() being called. Inside of _distributeReward(), it will loop through the reward tokens and transfer any rewards to the users. If a user becomes blacklisted from using USDC, _distributeReward() will revert. This, in turn, will lead to the tokens being stuck in the users wallet and become untransferable. Additionally, this prevents a user from calling claimRewards(). They will not be able to claim any other rewards tokens earned outside of USDC.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial-of-service style bug in the staking pool contract where rewards are pushed to users during a token transfer. When a user transfers the pool token, the internal function _setShares triggers _distributeReward, which iterates over all configured reward tokens and attempts to transfer each reward to the recipient. If the recipient is on the USDC blacklist, the USDC transfer inside _distributeReward reverts. Because the revert propagates back through the internal call chain, the original transfer of the pool token also reverts, leaving the pool tokens locked in the sender’s wallet and making them untransferable. In addition, the same revert blocks the public claimRewards function, so the affected address cannot claim any accrued rewards, even those denominated in other tokens. The issue occurs only for accounts that have been blacklisted for USDC usage; normal accounts are unaffected. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that traced the call flow from token transfer to reward distribution and observed the revert condition. It is hard to notice because the failure happens deep inside a library call, so the front‑end simply reports a generic transaction failure without indicating that a USDC blacklist caused the problem. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a transaction that “fails” when trying to send the pool token, a balance that appears unchanged, and an inability to claim any rewards, leading to the perception that “my funds disappeared” or “rewards are missing”. This violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that rewards can always be claimed and that token transfers are always possible. The vulnerability belongs to the class of push‑based reward distribution bugs where an external token’s transfer restrictions (such as blacklists, pausable contracts, or failing ERC‑20 implementations) can cause a cascade of reverts that lock user assets. The recommended mitigation is to switch from an automatic push model to a pull‑based model: let users explicitly call a claim function for each reward token they wish to receive, and skip or defer transfers of blacklisted tokens. Alternatively, the contract could check the blacklist before attempting the USDC transfer and either omit that token or route the reward to a fallback mechanism, ensuring that the primary token transfer never reverts because of an unrelated reward token.

title: M-23 | Uniswap Ticks Rounding
description: Multiple contracts in the system -[V3TwapUtilities](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/peapods-2/blob/cebeb47138e5f029cefd698328dfbd33e90fbbea/contracts/twaputils/V3TwapUtilities.sol#L94-L97), [V3AerodromeUtilities](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/peapods-2/blob/cebeb47138e5f029cefd698328dfbd33e90fbbea/contracts/twaputils/V3TwapAerodromeUtilities.sol#L96-L99), [UniswapV3SinglePriceOracle](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/peapods-2/blob/cebeb47138e5f029cefd698328dfbd33e90fbbea/contracts/oracle/UniswapV3SinglePriceOracle.sol#L60-L63) - fetch the TWAP price of a given asset. When calculating the TWAP, the delta of two CL ticks is divided by a given time period. Since solidity truncates when it divides, for negative ticks the result will be rounded up instead of rounded down resulting in a different price. For reference, see how is this handled in [OracleLibrary](https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-periphery/blob/697c2474757ea89fec12a4e6db16a574fe259610/contracts/libraries/OracleLibrary.sol#L36).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error that occurs when several contracts compute a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) using the difference between two Uniswap V3 tick values divided by a time interval. In Solidity, integer division truncates toward zero. When the tick delta is negative, this truncation effectively rounds the result up instead of rounding down, producing a slightly larger tick‑per‑second value and consequently a higher quoted price. The root cause is the use of plain signed integer division without compensating for the sign, which violates the mathematical expectation that a division of a negative numerator should round toward negative infinity for price calculations. An attacker can exploit this by forcing a negative tick delta—such as during a market swing—so that the oracle reports a price that is systematically biased upward. Protocols that rely on this oracle for pricing, liquidation thresholds, or fee calculations may then execute trades or liquidations at incorrect values, leading to potential loss of funds, unfair pricing, or arbitrage opportunities. The issue manifests only when the tick delta is negative and the division by the time period is performed; positive deltas are unaffected because truncation rounds down as intended. Users of the protocol, including traders, lenders, and liquidity providers, are impacted because the displayed price may differ from the true market price, causing unexpected slippage, failed liquidations, or missing refunds. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementation against Uniswap’s reference OracleLibrary, which explicitly handles signed division to ensure rounding down. The problem is subtle because the numerical discrepancy is often small and only appears under specific market conditions, making it easy to overlook in routine testing. To remediate, the contracts should adopt the same rounding‑down technique used in OracleLibrary, typically by adjusting the division to add one when the numerator is negative before truncating, or by using a library function that implements signed division with floor rounding. This change restores the intended price calculation, aligns the oracle with Uniswap’s reference implementation, and eliminates the risk of price manipulation due to rounding errors.

title: M-24 | Arbitrage From Deviation In Oracle Price
description:
The maximum a user can borrow is determined by the exchange rate returned by the oracle. However, all oracles are susceptible to front-running as their prices tend to lag behind an assets real price. For example, Chainlink oracles are updated after price crosses a threshold while Uniswap V3 TWAP returns price over past X blocks. An attacker could exploit the difference between the price reported by an oracle and the asset's actual price to gain a profit by front-running the oracle's price update. The likelihood of this condition is increased for Peapods due to the multiple layers that an underlying asset is wrapped in. Consider this example:
• Fraxlend Vault has a high maxLTV of 95%, with the collateral as aspTKN (pPEAS-WETH) and asset (WETH)
• 1 aspTKN is currently worth 0.002 WETH
• Price of aspTKN drops while WETH price increases, such that 1 aspTKN should be worth 0.0015 WETH
• Due to the lag in oracle update, price is not updated yet
• Attacker sees this opportunity and front-runs the oracle update to:
• Deposit 100 aspTKNs
• Max borrow 0.19 WETH (95% LTV)
• Afterwards, the oracle price is updated to 1 aspTKN = 0.0015 WETH
• The attacker's position is now unhealthy as his collateral is worth less than the loan amount
• Attacker back-runs the oracle update to liquidate himself:
• To seize 100 aspTKN he repay 0.15 WETH
• Gains back his original collateral plus 0.04 WETH
All profits gained result in bad debt socialized among lenders.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an oracle price deviation arbitrage that arises because the protocol determines a borrower’s maximum loan amount from a price feed that can lag behind the market price of the underlying asset. The root cause is the reliance on a single, potentially stale oracle value to calculate collateral value while allowing a very high loan‑to‑value ratio (95%). When the market price of the wrapped collateral moves sharply, the oracle may not reflect the new price immediately, creating a window where the reported collateral value is higher than its real value. An attacker can monitor this discrepancy, deposit the collateral, borrow up to the reported limit, and then wait for the oracle to update. After the price correction, the attacker’s position becomes under‑collateralised; the attacker can immediately trigger a self‑liquidation, repaying only a fraction of the borrowed amount and keeping the difference as profit. In the described scenario the attacker deposits 100 units of a wrapped token, borrows 0.19 ether at 95 % LTV, and after the oracle price drops from 0.002 to 0.0015 ether per token, liquidates the position by repaying 0.15 ether, thereby walking away with an extra 0.04 ether. The impact is that the attacker gains profit while the shortfall is socialised among lenders as bad debt, effectively eroding the protocol’s capital safety. This condition occurs whenever the oracle update frequency or methodology (e.g., threshold‑based updates or short‑window TWAP) cannot keep up with rapid price movements, especially for assets that are wrapped through multiple layers, which amplify the lag. All participants who rely on the borrowing function – borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the borrowing limit calculation does not incorporate safeguards against rapid price changes or front‑running. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the borrowing logic and identified that the protocol does not enforce any delay, fee, or sanity check before allowing a loan based on a potentially outdated price. The flaw can be hard to notice because the exploit can be executed within a single transaction sequence, leaving no obvious on‑chain trace of manipulation beyond the profit taken by the attacker, and because the protocol’s accounting may still appear balanced after the liquidation. To remediate, the protocol should treat this class of bug as an oracle‑price‑staleness vulnerability and introduce mitigations such as a borrowing fee that reduces the incentive for arbitrage, tighter LTV caps, longer or more robust price averaging windows, price‑change sanity checks, or a mandatory re‑valuation period before allowing a loan to be taken. These measures would align the collateral valuation more closely with the market price and prevent attackers from profiting by exploiting temporary oracle lag, thereby protecting lenders from unexpected bad debt.

title: M-07 | Improper Slippage And Deadline During Deposit
description: When calling deposit, a slippage of 0 and a deadline of block.timestamp is passed to _processRewardsToPodLp. Using 0 for slippage is dangerous as MEV bots could sandwich the swap to steal tokens. Similarly, setting block.timestamp as deadline is ineffective as the transaction could sit in the mempool until it's ready to be processed, at which time block.timestamp is set, therefore offering no protection from sandwich attacks.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper handling of slippage tolerance and transaction deadline in the deposit workflow of the contract. When a user calls the deposit function, the internal call to _processRewardsToPodLp is supplied with a hard‑coded slippage value of zero and a deadline equal to block.timestamp. Because the slippage tolerance is zero, the swap that converts the deposited assets into pool tokens is forced to execute at exactly the quoted price; any deviation caused by market movement or front‑running will cause the swap to revert or, more commonly, to be executed at a price that is unfavorable to the user. The deadline being set to the current block timestamp provides no time buffer: a transaction can sit in the mempool for an arbitrary period, and when it is finally mined the block.timestamp will have advanced to the same value used as the deadline, effectively disabling the deadline check. Under these conditions a malicious MEV bot can sandwich the deposit transaction – submitting a front‑run trade that moves the price before the victim’s deposit is processed and a back‑run trade that restores the price afterwards – thereby stealing a portion of the deposited tokens. From the user’s perspective the deposit appears to succeed, but the received LP balance may be dramatically lower than expected or even zero, leading to the impression that “my funds disappeared” or “the refund is missing”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the parameter flow into the reward‑processing routine and identified the hard‑coded values as a logical flaw. It is difficult to notice because the contract does not emit explicit error messages; the transaction does not revert, and the only symptom is an unexpected loss of value in the user’s balance. The root cause is the lack of user‑controlled slippage and deadline parameters, which violates the business assumption that deposits should be protected against price manipulation and should respect a reasonable time window. To remediate the issue the contract should expose slippage tolerance and deadline as configurable inputs, enforce a minimum non‑zero slippage (e.g., 0.5 % or higher) and require the deadline to be greater than the current block timestamp by a configurable offset, thereby restoring protection against sandwich attacks and ensuring that deposited funds are accounted for correctly.

title: M-25 | mint In Fraxlend Rounds In Users’ Favour
description: The mint function in the FraxlendPairCore contract rounds down in favour of the users and users pay fewer assets for corresponding shares.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding bias in the mint function of the FraxlendPairCore contract. When a user calls mint to receive protocol shares in exchange for depositing assets, the contract calculates the number of shares by dividing the deposited amount by the current share price and then applies integer division that rounds down. Because the rounding is performed in favour of the user, the user receives slightly more shares than the exact proportional value would dictate, effectively paying fewer assets for the same amount of shares. The root cause is the use of floor division without a compensating safety margin, which is a classic arithmetic rounding error. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly minting small amounts, where the rounding error per transaction is tiny but accumulates, allowing the attacker to acquire a larger share of the pool for less collateral. The impact is a gradual dilution of existing shareholders, a reduction in the total asset backing per share, and potential insolvency of the lending pool if the bug is exercised at scale. The condition under which it occurs is any call to the mint function that involves a division operation; the effect is more pronounced with small deposit amounts but is present for all minting actions. All participants in the Fraxlend protocol—depositors, borrowers, and token holders—are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each share is fully backed become violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the expected proportional minting logic with the actual implementation and noticed that the rounding direction favoured users. Because the per‑transaction discrepancy is often only a few wei, it can be difficult to notice in normal operation, especially when users only see that they receive the expected number of shares. The bug belongs to the class of rounding‑bias or arithmetic‑precision vulnerabilities that break financial invariants. To fix the problem the mint calculation should be changed to round up (ceil) or to include a small protocol‑level buffer so that the protocol never receives fewer assets than required for the minted shares. In user‑facing terms, a user may observe that after minting they receive more shares than anticipated while the pool’s total assets appear slightly lower than expected, leading to a situation where funds disappear from the protocol’s perspective even though individual users seem to get a better deal.

title: M-26 | Oracle Incompatible With Non-Standard Tokens
description: The current logic in getPrices will underflow when the BASE token has more than 18 decimals: uint256 _priceOne18 = _priceBaseSpTKN * 10 ** (18 - IERC20Metadata(BASE_TOKEN).decimals()); This will entirely prevent oracle compatibility with borrow tokens that have more than 18 decimal precision, which is problematic in Peapods which is a permissionless system.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the price oracle function that computes a token price by scaling the raw price with a factor derived from the token's decimal count. The code multiplies the raw price by 10 raised to the power of (18 minus the token's declared decimals). When the base token reports more than 18 decimal places, the subtraction 18 - decimals underflows because it is performed with unsigned integers, resulting in a very large exponent. This causes the multiplication to overflow or produce an incorrect zero value, effectively breaking the price calculation. The bug is triggered whenever a borrow token with a non‑standard precision (greater than 18 decimals) is queried, which can happen in permissionless environments where any ERC‑20 token may be supplied. From a user’s perspective the oracle returns no price, the borrowing transaction reverts, and the UI may show a missing or zero balance where a valid price was expected. The impact is that legitimate assets with higher precision become unusable in the protocol, leading to denial‑of‑service for those token holders and potentially reducing the protocol’s market coverage. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic handling of token decimals. It is subtle because the code compiles without warnings and only fails for a subset of tokens that are not commonly used, making it easy to overlook during testing. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of arithmetic underflow/overflow errors caused by incorrect scaling of token amounts. To remediate, the contract should first read the token's decimal value, compare it against the standard 18‑decimal scaling, and if the token has more than 18 decimals, adjust the scaling factor by dividing instead of multiplying (or by using a safe exponent calculation that never underflows). This change restores compatibility with high‑precision tokens and ensures that price queries always produce a meaningful result.

title: M-27 | Fee-on-transfer Tokens Are Not Supported
description:
Fee on transfer tokens are not supported correctly for:
• pod underlying token - bond() doesn't check the received amount of the transfer and mints shares based on the initial amount
• pod paired token - LeverageManager assumes it has received the whole amount of the flashloaned token
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the protocol’s implicit assumption that ERC20 tokens transfer the exact amount specified in the call. In two critical paths the contract does not verify the actual amount received after a transfer. First, when a user bonds an underlying token to a pod, the bond() function records the amount that was requested to be transferred and mints pod shares based on that value without checking how many tokens actually arrived. Fee‑on‑transfer tokens deduct a portion of the transferred amount as a fee, so the contract mints shares for a larger amount than it really holds, creating an accounting mismatch that can be exploited to inflate share balances. Second, the LeverageManager component receives a flash‑loaned token that is paired with the pod. It assumes the full loan amount is available for the subsequent operations, again without confirming the net amount after the fee. If the token charges a transfer fee, the manager will operate with fewer tokens than expected, potentially causing under‑collateralisation, failed repayments, or loss of funds. The issue is observable when a user deposits a fee‑on‑transfer token and either receives more shares than justified or sees the protocol fail to execute a leveraged position, leading to unexpected zero balances or missing refunds. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the lack of balance checks after external token transfers. Because the contract relies on events and the amount passed to the function rather than the post‑transfer balance, the bug can remain hidden unless a token with transfer fees is used. To remediate, the code should employ a safe‑transfer pattern that records the contract’s token balance before and after the transfer, calculates the exact received amount, and bases share minting or flash‑loan accounting on that real value. Supporting fee‑on‑transfer tokens at the protocol level eliminates the accounting discrepancy and restores the intended business logic that each deposited token corresponds to an equal share of the pod and that flash‑loaned amounts are fully available for leveraged operations.

title: M-28 | Missing Check For Sequencer Downtime
description: Chainlink recommends that all Optimistic L2 oracles consult the Sequencer Uptime Feed to ensure that the sequencer is live before trusting the data returned by the oracle. See https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds#l2-sequencer-uptime-feeds If the Arbitrum sequencer goes down for example, oracle data will not be updated and could become stale. Attackers could take advantage of the stale prices and carry out attacks, such as borrowing more against their collateral's true value.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of the contract’s failure to verify that the Optimistic Layer‑2 sequencer is operational before using price data from a Chainlink oracle. The root cause is the omission of a check against the Chainlink Sequencer Uptime Feed, which is designed to signal when the sequencer is down. Because the contract reads the price feed unconditionally, it may accept stale price values that have not been updated while the sequencer is offline. An attacker who observes a sequencer outage can submit transactions that rely on the outdated price, for example by opening or increasing a loan with collateral that appears over‑valued. The impact is that the protocol may lend more assets than the true collateral value justifies, leading to under‑collateralized positions and potential loss of funds for lenders or the protocol treasury. The condition occurs whenever the L2 sequencer experiences downtime – a scenario that can happen due to network upgrades, attacks on the sequencer, or infrastructure failures. All users who interact with the borrowing or liquidation logic are affected, including borrowers, lenders, and any third‑party contracts that depend on the oracle data. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s oracle usage pattern against Chainlink’s recommended best practices for L2 feeds. Because the contract still functions correctly when the sequencer is up, the problem is subtle and may only be noticed when a sudden drop in collateralization ratios or unexpected loan approvals appear during a sequencer outage. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a loan may be approved with a collateral value that seems correct in the UI, but later the position is liquidated or the protocol suffers a loss because the price used was stale. This class of bug belongs to missing external state validation or stale oracle data vulnerabilities, where a contract trusts a data source without confirming its freshness. The recommended fix is to query the Sequencer Uptime Feed before reading the price feed and to abort or fallback to a safe state when the feed reports that the sequencer is down, following the example code provided by Chainlink. Implementing this check restores the invariant that price data must be up‑to‑date, preventing attackers from exploiting periods of sequencer downtime.

title: M-29 | ASP Insufficient Liquidity DOS
description: When AutoCompoundingPodLp swaps the paired tokens for pod tokens, it adds them as liquidity. However, if the amounts are too small, this will result in minting 0 liquidity and a revert with INSUFFICIENT_LIQUIDITY_MINTED.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an insufficient‑liquidity minting error that occurs when the AutoCompoundingPodLp contract attempts to add liquidity after swapping the paired tokens for pod tokens. The contract forwards the swapped token amounts to the underlying AMM’s addLiquidity function, which calculates the amount of liquidity tokens to mint based on the pool’s current reserves. If the supplied token amounts are very small, the calculation rounds down to zero, causing the AMM to try to mint 0 liquidity tokens. The AMM then reverts with the error INSUFFICIENT_LIQUIDITY_MINTED. This situation creates a denial‑of‑service condition because any transaction that triggers a small‑amount swap will fail, preventing users from receiving pod tokens or rewards. The root cause is the lack of a minimum‑amount guard before invoking the liquidity‑minting step; the contract assumes that any positive amount will produce a positive liquidity mint, ignoring the rounding behavior of integer arithmetic in the AMM. An attacker or even a benign user can exploit the issue by submitting a transaction with a tiny swap amount, causing the minting step to revert and thereby blocking further reward distribution for that pod. The impact is that users see their transactions revert, receive no pod tokens, and observe unchanged balances in the UI, effectively losing the ability to claim accrued rewards. The problem manifests only when the swapped amounts fall below the implicit threshold defined by the AMM’s liquidity formula, which may be rare under normal usage and therefore easy to miss during testing. The affected parties are all participants who interact with the pod – liquidity providers, reward claimants, and the protocol itself, which may suffer reputational damage. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the contract does not enforce a minimum reward size similar to the pattern used in the DecentralizedIndex contract. Because the revert is triggered only for edge‑case amounts, it can be overlooked in functional tests that use typical transaction sizes. To remediate, the contract should introduce a check that the calculated liquidity to be minted exceeds a safe, non‑zero threshold before calling the AMM, and if the amount is below that threshold, the contract should skip the reward minting or revert with a clearer, user‑friendly message. This mitigation aligns the logic with a generic class of “insufficient liquidity mint” bugs, where rounding errors lead to zero‑output operations and potential denial‑of‑service.

title: M-30 | User's Lockup Period Should Not Change Midway
description: Owner can set the lockupPeriod variable via setLockupPeriod. However, this would affect all users who are already staked with the previous lockupPeriod value, which would be unfair.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract exposing a mutable global lockupPeriod that can be altered by the owner through a setLockupPeriod function. Because the contract checks the unlock eligibility of a stake against this single variable, any change to lockupPeriod retroactively applies to all existing stakes, regardless of when they were created. An attacker with owner privileges can extend the lockup period after users have already deposited tokens, causing those users to remain locked for a longer time than originally promised. This can be exploited by the owner calling setLockupPeriod to a larger value shortly before a large number of users are expected to unstake, effectively preventing them from withdrawing their funds on schedule. The impact is that users experience delayed access to their staked assets, potentially missing market opportunities or being unable to retrieve funds when needed, which violates the economic assumptions of the staking service. The condition occurs whenever the owner invokes the lockup period update after stakes have been made; it does not require any special user interaction. All participants who have staked tokens are affected, including regular users, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts that rely on the expected unlock time. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined state‑variable usage and identified that the lockupPeriod is not snapshot per stake. It can be hard to notice because the contract may appear to function correctly for new stakes, and the UI may simply show a longer countdown without indicating that the policy changed. The proper mitigation is to capture the current lockupPeriod value at the moment a user stakes and store it in the individual Stake record, then reference this stored value when calculating the unlock timestamp during unstake. This change isolates each stake from future policy adjustments, preserving the original agreement and preventing unfair extension of lockup periods.

title: M-31 | Asp Rewards Can Be Sandwiched
description:
The idea of AutoCompoundingPodLp is to swap the accumulated rewards into paired lp tokens and use them to generate new spTokens. When the current reward token of the asp doesn't match the reward token for its pod, 0 slippage is used for the swap so anyone can sandwich the transaction to benefit from it which will result in a loss for the asp holders. The following can be executed in one transaction:
• swap
• process rewards
• swap again
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the auto‑compounding mechanism of the pod that converts accumulated reward tokens into LP tokens and then mints new spTokens. When the reward token that the ASP contract distributes differs from the reward token expected by the pod, the contract performs the swap with a hard‑coded slippage tolerance of zero. This design assumes that the market price will not move between the moment the transaction is submitted and the moment it is executed. In reality an attacker can submit a transaction that front‑runs the swap, pushes the price unfavourably, lets the victim’s zero‑slippage swap execute at a worse rate, and then back‑runs to restore the price and capture the spread. Because the swap, reward processing and the second swap are all executed within a single transaction, the attacker can perform the entire sandwich in one atomic call, extracting value from the ASP holders without any visible error. The impact is a reduction of the value of the ASP holders’ positions – users may see their balances shrink or receive fewer spTokens than expected – and the protocol may suffer a loss of funds. The issue only manifests when the reward token mismatch condition is true and the contract uses a zero‑slippage parameter; otherwise normal operation is unaffected. It was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the unrealistic assumption of price stability. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert and appears to succeed, making the loss look like a normal market movement rather than an exploit. To remediate, the swap should be executed with a reasonable slippage tolerance that can be configured per pod, and the call should be wrapped in a try/catch block so that a failed swap does not revert the whole operation, thereby preventing both the sandwich profit and a potential denial‑of‑service vector.

title: M-32 | Incorrect Autocompounding Asset And Shares Conversions
description: In AutoCompoundingPodLp::withdraw(), it will convert the amount of assets to shares prior to calling _processRewardsToLp(). Then it will convert the shares back to assets. In between conversions, the _cbr() is likely to increase due to the increase in total assets that will occur when _processRewardsToLp() is called. This will lead to a larger output amount of assets than requested to be withdrawn. When AutoCompoundingPodLp::mint() is called, it will convert the amount of shares to assets. Then call _processRewardsToLp(), and proceed to convert the amount of assets back to shares. This will have the inverse effect, and provide a smaller amount of shares for the deposited user than requested. Ultimately, both of these functions will provide users with different amount of shares and assets respectively than expected.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the AutoCompoundingPodLp contract where the functions withdraw() and mint() perform asset‑to‑share and share‑to‑asset conversions in the wrong order relative to the internal reward processing routine _processRewardsToLp(). In withdraw(), the contract first converts the user‑requested asset amount into shares using the current conversion rate (cbr), then calls _processRewardsToLp() which adds newly earned rewards to the pool and consequently increases the total asset balance. Because the conversion rate is a function of total assets divided by total shares, the added rewards raise the rate before the contract converts the shares back to assets. This results in the user receiving more assets than they originally requested. Conversely, in mint(), the contract converts the deposited share amount into assets, then processes rewards, and finally converts the resulting assets back into shares. The reward addition again raises the conversion rate, so the final share amount calculated is smaller than what the depositor expected. The root cause is the misplaced call to _processRewardsToLp() after the conversion steps, causing the conversion rate to change between the two conversions. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly withdrawing or minting to capture the systematic over‑payment of assets or the systematic under‑allocation of shares, gradually draining value from the pool or diluting existing participants. The issue manifests whenever _processRewardsToLp() modifies the total asset balance – typically when rewards are accrued – and the contract performs a conversion before invoking that function. All users of the AutoCompoundingPodLp, including depositors, withdrawers, and the protocol’s accounting layer, are affected because the accounting invariants (total assets = total shares * conversion rate) are broken. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined the order of state‑changing calls and noticed that the conversion rate could shift between the two conversion steps. It is subtle because a single transaction may only show a small discrepancy that can be masked by rounding, making it hard to detect without systematic testing or balance audits. To remediate, the contract should invoke _processRewardsToLp() before any conversion, ensuring that the conversion rate is stable for the entire operation, or alternatively recalculate the conversion rate after rewards are processed before performing the second conversion. This restores the expected relationship between assets and shares, prevents users from receiving more assets than requested or fewer shares than expected, and preserves the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: M-33 | LendingAssetVault Asset/Share Conversion Error
description: Similarly to M-20, the LendingAssetVault::withdraw() and LendingAssetVault::mint() perform asset and share conversions with an update to _cbr() taking place in between. This takes place with the call to _updateInterestAndMdInAllVaults() happening in _withdraw() and _deposit(). This will lead to a similar scenario where the accounting for assets will be incorrect for withdrawals and the shares will be incorrect for mints compared to the amounts requested.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an asset‑share conversion error in the LendingAssetVault contract. When a user calls withdraw or mint, the contract first converts between the underlying asset amount and the vault share amount, then invokes the internal function _updateInterestAndMdInAllVaults before completing the conversion. Because the interest and market‑depth state are updated between the two conversion steps, the first conversion uses stale accounting data while the second conversion uses the freshly updated data. This mismatch leads to an incorrect calculation of the number of assets that should be returned on withdrawal and an incorrect number of shares that should be minted on deposit. The root cause is the placement of the interest‑update call in the middle of the conversion workflow rather than at the beginning of the operation. An attacker or any user can exploit this by initiating a withdrawal or mint transaction when the vault’s interest rate changes, causing the contract to credit fewer assets or issue fewer shares than the user is entitled to. The impact is a systematic under‑allocation of value: users may receive less than the amount they deposited or expect to withdraw, effectively causing a loss of funds that appears as missing balances or zero refunds in the UI. The bug manifests whenever the contract’s _updateInterestAndMdInAllVaults function is triggered during a withdraw or deposit, which can happen on any transaction that changes the vault’s interest state. All participants who interact with the vault – depositors, borrowers, and liquidity providers – are potentially affected because the accounting error propagates to their balances. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the expected accounting invariants with the actual state changes after each operation, revealing that the asset‑share conversion diverged from the intended formula. It is hard to notice because the discrepancy may be small for a single transaction and only becomes evident after multiple operations or when large interest adjustments occur. The recommended fix is to move the call to _updateInterestAndMdInAllVaults to the start of the withdraw and mint functions so that both conversion steps use a consistent, up‑to‑date view of the vault’s interest and market‑depth parameters. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistent accounting errors where mutable protocol state is read before it is fully synchronized, violating the assumption that asset‑share ratios remain constant throughout a single user operation. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that a withdrawal returns less than expected, sometimes even zero, and a deposit yields fewer shares than the amount of assets supplied, breaking the expectation that “deposit X tokens, receive X‑equivalent shares” and “withdraw Y shares, receive Y‑equivalent tokens”.

title: M-34 | VotingPool Pods Priced Equally
description: Currently, all pods are priced equally in the VotingPool contract (assuming the conversion factor is 1:1). This means users can stake cheap pods and receive the same amount of voting tokens they would have received with more expensive pods. For example, a pod with DAI as underlying token and a pod with WETH as underlying token would both be priced equally if their conversion factors are the same. There may also be a situation where the pod with DAI token has its conversion factor higher - this will lead to the DAI pod minting more voting tokens than the WETH one.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the VotingPool contract’s pricing logic, which treats every staking pod as having the same economic value when the conversion factor is set to a 1:1 ratio. This design assumes that the conversion factor alone accurately reflects the market worth of the underlying asset, ignoring the fact that different tokens such as DAI and WETH have vastly different prices. As a result, a user who stakes a low‑value pod (for example, a DAI pod with a modest market price) receives the same amount of voting tokens as a user who stakes a high‑value pod (such as a WETH pod) if both pods share the same conversion factor. The root cause is the omission of an external price reference or weighted conversion that would align voting token minting with the true economic value of the deposited assets. An attacker can exploit this by depositing large quantities of cheap pods that are priced equally to more expensive pods, thereby minting a disproportionate number of voting tokens for relatively little capital. This inflated voting power can be used to sway governance proposals, approve malicious upgrades, or otherwise manipulate protocol decisions without providing commensurate economic stake. The impact is a distortion of the protocol’s governance model: voting outcomes no longer reflect the actual value locked in the system, potentially leading to decisions that favor a minority of participants who exploit the pricing flaw. The condition for exploitation is the presence of pods with differing market prices but identical conversion factors, or a scenario where the conversion factor is manually set higher for a low‑value pod, causing it to mint more voting tokens than intended. All participants in the governance process—token holders, delegators, and the protocol itself—are affected because the integrity of voting results is compromised. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the contract’s economic assumptions, where the auditor noted that the pricing function did not incorporate any price oracle or market data, making the equal‑price assumption unrealistic. The flaw can be hard to notice because the user interface may display pod prices as identical, and there is no immediate error or revert; the problem manifests only in the distribution of voting power, which may appear normal on the surface. To remediate the issue, the contract should be updated to include a reliable price feed for each underlying asset, apply a weighted conversion that reflects real‑time market values, or restrict the pool to pods whose prices are within a narrow band, ensuring that voting tokens are minted proportionally to the actual economic value contributed. This class of bug falls under economic mispricing or tokenomics design flaws, where the lack of proper valuation leads to unfair advantage and potential governance attacks.

title: M-08 | AutoCompoundingPodLp Is Not EIP Compliant
description:
Some [EIP-4626](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4626) compliance issues have been observed in the AutoCompoundingPodLp contract:
1. According to EIP-4626, the mint function must mint exactly the user-inputted amount of shares, and the withdraw function must transfer exactly the specified assets amount. However, these functions mint or withdraw fewer tokens due to rounding down twice during the action flows. During the withdraw function in the codebase:
• User provides _assets amount.
• It is converted to shares with convertToShares function, which rounds down.
• Then, the internal _withdraw function is called with this shares amount.
• In this internal function, the shares amount is converted to assets again with convertToAssets, which also rounds down. As a result, the actual assets amount transferred to the user is not the same as the user-provided amount. The same issue can be observed in the mint function as well.
2. According to EIP-4626, withdraw and redeem functions must support transaction flows where the msg.sender has an approval from the owner. However, in the codebase, withdrawals and redeems can only be performed by the owner, and approved users cannot execute these actions.
bug_full: The AutoCompoundingPodLp contract deviates from the EIP‑4626 tokenized vault standard in two fundamental ways. First, the mint and withdraw entry points do not honour the exact amounts specified by the caller because the internal conversion helpers round down twice. When a user supplies an asset amount to withdraw, the contract first converts that amount to a share quantity using convertToShares, which truncates any fractional part. The resulting share count is then passed to an internal _withdraw routine that reconverts the shares back to assets with convertToAssets, applying another round‑down. Consequently the final asset transfer is strictly less than the amount the user requested, often by a small but measurable fraction. The same double‑rounding occurs in the mint path, causing the user to receive fewer shares than the deposited assets would dictate. Second, the contract enforces that only the token owner may invoke withdraw or redeem, ignoring the EIP‑4626 requirement that a spender with a valid allowance be able to act on the owner’s behalf. As a result, approved third‑parties cannot trigger withdrawals or redemptions, breaking expected delegation semantics. From a user perspective the symptoms are subtle: a withdrawal that should return 10.0 tokens may only deliver 9.9999, or a redemption may appear to succeed while the user’s balance is reduced by less than anticipated, leading to “missing” funds or zero‑value returns for very small amounts. The impact is two‑fold: users receive less value than promised, eroding trust and potentially allowing an attacker to accumulate rounding losses over many small operations, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated because the vault no longer guarantees a one‑to‑one correspondence between assets and shares. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit that compared the contract’s behaviour against the EIP‑4626 specification; the rounding discrepancy is easy to miss in casual testing because the differences are often below typical UI precision thresholds. To remediate, the mint and withdraw logic must be rewritten to perform a single conversion that respects the caller’s exact amount, for example by using round‑up semantics or by calculating the required shares/assets with exact arithmetic before transferring. Additionally, the withdraw and redeem functions should be extended to accept calls from approved spenders, checking allowance in the same way ERC‑20 permits transfers. Implementing these changes restores compliance, eliminates unexpected fund loss, and aligns the contract with the intended delegation model of EIP‑4626.

title: M-35 | VotingPool Incompatible With Non-Standard Tokens
description: If the underlying token of a pod is a Fee-on-Transfer token, the accounting when staking in VotingPool would be inaccurate. The balance of tokens after fees should be accounted for instead. Multi-asset pods are also incompatible as _calculateCbrWithDen assumes _asset[0] is the only token in the pod.
bug_full: VotingPool assumes that the amount of tokens transferred into the pool is equal to the amount that arrives in the contract. This assumption holds for standard ERC20 tokens that do not deduct a fee on transfer, but it breaks for fee‑on‑transfer (FoT) tokens where the token contract subtracts a percentage or fixed amount before the recipient’s balance is updated. When a pod uses an FoT token, the pool records the pre‑fee amount as the user’s stake, while the actual balance held by the contract is lower. The same problem appears in multi‑asset pods because the internal function _calculateCbrWithDen reads only the first element of the asset array and treats it as the sole token of the pod. Consequently, any additional assets are ignored in the calculation of the circulating balance ratio, leading to inaccurate voting power and reward distribution. An attacker can exploit this mismatch by depositing a token with a known transfer fee, causing the pool to credit more voting power than the real token balance supports. This inflated power can be used to sway governance proposals or to claim a larger share of rewards than entitled. The impact is a distortion of the protocol’s accounting model, potential loss of funds for honest participants, and erosion of trust in the governance mechanism. The vulnerability manifests whenever a pod is created with a non‑standard token that implements a fee on transfer, or when a pod contains more than one asset but the contract still assumes a single‑asset model. Users, token holders, and the protocol itself are affected because the displayed stake may not match the actual token holdings, leading to unexpected zero or reduced rewards, or to a situation where a user receives less than expected after withdrawal. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the contract’s internal accounting with on‑chain token balances and identified the hard‑coded reliance on _asset[0] and the lack of post‑transfer balance verification. It is difficult to notice because the token’s transfer event still reports the intended amount, and the UI typically shows the user‑entered amount, masking the discrepancy. To remediate, the contract should measure the actual token balance before and after each transfer (or use the return value of safeTransferFrom when supported) and adjust the recorded stake by the net amount received. Additionally, the CBR calculation should iterate over the full asset list and aggregate balances for all tokens in a pod, removing the single‑asset assumption. By handling fee‑on‑transfer tokens and multi‑asset pods explicitly, the protocol can maintain correct accounting, preserve accurate voting power, and ensure that rewards are distributed according to the true token holdings.

title: M-36 | redeemFromVault DOS
description: When LAV.redeemFromVault() is called, FraxlendPair.redeem() is called and the returned value (the assets received) are subtracted from the vaultUtilization. Since vaultUtilization is adjusted by dividing in _updateAssetMetadataFromVault, vaultUtilization may end up being 1 wei less than the received assets. Because of this the redeemFromVault transaction will fail.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one rounding error that leads to a denial‑of‑service condition in the LAV.redeemFromVault function. When a user calls redeemFromVault, the contract forwards the call to FraxlendPair.redeem and receives a certain amount of assets. The contract then attempts to reduce the internal accounting variable vaultUtilization by the exact amount of assets received. However, vaultUtilization is previously adjusted in the private helper _updateAssetMetadataFromVault using integer division, which truncates any fractional wei. As a result, after a series of operations vaultUtilization can be one wei smaller than the actual assets that will be returned. When the subtraction is performed, the contract tries to deduct more than the recorded utilization, causing the transaction to revert (or fail) because the internal balance check does not allow a negative utilization value. This failure blocks further calls to redeemFromVault, effectively locking users out of withdrawing their funds from the vault. The issue is triggered only under specific conditions: a redeem operation that leaves vaultUtilization marginally lower than the assets to be returned, which can happen after normal usage due to the rounding behaviour of integer division. All participants who rely on the vault – individual lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself – are affected because they cannot retrieve their deposited assets, leading to a loss of confidence and potential capital freeze. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic flow of vaultUtilization updates and noticed the mismatch between the recorded utilization and the actual asset amount. Because the discrepancy is only one wei, it is easy to overlook in testing and may not surface in typical transaction simulations that use larger amounts. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑precision errors where rounding or truncation creates a mismatch between logical state and real token balances, breaking invariants that assume the two are equal. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful redeem request but the transaction would revert, leaving the user with a “redeem failed” message and no change in their displayed balance, contrary to the expectation that the vault would return the requested amount. To remediate the issue the contract should cap the subtraction to the smaller of the received assets and the current vaultUtilization, for example by using the minimum of the two values. This prevents the internal accounting from ever becoming negative and restores the ability for users to redeem their funds without triggering a revert.

title: M-37 | Vaults' Utilization Not Updated After Bad Debt
description: During liquidation in FraxlendPair, if bad debt was incurred, whitelistUpdate is called which updates of all whitelisted vaults (except the calling vault). Then the bad debt is realized via: totalAsset.amount -= _amountToAdjust before LendingAssetVault is updated again to reduce its own internal tracking for _totalAssets. Instead, the whitelistUpdate of all vaults should be performed after the bad debt is realized in FraxlendPair. As a result, all other vaults will assume a higher amount of available assets (did not account for lost assets from bad debt) and charge a higher interest.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting order‑of‑operations error that occurs during the liquidation process of a FraxlendPair when a bad‑debt amount is realized. The contract first calls a whitelistUpdate routine that refreshes the utilization metrics of all whitelisted vaults except the one performing the liquidation. Immediately afterwards the bad‑debt is subtracted from the total asset amount (totalAsset.amount -= _amountToAdjust) and only then the LendingAssetVault updates its internal _totalAssets counter. Because the whitelistUpdate runs before the bad‑debt reduction, the other vaults are left with stale utilization data that still reflects the pre‑loss asset balance. Consequently those vaults calculate a higher available‑asset figure, which drives up the interest rate charged to borrowers. The bug is a classic state‑inconsistency or race‑condition style flaw where dependent contracts are updated in the wrong sequence, leading to mis‑priced loans. It can be exploited by triggering a liquidation that generates bad debt, causing the protocol to over‑estimate liquidity and charge borrowers more interest than warranted; the extra interest accrues to the protocol rather than to legitimate lenders. The impact is primarily on users of the affected vaults who see unexpectedly high interest rates, reduced returns, or mismatched utilization statistics, while the protocol’s accounting assumptions about asset availability become unreliable. The condition for the bug to manifest is any liquidation that results in bad debt while the whitelistUpdate is invoked prior to the debt adjustment. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the liquidation flow and noticed that the whitelistUpdate was placed before the asset balance was corrected. The issue is subtle because the UI typically shows only the resulting interest rate or utilization metric, not the internal sequence of state changes, making the discrepancy easy to miss. The proper fix is to move the whitelistUpdate call to the end of the liquidation routine, after the bad‑debt amount has been deducted and the LendingAssetVault’s internal totals have been updated, ensuring that all vaults see a consistent view of the remaining assets. This correction restores accurate utilization calculations, aligns interest rates with the true amount of available liquidity, and eliminates the over‑charging of borrowers caused by the premature update.

title: M-38 | Same TWAP For Multiple V3 Pools
description: spTKNMinimalOracle uses the same twapInterval for two different pools. Depending on the available liquidity on the two pools and the assets volatility, one twap period may not be sufficient to get accurate prices for both pools.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the design of the spTKNMinimalOracle, which aggregates price information from two distinct Uniswap V3 pools but applies a single time‑weighted average price (TWAP) interval to both. Because each pool can have markedly different liquidity depth and volatility characteristics, a uniform TWAP window may be long enough to smooth out price fluctuations in a deep, stable pool while being far too short to capture reliable price data in a shallow or highly volatile pool. Consequently, the oracle can return a price that deviates from the true market rate for one of the assets. An attacker who can influence the price in the low‑liquidity pool within the shared TWAP window can cause the oracle to publish a distorted price, which downstream contracts may use for critical operations such as collateral valuation, liquidation triggers, or trade execution. This can lead to users receiving incorrect trade quotes, premature liquidations, or loss of funds when positions are settled at an unfavorable price. The issue manifests whenever the oracle is queried during periods of low liquidity or heightened volatility in either pool, and it affects any participant that relies on the oracle’s price feed – typically traders, lenders, and the protocol itself. The flaw was identified during a manual audit that examined the oracle’s configuration and noted the reuse of a single interval parameter across heterogeneous pools. It is subtle because the price may appear correct for the well‑liquidity‑backed pool, masking the inaccuracy for the other pool, and because price deviations can be intermittent, making them hard to reproduce without targeted testing. The root cause is a misconfiguration of the oracle’s aggregation logic, a classic example of an “oracle price aggregation misconfiguration” where a single smoothing parameter is applied to heterogeneous data sources. To remediate, the oracle should maintain independent TWAP intervals for each pool, potentially adapting the interval length based on observed liquidity and volatility metrics, thereby ensuring that each price feed is sufficiently smoothed to reflect true market conditions. From a user perspective, the symptom may be a trade that executes at an unexpected price, a liquidation that occurs earlier than anticipated, or a balance that appears unchanged after a transaction because the underlying price feed was inaccurate. Users expect the oracle to provide a reliable average price, but the shared interval causes the reality of stale or skewed prices, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions and exposing it to financial risk.

title: M-39 | _getPairedTknAmt 0 Bond Slippage
description: LeverageManager._getPairedTknAndAmt uses 0 as slippage parameter when bonding tokens. In result, the received pToken amount may be too small that it causes significant loss for the user.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the LeverageManager contract where the internal function that bonds a user’s base token for a paired pToken is called with a hard‑coded slippage value of zero. Because the slippage parameter is fixed at zero, the contract does not enforce any minimum amount of pToken that must be received from the bonding operation. In practice, market conditions, price impact, or front‑running can cause the actual amount of pToken returned to be lower than the amount the user expects. Since the function does not check for this shortfall, the transaction completes successfully but the user ends up with fewer pTokens than anticipated, leading to a material loss of value when the position is later unwound or when the user expects a certain return. The issue manifests whenever a user initiates a bonding transaction through the LeverageManager, typically when opening a leveraged position or rebalancing assets. It affects all participants of the protocol who rely on the bonding mechanism, as their balances may be reduced without any explicit error. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit performed by the Guardian team, where the hard‑coded zero slippage was identified as a logical flaw that bypasses standard slippage protection. Because the transaction does not revert, the symptom is subtle: the UI may show a successful operation while the user’s pToken balance is unexpectedly lower, making the bug hard to notice without detailed balance checks. To remediate, the contract should expose a configurable slippage tolerance that the user can set, enforce a minimum acceptable pToken amount, and revert the transaction if the received amount falls below this threshold. This aligns the implementation with common slippage‑protection patterns and restores the expected accounting guarantees that the amount of pToken received should not be less than the user‑specified tolerance, preventing inadvertent loss of funds.

title: M-40 | getPairAccounting Includes LAV Assets
description: [FraxlendPair.getPairAccounting](https://github.com/peapodsfinance/fraxlend/blob/dc76f7b45b41fa75e175ca1b17dfb37f9d0f5ee2/src/contracts/FraxlendPair.sol#L142) includes the unlent assets from the LAV. External integrations that depend on that function will receive wrong information. For example, if they calculate the value of a single share using the output of that function, their result will be wrong because they account for assets not present in the pair.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the accounting routine of the FraxlendPair contract, specifically the getPairAccounting function. This function aggregates the total assets of a pair but mistakenly includes the assets that are held in the Liquidity Asset Vault (LAV) and are not actually lent to the market. The root cause is a logical oversight: the function does not filter out or subtract the unlent LAV balance before reporting the pair’s total assets, leading to a double‑counting style error. When external contracts, price oracles, or front‑end components call getPairAccounting to derive the value of a single share, they receive an inflated asset figure because the reported total includes assets that are not available for borrowing or redemption. An attacker or a careless integrator can exploit this mis‑reporting by assuming a higher per‑share value, potentially minting or withdrawing more shares than the real collateral supports, or by presenting users with misleading share‑price information that encourages over‑investment. The impact is economic: users may see a share price that appears higher than the underlying liquidity, causing them to deposit funds under false pretenses, and later suffer reduced returns or loss when the true asset pool is settled. The condition under which the bug manifests is any situation where the LAV holds a non‑zero balance and an external entity relies on getPairAccounting for valuation or accounting logic. All participants that depend on accurate pair accounting – including other smart contracts, DeFi aggregators, and end‑users – are affected because they receive incorrect data. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the accounting flow and identified that the LAV balance was not excluded. It can be hard to notice because the function name suggests a comprehensive accounting view, and the returned numbers look plausible at a glance; only a deeper inspection of the asset sources reveals the discrepancy. To remediate, the getPairAccounting implementation should be revised to exclude LAV assets from the total, either by subtracting the LAV balance or by providing a separate view that distinguishes lent from unlent assets, thereby ensuring that any downstream calculation reflects the true, withdrawable liquidity. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an "incorrect total asset accounting" or "double‑counting" vulnerability, which violates the fundamental accounting invariant that reported assets must equal the sum of assets actually available to the protocol. From a user’s perspective, the symptom may appear as a share price that seems unusually high, a dashboard showing more assets than can be withdrawn, or a situation where a withdrawal returns less than expected despite the displayed balance indicating otherwise.

title: M-41 | Donation Increases Share Supply
description: Function donate aims to increase the totalAssets of the LendingAssetVault without increasing the totalSupply of shares, hence a donation. The issue is that _burn(address(this), convertToShares(_assetAmt)); converts the _assetAmt to shares after _deposit(_assetAmt, address(this)); already minted shares, so the newly calculated share amount to burn will be less than the calculated and minted shares in _deposit. Ultimately, function donate increases the totalSupply even though it is not meant to.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/peapods-fuzzing/blob/504c79e9f12f6b586fe627b42dc9ac29df106ddf/test/invariant/helpers/ForgeTester.sol#L129
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the donate function of a vault contract that is supposed to act as a pure donation mechanism: it should increase the vault's total assets while keeping the total supply of share tokens unchanged, thereby preserving each holder's proportional ownership. The implementation first calls an internal deposit routine that converts the donated asset amount into shares and mints those shares to the vault itself. Immediately afterwards it attempts to neutralise the donation effect by burning shares using the expression _burn(address(this), convertToShares(_assetAmt)). The critical mistake is that convertToShares is evaluated after the deposit has already altered the vault's accounting state. Because the conversion rate is based on the new, higher total asset balance, the number of shares calculated for the burn is smaller than the number of shares that were just minted. Consequently the net effect of a donate call is a positive delta in totalSupply, meaning new shares are created unintentionally. This flaw can be exploited by any caller who invokes donate with any positive asset amount; each call inflates the share supply, diluting existing shareholders and effectively granting the donor a larger ownership stake than intended. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees: share holders see their relative claim on the vault’s assets shrink, the share price (assets per share) deviates from the expected constant, and the protocol may appear to reward donors with extra tokens, undermining trust. The bug manifests whenever donate is executed, regardless of the amount, and is visible from a user perspective as an unexpected increase in the donor’s share balance and a corresponding decrease in the value of other users’ shares. It is difficult to notice because the total assets rise as expected, masking the hidden increase in share supply; only a careful inspection of the share‑supply invariant reveals the discrepancy. The issue was discovered during a security audit that employed invariant‑based fuzz testing, which highlighted that totalSupply was not constant after donations. To remediate the problem, the contract should either burn exactly the number of shares that were minted during the deposit, compute the burn amount before the deposit, or redesign donate to avoid minting shares altogether, thereby ensuring that donations affect only the asset side of the balance sheet and leave the share supply untouched.

title: M-42 | Not Updating Pairs Will Break LAV
description: When a deposit or withdraw happens in the LendingAssetVault all pairs should be updated because the totalAssets are increased unilaterally which affects the pairs. There is a function which allows setting _updateInterestOnVaults to be set to false. If so, any updates to all pair at once will be skipped. This means users can manipulate pairs' utilization rates by depositing/withdrawing.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a design choice in the LendingAssetVault where a global flag, _updateInterestOnVaults, can be switched off to skip the batch update of all market pairs after a deposit or withdrawal. When the flag is false, the contract does not recalculate each pair’s utilization rate even though the total assets held by the vault have changed unilaterally. This creates a mismatch between the recorded total assets and the per‑pair accounting that drives interest rates. An attacker who can trigger deposits or withdrawals while the flag is disabled can artificially inflate or deflate a pair’s utilization metric, causing the protocol to apply incorrect interest rates or collateral requirements. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as unexpected zero or reduced rewards, a sudden drop in reported borrowing capacity, or a refund that does not reflect the actual amount deposited. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic for updating pair state and identified that the flag bypasses a critical invariant. Because the flag is intended to be used only in rare out‑of‑gas scenarios, the inconsistency can be subtle and may not surface until a malicious actor deliberately manipulates the vault state. The impact is medium‑severity: it does not directly steal funds, but it undermines the economic guarantees of the protocol, potentially leading to loss of yield or over‑collateralisation for honest users. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑state‑inconsistency vulnerabilities where batch updates are conditionally omitted, breaking the assumption that total assets are always reflected in per‑pair metrics. The proper remediation is to remove the ability to disable the pair‑wide update, or to enforce that any change to total assets must synchronously update all affected pairs, ensuring that utilization rates remain accurate regardless of gas constraints. This restores the invariant that the sum of per‑pair balances equals the vault’s total assets, preserving correct interest calculations and user expectations.

title: M-09 | Rewards Not Updated Prior To Fee Change
description: Owner can set a new protocol fee via setProtocolFee. However, because rewards are not updated prior to the fee change, the new fee will apply to previously accrued rewards. For example, 100 PEAS in rewards were accrued since the last update. Fees are increased from 1 to 2%. An additional 1% of fees are unjustly applied to the accrued rewards.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical accounting error that allows the contract owner to change the protocol fee without first settling pending reward balances. The root cause is that the function which updates the protocol fee does not invoke the internal reward‑processing routine before the fee variable is overwritten. As a result, any rewards that have accrued but have not yet been transferred to users are still subject to the new fee rate. An attacker who controls the owner role can increase the fee after rewards have built up, causing an extra portion of those pending rewards to be deducted as fees. For example, if a user has earned 100 reward tokens under a 1 % fee and the owner raises the fee to 2 % before the rewards are processed, the system will incorrectly apply the 2 % fee to the already‑accrued 100 tokens, effectively taking an additional 1 % from the user. This can be exploited simply by calling the fee‑setting function at a strategic moment, without any need for complex transaction ordering or re‑entrancy. The impact is a loss of user funds: users receive less than the amount they expect, seeing their reward balance reduced or even zeroed out after a fee change. The issue manifests whenever the owner invokes the fee‑update function after rewards have accumulated but before they are claimed or processed. All participants who rely on accurate reward accounting – token holders, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts – are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the sequence of state updates in the fee‑management logic. It can be difficult to notice because the fee change itself appears legitimate and the reward balances are only adjusted later, making the over‑deduction subtle and only observable when users claim their rewards. The correct mitigation is to ensure that the reward‑processing routine is executed before the fee variable is updated, for instance by calling the internal _processRewardsToPodLp function at the start of setProtocolFee, thereby locking in the old fee rate for any pending rewards. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a retroactive fee application or reward‑settlement ordering error, where the order of state changes leads to unintended financial loss.

title: M-10 | Vault Whitelist Can Be Set One Above Max
description: When whitelisting a new vault with setVaultWhitelist, even if maxVault value has been reached, the new vault is still added to the whitelist due to using <= maxValue instead of "< maxValue" in the check.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one boundary error in the function that adds new vault addresses to the protocol’s whitelist. The contract checks the current number of whitelisted vaults against a configured maximum using a "less‑than‑or‑equal" comparison (<= maxVaults). Because the check allows equality, an additional vault can be inserted after the limit has already been reached, effectively permitting one vault more than the intended cap. This occurs whenever the setVaultWhitelist routine is called after the whitelist length equals the maximum value. The root cause is the incorrect relational operator in the require statement, which does not enforce the strict upper bound required by the business rule. An attacker or a careless administrator can exploit this by submitting a transaction that adds a vault after the limit is hit, thereby bypassing the intended restriction. The impact is that the protocol may host more vault contracts than it was designed to manage, potentially leading to resource exhaustion, unexpected fee distribution, or the inclusion of malicious vaults that can siphon funds or disrupt accounting. Users may notice an extra vault appearing in the UI, see their expected list of approved vaults longer than advertised, or experience unexpected behavior when interacting with the newly added vault. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the whitelist management logic and identified the relational operator mismatch. Because the condition only fails when the whitelist length exceeds the maximum by more than one, the bug can remain hidden during normal operation until the limit is reached and an extra vault is added, making it difficult to spot without targeted testing. To remediate, the require statement should enforce a strict less‑than comparison (require(_vaultWhitelistAry.length < maxVaults, ...)), ensuring that the whitelist never exceeds the configured ceiling. This correction aligns the implementation with the intended business rule that the number of whitelisted vaults must never surpass the maximum allowed, restoring proper accounting and preventing unauthorized vault inclusion.

title: M-11 | Inflated Admin Fee
description: When a swap fails in depositFromPairedLPToken(), the amount that can be used in the next attempt is halved from the attempted swap amount. The next time depositFromPairedLPToken() is called the fee will be based off the current balance of the contract, which will include the balance from the failed swap. When _swapForRewards is called, it will reduce the _amountIn and _amountOut but still charge the admin fee based on the balance of the contract. This results in excessive admin fees paid over the multiple swaps.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a miscalculation of the admin fee in the depositFromPairedLPToken workflow. When a token swap performed inside this function fails, the contract halves the amount that can be retried and retains the failed amount in its balance. Subsequent calls compute the admin fee based on the contract's total token balance, which now includes the unrecovered amount from the failed swap. The internal _swapForRewards routine further reduces the nominal input and output amounts but still charges the fee using the inflated balance, causing the fee to be larger than the actual value swapped. This logic error can be exploited by deliberately causing swap failures – for example by providing unfavorable slippage parameters – so that the contract repeatedly accrues unrecovered tokens and continues to charge fees on them. The impact is that users who deposit paired LP tokens end up paying higher than expected admin fees, reducing their net rewards and potentially draining funds over multiple deposit attempts. The condition occurs only after a swap failure; normal successful swaps do not exhibit the problem because the balance matches the swapped amount. All participants who interact with the deposit function – typically liquidity providers – are affected because the fee is deducted from their deposited assets. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the fee calculation against the actual amount transferred and noticed a discrepancy after simulated swap failures. It is hard to notice in production because the fee appears as a normal administrative charge and the variance may be attributed to market conditions, while the underlying accounting assumption – that the contract balance equals the amount actually swapped – is silently violated. To remediate, the fee should be calculated from the real amount that was successfully exchanged, i.e., the delta of tokens moved to the rewards pool, rather than the contract's overall balance, and the retry logic should reset the amount to the original intended swap size instead of halving it after a failure. This aligns the fee with the economic reality of the transaction and prevents the accumulation of inflated charges that effectively steal value from users.

title: M-12 | Same Heartbeat For Multiple Oracles
