description: getPriceUSD18 makes requests to a base and quote asset oracles. If any of them has been updated more than maxOracleDelay seconds ago, _isBadData will be set to true. Since not all feeds have the same heartbeat, if the oracle uses two feeds with different ones, it may happen that one of the prices is stale, but it's accepted as a valid one.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the price aggregation function that queries two separate oracle feeds – one for a base asset and one for a quote asset – and validates their freshness using a single global delay parameter called maxOracleDelay. The contract assumes that both feeds update at the same rate, but in practice each oracle may have a different heartbeat, i.e., the maximum time between successive updates. Because the same delay is applied to both feeds, the validation logic can deem the combined price data as acceptable even when one of the feeds is stale. An attacker who can influence the stale feed (for example by withholding updates or feeding outdated data) can cause the contract to compute an incorrect USD price for the asset pair. This mis‑priced value may be used in downstream calculations such as collateral valuation, liquidation triggers, or token swaps, potentially leading to users receiving less than expected, liquidations occurring prematurely, or funds being transferred at an unfavorable rate. The issue manifests whenever the timestamp of one oracle exceeds its own expected heartbeat but remains within the shared maxOracleDelay threshold, a condition that can persist unnoticed because the contract does not emit explicit warnings for individual feed staleness. The problem was identified during a manual audit that compared the heartbeat specifications of the involved feeds against the contract’s single‑delay check. It is difficult to spot in normal operation because the contract continues to return a price value, and only the subtle drift in pricing reveals the flaw. To remediate, the contract should maintain separate freshness thresholds for each oracle – for instance, a baseDelay and a quoteDelay – and reject the price if either feed is older than its own allowed interval. This change aligns the validation logic with the heterogeneous update patterns of the feeds and restores the intended guarantee that all price components are recent, thereby preventing stale data from corrupting financial calculations.

title: M-13 | No Circuit Breaker Checks In ChainlinkOracle
description: getPriceUSD18 returns _isBadData if the oracle price is stale. However, it doesn't consider the price going outside of the price range for the oracle's aggregator. The price will be capped between minAnswer and maxAnswer of the aggregator. This will result in a wrong price being used in the protocol. Even though most feeds have disabled their circuit breaker feature, there are still some that haven't, for example [CVX/ETH](https://etherscan.io/address/0xf1F7F7BFCc5E9D6BB8D9617756beC06A5Cbe1a49#readContract)
bug_full: The contract’s price‑retrieval function getPriceUSD18 is designed to signal bad data when the Chainlink oracle price is stale, but it fails to verify whether the reported price lies within the aggregator’s configured bounds (minAnswer and maxAnswer). Chainlink aggregators include a circuit‑breaker mechanism that caps any price that drifts outside this range; when the circuit breaker is active the price is replaced by the nearest bound. Because the contract does not check for this condition, it may accept the capped value as a legitimate market price. An attacker who can influence the underlying feed – for example by causing a rapid price swing that pushes the value beyond the allowed range – can trigger the circuit breaker, causing the oracle to return a price that is artificially high or low. The protocol then uses this distorted price in its accounting logic, which can lead to mis‑pricing of assets, under‑collateralisation, unintended liquidations, or loss of funds for users. The flaw manifests whenever the oracle’s circuit‑breaker feature is enabled (or left at its default) and the price moves outside the defined range, even if the timestamp is fresh. It is difficult to notice because the stale‑data flag remains false, so monitoring tools that only watch for stale timestamps will not raise an alarm, and the UI may simply display a price that appears plausible but is actually capped. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s bad‑data detection logic with the official Chainlink documentation. To remediate, the price‑fetching routine should also compare the retrieved value against the aggregator’s minAnswer and maxAnswer and set the internal _isBadData flag when the price is out of bounds, thereby preventing the protocol from acting on a price that has been artificially constrained by the circuit‑breaker. This class of bug falls under improper validation of external data sources, specifically missing range checks on oracle outputs, which violates the protocol’s assumption that a fresh price is always within the expected market range.

title: M-14 | DOS Of Borrow & Redeem
description:
Each time borrow or redeem is called in FraxlendPairCore, if there are insufficient local assets, then _depositFromVault is called to pull assets from the vault. However, in _depositFromVault there is a check: if (depositLimit < _totalAsset.totalAmount(address(externalAssetVault))) revert ExceedsDepositLimit(); This check prevents the deposit from vault if the vault's allocated assets to the FraxlendPair exceeds the deposit limit. Consider this example:
• FraxlendPair has a deposit limit of 10 ETH
• Vault has 30 ETH and allocates 50% to FraxlendPair
• Borrow/redeem actions cannot go through as the depositLimit check would always fail
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs in the FraxlendPairCore contract when a user attempts to call borrow or redeem. The core logic tries to ensure sufficient liquidity by invoking an internal function _depositFromVault, which pulls assets from a shared LendingAssetVault. Inside _depositFromVault a guard clause checks whether the vault’s total allocated amount for the pair exceeds the pair’s configured depositLimit, and if so the call reverts with ExceedsDepositLimit. Because the check compares the allocated amount rather than the actual free balance, a situation can arise where the vault holds enough underlying tokens but the allocation percentage forces the allocated amount to be larger than the deposit limit. For example, if the pair’s deposit limit is set to 10 ETH, the vault contains 30 ETH and has allocated 50 % of its balance to the pair (15 ETH), the condition depositLimit < allocatedAmount is true and every subsequent borrow or redeem attempt fails. The root cause is the misuse of the deposit limit as a hard ceiling on the allocated amount, ignoring that the vault can still provide liquidity from its unallocated reserve. An attacker or a misconfigured governance action could increase the allocation percentage or set a low deposit limit, causing the check to always trigger. When the check reverts, the borrow or redeem transaction does not complete, the user receives no funds, their balance remains unchanged, and the protocol appears unresponsive. This impacts any participant who expects to borrow assets or redeem their collateral, effectively freezing user funds and breaking the core lending functionality. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the FraxlendPairCore contract where the control flow of borrow/redeem was traced and the deposit limit condition was found to be overly restrictive. It can be hard to notice because the deposit limit is intended as a safety mechanism, so developers may assume it only prevents over‑deposit, not that it can block legitimate withdrawals. To remediate, the deposit limit check should be removed from _depositFromVault or relocated to the vault’s allocation logic, where the vault validates that the total allocated amount never exceeds its own deposit limit before assigning percentages. This ensures that borrow and redeem operations can succeed as long as the vault holds sufficient free assets, preserving expected protocol behavior and preventing denial‑of‑service attacks.

title: M-43 | Leverage Doesn't Work When FOT Is Enabled
description: Pods have a property hasTransferTax which when enabled, a fee-on-transfer is taken from the value to be transferred and the recipient receives less tokens. This is a problem for the [LeverageManager.addLeverage()](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/peapods-2/blob/cebeb47138e5f029cefd698328dfbd33e90fbbea/contracts/lvf/LeverageManager.sol#L128) function because it assumes the whole amount has been received and assigns that amount to LeverageFlashProps.podAmount. Later, when the podAmount is requested from the IndexUtils, the transaction will revert because the LeverageManager contract doesn't have all the tokens.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/peapods-2/pull/1
bug_full: The vulnerability occurs in the leverage module of the protocol when a pod token is configured with the hasTransferTax flag, meaning the token applies a fee‑on‑transfer that reduces the amount actually received by the recipient. The addLeverage function in LeverageManager assumes that the full amount specified by the caller is transferred to the contract and directly records this amount in the internal LeverageFlashProps.podAmount field. Because the function does not verify the real amount received after the fee‑on‑transfer, it records a value that is larger than the contract’s token balance. Later, when the protocol queries the stored podAmount through IndexUtils to retrieve the tokens for the leveraged operation, the contract attempts to move more tokens than it holds, causing the transaction to revert with an insufficient‑balance error. This flaw is rooted in a missing accounting step: the contract does not account for the transfer tax that some pod tokens impose, treating the input amount as if it were the net amount received. An attacker or even an honest user can trigger the issue simply by enabling the transfer‑tax flag on a pod before calling addLeverage, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition where leveraged positions cannot be opened and funds may appear to be locked or disappear from the user’s perspective. From the user’s point of view the UI may show that the leverage request was submitted, but the transaction fails and the user receives no tokens, often seeing a zero balance or a reverted transaction without a clear error message. The problem is difficult to notice because fee‑on‑transfer tokens are common and the contract does not emit explicit warnings about the tax; the mismatch between expected and actual token amounts only surfaces later when the contract attempts to move the recorded amount. To remediate, the contract should either reject pods that have a transfer tax, or it should measure the actual amount received after the transfer (for example by checking the token balance before and after the call) and store that net amount in podAmount. Additionally, the logic that uses podAmount should be updated to work with the verified net amount, ensuring that subsequent token movements never exceed the contract’s balance. This class of bug is a token accounting mismatch caused by fee‑on‑transfer tokens, leading to incorrect state assumptions, transaction reverts, and potential loss of user confidence in the protocol.

title: M-44 | Swap Error Handling Causes DOS Of AutoCompounder
description: In _processRewardsToPodLp, if a swap of the main reward token fails, an override feature kicks in to halve and store the next _amountIn to swap in _tokenToPairedSwapAmountInOverride. A temporary DOS attack can be carried out as such: 1. Donate 50 wei of the main reward token (PEAS), assuming contract has no previous balance of PEAS. 2. Call deposit to trigger _processRewardsToPodLp where the small swap to Uniswap V3 would fail due to insuﬃcient amountOut. 3. Half of 50 wei (i.e. 25 wei) will then be stored in the override mapping. 4. Contract will attempt to swap for another 6 times before the override amount is set to zero — preventing actual rewards from being processed.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/peapods-1/pull/15/files
bug_full: The vulnerability is an error‑handling flaw in the reward‑processing routine of an auto‑compounder contract. When the function that converts accrued reward tokens into a paired token attempts a swap on Uniswap V3 and the swap fails – for example because the amount is too small to satisfy the minimum amountOut – the contract does not revert or emit a clear error. Instead it activates an override mechanism that stores half of the intended input amount in a mapping and schedules a retry. Because the stored amount is still insufficient, the contract repeats the swap attempt up to six times, each time using the halved amount, before finally resetting the override to zero. An attacker can exploit this by donating a minimal amount of the main reward token (PEAS) when the contract has no prior balance, triggering the failing swap on the next deposit call. The half‑amount (25 wei in the example) is recorded in the override, and the subsequent six retry cycles all fail, effectively blocking any further reward processing. The impact is a temporary denial‑of‑service: legitimate users see no rewards, balances appear unchanged, and the auto‑compounder ceases to distribute earnings for the duration of the retry loop. This condition occurs only when a swap fails due to insufficient output, which is easy to provoke with a tiny deposit. All participants in the auto‑compounder are affected because the override state is global to the contract, not scoped to the offending user. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the swap‑handling logic and identified the halving‑and‑override pattern as a potential dead‑end. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit failure event; the UI simply shows no reward accrual, leading users to think their deposit was ignored rather than the system being stuck. The bug belongs to the class of error‑handling and state‑management vulnerabilities that can cause denial‑of‑service by retaining a failing state. To remediate, the swap routine should either revert on failure, clear the override immediately, or implement a more robust retry strategy that validates the amount before scheduling another attempt, thereby preventing the contract from entering a loop that blocks reward distribution.

title: M-45 | DOS Of depositFromPairedLpToken
description: In depositFromPairedLpToken, if a swap of a reward token fails, an override feature kicks in to halve and store the next _amountIn to swap in _rewardsSwapAmountInOverride. A temporary DOS attack is possible by making use of this feature: 1. Deposit 50 wei of the reward token. The small swap to Uniswap V3 would fail due to insuﬃcient amountOut. 2. Half of 50 wei (i.e. 25 wei) will then be stored in _rewardsSwapAmountInOverride. 3. Contract will attempt to swap for another 6 times before the override amount is set to zero — preventing actual rewards from being processed.
poc: https://github.com/GuardianAudits/peapods-1/pull/15/files
bug_full: The vulnerability is a temporary denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition that arises in the depositFromPairedLpToken routine of the reward‑distribution contract. The function attempts to swap a small amount of a reward token on Uniswap V3; if the swap fails, the code falls back to an override mechanism that halves the original input amount and stores the result in a state variable called _rewardsSwapAmountInOverride. Because the override value is retained for a fixed number of subsequent calls (six attempts) before being cleared, an attacker can deliberately trigger the fallback with a minimal deposit that is guaranteed to fail (for example, 50 wei of the reward token, which cannot satisfy the pool’s minimum amountOut). The contract then records 25 wei in the override slot and, on each of the next six deposits, it re‑uses this override amount for a swap that will also fail, effectively preventing any legitimate reward swaps from being executed. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that deposits appear to succeed, but the expected reward tokens never arrive; balances remain unchanged or become zero, and the UI shows no error despite the underlying failure. The root cause is the design of the override logic: it does not immediately reset after a failed swap and it blindly re‑uses a halved amount without verifying that the amount is sufficient for a successful trade. This makes the contract vulnerable to a low‑value, repeatable attack that stalls the reward pipeline for a short window, impacting all participants who rely on timely reward distribution. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer exercised the deposit function with tiny amounts and observed that the override persisted across multiple calls, leading to repeated swap failures. The bug is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit a clear error; it simply consumes gas on failed swaps while silently discarding the reward amount. To remediate the problem the override design should be redesigned: either revert on swap failure, reset the override immediately, enforce a minimum amountOut check before attempting the swap, or limit the retry mechanism so that a single failed attempt cannot block reward processing for subsequent users. In generic terms the flaw belongs to the class of “state‑persistent fallback logic leading to denial‑of‑service” bugs, where an error handling path unintentionally creates a reusable state that can be abused to stall normal operation.

title: Updating `operatorRewardPercentage` incorrectly redistributes already accrued rewards
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reward‑distribution logic error in the L1Strategy/SequencerVault contract. The contract stores a single variable operatorRewardPercentage that determines how newly accrued rewards are split between operators and other recipients. When this percentage is changed, the updateDeposits function recomputes the operator share for the entire amount of pending rewards using the current percentage, regardless of the percentage that was in effect when those rewards were generated. As a result, rewards that have already been earned but not yet distributed are retroactively re‑allocated. If the percentage is increased, non‑operator recipients lose part of the tokens they were entitled to; if it is decreased, operators lose part of their earned share. The bug is triggered whenever the operatorRewardPercentage is modified and a subsequent call to updateDeposits occurs, which is the normal path for depositing or withdrawing. Any party that can propose a new percentage – typically the vault controller – can cause a mis‑allocation of previously accrued rewards, effectively stealing or depriving other participants. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that balances shown after an update are lower than expected: operators may see their reward balance drop, or regular recipients may receive fewer tokens than they anticipated, even though the total reward amount has not changed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward‑calculation code and noticed that the variable vaultController.operatorRewardPercentage() is used directly inside the depositChange branch without preserving the historic rate. The problem is subtle because the function appears to correctly calculate a share of the change in total deposits, but it ignores the fact that the change already includes rewards that were generated under a different split ratio. This makes the bug easy to miss in testing that only checks the immediate split after a percentage change. The vulnerability belongs to the class of incorrect accounting after parameter mutation or reward‑distribution snapshot bug. To fix the issue the contract should first settle any pending rewards using the percentage that was active at the time those rewards accrued, for example by distributing the pending amount before allowing the percentage to be updated, or by storing a per‑epoch percentage and applying it only to rewards generated in that epoch. Properly separating the reward‑distribution step from the parameter‑update step restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents unexpected loss of tokens.

title: Incorrect logic causes that SequencerVaults to not behave as expected when relocking or claiming rewards.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect conditional logic in the SequencerVault.updateDeposits function that causes reward processing to be completely skipped when the caller passes a _minRewards value of zero. According to the function’s documentation the parameter _minRewards is used to indicate that reward claiming should be omitted while any existing rewards should still be relocked into the MetisLockingPool. The implementation, however, wraps the entire reward handling block inside an if (_minRewards != 0 && rewards >= _minRewards) check and provides no else branch. As a result, when _minRewards is set to zero the contract neither claims nor relocks the accumulated rewards, leaving them permanently stuck in the external locking pool. The root cause is a missing code path and a misplaced condition that conflates the 'skip claiming' intent with 'skip all reward logic'. An attacker or honest user can trigger the bug simply by calling updateDeposits with minRewards set to zero, which is a legitimate operation according to the interface. The exploit does not require any special permissions beyond the vault controller role, and it manifests as rewards that never become part of the vault’s total deposits and cannot be withdrawn or restaked. From a user perspective the UI may still display the original principal balance, while the expected increase from rewards is absent; users may see 'rewards not processed' or 'balance stays the same' even though a reward event was recorded. The impact is a loss of expected yield, potential accounting mismatches for the protocol, and reduced confidence for sequencer operators who rely on automatic relocking of rewards. The issue occurs whenever the vault has a positive reward balance and the caller explicitly requests to skip claiming by passing zero as the minimum reward threshold. It was discovered during a formal audit by Cyfrin and reproduced with a unit test that verifies that rewards remain unchanged after an updateDeposits call with a zero threshold. The bug is hard to notice because the function still returns the total deposit amount unchanged and does not revert, so external observers may assume normal operation. The appropriate fix is to separate the claiming and relocking logic: when _minRewards is zero the contract should execute the relocking path (e.g., call lockingPool.relock) without attempting to claim, and when _minRewards is greater than zero and rewards meet the threshold the contract should claim as documented. This adjustment restores the intended business rule that rewards are either claimed or relocked but never silently ignored, aligning the implementation with its specification and preventing funds from becoming permanently inaccessible.

title: Cross-chain token transfer from `SpokeVault` fails due to approval from implementation contract instead of proxy
bug_full: The vulnerability is a cross‑chain token transfer failure caused by an incorrect ERC20 allowance being set on the wrong contract. When the SpokeVault contract is deployed through an ERC1967 proxy, its constructor runs on the implementation contract, not on the proxy that actually holds the M tokens. The constructor creates an infinite approval for the SpokePortal by calling IERC20(mToken).approve(spokePortal_, type(uint256).max). Because this call writes the allowance into the storage of the implementation contract, the proxy’s storage – which is the contract that later executes transferExcessM – never receives the allowance. Consequently, when transferExcessM attempts to move excess M tokens to the HubVault, the SpokePortal’s transferFrom call finds a zero allowance and reverts, leaving the tokens effectively locked in the proxy. The root cause is the misuse of a constructor in an upgradeable proxy pattern, leading to a mismatch between where state is written and where it is read. Exploitation is straightforward: any user or automated process that triggers transferExcessM will see the transaction succeed at the UI level but the token balance on the HubVault will not change, because the underlying token transfer never occurs. The impact is that excess M tokens cannot be migrated to the main‑net HubVault, breaking the intended cross‑chain accounting and potentially causing funds to appear missing from the user’s perspective. This condition occurs whenever SpokeVault is instantiated via the DeployBase::_deploySpokeVault routine, which always creates a proxy. The affected parties include protocol operators, token holders expecting their excess tokens to be transferred, and any downstream contracts that rely on the correct balance in HubVault. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the constructor logic with the proxy deployment flow and identified that the approval was being set on the implementation contract. It is hard to notice because the approval code appears correct in isolation and unit tests may interact with a non‑proxied instance, masking the storage discrepancy. The bug belongs to the class of proxy‑initialization errors where constructors are used to set mutable state instead of an initializer function, resulting in allowance misconfiguration. From a user’s point of view the UI may report a successful transfer, yet the balance on the destination chain remains unchanged, leading to confusion such as “my transfer did nothing” or “my funds disappeared”. The expected behavior is that the SpokePortal can pull the approved amount, but the reality is that no allowance exists, so the transfer fails silently. To remediate, the contract should avoid setting an infinite approval in the constructor; instead it should grant the exact amount of allowance right before calling the portal, or move the approval logic into an initializer that runs on the proxy. This eliminates the storage mismatch and removes the security risk of an unchecked infinite allowance on an upgradeable contract.

title: SpokeVault transfers will frequently revert due to Wormhole gas fee fluctuations
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the bridge component that forwards ETH to cover Wormhole gas fees. The contract function that initiates the transfer calculates a total price quote and expects the caller to send exactly that amount of ETH. After the transfer, any excess ETH is sent back to the original caller through a low‑level call. However, the receiving contract (SpokeVault) does not implement a payable fallback or receive function, meaning it cannot accept incoming ETH. When a user overpays even by a small amount – which is common because off‑chain fee estimates can differ from the on‑chain gas cost at execution time – the refund call fails, triggering a revert of the entire transaction. The root cause is therefore an improper handling of payable refunds: the contract assumes it can always send ETH back, but the target contract is non‑payable. Exploitation is straightforward: a user (or any caller) supplies a fee that is not precisely equal to the quoted Wormhole fee; the excess triggers the refund path, the call to the non‑payable SpokeVault fails, and the transaction reverts with a RefundFailed error. The impact is that legitimate bridge transfers become unreliable; users see their transactions revert, receive no token transfer, and may be confused because they expected the bridge to succeed even with a slight overpayment. This occurs whenever gas fee estimates fluctuate between the moment the fee is calculated off‑chain and the moment the transaction is mined, or when a caller mistakenly sends more ETH than required. All participants who rely on the bridge – end‑users, the protocol that routes assets, and any integrators – are affected because the bridge may appear to be broken or untrustworthy. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the _prepareForTransfer and _refundToSender logic and noticed that the refund target is SpokeVault, which lacks a payable receive function. The bug can be hard to notice because it only manifests when an excess fee is sent; many users may try to send the exact amount and therefore never encounter the failure, masking the underlying flaw. To remediate, the contract should be updated to include a payable receive (or fallback) function that can accept ETH refunds, and the refund logic should be adjusted to forward any excess ETH directly back to the original external caller rather than to the SpokeVault itself. This class of bug falls under improper handling of payable callbacks and refund mechanisms, a common pattern where contracts assume they can always receive Ether but omit the necessary fallback, leading to transaction reverts and degraded user experience. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a transaction failure, no tokens received, and possibly a generic “RefundFailed” message, contrary to the expectation that a slight overpayment would simply be returned.

title: Operator can finalize for non-existent `finalShnarf`
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked existence condition for the final shnarf identifier used during block finalization in the LineaRollup contract. In the original implementation, the function _finalizeBlocks verified that the shnarf supplied by the operator corresponded to a known block number by consulting the mapping shnarfFinalBlockNumbers and reverting if the association was missing. During a refactor this mapping was replaced with blobShnarfExists, a boolean‑style flag stored as a uint, and the explicit check was removed without adding an equivalent verification step. As a result, an operator can invoke the finalization routine with a computed finalShnarf value that has never been submitted or recorded in the contract state. The root cause is the absence of a guard that ensures the final shnarf exists before it is used to mark a block as finalized. An attacker controlling the operator role can craft a finalization payload containing an arbitrary shnarf hash, causing the contract to record a block as finalized even though the corresponding data blob was never posted. This breaks the protocol’s accounting assumptions because the system assumes that every finalized block has an associated data blob that can be later referenced for fraud proofs or state verification. Consequently, downstream components may attempt to retrieve a non‑existent blob, leading to failed proofs, potential loss of funds that rely on correct finalization, or the ability for a malicious operator to claim rewards for blocks that were never actually produced. The issue manifests whenever the _finalizeBlocks function is called after the refactor, i.e., any time an operator finalizes a batch of blocks. All participants that trust the rollup’s finality – users, delegators, and other contracts that depend on the rollup’s state – are affected because the rollup may appear to have progressed while its underlying data is missing. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s state‑transition logic, where the auditor noticed the removal of the shnarf‑to‑block check and the lack of a replacement. It can be hard to notice because the transaction may still succeed and emit normal events, giving the impression that finalization proceeded correctly, while the missing blob is only revealed later when other contracts attempt to access it. The proper remediation is to re‑introduce an existence verification step that checks blobShnarfExists[finalShnarf] is non‑zero before allowing finalization, mirroring the original safety check. This class of bug falls under “missing validation of identifier existence” or “unchecked state transition condition”, which commonly leads to inconsistent state and potential fund loss. From a user’s perspective, a transaction that should finalize a batch may appear successful, yet later actions such as withdrawals or state queries may fail or return zero, creating confusion where “my balance is zero after finalization” or “the rollup claims a block is final but no data is available”.

title: Blacklisted user can burn tokens during WHITELIST_ENABLED state
description: Blacklisted user can burn tokens during WHITELIST_ENABLED state. This breaks the main invariant from the [README](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-11-ethena-labs/tree/main#main-invariants). This could become an issue when the admin tries to redistribute the blacklisted user’s UStb balance using `redistributeLockedAmount()` but the blacklisted user frontruns it with a burn.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of allowing a blacklisted address to burn its tokens when the contract is in WHITELIST_ENABLED transfer state. The contract checks only that the caller and the source address have the WHITELISTED_ROLE before permitting a burn to address(0). Because the blacklist manager and whitelist manager are separate, an address can be granted both roles, either by being added to the whitelist after being blacklisted or vice‑versa. When this dual‑role condition occurs, the burn check passes and the blacklisted user can invoke the burn function. This breaks the invariant that blacklisted accounts must not be able to move or destroy collateral while the protocol is in whitelist mode. An attacker controlling a blacklisted account can front‑run a redistribution transaction (redistributeLockedAmount) that the admin intends to move the blacklisted balance to a safe pool, by burning the tokens first, thereby reducing the amount available for redistribution. The immediate symptom for honest users is that the protocol’s accounting shows a loss of collateral: the total supply decreases unexpectedly and the blacklisted user’s balance becomes zero, while other participants may see a temporary excess of collateral. The issue is discovered during a code audit that noted a comment allowing both roles on the same address and verified the burn condition. It can be hard to notice because the burn path is only reachable in a specific state (WHITELIST_ENABLED) and the role overlap is not prevented elsewhere, so normal operation appears correct. The fix is to ensure that neither the caller nor the source address holds the BLACKLISTED_ROLE when a burn is attempted, i.e., add explicit checks that blacklist and whitelist roles are mutually exclusive before allowing token destruction. This class of bug is a role‑conflict access control flaw that permits privileged actions to be performed by accounts that should be denied, leading to unintended token supply changes and potential disruption of protocol accounting.

title: Non-whitelisted users can burn UStb and redeem collateral during WHITELIST_ENABLED state
description: Non-whitelisted users can redeem collateral tokens and burn their UStb even when whitelist mode has been enabled on UStb contract. This breaks the main invariant mentioned in the [README](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-11-ethena-labs/tree/main#additional-context).
bug_full: The vulnerability is an access‑control bypass that allows addresses without the WHITELISTED_ROLE to burn UStb tokens and redeem the underlying collateral while the contract is in the WHITELIST_ENABLED transfer state. The root cause is a missing whitelist check on the 'from' address inside the internal _beforeTokenTransfer hook that is executed for ERC20 burns. The code only verifies that the caller (msg.sender) holds the MINTER_CONTRACT role, that the 'from' address is not blacklisted, and that the destination is the zero address, but it never confirms that the token holder is whitelisted. As a result, any user can submit a redemption request through the authorized Redeemer contract, which has the MINTER_CONTRACT role, and the burn will succeed even if the user is not on the whitelist. Exploitation requires the contract to be in WHITELIST_ENABLED state and the attacker to interact with the Redeemer (or any contract with MINTER_CONTRACT role). When successful, the attacker receives collateral that should be reserved for whitelisted participants, breaking the protocol invariant that only whitelisted users may send, receive, or burn tokens during this state. From a user perspective the symptom is that a non‑whitelisted address can initiate a redemption and receive the expected collateral, contrary to the expectation that the transaction would be rejected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the token’s transfer logic, where the auditors compared the on‑chain checks against the documented invariant in the README. The bug is subtle because the contract already performs several role checks and relies on an off‑chain RFQ system to enforce whitelist rules, making the missing on‑chain verification easy to overlook. To remediate, the WHITELIST_ENABLED branch should include an explicit hasRole(WHITELISTED_ROLE, from) condition, thereby enforcing the whitelist invariant on‑chain and preventing unauthorized burns and collateral redemptions.

title: Redemption of slashed registrations could result in DoS due to incorrect state update
description:
** Due to the logic surrounding Pay As You Go (PAYG) registrations, potential refunds associated with failed validators, and post-expiry redemptions of stake, a minimum balance of `AVAX` is required to remain within the `Ignite` contract. The [`IgniteStorage::minimumContractBalance`](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/IgniteStorage.sol#L97-L98) state variable is responsible for keeping track of this balance and ensuring that [`Ignite::withdraw`](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/Ignite.sol#L556-L572) transfers the appropriate amount of `AVAX` to start validation.

When the validation period for a given registration has expired, [`Ignite::releaseLockedTokens`](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/Ignite.sol#L574-L707) is called by the privileged `ROLE_RELEASE_LOCKED_TOKENS` actor along with the redeemable tokens. If the registration is slashed, `minimumContractBalance` is [updated](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/Ignite.sol#L695-L697) to include `msg.value` less the slashed amount. Finally, when [`Ignite::redeemAfterExpiry`](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/Ignite.sol#L402-L481) is called by the original registerer to redeem the tokens, the `minimumContractBalance` state is again updated to discount this withdrawn amount.

However, this [state update](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/Ignite.sol#L458) is incorrect as it should decrement the `avaxRedemptionAmount` rather than the `avaxDepositAmount` (which includes the already-accounted-for slashed amount). Therefore, `minimumContractBalance` will be smaller than intended, resulting in redemptions reverting due to underflow of the decrement or if a call to `Ignite::withdraw` leaves the contract with insufficient balance to fulfill its obligations.

** Redemptions could revert if the current redemption is slashed and the state update underflows or if an earlier redemption is slashed and more `AVAX` is withdrawn than intended.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting logic error in the Ignite contract that manages Pay‑As‑You‑Go (PAYG) validator registrations. The contract keeps a variable called minimumContractBalance that records the smallest amount of AVAX that must remain in the contract to satisfy future withdrawals. When a registration expires and is slashed, the contract calculates the amount that should be returned to the user (avaxRedemptionAmount) by subtracting the slashed portion from the original deposit (avaxDepositAmount). However, the state update that reduces minimumContractBalance mistakenly subtracts the full avaxDepositAmount instead of the reduced avaxRedemptionAmount. As a result the recorded minimum balance becomes smaller than it should be. If a user later calls redeemAfterExpiry for a slashed registration, the contract tries to decrement minimumContractBalance by the full deposit amount, which can be larger than the already‑reduced balance, causing an arithmetic underflow and a transaction revert. The same mis‑calculation can also make a subsequent call to withdraw leave the contract with insufficient AVAX to meet its obligations, effectively blocking further withdrawals. The bug manifests only when a non‑zero slash percentage is configured; the deployed version currently uses a zero percentage, so the issue is not observable in production but can be triggered in testing. From a user’s perspective the redemption transaction simply fails, the expected refund is not received, and the contract may appear to have a lower minimum balance than anticipated, leading to confusion and potential denial‑of‑service for other participants. The root cause is the use of the wrong variable in the balance adjustment, a classic example of an incorrect accounting update that leads to underflow. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin through code review of the releaseLockedTokens and redeemAfterExpiry functions and reproduced with a test that forces a 50 % slash. The bug is hard to notice because the default configuration avoids slashing, and the balance discrepancy is internal to the contract state rather than visible on‑chain. The proper fix is to decrement minimumContractBalance by avaxRedemptionAmount—the actual amount that will be returned to the user—rather than by avaxDepositAmount, thereby preserving the intended accounting invariant and preventing underflow reverts.

title: The default admin role controls all other roles within `StakingContract`
description:
** Within `StakingContract`, there is intended separation between the Zeeve and BENQI admin/super-admin roles as implemented in the [`grantAdminRole()`](https://code.zeeve.net/zeeve-endeavors/benqi_smartcontract/-/blob/b63336201f50f9a67451bf5c7b32ddcc4a847ce2/contracts/staking.sol#L986), [`revokeAdminRole()`](https://code.zeeve.net/zeeve-endeavors/benqi_smartcontract/-/blob/b63336201f50f9a67451bf5c7b32ddcc4a847ce2/contracts/staking.sol#L1017), and [`updateAdminRole()`](https://code.zeeve.net/zeeve-endeavors/benqi_smartcontract/-/blob/b63336201f50f9a67451bf5c7b32ddcc4a847ce2/contracts/staking.sol#L1048) functions. The intention is for admin roles to be managed by the corresponding super-admin; however, `AccessControlUpgradeable::_setRoleAdmin` is never invoked for any of the roles and the current implementation fails to consider the default admin role that is [granted to the BENQI super-admin](https://code.zeeve.net/zeeve-endeavors/benqi_smartcontract/-/blob/b63336201f50f9a67451bf5c7b32ddcc4a847ce2/contracts/staking.sol#L169) for pausing purposes when the contract is initialized. As a result, the BENQI super-admin can be used to manage all other roles by invoking `AccessControlUpgradeable::grantRole` and `AccessControlUpgradeable::revokeRole` directly. This behavior is used in `Ignite` and `ValidatorRewarder` to grant the appropriate roles; however, it is not desirable in `StakingContract`.

** The default admin role granted to the BENQI super-admin can be used to control all other roles.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a privilege‑escalation flaw caused by an incorrectly configured role hierarchy in the StakingContract. The contract uses OpenZeppelin AccessControlUpgradeable, which assigns a DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE that can manage any other role unless a specific admin role is set with _setRoleAdmin. During initialization the BENQI super‑admin is granted the default admin role for pausing, but the contract never calls _setRoleAdmin for the ZE​EVE and BENQI admin or super‑admin roles. As a result the BENQI super‑admin remains the admin of every role, including the ZE​EVE_SUPER_ADMIN_ROLE. An attacker who controls the BENQI super‑admin address can call the generic grantRole and revokeRole functions to add, replace or remove any privileged role, effectively taking over the entire permission system. This can be exploited at any time after deployment by sending a transaction from the BENQI super‑admin account that grants the ZE​EVE_SUPER_ADMIN_ROLE to an address of the attacker and revokes it from the legitimate holder. The impact is a loss of the intended separation of duties: the attacker can pause the contract, modify reward parameters, or otherwise manipulate protocol logic, potentially leading to loss of funds or disruption of service for users and token holders. The issue manifests when the contract is initialized and the default admin role is left unchanged; it is not obvious from the UI because the role‑management functions appear to enforce separate admin roles, yet the underlying hierarchy still gives full control to the default admin. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the role‑admin assignments and confirmed that getRoleAdmin returns DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE for every defined role. It is hard to notice because the OpenZeppelin library hides the admin relationship behind internal calls, and developers may assume that custom grantAdminRole and updateAdminRole functions enforce the correct hierarchy. To remediate, the contract should explicitly set the appropriate admin role for each custom role during initialization, remove reliance on the default admin role by creating a dedicated pauser role, or override the OpenZeppelin grantRole and revokeRole functions to prevent direct calls from the default admin. In essence, the bug is an improper role hierarchy configuration that enables privilege escalation and violates the protocol’s security model and accounting assumptions.

title: Inconsistent transfers of native tokens could result in unexpected loss of funds
description:
** Multiple protocol functions across both `Ignite` and `StakingContract` transfer native `AVAX` to the user and/or protocol fee/slashed token recipients.

Throughout `Ignite` [[1](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/Ignite.sol#L215), [2](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/Ignite.sol#L427), [3](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/Ignite.sol#L477), [4](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/Ignite.sol#L563), [5](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/Ignite.sol#L639), [6](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/Ignite.sol#L699)], the low-level `.call()` pattern is used; however, this same behavior is not followed in `StakingContract` – the `.transfer()` function is used on lines [433](https://code.zeeve.net/zeeve-endeavors/benqi_smartcontract/-/blob/b63336201f50f9a67451bf5c7b32ddcc4a847ce2/contracts/staking.sol#L433) and [484](https://code.zeeve.net/zeeve-endeavors/benqi_smartcontract/-/blob/b63336201f50f9a67451bf5c7b32ddcc4a847ce2/contracts/staking.sol#L484), and on line [728](https://code.zeeve.net/zeeve-endeavors/benqi_smartcontract/-/blob/b63336201f50f9a67451bf5c7b32ddcc4a847ce2/contracts/staking.sol#L728-L733) `_transferETHAndWrapIfFailWithGasLimit()` is used, all with a `2300` gas stipend.

While these other functions may have been used to mitigate against potential re-entrancy attacks, native token transfers using low-level calls are preferred over `.transfer()` to mitigate against changes in gas costs, as described [here](https://consensys.io/diligence/blog/2019/09/stop-using-soliditys-transfer-now/). The instances on lines 433 and 484 are particularly problematic as they have no `WAVAX` fallback and could result in an unexpected loss of funds as described [here](https://solodit.xyz/issues/m-01-swapsol-implements-potentially-dangerous-transfer-code4rena-tally-tally-contest-git) and in the linked examples.

** There could be an unexpected loss of funds if the recipient of a transfer (applicable to both users and the Zeeve wallet) is a smart contract that fails to implement a payable fallback function, or the fallback function uses more than 2300 gas units. This could happen, for example, if the recipient is a smart account whose fallback function logic causes the execution to use more than 2300 gas.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistent handling of native AVAX transfers in the Ignite and StakingContract contracts. Some functions use a low‑level .call with a configurable gas stipend, while others rely on .transfer or a wrapper that forwards only the fixed 2300‑gas stipend. Because .transfer and a 2300‑gas call assume the recipient can accept the funds with a simple payable fallback, any recipient contract that does not implement a payable fallback or whose fallback consumes more than 2300 gas will cause the transfer to fail. When the failure is not properly checked, the AVAX can become permanently locked in the contract or the intended recipient receives nothing. This situation can be triggered whenever the protocol distributes rewards, refunds, or fees to a user‑controlled contract, a smart‑account wallet, or the protocol’s own fee collector. From the user’s perspective the balance shown after the transaction may remain unchanged, a refund may be missing, or a fee appears to disappear, violating the expected accounting guarantees of the system. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, which noted the mixed use of .call and .transfer and the lack of a fallback handling path. The problem is subtle because a failed .transfer reverts the whole transaction, potentially halting other logic, while a .call that returns false may be ignored, making the loss silent. The root cause is the reliance on a fixed gas stipend and the absence of a uniform safe‑value‑transfer pattern. To remediate, all native AVAX transfers should be performed with a low‑level call that forwards enough gas (or uses Address.sendValue) and checks the return value, or the contract should adopt a pull‑payment model where recipients claim their funds. Aligning the transfer mechanism across the codebase eliminates the risk of unexpected fund loss and restores the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: Redemption of failed registration fees and pre-validated QI is not guaranteed to be possible
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of missing validation of the beneficiary's ability to receive AVAX when registering with a fee or when redeeming pre‑validated QI stakes. In the registerWithStake function the contract performs a low‑level call to msg.sender and requires success, ensuring that the caller can accept a zero‑value transfer. The analogous functions registerWithAvaxFee and registerWithPrevalidatedQiStake omit this check. Consequently, if the caller is a contract that does not implement a payable fallback or receive function, the low‑level call made during fee redemption or stake redemption will revert, causing the AVAX registration fee or the locked QI stake to remain permanently in the Ignite contract. The issue is triggered when a user registers through a contract that cannot receive AVAX, or when the redemption after expiry attempts to send AVAX to such a contract. The affected parties are users who interact via contracts, the protocol because funds become unrecoverable, and any role that expects refunds or stake withdrawals. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the code paths of registerWithStake and the other registration functions and verified the behavior with a Forge test that showed a zero‑value call to a non‑payable contract fails. The bug is subtle because the failure occurs only at redemption time, not at registration, and the contract does not emit an explicit error indicating that the beneficiary is unsuitable, making it easy to overlook. The impact is that AVAX registration fees and pre‑validated QI stakes can become permanently locked, breaking the accounting assumptions that every registration fee is refundable and that every stake can be redeemed after expiry. To remediate, the contract should perform the same low‑level call check in registerWithAvaxFee and registerWithPrevalidatedQiStake, and optionally protect the redemption function with a non‑reentrant guard to avoid re‑entrancy attacks. This class of bug is a beneficiary‑receiveability validation omission, commonly seen in contracts that rely on low‑level calls without confirming that the target address can accept ether.

title: Ignite fee is not returned for pre-validated `QI` stakes in the event of registration failure
description:
** The `1 AVAX` [Ignite fee](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/Ignite.sol#L387) applied to pre-validated `QI` stakes is [paid to the fee recipient](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/Ignite.sol#L388) at the time of registration. If this registration fails (e.g. due to off-chain BLS proof validation), the registration will be [marked as withdrawable](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/Ignite.sol#L620) once `Ignite::releaseLockedTokens` is called; however, since the fee has already been paid and [deducted from the user's stake amount](https://github.com/Benqi-fi/ignite-contracts/blob/bbca0ddb399225f378c1d774fb70a7486e655eea/src/Ignite.sol#L397), it will not be returned with the refunded `QI` stake. This behavior differs from the other registration methods, which all refund the usually non-refundable fee in the event of registration failure.

** Users who register with a hosted Zeeve validator will not be refunded the Ignite fee if registration fails.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of the one‑AVAX Ignite fee that is charged when a user registers a pre‑validated QI stake through the Ignite contract. The fee is transferred to a designated fee recipient at the moment of registration and is subtracted from the user’s stake amount. If the registration later fails – for example because an off‑chain BLS proof does not validate – the contract marks the stake as withdrawable and returns the QI tokens, but it does not return the previously transferred fee. Consequently the user receives back only the stake amount while the one‑AVAX fee remains permanently with the fee recipient. This behavior is inconsistent with other registration pathways, which do refund the fee when registration fails, and it only affects users who employ the pre‑validated QI stake method, notably those using a hosted Zeeve validator. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, which noted the discrepancy in fee handling. It can be hard to notice because the transaction appears successful from a UI perspective – the stake is shown as withdrawn – while the small fee loss may be overlooked. From the user’s point of view the expectation is that a failed registration results in a full refund, but in reality the fee disappears, leading to a loss of funds and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions. The root cause is that the fee is treated as a non‑refundable payment in the registration logic, and no refund path is implemented for the pre‑validated flow. To remediate, the contract should retain the fee in escrow until the registration outcome is known and, in the event of failure, return the fee to the user in the same manner as other registration methods. This would align the fee handling with the intended business logic, prevent unintended fund loss, and close a potential incentive for malicious actors to deliberately cause registration failures to capture fees.

title: Incorrect range validation in `quantAMMPackEight32` allows invalid values to be packed
description:
The `ScalarQuantAMMBaseStorage::quantAMMPackEight32` function contains incorrect validation logic that fails to properly check minimum bounds for six out of eight input parameters. The require statement incorrectly reuses `_firstInt` for minimum bound checks instead of checking each respective input parameter.

```solidity
require(
    _firstInt <= MAX32 &&
        _firstInt >= MIN32 &&
        _secondInt <= MAX32 &&
        _secondInt >= MIN32 &&
        _thirdInt <= MAX32 &&
        _firstInt >= MIN32 &&  // @audit should be _thirdInt
        _fourthInt <= MAX32 &&
        _firstInt >= MIN32 &&  // @audit should be _fourthInt
        _fifthInt <= MAX32 &&
        _firstInt >= MIN32 &&  // @audit should be _fifthInt
        _sixthInt <= MAX32 &&
        _firstInt >= MIN32 &&  // @audit should be _sixthInt
        _seventhInt <= MAX32 &&
        _firstInt >= MIN32 &&  // @audit should be _seventhInt
        _eighthInt <= MAX32 &&
        _firstInt >= MIN32,    // @audit should be _eighthInt
    "Overflow"
);
```
This function is called by `quantAMMPack32Array` which inturn is used in the `QuantAMMWeightedPool::setWeights` function to pack weight values.

While the `setWeights` function is protected by access controls (only callable by `updateWeightRunner`), allowing invalid values to be packed could lead to unexpected behavior in weight calculations.
poc: TBD
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in a packing routine that combines eight 32‑bit integers into a single 256‑bit word. The routine is supposed to enforce that each integer lies within the allowed range defined by MIN32 (the minimum acceptable value) and MAX32 (the maximum acceptable value). The implementation contains a require statement that correctly checks the upper bound for every parameter, but mistakenly reuses the first parameter, _firstInt, for the lower‑bound checks of the remaining seven parameters. As a result, only _firstInt is verified to be greater than or equal to MIN32, while _secondInt through _eighthInt can be arbitrarily low, even below the protocol’s minimum. This logical error was discovered during a manual audit when the repeated use of _firstInt in the require clause was flagged as a copy‑paste mistake. Because the condition syntax looks syntactically valid, the flaw can be easily overlooked, especially if tests only cover typical, in‑range values. The packing function is invoked by a higher‑level routine that sets weight values for a weighted automated market maker pool. When an attacker with permission to call the weight‑setting function supplies a value below MIN32 for any of the unchecked parameters, the packed weight word contains an out‑of‑range component. Subsequent weight calculations that rely on the packed data may produce incorrect ratios, division‑by‑zero errors, or negative weight interpretations, leading to distorted pricing and potentially causing users to receive fewer tokens than expected, see balances unexpectedly drop to zero, or experience failed trades. Although the function is protected by an access‑control check that limits calls to a designated updater contract, any compromise of that updater or a malicious insider can exploit the flaw. The impact is classified as medium because it does not allow arbitrary fund theft without additional privileges, but it can undermine the economic guarantees of the pool and erode user trust. To remediate the issue, the require clause should be rewritten so that each parameter is individually compared against MIN32, or the validation logic should be abstracted into a reusable helper that iterates over all inputs, ensuring both lower and upper bounds are correctly enforced for every value. Proper testing with edge‑case values below MIN32 should be added to prevent regression.

title: Lack of permission check allows unauthorized updates to `lastPoolUpdateRun`
bug_full:
The vulnerability consists of an unchecked permission path that allows any address to modify the timestamp stored in the pool’s lastPoolUpdateRun variable. In the QuantAMM weighted pool architecture each pool defines a bitmap of permissions at deployment; specific bits grant the ability to trigger weight updates (MASK_POOL_PERFORM_UPDATE) and to override the timing of those updates (MASK_POOL_DAO_WEIGHT_UPDATES or MASK_POOL_OWNER_UPDATES). The function InitialisePoolLastRunTime is intended to be callable only by a DAO‑designated runner or by the pool manager, but the contract only verifies the caller when one of the two override bits is set. When neither override bit is present the code falls through without a revert, meaning the subsequent assignment to lastPoolUpdateRun executes unconditionally. This logical omission creates a permission‑less entry point.

An attacker can exploit the flaw by calling InitialisePoolLastRunTime with an arbitrary timestamp. By setting the timestamp far in the past the attacker resets the interval counter, allowing performUpdate to be invoked earlier than the configured updateInterval, effectively bypassing the rate‑limiting safeguard. Conversely, by setting the timestamp far in the future the attacker can block legitimate updates, causing the pool’s weight‑adjustment algorithm to stall. From a user’s perspective the pool may appear to stop updating its internal weights, leading to stale pricing, unexpected slippage, or trades that execute against outdated weight ratios. In extreme cases the destabilised algorithm could produce price distortions that harm liquidity providers and token holders.

The issue manifests only for pools that have the perform‑update permission enabled but lack either the DAO‑update or owner‑update permission bits. Such a configuration is possible during deployment or through mis‑configuration of the permission bitmap. Because the function name suggests an administrative operation, developers and auditors may assume that only privileged actors can reach it, making the missing revert easy to overlook during code review. The flaw was identified during a systematic security audit performed by the Cyfrin team, which added a test case that demonstrated that an arbitrary address could successfully call InitialisePoolLastRunTime and then cause performUpdate to revert due to the manipulated timestamp.

To remediate the problem the contract should explicitly reject calls when none of the required permission bits are set. Adding an else clause that reverts with a clear error message ensures that only authorized entities can modify lastPoolUpdateRun, restoring the intended protection of the updateInterval and preserving the integrity of the weight‑adjustment logic. This fix aligns the function’s behaviour with the documented permission model and prevents unauthorized timing manipulation that could otherwise lead to stale or overly frequent weight updates, protecting both the protocol’s economic guarantees and its users’ expectations.

title: Faulty permission check in `UpdateWeightRunner::getData` allows unauthorized access
description:
Certain actions on a pool are protected by permissions. One such permission is `POOL_GET_DATA`, which governs access to the [`UpdateWeightRunner::getData`](https://github.com/QuantAMMProtocol/QuantAMM-V1/blob/7213401491f6a8fd1fcc1cf4763b15b5da355f1c/pkg/pool-quantamm/contracts/UpdateWeightRunner.sol#L315-L366) function:

```solidity
bool internalCall = msg.sender != address(this);
require(internalCall || approvedPoolActions[_pool] & MASK_POOL_GET_DATA > 0, "Not allowed to get data");
```

The issue lies in how the `internalCall` condition is enforced. The variable `internalCall` is intended to check if the call is made internally by the contract. However, this logic behaves incorrectly:

- `internalCall` will always be `true` because `UpdateWeightRunner` does not call `getData` in a way that changes the call context (i.e., `address(this).getData()`). As a result, `msg.sender` is never equal to `address(this)`.
- Consequently, the statement `msg.sender != address(this)` will always evaluate to `true`, allowing the `require` condition to pass regardless of the pool's permissions.

As a result, the `POOL_GET_DATA` permission is effectively bypassed.

The `UpdateWeightRunner::getData` function can be called on pools that lack the `POOL_GET_DATA` permission.
bug_full: An unauthorized‑access vulnerability exists in the UpdateWeightRunner contract’s getData function. The function is supposed to restrict reading of a pool’s internal data to callers that hold the POOL_GET_DATA permission. To implement this, the code defines a boolean internalCall that is true when the caller is not the contract itself (msg.sender != address(this)) and then requires that either internalCall is true or the pool’s permission bitmap contains the POOL_GET_DATA flag. Because UpdateWeightRunner never invokes getData via an internal call (it does not use address(this).call or a similar pattern), msg.sender is always an external address, making internalCall evaluate to true for every invocation. Consequently the require statement is satisfied regardless of the permission bitmap, effectively bypassing the access control check. An attacker can therefore call getData on any pool, even those that have not been granted the POOL_GET_DATA permission, and obtain sensitive state such as weight vectors, balances, or other accounting data that the protocol intended to keep private. The impact is information disclosure; while no ether is directly stolen, the leaked data can be used for strategic attacks, front‑running, or undermining the economic assumptions of the pool. The bug manifests whenever an external account calls getData, which is the normal usage pattern, so it is always exploitable. All users, pool operators, and third‑party contracts that rely on the permission model are affected because they assume that private pool data cannot be read without explicit approval. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test that expected a revert for an unapproved pool succeeded, indicating that the permission check was ineffective. The problem is subtle because the presence of the internalCall variable gives the impression of a dual‑mode guard, masking the fact that the condition is trivially true. The recommended remediation is to remove the internalCall variable entirely and require that the POOL_GET_DATA flag be set for the target pool before returning data. Making the function view and eliminating the unnecessary event emission also clarifies its intent and prevents future misuse. This vulnerability belongs to the class of improper access control bugs where an always‑true condition defeats the intended permission logic.

title: Stale Oracle prices accepted when no backup oracles available
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the contract may accept stale oracle price data when no backup oracles are configured. The getData function first checks whether the primary (optimised) oracle returns a timestamp newer than the allowed staleness threshold. If the data is fresh, it is used; if it is stale, the code attempts to iterate over a list of backup oracles. When the backup list is empty, the loop is skipped and the function proceeds to assign the previously rejected stale price to the output array. This logic flaw means that a stale price can be silently accepted and later used to calculate pool weight updates. The root cause is an insufficient fallback validation: the contract does not revert or signal an error when the primary oracle is stale and there are no alternative sources. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker who can cause the primary oracle to return outdated data, or who can wait until the data naturally becomes stale, can trigger weight calculations based on old market information. Because pool weights influence token swaps, the outdated weights can cause users to receive less value than expected, create arbitrage opportunities, or even lead to loss of funds if the pool is rebalanced on incorrect data. The issue manifests only when the staleness check fails and the pool has zero backup oracles for the affected asset, a situation that can occur in newly deployed pools or after misconfiguration. All participants in the pool—traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the accounting assumptions that weights reflect current market prices are violated. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that traced the control flow of the getData function and noticed that the stale‑data branch does not revert when the backup array length is one (the primary oracle only). It is hard to notice in normal operation because the function still returns a price and emits no error, so the UI shows a successful call and users see no immediate failure. From a user perspective the symptoms are a pool that appears to update weights normally but later yields unexpected slippage, missing or reduced balances, or trades that seem to give away more tokens than the market price would suggest. The vulnerability belongs to the class of oracle freshness validation bugs where fallback mechanisms are missing or incorrectly handled. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit revert when no fresh oracle values are available, for example by checking that the number of configured backup oracles is greater than one before attempting the fallback loop, and reverting with a clear error message if the primary data is stale and no alternative source exists.

title: Missing admin functions prevent execution of key `UpdateWeightRunner` actions
description:
Several functions in `UpdateWeightRunner` require the `quantammAdmin` role, but these functions are missing from `QuantAMMBaseAdministration`. The affected functions are:

* [`UpdateWeightRunner::addOracle`](https://github.com/QuantAMMProtocol/QuantAMM-V1/blob/7213401491f6a8fd1fcc1cf4763b15b5da355f1c/pkg/pool-quantamm/contracts/UpdateWeightRunner.sol#L182-L195)
* [`UpdateWeightRunner::removeOracle`](https://github.com/QuantAMMProtocol/QuantAMM-V1/blob/7213401491f6a8fd1fcc1cf4763b15b5da355f1c/pkg/pool-quantamm/contracts/UpdateWeightRunner.sol#L197-L203)
* [`UpdateWeightRunner::setApprovedActionsForPool`](https://github.com/QuantAMMProtocol/QuantAMM-V1/blob/7213401491f6a8fd1fcc1cf4763b15b5da355f1c/pkg/pool-quantamm/contracts/UpdateWeightRunner.sol#L205-L209)
* [`UpdateWeightRunner::setETHUSDOracle`](https://github.com/QuantAMMProtocol/QuantAMM-V1/blob/7213401491f6a8fd1fcc1cf4763b15b5da355f1c/pkg/pool-quantamm/contracts/UpdateWeightRunner.sol#L281-L287)

Since these functions rely on `quantammAdmin`, they cannot be executed unless the corresponding calls are included in `QuantAMMBaseAdministration`.

The `QuantAMMBaseAdministration` contract cannot execute the above functions. As a result, administrative actions such as adding or removing oracles, setting approved actions for pools, and updating the ETH/USD oracle cannot be performed, limiting the functionality and flexibility of the system.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing administrative interface in the QuantAMM protocol. Several functions that modify critical protocol parameters – adding or removing price oracles, setting which actions a pool may execute, and updating the ETH/USD price oracle – are defined in the UpdateWeightRunner contract with a requirement that the caller hold the quantammAdmin role. However, the QuantAMMBaseAdministration contract, which is intended to expose admin‑only functions to the designated admin, does not contain external wrappers for these UpdateWeightRunner functions. As a result, the admin address cannot invoke them, because the function selectors are not present in the contract’s ABI and any call to them will revert with an undefined function error. This omission stems from an incomplete inheritance or composition design where the base administration contract was assumed to forward all privileged calls but the forwarding code was never implemented. Exploitation is indirect: an attacker who gains the admin role would still be unable to perform essential governance actions, effectively locking the protocol’s ability to refresh oracle data or adjust pool permissions. Even without an attacker, the protocol suffers a denial‑of‑service condition – price feeds may become stale, pools may retain outdated approved actions, and the system loses flexibility to respond to market changes. From a user’s perspective the UI may show no option to add a new oracle, the admin dashboard may report “action not available”, or trades may execute with an outdated ETH/USD price, leading to unexpected slippage or loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract hierarchy, where the auditor compared the list of admin‑only functions declared in UpdateWeightRunner with the functions actually exposed by QuantAMMBaseAdministration and found several gaps. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles and the missing functions do not cause immediate runtime errors; they simply cannot be called, which may be mistaken for a fully functional system until an admin tries to perform an update. To remediate, the protocol should either add external wrappers for addOracle, removeOracle, setApprovedActionsForPool, and setETHUSDOracle in QuantAMMBaseAdministration, or replace the custom administration contract with a well‑tested OpenZeppelin Timelock that correctly enforces role‑based access and provides the necessary external entry points. In either case the fix restores the ability of the designated admin to manage oracles and pool permissions, eliminating the operational lock‑out and aligning the implementation with the intended governance model.

title: `QuantAMMBaseAdministration::onlyExecutor` modifier does not enforce a time lock on actions
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the administration contract of the QuantAMM protocol where a modifier named onlyExecutor is used to protect privileged functions. The modifier checks only that the caller holds the EXECUTOR_ROLE on the external TimelockController contract, but it does not require the call to originate from the timelock contract itself. Because the OpenZeppelin TimelockController allows any address with EXECUTOR_ROLE to execute scheduled operations directly, an attacker who is granted this role can bypass the intended delay and invoke the protected functions immediately. This flaw occurs whenever a function is guarded by onlyExecutor, which includes critical administrative actions such as parameter updates, fee changes, or fund withdrawals. From a user’s perspective the protocol may appear to respect a governance delay, yet changes happen instantly, leading to unexpected token price shifts, sudden fee adjustments, or unexplained movement of funds. The impact is that the governance timelock, which is supposed to give token holders a window to react, is effectively disabled, allowing a malicious executor to alter the protocol state without warning and potentially drain assets or manipulate market conditions. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that compared the modifier logic with the reference implementation of TimelockController and noticed the missing address check. It can be hard to notice because the require statement still references the timelock contract and the role check looks correct at a glance, masking the fact that the timelock’s delay enforcement is absent. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce that only the timelock contract itself can call the privileged functions, for example by replacing onlyExecutor with a modifier that requires msg.sender to equal the timelock address, or by delegating administration entirely to an OpenZeppelin TimelockController instance. This change restores the intended delay, aligns the contract with the security model of timelocked governance, and prevents immediate execution of high‑risk actions by any executor role holder.

title: Unauthorized role grants prevent `QuantAMMBaseAdministration` deployment
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unauthorized role assignment that occurs during the construction of the QuantAMMBaseAdministration contract. The contract’s constructor iterates over supplied proposer and executor address arrays and calls grantRole on an external TimelockController for the PROPOSER_ROLE and EXECUTOR_ROLE. However, the QuantAMMBaseAdministration contract itself does not hold the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE required by the TimelockController’s AccessControl mechanism, so each grantRole call reverts with an AccessControlUnauthorizedAccount error. This failure happens at deployment time, before any other logic can execute, and prevents the contract from being instantiated. As a result, the protocol’s break‑glass administration features remain unavailable, the DAO cannot initialize its governance infrastructure, and end‑users see the contract missing or transactions reverting. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case deliberately expected a revert and observed that the constructor could not complete. It is easy to miss because role‑granting patterns are common and often succeed when the caller is an admin; the missing admin privilege is only apparent when the constructor runs. The bug belongs to the class of AccessControl misuse where a contract attempts to assign privileged roles without possessing the necessary admin role, leading to a deployment‑time denial‑of‑service. From a user perspective the UI may report that the admin contract failed to deploy, show a transaction revert, or display empty balances where governance functions should be available, violating the expectation that the contract will be live after deployment. To remediate, the redundant grantRole calls should be removed from the constructor, relying on the TimelockController’s own constructor to set up the appropriate roles, or the QuantAMMBaseAdministration contract should be granted DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE before attempting any role assignments. This correction restores successful deployment and ensures that the protocol’s governance and emergency controls function as intended.

title: Auto redemption will not function due to slippage misconfiguration
description:
Both legacy and non-legacy vaults perform a call to `ISwapRouter::exactInput` when attempting to swap collateral to `USDs`, with the `amountOutMinimum` parameter being specified as the USD value of the collateral being swapped:

```solidity
calculator.tokenToUSD(
    ITokenManager(ISmartVaultManager(manager).tokenManager()).getTokenIfExists(_collateralAddr),
    _collateralAmount
)
```

However, this fails to account for slippage incurred during the swap.

The further `USDs` is below peg, the more `USDs` will be redeemed for a given amount of collateral and so this will not likely present any issues. When swapping through high fee, lower liquidity pools, auto redemption will be more likely to fail, especially if `USDs` is closer to peg.
