Because the receiver is responsible for pulling tokens from a Sablier stream, the contract’s omission means that any remaining streamed amount stays locked inside the Sablier lockup contract and cannot be retrieved by the council. This situation can arise whenever the GOVERNANCE_COUNCIL_ROLE – typically a multisig or governance contract – calls an update while the stream has not been depleted. If the stream is later cancelled, the sender can only recover the un‑streamed portion; the already streamed tokens remain claimable only by the original receiver, which in this case is the outdated CouncilMember contract that no longer holds a reference to the stream. Consequently, council members may see their expected token balance stay at zero or be reduced, and the protocol may lose funds that are effectively stranded. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the flow of stream updates and compared it with Sablier’s documentation, which states that the receiver must withdraw before a stream is cancelled. The problem is subtle because the contract’s state appears to change correctly – events are emitted and the new stream address is stored – yet the underlying token balance is invisible to users, making the loss easy to miss in UI displays. The bug belongs to the class of improper external asset settlement, where a contract updates its internal references without first reconciling external token holdings. To remediate, the contract should either implement Sablier’s onStreamCanceled hook so that any cancellation automatically triggers a withdrawal of the streamed amount, or explicitly check that the stream is depleted (or withdraw the remaining balance) before performing any state updates. Both approaches ensure that no streamed tokens remain idle and that council members receive the full amount they are entitled to.

title: JUSDBankStorage::getTRate(),JUSDBankStorage::accrueRa
bug_full: An inconsistency exists between the function that updates the accumulated borrowing fee rate (accrueRate) and the view function that reports the current rate (getTRate). The accrueRate function multiplies the previous tRate by a factor that includes the elapsed time and the borrow fee rate using a decimal multiplication helper, then stores the result. In contrast, getTRate simply adds a linear term (borrowFeeRate * timeDifference / Types.SECONDS_PER_YEAR) to the stored tRate without applying the same decimal multiplication. Because the two formulas are not mathematically equivalent, the value returned by getTRate diverges from the value stored in tRate after each call to accrueRate, especially when large time intervals are simulated. This divergence propagates to every contract routine that relies on the reported rate, such as the safety check (_isAccountSafe), flash loan eligibility, and bad‑debt handling. As a result, the protocol may incorrectly deem an account unsafe, reject legitimate flash loans, or miscalculate bad‑debt recoveries, leading to users receiving no funds, unexpected reverts, or loss of collateral. The bug appears only after the contract experiences a non‑trivial time gap; during normal short‑interval operation the difference is small and can be missed during manual testing. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit when the auditor added a test that warped the blockchain timestamp by many days, called accrueRate, and compared the two rate values, observing a measurable deviation. The problem is hard to notice because both functions are named as if they provide the same rate and the code paths are rarely exercised together in production. The appropriate fix is to make getTRate use the identical decimal multiplication formula that accrueRate uses, ensuring both functions compute the same value for any elapsed time. This aligns the contract’s accounting logic, restores correct safety checks, and prevents unintended fund loss.

title: Funding#requestWithdraw uses incorrect with-
bug_full: The vulnerability is an authorization‑identity mismatch in the requestWithdraw function of the Funding contract. Instead of recording a pending withdrawal for the address supplied in the from parameter, the implementation mistakenly uses msg.sender, the caller’s address, when updating the pendingPrimaryWithdraw, pendingSecondaryWithdraw and withdrawExecutionTimestamp mappings. This root cause stems from an incorrect reference to the transaction sender rather than the intended beneficiary, a classic case of improper use of msg.sender in delegated‑action functions. An attacker or any user attempting to initiate a withdrawal on behalf of another participant – for example, a relayer, operator, or a contract with an allowance – will trigger the function, pass a valid from address, and satisfy the isWithdrawValid check, but the contract will store the withdrawal request under the caller’s own address. Consequently, the intended recipient never sees a pending withdrawal entry, the UI may display a request event referencing the caller, and the funds remain locked because the contract expects the caller to later execute the withdrawal. The impact is that delegated withdrawals become non‑functional, leading to stranded or irretrievable funds for users who rely on third‑party initiated withdrawals, such as custodial services or meta‑transaction relayers. This condition occurs whenever requestWithdraw is invoked with a from argument that differs from msg.sender, which includes any scenario where an allowance is set for another address. The affected parties are the protocol’s users who delegate withdrawals, the operator who may unintentionally be charged, and any integrators expecting the contract to honor the from parameter. The issue was discovered during a manual audit review of the Funding.sol source, where the code path was examined and the mismatch between the function signature and the internal state updates was observed. It can be hard to notice because the function still succeeds for self‑withdrawals, and test suites that only cover direct withdrawals may not expose the bug. To remediate, all occurrences of msg.sender used for state updates in this function should be replaced with the from variable, ensuring that pending withdrawals are correctly attributed to the intended beneficiary. This aligns the contract with the expected business logic that a withdrawal request records the amount for the user specified by the from address, preserving accounting integrity and preventing funds from disappearing due to misattributed state entries.

title: FundRateArbitrage is vulnerable to inflation
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inflation attack on the index used to convert deposited USDC into earnUSDC shares. The contract computes the index as the net value of the contract (including all USDC held) divided by the total supply of earnUSDC tokens. Because the net value counts USDC that can be sent to the contract without minting any earnUSDC (for example through a donation or a direct transfer), an attacker can inflate the index by depositing a large amount of USDC that does not increase totalEarnUSDCBalance. When the index becomes extremely high, the calculation of earnUSDCAmount during a normal user deposit – amount divided by the inflated index – rounds down to zero due to integer division. The user’s USDC is still transferred to the contract, but the user receives no earnUSDC shares, effectively losing the deposited funds. The attacker can later withdraw their existing shares (or any shares that were already minted) and receive a disproportionate amount of USDC, stealing the victim’s deposit. This issue occurs whenever the contract allows arbitrary USDC to be added to its balance without a corresponding increase in the share supply, and when the deposit amount is smaller than the inflated index, causing the division to truncate to zero. It affects any user who tries to deposit USDC, the protocol’s token holders, and ultimately the trustworthiness of the platform. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by examining the getIndex and deposit functions and recognizing that the index calculation mirrors the classic ERC4626 inflation attack where external assets inflate the asset‑per‑share ratio. The bug is subtle because the contract’s public index appears to be a normal price feed, and donations may be perceived as legitimate contributions, making the rounding error easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should adopt a virtual offset or similar accounting mechanism as recommended by OpenZeppelin for ERC4626 contracts, ensuring that only assets backing issued shares are included in the index calculation, thereby preventing external inflation of the conversion rate.

title: External lending can exceed the threshold
description:
Due to an incorrect calculation of the max lending amount, external lending can exceed the external withdrawal threshold. If this restriction/threshold is not adhered to, users or various core functionalities within the protocol will have issues redeeming or withdrawing their prime cash.
External Withdraw Threshold: ensures that Notional has sufficient liquidity to withdraw from an external lending market. If Notional has 1000 units of underlying lent out on Aave, it requires 1000 * externalWithdrawThreshold units of underlying to be available on Aave for withdraw. This ensures there is sufficient buffer to process the redemption of Notional funds. If available liquidity on Aave begins to drop due to increased utilization, Notional will automatically begin to withdraw its funds from Aave to ensure that they are available for withdrawal on Notional itself.
To ensure the redeemability of Notional’s funds on external lending markets, Notional requires there to be redeemable funds on the external lending market that are a multiple of the funds that Notional has lent on that market itself.
Assume that the externalWithdrawThreshold is 200% and the underlying is USDC. Therefore, PERCENTAGE_DECIMALS/externalWithdrawThreshold = 100/200 = 0.5 (Line 83-84 below). This means that the number of USDC to be available on AAVE for withdrawal must be two (2) times the number of USDC Notional lent out on AAVE (A multiple of 2).
The externalUnderlyingAvailableForWithdraw stores the number of liquidity in USDC on the AAVE pool available to be withdrawn.
If externalUnderlyingAvailableForWithdraw is 1000 USDC and currentExternalUnderlyingLend is 400 USDC, this means that the remaining 600 USDC liquidity on the AAVE pool is not owned by Notional.
The maxExternalUnderlyingLend will be 600 * 0.5 = 300. Thus, the maximum amount that Notional can lend externally at this point is 300 USDC.
Assume that after Notional has lent 300 USDC externally to the AAVE pool. The currentExternalUnderlyingLend will become 400+300=700, and the externalUnderlyingAvailableForWithdraw will become 1000+300=1300
Following is the percentage of USDC in AAVE that belong to Notional 700/1300 = 0.5384615385 (53%).
At this point, the invariant is broken as the number of USDC to be available on AAVE for withdrawal is less than two (2) times the number of USDC lent out on AAVE after the lending.

The root cause is that when USDC is deposited to AAVE to get aUSDC, the total USDC in the pool increases. Therefore, using the current amount of USDC in the pool to determine the maximum deposit amount is not an accurate measure of liquidity risk.
To ensure the redeemability of Notional’s funds on external lending markets, Notional requires there to be redeemable funds on the external lending market that are a multiple of the funds that Notional has lent on that market itself.
If this restriction is not adhered to, users or various core functionalities within the protocol will have issues redeeming or withdrawing their prime cash. For instance, users might not be able to withdraw their assets from the protocol due to insufficient liquidity, or liquidation cannot be carried out due to lack of liquidity, resulting in bad debt accumulating within the protocol and negatively affecting the protocol's solvency.
bug_full: External lending can exceed the external withdrawal threshold due to an incorrect calculation of the maximum amount that may be deposited into an external market. The contract determines the limit by subtracting the current amount lent from the total liquidity reported by the external pool, multiplying by a constant and dividing by the configured withdraw threshold. This formula assumes that the pool liquidity remains static while the deposit is being made. In reality, depositing USDC into Aave mints aUSDC and increases the total USDC balance of the pool, so the denominator used in the calculation no longer reflects the post‑deposit state. As a result the contract may approve a deposit that pushes the ratio of Notional‑owned liquidity to total pool liquidity below the required multiple (for example, below 2× when the threshold is 200 %). When this invariant is broken, the protocol no longer guarantees that enough assets are available on the external market to satisfy withdrawals or redemptions. Users attempting to withdraw their prime cash may see transactions revert, receive zero tokens, or observe missing balances in the UI. Liquidations may fail because the external market cannot provide the needed funds, potentially creating bad debt and threatening the protocol’s solvency. The condition occurs whenever externalUnderlyingAvailableForWithdraw is greater than currentExternalUnderlyingLend and a new deposit is processed; the faulty calculation does not re‑evaluate the invariant after the deposit. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the ExternalLending.sol file, where the auditor constructed a numeric example that showed the ratio dropping from 0.5 to 0.538 after a permitted deposit, violating the 2× rule. The bug is subtle because the pre‑deposit check passes and the contract does not emit any warning, making the problem easy to miss in routine testing. The proper fix is to compute the maximum deposit using the formula D = (T·W – L) / (1 – T), where T is the withdraw threshold expressed as a fraction, W is the current external liquidity, and L is the amount already lent. This ensures that after the deposit the required multiple is preserved, preventing liquidity shortfalls and protecting user withdrawals. The vulnerability belongs to the class of threshold‑invariant arithmetic errors where mutable external state is used in a static calculation, leading to over‑allocation of assets.

title: Unexpected behavior when calling certain ERC4626
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the wfCash ERC4626 wrapper calculates the value of matured fCash tokens before the global settlement has been executed. When an fCash position reaches its maturity timestamp, the contract does not automatically perform the global settlement; instead, settlement is triggered lazily the first time an account attempts to settle its own balance. The internal helper _getMaturedCashValue checks the settlement rate returned by NotionalV2 and assumes that if the supplyFactor field of the returned PrimeRate struct is zero, the fCash has not yet been settled and therefore the cash value should be zero. This assumption is used directly by totalAssets(), which is the core accounting function for the ERC4626 interface. Consequently, during the narrow window after the maturity block but before any account has called settle, totalAssets() returns zero even though the wrapper still holds the underlying cash. All higher‑level ERC4626 view functions that rely on totalAssets – such as convertToAssets, previewRedeem, maxWithdraw and convertToShares – either report a zero asset amount or trigger a division‑by‑zero revert. From a user’s perspective the wrapper appears to have no assets: balances displayed in the UI become zero, withdrawals are rejected, and share‑to‑asset conversions fail. External protocols that query these functions for collateral valuation or withdrawal limits receive incorrect data, potentially causing liquidations or preventing legitimate operations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Notional update where the code path for matured fCash was examined and the interaction between hasMatured(), the lazy settlement model, and the supplyFactor check was found to produce an unexpected zero cash value. Because the problem only manifests in a short post‑maturity window, it can be easily missed by standard testing or by developers who assume that maturity automatically implies a settled cash balance. To remediate, the contract should either trigger the global settlement automatically at maturity, or modify the accounting logic to fall back to the actual cash balance when supplyFactor is zero, and add explicit guards against division‑by‑zero in convertToShares. Additionally, the behavior should be clearly documented so that integrators understand that asset queries may return zero or revert until settlement occurs.

title: Rebalance will be delayed due to revert
bug_full: The vulnerability is a timing‑dependent rebalancing failure in the protocol’s treasury action. The contract attempts to rebalance several currencies in a single transaction after a view function reports them as unhealthy. Because the health check is performed again inside the transaction with a require statement, if any of the reported currencies becomes healthy before the transaction is mined, the require reverts and the whole transaction is cancelled. As a result, other currencies that remain unhealthy are not rebanced, leaving excess liquidity lent to external markets. This delay can accumulate under volatile market conditions, causing the protocol to have insufficient on‑chain liquidity for user withdrawals or for liquidation of under‑collateralised positions. The issue appears when the automated Gelato bot schedules a rebalance based on stale data, submits the transaction, and the market moves before execution. Users may experience failed withdrawals, delayed liquidation, or balances that appear unchanged despite external activity. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that traced the rebalancing flow and observed that the require at line 326 aborts the entire batch when a single currency passes the health check. The problem is hard to notice because the revert only occurs intermittently and does not directly indicate that other currencies were left unbalanced. The proper fix is to treat each currency independently: skip the ones that are now healthy and continue processing the remaining unhealthy ones, for example by replacing the require with a conditional early‑return or by splitting the batch into separate transactions. This changes the failure mode from a single‑transaction abort to a graceful skip, preserving the intended liquidity management and preventing the protocol from unintentionally over‑lending assets.

title: Rebalance might be skipped even if the ex-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a miscalculation of the deviation between the protocol's target external lending amount and the actual amount that is currently lent out. The function that determines whether external lending is unhealthy computes an off‑target percentage using the formula abs(currentExternalUnderlyingLend‑targetAmount) divided by the sum of currentExternalUnderlyingLend and targetAmount. This denominator is incorrect; the deviation should be expressed as a ratio to the target amount only. Because the sum of the two values is roughly twice the target when the current amount is close to the target, the resulting percentage is underestimated by about half. The contract then decides whether a rebalance is required by checking that the current amount exceeds the target and that the off‑target percentage is greater than zero. In practice the intended safeguard is to trigger a rebalance when the deviation exceeds a small threshold (for example 1 %). The under‑estimated percentage may fall below that threshold even though the external lending is materially above the target, causing the condition to evaluate to false and the rebalance to be skipped. This can happen whenever the protocol’s external lending drifts upward but remains within a narrow band of the target, which is precisely the situation the health‑check logic is meant to catch. The impact is that excess external lending reduces the amount of liquid assets available in the protocol, potentially leading to failed withdrawals, forced liquidations, or other operations that require on‑chain liquidity. Users attempting to withdraw may see their transactions revert or receive zero tokens, while the protocol’s accounting appears healthy because the health‑check incorrectly reports a healthy state. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the TreasuryAction contract, where the auditor noticed that the percentage calculation did not match the documented intent and that the resulting value was consistently lower than expected. The bug is subtle because the contract only checks that the percentage is greater than zero, so the under‑estimation does not raise an obvious error flag, and the protocol may continue operating normally until liquidity pressure surfaces. To remediate the problem the off‑target percentage should be calculated as abs(currentExternalUnderlyingLend‑targetAmount) divided by targetAmount, optionally multiplied by a constant to express it as a percentage. Adjusting the threshold comparison to use the corrected percentage will ensure that any meaningful deviation triggers a rebalance, preserving liquidity and aligning the contract’s behavior with its intended risk‑management model.

title: getOracleData() maxExternalDeposit not ac-
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that reports the maximum amount of external assets that can be deposited, commonly called maxExternalDeposit. The routine calculates the remaining capacity by subtracting the current aToken supply from the pool's supply cap, but it ignores the amount that has already been accrued to the treasury and adjusted by the next liquidity index. Because the accrued interest that belongs to the treasury is not deducted, the reported maxExternalDeposit can be larger than the true remaining capacity. When a user or an automated agent attempts to deposit up to this inflated limit, the protocol’s supply‑cap validation, which includes the term reserve.accruedToTreasury multiplied by the next liquidity index, fails. The validation logic therefore reverts the transaction with a supply‑cap‑exceeded error and the Treasury.rebalance() function cannot complete. This situation occurs only when the pool has a non‑zero supply cap, the current aToken supply is below that cap, and there is a positive accruedToTreasury balance – a common state after interest has been generated. Users experience symptoms such as being told they can deposit a large amount, only to see the transaction revert or the UI show a zero maximum deposit after a failed rebalance, effectively making funds appear to disappear or become locked. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the oracle’s maxExternalDeposit calculation with Aave’s official ValidationLogic, revealing the missing subtraction of the accrued treasury amount. The bug is hard to notice because the oracle returns a seemingly reasonable number in many scenarios, and the discrepancy only surfaces when treasury accruals are present, which may be a small value that does not raise immediate suspicion. Conceptually, this is an accounting mismatch where the protocol’s external‑deposit limit does not account for internal treasury balances, leading to an over‑estimation of available capacity. The proper fix is to subtract the treasury’s accrued amount, after applying the next liquidity index, from the remaining supply‑cap space before exposing maxExternalDeposit, thereby aligning the oracle’s view with the actual validation performed during deposits and rebalancing. By correcting the calculation, deposits will be limited to the true remaining capacity, preventing unexpected reverts, preserving protocol safety, and ensuring that treasury accounting remains consistent with business logic.

title: getTargetExternalLendingAmount() when tar-
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal function that calculates the desired amount of external lending, getTargetExternalLendingAmount. When the rebalancing target specifies a utilization of zero, the function short‑circuits and returns a target amount of zero without evaluating whether the protocol can actually withdraw the currently lent amount. This omission means that if the external lending platform (for example AAVE) reports a current external lend that exceeds the amount that is presently available for withdrawal, the subsequent rebalance routine, _rebalanceCurrency, will attempt to withdraw more than is permitted and will revert. The bug is triggered when an operator calls setRebalancingTargets with all targets set to zero in order to exit all positions; the call chain proceeds through _rebalanceCurrency, _isExternalLendingUnhealthy, and finally getTargetExternalLendingAmount, which returns zero and causes the withdrawal to fail. In a concrete scenario, if the contract has 100 units lent externally and only 99 units are available for withdrawal, the correct target amount should be adjusted to 1 so that the excess can be redeemed, but the early return forces the target to zero, leading to an insufficient‑balance error. The impact is that the protocol cannot complete a full exit, causing user‑facing symptoms such as transactions reverting, balances appearing unchanged, and funds remaining locked in the external lending pool. The affected parties include protocol operators, liquidity providers, and any users whose deposits rely on the rebalancing mechanism. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noticed that the zero‑utilization shortcut bypasses the safety check that aligns target amount with externalUnderlyingAvailableForWithdraw. Because returning zero seems logically sound, the bug can remain hidden unless the specific condition of limited withdrawable liquidity is exercised, making it difficult to detect through standard testing. The appropriate remediation is to remove the early return for targetUtilization == 0, allowing the existing logic that adjusts targetAmount based on the difference between current external lend and available withdrawable amount to execute even when utilization is zero. This change ensures that the contract will attempt to withdraw the maximum possible amount, respecting the external platform’s constraints, and prevents the rebalance routine from reverting, thereby preserving the intended accounting invariants and user expectations of successful fund exits.

title: getTargetExternalLendingAmount() targe-
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting logic error in the calculation of the target amount for external lending. The function that determines how much of the underlying token should be supplied to an external pool first caps the target amount by the oracle‑provided maxExternalDeposit, but it fails to recognise that maxExternalDeposit is intended to limit only *additional* deposits, not the total amount already held by the protocol. Because the current external deposit (currentExternalUnderlyingLend) is already included in the oracle’s maxExternalDeposit value, the min‑operation can incorrectly shrink the target amount to a value far below the actual amount that should remain deposited. When the protocol’s rebalancing logic later sees a target amount that is lower than the current deposit, it interprets this as a signal to withdraw the excess, triggering an unnecessary withdrawal of funds that should have stayed invested. From a user’s perspective this may appear as a sudden drop in the protocol’s balance, missing yield, or a zero‑deposit state even though the protocol still holds assets. The bug occurs whenever the protocol attempts to rebalance while the current external deposit is non‑zero and the oracle’s maxExternalDeposit does not account for that existing balance – for example when maxExternalDeposit is reported as zero because the oracle aggregates the total deposit including the current one. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the rebalancing logic, where the auditor noticed that the min‑function combined three values without distinguishing between a cap on new deposits and a cap on total holdings. It is hard to notice because the function still returns a numeric value and the surrounding code does not raise an error; the problem only manifests as an unexpected withdrawal, which may be attributed to market conditions rather than a code defect. Conceptually, the fix is to apply the maxExternalDeposit restriction only when the calculated target amount exceeds the current external deposit, i.e., when a net deposit is required. The corrected logic first computes the minimum of the desired external amount and the protocol‑specific underlying limit, then checks if the result is greater than the current external balance; if so, it ensures that the incremental deposit does not surpass maxExternalDeposit. This change aligns the implementation with the intended business rule that the cap limits only new inflows, preventing unnecessary withdrawals and preserving the protocol’s capital and expected yields.

title: wfCashERC4626
bug_full: The wfCash ERC4626 vault incorrectly credits prime cash when the underlying asset is a fee‑on‑transfer token, yet it still mints wfCash shares on a 1:1 basis with the amount the user intended to deposit. The root cause is that the vault records the actual amount received after the transfer fee (using a balance‑before/after check) but calculates the number of shares to mint from the pre‑fee deposit amount, assuming a perfect 1:1 conversion. Because the vault’s accounting logic does not subtract the transfer fee from the share issuance, it ends up issuing more wfCash tokens than the prime cash it actually holds. An attacker or any user can exploit this mismatch simply by depositing a fee‑on‑transfer token such as USDT with a known transfer tax. The vault will mint the full requested amount of wfCash, while the underlying prime cash balance grows only by the net amount after the fee. When the depositor later redeems their wfCash at maturity, the vault lacks sufficient prime cash to satisfy all share redemptions; the last redeemers receive less than expected, potentially zero, and the overall vault becomes insolvent. This condition manifests whenever the vault processes deposits of fee‑on‑transfer tokens and does not adjust its minting formulas, which is typical during normal operation and is not limited to edge cases. All participants who hold wfCash – individual users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the shortfall directly reduces the redeemable value of their shares. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the minting path and token handling code, where the auditor noticed that the balance update uses the actual transferred amount but the share minting uses the requested amount, creating a hidden accounting gap. The problem can be hard to notice because the vault still records a successful deposit event and the fee is often small relative to a single deposit, so the deficit only becomes apparent after many deposits accumulate or when a large redemption is attempted. To remediate the bug, the vault should detect when the underlying token charges a transfer fee (for example by a dedicated flag) and adjust all preview and mint calculations to account for the net amount received, ensuring that the number of wfCash shares minted never exceeds the prime cash actually deposited. In other words, the share issuance must be proportional to the post‑fee balance change, preserving the invariant that each wfCash token is fully backed by prime cash. This correction restores the accounting integrity of the vault and prevents users from experiencing missing refunds, zero balances, or reduced redemption values that violate the expected 1:1 relationship between deposited assets and minted shares.

title: ExternalLending
bug_full: The vulnerability originates in the Treasury rebalancing logic that redeems aTokens from Aave V3. When the protocol needs to withdraw an underlying token it builds a call to Aave's withdraw function with a parameter called withdrawAmount, which is assumed to be the exact amount that will be transferred back to the Treasury. After the low‑level calls are executed the code checks that the change in the Treasury's token balance (underlyingBalanceChange) is greater than or equal to a value called data.expectedUnderlying. This expected value is calculated as the difference between the current amount held and the target amount, without taking into account any transfer fee that may be deducted by fee‑on‑transfer (taxed) tokens. Because fee‑on‑transfer tokens automatically subtract a portion of the transferred amount, the actual balance increase is always smaller than withdrawAmount. Consequently the require statement fails and the whole redemption transaction reverts. The bug manifests only when the underlying asset is a fee‑on‑transfer token, such as tokens that charge a 1‑2 % tax on each transfer. Under normal ERC‑20 tokens the check passes, making the problem easy to miss during routine testing. The impact is severe: any token deposited into Aave V3 that has a transfer fee can never be redeemed, causing the Treasury’s rebalancing process to stall and potentially leading to protocol insolvency because the funds become permanently locked. Users attempting to withdraw or expecting a refund will see their transaction revert or their balance remain unchanged, contrary to the expectation that the protocol will return the full amount. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the expectedUnderlying calculation with the actual token balance change after redemption and observed a systematic shortfall for fee‑on‑transfer assets. The root cause is an accounting mismatch – the contract assumes a 1:1 transfer relationship and does not incorporate the token’s transfer fee into its accounting model. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an “insufficient balance check for fee‑on‑transfer tokens” or “transfer‑fee accounting error”. To remediate the problem the expectedUnderlying value must be adjusted to reflect the net amount that will be received after fees, either by estimating the fee based on the token’s tax rate or by measuring the actual amount transferred and using that as the benchmark for the require check. Implementing such a correction will allow the Treasury to correctly verify that sufficient underlying assets have been received, restoring the ability to rebalance and withdraw fee‑on‑transfer tokens safely.

title: Wfcash deposit might give incorrect amount
description: Wfcash deposit might not give correct amount of wfcash when there is no fcash available on the markets. The preview function, which calculates the amount of share for minting, does not take the edge case, when there is not available fcash on the markets, into account. In this case, amount of shares should be equivalent to the amount of asset (ratio 1:1). However, the code will get amount of share on notionalv2 instead, which is incorrect. Users will get less/ incorrect amount of shares when using this deposit function.
bug_full: The contract contains an accounting flaw in the deposit workflow that can return an incorrect amount of wfcash shares to a user. The preview routine that determines how many shares to mint assumes that there is always some fcash liquidity on the underlying markets. When the market holds zero or insufficient fcash, the routine falls back to a generic notional‑v2 calculation instead of applying the expected 1:1 conversion between the deposited asset and the minted share. Because the edge case is not checked, the contract mints fewer shares than the amount of asset supplied. This can be triggered whenever the fcash reserve on the market is drained, for example after a large withdrawal or a market liquidation. Any user who calls the deposit function under those conditions will see a shortfall: the UI will show that the deposited amount was accepted but the resulting wfcash balance is lower than expected, often appearing as if the transaction gave back nothing or only a fraction of the input. The impact is a loss of value for depositors and a breach of the protocol’s accounting invariants, which rely on a 1:1 relationship when no fcash is available. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit when the reviewer noticed that the preview function did not contain a guard for a zero‑fcash scenario. It is easy to miss because normal test scenarios always have positive fcash balances, so the bug only surfaces in rare edge cases that are not covered by standard unit tests. To remediate, the contract should explicitly detect the situation where available fcash is zero (or below a safe threshold) and enforce a direct 1:1 minting rule, falling back to the notional‑v2 formula only when sufficient liquidity exists. This change restores the intended economic behavior, prevents users from receiving fewer shares than they paid for, and aligns the implementation with the protocol’s financial model.

title: _isExternalLendingUnhealthy() using stale fac-
bug_full: The issue originates from the rebalancing logic of the protocol, specifically the internal function that determines whether external lending for a given currency is unhealthy. The function retrieves a set of pricing factors using a call that returns a stale, not‑yet‑aggregated snapshot of the PrimeCashFactors. This stale data is then fed into the external lending module to compute the target amount of external lending that should be held. Because the factors are outdated, the calculated target amount can be inaccurate, causing the surrounding checkRebalance routine to incorrectly conclude that no rebalance is required. As a result, the rebalancing bot, which relies on checkRebalance to emit a list of currency identifiers that need adjustment, may omit currencies that actually need to be re‑balanced. The bug manifests only when the checkRebalance path is executed, i.e., during periodic rebalancing cycles, and it affects the protocol’s ability to maintain its intended liquidity and risk parameters. From a user perspective the symptom is that no rebalance events are observed even though the protocol’s accounting indicates a deviation from the desired external lending ratio; balances appear unchanged and expected yield adjustments do not occur. The root cause is the use of PrimeCashExchangeRate.getPrimeCashFactors instead of the up‑to‑date view returned by PrimeCashExchangeRate.getPrimeCashRateView, which aggregates the latest factors before they are used for calculations. This logical flaw was identified during a manual audit where the data flow was traced and the mismatch between the function used and the required fresh data was noted. The problem is subtle because the function still returns a boolean and a numeric target, so no explicit error is thrown, making it easy to miss in routine testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of stale‑data or time‑of‑check‑time‑of‑use (TOCTOU) bugs that break accounting assumptions and can lead to protocol drift, reduced yields, or increased exposure to external lending risk. To remediate, the code should be changed to fetch the latest aggregated factors via getPrimeCashRateView before computing the target amount, ensuring that the rebalance decision reflects the current state of the market and that the protocol’s risk management logic operates as intended.

title: recover() using the standard transfer may not
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the recover function of the SecondaryRewarder contract, which attempts to send arbitrary ERC20 tokens back to the contract owner by calling IERC20.transfer. The function assumes that every ERC20 token conforms to the standard interface that returns a boolean value indicating success. However, a class of tokens such as USDT implements a non‑standard transfer that does not return any value. When the contract calls IERC20.transfer on such a token, the Solidity compiler expects a bool return and treats the missing return data as a failure, causing the call to revert automatically. This root cause is the use of a standard transfer call without a safety wrapper that can handle tokens with no return value. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the mere presence of a non‑standard token in the contract’s balance makes the recover function unusable. When the owner invokes recover with a USDT‑like token, the transaction reverts, leaving the tokens permanently locked in the contract. The impact is that the contract owner cannot retrieve stray or excess reward tokens, which may represent significant value, and users may see their expected refunds or reward withdrawals disappear without explanation. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to recover where the token address points to a contract that does not return a bool on transfer, a situation that is common in the ecosystem because many stablecoins follow the USDT pattern. The affected parties include the contract owner, the protocol that relies on being able to clean up leftover tokens, and any token holder expecting to receive a refund or reward. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the recover implementation against known token behaviours. It can be hard to notice because most ERC20 tokens do return a bool, so the code appears correct at first glance, and the revert does not provide a clear error message indicating a missing return value. The appropriate remediation is to replace the direct IERC20.transfer call with a safe transfer utility, such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20.safeTransfer or a custom wrapper that performs a low‑level call and checks the success flag, thereby supporting both standard and non‑standard tokens. In abstract terms, this is a non‑standard ERC20 handling bug where the contract assumes compliance with the ERC20 specification and fails to account for tokens that deviate from the expected return semantics, leading to locked funds and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to accept a recover request but the balance of the token on the contract never changes, and the owner receives no tokens despite the expectation that recover should move them out.

title: Malicious users could block liquidation or per-
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a push‑based reward distribution mechanism implemented in the _claimRewards function of the SecondaryRewarder contract. After calculating the amount of secondary reward tokens owed to an account, the function immediately attempts to transfer those tokens using GenericToken.safeTransferOut while also updating the internal reward debt accounting. Because the transfer is an external call to an arbitrary ERC‑20 token, the contract implicitly trusts that token to behave correctly. Tokens that implement blacklisting, custom hooks, or that simply revert on transfer can cause the safeTransferOut call to fail. When such a revert occurs, the entire call stack – which includes claimRewards, Incentives.claimIncentives, BalancerHandler._finalize and ultimately core protocol actions such as deposit, withdrawal, and liquidation – is unwound. An attacker who controls an account can deliberately place themselves on a token’s blacklist or otherwise trigger a revert during the reward transfer, causing the liquidation of their unhealthy position to abort. This blocks the protocol from seizing collateral, leaves the borrower’s debt outstanding, and can accumulate bad debt that threatens solvency if repeated across many accounts. The issue manifests only when the protocol attempts to push rewards as part of a state‑changing operation; under normal conditions with well‑behaved tokens the function succeeds, making the problem easy to miss during routine testing. From a user perspective the symptoms are a transaction that reverts with no explicit error message when trying to liquidate, withdraw or claim rewards, and an expectation of receiving a reward that is never delivered. The class of bug is a push‑based external‑call failure that couples reward distribution with critical state updates, effectively creating an attack surface where malicious token contracts can disrupt protocol logic. The recommended mitigation is to decouple reward distribution from balance updates by adopting a pull‑based model: users should claim their rewards in a separate transaction after the protocol has safely updated internal accounting, thereby isolating external token transfers from core operations and preventing a single token revert from halting essential functions.

title: Low precision is used when checking spot
description:
Low precision is used when checking spot price deviation, which might lead to potential manipulation or create the potential for an MEV opportunity due to valuation discrepancy. Assume the following:
• The max deviation is set to 1%
• nTokenOracleValue is 1,000,000,000
• nTokenSpotValue is 980,000,001
File: Constants.sol
46:
```solidity
// Basis for percentages
47:
int256 internal constant PERCENTAGE_DECIMALS = 100;
```
File: nTokenCalculations.sol
61:
```solidity
int256 maxValueDeviationPercent = int256(
    uint256(uint8(nToken.parameters[Constants.MAX_MINT_DEVIATION_LIMIT]))
);
// Check deviation limit here
int256 deviationInPercentage = nTokenOracleValue.sub(nTokenSpotValue).abs()
    .mul(Constants.PERCENTAGE_DECIMALS).div(nTokenOracleValue);
require(deviationInPercentage <= maxValueDeviationPercent, "Over Deviation Limit");
```
Based on the above formula:
```solidity
nTokenOracleValue.sub(nTokenSpotValue).abs().mul(Constants.PERCENTAGE_DECIMALS).div(nTokenOracleValue);
```
((nTokenOracleValue - nTokenSpotValue) * Constants.PERCENTAGE_DECIMALS) / nTokenOracleValue
((1,000,000,000 - 980,000,001) * 100) / 1,000,000,000
(19,999,999 * 100) / 1,000,000,000 = 1,999,999,900 / 1,000,000,000 = 1.9999999 = 1
The above shows that the oracle and spot values have deviated by 1.99999%, which is close to 2%. However, due to a rounding error, it is rounded down to 1%, and the TX will not revert. The purpose of the deviation check is to ensure that the spot market value is not manipulated. If the deviation check is not accurate, it might lead to potential manipulation or create the potential for an MEV opportunity due to valuation discrepancy.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision loss in the calculation that checks the deviation between an oracle price and the on‑chain spot price. The contract stores the allowed deviation as a percentage with a constant called PERCENTAGE_DECIMALS set to 100, meaning that the deviation is computed using integer arithmetic and then divided by the oracle value. Because the calculation multiplies the absolute price difference by only 100 before dividing, any fractional part of the percentage is truncated. In the example where the oracle reports 1,000,000,000 and the spot price is 980,000,001, the true deviation is 1.9999999 % (just under 2 %). The integer division rounds this down to 1 %, which is exactly the configured maximum. Consequently the require statement does not revert even though the price deviation exceeds the intended limit. This rounding error can be exploited by an attacker who deliberately creates a spot price that is just above the allowed threshold; the contract will accept the transaction, allowing minting or other actions based on a manipulated price. The impact is that the protocol’s economic safeguards are bypassed, opening the door to market manipulation, over‑issuance of tokens, or MEV extraction where a bot profits from the valuation discrepancy. The bug manifests only when the deviation is between the integer‑rounded limit and the true limit, making it hard to notice because on‑chain logs show a deviation value of 1 % and the transaction succeeds, matching the developer’s expectation of a safe operation. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the percentage calculation and identified the insufficient decimal precision. The issue belongs to the class of rounding or truncation bugs caused by low‑precision integer arithmetic in financial contracts. From a user’s point of view, a transaction that should have been rejected (for example, a mint that exceeds the price deviation guard) proceeds silently, resulting in unexpected token balances or perceived “free” minting. The expected behavior is that the transaction reverts when the deviation exceeds 1 %; the actual behavior is that it does not revert due to the rounding down. The recommended fix is to increase the precision constant, for example by using a factor such as 1e8 instead of 100, so that the percentage calculation retains enough decimal places to correctly detect deviations above the threshold. This change eliminates the truncation, ensuring that any deviation greater than the allowed percentage triggers a revert and restores the intended economic protection.

title: The use of spot data when discounting is sub-
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s reliance on real‑time (spot) market data when calculating the cash amount to return to a user who redeems wrapped fCash (wfCash) before maturity. The discounting logic calls a view function that uses the current interest‑rate curve, which itself is derived from the market’s utilization rate – the ratio of total fCash to total underlying cash. Because utilization is a mutable on‑chain variable, an attacker can temporarily alter it by injecting additional prime cash into the Notional market, for example via a flash loan or a direct deposit. By increasing the denominator of the utilization formula, the attacker drives the utilization down, which moves the interest rate from a higher region (e.g., 4 %) to a lower region (e.g., 1.5 %). The lower rate reduces the discount applied to the fCash, causing the view function to compute a larger present‑value cash amount. When the attacker then redeems his wfCash, the contract transfers this inflated cash amount to him, while the protocol’s cash reserves are correspondingly reduced – a zero‑sum loss for the protocol. This exploit can only be triggered when the wrapper does not have enough fCash to sell on the AMM, causing the fallback path that invokes the spot‑based calculation. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a redemption transaction returns more cash than the protocol’s pricing model would suggest, and the protocol’s overall cash balance shrinks unexpectedly. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the redemption flow and identified the dependence on mutable spot data inside a view function, a pattern that is easy to overlook because the function is read‑only and appears to use legitimate market parameters. The bug belongs to the class of oracle‑manipulation or price‑manipulation vulnerabilities where on‑chain state is used directly for financial calculations without protection against short‑term distortion. To mitigate the risk the contract should replace the spot‑based interest‑rate input with a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) or another lagged oracle that cannot be altered instantly, ensuring that redemption values are based on a stable, historical rate rather than a manipulable instantaneous snapshot.

title: Rounds can not be immediately drawn after
description:
Users can deposit ETH to multiple future rounds. If the future round can be "drawn" immediately when the current round ends this execution will revert because of chainlink contracts reentrancy guard protection hence ending the current round will be impossible and it needs to be cancelled by governance.

When the round is Drawn, VRF is expected to call fulfillRandomWords to determine the winner in the current round and starts the next round.
3bb38b8a5daa3bdc03f7c/contracts-yolo/contracts/YoloV2.sol#L1293

fulFillRandomWords function is triggered by the rawFulfillRandomWords external function in the Yolo contract which is also triggered by the randomness providers call to VRF's fulFillRandomWords function which has a reentrancy check as seen and just before the call to Yolo contract it sets to "true".
https://github.com/smartcontractkit/chainlink/blob/6133df8a2a8b527155a8a822d2924d5ca4bfd122/contracts/src/v0.8/vrf/VRFCoordinatorV2.sol#L526-L546

If the next round is "drawable" then the _startRound will draw the next round immediately and by doing so it will try to call VRF's requestRandomWords function which also has a nonreentrant modifier
https://github.com/smartcontractkit/chainlink/blob/e4bde648582d55806ab7e0f8d4ea05a721ca120d/contracts/src/v0.8/vrf/VRFCoordinatorV2.sol#L349-L355

since the reentrancy lock was set to "true" in first call, the second calling requesting randomness will revert. Current "drawn" round will not be completed and there will be no winner because of the chainlink call will revert every time the VRF calls the yolo contract.

Already "drawn" round will not be concluded and there will be no winner. VRF's keepers will see their tx is reverted
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reentrancy‑guard conflict that occurs when the YoloV2 contract attempts to start a new lottery round immediately after the current round has been drawn. When the current round is drawn, the Chainlink VRFCoordinator calls the contract’s fulfillRandomWords function, which sets an internal non‑reentrant lock to true before invoking the Yolo contract. Inside the same transaction the Yolo contract’s _startRound logic checks whether the next round is already drawable; if it is, the function calls VRFCoordinator.requestRandomWords to obtain randomness for the new round. Because the non‑reentrant lock is still active from the first VRF callback, the second requestRandomWords call triggers the modifier in the VRFCoordinator and reverts the whole transaction. As a result the current round never reaches a final state, no winner is selected, and the round remains stuck until governance manually cancels it. Users who deposited ETH for that round see their funds locked and receive no payout, effectively experiencing a “funds disappear” or “no winner” symptom. The issue is triggered only when a future round is already eligible to be drawn at the moment the previous round finishes, a condition that can arise when participants deposit for multiple upcoming rounds. It was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s drawWinner and _startRound flow, where the interaction with Chainlink’s reentrancy guard was examined. The problem is subtle because the revert happens deep inside the VRFCoordinator and only under the specific timing condition, making it easy to miss in normal testing. To remediate, the contract should decouple the drawing of a round from the immediate start of the next round. A simple mitigation is to add a guard that prevents _startRound from being called inside the same drawWinner execution, or to require a separate external call to initiate the next round after the first transaction has completed, thereby ensuring the Chainlink non‑reentrant lock is cleared before a new randomness request is made. This aligns the contract’s business logic with the expectation that a round is fully resolved before a new round begins, restoring correct accounting of deposits and payouts.

title: The number of deposits in a round can be larger
bug_full: The vulnerability is an invariant violation that allows the number of deposits recorded for a lottery round to exceed the constant MAXIMUM_NUMBER_OF_DEPOSITS_PER_ROUND. The root cause is the absence of a boundary check in the internal deposit routine that is invoked by both depositETHIntoMultipleRounds() and rolloverETH(). When a round reaches the maximum participant count, the contract normally triggers a winner draw via a VRF callback. However, if the protocol is paused after the round is full but before the VRF response arrives, the automatic draw is suppressed. The VRF callback still executes fulfillRandomWords(), which starts the next round in an OPEN state without performing the draw because the paused flag prevents _drawWinner() from being called. Because the next round is now open while the pause flag is cleared later, users can call the deposit functions again and add extra deposits, pushing the deposit count beyond the intended limit. This can be exploited by an admin (or any entity with pause rights) who pauses the contract at the precise moment between a round reaching its maximum and the VRF response, then unpauses after the next round has been opened but not drawn, allowing malicious participants to flood the round with additional deposits. The impact is that the fairness and accounting assumptions of the lottery are broken: more participants may be eligible for a prize than the round was designed to support, the prize pool may be over‑allocated, and the contract’s internal accounting (e.g., expected payout ratios) no longer matches reality. The condition occurs only when the pause mechanism is used during the narrow window between a full round and the VRF callback, making it hard to notice because under normal operation the draw happens immediately and the deposit limit appears enforced. Users experience the symptom of being able to submit a deposit to a round that the UI reports as already full, and the on‑chain round data shows a deposit array length greater than MAXIMUM_NUMBER_OF_DEPOSITS_PER_ROUND. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that exercised the pause‑unpause flow and verified that the deposit count could be incremented beyond the limit. To remediate, a check should be added in the internal _depositETH() routine that reverts when round.deposits.length is greater than or equal to MAXIMUM_NUMBER_OF_DEPOSITS_PER_ROUND, thereby restoring the invariant and preventing extra deposits regardless of the contract’s paused state.

title: Nobody can cast for any proposal
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the governance contract’s internal voting routine, specifically the castVoteInternal function. This function attempts to determine a voter’s effective voting power by calling the external gOHM token contract twice: once with the proposal’s start block and once with the current block number (block.number). The gOHM getPriorVotes method contains a hard requirement that the supplied blockNumber must be strictly less than the current blockchain height; it reverts with the message "gOHM::getPriorVotes: not yet determined" if the condition is not met. Because castVoteInternal passes block.number directly, the requirement is always violated, causing an immediate revert on every voting attempt. The root cause is a logical misuse of the snapshot function: the contract assumes it can query the current block, while the token contract deliberately disallows that to prevent indeterminate state. Consequently, any call to castVoteInternal – which is the only path through which votes are recorded – fails, making it impossible for any participant to cast a vote on any proposal. From a user’s perspective, transactions that aim to vote revert, leaving the UI with no confirmation, no change in vote tallies, and often an error message referencing gOHM. Users expect their vote to be counted, but instead the transaction fails and their voting power appears to disappear. The impact is severe: the entire on‑chain governance mechanism becomes non‑functional, preventing proposal execution, fund allocation, or protocol upgrades that rely on community voting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the GovernorBravoDelegate contract, where the auditor traced the vote‑counting logic and reproduced the failure with a Foundry test that deliberately called getPriorVotes with block.number, confirming the revert. The bug is subtle because the surrounding code correctly fetches the voter’s prior votes at the proposal start block, giving the impression that voting logic is sound, while the hidden revert condition is only triggered by the second call. To remediate, the contract should query gOHM with a block number that satisfies the token’s requirement, such as block.number‑1, or redesign the vote‑weight calculation to rely solely on the snapshot taken at proposal creation. This adjustment aligns the call with the token’s contract constraints and restores the ability for participants to cast votes, re‑enabling the governance process.

title: High risk checks can be bypassed with extra
bug_full: The vulnerability is a classification bypass in the governance contract where proposals that invoke the kernel's executeAction function are incorrectly identified as low‑risk when the calldata contains any extra unused bytes. The _isHighRiskProposal function determines high‑risk status by checking that the calldata length is exactly 0x44 (or 0x40 for an alternative encoding). Solidity discards bytes that are not required to decode the declared arguments, so adding a single empty byte after the encoded parameters does not affect the execution of executeAction, but it makes the length check fail and the proposal is treated as non‑high‑risk. As a result the contract selects the normal quorum instead of the higher quorum reserved for critical actions. An attacker can craft a proposal with the correct selector and arguments, append a padding byte, and submit it through the governor. The proposal will be accepted once the lower quorum of votes is reached, allowing changes that should have required a stricter voting threshold. This bypass occurs whenever the proposal calldata is built with abi.encodeWithSelector or similar methods and then manually extended, and it affects any user who relies on the governance UI to enforce the high‑risk invariant, including token holders and protocol operators. The issue was discovered during a security audit by extending the calldata in a unit test, which showed that the executeAction call succeeded while the quorum calculation returned the low‑risk value. The bug is subtle because the extra bytes are invisible to the called function and the contract does not revert, making the mis‑classification easy to miss in normal operation. To remediate, the length comparison should be changed from strict equality to a greater‑than‑or‑equal check, or the code should avoid relying on calldata length altogether and decode the arguments directly, ensuring that additional padding does not alter the risk classification. This fix restores the invariant that high‑risk proposals always require the higher quorum, preventing unauthorized low‑quorum approvals and preserving the protocol’s security guarantees.

title: Post-proposal vote quorum/threshold checks
bug_full: The vulnerability is a governance quorum and threshold mis‑calculation that stems from storing the required vote counts at the moment a proposal is created, using the total gOHM supply at that time, instead of recomputing them against the current supply for each vote check. Because gOHM is an elastic token whose supply can increase or decrease dramatically through minting or burning, the static values become stale whenever the supply changes during the mandatory voting delay. An attacker or a severe bug that causes a rapid contraction of the token supply can therefore reduce the actual quorum needed to a value that is either unreachable for honest voters or, in extreme cases, zero, allowing any holder with a trivial amount of tokens to pass proposals. This situation can be exploited to freeze the entire governance process: proposals that originally met the stored quorum will fail to reach the outdated threshold after the supply drops, preventing execution and leaving the system unable to pass any future proposals. Conversely, when the supply falls below certain hard‑coded limits, the quorum calculation yields zero, meaning a malicious actor can submit and execute a proposal with virtually no support, potentially draining the treasury. The issue manifests when a proposal is created under a healthy supply, the voting period elapses, and the supply has since changed; users see their votes counted but the contract reports insufficient quorum, or they observe proposals being executed with no apparent backing. It affects all token holders, governance participants, and the protocol itself because the core decision‑making mechanism becomes either inoperable or trivially manipulable. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the GovernorBravoDelegate contract’s vote outcome logic and noticed that the quorum and threshold values are captured once at proposal creation rather than being derived from the live totalSupply() call. The problem is subtle because under normal, stable‑supply conditions the stored and current values match, so routine testing does not reveal the discrepancy. To remediate, the contract should calculate quorum and proposal thresholds dynamically at each vote evaluation using the current totalSupply(), or better, express requirements as a percentage of the total supply, following the pattern used in OpenZeppelin’s Governor implementation, thereby ensuring that voting power reflects the real token distribution at any point in time.

title: High-risk actions aren't all covered by the ex-
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the governance contract’s risk classification mechanism, which fails to treat several critical actions as high‑risk operations. Specifically, actions that modify the mapping of high‑risk modules (such as calls to _setModuleRiskLevel) and the MigrateKernel function, which can replace the core execution kernel, are not flagged by the _isHighRiskProposal check. The root cause is that the high‑risk detection logic only inspects a limited set of action identifiers – upgrading a module (action == 1) and installing or deactivating a policy (action == 2 or 3) – and then looks up keycodes in a static mapping. It does not consider state‑changing functions that alter the mapping itself or perform a kernel migration, so these operations are mistakenly classified as low‑risk. An attacker can exploit this oversight by submitting a governance proposal that either removes a previously high‑risk module from the high‑risk list or migrates the kernel to a malicious implementation. Because the proposal is not recognized as high‑risk, it can pass with the standard, lower quorum threshold. Once executed, the protocol may become bricked – the new kernel could disable essential functionality – or the security posture may be weakened as the required quorum for future high‑risk actions is effectively lowered. The impact includes loss of protocol integrity, potential inaccessibility of user funds, erosion of trust among token holders, and the ability for a malicious actor to seize control of governance decisions with minimal community support. This condition occurs whenever a proposal invokes functions that modify the risk mapping or perform kernel migration, under the assumption that the governance contract’s high‑risk guard is comprehensive. All participants who rely on the governance process – token holders, developers, and end‑users – are affected because the expected safety barrier is absent. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the GovernorBravoDelegate contract, where the auditor noted that the high‑risk invariant (high‑risk actions must be behind a higher quorum) was violated by missing entries in the detection routine. The bug is subtle because the contract appears to enforce risk checks, yet the omission of certain actions is not obvious without inspecting the full set of state‑changing functions. To remediate, the governance contract should be updated so that any function capable of altering the high‑risk module list or performing a kernel migration is explicitly marked as high‑risk. This can be achieved by extending the _isHighRiskProposal logic to include calls to _setModuleRiskLevel and MigrateKernel, or by introducing a separate access‑control layer that enforces a higher quorum for any modification of the risk mapping. Ensuring that all critical governance actions are subject to the appropriate quorum restores the intended security guarantees and prevents protocol bricking or inadvertent lowering of security thresholds.

title: Validator cannot set new address if more than
description:
If a validator has more than 300 accumulated unstakes associated with it, then it cannot set a new address for itself. The only way to decrease the length of the Unstaking array is through the setValidatorAddress() function, but will revert if it's array is longer than 300 entries. A malicious delegator could stake 1,000 tokens, and then unstake 301 times with small amounts to fill up the unstaking array, and there is no way to remove those entries from the array. Every time _unstake() is called, it pushes another entry to it's array for that validator.

A malicious validator could also set it's new address to another validator, forcing a merge of information to the victim validator. The malicious validator can do this even when it's disabled with 0 tokens. So it could get to 300 length, and then send all those unstakes into another victim validators unstaking array. This is the same to other validators, effectively creating a forceful merging of them.

The README.md suggests there is a mechanism to counteract this: "In case if there are more than 300 unstakings, there is an option to transfer the address without unstakings." But there appears to be no function in scope that can transfer the address of the validator without unstakings, or any other function that can reduce the unstakings array at all.

See Summary
Validator can be permanently stuck with same address if there are too many entries in it's Unstaking array.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the mechanism that allows a validator to change its registered address in a staking protocol. The contract stores pending unstake requests in an array attached to each validator. When a validator attempts to call setValidatorAddress to replace its address, the function first checks the length of the unstaking array and reverts if the array contains more than three hundred entries. Because every call to the internal _unstake function appends a new entry to this array and there is no separate function that can prune or batch‑process those entries, the array can grow indefinitely. A malicious delegator can repeatedly request tiny unstake amounts – for example, 1,000 tokens split into 301 separate unstake calls – thereby inflating the array beyond the 300‑entry threshold. Once the limit is exceeded, the validator is unable to execute setValidatorAddress, effectively locking the validator to its current address forever. In addition, a validator (or an attacker controlling a validator) can set its address to that of another validator, causing the two unstaking arrays to merge. This can be done even when the attacker’s validator holds zero tokens, allowing the attacker to force a victim’s unstaking array to swell and become unchangeable. From a user perspective the symptom is that a validator’s address change transaction fails with a revert, the UI may display an error such as “cannot change address – too many pending unstakes”, and any funds associated with that validator remain inaccessible or are unintentionally merged with another validator’s state. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for the affected validator, loss of control over validator identity, and potential misallocation of pending refunds, which violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each validator can freely manage its address and that pending unstakes are eventually processed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer compared the README claim that an address could be transferred even with many unstakings against the actual contract code, which lacked any such function. The problem is subtle because the 300‑entry limit is relatively high and the array growth is not visible in typical UI flows, making it easy to overlook until an attacker deliberately inflates the array. To remediate, the contract should either allow address changes without requiring the unstaking array to be empty, provide a safe batch‑processing or pruning method for pending unstakes, enforce a stricter limit on array growth, or outright forbid changing a validator’s address to that of another validator. Implementing a clear path to clear or migrate pending unstake entries would restore the intended flexibility and prevent validators from being permanently stuck.

title: OperationalStaking may not possess enough
bug_full: The OperationalStaking contract contains a rounding error bug in the two internal conversion functions that translate between token amounts and internal share units. Both _tokensToShares and _sharesToTokens perform integer division that always rounds down, effectively truncating fractional values. When a user stakes tokens, the contract calculates the number of shares by multiplying the token amount by a fixed divider and dividing by the current rate, discarding any remainder. Conversely, when the user unstakes, the contract multiplies the share balance by the rate and divides by the same divider, again discarding any remainder. This double‑flooring can leave a tiny “dust” amount of shares on the user’s balance after a full withdrawal because the rounding loss is not recoverable through the normal redemption path. The contract enforces a minimum redeemable amount via REWARD_REDEEM_THRESHOLD, so the dust is initially blocked from being withdrawn. However, if the staking multiplier (rate) later increases, the value of those leftover shares rises above the threshold, making the dust withdrawable. At that point the user can claim more tokens than the sum of their original stake and any legitimate rewards. Because the protocol’s accounting assumes that the total token balance will cover all withdrawals, the extra tokens extracted from the dust cause the contract’s final CQT transfer to revert due to insufficient balance. From a user’s perspective the contract may appear to reject a withdrawal with an “insufficient balance” error, or it may unexpectedly return a larger amount than expected, breaking the expectation that the contract will always return exactly the deposited amount plus earned rewards. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a Foundry proof‑of‑concept that showed repeated reverts unless the attacker deliberately reduced the withdrawal amount. The bug is subtle because the rounding loss is typically a few wei, which is easily dismissed as normal dust, and the threshold check masks the problem until the rate changes. The vulnerability belongs to the class of rounding‑off‑by‑floor arithmetic errors that violate accounting invariants in financial smart contracts. To remediate the issue the conversion functions should be changed to round up (or round to nearest) against the user, ensuring that the token‑to‑share and share‑to‑token calculations never give the user less than the mathematically exact value, and that any residual dust is either eliminated or safely handled without allowing excess withdrawals.

title: New staking between reward epochs will di-rectly affect the rewards distribution
description: In the Covalent Network, validators perform work to earn rewards, which is distributed through OperationalStaking. The staking manager is expected to regularly invoke rewardValidators() to distribute staking rewards accordingly to the validator, and its delegators. However, the function takes into account all existing stakes, including new ones. This makes newer stakes being counted equally to existing stakes, despite newer stakes haven't existed for a working epoch yet. An attacker can also then front-run rewardValidators() to steal a share of the rewards. The attacker gains a share of the reward, despite not having fully staked for the corresponding epoch. The function rewardValidators() is callable only by the staking manager to distribute rewards to validators. The rewards is then immediately distributed to the validator, and all their delegators, proportional to the amount staked. However, any new staking in-between reward epochs still counts as staking. They receive the full reward amount for the epoch, despite not having staked for the full epoch. An attacker can abuse this by front-run the staking manager's distribution with a stake transaction. The attacker stakes a certain amount right before the staking manager distributes rewards, then the attacker is already considered to have a share of the reward, despite not having staked during the epoch they were entitled to. This also applies to re-stakings, i.e. unstaked tokens that are re-staked into the same validator: Any stake recovers made through recoverUnstaking() is considered a new stake. Therefore an attacker can use the same funds to repeatedly perform the attack. Unfair distribution of rewards. New stakers get full rewards for epochs they didn't fully stake into.
poc:
0. Alice is a validator. She has two delegators:
• Alicia delegating 5000 CQT.
• Alisson delegating 15000 CQT.
• Alice herself stakes 35000 CQT, for a total of 50000.
1. The staking manager distributes 1000 CQT to Alice. This is then distributed proportionally across Alice and her delegators.
2. Bob notices the staking manager, and front-runs with a 50000 CQT stake into Alice.
• Alice now has a total stake of 100000, with half of it belonging to Bob.
• Bob's staking tx goes through before the staking manager's tx.
3. Bob now owns half of Alice's shares. He is distributed half of the rewards, despite having staked into Alice for only one second.
4. Bob can repeat this attack for as often as they wish to, by unstaking then restaking through recoverUnstaking().
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the staking contract calculates rewards for validators and their delegators. The reward distribution function takes the current total amount of stake at the moment it is called and treats every token that is currently staked as having been present for the whole reward epoch. Because the contract does not record a snapshot of the stake at the beginning of the epoch, any stake that is added after the epoch has started is counted equally to older stakes. This design flaw allows an attacker to front‑run the manager’s rewardValidators call: the attacker deposits a large amount of tokens just before the manager distributes rewards, the contract then includes the attacker’s fresh stake in the reward calculation, and the attacker receives a proportional share of the epoch’s reward even though the tokens were staked for only a few seconds. The same effect can be achieved repeatedly by unstaking and restaking through the recoverUnstaking path, because each restake is treated as a new stake. The impact is an unfair distribution of rewards: new stakers obtain the full reward for an epoch they did not actually participate in, while legitimate delegators receive a smaller share of the same reward pool. This can erode trust in the protocol’s economics, reduce delegator incentives, and allow malicious actors to siphon rewards over many epochs. The issue occurs every time the staking manager invokes rewardValidators, which is expected to happen at the end of each reward epoch.
