All validators, their delegators, and any token holder who relies on the staking rewards are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the reward calculation logic, where the lack of an epoch‑based checkpoint became apparent. It is difficult to notice because the total reward amount appears correct on‑chain and the UI shows a normal distribution, while the underlying share accounting is inflated for the attacker. The bug belongs to the class of time‑weighted accounting errors, specifically missing epoch snapshots that enable front‑running of reward distribution. From a user perspective, a new delegator may see a full reward for their first epoch, while existing delegators see their expected payout shrink or even become zero in extreme cases, contradicting the expectation that rewards are earned proportionally to the time the stake was held. To remediate the issue, the contract should adopt a checkpoint‑based share model: newly deposited tokens should be placed in a pending‑stake bucket and only converted into active shares after the current epoch’s rewards have been settled, while shares from unstaked tokens should be burned immediately. This ensures that only stakes that were present for the entire epoch participate in its reward calculation, eliminating the front‑running advantage and restoring fair reward distribution.

title: Frontrunning validator freeze to withdraw tokens
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing validation check that allows a validator to withdraw unstaked tokens even after the protocol has frozen the validator for malicious behavior. Covalent’s operational staking contract includes a freeze flag on each validator that is intended to block all interactions once the validator is deemed malicious. Most contract functions enforce this rule with a require(!v.frozen, "Validator is frozen") guard, but the two functions responsible for moving unstaked tokens out of the contract – transferUnstakedOut() and recoverUnstaking() – do not contain this guard. Because the contract also enforces a timelock that only permits withdrawals after a cooldown period, the protocol assumes that once a validator is frozen the stake will remain locked forever. In practice, a malicious validator can monitor the mempool, detect the pending freeze transaction, and submit an unstake transaction with a higher gas price so that it is mined before the freeze. The unstake succeeds, recording an unstaking entry. When the freeze transaction is later mined, the validator becomes frozen, but the previously recorded unstake is not reverted. After the cooldown expires, the validator can call transferUnstakedOut() or recoverUnstaking() and withdraw the full amount of tokens, effectively escaping the intended slashing mechanism. This attack results in the validator retaining both the illicit fees earned from the misbehavior and the original stake, causing a loss of funds for the protocol and breaking the economic guarantees of the staking system. The issue manifests only when a freeze transaction is pending and the validator is able to front‑run it; under normal conditions where no freeze is being issued, the missing check does not cause a problem, which makes it easy to overlook during testing. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the staking contract when the auditor noticed that the frozen flag was not referenced in the token‑withdrawal paths. To remediate, the contract should add a require(!v.frozen) guard to transferUnstakedOut() and recoverUnstaking(). If the designers wish to allow honest unstaking while still preventing withdrawals after a freeze, they can store the block number or timestamp of each unstake and modify the freeze logic to only affect unstaking entries created after the freeze block, thereby preserving previously initiated withdrawals. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a validator who has been reported as malicious can still pull out their stake after the cooldown, leading to unexpected zero balances in the protocol’s reserve and a mismatch between expected slashing outcomes and actual token flows.

title: No cooldown in recoverUnstaking(), opens up several possible attack vectors
description:
The function recoverUnstaking() allows a user to recover any of their unstaking to the same validator. However, the function has no cooldown, i.e. a user can unstake and restake to the same validator at any time they prefer. We describe several attack vectors that may arise from this issue. When a user unstakes, they must wait for a cooldown of 28 days (180 days if validator) before being able to withdraw. The user also has the choice to revert the action, and re-stake said amount back to the same validator by calling recoverUnstaking(). However, the function recoverUnstaking() has no cooldowns. In other words, a user can re-stake as many times as they like, at any time they prefer, without being subject to the unstaking cooldown. This opens up several possible attack vectors by abusing the lack of cooldown of this functionality. Next section we describe some of the possible attack vectors. Denying delegators for any validators An attacker with a large enough capital can do the following to deny a target validator from getting delegated stakings:
• Max stake to the target validator, up to staked * maxCapMultiplier, but immediately unstake.
• Whenever someone stakes, front-run them with a recoverUnstaking(), re-staking their max stake.
• The user's stake tx fails, as the attacker has taken up the maximum possible stake.
• The attacker then unstakes, able to repeat the attack when necessary. The impact is that a validator can be denied from getting delegators. Stealing of rewards This attack vector builds upon a separate issue we have submitted, about unfair distribution of rewards for mid-epoch stakers. An attacker can perform the following, while greatly de-risking themselves from staking.
• Stake an amount they want, but unstake.
• Listen to the staking manager's rewardValidators() with the intent of front-running.
• If the attacker choose to, front-run rewardValidators() calls, unfairly taking a share of the rewards.
• Unstake. The attacker benefits from the following:
• While unstaking, their 28-day cooldown still counts. They greatly de-risk themselves by being able to choose whether or not to steal rewards (and reset countdown), or to take profits.
• Unstakings from frozen validators can still be withdrawn once the cooldown has passed. By keeping themselves in an unstaking state, they bypass the freezing mechanism.
• They eliminate the risk from other standard staking mechanism, should they recoverUnstaking() can be abused, opens up several possible attack vectors, with varying impacts (shown above).
bug_full: The vulnerability is the absence of any cooldown enforcement in the recoverUnstaking function of the staking contract. When a delegator initiates an unstake, the protocol normally imposes a 28‑day (or 180‑day for validator) waiting period before the funds can be withdrawn. The recoverUnstaking function is intended to allow the delegator to cancel the unstake and move the amount back to the same validator, but because the function does not check or enforce the same waiting period, a user can immediately restake the same tokens any number of times. This design flaw originates from missing state checks that tie the cooldown timer to the unstake operation; the contract only records the cooldown for withdrawals, not for re‑staking. An attacker can exploit the missing cooldown by repeatedly unstaking a large amount, then calling recoverUnstaking to instantly restake, effectively monopolising the validator’s stake capacity. By front‑running legitimate delegators, the attacker can fill the validator up to its maximum cap, causing subsequent stake transactions from honest users to revert with insufficient capacity. The attacker can also keep the tokens in an unstaking state while still being able to re‑stake before the cooldown expires, allowing them to front‑run the reward distribution call and capture a disproportionate share of epoch rewards. The impact is twofold: denial of service for honest delegators who are unable to delegate to a targeted validator, and unfair reward extraction that reduces earnings for all other participants. The condition occurs whenever a user calls recoverUnstaking after an unstake, regardless of how much time has passed. Both delegators and the protocol’s economic model are affected because the expected accounting rule—that unstaked tokens are locked for a fixed period—is violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the lifecycle of unstaking and noticed that the cooldown variable was never consulted in the re‑stake path. Because the function executes successfully and does not emit obvious error messages, the problem can remain hidden until abnormal staking failures or missing rewards are observed. The appropriate mitigation is to enforce the same cooldown interval for recoverUnstaking as for withdrawals, or to introduce a short mandatory delay (e.g., a few days) before the amount can be restaked. This brings the bug into the class of missing time‑lock enforcement or re‑entrancy‑like state‑inconsistency vulnerabilities, where a contract allows state transitions that should be temporally restricted. From a user’s point of view the symptoms are stake transactions that unexpectedly fail, validators that appear full despite low overall delegation, and a sudden drop in expected reward payouts. The protocol’s business logic that assumes funds are locked during the cooldown is broken, leading to potential loss of trust and economic imbalance.

title: validatorMaxStake can be bypassed by using setValidatorAddress
poc:
0. Bob the validator has a self-stake equal to validatorMaxStake.
1. Bob has another address, B2, with some stake delegated to Bob's validator.
2. Bob migrates to B2.
3. Bob's stake is stacked on top of B2. B2 becomes the new validator address, but their stake has exceeded validatorMaxStake.
4. B2 can then repeated this procedure to addresses B3, B4, ..., despite B2 already holding more than the max allowed amount. Bob now holds more stake than he should be able to, allowing him to earn an unfair amount of rewards compared to other validators.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the validator address migration function, which allows a validator to move its stake from one address to another without enforcing the protocol‑wide maximum stake limit (validatorMaxStake). The root cause is that the function simply adds the shares and staked amount of the old address to the new address’s record and then deletes the old entry, without checking whether the resulting total stake for the new address exceeds the allowed maximum. An attacker can exploit this by first staking up to the maximum allowed amount, then creating or using another address that already holds some delegated stake, and finally calling the migration function to merge the two balances. Because the combined stake is not validated, the new validator address can hold more than validatorMaxStake, breaking a critical invariant that caps validator power and reward eligibility. This condition can be repeated across multiple addresses, allowing a single validator to accumulate arbitrarily large stake and consequently earn a disproportionate share of validator rewards and increase the maximum delegator capacity through the maxCapMultiplier formula. The issue manifests when a validator initiates a migration; from the user’s perspective the UI may show a validator’s total stake suddenly jumping above the documented limit, or rewards increasing without any additional delegation. The affected parties include validators who can unfairly boost their earnings, delegators who may receive reduced rewards, and the protocol itself, whose security and economic assumptions rely on the stake cap. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s migration logic, where the absence of a max‑stake check was noted. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to perform a legitimate address update and the stake increase may be attributed to normal delegation activity. To remediate, the migration routine should first compute the prospective total stake for the target address and reject the transaction if it would exceed validatorMaxStake, thereby preserving the intended invariant.

title: OperationalStaking::_unstake Delegators can reduce risk by unstaking instead of claiming rewards
description:
When rewards are distributed, they are distributed evenly across all of the shares held for a validator. However participants collecting rewards burn shares, and thus receive less rewards in subsequent rounds, compared to participants which have left rewards in the contract. This means that delegators can unstake instead of redeeming rewards, which will progressively replace the initial staked amount with claimable rewards. We can see in the function redeemRewards that the equivalent amount of shares is burned when rewards are withdrawn. This means that by redeeming rewards a validator will receive less of the future rewards than the stake he invested. Conversely, this means that delegators can progressively derisk their staking position by burning small quantity of shares from their stake (by calling unstake) instead of claiming rewards. When enough rewards accumulated, they have the equivalent of their initial amount in the contract, but it is less risky, since as rewards, they are not subject to the unstaking cooldown of 28 days and can be transferred out immediately. Scenario Alice is a validator staking 35000 CQT. Bob delegates 35000 CQT to Alice. Shares distribution:
• Alice owns 35000e18 shares
• Bob owns 35000e18 shares
Owner distributes rewards to the tune of 70000 CQT (an exaggerated amount to make the point here) Alice withdraws all her rewards, and burning half of her shares Bob unstakes all of his position, but does not redeem his rewards Shares distribution:
• Alice owns 17500e18 shares
• Bob owns 17500e18 shares
Alice and Bob still have the same number of shares, and have the same claim to future rewards. However Bob's position has less risk compared to a normal delegator, since he can get all of his funds out anytime by calling redeemRewards, and does not have to wait a cooldown period.
bug_full: During reward distribution the contract assigns reward amounts proportionally to each share owned by a validator or delegator. The redeemRewards function implements reward withdrawal by burning an amount of shares equal to the reward value, effectively reducing the caller’s share balance. Because future rewards are calculated on the remaining shares, a participant who claims rewards receives a smaller portion of subsequent distributions. Conversely, a delegator can achieve the same economic effect by calling unstake, which also burns shares but does not trigger the 28‑day cooldown that applies to normal unstaking. By repeatedly unstaking small amounts instead of redeeming rewards, a delegator can gradually replace the original stake with reward‑derived balance that can be withdrawn instantly via redeemRewards, thereby derisking the position. The vulnerability is a logical accounting flaw: burning shares on reward redemption changes the staking economics and creates an incentive to bypass the intended cooldown mechanism. It can be exploited by any delegator who wishes to convert accrued rewards into immediately withdrawable funds without waiting for the unstaking period, while preserving the same share count as other participants. The impact includes distortion of reward distribution, potential loss of future earnings for validators, and erosion of the protocol’s security assumptions that staked tokens remain locked for a defined period. The issue manifests whenever rewards have been accrued and a user calls redeemRewards or unstake; the UI may still display the same number of shares, making the reduction invisible to users. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the OperationalStaking contract when the reward‑redeeming logic was examined. It is hard to notice because burning shares is a subtle state change that does not produce an obvious error message or balance discrepancy. The recommended mitigation is to stop burning shares on reward redemption and instead record claimed rewards in a separate mapping, preserving the original share balance while still allowing users to withdraw their rewards. This fixes the accounting inconsistency and restores the intended risk model where rewards remain subject to the unstaking cooldown.

title: BlockSpecimenProofChain::submitBlockSpecimenProof can be abused to reduce session time
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way a block specimen production session is initialized in the submitBlockSpecimenProof function. The contract treats the first call that submits a specimen for a particular block height as the moment the session starts, regardless of whether that block actually exists on the chain. Because the only guard is a check that the requested block height is not more than a fixed number of blocks (allowedThreshold, default 100) ahead of the current block, a malicious producer can submit a proof for a future block that is still within this threshold. When this happens the session deadline is calculated from the current block number plus the fixed session duration (approximately 240 blocks). Consequently the session for that future block begins early, and the effective time window that honest producers have to submit their own specimens is cut roughly in half. The root cause is the coupling of session start time to the first submission rather than to the actual creation of the target block, combined with an allowedThreshold that is smaller than the intended session length. An attacker can exploit this by sending a deliberately malformed or dummy specimen for a block that will be mined later, causing the contract to record the session as started immediately. Honest producers, who can only submit after the block is mined, will then find the session deadline already close or passed, resulting in rejected submissions, missed rewards, or inability to participate. The impact is a denial‑of‑service‑like effect on legitimate specimen producers and a potential reduction in the security guarantees of the protocol because fewer specimens may be collected for a given block. This condition occurs whenever the contract is deployed with the default allowedThreshold and the session duration is longer than that threshold, which is the case in the current deployment. All participants who rely on the specimen submission process—block producers, delegators, and any downstream contracts that expect a full set of specimens—are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logical flow of session creation and identified that the session start logic does not verify that the block height is already finalized. The bug is subtle because the require statement appears to protect against far‑future submissions, yet it does not prevent the session from being opened prematurely, making the problem easy to overlook during testing. To remediate the issue the session should be anchored to the estimated timestamp of the target block rather than the current block number, or the contract should enforce that a session can only be started after the block has been mined. In practice this means calculating the session deadline using the expected time of the target block and the configured session length, ensuring that honest producers always receive the full intended window to submit their specimens.

title: In LeverageModule.executeOpen/executeAdjust, checkSkewMax is called before updateGlobalPositionData
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic‑ordering flaw in the LeverageModule contract where the function that enforces the maximum allowed long skew (checkSkewMax) is executed before the global position data is updated (updateGlobalPositionData). The check uses the variable stableCollateralTotal to compute the long skew fraction, but stableCollateralTotal is modified by updateGlobalPositionData based on the profit‑loss of the system. When profitLossTotal is positive, stableCollateralTotal decreases; when it is negative, it increases. Because the skew check is performed with the stale value of stableCollateralTotal, the calculated longSkewFraction can be artificially low, allowing a new or adjusted long position to be accepted even though the true post‑update skew would exceed the protocol‑defined limit. An attacker can exploit this by opening a large long position (or increasing an existing one) when the system is already close to the skew ceiling. The check passes, the global data is then updated, the collateral pool shrinks, and the actual skew surpasses the allowed threshold. This creates an unsafe exposure where the protocol may become overly biased toward longs, potentially leading to forced liquidations, inability to honor withdrawals, or loss of funds for other participants. The issue manifests during executeOpen and executeAdjust calls that add positive additionalSizeDelta. It affects all users of the protocol, especially those on the short side or holding collateral that could be depleted by unexpected liquidations. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that checkSkewMax was called before the state‑changing updateGlobalPositionData, contradicting the intended risk model. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert and the on‑chain event logs show that the skew limit was checked, giving a false sense of safety; only after the state change does the invariant become violated, which may not be obvious without inspecting internal variables. The appropriate remediation is to reorder the calls so that updateGlobalPositionData runs first, then invoke checkSkewMax with the additional skew already accounted for (for example by passing zero as the additionalSkew argument). This ensures the skew calculation uses the latest stableCollateralTotal and that the protocol’s risk parameters are correctly enforced. The bug belongs to the class of invariant‑verification errors caused by stale data usage, often described as a “check‑then‑act with outdated state” or “improper sequencing of state updates”. From a user perspective the symptoms can include opening a position that later appears to have no value, unexpected liquidation of long positions, or a sudden inability to open further longs despite the protocol’s advertised limits, effectively causing funds to disappear or balances to become zero when the skew limit is silently breached.

title: Oracle will not failover as expected during liquidation
bug_full: The vulnerability is a failure of the oracle fallback mechanism that prevents liquidations from being executed when the primary Pyth price feed is unavailable. The contract offers two liquidation entry points: one that updates the Pyth price and another that skips the price update, intending to rely on the last known Pyth price together with a Chainlink fallback. However, the internal _getPrice function always compares the on‑chain Pyth price with the off‑chain Chainlink price and reverts if their percentage difference exceeds a configured maxDiffPercent. When Pyth is down, its on‑chain price becomes stale while the Chainlink price continues to move, causing the deviation to grow until the check triggers a FlatcoinErrors.PriceMismatch revert. Because the second liquidate function still calls _getPrice, the deviation check is still performed, so the liquidation transaction fails even though the caller deliberately avoided a Pyth update. This situation can be exploited by any actor who can cause the Pyth feed to stop updating (for example by disabling the Pyth network or simply waiting for it to become stale). Once the price mismatch threshold is crossed, every liquidation attempt reverts, leaving underwater positions un‑liquidated and allowing bad debt to accumulate. The impact is a loss of the protocol’s core risk‑mitigation mechanism, which threatens overall solvency because the protocol can no longer prune risky positions. The issue manifests only when the Pyth feed is stale beyond the allowed deviation, a condition that may persist for an extended period, making it hard to notice during normal operation because the fallback path appears to work in tests where Pyth is healthy. The bug belongs to the class of oracle consistency checks that unintentionally block critical protocol actions when one data source becomes stale. From a user’s perspective, a liquidator expects the transaction to succeed and to receive the liquidation reward, but instead the transaction reverts with a price‑mismatch error, resulting in no funds transferred and the position remaining open. The protocol’s assumption that liquidation can proceed without a fresh Pyth price is violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the LiquidationModule and OracleModule, where the interaction between the two liquidate functions and the price‑validation logic was examined. To remediate, the price‑validation logic should be adjusted to bypass the deviation check when the Pyth source is known to be down, or to allow the Chainlink price to be used unconditionally after a certain staleness period, ensuring that the fallback liquidation path truly works without requiring a fresh Pyth price.

title: Large amounts of points can be minted multiple times
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic minting flaw that allows a user to create large amounts of protocol points without paying any cost. The contract mints points unconditionally on every stable‑coin deposit, while the withdraw fee that normally offsets point creation is skipped when the total supply of the stable token is zero. Because the fee exemption is tied to the condition totalSupply() > 0, a participant who is the sole liquidity provider can deposit rETH, receive a matching amount of UNIT and an equal amount of points, then immediately withdraw the same amount of UNIT and rETH without incurring a withdraw fee. The points remain in the attacker’s account, so each deposit‑withdraw cycle generates free points. This can be repeated as long as the attacker remains the only LP, which in practice may allow thousands of points to be minted within minutes. The root cause is the combination of (1) a check that bypasses the withdraw‑fee logic when totalSupply is zero, and (2) a separate call that mints points based solely on the deposit amount without any later reconciliation. Exploitation requires announcing a deposit, waiting for the minExecutabilityAge, executing the deposit to mint points, announcing a withdraw, waiting again, and executing the withdraw to retrieve the original collateral while keeping the points. The impact is that the attacker can accumulate a large balance of points that are intended to be exchanged for valuable assets, thereby extracting disproportionate value from the protocol and creating unfairness for other users. The issue manifests only when the protocol has no existing stable token supply, i.e., when the first LP is alone, and when the withdraw fee is not charged. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee‑exemption branch and the points‑minting call. The bug is subtle because the fee exemption appears legitimate for an initial system bootstrapping, and the points minting looks like a standard reward mechanism, making it easy to overlook that points are never burned or deducted on withdrawal. To remediate, the protocol should either charge a withdraw fee even when totalSupply is zero, or implement a mechanism that reduces or burns the points when a position is closed, or prevent points from being minted until the system has a non‑zero stable token supply. In user‑facing terms, a user expects that points represent value contributed to the vault, but after withdrawing their collateral they still see their points balance increase, effectively receiving “free” rewards that were never earned.

title: Vault Inflation Attack
description:
Malicious users can perform an inflation attack against the vault to steal the assets of the victim.
A malicious user can perform a donation to execute a classic first depositor/ERC4626 inflation Attack against the FlatCoin vault. The general process of this attack is well-known, and a detailed explanation of this attack can be found in many of the resources such as the following:
• https://blog.openzeppelin.com/a-novel-defense-against-erc4626-inflation-attacks
• https://mixbytes.io/blog/overview-of-the-inflation-attack
In short, to kick-start the attack, the malicious user will often usually mint the smallest possible amount of shares (e.g., 1 wei) and then donate significant assets to the vault to inflate the number of assets per share. Subsequently, it will cause a rounding error when other users deposit.
However, in Flatcoin, there are various safeguards in place to mitigate this attack. Thus, one would need to perform additional steps to workaround/bypass the existing controls.
Let's divide the setup of the attack into two main parts:
1. Malicious user mint 1 mint of share
2. Donate or transfer assets to the vault to inflate the assets per share
Part 1 - Malicious user mint 1 mint of share
Users could attempt to mint 1 wei of share. However, the validation check at Line 79 will revert as the share minted is less than MIN_LIQUIDITY = 10_000. However, this minimum liquidation requirement check can be bypassed.
File: StableModule.sol
```solidity
function executeDeposit(
    address _account,
    uint64 _executableAtTime,
    FlatcoinStructs.AnnouncedStableDeposit calldata _announcedDeposit
) external whenNotPaused onlyAuthorizedModule returns (uint256 _liquidityMinted) {
    uint256 depositAmount = _announcedDeposit.depositAmount;

    uint32 maxAge = _getMaxAge(_executableAtTime);

    _liquidityMinted = (depositAmount * (10 ** decimals())) / stableCollateralPerShare(maxAge);

    if (_liquidityMinted < _announcedDeposit.minAmountOut)
        revert FlatcoinErrors.HighSlippage(_liquidityMinted, _announcedDeposit.minAmountOut);

    _mint(_account, _liquidityMinted);

    vault.updateStableCollateralTotal(int256(depositAmount));

    revert FlatcoinErrors.AmountTooSmall({amount: totalSupply(), minAmount: MIN_LIQUIDITY});
```
First, Bob mints 10000 wei shares via executeDeposit function. Next, Bob withdraws 9999 wei shares via the executeWithdraw. In the end, Bob successfully owned only 1 wei share, which is the prerequisite for this attack.
Part 2 - Donate or transfer assets to the vault to inflate the assets per share
The vault tracks the number of collateral within the state variables. Thus, simply transferring rETH collateral to the vault directly will not work, and the assets per share will remain the same.
To work around this, Bob creates a large number of accounts (with different wallet addresses). He could choose any or both of the following methods to indirectly transfer collateral to the LP pool/vault to inflate the assets per share:
1) Open a large number of leveraged long positions with the intention of incurring large amounts of losses. The long positions' losses are the gains of the LPs, and the collateral per share will increase.
2) Open a large number of leveraged long positions till the max skew of 120%. Thus, this will cause the funding rate to increase, and the long will have to pay the LPs, which will also increase the collateral per share.
Triggering rounding error
The stableCollateralPerShare will be inflated at this point. Following is the formula used to determine the number of shares minted to the depositor.
If the depositAmount by the victim is not sufficiently large enough, the amount of shares minted to the depositor will round down to zero.
```solidity
_collateralPerShare = (stableBalance * (10 ** decimals())) / totalSupply;
_liquidityMinted = (depositAmount * (10 ** decimals())) / _collateralPerShare
```
Finally, the attacker withdraws their share from the pool. Since they are the only ones with any shares, this withdrawal equals the balance of the vault. This means the attacker also withdraws the tokens deposited by the victim earlier.
Malicious users could steal the assets of the victim.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inflation attack against an ERC4626‑style vault that allows a malicious actor to steal assets deposited by honest users. The root cause is a combination of an insufficient minimum‑liquidity guard and a rounding‑error in the share‑minting formula. The contract only checks that the total supply of shares is greater than a constant MIN_LIQUIDITY, but this check can be bypassed by first minting the minimum amount of shares and then withdrawing almost all of them, leaving the attacker with a single wei of share. Because the contract does not enforce that the share balance can never fall below MIN_LIQUIDITY, the attacker can reduce the supply to the smallest possible value. After that, the attacker inflates the vault’s collateral per share by moving a large amount of underlying assets into the vault through indirect mechanisms such as opening many leveraged long positions that generate losses paid to the liquidity providers, or by pushing the funding rate to its maximum skew. These actions increase the internal accounting of assets per share without changing the total supply, so the ratio of assets to shares becomes very large. When an honest user later deposits a modest amount, the contract computes the number of shares to mint by dividing the deposit amount by the inflated collateral‑per‑share value. Because of integer division, the result rounds down to zero, meaning the user receives no shares even though the transaction succeeds. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful deposit but the balance of vault shares remains unchanged, effectively losing the deposited funds. The attacker then withdraws the single remaining share, which now represents the entire inflated vault balance, thereby extracting both the assets they injected and the victim’s deposit. The impact is loss of user funds, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential depletion of the vault’s capital. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the MIN_LIQUIDITY enforcement and the share‑minting arithmetic. It is hard to notice because the deposit transaction does not revert and the rounding to zero shares produces no obvious error flag. To remediate, the contract should guarantee that a minimum number of shares always exists and cannot be reduced, for example by minting an immutable amount of shares to a dead address at deployment, and by rejecting any operation that would bring totalSupply below the threshold. Additionally, the share‑minting calculation should use rounding‑up or enforce a minimum deposit amount relative to the current total supply, and the vault should prevent external manipulation of collateral per share through untracked asset transfers.

title: Long traders unable to withdraw their assets
description:
Whenever the protocol reaches a state where the long trader's profit is larger than LP's stable collateral total, the protocol will be bricked. As a result, the margin deposited and gain of the long traders can no longer be withdrawn and the LPs cannot withdraw their collateral, leading to a loss of assets for the users.
Per Line 97 below, if the collateral balance is less than the tracked balance, the _getCollateralNet invariant check will revert.
File: InvariantChecks.sol
```solidity
/// @dev Returns the difference between actual total collateral balance in the vault vs tracked collateral
/// Tracked collateral should be updated when depositing to stable LP (stableCollateralTotal) or
/// opening leveraged positions (marginDepositedTotal).
/// TODO: Account for margin of error due to rounding.
function _getCollateralNet(IFlatcoinVault vault) private view returns (uint256 netCollateral) {
    uint256 collateralBalance = vault.collateral().balanceOf(address(vault));

    uint256 trackedCollateral = vault.stableCollateralTotal() + vault.getGlobalPositions().marginDepositedTotal;

    if (collateralBalance < trackedCollateral) revert FlatcoinErrors.InvariantViolation("collateralNet");

    return collateralBalance - trackedCollateral;
```
Assume that:
• Bob's long position: Margin = 50 ETH
• Alice's LP: Deposited = 50 ETH
• Collateral Balance = 100 ETH
• Tracked Balance = 100 ETH (Stable Collateral Total = 50 ETH, Margin Deposited Total = 50 ETH)
Assume that Bob's long position gains a profit of 51 ETH.
The following actions will trigger the updateGlobalPositionData function internally:
executeOpen, executeAdjust, executeClose, and liquidation.
When the FlatcoinVault.updateGlobalPositionData function is triggered to update the global position data:
```solidity
profitLossTotal = 51 ETH (gain by long)
newMarginDepositedTotal = marginDepositedTotal + marginDelta + profitLossTotal
newMarginDepositedTotal = 50 ETH + 0 + 51 ETH = 101 ETH
_updateStableCollateralTotal(-51 ETH)
newStableCollateralTotal = stableCollateralTotal + _stableCollateralAdjustment
newStableCollateralTotal = 50 ETH + (-51 ETH) = -1 ETH
stableCollateralTotal = (newStableCollateralTotal > 0) ? newStableCollateralTotal : 0;
stableCollateralTotal = 0
```
In this case, the state becomes as follows:
• Collateral Balance = 100 ETH
• Tracked Balance = 101 ETH (Stable Collateral Total = 0 ETH, Margin Deposited Total = 101 ETH)
Notice that the Collateral Balance and Tracked Balance are no longer in sync. As such, the revert will occur when the _getCollateralNet invariant checks are performed.
Whenever the protocol reaches a state where the long trader's profit is larger than LP's stable collateral total, this issue will occur, and the protocol will be bricked.
The margin deposited and gain of the long traders can no longer be withdrawn from the protocol. The LPs also cannot withdraw their collateral.
The reason is that the _getCollateralNet invariant checks are performed in all functions of the protocol that can be accessed by users (listed below):
• Deposit
• Withdraw
• Open Position
• Adjust Position
• Close Position
• Liquidate
Loss of assets for the users. Since the protocol is bricked due to revert, the long traders are unable to withdraw their deposited margin and gain and the LPs cannot withdraw their collateral.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting invariant violation that occurs when a long trader’s profit exceeds the total stable collateral supplied by liquidity providers (LPs). The contract tracks two separate values: the actual collateral held in the vault and a derived "tracked" collateral amount that is the sum of the LPs’ stable collateral total and the margin deposited by all open positions. When a long position generates a profit larger than the LPs’ stable collateral, the update logic reduces the stable collateral total by the profit amount but caps the result at zero, while the margin‑deposited total is increased by the full profit. This creates a situation where the tracked collateral (stableCollateralTotal + marginDepositedTotal) becomes greater than the real collateral balance held by the vault. The private function _getCollateralNet checks that the actual balance is not less than the tracked amount and reverts with an invariant violation if it is. Because this check is executed in every user‑facing function (deposit, withdraw, open, adjust, close, liquidate), any subsequent interaction with the contract triggers a revert, effectively bricking the protocol. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that withdrawals fail with a revert, balances appear unchanged, and funds that were previously deposited cannot be retrieved, giving the impression that assets have disappeared. The root cause is an asymmetric handling of gains and losses: the LP loss is capped at zero while the trader’s gain is not, breaking the accounting invariant that assumes the sum of LP collateral and trader margin always matches the vault’s actual balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the FlatcoinVault’s invariant checks. It is hard to notice because the invariant only fails after a profit larger than the LP pool is realized, a scenario that may be rare in normal operation. The conceptual fix is to align the trader’s profit with the available LP collateral, for example by capping the profit to the current stableCollateralTotal before updating the global position data, ensuring that the tracked collateral never exceeds the real vault balance. This restores the invariant, allowing deposits, withdrawals, and position management to function correctly and prevents funds from being locked.

title: Losses of some long traders can eat into the margins of others
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the global margin handling of long positions. The contract aggregates the profit and loss of all open long positions in the updateGlobalPositionData function, computes a single profitLossTotal and then adds this signed value directly to the shared marginDepositedTotal that represents the collateral pool of all long traders. Because the loss of a single trader is deducted from the collective pool, a negative profitLossTotal can reduce marginDepositedTotal for every long participant, even those whose individual positions remain profitable. This design causes the margin of one trader to be unintentionally shared with others, violating the expectation that each trader’s margin is isolated. The flaw is triggered whenever updateGlobalPositionData is called – during opening, adjusting, closing, or liquidating a position – after a price movement that creates a negative PnL for at least one long. In the illustrated scenario, two traders each hold a 6 ETH long position. When the price drops from $1000 to $600, both incur a –4 ETH PnL, resulting in a total profitLossTotal of –8 ETH. The function then subtracts this amount from the global marginDepositedTotal of 8 ETH, setting the pool to zero. Consequently, the trader with a positive settled margin (Bob) is unable to withdraw his remaining 1 ETH because the shared pool no longer contains any collateral. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a position that should be withdrawable, yet the withdrawal transaction returns zero or fails, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the vault’s accounting logic, where the auditors noticed that the loss of one long was being charged to the collective margin rather than to the liquidity provider’s stable collateral. The bug is subtle because the aggregated profitLossTotal matches the sum of individual PnLs, so the error only becomes apparent when traders have differing outcomes. Exploitation is possible by an attacker who opens a large losing long position, forcing the global profitLossTotal to become sufficiently negative to deplete the marginDepositedTotal and block withdrawals for all other long participants. The impact is a loss of accessible assets for honest traders, erosion of confidence in the protocol, and potential financial damage. The conceptual fix is to separate the accounting of trader margin from the LP collateral: negative PnL should be absorbed by the stable collateral pool owned by the liquidity providers, while each trader’s margin balance should be updated independently, ensuring that a loss incurred by one participant does not diminish the withdrawable margin of others. Implementing per‑trader margin isolation and adjusting the updateGlobalPositionData logic to credit or debit the appropriate pool will restore the intended economic guarantees of the system.

title: Oracle can return different prices in same transaction
description:
The Pyth network oracle contract allows to submit and read two different prices in the same transaction. This can be used to create arbitrage opportunities that can make a profit with no risk at the expense of users on the other side of the trade.
OracleModule.sol uses Pyth network as the primary source of price feeds. This oracle works in the following way:
• A dedicated network keeps track of the latest price consensus, together with the timestamp.
• This data is queried off-chain and submitted to the on-chain oracle.
• It is checked that the data submitted is valid and the new price data is stored.
• New requests for the latest price will now return the data submitted until a more recent price is submitted.
Data is updated every 400ms off-chain, so when a new price is submitted on-chain it is not necessary that the price is the latest one. Otherwise, the process of querying the data off-chain, building the transaction, and submitting it on-chain would be required to be done with a latency of less than 400ms, which is not feasible. This makes it possible to submit two different prices in the same transaction and, thus, fetch two different prices in the same transaction.
This can be used to create some arbitrage opportunities that can make a profit with no risk.
How this can be exploited
An example of how this can be exploited, and showed in the PoC, would be:
• Create a small leverage position.
• Announce an adjustment order to increase the size of the position by some amount.
• In the same block, announce a limit close order.
• After the minimum execution time has elapsed, retrieve two prices from the Pyth oracle where the second price is higher than the first one.
• Execute the adjustment order sending the first price.
• Execute the limit close order sending the second price.
The result is approximately a profit of adjustmentSize * (secondPrice - firstPrice) - (adjustmentSize * tradeFees * 2) from the two trades, as the trade size is the same in both cases. The profit would be proportional to the price delta between both executions and inversely proportional to the trade fees. The position will end with no change in size, which in any case can be insignificant compared to the adjustment size. The keeper fee is also not included, as is the owner of the position that is executing the orders.
The following things are required to make a profit out of this attack:
• Submit the orders before other keepers. This can be easily achieved, as there are not always enough incentives to execute the orders as soon as possible.
• Obtain a positive delta between two prices in the time frame where the orders are executable that is greater than twice the trade fees. This can be very difficult to achieve. This requirement can be lowered to a delta greater than once the trade fees if we take into account that there is currently another vulnerability that allows to avoid paying fees for the limit order.
In the case of not being able to obtain the required delta or observing that a keeper has already submitted a transaction to execute them before the delta is obtained, the user can simply cancel the limit order and will have just the adjustment order executed.
Another possible strategy would pass through the following steps:
• Create a leverage position.
• Announce another leverage position with the same size.
• In the same block, announce a limit close order.
• After the minimum execution time has elapsed, retrieve two prices from the Pyth oracle where the second price is lower than the first one.
• Execute the limit close order sending the first price.
• Execute the open order sending the second price.
The result in this case is having a position with the same size as the original one, but having either lowered the position.lastPrice or getting a profit from the original position, depending on how the price has moved since the original position was opened.
Different oracle prices can be fetched in the same transaction, which can be used to create arbitrage opportunities that can make a profit with no risk at the expense of users on the other side of the trade.
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the Pyth off‑chain oracle used by OracleModule.sol can be fed with two distinct price updates within a single transaction and the contract will return the first price for one call and the second price for a later call in the same transaction. This arises because the contract only checks that the timestamp of the stored price is older than the current block timestamp, but does not enforce that the price data corresponds to the latest consensus before the transaction is executed. Consequently an attacker can submit a price update, read the price, then submit a second update with a higher (or lower) price and read it again before the block is finalized. By combining this price‑manipulation with leveraged positions and limit orders, the attacker can execute an adjustment order at the lower price and a closing order at the higher price (or vice‑versa) in the same block, earning a profit equal to the position size multiplied by the price delta minus fees. The profit is risk‑free because the net position size after the two trades is unchanged. The issue manifests when the oracle is updated more frequently than the time required to fetch, sign and submit a transaction (≈400 ms), allowing two updates to be packed into one block. Users of the protocol who open leveraged positions or place limit orders are affected: they may see their counterparties profit while their own balance is reduced or they receive a worse execution price. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test where two different prices were read in the same transaction, confirming that the oracle contract does not enforce monotonic price updates. The bug is subtle because the contract emits the correct price events and the price feed appears valid; only the timing of multiple updates inside a single transaction reveals the inconsistency. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “oracle price‑staleness / intra‑transaction price manipulation” bugs, where the contract trusts a price that can be altered after it has already been used for a previous calculation. From a user perspective the symptom is that a trade that should have been executed at the market price instead settles at a price that is noticeably better for the counterparty, leading to unexpected loss of funds or a missing profit. The fix requires the contract to enforce that only the most recent price (by timestamp) can be used within a transaction, for example by storing the price at the beginning of the block and rejecting any further updates until the next block, or by requiring a single price read per block and rejecting multiple updates. Implementing a re‑entrancy guard around price reads or adding a check that the submitted price data’s publish time is not newer than the previously stored price within the same block would also mitigate the issue.

title: Fees are ignored when checks skew max in
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting omission that causes the protocol’s skew‑limit check to ignore fees that remain in the vault after a stable withdrawal, a leverage open, or a leverage adjust. The contract updates the vault’s stable collateral total by subtracting the withdrawn amount, then calculates a withdrawal fee and later settles that fee back into the vault. However, when the function that enforces the maximum allowed skew (checkSkewMax) is called, the fee amount is not included in the additionalSkew parameter, so the skew fraction is computed as if the fee‑related collateral were still available to the user. This mismatch means that the reported skew can exceed the configured skewFractionMax even though the real post‑fee collateral level would keep the skew within limits. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; any user attempting a legitimate withdrawal or a trader opening or adjusting a leveraged position when the fee is non‑zero and the current skew is close to the maximum will experience a revert with a high‑slippage error. The impact is that safe operations are incorrectly blocked, leading to user frustration, potential loss of liquidity, and reduced confidence in the protocol’s reliability. The condition occurs whenever the fee percentage is greater than zero and the vault’s skew is near the configured ceiling, which is a common scenario for small withdrawals or position adjustments. Both depositors and traders are affected because their expected balances are not transferred, and the protocol’s liquidity providers may see reduced activity. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that exercised withdrawal and leverage functions with fee parameters set to non‑zero values and observed that the skew fraction reported by the contract differed from the value calculated after accounting for the fee. The bug is subtle because the fee amount is typically small, the UI may display the post‑fee balance correctly, and the revert message references slippage rather than the underlying skew calculation, making it easy to misinterpret as a market‑price problem. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of validation bugs where state‑invariant checks omit recent state changes, similar to rounding or fee‑omission errors in financial contracts. To remediate, the protocol should incorporate the withdrawal or trade fee into the additionalSkew argument (or otherwise adjust the skew calculation) so that the invariant reflects the true collateral distribution after fees are settled, ensuring that the check only rejects operations that would genuinely violate the skew limit.

title: Pairs with "MAX_FEE" can revert due to round-
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one rounding mismatch that can cause a legitimate swap transaction to revert with a FeeTooLarge error. The fee controller computes the fee amount using a ceiling division (mulDivUp), which rounds the result up to the nearest integer. Immediately afterwards, the ProtocolFees abstract contract validates that the fee taken does not exceed the pair‑specific maximum fee (MAX_FEE) by recomputing the allowed fee using a floor division (mulDivDown), which rounds the result down. When the product of the order amount and the fee rate is not an exact multiple of the denominator, the ceiling‑rounded fee can be one unit larger than the floor‑rounded maximum fee. The contract then incorrectly interprets this as the fee being too large and reverts the transaction. This occurs only for certain order amounts and fee settings where the rounding discrepancy appears; for example, with a MAX_FEE of 1 000 and an order amount of 111111111111111111111 (111.11 tokens with 18 decimals), the fee controller calculates 1 1111111111111111112 (rounded up) while the max‑fee check computes 1 1111111111111111111 (rounded down), triggering the revert. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a transaction failure with a FeeTooLarge error, even though the fee charged appears reasonable; the user expects the swap to succeed and receive the quoted amount, but instead receives no token transfer and the transaction is rolled back. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Sherlock, who wrote a fuzz test that generated many amounts causing the mismatch. It is hard to notice because the fee values look correct and the error only appears for edge‑case amounts, making it easy to attribute the failure to network congestion or user error. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style problem: users cannot execute swaps for affected amounts, potentially leading to loss of confidence and reduced liquidity, although no funds are permanently stolen because the transaction reverts. The bug belongs to the class of rounding‑error inconsistencies in financial smart contracts, where different parts of the code apply opposite rounding directions to the same arithmetic expression. To fix the issue, the fee calculation and the max‑fee verification must use the same rounding method, or the comparison should be performed on the pre‑rounded exact value, ensuring that a fee that is mathematically within the allowed bound never triggers a false revert. Aligning the rounding semantics eliminates the spurious FeeTooLarge condition and restores expected swap behavior.

title: Attacker can make first time taker's loose their
bug_full: The vulnerability is an fee inflation bug that affects users who place a first‑time taker order on a spot market. The contract calculates a taker fee as the product of the base quantity and a taker fee rate, then adds an additional component that divides a fixed transaction fee by the execution price. Because the division routine multiplies by 1e18 before dividing, a very low execution price makes the added component extremely large. An attacker can deliberately submit a sell order with a tiny price and a small quantity, creating a situation where the first taker on the opposite side is forced to pay an exorbitant fee. This condition typically occurs when the order book is empty or has no opposite‑side orders, so the first taker has no price reference other than the attacker’s low price. The root cause is the use of the execution price as a divisor in the fee formula without any sanity checks or price floor, combined with the e18 scaling that magnifies the result. When exploited, the taker’s balance is reduced by an amount far greater than the trade value, often leaving the user with zero or negative effective balance, which appears to the user as a missing refund or funds that simply disappear after the trade. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the _matchSpotOrder function, where the fee logic for first‑time takers was examined and the division by price was identified as unsafe. The bug is hard to notice because the fee calculation looks normal for most orders and only triggers under the specific first‑time, low‑price scenario, which may not be exercised in routine testing. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a minimum price limit or cap the fee contribution, collect fees in a core collateral pool rather than using the price‑dependent formula, and preferably use an oracle‑derived price for any conversion that involves division. By applying these conceptual fixes, the fee calculation will no longer be manipulable, protecting users from unexpected loss of funds and preserving the intended accounting invariants of the market.

title: User can DOS its own ingresso transactions by
description:
```solidity
User can ERC20.approve deposit amount to ciao address, create deposit request via off-chain app, but then front-running ingresso transaction with removal or reduction of approved amount to ciao address. This will cause the deposit and whole ingresso transaction to revert. This can be repeated again (simply increase approved amount again, possibly re-creating off-chain deposit request again).
Such user behavior will cause lots of reverted transactions (with wasted/lost gas by operator), disruption of the protocol service to the other users (due to failed transactions) and moreover will allow user to selectively censor ingresso transactions (allowing what he "likes" to proceed and what he doesn't like to revert).
Ciao.deposit uses ERC20 transferFrom to transfer funds from the user:
// Pull resources from sender to this contract
SafeTransferLib.safeTransferFrom(
ERC20(asset),
account,
address(this),
quantity
);
This is also called from OrderDispatch.deposit action:
ICiao(Commons.ciao(address(addressManifest))).deposit(
depo.account,
depo.subAccountId,
depo.quantity,
depo.asset
);
This means that user must first approve Ciao address to spend this amount of asset. This should be checked by off-chain app before it sends ingresso transaction with deposit.
However, the user can front-run this transaction and reduce approved amount to cause ingresso transaction revert. This will waste operator's gas, and since ingresso might include the other transactions as well, this will also cause disruption to protocol service.
Alternatively, especially in L2 networks with no mempool - just figure out the time for off-chain to react to deposit request, and submit approve 0 transaction shortly before this reaction time to ensure ingresso transaction executes after approve 0 transaction to make it revert.
Operator will waste gas on reverted transactions, user can disrupt protocol service and can also selectively censor transactions/actions if they're batched together in 1 transaction with user's deposit action, allowing user to do all kinds of malicious things.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on a user‑provided ERC20 allowance that is checked only off‑chain before a deposit (ingresso) transaction is submitted. The Ciao.deposit function pulls tokens from the caller by invoking ERC20.transferFrom, which will revert if the allowance held by the Ciao contract is lower than the requested amount. Because the allowance can be changed at any time by the token holder, a malicious user can front‑run the pending deposit transaction and submit an approve(0) or a reduced allowance transaction targeting the same token and spender address. When the original deposit transaction is later mined, the transferFrom call fails, causing the entire ingresso transaction – which may also contain other batched actions – to revert. This behaviour allows the user to deliberately cause a denial‑of‑service (DoS) against the protocol: the operator loses gas on each reverted transaction, other users experience failed deposits, and the attacker can selectively censor specific ingressos by choosing which ones to let succeed and which to force to revert. The issue manifests whenever a deposit request is generated off‑chain based on a previously granted allowance, and the on‑chain execution does not re‑validate the current allowance before calling transferFrom. It affects any participant that relies on the deposit mechanism, the protocol’s service availability, and the operator’s economic incentives. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the off‑chain approval flow and the on‑chain deposit logic, noting that the contract does not guard against allowance changes after the request is created. The bug can be subtle because allowance manipulation is a normal user operation and is not typically considered a security risk; however, in a batch‑processing context it becomes an attack vector. To remediate the issue, the deposit routine should compute the amount to transfer as the minimum of the currently approved allowance and the amount requested, and should skip the transfer entirely when the allowance is zero. This prevents the transferFrom call from reverting due to insufficient allowance and eliminates the ability for a user to force a revert by manipulating the allowance after the request is issued. The fix aligns the on‑chain logic with the intended business rule that a user’s deposit should succeed only up to the amount they have explicitly authorized, preserving protocol continuity and preventing intentional censorship or gas waste.

title: User can DOS liquidation by front-running with
description:
```solidity
When user is liquidated, the system makes sure it's not "over-liquidated":
// check liquidatee's initial health is zero or below. If above, they have been liquidated for too much
if (_furnace().getSubAccountHealth(liquidateeSubAccount, true) > 0) revert Errors.LiquidatedTooMuch();
A rational liquidator will always liquidate maximum amount to be at exact 0 or just below 0 for liquidatee account health.
This means that a tiny deposit by the user which front-runs the liquidation will cause liquidation to revert due to the line above, keeping user account healthy when it should be liquidated for a tiny cost. This allows user to DOS liquidator and keep unhealthy account active for arbitrary time, potentially letting it drop down into bad debt and loss of funds for the other users of the protocol.
Scenario for the user:
• Open 2 opposite positions with minimum collateral
• Wait until either position is unhealthy
• Watch for mempool and front-run liquidation transaction with user's tiny deposit transaction
• OR alternatively (especially for L2 chains without mempool) - simply submit multiple small deposit transactions to ensure all liquidation transactions are front-run by user's deposit transactions
Liquidator(s) (or operator) will waste gas on reverted transactions, user can avoid liquidation and keep unhealthy position active for rather low cost for arbitrary time, which can easily cause bad debt and loss of funds for the other users in the system.
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running denial‑of‑service (DoS) against the liquidation mechanism. When a user’s account health falls to zero or below, a liquidator calls the protocol to seize collateral. The contract first checks that the liquidatee’s health after the liquidation would not be positive; if the health is greater than zero the transaction reverts with an over‑liquidation error. Because the health check is performed after any pending deposit, a malicious user can submit a tiny deposit transaction that raises the health just above zero right before the liquidator’s transaction. The front‑run deposit causes the health check to fail, the liquidation reverts, and the user’s unhealthy position remains open. This can be repeated by sending many small deposits or by monitoring the mempool and out‑bidding the liquidator’s gas price, leading to repeated failed liquidations. The impact is that liquidators waste gas on reverted calls, the protocol’s risk management is bypassed, and the unhealthy account may accrue further debt, potentially resulting in bad debt that harms other participants. The issue occurs only when the account is on the brink of liquidation and a deposit can be timed to precede the liquidation call, which is common on chains with a visible mempool or on L2s where users can flood the network with tiny deposits. The affected parties are the user who can exploit the front‑run, the liquidators who lose gas and fail to recover collateral, and the broader protocol whose solvency assumptions are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation logic, where the health‑check condition was identified as being evaluated after state‑changing deposits. It is subtle because a small deposit looks innocuous and the revert message only indicates “over‑liquidated”, which does not immediately suggest a timing attack. The bug belongs to the class of economic DoS or front‑running attacks that manipulate on‑chain state to invalidate critical operations. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a liquidation transaction repeatedly fails, the account stays active despite being unhealthy, and the liquidator sees repeated “revert” errors and gas loss. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a minimum deposit size expressed in USD (for example $10) or redesign the over‑liquidation guard so that the health check is performed before applying any user‑initiated deposit, thereby preventing a tiny front‑run deposit from altering the health outcome.

title: feeRecepient and insurance special addresses
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol distributes trading and liquidation fees to two privileged accounts, the feeRecipient and the insurance account. Both accounts are treated as normal sub‑accounts when the Ciao.incrementFee function is called. IncrementFee simply adds the fee amount to the asset balance of the recipient without checking whether the recipient already holds a debt position in the same asset, which may be the core collateral token used for health calculations. If either privileged account has an outstanding core‑collateral debt, the fee addition creates a state where the account simultaneously holds a positive balance and a negative debt for the same token. When the privileged account later withdraws the entire balance, the withdrawal logic removes the asset from the account’s asset set once the balance reaches zero. Consequently, the core‑collateral token disappears from the list of assets that are iterated during the health‑factor computation. The health calculation therefore skips the core‑collateral entry and never subtracts the outstanding debt, causing the reported health to be artificially high. Under these conditions the account can acquire additional borrowing capacity that is not reflected in its true risk profile, potentially leading to excessive leverage, bad debt, and loss of funds for other participants. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑distribution code, where the auditor noticed that incrementFee does not consider existing debt and that the withdrawal routine removes zero‑balance assets without reconciling outstanding liabilities. The bug is subtle because the balance and debt are stored in separate mappings, so a zero balance does not immediately raise an alarm, and the health‑factor function only looks at assets present in the set, silently ignoring the missing collateral. To remediate the problem the fee‑distribution logic should first check whether the asset being credited is the core collateral and, if the recipient has a debt in that asset, settle the debt by reducing it instead of merely increasing the balance, or otherwise ensure that the asset remains in the account’s asset list even when the balance is zero so that health calculations remain accurate. This class of bug can be described as an accounting inconsistency where fee crediting bypasses debt reconciliation, leading to health‑factor miscalculation and unintended borrowing capacity.

title: Users might not be able to withdraw perp profit and loss
description:
Users can deposit any collateral to support their perp positions, however settlement is done in core collateral asset. The problem is the mismatch between the realized profit and loss (which is forced to be in core collateral asset) and unrealized profit and loss (which is theoretical and is not forced to be in core collateral asset). When a lot of deposits are in non-core collateral assets and then some profit is realized, transactions to withdraw this profit will revert, because system won't have enough core collateral asset and there is no way to "force" conversion of deposited assets into core collateral asset.
This means that it's easily possible that users can't withdraw core collateral asset due to protocol not having enough of it, which can happen by itself or crafted by malicious user.
Possible scenario of the issue happening by itself:
1. Alice deposits 10 BTC, Bob deposits 100 ETH, Charlie deposits 5000 USDC (USDC = core collateral asset)
2. Alice opens 1 BTC long position with Bob being the maker (1 BTC short position), at the price of BTC = $10000
3. BTC price rises to $20000. Alice now has unrealized profit of $10000, Bob has unrealized loss of $10000.
4. Alice closes her position against Charlie, realizing 10000 USDC profit.
5. Alice now has 1 BTC + 10000 USDC, Bob has 100 ETH and 1 BTC short position with unrealized loss of 10000 USDC, Charlie has 5000 USDC and 1 BTC long position (with 0 unrealized pnl).
6. Alice tries to withdraw 10000 USDC profit, but transaction reverts, because the protocol only has 5000 USDC.
7. Alice withdraws 5000 USDC. Now Charlie wants to withdraw some of its deposit, but any amount will revert, because protocol has no core collateral deposited at all.
The issue arises when some profit is realized in core collateral, but the loss remains unrealized thus deposited assets are not forced to be converted to core collateral asset.
Possible scenario of the issue being forced by malicious user:
1. Protocol has 1 BTC, 10 ETH and 10000 USDC deposited (USDC = core collateral asset)
2. Malicious user Alice wants to cause panic for protocol users
3. Alice uses 2 subaccounts, depositing 10 BTC into acc#1 and 10 BTC into acc#2
4. Alice uses acc#1 to open 100 BTC long position, and at the same time uses acc#2 to open 100 BTC short position (price = $10000)
5. Alice waits for BTC to rise or fall until either acc#1 or acc#2 is in 10000 USDC profit.
6. For example, BTC has dropped to $9900, acc#1 has 10000 USDC unrealized loss, acc#2 has 10000 USDC unrealized profit.
7. Alice closes and immediately reopens 100 BTC short position in acc#2, withdrawing 10000 USDC of realized profit.
After these steps, Alice can go wreck havoc by saying to users to try to withdraw their core collateral asset, and when transactions revert, this can cause panic and everybody withdrawing and creating negative publicity and reputation: it's always bad when users can not withdraw their assets unexpectedly.
Users might be unable to withdraw any deposited assets or realized profit in core collateral asset. This can happen by itself, or caused by malicious user.
Health calculation includes any deposited asset:
/contracts/libraries/MarginDirective.sol#L94-L100
This means that users can deposit non-core collateral asset to support their open positions, but the profit is realized in core collateral asset:
/contracts/OrderDispatch.sol#L599-L607
This means that protocol might not have enough core collateral asset to pay out the realized profits, when the loss is not yet realized (and the loss can stay unrealized for a long time).
bug_full: The vulnerability is a liquidity mismatch that occurs when a perpetual trading protocol settles realized profit and loss (PnL) exclusively in a designated core collateral asset while allowing users to provide collateral in arbitrary non‑core assets. The root cause is that the settlement logic forces realized PnL to be paid out in the core asset, but unrealized PnL remains expressed in the assets originally deposited, and there is no automatic mechanism to convert those non‑core assets into the core asset when a shortfall appears. As a result, if a large share of the system’s deposits are non‑core assets and a position generates realized profit in the core asset, the contract may not hold enough core collateral to satisfy the withdrawal request. An attacker can amplify the problem by opening offsetting long and short positions with the same non‑core asset, realizing profit on one side while keeping the loss unrealized on the other, thereby draining the core reserve. When a user attempts to withdraw the realized profit, the transaction reverts because the protocol’s balance of the core asset is insufficient, even though the overall health calculation reports sufficient collateral by counting all assets. This leads to users being unable to withdraw any core collateral, including their own deposits or realized gains, which can cause panic, loss of confidence, and reputational damage. The issue manifests whenever the proportion of non‑core collateral is high and unrealized losses have not been settled, a condition that can arise naturally during market movements or be engineered by a malicious participant. All users with open positions, as well as the protocol’s liquidity pool, are affected because the mismatch breaks the fundamental accounting assumption that realized payouts are always covered by available core collateral. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by Sherlock, who identified the logical inconsistency between the health calculation in the margin directive library and the settlement flow in the order dispatch module. The problem is hard to notice because the health metric aggregates all deposited assets, giving a false impression of solvency, while the withdrawal path checks only the core asset balance. To remediate the issue, the protocol should introduce a forced settlement mechanism that can automatically convert a portion of non‑core collateral into the core asset when a shortfall is detected, similar to an auto‑deleveraging process, or establish a dedicated reserve fund in the core asset that can be used to cover realized payouts when the regular pool is depleted. Implementing either approach restores the invariant that realized profit can always be withdrawn, aligning the accounting model with the protocol’s business logic and protecting users from unexpected withdrawal failures.

title: Incorrect spread liquidation for assets with 1e18 spreadPenalty
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect application of the spread penalty during liquidation for assets whose maintenance spread weight is set to the maximum value (1e18). In the health‑calculation view the contract recognises that such assets do not support a spread and treats the position as a separate spot component and a perpetual component. However, the liquidateSubAccount routine does not perform the same check and calls the generic _getSpreadLiquidationPrice function. That function multiplies the oracle price by (1e18‑spreadPenalty) for the spot side and by (1e18+spreadPenalty) for a short perpetual side. When spreadPenalty equals 1e18 the spot multiplier becomes zero and the perp multiplier becomes two, so the spot asset is liquidated at a price of zero while the short perp is liquidated at twice the market price. An attacker who initiates liquidation on an under‑collateralised account can therefore extract the full value of the spot balance and profit from the inflated perp liquidation price, causing the liquidatee to lose their funds. The issue manifests only when a user holds a position in an asset with a maintenance spread weight of 1e18 and the position becomes eligible for liquidation; normal positions are unaffected. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the health‑view logic with the liquidation path and noticed the missing condition. The bug is subtle because the health view reports a correct, non‑spread health score, so the error is not visible until liquidation is attempted, and the resulting zero price does not raise an explicit error – the balance simply disappears. The class of bug is an edge‑case mishandling of a parameter in price calculation, leading to a mis‑priced liquidation that violates the protocol’s accounting assumption that liquidation prices are bounded by the market price plus a bounded spread. To remediate, the liquidation code should explicitly check for a maintenance spread weight of 1e18 and either forbid spread‑based liquidation for those assets or compute the liquidation price without applying the full penalty, thereby preserving the expected price relationship and preventing loss of user funds.

title: Stargate STG rewards are accounted incorrectly
bug_full: An accounting bug in the Stargate LP_STAKING_TIME contract causes rewards to be transferred but the internal accounting variable that tracks the last global reward for each asset is never reset. The contract’s mint() and increaseLiquidity() functions call a reward‑withdrawal routine that clears the pending emission token from the external Stargate staking contract, yet they leave assetState[asset].lastRewardGlobal unchanged. Subsequent operations – mint, increaseLiquidity, burn, decreaseLiquidity, claimRewards, or any view that calls _getRewardBalances() – compute the reward delta as currentRewardGlobal – lastRewardGlobal. Because lastRewardGlobal still holds the previous total, the subtraction either underflows (causing a revert) or yields a smaller delta, meaning the user receives fewer rewards than earned. The bug manifests only after a reward‑withdrawal action; until the external pending reward becomes equal to or larger than the stale lastRewardGlobal, any further interaction reverts, effectively locking the position. Users see their balances unchanged, attempts to claim or adjust liquidity fail with a revert, and the reported reward amount is zero or dramatically reduced, leading to loss of expected earnings.
