When the borrower reacts to a partial liquidation by calling increaseCollateralBalance to restore solvency, the stale accumulator forces the system to charge the borrower again for the fees that were already collected, effectively double‑charging. This can also make the collateral balance appear far lower than it truly is, so a later call to harvest or a second liquidation may trigger an additional liquidation even though the borrower has added sufficient collateral. The impact is that users lose more funds than required by the protocol’s economic model: they may see their fees balloon, their collateral balance drop to zero, or their position liquidated despite having restored the required collateralization ratio. The condition under which this occurs is a sequence of events where (1) a borrower becomes liquidatable, (2) an emergency partial liquidation is executed, (3) the borrower adds collateral before a full liquidation, and (4) any subsequent fee‑related operation (repay, harvest, or another liquidation) is performed while the accumulator remains unchanged. All borrowers who rely on the emergency liquidation path, as well as lenders and the protocol’s overall health, are affected because the mis‑calculation can erode trust and lead to unnecessary loss of capital. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the LiquidityBorrowingManager contract, where the auditor noticed that the accLoanRatePerSeconds variable was only updated in the full‑liquidation branch and not in the partial‑liquidation branch, and that the fee‑addition logic used the unchanged rate to compute fees. The bug is subtle because the contract still enforces a liquidation when the calculated collateral balance is negative, so the failure manifests as an unexpectedly high fee charge rather than an outright revert, making it easy to overlook during functional testing. To remediate the problem, the contract should update accLoanRatePerSeconds (or an equivalent interest accumulator) whenever a partial emergency liquidation occurs, ensuring that subsequent fee calculations reflect the true accrued interest and that borrowers are not charged fees on the full collateral amount after they have already repaid part of the debt. In broader terms, this is a classic example of an interest‑accrual state‑inconsistency bug that breaks the accounting invariants of a lending protocol, leading to over‑charging and unfair liquidation outcomes.

title: JalaPair potential permanent DoS due to overflow in `_update` function
description:
In the JalaPair::_update function, overflow is intentionally desired in the calculations for timeElapsed and priceCumulative. This is forked from the UniswapV2 source code, and it’s meant and known to overflow. UniswapV2 was developed using Solidity 0.6.6, where arithmetic operations overflow and underflow by default. However, Jala utilizes Solidity >=0.8.0, where such operations will automatically revert.
```solidity
uint32 timeElapsed = blockTimestamp - blockTimestampLast; // overflow is desired
if (timeElapsed > 0 && _reserve0 != 0 && _reserve1 != 0) {
    // * never overflows, and + overflow is desired
    price0CumulativeLast +=
        uint256(UQ112x112.encode(_reserve1).uqdiv(_reserve0)) * timeElapsed;
    price1CumulativeLast +=
        uint256(UQ112x112.encode(_reserve0).uqdiv(_reserve1)) * timeElapsed;
}
```
This issue could potentially lead to permanent denial of service for a pool. All the core functionalities such as mint, burn, or swap would be broken. Consequently, all funds would be locked within the contract. I think issue with High impact and a Low probability (merely due to the extended time required) should be considered at least as Medium.

References  
There are cases where the same issue is considered High.  
https://solodit.xyz/issues/h-02-uniswapv2priceoraclesol-currentcumulativeprices-will-revert-when-pricecumulative-addition-overflow-code4rena-phuture-finance-phuture-finance-contest-git  
https://solodit.xyz/issues/m-02-twavsol_gettwav-will-revert-when-timestamp-4294967296-code4rena-nibbl-nibbl-contest-git  
https://solodit.xyz/issues/trst-m-3-basev1pair-could-break-because-of-overflow-trust-security-none-satinexchange-markdown_
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unintended permanent denial-of-service condition in the JalaPair contract caused by arithmetic overflow checks introduced by Solidity version 0.8 and later. The _update internal routine calculates a uint32 timeElapsed as blockTimestamp - blockTimestampLast and then adds the product of a price ratio and timeElapsed to two uint256 cumulative price variables. In the original UniswapV2 code, which was written for Solidity 0.6.6, these operations were allowed to overflow silently; the overflow was considered part of the design because the values are meant to wrap around. When the same code is compiled with Solidity >=0.8, any overflow or underflow triggers an automatic revert. Consequently, when the timestamp difference exceeds the 32-bit range (approximately 136 years) or when the cumulative price addition exceeds the 256-bit limit, the subtraction or addition reverts, causing the _update function to fail. Because _update is invoked by every core action—mint, burn, and swap—any call to those functions will revert, effectively locking all liquidity and preventing any further interaction with the pool. The impact is that users see no ability to trade or withdraw, balances appear unchanged, and funds become permanently inaccessible until the contract code is upgraded or the overflow checks are disabled. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the Jala implementation with the original UniswapV2 source and noticed the mismatch in compiler behavior. It is hard to notice in normal testing because the overflow condition requires an unusually long period of inactivity, making it unlikely to surface in short-term test suites. The proper remediation is to wrap the arithmetic that is expected to overflow in an unchecked block, or to redesign the variables (for example, using a larger timestamp type) so that overflow cannot occur. By doing so the contract regains its intended behavior where price accumulators wrap around without reverting, restoring normal mint, burn, and swap functionality and preventing permanent fund lockup.

title: If the vault's side token balance is 0 or a tiny amount, delta hedge check fails
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect delta‑hedge validation that triggers a transaction revert when the vault’s side‑token balance is zero or extremely small. The contract calculates the amount of side token that must be sold (tokensToSwap) and then checks that the absolute value of this amount is greater than the current side‑token balance, allowing a tiny relative tolerance (balance/10000). The check is implemented as: if (abs(tokensToSwap) > sideTokensAmount) { if (abs(tokensToSwap) - sideTokensAmount < sideTokensAmount/10000) { tokensToSwap = revabs(sideTokensAmount,true); } }. The root cause is that when sideTokensAmount is zero, the relative tolerance sideTokensAmount/10000 also evaluates to zero, making the inner comparison (abs(tokensToSwap) - sideTokensAmount < 0) impossible to satisfy. Consequently, even a minimal non‑zero tokensToSwap such as 1 wei causes the condition to fail and the transaction reverts. This situation occurs when the vault holds no side token, which happens when the market price is above the high boundary (Kb) and the IG Bull liquidity is exhausted. In that state, IG Bear trades do not affect the hedge amount, but the delta‑hedge calculation still produces a tiny non‑zero sell amount, leading to a revert due to the faulty comparison. An attacker or any user can trigger this edge case simply by causing the price to move above the high boundary or by draining the IG Bull side token balance, after which any attempt to open or close IG Bear positions will fail. The impact is that core protocol functionality becomes unavailable for bear‑side users, preventing them from executing trades and potentially causing loss of expected profit or locking of funds in the vault. The bug was discovered during a formal audit and reproduced with a Forge test that deliberately set the side‑token balance to zero and observed a revert when buying IG Bear options. It is hard to notice because the failure only appears under specific market conditions and the revert does not provide a clear error message, making it look like a generic transaction failure. The issue belongs to the class of “incorrect boundary checks with zero‑division tolerance” or “relative‑tolerance checks that break on zero values”. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a normal transaction attempt but receives no options and the transaction is reverted, contrary to the expectation that the trade would succeed. To remediate, the validation should incorporate an absolute tolerance (for example a fixed minimal amount such as 1,000 wei or side‑token unit/10000) in addition to the relative one, or simply cap the sell amount to the actual side‑token balance before performing the comparison. This ensures that when the balance is zero the check does not rely on a zero denominator and the contract can handle the edge case gracefully.

title: Mint and sales can be dossed due to lack of approval to zero
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by the misuse of OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20.safeApprove function in the DVP and PositionManager contracts. The code attempts to set a non‑zero allowance for the base token without first resetting the existing allowance to zero. SafeERC20.safeApprove contains a require that the new allowance must be zero or the current allowance must be zero; otherwise it reverts with the message "SafeERC20: approve from non-zero to non-zero allowance". During the first mint or sell operation the contract successfully approves the fee manager to pull the fee amount, but any subsequent mint or sell that again calls safeApprove with a non‑zero value will hit the require and revert. As a result, the mint, sell and burn functions become unusable after the initial successful call, effectively DOS‑ing the protocol's core functionality. The issue is triggered whenever the PositionManager or DVP contracts try to approve the base token for the fee manager or the DVP contract after an allowance has already been set. Users attempting to mint new positions or sell existing ones experience transaction failures, see no tokens minted or burned, and their balances remain unchanged. The protocol’s fee collection and vault accounting are also broken because the fee manager cannot pull the required fees. The bug was discovered during a manual audit by inspecting the approval logic and noticing the missing zero‑approval step. It can be hard to notice because the first operation works as expected, while later operations fail sporadically, leading to confusion rather than an obvious constant error. To remediate, the contract should either reset the allowance to zero before each new approval, use SafeERC20.safeIncreaseAllowance / safeDecreaseAllowance, upgrade to a newer OpenZeppelin version that provides a forceApprove helper, or redesign the flow to transfer tokens directly without relying on repeated approvals. Correcting the approval pattern restores the expected behavior where users can continuously mint, sell, and burn positions and the fee manager can reliably collect fees, preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees.

title: Vault Inflation Attack
description:
An attacker can be the first and only depositor on the vault during the first epoch in order to execute an inflation attack that will steal the deposited funds of all depositors in the next epoch. A malicious user can perform a donation to execute a classic first depositor/ERC4626 inflation attack against the new Smilee vaults. The general process of this attack is well-known, and a detailed explanation of this attack can be found in many of the resources such as the following:
• https://blog.openzeppelin.com/a-novel-defense-against-erc4626-inflation-attacks
• https://mixbytes.io/blog/overview-of-the-inflation-attack

In short, to kick-start the attack, the malicious user will often usually mint the smallest possible amount of shares (e.g., 1 wei) and then donate significant assets to the vault to inflate the number of assets per share. Subsequently, it will cause a rounding error when other users deposit.

However, in Smilee there's the problem that the deposits are not processed until the epoch is finished. Therefore, the attacker would need to be the only depositor on the first epoch of the vault; after the second epoch starts, all new depositors will lose all the deposited funds due to a rounding error. This scenario may happen for newly deployed vaults with a short maturity period (e.g., 1 day) and/or for vaults with not very popular tokens. An attacker will steal all funds deposited by the depositors of the next epoch.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inflation attack on the ERC4626‑style vault used by Smilee Finance. Because the contract postpones the processing of deposits until the end of an epoch, the first user that deposits in a newly created vault can manipulate the share‑to‑asset ratio. The attacker deposits the smallest possible amount of shares (for example 1 wei) and then donates a large amount of the underlying token directly to the vault. This donation inflates the number of assets that each share represents. When the next epoch begins, normal users submit deposits that are converted to shares based on the inflated ratio. Due to integer division and rounding down, the conversion yields zero or a negligible number of new shares, effectively causing the assets they supplied to be recorded as belonging to the attacker’s share balance. After the epoch rolls, the attacker redeems the single share and withdraws the entire pool, which now contains both the original donation and the assets contributed by the later depositors. The impact is that all users who deposit in the second epoch lose their funds, while the attacker walks away with the stolen assets. The attack can only be carried out when the attacker is the sole depositor in the first epoch, a situation that is realistic for freshly deployed vaults with short maturity periods or for vaults that accept low‑volume tokens. The issue was discovered during a security audit by reproducing the classic ERC4626 inflation scenario in a unit test. It is hard to notice because the total supply of shares does not change, the vault’s accounting appears consistent, and the loss is manifested only as a rounding error that silently transfers value to the attacker’s share balance. To mitigate the problem, the contract should enforce a minimum liquidity threshold on deposit and withdraw operations, preventing the total deposited amount from being so small that rounding down can occur. More generally, the design should avoid delayed deposit processing or ensure that the share‑to‑asset conversion cannot be manipulated by external token transfers, thereby preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the vault.

title: Position Manager providing the wrong strike
bug_full: The vulnerability is a strike‑mismatch bug in the PositionManager contract that causes minted positions to become permanently non‑redeemable when the strike supplied by the user does not exactly match the current strike used by the underlying IG (Interest‑Generating) contract. The root cause is that PositionManager records the user‑provided strike value in its internal ManagedPosition struct, while the IG contract’s mint function internally substitutes the protocol’s currentStrike for the supplied strike. Consequently, the on‑chain record and the protocol’s internal accounting diverge. When a user later attempts to burn or sell the position, the burn logic reads the stored strike from PositionManager and passes it to the IG contract, which expects the current strike. Because the two values differ, the IG contract cannot locate the position and reverts (e.g., with PositionNotFound), leaving the NFT and the associated premium locked inside PositionManager. This situation can arise whenever a user mints a position close to an epoch transition and provides the old epoch’s strike, or simply provides any strike that is not the exact current price at the moment of minting. From the user’s point of view the transaction appears successful – the NFT is minted and the premium is transferred – but later attempts to sell, burn, or withdraw result in a failed transaction and the user sees no balance change, often receiving a generic revert error. The impact is that funds become effectively inaccessible; the user cannot recover the premium or the notional amount tied to the position, which violates the protocol’s financial guarantees and accounting assumptions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a targeted test that deliberately mismatched the strike, causing the burn call to revert. It is hard to notice because the mint operation does not emit an error and the mismatch only surfaces on subsequent operations. The proper fix is to ensure that PositionManager stores the protocol’s current strike (retrieved via IG.currentStrike()) rather than the user‑supplied value, thereby keeping the internal record consistent with the IG contract’s accounting. Aligning the stored strike with the protocol’s strike eliminates the mismatch, allowing positions to be burned or sold normally and preserving user funds.

title: Whenever swapPrice > oraclePrice, minting
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistent premium calculation in the mint flow of a position‑manager contract. The manager obtains a premium from the DVP contract by calling DVP.premium, which returns a value based only on the external oracle price. Later, when the DVP actually requires the premium to mint a position, it computes the amount as the greater of two market values: one derived from the oracle price and one derived from an internal swap price produced by the delta‑hedge routine. The manager, however, still transfers only the oracle‑derived premium it previously obtained. When the internal swap price exceeds the oracle price, the required premium (premiumSwap) is larger than the transferred amount (obtainedPremium). The DVP then attempts to pull the shortfall via IERC20Metadata.safeTransferFrom, which reverts because the PositionManager does not hold enough tokens. This revert aborts the entire mint transaction, preventing the creation of new positions. The issue manifests whenever market conditions cause the swap price to be higher than the oracle price, a situation that can arise in volatile markets. All users who try to open positions through the PositionManager are affected, as their transactions fail and no new positions can be minted, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the mint function, where the auditor noticed that the premium used for the actual transfer was calculated with a max() between two values, while the premium fetched earlier did not apply the same logic. The problem is subtle because both price sources are legitimate and the code appears consistent; only the mismatch in the two calculations leads to a silent shortfall that surfaces as a transaction revert. The impact is a service interruption rather than direct loss of funds, but prolonged blockage can halt trading activity and affect protocol revenue. To remediate, the contract should compute the obtained premium using the same max‑logic as the DVP—i.e., compare the oracle‑derived premium with the swap‑derived premium and use the larger value—or otherwise guarantee that the transferred amount always covers the premium required by the DVP. Aligning the premium calculation eliminates the mismatch, restores correct accounting, and prevents the denial‑of‑service condition. This class of bug belongs to inconsistent financial‑calculation errors where different components of a system use divergent formulas for the same economic quantity, leading to mismatched expectations and potential reverts.

title: Trading out of the money options has delta
description:
Smilee protocol fully hedges all traders pnl by re-balancing the vault between base and side tokens after each trade. This is the assumption about this from the docs:
This ensures Smilee has always the correct exposure to the reference tokens to:
• Cover Impermanent Gain payoffs, no matter how much money traders earn and when they trade.
• Ensure Liquidity Providers gets the same payoff of a DEX LP*
• Ensure the protocol is not exposed to any shortfall.
https://docs.smilee.finance/protocol-design/delta-hedging
In the other words, any profit for traders is taken from the hedge and not from the vault Liquidity Providers funds. LP payoff must be at least the underlying DEX (Uniswap) payoff without fees with the same settings.
However, out of the money options (IG Bull when price < strike or IG Bear when price > strike) have delta = 0, meaning that trading such options doesn't influence vault re-balancing. Since the price of these options changes depending on current asset price, any profit gained by traders from these trades is not hedged and thus becomes the loss of the vault LPs, breaking the assumption referenced above.
As a result, LPs payout can becomes less than underlying DEX LPs payout without fees. And in extreme cases the vault funds might not be enough to cover traders payoff.
When the vault delta hedges its position after each trade, it only hedges in the money options, ignoring any out of the money options. For example, this is the calculation of the IG Bull delta (s is the current asset price, k is the strike):
```solidity
/**
_bull = (1 / ) * F
F = {
@@@
* 0
if (S < K)
* (1 - (K / Kb)) / K
if (S > Kb)
* 1 / K - 1 / (S * K)
if (K < S < Kb)
}
*/
function bullDelta(uint256 k, uint256 kB, uint256 s, uint256 theta) internal pure returns (int256) {
    SD59x18 delta;
    if (s <= k) {
        return 0;
    }
}
```
This is example scenario to demonstrate the issue:
• strike = 1
• vault has deposits = 2 (base = 1, side = 1), available liquidity: bull = 1, bear = 1
• trader buys 1 IG bear. This ensures that no vault re-balance happens when price < strike
• price drops to 0.9. Trader buys 1 IG bull (premium paid = 0.000038)
• price raises to 0.99. Trader sells 1 IG bull (premium received = 0.001138). Trader profit = 0.0011
• price is back to 1. Trader sells back 1 IG bear.
• at this point the vault has (base = 0.9989, side = 1), meaning LPs have lost some funds when the price = strike.
While the damage from 1 trade is not large, if this is repeated several times, the damage to LP funds will keep increasing.
This can be especially dangerous if very long dated expiries are used, for example annual IG options. If the asset price remains below the strike for most of the time and IG Bear liquidity is close to 100% usage, then all IG Bull trades will be unhedged, thus breaking the core protocol assumption that traders profit should not translate to LPs loss: in such case traders profit will be the same loss for LPs. In extreme volatility, if price drops by 50% then recovers, traders can profit 3% of the vault with each trade, so after 33 trades the vault will be fully drained.
In some specific trading conditions (IG Bear liquidity used close to 100% if price < strike, or IG Bull liquidity used close to 100% if price > strike), all or most of the traders pnl is not hedged and thus becomes loss or profit of the LPs, breaking the core protocol assumptions about hedging and in extreme cases can drain significant percentage of the vault (LPs) funds, up to a point of not being able to payout traders payoff.
bug_full: The Smilee protocol claims to keep liquidity‑provider (LP) capital safe by delta‑hedging the vault after every trade, re‑balancing the base and side token holdings so that any trader profit is taken from the hedge rather than from LP funds. In practice the contract treats out‑of‑the‑money (OTM) options – IG Bull when the spot price is below the strike or IG Bear when the spot price is above the strike – as having a delta of zero. Because the delta calculation returns zero for these states, the vault’s re‑balancing routine skips any adjustment when an OTM option is bought or sold. Consequently, when a trader opens an OTM position, pays a premium, and later closes it after the price moves back across the strike, the trader realizes a profit while the vault’s token balances remain unchanged. The profit is therefore absorbed by the vault’s base token pool, reducing the amount that LPs can withdraw. Over a single trade the loss may be a fraction of a percent, but repeated trades – especially with long‑dated options that keep the price on one side of the strike for extended periods – can accumulate to a substantial erosion of LP capital. In extreme scenarios, such as a 50 % price swing followed by a reversal, each round‑trip can drain several percent of the vault, potentially leaving the protocol unable to honour trader payouts. The vulnerability stems from an oversimplified delta approximation that deliberately returns zero for OTM options, ignoring the fact that OTM option prices still change with the underlying asset and therefore carry a non‑zero exposure. It was discovered during a formal audit when a test contract repeatedly bought IG Bear at the strike, then bought and sold IG Bull at prices below the strike, observing that the vault’s base token balance fell while the side token balance stayed constant. The bug is subtle because each individual loss is small and the delta‑zero logic appears mathematically correct at a glance, making it easy to miss in routine testing. Affected parties include LPs, who see their share of the vault shrink (for example, an LP may notice that their token value is lower than expected or that the vault balance is decreasing despite no direct withdrawals), and the protocol itself, which may breach its guarantee that LP payoff is at least the underlying DEX LP payoff. To remediate, the delta calculation should be refined to produce a small but accurate exposure for OTM options, or the protocol should introduce a fee or adjustment that ensures the vault’s notional value never falls below the equivalent DEX LP value after a trade. This class of issue can be described as a delta‑hedging approximation bug that leads to unhedged exposure and unintended capital loss.

title: Ether can stuck when an operators validators
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fund‑locking defect that appears when an operator’s validators are shut down and the EigenPod attempts to withdraw the full validator balance. The contract calculates the amount to exit by taking the total EigenPod shares, rounding them down to the nearest Gwei, and then requesting that exact amount from the delegator. If a user (or an attacker) submits a withdrawal request for an amount that is slightly smaller than the total balance – for example 63 ether when the pod holds 64 ether – the withdrawal logic still triggers a full exit of the 64 ether share. The user receives only the requested 63 ether, leaving a residual 1 ether in the EigenPod. A subsequent call to the scrape function is supposed to move any excess ETH out of the pod, but the function contains a guard that only allows scraping when the excess exceeds a constant MIN_EXCESS_FULL_WITHDRAWAL_ETH_FOR_SCRAPE (set to 1 ether). Because the leftover amount is exactly 1 ether, the condition fails and the call reverts with INSUFFICIENT_EXCESS_FULL_WITHDRAWAL_ETH. Consequently the remaining ether becomes permanently stuck unless the owner re‑enables the validators and repeats the withdrawal, which defeats the original intention of shutting down the operator. The root cause is the combination of rounding to Gwei precision and a minimum‑excess threshold that does not account for small dust amounts left after a partial withdrawal. The issue can be exploited by front‑running the owner’s shutdown transaction: a malicious user can submit a withdrawal just below the total balance, causing the leftover to be trapped. The impact is that stakers may see less ETH than expected, the protocol loses usable capital, and the operator owner may be forced to restart validators to recover the dust, potentially violating governance decisions. The bug manifests only under the specific condition where the operator is being exited and a user‑initiated withdrawal occurs before the owner’s transaction, making it easy to miss because the leftover amount looks like a harmless rounding error. It was discovered during a manual audit of the EigenPod withdrawal and scrape logic, with a proof‑of‑concept test that triggers the revert. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “un‑scrapable dust” or “precision‑rounding withdrawal” bugs, where leftover funds cannot be reclaimed due to overly strict guard checks. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful withdrawal but the received amount would be lower than requested, and the on‑chain balance of the EigenPod would still contain a small amount of ETH that cannot be moved. To remediate, the contract should provide an emergency path that allows the owner to sweep any positive excess regardless of the MIN_EXCESS_FULL_WITHDRAWAL_ETH_FOR_SCRAPE threshold, or adjust the rounding and guard logic so that no dust can become permanently locked.

title: A part of ETH rewards can be stolen by sandwiching
description:
Rewards can be stolen by sandwiching the call to EigenLayer::DelayedWithdrawalRouter::claimDelayedWithdrawals(). The protocol handles ETH rewards by sending them to the rewards distributor. There are at least 3 flows that end-up sending funds there:
1. When the function RioLRTOperatorDelegator::scrapeNonBeaconChainETHFromEigenPod() is called to scrape non beacon chain ETH from an Eigenpod.
2. When a validator receives rewards via partial withdrawals after the function EigenPod::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals() is called.
3. When a validator exists and has more than 32ETH the excess will be sent as rewards after the function EigenPod::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals() is called.

All of these 3 flows end up queuing a withdrawal to the rewards distributor. After a delay the rewards can claimed by calling the permissionless function EigenLayer::DelayedWithdrawalRouter::claimDelayedWithdrawals(), this call will instantly increase the TVL of the protocol.

An attacker can take advantage of this to steal a part of the rewards:
1. Mint a sensible amount of LRTTokens by depositing an accepted asset
2. Call EigenLayer::DelayedWithdrawalRouter::claimDelayedWithdrawals(), after which the value of the LRTTokens just minted will immediately increase.
3. Request a withdrawal for all the LRTTokens via RioLRTCoordinator::requestWithdrawal().

Rewards can be stolen by sandwiching the call to EigenLayer::DelayedWithdrawalRouter::claimDelayedWithdrawals(), however this requires a bigger investment in funds the higher the protocol TVL.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a sandwich‑style race condition that allows an attacker to capture a portion of ETH rewards that are queued for distribution to the rewards distributor. The protocol aggregates rewards from three different sources – scraping non‑beacon‑chain ETH, partial withdrawals after validator processing, and excess ETH from validators – and queues them as delayed withdrawals. When the permissionless function claimDelayedWithdrawals is called, the queued rewards are transferred to the distributor and the protocol’s total value locked (TVL) increases instantly. Because the value of the LRTTokens that represent a user’s stake is derived from the current TVL, an attacker can mint LRTTokens, trigger claimDelayedWithdrawals to inflate the TVL, and then request a withdrawal of all their newly minted tokens in the same block. The withdrawal request pulls the inflated token value out of the system, effectively stealing a share of the rewards that were just claimed. This attack can be executed whenever rewards are pending and the claimDelayedWithdrawals function is callable, which is any time after a reward‑queuing event and before the next epoch’s withdrawal processing. Users, validators, and the protocol itself are affected because the expected reward distribution is altered: a user who expects to receive a proportional share of rewards may see their balance unchanged while the attacker’s balance grows, leading to missing or reduced refunds and a lower overall TVL for honest participants. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test where an attacker deposited ETH, claimed delayed withdrawals, and then withdrew all tokens, resulting in roughly a 50 % gain of the queued rewards. The bug is subtle because the reward claim appears to succeed and the TVL spike is a legitimate state change, making the loss of funds look like a normal reward distribution rather than an exploit. To remediate, the protocol should prevent rewards that are claimed in the current epoch from being used to calculate token value for withdrawal requests, for example by deferring reward distribution to a later epoch or by separating the accounting of newly claimed rewards from the withdrawal queue. This would close the race condition and ensure that token holders cannot profit from immediate TVL inflation, preserving the integrity of the reward accounting logic.

title: Execution Layer rewards are lost
description:
According to Rio Network Docs: "The Reward Distributor contract (RioLRTRewardDistributor) has the ability to receive ETH via the Ethereum Execution Layer or EigenPod rewards and then distribute those rewards". However, this is only true for EigenPod rewards. Execution Layer rewards are not accounted for and lost.

Execution Layer rewards are not distributed through plain ETH transfers. Instead the balance of the block proposer fee recipient's address is directly updated. If the fee recipient getting the EL rewards is a smart contract, this means that the fallback/receive function is not called. Actually, a smart contract could receive EL rewards even if these functions are not defined.

The RioLRTRewardDistributor contract relies solely on its receive function to distribute rewards. EL rewards which don't trigger this function are not accounted in the smart contract and there is no way of distributing them.

Execution Layer rewards are lost.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of execution‑layer (EL) rewards that are sent to the RioLRTRewardDistributor contract but never become part of the contract’s accounting or distribution logic. The contract assumes that any incoming ETH will trigger its receive function, where it records the amount and later forwards shares to the treasury, operator and deposit pool. However, EL rewards are not transferred via a regular ETH transfer; instead the protocol updates the balance of the fee‑recipient address directly at the consensus layer. When the fee recipient is a smart contract, this balance update does not invoke the fallback or receive function, meaning the contract’s internal bookkeeping never sees the incoming funds. As a result, the ETH sits in the contract’s balance without any event, cannot be split according to the predefined shares, and effectively becomes lost to the protocol. The issue appears whenever a block proposer’s fee‑recipient address is set to the RewardDistributor contract, which is the intended destination for EL rewards. All parties that rely on those rewards – validators, operators, the treasury and end users – receive less or no ETH than expected, breaking the economic model of the network. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the reward distribution code when the auditor noticed that the contract only handled ETH received through its receive function and did not consider balance changes that occur without a call. Because the balance increase is silent, there is no transaction log or UI indication that funds arrived, making the bug hard to spot; users may see a zero reward claim despite the protocol having credited ETH to the contract address. The class of bug is an accounting flaw where incoming native currency is not captured because the contract relies exclusively on a payable fallback, a pattern that fails for direct balance updates. To remediate, the contract should include a mechanism that can be called after EL rewards are credited – for example a function that reads the contract’s total balance, calculates each party’s share using the configured basis points, and transfers the appropriate amounts. Such a method would allow the protocol to recover any ETH that arrived without triggering receive, ensuring that rewards are correctly distributed and that the accounting invariants of the system are restored.

title: The protocol can't receive rewards because
description:
The hardcoded gas limit of the Asset::transferETH() function, used to transfer ETH in the protocol, is too low and will result unwanted reverts.

ETH transfers in the protocol are always done via Asset::transferETH(), which performs a low-level call with an hardcoded gas limit of 10_000:
```solidity
(bool success,) = recipient.call{value: amount, gas: 10_000}('');
if (!success) {revert ETH_TRANSFER_FAILED();}
```
The hardcoded 10_000 gas limit is not high enough for the protocol to be able receive and distribute rewards. Rewards are currently only available for native ETH, an are received by Rio via:
• Partial withdrawals
• ETH in excess of 32ETH on full withdrawals

The flow to receive rewards requires two steps:
1. An initial call to EigenPod::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals(), which queues a withdrawal to the Eigenpod owner: an RioLRTOperatorDelegator instance
2. A call to DelayedWithdrawalRouter::claimDelayedWithdrawals().

The call to DelayedWithdrawalRouter::claimDelayedWithdrawals() triggers the following flow:
1. ETH are transferred to the RioLRTOperatorDelegator instance, where the receive() function is triggered.
2. The receive() function of RioLRTOperatorDelegator transfers ETH via Asset::transferETH() to the RioLRTRewardDistributor, where another receive() function is triggered.
3. The receive() function of RioLRTRewardDistributor transfers ETH via Asset::transferETH() to the treasury, the operatorRewardPool and the RioLRTDepositPool.

The gas is limited at 10_000 in step 2 and is not enough to perform step 3, making it impossible for the protocol to receive rewards and leaving funds stuck.

The protocol is unable to receive rewards and the funds will be stuck.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a gas‑limit misconfiguration in the contract function that forwards native ETH. The protocol uses a low‑level call with a hard‑coded gas stipend of 10,000 when executing Asset.transferETH, assuming this amount is sufficient for a simple value transfer. In reality the call chain that distributes rewards involves several receive() functions in protocol‑controlled contracts (the delegator, the reward distributor, the treasury and pool contracts). Each receive() execution consumes more than 10 k gas, especially when the second hop forwards the ETH again. When a user or operator triggers the reward‑claim flow – first by queuing a withdrawal via EigenPod.verifyAndProcessWithdrawals and then by calling DelayedWithdrawalRouter.claimDelayedWithdrawals – the protocol attempts to move the reward ETH through two nested Asset.transferETH calls. The first call succeeds, but the second call runs out of the hard‑coded gas limit, causing the low‑level call to return false and the transaction to revert with ETH_TRANSFER_FAILED. As a result the reward amount never reaches the treasury, operator reward pool or deposit pool, and the funds remain locked in the delegator contract. The impact is that rewards that should be automatically distributed become unavailable; users see a pending reward balance but receive zero after claiming, breaking the expected accounting and incentive model. The issue manifests only when rewards are paid in native ETH and the destination is a protocol‑controlled contract; it does not affect other asset types. It was discovered during a formal audit and reproduced with a unit test that simulates a full withdrawal and observes an out‑of‑gas revert on claimDelayedWithdrawals. The problem is hard to notice because the failure occurs deep in the call stack, the UI may still display a non‑zero reward balance, and the revert message is generic. The bug belongs to the class of insufficient‑gas‑stipend or gas‑limit misconfiguration vulnerabilities that can cause denial‑of‑service for fund transfers. To remediate, the hard‑coded 10 k gas limit should be removed for ETH transfers to protocol contracts, allowing the call to forward all available gas or using a sufficiently high stipend, and the contract should handle call failures gracefully. This change restores the intended flow where rewards are automatically forwarded, aligning the implementation with the protocol’s business logic that rewards must be received and distributed without manual intervention.

title: RioLRTIssuer::issueLRT reverts if deposit asset
description:
Using ERC20::approve will not work with ERC20 tokens that do not return a bool. The contest's README states that tokens that may not return a bool on ERC20 methods (e.g., USDT) are supposed to be used.

The RioLRTIssuer::issueLRT function makes a sacrificial deposit to prevent inflation attacks. To process the deposit, it calls the ERC20::approve method, which is expected to return a bool value.

Solidity has return data length checks, and if the token implementation does not return a bool value, the transaction will revert.

Issuing LRT tokens with an initial deposit in an asset that does not return a bool on an approve call will fail.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the contract's reliance on the standard ERC20 approve function returning a boolean value. In the RioLRTIssuer::issueLRT workflow a sacrificial deposit is performed to protect against inflation attacks, and the implementation calls ERC20.approve expecting a bool result. Certain widely used tokens, such as USDT, deviate from the ERC20 specification and do not return any data on approve. Solidity automatically checks the length of the returned data; when the call returns no bytes the runtime reverts the transaction. Consequently, if a user supplies a deposit asset that is a non‑standard token, the approve call fails, the whole issueLRT transaction reverts, and no LRT tokens are minted. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome – receiving newly issued LRT – does not happen; instead the transaction is dropped and the user only loses the gas spent, often seeing a zero balance change or an empty receipt. The issue is discovered during an audit by reproducing the approve call against USDT in a Forge test, which demonstrated a revert, while a SafeERC20.forceApprove call succeeded. The bug is subtle because most ERC20 tokens behave as expected, so developers may not notice the incompatibility until a non‑standard token is used. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for any deposit asset that does not return a bool, potentially preventing legitimate users from acquiring LRT and reducing the protocol’s usability. The affected parties include token holders attempting to issue LRT, the protocol’s issuance mechanism, and any downstream services that rely on successful token minting. To remediate the problem the contract should avoid direct calls to approve and instead employ OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library, specifically the forceApprove helper, which performs a low‑level call and tolerates missing return data, thereby restoring compatibility with all ERC20 implementations.

title: ETH withdrawers do not earn yield while waiting
description:
In the Rio doc we can read the following:
"Users will continue to earn yield as they wait for their withdrawal request to be processed."
This is not true for withdrawals in ETH since they will simply receive an equivalent to the sharesOwed calculated when requesting a withdrawal.
When requestWithdrawal() is called to withdraw ETH, sharesOwed is calculated:
```solidity
sharesOwed = convertToSharesFromRestakingTokens(asset, amountIn);
```
The total sharesOwed in ETH is added to epochWithdrawals.assetsReceived if we settle with settleCurrentEpoch() or settleEpochFromEigenLayer().
Below are the places where assetsReceived is set and accumulated:
```solidity
epochWithdrawals.assetsReceived = SafeCast.toUint120(assetsReceived);
```
```solidity
epochWithdrawals.assetsReceived = SafeCast.toUint120(assetsReceived);
```
```solidity
epochWithdrawals.assetsReceived += SafeCast.toUint120(assetsReceived);
```
When claiming rewards, this is used to calculate user share:
```solidity
amountOut = userSummary.sharesOwed.mulDiv(epochWithdrawals.assetsReceived, epochWithdrawals.sharesOwed);
```
The portion of staking rewards accumulated during withdrawal that belongs to LRT holders is never accounted for, so withdrawing users do not earn any rewards when waiting for a withdrawal to be completed.
Since a portion of the staking reward belongs to the LRT holders and since the docs mention that yield is accumulated while in the queue, it is fair to assume that withdrawing users have a proportional claim to the yield.
As shown above, this is not true: users withdrawing in ETH do not earn any rewards when withdrawing.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the accounting of staking rewards for users who request an ETH withdrawal on the Rio network. When a user calls requestWithdrawal() the contract records a fixed amount of sharesOwed based on the amount of ETH they wish to withdraw. This value is stored and later used together with epochWithdrawals.assetsReceived to calculate the final payout when the withdrawal is settled. However, the implementation only adds the principal amount to assetsReceived and never incorporates the portion of staking rewards that accrue to the liquidity restaking token (LRT) pool during the waiting period. As a result, the formula amountOut = userSummary.sharesOwed * epochWithdrawals.assetsReceived / epochWithdrawals.sharesOwed yields a payout that reflects only the original deposit, while any yield that should have been earned while the request was pending is omitted. The bug originates from missing reward accounting in the withdrawal queue logic, a mismatch between the protocol’s documentation – which promises that users continue to earn yield while waiting – and the actual code path that settles withdrawals. Exploitation is straightforward: a user submits an ETH withdrawal request, waits for the epoch to settle, and receives exactly the amount they requested, with no additional rewards, contrary to expectations. The impact is that users lose the yield they were led to believe they would earn, effectively causing “funds disappear” from the perspective of expected earnings. This condition occurs for any ETH withdrawal that goes through requestWithdrawal() and is later settled via settleCurrentEpoch() or settleEpochFromEigenLayer(). It affects all ETH withdrawers and, indirectly, LRT holders who rely on accurate reward distribution. The issue was discovered during a security audit by comparing the protocol’s public statements with the on‑chain accounting logic and noticing that the assetsReceived variable never receives reward amounts. Because the withdrawal still returns the correct principal, the missing yield is subtle and may not be immediately visible in the UI, making it hard to detect without detailed analysis of the reward calculation. To remediate, the contract should adjust the assetsReceived accounting to include the proportional share of rewards that accrue during the withdrawal period, for example by pulling the relevant data from the DelayedWithdrawalRouter on Eigenlayer and adding it to the pending withdrawal’s assetsReceived before the final payout calculation. This change would align the implementation with the promised behavior that users continue to earn yield while their withdrawal is pending, restoring correct accounting and preventing users from receiving less than expected.

title: Slashing penalty is unfairly paid by a subset
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unfair distribution of slashing penalties in the EigenPodManager component of the EigenLayer protocol. When a validator is slashed while ETH is queued for withdrawal, the protocol records a negative balance (deficit) in the internal accounting variable that tracks each pod owner's shares. The root cause is that the settlement function settleEpochFromEigenLayer() assumes that the assets received for a withdrawal cohort will always cover the owed shares. If the deficit exceeds the amount queued for the current cohort, the calculation of assetsReceived becomes zero and the entire shortfall is charged to the first cohort that completes a withdrawal. Consequently, users in that cohort receive no ETH (or a reduced amount) while later cohorts receive the full amount, effectively shifting the full slashing loss onto a subset of LRT holders instead of spreading it proportionally among all token holders. This can be exploited by triggering a slashing event during the withdrawal window, then initiating withdrawals in multiple epochs; the first epoch will absorb the whole penalty, potentially receiving zero funds, while subsequent epochs are unaffected. The impact is a breach of economic fairness: some participants lose their expected refunds, see their balances drop to zero, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about proportional loss sharing are violated. The condition occurs whenever a deficit is created before the first withdrawal settlement, typically during periods of active slashing and pending withdrawals. All users who have deposited LRT tokens are affected, but the immediate victims are those whose withdrawal request is processed first. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that simulated slashing and observed that the first cohort’s claim returned zero ETH while later cohorts claimed the full amount, revealing that the penalty was not distributed as intended. The bug is subtle because the contract’s logic correctly updates share balances, yet the settlement routine does not check for a negative share balance before applying the assetsReceived calculation, making the problem easy to miss in standard testing. To remediate, the settlement logic should detect a deficit and allocate the penalty proportionally across all outstanding LRT holders, for example by adjusting the share value of assetsReceived for each cohort or by introducing a global deficit pool that is amortized over future withdrawals. This would restore the intended fairness and prevent any single cohort from bearing the entire slashing loss.

title: requestWithdrawal doesn't estimate accurately
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inaccurate estimation of withdrawable shares in the requestWithdrawal function. The function determines how many shares are available by converting the protocol's total asset balance to shares using the asset registry. However, the total balance reported by getTotalBalanceForAsset aggregates both assets that have already been deposited into EigenLayer and assets that are still sitting in the deposit pool. Assets that remain in the deposit pool have not been converted to EigenLayer shares yet, so applying the current share‑to‑asset price to them yields a misleading share count. As a result the calculated availableShares can be higher or lower than the real number of shares the protocol controls. When a user calls requestWithdrawal, the function queues the withdrawal based on this inflated (or deflated) share estimate. An attacker can submit a large withdrawal request that appears to be fully backed by shares, causing the withdrawal queue to exceed the actual share reserve. Subsequent legitimate users may then find their withdrawals blocked or receive less ETH/token than their share entitlement, effectively losing funds. The issue manifests whenever the deposit pool holds a non‑zero balance, i.e., after new deposits have been made but before they are transferred to EigenLayer. All participants who rely on the withdrawal mechanism—regular users, delegators, and the protocol itself—are affected because the accounting invariant that “total shares = total deposited assets” is broken. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the Rio Network contracts, where the auditor noticed that getTotalBalanceForAsset adds depositPool balance to the amount already deposited in EigenLayer, contradicting the intended share conversion logic. The bug is subtle because the function name and return value suggest a complete view of assets, making the mis‑count easy to overlook in testing. To remediate, the share estimation should be based solely on assets that have been converted into EigenLayer shares; the deposit pool balance must be excluded or accounted for separately, and the requestWithdrawal logic must be updated to use a corrected share‑availability calculation. In generic terms this is an accounting‑logic error where pending deposits are mistakenly treated as fully vested shares, leading to withdrawal queue overflow, fund shortfall, and broken financial guarantees.

title: All operators can have ETH deposits regardless
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the Rio LRT protocol aggregates Ether (ETH) holdings for its Total Value Locked (TVL) calculation. The contract treats every registered operator as if it can contribute ETH to the beacon‑chain strategy, regardless of whether the operator has been assigned a validator cap or is actively participating in the BEACON_CHAIN_STRATEGY. An operator can acquire ETH simply by staking on the beacon chain without invoking the EigenPods stake function, and the operatorDelegator contract can call verifyWithdrawalCredentials to increase its EigenPod shares. The TVL function getTotalBalanceForAsset sums the balance of the deposit pool with the result of getETHBalanceInEigenLayer, which iterates over *all* operator IDs and adds each operatorDelegator’s getETHUnderManagement value. Because getETHUnderManagement returns the sum of EigenPod shares and queued ETH, the TVL includes ETH that is technically locked in EigenPod shares of operators that are not part of the active validator heap. Consequently, the protocol reports a higher ETH TVL than the amount that can actually be withdrawn. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a larger ETH balance and a more favorable exchange rate, leading users to expect that they can withdraw the displayed amount. In reality, withdrawals may fail or return zero because the underlying ETH does not exist in a withdrawable pool. The issue is triggered when an inactive operator (one without a cap) deposits ETH or verifies withdrawal credentials; the TVL calculation still counts this ETH, but the withdrawal path cannot access it because the operator is not in the heap order. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the TVL aggregation logic and the operator eligibility checks. It is subtle because the TVL numbers appear plausible and the discrepancy only surfaces during edge‑case withdrawals, making it easy to miss in routine testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where assets are double‑counted or counted without proper eligibility verification, violating the protocol’s financial invariants. To remediate, the verifyWithdrawalCredentials function should reject calls from operators that are not actively participating in the BEACON_CHAIN_STRATEGY, and the TVL aggregation should filter out ETH contributions from inactive operators or adjust the EigenPod share calculation to reflect only withdrawable assets. This ensures that reported TVL matches the actual, withdrawable ETH balance, restoring trust and preventing failed withdrawals.

title: Stakers can avoid validator penalties
description:
Stakers can frontrun validator penalties and slashing events with a withdrawal request in order to avoid the loss, this is possible if the deposit pool has enough liquidity available.
Validators can lose part of their deposit via penalties or slashing events:
• In case of penalties Eigenlayer can be notified of the balance drop via the permissionless function EigenPod::verifyBalanceUpdates().
• In case of slashing the validator is forced to exit and Eigenlayer can be notified via the permissionless function EigenPod::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals() because the slashing event is effectively a full withdrawal.
As soon as either EigenPod::verifyBalanceUpdates() or EigenPod::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals() is called the TVL of the Rio protocol drops instantly. This is because both of the functions update the variable podOwnerShares[podOwner]:
• EigenPod::verifyBalanceUpdates() will update the variable here
• EigenPod::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals() will update the variable here
This makes it possible for stakers to:
1. Request a withdrawal via RioLRTCoordinator::rebalance() for all the LRTTokens held.
2. Call either EigenPod::verifyBalanceUpdates() or EigenPod::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals().
At this point when RioLRTCoordinator::rebalance() will be called and a withdrawal will be queued that does not include penalties or slashing.
It's possible to withdraw LRTTokens while avoiding penalties or slashing up to the amount of liquidity available in the deposit pool.
Stakers can avoid validator penalties and slashing events if there's enough liquidity in the deposit pool.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch that allows a staker to withdraw LRTTokens without suffering the loss that should be applied when a validator incurs a penalty or a slashing event. The root cause is that the RioLRTCoordinator::rebalance function creates a withdrawal queue based on the current total value locked (TVL) before the protocol processes the penalty notification, while the EigenPod::verifyBalanceUpdates and EigenPod::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals functions, which are permissionless, can be called afterwards to instantly reduce the TVL by updating the podOwnerShares mapping. Because the withdrawal amount is calculated prior to the TVL drop, the queued withdrawal does not include the penalty or slashing deduction. An attacker can monitor validator performance, detect an upcoming penalty, submit a withdrawal request for the desired amount, and then trigger the penalty notification (or a slashing event) that lowers the TVL. When the rebalance is finally executed, the queued withdrawal is processed and the attacker receives the full amount requested, effectively avoiding the penalty. This exploit works only when the deposit pool contains enough liquid ETH to satisfy the withdrawal request, and when the attacker can invoke the EigenPod verification functions after the request. The impact is that honest stakers and validators bear the full penalty while the attacker keeps their funds, leading to an unfair redistribution of losses, potential under‑collateralisation of the protocol, and erosion of economic incentives. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a normal withdrawal request and later a successful claim with the expected amount, while the pool’s TVL has decreased, making the discrepancy subtle and hard to notice. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Sherlock, who built a proof‑of‑concept that demonstrated a withdrawal made before an instant TVL drop returns the full amount. The bug is difficult to detect because the contract does not reject the withdrawal and no error is emitted; the only symptom is a mismatch between the pool’s reported TVL and the amounts received by users. To fix the problem the protocol should ensure that penalties and slashing events are accounted for in all pending withdrawals, either by adjusting the withdrawal amounts after a TVL change or by distributing the penalty proportionally across all LRTTokens, including those already queued, and by preventing the separation of TVL updates from withdrawal accounting.

title: The current idea of creating reETH and accepting different staked assets may lead to “withdrawals before price drop” attack
description:
After the release of LRT, which will include the ability to deposit native eth and wrapped staking tokens like cbETH or wstETH, Rio users will be exposed to additional economic risks that may lead to loss of capital. In case of a predictable price drop (e.g. caused by a slashing event in an external liquid staking provider), external users can deposit their funds into Rio before the price drop. They will receive the LRT (corresponding to the value before the price drop, as priceFeed displays the changed price only when it actually happens) and withdraw them once the price drops, sharing their loss with Rio users.
Rio creates a network for issuing Liquid Restaking Tokens (LRTs) that have an underlying asset mix. The idea is to have multiple LRTs like: reUSD, reETH, reXXX, where for reUSD underlying asset mix will include e.g. USDC, DAI, USDT and for reETH underlying asset mix will include native ETH and e.g. cbETH (as it is used in tests), or wstETH.
Users depositing their funds into Rio are encouraged by the rewards of staking and re-staking through EigenLayer, but they also bear the risk of penalties and slashing of their deposited funds. However, in case of reETH, the 3rd party users who are not associated in any way with Rio ecosystem can take advantage of such LRT and make Rio users bear their losses.
Keeping in mind these things:
• value of assets like wstETH, cbETH generally increase over time,
• there are price drops for assets like wstETH, cbETH, but most of the time these are temporary,
• things that can cause price drops for assets like wstETH, cbETH include: slashing, lower demand / lack of trust for particular asset, withdrawal caused by people who accumulated big rewards over time,
• lower demand / lack of trust is unpredictable, however, big withdrawals can be monitored and slashing is a process spread over time, so there is a time when you know the value of asset will drop,
• liquid staking providers like LIDO etc., protects themselves from "withdrawal before slashing" by making withdrawal process long enough so that slashing can affect the users who request to withdraw,
• user within Rio ecosystem can deposit asset1 to get LRT, and then request to withdraw asset2.
Consider the following scenario (values used for ease of calculation and to illustrate the attack, real values will be presented later in this description):
Rio issues LRT (reETH) that supports two assets (cbETH and native ETH).
1. 200 ETH is deposited inside RIO by users and 200 reETH were minted.
2. The attacker (cbETH staker) has 100 cbETH (price is e.g. 1 cbETH = 2 ETH, their cbETH is worth 200 ETH)
The attacker knows through monitoring slashing events and big withdrawalas that price will drop soon.
3. The attacker deposit their 100 cbETH to Rio to get 200 reETH (as current price is still 1 cbETH = 2 ETH)
Total value locked on Rio will increase from 200 ETH to 400 ETH (200 eth and 100 cbETH)
Price of cbETH now drops by 50% (so now 1 cbETH = 1 ETH)
Total value locked on Rio will decrease from 400 ETH to 300 ETH (as 200cbETH is now worth only 100 ETH).
4. The attacker decides to request withdraw all of their cbETH by burning only 150 reETH and they also request to withdraw 50 ETH by burning another 100 reETH.
5. Attacker gets 200 cbETH back (current price is 100 ETH) and additional 50 ETH.
6. Attacker buys additional cbETH for their additional 50 ETH, so know they have 250 cbETH (from another source)
Now price recover, so its again 1 cbETH = 2 ETH.
Attacker now have 250 cbETH worth 500 ETH, and Rio users have 150 ETH (lost 50 ETH, as attacker delegeted their risk to rio users).
However, the price will not drop by 50%. The real numbers could be up to 10%.
Looking at 2 examples of assets that are considered to be added to reETH (cbETH and wstETH) we can observe the following:
1. cbETH (https://coinmarketcap.com/currencies/coinbase-wrapped-staked-eth/)
• there are price drops
• based on data from last 365 days the biggest percentage drop in price occurred on March 11, 2023, with a drop of approximately 8.25% (https://coinmarketcap.com/currencies/lido-finance-wsteth/historical-data/) (https://coinmarketcap.com/currencies/coinbase-wrapped-staked-eth/historical-data/)
2. wstETH (https://coinmarketcap.com/currencies/lido-finance-wsteth/)
• there are price drops
• based on data from last 365 days the biggest percentage drop in price occurred also on March 11, 2023, with a drop of approximately 9.28% (https://coinmarketcap.com/currencies/lido-finance-wsteth/historical-data/)
MEDIUM - as it require conditions that needs to be satisfied (observed in advance price drop) and funds which cannot be possed in flash-loan to increase the impact of the vulnerability.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic attack on the Liquid Restaking Token (LRT) called reETH that mixes native ETH with wrapped staking assets such as cbETH or wstETH. The protocol mints reETH based on the current price reported by a price feed, but the price feed only reflects a change after the underlying asset actually drops in value. Because the token is backed by a basket of assets, an attacker who can anticipate a predictable price decline— for example a slashing event or a large withdrawal that depresses the market price of cbETH— can deposit the vulnerable asset just before the drop, receive reETH at the pre‑drop valuation, and later withdraw the same amount of reETH after the price has fallen. By doing so the attacker extracts the loss from the pool, leaving the remaining honest Rio users with a reduced share of the underlying assets. The attack works because the protocol permits users to withdraw any asset from the pool regardless of what they originally deposited, and because there is no lock‑up period or price‑drop detection that would prevent rapid deposit‑withdraw cycles around a known price event. The impact is a direct loss of capital for honest participants; in the illustrative scenario the honest users lose the equivalent of 50 ETH while the attacker ends up with a net gain. The condition for exploitation is the ability to predict or observe an upcoming price drop and to hold enough of the vulnerable asset to influence the pool size; the attack does not require flash loans but can be amplified with sufficient capital. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the accounting logic of mixed‑asset LRTs and identified that the price oracle’s delayed update creates a window where the minting price and redemption price diverge. The problem is subtle because temporary price dips are common in liquid staking markets and the protocol’s accounting appears correct at a glance; only after a withdrawal does the hidden loss become visible to users, who may notice that their reETH balance converts to less ETH than expected or that their redemption yields zero or unexpectedly low amounts. To remediate the flaw the protocol should enforce asset‑specific withdrawals, introduce a minimum holding period between deposit and withdrawal, monitor for large price movements and temporarily pause deposits, or issue separate LRTs for each underlying asset so that a single price shock cannot affect a mixed basket. In essence the bug belongs to the class of “withdraw‑before‑price‑drop” or “oracle‑timing” vulnerabilities that arise when a token’s value is derived from a composite of assets whose prices can change independently and the system does not synchronize minting and redemption prices.

title: Depositing to EigenLayer can revert due to rounding down
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding‑down precision error that occurs when the deposit pool converts an underlying token amount into EigenLayer strategy shares and then back into tokens during a rebalance operation. The root cause is the use of integer division in the conversion functions underlyingToSharesView and sharesToUnderlyingView, which multiply the amount by a virtual total share value and then divide by a virtual token balance that includes small offset constants. Because Solidity integer division always rounds toward zero, the two conversions are not exact inverses when the division does not produce a whole number. In the described scenario, 111 * 1e18 stETH is converted to 107636363636363636364 shares, but converting those shares back yields 110999999999999999999 tokens, one token unit short of the original amount. The deposit routine later checks that the number of shares received from the operator matches the number of shares allocated; the off‑by‑one caused by the rounding mismatch triggers a revert (INCORRECT_NUMBER_OF_SHARES_RECEIVED). This can be exploited by any actor who initiates a deposit that falls into the non‑divisible case, causing the transaction to fail and effectively denying service to users who wish to stake. The impact is that legitimate deposits are rejected, users see no change in their balances, and the protocol may lose liquidity because operators cannot receive new stakes. The issue manifests whenever the token amount is not perfectly divisible by the virtual token balance‑to‑share ratio, which is common given the presence of the offset constants. It affects depositors, operators, and the overall protocol health. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that constructed a concrete numeric example and observed the mismatch, and it is hard to notice because the rounding error is typically a single token unit, which does not appear in high‑level balance checks but only surfaces in the strict equality revert. To fix the problem, the conversion logic should be made mathematically symmetric: either use a rounding‑up method, remove or adjust the offset constants, employ a mulDiv function that preserves precision, or add a tolerance check before the final equality assertion. Ensuring that the share‑to‑token and token‑to‑share conversions are exact or that the contract tolerates the minimal rounding difference will prevent the revert and restore correct deposit functionality.

title: Blacklisted accounts can still transact
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an ineffective blacklist mechanism in an ERC‑20 stablecoin where accounts that have been added to the blacklist continue to be able to send and receive tokens. The root cause is that the contract only implements a hook (_onceBlacklisted) that transfers the entire balance of the blacklisted address to the caller at the moment of blacklisting, but it does not add any validation in the core transfer logic to reject future transfers involving a blacklisted address. Because the internal _update function, which is responsible for moving balances, lacks a check for the blacklist status of the sender or recipient, the blacklist operation becomes a no‑op for ongoing activity. An attacker (or any privileged role) can call addBlackList on a target address, but the target can still execute transfers before the seizure transaction is mined, and can continue to transact afterwards without receiving any revert error. This can be exploited by front‑running the blacklist transaction to move funds out of the target address before the balance seizure occurs, or simply by ignoring the blacklist and continuing normal operations, thereby defeating the intended compliance control. The impact is that the protocol cannot rely on the blacklist to enforce sanctions, allowing sanctioned or malicious accounts to retain full token functionality, which may lead to regulatory violations, loss of trust, and potential financial loss if funds are moved out of compliance‑restricted accounts. The issue manifests whenever the addBlackList function is invoked; any subsequent transfer involving the blacklisted address will succeed because the transfer path does not verify blacklist status. Users, compliance officers, and the protocol itself are affected because the expected behavior (blocked transfers) does not occur, and the UI may misleadingly indicate that an address is blocked while the blockchain still permits activity. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit review of the blacklist implementation, where the auditor noted that the only observable effect was an immediate balance transfer and that no further restrictions were enforced. The problem can be hard to notice because there is no explicit error message; transactions appear normal, and only the balance seizure is visible, which may be interpreted as a successful sanction. To remediate, the contract should incorporate blacklist checks directly in the token’s transfer hook, for example by overriding _update to revert when either the sender or the recipient is listed in the blacklist, thereby ensuring that blacklisted accounts are truly unable to move tokens. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an access‑control bypass or missing validation in a security‑critical function, where a manually administered feature fails to enforce its intended policy, leading to unexpected token movement and a breakdown of accounting assumptions such as “sanctioned accounts cannot transfer”. From a user’s perspective, a blacklisted account may still see outgoing transfers succeed, may receive new tokens despite being flagged, and may notice that their balance can be drained without any error, contrary to the expectation that the contract would block all activity for that address.

title: Not all ERC20 tokens can be bridged because of hardcoded predicate
bug_full: The vulnerability is a hard‑coded predicate address in the BridgeRelay contract that is used when an ERC20 token is transferred to the Polygon bridge. The function transferERCToBridge always approves a single hard‑coded ERC20Predicate contract, regardless of the actual predicate that the bridge expects for the specific token type. The bridge architecture stores a mapping from token type to a predicate address and calls that predicate’s lockTokens method. Because the approval is granted to the wrong predicate, tokens whose legitimate predicate differs from the hard‑coded one cannot be moved by the bridge. When a user initiates a bridge transaction with such a token, the contract zeroes any previous allowance, then increases the allowance only for the hard‑coded predicate. The subsequent deposit call succeeds, but the later lockTokens call fails to transfer the tokens, leaving the tokens permanently locked in the BridgeRelay contract. The issue can be triggered simply by sending any ERC20 that uses a non‑ERC20Predicate, or by a token that later changes its predicate, causing previously bridged funds to become irretrievable. The impact is that users lose access to the bridged assets; the protocol’s accounting assumes that deposited tokens will be transferred to the correct predicate and become available on the destination chain, which is violated. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the bridge code where the constant PREDICATE_ADDRESS was observed. It is hard to notice because the function appears to approve and deposit tokens correctly, and the failure only manifests later when the bridge attempts to lock the tokens. The proper fix is to query the bridge for the token’s type and retrieve the corresponding predicate address at runtime, then approve that predicate instead of the hard‑coded one. This change restores the intended dynamic mapping and prevents tokens from being permanently stuck.

title: The repaying action in BBLeverage.sellCollateral
description:
The sellCollateral function is used to sell a user's collateral to obtain YieldBox shares of the asset and repay the user's loan. However, in the BBLeverage contract, it calls _repay with the from parameter set to the user, even though the asset shares have already been collected by this contract beforehand.
In BBLeverage.sellCollateral, the from variable (user) is used as the repayer address.
Therefore, asset shares of user will be pulled in BBLendingCommon._repay function.
This is incorrect behavior since the necessary asset shares were already collected by the contract in the BBLeverage.sellCollateral function. The repayer address should be address(this) for _repay.
Mistakenly pulling user funds while the received asset shares remain stuck in the contract will result in losses for users who have sufficient allowance and balance when using the BBLeverage.sellCollateral functionality.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the BBLeverage contract's sellCollateral function. After the function swaps a user's collateral for YieldBox asset shares, it immediately calls the internal _repay routine and passes the caller's address as the repayer (the from parameter). Because the asset shares have already been transferred to the BBLeverage contract earlier in the same call, using the user address causes the _repay logic to pull the same shares from the user's wallet a second time. The contract therefore attempts to debit the user for shares that are no longer available, while the previously collected shares remain locked inside the contract. This double‑pull results in a net loss of funds for the user: the loan may be marked as repaid, but the user's balance of YieldBox shares is reduced or becomes zero, and the reclaimed shares are stuck in the contract with no mechanism to return them. The issue occurs whenever a user invokes sellCollateral with sufficient allowance and balance, because the _repay call does not verify that the required shares are already held by the contract. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of assets through sellCollateral and identified the mismatch between the source of repayment and the location of the collected shares. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert and appears successful from a UI perspective; the user sees the loan repayment event but does not notice that their share balance has disappeared. The root cause is a logical error in selecting the repayer address; the correct source should be the contract itself (address(this)) rather than the external user. To remediate, the _repay invocation must be changed to use the contract's address as the from parameter, and additional checks should be added to ensure that shares are not pulled from a user who has already transferred them. This class of bug falls under improper asset accounting and double‑withdrawal due to incorrect caller context, violating the protocol's accounting assumptions that each asset movement is accounted for exactly once.

title: leverageAmount is incorrect in SGLLeverage.sellCollatera
description:
See vulnerability detail
SGLLeverage.sellCollateral function attempts to remove the user's collateral in shares of YieldBox, then withdraws those collateral shares to collect collateral tokens. Subsequently, the received collateral tokens can be used to swap for asset tokens.
However, the leverageAmount variable in this function does not represent the actual withdrawn tokens from the provided shares because it is calculated after the withdrawal.
yieldBox.toAmount after withdrawal may return different from the actual withdrawn token amount, because the states of YieldBox has changed. Because the token amount is calculated with rounding down in YieldBox, leverageAmount will be higher than the actual withdrawn amount.
For example, before the withdrawal, YieldBox had 100 total shares and 109 total tokens.
