In the worst case, in the example above, if Bob opens maker = 40 (adiabatic fees Given that Alice's position is 10 at price = 2 (notional = 20), a loss of -0.4 is a loss of -2% at 1x leverage, which is quite significant.
Individual makers bear an additional undocumented price risk due to adiabatic fees, which is quite significant (can be several percentages of the notional).
bug_full: The protocol introduces adiabatic fees that are intended to net to zero in USD terms across the entire makers pool. In the current implementation the fee exposure adjustment is distributed proportionally to each maker’s position size rather than to each maker’s individual fee exposure. As a result, when multiple makers are active and the market price changes, the total fee adjustment is split evenly by position amount, causing each maker’s collateral to be altered by a component that does not correspond to their own accrued adiabatic fee. The aggregated pool still nets to zero, so the discrepancy is hidden at the global level, but individual makers can experience a net profit or loss that is unrelated to any long or short positions. This effect appears even when there are no open longs or shorts; a maker may see their collateral increase or decrease solely because of the price‑dependent fee redistribution. The loss can be several percent of the notional amount, which is significant for participants expecting only the advertised fee behavior. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit where a test scenario with two makers (Alice and Bob) showed that after a price move from 1 to 2 the combined fee exposure was correctly balanced, yet each maker’s collateral changed in an unexpected direction, leading to a net loss for one of them. The bug is hard to notice because the pool‑level accounting remains correct, masking the per‑user imbalance. The root cause is the weighting of the exposure adjustment by raw position size instead of by each maker’s individual fee exposure. To remediate, the contract should track a separate accumulator for total fee exposure and store each maker’s own exposure in local state, then apply the global adjustment proportionally to the stored individual exposures. This change ensures that the adiabatic fee paid when a maker closes a position exactly offsets the fee received when the position was opened, eliminating the undocumented price risk and preventing individual makers from losing funds due to fee misallocation.

title: Orders on Optimism chains can not be settled
bug_full: The vulnerability is a deprecated function call that breaks fee calculation on Optimism‑compatible chains. After the Ecotone upgrade the OptGasInfo contract at address 0x420000000000000000000000000000000000000F removed support for the scalar() view function. The Kept_Optimism contract still invokes OPT_GAS.scalar() inside its internal _calldataFee routine to compute the L1 data fee as l1BaseFee * scalar / (10 ** …). Because scalar() now reverts with the error message "GasPriceOracle: scalar() is deprecated", any transaction that triggers _calldataFee immediately reverts. This occurs whenever an order settlement attempts to charge the calldata fee on Optimism or Base mainnet, i.e. after the block height where the Ecotone upgrade was activated. From a user perspective the order appears to be submitted but never reaches a settled state; the UI may show a pending or failed status, and the expected refund or execution never happens, leading to the impression that funds have disappeared or that the protocol is unresponsive. The root cause is a hard‑coded dependency on a now‑invalid external contract interface, a classic case of an external‑dependency breakage or deprecated‑API bug. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors executed a Forge test that explicitly called OPT_GAS.scalar() and observed the revert. Because the revert originates deep inside a fee‑calculation helper, the failure can be mistaken for a generic order‑execution error, making it hard to diagnose without inspecting the call stack. The impact is medium severity: core order‑settlement functionality on Optimism‑based chains is non‑functional, preventing users from completing trades and potentially locking funds in the contract until the bug is fixed. The affected parties include any user placing orders on Optimism or Base, the protocol’s order‑matching engine, and any downstream contracts that rely on the Kept_Optimism fee logic. To remediate, the contract should be updated to stop calling the deprecated scalar() function and instead adopt the new fee‑calculation methodology described in the Optimism documentation for the Ecotone upgrade, such as using the L1 base fee directly or the new getL1GasUsed interface without the scalar multiplier. Once the formula is corrected, orders can be settled again and the protocol regains its expected accounting guarantees.

title: All transactions to claim assets from the vault
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the vault’s asset‑claim routine, where the contract incorrectly subtracts the amount a user is withdrawing (the "withdrawal") twice when it computes the vault’s total assets after a claim. The function that determines the assets that are ineligible for redemption adds the withdrawal value at the end of its calculation, and this value is also subtracted earlier as part of the collateral adjustment. As a result the derived assets figure is smaller than the real amount held by the vault. When the mis‑computed assets drop below the protocol‑defined minimum assets threshold (minAssets), the contract triggers a revert (StrategyLibInsufficientAssetsError) even though the user is only trying to claim already‑redeemed funds. This double‑counting error becomes visible only in a specific market condition: if one of the underlying markets has a high long‑short skew that forces the maker position to sit at the market’s minimum position, a large redemption can push the vault’s position to that limit. After that point any further claim – even for users who have already redeemed – will hit the assets‑under‑minimum check and revert, effectively locking all users’ funds in the contract. The issue was uncovered during an audit by reproducing a failing claim in an integration test that simulated a market with a constrained maker position. It is hard to notice from a UI perspective because the transaction simply fails with a generic error, giving the impression that the claim function is broken rather than that the accounting logic is flawed. Users experience the symptom of “my claim transaction reverts, I receive nothing, my balance stays the same” which contradicts the expectation that a claim should always succeed once assets are redeemed. The bug belongs to the class of accounting miscalculations caused by double‑counting of a variable, leading to insufficient‑asset checks. The proper remediation is to remove the extra addition of the withdrawal amount from the ineligible‑assets calculation, ensuring that assets are only reduced once for the claimed amount and that the minAssets guard reflects the true vault balance. By correcting the formula the vault will allow legitimate claims and prevent permanent or temporary fund lock‑up.

title: If referral or liquidator is the same address
bug_full: The vulnerability is that when the same address is used as both the market participant and the liquidator or referral, the fees that should be added to the participant’s claimable balance are silently discarded during the settlement routine. The contract loads the participant’s local state into a temporary memory struct (context.local), then during settlement it calls an internal _credit function that writes the liquidationFee and referralFee into the storage mapping _locals[account].claimable. However the mapping entry that was loaded earlier is cached in memory and later written back to storage by _storeContext, which overwrites the entire local struct with the original copy that does not contain the newly increased claimable amount. As a result the fees are effectively lost: they are subtracted from the user’s collateral but never become withdrawable. The bug occurs only when the fee recipient is the same address that is being settled, i.e., self‑liquidation or self‑referral. Any other participant receives the fees correctly because their local struct is not overwritten. The impact is that users can unintentionally forfeit the incentive fees that should compensate them for liquidating or referring, leading to a reduction of their withdrawable balance and a permanent lock of those tokens inside the contract. From a user’s perspective the UI would show that a liquidation was performed and that a fee was supposed to be earned, but the claimable balance remains zero, creating confusion and the impression that “funds disappeared”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the test suite demonstrated that after a self‑liquidation the claimable field stayed at zero despite the contract logic that should have credited it. The problem is subtle because the credit operation appears to succeed and no event is emitted indicating a failure; the loss only becomes visible after the settlement transaction finishes and the state is read again. The root cause is the ordering of state updates: the contract writes the updated local struct back to storage after the settlement logic has already modified the claimable field, thereby discarding the modification. The class of bug is a state‑caching or stale‑memory overwrite bug, common in contracts that keep a copy of storage in memory and later overwrite it without merging incremental changes. The recommended fix is to adjust the internal credit routine so that when the recipient address matches the account whose local state is being stored, the claimable increase is applied directly to the context.local struct before it is written back, ensuring the fee is persisted. Alternatively, the contract could avoid caching the whole local struct or could merge the pending claimable changes into the cached copy before persisting.

title: _loadContext() uses the wrong pendingGlobal.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect source of pending order data inside the strategy library function that builds the market context for a rebalance operation. The function retrieves a variable named pendingGlobal by calling registration.market.pendings(address(this)), which actually returns the pending orders that belong to the strategy contract itself (a local pending view). The intended data is the global pending order book, which should be obtained via registration.market.pending(). Because the function uses the local pending view, the subsequent calculations of currentPosition, minPosition and maxPosition are based on stale or incomplete information. This mis‑calculation propagates to the rebalance logic, causing the target position to be derived from wrong bounds. In practice the protocol may attempt to rebalance with a position that is either too large or too small, violating risk limits, exposing the market to unintended leverage, or simply failing to execute a needed trade. The bug manifests whenever the _loadContext routine is invoked, typically at the start of each rebalance cycle, and therefore affects every strategy that relies on this library. Users of the market see the expected balances on‑chain, but the strategy may submit orders that do not match the actual market state, leading to symptoms such as “my trade size is zero”, “the strategy does not adjust my position”, or “unexpected loss of capital”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the auditor noticed that the pending order query used the contract’s own address instead of the global view, a subtle logic error that does not raise compiler warnings and can be easily missed in testing because the contract’s local pending state may often be empty, making the bug appear harmless until a rebalance is triggered. The class of bug is an incorrect state derivation caused by confusing local versus global data sources, a common pattern in financial smart contracts where accounting assumptions rely on precise market snapshots. To remediate the problem the function should be changed to call registration.market.pending() so that the global pending order book is used, and the downstream position calculations will then reflect the true market state, restoring correct rebalance behavior and preserving protocol safety.

title: Large amount of points can STILL be minted
description:
Out that the points could be minted without any cost, this issue still remains, and now the attacker can prevent other users from earning points. Following attack to mint a large number of points:
1. Deposit liquidity
2. After a short amount of time, withdraw it
3. Repeat the attack, minting a huge amount of points
This attack can still be executed to mint a large number of points at almost no cost. On the minted points. Even though this mitigation would reduce the profit of an attacker, it won't prevent the attacker from minting the maximum amount of points until the rate limit is reached.
Moreover, an attacker could use the rate limit to prevent other users from minting points. By constantly depositing and withdrawing liquidity, it would mint all points for himself until the rate limit is reached. Then, when other innocent users deposit liquidity or make trades, they won't receive any points.
The attacker can still mint a large amount of points, and prevent other users from receiving them.
bug_full: An attacker can repeatedly deposit liquidity and withdraw it in rapid succession to trigger the contract's point‑minting logic without incurring any cost. The contract awards points on each withdrawal based on a fixed formula and does not charge a fee, so each cycle creates new points out of thin air. Because the system only enforces a global rate‑limit on the total number of points that can be minted in a given period, the attacker can continue the deposit‑withdraw loop until that limit is reached, accumulating a large balance of points at almost zero expense. Once the limit is exhausted, any subsequent legitimate user who deposits liquidity or performs a trade will find that no points are credited to their account, effectively starving them of rewards. The vulnerability originates from the combination of (1) a reward‑minting mechanism that does not require any payment or collateral when liquidity is withdrawn, and (2) a rate‑limit that caps total points but does not differentiate between honest users and malicious actors. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward calculation path and identified that the withdrawal function calls the mint routine without any cost check. Because the contract appears to work correctly under normal conditions, the problem can be subtle: users see normal point accrual until an attacker repeatedly triggers the minting loop, at which point the reward balance for honest participants abruptly stops increasing. The impact includes inflation of the point supply, loss of economic incentives for genuine participants, and potential reputational damage to the protocol if users perceive that rewards are being hoarded by a single entity. The attack can be carried out with minimal gas costs, making it economically viable. Mitigation requires either reducing the amount of points minted on withdrawal, introducing a withdrawal fee that is collected even when the liquidity provider is the last one in the market, or redesigning the reward logic to tie point creation to actual economic activity rather than to a free withdrawal event. By ensuring that each minted point is backed by a proportional contribution or fee, the protocol can prevent unlimited point creation and protect honest users from being locked out of rewards.

title: Code asymmetry of
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency caused by asymmetric handling of the globalPositions.marginDepositedTotal variable across two core functions of the vault contract. In the settleFundingFees function the protocol deliberately adds the net funding fee to marginDepositedTotal, allowing the value to become negative when the accrued funding exceeds the total margin deposited by traders. The code comment even acknowledges this possibility, expecting a later liquidation to restore the balance to a positive amount. By contrast, the updateGlobalPositionData function enforces a non‑negative invariant: if the computed newMarginDepositedTotal would be below zero it is forced to zero. This mismatch creates a state‑invariant violation. An attacker (or any user, because settleFundingFees is permissionless) can trigger settleFundingFees when funding fees are larger than the existing margin, pushing marginDepositedTotal into the negative region. If a subsequent transaction updates global position data without performing a liquidation – for example an order placement, adjustment, or closure – the clamping logic will silently reset the negative total to zero, effectively erasing the deficit. Later, when a liquidation finally occurs, the liquidation module supplies a positive marginDelta that compensates the previously erased negative amount, causing marginDepositedTotal to be increased by the amount of the erased deficit. The net result is an inflated marginDepositedTotal that is not backed by any real collateral. From the user’s perspective the liquidity provider may see an unexpected credit or a sudden increase in their claimable collateral, while traders may observe their margin being “restored” after a loss, and the protocol’s total ETH balance can appear correct even though assets have been mis‑allocated. The impact is a breach of accounting integrity that can lead to loss of assets for liquidity providers and a broken economic model for the protocol. The issue manifests whenever funding fees exceed the total trader margin and liquidation does not immediately follow the fee settlement – a situation that can arise under normal market volatility. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the two functions and identified the contradictory treatment of negative totals. The bug is subtle because the protocol eventually restores a positive balance, masking the intermediate inconsistency, and because the variable is internal and not directly exposed to users. The proper remediation is to enforce a consistent policy for marginDepositedTotal: either forbid negative values in all code paths and adjust fee settlement logic accordingly, or allow negatives everywhere and remove the zero‑clamping in updateGlobalPositionData, adding explicit checks to prevent unintended inflation. Aligning the invariant across the contract eliminates the accounting error and restores correct asset accounting.

title: Attacker can steal LPs funds by using differ-
description:
Prevent the attack path described there, but a malicious LP can steal funds using a similar attack path.
The attack path is as follows:
1. The attacker has some liquidity deposited as an LP with address A.
2. The attacker announces the withdrawal of all liquidity with address A.
3. In the same txn, the attacker announces the deposit of liquidity (same amount as the withdrawal) with address B.
4. After the minimum execution time has elapsed, retrieve two prices from the Pyth oracle where the second price is lower than the first one.
5. Execute the withdrawal of address A sending the higher price.
6. Execute the deposit of address B sending the lower price.
As a result, the attacker will have the same deposited liquidity in the protocol, plus a profit from the price deviation.
Even though the withdrawal may reduce the profits of this attack, it doesn't completely prevent it. Moreover, if the attacker is the only LP on the market, there's not going to be a withdrawal fee, increasing the profits of such an attack at the expense of the traders.
The requirements of this attack are the same as the ones described in the original issue, hence the medium severity.
Another possible strategy would pass through the following steps:
• Create a leverage position.
• Announce another leverage position with the same size.
• In the same block, announce a limit close order.
• After the minimum execution time has elapsed, retrieve two prices from the Pyth oracle where the second price is lower than the first one.
• Execute the limit close order sending the first price.
• Execute the open order sending the second price.
The result in this case is having a position with the same size as the original one, but having either lowered the position.lastPrice or getting a profit from the original position, depending on how the price has moved since the original position was opened.
I don't have access to the exact pull request of the fix but I'm pretty sure the attack path described above is still feasible.
Different oracle prices can be fetched in the same transaction, which can be used to create arbitrage opportunities that can make a profit with no risk at the expense of users on the other side of the trade.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a cross‑price manipulation flaw that allows a liquidity provider (LP) to extract value from the protocol by exploiting the fact that the contract reads oracle prices independently for withdrawal and deposit operations within the same transaction or block. The root cause is that the protocol does not enforce a single, immutable price reference for the entire execution window; it permits two separate calls to the Pyth oracle after the minimum execution time has elapsed, and it applies the first (higher) price to the withdrawal of the attacker’s original liquidity while applying the second (lower) price to a newly announced deposit under a different address. An attacker can therefore announce a full withdrawal of their LP position, simultaneously announce a deposit of the same amount under a fresh address, wait for the oracle to update to a lower price, and then execute the withdrawal using the stale higher price and the deposit using the new lower price. The result is that the attacker retains the original liquidity amount and also pockets the price differential as profit. This attack works especially when the attacker is the sole LP, because no withdrawal fee is charged, maximizing the net gain. The impact is a loss of funds for other market participants, distorted pricing for traders, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees that the value of deposited liquidity should be conserved. The flaw manifests only when the oracle price can change between the two reads within the same block and when the contract allows the attacker to schedule both withdrawal and deposit in the same transaction without price locking. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the ordering of oracle reads and the withdrawal/deposit flow. The issue is subtle because price updates are a normal part of the system, so a divergent price read may not raise an alarm, and the profit appears as a legitimate LP gain rather than an obvious theft. To remediate, the protocol should bind a single price reference for the entire execution period, prevent multiple oracle reads from being used in a single settlement cycle, enforce a minimum time lock that disallows price changes between withdrawal and deposit, or apply a consistent price snapshot across all LP state transitions. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of oracle‑price‑inconsistency and same‑block manipulation vulnerabilities that break the invariant that a user’s deposited value cannot be increased without providing equivalent value to the system.

title: L1 data fees are not reimbursed
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a systematic omission of L1 data fee reimbursement in the OpenRelay (and similarly in Keep3r) implementation on Optimism and other roll‑up chains. The contract records the amount of L2 gas consumed with gasleft(), multiplies it by block.basefee and a fixed multiplier, and then pays the relayer only that amount. On Optimism, publishing calldata from L2 to L1 incurs a separate L1 data fee that can be orders of magnitude larger than the L2 gas cost. Because the reimbursement formula does not include this fee, the relayer receives far less than the actual cost of executing the job. As a result, relayers are economically disincentivised to submit transactions, causing automation jobs to remain pending for hours or indefinitely. Users expecting timely execution, such as order closures on an exchange, experience missing refunds, zero balances, or stuck orders, which translates into potential loss of funds. The issue appears only when a job is executed on a chain where L1 data fees are significant; it was discovered during an audit by comparing the total transaction cost (≈0.000305 ETH) with the reimbursed amount (≈0.00000009 ETH) and noting that the L1 data fee (≈0.000304 ETH) was never accounted for. The problem is subtle because transaction receipts normally highlight gas used, while L1 data fees are hidden in the calldata cost, making the under‑payment easy to overlook. To remediate, the payment calculation must be extended to add the L1 data fee using the appropriate per‑chain formula (for Optimism, the fee can be obtained from the L2‑to‑L1 message receipt) and then include it in the FeeData sent to the automation vault. This change restores economic parity, ensures jobs are executed promptly, and aligns the protocol with its promise of reimbursing all execution costs.

title: Keep3r Relay Implementations are Not Com-
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the Keep3r relay contracts (Keep3rRelay and Keep3rBondedRelay) and the Keep3r side‑chain implementation deployed on Optimism. Keep3r’s side‑chain contract deprecates the original worked(address) function and replaces it with a new worked(address _keeper, uint256 _usdPerGasUnit) that requires a USD‑per‑gas‑unit parameter for accurate reward calculation. The relay contracts, however, still encode and invoke the old selector worked(address) when they build the ExecData structure for a keeper’s execution. Because the side‑chain contract deliberately reverts any call to the deprecated signature, every exec() call issued by a keeper on Optimism triggers a revert. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that compared the ABI of the relay contracts with the side‑chain Keep3r implementation and observed the explicit revert in the deprecated function. It is subtle because the contracts compile without errors and the vault creation transaction succeeds, giving the impression that the job is correctly registered. From a user’s perspective, a keeper sees a job appear in the UI, attempts to execute it, and receives a transaction failure with no reward; the protocol’s accounting shows the job as pending while no work is actually performed, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service and potentially leaving funds unclaimed. The impact is medium severity: keepers cannot earn rewards, jobs remain unexecuted, and the protocol’s incentive model is broken on the side‑chain, which may lead to reduced participation or loss of value for users relying on automated execution. The root cause is an interface incompatibility: the relay contracts were not updated to match the new function signature required by the side‑chain Keep3r contract. To remediate, the relay should be modified to call the new worked(address,uint256) selector, passing an appropriate usdPerGasUnit value, or a compatibility shim should be added that forwards the old call to the new function. Alternatively, the protocol could avoid using Keep3r on side‑chains until a compatible version is deployed. The bug belongs to the class of “incompatible interface / deprecated function call” errors that cause runtime reverts and break business logic expectations such as reward distribution and job execution.

title: Donating (and syncing) tokens to an Aero-
description:
An attacker can bypass the exposure limits by donating tokens to an Aerodrome pool in which he owns ~100% of the liquidity, this will inflate reserves which will increase the value of the collateral and the attacker won't lose capital because he owns ~100% of the liquidity.
Attack scenario:
1. Create a new Aerodrome pool, let's suppose an STG/WETH pool
2. Provide liquidity to the pool and mint LPs, let's suppose we mint ~1000$ worth of liquidity
3. Deposit the LP in an Arcadia account, the collateral is worth ~1000$
4. Send STG and WETH directly to the Aerodrome pool, let's suppose we send ~500_000$ worth of tokens
5. Call sync() on the Aerodrome pool
6. The pool reserves are increased and the collateral is now worth ~501_000$ use of any volatile Aerodrome pool LPs as collateral, as long as the underlying tokens are allowed.
An attacker can bypass the exposure limits set by a creditor.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inflation of collateral value caused by the ability to manipulate the reserve accounting of an Aerodrome liquidity pool through direct token transfers followed by a call to the pool’s sync() function. The root cause lies in the pool’s design, which updates its internal reserve balances solely based on the token balances held by the contract, without verifying that the tokens were added through the official addLiquidity flow or that the caller owns a proportional share of the liquidity. An attacker can exploit this by first creating a new pool, providing a small amount of liquidity and receiving the corresponding LP tokens, then depositing those LP tokens as collateral in a lending protocol such as Arcadia. Because the attacker controls almost all of the LP supply, they can subsequently send a large amount of the underlying tokens directly to the pool contract, bypassing the normal minting process, and invoke sync(). The sync call forces the pool to recount its reserves, which now include the freshly transferred tokens, inflating the reported reserve values. As the value of the LP tokens is derived from these reserves, the attacker’s collateral appears to have grown from roughly $1,000 to over $500,000, allowing them to borrow far beyond the exposure limits set by the creditor. This attack can be carried out on any Aerodrome pool whose underlying assets are accepted as collateral, and it requires the attacker to own an overwhelming share of the LP tokens so that the inflated reserve value is attributed almost entirely to their position. From a user’s perspective, a lender would see a borrower’s collateral suddenly jump to a very high amount while the actual liquidity in the pool remains unchanged, leading to a false sense of security and potentially resulting in the borrower withdrawing the inflated assets and leaving the pool under‑collateralized. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between Aerodrome pool mechanics and Arcadia’s collateral valuation logic; it is subtle because the sync function is publicly callable and token transfers to the pool are not restricted, making the abnormal reserve growth appear as a legitimate state change. To remediate the problem, the protocol should enforce that reserve updates only reflect liquidity added through the pool’s official addLiquidity interface, restrict who can call sync or make it internal, and/or adjust the collateral valuation to consider the proportion of LP tokens actually backed by genuine liquidity rather than raw reserve numbers. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “reserve‑inflation via unsanctioned token injection” vulnerabilities that break accounting assumptions and enable borrowers to bypass risk controls.

title: Swapping large amounts of assets back and
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the WrappedAerodromeAM contract evaluates the value of a wrapped Aerodrome liquidity‑provider (LP) position when it is used as collateral in an Arcadia account. The wrapper extracts the amount of LP tokens that were originally deposited and adds the two fee counters (fee0Position and fee1Position) that represent trading fees accumulated by the underlying Aerodrome pool. Because these fee counters are read directly from the pool at the moment the collateral value is queried, an attacker who controls the entire liquidity of a newly created Aerodrome pool can repeatedly swap large volumes back and forth inside that pool after the LP position has already been deposited as collateral. Each swap generates additional fees, which increase the fee counters, and consequently the reported collateral value rises even though no extra LP tokens have been added. The protocol’s exposure‑limit checks rely on this reported collateral value, so the inflated figure allows the attacker to borrow more assets than the intended limit would permit. The attack can be performed indefinitely, limited only by gas costs, and does not require any external contracts or privileged permissions beyond ownership of the pool’s liquidity. From a user’s perspective the collateral balance appears to grow automatically, and the borrowing capacity suddenly expands, contradicting the expectation that only the amount of LP tokens originally supplied determines exposure. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors noticed that the wrapper’s valuation logic does not snapshot the fee amounts at deposit time, allowing post‑deposit fee accrual to affect collateral. This behavior is subtle because fee accumulation is a normal and expected outcome of trading, making it easy to overlook that the value of already‑deposited collateral can be artificially inflated. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “dynamic collateral valuation” bugs where on‑chain accounting assumes that a collateral’s value is static after deposit, but the contract mistakenly treats mutable state (such as accrued fees) as part of the immutable collateral. To remediate the problem the protocol should either snapshot the fee counters at the moment the LP is wrapped, ignore fee accrual when computing exposure limits, or impose a cap on how much the collateral value can increase after deposit, following the safety guard already implemented for UniswapV3 positions. Implementing such a guard would prevent attackers from repeatedly swapping to generate fees and thereby bypassing exposure limits, restoring the intended risk model of the Arcadia system.

title: WrappedAerodromeAM.sol is not compatible
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the WrappedAerodromeAM contract’s decreaseLiquidity and claimFees functions, which unconditionally attempt to transfer fee amounts to the position owner using ERC20.safeTransfer. The code assumes that transferring a zero‑value amount is always a no‑op, but some ERC20 implementations deliberately revert when the transfer amount is zero (a “revert on zero transfer” token). This mismatch creates a denial‑of‑service condition: when the calculated fee for a position is zero, the safeTransfer call reverts, causing the entire decreaseLiquidity transaction to fail. As a result, the user who initiates the call receives a transaction revert instead of the expected fee payout, and the liquidity that should have been withdrawn remains locked in the pool. The issue is triggered whenever a position’s pending fees are zero or when the underlying token implements the zero‑transfer revert behaviour, which can happen naturally for newly opened positions or after fee collection. All users holding positions in the affected pool are impacted because they cannot decrease liquidity or claim fees, effectively freezing their assets. The problem was identified during a manual audit that referenced the README’s note about “weird behaviours” of minimal ERC20 tokens and verified that the contract does not guard against zero‑value transfers. It is subtle because most popular tokens accept zero transfers, so developers often overlook the need for an explicit check. The correct mitigation is to guard each transfer with a condition that the amount is non‑zero before invoking safeTransfer, thereby aligning the contract’s logic with the token’s transfer semantics and restoring the ability for users to withdraw liquidity and receive fees as intended. This class of bug falls under improper handling of edge‑case token behaviours and can be described as a zero‑value transfer revert leading to a denial‑of‑service in fee‑payout functions.

title: distributeYield() calls earningsTrancheuse()
bug_full: The contract’s distributeYield function calculates the protocol’s yield and then calls earningsTrancheuse to split that yield between senior and junior tranche holders. However, the exponential moving average variables emaSTT and emaJTT, which are required to compute the target yield and the senior‑proportion, are only refreshed after earningsTrancheuse returns. As a result the yield‑splitting logic runs with stale EMA values that reflect the supply state of the previous distribution period instead of the current adjusted supplies. This ordering mistake creates a classic stale‑state accounting bug: the senior and junior tranche allocations are based on an outdated view of token supply, so when the supply of junior tranche tokens changes because of defaults or new loans, the protocol may over‑pay one tranche and under‑pay the other. The impact is a mis‑allocation of yield that can lead to junior holders receiving less than their entitled share or, conversely, receiving more than they should, while senior holders may be over‑compensated. The error manifests each time a distribution occurs after a change in the adjusted supplies within the EMA look‑back window (approximately 2.5 months). All participants who rely on the promised APY – senior and junior tranche investors as well as the protocol’s revenue model – are affected because the accounting assumptions that the yield target is based on the current EMA are violated. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that inspected the call order and noticed that emaSTT and emaJTT are updated only after the call to earningsTrancheuse. It is hard to spot in testing because the transaction does not revert and the YieldDistributed event is emitted, so the contract appears to work, but the numbers are subtly wrong. The proper fix is to update the EMA values before invoking earningsTrancheuse, either by moving the ema update statements above the call or by calculating the fresh EMA locally and passing it to the tranche‑splitting logic. This ensures that the yield distribution uses the correct, up‑to‑date supply data and restores the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Forwarding yield in OCL_ZVE is possible a lot
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the periodic yield forwarding mechanism of the OCL_ZVE contract. The function forwardYield is intended to be callable only once every thirty days, enforced by a require statement that checks block.timestamp against a stored timestamp called nextYieldDistribution (or a 12‑hour earlier value for keepers). However, nextYieldDistribution is initially zero and is only set to a future value when pushToLockerMulti is executed for the first time. If forwardYield is called before any function that initializes nextYieldDistribution, the require condition passes because block.timestamp is always greater than zero. After the call, the contract increments nextYieldDistribution by a fixed 30‑day offset (nextYieldDistribution += 30 days) rather than setting it relative to the current block timestamp. Since the initial value was zero, the new value becomes exactly thirty days after the Unix epoch, which is far in the past compared to the current block.timestamp. Consequently, the timestamp check remains true on every subsequent block, allowing forwardYield to be invoked repeatedly. The exploit consists of repeatedly calling forwardYield, which may trigger the internal _forwardYield logic when the fetched amount exceeds the stored basis, or at least repeatedly update the nextYieldDistribution counter without any real yield being distributed. This breaks the protocol’s accounting assumptions that yield should be distributed at most once per month, leading to potential over‑payment, unexpected token balances for users, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s economic model. The issue manifests when a user or keeper observes that yield can be forwarded many times in quick succession, contrary to the documented behavior; UI dashboards may show repeated reward events, balances increasing unexpectedly, or a lack of the expected 30‑day cooldown. The bug was discovered during a security audit when a test loop repeatedly called forwardYield and observed that the timestamp condition never blocked further calls. It is subtle because the require statement appears correct at first glance, and the increment of nextYieldDistribution seems harmless; however, the special‑case initialization to zero creates a loophole that bypasses the intended timing guard. To remediate, the contract should either prevent forwardYield from executing when nextYieldDistribution is zero, initialize nextYieldDistribution to block.timestamp + 30 days at deployment, or replace the incremental update with an assignment that always sets nextYieldDistribution to the current block.timestamp plus the required interval, thereby guaranteeing that the next call cannot occur before the intended period has elapsed.

title: When APR late rate is lower than APR, an OCC
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the settlement logic of a bullet‑style loan in the OCC_Modular contract. In a bullet loan the borrower only repays periodic interest and the principal at the final term. The contract provides a callLoan function that allows the borrower (or an authorized locker) to settle the entire loan in a single transaction. callLoan obtains the amount owed by invoking amountOwed once and then transfers the principal, the interest for the current interval, and a single late‑fee amount calculated for that interval only. Because amountOwed does not aggregate late fees accrued over all missed intervals, the total interest component is limited to the interest of the most recent interval while the late‑fee component reflects only one interval’s penalty. When the loan’s APR (annual percentage rate) is higher than the APRLateFee rate, a borrower who lets the loan fall many intervals behind can invoke callLoan after a long delay and pay substantially less interest than is actually owed, covering the shortfall with only a small late‑fee charge. This situation can occur whenever the loan is in the Active state, the payment schedule is bullet (paymentSchedule == 0), the borrower is still allowed to call callLoan, and the underwriter does not move the loan to Default despite the overdue status. The impact is a loss of expected interest revenue for the protocol and a breach of the accounting assumptions that interest accrues each interval. From the user’s perspective the UI may indicate that the loan is fully repaid, while the protocol’s balance shows a missing amount of interest; the borrower receives a “settled” status even though they have effectively avoided paying most of the interest. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the normal payment flow with the callLoan shortcut and observed that the total amount transferred in the latter case was lower than the sum of all interval interests. It is hard to notice because the callLoan function appears to settle the loan correctly and emits an event with the total amount, but the underlying calculation silently omits earlier late fees. The bug belongs to the class of “incomplete accrual calculation” or “partial settlement under‑payment” vulnerabilities, where a financial contract fails to aggregate all accrued obligations before settlement. To remediate, the protocol should either prohibit callLoan when the loan is overdue and more than one payment interval remains, or modify amountOwed (or a dedicated settlement routine) to compute the cumulative interest and late‑fee amounts for all missed intervals before allowing a full repayment. This ensures that borrowers cannot bypass the intended interest schedule and that the protocol receives the full amount owed according to its business logic.

title: Rewards are calculated as distributed even if
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the reward‑distribution contracts that causes reward tokens to be considered distributed during periods when no users are staking, even though the contract never actually transfers those tokens to any participant. The root cause is that the contract updates the global timestamp used for reward accrual regardless of whether the total staked supply (_totalSupply) is zero, while it deliberately skips updating the cumulative reward rate only when the supply is zero. Because the timestamp continues to advance, the reward calculation assumes that a certain amount of rewards has been earned for the elapsed time. When a reward deposit is made while the pool is empty, the deposited tokens are transferred into the contract but the accounting logic does not credit any future staker with those tokens; instead the accrued reward amount is recorded as if it had been paid out to a non‑existent user. Consequently the deposited tokens become permanently locked in the contract and are never added to the reward pool for later periods. This can be exploited by anyone who can trigger a reward deposit before any stake exists – the deposited tokens will be lost forever, reducing the total incentive pool and potentially allowing a malicious actor to lock away competitor’s reward tokens. The impact is that stakers receive less than the advertised reward, the protocol loses valuable token balances, and users may see a non‑zero residual balance in the contract after withdrawing all earned rewards, which appears as “missing” or “locked” funds. The condition occurs whenever depositReward is called while the staking pool is empty, which can happen during contract initialization, after a complete withdrawal of all stakes, or any time the pool temporarily has zero participants. All users who later stake and withdraw are affected because part of the reward they expect is permanently unavailable. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that added a test case where a reward was deposited two days before any stake; after a full staking cycle the contract still held a small amount of the reward token, confirming that the funds were locked. The bug is subtle because the contract’s external behavior (successful deposits, withdrawals, and balance updates) looks normal, and only a detailed accounting check reveals the leftover tokens. To remediate, the contract should either (1) avoid transferring reward tokens on each deposit and instead require the contract to hold sufficient balance before distribution, as done in the original Synthetix implementation, or (2) modify the timestamp update logic to skip accrual when the total supply is zero, ensuring that no reward is considered earned during empty periods. This correction restores the invariant that all deposited rewards are either claimable by stakers or remain available for future distribution, eliminating the permanent loss of funds.

title: EMA Data Point From Unlock Is Discarded
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the exponential moving average (EMA) calculation used for the STT and JTT yield distribution. During an unlock operation the contract stores the current totalSupply values as the first EMA data point (emaSTT and emaJTT). The distributionCounter is incremented before being supplied to the MATH.ema() function, so on the first call to distributeYield the function receives N = 1. With N = 1 the EMA formula reduces to returning only the latest value (cV) and discarding the previously stored data point (bV). As a result the EMA used for the first yield distribution does not incorporate the unlock data point, producing an incorrect EMA value and consequently an inaccurate yield amount. This error manifests only on the first distribution after an unlock, meaning that users who have just unlocked their tokens may receive a smaller reward than the protocol intends, or in some cases receive no reward at all. The bug was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor examined the interaction between unlock, distributionCounter and the EMA helper and noticed that the first data point was never averaged. Because the EMA function itself looks mathematically sound, the loss of the initial observation is subtle and may go unnoticed unless specific edge‑case tests are performed. The impact is a breach of the accounting assumptions of the protocol: the protocol assumes that the EMA reflects all historical supply values, but the calculation violates this assumption, leading to mis‑allocation of yield and potential loss of trust. The affected parties are token holders of STT and JTT, the protocol’s reward logic, and any downstream contracts that rely on the reported EMA. To remediate the issue the distributionCounter (or the value passed to the EMA function) should be adjusted so that the first call uses N = 2, or the EMA helper should be rewritten to treat the initial data point correctly. Renaming the counter to reflect that it represents the number of observations rather than the number of distributions would also improve clarity. After the fix the EMA will correctly average the unlock data point with subsequent supply values, ensuring that users receive the yield they are entitled to and that the protocol’s accounting remains sound.

title: ZivoeTranches#rewardZVEJuniorDepositfunction
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward calculation logic of the ZivoeTranches contract for both junior and senior deposits. The function determines a reward rate (avgRate) by first computing the average of the pre‑deposit and post‑deposit junior‑to‑senior supply ratios (avgRatio) and then selecting a rate from a piecewise linear incentive curve that is bounded by lowerRatioIncentiveBIPS and upperRatioIncentiveBIPS. When a deposit causes the ratio to cross one of these bounds, the algorithm still uses the average ratio to pick a single rate, effectively applying either the maximum or minimum rate to the whole deposit. Because the incentive curve is not linear across the breakpoint, the average‑ratio approximation does not represent the true marginal rates that would apply to each infinitesimal portion of the deposit. Consequently, a single large deposit can yield a different total reward than the sum of rewards from several smaller deposits that together amount to the same total amount. In the example where juniorSupply is initially zero, a 2000‑unit deposit receives a reward of 800 ZVE, while two consecutive 1000‑unit deposits receive 400 and 300 ZVE respectively, totalling only 700 ZVE. This discrepancy means the protocol may over‑pay (or under‑pay) relative to its intended incentive schedule, leading to a loss of funds for the protocol or an unfair advantage for a depositor who splits the deposit. The issue manifests whenever the deposit moves the supply ratio across the lower or upper incentive thresholds, which can happen for both junior and senior tranche deposits. It affects any user who interacts with the deposit functions as well as the overall protocol treasury that holds the ZVE tokens used for rewards. The flaw was uncovered during a manual audit by examining the mathematical relationship between the ratio and the reward rate and testing edge cases where the ratio traverses the incentive bounds. Because the function is marked view and appears to return a deterministic value, the inconsistency is subtle and may be missed by superficial testing that does not consider boundary‑crossing scenarios. To remediate the problem, the reward calculation should be rewritten to account for the piecewise nature of the incentive curve: the deposit amount must be split into portions that stay within each segment, or the algorithm should integrate the marginal rate over the entire interval, thereby applying the correct rate to each portion of the deposit. This change restores the intended linear relationship between deposited amount and reward and prevents unintended over‑ or under‑payment.

title: Time calculation issues with exponential de-
description: OCE_ZVE is a locker that distributes rewards based on a exponential decay model. When a distribution starts, the whole balance of the contract should be unclaimable. As time moves forward, more and more of it should be unlocked for distributing. The calculations are made using the lastDistribution variable which is initially set in the constructor and then changed on each distribution. This is problematic because the "idle" periods where no distribution is happening will be considered as passed time when a real distribution starts. In the constructor, the lastDistribution variable is set to block.timestamp. lastDistribution = block.timestamp; When forwardEmissions() gets called, the calculation block.timestamp - lastDistribution will return a large value because the timer has started at the time of deployment. function forwardEmissions() external nonReentrant { uint zveBalance = IERC20(IZivoeGlobals_OCE_ZVE(GBL).ZVE()).balanceOf(address(this)); _forwardEmissions(zveBalance - decay(zveBalance, block.timestamp - lastDistribution)); lastDistribution = block.timestamp; } As we can see in the Figma file, the OCE locker will be deployed at Phase One and funding will start after ITO ends, which is at least 30 days. This results in a wrong calculation and instead of decaying, a big amount of the rewards can be forwarded as soon as the distribution starts. The issue persists for further distributions also. If distribution 1 ends on 1 January months will be claimable from the very beginning. Clearing the timestamp before a distribution starts is not an option because it requires at least 100e18 assets to be forwarded. require(amount >= 100 ether, "OCE_ZVE::_forwardEmissions amount < 100 ether"); Instead of decaying, a big part of the rewards is claimable from the beginning.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a time‑calculation flaw in a reward locker that uses an exponential decay schedule to gradually unlock tokens. The contract stores the timestamp of the last distribution in a variable that is set to the block timestamp at deployment. Because the locker is deployed long before the first distribution – often weeks after an ITO – the idle period is mistakenly counted as elapsed time when forwardEmissions() is called for the first time. The function computes the amount to unlock as the current balance minus the decay of the balance over (block.timestamp‑lastDistribution). When lastDistribution still reflects the deployment time, the subtraction yields a very large interval, causing the decay function to return a near‑zero value and the contract to forward almost the entire reward balance immediately. An attacker or any caller can therefore trigger forwardEmissions after the idle period and claim a disproportionate share of rewards far earlier than the protocol intends. The impact is that users receive a large lump‑sum of tokens instead of a smooth, time‑based release, breaking the economic model, potentially draining the reward pool, and undermining trust in the protocol. The issue manifests only when there is a gap between contract deployment and the first legitimate distribution, which is the expected workflow for this locker (deployment in Phase One, funding after at least 30 days). It affects all participants who rely on the gradual vesting – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – because the accounting assumptions about how much is claimable at any moment are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s state‑transition logic; it is subtle because the forwardEmissions function appears to work correctly after the first call, and the large initial unlock can be mistaken for a legitimate reward spike. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a huge balance becoming claimable instantly, contrary to the expectation of a slow release, leading to confusion or suspicion. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect time‑based accounting” or “epoch‑initialisation” errors where a timestamp is set before the relevant process starts. To remediate, the contract should not initialise lastDistribution at deployment. Instead a guarded startDistribution() function (or similar mechanism) should be called by the authorized entity when the reward schedule is meant to begin, resetting lastDistribution to the current block timestamp. Alternatively, the logic could detect a zero‑initialisation state and treat the first call specially, ensuring that only the elapsed time after the official start is considered in the decay calculation.

title: OCL_ZVE.sol::forwardYield relies on manip-
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the forwardYield function of the OCL_ZVE contract, which is responsible for distributing excess yield based on a value called basis. The function obtains the current claimable USDC amount by calling fetchBasis, then compares this amount to the stored basis. If the amount is greater than the basis, the contract forwards the difference as yield; otherwise it simply updates the stored basis to the returned amount. Because the contract trusts the amount returned by fetchBasis – which is derived from the price of a Uniswap V2 ZVE/USDC pool – an attacker can manipulate that pool, for example with a flash‑loan, to artificially depress the USDC price and cause fetchBasis to return a very small amount. When forwardYield is called during this manipulated state, the amount is less than the current basis, so no yield is forwarded, but the contract still overwrites the basis with the tiny manipulated value. After the attacker restores the pool price, a subsequent call to forwardYield (typically after the 30‑day interval) sees a large amount relative to the artificially low basis and forwards an excessive amount of USDC to the attacker. This results in a loss of funds for the protocol and its users. The issue occurs whenever forwardYield is executed while the underlying Uniswap pool price can be temporarily distorted, and it affects any participant who relies on the correct distribution of yield, including token holders and the protocol itself. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of forwardYield and identified that the basis is updated even when the amount is not greater than the current basis, creating an opportunity for price‑manipulation attacks. The problem is subtle because the function appears to behave correctly – it only forwards yield when amount > basis – but the silent update of basis on a low amount is not obvious from the UI or typical transaction logs, making the exploit hard to detect. To remediate, the contract should either revert the transaction when amount <= basis, avoid updating the basis in that case, or replace the direct Uniswap pool query with a more robust price oracle or time‑weighted average that cannot be manipulated in a single block. This class of bug is an oracle manipulation vulnerability where on‑chain accounting relies on a manipulable market price without sufficient safeguards, leading to incorrect accounting, unexpected zero payouts, and later oversized payouts that violate the protocol’s financial assumptions.

title: ZivoeYDL::distributeYield yield distribution
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the yield distribution function of the ZivoeYDL contract, which allocates protocol earnings to stZVE and vestZVE holders based on the current totalSupply of the stZVE token. Because the function reads the live totalSupply directly, an attacker can temporarily inflate that supply by acquiring a large amount of ZVE through a flash‑loan, staking it, and invoking the distribution in the same block. The root cause is the reliance on a mutable on‑chain state (totalSupply) without any time‑locking or snapshot mechanism, allowing the reward calculation to be gamed. An exploit proceeds as follows: the attacker obtains a flash‑loan of ZVE, stakes the borrowed tokens to increase stZVE’s totalSupply, calls the distributeYield function, receives a disproportionately large share of the earnings, then withdraws the staked tokens and repays the flash‑loan, keeping the excess yield. This results in the protocol losing funds that should have been shared among legitimate stakers, while honest users see their expected rewards reduced or disappear entirely. The issue manifests when the protocol permits staking and unstaking within the same block and does not enforce a minimum holding period before rewards are calculated. It affects all participants in the Zivoe ecosystem, including token holders, stakers, and the protocol’s treasury, because the accounting assumptions that rewards are proportional to a stable supply are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the reward‑distribution logic, where the use of totalSupply was flagged as potentially manipulable. It can be hard to notice because the totalSupply value appears correct at the moment of the call, and the distribution code looks mathematically sound, masking the economic manipulation. To remediate, the contract should base reward calculations on a past snapshot of totalSupply (e.g., the value from the previous block), enforce a minimum staking period so that tokens cannot be deposited and withdrawn within the same block, or employ a dedicated snapshot mechanism that records supply at a fixed point before distribution. This class of bug is an economic manipulation vulnerability where reward formulas depend on mutable state that can be altered by flash‑loan attacks, leading to unintended fund loss and broken accounting guarantees.

title: OCC_Modular::applyCombine will round APR
description:
OCC_Modular::applyCombine calculation of APR APR = APR / notional rounds in defavor of the protocol, and a user can game this feature to shave of a point of APR from one of his loans. OCC_Modular::applyCombine is used to combine multiple loans into a single loan. We can see that the APR for the new loan is computed as a weighted average of combined APRs. However since the division rounds down, the APR can be underestimated by 1 point. Since the APR is expressed as BIPS, a point represents a significant amount of interest. OCC_Modular.sol#L781
```solidity
APR = APR / notional;
```
off-chain that the APR would not be rounded down before approving a combination, a user can make sure it rounds down by making some payments on his loans. Loss of funds for the borrowers of the protocol, since a user can reduce APR on his loans by 1 point.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the loan‑combination routine of the OCC_Modular contract, specifically in the applyCombine function that computes the annual percentage rate (APR) for a newly created loan by taking a weighted average of the APRs of the constituent loans. The calculation is performed using integer arithmetic: the sum of APR‑times‑notional values is divided by the total notional amount, and Solidity’s division operator truncates any fractional part. Because the APR is expressed in basis points (BIPS), a single point represents a noticeable amount of interest. When the division rounds down, the resulting APR can be underestimated by exactly one BIPS. This rounding error is subtle and may appear correct at a glance, but it creates a systematic bias in favor of the borrower. An attacker who controls multiple loans can deliberately adjust the outstanding balances (for example by making small payments) so that the division truncates down, then invoke applyCombine to merge the loans. The combined loan will carry an APR that is one BIPS lower than the mathematically correct weighted average, reducing the interest owed by the protocol. The impact is a loss of interest revenue for the protocol and lenders, while borrowers receive a slightly better rate than intended. The bug manifests only when the combine operation is executed after the attacker has shaped the loan balances; it does not affect normal loan creation or repayment paths. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic of applyCombine and identified the use of plain division without rounding safeguards. The issue is hard to notice because the deviation is only one BIPS, which may be within normal variance and does not raise obvious red flags in test suites that check for exact APR values. To remediate, the contract should either enforce exact division (e.g., require(APR % notional == 0)) or employ a rounding‑up or fixed‑point arithmetic scheme that preserves precision, thereby eliminating the floor‑division bias. In broader terms, this is a classic integer‑division rounding error, a class of bugs where financial calculations lose fractional precision, leading to under‑ or over‑payment. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that after combining loans the displayed APR is slightly lower than expected, and the protocol’s accounting shows a small shortfall in accrued interest, contrary to the business rule that the combined loan should retain the exact weighted average rate.

title: ZivoeYDL::earningsTrancheuse()always assumes
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the earningsTrancheuse function calculates the target yield and the senior proportion for the senior and junior tranches. The function uses the constant daysBetweenDistributions, expressed in days, as the time basis for the yield target, while the distributeYield function only checks that the current block timestamp is greater than or equal to lastDistribution plus daysBetweenDistributions multiplied by 86400 seconds. Because the contract does not enforce that distributeYield is called exactly at the moment when the interval expires, callers can invoke distributeYield significantly later. When this happens, the earningsTrancheuse calculation still assumes the original number of days, ignoring the extra elapsed seconds, and therefore distributes a smaller amount of yield to the senior and junior tranches than the advertised APY. The residual pool receives the unallocated portion, effectively reducing the returns for tranche holders. The bug is triggered whenever block.timestamp exceeds lastDistribution + daysBetweenDistributions*86400 by more than a negligible amount, which is allowed by the require statement. It affects all participants holding senior or junior tranche tokens, as their expected returns are lower than promised, and it also undermines the protocol’s accounting assumptions that the yield distribution matches a fixed APY over the defined interval. The issue was discovered during an audit when a test warped the blockchain time beyond the exact distribution point and observed that the senior tranche balance did not increase proportionally to the longer waiting period. The problem is subtle because the contract still passes the timestamp check and appears to function normally; only a careful comparison of expected versus actual yields reveals the discrepancy. From a user perspective, the UI would show the same senior tranche balance after a month even though the user expected a higher return, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust. The bug belongs to the class of time‑dependent financial calculation errors where fixed intervals are used instead of the actual elapsed time, causing under‑payment of rewards. To remediate the issue, the seniorProportion and yieldTarget calculations should be based on the exact number of seconds elapsed (block.timestamp - lastDistribution) rather than the preset daysBetweenDistributions value, and the lastDistribution timestamp should be updated after the earningsTrancheuse computation so that future calls use the correct reference point.

title: Title: Inadequate Allowance Handling in con-
description: The OCT_DAO:convertAndForward and OCT_YDL:convertAndForward function suffers from inadequate handling of token allowances for the 1inch router. Although allowances are set correctly before converting assets, they are not reset afterward. This can lead to failed transactions if the 1inch router does not utilize the entire allowance due to slippage or other factors. the issue arises from the lack of allowance reset after interacting with the 1inch router. If the router does not utilize the entire allowance specified due to slippage or other reasons, the allowance will remain unchanged, potentially causing the assertion to fail and the transaction to revert. The impact of this vulnerability is that transactions may fail due to incorrect allowance management. This could result in inefficiencies in liquidity provision, loss of gas fees because due to asset statement it consume all the gas and won't return anything and convertandTransfer will never be able to transfer asset to DAO.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the convertAndForward functions of the OCT_DAO and OCT_YDL contracts, where token allowances granted to the 1inch router are not cleared after the router finishes processing a conversion. The code correctly calls approve to give the router a sufficient allowance before swapping assets, but it never resets that allowance to zero once the operation is complete. If the router consumes only a portion of the approved amount – for example because the trade experiences slippage, partial fills, or other execution constraints – the remaining allowance stays active on the token contract. This stale allowance can cause two distinct problems. First, the contract contains an internal assertion that expects the allowance to be fully consumed; when the leftover allowance is detected the assertion fails and the whole transaction reverts, wasting all gas and leaving the user’s assets unmoved. Second, the persistent approval creates an unnecessary permission that could be abused by a malicious actor who gains control of the router address or is able to trigger a transfer using the leftover allowance, effectively allowing unauthorized token movement. The issue manifests only under conditions where the router does not use the entire approved amount, which may be rare and therefore easy to miss during normal testing. Users experience a failed transaction with no asset transfer, see their balances unchanged, and incur the full gas cost of the call. The problem was identified during a manual security audit performed by the auditor Sherlock, who noted the missing allowance reset as a logical flaw in the token handling flow. Because allowance state is stored on the token contract and not directly visible in the DAO’s UI, the bug can remain hidden until a specific slippage scenario triggers the revert. To remediate the issue, the contract should explicitly set the allowance back to zero after the router call, or employ a pattern such as safeApprove that first resets to zero before granting a new allowance. This ensures that no excess permission remains, prevents unexpected reverts, and aligns the implementation with the expected accounting model where each conversion consumes exactly the approved amount and no residual approvals persist.

title: DAO unable to withdraw their funds due to
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an unrestricted admin function in Convex's BaseRewardPool contract that allows the reward manager to add an arbitrary number of extra reward contracts via addExtraReward. Zivoe’s DAO interacts with this pool through its pullFromLocker function, which internally calls claimRewards(false). ClaimRewards iterates over the entire extraRewards array and invokes external calls on each reward contract. Because the admin can push a malicious token or a very large list of tokens into extraRewards, the claimRewards loop can be forced to execute code that reverts, consumes all gas, or otherwise fails. When claimRewards fails, the surrounding pullFromLocker transaction reverts, preventing the DAO from pulling assets from the Convex locker. Consequently, the protocol’s funds and the users’ deposited assets become locked, and users see no balance change or are unable to withdraw, contrary to the expectation that a withdrawal request will succeed. This condition occurs whenever the Convex admin adds or modifies extra rewards, a situation that may not be obvious during normal operation because the extraRewards mechanism is intended for legitimate incentive tokens. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the admin‑controlled addExtraReward function and its downstream effect on Zivoe’s withdrawal flow. It is difficult to notice because the failure only manifests when the DAO attempts to withdraw, and the extra reward contracts may appear benign at first glance. The bug belongs to the class of “untrusted external call” or “admin‑controlled dependency” vulnerabilities, where a privileged external contract can inject malicious logic that breaks core protocol functions. To remediate, the protocol should either restrict the Convex admin’s ability to add extra rewards, enforce a cap on the number of extra rewards, validate that added contracts conform to a safe interface, and/or wrap each external call in a try/catch block so that a failing reward does not abort the entire withdrawal. Additionally, an emergency withdrawal path that bypasses claimRewards should be provided to allow users to recover funds if the normal pullFromLocker flow is blocked.

title: ZivoeYDL::distributeYield() will revert if protocol recipients length is less than residual recipients
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the yield‑distribution routine of the ZivoeYDL contract. The function distributeYield builds two parallel arrays, _protocol and _residual, whose lengths are derived from the number of protocolRecipients and residualRecipients respectively. No invariant is enforced to guarantee that these two recipient lists have the same size. Consequently, when residualRecipients contains more entries than protocolRecipients, the second loop that iterates over residualRecipients accesses the element _protocol[i] while emitting the YieldDistributedSingle event. Because _protocol was allocated with the shorter length, the index i eventually exceeds its bounds, causing an out‑of‑range exception and a revert of the entire transaction. The root cause is the missing length‑consistency check and the mistaken use of the protocol‑array index in the residual‑distribution loop. An attacker or any participant can exploit this by updating the residualRecipients list (through the authorized timelock contract) to be longer than the protocolRecipients list and then invoking distributeYield. The call will revert as soon as the first residual recipient that matches a reward contract (stSTT or stJTT) is processed, preventing the allowance increase and reward deposit for that recipient. The impact is that the core yield‑distribution mechanism becomes unavailable, fees and rewards are not transferred, and funds that should have been allocated to users or protocol participants remain locked in the contract. This condition can be triggered under normal protocol operation because the updateRecipients function only validates that each individual recipient list matches its proportion array, not that the two lists are of equal length. The issue may be hard to notice during testing because typical deployments keep the two lists synchronized, so the out‑of‑bounds path is never exercised. The bug belongs to the class of array‑index‑out‑of‑bounds errors caused by mismatched data structures and incorrect event emission logic. From a user’s perspective, expected yield payments disappear, balances appear unchanged after a distribution attempt, and the UI may show a transaction failure without a clear error message. To remediate, the contract should either enforce that protocolRecipients and residualRecipients always have the same length when they are updated, or the distribution loops should be written to iterate over the minimum of the two lengths and use the correct residual value when emitting events. Additionally, the event emission line should reference _residual[i] instead of _protocol[i] to reflect the actual amount being distributed to residual recipients.

title: OCL_ZVE::pushToLockerMulti() will revert due to allowance not being zero
bug_full: The vulnerability is an allowance‑reset logic error in the pushToLockerMulti function of the OCL_ZVE contract. The function increases the ERC20 allowance of both the pair asset and the ZVE token for the UniswapV2/Sushi router, then calls the router’s addLiquidity method with the full balances as the desired amounts and a 90 % of those balances as the minimum amounts. Because the router only transfers the actual amounts that satisfy the minimum constraints, the amount actually taken from the contract can be lower than the allowance that was granted. After the external call the code asserts that the allowance for each token is exactly zero. In most cases the allowance will still contain the difference between the granted amount and the amount actually transferred, so the assert fails and the transaction reverts. This happens whenever the router does not consume the full allowance, which is common due to the 90 % minimum‑liquidity check. The bug affects the DAO and any user trying to add liquidity through the locker: the transaction reverts, no liquidity tokens are minted, and the UI may show an unexpected failure or a missing LP token balance. The impact is a loss of core functionality – the locker cannot provide liquidity and becomes effectively unusable, potentially locking funds that cannot be moved until the bug is fixed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the allowance handling after external calls. It is hard to notice because the allowance increase and the subsequent assert look correct in isolation, and the router’s internal logic that may leave a residual allowance is not obvious from the caller’s perspective. The vulnerability belongs to the class of improper post‑call state validation or allowance‑reset bugs, where a contract assumes an external call will consume the entire allowance it set. To remediate, the contract should explicitly reduce the remaining allowance after the addLiquidity call, for example by calculating the leftover amount (granted allowance minus amount actually transferred) and calling safeDecreaseAllowance, or by resetting the allowance to zero using safeApprove. This ensures the post‑condition matches the contract’s expectation and prevents the revert.

title: Excess ETH will be stuck in the Fee Manager
description:
Excess ETH will be stuck in the Fee Manager contract and not swept back to the users. Per Line 236 below, it is expected that there will be excess ETH residing on the contract with the intention of sweeping excess ETH back to the caller of the mint function at the end of the transaction. Assume Bob transfers 0.05 ETH to the Edition contract, but the minting fee ends up being only 0.03 ETH. The _refundExcess function at the end of the function (Line 241 below) is expected to return the excess 0.02 ETH back to Bob. However, it was found that such a design does not work. When the collectMintFee function is executed on Line 236 below, the entire amount of ETH (0.05 ETH) will be forwarded to the Fee Manager contract. 0.03 ETH out of 0.05 ETH will be forwarded to the fee recipients, while the remaining 0.02 will be stuck in the Fee Manager contract.
