The excess 0.02 is not being returned to the Edition contract. Thus, when the _refundExcess function is triggered at the end of the function, no ETH will be returned to Bob.

File: Edition.sol

```solidity
228:
function mint(
229:
address to_,
230:
uint256 tokenId_,
231:
uint256 amount_,
232:
address referrer_,
233:
bytes calldata data_
234:
) external payable override {
235:
// wake-disable-next-line reentrancy
236:
FEE_MANAGER.collectMintFee{value: msg.value}(
237:
this, tokenId_, amount_, msg.sender, referrer_, works[tokenId_].strategy
238:
);
239:
240:
_issue(to_, tokenId_, amount_, data_);
241:
_refundExcess();
242:
}
```

[!IMPORTANT] Edition.mintBatch functions. The write-up is the same and is omitted for brevity. In addition, the Contest's README mentioned that the protocol aims to aims to avoid any direct TVL in this release:

Please discuss any design choices you made. Fund Management: We chose to delegate fee payouts to 0xSplits v2. The protocol aims to avoid any direct TVL in this release.

In other words, this means that no assets should be locked within the protocol. However, as shown in the earlier scenario, some assets will be stored in the Fee Manager, breaking this requirement. Excess ETH will be stuck in the Fee Manager contract and not swept back to the users.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic error in the minting flow that causes any ETH sent in excess of the required minting fee to become permanently locked in the Fee Manager contract instead of being returned to the caller. When a user invokes the mint function and supplies msg.value, the implementation forwards the entire amount to the external Fee Manager via collectMintFee. The Fee Manager then distributes only the exact fee amount to the designated recipients and retains the remainder, because it has no mechanism to send the surplus back to the Edition contract. After the fee collection, the mint function calls an internal _refundExcess routine that is supposed to transfer any leftover ETH back to the original sender. However, because the surplus was already absorbed by the Fee Manager, the Edition contract’s balance is zero and the refund call sends nothing, leaving the user with a missing amount of ETH. This situation occurs whenever the user overpays the mint fee – for example, sending 0.05 ETH while the required fee is 0.03 ETH – and results in the user receiving no refund, effectively losing the 0.02 ETH. The impact is two‑fold: users lose funds they expected to be returned, and the protocol unintentionally holds ETH, violating its design goal of having no direct TVL. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the mint implementation, where the flow of value from the caller through the Fee Manager to the refund step was examined. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and appears successful; the missing funds are only observable by checking balances after minting. The bug belongs to the class of “excess payment lock” or “refund logic failure” vulnerabilities, where a contract forwards more value than needed to a downstream contract that does not forward the surplus back. To remediate, the mint function should first query the exact fee amount from the Fee Manager and forward only that amount, allowing any unspent ETH to remain in the Edition contract and be reclaimed by the _refundExcess call. Alternatively, the Fee Manager could be modified to return any surplus to the caller. Either approach restores the intended behavior where users receive a refund of any over‑paid ETH and the protocol maintains a zero‑TVL stance.

title: Malicious users can block creators from acknowledging or deacknowledging an edge, affecting the sanctity of the data in the Graph.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a signature‑replay denial‑of‑service that allows a malicious actor to block a creator from acknowledging or de‑acknowledging an edge in the TitlesGraph. Both acknowledgeEdge and unacknowledgeEdge functions share a single modifier, checkSignature, which verifies a signature against a single type hash (ACK_TYPEHASH) and then records the signature hash in a global _isUsed mapping. Because the same digest format is used for both actions, a signature that was generated for an acknowledgment can be submitted to the unacknowledge function, or vice‑versa. An attacker can front‑run the legitimate creator, submit the creator’s valid signature to the opposite function, and cause the _isUsed entry to be set to true. When the creator’s original transaction later executes, the modifier detects the signature as already used and reverts, preventing the intended state change. This occurs under normal blockchain conditions where transactions are ordered by gas price, especially on low‑cost L2 networks where front‑running is cheap. The affected parties are the creators who rely on the protocol to record their acknowledgments, the protocol itself because the integrity of the graph data is compromised, and any downstream users who trust the graph’s truthfulness. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the permissioning logic and noticed that the same signature verification was applied to two semantically different operations. It can be hard to notice because the signature itself is valid and the revert only happens after the attacker’s transaction, making the failure appear as a generic “unauthorized” error rather than a deliberate sabotage. The impact is a loss of data sanctity: edges may remain unacknowledged or cannot be de‑acknowledged, breaking the hierarchy of truth that the protocol promises. To fix the problem, the contract should distinguish the two actions at the cryptographic level, for example by defining separate type hashes for acknowledgment and de‑acknowledgment and using distinct modifiers that compute separate digests. Including an explicit action identifier in the signed payload or using separate nonces per action would also prevent a signature intended for one function from being replayed in the other, thereby restoring the ability of creators to update the graph without interference.

title: Signature is malleable
bug_full: The vulnerability is a signature‑malleability flaw that allows an attacker to produce a second, distinct ECDSA signature that still validates against the same message digest. The contract relies on Solady's SignatureCheckerLib to verify signatures and then records the raw signature hash (keccak256(signature)) in a mapping called _isUsed to prevent replay. Because the library does not enforce the low‑s rule, a signer can create a malleable variant of the original signature – for example by replacing the s value with its secp256k1 complement or by toggling the recovery identifier – which yields a different byte representation while still being accepted as valid for the same digest. When the attacker submits this alternate signature, the verification step succeeds, but the _isUsed check fails because the hash of the new signature differs from the stored hash of the original one. Consequently the contract marks the new signature as unused and permits the same edge to be acknowledged again. This can be exploited repeatedly, allowing the creator or any party with the signing key to replay the acknowledgment logic, potentially inflating rewards, double‑counting actions, or corrupting protocol state. The issue manifests whenever the protocol uses a signature as a unique identifier for a one‑time operation without adding a nonce to the signed message or without checking that the signature is non‑malleable. Users may notice that an edge that should be acknowledged only once can be processed multiple times, leading to unexpected balance increases or duplicate reward payouts. The problem was discovered during a security audit that highlighted the library’s warning about non‑malleable signatures and observed that the contract stores the raw signature hash rather than the message digest. It is hard to detect because standard signature verification passes and the replay protection appears to work for identical byte strings, while the malleable variant bypasses the check silently. To remediate, the contract should enforce the low‑s requirement (e.g., by rejecting signatures with s > secp256k1n/2 as shown in the recommendation), include a unique nonce or use EIP‑712 typed data in the digest, and store used digests instead of raw signatures. By ensuring signatures are non‑malleable and that replay protection is tied to the message hash, the protocol can reliably enforce single‑use semantics and prevent duplicate acknowledgments.

title: Broken batch minting feature
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee‑handling logic error in the batch minting function of the protocol. The function receives a single msg.value that represents the total minting fee for all requested tokens, but inside a for‑loop it forwards the entire msg.value to the fee manager on every iteration. Because msg.value is immutable and does not decrease after each transfer, the first iteration drains the contract’s balance by sending the full fee amount to the fee manager. When the loop proceeds to the second token, the contract no longer holds any ether, yet it attempts to forward the same full amount again. This second transfer fails with an out‑of‑gas or insufficient‑balance revert, causing the whole transaction to revert. The root cause is the misuse of msg.value as a mutable counter rather than calculating and forwarding a per‑token fee. An attacker or honest user can exploit this by simply calling mintBatch with a valid fee; the transaction will revert after the first iteration, resulting in the fee manager receiving the fee for the first token while the user receives no minted tokens. The impact is that users cannot successfully batch‑mint multiple tokens, leading to a loss of the fee already transferred and a broken user experience where the transaction appears to have succeeded in sending ether but ends with no tokens and possibly missing funds. The bug manifests whenever mintBatch is called with more than one token ID, i.e., when tokenIds_.length > 1, and the caller supplies the correct total fee. It affects any user attempting to batch mint, as well as the protocol’s revenue model because fees may be collected without delivering the corresponding assets. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of ether inside the loop and noticed that msg.value was never adjusted. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not explicitly check the remaining balance, and the first fee transfer succeeds, giving a false impression that the operation is proceeding correctly. The appropriate fix is to compute the exact minting fee for each token (for example by calling a fee manager view function) and forward only that amount in each iteration, or to deduct the used portion from a local variable that tracks the remaining fee. This changes the bug class from an immutable‑value misuse to a correct per‑iteration fee accounting, restoring the intended business logic that each token’s fee is charged once and that batch minting either succeeds entirely or fails without partial fee loss. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are a transaction that reverts after sending ether, a balance that appears to be reduced to zero, and no tokens appearing in the wallet, contrary to the expectation that sending 0.004 ETH would mint four tokens and leave the remaining balance unchanged.

title: New creators unable to update the royalty
description:
The new creators are unable to update the royalty target and the fee route for their works. As a result, it could lead to a loss of assets for the new creator due to the following:
• The work's royalty target still points to the previous creator, so the royalty fee is routed to the previous creator instead of the current creator.
• The work's fee is still routed to the recipients, which included the previous creator instead of the current creator.
The creator can call the transferWork to transfer the work to another creator.
However, it was observed that after the transfer, there is still much information about the work pointing to the previous creator instead of the new creator.
```solidity
function transferWork(address to_, uint256 tokenId_) external {
    Work storage work = works[tokenId_];
    if (msg.sender != work.creator) revert Unauthorized();
    // Transfer the work to the new creator
    work.creator = to_;
    emit WorkTransferred(address(this), tokenId_, to_);
}
```
Following are some instances of the issues:
• The work's royalty target still points to the previous creator, so the royalty fee is routed to the previous creator instead of the current creator.
• The work's fee is still routed to the recipients, which included the previous creator instead of the current creator.
To aggravate the issues, creators cannot call the Edition.setRoyaltyTarget and FeeManager.createRoute as these functions can only be executed by EDITION_MANAGER_ROLE and [Owner, Admin], respectively.
Specifically for the Edition.setRoyaltyTarget function that can only be executed by EDITION_MANAGER_ROLE, which is restricted and not fully trusted in the previous creator, but only to find out that the malicious edition manager decided not to update the royalty target to point to the new creator's address for certain reasons, leading to the royalty fee continuing to be routed to the previous creator.
In this case, it negatively impacts the new creator as it leads to a loss of royalty fee for the new creator.
The following is an extract from the contest's README stating that the EDITION_MANAGER_ROLE is restricted. This means that any issue related to EDITION_MANAGER_ROLE that could affect TITLES negatively will be considered.
EDITION_MANAGER_ROLE (Restricted) =>
Loss of assets for the new creator due to the following:
• The work's royalty target still points to the previous creator, so the royalty fee is routed to the previous creator instead of the current creator.
• The work's fee is still routed to the recipients, which included the previous creator instead of the current creator.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incomplete ownership transfer for digital works where only the creator address stored in the work struct is updated, while the royalty target and fee routing information remain bound to the previous creator. This mismatch occurs because the contract provides a public transferWork function that changes work.creator but does not modify the associated royalty configuration, which is stored separately and can only be altered by privileged roles such as EDITION_MANAGER_ROLE or Owner/Admin. As a result, after a creator transfers a work to a new address, any royalty fees that are supposed to be paid to the new creator are still sent to the old creator, and the fee distribution list continues to include the previous creator. The root cause is a separation of concerns in the contract’s state: ownership and royalty metadata are not synchronised, and the permission model deliberately restricts royalty updates to roles that may not act in the new creator’s interest. An attacker controlling the edition manager role could deliberately refuse to update the royalty target, ensuring that all future royalty income is siphoned to the original creator. The impact is a loss of expected revenue for the new creator; from a user perspective the UI shows that they own the work, yet their balance never increases when sales occur, leading to confusion such as “my royalty balance stays at zero” or “I receive no payment despite being listed as the owner”. The issue manifests whenever transferWork is called and the royalty configuration is not subsequently updated, which may be after any transfer of ownership. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the fields modified by transferWork with the fields used by the royalty payout logic and noted the restrictive access control on setRoyaltyTarget and createRoute functions. The bug can be hard to notice because the transfer event emits the correct new owner address, giving the impression that all rights have moved, while the hidden royalty mapping silently continues to point to the old address. To remediate, the contract should either grant creators the ability to update royalty targets and fee routes for their works, or automatically synchronize those fields to the new creator within the transferWork function, ensuring that royalty and fee distribution always reflect the current owner. This aligns the implementation with the business expectation that ownership transfer includes full rights to receive royalties and fees.

title: Malicious EDITION_MANAGER_ROLE can front-run victims to increase royalty, leading to a loss of assets for the victim.
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the EDITION_MANAGER_ROLE being granted the ability to modify royalty information for an NFT edition. Because this role is not sufficiently restricted, a holder of the role can change the royalty percentage or the royalty receiver immediately before a secondary‑market sale is executed. In a typical scenario, a buyer (for example Bob) submits a transaction to purchase an NFT from CollectionX. The transaction sits in the mempool while a malicious actor who possesses EDITION_MANAGER_ROLE observes it and quickly submits a transaction that calls the royalty‑setting function, raising the royalty from the expected 5 % to a much higher value such as 95 %. When the marketplace later calls the edition’s royaltyInfo function to calculate the fee, it uses the newly‑set royalty rate, causing the buyer to pay an unexpectedly large royalty amount. From the buyer’s perspective the UI may still display the original 5 % royalty, but the actual transfer includes a far larger fee, resulting in a loss of funds that appears as “my purchase cost more than advertised” or “my balance dropped unexpectedly”. The issue is discovered during a security audit that examined role permissions and identified that the EDITION_MANAGER_ROLE is able to alter a critical economic parameter without additional safeguards. The problem is hard to notice because the royalty change happens on‑chain and can be executed in the same block as the purchase, leaving little time for the buyer or the marketplace to verify the royalty rate before the transfer. The impact is financial loss for any user buying NFTs during the window in which a malicious manager can front‑run the transaction, and it undermines trust in the protocol’s royalty mechanism. The vulnerability belongs to the class of privileged‑parameter‑manipulation and front‑running bugs, where an authorized role can alter economic settings that are later used by other contracts. To mitigate the risk, the protocol should limit EDITION_MANAGER_ROLE to trusted, possibly multi‑signature controlled accounts, make royalty parameters immutable after initial configuration, or introduce a time‑locked governance process that requires community approval before royalty rates can be changed. Such controls would prevent a single actor from arbitrarily raising royalties and protect buyers from unexpected fee extraction.

title: Edition.supportsInterface is not EIP1155 compatible
description:
According to the ERC-1155 specification, the smart contracts that are implementing it MUST have a supportsInterface(bytes4) function that returns true for values 0xd9b67a26 and 0x0e89341c. The current implementation of Edition.sol will return false for both these values.
The contract inherits from ERC1155 and ERC2981.
```solidity
contract Edition is IEdition, ERC1155, ERC2981, Initializable, OwnableRoles
```
The supportsInterface() function of Edition returns the result of executing super.supportsInterface()
```solidity
function supportsInterface(bytes4 interfaceId)
    public
    view
    override(IEdition, ERC1155, ERC2981)
    returns (bool)
{
    return super.supportsInterface(interfaceId);
}
```
Since both ERC1155 and ERC2981 implement that function and ERC2981 is the more derived contract of the two, Edition.supportsInterface() will end up executing only ERC2981.supportsInterface().
Medium. The contract is to be a strict implementation of ERC1155, but it does not implement the mandatory ERC1155.supportsInterface() function.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect implementation of the ERC‑1155 interface detection function supportsInterface(bytes4). According to the ERC‑1155 standard a contract that claims to implement the token type must return true when queried with the interface identifiers 0xd9b67a26 (ERC‑1155) and 0x0e89341c (ERC‑1155 metadata). The Edition contract inherits from ERC1155 and ERC2981 and overrides supportsInterface by delegating to super.supportsInterface(interfaceId). Because ERC2981 is the most derived base in the linearization, the super call resolves only to ERC2981’s implementation, which does not recognise the ERC‑1155 identifiers. Consequently the function returns false for both required IDs. The root cause is the reliance on Solidity’s super keyword in a multiple‑inheritance hierarchy where the more derived base does not forward the call to its sibling. An attacker or any integration tool that checks for ERC‑1155 compliance will receive a negative response and may refuse to interact with the contract, leading to loss of interoperability. Users attempting to trade, transfer or query the token through standard ERC‑1155 marketplaces may see their transactions rejected or their balances appear unchanged, even though the token logic itself works. The issue manifests whenever an external contract or off‑chain client calls supportsInterface with the ERC‑1155 identifiers; it does not affect the core token functionality but breaks the contract’s advertised compliance. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s interface support against the specification. It can be hard to notice because the function executes without reverting and returns a simple boolean, so developers may assume compliance without testing the specific identifiers. The correct fix is to implement supportsInterface so that it returns the logical OR of the ERC1155 and ERC2981 checks, thereby acknowledging both interface IDs. This change restores the contract’s ability to be recognised as an ERC‑1155 token by wallets, marketplaces and other tooling, aligning the implementation with the standard’s mandatory requirements.

title: Incompatibility of Upgradeability Pattern in TitlesGraph
description:
The TitlesGraph contract is designed to be upgradeable, utilizing the UUPSUpgradeable pattern. However, it's instantiated via a constructor in the TitlesCore contract setup.
In the TitlesCore contract, TitlesGraph is instantiated directly using a constructor rather than being set up as a proxy. This could lead to unexpected behavior when attempting to upgrade the contract, as the proxy would not have access to the initialized state variables or might interact incorrectly with uninitialized storage.
Inability to leverage the upgradeability.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mismatch between the upgradeability design of the TitlesGraph contract and the way it is deployed. TitlesGraph is written to follow the UUPSUpgradeable pattern, which requires the contract to be deployed as an implementation behind an ERC1967 proxy and to be initialized through an external initializer function rather than a constructor. In the current system the TitlesCore contract creates a TitlesGraph instance directly with a constructor call, bypassing the proxy entirely. This root cause means that the storage layout expected by the UUPS pattern is never correctly set up, the initializer is never executed, and the proxy‑specific upgrade functions are not reachable. An attacker cannot directly exploit a code execution flaw, but the practical effect is that any attempt to upgrade the graph contract will fail or behave unpredictably because the upgrade mechanism assumes a proxy context that does not exist. The impact is that the protocol loses the ability to patch bugs, add features, or migrate state in the TitlesGraph component, potentially locking functionality or causing stale logic to persist. The condition occurs at deployment time when TitlesCore instantiates TitlesGraph; any later upgrade call will either revert or interact with uninitialized storage, leading to default‑zero values for critical variables. Users of the protocol, developers, and any parties relying on the graph’s data are affected because the contract may return empty or incorrect information, and the expected upgrade path is unavailable. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s source code against its deployment pattern. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles and appears functional, yet the upgrade functions are silently ineffective until an upgrade is attempted. From a user perspective the UI may show missing graph data, zero balances, or failed upgrade transactions, contradicting the expectation that the contract can be upgraded. The bug belongs to the class of upgradeable‑contract misconfiguration where a contract using a proxy‑based pattern is instantiated directly, leading to uninitialized state and broken upgrade paths. The recommended remediation is to deploy TitlesGraph as a pure implementation without constructor‑based state initialization, then create an ERC1967 (or LibClone) proxy that points to this implementation and invoke the initialize function through the proxy, thereby aligning the deployment with the UUPS pattern and restoring proper upgradeability.

title: Incorrect encoding of bytes for EIP712 digest
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect construction of the EIP712 message digest in the TitleGraph contract. The checkSignature modifier rebuilds the digest by encoding the edgeId and the raw data bytes directly with abi.encode, but according to the EIP712 specification dynamic types such as bytes must first be hashed with keccak256 and the hash value included in the encoding. Because the contract omits the keccak256 step for the data field, a signature produced with standard EIP712 tooling (for example ethers.js signTypedData or Solady’s EIP712 helper) does not match the digest that the contract expects. An attacker does not gain any additional capability, however any legitimate user who signs the correct typed data will see their signature rejected, causing functions like acknowledgeEdge and unacknowledgeEdge to revert or return false. The bug appears when the checkSignature modifier is executed, i.e., whenever a transaction supplies a bytes calldata argument together with a signature. Users, integrators, and the protocol itself are affected because edge acknowledgement is a core operation for the TitlesGraph publishing workflow; the UI may display messages such as signature verification failed or simply show that the edge was not recorded, leading to confusion and potentially halted workflows. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who reproduced the mismatch with a proof‑of‑concept that generated a valid EIP712 signature using ethers.js and compared it against the digest computed by the contract, observing a mismatch. The problem is subtle because the signature appears syntactically correct and the contract does not emit an explicit error indicating an encoding problem, making it easy to mistake the failure for a network or wallet issue. The correct fix is to follow the EIP712 encoding rules for dynamic types: compute keccak256(data) and include that hash in the abi.encode call before passing the result to _hashTypedData. In abstract terms the bug belongs to the class of “EIP712 encoding mismatches for dynamic bytes” and violates the assumption that the on‑chain verifier reconstructs the exact same message hash that off‑chain signers produce. Once the encoding is corrected, signatures generated by standard tools will be accepted and the protocol’s business logic for edge acknowledgement will function as intended.

title: CREATE opcode works differently in the zkSync
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of the generic CREATE opcode inside a cloning routine that is compatible with the Ethereum Virtual Machine but not with zkSync Era. The TitlesCore::createEdition function calls Solady's LibClone.clone, which assembles a small piece of creation bytecode and invokes the CREATE opcode to deploy a new Edition contract. On zkSync Era the CREATE opcode is restricted: the compiler must know the exact bytecode of the contract being created, otherwise the deployment is rejected. Because the clone routine supplies raw bytecode that the zkSync compiler has not seen, the deployment transaction does not revert but silently fails to produce a contract instance. The createEdition function is payable, so users send a fee expecting a new edition to be minted. In practice the transaction succeeds, the event EditionCreated is emitted, but the returned address points to a zero or non‑existent contract and no edition is actually created. From the user’s perspective the UI may indicate success while the balance of the newly‑supposed edition remains zero, leading to missing NFTs or unavailable functionality. The impact is loss of funds and an inability to create editions on zkSync Era, breaking the core business logic of the publishing protocol. The issue occurs whenever createEdition is called on zkSync Era, i.e., under the condition that the underlying chain enforces the CREATE restriction. It affects any user who pays the creation fee, the protocol operators who rely on edition deployment, and any downstream contracts that assume the edition exists. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor compared the documented CREATE behaviour in zkSync Era with the implementation that uses Solady's generic clone. The problem is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and emits expected events, so developers may assume the deployment succeeded. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of deployment‑bytecode‑awareness errors where a contract attempts to create arbitrary code without the target chain’s compiler support. The recommended remediation is to replace the generic CREATE‑based clone with a CREATE2 deployment that uses the known creation code of the Edition contract (type(Edition).creationCode), as described in the zkSync Era documentation, thereby ensuring the compiler is aware of the bytecode at deployment time and preventing silent failures.

title: ERC2981 royalties discrepancy with strategy
bug_full: The vulnerability is a royalty synchronization error between a custom fee strategy stored in the work record and the ERC2981 royalty mechanism built into the Edition contract. When a creator or an authorized manager updates the strategy for a token via setFeeStrategy, or when a new work is created with publish, the contract stores the royalty basis points (royaltyBps) in works[tokenId].strategy but never calls the internal ERC2981 function _setTokenRoyalty to update the standard royalty mapping. Because ERC2981’s royaltyInfo function reads from its own storage, the value returned by royaltyInfo(tokenId,salePrice) can differ from the royaltyBps displayed in the UI or reported by the strategy. This discrepancy can cause royalty payments to be calculated with an outdated or incorrect rate, leading to creators receiving less (or potentially more) than intended. The issue manifests whenever the strategy’s royaltyBps is changed after the token has been minted, or when a token is minted directly through Edition without the additional TitlesCore helper that later calls setRoyaltyTarget. Users may see the expected royalty percentage in the marketplace UI, but the actual payout on secondary sales will follow the stale ERC2981 value, resulting in missing or reduced royalty funds. The bug is hard to notice because the contract does not emit any warning, and the UI typically reads the strategy field, giving a false sense of correctness. It was discovered during a manual audit of the Edition contract’s fee management functions, where the absence of a call to _setTokenRoyalty after updating works[tokenId].strategy was observed. The root cause is a missing synchronization step between the custom strategy storage and the ERC2981 internal royalty storage, a classic case of inconsistent state across contract modules. To remediate, the setFeeStrategy function (and any other entry point that modifies royaltyBps) should invoke _setTokenRoyalty with the updated royaltyBps and the appropriate fee receiver address, ensuring that ERC2981’s royaltyInfo reflects the intended rate. This aligns the contract’s accounting logic with business expectations that the displayed royalty percentage matches the actual payout on sales.

title: FeeManager's admin cannot grant or revoke
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing administrative interface in the FeeManager contract that prevents the designated ADMIN_ROLE from granting or revoking any roles. The contract inherits from solady's OwnableRoles and only exposes functions that are guarded by the onlyOwner modifier, meaning that only the contract owner (the TitlesCore contract) can call grantRoles and revokeRoles. Although the project README documents an ADMIN_ROLE that should be able to manage roles, the contract does not implement any functions that check for this role, nor does it provide a onlyOwnerOrRoles(ADMIN_ROLE) guard. As a result, when an address holding the ADMIN_ROLE attempts to assign or remove permissions, the transaction either reverts due to the onlyOwner restriction or silently does nothing because no public entry point exists. This limitation is permanent because the contract is not upgradable, and the TitlesCore contract that owns FeeManager also lacks the required role‑management functions. The impact is functional rather than a direct code execution exploit: the protocol’s governance and permission model break down, preventing the admin from onboarding new participants, updating fee structures, or revoking compromised accounts. Users may observe that role‑related actions they expect to succeed simply have no effect, leading to missing permissions, stalled fee distribution, or an inability to recover from a compromised admin key. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer compared the documented capabilities of ADMIN_ROLE with the actual Solidity interface and noticed the absence of any admin‑authorized grant or revoke functions. Because the problem manifests as an absence of functionality, it can be hard to notice unless the role management workflow is exercised. The correct remediation is to add public functions that allow callers possessing either the contract owner or the ADMIN_ROLE to call the internal _grantRoles and _removeRoles helpers, typically by adding an onlyOwnerOrRoles(ADMIN_ROLE) modifier to the existing grantRoles and revokeRoles functions or by introducing new admin‑specific wrappers. This change restores the intended permission hierarchy and aligns the contract behavior with the documented business logic, ensuring that role management can be performed by the designated admin without requiring a contract upgrade.

title: TitlesGraph::acknowledgeEdge() methods do
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the acknowledgeEdge function of the TitlesGraph contract, where the edge data is loaded from the edges mapping into a local variable declared as memory. Because memory variables are temporary copies, any modifications performed on this copy – such as setting the acknowledgement flag or updating attached data – are not written back to the persistent storage slot that holds the original Edge struct. Consequently, when the transaction finishes the state of the edge remains unchanged, even though the function appears to have succeeded. The root cause is a misuse of Solidity’s data location semantics: the internal helper returns an Edge memory reference instead of a storage reference, and the public acknowledgeEdge function also declares its return variable as memory. This pattern causes a logical disconnect between the intended state change and the actual on‑chain state. An attacker or honest user can invoke acknowledgeEdge expecting the edge to be marked as acknowledged; the call will emit events and return a seemingly updated Edge, but the underlying mapping still records the edge as unacknowledged. The impact is that protocol participants – creators, entities, or any user relying on edge acknowledgement for downstream logic – will observe inconsistent behavior: UI components may show a successful acknowledgement while the contract’s accounting still treats the edge as pending, leading to failed workflows, missing permissions, or stalled reward distribution. The bug manifests only when the acknowledgeEdge path is exercised; normal edge creation works because it writes directly to storage. It was discovered during a formal audit when a test (test_acknowledgeEdgeFailure) asserted that the acknowledgement flag should become true after calling acknowledgeEdge, but the assertion failed and the logged value remained false. The issue is subtle because the function compiles without warnings and the transaction does not revert, making it easy to miss during manual testing. To remediate, the function should return a reference to storage (Edge storage) or directly modify the edges mapping without copying to memory, ensuring that state changes persist after execution. This class of bug is commonly known as a “memory‑vs‑storage write loss” or “state‑mutation on a copy” and violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a successful call results in a durable state transition. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after acknowledging an edge, the UI still shows the edge as unacknowledged or the expected permission is not granted, creating confusion and potentially causing funds or rights to be unavailable.

The collected minting fee will be routed or transferred to one or more of the following parties directly (Using a push mechanism):

This approach introduced the risk of DOS to the minting process. As long as any of the parties above intentionally revert upon receiving the ETH minting fee, they could DOS the entire minting process of work.

The minting process might be DOS by malicious fee recipients, breaking the protocol's core functionality. This would also result in the loss of fee for the rest of the innocent fee recipients as the minting cannot proceed, resulting in the minting fee not being collected.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the minting workflow caused by a push‑payment design for distributing the minting fee. When a new token is minted the contract calls a fee manager that immediately forwards the received ETH to a set of recipients – the edition creator, any attribution wallets, the collection referrer, the minting referrer and the protocol fee receiver – using a single atomic transaction. Because each transfer is performed with a direct external call, the entire minting call reverts if any of those recipients revert or otherwise fail to accept the payment. This creates a classic push‑payment DOS: a malicious or faulty fee recipient can deliberately revert in its fallback or receive function, causing the whole mint transaction to fail. The failure occurs every time a mint is attempted while at least one recipient is refusing the payment, which means the token is never issued, the user’s transaction reverts, and no fee is collected for the other honest parties. From the user’s point of view the mint operation appears to “fail” or “revert” with no token minted and the expected fee distribution does not happen, contrary to the expectation that minting succeeds and fees are split. The impact is a loss of core protocol functionality – users cannot mint new editions, revenue for creators and referrers is halted, and the protocol appears broken. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the fee distribution logic and recognized the unsafe push‑payment pattern. It can be hard to notice because normal operation works when all recipients behave correctly; the problem only surfaces when a recipient is malicious or a contract upgrade introduces a revert. The recommended mitigation is to replace the push model with a pull model, where fees are accrued per recipient and can be claimed in separate transactions, or to wrap each external transfer in a try/catch and continue even if a recipient fails, thereby decoupling fee distribution from token issuance.

title: Malicious borrower can pay each payment and
bug_full: The contract calculates the next payment due date based on the timestamp of the last repayment and the original accepted timestamp. The logic adds one payment cycle (normally one month) to the due date, but it contains a conditional that checks whether the day component of the last repayment timestamp is greater than the day component of the accepted timestamp. If this condition is true, the algorithm increments the payment cycle counter by two instead of one. A similar path uses a ceiling division of the time delta between the last repayment and the accepted timestamp, then multiplies the resulting repayment cycles by the payment cycle length before adding it to the due date. Because the comparison is performed on the day of the month rather than the exact elapsed time, a borrower who makes a partial repayment just one day and one second after the accepted timestamp triggers the "greater day" branch. The contract then schedules the next due date two months ahead instead of one. This edge case can also be triggered when the repayment occurs slightly later than a full payment cycle, causing the ceiling division to round up and add an extra cycle. The vulnerability allows a malicious borrower to deliberately delay payments, effectively halving the interest accrued over the loan term. From a user perspective the borrower sees a longer interval before the next payment is required, while the lender receives fewer interest payments than expected. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the V2Calculations library by examining the calculateNextDueDate function and reproducing the behaviour with unit tests that warped the blockchain timestamp. It is subtle because the code appears to handle normal repayment timing correctly, and the extra month is only added under a narrow timing condition that may not be obvious during casual testing. The impact is a reduction in lender earnings (medium severity) rather than direct loss of principal, as the loan remains technically in good standing. To remediate the problem the calculation should always advance the due date by exactly one payment cycle, removing the day‑based conditional and avoiding multiplication by the repayment cycle count after a non‑zero delta. In other words, the next due date should be computed as the previous due date plus a single payment cycle regardless of the exact repayment timestamp, thereby preserving the intended interest schedule and preventing borrowers from gaming the payment schedule.

title: LenderCommitmentGroup pools will have incor-
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch that occurs when the LenderCommitmentGroup contract accepts a fee‑on‑transfer token as its principal asset. The addPrincipalToCommitmentGroup function records the amount supplied by the caller (_amount) as the amount actually deposited, but it does not verify how many tokens the contract really received after the token’s transfer fee is applied. Because fee‑on‑transfer tokens deduct a portion of the transferred value, the contract’s internal variable totalPrincipalTokensCommitted becomes larger than the real token balance. This inflated figure propagates to the pool’s total estimated value calculation, which in turn skews the sharesExchangeRate used for minting pool share tokens and for converting shares back to principal tokens. As a result, users may receive fewer share tokens than they expect when depositing, or they may receive an incorrect amount of principal when withdrawing, effectively causing funds to disappear or be mis‑allocated. The bug manifests only when the principal token implements a transfer fee; with a standard ERC‑20 token the accounting remains correct. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the accounting logic and noticed that the contract relied on the caller‑provided amount instead of the actual received amount. The issue is subtle because the transferFrom call succeeds and the contract’s external balance appears consistent, so the discrepancy is hidden inside internal accounting and only becomes visible through abnormal exchange rates or unexpected share balances. To remediate, the contract should measure the token balance before and after the transfer (or use a safeTransfer function that returns the actual amount received) and update totalPrincipalTokensCommitted with the net amount received, or alternatively reject fee‑on‑transfer tokens altogether. This class of bug falls under incorrect token accounting for fee‑on‑transfer assets, violating the protocol’s assumption that deposited tokens equal the amount recorded, and it can lead to loss of user funds, unfair share distribution, and a broken economic model for the lending pool.

title: Issue #497 'Add parameter to lender accept
description:
is still present. The vulnerability is well explain in the mentioned link above, essentially any market owner may change the marketplace fee while frontrunning a borrower and getting more funds in return. From the docs, the issue is valid as long as there is not a won't fix label. Borrower pays more marketplace fees than expected due to malicious market owner. TellerV2::lenderAcceptBid():
```solidity
function lenderAcceptBid(uint256 _bidId)
...
{
    ...
    amountToMarketplace = bid.loanDetails.principal.percent(
        marketRegistry.getMarketplaceFee(bid.marketplaceId)
    ...
}
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a fee manipulation or front‑running flaw in the TellerV2 marketplace contract. When a borrower creates a bid, the marketplace fee that will be deducted is not stored with the bid; instead the contract reads the fee from the MarketRegistry at the moment the lender calls lenderAcceptBid. Because the market owner (or any entity with permission to call setMarketFeePercent or setProtocolFee) can change the fee at any time, they can increase the fee after the borrower has submitted the bid but before the lender accepts it. By doing so the borrower ends up paying a higher marketplace fee than was displayed when the bid was created. The exploit consists of the market owner submitting a transaction that raises the fee, then front‑running the lender’s acceptance transaction. The borrower sees a larger deduction from the loan principal, receives less net proceeds, and the excess fee is transferred to the market owner’s address. This occurs whenever the fee‑setting functions are callable without a delay or without requiring the borrower’s consent. The affected parties are borrowers who rely on the advertised fee, lenders who may be unaware of the fee change, and the protocol which loses trust in its fee accounting. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the Teller Finance codebase, where the logic of lenderAcceptBid was examined and the dynamic fee lookup was noted. The problem is subtle because the UI shows the fee at bid creation, and the contract does not emit a warning when the fee changes later, making it easy to miss during normal testing. To remediate, the fee should be locked at the time the bid is created, or the borrower should be required to pass the expected fee as an explicit parameter that is validated against the registry, and any changes to fee parameters should be subject to a timelock. This prevents a market owner from arbitrarily increasing fees after a bid is placed and protects borrowers from unexpected fee loss.

title: _repayLoan now allows for overpaying of loan
bug_full: An overpayment vulnerability exists in the internal repayment routine. The function calculates the total amount to be sent as the sum of principal and interest, compares it with the amount owed and, if the supplied amount is larger, replaces the local variable with the exact owed amount. However the original Payment struct that contains the caller‑provided principal and interest values is never modified. The subsequent call that transfers funds uses the unchanged struct, so the contract actually moves the full over‑paid amount out of the caller’s wallet. Because the accounting variables that track how much principal has been repaid are updated based on the values in the Payment struct, the protocol records a repayment that is larger than the outstanding principal. When the total repaid principal exceeds the total lent principal, the view function that returns totalPrincipalTokensLended minus totalPrincipalTokensRepaid underflows and reverts. This makes any subsequent borrow transaction fail, effectively creating a permanent denial‑of‑service condition for the lending pool. The bug is triggered whenever a borrower (or any caller) supplies a repayment request with a principal or interest value greater than the amount still owed, which can happen unintentionally or be crafted by an attacker. From the user’s perspective the loan is marked as repaid and an event is emitted, but the wallet balance is reduced by more than expected and later attempts to borrow simply revert with an arithmetic error. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the repayment logic, where the mismatch between the capped paymentAmount variable and the unchanged Payment struct was observed. It is hard to notice because the contract still behaves as if a correct repayment occurred – the state transition and events are correct – while the hidden overpayment only surfaces later in the accounting view. The vulnerability belongs to the class of input‑validation and accounting bugs where user‑controlled monetary values are not properly bounded before being used for transfers and state updates. The recommended remediation is to either reject repayments that exceed the owed amount or to adjust the Payment struct (or the values used for accounting and fund transfer) to the capped amount before any external call or state change, ensuring that the recorded repayment and the actual transferred funds are identical.

title: Missing __Ownable_init() call in
description: __Ownable_init() is not called in LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart::initialize(), which will make the contract not have any owner. LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart::initialize() does not call __Ownable_init() and will be left without owner. Inability to pause and unpause borrowing in LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart due to having no owner, as these functions are onlyOwner.
bug_full: Missing call to the Ownable initializer in the contract's initialize function leaves the contract without an owner. The contract inherits from OpenZeppelin OwnableUpgradeable, which requires __Ownable_init() to be executed during initialization to set the owner variable. Because LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart.initialize does not invoke this parent initializer, the internal owner slot remains zero. As a result, any function protected by the onlyOwner modifier, such as pauseBorrowing and unpauseBorrowing, cannot be executed by any address. Users interacting with the protocol will see that borrowing cannot be paused even when a risk event occurs, and the admin interface will show disabled or failing pause controls. The bug is discovered during a manual audit that inspected the initializer sequence. It is hard to notice because the contract compiles and deploys successfully, and the missing owner does not cause an immediate revert; only privileged actions fail silently or revert with an onlyOwner error. The impact is a loss of emergency control: the protocol cannot halt borrowing, potentially allowing unchecked debt accumulation after a market shock. The affected parties include protocol administrators, lenders, and borrowers who rely on the ability to pause the system. The vulnerability belongs to the class of initialization bugs where a parent contract's initializer is omitted, leading to uninitialized state variables. To remediate, the initialize function should invoke __Ownable_init() before any other setup, thereby establishing a proper owner and restoring the functionality of onlyOwner protected methods.

title: LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart does not use mulDiv
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic overflow in the calculation of the share exchange rate and the underlying value inside LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart. The contract computes the rate as (poolTotalEstimatedValue * EXCHANGE_RATE_EXPANSION_FACTOR) / totalSupply without using a full‑precision mulDiv routine. Because the multiplication is performed first, the product can exceed the 256‑bit limit when poolTotalEstimatedValue is large or when the token supported by the pool has an extreme decimal factor (for example 1e36). When the product overflows, the division yields an incorrect, often zero, rate. This incorrect rate can be used by a malicious actor or can arise naturally when the pool grows beyond roughly 115 792 units of a token with 1e36 decimals, which corresponds to about $115 k at a $1 price. An attacker can trigger the overflow by depositing a token with very high decimals or by inflating the pool value, causing sharesExchangeRate() to wrap and _valueOfUnderlying() to return wrong amounts. As a result, users attempting to withdraw may receive no shares, see their balances unchanged, or be unable to complete the withdrawal, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service and potentially locking funds in the contract. The issue is discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who noted the absence of OpenZeppelin’s Math.mulDiv and the risk of overflow. The bug is subtle because normal test values with typical ERC20 decimals (18) never reach the overflow threshold, so it may remain unnoticed until a high‑decimal token is used or the pool grows large. The affected parties include any lender or borrower interacting with the commitment group, as well as the protocol’s overall liquidity and reputation. To remediate, the arithmetic should be rewritten using OpenZeppelin’s Math.mulDiv (or an equivalent full‑precision multiplication‑then‑division) so that the intermediate product never overflows, and additional checks on token decimal ranges could be added. By fixing the calculation, the contract will correctly preserve the accounting relationship between deposited tokens and issued shares, preventing funds from disappearing, refunds from being zero, and the protocol from being rendered unusable.

title: LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart_test::
bug_full: The vulnerability is a slippage‑related logic flaw in the lender contract’s functions that add principal to a commitment group and burn shares to withdraw earnings. Because the contract doesnot enforce a minimum amount‑out (or any slippage protection), an attacker can manipulate the internal share price by forcing the pool’s estimated total value to drop to zero. The attack proceeds as follows: the attacker first deposits a normal amount of DAI and receives a corresponding amount of pool shares. Then the attacker takes out a loan of the same size, lets the loan default, and liquidates it with the maximum incentive, which reduces the pool’s estimated total value to zero while the share supply remains unchanged. When the pool value is zero, any subsequent deposit through the add‑principal function calculates the number of shares based on a zero price and therefore issues zero shares to honest users. The attacker, who still holds the entire share supply, can then call the burn‑shares function to withdraw earnings, receiving the full amount of DAI that other users later deposited. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that a deposit appears to succeed but the user receives no shares, and later the user’s balance is drained without any on‑chain error. The impact is a complete loss of deposited funds for all users who interact after the price manipulation, effectively allowing an attacker to steal the pool’s assets. The flaw occurs under the condition that an adversary can default a loan with an incentive equal to the borrowed amount, which is possible in the current protocol design. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a concrete proof‑of‑concept test reproducing the attack. It is hard to notice because the share price calculation looks correct in normal operation, and the zero‑share issuance only manifests after the pool value has been artificially driven to zero. The vulnerability belongs to the class of slippage or price‑oracle manipulation bugs where the contract trusts internal accounting without bounding the acceptable change in exchange rate. To remediate, the contract should introduce slippage protection by requiring callers to specify a minimum acceptable amount‑out (or share amount) when adding principal or burning shares, similar to the safeguards used by decentralized exchanges to prevent sandwich or deflation attacks. This ensures that any drastic change in the pool’s estimated value will cause the transaction to revert rather than allow an attacker to extract funds.

title: Borrowers can surpass liquidityThresholdPercent
description:
Borrowers can borrow up to 100% of the principal due to getPrincipalAmountAvailableToBorrow relying on deposited principal. This will in tern lock LPs and prevent them from withdrawing. acceptFundsForAcceptBid includes a check that prevents borrowers from borrowing more than the liquidityThresholdPercent of the principal. This measure is intended to ensure safe withdrawals for LPs even when demand for borrowing exceeds the available principal. If this threshold is reached, no more assets can be borrowed, though LPs are still free to deposit and withdraw. However, this check relies on getPoolTotalEstimatedValue, which includes totalPrincipalTokensCommitted - the total tokens deposited.
```solidity
function getPrincipalAmountAvailableToBorrow() public view returns (uint256) {
    return (uint256(getPoolTotalEstimatedValue())).percent(liquidityThresholdPercent) - getTotalPrincipalTokensOutstandingInActiveLoans();
}
```
With this in mind, if liquidityThresholdPercent is reached, borrowers can simply deposit some collateral to increase the getPrincipalAmountAvailableToBorrow ratio, borrow the newly available collateral, and withdraw their original stake. Example:
• liquidityThresholdPercent is 80%, expected to be sufficient to ensure normal LP withdrawals.
• Pool value (getPoolTotalEstimatedValue) is $100k.
• Assets borrowed are $80k.
• getPrincipalAmountAvailableToBorrow returns (100k * 80%) - 80k = 0 -> no borrowing allowed.
Steps:
1. Alice deposits $25k principal (flash loans can be used, but are not required).
2. getPrincipalAmountAvailableToBorrow calculates $20k available (125k * 80% - $80k = 20k).
3. Alice borrows $20k.
4. Alice withdraws her $25k principal.
In the example above, our borrower surpassed the liquidityThresholdPercent, causing the market to be at 100% utilization, essentially locking LPs until a borrow is repaid or another LP deposits. Pools will be in a locked state, where every new deposit will be instantly borrowed or used as exit liquidity by another LP. This also break core contract functionality - borrowers should not be able to borrow past liquidityThresholdPercent.
bug_full: The contract is intended to limit borrowing to a configurable percentage of the pool’s total estimated value, called liquidityThresholdPercent, so that liquidity providers (LPs) can still withdraw their deposits even when borrowing demand is high. The enforcement is performed by the function that returns the principal amount available to borrow, which calculates (pool total estimated value * liquidityThresholdPercent) minus the amount already outstanding in active loans. The flaw originates from the fact that the pool total estimated value is derived from the sum of all principal tokens committed, which includes any new principal that a borrower may deposit as collateral. Because the calculation does not exclude freshly deposited collateral, a borrower can artificially increase the pool value, causing the available‑to‑borrow formula to become positive even after the threshold has been reached. By depositing collateral, borrowing the newly created available amount, and then withdrawing the original deposit, the borrower can push the utilization of the pool beyond the intended 80 % limit up to 100 % or higher. In practice this means that once the threshold is hit, a malicious borrower can still extract additional funds, leaving the pool fully utilized and preventing honest LPs from withdrawing any of their capital. From the user’s perspective an LP who expects to be able to withdraw a portion of their balance sees the withdrawal transaction revert or return zero, while the pool’s accounting shows no available liquidity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the borrowing logic, where the relationship between getPoolTotalEstimatedValue and the threshold check was examined. It is difficult to notice because the check appears to enforce the limit, yet the underlying accounting mixes new deposits with existing liquidity, creating a subtle accounting loophole. The vulnerability belongs to the class of threshold‑enforcement or liquidity‑exhaustion bugs, where the protocol’s invariant that “borrowed amount ≤ liquidityThresholdPercent of pool value” can be violated through self‑service deposits. To remediate the problem the protocol should separate the accounting of existing pool liquidity from newly deposited collateral when computing the borrowable amount, or enforce the threshold on a net‑available liquidity metric that does not count deposits made in the same transaction. This would restore the guarantee that LPs can withdraw funds up to the defined safety margin and prevent borrowers from draining the pool beyond the intended limit.

title: Utilization math should include
description: Utilization math should include liquidityThresholdPercent, as this represents the maximum value that can be borrowed. This means that if borrowing reaches principal * liquidityThresholdPercent, then 100% of the available assets are considered borrowed. getPoolUtilizationRatio is used within getMinInterestRate to calculate the interest rate at which borrowers borrow. Higher utilization equates to a higher APR. However, in the current case, getMinInterestRate fails to include liquidityThresholdPercent in its calculation. This variable is crucial as it caps the maximum borrowing allowed (e.g., if it's 80%, then a maximum of 80% of the assets can be borrowed). Not including this variable means that the utilization (and thus the APR) will appear lower than it actually is. An example of this is a more risky market with a lower liquidityThresholdPercent, such as 40%. In these markets, even though there is some risk that the LPs take, the maximum utilization will be 40%, as borrowers cannot borrow above that, even if there is demand for this token. This in tern will decease the profits LPs make from staking in risky markets. This results in a breakdown of core contract functionality. Utilization above liquidityThresholdPercent is unreachable, leading to lower LP profits.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the protocol calculates the pool utilization ratio, which is a key input for determining the minimum interest rate offered to borrowers. The current implementation computes utilization as the total principal tokens outstanding divided by the total estimated pool value, expressed as a percentage. However, it omits the liquidityThresholdPercent parameter, a configurable cap that defines the maximum proportion of assets that may be borrowed (for example, an 80% threshold means only 80% of the pool can be loaned out). Because this cap is not factored into the formula, the reported utilization can never exceed the theoretical 100% limit, even when the actual borrowable amount is lower due to the threshold. Consequently, the utilization metric appears artificially low, leading the getMinInterestRate function to produce a lower APR than should be applied. This mis‑pricing harms liquidity providers (LPs) who expect higher returns in riskier markets where the threshold is set lower (e.g., 40%). From a user’s perspective, LPs see their expected rewards shrink or disappear, while borrowers may obtain loans at rates that do not reflect the true scarcity of capital. The issue manifests whenever a pool’s liquidityThresholdPercent is below 100%, which is common for markets that aim to limit exposure. It was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s financial logic, where the auditor noticed that the utilization ratio never exceeded the threshold and that the APR calculation did not align with the protocol’s economic model. The bug is subtle because the contract still compiles and functions, and the discrepancy only becomes evident when comparing expected versus actual LP earnings or when analyzing the interest‑rate curve. To remediate, the utilization calculation must incorporate the liquidityThresholdPercent, typically by dividing the outstanding principal by the product of the total pool value and the threshold percentage, and then capping the result at 100%. This adjustment restores the intended relationship between utilization, risk, and APR, ensuring that LPs receive compensation that matches the underlying borrowing constraints.

title: APRs are lower than they should
description:
LenderCommitmentGroup (LCG) calculates the APR borrowers can borrow on using getMinInterestRate. However, this math doesn't include the amount that the borrower is currently borrowing. As a result, interest rates are lower in every market, and the MAX APR becomes unreachable. When borrowers borrow from LCG using acceptFundsForAcceptBid, they can choose the interest rate they are going to pay. Considering that borrowers will always choose the lowest APR available, loans are always made with _interestRate >= getMinInterestRate(). However, getMinInterestRate does not factor in the new amount that the borrower is going to borrow. Instead, it provides the pool's current APR. If the borrower borrows a significant amount of the pool, they will get a very favorable APR. This significantly reduces LP profits because the APR borrowers pay is always lower than the pool's current calculated interest. Example:
1. APR ranges from 4% to 40% depending on utilization.
2. The pool currently has 70k principal, resulting in 70% utilization and an APR of 40% * 70% = 28%.
3. Alice borrows 25k (25%) of the pool, raising utilization to 95%.
4. Despite the pool being at 95% utilization, Alice only pays 28% APR because her minimum interest was calculated without considering the newly borrowed amount.
LPs earn 28% APR from Alice's loan even though the pool is 95% utilized. If Alice borrowed 100%, the pool's maximum APR would have been 28% instead of 40% (as no more loans would be given and 28% would be the highest interest), resulting in LPs profits significantly decreasing. Lower interest and lower profits for LPs, making the maximum APR unreachable and breaking core functionality.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect calculation of the minimum interest rate (APR) that borrowers must pay when taking a loan from the LenderCommitmentGroup (LCG). The contract’s getMinInterestRate function determines the APR based solely on the pool’s current utilization ratio, but it does not incorporate the amount that the borrower is adding to the loan in the same transaction. Because the new loan amount is omitted, the utilization used for the APR formula remains at its pre‑borrow level, causing the returned APR to stay at a lower value even after the pool becomes highly utilized. This root‑cause is a missing state update in the financial formula: the function calculates interest using stale data, effectively an off‑by‑one error in utilization accounting. An attacker can exploit the bug by submitting a large borrow request through acceptFundsForAcceptBid, observing the current APR (for example 28 % at 70 % utilization), and then borrowing a substantial portion of the pool (e.g., 25 k of a 70 k pool) which raises utilization to 95 % while still receiving the previously calculated 28 % APR. The borrower benefits from a disproportionately low rate, while liquidity providers (LPs) receive less interest than the protocol’s economic model predicts. The impact is a systematic under‑payment of interest, making the maximum APR unreachable, reducing LP profits, and breaking the core incentive alignment of the protocol. The issue manifests whenever a borrower calls the loan‑acceptance function and the contract queries getMinInterestRate without passing the prospective loan amount; it therefore occurs in all markets that rely on this calculation. Affected parties include borrowers (who receive unexpectedly low rates), LPs (who earn less than expected), and the protocol itself (which cannot achieve its designed APR curve). The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the interest‑rate logic, where the auditor noted that the APR displayed to users did not increase after large borrow actions despite the utilization metric rising. The problem is hard to notice because the UI may correctly show a high utilization percentage while still displaying the old APR, giving the impression that the system is functioning normally. From a user’s perspective, a borrower may see a loan approved at a low APR even though the pool is nearly full, and an LP may observe a drop in yield without an obvious cause, such as “my earnings are lower than before” or “the APR stays at 28 % while utilization is 95 %”. This bug belongs to the class of financial mis‑pricing errors where a formula fails to account for a state change, similar to missing‑parameter or stale‑state bugs in interest‑rate calculations. To remediate, the contract should include the prospective borrowing amount when computing utilization, either by adding a newAmount parameter to getMinInterestRate or by averaging the utilization before and after the loan, thereby ensuring that the APR rises appropriately with utilization and that the maximum APR remains reachable.

title: Incorrect selector in
description:
FlashRolloverLoan_G5::_acceptCommitment() allows picking the SmartCommitmentForwarder, but the selector is incorrect, making it unusable for LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart. FlashRolloverLoan_G5::_acceptCommitment() accepts the commitment to SmartCommitmentForwarder if _commitmentArgs.smartCommitmentAddress != address(0). However, the selector used is acceptSmartCommitmentWithRecipient(), which does not match SmartCommitmentForwarder::acceptCommitmentWithRecipient(), DoSing the ability to rollover loans for LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart. FlashRolloverLoan_G5 will not work for LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart loans.
```solidity
FlashRolloverLoan_G5::_acceptCommitment()
function _acceptCommitment(
    address lenderCommitmentForwarder,
    address borrower,
    address principalToken,
    AcceptCommitmentArgs memory _commitmentArgs
)
    internal
    virtual
    returns (uint256 bidId_, uint256 acceptCommitmentAmount_)
{
    uint256 fundsBeforeAcceptCommitment = IERC20Upgradeable(principalToken)
        .balanceOf(address(this));
    if (_commitmentArgs.smartCommitmentAddress != address(0)) {
        .functionCall(
            abi.encodePacked(
                abi.encodeWithSelector(
                    ISmartCommitmentForwarder
                        .acceptSmartCommitmentWithRecipient
                        .selector,
                    _commitmentArgs.smartCommitmentAddress,
                    _commitmentArgs.principalAmount,
                    _commitmentArgs.collateralAmount,
                    _commitmentArgs.collateralTokenId,
                    _commitmentArgs.collateralTokenAddress,
                    address(this),
                    _commitmentArgs.interestRate,
                    _commitmentArgs.loanDuration
                ),
                borrower //cant be msg.sender because of the flash flow
            )
        );
...
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the flash‑loan rollover contract when it attempts to forward a commitment to a smart‑commitment forwarder. The internal function checks whether a smart‑commitment address is supplied and, if so, builds a low‑level call using abi.encodeWithSelector. However, the selector that is encoded is acceptSmartCommitmentWithRecipient, which belongs to the ISmartCommitmentForwarder interface, while the actual forwarder contract implements acceptCommitmentWithRecipient. Because the selector does not match any function in the target contract, the call silently fails – the forwarder does not execute the expected acceptance logic and no revert is triggered. This mismatch prevents the FlashRolloverLoan_G5 contract from successfully rolling over loans that belong to a LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart group. From a user’s perspective a borrower who initiates a flash rollover expects the loan to be extended and the commitment to be accepted, but the transaction completes without any visible error and the loan remains unrolled, effectively leaving the borrower without the anticipated new loan term. The impact is that the rollover feature is unusable for the affected loan type, potentially causing missed refinancing opportunities, stranded capital, or even default if the borrower cannot meet the original loan deadline. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to _acceptCommitment where the smartCommitmentAddress field is non‑zero and the lender commitment group is of the Smart variant. The affected parties are borrowers, lenders and the protocol itself because the intended business logic – seamless loan rollover – is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s flash‑loan flow, where the selector used in the low‑level call was compared against the forwarder’s ABI and found to be incorrect. Because the call does not revert, the failure can be hard to notice without explicit event logging or return‑value checks; the contract simply proceeds as if the acceptance succeeded. To remediate the problem the contract should replace the incorrect selector with the correct one – SmartCommitmentForwarder::acceptCommitmentWithRecipient – ensuring that the forwarder receives a valid function call and can process the commitment as intended. This change restores the intended accounting flow, allowing the rollover to succeed and preserving the protocol’s financial guarantees.

title: FlashRolloverLoan_G5 will fail for
description: FlashRolloverLoan_G5 calls SmartCommitmentForwarder::acceptCommitmentWithRecipient(), which will have CollateralManager committing tokens from FlashRolloverLoan_G5, which will revert as it does not approve it nor have the funds. The issue lies in the fact that FlashRolloverLoan_G5 assumes SmartCommitmentForwarder gets the borrower from the last 20 bytes, but it sets the borrower to msg.sender instead. Thus, in SmartCommitmentForwarder::acceptCommitmentWithRecipient(), TellerV2::submitBid() is called with the borrower being FlashRolloverLoan_G5, which will end up having the CollateralManager pulling collateral from FlashRolloverLoan_G5, which will fail, as it does not deal with this. FlashRolloverLoan_G5 will never work for LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart loans.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a borrower‑address mismatch that causes a flash‑rollover loan contract to fail when it attempts to accept a commitment through the SmartCommitmentForwarder. FlashRolloverLoan_G5 calls SmartCommitmentForwarder.acceptCommitmentWithRecipient, expecting the forwarder to extract the borrower address from the last 20 bytes of the calldata. In reality the forwarder overwrites the borrower with msg.sender, which means the borrower becomes the FlashRolloverLoan_G5 contract itself. When SmartCommitmentForwarder then invokes TellerV2.submitBid, the CollateralManager is instructed to pull the required collateral from the borrower address – now the FlashRolloverLoan_G5 contract. Because FlashRolloverLoan_G5 never holds the borrower’s tokens and does not grant the CollateralManager an allowance, the collateral transfer reverts. The root cause is the incorrect assumption about how the borrower is determined, leading to an approval and balance mismatch. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; simply triggering the normal loan rollover flow will cause the transaction to revert, preventing the loan from being executed. The impact is that any LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart loan that relies on FlashRolloverLoan_G5 cannot be rolled over, leaving borrowers unable to refinance and potentially causing stale or dead loan positions. The issue is observed only when the flash‑rollover path is used; normal loan creation works because the borrower address is set correctly elsewhere. Users of the contract see the transaction fail with a revert, often without any token movement, which can be confusing because the UI may indicate that the loan was submitted but no funds are transferred. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that traced the call chain from FlashRolloverLoan_G5 through the forwarder to the CollateralManager and identified the mismatched borrower handling. It is hard to notice because the failure occurs deep in a third‑party manager contract, and the revert message does not directly point to the missing approval. To remediate, the FlashRolloverLoan_G5._acceptCommitment function should be updated to pull the collateral from the actual borrower and explicitly approve the CollateralManager for the required amount before calling the forwarder, ensuring that the CollateralManager can successfully transfer the tokens. Conceptually, the fix aligns the borrower identity used throughout the call chain and guarantees that the necessary token allowance is in place, restoring the intended flash‑rollover functionality.

title: FlashRolloverLoan_G5 will not work for certain
description: FlashRolloverLoan_G5::_repayLoanFull() approves TELLER_V2 for _repayAmount, but TELLER_V2 always pulls the principal and interest, possibly leaving some dust approval left. Some tokens revert when trying to set approvals from non null to non null, which will make FlashRolloverLoan_G5 revert. Some ERC20 tokens must have 0 approval before setting an approval to a non 0 amount, such as USDC. The interest rises with block.timestamp, so borrowers will likely take a flash loan slightly bigger than _repayAmount to take this into account, or repay will fail. Thus, when the approval is set for TellerV2 of the _principalToken, principal + interest may be less than the approval, which will leave a dust approval. FlashRolloverLoan_G5::executeOperation() later on approves POOL, which will revert as a dust amount was left. FlashRolloverLoan_G5 will not work and be DoSed.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper handling of ERC20 allowance resets in the FlashRolloverLoan_G5 contract. After a flash loan is repaid, the contract calls _repayLoanFull() which sets an allowance for the TellerV2 contract equal to the total amount that must be transferred (principal plus accrued interest).
