To remediate, the contract should guard each external token transfer by checking that the amount is greater than zero before invoking the transfer function, or adjust the fee logic to enforce a minimum non‑zero fee when zero‑fee promotions are not required. This class of bug – improper handling of zero‑value external calls – can cause unexpected reverts, break business logic that assumes free operations, and undermine user trust if left unaddressed.

title: Maradona: Excess msg.value not refunded to
description: In Maradona.takeTokensAndTrade(), excess msg.value is not refunded to the user, which may leave some Ethers stuck in the contract. In Maradona.takeTokensAndTrade(), excess msg.value is not refunded to the user. If the output token is not ETH, the contract will send the user the entire balance of the output token only, but not ETH. Per the contest README: We need to monitor specially that there is no set of inputs that allows a transaction to succeed if the balance of the contracts involved in after the transaction is greater than before the transaction. This means that we want that always balance before trading is equal to balance after trading for all contracts for all tokens. language that indicates the codebase's restrictions and/or expected functionality. Issues that break these statements, irrespective of whether the impact is low/unknown, will be assigned Medium severity. Thus, this issue breaks an invariant defined by the protocol Breaks invariant defined by the protocol, funds may remain in the contract

Which will make the tx sends twice the amount of Ethers required. Running the test with make tests/Maradona gives the following failed test: Which shows that the tx does indeed go through, and the assertion at line 543 shows that ETH indeed remains in the contract
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improper handling of excess Ether sent to the Maradona contract during the execution of the takeTokensAndTrade function. When a caller supplies more msg.value than required for a trade, the contract does not return the surplus Ether. Instead, after performing the token swap, the contract only transfers the acquired output token balance to the caller and leaves any remaining Ether locked in its own balance. This occurs because the function lacks a final step that refunds the contract's Ether balance to the transaction sender. The root cause is a missing refund logic that violates the protocol’s invariant that the total balance of each token for every involved contract must be unchanged after a successful trade. An attacker or any user can exploit this by deliberately over‑paying Ether in a trade; the transaction will still succeed, the user will receive the expected output token, but the extra Ether will remain trapped in the contract. The impact is that funds may become permanently inaccessible, reducing the protocol’s economic safety and breaking the expectation that a trade does not alter the contract’s Ether holdings. The issue manifests whenever the output token of the trade is not Ether, which is the common case for token‑to‑token swaps. All participants who interact with the contract—regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the contract’s balance can accumulate stray Ether over time. The flaw was discovered during a security audit when the auditor modified a test to send twice the required Ether amount; the test showed that the transaction succeeded while the contract’s Ether balance increased, confirming the invariant breach. The problem is subtle because the contract still performs the intended token transfer, so the missing refund may not be immediately visible in normal UI flows, and no explicit error is raised. To remediate, the contract should, after all internal operations have completed successfully, transfer the entire remaining Ether balance back to msg.sender, thereby restoring the pre‑trade balance and preserving the invariant. This class of bug is commonly known as an “excess payment not refunded” or “missing refund” vulnerability, which can lead to funds disappearing from the user’s perspective while the contract retains them unintentionally.

title: Bridging without any swap ops is fee free in
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the fee‑charging routine of the Maradona contract when a user invokes the takeTokensAndTrade function with a bridge operation but without any swap operations. The code iterates over an array called swapOps to accumulate a computableFeeAmount, but if swapOps is empty the loop never runs and computableFeeAmount remains zero. Subsequent fee calculations use this amount to decide whether a fee transfer should occur. Because the computed fee values are derived from a zero base, the contract treats the fee charge as successful with a zero amount and records the operation as succeeded. The logic then skips any further attempts to collect fees, meaning that the protocol never receives the expected fee for a pure bridge transaction. This flaw occurs only when the transaction contains no swap steps, i.e., when a user simply bridges assets from one chain to another. It affects the protocol’s revenue model because every such bridge bypasses the fee mechanism, allowing users to move value without paying the intended terrace or fee‑receiver fees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑charging flow, where the auditor noticed that the fee‑computation loop depends on the presence of swapOps and that the success flag prevents a second charge attempt. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an error; it silently records a successful fee charge of zero, making it easy to miss in testing. To remediate, the contract should either require at least one swap operation before attempting a fee charge or, when swapOps is empty, compute the fee based on the bridged amount (for example, using the contract’s balance after the bridge and subtracting any bridge‑specific costs). This ensures that a non‑zero fee is always deducted according to the protocol’s fee schedule, preserving expected revenue and preventing fee‑free bridging.

title: setStartBlock() doesn't change the block at
description: The function setStartBlock() can be called by the owner to change the block number at which points will start accumulating. When it's called, the block at which already existing pools will start accumulating points will not change. Already existing pools will: 1. Start accumulating points from the old startBlock if the new startBlock is set after the old one. 2. Not accumulate rewards until the old startBlock is reached if the new startBlock is set before the old one. This happens because updatePool() considers the pool lastRewardBlock as the block number from which points should start accumulating and setStartBlock() never updates the lastRewardBlock of the already existing pools to the new startBlock. When setStartBlock() is called the block at which already existing pools will start accumulating points will not change.
bug_full: The contract allows the owner to change the block number at which reward points start to accrue by calling setStartBlock(). The function updates a global startBlock variable but does not modify the lastRewardBlock field stored in each pool that has already been created. The reward‑calculation routine updatePool() uses the pool’s lastRewardBlock as the reference point for determining how many blocks have passed and therefore how many points should be minted. Because setStartBlock() never synchronises lastRewardBlock with the new startBlock, pools that existed before the change continue to calculate rewards from the old block number. Consequently, if the owner raises the startBlock to a future block, users who deposit after the original startBlock but before the new one will still earn points, violating the intended “no rewards before startBlock” rule. Conversely, if the owner lowers the startBlock, existing pools will not begin rewarding until the old startBlock is reached, effectively delaying rewards. The bug manifests whenever the owner invokes setStartBlock() after at least one pool has been initialized. All participants who interact with those pools are affected because the accounting of pending points becomes inconsistent with the protocol’s economic model; users may see non‑zero pending points when they expect none, or may miss rewards they should have earned. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit by executing a test that changed the startBlock from 1 to 100, deposited after block 90, and observed that pending points were already accruing at block 99, even though the global startBlock had not been reached. The problem is subtle because the UI typically displays the current startBlock value, giving the impression that rewards are paused, while the underlying pool state still generates points, making the discrepancy easy to miss. To remediate, setStartBlock() should iterate over every existing pool and set each pool’s lastRewardBlock to the new startBlock, ensuring that reward calculations align with the updated schedule. Additionally, the function should revert if the supplied startBlock is lower than the current block number, preventing retroactive start times that could break the reward timeline. This correction restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents users from receiving points they should not earn, preserving the fairness and predictability of the farming protocol.

title: Accounting will be broken if output token is
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the strategy contract calculates its total token balances. The balances() view function adds together the amounts of token0 and token1 that are held directly by the contract (retrieved via ERC20.balanceOf) and the amounts that are locked in the liquidity‑pool positions (retrieved from the pool). This calculation assumes that the two token types are distinct from the output token that the strategy reports to the vault. When the output token happens to be one of the LP tokens – for example, the strategy’s reward token is the same ERC20 contract as token0 or token1 – any fees that have accrued in the pool but have not yet been harvested are still counted as part of the contract’s direct balance. Consequently, the reported total includes both the real underlying assets and the unharvested fees, inflating the apparent share value. Users depositing through the vault therefore receive more shares than they should, based on an overstated asset valuation. When the protocol later harvests the pending fees, the previously counted amount disappears from the balance, causing the share price to drop and resulting in a loss for those depositors. In extreme cases the double‑counted fees can make the accounting appear solvent while the actual liquid assets are insufficient, potentially leading to insolvency of the strategy. The issue manifests whenever the output token is identical to one of the LP tokens and there exist unharvested fees in the pool. It affects all participants who interact with the vault – depositors, withdrawers, and the protocol itself – because the accounting mismatch breaks the fundamental invariant that total assets equal the sum of user balances. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the balance‑aggregation logic and identified that the code does not exclude pending fees when the output token overlaps with the LP tokens. The bug is subtle because the balances() view returns non‑zero values that look plausible; only after fee accrual does the discrepancy become visible, making it hard to detect through casual testing or UI observation. To remediate the issue, the strategy must detect when the output token is one of the LP tokens and subtract any unharvested fees from the token balance before adding the pool position amounts. This adjustment restores correct accounting, prevents share‑price inflation, and ensures that the protocol cannot become insolvent due to double‑counted assets. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting errors caused by double counting of assets, especially when reward or output tokens overlap with underlying token contracts, and it violates the core business logic that each user’s share should represent a proportional claim on the actual, harvest‑ready assets.

title: Corruptible Upgradability Pattern
description: Storage of DepositVault/RedemptionVault/mTBILL contracts might be corrupted during an upgrade. Following are the inheritance of the DepositVault/RedemptionVault/mTBILL contracts. defined. The contracts highlighted in Green mean that gap slots have been defined. The DepositVault/RedemptionVault/mTBILL contracts are meant to be upgradeable. However, it inherits contracts that are not upgrade-safe. DepositVault/RedemptionVault/mTBILL/ERC20PausableUpgradeable. ManageableVault/Pausable/Greenlistable/Blacklistable/WithMidasAccessControl. Among these contracts, ManageableVault and WithMidasAccessControl are contracts with defined variables (non pure-function), and they should have gaps as well. Without gaps, adding new storage variables to any of these contracts can potentially overwrite the beginning of the storage layout of the child contract, causing critical misbehaviors in the system. Storage of DepositVault/RedemptionVault/mTBILL contracts might be corrupted during upgrading.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a storage‑layout corruption risk inherent to the upgradeable DepositVault, RedemptionVault and mTBILL contracts. These contracts inherit from several base contracts, including ManageableVault and WithMidasAccessControl, which contain state variables but do not reserve reserved storage slots (the typical 50‑slot gap). In an upgradeable proxy pattern, the storage layout of the implementation contract must remain compatible with all previous versions. Because the parent contracts lack a storage gap, adding new variables in a future implementation can shift the positions of existing variables in the child contracts. When such a shift occurs, the proxy continues to read and write at the old slot indices, causing the values of critical fields—such as vault balances, pausing flags, green‑list/black‑list status, and access‑control roles—to be overwritten with unrelated data. An attacker or even an honest upgrade can therefore cause the contract to mis‑report balances (for example a user sees a zero balance after a deposit), reject legitimate withdrawals, or allow unauthorized parties to perform privileged actions. The impact is loss of user funds, broken accounting, and potential breach of the protocol’s security guarantees. The issue manifests only when a new implementation introduces additional storage variables in any of the non‑gap‑protected base contracts; it does not appear in the initial deployment. It affects every participant that interacts with the vaults—depositors, redeemers, and the protocol’s governance—because the corrupted state can affect all financial operations. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the contract inheritance tree, where the auditor noted the absence of the standard storage gap in the two base contracts. The bug is subtle because the contract compiles and runs correctly until an upgrade changes the storage layout, at which point the failure is silent and only observable through unexpected UI symptoms such as missing balances or failed transactions. The recommended remediation is to add a reserved storage gap (for example uint256[50] private __gap;) to each non‑pure‑function base contract, ensuring that future upgrades can add new variables without colliding with existing slots. This aligns the contracts with the established upgrade‑safe pattern and restores confidence that accounting and access‑control logic remain intact.

title: DEPOSIT_VAULT_ADMIN_ROLE/REDEMPTION_-
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an over‑privileged admin role in the DepositVault and RedemptionVault contracts. The roles DEPOSIT_VAULT_ADMIN_ROLE and REDEMPTION_VAULT_ADMIN_ROLE are documented to manage deposit parameters and token withdrawals, but the contract code also grants them the ability to pause and unpause the vaults. This occurs because the vaultRole() function, which defines the admin role for each vault, is implemented to return the same identifier that pauseAdminRole() returns, and pauseAdminRole() simply forwards to vaultRole(). Consequently, any address that holds the documented admin role can invoke the pause() and unpause() functions protected by onlyPauseAdmin. The root cause is a circular role definition that unintentionally merges the administrative and pausing permissions. An attacker or a malicious admin can exploit this by calling pause() to halt deposits and redemptions, effectively freezing user funds and preventing normal operation of the protocol. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: users attempting to deposit or redeem will receive no transaction effect, balances remain unchanged, and the UI may show that the vault is unavailable or that deposits/redeems are rejected. This situation can arise at any time the admin decides to call pause, and it affects all participants who rely on the vault for liquidity, including token holders and downstream contracts. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditor compared the contest readme’s description of role capabilities with the actual Solidity implementation and noticed that the pause functions were accessible to the same role identifiers. Because pausing is often hidden behind role abstractions, the over‑privilege may not be obvious without a detailed review of the role‑resolution logic. To remediate, the pauseAdminRole should be defined as a distinct role that is not equal to DEPOSIT_VAULT_ADMIN_ROLE or REDEMPTION_VAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, and the vaultRole() implementation should return only the intended admin identifier. Removing the pause permission from these admin roles or assigning a separate, tightly controlled pauser role will align the contract behaviour with the documented expectations and prevent unauthorized vault shutdowns.

title: CCTPManager does not support bridging to Ethereum
bug_full: The vulnerability is a validation logic error in the CCTPManager contract that prevents users from bridging USDC to the Ethereum mainnet. The contract’s bridge routine checks the destination identifier supplied in the extraUInts array and explicitly requires that it be non‑zero (require(destination != 0, "CCTPManager: invalid destination")). According to the official Cross‑Chain Transfer Protocol (CCTP) specification, a destination value of zero is a legitimate identifier that represents the Ethereum mainnet. Because the contract treats zero as an invalid sentinel, any attempt to bridge assets to Ethereum triggers a revert, causing the transaction to fail before any token transfer occurs. This issue arises whenever the operation type is BRIDGE and the caller passes 0 as the destination chain ID, which is the exact scenario required for Ethereum bridging. The affected parties are end‑users and integrators who rely on the contract to move USDC from the source chain to Ethereum; they experience a failed transaction, see an error message about an invalid destination, and receive no funds on the target chain. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s source code against the CCTP documentation and identified the mismatch in expected destination values. The bug can be hard to notice because a zero value is often used in smart contracts as a placeholder for “null” or “unset”, leading developers to assume it should be rejected. In practice, however, the protocol defines zero as a valid chain identifier, so the contract’s defensive check is incorrectly restrictive. The impact is effectively a denial‑of‑service for the Ethereum bridge path: users cannot complete cross‑chain transfers to Ethereum, which breaks the intended business logic of the protocol and may cause loss of confidence or revenue. To remediate the issue, the contract should either remove the require statement that blocks destination zero or replace it with a proper whitelist that includes zero as an allowed destination, ensuring alignment with the CCTP specification. Conceptually, the fix is to correct the input validation to accept all documented chain identifiers rather than arbitrarily rejecting zero.

title: Users are heavily overcharged for gas fees if
description:
Users are heavily overcharged for gas fees if they're bridging ETH. In Messi, the amount of gas we charge fees on is the gas used for claim and swap operations plus valueToSend (the ETH to bridge, not including the bridging fee, so this will only be non-zero if we're bridging with ETH).
```solidity
(gasCharged, gasAmountCharged) = tryToChargeForGas(
    (initialGas - gasleft()) * tx.gasprice + valueToSend, <-- gasAmount
    gasToFeeTokenExchangeRate,
    feesTokenAddress,
    receivingUser,
    true,
    gasCharged,
    bridgeFound? bridgeOp.inputToken != feesTokenAddress: swapOps.length > 0? swapOps[swapOps.length - 1].outputToken != feesTokenAddress: claimOp.outputToken != feesTokenAddress
);
```
We directly calculate the fee amount to be paid using the uint256 feeValue = (gasAmount * gasToFeeTokenExchangeRate) / 10 ** 18; Since gasAmount includes valueToSend, if we're bridging with ETH (e.g. using StargateManager), we will have to pay fees for gas + the full value of the amount we're bridging. When the fee token is not ETH, the fee amount will be transferred from the receivingUser to feeCollector which is not unlikely since the receivingUser could have approved a large amount (or even max amount) to the Messi contract for convenience. Loss of funds for users due to heavily overpriced gas fees when bridging ETH.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑charging of gas fees that occurs when a user bridges ETH through the Messi contract. The contract builds the fee amount by taking the gas used for claim and swap operations, multiplying it by the transaction gas price, and then adding the variable valueToSend, which represents the amount of ETH being bridged. This sum, called gasAmount, is then multiplied by a gas‑to‑fee‑token exchange rate to obtain the fee value. Because valueToSend is included, the fee calculation mistakenly treats the entire bridged principal as part of the gas cost. When the fee token is not ETH, the contract transfers the computed fee from the receiving user’s allowance to the fee collector. If the user has approved a large or unlimited allowance for the Messi contract, the fee collector can drain a substantial portion of the user’s balance. The bug is triggered only when the bridge operation uses ETH as the input token and the fee token differs from ETH, and it requires that the user has previously approved the contract to spend fee tokens. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed, but the user receives far less ETH on the destination chain, or the balance may become unexpectedly low, because the fee taken is far larger than the expected gas cost. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑charging logic, where the inclusion of valueToSend in the gasAmount parameter was identified as a logical error. It is hard to notice because the contract reports a normal gas price, and the excessive deduction is hidden in the fee transfer, making the UI show only a standard gas cost while the actual token transfer is much higher. This class of bug can be described as a fee‑calculation error or double‑counting of transferred value, violating the accounting assumption that fees should be based solely on gas consumption. To remediate the problem the contract should replace valueToSend with the explicit bridge fee amount (bridgeFeeEth) when constructing the gasAmount, ensuring that only the gas used is charged and the bridged principal is excluded from the fee computation.

title: Round-off errors during ratioBPs splits will
description:
Per the contest README:
We need to monitor specially that there is no set of inputs that allows a transaction to succeed if the balance of the contracts involved in after the transaction is greater than before the transaction. This means that we want that always balance before trading is equal to balance after trading for all contracts for all tokens.
language that indicates the codebase's restrictions and/or expected functionality. Issues that break these statements, irrespective of whether the impact is low/unknown, will be assigned Medium severity.
We show that for multi-hop trades with valid inputs, the ratioBPS round-off errors for realistic UniV2/UniV3/Balancer swaps will almost always leave the contract with some dust amounts of middle tokens.
The contract Maradona (and Messi but permissioned) allows performing multi-hop trades, where each hop can be split across multiple markets with different ratio.
From the second hop onwards, the operation's amountIn is overriden by the previous hop's output, multiplied by the ratio intended for this particular swap market.
dit-v1/contracts/Paymaster/Maradona.sol#L389
```solidity
if (op.useContractFunds) {
    op.amountIn = (prevCumOutputAmount * ratioBPs) / 10000;
}
```
However, most (if not almost all) of the time, a swap on UniV2/UniV3/Balancer does not return an amount out perfectly divisible by 10000, which causes truncation of at most 0.9999 wei in the above division. If the hop contains two or more swaps, the truncation will total to 1 wei or more that remains in the contract, scaled by the number of operations for that hop.
Because the amountIn is always calculated that way, and the round-off amounts are never swept, the round-off amounts remains in the contract.
• Breaks invariant defined by the protocol, that the contract should not hold any balance after trades
– Specifically, Gemini USD has only 2 decimals. Therefore any precision loss may be material if accumulated.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the Maradona contract computes the input amount for each hop of a multi‑hop trade when the operation is configured to use contract funds. For every hop the contract multiplies the cumulative output amount of the previous hop by a ratio expressed in basis points (ratioBPs) and then divides by 10,000 using integer division. Because Solidity discards any fractional remainder, the division truncates up to 0.9999 wei whenever the previous hop’s output amount is not perfectly divisible by 10,000 – a condition that occurs in almost every realistic Uniswap V2, Uniswap V3 or Balancer swap. When a hop contains more than one market split, the truncation error is applied to each split, causing one or more wei of the intermediate token to remain in the contract after the trade completes. This leftover dust violates the protocol‑level invariant that the contract’s token balances must be identical before and after a trade, effectively meaning the contract should not retain any funds. The issue is most visible for tokens with low decimal precision such as Gemini USD (2 decimals), where even a single wei of loss can be material. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to keep a tiny amount of the middle token, so the expected balance after a trade is not zero; the user may see a small, unexplained token balance in the contract’s address. The problem was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors constructed a proof‑of‑concept test that deliberately split a second hop into two markets with ratios 66.66 % and 33.34 %. The test showed that, because the first hop’s output was not divisible by 10,000, each split introduced a rounding loss that accumulated as dust in the contract. The bug is subtle because the amount lost is typically only a few wei, making it easy to overlook during manual inspection or standard testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should detect when the cumulative ratio reaches the full 10,000 basis points and, instead of recomputing amountIn via division, assign amountIn the exact remaining amount (prevCumOutputAmount minus the amount already accounted for). This eliminates the truncation error and restores the invariant that no residual token balance remains after a trade. The vulnerability belongs to the class of rounding‑error or integer‑division bugs that cause accounting mismatches in financial smart contracts.

title: prevLastOutBalance/prevSwapEthBalance should
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the contract records the ETH balance before executing a series of swaps in the takeTokensAndTrade function. When the final swap is expected to deliver ETH, the code snapshots the contract’s current balance using address(this).balance and stores it in prevLastOutBalance. However, the transaction that calls the function also transfers msg.value ETH to the contract, and this incoming amount is unintentionally included in the snapshot. Consequently, the subsequent check that verifies the output amount – lastOutBalance - prevLastOutBalance >= minAmountOut – is performed against a baseline that is artificially high by exactly the amount of msg.value. In scenarios where the trade both starts and ends with ETH (for example an MEV arbitrage that begins with ETH, swaps through intermediate tokens, and finally returns ETH), the calculated difference is reduced by the value of msg.value, causing the requirement to fail even though the swap produced the expected profit. From a user’s perspective the transaction reverts with the message “Maradona: last output amount is less than minAmountOut”, the user receives no tokens, and the expected refund or profit disappears. The issue is triggered only when the output token of the last swap is ETH and the input token of the first swap is also ETH, i.e., when ops[0].inputToken == ops[last].outputToken. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined balance accounting logic and noticed that prevLastOutBalance was never adjusted for the incoming ETH. The bug is subtle because balance checks are common and the extra msg.value is easy to overlook, especially when testing only token‑to‑token paths. The impact is medium: legitimate trades are incorrectly rejected, leading to loss of gas and missed arbitrage opportunities, and it could be abused to cause a denial‑of‑service on the contract’s trading functionality. The proper fix is to subtract msg.value from the recorded prevLastOutBalance when the final output is ETH (or, equivalently, to record the balance before the payable call) and to apply a similar correction in related contracts such as Messi.sol where claimedAmount must be deducted. By correcting the accounting, the minAmountOut check will reflect the true net ETH received from the swap, restoring expected behavior and preventing false reverts.

title: tryToChargeForGas() return gasAmountCharged
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the helper routine that charges the caller for gas fees, tryToChargeForGas. When the contract is instructed to charge gas using the native blockchain token (feesTokenAddress equals the zero address) and the flag needToBringTokens is false, the code executes a branch that transfers the required ETH to the fee collector but never assigns a value to the local variable that is later returned as gasAmountCharged. Consequently the function always returns zero for gasAmountCharged in this specific execution path. The calling function, takeTokensAndTrade, uses the returned gasAmountCharged to reduce the amount of tokens that will be supplied to a downstream bridge operation (bridgeOp.amountIn -= gasAmountCharged). Because the returned value is incorrectly zero, the bridge operation receives an amount that is larger than intended, which can cause the bridge to either fail due to insufficient token balance after the fee transfer or to execute with a wrong accounting of fees. From a user perspective the transaction may revert with an unexpected error, or the user may see that the expected refund or token amount is missing or that the bridge does not complete, effectively resulting in funds being locked or lost. The issue occurs only when the fee token is the native currency and the contract does not need to pull tokens from the user, a scenario that is common in ETH‑based fee models. It was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noticed that the branch handling native ETH does not set the amount variable before returning. The bug is subtle because the function returns a tuple and other branches correctly populate the amount field, so automated tests that only cover token‑based fee paths may miss the problem. To remediate the issue the function should assign amount = feeValue (or the appropriate calculated fee) before emitting the GasCharged event and returning, ensuring that gasAmountCharged always reflects the actual fee transferred regardless of the fee token type. This correction restores proper accounting, prevents incorrect bridge input amounts, and aligns the contract’s behavior with its business logic that expects the fee to be deducted from the bridge input amount.

title: It is impossible to bridge USDC via CCTPManager
description:
Attempts to bridge USDC after swapping via CCTPManager will revert if the fee token is USDC.
At the start of takeTokensAndTrade for both paymaster contracts, we validate that the fee token is either the input token of the first operation or the output token of the last operation (for Maradona, we check for ETH since the input is always ETH).
dit-v1/contracts/Paymaster/Messi.sol#L89-L91
```solidity
function validateFeeToken(address feeTokenAddress, OperationParameters[] memory ops) internal pure returns (bool) {
    return (feeTokenAddress == ops[0].inputToken || feeTokenAddress == ops[ops.length - 1].outputToken);
}
```
If we're bridging USDC after swapping to USDC tokens and the fee token is USDC, the output token of the bridge op must be USDC due to this check since the bridge op is always last (implies we're paying fees with the output USDC). If we're using CCTPManager, the issue is the output token must be address(0).
dit-v1/contracts/CCTP/CCTPManager.sol#L109
```solidity
require(opParams.outputToken == address(0), "CCTPManager: invalid output token");
```
This contradicts the necessity of setting the output token to USDC to satisfy the original validation against the fee token.
It is impossible to bridge USDC after swapping via CCTPManager if the fee token is USDC due to over-restrictive validation of outputToken in CCTPManager.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical conflict between two validation rules that makes it impossible to bridge USDC when the fee token is also USDC. The Paymaster contracts contain a function that checks the fee token against the first input token or the last output token of a series of operations. This rule is intended to ensure that the token used to pay fees is actually available at the start or end of the transaction flow. Separately, the CCTPManager contract, which handles cross‑chain transfers, enforces that the output token of a bridge operation must be the zero address (address(0)). When a user swaps assets and then attempts to bridge the resulting USDC using CCTPManager while also designating USDC as the fee token, the Paymaster validation requires the bridge operation’s output token to be USDC, but the CCTPManager check forces it to be address(0). The contradictory requirements cause the transaction to revert before the bridge can be executed. This issue manifests only when the fee token is USDC and the bridge operation is performed through CCTPManager, which is a common pattern for users who want to pay fees in the same stablecoin they are moving. Affected parties include any user trying to bridge USDC, the protocol’s paymaster logic, and any role that relies on successful fee payment in USDC. From a user’s perspective the UI will show a failed transaction or a generic revert message, and the expected outcome – a successful USDC bridge – does not occur, effectively making the bridge function unusable for that token. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the validation logic, where the auditor noticed that the output token check in CCTPManager contradicts the fee‑token validation in the Paymaster. Because each check looks reasonable in isolation, the conflict is subtle and may be missed without a holistic view of the call flow. The bug belongs to the class of contradictory validation constraints or mismatched interface contracts, where two modules impose incompatible requirements on a shared parameter. To remediate the issue the CCTPManager should either remove the hard‑coded requirement that the output token be address(0) or relax it to allow USDC when the fee token is USDC, thereby aligning the validation logic across contracts and restoring the ability to bridge USDC.

title: Messi paymaster should approve to zero first
description:
Some tokens like USDT revert in case the prior approval is non zero.
The messi paymaster approves tokens twice to bridge, which will lead to a revert in case a user tries to bridge tokens like USDT
In addition to this the first approve does not include fees, and on its own is incorrect.
The messi paymaster approves tokens first in line 420:
```solidity
tokenToBridge.approve(markets[bridgeOp.exchangeID], bridgeOp.amountIn);
```
After this messi tries to approve tokens again in line 520:
```solidity
tokenToBridge.approve(markets[bridgeOp.exchangeID], bridgeOp.amountIn);
```
The second approve is made in case the fee token should be bridged, and fees are deducted.
As we can see we try to approve tokens twice without approving to zero first, which will lead to an revert.
Messi paymaster cant bridge tokens like USDT which revert on non zero approval.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a non‑standard ERC20 allowance handling bug in the Messi Paymaster contract. The contract calls the token's approve function twice in succession – first to grant the bridge contract the amount to be transferred, and later a second time to cover the fee amount – but it never resets the spender's allowance to zero before issuing the second approval. Tokens such as USDT implement a stricter version of ERC20 where a call to approve with a non‑zero value is required to first set the allowance to zero; otherwise the call reverts. Because the Paymaster assumes that multiple non‑zero approvals are always accepted, the second approve reverts when the token enforces the zero‑first rule. This occurs during the bridging flow when a user attempts to bridge a token that follows the USDT pattern. The immediate impact is that the bridging transaction fails, the user sees a revert error (for example USDT reverts here), and no funds are transferred. From the user's perspective the UI reports a failed bridge, the expected receipt of tokens never arrives, and the balance appears unchanged, which can be confusing and may be perceived as a loss of funds. The issue was discovered during an audit by Sherlock, who added a mock ERC20 that mimics USDT's approve behaviour and observed that both bridge tests reverted. The bug is hard to notice because the majority of ERC20 tokens allow repeated non‑zero approvals, so standard testing with common tokens does not expose the problem. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of allowance‑reset bugs where contracts do not account for tokens that require a zero‑allowance reset before changing the allowance. The correct mitigation is to remove the redundant first approve and to ensure that any new allowance is preceded by an explicit approve of zero, either directly in the Paymaster or via a helper library that always performs a zero‑first approval. This change eliminates the revert, restores correct bridging functionality, and aligns the contract with the accounting assumptions of all ERC20‑compatible tokens.

title: minAmountOut check must be done after charg-
bug_full: The vulnerability is an ordering flaw in the contract’s output validation logic. The code checks that the amount of the last output token that will be transferred to the user meets the caller‑provided minAmountOut requirement before any protocol fees are taken from that same token. Because the fee deduction occurs after the require statement, the contract can satisfy the minAmountOut check while still sending the user a smaller net amount after the fee is subtracted. This happens when the fee token is identical to the output token, which is a common case for many swaps or bridge operations. An attacker or a malicious user can exploit the flaw by specifying a minAmountOut that is just above the expected fee amount; the contract will pass the check, then deduct the fee, leaving the recipient with less than the promised minimum. The impact is that users receive fewer tokens than they were guaranteed, breaking a core invariant that the protocol must never deliver less than the minimum amount declared by the caller. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful – the UI shows a “swap completed” message – but the received balance is unexpectedly lower, sometimes even zero if the fee exceeds the output. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the sequence of checks and fee handling. It can be hard to notice because the require statement does not fail, so standard test cases that only verify the require pass will miss the subsequent reduction. The proper fix is to move the minAmountOut validation to after the fee‑charging step, or to adjust the required amount to account for the fee before the check, ensuring that the net amount transferred always satisfies the caller’s minimum expectation. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “incorrect order of operations in financial checks”, where validation is performed on a pre‑fee value while the post‑fee value is actually transferred, leading to under‑payment and broken accounting guarantees.

title: Usage of transfer to send eth might silently
description:
Usage of transfer to send eth might silently fail
Within the contracts, transfer is used to send eth. This is a problem as transfer limits gas consumption to 2300 gas. If the receiving address has a fallback/ receive function which consumes more than 2300 gas, it would cause the transfer to silently fail and the eth will remain within the Maradona contract.
```solidity
payable(receivingUser).transfer(address(this).balance);
```
Loss of funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the use of Solidity's built‑in transfer function to move Ether from the contract to an arbitrary recipient. Transfer forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas to the recipient’s fallback or receive function. If the receiving address implements a fallback/receive routine that requires more than this gas limit – for example because it performs storage writes, emits events, or calls other contracts – the stipend is insufficient and the transfer operation reverts. Because the contract does not capture or handle the revert, the Ether remains locked inside the contract instead of being delivered to the intended user. This situation can be triggered whenever a user withdraws funds, receives a refund, or any logic that relies on transfer to forward the contract’s balance. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears to have succeeded (the transaction hash is recorded, gas is paid) but the expected balance increase never occurs; the UI may show a successful withdrawal while the recipient’s wallet balance stays at zero. The impact is a loss of funds for the affected users and a potential denial‑of‑service vector, as an attacker could deliberately deploy a contract with a costly fallback to block withdrawals from the vulnerable contract. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected Ether‑sending patterns and identified the hard‑coded gas stipend as a risk. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not emit an explicit error and the contract’s state does not change, leaving developers with no obvious on‑chain indicator that the transfer failed. The bug belongs to the class of gas‑stipend or “transfer‑failure” vulnerabilities, which violate the assumption that Ether can always be sent with a simple transfer call. The correct mitigation is to replace transfer with a low‑level call, forwarding all available gas and explicitly checking the returned boolean value, reverting or handling the failure as appropriate. This change ensures that even contracts with expensive fallback logic receive the Ether, and that any failure is detected and can be acted upon, restoring the intended accounting behavior of the protocol.

title: Swap will unnecessarily revert in some cases
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the fee‑charging routine of a token swap function that can cause the entire transaction to revert when the swap is split across multiple swap operations (swapOps). The contract charges the protocol fee in ETH before executing any swapOps and assumes that the fee can be deducted from the input amount of the first swapOp. If the first swapOp provides less ETH than the required fee, the require statement `swapOps[0].amountIn > feesCharged` fails, triggering an underflow‑like revert with the message "Maradona: cannot substract fee from input swap". This situation arises when the swap logic distributes the total input across several exchanges to obtain better prices, a common pattern in decentralized aggregators. Because the fee deduction is hard‑coded to the first leg, any split that places a small amount in the first leg will cause the transaction to abort even though the overall input is sufficient to cover both the fee and the desired token purchase. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: users attempting to swap ETH for a token may see their transactions revert unexpectedly, receiving no tokens and no ETH transferred, while still paying gas. The bug is discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee‑charging flow and identified the mismatch between fee deduction and multi‑leg swap execution. It can be hard to notice because the revert only occurs for specific input patterns; typical single‑leg swaps succeed, so the failure appears intermittent and may be attributed to market conditions rather than a contract flaw. The affected parties are any users who trade with ETH‑denominated fees and rely on multi‑exchange routing, as well as the protocol that could lose credibility due to unexplained transaction failures. To remediate, the fee‑charging logic should be adapted to either (a) charge fees proportionally across all swapOps, (b) ensure the first swapOp always contains enough ETH to cover the fee, or (c) perform fee deduction after the full swap amount is known, thereby eliminating the assumption that the first leg can always pay the fee. This class of bug falls under improper input validation and incorrect accounting of fees in multi‑step financial operations, where the contract’s accounting assumptions do not hold for all execution paths, leading to unexpected reverts and loss of user confidence.

title: getBridgeFee() may can't work properly
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the getBridgeFee function of the StargateManager contract. This view function is intended to return the exact LayerZero message fee that will be required when the contract later calls swapRouter.swap to bridge assets. However, the parameters passed to swapRouter.quoteLayerZeroFee inside getBridgeFee are not identical to the parameters that swapRouter.swap actually uses. Specifically, the function encodes the destination address with abi.encode instead of abi.encodePacked, supplies an empty string "0x" as the payload while swap uses a non‑empty bytes payload, and constructs dstNativeAddr by abi.encode(opParams.extraAddresses[1]) even though the swap call expects a plain address or a zero value. Because extraAddresses[1] may be undefined for certain calls, the encoding can read out of bounds and cause the view function to revert, or it can return a fee that is lower or higher than the real cost. When the subsequent swapRouter.swap is executed with the fee returned by getBridgeFee, the transaction may run out of gas, be rejected by the LayerZero relayer, or simply revert, leaving the user’s funds locked in the contract. The bug manifests only when a user initiates a cross‑chain bridge; from the user’s perspective the UI shows a quoted fee, the user confirms the transaction, and then the transaction fails or completes with an unexpected fee, often resulting in a “transaction reverted” message or a missing balance on the destination chain. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s logic, where the auditor compared the arguments of quoteLayerZeroFee with those of swap and noticed the mismatches. It is hard to detect because getBridgeFee is a view function that does not change state, so a developer may assume the returned value is safe without testing the exact execution path of swap. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect fee estimation due to mismatched encoding and out‑of‑bounds array access”, which violates the protocol’s accounting assumption that the quoted fee equals the actual fee required for a successful bridge. The recommended fix is to align the arguments of quoteLayerZeroFee with those of swap: use abi.encodePacked for the recipient address, provide the same payload format, and set dstNativeAddr to a static zero address (or the proper destination address) instead of encoding an unchecked array element. By doing so the function will return a reliable fee and prevent swaps from failing unexpectedly.

title: StargateManager.bridge() when isFromEth ,
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the bridge function of the StargateManager contract when the transaction originates from native ETH (isFromEth is true). In this execution path the contract skips any validation of the outputToken field supplied in the operation parameters. The validateFeeToken logic later permits the fee‑payment token to be either the input token or the bridge operation’s output token. Because the output token is not checked for the ETH‑origin case, an attacker can supply an arbitrary address—such as a mock token with zero value—as the outputToken and also set the feesTokenAddress to that same address. Consequently the fee calculation uses a token that carries no economic value, allowing the attacker to evade the required bridge fees entirely. Exploitation consists of calling bridge with inputToken set to address(0), providing a legitimate destination and recipient, but inserting a dummy outputToken (e.g., a freshly deployed ERC‑20 with no supply) and pointing the fee token to it. The contract then proceeds with the swapRouterETH.swapETH call without charging any fee. From a user perspective the transaction appears to succeed, the ETH is transferred to the destination, but the protocol receives no fee revenue; a malicious user may notice that no fee is deducted while honest users see normal fee deductions. The issue manifests only when bridging from ETH; bridging from an ERC‑20 token includes a require that outputToken equals the input token, preventing the same evasion. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the ETH branch with the ERC‑20 branch and identified the missing require statement. It can be hard to notice because the function otherwise executes successfully and the missing check does not cause a revert, making the behavior indistinguishable from a correctly funded bridge except for the absent fee transfer. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked input validation leading to fee‑evasion or economic‑logic bypass. To remediate, the contract should enforce that opParams.outputToken is address(0) (or otherwise a valid fee token) in the isFromEth branch, mirroring the validation performed for ERC‑20 bridges, thereby ensuring that fee calculations always reference a token with real value and that the protocol’s accounting assumptions remain intact.

title: Paymaster will always revert when trying to bridge ETH due to incorrect balance calculation
description: Messi Paymaster allows users to swap any token into ETH, and bridge this ETH using Stargate. This operation will not work because the paymaster tries to send more eth to the bridge than the actual balance. This is due to missing the subtraction of bridge fees in case of ETH bridge. A similar issue exists on Maradona as well, there in case the user does not send the bridge fee in addition to ETH used for trade, the transaction will revert. This bridge fee will never be refunded to the relayer, leading to the same problem as described here. Messi paymaster tries to bridge ETH in line 524: bridge(bridgeOp, bridgeFeeEth + valueToSend); In this case it tries to send bridgeFeeEth + valueToSend. The reason for this is because for example stargate uses the native token as fee token. The problem with this is that valueToSend and bridgeOp.amountIn does not exclude bridgeFeeEth, in case we want to bridge ETH. In case we trade 1 ETH worth of USDC to 1 ETH, and try to bridge this 1 ETH (with 5000 wei bridge fee), it will result in revert. The paymaster tries to transfer 1000000000000005000 wei, even if his balance is only 1000000000000000000 wei (the output of last trade). In this case for the transaction to succeed the sponsor would have to send more eth to the contract, which is not refunded. In case user wants to bridge ETH the transaction will always revert.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect balance calculation in the Paymaster contract when bridging native ETH through Stargate. The contract adds the bridge fee to the amount of ETH that it attempts to send, but it does not subtract that fee from the amount obtained from the preceding token swap. As a result the contract calls the bridge function with value = bridgeFeeEth + valueToSend while its internal ETH balance only contains valueToSend. When the sponsor does not provide extra ETH to cover the fee, the call exceeds the contract's balance and the transaction reverts. This condition occurs whenever a user swaps any token for ETH and then requests the Paymaster to bridge that ETH; the same logic flaw exists in a related Maradona Paymaster. The impact is that the user’s intended bridge never completes, the sponsor may have to send additional ETH that is never refunded, and the protocol suffers a denial‑of‑service condition for ETH bridges. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the bridge invocation code and noticed that the fee variable was added instead of being excluded. It can be hard to notice because the fee amount is typically very small (a few thousand wei) and the revert only happens in the specific ETH‑bridge path, so normal token‑bridge tests pass. From the user’s point of view the UI may show that the swap will produce 1 ETH and that the bridge will succeed, but the transaction fails and no ETH is transferred, leaving the user with no funds received and the sponsor potentially losing the extra ETH they sent. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect fee accounting” or “insufficient balance due to fee double‑counting”. To fix the problem the contract must calculate the amount to send to the bridge as valueToSend (or amountIn) minus the bridge fee, or handle the fee as a separate transfer, ensuring that the total ETH deducted from the contract never exceeds its actual balance.

title: Fee-on-transfer token is not integrated correctly
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the contract assuming that a token transfer delivers exactly the amount specified in the bridge or swap request, while some ERC20 tokens deduct a fee on each transfer (fee‑on‑transfer tokens). The code uses safeTransferFrom and the standard swapExactTokensForTokens function, both of which expect the recipient to receive the full amount. Because the implementation does not check the actual balance after the transfer, it proceeds with the original amount value (bridgeOp.amountIn) even when the token has taken a fee, causing the contract to believe it holds more tokens than it actually does. This mismatch leads to two concrete failure modes. First, when a fee‑on‑transfer token is swapped through the router, the call to swapExactTokensForTokens may revert with the generic INSUFFICIENT_OUTPUT_AMOUNT error because the amount received after the fee is lower than the minimum output required. Second, in the Messi contract’s bridging logic, the contract calls tokenToBridge.safeTransferFrom expecting to receive bridgeOp.amountIn tokens; if the token charges a fee, the contract receives less (for example 9900 instead of 10000) and later attempts to bridge the full 10000, causing the operation to revert. The root cause is the lack of integration for fee‑on‑transfer tokens: the code never measures the actual amount received nor uses the router function that is designed to support such tokens (swapExactTokensForTokensSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens). The issue can be exploited by any user who supplies a fee‑on‑transfer token to the bridge or swap interface; the transaction will appear to succeed at the transfer step but will fail later, resulting in a reverted transaction, loss of gas, and potentially tokens being locked in the contract if the revert does not unwind the transfer. From a user’s perspective, the expected outcome – receiving the bridged amount or a successful swap – does not happen; the UI may show that the transaction was submitted but the token balance remains unchanged or an error message appears, leading to confusion and panic. The impact is medium severity because it does not directly allow an attacker to steal funds, but it can cause denial‑of‑service for users attempting to use fee‑on‑transfer tokens, and may result in funds being temporarily inaccessible. The bug manifests whenever a token that charges a transfer fee is used, including tokens that currently have no fee but could add one in the future, making the contract brittle against future token upgrades. The problem was discovered during a security audit that reviewed token handling paths and identified that the router call and the bridging logic do not account for fee‑on‑transfer behavior. The issue is subtle because the transfer itself succeeds and the fee is deducted silently, so standard testing with fee‑exempt tokens would not reveal it. To remediate, the contract should replace calls to swapExactTokensForTokens with swapExactTokensForTokensSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens when dealing with tokens that may charge a fee, and every safeTransferFrom should be followed by a balance‑before/balance‑after check to compute the actual amount received and adjust internal accounting accordingly. Alternatively, the contract could enforce that only fee‑exempt tokens are allowed, but the more robust solution is to explicitly support fee‑on‑transfer tokens throughout the codebase, ensuring that business logic such as minimum output checks and bridge amount calculations use the real received amount rather than the nominal amount specified by the caller.

title: Gas fee is charged too early and make sponsor lose fund when trigger setupAndTrade if there are bridging transaction
bug_full: The Messi contract implements a function that lets a designated sponsor trigger a series of operations, including token swaps and cross‑chain bridges, on behalf of a receiving user. Before any bridge call is executed the contract attempts to charge a gas fee by calculating (initialGas‑gasleft()) * tx.gasprice plus any value that will be sent, and it records this amount in the variable gasAmountCharged. The charge is performed immediately after the function records the initial gas amount, without waiting for the bridge transaction to finish. When the bridge operation uses a token that is not the designated fee token, the code that deducts the gas amount from the bridge input amount is skipped, so the gas cost is never sub‑tracted from the bridge payload. Consequently the sponsor, who is required to be the caller of the function, ends up paying the full gas cost of the bridge execution even though the protocol’s accounting assumes the fee would be covered by the fee token. This situation occurs only when a bridging operation is present and the bridge’s input token differs from the fee token, which is a common pattern for cross‑chain bridges such as Stargate that consume large amounts of gas. From a user’s perspective the receiving user sees their expected tokens transferred, but the sponsor’s balance is reduced by an amount that appears unrelated to any token movement, effectively “money disappears” from the sponsor’s account. The impact can be severe: on mainnet each bridge may cost roughly twenty US dollars in gas, so executing ten thousand such operations would drain around two hundred thousand dollars from the sponsor’s funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑charging logic, where the auditor noticed that the gas fee calculation is performed before the bridge call and that the subsequent deduction logic is conditional on the fee token matching the bridge input token. The bug is subtle because the contract does enforce a require(gasCharged) check, giving the impression that the fee has been accounted for, yet the actual token balance adjustments omit the gas cost in many realistic scenarios. To remediate the problem the contract should either defer the gas fee charge until after the bridge call completes, or ensure that the gasAmountCharged is always deducted from the bridge payload regardless of the token used, or alternatively shift the responsibility for paying the bridge gas to the receiving user as intended by the protocol’s economic model. In short, the vulnerability is an early‑gas‑charging logic error that leads to unintended sponsor fund loss during bridging operations, violating the expected accounting guarantees of the system.

title: USDT is not supported
description:
When approving USDT, the allowance value needs to be set to 0 first before it can be used correctly. However, the 4.9.5 version of OpenZeppelin does not internally call forceApprove.
Users can perform swap operations using RouterSwapExecutor, but the actual amount used in params_.swapData.amountInSwap and params_.swapData.swapPayload can differ. For USDT, this will result in the contract being unable to use the pool again.
Additionally, other parts of the protocol are also affected. For example, in ValantisHOTModule.swap, setting the router to a specific SovereignPool and passing parameters that cause the actual balance used to be less than amountIn will result in the allowance not being 0. This prevents the module from directly interacting with the SovereignPool again.
The contract may not work properly
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the interaction between the protocol’s swap modules and the USDT token, which implements a non‑standard ERC‑20 approve flow. USDT requires that an existing allowance be set to zero before a new allowance can be granted; otherwise the approve call is ignored or reverts. The protocol relies on OpenZeppelin version 4.9.5, which does not automatically invoke the forceApprove helper that would reset the allowance to zero before setting a new value. Consequently, when a user or a contract attempts to approve USDT for a swap through RouterSwapExecutor or through ValantisHOTModule.swap, the allowance may remain at a non‑zero value that does not match the amount needed for the next operation. The swap functions calculate the amount to be transferred (params_.swapData.amountInSwap) based on the caller’s expectation, but the actual amount transferred can be lower because the allowance was not correctly reset. This mismatch prevents the contract from pulling the required USDT from the pool, causing the pool interaction to fail and leaving the module unable to perform further swaps with that pool. The issue manifests as failed swap transactions, missing refunds, or balances that appear to drop to zero after a swap attempt. Users experience a denial‑of‑service where their USDT cannot be swapped, and funds may become temporarily locked in the contract because the allowance state blocks further token transfers. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended swap amount with the actual token movement and observed that the allowance was not cleared for USDT. It is subtle because most ERC‑20 tokens do not require a zero‑allowance step, so the failure only appears with USDT and similar tokens, making it easy to overlook in generic testing. To remediate the issue, the protocol should upgrade to a newer OpenZeppelin release that includes forceApprove or explicitly reset the allowance to zero before setting a new allowance for USDT. Alternatively, the swap logic can be modified to detect the token’s non‑standard behavior and handle allowance resets accordingly. By ensuring the allowance is correctly set, the protocol restores its ability to pull the exact amount of USDT needed for swaps, preventing transaction failures and protecting user funds.

title: AdvancedDistributorInitializable sets claim data
description:
AdvancedDistributorInitializable.claim overrides the passed-in data with new bytes(0). This data is needed by both PerAddressTrancheVestingMerkleDistributor and PerAddressContinuousVestingMerkleDistributor for claims to work. Therefore, claims do not work.
Claims do not work
Both PerAddressTrancheVestingMerkleDistributor and PerAddressContinuousVestingMerkleDistributor also pass in new bytes(0) to this argument, causing the same issue. However, this is a separate issue per my
AdvancedDistributorInitializable calls DistributorInitializable._executeClaim with data=new bytes(0)
e/blob/main/contracts/packages/hardhat/contracts/claim/factory/AdvancedDistributorInitializable.sol#L106-L113
```solidity
function _executeClaim(address beneficiary, uint256 totalAmount, bytes memory)
    internal
    virtual
    override
    returns (uint256 _claimed)
{
    _claimed = super._executeClaim(beneficiary, totalAmount, new bytes(0));
    _reconcileVotingPower(beneficiary);
}
```
DistributorInitializable._executeClaim forwards this data to getClaimableAmount, which forwards it to getVestedFraction
e/blob/main/contracts/packages/hardhat/contracts/claim/factory/DistributorInitializable.sol#L113
Many implementations of getVestedFraction attempt to decode this data in ways that break if the data is empty.
E.g.:
e/blob/main/contracts/packages/hardhat/contracts/claim/factory/PerAddressContinuousVestingInitializable.sol#L30-L35
```solidity
function getVestedFraction(
    address beneficiary,
    uint256 time, // time is in seconds past the epoch (e.g. block.timestamp)
    bytes memory data
) public view override returns (uint256) {
    (uint256 start, uint256 cliff, uint256 end) = abi.decode(data, (uint256, uint256, uint256));
```
Putting these together, attempting to claim will be a lot like this Chisel section.
```solidity
bytes memory data = new bytes(0)
(uint256 start, uint256 cliff, uint256 end) = abi.decode(data, (uint256, uint256, uint256));
```
Traces:
[805] 0xBd770416a3345F91E4B34576cb804a576fa48EB1::run()
←"EvmError: Revert"
Chisel Error: Failed to execute REPL contract!
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the claim execution path of the AdvancedDistributorInitializable contract. When a beneficiary calls the claim function, the contract overrides the data argument that is supposed to carry vesting schedule parameters with an empty byte array (new bytes(0)). This overridden data is then forwarded to DistributorInitializable._executeClaim, which in turn passes it to the getClaimableAmount logic of downstream distributors such as PerAddressTrancheVestingMerkleDistributor and PerAddressContinuousVestingMerkleDistributor. Those implementations expect the data field to contain an ABI‑encoded tuple of three uint256 values (start, cliff, end) and decode it using abi.decode. Because the data is empty, the decode operation reverts, causing the entire claim transaction to fail. The root cause is an incorrect parameter forwarding – the contract discards the caller‑provided data instead of propagating it. Exploitation is straightforward: any attempt to claim vested tokens triggers a revert, effectively denying service to all beneficiaries. The impact is that users cannot receive the tokens they are entitled to; from a user’s perspective the UI shows a failed claim, no tokens are transferred, and balances appear unchanged, which may be interpreted as funds disappearing. The issue manifests whenever the claim function of AdvancedDistributorInitializable or any contract that inherits it (including the two Merkle distributors) is used, i.e., under normal claim conditions. All token holders who rely on the vesting schedule are affected, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about gradual token release are violated. The problem was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the claim function replaces the data parameter with an empty byte array and traced the subsequent revert in the downstream decode logic. It is hard to notice because the contract compiles and deploys without error; the failure only appears at runtime when a claim is attempted, and the revert message does not clearly indicate the missing data. To remediate, the contract should forward the original data argument unchanged to the parent _executeClaim function, or the downstream contracts should be modified to handle an empty data payload gracefully. In generic terms, this is a classic case of improper argument forwarding leading to ABI‑decoding failures, which breaks business logic that depends on correctly supplied parameters for vesting calculations.

title: PerAddressTrancheVestingMerkleDistributor.claim
description:
Both the claim and initializeDistributionRecord methods of PerAddressTrancheVestingMerkleDistributor do not include the tranches when checking the Merkle proof (and do not even accept the tranches as a parameter). Both methods therefore always revert, before the function body is even entered.
We know from PerAddressTrancheVestingMerkle that the Merkle trees for this kind of distributor include the list of tranches for each address (and also because they have to be; there's no other way to specify the tranches). However, PerAddressTrancheVestingMerkleDistributor omits the tranches when checking the Merkle proofs. The Merkle proofs therefore always revert.
PerAddressTrancheVestingMerkleDistributor is completely inoperable.
Notice the lack of tranches here:
e/blob/main/contracts/packages/hardhat/contracts/claim/factory/PerAddressTrancheVestingMerkleDistributor.sol#L42-L58
```solidity
function initializeDistributionRecord(
    uint256 index, // the beneficiary's index in the merkle root
    address beneficiary, // the address that will receive tokens
    uint256 amount, // the total claimable by this beneficiary
    bytes32[] calldata merkleProof
) external validMerkleProof(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(index, beneficiary, amount)), merkleProof) {
    _initializeDistributionRecord(beneficiary, amount);
}

function claim(
    uint256 index, // the beneficiary's index in the merkle root
    address beneficiary, // the address that will receive tokens
    uint256 totalAmount, // the total claimable by this beneficiary
    bytes32[] calldata merkleProof
)
    external
    validMerkleProof(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(index, beneficiary, totalAmount)), merkleProof)
```
Contrast the code in PerAddressTrancheVestingMerkle, which checks the Merkle proof like this:
e/blob/main/contracts/packages/hardhat/contracts/claim/PerAddressTrancheVestingMerkle.sol#L45
```solidity
validMerkleProof(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(index, beneficiary, amount, abi.encode(tranches))), merkleProof)
```
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the PerAddressTrancheVestingMerkleDistributor contract where the claim and initializeDistributionRecord functions perform Merkle proof verification without including the tranche information that is required to reconstruct the leaf node. The root cause is that the function signatures do not accept a tranches parameter and the validMerkleProof modifier hashes only index, beneficiary and amount (or totalAmount), omitting the encoded tranches array that is part of the Merkle tree used by the corresponding PerAddressTrancheVestingMerkle contract. Because the leaf hash does not match any node in the stored Merkle root, every Merkle proof supplied to these functions fails verification and the modifier forces the transaction to revert before any internal logic is executed. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; any legitimate user attempting to claim their vested tokens will experience an immediate revert, receiving no tokens and seeing no change in their balance. The impact is that the distributor becomes completely inoperable: beneficiaries cannot claim their allocations, and the protocol’s token distribution schedule is effectively broken, potentially locking funds indefinitely. This condition occurs whenever a caller invokes claim or initializeDistributionRecord on the PerAddressTrancheVestingMerkleDistributor with any Merkle proof, regardless of its correctness, because the verification step is fundamentally flawed. The affected parties are the token holders who are meant to receive vested tokens, the protocol that relies on the distribution mechanism, and any downstream contracts that assume successful vesting. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit when the auditor compared the Merkle proof validation logic of this contract with the reference PerAddressTrancheVestingMerkle implementation and noticed the missing tranches argument. The bug can be hard to notice because the functions compile and appear to accept a Merkle proof, yet all calls silently revert, giving no obvious indication that the problem lies in the proof construction rather than in external factors. To remediate the flaw, the contract should be updated to accept a tranches parameter in both functions and incorporate abi.encode(tranches) into the leaf hash used by the validMerkleProof modifier, thereby aligning the verification process with the actual Merkle tree structure. This change restores the ability for beneficiaries to successfully prove their entitlement and claim their vested tokens, re‑enabling the intended distribution flow.

title: Potential ETH Loss Due to transfer Usage in
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the use of Solidity's built‑in transfer method to return ETH from the Requestor contract. Transfer forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas to the recipient, which is sufficient for a simple external‑owned account but insufficient for contracts that execute any logic in their receive or fallback functions, and it can also be insufficient on layer‑2 solutions such as zkSync where the intrinsic gas cost of a basic transfer may exceed the stipend. When a user or an automated draw bot supplies ETH to request a random number, any unused portion of that payment is meant to be withdrawn later via the withdraw function. The withdraw function calls _to.transfer(balance), sending the entire contract balance to the caller‑specified address. If the destination address is a contract with a non‑trivial receive/fallback, or if the underlying chain imposes higher gas requirements (as documented for zkSync), the transfer will revert, leaving the ETH locked inside the Requestor contract. This failure can be triggered whenever the withdraw function is invoked, which is restricted to the contract creator but can be called on behalf of any user who deposited funds. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – a refund of the unused ETH – does not materialise; the UI may show a pending withdrawal or a zero balance change, and the user receives no funds despite the contract holding them. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined cross‑chain deployment assumptions and noticed that the transfer pattern does not conform to best practices on modern roll‑up networks. It is hard to notice because on most EVM‑compatible mainnets the transfer succeeds, masking the problem until the contract is deployed on a chain with stricter gas limits. The impact is medium severity: funds can become effectively irretrievable, breaking the economic model of the draw system and potentially causing loss of confidence in the protocol. The recommended remediation is to replace transfer with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas (or a configurable amount) and checks the returned success flag, e.g., (bool sent, ) = _to.call{value:balance}(''); require(sent, 'ETH transfer failed'); This approach respects the varying gas requirements of different execution environments and ensures that refunds are reliably delivered.

title: Claimers Cannot Claim Prizes When Last Tier
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the claimPrizes function of the Claimer contract, which reverts when the prize amount for the tier identified as numberOfTiers‑3 is zero. The function computes a fee for the claimer bot by calling an internal routine _computeFeePerClaim, which in turn invokes _computeDecayConstant. This routine fetches the maximum fee from the PrizePool via getTierPrizeSize(numberOfTiers‑3) and passes it to LinearVRGDALib.getMaximumPriceDeltaScale. The library ultimately calls wadLn on the ratio of the maximum fee to the time parameter. The wadLn function contains a require statement that the input be greater than zero; when the maximum fee is zero, the require fails and the whole transaction reverts. The root cause is the implicit assumption that the last regular tier always holds a positive prize amount, an assumption that breaks when liquidity for that tier is exhausted or no contributions were made in a draw, causing the tier prize to round to zero. An attacker does not need to act maliciously – any caller (typically an off‑chain claimer bot) that attempts to claim prizes for legitimate winners will trigger the revert, preventing the prize distribution for all winners in that draw. From the user’s perspective the claim transaction fails, the UI reports that no prize was received, balances remain unchanged and winners see “claim failed” or “no reward” messages even though they are entitled to a prize. The impact is that legitimate winners do not receive their rewards, the protocol’s incentive mechanism is broken, and funds remain locked in the PrizePool until a manual claim with a zero fee is performed or the contract is patched. The issue occurs only when the last regular tier has zero liquidity, which can happen after draws with no contributions, after liquidity is reclaimed, or when the tier’s prize calculation rounds down to zero. It was discovered during a security audit that traced the fee‑calculation path and identified the unchecked division by zero in the library call. The bug is hard to notice because it manifests only in edge‑case draws and the revert originates deep inside a mathematical library, not directly in the claimPrizes code. To remediate, the contract should guard against a zero maximum fee – for example by bypassing the fee calculation and setting feePerClaim to zero when getTierPrizeSize(numberOfTiers‑3) returns zero, or by ensuring the library can handle a zero input safely. This change restores the ability of honest claimers to claim prizes for all winners regardless of tier liquidity, aligning the implementation with the intended business logic that every winner should be able to receive their reward.

title: DoSed liquidations as
description:
