To remediate, the calculation must be adjusted to reverse the 63/64 reduction, for example by multiplying the gasleft value by 64/63 before subtracting it from startGas, or by using a more direct measurement of actual gas used. In user‑facing terms, a user expects to pay an execution fee and later receive a partial refund of any unused portion, but due to the bug the refund can be zero, making the fee disappear from the user’s balance. This class of bug is a gas‑accounting miscalculation caused by ignoring EIP‑150’s gas forwarding rules, leading to over‑charging and fee theft.

title: If the accounted token balance is higher than
description:
In extreme cases, such as when late liquidations incur losses to liquidity providers, the actual balance will not exist in the vaults. The transfer will not revert due to how remains unchanged. This will lead to insolvency. When tokens are insufficient in the vaults, the token amount might never be sent to the users/pools without a revert.

For example, in cases of late liquidation during extreme market conditions, closing the liquidated positions will update the corresponding storage balances in pools and vaults. However, if there are insufficient funds in the pool, the tokens are not transferred to their destination, and the amount not sent is not checked. As seen in the DecreasePositionProcess::_settleCrossAccount and _settleIsolateAccount functions, VaultProcess.transferOut is called with the boolean set to "true," which will skip the token transfer if the contract's token balance is insufficient.

Consequently, the tokens are assumed to be sent in the exact amount reflected in the storage variables. However, the actual tokens transferred (0) can be significantly different, leading to insolvency.

This is definitely a problem in extreme market conditions where the pool incurs losses from undercollateralized borrowed positions or very high funding fees. In such cases, closing positions will not be tracked, and the actual balance transferred might be "0" for some users because there are not enough tokens in the vault. Since this would require a volatile market for the asset, I will label this as medium.

a04d794bf6b8104528681ad/elfi-perp-contracts/contracts/process/VaultProcess.sol#L13-L31  
a04d794bf6b8104528681ad/elfi-perp-contracts/contracts/vault/Vault.sol#L16-L2  
a04d794bf6b8104528681ad/elfi-perp-contracts/contracts/process/DecreasePositionProcess.sol#L338-L444  
a04d794bf6b8104528681ad/elfi-perp-contracts/contracts/process/IncreasePositionProcess.sol#L83-L104  
a04d794bf6b8104528681ad/elfi-perp-contracts/contracts/process/MarketProcess.sol#L118-L126
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch that occurs when the contract records a token transfer in its internal storage but the actual ERC20 transfer does not happen because the vault’s token balance is insufficient. The root cause is a logic flaw in the VaultProcess.transferOut function, which is invoked with a flag that deliberately skips the revert on insufficient balance. Consequently, the function updates the pool and position balances as if the full amount was sent, while the low‑level token transfer silently fails and returns zero. This can be exploited in extreme market conditions such as late liquidations, severe funding‑fee accruals, or large losses that drain the vault. An attacker or a regular user can trigger a position close when the vault is under‑collateralised; the contract will mark the position as settled, update storage variables to reflect the expected payout, but the actual token transfer will be omitted. The impact is that users receive no funds – their UI shows a successful closure and a positive balance change, yet their wallet balance remains unchanged, effectively causing funds to disappear and potentially rendering the pool insolvent. The issue manifests only when the on‑chain token balance of the vault is lower than the amount recorded in storage, which typically happens after extreme price moves or when multiple liquidations exhaust the pool’s liquidity. All participants who rely on the protocol – traders, liquidity providers, and downstream contracts – are affected because the protocol can no longer honour withdrawals or settlements. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the DecreasePositionProcess and IncreasePositionProcess flows and noticed that VaultProcess.transferOut is called with the boolean parameter set to true, bypassing the usual balance check and revert. Because the transaction does not revert, the problem is subtle and may go unnoticed; the contract’s events and storage appear consistent, while the actual token balance is reduced to zero. To remediate, the transferOut routine should verify that the vault holds enough tokens before updating storage, revert on insufficient balance, or at least adjust the recorded amount to the real transferred value. Alternatively, the protocol could implement partial payouts using the available balance or socialize the loss among participants, ensuring that no position can be closed without a corresponding token movement that matches the accounting state.

title: Unbacked tokens can be used for opening
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol treats funding‑fee adjustments as part of a pool’s available liquidity. When a position is increased, the FeeProcess updates an unsettled amount in the pool’s balance sheet. The pool’s borrow limit is calculated as (baseAmount + unsettledAmount) × liquidityFactor, so the unsettled amount – which represents funding fees that have not yet been transferred to any user – is mistakenly counted as real, withdrawable assets. Because these fees are only settled when a position is closed, the pool can appear to have more ETH than it actually holds. An attacker can exploit this mismatch by opening a new leveraged position after the unsettled amount has been added but before it is settled. The contract will allow borrowing up to the inflated limit, effectively granting the attacker “unbacked” tokens that exceed the pool’s true reserves. In the described scenario, Alice’s small top‑up creates a 10 ETH unsettled balance, inflating the pool’s available liquidity to 107.8 ETH even though only 100 ETH is truly deposited. Carol then borrows the extra 12.8 ETH, a amount that should be impossible, and later closes her position while the protocol still believes the pool is solvent. The impact is that the protocol can issue more tokens than it can redeem, leading to loss of funds for other traders (short positions incur unexpected ETH losses) and potential insolvency of the pool. This condition occurs whenever funding‑fee updates add unsettled amounts and the borrow‑limit formula does not exclude them, typically during position‑increase or funding‑fee‑update calls. All market participants – liquidity providers, long and short traders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting invariant that total borrowed assets must be ≤ actual pool reserves is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of funding fees through IncreasePositionProcess, FeeProcess, and MarketProcess and noticed that the unsettled amount was added to the liquidity calculation without being backed by real tokens. The bug is subtle because the on‑chain state still shows a non‑negative balance and the pool’s reported liquidity looks correct; only a deeper inspection of how unsettled fees are accounted reveals the over‑allocation. To remediate, the protocol should exclude unsettled funding fees from the liquidity‑available calculation, enforce settlement of fees before they contribute to borrow limits, or redesign the borrow‑limit formula to rely solely on actual free assets. In essence, the contract must treat funding‑fee accruals as a liability rather than an asset until they are transferred, thereby preventing the creation of unbacked tokens and preserving the integrity of the pool’s accounting model.

title: Users can gas grief or completely block keep-
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked Ether refund that is sent to the user with an unlimited gas stipend after a keeper executes or cancels an order. The contract calls a low‑level withdraw function that forwards all remaining gas to the recipient address. Because the refund is performed without verifying whether the destination is a contract or handling a possible revert, a malicious user can deploy a contract with a fallback function that either reverts or deliberately consumes all the remaining gas. When the keeper’s transaction reaches the refund step, the malicious fallback either triggers a revert that bubbles up and causes the whole keeper transaction to fail, or it exhausts the gas supplied to the keeper, resulting in a gas‑griefing situation. This can happen whenever the refund amount (refundFee) is greater than zero, which includes order cancellations that are only callable by keepers. The affected parties are the keepers, who lose the execution fee they paid and may be unable to complete future cancellations, and the protocol, whose order‑cancellation mechanism can be permanently blocked. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the pattern of sending refunds with infinite gas in the GasProcess.processExecutionFee function. It is hard to notice because typical tests use externally owned accounts that accept Ether without reverting, so the failure only appears when a contract with a malicious fallback is used. The impact is economic loss for keepers and a denial‑of‑service condition for the protocol, effectively allowing a user to block keepers from performing required actions. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of unchecked external calls that enable denial‑of‑service or gas‑griefing attacks. To remediate, the contract should first check whether the recipient address contains code and, if so, either use a limited‑gas call (e.g., call{value: amount, gas: 2300}()) or adopt a pull‑payment model where the user withdraws the refund themselves. Additionally, the refund logic should be wrapped in a try/catch block so that a revert from the recipient does not revert the entire keeper transaction, and the execution fee should be accounted for even if the refund fails. This change restores the intended business logic that keepers are reimbursed for gas costs while preventing a user from causing the transaction to fail or consume all gas.

title: Keepers loss gas is never accounted
bug_full: The vulnerability is a loss‑accounting bug in the GasProcess::processExecutionFee routine used by many facets of the Diamond contract. The function is intended to track three values after a keeper executes a transaction: the execution fee actually spent, a refund to the user when the spent fee is lower than the prepaid amount, and a loss fee that should be recorded when the spent fee exceeds the prepaid amount. The root cause is a logical error in the calculation of lossFee. After measuring used gas and computing executionFee = usedGas * tx.gasprice, the code checks if executionFee > cache.userExecutionFee. If true, it clamps executionFee to cache.userExecutionFee and then sets lossFee = executionFee - cache.userExecutionFee. Because executionFee has just been overwritten with the same value as cache.userExecutionFee, the subtraction always yields zero, so lossFee is never positive. Consequently the subsequent call to CommonData.addLossExecutionFee is never executed with a non‑zero amount, and any excess gas paid by the keeper is never recorded. This flaw can be exploited implicitly: a keeper that spends more gas than the amount it prepaid will not receive any compensation for the surplus, and the protocol’s accounting will silently lose those funds. Over many executions, especially in a scaled system, the unaccounted loss can accumulate to a substantial amount, eroding keeper incentives and potentially reducing the reliability of the service. The condition for the bug to manifest is any execution where usedGas * tx.gasprice exceeds the user‑provided execution fee. The affected parties are the keepers who supply gas, the protocol that relies on accurate fee‑accounting, and indirectly any users whose transactions depend on timely keeper execution. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s fee‑processing logic, where the reviewer noted that the lossFee variable is annotated with a comment “@review always 0”. The bug is hard to notice because the function does not revert or emit events when the loss fee is zero, and the overall system may still appear to work correctly from a functional standpoint, masking the financial discrepancy. To remediate, the lossFee should be computed before the executionFee is capped, or the logic should directly calculate lossFee as max(0, usedGas * tx.gasprice - cache.userExecutionFee) and then add that amount to the loss accounting. This change restores proper accounting of excess gas, aligns the contract with its intended economic model, and prevents silent erosion of keeper compensation.

title: Contract will reach a point where users will
description:
With the contract working as intended, after a long enough period of time the perceived amount of collateral for a specific point will cross collateralTotalCap resulting in the fact that users will not be able to deposit more tokens of that type.

When deposit is called, after the necessary checks the method commonData.addTradeTokenCollateral is called which increases the total amount of collateral for a specific token in order to track how much collateral of this type of token exists and so that it does not cross the collateralTotalCap.

On the other hand, the function subTradeTokenCollateral which is used to reduce the amount of total collateral per token is never called anywhere in the project resulting in an inaccurate value for self.tradeCollateralTokenDatas[token].totalCollateral as it tracks the amount of tokens that have entered the contract and not how many tokens are currently present inside the vault of the contract. And because there is a check whether the calling deposit would pass this cap it will eventually make it so that calling deposit with specific tokens would revert every time.

Eventual denial of service for deposit
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the contract’s collateral tracking mechanism that can lead to a denial‑of‑service condition for deposits of a particular token type. The contract maintains a variable that records the total amount of collateral for each token and checks this value against a hard‑coded collateralTotalCap before allowing new deposits. When a user deposits tokens, the function commonData.addTradeTokenCollateral is invoked, correctly increasing the recorded totalCollateral. However, the complementary function subTradeTokenCollateral, which should be called whenever collateral is removed (for example during a withdrawal), is never invoked anywhere in the code base. As a result, the totalCollateral value only ever grows, even though tokens may have been withdrawn from the vault. Over time, or after a series of deposits and withdrawals, the recorded totalCollateral can exceed the collateralTotalCap. Because the deposit routine checks the recorded total against the cap, any subsequent deposit attempt for that token will hit the cap check and revert, preventing the transaction from completing. From a user’s perspective this appears as a sudden inability to add more tokens: the UI shows a failed transaction or a “deposit reverted” error, even though the user expects to be able to increase their collateral. The impact is that legitimate users are blocked from adding further collateral, effectively freezing the deposit functionality for that token and undermining the protocol’s ability to accept new participants or increase liquidity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of collateral updates and noticed that the decrement function existed but was never called. It can be hard to notice because normal operation with a modest amount of deposits may never reach the cap, and unit tests often focus on successful paths rather than long‑term state evolution. The root cause is the missing invocation of subTradeTokenCollateral, leading to an inaccurate totalCollateral that does not reflect the actual token balance inside the contract. To remediate, the contract should invoke subTradeTokenCollateral whenever collateral is reduced, such as in the withdraw function, or otherwise ensure that the stored totalCollateral is recomputed from the real token balance before performing the cap check. This correction restores the invariant that totalCollateral accurately represents the amount of tokens held, preventing the cap from being erroneously reached and allowing deposits to continue as intended.

title: The keeper will suffer continuing losses due
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an under‑compensation of the keeper that submits transactions to rollup‑based L2 chains such as Arbitrum, Base or Optimism. The contract function that settles the execution fee calculates the amount to be paid to the keeper solely from the L2 gas used (usedGas * tx.gasprice) and then either refunds the user or records a loss based on the difference between the user‑provided fee and the calculated execution fee. However, each L2 transaction also incurs a mandatory L1 rollup or data fee that must be paid to the underlying L1 for publishing the transaction batch. Because the current implementation never queries or adds this L1 fee to the keeper’s compensation, the keeper receives only the L2 portion while still bearing the L1 cost. This omission originates from a logical flaw in the fee accounting logic: the processExecutionFee routine assumes that the total cost is represented by L2 gas alone, ignoring the separate accounting rule described in the Arbitrum and Optimism documentation. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the code; the loss occurs automatically whenever a keeper executes a transaction, making the issue a systemic economic bug rather than a classic security breach. The impact is that keepers experience a net loss on every transaction, which can erode their incentive to provide service, potentially leading to reduced reliability of the protocol. The problem manifests under the condition that the contract is used on any L2 that requires an L1 data fee, and it affects any address acting as a keeper, as well as downstream users who may see degraded service. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s fee logic with the official rollup fee models and noticed the missing L1 component. It can be hard to notice because the L1 fee is not visible in the Solidity code and the contract’s events only show L2 gas reimbursement, giving a false impression that the keeper is fully compensated. To remediate, the fee calculation should be extended to include the L1 rollup fee, for example by reading the L1 data fee from the rollup’s system contract or by passing it as a parameter, and then adjusting the executionFee, refundFee and lossFee calculations accordingly. This change restores the economic balance, ensuring that the keeper receives a payment that covers both L2 execution and L1 publishing costs, and prevents the systematic drain of keeper funds.

title: Missing compensation for the 21,000 intrin-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a systematic under‑payment of the keeper’s execution fee caused by the contract’s fee‑calculation routine not accounting for the 21,000 gas units that the EVM deducts as intrinsic cost before any Solidity code runs. The function records the remaining gas with gasleft() after the intrinsic cost has already been subtracted, then passes that value to GasProcess.processExecutionFee to reimburse the caller. Because the intrinsic cost is omitted, the reimbursement is short by exactly the intrinsic amount (or by the amount of additional gas required for calldata and diamond fallback as noted in the audit). This can be exploited simply by invoking executeOrder as a keeper; each call will result in the keeper receiving less ether than required to cover the true gas spent, effectively losing 21 k gas per transaction. Over many executions the loss accumulates, reducing the economic incentive for keepers, potentially causing orders to go unexecuted and harming the protocol’s reliability. The issue manifests whenever a keeper calls executeOrder on any chain (L1 or L2) because the intrinsic cost is universal. Users of the protocol see no direct UI symptom, but keepers notice that their balance after execution is lower than expected, often observing “my gas reimbursement is missing 21 k” or “the fee paid does not cover the gas I spent”. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the startGas snapshot with the known intrinsic cost and realized the compensation logic omitted that portion. It is easy to miss because gasleft() appears to give a complete picture of gas usage, yet the EVM subtracts the intrinsic cost before the first opcode, so the snapshot is already reduced. The proper fix is to add the intrinsic gas amount (or an appropriate constant covering calldata and diamond fallback overhead) to the recorded startGas before fee calculation, or to modify GasProcess.processExecutionFee to add the intrinsic cost internally. This aligns the reimbursement with the actual gas consumed, restores the intended economic model, and prevents systematic loss of funds for keepers.

title: A significant 105,983 gas cost of
bug_full: The vulnerability is an under‑accounted gas cost in the fee‑compensation routine that is executed after an order is processed. When executeOrder records the gas remaining at the start of the function (startGas) it later calls processExecutionFee to calculate the keeper's execution fee based on the difference between startGas and the current gas left. However, the gas consumed by the internal logic of processExecutionFee itself – including token transfers, ether withdrawals and bookkeeping – is not added to the usedGas calculation. As a result the executionFee variable is computed with a value that is lower than the actual gas spent, typically by about 105,983 gas units in the current implementation. The keeper therefore receives less ether than required to reimburse the gas it actually used, leading to a systematic loss of roughly 100 k gas per order execution. This issue manifests whenever an order is executed and the fee‑processing function is invoked, affecting the keeper (the entity that calls executeOrder), the protocol’s economic model and indirectly the users who may see higher effective fees or reduced incentives for keepers. The problem was discovered during a security audit by measuring the gas consumption of processExecutionFee with a dedicated event and observing a significant unaccounted portion. It is hard to notice because the fee calculation appears syntactically correct and the missing gas is hidden inside a helper function, making the discrepancy subtle and only visible through precise gas profiling. The bug belongs to the class of gas‑accounting errors where internal execution costs are omitted from reimbursement calculations, violating the protocol’s assumption that the recorded startGas fully covers all subsequent operations. To remediate, the contract should either add a calibrated constant (approximately 101 000 gas) to the usedGas computation, compute usedGas after the internal logic, or redesign the fee calculation to include the gas spent by processExecutionFee itself, ensuring the keeper is fully compensated for the true gas consumption.

title: Future upgrades may be difficult or impossible
bug_full: An upgradable contract stores its state using nested structs. The outer structs contain inner structs that themselves hold mappings, sets and primitive variables. Because the Solidity storage layout is fixed at compile time, each field occupies a specific slot sequence. When a struct is placed inside another struct, the compiler lays out the inner fields directly after the outer fields. Adding a new variable to the inner struct in a later implementation shifts the position of all subsequent fields in the outer struct, so the data that was written to those slots during the original deployment is interpreted incorrectly after the upgrade. This situation is analogous to the well‑known storage‑gap problem but is more subtle because the gap is hidden inside a nested struct. The vulnerability manifests when the proxy pattern is used and the contract is upgraded to a version that modifies any inner struct. Under those conditions the upgrade may overwrite or misread existing balances, fee reward records, APR values or other financial parameters. Users may see their token balances become zero, rewards disappear, or APR values change unexpectedly, even though no transaction was performed. The protocol’s accounting logic relies on the integrity of these stored values, so corrupted storage can lead to incorrect payouts, loss of claimable rewards, or even a complete breakdown of the pool’s operation. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the storage definitions, where the nested structs were observed and the inability to safely extend them was noted. It is hard to detect in normal testing because the contract behaves correctly before any upgrade; the problem only appears when a future change attempts to add fields to the inner structs. The proper mitigation is to avoid placing structs directly inside other structs for upgradable contracts. Instead, each logical component should be stored in its own mapping or separate storage contract, optionally reserving explicit storage gaps. This approach allows new variables to be added by extending the mapping keys without shifting existing slots, preserving data consistency across upgrades.

title: Use of outdated liability value in decreasePosition
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency that occurs when a cross‑margin position with an outstanding liability is settled and the user’s token balance subsequently increases, for example through a deposit or a post‑settlement token credit. The protocol first calls a function that repays the user’s previous liability (accountProps.repayLiability) and then invokes LpPoolProcess.updatePnlAndUnHoldPoolAmount, passing the newly generated liability value (addLiability) as the amount to adjust the pool’s PnL and un‑held funds. Because the repayment is performed before the pool update but the updated liability amount does not reflect the amount that has just been repaid, the pool continues to treat the old liability as outstanding. This outdated liability value is used to calculate fees and pool balances, leading to an over‑charge on the user and a mismatch between the pool’s internal accounting and the actual funds held. The issue manifests only when there is a non‑zero liability and a subsequent token increase; it does not affect positions without liability. Users experience symptoms such as seeing a higher fee than expected, receiving a smaller net deposit, or observing a missing refund after a position is closed. From a developer’s perspective the bug is a classic case of using stale state in a financial calculation – the contract fails to incorporate the effect of a repayment before adjusting pool metrics. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of liability repayment and pool updates and identified that the repayment result was never fed back into the pool‑update call. The flaw can be hard to notice because the UI may still display the correct token balance, while the hidden accounting layer records an inflated liability, causing subtle fee inflation. To remediate the issue the pool‑update function should be supplied with the net liability after repayment, or the repayment amount should be subtracted from the liability argument passed to updatePnlAndUnHoldPoolAmount. In conceptual terms the fix requires synchronising the liability state across the repayment and pool‑adjustment steps so that the pool’s accounting reflects the true outstanding debt, eliminating the fee over‑charge and ensuring that users receive the expected amount after deposits or settlements.

title: The balance.unsettledAmount is missing in getMaxWithdraw
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting omission in the USD pool contract where the field representing fees that have been earned but not yet transferred (unsettledAmount) is not taken into account when calculating the maximum amount a user can withdraw (getMaxWithdraw) and when checking whether a subtraction amount is allowed (isSubAmountAllowed). Because the functions only consider the settled balance (amount) and the hold amount, any positive unsettledAmount reduces the computed withdrawable amount artificially. This happens whenever the pool has accrued fees, i.e., when unsettledAmount > 0. As a result, higher‑level functions that rely on these helpers incorrectly conclude that a withdrawal or a subtraction is not permitted, causing the transaction to revert or to return zero. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that no funds are available for withdrawal or that a withdrawal request fails even though the account balance appears sufficient, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the financial logic of the pool contract and noticed that the unsettledAmount variable was never referenced in the relevant calculations. The bug is hard to notice because the primary balance fields (amount and holdAmount) look correct, while the missing component subtly skews the limit calculation. The impact is that liquidity providers or users cannot retrieve the full amount they are entitled to, effectively locking fees inside the contract until the bug is fixed. The class of bug is an accounting logic error – a missing state variable in a financial formula – which violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that total available assets equal settled balance plus pending fees. The recommended fix is to include unsettledAmount in both getMaxWithdraw and isSubAmountAllowed calculations, adding it to the balance before applying hold and liquidity‑limit adjustments, thereby restoring the correct withdrawable amount and allowing legitimate withdrawals to succeed.

title: Users can have positions with a margin lower than the minimum margin
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of allowing a trader to end up with a position whose remaining margin falls below the protocol‑defined minimum margin threshold. The contract enforces the minimum margin only when a new position is opened, rejecting orders whose initial margin is lower than the configured limit. However, when a position is partially closed, the implementation does not verify that the leftover margin after the decrease still satisfies the minimum requirement. As a result, a user can close a large portion of a position and leave a tiny amount of collateral – often called “dust” – that is smaller than the minimum order margin. This dust margin creates rounding discrepancies in fee, profit‑and‑loss and liquidation calculations. Because the accounting logic assumes every active position holds at least the minimum margin, the rounding errors may cause the liquidation engine to mis‑detect profitability or to be unable to execute a liquidation, effectively locking the remaining funds. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a very small position size and a near‑zero margin, yet the user cannot withdraw the residual amount because the protocol treats the position as still open but under‑collateralised. The impact includes loss of funds that become unrecoverable, inaccurate accounting, and a potential denial‑of‑service where small positions cannot be liquidated. The issue manifests whenever a trader uses a decrease‑position order on a cross‑margin account without a safeguard on the post‑trade margin balance. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the order‑validation logic and then exercised a sequence of open‑order followed by a partial‑close transaction, observing the leftover margin drop below the threshold. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error for the dust case; the only symptom is the unexpected small balance and failed liquidation, which can be mistaken for normal rounding noise. The proper remediation is to add a post‑trade validation step that checks the remaining margin against the minimum allowed margin and rejects the trade if the residual collateral would be insufficient, thereby preserving the invariant that every active position holds at least the minimum margin and preventing dust‑margin scenarios.

title: The User will receive less amount than user expected
bug_full: The vulnerability is an ordering flaw in the redemption flow of a staking protocol where the user‑specified minimum redeem amount (minRedeemAmount) is validated before the protocol fee is deducted. The contract first converts the unstaked USD value to a token amount, stores it in a temporary variable, and then checks whether this amount is at least the user‑provided minimum. Because the fee is subtracted only after this check, the final amount transferred to the user can be lower than the minimum they expected, violating the guarantee that the transaction will either deliver at least the specified amount or revert. This occurs whenever a user initiates a redemption request with a non‑zero minRedeemAmount and the fee is non‑negligible relative to the redeem amount. An attacker does not need to act actively; the bug is triggered automatically by the protocol’s own fee calculation. The impact is that users receive fewer tokens than promised, leading to unexpected balance reductions, failed expectations (e.g., “I expected to receive 9 tokens but got 8.9”), and potential loss of trust in the protocol’s accounting logic. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the RedeemProcess library, where the auditor noticed that the slippage check was performed before fee deduction, a pattern that can easily be missed because the transaction still succeeds and only the final transferred amount is slightly lower. The problem is hard to notice because the difference may be small and the transaction does not revert, so users may attribute the shortfall to market movement rather than a contract bug. Conceptually, this is a fee‑ordering or slippage‑check bug: the contract should verify that the amount remaining after fee deduction still satisfies the user’s minimum requirement. The recommended fix is to move the minRedeemAmount validation to after the fee is calculated, ensuring that the net amount transferred meets the user’s expectation, or to adjust the check to compare the net amount (redeemTokenAmount minus redeemFee) against the minimum. By correcting the order of operations, the protocol restores the intended guarantee that users either receive at least the amount they specified or the transaction reverts, preserving accounting integrity and user confidence.

title: isHoldAmountAllowed and isSubAmountAllowed logic inconsistency
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inconsistency between two accounting checks that govern how stable token balances are held and later deducted. The HoldStableToken routine uses a condition that adds the current amount, any unsettled amount and then subtracts the already‑held amount to decide if a new hold is permissible. This logic permits a holdAmount that can be larger than the actual token balance because it does not verify that balance.amount is at least as large as the new hold. Later, when the contract attempts to subtract tokens via subStableToken, it relies on a different check that only ensures balance.amount is greater than the requested subtraction amount and that the pool liquidity limit is satisfied. Crucially, it does not confirm that balance.amount is greater than or equal to the existing holdAmount. If a holdAmount exceeds balance.amount, the subtraction expression balance.amount - balance.holdAmount underflows, causing the transaction to revert under Solidity 0.8’s built‑in safety checks. This situation can be triggered when poolLiquidityLimit is zero, allowing a hold of, for example, 12e18 tokens while the actual amount is only 10e18. The subsequent subStableToken call then fails with an underflow error, effectively blocking any operation that depends on token subtraction such as redemption, profit‑and‑loss updates, or rebalance calls. From a user’s perspective the UI will show a transaction that “reverts” or “fails” without any change to balances, leading to confusion as the expected refund or redemption never arrives. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate users cannot withdraw or the protocol cannot rebalance, potentially freezing liquidity and harming confidence. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the UsdPool library, where the auditor noticed that the two checks were not symmetrical and that the subtraction could overflow when holdAmount is larger than the stored amount. The bug is hard to notice because the hold check passes, giving a false sense of safety, while the later subtraction silently reverts only when executed. The flaw belongs to the class of inconsistent accounting validations that lead to arithmetic underflow. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit guard in isSubAmountAllowed that ensures balance.amount is not less than balance.holdAmount before performing the subtraction, thereby aligning the two checks and preventing the underflow scenario.

title: User Collateral Cap Check Issue
description: User Collateral can exceeds the cap and deposit will still be processed. The check accountProps.getTokenAmount(token) > tradeTokenConfig.collateralUserCap is designed to ensure that a user's collateral does not exceed their specific cap. However, this validation occurs before the new deposit amount is added, thereby only verifying the current balance. Consequently, this can result in the user's collateral exceeding the cap once the deposit is processed.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect collateral cap validation in the deposit function. The contract checks the user's existing token amount against a per‑user collateral cap, but the check is performed before the new deposit amount is added. As a result the condition only guarantees that the current balance is below the limit, not that the balance after the deposit will stay within the limit. An attacker (or any user) can submit a deposit that pushes the total collateral above the configured cap, and the transaction will still succeed because the require statement evaluates the pre‑deposit balance. This allows the user’s collateral to exceed the intended maximum, breaking accounting assumptions that the protocol relies on for risk management, margin calculations, and liquidation thresholds. The issue manifests when a user already holds a collateral amount close to the cap and then makes an additional deposit; the contract will accept the deposit and record a total that is higher than allowed. The bug was discovered during a manual audit by inspecting the order of operations in the deposit logic and confirmed with a unit test that deliberately deposits an amount that would overflow the cap. Because the contract does not emit an explicit error and the UI may simply show a higher balance, the problem can be hard to notice unless the developer compares the recorded balance with the configured cap. The impact is medium: it may allow a user to lock more assets than permitted, potentially affecting the protocol’s risk parameters and exposing other participants to higher leverage or insufficient collateral coverage. The class of bug is an off‑by‑one‑or‑order‑of‑operations validation error, where a limit check is applied to stale state. To remediate, the contract should compute the prospective total collateral (current amount plus the incoming deposit) and require that this sum does not exceed the user cap, emitting a clear error such as CollateralUserCapOverflow if it does. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that after a deposit the displayed collateral balance can be larger than the maximum advertised limit, or that a transaction that should have been rejected succeeds, leading to confusion when the protocol later rejects actions that depend on the cap. The bug violates the business rule that each participant may only provide a bounded amount of collateral, breaking the accounting invariant that total collateral ≤ user cap.

title: Private vaults don't prevent non-whitelisted
bug_full: The vulnerability is that a vault marked as private does not enforce the whitelist on subsequent token transfers, allowing any holder of shares to send them to non‑whitelisted addresses. The root cause is that the only access control is applied in the deposit function via the onlyAllowed modifier, which checks that the recipient is either the manager, the vault is public, or the address is whitelisted. However, the ERC‑20‑like share token implements _beforeTokenTransfer that only blocks transfers when the vault is paused or when a cooldown is active, but it does not re‑check the whitelist for the destination address. Consequently, a whitelisted investor can deposit, receive shares, and then transfer those shares to an arbitrary address, effectively bypassing the private‑pool restriction. An attacker can exploit this by first depositing through a whitelisted account (or by having a trusted participant do so) and then calling transfer or transferFrom to move the shares to a non‑whitelisted wallet. The impact is that the privacy guarantee advertised in the README – that only selected members may participate in a private vault – is broken; anyone can gain exposure to the vault’s assets, potentially leading to unauthorized profit sharing, dilution of intended participants, or regulatory compliance issues. The condition under which the bug manifests is any time the vault is configured as private (privatePool == true) and a transfer of shares is performed; the bug does not depend on the amount transferred or on any special cooldown state. All users of the protocol, especially managers who rely on the private setting to restrict participation, are affected because the whitelist can be circumvented. The issue was discovered during a manual code review that compared the documented behavior in the README with the actual access‑control logic in PoolLogic.sol and observed that the transfer hook does not enforce the whitelist. It can be hard to notice because the deposit path correctly rejects non‑whitelisted callers, so initial testing may only involve deposits and not subsequent transfers, giving a false sense of security. The proper fix is to extend the whitelist check to the token‑transfer hook, requiring that the recipient of any share transfer is either the vault itself (minting) or a whitelisted member when the vault is private, and to keep the existing cooldown and pause checks. This class of bug is a “missing authorization on state‑changing transfer” or “whitelist bypass via token transfer”, similar to other cases where access control is applied only on entry functions but not on subsequent token movements. From a user’s perspective, a participant who expects that only approved members can hold vault shares may see their shares appear in an address that was never approved, or a non‑approved address may suddenly hold a balance, contradicting the expectation that ‘only whitelisted members can invest’. The failure mode is that money or share ownership can be moved to anyone, breaking the accounting assumption that private vaults have a closed set of participants.

title: Lack of slippage parameters on deposits
description:
The lack of slippage parameters on deposits will allow minting fewer shares than expected if prices have changed between the time the user sends the transaction and when the transaction gets included in a block. When a user makes a deposit in a Vault, the _depositFor first calculates the amount in USD that represents that deposit. Then, it uses a formula to calculate the shares to mint for that user making the deposit:  
liquidityMinted := usdAmount \* totalSupply / totalAssets \* (1 - entryFee)  
*The names of the variables may be different on the code but the underlying formula is the same. Just to clarify, usdAmount represents the deposit value in USD, and totalAssets represent the total value of the Vault in USD. In the period between the user submitting a deposit transaction and that transaction getting included in a block, the prices could change and that can cause the user to receive fewer shares than expected. For example, when a Vault uses different tokens to deposit and to invest, it's possible that a change in value on one of those tokens will alter the shares minted to a user. Imagine a Vault has almost all the assets invested in ETH and they accept stablecoins as deposit assets. In that case, if the price of ETH suddenly rises when the deposit transaction is still pending, the value of totalAssets will be bigger, thus resulting in a lower value for liquidityMinted. Another example is if a Vault has almost all the assets in stablecoins and accepts ETH as a deposit asset, a sudden fall of the ETH price while a deposit transaction is pending will cause the minting of fewer shares than expected. In this case, the value of usdAmount will be lower, resulting in fewer shares minted. Users depositing into Vaults will receive fewer shares than expected, thus causing a loss of funds.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the absence of any slippage protection on vault deposit functions. When a user initiates a deposit, the contract first converts the incoming token amount into a USD‑denominated value (usdAmount) and then computes the number of vault shares to mint using a formula that multiplies usdAmount by the total supply of shares and divides by the total assets held by the vault, optionally applying an entry fee. Because the calculation uses the on‑chain values of totalAssets and the price conversion at the exact moment the transaction is executed, any change in market prices between the moment the user signs the transaction and the moment the transaction is included in a block will directly affect the resulting share amount. If the price of an asset that constitutes a large portion of the vault’s holdings moves unfavourably during this window, the denominator (totalAssets) can increase or the numerator (usdAmount) can decrease, causing the contract to mint fewer shares than the user expected. This effect is especially pronounced for vaults that hold a single volatile asset (e.g., mostly ETH) while accepting a different deposit token (e.g., a stablecoin) or vice‑versa. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, but the balance displayed after the deposit is lower than anticipated, leading to a perception that funds have disappeared or that the vault is unfair. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the deposit logic, where the lack of a minimum‑share or slippage parameter was noted as a deviation from standard DeFi best practices. It is difficult to notice because the transaction does not revert; the only symptom is a smaller share balance, which may be attributed to normal market fluctuations rather than a contract flaw. The class of bug can be described as a price‑oracle race condition or slippage omission, where the contract trusts instantaneous price data without bounding the acceptable deviation. To remediate, the deposit functions should accept a user‑specified slippage tolerance or a minimum acceptable share amount; the transaction must revert if the computed shares fall below this threshold, thereby protecting depositors from adverse price movements occurring between transaction submission and execution. Implementing such a check restores the expected accounting relationship between deposited value and minted shares and aligns the contract with typical safety guarantees expected by users and auditors.

title: Incorrect implementation of the slippage pa-
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the way a vault contract validates slippage tolerance during a multi‑asset withdrawal. The contract allows a caller to specify a maximum acceptable slippage percentage, expecting that the total value received after withdrawing all underlying assets will not deviate from the expected amount by more than that percentage. However, the implementation checks the slippage condition separately for each individual asset inside the internal _withdrawProcessing function. For every asset the code requires that the on‑chain valuation of the withdrawn amount be at least the expected value multiplied by (10000‑slippageTolerance)/10000. If any single asset experiences a price impact that exceeds the user‑provided tolerance, the require statement triggers and the whole withdrawal reverts, even when the aggregate slippage across all assets stays within the allowed bound. This mismatch between per‑asset enforcement and the user’s expectation of an overall tolerance creates a denial‑of‑service vector: an attacker or market movement that pushes one asset’s price just above the tolerance can block all withdrawals, effectively freezing user funds. The issue appears when a vault holds heterogeneous positions, such as a stablecoin and a yield‑bearing position on Aave, and the user sets a modest slippage limit (for example 2%). In the described scenario the WETH portion incurs 0 % slippage while the Aave portion suffers 3 % slippage; the weighted average slippage is only 1.5 %, which should be acceptable, yet the transaction reverts because the Aave leg alone violates the per‑asset check. Users experience a failed transaction with the error message “high withdraw slippage”, see no funds transferred, and may be unable to withdraw until the market stabilises or the contract is patched. The problem was uncovered during a manual audit of the withdrawal logic, where the auditor noticed that the slippage check was placed inside the loop that processes each asset rather than after aggregating the total value. Because the contract’s UI and documentation present the slippage parameter as a global tolerance, the bug can be hard to spot: the overall withdrawal value often looks correct, but the hidden per‑asset validation silently aborts the operation. To remediate, the contract should compute the total expected withdraw value across all assets, sum the actual received value, and then compare the aggregate against the user’s tolerance. Alternatively, the logic could allow each asset to have its own tolerance or use a weighted average that respects the user‑specified global limit. By moving the slippage verification out of the per‑asset loop and applying it to the combined result, the vault will honour the user’s expectation that the total withdrawal stays within the declared slippage range, eliminating the denial‑of‑service condition and restoring correct financial accounting.

title: First depositor can effectively disable the per-
bug_full:
The vulnerability consists of a manipulation of the vault's performance‑fee high watermark that can be performed by the very first depositor of a newly created vault. The contract stores the last token price at which a performance fee was minted in the variable tokenPriceAtLastFeeMint. When a fee is minted, the current token price is calculated from the total fund value and the total supply of vault shares, and this price is written to the high‑watermark variable. Because the code does not reset or bound this value when the vault becomes empty, an attacker who is able to make a tiny initial deposit, inject additional funds directly into the vault, and trigger a fee mint can force tokenPriceAtLastFeeMint to an astronomically high number (for example 1e28). After the attacker withdraws the initial shares and later deposits a normal amount, the observable token price returns to a normal range (e.g. 1e18) while the stored high watermark remains at the inflated value. The performance‑fee calculation only mints a fee when the current token price exceeds the stored high watermark, so the condition will never be satisfied again. Consequently the manager never receives any performance fee for the lifetime of the vault.
The root cause is the lack of a safeguard that resets or validates the high‑watermark after the vault is emptied or after a very small initial supply is created. The fee‑minting logic trusts the stored tokenPriceAtLastFeeMint without checking that it is realistic relative to the current supply and fund value.
An attacker can exploit the issue by: (1) depositing a minimal amount of tokens to obtain a tiny share supply, (2) sending an extra amount of tokens directly to the vault contract, (3) invoking the fee‑minting function (or any operation that triggers _mintManagerFee) so that the inflated token price is recorded as the new high watermark, (4) withdrawing the initial shares after any cooldown, and (5) depositing a regular amount of tokens. From that point onward, every subsequent deposit or withdrawal will calculate a current token price far below the stored high watermark, preventing any performance fee from ever being minted.
The impact is economic rather than functional: the vault continues to operate, users can deposit and withdraw normally, but the manager loses all future performance‑fee revenue. Users may notice that no fee is ever deducted from their balances, which contradicts the protocol’s advertised fee model. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑calculation functions, where the relationship between tokenPriceAtLastFeeMint and the current token price was examined and the possibility of an initial‑state manipulation was identified. It is hard to notice because the token price displayed to users appears normal and the high‑watermark variable is internal, so no error or warning is emitted.
The issue belongs to the class of high‑watermark manipulation or fee‑disable bugs, where an economic invariant is broken by an attacker controlling the initial state. The recommended remediation is to reset tokenPriceAtLastFeeMint whenever the vault is completely emptied or when the total supply falls below a safe threshold, and to enforce that the high watermark cannot be set to a value that is unrealistically higher than the current token price. This prevents the first depositor from permanently disabling the performance fee and restores the intended fee‑collection behavior.
From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after depositing, the manager’s performance fee never appears, and the user’s balance does not decrease by the expected fee amount, even though the protocol documentation states that a fee should be taken on gains. The expectation of a fee being collected is therefore violated, while the actual behavior is that the fee is effectively disabled.

title: Manager can steal up to 10% of the Vault's
description:
The manager of a Vault can use the 1Inch protocol to swap tokens, but some checks prevent the manager from taking too much slippage on those swaps. However, the slippage checker currently allows the manager to steal up to 10% of the Vault's funds daily. When a Vault's manager wants to perform a swap using 1Inch, the contract guard OneInchV6Guard makes some checks to ensure that the manager doesn't steal any funds in the swapping process. One of those checks is done by calling the contract SlippageAccumulator, which calculates the slippage accumulated of that Vault's swaps and reverts the transaction if the accumulated slippage is above some maximum value. Here's the main snippet that checks that the slippage isn't too high:  
s/utils/SlippageAccumulator.sol#L94-L101  
```solidity
if (dstAmount < srcAmount) {
    uint128 newSlippage = srcAmount.sub(dstAmount).mul(SCALING_FACTOR).div(srcAmount).toUint128();
    uint128 newCumulativeSlippage = (
        uint256(newSlippage).add(getCumulativeSlippageImpact(swapData.poolManagerLogic))
    ).toUint128();
    require(newCumulativeSlippage < maxCumulativeSlippage, "slippage impact exceeded");
}
```
In the SlippageAccumulator contract, there are two key values set by the dHEDGE admins that determine if a swap is valid based on the slippage:  
1. maxCumulativeSlippage: This is the maximum cumulative trade slippage within a period.  
2. decayTime: This is the decay time for the accumulated slippage. E.g. If a swap has 5% slippage, it will accumulate until the decay time has passed. Currently, the deployed SlippageAccumulator contract has the following values for the mentioned variables:  
1. maxCumulativeSlippage: 10%  
2. decayTime: 1 day  
With these values, a manager of a Vault can take a maximum of 10% of slippage on all swaps in a Vault every 24 hours. This means that each day, the manager can make a swap on the Vault allowing 10% of slippage at most. With this configuration, a manager can self-sandwich a Vault's swap to extract up to 10% of the funds used for the swap. The attack sequence would look as follows:  
1. [Frontrun] The manager uses his address to take a flash loan and make a huge swap in some Uniswap pool to unbalance it.  
2. The manager uses all the Vault's funds to make a swap in the same uniswap pool allowing 10% of slippage.  
3. [Backrun] The manager uses the funds from the first transaction to reverse the swap in the pool, pocketing the 10% slippage taken by the Vault.  
4. The manager returns the flash loan with the profits.  
*All these steps will happen in a bundle so that the attack is executed in the same block. With this sequence, the manager can steal up to 10% of the Vault's funds in a single block, and this attack can be repeated every 24 hours. This means that in a week, a manager can steal up to 65.13% of the Vault's funds. This issue breaks a restriction stated in the README: Manager or trader under any circumstances should not be able to take out depositors funds put in the vaults they manage. The Vault's manager can steal up to 10% of the Vault's funds daily, 65.13% weekly. This attack doesn't need any external conditions so I think it warrants high severity.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a cumulative slippage abuse that lets a vault manager extract a portion of the vault's assets by exploiting the slippage accumulator logic. The guard contract checks that the slippage percentage of a swap stays below a hard‑coded maximum (10% per day) and that the accumulated slippage decays over a 24‑hour period, but it does not verify who caused the slippage or whether the trade is beneficial to the manager. Because the manager has permission to initiate swaps through the 1Inch integration, they can deliberately create a large price impact using a flash loan, then execute the vault's swap with the allowed 10% slippage, and finally reverse the initial price‑moving trade in the same block. This self‑sandwich sequence stays within the cumulative slippage limit, so the contract does not revert, yet the manager pockets the price difference, effectively stealing up to 10% of the vault's funds each day and potentially more than 60% over a week. The attack can be performed at any time, does not depend on external market conditions, and is repeated daily because the slippage accumulator resets after the decay time. Depositors experience an unexpected drop in their vault balance or share price, seeing less value than anticipated without any error messages, violating the expectation that a manager cannot withdraw depositor funds. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the slippage check was examined and found to allow systematic extraction. It is hard to notice because the slippage check appears to protect against excessive loss, yet it silently permits a controlled amount of loss that can be repeatedly abused. To remediate, the slippage guard should be redesigned to enforce per‑swap slippage caps, require multi‑signature or community approval for high‑slippage operations, or replace immediate execution with a commit‑reveal scheme that gives users time to react, thereby preventing a manager from repeatedly abusing the daily slippage allowance.

title: Precision loss at AaveLendingPoolAssetGuard will
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision‑loss rounding error that occurs when the vault calculates the amount of collateral to withdraw or the amount of debt to repay on Aave. The contract multiplies the total token balance held by the vault with a user‑specified portion (expressed with 18‑decimal fixed‑point precision) and then divides by 10**18. When the underlying token balance is extremely small – for example a single wei of LINK or WETH – the multiplication followed by integer division rounds the result down to zero. Aave’s core validation logic rejects any withdraw or repay call with an amount of zero, causing the transaction to revert with the INVALID_AMOUNT error. This situation can be triggered deliberately by an attacker who deposits a minimal amount of collateral on behalf of the vault, or by a manager who creates a tiny debt position, because the subsequent withdrawal flow will always attempt to withdraw or repay a zero amount. From the user’s perspective the vault appears to freeze: a user initiates a withdrawal expecting to receive a proportional share of their assets, but the transaction reverts and no funds are transferred, often showing an error code (e.g., 26) or simply “transaction failed”. The impact is that all withdrawals from the affected vault are halted as long as any asset balance or debt amount is subject to this rounding‑to‑zero condition. The bug was discovered during a security audit by inspecting the internal _calculateCollateralAssets and _calculateBorrowAssets functions and observing that the amount calculation could produce zero for tiny balances, then confirming the failure on a forked Optimism network. The issue is hard to notice because the contract works correctly for normal balances and only fails for edge‑case amounts that are rarely exercised in typical usage. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of arithmetic precision or rounding bugs where integer division truncates fractional values, leading to zero‑value operations that violate external protocol invariants. The recommended mitigation is to add a guard that skips the Aave withdraw or repay call when the computed amount is zero, thereby preventing the INVALID_AMOUNT revert and preserving the vault’s ability to process withdrawals for normal balances.

title: DoS on withdrawals when the slippage in swaps
description:
When a withdrawal is initiated and the Vault has some loans in Aave, the slippage in swaps to repay the debt can end up being higher than the flash loan repayment, thus reverting the whole withdrawal transaction. When a user initiates a withdrawal, if the Vault has some collateral and debt in Aave, the following steps are going to be followed to process that withdrawal:
1. The Vault is going to request a flash loan from Aave.
2. The Vault will repay the pro-rated debt using the flash loan funds.
3. The Vault will withdraw the pro-rated collateral from Aave.
4. The Vault will swap the withdrawn collateral to WETH.
5. The Vault will swap the WETH to the relevant tokens to repay the flash loan + the flash fees.
When the market is volatile and a user tries to initiate a withdrawal from the Vault, the slippage incurred on those swaps can be higher than the flash loan to repay, thus reverting the whole transaction. Let's look at an example:
1. Vault has 100 USD collateral in LINK and 80 USD debt in OP deposited in Aave (apart from more assets outside Aave).
2. User initiates a withdrawal using half of the total Vault liquidity:
• Vault gets a flash loan of 40 USD in OP and repays the debt.
• Vault withdraws 50 USD in LINK and swaps it all to WETH, incurring 10% in slippage, so the output is 45 USD in WETH.
• Vault swaps 45 USD in WETH to repay the flash loan (40 USD in OP) but the slippage incurred is 13% so there are not enough tokens to get the 40 USD in OP.
3. The whole withdrawal gets reverted because the flash loan cannot be repaid due to the high slippage in swaps.
This issue will halt withdrawals as long as the slippage incurred in the swaps is high. Having on-time withdrawals is critical for the users because when the market is volatile, delayed withdrawals may imply a loss of funds for the users given that Vault share price may be decreasing at a fast rate. Moreover, the manager can trigger this bug by himself to halt withdrawals even if the slippage is null. To do that, a manager can deposit collateral directly in Aave on behalf of the Vault using a non-supported asset by the Vault. When a withdrawal is initiated, the collateral on supported tokens won't be enough to repay the flash loan because the debt to repay is bigger than the accounted collateral. The attack path could be the following:
1. The Vault has 1 WETH as collateral in Aave.
2. The manager deposits directly in Aave 1 rETH on behalf of the Vault.
3. The manager uses the Vault to borrow an amount higher than the accounted collateral, like 5,000 USDC.
4. When the withdrawal is initiated, the flash loan to repay will be 5,000 USD but the collateral withdrawn will only be 1 WETH. Because 1 WETH is less valuable than 5,000 USDC, the flash loan won't be fully repaid, halting the withdrawal.
In step 4, the collateral withdrawn will only be 1 WETH instead of 1 WETH + 1 rETH because the rETH token isn't a token supported by the Vault so it's not available to withdraw from the Vault. DoS on withdrawals when the slippage incurred is high so there are not enough tokens to repay the flash loan on Aave. The manager can also trigger this bug easily to halt withdrawals whenever he desires. This issue breaks a protocol restriction stated in the README:
Depositor under any circumstances should be able to withdraw funds they've invested according to the value of their vault shares given that no lock up is applied. Moreover, given that the manager can trigger this bug without external conditions or requirements, I believe this warrants high severity.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when a user attempts to withdraw from a vault that holds both collateral and debt on Aave and the withdrawal logic relies on a flash loan to repay the proportional debt, withdraw the proportional collateral, and then swap the withdrawn assets back to the flash‑loan token. The root cause is that the contract assumes the series of swaps will always yield enough tokens to fully repay the flash loan plus fees, but it does not account for slippage or for collateral that is not recognised by the vault’s asset list. In a volatile market the price impact on the swap from the withdrawn collateral to WETH and then to the flash‑loan token can be larger than expected, so the amount received after the swap is insufficient to cover the flash loan repayment. When this happens the whole transaction reverts, preventing the withdrawal from completing. A malicious manager can also trigger the same failure by depositing an unsupported asset directly into Aave on behalf of the vault; because the vault’s accounting only recognises supported assets, the withdrawn collateral is insufficient to cover the flash loan, causing an immediate revert regardless of market conditions. The impact is that users are unable to retrieve their funds when they request a withdrawal; from the user’s perspective the UI may show a transaction failure, no tokens received, or a balance that appears unchanged despite a withdrawal attempt. This violates the protocol’s stated guarantee that any depositor can withdraw their share value at any time without lock‑up. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the withdrawal flow and identified that the flash‑loan repayment step lacks slippage protection and that asset accounting excludes tokens that can be introduced by a manager. The problem can be hard to notice because it only manifests under specific market volatility or when a manager deliberately adds unsupported collateral, conditions that are not exercised in normal testing. To remediate the issue the contract should allow the caller to specify assets that may be excluded from the withdrawal path, enforce a slippage tolerance on the swaps, and ensure that all collateral deposited on Aave is accounted for in the vault’s asset list before attempting the flash‑loan repayment, thereby guaranteeing that a withdrawal either succeeds or fails gracefully without locking out all users.

title: Manager can remove the Aave Lending Pool
bug_full: The vulnerability allows a vault manager to remove the Aave V3 lending pool from the list of supported assets even when the vault still holds collateral and an outstanding borrow, by exploiting a flaw in the balance calculation routine. The guard that protects asset removal computes the vault's Aave balance as the difference between total collateral value and total debt value, but it only aggregates assets that are currently marked as supported. If the manager deposits collateral into Aave using a token that is not listed as supported at that moment, that collateral is invisible to the guard. Consequently, the net balance reported by the guard can be zero when the visible collateral equals the visible debt, even though hidden collateral and debt exist in the Aave position. An attacker can therefore follow a sequence: first deposit a supported token such as WETH, then directly deposit an unsupported token like rETH on behalf of the vault, borrow an amount of stablecoin that matches the value of the visible collateral, and finally invoke the asset‑removal function, which passes because the computed balance is zero. After the removal, the manager can wait for market movements; if the price of the underlying asset rises, re‑adding the Aave pool inflates the vault’s token price, allowing the manager to withdraw a larger share of the underlying assets than entitled. Conversely, if the price falls, the manager can re‑add the pool to imprint losses on the token price, effectively griefing users. From a user perspective the vault’s token price may jump unexpectedly or drop sharply, and the asset list may show that the Aave pool is no longer supported even though the vault still holds a hidden position. The issue was discovered during a security audit through static analysis of the asset‑guard contracts and confirmed with a Foundry test that reproduces the removal of the Aave pool while a non‑zero Aave position exists. The bug is subtle because the guard’s zero‑balance check succeeds, giving the impression that the vault is empty of Aave exposure, while in reality funds are still locked in the protocol. The root cause is the incomplete accounting of collateral and debt, relying on a net‑zero condition rather than verifying that both collateral and debt are individually zero. To remediate, the removal logic should enforce that the vault has no outstanding collateral and no outstanding debt in the Aave pool before allowing the asset to be removed, or the guard should include all assets—supported or not—in its balance calculation, and direct deposits of unsupported tokens on behalf of the vault should be prohibited.

title: Manager can mint performance fees even when
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical accounting flaw that allows a fund manager to mint performance fee shares even when the fund’s per‑share price has decreased overall. The root cause lies in the way the contract tracks the reference price used for performance fee eligibility: a variable called tokenPriceAtLastFeeMint is only updated when the current token price is higher than the stored value. After the manager mints performance and streaming fee shares, the total token supply rises while the fund value stays constant, which lowers the token price. Because the update condition fails (the new price is lower), tokenPriceAtLastFeeMint remains at the old higher value, so the next fee‑minting period still sees the current price as higher than the stale reference and permits another performance fee mint. This can be exploited by a manager who calls the fee‑minting function each period; even if streaming fees exceed the fund’s growth and the net token price drops, the contract still treats the situation as profitable and mints additional performance shares. The impact is that investors see their per‑share value decline – they may notice that the fund’s total value appears unchanged while their share price drops, resulting in an effective loss of value despite paying performance fees. The issue occurs whenever streaming fees are large enough to offset or surpass the fund’s appreciation, causing token dilution after fee minting. All token holders of the affected fund are affected, as the protocol’s economic model is compromised and users receive fewer underlying assets for the same number of shares. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the fee calculation logic, where the interaction between share minting, token price recomputation, and the stale reference price was identified. It is hard to notice because the fees are minted as new shares rather than transferred, so standard balance checks may not reveal the dilution, and UI dashboards often display total fund value without highlighting per‑share price erosion. The correct mitigation is to update tokenPriceAtLastFeeMint to the token price that was used for the performance fee calculation (i.e., the pre‑dilution price) or to recompute the reference after minting, ensuring that a manager can only collect performance fees when a genuine increase in token price remains. This class of bug falls under improper state‑dependent fee accounting, where mutable variables are used to gate profit‑based rewards without accounting for the side‑effects of the reward itself.

title: A manager benefits immediately when there
bug_full: An on‑chain accounting bug allows the pool manager to collect a performance fee immediately after a user deposits, even though no time has elapsed. The contract records the token price (total fund value divided by total share supply) at the moment a fee is minted. When a deposit is processed the entry fee reduces the amount of shares minted for the depositor, which makes the post‑deposit token price higher than the pre‑deposit price. The implementation then overwrites the stored tokenPriceAtLastFeeMint with this inflated price before the manager fee can be minted. Because the fee‑minting logic calculates the available manager fee as the difference between the current token price and the stored price, a subsequent call to mintManagerFee in the same block sees a positive price delta and mints an additional fee. This extra fee is taken from the newly created shares, causing the effective token price for the depositor to drop within the same block. From a user’s perspective the deposit appears to succeed but the share value immediately falls, leading to a situation where “my balance is lower than expected” or “the token price drops right after I deposit”. The bug occurs whenever a deposit that incurs an entry fee is followed by a manager‑fee mint in the same block, and it affects any investor who deposits during that window as well as the overall fairness of the protocol. The issue was uncovered during a security audit when the tester performed two consecutive deposits and called mintManagerFee in the same block, observing an unexpected increase in the manager’s share balance. The problem is subtle because the price change is small and only manifests when the fee‑mint function is invoked immediately after a deposit, a pattern that may not happen in normal operation and therefore can be missed in casual testing. The root cause is the incorrect ordering of state updates: the token price snapshot is taken after the entry‑fee adjustment instead of before, allowing the fee calculation to use an artificially high price. To remediate the vulnerability the contract should record the token price before applying the entry fee, or prevent fee minting in the same block after a deposit, or adjust the fee formula to exclude the entry‑fee‑induced price inflation. Fixing the bug restores the intended accounting invariant that manager fees accrue only over elapsed time and not from a single deposit, thereby protecting investors from immediate, unfair fee extraction.

title: lastFeeMintTime is updated even when streamingFee
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting state‑update error in the manager fee minting routine. The contract calculates a streaming fee based on token supply, elapsed time and a manager fee rate. When the calculation results in zero – for example because the token supply is low, the fee rate is zero, or the elapsed time is insufficient – the function still updates the global variable lastFeeMintTime to the current block timestamp. Because lastFeeMintTime records the moment at which fees were last minted, advancing it while no fee was actually minted causes the next call to _mintManagerFee to treat the elapsed interval as already accounted for. Consequently the manager receives no tokens for that period and the lost time is never reclaimed, leading to a systematic reduction of manager fees over time. The issue occurs whenever the streaming fee expression evaluates to zero, which can happen regularly in pools with small supplies or during short intervals. It affects the pool manager, the DAO that receives a share of the fee, and ultimately token holders who expect the fee distribution to reflect the true time‑based accrual. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑minting logic, where the unconditional assignment to lastFeeMintTime stood out as inconsistent with the conditional minting of fee tokens. It is hard to notice because updating a timestamp is a benign‑looking operation and a zero fee may be a legitimate outcome, so no error is emitted and the contract state appears normal. From the user’s perspective the manager’s fee balance remains unchanged after a period where fees should have been minted, and the token price at last fee mint does not move as expected, creating a discrepancy between the expected fee accrual and the actual token distribution. The proper fix is to conditionally update lastFeeMintTime only when a positive streaming fee is minted, or to separate the timestamp update from the fee‑minting path so that time is only recorded when an actual fee accrual occurs. This aligns the state update with the economic reality of fee generation and prevents silent loss of manager fees.

title: A malicious user can delay any user's with-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service style flaw that allows any participant to delay another user’s ability to withdraw or transfer assets from the pool. The root cause lies in the deposit routine, which accepts an arbitrary recipient address and, after minting liquidity, updates two state variables – lastDeposit[recipient] and lastExitCooldown[recipient] – based on the current block timestamp. The cooldown calculation guarantees a minimum cooldown of one block, and the function only requires a very small amount of liquidity (at least 100000 shares) to be minted, making the attack cheap. An attacker can call the internal deposit function on behalf of a victim, causing the victim’s lastDeposit timestamp to be set to the current block and the cooldown to be set to at least one block.
