shares, which is the root cause why simple double-conversion is not enough to
mint exact shares amount via deposit.
Internal pre-conditions
Certain combination of total lender assets, totalSupply and user requested mint
amount. The higher the supply/assets ratio, the higher the probability of incorrect
withdrawal amount. This can never happen if assets >= supply. Even though the
protocol is designed such that assets >= supply, it's still possible to have assets <
supply in some tricky edge cases.
External pre-conditions
None
Attack Path
Since protocol is designed for assets >= supply, the first part of the attack is to
show scenario when assets can actually be below supply. One possible way to
achieve this is to exploit borrow rounding error:
• Lender.borrow calculates the borrow units rounding them down:
units = (amount * BORROWS_SCALER) / cache.borrowIndex;
• However, when the borrow inventory is calculated in _previewInterest, the
units => asset amount conversion rounds down too:
uint256 oldBorrows = (cache.borrowBase * cache.borrowIndex) / BORROWS_SCALER;
This means that if we borrow exactly 1 wei (when borrowIndex is greater than ONE,
if it's exactly ONE, then division by borrowIndex is always exact due to
BORROW_SCALER being ONE « 72), then the oldBorrows (borrow inventory) will be
0 (because our integer borrowing units amount is slightly less than exact amount of
units needed for 1 wei of assets due to rounding it down).
This borrow feature allows to reduce assets while keeping totalSupply the same. So
the exact steps to make assets < totalSupply:
1. Make sure that borrowIndex is greater than ONE (deposit, borrow, wait, repay,
redeem to make it so)
2. Deposit some assets (since this is a deposit into an empty Lender, totalAssets
= totalSupply)
3. borrow exactly 1 wei of assets from the Lender (totalAssets decrease by 1)
4. mint the amount of shares equal to current totalSupply - 1 => the actual
minted amount will be equal to totalSupply instead.
the other ways to have assets < totalSupply.
Lender is not ERC4626-compliant. Since this compliance is specifically stated in
contest README, this should make this issue a valid medium.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a deviation from the ERC‑4626 specification in the Lender contract’s mint function. According to the standard, mint must issue exactly the number of shares requested by the caller. In this implementation the function first converts the desired share amount into an asset amount using a rounding‑up division, then immediately converts that asset amount back into shares using a rounding‑down division. Because the two conversions use opposite rounding directions, the final share amount can be larger than the original request when the contract’s total assets are slightly lower than its total supply. This situation can be triggered by exploiting the borrow logic: by borrowing a single wei when the borrow index is greater than one, the contract’s internal accounting reduces total assets by one while leaving total supply unchanged, creating the condition assets < supply. When a user then calls mint with a share amount equal to totalSupply‑1, the double‑conversion yields totalSupply shares, effectively minting one extra share. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to give more shares than expected, breaking accounting assumptions and potentially allowing profit extraction or dilution of existing holders. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test showing the asset‑to‑share mismatch and the resulting over‑mint. It is hard to notice because the rounding error only manifests in rare edge cases where assets fall below supply, a state that the protocol normally tries to avoid. To remediate the bug the mint function must be rewritten to avoid the double conversion; instead it should calculate the required asset amount with rounding up and then mint the exact requested shares, or otherwise ensure that the final share count matches the caller’s request regardless of rounding direction. This class of bug falls under “incorrect rounding in token accounting” and violates the ERC‑4626 compliance requirement for deterministic minting.

title: Uniswap governance increase of protocol fees
description:
There is a conceptual issue with protocol math, which will permanently reduce IV if
uniswap governance increases protocol fees. This, in turn, will significantly increase
a risk of bad debt liquidations since IV is used for borrowers health calculations and
borrowers will be allowed more risky positions than designed by the protocol.
Aloe uses the following formula to calculate IV: IV = 2 * sqrt( 20000 * (fgg0 ·
gamma1 · sqrt(P)
+
fgg1 · gamma0 / sqrt(P)) / tickSpacing )
where fgg is the fees per liquidity unit collected over the FEE_GROWTH_AVG_WINDOW (72
hours) and gamma is the percentage of fees received by LPs from the trading volume
(gamma = trading fee - protocol fee). As seen from the formula, IV is in direct
proportion to sqrt(fgg) and to sqrt(gamma).
Increase of protocol fees decreases gamma. In such case in efficient market fgg
must stay about the same (since fgg is basically APR% earned by LPs, so if they
start earning less than before due to increased protocol fees / decreased gamma,
it's likely some liquidity will withdraw for better opportunities elsewhere which will
bring per-liquidity earnings (fgg) back to about the same value). In reality things are
more complex (reduced liquidity will cause reduced trading volume and reduced
fees, which in turn can cause more liquidity to withdraw) are fgg can slightly
decrease, but in these circumstances it can never increase.
All in all, if uniswap governance increases protocol fees, this causes gamma to
decrease and fgg to either stay the same or slightly decrease, meaning IV will
permanently decrease (even though actual volatility doesn't change).
it/2024-06-aloe-update/blob/main/aloe-ii/core/src/libraries/Volatility.sol#L61-L85
If protocol fees are increased, gamma permanently decreases and fgg stays the
same or decreases (but never increases), leading to permanent IV decrease.
The root cause is conceptual issue with the IV calculations math. In my
understanding it must not depend on gamma, only on fgg, because intuitively IV
shouldn't depend on how much fee percentage is taken from trading, as change of
fee will just adjust liquidity to keep fgg about the same. But this requires further
research.
Internal pre-conditions
The only condition is for any user to call VolatilityOracle.prepare to reflect
uniswap protocol fees in the internal cache. Since this is permissionless function,
it's very easy for anyone to call it.
External pre-conditions
Uniswap governance increases protocol fees.
Attack Path
Once pre-conditions are met, nothing is needed to do - IV will always permanently
decrease compared to actual volatility.
In worst case, if protocol fees are set to its max value of 1/4, new gamma is then 3/4
of old gamma, and new IV will be sqrt(3/4) = 87% of the old IV permanently. So the
impact is permanent reduction of IV by 13%. Per-second and per-update IV change
limitations are irrelevant, because this is the long-term IV so it will slowly come
down to the new (reduced) amount and will stay there.
This deflated IV will allow borrowers to open more risky positions than they should
be allowed by protocol, thus the risk of bad debt significantly increases, and in
case of bad debt, lenders will lose funds as not all lenders will be able to withdraw
due to bad debt, and this can cause bank run since the last to withdraw will be
unable to do so.
important to the protocol, so IV calculations should be correct, and this issue
demonstrates a permanent error in IV calculation by 13%.
poc: Not needed as this is conceptual math issue.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a conceptual flaw in the way the protocol calculates the implied volatility (IV) that is used to assess borrower health. The IV formula multiplies a term that contains the fee‑growth per liquidity unit (fgg) by the square root of the LP fee share (gamma). When Uniswap governance raises the protocol fee, gamma – the percentage of trading fees that remain for liquidity providers – decreases. Because the formula ties IV directly to sqrt(gamma), a permanent reduction of gamma causes IV to drop even though the underlying market volatility has not changed. The root cause is the inclusion of gamma in the IV calculation; the design assumes that IV should be independent of how much of the trading fee is taken by the protocol. The drop in IV is not triggered by any malicious transaction; it occurs automatically after the fee change and after any caller invokes the permission‑less VolatilityOracle.prepare function to refresh the cached values. As a result, borrowers appear healthier than they actually are, allowing them to open positions that exceed the risk limits intended by the protocol. This mis‑pricing increases the probability of bad‑debt events, potentially leading to lender losses and a cascade of withdrawals that could resemble a bank run. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are subtle: health factors remain high, liquidation thresholds seem too lenient, and the UI may show a lower volatility number without any obvious market movement. The issue is hard to notice because the IV value drifts slowly and stays within normal variance, and there is no explicit on‑chain error flag. The impact is permanent: with a maximum protocol fee of 25 % the new gamma is three‑quarters of the previous value, reducing IV to roughly 87 % of its former level, a 13 % under‑estimation of risk that persists indefinitely. The vulnerability was identified during a formal audit of the Aloe II core library, where the mathematical relationship between fee parameters and IV was examined. To remediate the problem the IV calculation should be redesigned to remove the dependence on gamma, relying solely on the fee‑growth per liquidity (fgg) or an alternative metric that does not vary with protocol fee adjustments. Ensuring that IV reflects true market volatility rather than fee policy will restore correct borrower health assessments and protect lenders from unintended exposure.

title: Long time delay between transactions causes
description:
Protocol Q&A mentions the RESERVE address:
There is a RESERVE address to which a portion of all interest accrues. It should be able to take any action and behave normally.
However, when RESERVE address receives its portion of all interest, it also receives rewards, but the rewards are calculated incorrectly, adding less rewards to RESERVE than it should receive, thus the RESERVE account loses rewards. This happens because RESERVE receives its portion of all interest continuously (each second), but the rewards are calculated with RESERVE balance only at the start of the interval (RESERVE balance at the time of last transaction) ignoring any RESERVE balance accural inside the interval.
Example: transaction at t=0: RESERVE balance = 0, reward rate = 1 per second per unit balance, total borrows increases at such a rate, the RESERVE receives 10 new tokens per second. t=1: RESERVE balance = 10, rewards should be 0 (not updated in storage) t=2: RESERVE balance = 20, rewards should be 10 (not updated in storage) t=3: RESERVE balance = 30, rewards should be 10+20=30 (not updated in storage) t=4: RESERVE balance = 40, rewards should be 30+30=60 (not updated in storage). Transaction at t=5: first the rewards are updated for the time interval [0;5] with the stored balance (0), so RESERVE rewards are 0, only then the RESERVE balance is set to 50.
RESERVE receives its portion of all interest by minting new shares:
/Lender.sol#L527
However, when minting, the rewards are calculated by multiplying user's balance before the mint by the accumulated rewards per unit balance:
lob/main/aloe-ii/core/src/libraries/Rewards.sol#L92
This is correct for all accounts except RESERVE: all accounts have static balances between updates, so the rewards formula is correct, but RESERVE has continously increasing balance over time, meaning the formula to calculate the reward should take this into account, but it doesn't.
Internal pre-conditions
Always happens by itself, the longer the time between transactions, the larger the rewards loss for the RESERVE account.
External pre-conditions
None
Attack Path
None, always happens by itself.
RESERVE account always losing rewards, the longer the time between transactions, the larger the rewards loss. For example, if the protocol has $10M borrowed at the rate of APR of 10%, and reserve factor is 10%, this means that RESERVE account receives $0.003 per second. Let's say there is a reward at the rate of 1 reward token per unit balance per second. Then:
• if transactions are going every second for 1 hour, the RESERVE account receives reward of 0.003 * (0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + ... + 3599) = 0.003 * 6478200 = 19434.6 tokens (this is the correct amount it should receive)
• if there are just 2 transactions (at t = 0 and at t = 1 hour), then RESERVE account receives reward of 0. If both scenarios continue for 1 day (transactions every second vs every 1 hour), then in scenario 1 the RESERVE account will receive 11.197M tokens, in scenario 2 the RESERVE account will receive 10.731M tokens, a loss of 466K reward tokens or a 4.3% loss.
The RESERVE account total rewards accured in time is quadratic, while the rewards loss is linear in time, so the longer time period, the higher the absolute loss and the smaller the relative (percentage) loss.
poc: N/A
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reward‑calculation error affecting the special RESERVE account of the protocol. The RESERVE account is designed to receive a proportion of all accrued interest continuously, and it also participates in the protocol’s reward distribution. The contract updates rewards by multiplying the account’s balance at the moment of the last state‑changing transaction by the accumulated reward‑per‑unit‑balance. This method works for ordinary users whose token balance remains constant between updates, but the RESERVE balance grows every second because new interest shares are minted into it. Because the reward formula does not take the intra‑interval increase of the RESERVE balance into account, the protocol records a reward amount based on the stale balance at the start of the interval. Consequently, the RESERVE account receives fewer reward tokens than it is mathematically entitled to. The error becomes larger the longer the time gap between transactions that trigger a reward update, leading to a quadratic shortfall in the RESERVE’s total rewards while the loss grows linearly with time. From a user’s point of view the symptom is that the reserve’s share of reward tokens is lower than expected; the protocol may appear to under‑pay incentives, and the overall accounting of distributed rewards diverges from the intended model. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the reward‑distribution library, where the auditor noticed that the RESERVE balance is updated continuously but the reward calculation only reads the stored balance. The bug is subtle because the protocol still functions and no transaction reverts; the discrepancy only shows up over extended periods and is hidden by the normal flow of interest accrual. The impact is a systematic loss of reward tokens for the RESERVE account, which can reduce the protocol’s profitability, affect tokenomics, and potentially mislead stakeholders about the health of the reward pool. There is no direct attack vector; the loss occurs automatically as time passes without intervening transactions. To remediate the issue the reward‑accumulation logic for the RESERVE account must be changed to account for the continuously increasing balance, for example by applying an arithmetic‑progression formula or by updating the RESERVE’s reward balance on each mint operation. This brings the calculation in line with the class of bugs known as incorrect reward accrual for dynamically changing balances and restores the intended linear (or near‑linear) growth of rewards for the reserve.

title: Any user can DOS BorrowNFT.modifyof any other
description:
ETH balance is required to be 0 at the end of modify:
require(address(this).balance == 0, "Aloe: antes sum");
This allows any user to front-run this transaction, deposit 1 wei of ETH (for example via calling payable multicall function with 1 wei and empty array), and the modify transaction will revert in the require referenced above.
This can be kept forever only at the gas cost, DOS'ing the modification of position, making it impossible for the other user(s) to do anything with their accounts, especially withdrawing/borrowing, which can be a lost opportunity or loss of funds for the user (for example, user wanted to withdraw collateral to fund another position to avoid liquidation, but due to DOS he can't withdraw + deposit and is liquidated).
BorrowNFT.modify sends out ETH to all user borrower accounts for ante, requiring remaining balance in the BorrowNFT contract to be exactly 0:
y/src/borrower-nft/BorrowerNFT.sol#L111
Since user doesn't control amount of ETH in the contract (and it's easy to send ETH to the contract via payable multicall or mint functions), it's easy to DOS the modify non-zero and revert.
Internal pre-conditions
Any user call BorrowNFT.modify
External pre-conditions
None
Attack Path
Front-running BorrowNFT.modify with depositing 1 wei of ETH to BorrowNFT via multicall payable function with empty array.
DOS the NFT borrow position modification of any user. This makes it impossible for the user(s) to do any actions with their accounts, such as withdrawals, borrows etc.
This can be a lost opportunity or loss of funds for the user (for example, user wanted to withdraw collateral to fund another position to avoid liquidation, but due to DOS he can't withdraw + deposit and is liquidated).
poc: N/A
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the BorrowNFT contract that stems from an invariant check on the contract’s ETH balance. The modify function ends with a require statement that asserts address(this).balance == 0, meaning the contract must hold no ether after the operation. Because the contract does not restrict who can send ether to it, any external account can deposit a tiny amount of ETH (for example 1 wei) before the modify call is executed. An attacker can front‑run a legitimate modify transaction by invoking a payable multicall or mint function with an empty payload and a non‑zero value, thereby leaving the contract balance non‑zero. When the original modify transaction reaches the require check, the condition fails and the transaction reverts with the message “Aloe: antes sum”. This reverts the whole modify flow, preventing the caller from updating their NFT borrow position, withdrawing collateral, borrowing more assets, or performing any other state‑changing action that depends on modify. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – such as a successful withdrawal or a position adjustment to avoid liquidation – is replaced by a failed transaction and an error message, often without an obvious indication that the failure is caused by a stray wei in the contract. The impact can be severe: users may miss time‑critical opportunities, be forced into liquidation, or lose access to funds that remain locked in the contract. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the pre‑ and post‑conditions of modify and noticed that the balance check could be violated by external deposits. It is hard to notice because the offending amount can be as small as a single wei, which does not raise suspicion in transaction logs, and the revert message does not clearly explain the root cause. The bug belongs to the class of balance‑invariant violations where a contract assumes a certain ether balance that can be altered by anyone, leading to a DoS. The proper mitigation is to avoid requiring a zero balance; instead the contract should return any excess ether to the caller or use a pull‑payment pattern, ensuring that the invariant cannot be broken by external deposits. By eliminating the strict zero‑balance requirement, the modify function can execute safely even if stray ether is present, removing the attack surface for front‑running DoS attacks.

title: Address approved by user in BorrowerNFT for
poc: N/A
bug_full: The vulnerability is an insufficient data verification flaw in the Permit2Manager used by the BorrowerNFT system. The manager accepts a Permit2 permit that authorises a token transfer but only validates the function selector, the signer address and that the destination (the to field) matches the caller contract. Becausethe to field is not part of the signed data, an attacker who is approved to control one NFT can take a permit that the user included in a modify call for a different NFT, change the to address to the NFT the attacker controls, and front‑run the user’s transaction. The modify function first checks that the caller is either the owner or an approved operator for the specific token, and then forwards the permit to Permit2Manager. All of these checks pass because the attacker is approved for the token he will use, and the permit signature is still valid for the owner. As a result the Permit2 call transfers the user’s funds to the attacker‑controlled NFT, after which the attacker can immediately withdraw them. The bug is triggered when a user holds several BorrowerNFTs, approves an address for only one of them, and later invokes modify with a Permit2 permit for another NFT. From the user’s perspective the expected deposit never arrives, the balance of the intended NFT remains unchanged, and the user may see a sudden loss of funds with no error message. The issue is hard to notice because the contract performs several seemingly correct authorization checks, yet none of them verify that the permit’s destination corresponds to the NFT being modified. The root cause is the lack of a direct check that the permit’s to field matches the NFT for which the modify call is executed, and the reliance on a signature that does not cover that field. To remediate the problem the manager should require the owner to sign the full permit data, including the destination address, or add an explicit verification that the to address in the permit equals the borrower contract associated with the token being modified. This class of bug falls under improper authorization and unchecked external data, where a signature does not bind all relevant parameters, allowing an attacker to replay or tamper with the permit and steal funds.

title: Address approved by user in BorrowerNFT for
description:
Insufficient data verification in UniswapNFTManager and BoostManager allows attacker to break security control and use the approval the user gives to his Uniswap NFTs to UniswapNFTManager and BoostManager to steal this position funds.
In more details: BorrowerNFT allows any user to mint NFT's, which creates a borrower account and allows the user to control this account via the BorrowerNFT.modify calls. User can either call modify himself, or approve any address to call it on his behalf. The user can either approve address for all of his NFTs, or he can approve address for his individual NFTs. Notice: if the user approves some address to one of his NFTs, this address must not have any control condition, allowing the address approved by user to one NFT to steal user funds from the other NFTs (even when not approved for them).
Suppose attacker address is approved by user to NFT1. And then the same user wants to use UniswapNFTManager and/or BoostManager to transfer his existing uniswap NFT position into NFT2 (which the attacker is not approved to). Before using these managers, user must first approve his uniswap NFT position to be managed by the UniswapNFTManager or BoostManager. However, the issue is that the user can not specify which of his NFTs this is supposed to be used. If the user intended to deposit this position into NFT2, any address approved for any of his other NFTs (like attacker who is approved for NFT1) can use this approval to deposit this position into another NFT. So once user approves his position, attacker can immediately use this approval to deposit this into NFT1 and immediately withdraw the funds to steal them.
Here are all the security control checks, all of them will be passed by the attacker's transaction:
1. modify first verifies if attacker is authorized, he is not, so authorized is set to false:
bool authorized = msg.sender == owner || isApprovedForAll[owner][msg.sender];
2. modify checks if attacker is approved to control the NFT1, he was approved, so this require passes correctly:
if (!authorized) require(msg.sender == getApproved[tokenId], "NOT_AUTHORIZED");
3. Next modify calls borrower.modify (where borrower corresponds to NFT1) with UniswapNFTManager.callback and liquidity < 0 or BoostManager.callback with action = 0, which perform its own checks. First check in both passes (msg.sender is NFT1 borrower which is registered as borrower in the FACTORY and the owner of this borrower is BORROWER_NFT):
require(FACTORY.isBorrower(msg.sender) && owner == BORROWER_NFT, "Aloe: bad caller");
4. Next check in both passes (uniswap NFT owner matches NFT1 owner):
require(owner == UNISWAP_NFT.ownerOf(tokenId));
5. Finally, the liquidity is withdrawn from uniswap NFT and transferred to attacker's controlled NFT1 (with additional borrow in case of BoostManager, which can be immediately cancelled by the attacker).
_withdrawFromNFT(tokenId, uint128(-liquidity), msg.sender);
borrower.uniswapDeposit(lower, upper, uint128((uint256(uint128(-liquidity)) * 999) / 1000));
6. Since attacker has full control over NFT1, he can immediately withdraw the funds he just stole.
There is no way for UniswapNFTManager and BoostManager to distringuish which user's NFT the uniswap NFT is supposed to be for, thus any address approved for any of user's BorrowerNFTs can use/steal the uniswap NFT approved by the user to in/aloe-ii/periphery/src/managers/UniswapNFTManager.sol#L26-L54 y/src/managers/BoostManager.sol#L37-L53 however it's different as both the fix and attack path are different.
Internal pre-conditions
User has several BorrowerNFTs and approves attacker for only one of the NFTs, then approves his uniswap NFT to either UniswapNFTManager or BoostManager
External pre-conditions
None
Attack Path
1. Attacker listens to the user transaction, and as soon as user gives approval to any of his uniswap NFTs to either UniswapNFTManager or BoostManager, immediately call BorrowerNFT.modify with NFT1, corresponding manager and user's uniswap NFT.
2. Attacker immediately withdraws these funds from the NFT
Usage of UniswapNFTManager and BoostManager requires user to approve his uniswap NFT to these managers, but this immediately makes it possible for any address approved for any of user's BorrowerNFTs to steal this uniswap NFT.
poc: N/A
bug_full: The vulnerability is an insufficient data verification flaw in the interaction between BorrowerNFT, UniswapNFTManager and BoostManager that allows an attacker who is approved for a single BorrowerNFT to steal liquidity that the user intended to move to a different BorrowerNFT. The root cause is that the manager contracts accept a generic approval of a Uniswap NFT position without requiring the caller to specify which BorrowerNFT the position should be associated with. Consequently, any address that holds an approval for any BorrowerNFT owned by the same user can invoke BorrowerNFT.modify, trigger the manager callback, and withdraw the approved liquidity into the NFT it controls. Exploitation proceeds as follows: the user, who owns multiple BorrowerNFTs, approves an attacker address to manage NFT1. Later the user approves a Uniswap NFT position to UniswapNFTManager or BoostManager, intending to deposit it into NFT2. Because the manager contracts only check that the caller is a registered borrower and that the Uniswap NFT owner matches the caller’s owner, the attacker’s approved NFT1 satisfies these checks. The attacker monitors the approval transaction, immediately calls BorrowerNFT.modify with NFT1, passes the manager’s callback, and executes the internal _withdrawFromNFT function, moving the liquidity to NFT1. The attacker can then withdraw the funds, leaving the user’s intended NFT2 empty. The impact is a loss of the user’s deposited liquidity; from the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful deposit but the balance of the target NFT becomes zero and no funds are received. This occurs whenever a user holds several BorrowerNFTs, grants approval to an address for at least one of them, and then approves a Uniswap NFT position to the manager contracts. The affected parties are any users of the protocol who manage multiple BorrowerNFTs and rely on the manager contracts for position migration. The issue was discovered during a security audit performed by Sherlock, and it is subtle because the manager contracts appear to enforce ownership checks, yet they do not bind the approved Uniswap NFT to a specific BorrowerNFT, making the misuse non‑obvious. To remediate, the protocol should replace generic approvals with permit‑style authorisations that are signed for a specific target BorrowerNFT, and the manager contracts should require the user to explicitly bind the Uniswap NFT to the intended BorrowerNFT, rejecting calls that originate from an approved NFT that does not match the target. This would prevent an approved third party from hijacking the position and ensure that funds are transferred only to the intended NFT.

title: BorrowerNFT can mint at most 65536 NFTs which
poc: N/A
bug_full: The vulnerability is a hard‑coded maximum supply of 65536 NFTs caused by the contract limiting the internal token index to two bytes. The root cause is the function that returns a fixed index size of 2, which is then used to compute the maximum supply as 1 shifted left by (indexSize multiplied by 8), resulting in a supply ceiling of 2^16. When the totalSupply reaches this value, the mint function checks that the new totalSupply is less than the maximum and reverts with the error "MAX_SUPPLY". This check triggers on every mint attempt after the cap is hit, causing the transaction to fail and preventing any further NFTs from being created. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate users who try to mint after the cap is reached receive a revert, see no new token, and the protocol’s core borrowing functionality that depends on minting BorrowerNFTs becomes unavailable. The condition occurs once 65536 NFTs have been minted, which can happen during normal growth – for example, if each user mints an average of ten borrowers, the system would stop accepting new users after roughly 6,500 participants – or it can be forced by an attacker who deliberately mints the entire supply. Because minting each NFT only costs gas, an attacker could exhaust the supply in about one to two days by submitting ten mint transactions per block. The issue may be hard to notice because the limit appears large and there is no explicit warning; the contract simply reverts when the limit is reached, giving the impression of a generic error rather than a systemic cap. The bug belongs to the class of supply‑capping or integer‑size limitation vulnerabilities that break business logic assumptions about unlimited or sufficiently large token issuance. From a user’s perspective, the UI would show a transaction failure with a generic "MAX_SUPPLY" message, and users would see that no new NFT is received even though they expected a successful mint. To remediate, the index size should be increased to at least four to eight bytes, thereby raising the maximum supply to a value that aligns with the protocol’s expected user base, or the limit should be made configurable and accompanied by proper checks and warnings before the cap is approached.

title: Lender ERC4626 broken compliance for the
description:
README states the following about ERC4626 compliance:
Q: Is the codebase expected to comply with any EIPs? Can there be/are there any deviations from the specification? The Lender complies with here: https://coda.io/d/_dJtHvRlIBOx/Standard-Compliance_su6Wx
The link referenced provides the following compliance item in the checklist for maxRedeem and maxWithdraw functions:
[x] MUST return the maximum amount of shares that could be transferred from owner through redeem and not cause a revert, which MUST NOT be higher than the actual maximum that would be accepted (it should underestimate if necessary).
This condition doesn't hold in the following edge case: redeem (and withdraw) reverts if the totalSupply after the operation is between 1 and 1e5, but this case is not handled when calculating maxRedeem (and maxWithdraw):
require(cache.totalSupply == 0 || cache.totalSupply > 1e5);
If the lender has only 1 user with deposit (who has, say, 1000000 shares) and there is a dust amount borrowed (say, 100 tokens), then maxRedeem will return something like 999900 shares (if borrowBase is 1), however if user tries to redeem with this amount, the operation will revert, because remaining totalSupply will be 100, failing the require above. The correct maxRedeem amount in this case is 900000 shares, as this is the max amount which can be redeemed without revert.
maxRedeem function doesn't take into account a special case when remaining -update/blob/main/aloe-ii/core/src/Ledger.sol#L305-L312
In such edge case the value returned by maxRedeem will revert the redeem operation:
/Lender.sol#L200
maxWithdraw and withdraw functions simply use maxRedeem and redeem, so they have
Internal pre-conditions
Only 1 user deposit into lender, dust amount (<1e5) borrowed from this lender.
External pre-conditions
None
Attack Path
1. User calls maxRedeem and tries to redeem with this amount (or alternatively, user calls redeem with shares = type(uint256).max)
2. redeem reverts, breaking the ERC4626 condition (redeem with amount returned by maxRedeem must not revert).
Lender is not ERC4626-compliant. Since this compliance is specifically stated in contest README, this should make this issue a valid medium.
poc: N/A
bug_full: The vulnerability is a violation of the ERC‑4626 specification in the Lender contract’s maxRedeem and maxWithdraw functions. According to the ERC‑4626 checklist, maxRedeem must return the greatest number of shares that can be redeemed without causing a revert, and the returned value must never be higher than the true maximum. In this implementation the function calculates the amount based solely on the current totalSupply and the borrow balance, but it ignores a special internal requirement that the totalSupply after a redeem operation must be either zero or greater than 100 000 units. When a lender has only a single depositor and a small “dust” amount of tokens (less than 100 000) has been borrowed, redeeming the amount suggested by maxRedeem would leave the totalSupply in the prohibited range (1‑100 000). The contract therefore reverts with the require statement require(cache.totalSupply == 0 || cache.totalSupply > 1e5). Because maxRedeem does not account for this edge case, it overestimates the redeemable shares; for example it may return 999 900 shares while only 900 000 can be safely redeemed. This breaks the ERC‑4626 guarantee that a call to redeem with the value returned by maxRedeem must succeed. The bug can be triggered by calling maxRedeem and then redeeming the returned amount, or by directly calling redeem with an excessively large share amount such as type(uint256).max. The impact is that users see a non‑zero maxRedeem value, attempt to withdraw or redeem, and experience a transaction revert, resulting in wasted gas and a confusing user experience where the UI shows a possible withdrawal but the operation fails. The issue primarily affects users of the Lender contract when the pool contains a single depositor and a dust borrow exists; other participants are not directly impacted. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s behavior against the ERC‑4626 compliance checklist and exercised the edge case with a small borrowed amount. It is hard to notice because the revert only occurs in the rare situation where the remaining totalSupply falls into the small dust range, which many tests with larger balances do not cover. The correct fix is to modify maxRedeem (and consequently maxWithdraw) to cap the returned share amount at totalSupply - 1e5 when the post‑redeem totalSupply would otherwise fall below the 100 000 threshold, or to return zero in that scenario, thereby ensuring the returned value never leads to a revert. By aligning the calculation with the internal supply constraint, the contract regains full ERC‑4626 compliance and users can rely on the maxRedeem figure to safely withdraw their funds.

title: Lender ERC4626 broken compliance for the
bug_full:
The vulnerability is a deviation from the ERC4626 specification in the withdraw function of the Lender contract. According to the ERC4626 standard, a withdraw call must transfer exactly the amount of underlying assets that the caller specifies. In this implementation the function first converts the requested asset amount into a share amount using a rounding‑up conversion, then immediately converts those shares back into assets using a rounding‑down conversion. Because the two conversions use opposite rounding directions, the final asset amount can differ from the original request. For example, with an inventory of 1,000,000 tokens and a totalSupply of 990,000, a request to withdraw 99 assets is converted to 99 shares (rounded up from 98.01) and then back to 100 assets (rounded down from 100.0). The contract therefore sends 100 assets, one more than requested. This behavior violates the ERC4626 compliance clause that withdraw must send exactly the requested amount, making the contract non‑compliant as advertised in the project README.
The root cause is the reuse of the redeem conversion logic for withdraw, which assumes a symmetric conversion between assets and shares. When the ratio of total assets to totalSupply exceeds one – a condition that naturally arises as the protocol accrues interest and inventory grows – the asymmetric rounding can produce a mismatch. The issue manifests only when assets are greater than totalSupply; it cannot occur when assets are less than or equal to totalSupply. Consequently, the problem becomes more likely later in the protocol’s lifecycle, when the inventory has expanded relative to the share supply.
An attacker or any user can exploit this by repeatedly calling withdraw with amounts that trigger the rounding discrepancy, receiving slightly more assets than requested each time. Although each individual over‑payment may be as small as one token, the effect can accumulate, leading to a measurable loss of funds from the pool and breaking the accounting invariants that the protocol relies on. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a withdraw the token balance increases by more than the amount they asked for – for instance a call withdraw(2667) results in an actual increase of 2668 tokens. Users may perceive this as a bug or an unexpected bonus, but it undermines the trust model of the protocol.
The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case was added that logged the actual withdrawn amount and observed the off‑by‑one discrepancy. Because the deviation is only a single token in many cases, it can be easy to miss during manual testing or casual use, especially when the contract is handling large numbers where a one‑token difference is not immediately obvious.
To remediate the problem the withdraw function must be implemented independently of redeem. Instead of converting the requested assets to shares and then back, the contract should calculate the minimal number of shares to burn (rounding up) and then transfer exactly the requested asset amount, ensuring that the final transfer matches the caller’s request. This change restores ERC4626 compliance and prevents the rounding‑induced over‑payment.
In summary, the bug is a rounding‑error class issue caused by double conversion between assets and shares with opposite rounding directions, triggered when the asset‑to‑share ratio exceeds one. It leads to users receiving more assets than requested, violates the ERC4626 withdraw guarantee, can be exploited to drain funds over time, and is hard to notice because the discrepancy is often a single token. The proper fix is to separate withdraw logic from redeem and enforce exact asset transfer as required by the standard.

title: UniswapV3PoolTwapObserver uses the slot0
bug_full: The vulnerability is an oracle manipulation flaw in the UniswapV3PoolTwapObserver contract. When the time elapsed since the last checkpoint (duration) is zero, the observer falls back to returning the current spot price from the Uniswap pool slot0 instead of a time‑weighted average price (TWAP). Because the spot price can be altered by a large swap, an attacker can temporarily push the price to an extreme value and then use the observer’s getTwapSinceLastCheckpoint function to obtain a quote based on that manipulated price. The root cause is the special‑case branch that directly reads slot0 when duration equals zero, combined with the logic in TorexCore that allows a non‑zero amount of inTokens to be available after a user reduces their flowRate. Reducing the flowRate lowers the minimumDeposit required for the fee distribution pool, which frees up a buffer of tokens (availableInTokens) that the attacker can move. The exploit proceeds as follows: 1) The attacker monitors the mempool for a transaction that will close a user’s flow with a reduced flowRate. 2) Before that transaction is mined, the attacker calls moveLiquidity to transfer any remaining inTokens and then performs a large swap on the Uniswap pool to push the spot price far away from the market price. 3) The user’s transaction executes, closing the flow and causing the contract’s availableInTokens calculation to release a large amount of tokens (the buffer amount). 4) Immediately after the user’s transaction, the attacker calls moveLiquidity again. Because duration is zero, the observer uses the manipulated spot price from slot0, resulting in a quote that lets the attacker buy the newly released tokens at a dramatically reduced cost. 5) The attacker then restores the Uniswap price to normal. The impact is that the attacker can acquire a substantial quantity of tokens for near‑zero cost, effectively draining value from the protocol and potentially allowing the recovery of back‑charged fees that are otherwise not refunded when a flowRate decreases. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected token balances: the attacker’s wallet shows a sudden increase in token holdings while other participants see a loss of value or receive far fewer tokens than expected. The protocol’s accounting assumptions – that the TWAP reflects a fair market price over the elapsed interval – are violated because the contract trusts a manipulable spot price for zero‑duration intervals. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the moveLiquidity flow and the observer’s price calculation logic. It is hard to notice because the zero‑duration branch is rarely exercised and the price manipulation can be brief, leaving little trace in normal operation. The recommended remediation is to always use a TWAP price regardless of duration, or to enforce a minimum non‑zero interval before quoting a price, thereby eliminating the fallback to the manipulable slot0 value.

title: Updating stake or updating flow may DoS if
bug_full: The vulnerability is an underflow‑based denial‑of‑service condition that appears when a Torex instance is created without QuadraticEmission (QE) being enabled and a user later updates their stake or token flow while QE is still disabled. The QuadraticEmissionTIP hooks onStakeUpdated and onInFlowChanged are guarded by a check isQEEnabledForTorex(torex). When the check returns false, the functions simply return without performing any state updates, but they still rely on previously stored values such as the quadratic emission accumulator (q0) and the trader’s emission units in the emission pool. If QE is subsequently enabled by the admin, the next call to either hook will attempt to compute a delta using the old stored values that were never adjusted while QE was disabled. For example, when a user reduces a flow rate from 100 to 50 units, the code evaluates emissionPool.getUnits(trader) + newTraderUnits - prevTraderUnits, which becomes 0 + 50 - 100. Because the variables are unsigned integers, the subtraction underflows, causing the transaction to revert. The same pattern applies to stake updates where q0 + sqrt(new) - sqrt(old) can underflow if the new stake is smaller than the old one. The revert stops the update function, effectively locking the user out of modifying their stake or flow and preventing the contract from processing further emissions for that Torex. This situation can be triggered whenever QE is enabled after the Torex has been active for a period during which users have performed stake or flow changes. The affected parties are the users who hold stakes or active flows, the protocol that relies on continuous emission calculations, and any downstream contracts that expect successful updates. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the SuperBoring protocol, where the logical flow of the QE gating was examined and the mismatch between stored values and actual updates was identified. It is hard to notice because the gated functions appear to be harmless no‑ops when QE is disabled, leading developers to assume no state is altered, while the hidden state later causes arithmetic failures. To remediate, the contract should either prevent recording of stake or flow values while QE is disabled, reset or guard the stored emission variables before QE is turned on, or add explicit underflow checks (e.g., using SafeMath or conditional branches) that handle the case where the new amount is smaller than the previous amount. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of arithmetic underflow errors caused by inconsistent state initialization across feature‑gated code paths, resulting in funds appearing to disappear or updates being blocked, which violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that emission shares are always non‑negative and continuously updatable.

title: AdjustmentFlow for feeDistributionPool is streamed
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of the adjustment flow in a General Distribution Agreement (GDA) when the calculated flowRate for a fee distribution pool cannot be evenly divided among the total number of units. In such cases the protocol specification dictates that the remainder of the flowRate is streamed to the pool administrator. In the SuperBoring implementation the administrator of the feeDistributionPool is the SuperBoring controller contract itself. The contract receives the remainder as a continuous token stream, but it does not expose any function that allows the controller to withdraw or otherwise rescue those streamed tokens. Consequently, any remainder that is streamed becomes permanently locked inside the SuperBoring contract. The issue arises whenever the pool’s total unit count does not perfectly divide the desired flowRate – a situation that is common when many users stake large numbers of units. For example, with 100,000 users each holding 100,000 units, the total unit count reaches the protocol’s upper limit of 1e10, which can generate a remainder flow of up to 1e10 tokens per second. If the stream runs for a day, billions of tokens may be trapped. From a user perspective the symptom is that funds that should be distributed as fees simply disappear from the pool balance and never reach the intended recipients; the UI may show a decreasing pool balance with no corresponding withdrawals. The impact is a loss of value for token holders and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that all distributed fees are eventually claimable. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the SuperBoring code where the adjustment‑flow logic was examined and the absence of a rescue mechanism was noted. It can be hard to notice because the contract’s balance increases as expected, yet there is no observable way to move those tokens out, and no events are emitted to signal the lock‑up. The appropriate remediation is to add an admin‑only rescue function (or a similar mechanism) that allows the controller to withdraw the remainder tokens, or to redesign the rounding logic so that no remainder is ever streamed to an address without an exit path. This class of bug falls under “unrecoverable token lock‑up due to missing withdrawal path” and violates the fundamental business rule that distributed fees must remain accessible to the protocol or its participants.

title: Silent Failure in Must- NewDecFromString Can Lead to Node Crashes The protocol has acknowledged this issue. Found by defsec
description:
The use of MustNewDecFromString in the AlloraExecutor's ExecuteFunction method ignores potential errors, which can lead to invalid parameters being passed to the node, causing crashes.
In the ExecuteFunction method of the AlloraExecutor, MustNewDecFromString is used to convert string values to decimal types. This function panics if it encounters an error during conversion, rather than returning an error that can be handled gracefully. The code doesn't have any error handling or recovery mechanism for these potential panics.
For example:
can crash the node if not caught.
Similar issues exist for other conversions in the code, such as those for forecaster values and various attributed values.
• Malicious actors could potentially exploit this to crash nodes by providing invalid input data.
• Unexpected panics can cause the node to crash.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unchecked panic caused by the use of a conversion routine that aborts execution when it encounters an invalid decimal string. In the AlloraExecutor contract the ExecuteFunction method calls MustNewDecFromString to turn incoming string values into decimal types. MustNewDecFromString does not return an error; instead it triggers a Solidity panic if the string cannot be parsed. Because the surrounding code does not catch this panic or perform any validation, an attacker who supplies a malformed decimal string can cause the routine to panic, which propagates up to the node process and forces the node to terminate. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: the affected node crashes, stops processing further transactions, and appears unresponsive to users. From a user’s perspective the expected behaviour – a successful execution or a clear error message – is replaced by a silent failure where the node simply stops, balances may appear unchanged, and no refund or result is returned. The bug manifests whenever ExecuteFunction receives external input that includes inferer, forecaster, or other attributed values expressed as strings, which is a normal part of the protocol’s workflow. All nodes running the Allora software are therefore exposed, and any participant relying on those nodes experiences reduced availability. The issue was discovered during a security audit performed by the defsec team, who noted that the code lacks any error handling for the conversion calls. Because normal inputs are well‑formed, the panic may not surface during routine testing, making it easy to overlook. The proper remediation is to replace MustNewDecFromString with a non‑panicking variant such as NewDecFromString, check the returned error, and propagate a descriptive error message back to the caller instead of allowing a panic to unwind the call stack. Adding explicit validation of input strings before conversion also mitigates the risk. In broader terms this is a class of unchecked exception or panic bugs where a library function aborts the program on bad input, leading to potential denial‑of‑service attacks.

title: Topics wont activate even with
description:
Topics wont activate even with a sufficient stake
The AddStake function is used to add stake to a topic. If the stake amount reaches a certain threshold, the topic gets activated.
err = activateTopicIfWeightAtLeastGlobalMin(ctx, ms, msg.TopicId, msg.Amount)
This function however uses the GetCurrentTopicWeight function to get the current topic weight. This is calculated with an EMA filter, so the current deposit does not have the full weight. The result is a weighted average of the last topic weight and the current weight including the fresh stake.
weight, err = alloraMath.CalcEma(topicRewardAlpha, targetWeight,
previousTopicWeight, noPrior)
The topic is only activated if this new weight is higher than the setting in the params.
if newTopicWeight.Gte(params.MinTopicWeight) {
err = ms.k.ActivateTopic(ctx, topicId)
if err != nil {
return err
}
}
So due to the topic using an EMA filter, even if the actual weight of the topic exceeds the threshold, the topic wont get activated since the EMA value will still be below threshold.
At the end of the block, the EMA weights are updated in the EndBlocker function.
weights, sumWeight, totalRevenue, err :=
rewards.GetAndUpdateActiveTopicWeights(sdkCtx, am.keeper, blockHeight)
This is where the weights are updated, and after a few blocks the EMA will rise enough to clear the threshold.
However, while the EndBlocker function has the functionality to de-activate topics if their weight is below the threshold, it does not have the functionality to activate topics which cross the threshold.
The scenario looks like the following:
Assume the current stake is 0. Alice stakes 100 tokens. The threshold is 0.5. alpha for EMA is 0.8.
1. In block 1, Alice deposits 100 tokens. Current weight is = 0x0.8 + 100x0.2 = 20. Since this is below threshold, the ActivateTopic function never gets called.
2. Block 2, EMA = 20x0.8 + 100x0.2 = 36.
3. Block 3, EMA = 36x0.8 + 100x0.2 = 48.8. Now the threshold is cleared. However, the endblocker has no functionality to activate the topic.
Thus Alice deposits the necessary tokens but the topic never gets activated.
Topic does not get activated immediately on stake deposit due to EMA not clearing the threshold. Since the EndBlocker function does not turn on topics automatically, the topic will stay deactivated even though its weight is above the threshold.
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the activation logic of topics that rely on a weighted stake metric. When a user adds stake to a topic, the contract calls a function that calculates the current topic weight using an exponential moving average (EMA) filter. The EMA combines the previous weight with the newly deposited amount, applying a smoothing factor (alpha). The activation condition checks whether this EMA‑derived weight is greater than or equal to a globally configured minimum weight. Because the EMA smooths the contribution of fresh stake, the calculated weight can remain below the threshold even though the raw, unsmoothed stake already exceeds the required amount. Consequently, the ActivateTopic routine is never invoked at the moment the raw stake crosses the threshold. The end‑block processing routine updates the EMA values for all active topics, and it contains logic to deactivate topics whose EMA weight falls below the minimum, but it lacks any counterpart that would activate topics whose EMA weight has risen above the threshold. As a result, a topic may stay permanently inactive despite having sufficient stake, only becoming active after enough blocks have passed for the EMA to catch up, or never becoming active at all if the end‑block code never triggers activation. This flaw was discovered during a systematic audit of the staking and end‑block modules, where the mismatch between the activation check and the EMA update path was observed. The issue is subtle because the EMA calculation is a common technique for smoothing metrics and the UI typically shows the deposited amount correctly, leading users to expect immediate activation. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are a stake transaction that succeeds, a topic status that remains “inactive”, zero rewards, and an apparent loss of functionality despite meeting the economic requirement. The bug belongs to the class of state‑transition logic errors where a delayed or smoothed metric is used for a critical gating condition, and the state‑change handler does not account for the delayed metric. The impact includes denial of service for topic creators, locked incentives, and a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions about stake‑driven activation. To remediate the problem the activation condition should be based on the raw stake amount, or the end‑block routine should be extended with a queue that activates topics once their EMA weight finally exceeds the threshold, ensuring that topics become active as soon as the underlying economic condition is satisfied.

title: Depositing to another receiver other than msg.sender
description: StakedEXA::_update() is called when minting and if the time staked is smaller than the reference time, it calls _claim(reward), which claims the rewards for the msg.sender. However, the mint may be to someone else other than msg.sender, so avgStart[to]‘ will increase without first claiming, which will lead to loss of rewards for the receiver of the new deposit. In StakedEXA.sol::146 on claim(reward), it claims to the msg.sender, but the deposit is done to the to address, which may be different. Internal pre-conditions 1. Anyone must do a deposit to a different address. External pre-conditions None. Attack Path 1. User has some StakedEXA from previous deposits. 2. Another user deposits/mints to user 1, which increases avgStart[user1], but does not claim first for user1, making the funds stuck. The funds are stuck for much longer than they are supposed to. The duration is 24 weeks in the tests, so users can have to wait up to 24 weeks more if they do a really big deposit while having fully claimable rewards. Additionally, in case they decide to withdraw after depositing, before the rewards vest again, they will lose these funds to savings.
bug_full: An improper accounting flow occurs when the staking contract processes a mint that is directed to an address different from msg.sender. The internal function _update is invoked during minting and, if the elapsed staking time is less than the reference period, it automatically calls _claim for msg.sender. However, the subsequent deposit operation records the new stake under the 'to' address supplied by the caller. When the caller is not the same as the original staker, the contract updates the average start timestamp (avgStart) for the beneficiary without first claiming the rewards that were already accrued for that beneficiary. Because reward entitlement is calculated from avgStart, increasing this value without a prior claim effectively resets the claimable amount to zero. An attacker can exploit this by depositing or minting tokens on behalf of an existing staker; the victim’s previously earned rewards become inaccessible until the next vesting period, which in the test suite is up to 24 weeks. From the user’s perspective the UI shows no pending rewards, the balance of earned tokens remains zero, and the expected refund or claim transaction returns nothing. The issue is hard to notice because the deposit transaction succeeds and the staker’s principal balance appears unchanged, while the hidden accounting variable avgStart is silently altered. The bug belongs to the class of reward‑accounting mismatches caused by mismatched caller and beneficiary contexts. It was discovered during a systematic audit that exercised cross‑address deposits and observed that rawClaimable returned zero after a third‑party deposit. To remediate, the contract should ensure that any change to a beneficiary’s avgStart is preceded by a claim for that beneficiary, or the claim logic should be executed for the 'to' address rather than msg.sender. Proper separation of minting and depositing responsibilities or explicit checks that prevent deposits on behalf of others without an explicit claim would close the vulnerability.

title: Liquidations will leave dust when repaying
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding error that occurs during the liquidation of expired maturities in the market contract. When a position’s debt exceeds the maximum assets that can be repaid, the contract computes the actual repayment amount with a mulDivDown operation that always rounds down. Because the rounded value is smaller than the intended maximum, the liquidator repays fewer assets than allowed, leaving a small residual amount of collateral – often called dust – on the liquidated account. This dust remains even after repeated liquidation attempts, preventing the protocol from ever reducing the debt to zero and consequently blocking the clearBadDebt routine that would normally erase the bad debt entry. The issue manifests only when a borrower lets a loan mature, the debt grows larger than the supplied collateral, and the liquidation function is invoked. Under these conditions the rounding down of the repayment calculation produces a shortfall, the liquidatee ends up with a non‑zero collateral balance that cannot be withdrawn, and the protocol’s accounting assumes the bad debt is still outstanding. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by Sherlock, who observed that successive calls to liquidate a position with expired maturities never cleared the debt and eventually caused a revert with a “ZERO WITHDRAW” error. The problem is subtle because the leftover amount can be very small, making it appear as normal rounding noise rather than a systemic flaw. To fix the issue the repayment calculation should either use a rounding‑up variant (mulDivUp) or include explicit handling of the residual dust, ensuring that the liquidator can always repay up to the maximum assets and that clearBadDebt is triggered when the debt becomes effectively zero. In broader terms this is a classic example of a rounding‑down arithmetic bug in financial smart contracts that breaks the invariant that liquidation must be able to fully extinguish a debt when sufficient collateral exists, leading to funds that appear to disappear from the user’s perspective and violating the protocol’s accounting guarantees.

title: Liquidator will leave a pool with unassigned
description:
The issue is that in Market::clearBadDebt(), when a maturity is repaid, the unassigned earnings of this pool only go to the earnings accumulator when the last maturity is liquidated. However, if it's not the last maturity, the problem remains in case there is another borrowed maturity, and some user can claim these unassigned earnings just by supplying a few funds. Or if all floatingBackupBorrowed was due to the repaid maturity, and now it is 0, so users can borrow and deposit 1 wei to steal the unassigned earnings. In Market:661, the earningsAccumulator is only increased (contracts/blob/main/protocol/contracts/Market.sol#L652-L655) becomes null after a repayment. This means that as long as there are other borrowed maturities, the unassigned earnings may be stolen.

Internal pre-conditions  
1. Unassigned earnings must exist.

External pre-conditions  
None.

Attack Path  
1. Deposit funds to Market via Market::deposit() for the maturities to borrow, increasing floatingBackupBorrow and generating unassigned earnings.  
2. 1 maturity is borrowed which will be liquidated.  
3. At least 1 other maturity is borrowed so after liquidating the first,  
4. Liquidate one of the maturities, so the unassigned earnings resulting from this maturity will not go to the earningsAccumulator.  
5. Deposit at maturity to capture the unassigned earnings from both maturities, while only contributing liquidity to the other non liquidated one, which may be a dust amount, but the full unassigned earnings are captured to a single user.  
Attacker can claim a lot of unassigned earnings just by depositing at maturity enough (may be as small as 1 wei) to cover remaining floatingBackupBorrowed.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting leakage that occurs in the market contract when clearing bad debt for a maturity that is not the final outstanding maturity. When a borrowed maturity is repaid, the contract generates unassigned earnings – revenue that should be added to the global earnings accumulator and later distributed to liquidity providers. The implementation only updates the earnings accumulator if the repaid maturity happens to be the last one with outstanding borrowed positions. If other maturities remain borrowed, the unassigned earnings stay in a temporary variable and are never transferred. This logical flaw allows an attacker to capture the entire pool of unassigned earnings by making a minimal deposit at the affected maturity. The attack flow is: (1) a user deposits funds, creating floatingBackupBorrowed and generating unassigned earnings; (2) one maturity is liquidated while at least one other maturity stays borrowed; (3) because the liquidation does not clear the last borrowed maturity, the unassigned earnings are left orphaned; (4) the attacker deposits a dust amount (as little as 1 wei) at the same maturity, which triggers the contract to assign the orphaned earnings to the attacker’s account, effectively stealing revenue that should have been shared among all lenders. The impact is a loss of protocol revenue and an unfair profit for the attacker; legitimate lenders receive less than expected, and the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken. The condition for exploitation is the presence of unassigned earnings together with at least one other active borrowed maturity after a repayment or liquidation. Anyone providing liquidity can be affected because the stolen earnings reduce the total pool size, harming all participants. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when a test case showed that depositing only 10 wei after a liquidation cleared all unassigned earnings. It is hard to notice because the earnings accumulator appears unchanged, and the orphaned earnings are not emitted in events, making the loss invisible without deep state inspection. The bug belongs to the class of revenue‑misallocation or accounting‑state‑inconsistency vulnerabilities, where internal bookkeeping fails to reflect earned fees. To remediate, the contract should allocate unassigned earnings to the earnings accumulator proportionally to the amount of floatingBackupBorrowed that is cleared during each bad‑debt clearance, ensuring that no earnings remain orphaned regardless of the order in which maturities are liquidated. From a user’s perspective, the protocol promises that a deposit returns only the deposited amount plus a share of accrued fees; instead, a user may see a tiny deposit suddenly yield a large fee, contradicting the expectation that fees are distributed fairly among all liquidity providers.

title: Liquidating maturies with unassigned earn-
description:
Market::liquidate() calculates the amount to liquidate in Auditor::checkLiquidation(), which does not take into account floating assets accrual due to unassigned earnings in Market::noTransferRepayAtMaturity(). Thus, it will underestimate the collateral a certain account has and liquidate less than it should, either giving these funds to the liquidatee or in case the debt is bigger than the collateral, leave this extra untracked collateral in the account which will not enable clearBadDebt() to work. In Auditor::checkLiquidation(), the collateral is computed just by looking at the shares of an account, without taking into account maturities accruing unassigned earnings. In Market::noTransferRepayAtMaturity(), maturities are repaid and floating assets are increased due to backup earnings. Thus, when it seizes the collateral, it will seize at most the collateral without taking into account the new amount due to the floating assets sudden increase, as Auditor::checkLiquidation() is called prior the floating assets increase.

Internal pre-conditions  
1. Pool has unassigned earnings and user is liquidated.

External pre-conditions  
None.

Attack Path  
1. Users borrow at maturity and generate unassigned earnings.  
2. One of these users is liquidated but the collateral preview is incorrect and the liquidation is incomplete and the funds are lost.  
If the user has less debt than collateral but the debt would require most of its collateral, it would not be possible to seize it all. If the user has more debt than collateral a portion of the collateral will be leftover which will not allow bad debt to be cleared right away via clearBadDebt() and stays accruing.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an under‑seizure of collateral during the liquidate() operation caused by the Auditor::checkLiquidation() routine calculating required collateral without considering the increase in floating assets that results from unassigned earnings accrued when a maturity is repaid in Market::noTransferRepayAtMaturity(). Because the auditor preview is performed before the earnings accumulator updates the pool’s floating assets, the computed collateral amount is lower than the actual amount that should be available. An attacker can trigger a liquidation after a borrower has generated unassigned earnings but before the earnings are reflected in the pool balance, causing the protocol to seize only a fraction of the borrower’s collateral. The impact is that the borrower retains a small residual collateral that cannot be withdrawn and that the protocol’s clearBadDebt() function cannot clear the remaining bad debt, effectively leaving funds stuck or lost. The issue occurs only when the pool holds unassigned earnings and a user with a maturity‑based loan is liquidated after the maturity has passed. It affects borrowers, liquidators, and the overall accounting of the protocol because the accounting assumption that collateral fully covers debt is violated. The problem was discovered during a manual audit when a test case showed that after liquidation the borrower’s collateral balance was not reduced to zero even though the debt exceeded the original collateral. The bug is hard to notice because the accountSnapshot view of collateral before liquidation appears correct, while the liquidation step silently under‑estimates the seize amount. The correct fix is to modify the auditor’s collateral preview to include a simulation of the floating‑asset increase caused by the pending unassigned earnings, or to compute the collateral after the earnings accumulator has been applied. In generic terms this is a liquidation‑preview accounting miscalculation, a class of bug where state‑dependent earnings are omitted from collateral valuation, leading to unexpected “funds disappear” or “partial liquidation” symptoms where users expect their entire collateral to be taken but receive a leftover amount.

title: Rewards Can Be Harvested Even When Dis-
bug_full: The StakedEXA contract contains a logic flaw that allows reward tokens to be harvested even after the administrator has called finishDistribution, which is intended to terminate the reward emission schedule. The finishDistribution function records the current block timestamp as the finish time (finishAt) and transfers any remaining reward balance to a savings address, but it does not disable the harvest pathway. When a regular user subsequently invokes harvest, the function calculates the amount of assets to withdraw from the market based on the distributor’s allowance and then calls notifyRewardAmount. Inside notifyRewardAmount the code checks if block.timestamp is greater than or equal to rewardData.finishAt; if true, it recomputes rewardData.rate and, crucially, resets rewardData.finishAt to block.timestamp plus the original duration. This effectively starts a new distribution period, undoing the administrator’s intention to stop rewards. Because the provider’s token allowance remains unchanged, the market continues to release reward tokens that are then harvested and claimed by users. The impact is that the reward provider loses assets that were supposed to be locked after finalisation, breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol and allowing unintended token emission. The vulnerability manifests only after finishDistribution has been executed; any subsequent harvest call re‑opens the distribution window. It affects all parties that rely on the reward schedule: the provider (who loses tokens), users (who receive unexpected rewards), and the protocol’s integrity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced state changes across finishDistribution, harvest, and notifyRewardAmount, revealing that the finishAt timestamp is overwritten rather than enforced. The bug is subtle because the finishDistribution function appears to perform the correct finalisation, yet the later logic silently revives the schedule, making it easy to miss without a thorough state‑flow analysis. To remediate, the contract should either block calls to harvest after finalisation, revoke or set the distributor’s allowance to zero, or modify notifyRewardAmount so that it does not reset finishAt when a distribution has been marked as finished. In essence, the contract needs a definitive guard that enforces the termination of reward emissions, aligning the implementation with the intended business rule that rewards stop after the admin’s explicit finalisation.

title: Some bad debt will not be cleared when it
description:
In Market::clearBadDebt(), it only clears bad debt if the earningsAccumulator is unassigned earnings which would be added to the earnings accumulator. Thus, the accumulator would have funds to handle the bad debt, but due to checking if it is enough before taking into account its increase, it will not clear the bad debt and will decrease protocol solvency. In Market:641, it first checks if accumulator >= badDebt and then in Market:653 it increases the accumulator. This should be done in the opposite order as the accumulator may actual be big enough with the added unassigned earnings to clear the bad debt.

Internal pre-conditions  
2. User is liquidated.  
3. Accumulator is bigger than the bad debt if it takes into account unassigned earnings.

External pre-conditions  
None.

Attack Path  
1. User borrows maturities but lets them expire and accrues more debt than collateral.  
2. User is liquidated, but the accumulator is not enough to cover the bad debt without the unassigned earnings increase, so bad debt keeps accruing.  
Bad debt accrual which harms protocol users as it increases the risk of insolvency.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an ordering flaw in the debt‑clearance routine of the market contract. When a borrower is liquidated, the function responsible for clearing bad debt first checks whether the current earnings accumulator is greater than or equal to the outstanding bad debt, and only afterwards adds any unassigned earnings to the accumulator. Because the check is performed before the accumulator is increased, the condition can evaluate to false even though the accumulator would be sufficient after the pending earnings are accounted for. This logical mistake prevents the protocol from clearing the bad debt, allowing the debt balance to keep growing after liquidation. The issue manifests only when there are unassigned earnings that would raise the accumulator above the bad‑debt threshold; under those circumstances the protocol incorrectly assumes it lacks enough funds and leaves the debt uncleared. As a result, the protocol’s solvency metric deteriorates, exposing lenders and other users to higher risk of insolvency. From a user’s point of view, a liquidation that should wipe out the borrower’s debt instead leaves the debt outstanding, so the borrower’s position may appear to be “still in debt” or the protocol may show a sudden drop in available liquidity. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑order errors where state updates are applied after a condition that depends on the updated state, a pattern that can be hard to spot because the code reads as if the check is correct and the accumulator update seems harmless. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the clearBadDebt logic and traced the execution path through the accumulator comparison and subsequent update. To remediate the issue, the contract should first incorporate the unassigned earnings into the accumulator and only then compare the resulting value against the bad‑debt amount, ensuring that any debt that can be covered is actually cleared. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that the protocol’s earnings buffer is always used to offset bad debt before it is declared insolvent.

title: Precision Loss in notifyRewardAmount Func-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision loss in the reward‑rate calculation of the StakedEXA contract's notifyRewardAmount function. The function computes rewardData.rate by dividing the supplied reward amount by the reward duration using integer division. Because Solidity truncates any fractional part, the resulting rate is rounded down. When the contract later multiplies this rate by the duration to determine the total distributable reward, the product can be smaller than the original amount. If a previous reward period is still active, the function adds the remaining rewards to the new amount before dividing, but the same rounding down occurs, leaving a residual amount that is never accounted for in subsequent claims. This residual amount remains locked in the contract because there is no mechanism to withdraw or redistribute it. The issue manifests when the reward amount is not an exact multiple of the duration, or when the combined amount (new amount plus leftover) is not divisible by the duration. Under these conditions, stakers who call the claim function receive slightly less than the theoretical total; for example, a user expecting 10 WBTC may receive only 9.9976 WBTC while a small balance (≈0.0026 WBTC) stays in the contract. From a user perspective the UI shows a successful claim but the reward balance is marginally lower than expected, and the contract's token balance shows an unexplained residual. The bug was discovered during a formal audit when a unit test measured the contract balance after many weeks of reward distribution and observed a non‑zero remainder. The problem is hard to notice because the leftover can be a tiny fraction of the total reward, easily masked by normal rounding noise, and the contract does not expose the hidden balance to users. The economic impact is a loss of funds that become effectively unrecoverable for stakers, violating the protocol's accounting assumption that all notified rewards will eventually be claimable. To remediate, the contract should avoid integer division for rate calculation, for instance by using a fixed‑point scaling factor (e.g., multiplying the amount by 1e18 before division) or by tracking rewards per share with high‑precision arithmetic. Additionally, an administrative withdrawal function should be added to allow the protocol owner to recover any undistributed tokens caused by rounding, ensuring that no reward funds remain permanently locked.

title: Attackers will reset avgStart of any user mak-
description:
StakedExa::_update() resets avgStart[to] whenever the time passed is bigger than the reference time.
