An attacker can deposit 1 wei to some user and reset the avgStart, which will make claiming for the to address return 0 rewards until at least minTime and/or the to address loses the rewards to savings when withdrawing. In StakedExa.sol::151, if (time > memRefTime) avgStart[to] = block.timestamp * 1e18; resets the average start time to the current block timestamp, which may be performed by an attacker donating just 1 wei to the to address.

Internal pre-conditions  
1. User must stake for at least refTime, which is expected as this the moment the user can claim the maximum rewards.

External pre-conditions  
None.

Attack Path  
1. User stakes until reaching at least the reference time + 1.  
2. Attacker deposits 1 wei to the user forcing avgStart to reset and discount all rewards to 0 until minTime passes.  
User will not receive any rewards until minTime and will lose to savings when withdrawing as no rewards would have vested due to avgStart[to] having been reset.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the staking contract’s internal accounting routine that updates the average start timestamp (avgStart) for a beneficiary. When the contract processes a deposit for any address, it checks whether the elapsed time since a reference point exceeds a stored reference time; if it does, the routine overwrites avgStart[to] with the current block timestamp multiplied by 1e18. Because the check does not verify that the deposit originates from the same user who originally staked, an attacker can send a trivial amount – as little as one wei – to the victim’s address through the staking contract. This single‑wei deposit triggers the condition time > memRefTime, causing avgStart for the victim to be reset to the present block time. The reward formula later uses avgStart to calculate vested rewards, so resetting it effectively discards the time that the victim had already accrued. As a result, the victim’s claimable reward drops to zero until the minimum staking period (minTime) elapses, and any subsequent withdrawal yields only the principal without the expected earnings. The issue manifests only after a user has already staked for at least the reference time, which is the moment the protocol expects maximum rewards to be claimable. From a user’s perspective the UI still shows the staked balance, but the reward balance appears empty or the claim transaction returns no tokens, contradicting the expectation of receiving accrued rewards. The flaw was uncovered during a manual audit by constructing a test that deposits a single wei on behalf of another address and observes the avgStart reset and the resulting zero claimable amount. The problem is subtle because the state change is a single timestamp update and the deposited amount is negligible, making it easy to miss in normal operation. Conceptually, this is a state‑mutation bug that allows external actors to manipulate accounting variables that should be immutable for a given staking period. The proper mitigation is to stop overwriting avgStart on arbitrary deposits, for example by only updating avgStart when the beneficiary themselves initiates a deposit or withdraw, or by preserving the original timestamp once the reference period has been reached. Removing the reset eliminates the attack surface that lets an adversary nullify another user’s earned rewards.

title: Frozen/paused Market that is harvested from
description:
StakedEXA::harvest() withdraws from the market of the StakedEXA contract if the provider has assets there and has approved StakedEXA. However, the market may be paused/frozen, but StakedEXA::harvest() will try to withdraw anyway, which will make it revert. As it is part of the deposit flow, it means all deposits will revert and new users will not be able to collect yield. In StakedEXA::_update(), StakedEXA::harvest() is called if it is a mint (from == address(0)), here. Then. in StakedEXA:harvest(), it withdraws from the market regardless of its state, reverting if frozen or paused.

Internal pre-conditions  
None.

External pre-conditions  
1. Market is frozen or paused.

Attack Path  
1. Market is frozen or paused.  
2. StakedEXA deposits are frozen.  
Frozen StakedEXA deposits which means new users will miss out on the yield and current users will enjoy a guaranteed higher yield.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the staking contract’s harvest routine, which attempts to withdraw assets from an external market without first verifying the market’s operational state. When a user deposits into the staking contract, the internal _update function triggers harvest as part of the mint flow. Harvest unconditionally calls the market’s withdraw function even if the market has been paused or frozen. Because the market contract reverts on any withdraw attempt while in a paused or frozen state, the entire deposit transaction reverts, preventing the user from completing the deposit and from receiving any yield. This situation occurs only when the external market is in a paused or frozen condition, which can be triggered by any account possessing the market’s pauser role. An attacker or a legitimate pauser can therefore freeze the market, causing all subsequent deposit attempts to fail and effectively locking out new participants. Existing stakers may continue to earn yield, but they cannot add more assets, and new users experience a mismatch between the expectation of a successful deposit and the reality of a reverted transaction, often manifested as a generic “transaction reverted” error with no obvious indication of the underlying cause. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that included a test case where the market was paused before a deposit, confirming that the deposit call reverted. The bug is hard to notice because the harvest function is internal and only invoked during deposit, so the pause condition may not be exercised in normal operation, and the revert message does not explicitly reference the market’s paused state. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of missing state validation or business‑logic checks, where a contract assumes an external dependency is always available. The proper remediation is to add an explicit check of the market’s paused or frozen flag before invoking harvest, and to skip or defer the harvest call when the market is not active, thereby aligning the contract’s behavior with the expected accounting logic that deposits should only succeed when the underlying market can accept withdrawals.

title: Setting a new market will make depositing
description:
In StakedEXA::harvest(), it deposits to the market the resulting savings that are not notified as rewards from the provider. The approval of the asset of the Market to the Market is only performed in the constructor, which means that if a new Market is set via StakedEXA::setMarket(), it currently does not approve it and will DoS deposits and make it impossible to correctly switch markets. In StakedEXA.sol::460, setMarket(), a new market is set but an approval is not given of the market.asset() to the market, which will DoS deposits.

Internal pre-conditions  
1. A new market is set.

External pre-conditions  
None.

Attack Path  
1. StakedEXA::setMarket() is called, setting a new market.  
2. Deposits are DoSed because it tries to deposit to the new market without approving it first and reverts.  
DoSed deposits and impossability of correctly changing markets.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing token allowance initialization when the StakedEXA contract switches to a new market via the setMarket() function. In the constructor the contract grants an unlimited approval (type(uint256).max) for the market’s underlying asset to the market itself, which enables the internal harvest() routine to deposit any surplus tokens without further checks. However, setMarket() only updates the market reference and does not repeat this approval step. As a result, when a new market is set, the StakedEXA contract attempts to call market.deposit() with the underlying asset but the market has no allowance to transfer those tokens from StakedEXA, causing the ERC20 transfer to revert. This logical omission creates a denial‑of‑service condition: any subsequent deposit transaction reverts, users see a failed deposit or a zero balance change, and the protocol cannot correctly migrate to a different market. The issue manifests only after a market change, which is why it may be overlooked during standard testing that only exercises the initial market. It was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s state‑transition functions, where the auditor noticed that the approval logic present in the constructor was not duplicated in setMarket(). Exploiting the bug is straightforward – an attacker (or even a benign user) can call setMarket() with a freshly deployed market contract, after which all deposit attempts will revert, effectively locking out users from adding new funds. The impact is limited to the deposit functionality; existing balances remain intact, but new funds cannot be added, breaking the expected business logic of staking and potentially eroding user trust. The affected parties are all users of the StakedEXA contract who wish to deposit after a market switch, as well as the protocol operators who rely on the ability to upgrade markets. To remediate, the setMarket() implementation should replicate the constructor’s approval step by calling the underlying asset’s approve() method with an unlimited allowance for the new market, ensuring that subsequent harvest and deposit calls succeed. This class of bug falls under improper initialization or missing permission grant during a state transition, a common source of functional denial‑of‑service in token‑handling contracts.

title: Market utilization ratio near 100% will DoS de-
description:
StakedEXA::_update() harvests when depositing, withdrawing assets from the provider in the given market. However, due to the utilization ratio check in the market, it may not be possible to withdraw these assets, reverting. This will halt deposits and secure some extra yield for users that potentially make this happen. In StakedEXA::356 it withdraws without checking if there is enough protocol liquidity in the market such that it is possible to withdraw. If there is too much debt, it will revert and halt deposits.

Internal pre-conditions  
None.

External pre-conditions  
1. Market needs to be close to maximum utilization ratio.

Attack Path  
1. Users borrow a lot from the underlying market, making the utilization ratio reach 100%  
2. Users try to deposit but revert due to trying to withdraw assets from the provider in the market that would leave the market with less deposits than borrows.  
Deposits are DoSed leading to extra yield for current depositors and loss of yield for future ones that can't stake.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic error in the StakedEXA contract where the internal _update routine attempts to withdraw assets from the underlying market without first verifying that the market has sufficient free liquidity. The market enforces a utilization ratio that measures borrowed assets against total deposits, and when this ratio reaches or exceeds 100 % the market rejects any withdrawal request. Because the contract does not check this condition, a call to deposit triggers a withdrawal that reverts if the market is fully utilized. An attacker can exploit this by borrowing a large amount from the underlying market until the utilization ratio is close to the maximum, then any subsequent deposit to StakedEXA will fail, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service on new deposits. The impact is that users attempting to stake see their transactions revert with no explicit error, their balances remain unchanged, and they receive no receipt of the deposit. Existing stakers continue to earn yield, potentially at a higher rate because no new deposits dilute the pool, while future users are unable to participate and lose expected yield. The condition occurs only when the external market is at or above its maximum utilization, a state that may not be exercised in routine unit tests, making the bug hard to notice. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the withdrawal path in StakedEXA::_update and identified the missing liquidity check. It belongs to the class of unchecked external calls that can revert due to state constraints, leading to a DoS vector. To remediate, the contract should cap the withdrawal amount to the maximum that keeps the utilization ratio at or below 100 %, or explicitly query the market’s available liquidity before attempting the withdrawal, ensuring that a deposit never triggers a revert because of insufficient market liquidity.

title: Anyone will DoS setting a new rewards dura-
description:
Rewards are destributed via StakedEXA::notifyRewardAmount() over a certain duration and amount, which originates a rate. The protocol may intend to change this rate by altering the duration, making users receive more or less rewards depending on intent. The duration of the rewards is set in StakedEXA::setRewardsDuration(), but it will be near impossible to set as there is an automatic mechanism to harvest rewards from the provider. In StakedEXA::443, it's not possible to set a new duration if the current rewards are still not finished. This will always be the case as the automated provider harvesting will keep notifying new rewards and resetting the finish time of the rewards.

Internal pre-conditions  
None.

External pre-conditions  
None.

Attack Path  
1. Provider harvests new rewards.  
2. StakedEXA::harvest() is called, which notifies new rewards and updates the finish time.  
3. StakedEXA::setRewardsDuration() reverts as block.timestamp has not reached rewardData.finishAt.  
The ability to change the duration of rewards is DoSed which will impact the amount of rewards users get over time.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that prevents the contract administrator from changing the rewards distribution duration once the reward period has started. The contract calculates a reward rate from a total amount and a duration, and stores a finish timestamp. The function that updates the duration checks whether the current block timestamp is greater than or equal to the stored finish timestamp; if it is not, the call reverts. At the same time the contract contains an automated harvesting routine that, whenever new rewards are supplied, calls a notify function which resets the finish timestamp to a future value. Because the harvest is continuously triggered by the reward provider, the finish timestamp is constantly extended and never reaches the point where the duration‑change check passes. Consequently any attempt by an admin to call setRewardsDuration will always revert, effectively locking the reward schedule. This logic coupling creates a situation where the protocol cannot adjust its incentive parameters, meaning that the intended increase or decrease of reward rates cannot be enacted. Users who expect a change in reward accrual see no difference, while the protocol may continue to distribute rewards at an outdated rate, potentially leading to over‑payment or under‑payment. The issue is discovered during a security audit by inspecting the reward‑duration setter and noticing that it depends on a condition that is never satisfied because of the automatic harvest that updates the finish time. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the contract functions correctly while rewards are being distributed; the problem only surfaces when an admin attempts to modify the duration, a relatively rare action. The bug belongs to the class of governance‑parameter update denial‑of‑service bugs where state updates are unintentionally coupled with external triggers. From a user perspective the UI may show the reward rate unchanged after a governance vote, or an admin transaction may revert with a generic “reward period not finished” error, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. To fix the issue the setter should be redesigned to allow a new duration to be applied by recalculating the remaining reward rate based on the leftover rewards, or by separating the harvest notification from the duration‑change logic, or by providing a pause mechanism that lets the admin update parameters before the next harvest. In any case the fix must break the tight dependency between harvest‑induced finish‑time updates and the duration‑change guard so that the protocol can safely adjust its incentive schedule without being locked out.

title: Having no deposits in StakedEXA will lead to
description:
The provider in StakedEXA is free to distributed rewards as it pleases and there is an automated way to distribute via StakedEXA::harvest(). The harvest setup may be started but no actual deposits have been made to StakedEXA or users may withdraw from StakedEXA while automated ongoing rewards are happening, which will lead to stuck rewards inside StakedEXA. In StakedEXA::globalIndex() it returns a stale index if the totalSupply() is null (no deposits), but it should instead calculate the amount (rate x deltaTime) and send it to savings. This way rewards will never be stuck.

Internal pre-conditions  
1. No deposits are present in StakedEXA.

External pre-conditions  
None.

Attack Path  
1. Deposits were not yet made and rewards are harvested or users withdraw all deposits while rewards are rolling out.  
Stuck rewards as the index is not increased but rewardData.updatedAt increases.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑distribution logic of the StakedEXA contract. When the contract’s total token supply is zero – either because no deposits have been made yet or because all users have withdrawn their stakes – the function that calculates the global reward index deliberately returns the previously stored index without adding any newly accrued rewards. At the same time, the timestamp that records the last time rewards were applicable (rewardData.updatedAt) is still advanced. Because the index is not increased, the amount of rewards that should have been generated during the elapsed time is never accounted for and is effectively removed from the contract’s accounting. This situation can be triggered deliberately by calling the harvest routine or by withdrawing all deposits while the automated reward schedule is still running. An attacker or any user can therefore cause the contract to “lock” or “lose” rewards that were supposed to be distributed, resulting in funds that are permanently inaccessible. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – a positive reward balance after a harvest – is replaced by a zero or unchanged balance, giving the impression that the rewards have vanished. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the StakedEXA contract when the auditor observed that globalIndex returns a stale value when totalSupply() equals zero, while rewardData.updatedAt continues to increase. The bug is subtle because it only manifests when the pool is empty; under normal operating conditions with a positive supply the index updates correctly, so the loss of rewards can go unnoticed until the pool is emptied. Conceptually, the fix is to handle the zero‑supply case by still calculating the pending reward amount as rate multiplied by the elapsed time (deltaTime) and either crediting it to a savings pool or adding it to the index before returning. This ensures that no reward accrues silently disappears, preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees and the users’ expectation of receiving earned incentives.

title: First liquidity provider of a newly created sta-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding‑down error in the stable‑pair pricing curve used by the Pair contract. The internal function that computes the invariant, called _k, multiplies the normalized reserves of the two tokens and then divides by 1e18. When the product of the scaled reserves is smaller than 1e18, integer division truncates the result to zero, causing the computed invariant k to be zero. The swap function checks that the current invariant is at least as large as the previous invariant (require(_k(_balance0,_balance1) >= _k(_reserve0,_reserve1))), so a zero value bypasses this check entirely. Because the pool is newly created and has no prior reserves, an attacker who is the first liquidity provider can deposit a tiny amount of each token such that the product of the scaled amounts is below the 1e18 threshold, mint LP tokens based on a near‑zero k, and then perform swaps that satisfy the amount‑in requirement with only a single token unit. The invariant check passes because both the old and new k values are zero, allowing the attacker to extract almost all of the pool’s liquidity while the LP token totalSupply inflates dramatically. Repeating the deposit‑mint‑swap cycle drives the totalSupply close to the uint256 overflow limit, after which any further mint attempts revert, effectively denying service to legitimate users. The issue only manifests on newly created stable pairs, requires the attacker to be the first liquidity provider, and is triggered by extremely small initial deposits that are unlikely to be covered by standard test vectors. Users experience symptoms such as the pool balance dropping to a single wei after a swap, LP token balances exploding, and later inability to add liquidity because the contract reverts on overflow. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the Pair contract’s invariant logic, where the mathematical expression for the stable curve (x³y + y³x) was examined and a proof‑of‑concept test demonstrated the drain. The problem is hard to notice because the invariant appears correct for normal reserve sizes; only the edge case of very small amounts reveals the rounding error. The vulnerability belongs to the class of integer‑division rounding bugs that break financial invariants, leading to invariant bypass and fund loss. A conceptual fix is to enforce a minimum invariant value during minting (for example, a MINIMUM_K constant) or to redesign the curve calculation to avoid division that can truncate to zero, ensuring that k is never zero for any valid deposit. This prevents the attacker from minting LP tokens with negligible collateral and stops the pool from being drained or from reaching an overflow state.

title: swap may be reverted if the input amount is
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way swap fees are calculated and forwarded to an external bribe contract in a liquidity pool that supports gauge rewards. When a user initiates a swap, the pool computes a fee proportional to the input token amount. For tokens with a low number of decimals (for example a stablecoin with 2 decimals) the fee calculation can be rounded down to zero because the fee rate (e.g., 0.03 %) multiplied by a small amount yields a value smaller than one token unit. The pool contract still attempts to send this fee to the external bribe via the function notifyRewardAmount, which contains a require(amount > 0) guard. Because the fee amount is zero, the require statement fails and the entire swap transaction reverts. This situation occurs only when the input amount is positive but insufficient to generate a non‑zero fee, which is unlikely for high‑decimal tokens but common for low‑decimal assets such as GUSD when swapping modest sums (e.g., 30 USD). From a user’s perspective the swap simply fails; the UI may show a generic “transaction reverted” or “swap failed” message, and the expected output tokens are never received, giving the impression that the protocol is broken or that funds have disappeared. The impact is limited to the inability to complete swaps involving low‑decimal tokens with small amounts, effectively denying service to those users and potentially reducing liquidity utilisation. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit when a test case that swapped a small amount of a 2‑decimal token caused the transaction to revert. It can be hard to notice because the fee amount is invisible to the user and the revert message does not explicitly mention a zero‑fee condition. The bug belongs to the class of “fee‑transfer rounding errors leading to contract reverts” and violates the business assumption that a fee calculation will always produce a positive amount that can be safely transferred. The recommended remediation is to add a guard that skips the fee transfer when the calculated fee is zero, or to modify the external bribe contract to accept a zero amount, thereby preventing the revert while preserving the intended fee distribution logic.

title: update_period(..) leads to wrong calculation
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the Minter contract’s update_period function, which is responsible for calculating the amount of tokens that must be minted each week and distributing them to voters. The function determines the current period, checks that a new week has started, and then calls weekly_emission() to obtain the expected weekly reward. However, the required amount is computed without applying the protocol’s precision scaling factor, causing the _required variable to be far larger than the intended 5 % emission. As a result, when the contract’s balance is lower than this inflated requirement, it mints the difference directly to its own balance. This over‑minting occurs every time update_period is triggered, i.e., at the beginning of each week, and it accumulates as the number of gauges grows, because each gauge’s reward calculation suffers from the same error. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that rewards appear larger than advertised, or that the protocol’s reported circulating_supply grows faster than expected, potentially showing a balance that is higher than the sum of user holdings. The impact is two‑fold: protocol accounting becomes inaccurate, third‑party contracts that rely on circulating_supply for fee or incentive calculations receive incorrect data, and the total token supply inflates beyond the economic model, undermining trust in the system. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Minter.sol source, where the auditor noticed that the weekly emission value was 2000e18 instead of the documented 5 % rate and that the circulating_supply function simply subtracts ve tokens from totalSupply, making the inflation visible. The bug is subtle because the extra tokens are minted to the contract itself, not directly to external accounts, so ordinary transaction logs may not reveal the discrepancy without inspecting the supply functions. The proper fix is to incorporate the PRECISION constant (or the equivalent scaling factor) into the calculation of the required mint amount, ensuring that the minted amount matches the intended emission rate and that circulating_supply reflects the true economic supply. In summary, the contract suffers from an over‑minting arithmetic error in its period update logic, leading to inflated token supply and broken accounting assumptions.

title: Voting power does not decay when calculat-
description:
Voting power does not decay when calculating shares of flow emissions earned by a pool/gauge, if the user does not vote again. The votes are still counted, but assigned too much power. The documentation linked in the README states that voting power should decay linearly based on time to unlock. However, this decay is not taken into account when calculating shares of flow emissions in Voter._updateFor() if the user does not call Voter.vote again. Their votes are still counted, but with the weights unchanged. This leads to an unfair distribution of weekly emissions and a loss of funds for the liquidity providers who do not get their fair share. Liquidity providers does not get their fair share of weekly emissions. Voter.vote() calls Voter._vote, which updates weights[_pool]. This is where the calculation of the voting power based on time to unlock happens. 
https://80eff4bd12578146a844cfd/v4-contracts/contracts/Voter.sol#L287-L292
https://80eff4bd12578146a844cfd/v4-contracts/contracts/Voter.sol#L249-L285
Voter._updateFor() uses weights[_pool] to calculate the share of emissions earned by the pool/gauge. The user's contribution to weights[_pool] remains unchanged until the user calls Voter.reset or Voter.vote. 
https://80eff4bd12578146a844cfd/v4-contracts/contracts/Voter.sol#L517-L534
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the calculation of voting power that determines how weekly flow emissions are split among pools (gauges). According to the protocol documentation, a user’s voting power should decrease linearly over time as the lock period approaches its unlock date. The decay is implemented in the function that processes a vote, where the weight assigned to a pool is reduced based on the remaining lock time. However, the emission distribution routine reads the stored weight directly without re‑applying the decay logic. If a user casts a vote once and never calls the vote function again, the stored weight remains unchanged even though the lock time is advancing. Consequently the protocol continues to treat the user’s voting power as if it were at its original maximum, while other users who vote again have their weight correctly reduced. This mismatch leads to an unfair allocation of weekly emissions: gauges associated with users who repeatedly vote receive a smaller share, while gauges linked to users who do not vote again receive a larger share than they are entitled to. The impact is a systematic loss of rewards for liquidity providers who rely on the documented linear decay, effectively causing their expected share of emissions to disappear over time. The issue manifests during normal weekly emission cycles, specifically after the first epoch when the lock period has progressed but no new vote has been submitted. It affects any participant who locks tokens, votes, and then remains idle, as well as the overall protocol economics because the emission distribution no longer matches the intended incentive model. The bug was uncovered during a security audit through a targeted test that simulated two users voting for different pools, advancing time, and observing that only the user who voted again experienced decay, resulting in a measurable skew in gauge balances. The problem is subtle because the UI still shows the vote as active and the total emissions are still distributed, making the discrepancy hard to notice without detailed balance checks. To remediate the issue, the contract should either enforce voting on every epoch so that decay is always recomputed, or redesign the share calculation to use a bias‑and‑slope model similar to the RewardsDistributorV2 contract, which inherently accounts for time‑based decay regardless of whether a new vote is submitted. Implementing either approach restores the intended linear decay of voting power and ensures a fair distribution of rewards across all liquidity providers.

title: User can make their veNFT unpokeable by vot-
description:
In order to understand the impact of the issue, we need to first understand why poke is critical to the system. When users vote for a pool of their choice, they contribute with the current balance of their veNFT. As the veNFT balance is linearly decaying, this results in possible outdated votes. For example: if a user has voted with a veNFT which has 10 weeks until unlock_time and 9 weeks have passed without anyone poking or revoting the veNFT, it will still be contributing with the balance from 9 weeks ago, despite the current balance being 10x less. For this reason poking is introduced, so if a NFT has not been updated in a long time, admins can do it (usually in other protocols like Velodrome, poking is unrestricted and anyone can do it to make it fair for all users). A user can make their veNFT unpokeable in the following way:
1. Gauge is known that it will soon be killed
2. User votes most of their weight to the pool they'd like and a dust amount to the to-be-killed gauge.
3. As soon as the gauge is killed, user's veNFT becomes unpokeable due to the following check in _vote:
```solidity
if (isGauge[_gauge]) {
    require(isAlive[_gauge], "gauge already dead");
```
User's gauge of choice will receive more emissions than supposed to. User will receive more bribes than supposed to.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic flaw that allows a veNFT holder to render their voting position permanently unpokeable after a gauge is killed, causing the contract to keep using an outdated, decayed voting balance for reward calculations. The system relies on a periodic "poke" operation to refresh the linear decay of a veNFT’s voting power; without a poke, a vote would continue to count the old balance, which can be many times larger than the current balance. In the current implementation the internal _vote function first checks whether the target gauge is registered (isGauge) and then requires that the gauge is still alive (isAlive). When a user votes the majority of their weight to a desired gauge and a small amount to a gauge that is known to be killed shortly afterwards, the subsequent kill flips isAlive to false. Because the same _vote logic is also used by the poke mechanism, any later attempt to poke the veNFT for that gauge triggers the require statement and reverts, effectively blocking any further balance updates for that NFT. The attacker therefore locks the stale voting weight in place, and the protocol continues to allocate emissions and bribes based on the inflated, outdated balance. This results in the attacker receiving more token emissions and bribe rewards than they are entitled to, while other participants receive less. The issue manifests only after a gauge has been killed and a poke would normally be required; it is hard to notice because the contract does not emit a specific warning and the symptom is simply an unexpectedly high reward payout. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the voting and gauge‑kill logic, where the interaction between the isAlive check and the poke path was examined. It belongs to the class of state‑update denial bugs where a condition meant for one operation (preventing votes on dead gauges) unintentionally blocks a maintenance operation (poke) that is essential for correct accounting. From a user’s perspective the UI would show the gauge still receiving votes and the user’s balance increasing, while the expectation that rewards decay over time is violated. The recommended remediation is to separate the alive‑gauge check from the poke path, for example by allowing the poke to continue even if the gauge is dead or by moving the check to a dedicated voting function, thereby ensuring that veNFT balances are always refreshed regardless of gauge status.

title: Rewards supplied to a gauge, prior to its first
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a permanent loss of reward tokens when they are sent to a gauge that has not yet received any deposits. The distribute function in the Voter contract automatically calculates a claimable amount for each gauge each week and, if certain conditions are met, forwards that amount to the gauge via IGauge.notifyRewardAmount. However, the function does not verify whether the gauge currently holds any staked supply. When a gauge’s total supply is zero – meaning no user has deposited tokens – the claimable amount is still transferred, but the gauge’s internal accounting cannot distribute the reward because there are no participants to receive it. As a result, the tokens become irretrievable and remain locked in the gauge forever. This occurs every time the weekly distribution runs for a newly created gauge that has not yet been activated by a depositor, which is a common scenario given that rewards are distributed automatically without regard to gauge activity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Voter contract where the logic of _updateFor and the subsequent claimable check were examined and it was observed that no guard exists for a zero‑supply gauge. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert and emits a normal DistributeReward event, giving the impression that the distribution succeeded, while the funds silently disappear from the protocol’s accounting. Users expecting a reward may see their balance remain unchanged or become zero, leading to confusion. The impact is a loss of protocol‑owned reward tokens, reducing the overall incentive pool and potentially undermining trust in the reward mechanism. To remediate, the contract should include a check that the gauge’s current supply (or an equivalent indicator of activity) is greater than zero before calling notifyRewardAmount, and revert or skip the distribution when the gauge is empty. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that rewards are only meaningful when there are participants to claim them, preventing permanent fund loss.

title: Incorrect calculation of TWAP in OptionTo-
description: The average price returned by OptionTokenV4.getTimeWeightedAveragePrice() can be up to 30 minutes outdated and does not reflect the current Token price. In the getTimeWeightedAveragePrice() function, the average price is calculated using the last X known price observations from the Pair contract. However, this approach has a flaw because it does not consider the current price, which could be as much as 30 minutes old. Consider a scenario where the price of the Token significantly increases during this 30-minute window. The resulting maximum discount might not adequately cover the percentage increase in price. This could lead to the protocol failing to collect proper fees when exercising the Tokens. The use of an outdated TWAP price could result in losses for the protocol or users.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the way the contract computes a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) for the underlying token when exercising options. The getTimeWeightedAveragePrice function aggregates only the last X price observations that are stored in the Pair contract and then divides the sum by the number of points. Because the function never incorporates the most recent price returned by Pair.current, the calculated average can be as much as thirty minutes older than the actual market price. This stale price is used to determine the discount applied to option holders and the fee that the protocol collects on exercise. If the token price rises sharply within the thirty‑minute window, the discount will be calculated on an outdated lower price, causing the protocol to collect insufficient fees and potentially allowing users to exercise options at a price that no longer reflects market reality. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that exercising an option yields a higher payoff than expected, or that the protocol appears to lose money on each exercise. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer compared the TWAP output against the live price feed and noticed a systematic lag. It is hard to notice because the contract still returns a numeric price and the price feed appears functional; only a careful comparison with the current market price reveals the discrepancy. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or oracle‑staleness errors where historical data is used without accounting for the latest observation, violating the business assumption that the price used for fee calculation reflects the current market. To remediate the issue the TWAP calculation should be amended to add the current price from Pair.current to the sum of historical observations before dividing by the number of points, ensuring that the average price never lags behind the real market price. This conceptual fix restores correct fee collection and aligns exercised option pricing with up‑to‑date market conditions.

title: Voter.replaceFactory()and Voter.addFactory()
description:
The Voter.replaceFactory() and Voter.addFactory() functions are broken due to invalid validation.
1. In the addFactory() function, the line require(!isFactory[_pairFactory], 'factory true'); is missing.
2. In the replaceFactory() function, the isFactory and isGaugeFactory checks are incorrect:
```solidity
require(isFactory[_pairFactory], 'factory false'); // <=== should be !isFactory
require(isGaugeFactory[_gaugeFactory], 'g.fact false'); // <=== should be !isGaugeFactory
```
These issues lead to the invariant being broken, allowing multiple instances of a factory or gauge to be pushed to the factories and gaugeFactories arrays. Broken code. DoS when calling Voter.createGauge().
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the factory management functions of the Voter contract. The addFactory() routine is supposed to prevent the same pair factory from being registered more than once, but it lacks the required validation check that would reject an already‑registered address. Consequently, any caller can invoke addFactory() with a factory address that is already marked as a factory, and the contract will silently push a duplicate entry into the factories array. The replaceFactory() routine suffers from inverted logic: it checks that the supplied pair factory and gauge factory are already known (require(isFactory[_pairFactory]) and require(isGaugeFactory[_gaugeFactory])) when it should be asserting that they are *not* already present. This mistake allows an attacker to replace a factory with an address that is already registered, again creating duplicate entries. The root cause is improper use of the isFactory and isGaugeFactory mappings, either missing a negation or using the wrong condition entirely. When duplicate factories accumulate, the invariant that each factory appears only once in the internal arrays is broken. The Voter.createGauge() function iterates over the factories array to locate a matching factory for a given token pair; with duplicated entries the loop can encounter unexpected state, potentially reverting or consuming excessive gas, which results in a denial‑of‑service condition where new gauges cannot be created. From a user’s perspective, attempts to create a gauge simply fail, returning no gauge address and leaving the caller with no indication that the failure is due to duplicated factory entries. The impact is that the protocol’s ability to launch new liquidity gauges is halted, preventing reward distribution and harming token holders who rely on gauge creation for staking or incentive programs. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s governance logic, where the auditor noticed that the require statements in addFactory() and replaceFactory() did not enforce the intended uniqueness constraint. Because the functions do not emit explicit events on duplicate insertion and the failure only manifests later during gauge creation, the bug can remain hidden until a user experiences a silent failure. The recommended remediation is to add a require(!isFactory[_pairFactory]) check to addFactory() and to correct the replaceFactory() checks to require(!isFactory[_pairFactory]) and require(!isGaugeFactory[_gaugeFactory]), thereby restoring the uniqueness invariant and preventing the DoS scenario.

title: The circulating_supply() of the Minter contract may revert, causing the Minter to fail to periodically emit Flow tokens, leading to systemic DOS risks.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way the Minter contract calculates the circulating supply of the Flow token. The function circulating_supply() subtracts the total amount of tokens locked in the veEscrow contract from the total supply of the Flow token without first checking which value is larger. When the veEscrow balance (_ve.totalSupply()) exceeds the Flow token total supply (_flow.totalSupply()), the subtraction underflows and the function reverts. This revert occurs inside the weekly emission routine update_period(), specifically at the line emit Mint(msg.sender, weekly, circulating_supply()); because the event emission evaluates the circulating_supply() return value. The root cause is an unchecked arithmetic operation that assumes totalSupply is always greater than or equal to the ve‑locked supply, an assumption that can be violated when the Flow‑WETH liquidity pool mints more LP tokens than the existing Flow supply, especially when Flow’s market price is high and large amounts are staked into veEscrow. An attacker or even a legitimate user can trigger the condition by providing enough liquidity and staking the resulting LP tokens, causing veEscrow’s total supply to surpass the Flow total supply. When this state is reached, the next call to update_period() reverts, preventing the contract from minting the scheduled weekly Flow tokens, skipping the approval and reward notification steps, and ultimately halting the distribution of new tokens. From a user’s perspective the weekly reward amount appears to be zero, the Mint event is not emitted, and the UI may show missing or stale balances, leading users to believe that their rewards have disappeared. The impact is systemic: any protocol component that relies on the periodic emission – such as voting power accrual, fee distribution, or incentive programs – stops functioning, creating a denial‑of‑service condition for the whole ecosystem. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s emission logic, where the auditor noted that circulating_supply() could revert under certain supply configurations. It is hard to notice in normal testing because the condition only manifests when the veEscrow balance overtakes the total supply, a scenario that may not be covered by typical unit tests. The recommended mitigation is to make circulating_supply() return zero when the subtraction would underflow, for example by using a conditional expression that returns max(0, totalSupply‑veSupply). This change restores the invariant that circulating supply is never negative, prevents the revert, and ensures that the Minter can continue emitting tokens even when veEscrow temporarily holds more tokens than the total supply, thereby preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees and eliminating the DOS risk.

title: Attacker will prevent distribution of USDC to stakers
description:
USDC's lower precision of 6 decimals and frequent reward updates will cause stakers to receive 0 of the allotted 10K USDC weekly rewards. distributions should be done at the pace of 10k per week until fully distributed. Using the same reward-per-token calculation for USDC used for KWENTA is a mistake as USDC only has 6 decimals of precision compared to KWENTA's 18 decimals.
Internal pre-conditions
1. The rewardsDuration is 1 week. This is the default duration.
2. The StakingRewardsNotifier sends 10_000e6 USDC of rewards to StakingRewards. Kwenta Governance will be distributing 10K USDC per week as rewards.
KWENTA's current total supply is at ~631_000e18.
External pre-conditions
Attack Path
1. The StakingRewardsNotifier sends 10_000e6 USDC to StakingRewards via notifyRewardAmount(). The rewardRateUSDC is now equal 16534 (10_000e6 / 1 weeks). This is scheduled to happen every week.
2. Every 1 to 3 blocks, the attacker will trigger an update of rewards by calling stake or unstake in StakingRewards. The reward-per-token for USDC is calculated:
```solidity
((lastTimeRewardApplicable() - lastUpdateTime) * rewardRateUSDC * 1e18) / allTokensStaked
```
When 3 blocks have passed, the time since the last update would be 6 seconds because block time in Optimism is 2 seconds per block.
```solidity
(6 * rewardRateUSDC * 1e18) / allTokensStaked
```
rewardRateUSDC is 16534 and allTokensStaked is 100_000e18.
```solidity
(6 * 16534 * 1e18) / 100_000e18
// ==> this will return 0
```
Since the reward-per-token for USDC is 0, none of the 10_000e6 USDC will be distributed to the stakers. organic activity on every block from users interacting with StakingRewardsV2 and trigger the rewards update. All stakers will receive 0 USDC rewards of the 10_000e6 USDC weekly rewards.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an arithmetic precision error that prevents weekly USDC rewards from being distributed to stakers. The contract reuses the reward‑per‑token formula that was designed for a token with 18 decimal places (KWENTA) and applies it unchanged to USDC, which only has 6 decimals. The formula multiplies the elapsed time, the reward rate and a 1e18 scaling factor, then divides by the total amount of staked tokens, which is also expressed with 18 decimals. Because the USDC reward rate is expressed in 6‑decimal units, the intermediate product becomes far smaller than the divisor when the elapsed time between updates is only a few seconds. Integer division therefore truncates the result to zero, so the computed reward‑per‑token for USDC is zero. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly invoking stake or unstake operations every few blocks, forcing the contract to perform the reward update with a very short time interval (for example six seconds on Optimism). Each update yields a zero per‑token reward, meaning none of the 10 000 USDC that the rewards notifier sends each week is credited to any staker. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a reward balance of 0 USDC despite having staked tokens and despite the contract receiving the weekly reward allocation. The impact is that stakers receive no USDC, the promised incentive distribution fails, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about reward accrual are violated. The issue is discovered during audit testing, where a unit test that checks rewardPerTokenUSDC after a short warp returns zero, confirming that the rewards are never accounted for. The bug is subtle because the contract accepts the reward transfer, emits expected events, and the arithmetic looks correct at a glance; only the interaction of differing decimal precisions and integer division reveals the flaw. The correct mitigation is to normalize USDC amounts to 18‑decimal precision before performing the reward‑per‑token calculation, or to accumulate fractional USDC rewards in a higher‑precision accumulator and only transfer whole units when they become available. Storing unclaimed fractional values until they sum to a whole USDC amount also prevents loss of reward value. In summary, the flaw is a precision‑related integer‑division bug that causes reward calculations to round down to zero, blocking USDC distribution to all participants.

title: Anyone can cancel a raffle with tickets == minTicketsThreshold
bug_full: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one logic error in the raffle contract that determines whether a raffle may be cancelled after ticket sales have ended. The internal function _checkShouldCancel examines the total ticket supply and only reverts when the supply is greater than the configured minTicketsThreshold. Consequently, when the exact number of tickets equal to minTicketsThreshold have been sold and the raffle end time has passed while the raffle status remains IDLE, the contract does not block the cancelRaffle entry point. An attacker – which can be any participant or a griefer – can invoke cancelRaffle before the drawWinner function is called, causing the raffle to be cancelled instead of drawing a winner. This situation occurs only under the narrow condition that currentTicketSold == raffle.minTicketsThreshold, block.timestamp >= raffle.endsAt, and raffle.status == IDLE. The impact is that the expected winner selection never happens, participants lose the opportunity to claim the prize, and depending on the contract’s cancellation logic, funds may be refunded incorrectly or become locked, breaking the accounting assumption that reaching the minimum ticket threshold guarantees a draw. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the raffle logic, and it is hard to notice because the edge case triggers only when the ticket count matches the threshold exactly, which may be rare in normal operation. To remediate, the cancellation check should reject the transaction when the supply is greater than or equal to the minimum threshold (supply >= minTicketsThreshold), ensuring that once the threshold is met the raffle can only proceed to drawing a winner. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of boundary‑condition errors that allow unintended state transitions, leading to user‑facing symptoms such as my raffle was cancelled even though we reached the required number of tickets or no winner was selected and my balance shows no reward.

title: The setRole() function grants role instead of revoking
description:
Access control in the Winnables Raffles protocol is handled with the Roles contract. It works similarly to OpenZeppelin's access control but uses bit flags to determine whether a user has a role. Each user has a bytes32 representing the bitfield of roles. Role 0 is an admin role, allowing its members to grant or deny(remove) roles to other users.  
The setRole(address user, uint8 role, bool status) function, as it stands, always adds a role by performing a bitwise OR operation. However, it does not handle the removal of roles if the status parameter is false. This oversight results in incorrect role management within the contracts, potentially leading to accidental privilege grants or the inability to revoke privileges from compromised or revoked accounts.  
In Roles.sol:L29 the _setRole() function always adds a role by performing a bitwise OR operation:  
[contracts/contracts/Roles.sol#L29-L33](contracts/contracts/Roles.sol#L29-L33)  
This internal function is used in the setRole() function:  
[contracts/contracts/Roles.sol#L35-L37](contracts/contracts/Roles.sol#L35-L37)  

Internal pre-conditions  
The setRole() function can only be called by the Admin.  
External pre-conditions  
Attack Path  
1. Admin deploys the WinnablesTicketTest contract.  
2. Admin grants role 1 to Alice by calling the setRole() function of the WinnablesTicketTest contract. The role is granted to Alice.  
3. Alice mints 10 tickets to Bob using the role.  
4. Admin revokes role 1 from Alice by calling the setRole() function.  
5. The role is not removed from Alice. She can still mint tickets to Bob.  
The improper implementation results in incorrect role management within the contracts, potentially leading to accidental privilege grants or the inability to revoke privileges from compromised or revoked accounts.
bug_full: The vulnerability lies in the role‑management routine of the Winnables Raffles protocol. The internal _setRole function is designed to update a user’s permission bitfield based on a boolean status flag, but the implementation only performs a bitwise OR operation, which always adds the specified role regardless of whether the caller requested a revocation. Because the status parameter is ignored when false, the contract never clears the corresponding bit in the user’s role mask. This logical flaw means that an admin who calls setRole(user, role, false) believes the role has been removed, yet the user’s permissions remain unchanged. An attacker who has previously been granted a privileged role (for example, the ability to mint tickets) can continue exercising that privilege even after the admin attempts to revoke it. The impact is a breach of the intended access‑control model: unauthorized accounts may keep minting tickets, potentially draining funds or violating the protocol’s business rules. The issue manifests whenever the admin tries to deny a role; the contract silently accepts the request, emits no error, and the user’s UI may still indicate the role is present, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual permissions. The bug was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a test that called setRole with false and then attempted a privileged action, which unexpectedly succeeded. It is hard to notice because the function signature suggests revocation is supported, and the test suite only checks the positive path. The vulnerability belongs to the class of improper bitmask handling or incomplete role‑revocation logic. To remediate, the _setRole routine must conditionally apply a bitwise AND with the complement of the role mask when status is false, thereby clearing the bit and correctly reflecting the revocation. After the fix, attempts to perform privileged actions without an active role will revert with the expected MissingRole error, aligning the contract’s behavior with the protocol’s security assumptions.

title: Admin can unrestrictedly affect the odds of a raffle
description:
A core invariant defined in the contest README is that:  
Admins cannot affect the odds of a raffle  
The existence of max ticket supply and max holdings however guarantees a minimum level of fairness.  
By setting themselves up with role(1) directly in the WinnablesTicket token contract, the admin can bypass all these assumptions (max ticket supply, max holdings), and affect the winning odds with no limit.  
First of all, let's look at mint() in WinnablesTickets contract:
```solidity
function mint(address to, uint256 id, uint256 amount) external onlyRole(1) {
```
[contracts/contracts/WinnablesTicket.sol#L182-L199](contracts/contracts/WinnablesTicket.sol#L182-L199)  
It is clear that role(1) can mint unlimited tickets. Furthermore, the admin can also grant themselves the role, bypassing any restrictions in buyTicket(). We now investigate the impact (how the results are affected by the admin minting tickets to themselves).  
When the raffle results are created, the winner is calculated using the supply from the ticket storage.
```solidity
function _getWinnerByRequestId(uint256 requestId) internal view returns(address) {
    RequestStatus storage request = _chainlinkRequests[requestId];
    uint256 supply = supplyOf is taken from the ticket;
    uint256 winningTicketNumber = request.randomWord % supply;
    return IWinnablesTicket(TICKETS_CONTRACT).ownerOf(request.raffleId, winningTicketNumber);
}
```
[contracts/contracts/WinnablesTicketManager.sol#L472](contracts/contracts/WinnablesTicketManager.sol#L472)  
By minting (virtually) unlimited tickets to themselves, the admin bypasses all restrictions imposed in ticket purchase, granting themselves victory odds far exceeding the restrictions imposed.  

Internal pre-conditions  
External pre-conditions  
Attack Path  
1. The admin locks a prize, and starts a raffle as normal. People starts buying tickets to enter the raffle.  
2. Admin grants themselves role(1) on the WinnablesTickets (not the ticket manager), and mints themselves (or any related party) almost unlimited tickets.  
3. Admin bypasses all max ticket restrictions, and said party is virtually guaranteed to be the winner.  
Admin can unrestrictedly affect the odds of a raffle, breaking protocol invariant.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a privileged mint capability that allows an administrator to arbitrarily increase the number of raffle tickets owned by a chosen address, thereby distorting the probability distribution used to select a winner. The contract’s design assumes that ticket supply is limited by a maximum total supply and per‑address holding caps, which together form a fairness invariant: no participant, including the admin, should be able to influence the odds beyond what the purchase logic permits. This invariant is broken because the token contract exposes a mint function that can be called by any account holding a specific role (role 1). The admin can either already possess this role or grant it to themselves, bypassing the purchase restrictions entirely. When the raffle draws a winner, it computes a random index modulo the current total ticket supply and then resolves the owner of the ticket at that index. By minting a very large number of tickets to themselves, the admin inflates their share of the total supply, making the random index almost certainly point to one of their tickets. The impact is that the admin, or any party they mint tickets for, can virtually guarantee victory, causing other participants to lose their expected prize while the contract appears to function correctly from a randomness perspective. This condition occurs whenever the admin exercises the mint privilege before the winner is calculated; it does not depend on the admin being the raffle creator, only on possessing the mint role. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented invariant with the actual access control on the mint function, revealing that the role‑based restriction is insufficient to enforce the intended fairness. The problem is subtle because the contract still emits a valid random number and the winner selection logic is unchanged, so the manipulation is not obvious from the outside and may only be noticed by an abnormal spike in total ticket supply or repeated wins by the same address. To remediate, the mint function should be either removed or restricted so that only the ticket‑manager contract can create tickets through the defined purchase flow, and any privileged role that can mint should be excluded from participating in active raffles. Additional checks that enforce the maximum supply and per‑address limits at the moment of winner selection would also restore the intended invariant and prevent the admin from unilaterally affecting raffle odds.

title: Admin can prevent raffle winner from claiming prize
description:
By whitelisting their address and sending a WINNER_DRAWN CCIP message to PrizeManager, Admin can steal the raffle prize, which breaks the invariant from README:  
Winnables admins cannot do anything to prevent a winner from withdrawing their prize  
In WinnablesPrizeManager, Admin can add/remove any address as CCIP counterpart at any time.  

Internal pre-conditions  
A raffle is able to reach REQUESTED stage (enough tickets were sold).  
Attack Path  
1. Admin sends NFT (or token/ETH) to PrizeManager.  
2. Admin calls PrizeManager#lockNFT.  
3. Admin calls TicketManager#createRaffle.  
4. Raffle (ticket sale) ends successfully.  
5. drawWinner is called.  
6. Admin adds himself as PrizeManager's CCIP counterpart and sends WINNER_DRAWN CCIP message with his own address as winner to PrizeManager; Admin removes TicketManager from PrizeManager's CCIP counterparts.  
7. Chainlink VRF request from step 5 is fulfilled.  
8. TicketManager#propagate is called, which propagates Alice as the winner of the raffle, but CCIP message reverts on the destination chain with UnauthorizedCCIPSender().  
9. Admin claims reward from PrizeManager.  
Admin steals the raffle reward.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an access‑control flaw that allows the contract administrator to intervene in the cross‑chain communication path used to deliver raffle winnings, effectively preventing the legitimate winner from claiming the prize and enabling the admin to claim it instead. The root cause is that the PrizeManager contract exposes privileged functions that let an admin add or remove any address from the list of CCIP counterparts at any time, and the contract trusts the sender of a WINNER_DRAWN CCIP message without verifying that the counterpart list remained unchanged after a raffle has been created. When a raffle reaches the REQUESTED stage and the ticket sale ends, the system draws a winner and expects a CCIP message from the pre‑registered counterpart to forward the winner’s address to the TicketManager. An attacker who is also the admin can first lock an NFT or token in the PrizeManager, then create a raffle, let the ticket sale finish, and after the winner is drawn add their own address as the CCIP counterpart while simultaneously removing the legitimate TicketManager from the counterpart list. When the Chainlink VRF request is fulfilled, the TicketManager propagates the real winner (for example Alice) but the CCIP call on the destination chain reverts with an UnauthorizedCCIPSender error because the sender is no longer recognised. The admin can then call the claim function on PrizeManager and withdraw the prize that should have gone to the winner. This breaks the invariant stated in the README that “Winnables admins cannot do anything to prevent a winner from withdrawing their prize”. The impact is that participants who win a raffle receive no reward, their balances remain unchanged, and the admin can steal the funds, compromising the fairness of the protocol. The condition under which the bug manifests is any raffle that reaches the winner‑draw stage while the admin modifies the CCIP counterpart list before the cross‑chain message is processed. The affected parties are the raffle participants, especially the declared winner, and any users relying on the protocol’s promise of unbiased prize distribution. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the privileged admin functions and the flow of CCIP messages, noting that the counterpart list is mutable and not locked during an active raffle. It can be hard to notice because the failure appears as a generic CCIP sender authorization error, which may be attributed to network issues rather than malicious admin behavior. To remediate, the contract should prevent admins from adding or removing CCIP counterparts while a raffle is active, or it should lock the counterpart list at raffle creation and enforce that only the originally registered counterpart can send winner messages. Alternatively, the contract could verify the integrity of the winner‑drawn message against an immutable source or require multi‑party approval before changing trusted addresses, thereby preserving the business logic that winners must be able to claim their prize without interference.

title: Users buying too many tickets will DoS them
description:
WinnablesTicket stores nft ownership by setting the first minted nft id ownership to the user minting and all the next minted nfts remain as 0. This means it always costs the same to mint, but the ownerOf() function becomes much more expensive, to the point where it may cause OOG errors. In this case, the user is able to buy tickets via WinnablesTicketManager::buyTickets(), the draw is made in WinnablesTicketManager::drawWinner() and the chainlink request is fulfilled with the winner in WinnablesTicketManager::fulfillRandomWords(). However, in WinnablesTicketManager::propagateWinner(), it reverts due to OOG when calling WinnablesTicket::ownerOf(). In WinnablesTicket:97-99, it may run out of gas if enough tickets were bought.
Internal pre-conditions
1. Admin sets max holdings and max tickets to a number of at least 4000 or simillar.
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. Users buy tickets via WinnablesTicketManager::buyTickets()
2. The draw is made in WinnablesTicketManager::drawWinner()
3. The chainlink request is fulfilled with the winner in WinnablesTicketManager::fulfillRandomWords()
4. In WinnablesTicketManager::propagateWinner(), it reverts due to OOG when calling WinnablesTicket::ownerOf().
DoSed winner and protocol ETH from the raffle.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by an inefficient ownership lookup in the ticket NFT contract. The contract records the owner only for the first minted token and leaves the ownership entry of every subsequent token at the default value 0. Consequently the public ownerOf function cannot read a direct mapping; instead it iterates over a range of token identifiers, checking each entry until it finds a non‑zero owner. This linear scan has a gas cost that grows proportionally with the number of tickets that have been minted. When the admin configures the raffle to allow a large maximum number of holdings or tickets (for example 4000 or more) a single user can purchase that many tickets in one transaction via the manager’s buyTickets function. Later, when the drawWinner function is executed and the Chainlink callback triggers propagateWinner, the manager calls ownerOf with a range that now spans thousands of tokens. The gas required for this loop exceeds the block gas limit, causing the call to revert with an out‑of‑gas error. From the user’s perspective the transaction that should announce the winner fails, the UI may show “winner not found” or simply no prize is transferred, and the protocol’s ETH that should be paid to the winner remains locked in the contract. The impact is that the raffle cannot complete, participants cannot receive their winnings, and the protocol’s reputation is damaged. The issue is discovered during a formal audit and reproduced with a test that consumes about nine million gas, more than the block limit on Avalanche. It is hard to notice because the contract works correctly for small ticket counts; the gas explosion only appears when the ticket count crosses a high threshold, which is not obvious from the code. The root cause is the misuse of a storage pattern that forces a linear search instead of a constant‑time mapping, combined with unchecked admin‑controlled limits. To fix the problem the contract should store a direct mapping from each token ID to its owner (as in the standard ERC‑721 implementation) or otherwise enforce a reasonable cap on the number of tickets a single transaction can mint, ensuring that ownerOf remains a constant‑time operation and cannot be forced into an OOG state.

title: RedStone oracle is vulnerable be-
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the Redstone price oracle returns stale or user‑selected prices because the state variables that hold the USD price of the asset and the USD price of ETH are never refreshed inside the view function that calculates the asset value in ETH. The root cause is that the contract defines an external updatePrice function that fetches fresh data from the Redstone data feed, but this function is never invoked by getValueInEth and is also callable by any address. Moreover, updatePrice deliberately sets the internal priceTimestamp to block.timestamp minus three minutes, which satisfies the stale‑price check (priceTimestamp < block.timestamp - STALE_PRICE_THRESHOLD) as an equality, allowing the stale values to be considered fresh. An attacker can therefore call updatePrice with a price that is up to three minutes old, or simply rely on the existing stale values, and then invoke getValueInEth to obtain an incorrect ETH valuation. By borrowing assets based on the artificially low valuation and later repaying when the true market price has risen, the attacker can return less ETH than was effectively borrowed, creating a profit. The impact is incorrect asset‑to‑ETH conversion, potential under‑collateralisation of loans, and loss of funds for honest users who trust the oracle output. The issue manifests whenever a contract queries the oracle for a price; the user sees a normal UI response but the returned ETH amount may be zero or far from the expected value, leading to failed trades or unexpected balance changes. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the contract source, where the reviewer noticed that updatePrice is not called from any other function and that the priceTimestamp is artificially back‑dated. Because the function is view‑only and does not emit events, the problem can remain hidden until a transaction that depends on the price behaves incorrectly. The vulnerability belongs to the class of stale‑price oracle or unauthenticated price update bugs, where price data is not guaranteed to be fresh and can be supplied by arbitrary callers. To remediate, the contract should either call updatePrice internally before performing the conversion, restrict updatePrice to a trusted oracle signer, or redesign the oracle to pull fresh data on each query and verify timestamps against the actual feed. Ensuring that the price used for calculations reflects the most recent market data restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents users from receiving zero or unexpectedly low ETH amounts.

title: SuperPool fails to correctly de-
poc:
Lets look at the following example:
1. Owner of poolId=1 creates the pool and sets poolCap=2000USDC
2. In SuperPool poolId=1 is added to the contract with poolCapFor[poolId]=1500.
3. Alice deposits 1000 USDC to poolId=1 by calling SuperPool.deposit(). a) Now the poolCapFor[poolId] free space is 500 USDC. b) And poolCap free space for poolId=1 is 1000 USDC.
4. Bob calls directly Pool.deposit() for poolId=1 with 600 USDC, and poolCap free space for poolId=1 is 400USDC.
5. John calls SuperPool.deposit() with 500 USDC and it will try to deposit into poolId=1 because poolCapFor[poolId] free space=500, but poolCap free space=400, the tx will revert for that poolId and will move forward and try to deposit into the next pool even when there is free space for 400 USDC.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical allocation error in the SuperPool contract that prevents deposited assets from being correctly supplied to underlying pools when the real pool capacity is reduced by external deposits. The root cause is that the internal function _supplyToPools uses a mapping called poolCapFor, which stores a capacity value set by the SuperPool owner, to decide how much free space a pool has. It compares the amount of assets already held by the SuperPool in a pool (assetsInPool) against poolCapFor and calculates a supply amount based on the difference. However, the actual free space of the pool is determined by the pool's own cap (poolCap) minus its total assets, which can be changed by direct deposits to the pool that bypass SuperPool. When an external deposit fills the real pool capacity beyond the value stored in poolCapFor, the supply amount computed by SuperPool may exceed the true remaining capacity. The subsequent call to POOL.deposit then reverts. The revert is caught by a try‑catch block, the assets variable is not reduced, and the loop moves on, leaving the original assets idle in the SuperPool contract. This can be exploited by an attacker who deliberately deposits directly to a pool to consume its real capacity, causing later SuperPool deposits to fail partially and leaving user funds stuck without earning yield. The impact is that users see their deposit transaction succeed, receive a Deposit event, but a portion of their assets remains unallocated, resulting in lower expected returns or apparent loss of funds. The issue occurs whenever the pool receives deposits outside of SuperPool after the poolCapFor value has been set, i.e., under mixed‑source deposit scenarios. All depositors, the protocol’s yield calculations, and any role that relies on accurate asset allocation are affected. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the allocation loop and simulated a scenario where a direct pool deposit reduced the real capacity, causing the SuperPool allocation to revert silently. Because the revert is swallowed, the problem is hard to notice; the contract appears to have processed the deposit, yet the assets stay idle. The correct fix is to query the pool’s true cap and total assets (for example via a getPoolCap function) and compute the remaining capacity as poolCap minus total assets, then cap the supply amount to this true free space before calling POOL.deposit. This aligns the source of truth for capacity and prevents silent reverts, ensuring that deposited assets are always forwarded to a pool that has genuine space, or otherwise returned to the depositor.

title: Lack of slippage protection during withdrawal
bug_full: The vulnerability is a lack of slippage protection in the withdrawal and redemption paths of both the Pool and SuperPool contracts. When a user calls withdraw() (or redeem()) the contract converts the requested share amount to assets based on the current totalAssets and totalShares of the pool at the moment the transaction is executed. Because the conversion uses the live pool state and does not enforce a minimum amount out or a maximum share input, an attacker or any external event that reduces the pool’s total assets after the user’s transaction has been signed but before it is mined can change the exchange rate unfavourably. In a typical bad‑debt liquidation the pool’s totalAssets drop, so the same number of shares now represents fewer assets. As a result the user burns more shares than expected or receives fewer assets than anticipated, effectively losing value even though the transaction does not revert. The issue appears only when the pool experiences a reduction in assets while a withdrawal is pending – for example, a liquidation that lowers totalAssets from 2000 to 1500 while a user expects to withdraw 500 assets. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful withdrawal but the received amount is lower than the quoted amount, or the share balance is reduced more than the user calculated. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the withdraw() and redeem() implementations, where the conversion logic was found to lack any slippage guard. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an error; the loss is silent and only visible by comparing expected versus actual balances after the transaction. This class of bug belongs to the “missing slippage protection” or “price‑impact” category common in DeFi protocols that rely on internal accounting ratios. To remediate, the functions should accept a user‑specified minimum amount out (for redeem) or maximum shares to burn (for withdraw) and revert if the actual conversion falls outside these bounds, effectively snapshotting the exchange rate at call time or otherwise protecting against adverse state changes.

title: Liquidators may repay a posi-
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from the protocol’s assumption that each base pool operates with isolated financial risk, while the actual implementation aggregates collateral requirements across all pools that share a single position. A position is considered healthy only if the total value of its recognized collateral exceeds a globally calculated minimum required asset value. This minimum is derived by iterating over every debt pool and every collateral token, multiplying the debt amount by the token weight and dividing by the loan‑to‑value (LTV) setting that each pool has configured for that token. Because the calculation does not allocate collateral to individual pools, the LTV parameters of one pool directly influence the health assessment of a position that also holds debt in other pools. Consequently, a pool owner can change the LTV for an asset in their pool, and that change can cause a position that is otherwise within the risk tolerance of another pool to become unhealthy and subject to liquidation. The exploit can be carried out without any change in the price of the underlying collateral and without the affected pool’s owner modifying its own risk settings. An adversarial pool can deliberately lower its LTV, wait for the timelock, and trigger liquidations in other pools that share the same borrower, thereby seizing collateral and repaying debt from the targeted pool. This reduces the borrow volume and utilization of the victim pool, lowering interest earnings for its depositors and potentially allowing the attacker to capture liquidation incentives. The issue occurs whenever a position holds debt in multiple pools and any of those pools updates its LTV, which is unrestricted and can be done permissionlessly. All participants who open multi‑pool positions—borrowers, depositors, and liquidators—are affected, as borrowers may see unexpected liquidations, depositors may lose expected yield, and liquidators may gain incentives from forced liquidations.
