The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the protocol’s documented isolation guarantees with the actual risk‑engine code and was reproduced with a proof‑of‑concept test that showed a position becoming unhealthy solely due to an LTV change in a different pool. The bug is subtle because the health check appears to consider only the position’s own collateral and debt, masking the hidden cross‑pool dependency, and because the timelock on LTV updates gives a false sense of safety. To remediate, the protocol should compute the required collateral on a per‑pool basis or apportion the position’s collateral proportionally to each pool’s share of the debt when evaluating health, thereby restoring true isolation of risk between base pools. This change aligns the implementation with the documented guarantee that each base pool’s financial activities remain independent, eliminating the ability for one pool’s risk parameters to jeopardize another’s borrowers and depositors.

title: Base pools can get bricked if
description: In case depositors pull their funds out of the pool, due to rounding, there can be TotalDepositAssets>0 while TotalDepositShares==0. This would completely brick the deposit function of the pool and the pool would not be functional anymore. This can lead to attackers being able to disable a pool since the start of it's initialization. in , the asset to share conversion is rounded up. This can allow the subtraction in to reduce the share amount to zero while assets can stay more than zero. This state causes every to lead to zero for deposit assets, hence, bricking the function with the error Pool_ZeroSharesDeposit. Internal pre-conditions 1. No other depositors should be present in the pool 2. At least one accrual should have happened so that totalDepositAssets > totalDepositShares External pre-conditions N/A Attack Path 1. An attacker sees a pool initialization in the mempool 2. Attacker initializes the pool herself so that the other transaction from the victim fails. (in case it is trying to deposit right after initialization) 3. The attacker deposits some amount in the pool right after initialization 4. In the next block, attacker takes all the deposit assets out and leaves only 1 in 5. Now the TotalDepositAssets==1TotalDepositShares==0 holds true 6. The pool is bricked • Since the initialized pools for each address are limited and can be triggered by anyone: poolId = uint256(keccak256(abi.encodePacked(owner, asset, rateModelKey))); Attacker can create all the possible pools for a certain address and brick them all. This stops the target address from creating any more pools. However, new pools can be created from other addresses and be transferred too the victim. This bug can break certain usecases and allow adversaries to target certain users/protocol and launch DoS against them. • No loss of funds happen since this situation only happens if there are 0 depositors in the pool, which means 0 borrowers.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a rounding‑induced state inconsistency in the base pool contract that can leave the pool with a positive total deposit asset balance while the total deposit share counter is zero. The root cause is the asset‑to‑share conversion routine that rounds up when a deposit is made; later, when a withdrawal subtracts shares, the rounding can reduce the share count to zero even though a small amount of assets remains. This violates the invariant that assets and shares should become zero together. An attacker can exploit the condition by initializing a pool for a target address, making a modest deposit, and then withdrawing almost all of the assets so that exactly one unit of the underlying asset stays in the pool while the share balance drops to zero. After this transition the deposit function checks that totalDepositShares is non‑zero and reverts with the error Pool_ZeroSharesDeposit, effectively bricking the pool for any further deposits. Because the pool identifier is deterministic (derived from owner, asset and rate model key), the attacker can pre‑create and brick every possible pool for the victim, causing a denial‑of‑service that prevents the victim from opening new pools under that address. No funds are lost because the state only occurs when there are no remaining depositors; the remaining asset is locked but belongs to no borrower. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a proof‑of‑concept test that logged the pool’s totalDepositAssets and totalDepositShares before and after the exploit. The bug is hard to notice because the pool still reports a non‑zero asset balance, yet any deposit attempt fails with a generic revert, giving the impression of a mysterious “deposit not working” error. To remediate, the protocol should enforce that any state transition that would set assets or shares to zero must also set the counterpart to zero, or adjust the conversion logic to avoid rounding that can produce a zero‑share outcome while leaving assets. In practice this means adding a guard before withdrawals that prevents the share count from dropping to zero unless the asset count is also zero, or using a rounding‑down conversion for withdrawals, thereby preserving the assets‑shares invariant and preventing the pool from becoming unusable. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a deposit transaction that reverts with an unexpected error, the UI shows no change in balance, and the user receives no confirmation that their funds were accepted, contrary to the expectation that a deposit should succeed and increase their share balance.

title: Protocol's interestFees + Inter-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision‑loss bug in the protocol’s interest‑fee accounting that appears when the pool handles assets with fewer than 18 decimals, such as USDT or USDC, and when accrue() is invoked over short time intervals (seconds to a few minutes). The core of the problem lies in the calculation of feeShares: the contract multiplies the accrued interest (interestAccrued) by the protocol fee (interestFee) and divides by 1e18 using mulDiv. Because interestAccrued is derived from the rate model using the raw asset balances, low‑decimal assets produce very small integer values for short periods; the division therefore rounds down to zero. When feeShares is zero, the protocol does not mint any fee tokens for the feeRecipient and does not increase totalDepositShares, meaning the protocol’s fee revenue for that period is permanently lost – the timestamp is updated, so the missing amount cannot be recovered on the next accrue call. This rounding error can be triggered unintentionally by normal low‑value transactions, but it can also be exploited deliberately. An attacker can repeatedly deposit or borrow tiny amounts of a 6‑decimal token in rapid succession, causing each accrue() call to generate zero feeShares and thereby avoiding the protocol’s interest fee. Lenders are especially able to do this without a minimum‑deposit guard, while borrowers can also exploit it if the pool’s minBorrow threshold is low enough. The impact is a gradual erosion of the protocol’s revenue: lenders receive fewer interest shares than expected, borrowers may benefit from reduced fees, and over many compounding periods the loss can become material, especially on chains where transaction costs are low. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditor replaced a mock ERC20 with 6‑decimal precision and observed that after a 45‑second skip the feeShares minted were zero, confirming that the fee calculation had rounded away. The bug is hard to notice because the protocol’s accounting appears to work correctly for 18‑decimal assets and for longer accrual periods; only specific combinations of low‑decimal tokens and short intervals expose the rounding to zero. To remediate, the protocol should normalise all asset amounts to 18‑decimal precision before performing interest and fee calculations, for example by scaling totalBorrowAssets and totalDepositAssets to 18 decimals regardless of the underlying token’s native decimals. This prevents the mulDiv operation from truncating to zero. Adding a minimum deposit amount or a minimum fee threshold can also mitigate intentional abuse. In summary, the flaw is a rounding‑error class of bug in financial smart contracts that arises from mismatched token decimal precision and frequent interest accrual, leading to lost fees and distorted accounting.

title: Attacker Can Manipulate Interest System Multiple Times
bug_full: The vulnerability is an interest‑allocation manipulation in the SuperPool contract. The pool is initialized with a share owned by the canonical dead address (0x000000000000000000000000000000000000dEaD). When the pool accrues interest, the contract calculates a fee portion of the newly accrued assets and converts that fee amount into pool shares using the total asset balance after the fee has been added. Because the dead address already holds a large number of shares from initialization, any fee shares minted are assigned proportionally to existing shares, which includes the dead address. An attacker can exploit this by sending a large amount of assets to the pool before a regular user makes a deposit. The attacker’s deposit inflates the total assets, causing the fee calculation to generate a substantial fee amount. When accrue() is called, the fee shares are minted and, due to the dead address’s pre‑existing share balance, a disproportionate portion of those shares is credited to the dead address. Consequently the dead address receives far more interest than its actual contribution warrants, while legitimate users receive a reduced share of the accrued interest. From a user’s point of view the expected return on their deposit is lower than anticipated; the UI may show a normal share balance but the interest earned per share is diminished, effectively funds disappear from their perspective. The issue occurs only when the fee parameter is non‑zero, interest has accrued, and the pool contains the dead address share from initialization. It was discovered during a security audit by constructing a test where an attacker transfers a large token amount to the pool before a normal user deposits, then triggers accrue and observes that the dead address’s share balance exceeds 40 % of total supply. The bug is subtle because the share‑to‑asset conversion functions appear mathematically correct, and the dead address is a legitimate address in the contract’s state, so the misallocation is not obvious from simple balance checks. The class of bug is an unfair share‑allocation or fee‑distribution flaw caused by including a privileged address in the share pool during fee minting. To remediate, the contract should exclude the dead address from fee‑share calculations or cap the number of shares that can be assigned to it during interest accrual, ensuring that fee shares are minted only for active contributors and that the interest distribution remains proportional to actual deposits.

title: Attacker can inflict losses to other Superpool users during a bad debt liquidation depending on the deposit/withdraw queue order
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the way a SuperPool handles bad‑debt liquidation together with the ability to arbitrarily reorder the internal deposit and withdraw queues. The pool keeps a list of sub‑pools (or “pools”) that receive deposits and a separate list that determines the order in which withdrawals are satisfied. During a bad‑debt liquidation the contract reduces the total amount of deposited assets by the amount of borrowed assets (totalDepositAssets = totalDepositAssets > borrowAssets ? totalDepositAssets - borrowAssets : 0). Because the loss is applied to the pool that is currently at the front of the deposit queue, an attacker who can control the queue order can force the loss onto a pool that does not contain his own funds. By first depositing a large amount into the pool that will be placed at the front of the deposit queue, then reordering the withdraw queue so that his own withdrawal comes from a different pool, the attacker can withdraw his fresh deposit without suffering any reduction while the other depositors in the affected pool absorb the full loss. The attack scenario proceeds as follows: (1) the attacker deposits assets into the SuperPool; (2) the attacker calls the onlyOwner function reorderDepositQueue to move the pool that now holds his deposit to the front of the deposit order; (3) a bad‑debt liquidation event occurs, causing the front‑most pool’s assets to be reduced by the borrowed amount; (4) the attacker calls reorderWithdrawQueue to prioritize withdrawals from a different pool; (5) the attacker withdraws his previously deposited assets, which were not reduced by the liquidation, while the other users see their balances shrink or become zero. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a sudden drop in the value of their deposited shares, a missing refund, or a balance that no longer matches the expected amount after a liquidation event. The impact is that honest depositors lose value that should have been shared proportionally across the pool, breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol and potentially eroding trust. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the rebalanceBadDebt function together with the queue‑reordering functions and noticed that the queue manipulation could change which pool bears the loss. It is hard to notice because the reduction in totalDepositAssets looks like a normal liquidation loss, while the underlying cause – the attacker’s control over queue ordering – is not visible on‑chain without deep inspection. To remediate the problem the protocol should either remove the ability for anyone (including the owner) to arbitrarily reorder the queues, or at least lock the queue order during any liquidation process. A more robust fix is to calculate loss distribution based on each depositor’s share of the total pool rather than on queue position, ensuring that no single participant can shift the loss onto others. Monitoring for bad‑debt events and limiting queue manipulation are also recommended as mitigations.

title: ChainlinkOracle doesn't validate for minAnswer/maxAnswer
bug_full: An analysis of the ChainlinkOracle implementation reveals that the contract retrieves a price from a Chainlink aggregator but does not enforce the minAnswer and maxAnswer bounds that many aggregators expose. The function _getPriceWithSanityChecks checks only that the price is positive and that the timestamp is recent, then returns the raw price. Because the contract never compares the returned value with the oracle’s configured minimum and maximum limits, a feed that is allowed to report values outside its intended range can supply an arbitrarily high or low price during abnormal market conditions such as a flash crash. An attacker can exploit this omission by depositing an asset when the oracle temporarily reports an inflated price, borrowing against the over‑valued collateral, and then allowing the price to revert or crash. The protocol will continue to value the collateral using the out‑of‑range price, causing lenders or other counterparties to suffer losses when the loan is liquidated or repaid at the true market price. The vulnerability manifests whenever a Chainlink feed that defines minAnswer/maxAnswer is used on a chain where the oracle contract does not perform the corresponding checks – for example the BNB/USD and ETH/USD feeds on BSC that still expose these limits. Users of the protocol see the expected UI behaviour (they can borrow against their deposit) but the underlying accounting is wrong: the protocol believes the collateral is worth more than it actually is, leading to situations where a borrower receives funds while the protocol’s balance appears unchanged or even negative. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the oracle’s public interface with the contract’s validation logic. It can be difficult to notice because the price value is still positive and the timestamp passes the freshness test, so standard monitoring that looks only for stale or negative prices will not flag the problem. The recommended mitigation is to read the minAnswer and maxAnswer from the aggregator and reject any price that falls outside this interval, or to trigger a circuit‑breaker that pauses borrowing when the price deviates beyond the allowed bounds. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of missing sanity checks on external data sources, which can lead to incorrect financial calculations, over‑valuation of assets, and ultimately loss of funds.

title: Setting minDebt and minBorrow to low values can cause protocol to accrue bad debt as liquidators won't find enough incentive in clearing the low debt and also depending on the price, users may be able to borrow dust without providing collateral
description:
Setting minDebt and minBorrow to low values can cause protocol to accrue bad debt as liquidators won't find enough incentive in clearing the low debt and also depending on the price, users may be able to borrow dust without providing collateral.
minDebt and minBorrow are supposed to be settable from 0.
link
Min Debt = from 0 to 0.05 ETH = from 0 to 50000000000000000
Min Borrow = from 0 to 0.05 ETH = from 0 to 50000000000000000
Setting these to low values will allow positions to be created with low debts and liquidations won't happen on small positions due to it not generating enough profit to cover the costs of the liquidator. This will cause the protocol to accrue bad debt. Also if both are set to dust, the roundings will become significant and allows one to borrow dust amounts without proper collateral. Eg, if both are set to 0 and the price of assets is less than that of eth, the borrowing 1 wei of the assets will require no collateral as the value in eth will be rounded to 0.
Protocol can accrue bad debt leading to depositors loosing their assets in case the values are set low.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from allowing the protocol parameters minDebt and minBorrow to be set to extremely low values, including zero. These parameters define the smallest permissible debt and borrow amounts for a position. When they are configured below a safe threshold, two related problems appear. First, the rounding logic used to convert asset values to the native token (ETH) can reduce a tiny debt to zero, meaning a borrower can request a dust amount such as 1 wei of an asset without providing any collateral because the calculated collateral requirement rounds down to zero. Second, liquidators receive profit only from the difference between the collateral value and the debt value. For very small debts the profit is insufficient to cover the gas costs and any required incentive, so liquidators have no economic reason to trigger liquidation. As a result, positions with dust debt can remain under‑collateralised and eventually default, causing the protocol to record bad debt. The impact is that the protocol’s asset pool is slowly eroded; depositors may see their balances shrink or even disappear because the system cannot recover the unpaid dust amounts. This condition manifests whenever governance or an upgrade lowers minDebt or minBorrow to values that are comparable to the smallest unit of the token, especially when the price of the borrowed asset is lower than ETH, amplifying rounding to zero. The affected parties include borrowers who can exploit the loophole, liquidators who are disincentivised, and ultimately the depositors and the protocol itself. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the economic incentive model and the handling of edge‑case values. It is difficult to notice because the amounts involved are tiny and may appear harmless, yet the cumulative effect can be significant. The bug belongs to the class of dust‑borrowing or rounding‑incentive mismatches, where economic parameters allow under‑collateralised positions to persist. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a non‑zero lower bound on minDebt and minBorrow that is high enough to keep rounding errors negligible and to guarantee that any liquidation yields a profit that exceeds the liquidator’s cost. Additional safeguards such as minimum collateral requirements independent of rounding and checks that prevent creation of positions with debt below a safe threshold would close the attack surface.

title: User's can create non-liquidateable positions by leveraging rebalanceBadDebt to decrease share price
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the rebalanceBadDebt routine, which is intended to adjust the pool’s accounting after a borrower falls into bad debt. The function subtracts the borrowed asset amount from the pool’s totalDepositAssets while leaving totalDepositShares unchanged. This breaks the fundamental invariant that the ratio of assets to shares reflects the true value of each share. By artificially deflating the asset side, the price of a share drops dramatically. When a user subsequently deposits assets, the contract mints shares based on the new, much lower share price, resulting in an explosion of the total share count. An attacker can repeat this cycle – borrowing almost all assets to trigger bad debt, invoking rebalanceBadDebt to shrink the asset pool, then depositing a large amount to receive an enormous number of shares – until the total share counter approaches the maximum uint256 value. Once the share total is near the overflow boundary, any later operation that adds fee shares or calculates interest can cause an arithmetic overflow, causing core view functions such as getBorrowsOf and isPositionHealthy to revert. Because these health‑check functions revert, the protocol is unable to determine that the position is under‑collateralised, and liquidation logic cannot be executed. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are striking: after a deposit the user receives an unexpectedly huge amount of pool tokens, later attempts to query borrow information or trigger liquidation fail with a revert, and the protocol appears to “lose” funds because bad debt cannot be recovered. The issue affects any participant who can create a position that enters bad debt, but the primary victim is the protocol and honest lenders whose deposits become exposed to unrecoverable loss. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that rebalanceBadDebt reduces deposit assets without a corresponding reduction in deposit shares, a pattern that enables share‑price manipulation and eventual overflow. The problem is subtle because the function’s name suggests a benign rebalancing operation, and the overflow only manifests after many iterations, making it easy to miss in standard testing. To remediate the issue the contract must preserve the assets‑to‑shares invariant: either adjust both sides proportionally when rebalancing, cap the total share supply, or add explicit checks that prevent the share price from falling below a safe threshold and that guard against arithmetic overflow in fee and interest calculations. In essence, the bug is an accounting invariant violation that enables share price manipulation leading to integer overflow and un‑liquidatable positions, breaking the core economic guarantees of the lending protocol.

title: Super pool uses ERC20.approve in initialization and reallocate, some tokens don't return a value on approve
description:
Super pools that get created on a specific asset then leverage its positions and deposit them in the ”main” pools. Super pools get created in SuperPoolFactory::deploySuperPool, where some initial amount is sent from the user, and then deposited in the deployed super pool. When the assets are sent from the user, the factory approves the deployed.
2024-08-sentiment-v2/blob/main/protocol-v2/src/SuperPoolFactory.sol#L73:
```solidity
IERC20(asset).approve(address(superPool), initialDepositAmt);
```
And the ”default” ERC20 behavior expects the approve function to return a boolean, however, some ERC20s on some chains don't return a value. The most popular example is USDT on the main net, and as the docs mention it should be compatible on any EVM chain and will support USDT:
Q: On what chains are the smart contracts going to be deployed? Any EVM-compatbile network
Q: If you are integrating tokens, are you allowing only whitelisted tokens to work with the codebase or any complying with the standard? Are they assumed to have certain properties, e.g. be non-reentrant? Are there any types of weird tokens you want to integrate? Tokens are whitelisted, only tokens with valid oracles can be used to create Base Pools. Protocol governance will ensure that oracles are only set for standard ERC-20 tokens (plus USDC/USDT)
Another occurrence of this is SuperPool::reallocate, here.
This causes Super pool to never work on these chains/tokens.
Some known tokens don't return a value on approvals, more info here, an example of this is USDT, which is mentioned that the protocol will use it.
Standard ERC20s return a boolean on approval, https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/oz-contracts/blob/master/contracts/token/ERC20/IERC20.sol#L67.
USDT on the main net doesn't return a value, https://etherscan.io/token/0xdac17f958d2ee523a2206206994597c13d831ec7#code.
Super pools can never be created and used for assets that don't return a value on approval, an example of this is USDT on Ethereum main net.
bug_full: SuperPoolFactory and SuperPool contracts call IERC20(asset).approve(...) assuming the ERC20 approve function returns a boolean as defined in the standard interface. Some widely used tokens, most notably USDT, implement approve as a non‑returning function. When the Solidity compiler generates a call that expects a 32‑byte return value, the EVM returns an empty byte array. Decoding this empty data as a bool causes the call to revert, so the approval transaction fails. Because the factory uses this approval step during the initial deposit and the reallocate function repeats the same call, any super pool that is created for a token without a return value cannot be initialized or rebalanced. From a user perspective the transaction reverts, no super pool appears, and the deposited tokens remain in the user's wallet while gas is spent, leading to the impression that funds disappear or the pool never works. The issue is triggered only when the asset token deviates from the ERC20 specification, i.e., when its approve function does not return a bool. It affects any user or liquidity provider who tries to create a super pool with such a token, and it also limits the protocol’s ability to support popular stablecoins like USDT across all EVM‑compatible chains. The problem was discovered during a security audit when a mock USDT contract that omits the return value caused the deploySuperPool call to revert. The bug is hard to notice because most tokens follow the standard and the missing return does not produce a compile‑time error; it only manifests at runtime. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “non‑standard ERC20 token handling” or “approve return‑value mismatch”. The recommended fix is to replace direct calls to approve with OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20.safeApprove (or an equivalent low‑level call that checks success without relying on a return value), ensuring compatibility with tokens that do not return a boolean. By using safeApprove, the contract will treat a missing return as success, allowing super pools to be created and reallocated for all whitelisted tokens, preserving user funds and protocol functionality.

title: Liquidation fee is incorrectly calculated
description:
Incorrect liquidation fee calculation makes liquidations unprofitable, leading to insolvency.
During PositionManager.liquidate() , two things happen:
1. An amount x of the position’s collateral is paid to the liquidator (link)
2. The liquidator pays off the debt of the position (link)
During step 1, the liquidation fee is effectively calculated as liquidationFee.mulDiv(x,1e18)
This is incorrect- the correct way would be to take the liquidation fee from the profit of the liquidator, rather than from the entire amount x
Due to this inaccuracy, a large majority of liquidations will be unprofitable:
Example scenario
Consider a situation where liquidation fee is 30% (as stated in the contest README)
Say LTV = 90%, Debt value = $90, Collateral value drops from $100 to $98
Now, since the position LTV (90/98) is greater than the set LTV (90/100), the position is liquidatable
A liquidator aims to pay off the debt and receive the $98 worth of collateral, effectively buying the collateral at a discount of ~8%
However, They will only receive 70% of the $98 (due to the 30% liquidation fee), so they can only receive $68.6
This is extremely unprofitable since they have to pay off $90 worth of debt, and only receive $68.6 as a reward.
The correct approach to calculating fee would be the following:
1. Calculate liquidator profit = Reward - Cost = $98 - $90 = $8
2. Calculate liquidator fee = feePercentage*profit = 30% of $8 = $2.4
This ensures that liquidations are still incentivised.
Internal pre-conditions
External pre-conditions
Attack Path
Liquidations are unprofitable due to liquidation fee being calculated incorrectly.
This leads to bad debt and insolvency since there is no incentive to liquidate.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect economic calculation of the liquidation fee in the PositionManager.liquidate() routine. Instead of charging the fee on the net profit that a liquidator earns from closing an under‑collateralised position, the contract applies the fee to the entire amount of collateral transferred (x) by using the expression liquidationFee.mulDiv(x,1e18). This mis‑interpretation of the fee semantics means that the liquidator is charged a percentage of the full collateral value rather than a percentage of the difference between the collateral received and the debt repaid. The root cause is a flawed formula that does not subtract the debt before applying the fee, effectively turning a fee that should be a small slice of profit into a large slice of the total collateral. When a liquidation is triggered – for example, when the loan‑to‑value (LTV) of a position exceeds the protocol‑defined limit – the liquidator pays off the outstanding debt and expects to receive the collateral minus a modest fee. Because the fee is taken from the whole collateral amount, the liquidator often ends up receiving far less than the debt they have paid, making the operation unprofitable. In a typical scenario with a 30 % fee, a position with $90 debt and $98 collateral would yield only 70 % of $98 (≈$68.6) after the fee, while the liquidator must still cover the $90 debt, resulting in a loss of more than $20. This economic loss discourages liquidators from performing needed liquidations, allowing under‑collateralised positions to persist and eventually generating bad debt that can render the protocol insolvent. The issue manifests as liquidators receiving unexpectedly low or even zero rewards, users seeing liquidations that do not improve their position, and the protocol’s accounting showing growing deficits. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the liquidation flow and compared the fee calculation against the documented economic model. The problem is subtle because the transaction still succeeds and emits the expected events, so a casual observer may not notice the negative profit. To remediate, the fee should be calculated on the liquidator’s profit: first compute profit = collateralValue – debt, then apply the fee percentage to that profit, and finally subtract the fee from the profit before transferring the remainder to the liquidator. This adjustment restores the intended incentive structure, ensuring liquidations remain economically viable and protecting the protocol from insolvency.

title: Griefer can DOS the SuperPool by frontrunning creation and donating to predictable address
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises from the predictability of the address of a SuperPool contract created by the SuperPoolFactory using the CREATE opcode. The factory requires the caller to deposit a minimum amount of assets and immediately mint at least 1000 shares, which are then burned to a dead address. The number of shares minted is calculated by a conversion function that divides the deposited assets by the current total assets of the pool (plus one) and multiplies by the total supply (plus one). Because the address of the contract to be deployed can be computed in advance, an attacker can front‑run the creation transaction, send a small amount of the chosen asset to that future address, and thereby increase the pool’s total assets before the legitimate user’s deposit is processed. When the user’s deposit is later executed, the inflated total assets cause the conversion formula to return zero or far fewer shares than required, causing the factory’s check for a minimum of 1000 shares to revert. The user sees a transaction revert with an error indicating too few initial shares, and the expected refund or pool creation never occurs, effectively making the pool impossible to create without supplying a much larger amount of assets. This attack can be performed by anyone who can calculate the future address, which is trivial given the known factory address and its nonce, and it only requires a tiny token transfer, making it inexpensive. The impact is that new SuperPools cannot be launched, preventing users from accessing the intended functionality and potentially stalling the protocol’s growth. The issue affects pool creators, token holders, and the protocol itself. It was discovered during an audit through a proof‑of‑concept test that deliberately transferred tokens to the predicted address before calling deploySuperPool. The problem is subtle because the address appears uninitialized and a small token transfer seems harmless, so the failure manifests only when the minimum deposit is attempted. To remediate, the factory should not rely on minting dead shares from an actual deposit; instead it can hard‑code a constant offset in the totalAssets and totalSupply queries or adjust the conversion logic to ignore any pre‑existing balance, or use a deployment method that yields an unpredictable address such as CREATE2 with a random salt. By removing the dependency on a clean initial balance, the denial‑of‑service vector is eliminated.

title: LTV of 98% would be extremely dangerous as it doesn't take into account oracle deviation
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the maximum loan‑to‑value (LTV) parameter that a pool can set to 98 percent while ignoring the possible deviation of the price oracles used for collateral valuation. The root cause is that the protocol’s risk engine assumes the oracle price to be exact and does not add a safety margin for the known deviation range, which can be between 0.25 percent and 2 percent for each asset. When a borrower supplies an asset whose reported price is slightly lower than its true market price and simultaneously borrows an asset whose reported price is slightly higher, the combined oracle deviations are added to the nominal LTV. Consequently the effective LTV becomes LTV + oracle1deviation + oracle2deviation, which can exceed 100 percent. This situation can be exploited by depositing a stablecoin such as USDC, whose oracle may under‑report its value by up to 1 percent, and borrowing another stablecoin such as USDT, whose oracle may over‑report by a similar amount. In the worst case the pool appears to have a 98 percent LTV on‑chain, but the real economic exposure is 100 percent or more, allowing the borrower to extract the entire pool value without providing sufficient collateral. The impact is severe: lenders may lose their funds because borrowers are not incentivised to repay, liquidators receive no profit and may even incur a loss when the price normalises, and the protocol can accrue bad debt or suffer a denial‑of‑service condition as the pool becomes fully drained. The condition occurs whenever the oracle deviation for the two assets involved reaches the upper bound of its range and the pool’s max LTV is set at the high end of the allowed interval. All participants – borrowers, lenders, liquidators and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the risk engine code and the accompanying README, where the stated LTV range (10 percent to 98 percent) was found to be inconsistent with the documented oracle deviation values. The problem is subtle because the on‑chain LTV value looks within the permitted range, yet the hidden deviation pushes the effective exposure over the safety threshold, making it easy to overlook in routine testing. To remediate the flaw, the protocol should enforce a lower maximum LTV, incorporate a conservative buffer that accounts for the worst‑case oracle deviation, or redesign the LTV calculation to include the deviation margin explicitly. By doing so the effective LTV will remain safely below 100 percent even in the presence of oracle error, preserving lender capital and ensuring that liquidators retain a viable incentive.

title: The SuperPool vault is not strictly ERC4626 compliant
bug_full: The SuperPool vault advertises strict ERC4626 compliance but its convertToShares and convertToAssets view functions incorporate pending fee accruals before performing the conversion. According to the ERC4626 specification, the convertTo functions must provide a rough estimate of shares or assets and must not be inclusive of any fees that are charged against the vault’s assets. By calling an internal simulateAccrue routine that adds newly accrued fee shares and adjusts the total assets, the contract returns values that already reflect fees, violating the standard’s requirement that these functions be fee‑agnostic. This discrepancy can be exploited by users or front‑end applications that rely on the convertTo outputs to display expected returns or to calculate slippage. Because the functions over‑state the amount of shares received for a given asset deposit (or under‑state assets redeemable for a given share amount), a user may be led to believe they will receive more value than is actually obtainable after fees are applied, resulting in unexpected loss of assets or reduced returns. The issue manifests whenever a caller invokes convertToShares or convertToAssets, which are typically used by UI components, price oracles, and other contracts to estimate conversion rates. All participants that trust the advertised ERC4626 behavior—depositors, withdrawers, and integrators—are affected. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that cross‑checked the contract’s README claim of strict compliance against the ERC4626 normative text and observed the inclusion of fee calculations in the preview functions. The problem is subtle because the functions are view‑only and do not revert, so the contract appears to operate normally, yet the returned numbers are misleading. To remediate, the convertTo functions should be rewritten to call the base totalAssets and totalSupply values directly, without invoking any fee‑accrual simulation, thereby aligning with the ERC4626 requirement that preview calculations exclude fees. This adjustment restores accurate, fee‑agnostic estimates and ensures that the vault’s behavior matches the expectations of ERC4626‑compliant applications.

title: The RedstoneCoreOracle has a constant STALE_PRICE_THRESHOLD for all tokens
description:
Different tokens have different STALE_PRICE_THRESHOLD. The protocol uses a constant STALE_PRICE_THRESHOLD=3600 for all tokens in the RedstoneCoreOracle.
The issue arises when the token actually has a STALE_PRICE_THRESHOLD < 3600. Here are some tokens whose redstone priceFeed has a STALE_PRICE_THRESHOLD < 3600 (1 hour):
1. TRX/USD 10 minutes
2. BNB/USD 1 minute
Using a constant STALE_PRICE_THRESHOLD=3600, rather than setting one for each token.
Internal pre-conditions
External pre-conditions
Token has a threshold < 3600
Attack Path
Stale prices.
It will lead to unfair liquidations due to stale price valuation of collateral AND/OR a position not being liquidated due to stale price valuation of collateral.
It will also lead to borrowing a wrong amount due to stale price valuation of collateral.
bug_full: During the audit it was observed that the RedstoneCoreOracle contract stores a single constant STALE_PRICE_THRESHOLD set to 3600 seconds and applies it to every supported token. Different tokens published by Redstone have their own freshness requirements; for example the TRX/USD feed is considered stale after 10 minutes and the BNB/USD feed after 1 minute. Because the oracle ignores these token‑specific limits, a price that is older than the token’s real threshold but younger than 3600 seconds is still accepted as valid. This mismatch can be triggered whenever a token with a lower threshold does not receive an update within its short window. An attacker or simply a network delay can cause the feed to become stale, after which the protocol continues to use the outdated price for collateral valuation. The stale price may overstate or understate the value of the collateral, leading to two opposite failure modes: (1) a borrower may be liquidated while the true market price would keep the position healthy, and (2) a severely under‑collateralised position may escape liquidation because the oracle refuses to use the stale price. Both outcomes distort borrowing limits, cause users to receive or lose funds unexpectedly, and break the accounting assumptions that the protocol relies on for safe lending. The issue is subtle because the UI typically shows only the timestamp of the last price update, which appears recent relative to the 3600‑second window, so users do not see that the feed is already stale for that particular asset. The vulnerability was discovered by comparing the documented STALE_PRICE_THRESHOLD values of individual Redstone feeds with the hard‑coded constant in the oracle code. It belongs to the class of oracle freshness misconfiguration bugs, where a generic parameter is applied uniformly despite heterogeneous requirements. To remediate the problem the contract should store a separate freshness threshold for each token, similar to the design used by Chainlink oracles, and enforce the token‑specific limit when deciding whether a price is stale. Updating the contract to reference per‑token thresholds will prevent stale prices from being used, restore correct liquidation logic, and ensure that borrowing calculations reflect the true market value of collateral.

title: First depositor could DoS the pool
description:
Currently, when adding liquidity to a pool, the way LP tokens are calculated is the following:
1. If LP total supply is 0, mint LP tokens equivalent the mint value
2. If LP total supply is not 0, mint LP tokens equivalent to mintValue * lpSupply / poolValue

However, this opens up a problem where the first user can deposit a dust amount in the pool which has a value of just 1 wei and if the price before the next user deposits, the pool value will round down to 0. Then any subsequent attempts to add liquidity will fail, due to division by 0.

Unless the price goes back up, the pool will be DoS'd.
bug_full: An attacker can render a liquidity pool unusable by exploiting the way LP tokens are minted during the first deposit. The contract calculates newly minted LP tokens as mintValue * totalSupply / poolValue when the pool already has liquidity. Because Solidity uses integer division, if the pool value becomes less than one wei after a tiny initial deposit and a subsequent price change, the division rounds down to zero. When a later user tries to add liquidity, the formula attempts to divide by a pool value of zero, causing a revert due to division‑by‑zero. This situation can be triggered by the first depositor intentionally adding a dust amount (e.g., 1 wei) and then waiting for the market price to move such that the total value of the pool, expressed in the accounting token, drops to zero after rounding. The immediate symptom for a legitimate liquidity provider is a failed transaction with a “division by zero” error and no LP tokens received, even though the UI indicates that the add‑liquidity operation should succeed. The protocol loses the ability to accept new liquidity, effectively a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition, and any funds already in the pool become inaccessible for further growth. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the LP‑minting logic, where the special‑case handling for a zero total supply was found to ignore the possibility of a zero pool value after the first deposit. The bug is subtle because the contract works correctly for normal deposit sizes; only an extreme edge case involving rounding to zero triggers the failure, making it easy to overlook in testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “initial liquidity rounding/zero‑division” bugs, where arithmetic assumptions break down when the pool’s accounting balance can become zero. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum initial liquidity amount, add a guard that prevents division when poolValue is zero, or redesign the minting formula to handle a zero‑value pool safely (for example, by using a fixed‑point scaling factor or by requiring a non‑zero pool value before minting additional LP tokens).

title: Whale LP providers can open positions on both sides to force users into high fees
description:
LP fees within the protocol are based on utilization percentage of the total funds in the pool. The problem is that this could easily be abused by LP providers in the following way.
Consider a pool where the majority of the liquidity is provided by a single user.
1. Users have opened positions at a relatively low utilization ratio
2. The whale LP provider opens same size positions in both directions at 1 leverage.
3. This increases everyone's fees. Given that the LP provider holds majority of the liquidity, most of the new fees will go towards them, making them a profit.

As long as the whale can maintain majority of the liquidity provided, attack remains profitable. If at any point they can no longer afford maintaining majority, they can simply close their positions without taking a loss, so this is basically risk-free.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic manipulation flaw in the fee‑calculation mechanism of a perpetual DEX that bases liquidity‑provider (LP) fees on the utilization percentage of the total pool funds. The root cause is that utilization is defined as the ratio of capital locked in open positions to the total liquidity, without any safeguard against a single LP artificially inflating that ratio. A whale LP that controls the majority of the pool can open equal‑sized long and short positions at 1× leverage. By doing so the whale consumes a large portion of the pool’s capital, raising the utilization metric and consequently the fee rate applied to every trader’s position. Because the fee revenue is distributed proportionally to LP shares, the whale—holding most of the shares—captures the additional fees as profit. The attack can be carried out repeatedly: as long as the whale maintains a majority of the liquidity, the elevated utilization persists, and the extra fees continue to accrue to the whale. If the whale’s share drops below the majority threshold, it can simply close the opposing positions without incurring a loss, having already extracted the fee surplus. This results in ordinary users experiencing unexpectedly high trading fees, lower net returns, or even failed transactions when the fee exceeds the user‑specified maximum. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the fee‑logic and identified that utilization‑based fees are directly manipulable by position size. The problem is subtle because the fee increase appears as a normal market condition; the whale’s balanced long/short exposure may look benign, making the manipulation hard to detect from the UI or on‑chain analytics. The flaw belongs to the class of “utilization‑based fee abuse” or “economic manipulation” bugs, where a protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated by a participant who can control the denominator of a fee formula. To remediate, the protocol should redesign the fee model so that fees are not a simple function of instantaneous utilization, for example by using a time‑weighted average utilization, capping fee spikes, or separating fee accrual from LP share ownership. Such changes would prevent a single LP from inflating fees and ensure that fee distribution reflects genuine market activity rather than engineered utilization spikes.

title: User could have impossible to close position if funding fees grow too big
description:
User could have impossible to close position if funding fees grow too big.
In order to prevent positions from becoming impossible to be closed due to funding fees surpassing collateral amount, there's the following code which pays out funding fees on a first-come first-serve basis.
However, this wrongly assumes that the order of action would always be for the side which pays funding fees to close their position before the side which claims the funding fee.
Consider the following scenario:
1. There's an open long (for total collateral of X) and an open short position. Long position pays funding fee to the short position.
2. Eventually the funding fee grows larger than the whole long position (X + Y). it is due liquidation, but due to bot failure is not yet liquidated (which based on
3. A new user opens a new long position, once with X collateral. (total quote collateral is currently 2X)
4. The original long is closed. This does not have an impact on the total quote collateral, as it is increased by the funding_paid which in our case will be counted as exactly as much as the collateral (as in these calculations it cannot surpass it). And it then subtracts that same quote collateral.
5. The original short is closed. funding_received is calculated as X + Y and therefore that's the amount the total quote collateral is reduced by. The new total quote collateral is 2X - (X + Y) = X - Y.
6. Later when the user attempts to close their position it will fail as it will attempt subtracting (X - Y) - X which will underflow.
Marking this as High, as a user could abuse it to create a max leverage position which cannot be closed. Once it is done, because the position cannot be closed it will keep on accruing funding fees which are not actually backed up by collateral, allowing them to double down on the attack.
Loss of funds
bug_full: An underflow vulnerability arises in the funding‑fee settlement logic of the perpetual futures contract. The contract settles funding fees on a first‑come‑first‑serve basis and implicitly assumes that the side that owes the fee will close its position before the side that receives the fee. When the accumulated funding fee for a position grows larger than the total collateral backing that position, the assumption no longer holds. An attacker can trigger this condition by allowing a long position’s funding obligation to exceed its collateral (for example, by delaying liquidation) and then opening a new long with additional collateral. When the original long is closed, the contract credits the funding fee but does not reduce the global quote‑collateral pool because the fee amount is capped at the original collateral. Subsequently, when the short that is owed the fee is closed, the contract deducts the full funding amount (which is larger than the original collateral) from the global quote‑collateral pool. This leaves the pool with a negative effective balance (X‑Y) that is insufficient to cover the new long’s collateral X. When the new long attempts to close, the contract tries to subtract X from a pool that only contains X‑Y, causing an unsigned integer underflow and reverting the transaction. From the user’s perspective the position appears stuck: the UI shows the position as open, but any attempt to close it fails with an error or reverts, and the user sees no funds returned. The impact is that a malicious actor can create a position that cannot be closed, causing perpetual accrual of unfunded funding fees and potentially draining the protocol’s liquidity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the funding‑fee settlement flow, where the auditor noticed that the ordering assumption was not enforced and that the accounting of global quote collateral could become negative. The bug is subtle because the contract’s normal operation (closing positions in the expected order) masks the problem, and the underflow only manifests under a specific sequence of events involving large funding fees and delayed liquidation. The vulnerability belongs to the class of incorrect accounting leading to arithmetic underflow and violates the fundamental business rule that total collateral must always be sufficient to cover all outstanding positions and fees. A proper fix requires redesigning the funding‑fee settlement to ensure that fee payments cannot exceed the available collateral, for example by capping the fee to the remaining pool balance, performing a pre‑check before closing, or by separating fee settlement from position closure so that ordering assumptions are no longer required.

title: Funding fee will be zero because of precision loss
description:
funding fee in some cases will be zero because of precision loss
long_utilization = base_interest / (base_reserve / 100) short_utilization = quote_interest / (quote_reserve / 100)
borrow_long_fee = max_fee * long_utilization [min = 10] borrow_short_fee = max_fee * short_utilization [min = 10]
funding_fee_long = borrow_long_fee * (long_utilization - short_utilization) /
funding_fee_short = borrow_short_fee * (short_utilization - long_utilization) /
let's assume alice open a long position with min collateral[5e6] and leverage 2x when btc/usdt $50,000
long_utilization = 0.0002e8 / (1000e8 / 100) = 2e4 / 1e9 = 0.00002[round down => 0]
short_utilization = 0 / 1e12 /100 = 0
borrowing_long_fee = 100 * (0) = 0 [min fee = 1] ==> 10 borrowing_short_fee = 100 * (0) = 0 [min fee = 1] ==> 10
funding_fee_long = 10 * (0) = 0 funding_fee_short = 10 * 0 = 0
1000 block passed
funding_paid = 5e6 * 1000 * 0 / 1_000_000_000 = 0 borrowing_paid = (5e6) * (1000 * 10) / 1_000_000_000 = 50
** long_utilization and short_utilization are zero until base_reserve / 100 >= base_interest and quote_reserve / 100 >= quote_interest
Internal pre-conditions
pool status: ”base_reserve” : 1000e8 BTC ”quote_reserve” : 1,000,000e6 USDT "collector" : "0xCFb56482D0A6546d17535d09f571F567189e88b3", "symbol" : "WBTCUSDT", "base_token" : "0x03c7054bcb39f7b2e5b2c7acb37583e32d70cfa3", "quote_token" : "0x05d032ac25d322df992303dca074ee7392c117b9", "base_decimals" : 8, "quote_decimals": 6, "blocktime_secs": 3, "parameters" : { "MIN_FEE" : 1, "MAX_FEE" : 100, "PROTOCOL_FEE" : 1000, "LIQUIDATION_FEE" : 2, "MIN_LONG_COLLATERAL" : 5000000, "MAX_LONG_COLLATERAL" : 100000000000, "MIN_SHORT_COLLATERAL" : 10000, "MAX_SHORT_COLLATERAL" : 200000000, "MIN_LONG_LEVERAGE" : 1, "MAX_LONG_LEVERAGE" : 10, "MIN_SHORT_LEVERAGE" : 1, "MAX_SHORT_LEVERAGE" : 10, "LIQUIDATION_THRESHOLD": 5 }, "oracle": { "extractor": "0x3DaF1A3ABF9dd86ee0f7Dd13a256400d01866E04", "feed_id" : "BTC", "decimals" : 8 }
Funding fee always is lower than what it really should be
poc:
Place below test in tests/test_positions.py and run with pytest -k test_precision_loss -s
```solidity
def test_precision_loss(setup, open,VEL, STX, long, positions, pools):
setup()
open(VEL, STX, True, d(5), 10, price=d(50000), sender=long)
chain.mine(1000)
fee = positions.calc_fees(1)
assert fee.funding_paid == 0
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a precision loss in the calculation of the funding fee for perpetual positions. The contract computes long_utilization and short_utilization by dividing the accrued interest by the reserve divided by 100, using integer arithmetic. When the interest amount is smaller than the scaled reserve, the division truncates to zero, so both utilizations become zero. The borrowing fee logic applies a minimum fee after the utilization multiplication, but the funding fee is calculated as borrowing_fee multiplied by the difference between long_utilization and short_utilization. Because the utilizations are zero, the difference is zero and the funding fee collapses to zero even though a non‑zero fee should be accrued over time. This occurs whenever base_reserve divided by 100 is greater than or equal to base_interest and similarly for the quote side, which is the typical state for a healthy pool with modest interest rates. As a result, traders who open positions with small collateral or when the market price is such that interest is low receive no funding fee after any number of blocks. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a funding payment of 0 while borrowing fees are still deducted, violating the expectation that funding fees offset borrowing costs. The protocol therefore loses revenue that should have been collected, and an attacker could repeatedly open and close positions to avoid funding charges, gaining an economic advantage. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when a test case that mines 1000 blocks reported a funding_paid value of 0 despite non‑zero borrowing fees. The bug is subtle because the zero value is a legitimate result of integer truncation and does not trigger a revert, making it easy to overlook in normal operation. The proper fix is to increase the precision of the utilization calculation, for example by scaling the numerator before division or using a fixed‑point library with more decimals, and to enforce a minimum non‑zero utilization or apply the minimum fee logic before the utilization multiplication. In short, the flaw belongs to the class of rounding‑error or precision‑loss bugs in financial smart contracts, where integer division causes fee formulas to under‑charge.

title: Invalid Redstone oracle payload size limit
description:
In api contract, it uses 224 bytes as maximum length for Redstone's oracle payload, but oracle price data and signatures of 3 signers exceeds 225 bytes thus reverting transactions.
In every external function of api contract, it uses 224 bytes as maximum size for Redstone oracle payload.
However, the RedstoneExtractor requires oracle data from at least 3 unique signers, as send token price information like token identifier, price, timestamp, etc and 65 bytes of signature data. Just with basic calculation, the oracle payload size exceeds 224 bytes.
Here's some proof of how Redstone oracle data is used:
• Check one of transactions from here that uses Redstone oracle.
• One of transaction is this one on Avalanche, which has 9571 bytes of data.
• Check this Blocksec Explorer, and it also shows the oracle data of 3 signers are passed.
As shown from the proof above, the payload size of Redstone data is huge, so setting 224 bytes as upperbound reverts transactions.
Protocol does not work because the payload array size limit is too small.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an improperly bounded payload size for Redstone oracle data in the API contract. The contract enforces a hard‑coded maximum of 224 bytes for the oracle payload, but the RedstoneExtractor requires data from at least three distinct signers, each providing token identifier, price, timestamp and a 65‑byte ECDSA signature. The combined size of these fields inevitably exceeds the 224‑byte limit, causing any transaction that supplies a valid Redstone payload to revert. The root cause is the static size check that does not account for the actual structure of Redstone data, leading to a mismatch between expected and real payload length. An attacker or even a legitimate price update can trigger the revert simply by submitting a correctly formatted payload that is larger than the hard‑coded limit, resulting in a denial‑of‑service condition for any function that depends on the oracle. The impact is that price feeds cannot be refreshed, trades, liquidations or any operation that relies on the oracle will fail, and users may see transactions revert with no obvious reason, potentially leaving positions open or funds effectively frozen. This occurs in every external function of the API contract that validates the payload size, so the failure mode is systemic across the protocol. The affected parties are all users of the PerpDEX – traders, liquidity providers and anyone interacting with the contract – because the core business logic (price discovery and settlement) is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor inspected the size constraint and compared it with real transaction data on Avalanche, which showed payloads of several kilobytes (for example a transaction with 9 571 bytes of data). The problem is subtle because the size limit is an internal constant and the revert only happens when the payload exceeds it, which may not be obvious during normal testing with smaller data sets. To remediate, the contract should either remove the arbitrary 224‑byte ceiling, increase it to a value that comfortably accommodates the full Redstone payload (including three signatures), or implement a dynamic check based on the actual calldata size. Aligning the payload validation with the true format of Redstone data restores the intended functionality, prevents unnecessary reverts, and ensures that price updates and downstream financial operations can proceed as designed.

title: Usage of tx.origin to determine user is prone to attacks
description:
Usage of tx.origin to determine the user is prone to attacks
Within core.vy to user on whose behalf it is called is fetched by using tx.origin.
This is dangerous, as any time a user calls/ interacts with an unverified contract, or a contract which can change implementation, they're put under risk, as the contract can make a call to api.vy and act on user's behalf.
Usage of tx.origin would also break compatibility with Account Abstract wallets.
Any time a user calls any contract on the BOB chain, they risk getting their funds lost.
Incompatible with AA wallets.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists ofusing the global variable tx.origin as the identifier of the caller in the core contract. tx.origin returns the original external account that started the transaction, not the immediate caller. This design is insecure because a malicious contract can be placed in the call chain, causing tx.origin to point to a victim’s wallet while the malicious contract executes privileged functions on its behalf. An attacker can lure a user to interact with a seemingly harmless contract, which then forwards a call to the vulnerable core contract. Because the core contract trusts tx.origin, it treats the victim as the authorized user and may transfer assets, update positions, or execute privileged API calls. The impact is that funds can be moved out of the victim’s account, positions can be liquidated, or other state changes can occur without the user’s consent. The issue manifests whenever any user interacts with any contract on the BOB chain that subsequently calls the vulnerable core contract, including when using abstract account wallets that rely on delegated calls; such wallets become incompatible because they do not appear as tx.origin. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the core.vy source where the author noted the use of tx.origin to fetch the user address. The bug is subtle because the contract appears to work correctly when called directly, and the misuse of tx.origin does not raise compiler warnings. From a user perspective the symptom is that after interacting with an unrelated contract, the user may see their balance reduced to zero or unexpected trades executed, without any visible transaction from their address. This violates the fundamental accounting assumption that only the direct caller can authorize asset movement. The vulnerability belongs to the class of origin authentication or tx.origin misuse bugs, where authentication is performed on the transaction origin rather than the immediate caller. The recommended mitigation is to stop using tx.origin and instead pass the caller’s address explicitly, for example via msg.sender supplied from the API layer, ensuring that only the contract that directly invoked the core logic is authorized.

title: Using the same heartbeat for
description:
Chainlink price feeds usually update the price of an asset once it deviates a certain percentage. For example the ETH/USD price feed updates on 0.5% change of price. If there is no change for 1 hour, the price feed updates again - this is called heartbeat: https://data.chain.link/feeds/ethereum/mainnet/eth-usd.
According to the docs, the protocol should be compatible with any EVM-compatible chain. On the other hand, different chains use different heartbeats for the same assets.
Different chains have different heartbeats:
USDT/USD:
• Linea: ~24 hours, https://data.chain.link/feeds/linea/mainnet/usdt-usd
• Polygon: ~27 seconds, https://data.chain.link/feeds/polygon/mainnet/usdt-usd
BNB/USD:
• Ethereum: ~24 hours, https://data.chain.link/feeds/ethereum/mainnet/bnb-usd
• Optimism: ~20 minutes, https://data.chain.link/feeds/optimism/mainnet/bnb-usd
In, the protocol is using the same heartbeat for all assets/chains, which is 30 minutes.
This causes the protocol to regularly revert unexpectedly (DOS).
The same heartbeat is being used for all chains/assets, in PoolGetters::getAssetPrice.
Either constant downtime leading to transactions reverting or insufficient staleness checks leading to the possibility of the old price.
poc:
1. User calls withdraw, to withdraw his collateral (in USDT) from a certain pool on Linea
2. The withdraw function calls other multiple functions leading to GenericLogic::calculateUserAccountData (which gets the price of an asset)
3. The contract calls the Oracle USDT/USD feed on Linea
4. At the moment the heartbeat check for every price feed on every chain is set to 30 minutes
5. The price was not updated for more than 2 hours since the heartbeat for the pair is 24 hours and also not changed 1% in either direction
6. The transaction reverts causing DoS
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of a hard‑coded heartbeat value of 30 minutes that is applied uniformly to every Chainlink price feed regardless of the chain or asset. Chainlink feeds are configured with different maximum intervals between updates (for example USDT/USD on Linea updates roughly every 24 hours, while on Polygon it updates every 27 seconds). The protocol’s PoolGetters::getAssetPrice function checks the timestamp of the latest round against the fixed 30‑minute threshold and reverts if the feed is older. On chains where the legitimate heartbeat is longer than 30 minutes, the price may become stale without any price movement, causing the check to fail and the transaction to revert. Conversely, on chains with very short heartbeats the contract may accept a price that is older than the feed’s intended freshness, exposing the system to outdated pricing data. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the constant heartbeat was observed and cross‑referenced with the documented feed intervals. It is difficult to notice because price feeds usually return a value and the contract does not emit a specific “stale price” event; the failure manifests only as an unexpected revert when no price change occurs for a period longer than the hard‑coded limit. An attacker can exploit the condition by simply waiting until a feed on a given chain has not updated for more than 30 minutes and then triggering any function that reads the price, causing a denial‑of‑service that blocks withdrawals, deposits or other critical actions. Users experience the symptom of transactions reverting with no state change, often seeing their balance remain unchanged or receiving a generic “execution reverted” error. The impact is a medium‑severity service interruption that can freeze user funds and erode confidence in the protocol. The bug affects all participants that rely on price data – borrowers, lenders and the protocol itself – on any chain where the real heartbeat differs from 30 minutes. The proper mitigation is to store or retrieve the specific heartbeat associated with each feed and compare the feed’s updatedAt value against that per‑feed threshold, or to use the feed’s round data to enforce staleness checks that respect the feed’s configured interval. This change aligns the contract’s accounting assumptions with the actual oracle behavior and prevents both unintended reverts and the acceptance of outdated prices.

title: CuratedVaults are prone to in-
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inflation‑type accounting bug in the CuratedVault implementation. The vault uses a SharesMathLib library that defines two constants, VIRTUAL_SHARES and VIRTUAL_ASSETS, which in the reference Morpho implementation are non‑zero to provide a small amount of virtual liquidity that stabilises the share‑to‑asset conversion. In ZeroLend One these constants are set to zero, removing the protective buffer. When an attacker first supplies a small amount of the underlying token to the vault (a donation), the total assets increase while the total share supply remains zero, causing the internal share price to become arbitrarily large. Because the share price is inflated, a subsequent legitimate deposit by a user is rounded down to zero shares – the arithmetic truncates the fractional share amount to zero. The attacker can then front‑run the user’s deposit, receive at least one share for their own assets, and later redeem that share for the combined assets of both the attacker’s donation and the victim’s deposit. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed (the deposit call does not revert) but the returned share balance is zero, the UI shows no new vault balance, and the underlying tokens disappear from the user’s wallet. The impact is a total loss of the victim’s deposited tokens, effectively a 100 % theft of the underlying amount. The condition occurs whenever the vault is instantiated with zero virtual shares/assets and an attacker can execute a donation before any legitimate deposit. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by inspecting the SharesMathLib constants and reproducing the scenario with a Foundry test that logged a supplier receiving zero shares while the attacker obtained a share. The bug is subtle because the deposit function does not revert and the zero‑share result can be mistaken for a normal outcome in a low‑liquidity pool. The proper mitigation is to restore non‑zero virtual share and asset constants (for example 1e6 virtual shares and 1 virtual asset) or otherwise enforce a minimum share price that prevents rounding to zero. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of share‑price inflation or rounding‑error attacks in ERC‑4626 style vaults, where manipulation of the virtual liquidity parameters leads to incorrect accounting and fund loss.

title: Malicious actors can execute
bug_full: The vulnerability is an asset‑share ratio manipulation that occurs when a vault administrator adds or re‑adds a market that already holds a non‑zero balance for the vault. The contract updates the vault's totalAssets value immediately by summing the balances of all markets in the withdraw queue, including the newly added market, and does so without applying any fee or delay. Because share‑to‑asset conversions later use this totalAssets figure, the sudden increase in assets inflates the asset‑per‑share ratio. An attacker can observe the pending acceptCap transaction, deposit assets just before the market addition, and then withdraw the same amount of shares after the addition. The inflated ratio causes the attacker to receive more underlying assets than were originally deposited, effectively extracting value from the vault. Existing vault users suffer a proportional loss that depends on the size of the newly added market’s assets relative to the vault’s prior total assets. The flaw is triggered only when the admin calls acceptCap to add a market and the market has existing funds, conditions that are realistic because markets can be re‑integrated after removal or can receive direct donations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the _setCap logic and the totalAssets view function. It is hard to notice because the market addition appears legitimate and the fee exemption is intended for legitimate scenarios, masking the subtle shift in accounting. From a user perspective the UI may show their share balance unchanged while other users receive unexpectedly large withdrawals, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual payouts. The bug belongs to the class of “instant asset inclusion” or “share‑ratio manipulation” vulnerabilities, where accounting assumptions about constant total assets are violated. To remediate, the contract should avoid immediate inclusion of new market assets; instead it should unlock those assets gradually over a defined period or apply the standard fee mechanism, thereby preventing abrupt changes to the share conversion rate.

title: GenericLogic.sol contract as-
description:
Mixing price feeds decimals when doing the calculation of totalCollateralInBaseCurrency and totalDebtInBaseCurrency will cause an incorrect healthFactor affecting important operations of the protocol such as liquidation, borrow and withdraw. GenericLogic.sol contract assumes all price feeds have the same decimals but is a wrong assumption as is demonstrated in the Root cause section.
acts/core/pool/logic/GenericLogic.sol#L106-L128
GenericLogic.sol:69 calculateUserAccountData calculates the totalCollateralInBaseCurrency and the totalDebtInBaseCurrency doing a sum of all the differents reserve assets as collateral or debt in base currency but the problem is a wrong assumption that all chainlink price feeds has the same decimals. Most USD price feeds has 8 decimals but for example AMPL / USD feed has 18 decimals. So totalCollateralInBaseCurrency and the totalDebtInBaseCurrency will be incorrect because calculateUserAccountData will sum asset prices with different decimals leading to a wrong calculation of the health factor and incorrect function of many protocol operations.
Internal pre-conditions
1. Price feeds for collateral or debt assets in a given position needs to have different decimals.
External pre-conditions
None
Attack Path
Is a wrong assumption proven by example
1. Liquidation: Mixing Price decimals lead to incorrect calculation of the healthFactor that is a result of wrong totalCollateralInBaseCurrency and the totalDebtInBaseCurrency.
2. Borrow: Wrong healthFactor also affects borrowing when doing validations to make sure that the position is not liquiditable.
3. Withdraw: Also uses healthFactor via ValidationLofic::validateHFAndLtv
4. executeUseReserveAsCollateral: Also uses healthFactor via ValidationLofic::validateHFAndLtv
5. Any other operation that uses the health factor.
poc: none
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect assumption in the GenericLogic contract that all Chainlink price feeds provide values with the same number of decimal places. In reality, most USD price feeds use eight decimals while some assets, such as AMPL/USD, use eighteen decimals. The contract aggregates collateral and debt values by converting each asset price directly to a base currency without first normalising the differing decimal precisions. As a result, the calculated totalCollateralInBaseCurrency and totalDebtInBaseCurrency are distorted, which leads to a health factor that does not reflect the true risk of the position. The health factor is used by many protocol operations – liquidation, borrowing, withdrawing, and the function that toggles a reserve as collateral – to decide whether a user’s account is safe. When the health factor is artificially low because of the decimal mismatch, a user may be liquidated despite having sufficient collateral, may be prevented from borrowing additional funds, or may be blocked from withdrawing assets that should be available. Conversely, an artificially high health factor could allow unsafe borrowing, potentially endangering the protocol’s solvency. The issue manifests only when a user’s portfolio contains assets whose price feeds have different decimal settings; it does not appear in simple cases where all assets share the same eight‑decimal feed. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the calculation logic in calculateUserAccountData and identified the hard‑coded assumption about feed precision. The bug is subtle because the health factor may still appear reasonable in the UI, masking the underlying arithmetic error until an operation fails or an unexpected liquidation occurs. To remediate the problem, the contract should either enforce a uniform decimal precision for all price feeds (for example, by rejecting assets with non‑standard decimals) or, more flexibly, retrieve each feed’s decimals via AggregatorV3Interface::decimals and normalise every price to a common scale before performing the aggregation. This ensures that the health factor accurately reflects the true collateralisation of each user’s position, restoring correct behaviour for liquidation, borrowing, withdrawing, and related validation logic.

title: After a User withdraws The interest Rate is not updated accordingly leading to the next user using an inflated index during next deposit before the rate is normalized again Found by A2-security, Bigsam, Obsidian, iamnmt
description:
A bug in Zerolend's withdrawal mechanism causes the interest rate to not be updated when funds are transferred to the treasury during a withdrawal. This failure leads to the next user encountering an inflated interest rate when performing subsequent actions like deposit, withdrawal or borrow before the rate is normalized again. The issue arises because the liquidity in the pool drops due to the funds being transferred to the treasury, but the system fails to update the interest rate to reflect this change.
Examples of update rate before transferring everywhere in the protocol to maintain Rate
acts/core/pool/logic/SupplyLogic.sol#L69-L81
acts/core/pool/logic/SupplyLogic.sol#L125-L146
acts/core/pool/logic/BorrowLogic.sol#L88-L99
acts/core/pool/logic/BorrowLogic.sol#L139-L158
The same process can be observed in Aave v3.
1. https://github.com/aave/aave-v3-core/blob/782f51917056a53a2c228701058a6c3fb233684a/contracts/protocol/libraries/logic/SupplyLogic.sol#L130
2. https://github.com/aave/aave-v3-core/blob/782f51917056a53a2c228701058a6c3fb233684a/contracts/protocol/libraries/logic/SupplyLogic.sol#L65
3. https://github.com/aave/aave-v3-core/blob/782f51917056a53a2c228701058a6c3fb233684a/contracts/protocol/libraries/logic/BorrowLogic.sol#L145-L150
4. https://github.com/aave/aave-v3-core/blob/782f51917056a53a2c228701058a6c3fb233684a/contracts/protocol/libraries/logic/BorrowLogic.sol#L227-L232
Looking at the effect of updating rate
acts/core/pool/logic/ReserveLogic.sol#L134-L182
acts/periphery/ir/DefaultReserveInterestRateStrategy.sol#L98-L131
This rates are used to get the new index
acts/core/pool/logic/ReserveLogic.sol#L225-L227
acts/core/pool/logic/ReserveLogic.sol#L235-L237
Internal pre-conditions
External pre-conditions
Attack Path
