An attacker can front‑run the keeper’s transaction, call placeOrder with the identical orderId and set maxFee to zero (or any lower value). When the keeper finally calls executeOrder, the fee calculation yields zero and the keeper is paid nothing. This occurs only when the protocol permits order overwriting and does not enforce a minimum fee or an immutable maxFee. The affected parties are the keepers who rely on the compensation to offset gas costs and earn revenue; they may see a successful order execution but receive no reward, effectively losing expected income. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the fee handling logic, where the auditor noticed that the maxFee parameter is user‑controlled and can be altered after order creation, a scenario that is not covered by typical unit tests and therefore easy to miss. The bug belongs to the class of mutable‑parameter fee manipulation vulnerabilities, where a business rule (the keeper must be compensated) is broken by allowing a participant to reduce the payable amount after the fact. From a user perspective the UI would show the order being fulfilled, but the keeper’s balance would remain unchanged, contradicting the expectation that a fee is transferred. To remediate the problem the contract should either make maxFee immutable once the order is placed, enforce a lower bound on the fee during execution, or add a minimum‑fee parameter to the executeOrder function so that the keeper cannot be paid less than a predefined amount.

title: MultiInvoker and Manager orders execution can
description:
panprog Summary Perennial contracts rely on the DSU token, which is essentially a wrapper for the USDC token. There are 2 in-scope implementations of DSU wrappers (reserve) which use part of the protocol reserves to deposit into external protocols (AAVE and Compound). Any time the protocol tries to unwrap (redeem) from the reserve (basically convert DSU to USDC), some funds are withdrawn from the AAVE or Compound.
The issue is that both AAVE and Compound allow to withdraw only the difference between the pool's supply and debt. This means that the withdrawal operation might revert in case of 100% utilization (supply ~= debt). This can happen by itself (and has happened in the past during some periods) or be intentionally forced by anyone by temporarily taking out all available AAVE/Compound funds as a debt, and then later repaying it to DOS certain operations to Perennial users.
In particular, all MultiInvoker and Manager withdrawals with unwrap flag set are vulnerable to this DOS. Each MultiInvoker or Manager action charges interfaceFee by withdrawing it from user's market balance and if unwrap flag is set, it's converted to USDC via batcher or reserve (if batcher is not set or empty). Since this conversion to USDC will revert in reserve, entire MultiInvoker or Manager transaction will revert as well. The most impactful operation seems to be the stop loss or take profit orders execution - attacker can monitor the MultiInvoker and Manager limit orders and when the stop loss price is near, execute this attack to delay the execution of these orders until the price becomes much worse, thus users will lose funds due to delay in their orders execution, getting much worse price than what they could get if not for the attack.
Root Cause MultiInvoker charges interface fee in _update:
nnial-v2/packages/perennial-extensions/contracts/MultiInvoker.sol#L241-L242
_chargeFee unwraps DSU if unwrap is set to true:
nnial-v2/packages/perennial-extensions/contracts/MultiInvoker.sol#L310
_unwrap redeems from reserve:
nnial-v2/packages/perennial-extensions/contracts/MultiInvoker.sol#L370
redeem allocates:
tyset-mono/packages/emptyset-reserve/contracts/reserve/ReserveBase.sol#L81
_allocate calls _update to allocate/deallocate to match allocated amount to target amount according to strategy:
tyset-mono/packages/emptyset-reserve/contracts/reserve/ReserveBase.sol#L137
024-08-perennial-v2-update-3/blob/main/emptyset-mono/packages/emptyset-reserve/contracts/reserve/strategy/AaveV3FiatReserve.sol#L66-L67
udit/2024-08-perennial-v2-update-3/blob/main/emptyset-mono/packages/emptyset-reserve/contracts/reserve/strategy/CompoundV3FiatReserve.sol#L61-L62
al-v2-update-3/blob/main/perennial-v2/packages/perennial-order/contracts/Manager.sol#L218
Internal pre-conditions
1. Reserve uses either AAVE or Compound strategy
2. Reserve.allocation is not 0
3. User has created a MultiInvoker or Manager order with interfaceFee.unwrap or interfaceFee2.unwrap set to true.
External pre-conditions Market price is within the order's execution range
Attack Path
1. Attacker empties the batcher if it's set in MultiInvoker and Manager and not empty. Exact steps depend on the batcher implementation which is out of scope, but should be possible according to current implementation (depositing large amount of USDC to batcher, then immediately withdrawing it). Alternatively (if not possible), this should be additional pre-condition (no batcher set or batcher is empty).
2. Attacker deposits some token other than USDC into AAVE/Compound and takes out USDC debt to make AAVE/Compound USDC balance almost 0. Alternatively, this can happen by itself (and has happened in the past), in such case this is additional external pre-condition.
3. Attacker waits for some time, taking out more debt if needed to keep AAVE/Compound USDC balance close to 0.
4. All this time MultiInvoker and Manager orders execution is blocked
5. Once the price is far enough from where it was, attacker repays the debt and withdraws amount supplied to AAVE/Compound
• User order is executed at a much worse price
• Or position is liquidated (in case the order was a stop-loss and price moved beyound liquidation price)
• Or user order is not executed (in case the order is take profit and the price had moved away from the execution range)
In all 3 cases user losses funds.
This attack can be intentionally caused by attacker, or can happen by itself (but much less probable). If it is caused by attacker, this is then mostly a griefing attack as there is no profit for the attacker, although the attacker might be a maker and want to avoid closure of the large position which has an order in MultiInvoker.
The same issue also causes all user attempts to exit DSU to USDC revert for some time, including MultiInvoker withdrawal orders (but probably less severe as not as time-critical as positional orders execution).
PoC Not needed
Mitigation It's probably impossible to do anything in such circumstances to convert DSU to USDC, however it's still possible to keep orders execution, keeping all funds in DSU. So one possible mitigation is to force all interface fee to be in DSU only (so remove the unwrap field from interface fee). Alternatively, if some interfaces only support USDC, maybe accumulate their fee in DSU and let them manually claim USDC if needed (so that it's not time-critical and can be done when unwrapping is available again)
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises when the Perennial protocol attempts to convert its DSU wrapper token back into USDC (the “unwrap” operation) while the underlying lending protocol – either AAVE or Compound – is at full utilization. The reserve contract that holds DSU delegates the actual USDC withdrawal to the external protocol, which only permits a withdrawal of the difference between the total supplied USDC and the outstanding debt. When supply and debt are almost equal, the external protocol’s withdraw call reverts, causing the reserve’s redeem function to fail. MultiInvoker and Manager contracts charge an interface fee during order execution; if the fee’s unwrap flag is set, the fee is converted to USDC in the same transaction. Because the conversion now reverts, the entire order transaction reverts as well. This situation can occur naturally when the protocol’s reserves become fully utilized – a state that has been observed historically – or it can be forced deliberately by an attacker who temporarily borrows all available USDC from AAVE or Compound, keeping the debt outstanding long enough to block subsequent unwrap calls. While the attacker maintains the high‑utilization state, any pending MultiInvoker or Manager order that relies on unwrapping (including stop‑loss and take‑profit orders) cannot complete. From the user’s perspective the order appears to be stuck or to revert, the expected USDC fee is not received, and the execution price may drift far from the intended level, potentially causing liquidation or a much worse fill. The impact is loss of value for users who rely on timely order execution, even though the attacker does not directly profit from the blockage. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that traced the fee‑charging path and identified that the reserve’s redeem call propagates the external protocol’s revert, a condition that is easy to miss because it only manifests under a transient full‑utilization state. The bug is hard to detect in normal operation because the contracts assume that the external protocol always has spare liquidity for withdrawals. Mitigation involves removing the automatic unwrap of DSU to USDC from the fee‑charging flow – for example, keeping fees in DSU and allowing a separate, non‑time‑critical claim of USDC when liquidity is available – thereby breaking the dependency on an external protocol that can revert. In broader terms, this is a liquidity‑availability denial‑of‑service flaw caused by reliance on external withdraw functions that may fail when the external pool is fully utilized, violating the business assumption that fee conversion is always possible.

title: MultiInvoker, Manager and Account unexpected
description:
panprog Summary AAVE v3 pool implementation reverts when trying to deposit or withdraw amount = 0:
```solidity
function validateSupply(DataTypes.ReserveCache memory reserveCache, uint256 amount)
    internal
    view
{
    require(amount != 0, Errors.INVALID_AMOUNT);
```
AaveV3FiatReserve._update still allows deposits to and withdrawals from AAVE with amount = 0:
```solidity
{
    if (collateral.gt(target))
        address(this));
    if (target.gt(collateral))
        address(this), 0);
}
```
All amounts relevant for this issue are calculated from 6-decimals amounts (unallocated amount is balance of 6-decimals USDC token, allocated amount is MultiInvoker, Manager and Account), however the target value is calculated as:
target = unallocated.add(allocated).sub(amount).mul(allocation);
Since unallocated, allocated and amount all will be converted from 6 to 18 decimals - all of them will be divisible by 1e12. But target amount will very likely not be divisible by 1e12. For example, unallocated + allocated - amount = 111e12, allocation = 10% = 0.1e18 = 1e17, then target = 111e12 * 1e17 / 1e18 = 111e11 = 11.1e12.
This means that collateral will almost always be either greater or less, but not equal to target.
Now, the situation when abs(collateral - target) < 1e12 might happen:
and Account DSU balance is 0.
• In MultiInvoker and Manager: if the allocated amount (aUSDC) grows by exactly the user's order amount over the time without transactions
• or if admin changes allocation percentage and order's amount matches the difference between collateral and new target exactly
The most likely situation is in the Account: when user tries to withdraw full amount in USDC (setting unwrap = true) (either directly from Account or with signature via Controller), and the account doesn't have any DSU (only USDC), such transactions will almost always revert, denying the user core protocol functionality. This might be time-critical for the user as he might need these funds elsewhere and the unexpected reverts (which will keep happening in consecutive transactions) might make him lose funds from the positions opened or not opened elsewhere.
Much less likely condition for MultiInvoker and Manager: withdrawals with unwrap flag set are vulnerable to this DOS. MultiInvoker or Manager action charges interfaceFee by withdrawing it from user's market balance and if unwrap flag is set, it's converted to USDC via batcher or reserve (if batcher is not set or empty). Since this conversion to USDC will revert in reserve, entire MultiInvoker or Manager transaction will revert as well.
Root Cause AaveV3FiatReserve._update doesn't verify amount passed to 8-perennial-v2-update-3/blob/main/emptyset-mono/packages/emptyset-reserve/contracts/reserve/strategy/AaveV3FiatReserve.sol#L66-L69
Internal pre-conditions
1. Reserve uses AAVE strategy
2. Reserve.allocation is not 0
3. (allocated + unallocated - interfaceFee.amount) * reserve.allocation is not divisible by 1e12.
Account: 4a. User's account has some USDC and none DSU 5a. User calls MultiInvoker and Manager: 4b. User has created a MultiInvoker or Manager order with interfaceFee.unwrap or interfaceFee2.unwrap set to true. 5b. The allocated amount in reserve has grown exactly by the amount charged by interface over the time without transactions
External pre-conditions Account: None
MultiInvoker and Manager: Market price is within the order's execution range
Attack Path Happens by itself:
• Account user: all such withdrawal transactions will revert denying user withdrawal of his funds (the funds can still be withdrawn if unwrap is set to false, or exact amount is specified, but if it's another contract, this might not be possible at all).
• MultiInvoker/Manager: user's order can not be executed temporarily due to revert.
Impact Account: User is unable to withdraw his funds and can not allocate them in the other positions, losing funds from liquidation or not benefiting from the position he intended to open.
MultiInvoker / Manager:
• User order is executed at a worse price
• Or position is liquidated (in case the order was a stop-loss and price moved beyound liquidation price)
• Or user order is not executed (in case the order is take profit and the price had moved away from the execution range)
PoC Not needed 0, instead of directly comparing target with collateral in AAVE strategy.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that appears when a user attempts to withdraw USDC from an Aave V3 based reserve with the unwrap flag set to true while the amount passed to the reserve’s internal update function is zero. The Aave core contract enforces a non‑zero amount check (require(amount != 0, Errors.INVALID_AMOUNT)), but the AaveV3FiatReserve._update implementation does not perform the same validation. Because USDC is a 6‑decimal token, the contract converts unallocated, allocated and amount values to 18‑decimal precision by multiplying by 1e12. The target collateral is then calculated as (unallocated + allocated – amount) * allocation / 1e18. Even though the three inputs are multiples of 1e12, the multiplication by the allocation factor (typically 0.1e18) produces a target that is often not a multiple of 1e12. Consequently the on‑chain comparison between the actual collateral and the computed target fails, causing the reserve to revert the transaction. This situation is most likely to occur when a user’s account holds only USDC and no DSU tokens, and the user tries to withdraw the full USDC balance with unwrap=true, or when the allocated amount grows exactly by the interface fee amount or when an admin changes the allocation percentage such that the difference between collateral and target is less than 1e12. Under these precise conditions the transaction reverts repeatedly, preventing the user from retrieving his funds and breaking core protocol functionality such as MultiInvoker and Manager order execution. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a normal balance before the call, but after the transaction the balance appears unchanged and the transaction fails with an “invalid amount” error, giving the impression that funds have disappeared. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the Perennial V2 Update 3 codebase when the auditor noticed that AaveV3FiatReserve._update lacks an amount‑zero guard and that the decimal‑scaling mismatch could lead to a collateral‑target mismatch. The bug is hard to spot because it only manifests for edge‑case values (zero amount combined with specific allocation ratios) that are not exercised in typical test suites. To remediate the problem the reserve’s update function should enforce the same non‑zero amount requirement as the Aave core, or it should round the target calculation to the 1e12 granularity used by the token, and handle zero‑amount unwrap paths gracefully, thereby restoring the expected withdraw behaviour and eliminating the denial‑of‑service vector.

title: Previous beneficiary will not be able to claim beneficiaryFees
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic error that prevents a former fee beneficiary from withdrawing accrued fees after the contract owner changes the beneficiary to a pool address. The contract stores a single boolean flag beneficiaryIsPool that reflects only the current beneficiary’s pool status. The claim() function checks this flag unconditionally and reverts with BeneficiaryPoolCannotClaim when the flag is true, regardless of which address is attempting to claim. Because the flag is updated when setBeneficiary() is called, any subsequent claim – even from a previous beneficiary that is not a pool – will hit the revert condition. This occurs when the owner calls setBeneficiary() with a pool address, causing beneficiaryIsPool to become true. The previous beneficiary, who still has a non‑zero entry in the beneficiaryFees mapping, calls claim() expecting to receive their fees, but the transaction reverts and no funds are transferred. From the user’s perspective the claim transaction fails, the UI shows no change in balance, and the user receives an error instead of the expected refund. The impact is that fees earned by the previous beneficiary become locked, violating the documented contract behavior that the old beneficiary should be able to claim any fees generated while they were active. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the claim logic and the setBeneficiary documentation, which explicitly states that the old beneficiary can claim fees. The bug is subtle because the revert only triggers when the global pool flag is true, and the claim function returns silently when the amount is zero, making it easy to miss during testing. The problem belongs to the class of state‑dependent access‑control or business‑logic flaws where a global state variable is used to gate functionality for multiple actors. To fix the issue the claim() function should verify the pool status of the specific beneficiary being claimed, or separate pool fee handling into its own mapping and allow pool beneficiaries to withdraw via a dedicated function. Removing the unconditional beneficiaryIsPool check or conditioning it on the caller being the current beneficiary will restore the intended ability for previous beneficiaries to claim their fees.

title: Malicious user can bypass execute shutdown prevention
bug_full: The vulnerability is a shutdown‑bypass flaw in the collection‑shutdown module. The contract provides a preventShutdown function that is intended to stop a shutdown process by checking that the shutdownVotes counter is zero before allowing a manager to set a shutdownPrevented flag. However, the check only looks at the numeric counter and does not verify whether a shutdown has already been initiated. An attacker can first call the start function, which records a vote and increments shutdownVotes, and then immediately call reclaimVote, which subtracts the same amount of votes and resets shutdownVotes back to zero. Because the counter is again zero, a subsequent call to preventShutdown passes its require‑style check, even though a shutdown has already been started. This sequence can be performed as a front‑run or after the manager’s transaction, effectively rendering the preventShutdown protection useless. The impact is that a locker manager (or any privileged role) believes the collection is protected from shutdown, while a malicious participant can later complete the shutdown, potentially freezing assets, breaking governance expectations, or causing loss of funds for users who assumed the collection would remain active. The issue occurs whenever the contract allows any user to invoke start and reclaimVote without additional state validation, i.e., under normal operating conditions when the contract is not paused. It primarily affects collections that rely on the shutdownPrevented flag for security, the locker manager role that calls preventShutdown, and any users of the collection who expect the shutdown to be blocked. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logical flow of the shutdown lifecycle and identified that the preventShutdown guard does not consider the existence of a pending shutdown beyond the vote count. The bug is subtle because the vote counter appears to be cleared, giving the impression that no shutdown is in progress, while internal state elsewhere may still indicate an active shutdown request. To remediate, the contract should check a dedicated shutdown‑in‑progress flag or verify that quorumVotes (or another immutable indicator) is zero, rather than relying on the mutable shutdownVotes counter. In broader terms, this is a classic example of an insufficient state‑validation bug where a function assumes a numeric counter fully represents a process’s existence, allowing an attacker to manipulate the counter and bypass security checks. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show that shutdown has been prevented, yet later the collection becomes inaccessible or funds are locked, contradicting the expectation that the collection remains operational.

title: ERC721 Airdrop item can be redeemed/swapped out
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns the handling of ERC721 airdropped items in the Locker contract. When the contract owner invokes requestAirdrop to claim an airdrop, the received ERC721 token is held by the Locker contract and is supposed to be transferred only to an authorised claimant. However, the redeem and swap functions that allow a user to exchange a token from a personal collection for the airdropped token do not verify that the caller is the authorised claimant for the airdropped token. The logic only checks that the caller owns the token they are offering in the swap, leaving the airdropped token unrestricted. An attacker can therefore create a collection that references the airdropped ERC721 contract, approve a token they own, and call swap with the identifier of the airdropped token. The contract will transfer the airdropped NFT to the attacker even though they have no claim to it. This results in the unauthorized transfer of valuable NFTs, effectively stealing them from the intended recipient. The issue manifests only when the airdropped asset is an ERC721; ERC20 and ERC1155 paths include proper claimant checks, making the flaw subtle and easy to miss during casual testing. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by Sherlock, who wrote a test case in Locker.t.sol that demonstrates the exploit. From a user perspective the symptom is that an expected airdropped NFT never arrives, or appears in an unexpected address, while the user’s own token is transferred out as part of the swap. The business logic of the airdrop protocol—namely that each airdropped item is reserved for a specific claimant—gets violated, breaking accounting assumptions and exposing users to loss. To remediate, the contract must enforce an explicit authorisation check in redeem and swap for ERC721 items, ensuring that only the designated claimant can trigger the transfer of the airdropped token. This can be achieved by storing the authorised claimant for each airdrop and validating msg.sender against that record before allowing any redemption or swap operation.

title: Admin can not set the pool fee
bug_full: The vulnerability is that the function intended to allow an admin to set a per‑pool fee writes the new fee into a temporary memory copy of the pool parameters instead of updating the persistent storage slot. Because the struct is loaded into a memory variable, the assignment only changes the in‑memory representation, which is discarded at the end of the call. Consequently the fee stored in the contract’s state remains unchanged and the default fee defined elsewhere is always used when swaps are executed. The root cause is a misuse of the Solidity data location specifier: the code declares `PoolParams memory poolParams = _poolParams[_poolId];` and then sets `poolParams.poolFee = _fee;`. The correct approach would be to obtain a storage reference (`PoolParams storage poolParams = _poolParams[_poolId];`). The bug can be exploited by any actor who believes they have changed the fee – for example an admin may call the function with a reduced fee expecting lower costs for users, but the contract will continue to charge the original default fee. From a user perspective swaps will appear to charge an unexpected fee, or the protocol may collect less revenue than intended if the default fee is lower than the intended custom fee. The impact is primarily economic: the protocol cannot enforce pool‑specific fee tiers, leading to revenue loss, fee‑model inconsistency, and potential trust issues for liquidity providers who expect their pool to have a particular fee. The condition occurs every time the admin calls the fee‑setting function; there are no external pre‑conditions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑management code, where the auditor noticed that the function manipulates a memory variable and does not write back to storage. Because the transaction does not revert and emits no error, the problem can be hard to notice without inspecting the data locations. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑update not persisted” or “storage‑memory confusion” vulnerabilities, where a contract updates a temporary copy instead of the persistent state. To remediate, the function should obtain a storage pointer to the pool parameters and write the fee directly to storage, or use a dedicated setter that updates the mapping entry. After the fix, calls to set a pool fee will correctly persist the new value, and `getFee()` will return the updated fee for that pool. Until fixed, users may see the fee remain at the default value even after an admin transaction, leading to mismatched expectations versus reality.

title: ERC1155Bridgable is not EIP-1155
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from a deviation between the declared compliance of the ERC1155Bridgable contract and the actual behaviour required by the ERC‑1155 standard, specifically the optional ERC1155Metadata_URI extension. The contract implements the supportsInterface function so that it reports support for the metadata interface, and it stores a per‑token URI in a mapping that can be updated through the setTokenURIAndMintFromRiftAbove function. However, when the URI is changed the contract does not emit the URI event defined in EIP‑1155, which must be fired whenever a token’s metadata URI is altered and the change can be expressed by an event. The root cause is the omission of an event emission after the internal uriForToken mapping is updated. This omission can be exploited by an attacker who updates a token’s URI to point to malicious or misleading metadata without triggering any off‑chain listeners; because the event is missing, indexers, marketplaces, and bridge relayers that rely on the URI event will not become aware of the change. Consequently, users may continue to see stale or incorrect metadata, experience missing images, or be presented with wrong token information, violating the expectation that the token’s visual representation matches its on‑chain state. The issue manifests whenever the bridging flow calls setTokenURIAndMintFromRiftAbove – a legitimate operation for authorized bridge components – and the token’s URI differs from its previous value. All token holders, integrators, and any protocol that consumes the ERC1155 metadata through events are affected, as they may display incorrect data or fail to synchronize state across chains. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s behaviour against the EIP‑1155 specification; the missing event is subtle because the token still transfers correctly and the URI can be read directly from the contract, so functional testing of transfers does not reveal the defect. The bug is hard to notice for developers who focus on on‑chain logic and ignore off‑chain event handling. To remediate the issue, the contract should compare the new URI with the existing one and, if they differ, emit the standard URI event with the token ID and the new URI, thereby restoring full compliance with the ERC‑1155 metadata extension and ensuring that external observers can reliably track metadata updates.

title: The unused tokens from the user’s initialization of UniswapV4‘s pool will be locked in the UniswapImplementation contract. Found by 0x37, 0xHappy, 0xNilesh, 0xc0ffEE, 0xlucky, BADROBINX, BugPull, ComposableSecurity, Ironsidesec, KingNFT, Ollam, ZeroTrust, blockchain555, h2134, merlinboii, novaman33, shaflow01, wickie, zarkk01, zzykxx
bug_full: During the initialization of a UniswapV4 pool, the contract function initializeCollection forwards the caller‑provided token amounts to the pool manager via an unlock callback. The callback computes the amount of liquidity that can be created from the supplied amounts using UniswapV4’s LiquidityAmounts.getLiquidityForAmounts routine. Because the price range and the discrete nature of the liquidity formula rarely consume the exact supplied quantities, one of the two tokens (either the native token or the collection token) is left over after the liquidity is minted. The implementation of the unlock callback (_unlockCallback) only checks that the leftover amount of the collection token does not exceed a user‑specified slippage tolerance; it never transfers any remaining tokens back to the caller. Consequently, any unused portion of the supplied amounts stays permanently locked inside the UniswapImplementation contract. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears successful – the pool is created and events are emitted – but the user’s wallet shows a reduction in balance that is larger than the amount actually used as liquidity, and no refund event is emitted. This discrepancy can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit warning and the UI typically only displays the pool’s existence, not the exact token accounting. The vulnerability is a classic case of “locked‑asset” or “refund‑missing” bug, where leftover assets are unintentionally retained by the contract due to missing return logic. It affects any entity that initializes a pool through the Locker, leading to loss of the unused token portion and reducing overall protocol capital efficiency. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit by multiple researchers who traced the flow of tokens through the unlock callback and observed that the leftover amount is never sent back. To remediate the problem the contract should be extended to calculate the exact unused token amounts after liquidity minting and explicitly transfer those amounts back to the caller (or to a designated refund address), or alternatively adjust the slippage check to allow the transaction to succeed while still returning the surplus. Implementing a proper refund mechanism restores the expected accounting invariant that all tokens supplied by the user are either used as liquidity or returned, thereby preventing silent fund loss and aligning contract behavior with user expectations.

title: ERC721Bridgable and ERC1155B
description:
According to the README:
The Bridged721 should be strictly compliant with EIP-721 and EIP-2981 The Bridged1155 should be strictly compliant with EIP-1155 and EIP-2981
EIP-2981 states the following:
Marketplaces that support this standard MUST pay royalties no matter where the sale occurred or in what currency, including on-chain sales, over-the-counter (OTC) sales and off-chain sales such as at auction houses.
As royalty payments are voluntary, entities that respect this EIP must pay no matter where the sale occurred - a sale conducted outside of the blockchain is still a sale.
The crux of the standard, is that if a contract is EIP-2981 compliant, the royalty should be paid to the artist who created the NFT no matter where the sale occurred. For that it first needs to be correctly reported to marketplaces, and attributed to the artist. It's worth noting that as returned by the EIP-2981 function royaltyInfo, both the royalty recipient and the royalty amount are specific to each NFT:
```solidity
function royaltyInfo(uint256 _tokenId, uint256 _salePrice) external view returns (address receiver, uint256 royaltyAmount);
```
The problem is that both ERC721Bridgable and ERC1155Bridgable completely violate this crucial property via both setting a uniform royalty amount across all NFTs, and designating themselves as the royalty recipient, thus reporting wrong amounts, and mixing them together in a single bucket. This makes it impossible to either correctly collect the appropriate royalty amounts, or to attribute the collected royalties to artists.
Both ERC721Bridgable and ERC1155Bridgable perform the following in their initialize function:
```solidity
// Set this contract to receive marketplace royalty
_setDefaultRoyalty(address(this), _royaltyBps);
```
As per-NFT royalties are not set, this makes the contract a single recipient of the same _r happens next, it's impossible to either correctly collect the appropriate royalty amounts at marketplaces, or to correctly attribute the royalties to different artists.
Definite loss of funds (NFT creators won't receive the appropriate royalties):
• Marketplaces who sell NFTs on L2s are not able to pay correct amounts of royalties
• Artists who created the NFTs in collections on L1, which are bridged to L2, are not able to track the amounts of royalties they have the right to receive (which effectively deprives them of said royalties)
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the ERC721Bridgable and ERC1155Bridgable contracts that are intended to represent NFTs bridged from layer‑1 to layer‑2. Both contracts claim to be fully compliant with EIP‑721/EIP‑1155 and with the royalty standard EIP‑2981, yet they violate a core requirement of that standard: the royalty information must be specific to each token and must point to the original creator (or another designated recipient). In the initialize function of each contract the code calls _setDefaultRoyalty(address(this), _royaltyBps), which registers the contract itself as a single royalty recipient and applies the same basis‑point value to every token. Because no per‑token overrides are ever set, the royaltyInfo function always returns the same receiver address and the same royalty amount regardless of the token identifier. This design flaw means that when a marketplace on layer‑2 queries royaltyInfo to determine how much royalty to pay and to whom, it receives a uniform, incorrect answer. The marketplace will then forward the royalty payment to the contract address instead of the artist who created the NFT, or it may even skip the payment if the contract does not expose a withdrawal mechanism. Consequently, creators lose the royalties they are legally entitled to, and the protocol fails to satisfy the business logic that royalties must follow the asset wherever it is sold. The issue manifests for any bridged NFT that is sold on layer‑2, because every sale triggers a call to royaltyInfo. It affects NFT creators, buyers, marketplaces, and any user relying on the royalty guarantee of EIP‑2981. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the initialization routine and compared it against the EIP‑2981 specification. The bug is subtle because the contract still returns a valid address and amount, so a marketplace may assume compliance and continue operating without obvious errors, while the funds are silently redirected. To remediate the issue the contracts need to store and expose per‑token royalty data, either by using ERC2981’s _setTokenRoyalty for each token or by implementing a custom mapping that returns the original creator and the correct royalty amount for the given token ID. The royalty collection mechanism must also be designed to forward the received royalties to the appropriate artists on layer‑1, although the cross‑chain distribution is outside the scope of this finding. In user‑facing terms, a seller will see a constant royalty fee regardless of which NFT is sold, and the artist will receive nothing or an unexpected payment to the bridge contract, breaking the expectation that royalties are automatically paid to the creator on every sale.

title: There is a logical error in the re-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the fee exemption removal function of a smart contract that manages per‑beneficiary fee overrides. The contract stores a 48‑bit value where the upper 24 bits hold a custom flat fee and the lower 24 bits are used as a boolean flag. The setFeeExemption() routine writes the flag value 0xFFFFFF, meaning “exemption active”. The removeFeeExemption() routine attempts to verify that an exemption exists by extracting the lower 24 bits and comparing them to the literal value 1. Because the stored flag is 0xFFFFFF, the comparison never succeeds, causing the function to revert with NoBeneficiaryExemption every time it is called. As a result the delete operation is never reached and the feeOverrides entry cannot be cleared. This bug can be triggered by any owner who tries to revoke a beneficiary’s fee exemption; the transaction will fail and the exemption will remain permanently active. The impact is that the beneficiary continues to receive the reduced fee rate even after the protocol intends to remove it, which leads to unintended fee revenue loss for liquidity providers and the protocol. The condition occurs whenever the contract owner calls removeFeeExemption() for an address that has previously been granted an exemption. The affected parties are the protocol (loss of expected fee income), liquidity providers (partial fee erosion), and potentially users who expect their fee status to be updated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the bit‑mask logic used to encode the exemption flag. It is easy to miss because the code compiles without warnings and the flag value is a valid 24‑bit number; only a careful inspection of the intended flag semantics reveals the mismatch. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect flag or bitmask validation” errors, where a stored sentinel value is compared against the wrong constant. From a user’s perspective the UI may still show the beneficiary as exempt, but the protocol’s dashboard might indicate that the exemption was removed, creating a discrepancy where users expect the fee to revert to normal but it stays reduced. The correct fix is to compare the extracted flag against the actual sentinel value (0xFFFFFF) or to store a simpler boolean flag (e.g., 1) that matches the removal check. After fixing the condition, the delete statement will execute and the feeOverrides entry will be cleared, restoring the intended fee schedule.

title: It is possible to prevent the ex-
description:
It is possible for everyone to front-run the calls to the execute() function, by listing an NFT in the Listings.sol contract, right after the quorum is reached.
In the CollectionShutdown.sol, there is the possibility to start a voting system to delete a specific collection from the platform. The logic of the voting system is simple: There is a quorum to reach. After that, it is possible to call the execute() function that will delete the collection.
The function that will initialize this voting system is the start() function that is possible to check here.
Supposing that the Voting system for a collection starts, and the quorum is reached.
At this point, the Owner of the CollectionShutdown.sol contract, could call the execute() function to delete the collection from the platform.
In the meantime, a malicious actor who doesn't want the collection to be deleted lists an NFT of the same collection.
At this point, when the Owner of the CollectionShutdown.sol tries to call the execute() function, there is a call on the _hasListing() function to check if the collection is listed.
The collection is listed, so the execute function will go in revert due to the previous check.
Internal pre-conditions
External pre-conditions
Attack Path
There are 2 different users: User2, Hacker
1) Hacker creates and initializes Collection with 10 NFTs.
2) User2 owns the same NFTs (5 in total) and after some time, wants to start a voting system to delete the collection from the platform.
3) User2 calls start() in CollectionShutdown.sol and reaches the quorum to delete the collection.
4) Hacker has one more NFT, and lists it in Listings.sol
5) Owner of CollectionShutdown.sol calls the execute()
6) Reverts, due to the _hasListing() check, that attests that there is one token listed already.
Everyone can prevent the execution of the execute() function. This will make the voting system useless
bug_full: The vulnerability is a race condition that allows any participant to block the deletion of a collection by front‑running the governance execution step. The platform provides a CollectionShutdown contract that lets token holders start a vote, reach a quorum and then call execute() to permanently remove the collection. The execute() function first checks whether the collection is currently listed in the Listings contract via an internal _hasListing() call. If a listing exists, the function reverts. Because the contract does not prevent new listings while a shutdown vote is pending, an attacker can submit a listing for the same collection after the quorum is reached but before the owner invokes execute(). The attacker’s listing causes the _hasListing() check to succeed, forcing execute() to revert and leaving the collection on the platform. This defeats the intended governance flow and creates a denial‑of‑service condition for the collection owner and any users expecting the collection to be removed. The issue occurs only when the following conditions are met: a shutdown vote has been started, the quorum has been satisfied, and a malicious actor can list at least one token of the targeted collection before the owner calls execute(). The affected parties are the collection owner, token holders who rely on the shutdown mechanism, and the overall protocol which loses a functional governance tool. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that exercised the start‑vote and execute path and observed that a listing could be introduced in the narrow window between quorum achievement and execution. It is subtle because the listing logic resides in a separate contract and the shutdown contract only performs a simple existence check; the lack of cross‑contract state coordination makes the problem easy to overlook. To remediate, the platform should enforce a lock on the collection while a shutdown vote is active, preventing any new listings, or the execute() function should first clear existing listings or incorporate a more robust state transition that does not rely on a single _hasListing() guard. In practice, the user experience would be that after voting to delete a collection, the UI still shows the collection as present, and attempts to delete it repeatedly fail with no obvious error, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust in the protocol’s governance. The bug belongs to the class of “race condition / front‑runable state‑inconsistency” vulnerabilities where separate contracts can modify shared state in a way that invalidates a pending privileged operation.

title: If a collection has been shut-
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑reset flaw in the collection shutdown workflow. When a collection reaches the required quorum of shutdown votes, the admin can trigger a shutdown that deletes the collection token and clears the collectionInitialized flag, allowing the collection to be re‑registered later. However, the internal counter that tracks the number of shutdown votes (params.shutdownVotes) is never set back to zero after the shutdown completes. The contract only checks that this counter is zero before allowing a new shutdown to start, using a guard that reverts with ShutdownProcessAlreadyStarted if the value is non‑zero. Because the counter remains at the value accumulated during the first shutdown, any subsequent attempt to shut down the same collection after it has been re‑initialized will always revert, even though the mapping entries have been cleared. This bug occurs whenever a collection is shut down, its assets are claimed, and the collection is later re‑added to the protocol. It affects the protocol’s administrators and collection owners because it prevents a second shutdown, potentially leaving sale proceeds or other assets inaccessible if the collection needs to be closed again. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the shutdown logic and noticed that the vote counter was never reset. It can be hard to notice because the mappings that store the token and initialization flag are deleted, giving the impression that the shutdown state is fully cleared, while the hidden vote counter persists. The impact is functional rather than directly financial: the protocol cannot enforce a second shutdown, which may lead to locked funds, inability to reclaim proceeds, or a broken user experience where owners cannot exit the collection. To remediate, the shutdown routine should explicitly reset params.shutdownVotes to zero after all votes have been processed and the shutdown finalization steps are completed, ensuring that a re‑initialized collection can be shut down again without hitting the guard condition. This class of bug is a typical state‑management error where a mutable variable is not restored to its initial value after a lifecycle transition, violating the expected invariant that a shutdown process can be started only when no prior shutdown is in progress.

title: There is a logical error in the
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical error in the fee distribution routine of a liquidity pool contract. When the contract distributes collected fees it is supposed to split the total amount into a pool portion (typically 95 %) that goes to the liquidity providers of the collection token and a beneficiary portion (typically 5 %) that goes to the beneficiary address, which in this case can be another pool belonging to the Flayer protocol. The root cause is that, for the special case where the beneficiary is itself a pool, the identifier of the beneficiary pool (derived from _poolKeys[beneficiary].toId()) is identical to the identifier of the pool that is currently receiving the fees (derived from _poolKey.toId()). Because the code treats the two identifiers as distinct, it first resets the pool’s fee balance to zero, then attempts to add the beneficiary fee to the beneficiary pool’s balance. Since both identifiers refer to the same storage slot, the beneficiary fee is effectively written to the same pool that has just been cleared, and later the emitted event reports a zero beneficiary amount. As a result, 5 % of the fees that should be allocated to the beneficiary remain unassigned and are not transferred to any party. This leaves a portion of the collected fees “missing” from the accounting view. The impact is that original liquidity providers receive only the pool portion of the fees, while new liquidity providers who join after the mis‑allocation inadvertently receive a share of the unassigned 5 % fee, creating an unfair advantage. Users observing their reward balances may notice that the expected 5 % royalty is never credited, or that their total earnings are lower than the protocol’s documentation promises. The issue manifests only when the beneficiary flag beneficiaryIsPool is true and the pool being processed is the Flayer protocol’s own NFT collection; under all other configurations the split works as intended. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the _distributeFees function, where the auditor traced the flow of variables and identified that the same pool identifier is used for both the pool and the beneficiary, causing the fee split logic to collapse. Because the contract still emits a successful distribution event, the problem can be subtle and may not trigger a revert or obvious error, making it hard to detect through simple testing. The recommended remediation is to add a conditional check that zeroes out the beneficiary fee when the pool identifier matches the beneficiary pool identifier, ensuring that the full amount is allocated to the pool and no fee is left dangling. Conceptually, the fix restores the intended accounting invariant that the sum of pool fees and beneficiary fees equals the total collected fees, eliminating the hidden loss of funds and preserving fairness for all liquidity providers.

title: A user loses funds when he mod-
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect tax accounting logic that occurs when a listing owner modifies only the price (floorMultiple) of an existing liquid listing without changing its duration. The contract’s modifyListings function first resolves the tax for the current listing by calling _resolveListingTax, which calculates a refund based on the remaining time of the listing using the original creation timestamp. After the optional duration update, the function always adds the full tax required for the (potentially unchanged) listing by calling getListingTaxRequired. However, when params.duration is zero the code does not update listing.created, so the later taxRequired calculation assumes the full original duration even though the refund was already computed for the remaining time. As a result, the net tax payable is higher than it should be, causing the user to lose funds that should have been refunded. This bug manifests only when the duration field is left unchanged while the price is altered, which is a common operation for sellers adjusting market prices. It is discovered during a manual audit of the Listings.sol contract where the auditor noticed a mismatch between the refund formula and the subsequent tax requirement aggregation. The issue is subtle because the function appears to handle tax consistently, and the extra tax is deducted silently, making it hard to notice without inspecting the accounting flow. The impact is financial loss for the listing owner: the user expects to pay tax proportional to the remaining listing time and to receive a proportional refund, but instead receives a smaller refund or pays the full tax for the whole period, leading to unexpected balance reductions or “funds disappearing”. The bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistent fee calculation errors, where mutable state (listing.created) is not refreshed before a dependent computation, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions. To fix the issue, the contract should update the listing’s creation timestamp regardless of whether the duration changes, or recompute the tax based on the same snapshot used for the refund, ensuring that the tax required and the refund are calculated from a consistent state. This adjustment restores the intended economic model where modifying only the price does not increase the tax burden beyond the proportional remaining time.

title: Price limit is used as the price
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way the Uniswap V4 implementation treats the user‑provided price limit during a swap. In the public API a trader supplies a sqrt price limit that is intended to act as a stop‑condition: if the pool price reaches this limit the swap should halt. Internally the swap step calculation expects a *price target* that represents the next price boundary for the current step. The code mistakenly passes the raw price limit directly as the price target without first converting it to the appropriate range using the library function that derives the target from the limit. This mismatch causes the swap math to compute input and output amounts based on an incorrect price boundary. As a result the computed token amounts often become infeasible, leading the swap transaction to revert. From a user’s perspective the transaction simply fails – the UI shows a submitted trade, but the transaction reverts and no tokens are transferred, giving the impression that the trade “disappeared” or that the protocol is refusing to execute. The issue manifests whenever a swap is executed with a non‑trivial price limit, which is the common case for limit orders or slippage protection. It affects any participant who attempts to trade through the affected Uniswap implementation, regardless of the token pair or direction of the trade. The bug was discovered during a systematic audit of the UniswapImplementation contract when the auditors observed that swaps with a price limit consistently reverted, and tracing the call stack revealed the misuse of the price limit as the price target. The problem is subtle because the function signatures appear correct and the price limit value is a legitimate uint160, so static analysis may not flag it; only a functional test that exercises limit‑based swaps exposes the failure. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on limit‑order style swaps and a broken user experience, as traders cannot rely on price limits to protect against adverse execution. Conceptually, the fix is to translate the supplied price limit into a proper price target before invoking the swap step computation, using the library routine that derives the target from the limit and the direction of the trade. By applying this conversion, the swap math will respect the intended stop‑condition, allowing swaps to succeed when the price stays within the limit and to revert only when the limit is truly crossed, restoring correct accounting and preventing unexpected reverts.

title: In the unlockProtectedListing()
bug_full: UnlockProtectedListing contains a logic error where the function burns the full amount of tokens that remain after the principal is repaid, including the accrued interest that should be allocated to liquidity‑provider (LP) holders. The root cause is that the code calls collectionToken.burn((1 ether - tokenTaken) * 10 ** denomination) without separating the interest component, while the unlockPrice() function calculates a fee that already incorporates the compound interest. Consequently, when a user unlocks a protected listing, the interest portion is destroyed instead of being distributed, leading to a reduction in the total supply of the collection token. This deflation creates a mismatch between the number of NFTs held in the Locker contract and the available token supply, causing the utilizationRate() calculation to exceed 100 % and driving the protocol’s interestRate_ to unsustainably high values. Under these conditions new protected listings may become impossible to create, and existing LP holders receive less than the expected return, effectively losing funds. The vulnerability is triggered each time unlockProtectedListing is executed with sufficient collateral, affecting any LP participant, the protocol’s accounting integrity, and users who rely on the protected‑listing feature. It was discovered during a manual audit by comparing the unlock flow with liquidateProtectedListing, which correctly transfers the remaining collateral to the implementation for fee distribution. The bug is subtle because the burn operation does not emit an obvious error and the UI simply shows the listing as unlocked, while the hidden loss appears as a gradual shrinkage of LP balances. The proper remediation is to replace the burn of the residual amount with a transfer of the accrued interest to the LP pool, for example by calling the same depositFees logic used in liquidation, and to ensure that only the principal fee is burned if required.

title: Users can dodge createListing
description:
Users can abuse a loophole to create a listing for 5% less tax than intended, hijack others' tokens at floor value and perpetually relist for free.
For the sake of simplicity, we assume that collection token denomination = 4 and floor price = 1e22
Users who intend to create a dutch listing for any duration <= 4 days can do the following:
1) Create a normal listing at min floor multiple = 101 and MIN_DUTCH_DURATION = 1 days, tax = 0.1457% (tokensReceived = 0.99855e22)
2) Reserve their own listing from a different account for tokenTaken 0.95e18, collateral 0.05e18, collateral is burnt, protected listing is at 0 health and will be liquidatable in a few moments (remainingTokens = 0.94855e22)
3) Liquidate their own listing through liquidateProtectedListing, receive KEEPER_REWARD = 0.05e22 (remainingTokens = 0.99855e22)
4) createLiquidationListing is invoked with us as owner and hardcoded values floorMultiple = 400 and duration = 4 days
User has paid 0.14% in tax for a listing that would've normally cost them 5.14% in tax.
This process can be repeated any number of times even after the liquidationListing expires to constantly reserve-liquidate it instead of calling relist and paying further tax.
There are numerous other ways in which this loophole of reserve-liquidate can be abused:
1) Users can create listings for free out of any expired listing at floor value, they only burn 0.05e18 collateral which is then received back as KEEPER_REWARD
2) Users can constantly cycle NFTs at floor value (since it is free) and make liquidationListings, either making profit if the token sells or making the token unpurchasable at floor since it is in the loop
3) Any user-owned expired listing can be relisted for free through this method instead of paying tax by invoking relist
Tax evasion
```solidity
_listings.createLiquidationListing(
    IListings.CreateListing({
        collection: _collection,
        tokenIds: tokenIds,
        listing: IListings.Listing({
            owner: listing.owner,
            created: uint40(block.timestamp),
            duration: 4 days,
            floorMultiple: 400
        })
    })
);
```
bug_full: The vulnerability is a tax‑evasion loophole that allows a user to create a Dutch auction listing while paying far less than the intended marketplace tax. The root cause lies in the combination of three contract mechanisms: (1) the ability to reserve a protected listing by supplying a small amount of collateral that is immediately burned, (2) a keeper reward that is paid to the caller of the liquidation function and is equal to the amount of collateral that was burned, and (3) the createLiquidationListing function that can be invoked by any address with hard‑coded parameters (floorMultiple = 400 and duration = 4 days) without checking that the caller is distinct from the original listing owner. Because the reward reimburses the burned collateral, an attacker can create a normal listing that incurs the full 5.14 % tax, then immediately reserve their own listing from a second account, burn only a tiny collateral amount, liquidate the protected listing to collect a keeper reward that covers the burned collateral, and finally call createLiquidationListing with the attacker as owner. The net tax paid is reduced to roughly 0.14 % instead of the expected 5 %, effectively allowing free or near‑free listings. This sequence can be repeated indefinitely, even after the liquidation listing expires, by repeatedly reserving and liquidating the same listing. The impact is a loss of revenue for the protocol, the ability for malicious actors to flood the market with listings at floor price without paying fees, and the potential to manipulate token availability and pricing because tokens can be cycled at floor value without cost. The flaw manifests whenever a user creates a listing with a duration of four days or less and a floorMultiple of 400, and when the attacker controls both the original owner address and a secondary address used for reservation. Any participant in the marketplace can be affected because the economic model assumes that each listing contributes tax revenue; the loophole breaks that assumption and can lead to a situation where users see listings appear for free, balances that should have been reduced by tax remain unchanged, and expected fees disappear. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the reserve‑protected‑listing, liquidateProtectedListing, and createLiquidationListing functions and identified that the keeper reward calculation does not account for the collateral burn, allowing self‑exploitation. The bug is subtle because each individual function appears correct in isolation, and the reward‑for‑collateral pattern is a common incentive mechanism, making the net tax reduction easy to overlook. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a higher minimum collateral that is not fully reimbursed by the keeper reward, adjust the tokenTaken ratio so that the reward does not cover the burned collateral, restrict self‑reservation and self‑liquidation, and add validation that the caller of createLiquidationListing cannot be the same entity that supplied the collateral. These changes would restore the intended tax collection and prevent free‑listing abuse, aligning the contract’s behavior with its economic design.

title: manipulation of the Utilization
bug_full: The vulnerability is an economic manipulation flaw that allows a participant who holds a large number of NFTs to artificially inflate or deflate the total supply of the protocol’s ERC20 token by using the deposit and redeem functions, which mint and burn tokens without any fee or restriction. Because the protocol calculates the utilization rate – the ratio that drives the protected‑listing interest rate – directly from the total token supply, an attacker can change the utilization rate at will. By depositing many NFTs, the attacker mints a huge amount of ERC20, which lowers the utilization rate and consequently alters the protected interest calculation used in the compounded factor formula. Conversely, by redeeming NFTs the attacker burns tokens, raising the utilization rate and driving the interest rate upward. The compounded factor feeds the health check of protected listings; when the health factor falls below the liquidation threshold, the contract’s liquidateProtectedListing function can be called. An attacker who controls a substantial share of the NFT collection can therefore push other users’ listings into liquidation, trigger the liquidation, collect the keeper reward, and subsequently acquire the liquidated NFT at a discounted auction price. The impact is that honest participants can lose their protected assets, suffer financial loss, and see the protocol’s stability and fairness eroded. The issue manifests when a user with many NFTs performs deposit or redeem actions; from the user’s perspective the protected listing is suddenly flagged as unhealthy, a liquidation event occurs, and the NFT disappears from their wallet, often leaving a zero balance where they expected safety. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that traced the direct dependency between the ERC20 totalSupply and the liquidation health logic, noting that the mint/burn operations are fee‑free and therefore exploitable. The problem is hard to notice because the minting and burning appear to be normal collateral handling, while the downstream effect on utilization and liquidation is indirect and hidden in the interest‑rate calculation. The bug belongs to the class of supply‑manipulation or interest‑rate manipulation attacks, where an attacker leverages unchecked token creation or destruction to influence protocol economics. To remediate, the contract should introduce proportional fees on deposit and redeem, impose caps or governance checks on the amount of tokens that can be minted or burned per operation, or decouple the utilization calculation from the raw totalSupply so that token supply changes cannot directly affect liquidation thresholds.

title: CollectionShutdown::execute(
description: CollectionShutdown::execute() doesn't ensure that all tokens of the collection being shutdown are added to the sudoswap pool in order to be sold. This function takes as input an array of the token IDs to be sold via sudoswap pool. In case an NFT ID that's locked in the protocol is not in this array the NFT will stay locked and not sold. Even if the function is only callable by admins the admins have no control on the order and the moment transactions are executed and such scenarios should be handled at the moment of execution. Internal pre-conditions External pre-conditions Attack Path 1. The protocol currently holds NFTs 55 and 56, admin calls CollectionShutdown::execute() by passing as a parameter [55,56]. 2. While the CollectionShutdown::execute() transaction is in the mempool a deposit of NFT 60 is done via Locker::deposit(). 3. The CollectionShutdown::execute() transaction goes through and a sudoswap pool selling 55 and 56 is created 4. NFT 60 is locked in the protocol NFTs that should be sold are locked in the procotol, which leads to an indirect loss of funds to collection tokens holders.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the shutdown routine of a collection contract that creates a sudoswap pool to sell all NFTs currently locked in the protocol. The routine accepts an explicit array of token identifiers that the caller (an admin) claims should be sold. Because the function does not verify that the supplied list matches the full set of locked tokens at the moment of execution, a race condition can be introduced: an attacker or any user can deposit a new NFT into the locker after the shutdown transaction has been signed and placed in the mempool but before it is mined. When the shutdown transaction finally executes, it only creates a pool for the IDs that were listed, leaving the newly deposited NFT locked and unsold. The root cause is the absence of an atomic pre‑condition that all locked tokens are enumerated or that deposits are blocked during shutdown. Exploitation consists of broadcasting a shutdown call with a known list of IDs, then quickly depositing additional NFTs; the protocol will silently ignore those extra tokens, resulting in an indirect loss of value for the collection’s token holders because their assets remain trapped. This issue manifests whenever the admin initiates a shutdown while the contract still permits deposits, which is a typical operational scenario. The affected parties are the owners of the collection’s NFTs and any downstream users who rely on the shutdown to liquidate assets, as they may see their balances unchanged or NFTs disappear from the marketplace without a sale. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended business logic (sell every locked NFT) with the actual implementation (sell only the caller‑provided IDs). It can be hard to notice because the function appears to succeed – a pool is created and events are emitted – yet the missing tokens leave no explicit error, making the loss subtle. The recommended remediation is to make the shutdown routine compute the current set of locked token IDs on‑chain at execution time, or to enforce that no new deposits can occur after the shutdown is scheduled, thereby guaranteeing that every locked NFT is included in the sudoswap pool and sold according to the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: If the royalties receiver it's a
bug_full: An authorization restriction in the InfernalRiftAbove contract prevents the royalty receiver from claiming accumulated royalties when the receiver is a smart contract that does not have a function to invoke claimRoyalties. The function claimRoyalties first queries the ERC‑2981 royaltyInfo for the collection, extracts the receiver address, and then checks that msg.sender equals this receiver. If the receiver is an externally owned account the check passes, but if the receiver is a contract the check fails unless the contract itself calls claimRoyalties. Because many contracts are not designed to call this external function, the royalty balance remains locked in the bridge contract. An attacker does not need to exploit a vulnerability; the issue is a logical design flaw that results in funds being inaccessible. The impact is that royalty payments for NFTs bridged to L2 are never transferred to the intended recipient, leading to missing payouts, zero balances for the receiver, and a breach of the expected accounting model where royalties should be claimable by the designated party. The condition occurs whenever the royaltyInfo returns a contract address as the receiver and that contract lacks a method to trigger claimRoyalties. Users experience the symptom of receiving no royalty funds despite the system indicating that royalties have been accrued. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the access control logic of claimRoyalties and identified the mismatch between the receiver type and the required caller. The issue can be hard to notice because the contract compiles and works for typical EOA receivers, and no explicit error is emitted when royalties are simply unclaimed. The recommended remediation is to relax the caller restriction: allow any address to invoke claimRoyalties when the designated receiver is a contract, and forward the funds to the receiver, or provide a separate mechanism for contracts to claim royalties. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “authorization lock” or “receiver‑cannot‑claim” defects, where business logic assumes the receiver can act but the contract’s access control prevents it, resulting in locked assets and broken financial expectations.

title: UniswapImplementation::befo
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the UniswapImplementation contract’s beforeSwap hook, where the function performs an incorrect validation when a user initiates an exact‑input swap of native tokens (ETH) for a collection token. The hook is designed to convert any collection‑token fees that have accumulated in the contract into native tokens before the user’s swap is settled. The root cause is that the code compares the computed tokenOut amount against the absolute value of the user‑specified input (‑params.amountSpecified) instead of comparing the amount of native token that will actually be spent (ethIn). When the hook has at least one wei of collection‑token fees, the swap is executed with amountSpecified negative (exact input), and the computed tokenOut is smaller than the required amount while ethIn is larger, the condition tokenOut <= uint(-params.amountSpecified) evaluates to false and the function forces ethIn and tokenOut to zero, causing the surrounding swap to revert. This specific combination of conditions – a native‑to‑collection swap, accumulated collection‑token fees, and an exact‑input amount – triggers the revert. An attacker can exploit the bug simply by performing a legitimate swap after the contract has collected any amount of collection‑token fees; the transaction will revert, denying service to honest users. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on swaps that would otherwise succeed, leading to user frustration, apparent loss of funds (the transaction reverts so the ETH remains with the sender but no tokens are received), and reduced confidence in the protocol’s reliability. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and unit‑test execution that exercised fee accumulation followed by an exact‑input swap, revealing that the transaction consistently reverted under those pre‑conditions. The bug is subtle because it only manifests after fees have been collected, a state that may not be exercised in routine testing, and the revert does not produce a clear error message indicating the underlying logic flaw. To remediate, the beforeSwap logic should validate that the amount of native token required to cover the fee conversion (ethIn) does not exceed the user‑specified input amount, i.e., replace the tokenOut comparison with an ethIn comparison. This aligns the check with the intended accounting model, ensuring that the protocol only performs the internal fee conversion when sufficient ETH is supplied, and restores normal swap functionality.

title: User can cancel or modify Dutch auctions, compromising market in- tegrity and user trust Found by 0xNirix
bug_full: An auction‑type preservation bug exists in the contract that manages NFT listings. The relist function does not verify the original listing type before overwriting an existing entry, allowing a caller who is not the owner to replace a Dutch auction or liquidation listing with a new listing of a different type, typically a liquid listing. The root cause is the absence of the same listing‑type checks that are present in modifyListings and cancelListings, combined with a tax‑refund calculation that returns a proportional amount of the original tax when the listing is cancelled before its expiry. An attacker can exploit the flow by first creating a Dutch auction, then using a second address to call relist, changing the duration and type, and immediately calling cancelListings to obtain a near‑full refund of the newly paid tax while keeping the original tax refund from the old listing. This results in the auction becoming mutable, breaking the immutability guarantee of Dutch auctions and allowing the market to be manipulated. From a user’s perspective the auction may suddenly disappear or change to a different sale mode, bidders see the price no longer decreasing, and the seller may receive an unexpected refund, leading to loss of trust and market efficiency. The vulnerability manifests whenever a non‑owner invokes relist on an existing Dutch or liquidation listing; the contract does not enforce that only the original owner can modify the listing type, and it fails to clear liquidation flags on cancellation. It was discovered during a manual audit of the Listings.sol source code, where the missing checks were identified as a logical oversight. The issue is subtle because the relist operation appears to be a normal marketplace feature and the tax‑refund logic seems benign, making the unintended type switch easy to overlook. To remediate, the relist function should include the same listing‑type validation as modifyListings and cancelListings, restrict relisting to the original owner or a designated authority, and ensure that liquidation flags are cleared when a listing is cancelled. In broader terms, this is a type‑switching and immutability violation that allows unauthorized modification of auction parameters, compromising protocol integrity and user confidence.

John sees the NFT and wants to reserve it, putting up 0.9e18 amount of CollectionTokens as _collateral. 3. The _collateral is burned. 4. The math will remain mostly the same with little updates and we will first run the math with the wrongly computed previousCompoundedFactor and then will compare it to the correct one. collection token total supply = 5e18 (because the burned _collateral amount of CollectionTokens has been essentially minted to the ProtectedListings contract hence as we said reserve() does not affect the total supply after the function is executed). collection protected listings count = 2 (now 1 more due to the created protected listing) previousCompoundedFactor = 1005232876711984000 (the wrong one, as we derived it a bit earlier) utilizationRate = collection protected listings count ∗1e36 ∗10denomination / CT total supply utilizationRate = 2 ∗1e36 ∗100 / 5e18 = 2e36 / 5e18 = 0.4e18 interestRate = 200 + utilizationRate ∗600 / 0.8e18 = 200 + 0.4e18 ∗600 / 0.8e18 = 500 (5 %) perSecondRate = interestRate ∗1e18 / 365 ∗24 ∗60 ∗60 = 500 ∗1e18 / 31 536 000 = 15854895991882 timePeriod = 432000 (5 days) (the previous checkpoint was made 5 days ago) compoundedFactor = 1005232876711984000 ∗(1e18 + (15854895991882/1000 ∗432000)) / 1e18 compoundedFactor = 1005232876711984000 ∗1006849315068112000 / 1e18 = 1012118033401408964 or 0.68% accrued interest for that collection for the past 5 days. Now let's run the math but compounding on top of the correct compound factor: compoundedFactor = 1004794520547808000 ∗1006849315068112000 / 1e18 = 1011676674797752473 or 0.21% of interest should've been accrued for that collection for the past 5 days, instead of 0.68% which in this case is 3 times bigger.
bug_full: Vulnerability: In the reserve function of the Listings contract, the sequence of token operations (transfer, transfer, burn, mint, transfer, burn) causes the contract to create a protected listing and checkpoint the collection’s compoundFactor while the totalSupply of the CollectionToken is temporarily reduced. The checkpoint routine reads the utilization rate, which is defined as (protected listings count * 1e36 * 10^denomination) / totalSupply. Because the second burn has not yet been executed, totalSupply is lower than it will be after the function finishes, so the utilization rate is artificially inflated. The inflated utilization rate is then used to compute a compoundedFactor that is stored in the current block’s checkpoint. All loans that reference this checkpoint therefore start with a higher compoundedFactor and accrue more interest than they should. The bug manifests only during the execution of reserve; after the function returns the totalSupply is restored, so external observers see no change in token balances, making the problem hard to notice. Borrowers of NFTs in the affected collection experience higher interest charges, while the protocol’s accounting assumes a correct utilization rate. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the order of token burns and the point at which protected listings are recorded. It is difficult to detect because the totalSupply variable ends unchanged and the checkpoint is written in the same transaction, so standard balance checks do not reveal the discrepancy. The proper fix is to reorder the operations so that the collateral burn occurs after the protected listing has been created and the checkpoint taken, or to defer the burn until after the checkpoint, ensuring that the totalSupply used for the utilization calculation reflects the final state of the transaction. This class of bug belongs to “intermediate state checkpointing” where a protocol records a value based on a transient state of a shared resource, leading to accounting errors and unintended financial consequences.

title: FTokens are burned after quor
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect ordering of operations during the shutdown of a collection. When the admin initiates the shutdown, the contract first calculates a new quorum value by multiplying the current total supply of the collection token (the fToken) by a fixed percentage. This value is stored in params.quorumVotes. Immediately after this calculation the contract calls Locker.sunsetCollection, which burns all remaining fTokens for the collection. Because the burn reduces the totalSupply, the previously stored quorumVotes is now larger than the actual number of votes that can be represented by the remaining token supply.
