The claim formula used later – availableClaim * claimableVotes / params.quorumVotes * 2 – divides the claimable ETH by this inflated quorum value, so each vote receives a smaller share of the auction proceeds. As a result a portion of the ETH that should be distributed to voters becomes permanently unclaimable, effectively reducing the payout for every participant. The issue occurs every time the shutdown function is executed, provided the pre‑condition that at least half of the holders have voted for shutdown is satisfied. It affects all token holders who voted for the shutdown, as well as the overall fairness of the protocol’s profit‑sharing mechanism. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of state changes and identified that the token burn happens after the quorum calculation. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error; users simply see a lower-than‑expected refund or a zero balance after claiming, which may be attributed to market conditions rather than a bug. To remediate the issue the quorum calculation should be performed after the token burn, for example by calling Locker.sunsetCollection before setting params.quorumVotes, or by recomputing quorumVotes after the burn. This ensures that the denominator in the claim formula accurately reflects the actual token supply, preserving the intended distribution of ETH profits and preventing funds from disappearing unexpectedly.

title: SEV 5: The getAccountMarginRequirementUsdAndUnrealizedPnlUsd function returns incorrect margin requirement values when a position is being changed
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the function that calculates an account's margin requirements after a trade is executed. Instead of using the market price that would be observed after the trade’s impact on market skew, the implementation mistakenly re‑uses the fill price of the current order as the mark price for the after‑trade margin check. Because the mark price depends on the market skew and the trader’s position size, the price that should be used by the liquidation logic (the price after the trade) differs from the price used by the margin‑checking code. When a position is increased or decreased, the skew changes, causing the used mark price to be higher for long positions and lower for short positions than the correct post‑trade price. Consequently the computed initial and maintenance margin requirements are inflated for long positions and deflated for short positions. This mis‑calculation leads to two classes of observable failures: (1) a trader with sufficient margin may have a legitimate size‑increasing order rejected because the protocol thinks the required initial margin is larger than the actual margin balance; (2) an account that is not truly liquidatable may be flagged as liquidatable, causing the protocol to reject order reductions or to force liquidation, while conversely a genuinely liquidatable account may be allowed to trade because the required maintenance margin is underestimated. The bug manifests only when a position is being changed (sizeDelta ≠ 0) and the target market identifier is non‑zero, i.e., during normal market orders. Affected parties include any trader interacting with the perpetual market, the protocol’s risk engine, and ultimately users’ funds because orders may be blocked or liquidations may be triggered incorrectly. The issue was discovered during a security audit through a targeted unit test that compared the margin values produced by the function against those computed by the liquidation routine, revealing a systematic offset proportional to the position size and market skew scale. The problem is subtle because the margin check itself succeeds – the contract believes the account meets the requirement – yet the downstream liquidation logic uses a different price, causing inconsistent behavior that is not obvious from a single transaction view. To remediate, the margin‑calculation routine must obtain the mark price based on the market skew and position size *after* applying the trade, typically by calling a dedicated price‑oracle function with the updated skew and using that price to compute notional value and margin requirements. This aligns the margin check with the liquidation logic and restores correct enforcement of initial and maintenance margin rules. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect state‑dependent pricing in risk calculations” and violates the fundamental accounting assumption that margin requirements are derived from the same market price used for liquidation. From a user perspective, the symptoms are orders being rejected despite having enough collateral, unexpected “account liquidatable” warnings, or the ability to trade when the account should be liquidated. Users expect their trades to be accepted when they have sufficient margin, but the contract’s flawed calculation makes the system behave otherwise, effectively causing funds to be locked or liquidated incorrectly.

title: Potential accounting problems due to issue
description:
Potential issue in ClearingHouse.updatePositions() when lastFundingTime is not being updated by ClearingHouse.settleFunding.
ClearingHouse.lastFundingTime is only updated when _nextFundingTime is not zero:
otocol/contracts/ClearingHouse.sol#L281-L282
_nextFundingTime is determined a few lines above by a call to amms[i].settleFunding():
otocol/contracts/ClearingHouse.sol#L267
The return value of amms[i].settleFunding() can be zero for _nextFundingTime, if the block.timestamp is smaller than the next funding time:
otocol/contracts/AMM.sol#L236-L249
That means that if the last market inside the amms array has not reached the next funding time at block.timestamp, _nextFundingTime will be zero and lastFundingTime will not be updated.
Then when ClearingHouse.updatePositions() is called, it will not process fundingPayment because lastFundingTime was not updated:
otocol/contracts/ClearingHouse.sol#L241-L250
Unrealized funding payments are not settled correctly, potentially leading to incorrect margin accounting when opening a position. Also marginAccount.realizePnL() (line 255 ClearingHouse.sol) won't get called, so the trader won't receive funds that they should receive.
(line 141 ClearingHouse.sol).
ClearingHouse._openPosition
There can be multiple potential issues with accounting that can result due to this issue, both when liquidating and when opening a position.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logical accounting flaw in the clearing‑house contract that can cause funding payments and profit‑and‑loss (PnL) realization to be skipped. The contract updates a global variable called lastFundingTime only when a temporary value named _nextFundingTime is non‑zero. _nextFundingTime is obtained by calling settleFunding on each automated market maker (AMM) in the amms array. If the last AMM in the array returns zero because the current block timestamp is still earlier than that market’s scheduled funding time, the aggregated _nextFundingTime becomes zero and the clearing‑house deliberately does not update lastFundingTime. Consequently, when updatePositions is later invoked – for example during the opening of a new position, a liquidation, or any routine position update – the function believes that no funding interval has elapsed and therefore does not process the pending fundingPayment. This omission leaves unrealized funding payments unsettled, prevents marginAccount.realizePnL from being called, and can cause a trader’s expected payout to disappear. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a missing refund, a balance that stays unchanged after a funding event, or a liquidation that fails because the protocol thinks the margin is insufficient even though the trader actually holds enough collateral. The issue occurs only under the specific timing condition where the final market in the amms list has not yet reached its next funding timestamp at the moment updatePositions runs; typical test scenarios that exercise all markets simultaneously may not trigger it, making the bug hard to notice. The root cause is the reliance on a single _nextFundingTime flag that can be zero, leading to an incorrect decision to skip the accounting update. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the clearing‑house logic, where the auditor traced the flow from settleFunding through updatePositions and identified the conditional that prevents lastFundingTime from being refreshed. To fix the issue the contract should either track each market’s funding event independently, ensure that lastFundingTime is updated whenever any market settles funding, or introduce a boolean flag that records whether at least one market produced a non‑zero nextFundingTime before deciding to skip the update. By guaranteeing that funding payments are always settled and that realizePnL is invoked, the protocol will maintain correct margin accounting and prevent funds from disappearing unexpectedly.

title: User's might be able to claim their prizes even
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the prize‑claiming function of the prize pool contract, which does not verify whether the pool has been shut down before allowing a winner to claim a prize. The contract tracks two independent time‑bases: the draw period, which determines when a draw opens and closes, and the TWAB (time‑weighted average balance) period, which determines when the pool may be shut down based on the last observation timestamp. When these periods differ, the shutdown can occur in the middle of an active draw – specifically after the last observation timestamp but before the draw is marked as finalized. Because the claimPrize function only checks that the draw has not been finalized (using isDrawFinalized) and lacks a check that the pool is not in shutdown, a winner can invoke claimPrize after the shutdown timestamp. The claim transfers the prize amount to the winner, and the same winner can subsequently call withdrawShutdownBalance to retrieve their share of the remaining pool balance, which should have been allocated only once. This results in a double‑claim scenario where the same assets are withdrawn twice, effectively stealing funds from other participants. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a winner can still receive a prize after the pool is announced as shut down, and then the pool balance for other users appears reduced or even zero, contrary to the expectation that no further claims are possible after shutdown. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case simulated a mismatch between draw and TWAB periods and observed that claimPrize succeeded after the shutdown timestamp, followed by a successful shutdown balance withdrawal that reverted only because the funds had already been taken. The bug is subtle because the shutdown condition is extremely rare – it only occurs when the TWAB controller reaches its maximum uint32 timestamp (approximately 82 years) and when the draw period is not a multiple of the TWAB period – making it easy to overlook in normal testing. The root cause is the missing shutdown guard in claimPrize; the contract should enforce that no prize can be claimed after a shutdown, for example by adding a notShutdown modifier or by aligning the draw and TWAB periods so that shutdown can only happen after a draw is finalized. Conceptually, this is a classic case of improper state validation leading to double‑spending of assets, violating the accounting assumptions that each prize and each shutdown share can be withdrawn exactly once.

title: ERC20VotesUpgradeable::getPastTotalSupply overestimates the value
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns an accounting mismatch between the public totalSupply view of the Karma token and the internal checkpointing mechanism provided by ERC20VotesUpgradeable. Karma overrides balanceOf and totalSupply to exclude tokens that have been minted to reward distributors but are not yet distributed, ensuring that only circulating tokens are counted for voting power and quorum calculations. However, ERC20VotesUpgradeable records totalSupply checkpoints in its _mint and _burn functions by simply adding or subtracting the minted amount, without invoking the overridden totalSupply logic that subtracts undistributed rewards. Consequently, each checkpoint stores a totalSupply value that includes tokens held by reward distributors, inflating the historical supply figure. This overestimation becomes critical because governance quorum is typically defined as a percentage of totalSupply; an inflated supply lowers the absolute number of votes required to meet quorum. In practice, proposals may be marked as passing even though the actual voting power represented by token holders is insufficient, violating the intended governance rules. The issue manifests when reward distributors hold large amounts of undistributed tokens, causing the discrepancy between the displayed totalSupply (which correctly subtracts those balances) and the checkpointed totalSupply (which does not). Users may observe that their voting power appears as zero if they are a distributor, while the overall supply shown by the contract remains high, leading to confusion and potential manipulation. The bug was discovered during a security audit that compared the contract's public totalSupply implementation with the internal checkpoint updates and identified that the checkpoint logic does not respect the custom supply accounting. It can be hard to notice because the contract still reports a plausible totalSupply value, and the mismatch only affects historical snapshots used for quorum, not the immediate balance queries. Exploitation does not involve direct fund loss but can be leveraged by an attacker who can trigger additional minting to distributors, artificially inflating the checkpointed supply and thereby reducing the quorum threshold. The appropriate mitigation is to align the checkpoint updates with the overridden totalSupply calculation, for example by preventing _mint and _burn from writing checkpoints when the minted amount is destined for a reward distributor, or by adjusting the checkpoint logic to subtract undistributed balances before recording the totalSupply snapshot. This correction ensures that quorum calculations reflect the true circulating token supply, preserving the integrity of the governance process.

title: Fees never deducted in AccountableOpenTerm loan
description:
In AccountableOpenTerm, interestData() returns non-zero performanceFee and establishment-
Fee, but no path ever charges these fees. _accrueInterest() only updates _scaleFactor for base interest and
none of supply or repay calls FeeManager (unlike FixedTerm’s collect). As a result, fees are never charged.
Impact: Protocol/manager fees are effectively never taken.
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability in the AccountableOpenTerm loan contract is an accounting omission where advertised performance and establishment fees are never actually deducted from borrowers. The contract’s interestData function correctly calculates non‑zero fee amounts based on elapsed time, but the internal _accrueInterest routine only updates the scale factor for base interest and does not incorporate any fee logic. Moreover, the public supply and repay functions, which in comparable FixedTerm contracts call a FeeManager to transfer the calculated fees, contain no such calls. As a result, when a user supplies collateral or repays a loan, the contract updates interest balances but skips the step that would move the fee amounts to the FeeManager. This flaw can be exploited by opening and closing loans without ever paying the intended fees, effectively allowing free borrowing and causing the protocol to lose expected revenue. The issue manifests whenever a loan is created, supplied to, or repaid, because each of those pathways omits the fee collection step. It affects the protocol’s fee manager, the protocol’s treasury, and any stakeholders relying on fee income, while borrowers may notice that no fee is taken despite the contract reporting a fee value. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the fee handling logic of AccountableOpenTerm with the reference FixedTerm implementation and observed the missing FeeManager invocation. Because the contract still reports non‑zero fees, the discrepancy can be subtle and may not be evident from simple transaction logs, making it hard to notice without a detailed code review. To remediate, the fee calculation should be performed during supply and repay, the appropriate fee amounts for the elapsed period should be transferred to the FeeManager before any other state changes, and the contract’s accounting should be updated to reflect the deducted fees, aligning the implementation with the advertised fee policy. This class of bug falls under fee omission or accounting inconsistency, where a system reports a charge but fails to enforce it, leading to revenue leakage and potential trust issues.

title: FiveFiftyRule::_removeFromEntity will revert or not work in some cases
bug_full: The vulnerability is an out‑of‑bounds index error in the internal function that removes an entity from each investor’s list. The function receives an array of investor addresses and iterates over it with a variable `len`. For each investor it retrieves the stored list `ens` and determines its actual length `eLen`. However, the inner loop that searches for the target entity incorrectly uses the outer length `len` as its bound instead of `eLen`. When the supplied investors array is longer than the stored list, the inner loop accesses `ens[j]` for indices that do not exist, causing the Solidity runtime to revert with an index‑out‑of‑bounds error. This bug manifests when callers provide an investors array that does not exactly match the number of investors associated with the entity, which can happen unintentionally or be crafted maliciously. The impact is that calls to `removeFromEntity` and `deleteEntity` may revert, preventing the removal of entities or investors and leaving stale entries in the `findEntity` mapping. From a user’s perspective, a transaction that should delete an entity fails with a generic revert, and the UI may show that the entity still exists or that no funds are moved. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by reviewing the loop logic and reproducing the failure with a test that supplies a mismatched investors array, resulting in a `stdError.indexOOBError`. The bug is subtle because the outer loop appears correct and the inner loop condition looks plausible, making it easy to overlook that the two lengths differ. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of “incorrect loop bounds leading to out‑of‑bounds access” bugs, which violate the protocol’s accounting invariant that each investor’s entity list accurately reflects current state. To remediate, the inner loop should iterate up to `eLen` (the actual length of the stored list) rather than `len`. Updating the loop condition to `for (uint256 j; j < eLen; ++j)` ensures that only valid indices are accessed, preventing spurious reverts and preserving the integrity of the entity‑removal logic.

title: FiveFiftyRule::_removeFromEntity will revert or not work in some cases
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the internal function that removes an entity reference from each investor’s list. The function receives an array of investor addresses and stores its length in a variable called len. It then iterates over each investor and retrieves the investor’s stored list of entities, whose length is stored in eLen. The inner loop, which is supposed to scan the investor’s entity list, mistakenly uses len as its upper bound instead of eLen. When the supplied investors array is longer than the actual entity list for any investor (len > eLen), the inner loop attempts to read ens[j] for indices that do not exist. This out‑of‑bounds access triggers a Solidity index‑out‑of‑range revert. The bug manifests during calls to removeFromEntity and deleteEntity, both of which rely on _removeFromEntity. In practice, a caller may provide a correctly formatted investors array, but if the array length exceeds the stored entity count for any investor, the transaction reverts with an index error, leaving the state unchanged. From a user perspective the transaction simply fails; the UI may show that the entity was not removed or that a refund was not processed, even though no funds are lost. The issue was discovered during a security audit and reproduced with a Forge test that deliberately supplied a mismatched investors array, causing an expected revert. Because the loop condition looks syntactically correct, the bug can be hard to spot without targeted testing of edge cases where the input length differs from the stored list length. The underlying class of bug is an array‑indexing error caused by using an incorrect loop bound, a common source of out‑of‑bounds exceptions in smart contracts. To remediate, the inner loop should iterate up to eLen, the actual length of the investor’s entity array, or include an explicit bounds check before accessing ens[j]. This change aligns the loop with the data structure’s size, preventing spurious reverts and ensuring that entity removal behaves as intended, preserving protocol correctness and preventing denial‑of‑service scenarios.

title: Frontrun resolve user
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic flaw in the ChildToken contract that causes the totalInvestors counter to be decremented incorrectly when a user is resolved to a new address. The root cause is that resolveUser invokes super._transfer directly, bypassing the overridden _transfer function that contains a protection returning early for zero‑value transfers. By skipping this guard, the internal _update routine is executed with a from address that already has a zero balance and a transfer amount of zero. The _update logic checks whether the sender’s balance will become zero after the transfer and, if so, decrements totalInvestors. Because the condition is satisfied both when the user first transfers all of its tokens (front‑run) and again when resolveUser is called with the already‑empty old address, the counter is decremented twice. This leads to an inaccurate count of active investors; the UI may show fewer investors than actually exist, and in extreme cases the counter can underflow to zero, causing subsequent legitimate transfers that would zero out a balance to revert. The impact is primarily a denial‑of‑service risk: other investors may be unable to transfer their full balances because the system believes there are no investors left, although token balances themselves remain correct. The issue manifests when a migration transaction is preceded by a front‑running transfer that empties the old address, and it is hard to notice because the token transfer succeeds and no explicit error is thrown, only the investor count changes silently. It was discovered during an audit that exercised the resolveUser flow with a front‑run scenario and observed the counter decrementing twice. Fixing the bug involves adding a validation step before calling super._transfer, such as reverting if the old address balance is zero, or using the overridden _transfer that includes the zero‑value guard, thereby ensuring that _update is not invoked with a zero‑value transfer from an empty account. This correction restores the integrity of the totalInvestors accounting and prevents the potential DoS condition.

title: Fr Resolve users
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the ChildToken contract that causes the totalInvestors counter to be decremented twice when a user is resolved from an old address to a new address. The root cause is the use of super._transfer inside the resolveUser function, which bypasses the ChildToken overrides that contain a protection returning early for zero‑value transfers. Because this guard is skipped, the internal _update hook is executed even when the transferred amount is zero and the sender’s balance is already zero. The _update logic interprets a zero‑balance sender as an investor exiting the system and decrements totalInvestors; it also increments the counter when a recipient’s balance moves from zero to non‑zero. When resolveUser is called after the old address has already transferred its full balance (often via a frontrunning transaction), the super._transfer call with a zero amount triggers the decrement a second time, resulting in an inaccurate investor count. This can be exploited by an attacker who front‑runs the resolveUser call, first emptying the old address’s balance, then allowing the resolveUser transaction to execute and cause the double decrement. The impact is that the protocol’s view of how many investors are active becomes wrong, potentially reaching zero or underflowing, which may cause subsequent transfers of full balances to revert, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition for legitimate users. The issue occurs only when resolveUser is invoked for an address whose balance is already zero, and only because the contract’s internal accounting does not guard against zero‑value transfers after the balance has been cleared. It was discovered during a security audit that included fuzzing and manual inspection of the resolveUser flow, and it is subtle because the transfer of zero tokens does not revert and therefore does not raise an obvious error. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show that the number of investors drops unexpectedly, or that transfers that should succeed fail with an underflow error. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect state update due to bypassed overrides” and violates the business logic that the totalInvestors counter must accurately reflect active token holders. The recommended mitigation is to add an explicit check before invoking super._transfer that reverts if the old address balance is zero, or to avoid using super._transfer altogether and call the overridden transfer function that includes the zero‑value guard, thereby ensuring that _update is not called with a zero amount when the sender’s balance is already zero.

title: Griefer can block user from claiming airdrop
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability is a front‑running signature replay issue in the claim function of the KarmaAirdrop contract. The function transfers the airdrop tokens and, when the recipient has no prior token balance, attempts to delegate voting power by calling delegateBySig with a user‑provided signature, nonce and expiry. Because the signature is included in the same transaction, it is visible in the mempool before execution. An attacker monitoring the mempool can extract the signature and submit a separate delegateBySig transaction that consumes the same nonce. When the original claim transaction later executes, the delegateBySig call fails the nonce check, causing the entire claim transaction to revert. As a result the user receives no tokens and the airdrop claim is blocked. This occurs only when the account has zero balance before the claim, and when the attacker can front‑run the transaction before it is mined. The affected parties are the airdrop recipients and the protocol that relies on the airdrop distribution, as funds that should be transferred remain unclaimed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the claim logic and the Erc20Votes delegateBySig implementation, noting that the nonce handling mirrors the known EIP‑2612 permit replay problem. The bug is subtle because the revert happens after the token transfer step, making it appear as if the transfer succeeded, and the UI may incorrectly report success. The vulnerability belongs to the class of replayable signature attacks where a public signature can be reused to invalidate a later dependent call. To remediate, the delegateBySig call should be isolated from the claim flow, for example by wrapping it in a try‑catch block and proceeding only if the delegation succeeds, or by using a separate nonce or off‑chain delegation mechanism that cannot be front‑run. Ensuring that a failed delegation does not revert the whole claim prevents users from being blocked from receiving their airdrop.

title: Removing Individuals from groups doesn't properly decrement the groups.numCatalyst
bug_full: The vulnerability concerns an accounting mismatch in the way a group-level catalyst counter is updated when individuals are removed from a group. Each time an individual is assigned as a catalyst on an entity, the contract increments the group’s numCatalyst field, potentially multiple times for the same individual if they serve as a catalyst on several entities. However, when the individual is later removed, the removal routine only checks whether the individual’s personal catalyst count is non‑zero and then decrements the group counter by a single unit, regardless of how many catalyst assignments the individual held. This asymmetric update causes the group.numCatalyst value to remain higher than the actual number of active catalysts. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that exercised the createEntity and removeIndividual functions: after adding a user as a catalyst on two entities and then removing that user, the group counter stayed at one instead of returning to zero. The issue is subtle because the counter appears plausible and the discrepancy may be small, making it hard to notice without targeted tests that verify the counter after removal operations. The incorrect counter feeds into the FiveFiftyRule::canTransfer function, which uses the group.numCatalyst metric to decide whether a transfer is permissible. An inflated counter can allow transfers that should be blocked, while an underestimated counter can reject legitimate transfers, leading to unexpected rejections, potential loss of funds, or unauthorized asset movement. Users experience symptoms such as transfers being unexpectedly denied despite sufficient balances, or transfers succeeding when business rules suggest they should fail, creating confusion and possible financial risk. The bug violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that the group-level catalyst count accurately reflects the sum of all entity‑level catalyst assignments. To remediate, the contract should maintain a precise mapping of each individual’s catalyst assignments and adjust the group counter symmetrically: when removing an individual, decrement the group.numCatalyst by the exact number of catalyst roles the individual held, or recompute the counter from scratch. Ensuring that add and remove operations are mirror images restores the integrity of the accounting logic and prevents the downstream transfer rule from being misled.

title: Allowance check in FiveFiftyRule::canTransfer is inverted
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inverted allowance check in the function that determines whether a token transfer to an entity is allowed. Instead of verifying that the entity's remaining allowance is at least the amount to be transferred, the code mistakenly uses a less‑than‑or‑equal comparison. As a result, when the allowance is greater than the requested amount the function follows the else‑branch and reverts, and when the allowance is smaller the subtraction underflows, also causing a revert. This logic error prevents any transfer to an entity unless the allowance exactly matches the amount, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition. The bug occurs only when the destination address is flagged as an entity and the allowance does not equal the transfer amount. Users attempting such transfers experience transaction failures, see no change in their balances, and may lose gas fees, contrary to the expectation that a sufficient allowance would permit the transfer. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the conditional statements governing allowance validation. It is hard to notice because the revert does not provide a specific error message and the condition appears syntactically plausible. The class of bug is an inverted conditional or off‑by‑inequality error, common in permission checks where the relational operator is reversed. To fix the problem the comparison must be changed to allowance >= amount before performing the subtraction, and the return logic should reflect the same condition. After correction, the contract will correctly enforce allowance limits, allowing legitimate transfers and restoring the intended accounting behavior where the allowance represents the spendable balance for an entity.

title: Karma.sol doesn't initialize signature variables
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability stems from an incomplete initialization sequence in the Karma upgradeable token contract. Karma inherits ERC20VotesUpgradeable, which itself inherits ERC20PermitUpgradeable, a module that defines the EIP712 domain separator used for off‑chain signature verification. The contract’s initialize function calls __ERC20_init, __ERC20Votes_init, __UUPSUpgradeable_init, and __AccessControl_init, but it never invokes __ERC20Permit_init. As a result, the EIP712 domain is created with an empty name string and a version value of 0 instead of the expected token name and version \"1\". This mismatch causes any signature generated by wallets for the delegateBySig function to be considered invalid because the signed domain data does not align with the contract’s stored domain. Consequently, users attempting to delegate voting power via a signed message experience transaction reverts or silent failures, seeing UI symptoms such as a “delegate” button that appears to do nothing or error messages like “invalid signature”. The issue occurs whenever the contract is initialized without the missing call, affecting all token holders who rely on off‑chain delegation, the governance process of the protocol, and any external applications that expect standard ERC20Permit behavior. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s initializer list against its inheritance chain and identified the absent __ERC20Permit_init invocation. It can be hard to notice because the token’s basic ERC20 functionality works correctly, and the failure only manifests when signature‑based features are used, which may be exercised infrequently. The impact is functional rather than a direct loss of funds: the governance mechanism that depends on signed delegations is broken, reducing decentralisation and potentially causing confusion among users. To remediate, the contract should be upgraded (using its UUPS upgradeability) to include a call to __ERC20Permit_init with the proper token name during initialization, thereby establishing a correct EIP712 domain with version \"1\". This aligns the contract with the ERC20Permit specification, restores compatibility with digital wallets, and enables delegateBySig to operate as intended. The bug belongs to the class of missing‑initialization or inheritance‑related configuration errors that lead to incorrect protocol state and broken business logic.

title: Migrating the existing locks for an investor when is resolved can be gamed causing the existing locks to last longer than they should
bug_full: The vulnerability is a lock‑ordering and short‑circuit flaw that appears when an investor’s account is resolved and its token locks are migrated to a new address. The migration function copies the old address’ lock entries and appends them after any existing locks of the new address without re‑ordering by timestamp. The contract’s unlock routine and the view function that reports available tokens iterate over the lock array in order and break as soon as they encounter a lock whose elapsed time is less than the required lockUpTime. Because of this early‑exit, any locks that appear later in the array are never examined, even if their lock periods have already expired. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running the resolveUser transaction and sending a token to the new address before the migration occurs. The donation creates a fresh lock with the full lock‑up duration, which becomes the first entry in the new address’ lock list. When the migration appends the old locks after this fresh lock, the unlock loop stops at the fresh lock, causing all previously unlocked tokens to remain frozen until the attacker’s lock expires. This results in users seeing zero available balance or experiencing delayed token releases, even though the original lock periods have passed. The issue is discovered through audit testing that simulates a front‑run donation followed by a resolveUser call, revealing that migrated tokens stay locked for an entire year instead of unlocking quarterly as expected. It is hard to notice because the contract correctly records lock timestamps and the total locked amount appears unchanged; only the ordering bug prevents the unlock logic from reaching the eligible entries. The impact is a griefing attack that forces funds to stay locked longer than intended, affecting any user whose account is migrated. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect ordering of time‑based lock entries combined with premature loop termination”. To remediate, the migration logic should merge the two lock arrays in chronological order, or the unlock and available‑tokens functions should be rewritten to scan the entire list without breaking on the first unexpired lock, ensuring that each lock is released as soon as its own lock period ends.

title: User can loseaccrued rewards during migration
poc: Information not provided
bug_full:
The vulnerability is a reward‑loss bug in the staking contract’s migrateToVault function. When a user migrates a staking position from an old vault to a new vault, the implementation copies the entire VaultData struct from the source to the destination, including the rewardsAccrued field. The function only validates that the destination vault’s stakedBalance is zero before allowing the migration, but it does not verify whether the destination already holds any accrued rewards. As a result, if the target vault has non‑zero rewardsAccrued – for example, because the user previously deposited into that vault, earned rewards, and then unstaked – the migration overwrites those pending rewards with the source vault’s rewardsAccrued value, which is typically zero. This overwriting causes the user’s pending reward balance to disappear, leading to a loss of earned tokens.
The root cause is the missing check for existing rewards in the destination vault and the unconditional assignment newVault.rewardsAccrued = oldVault.rewardsAccrued. The bug can be exploited by any actor who can trigger a migration into a vault that already contains rewards, intentionally or unintentionally, causing those rewards to be erased. The impact is monetary loss for users who rely on the migration feature to move stakes between vault versions; the loss is silent – the transaction succeeds, but the UI will show a zero reward balance after migration, which can be confusing and hard to detect.
The condition occurs whenever a user performs the following sequence: (1) stakes in an old vault, (2) a new vault version is deployed, (3) the user creates a stake in the new vault and accrues rewards, (4) the user unstakes from the new vault, (5) the user migrates the old vault’s stake into the new vault. Steps 3‑4 generate rewards in the new vault, and step 5 overwrites them, causing the loss.
All participants who use the migration functionality are affected, as any migration into a vault with existing rewards will suffer the same issue. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the migration logic, where the auditor noticed that the rewardsAccrued field is copied without any safeguard.
Because the contract does not emit a specific error for reward loss and the UI may simply display a reduced or zero reward balance, the bug can remain unnoticed until users compare expected versus actual rewards. The recommended mitigation is to extend the validation to also reject a target vault that has a non‑zero rewardsAccrued value, or to implement a merging strategy that preserves both the source and destination rewards. By ensuring the destination vault is truly empty of both stake and pending rewards before migration, the protocol can prevent accidental destruction of accrued rewards and maintain the integrity of users’ earnings.

title: calling paymentsettler::setstablecoin can lead to inability of holders to claim funds and old stablecoin being trapped in the contract
description:
An admin can call PaymentSettler::setStablecoin at any time. As the code is currently design this should only be done when the stablecoin balance of the contract is zero, which is a very rare occurrence given that many tokens will be at various stages of the their lifecycle.
For instance, if setStablecoin were called in the middle of the burning phase of a central token, it would lead to the inability of some users to burn their tokens. This also holds if there are outstanding payouts to claim before burning is enabled.
As it is not unknown for stablecoins to become de-pegged (even USDC de-pegged for a few hours), a method for migrating from one stablecoin to another must be implemented.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a logic and accounting flaw in the PaymentSettler contract that allows an admin to call setStablecoin at any moment, even when the contract holds a non‑zero balance of the currently configured stablecoin. The intended design assumes the function is only invoked when the stablecoin balance is zero, a condition that is rarely met because tokens are often in various lifecycle stages such as burning or pending payouts. When setStablecoin is executed during an active burning phase or before all payouts are claimed, the contract updates its internal reference to a new stablecoin address while still retaining the old stablecoin balance. Consequently, subsequent calls to burn or claim payouts reference the new token, find no balance, and revert with errors such as ERC20InsufficientBalance. From a user’s perspective, expected actions like burning tokens or receiving a refund result in zero payouts, failed transactions, or balances that appear empty, violating the expectation that funds are always claimable. The impact is two‑fold: existing stablecoins become trapped inside the contract, and users are unable to either claim their entitled payouts or burn their central tokens, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service condition. This issue may be hard to notice because the setStablecoin function appears benign and is restricted to an admin role, so ordinary users do not see the state change until a transaction fails. The bug was discovered during a security audit through a proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrated a user’s burn transaction reverting after the stablecoin was switched. Mitigation requires either enforcing that setStablecoin can only be called when the contract’s stablecoin balance is zero, storing the stablecoin address per payout or per enable‑burn operation, implementing a migration path that withdraws or converts the old stablecoin before the change, or otherwise redesigning the accounting to prevent mismatched token references. These fixes restore the invariant that the contract’s stablecoin reference always matches the actual token balance, ensuring users can reliably claim payouts and burn tokens without risk of funds becoming inaccessible.

title: Calling PaymentSettler::setStableCoin can lead to inability of holders to claim funds and old stablecoin being trapped in the contract
description:
Description: An admin can call PaymentSettler::setStablecoin at any time. As the code is currently design this should only be done when the stablecoin balance of the contract is zero, which is a very rare occurrence given that many tokens will be at various stages of the their lifecycle.  
For instance, if setStablecoin were called in the middle of the burning phase of a central token, it would lead to the inability of some users to burn their tokens. This also holds if there are outstanding payouts to claim before burning is enabled.  
As it is not unknown for stablecoins to become de-pegged (even USDC de-pegged for a few hours), a method for migrating from one stablecoin to another must be implemented.
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from an admin‑controlled function that changes the address of the stablecoin used by the PaymentSettler contract. The contract was designed to hold a single global stablecoin reference, assuming that the address would only be updated when the contract’s stablecoin balance was zero. In practice, the admin can invoke setStablecoin at any moment, including while the contract holds a non‑zero balance of the current stablecoin or while users have active central tokens that are in the burning phase or awaiting payout. Because the contract does not enforce a zero‑balance check or verify that no tokens are active, changing the stablecoin address breaks the accounting logic that underpins both the burn and payout mechanisms. When the address is switched, subsequent calls to burn or claim payouts attempt to transfer the newly set stablecoin, which holds no funds for those pending operations. This results in ERC20InsufficientBalance reverts, preventing users from burning their tokens or receiving their entitled payouts. From the user’s perspective, the UI may show a zero balance even though they previously deposited stablecoins, and attempts to execute a burn transaction fail with an unexpected revert, leading to confusion and panic. The impact is two‑fold: existing stablecoin funds become trapped inside the contract, and token holders are effectively denied service, constituting a denial‑of‑service condition with medium severity. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test where an admin changed the stablecoin after one user had already burned tokens, causing the second user’s burn to revert. The bug is subtle because the function is restricted to an admin role, leading developers to assume it is safe, and the failure only manifests under specific state conditions that are not obvious during normal operation. To remediate, the contract should either forbid setStablecoin unless the stablecoin balance is zero and no central tokens are active, or it should store the stablecoin address on a per‑payout and per‑enable‑burn basis, ensuring that each financial operation continues to reference the correct token. Alternatively, a migration mechanism could be introduced to safely withdraw the old stablecoin and replace it with an equivalent amount of the new one, thereby preserving user funds while allowing a stablecoin transition. Implementing any of these mitigations restores the integrity of the accounting model, prevents funds from becoming locked, and eliminates the denial‑of‑service vector.

title: Misconfigured decimal scale can skew vault accounting
description:
Description: The vault’s math assumes the same decimal scale as the wrapped asset (USDC, 6 decimals) and as the globalPricePerShare fed by ops. While deployment sets vaultParams.decimals = 6 and the wrapper enforces USDC’s 6 decimals, a misconfiguration will skew conversions.
Impact: Configuring the vault with more than 6 decimals can cause incorrect accounting, and follow‑on reverts in rebalancing.
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability is a misconfiguration of the decimal scale used by a vault that holds a wrapped stablecoin with six decimal places, such as USDC. The vault’s internal accounting logic assumes that both the underlying token and the global price‑per‑share value share the same six‑decimal precision. When the vault is deployed with a different decimal setting— for example, a higher number of decimals— the conversion formulas that translate token amounts to vault shares and vice‑versa apply an incorrect scaling factor. This root cause stems from the lack of a hard‑coded or validated decimal constraint in the contract’s initialization parameters. An attacker or a careless operator could set the vault’s decimals to a value greater than six, causing the contract to under‑ or over‑represent user balances. Exploitation follows a simple flow: a user deposits a known amount of USDC, the contract computes the number of shares using the mismatched decimal factor, and the resulting share balance is either too small or too large. Subsequent operations such as withdrawals, rebalancing, or price calculations rely on these distorted share values, leading to arithmetic errors, unexpected reverts, and ultimately an accounting mismatch where the protocol appears to lose or gain funds. The impact includes incorrect user balances displayed in the UI (e.g., a user sees a zero or reduced balance after a successful deposit), failed rebalancing transactions, and potential loss of trust because the protocol can no longer guarantee that each share corresponds to the correct amount of the underlying asset. The issue manifests only when the vault’s decimal configuration deviates from the six‑decimal standard, which may happen during deployment or through an upgrade that does not enforce the original setting. All participants who interact with the vault—depositors, withdrawers, and the protocol’s operators—are affected because the accounting invariants are broken. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that reviewed the vault’s initialization parameters and identified that the decimals field was not immutable. It can be hard to notice because the numbers may still look plausible; the discrepancy often only surfaces when large rebalancing operations trigger a revert or when users observe unexpected balance changes. To remediate, the vault should lock its decimal precision to six at deployment, enforce this constraint in any future upgrades, and add explicit checks that reject any attempt to set a different decimal value. By aligning the contract’s arithmetic with the known decimal scale of the wrapped asset, the accounting logic regains its correctness and the protocol’s financial guarantees are restored.

title: CompensationPriceFinder::getZeroForOne may compute smaller effective prices than expected
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the compensation price calculation routine for zero‑for‑one swaps. The function `CompensationPriceFinder::getZeroForOne` contains a guard `if (sumAmount0Deltas > taxInEther)` that determines whether the effective price validation is performed. Because the guard requires the accumulated token0 delta to exceed the tax amount, the validation is skipped whenever `sumAmount0Deltas` is less than or equal to `taxInEther`. In those cases the code proceeds to a fallback path that computes a simple price using `simplePstarX96 = sumAmount1Deltas.divX96(sumAmount0Deltas + taxInEther)`. This simple price can be lower than the price that would have been accepted by the original validation, leading to a smaller effective price being used for compensation. Additionally, after iterating over all ticks, the final price check uses a strict greater‑than comparison (`if (simplePstarX96 > priceLowerSqrtX96^2)`) instead of a non‑strict comparison. When the computed price equals the lower bound, the condition fails and the routine returns a 512‑bit square‑root price rather than invoking `_zeroForOneGetFinalCompensationPrice`, again resulting in a lower price. The root cause is an overly restrictive conditional branch and an asymmetrical final comparison, both of which were introduced to avoid underflow or division‑by‑zero errors but inadvertently bypass legitimate price checks. An attacker or a malicious swap can trigger the bypass by ensuring `sumAmount0Deltas` does not exceed the tax, causing the contract to skip the proper compensation calculation and award liquidity providers a price that is smaller than the market price. The impact is that liquidity providers may receive excess compensation, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions and potentially inflating token balances. This occurs during the execution of zero‑for‑one swaps when the token0 delta is low relative to the tax, and it affects any liquidity provider participating in such swaps. The issue was discovered through a manual audit that examined the conditional logic and identified the mismatch between the guard and the intended price range validation. It can be hard to notice because the contract still executes without reverting, and the over‑compensation manifests as a subtle increase in LP balances rather than an outright failure. To remediate, the guard should be removed or relaxed so that the price validation runs regardless of the relation between `sumAmount0Deltas` and `taxInEther`, and the final comparison should be changed to a non‑strict `>=` to ensure the compensation routine is invoked when the price equals the lower bound. Conceptually, the fix restores the invariant that the effective price must always be validated against the tick range before any compensation is applied, preventing the calculation of a smaller-than‑expected price and preserving correct accounting for all participants.

title: Incorrect EIP-712 TXTYPE_HASH in SecuritizeSwap
description:
SecuritizeSwap::TXTYPE_HASH does not match the actual message structure being encoded for EIP-712 signature verification. The constant is defined as the hash of:

```
"ExecutePreApprovedTransaction(string memory _senderInvestor, address _destination,address _executor,bytes _data, uint256[] memory _params)"
```

But the actual `abi.encode` call in `SecuritizeSwap::doExecuteByInvestor` encodes a different structure:

```solidity
function doExecuteByInvestor(
    uint8 _securitizeHsmSigV,
    bytes32 _securitizeHsmSigR,
    bytes32 _securitizeHsmSigS,
    string memory _senderInvestorId,
    address _destination,
    bytes memory _data,
    address _executor,
    uint256[] memory _params
) internal {
    bytes32 txInputHash = keccak256(
        abi.encode(
            TXTYPE_HASH,
            _destination,
            _params[0], //value
            keccak256(_data),
            noncePerInvestor[_senderInvestorId],
            _executor,
            _params[1], //gasLimit
            keccak256(abi.encodePacked(_senderInvestorId))
        )
    );
    ...
}
```

The type string declares 5 parameters in this order:
1) string _senderInvestor  
2) address _destination  
3) address _executor  
4) bytes _data  
5) uint256[] _params  

But the actual encoding has 7 parameters:
1) address destination  
2) uint256 value (from `params[0]`)  
3) bytes32 dataHash (keccak of `_data`)  
4) uint256 nonce  
5) address executor  
6) uint256 gasLimit (from `params[1]`)  
7) bytes32 investorIdHash (keccak of `_senderInvestor`)

This is a significant mismatch between the expected message type and the actual encoded parameters that violates EIP-712 structured data standards.

Another problem is that the EIP-712 spec does not have storage qualifiers like `storage` and `memory` in the type hash string. So even if the above mismatch didn't occur, the current hash is still incorrect as it has been created using an incorrect type hash string.
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability is a mismatch between the EIP‑712 type hash constant (TXTYPE_HASH) and the actual data structure that the contract encodes when verifying off‑chain signatures. The constant was generated from a type string that includes a memory qualifier and lists five parameters (string, address, address, bytes, uint256[]), while the doExecuteByInvestor function encodes seven fields: destination address, value, data hash, nonce, executor address, gas limit, and a hash of the investor identifier. Because the hash does not represent the real encoded layout, the on‑chain keccak256 of the encoded message never matches the hash that was signed off‑chain. The root cause is an incorrect type‑hash definition that does not follow the EIP‑712 specification, which forbids storage qualifiers and requires the type string to exactly mirror the encoded fields. An attacker cannot directly steal assets, but the bug can be exploited to cause denial‑of‑service by repeatedly submitting transactions that will always fail signature verification, preventing legitimate users from executing swaps. The impact is that any user attempting to execute a pre‑approved transaction experiences a revert or a transaction that appears pending, leading to confusion as balances remain unchanged and expected refunds or swaps never occur. This occurs whenever doExecuteByInvestor is called, affecting all investors and any external wallet or signing tool that relies on standard EIP‑712 signatures. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the declared type string with the actual abi.encode call and noted the presence of memory keywords, which are not part of the EIP‑712 schema. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles and the mismatch only surfaces at runtime during signature verification, often producing generic error messages. To remediate, the TXTYPE_HASH constant must be regenerated from a corrected type string that omits memory qualifiers and lists the exact seven parameters in the order they are encoded. Updating the constant and redeploying the contract (or using a proxy upgrade) will align the on‑chain hash with the off‑chain signed data, restoring proper signature validation and allowing transactions to succeed as intended.

title: Insufficient fee validation in STBL_Register::setupAsset can cause underflow
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability is an insufficient cumulative fee validation in the asset registration and fee‑setting functions of the stablecoin protocol. Individual fee parameters—deposit fee, haircut and insurance fee—are each checked for range, but the contract never verifies that their combined value expressed in basis points does not exceed the 100 % threshold (10000 basis points). In the calculateDepositFees routine each fee amount is derived from the gross stable value, and later the issuer contracts compute the net stable value by subtracting the sum of these three amounts from the gross value. When the total of the three fees is greater than 100 %, the subtraction yields a negative intermediate result, which in unsigned arithmetic causes an underflow and triggers a revert. This error can be exploited simply by configuring an asset with a fee schedule whose combined deposit‑time fees exceed 100 %, causing any deposit transaction to fail. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: users attempting to deposit receive a transaction revert, their balances remain unchanged, and the protocol cannot issue net stable tokens for that asset. The condition occurs at asset setup or fee update time, because the functions that store fee values lack a cumulative check, and it manifests during the first deposit after such a configuration. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined fee calculations and identified that the sum of fees was never bounded. It is hard to notice because each fee individually passes its own validation, so only specific fee combinations reveal the problem. The appropriate mitigation is to add a validation step in the setupAsset and setFees functions that ensures depositFee + hairCut + insuranceFee ≤ 10000 basis points before accepting the parameters. This prevents the underflow, aligns the contract with the business logic that fees cannot exceed the total value, and restores correct accounting where users expect a positive net balance after depositing.

title: Licredity::decreaseDebtShare bypasses interest accrual
description: A borrower can call Licredity::decreaseDebtShare to repay their loan. Because this call can only reduce debt, it’s treated as “safe” and allowed outside the Licredity::unlock flow. However, interest accrues only during unlock, swap, and liquidity add/remove operations. Therefore calling decreaseDebtShare directly therefore uses the last totalDebtBalance/totalDebtShare without first accruing interest, so the repayment is computed from a stale state.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an interest‑accrual bypass in the decreaseDebtShare function of the Licredity contract. Borrowers are allowed to call decreaseDebtShare directly to repay a portion of their loan because the function only reduces debt and was considered safe to be used outside the normal unlock flow. However, the contract only accrues interest during specific operations such as unlock, swap, and liquidity add or remove. When a borrower calls decreaseDebtShare without first triggering one of those operations, the contract uses the previously stored totalDebtBalance and totalDebtShare values, which do not reflect any interest that should have accumulated during the elapsed time. Consequently, the repayment amount is calculated from a stale state and the borrower effectively skips the interest that would normally be owed. This can be exploited by opening a borrowing position, allowing time to pass so that interest would accrue, and then repaying via a direct decreaseDebtShare call. The attacker walks away having paid only the principal while the protocol loses the expected interest revenue. The impact is primarily economic: liquidity providers receive less yield, the protocol’s net APY is reduced, and accounting records become inconsistent because interest remains unrecorded until another participant triggers an accrual hook. The issue was discovered during a security audit by adding a test that warps the blockchain timestamp, changes the oracle price, and calls decreaseDebtShare directly, confirming that no interest is accrued and the repayment equals the original borrowed amount. The bug is subtle because the function is labeled as “safe” and does not modify any external state besides the debt share, making it easy to overlook that interest must be pulled first. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show that the loan balance drops to zero after repayment, yet the protocol still holds an unpaid interest component, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual outcomes. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting or state‑update bugs where a necessary side‑effect (interest accrual) is omitted. To remediate, the contract should either pull interest at the beginning of decreaseDebtShare (a “pull‑accrual” pattern) or restrict decreaseDebtShare to be callable only within the unlock context where interest is guaranteed to be up‑to‑date.

title: Token value locks done as part of issuance restrict subsequently transferred unlocked tokens after negative rebasing
description:
Description: When a token issuance occurs, as part of that token issuance two types of locks can be enacted:
• share value based lock via:
TokenIssuer::issueTokens
-- DSToken::issueTokensWithMultipleLocks
---- TokenLibrary::issueTokensCustom
------ ComplianceService::validateIssuance
-------- ComplianceServiceRegulated::recordIssuance -> createIssuanceInformation
• token value based lock via:
TokenIssuer::issueTokens
-- DSToken::issueTokensWithMultipleLocks
---- TokenLibrary::issueTokensCustom
------ InvestorLockManager::addManualLockRecord -> createLock -> createLockForInvestor

Impact: In a scenario where:
• Investor1 has a token issuance for 1000 tokens with both shared-base and token-value based locks for that issuance
• Negative rebasing occurs
• Investor2 transfers 1000 unlocked tokens to Investor1
The token value lock from Investor1's original token issuance will restrict the transfer of the unlocked tokens which Investor2 subsequently transferred to Investor1.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an over‑locking bug that occurs when token‑value based locks are recorded in absolute token units at issuance and a negative rebasing event reduces the holder's token balance. Because the lock amount is not scaled with the rebasing multiplier, the lock can exceed the actual balance after the rebasing, causing the lock manager to treat a portion of the balance – including any subsequently received unlocked tokens – as non‑transferable. In the described scenario, Investor1 receives 1000 tokens with a full token‑value lock, then a negative rebase halves the balance to 500 tokens while the lock remains at 1000 tokens. When Investor2 later transfers 1000 unlocked tokens to Investor1, the lock still applies to the total token amount, so only the 500 rebased tokens are considered transferable and the newly received 1000 tokens are partially locked. This leads to a user‑visible symptom where the account balance shows a higher amount (e.g., 1500 tokens) but the transferable amount is much lower (e.g., 500 tokens), breaking the expectation that received tokens can be freely moved. The issue was discovered through a targeted test case that simulated issuance, locking, negative rebasing, and subsequent transfer, revealing that the lock manager reports zero or reduced transferable tokens despite a positive balance. The bug is hard to notice because the lock behaves correctly before rebasing; only after the multiplier changes does the mismatch become apparent, and the over‑locking may be mistaken for a protocol restriction rather than a flaw. The root cause is the lock system’s design: it stores lock amounts in token units instead of share units that automatically adjust with rebasing. To fix the problem, the lock accounting should be refactored to store all lock amounts in shares, or the contract should recalculate token‑value locks whenever the rebasing multiplier changes, ensuring that locks always reflect the current token balance and do not unintentionally restrict transferred tokens.

title: All swaps other than the top-of-block swap will revert
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the afterSwap hook of the AngstromL2 contract, where the function _getSwapTaxAmount is called without considering whether the current swap is the top‑of‑block swap. For the first swap in a block, the protocol tax is correctly collected and the block number is stored in _blockOfLastTopOfBlock. However, for subsequent swaps in the same block the code still retrieves a non‑zero taxInEther value and passes it to _computeAndCollectProtocolSwapFee. Because the check for a zero tax is performed only after the fee collection, a debt is unintentionally created and the hook returns a non‑zero hookDeltaUnspecified. This violates the invariant that the hook must maintain zero balance deltas for all currencies (hookDeltaNeutrality). As a result, any swap that is not the top‑of‑block swap reverts with an error such as CurrencyNotSettled, effectively allowing only a single swap per block to succeed. The issue was discovered through a unit test that performed two swaps in the same block with different priority fees; the second swap consistently reverted. The bug is subtle because a single swap works correctly, and the failure only appears under the specific condition of multiple swaps within one block, making it easy to miss during casual testing. The impact is that users attempting to execute multiple trades in a single block experience unexpected reverts, leading to a poor user experience and potential loss of trading opportunities, though funds are not permanently stolen because the transaction reverts. The affected parties include any user or protocol component that relies on executing multiple swaps per block, as well as liquidity providers whose fees may be mis‑applied. The root cause is the lack of block‑context awareness in the tax calculation, causing double charging of the protocol fee. The recommended mitigation is to make taxInEther zero for non‑top‑of‑block swaps by checking whether the current block number equals _blockOfLastTopOfBlock before calling _computeAndCollectProtocolSwapFee. This restores the delta‑neutral property and allows multiple swaps per block without reverting.

title: TrustService::changeEntityOwner can overwrite existing _newOwner record, breaking 1-1 relationship between owners and addresses
description:
Description: TrustService::changeEntityOwner can overwrite existing _newOwner record, breaking 1-1 relation-
ship between owners and addresses.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the TrustService contract’s changeEntityOwner function, which updates the mapping that links an entity to its owner without enforcing the invariant that each owner may be associated with only one entity. The root cause is the absence of a check on the _newOwner address before overwriting the internal _newOwner record; the function simply writes the new association, thereby destroying any previous reverse mapping entry for that address. An attacker or any caller with permission to invoke changeEntityOwner can exploit this by selecting a new owner that already controls another entity. The exploit proceeds step‑by‑step: first, two distinct entities are created with separate owners; second, changeEntityOwner is called to transfer one entity to the address that already owns the second entity; third, the contract overwrites the owner‑to‑entity reverse mapping for the new owner, so the forward mapping now shows the new owner as controlling both entities, while the reverse mapping retains only the most recent association. As a result, the previously owned entity becomes orphaned—its owner cannot be retrieved through getEntityByOwner, and the original owner loses any reference to an entity. This breaks the business logic that assumes a one‑to‑one relationship between owners and entities, leading to accounting inconsistencies, potential denial‑of‑service for legitimate owners, and the possibility of hiding or misrepresenting ownership rights. The issue manifests when changeEntityOwner is called with a _newOwner that already has an entry in the owner‑to‑entity map; under those conditions the contract silently corrupts its state. Users experience symptoms such as seeing two entities listed under the same address in the UI while the lookup function returns only one, or finding that an entity they previously owned is no longer reachable, giving the impression that funds or rights have disappeared. The bug was discovered through a targeted unit test that performed the ownership transfer and asserted the expected one‑to‑one mapping, which failed after the transfer. Because the forward mapping still appears correct, the inconsistency can be subtle and may go unnoticed until reverse lookups are performed. The recommended remediation is to enforce uniqueness of the new owner, for example by adding a modifier (onlyNewEntityOwner) or an explicit require statement that checks the reverse mapping is empty before allowing the change, and to update both mappings atomically to preserve the invariant. This conceptual fix restores the intended one‑to‑one relationship and prevents orphaned entities and ambiguous ownership states.

title: Operators can lose their reward share
description: Description: The Rewards::distributeRewards function distributes rewards for epochs that are at least two epochs older than the current one. However, when calculating and distributing these rewards, the contract fetches the list of operators using l1Middleware.getAllOperators(), which returns the current set of operators. If an operator was active during the target epoch but has since been disabled and removed before the rewards distribution, they will not be included in the current operator list. This can occur if the SLASHING_WINDOW in AvalancheL1Middleware is shorter than 2 * epochDuration.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a reward‑distribution inconsistency that can cause operators to lose their entitled share of protocol rewards. The root cause lies in the Rewards::distributeRewards function, which obtains the list of operators by calling l1Middleware.getAllOperators(). This call returns the current set of operators, not the set that was active during the epoch for which rewards are being settled. Because rewards are only distributed for epochs that are at least two epochs older than the current one, an operator that was active in the target epoch may be disabled and subsequently removed before the distribution occurs. If the SLASHING_WINDOW parameter in AvalancheL1Middleware is shorter than twice the epoch duration, the removal can happen within the reward‑distribution delay window. When the contract later iterates over the current operator list to calculate and allocate shares, the removed operator is absent, resulting in a zero share entry for that epoch. From a user’s perspective, the affected operator sees no increase in their balance after a reward period, contrary to the expectation that they should receive a proportional payout. The impact is an unfair loss of rewards for legitimately active operators and a potential avenue for a privileged party to manipulate the operator set to exclude competitors. The issue was discovered through a targeted test that disabled and removed an operator before the delayed distribution and then verified that the operator’s share was zero while other operators received rewards. The bug is subtle because the discrepancy only appears after the delayed distribution, making it easy to attribute to normal variance or UI glitches. It belongs to the class of state‑inconsistent accounting bugs where mutable current state is incorrectly used for historical calculations. To remediate, the contract should maintain a historical snapshot of operator status per epoch or query the operator set as it existed at the target epoch, ensuring that reward eligibility is evaluated against the correct historical data. Additionally, configuring SLASHING_WINDOW to be at least 2 × epochDuration prevents premature removal of operators before their rewards are processed.

title: Curator Rewards Ownership Transfer
description:
Curators lose reward if they lose ownership of vault after epoch but before distribution  

The Rewards contract calculates and assigns curator shares for each epoch by calling `VaultTokenized(vault).owner()` to determine the curator (vault owner) who should receive rewards. However, this fetches the current owner of the vault at the time of reward distribution, not the owner during the epoch for which rewards are being distributed. Since `VaultTokenized` inherits from `OwnableUpgradeable`, ownership can be transferred at any time using `transferOwnership`. This means that if a vault changes ownership after an epoch ends but before rewards are distributed for that epoch, the new owner will receive the curator rewards for past epochs, even if they were not the owner during those epochs.
bug_full: The vulnerability is a historical ownership snapshot omission in the curator rewards mechanism of a DeFi protocol. The rewards contract calculates each epoch's curator share by calling the vault's owner() function at the moment rewards are distributed, rather than using the address that owned the vault during the epoch itself. Because VaultTokenized inherits from OwnableUpgradeable, ownership can be transferred at any time via transferOwnership. Consequently, if a vault changes hands after an epoch ends but before the distribution transaction runs, the contract will credit the curator rewards for that past epoch to the new owner, even though the new owner did not contribute to the vault during that period. This flaw arises from the root cause that the contract does not record or snapshot the vault owner at epoch boundaries, relying instead on a mutable state variable. An attacker or opportunistic buyer can exploit this by acquiring a vault immediately after an epoch concludes and before the protocol processes rewards, thereby retroactively claiming curator fees that rightfully belong to the previous owner. The impact is a misallocation of incentive payments: the original curator loses the expected reward, while the new owner receives unearned fees, breaking the protocol’s fairness and economic assumptions. The issue manifests when the reward distribution window is delayed relative to epoch finality, a common pattern in many staking or reward systems, and it affects any participant who transfers vault ownership in that interval. It was discovered through a targeted test that transferred ownership between epoch end and reward distribution, observing that curatorShares for the original owner were zero while the new owner received a positive share. The bug can be subtle because the contract’s external behavior—reward claims—appears to work correctly for the current owner, and there is no immediate on‑chain indication that a historical owner was bypassed. From a user’s perspective, a curator who expects to receive a payout after an epoch may see their balance remain zero, while the new vault holder unexpectedly receives a token transfer. This violates the business logic that rewards should be tied to the entity that managed the vault during the rewarded period. The recommended remediation is to introduce a snapshot mechanism that records the vault owner at the end of each epoch (or at each ownership transfer) and to reference this immutable snapshot when assigning curator shares during distribution. By doing so, the contract will correctly attribute rewards to the historical owner, restoring fairness and preventing retroactive reward theft.

title: Inaccurate stake calculation due to decimal mismatch across multitoken asset classes
bug_full: The vulnerability is an inaccurate operator stake calculation caused by a decimal mismatch across multiple token types within a single asset class. The root cause is that the getOperatorStake view iterates over all vaults belonging to an asset class and adds the raw token amounts returned by each vault without first normalizing them to a common decimal base. Tokens such as USDC that use six decimals and tokens such as DAI that use eighteen decimals therefore contribute values that are not comparable; the six‑decimal amount is effectively treated as negligible or zero when summed with an eighteen‑decimal amount. An attacker or honest user can trigger the bug whenever an asset class contains at least two collaterals with different decimal precisions and the stake query is executed for an epoch in which those vaults are active. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that the displayed operator stake is far lower than the amount actually deposited, sometimes appearing as zero even though the vault balances show the correct token amounts. This discrepancy violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions, leading to under‑reported stake, potentially skewed reward distribution, and incorrect slashing logic. The issue was discovered during a security audit that added a test case depositing both a six‑decimal token and an eighteen‑decimal token into separate vaults and then asserting that the summed stake does not match the expected total. The bug is subtle because each individual vault reports the correct raw balance, and only the aggregated view is wrong, making it easy to miss in standard unit tests that do not mix token decimals. The correct mitigation is to normalize each vault’s raw stake to a common precision—typically eighteen decimals—by multiplying when the token’s decimals are lower than eighteen or dividing when they are higher, before adding the value to the total stake. This conceptual fix restores accurate accounting without altering the underlying vault logic and ensures that users see a stake value that truly reflects the value of all deposited assets.

title: Rewards distribution DoS due to uncached secondary asset classes
