bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the rewards distribution routine caused by the contract reading an uncached total‑stake value for secondary asset classes. The root cause is that the internal function that calculates an operator’s share accesses the totalStakeCache mapping directly instead of invoking the getter that falls back to a recalculation when the cache entry is missing. Only the primary asset class is automatically cached by regular node‑addition and slashing operations; secondary classes are cached only when a slash occurs for that class or when an explicit calcAndCacheStakes call is made. Consequently, when distributeRewards iterates over all asset class identifiers, it may encounter a zero entry in totalStakeCache for a secondary class that has never been cached. The subsequent division of the reward amount by this zero totalStake triggers a division‑by‑zero revert, causing the whole rewards distribution transaction to fail. This failure manifests to users as rewards not being distributed for the affected epoch – operators see no increase in their balances, and the UI may show “no rewards” or “distribution failed”. The condition occurs only for epochs where at least one secondary asset class has never been cached, which is typical when no slashing or manual caching has been performed for that class. The affected parties are the protocol participants who rely on timely reward payouts and the protocol itself, because a halted distribution can erode trust and require manual intervention. The issue was discovered during a security audit that inspected the reward‑calculation code and identified the direct cache access pattern. It is subtle because the primary asset class works correctly, so the bug only appears under specific asset‑class configurations, making it easy to miss in routine testing. The proper fix is to replace the direct cache read with a call to the getter that performs a fallback calculation, or to add logic that checks for a zero cache entry and invokes calcAndCacheStakes before using the value. This change restores the invariant that totalStake is always non‑zero for a valid epoch and prevents the division‑by‑zero revert, eliminating the temporary DoS condition.

title: MajorityChoicePrompt SessionManager Instance Conflict
description:
Description: MajorityChoicePrompt is supposed to support multiple instances of SessionManager, however every instance of SessionManager starts with `QuestionManager::nextQuestionId = 0`. This is problematic as `MajorityChoicePrompt::revealReaction` does this:  

```solidity
Reaction storage r = reactions[_questionId][_user];
require(!r.baseReaction.reactions[_questionId][_user], AnswerAlreadyRevealed(_user, _gameId, _questionId));
```  

When a user plays `questionId = 0` on the first instance of SessionManager everything will work ok and `reactions[_questionId][_user].revealed` will be set to true. If that same user plays `questionId = 0` on a second instance of SessionManager which uses the same instance of MajorityChoicePrompt, then `MajorityChoicePrompt::revealReaction` will revert with `AnswerAlreadyRevealed`.  

Another potential issue is that `results[questionId][player]` will have valid results stored for a player from games on the first instance and this mapping doesn't differentiate between the different instances of SessionManager.
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability is a state‑collision bug that arises when multiple SessionManager contracts share a single instance of MajorityChoicePrompt (or the related SPBinaryPrompt and TriviaChoicePrompt). Each SessionManager starts its QuestionManager with nextQuestionId set to zero, so the first question in every new session has the same identifier as the first question in previous sessions. The prompt contracts keep internal mappings—reactions[questionId][user] and results[questionId][player]—that are keyed only by questionId and user address, without any session or game identifier. Because the prompt instance is reused, these mappings retain data from earlier sessions. When a user who answered questionId 0 in the first session attempts to answer questionId 0 in a second session, the revealReaction function reads the stale flag in reactions and the require statement fails, reverting with AnswerAlreadyRevealed. Similarly, results[questionId][player] may return or overwrite scores from a previous game, leading to incorrect or missing results. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a refund or answer cannot be submitted, that their balance appears unchanged, or that scores remain zero despite participation. The protocol’s business logic assumes that each question identifier is unique within the lifetime of the prompt contract; this assumption is violated when identifiers are reused across sessions, breaking accounting and game flow. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between SessionManager and the prompt contracts and noted that the mappings were not scoped per session. It is subtle because the same contract address is used, and tests that only cover a single session do not expose the collision. The impact includes transaction reverts, inability to replay games, potential loss of deposited funds, and corrupted result data, affecting all users of the affected prompts and the overall protocol reliability. The recommended remediation is to instantiate a fresh prompt contract for each SessionManager, or enforce a single active SessionManager at any time and ensure that gameId, sessionId, and questionId are strictly increasing across sessions. Adding dedicated tests that simulate multiple SessionManager instances sharing a prompt will help prevent regression.

title: Hardcoded gas limit for hook in onSlash may cause reverts
description:
The onSlash function in the BaseDelegator contract conditionally invokes a hook via a low-level call if a hook address is set:
```solidity
assembly ("memory-safe") {
    pop(call(HOOK_GAS_LIMIT, hook_, 0, add(calldata_, 0x20), mload(calldata_), 0, 0))
}
```
This call uses a hardcoded gas limit (HOOK_GAS_LIMIT), and the function enforces that at least HOOK_RESERVE + HOOK_GAS_LIMIT * 64 / 63 gas is available before proceeding. If this requirement is not met, the function reverts with `BaseDelegator__InsufficientHookGas`.

This rigid gas enforcement introduces a fragility: if the hook's execution requires more gas than allocated by HOOK_GAS_LIMIT, the call may silently fail or the transaction may revert entirely.

Impact: Hooks that require more gas than the hardcoded limit will consistently fail, potentially breaking integrations. As protocol complexity grows, hardcoded gas limits become brittle and may hinder composability or future extensions.
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability is a hard‑coded gas limit used when BaseDelegator’s onSlash function invokes an optional external hook via a low‑level call. The contract reserves a fixed amount of gas (HOOK_GAS_LIMIT) and checks that at least HOOK_RESERVE + HOOK_GAS_LIMIT*64/63 gas remains; if not, it reverts with BaseDelegator__InsufficientHookGas. Because the limit is immutable, any hook whose execution consumes more gas than the preset stipend will cause the call to return false or trigger the revert condition. An attacker or developer can exploit this by deploying a hook that deliberately exceeds the gas budget, causing the slash operation to fail and potentially denying service to users who rely on the hook for reward distribution or state updates. The impact is that legitimate integrations see missing refunds, zeroed balances, or failed slash processing, breaking business logic that assumes the hook always succeeds. The issue manifests whenever onSlash is called with a non‑zero hook address and the hook’s code grows in complexity, which is common as the protocol evolves. All participants—delegators, slashing victims, and downstream contracts—are affected because the failure aborts the entire transaction, leaving users with unexpected “nothing happened” UI feedback. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the assembly block and noted the static gas constant, a pattern known to cause brittleness in composable contracts. It is hard to notice because the low‑level call silently discards the return value, so developers may not see an error unless the explicit gas‑reserve check triggers a revert. The correct mitigation is to replace the fixed HOOK_GAS_LIMIT with a configurable parameter controlled by the contract owner or governance, or to forward all remaining gas and explicitly handle the call’s success flag, thereby aligning the hook’s gas budget with actual execution needs. In generic terms, this is a classic “hard‑coded gas stipend” bug that violates the assumption that external callbacks have sufficient resources, leading to denial‑of‑service style failures and broken accounting.

title: In the RedemptionManager::executeTwoStepRedemption function
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the redemption workflow of the RedemptionManager contract, specifically in the executeTwoStepRedemption function. The function calls a liquidity provider’s supplyTo method with a parameter called minOutputAmount that represents the smallest amount of output tokens the caller expects to receive. After the supplyTo call, the contract reads the balance of the received liquidity token, calculates a protocol fee using an internal _getFee helper, and then checks that the balance minus the fee is still at least the original minOutputAmount. If the condition fails, the contract reverts with a SlippageControlError. The root cause is that the minOutputAmount supplied to the liquidity provider does not include the fee that will be deducted later. Consequently, when the provider returns exactly the requested minOutputAmount, the subsequent fee subtraction reduces the net balance below the original threshold, causing a false slippage error. This mismatch can be exploited by simply providing a scenario where the provider meets the nominal minimum but the fee pushes the net amount under the limit, leading to unnecessary transaction reverts. The impact is that legitimate redemptions may fail, users see refunds or withdrawals reported as failed, balances appear unchanged or zero in the UI, and the protocol experiences a denial‑of‑service effect because users cannot complete expected operations. The condition occurs whenever the provider’s output equals the unadjusted minOutputAmount and a non‑zero fee is applied, which is a common case in normal operation. All participants who interact with the redemption function—users, integrators, and the protocol itself—are affected because the bug breaks the accounting assumptions that the net output after fees must meet the user‑specified minimum. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the parameters passed to supplyTo with the later slippage check and identified the inconsistency. It can be hard to notice because the slippage check itself is correctly implemented; the problem lies in the earlier input value, which may appear reasonable at first glance. To remediate the bug, the contract should compute the expected fee before calling supplyTo and add that fee to the minOutputAmount argument, ensuring that the post‑fee balance will still satisfy the slippage condition. This adjustment aligns the economic expectations of the caller with the protocol’s fee model and prevents legitimate transactions from being incorrectly reverted.

title: CollateralLiquidityProvider AvailableLiquidity Miscalculation
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the CollateralLiquidityProvider contract where the availableLiquidity view function returns the raw balance of the collateral asset held by the provider and assumes a one‑to‑one conversion to liquidity tokens. This assumption is incorrect because the actual liquidity that can be delivered to redeemers is determined by the externalCollateralRedemption contract, which may apply fees, exchange rates, or other conversion mechanisms that reduce the amount of liquidity tokens minted. The root cause is the omission of a call to externalCollateralRedemption.calculateLiquidityTokenAmount when computing available liquidity, leading to an over‑estimation of the pool’s capacity. An attacker does not directly profit, but a user can be misled: the UI or other callers see a high availableLiquidity value, attempt to redeem a certain amount, and the supplyTo function first checks the inflated figure. When the external redemption step executes, the actual token amount is lower, causing the transaction to revert with InsufficientLiquidity or to transfer fewer tokens than expected. From the user’s perspective this manifests as a situation where the contract reports sufficient funds, yet the redemption either fails or results in zero or unexpectedly small token balances, violating the expectation that a redeem call yields a proportional amount of liquidity tokens. The issue occurs whenever the external redemption contract does not maintain a 1:1 ratio, which is common when fees or market rates are involved. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the view’s return value with the logic inside supplyTo and noticed the mismatch. The bug can be hard to notice because the balance check passes, and only after the redemption step does the discrepancy surface, often only in edge cases with non‑trivial fee structures. The problem belongs to the class of accounting or conversion bugs where internal state is reported without applying the same transformation as the execution path. To remediate, the availableLiquidity function should delegate to a private _availableLiquidity helper that first reads the collateral balance and then invokes externalCollateralRedemption.calculateLiquidityTokenAmount to obtain the true amount of liquidity tokens that can be supplied. Additionally, the external availableLiquidity function should call this internal helper instead of duplicating the raw balance logic, eliminating code duplication and ensuring consistent calculations across the contract.

title: Unsafe external calls made during proportional LP fee transfers can be used to reenter wrapper contracts
bug_full: The vulnerability is an unsafe external call performed during the proportional liquidity‑provider (LP) fee transfer in the ERC721WrapperBase partial unwrap routine. When a user calls the `unwrap` function, the contract first invokes an internal `_unwrap` routine that transfers fee tokens directly from the underlying Uniswap pool to the caller‑specified `to` address. If the underlying position holds assets that trigger external callbacks—such as native ETH in Uniswap V4 or ERC‑777 tokens with transfer hooks—the recipient contract can execute code in its fallback function before the wrapper finishes its own state updates. The wrapper then proceeds to burn the specified amount of ERC‑6909 tokens and reduce the caller’s balance, but because the external call occurred earlier, the re‑entrancy can happen while the balance and total supply are still unchanged. The `callThroughEVC` modifier and the `nonReentrantChecksAndControlCollateral` modifier appear to protect against re‑entrancy, yet the execution context defers the re‑entrancy checks, allowing the callback to bypass them. An attacker can therefore re‑enter the wrapper contract, potentially invoking another unwrap or borrowing from the vault before the original burn is applied. This can lead to inconsistent accounting, unexpected fee distribution, or a situation where the user’s LP token balance is reduced more than intended, sometimes appearing as if funds disappear or refunds are missing. From a user’s perspective, a call to unwrap may result in the balance staying the same, dropping to zero, or the user receiving no refund despite expecting a partial return. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test where a malicious contract re‑entered the wrapper via its fallback during the fee transfer. The bug is hard to notice because the external call is embedded in a seemingly innocuous internal function and the modifiers give a false sense of safety. The vulnerability belongs to the class of re‑entrancy bugs caused by external calls before state changes (checks‑effects‑interactions violation). Mitigation involves applying a proper re‑entrancy guard around the entire unwrap flow or restructuring the code so that all internal accounting (balance updates, token burns) occurs before any external transfer, thereby preventing a malicious callback from influencing the contract’s state.

title: users_can_enable_tokenids_as_collateral_even_if_they_do_not_own_any_of_the_erc-6909_supply
description: It is possible for users to enable tokenIds that that they do not own as collateral. Based on the cur‑rent remediated logic, it does not appear possible for this to be further weaponized beyond the blocking of liquidations, as described in C-01, stemming from the incorrect implementation ERC721WrapperBase::normalizedToFull as described in H-02. That said, this ability for a borrower to add a tokenId as collateral for which they have zero ERC-6909 balance should be explicitly forbidden. Liquidators who do not already own a share of the position but need to enable the tokenId as collateral to pass account liquidity checks should still be able to do so by utilizing the deferred checks of EVC batch calls.
bug_full: The vulnerability consists of allowing users to enable ERC‑6909 tokenIds as collateral even when they hold no balance of the underlying token. The root cause is the absence of an ownership verification step in the enableTokenIdAsCollateral function; the contract records the tokenId as collateral without checking balanceOf(sender, tokenId). This omission stems from an incorrect implementation of the normalizedToFull conversion in the ERC721WrapperBase, which fails to enforce the invariant that collateral must be backed by actual token supply. An attacker or any borrower can exploit the flaw by calling enableTokenIdAsCollateral with a tokenId whose total ERC‑6909 supply is zero. The contract then adds the tokenId to the borrower’s enabled collateral list, causing the protocol’s liquidity and liquidation checks to treat the position as sufficiently collateralised despite the lack of real assets. The impact is that liquidations can be blocked because the system believes there is collateral to seize, while in reality there is none. This can lead to frozen positions, inaccurate risk metrics, and potential protocol instability. The condition under which the bug manifests is when a tokenId has zero total supply (e.g., the token has not been wrapped) and a user invokes the enable function. Both borrowers and liquidators are affected: borrowers can unintentionally or maliciously prevent their positions from being liquidated, and liquidators may be unable to execute legitimate liquidations, undermining confidence in the protocol’s safety. The issue was discovered through an audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test: the test enabled a tokenId with zero supply and verified that the enabled token list grew, confirming the missing check. The bug is subtle because the UI may show the token as enabled collateral, giving the impression that the user’s balance is being used, while the underlying balance remains zero, leading to a mismatch between displayed collateral and actual holdings. To remediate, the contract should enforce a non‑zero balance requirement when enabling collateral, reverting with a clear error if balanceOf(sender, tokenId) equals zero. This aligns the contract’s state with the business logic that collateral must be backed by real token holdings, restores correct liquidation behavior, and prevents the protocol from being gamed by false collateral entries.

title: Hardcoding deadline for permit() will mess up the structHash leading to an invalid signature
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability is a hard‑coded deadline used when invoking ERC20Permit’s permit function, which causes a mismatch between the deadline embedded in the user’s signed message and the deadline supplied to the contract. In EIP‑2612, the deadline is part of the struct that is hashed and signed; any difference, even a single second, produces a different structHash. The contract recomputes the hash using the hard‑coded block.timestamp+300 value, then attempts to recover the signer with ECDSA.recover. Because the hash does not correspond to the one the user signed, the recovered address differs from the owner, triggering an ERC2612InvalidSigner revert. This bug manifests whenever a function such as pledge or refundToken tries to approve ERC20 tokens via permit. From the user’s perspective, a transaction that appears to succeed on the UI results in no token approval: the expected outcome is that the contract records an allowance, but in reality the allowance remains unchanged, leading to missing balances, failed refunds, or stalled pledges. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the permit call flow and identified the hard‑coded deadline as a deviation from the signed data. It can be hard to notice because the transaction may not revert outright; instead, downstream logic that expects an approved allowance simply does not execute, producing silent failures. The root cause is a logical error in parameter handling rather than a cryptographic flaw. To fix the problem, the contract should accept the deadline as an explicit argument supplied by the caller (e.g., data.deadline) and pass that exact value to the permit function, ensuring the structHash matches the signed message. This correction restores proper signature verification, allowing permit‑based approvals to function as intended and preventing denial‑of‑service conditions where users cannot grant allowances through signed permits.

title: Don't add duplicate documentHash to DocumentManager::DocumentStorage::_docHashes when overwriting via _setDocument as this causes panic revert when calling _removeDocument
bug_full: The vulnerability is a duplicate‑hash logic error in the DocumentManager contract. When the internal function _setDocument is invoked to overwrite an existing document, it unconditionally appends the supplied documentHash to the private array _docHashes. Because the function does not verify whether the hash is already present, overwriting creates two identical entries in the array. The removal routine _removeDocument assumes each hash appears only once; it iterates over the entire array, swaps a matching element with the last entry, and then calls pop() to shrink the array. If duplicate hashes exist, the loop continues after the first deletion and eventually accesses an index that no longer exists, triggering a Solidity panic due to an out‑of‑bounds array access. From a user’s perspective, updating a document appears to succeed, but the UI may show the same document listed twice, and any subsequent attempt to delete the document reverts with a panic error, effectively locking the document data. The issue was discovered through unit testing that deliberately overwrote a document and then called the removal function, reproducing the panic. It is hard to notice in production because the contract does not emit an explicit error for duplicate entries, and the revert only occurs during removal, a path that may be exercised infrequently. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for document management: legitimate users cannot delete or replace documents, breaking business logic that relies on accurate accounting of stored documents. The affected parties include any user or protocol component that interacts with DocumentManager, such as token holders relying on document provenance. To remediate, the _setDocument function should check for the existence of the hash before pushing it, or the storage structure should be replaced with an EnumerableSet that enforces uniqueness. Additionally, the removal loop should break after successfully deleting an entry to avoid further iteration over a shortened array. This class of bug falls under duplicate entry insertion leading to array‑index errors, a common pattern in smart contracts that manage dynamic collections without proper uniqueness checks.

title: Payout distributions to Remora token holders are diluted by initial token owner mint
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability originates from the way dividend payouts are calculated in the Remora token system. When the token contract is initialized, the entire initial supply is minted to a single tokenOwner address. The dividend manager records the total token supply at the moment a payout is created and later distributes the payout by dividing the payout amount by this recorded totalSupply. Because the owner’s large balance is part of the totalSupply, each token – including those held by regular users – receives a proportionally smaller share of the payout. This results in reward dilution for all non‑owner holders, especially when the owner holds a significant percentage of the supply. The issue can be exploited simply by the token owner retaining or acquiring a large amount of tokens; no special transaction or code execution is required. The impact is that users who expect a certain dividend amount receive less, sometimes dramatically less, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual rewards, which may appear as missing or near‑zero balances after a claim. The flaw manifests whenever a payout is distributed after the initial mint, and it affects every token holder except the owner, as well as the overall perception of fairness in the protocol. The problem was discovered during a security audit that compared the token’s initialization logic with the dividend manager’s payout calculation and identified that the denominator used for distribution includes non‑circulating tokens owned by the protocol. This type of bug is hard to notice because the arithmetic itself is correct; the error lies in the business logic of which supply should be considered for dividend allocation. To remediate, the contract should exclude the owner’s tokens from the payout denominator, either by subtracting the owner’s balance from totalSupply at distribution time or by maintaining a separate circulating‑supply variable that can be set by an admin. Alternative mitigations include tracking the owner’s holdings in a dedicated variable and using it to adjust the divisor, though this still requires trust in the owner to update the value correctly. Acknowledging the dilution is also an option if the protocol accepts the economic consequence, but a proper fix restores the intended reward distribution and aligns the system with user expectations that each token receives an equal share of dividends.

title: Burning ALL PropertyTokens of a frozen holder results in the holder losing the payouts distribution while he was frozen
description:
Burning PropertyTokens from frozen holders has an edge case when all the tokens owned by a frozen holder get burned. This is how burning PropertyTokens impacts the payouts for distributions of frozen holders:
- If not all the PropertyTokens owned by a frozen holder are burned, the holder can still have access to the payouts for the distributions while he was frozen.
- If all the PropertyTokens owned by a frozen holder are burned, the holder would lose the payouts for the distributions while he was frozen.  

The discrepancy in the behavior when burning PropertyTokens of Frozen Holders demonstrates an edge case that can result in frozen holders losing payouts.  

For example – (Assume holders were frozen at the same index and got their tokens burned at the same index too):
- UserA has 1 PropertyToken and is frozen
- UserB has 2 PropertyTokens and is frozen too
- UserA and B get burned each a PropertyToken.  
  – UserA loses the payouts distributions while he was frozen, whilst UserB still has access to the payouts for the 2 PropertyTokens that he owned during those distributions.  

**Impact:** Burning ALL the PropertyTokens owned by a frozen holder causes the holder to lose the payouts for the distributions while he was frozen.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting edge case in a token contract that distributes periodic payouts to holders. When a holder is frozen, the contract continues to accrue payout credits for that holder based on the number of PropertyTokens owned at each distribution. The payout entitlement is stored in a mapping that is keyed to the holder’s current token balance. The root cause is that the burnFrom (and burn) functions do not consider the frozen status when a burn reduces the holder’s balance to zero. As a result, if a frozen holder’s entire token balance is burned before the holder is unfrozen, the contract removes the holder from the payout ledger, discarding all payouts that were earned while the holder was frozen. An attacker or any actor that can trigger a full burn on a frozen account can cause that account to lose its pending payouts, effectively denying the rightful owner their claimable funds. The impact is that frozen users who later have all their tokens burned see their payout balance drop to zero, even though they expected to receive the accumulated payouts after unfreezing. This manifests in the user interface as a missing or zero payout claim, contrary to the expectation that “my frozen account should still receive the payouts earned during the freeze”. The condition required for the bug to appear is a holder being in a frozen state and then having all of its PropertyTokens burned before being unfrozen. The issue was discovered during an audit test that simulated freezing a holder, distributing payouts, burning all tokens while still frozen, and then unfreezing the holder; the test showed that the payout balance was cleared. The bug is hard to notice because normal burning of non‑frozen holders works as intended, and the loss only occurs in the specific combination of freeze plus full burn, which may not be exercised in routine testing. To fix the problem, the contract should either prevent burning when the holder is frozen and the burn would leave a zero balance, or it should adjust the payout bookkeeping so that accrued payouts are retained even if the holder’s token balance becomes zero. Adding a check in burnFrom to revert when balanceOf(account) == 0 && isHolderFrozen(account) restores the intended business logic that frozen holders retain their payout rights until they are unfrozen.

title: Overriding fees can't be switched back once set
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability is a permanent fee‑override lock in the TokenBank contract. The contract is designed to allow an administrator to charge either a global base fee for all PropertyToken purchases or individualized per‑token fees. A boolean variable, overrideFees, controls which fee model is active: when true, the base fee is applied to every token; when false, the per‑token fee configuration is used. The root cause is a conditional update in the setBaseFee function that only writes the overrideFees variable when the supplied overrideFee argument is true. The code fragment if (overrideFee) { overrideFees = overrideFee; emit FeeOverride(overrideFee); } means that once overrideFees has been set to true, any subsequent call with overrideFee set to false does not modify the stored flag because the condition fails and the assignment is skipped. Consequently, the system cannot be switched back to per‑token fee mode. An attacker or any privileged user who can invoke setBaseFee can enable the override, after which the contract will forever charge the base fee, preventing the intended per‑token fee logic from ever being restored. This leads to an impact where the protocol loses flexibility in fee management, potentially overcharging users who expect token‑specific fees, and breaking business assumptions about fee accounting. The issue manifests only after the override flag has been set; attempts to reset it appear to have no effect, which can be confusing from a user interface perspective where fees suddenly become uniform across all tokens. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the one‑way conditional assignment. It may be hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly on the first activation of the override, and the lack of a revert path only becomes apparent later when administrators try to disable it. The recommended remediation is to assign the overrideFees variable unconditionally with the value of the overrideFee parameter and emit the corresponding event, thereby allowing the flag to be toggled both ways and restoring the intended fee selection mechanism.

title: Changing stablecoin on TokenBank can mess up fees collection
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability is a decimal‑normalization error in the TokenBank contract’s fee handling logic. Fee amounts are calculated and stored using the decimal precision of the stablecoin that is active at the moment the fee is generated. The contract assumes a six‑decimal stablecoin (such as USDC) and does not adjust the stored raw fee values when the stablecoin reference is later changed to a token with a different number of decimals. Consequently, pending fees that were computed under the old decimal regime are transferred later using the new token’s decimals without conversion. For example, a pending fee of 10 USDC (10 × 10⁶) becomes 0.1 USDT (10 × 10⁶ interpreted with 8 decimals) when the stablecoin is switched to USDT. This mismatch can also affect fees generated after the switch, because the fee calculation uses the new decimals but the transfer still uses the raw amount. The impact is that the protocol’s fee collector (custodial wallet) receives a different amount of value than intended, leading to under‑collection of revenue or, in some cases, over‑collection. The bug manifests when there are any unclaimed fees at the moment the stablecoin address is updated, which can happen during normal operations, for instance if a buyToken transaction occurs between a fee claim and a stablecoin change. Users may see the UI display the expected fee amount while the actual token transferred is significantly lower, creating the impression that fees have disappeared. The issue was discovered during an audit that flagged the claimAllFees loop with a comment indicating that pending fees were computed with the old stablecoin’s decimals. It is hard to notice because internal accounting appears correct; only the external transfer reveals the discrepancy. The root cause is the lack of a normalization step that converts stored fee values to the decimal precision of the currently configured stablecoin before any transfer. The recommended remediation is to introduce a helper function that scales the fee amount up or down based on the difference between the stored baseline (6 decimals) and the current stablecoin’s decimals, and to apply this conversion in the claimAllFees function (and any other place where fees are transferred). This aligns the contract with the same approach used in the PledgeManager and ensures that fee collection remains accurate regardless of which stablecoin is used.

title: Missing staleness check in PriceOracle::getTokenPrice
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability is a missing staleness validation in the price‑oracle wrapper function that relays data from an external Pyth oracle. The function retrieves a price using getPriceUnsafe, which returns the raw price together with its publish timestamp and confidence interval, but the wrapper never checks whether the timestamp is recent or whether the confidence interval meets a safety threshold. Because of this omission, a price that is hours old, or deliberately frozen by an attacker, is accepted as if it were current. An attacker who can delay oracle updates or submit a stale price can cause the contract to compute fees, collateral requirements, or other financial parameters based on outdated market information. This can lead to users being over‑charged, under‑paid, or otherwise experiencing incorrect accounting outcomes. The issue manifests whenever the contract calls getTokenPrice, which occurs during fee calculation, trade execution, or any operation that depends on the token’s market price. All participants that rely on accurate pricing—traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the business logic assumes that each price reflects the latest market state. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the oracle‑fetching code with the Pyth documentation and noted the absence of any timestamp or confidence checks. It can be hard to notice because the contract still returns a numeric price and does not revert, so normal operation appears to succeed even though the underlying data may be stale. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected fee amounts, trades that seem to execute at a price that does not match the UI, or balances that change in ways that do not align with current market rates. The vulnerability belongs to the class of oracle‑validation bugs where freshness or integrity checks are omitted, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that prices are up‑to‑date. To remediate, the wrapper should replace the unsafe call with a function that enforces a maximum age, such as getPriceNoOlderThan, and optionally verify that the confidence interval is within acceptable bounds before scaling and returning the price. This ensures that only recent, reliable price data influences protocol calculations, restoring the intended economic guarantees.

title: MetaVault::redeemRequiredBaseAssets
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the MetaVault::redeemRequiredBaseAssets function, which is intended to collect a specified amount of base tokens by iterating over a list of supported vaults and redeeming assets until the requirement is met. The root cause is a flawed withdrawal condition: the code checks whether a single vault can redeem an amount greater than or equal to the total requested baseTokens and, if so, performs a full withdrawal from that vault and breaks out of the loop. This logic ignores the possibility of aggregating smaller amounts from multiple vaults and does not limit the withdrawal to the exact remaining amount, leading to two main failure modes. First, when no individual vault holds enough balance to satisfy the whole request, the loop skips all vaults, the function exits without redeeming any assets, and the calling routine later reverts due to insufficient funds even though the combined balances of several vaults would have been sufficient. Second, if a vault can redeem more than the needed amount, the function still withdraws the full requested amount, potentially leaving excess USDe tokens inside the vault contract; those tokens remain idle and do not earn yield because the contract lacks a mechanism to restake or retrieve them after the yield phase begins. From a user’s perspective, this manifests as redemption transactions that either fail with no tokens received or result in unexpected zero balances, and as idle funds that do not generate expected returns. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where a comment highlighted the “only withdraw if a single withdraw can satisfy desired amount” check, and testing of multi‑vault scenarios revealed the problem. It can be hard to notice because the function superficially appears to loop over vaults, yet the early break condition prevents partial withdrawals, and typical unit tests may only cover cases where a single vault suffices. The vulnerability does not directly enable theft but causes economic loss, protocol liquidity shortfalls, and broken accounting assumptions. The recommended remediation is to track the cumulative amount redeemed, compute the remaining amount after each iteration, and withdraw either the exact remaining amount if the current vault can satisfy it or the maximum possible amount otherwise, updating the redeemed total each step. This approach allows the contract to aggregate small redemptions across multiple vaults, avoids over‑withdrawal, and ensures that no USDe tokens remain stranded, thereby aligning the implementation with the intended business logic of precise, yield‑preserving asset redemption.

title: Duplicate vaults can be pushed to assetsArr
bug_full: The vulnerability is a duplicate‑vault addition flaw in the MetaVault contract. The addVault function, although restricted to the contract owner, lacks a guard against inserting the same vault address more than once. Each call to addVaultInner creates a TAsset struct, stores it in the assetsMap mapping, and pushes it onto the assetsArr array without verifying whether the address already exists. Consequently, the same vault can appear multiple times in assetsArr while the mapping entry is overwritten each time. When the contract later executes its redemption routine (redeemMetaVaults) or attempts to remove a vault, the logic assumes a one‑to‑one relationship between the mapping and the array. During removal, the function removeVaultAndRedeemInner clears the assetsMap entry and removes one copy from assetsArr. If a duplicate entry remains, a subsequent call to removeVault triggers requireSupportedVault, which reads the now‑cleared mapping entry (address(0)) and reverts, leaving the duplicate element stranded. This situation can arise whenever the owner adds a vault twice, either inadvertently or maliciously. Exploitation consists of the owner adding a vault repeatedly and then trying to remove it; the second removal fails, causing the contract to be unable to cleanly delete the vault. The impact is that assets associated with the duplicated vault may not be redeemed promptly, and users attempting to withdraw during the transition to the yield phase may experience delayed or blocked withdrawals. From a user’s perspective, deposits may appear to succeed, but later withdrawal attempts return nothing or revert, leading to confusion and a perception that funds have disappeared. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the vault management functions and identified the missing uniqueness check. It is hard to notice because normal operation (adding a vault once) works correctly, and the duplicate only manifests when removal is attempted, at which point the contract silently skips redemption for the zero‑balance second entry. The bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency errors caused by unchecked duplicate entries in collections. To remediate, the contract should enforce uniqueness by reverting if assetsMap[vaultAddress].asset is already non‑zero before pushing to assetsArr, or by using a set‑like data structure that prevents duplicates. This ensures that each vault can be added only once, keeping the mapping and array in sync and allowing reliable removal and redemption of assets.

title: Impossible to claim rewards when XPTiers are not set, resulting in permanently locked tokens once game has concluded
bug_full: The vulnerability is a business‑logic validation error that allows a game to be started without first configuring the XP tier array, which is required for reward calculation. The function setXPTiers is deliberately restricted to the Created state, but the startAndRevealGameQuestion routine does not verify that XP tiers have been set before transitioning the game to the Started state. As a result, a game can progress through all phases and reach the Concluded state while the xpTiers mapping for that game remains empty or zero. When the reward‑distribution contracts query the XP tiers to compute a Result struct, they receive a zero value for both the winning and losing branches. The ProportionalToXpReward strategy then distributes rewards proportionally to these XP values, which are all zero, so every claim transaction transfers no tokens. From a user’s perspective the expected reward is missing; the UI shows a successful claim but the balance remains unchanged, creating the impression that tokens are permanently locked. The impact is that winners cannot receive any payout after the game ends, effectively forfeiting their earned tokens. The issue occurs whenever a creator starts a game without first calling setXPTiers, which can happen because the start function lacks a prerequisite check. It affects all participants, the protocol’s economic model, and any token held for rewards. The bug was discovered during an audit that exercised the game lifecycle without setting XP tiers and observed zero reward outcomes. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the claim succeeds silently with a zero amount. The proper fix is to enforce that XP tiers are set before a game can be started, either by adding a require statement in startAndRevealGameQuestion or by allowing XP tiers to be set later but ensuring they are non‑empty before any reward calculation. This aligns the contract’s state transitions with its business rules and prevents the zero‑reward scenario.

title: Incorrect summation of curator shares in claimUndistributedRewards leads to deficit in claimed undistributed rewards
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect summation of curator shares inside the claimUndistributedRewards function of a rewards distribution contract. The root cause is a logical error in the aggregation step: the contract stores each curator’s total share for a given epoch in a mapping (curatorShares[epoch][curator]) that already represents the sum of all shares earned by that curator across every vault they own. When claimUndistributedRewards later iterates over the list of vaults for the epoch, it retrieves the owner of each vault and adds the entire curatorShares entry to the totalDistributedShares variable. If a curator controls multiple vaults, their aggregated share is added multiple times—once for each vault—resulting in an inflated totalDistributedShares value. This inflated sum is used in the formula undistributedRewards = totalRewardsForEpoch - Math.mulDiv(totalRewardsForEpoch, totalDistributedShares, BASIS_POINTS_DENOMINATOR). Because totalDistributedShares is too large, the computed undistributedRewards is smaller than the actual amount that remains unclaimed. Consequently, when a caller with the REWARDS_DISTRIBUTOR_ROLE invokes claimUndistributedRewards, they receive a reduced amount of tokens, and the remainder stays locked in the contract indefinitely. The bug manifests only when a curator owns two or more vaults that were active in the same epoch; under single‑vault ownership the calculation is correct. Users of the protocol, especially the rewards distributor and any curators with multiple vaults, are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated and funds become inaccessible. The issue was discovered during a security audit and confirmed with a proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrated the total of operator, vault and curator shares exceeding 10 000 basis points (the 100 % limit). The problem is subtle because the contract still appears to distribute rewards correctly for most participants, and the discrepancy may only be noticed when large curator holdings are involved or when the undistributed reward pool is inspected. To remediate, the contract must ensure that each curator’s share is counted only once per epoch. A common mitigation is to maintain a set of unique curator addresses during the initial share calculation (for example using an EnumerableSet) and then iterate over that set when summing curator shares in claimUndistributedRewards. This change restores the intended accounting logic, prevents under‑payment of undistributed rewards, and eliminates the hidden fund lock‑up.

title: Not all reward token rewards are claimable
description: The lastEpochClaimedStaker, lastEpochClaimedCurator and lastEpochClaimedOperator mappings in the Rewards contract track the last epoch for which a staker/curator/operator has claimed rewards, but it is keyed only by the staker's/curator's/operator's address and not by the reward token. This means that when a staker/curator/operator claims rewards for a given epoch and reward token, the contract updates the mappings for all tokens, not just the one claimed. As a result, if a staker/curator/operator is eligible for rewards from multiple tokens for the same epoch(s), claiming rewards for one token will prevent them from claiming rewards for the others for those epochs.
bug_full: The vulnerability is an accounting‑state tracking flaw in the Rewards contract where the mappings that record the last epoch a staker, curator, or operator has claimed rewards are keyed only by the participant’s address and not by the reward token. Because the contract updates these mappings whenever a claim is made, a claim for any token overwrites the stored epoch for all tokens associated with that address. As a result, when a participant is eligible for rewards from multiple tokens for the same epoch(s), claiming one token causes the contract to believe the latest epoch has already been claimed for the other tokens as well. This prevents subsequent claims for those tokens, leading to loss of rewards. The bug occurs under the condition that multiple reward tokens are distributed for the same epoch and a participant attempts to claim more than one of them. It affects any staker, curator, or operator who holds positions that earn multi‑token rewards, causing their balances to remain unchanged for the omitted tokens while they may receive the first token they claim. The issue was discovered during a security audit that added a second reward token in the test suite; the test showed that after a successful claim for the first token, the second token claim reverted with an AlreadyClaimedForLatestEpoch error. The problem is subtle because the contract’s logic appears correct when only a single token is used, so basic tests may not expose it. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions: rewards that should be distributable become permanently inaccessible, violating user expectations that each token’s rewards are claimable independently. The appropriate mitigation is to redesign the claim‑state mappings to be double‑keyed by both participant address and reward token (e.g., mapping(address => mapping(address => uint48)) for stakers, curators, and operators). All claim‑related functions must be updated to reference the new structure, ensuring that each token’s claim epoch is tracked separately. This change isolates state per token, restores correct reward distribution, and eliminates the loss of funds caused by the current implementation.

title: Vault initialization allows deposit whitelist with no management capability
bug_full: The vulnerability is an access‑control misconfiguration that occurs during the initialization of the VaultTokenized contract. When a vault is created with the deposit whitelist flag enabled, the contract is expected to have two distinct roles: one that can toggle the whitelist on or off (depositWhitelistSetRoleHolder) and another that can add addresses to the whitelist (depositorWhitelistRoleHolder). The initialization code only validates the consistency of these roles if depositWhitelistSetRoleHolder is the zero address. Consequently, if a caller supplies a non‑zero address for the toggle role but leaves the add‑to‑whitelist role as address(0), the validation is bypassed. The vault then enters a state where the whitelist is active but no address possesses the permission to populate it. As a result, every deposit attempt is rejected with a NotWhitelistedDepositor error because the sender is not on the whitelist, and no one can add new entries. Users experience symptoms such as transactions reverting, balances remaining zero after a deposit call, and UI messages indicating that deposits are not possible. The impact is that deposits are effectively frozen until the toggle role is used to disable the whitelist; if that role is also inaccessible, the vault becomes unusable. This condition can be triggered by any party that can call the factory’s create function with the described parameters, meaning an attacker could deliberately deploy a vault that blocks all user deposits. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised the initialization paths and observed that the role‑consistency check was conditional on a specific role being zero. It is hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors and the role checks appear to function correctly in other scenarios, yet the specific combination of parameters creates a deadlock. The proper fix is to enforce role consistency unconditionally: if the whitelist is enabled, a non‑zero depositorWhitelistRoleHolder must be provided; if the whitelist is disabled, no depositorWhitelistRoleHolder should be set. This change prevents the creation of a vault where deposits are blocked by design and restores the intended business logic that whitelisted deposits are allowed only when a valid whitelist management mechanism exists.

title: Wrong value is returned in upperLookupRecentCheckpoint
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect value handling in the upperLookupRecentCheckpoint function of the checkpoint library. The function is supposed to locate the most recent checkpoint whose key is less than or equal to a given search key and return the checkpoint key, the stored value and the position. Internally it calls the helper at which already resolves the stored value by reading self._values[checkpoint._value] and returns a struct with the concrete value in the _value field. The upperLookupRecentCheckpoint implementation, however, dereferences the returned _value a second time by accessing self._values[checkpoint._value] again. When a valid hint (position) is supplied, the function obtains the checkpoint via at, then mistakenly indexes the values array a second time. This double‑lookup either returns a completely unrelated number or, if the second index is out of range, triggers an array‑bounds revert. The bug is therefore a classic case of improper handling of already‑resolved data, a logic error that violates the contract’s accounting assumptions. An attacker or a regular user can trigger the bug simply by calling upperLookupRecentCheckpoint with a hint that points to an existing checkpoint; the call may revert or return a value that does not correspond to the checkpoint’s stored amount. From the user’s perspective the contract may appear to “lose” a value, return zero or an unexpected number, or the transaction may fail unexpectedly. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test that supplied a valid hint caused a revert due to an out‑of‑bounds array access. Because the function works correctly when no hint is provided, the problem can be easy to miss in normal operation. The impact is that any protocol logic that relies on historical checkpoint values – for example token vesting, voting power snapshots, or price oracles – may receive wrong data or experience unexpected reverts, potentially breaking accounting or causing loss of funds. The fix is to stop the second dereference and return the _value field that the at helper already provides, i.e., replace self._values[checkpoint._value] with checkpoint._value in all return paths.

title: Wrong value is returned in upperLookupRecentCheckpoint
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect value handling in the upperLookupRecentCheckpoint function of a checkpoint library. The function is supposed to return the key, stored value and position of the most recent checkpoint whose key is less than or equal to a supplied search key. It can receive an optional hint that points to a candidate position to speed up the search. The root cause is that the function calls the internal at helper, which already resolves the checkpoint value, but then it looks up the value again through self._values[checkpoint._value]. Because checkpoint._value is already the concrete value, treating it as an index into the internal _values array yields either a completely wrong numeric result or an out‑of‑bounds access that triggers a revert. When a valid hint is supplied, the function therefore returns a wrong value or reverts, breaking the expected lookup behaviour. An attacker or a malformed client can trigger the bug by providing a hint that points to any existing checkpoint; the call will either return an unexpected value (e.g., a balance of 0 instead of the real amount) or cause the transaction to fail with an array‑bounds error. The impact is that any protocol logic that relies on correct checkpoint retrieval – such as vesting schedules, voting power calculations, or historical price queries – may receive incorrect data or become unavailable, leading to missing funds, zero refunds, or denial‑of‑service for users. The condition occurs only when the hint argument is non‑empty; calls without a hint work correctly. The bug affects all callers of the library, including end‑users who expect a correct balance or refund, and the protocol that assumes the checkpoint value is accurate. It was discovered during a formal audit when the test suite exercised the function with a valid hint and observed a revert due to array bounds. The issue is subtle because the at helper already returns the correct value, so the extra array lookup looks harmless at first glance and does not affect the no‑hint path. The fix is to stop dereferencing self._values and return checkpoint._value directly, ensuring the function uses the value already resolved by at. Conceptually this is a classic “double‑lookup” or “index‑as‑value” bug, where a value is mistakenly treated as an index, leading to wrong accounting and potential loss of funds.

title: Incorrectinclusion of removed nodes in _requireMinSecondaryAssetClasses during forceUpdateN-odes
description:
Description: The function _requireMinSecondaryAssetClasses is utilized within the forceUpdateNodes process.  
During execution, if a node is removed in the first iteration, the subsequent iteration still includes the removed node in the _requireMinSecondaryAssetClasses computation because the node remains in the list until the full removal process completes.  

```solidity
if ((newStake < assetClasses[PRIMARY_ASSET_CLASS].minValidatorStake)
    || !_requireMinSecondaryAssetClasses(0, operator)) {
    newStake = 0;
    _initializeEndValidationAndFlag(operator, valID, nodeId);
}
```

Example Scenario:  
1. forceUpdateNodes is invoked for an operator managing 5 nodes and the operator stake dropped from the last epoch.  
2. On the first iteration, the first node is removed due to a drop in the value of _requireMinSecondaryAssetClasses is executed.  
3. On the second iteration, while checking if the second node should be removed, _requireMinSecondaryAssetClasses incorrectly includes the previously removed first node in its calculations, even though it is slated for removal. This will ultimately remove all five nodes.  

This problem will occur only if the last epoch's operator stake dropped and the limitStake is a small value.  

Impact: This behaviour can lead to inaccurate evaluations during node removal decisions. The presence of nodes marked for removal after the _requireMinSecondaryAssetClasses calculations can cause the system to misjudge whether the minimum requirements for secondary asset classes are met. This may result in either:  
• Preventing necessary node removals, thereby retaining nodes that should be removed, or  
• Causing inconsistencies in node state management, potentially affecting operator performance and system integrity.
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the node removal routine of the contract, specifically in the interaction between forceUpdateNodes and the helper function _requireMinSecondaryAssetClasses. When forceUpdateNodes iterates over an operator's node list, it may remove a node in the first iteration because the operator's stake fell below the required threshold. However, the list of nodes (operatorNodesArray) is not updated until the loop finishes, so the removed node remains counted in the subsequent iteration. _requireMinSecondaryAssetClasses computes the minimum secondary asset class requirement by dividing each class's stake by the total node count plus an extraNode parameter. Because extraNode is always passed as zero and the function uses an unsigned integer, it cannot represent the negative adjustment needed for nodes already removed. As a result, the denominator includes the stale node, making the stake‑per‑node ratio appear lower than it actually is. This miscalculation can cause the contract to believe the minimum requirement is violated for every remaining node, leading to a cascade where all nodes are removed, or conversely it may prevent necessary removals if the ratio is incorrectly satisfied. The bug only manifests when the operator's stake dropped in the previous epoch and the limitStake is small enough that the ratio check is sensitive to the extra node count. Affected parties include operators, delegators, and the overall protocol, because node state inconsistencies can degrade validator performance and undermine system integrity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a test that forces a stake drop and calls forceUpdateNodes. It is hard to notice because the removal loop appears to execute normally, yet the hidden counting error silently corrupts the node set. From a user perspective, the UI may show all validator nodes disappearing or, alternatively, nodes that should have been removed remaining active, leading to unexpected zero rewards or missing validators. The bug violates the business logic that the number of active nodes must reflect the actual validator set and that secondary asset class ratios must be calculated on the current active count. To remediate, the contract should adjust the node count used in the ratio calculation to exclude nodes already marked for removal. This can be achieved by changing the extraNode argument to a signed integer and passing a negative value equal to the number of removed nodes, or by maintaining a separate counter of pending removals and subtracting it before the division, thereby ensuring the minimum‑stake check reflects the true active node set.

title: Rewards distribution DoS due to uncached secondary asset classes
bug_full: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the rewards distribution mechanism caused by an unchecked direct read of a cached total‑stake mapping for each asset class. The root cause is that the contract accesses the totalStakeCache mapping instead of a getter that falls back to a calculation when the cache entry is missing. Only the primary asset class is automatically cached by routine node‑addition and update functions; secondary asset classes are cached only when a slash operation targets them or when an operator manually invokes a cache‑update function. Consequently, when the rewards distributor iterates over all asset classes and encounters a secondary class whose cache entry is still zero, the share calculation divides by that zero value, triggering a revert. This revert aborts the entire distributeRewards call, so no rewards are transferred for the affected epoch. The issue manifests when an epoch includes a secondary asset class that has never been slashed or manually cached, which can happen in normal operation because slashing of secondary classes is infrequent. Users experience missing rewards or see transactions fail without a clear error message, leading to confusion or the perception that funds have disappeared. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the reward‑calculation path and identified the direct mapping access as lacking fallback logic. It is subtle because the primary asset class works correctly, masking the problem until a secondary class is involved. To remediate, the code should verify that the cached total stake is non‑zero before using it; if it is zero, it should invoke the cache‑calculation routine for that epoch and asset class and then read the updated value. This change ensures a valid divisor and prevents the division‑by‑zero revert, restoring reliable reward distribution while preserving the intended accounting logic.

title: Incorrect owner passed to Manager::redeem in YToken withdrawal flow
bug_full: An incorrect address is supplied to the manager.redeem call inside the YToken withdrawal routine. The function _withdraw receives parameters caller, receiver, owner, assets, shares. When delegating a withdrawal, the caller may be a third‑party contract or user that has allowance to act on behalf of the owner. The code mistakenly passes msg.sender as the owner argument to manager.redeem instead of the owner variable that was already provided. This mismatch only manifests when caller != owner. In that case the manager contract validates the owner against the shares to be burned; if the supplied owner does not hold the required shares the call reverts, preventing the redemption. If the caller also holds shares, the manager may burn the caller’s tokens instead of the intended owner’s, leading to loss of the caller’s balance. The bug is a classic authorization parameter mix‑up, a form of improper access control where the wrong principal is used in a downstream call. It was discovered during a manual audit of the withdrawal flow and reproduced with a test that invokes redeem through a third party. The issue is subtle because the same code works when the caller is the owner, so normal user‑initiated withdrawals appear correct, hiding the problem from casual testing. The impact is that delegated withdrawals can fail or cause unintended token burning, affecting users who rely on allowance‑based withdrawals and potentially the protocol’s liquidity accounting. The fix is to replace msg.sender with the owner parameter when invoking manager.redeem in both YToken and YTokenL2 contracts, ensuring the correct account is credited for the burn and that the manager’s accounting remains consistent. This aligns the implementation with the ERC‑4626 expectation that the owner argument represents the token holder whose shares are being redeemed.

title: Manager::_transferFee returns invalid feeShares when fee is zero
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability is an incorrect fee calculation in the Manager contract’s internal _transferFee function. When the protocol fee parameter (_fee) is zero, the function returns the full amount of shares (_shares) instead of returning zero fee shares. This logical error originates from a faulty conditional branch that treats a zero fee as a full‑share fee. During a deposit, the contract calls _transferFee to compute the protocol fee and then subtracts the returned fee shares from the adjusted share total along with any gas fee shares. Because adjustedFeeShares incorrectly equals adjustedShares when the fee is zero, the subsequent subtraction `adjustedShares - adjustedFeeShares - adjustedGasFeeShares` attempts to subtract more than the available amount, causing an arithmetic underflow that triggers a revert. The impact is that deposits with a zero protocol fee and a non‑zero gas fee fail; the transaction reverts and the user receives no shares, while only the gas spent is lost. In the unlikely event that the subtraction were unchecked, the user could end up with zero shares credited despite having supplied tokens, effectively losing their position. The bug is discovered through code review and testing of zero‑fee deposit paths, and it can be hard to notice because zero‑fee scenarios are less common and the revert may be attributed to other reasons such as insufficient gas. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show a transaction failure, no change in balance, or an unexpected zero share balance after a successful token transfer, contradicting the expectation that a deposit should always result in a positive share allocation. This class of bug falls under “incorrect accounting logic” or “fee calculation error” where a function returns an unexpected value, violating the contract’s accounting assumptions. The correct fix is to modify the conditional in _transferFee so that it returns 0 when _fee is zero, ensuring downstream calculations receive the proper fee share amount and preventing underflow conditions.

title: YtokenL2::previewMint and YTokenL2::previewWithdraw round in favor of user
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability resides in the YTokenL2 implementation of the previewMint and previewWithdraw helper functions, which are part of an ERC‑4626‑style vault that relies on an oracle‑provided L1 exchange rate instead of internal accounting. Both functions perform integer arithmetic that rounds in favor of the caller: previewMint multiplies the desired share amount by the exchange rate and then divides by a constant, while previewWithdraw multiplies the requested asset amount by the constant and divides by the exchange rate. Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, the order of operations causes any fractional remainder to be discarded in a way that gives the user a slightly larger asset amount for minting or requires fewer shares for withdrawing. This behavior contradicts the EIP‑4626 recommendation to round toward the vault, which is intended to prevent value leakage. The flaw can be exploited whenever a user queries these preview functions to determine how many assets to supply for a given share amount or how many shares are needed for a withdrawal. By repeatedly minting and withdrawing, an attacker can accumulate a small excess of shares or assets on each transaction, leading to a slow but continuous drain of the vault’s value, especially when automated scripts execute many operations. The issue manifests under normal usage conditions whenever the preview calculations are used, and it affects all participants of the protocol: token holders, the vault’s liquidity, and any downstream contracts that rely on accurate accounting. The problem was identified during a security audit that compared the contract’s rounding logic against the EIP‑4626 specification and noticed the deviation. Because the discrepancy is only a few wei or token units per transaction, it is easy to miss in casual testing and only becomes apparent after many interactions or when balances appear to increase unexpectedly. To remediate the issue, the conversion helpers should be rewritten to explicitly round down when converting shares to assets and round up when converting assets to shares, following the pattern used in OpenZeppelin’s ERC‑4626 implementation. This change restores the intended accounting invariants, prevents the vault from leaking value, and aligns the contract with established standards. From a user’s perspective, the bug may appear as “extra tokens” being minted or withdrawals succeeding with less loss, which contradicts the expectation that the amount received matches the precise exchange rate. The rounding bias therefore violates the core business logic that the vault’s share‑to‑asset conversion be lossless for the protocol.

title: Direct YToken deposits can lock funds below minimum withdrawal threshold
description:
In Manager::deposit, there is a check enforcing a minimum deposit amount inside Manager::_validate:
```solidity
uint256 normalizedAmount = _normalizeAmount(_yToken, _asset, _amount);
require(IERC4626(_yToken).convertToShares(normalizedAmount) >= minSharesInYToken[_yToken],
"!minShares");
```
A similar check exists in the redeem flow, again via Manager::_validate:
```solidity
require(_amount >= minSharesInYToken[_yToken], "!minShares");
```
However, no such minimum is enforced when depositing directly into a YToken. In both YToken::_deposit and YTokenL2::_deposit, the only requirement is:
```solidity
require(receiver != address(0) && assets > 0 && shares > 0, "!valid");
```
As a result, a user could deposit an amount that results in fewer shares than `minSharesInYToken[_yToken]`, which cannot be withdrawn through the Manager due to its minimum withdrawal check, effectively locking their funds.
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: Direct deposits into a YToken can bypass the minimum‑share validation that the Manager contract enforces for both deposits and redemptions. The Manager’s internal _validate function requires that the number of shares obtained from a deposit, as calculated by IERC4626.convertToShares, be greater than or equal to a protocol‑defined minSharesInYToken value, and it also requires that any redemption amount be at least that same threshold. By contrast, the YToken::_deposit and YTokenL2::_deposit functions only check that the receiver address is non‑zero and that both assets and shares are greater than zero. Consequently, a user who deposits a very small amount directly into the YToken can receive a share count that is below the minimum threshold. When the same user later attempts to withdraw through the Manager, the Manager’s redemption check fails with the \"!minShares\" revert, preventing the user from exiting the position. From the user’s perspective the deposit appears successful, but the balance displayed by the UI may show a non‑zero amount that cannot be redeemed, leading to confusion, panic, or the impression that funds have vanished. The issue is a classic case of inconsistent validation across contract layers, creating a “dust” condition where assets are locked because they do not satisfy the withdrawal accounting rules. The vulnerability was identified during a manual audit that compared the validation logic of the Manager and the YToken contracts and noticed the missing check. It may be hard to notice because the deposit transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted at the time of deposit. The impact is limited to user funds that become non‑withdrawable; the protocol’s overall security is not compromised, but user trust can be damaged. The recommended remediation is to enforce the same minSharesInYToken threshold inside YToken::_deposit and YTokenL2::_deposit, and optionally to add a post‑withdrawal balance check that ensures any remaining shares are either zero or above the minimum, thereby eliminating non‑withdrawable dust.

title: Chainlink router configured twice
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability is a configuration mismatch caused by having two separate router addresses in the BridgeCCIP contract: a mutable storage slot called router that can be changed by an admin, and an immutable router address inherited from the CCIPReceiver base contract (i_ccipRouter). The root cause is that the contract’s send function forwards outbound CCIP messages using the mutable router, while the inbound validation logic in CCIPReceiver checks that incoming messages originate from the immutable router. When the admin calls setRouter and updates the mutable address, outbound messages are routed to the new router, but replies are still expected from the original immutable router. This inconsistency can break cross‑chain communication, causing messages to be dropped or ignored, which in turn leads to funds appearing to disappear, refunds not being received, or balances remaining zero on the destination chain. The issue occurs only after the router is changed after deployment; before any change the two addresses are identical and the contract works as intended. Users who initiate cross‑chain transfers expect their assets to arrive on the target chain, but due to the mismatch they see a successful transaction on the source chain while the destination balance stays unchanged, creating confusion and potential loss of trust. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined storage layout and inheritance, noticing that the same logical component (the CCIP router) was defined both as a mutable variable and as an immutable constant. Because the two variables are used in different code paths, the bug can be subtle and may not surface until an admin actually changes the router address. The vulnerability belongs to the class of configuration duplication and state inconsistency bugs, where redundant state variables lead to divergent behavior. To remediate, the mutable router variable and its setter should be removed, and the contract should rely solely on the immutable i_ccipRouter inherited from CCIPReceiver. If a router change is ever required, the contract must be redeployed with the new address, ensuring that both sending and receiving logic reference the same router and preserving the integrity of cross‑chain accounting.

title: [M-07] isGenesis flag is ineffective to control add liquidity flow in RouterV2.addLiquidity()
poc: Information not provided
bug_full: The vulnerability is an ineffective protection mechanism for Genesis pools that are supposed to be locked until an official launch. The router function that adds liquidity contains a guard that rejects calls only when the pair is marked as Genesis and its total supply is exactly zero. Because the check is combined with a totalSupply condition, any non‑zero supply—whether created by the legitimate launch or by a tiny dust mint from an attacker—makes the guard evaluate to true and the require passes. Consequently, external users can add liquidity to a Genesis pair before the flag is cleared. The Pair contract’s mint function does not verify the Genesis status at all, allowing an attacker to transfer minimal amounts of the two tokens to a fresh Genesis pair, call mint directly, receive LP tokens, and increase totalSupply. After this dust mint, the router’s check is bypassed, opening the pool to unrestricted liquidity. The impact is not an immediate loss of funds, but it enables price manipulation, unfair advantage, and disruption of the intended controlled launch, breaking the business logic that no one should be able to provide liquidity until the pool is officially opened. The issue manifests whenever a Genesis pair exists with the isGenesis flag set to true and any LP token—however small—has been minted. It affects token issuers, liquidity providers, and users who rely on a fair launch, and it may be hard to notice because the pool appears to function normally after the first mint, masking the earlier breach. The flaw was discovered through manual audit of the router’s addLiquidity guard and the pair’s mint implementation, revealing the missing Genesis check. To remediate, the router should reject any addLiquidity call for a Genesis pair regardless of totalSupply, and the pair’s mint function should also enforce the Genesis flag, preventing any initial liquidity before the launch flag is cleared.

title: [M-12] Epoch voting restrictions bypassed via deposit_for() for blacklisted/non-whitelisted tokenIDs
description:
The vote function in VoterV3.sol restricts voting after the epoch ends, allowing only whitelisted tokenIds (NFTs) or those meeting specific conditions (i.e., IAutoVotingEscrowManager(avm).tokenIdToAVMId(_tokenId) == 0) to continue voting. However, this restriction can be bypassed because the deposit_for function, which internally calls poke—does not enforce these same checks. As a result, even holders of non-whitelisted or blacklisted tokenIds can call deposit_for after the epoch has ended.
